# Patrologia Latina, volume 220 — English translation

*Patrologia Latina*, vol. 220

*Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library … of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III … Earlier Latin Series.*

**Volume CCXX of the Latin Patrology**

**Third Volume**

Printed and sold by J.-P. Migne, publisher, in the street called d’Amboise, formerly near the gate of Paris commonly called d’Enfer, or Petit-Montrouge, but now within the walls of Paris. 1863.

Volume front matter

Series title page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library, complete, uniform, convenient, economical, of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical Writers, whether Latin or Greek, who flourished from the apostolic age to the times of the Council of Trent (1545) for the Latins, and of the Council of Florence (1439) for the Greeks: a chronological reprinting of all surviving monuments of Catholic tradition through the first fifteen centuries of the Church and beyond, according to the most accurate editions, compared with one another and with certain manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest care; continually elucidated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the completion of the most extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following individual volumes or authors of some importance; arranged with chapters properly disposed within the text itself, and likewise with headings distinguishing the upper margins of individual pages and indicating the matter beneath; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal, yet possessing some authority with respect to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with more than two hundred indexes of authors and works—alphabetical, chronological, statistical, synthetic, analytical, analogical—covering every dogmatic, moral, liturgical, canonical, disciplinary, and historical point of religion, and every other subject without exception; but especially with two immense and general indexes: one, namely, of subjects, through consultation of which one may see at a glance whatever not merely this or that Father, but every single Father, without even one omitted, has written on any given theme; the other, of Sacred Scripture, through which the reader may readily discover which Fathers, and in which places in their works, have commented upon the individual verses of every book of Scripture, from the first of Genesis to the last of the Apocalypse. A most accurate edition, readily to be preferred to all others, if one considers the clearness of the type, the quality of the paper, the completeness of the text, the perfection of the correction, both the variety and number of reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently alike throughout the whole course of the Patrology, the modest price, and especially this single, methodical, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and shorter works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time gathered in our library from works and manuscripts pertaining to every age, place, language, and form.**

**Earlier Latin Series**, in which appear the Latin Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical Writers from Tertullian to Innocent III; prepared by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Clergy Library, or Complete Courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning. Patrology, after the pattern of the Church itself, is divided into two parts: one Latin, the other Greco-Latin. The Latin part, now entirely completed, comprises in its first series two hundred and twenty-five volumes, and will shortly stand complete after the indexes have been finished; it is sold for one thousand one hundred and twenty-five francs. The Greek part has been issued in two typographical editions. The first contains the Greek text together with a parallel Latin translation and reaches one hundred and nine volumes, but lacks indexes. The second presents this translation alone and is therefore contained within fifty-five volumes. Both had appeared in full by 24 December 1860. Each Greco-Latin volume is sold for eight francs, and each purely Latin one for only five francs; but in either case, for a purchaser to enjoy this price, it is necessary to buy the complete collection, Greek or Latin, consisting of 326 volumes for the larger edition and 272 for the smaller without indexes. Otherwise, the size and difficulties of each volume will establish different prices. Nevertheless, if someone buys entire and separately either the Greco-Latin collection or the same collection translated from Greek into Latin, each volume will then be obtained for nine or six francs respectively. These conditions apply to the Patrology series not yet printed.

**List of the Indexes contained in this Volume CCXX**

**Thirteenth Series of Indexes** (continuation), containing the indexes: On Civil Legislation; On Immunities; On the Power of the Holy Pontiff, cols. 10–111. **Fourteenth Series of Indexes**, containing the indexes: On Death; On the Particular Judgment after Death; On Heaven; On Hell; On Purgatory; On Worship toward the Departed; On Antichrist; On the Resurrection of the Dead; On the Last Judgment, 198–291. **Fifteenth Series of Indexes**, containing the Moral Index; the Moral Library of the Fathers; the same arranged analogically; the same arranged alphabetically; the Ascetic Index of the Fathers; the Ascetic Library of the Fathers; the same arranged analogically; the same arranged alphabetically; the Index on Conscience, 307–351. **Sixteenth Series of Indexes**, containing the indexes: On the Decalogue; On Love of Enemies; On Almsgiving; On Fraternal Correction; On the Precepts of the Church; On Feasts; On Fasting; On the Mortification of the Senses, 355–555. **Seventeenth Series of Indexes**, containing the indexes: On Faith; On Hope; On Charity; On Virtues; On Priestly Virtues; On Clerical Continence; On the Duties of Monks; On Virgins; On Nuns; On Widows; On Kings; On Poverty; On Unpublished Writings; On Memorable Sayings; On the Virtues of Pagans, 571–783. **Eighteenth Series of Indexes**, containing the indexes: On Sins; On Vices; On Homicide; On Simony; On Unlawful Pleasures; On the Vices and Errors of Pagans, 787–937. **Nineteenth Series of Indexes**, containing the indexes: On Prayer in General; On the Lord’s Prayer, 942–959. **Twentieth Series of Indexes**, containing the indexes: On Historiographers; On Jews; On Chronicles; On Monasteries; On Dioceses; On Episcopal Cities and Abbeys; Biographical Index; Second Biographical Index, 962–1283.

**Special Indexes of the Latin Patrology**

**Thirteenth Series of Indexes.** (Continuation.)

### CXXIII. INDEX ON CIVIL LEGISLATION, ARRANGED ALPHABETICALLY BY SUBJECT, REPORTING VARIOUS LAWS AND DECREES INSOFAR AS THEY RELATE TO RELIGION

**ABBOT.** Letter of an abbot or rector of a church, *Ancient Formularies of an Unknown Author*, LXXXVII, 793.

**ABOLITION.** On abolitions, Constitution of Constantine the Great (312–366), VIII, 183.

**ABSENT PERSON.** An absent person cannot accuse in capital cases, nor can an accused person be defended through another, Angelramnus, XCVI, 1063.—Against the seizure of an absent person’s property, Constitution of Constantine the Great (312–366), VIII, 322.—If an absent person’s possession has been disturbed by force or otherwise, ibid., 285.—Persons absent can neither be accused nor judged, St. Ivo, bishop of Chartres, CLXI, 1193.

**ACACIUS.** Edict containing the judgment of Pope Felix concerning the condemnation of Acacius, LVIII, 934.

**ACCUSER.** The persons of accusers must be carefully examined, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1295.

**TO ACCUSE.** One cannot accuse through another, nor be accused while absent, St. Ivo, bishop of Chartres, CLXI, 1194.—The laws oblige no one to accuse, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 238.

**ACCUSATION.** On the accusation and trial of clerics, in material attributed to Pope St. Sylvester, VIII, 839; in the fragments of Pope Julius, ibid., 889.—Form of entering an accusation of homicide, *Ancient Formularies of an Unknown Author*, LXXXVII, 790.—An accusation ought not to be made in writing, St. Ivo, bishop of Chartres, CLXI, 1193, 1194.—Under how many witnesses an accusation ought to be made, ibid., 513.—Those who are not to be admitted in an accusation, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 675, 676.—That persons implicated in crimes are not to be admitted either to accusation or to testimony, Angelramnus, XCVI, 1060, 1065.

**ACCUSATIONS.** Which accusations ought to be rejected, St. Ivo, bishop of Chartres, CLXI, 512, 513.—On accusations, Constitution of Constantine the Great, VIII, 143, 153, 234, 293, 310; St. Ivo, bishop of Chartres, CLXI, 1193.

**ACCUSER.** No one can simultaneously be accuser, witness, or judge, St. Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 511, 514, 1199.—On the accuser, Pope Nicholas I, CXIX, 1123.—On the false accuser, ibid., 1010.—A false accuser must be condemned, St. Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 497, 956.—Penalty for an accuser who fails in proof, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 699, 809; Innocent III, CCXV, 1271.

**ACCUSERS.** Accusers must be examined, St. Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 509.—Which accusers are to be excluded, ibid., 513, 918.—Enemies cannot be accusers, ibid., 345, 395, 1196; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 677; nor can an infamous person, ibid., 824; nor an excommunicated person, ibid., 966.—What kind of persons accusers ought to be, Laws of St. Stephen, CLI, 1246.—Accusers ought to be free from suspicion, Pope St. Felix I, V, 145.—On accusers, Charlemagne’s Diplomatic Codex, XCVII, 523, 753, 810, 811, 821, 827; Pope Nicholas I, CXIX, 1184, 1185; St. Leo to Emperor Charles, XCVIII, 523 (800–814); Burchard, CXL, 909; St. Ivo, bishop of Chartres, CLXI, 411, 522.—On the acceptance and rejection of accusers, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 54.

[Col. 0010]

**ACCUSED PERSON.** An accused person ought not to accuse his accuser before clearing himself of the crime laid against him, St. Ivo, CLXI, 408.—On two persons accused of adultery, ibid., 895, 896.

**ACQUISITION.** On acquiring and recovering possession, Constitution, VIII, 117.—That a landed estate cannot be bought without registration for tax, VIII, 165.

**ACTIONARII [record-keepers].** St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 569, 570, 571, 625, 1150, 1221.

**ACTORES.** St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 569, 570, 571, 625, 639, 1150, 1221.—That *actores fisci* [administrators or agents of the treasury] be present at the annual synod, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 355.—On the *actores* of private property, Constitution of Constantine the Great, VIII, 95.

**ACTUARII.** On treasurers and *actuarii* [accounting officers], Constitution of Constantine the Great, VIII, 164, 372, 377 (312–366).

**ASSISTANTS.** On choosing assistants and ministers of private property, Charlemagne’s Diplomatic Codex, XCVII, 870.

**ADMINISTRATION.** On property alienated or donated through administration, Constitution of Constantine the Great, VIII, 377.—Various formularies of administration, Cassiodorus, LXIX, 679.—On the administrations of secular courts, Bishop Cresconius, LXXXVIII, 904.

**ADMINISTRATOR.** On administrators, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 650.

**ADMONITION** to the king and ministers of the commonwealth, Hincmar, CXXV, 1077.

**ADOPTION.** Letter used when grandchildren are appointed by their grandfather in the place of children, Marculf the monk, LXXXVII, 735.

**ADOPTION.** The extent to which adoption impedes marriage, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1444.—How an outsider is adopted in the place of a son, Marculf, ibid., 737, 818; *Ancient Formularies of an Unknown Author*, ibid., 787.

**ADULTERER.** On adulterers, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 77, 108, 273, 584; Works of Charlemagne, XCVII, 731; Pope Nicholas I, CXIX, 992; in Adrevald (877, 881), CXXIV, 1087.—On adulterers who take refuge in a church, St. Isidore, LXXXIV, 274, 636.—The Julian law on adultery, allowing concubines and prostitutes, is exceedingly unjust, St. Zeno, XI, 297.—The law of Antoninus on adulterers, St. Augustine, XL, 474; Hincmar, bishop of Reims, CXXV, 1024.—Against adulterers, Cassiodorus (555–560), LXIX, 782; Charlemagne’s Diplomatic Codex, XCVII, 149.—On the law enacted against adulterous women, Cassiodorus, LXIX, 1041.—How a husband ought to proceed against a suspected adulterer, St. Ivo, CLXI, 935.—A marriage ought not to be dissolved when both spouses are adulterers, Innocent III, CCXV, 1418.

**COUNTERFEITER.** On coin counterfeiters, Charlemagne’s Diplomatic Codex, XCVII, 409, 577.

**ADULTERY.** On adultery, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 75, 77; Works of Charlemagne, XCVII, 756; appendix to Pope Nicholas I, CXIX, 1185; Isaac, bishop of Langres, CXXIV, 1087; Regino, abbot of Prüm, CXXXII, 303 ff., 307; Laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1301.—Against adultery on the ground that it disrupts social order and family life, St. Ambrose (387), XIV, 428, 442; in the Code of Canons, LVI, 441.—Against adulteries, in St. Caesarius, LXVII, 1085; in the constitution of Emperor Henry III (1099), CLI, 1180.—How adultery is to be proved or purged, St. Ivo, CLXII, 254.—On the penalty for adultery, Irish Canons, XCVI, 1322 ff.

**ADVENTITIOUS PROPERTY.** On adventitious property, Works of Charlemagne, XCVII, 306, 585.

**OPPONENT.** In judicial proceedings the opposing party must be notified to come to hear the witnesses, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1255.

**ADVOCATE.** St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 357.—On the advocate of the treasury, Constantine the Great, VIII, 116, 378.—On advocates, Works of Charlemagne, XCVII, 286, 553, 557, 560, 655.—What advocates ought to be like, Diplomatic Codex, ibid., 560.—Corrupt advocates should be removed, Works of Charlemagne, ibid., 778.—On the faults of advocates, Constitution of Constantine the Great, VIII, 200.—Those excluded from the profession of advocate, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 691, 692.—Against advocates, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 159.

**BUILDING.** On the building and endowment of a church composed of villages, Laws of St. Stephen, CLI, 1251.

**BUILDING.** On private buildings, Constitution of Constantine the Great (312–366), VIII, 233.

**AELIASANCTA LAW.** Boethius, LXIV, 1062.

**EQUALITY** or compact, unknown author, LXXXVII, 771.

**EQUALITY.** On equality to be secured by the royal envoys, Works of Charlemagne, XCVII, 554.

**ÆTHELRED.** Charter of Æthelred, duke of the Mercians, appendix to Bede, XCV, 370, 376.—Ecclesiastical laws of Æthelred II, CLI, 1165, 1172.

**ÆTHELSTAN.** Laws of Æthelstan, anonymous works, CXXXVIII, 461, 472.

**FIELD.** On every deserted field, and when barren lands are assessed together with fertile ones, Constitution of Constantine the Great (312–366), VIII, 394.—On boundaries of fields: that a dispute be settled by possession of forty years, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 455.

**AGNATION.** Charter of agnation when a slave marries a freeborn woman, Marculf, LXXXVII, 745.—Charter of agnation, ibid., 765.

**CHARTER OF AGOBARD**, CIV, 319.

**FARMER.** On farmers, registered taxpayers, and tenant farmers, Constitution, VIII, 327, 398.—On farmers and the lord’s slaves, ibid., 398.

**DIPLOMAS OF ST. ALDHELM**, LXXXIX, 309–314.

**ALDIO.** On the *aldiones* of the palace, Capitularies of the Franks, XCVII, 143; Capitularies of the Lombards, ibid., 144.—On public *aldiones* belonging to public law, Capitularies of Pavia, XCVII, 213.

**CHARTERS OF ALEXANDER I, KING OF SCOTLAND**, appendix to Bede, XCV, 367.

**ECCLESIASTICAL LAWS OF KING ALFRED**, CXXXVIII, 447–458.

**CHIROGRAPH OF BISHOP ALHWIN OF THE HUICCI AND DUKE ÆTHELWULF**, appendix to Bede, XCV, 374.—Charter of Alhwin, ibid.

**ALIENATION.** A thing is not alienated when it is sold for less than the amount ordered, St. Ivo, bishop of Chartres, CLXI, 939.

**MAINTENANCE.** On maintenance, Constitution of Constantine the Great, VIII, 236.—On maintenance which impoverished parents ought to request from the public treasury, ibid., 121.

**PLEADINGS** of litigants must suffer no prejudice owing to the occupations of the prince, St. Ivo, CLXI, 928.

**ALLODS.** On an allod, Works of Charlemagne, XCVII, 365.—On an allod vindicated, unknown author, LXXXVII, 796.

**CHARTER OF ALRED, UNDER-KING OF THE HUICCI**, appendix to Bede, XCV, 371.

**ALTAR.** One who kills ministers of the altar, diplomatic monuments of Cnut I, CLI, 1178.

**INSANE PERSON.** If one spouse becomes insane, the marriage is not dissolved, St. Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 619.

**FEMALE SLAVE.** On a female slave made free by charter, Works of Charlemagne, XCVII, 412.—Whoever puts out the eye of a female slave shall set her free, ibid., 753.—On those who seek other persons’ female slaves as wives, Laws of St. Stephen, CLI, 1249.—It is not lawful voluntarily to dismiss a female slave taken in marriage, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1433.

**THE PEOPLE OF ANCONA.** On a law established by the people of Ancona, Pope Clement III, CCIV, 1479.

**ANIMALS.** On the redemption of animals, Laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1297.

**ANNATE.** On annates, Innocent III, CCXIV, 189.

**GRAIN ALLOWANCE.** On the grain allowance, Constitution of Constantine the Great, VIII, 99, 391.—On the disbursement of the military grain allowance, ibid., 294.—On grain supplies seized or stolen in enemy territory, Works of Charlemagne, XCVII, 561.

[Col. 0012]

**ANTIA LAW.** Tertullian, I, 298.

**LAW OF ANTONINUS** on adulterers, St. Augustine, XL, 474; Hincmar, CXXV, 1024.—On repudiations, ibid., 737.

**ANTRUSTION.** On the king’s *antrustion* [admission to royal protection], Marculf, LXXXVII, 711.

**APENNIS.** See **APPENNIS**.

**BEES.** On bees, Laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1334; Laws of Edward III, CLI, 1192.

**APOSTATE.** On apostates, Theodosius the Great, XIII, 538; Laws of Edward the Elder, CXXXVIII, 459.

**TO APPEAL.** It is lawful to appeal even in criminal cases, Angelramnus, XCVI, 1063.—Appellants are not to be obstructed by any detention, ibid.—On those who did not appeal through fear of the judge, Constitution, VIII, 358.—Though there is no appeal from a judgment and adjudicated matter, a suspected judge may always be challenged, Innocent III, CCXIV, 805.—Following the example of St. Paul, who appealed to Caesar, it is lawful for servants of God to protect themselves against unjust laws, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 668, 669.

**APPEAL.** Unless an appeal is lodged within ten days, the judgment becomes res judicata, Innocent III, CCXIV, 497.—On a pending appeal, Constitution of Constantine the Great, VIII, 233.—If death intervenes while an appeal is pending, ibid., 219, 233.

**APPEALS** to the emperor, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 606, 607, 609.—Whose appeals are not to be received, Constitution of Constantine the Great, VIII, 104, 118, 308.—Reckless appeals are not to be received, Innocent III, CCXIV, 546.—Vexatious appeals are not to be received, ibid., 180.—On appeals, Constitution of Constantine the Great, VIII, 93, 103 ff., 129, 131, 142, 147, 156, 199, 204, 251, 308, 318, 319, 351, 374; St. Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1207, 1212; Pope Clement III, CCXIV, 1481; Pope Celestine, CCVI, 1260; Innocent III, CCIV, 975, 986; CCXV, 310, 1257.—The Julian law concerning appeals to Caesar, Bl. Alcuin, C, 413.—On appeals by bishops and presbyters, Hincmar, CXXVI, 230.—On vexatious appeals, Pope Alexander III, CC, 929.

**APPENNIS.** St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 1162; *Ancient Formularies of an Unknown Author*, LXXXVII, 773, 790; Angevin Formularies, ibid., 846, 847.

**WATER.** Judgment by cold water, Hincmar, CXXV, 161.

**AQUEDUCT.** On aqueducts, Constitution of Constantine the Great, VIII, 347.

**ARBITER.** On arbiters, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 511.

**ARIUS.** Constantine orders the books of Arius to be burned, VIII, 505, 506.

**ARMS.** Arms are not to be borne against one’s country, Works of Charlemagne, XCVII, 777, 906.—On arms, ibid., 284, 285.—On not carrying arms, ibid., 551, 555.—The sale of arms outside the kingdom is forbidden, Capitularies of Mantica, ibid., 135, 906.—Clerics must not bear arms, Regino, abbot of Prüm, CXXXII, 222.—Arms are not to be supplied to unbelievers, Innocent III, CCXIV, 163.—Not even under the pretext of trade, ibid., 493.

**ARMAMENT.** On armament to be possessed for an expedition against the enemy, Works of Charlemagne, XCVII, 551, 732.

**CRAFTSMAN.** On exemptions for craftsmen, Constitution, VIII, 381, 394.

**ASSIZES OF JERUSALEM**, Godfrey, king of Jerusalem, CLV, 397–430.

**ASYLUM.** Clovis preserved the right of asylum for churches, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 484.—On those who take refuge in a church, Works of Charlemagne, XCVII, 257.—On the right of asylums, Laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1293.

**ATTIC LAWS.** Sidonius Apollinaris, LVIII, 534.

**AUTHOR.** On the instigators of seditions or riots, Works of Charlemagne, XCVII, 844.—That someone may have permission to undertake the causes of his clients, Marculf, LXXXVII, 721.

**CHARTER OF HEARING.** Marculf, LXXXVII, 716.

**AUGUR.** On augurs, Burchard, CXL, 791; St. Ivo, bishop of Chartres, CLXI, 745 ff.

**AUGURY.** On auguries, Works of Charlemagne, XCVII, 516.

**COURT.** On the household members of the court, Laws of St. Stephen, CLI, 1254.

**LAWS OF AUNARIA.** Arnobius, V, 916.

**AVARICIOUS PERSONS; AVARICE.** Against wealthy avaricious persons, because they disturb the order of society, St. Ambrose, XIV, 731, 795.—Avarice is condemned, idem, XVI, 130, 137.

**BAVARIANS.** Chapters added to the law of the Bavarians, Charlemagne, XCVII, 277.

**TO PROCLAIM BY BAN.** Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 265, 439.—On those who ought to be summoned by ban to the court assembly, ibid., XCVII, 557.

**BAN OF A BISHOP OR PRIEST.** Regino, abbot of Prüm, CXXXII, 286, 341, 363.—On the ban, Works of Charlemagne, XCVII, 904.—On payment of the ban, ibid., 895.—On observance of the ban, ibid., 231.

[Col. 0013]

**ROYAL BAN.** Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 199, 291, 321, 336, 337, 542, 374.—Lordly ban, ibid., 201, 236, 364, 416, 448.—On the lordly ban, Charlemagne, XCVII, 125.—On one’s own property placed under ban, ibid., 406, 574.

**BARONS.** On barons who have their own courts and customs, Laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1336; Laws of Edward III, CLI, 1194.—On barons of the ports, Laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1340.

**BASTAGARII.** On the *bastagarii* [carriers], Constitution of Constantine the Great, VIII, 148.

**BECHARII.** On the *becharii* [term uncertain], Erkembald, CXXXVII, 596.

**WAR.** On wars, St. Ivo of Chartres, LXXXII, 639; appendix to Pope Nicholas, CXIX, 1200.—Justice must be observed even in war, St. Ambrose, XVI, 63.

**DIPLOMA OF BENEDICT III**, CXV, 701.

**BENEFICE.** Chapters on benefices, monuments of Conrad II, CLI, 104; Edict, ibid., 1042.—On ruined benefices, Charlemagne, XCVII, 410, 418.—Formularies for describing benefices and royal fiscal estates, ibid., 339, 340.—On those holding royal benefices, ibid., 554.—On those who commit fraud in royal benefices, ibid.

**PROPERTY.** On vacant property, Constitution of Constantine the Great, VIII, 97, 156, 317.

**PROPERTY OF THE CHURCH.** That, when relatives fail, the Church may receive the inheritance, and that bequests remain valid, Constitution of Constantine the Great, VIII, 265.—That those who have bought or received as gifts the Church’s property restore it, Constitution of Constantine the Great, VIII, 269.—That bishops remove nothing from Church property, St. Isidore, LXXXIV, 400.—If it is said that something is given from Church property as compensation, the grounds of the compensation must be examined, ibid., 435.—What division is to be made, from acquired property, between the Church and the heirs of a priest, ibid., 436.—If a bishop establishes a monastery or endows a parish church, what portion of Church property he may confer, ibid.—That a bishop may confer upon whomever he chooses the third part of ecclesiastical property due to himself, ibid.—That the heirs of a deceased priest do not presume, apart from the established order, to enter upon his property, ibid., 437.—On invaders of Church property, ibid., 826.—On the administration of Church property, ibid., 576.—On the money offered in the Church of God, to be faithfully collected and divided, ibid., 621.—How that which a bishop wishes to donate from Church property to his friends, slaves, or freedmen is to remain confirmed, ibid.—That Church revenues or the offerings of the faithful should be divided into four portions, ibid., 806.—On the proper administration of Church property by bishops, ibid., 805.—That Church property is not to be alienated, but granted only for use to clerics, monks, or pilgrims, in the letter of Pope Symmachus, ibid., 811.

**MATERNAL PROPERTY.** On maternal property, Constitution, VIII, 123, 169, 375.

**OX.** On an ox that gores, Charlemagne, XCVII, 755.—On an ox that wounds another ox, St. Ivo, CLXI, 966.—One who steals an ox must restore five oxen for one, ibid., 966.

**WRIT OF OATH.** *Ancient Formularies of an Unknown Author*, LXXXVII, 792.—Writ of oath according to the judgment itself, ibid., 796.

**BREVIS.** A *brevis* is called an inventory or a brief document containing a summary of any kind of property, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 638, 639, 900, 901.

**BRUNIAE.** On *bruniae* [body armour], Capitularies of the Franks under Charlemagne, XCVII, 131.—On possessing *bruniae*, Charlemagne, XCVII, 732.

**BURDA; BURDATIO.** St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 501, 502.

**BURGENSES.** On burgesses, Laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1341.

**CAESARIANI.** On the *Caesariani*, Constantine the Great, VIII, 148.

**CALCIARIUM.** A *calciarium* is an assessment for assistance with food and clothing, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 493.

**HOT WATER.** Judgments by hot water, St. Agobard, CIV, 119, 120.

**CALUMNIATORS.** On slanderers at court, Laws of St. Stephen, CLI, 1253.

**CHANCELLORS.** On chancellors, Charlemagne, XCVII, 452.—On chapters to be received from the chancellor of the palace by archbishops and counts, ibid., 542.

**GLOWING IRON.** Judgment by glowing iron is forbidden to take place in church, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 612.

**DOGS.** Compensation for damage inflicted by dogs, Abedoc and Æthelvolf, XCVI, 1305.

[Col. 0014]

CUSTOM, Charlemagne, XCVII, 804.---What custom is, St Ivo, CLXI, 1120; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 30.---On the authority of law and custom, Frankish Capitulary, XCVII, 143; Lombard Capitulary, ibid., 144.---Custom is vainly opposed to reason, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 46.---When truth has been revealed, custom ought to yield to it, ibid., 46.---A harmful custom must be rooted out, ibid.---Every custom must be subordinated to truth, ibid., 46, 47.---Custom cannot overcome law and reason, St Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 309, 1120; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 58.---On unjust customs, Charlemagne, XCVII, 408, 414, 576, 579.---Collection of customs, in Richard, abbot of Fleury, CXXXVI, 1303.---Ancient customs of the Northmen, confirmed at the council held at Lillebonne in 1080, in the Laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1229.

CONSUL. On consuls, Innocent III, CCXIV, 218.

CONSULAR. Consular officials and consuls were formerly appointed by codicils, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 446.---On consular laws, St Isidore, LXXXII, 201.

CONSULSHIP. Justin unsuccessfully attempted to restore the consulship abolished by Justinian, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 446, 599, 1329 (note).

CONSULTATION. On consultations, Constantine the Great, VIII, 93, 374.

CONTEMPT. Contempt for the laws is denounced, St Agobard, CIV, 187 ff.---On contempt for the count’s just judgment, Laws of St Stephen, CLI, 1252.

CONTROVERSY. To settle a dispute between parties, one oath is sufficient, St Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 930.

CONTUMACIOUS PERSON. On the contumacious, Charlemagne, XCVII, 767.

[Col. 0020] DISTURBER. On suppressing disturbers of the Church, Charlemagne, XCVII, 804.

ASSEMBLY OF MAINZ, Constitutions of Henry IV, CLI, 1128.---Assembly of Oppenheim, ibid., 1125.---Assembly of Regensburg, ibid., 1140.---Assembly of Pavia, ibid., 1126.

CONVOCATION. On summoning bishops to a conference, St Optatus, XI, 818.

CORNELIAN testamentary law, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 978.---Under the Cornelian law concerning forgery, Constantine, VIII, 133, 304.

CORNICULARII. On *cornicularii*, Constantine, VIII, 120.

CORNUTIAN CHARTER, Prolegomena to Anastasius, CXXVII, 971.

CORONATION of Charles the Bald, Hincmar, CXXV, 803.---Coronation of Louis II, ibid., 809.---Coronation of Judith, daughter of Charles, ibid., 811.---Coronation of Queen Ermentrude, CXXXVIII, 727.---Coronation of Emperor Arnulf, ibid., 809.

CORRECTION. On correcting one who has committed an offence by magical art, Pope Gelasius, LIX, 146.

CO-DEBTOR means a surety, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1136.

CREDITOR. The creditor’s right against a debtor is variously established by different laws, St Gregory the Great, LXXXII, 656, 719.---What a creditor ought to do when a debt is not paid on the appointed day, St Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 927.---Creditors must not unjustly despoil another’s property, St Gregory the Great, LXXXII, 504.---The laws forbid creditors to hold the debtor’s son, ibid., 719.---Creditors must not compel the sons of a debtor whose inheritance they have entered upon to accept it, ibid., 826.---What penalties are imposed upon creditors who have detained a free person for debt, ibid., 718, 719.---What punishment a creditor ought to suffer who harasses his sick debtor, St Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 930.

CRETIO, St Isidore of Seville, LXXXII, 204.

CRIME. On remissions of crimes, Constantine, VIII, 223.---On crimes set down in the law, St Isidore, LXXXII, 209.---On the crime of treason, Charlemagne, XCVII, 209.

CRIMINAL matters are to be concluded within a year, St Ivo, CLXI, 951.

CROSS. On a recovered cross, Ancient Formularies, LXXXVII, 802.

COOPERS. On coopers, Erkembald, CXXXVII, 596.

CURATOR. A guardian of minors must swear that he will manage everything that he judges advantageous to the minors, St Ivo, CLXI, 931.---What a curator of a city is, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1022, 1302.---On appointing guardians, Constantine, VIII, 176, 326.---On curators of the *Kalendarium* (debt-register), ibid., 110.---On the administration and liability of curators, ibid., 113, 135, 355, 370.

COURT OF MAINZ, Constitutions of Henry IV, CLI, 1135, 1136.

POSTAL SERVICE. On the public post, Constantine, VIII, 117, 118, 142, 299, 314.---On the course of time, ibid., 216.

MANOR, COURT, ESTATE. On the lord’s manor, Erkembald, CXXXVII, 594.---Capitulary concerning imperial estates, Charlemagne, XCVII, 349.

CUSTODY. On the protection of kings’ safety and the defence of the offspring of reigning princes, St Isidore, LXXXIV, 389.---On night watches, Laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1319.---On custody of accused persons, Constantine, VIII, 198, 389.

GLOVE-MAKERS. On glove-makers, Erkembald, CXXXVII, 536.

DAGOBERT I, king of the Franks. Diplomas, LXXX, 490–564.

DAGOBERT II. Diplomas, LXXXVII, 1301–1314.

DAGOBERT III. Diplomas, LXXXVIII, 1111–1155.

CONDEMN; CONDEMNED. No one is to be condemned without a lawful accuser, St Isidore, LXXXIV, 399.---The property of condemned slaves belongs to their master, St Ivo, CLXI, 98.---On the property of condemned persons, Constantine, VIII, 208.---What should be done with the property of one condemned to death, St Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 928.---The property of those condemned for a capital crime is to pass to their relatives, ibid., 1222.

DAMAGE. On damage inflicted, Hincmar, CXXV, 1078.---On compensation for damage caused by cattle, Irish Canons, XCVI, 1322 ff.---Damage occurring by accident falls, more or less, upon the owner of the thing causing it, St Ivo, CLXI, 1226.

DANEGELD. On Danegeld, Laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1335; Edward III, CLI, 1193.

CHARTER of David, count and later king of the Scots, XCV, 368.

MAIMING. On maiming limbs with the sword, Laws of St Stephen, CLI, 1253.

DEBTOR. Various penalties were inflicted upon debtors by laws and emperors, St Gregory, LXXXVII, 656.---Debtors were formerly excluded from clerical status and every office of honour, ibid., 663.---What a debtor who has nothing with which to pay his debts ought to do, St Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 927.---What a debtor suffers who, at the time of payment, seeks to frustrate his creditor, ibid., 928.---No one is to harass a sick debtor, ibid., 930.---How debtors’ evasions are to be judged, ibid., 933.---On debtors, ibid., 908, 962.

DEBT. One who promises is bound to payment, St Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 962.---On how royal debts ought to be paid, Charlemagne, XCVII, 259, 557.---On paying debts, things advanced on credit, and set-off, St Ivo, CLXI, 947.---Claim for a debt by oath, ibid., 899.

TITHING. On the tithing of *thegns*, Diplomatic Records of Æthelred II, CLI, 1166; Laws of St Stephen, CLI, 1253.

TITHES. On tithes, St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 901; Abedoc and Æthelwealh, XCVI, 1319, 1320; Charlemagne, XCVII, 127, 128, 411, 451, 577, 579, 844, 875, 905, 908; Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 190, 197, 201, 202, 257, 259, 417, 418; St Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1093, 1096; Innocent III, CCXIV, 189; CCXVI, 1205.---On tithes from bees and many other small things, Laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1334; CLI, 1192.---On tithes and ecclesiastical tribute, Charlemagne, XCVII, 725.---Unowned labour, id., CXXXVIII, 480.---On the obligation to render tithes, id., XCVII, 127.---On rendering tithes, ibid., 146, 196.---On rendering to the Church tithes of sheep and small parcels, Laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1334; Laws of Edward III, CLI, 1192.---On rendering tithes, maintaining the poor, and annually distributing alms from royal estates, Laws of Æthelstan, CXXXVIII, 461, 465.---On exacting tithes, capitularies of the Frankish kings, CXXXVIII, 582.---On rendering tithes, Diplomatic Records of Cnut, CLI, 1174.---On paying tithes, Innocent III, CCXVI, 163, 302.---On tithes belonging to the Church of Tehani, Diplomatic Records of Cnut, CLI, 1174.---On the tithes of the Templars, Records concerning the Holy War, CLV, 1237.

DECREE concerning slaves and places of asylum, ecclesiastical injunctions of Chlothar II, king of the Franks, LXXX, 449–452.

DECREE. The decrees of the ancestors must be observed, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 596, 697, 598, 618.---That the decrees of councils and Roman prelates be observed, St Isidore, LXXXIV, 351.---Decree of the universal judgment issued in the prince’s name, ibid., 430.---Decree made for the benefit of the public palace, diplomas of Pippin, XCVI, 757.---Decree of Charlemagne, Charlemagne, XCVII, 673.

DECURION. On decurions, Constantine, VIII, 97, 130, 134, 144, 148, 185, 191, 251, 284, 290, 294, 295, 309, 324–329, 359, 384–390.

DEFENDER. The office of defender was entrusted by codicils, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 999.---The duties of defenders, both civil and ecclesiastical, ibid., 480.---The duties of defenders in settling disputes, ibid., 354, 630, 1126, 1150, 1221, 1227.---The duties of defenders in punishing accused persons, ibid., 637, 672, 1170.---The duties of defenders concerning testaments, ibid., 852, 853, 863, 977, 978, 1009, 1069.---The cases of laypersons were sometimes entrusted to bishops acting as defenders, ibid., 963.---One defender’s case is entrusted to another defender for judgment, ibid., 993.---Defenders were requested from the emperors, ibid., 480.---Who the defenders of the Church were, and what their office and institution were, ibid., 200.---Formula for appointing a defender, ibid., 754, 954, 1149.

INFORMER. On informers, St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 53; Charlemagne, XCVII, 819, 894.---What penalty informers are to be fined, Angilram, XCVI, 1064.

DENARIAL precept, Marculf, LXXXVII, 713.

DENARIAL charter before the king, Ancient Formularies, LXXXVII, 767.---On denarial charters, Charlemagne, XCVII, 773.

PENNY. On St Peter’s penny (*Romescot*), Laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1303, 1335, 1338.---On giving the penny of the holy Church, Diplomatic Records of Æthelred II, CLI, 1166.---On those who refuse to accept good denarii, Charlemagne, XCVII, 408, 576.

DENDROPHORI. On the *dendrophori*, Constantine the Great, VIII, 129.

DESIGNATION. Charter of designation to a church of land and slaves, Ancient Formularies, CLI, 1438.

DENUNCIATION. On denunciation or proclamation, Constantine, VIII, 154.---On denunciation or proclamation of a rescript, ibid., 235.---On the renewal of denunciations, ibid., 141.

DEPOSIT. On deposit, St Isidore, LXXXII, 207, 208; Charlemagne, XCVII, 756; St Ivo, CLXI, 931.---If anyone gives another a deposit, he is to employ three witnesses, ibid., 931.

[Col. 0022] DESERTERS. On deserters, Capitulary of Pavia, XCVII, 213.

BETROTHAL. On the betrothal of those below puberty, Innocent III, CCXIV, 290, 539, 791.

DEACONESS, Charlemagne, XCVII, 881.

DIGEST. The code of the Digest, or Pandects, Paul the Deacon, XCV, 468.

DIGNITIES. On dignities, Constantine, VIII, 394.---Dignities of the Frankish palace, Carolingian Code, XCVIII, 587.---On the fine to be paid for the dignity of the Church, CLI, 1171.

GODS. Laws concerning the establishment of new gods, Tertullian, I, 290.---The laws of the nations punish gods, In the Lives of the Fathers, LXXIII, 553.

DELAY. On delays, Constantine, VIII, 112, 330; St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 577, 802.

DIPLOMA. Diploma of Otto I, XCVIII, 30.---On Henry’s diploma, ibid., 32.---Diplomas, ibid., XCVII, 913–1084.---Diplomas of Sigebert, LXXXVII, 319–326.---Genuine diplomas of Clovis, ibid., 681–686.---Diplomas granted to or by St Willibrord, LXXXIX, 535–356.---On the diplomas of Rudolf, king of the Romans, XCVIII, 41, 863.

PLUNDER. What one who invites others to plunder ought to suffer, St Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 311.

SEPARATION. Regino, abbot of Prüm, CXXXII, 304.---Oath concerning an incestuous separation, ibid., 329.

DISCERNMENT. On the discernment of cases, St Isidore, LXXXXIV, 375.

EXPENSES of royal envoys, Charlemagne, XCVII, 443, 583.

DISSOLUTION of marriage. Formula for dissolving a marriage, Andecavian Formularies, LXXXVII, 854.

DIVINE laws rest upon nature; human laws upon customs, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 29.

DIVISION. Andecavian Formularies, LXXXVII, 853.---On a division when the king’s envoy is present, ibid., 712.---Agreement for division between brothers, ibid., 804.---Division of the empire, Diplomatic Code, XCVII, 295, 373, 641.---Formula for division of the empire, ibid., 669.

DIVORCE. On divorce, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 247; Innocent III, CCXVI, 238, 258.---On the ground of divorce, ibid., 749.---For three causes a wife may separate from her husband, Laws of Haelidha, CXXXVIII, 474.---A woman may not dismiss a man whom she knowingly accepted as a slave for a husband, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1434.---A marriage ought not to be dissolved when both spouses are adulterers, Innocent III, CCXV, 1418.---On divorce on account of spiritual kinship, ibid., CCXIV, 360, 361.---On the divorce of King Philip, ibid., 617, 881–896.---On the divorce of King Lothar and Queen Tetberga, Hincmar, CXXV, 612–760.---Against divorce, St Augustine, XL, 100; Diplomatic Code, XCVII, 739.---On those who abandon wives following a divorce, In St Isidore’s Extracts of Canons, LXXXIV, 476.---If they bind themselves in marriage, they are shown to be adulterers, ibid., 651.---What ought to be decided concerning those who wish, on the ground of fornication, to leave their wives and take others to themselves; likewise concerning one who denies that he has betrothed her whom he is thought to have betrothed, Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, CL, 518.---A man may not dismiss his wife unless consanguinity has been proved before the Church, Pope Alexander II, CXLVI, 1388.---A man cannot take another wife while his wife is alive, as Scripture testifies, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1428.

FRAUD. On malicious fraud, Constantine, VIII, 170.---Whoever uses fraud or fear in order that a thing may pass to another is liable for both force and fraud, St Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 944.

THE LORD’S DAY. On observance of the Lord’s Day, St Isidore, LXXXIV, 285.---Observance of the Lord’s Day is commanded, Charlemagne, XCVII, 196, 239.---On servile works which must not be done on Sundays, ibid., 519.

OWNERSHIP. Some ownerships of things are acquired by natural law, others by civil law, St Ivo, CLXI, 1226.

LORD. A distinction exists between an owner and a possessor, St Gregory the Great, LXXXVII, 685.---If a slave kills with his master’s knowledge, both remain culpable, St Ivo, CLXI, 921.---The master, not the slave, is to be sued for recovery, ibid., 922.---On lords, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 174.

TO GIVE. On the capacity of a free person to give, Charlemagne, XCVII, 572.---On a woman’s power to sell and give, Frankish Capitulary, XCVII, 144; Lombard Capitulary, ibid.---The house given by Ammonia to the Roman Church is to be restored to Calicenus, her nephew, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 954.

DONATION. St Isidore of Seville, LXXXII, 206; Anamod, CXXIX, 905.---Precept of donation, Marculf, LXXXVII, 707.---Precept concerning Loesiverpo, issued by the king’s hand, [Col. 0023] ibid., 708.---Donation to the house of God, Ancient Formularies, ibid., 772, 804; (Marculf?) ibid., 811, 812.---Donation to the house of God for masses to be sung, ibid., 857.---Donation to a church, ibid., 779.---Cession to a church, ibid., 767.---Cession from the present day to a church, ibid., 731, 810.---Donation of a small thing to a church, ibid., 732, 810.---Donation to a church after death, ibid., 793.---If any persons have a thing of the Church for use and give something from their own property, ibid., 750.---That every free person should have the power, wherever he wishes, to give his property for the salvation of his soul, Charlemagne, XCVII, 404.---On a cleric who is tonsured in a monastery and gives his property to that place, Marculf, LXXXVII, 729.---Charter of donation to a monastery in precarial tenure, ibid., 875.---Donation from the present day, ibid., 862.---Cession from the present day, ibid., 794.---Another cession, ibid., 810.---Cession to laypersons, ibid., 816.---One who has made a donation for a weighty cause, ibid., 728.---Charter of donation between a man and a woman of their property, ibid., 733.---Likewise another, without any diminution, ibid.---Donation between husband and wife, provided that it is entered in the public records, ibid., 785.---Donation made to a betrothed woman, ibid., 785.---Donation to a betrothed woman, ibid., 799.---Donation to children, Ancient Formularies, ibid., 777.---Donation which a father makes to his son, ibid., 801, 802, 817.---Another donation of the same thing, ibid., 817.---Donation to natural children, ibid., 819.---Donation which a person gives to his parent, ibid., 804.---If anyone wishes to grant something to his slave or his *gasindus* (retainer), ibid., 749.---A donation must be confirmed in writing, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 618.---Letter of donation, Marculf, LXXXVII, 810.

DONATIONS. *Codex Carolinus*, XCVIII, 565.---Donations and testaments, LXXXVIII, 1155–1518.---How donations or testaments are to be read, Marculf, LXXXVII, 749.---On donations, Constantine the Great, VIII, 135, 140, 176, 232, 371; Charlemagne, XCVII, 840.---Charters of donation, *Codex diplomaticus*, ibid., 212.---Charter of Countess Matilda, or donation to the Holy See made once and again, XCVIII, 659, in Pope Leo’s letter to Emperor Charles.

DONATISTS. On indulgence and freedom of choice granted to the Donatists by Constantine, VIII, 775.---Imperial laws against the Donatists, St. Optatus, XI, 805.---Constantine’s laws against the Donatists, ibid., 794.---Honorius’s laws against the Donatists, ibid., 817, 1194, 1212, 1216, 1420, 1424, 1428, 1430.---Law of Theodosius the Younger against the Donatists, ibid., 823.---The law of Theodosius imposing a fine of ten pounds of gold upon heretics, extended to the Donatists, St. Augustine, XXXII, 804.---Very many Donatists corrected through the laws of the emperors, id., XXXIII, 796, 806.---Donatists ordered to lose their possessions under the laws of earthly rulers, ibid., 345.---Usefulness of imperial laws against the Donatists, ibid., 796, 798, 802, 806; XLIII, 315, 425, 733.---Pope St. Gregory complains that laws enacted against the Donatists are neglected, LXXVII, 848.

DOWRY. Conveyance as dowry, Andegavian Formulae, LXXXVII, 849.---Establishment of a dowry, Marculf, ibid., 823, 876.---Solemn formula concerning a dowry, St. Gregory, bishop of Tours, LXXI, appendix, 1160; Andegavian Formulae, LXXXVII, 839.---Dowry document, Marculf, id., 738; anonymous author, id., 771; (Marculf?), id., 822, 823; Andegavian Formulae, id., 848; ancient formulae, CLI, 1436, 1437.

DOWER of the queen of the English, Innocent III, CCXVI, 268.

DUCHY. Charter concerning a duchy, Marculf, LXXXVII, 705, 815.

DUEL. On the duel, Clement III, CCIV, 1501.---Against the duel, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 581.

CHARTER OF KING DUNCAN OF THE SCOTS, Appendix to Bede, XCV, 366.

DUKES. City dukes, *Codex diplomaticus*, XCVIII, 370.---Dukes serving as judges in Gaul, ibid., 313.---Counts and dukes alike preside over cities, ibid., 571.

CHARTERS OF EDGAR, KING OF THE SCOTS, Appendix to Bede, XCV, 366.---Charters of Edgar, king of the English, ibid., 379.---Edgar’s statutes, St. Germanus of Paris, LXXII, 403.

CHARTERS OF EDGAR, KING OF THE ENGLISH, Appendix to Bede, XCV, 377.

DRUNKENNESS. The vice of drunkenness is prohibited by law, Charlemagne, XCVII, 187.

CHURCH. The Church observes the laws of the Roman emperors, St. Ivo, CLXII, 279.---On churches, Constantine the Great, VIII, 101, 180; Theodosius, XIII, 531.---On the honor due to churches, *Codex diplomaticus*, XCVII, 414, 570, 579, 746.---On breaking into a church, laws of Athelstan, CXXXVIII, 463, 466.---On restoring and building churches, Constantine, VIII, 491.---On repairing churches, St. Isidore, LXXXIV, 539.---On the restoration of churches, [Col. 0024] *Codex diplomaticus*, XCVII, 541; Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 199, 417.---What is to be observed in the restoration of churches, whether in construction or dedication, St. Isidore, LXXXIV, 832.

CHARTER OF BISHOP ECQUINUS, Appendix to Bede, XCV, 371.

EDICT. Baluzian Formulae, LXXXVII, 860.

EDICT. St. Isidore of Spain, LXXXII, 201.---What an edict is, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 32.---An edict of prefects is to be ranked below the emperor’s law, Marius Mercator, XLVII, 391.---Copy of an edict of the praetorian prefects, ibid., 392.---Why use edicts? ibid., 528.---General edicts customarily inscribed with the names of the praetorian prefects, ibid., 381 (note).---Edicts were not promulgated in provinces unless furnished with a proclamation of the provincial governors, ibid., 566, 785, 827, 833.---What distinction exists between edicts and imperial letters to governors, ibid., 833.---On edicts, Constantine the Great, VIII, 242.---When Galerius’s edict in favor of Christians was issued and posted at Nicomedia, Lactantius, VII, 250, 781, 786.---On what day and in what year the edict of Diocletian and Maximian against Christians was promulgated, ibid., 213, 317, 506, 687.---Edict of Constantine and Licinius in favor of Christians, ibid., 267.---Edict for religious liberty, id., VIII, 105.---Edict by which Constantine hands over the city of Rome, etc., etc., to Pope Sylvester and his successors, Constantine, VIII, 567, 578.---Edict issued by Volusianus, prefect of the city, St. Leo, LVI, 500.---Edict addressed to bishops and patriarchs established everywhere, Justinian, LXXI, 957.---Edict of the emperors confirming the Council of Chalcedon, St. Isidore of Spain, LXXXIV, 173 ff.---Edict concerning the Corsican expedition, Charlemagne, XCVII, 461.---Otto’s edict for Ratherius, in the Life of Ratherius, CXXXVI, 88.

EMILIAN LAW, Tertullian, I, 298.

EMPHYTEUTIC. On emphyteutic right, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 526.

St. Isidore, LXXXII, 205; *Codex diplomaticus*, XCVII, 766; Folcuin, CXXXVI, 1198, 1199, 1205, 1212, 1217.---On entering into a purchase, Constantine, VIII, 173, 391.---On buying on the Lord’s Day, laws of Athelstan, CXXXVIII, 464, 468.---On purchases, *Codex diplomaticus*, XCVII, 313.---That sale and purchase must not occur except before witnesses and in towns, laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1313, 1319.---On goods bought from a thief, from an uncertain council, LXXX, 829.---If anyone buys something from a slave without the master’s knowledge, the sale may be rescinded, St. Ivo, CLXI, 924, 1221.---Nothing is to be bought from an unknown person, St. Ivo, CLXI, 959.---On one who has sold property bought by fraudulent contrivance from another, ibid., 964.

MARKET. On markets, laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1319.

ROYAL IMMUNITY. Marculf, LXXXVII, 701, 808.---Immunity of saints, ibid., 773.---Confirmation concerning immunity, ibid., 702.

BISHOPRIC. Precept concerning a bishopric, Marculf, LXXXVII, 704.---Grant of citizens concerning a bishopric, ibid., 705.---Another grant of citizens concerning a bishopric, ibid., 807.

ENVOY. On the office of proconsul and envoy, Constantine, VIII, 99, 186, 201, 398.---Travel-warrant for envoys, id., LXXXVIII, 706, 815.---On the admonition addressed to those performing an embassy, id., XCVII, 543.

LEGISLATOR justly amends or abolishes a law for good cause, XCVIII, 804.---The first legislators of the Franks, St. Ivo, CLXI, 611.---On legislators, Laws of Æthelstan, CXXXVIII, 464.---On the authors of laws, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 197.---On makers of laws, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 43.---Ecclesiastical and civil legislators often abuse their authority, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1346.

ON THE LEGITIMATION of children, Innocent III, CCXIV, 1130.

PIMP. Pimps are to be expelled from cities, St. Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 651, 928.---Praetors ought to prevent anyone from being a pimp, ibid., 1222.

PIMPING. On pimping, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 311, 312.---He who keeps slaves for prostitution practices pimping, St. Ivo, CLXI, 311, 312.

CHARTER OF BISHOP LEOFSIGE, Appendix to Bede, XCV, 383.

THAT *LEUDESAMIA* [pledges of loyalty] be promised to the king (Marculf?), LXXXVII, 816.

LEUDES. That the oath of the *leudes* [royal retainers] be promised to the king, Marculf, LXXXVII, 724.

LAW. On laws, St. Ivo, CLXI, 1115.---What is understood by the name “law,” Gratian, CLXXXVII, 667.---Law is so called from reading or choosing, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 681.---Law (from *legere*, “to read” or “to choose”) is a written ordinance, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 199, 200.---Law is understood in a general and in a special sense, St. Augustine, XXXV, 2087, 2088.---What an honorable law is, St. Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 303.---Why law was made, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 202; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 35.---What law can do, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 202.---What sort of law ought to be made, ibid., 203; St. Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1116; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 35.---Law [Col. 0036] presupposes free choice, Tertullian, II, 289, 290.---Law distinguishes a human being from a beast, ibid.

The usefulness of law, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 676.---Law binds human beings to God, Tertullian, II, 289.---Laws are enacted with the intention that they benefit, not harm, Lactantius, VII, 308 (note).---It is prejudged that what is done well is not done contrary to law, Tertullian, I, 285.---All laws aim at happiness, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 393.---Laws fortify and defend, Juvencus, XIX, 171.---On divine and human laws, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 198.---Divine laws rest upon nature; human laws, upon customs, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 29.---On secular laws, Charlemagne, XCVII, 233.---Law handed down by men is a good shield, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 137.---The best laws of the ancients were borrowed from divine law, Tertullian, I, 499.---Law is a written ordinance, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 30.---Law is an ordinance of the people, ibid., 31.---Law is called a divine sanction of the emperor, Marius Mercator, XLVIII, [page not printed].---Whatever the emperor establishes by letter, decrees when hearing a case, or promulgates by edict, is law, St. Ivo, CLXI, 304, 305.---The human law is called the prefect’s edict, Marius Mercator, XLVIII, 409.---How law, statutes, and customs differ from one another, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 199.---On law and custom, Charlemagne, XCVII, 804.---Long-established customs resemble law, St. Ivo, CLXI, 940.---Things established for lasting benefit ought to remain unshaken, ibid., 961.---Customs pass into laws, ibid., 308. Yet they do not prevail over laws, ibid., 309.---Good laws and customs are not easily to be changed, ibid., 309, 311.---Bad ones, however, are to be uprooted, ibid., 309, 311, 949.

Equity alone commends a law, Tertullian, I, 288, 289.---A law which is not just is not law, St. Augustine, XXXII, 1231.---An unjust law demands no honor or obedience, Tertullian, I, 286, 566.---No law ought to owe the justification of its justice to itself alone, but to those from whom it expects obedience, ibid., 289, 566.---A law is suspect if it does not wish to be tested; it is wicked if, untested, it rules, ibid.---If a law errs, it comes from human beings, not from heaven, ibid., 285.---Why human laws are imperfect, ibid., 289, 499.---It is not justice but expediency that devised laws, Lactantius, VI, 662.---Every nation has established for itself what it judged useful to its own affairs, ibid.---Human laws are often harmful or useless, Tertullian, I, 285.---Unjust laws are foolish, ibid., 289.---Those deceived by the unjust impunity of human laws do not know true justice, St. Zeno, XI, 297.---Under human law certain things are permitted which divine law forbids and punishes, St. Augustine, XXXII, 1232.---Laws are to be enforced by a just ruler, Hincmar, CXXV, 851.---Kings are to be bound by their own laws, St. Ivo, CLXI, 914.---Human law is necessarily manifold and variable; divine law is one and everlasting, Lactantius, VI, 661.---Positive law is especially mutable, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 164.---Temporal law can be changed, ibid., 449.---Laws mitigated by public consent, Tertullian, I, 287.---Laws amended and made obsolete, ibid., 566; Arnobius, V, 914 ff.---Law released by necessity, Lactantius, VII, 205.---The authority of human laws, Tertullian, I, 499.---Human laws, when connected with divine law, bind, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1346.---He who does not love laws is subject to laws, St. Augustine, XXXII, 1188.---What is done contrary to law is dissolved by the authority of law, Hincmar, CXXVI, 655; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 55.---Laws are invalid without a date and consul, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 271.---Those provisions prevail in laws which agree with the rationale of right and law, St. Ivo, CLXI, 308.---Many laws are evidence of corrupted morals, Lactantius, VI, 574.---No law forbids inquiry, Tertullian, I, 566.---No law forbids examination of what it forbids being admitted, ibid., 289.---No law ought to condemn a person unless convicted of a crime or confessing it, ibid., 566, 702.---Laws indeed attack laws through an eloquence favoring injustice, St. Zeno, XI, 284.---To act against justice through legal circumventions is worse than any violence, ibid., 286.---Secular laws and rights are sold and corrupted through inveterate malice, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 520.---The diversity of laws obstructs Christian unity, St. Agobard, CIV, 116 ff.---Law grants pardon for the past and forbids for the future, St. Ivo, CLXI, 941.

Human laws are to be learned, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 62.---No one may be allowed not to know the laws, Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius; Hincmar, CXXV, 1106.---On observing laws, St. Ivo, CLXI, 307.---The observance of laws is an indication of civilization, Cassiodorus, LXIX, 630.---Temporal laws, once established, are to be observed, St. Ivo of Chartres, bishop, CLXI, 304, 307, 949.---The laws are to be observed by all Roman rulers, ibid., 1118.---He who does not obey the just laws of emperors incurs punishment, ibid.---The emperors’ laws ought to be observed, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 55, 56.---The laws of rulers are not to be despised by anyone, St. Ivo, [Col. 0037] CLXI, 306; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 56.---Breakers and despisers of laws are to be punished, St. Ivo, CLXI, 306.---The laws of rulers prevail over natural law, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 47.---Imperial laws are to be observed in ecclesiastical judgment, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1296.---The laws of rulers are sometimes rightly invoked in aid of canons, ibid., 1298.---The law of emperors is not above the law of God, Charlemagne, XCVII, 870.---The laws of rulers must be subject to God’s law, St. Ivo, CLXI, 287, 307.---The laws of God are to be of greater concern to prelates than Justinian’s laws, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 719.---The laws of Christians, enacted by God and Christ, surpass all others, Tertullian, I, 489.---The laws of Christian kings are to be accepted by churches, St. Ivo, CLXI, 305.---The Church benefits from both good and bad laws of emperors, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 399, 796.---On consular and tribunician laws, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 201.---What the laws of tyrants are, Rupert, abbot, CLVIII, 561.---By which emperors laws against Christians were enacted, Tertullian, I, 292 ff.---Law concerning the establishment of new gods, ibid., 290.---What was decreed at the Council of Carthage concerning requesting laws from emperors against Donatists, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 805.---Law abolishing gladiators and concerning the priests of the Nile, Eusebius Pamphilus, VIII, 75.---Laws against heretics. See HERETICS.---Law confirming the Fourteenth Council of Toledo, St. Isidore, LXXXIV, 503.---Law confirming the Sixteenth Council of Toledo, ibid., 547.---Law confirming the Seventeenth Council of Toledo, ibid., 561.---Law conferring upon the Roman pontiff authority to judge matters of religion, Theodosius, XIII, 577 ff.---Law against Jews, Samaritans, and heretics, Justinian, LXXII, 986.---Laws and cases are to be decided according to the laws, St. Ivo, CLXI, 308, 933.---Different laws do not dissolve a marriage once contracted, St. Ivo, CLXI, 628.---What Agellius wrote concerning the laws of cities, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 164.

Lex Aehasancta, Boethius, LXIV, 1062.---Lex Antia, Tertullian, I, 298.---Law of Antoninus against adulterers, St. Augustine, XL, 474; Hincmar, CXXV, 1024.---Law of Antoninus on repudiations, ibid., 737.---Attic laws, Sidonius Apollinaris, LVIII, 534.---Aunarian laws, Arnobius, V, 916.---Cincian laws, ibid., 917.---Law of Constantine on piety toward God and the Christian religion, Constantine, VIII, 253 ff.---On the laws which Constantine enacted for Christians, Cassiodorus, LXIX, 891.---Cornelian law on forgery, Constantine, VIII, 133, 304.---Cornelian testamentary law, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 978.---Laws drawn up by Hadrian from the Athenian books of Draco and Solon, Cassiodorus, LXIX, 1232.

Ecclesiastical laws of Alfred, king of the English, CXXXVIII, 447 (999).---Of Edward the Elder, king of the English, ibid.; and of Guthrum, king of the Danes, ibid., 459.---Of Æthelstan, king of the English, ibid., 461.---Of Haelidha, prince of all Wales, ibid., 471.---Of Edmund, king of the English, ibid., 480.---Of Edgar, king of the English, ibid., 496.---Assemblies and laws of Lothar I, ibid., 525; of Louis II and Charles II, ibid., 527; of Lothar I, Louis II, and Charles II, ibid., 533; of Louis II, ibid., 546.---Constitutions and ecclesiastical laws of the three Ottos, ibid., 821.---Laws of King St. Edward which he maintained in England, and which William, his heir and kinsman, confirmed, CXLIX, 1331 (1083, 1087).---Other laws of King Edward, written in the Norman language, ibid., 1334.---Ancient statutes setting forth the assemblies of the whole realm of England, ibid., 1339.---Laws of Stephen I, king of the Hungarians, CL, 1243.---Laws of Břetislav, duke of Bohemia, ibid., 1257.

Lex Aemilia, Tertullian, I, 298.

Lex Fabia, Constantine, VIII, 126.

Laws of the Franks, Alamanni, and Bavarians, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 1163 appendix.---Dagobert revises the laws of the Franks, ibid., 1163.---The laws of the Franks and Lombards supplemented by Charles, XCVIII, 502.---In the kingdom of the Franks, as there were different peoples, so there were different laws: the Franks lived by their own law, the Lombards by theirs, likewise the Burgundians and Saxons by theirs, and the Goths by theirs, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 416.

Lex Gundobada, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 230; St. Agobard, CIV, 113, 120, 121; Hincmar, CXXV, 1026. See GUNDOBADA.

Laws of St. Henry, CXL, 223–258.

Laws promulgated by Emperor Louis II, CXXXVIII, 573, 614.

Julian law, Tertullian, I, 286; St. Augustine, XL, 475.---Julian law on adulteries, Constantine, VIII, 298, 307; Theodosius, XIII, 526; St. Eugyppius, abbot, LXII, 732; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 977.---The utterly unjust Julian law on adultery, permitting concubines and prostitutes, St. Zeno, XI, 297.---Julian law on appeals to Caesar, Blessed Alcuin, C, 413.---Julian law on the marriage of younger persons, repealed by Severus, [Col. 0038] Tertullian, I, 286.---Julian law of treason, Constantine, VIII, 109, 145.---Julian law, or law concerning public and private violence, ibid., 146, 174.

Laws of Julian against Christians, Cassiodorus, LXIX, 1040.

Laws of Lycurgus amended by the Lacedaemonians, Tertullian, I, 286.

Mantian Law concerning the oath of clerics, CIII, 811 (note).

Appian Law, Orosius, XXXI, 907.

Papia Law repealed by Severus, Tertullian, I, 286.

Roman Law, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 1160, 1161.---When Roman laws were introduced into collections of canons, St. Leo, LVI, 316 et seq. (note).---Roman law accords with canonical authority, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 301.---Roman laws corrected by the Emperor Justinian, Paul the Deacon, XCV, 467; Ado, CXXIII, 118; St. Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 304.---Roman law ought not to be corrupted by anyone’s rashness, St. Ivo, CLXI, 1118; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 56.---Roman law concerning consanguinity, St. Ivo, CLXI, 669.

Laws were brought to the Romans from Athens, as also to the Greeks and Hebrews, St. Ambrose, XVII, 105.---The laws of the Romans enormously increased, Tertullian, I, 286, 572.

Satira Law, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 34.

Theodosian laws, Sidonius Apollinaris, LVIII, 473.

Theodosian Law, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 308.---Theodosian laws, Sidonius Apollinaris, LVIII, 472; St. Ivo, CLXI, 1116.

Laws of the Twelve Tables. Names of those who expounded the laws of the Twelve Tables, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 44.

**PETITION** (*libellus*) of complaint or applications, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 391.---Concerning defamatory pamphlets, Constantine, VIII, 157, 191, 202, 334.

**FREE PERSON, FREE PERSONS.** Free persons are not to be compelled to perform servile works, Charlemagne, XCVII, 143, 144.---Let no one reduce a free person to slavery, Laws of St. Stephen, CLI, 1248.---Concerning free persons who wish to devote themselves to God’s service, Charlemagne, XCVII, 287, 292.---That every free person may have the power, wherever he wishes, to give his goods for the salvation of his soul, ibid., 404.---Concerning free persons who must be compelled to come to the *mallus* [public court], ibid., 559.---Concerning a free person summoned for military service, ibid., 562.---How a free person may clear himself of theft, St. Ivo, CLXI, 949.---How a free person may distribute his goods as he wishes, ibid., 955.---The right of free persons, Formulae of Angers, LXXXVII, 849.

**CONCERNING A CASE OF FREE STATUS.** Constantine, VIII, 235, 237, 246, 369.

**LIBERALITY.** Concerning liberality and the dispensing of alms, St. Ambrose, XVI, 123.

**CHILDREN.** Concerning the legitimation of children, Innocent III, CCXIV, 1130.---Parents may not disinherit children, nor children parents, because they have become monks, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1098.---That slaves, free persons, and every class of infamous persons ought not to bring accusations, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 222.---Concerning those who obtained exemption by reason of the number of their children or poverty, Constantine, VIII, 283.

**LIBERTY.** Charter of liberty, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 190, 269, 272, 393, 457.---Concerning a person who has obtained liberty through a charter, Charlemagne, XCVII, 258, 556.---Liberty of Roman citizens, (Marculf?), LXXXVII, 827.---Concerning prescription by long lapse of time, which is pleaded in favor of liberty and not against liberty, Constantine, VIII, 117.---Form of a charter of liberty, LXXXVII, 872.

**LIBERTIES OF THE CHURCH.** Edict for religious liberty, Constantine, VIII, 105.---Expositions in defense of the liberties of the Church, Hincmar, CXXV, 1035.

**FREEDPERSON.** Concerning freedpersons and their children, Constantine, VIII, 187, 368.---Concerning freedpersons of the Church, St. Isidore, LXXXIV, 381, 382, 383.---Freedpersons are not to be promoted to the clergy while their patrons live, ibid., 310.---That freedpersons from the household of the Church may be made by priests in compensation for property acquired, ibid., 382.---Concerning the declaration of freedpersons of the Church, ibid.---Concerning freedpersons of the Church who abandon its patronage, ibid.---Concerning freedpersons commended to the patronage of the Church, ibid.---Concerning the declarations and obedience of freedpersons of the Church, ibid., 398.---Concerning the descendants of freedpersons of the Church: they may not wander away from the Church, even on the pretext of maintenance, ibid., 399.---That those born of freedpersons of the Church and of freeborn persons may not withdraw from the Church’s obligations of service, ibid., 438.---Concerning the service and discipline of freedpersons of the Church, ibid.---That freedpersons of the Church may not transfer any of their property into another’s ownership, ibid., 439.---How bishops are to make freedpersons, and how freedpersons are never to depart from the Church’s patronage, ibid., 623.---That freedpersons are not to be witnesses, LXXXIX, 828.---The Church is to protect freedpersons in their liberty, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 416.---Freedpersons are to be defended by priests lest they be recalled into slavery, ibid.---Which freedpersons are called freeborn, and which may or may not make a will, St. Ivo, CLXI, 1225.---Ungrateful freedpersons who accuse their patrons are to be punished, ibid., 918, 923, 932, 933.---A marriage between patron and freedwoman is recognized as lawful, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1433.

What is public, that is, what is commonly done, seems lawful, St. Agobard, CIV, 187.

**LOIRE.** Concerning the making of embankments along the Loire, Charlemagne, XCVII, 570.

**LAWSUIT.** Concerning the limits of lawsuits, Charlemagne, XCVII, 562.---How all lawsuits ought to be settled, St. Ivo, CLXI, 933.---All lawsuits ought to be abbreviated according to the laws, ibid., 308.

**LITIGANT.** Concerning litigants, Charlemagne, XCVII, 752, 829.

**CONCERNING LITIGIOUS MATTERS.** Constantine, VIII, 356.---Things placed in litigation must not be transferred to any person before the outcome of the hearing, LIX, 146.

**LETTERS.** Concerning contempt for royal letters, Charlemagne, XCVII, 408, 575.---Letters of the rulers of the empire concerning the confirmation and observance of peace between the Church and the empire, Alexander III, CC, 55.---Concerning literary studies, Charlemagne, XCVIII, 895.

**LOMBARDS.** Diplomas of the Lombard kings, LXXXVII, 1347–1444.---Lombard capitula, Charlemagne, XCVII, 441.---Lombard law was highly favorable to wives, St. Agobard, CIV, 317.

Roman constitution of Lothair I, Charlemagne, XCVII, 457.---Constitutions of Lothair I at Maringo, ibid., 461.---Lombard capitula of the Emperor Lothair I, ibid., 668.

**LAMP.** Concerning money for lamps, Diplomatic Monuments of Cnut, CLI, 1174.

Assembly of the Emperor Louis I at Compiègne, Charlemagne, XCVII, 665.---Capitularies of Louis I and Lothair, ibid., 371–672.---Agreement of the Emperor Louis I with Pope Paschal, ibid., 679.

**CONCERNING MALEFACTORS.** Constantine, VIII, 153, 162; Charlemagne, XCVII, 511, 756, 821; Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 349; Laws of St. Stephen, CLI, 1251.

**MALLUS** [public court]. Concerning the public *mallus*, Charlemagne, XCVII, 660; Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 219, 271, 307, 344, 346, 347, 348.---Concerning one who has been lawfully summoned to the *mallus* and has not appeared, Charlemagne, XCVII, 773.

**SLAVES.** Concerning slaves, Ancient Formulae of an Unknown Author, LXXXVII, 800; Charlemagne, XCVII, 131, 653, 906.---Concerning slaves of the palace and of churches, ibid., 143, 144.---Edict concerning slaves of churches, Laws of St. Stephen, CLI, 1039.---Concerning agricultural workers and slaves belonging to public or private royal estates and fiscal lands, Constantine, VIII, 398.---Concerning slaves seized by the royal treasury, Charlemagne, XCVII, 567.---Concerning slaves and coloni of patrimonial, forest, and emphyteutic estates, Constantine, VIII, 187.---Concerning the sale of slaves, ibid., 725.---Order concerning the exchange of a slave, *Liber Diurnus* of the Roman Pontiffs, CV, 100.---Concerning slaves taking refuge in royal estates, Charlemagne, XCVII, 411, 577.---Why slaves were formerly sold in the presence of ecclesiastical persons or judges, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1037.---A slave is redeemed for fifteen solidi, ibid., 676.---For the sake of faith, slaves were asserted into freedom against their owners’ will, with no price paid, ibid., 675.---This practice was not in force everywhere, ibid., 675, 676, 683.---A slave manumitted on the condition that he become a monk was not permitted to leave the monastery, ibid., 971.---It was forbidden to sell slaves and weapons outside the kingdom, Charlemagne, XCVII, 135.---A pagan, Jew, or heretic may not possess a Christian slave, ibid., 635, 680, 876, 877.---The laws forbid Jews to circumcise pagan slaves, ibid., 823, 824.---If Samaritans circumcise pagan slaves, let those slaves be claimed for freedom, ibid., 824; Isaac, Bishop of Langres, CXXIV, 1109.
