WEIGHT. On weights, *Codex Diplomaticus*, XCVII, 566; laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1319.

BRIDGE. On public bridges, Charlemagne, XCVII, 581, 904.---On the construction of all bridges, ibid., 576.---On renewing bridges where they existed in ancient times, ibid., 541.---On repairing bridges in various places, ibid., 577.---On restoring twelve bridges over the Seine, ibid., 570.---On not compelling anyone to go to a bridge for the sake of toll, ibid., 560.

PONTIFF. On the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, Pope Nicholas, Appendix, CXIX, 1187.

POSSESSION. On possession, St Ivo, CLXI, 1095–1098.---On acquiring and recovering possession, Constantine, VIII, 117.---By what arguments possession is proved, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 651.---How possession is valid, St Ivo, CLXI, 239.---It appears that St Gregory first extended possession to forty years in ecclesiastical matters, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 455.---How possession is interrupted, ibid., 456.---On possession of thirty years, *Codex Diplomaticus*, XCVII, 661; Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 196.---Possession of thirty years suffices in secular matters and formerly prevailed in ecclesiastical matters, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 455.---Possession of forty years is valid, Innocent III, CCXIV, 546; St Ivo, CLXI, 232.---Possession for three years excludes objections, ibid., 232.---Three-year possession must be maintained within a single province, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1028.---Possession of a boundary cannot be acquired by prescription, ibid., 1029.---What emphyteutic possession is, St Gregory the Great, LXXXVII, 502.---Church possessions are exempt from payment of taxes and imposts, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 197, 416.

POSSESSOR is not the owner, but has a right in the thing, St Gregory, LXXVII, 684.---Proof is to be required not from the possessor but from the claimant’s party, St Ivo, CLXI, 943.---No one ought to sell anything without the possessor’s consent, ibid., 946.---On a possessor expelled by force, Charlemagne, XCVII, 767, 786; St Ivo, CLXI, 960.

POSSESSORY ACTION. On the right of election with regard to possessory and petitory action, Innocent III, CCXIV, 851.

POSTERITY. What all posterity ought to have, Appendix to the tenth century, CLI, 1421.

On POSTLIMINIUM (restoration of rights upon return), Theodosius, XIII, 525.

On MAKING A CLAIM, Constantine, VIII, 182, 283, 300.

PETITIONS, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 391.

POWER. Power should not be weakened, nor should it lend its ears to flattery, St Ambrose, XVI, 86.---The power of the prince, St Augustine, XXXVIII, 109.---On royal power, Hugh, CLXIII, 941.

ORDERS of King Theodoric, LXXII, 1112, 1114, 1115.

CHARTER of donation, Marculf, LXXXVII, 707.---Charter concerning Laesiwerp, issued through the king’s hand, ibid., 708.---Charter of King Pippin obtained by Abbot Sigobald, XCVI [reference omitted in source].---Charter of King Pippin confirming the estate of Taberniacum in the district of Paris, XCVI, 1526.---Charter of Louis, King of the Franks, St Odo of Cluny, CXXXIII, 839.---Charter of Emperor Conrad, ibid., 842.

ESTATES. On the estates of shipowners, Constantine, VIII, 323; XCVII, 561.

PREFECT. A magistracy distinct from the exarch, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 484.---Who in former times was called cardinal prefect, ibid., 460, 461.---The urban prefect required accounts from the prefect of the grain supply, ibid., 484.---The prefects’ deputy, ibid., 412.---On the office of the praetorian prefects, Constantine, VIII, 292, 327, 361.

On OVERSEERS and treasurers, Constantine, VIII, 210.---On overseers appointed by the emperor, Innocent III, CCXVI, 147.

PRESCRIPTION. On prescription, St Ivo, CLXI, 1095–1098; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1027–1038.---Prescription is one of the exceptions derived from the passage of time, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 455.---When prescription runs where the fury of hostile invasion presses, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1033.---Things granted to some persons out of regard for humanity cannot be prescribed, ibid., 1032.---On prescription by long time, Constantine, VIII, 132.---On prescription by long time, which is raised in favour of liberty and not against liberty, ibid., 117.

On various prescriptions, Roger, CXLVI, 1485–1498.---Whether centennial prescription is reserved to the Roman Church alone, St Gregory the Great, CLXXVII [probably LXXVII], 455.---Centennial prescription is not to be admitted against the Roman Church, Innocent III, CCXVI, 959.

Prescription of fifty years: in what matters and between whom it is or is not valid, Abedoc and Aethelwulf, XCVI, 1293, 1294, 1299.---Prescription of forty years, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 897; Charlemagne, XCVII, 752; Roger, CXLVI, 1491.---Only prescription of forty years may be pleaded against religious houses, Charlemagne, XCVII, 367.---On observing prescription of forty years even against the Holy Roman Church, ibid., 455, 456.---A dispute concerning the boundaries of fields is to be settled by the prescription of forty years, ibid., 455.

Prescription of thirty years, St Isidore, LXXXIV, 806; Regino, Abbot of Prüm, CXXXII, 196; Roger, CXLVI, 1491.---Things quietly possessed for thirty years cannot be reclaimed, Pope Gelasius, LXX, 137; Gratian, CLXXXVIII, 1031.---Rural parishes are to remain undisturbed under those bishops who have possessed them for thirty years without violence, ibid., 1027.

On prescription of twenty years, Roger, CXLVI, 1488.---On five-year prescription, ibid.---On four-year prescription, Constantine, VIII, 398; Roger, CXLVI, 1488.---On two-year prescription and its effects, ibid., 1487.---On annual prescription, ibid., 1486, 1487.---Dialogue on prescriptions, ibid., 1491–1502.---Catalogue of prescriptions, ibid., 1501–1504.

On PRESENTATIONS, Celestine III, CCVI, 1253.

Church presidents are ordered to be exempt from public services, Constantine, VIII, 481.

PRAESTARIA. Old formulae of uncertain authorship, LXXXVII, 773; (Marculf?), ibid., 813, 814.---A *praestaria* concerning church property executed by a bishop, Marculf, ibid., 751.---A *praestaria* to the Church, Old Formulae, ibid., 768.---A *praestaria* to the house of God (Marculf?), ibid., 811.

PRAETOR. From whom he ought to guard himself while administering a province, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 443.---Among the ancients, any commander of soldiers was called praetor, ibid., 1073.---On praetors, Constantine, VIII, 194, 328.

PRECARIA. Old formulae of uncertain authorship, LXXXVII, 767, 805; (Marculf?), ibid., 814.---Unpublished formulae, ibid., 897.---Appendix to the tenth century, CLI, 1415, 1430, 1424, 1440.---A *precaria* to the house of God (Marculf?), LXXXVII, 811.

PRECARIOUS GRANT, St Isidore, LXXXII, 207.

PRECATURIA, Old formulae of uncertain authorship, LXXXVII, 782.

PRESBYTER. On the compensation for a presbyter if he is killed, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 293, 294.

On PRIMIPILARES, Constantine, VIII, 120, 148.

On FIRST-FRUITS of seed, Canute, *Diplomatic Monuments*, CLI, 1174.

PRINCE. On princes, Constantine, VIII, 120.---On those who presume to curse princes, St Isidore, LXXXIV, 391.---Princes themselves are bound by their own laws, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 49.---In the *Book on the Deaths of the Persecutors*, Lactantius shows that princes who resist true religion bring about both their own unhappiness and the ruin of their peoples, VII, 189 (308, 328), in Lactantius.---In the *Life of Constantine*, Eusebius Pamphilus shows that the pious emperor provides for the happiness of his subjects, VIII, 9 (312, 566), in Eusebius Pamphilus.---On reverence toward princes, LXXXIV, 79 (636), in the *Excerpts of Canons*, in St Isidore.---On admonishing the people not to offend against princes; on the election of princes; on admonishing princes how they should judge, ibid., 383.---On safeguarding the welfare of kings and defending the offspring of reigning princes, ibid., 389.---On the safety and due esteem to be accorded to royal offspring, ibid., 400.---On those who, while the king is alive, provide a future kingdom either for themselves or for others, and on persons prohibited from attaining the kingdom, ibid., 401.---On guarding the lives of princes and on the protection which succeeding kings must afford to preceding kings, ibid.---On the honour of the chief dignity of the palace, ibid., 399.---On the reward bestowed upon the faithful servants of kings, ibid.---That princes should have humility of heart, ibid., 838, in the Letter of Pope Gregory.---If anyone acts against the king’s will, a safe-conduct for the person whom he has ordered to be pursued, LXXXVII, 718 (646, 680), in the Formulae of Marculf the monk.---On Christian princes: their duties and glory, CIII, 293 (820, 821), in Sedulius Scotus’s *Book on Christian Rulers*.---On the duty of secular princes and the obedience to be rendered to bishops, CXXXII, 947 (942, 963), in Odo, Bishop of Canterbury.---Princes themselves are bound to live by their own laws, CLXXXVII, 49 (1152, 1153), in the first part of Gratian’s *Decretum*.---On the difference between a prince and a tyrant, and on what a prince is, CXCIX, 513 (1180, 1182), in the *Polycraticus* of John of Salisbury, Bishop of Chartres.---That although a prince is free from the bonds of the law, he is nevertheless the servant of law and equity; that he bears a public person; and that he sheds blood without guilt, ibid., 514.---That the prince is the minister of priests and inferior to them; and what it is faithfully to discharge the ministry of rulership, ibid., 516.---That, by the authority of divine law, it is established that the prince is subject to the law of justice, ibid., 518.---That a prince must be chaste and avoid avarice, ibid., 520.---That he ought always to have the law of God in his mind and before his eyes, be skilled in letters, and be guided by the counsels of learned men, ibid., 522.---That he must be taught the fear of God and be humble, and preserve humility in such a way that public authority is not diminished; and that some commands are immutable and others mutable, ibid., 526.---On the balance of a prince’s justice and clemency, which ought to be tempered in him for the benefit of the commonwealth, ibid., 529.---What it is to turn to the right or to the left, which is forbidden to a prince, ibid., 531.---What benefit princes obtain from the cultivation of justice, ibid., 532.---What the other reward of princes is, ibid., 533.---For what causes principalities and kingdoms are transferred, ibid., 537.---Princes themselves are bound to live by their own laws, ibid., 49.---Certain general precepts concerning the office of a prince, and a brief epilogue on the great reverence to be shown him, ibid., 628.---That the people are shaped according to the prince’s merit, and the principality is shaped according to the people’s merit, ibid., 633.

PRISCILLIANISTS. Rescript of Emperor Maximus in the case of the Priscillianists, Pope St Damasus, XIII, 260 (note).

A PRIVATE law cannot make a common law, Bishop Placidus, CLXIII, 664.

PRIVILEGE of King Theodoric, Folcuin, CXXXVI, 1192.---On the privileges of those who served in the sacred palace, Constantine, VIII, 115, 159, 172, 210, 311.---On the privileges of emperors in the Roman Empire, Eutropius, CXXIX, 961–968.

PROOF in all cases of theft requiring proof, Marculf, Appendix, LXXXVII, 942.---Those who in proof become bronze, tin, iron, and lead, St Gregory the Great, LXXXII, 70.---Proof is more certain in those regions where the act was done, ibid., 1308.---Rite of proof by cold water, Pope Eugenius II, CXXIX, 985–987.

PROCONSUL. On the office of proconsul and legate, Constantine, VIII, 99, 186, 201, 398.

PROCURATION. On restraining excessive procurations, Innocent, CCIV, 674.---On not increasing procurations, the same, CCXVI, 1203.

PROCURATOR. On procurations, Constantine, VIII, 95, 187; St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1267.---Through a slave acting as procurator, prejudice cannot be caused to the master against his will, St Ivo, CLXI, 1221.

PROFESSION of the Count of Foix, Innocent III, CCXVI, 847.---Profession of the Count of Comminges, ibid., 848.---Profession of Gaston of Béarn, ibid., 848.

On PROFESSORS, Constantine, VIII, 225, 310, 373.

A PROMISE becomes a debt, laws of St Stephen, CLI, 1253.

On KINSHIP, Charlemagne, XCVII, 767.

PROPERTY. How one ought to proceed when property is at issue, Innocent III, CCXIV, 998.---Ownership is acquired by delivery, possession alone by tradition, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 617, 618.---If anyone wishes, but is unable, to have as property another’s thing which he cultivates, and later obtains it by a *precaria*, LXXVII, 752, 833.

PROSCRIBED PERSONS. On the goods of proscribed or condemned persons, Constantine, VIII, 208.

On FORGERIES and doubtful narratives, Charlemagne, XCVII, 518.

GIRL. Charter of composition if anyone has carried off a girl against her will (Marculf?), LXXXVII, 824.---A girl cannot contract betrothal before her seventh year, Innocent III, CCXIV, 299.---Until her twelfth year a girl shall be subject to her father’s will, Gratian, CLXXXVIII, 1104.---On girls veiled against their parents’ wishes, the same, XCVII, 410.

BOY. Charter for donating a boy, *Liber Diurnus of the Roman Pontiffs*, CV, 101.---No one may claim exposed children of whatever status as his own property, St Ivo, CLXI, 921.---On boys tonsured or girls veiled against their parents’ wishes, *Codex Diplomaticus*, XCVII, 410.

CHILDBIRTH. The law did not wish an unformed fetus to count as homicide, St Ivo, CLXI, 706.

[Col. 0049] FIGHT. On a fight before a senator, laws of Alfred, CXXXVIII, 554.---On fights, laws of Alfred, ibid., 434.

On WARDS, *Codex Diplomaticus*, XCVII, 404, 414, 571, 579, 730.---Letter on how wards are to be received, Old Formulae of uncertain authorship, LXXXVII, 788.---On the care of wards and poor persons, St Isidore, LXXXIV, 375.---Wards are to be protected by counts, XCVII, 185.

PURGATION. On the purgation of persons ordained, Canute, *Diplomatic Monuments*, CLI, 1172.---On the purgation of one accused of theft, laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1301.

On SWORD-POLISHERS, Erkembald, CXXXVII, 596.

QUESTION / INQUIRY. On judicial inquiry, Pope Nicholas, CXIX, 1010.---On inquiries, Theodosius, XIII, 527.

On QUAESTORS, Constantine, VIII, 194.

QUANTITY. Laws establish the measure of punishments according to the measure of offenses or crimes, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 334.

On RAPACIOUS PERSONS, Isaac of Langres, CXXIV, 1096 ff.; Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 341.

ROBBERY, on, Charlemagne, XCVII, 895; Regino of Prüm, CXXXI, 335, 337 ff.; St Ivo, CLXI, 803, 954.---On robberies, Hincmar, CXXV, 1078.---On robberies committed within the kingdom, Charlemagne, XCVII, 761.---What difference there is between robbery and theft, St Ivo, CLXI, 804.---On those who commit theft and robbery, ibid., 962.

ABDUCTOR. On abductors, St Isidore, LXXXIV, 74, 171, 273, 811; Pope Nicholas I, CXIX, 992; Isaac of Langres, CXXIV, 1093, 1094, 1095, 1096; Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 273; St Ivo, CLXI, 803.---On abducted women and their abductors, Charlemagne, XCVII, 525, 728.---On abductors and abducted virgins and widows, ibid., 758.---Collection concerning abductors, Capitularies of the Kings of the Franks, CXXXVIII, 645.---Justinian’s law against abductors of virgins, CLXXVIII, 253.---The abductor of another man’s wife must be severely punished, St Gregory, LXXVII, 682.

ABDUCTION. On abduction, St Ivo, CLXI, 589.---On the abduction of virgins or widows, Constantine, VIII, 194.---On the abduction of another’s betrothed women, Charlemagne, XCVII, 405, 731.---On the abduction of girls, laws of St Stephen, CLI, 1249.---On restraining and rooting out the abduction of widows, girls, etc., Hincmar, CXXV, 1017.---If at any time husband and woman have jointly consented to abduction, suit must be brought within five years, Old Formulae, LXXXVII, 792.

Proceedings in the affair of Raymond, Count of Toulouse, Innocent III, CCXVI, 89–98.

REBAPTIZER. Laws of Honorius against rebaptizers, XI, 1204, 1205, 1208.

Edict of King Reccared confirming the Council of Toledo, LXXII, 1121, 1122.

Law issued by Prince Recceswinth, St Isidore, LXXXIV, 432.

HARBOURERS of thieves are to be regarded as thieves, St Ivo, CLXI, 946.

Bill of complaint, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 391.

On COMPLAINANTS, *Codex Diplomaticus*, XCVII, 650.

Laws of RECONCILIATION, Innocent III, CCXVI, 774.

RECTOR, among jurists, means the person who governs provinces under any title whatsoever, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 569.---On the office of a provincial governor, Constantine, VIII, 150, 334, 350, 362, 386.

REDEMPTION. On the redemption of a homicidal slave, laws of St Stephen, CLI, 1252.

REDEMPTION CHARTER, Old Formulae of uncertain authorship, LXXXVII, 776.

On REFUGES at churches, laws of Alfred, CXXXVIII, 453.

REGALIA. On confirming regalian rights, *Codex Diplomaticus*, XCVIII, 579.---On regalian rights granted to blessed Peter, ibid., 625.---Regalia of Benevento in the twelfth century, ibid., 620.---Regalian rights and the property of the treasury are to remain untouched, laws of St Stephen, CLI, 1246.---Agreement between Clement III and the senators and people of Rome concerning regalia, CCIV, 1507–1510.

Subjects ought to strive to preserve the royal rights unimpaired, laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1319.

KINGDOM. On those who flatter themselves with the hope of the kingdom while the king is still alive, St Isidore, LXXXIV, 391.---On the disqualification of persons prohibited from attaining the kingdom, ibid., 390.

REPORT together with judgment, Old Formulae, LXXXVII, 790.---On reports, Constantine, VIII, 155.

The report called an *apennis*, Old Formulae, LXXXVII, 773.

RELIEF. On a count’s relief, laws of William the Conqueror, [Col. 0050] CXLIX, 1303.---On a baron’s relief, ibid., 1305.---On tenants’ relief, ibid., 1307.

RENUNCIATION. Letters of the Queen of Cyprus concerning her renunciation of the counties of Champagne and Brie, Innocent III, CCXVI, 988.---Letter of King Louis concerning the renunciation of the Queen of Cyprus, ibid., 991.

On the REPAIR of notices, Constantine, VIII, 141.

On the DISQUALIFICATION of persons prohibited from attaining the kingdom, St Isidore, LXXXIV, 390.

REPUDIATION. On repudiations, Constantine, VIII, 353; Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 303; St Ivo, CLXI, 935; Innocent III, CCXIV, 148–150.---Bill of repudiation, Marculf, LXXXVII, 746; Old Formulae of uncertain authorship, ibid., 787.---When a wife may send repudiation to her husband, St Ivo, CLXI, 935.---Law of Antoninus concerning repudiations, Hincmar, CXXV, 737.

THING / PROPERTY. On not purchasing, upon some wrongful pretext, the goods of poor or less powerful persons, Charlemagne, XCVII, 546.---On things found by chance, laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1297.---On one who has sold another’s property for less [than its value], St Ivo, CLXI, 948.---Ecclesiastics ought not receive goods from persons whose children or relatives would thereby be disinherited, ibid., CLXI, 952.

RESCRIPT TO THE KING, Marculf, LXXXVII, 706.

RESCRIPT. The rescripts or commands of emperors are called sacred mandates, imperial sacred documents, or simply sacred documents, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 512.---On various rescripts, Constantine, VIII, 117, 128, 143, 185, 288, 373.---On rescripts and their interpretations, Innocent III, CCXVI, 1221.---Rescript of Honorius Augustus, establishing that, if two bishops have been ordained at Rome, both are to be expelled from the city, St Isidore, LXXXIV, 677.

RESPONSES OF JURISTS, Constantine, VIII, 332.---What the responses of jurists are, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 32.

COMMONWEALTH. What the commonwealth is according to Plutarch, and what occupies in it the place of soul or of limbs, CXCIX, 540 (1180, 1182), in the *Polycraticus* of John of Salisbury, Bishop of Chartres.---On the prince, who is the head of the commonwealth, and on his election and privileges, and the reward of virtue and punishment of fault, ibid., 518.---What evils or goods accrue to subjects from the character of princes, ibid., 554.---On those who hold the place of the heart in the commonwealth; that wicked persons must be excluded from the counsels of rulers; and on the fear of God, wisdom, and philosophy, ibid., 560.---On the sides of rulers, whose needs must be supplied and whose wickedness restrained; on advocates, whose tongue is harmful unless it is bound with silver cords; on recipients of gifts; and on what constitutes a gift by reason of hand, cause, time, place, or manner, ibid., 563.---Who are the feet of the commonwealth, and on the care to be bestowed upon them, ibid., 618.---On ordering the commonwealth after the likeness of nature and borrowing its order from bees, ibid., 619.---That without prudence and diligence no magistracy remains sound, nor does a commonwealth flourish whose head is infirm, ibid., 620.

On RESTITUTION, Alexander III, CC, 452; Innocent III, CCXIV, 174; CCXVI, 1238.---On restitution in integrum, Constantine, VIII, 301.

ACCUSED PERSON. On seeking out accused persons, Constantine, VIII, 233.---No one is to be made an accused person unless a formal accusation has been lodged, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 372.---On an accused person seeking a confessor, Canute I, *Diplomatic Monuments*, CLI, 1179.---On accused persons fleeing to the Church, laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1333; laws of Edward, CLI, 1192.---An accused person is by no means to be brought outside his province, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 683.

On REVELATIONS, Constantine the Great, VIII, 93.

REVERENCE. On reverence to be shown to priests, Canute, *Diplomatic Monuments*, CLI, 1172.---On the reverence of emperors toward clerics, Bishop Placidus, CLXIII, 687.

To re-pledge (*rewadiare*) a ban, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 236, 431.

KING. What the office of a king is, laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1336; laws of Edward III, CLI, 1194.---On kings, Pope Nicholas, CXIX, 1188.---A king ought to punish evils, St Ivo, CLXI, 721.---Kings ought to be subject to divine laws, ibid., 307, 903.---Kings are bound by their own laws, ibid., 908.---While a king lives, another is not to be elected, ibid., 908.---On aid to the king, laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1347.---On faith and obedience toward the king, ibid., 1317.---Kings commanding anything contrary to God are not to be obeyed, St Ivo, CLXI, 324, 907, 908.---On the privilege of the king’s men, laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1295.

RHODIAN laws, St Isidore, LXXXII, 202; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 34.

RIPUARIAN law. Chapters to be inserted into the Ripuarian law, Charlemagne, XCVII, 263.---Chapters concerning Ripuarian law, Capitularies of the Kings of the Franks, CXXXVII, 630.

When the strictness of laws is to be tempered, St Ivo, CLXII, 256.

[Col. 0051] RITE of the coronation of the German king, *Codex Carolinus*, XCVIII, 674.

On QUARRELLERS, if either has been struck, St Ivo, CLXI, 965.

On *roborias*, Diplomatic Monuments of Æthelred II, CLI, 1168.

On ROCKS, *Codex Diplomaticus*, XCVII, 311.

ROMAN law. St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 1160, 1161, Appendix; Roman laws, Hincmar, CXXV, 1026.

SACELLARIUS: the quaestor who is in charge of the treasury is so called, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 749, 750.

PRIEST. Law of King Theodoric against priests who presume to sell or give away Church property, Justinian, LXXII, 1118.---On injuries committed against priests in churches, Charlemagne, XCVII (800), 403, 571, 730.---On a priest’s fight, laws of Alfred, CXXXVIII, 454.

On SACHA, laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1336; laws of Edward III, CLI, 1194.

SACRAMENTAL, Formulae of Angers, LXXXVII, 843.

OATH. St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 1161, 1162 (Appendix); St Isidore, LXXXII, 206.---On oaths, Charlemagne, XCVII, 575, 653, 773, 897.---The king’s oath, Capitularies of the Kings of the Franks, CXXXVIII, 652.---Oath of the kings of Jerusalem, Monuments of the Holy War, CLX, 1238.---Oath of fidelity rendered by Otto, Innocent III, CCXVI, 1169.---On oaths sworn in the palace, Charlemagne, XCVII, 560.---On the oath to be rendered by bishops, abbots, and counts, ibid., 149.---Oath of laymen, Capitularies of the Kings of the Franks, CXXXVIII, 745.---General oath of all the faithful, ibid., 651, 746.---Oath of fidelity, Marculf, LXXVII, 816; XCVII, 185; *Codex Carolinus*, XCVIII, 502, 505, 514, 525, 676, 681, 710.---Where oaths are to be sworn, *Codex Diplomaticus*, XCVII, 407.---Oath of the Romans, etc., ibid., 460.

SACRIFICE. On pagan sacrifices, Constantine, VIII, 202.---Laws of Constantine against sacrifices, Eusebius Pamphilus, VIII, 44.

SACRILEGE. On sacrilege, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 283; laws of King Alfred, CXXXVIII, 453.---Penalty for sacrilege: death, Saxon capitulary, XCVII, 145.

SACRILEGIOUS PERSON. On sacrilegious persons, *Codex Diplomaticus*, XCVII, 797.---Sacrilegious persons are not to be admitted to testimony, Pope St Felix, XIII, 20.---Law concerning sacrilegious persons, added to the Gothic laws by Pope John in the Council of Troyes, Pope John VIII, CXXVI, 795.

WITCH. On witches, *Codex Diplomaticus*, XCVII, 311; laws of Edward the Elder, CXXXVIII, 462; laws of Æthelstan, ibid., 463, 466.---On expelling witches, Canute I, *Diplomatic Monuments*, CLI, 1178.

SALT. On those who make salt on the seashore, *Codex Diplomaticus*, XCVII, 569.

On not providing *salgamo* for guests, Constantine, VIII, 399.

SALIC law. Chapters of Salic law, Capitularies of the Kings of the Franks, CXXXVIII, 627.---Salic laws, Hincmar, CXXV, 1026.---Chapters added to Salic law, *Codex Diplomaticus*, XCVII, 437.---Chapters to be added to Salic law, ibid., 255, 439, 780.

SALIGA law, Capitularies of Ticino, XCVII, 215.

On SAMARITANS, Constantine, VIII, 130; Theodosius, XIII, 540.---Novella, or law, concerning Samaritans, Justinian, LXXII, 1050.---Law against Samaritans, ibid., 986.

BLOOD-STAINED PERSONS. On those who have received blood-stained persons by purchase or to be reared, Constantine, VIII, 341.

On SATIRICAL law, St Isidore, LXXXII, 202.

SCABINI. On *scabini* (judgment-finders), *Codex Diplomaticus*, XCVII, 781.---On expelling bad *scabini*, ibid., 903.

On ACTORS, Theodosius, XIII, 528; *Codex Diplomaticus*, XCVII, 752.

On LADDERS to be kept in every city, *Codex Diplomaticus*, XCVII, 862.

On SCRIBES, *Codex Diplomaticus*, XCVII, 283.

The duty of SCRIBONES was to select and examine recruits in the provinces, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 568, 569.

WRITING of Philip and embassy to the pope, Innocent III, CCXVII, 298.

On SCULDASSI, Lombard Capitularies, XCVII, 138.

On the RIGHT of *scultheti*, Erkembald, CXXXVII, 585.

Innocent III writes that scutage is to be rendered to the King of England, CCXVII, 247.

SECRETARIUM, among jurists, means the place in which judges hear cases, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 463, 464.

SECULAR laws, St Augustine, XXXIII, 106.

SECURITY / SAFE-CONDUCT. Old Formulae, LXXXVII, 766, 777; (Marculf?), ibid., 830; Formulae of Angers, ibid., 841, 845, [Col. 0052] 849, 850; Unpublished Formulae, ibid., 894, 898; *Liber Diurnus of the Roman Pontiffs*, CV, 102, 103.---Safe-conduct concerning homicide, Marculf, LXXXVII, 741; Old Formulae of uncertain authorship, ibid., 795, 1801.---Safe-conduct concerning abduction, Formulae of Angers, LXXXVII, 850.---Safe-conduct concerning *supersallicio*, ibid., 841.---If anyone has acted against the king’s will: safe-conduct for the person whom he has ordered to be pursued, Marculf, LXXXVII, 718.

SEDITIONARIES. Against seditionaries, St Isidore, LXXXIV, 273.

On SADDLERS, Erkembald, CXXXVII, 595.

SENATORS. Where senators or *clarissimi* are sued in civil or criminal matters, Constantine, VIII, 151.

What a SENATORIAL DECREE is, St Isidore, LXXXII, 201; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 32.

JUDGMENT. On persons sentenced, restored, and their children, Constantine, VIII, 227.---Judgment (*Doubtful*): St Henry on the marriage of clerics, CXL, 232.---On judgment and the matter adjudicated, Innocent III, CCXVI, 1242.

BREAKERS and violators of tombs, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 265, 335, 368.---How they are to be punished, ibid., 216.

On BURIAL, *Codex Diplomaticus*, XCVII, 145, 548, 550.

SERVICE. One who binds himself into another’s service, Marculf, LXXXVII, 745.---On the right to devote oneself to God’s service, XCVII, 655.

SLAVE, SLAVES. On slaves, Constantine, VIII, 295; St Isidore, LXXXIV, 275; Old Formulae of uncertain authorship, LXXXVII, 758, 766; *Codex Diplomaticus*, XCVII, 514; laws of Alfred, CXXXVIII, 448; laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1320.---On slaves and their manumission, ibid., 1320.---On a slave whom a tenant buys, Old Formulae of uncertain authorship, LXXXVII, 759.---On the freedom of slaves, laws of St Stephen, CLI, 1248.---Letter to be sent to a king to obtain the freedom of one’s slave (Marculf?), LXXXVII, 827.---On the correction of slaves, Constantine, VIII, 161, 305.---No one is to judge another’s slave, St Ivo, CLXI, 926.---On a slave killed by another slave, laws of St Stephen, CLI, 1252.---Penalty for a slave who denounces his master, St Ivo, CLXI, 963, 966.---The owner may reclaim without payment a slave unjustly carried off, ibid., 962.---The slaves of others are not to be corrupted or enticed, laws of St Stephen, CLI, 1249; St Ivo, CLXI, 925.---Whoever puts out a slave’s eye shall set him free, *Codex Diplomaticus*, XCVII, 753.---Except for fiscal slaves, no one is to pass from servile condition into palatine office, St Isidore, LXXXIV, 493.---Notice concerning children born to slaves, Formulae of Angers, LXXXVII, 854.---On fugitive slaves, Constantine, VIII, 150, 370, 394; *Codex Diplomaticus*, XCVII, 214; Pope Nicholas, CXIX, 990; St Ivo, CLXI, 813, 916, 920, 924, 940.---On slaves fleeing to the royal treasury, *Codex Diplomaticus*, XCVII [reference omitted in source].---Fugitive slaves ought to seek their masters’ intercession at church, not hiding places, Gelasius, LIX, 152.---A person who conceals a fugitive slave is to be punished, St Ivo, CLXI, 919.---On slaves committing crimes, St Ivo, CLXI, 924.---On a slave who has caused damage, *Codex Diplomaticus*, XCVII, 558, 773.---On slaves who, without their masters’ knowledge, inflict harm, St Ivo, CLXI, 922, 923, 924.---On slaves who through contumacy use force against someone, *Codex Diplomaticus*, XCVII, 567.---One who kills another’s slave who lies in wait for him is to be secure, St Ivo, CLXI, 938.---On conspiracies of slaves in Flanders and in Mempiscus, *Codex Diplomaticus*, XCVII, 569.

On marriages of slaves. (See MARRIAGE.) St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 1163, Appendix; *Codex Diplomaticus*, XCVII, 367; St Ivo, CLXI, 595.---The marriages of slaves are lawful, ibid., 619.

On the ordination of slaves, *Codex Diplomaticus*, XCVII, 522.---On slaves ordained without their masters’ consent, Gelasius, LIX, 144.---On slaves not to be admitted to sacred orders, *Codex Diplomaticus*, XCVII, 409.---Slaves are not to be admitted to the religious habit without their master’s consent, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1636, 637, 663.---Justinian enacted a contrary law, ibid., 663.

The testimony of slaves against their masters is not to be received, laws of St Stephen, CLI, 1248; St Ivo, CLXI, 917, 924, 947, 1218, 1220. See TESTIMONY, THIRD.

SEXTARIATICUM was a burden levied from tenants in addition to every *sextarius*, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 498, 499.

On SEALS, letters, and the safeguarding of port-tolls, *Codex Diplomaticus*, XCVII, 143, 144.

On SIGMATA, Charlemagne, XCVII, 587.

SIMONY. Decrees of Athalaric against simoniacs, Cassiodorus, LXIX, 778.

Laws of SOBRIETY among the Romans, Tertullian, I, 302.

On SOCA, laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1336; laws of Edward III, CLI, 1194.

A PARTNERSHIP formed through deceit and fraud is of no force, St Ivo, CLXI, 938.

[Col. 0053] On SODOMITES, St Isidore, LXXXIV, 538.

On the SOLEMNITY of a feast day, laws of Alfred, CXXXVIII, 456.

SOLSADIA, on, St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 1162, Appendix; Formulae of Angers, LXXXVII, 843.

PAYMENT. On payments, *Codex Diplomaticus*, XCVII, 583; St Ivo, CLXI, 937.

SUMPTUARY laws, Tertullian, I, 298.---The Aemilian and Antian laws fixed the expenses of dinners, ibid.

On DIVINERS, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 284, 349; Canute, *Monuments*, CLI, 1178; laws of St Stephen, CLI, 1251; St Ivo, CLXI, 745 ff.

SPECTACLES. Against spectacles on moral grounds, Tertullian, I, 627; St Cyprian, IV, 779; Lactantius, VI, 1074; Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 202.

BETROTHED WOMAN. On another man’s betrothed women, *Codex Diplomaticus*, XCVII, 472.---Delivery to a betrothed woman, Marculf, LXXXVII, 821.

BETROTHAL. On betrothals, Constantine, VIII, 161, 177, 346, 365, 387.---How betrothals ought to be made, St Ivo, CLXI, 939.---Betrothals are not to be contracted before the seventh year, Innocent III, 290, 791.

ESTABLISHMENT of crusaders, Innocent III, CCXVII, 239.

From whom stable-keepers are to receive payment, St Ivo, CLXI, 937.

Statutes of the pious must be observed, Gelasius, LIX, 148.---Statutes of Rispach and Freising (year 799), *Codex diplomaticus*, XCVII, 20.---Salzburg Statutes (799), ibid., 208.---Statutes of Emperor Louis II enacted as law, *Capitularies of the Frankish Kings*, CXXXVIII, 619.

Laws of St. Stephen, CLI, 1243–1254.

STIPULATION, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 206.---On the rationale of stipulations and witnesses, Abedoc and Aelhelwulf, XCVI, 1293.

On witches (*striges*), Laws of St. Stephen, CLI, 1250.

On violators of boys, LXXXIV, 76.

On sexual violation, Laws of Alfred, CXXXVIII, 454.

On swineherds, Constantine, VIII, 304.---On swineherds, wine-receivers, and the other incorporated trades, ibid., 374.

An emperor’s order obtained by fraud, to be annulled on its own account, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV; St. Gregory the Great, LXXXVII, 1311, 1312.

On those evading judgment, St. Ivo, CLXI, 1203.

SUCCESSION. A person who renounces an inheritance is not to be harassed by creditors, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 286.---On the intestate succession of Chlothar, LXXV, 452.---That the king’s faithful men are not to be defrauded by the successors to the kingdom of their property rights as payment for servitude, St. Isidore, LXXXIV, 394.

Constitutions of Suger, CLXXXVI, 1445.

Supplication to the king, Baluzian Formulae, LXXXVII, 858.

Petition on behalf of one who desires to enter into monastic life, Marculf, LXXXVII, 754.

PUNISHMENT. On the manner of punishments, Laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1321.---On the punishment of one who swears by God’s hair or beard, St. Ivo, CLXI, 788.

*Suppositorium* or *suppostarium*, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 504.

A deaf person may contract marriage, Innocent III, CCXIV, 304.

On receivers, Constantine, VIII, 210, 290.

On shoemakers, Erkembald, CXXXVII, 596.

On transferring a synagogue of the Jews if it obstructs the offices of the Church, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 457.

NOTARY. On the office of a notary, St. Ivo, CLXI, 931.---Clerics are not to be notaries, Innocent III, CCXVI, 486.

THE TWELVE TABLES, Lactantius, VI, 663.---Names of those who expounded the laws of the Twelve Tables, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 44.---The law of the Twelve Tables permits the killing of a thief caught at night, St. Ivo, CLXI, 938.

On record-keepers, Charlemagne, XCVII, 129, 653.

On a butting bull if it kills someone, St. Ivo, CLXI, 702.

TOLL. On toll, Synod of Paris, LXXX, 452; St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 718.---On tolls, *Codex diplomaticus*, XCVII, 132, 287, 553, 653, 733, 779, 906, 908.---On unjust tolls, ibid., 408, 414, 540, 576.---Which tolls are prohibited, St. Ivo, CLXI, 959.---Tolls may be levied from merchants, ibid., 953.---Where tolls should be levied, *Codex diplomaticus*, XCVII, 443.---No one is to be compelled to go to a particular place in order to pay toll, *Codex diplomaticus*, XCVII, 560; St. Ivo, CLXI, 954.

Weather-makers, St. Agobard, CIV, 147.

On pagan temples, Constantine, VIII, 202.

[Col. 0054] On times of justice, Monuments of Cnut, CLI, 1176.

TENANTS. On all those holding from the Church, Laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1333; Laws of Edward III, CLI, 1192.

On boundaries not to be moved, St. Isidore, LXXXIV, 655.

LAND. On rent-paying land, *Codex diplomaticus*, XCVII, 410, 577, 739; St. Ivo, CLXI, 956; St. Bernard, CLXXXVI, 718.---On tributary land, *Codex diplomaticus*, XCVII, 410, 577, 739; St. Ivo, CLXI, 956.---On dedicated land [reading uncertain: *eo si dicata*], Ancient Formulae, LXXXVII, 759.---On hereditary land, Laws of Alfred, CXXXVIII, 456.

WILL. St. Isidore, LXXXII, 203.---On wills, *Codex diplomaticus*, XCVII, 840.---On wills, Constantine, VIII, 325.---“Will” is sometimes used for a written document validated by the presence of witnesses, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1102.---On an undutiful will, Constantine, VIII, 158, 206, 357.---On the will of a sick person, Abedoc and Aethelwulf, XCVI, 1291.---On the will of a soldier, Constantine, VIII, 382.---Holograph will, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 204.---Will to a holy place, Baluzian Formulae, LXXXVII, 864.---Tablets of a will, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 203–204.

How a person should make a will, Marculf, LXXXVII, 820.---Formula for making a will, Baluzian Formulae, ibid., 863.---How the will of two persons is to be drawn up in one document, Marculf, ibid., 739.---Proceedings according to Roman custom: how donations and wills are to be read, ibid., 749.---A will under civil law, validated by the subscriptions of five witnesses, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 204.---A will under praetorian law, sealed with the marks of seven witnesses, ibid.

Authority granted to make a will, Innocent III, CCXIV, 1033.---Who may make a will, St. Ivo, CLXI, 941.---Freedmen who are called freeborn, and who may and may not make a will, ibid., 1225.---Persons subject to ecclesiastical jurisdiction are not to make out a testamentary document for themselves, Gelasius, LIX, 147.---Persons under ecclesiastical jurisdiction cannot make a will, St. Ivo, CLXI, 926.---Invalid will, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 945.---The property of father and mother dying without a will belongs to their son, ibid., 711.---The will of a deceased natural father must be confirmed for his children by the prince, St. Ivo, CLXI, 931.

Correction of the law concerning wills, Eusebius Pamphilus, VIII, 76.---Donations and wills of bishops, abbots, etc., LXXXVIII, 1155–1318.---Will of St. Aredius, abbot, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 1143.---Will of Lord Berno, abbot, St. Odo, Appendix, CXXXIII, 853.---Will of St. Berthichamnus, LXXX, 387–410.---Will of Burgundofara, LXXXVII, 1137.---Fragment of the will of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, LXXX, 542.---Will of Perpetuus, bishop of Tours, St. Gregory of Tours, Appendix, LXXI, 1149.---Will of Tello, bishop, eighth century, *Monuments*, XCV, 1555.---Will of William, St. Odo, Appendix, CXXXIII, 843.

TO MAKE A WILL. On the free power of making a will in favor of churches, Innocent III, CCVI, 296, 302, 487, 597.---Monks were sometimes permitted by human laws to make wills, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 506, 945, 946.

TESTATOR. The testator’s intention must be observed, Gelasius, LIX, 154.---On the property of a deceased testator, St. Ivo, CLXI, 927.

On a certificate from tribunes and protectors, Constantine, VIII, 99.

TESTIMONY. On testimonies, Celestine III, CCVI, 1260.---On the person called to bear testimony and the character he ought to possess, Charlemagne, XCVII, 260.---The testimony of one person is by no means to be received, St. Ivo, CLXI, 945.---Who are not to be admitted to give testimony, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 223; Abedoc and Aethelwulf, XCVI, 1286.---Murderers, evildoers, thieves, sacrilegious persons, abductors, poisoners, adulterers, and false witnesses are never to be admitted to testify, Angelram, XCVI, 1066.---Accomplices in crimes cannot bear testimony, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 634.---Judges should not readily admit persons of low status to testify, St. Ivo, CLXI, 1217.---No person’s testimony is to be received unless good repute or rank recommends him, ibid.---On accepting the testimony of persons who have lost the right to testify under the law concerning promotion in military service, St. Isidore, LXXXIV, 476.---On not receiving slaves as witnesses against their masters, Laws of St. Stephen, CLI, 1248.---On the testimony of slaves appointed over the court, ibid., 1253.---The testimony of slaves is not to be accepted, St. Ivo, CLI, 947, 924, 947; invalid, ibid., 934.---In criminal cases, the testimony of women is not admitted, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 633, 634.---Under canon and Gallican law women are admitted to bear testimony, ibid.---Women have the right to give testimony in court, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 977.---No one is to receive a cleric’s testimony against a layman, Constantine, VIII, 839.---Testimony is invalid without an oath, St. Ivo, CLXI, 1218.---On false testimony, Regino of Prüm, LXXXII, 284.

WITNESS. On witnesses, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1296, 1299, 1300; St. Isidore, LXXXII, 203; *Codex diplomaticus*, XCVII, 214, 738, 753, 785, 821, 829; Isaac of Langres, CXXIV, 1108; St. Ivo, CLXI, 930, 941; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 616, 617; Innocent III, CCXV, 95.---On public witnesses, Celestine III, CCVI, 1260.---On the number of witnesses, Laws of Haelidha, CXXXVIII, 476.---Decrees concerning witnesses, Burchard, CXI, 909.---On rejection of witnesses, St. Isidore, LXXXIV, 54.---Oath-witnesses, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 872.---On the oath of witnesses, St. Ivo, CLXI, 670, 943.---Formula for sworn witnesses, the same author, CLXII, 322.---Witnesses must not be produced except in the presence of the opposing parties, St. Ivo, CLXI, 934.---On witnesses produced before joinder of issue, Innocent III, CCXVI, 1234.---Witnesses are not to give testimony except concerning matters which they know personally and truthfully, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 701.---On choosing witnesses, *Codex diplomaticus*, XCVII, 362.---On examining them, St. Isidore, LXXXIV, 54; Innocent III, CCXVI, 33.---What sort of persons witnesses should be, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1299, 1300; Laws of St. Stephen, CLI, 1246; St. Ivo, CLXI, 411, 522, 933, 934.---How witnesses are to be called to give testimony, *Codex diplomaticus*, XCVII, 560.---On witnesses to be received in an accusation, St. Ivo, CLXI, 1199–1202.---A witness ought to be of reputable life, ibid., 933.

Who are, and are not, to be compelled to testify, St. Ivo, CLXI, 939.---Who cannot be accusers or witnesses, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 677, 678, 680.---A hostile witness is not to be heard, St. Ivo, CLXI, 934.---Slaves are not to be accepted as witnesses against masters, ibid., 1218, 1220.

On a witness acting as mediator between parties, St. Ivo, CLXI, 931.---On differences in witnesses corresponding to differences of persons, ibid., 930.---Against outsiders, parents or kinsmen ought not to be witnesses, ibid., 967.---Several persons from one household may be used as witnesses in another person’s affair, ibid., 941.

On admitting witnesses in a matrimonial case, Innocent III, CCXV, 192; CCXVI, 43.---On receiving witnesses regarding prescription, ibid., 262.---On witnesses to be employed in a case of separation because of closeness of kinship, Pope Eugenius III, CLXXX, 1566.

On false witnesses, St. Isidore, LXXXIV, 77; *Codex diplomaticus*, XCVI, 311, 558, 737, 775, 858.---On convicting false witnesses, ibid., 406, 573, 731, 738.---Witnesses being examined concerning someone’s falsity must not be prevented from speaking the truth, Innocent III, CCXIV, 502.

On *theano* [term uncertain], Laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1336; Laws of Edward III, CLI, 1195.

Diplomas of Theodoric III, king of the Franks, LXXXVII, 1319–1542.

Diplomas of Theodoric IV, LXXXVIII, 1132–1146.

The Theodosian Law, Hincmar, CXXV, 737.

THEODOSIAN CODE, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 271.---Laws of the Theodosian Code, St. Leo, LVI, 679.

Constitution of Emperor Theodosius, Bishop Placidus, CLXIII, 685.

Capitulary of Theodulf, CV, 207 ff.

On the office of toll-collectors, Erkembald, CXXXVII, 591.

On treasures, Constantine, VIII, 120.---On discovered treasures, Laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1335; Laws of Edward III, CLI, 1194.

On *thol* [toll], Laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1336; Laws of Edward III, CLI, 1194.

Charter of Thor Longi, Appendix to Bede, XLV, 369.

The levy for recruits was a burden upon provinces on account of their possessions and estates, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 368.

*Tituli* are wooden tablets placed on estates, *corbanis* [term uncertain], or rural holdings as a sign of possession, ibid., 522, 768.

Safe-conduct document for envoys, or one of the smallest kind made after this model, Marculf, LXXXVII, 706.

Travel warrant for undertaking a journey, Ancient Formulae, LXXXVII, 761.

TO DELIVER. What a man conveys in return for food and clothing, Appendix to the Tenth Century, CLI, 1422.---A contract made solely for the benefit of the person delivering is lost at his risk, St. Ivo, CLXI, 1225.

DELIVERY/CONVEYANCE. Anamod, CXXIX, 901, 915, 920, 921, 922, 924, 927, 929, 931, 932, 933, 939, 940, 947; diplomas of Emperor St. Henry, [Col. 0056] CXL, 294, 295, 296.---Conveyances (Marculf?), LXXXVII, 837.---Conveyance to whomever he wishes to convey, ibid., 833.---Conveyance to a bride, author unknown, ibid., 785.---Confirmation of a conveyance to a monastery, Baluzian Formulae, ibid., 865.---Charter of conveyance, Ancient Formulae, CLI, 1439.---Charter of conveyance made by husband and wife of both their possessions without any rent, Appendix to the Tenth Century, ibid., 1411.---Charter of conveyance made by husband and wife of all their possessions, with rent to be paid throughout their lives, ibid., 1414.---Charter of conveyance made by a husband of his property, which he wishes his wife to have after him, and conversely, ibid., 1417.---Charter of conveyance made by a man who wishes his children to have it after him subject to a rent, ibid., 1418.

On a deed of conveyance, author unknown, LXXXVII, 780.---Conveyance of land, ibid., 768, 773.---Conveyance by sale, ibid., 766.

On settlements, Constantine, VIII, 161; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 994.

TRUCE. Innocent III, CCXIV, 509, 510; CCXVI, 54, 61.---On truces, the same author, CCXIV, 553, 554.---On making a truce between the kings of England and France, the same author, CCXVII, 227.---Documents concerning the Truce of God, Anonymous, CLI, 737–752.

There were various ranks of tribunes, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 458.

TRIBUTE. On tributes, Constantine, VIII, 99, 391.---Formerly ecclesiastical possessions were exempt from every tribute, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1040.---On the remission by the ruler of tributes for the people, St. Isidore, LXXXIV, 491.

Dioceses possessed by bishops for thirty years are to remain undisturbed, Gratian, CLXXXVIII, 1027.

Charter of *triscabina* (Marculf?), LXXXVII, 825.

Law concerning triumphing, Paulus Orosius, XXXI, 925.

On mutilation of limbs, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 296.

On establishing a *trustis* [protective association], *Codex diplomaticus*, XCVII, 129, 653.

GUARDIAN. On guardians and curators, Constantine, VIII, 187; Charlemagne, XCVII, 138.---On guardians of minors, St. Ivo, 931.---On appointing guardians, Constantine, VIII, 176, 326.---On guardians’ administration and liability, ibid., 113, 135, 302, 355, 370.---A guardian must not deprive wards of their property, St. Ivo, CLXI, 488.---A guardian is prohibited from marrying his female ward, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 546.---If anyone seduces her of whom he has been guardian, Constantine, VIII, 197.

Charter of Uictred, Appendix to Bede, XCV, 390, 395.

UNITY. Edict on unity issued by Honorius, St. Optatus, XI, 817.---Law of Honorius concerning the Edict of Unity, ibid., 1211.

USUCAPION, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 208.

USUFRUCT, ibid.

USURY, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 207.---On usuries, Constantine, VIII, 151, 287, 395, 397; St. Isidore, LXXXIV, 583; *Codex diplomaticus*, XCVII, 154, 509; St. Ivo, CLXI, 1167–1168.---On the crime of usury, Innocent III, CCXVI, 1237.---Against usury, St. Leo, LIV, 613.---On prohibiting usury, Innocent III, CCXVII, 229.---When more than what was given is demanded, it is usury, St. Ivo, CLXI, 1168.---On the plague of partnership-usury, 968, in the Fragments of Pope Julius.---Against the moneylender, a plague in the commonwealth, XIV, 762, 763, 777 (387), in St. Ambrose.---Against clerical moneylenders, LVI, 398 (447, 461), in the *Code of Ecclesiastical Canons and Constitutions of the Apostolic See*.---Against clerical moneylenders, LXXXIV, 184 (636), in the *Extracts of Canons* in St. Isidore.---Against usurers, ibid., 304.---That not only clerics, but neither Christian laypersons, ought to exact usury, ibid., 762, letter of Pope Leo to all bishops.---On usury and lending at interest, XCVII, 529 (800), in Charlemagne’s *Codex diplomaticus*.---Royal decree on usuries, CLI, 1196 (1099), in Edward the Confessor.

USURERS. On usurers, Laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1338; Laws of Edward III, CLI, 1196.---That usurers are to be punished notwithstanding any appeal, Innocent III, CCXIV, 376.---Against usurers, the same author, CCXV, 1308.

USE, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 208.---Use cannot prevail over law and reason, St. Ivo, CLXI, 1120; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 58.

WIFE. Lombard law was highly favorable to wives, St. Agobard, CIV, 317.---After the death of her husband, a wife ought to possess her dowry, and it does not belong to the heirs of the deceased, Ivo, CLXI, 950.---On what share of the jointly acquired property wives of deceased persons should receive after their husbands’ deaths, *Codex diplomaticus*, XCVII, 570.---The crime by which a certain man’s wife was abducted and sold to another must be punished, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 681.---On those who kill their wives, Laws of St. Stephen, CLI, 1247.---Those who flee abroad from their wives, ibid., 1250.---On a wife dismissed by her husband, *Codex diplomaticus*, XCVII, 513.---On the wives of captives, ibid., LXXXIV, 773, 774.

Deed of vacancy, Andecavian Formulae, LXXXVII, 843, 844.

BAIL. On breach of an undertaking to appear, Laws of Alfred, CXXXVIII, 453.---On failure to appear after bail has been given, Laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1315.

PLEDGE. On oaths and pledges, Laws of Alfred, CXXXVIII, 451.---On a free man who gives himself as a pledge, the same author, XCVII, 556.

Constitution of Emperor Valentinian against Hilary, St. Leo, LIV, 461, 462 (note).---By a decree of Theodosius, Valentinian is called Augustus, St. Prosper, LI, 593.

VASSAL. On the obligations of vassals, Laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1319.

On vassals, *Codex diplomaticus*, XCVII, 725.---On the king’s vassals, ibid., 582.---On the king’s vassals appointed to guard the seas, ibid., 569.---Complaint concerning a vassal who refuses to do justice, Marculf, LXXXVII, 856.

On false prophets, *Codex diplomaticus*, XCVII, 825.

Relief of a vavasour, Laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1305.

On taxes, Constantine, VIII, 221; Hincmar, CXXV, 981.

On things for sale, St. Ivo, CLXI, 969.

SALE. St. Isidore, LXXXII, 205; author unknown, LXXXVII, 782, 783, 784; Andecavian Formulae, LXXVII, 844; *Codex diplomaticus*, XCVII, 313; Appendix to the Tenth Century, CLI, 1422.---Sale of a thing, Marculf, LXXXVII, 830.---Sale of a field, ibid., 742.---Sale of a village/estate, ibid., 741, 742.---Sale of ownership, Andecavian Formulae, ibid., 846.---Sale of land, author unknown, LXXXVII, 799; Andecavian Formulae, ibid., 840.---Sale of a man placed in *escenum* [term uncertain], ibid.---Sale of a slave, Marculf, ibid., 743; author unknown, ibid., 783, 799.---Sale by one who sold himself, ibid., 840, 841, 845.---Sale of oneself: how a free man is sold, author unknown, LXXXVII, 783.---Sale of a house within a city, Marculf, ibid., 742; author unknown, ibid., 796.---Sale to the Church, ibid., 794.---Sale to a monastery, ibid., 805.---Sale within the immunity of the Church or fisc, Marculf, ibid., 831.---On sales in which the price is reduced or the thing is defective, *Codex diplomaticus*, XCVII, 749.---No sale is to take place except before witnesses and in towns, Laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1319.---No one is to be sold outside his native country, Diplomatic Monuments of Æthelred II, CLI, 1167.---Sales to be regarded as void, Innocent III, CCXIV, 103.---Charter of sale, Ancient Formulae, CLI, 1439.

On poisoners, *Codex diplomaticus*, XCVII, 821.---Poisoners are to be punished capitally, St. Ivo, CLXI, 752.

[Col. 0058] PARDON. On those who have obtained dispensation on account of age, Constantine, VIII, 210.

BLOWS. Compensation for blows, XCVI, 1321 ff.

On veterans, Constantine, VIII, 151, 192, 201, 288.

ROAD. On public roads, Laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1307.---On a neighborhood road, LXXXIX, 829.

VICAR. On vicars, *Codex diplomaticus*, XCVII, 553.---On admonishing vicars concerning enactment of a law, ibid., 581.---On the office of vicar, Constantine, VIII, 285.

What a viscount is, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 921.

VICE-LORD. St. Gregory, LXXVII, 457, 458, 838, 1210; *Codex diplomaticus*, XCVII, 553.---That corrupt vice-lords be removed, ibid., 778.

WIDOW. On widows, Charlemagne, XCVII, 138, 404, 414, 571, 579, 730.---On abduction of widows, ibid., 404, 572, 730, 758.---Charlemagne abrogates the Lombard law concerning widows, ibid., 366.

WATCHES. No one is to be excused from guard duty on the walls, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 921.

ESTATE/VILLAGE. Capitulary concerning imperial estates, *Codex diplomaticus*, XCVII, 349.---On one who occupies another’s estate, ibid., 440.

On those striving to acquire freedom by manumission, Laws of St. Stephen, CLI, 1252.

VINEYARD. Guarantee concerning a vineyard, author unknown, LXXXVII, 776; Andecavian Formulae, ibid., 844.

On violators of tombs, *Codex diplomaticus*, XCVII, 822; Isaac of Langres, CXXIV, 1108.

On violence, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 337 ff.

MAN. Decrees concerning men and women consecrated to God, Burchard, CXL, 701.

FORCE. Public and private force, Constantine, VIII, 174.---On a woman joined by force to another’s slave, ibid., 113, 296, 361.---On a woman subjected to violence, Laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1303.---Things done by force are held invalid in law, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 849. See FEAR.

The Voconian law is unjust, St. Augustine, XLI, 103.

The will of a deceased person concerning construction of a monastery must be fulfilled, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 674.

WOUND. On wounds, Laws of Alfred, CXXXVIII, 449.---On a wound inflicted, Laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1299.---On a sword-wound, Laws of St. Stephen, CLI, 1253.---Compensation for wounds, Abedoc and Aethelwulf, XCVI, 1321 ff.

On *wera*, Laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1299.---On *weras* or *wergilds*, that is, valuations of persons, Laws of Æthelstan, CXXXVIII, 469.

Laws of King Wido, CXXXVIII, 801.

Laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1291.

WEREGILD. On composition for wergild, *Codex diplomaticus*, XCVII, 405, 573, 731.

HOSPICE. Administration of hospices (*xenodochia*) was, by ancient custom, in the hands of bishops, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 697.---What kind of persons those who preside over hospices ought to be, ibid., 697.---On one who wishes to build a hospice from substantial property, Marculf, LXXXVII, 725.

# CXXIV. INDEX OF IMMUNITIES, EXEMPTIONS, AND PRIVILEGES GRANTED BY ECCLESIASTICAL AND CIVIL AUTHORITIES TO CHURCHES, CLERGY, MONASTERIES, ETC., ARRANGED ALPHABETICALLY BY GRANTOR, WITH A SUMMARY ACCOUNT OF THE NATURE OF THE PRIVILEGES AND IMMUNITIES

[Col. 0059] ABSALON, bishop of Roskilde.---Receives the church of Blessed Thomas of Eskil under his protection, confirms to it its possessions, and confers many benefits and privileges upon it, CCIX, 745.---Confirms to William, abbot of St. Thomas of Paraclete, and to the brothers of that church, what they had obtained from him by exchange or donation, ibid., 748, 751.---Will by which the dying archbishop of Lund left his property for distribution among various persons, ibid., 757.

ADALBERO, bishop of Liège.---Charter in favor of the monastery of Cluny, CLXXXIX, 1055.

ADEFONSUS, emperor of Spain.---Charter concerning St. Vincent of Salamanca, CLXXXIX, 1069.

ADRIAN I, pope.---Grants the monastery of St. Denis at Paris the privilege of being permitted to have its own bishop, XCVI, 1211.---Confirms by a new privilege the ancient rights of the church of Rheims, ibid., 1212.---Bull confirming the agreement concerning the diocese of Strasbourg and other rights, ibid., 1213.

ADRIAN II, pope.---Letter to King Lothair: admonishes Lothair to receive his wife Theutberga into marital fellowship, etc., CXXII, 1259.---Letter to Ado, archbishop of Vienne: praises his zeal and acuteness of mind in forestalling the snares of the ungodly, ibid., 1261.---Letter to the Synod of Troyes: approves their diligence in collecting the proceedings, and grants the pallium to Wulfad, etc., ibid., 1261.---Letter to the bishops of Germany: states that he has absolved Waldrada and instructed her with appropriate admonitions, ibid., 1266.---Grants Bishop Aetard use of the pallium for consolation in his afflictions, ibid., 1269, 1272.---Directs Herard, archbishop of Tours, to grant Bishop Aetard the monastery which he had formerly held in Herard’s diocese, etc., ibid., 1273.---Letter to Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims: commends the church of Laon to him, ibid., 1280.---Other commendations concerning various matters, ibid., 1281, 1282.---Confirms the marriage of a certain couple contracted in the absence of a priest, ibid., 1318.---Bull granted for the foundation of the monastery of St. Mary at Bagno in Emilia, CXXIX, 1015.---Bull for the monastery of Corbie, by which he receives Corbie into apostolic protection and confirms donations made to it, ibid., 1018.

ADRIAN III, pope.---Privilege for the monastery of Piacenza, CXXVI, 971.

ADRIAN IV, pope.—Takes the monastery of Toul under the protection of Blessed Peter and confirms its possessions and rights, CLXXXVIII, 1369.—Concerning the Premonstratensian monastery, ibid., 1375.—Concerning the church of St. Mary and St. Evodius at Brannes, ibid., 1378.—Concerning the monastery of Vallis Serena, ibid., 1381.—Grants to the canons of this church one fourth of all offerings arising from the altar of Blessed Peter of the Roman Church, ibid., 1382.—Takes the monastery of St. Mansuetus at Toul into his protection and confirms its rights and possessions, ibid., 1384.—Grants to Henry, Patriarch of Grado, and his successors the primacy over the archbishopric of Zara and the right to consecrate its archbishops, ibid., 1387–1388.—Takes the monastery of Corbie into his protection and confirms its goods and rights, ibid., 1389.—A privilege in favour of Roger, Archbishop of York, by which he invests him with the pontifical pallium and subjects to him the bishops of Scotland, ibid., 1391.—Grants Hubert, provost of Prato, the right of appeal to the Apostolic See, ibid., 1393.—Takes under protection the church of St. Mary of Porto near Ravenna and confirms its rights, ibid., 1393.—Concerning the Camaldolese congregation, ibid., 1396.—Commends to Wibald, abbot of Stavelot, the Camaldolese houses of Berading and St. Peter of Rota, ibid., 1400.—Takes the monastery of Benediktbeuern under his patronage and confirms its rights, ibid., 1403.—Concerning the church of St. Mary at Czerwińsk, ibid., 1404.—Concerning the monastery of Floreffe, ibid., 1405.—Concerning the monastery of Rosenfeld, ibid., 1409.—Concerning the church of St. Mary at Martura, ibid., 1411.—Concerning the monastery of St. Salvant, ibid., 1413.—Confirms to Peter, abbot of Cluny, and his successors the monastery of Baume, ibid., 1415.—Commends the canons of Orléans to Louis, king of the Franks, ibid., 1417.—Takes the convent of nuns at Herford under protection and confirms its privileges and goods, ibid., 1415.—Takes the monastery of Stavelot under the protection of the Apostolic See and confirms all its possessions and privileges, ibid., 1419.—Concerning the church of Goslar, ibid., 1420.—Letter of recommendation for Hugh, Archbishop of Dol, ibid., 1422.—A privilege for the monastery of Cluny: in parishes belonging to its jurisdiction, no order or religious community other than the Cluniac order is to be established, ibid., 1126.—Orders certain bishops and abbots to commend the monastery of Farfa to Frederick, king of the Romans, ibid., 1427.—Concerning the monastery of Stavelot, ibid., 1428.—Takes the monastery of St. Mary of the Prison under protection and confirms its goods, ibid., 1428.—Concerning the monastery of Hardehausen, founded by Bernard, bishop of Paderborn, ibid., 1429.—For the church of Trier, ibid., 1431.—Concerning the monastery of Heidenheim, ibid., 1432.—A privilege for Hillin, Archbishop of Trier, to perform church consecrations, confirmations of persons, and the correction of offences according to synodal justice, ibid., 1433.—Takes the monastery of St. Michael at Pisa under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges, ibid., 1436.—Grants King Henry II of England a privilege to occupy Ireland, ibid., 1441.—At the request of Bishop John, confirms the privileges of the church of Olivolo, or Castello, Venice, ibid., 1445.—Confirms to John, Archbishop of Toledo, the primacy of the Spains, ibid., 1447.—Confirms to the same man the parish of Complutum [Col. 0062] and the use of the pallium, ibid., 1449.—Takes the church of Tortosa under the protection of the Apostolic See and confirms its statutes and possessions, ibid., 1453.—Concerning the monastery of St. Stephen at Dijon, ibid., 1456.—Concerning the monastery of St. Lambert at Liège, ibid., 1461.—Concerning the monastery of St. Paternianus at Fano, ibid., 1461.—Concerning the monasteries of Steingaden and St. Afra at Augsburg, and the church of St. Vincent, ibid., 1663–1666.—A privilege for the church of Palermo, to which he subjects Agrigento, Mazara, and Malta, ibid., 1471.—Takes under protection the monastery of Haysburg and the churches of Bâle and Minden, of St. Constantius at Orvieto, of Aachen, of St. Mary at Pinetum, and of Nemans, ibid., 1472–1483.—Confirms the privileges and possessions of the monasteries of St. Denis, St. Bavo at Ghent, and St. Peter at Aldenburg, ibid., 1483–1488.—Confirms the election of Archbishop Berengar, ibid., 1498.—Confirms to the hospital house at Canterbury the church of Northbourne, granted by Silvester, abbot of St. Augustine’s, for the relief of pilgrims and the poor, ibid., 1499.—Grants the convent of St. Mary at Caramagna to Anselm, bishop of Asti, ibid., 1491.—Takes under protection the Venetian convent of St. Zacharias, the Scottish monasteries of St. James at Regensburg and St. Vitalis at Ravenna, and the church of St. Peter at Guastalla, ibid., 1493–1497.—Takes under the protection of the Apostolic See the monasteries of Canusium in the district of Reggio and of St. Mary of Pontigny, the convent of St. Mary at Corolicastrum, and the church of Genoa, ibid., 1498–1508.—Concerning the convent at Remiremont and the monasteries of St. Blaise in the Black Forest and of Engelberg, ibid., 1508–1515.—Confirms Henry of Grado in patriarchal dignity and in primacy over the archbishopric of Zara, ibid., 1516.—Grants him the right to ordain and consecrate bishops at Constantinople and in other cities of the Empire, ibid., 1519.—Confirms to Rudolph, Camaldolese prior, and his successors the monastery of Prato, ibid., 1521.—Takes under protection the churches of Ravello, Benevento, and St. Rupert, the Milanese monastery of St. Denis, and the convent of the Holy Spirit of the Paraclete, ibid., 1522–1529.—Grants certain benefice lands to Aldebrandinus and Bernardinus, ibid., 1532.—Commends Anselm, abbot of Compiègne, to Henry, bishop of Beauvais, ibid., 1538.—Counsel and assistance are to be supplied to the Church of Jerusalem and to the Knights Templar, ibid., 1537.—Commends Hugh, Archbishop of Dol, to the counts of Léon and Lamballe, ibid., 1546.—Concerning confirmation of the grant of the first year’s revenue of prebends of Auxerre cathedral church, and concerning the liberty and customs of the church of Soissons, ibid., 1547.—Takes under protection the churches of St. Mary at Utrecht, Ferrara, Ratzeburg, and St. Mary of Gariberto, ibid., 1548–1552.—Takes the monastery of St. Pancras at Ranshofen and the churches of SS. John and Paul and St. Martin under the protection of the Roman See, ibid., 1554–1557.—Takes under protection the churches of St. Fericula at Parma and St. Samson at Orléans, the convent at Visbecc, and the monastery of SS. Nazarius and Celsus at Verona, ibid., 1562–1567.—Takes under protection of the Apostolic See the church of St. John at Selbold and Raymond, count of Barcelona, ibid., 1563–1570.—A privilege granted to Hugh, bishop of Piacenza, to ordain and to prepare chrism and holy oil, etc., for churches belonging to the parish of Piacenza, ibid., 1578.—Commends Baldwin and Balditzonius, messengers sent to Emperor Manuel, ibid., 1580.—To Louis, king of the Franks: he commends the king’s especially favourable affection toward religious men, asking that the Premonstratensian brethren may experience it out of reverence for Blessed Peter and for himself, ibid., 1582.—Takes the church of St. John in the Vines under Blessed Peter’s protection and confirms its privileges, ibid., 1585.—Takes under protection the church of St. Omer and the monasteries of St. Michael in Peril of the Sea and St. Denis, ibid., 1589, 1593.—Takes under the guardianship of the Holy See the monastery of the Holy Trinity of Mont-Sacré, the collegiate church of St. Stephen, and the abbey of St. Augustine at Limoges, ibid., 1613.—Concerning the church of Hamburg, the monastery of Jerichow, and the monastery of St. Magloire at Paris, ibid., 1617–1621.—Concerning the monasteries of St. Clement at Poissy, Prüfening, St. John at Blaubeuren, and St. Opportuna at Paris, ibid., 1625–1634.—Concerning the churches of Utrecht and St. Mary of Ressensis, and the monastery of Reichersberg, ibid., 1639.—Diploma concerning the abbey of Ralmensis [reading uncertain], in the archbishopric of Besançon, with its appurtenances, CLXXXIX, 107.

AENGILBALD, illustrious man.—Charter by which he grants to Willibrord, bishop of Utrecht, whatever belongs to him in the estate of Waderlo, LXXXIX, 538.

AENGELBERT, illustrious man.—Makes gifts to Willibrord, bishop of Utrecht, at Alfheim, a place in Toxandria, LXXXIX, 542–546.

AETHELRED II, king of the English.—Privilege for the Church of Canterbury, in which he rejoices at and confirms the expulsion of clerics from Christ Church, Canterbury, and the introduction of monks; he confirms for it numerous estates and grants very extensive privileges, CLI, 1169.

AGAPETUS II, pope.—A privilege for the monastery of the Saviour at Fulda, that it be subject to the jurisdiction of no other church save the Roman Church, CXXXIII, 800.—Confirms the privileges of the convent of nuns at Essen, ibid., 893.—Receives under protection of the Apostolic See the monastery of Gandersheim, built in Saxony, and endows it with various privileges, ibid., 896.—Confirms the privileges of the recently restored monastery of Fulda, ibid., 897.—Settles the dispute between the churches of Lorch and Salzburg, and grants them authority freely to preach throughout all Slavic lands, to ordain bishops there, and to establish all things by apostolic authority, ibid., 898.—A privilege for the abbey of Cluny, that it be free from the dominion of any king, bishop, count, etc., ibid., 900.—Confirms the immunities of St. Maximinus, ibid., 902.—Confirms the privileges and possessions of the monasteries of SS. Germanus and Michael at Cuxa, and of the church of Urgell, ibid., 905.—Concerning the monasteries of St. Mary at Ripoll, Cruas, Capua, and the church of St. Vincent at Mâcon, ibid., 907–913.—Concerning the monasteries of SS. Stephen, Denis, and Sylvester; St. Martin of Lérins; and Monte Cassino, ibid., 916–929.

ALAN, bishop of Auxerre.—Charter for the monastery of St. Marianus, CCI, 1387.—The priory of St. Amator is united to the monastery of St. Satyrius at Bourges, ibid., 1389.—Confirms certain churches to the monks of Douzy, ibid., 1390.

ALEXANDER II, pope.—Bull for the security of the property of the monastery of Ripoll against harassment by any person, CXLVI, 1282.—Orders Gervase, Archbishop of Reims, to protect the monastery of Corbie against the injuries of Guy of Amiens, ibid., 1283.—Confirms the canonry established in the Pisan church and the goods belonging to it, ibid.—Bull for the church of St. Donatus at Lucca, ibid., 1284.—Commends the merits of Burchard, bishop of Halberstadt, and grants him the pallium in recognition thereof, ibid., 1286.—Receives the monastery of Fruttuaria under the protection of the Apostolic See and confirms an exchange of certain land made between the abbot and Bishop Albert, ibid., 1288.—Privilege for the monastery of Vendôme, ibid., 1291.—Takes under protection the monastery built at Caen by Abbot Lanfranc, ibid., 1299.—Confirms the donations and privileges granted by King Edward to the monastery of Coventry, ibid.—Privilege for the monastery of the Saviour and St. Boniface at Fulda, ibid., 1301.—Grants a privilege to the monastery of San Miniato, ibid., 1303.—Constitution for the monastery of St. Peter at Perugia, ibid., 1304.—Privilege for the abbey of St. Denis, ibid., 1306.—Confirms the privileges granted by his predecessors to the monastery of St. Denis against the bishop of Paris, ibid., 1309.—Bull to the clergy of Velletri, ibid.—Privilege for the monastery of Dervent, ibid., 1310.—Bull for the monastery of Gellone, ibid., 1311.—Confirms the monastery of St. Michael at Siegburg by apostolic protection, ibid., 1312.—Grant of the monastery of St. Prisca to the monks of Vendôme, ibid., 1313.—Confirms the possessions and rights of the church of Cremona, ibid., 1314.—Confirms the entire ordering and disposition of the monastery of Gellone to the abbot and congregation of Aniane, ibid., 1315.—Why he exempted the monastery of Corbie from episcopal jurisdiction, ibid., 1321.—Privilege for the church of St. Peter at Lille, ibid., 1325.—Bull for the monastery of Monte Cassino, ibid.—Confirms the convent of St. Peter at Florence, ibid., 1330.—Privilege for the monastery of SS. Denis, Rusticus, and Eleutherius at Reims, ibid.—Privilege for the monastery of St. Nicasius at Reims, ibid., 1332.—For the monastery of St. Sylvester at Nonantola, ibid., 1333.—Confirms the goods of the church of Salerno restored by William, son of Tancred, ibid., 1335.—Confirms the rights and possessions of the church of Salerno, ibid., 1337.—Takes the monastery of St. Stephen at Caen under protection and adorns it with privileges, ibid., 1339.—Takes the monastery of Gellone under the defence of the Apostolic See, ibid., 1341.—Grants Arnold, Archbishop of Acerenza, use of the pallium, ibid., 1313.—Takes the church of St. Mary Magdalene at Verdun under protection and confirms its goods, ibid., 1344.—Takes under protection the chapter of canons of Ferrara at Padua and confirms its possessions, ibid., 1345.—Takes the canonry of St. Mary at Spoleto under protection and confirms its goods, ibid., 1351.—Confirms the property of the canons of the church of Narni, ibid., 1352.—Confirms the privileges of the monastery of St. Peter in Ciel d’Oro at Pavia, [Col. 0064] ibid.—Confirms the foundation of the college of canons at Harlebeke, ibid., 1353.—Grants Gebhard, Archbishop of Salzburg, authority to establish one bishopric in his province, ibid., 1354.—The collegiate church of St. Mary of Belle-Lieu in the diocese of Mâcon is received under protection of the Apostolic See, and all its goods and privileges are confirmed, ibid., 1355.—Confirms the privileges of the abbey of St. Benignus at Fruttuaria, ibid., 1356.—Confirms the possessions of the church of Arezzo, ibid., 1357.—Privileges for the monastery of St. Mary at Florence, ibid., 1358.—Privilege for the bishops of Lucca, ibid., 1360.—Receives under guardianship the abbey of St. Rigaldus and grants the brethren authority to elect an abbot according to the Rule of St. Benedict, ibid.—Takes the monastery of St. John at Penne under protection and restores its privileges, ibid., 1362.—The monastery of St. Edmund is received under protection of the Apostolic See, and all its goods are confirmed, ibid., 1363.—Bull granting the pallium to the Archbishop of York, ibid., 1364.—Privilege for the church of St. Mary at Florence, ibid., 1367.—Privilege for the church of St. Peter Damian, ibid., 1369.—Takes the church of Furcon under protection and confirms its possessions, ibid.—Privilege for the monastery of St. Prosper at Reggio, ibid., 1370.—Approval of the congregation of Camaldolese hermit monks, ibid., 1373.—Grant of privileges to the monastery of York and confirmation of the goods pertaining to it, ibid., 1375.—Letters in favour of the church of Chalon, ibid., 1377.—Bull protecting and confirming Gerald, bishop simultaneously of the churches of Saint-Paul-Trois-Châteaux and Orange, ibid., 1385.—Privilege for the church of Lucca; it forbids alienation of its goods, ibid., 1393.—Grants to Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino, the abbey of SS. Sebastian and Zosimus, ibid., 1395.—Confirms perpetual exemption and liberty to the monastery of St. Saviour of Magella and its churches and goods, ibid.—Confirms the bishopric of Troyes, ibid., 1400.—Decretal letter against wrongdoers against the church of St. Clement, ibid., 1401.—Letter to William, king of the English, concerning exaction of St. Peter’s Pence, ibid., 1413.—Confirms the decrees of his predecessors permitting monks to hold cathedral churches, ibid., 1415.—Letter to Lanfranc, Archbishop of Canterbury, warning him to safeguard the condition of the monastery at Winchester, ibid., 1416.—Privilege for the church built by Altmann, bishop of Passau, for the regular life of canons, ibid., 1417.—Privilege for the church of St. Mary Magdalene at Besançon, ibid., 1418.—Letter to Liemar, Archbishop of Hamburg; he sends him the pallium and confirms the privileges of his church, ibid., 1419.—Privilege for the monastery of the Saviour and St. Julia at Brescia, ibid.—Bull confirming all the privileges and rights of the monastery of sacred virgins at Trier, called the Senator’s, ibid., 1421.—Privilege for the church of the Saviour at Vyšehrad, ibid., 1423.—Privilege for the abbey of Monte Cassino, ibid., 1425.—Bull confirming the goods of the monastery of St. Severus in Classe, ibid., 1426.

ALEXANDER III, pope.—Takes under protection, and confirms the possessions and privileges of, the church of the Holy Sepulchre at Jerusalem, CC, 73; the monastery of Monte Cassino, which he declares the foremost in all Italy, ibid., 75; the Church of Grado, ibid., 118; the monastery of St. Martin, ibid., 122; the castle of Scuria, ibid., 150; the monastery of Blessed Peter at Montpellier, ibid., 154; the monastery of La Populeuse, ibid., 166; the church of St. Geneviève at Paris, ibid., 211; the monastery of SS. Facundus and Primitivus, ibid., 244; the monastery of Vallis Vicariae, ibid., 295; the monastery of St. Mary at Orthez, ibid., 312; the church of St. Mary at Liskeard, ibid., 315; the monastery of Cîteaux, ibid., 340; the monastery of Dunes, ibid., 343; the monastery of St. Martin at Autun, ibid., 346; the church of Paris, ibid., 353; the church of St. Mark at Venice, ibid., 362; the monastery of St. Illidius, ibid., 380; the monastery of St. Daniel, ibid., 388; the monastery of St. John at Poissy, ibid., 409; the monastery of St. Savin at Tarbes, ibid., 461; the Church of Modena, ibid., 453; the convent of St. Victorinus at Benevento, ibid., 479; the monastery of Nonantola, ibid., 493; the monastery of SS. Felix and Fortunatus, ibid., 499; the churches of SS. Hippolytus and Cassian and St. John the Baptist at Fucecchio, ibid., 502; the church of St. Peter at Bologna, ibid., 504; the church of Montefalcone, ibid., 513; the monastery of St. Peter at Cava, ibid., 565; St. Nicasius at Reims, ibid., 567; the monastery of Vallombrosa, ibid., 369; the church of Ferrara, ibid., 578; the church of Asti, ibid., 597; the convent of SS. Fabian and Damian, ibid., 602; the church of St. Medard at Tremblay, ibid., 629; the monastery of Admont, ibid., 718; the episcopal see of Cefalù, ibid., 723; the church of St. Mary at Scuthell, ibid., 731; the church of Southwell, ibid., 732; the church of Strana, [Col. 0065] ibid., 848; the church of Saragossa, ibid., 867; the monastery of St. Mary of Monte Laeto, ibid., 878; the monastery of St. Mary of Trinity, ibid., 880; the church of Padua, ibid., 886; the monastery of Cona, ibid., 889; the church of St. Eustorgius at Milan, ibid., 907; the monastery of Belle-Lieu, ibid., 911; the monks of St. Peter at Modena, ibid., 912; the church of St. Donatian at Bruges, ibid., 913; the church of Castello, ibid., 924; the abbey of St. John, ibid., 926; the monastery of St. Remigius at Reims, ibid., 934; the monastery of Cyri, ibid., 949; the church of St. Mary at Montdésir, ibid., 969; the monastery of St. Mary at Liskeard, ibid., 971; the monastery of St. Mary at Nogent, ibid., 983; [lacuna] and others as far as 1319.

Privileges, bulls, diplomas, immunities, etc., for the monastery of Pontigny, CC, 85; for the monastery of St. Mary at Rievaulx, ibid., 92; for the church of Thérouanne, ibid., 98; for the church of St. Cuthbert at Radford, ibid., 103; for the monastery of Phalempin, ibid., 110; for the church of Grado, ibid., 118; for the church of St. Mary the New, ibid., 126; for the church of SS. Peter and Ursus at Aosta, ibid., 131; for the canons of the Church of Piacenza, ibid., 132; for the monastery of Aniane, ibid., 142; for the monastery of St. Mary at Stivens, ibid., 143; for the monastery of St. Stephen at Nevers, ibid., 145; for the monastery of St. Arnulf at Crépy, ibid., 147; for the church of St. Eusebius, ibid., 151; for the monastery of Curia Dei, ibid., 155; for the church of St. Stephen at Toulouse, ibid., 156; for the church of St. Aignan at Orléans, ibid., 159; for the monastery of St. John at Kaltenborn, ibid., 171; for the church of St. Ambrose at Milan, ibid., 174; for the monastery at Compiègne, ibid., 180; for the monastery of St. Mary and St. Rotulf at Thorn, ibid., 190; for the monastery of Fontevraud, ibid., 197; for the monastery of Savigny, ibid., 200; for the monastery of St. Mary, ibid., 201; for the convent of the Holy Spirit of the Paraclete, ibid., 207; for the church of St. Mary at Hérivaux, ibid., 210; for the church of Gerberoy, ibid., 215; for the church of St. Peter at Douai, ibid., 217; for the church of León, ibid., 219; for the church of St. John at Amiens, ibid., 222; for the monastery of St. Faith at Horsham, ibid., 225; for the monastery of St. Bertin at Saint-Omer, ibid., 227; for the church of St. Mary at Sulap, ibid.; for the monastery of St. Salvius at Florence, ibid., 229; for the monastery of St. Mary at Sherborne, ibid., 231; for the church of Genesson, ibid., 233; for the monastery of St. Martin at Canigou, ibid., 236; for the monastery of St. Mary at Vitteaux, ibid., 241; for the monastery of Gix, ibid., 245; for the monastery of St. Mary at Mont-Ramey, ibid., 267; for the priory of St. Mary of the Field in the district of Roussillon, ibid., 284; for the Carthusian order, ibid., 293; for the monastery of St. Peter at Chartres, ibid., 294; concerning the establishment of the metropolitan see of Uppsala, ibid., 303;
