ibid.—Concerning the Church of Lucca, ibid., 1074.—Concerning the monastery of Stegburg, ibid., 1077.—Concerning the monastery of St. Peter of Cerreto, ibid., 1079.—Concerning the Church of St. Saviour at Venice, ibid., 1091.—Concerning the monastery of Bonifagetum, ibid., 1094.—Concerning the Church of St. Peter at Juvilly, ibid., 1100.—Concerning the monastery of St. Mary of Sorø, ibid., 1104.—Concerning the monastery of St. Mary of the Wood, ibid., 1110.—Concerning the Church of St. Mary at Gubbio, ibid., 1115.—Concerning the Church of Waldetrudis at Mons, ibid., 1116.—Concerning the nunnery of St. Mary and St. Peter at Charlemont, ibid., 1118.—Concerning the priory of St. Peter at Rumilly, ibid., 1133.—Concerning the monastery of Reichenbach, ibid., 1134.—Concerning the monastery of St. Mary at Würzburg, ibid., 1136.—Concerning the Church of St. Mary of Rheno, ibid., 1138.—Concerning the monastery of Dudley, ibid., 1144.—Concerning the Church of St. Mary Magdalene at Besançon, ibid., 1150.—Concerning the Church of St. Mary at Lausanne, ibid.—Concerning the monastery of St. Mary of Murel, ibid., 1158.—Concerning the Church of Sagne, ibid.—Concerning the Church of Ravello, ibid., 1160.—Concerning the monastery of St. Mary of Baumgarten, ibid., 1163.—Concerning the monastery of St. Remigius at Reims, ibid., 1168.—Concerning the monastery of St. Mary of Clairvaux, ibid., 1173.—Concerning the Church of St. Denis of the Pass, ibid., 1176.—Concerning the Church of St. Eusebius at Vercelli, ibid., 1177.—Concerning the Church of St. Stephen at Prato, ibid., 1184.—Concerning the monastery of St. Lawrence, ibid., 1188.—Concerning the Church of Isernia, ibid., 1190.—Concerning the Church of St. Peter at Regensburg, ibid., 1203.—Concerning the monastery of St. Martin on the island of Barbara, ibid., 1202.—Concerning the monastery of St. Denis, ibid., 1205.—Concerning the monastery of SS. Flora and Lucella of Arezzo, ibid., 1208.—Concerning the monastery of St. Himerius, ibid., 1210.—Concerning the Church of St. Anianus at Orléans, ibid., 1213.—Concerning the monastery of Ebersheim, ibid., 1217.

Concerning the monastery of St. Nicholas at Hermer, CCI, 1220.—Concerning the chapter of Terracina, ibid., 1225.—Concerning the monastery of St. Peter at Thierhaupten, ibid., 1226.—Concerning the monastery of Lehon, ibid., 1234.—Concerning the monastery of the Holy Trinity at Florence, ibid.—Concerning the Premonstratensian order, ibid., 1238.—Concerning the priory of St. Arnulf at Crépy, ibid., 1245.—Concerning the Church at Caput Ursuli, ibid., 1251.—Concerning the collegiate Church of Blessed Mary at Bruges, ibid., 1252.—Concerning the monastery of Laët, ibid., 1254.—Concerning the monastery of Carpi, ibid., 1255.—Concerning the canonry of St. Ursus at Aosta, ibid., 1257.—Concerning the monastery of St. Mary of Nieuwpoort, ibid., 1262.—Concerning the monastery of St. Benignus at Dijon, ibid., 1266.—Concerning the Church of St. Peter at Nesson, ibid., 1268.—Concerning the nunnery of SS. Saviour and Julia at Brescia, ibid., 1269.—Concerning the monastery of Altaich, ibid., 1273.—Concerning the monastery of St. Peter at Radolfzell, ibid., 1280.—Concerning the canons of Treviso, ibid., 1285.—Concerning the monastery of St. Peter at Vienne, ibid., 1288.—Concerning the Church of Feltre, ibid., 1292.—Concerning the abbey of Corbie, ibid., 1294.—Concerning the Carthusian house, ibid., 1306.—Concerning the Church of St. Mary at Regensburg, ibid., 1336.—Concerning the monastery of Paris in the district of Alsace, ibid., 1339.—Concerning the monastery of St. Mary of Charity, ibid., 1343.—Concerning the Roman monastery, ibid., 1345.—Concerning the monastery of the Scots, ibid., 1349.—Concerning the Church of St. Mary at Garz, ibid., 1371.—Concerning the Church of Uppsala, ibid., 1373.

Privileges: for the abbey of St. Mary at Soissons, CCI, 1077; for the nunnery of St. Hilary, ibid., 1083; for the Church of SS. Crispin and Crispinian at the Cave of Soissons, ibid., 1086; for the abbey of St. Germanus at Paris, ibid., 1088; concerning the redemption of tithes of the Church of Osnabrück, ibid., 1120; concerning tithes not to be granted to a layperson, ibid., 1121; concerning burial in the Church of Osnabrück, ibid.; for the Church of Modena, ibid., 1124; for the canons of the Church of Piacenza, ibid., 1126; for the monastery of St. Quentin at Mons, ibid., 1130; for the Church of St. Mary of Alterrac, ibid., 1146; for the monastery of Wilbach, ibid., 1186; for the abbey of St. Ghislain, ibid., 1192; for the nunnery of St. Zacharias at Venice, ibid., 1215; for the canons of Regina, ibid., 1222; for the abbey of Longport, ibid., 1227; for the monastery of St. Matthew of the Castle, ibid., 1229; for the monastery of St. Severus at Ravenna, ibid., 1249; concerning use of the mitre by the abbots of St. Michael at Bamberg, ibid., 1275; for the Church of St. Thomas at Reggio, ibid., 1276; for the Church of St. Evasio at Casale, ibid., 1278; for the Church of Treviso, ibid., 1284; for the Church of Magdeburg, ibid., 1288; for the monastery of SS. Peter and Paul at Münster, ibid., 1290; for the Church of St. Martin at Tours, ibid., 1296; for the congregation of Verona, ibid., [Col. 0098] 1301; for the Church of St. Ursus at Augsburg, ibid., 1303; for the monastery of St. Bertin at Sithiu, ibid., 1307; for the Church of St. Germanus at Mons, ibid., 1313; for the Church of Holy Cross, ibid., 1316; for the monastery of the Court of God, ibid., 1317; for the monastery of Reomay, ibid., 1321; for the monastery of St. James at Liège, ibid., 1323; for the abbot and monks of Lac, ibid., 1325; for the Carthusian prior, ibid., 1331; for the monastery of St. Ghislain, ibid., 1332; for the monastery of Raitenhaslach, ibid., 1338; for the monastery of the Valley of St. John at Seitz, ibid., 1342; for the monastery of St. Minias, ibid., 1345; for the chapter of Pistoia, ibid., 1347; for the monastery of St. Mary of Holm Cultram, ibid., 1354; for the monastery of SS. Peter and Vitus at Calavena, ibid., 1357; for the nunnery of Épinal, ibid., 1360; concerning the liberty of the borough of St. Remigius, ibid., 1369; for the brothers of the Order of St. John of Jerusalem, ibid., 1364; for the monastery of Burton, ibid., 1366; for the canons of the Church of Épinal, ibid., 1368; for the Church of Belluno, ibid., 1368.

Bulls: for the brothers of the Hospital of Jerusalem, CCI, 1081; for the chapter of St. Martin at Tours, ibid., 1259, 1260, 1321; for the monastery of Bon-Repos, ibid., 1272; for Hermann, abbot of Reinhardsbrunn, ibid., 1301, 1305; for the canons of St. Peter at Soissons, ibid., 1322.—Grants the abbot of Vézelay and his successors the use of the mitre, 1093.—Confirms peace between the monks and townspeople of Tournus, ibid., 1094.—Between the count of Joigny and the abbess of St. Julian at Auxerre, ibid., 1098.

Confirms the statutes of Burgundius, bishop of Strasbourg, concerning the rights of the provost of Haselach and of the canons there, CCI, 1140.—Secures to the monastery of Repsholt an income granted by Liemar, formerly archbishop of Hamburg, ibid., 1143.—Confirmation of the possessions of the Church of Senlis, ibid., 1151.—Secures to Peter, abbot of Monte Cassino, the Church of St. Nicholas of Gurgo, bestowed by Baraso, ibid., 1155.—Secures to the canons of Asti the Church of St. Michael of Intercisio, ibid., 1165.—Ratifies the judgment rendered between the Church of Piacenza and Alfonso, former bishop of Pavia, ibid., 1166.—Secures to the monastery of St. Denis churches granted by the archbishops of Sens, ibid.—Grants various privileges to the monastery of St. Remigius at Reims, ibid., 1168.—Confirms the judgment rendered by the archbishop of Vienne and the bishop of Geneva against the count of Geneva, ibid., 1172.—Confirms certain churches to Peter, bishop of Maguelone, ibid., 1177.—Secures to the canons of Modena the chapel of St. Dalmatius, ibid., 1237.—Confirms to the monastery of St. George in the Black Forest the cell of St. Marius, ibid.—Confirms donations made in favor of the Knights Templar by Godfrey I, Henry I, and Godfrey II, dukes of Brabant, ibid., 1262.—Ratifies the election by which the bishop of Lincoln was chosen archbishop of Rouen, ibid., 1300.—Commends the Carthusian order to Robert, archbishop of Vienne, and his suffragans, ibid., 1303.—Confirms the privileges of the regular canons of the monastery of St. Mary ad Carceres, ibid., 1309.—Secures to Arnald of Blois, canon of the Church of Reims, the village of Fraillicourt, ibid., 1322.—Confirms the customs and liberties of the citizens of Reims granted by Archbishop William, ibid., 1324.—Secures to the monastery of Cluny a place granted by Jocerannus Grossus, ibid., 1326.—Secures to the monastery of Altenberg the village of Isacherode, ibid., 1327.—Grants the abbots of the monastery of St. George in the Black Forest the use of the mitre, gloves, and sandals, ibid., 1328.—Secures to the convent of St. Remigius at Reims the tithe of Besenes and certain privileges, ibid., 1329.—Commends the monastery of Rott to Archbishop Adalbert of Salzburg and his suffragans, ibid., 1335.

LOUIS THE PIOUS, king.—Privilege confirming the papal regalian rights of Pope Paschal, XCVIII, 579.—For the monasteries of Nobiliacum, CIV, 979; Cormaricum, 981; Gellone, 982; Duse, 983; St. Severinus at Bordeaux, 984; Anisole, 986; Crasse, 992, 993; Marmoutier, 998; Ebersholmen, 1000; St. Anthymus at Sens, 1003; St. Maximinus at Trier, 1005; Nicaise, 1014; Carro, 1016; Der, 1017; Gorze, 1019; Aniane, 1020; St. Maxentius, 1021; Farfa, 1023; Bagneux, 1024; Fontenelle, 1025; Île-Barbe, 1026; St. Zeno at Verona, 1027; Psalmodi, 1030; Montolieu, 1031; Prüm, 1033; St. Hilary, 1037; St. Germanus at Auxerre, 1039; Cormaricum, 1040; St. Méen, 1042; Saint-Maur-des-Fossés, 1044; Bodon, or Bonmoutier, 1046; Mount Amiata, 1047; Murbach, 1049, 1051; Saint-Maur-des-Fossés, 1054; Fulda, 1056; Soricium, 1059; Crudat, 1063; Solignac, 1064; St. Germanus of the Meadows, 1065; Tournai, 1070; St. Gall, 1075, 1076, 1077; Fleury, 1078, 1080; Magnilocus, [Col. 0099] 1080; Como, 1087; Déols, 1089; Conques, 1090; St. Bavo at Ghent, 1092; Grafschaft, 1095; Farfa, 1097; Arles, 1097; Prüm, 1098; Nonantola, 1103; Inda, 1105; Burchard, 1106; Horbach, 1107; St. Gall, 1108; St. Sulpicius at Bourges, 1109; Fulda, 1110; the City of Sens, 1111; Elnone, 1113; Sainte-Christine, 1115; St. Amand, 1117; Prüm, 1120, 1122; Sainte-Grâce, 1125; Masevaux, 1126; New Corbie, 1128; Corbie in Saxony, 1129; Maastricht, 1131; St. Florentius of Clon, 1132; Farfa, 1134; St. Medard, 1135; Como, 1136, 1137; Saint-Denis, 1141; New Corbie, 1150; Aniane, 1155; St. Gregory’s, 1157; St. Maxentius, 1160; Nonantola, 1161; Der, 1162, 1164; St. Maximinus at Micy, 1165; Eremifontaine, 1173; St. Gall, 1174; Saint-Germain, 1175; Farfa, 1177; St. Andrew of Jure, 1179; Ebersheim, 1180; Centula, 1182; St. Philibert, 1183; Bèze, 1186; Carro, 1188; Sithiu, 1190; Prüm, 1492; St. Andrew, 1194; Cormaricum, 1195; Faverney, 1199; Der, 1204; New Corbie, 1205; St. Martin at Tours, 1214; Marmoutier, 1215; Saint-Denis, 1224; St. Columba, 1227; New Corbie, 1228, 1229; St. Zeno, 1238; Kempten, 1248; Grumi, 1248; Duse, 1252; Prüm, 1254; Le Mans, 1255; Auxerre, 1260; Sithiu, 1263; St. Carilefus, 1278; St. Columba, 1280; Longevilliers, 1283; Hohenburg, 1285; Nonantola, 1289; Cormeriacum, 1301; Kempten, 1305; Déols, 1305; Anisole, 1330; for the Churches of Le Mans, 985; Vienne, 1011, 1015; Viviers, 1020; Mâcon, 1036; Orléans, 1038; Cambrai, 1044; Trier, 1054; Reims, 1858; St. Stephen at Limoges, 1062; St. Martin at Tours, 1067; Strasbourg, 1073; Paris, 1100; St. Victor at Marseilles, 1116; Reims, 1144; Brioude, 1149; Strasbourg, 1197; Arezzo, 1232; Le Mans, 1255; St. Marcellus at Chalon, 1261; and Elne, 1270; for the abbeys of Aprimonasterium, 1082; St. Vincent, 1217; Hohenburg, 1287; Kempten, 1304; for Betio, bishop of Langres, 987; for Hildegrin, bishop of Halberstadt, 989; for Hildebald, bishop of Mâcon, 990; for Wirund, abbot of Stavelot, 991; for Christian, bishop of Nîmes, 994; for Nefridius, archbishop of Narbonne, 999; for Victor, bishop of Chur, 1154; for Frodegarius, bishop of Angers, 1178; for Epiphanius, abbot of the monastery of St. Vincent on the Volturno, 1196; for Victor, bishop of Chur, 1202; for the bishop of Arezzo, 1233; for Maxentius, patriarch of Aquileia, 1240; for Alberic, bishop of Langres, 1249; for Aldric, archbishop of Sens, 1267.

The exchange made between Peter, abbot of Nonantola, and Rodulf, rector of the monastery of St. Saviour at Brescia, is confirmed, CIV, 1007.—The testament of Abbo, founder of the monastery of Novalesa, and other rights of that monastery are confirmed to Abbot Frodoin, ibid., 1009.—The agreement concluded between the bishop of Constance and the monastery of St. Gall is ratified, ibid., 1048.—The exchange made between Bernold, bishop of Strasbourg, and Erchangar, count of Nordgau, is confirmed, ibid., 1123.—Makes a donation to Ricbod, abbot of Sens, ibid., 1149.—The exchange of certain estates between Hilduin, abbot of Saint-Denis, and Ermentrude, abbess of Jouarre, is confirmed, ibid., 1302.

LOUIS THE PIOUS, emperor.—Grants various privileges to the monastery of Aniane, CII, 1421–1437.—Charter for the monastery of St. Michael, ibid., 975.—Charter concerning the liberty and immunity of the monastery of St. Michael, ibid., 978.—Charter concerning the liberty of the people of Carres and Sagmari, ibid., 979.

LOUIS VI, king.—Enlarges and confirms the privileges of St. Denis in France, on the occasion of receiving the banner from the altar of the blessed martyrs, CLXXXVI, 1461.—Another privilege is granted, ibid., 1463.

LOUIS VII, king.—Grants various privileges to the same monastery of St. Denis, CLXXXVI, 1465, 1466, 1468.

LOUIS, king (A.D. 1130).—Charters for the monastery of Cluny, CLXXXIX, 1060, 1061.

MARINUS, pope.—Privilege for the monastery of Solignac, CXXVI, 967.—For the monastery of Savigny, ibid., 968.

MARINUS II, pope.—Privileges for the monasteries of Vézelay, St. Boniface at Fulda, Monte Cassino, St. Vincent on the Volturno, and St. Sylvester; and for the Churches of Benevento, Sabina, and Hamburg, CXXXIII, 863–879.

MATTHEW, cardinal.—Diploma concerning the agreement between Henry, archbishop of Sens, and the canons of Étampes, CLXXIII, 1262.—Instrument concerning the settlement made between Stephen, bishop of Paris, [Col. 0100] and Theobald, archdeacon, ibid., 1263.—Confirms the election of Odo, abbot of St. Peter at Chartres, ibid., 1264.—Charter for the Church of St. Martin of the Fields, ibid., 1267.

NICOLAS I, pope.—Orders that an account of the condition of the monastery of Fulda be repeatedly rendered to him, CXIX, 770.—Grants Adelwin, archbishop of Salzburg, the use of the pallium, ibid., 771.—Absolves Theutgaud, archbishop of Trier, and his clergy from an oath, ibid., 782.—Sends the pallium to Ado, archbishop of Vienne, ibid., 796.—Confirms to the Church of Beauvais the monasteries of Oratory and Flavigny, granted by King Charles the Bald, ibid., 813.—Privilege for the monastery of Corbie, ibid., 815.—Privilege for the monastery of Saint-Denis, ibid., 819.—Confirmation of the Synod of Soissons (A.D. 853), with a privilege for Archbishop Hincmar and the Church of Rheims, ibid., 821.—A privilege of liberty is confirmed for the monastery of Saint-Calais, ibid., 846.—Approves the profession of Adventius, bishop of Metz, and grants him the pardon and peace which he sought, ibid., 887.—Letter to the clergy and people of the Roman Church; absolution and restoration of Rothad, bishop, ibid., 892.—Grants Rembert, archbishop of Hamburg, the use of the pallium, ibid., 962.—Grants the pallium to Egilo, archbishop of Sens, although he says that he does not approve of his having been taken from another church and monastery, ibid., 973.—Privilege for the nunnery of Vézelay, ibid., 1116.—No one is to be subjected unwillingly to monastic discipline, ibid., 1120.—Confirms the ancient privilege of the metropolitan see of Vienne, by which four cities are subject to the Church of Vienne, ibid., 1151.—Privilege for the monastery of the Saviour at Fulda, CXXIX, 1011.—Bull confirming Charlemagne’s diploma for the monastery of Saint-Denis, ibid., 1013.—Bull for the monastery of Subiaco, ibid., 1015.

NICOLAS II, pope.—Confirms the goods and possessions of the monastery of Saint Peter at Perugia, CXLIII, 1301.—Bull by which he confirms to the monastery of Saint Vincent at Volturno and its abbot all its goods and rights, ibid., 1304.—Confirms all the goods and privileges granted to the monastery of Monte Cassino by Pope Leo IX, ibid., 1305.—Confirms the establishment of the chapter of the Blessed Virgin Mary *ad Gradus*, ibid., 1309.—Confirms the goods of the Church of Genoa, ibid., 1312.—Confirms the possessions and boundaries of the Church of Chieti, ibid., 1312.—Confirms to the monastery of Saint Peter at Perugia the tithes of the castles of Arni, Civitella, and Pilonico, ibid., 1324.—Privilege for the monastery of Saint Martin at Autun, ibid., 1327.—For the monastery of Saint Felicity, ibid., 1328.—For the Church of Saint Michael and Saint Eusebius of Pô, ibid., 1330.—Confirms the goods and privileges of the Church of Saint Andrew at Mussy, ibid., 1332.—Bull concerning the consecration of the basilica of Saint Lawrence at Florence, ibid., 1334.—Bull for the canons of Pesaro, ibid., 1336.—Confirms the foundation of the abbey of Saint Peter in the city of Ager, and grants certain privileges for its liberty, ibid., 1337.—Bull confirming the rights and goods of the monastery of Saint Thomas of Aposella, ibid., 1339.—Privilege for the nunnery of Saint Julia at Brescia, ibid., 1341.—For the royal monastery of the Most Holy Saviour, etc., ibid., 1343.—Consecration of the altars of the basilica of Farfa, ibid., 1345.—Bull for the monastery of Saint-Denis, ibid., 1351.—Privilege for the monastery of the Holy Trinity at Vendôme, ibid., 1352.—Bull confirming the privileges of the chapter of canons of Sovana, ibid., 1355.—Confirms the possessions and privileges of the Church of Dorchester, ibid., 1356.—Letter to Edward, king of the English, by which he confirms the privileges and possessions of the monastery of Blessed Peter at Westminster, ibid., 1358.—Privilege for Aldred, archbishop of York, ibid., 1359.

NORBERT, archbishop of Magdeburg.—Charter for the Church of Saint Mary at Magdeburg, CLXX, 1357.—Transfers a certain hospital house to the Premonstratensian brethren established in the Church of Blessed Mary at Magdeburg, ibid.—Charter in favour of hospitality for the poor, ibid., 1357, 1359.

ODO, bishop of Cambrai.—Confirms donations made to the abbey of Jette of the Premonstratensian order, CLX, 1151.—Privilege for the church of the canons of Saint John the Baptist, ibid.—Confirms the abbey of Saint Peter of the Order of Saint Benedict, ibid., 1152.—Confirmation of the college of canons of Ternemonde, ibid., 1153.—Grants various free churches and other benefices to the abbey of Jette, ibid., 1156.—Privilege for the Church of Nivelles, ibid., 1157.—Confirms the foundation and endowment of the abbey of Bornheim, made by Wenemar, castellan of Ghent, ibid., 1158.

OTTO (Saint), bishop of Bamberg.—Foundation charter for the monastery of Michelfeld, CLXXIII, 1328.—Raises the parish of Michelfeld to a higher status, ibid., 1330 [Col. 0101].—Foundation charter of the monastery of Uraug, ibid., 1331.—Confirms a donation made to the convent of Michelfeld, ibid., 1338.—Letters concerning the restoration of the monastery of Banz, ibid., 1340.—Foundation letters for the monastery of Heilsbronn, ibid., 1346.—Gives to the convent of Saint Michael the chapel or cell of Saint Faith, ibid., 1357, 1349.—Charter concerning the foundation of the convent of Vessera, ibid., 1350.

OTTO I, emperor.—Concerning the royal rights granted to Saint Peter, XCVIII, 603.

OTTO, emperor.—Confirms the rights, privileges, and possessions of the monastery of Saint Maiolus, CXLII, 1039.

PASCHAL I, pope.—Bull for the monastery of Farfa, CXXIX, 977.—Bull for the monastery of Saint Vincent at Volturno, ibid., 980.—Letter to all Christians in the northern regions. He commends Ebbo, archbishop of Rheims, and Halitgar, sent to spread the faith of Christ, ibid., 982.

PASCHAL II, pope.—Assures the monks of Cluny of the altar of a parish church donated by Pibo, CLXIII, 31.—Assures Bertrand, archbishop of Narbonne, of primacy over the metropolitan see of Aix, and confirms unshakenly to him whatever dignity or honour the Church of Narbonne possesses, ibid.—Confirms the privilege of the monastery of Vendôme concerning a profession not to be made by the abbot, ibid., 36.—Assures to the monastery of Reinhardsbrunn the church of Titteborn, ibid., 37.—Takes the monastery of Der, or Saint Bercharius, under his protection; confirms its possessions and privileges; and further decrees that no secular or ecclesiastical person may summon its abbot or his successors before a secular court, that no bishop may compel them to attend a synod except for a matter of faith, or finally compel them to leave the solemnities of their own monastery and attend urban observances, ibid.—Bull and privilege concerning the union of the Church of Orange with that of Tricastin, ibid., 38, 58.—Confirms the election of Norigald, bishop of Autun, and all the possessions of his church, and makes certain other decrees, ibid., 39.—Privilege for the Church of Mâcon, ibid., 40.—To the army fighting in Palestine: he congratulates it on its victory and at the same time urges it to advance, ibid., 42.—Confirms the boundaries of the bishopric of Mazara in Sicily, ibid., 45.—Concerning the privilege granted to Alberic, abbot of the new monastery of Chalon, ibid., 47.—Privilege by which he takes the monastery of Souvigny, as a member of the Cluniac convent, under the protection of the Apostolic See, ibid., 50.—Privilege confirming all the goods and rights of the monastery of Cluny, ibid., 51.—Commends the convent of Cluny, ibid., 53.—Takes the Greater Monastery under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges, ibid., 54.—Cluniac privilege, ibid., 56.—Privilege for the monastery of the Holy Saviour at Pavia, ibid., 59.—Grants the pallium and a privilege to Gerald, archbishop of Braga, ibid., 60.—Confirms the primacy of the Church of Toledo, ibid.—Privilege for the monastery of Saint-Savin of Piacenza, ibid., 62.—For the monastery of Monte Cassino, ibid., 65.—To the people of Velletri: he abrogates what Guibert had unlawfully established among them; he defines their boundaries, ibid., 66.—Confirmation of the donation of the monastery of Saint Benedict at Alpirsbach, ibid., 67.—Confirms the bishopric of Arras, ibid., 69.—To Henry, king of England, against ecclesiastical investitures, ibid., 70, 94.—Privileges for the churches of Chaumousey and Saint Vincent of Bergamo, ibid., 72, 73.—Abolishes the bishopric of Lavello; confirms the possessions and rights of Melfi, ibid., 73.—Confirms the privileges and possessions of the Church of Bavel, ibid., 74.—Privileges for the convent of Saint Sophia and the monastery of Monte Cassino, ibid., 75, 77.—Confirms the privileges and possessions of the Church of Saint James at Compostela, ibid., 78.—Grants the pallium to Gerard, archbishop of York, ibid., 82.—Privileges for the monasteries of Jesus of Nazareth and Saint Ambrose at Milan, ibid.—Confirms the privileges of the monastery of Saint Peter in the Golden Heaven at Pavia, ibid., 84.—Confirms the privileges of the monastery of Montmajour near Arles, ibid.—Concerning the goods of the Church of Fiesole, ibid.

Confirms an exchange made between Gerunton, abbot of Saint Benignus at Dijon, and Gilbert, abbot of Caen, and the possessions of the monastery of Dijon, ibid., 86.—Confirms the privileges of the monastery of Saint-Denis, ibid., 88.—Takes the monastery of Saint Mary at Rosenfeld under protection and endows it with privileges, ibid.—Assures to the monastery of Bec the churches granted as a provision by William, archbishop of Rouen, and others, ibid., 90.—That monks are not to be forbidden to have a cemetery in their monastery for burying their own members, ibid., 95.—To Crescentius, archbishop of Salona: confirms his metropolitan rights and grants him the pallium, ibid., 96.—Confirms the rights and privileges of the abbey of Saints Philip, James, and Walburga in the Hagenau Forest, ibid., 97 [Col. 0102].—Bull concerning the foundation of the monastery of Cheminon, ibid., 99.—Privilege for the monastery of Vichpach, ibid., 101.—Privilege for the abbey of Vézelay, ibid., 102.—Bull for the abbey of Saint John in the Valley, ibid., 104.—Confirms the privileges of the monastery of Saint Martin on Mount Pannonia, ibid., 105.—Grants the use of the pallium to Peter, archbishop of Aix, ibid., 108.—Confirms donations made to the abbey of Saint Aubert at Cambrai, of regular canons of the Order of Saint Augustine, ibid.—Confirms the privileges and exemption of the abbey of Saint Peter on Mount Blandin, of the Order of Saint Benedict, ibid., 111.—Confirms the possessions of the Church of Compostela, ibid.—Privilege for the convent of Saint Mary near Banz, ibid., 114.—Takes the monastery of Marbach under the protection of the Apostolic See, ibid., 116.—Confirms the primacy of Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, ibid., 119.—Confirms the privileges of the monastery of Casale Benedicti, ibid., 120.—Takes under protection the Church of the Holy Cross and Blessed Eulalia at Barcelona, and confirms its possessions and privileges, ibid., 125.—Takes the monastery of Pargau under protection and confirms its privileges, ibid., 126.—Takes the monastery of Saint Mary at Bornheim under protection and confirms its goods and privileges, ibid., 129.—Concerning the monasteries of Göttweig, Saint Blaise, Saint Orientius, and the Church of Saint Fridianus, ibid., 129, 132.—Grants the use of the pallium to Didacus, bishop of Compostela, ibid., 132.—Privileges for the monastery of Usenhofen, ibid., 134.—Confirms the privileges and possessions of the collegiate church of Saint Amatus at Douai, ibid., 136.—Sends the pallium to Ascer, archbishop of Lund and primate of Sweden, ibid., 138.—Strengthens the immunity of the Church of Affligem, ibid., 142.—Confirms the possessions and rights of the convent of Bez, ibid.—Concerning the monasteries of Monte Cassino, Saint Peter in the Golden Heaven at Pavia, and Saint Benedict at Polirone, ibid., 144, 148, 155.

Confirms the privileges, possessions, and rights of the bishopric of Pavia, ibid., 151.—Takes under protection the monasteries subject to the hermitage of Camaldoli, ibid., 152.—Confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of Altomünster, ibid., 155.—Confirms the privileges of Pontius, bishop of Le Puy, ibid.—To Daimbert, archbishop of Sens: commends to him the bishop of Paris, consecrated by himself, ibid., 158.—The establishment of the collegiate Church of Saint Mary at Bruges is confirmed, ibid.—Confirmation of goods belonging to the Church of Ferrara, ibid., 159.—Privileges for the monastery of Tournus and for the nunnery of Fontevraud, ibid., 164.—Takes the monastery of Saint Michael in the diocese of Verdun under protection and confirms its possessions, ibid., 165.—Confirms the ancient exemption of the see of Oviedo, ibid., 168.—Confirms the goods and privileges of the monasteries of Tulle and Saint George in the Black Forest, ibid., 171, 172.—Confirms certain possessions of the Church of Saint Walburga at Veurne, ibid., 175.—Privilege for the bishopric of Pistoia, ibid.—Privilege for the abbey of Saint Nicholas, ibid., 178.—Charter confirming the churches held by the canons of Langres, ibid., 181.—Bulls for the convents of Saint Peter at Chartres and Saint Valery, ibid., 183, 184.—Confirms the privileges of the monastery of Saint Faith at Sélestat, ibid., 185.—Privilege for the monastery of the Holy Saviour and Saint Julia at Brescia, ibid., 189.—Confirms the privileges of the Church of Saint Fridianus at Lucca, ibid., 193.—Confirms the election of Peter, archbishop of Acerenza, and the rights of the metropolitan see of Acerenza, and sends the pallium, ibid., 194.—Bull for Benedict, abbot of the monastery of the Holy Saviour at Moxi, ibid., 195.—Confirms to Hugh, abbot of Saint Giles, the abbey of Seumich, founded by Ladislaus, king of the Hungarians, ibid., 198.—Privilege of the monastery of Saint Stephen, ibid., 199.—Privilege for the Church of Coimbra, ibid., 201.—Confirms the rights and goods of the monastery of Casa Dei, ibid., 202.—Confirms the rights and possessions of the Cluniacs, ibid., 204.—Confirmation, made for Abbot Gaucerannus, of the churches and possessions of the monastery of Athanac, ibid., 205.—Privilege for the monastery of Saint Germain-des-Prés, ibid., 207.—Confirms the privileges of the monasteries of Saint Launomar at Blois and Saint John at Chartres, ibid., 208, 209.—Privileges for the abbey of Saint Martin of the Fields and the monastery of Saint Arnulf, ibid., 209, 210.—Confirms the possessions of the abbey of Elnone, or Saint Amand, of the Order of Saint Benedict, and fortifies them with apostolic privileges, ibid., 211.—Confirms certain privileges of the monastery of Saint Remigius at Rheims, ibid., 216.—Confirms the goods of the Church of Auxerre, ibid., 217.—Privilege for the monastery of the Isle of Agen, ibid., 218.—Bull confirming the exemption, already granted by a bull of Pope Nicolas II, of the convent of Corbigny from subjection to Flavigny, ibid., 220.—Awards the Cluniacs the cell of Saint Denis at Nogent, ibid.—Confirms the possessions and rights of the Church of Narbonne, ibid., 222.—Grants certain privileges to the monastery of Saint Benedict at Polirone, ibid., 226 [Col. 0103].—Confirms the privileges of the Church of Lucca, ibid.—Confirms certain privileges of Gregory the archdeacon, Hubert the archpriest, Rainerius the primicerius, and Guido the cantor, brethren of the Church of Lucca, ibid., 227.—Privilege of the convent of Florence, ibid.—Privilege for the nunnery of Saint Peter of Lucca, CLXIII, 228.—Subjects certain monasteries to the monastery of Casa Dei, ibid., 232.—Privilege for the Church of Saint Martin, ibid.—Entrusts Bruno, archbishop of Trier, with the absolution from excommunication of the bishop of Liège, ibid., 234.—Assigns the monastery of Saint Germain at Auxerre to Hugh, abbot of Cluny, ibid., 235.—Commends the canons of Saint Fridianus to Rangerius, bishop of Lucca, ibid.—Confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of Saint Michael at Siegburg, ibid., 237.

Privilege for the Church of Evasius, CLXIII, 237.—Confirms the boundaries of the diocese of Burgos, ibid., 239.—Privilege for the Church of Saint Mary at Vasera, ibid., 241.—Confirms the liberty, privileges, and possessions of the monastery of Saint Bertin at Saint-Omer, ibid., 243.—Privilege for the monastery of Selbold, ibid., 246.—Confirms the exemption of the Church of Burgos and its boundaries established in a council, ibid., 248, 249.—Privilege of Baldwin, archbishop of Dol, concerning the pallium, ibid., 251, 252.—Confirms the possessions and privileges of the Church of Saint Fridianus at Lucca, ibid., 253.—Bull protecting and confirming the goods of the monastery of Chaumousey, ibid., 254.—Takes the monastery of Saint Lambert under protection and confirms its goods, ibid., 256.—Privilege for the Church of Saint Deodatus, ibid.—Takes the monastery of Weissenau under protection and confirms its possessions and rights, ibid., 257.—Bull for Saint Martin at Amiens, ibid., 258.—Privilege for the Greater Monastery, ibid., 259.—Confirms to Pontius, abbot of Cluny, and his successors all things granted, bestowed, and confirmed to the monastery of Cluny by his predecessors, the popes, ibid., 260.—Confirms the privileges of the monastery of Cluny, ibid., 262.—Privilege addressed to Pontius, abbot of Cluny, to whom he sends a white pallium so that he may make dalmatics from it for use in the Church of Cluny, granting him the use of pontifical insignia on the eight principal feasts of his monastery, ibid.—Privilege for the monastery of Siegburg, ibid., 263.—Privilege concerning the market and the meal given on the two feasts of Saint Remigius, and likewise concerning the immunity of that church, ibid.—Privilege for the monastery of Saint Mary at Florence, ibid., 266.—Confirms the boundaries of the diocese of Sora and the possessions of its church, ibid., 267.—Confirmation of the endowment and goods of the monastery of Saint Benignus at Fruttuaria, ibid., 268.—Confirms the liberty, privileges, and possessions of the Church of Squillace, ibid.—Privilege for the Church of Saint Christopher at Phalempin, ibid., 270.—Privilege for the monastery of Saint Peter at Melk, ibid.—Confirms the possessions of the Church of Saint James at Compostela, ibid., 272.—Takes the convent of Saint Maxentius under the protection of the Holy See, ibid., 274.—Takes the monastery of Saint Vincent at Copersano under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges, ibid., 277.—Confirms the possessions and privileges of the Church of Sonnebecq, ibid., 278.—Confirms the possessions of the Church of Saint Donatian at Bruges, ibid., 279.—Privilege concerning investitures extorted by force, ibid., 284.—Privilege for the monastery of Hersfeld, ibid., 287.—Confirms the privileges of the monastery of Corbie, ibid., 293.

He confirms that the monastery of Monte Cassino is to be preferred to the other monasteries throughout the West, free from every jurisdiction whatsoever, and subject to the Holy Roman Church alone; and, under anathema, decrees that the abbot of that convent is to hold, in every assembly of bishops and princes, a place superior to all other abbots, and to give the first opinion before all others of his order, CLXIII, 295.—Privilege for the nunnery of Fontevraud, ibid., 296.—Confirms privileges granted to the bishop of Arras, ibid., 297.—For the monastery of Saint Martin in the Valley, to which he grants the safeguard of apostolic protection: he designates its churches and enumerates its privileges, ibid., 298.—Takes the monastery of Saint Bertin at Saint-Omer under protection and confirms its goods, ibid., 301.—Assures to the monastery of Anchin the church of Saint George near Hesdin, given by John, bishop of Thérouanne, ibid., 303.—Confirms the liberty of the Church of Orange, separated from that of Tricastin, ibid., 304.—Confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of Nonantola, ibid., 306.—Privilege for the monastery of Aréval, ibid., 308.—Bull by which he grants the protection of the Apostolic See to the hospice of Saint John of Jerusalem, ibid., 314.—Privilege for the monastery of Saint Nicasius at Rheims, ibid., 317, 318.—Subjects the cell of Gordanice to the monastery of Aniane, ibid., 320.—Confirms the possessions of the monastery of Saint Victor at Marseilles, ibid., 327.—Bull listing the Camaldolese monasteries and receiving them under apostolic protection, ibid., 330 [Col. 0104].—Grants the clergy of the Church of Tournai the right to have a bishop, having shaken off the yoke of the Church of Noyon, ibid., 332.—Defends the liberty of the monastery of Saint Bertin at Saint-Omer against Pontius, abbot of Cluny, ibid., 334.—Privilege for the monastery of Saint Rufus at Avignon, ibid., 336.—Privilege for the Church of Ayt, ibid., 337.—Confirms the possessions of the Church of the Marsi, ibid., 338.—Concerning the preservation of the liberty of the monastery of Saint Bertin at Saint-Omer, ibid., 338, 340.—Privilege for the monastery of Tulle, ibid., 341.—Bull for the monastery of Évreux, ibid., 343.—Confirms all the possessions and privileges of the monastery of Subiaco, ibid., 345.—Privilege for the Church of Blessed Lawrence at Florence, ibid., 349.—Privilege for the Church of Saint Evasius at Casale, ibid., 350.—Privilege for the bishopric of the Church of Bologna, ibid., 351.—Privilege for the Church of Lescar, ibid., 354.—Confirms the possessions and rights of the Church of Blessed Mary in the harbour of Ravenna, ibid., 356.—Concerning the monastery of Saint Mary of Charity, ibid., 357.—Privileges for Pontius, abbot of Cluny, ibid., 358, 359.—Privilege for the monastery of Saint Victor at Paris, confirming to the canons of Saint Victor what had been granted by royal diploma, ibid.—Confirmation of the first foundation of the monastery of Saint Margaret at Baumburg, offered by its founder Peter, ibid., 363.—Privilege confirming donations to the Church of Berchtesgaden, ibid., 368.—Concerning the privileges of the Church of Girona, ibid., 371.—Privilege for the monastery of Vallombrosa, ibid., 372.—Confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of Saint Peter at Perugia, ibid., 374.—Confirms the judgment of Urban II concerning the agreement concluded between the monks of Saint Alban and those of Vendôme, ibid., 382.

Bull for Maurice, archbishop of Braga, CLXIII, 283.—Confirms certain possessions of the Church of Chieti, ibid., 385.—Exempts the Church of Portugal from metropolitan jurisdiction and asserts and confirms the boundaries of its diocese, ibid.—Takes under protection the oratory of Saint Mary near Nieuwburg at Oudenaarde, a member of the Church of Ename, ibid., 390.—Confirms the privileges of the monastery of Sinsheim, ibid., 391.—Privilege for the canons of Saint Faith, ibid., 393.—To Bernard, primate of Toledo: he grants him the city of Segovia personally and gives him the monastery of Saint Servandus, ibid.—Frees the monastery of Faverney from the authority of the bishop of Basel and confirms its goods, ibid., 397.—To the clergy and people of Florence: declares their bishop innocent and deprives his accusers of offices and benefices, ibid.—Confirms to Gozaran, archbishop of Lyons, primacy in the province of Lyons, ibid., 399.—Privilege for the Church of Saint Pancras at Hadmersleben, ibid.—Bull for the monastery of Saint Thibéry, ibid., 401.—Confirms certain possessions and privileges of the monastery of Saint Facundus at Sahagún, ibid., 400.—Takes the Neapolitan monastery of Saint Archangel of Morfisa under protection and confirms its goods and privileges, ibid., 401.—Grants Anselm, abbot of Saba, authority to exercise apostolic functions in England, ibid., 408.—Declares that Robert, abbot of Vézelay, is under the protection of the Apostolic See, ibid., 410.—Decree by which, against the abbot of Cras, the monastery of Saint Polycarp is confirmed to the abbot of Alet, ibid., 410.—Privilege given for confirmation of all the goods of the monastery of Saint Bartholomew, ibid., 412.—Privilege for the Church of Saint Mary in Port, ibid., 414.—Takes the Church of Saint Pancras at Backnang under protection and confirms its possessions, ibid., 415.—Privilege for the monastery of Saint Bertin at Saint-Omer, ibid.—Privilege for the canons of Saint Faith, ibid., 417.—Confirms the possessions of the monastery of Micy, ibid.—Assures to Abbot Albin and the canons of Saint Mary of the Wood the chapel of Blessed Nicholas at Crécy, ibid., 419.—Privilege for the abbey of Fontevraud, ibid.—Confirmation of King Louis’s privilege for the Church of Chartres, ibid., 421.—Grants privileges to Anthony, provost of Saint Peter at the oratory of Campistrano, cardinal-priest, ibid., 222.—Privilege of Saint Peter of Murki and Saint Nicholas of Mugubi, ibid., 423.—Confirms certain possessions of the monastery of Subiaco, ibid., 424.—Privilege for the Church of the Holy Trinity at Norwich, ibid., 432.—Takes the monastery of Andres under protection and confirms its goods and privileges, ibid., 434.—Privilege for the Church of Belleloc, ibid., 435.—Confirms the monastery of Othon and its possessions, ibid., 439.—Bull for Gerard of Ilam, dean of the Church of Saint Quentin, ibid., 443.

PETER, bishop of Burgos.—Grants and confirms to the monastery of Cluny the church of Carandigna, CLXVI, 855.

PHILIP, king of the Franks.—Concerning the Saladin tithe: that nothing further is to be exacted in any manner on the pretext of restoring the Holy Land, CCIX, 869 [Col. 0105].

PHILIP OF ALSACE, count of Flanders.—Benefits the abbey of Aldenburg, of the Order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Bruges, CLXXIV, 1576.

PHILIP, count of Flanders and Vermandois.—Confirms donations of tithes from Oudenburg, etc., CLXXIV, 1577.—Concerning the tithes of the whole parish of Aldenburg, ibid., 1579.

PIBO, bishop of Toul.—Privilege for the monastery of Saint Aper, CLVII, 419.—Confirmation of the privileges of the priory of Asmantia, ibid., 422.—Charter for the Church of Saint Deodatus, ibid., 424.—Foundation of the monastery of Saint Leo at Toul, ibid., 427.—Privilege for the abbey of Saint Leo at Toul, ibid., 431.—Foundation of the priory of Saint Theobald, ibid., 433.—Privilege for the Church of Saint Mary, ibid., 435.—Foundation of the priory of Saint James at Chastel-Neuf for the abbey of Saint Mansuetus at Toul, ibid., 436.—Foundation of the priory of Laudecourt, ibid., 439.—Charter concerning the consecration of the Church of Port, ibid., 440.—Privilege for the Church of Saint Gengulf, ibid., 442.

PIPPIN, illustrious man.—Charter by which he grants the monastery of Echternach one half of Echternach itself, LXXXIX, 539.—Charter by which he takes the monastery of Echternach under his protection and grants the brethren assembled there the right, upon the death of Willibrord, bishop of Utrecht, to appoint an abbot for themselves from among their own number, ibid., 541.

PIPPIN, king.—Gives the monastery of Saint-Denis a castle at Mont-Saint-Michel in the district of Verdun, XCVI, 1528.—Judicial settlement concerning tolls in the market of Saint-Denis, vindicated for that monastery, ibid., 1530.—Decree confirming the possessions of the monastery of Prüm to the abbey of Murbach, etc., ibid., 1531.—Diploma by which he gives the village of Tirmingen to the Church of Fulda, ibid., 1536.—Donations in favour of the abbey of Prüm, ibid., 1537–1546.—Privilege for the monastery of Saint Maximin, ibid., 1554.

RADBOD, bishop of Tournai.—Diploma concerning the liberty of the Church of Saint Aldegundus of the Apostle Peter, CLXXIV, 1567.

RAIMBALD, archbishop of Arles.—Privilege for the monastery of Saint Victor, CXLIII, 1393.—Grants absolution from penances at the consecration of the endowed Church of Saint Mary of Correno, ibid., 1394.—Charter by which he gives the Church of Saint Genesius and Saint Honoratus to the Victorine monks, ibid., 1396.

RAINALD II, archbishop of Rheims.—Confirmation of the foundation of Saint Josse of the Wood, CLXXII, 1343.—Foundation charters of the monastery of Igny, ibid., 1350.—Charter confirming Saint Wimar, ibid., 1352.—Confirms all possessions of the monastery of Silincourt, ibid., 1354.—Privilege concerning the water of the Vidula, marshland, pasture-right, and jurisdiction of Saint Theodoric as far as Raymond’s Cross, ibid., 1356.—Charter for the monastery of Cluny, CLXXXIX, 1058.

REMIGIUS, bishop of Strasbourg.—Testamentary deed donating the monasteries of Aschoria and Werth to the Church of Strasbourg, XCVI, 1582.

RICHARD, bishop of Constance.—Charter concerning the church of Morsalines, CLXXXIX, 1071.

RIQUINUS, administrator of Toul.—Charter concerning the cell of Frondon for the monastery of Cluny, CLXVI, 849.

RODULPH, king.—Gives certain estates to the monastery of Cluny, CXLII, 1040.—Charter for the convent of Saint Peter at Cluny concerning the donation of Saint Blaise at Viculis with its appurtenances, CXLII, 1041.

ROHINGUS, nobleman.—Charter by which he gives Willibrord, bishop of Utrecht, the Church of Saints Peter and Paul at Antwerp, LXXXIX, 553.

RUDOLPH I, king of the Romans.—Thanks a certain cardinal because he has uniquely supported his cause in the Roman Curia, XCVIII, 718.—Remits services not rendered during the vacancy of the Empire, ibid., 721.—Promises the pontiff that he will carry out his reform against the wayward bishops of Germany, ibid., 737.—Thanks a certain prince for letters sent and states that he held a familiar conference with the pontiff at Lausanne, ibid.—Entrusts to a certain person the defence of a devastated monastery, ibid., 800.—Provides for a certain religious house of the Order of Penitents, ibid., 806.—Commends to counts, barons, etc., a newly elected bishop, ibid., 808.—Privilege of the city of Halle, ibid., 810.—Commends a certain canon to the Church of Liège, asking that he be sent back to the court as soon as possible, ibid., 814.—Confirms the judgment of the bishop of Liège concerning the fixing of the limits of judicial duels, ibid., 815.—Commends the monastery of Golden Valley to the king of the Franks, ibid., 816.—Receives the Hospitallers of the Teutonic House into his special protection, ibid., 817.—Receives into protection the brethren of the Hospital of Saint John in Jerusalem and confirms their privileges, ibid., 819 [Col. 0106].—Grants a certain person the right to cultivate certain mountains, ibid., 826.—Commends a certain abbot to a certain bishop, ibid.—Grants a certain prince authority to mint coinage, ibid., 827.—Confirms the privileges of a certain monastery, ibid., 829.—Receives under protection a five-year-old orphan, ibid., 836.—Writes against persons unlawfully exacting tolls, ibid., 838.—Commends a certain person for a certain ecclesiastical benefice, ibid., 839.—Diploma by which he protects ecclesiastical rights through a severe edict, ibid., 872.

SERGIUS II, pope.—Grants Ansgar, bishop of Hamburg, the use of the pallium and other privileges, CXXIX, 997.

SERGIUS III, pope.—Bull for the monastery of Saint Gall, CXXXI, 971.—Privilege for the Church of the White Forest, ibid., 973.—Vindicates the rights of the Church of Bremen, ibid., 974.—Privilege for the chapter of Asti, whose possessions he confirms, ibid., 976.—Confirms the privileges of the monastery of Nonantola, ibid., 977.—Confirms the privileges and possessions of the Church of Vienne, and expressly assures to it the churches of Maurienne and Susa, ibid., 978.—Letter to Hoger, bishop of Hamburg, by which he sends him the pallium, ibid., 980.—Privilege for the monastery of Saint Martin at Tours: after the devastation inflicted upon Tours by the Normans, he confirms the privileges of the monastery, ibid.

SERGIUS IV, pope.—Assures Andrew, bishop of Poreč, possession of the parish of Bavin and two castles, CXXXIX, 1499.—Letters by which he grants to a certain Vedian the castle of Scure under emphyteutic tenure, ibid., 1501.—Confirms the foundation of the parish Church of Saint Michael near the monastery of Nonantola in the territory of Modena, made by Radulph, abbot of that monastery, ibid., 1502.—Confirms all goods belonging to the monastery of Cuxa, ibid., 1594.—Concerning the monastery of Ripoll, ibid., 1509.—Confirms the foundation of the monastery of Saint Peter of Fenillotes and the goods belonging to it, ibid., 1514.—Privilege for the monastery of Canigou, by which he confirms privileges and rights formerly granted to it, ibid., 1516.—Receives the monastery of Arles under the protection of the Apostolic See and exempts it from the jurisdiction of every person whatsoever, even of its ordinary bishop, ibid., 1517.—Privilege of gaining indulgences for those who come to the consecration of the church of the monastery of Montmajour, ibid., 1520.—Confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of Saint Vincent at Volturno, ibid., 1522.—Concerning the monastery of Belleloc, ibid., 1525, 1527.—Confirms the metropolitan rights of Michael, archbishop of Salerno, ibid., 1528.

SYLVESTER II, pope.—Confirms and endows with rights the monastery of Saint Lambert at Seeon, ibid., 269.—Concerning the monastery of Fulda, ibid., 272.—Grants Arnulf, archbishop of Rheims, authority, after receiving staff and ring, to exercise the archiepiscopal office and enjoy all insignia in the customary manner, after he had for a time been deprived of them, ibid., 273.—Sends the sacred crown to Stephen, duke of the Hungarians, whom he also honours with the royal title; and, having granted various privileges, establishes the Church of Esztergom as metropolitan of the kingdom, ibid., 274.—Confirms the goods and rights of the Church of Urgell, ibid., 278.—To Robert, abbot of Vézelay: confirms the privileges of the monastery of Vézelay, ibid., 279.—To Odo, bishop of Girona: receives the bishopric of Girona under his protection and confirms its privileges and rights, ibid., 281.—Bull by which he takes both monasteries, Stavelot and Malmedy, under his protection, and orders that, in the election of an abbot, one from Stavelot is to be chosen if a worthy person is found, ibid., 282.—Endows with privileges the monastery of the Holy Trinity and Saint Peter at Bourgueil, ibid., 285.

SIMON, bishop of Tournai.—Diploma concerning the donation of the Church of the Blessed Virgin Mary at Aldenberg, together with the entirety of the parish of Aldenberg, CLXXIV, 1570.

STEPHEN II, pope.—Concerning the hospital and house at Rome granted to Abbot Fulrad, LXXXIX, 1013.—Bull to Fulrad, abbot of Saint-Denis, by which he grants to the monks of Saint-Denis several things wholly new and unprecedented, ibid., 1013.

STEPHEN IV, pope.—Bull for the monastery of Farfa, CXXIX, 973.

STEPHEN V, pope.—Diploma for the monastery of Corbie, CXXIX, 794.—To Dominic, archbishop of Ravenna, he signifies that he has consecrated the bishop of Piacenza; nevertheless, that he wishes in no respect to prejudice the right of the metropolitan of Ravenna, ibid., 798. To the clergy and people of Piacenza. He gives them Bishop Bernard and commends submission to the metropolitan of Ravenna, ibid., 799.—Privilege for the church of Piacenza, ibid., 812.—Privilege granted to Abbot Huoggo, ibid., 813.—Privilege for the monastery of St. Liudger, ibid., 814.—Privilege for the monastery of Herten, ibid., 815.

STEPHEN VI, pope.—Privilege of the archbishopric of [Col. 0107] Narbonne, CXXIX, 855.—Privilege for the monastery of Vézelay, ibid., 858.

STEPHEN VII, pope.—He confirms to the monastery of St. Vincent on the Volturno and to its abbot Raimbald all rights and property, CXXXII, 1051.—He confirms the foundation of the abbey of Brogne, in the county of Namur, ibid., 1053.

STEPHEN VIII, pope.—The monastery of Tulle in the diocese of Piacenza is received under the protection of the Apostolic See and is declared wholly subject to its abbot alone, CXXXII, 1089.—He confirms the privileges and possessions of the monastery of Buxières, founded by Gauslin, abbot of Tulle, ibid., 1090.

STEPHEN X, pope.—Letter to Gervasius, archbishop of Reims, in which he promises assistance to one acting vigorously for religion, etc., CXLIII, 869.—Bull by which he confirms the immunity of the secular clergy from the courts and burdens of secular powers, ibid., 871.—Confirmation of grants and other indulgences of the sacred monastery of St. Peter at Perugia, ibid.—He confirms the property of the canons of Arezzo, ibid., 874.—Constitution for the monastery of St. Prosper of Reggio, ibid., 876.—Privilege by which he confirms all monasteries, property, rights, and privileges previously granted to the monastery of Cluny, ibid., 879.

STEPHEN, bishop of Paris.—Charter for the canons of St. Mary of Paris, CLXXIII, 1421.—Charter for the regular canons of St. Victor of Paris, ibid.—Charter for the canons of St. John the Round, ibid., 1423.—Charter concerning the church of St. Dionysius of the Prison, ibid.—Charter concerning the Church of Fosses, ibid., 1424.—Charter of the foundation of the abbey of Hédère, ibid., 1427.

STEPHEN, king of the English.—Charter for the monastery of Cluny, CLXXXIX, 1063.

TELLO, bishop of Chur.—He grants possessions to the churches of St. Mary and St. Martin, XCVI, 1555.

THEODORIC, count of Flanders.—Diploma confirming the donations made by Conon and Walter to the church of Aldenberg, CLXXIV, 1569.—He remits an annual rent from certain properties, etc., ibid., 1571.

URBAN II, pope.—The primacy of the Church of Toledo in Spain is restored, CLI, 288.—Letter to Ildefonsus, king of Galicia. He rejoices that the church of Toledo has been wrested from the Saracens. He commends Bernard, archbishop of Toledo, upon whom he has bestowed the pallium and whom he has established as primate throughout all the kingdoms of the Spains, ibid., 289.—He confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of Cluny and grants Abbot Hugh the use of the mitre, dalmatic, gloves, and sandals, ibid., 291.—Privilege for the abbey of St. John of the Vines, ibid., 295.—Letter to Gebehard, bishop of Constance, by which he entrusts and confirms to him an apostolic legation and the administration of the churches in Saxony and Germany, ibid., 297.—Privilege for the monastery of Jesus of Nazareth, ibid., 301.—He grants to Frotard, abbot of St. Pontius of Tomières, a privilege exempting that place from the jurisdiction of any bishop whatever and adorning it with many other prerogatives, ibid.—Privilege for the clergy and laity of Velletri, ibid., 304.—Letter to Rainold, archbishop of Reims. He grants him the pallium and maintains the primacy of the whole province of Belgica Secunda, extending even to the consecration of the kings of the Franks, ibid., 309.—He confirms to the archbishop of Besançon the possessions of the monastery of Baume among the Sequani, ibid., 311.—Bull for the canons of Pistoia, ibid., 317.—For the canons of St. Antoninus in the diocese of Rodez, ibid., 319.—For the church of Grenoble, ibid., 320.—He confirms the property of the monastery of St. Theofred of Chaumont, ibid., 322.—He undertakes the protection of Marmoutier and confirms its possessions, ibid., 324.—Concerning the nunnery of Holy Cross at Poitiers, ibid., 328.—Concerning the monastery of St. Bartholomew in Lipari, ibid., 329.—Confirmation of the canonical establishment of St. Mary at Rettembach, which is received under the protection of the Apostolic See; after all property belonging to it has been confirmed, certain privileges are granted to it, ibid., 337.—He undertakes the protection of the monastery of St. Sophia at Benevento and confirms its possessions and rights, ibid., 341.—Concerning the monastery of Reinhardsborn, ibid., 342.—Privilege for the church of Pisa, to which, on account of its citizens’ merits toward the Roman Church, he subjects the Corsican bishoprics, ibid., 344.—He grants Guarinus, abbot of the monastery of St. Lawrence at Aversa, the use of the mitre and ring, ibid., 346.—Concerning privileges granted to the monastery of Cava, ibid., 347.—He assures St. Bruno, founder of the Carthusians, and Lanuin of the place granted by Count Roger and confirmed by Theodore, bishop of Squillace, ibid., 353.

Letter to all the bishops of Brittany. He grants the pallium to the bishop of Dol, saving the right of the church of Tours, ibid., 359.—He confirms the purpose of the canons of St. Paul at Narbonne to profess the regular life, ibid., 360.—Letter to all the faithful. Concerning the church of St. Mary of the monastery of Monte Cassino, consecrated by him and fortified with a privilege, [Col. 0108] ibid., 363.—He confirms to the New Monastery of Poitiers the church of St. Nicholas beside the walls of the city of Poitiers, ibid., 367.—Bull by which he confirms a donation made by Countess Matilda to the monastery of St. Blaise, ibid., 374.—He confirms the rights and possessions of the monastery of Vendôme, ibid., 380.—Privilege for the Church of Tours, that the Church of Dol should be subject to it, ibid., 385.—He commands all bishops established throughout Brittany to obey the archbishop of Tours as their metropolitan, ibid., 387.—Privilege for the canons of Pistoia, ibid., 399.—Bulls for the monasteries of St. Peter at Pozzuoli and St. Giles, ibid., 398, 399.—He receives the monasteries of St. George in the Black Forest and Hirsau under the protection of the Apostolic See, and their property is confirmed to them, ibid., 402. Bull for the abbey of St. Peter in the Black Forest, ibid., 403.—Privilege for the monastery of Cluny, ibid., 410.—For the church of St. Peter at Guastalla, ibid., 412.—For the monastery of St. Abundius at Como, ibid., 417.—He undertakes the protection of the church of St. Peter at Standalmont, handed over to St. Peter by Countess Matilda, and confirms its property, on condition that the clergy pay to the Lateran palace each year a gold denarius, or every fourth year a Byzantine coin, ibid., 419.—Privilege for the Church of Besançon, ibid., 421.—Privilege for the convent of nuns of St. Peter at Blazilis, ibid., 422.—The canons of the church of Cahors are confirmed in the profession of the regular life which they had recently professed, ibid., 423.—Privilege for the monastery of La Chaise-Dieu, ibid., 424.—Bull for the monastery of St. Giles, ibid., 425.—He confirms the regular discipline of the canons of the church of St. Avignon, who, together with all the property belonging to that canonry, are received under the protection of the Apostolic See, ibid., 426.—Privileges for the churches of St. Rufus and Mâcon and for the monastery of Savigny, ibid., 430.

[Col. 0111]

## CXXV. INDEX CONCERNING THE TEMPORAL POWER OF THE SUPREME PONTIFF

IN THIS INDEX WE SET OUT TWO PARTS, NAMELY:

1. Concerning the right of this power; 2. Concerning its exercise.

In the first part, under one article, are explained Christ’s words by which the authority of the Roman pontiff is established in the person of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and whether those words deal with temporal power.

In the second part, under two articles, the question is brought forward: 1. By historical notions and monuments concerning this human power; 2. By arguments drawn from natural law, from the oath issued by the supreme pontiffs on this matter, from advantage and disadvantage, and from the donations over which it is exercised.

## PART ONE. Concerning the privileges granted by Christ himself to the supreme pontiffs in the person of Blessed Peter, and whether they concern temporal power

It is utterly incredible and inexplicable how many men burn with an incurable hatred toward Roman pontiffs, both ancient and recent, and in how many ways they display and make public this hatred of theirs—not human, but plainly infernal. Lies, curses, insults, inventions, and innumerable fabrications hold first place among these means; with them they fill and stuff almost all their books, so excessively and uncontrollably that many books issuing from this workshop seem to be nothing other than one single lie, insult, and calumny woven on a perpetual and unbroken thread [Col. 0112]. Though utterly remote from all truth, they introduce, heap up, chant, repeat, and reiterate these accusations privately and publicly, in order to make the Roman pontiffs hated and detested by all, mindful of the saying: “Whether deceit or valour, falsehood or truth—who asks in an enemy?”

Now a single cry is heard: “Come now, O Caesar, kings, princes, and magnates, and all who can lay hold: seize them. Cursed be the idle and slothful hand. First, take from the pontiff Rome, Romagna, Urbino, [Col. 0113] Bologna, and everything which he holds and possesses under the title of being pontiff; for he is a possessor in the worst faith; by lies and frauds he acquired everything. But what do I say—by lies and slaughter? Rather, by his blasphemies and idolatries he withdrew the Roman Empire from its allegiance, snatched it away, subjected it to himself, and, as the price of his superstition, led innumerable souls down to hell. Next, the magistrate ought to seize the pontiff, the cardinals, and the rest of those who share their order, superstition, and impure sanctity; and, as blasphemers are customarily punished, draw out their tongues through the nape of the neck, cut them off, and dispatch them in order to the gallows, in exactly the manner in which they themselves are accustomed to attach seals to their bulls—although this punishment would be far less and milder than their blasphemies and idolatries. When this has duly been done, permission might indeed be granted them to celebrate, at the gallows among the ravens or in hell among the devils, one council, or as many as they might wish at their pleasure,” CXLVIII, 196.

Luther himself, that mad apostate, had already said in his book *Against the Papacy*: “But if I were in Caesar’s place, I would immediately do this: I would drive all those wicked scoundrels—the pontiff, the cardinals, and all men of their ilk—bound and girded together as if by one chain, no farther than three miles away, namely to Ostia; for, once loosed and unbound, they would go so far off into life as they pleased. There is in that place a certain pool which the Latins call the Tyrrhenian Sea, a healthful bath against all plagues, infirmities, and diseases of the pontiff’s unclean sanctity, of all cardinals, and of the pestilence of the whole see. I would vigorously wash those persons there, most gently placed within it. And if it happened that they shrank from bearing the water, as madmen and the possessed usually tremble at water, I would add for them something from the rock upon which they and their Church are founded; indeed, I would attach something to those keys by which they can loose all things in heaven and on earth, and would command the waters whatever they wished. Their pastoral crook and club also ought to be at hand, so that they might strike the waters with such heavy slaps that blood would pour from their mouths and nostrils. Finally, their pastures too would go with them, by which they might refresh and restore themselves in the bath: namely, all the Decrees, Decretals, the *Sext*, Clementines, Extravagants, bulls, indulgences, buttery, cheesy, and milky letters hanging from their necks, for every kind of security,” CXLVIII, 196.

But let the greater number rage, gnash their teeth, go mad, and finally dash their hands, feet, heels, and heads against the rock upon which the Apostolic See is founded; let them thunder, hurl lightning, and flash with insults; let them tear and lacerate the bishops of the Apostolic See with a thousand curses and utterly mendacious fabrications: “He who dwells in heaven shall laugh at them, and the Lord shall mock them” (Ps. II). And we, with Saint Augustine (XLIII, 300), openly and fearlessly repeat to them: “What has the chair of the Roman Church done to you, in which Peter sat and in which Anastasius—now Pius IX—sits today? Why do you call the Apostolic Chair a chair of pestilence? If it is because of men whom you think speak the law and do not perform it, did our Lord Jesus Christ inflict any injury upon the chair in which the Pharisees sat, concerning whom he said, ‘For they say and do not do’? Did he not commend that chair of Moses, and, while preserving the honour of the chair, rebuke them? For he said: ‘They sit upon the chair of Moses; what they say, do,’ etc. If you considered these things, you would not, because of men whom you defame, blaspheme the Apostolic Chair with which you do not communicate. But what else is this than not to know what one is saying, and yet to be unable to do anything but curse?”

Moreover, if some persons less praiseworthy and commendable in life and morals have obtained or held Peter’s chair, what follows from that? For, as Saint Augustine says (XXXIII, 403), God made his people secure concerning evil prelates, so that the chair of saving doctrine may not be abandoned on their account, a chair in which even evil men are compelled to say good things. For what they say is not their own, but God’s, who has placed the teaching of truth in the chair of unity.—“Even if,” the same Augustine continues (XXXIII, 196, 197), “some traitor [wicked man] had crept in during those times into that order of bishops which is led from Peter himself down to Anastasius [Pius IX], who now sits upon that same chair, he would do no prejudice to the Church or to innocent Christians, for whom the Lord, providing beforehand, said concerning evil prelates: ‘What they say, do,’ etc.”

“But the claims of the Popes, it is said, have at all times been excessive, even in matters touching only spiritual power; they have often been attacked and opposed by the most orthodox Catholics. Bishops such as St. Cyprian of Carthage, Isidore of Seville, and others have seemed to deny them to the Popes in the name of the Gospel. The Church of France, in the time of [Col. 0114] Louis XIV, held this view. Yet is the Pope’s jurisdictional primacy merely a matter of ecclesiastical and human law, rather than divine law? This is the question at issue in this part of our INDEX; for as regards the Popes’ temporal power, *videtur dici posse* [it seems possible to say] that the temporal papacy is not established by God, and that, even if all the Pope’s spiritual powers were admitted, however unlimited one might wish them to be, it would by no means follow that the Papal States were his property by the sole title of the temporal papacy.”

Since these matters are set forth more or less clearly in what follows, it seemed appropriate to note them here beforehand by way of analysis.

But whatever may be or may happen in the end, the patrimonies of the Apostolic See must be defended by the supreme pontiffs, both by right of patrimony and by another, higher right flowing from the divine laws: namely, that things sacred to God are to be administered, possessed, retained, defended, and reclaimed by the high priest from sacrilegious usurpers whenever they are occupied. Hence among the greatest pontiffs who vigorously defended these rights, some were especially notable—among them Gregory III and Zacharias, to name these two while passing over Gregory VII and Boniface VIII, and, in our own times, Pius IX, the most illustrious of them all. Gregory III by force of arms, and Zacharias—like him celebrated for innocence of character and holiness of life—endeavoured by action to recover cities taken from the Apostolic See. But questions may be raised, and the reader shall judge.

**Pope Adrian II says:** He to whom our Lord entrusted His sheep—that is, the whole Church, already redeemed by His precious blood—namely blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, after the bonds of His Passion, after the wounds of the nails, the mockery of the cross, and the glory of the resurrection, entrusted them to him a third time, saying: “Feed my sheep; feed my lambs” (John XXI): we, indeed, exercising the office of that apostolate, with the Lord cooperating in all things, have received by the divine will the flock of the Lord, to be fed with the pasture of spiritual life and guarded with diligent care, with the rod of equity and justice, with the forbearance of kindly humility and patience. . . . May you, O illustrious King Lothair, open the ear of your heart to blessed Peter, the true keeper of the keys, speaking in us from heaven—the mouth of our apostolate being full of the grace of the sevenfold Spirit. CXXII, 1259.

We, Celestine, shall undoubtedly deserve to attain the joy of the blessed if we keep careful watch over the Lord’s sheep, lest either the ravening wolf assail them through the snares of hatred or discord, or that greedy lion devour them, who, as the prince of the Apostles teaches, prowls about seeking someone to devour. CXXII, 1263.

No one at all doubts that there is no crime from which the Church, by the divinely given power entrusted to her, cannot absolve those who desist and release those who repent—to whom it is said: “Whatever you shall forgive upon earth,” etc. . . . in all such matters, whatever and however great or of whatever kind they may be.

But you (in the letter to Hincmar of Rheims), because you kept silent and did not rise even slightly against this crime, appear to be not merely an accomplice but, what is worse, an instigator of this tyranny. Therefore, lest we ourselves seem blameworthy before God, who renders to each according to his work, because of the silence of our own silence, we rouse your slumber by apostolic words; and, as otherwise we ought not, we command you to return to yourself. 1301, 1302.

**Anastasius the Librarian.**—Both sacred Scripture and the constant tradition of the Fathers affirm that the power of kings and princes over peoples subject to them proceeds from God alone. Yet there is no dominion on earth whose institution and jurisdiction are more plainly evident from the utterances of Scripture, or whose exercise is confirmed by fuller patristic authority, than that of Saint Peter and of the Roman pontiffs who followed him.

Sacred Scripture consists of the Old and New Testaments. The Old bore beforehand the image of the New. Its various ministers foreshadowed the ministers of the latter; and therefore the high priest of the Jews indicated the supreme pontiff of Christians. For the high priest of the Jews possessed a definite and supreme tribunal for pronouncing judgment on all matters pertaining to religion, for seeking the true meaning of the laws, and for settling every controversy. In the same way the supreme pontiff of Christians occupies a fixed and supreme see, since he exercises the same authority in the Church. At one time, in the Synagogue, the same pontiff exercised temporal administration together with spiritual administration. Thus, after the Church had been established and made firm, when the empire at Rome—which had ruled almost all nations—had been entirely destroyed after being divided among many kings, divine Providence made Peter’s successors absolute and supreme rulers even in temporal affairs, [Col. 0115] in that portion of lands and peoples where their see is situated. Therefore the royal priesthood, foreshadowed both by written law and by the law of nature—in which afterward fathers, elders, and heads of patriarchal families performed the office both of priest and of king—is found complete in every respect. Moreover, the head and parent of all Christians, free from the power of every prince of this world, can exercise his authority with greater dignity and liberty, being suspected by no one whatever.

In the New Testament, where the founding of the Church is concerned, this first appears: namely, that Peter and each of his successors are designated the head and foundation of the Church. Formerly called Simon, he receives the name Peter; he occupies the foremost place; through him the eternal Father reveals to human beings Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God. The Saviour makes him and his successors participants in his dignity as the cornerstone, for the establishment of the Church, so that the gates of hell may not prevail against it. Finally, He gives to him and his successors the keys of the kingdom of heaven, that is, the supreme power of governing the Church.

The Saviour Himself declares that He prayed for these same persons, that their faith might not fail; indeed, that they might strengthen their brethren in the faith.

The same divine Saviour, after His resurrection and before ascending into heaven, established Peter and his successors as supreme governors of the whole Church, when He commanded them to feed the lambs and sheep, of which the universal body of the Church is composed. For the lambs are Christian peoples, and the sheep, mothers of the lambs, are the various pastors, to whose care different portions of the flocks are entrusted. Thus, to commit the lambs and sheep—that is, peoples and pastors—to Peter and his successors for their safekeeping is the same as declaring them supreme governors of the entire Church, whose one fold depends upon one shepherd.

Scarcely had Jesus Christ ascended into heaven when Peter began to perform his office. Since a large part of the nascent Church had gathered at Jerusalem, he wished that another apostle should be appointed in the traitor Judas’s place, in order that all the seats of that sacred college might be filled, and thus to prepare the Church for receiving the Holy Spirit. After Pentecost Peter was the first of all to begin preaching the Gospel, unlocking the mysteries of the Old Testament in which Jesus Christ was prefigured. The first to proclaim the word of God, again and at the same time, he caused eight thousand persons converted to God to be baptized. He was the first to show himself the supreme dispenser of graces by working miracles, and the judge of sins by imposing anathemas. Peter himself makes James the Less bishop of Jerusalem; and Paul himself approaches him as head of the Church not long after his conversion. When the Gospel had already spread widely through all Judaea and the neighbouring provinces, this same Peter visited churches founded both by the other apostles and by other preachers of the Gospel, and extended them immensely, winning for Jesus Christ villages everywhere and entire districts. Moreover, Peter is the first to proclaim salvation to the Gentiles, as he had first proclaimed it to the Jews. For since he was to be the common father and supreme shepherd of both peoples, he accordingly opens for each the door into the fold. Finally, when he is held in prison in chains for the faith, the Church—being especially concerned for the safety of him as its head, a thing which is known never to have been done for any other apostle—appoints public prayers for his preservation. Now it is proved that the Church’s tradition was unanimous and constant in recognizing in the supreme pontiffs succeeding in the Roman See the same privileges enjoyed by Peter. CXXVIII, 937–970.

**Anselm, bishop of Lucca.**—Since the Lord says to Peter, “And to thee I will give the keys,” etc.; “Upon this Rock,” etc.; “Feed,” etc.; whatever church is corrupted by the usurpation of another’s jurisdiction is proved to be no longer the bride of Christ but an adulteress, no longer free but a slave. As blessed Ambrose says:

> “I was approached by counts and tribunes, that through me the basilicas might be promptly handed over; they said that the emperor had rightfully commanded that all things within his power ought to be surrendered. I replied: If he asked of me what was mine—my estate, my silver, some right of mine of that sort—I would not oppose him, although all that is mine belongs to the poor. But things that are divine are not subject to imperial power.”

And shortly afterward:

> “It is neither lawful for me to surrender them nor expedient for you, Emperor, to receive them. The house of a private person cannot lawfully be violated. Do you think that the house of God is to be taken away? It is alleged to the emperor that all things are lawful to him, that the universe is his. I answer: Do not burden yourself, Emperor, by thinking that you possess any imperial right in matters divine. Do not exalt yourself; rather, if you wish to reign longer, be subject to God. [Col. 0116] For it is written: ‘Render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar’s,’ etc. Palaces belong to the emperor; churches to the priest. The right over public walls has been entrusted to you, not over sacred things. Again it is said to me that the emperor commanded: ‘I too ought to have one basilica.’ I answer: You are not permitted to have any at all.” CXLIX, 448.

**Augustine, bishop of Hippo.**—“And I say unto thee that thou art Peter,” etc. For Peter himself had said: “Thou art the Christ, the Son,” etc. “Upon this Rock I will build” the faith which you confess, upon that which you have said: “Thou art the Christ,” etc. “I will build my Church.” “For you are Peter. Peter is from rock (*petra*), not rock from Peter. Thus Peter is from the rock, just as a Christian is from Christ. Do you wish to know from what rock Peter is called? Hear Paul: ‘I would not have you ignorant,’ etc. ‘And the Rock was Christ.’”

Before His Passion, the Lord Jesus chose His disciples, whom He called apostles. Among these, Peter alone, almost everywhere, deserved to bear the person of the whole Church. Because of that person, which he alone bore for the whole Church, he deserved to hear: “To thee I will give the keys,” etc. For it was not one man but the unity of the Church that received these keys. Thus Peter’s pre-eminence is proclaimed because he bore the figure of the universality and unity of the Church when it was said to him: “To thee I will give,” etc.—what was given to all. For, that you may know that the Church received the keys of the kingdom of heaven, hear what the Lord says elsewhere to all His apostles: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive,” etc. This pertains to the keys, concerning which it was said: “Whatever you shall loose on earth shall be loosed,” etc. Yet He said this to Peter. To know that Peter then bore the person of the universal Church, hear what is said to him and what is said to all holy believers: “If your brother shall sin against you,” etc. The dove—the Church—binds; the dove looses. The building upon the Rock binds and looses. XXXV, 544.

Concerning the two apostles Peter and John, the question is asked why the Lord loved John more, although Peter loved the Lord Himself more. Whenever John mentions himself, so that he may be understood while suppressing his own name, he adds that Jesus loved him, as though Jesus loved him alone, so that by this sign he might be distinguished from the others, whom He certainly loved. What, then, did he wish to be understood by saying this, except that he was loved more? Far be it that he should say this falsely. What greater indication of His greater love toward him could Jesus have given than that, although he was a man sharing so great a salvation with his fellow disciples, he alone reclined upon the breast of the Saviour Himself?

Many proofs may indeed be offered that the apostle Peter loved Christ more than the others. But, not to go far afield, this is evident in the Lord’s third manifestation, where He says: “Do you love me more than these?” The Lord certainly knew what He was asking, and yet He asked it. But because Peter, when he answered, “I love you,” did not add “more than these,” he answered only what he knew concerning himself. For he could not know how much any other person loved Christ, since he could not see another’s heart. Yet by saying, “Yes, Lord, you know,” he sufficiently declared that the Lord knew what He asked; therefore the Lord knew not only that Peter loved Him, but also that Peter loved Him more than they did.

And yet, if we ask which of the two is better—one who loves Christ more or one who loves Him less—who would hesitate to answer that the one who loves more is better? Again, if we ask which of the two is better—one whom Christ loves less or one whom Christ loves more—we shall undoubtedly answer that the one more loved by Christ is better. In the first comparison, therefore, Peter is preferred to John; but in this second, John is preferred to Peter. We therefore propose a third comparison: which of two disciples is better—one who loves Christ less than his fellow disciple but is loved by Christ more than that fellow disciple, or one whom Christ loves less than his fellow disciple, while he himself loves Christ more than his fellow disciple? Here the answer plainly hesitates, and the question grows greater. But so far as I understand, I should readily answer that the one who loves Christ more is better, whereas the one whom Christ loves more is happier. How I should defend the justice of our Deliverer in loving less the one who loves Him more, and loving more the one who loves Him less, I do not see. XXXV, 1971, 1972.
