But the Lord asks what He knew, and not once but again and a third time, whether Peter loves Him; nor does He hear anything else from Peter the third time than that He is loved; nor does He so often entrust anything else to Peter except the feeding of His sheep. A threefold confession is rendered for the threefold denial, lest the tongue serve love less than it had served fear. Let feeding the Lord’s flock be the office of love, since denying the shepherd had been the sign of fear. Those who feed Christ’s sheep with the intention that they should be their own and not Christ’s are convicted of loving themselves, not Christ—whether through the desire for boasting, domination, or gain—rather than through the love of obedience, helpfulness, and pleasing God. Against such persons, therefore, this frequently repeated voice of Christ keeps watch; concerning them the Apostle laments that they seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ. For what else does “Do you love me? Feed my sheep” mean, than this: If you love me, do not think of feeding yourself, but feed my sheep; feed them as mine, not as yours; seek my glory in them, not yours; my dominion, not yours; my gains, not yours; lest you be among those who belong to perilous times, lovers of themselves, and all the other things connected with this beginning of evils.

Rightly it is said to Peter, “Do you love me?” and he answers, “I love you”; and the reply is made to him, “Feed my lambs,” and this a second and a third time. Here too it is shown that *amor* and *dilectio* are one and the same; for even the Lord at the end does not say, “Do you cherish (*diligis*) me?” but “Do you love (*amas*) me?” Therefore let us love not ourselves but Him; and, in feeding His sheep, let us seek what is His, not what is ours. XXXV, 1967, 1968.

“To thee I will give the keys,” etc. For it is not rock from Peter, but Peter from rock, just as Christ is not named from Christian, but Christian from Christ. The Lord therefore said, “Upon this Rock,” because Peter had said: “Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God.” Therefore, “Upon this Rock,” He says, “which you have confessed, I will build my Church.” “For the Rock was Christ,” and Peter himself was built upon that foundation. “For no other foundation can anyone lay besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus.” Therefore the Church founded upon Christ received from Him, in Peter, the keys of the kingdom of heaven—that is, the power of binding and loosing sins. For what the Church is by propriety in Christ, Peter is by signification in the rock: by this signification Christ is understood as the Rock and Peter as the Church. XXXV, 1973, 1774.

**Bruno, bishop of Segni.**—“But whom do you say that I am?” etc. It was fitting that Peter should answer this, since he was to be prince of the apostles. “Peter himself,” says Saint Augustine, “first in the rank of apostles, most ready in love for Christ, often answered alone for all.” Christ asks concerning Himself as man; Peter says that the Son of God is Son of Man. Therefore He who is the Son of God is Himself also the Son of Man. Hence the blessed Virgin is called one who bears God and man alike, or Theotokos, “God-bearer”; and because Nestorius refused to confess this, he was expelled and condemned by the Church. . . .

Barjona—that is, “son of the dove.” But why is Peter called son of the dove? For we read that the Holy Spirit appeared over Christ the Lord in the form of a dove. He, then, is the son of this dove who possesses so holy and spiritual an understanding. “Because flesh and blood,” etc. This knowledge is not carnal; this faith is not of flesh and blood; neither your parents nor your flesh taught you these things. “And I say unto thee,” etc. You speak, and speak truly, that I am Christ, the Son of the living God; and I say to you that you are Peter, strong in faith and steadfast in doctrine. Unless Christ had understood strength and stability in this name, He would not immediately have added what follows: “And upon this Rock,” etc. Do not understand Saint Peter [as the rock]; look to the rock; and the Rock was Christ. Thus Peter is from rock, just as Christian is from Christ; for I am the rock, you are Peter. “Upon this Rock,” which you have now set forth as the foundation of faith; upon this faith which you have now taught in saying: “Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God”—upon this Rock and this faith “I will build my Church.”

For the Apostle, agreeing with this interpretation, says: “No other foundation,” etc., as if to say: there is no other foundation, unless he meant that Rock which Peter placed as the foundation when he said: “Thou art the Christ, the Son,” etc. Upon this Rock, moreover, the whole Church of God is built. “And the gates of hell,” etc. “For whoever falls upon this stone shall be broken; but upon whomever this stone falls, it shall crush him.” For this Rock is borne with such force and strength that it breaks down walls and shatters gates, and no power or strength can resist it.

But if you wish to understand “the gates of hell” otherwise, first recognize the gates of heaven. For the gates of heaven are apostles, bishops, priests, and others through whose teaching and examples the souls of believers enter the palace of heaven. On the contrary, the gates of hell are Jews and heretics, and all deceivers and corrupters of the Catholic faith; through these, the souls of unbelievers enter hell and are plunged into darkness. These, indeed, shall not prevail against this Rock and against the Church built upon it. What is said principally to Peter must be understood as said also to the other apostles, and not only to the apostles but also to bishops and priests. For to these the Lord gave both the keys and the power, so that they may open not only the Church but also heaven to others. CLXV, 211, 214.

**Cyprian, bishop of Carthage.**—For Peter, to whom the Lord entrusted His sheep to be fed and guarded, and upon whom He placed and founded the Church, denies that he possesses gold and silver, but says that he is rich by the grace of Christ, abundantly supplied through faith in Him and His power. By these riches he performed many great deeds with miracles, and by these spiritual goods he had abounded unto the grace of glory. The virgin who prefers to be rich in the world rather than in Christ cannot possess these riches and this wealth. IV, 449.

Saint Cyprian held deeply fixed in his mind that the apostles, in whom the Church rested and was built, were by no means separated from one another, each having his own rights and authority separately from the one Christ. Rather, all and each were fused into one and the same body, united by the same will, in the same power, toward one end; and Peter alone was the head of the entire apostolic body, the centre and summit of unity. Thus not only is there one head of the apostolic college, but also one apostolic person. Hence he says: “The Lord first gave to Peter, upon whom He founded the Church and from whom He established and displayed the origin of unity, this power: that what he loosed on earth should be loosed in heaven.” III, 1114.

Hence, in order to manifest unity, He established one chair; by His authority He ordained that the origin of that same unity should begin from one. Certainly the apostles were what Peter was, endowed with an equal partnership of honour and power; but the beginning proceeds from unity, and primacy is given to Peter, so that the one Church of Christ and the one chair may be shown. All are shepherds, and one flock is shown, fed by all the apostles in unanimous agreement, so that the Church of Christ may be shown to be one. IV, 499, 500.

We must firmly hold and defend this unity, especially we bishops who preside in the Church, in order that we may prove that the episcopate itself too is one and undivided. The episcopate is one, of which each bishop holds a share in its entirety. IV, 501.

In many passages of Saint Cyprian, it is clear that the principle of unity cannot exist without primacy. For who would deny primacy to him from whom unity begins and through whom the Church is shown to be one? Just as unity did not cease after Peter, so neither did primacy and the principle of unity, which Christ ordained by His authority and instituted with the purpose that the Church might be shown to be one. It is therefore necessary that, as unity, so also the principle and bond of unity should remain in the Church. From this one may judge how highly Cyprian valued the Roman Church, and how closely he was attached to the principle of unity, he who was animated by so great a love for unity. Further, he expressed his whole mind concerning the question in our Index: he weakened Peter’s power even in spiritual matters, much less extended it to temporal matters; nor [*Arianum*, a syntactically uncertain printed reading]; and yet, although at that time there was being debated the very serious question of rebaptizing heretics, concerning which the supreme pontiff Stephen was spreading erroneous views, and although he defended the rights of bishops most vehemently, he nevertheless firmly acknowledged the lawful primacy of the Roman See. IV, 494, 520.

Nor did Peter, whom the Lord first chose and upon whom He founded His Church, when Paul afterward disputed with him concerning circumcision, claim anything for himself insolently or arrogantly assume anything, so as to say that he held the primacy and ought rather to be obeyed by those who came later and followed him. Nor did he despise Paul because Paul had formerly persecuted the Church; rather, he accepted the counsel of truth and readily consented to the lawful reasoning which Paul maintained, thereby giving us examples both of concord and patience: that we should not stubbornly love our own opinions, but should rather regard as our own those things which are at times usefully and salutarily suggested by our brethren and colleagues, if they are true and lawful. IV, 410.

Saint Cyprian: “The Lord first gave to Peter, upon whom He built the Church and from whom He established and displayed the origin of unity, this power: that what he loosed on earth should be loosed in heaven.” III, 1114.

In the Gospel, when the disciples abandoned the Lord as He was speaking, He turned to the Twelve and said: “Do you also wish to go away?” Peter answered Him: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the word of eternal life, and we have believed and known that you are the Son of the living God.” Peter speaks here, he upon whom the Church was to be built, teaching and showing in the name of the Church that, even if a stubborn and proud multitude unwilling to obey departs, the Church nevertheless does not depart from Christ. And they are the Church: the people united to their priest and the flock clinging to its shepherd. Hence you ought to know that the bishop is in the Church and the Church in the bishop; and if anyone is not with the bishop, he is not in the Church. Those who do not have peace with God’s priests flatter themselves in vain when they creep in and believe that they communicate secretly with certain persons, since the Church, which is Catholic and one, is not torn or divided but is certainly connected and joined together by the bond of priests clinging mutually to one another. IV, 406.

**Firmilian, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia.**—What kind of error and how great a blindness belongs to one who says that remission of sins can be given in the synagogues of heretics remains established upon the foundation of the one Church, which Christ once for all made firm upon the Rock. From this it may be understood why Christ said to Peter alone: “Whatever you shall bind,” etc.; and again in the Gospel, when Christ breathed upon the apostles alone, saying: “Receive the Holy Spirit,” etc. Therefore the power of forgiving sins was given to the apostles, to the churches which they, sent by Christ, established, and to the bishops who succeeded them by vicarious ordination. III, 1168.

**Gregory the Great, pope.**—When the apostle Peter wished the custom of circumcision under the Law still to be observed, Paul opposed him to his face and says that he was blameworthy in this matter. Speaking to the disciples, he calls this conduct not merely a fault but, what is greater, hypocrisy—that is, pretence—saying: “When Peter came to Antioch, I opposed him, because he was blameworthy.” And shortly afterward: “The other Jews also joined in his pretence.”

Again, the first of the apostles, when he gave many admonitions to the disciples and learned that some were disparaging Paul’s writings, said: “As our most illustrious brother Paul, according to the wisdom given him, wrote to you, speaking in them of matters in which there are some things difficult to understand, which the unlearned and unstable distort, as they do the other Scriptures, to their own destruction.”

See: Paul in his Epistles wrote that Peter was blameworthy, and Peter in his Epistles declares Paul admirable in what he wrote. Certainly, unless Peter had read Paul’s Epistles, he would not have praised them. But having read them, he found that he himself was called blameworthy there. Therefore the friend of truth praised even that for which he had been reproved; and he was pleased even by this: that in those matters he had not been pleasing, because he had thought otherwise than he ought. He yielded himself to agreement with his lesser brother, and in that matter became a follower of one beneath him, in order that in this also he might lead: so that, being first in the summit of the apostolate, he might be first also in humility. Thus, lest he disdain to hear words of rebuke, he dismissed from memory, as it were, all the gifts he had received, so that he might hold firmly the single gift of humility. LXXVI, 1002, 1003.

**Jerome, presbyter of Stridon.**—His letter to Pope Damasus is well known; let us attend to its words and meaning:

> “Since the East, shattered against itself by the long-standing fury of peoples, is tearing the Lord’s seamless, woven-from-above tunic piecemeal into fragments; and since foxes are ravaging the vineyard of Christ, so that among broken cisterns which hold no water it is difficult to discern where the sealed fountain and enclosed garden may be: I have therefore judged that I should consult the Chair of Peter and the faith praised by the apostolic mouth. I now seek food for my soul from that place from which I formerly received the garment of Christ. Neither the vast expanse of liquid element nor the intervening distance of lands has been able to prevent me from seeking the precious pearl. ‘Wherever the body is, there shall the eagles be gathered.’
>
> “The inheritance being squandered by an evil offspring, among you alone the incorrupt inheritance of the Fathers is preserved. There, the rich soil produces the purity of the Lord’s seed with a hundredfold fruit; here, grain buried in furrows degenerates into tares and wild oats. Now, in the West, the Sun of righteousness rises; but in the East that Lucifer who fell set his throne above the stars. ‘You are the light of the world; you are the salt of the earth’; you are vessels of gold and silver; here, earthenware or wooden vessels await the iron rod and eternal fire. Although your greatness terrifies me, your kindness nevertheless invites me. From the priest I seek the salvation of the victim; from the shepherd, protection for the sheep. Let envy depart; let the ambition of the Roman height withdraw. I speak with the successor of the fisherman and disciple of the cross. Following no first leader except Christ, I am joined in communion with your Blessedness, that is, with the Chair of Peter. I know that the Church is built upon that Rock. Whoever eats the Lamb outside this house is profane. If anyone is not in Noah’s ark, he shall perish when the flood prevails. . . . I do not know Vitalis; I reject Meletius; I am ignorant of Paulinus. Whoever does not gather with you scatters; that is, whoever is not of Christ is of Antichrist.”

Therefore I beseech your Blessedness, by the salvation of the world crucified, by the *homoousian* Trinity—“of one substance”—to grant me authority by your letters either to be silent about or to speak of the hypostases. XXII, 335, 358.

[Col. 0120] **Henry of Augsburg, presbyter.**—Peter answered for all: “Because you are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” And the Lord pronounced blessed his faith, which, He said, not carnal descent but My Father had revealed to you. Therefore I shall change your name to Peter; upon the rock of your faith I shall also found My Church, against which the gates of hell shall not prevail, nor shall the rivers of persecutions be able to overthrow it. And I make you keeper of the gate of life, giving you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and power is conferred upon you so that whatever shall have been bound by you on earth may remain entangled by bonds in heaven also, and whatever shall have been loosed by you on earth may in heaven also be free from bonds. CLXXII, 970.

Although the priesthood surpasses kingship, nevertheless, for the bond of peace and concord, evangelical and apostolic authority teaches that honour must be rendered to kings in secular affairs only: “Render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar’s,” etc. Therefore in matters belonging to the right of kingship, the people also ought to obey kings; but in matters pertaining to the right of the divine law, they ought to please God. Thus Sebastian, thus Maurice, etc. “Behold, here are two swords.” The Lord confirmed the disciples’ words by His authority, because He showed beforehand that two swords are necessary for governing the Church in the present life: one spiritual, namely the word of God, which the priesthood uses to enlighten sinners; the other material, which kingship uses to punish those persisting in evil. For it is necessary that royal power subdue by the material sword those who, rebelling against God’s law, cannot be corrected by the priestly stole. CLXXII, 1266, 1267.

A king, or secular authority, ought and can grant only secular dignities, such as duchies, prefectures, and countships; the Church alone, however, ought to entrust spiritual things to spiritual persons. If it is objected that the emperor Valentinian said to Ambrose: “I entrust bodies to you; God, however, entrusts souls,” one should know that Ambrose had previously been a provincial judge; but, after he canonically received the episcopate, the king additionally delegated to him the administration of the province. We know that this custom is still observed in certain churches: namely, that a bishop bears the care of both a bishopric and a duchy. Yet we know that this is wholly unsuitable for priests of Christ, because “no one who serves as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs.” CLXXII, 1228.

Our Lord Jesus Christ, true king and priest according to the order of Melchizedek, established laws and rights for His bride; and for governing her He instituted not kingship but priesthood. Over this He set the apostle Peter, to whom He also said: “You are Peter,” etc. Peter received this power of priesthood from the Lord and left it to his successors. Therefore, just as from the time of Moses to Samuel priests presided over the people of God, so from the time of Christ to Sylvester the priests of God alone ruled the Church. She was excellently instructed by them in the best morals and laws; but she was attacked on every side by kings, who strove by every means to turn her away from the worship of truth and to convert—indeed compel—her to the worship of demons.

But after the stone cut from the mountain without hands, rejected indeed by the builders of the wall of iniquity but raised by God as the head of the corner, grew into a great mountain and filled the whole earth with its greatness, it immediately changed times and transferred kingdoms. The height of kingship began to bow before the feet of Christ, and the summit of empire to incline in the assembly of the Church. For the God of peace, the great priest, exchanged the time of persecution for a time of peace; and the great King above all gods transferred the rebellious empire of pagans into the kingdom of Christians.

Constantine, therefore, the prince of the princes of the realm, is converted to the faith of Christ through Sylvester, the prince of the priests of the Church; and the whole world is clothed in the new rite of the Christian religion. Constantine placed the crown of the kingdom upon the Roman pontiff and decreed by imperial authority that thereafter no one should assume the Roman Empire without the consent of the Apostle. Sylvester received this privilege from Constantine and left it to his successors. And since the care of the priesthood and the supreme authority of the kingdom depended upon Sylvester’s judgment, this man filled with God, understanding that those rebellious against priests could not be restrained by the sword of the word but by the material sword, took Constantine himself as his helper in God’s husbandry and as defender of the Church against pagans, Jews, and heretics. To him he also granted the sword for the punishment of evildoers, and placed upon him the crown of the kingdom for the praise of the good.

From this point the Church at once began to have kings or judges for secular judgments, who might forcefully repel pagans harassing the Church, or its other enemies attacking it; while within, they subjected to the Church, through fear of punishments, those rebellious against the divine laws. Thus secular judgments alone belong to kings. Hence, when certain bishops brought their [Col. 0121] fellow bishops to trial before the Emperor Constantine, he, knowing that the matter did not belong to his jurisdiction, replied: “Go, because you belong to Christ; see to this matter yourselves among yourselves. I shall not be your judge,” CLXXII, 1263, 1264.

IVO (St), bishop of Chartres.—In the New Testament, after Christ the Lord, the priestly order began with Peter, because the pontificate in Christ’s Church was first given to him, the Lord saying to him: “You are Peter,” etc. Therefore he was the first to receive from the Lord the power of binding and loosing, and the first to bring the people to faith by the power of his preaching. The other apostles, however, received honour and power in equal fellowship with him. They also wished him to be their prince; and, at the Lord’s command, they were scattered throughout the whole world and preached the Gospel.

When they departed this life, bishops arose in their place, whose ordination ought to take place in the aforesaid order and manner. Whoever receives them and their words receives the Lord; but whoever despises them despises him by whom they were sent and whose embassy they perform, and he himself will without doubt be despised by the Lord. By heavenly favour Peter’s see is the Roman Church, which Peter and Paul consecrated by their martyrdom. [lacuna] Christ gave bishops power, and he also gave a primacy far more perfect than the principalities of the earth. Or does it seem just to you that spirit should yield to flesh, that heavenly things should be separated from earthly, that human things should be preferred to divine?

The Lord willed the sacrament of evangelical preaching to belong to the office of all the apostles in such a way that he placed it pre-eminently in the most blessed Peter, chief of all the apostles, and that from him, as from a certain head, he might diffuse his gifts, as it were, into the whole body; so that anyone who had dared to depart from Peter’s firmness might understand himself to be excluded from the divine mystery [variant: ministry]. For, having been taken into the fellowship of indivisible unity, Christ wished him to be called what he himself was, saying: “You are Peter,” etc., so that the building of the eternal temple might rest, by the wondrous gift of God’s grace, upon Peter’s firmness. Thus he strengthened his Church with this stability, so that neither human rashness might assail it nor the gates of hell prevail against it.

Whoever in any way separates himself from the unity of faith or fellowship of Peter the Apostle can neither be absolved from the bonds of sins nor enter the gate of the heavenly kingdom. The Roman Church has so shared its offices with the other Churches that they are called to a share in the burden of care, not to the fullness of power, CLXI, 322–330.

LACTANTIUS FIRMIANUS.—When Nero had already become emperor, Peter came to Rome; and, performing certain miracles by the power of God himself, granted him by God, he converted many to righteousness. And he established for God a faithful and steadfast temple. When this was reported to Nero, he perceived that not only in Rome but everywhere a great multitude was daily deserting the worship of idols and, condemning the old order, passing over to a new religion. Being the abominable and harmful tyrant that he was, he rushed forth to destroy the heavenly temple and annihilate righteousness. He was the first of all to persecute God’s servants and fastened Peter to the cross.

Yet he did not escape punishment. For God looked upon the affliction of his people. Cast down from the height of imperial power and hurled from his summit, the powerless tyrant suddenly appeared nowhere, so that not even a place of burial on earth was found for so evil a beast, VII, 195, 196, 197, 303, 438, 589, 619, 621.

LEO THE GREAT (St), pope.—“Blessed are you, Simon,” etc.; that is, blessed are you because my Father has taught you. Earthly opinion has not deceived you, but heavenly inspiration has instructed you; and neither flesh nor blood, but he whose Only-begotten I am, has revealed me to you. “And I say to you,” etc.; that is, as my Father has revealed my divinity to you, so I make known to you your exalted dignity: “because you are Peter.” That is: although I am the inviolable rock, I the cornerstone, who make both one, nevertheless you too are a rock because you are made firm by my power; so that what is proper to me by power may become common to you through participation in me.

“Upon this rock,” etc. Upon this strength, he says, I shall build an eternal temple; and the loftiness of my Church, which is to be joined to heaven, shall rise upon the firmness of this faith. The gates of hell shall not hold this confession; the bonds of death shall not bind it. For this voice is the voice of life: as it leads its confessors to heavenly things, so it casts deniers down to hell. “I will give to you,” etc.

The right of this power did indeed pass also to the other apostles, but it is not without reason that what is communicated to all is entrusted to one. For this is entrusted uniquely to Peter because Peter’s pattern is set before all rulers of the Church. Therefore Peter’s privilege remains wherever judgment is rendered according to his equity; and neither severity nor leniency is excessive where nothing is bound and nothing loosed except what blessed Peter has bound or loosed, LIV, 429, 430.

But when his Passion was imminent—the Passion that was to disturb the steadfastness of his disciples—the Lord said: “Simon, [Col. 0122] Simon, behold, Satan,” etc. The danger arising from the temptation of fear was common to all the apostles, and they alike needed the aid of divine protection, because the devil desired to assail all and crush all. Yet the Lord undertakes a special care for Peter, and prayer is made particularly for Peter’s faith, as though the condition of the others would be more secure if the leader’s mind were not overcome.

Thus in Peter the strength of all is fortified, and the help of divine grace is so ordered that the firmness bestowed upon Peter through Christ is conferred through Peter upon the apostles. For after his resurrection the Lord said three times to the blessed Apostle Peter—after the keys of the kingdom, through the mystical implication of a threefold profession of eternal love—“Feed my sheep,” etc. This he undoubtedly does even now, and the devout shepherd fulfills the Lord’s command, strengthening us by exhortations and never ceasing to pray for us, that we may not be overcome by any temptation.

Since, therefore, we see that so great a protection has been divinely established for us, we reasonably and justly rejoice in the merits and dignity of our leader, giving thanks to the everlasting King, our Redeemer Jesus Christ, because he gave such great power to him whom he made prince of the whole Church, to the glory of his name, LIV, 431, 432.

It should be observed that, although St Leo says concerning St Peter and St Paul: “For these are the men through whom, Rome, the Gospel of Christ shone forth for you; these are your holy fathers and true shepherds,” LIV, 422, nevertheless at col. 423 he assigns the episcopal see to Peter alone: “Through the sacred see of blessed Peter, having been made head of the world, [Rome] might exercise a wider presidency by divine religion than by earthly dominion.” In saying “episcopal see,” he assigns it to Peter alone, and declares that through it Rome was made head of the world. By reason of that see Rome presides over the whole world, so that henceforth it presides more widely by divine religion than by earthly dominion.

These verses of Prosper in his poem *Against the Ungrateful* accord with this:

> Rome, Peter’s see, which by pastoral honour,  
> Made head of the world, holds by religion  
> Whatever it does not possess by its armies.

Therefore the primacy, dignity, and authority extending over the whole world, even beyond the boundaries of the Roman Empire, could not have originated from the imperial city to which Peter’s episcopate was attached, as certain heterodox persons still dream even today.

What is also said in St Leo, LIV, 428—“because election made them equal, labour similar, and their end equal,” concerning them, that is, St Peter and St Paul—must be explained.

1. The words “and election [made them] equal” are absent from the most ancient Vatican manuscripts. Yet, if they are to be explained, “election” means election to the apostleship, in which Peter and Paul were equal because each was chosen as an apostle by Christ. This does no prejudice to the primacy, for, as St Leo teaches, LIV, 149: “Peter alone is chosen, that [lacuna] he may be set over all the apostles.” And in LIV, 629, speaking of the apostleship to which all the apostles were called: “The Lord willed the sacrament of this office to belong to the office of all the apostles in such a way that he placed it pre-eminently in the most blessed Peter, chief of all the apostles.”

2. Leo describes them as “similar and equal” not in the power of primacy, but in their end—that is, in death or martyrdom.

These matters should be noted in refuting the marginal note attached to this passage in the Quesnellian editions, where one reads: “Peter and Paul, the Church’s twin eye, one equal to the other.” Quesnel himself, moreover, in the work entitled *La discipline de l’Eglise*, after citing those words of St Paul the Apostle, “I was in no way inferior to the superlative apostles,” admits that all this equality concerns precisely the apostleship alone, and not the primacy of the apostleship: “In all this, equality concerns precisely the apostleship alone, not the primacy of the apostleship.”

And even the Gallican theologians themselves confess with the Catholic Church that this primacy is not merely one of honour but especially a primacy of power and jurisdiction. Thus Leo also acknowledged, LIV, 425, that not mere honour but an honour of power was assigned to Peter by divine preordinations, LIV, 428.

In order that the effect of the ineffable grace of the redemption of the whole human race might be spread throughout the whole world, divine Providence prepared the Roman Empire, whose growth had been brought to those limits at which it bordered upon and lay adjacent to the universality of all nations on every side. For the work divinely ordered was most fittingly served by the confederation of many kingdoms under one empire, and by the availability of a swift passage for universal preaching among peoples held under the rule of one city.

Yet this city, ignorant of the author of its advancement, although it ruled almost all nations, was enslaved to the errors of all nations. It seemed to itself to have embraced a great religion because it had rejected no falsehood. Therefore, as much as it was more tenaciously bound through the devil, so much more wonderfully was it freed through Christ.

For when the twelve [Col. 0123] apostles, having received through the Holy Spirit the speech of all languages, had undertaken to instruct the world with the Gospel, assigning regions of the earth among themselves, the most blessed Peter, prince of the apostolic order, was sent to the citadel of the Roman Empire, so that the light of truth, revealed for the salvation of all nations, might flow more effectively from that head throughout the body of the world. What people were not then present in that city? Or what nations anywhere did not know what Rome had learned?

There the opinions of philosophy were to be trampled down; there the alleged truths of earthly wisdom were to be dissolved; there the worship of demons was to be refuted; there the impiety of every sacrifice was to be destroyed, where, with most diligent superstition, everything that had anywhere been established by various errors had been gathered together.

Therefore, most blessed Apostle Peter, you did not fear to come to this city [lacuna] and you entered this forest of roaring beasts and ocean of most turbulent depth with greater constancy than when you walked upon the sea. You did not fear Rome, mistress of the world, though in Caiaphas’s house you had been terrified by the maidservant of the high priest. Was either the authority of Claudius less than Pilate’s judgment, or Nero’s cruelty less than the savagery of the Jews? The power of love, therefore, conquered the material of fear; and you did not judge those whom you had undertaken to love to be objects of fear.

You had certainly already conceived this affection of fearless love when your profession of love for the Lord was established by the mystery of a threefold question. Nor was anything else sought from this purpose of your mind than that you should expend upon feeding the sheep of him whom you loved the food with which you yourself had been enriched.

So many signs of miracles, so many gifts of charisms, so many proofs of powers also increased your confidence. You had already instructed the peoples who had believed from the circumcision; you had already founded the Church of Antioch, where the dignity of the Christian name first arose; you had already imbued Pontus, Galatia, Asia, and Bithynia with the laws of evangelical preaching. Neither uncertain of the work’s outcome nor ignorant of the span of your life, you bore the trophy of Christ’s cross into the Roman citadels, whither the honour of power and the glory of suffering went before you by divine preordinations, LIV, 430 and passim.

MAXIMUS (St), bishop of Turin.—When St Leo and St Maximus proclaim Peter and Paul to have been peers, alike, and equal, so that it cannot be determined which was set before the other, this must be understood not of dignity and power—in which both confess Peter to have been superior to Paul—but of their wondrous election, virtue, merit, and the glory of martyrdom, LVII, 111–115.

St Maximus, in Homily 72, once seemed to have divided the unity of the Church’s head when he divided the keys signifying supreme power, assigning one to Peter and another to Paul. But such an interpretation must be judged wholly foreign to Maximus’s mind. For, speaking as an orator, he had earlier commended now Peter’s admirable confession of Christ’s divinity, now his election to found and raise up the Church, and elsewhere his courage in undergoing the punishment of the cross. Having also discoursed at length about Paul—especially about how he was made a teacher from a persecutor of the Church and with what lights he was illumined—he derived a new argument for speaking from the double key.

Maximus first states that all the apostles obtained from the Lord an equal grace of holiness, because all were elected and called to the same work of spreading the truth. Nevertheless, he proclaims Peter and Paul more eminent than the rest because Christ enriched them with greater gifts and privileges. To prove his point, Maximus devised the double key as signifying two things: one, the supreme authority of governing; the other, the knowledge of teaching heavenly truths.

For Maximus says: “To Peter, as a good steward, he gave the key of the kingdom of heaven; to Paul, as a capable teacher, he entrusted the teaching office of ecclesiastical instruction, so that those whom the latter has instructed for salvation may be received by the former into rest, and that Peter may receive into the heavenly kingdoms the souls of those whose hearts Paul has opened by the teaching of words.”

Maximus, therefore, was far from wishing to divide the primacy of governing the Church between Peter and Paul; rather, he professed to teach the unity of the head and Peter’s pre-eminence. Since access to God is certainly obtained through faith alone, and faith is produced by hearing, knowledge is the first disposition and, as it were, the key which unlocks the hearts of unbelievers and sinners and floods them with the light and power of grace. Whenever, therefore, people have been established in doctrine and the law of God, the key of power is then ready for them, by which they are absolved from sins and made capable of the eternal inheritance. For the ministry of the divine word must precede every path to salvation.

The first office of knowledge, therefore, is to provide the light by which the things to be believed are perceived; [Col. 0124] but the office of granting pardon for sins belongs to the higher power handed down by God. The former prepares souls; the latter opens the heavenly kingdom to believers who have been disposed and made ready. That this, and no other, was St Maximus’s teaching is further clear from the fact that he requires an inward foundation of faith and promises the possession of God’s favour to those who persevere therein in holiness.

“Therefore,” says St Maximus, “both received keys from the Lord: this man [Paul] the key of knowledge, that man [Peter] the key of power. The latter dispenses the riches of immortality; the former bestows the treasures of knowledge. For there are treasures of knowledge, as it is written: ‘In whom are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.’”

Maximus also calls this office of opening truth not simply “the key,” but “in a certain manner,” so that it may be understood that he speaks allegorically and is far from making Christ’s Church two-headed—something which certain writers of later times have most unjustly attributed to him. St Maximus therefore knew that the personal prerogative of primacy in Peter was expressed in the keys handed to him by Christ, and he did not make it common with Paul. To Paul, he says, was entrusted the dispensation of wisdom and God’s mysteries, to which the other apostles were called; but Paul excelled above them in teaching and heavenly illuminations, LVII, 401–404.

NICHOLAS I, pope.—The Creator of all bestowed the primacy of divine power upon his chosen apostles, establishing it upon the firm solidity of the faith of Peter, prince of the apostles, and ordained its eminent—indeed, first—see: “You are Peter,” etc. Finally, Peter, from the firmness of the rock which is Christ, does not cease by his prayers so to fortify the unshaken structure of the universal Church and faith strengthened in firmness that he hastens to reform the madness of those who stray according to the rule of right faith, and diligently seeks to reward those who intrepidly strengthen it, so that the gates of hell—that is, the suggestions of wicked spirits and the assaults of heretics—may not prevail to break the unity of that Church, CXIX, 773.

After the Lord gave blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, the power of binding and loosing in heaven and on earth and granted him the opening of the gates of the kingdom of heaven, he deigned to establish his holy Church upon the solidity of Peter’s faith: “You are Peter,” etc. In accordance with this promise, the foundations of the holy apostolic institution began to rise from precious stones under the cement of this foundation; and, by the favour of divine mercy, through the labour of its builders and the care of apostolic authority, they were brought without dissolution to the summit, to stand forever without the blast of a hostile wind. Blessed Peter deservedly obtained its primacy.

After him, his vicars, serving God with the greatest sincerity and free from the mists which commonly impede the straight path, worthily received it and remained diligent in the care of government which they undertook for the Lord’s sheep. Among them the mercy of almighty God has deigned to number even our lowliness. Since the whole body of believers seeks teaching from this holy Roman Church, which is the head of all Churches, demands integrity of faith, and entreats absolution from sins for those worthy of it and redeemed by God’s grace, it is fitting, etc. [lacuna]

For it is established that the holy Roman Church, through blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, is head of all Churches; and that from it [the Churches] should seek and follow rectitude and order in all useful matters and ecclesiastical institutions, which they must retain inviolably and incontrovertibly according to the canonical and synodical enactments of the holy Fathers. Consequently, what is decreed by the rulers of this see with full authority must not, on the pretext of any custom and in pursuit only of private wishes, be set aside, but must be held all the more firmly and unshakenly, CXIX, 785, 786.

PASCHASIUS RADBERTUS (St), abbot of Corbie.—When the Lord Jesus said, “Whom do men say that the Son of Man is?” he immediately added, “But whom do you say that I am?” You, because you are gods, whom do you testify me to be? A marvellous and astounding question. For before their eyes he appeared as nothing other than a man; he even said that he was the Son of Man, which he truly was, yet he sought something else from them.

Therefore I would by no means say that he asked concerning himself what he himself confessed, what was before their eyes and present in the same place, what could be touched by the hand. Rather, hidden was the matter about which he asked, in which and up to what point the foundations of the Church were to be made and the faith commended to all. Hence the marvellous and unheard-of answer of blessed Peter shone forth, so that he might discern all that was in the Lord and all that was in Christ, who was God. [lacuna]

“Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona.” There are some who understand this simply, so that Simon Peter is understood to be John’s son according to the flesh, in accordance with the question in another passage, “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” They maintain [Col. 0125] that the text has been corrupted through the copyist’s fault, so that *Bar-Jona* is read corruptly instead of *Bar-Joanna*, one syllable having been removed.

“And I say to you that you are Peter,” etc. It is as though he said openly: not with an empty word having no effect in action, but I say to you—I whose speaking is doing, because my word is full of omnipotence—“because you are Peter,” a name derived from *petra*, “rock,” that is, from me, upon whom the whole Church is built. For Peter is not, as some wrongly think, the foundation of the whole Church: “For no one can lay another foundation than that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus.” [lacuna]

And it should be noted that this name was not first imposed upon him here, but much earlier, according to John, when Andrew brought him to Christ: “You are,” he said, “Simon, son of John; you shall be called Cephas,” which is translated Peter. He did not say, “You shall be called Peter,” since he had already been called by that name; but he significantly said: “You are Peter, and upon this rock,” from which rock he was made, “I shall build my Church.” Not because he was then already so firm, but because he was to become so through Christ.

Nathanael had earlier held the same confession when he said: “Rabbi, you are the Son of God, you are the King of Israel.” But he was still in the disposition of one inquiring and doubting, seeking rather to see than to establish; and this was because he had been seen beneath the fig tree. Peter, however, expressed from his heart so great and such a confession that his confession is the confession of all the apostles. And as all were questioned together, so in him there is the one answer of all, upon which the Church is founded and against which the gates of hell shall not prevail. For whether one says that they do not prevail against this faith, or that they do not prevail against the Church founded and made firm by this faith upon Christ, it is one and the same; because neither is the foundation dissolved, nor is such and so great a faith weakened, nor shall the Church be overthrown amid innumerable storms of winds and blasts, CXX, 557–561.

“The gates of hell shall not prevail against it,” or, as some manuscripts have, “shall not prevail over it.” It is rightly asked: over whom? Or against what? Shall they not prevail against the rock upon which God’s Church is built, or against the Church which Christ builds upon the rock? Although this is not expressed openly, it must nevertheless be believed without doubt: for they shall prevail neither against the rock upon which the Church is built, nor against the Church built upon such a rock. Otherwise, anyone against whom the gates of hell prevail is neither to be called the rock upon which the Church is built by Christ nor the Church built upon the rock, CXX, 557–561.

“And whatever you bind on earth,” etc. Whoever wishes to claim this grace for himself ought to hold Peter’s weakness in the rock, and preach the faith in conduct and speech; then he ought, as a heavenly doorkeeper, to guard the keys of the kingdom which he possesses—keys received not from himself, but from the Lord and through the Lord. Otherwise, unless his judgments remain firm in Christ, as though God were judging through him, he must fear lest the gates of hell prevail against him who binds or looses, if he judges unjustly and not according to God’s word. But he against whom the gates of hell have not prevailed judges justly, because he bears with him the keys already received from the Lord. Therefore he opens to those who have been loosed upon earth, so that they may be loosed and free in heaven. And he shuts against those who have been bound on earth by his just judgment, so that they may be bound, as it were, in heaven and judged, CXX, 563.

PAUL THE DEACON.—“You are Peter,” etc. It should not be believed that Peter first received this name now, but rather when, at the beginning of the Lord’s preaching, he was brought to Jesus by Andrew and heard from him, as a great foretoken of his faith: “You are Simon, son of John; you shall be called Cephas,” which is translated Peter. Therefore the Lord now addressed him by this name, saying, “You are Peter”; for he did not say, “You shall be called Peter,” but “You are Peter,” which had been said before.

For just as Christ gave the apostles names, so that they might be called the light or salt of the earth, so he gave this outstanding confessor of his—formerly called Simon, that is, “obedient”—the name Peter because of the strength of his unconquered faith. Peter, that is, clung with steadfast mind to him of whom it is written: “And the rock was Christ.” He is a rock not by essence but by signification; just as he is called a lion because of strength or a lamb because of innocence, so he is called a rock because of firmness—the one who is a tower of strength from the face of the enemy to those who work in him.

“And upon this rock,” that is, upon me whom you confessed with your mouth, saying, “You are Christ, the Son of the living God.” For he is the precious stone placed in the foundation of the Church, of whom Paul says: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, Christ Jesus.” Or, “upon this rock,” that is, [Col. 0126] upon this faith by which he confessed me to be the Son of the living God, I shall build my Church. “And the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.” He did not say this of the temporal condition of death, by which we read that nearly all the apostles were brought to completion by martyrdom; rather, he calls vices and sins the gates of hell. The gates of hell are the deadly doctrines of heretics, by which they entice the unwary and draw them to the condemnation of everlasting death, XCV, 1481, 1482.

“Whatever you bind on earth,” etc. Although this power of loosing and binding appears to have been granted by the Lord to Peter alone, it was also granted generally to all the apostles under his person. For after the noble triumph of his resurrection, appearing openly to them all, he said: “Whose sins you forgive,” etc. For just as Peter answers on behalf of all when all are questioned collectively, so the Lord’s answer to Peter was an answer in Peter to all. Indeed, the same office is entrusted to all bishops and presbyters in the Church: once the cases of sinners have been examined, they are to exercise the power of binding and loosing according to the measure of sins or penance—provided only that, as is found even in certain priests in this age, they neither condemn those who are innocent or harmless nor, as though presuming absolution, render secure those who deserve condemnation, XCV, 1184, 1185.

“You are Peter; upon this rock,” he says, that is, upon the Lord and Saviour, who gave to his faithful confessor a share in his own name: “The gates of hell shall not prevail,” etc. The gates of hell are the torments and blandishments of persecutors, which by deterring some from the firmness of faith open the entrance of eternal death. Thus there are many gates of hell, but none of these prevails against the Church founded upon the rock. He is therefore deservedly to be honoured by all Churches who, following the head of the Church and the firmness of the most steadfast rock, confounded Christ’s enemies through the authority of the Holy Spirit and triumphed by the strength of untiring patience. No gate of hell prevailed against him who, by confessing the King of glory, opened for himself the gate of eternal entrance, XCV, 1463, 1464.

PETER (St), apostle and first pope.—Blessed Peter the Apostle, prince of the apostles and first pope, first sat in the episcopal chair at Antioch for seven years. Then, entering Rome to oppose Simon Magus, in the second year of Claudius, he sat in the episcopal chair for twenty-five years, two months, and three days. At one and the same time and on one and the same day—namely, in the thirty-eighth year after the Lord’s Passion, and in the final year of Nero, on the third day before the Kalends of July [29 June]—he completed martyrdom with Paul.

He wrote two Epistles, called canonical. In the first, he first instructs the Church generally, explaining the benefits by which divine mercy deigned to call us to salvation and the gifts by which it once deigned to honour the Jews but now honours us. Afterwards he diligently exhorts the various classes of the faithful not, by living carnally, to make themselves unworthy of so great a grace of the Spirit; and not, though distinguished by the title of royal and priestly, to degenerate from the glory of the nobility bestowed or promised to them by becoming subject to the wickedness of vices. He addresses first free persons and slaves, then women and men specifically; and after a section of general exhortation, he also shows how elders and younger persons ought to conduct themselves.

In the second Epistle, written to the same persons as the first, he has compassion on them and repeatedly admonishes and exhorts them, now as more perfect persons, to greater and more perfect things. He is also said to have produced Mark’s Gospel, because Mark was his assistant and his son through baptism. He ordained three bishops—Linus, Cletus, and Clement—ten presbyters, and seven deacons. [lacuna]

Although Clement is found third after blessed Peter in the order of the catalogue, in truth, as he himself wrote in his Epistle to James, bishop of Jerusalem, he doubtless held the helm of the Roman see first after blessed Peter, with no one intervening. Linus and Cletus are counted as Peter’s successors because Peter himself made them his assistants during his lifetime, so that he might more freely devote himself to prayer, CXXIX, 1151, 1152.

PETER LOMBARD.—From the passage of Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians: “I said to Cephas before them all,” etc. Porphyry objects that Peter was rebuked by Paul, seeking both to stain the former with the blot of error and to charge the latter with insolence, and to accuse both jointly of the falsehood of a feigned doctrine, since the leaders of the Churches disagreed among themselves. He does this because he does not understand in what sense Peter was blameworthy, or in what sense the Apostle Paul is said to have resisted him to his face.

For both rightly held that the Law need not be observed, and that in every nation whoever fears God and works righteousness is acceptable to him. But both administer a cautious dissimulation: [Col. 0127] Peter, by withdrawal; Paul, by rebuke, so that pride might be taken from the Jews and despair from the Gentiles. Thus Peter was not truly blameworthy either to Paul or to those from whom he afterwards separated himself after previously eating with them; nor did Paul insolently resist him. For Paul could not rebuke in Peter what he himself had done, nor accuse a dissimulation of which he too was guilty. This rebuke, therefore, was not genuine but administrative; Peter did not sin, nor did Paul rebuke insolently.

But Peter, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles, was the author of the decree that the Law should not be observed after the Gospel. After the vision of the sheet, on which were animals of various kinds, he entered Cornelius’s house and ate with Gentiles. He also settled the question in this matter, as appears in Acts 15. Peter therefore held correctly concerning release from the Law, but he dissembled out of fear of the Jews, lest they should withdraw from the faith on account of the Gentiles and he should thus lose his flock. Paul likewise dissembled through a similar fear, as in Timothy’s circumcision; and he who had grown [his hair] by a vow, as a Nazirite, cut his head [i.e. his hair] at Cenchreae according to the Law, CXCII, 110, 111.

RADBERTUS (St), abbot of Corbie.—“And I say to you,” etc.: Peter is a name derived from *petra*, “rock,” that is, from me, upon whom the whole Church is built. For Peter is not, as some wrongly think, the foundation of the entire Church, “because no one can lay another foundation than that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus.” Although Peter may rightly be believed to be placed first upon that same foundation, as though its head, nevertheless the whole heavenly Jerusalem—that is, [the Church]—is built and made firm upon that rock from which Peter drew his name as a gift, namely upon Christ, so that the pattern may endure forever.

Nor is it surprising that Peter was called from the rock, because through the Holy Spirit he was to be firm in the firmness of faith, since he too is called the light of the world from the light which is Christ. [lacuna] Thus Peter was not yet blessed in himself, but only in God’s predestination; for the Lord loved him not as he then was but as he was to become. [lacuna] Bishops, to whom the Lord has given the same power as Peter of forgiving sins, etc., ought to hold their own weakness in Peter and recognize him as their head, CXX, 562, 563.

RUPERT OF DEUTZ, abbot.—Moreover, concerning Peter’s fall and his being permitted to deny, this too is devout and fitting within the dispensation of the Spirit of wisdom. For Peter had been destined to be prince of the apostles, and to him especially great power after Christ was to be given, or had already been given, when Christ, the Son of the living God whom he had confessed, said: “Blessed are you,” etc.; “Feed,” etc. Preceded by such great and weighty authority of evangelical truth, the most Christian emperors, after a long time, and all the princes of the Churches, determined this and confirmed it by a perpetual law: that, just as all prefects or judges are subject to the emperor, so the other bishops of the Churches should be subject to blessed Peter and, according to the excellence of his rank, to the Roman pontiff.

A great honor, a lofty elevation; but the very author of that honor or elevation says: “He who is greater among you shall be as the lesser, and he who goes before as one who serves.” Likewise, by great zeal he instructs those greater ones, or ministers, toward mercy, a lesson which he plainly draws from Peter’s most humble deeds. For when or how could a man placed in the height of honor know, amid a great consciousness of holiness, to stoop to the lowly and to suffer with the wretched? God alone is humble, merciful, and compassionate by nature; indeed, he is humility itself and mercy itself. A human being, however, is humble or merciful only accidentally. Therefore there had to be in the apostle Peter, predestined and called to such an elevation, a cause which should precede the greatness of his honor and from which the knowledge of humility and compassion might continually arise for him.

For this reason he was permitted to fall; for this reason he was abandoned even to a threefold denial—by a beautiful and conspicuous ordering of wisdom—so that we, all of us who are skilled spectators of that same wisdom and have the eyes of discernment opened, may rightly wonder. And observing this, we believe it altogether expedient for those who preside, both for their own sakes and for the sake of those over whom they preside, that they be taught humility or compassion through the great and memorable experience of past weakness. Otherwise, they scarcely, or in no way, know how to bear the weaknesses of their subjects. CLXVII, 1638–1639.

On this subject, the author of the *Historical and Chronological Dissertation on the Works of Rupert* expresses himself as follows:

> “Rupert explains that, although all the apostles received in common the power to bind and loose sinners, Saint Peter nevertheless received a particular privilege because he was the first to confess the divinity of Jesus Christ. This particular privilege granted to Saint Peter consists in the fact that Saint Peter [Col. 0128] was destined to be prince of the apostles: *Princeps quippe apostolorum destinatus fuerat*—‘For he had been destined prince of the apostles.’ He was specially to receive, or had already received, a great power which Jesus Christ gave him when he said: ‘You are blessed, Simon, son of Jona . . . and I say to you,’ etc. Rupert also reports what Jesus Christ said after his resurrection to the same apostle: ‘Simon, do you love me more than these? Feed my lambs; feed my sheep.’
>
> “He then continues: ‘The Christian emperors and the princes of the Church, founded upon the authority of this evangelical truth—*tali et tanta prae eunte evangelicae veritatis auctoritate*—long afterward established by an unchangeable law that, just as all governors and judges obey the emperor, so all the prelates of the other churches should be subject to Peter and to the Roman Pontiff, because of the excellence of his dignity. This is a great honor and a great elevation: *Magnus honor, magna celsitudo*.’
>
> “Cyprians, Basils, and the other Fathers, especially in the first centuries of the Church, did not hold such an idea of Saint Peter’s particular privilege; nor did even the holiest Popes, such as Saint Gregory the Great, hold it. . . . To this observation it may be answered that humility caused the Popes to be silent concerning their right; but, in the end, all of them, Popes or bishops alike, nevertheless recognized supremacy in the person of Saint Peter’s successors.
>
> “And, to draw from this some practical conclusion: let us recognize Saint Peter’s real prerogatives, which passed to his successors; let us recognize his primacy by divine right; but let us beware of degrading his colleagues and brothers in the episcopate. Let us beware of believing that they owe him the same submission and obedience that governments and judges owe to superiors and kings. Rupert seems to soften somewhat what he had advanced by adding that he who conferred so high a dignity upon Saint Peter gave him this warning: ‘Let him who is greatest among you become as the least, and he who rules as one who serves.’
>
> “There, as may be seen, Rupert’s purpose is to show that God permitted Saint Peter’s enormous fall only in order to keep him humble in the high degree of elevation to which he intended to raise him, and in order to give, in his person, to all who are raised above others a striking example teaching them to be humble and to bear kindly and compassionately the weaknesses of those under their care.” CLXVII, *passim*.

TERTULLIAN, presbyter of Carthage.—If you still think heaven closed, remember that the Lord here left its keys to Peter, and through him to the Church—keys which each person, once questioned and having confessed, will bear with him. II, 142. “The whole key of paradise is your blood, O martyr.” II, 745.

In him, that is, in Peter, the Church was built—that is, through him; he received the key. He was the first to open, in Christ’s baptism, the entrance to the heavenly kingdom, whereby former sins that are bound are loosed, and those that have not been loosed according to true salvation are bound. He bound Ananias with the bond of death and freed the lame man from the defect of bodily infirmity. Likewise, in that controversy concerning whether the Law was to be kept or not, Peter, first of all, inspired by the Spirit and having spoken beforehand concerning the calling of the nations, Acts 15:10–11, then by his judgment loosed what had been omitted from the Law and bound what had been retained. II, 1025–1026.

Something was unknown to Peter—he who was called the rock for the building of the Church, who had received the keys of the kingdom of heaven and the power of loosing and binding in heaven and on earth. II, 34.

The rebuke Peter underwent from Paul does not detract from the privileges of Peter mentioned above: after having lived with Gentiles, he afterward separated himself from their company out of regard for persons. II, 35–36. For in this rebuke the sole question concerned the ancient Law, in showing what of it ought to be observed. This came about on Peter’s part through a certain inconsistency, through the character of persons, through an ambiguous manner of conduct only, and not through any perversion concerning divinity. II, 474.

The apostolic Churches transmit their registers of succession; the Church of Rome declares that Clement was ordained by Peter. II, 44–45.

Peter is struck; then he is girded by another when he is bound to the cross. II, 151. Peter is made equal to the Lord’s Passion. II, 49.

You are commanded to forgive seventy times seven in the person of Peter. Thus, if it is established that even the blessed apostles forgave something whose pardon belonged to God, not to man, they did so not by discipline but by power. For they raised the dead—which God alone does—and restored the infirm—which no one but Christ does. Indeed, they also inflicted plagues, which Christ was unwilling to do; for it did not befit him who had come to suffer to rage. Ananias was struck with death . . . so that by this very fact it might be proved that Christ also could have done these things. Tertullian, II, 1024.

ZACHARIAS CHRYSOPOLITANUS, bishop.—“And Jesus answered and said: Blessed are you, Simon Barjona,” etc. (St. Jerome.) In Peter he answers all, granting the reward of true confession, as though saying: “What flesh and blood could not reveal, the grace of the Holy Spirit has revealed.” Therefore from his confession he receives his name, because *Barjona* means “son of the dove.” Others say that Simon, that is Peter, was the son of John, as in: “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” They maintain that this has been corrupted through scribal error, so that *Barjona* has been written for *Barjoanna*, that is, “son of John,” with one syllable removed. *Joanna* is interpreted “the grace of the Lord.” Both names are understood mystically, because the dove signifies the Holy Spirit and the Lord’s grace signifies the spiritual gift. For the Father revealed to the son of the dove, because the grace of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one. *Barjona* is Syriac and Hebrew.

“You are Peter,” etc. (St. Jerome.) You have said that I am the Son of the living God, and I, whose speaking is doing, say to you that, etc. The prince of the apostles is now called Peter, now Cephas—not in a different sense, but because what we call *petra*, “rock,” in Latin and Greek, the Hebrews and Syrians call *Cephas*. Peter rightly receives this name because he believed in Christ the Rock; and according to the metaphor of the rock it is said to him: “I will build my Church upon this rock,” [Col. 0130] that is, upon this foundation of faith; or thus, upon this rock which you have confessed, that is, upon myself. The apostle says of this: “No one can lay another foundation,” etc.

“And the gates of hell,” etc. Sins and the teachings of heretics are the gates of hell. By “the keys of the kingdom of heaven” he means the very knowledge and power of discernment by which Peter ought to admit the worthy into the kingdom and exclude the unworthy from it. “Whatever you bind,” etc. . . . The sense is: whomever you bind upon earth—that is, while he is living—by expelling him from the Church, shall be bound in heaven; that is, all Churches to which this becomes known will avoid him. Or he shall be bound in heaven, that is, the heavenly judgment will confirm that the present Church avoids him. And whomever, while he is living, you loose from excommunication by reconciling him, shall be loosed in heaven; that is, the Churches which communicate this knowledge to him will receive him. Or he shall be loosed in heaven, that is, the heavenly judgment will confirm that he is to be received by the present Church.

A great honor, but a heavy burden. . . . Therefore Peter receives specially the keys of the kingdom of heaven and the primacy of judicial power, so that all believers may understand that whoever separates themselves from the unity of faith and fellowship with him can neither be loosed from the bonds of sins nor enter the gate of the kingdom of heaven. . . . This takes place through episcopal ministry in the ordination of presbyters, or—what seems truer—when the care of souls is entrusted to presbyters. CLXXXVI, 285–287.

## Part Two

[Col. 0129]

## First Article.—Concepts concerning the temporal power of the pontiff

The emperor Constantine, as is known, was wholly intent on offering offerings to God, so that they might be assigned by right of patrimony to the holy Roman Church and to its bishop, Peter’s successor, as things sacred to God, to be retained and administered under the complete power of the supreme pontificate through Silvester and his legitimate successors. Newly baptized, after he had most lavishly enriched the Church with gifts, he devoutly supplied the necessary expenses for the Roman council convoked by the holy pontiff Silvester.

And judging it unworthy that the city of Rome, in which the monarch of the whole Church and Christ’s vicar on earth resided, should be subject to the rule of a secular prince, he most lavishly granted to Silvester and to his legitimate successors in Peter’s Chair temporal dominion and jurisdiction not only over the city of Rome but over nearly all Italy and other provinces as well. VIII, 795.

Rome! Rome! It has rightly been called the head of the world, mistress and queen of cities. It is reported of this emperor that, while gazing with admiration upon the Campus Martius, the tomb of Caesar Augustus, the Roman Forum, the shrines of Jupiter on the Tarpeian Rock, the baths, porticoes, amphitheater, Pompey’s theater, the Circus Maximus, and so forth, he was astonished and finally said: “Nature has poured all her powers into one city.” Most truly, even now it may be said of Rome: “Just as nothing in the whole order of nature is better or more excellent than the world, so on earth nothing better or more excellent than Rome can be found.” VIII, 827.

The magical splendor of Rome is no less today than of old:

> “It was 8 December 1854. The Eternal City was entirely astir; from early morning people hurried from every quarter toward the gigantic Square of Saint Peter. Soon the great basilica of Saint Peter was filled with people. Such a gathering was unheard of. There was a crowd in that immense church; for Saint Peter’s is immensity in length, breadth, depth, and height. When one enters it, the eye is lost in that expanse, and the farther one advances, the more space seems, in a manner of speaking, to withdraw before one. When there are only 30,000 people in Saint Peter’s, one is quite at ease in the great nave, and there is no one in the lateral chapels. Yet on that day there was a crowd, and the feeling of gratitude toward God prevailed everywhere.
>
> “But the sacred ceremonies were being prepared. The Pope-King, Pius IX, intones the office in a strong and majestic voice; he begins Mass, and after the Gospel, after the singing of the *Veni Creator*, rising upon his throne, he reads, despite the liveliest emotion, the decree declaring the Immaculate Conception of the Blessed Virgin a dogma of faith, worded as follows:
>
> ‘We declare, pronounce, and define that the doctrine which holds that the most blessed Virgin Mary, in the first instant [Col. 0130] of her conception, by a singular grace and privilege of almighty God, in view of the merits of Christ Jesus, Savior of the human race, was preserved free from every stain of original sin, is revealed by God and therefore must be believed firmly and constantly by all the faithful.’
>
> “At that moment the cannon of the Castle of Saint Angelo is heard, all the bells of Rome’s 365 churches begin to ring, and so forth. . . . Oh, it was beautiful to be in Rome that day.”

This triumph of the spiritual papacy, from which the temporal papacy is nevertheless not excluded, may be set alongside the triumph of the temporal papacy of Boniface VIII. This spiritual triumph is fully equal to the triumph of man—the triumph in which the latter appeared during the great Jubilee of 1300 with the double insignia of spiritual and temporal authority, repeating aloud: “Behold the two swords; here, O Peter, you see your successor; you, saving Christ, behold your vicar.”

To these two spectacles Europe has hastened to Rome. “And today, now 8 June 1862, on the holy day of Pentecost,” it may be said that a third universal spectacle of Christendom was displayed at Rome. A religious journal, the *Rosier de Marie*, dated yesterday, 7 June, tells us:

> “To find in Rome a number of bishops greater than that of this day—during the last eight days more had still been arriving daily—we must go back to the Fourth Lateran Council under the pontificate of Innocent III. At no time has the Mediterranean been crossed by vessels carrying more than 200 ecclesiastics, as was a steamer arriving from Marseilles last week. Revolutions may indeed continue on their course, but God knows how, in their midst, to make his Church stronger and more powerful. The papacy is violently attacked, yet it always resists and becomes more and more unshakable. It is useless, let us confidently say, to fight it; God’s work cannot be conquered or destroyed.”

What will happen in the future, and now with regard to the Pope’s temporal dominion, is unknown. God knows; for the present, let us only recount the past. God will provide for the future. Amen.

AMBROSE, Saint, bishop.—In his sermon against Auxentius, XVI, 1012, he showed himself high-spirited in refusing to surrender the basilicas.

“You, Lord Jesus,” he says, “redeemed the world in one moment; Auxentius in one moment will, insofar as lies in him, slaughter so many peoples—some by the sword, others by sacrilege. He demands my basilica with a bloody mouth and bloodstained hands. To him the reading just heard rightly replies: ‘But God said to the sinner: Why do you recount my ordinances?’ That is, peace and fury do not agree; Christ and Belial do not agree. For you remember what was read today: Naboth, that holy man who possessed his vineyard, was approached by a royal request that he should give up his vineyard, where the king, after cutting down the vines, might plant worthless vegetables; and Naboth answered: ‘Far be it from me that I should surrender the inheritance of my fathers!’ [Col. 0131] The king was grieved because a right that was not his had been denied him by a just answer, but he was deceived by a woman’s counsel. Naboth defended his vines even with his own blood. If he did not surrender his vineyard, shall we surrender the Church of Christ?

“What answer, then, was given by me with contumacy? For the assembly said: ‘Far be it from me that I should surrender Christ’s inheritance!’ If he did not surrender the inheritance of his fathers, shall I surrender Christ’s inheritance? And I added this also: ‘Far be it from me that I should surrender Christ’s inheritance—the inheritance of the fathers: that is, the inheritance of Dionysius, who died while assisting in the cause of faith; the inheritance of Eustorgius the confessor; the inheritance of Myrocles; and the inheritance of all the faithful bishops of former times!’ I answered as becomes a priest: let the priest do what belongs to the priest; let the emperor do what belongs to the emperor. It is sooner possible for him to take my life from me than my faith.

“But to whom should I surrender it? The Gospel reading before us ought to teach us what is being demanded and by whom it is being demanded. You heard read, surely, that when Christ sat upon the colt of an ass, the children cried out and the Jews were annoyed. Finally they appealed to the Lord Jesus, asking him to make them silent; he answered: ‘If these are silent, the stones will cry out.’ Then, entering the temple, he drove out the money-changers and the seats, and those selling doves in God’s temple. . . . Therefore the praises of Christ are always the scourges of the faithless. And now, when Christ is praised, the heretics say that sedition is being stirred up; the heretics say that death is being prepared for these people—and truly they have death in the praises of Christ. For how can they bear his praises when they proclaim his weakness?

“The Gerasenes could not endure Christ’s presence; these men are worse than the Gerasenes, for they cannot even endure Christ’s praise. They see children singing the glory of Christ, and mock this tender age that is full of faith, saying: ‘See what they are shouting!’ But Christ answered them: ‘If these are silent, the stones will cry out.’ That is, the stronger will cry out; the young men will cry out; those of maturer age will cry out; the old men will cry out—these stones now joined to that solid stone of which it is written: ‘The stone rejected by the builders has become the head of the corner.’” XVI, 1012–1013; CLXIII, 678–679.

ANASTASIUS THE LIBRARIAN.—The blessed apostle Peter, prince of the apostles, first held the episcopal chair at Antioch for seven years. This Peter entered the city of Rome under Nero Caesar and there held the episcopal chair for twenty-five years, one month, and eight days. . . . He was crowned with martyrdom with Paul thirty-eight years after the Lord’s Passion. . . .

The older catalogues of Roman pontiffs and the manuscripts of the *Liber Pontificalis* for the most part prefix the title “blessed” to Peter alone; in this they seem to have had regard to the Redeemer’s saying: “Blessed are you, Simon Barjona,” etc. With reference to these words Basil wrote that Saint Peter obtained a blessedness far greater than that of all the rest. For in the New Testament two persons are honored with that title: the Mother of God, who under the divine inspiration of the Spirit said, “From this time all generations will call me blessed,” and Peter, by the voice of the Redeemer. Hence is the true origin of the term “Beatitude” and “Most Blessed,” bestowed upon Roman Pontiffs by Fathers and councils, so that the Roman Pontiff was designated by that title antonomastically.

By divine institution there is one chair, entrusted to Peter alone and transmitted to his successors; Peter does not admit an alien associate. Christ builds his Church upon one, in order to manifest unity; by his authority he established the origin of that same unity as beginning from one. God is one, Christ is one, the Church is one, and the chair is one, founded upon Peter by the Lord’s word. Another altar cannot be erected, nor can a new priest be made apart from the one altar and the one priest. . . .

That Peter sat in this Roman chair until death must be understood of the authority, power, and office of governing all Churches, not of local residence. For it is established that, after he had administered this chair for seven years, when all Christians and Jews were expelled from Rome by Claudius’s edict, Peter too was expelled and returned to Jerusalem. Nevertheless, when Claudius died, he returned to Rome and ended his life there.

The characteristic of the supreme and universal shepherd is that he should be infallible in feeding the whole flock, since no superior has been appointed over him to direct him, except Christ Jesus himself, who says to him, without any capacity for censure or power being exercised over him by another: “Feed my sheep,” etc. CXXVIII, 1004–1044. Paul is here named as Peter’s associate, but only in the partnership of preaching, not in the partnership of the chair—a point to be noted, etc.

It should be observed, with blessed Leo the Great, that Saint Peter’s arrival at Rome was not accidental, but was prepared by the counsel of divine Providence, which sweetly and strongly orders all things. Thus too the magnitude and unity of the Roman Empire, and the treaties concluded by Roman rulers with the remotest regions of the earth, were prepared as though a vehicle for carrying the Gospel [Col. 0132] throughout the whole world.

For the divine ordering was most fitting for the work, so that the general preaching might quickly find open access to peoples whom the government of one city held.
