At the Lord’s birth, according to the prophecies of the prophets, while the world was settled in peace, and during those years of Augustus in which the same Caesar’s decree was published that the whole world should be enrolled, the ordering of provinces under one ruler not only prepared easy access for the appointed heralds of the Gospel, but also began, in the civil arrangement of regions and in the network woven town by town through them, a kind of image of that more sacred ordered government which the Lord Christ, Prince of Peace, was shortly to establish through his apostles and their successors in the hierarchy of the Christian episcopate.

Since the prince of the apostolic company, Simon Peter, chosen by the Lord Christ as the first hierarch of his Church, thoroughly understood this design of divine counsel before Leo the Great, he established principal sees in East and West and added a third in Egypt, from which most extensive regions of the South might receive Christ’s envoys, who would extend the boundaries of his authority as far as India and Ethiopia. Yet, in order that all these might understand that the authority of that chair was preferred, which he, while living and dying, had endowed with the privilege of his succession in the most extensive power—such power as the Redeemer of humankind had conferred upon him above all assemblies of the faithful—he wished to fix it in the city of Rome, the head of the world and long since the seat of empire, spreading through Europe, Asia, and Africa. From there both he and his successors could more readily transmit their laws and embassies into whatever regions of the earth.

Not only peace, the organization of provinces, the census of citizens, and Augustus’s treaties with most distant kings served the design of the divine work, but wars also and victories, journeys, divisions of provinces, military expeditions, the establishment of colonies, the transfer of legions, the allotment of governors, and nearly all the acts of the republic and subsequent Caesars. Whether Gaius, Caligula, and Claudius moved into Britain; Nero into Armenia; Vespasian into Judaea; Trajan into Dacia, Parthia, and Mesopotamia; Hadrian restored to the barbarians what Trajan had taken; he himself, and Antoninus after his example, surveyed the provinces and made the whole empire passable by frequent journeys; he strengthened it by Roman legions; he joined seas and islands to the mainland by fleets equipped in Italy, on the Upper and Lower Seas, at Ravenna and Misenum; or he secured the borders of the empire by stationed armies—British, Cappadocian, Dacian, Germanic, Spanish, Illyrian, Mauritanian, Moesian, Raetian, Sarmatian, and Syrian—depicted on Hadrian’s coins: all these were equipment, escort, and assistance for conveying the Gospel. They were not prepared by the vain plan of human beings, who granted such things for the temporary life of this world, but were ordered and administered by the will and power of divine wisdom for Christ’s glory and the salvation of the elect. He commands every creature to be at hand and serve that end, even without thinking of it, even while kicking against the goad.

For how much facility was afforded to apostolic missions sent from the City by the supreme hierarch of the Church into every distant region through the frequent transfer of legions and the almost daily departure of greater and lesser magistrates to govern provinces and forces! Hence, while the prince of the apostles had not yet, or scarcely, been crowned with martyrdom, Trier, Lyons, Vienne, Mainz, and so forth received bishops sent from Rome: Pothinus, Telesphorus, Severus, Crescens, and so forth. CXXVIII, 1256–1257.

The holy and universal eighth synod, celebrated at Constantinople, holds concerning the Lord’s saying which Christ spoke to his holy apostles and disciples—“He who receives you receives me, and he who despises you despises me”—that it was said also to all those who after them became supreme pontiffs in the Catholic Church. We define that absolutely none of the powerful persons of the world may dishonor, or attempt to remove from his own throne, any one of those who preside over patriarchal sees, but that they are to be judged worthy of all reverence and honor—especially the most holy Pope of elder Rome, and next the patriarch of Constantinople. . . . Nor may anyone compose or circulate writings against the most holy Pope of elder Rome under the pretext of certain allegedly defamatory charges. If anyone enjoying or wielding any secular power attempts to expel the aforesaid Pope of the Apostolic See, let him be anathema. . . . Moreover, if an ecumenical synod has been convened and any ambiguity or controversy has arisen concerning the holy Roman Church [Col. 0133], the proposed question must be investigated reverently and with fitting respect, and an answer received or progress made; yet no one may rashly pronounce judgment against the supreme pontiffs of elder Rome. CXXIX, 159–160.

The medical art has produced many physicians for wounds and bruises found in the limbs of a human being, one taking on this affliction and another that, cutting away and healing by experience. But for the afflictions in the members of Christ and God the Savior—who is the head of us all—and of his bride, the Catholic and Apostolic Church, the supreme prince, the mighty Word, the organizer and healer, God, the sole teacher in every respect, has produced one singular, eminent, and most catholic physician: namely, the Pope of elder Rome. For this reason he said to Peter, the great and supreme apostle: “You are Peter,” etc.; “I give to you the keys,” etc. . . .

For he did not restrict and define such blessed words merely for the prince of the apostles according to some particular lot, but through him transmitted them to all who after him were to become supreme shepherds and most divine and sacred pontiffs of elder Rome. Therefore, from ancient times and from the beginning, during the rise of heresies and transgressions, many who preceded there in the holiness and supreme fatherhood of the supreme pontiffs have repeatedly become uprooters and destroyers of evil tares and of diseased members that were corrupting and utterly incurable. CXXIX, 60–61.

Stephen VI succeeded Formosus. Boniface, who seized the Apostolic See and held it for fifteen days, is not to be counted among the pontiffs, since, as a wicked man, he had already twice been deposed from rank—first from the diaconate and then from the priesthood—and condemned at a Roman synod under Pope John IX. Although both obtained the see by force, fear, and tyranny, so that one intruder likewise expelled another intruder, Stephen is nevertheless counted in the number and succession of pontiffs by common consent, because, to avert the danger of schism, the whole clergy approved him, wicked man though he was, and the whole Catholic Church acknowledged him as Christ’s vicar and Peter’s successor.

He began his pontificate with that sacrilege by which he had the body of Pope Formosus exhumed, clothed in priestly vestments, mutilated by cutting off three fingers, and thrown into the Tiber; and he commanded that all whom Formosus had ordained should be consecrated and ordained again. The deed of the sacrilegious pontiff—by which he unjustly exacted punishment from a dead man and repeated orders lawfully conferred, against Christ’s institution and God’s command—is rightly refuted and detested by the innovating heretics of our own age. But they wrongly rise up against Christ’s promises to Peter and to the Church on account of that impious deed, and boast far too prematurely of victory and celebrate a triumph.

For everything Stephen said or did against Formosus was done by a man driven by fury, carrying out what seething rage had suggested. Yet, by papal authority lawfully exercised, he defined nothing contrary to faith or good morals. Therefore, in this matter we acknowledge violent tyranny in the act itself; but we steadfastly deny that an error in faith was defined or approved by Stephen while lawfully exercising pontifical authority. This would in no way prejudice the Apostolic See even if we granted that an invader, not legitimately elected but an intruded pseudo-pontiff, had erred in asserting articles of faith. CXXIX, 855–856.

In the year nine hundred and four after the Lord’s birth, Pope Formosus sent letters to England by which he pronounced excommunication and a curse upon King Edward and all his subjects. . . . King Edward reformed himself and appeased the Pope with great humility; this greatly pleased the Apostolic See, and it restored him to the bosom of the Church. CXXIX, 845–846.

POPE ANASTASIUS.—Do not receive the Manichaeans whom we have found in the city of Rome, nor their followers; do not communicate with them or have any fellowship with them before they are converted to the right faith. Let not their perniciously sprouting seeds, which we extinguish in our city, be sown or germinate among you with most evil roots. Our investigation found very many of them and adherents of their impiety, as well as their teachers; our vigilance exposed them, and our authority and discipline restrained them. We corrected those whom we were able to reform.

We compelled them publicly in the Church, by profession and by the subscription of their own hand, to condemn Mani with his preaching and teachings; and thus, when they had confessed, we relieved them from the abyss of their impiety by granting penance. But some had sunk themselves so deeply that no remedy of aid could avail them. Subjected to the laws according to the ordinances of Christian rulers, lest they should pollute the holy flock with their contagion, they were banished into perpetual exile [Col. 0134] by public judges. And all the profane or shameful things which they possess both in their writings and in their secret traditions we displayed by a definite disclosure before the eyes of the Christian people, so that the people might know what to flee or avoid—to such an extent that the man called their bishop, whom we held in custody, revealed the shameful practices he maintained in their mysteries, as the sequence of the official acts will be able to teach you. CXXX, 691–692.

ANSELM OF LUCCA, bishop.—In the letter which Bishop Anselm wrote to Wibert, the antipope called Clement III, in which he calls him a transgressor and a proud man, he adds among other things:

> “Therefore, to speak of blessed Gregory our father”—this is Gregory VII—“what blessed Cyprian wrote of Cornelius: he was made bishop by the judgment of God and his Christ, by the testimony of nearly all the clergy—or rather, to speak more truly, of absolutely all of them—by the vote of the people, who then hated him, and by the assembly of ancient priests and good men; when no one had been made bishop before him; when Alexander’s place, that is, the place of Peter and the rank of the sacerdotal chair, was vacant. Once that place has been occupied and its holder ordained by God’s will and by the consent of us all, whoever wishes thereafter to become bishop must necessarily be outside; he does not possess ecclesiastical ordination who does not maintain the unity of the Church. Whoever he may be, though boasting greatly of himself and claiming very much for himself, he is profane, he is alien, he is outside. Since after the first there cannot be a second, whoever has been made after him who alone ought to exist is no longer a second, but is nothing.”

Thus speaks Saint Anselm, bishop of Lucca, a man most thoroughly learned in letters, of most acute intellect, outstanding eloquence, and—what surpasses all else—most renowned for fear of God and holy conduct; so much so that both in life and after death he is reported to have been illustrious for miracles. From Ekkehard of Uraugiens. CLIV, 952.

It is clear, after reviewing the authorities of the holy Fathers, Latin as well as Greek, that they attributed no right whatsoever to imperial power in the election or promotion of pontiffs; indeed, some of them prohibited under anathema any lay power from claiming anything for itself in these matters. CXLIX, 462.

There are those who maintain that Gregory and Ambrose were promoted to the pontificate by secular rulers; this is false. For thus their election or promotion is described, or recorded, in their Acts:

“Although Gregory resisted with all his strength, the clergy, senate, and Roman people unanimously chose him as their pontiff. But when he could not escape the general decree, he at last pretended that he would consent, and secretly sent letters to the Emperor Maurice, whose son he had received from the holy font, entreating him never to grant the people an opportunity of raising him to the glory of this honour. But Germanus, prefect of the city, intercepted his messenger and, after opening the letters, sent to the emperor the consent which the people had made.” (From the *Acts of Gregory*), CXLIX, 463.

Likewise, in the *Acts of Ambrose*, LXXV, 381, 382:

“When the people shouted ever more loudly, ‘Your sin be upon us,’ and when he saw that his purpose could achieve nothing, he prepared to flee. Leaving the city in the middle of the night, he thought that he was making for Ticinum; but in the morning he was found at the gate of the city of Milan called the Roman Gate. When he had been found and was kept under guard, a report having been sent by the people to the Emperor Valentinian, the emperor received it with the greatest joy: that judges sent to him should be sought for the priesthood.” CXLIX, 463.

Very many matters of this kind confirm that imperial power did not directly intervene in the election or promotion of the supreme pontiffs, CXLIX, 446–466.

As to the number of years during which this damnable custom is said to have endured—namely, that secular power promoted pontiffs at will—no argument can rightly be made from it. For among differing customs, that is especially to be followed which, from its origin, had as its authors Catholic Fathers following in the footsteps of their earlier Fathers; just as the Fathers of the Seventh and Eighth Synods followed the decrees of the holy Fathers, the Roman pontiffs, and that custom observed in all churches from apostolic times. But that perversion introduced by secular rulers does not prejudice that holy custom, however long a course of time it may have prevailed, CXLIX, 466–476.

BENEDICT, deacon.—In his collection of capitularies one reads:

“Secular princes sometimes hold the heights of power within the Church, in order that by that same power they may safeguard ecclesiastical discipline. Otherwise, powers within the Church would not be necessary, except so that what the priest cannot accomplish by the word of doctrine, power may command through the terror of discipline. Often through the earthly kingdom the heavenly kingdom advances, so that [Col. 0135] those placed within the Church who act against the faith and discipline of the Church may be crushed by the severity of princes; and so that princely power may impose upon the necks of the proud that discipline which the Church’s own advantage is unable to enforce.” XCVII, 869.

“On the property of the Church.” Since, according to the tradition of the holy Fathers, we know that the property of the Church consists in the vows of the faithful, the payments of sinners, and the patrimony of the poor—and since we desire not only to preserve what it possesses, but, with God’s help, to contribute much to it—we have nevertheless decreed, in order wholly to remove the long-entertained suspicion that the property of that Church would not be divided, that neither in our time nor in the time of our sons and, by God’s dispensation, our successors—whoever may wish to imitate our will or the example of our forebears—shall it suffer any division or loss whatsoever, XCVII, 321 and 873.

“We know that the property of the Church is consecrated to God; we know that it consists in the offerings of the faithful and the payments of sinners. Therefore, if anyone transfers it away from the churches to which it was contributed by the faithful and consecrated to God, he unquestionably commits sacrilege; for blind indeed is he who does not see this. Whoever, therefore, among us conveys his own property to the Church, offers and dedicates it to the Lord God and to His saints, and not to another, saying and doing such things as these. For he draws up a document concerning the property which he desires to give to God, and holds that document in his hand before or upon the altar, saying to the priests and guardians of that place:

‘For the remission of my sins and those of my parents and children, etc., I offer to God and dedicate all the property entered in this little charter, that from it God may be served in sacrifices, the solemnities of Masses, prayers, lights, almsgiving to the poor and clergy, and the other divine services and needs of that Church. But if anyone should take it away from there—which I by no means believe will happen—let him render the strictest account to the Lord God, to whom I offer and dedicate it, under the penalty of sacrilege.’

He also sets down other imprecations in it. What does one who afterward removes this property from there do except commit sacrilege? If, then, it is theft to seize anything from a friend, it is unquestionably sacrilege to defraud or take away the Church’s property. Hence it is also laid down in the sacred canons framed by the Spirit of God:

‘If anyone wishes, apart from the knowledge of the bishop or of him to whom such duties have been entrusted, to receive or give the offerings of the Church outside the Church, and is unwilling to act with his counsel, let him be anathema.’

Far be it from us to become sacrilegious or anathema through desire for, or seizure of, ecclesiastical property, or ever to be entangled in such snares. For we know that persons under anathema or guilty of sacrilege are not only infamous and excluded from the communion of the faithful, until they amend these matters by public satisfaction to the Church, reconciliation with the bishops, and the laying on of hands; we do not doubt that, if they persist in such conduct, they become excluded from the kingdom of God as well.

Therefore, that every suspicion may be utterly removed from us before all priests and all the faithful of Christ and of the holy Church of God, we all profess—holding straws in our right hands and casting them from our own hands before God and His angels, before you, and before all the priests and peoples standing around—that we will neither do such things nor consent to those wishing to do them, but will rather, with God’s help, resist them.

We also wish it to be known to you and to all faithful members of the holy Church, and to our own people, that with those who, without the will, consent, or grant of the ruler of the church to which the property rightfully belongs, and especially without that of its own bishop, presume to ask kings for, retain, take away, seize, or ravage Church property, we ought never knowingly or willingly to go against an enemy, go to battle, take food, go to church or palace, travel upon the road, let our men associate with their men, let our horses or other livestock pasture with theirs, dwell or remain together with them, or have any participation with them whatsoever—except for the purpose of correction—before public amendment and satisfaction to the Church; lest, because of their iniquities and crimes, we and ours perish together with them, which God forbid. For we know that the righteous person perishes because of the impious. Therefore, if you wish to regard us as faithful, separate such persons from us, reduce them to confinement under public penance, and grant the requests made.” XCVII, 789, 790.

BERNARD (St.), abbot.—In his letter to Conrad, King of the Romans, he says:

“Nothing sweeter, nothing more friendly, nor indeed anything more closely united, could kingship and priesthood be joined or planted together than in the person of the Lord, in whom both met alike; for according to the flesh He was made for us, from both tribes, both High Priest and King. Nor did He merely unite them: He also blended and allied them in His body, which is the Christian people, He Himself being its head; [Col. 0136] so that this race of men is called by the apostolic voice ‘a chosen race, a royal priesthood’ [1 Peter 2:9]. In another Scripture all who are predestined to life are named alike kings and priests [Revelation 1:6; 5:10]. Therefore let not man separate what God has joined; rather, let human will strive to fulfil what divine authority has ordained. Let those joined in institutions be joined in heart. Let them cherish one another, defend one another, and bear one another’s burdens. The Wise Man says: ‘A brother helping a brother: both shall be comforted’ [Proverbs 18:19].” [lacuna]

On this passage Suger says:

“Since the glory of Christ’s body, that is, the Church of God, consists in the indissoluble unity of kingship and priesthood, it is certainly clear that he who provides for the one assists the other; for all discerning persons evidently recognize both that the temporal kingdom stands through the Church of God and that the Church of God advances through the temporal kingdom.” CLXXXII, 440–441.

St Bernard discusses the excellence of pontifical dignity and power:

“Come, let us inquire yet more diligently who you are; that is, what person you bear for the time being in the Church of God. Who are you? A great priest, the supreme pontiff. You are prince of bishops, heir of the apostles: Abel in primacy, Noah in governance, Abraham in patriarchal rank, Melchizedek in order, Aaron in dignity, Moses in authority, Samuel in judgment, Peter in power, Christ in anointing. You are he to whom the keys were given, to whom the sheep were entrusted. There are indeed other doorkeepers of heaven and shepherds of flocks; but you have inherited both titles in so much the greater glory as they are distinctively yours above the rest. They have flocks assigned to them, each one one flock; all are entrusted to you, one flock to one man. Nor are you shepherd only of the sheep, but also the one shepherd of all shepherds. You ask how I prove this? From the Lord’s word. To whom—not, I say, of the bishops, but even of the apostles—were the whole sheep so absolutely and without distinction entrusted: ‘Feed my sheep’?” CLXXXII, 751.

“You say that I bid you feed dragons and scorpions, not sheep. For that very reason, I say, attack them—but with the word, not with the sword. Why do you again attempt to usurp the sword which you were once commanded to put back into its sheath? Yet whoever denies that it is yours seems to me not to heed sufficiently the Lord’s saying, ‘Put your sword back into its sheath.’ It is therefore yours also, perhaps to be drawn at your nod, though not by your hand. Otherwise, if it did not in any way pertain to you, when the apostles said, ‘Here are two swords,’ the Lord would not have answered, ‘It is enough,’ but, ‘It is too much.’ Both swords, therefore, are the Church’s: the spiritual sword and the material sword. The former is to be wielded by the Church; the latter for the Church. The former by the hand of the priest, the latter by the hand of the soldier—but certainly at the priest’s nod and at the emperor’s command.”

St Bernard teaches that both swords belong to the Church, namely the spiritual and the material. But the former is to be wielded by the Church, the latter for the Church; the former by the priest’s hand, the latter at his nod, but by the soldier’s hand and at the emperor’s command. For a long succession, political writers—not to mention sectarians—and indeed many theologians and canonists have employed these words. Formerly, and even today, they have aided emperors and princes who took arms against the pontiff; and, while elsewhere men fought with steel, these writers pursued the matter no less with the pen. They contend that the material sword does not belong to the pontiff; rather, that as supreme head of the Church he may call upon the emperor—as a more worthy and powerful member of the Church—and similarly upon other princes, to lend arms to the Church and defend her against enemies; but that he cannot wage war by his own authority. For this they rely on the present passage of St Bernard, wishing the temporal sword to be wielded not by the pontiff’s hand but only at his nod and by the emperor’s command.

They adduce similar words by the same author from Letter 256 to Pope Eugenius:

“Both swords must now be drawn, Christ suffering again where He suffered also the other time. But by whom, if not by you? Both belong to Peter: the one to be drawn at his nod, the other by his own hand, whenever necessity requires. For concerning the sword which seemed less clearly his, it was said to Peter, ‘Put your sword back.’ It was therefore his, but certainly was not to be drawn by his own hand,” etc. CLXXXII, 775–777.

CHARLEMAGNE, emperor.—Assuredly nothing is more celebrated among historians, ancient and recent alike, than the madness of the iconoclasts during the eighth century of the Church. From it came Italy’s defection from the Eastern Augusti, the dominion of the Roman Church, the transfer of the exarchate, the destruction of the Lombard kingdom, and especially the beginnings and power of the Carolingian kings, which they ascribed to the Prince of the Apostles and his successors. The orthodox faith and the tradition of the Fathers—that is, the veneration of sacred images—are earnestly commended to the Frankish kings. Above all, these pious kings are urged to defend the image of St Peter, renowned throughout the world. For the Isaurian emperor, at the very beginning of his impiety, had threatened Gregory II [Col. 0137] in blasphemous words that he would break it:

“I shall send to Rome and break the image of St Peter; and I shall see that Gregory the pontiff is carried off from there in chains.”

Accordingly, in the first embassy sent to the Frankish prince Charles Martel, Peter’s keys—the symbol, that is, of the power to open and close the kingdom of heaven—were dispatched, with such success that what Charles could not do, his son Pippin, the first Carolingian king, accomplished: by Peter’s authority through his vicar or successor he was made king together with his son Charlemagne; and they were designated patricians, or defenders, of Peter and his successors, and of his special people—the Romans, namely, and all inhabitants of the Roman duchy. They held nothing more ancient, nothing more sacred, than the defence and exaltation of the Apostolic See, of “the key-bearer of the kingdom of heaven and his special people.” How greatly and fruitfully each king fulfilled this duty is abundantly shown by the overthrow of so many barbarian nations, the extension of the Catholic faith, and the great terror struck into those impious men in their distress.

Moreover, Hadrian held up as an example the extraordinary veneration with which Charlemagne honoured the Prince of the Apostles above other saints. In his letter to Constantine and Irene, he admonished them to seek Peter’s protection after the example of “Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans.” For he says:

“With the blessed Prince of the Apostles Peter accompanying you, you shall rule as victorious conquerors in triumph over all barbarian nations, just as our lord Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, our son and spiritual co-godfather, obeying our admonitions and fulfilling our wishes in all things, has cast down beneath his feet all the barbarian nations of the western Hesperia and the western region, subdued their powers, and united them under his kingdom. Therefore, through his laborious struggles and through excessive love for the Church of that apostle of God, he has bestowed upon it for perpetual possession many gifts: provinces, cities, castles, and other territories, indeed also patrimonies held by the treacherous Lombard people, by a strong arm restoring them to that apostle of God, whose rights they were known to be. Nor does he cease daily to offer gold and silver for the provision of lights and the sustenance of the poor, so that the memory of his king may not be abandoned for ever and ever.”

From this it is already evident that by the end of the eighth century Greek dominion at Rome had been utterly effaced. The patriciate comprised two things: the jurisdiction exercised by the Frankish kings in the city of Rome itself, with the consent of the pontiff and Roman people; and the defence of the Roman Church. To these must certainly be added the protection of orthodox faith, which was the patriciate’s chief office.

What Charlemagne promised in word, he proved in deed. For Pope Leo III required the defence which was the peculiar office of the patrician of the Romans. Great violence was inflicted upon him during a procession near the monastery of St Silvester in Capite. He then fled to Francia, and Charlemagne soon came to Rome; peace was arranged, and “in the year 799, on the vigil of the Apostle St Andrew, all the Romans in general received Pope Leo returning from Francia with exceeding great joy.”

All ancient authorities unanimously affirm that on this occasion Charlemagne was unexpectedly and almost unwillingly adorned with the imperial crown:

“As he rose from prayer during Mass before the Confession of the blessed Apostle Peter, Lord Pope Leo placed a crown upon his head; and the whole Roman people cried out: ‘To Charles Augustus, crowned by God, great and peace-making emperor of the Romans: life and victory!’”

The *Liber Pontificalis* (§376) adds the unmixed reason for the acclamations of all the people:

“All the faithful Romans, seeing such great defence and love as he had shown toward the holy Roman Church and its vicar, with one accord and in a loud voice, by God’s will and that of blessed Peter, key-bearer of the kingdom of heaven, cried: ‘To Charles Augustus,’ etc.”

It is therefore certain that Charlemagne’s imperial majesty arose from the aforementioned crime of the Romans, and that Leo III was the originator of this new dignity, receiving the crown from the altar before the most holy body of the Apostle Peter. Eleven Augusti are counted before the anarchy of the tenth century, which Otto the Great, first emperor of the Germans, removed: seven, namely, of the Carolingian line—Charlemagne, Louis the Pious, Lothair I, Louis II, Charles the Bald, etc.—XCVIII, 490–505.

I would not deny that the ancient ardour which for more than one hundred and twenty years animated Pippin, Charlemagne, and their descendants toward the Prince of the Apostles and his successors grew cool. Yet, if the emperors departed from the examples of their ancestors, we certainly learn that, in order to attain the full character of renewed majesty, [Col. 0138] at the very act of coronation they caused to be read publicly the pact of confirmation, or diploma, by which all donations and rights of the Holy See were confirmed, XCVIII, 505–506.

The capitularies of the Frankish kings, by which the institutions of sacred councils and decrees of the holy Fathers were reinforced with authority, and to which even the Roman pontiffs formerly declared in writing before princes that they wished to submit—by whose protection and authority sound discipline was preserved in the Gallican, German, Italian, and other Churches—are to be consulted here. Capitularies are laws, partly ecclesiastical and partly secular. Yet Pippin, Charlemagne, and the other Frankish kings who framed ecclesiastical laws or capitularies to restore ecclesiastical discipline did not do so by their own authority alone, but by the direction and permission of bishops, with the bishops and councils approving. Indeed, some say that most of these chapters were enacted by authority of the Roman pontiffs; but others deny this—that is, they say that certain capitularies were made by princes in their own right, outside the presence of synods and ecclesiastical assemblies. For example, they say that Charlemagne sanctioned laws of this kind by royal right.

Others, however, taking a wholly contrary path and plainly abusing the words of Christ the Lord by which He promised the keys of the kingdom of heaven to Peter and his successors, remove from princes all authority to decree concerning ecclesiastical affairs. They assert that neither an emperor nor a king, as such, has any ecclesiastical jurisdiction, and that Charlemagne claimed no right for himself over ecclesiastical affairs or persons. That this is false is clear to all, especially since it is established that in Charlemagne’s age ecclesiastical constitutions of bishops were customarily examined in the princes’ court and required their confirmation in order to have force.

Certainly our kings then thought that they were lords of the land, not lords in the bishops’ place, nor stewards and ministers—as Gretser seems expressly to have wished to make them. Charles the Bald bears witness in a letter written to Pope Hadrian II in 871, in the case of Hincmar, bishop of Laon (vol. II, 706):

“We Frankish kings, born of royal stock, have hitherto been regarded not as lords in the place of bishops but as lords of the land. And, as Leo and the Roman synod wrote, kings and emperors, whom divine power commanded to preside over lands, permitted to holy bishops, according to divine enactments, the right of deciding cases; but they have not been stewards of bishops.—And St Augustine said: ‘Possessions are held under the laws of kings’; kings do not, however, become stewards and agents of bishops through episcopal command.” XCVII, 63–69, in the Prolegomena.

To confirm the authority of Frankish princes and Frankish laws even in cases concerning bishops of the eternal city, whether they were plaintiffs or defendants, the letter of Pope Leo to Emperor Louis must not be omitted. A fragment of it survives in Ivo and Gratian. But first it should be noted that at that period there were imperial judges in the city of Rome, permanently residing there to determine disputed controversies; and royal dignity always remained at Rome within its boundaries until the end of the days of Louis the Pious. Thus, whenever other cases arose, light or serious, they were judged by imperial judges. If anyone complained of having suffered an injury, an envoy was sent by the emperor to investigate carefully the truth of the matter.

Accordingly, when certain Romans had been treated badly by Pope Leo contrary to the order of law, and for that reason brought their complaint against him before Louis the Pious as their supreme lord, and when Louis had undoubtedly rebuked Leo and written that he would send envoys to investigate the truth of the matter, Leo replied that he would obey their judgment, while asking the prince to send wise and God-fearing men:

“If we have done anything improperly, and have not preserved in our subjects the course of just law, we wish everything to be corrected by your judgment and that of your envoys; for if we, who ought to correct the sins of others, commit worse things, then assuredly we shall be, as we say with sorrow, not disciples of truth but above all others teachers of error. Therefore we earnestly implore the clemency of Your Greatness to dispatch to these regions envoys to investigate these matters, men who fear God in all things. [lacuna] And we ask not only that they scrutinize these matters alone with exactitude, but that, whether lesser or even greater charges concerning us are reported to them, all may be concluded by their lawful examination, so that henceforth nothing may remain from them unexamined or undecided.” XCVII, 80, in the Prolegomena.

There are opponents of this view who say that it is certain that no one can be judged by an inferior; that the pope is superior to the emperor and all kings and princes; [Col. 0139] that he is answerable to no judgment except the divine; and that he himself ought to judge all things. But these persons confuse the spiritual authority of the Roman pontiff with temporal authority, and do not distinguish his civil causes from criminal ones, although there is the greatest difference among all these matters.

For although it must be admitted that he is the spiritual father of Christian kings and princes, and that his person cannot be judged by secular judges—this is entirely true after a large part of Italy had been reduced under the pope’s power—yet when the Roman pontiff obeyed emperors, his person, like that of other faithful persons, was subject to civil jurisdiction. And if some Roman pontiff had perhaps been guilty of high treason or any other public crime punishable by death, he could have been condemned to punishment by the authority of the prince; this could readily be proved. But, to make this clearer, it must be considered what absurdities would have followed if, while the Roman pontiff obeyed emperors, his person had been free from their jurisdiction and supreme power.

For it would then follow that the persons of all other bishops also—who, as St Cyprian says, together with the pope, head of the Church, share one episcopate, of which each holds a part in its entirety—could not be subject to the jurisdiction of the princes to whom they are subordinate, whatever crimes might stain them. Who would defend such an opinion, when Christ said: “My kingdom,” etc.; “The disciple is not above the master,” etc.; “Every soul [be subject] to the powers,” etc.; “There is no power except,” etc.? Thus falls the opinion that the pope’s person could never be judged by emperors.

As we have already said concerning secular judges, it is certain that the civil cases of Roman pontiffs anciently belonged to the secular forum as long as kings and emperors held Rome in their power—that is, until the death of Emperor Louis II. Examples are cited, XCVIII, 80–83.

Capitularies were frequently partly civil and partly ecclesiastical; they were laws of the realm. A law is made by the consent of the people and the enactment of the king. By “consent of the people” is meant that of princes, nobles, great men, bishops, abbots, dukes, and counts. Hence bishops were then present in the kings’ counsels along with the magnates of the realm; all were admitted to public assemblies summoned by kings. In these, decrees of councils were examined, matters relating to ecclesiastical polity were arranged, and chapters or laws for the common good were promulgated by the consent of all ranks.

Accordingly, after chapters had been established by the prince, they were read before the people; and when all had assented, all subscribed to those new chapters. Thus all the *scabini* [judicial assessors], bishops, abbots, and counts signed with their own hands the chapters appended in 803 to the Salic Law. Yet, although it is certain that capitularies were enacted by kings in public assemblies of the realm, amid a numerous attendance of noblemen and magistrates, it must nevertheless be admitted that not all were established in assemblies of this kind. Many capitularies were also drawn from episcopal councils and synods.

These extracts of synodal chapters, however, were not always made in public assemblies or synods, but by delegation of the prince in private gatherings of bishops and ecclesiastical men who happened at that time to be in the royal retinue; as it is said somewhere: “Chapters drawn up by Lord Charles and his son, together with their most wise bishops.” The kings were indeed then so concerned, desiring the Christian religion to remain safe and sound and Christian morals to be shaped after the best model, that they had chapters of most holy institutions collected from the decrees of ancient Fathers and the canons of councils, and commanded them to have the force of law throughout the kingdom of the Franks. Yet it cannot be denied how many capitularies our princes established in their own right, outside a synod and the presence of public assemblies; afterward, if circumstances seemed to require it, they arranged for these to be reread in the same assemblies and received by the public consent of all, XCVII, 67–69, in the Prolegomena.

There follow innumerable capitularies which seem rather to be decrees of councils than laws of princes and kings. In almost all there are similar inscriptions:

“Charles, by the grace of God king and ruler of the kingdom of the Franks, devout defender of the holy Church, and helper in all things of the Apostolic See,” XCVII, 121–1084.

CLEMENT III, antipope (WIBERT).—Clement III, previously called Guibert of Corrigia, was made archbishop of Ravenna by Alexander II; formerly chancellor of Emperor Henry IV, he was made Roman antipope in schism through Henry’s influence, against Gregory VII and his successors Victor III, Urban II, and Paschal II. [Col. 0140] He held office for twenty-one years while Henry ruled. Created at Brixen in Noricum by thirty schismatic bishops, he was crowned at St Peter’s in Rome in 1084. He made twenty-nine cardinals, four bishops, and ten priests. He died at Rome in 1101. Buried in the cathedral church at Ravenna, his body was not long afterward exhumed and burned at the command of Paschal II. This was the worst and the twenty-third schism in the Roman Church, CXLVIII, 826.

KING HENRY IV celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Rome, at St Peter’s, and soon afterward crossed into Campania and took a great part of Apulia. Thereafter, asked by Roman envoys to return peacefully, he returned to Rome. Pitching camp at the Lateran Gate, he received the submission of all; and, at their request, because Hildebrand had been deposed by them and had fled, he set Wibert, bishop of Ravenna, over them as apostolic bishop. In that same year, 1084, accompanied by many men and with great glory, he entered Rome, bringing with him the aforementioned bishop. On the following Sunday, this bishop, consecrated to the apostolic title by many pontiffs and taking the name Clement, was reverently enthroned. By him the king, together with the queen, was exalted with the imperial title. In 1085 a synod was held at Mainz, attended by Henry IV; there, with Roman envoys present, all bishops rebellious against the emperor were judged to be deposed, while the rest were, as it seemed, condemned by anathema, CLIV, 953–954.

CONSTANTINE THE GREAT.—This emperor gave, over the bodies of the saints Marcellinus and Peter, the island of Sardinia with all possessions pertaining to it, CXXVIII, 1524.

Accordingly, this prince offered the island of Sardinia as the dowry of the church to the basilica of Saints Marcellinus and Peter founded by himself; and thus that island belonged by right and ownership to the Roman Church, CXXVIII, 1548.

In every section of the Life of St Silvester, Anastasius the Librarian is wholly occupied in enumerating the gifts offered by Constantine to God, so that they might be assigned by patrimonial right to this holy Roman Church and to its bishop, Peter’s successor, as things sacred to God, to be retained and administered under the complete authority of the supreme pontificate by Silvester and his lawful successors. Therefore, lest we dwell upon every section by tedious and quite superfluous investigation, pursuing the locations, names, revenues, and transfers of the individual estates, it is enough to note that great patrimonies were established by Constantine under the name of the SACRED PATRIMONY, etc., CXXVIII, 1512–1513 and 1591–1593.

When St. Sylvester obtained the Roman episcopate in the year 314, the ninth year of the Emperor Constantine, Maximinus and Licinius—the enemies and persecutors of the Eastern Church—having been defeated, and the Jews, who were stirring up sedition, having been successfully suppressed by Constantine, who cut off their ears and branded their bodies with the mark of rebellion, peace and tranquillity were granted to the whole world, and especially to the universal Church. Once this peace had been obtained, the ruined churches immediately began to be rebuilt, and most holy laws began to be promulgated by the rulers of the ecclesiastical and secular commonwealth for the correction of corrupt morals. Finally, in order to curb the obstinacy of the schismatic Donatists, who appealed three or four times in the case of Caecilian; to quench the blaze of the Arian heresy which had arisen at Alexandria; and to confirm the election of Athanasius against the faction of the Arians and Meletians, the councils of Arles, Ancyra, Neo-Caesarea, Alexandria, Laodicea, Rome, Nicaea, and many others were convened, assembled, and celebrated at different places and times.

Among the laws which the emperor, still a catechumen and unbaptized, most piously enacted and promulgated, the following are especially worthy of notice: those by which he restored to freedom freeborn persons reduced to slavery by the tyrant; forbade sexual relations with boys; relieved the poverty of parents in feeding and bringing up their children; abolished the punishment by which the faces of wretched people were branded; recalled Christians who had been exiled or condemned to the mines, after the defeat of Licinius; restored persons reduced in rank and stripped of all their goods; abolished the Julian and Papian laws, once enacted against disgraceful, feigned, and sterile celibacy, but turned against the true, holy, and fruitful celibacy of Christians; and finally, his rescript to Maximus, prefect of the City, concerning diviners (*haruspices*), forbidding them to enter private houses, since on that pretext they instilled the poisons of clandestine idolatry.

But when he saw that many minds were deeply embittered by this decree and that a sedition was almost being stirred up, under the appearance of calming the sedition he issued to the same Maximus a rescript contrary to the former one. By it he decreed that diviners should be consulted if lightning struck some building, and that what they answered should be reported to him. Therefore, in order that the emperor himself might learn, and by his example teach others, how great an offence [Col. 0141] against God is involved in concealing religion for the sake of temporal advantage, God, as avenger, permitted his empire, hitherto most prosperous, to relapse into the utmost misfortune, and in some respects the Neronian ages themselves seemed to revive.

For after he had put to death the younger Licinius, suspected of rebellion, he then most cruelly killed the excellent Christian Caesar Crispus—distinguished by splendid victories, truly great through his brave achievements, eminent for chastity and other virtues—together with his own Fausta, on the charge that Crispus had attempted to violate his stepmother; he also killed many men of conspicuous virtue besides. For these crimes the emperor was struck with leprosy by God. When he was deterred, by the answers of the diviners—who advised that, in order to cure the leprosy, the blood of innocents should be added to blood innocently shed—and by the lamentations of mothers and infants, he came to his senses, detested his deed, and sought expiation both for the crime and its punishment.

From Hosius, bishop of Corduba, and from an apparition of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, he learned that Sylvester must be recalled from his hiding-place in exile and that he must seek from him the washing of baptism. They promised the emperor that, if he did so, he would be cleansed from the contagion alike of soul and body. He obeyed the admonitions of the apostles and the bishop, recalled Sylvester from exile, and, after being instructed in the faith by him for several days, was baptized and immediately cleansed of leprosy. Mindful of this benefit received, in order to make known his affection toward God and the Church, he at once demolished the shrines of the pagan gods, built very many churches to be consecrated to divine worship, and most lavishly adorned them with exceedingly ample gifts.

And since he judged it unworthy—as has already been stated in the *Monitum*—that the city in which the monarch of the whole Church and Christ’s vicar on earth resided should be subject to the rule of a secular prince, he most generously bestowed upon Sylvester and his legitimate successors in Peter’s chair not merely the lordship and temporal jurisdiction of the city of Rome, but of nearly all Italy and other provinces as well; in the Notes, VIII, 795, 796, 797.

This venerable emperor, grieving that the faith of Christ was being disturbed by the attacks of the Arians, sent leading men from his court and assembled bishops from the whole world, establishing a universal council. There the faith of Christ, preached by the apostles and prophets, was firmly confirmed by the mouths of the saints, as the grace of the Holy Spirit enlightened them. There he showed such humility that in the council itself he sat in a lower seat than all the bishops. And when some of them accused others, he said: “You are gods; I am a man. Therefore it is not fitting that a man should judge gods. Hear the case among yourselves and make peace; for if I saw a priest of God sinning, I would cover him with my own cloak.”

This most religious man, the first of the Roman emperors openly to embrace the faith of truth, granted permission throughout the world while his empire endured not only for people to become Christians, but also ordered that churches should be built and assistance furnished. Finally, the same aforesaid prince established immense gifts and the construction of the church of the prince of the apostles, the first see, so that he abandoned the imperial seat over which Roman rulers had presided and granted it for the benefit of blessed Peter and his bishops. From that time onward religious men consecrated not only the possessions and estates which they owned, but themselves as well, building basilicas on their own lands in honour of saints throughout cities, and innumerable monasteries in which communities of servants of the Lord might gather. Finally, kings, governors, and magistrates not only granted this permission, but themselves bestowed their own property throughout all the kingdoms of the earth and upon that Church . . . . . . On Constantine’s leprosy and the cure effected by baptism, see VIII, 800, the notes of Severinus Binius.

### CUNIBERT, king of the Lombards

We see that a charter of Felix, bishop of Lucca, confirmed for the monastery of St. Frigidian, was confirmed by Cunibert, king of the Lombards, in the year 700. With even greater zeal than he, other princes and bishops of Italy founded new monastic communities for the remission of their sins. Many are listed as having been built by Roman pontiffs and other bishops; many by the princes of Benevento; and many, finally, by the dukes of Friuli and Tuscany, and by other magnates of Italy. Yet the arrival and devastation of the Lombards caused monastic foundations in Italy during the sixth and seventh centuries not to be as frequent as in Gaul and Britain. Indeed, not a few of those founded earlier were destroyed, so that not even their memory survives.

But those monasteries became especially famous and wealthy which were begun by someone distinguished either by nobility of birth or holiness of life. The virtue of the founder who established his household there drew, by the renown of his name, the frequent offerings of a devout people and a great multitude of disciples and companions to itself [Col. 0142]. Thus St. Benedict for the monasteries of Monte Cassino and Subiaco, St. Columbanus for Bobbio, St. Anselm, etc., etc. Nor were other kings and nobles outside Italy less zealous in such activity. How many monastic dwellings, for example, Charlemagne and his son Louis the Pious built, etc., etc.: LXXXVII, 1349, 1350.

### EKKEHARD of Aura

His universal chronicle gives a chronological history of the disputes between Pope Gregory VII and King Henry IV, CLIV, 946–1012. It is almost the same history as that related in the *Saxon War* of Bruno, clerk of Magdeburg, CXLVII, 491–586. This history is given by us in brief under the name **GREGORY VII, pope**.

### EUGENIUS III, pope

Eugenius was made pontiff in the year of the Lord 1145, in the time of Emperor Conrad. “At the beginning,” says Otto of Freising, book VII, chapter 31, “of the dignity which he had undertaken, because the people, at Arnold’s instigation, wished to press him, as they had pressed his predecessors, to surrender the regalian rights to the City, he left the City with the bishops and cardinals. On the following Sunday, because of the violence of the persecution, he changed the custom and was elevated by pontifical consecration in the monastery of Farfa. Thereafter, avoiding the fury of the Roman people after his consecration, he withdrew to fortified places; later, coming to Viterbo, he stayed there for some time.

“But the Roman people, together with their patrician Jordan, having turned to fury, abolished the office of prefect, compelled all princes and nobles among the citizens into subjection to the patrician, demolished not only the towers of certain distinguished laymen but also the houses of cardinals and clerics, and carried off immense plunder. They did not fear sacrilegiously and most profanely to fortify as a castle the church of blessed Peter, head of all churches. They compelled pilgrims arriving for prayer to make offerings for the sake of gain by blows and beatings; and they did not shrink from killing some who refused to offer, by a wicked audacity, in the very portico and vestibule of the church.

“The venerable pontiff, having first struck Jordan with the sword of anathema together with certain of his supporters, restrained them by joining forces with the people of Tivoli, the ancient enemies of the Romans, and finally compelled them to seek peace. He granted that peace on the condition that they should abandon the dignity of the patriciate and restore the prefect to his former dignity, while the senators should hold office by his authority. Thus, returning to the City, he celebrated the Nativity of the Lord in the year 1146.”

Thus Eugenius’s entry into the City is narrated in a Vatican manuscript: “Therefore, through God’s agency, great joy arose throughout the whole City at the unexpected arrival of the pontiff himself. A very great throng of people came out to meet him with branches. Running at once to his footsteps, after kissing his feet they were raised to kiss his face. Standard-bearers advanced with banners; scribes and judges followed. Nor were the Jews absent from so great a rejoicing, carrying the Mosaic Law upon their shoulders. For the whole Roman choir sang together, saying: ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.’ Thus, with great joy of the people, the same pontiff was able to ascend the Lateran palace.” CLXXX, 1004–1007.

### FREDERICK, emperor

With the consent of the archbishops and bishops of the German kingdom, this emperor unjustly dismissed his wife and thereby brought great calamity upon himself. He was sharply reproved by Pope Adrian and Chancellor Roland for divorcing his first wife. Resenting this, he forbade Roman cardinals entry into the cities and churches of his kingdom. Thereupon Pope Adrian and Emperor Frederick wrote letters to one another in exceedingly biting language.

Adrian’s letter was as follows:

> “As the divine law promises long life to those who honour their parents, so it likewise pronounces a sentence of death upon those who curse father and mother. Moreover, by the voice of Truth we are taught that everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and he who humbles himself shall be exalted. Therefore we are not a little astonished at your prudence, since you appear not to show to blessed Peter and to the holy Roman Church entrusted to him the reverence which you ought. For in the letter sent to us you place your name before ours, thereby incurring the reproach of insolence—if I may not say arrogance.
>
> “What shall I say of the fidelity promised and sworn by you to blessed Peter and to us, and how you observe it? You demand homage from those who are gods and all sons of the Most High—that is, bishops; you exact fealty; you join their consecrated hands to your own; and, openly setting yourself against us, you close not only churches but even the cities of your kingdom to cardinals sent from our side. Come to your senses, therefore; come to your senses, we advise you. Since you have received consecration and the crown from us, while you seize what has not been granted, we fear lest you lose what has been granted, to the detriment of your nobility.”

Here is the emperor’s reply to him:

> “The law of justice restores to each person what is his own. For we do not disparage the parents to whom in this our kingdom we render due honour—namely our forefathers, from whom we received both the dignity and the honour of the kingdom. For nowhere before the time of Constantine [Col. 0143] is Sylvester known to have possessed anything royal; but through Constantine’s piety peace was granted to the Church, liberty restored, and whatever royal possession your papacy is known to possess today it holds by the generosity of princes.
>
> “Accordingly, when we write to the Roman pontiff, we rightly and according to ancient custom place our name before yours. And why should we not demand homage and oaths of fealty from those who are gods by adoption and who hold our regalian rights? For he who is the true teacher of both you and us, receiving nothing from a human king, yet bestowing all good things upon all, paid Caesar’s tribute for himself and for Peter, and gave you an example that you too should act thus. He teaches you by saying: ‘Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart,’ etc., etc.”

When these had been read, the pope launched himself wholly against the emperor; and, after holding a council with his cardinals, he excommunicated Emperor Frederick, who while his wife was living had taken another wife, etc., CLX, 297–299.

### GRATIAN, monk of St. Benedict

(From various decrees.) Although the other apostles are commanded to let down their nets, to Peter alone it is said: “Put out into the deep,” that is, into the depth of disputations. For what is so high as to behold the height of riches, to know the Son of God, and to embrace the confession of the divine generation—something which the human mind cannot comprehend by a full investigation of reason, but which the fullness of faith nevertheless embraces? There is another apostolic kind of fishing, by which the Lord commands Peter alone to fish, saying: “Cast the hook, and take the first fish that comes up.”

Do not depart from the right faith and the apostolic path on account of any persecution, knowing that, according to the Saviour’s sentence, blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake. This is the living tradition of the apostles; this is the holy and apostolic mother of all the churches of Christ, the Church which, by the grace of almighty God, is proved never to have erred from the path of apostolic tradition and has not succumbed to corruption by heretical novelties. Rather, as at its beginning it received the rule of Christian faith from its founders, the chief apostles of Christ, so it remains inviolate to the end.

In the Apostolic See the Catholic religion has always been preserved free from stain. Since the question of faith is under discussion, I judge that all our brethren and fellow bishops ought to refer only to Peter—that is, to the author of their name and honour—what may benefit all churches throughout the world in common, CLXXXVII, 1267, 1268, 1269.

The holy Roman Church, which has always remained immaculate, will remain so in the future, by the Lord’s providence and with the assistance of blessed Peter the apostle; firm and immovable, it will endure at all times without any assault by heretics.

Pope Marcellus, to bishops established throughout Antioch:

> “We ask you not to teach or think anything other than what you received from blessed Peter the apostle and the remaining apostles and Fathers. For you were first instructed by him. Therefore you ought not to abandon your own father and follow others. For he is the head of the whole Church, to whom the Lord said: ‘You are Peter,’ etc. His see was first among you, but was afterwards transferred to Rome at the Lord’s command; by the aid of divine grace we preside over it today. Nor ought you to depart from its ordinance, since all the greater ecclesiastical affairs have, by God’s disposing grace, been ordered to be referred to it, so that they may be regularly arranged by that see from which they took their beginning.
>
> “If, moreover, your Antiochene see, which was formerly first, yields to the Roman see, there is none which is not subject to its authority. Since the most blessed Peter received apostolic primacy from the Lord, and the Roman Church remains in his ordinances, it is impious to believe that his holy disciple Mark, who was the first to govern the Alexandrian Church, framed the decrees of his traditions by rules different from his master’s. For without doubt one Spirit was of the same fountain of grace in disciple and teacher, and the ordained man could not have handed down anything other than what he received from the one who ordained him.”

If Peter deliberately struck off the ear, he taught that they should not have in bodily form an ear which they did not possess in ministry. But the good Lord restored hearing even to him, showing according to the prophetic sayings that those wounded in the Lord’s passion may also be healed if they turn back, because every sin is washed away by the mysteries of faith. Peter therefore removes the ear. Why Peter? Because he is the one who received the keys of the kingdom of heaven. For he condemns who also absolves, since he received the same power of binding and loosing. He removes the ear of one who hears wrongly; with the spiritual sword he removes the inward ear of one who understands wrongly.

Let us beware lest anyone’s ear be removed while the Lord’s passion is being read. If we attribute the weakness of his bodily passion to his divinity, the ear is cut off—and it is cut off by Peter, who [Col. 0144] did not allow Christ to be judged a prophet, but taught by his faithful confession that he must be acknowledged as the Son of God, CLXXXVII, 1270, 1271.

### GREGORY II, pope (in the year 714)

In the time of Pope Gregory III, Liutprand, king of the Lombards, confirmed the donation to the Roman Church of the patrimony of the Cottian Alps which King Aripert had made, CXXVIII, 975, 992. Soon afterward, by this king’s command, the fortress of Narni was seized by the Lombards; and he himself, having ordered a general mobilisation, advanced upon Ravenna, besieged it for several days, seized the fortress, carried off captured fleets, and took countless riches.

After a few days Basil the duke, Jordanes the *chartularius*, and John the subdeacon formed a plan to kill the pontiff. Marinus, the imperial *spatharius*, who held the Roman duchy, sent from the imperial city by command of the emperor, approved their plan. But the undertaking had no effect. Afterwards certain persons plotted to carry out the same plan. But at last it was disclosed by the Romans, who killed the aforesaid Jordanes and John, the principal authors of the plot. Then Pope Gregory II was harassed in various ways by the aforesaid Liutprand. But the Romans, moved to defend the supreme pontiff, prepared themselves.

Subsequently orders having been sent, the emperor decreed that no image of any saint, martyr, or angel should be kept; for he asserted that all such things were accursed. If the pontiff agreed to this, he would have the emperor’s favour; but if he hindered its being done, he would fall from his rank. Therefore, beholding the profane command of the prince, the pious man armed himself against the emperor as against an enemy, rejecting his heresy and writing everywhere that Christians should beware, because such impiety had arisen.

Accordingly, all the forces of the Pentapolis and of Venice resisted the emperor’s order, saying that they would never consent to the death of that pontiff, but would rather fight bravely for his defence. Thus they subjected to anathema Paul the exarch, or the one who had sent him, and his adherents; despising the emperor’s ordinance, they all everywhere in Italy elected dukes for themselves; and other such measures, CXXVIII, 976, 977, 978, 979, 980.

But certain explanations must now be given concerning these matters. From Gregory II dates the first period of Italian liberty, in which Italy, beginning to free itself from the yoke of barbarians and Greeks, laid the foundations of the subsequently restored Western Empire. Theophanes speaks thus of this movement in Italy:

> “Moreover, that sacred and divine Germanus, defender of the decrees of true religion, flourished at Byzantium, fighting against Leo—who had a name derived from a wild beast—and his followers as against wild beasts; just as in ancient Rome Gregory, a man altogether sacred and apostolic, confessor of Peter, chief of the apostles, shone forth through learning and illustrious deeds. He withdrew Rome, Italy, and the entire West from obedience to Leo the Isaurian, both civil and ecclesiastical, and from his empire.”

CXXVIII, 994.

After this it is said that all Italy formed a plan to choose an emperor for itself and lead him to Constantinople; but the pope checked such a plan, hoping for the prince’s conversion. That we have certainty on this matter is clear from Pope Gregory’s letter to Emperor Leo:

> “We shall invoke Christ, prince of the army of every creature, seated in heaven, who is above all the hosts of the heavenly powers, that he may send you a demon, as the Apostle says: ‘to hand such a one over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved.’”

From this nothing else seems capable of being understood than excommunication, CXXVIII, 1014.

The causes which gave occasion for the aforesaid acts of St. Gregory, pope, against Emperor Leo are these. Thereafter the wickedness of Leo the Isaurian became manifest, so that by force and persuasion alike he compelled all inhabitants of Constantinople to take down wherever they were found images of the Saviour, of his holy Mother, and of all saints; to burn them in the middle of the city—cruel even to say—and to whitewash all painted churches, CXXVIII, 984.

These matters are explained as follows. In the earliest times after the rise of the Christian religion, when pagan fury still raged against it and the superstition of idols still lay hidden in human minds, the use of sacred images was not as frequent as that of churches and basilicas. Since images belong to the class of things which are not absolutely necessary to salvation and do not pertain to the very substance of religion, it lies within the Church’s power to employ or remove them, according to what it judges more expedient; they are of the kind commonly called matters of positive law.

Hence arose that reproach of unbelievers expressed in these words by Minucius Felix: “Why do they have no altars, no temples, [Col. 0145] no recognised images?” Therefore some held it sinful and unlawful to possess images. But Christians gradually learned that the veneration of images was not to be condemned and could greatly promote piety. Therefore, just as Christians did not hesitate to build basilicas or churches and altars in God’s honour and worship, so at the same time the Church adopted images of Christ and the saints—whose use had not hitherto become widespread—when there was no longer any danger of idolatry, and when this seemed useful both for preserving the memory of Christ, the martyrs, and the other saints and for encouraging the faithful by their example to steadfastness in piety.

Thus it came to be believed that the use and veneration of images of Christ and the saints not only did not conflict with God’s law but were consonant with religion and useful for stirring up the piety of the faithful. In the eighth century there arose in the East a dreadful monster: the heresy of the Iconoclasts, which declared war on venerable images. Leo the Isaurian burned with rage against images. St. Germanus, patriarch of Constantinople, opposed this emperor’s impiety with all the steadfastness he could; afterwards Pope Gregory II likewise resisted and, as we have seen, freed Italy from the yoke of barbarians and Greeks, CXXVIII, 1005, 1006, 1007, 1008.

### GREGORY III (St.), pope

He lived in the time of the emperors Leo and Constantine, when the persecution instigated by them for the removal and destruction of the sacred images of our Lord Jesus Christ, of the holy Mother of God, of the holy apostles, and of all saints and confessors was raging. For this reason the same most holy man, in order that they might come to their senses and withdraw from this error, sent through Gregory the priest admonitory letters established by the authority of the Apostolic See, just as his predecessor of holy memory had sent, etc., CXXVIII, 1023–1030.

Among the acts of this pontiff, the following should be noted. In the year 740 Liutprand, king of the Lombards, surrounded Rome with a siege, because Trasamund, duke of Spoleto, and Godescalc, duke of Benevento, hostile to him, were friends of the supreme pontiff. Therefore Pope Gregory III, in 741, sent a double embassy to Charles Martel, mayor of the royal house of the Franks, together with the keys of St. Peter and portions of the chains; he also wrote him two letters, intending that Charles might free them from so great an oppression by the Lombards . . . . . . It appears that the pope proposed a compact to Charles: if Liutprand fell, he would confer upon Charles the Roman consulship, or patriciate.

Charles received the embassy with extraordinary and magnificent honour and bestowed precious gifts. Since this embassy was so pleasing to Charles, there is no doubt that he declared war upon King Liutprand through envoys unless he immediately withdrew from Roman territory; and Liutprand, deterred from his undertaking by the threats, returned to Pavia, whence he had come, retaining nevertheless the four towns which he had occupied. These were later restored under Zachary, Gregory’s successor. There is likewise no room for doubt that Charles promised aid to the pontiff; but because he died in the same year, 741, he could not furnish it.

From the history of these times it is inferred and explained that Gregory III offered Charles the consulship or patriciate, when it is said that the Roman people, abandoning the emperor’s dominion, called Charles to their defence. For the dignity of patronage was conferred upon those chosen to defend churches and the poor from the violence of the powerful, as is clear from the formula by which the prince proclaimed a man patrician. The formula was:

> “Hence we grant you this honour: that you may administer justice for the churches of God and the poor, and thereafter render an account to the highest Judge. Then let the emperor clothe him with a mantle, place a ring upon the index finger of his right hand, and give him with his own hand a written document on cotton: ‘Be a merciful and just patrician.’ Then let him place a golden circlet upon his head and dismiss him.”

The patriciate entailed a certain extraordinary right of protection, which those who are not otherwise bound by their office to do so are accustomed to grant to churches not subject to them against public or private violence by the powerful. Although princes are bound by office to protect churches established within their kingdoms, that right of protection is ordinary and depends upon jurisdiction. But this extraordinary right of protection was granted to distinguished men called patrons, defenders, protectors, and advocates, who furnished singular protection and defence to particular churches beyond that expected from kings under the order of public discipline.

But the patriciate of the Roman Church, or the title “patrician of the Romans,” embraced two things: the jurisdiction which the kings of the Franks exercised in the City by consent of the pope and Roman people; and the protection or defence which they had promised to the Roman Church. This defence [Col. 0146] had been established through agreements entered into with the Roman pontiffs. The writer Marca assigns the beginning of those agreements concerning protection concluded with the Roman Church to these times, when Gregory III committed himself and his Church to the guardianship of Charles, duke of the Franks. He writes that this protection was confirmed by certain new laws enacted by Pippin, king of the Franks, and Pope Stephen II of Rome, who conferred the dignity of patrician upon Pippin and his sons.

That Charles Martel was called patrician of the Romans and defender of the Church in these most difficult times is clearly suggested, besides the continuator of the historian Fredegar, by the emperors Charlemagne and Louis the Pious. In the division of his kingdom among his sons in 806, Charlemagne says:

> “Above all, we command that these three brothers jointly undertake the care and defence of the Church of St. Peter, just as it was formerly undertaken by our grandfather Charles, by our father King Pippin of blessed memory, and afterwards by ourselves; and that with God’s help they endeavour to defend it from enemies and cause it to have its rights, insofar as concerns them and reason requires.”

Louis the Pious has the same provision in the division of his kingdom, and also says:

> “Above all, we command and order that these three brothers jointly undertake the care and defence of the Church of St. Peter, just as it was formerly undertaken by our great-grandfather Charles, our grandfather Pippin, our father the Emperor Charles of blessed memory, and afterwards by ourselves.”

From this we must conclude that Charles Martel was the first of all princes of the Franks, or of any other people, to undertake the patronage of the City and Church of Rome.

From that embassy of Gregory III to Charles Martel, in whose hands the entire administration of Francia then lay, there seems to have arisen the origin of apostolic envoys in Francia. For then the *apocrisiarii*—representatives—of the Roman See appeared in Francia, and twice dealt with Charles Martel so that he might assist the Romans with aid and counsel. Those who held the Roman pontificate after Gregory III sent envoys to Francia more often, and the matter came to this: besides legates sent from Rome as new cases arose, an *apocrisiarius* of the Apostolic See remained continually at the king’s court. Not infrequently this office was conferred by the Roman pontiff upon the person whom the king had made archchaplain of his palace, CXXVIII, 1039, 1040, 1046.

### GREGORY VII, pope

After Aistulf, king of the Lombards, and Pippin, king of the Franks, had died, Charles ruled the Franks and Desiderius the Lombards. The former inherited obedience toward the Roman Church, the latter hatred. Desiderius began so grievously to harass and attack the Romans under Pope Adrian that the pontiff, far inferior to the Lombards in power and deprived of Eastern assistance, was compelled, following the example of Stephen II, to summon into Italy Charlemagne, son of Pippin and king of the Franks, then engaged in the Saxon war, to aid the Roman Church.

Obeying the pontiff, Charlemagne came into Italy with a great army after crossing the Alps. There, having defeated Desiderius in battle and captured him shortly afterward, he transferred the kingdom of the Lombards into Frankish possession. In order to show himself grateful to the Roman Church, for whose defence he had acquired a most wealthy kingdom, he divided the Lombard kingdom into three parts. One part—namely Pavia, the seat of the Lombard kingdom itself, and all that the Lombards had anciently acquired in Italy—he kept for himself. Another part, comprising what the Lombards had shortly before taken in Italy from the Eastern Roman emperors—that is, the exarchate, Umbria, and part of Picenum—he confirmed to the Roman Church, or granted anew. Having arranged these matters, he was the first of all princes to enlarge the Roman Church very greatly in dignity, secular dominion, and vast wealth.

Therefore Pope Adrian, not unmindful of so many and such great benefits, under whom Charles had deserved so magnificently of the Roman Church, assembled at the Lateran in the basilica of St. Saviour, in the year of salvation 785, a synod of 153 bishops, abbots, and many other prelates. By the consent of the whole synod, it gave Charles the right and power to elect a pontiff and to arrange the Apostolic See—although at that time it was customary for the Roman pontiff to be created by the free votes of the Roman clergy and people [“Baronius refutes this whole fabrication under the year 774. What? Is it established, or is its acceptance disputed among scholars?”]—and furthermore decreed that bishops, etc., should receive investiture from him, so that no bishop or abbot could be consecrated by anyone unless he had been wonderfully commended and invested by the king. Anastasius the Librarian is witness to this, as is read in Gratian, Distinction 63.

But the emperors who succeeded Charlemagne sank into such sloth that they were unwilling not only to protect such a privilege but even to concern themselves with any rights of the empire. [Col. 0147] Pope Adrian III, taking advantage of this occasion under Emperor Charles III in the year of salvation 884, convened a synod and entirely abolished and annulled that privilege, which under earlier pontiffs had gradually fallen into disuse, establishing that the emperor should not intervene in the election of a pope. Leo VIII, the antipope, restored this privilege to Emperor Otto I, who had deserved excellently of the Roman Church; he renewed it after the example of Adrian I, who had granted it to King Charlemagne, and confirmed it anew.

Moreover, against this decree of the antipope Leo VIII no Roman pontiff thereafter protested or openly contradicted it until Gregory VII. He was the first who, offended by the emperor’s simony, issued decrees to the contrary and wholly abrogated these two privileges of Adrian I and Leo VIII. It is sufficiently clear that John XIII, who immediately succeeded Leo VIII, Gregory V, and Sylvester II were installed in the apostolic see solely by the authority of the emperors, no votes of the Roman clergy or people having been sought. As for the other Roman pontiffs who stood between John XIII and Sylvester II, although we do not read that they were elected by the emperors, but by the Roman clergy, senate, and people, this happened because, at the time of the election, the emperors were absent from the City and so entangled in very great wars in Germany and elsewhere that they could not provide the Roman see with a new pontiff.

Yet this is certain: whenever the emperors—I mean the three Ottos—were in Rome or nearby, or at least in Italy, and it happened that the Roman Church lacked a shepherd, they appointed a new supreme pontiff. But if at the time of a new election they happened to be far from Italy, it is certain that the Roman pontiffs then elected by the Roman clergy, senate, and people were consecrated not without the emperors’ consent.
