Such were Benedict VI and VII, Boniface VII, an invader of the apostolic see, who was also expelled, and John XIV, XV, and XVI. The last of these, as some write, because he had been elected and consecrated without the consent of Emperor Otto III, was driven from Rome and deprived of the priesthood, Gregory V being substituted for him.

Therefore, from Leo VIII until Gregory VII, no pope ever protested against this privilege, although it was not observed altogether because of the emperors’ negligence. Thus eight or nine Roman pontiffs had already been created by the clergy, senate, and Roman people without election by the emperors. But when Henry III came into Italy, he splendidly asserted this privilege of the Empire for himself . . . he created a new pontiff, Clement II, having deposed three pontiffs—Benedict VIII, Sylvester III, and John XX—and he bound the cardinals, clergy, senate, and Roman people by oath to his will, compelling them to swear that they would not accept as Roman pontiff anyone created otherwise than by his command. So long as he lived, he held this most eminent right of the Empire tenaciously; and at his own discretion he designated Clement II, Damasus II, Leo IX, and Victor II as Roman pontiffs, CXLVIII, 164, 167.

After some rather obscure matters concerning the Roman pontiffs, Gregory VI, himself supreme pontiff, after the abdication of three schismatic pontiffs and himself exiled to the monastery of Cluny, where Hildebrand was, to avoid schism, is reproved by Hildebrand concerning the manner of his election. Hildebrand told him that it was altogether unfitting and contrary to the institutions of the holy Fathers for the pontiff of the entire Christian world to be forcibly imposed upon the government of the whole Church by a lay hand. But, if Gregory would follow his counsel, he promised him both results: that he would not incur the emperor’s indignation on that account, and that ecclesiastical liberty would remain unimpaired and preserved in the lawful and just ordination of the pontiff.

Gregory VI, a pious and holy man, humbly obeyed these admonitions. He immediately laid aside his purple garment and other pontifical vestments, assumed the dress of a pilgrim, took with him as companion Hildebrand the monk, who had given him the salutary counsel, and set out for Rome with Roman envoys and other accompanying bishops. Received at Rome with the highest honour, on the second day after his arrival, having assembled in the basilica of St Peter the cardinals, clergy, senate, and Roman people, he addressed them, instructed by Hildebrand, in these words:

> Brothers, having learned of your embassy, I went to the emperor in order to discover his will and purpose—not in order to be elected Roman pontiff by him, for I know that he has no right in an election of this kind, but that it belongs freely to you. I have come, however, for no other reason than that I might visit the thresholds of the apostles. And since this apostolic see has now long lacked a shepherd, it is not expedient for it to remain thus any longer. Therefore I exhort and admonish you all to choose for yourselves, without any delay, as soon as possible a suitable shepherd and bishop.

Immediately, by Hildebrand’s counsel, all the bishops, cardinals, and other nobles [Col. 0148] replied to him: “We want you alone, and no other; we elect you Roman pontiff.” Then the archdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, according to ancestral custom, cried out: “Blessed Peter has chosen Bishop Bruno,” etc., CXLVIII, 153, 154.

Having therefore been consecrated pontiff, he created the monk Hildebrand himself, by whose counsel all this had been done, cardinal subdeacon, etc. But after his death Hildebrand was sent by the clergy, senate, and Roman people as envoy to the emperor, to demand a new pontiff from him. Victor II was elected, and Hildebrand brought him to Rome. With him also, as with Leo IX, Hildebrand had very great influence in all matters, for he was a man highly distinguished by practical ability.

After Victor II’s death Stephen IX was elected, the right established by Hildebrand being observed. Afterwards Nicholas II was proclaimed supreme pontiff, and Hildebrand himself was made archdeacon by him. When Nicholas II died, Hildebrand, anxious for ecclesiastical liberty and now aspiring to wrest the election of the Roman pontiff from the emperors’ hands, was the principal author of the Roman Church’s beginning to recover the liberty which it had long lost in the election of its pontiffs. Through his efforts the appointment of Alexander II to the papacy was approved as having been made by lawful votes; and he recovered for him the patrimony of Blessed Peter in Campania, which the Normans had occupied.

When Alexander II died in 1073, Hildebrand, being occupied on the very day of his death and burial with the funeral rites, suddenly saw a vast gathering of clergy and Roman people in the Lateran basilica, who loved him and cried: “Peter has chosen Archdeacon Hildebrand.” He was then carried off by force and, on that same day, was made pontiff there in the place of Pope Alexander by the cardinals, clergy, senate, and Roman people, Emperor Henry IV neither consulted nor any authority of his—or of the bishops and princes of Germany—interposed or awaited, CXLVIII, 155–159.

Nevertheless, Hildebrand refused to be consecrated and crowned until he had sought the emperor’s and princes’ will concerning his election. Immediately after his election, therefore, he first wrote to the imperial prelate in Italy concerning his appointment. Likewise, through his envoys, he informed Emperor Henry IV, then in Germany, of the cause and manner of his violent election by the Romans. He asserted that, although elected, because he could not resist the will of an enraged people, he nevertheless had never wished, nor did wish, to be consecrated; nor would he ever undertake the administration of the pontificate unless the consent of the emperor and of the bishops and princes of Germany were first present. For this reason, after his election he was left very free by the people; and he immediately withdrew to Albano outside the City, lest he be compelled, contrary to custom, to receive the hands of consecration from that same people.

When letters from the emperor had been received and an assembly of bishops convened, the election of Gregory VII was carefully examined. When the emperor learned that it was lawful and had been carried out by the free votes of all, both clergy and Roman people, he and the other princes wished it to stand and consented to it. And when soon afterwards certain clouds arose, Gregory easily dispersed them. The king, divine will thus disposing matters, since the Roman Empire was to be diminished by priestly power and reduced almost to nothing, willingly accepted the explanations which Gregory offered.

Gregory, therefore, having attained beyond hope what he so greatly desired—that the emperor should consent to his election—judged that nothing should be delayed. At the approaching feast of Pentecost he had himself ordained priest; and on the feast-day of the apostles Peter and Paul he was consecrated Roman pontiff and received the insignia of his coronation. Thus confirmed in the Roman see, as though no further hesitation could enter people’s minds concerning the lawfulness of his appointment—for he had already been elected and consecrated by the cardinals, clergy, senate, and Roman people, with the emperor’s and princes’ consent and will added, and was then held to be the lawful, true, and unquestioned pontiff—not long after his consecration he resolved to execute what he had long conceived in his mind, CXLVIII, 159, 160, 161.

Accordingly, in 1074, still the first year of his pontificate, he laid the foundations at the appointed time for recovering ecclesiastical liberty in this manner. A synod was assembled and canons issued, most of which had previously been little used and had never been attempted by any of his predecessors. By these decrees he made them favourable to himself and opened the way for accomplishing all that he had conceived. Having laid and established these foundations in the synod, as a means of attempting what he had planned, he first kindly and courteously entreated King Henry by letter [Col. 0149] not to reject subjection to the Roman Church, but to show himself a devoted son of that Church as a Catholic prince. He exhorted him wholly to abstain from the Simoniacal heresy—that is, from the sale or traffic in bishoprics and abbacies, which he conferred after being bribed by gifts—and to refrain from the remaining vices of which he had been defamed and accused before the apostolic see, both under his predecessor Pope Alexander II and after Gregory himself had been proclaimed pontiff; otherwise, he said, he would employ ecclesiastical censures against him and the offenders.

For understanding the foregoing, it must be said that since the time of Emperor Charlemagne there had been a custom, first introduced by the authority of Adrian I, Roman pontiff: whenever the bishop or abbot of a city or abbey died, the clergy or monks immediately assembled and sent envoys to the reigning emperor. Carrying to him the deceased prelate’s pastoral staff and ring, they petitioned him, in the name of their community, to choose a new prelate. He then immediately assembled his senate and, usually according to its advice, bestowed upon someone chosen at his own discretion—either from the communities themselves or from among his friends, chaplains, and other household attendants and intimates, according to the dignity of the place—the deceased prelate’s ring and pastoral staff which had been sent to him. By his imperial diploma he invested that man with that priestly office—that is, endowed him with that dignity—and ordered him to be consecrated bishop or abbot, without any election by clergy or monks.

Thus John XIII, Gregory V, Sylvester, Clement, Damasus, Victor, Nicholas II, and Leo IX were elected and consecrated supreme pontiffs by decision of the emperors, without votes of the Roman clergy; and they had been invested by the emperors in the Roman papacy through ring and staff.

At last Gregory VII, finding an opportunity because the emperor everywhere and always asserted for himself the Church’s rights, and because moreover it happened that the aforesaid Emperor Henry IV, involved in many and very great military undertakings, needed immense sums of money and commonly granted bishoprics and abbacies to those offering him more, summoned Henry to a Roman synod to answer concerning the crimes alleged against him. There now appears the antipope Clement III, named Guibert the Cook, CXLVIII, 175, 176, 180, 181.

But Henry did not come to the council. Indeed, with then unheard-of audacity and astonishing pride, he assembled at Worms bishops who were accomplices of his crime and ought not even to be called bishops, and, after holding their little conventicle, they proscribed the bishop of the first see. Since the apostolic pontiff could not conceal the malice of so great a crime, he excommunicated both Henry and all his supporters, deprived him of every royal dignity, and released from every obligation of fidelity those bound to him by oaths. For—to say what it is shameful even to say—there were present at that holy council envoys of Henry IV who dared to bark thus: “Our lord the king commands you to abandon the apostolic see, the papacy as his own, and no longer obstruct this holy place.” O wickedness! Behold, he declared to be his own what Christ the Lord entrusted solely to Peter, prince of the apostles! For this reason the entire third holy Roman synod, justly indignant, cried anathema against him and confirmed it.

Therefore, after Gregory had struck King Henry and all who had been authors of the perpetrated crime with the sentence of anathema in the synod, he issued this letter to all Christ’s faithful, appending the sentence of excommunication pronounced against them, CXLVIII, 792.

Behold Gregory VII’s letter to all Christians concerning the excommunication pronounced against Henry IV:

> You have heard, brothers, a new and unheard-of presumption; you have heard the wicked chatter and audacity of schismatics blaspheming the name of the Lord in Blessed Peter; you have heard pride directed to the injury and insult of the holy and apostolic see—such as your fathers have neither ever seen nor heard, nor has the course of the Scriptures ever recorded as having arisen among pagans or heretics. . . . Therefore, if you believe that the keys of the kingdom of heaven were entrusted to Blessed Peter by our Lord God Jesus Christ, and if you desire that through his hands an entrance into the joys of eternal life may be open to you, you must consider how greatly you ought now to grieve over the injury inflicted upon him, etc., CXLVIII, 434.

Meanwhile, in the German regions Duke Rudolf was chosen king to defend the unity of the Catholic Church. Henry, increasingly enraged on this account, despised the counsel and assistance of the lord pope and unjustly raged against all Catholics. At length these events had not yet come to an end, etc.; but we must put an end to them here. Whoever desires fuller information should consult CXLVIII, 913, 914, 915, 916, 917, 918, and almost the whole of volume CXLVIII, in which [Col. 0150] Gregorian documents concerning these and other actions of St Gregory VII are collected.

The question concerning Henry IV and Gregory VII is treated at length in Ekkehard’s *Universal Chronicle*, CLIV, 946–1012.

Some further matters concerning Pope Gregory VII (year 1076). Pope Gregory attacks Emperor Henry on every side and turns away from him, by words and writings, all whom he can; he even alienates from him the mind of his mother Agnes. The Saxon princes who were in the emperor’s submission, being released by those to whose custody they had been entrusted, rebel at Gregory VII’s instigation. The pope himself, meeting the emperor in Lombardy (in 1071), absolves him under a false peace. For all who had earlier renounced Hildebrand, or Gregory VII, add perjury to perjury, renounce the emperor, and set over themselves as king Duke Rudolf of Burgundy. A crown had been sent to him by the pope, bearing the inscription: “The Rock gave to Peter; Peter gave the diadem to Rudolf.” Sigfrid, archbishop of Mainz, blessed him as king; and when the people of Mainz rebelled against them, Rudolf and the archbishop escaped by night. Pope Hildebrand absolves all those opposing the emperor from disloyalty and perjury. Henry soon frustrated all their plots, attacked Rudolf, and compelled him to flee . . .

Hildebrand, in 1080, as though it had been divinely revealed to him, foretold that in that year the false king would die. For he wrote to the bishop of Trent: “The feast of Blessed Peter must not pass before it becomes most certainly clear and plain to everyone that he has been most justly excommunicated.” Bonizo is wholly devoted to Gregory VII:

> On the Monday after Easter, at St Peter’s, after he had excommunicated the king, he added: “Let it be known to you all that, unless Henry repents by the feast of St Peter, he will be dead or deposed. And if this does not happen, I ought no longer to be believed.”

And indeed he foretold truly; but his conjecture concerning the false king, interpreted according to his own wish as referring to King Henry, deceived him. For King Henry engages the Saxons in a severe battle, and in the encounter the false king Rudolf is killed with many Saxon princes. From Sigebert, monk of Gembloux, CLX, 219, 220.

Gregory VII, wishing to oppose the innumerable evils arising from appointments made by imperial authority, held a Roman synod attended by fifty bishops and a multitude of priests and abbots, and established these decrees:

> If anyone henceforth receives a bishopric or abbey from the hand of any lay person, let him by no means be regarded as among the bishops, nor let any hearing be granted him as bishop or abbot. Moreover, we prohibit him from the favour of Blessed Peter and from entry into the Church.

Likewise:

> If any emperor, king, duke, margrave, count, or any secular power or person presumes to confer the investiture of bishoprics or of any ecclesiastical dignity, let him know that he is bound by the bond of the same sentence,

CXLIX, 468.

**HENRY IV, emperor.**—When an assembly of thirty bishops at Brixen in Noricum, together with an army of nobles from not only Italy but also Germany, was gathered at King Henry’s command, all agreed against Pope Hildebrand, surnamed Gregory VII. Declaring him to be a pseudo-monk, the pestiferous prince of all madness, and the chief invader of the holy apostolic see, they judged that he ought to be driven from the apostolic see, although absent, and elected Archbishop Wigbert of Ravenna to be installed in his place. The conclusion of this decree is as follows:

> Because, they say, it is evident that he was not elected by God but most rashly thrust forward by himself through deceit and money; because he overturns ecclesiastical order, disturbs the realm of the Christian Empire, threatens a Catholic and peaceable king with death of body and soul, defends a perjured king, sows discord among those in harmony, quarrels among the peaceful, scandals among brothers, divorces among spouses, and has shaken whatever appeared established for peace among those living piously: we, assembled into one body under God’s authority, relying upon the envoys and letters of nineteen bishops assembled at Mainz on the holy day of the past Pentecost, judge that this same most insolent Hildebrand—who preaches sacrileges and arsons, defends perjuries and murders, calls into question the Catholic and apostolic faith concerning the Lord’s body and blood, is an old disciple of the heretic Berengar, a worshipper of divinations and dreams, an evident necromancer, afflicted by a pythonic spirit, and therefore wandering from the true faith—must canonically be deposed and expelled; and unless, after hearing these things, he descends from the see itself, must be condemned forever,

CLIV, 951. After this Anselm of Lucca wrote, etc. See **ANSELMUS, LUC.** and, in the present Index, **GREGORY VII**.

[Col. 0151] **HENRY, prince of Trier, and other princes.**—Charter:

> We, N. N., princes of the Empire, to all who inspect this present document. From of old the Roman Mother Church embraced Germany with a certain almost sisterly love, and adorned her with that earthly name of dignity which is above every name of those who preside only temporally upon earth. Planting in her princes like chosen trees and watering them with singular grace, she gave them such increase of wondrous power that, supported by the authority of that Church as by a chosen shoot, they might through their election bring forth the one who should hold the reins of the Roman Empire. This is the lesser luminary in the firmament of the Church militant, illuminated by the greater luminary, Christ’s vicar. This is he who draws and wields the material sword at the vicar’s command, so that the shepherd of shepherds, aided by his protection, may defend and strengthen by the spiritual sword the sheep entrusted to him, restrain and correct them by the temporal sword for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of believers and good persons.

> Therefore, in order that every cause of dissension and scandal, or even occasion of rancour, between that Church and the Empire may be removed; that the two swords established in the house of the Lord may, united in their proper covenant, exercise themselves for the beneficial reform of universal government; and that we may be found sons of devotion and peace in will and deed, who are bound to foster both Church and Empire: whatever has been acknowledged, confirmed, ratified, renewed, newly granted, declared, or conceded, sworn, enacted, or done by our lord Rudolph, by God’s grace ever august king of the Romans, to the most holy father and our lord Pope Nicholas III, to his successors, and to the Roman Church itself, through privileges or any other writings of whatever tenor, concerning acknowledgments and ratifications, approvals, renewals, confirmations, donations, concessions, and deeds or acts of the other emperors and kings of the Romans, predecessors of the same king, as well as of the king himself; and especially concerning the fidelity, obedience, honour, and reverence to be rendered by Roman emperors and kings to Roman pontiffs and that Church; and concerning the possessions, honours, and rights of the same Church, specifically concerning all the land from Radicofani to Ceprano, the March of Ancona, etc., etc.—we, in the name of our principality, approve and ratify in all things and through all things. We unanimously and harmoniously offer our will, assent, and consent to all and every one of these matters, and to all other acts concerning them made in whatever manner by the same king or to be made in the future. And we promise that at no time shall we act against the foregoing or any part of it; rather, to the best of our ability, we shall procure that every one of these provisions be inviolably observed. . . . Done in the year 1279, indiction VII, in the reign of the aforesaid our lord, Lord Rudolph, king of the Romans, the glorious sixth year of his reign, XCVIII, 870–872.

**HINCMAR, archbishop of Rheims.**—There are two powers by which this world is chiefly governed: the sacred authority of pontiffs and royal power. For our Lord Jesus Christ alone could become both king and priest. But after his incarnation, resurrection, and ascension into heaven, neither has a king presumed to usurp pontifical dignity nor a pontiff royal power. Thus their actions and dignities were distinguished by him as proper to each, so that Christian kings might need pontiffs for eternal life, while pontiffs might employ the kings’ ordinances for the course of temporal affairs; in order that spiritual action might be distinct from carnal assaults, and that one serving God might not involve himself at all in secular business; and conversely, that one involved in secular affairs might not appear to preside over divine matters.

The dignity of pontiffs is greater than that of kings by so much as kings are consecrated to royal rank by pontiffs, whereas pontiffs cannot be consecrated by kings. The burden of priests is more weighty than that of kings by so much as they will render an account at the divine judgment even for kings themselves. Yet kings’ concern for human affairs is more extensive than that of priests, by so much as the King of kings has imposed upon them the burden of care for the honour, defence, and peace of the holy Church and its rulers and ministers, by promulgating laws and waging war.

And in the old Law, when priests anointed kings to rule the kingdom and placed diadems upon their heads, they gave them the Law in their hands, so that they might learn and know how they ought to govern themselves and those subject to them, and honour the priests of the Lord. And because King Uzziah presumed to offer incense, which belonged not to royal but to priestly ministry, he was struck with leprosy by God, expelled from the Temple by the priests, and confined in his house until death, CXXV, 1071.

[Col. 0152] **HUGH OF ST VICTOR, Parisian canon.**—The whole body of Christians, or the Church, comprises two orders, laity and clergy, like the two sides of one body. The laity are, as it were, on the left, because they serve the necessities of this present life. I do not call them “on the left” in the sense in which those will be set at the left to whom it will be said: “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire.” Far be it from me to presume to place good laypeople there! For those who are good, whether laypersons or clerics, will not be there; and those who are evil, whether laypersons or clerics, will be there. In the true Christian layperson there is also right and left. What is on the left in his body is of the body and is good, although it is not as excellent as what is at his right: “Length of days is in her right hand; but in her left are riches and glory” (Prov. III).

Christian laypeople, therefore, who administer earthly matters and the necessities of earthly life, are the left part of Christ’s body. Clerics, because they administer matters belonging to spiritual life, are as it were the right part of Christ’s body. Faithful Christian laypeople are permitted to possess earthly things; clerics, however, are granted spiritual things only. Thus formerly, in that earlier people, the other tribes, which bore the type of laypeople, received portions in inheritance; only the tribe of Levi, which represented ecclesiastics, was supported by tithes, offerings, and sacrificial victims.

Thus among laypeople, whose care and provision concern matters necessary for earthly life, there is earthly power. Among clerics, whose office concerns the goods of spiritual life, there is divine power. The former power is called secular; the latter is called spiritual. In both powers there are different ranks and orders of authorities, yet both are arranged under one head and are, as it were, derived from one prince and referred to one end. Earthly power has the king as its head; spiritual power has the supreme pontiff. Matters earthly and all things made for earthly life belong to the king’s power. Spiritual matters and all things assigned to spiritual life belong to the supreme pontiff’s power.

But as spiritual life is worthier than earthly life, and spirit than body, so spiritual power surpasses earthly or secular power in honour and dignity. For spiritual power has authority to establish earthly power, that it may exist, and to judge it if it is not good. Spiritual power itself was first established by God and, when it strays, can be judged by God alone, as it is written: “The spiritual person judges all things, and is judged by no one.” That spiritual power, insofar as divine institution is concerned, is both earlier in time and greater in dignity is plainly declared in the Old Testament, where the priesthood was first established by God; afterwards royal power was appointed through the priesthood at God’s command, CLXXVI, 417, 418.

Earthly power belongs to earthly life, and all things pertaining to earthly life are subject to earthly power. These all belong to the right of earthly power in two ways: earthly power itself distributes them justly to those who are to possess them, and defends them against the injustice of attackers. Just as it is the duty of prelates to administer justly to subjects the things they are to possess and defend them against injustice, so it is the duty of subjects, according to the provisions of laws and reasonable customs, to render service to their prelates both in their own persons and in their possessions.

**How the Church possesses earthly property.**—Of earthly goods belonging to earthly life, whether prelates possess them in their subjects or subjects possess them from prelates, some have been granted by the devotion of the faithful to Christ’s Churches for possession, yet with the right of earthly power preserved. This is reasonable and good, since our God is a lover of peace and true justice can approve nothing disorderly. Spiritual power does not preside in order to prejudice earthly power in its right; just as earthly power never usurps without fault what is owed to spiritual power.

Accordingly, when things belonging to earthly power are granted to Christ’s Churches, the donors are indeed bestowers of the gift, but can grant only what they possess. For subjects cannot transfer to another power what is owed to their superiors, nor may prelates introduce other possessors into things which subjects justly possess. That is, prelates must not bestow upon others what belongs to their subjects, nor may subjects presume to alter what belongs to their prelates.

Yet it should be observed that princes sometimes grant to the Church, in earthly possessions which they possess either in subjects or without subjects, only the usufruct, and sometimes both usufruct and jurisdiction. They grant usufruct without jurisdiction when they decree that the revenue of a possession be transferred to the Church’s use, but do not allow the authority to administer justice in that possession to pass under its jurisdiction. At other times they grant both jurisdiction and usufruct together. But here it must be carefully noted that, although the Church receives the revenue of an earthly possession for its use, it cannot exercise the authority of administering justice through ecclesiastical persons or secular courts; it may, however, have lay persons as officials, through whom it exercises, according to the tenor of the laws and the requirement of earthly law, the rights and judgments belonging to earthly power.

This must be understood in such a way that it recognizes that it has this authority from an earthly prince; and it must understand that these possessions can never be so separated from royal power that, when reason and necessity require it, that power does not owe protection to them and those possessions do not owe service in time of need. For just as royal power cannot give away the protection which it owes to another, so a possession held even by ecclesiastical persons cannot lawfully refuse the service owed to royal power in return for its protection, as it is written: “Render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar’s,” etc., CLXXVI, 419, 420.

**JONAS, bishop of Orléans.**—All the faithful should know that the universal Church is Christ’s body and that Christ himself is its head; and that within it there are two principal and eminent persons, namely, priestly and royal. The priestly is superior by so much as it must render an account to God even for kings themselves, as St Gelasius says. And St Fulgentius says: “As regards the life of this present time, no one in the Church is greater than the pontiff, and no one in the Christian world is found higher than the emperor.” The nature of priestly power and authority is readily evident from the Lord’s words: “Whatever you bind,” etc. Hence Emperor Constantine says: “God has appointed you priests and given you power to judge even us; and therefore we are rightly judged by you. But you cannot be judged by human beings,” etc.

Much is set forth concerning the duties and ministries of kings, CVI, 285–294. After much discussion, the following is read there:

> The royal ministry consists especially in governing and ruling God’s people with fairness and justice, and striving to ensure that they have peace and concord. A king must be the foremost defender of Churches and servants of God; it is also his office to provide diligently for the welfare and ministry of priests, and he must defend Christ’s Church by their arms and protection. . . . St Isidore says: “The rulers of the world sometimes hold the heights of power within the Church, in order that by that same power they may strengthen ecclesiastical discipline. Otherwise powers would not be necessary within the Church, except so that what a priest is unable to accomplish by the word of teaching, earthly power may command through the terror of discipline. Often through an earthly kingdom the heavenly kingdom advances, so that those who, being within the Church, act against faith and ecclesiastical discipline may be subdued by the rigour of princes; and that the ruling power may impose upon proud necks the very discipline which the Church’s benefit is unable to enforce, and may impart force so that it receives reverence.”

From the many authorities cited—in which it does not appear that kings ought to be rebuked by the supreme pontiff or deprived of their kingdom, etc.—it is declared that those who ought to govern God’s people after the king, namely dukes and counts, must necessarily be selected for appointment in such a way that they can be appointed without danger to the person appointing them. They must know that they have been placed in office in order to recognize the people of Christ as equal to themselves by nature, to preserve them mercifully and govern them justly; not to lord it over them and oppress them, nor to regard the people as their own property or subject them to themselves for their own glory. Such conduct belongs not to justice but rather to tyranny and unjust power.

The sole conclusion, therefore, is:

> Necessity strongly requires that, since the king himself will undoubtedly render an account to the most just Judge for the ministry entrusted to him, he should most diligently investigate each of the ministers placed under him, lest he himself incur divine judgment on their account. The ministers themselves must also be warned that whatever judgments they make will rebound upon them, etc.,

CVI, 290–294.

JUSTINIAN, emperor.—Since this emperor left us Novels relating to religion and selected laws, LXXII, 921–1110—laws which, like the Capitularies of Emperor Charlemagne, are partly ecclesiastical and partly civil—some matters concerning that emperor must be reported. In our judgment, whatever is blameworthy in him is likewise blameworthy in Emperor Charlemagne, who, though kings, nevertheless involved themselves too deeply in ecclesiastical affairs. Let us hear Cave’s judgment on Justinian; in such matters, as is known, each abounds in his own opinion. Baronius judged otherwise, as did we.

Justinian was born in the year 483. He had as his uncle the Emperor Justin, by whom he was educated and adopted as a son. Before becoming emperor he took as his wife Theodora, [Col. 0154] desperately devoted to the Eutychian heresy. In 519 he was made master of the soldiers by Emperor Justin and sent with an army to the East, where he conducted operations successfully against the Persians [lacuna]. In 527, being proclaimed Augustus, he began to reign with his uncle. In 528 he promulgated an edict by which he decreed that Nestorians and Eutychians, as heretics, should be punished by civil penalties; this edict was renewed five years later. In 541 he himself condemned Origen by edict, etc., etc. [lacuna] He died in 565.

There were formerly, and are still today, persons who unload whole cartloads of calumnies and insults upon that most sacred prince, distinguished no less by learning and piety than by power and the glory of his achievements. Yet no one, some say, has ever raged against Justinian’s memory with a judgment more unjust and an impudence—far beneath the station of a supreme ruler—directed against the most august, than Cardinal Baronius, exerting every power of his eloquence to present the emperor to us not as a man but as a devil. “Justinian,” says Baronius, “was a man utterly unlearned, so much so that he had never even learned the alphabet. A sacrilegious emperor, who stirred up no slight persecution; driven by madness, deranged in mind, corrupted by an evil spirit, agitated by Satan, and one who dissolved every order in the Church and made the kingdom of heaven a prison-house of hell” (*Annals*, under the year 551).

He is defended, first, with respect to his learning and piety. Procopius says: “Justinian was accustomed both to peruse books treating divine matters and to prolong discussions on them with bishops and presbyters far into the night; it was always his practice, for many weeks before Easter, to mortify his body by vigils and fastings more than ascetic—taking food once in two days, abstaining altogether from bread and other foods, and being content only with herbs seasoned with salt and vinegar and with water.” But let us hear Pope Agatho on his remarkable zeal for the Catholic faith: “Above all,” he says, “the Augustus Justinian, of pious memory, was a champion of the true apostolic faith; the uprightness of whose faith, as much as it pleased God by its sincere confession, so much did it exalt the Christian commonwealth, and its religious memory is regarded by all nations as worthy of veneration. The uprightness of his faith, disseminated throughout the whole world through his most august edicts, is praised.”

From this it is clear that, according to Baronius, the Novels are at fault because they seem, like papal bulls, to involve themselves here and there in ecclesiastical matters as though they were secular affairs; whereas, according to others, they are nothing but confirmations of papal decrees, even though the popes are not named, LXXII, 919–1110.

LEO THE GREAT (Saint), pope.—He went to Attila, king of the Huns, and delivered the whole of Italy from the danger of the enemy. After the defeat suffered on the Catalaunian Plains, Attila, bloodstained, attacked Italy. He besieged Aquileia, situated on the frontier of the province, for three years; and when, despairing of success, he was considering lifting the siege, he saw storks leaving the city for the fields with their young. Moved by this omen, he attacked the city more fiercely, finally captured it, plundered it, and burned it, sparing no class of persons; he called himself the Scourge of God. He destroyed Pavia and Milan, royal cities. Then, after devastating many places round about, as he was preparing to overthrow Rome also, Pope Leo the Great, at the urging of Emperor Valentinian, went out to meet him and rendered him so mild that he immediately departed, having promised the firmest peace, intending not to return beyond the Danube—terrified by two men who threatened him with death, swords drawn above his head, unless he yielded to the words of the holy pontiff [lacuna].

After his unsuccessful campaign on the Catalaunian Plains, Attila came through Pannonia into Italy and captured and plundered the royal cities Aquileia, Pavia, and Milan. Then, elated by success, he hastened toward Rome. Already the whole city was in alarm. Then the Roman emperor Valentinian, since he could not repel the enemy by force and arms, began to avert the danger by counsel. He sent Saint Leo the Great and gave him men of highest distinction as companions. Behold: the great pontiff came to Attila, soothed his savage spirit with words, broke his anger by eloquence, persuaded him to accept peace, and compelled him to withdraw from Italy. Historians say that, when Attila was asked why he had yielded so easily, he replied that he had been frightened by a portent: while Leo was speaking, he had seen an old man of venerable appearance, in priestly dress, threatening him with a sword unless he obeyed Leo; shaken by terror, he had collapsed as though his strength had failed, LV, 280–281.

We are stirred by divine precepts and apostolic admonitions to keep tireless watch, with active concern, over the condition of all Churches, so that, if anything anywhere is found liable to reproach, it may be recalled, through the vigilance of the clergy, either from the incompetence of ignorance or from the usurpation of presumption. For, while the command of the Lord’s voice remains in force—that command by which the most blessed Apostle Peter was instructed, through the threefold repetition of a mystical injunction, that whoever loves Christ should feed Christ’s sheep—we are constrained by reverence for that see over which, through the abundance of divine grace, we preside, [Col. 0155] to avoid, as far as we can, the danger of negligence; lest the profession of the chief apostle, who declared himself a lover of the Lord, be found lacking in us, when one who feeds negligently the flock so often entrusted to him is convicted of not loving the supreme Shepherd, LXVII, 281.

LEO III, pope.—Pope Leo III to Charles Augustus: “It is necessary that we make known to your imperial authority all that happens to us in every quarter. In the present year the monks who dwell on the holy Mount of Olives sent us a letter containing the dispute concerning faith which they had among themselves. We therefore sent them the creed of the orthodox faith, in order that all may hold, in accordance with it, our holy, Catholic, apostolic, sound, and inviolable faith. We have also sent that letter to your imperial power for your reading,” CXXIX, 1259.

LIBERIUS, pope.—Liberius was carried into exile by Constantius because he had refused to assent to the Arian heresy, and he spent two years in exile. But after the two years had passed, Constantius came to Rome. There, when Roman ladies asked him to command Liberius’s return from exile, the emperor, after consulting with his bishops, promised them that the man would return if he agreed with his bishops’ judgment. Liberius, therefore, overcome both by weariness and by an uncontrollable longing to recover his see, having also suffered force and beatings, condemned Athanasius, subscribed to the formula of faith offered him by the Arians, and entered the city of Rome.

Yet that Liberius, who seemed to have been weakened by the filth of the Arians, afterward returned to a better course, stood fearlessly for the Catholic faith, and refused to subscribe to Arian perfidy, is clear from various records. But why do we hesitate, when Pope Siricius, in his letter to the bishop of Tarragona, supplies us with a most certain proof of Liberius’s orthodoxy? For there it is maintained not merely that Liberius, with great confidence of spirit, resisted Arian audacity during those most disastrous times, by not signing the Arian formula of faith recited at the Council of Rimini—as almost everyone writes—but that he went further and rendered that council null and void, CXXVIII, 44–46.

LUCIUS III, pope.—When the emperor was making for Italy, Pope Lucius III left the city of Rome in order to go out and meet him, intending to discuss with him, in 1184, the affairs of the Christian commonwealth, which had begun to decline greatly in Asia. The emperor began to negotiate with him concerning the patrimony of the powerful lady Matilda in Italy, who, under the Emperors Henry father and son, had done much for the Church, and who, when departing this life, had left much property for that same Church to possess; the emperor was claiming it as belonging to imperial right, CCI, 1067.

LOUIS THE PIOUS, emperor.—Under this emperor, or king, although the supreme papal dominion in the City and consequently in its duchy is established from several letters in Charlemagne’s code, it must be said and acknowledged that the imperial dominion of Louis the Pious, Charlemagne, and others in the City was a participation in the same supreme authority belonging to the pontiffs. Thus, although the Roman pontiffs were lords in Rome, their rule was not free from the participation of the senate and people of Rome, who rendered an oath of fidelity to the pontiff as supreme ruler, without prejudice nevertheless to the Roman civil law or right. At that time the Roman pontiff was indeed supreme ruler, but by no means absolute in administering the commonwealth.

Nor did Stephen IV or Saint Pope Paschal devise anything new concerning the senate and people when they afterward wished their own supreme authority in the imperial city to rest upon imperial authority. The Roman pontiffs had never been accustomed to this; rather, they always wished that very administration of the Senate and People of Rome which their predecessors had employed, in no respect diminished, to be confirmed. For there are various diplomas expressed in these words: “Just as from your predecessors until now you have held and administered these things in your power and jurisdiction,” CVIII, 567–568.

There were, however, many dominions deriving from the generosity of princes in which the Roman pontiff alone ruled as an absolute prince, without any participation by senate and people; for their dominion had been granted to Peter alone and to his successors. But in these cases it was said: “Which you bestowed upon blessed Peter for the great reward of your soul,” etc., etc. Elsewhere, concerning many such patrimonies, it is said: “Which through various emperors, patricians also, and other God-fearing persons, for the reward of their souls and remission of sins, were granted in the regions of Tuscany, Spoleto, and Corsica—as also the Sabine patrimony—to blessed Peter the apostle and to the holy Church of God and apostolic Roman Church,” XCVIII, 568.

OTTO I, king.—It is not surprising that this emperor’s diploma is said to have been written in letters of gold. [Col. 0156] The donation of Aripert, king of the Lombards, had already been written in the same manner. It is said that “Aripert, in letters of gold, restored by his own right to the blessed prince of the apostles the donation of the patrimony of the Cottian Alps, which for a long time had been deprived of the Church’s right and held by that same people,” XCVIII, 589. “Otto I’s diploma concerning several donations of Charlemagne differs somewhat from the diploma of Louis the Pious,” XCVIII, 594.

This diploma nevertheless contains certain particulars, namely: “Moreover,” he adds, “we offer to you, blessed Peter, apostle, and to your vicar, Lord Pope John, and to his successors, for the remedy of our soul, that of our son, and those of our parents, from our own kingdom, cities and towns with their fisheries: namely Rieti, Amiternum, Furconium, Norcia, Balva, and Marsi; and elsewhere the city of Teramo with its patrimonies,” etc., XCVIII, 606–610.

PAUL (Saint), pope (A.D. 757).—He lived in the times of the emperors Constantine and Leo, etc., CXXVIII, 1136, etc.

Constantine had adopted the plan, against the Apostolic See, of recovering possession of the Exarchate of Ravenna, which Pippin, having defeated the Lombards, had lawfully reduced under his own power and had granted to the Roman pontiff to possess with supreme authority and beneficial ownership. Understanding very well that the emperor could never attain his desired end so long as the resources of the Franks aided the pontiff, and unless he drew the king of the Lombards over to his side by the lure of advantage, he left nothing untried in order to accomplish both objects. Accordingly, he sent envoys into Francia, who left no stone unturned in order to injure the pontiffs’ reputation and draw King Pippin away from the alliance concluded with the pope.

At the same time, he had agents at Ravenna and throughout the Exarchate who incited the peoples to revolt against the pontiff. He also ordered a marriage to be proposed between Leo, his son, whom he had associated with himself in the empire, and Giselda, Pippin’s daughter [lacuna]. But he could not detach Pippin from the Catholic faith and the defense of the Holy See. Constantine therefore turned elsewhere and lent his ear to the king of the Lombards, who promised to join alliance with him against the pope. They stipulated a treaty on these terms: that both would fight with united forces in order to bring Ravenna and Otranto under their control; that the Lombards would possess the former, while the Greeks would possess the latter together with the adjacent region; and that the emperor would promptly dispatch a very strong fleet to Italy for the stated purpose.

Copronymus, however, did not do this, persuading himself that the forces he possessed in Sicily and neighboring places would be sufficient to recover Ravenna without Lombard help, at a time when King Pippin could not aid the pontiff because he was occupied by war with the dukes of Bavaria and Aquitaine, who were subject to him. But the pontiff, having opportunely discovered Constantine’s plans, immediately disclosed them to King Pippin, so that he might compel the king of the Lombards, the dukes of Spoleto and Benevento, and other neighboring powers to defend the Holy See should the Greeks perhaps take up arms against it.

When the emperor learned this, he undertook none of the measures he had planned. On the contrary, the king of the Lombards caused Paul trouble throughout his pontificate. First, he refused to restore to the Holy See the cities of Bologna, Imola, Ancona, and others, which he had promised to restore in return for papal support against Ratchis, his rival for the Lombard kingdom. Then he brought arms into the Pentapolis and devastated it. Finally, he expelled the dukes of Spoleto and Benevento, who were dependent upon the Holy See, and installed others subject to himself [lacuna]. But, frightened by some unexpected event, the Lombard restored to Paul part of what was due to the pontiff by right and promised to restore whatever else he had withheld. Yet the king, or his minister Desiderius, did not keep his promises. Therefore, so long as he lived, the king of the Lombards was troublesome to the holy pontiff, as the pontiff’s last letter openly shows: “Let your most excellent Christianity know for certain that, if the territories of our cities invaded by those same Lombards and the patrimonies not restored are not returned to us, they will plot to invade even those which they restored at first,” CXXVIII, 1145–1147.

PETER DAMIAN (Saint).—“But since, among the other evils which arise in our times, violent men also insolently oppress the Churches themselves and seize estates or whatever goods belong to sacred right, some are troubled by the question whether the rulers of Churches ought to seek vengeance, repaying evils with evils after the manner of secular people. For most men, as soon as the violence of injury is inflicted upon them, immediately rush to declare wars, marshal ranks of armed men, and thus perhaps avenge themselves upon their enemies more harshly than they were injured.

“This seems plainly absurd enough to me: that the Lord’s own priests should attempt what is forbidden to vulgar crowds, and should uphold by their deeds what they attack in words. For what seems more contrary to Christian law than the requital of injuries? Where, I ask, are the many proclamations of Scripture? Where is what the Lord says: ‘If anyone takes what is yours, do not demand it back’? etc., etc.

“Indeed, the life which our Savior lived in the flesh no less than evangelical preaching is set before us as a rule of discipline to be observed. Therefore, just as he overcame all the obstacles of a raging world not through vengeance of strict judgment but through the invincible majesty of unshaken patience, so he teaches us rather to endure the world’s fury equably than either to seize arms or to answer one injury with another—especially since kingship and priesthood are distinguished by their respective duties: the king uses the arms of this world, while the priest girds himself with the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God [lacuna].

“Through charity the Son of God descended from heaven; through patience he conquered the devil. Equipped with these virtues, the founding apostles established the holy Church, and its champions, the holy martyrs, triumphantly endured diverse punishments of death. If, therefore, nowhere is it permitted to seize weapons of iron for the faith by which the universal Church lives, how can armored ranks rage with swords for the earthly and transitory resources of the Church? Moreover, when holy men prevail against heretics and worshippers of idols, they do not kill them; rather, they do not shrink from being killed by them for the Catholic faith. How then can one believer attack another with swords over the loss of insignificant things, when he knows that the other has likewise been redeemed with him by Christ’s blood?” CXLIV, 314–316 [lacuna].

These words must be read attentively, lest anyone either take occasion for error or suppose the author to have strayed in doctrine. For he may seem to have held that the pope or other ecclesiastical rulers cannot defend ecclesiastical goods by war, if necessary, because the Church possesses no temporal sword, but only a spiritual one; hence he wishes the offices of kingship and priesthood to be divided so that the king uses the arms of the world and the priest girds himself with the spiritual sword [lacuna].

But before we draw Damian’s words, and other things which he states with considerable emphasis and without distinction, to a pious and true meaning from the words themselves rather than from an alien sense, it is necessary briefly to set forth the true and Catholic doctrine.

First, it must be laid down that this discussion concerns an ecclesiastical ruler as such, or the pontiff insofar as he is pontiff. For if he is considered as a temporal lord, by reason of the proper and direct temporal dominion and jurisdiction which he possesses in his lands, there is no doubt that he possesses the same right of war as other supreme kings and temporal lords, so far as justice is concerned—although, in conducting war, he ought to preserve the religious character and decorum due to pontifical dignity, which is his chief dignity and obliges him, in using the temporal sword, to observe a manner suited to pontifical dignity [lacuna]. But Peter Damian does not treat this point.

Second, it must be laid down that, by virtue of pontifical dignity, the pope possesses not only a spiritual sword but also, in some manner, a temporal sword, as very many Fathers understood from the Gospel words: “Behold, here are two swords.” The Church also speaks thus of Peter: “You are shepherd of all, prince of the apostles; God entrusted to you all the kingdoms of the world.” The reason is that spiritual power, unless it had temporal power in some manner joined to it, would be ineffective and weak; and therefore, since God’s works are perfect and rightly ordered, when he gave Peter supreme spiritual authority, or the spiritual sword, he also gave him the temporal or material sword insofar as it is appropriate to the end of the other power. Thus Pope Nicholas said to the archbishop of Trier and the defenders of the Church that they should use the spiritual and material sword until ecclesiastical goods were recovered.

Alas, these things recall the battle of Castelfidardo [lacuna]. “Castelfidardo, holy land, land reddened by the blood of martyrs; battlefield where the vanquished was greater than the victor, who will never be properly absolved of his victory; holy hill, from which the eternal groaning of stricken right will rise forever toward God.”

Hence, third, it must be laid down that the pope possesses the spiritual sword in one way as pope and the temporal sword in another. For he possesses the spiritual sword in himself and directly; but the temporal sword only indirectly, that is, by reason of the spiritual power and insofar as it is appropriate to its end. Thus he alone receives the spiritual sword immediately from God, and through him it is derived to ecclesiastical persons who share in it; it is found in laymen in no way. But the temporal sword exists in itself and directly in the emperor and temporal kings or rulers, not by derivation from the pontiff, but through other titles and means [Col. 0158] by which such power is customarily justly acquired or obtained by hereditary right. For that supreme authority which the pope has indirectly in temporal matters does not take away the proper rights of other rulers or deprive them of their direct dominions and power. For this reason jurists commonly say that the pontiff, by reason of his pontificate, has no jurisdiction in temporal affairs, etc. [lacuna].

Finally, it must be laid down that, although by virtue of his power the pope possesses the material sword in the manner already explained, he nevertheless ought not to use it himself, nor through ecclesiastical persons, except in self-defense in a case of extreme necessity; rather, he should use it through secular rulers, whom he can command to employ it in his defense or for just vengeance when necessary, etc. [lacuna]. Yet, in our judgment, these matters are not clear; and though we understand them as concerning fact, the question of right still remains ambiguous [lacuna]. Let the reader judge, CXLIV, 317–320.

RUPERT, abbot of Deutz.—In sending out the apostles, Jesus Christ forbade them to have either gold or silver [lacuna] or a staff (Matthew 10:9); yet in Mark 6:8 he commanded them to carry nothing except a staff. To resolve this difficulty, Rupert distinguishes two kinds of staffs: one belonging to the kings of the nations, the other to the disciples of Jesus Christ. The staff of the kings of the nations is a staff of domination; the staff of Christ’s disciples is a staff of charity, a staff of pastoral duty that watches attentively over the salvation of souls. The staff of domination was not given to the ministers of the Gospel of peace; it is this domination that Jesus Christ forbids them here in saying, “Carry no staff.” He forbids it still more expressly by these words: “The kings of the nations lord it over them, and those who exercise authority over them take the title of benefactors. But you are not to do so” (Luke 22:25). This is the staff, or domination, that Jesus Christ forbids his disciples. Saint Peter, instructed in this truth, forbids pastors to lord it over the Lord’s inheritance. Likewise Saint Paul declares to the Corinthians that he is very far from exercising dominion over their faith, CLXX, 756.

Rupert expressed himself thus, CLXVIII, 1489–1490: “‘Do not possess [lacuna] nor a staff’;” and elsewhere: “‘He commanded them to take nothing on the way except a staff only.’” Indeed, if we knew of only one staff, this question would be more difficult to resolve. But now there are two staffs: one of the kings of the nations, the other of Christ’s disciples. The staff of the kings of the nations is a staff of domination; the staff of Christ’s disciples is a staff of love, a staff of pastoral office, keeping diligent watch over the care of souls. That staff which is domination was not granted to the ministers of the Gospel of peace, and it is forbidden here by the words, “nor a staff.” Moreover, elsewhere: “The kings of the nations lord it over them, and those who have authority over them are called benefactors; but you are not so.”

But the staff of discipline, the staff of pastoral concern and watchfulness, he not only never forbade, but even commanded from the beginning—“from the beginning,” I say, that is, from the time when he first began to send shepherds of souls. Such indeed were Moses and Aaron. When the Lord sent them, he commanded them to take nothing on their way except a staff only: “‘What,’ he says to Moses, ‘do you hold in your hand?’ He answered, ‘A staff.’ He said: ‘Throw it on the ground.’ He threw it down, and it was changed into a serpent,” etc. “‘Take also this staff in your hand, with which you shall perform the signs.’”

What else did he command Moses or his brother Aaron to take on their journey except that staff alone? Thus, certainly, he commanded all evangelists, all preachers of the Gospel, to take nothing else on their journey except the vigor of pastoral care, the law of life and discipline, and, as a sign of this thing, sometimes to carry a material staff in the hand. But in this evangelist he forbade the staff of domination, CLXVIII, 1489–1490.

URBAN II, pope.—After the Synod of Toulouse had been dissolved, Raynerius, Urban’s legate, traveling to Spain passed through Catalonia. There Raymond, count of Barcelona, having gathered the nobles of the province, solemnly donated the city of Tarragona to the Apostolic See on the condition that he and his descendants should “hold it, together with all that pertained to it, by the hand and word of Saint Peter and of his vicar, the apostolic bishop of the Roman See, paying him for five years an annual tribute of twenty-five pounds of the purest silver.” This donation was made through the hand of Lord Raynerius, cardinal of the Roman Church, “who,” says Raymond, “now exercises the legation in our regions,” in 1097. The instrument of this donation was published by Labbe, Aguirre, and other collectors of councils, CLI, 71.

ZACHARIAS (Saint), pope.—He found the whole province of Italy greatly disturbed, together with the Roman duchy, etc. [lacuna]. But in a remarkable embassy to Liutprand, king of the Lombards, he preached those saving truths; and Liutprand, moved by the admonitions of that holy [Col. 0159] man, promised to restore the four aforesaid cities which he had taken from the Roman duchy, and afterward did restore them. These cities are Horta, Polimartium, Ameria, and Bleda, CXXVIII, 1049.

The king of the Lombards restored to Zacharias, Roman pontiff, by title of donation to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, the Sabine patrimony, which had been taken away for almost thirty years; likewise the territories of Narni, Osimo, and Ancona; also Numana, and the valley called Magna, situated in the territory of Sutri.

First the city of Ameria; then Horta; and when they had met at the fortress of Polimartium and the king had received Zacharias, Grimoald, the king’s envoy, delivered the city of Blera to Pope Zacharias, CXXVIII, 1051.

At the same time, Ratchis, king of the Lombards, advanced in violent anger to capture the city of Perugia, as he had the other towns of the Pentapolis, and vigorously attacked it after encircling it. When the most holy pope heard this, immediately trusting in divine hope, he took some members of his clergy together with leading men and hastened as quickly as possible to that city. Having bestowed many gifts on the king and earnestly begged him, he removed him, with the Lord’s help, from the siege of the city. Preaching saving doctrine to him, with God as author, he desired to incline his mind toward a special devotion.

A few days later King Ratchis, abandoning royal dignity, came devoutly with his wife and children to the thresholds of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. Having received prayer from the aforesaid most holy pope and having become a cleric, he put on the monastic habit with his wife and children, CXXVIII, 1058.

In his time, Carloman, son of Charles, king of the Franks, abandoning the glory of this present life and earthly power, arrived devoutly at blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, with some of his followers; he entrusted himself to that apostle of God, pledged that he would remain in a special religious habit, and received from that most holy pope the yoke of the clerical state. Among many other gifts, he offered to the blessed Apostle Peter, before the Confession, a silver arch, etc. After some time he went to the monastery of Saint Benedict, situated in the territory of Aquino, where he solemnly professed by oath that he would end his life.

Rome and its duchy readily passed from the Greeks to the Roman pontiff because the people refused obedience to the heretical emperor on account of Leo’s heretical edicts. The Roman duchy, of which frequent mention is made and whose governors were chosen by the emperors, consisted of the city of Rome together with fortresses, towns, and villages, including those in parts of Tuscany. These were Porto, Centumcellae, Caere, Bleda, Maturana, Sutri, Nepi, the Castle of Gallese, Horta, Polimartium, Ameria, Todi, Perugia, Narni, Otricoli, Segni, Anagni, Ferentino, Alatri, Patrica, Frosinone, and Tivoli.

That this duchy was under the control of the Roman See in Gregory II’s time is apparent even from the fact that the Roman army, with the pontiff himself in command, suppressed rebels and the tyrant Tiberius, and compelled Liutprand to restore the places that he had usurped in this duchy. Therefore, from the time of Gregory II, in A.D. 714, and of his successors, clearer indications of supreme temporal power occur, CXXVIII, 1067. (In A.D. 708, CXXVIII, 960, the Roman duchy and the Roman commonwealth were governed by dukes sent by the emperors.)

We read in the *Life of Emperor Charles*: “The Merovingian family, from which the Franks had customarily made kings for themselves, is believed to have lasted down to King Childeric, who by command of Stephen, Roman pontiff, was deposed, shorn, and thrust into a monastery.” This means that, after Pope Zacharias had died, as will be explained below, before Pippin was crowned by Zacharias’s command, Stephen is to be understood to have confirmed the instruction of his predecessor Zacharias. For this does not concern Pippin’s second coronation, XCVIII, 27. An explanation of these matters follows, CXXVIII.

Charles Martel, who had received from Gregory II the title of patrician of the Romans, had two sons, Carloman and Pippin. The former, abandoning the glory of the present life, received the yoke of clerical office from the supreme pontiff, afterward went to a monastery, and ended his life there. Pippin still remained in the palace of the Franks. Popes Gregory II and III had long before entered into alliances with the Franks, and Pope Zacharias had renewed them. Moreover, since the mayors of the palace of the Franks had long arrogated supreme power to themselves, nothing was left to the descendants of the great Clovis except the royal name.

Pippin, surnamed the Short, the last of the mayors of the palace, at last undertook the great enterprise of assuming royal dignity, title, and right for himself. [Col. 0160] In order to carry out this plan and ensure its firm and ratified outcome, he understood that, besides the assent of the magnates of the kingdom, it was necessary to establish it by the authority of the Apostolic See, lest subject peoples should suppose that they could change kings at their own discretion.

A very suitable opportunity offered itself for securing the Holy See’s support for Pippin’s cause, since he alone could suppress the Lombards and sustain religion, endangered on every side. A very recent author (P. Daniel, *History of France*) says that Pippin used the assistance of Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, to undertake the matter and to test Zacharias’s disposition as to what his judgment would be in the affair. Pippin therefore asked that it be determined which of the two ought justly to be called and be king: the man who sat securely at home, or the man who bore the care of the whole kingdom and the burdens of every business. Pope Zacharias declared that it was better for the one in whom supreme power resided to be called king; and, by his authority, commanded Pippin to be made king.

In accordance with the Roman pontiff’s decree, Pippin was called king of the Franks; he was anointed with sacred anointing for this honorable dignity by the hand of Saint Boniface of blessed memory and, in the Frankish manner, raised to the throne in the royal city of Soissons. Childeric, who falsely bore the title of king, was shorn and sent to a monastery, and he was the last Merovingian to rule the Franks. Then the land rested from battles, when Pippin, together with the counsel and consent of all the Franks, after a report had been sent to the Apostolic See and authority received, was elevated to the royal throne by the election of all Francia, with the consecration of bishops and the submission of princes, together with Queen Bertrada.

The rationale of these acts will appear from what follows. Zacharias succeeded Pope Gregory III. At the same time, Chilperic succeeded King Charles Martel—or rather Pippin succeeded him in fact, since Chilperic was less than even an inactive king. Hardly had Zacharias been raised to Peter’s see when he negotiated through envoys with the king of the Lombards for the restoration of cities. The king promised what he had already promised Gregory III, but did not keep his promises. Yet Zacharias, energetic and fearless, went to the Lombard camp within the territory of Spoleto and did not return to Rome until the patrimonies taken long before had been restored, together with the four cities taken two years earlier, of which he himself entered into possession. Then he entered Rome.

From these things it appears that the Roman pontiff then needed a strong and powerful protector. Pippin was that protector, who already then, and afterward, by the glory of his arms, extended the patrimonies of the Holy See in every direction, CXXVIII, 1068–1069.

The Annals of Bertin state: “Pope Stephen confirmed Pippin with holy anointing, and with him anointed his two sons, Charles and Carloman”; therefore, if he “confirmed” him, Pippin had previously been inaugurated. The Annals of Fulda read: “Pope Zacharias, by the authority of Saint Peter the Apostle, commanded the Frankish people that Pippin, who exercised royal power, should also enjoy the dignity of the royal name. Thus King Childeric, the last of the Merovingians to rule the Franks, was deposed and sent into a monastery. But Pippin, in the city of Soissons, was anointed as king by Saint Boniface, Archbishop, and raised to the royal dignity,” CXXVIII, 1070, 1071.

Was Stephen, or Zacharias, the author in fact of Childeric’s deposition and Pippin’s elevation? It cannot be attributed to Stephen II, since when Stephen II was inaugurated Pippin was already reigning. Then to Zacharias? Not at all, even though that same Zacharias did not know who was the true king of the Franks; indeed, even though in his letter to Boniface, Archbishop of Mainz, he indicates that he regarded Charles Martel, Pippin’s father, as king . . . Yet since almost all writers ultimately make Stephen the author of Childeric’s deposition and of Pippin’s release from his oath in order to become king, what is to be decided?

Finally, in order to reach a conclusion, we shall say that King Pippin had been raised to the royal throne three years earlier by the authority and command of Pope Zacharias of holy memory, by the anointing with holy chrism at the hands of the most blessed priests of Gaul, and by the election of all the Franks. Afterwards, at the hands of the same Pope Stephen, on one day in the church of the aforesaid blessed martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, he was anointed and blessed as king and patrician. Thus Childeric’s deposition and Pippin’s elevation to the throne must be referred both to Zacharias and to Stephen. For Pope Zacharias assented to the envoys sent to him by the Frankish nation—namely Burchard, Bishop of Würzburg, and Fulrad the chaplain—who requested that he declare whom he judged worthy of the kingdom: the man who bore the name of king while doing nothing besides, like Childeric, or rather the man who discharged all the business of the kingdom, like Pippin. By the authority of the blessed Apostle Peter, he declared Pippin king and [Col. 0161] ordered that he be anointed king by Boniface, Archbishop of Mainz; this was done in the city of Soissons. Again, after three years, the same Pippin was anointed with chrism and crowned by Pope Stephen in the monastery of Saint Dionysius, together with his wife Bertrada and his sons Charles and Carloman. By this, the writers are reconciled: some attribute Pippin’s elevation to the throne to Zacharias, others to Stephen. If any chronological discrepancy occurs in the annals of writers from different peoples, although all agree most fully on the substance of what was done, it should either be disregarded or may be reconciled if the various events preceding and following this matter are carefully assigned to their proper years, CXXVIII, 1081, 1082.

## ARTICLE II.—On the Exercise of Pontifical Power in Temporal Matters

Reasons from natural law.—“Neither eminent domain nor any law can make a sovereign master of a prince’s state or of citizens’ property without prior compensation. He cannot take for himself what does not belong to him, nor give to one person what belongs to another. If a king alone, or a king together with a political body, or political bodies without a king, can at any time despoil states or despoil the properties of that state, tomorrow they will be able to do what they have been able to deny. In that case no one could feel secure in his social position . . . If the right of property is not sacred, liberty is violated; for property is liberty’s bulwark. Liberty in turn defends property . . . If he who possesses something this morning may possess nothing this evening and fall back into dependence, then there are no longer national morals; for morals are formed only through the permanence of things. At the same time there will no longer be any enduring society. A wise and just government must be restrained by ideas of morality and equity.” (CHATEAUBRIAND, *To a Peer of France*.)

Reasons from the sacred character of the oath. (Pontifical profession.)—“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Amen. I, N., elected and now, by God’s grace, the humble master of this holy Church of the Roman apostolic see, profess to you, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, to whom the keys of the kingdom of heaven [were given], etc. . . ., and to your holy Church, which today I undertake to govern under your protection, that, so long as I live, I shall not abandon it, etc.; but [I shall preserve] the integrity of the right faith, with every effort even unto blood . . . and I shall guard and preserve the unimpaired possessions of the Church, neither alienating them nor giving them, in fief, rent . . . or in any manner whatsoever, for any cause; and I shall take care that they be kept unimpaired. I shall diminish or alter nothing of the tradition which I have found canonically handed down and observed by my most approved predecessors, nor admit any novelty; but, as their disciple and follower, I shall with all the efforts of my mind preserve and venerate what I find canonically handed down . . . I, the aforesaid, by God’s grace elected bishop of this apostolic see of the Roman Church, in making this my profession, have bodily offered this oath to you, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, with a ready mind and conscience . . .” (*From Book Ten*, CV, 40–44.)

Reasons of expediency.—Gregory VII (Hildebrand) was the first pope to use the lever of spiritual authority to move and shake the world. As a monk of Cluny, Hildebrand had seen reigning around him only the blind and brutal violence of the great, or deceitful perversity, the companion of ignorance. Endowed with one of those supple and proud souls that dream great things and know how to prepare them, he hoped to reform all this. He therefore set his sights upon the papacy, and attained it on 20 April 1073. Having become master of spiritual power, this pope sought to impose his iron will upon the masters of the earth, and launched excommunications in order to dispose of empires, kingdoms, duchies, marquisates, and counties; his reign was nothing but a struggle with sovereigns. Yet he had the advantage of freeing the Church from the servitude to which earthly powers wished to subject it. He died on 24 May 1083. The same has been said of Boniface VIII, whose history we also give.

Reasons of disadvantage.—“From our imperial camp at Vienna, 17 May 1809. Napoleon, Emperor of the French, King of Italy, Protector of the Confederation of the Rhine;

“Considering that when Charlemagne, Emperor of the French and our august predecessor, made a gift of several counties to the bishops of Rome, he gave them only as fiefs and for the good of his states, and that by this gift Rome did not cease to be part of his empire;

[Col. 0162] “Considering that, since this mingling of a spiritual power with temporal authority, there has been, as there still is, a source of disputes, and that it has too often led the pontiffs to employ the influence of the former in support of the claims of the latter; so that spiritual interests and the affairs of heaven, which are immutable, have become entangled with earthly affairs, which by their nature change according to circumstances and the politics of the times;

“That everything we have proposed in order to reconcile the security of our armies, the tranquility and welfare of our peoples, and the dignity and integrity of our empire with the temporal claims of the Popes has not been capable of realization, we have decreed, etc. . . .—ART. I. The States of the Pope are united to the French Empire, etc. . . NAPOLEON.”

With these preliminaries stated, let the question be brought under examination.

ADRIAN IV, Pope.—Frederick, by God’s grace Emperor of the Romans and ever Augustus, to all the citizens of Tivoli. We wish your community to know that, out of reverence for blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we have relinquished the city of Tivoli to our most beloved and reverend father in Christ, Pope Adrian, while in every respect preserving imperial right. Therefore we release all and each of the citizens of Tivoli from the allegiance which you recently swore to us, earnestly commanding and enjoining you to stand faithfully by that venerable Pope Adrian, serve him devoutly, and strive to obey him devoutly as the Lord, knowing that, as has been said, you are released from the oath of allegiance which you recently made, while imperial right is preserved in all respects, CLXXXVIII, 1356.

William, King of Sicily, presumptuously raised his horns against his mother and lady, the most holy Roman Church, and, having assembled an army, caused the land of Saint Peter to be invaded in hostile fashion. His army accordingly besieged the city of Benevento for some time and burned its suburbs. Then, violently entering the borders of Campania, it likewise burned the town of Ceprano, the castle of Babucum, and other undefended places. For these and other offenses, therefore, the aforesaid Pope Adrian, drawing Peter’s sword, struck that king with the sword of excommunication, CLXXXVIII, 1353.

BENEDICT, monk of Saint Andrew.—In ancient times imperial splendor flourished at Rome. Under its dominion various kingdoms stood, and all nations bent their own necks in submission to it. It therefore established consuls, who by daily practice directed the reins of government through counsel. Offices were distributed among senators and magistrates. Imperial majesty, however, was honored and extolled by all solely with praises and honors. After Christ’s coming and the glory of his ascension, the Roman Empire transferred itself to Byzantium, which was called Constantinople after Constantine the Great Caesar. Because it gloried in the Roman Empire, it was called New Rome, though in such a way that glorious Old Rome was set before the rest. There blessed Peter and Paul, teacher of the nations, were crowned with martyrdom, so that, just as Rome through its ancient walls had been the head of many nations amid the division of idols, so it might be called the head and mistress of all Christians in the unity of the true faith and undivided Deity, possessing primacy over all Christendom through the privilege received from Christ, where he says: “You are Peter, etc.,” CL, 97.

BONIFACE VIII, Pope.—See PHILIP THE FAIR.

CONSTANTINE AUGUSTUS THE GREAT, Emperor.—Besides the innumerable gifts that Constantine bestowed upon Pope Saint Sylvester for building and adorning the churches which he founded, he further granted him very many lordships, CXXVIII, 1514–1518. Among them were: the house of Datianus; Coele in Amphrodisia; Pristinus; Popina; the garden of Maro; the estates of Sibylla, Timialia, Euthimica, Potinopolis, etc.; Patras, Anglesis, Terega, Falisca, Nymphas, Angulas, etc., CXXVII, 1520–1522; the estates of the counts, Timia, Fronimusa, Cyprias, Basilea, Sponsas, etc., CXXVII, 1523, 1524. He also assigned to the Roman pontiff the estate of Veranum, the water of Turia, the Sabine territory, the estate of Suturatae, Micina, Thermulae, Aranae, etc., CXXVII, 1525; moreover, the island of Sardinia, Mesenum, Attitiae, the Two Houses; Massa Milliana, the estate of Suri, the estate of Gargilianus, Massa Nemus, Armationum, etc., CXXVII, 1525, 1526.
