Constantine bestowed very many lands upon the Churches of God, now granting grain allowances for the support of poor widows and orphans, VIII, 77.

FREDERICK, Emperor of the Romans.—Frederick, by God’s grace Emperor of the Romans and ever Augustus, to all the citizens of Tivoli, his favor and goodwill.

We wish your community to know that, out of reverence for blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we have relinquished the city of Tivoli to our most beloved and reverend father in Christ, Pope Adrian, while in every respect preserving imperial right. Therefore we release all and each of the citizens of Tivoli from the allegiance which you recently swore to us, earnestly commanding and enjoining you to stand faithfully by that venerable Pope Adrian, serve him devoutly, and strive to obey him devoutly as the Lord, knowing that, as has been said, you are released from the oath of allegiance which you recently made, while imperial right is preserved in all respects. CLXXXVIII, 1356.

GARNIER, Abbot.—(Morin, *History of the Origin and Progress of the Sovereignty of the Popes*.) Pope Stephen III, more urgently pressed than ever by the king of the Lombards, had no hope left except in the valor and piety of the French. At the beginning of these new troubles, he therefore wrote to King Pippin and his children to warn them of Aistulf’s perfidy, set before them the outrages which he inflicted daily upon the Romans, and especially to entreat them to compel him by their authority to carry out the donation they had made to the Holy See, not one article of which he had fulfilled. In response to these complaints, Pippin sent an abbot of great authority named Garnier, to ascertain the truth and invite the Lombards to keep their promise. Garnier went to Aistulf to demand satisfaction for the See of Rome and addressed him thus: “Sire, the King of France, my master, has sent me to Your Majesty to request that you no longer harass the Pope or the Romans, and that you fulfill your promise by placing the exarchate of Ravenna in the hands of His Holiness, under the conditions agreed upon between him and Your Majesty,” etc., XCVI, 1370, 1371.

GREGORY II, Pope.—In the time of this holy pontiff many supreme rulers showed singular reverence toward the Holy See. For Theodo II, Duke of Bavaria, whom Saint Rupert, Bishop of Salzburg, had converted to the Catholic faith, was the first of all German princes who, for devotion’s sake, came to Rome to visit Saint Peter and his successor, the supreme pontiff. Yet in piety Theodo is surpassed by Ina, King of the English, who not only came to Rome to see the tombs of the apostles, but, before departing from the City, is said to have granted blessed Peter a penny from every household in his kingdom. This was long called by the English *Romescot*, but in Latin *Peter’s penny* (*denarius Petri*). Anastasius speaks, in passing, of Eudo, Duke of Aquitaine, imploring the Holy See’s aid against the Saracens and of his remarkable victory following the pontifical blessing; of the Lombard King Liutprand restoring to the Apostolic See the Cottian Alps, recently invaded anew; and finally of Lombard usurpations at Benevento, etc. The most illustrious Archbishop Sommier renders him into French, in order to relate together rulers’ acts of service toward the Holy See, LXXXIX, 463, 464.

GREGORY VI, Pope.—Since the history of this pontiff belongs in some measure to the history of Gregory VII, it seems appropriate to set it forth here so that the persons, affairs, and times of that period may be rightly judged.

When three usurpers of the sacred throne—Benedict VIII, Sylvester III, and John XX—had been expelled, Gregory VI was acclaimed supreme pontiff in 1045 by the votes of the Roman clergy and people.

He was considered a truly genuine and legitimate pontiff by the holiest and most learned men of his age: namely Hildebrand, later Gregory VII, Peter Damian, and others like them, implacable enemies of simoniacs. For Gregory persuaded the pseudo-pontiffs to withdraw from the Holy See not through ambition, but through zeal for piety—albeit by means of money. The Roman citizens, and especially the clergy, therefore chose him as supreme pontiff, mindful of the benefit bestowed upon them and regarding him as the liberator of God’s Church. Gregory VII himself, at the Roman council held in 1080, acknowledges this Gregory as a legitimate pontiff. Glaber, an author of that time, says of this pontiff: “Then Benedict was expelled from the See with the consent of the entire Roman people and by command of the Emperor; and in his place was appointed Gregory, a most religious man conspicuous for holiness, a Roman by nation, whose good reputation restored for the better whatever his predecessor had defiled.”

But let us see what Gregory did after becoming pope. William of Malmesbury, who flourished and wrote shortly afterwards, says: “Pope Gregory VI was a man of great piety and severity. He found the condition of the Roman apostolate so diminished through the neglect of his predecessors that, apart from a few towns near the City and the offerings of the faithful, he had almost nothing with which to support himself. Cities and distant possessions belonging by right to the Church had been seized by robbers; public ways and highways throughout Italy were crowded with bandits, [Col. 0164] so that no pilgrim could pass with impunity except with a larger company . . . Over the very bodies of the holy apostles and martyrs, above the sacred altars, swords were drawn; offerings of those approaching were scarcely laid down before they were snatched from their hands, and, when seized, were consumed in feasting and the abuses of prostitutes . . .” Gregory VI put an end, so far as he was able, to many of these evils.

Finally, however, when Emperor Henry III had chosen the antipope Clement III, Gregory VI himself, after having in some measure established the true pontificate, went to Sutri at Henry’s request. In a full council held there, in order to procure for the Roman Church its long-desired peace and to set a memorable example before the other three who had invaded the Holy See, he voluntarily abdicated in 1047 the pontificate which he had commendably governed for two years and eight months; and Gregory VII was elected in his place, CXLII, 569–572.

GREGORY VII (Saint), Pope.—Henry, King of the Germans and likewise Emperor of the Romans, had endured no slight dispute and controversy with Lord Pope Gregory VII over the ring and staff of deceased bishops. For a custom had taken root, especially in the Empire, that when prelates of churches died, the ring and pastoral staff were sent to the lord Emperor. Thereupon he invested one or another of his household servants and chaplains, and sent him to the vacant church to discharge there the office of pastor, without awaiting the election of the clergy. Considering that this was done contrary to all propriety and perceiving that ecclesiastical rights were trampled underfoot in the process, the lord Pope admonished the same Emperor once, twice, and three times to desist from so detestable a presumption. When he could not bring him back despite his admonition by salutary commands, he bound him with the bond of anathema. The Emperor, taking this deed most indignantly, began to persecute the Roman Church and raised up against the lord Pope as an adversary Guibert, Archbishop of Ravenna, a very learned and wealthy man. Relying on the Emperor’s power and trusting in his abundant riches, Guibert violently expelled the aforesaid venerable man and seized the Apostolic See, so mad and so devoid of sound understanding that he believed himself to be what he was falsely called. On the occasion of this schism, the world, slipping toward worse things, cast every reverence for God and human beings behind its back, pursuing harmful things and rejecting saving ones. Pontiffs and every prelate of churches were seized; those who did not agree with the Emperor in this perversity were committed to prison as if guilty of homicide, their goods confiscated. Injuries were inflicted on them not merely for a time, but successors were forced upon them permanently after their expulsion. Pope Gregory therefore fled the Emperor’s wrath and withdrew to Apulia, where he was kindly received by Duke Robert of Apulia, through whose assistance he escaped the hands of the aforesaid Emperor. Finally he came to Salerno, where he died and was buried, CCI, 229.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1075, indiction XIV, Lord Pope Gregory himself held a synod at Rome in the church of the Lord Savior, called the Constantinian [church]. A great number of bishops, abbots, clerics of various ranks, and laymen attended it. Among the other decrees enacted there, he excommunicated Henry IV, King of the Germans. Here is the form or text of this excommunication:

“Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, incline, we beseech you, your gracious ears to us and hear me, your servant, whom you have nurtured from infancy and up to this day delivered from the hand of wicked men who have hated and hate me for my fidelity to you. You are my witness, as are my lady the Mother of God, your brother blessed Paul, and all the saints, that your holy Roman Church drew me, unwilling, to its governance. I did not regard ascending to your See as robbery; rather, I preferred to end my life in pilgrimage than, by worldly cunning, to seize your place for the glory of this world. Therefore, by your grace and not through my own works, I believe it has pleased and does please you that the Christian people especially entrusted to you should obey me, especially through the authority entrusted to me in your stead. By your grace, power has been given me by God to bind and loose in heaven and on earth. Therefore, strengthened by this confidence, for the honor and defense of your Church, on behalf of almighty God—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—through your power and authority I prohibit Henry, king, son of Emperor Henry, who has risen against your Church with unheard-of pride, from governing the whole kingdom of the Germans and Italy. I release all Christians from the bond of the oath which they have made or shall make to him, and forbid anyone to serve him as king. For it is fitting that he who strives to diminish the honor of your Church should himself lose the honor which he seems to possess. And since, as a Christian, he has scorned obedience, has not returned to the Lord whom he abandoned, has shared with the excommunicated, has committed many iniquities, has despised my admonitions—which I sent him for his salvation, as you are witness—and has separated himself from your Church while attempting to rend it, I bind him in your stead with the bond of anathema. I bind him thus in confidence in you, so that the nations may know and prove that you are Peter, and that upon your rock the Son of the living God built his Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.” (Matthew XVI), CXLVIII, 72 and 790.

As for those who say that a king ought not to be excommunicated: although, because of their great folly, we ought perhaps not even to answer them, nevertheless, lest we appear to pass over their stupidity impatiently, we refer them to the sayings and deeds of the holy Fathers, so that we may recall them to sound doctrine. Let them therefore read what blessed Peter commanded the Christian people, at the ordination of Saint Clement, concerning one whom they knew not to possess the grace of a pontiff. Let them learn why the Apostle says: “Being ready to avenge all disobedience” (I Corinthians V), and of whom he says: “With such a one, not even to take food” (I Corinthians V). Let them consider why Pope Zacharias deposed the king of the Franks and released all the Franks from the bond of the oath which they had sworn to him. In the Register of Blessed Gregory, let them learn that in the privileges he granted to certain churches, he not only excommunicated kings and dukes who contravened his decrees, but also judged that they should be deprived of their rank. Nor should they overlook that blessed Ambrose excommunicated not only a king but indeed Emperor Theodosius, in respect both of morals and of power, and even forbade him to presume to remain in the church in the place of priests. But perhaps those men wish to understand that, when God entrusted his Church three times to most blessed Peter, saying, “Feed my sheep,” he excepted kings. Why do they not perceive—or rather, confess with shame—that when God principally gave blessed Peter the power to bind and loose in heaven and on earth, he excepted no one and subtracted nothing from his power? For he who denies that he can be bound by the bond of the Church must consequently deny that he can be loosed by its power. Whoever shamelessly denies this wholly separates himself from Christ. But if the holy Apostolic See, deciding spiritual matters by the chief power divinely bestowed upon it, judges them, why should it not also judge temporal matters? Your charity does not fail to know whose members they are and to whom they cling: namely, the kings and princes of this world who set their own honor and temporal profits before God’s justice, and, neglecting his honor, seek their own. For just as those who place God before every desire of their own and obey his command more than human beings are members of Christ, so also those of whom we have spoken are members of Antichrist, CXLVIII, 454, 455.

If, then, spiritual persons are judged when necessary, why should secular persons not the more be constrained concerning their evil deeds? But perhaps they think that royal dignity surpasses episcopal dignity. From their origins they may infer how far the two differ. The former was discovered by human pride; the latter was established by divine mercy. The former ceaselessly pursues empty glory; the latter always aspires to heavenly life. Let them also learn what Saint Anastasius, Pope, wrote to Emperor Anastasius concerning these dignities, and what Saint Ambrose decreed in his *Pastoral* concerning the difference between them. “The honor and eminence of episcopal office,” he says, “can be equaled by no comparisons. If you compare it with the splendor of kings and the diadem of princes, it will be far inferior, as if you compared lead ore to the brightness of gold. For you see kings’ and princes’ necks bow before the knees of priests; and, having kissed their right hands, they believe themselves fortified by their prayers” (Saint Ambrose, XVII, 569, 570). Constantine the Great, knowing this, chose not the first but the last place of sitting among the apostles. For he knew that “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James IV). Meanwhile, let your brotherhood [Herman, Bishop of Metz] know that, after receiving letters from certain of our brother bishops and dukes, by the authority of the Apostolic See we have given those bishops permission to absolve persons excommunicated by us who did not fear to abstain from communion with the king. But concerning the king himself, we have absolutely forbidden anyone to presume to absolve him until his definite penitence and sincere satisfaction have been made known to us through suitable witnesses, so that we may together determine how, if divine mercy has looked upon him, we may absolve him for God’s honor and his salvation. For we are not unaware that some among you, under a pretext supposedly received from us and misled by fear or human favor, would presume, if we did not forbid it, to absolve him and apply a wound to a wound instead of a remedy. If any truly episcopal persons opposed them, they would judge them to be pursuing not justice but enmities. But the ordination and consecration before God of bishops who presume to communicate with an excommunicated king becomes, according to the testimony of Saint Gregory, an execration. For when they proudly scorn obedience to the Apostolic See, they incur the crime of idolatry, as Samuel testifies (I Samuel XV). For if one is called God’s man who is stirred by zeal of divine love to strike at vices, assuredly he denies that he is God’s man who refuses, as far as he is able, to rebuke the life of carnal people. And if he is cursed who withholds his sword from blood—that is, the word of preaching from the destruction of carnal life—how much more cursed is he who, through fear or favor, drives his brother’s soul into eternal perdition? CXLVIII, 455, 456.

It became your royal dignity, since you confess yourself a son of the Church, to look with greater honor upon the teacher of the Church—that is, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. If you are one of the Lord’s sheep, you have been entrusted by the Lord’s word and power to his feeding; for Christ says to him: “Feed my sheep”; and, “To you have been entrusted the keys of the kingdom of heaven,” etc.; and, “Whatever you bind,” etc. Since, in his See and apostolic administration, we—though sinners and unworthy—by divine disposition exercise the office of his power, he himself certainly receives whatever you send to us either in writing or in plain spoken words. And while we scan written characters or listen to speakers’ voices, he, under whose scrutiny this occurs, discerns from what heart the commands have proceeded. Therefore your Highness should take care that no discrepancy of will be found toward the Apostolic See in your words and embassies, and that in matters through which the Christian faith and the condition of the Church chiefly advance toward eternal salvation, you do not deny to us—but to almighty God—the reverence that is due, although the Lord deigned to say to the apostles and their successors: “He who hears you hears me,” etc. Thus there can be no doubt that apostolic and evangelical doctrine, whose seat and foundation is Christ, must be received and held with every reverence by believers through those chosen for the ministry of preaching. For this year, when a synod had been gathered at the Apostolic See, over which the heavenly dispensation wished us to preside, and at which some of your faithful also attended, we saw the order of Christian religion already shaken for many ages, and the chief and proper means of gaining souls long fallen into decay and, at the devil’s urging, trampled down. Distressed by the danger and manifest destruction of the Lord’s flock, we had recourse to the decrees and teaching of the holy Fathers, establishing nothing new and nothing devised by ourselves, but judging that the first and only rule of ecclesiastical discipline, and the well-trodden path of the saints, must be resumed and followed after error has been abandoned. For we know of no other entrance into salvation and eternal life open to Christ’s sheep and their shepherds than that shown by him who said, “I am the door,” etc., preached by the apostles, and observed by the holy Fathers, as we have learned in the Gospel and in every page of the divine Scriptures, CXLVIII, 440, 441.

For a full understanding of all these matters, read in its entirety the *Saxon War*, by Bruno, cleric of Magdeburg, CXLVII, 491–586.

(On the feast of Saint Gregory VII, in the Nocturns.) Formerly Hildebrand . . . after the death of Alexander II, was elected Supreme Pontiff, unwilling and grieving, by the unanimous consent of all, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May [22 April], in the year of Christ 1073. He shone like the sun in the house of God. Powerful in deed and word, he applied himself with such zeal to restoring ecclesiastical discipline, spreading the faith, restoring the Church’s liberty, and rooting out errors and corruptions, that no pontiff since the age of the apostles is said to have endured greater labors and troubles for God’s Church, or to have fought more fiercely for its liberty. He cleansed several provinces from the stain of simony. Against the impious attempts of Emperor Henry he remained in every respect a strong and fearless champion; he did not fear to set himself as a wall for the Lord’s Israel. He deprived the same Henry, who had sunk into an abyss of evils, of communion with the faithful and of his kingdom, and released the peoples subject to him from the allegiance they had sworn. Gregory’s final dying words were: “I have loved justice and hated iniquity; therefore I die in exile.” Innumerable are the things which he either bore bravely or wisely established through many synods convened in the City: a man truly holy, the avenger of crimes and the Church’s most vigorous defender.” CXLVIII, 246, 247, 248.

“As soon as this Legend appeared,” says the republican Grégoire, “it aroused the horror of all persons attached to Gallican liberties,” CXLVIII, 249. Immediately the Parlement of Paris, supreme judge in liturgical matters, assembled; and its advocate-general, disguising the ill will [Col. 0167] with which he and his body were animated against Rome, sought to make people believe that, by the mere publication of the office of Saint Gregory VII, the French nation was on the verge of shaking off the yoke of its former kings. It is true that this happened before the close of the century in which the honorable magistrate spoke; but it is very doubtful that the legend had anything to do with it. “It was well enough known,” says the advocate-general, “that Gregory VII, so famous for his disputes with Emperor Henry, was the man who carried furthest those ambitious claims, unheard of in the Church’s first centuries, which caused such long disturbances and kindled such cruel wars in his time.

“But, he adds, let it be permitted to say that there was no reason to expect to see, introduced into his praise and celebrated in an ecclesiastical office, the excesses to which such dangerous principles finally led him. Is it then the masterpiece of his zeal that he undertook to deprive a king of his crown and to release his subjects from their oath of allegiance? And can we behold without grief that titles such as defender of the Church, restorer of its liberty, and bulwark of the house of Israel are based upon a deed so worthy of being buried in oblivion?

“Why must the traces of an enterprise whose memory time seemed to weaken reappear today even before our eyes, still to stir up our duty and zeal? Would we tolerate that, under cover of this alleged supplement to the Roman Breviary, there should be placed in the hands of the faithful, in the mouths of ministers of religion, even in the midst of our holy temples and the solemnity of divine worship, that which tends to shake the inviolable and sacred principles of subjects’ attachment to their sovereign?”

The bishops of Auxerre, Montpellier, Metz, Verdun, Troyes, Castres, and others besides, displayed their zeal against the said legend. The Parlement of Brittany hastened to follow in the footsteps of that of Paris. There too the procureur général spoke as follows:

> “Permit me to remind you, Gentlemen, that Gregory VII was the first of all Popes to dare to make manifest his claims over the temporal authority of kings, openly arrogating to himself the imaginary right to depose them and release their subjects from their oath of fidelity. A disastrous fiction which has only too long perpetuated itself beyond the mountains . . . . . The Parlement of Bordeaux requests that certain precautions be taken to ensure for the future that nothing may slip into books intended for divine service and other books of devotion which could injure the rights of the king and disturb the tranquillity of the State . . . . .”

The bishop of Verdun said in his pastoral charge:

> “No: whatever may have been the faults of Emperor Henry IV, the Pope had no right to take away his crown, nor to loosen the sacred bonds which attached his subjects to his service. This act, in which that Pope so unjustly exceeded his authority—an act which it may be presumed that he expiated by penance—cannot be one of the grounds for his canonization; and, if it is regarded merely as an historical fact, it ought not to be cited in a saint’s legend or amid a divine office.”

All these invectives against the legend came from the Jansenist camp and tended to prescribe to bishops that the Declaration of the Clergy of France of 1682 must be inviolably maintained and exactly observed. It was simply Gallicanism continuing its system of audacity.

While these things were taking place in France, Rome—outraged in what she holds most dear, the honour of the saints whom she invokes, and her own dignity, which, not being of this world, ought not to be sacrificed to human and personal considerations—set herself to defend herself with the weapons which the King of kings had placed in her hands. In 1729 Benedict XIII issued three vigorous briefs, condemning the pastoral charges of the bishops of Auxerre, Metz, Troyes, Castres, and Montpellier, and inflicted upon the Parlements of Paris and Bordeaux the punishment which they had deserved by their decrees injurious to the authority of the Holy See and to the honour of a glorious servant of God.

Yet the maxims which had long prevailed at the court of Versailles did not allow the use of the legend of St Gregory VII to be tolerated in the churches of the kingdom; but, on the other hand, an open conflict with Rome would have stirred up the Jansenist party, which asked only to rush against that sacred authority which the crown of France still thought worth preserving . . . [Col. 0168] Thus it needed neither declamatory pastoral charges nor fanatical decrees, but simply a resolution, amicably adopted by the clergy, to suppress the legend quietly. This was the court’s intention; this was obediently understood throughout the Church of France, so that, until the destruction of the old society in 1789, not one secular or regular church had been able to inaugurate the cult of the great pontiff Gregory VII.

A deplorable address to Louis XV, king of France, signed by fourteen archbishops and nineteen deputies of the second order, discussing the legend of St Gregory VII, calls him merely “Gregory VII” on an occasion precisely concerning the cult accorded to that holy pontiff—thus protesting against the Martyrology and against the authority which promulgates the Catholic calendar. There were no individual and impassioned pastoral charges; rather, the assembly, corporately, coolly, and authoritatively resolved to stifle this cult and arrest the effect of apostolic decisions. Rome concealed the insult, but courageously maintained the legend. All this occurred during the reign of Louis XV; and, in an address of the French clergy to that monarch, the episcopate, through the mouth of the bishop of Nîmes, expressed itself in these strong words: “Your Majesty, whose reign is founded upon Catholicity.” One could not with greater delicacy disavow all that had been done against the heroic pontiff than by recalling, in the presence of the king himself, that there was still something above his crown: the interest of Catholicity—the sole allusion in the address to the affair of the legend of St Gregory VII. This was in 1730; and before the end of the same century, that monarchy which had wished to be incapable of forfeiture was declared abolished for ever. The successor of Louis XV, stricken with the vertigo with which God seemed to have smitten those of his race, after finding himself drawn into sanctioning acts which annihilated the Church, mounted a scaffold, without his loyalty, his virtue, or his repentance being able to save the monarchical principles eclipsed for many more years; whereas St Gregory VII, brought back in triumph, reappears with unprecedented majesty and henceforth will share with Charlemagne the sublime title of founder of European society, CXLVIII, 247–269.

If we now inquire into what happened in several other countries of Europe concerning the legend, we encounter facts analogous to those which occurred in France in this matter: in Naples, in the States of Holland and West Frisia, in the Netherlands, in Belgium, in Austria, and in Portugal, there were the same doubts and the same tergiversations for or against the contents of this legend concerning the words of the fifth lesson:

> *Contra Henrici imperatoris impios conatus, fortis per omnia athleta impavibus permansit, seque pro muro domui Israel, etc.*  
> “Against the impious assaults of Emperor Henry, he remained in every respect a courageous and fearless champion, and [set] himself as a wall for the house of Israel, etc.”

Under the date 1787 there is cited an ordinance of the regency of Lower Austria suppressing from the breviary of the regular canons various passages from the offices of several holy popes, including this one in the fifth lesson for St Zachary, on 15 March:

> *Consultus a Francis, regnum illud a Chilperico viro stupido et ignavo, ad Pippinum pietate et fortitudine praestantem auctoritate apostolica transtulit.*  
> “When consulted by the Franks, by apostolic authority he transferred that kingdom from Chilperic, a foolish and indolent man, to Pippin, outstanding in piety and courage.”

This office of St Zachary is not properly in the Roman Breviary, but merely forms part of the proper offices of the clergy of the city of Rome.

The nineteenth century too furnished certain insults to the memory of the holy pontiff. Not to mention the blasphemies which more than once, in the English Parliament, proceeded from the bench of the ecclesiastical peers against the person of “the fiery Hildebrand,” there were some of which Catholic countries were the scene . . . Let us speak of Italy.

Until 1810 the office of St Gregory VII had never ceased to be celebrated in the churches of the various dioceses composing the kingdom of Italy. The excommunication incurred by Napoleon in 1809 made him exceedingly uneasy, and it is generally known how many persecuting measures bore upon the clergy of that period. What is less known is that the great emperor, while raising his hand against Pius VII, dared also to defy the majesty of a pontiff once, as it were, besieged and captive, but thereafter and for ever crowned—Pius VII—by Him “who first drank of the brook before lifting up His head.” A letter by the minister of religious affairs, Bigot de Préameneu, written in February 1810, ordered the bishops of Italy to imitate the silence of the Gallican Church concerning the name and acts of Hildebrand. Several bishops of Italy preferred to obey Caesar rather than the Church, among them the archbishop of Turin, Mgr Hyacinthe de [Col. 0169] la Tour, who sent the minister “the pastoral charge which he had considered it his duty to issue in order to forbid the office of St Gregory VII, and of which he declares that a copy is posted in all the sacristies of the churches in his diocese.” The letter is dated 1 March 1810, CXLVIII, 270–275.

Hardly escaped from the violence of the formidable eagle which gripped Europe, but still standing in the same place, the heroic Hildebrand fell prey to those anarchists whose desires are likewise desires of tyranny. In France, the regicide Grégoire, in his *Historical Essay on the Liberties of the Gallican Church*, published in 1818, accumulated against the holy Pope and his legend all the blasphemies of Protestants and Jansenists. In Spain, in March 1822, a proposal was made in the Cortes to suppress part of the office of Gregory VII “as prejudicial to the rights of the nation.”

One more outrage: it shall be the last we mention. At the beginning of 1828, a new edition of the Roman Breviary appeared in Paris, from the bookseller Poussielgue-Rusand. The editor had thought himself able to insert the office of St Gregory VII, though he placed it only at the end of the volume, not feeling fully reassured by the promise of religious liberty guaranteed to all by the Charter of 1815. A few days after publication of the Breviary, certain newspapers, calling themselves liberal and fraternizing in all things with the Spanish Cortes of 1822, began to cry out against Ultramontanism, which, they said, overflowed among us to the point that in 1828 people dared to print and offer for sale the legend of Gregory VII. Their cries were heard, and in Paris, in 1828, the legend of St Gregory VII was subjected, by order of the archbishopric, to the mutilations inflicted upon it by Austria in her dominions—that is, the removal of the words, *Contra Henrici imperatoris impios conatus*, etc.—without forgetting the charitable suppression of the epithet *iniqui* (“wicked”) applied to Henry IV, which is read in the sixth lesson, where it is said, *Cum ab iniqui Henrici exercitu*, etc. (“When [he was pursued] by the army of the wicked Henry,” etc.), an epithet so justly assigned to Henry IV by the Church. But since that time several editions of the Roman Breviary have been issued both at Lyons and in Paris, and the office of St Gregory VII is read in them in its proper place and in its entirety; while the Paris edition of 1828 is daily being exhausted, retaining to this day the trace of that final weakness which we could not have passed over without partiality.

But let us pass over a few years. On 4 March 1838 there was issued at Le Puy, by Mgr Louis-Jacques-Maurice de Bonald, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, archbishop of Lyons, primate of the Gauls, that magnificent and courageous pastoral letter on the visible head of the Church which will remain in the annals of the Church of France as one of the gravest events seen by our century, which has seen so many. On that memorable day one heard, proclaimed from the episcopal pulpit with no less eloquence than learning, faith in the infallibility of the Roman Pontiff speaking to the Churches, and the lofty mission imposed by Providence upon St Gregory VII and so worthily fulfilled by his great soul:

> “The irruption of the barbarians,” said the Prelate, “was only the image of an invasion more dangerous to the Church and to the civilized world; it was merely the figure of that triple coalition of ignorance, vice, and cupidity, leagued together to extinguish every light, stain every virtue, and stifle every justice. The Middle Ages saw this abyss open wide its entrails to swallow up society as a whole. And where will society take refuge in its distress? Once more at the feet of the Chair of St Peter. There it will find its support and its salvation in a poor monk raised to the sovereign pontificate, but who concealed beneath the coarse garment of the cloister a soul whose elevation has not been understood and would scarcely be understood in our days of speculation and indifference. Hildebrand measures the depth of the wound in the social body. To anyone else, the obstacles to curing it would appear insurmountable; for Gregory VII, it is from these very obstacles that he draws new courage and rekindles the energy of his character. Armed with unshakable strength and an inflexible rectitude of will; yielding also to the maxims of his contemporaries and to the spirit of his age, he undertakes a terrible struggle against his century and all its powers. Learning has deserted the sanctuary: he will bring it back. Virtue seems banished from every heart: he will restore it to its rights. Justice is trampled underfoot: he will make it triumph. He believes himself sent to oppose a brazen front to vice, whether he finds it at the altar or upon the throne. Ever [Col. 0170] inaccessible to fear, ever above human considerations, Gregory will give his zeal no rest until he has reformed the palace of the great, the sanctuary of justice, the cloister of cenobites, and the house of God; until he has rekindled the torch of learning, the heavenly flames of piety, and instilled into the hearts of sovereigns and priests that love of justice and hatred of iniquity which, overflowing in his soul, are poured forth with holy profusion in his writings, his actions, his words, in his entire pontificate. Calumnies, persecution, and death matter little to him, provided that he may cast down every height and make every knee bow before the eternal laws of justice and truth. In his disputes with the princes of the earth, people have chosen to see only unjust encroachments; they have denounced as abuses the holy undertakings of this great Pope. What could he do when peoples crushed beneath the press of the senseless despotism of their masters came to demand on their knees, as a last resource and an extreme remedy for their evils, the severe exercise of his jurisdiction and the thunderbolts of his spiritual sentences? What astonishes us, and almost scandalizes us, was in the eyes of the Middle Ages only the exercise of a just right and the necessary fulfilment of a divine mission. Now, to fight in order to establish everywhere the reign of justice, learning, and virtue—what else is that than to fight in order to civilize the world? Such were the struggles of Gregory VII, and the source for him of immortal glory.”

When reading these lines, so calm and so episcopal, in which the name of this Gregory—whom we have seen pursued so fiercely in the preceding popes—is blessed with so much love, does not the Catholic reader seem to rest sweetly in a peace which will no longer be disturbed? After this pastoral charge, it may be said, the battle is won; there are no more Alps: Rome and France are unanimous in celebrating the glory and virtues of Gregory, father of Christendom. Everything is forgotten, renewed; Christ is glorified in His servant . . . . , CXLVIII, 276–278.

## HENRY I, Emperor

—Concerning the royal rights granted to St Peter:

> “In the name of the Lord God almighty, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. I, Henry I, by the grace of God Emperor Augustus, pledge and promise by this pact of our confirmation to you, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles and keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and through you to your vicar, lord Benedict, supreme pontiff and universal pope, that, as you have held and administered until now, in your power and dominion, from your predecessors, the city of Rome with its duchy, its suburbs, and all its villages, etc.—Portus, Centumcellae, Cære, Bleda, Marturanum, Sutrium, Nepi, Castellum, Gallese, Orte, Polimartium, Amelia, Todi, Perugia with its three islands, Pulvese, Narni, and Otricoli—with all boundaries and territories belonging to the aforesaid cities.
>
> “And likewise the Exarchate of Ravenna in its entirety, with the towns, cities, boroughs, and castles which our predecessors of pious memory—lord Pippin, lord Charles, lord Louis, and Otto his son—had long ago bestowed by a charter of donation upon blessed Peter the Apostle and upon your predecessors: namely, the city of Ravenna and Emilia, Bobbio, Cesena, Forlimpopoli, Forlì, Faenza, Imola, Bologna, Ferrara, Comacchio, Adria, and Gabello; together with the Pentapolis, namely Rimini, Pesaro, Fano, Senigallia, Ancona, Osimo, Umana, Iesi, Fossombrone, Montefeltro, Urbino, and the territory of Balneum, Cagli [*Callis*], Lucioli, and Gubbio, with all boundaries and territories belonging to those same cities.
>
> “Likewise, in the parts of Tuscany: Castel della Felicità, Orvieto, Bagno Regio, Ferento, Viterbo, Orte, Marta, Bleda, Tuscania, Sovana, Populonia, Roselle with Urbanis, etc. Likewise, together with the island of Corsica, in Suriano, then at Monte Bardone, then at Berceto, thence at Parma, then at Reggio, and thence at Mantua, Monte Silicis, and the province of Venetia and Istria, the whole duchy of Spoleto and Benevento. Likewise, in the parts of Campania: Sora, Arce, Aquino, Ariminum, Teano, Capua, the patrimony of Sicily, the city of Gaeta, etc., etc. In addition, we confirm the monastery of Fulda and all that land which we possessed on the side of our kingdom between Narni, Teramo, and Spoleto. Moreover, under the protection of St Peter and of you and your successors, we offer the bishopric of Bamberg. We further offer . . . etc.
>
> “All these aforesaid provinces, towns and cities, [Col. 0171] boroughs and castles, villages and territories, together with estates, for the preservation of our kingdom and of the whole Christian people, we confirm to your aforesaid Church, blessed Peter, and to your vicar Benedict and his successors until the end of the age, in such manner that they may hold them in their own right, sovereignty, and dominion, etc., etc. . . . . .”

XCVIII, 625, 626, 637.

## HENRY II (St), Emperor

> “In the name of God almighty, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. I, Henry, by the grace of God Emperor Augustus, pledge and promise, through this pact of our confirmation, to you, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles and keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and through you to your vicar, lord Benedict VIII, supreme pontiff and universal pope, that, as you have held and administered until now, in your power and dominion, from your predecessors, the city of Rome with its duchy and suburbs, and all its villages and territories, etc., etc.—namely Portus, Centumcellae, etc., etc.—together with the towns, cities, boroughs, and castles which the lords Pippin, Charles, Louis, Otto, and likewise Otto his son, our predecessors of pious memory, had long ago bestowed by a charter of donation upon blessed Peter and your predecessors: namely the city of Ravenna, etc., etc. We further offer, establish, and confirm to you, blessed Peter, and to your vicar lord Benedict and his successors, as was done for Pope John of good memory and his successors by the Ottos, our predecessors, the cities of Rieti, Amiternum, etc. In the same manner, by this pact of our delegation, we confirm the donations which King Pippin of pious memory, and afterwards lord Charles, and the most pious Ottos, spontaneously bestowed upon blessed Peter, Christ’s Apostle, as is contained in those donations and as was agreed between Pope Adrian of holy memory and lord Charles the Emperor, when that pontiff confirmed to that emperor his decree of authority concerning the duchies of Tusculum and Spoleto, namely on the condition that every year the aforesaid tribute should be paid to the share of the Church of St Peter, etc., etc.”

CXL, 233–238.

## HENRY IV, King, A.D. 1068

Henry the king, availing himself of the liberty of youth, began to inhabit Saxony alone out of the whole Roman Empire; to despise princes, oppress nobles, exalt inferiors, devote himself, as he was accused, more to oppression, amusements, and other exercises of this kind than to the administration of justice; to give daughters of illustrious men in marriage to persons of obscure birth; and to establish private strongholds, evidently not sufficiently trusting the powerful men of the realm. From these seeds of discord it came about that very many plotters against both the king’s life and his kingdom arose, CLIV, 944.

King Henry attacked the Saxons with a strong hand, fought them, and gained the victory . . . Duke Rudolf, who afterwards usurped the kingdom, is recorded to have fought bravely with his men for the king. A council was held at Worms, where, in the presence of King Henry, almost all the German bishops, except the Saxons, deposed Pope Hildebrand, sending him a letter which, after making many accusations against him, concluded thus:

> “Since, therefore, your accession was inaugurated by so many perjuries; since the Church of God is endangered by so grave a tempest through the abuse of your innovations; and since you have dishonoured your life and conduct with such manifold infamy, we renounce the obedience which we never promised you, and declare that we shall not observe it henceforth; and, since none of us has hitherto been your bishop, as you publicly proclaimed, you likewise shall henceforth be apostolic to none of us.”

In the same year a great assembly was held at Oppenheim, where the princes of almost the whole kingdom renounced their submission to the king, alleging as their reason that, having been summoned by two successive Popes to make satisfaction, he had not appeared, and that for this contempt he had received from the Pope a sentence of excommunication in a Roman synod, although he had been unheard and absent. Compelled by this disturbance, the king humbly made his way to Rome, as one about to seek pardon from the Apostolic See, contrary to the expectation of his enemies; and, having found the Pope in the town of Canossa, he remained there for three days before the castle gate, having laid aside all royal attire, barefoot and clothed in woollen garments. Nor did he cease, with many tears, to implore the aid and consolation of apostolic mercy until, through the intercession of the prayers and tears of all who were present, the bond of anathema was at last relaxed and he was received into the grace of communion and the bosom of mother Church, after giving many assurances of the future amendment of his life. But how this peace, made between kingdom and priesthood, was soon broken, the whole world, greatly agitated by it, has now learned, etc.

But because some say that Rudolf was elevated to the kingdom by this Pope’s authority and counsel, while others deny that King Henry was excommunicated by him, it seems especially fitting to set down certain statements of that Pope upon these matters. For in a letter sent to all the princes of the German kingdom, he says:

> “We have heard that some among you doubt and inquire concerning the excommunication which we pronounced against the king, whether he was justly or unjustly excommunicated. We admonished him to do penance for his deeds; but he, resenting that he should be reproved by anyone, not only could not be recalled from what he had perpetrated to amendment, but, seized by greater fury, did not cease until he had caused almost all the bishops of Italy, and in the German lands as many as he could, to make shipwreck of the faith of Christ, by causing them to deny to blessed Peter and to the Apostolic See the obedience and honour granted by our Lord Jesus Christ. For these reasons, first because he refused to abstain from communion with those who were excommunicated for sacrilege and the guilt of the simoniacal heresy; then because, for criminal acts, he refused not merely to undertake penance but even to promise it, we excommunicated him by synodal judgment.”

Likewise, in another letter, after the reconciliation had been granted:

> “I restored to him communion alone,” he says, “but did not restore him to the kingdom from which I had deposed him in the Roman synod.”

And, after some intervening words:

> “The bishops and princes beyond the mountains, hearing that he did not keep what he had promised me, in a manner despairing of him, chose Rudolf as king for themselves without my counsel.”

CLIV, 947, 948.

When, at Brixen in Noricum, a gathering of thirty bishops and also an army of nobles, not only from Italy but also from Germany, was convened by order of King Henry, all agreed against Pope Hildebrand, surnamed Gregory VII. Declaring him a pseudo-monk, a pestiferous prince of every madness, and especially an invader of the see of the holy Roman Church, they judged that he ought to be driven from the Apostolic See, although absent, and chose Archbishop Wibert of Ravenna to be substituted for him. The conclusion of this decree is as follows:

> “Since,” they say, “it is clear that he was not chosen by God, but most foolishly thrust forward by himself through fraud and money; since he has overthrown ecclesiastical order, disturbed the realm of the Christian Empire, threatened a Catholic and peaceful king with death of body and soul, defended a perjured king, sown discord among those at concord, quarrels among the peaceful, scandals among brothers, divorces among spouses, and shaken whatever seemed to stand secure among those living piously: we, assembled together under God’s guidance, relying on the envoys and letters of nineteen bishops gathered at Mainz on this present holy day of Pentecost against that most insolent Hildebrand, who preaches sacrileges and conflagrations, defends perjuries and murders, calls into question the Catholic and apostolic faith concerning the body and blood of the Lord, [and is] an old disciple of the heretic Berengar, a worshipper of divinations and dreams . . . judge him canonically to be deposed and expelled; and, unless upon hearing these things he descends from that see, [we judge him] to be condemned for ever.”

CLIV, 951.

## HENRY IV

—See **GREGORY VII**.

## HENRY V, Emperor

> “I, Henry, by the grace of God Emperor Augustus of the Romans, for the love of God and of the holy Roman Church and of lord Pope Calixtus, and for the remedy of my soul, relinquish to God and to His holy Apostles Peter and Paul and to the holy Catholic Church every investiture by ring and staff, and grant that in all churches election and free consecration may take place. The possessions and regalian rights of blessed Peter which, from the beginning of this discord until the present day, whether in the time of my father or in my own, have been taken away, and which I possess, I restore to the same holy Roman Church; those which I do not possess, I shall faithfully assist to have restored. I shall likewise restore, by the counsel of the princes and according to justice, the possessions of all other churches, princes, and others, both clergy and laity, which I possess; and I shall faithfully assist to have restored those which I do not possess. And I grant true peace to Calixtus and to the holy Roman Church and to all who are or have been on its side. And in all matters in which the holy Roman Church shall request assistance, I shall faithfully assist it. Given in the year 1122.”

## INNOCENT III, Pope

> “In the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Amen. Since it pleased our Lord Jesus Christ to make me lord and emperor of all Bulgaria and Vlachia, I searched the writings and books of our ancestors, and the laws of our predecessors, the emperors of blessed memory, to learn whence they had received the kingdom of the Bulgarians, the imperial establishment, the crown upon their heads, and patriarchal blessing. Searching diligently, we found in their writings that those emperors, our predecessors of blessed memory, received the crown of their empire and patriarchal blessing from the Roman Church, from Peter, prince of the apostles of the Apostolic See, and from our most holy father, Pope Innocent III, the universal pope.
>
> “And to whomever patriarchal blessing and authority shall have been given and granted by the lord Pope in Trnovo, the city of my empire, for making and consecrating archbishops, metropolitans, and bishops, and for the other sacramental ecclesiastical ministries, my empire grants that they may have most complete authority throughout every possession and appurtenance of my empire. For all the churches of my whole empire and possession, and my patriarch, metropolitan, bishops, archbishops, and all priests, shall be subject to the Roman Church and shall maintain the law, custom, and observance maintained by the emperors of all Bulgaria and Vlachia of blessed memory, those ancient predecessors of ours; and we shall likewise imitate their footsteps.
>
> “Moreover, for security my empire confirms this its golden bull, that my empire itself shall never depart from the Roman Church and from the Apostolic See, from Peter, prince of the apostles; neither shall other rulers of my empire be separated, but I shall be, as one called, a beloved son of the most holy and apostolic Roman See of Peter, prince of the apostles. And henceforth whatever lands of Christians or pagans my empire may acquire shall be under the power and authority of that same most holy Roman Church and Apostolic See.”

CCXXV, 287, 288.

## LEO III, Pope

Leo, servant of the servants of God, etc., to the abbot of the venerable monastery of the holy martyr of Christ Dionysius:

> “Since you have requested that the privilege be renewed by the Apostolic See, which our predecessor Pope Stephen, of good and holy memory, hitherto confirmed for the monasteries constructed by you, we ought again to renew and confirm it by our authority for you and all your successors as abbots, so that they may in every way subsist and remain under the dominion of the Holy See of the Roman Church in perpetual preservation; namely, on this condition: whatever you are now seen to possess and hold from the donation of our most excellent son King Charles, or of other kings, good men, and your kinsmen, and from your own property and exchanges, or whatever you and your successors may acquire hereafter, whether in monasteries to be built, or villages, or slaves, situated in whatever districts, places, and lands, shall remain thus established and valid for ever. And in the aforesaid monasteries no bishop or priest shall have licence to celebrate masses without the consent of our most excellent son King Charles or of yourself, except when summoned by you; but [they shall] have their own bishop . . . . .
>
> “And we support this by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles . . . . , so that what has been handed over and confirmed may endure in the future, ordaining by this written instrument and forbidding that whoever, or whatever person of any rank, from the highest degree to the lowest, shall attempt or accomplish the violation of this privilege, shall be known by the universal Church to be bound by the bond of anathema through the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and our own authority, unless he shall do penance by worthy satisfaction before God and His saints.”

CXXIX, 967, 968.—Everywhere there are innumerable privileges of this kind issued by the supreme pontiffs, from which it appears that both spiritual and temporal power had been exercised by them.

## Louis I, Emperor (A.D. 817)

**Pact of Louis I, Emperor, with Pope Paschal.** In the name of God the almighty Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. I, Louis, Augustus and emperor, establish and enact by this pact of our confirmation, for you, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and through you for your vicar, Lord Paschal, supreme pontiff and universal pope, and for his successors in perpetuity, that you shall hold and administer—as you have held and administered, under your authority and jurisdiction, from your predecessors until now—the city of Rome with its duchy and suburbs, all its villages and territories, mountainous and maritime, shores and ports, and all cities, fortresses, towns, and villages in the regions of Tuscany: namely Porto, Centumcellae, Ceri, Bleda, Manturano, Sutri, Nepi, Castellum Gallese, Orte, Polimartium, Amelia, Todi, Perugia with its three islands—that is, the greater and lesser islands and Pulvese—Narni, and Otricoli, with all boundaries and territories belonging to the aforesaid cities.

Likewise, in Campania: Segni, Anagni, Ferentino, Alatri, Patrica, and Frusino, with the boundaries of Campania; also Tivoli, with all boundaries and territories belonging to those same cities; and likewise the Exarchate of Ravenna in its entirety, with its towns, cities, boroughs, and fortresses, which King Pippin of pious memory and our father Charles, emperor of blessed memory, formerly restored to the blessed apostle Peter and to your predecessors by deeds of donation: namely the city of Ravenna, Emilia, Bobbio, Cesena, Forlimpopoli, Forlì, Faenza, Imola, Bologna, Ferrara, Comacchio, [Col. 0174] Adria, and Gabello, with all boundaries, territories, and islands belonging by land and sea to the aforesaid cities.

Together with the Pentapolis: Rimini, Pesaro, Fano, Senigallia, Ancona, Osimo, Iesi, Umana, Fossombrone, Montefeltro, Urbino, the territory of Valva, Cagli, Lucioli, and Gubbio, with all boundaries and lands belonging to those same cities.

In the same manner, the Sabine territory, as it was granted in its entirety by a deed of donation from our father Charles, emperor, to the blessed apostle Peter, as it was delimited between that Sabine territory and the territory of Rieti by the abbots Itherius and Magenarius, his envoys.

Likewise, in the Lombard Tuscan regions: Castellum Felicitatis, Ubivetum, Bagno Regio, Ferento, the fortress of Viterbo, Orta, Marca, Tuscania, Sovana, Populonia, Roselle, and the islands—Corsica, Sardinia, and Sicily—in their entirety, with all adjoining places and territories, maritime districts, shores, and ports belonging to the aforesaid cities and islands.

Likewise, in Campania: Fondi, Arce, Aquino, Arpino, Teano, Capua, and the patrimonies belonging to your authority and jurisdiction, such as the patrimony of Benevento and Salerno, the patrimony of lower and upper Calabria, the Neapolitan patrimony, and wherever your patrimonies are known to exist within the regions of the kingdom and empire entrusted to us by God.

All these aforesaid provinces, towns, cities, boroughs, fortresses, villages, territories, and likewise the patrimonies of your aforesaid Church, blessed apostle Peter, and through you of your vicar, our spiritual father Lord Paschal, supreme pontiff and universal pope, and of his successors until the end of the age, we confirm in the same manner, so that they may hold them in their own right, principality, and jurisdiction.

Likewise, by this decree of our confirmation we ratify the donations which our grandfather, King Pippin of pious memory, and afterward our lord and father Charles, emperor, voluntarily conferred upon the blessed apostle Peter. We likewise confirm the tribute and payment, and the other donations, which were annually customarily brought into the palace of the king of the Lombards, whether from Lombard Tuscany or from the duchy of Spoleto, as contained in the aforesaid donations and as was agreed between Pope Adrian of holy memory and our lord and father Charles, emperor. For that pontiff confirmed to him his authoritative decree concerning the aforesaid duchies—namely Tuscany and Spoleto—in such a manner that the aforesaid tribute should be paid annually to the Church of the blessed apostle Peter, while our jurisdiction over those same duchies in all respects, and their subjection to our side, should remain unimpaired.

Moreover, as we have said, by this decree of our confirmation we strengthen all the things named above for your benefit, so that they may remain under the right, principality, and jurisdiction of you and your successors; so that neither by us nor by our sons or successors may your authority be diminished by any device or contrivance whatsoever, nor may anything be taken away from you or your successors from all the aforesaid matters: namely, from the aforesaid provinces, towns, cities, boroughs, fortresses, villages, territories, and patrimonies, and likewise from payments and tributes. Thus neither shall we take them away nor consent to anyone wishing to take them away.

Rather, we promise, insofar as we are able, to defend all that is read above—namely provinces, cities, towns, boroughs, fortresses, territories, patrimonies, islands, tributes, and payments—of the Church of the blessed apostle Peter and of the pontiffs perpetually presiding in his most sacred see, in order that all these things may firmly remain in his jurisdiction for use, enjoyment, and disposal.

We claim for ourselves no share or authority in them for disposing, judging, taking away, or diminishing, except insofar as we may be asked by him who at that time holds the government of this holy Church. And if any person from the aforesaid cities belonging to your Church comes to us wishing to withdraw himself from your jurisdiction and authority, or fleeing through fear of any wrongful plot whatever or of an offence committed, we shall in no way receive him, except in order to make a just intercession for him—provided only that the offence he has committed is found pardonable; otherwise, once apprehended, we shall return him to your authority.

Excepted are those who have come to us because they have suffered violence or oppression from more powerful persons, in order that they may deserve to receive justice through our intercession; their case is different and is very distinct from those above.

And when, by divine summons, the pontiff of this most sacred see has departed from this world, no man from our kingdom—whether Frank, Lombard, or of whatever people placed under our authority—shall have permission to come against the Romans, either publicly or privately, or to conduct an election; nor shall anyone dare, in the cities or territories belonging to the authority of the Church of the blessed apostle Peter, to inflict any evil upon any person. Rather, the Romans shall be permitted, with every reverence and without any disturbance, to provide an honourable burial for their pontiff.

And when all the Romans, by divine inspiration and the intercession of blessed Peter, have unanimously and concordantly, without any promise, elected someone to the pontifical office, he shall without ambiguity or contradiction be consecrated according to canonical custom. When he has been consecrated, envoys shall be sent to us or to our successors, the kings of the Franks, to unite friendship, charity, and peace between us and him, as it was customary to do in the times of Charles, our ancestor of pious memory, of our grandfather Lord Pippin, and also of our father Charles, emperor.

That this may be believed firm by all the faithful of God’s holy Church and of ours, and may be guarded more firmly for future generations and coming ages, we have strengthened this pact of our confirmation by the seal of our own hand and by the oaths, promises, and subscriptions of venerable bishops, abbots, and also our nobles. We sent it through Theodore, nomenclator and envoy of the holy Roman Church, to Lord Pope Paschal. I, Louis, emperor by the mercy of God, have subscribed. And his three sons subscribed, together with ten bishops, eight abbots, fifteen counts, one librarian, and one mansionary: XCVII, 682–686; and XCVIII, 579–588.

## Louis the Pious, Emperor

In the name of God the almighty Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. I, Louis, Augustus and emperor, establish and grant by this pact of our confirmation to you, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and through you to your vicar Lord Paschal, supreme pontiff and universal pope, and to his successors in perpetuity, that you shall hold and administer—as you have held and administered under your authority and jurisdiction from your predecessors until now—the city of Rome with its duchy and suburbs, all villages and territories, mountainous and maritime, shores and ports, and all cities, fortresses, boroughs, and villages in the Tuscan regions: namely Porto, Centumcellae, Ceri, Bleda, Manturano, Sutri, etc., etc., with all boundaries and territories belonging to the aforesaid cities, etc., etc., XCVIII, 579–583.

Likewise, by this decree of our confirmation we ratify the donations which our grandfather, King Pippin of pious memory, and afterward our lord and father Charles, emperor, voluntarily conferred upon the blessed apostle Peter; likewise the tribute and payments, and other donations annually customarily brought into the palace of the king of the Lombards, whether from Tuscany, etc., XCVIII, 583, 584, 585.

And we claim for ourselves in them no share or authority to dispose, judge, take away, or diminish, except when requested by him who at that time holds the government of this holy Church. And if, etc., etc., XCVIII, 584, 585, 586, 587, 588.

In this diploma Louis the Pious reserved for himself no dominion over the city of Rome; for it is most plainly read here that he yielded jurisdiction over the Roman duchy to the pontiff, reserving for himself only the right of intercession on behalf of persons having recourse to him, and the defence and protection of the Church, which those kings reserved for themselves and their successors with the attached rights and privileges—namely the patriciate or patronage: XCVIII, 504, 505.

## Countess Matilda

**Donation.** In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1102. I, Matilda, countess by the grace of God, for the remedy of my soul and those of my parents, have given and offered to the Church of St Peter, through the intervention of Pope Gregory VII, all my goods by right of ownership, both those which I then possessed and those which I later acquired, whether by right of succession or by any other right belonging to me. And all that I possessed on this side of the mountains, as well as all that appeared to belong to me in the transalpine regions, I gave and delivered, as stated, through the hand of Pope Gregory VII to the Roman Church, and I requested that a charter thereof be drawn up.

But because the charter appears nowhere, and I fear that my donation and offering may be called into doubt, I, the aforesaid Countess Matilda, from this present day again give and offer to the same Roman Church, through the hand of Bernard, cardinal and legate of the same Roman Church—as at that time I gave through the hand of Pope Gregory VII—all my goods, both those which I now possess and those which, God favouring, I shall acquire hereafter; and both those which I have, or shall have, on this side of the mountains and those in the transalpine regions, whether by hereditary right or by any other right, for the benefit and remedy of my soul and of my parents’ souls.

All those aforesaid goods of mine, belonging to me by right, together with their additions and appurtenances, and their upper and lower appurtenances, which I previously bequeathed in their entirety as stated above, I give and offer from this day to the same Church, and I confirm, by this present charter of offering, that they are to be held there. Moreover, by the knife, etc. … May this present charter of offering remain firm and enduring for all times, etc., XCVIII, 631–662.

## Melchiades, Pope

In the letter which he sent to the Spanish bishops, he instructed them by request and entreaty always first to investigate everything diligently, to decide with justice and charity, to condemn no one before a true and just judgment, to judge no one by the discretion of suspicion, but first to prove the matter and afterward to pronounce sentence charitably; and not to inflict on another what they would not wish done to themselves. They were not to judge or condemn bishops without the authority of the Roman see; if they did so, it would be void and those acting thus would be condemned. For this privilege was ordained to be preserved for the Roman see itself from the times of the apostles: although all the apostles had equal election, it was nevertheless granted to blessed Peter to take precedence over the others and prudently to dispose of cases and questions brought before him as complaints, CXXIX, 1180.

## Damasus, Saint and Pope

He established the Papirian estate in the territory of Ferentino, with its ancient adjoining lands; and the Antonian estate in the territory of Cassino, CXXVIII, 73.

It is also generally believed among Catholics that, when Charlemagne made donations to the Roman pontiff of very many counties, he granted him only their revenues and certain payments for the benefit of spiritual government:

> “He gave them to him only as fiefs and for the good of his states; and by these donations Rome and the territories granted did not cease to form part of his Empire.”

For it is said very often in these concessions that imperial authority was preserved.

## Nicholas III, Pope

In the year 1278, on the Nones of June [5 June], Nicholas III inserted in his letters the privileges of Louis, Otto, and Henry I, and sent them to Rudolph:

> “Lest, therefore, you should suppose that by these matters we are seeking anything new from you, or asking anything unusual from your predecessors, the Roman emperors, we send you under our bull, word for word, the texts of the privileges of those emperors, as we have found them in the archives of the Roman Church, in order more fully to enlighten your conscience as to how your predecessors, the Roman emperors, expressly set forth these things and declared, under express territorial distinctions, that they belonged to the Roman Church.”

He also communicated much to Conrad, the Franciscan ambassador of Rudolph, to be reported to the same king of the Romans for fuller assurance. Moreover, in other letters he prescribed for him the form which he should use in the privilege. For the form employed by Rudolph’s envoys at Lyons in 1274, and by Rudolph himself at Lausanne in 1275 before Gregory X, had been a source of error because it did not specifically enumerate the cities and the Exarchate, although, according to the usage of that age, it expressed the ecclesiastical dominions thus:

> “To these belongs the whole land which lies from Radicofani to Ceprano, the March of Ancona, the duchy of Spoleto, the land of Countess Matilda, the county of Bertinoro, the Exarchate of Ravenna, the Pentapolis, Massa Trabaria with the adjoining lands, and all other things belonging to the Roman Church.”

Nicholas III therefore sent the following to be inserted between “Matilda” and “the Pentapolis”:

> “The city of Ravenna and Emilia, Bobbio, Cesena, Forlimpopoli, Forlì, Faenza, Imola, Bologna, Ferrara, etc.”

And after many other things:

> “Therefore all the aforesaid things, whether expressed by the proper or special names of provinces, lands, cities, and places, or not expressed, and whatever other things belong to the Roman Church, we freely release, renounce, and restore to it by the will and knowledge, counsel and consent of the princes of the Empire. Indeed, so that every scruple may be removed, we anew grant, confer, and donate them, insofar as this can be understood more effectively and fully, so that, with every ground of contention and dissension removed, firm peace and full concord may endure between the Church and the Empire.”

XCVIII, 863.

## Orderic Vitalis, Monk

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1084, Henry, king of the Germans, assembled Saxons, Alemanni, and other peoples; he violently entered Italy, besieged and captured Rome, expelled Gregory VII from the apostolic see, and wickedly substituted for him Wibert, metropolitan of Ravenna. Gregory then withdrew to Benevento, and a great dissension arose in the city, bringing grave harm to the children of the Church and lasting long to the ruin of many.

Gregory, who at baptism had been called Hildebrand, was inflamed with zeal for truth and justice. He reproved every crime and, from fear or favour, spared no one who acted against rectitude. Accordingly, he suffered persecution and exile from men untamed and opposed to the Lord’s yoke; yet no artifice of theirs could overcome him until his death. He repeatedly admonished and rebuked Henry and at last excommunicated him, because he was an incorrigible transgressor of divine law. For the aforesaid prince left his wife and clung to the filthy pleasures of adultery, like a pig delighting in mud. The same king often deceitfully summoned to his court nobles whose wives, daughters, or estates he desired; then, having secretly sent his retainers ahead, he killed them unsuspectingly on the road.

Pope Gregory excommunicated Henry, often admonished and stubbornly persisting in his crimes, by the judgment of a synod; under an anathema, he stripped him of a kingdom damnably usurped while hardened in sin, and by apostolic authority, through the hands of many bishops, consecrated Count Conrad as king. Thus deprived, Henry remained silent for one year in his own house and hid himself while retaining the county which he had received from his parents by hereditary right. But he procured much assistance, lavishly giving funds from the treasure which he had once amassed in abundance. Then, after gathering many thousands of accomplices, he despised the common decree, rebelled as a public enemy, fought against King Conrad, cast him down and murdered him, and shattered his army with various disasters.

Henry, elated by this victory, seized the empire which he had lost, restrained rebels, greatly increased his forces, besieged Rome, and exerted every effort against Pope Gregory. When asked why he had dared such horrors against the head of the Church, he declared with a laugh that the cause of this immense discord between himself and the pope was that a physician had attempted too severely to cure an impatient sick man.

The unbridled king therefore laid a strong siege against Rome. He terrified the Romans with threats and force, soothed them with gifts and promises, and by these means won over the citizens and obtained the city. When the Romans failed him, Pope Gregory made for Apulia; there, honourably received by the Normans, he lived for four years and, imparting the commands of life to the children of the Church, completed the course of his labours.

Then Henry Augustus unlawfully introduced into the Lord’s sheepfold Wibert, metropolitan of Ravenna, whom they called Clement. Because of this a grave and lasting dissension in the world punished many with a twofold death. The Milanese, the men of Mainz, and many others who favoured Wibert anathematized all the Gregorians and cruelly attacked them with arms. Conversely, Gregory and his party summoned the erring Wibertines back to the unity of the Church, and excommunicated according to ecclesiastical law those who refused to return.

Then envoys of the Romans came with apostolic letters to Robert Guiscard, who had assembled from the whole duchy of Apulia and Calabria a strong army of Normans and Lombards; they begged his aid for Pope Gregory against Henry, king of the Germans. Robert was at first anxious, but finally said:

> “One must always obey God, who speaks through the common pastor of the Catholic Church. With God’s help, I shall obey the pope’s command.”

After these words, the warlike knight immediately crossed the sea with a few fellow-soldiers and, guided by God, proceeded into Apulia. From there, having collected armed bands, he advanced against Rome. Emperor Henry, learning that Duke Robert had already overcome the emperor of Constantinople, was greatly afraid and withdrew to the western parts of his kingdom. Yet, when Robert drew near, the proud Romans assembled and came out armed to meet him. But they were repulsed, and Robert opened for himself a way into Rome by sword and fire; no citizen afterwards dared mutter against him.

Then, when he reached the Tower of Crescentius, the pope came out to meet him with the clergy … The pope calmed the angry duke against the Romans; having taken counsel, he came down from the Tower of Crescentius with the clergy who followed him and, escorted by the duke with a strong force, went to Alba. Ascanius Julius, son of Aeneas, founded that city, and Emperor Constantine gave it to Pope St Sylvester. Having received the apostolic blessing, the duke hastened toward the sea and quickly crossed it to join his forces, as he had sworn to them, CLXXXVIII, 516, 517, 518, 521, 522, 523, 524.

## Otto, Emperor

**On regalian rights granted to blessed Peter.** Emperor Otto I confirms the jurisdictions and cities of the Roman Church established by his predecessors and adds certain others:

> “In the name of God the almighty Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. I, Otto, emperor by the grace of God, together with Otto, our glorious son and king, by the ordinance of divine providence pledge and promise by this pact of our confirmation to you, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles and key-bearer of the kingdom of heaven, and through you to your vicar Lord John, supreme pontiff, Pope John XII, that you shall hold and administer—as you have held and administered under your authority and jurisdiction from your predecessors until now—the city of Rome with its duchy and suburbs, all its villages, its mountainous and maritime territories, shores and ports, and all cities, fortresses, boroughs, and villages in the Tuscan regions: namely Porto, Centumcellae, Ceri, Bleda, Marturiano, Nepi, Castellum Gallese, Orte, Polimartium, Amelia, Todi, Perugia with its three islands, etc., etc.”

XCVIII, 804, 805, 806.

Moreover, we offer you, blessed apostle Peter, and your vicar Lord Pope John and his successors, for the remedy of our soul, that of our son, and those of our parents, from our own kingdom, cities and towns with their fisheries: namely Rieti, Amiternum, Forcona, Norcia, Balva and Marsia, and elsewhere the city of Teramo with its appurtenances.

All these aforesaid provinces, cities, etc., we confirm to your aforesaid Church, blessed apostle Peter, and through you to your vicar John, supreme pontiff, and to his successors until the end of the age, in such a manner that they may hold them in their own right, principality, and jurisdiction.

Likewise, by this pact of our grant we confirm the donations which King Pippin of pious memory and afterward Lord Charles, most excellent emperor, voluntarily conferred upon the blessed apostle Peter; likewise the tribute or payment annually customarily brought into the palace of the king of the Lombards, whether from Tuscany or from the duchy of Spoleto, as is contained in the aforesaid donations and as was agreed between Pope Adrian of holy memory and Lord Charles, when that pontiff confirmed to him his decree regarding those duchies, while our authority in all things over those same duchies and their subjection to our side remain unimpaired.

From this it appears that all the remaining jurisdictions were subject to the supreme right of the pontiffs, though certain conditions are imposed upon this portion; these, together with other matters, are to be examined. XCVIII, 806, 807, 808, 809, 810.

## Philip the Fair, King of the Franks

If the reign of Philip the Fair occupies a distinct place in the history of France in the Middle Ages, it is because that reign saw the attempt at once most astute and most audacious to free itself from every law, whether founded upon sacred bonds or deriving its origin from the traditional law of the nation. In this period we see royalty struggle against the papacy in order to acknowledge nothing above itself, even a warning given in God’s name; then fight the great vassals in order to find no equals at its side.

Guy of Dampierre, Count of Flanders, was the most illustrious representative of the resistance of the great vassals. Religious authority was upheld by the Order of Cîteaux. There existed, on both sides, connection, friendship, and shared memories in their opposition to the ideas of the age, while each remained united in its own sphere, religious or civil.

In October 1285, the date of Philip the Fair’s accession, although far removed from the time when the king of France would violently confiscate the county of Flanders from Guy of Dampierre, etc., we see appearing on the throne the most insatiable and excessive thirst for power. Philip the Fair demanded tithes; the Order of Cîteaux, though exempt from paying any by ancient privileges, paid its own, though with some settlement. In 1292 Philip the Fair demanded from the Order of Cîteaux an old tithe imposed seventeen years earlier by Gregory XV for the king of France. The abbot of Cîteaux protested … in 1294. Nevertheless, at Philip the Fair’s request, the Order of Cîteaux granted him a tithe for two years, to preserve the monasteries from the horrors of war and the exactions of the English, etc. … By means of this tithe the English were repulsed.

But Philip always needed money. Guy of Dampierre was brought as a prisoner to the Louvre, and extraordinary taxes were imposed by Philip the Fair on clerical and lay movable and immovable property alike. All France was disturbed by it.
