Here the Order of Cîteaux first undertook the defence of ecclesiastical immunities, alleging that by papal privileges it was exempt from such taxes imposed by royal authority. That in this circumstance the Order of Cîteaux understood the gravity of the situation in openly opposing Philip the Fair’s will; that, called to choose between the duty speaking to its conscience and the peril threatening its person and property, it courageously preferred the [Col. 0179] peril—of this there can be no doubt. Already, in 1128, the Order had shown similar firmness toward Louis VI. Thus in 1296 a general chapter was convened.

It first replied to the admonition addressed by a prelate who was a friend of Philip the Fair, Peter Barbet, archbishop of Reims, that the Order of Cîteaux was ready to submit to every tax imposed because of its possessions or for the defence of the country, but that it emphatically rejected extraordinary imposts not approved by the apostolic see.

> “The greatest rights bestowed upon human beings by God’s gift have been conferred by heavenly mercy: namely, the priesthood and the Empire. The former presides over divine things, while the Empire presides over human affairs. Elsewhere they are called the two great lights, like the sun and moon, so that the greater light is spiritual jurisdiction and the lesser light temporal jurisdiction. And just as gold is more precious than lead, the sun nobler than the moon, and divine things nobler and more worthy than earthly things, so priestly dignity surpasses royal dignity; and the lesser has no right to judge the greater when the latter is unwilling and refuses. Therefore the king has no right to compel unwilling and resisting priests to give assistance, since they are not subject to his Empire; for ecclesiastical property is dead to the world and exempt from temporal jurisdiction, and the said assistance plainly has the character of a tithe, with which the king has no business … Moreover, if priests and clerics were bound to the said assistance, they would be placed in a worse condition than other persons; and there would follow the indefensible abuse that, under the most Christian king, priests would be treated more harshly than under King Pharaoh, under whom, although all were subjected to servitude, the priests alone and their property were endowed with liberty.”

Thus the chapter of Cîteaux dared to tell the archbishop of Reims that Philip the Fair showed himself harsher than Pharaoh; it repeated this in the memorable protest which it sent to Rome. The pope’s legate in France convoked a council in Paris on 22 June 1296. The clergy complained to some extent of Philip the Fair’s conduct. But before Boniface VIII, the supreme pontiff, had received the decisions of this council, he granted the complaints of the Order of Cîteaux by placing Peter Barbet, archbishop of Reims, under interdict and, on 18 August 1296, publishing the famous bull *Clericis laicos*.

It is known that in it Boniface VIII pronounced excommunication against clerics who paid tithes without the pope’s prior assent. The bull *Clericis laicos* was confirmed by the bull *Ineffabilis amoris*, in which Boniface VIII reproached the king of France for having lost a precious possession—the love of his subjects—and declared that he was ready to suffer persecution, exile, and even death for the liberty of the Church.

Philip the Fair’s answer began with the words: “Before there were clerics, the king of France had custody of his kingdom”; and what followed was of the same kind and in the same tone. By sheer intrigue Philip the Fair made timid the Boniface VIII who had lately been so proud in his bulls, *Clericis laicos*, etc. … Before a deputation of twenty-three prelates devoted to Philip the Fair, Boniface VIII yielded unarmed. He even complained bitterly of the defection of Guy of Dampierre, duke of Flanders, and offered the king of France all the goods of the Church and his own person, etc. From this point, the reconciliation between the pope and the king of France was complete. Taxes to be collected were permitted by the pope to Philip the Fair … etc. … Complete agreement prevailed among all …

But the Order of Cîteaux gives a most grievous account of the sad condition in which it was oppressed by the incessant levying of tithes upon tithes. The duke of Flanders likewise saw Philip the Fair’s hand weigh heavily upon him. Seizure of the county of Flanders was decreed twice. Guy of Dampierre, count of Flanders, brought his complaints to the pope. Upon receiving all this news, Boniface VIII caused to be delivered to him a declaration by which the sons of the count of Flanders recognized his right to give sovereign judgment upon their claims and grievances.

In the palace of St Peter, the pope pronounced the arbitral judgment which he had refused to postpone any longer. This arbitral sentence of the pope contained no reservation in favour of the count of Flanders … the case was, as it were, appealed in order to resolve all the difficulties more promptly … Guy of Dampierre more strongly than ever demanded the protection of Edward I, king of England, so that justice might be rendered to him from Rome … But nowhere did he receive a favourable answer. Philip the Fair’s influence strongly predominated at the Roman court in the affair of Guy of Dampierre. Finally, precisely when the cause of Guy of Dampierre, count of Flanders, appeared lost forever, the difficulties which were to separate Boniface VIII from the king of France began to appear [Col. 0180].

After great political disputes, the alliance of Boniface VIII and Philip the Fair was broken beyond repair.

When Boniface VIII refused Philip the Fair approval of a treaty which he had just concluded with Albert of Austria, the Flemish ambassadors at Rome, fully understanding the circumstances, took the initiative in the great struggle which was being prepared. They invoked the rights of oppressed Flanders as the noblest and most legitimate field in which papal sovereignty, uniting temporal with spiritual power, might combat the injustices and usurpations of the king of France. The memorandum which they submitted to the pope for this purpose is one of the unpublished documents shedding the greatest light upon the history of the final years of Boniface VIII’s pontificate.

This memorandum begins by giving a most grievous account of the miseries in which Flanders found itself as a result of the vexations and tortures of every kind practised there by Philip the Fair. Not content with taking revenge on Guy of Dampierre, count of these provinces, he also attacked his subjects … The memorandum recalls that Philip the Fair refused, during conciliation, to comply with the summons notified to him by the Holy See; that he broke sworn treaties with the king of England for the purpose of reaching an amicable settlement with the count of Flanders; and it concludes that, at the present time, no judge remains to be sought in this grave affair except the Apostolic See, rightly regarded as the sole competent judge in such a matter.

That the most holy father, the pope, is the competent judge in the aforesaid matters, and no other, is proved:

1. For the same supreme pontiff is the judge of all, both in spiritual and temporal matters, among those who have other secular judges. For he is the vicar of Christ Almighty . . . . . , and this kind of vicarship has been entrusted to him in its fullness, explicitly and expressly entrusted to his successors in the person of Peter; he is, by every law, successor of the earthly and heavenly empire: “Whatever you shall bind,” etc.; and according to that saying, “Behold, two swords,” etc.; and according to that saying, “I have appointed you over nations.” And although kings exercise temporal jurisdiction, and men are subject to the king as pre-eminent and to dukes sent by him, nevertheless this was given by Peter and granted by God, the supreme prince—God, not a mere human child—whose office the pontiff performs on earth. And thus, since all power is from the Lord God, it is apparent that the jurisdiction of all persons, temporal as well as spiritual, has been fully given to him as God’s sole vicar. And just as Lord Pope does not lose his ordinary jurisdiction if he entrusts an ecclesiastical prelacy somewhere, but may be approached by a simple complaint by everyone, as the laws say, so it will be in the case of other powers, because they are from him: for whether the law grants an inheritance or approves one already granted, it appears to grant it, according to that divine saying: “By me kings reign,” etc. Of this highest and most complete power, because it resides in the supreme pontiff, there ought to be no doubt among any of the faithful.

The second reason is that, against those who acknowledge no judges, the supreme pontiff will without any hesitation be judge. Hence the supreme pontiff judges and deposes the emperor, than whom none among secular princes is superior. Likewise the king of France, who recognizes no superior, is nevertheless judged and deposed by the venerable pontiff on account of his demerits. Therefore it was said of the Roman pontiff: “I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms”; and he must be judge over the great as well as the small. Nor can anyone be acephalous, having no judge appointed above him; otherwise laws and justice would perish if there were no one to render them.

The third reason is that the count has already lawfully appealed to this See, since it is established by law that every oppressed person may freely appeal to the Roman See. In the present case, moreover, a judge is lacking, because the king acknowledges no superior . . . .

The fourth reason is that the king of France has notoriously and openly sinned against the count; and it is known that it belongs to the supreme pontiff to rebuke anyone for sin . . . .

The fifth reason is the sacrilege committed in the burning of churches and the killing of clerics and religious, which is an ecclesiastical crime and must be heard before an ecclesiastical judge. Furthermore, because the count’s daughter is detained, ecclesiastical judgment must especially be invoked on grounds of compassion and liberty, which the laws favor; and especially if she intends to marry, she must be placed in a safe and secure location, lest through fear she say that what she hates pleases her . . .

[Col. 0181] The sixth reason is that, before the lord king proceeded to so many and such great unlawful acts against the count, and began to wrong the lord count personally and with respect to the county, the count requested that the king grant him judgment by his peers, which was competent in this matter. The king, though repeatedly asked, refused to provide it; and although he had at one point promised to observe justice through judgment by peers, in the end he denied it to him. Therefore ecclesiastical justice intervened, and the king himself was deprived of the right which he had in the county by reason of the fief. Nor can the lord king say that he is judge in these matters, since no one can be judge in his own cause.

Judgment is therefore invoked against kings and their adherents, etc. . . . Likewise our lord pope can compel the king of France to make peace with the count . . . . This was always taught, in word and deed, by that supreme master, who always said: “Peace be with you; I give you my peace; I leave you peace.” These words must be heeded, because they convey a command which must be carried out by the vicar; and such an inheritance, left behind, is not to be rejected or neglected, but held firmly and approved.

One cannot doubt how favorably this solemn declaration was received at Rome, where pontifical authority—placed by God above all nations and armed with the two swords found on the Mount of Olives, that is, with spiritual and temporal power—was invoked not only as the sole refuge of the oppressed against princes who recognized no judge above themselves, but also as the supreme power endowed with the right to depose the king of France and the emperor. This Memorandum soon received a striking ratification. The pope appeared amid the great Jubilee of the year 1300 with the double insignia of spiritual and temporal authority, repeating aloud: “Behold two swords; here, O Peter, you see your successor; you, saving Christ, behold your vicar.” All Europe had flocked to Rome, and the number of pilgrims crowding at the gates of the holy basilicas eclipsed the most magnificent memories of the city twice queen of the world. It was at once the manifestation of immense religious enthusiasm and the manifestation of the power with which pontifical authority still appeared armed in the eyes of the peoples.

Boniface VIII sent the bishop of Pamiers to order the king of France to restore Guy of Dampierre to freedom; but Philip the Fair answered only by throwing the pope’s legate into prison, etc. . . . While receiving the complaints of the count of Flanders, Boniface VIII also remembered the no less vivid and no less frequent complaints of the Order of Cîteaux. On 4 December 1301 he suspended all privileges granted to the king for the collection of tithes. On the following day two other bulls were published. By the bull *Ausculta filii* (“Listen, son”), he set forth the power entrusted to him as vicar of Jesus Christ and successor of Saint Peter: “God has appointed us over kings and kingdoms, to root up, destroy, scatter, and build up in his name and doctrine. Dearest son, let no one persuade you that you have no superior.” But one must not believe, as modern historians have too often repeated, that in Boniface VIII’s eyes the papacy was to be the union—or, rather, the confusion—of the two powers exercised simultaneously. Boniface VIII himself said that no one could attribute to him such great ignorance or blindness as not to know the distinction between the two powers: “We know that there are two powers ordained by God. Who, then, ought to believe that there was such folly, such stupidity, in our head?” The emperor and kings alone exercised temporal power; to them belonged use, action, and the domain of facts. Right, nevertheless, remained subordinate to spiritual authority, called upon to distinguish what was just from what was unjust and endowed with incontestable jurisdiction *by reason of sin* (*ratione peccati*), whether it was fitting to recall an obscure Christian to penance or necessary to break the crown of the most powerful princes. This theory rested on the then universally accepted principle that, society being founded upon religion, religion was at once a moderating force for princes and a protector for peoples, to whom it offered equality before the supreme tribunal that represented on earth the tribunal of God.

The bull *Ausculta, filii* moreover has a very special interest for the questions previously discussed: the two grievances brought against the government of Philip the Fair, namely, on the one hand, the oppression of Guy of Dampierre—that is, of the great vassals—and, on the other, the oppression of the clergy and religious orders. Once the bull *Ausculta, filii* reached the king, it was publicly burned by his order on Sunday, 11 February [Col. 0182] 1301: “The apostolic letters were burned in the presence of the king himself and the magnates—an act which we do not read of any heretic, pagan, or tyrant having committed.” The Estates-General were summoned by the king for 10 April 1301. A memorandum, more or less respectful, was addressed to the pope; even the clergy adhered to it. Boniface VIII answered, either directly or through the cardinals, the complaints of the three estates composing the Estates-General. At the same time he issued a great bull forbidding bishops henceforth to leave their dioceses. In August a great consistory was held at Rome, presided over by the pope, in the presence of the bishop of Auxerre, envoy of the king, and the deputies of the clergy. Boniface VIII stated in explicit terms that he had the right to depose Philip the Fair, and seemed to predict the very imminent defeat of the French army beneath the walls of Courtrai. News of it arrived a few days after this consistory, followed by the triumph of Flanders, which brought about the uprising of Languedoc.

Boniface VIII had summoned a council at Rome for November 1302. Despite Philip the Fair’s threats, there were seen there four archbishops, thirty bishops, and superior abbots of various monasteries, such as Cîteaux, Cluny, and so on. Immediately after their departure, Philip the Fair ordered his bailiffs to take possession of the property of the prelates and abbots who had gone to Rome. This measure appears to have been directed chiefly against the Order of Cîteaux. At the same time, the bishop of Tournai, obeying Philip the Fair’s secret instructions, ordered all the ecclesiastical authorities of Flanders to cease the functions of their ministry.

In these continual conflicts, on 14 June 1303, at an assembly convened in the church of Notre-Dame, Philip the Fair received—not as king, but as champion of the faith and defender of the Church (Henry VIII also invoked this title in the eleventh century)—the indictment in which William of Plaisians reproached the pope with having sought to unite temporal and spiritual power. The deputies of the three estates of the realm heard the enumeration of all the charges, most of them so infamous that they cannot be reproduced. Then Philip the Fair, grandson of Louis IX, whose beatification that same Boniface VIII had proclaimed, declared that although, as a dutiful son, he had wished to conceal Noah’s nakedness from the people, conscience obliged him to accede to William of Plaisians’s request for the convocation of a council that would judge the pope. The bishops present gave their assent after some hesitation. Only one voice had courageously risen to defend the honor of the papacy and protest against the sacrilegious usurpation of the Church’s rights and liberties: that of the abbot of Cîteaux. The king punished him for it: he was dragged to the towers of the Châtelet. Boniface VIII wished to honor the devotion of this abbot, John of Pontoise; he granted him two privileges which passed to his successors. The first was to seal in white wax; the second, to place on his seal the image of the pope seated in Saint Peter’s chair and clad in pontifical vestments. Boniface VIII explained this privilege in these memorable words addressed to John of Pontoise: “You sat with me; you shall sit with me.”

Boniface VIII lived only a short while after these events. His contemporaries had accused him of ambition and avarice; he rehabilitated himself in the eyes of posterity by offering up to martyrdom a brow burdened with eighty-six years. Hardly was his tomb opened when the count of Flanders and the abbot of Cîteaux followed him there. It seems that the last representative of the temporal power of the papacy drew with him the last representatives of the power of the great vassals and religious orders.

As for Philip the Fair, one must descend to the final years of his life to find traces of a reparation prompted either by remorse or by fear of a general uprising. He had not ceased to harass the Order of Cîteaux and the others by the most vexatious tithes; a biennial levy imposed in May 1304 is found, and another tithe of one fifth imposed in 1305. Finally, a document preserved in the archives of Lille tells us that, in September 1312, the king exempted the Order of Cîteaux from all tithes that might be levied in the future. It was somewhat late, for already in 1303 one reads in the statutes of that Order: “Since the Order is in great debt and bound to various creditors.” And on 20 March 1313 he announces in a letter that he wishes to assist the abbey of Clairvaux, formerly so celebrated for the pomp and splendor of its religious ceremonies but already threatened with complete ruin: “This monastery, [Col. 0183] illustrious and noble among other monasteries, is oppressed by the burden of so many and such great debts that, unless a speedy remedy be provided, those serving this monastery will have to be miserably scattered to various places; and consequently the divine office, which until now has been celebrated there so devoutly and so solemnly, will be wholly destroyed, and the monastery itself will come to the misery of irreparable desolation.”

And it was Philip the Fair himself who, before dying, thus wrote the sorrowful history of his reign! It was the same supreme and prolonged complaint—“worn down by old age and long illness”—which was true of the abbot of Cîteaux, the abbot of Clairvaux, the count of Flanders, and the pope. Such was the sad and unhappy history of the end of the thirteenth century, a century remarkable among all those of the Middle Ages for its learning and glory, its virtues and genius. CLXXXV, 1833–1920. (*Studies on the History of the Thirteenth Century, or Researches concerning the Part Taken by the Order of Cîteaux and the Count of Flanders in the Struggle between Boniface VIII and Philip the Fair*, by Kervyn de Lettenhove.)

PLACIDUS, bishop of an unknown see.—“In what matter earthly princes ought to have power in the Church.” In what matter earthly powers ought to have a place within the Church, and whether by their own authority or at the Church’s summons, is to be noted from the words of Saint Gregory, who says:

> “Holy Church, in order to break the hardness of wicked men who oppress the humble, sometimes seeks the assistance of an earthly prince because her own strength does not suffice. When earthly princes act thus, they serve not themselves but God. Therefore, in the election of pastors of holy Church, earthly princes ought to exercise their powers in God’s service when, as often happens, discord arises between parties over an election and cannot be restrained by the authority of priests; then they ought to assist the judgment of the priests and in every way pursue wicked men. This we also read to have occurred in the Apostolic See itself, when dissident peoples had ordained two men, Eulalius and Boniface. At the request of the priests and Catholic peoples, the Emperor Placidius, with his son, established Boniface and expelled Eulalius from the City. Yet by this act they did not subject the Church to their own right; rather, they rendered their service to it, because afterwards they claimed no right in the election of the Roman pontiff. Catholic emperors ought to act similarly in bishoprics and abbeys, if they have been summoned by the Church. But if the Roman emperor is not Catholic, the Church ought not only not to seek his assistance, but rather to oppose him in all things. And if he is so arrogant as to cause another person to be ordained bishop at Rome, as though by his own power or authority, that man must not be regarded as bishop; rather, the bishop is the one whom the Catholic Church has chosen for herself. All Catholics who fear God ought not only to refuse service to an emperor doing this, but also, insofar as they are able, to resist him, knowing that they will receive an eternal reward from God for this, if they do it chastely and with zeal for God—as, conversely, it is sin if they neglect it.”

“On Pope GREGORY VII.” We have an example of this matter in modern times: when the Roman emperor, resisting the Catholic faith, had sent his own bishop there, all Catholics rejected and anathematized him; but they loved Gregory VII, ordained in accordance with the Catholic faith, and acknowledged him as the vicar of Blessed Peter. God also confirmed his teaching after his death, and did not permit the gates of hell to prevail against his Church, CLXIII, 666.

“That we benefit not only ourselves but also the emperor if we do not consent to his wrongdoing.” Blessed Ambrose, when he was compelled to surrender the vessels of the Church, said (*Sermon against Auxentius*, XVI, 1007–1008):

> “If something of my own were demanded or forcibly required from me—an estate, a house, gold, silver—whatever belonged to my own right, I would willingly offer it. I cannot take anything away from, or surrender, the temple of God. I had received it to be kept, not surrendered. Moreover, I also take thought for the emperor’s safety, because it would not be expedient for me to surrender it or for him to receive it. Let him accept the voice of a free priest: if he wishes to provide for his own welfare, let him withdraw from injury to Christ.”

These words, I think, are full of humility, full of the affection that a priest owes to the emperor. “Now let us consider these things, and, following the example of the holy Father Ambrose, far be it from us to shave away Christ’s inheritance; far be it from us to surrender the inheritance of the blessed apostle Peter, to whom Christ deigned to say: ‘To you I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven.’ At the Savior’s command, Peter himself and all the bishops, our Fathers, handing down the Holy Spirit to bishops, handed over this inheritance in perpetuity to all his successors; they gave them staff and ring, in order that through a bodily sign they might signify something spiritual. But now, far be it from us that lay and secular persons, serving vain glory and avarice, should dare, with our permission, to hand over what is spiritual. For what remains for them except to lay hands on persons? And if this is believed to be impious not only in deed but even in word, how much more must we refrain from such great wickedness! For one must hold firmly what the same blessed Ambrose goes on to say:

> ‘Christ enters his temple, takes up a whip, and drives the money-changers out of the temple. For he does not allow those who sell seats of office to be in his temple; he does not allow dealers in money to be in his temple. What are sacred seats except honors? What are doves except the simple minds of the faithful, or souls following faith white and pure? Shall I, then, bring into the temple one whom Christ excludes? For he commands him to go out who sells dignities and honors; he commands him to go out who wishes to sell the simple minds of the faithful.’”

CLXIII, 678–679.

RUDOLPH, King of the Romans.—Diploma. To the most holy father in Christ and lord, Pope Nicholas III, Rudolph, by the grace of God King of the Romans, ever August, for perpetual remembrance of the matter.

The highest protection of the commonwealth, springing by divine institution from the stock of two things, priesthood and empire, and thence strengthening its force, has beneficially governed humankind in the past and will govern it, God favoring, forever. These are the two gifts of God, indeed the greatest of all gifts bestowed from on high: namely, the sacred authority of pontiffs and the royal excellence of power. Our Savior Jesus Christ, mediator between God and men, himself exercised these two through distinct acts and dignities, so that he plainly showed to all that both proceed from him as from one and the same source.

Therefore, acknowledging all things from him alone, the living and true God from whom kings and kingdoms have received their beginning, and recalling the innumerable benefits of the most holy Roman Church toward us, we are stirred by full affection to repay, insofar as we can, what is due to her, from whom we perceive that such great and excellent gifts have been bestowed upon us and our predecessors, the kings of the Romans.

Accordingly, the aforesaid predecessors, among the other things which they confirmed, relinquished, or also granted to the Roman Church, relinquished, renounced, restored, and confirmed to Saint Peter, key-bearer of the heavenly kingdom, and to his successors and the Roman Church, the whole land from Radicofani to Ceprano; the March of Ancona; the Duchy of Spoleto; the lands of Countess Matilda; the county of Bretinoro; the Exarchate of Ravenna; the Pentapolis; Massa Trabaria with the adjacent lands; and all other goods, lands, possessions, and rights belonging to the Roman Church which are set forth or contained in the many imperial privileges from the time of Louis onward. To remove every scruple, insofar as it could be understood more fully and effectively, they bestowed, granted, and even donated these things, as is contained in their privileges or letters.

And afterwards, when, as it pleased the Lord, we were raised to the height of royal excellence, so that we might discharge no lesser debt of acknowledgment for the innumerable gifts we had received from the hands of the said Mother, we acknowledged all the aforesaid things in the presence of Pope Gregory X, of revered memory; and we confirmed, renewed, and newly granted and donated every one of them to him, receiving them for the Roman Church for himself and his successors, strengthening them nonetheless by our own oath sworn bodily, etc. . . .

And because royal acts ought to proceed in complete clarity, so that our royal declaration may remove every obscurity which generality often tends to introduce, and so that the rights of Mother Church herself may be fully established by our declaration, which we decree shall endure perpetually, we acknowledge, confess, and declare by the pronouncement of this present edict, for perpetual remembrance, that the city of Ravenna and Emilia, Bobbio, etc., etc., belong fully and entirely, by complete right, not only in spiritual matters but also in temporal matters, to Saint Peter, key-bearer of the heavenly kingdom, to you, most blessed father and lord Pope Nicholas III, to your successors the Roman pontiffs, and to the Roman Church itself; and that they are under the full right, jurisdiction, and lordship of you and of that Roman Church, XCVIII.

And, to abolish every scruple of doubt for the future and to make our devotion toward Mother Church herself shine forth more clearly, all and each of the aforesaid things—whether expressed by their proper or special names of provinces, lands, cities, and places, or not expressed—we newly, freely, and fully [Col. 0185] grant, confer, and donate, in the sense in which this is more fully and effectively understood, to most blessed Peter, to you, most holy father Pope Nicholas III, through you to your successors the Roman pontiffs, and to the Roman Church itself, so that, all matter of contention and discord having been removed, firm and complete peace and concord may endure between Church and empire, XCVIII, 863–868 and 844–863.

SILVESTER, Saint, pope.—In the Life of Saint Pope Sylvester and in the Lives of other Roman bishops, donations of every kind and description occur very frequently, after the donations of Constantine the Great, made to the Apostolic See or to other places specially consecrated to religion. Thus, in the Life of Saint Pope Stephen III, it is said that, concerning all the cities recovered, he sent a written grant to Saint Peter, to the holy Roman Church, and to all pontiffs of the Apostolic See in perpetuity, to possess them, CXXVII, 218.

In the Life of Pope Saint Adrian it is said: “As is shown to be contained in that same donation.” A copy of the same donation was placed upon the body of Blessed Peter, CXXVII, 218.

Thus divine providence won for the holy See ever greater veneration day by day, increasing its temporal power and splendor before the eyes of all. The faithful exalted this divine plan with the highest praises. And the Apostolic See always guarded its paternal inheritance faithfully; it increased the grain therein a hundredfold, CXXVII, 950.

To establish donations, one single and most ancient document would suffice: namely, the Charter of Cornutum, signed by public authority. From it one may conclude that, for five centuries following the year 471, solemn donations of both movable and immovable property were made to churches, CXXVII, 971.

Well known is this saying of Clovis and his successors: “Christ gave me the scepters; to Christ I return the crown.” For this was the zeal of most devout princes: to subject and dedicate royal insignia to Christ, Lord of kings, etc., CXXVII, 502.

STEPHEN II, pope.—Stephen II was made pontiff in most difficult times. At the very beginning of his pontificate, Aistulf, king of the Lombards, having broken the treaty which he had made with the Roman Church, resolved to attack Rome, at a time when the Romans had not yet abandoned obedience to the emperor. For the Roman pontiffs, after the seizure of their extensive estates and the heresy of Emperor Leo, had remained loyal to the empire of Leo and Constantine Copronymus and had not abandoned care of the commonwealth; and the Roman city, although afflicted by the calamities of war inflicted by King Aistulf, recognized the sovereignty of Constantine himself . . . . When King Aistulf was besieging Rome in order to subject it to his own rule and invading the cities of the Roman Church, Stephen sent letters to Pippin to urge him to send assistance. Then King Pippin sent an embassy to Aistulf, king of the Lombards, asking that, out of reverence for the most blessed Peter and Paul, he should not advance in hostility in the regions of Rome, and that at Pippin’s request he should not commit the superstitious and impious acts contrary to the order of law which he had never before committed at Rome. But Aistulf scorned to do this, and Pippin summoned all the Franks to arms against Aistulf and ordered them to come to him at the river Vidula. War was therefore prepared everywhere against King Aistulf, but the expedition was delayed for a while owing to the grave and dangerous illness of Pope Stephen. Yet Stephen was soon cured by a remarkable miracle through the intercession of Saint Dionysius the martyr, and he anointed Pippin and his sons, Charles and Carloman, and his wife Bertrada as kings of the Franks. Thus Pippin was anointed king twice: first by Saint Boniface, legate of the Apostolic See, as seems to appear in the acts of Pope Zachary; secondly by Pope Stephen. In anointing them kings, he called them patricians of the Romans.

After this, no satisfaction having been obtained from Aistulf, Pippin crossed the Alps with his entire army, defeated Aistulf in battle in the very passes of the mountains, pursued him in flight, and besieged him at Pavia. Then the pontiff, fearing a new shedding of Christian blood, negotiated with him; and, having received from Aistulf an oath and hostages for the restoration of Ravenna and other cities, he returned to Rome, while King Pippin returned victorious with his men to Gaul. Soon Pope Stephen complained to Pippin that King Aistulf had by no means kept his promises and had restored nothing either to the Roman Church or to the Roman commonwealth. In his letters the pontiff says of Aistulf: “He permitted not even a space of one palm’s breadth of land to be restored to Blessed Peter, the holy Church of God, or the Roman commonwealth, although they—that is, Pippin and his sons—had, of their own will, confirmed by a charter of donation that the cities and places were to be restored to Blessed Peter, the holy Church of God, and the commonwealth.” From these words one may infer that, when peace was concluded between Stephen and Aistulf, Pippin imposed upon the latter the condition that he restore what had been taken from both the Roman Church and the Roman commonwealth, not to the Roman Empire, as some wrongly maintain.

Indeed, King Aistulf again assembled a huge army and encircled the city of Rome itself with a siege. Then Pippin moved with his army against the Lombards, besieged Aistulf, driven to the Alpine passes, at Pavia, and refused ever to grant pardon to him when he begged for it after breaking the treaty, until he had handed over to the Roman pontiff Ravenna together with the entire exarchate, the Pentapolis, and twenty cities included in those provinces. From this time Roman pontiffs exercised full civil administration both in Rome and in the Exarchate of Ravenna, unless they were at times hindered by rebellion and other disturbances. Behold how the Romans, from the time when Pippin granted the Exarchate of Ravenna to the Prince of the Apostles and his successors, entirely cast off the domination of the heretical Emperor Constantine Copronymus, who could not defend them against the Lombards, and established a commonwealth whose head was called the Roman pontiff and whose defender and protector was called Pippin, king of the Franks. Hence, when Stephen II speaks in his letters of Aistulf and the harassment of the city of Rome, he nowhere mentions the emperor and calls the Romans his own people. Pope Paul, Stephen’s successor, and Adrian I use the same forms of speech. Contrary to the agreement, Aistulf retained until his death certain cities comprised in Pippin’s donation—such as Faenza, Ferrara, Osimo, Ancona, Umana, Bologna, etc.—and these cities were later likewise restored to the supreme pontiff with their territories and boundaries, CXXVIII, 1119–1133.

As is apparent from what has been said, agreements were entered into and solemnly confirmed by oath between Pope Stephen and King Pippin concerning the defense and protection of the Roman Church; but Stephen did not grant Pippin jurisdiction over the city of Rome and the Roman duchy. Two things, meanwhile, were agreed between Stephen and Pippin: first, that Stephen should confer upon Pippin the singular and distinguished honor, granted to no one before him, of the Roman patriciate, by virtue of which Pippin should undertake the guardianship, defense, and advocacy of the Roman Church, of the patrimonies of Blessed Peter, and of all the rights and plenary jurisdictions of the Apostolic See; second, that Pippin, by virtue of such protection, should strive with all his power to have the Church’s rights restored and the Exarchate of Ravenna wrested from Lombard hands and handed over to the Roman pontiff. The first is clearly shown by Stephen’s letter to Pippin: “What none of your parents deserved to receive, you have received; and the Prince of the Apostles, making you his special ones above other kings and nations, has entrusted all his causes to you; and you will render account to God of how you have fought for the justice of that gatekeeper of the heavenly kingdom.” The second is likewise clear from Stephen’s letters: “For when we were brought before your honey-sweet countenance, we commended into your hands all the causes of the Prince of the Apostles, since, inspired by God, you deigned to lend an ear to our petitions; and you promised Blessed Peter to demand his justice and procure the defense of the holy Church of God.” And: “Swiftly and without impediment restore to Blessed Peter the cities and places, all hostages and captives, which you promised Blessed Peter by your donation—or everything that the donation itself contains.”

These alone were the agreements established between Stephen and Pippin, and no others. Nowhere in their letters is any word to be found concerning an empire over the City or a Roman duchy granted to Pippin. There is frequent discourse of the oath and promise made by Pippin to Stephen to fight for the Church of God and to restore or donate the Exarchate of Ravenna to the Roman Church, but never a word of that imagined grant of jurisdiction which some assert. What more need be said? If, in conferring the patriciate upon Pippin, Stephen had granted him some right over the city of Rome, could he afterwards, in letters addressed to Pippin, have continued to use the words and terms by which he testified to his own full dominion over the City and Roman citizens? Yet he speaks of his Roman commonwealth, his people, and his Roman city: “For all our people of the Roman commonwealth,” says Stephen, “are afflicted with us by great sorrow and most bitter tears,” etc., etc. This mode of speech is clear evidence that jurisdiction was not alienated or divided, but always retained and preserved intact by the pope. Moreover, the earliest Frankish emperors themselves spoke in their acts indeed of the guardianship and defense of the Roman Church, but never of jurisdiction over the City or Roman duchy granted to them by the popes, CXXVIII, 1133–1136.

[Col. 0187] [Additions to Stephen II.]

In the year 753, in the month of October, Pope Stephen II, at the command of the Emperor of Constantinople, set out for Aistulf, king of the Lombards, intending to demand back from him the Ravennate exarchate and the other places he had seized. When he had attempted this in vain, he approached King Pippin; and, first, on 6 January 754 at Ponthion, having received a promise of assistance, he concluded at the public assembly of Quierzy an agreement concerning the defense of the Roman Church and the coronation of Pippin and his sons. By this agreement Pippin promised that he would confer upon the Roman Church those things which Aistulf had taken from the Greeks. This condition was expressed in these words:

> “From Luna with the island of Corsica; then at Suriano; then at Mount Bardon; thence at Berceto; then at Parma; then at Reggio; and thence at Mantua and at Monte Silicis; together with the whole exarchate of Ravenna as it had formerly been, and the provinces of Venetia and Istria, and likewise the whole duchy of Spoleto and Benevento.”

Yet the war, undertaken with great difficulty, was brought only so far, and ended in 755, that the Lombards restored the Pentapolis, Narni, Ceccano, the cities of Tuscia and Roman Campania which they had invaded, and the remaining places concerning which the Roman people complained. When the war was renewed, Comacchio was added in the year 756. Hence the completed donation of Pippin included these cities: Ravenna, Rimini, Pesaro, Conca, Fano, Cesena, Senigallia, Jesi, Forlimpopoli, Forlì with Sarsina, Montefeltro, Acquarola, Aggiomonte, Monte Lucati, Serra, the Castle of Saint Marinus, Bobbio, Urbino, Cagli, Luceoli, Gubbio, and Comacchio. Moreover, that Faenza, the duchy of Ferrara, Imola, Bologna, and Gabello were likewise handed over is clear from what follows; nor do we ever find that the pope subsequently obtained anything further from Pippin.

Eighteen years later, after Desiderius had first been defeated, the people of Spoleto and Rieti, the inhabitants of the duchies of Fermo, Osimo, and Ancona, and the inhabitants of the castle of Felicitas placed themselves under Pope Hadrian. King Charles, at Rome, promised Hadrian restitution of the exarchate invaded by Desiderius and, besides this, confirmed Pippin’s donation at Quierzy. On the basis of these promises, Pope Hadrian in 774 or 775 received part of the exarchate; but the remainder—namely Imola, Bologna, Gabello, Faenza, the duchy of Ferrara, Comacchio, Forlì, Forlimpopoli, Cesena, Bobbio, the tenth district of Tribunatus, which the Archbishop of Ravenna resisted, and the castle of Felicitas, seized by the Duke of Chiusi—he was unable to recover until 775 or 776.

But Hadrian went further. From the year 777 onward he began to demand lands never possessed either by himself or by Stephen or Paul, but which, he maintained, had formerly been taken from the popes by Lombard kings or others and ought to be restored to him under the donation of Quierzy. First, from 777 onward, he sought certain cities situated in Lombard Tuscia, the duchies of Spoleto and Benevento, Corsica, and the Sabine patrimony; then Terracina, which had been occupied and lost again, Gaeta, Naples, and the patrimonies in those regions. In 781, at Rome, in the presence of Charles and of his sons Pippin and Louis, consecrated kings respectively of the Lombards and Aquitaine, he obtained the grant of the Sabine patrimony for the endowment of lamps and the support of the poor. Yet this was not handed over by Charles’s envoys to Saint Peter until 783.

At the same time, or certainly in 787, the cities in Lombard Tuscia—Suana, Tuscania, Viterbo, Bagnoregio, and the rest, namely the Castle of Felicitas, Orvieto, Ferento, Orte, and Marca—were restored. In 787 he demanded that Populonia and Roselle, as well as cities in the region of Benevento and then Capua, should be added to these. On Charles’s third journey to Rome he obtained a promise that Benevento would be handed over; this promise, however, proved void, because the king, influenced by favor toward Duke Grimoald, granted that bishoprics, monasteries, public estates, and cities without inhabitants should indeed be delivered to the pope, but allowed their inhabitants to remain under Grimoald’s allegiance.

This was the end of Hadrian’s demands and of Charles’s favors. For we find neither that Hadrian obtained anything further, nor that his successor Leo III, when in 808 he demanded the island of Corsica under the agreement of Quierzy, met with better success. It is therefore established that Charles neither wished nor was able to keep intact the things which, while Desiderius still held Pavia and the outcome of the war was uncertain, he had promised the pope in the renewed agreement of Quierzy—perhaps because the popes could not prove their rights to the individual territories situated south of the line described, as they seem to have been bound and to have promised.

Accordingly, at Charles’s death the situation was such that, under Frankish rule, the popes possessed:

1. By ancient right, the city of Rome with its duchy—that is, Campania with Maritima as far as Ceprano and Terracina, and Roman Tuscia: namely the cities of Porto, Centumcellae, Cære, Blera, Marturanum, Sutri, Nepi, Castel, Gallese, Orte, Bomarzo, Amelia, Todi, Perugia with its three islands, Narni, and Otricoli.

2. By the donation of Pippin and Charles, the exarchate of Ravenna, the Pentapolis, and Emilia with the cities mentioned above.

3. By the agreement of Quierzy and by a right proved to King Charles, the Sabine territory, the cities in Lombard Tuscia mentioned above—perhaps with Populonia and Roselle added—and the rights delivered to them in the duchy of Benevento.

They claimed, but could not establish, moreover:

4. Very many territories extending southward from Luna with the island of Corsica through Suriano, Mount Bardon, Berceto, Parma, Reggio, Mantua, and Monte Silicis—especially Corsica, Populonia and Roselle, the duchies of Spoleto and Benevento, Capua, Gaeta, Naples, and the patrimonies situated there, partly held by the Franks, partly by the dukes of Benevento, and partly by the Greeks.

Nothing was added to these by Emperor Louis except the “legal estate” (*curtem legalem*) in Germany. Hence it plainly appears beyond doubt that the confirmation circulated under his name is fabricated—not only because of defects of form, but because Sardinia and Sicily, and a part of Beneventan Campania with the cities of Sora, Arce, Aquino, Arpino, Teano, and Capua, together with the Beneventan, Salernitan, Neapolitan, Upper-Calabrian, and Lower-Calabrian patrimonies, which were not even under Frankish power, are said to have been granted to the pope. The oldest surviving copy of the charter is found in a Vatican codex written in the twelfth century, XCVII, 679, 680, 681.

ZACHARIAS, Saint, Pope.—Popes Gregory II and III had long since entered into agreements with the Franks when Pippin, brother of Carloman, both sons of Charles Martel, consulted Zacharias as to which of the two seemed to him more worthy of royal eminence: the man who, languishing in idleness, contributed nothing to the common welfare of the peoples, or the man who thought day and night about the safety and protection of the kingdom. Zacharias declared that he wholly considered the man who served the interests of the kingdom and the safety of the peoples to be the one who should be chosen king; and, being asked, he issued a decree that they should substitute Pippin as king.

This is recorded as follows in the notice on Pope Saint Zacharias:

> “Carloman, son of Charles, king of the Franks, abandoning the glory of this present life and earthly power, came in devotion to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, with some of his faithful men, and devoted himself to that apostle of God. Promising that he would remain in a distinctive habit, he received from that most holy pontiff the yoke of clerical office. Among many other gifts, before the grant, he offered to blessed Peter the Apostle a larger silver arch, weighing seventy pounds; and after some time he departed for the monastery of blessed Benedict situated in the territory of the people of Aquino, where he professed under oath that he would end his life.” LXXXIX, 906.

The Annals of Saint-Bertin, under the year 749, report that Burchard and Fulrad were sent concerning the conferral of kingship upon Pippin:

> “Burchard, bishop of Würzburg, and Fulrad the chaplain were sent to Pope Zacharias to inquire concerning the kings in Francia who at that time did not possess royal power . . . whether this was right or not. And Pope Zacharias directed Pippin that it was better for him who possessed power to be called king than for him who remained without royal power, so that order might not be disturbed. Therefore, by apostolic authority, he commanded Pippin to be made king.”

And under the year 750:

> “Pippin was elected king according to the custom of the Franks, anointed by the hand of Boniface, archbishop of holy memory, and raised to kingship by the Franks in the city of Soissons. Hilderic, however, who was falsely called king, was tonsured and sent to the monastery of Saint-Bertin.”

Likewise the Continuator of Fredegar wrote under the year 751:

> “And indeed the land rested from wars. At that time, with the counsel and consent of all the Franks, after an embassy had been sent and authority received from the Apostolic See, the illustrious Pippin was raised, by the election of all Francia, to the royal throne, with the consecration of the bishops and the submission of the princes, together with Queen Bertrada, as ancient order requires.”

And the Annals published by Pithou have:

> “In the year 732 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Pope Zacharias, by the authority of blessed Peter the Apostle, directed the people of the Franks that Pippin, who exercised royal power, should also enjoy the dignity of the name. Accordingly King Hilderic, the last of the Merovingians to rule the Franks, was deposed and sent into a monastery. Pippin, however, was anointed in the city of Soissons by Saint Boniface the archbishop and exalted to the honor of kingship.”

The same Pope Zacharias granted Pippin the authority to nominate bishops of the kingdom of the Franks, so that he might apply a healing hand to the abuses and excesses of those times when elections had to take place. This was done while Pippin was still mayor of the palace; for he received such an indulgence at the Council of Soissons, held in 744, eight years before he ascended the royal throne.

> “Pippin, having laid before Zacharias, Roman pope, the necessity of this kingdom, received his consent at the synod in which Boniface the martyr took part, that, by the exertions of those most approved by him, he might provide for the severity of the times when bishops died.” Lupus, Abbot of Ferrières, Epistle 81, to Amulo of Lyons, LXXXIX, 966, 967, 968.

ZOSIMUS, Pope.—Although the tradition of the Fathers has attributed such great authority to the Apostolic See that no one would dare to dispute its judgment, and although that same See has always preserved this through the canons and rules, so that ecclesiastical discipline, still proceeding according to its own laws, may render to the name of Peter—from whom it too descends—the reverence which it owes: for canonical antiquity, by the judgments of all, has willed that this apostle possess such power, even by the promise of Christ our God himself, that he might loose things bound and bind things loosed; and an equal condition of authority has been given to those who, by his consent, deserved to inherit the See. For Peter himself has care both of all the Churches and especially of this one in which he sat; nor does he permit any privilege or any breath of judgment to waver, he whose own name established foundations firm and unblunted by any disturbances, and which no one rashly attacks without peril to himself.

Since, therefore, Peter is the head of so great an authority, and the succeeding endeavors of all the elders have confirmed that the Roman Church, whose place we govern and whose authority of name we hold—as you are aware—should be strengthened by all human and divine laws and disciplines: yet, dearest brethren, as priests ought to know, although we possessed such authority that no one could call our judgment into question, we have done nothing without voluntarily reporting it to your knowledge by our letters, etc. . . . XX, 676.

Before concluding this Index, we have decided to append here addresses both of the Supreme Pontiff to bishops and of bishops to the Supreme Pontiff, which strongly confirm our thesis, especially in these times.

## Address of Our Most Holy Lord Pius IX, Pope by Divine Providence

Delivered in Consistory on 9 June 1862, with patriarchs, primates, archbishops, and bishops also present, assembled at Rome for the canonization solemnities of the holy martyrs in Japan and Michael of the Saints.

Venerable Brethren,

We were indeed filled with the greatest joy, venerable brethren, when yesterday, with God’s gracious assistance, we were able to decree the honors and cult of the saints for twenty-seven most unconquered heroes of our divine religion, with you standing at our side—endowed as you are with outstanding devotion and virtue, called to share our solicitude, and in this great harshness of the times courageously contending for the House of Israel, a supreme comfort and consolation to us.

Would that, while we are filled with joy of this kind, no cause of sorrow and mourning from elsewhere afflicted us. For we cannot but grieve and be deeply distressed when we see the most grievous and never sufficiently lamented evils and losses by which, with immense harm to souls, the Catholic Church and civil society itself are now miserably oppressed and harassed. You know very well, venerable brethren, that a most foul war against the entire Catholic cause has been stirred up by those men who, as enemies of Christ’s cross, unable to endure sound doctrine, joined together in a wicked conspiracy, blaspheme whatever they do not know; and by depraved arts of every kind strive to undermine—indeed, if it could ever be done, wholly overthrow—the foundations of our most holy religion and of human society, and to imbue and corrupt all minds with every most destructive error and tear them away from the Catholic religion.

These most cunning craftsmen of fraud and fabricators of falsehood do not cease to summon forth from darkness every monstrous portent of ancient errors, so often defeated and repelled by most wise writings and condemned by the gravest judgment of the Church; they magnify them, expressed in new, diverse, and most deceitful forms and words, and disseminate them everywhere in every possible way. By this most disastrous and utterly diabolical art they contaminate and disfigure every branch of knowledge; they spread deadly poison for the ruin of souls; they foster unrestrained license in living and every depraved desire; they overturn religious and social order; they endeavor to extinguish every idea of justice, truth, right, uprightness, and religion; and they ridicule, despise, and attack the most holy dogmas and doctrine of Christ.

The mind recoils in horror and shrinks from even lightly touching upon the principal and pestilential errors by which men of this sort, in these most wretched times, throw all divine and human things into confusion.

None of you, venerable brethren, is unaware that these men utterly destroy that necessary coherence which, by God’s will, exists between the two orders, the natural and the supernatural; and that they wholly alter, overthrow, and obliterate the proper, true, and genuine character and authority of divine revelation, and the constitution and power of the Church. They proceed to such rashness of opinion that they do not fear most boldly to deny every truth, law, authority, and right of divine origin. For they are not ashamed to assert that philosophical and moral science, and civil laws also, can and ought to depart from divine revelation and the authority of the Church; that the Church is not a true and perfect society fully free, nor possessed of its own proper and permanent rights conferred on it by its divine Founder; but that it belongs to civil power to define what the Church’s rights and limits are, within which it may exercise those rights.

From this they perversely devise that civil power may interfere in matters relating to religion, morals, and spiritual government, and may even hinder bishops and the faithful from communicating freely and mutually with the Roman Pontiff, divinely established as supreme Pastor of the whole Church, so that the necessary and closest union which, by the institution of Christ the Lord himself, must altogether exist between the members of Christ’s mystical body and its visible head may be completely dissolved. Nor do they hesitate, by every fraud and deception, to proclaim publicly that the sacred ministers of the Church and the Roman Pontiff must be wholly excluded from every right and dominion in temporal affairs.

Moreover, with the utmost shamelessness, they do not hesitate to assert that divine revelation not only offers no advantage but even harms human perfection; that divine revelation itself is imperfect and therefore subject to a continuous and indefinite progress corresponding to the progress of human reason. Consequently, they are unashamed to boast that the prophecies and miracles set forth and narrated in Holy Scripture are inventions of poets; that the most sacred mysteries of our divine faith are the outcome of philosophical inquiry; that mythical inventions are contained in the divine books of both Testaments; and that our Lord Jesus Christ himself—horrible to say!—is a mythical fiction.

Therefore these most turbulent worshippers of perverse doctrines babble that moral laws do not need divine sanction, that human laws need not conform to natural right or receive binding force from God, and that consequently no divine law exists. They further dare to deny every action of God upon human beings and the world, and rashly affirm that human reason, with no regard whatever for God, is the sole judge of truth and falsehood, good and evil; that human reason is a law to itself and sufficient through its natural powers to secure the good of individuals and peoples. And while they perversely dare to derive all religious truths from the native force of human reason, they also attribute to each person a sort of primary right by which he may freely think and speak about religion and render to God the honor and worship which he judges best according to his own preference.

Indeed, they reach such a degree of impiety and shamelessness that they endeavor to storm heaven and remove God himself altogether. With remarkable wickedness and equal folly, they do not fear to assert that no supreme, most wise, and most provident divine Being exists distinct from the universe of things; that God is identical with the nature of things and is therefore subject to change; that God in fact comes into being in humanity and in the world; that all things are God and possess the very substance of God; and that God and the world are one and the same thing—thus spirit and matter, necessity and freedom, truth and falsehood, good and evil, justice and injustice. Nothing more insane, more impious, or more opposed to reason itself could ever be imagined or devised.

Concerning authority and right, they babble so rashly as shamelessly to say that authority is nothing other than the sum of numbers and material forces; that right consists in material fact; that all human duties are an empty name; and that all human acts have the force of right.

Then, heaping fiction upon fiction and delusion upon delusion, trampling underfoot all legitimate authority and every legitimate right, obligation, and duty, they do not hesitate to substitute false and counterfeit rights of force for true and legitimate right, and to subject moral order to the order of material things. They recognize no forces except those founded in matter; and they place all moral discipline and uprightness in accumulating and increasing wealth by whatever means and in satisfying every depraved pleasure. By these wicked and abominable principles they uphold, foster, and exalt the reprobate inclination of the flesh rebelling against the spirit; to it they attribute natural gifts and rights, which they say are trampled upon by Catholic teaching—altogether disregarding the warning of the Apostle:

> “If you live according to the flesh, you shall die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you shall live.” [Romans 8:13.]

They further strive to invade and destroy all rights of legitimate property, and wrongly devise and imagine a certain right without any prescribed limits, with which they suppose the State to be endowed, rashly judging it to be the origin and fountain of every right.

While sorrowfully and briefly touching upon these principal errors of our most unhappy age, venerable brethren, we omit to enumerate the almost innumerable other falsehoods and deceits, very well known and fully apparent to you, by which the enemies of God and humankind seek to disturb and overthrow both sacred and civil society. We pass over in silence the many and most serious injuries, calumnies, and insults by which they never cease to tear apart and persecute the sacred ministers of the Church and this Apostolic See.

We say nothing of the truly unjust hypocrisy by which the leaders and followers of the most disastrous disturbance and rebellion, especially in Italy, proclaim that they wish the Church to enjoy her liberty, while with utterly sacrilegious audacity they daily trample more and more upon every right and law of the Church, plunder her goods, harass in every way bishops and ecclesiastics who fulfill their office nobly, cast them into prison, violently expel members of religious orders and virgins consecrated to God from their monasteries, despoil them of their own property, and leave nothing unattempted in order to reduce the Church herself to a most shameful servitude and oppress her.

And while we receive a singular pleasure from your most welcome presence, you yourselves see, venerable brethren, what freedom the bishops of Italy now possess. Although courageously and steadfastly fighting the battles of the Lord, through the action of opponents they have been unable, to our profound grief, to come to us, associate with you, and attend this gathering, as they earnestly wished—as the archbishops and bishops of unhappy Italy have testified in letters overflowing with the highest love and obedience toward us and this Holy See. You likewise see no bishops from Portugal present here, and we grieve not a little when we consider the nature of the difficulties that prevented them from undertaking the journey to Rome.

We omit to recount the many other truly sad and dreadful acts perpetrated by these adherents of perverse doctrines, to the incredible mourning of ourselves, yourselves, and all good people. We say nothing likewise of the impious conspiracy and of the machinations and deceits of every kind by which they seek utterly to overthrow and destroy the temporal sovereignty of this Apostolic See.

Rather, we gladly recall the truly remarkable unanimity with which you yourselves, together with the other venerable brethren, bishops of the whole Catholic world, have never ceased, both in letters addressed to us and in pastoral letters written to the faithful, to expose and refute such deceptions, and at the same time to teach that this temporal sovereignty of the Holy See was given to the Roman Pontiff by a singular design of divine providence, and that it is necessary so that the Roman Pontiff, subject to no prince or civil power whatsoever, may exercise throughout the whole Church in fullest freedom the power and authority divinely received from Christ the Lord himself to feed and govern the entire flock of the Lord, and may provide more effectively for the good, advantage, and needs of the Church and the faithful.

What we have so far lamented, venerable brethren, presents a truly mournful spectacle. For who does not see that, through the iniquity of depraved doctrines and so many most wicked delusions and schemes, the Christian people are more miserably corrupted and driven toward ruin day by day; that the Catholic Church, her saving doctrine, venerable rights and laws, and sacred ministers are attacked; and that therefore every vice and crime grows and spreads, while civil society itself is agitated?

Therefore, mindful of our apostolic ministry and especially solicitous for the spiritual good and salvation of all peoples entrusted to us by God, since—using the words of our most holy predecessor Leo—“we cannot otherwise govern those entrusted to us unless we pursue with zeal for the Lord’s faith those who are destroyers and destroyed, and, lest this pestilence spread more widely, cut them off from sound minds by such severity as we can” [Epistle 7 to the Bishops throughout Italy, ch. 2, Ballerini edition], in this most distinguished assembly of yours, raising our apostolic voice, we reprove, proscribe, and condemn all the errors mentioned above, especially as altogether repugnant and supremely contrary not only to Catholic faith and doctrine and to divine and ecclesiastical laws, but also to eternal and natural law, justice, and right reason itself.

But you, venerable brethren, who are the salt of the earth and guardians and pastors of the Lord’s flock, we exhort and beseech again and again: in accordance with your eminent piety and episcopal zeal, continue—as hitherto you have done to the great honor of your order—to employ every care, diligence, and effort to keep the faithful entrusted to you away from these poisonous pastures, and by speech and suitable writings to refute and defeat the monsters of so many perverse opinions. For you know very well that the matter is of the highest importance, since it concerns our most holy faith and the Catholic Church and her doctrine, the salvation of peoples, and the good and tranquility of human society.

Therefore, insofar as lies in you, never cease to turn the faithful away from the contagion of so dreadful a pestilence: that is, to take harmful books and newspapers from their eyes and hands; continually to instruct and train the faithful in the most holy precepts of our august religion; and to warn and exhort them to flee these teachers of iniquity as from the face of a serpent. Continue to direct all your care and thought chiefly to ensuring that the clergy be formed holily and learnedly and shine in every virtue; that young people of both sexes be diligently trained in moral uprightness, piety, and every virtue; and that the system of studies be salutary. Keep most careful watch and see that nothing ever creep into the teaching of humane letters and more rigorous disciplines which might oppose faith, religion, and good morals.

Act manfully, venerable brethren, and never lose heart amid this great turmoil and wickedness of the times. Trusting wholly in divine help, taking up in all things the unconquerable shield of righteousness and faith, and taking the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, do not cease to withstand the attempts of all the enemies of the Catholic Church and of this Apostolic See, to blunt their weapons, and to break their assaults.

Meanwhile, venerable brethren, with our eyes raised to heaven day and night, let us not cease to pray and entreat unceasingly, in the humility of our hearts, the most merciful Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who makes light shine out of darkness and is able to raise children of Abraham from stones, that through the merits of his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, he may stretch forth a helping right hand to Christian and civil society, scatter all errors and impieties, enlighten by the light of his divine grace the minds of all who err, and convert and recall them to himself, so that his holy Church may attain the peace most earnestly desired, receive ever greater increase throughout the earth, and flourish and prosper.

And that we may more easily obtain what we ask and seek, let us not cease to invoke first of all as our intercessor before God the Immaculate and most holy Virgin Mary, Mother of God, who, as our most merciful and loving mother, has always destroyed all heresies, and whose patronage with God is second to none in promptness. Let us also seek the prayers of Saint Joseph, spouse of that same Virgin; of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul; of all the heavenly saints; and especially of those whom we have lately enrolled among the saints and whom we honor and venerate.

Before concluding our address, we cannot refrain from again testifying and affirming that we are filled with the greatest consolation as we enjoy the most welcome sight of you all, venerable brethren. Bound firmly to us and to this Chair of Peter by such faith, devotion, and reverence, you glory in carrying out your ministry and in seeking with every effort the greater glory of God and the salvation of souls. With hearts most united, and with truly remarkable care and love, together with the other venerable brethren, bishops of the whole Catholic world, and the faithful entrusted to your and their care, you do not cease in every way to alleviate and relieve our most grave distresses and afflictions.

Accordingly, on this occasion also, we publicly and openly profess in the fullest terms the sentiments of our equally loving and grateful heart toward you, all the other venerable brethren, and the faithful themselves. We ask you, when you have returned to your dioceses, to convey in our name these sentiments of our heart to the faithful entrusted to your vigilance, to assure them of our paternal love for them and of the Apostolic Blessing which, proceeding from the depths of our heart and joined with the wish for every true happiness, we most gladly impart to you yourselves, venerable brethren, and to those faithful.

## To Our Most Holy Lord Pius IX, Supreme Pontiff

The bishops present at Rome for the sacred solemnities of the twenty-six newly canonized holy martyrs of Japan and of Michael of the Saints, on the feast of Pentecost, 1862.

Most Blessed Father,

From the time when, on the sacred day of Pentecost, the apostles of Jesus Christ, united with Peter, head of the Church, in prayer, received the Holy Spirit, and, moved by his divine impulse, announced the wonderful power of God, each in his own language, to men of almost every nation assembled in the Holy City, never, as we believe, until this day have so many of their heirs, at the recurrence of these same solemnities, stood around the venerable successor of Peter while he prayed, heard him while he decreed, and strengthened him while he governed.

And just as, amid the dangers surrounding the nascent Church, nothing more joyful could have happened to the apostles than to stand beside the first Vicar of Christ on earth, newly inspired by the divine Spirit, so amid the present distresses of the holy Church nothing could be more fitting or sacred for us than to lay at the feet of Your Blessedness all the reverence and devotion contained in our hearts toward Your Holiness, and at the same time unanimously to declare with what admiration we regard the eminent virtues by which our Supreme Pontiff excels, and with what resolve we adhere to the things which this other Peter has taught, or which he has so firmly willed to stand established and ratified.

A new ardor inflames our hearts; a livelier light of faith illuminates our minds; a holier love possesses our souls. We feel our tongues quiver with the flames of that sacred fire which kindled the most gentle heart of Mary, around whom the apostles gathered, with a more burning desire for the salvation of humankind, and which impelled the apostles themselves to proclaim the mighty works of God.

Therefore, giving Your Blessedness abundant thanks because you have allowed us, in these most difficult times, to hasten to the pontifical throne, to console you in affliction, and to reveal to you the sentiments of our own hearts and likewise of the clergy and people entrusted to our care, we acclaim you with one voice and one mind, wishing you all prosperity and every good:

> Live long, Holy Father, and be strong to govern the Catholic Church. Continue, as you do, to protect her by your strength, guide her by your prudence, and adorn her by your virtues. Go before us as a good shepherd; by your example feed the sheep and lambs with heavenly food, refresh them with the waters of heavenly Wisdom. For you are our teacher of sound doctrine; you are the center of unity; you are an unfailing light prepared by divine Wisdom for the peoples. You are the rock and the foundation of the Church itself, against which the gates of hell shall never prevail. When you speak, we hear Peter; when you decree, we obey Christ. We admire you, amid so many troubles and storms, fulfilling the duties of your sacred office with serene brow and undisturbed mind, unconquered and unshaken.

Yet while we have the most just grounds for glorying in these things, we cannot but turn our eyes also toward what is sorrowful. For on every side there present themselves to our minds the monstrous deeds of those who have miserably ravaged the most beautiful land of Italy, of which you, Most Blessed Father, are the support and glory, and who strive to undermine and utterly overthrow your own temporal sovereignty and that of the Holy See—a sovereignty from which every noble benefit to civil society has flowed, as it were, from its fountainhead.

For neither the perpetual rights of centuries, nor the long and peaceful possession of government, nor finally treaties sanctioned and confirmed by the authority of all Europe, could prevent all things from being turned upside down, with contempt for all those laws by which states had hitherto stood supported.

But to come nearer to our own case: we see you, most blessed Father, despoiled by the wicked crime of usurping men of those provinces by whose aid most equitable provision was made both for the dignity of the Holy See and for the administration of the whole Church—men who [Col. 0194] have liberty only as a cloak for malice. Since Your Holiness has opposed their unjust violence with a most unconquered spirit, we judge that the thanks of all Catholics are owed to you in the fullest measure.

For we acknowledge the civil sovereignty of the Holy See as something necessary and manifestly established by the providence of God; nor do we hesitate to declare that, in the present state of human affairs, this very civil sovereignty is altogether required for the good and free governance of the Church and of souls. It was indeed fitting that the Roman Pontiff, head of the whole Church, should be subject to no prince—indeed, should be the guest of none—but, seated within his own dominion and kingdom, should be independent in his own right, and in noble, peaceful, and fostering liberty should protect and defend the Catholic faith and govern and direct the whole Christian commonwealth.

And who can deny that, amid this conflict of human affairs, opinions, and institutions, it is necessary that there be preserved in the midst of Europe, among the three continents of the old world, a kind of sacred place and most august See, from which there may arise in turn for peoples and princes a great and powerful voice: namely, the voice of justice and truth, favoring none above the rest, obeying the will of none, a voice which no one can restrain by threats or circumvent by any devices?

Moreover, how on this occasion could it have happened that the bishops of the Church might come here safely from the whole world to deliberate with Your Holiness concerning matters of the greatest gravity, if, gathering from so many and such diverse regions and nations, they had found some prince ruling these lands who either regarded their own sovereigns with suspicion or, himself suspected by them, opposed them? For there are duties belonging both to the Christian and to the citizen: duties not indeed opposed to one another, but nevertheless distinct. How could bishops fulfill them unless there remained at Rome a civil sovereignty such as that of the pontiffs, wholly free from subjection to another’s jurisdiction and, as it were, a center of universal concord—breathing nothing of human ambition and plotting nothing for earthly dominion?

Therefore we come freely to the free Pontiff-King: as pastors, taking fitting and equitable care for the affairs of the Church; as citizens, for the affairs of our country; and neglecting neither the duties of pastors nor those of citizens.

Since these things are so, who would dare to attack that sovereignty, so ancient, founded with such authority and such force of necessity? If one considers even that human law upon which the security of princes and the liberty of peoples rest, what other power can be compared with it? What power is so venerable and holy? What monarchy or republic, whether in former or more recent ages, can boast rights so august, so ancient, so inviolable? If all these things are once despised and trampled underfoot even in this Holy See, what prince can be secure in his kingdom, or what republic in its territory? Therefore, most holy Father, you contend and struggle indeed for religion, but also for justice and for those rights which are the foundations of human affairs among nations.

But it scarcely becomes us to say more on so grave a cause, since we have heard you very often not so much discoursing upon it as teaching it. For your voice, like a priestly trumpet sounding throughout the whole world, has proclaimed that “it was brought about by a wholly singular design of divine Providence that the Roman Pontiff, whom Christ established as head and center of His whole Church, should acquire civil sovereignty” [Apostolic Letter, 26 March 1860, pp. 3, 5; Allocution, 20 June 1859, p. 6; Encyclical, 19 June 1866, p. 4; Allocution, 17 December 1860]. Therefore all of us must hold it as most certain that this temporal government did not accrue to the Holy See by chance, but was granted to it by a special divine disposition, and through a long succession of years was strengthened and preserved by the unanimous consent of all kingdoms and empires, almost as by a miracle.

In lofty and solemn language you likewise declared: “That you will constantly defend and preserve whole and inviolate the civil sovereignty of the Roman Church and its temporal possessions and rights, which concern the whole Catholic world; indeed, that the defense of the sovereignty of the Holy See and of the patrimony of blessed Peter belongs to all Catholics; and that you are prepared rather to lay down your life than in any way to abandon this cause of God, of the Church, and of justice.” [Encyclical Letter, 19 January 1860, pp. 7–8.] To these illustrious words we respond with acclamation and applause: that we are prepared to go with you even to prison and to death; and we humbly ask you to remain unmoved in this constancy and most steadfast resolve, made a spectacle to angels and men of unconquered courage and highest virtue.
