This is also required of you by the Church of Christ, for whose happier governance civil sovereignty was most providently assigned to the Roman Pontiffs. The Church so regarded its defense as belonging to herself that, when the Apostolic See was once vacant and she was in the gravest straits, the Fathers of the Council of Constance, as public documents show, administered all the temporal possessions of the Roman Church jointly. Christ’s faithful, scattered through every region of the earth, also demand it: they long to come to you freely and freely to provide for their consciences. Finally, civil society itself demands it, for in the overthrow of your government it feels its own foundations shaken.

But why say more? You at last condemned by a just judgment wicked men and plunderers of ecclesiastical goods, proclaiming all that they had done “void and null” [Allocution, 26 September 1859, p. 7]. You decreed that all acts attempted by them were “wholly illegitimate and sacrilegious” [Allocution, 20 June 1859, p. 8]; and you declared, rightly and deservedly, that those guilty of such crimes were subject to ecclesiastical penalties and censures. [Apostolic Letters, 26 March 1860.]

It is ours reverently to receive these most weighty utterances of your mouth and these most illustrious deeds, and to renew our full assent to them. For as a body, joined to its head by the union of its members and by one life, suffers with it in all things, so we too must agree with you. In every one of your most bitter afflictions we are so united with you that whatever you are made to suffer, we also suffer through the concord of love. Meanwhile we humbly invoke God to put an end to so unjust a disturbance of affairs and to restore the Church, the bride of His Son, so miserably despoiled and oppressed, to her former splendor and liberty.

Yet we are not surprised that the rights of the Apostolic See are so fiercely and relentlessly assailed and attacked. For some years now the madness of certain persons has gone so far that they no longer merely attempt to reject or call into doubt individual doctrines of the Church, but purpose utterly to overthrow the whole of Christian truth and the Christian commonwealth. Hence come the most impious attempts of vain science and false learning against the doctrines of Holy Scripture and its very inspiration; hence the unhealthy zeal to imbue youth, withdrawn from the guardianship of Mother Church and often deprived of every religious instruction, with every error of the age; hence new and most pernicious theories concerning the social, political, and religious order, freely disseminated everywhere; hence the now familiar practice, especially in these regions, of despising the authority of the Church, arrogating rights to oneself, trampling upon her commands, scorning her ministers, mocking worship, and even praising and honoring religious errors themselves—indeed, even ecclesiastics miserably proceeding along the path of perdition. Venerable bishops and priests of God are stripped of office, compelled into exile, or cast into prisons; indeed, they are insultingly dragged before civil tribunals for steadfastly carrying out their sacred ministry. The brides of Christ groan, expelled from their homes, almost consumed by hunger or soon to be so consumed. Religious men are unwillingly forced back into secular life. Violent hands are laid upon the sacred patrimony of the Church. By the flood of most evil books, newspapers, and images, a continual and most bitter war is waged against faith, morals, truth, and modesty itself.

But those who devise such things know very well that in the Holy See, as in an impregnable citadel, reside the strength and powers of all truth and justice by which the assaults of enemies are repelled; that there is a watchtower there from which the vigilant eyes of the supreme Guardian behold prepared ambushes from afar and announce them to their fellow-soldiers. Hence their implacable hatred; hence their incurable envy; hence the continual effort of most wicked men to cast down the holy Roman Church and her [Col. 0196] See and, if it could ever be done, to destroy them utterly.

Who, most blessed Father, beholding such things, or even hearing them recounted, can restrain himself from tears? Seized, therefore, by just sorrow, we lift eyes and hands to heaven, imploring with all our hearts that divine Spirit who on this day of old sanctified and strengthened the Church at its birth under Peter’s rule: may He now, with you as her shepherd and leader, protect, enlarge, and glorify her. May Mary, whom through you was solemnly honored in this very place with the title of Immaculate, be witness to the vows we utter. May these sacred ashes which we venerate—the ashes of Peter and Paul, holy patrons of the Roman Church—be witnesses. May the venerable remains of so many pontiffs, martyrs, and confessors, which make holy this very ground upon which we tread, be witnesses. Finally and especially, may those saints stand as witnesses for us who, enrolled this very day by your supreme judgment among the company of heaven, are today to undertake the Church’s protection under a new title and from their altars first offer prayers to almighty God also for your safety.

With all these standing by, we bishops—lest impiety pretend ignorance of this, or dare deny it—condemn the errors which you have condemned; we detest and reject the new and foreign doctrines everywhere proclaimed to the injury of the Church of Jesus Christ; we reprove and condemn sacrileges, robberies, violations of ecclesiastical immunity, and other abominations committed against the Church and the See of Peter.

This protestation, which we request may be entered in the public records of the Church, we confidently make also in the name of our absent brethren: whether those who, amid so many distresses, are forcibly confined at home and today keep silence and weep, or those who, prevented by grave business or ill health, have been unable to be present with us today. We further unite with ourselves our faithful clergy and people, who, animated by the same love for you and the same devout reverence as ourselves, have most clearly demonstrated their devotion to you both by unceasing prayers and by their offerings, generally made with remarkable generosity, in Peter’s Pence. They know well that by their sacrifices this also is being secured: that while provision is made for the needs of the supreme Shepherd, provision is at the same time made for preserving his freedom.

Would that all peoples might join together in placing in safety this common cause of the whole Christian world—indeed, of the entire social order!

Would that kings and the powers of the age might understand and be instructed that the cause of the Pontiff is the cause of all princes and kingdoms; that they might see whither the wicked efforts of his adversaries tend, and at last foresee the ultimate consequences!

Would that those unhappy few ecclesiastics and religious men might come to their senses, who, forgetful of their vocation, deny the obedience due to the prelates of the Church and rashly usurp the Church’s own teaching office, and have gone onto the path of perdition!

Weeping with you, most blessed Father, we earnestly and from the heart implore this from the Lord, while, prostrate at your sacred feet, we seek from you that heavenly strength which your apostolic and paternal blessing is able to impart. May it be abundant and flow forth generously from the innermost sanctuary of your heart, so as to water and suffuse not only us but also our most beloved absent brethren and the faithful entrusted to us. May it be such as to soothe and alleviate our sorrows and those of the whole world, to sustain weakness, to make labor and effort fruitful, and finally to hasten happier times for the holy Church of God.

Rome, this eighth day of June, in the year of the Lord 1862.

## FOURTEENTH SERIES

[Col. 0197]

[PREFACE.]

Thus far we have discussed dogmas; but before proceeding to morals, we have decided to append here indexes concerning the Last Things of human beings, which pertain to both dogmatic and moral science. Accordingly, in this Fourteenth Series we present in succession indexes concerning Death and its day, both certain and uncertain; the particular and private judgment after death; Heaven and heavenly blessedness; Hell and the eternal punishments of the damned; Purgatory and the suffrages by which the souls of the righteous detained there can be aided; the cult of the dead; Antichrist and the signs which must precede, accompany, and follow him; the final end of this world; the supreme resurrection of the dead; and the general judgment, in which all human beings together will stand before the tribunal of the Supreme Judge.

[Col. 0197]

## CXXVI. INDEX CONCERNING DEATH, LOGICALLY SETTING FORTH WHATEVER THE FATHERS WROTE CONCERNING ITS NATURE, CAUSES, AND EFFECTS, ETC.

### NOTICE

For the benefit of all, and especially of those who fulfill the office of proclaiming the divine word or have the governance of souls, we have wished, in this Index, to recount the opinions of the holy Fathers on a matter of such great importance, not only in substance but very often in their very words; and we do so in the following order.

I. On the nature, causes, and effects of death.  
II. On the certainty and uncertainty of death.  
III. On means of dying well, especially those drawn from consideration of the death of the righteous or the wicked.  
IV. On some notable examples of a good or bad death.

## [INDEX CONCERNING DEATH]

### CHAPTER ONE.—The nature, causes, and effects of death

**TERTULLIAN.**—Death is the separation of body and soul, II, 736. Its kingdom effects nothing but the dissolution of the flesh, 862. Death is what not only corrupts but also consumes flesh and blood, 869. Although deaths have various outcomes, none is so mild that it does not occur by force, 739. That very operative principle of death is force, ibid. Untimely and cruel deaths are the work of demons, 748. Sleep is an image of death, 724. The death which you suppose is a departure, I, 1264. It followed humanity not by nature, but by fault—and not even by natural fault, 738. The pagans thought that those overtaken by untimely death wandered here until the remainder of their allotted years should be completed, 746.

**ST. CYPRIAN.**—Death is not an exit but a passage; and, when the temporal journey has been completed, a crossing over into eternity, IV, 597.

**LACTANTIUS.**—Death is the dissolution of the nature of living beings, VI, 321. Death is the endurance of eternal pain: the condemnation of souls, according to their deserts, to eternal punishments, 321. Two deaths are set forth: one belonging to the body, which must be undergone according to nature; the other belonging to the soul, which is acquired through wickedness, 769. The body, formed from a weighty and corruptible element, must decay and die, 771–772. As moisture spills out when a vessel is broken, so the soul vanishes from the dissolved body, 773. Death followed humanity in accordance with God’s sentence, 324.

**ST. HILARY, bishop of Poitiers.**—Death is customarily signified by sleep, X, 361, 451. The abode of death is designated by the depths of the sea, 273. Death follows from the law of sin, 404. Death is not the destruction of the soul, but its departure from the body, 411. Death ceased after it had assailed God, 478. The death of the saints is sleep, 700–701. By death the soul is stripped of the burden and companionship of weak and perilous flesh, 651.

[Col. 0198] **ST. ZENO.**—The righteous person, about to ascend to the height of heaven, leaves behind the impediments of his body, XI, 405.

**ST. AMBROSE.**—Death is the release of soul and body and a kind of separation of the human being, XIV, 543; XVI, 1324. It is more an escape from sin than a loss to the dying person, XIV, 140, 1173. Bitterness belongs not to death but to guilt, 556. Death is not an evil dissolution, because to be with Christ is better, ibid. Death is good in every respect, 546. Why then do we accuse death, which either pays life’s price or abolishes its pain and torment? ibid. Death is the proof of life, 556. Death is an honorable redemption from life, and also a support of honor or innocence, 1036. By it life is not taken away but transferred to better things, 358. Through life there is a passage to death; through death, a return to life, 555. For the righteous death is a harbor of rest; for the guilty, shipwreck, ibid. Death is the end not of nature but of guilt, 1174. Death is the completion of service, the sum of reward, the grace of discharge, 556. Nature and merits do not have the same end; nor does the reward of virtue die with the body, XVI, 1310. Christians possess far greater consolations than pagans concerning the death of their own, 1312. Death does not release one from the miseries of this world, 1315. Death is a refuge from all troubles and evils, a faithful station of safety, and a harbor of rest, 1320. Some customarily observe the third and thirtieth day for the dead; others the seventh and fortieth, 1386.

**ST. JEROME.**—The earth receives the body; the soul is restored to Christ, XXII, 598. Human bodies have one condition with beasts and cattle, 903. The death of the saints is sleep, XXIV, 304. Death is called mistress, 291. The Lord does not make death, but sin does, 884–885. Death is the last of evils, XXV, 1004. No one was more miserable than man before death was conquered, XXII, 590. O death, you who divide brothers and cruelly and harshly separate those joined in love, 590. By Christ’s [Col. 0199] death, you have died: you devoured and were devoured, XXII, 590. You reigned from Adam to Moses, ibid.

**ST. AUGUSTINE.**—Death is the separation of soul from body, XXXVI, 556, 893. Bodily death too is penal, XLV, 1222. Death is a punishment that separates the soul from the body, 1593. Some philosophers refuse to regard death as a punishment, XLI, 387. Julian maintains that bodily death would have occurred in paradise even if no one had sinned, XLV, 1585. Julian introduced into paradise not the rest of the good who had died, but the torments of the dying, 1575. According to Julian, death is penal and due to sin only when it is eternal, 1222. Bodily death, which ordinarily occurs by reason of sin, 1596, 1603–1604. According to the Pelagians death is not an evil, XLIV, 610. Death is sleep because of the future resurrection, as though an awakening, XXIII, 572. Death received its name from biting (*morsus*), XLV, 1617. It is called sleep, XXXIX, 2063. Death is a privation, having only a name and no essence, XLV, 1616. If it is nothing, how can it be seen, held, insulted, conquered, and condemned? 1618. The Pelagians teach that Adam would have died whether he sinned or not, 1613–1614. Death is not a condition of nature but the punishment of sin, 1667. It was not made in the tree, but found through man, XXXIX, 1737. Death is truly a debt, XL, 1159. That human beings die is the punishment of sin, XLV, 1616. Death is twofold, XLII, 890, 900; XLV, 1171. There are two deaths: one of the body, shared by good and bad; the other of the soul through sin, XLV, 1584. The first death drives the unwilling soul from the body, 1873. Death itself in humanity indicates that humanity would not have died had it not sinned, XXXIV, 552. The cause of death is the frail union of the limbs, XLI, 710. Death was sown by the serpent, XXXVI, 933. Death is the devil—not because he himself is death, but because death is through him, 556. Death comes from sin, XXXIII, 873; XXXIV, 353; XLI, 377, 378, 380, 387, 391, 396, 403; XLIV, 111, 197, 406, 826. Death is not from God, XXXII, 919. The sting of bodily death is sin, XLV, 1604. Death is called sin because it is the punishment of sin, XLII, 296–297. It came about through the sin of the first human being that we should die, XLIV, 992. Death reigned in the world because of original sin, XLV, 1221, 1224. Death would not have followed if sin had not preceded it, XL, 160. Death is the just vengeance for sin, yet showing more of God’s mercy than of His severity, XXXIV, 134. Each person’s day of death is that person’s last day, XXXVIII, 932. Death is a vehicle to the kingdom, XL, 668. Through the temporal deaths of mortals God imposes on peoples the salutary benefit of fear of Himself, XLII, 412. God has sometimes punished even those who had committed no sins by bodily deaths, 660–662. In all who are dying, death is evil; but among the dead it is evil for some and good for others, XLV, 1575. It is the beginning of blessedness and the end of labors, XXXII, 1471. Whether they are to die or not, those whom the day of judgment finds alive, XLII, 1215. Those surviving at Christ’s final coming will not die, XL, 1161.

**FASTIDIUS, British bishop.**—Through death the good are delivered from the fellowship and persecutions of the wicked; but punishment and penalty await the wicked, L, 388.

**ST. PROSPER OF AQUITAINE.**—From sin arise death and all things belonging to death, LI, 181. The different causes of death and why it comes at different ages are unknown, 708. Death takes away riches, ancestral nobility, country, and beauty, 496. Look about at those who shone before you with like splendors: where are the unconquerable emperors? Where are the commanders of armies, satraps, tyrants? Are not all things dust? Are not all things ashes? ibid. Look at the tombs and see: who is slave, who master, who poor, who rich? ibid.

**ST. PETER CHRYSOLOGUS.**—The gateway of harsh death is harsher still, LII, 380. The death of bodies makes life everlasting out of what was temporal, 484. Among human beings death becomes a restoration of piety, 503.

**GENNADIUS OF MARSEILLE.**—Bodily death is the punishment of sin, but not itself the sin which is the death of the soul, LVIII, 990.

**VIGILIUS OF TAPSO.**—Death occurs when things of diverse kinds, whose harmony produces life, depart from one another as though through a certain discord, LXII, 351. Therefore death does not consume what has been joined, but divides it and restores each part to its origin, ibid.

**EUGYPPIUS, African abbot.**—Death is the corruptibility of the body, LXII, 589. The body decays through age, illness, or various afflictions, until it reaches the final state called death, 589.

**CASSIODORUS.**—Death is the dissolution effected between soul and body, LXX, 1301. The years of human beings are compared with the fleeting seasons of grasses, 646.

**Lives of the Holy Fathers.**—After death all things are handed over to oblivion, LXXIII, 459. The first definition of philosophy is meditation on death, 297. Temporal death is not properly death, 511.

[Col. 0200] **ST. GREGORY THE GREAT.**—Death separates flesh from soul, LXXV, 652–654, 912–913.

**COLUMBANUS, abbot.**—The earth receives the naked corpse, to be dissolved by worms and decay, LXXX, 38. At death, extravagance, jesting, lust, and luxury fall silent, 237.

**ST. JULIAN, bishop of Toledo.**—Death comes to human beings from the propagation of sin, XCVI, 461. The first human being was justly condemned after sin to the punishment of death, ibid. Death is so called either because it is bitter or because it took its name from the bite of the first human being, 462. There are three kinds of death: cruel, untimely, and natural, ibid. Although death is not good, it is good for the good, 463. Death is the laying aside of a heavy burden, namely, the body, 466.

**ALCUIN.**—The death of the body occurs when, for whatever necessary cause, the body is deserted by the soul, C, 522. The kingdom of death was destroyed by the coming of grace, 432. The name “death” also denotes the devil and sin, 431.

**RABANUS MAURUS.**—Sin is the cause of death, CIX, 877. Death prevails over bitter life, 984. Death entered the world and all human beings together with sin, CXI, 1359. At the end of the world it will be destroyed, CVIII, 1138.

**HAYMO, bishop of Halberstadt.**—Bodily death is the exhalation and departure of the soul, CXVI, 841.

**LANFRANC, archbishop of Canterbury.**—Death greatly benefits the good, CL, 166–167. Death signifies the devil, 167. The cause of death is sin, 213–214, 271–272. Death is bitter, 230.

**ST. BRUNO, founder of the Carthusians.**—Death is called darkness, CLII, 879. The dominions of death are hunger, famine, fevers, and every kind of misery, CLIII, 58. Death is the chief and completion of all miseries, 58.

**GUIBERT, abbot of Nogent.**—The necessity of dying was imposed upon us because of sin, CLVI, 644. If the event of sin had not intervened, no encounter with suffering or death could have occurred, 645.

**ST. ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury.**—It is contrary to God’s wisdom and justice that a human being should die if he had not sinned, CLVIII, 401. By a just judgment it was decreed that the human being who had sinned could not escape the punishment of sin, 368, 401–402. Death is the beginning of rest, the end of labors, and the destroyer of vices, 795–797. The body will dissolve into most abject dust, 720.

**ST. IVO, bishop of Chartres.**—If man had remained obedient, he would have passed into the heavenly homeland without the death of the flesh, CLXI, 976. For the wretched, death comes without death, ibid.

**RUPERT, abbot of Deutz.**—Death is twofold: of soul and body, CLXVIII, 1473. Death was mercifully bestowed by God, 583. The death of the soul preceded the death of the body, 906. Death was invented by the devil, 1622. But mortality was imposed by God’s providence, CLXX, 390. Even after the Redeemer’s restoration, death overtakes human beings, so that they may not, like the demons, possess a miserable eternity, 390; CLXVII, 1668.

**HUGH OF ST. VICTOR.**—The devil, author of death, is said to possess the dominion of death, CLXXV, 616. Death prevails in three ways: naturally, accidentally, and cruelly, 784.

**ST. BERNARD OF CLAIRVAUX.**—Death is the just punishment of sin, CLXXXII, 934. It is the work of the devil, the punishment of sin overcome by Christ, CLXXXIII, 484. Christ routed death and sin, humanity’s two enemies, 116–117.

**ROBERT PULLUS, cardinal.**—Had the first human being not sinned, he would not have deserved the punishment of death, CLXXXVI, 746. The body is consumed by various diseases, 754.

**PETER LOMBARD.**—Because the soul deserted God by sinning of its own accord, it was compelled unwillingly to desert the body, CXCII, 301. Those who are alive at Christ’s coming will die, 304. The kingdom of death is destroyed by Christ’s grace alone, CXCI, 1388–1389. Death is conquered, not utterly destroyed, 1403. God did not make death, but humanity summoned it upon itself through sin, 1406–1407. Death comes not from the law itself but from human fault, 1420. The light of wisdom departed from the human being who sinned, and he was condemned to death, 294. If death had no bitterness, martyrs would have no fortitude, CXCII, 301.

**RICHARD OF ST. VICTOR.**—Mourning, pain, crying, and death will not exist in the eternity to come, CXCVI, 861.

**PHILIP OF HARVENG.**—Death is a passage, CCIII, 126. To die is nothing other than no longer to be what one was, 127.

**THOMAS THE CISTERCIAN.**—There are various ways of dying, CCVI, 169. Human death is threefold, 104–106. There will be three messengers of death: accident, illness, and old age, 695.

**PETER OF BLOIS.**—Death is the end of pilgrimage, the end of misery, the goal of labors, the gateway to the homeland, and the first-fruits of rewards, CCVII, 473.

### CHAPTER II.—Death certain and uncertain

**TERTULLIAN.**—Death is everywhere, and everywhere are awareness and evidence of death, I, 618. Frequent deaths lay waste most things, 390. All things die in order to live again, 324. We fear the death from which we cannot escape, 615.

[Col. 0201] **ST. CYPRIAN.**—The condition of dying is one, IV, 550. Death is common to all, 437–438. Without any distinction of the human race, the righteous die with the unrighteous, 592.

**LACTANTIUS.**—Man was created mortal, formed with an earthly and frail body, VII, 21. Therefore it is perishable and mortal, ibid. It is not invulnerable against diseases and external blows, ibid. A human being must die because he is not God, 22. It is falsely said that no one ought to die except an old person, ibid. He maintains the uncertainty of the hour of death, 23. If death were fixed for a certain age, a human being would become most insolent and lack every quality of humanity, ibid.

**ST. HILARY.**—Death is lawful only against those against whom it has been decreed, X, 318.

**ST. AMBROSE.**—Death is equal for all, indiscriminate toward the poor, making no exception for the rich, XVI, 1317. No one has redeemed himself from death—not the rich, not kings themselves; indeed, they are subject to heavier burdens, 1373. Who should suppose himself exempt from the condition of dying when he is not exempt from the condition of being born? 1291. Death cannot be postponed at the price of money, and the final day carries off poor and rich alike, 1292. Death is neither bitter to the needy, nor more burdensome to the rich, nor unjust to the old, nor cowardly toward the brave, 1326. It is not to be mourned, because it is common and owed by all, 1315.

**ST. JEROME.**—The moments of our life are diminished through each individual action, XXII, 601–602. All things are subject to death, 600. Death devastates, drags away, and snatches kings, leaders, cities, and kingdoms, ibid. Consider the ruins of the whole world: nations dashed against nations and kingdoms against kingdoms; some killed, others swallowed by the waves; these born, those dying, 601–602. All people in the world now living will be gone within a short time, ibid. We die daily, we are changed daily, and yet believe ourselves eternal, 602. Do you perceive when you became an infant, a child, a youth, of vigorous age, an old man? 602. Whatever I dictate, write, or reread … is taken from my life, ibid. O wretched human condition, and without Christ all that we live is vain, 597! For the person whose life’s end has come and whose necessity of death is irresistible, all things have passed away, 598. The present age will pass; ages yet to come will follow, 473. Death is near, at the doors; whether we wish it or not, we grow old, 557. Human beings and beasts dissolve into ashes and dust, 904. The day of death is fixed for each person not by fate but by God’s will, XXIV, 390. There is no living human being who shall not see death, XXV, 937. It must be understood that flourishing age quickly falls, XXIV, 412. Then where will that comely face be, where the dignity of the whole body? XXII, 597. Those who rejoice in bodily health and suppose youth and childhood to be perpetual are deceived, XXIX, 412. One must not rejoice in power, riches, or prosperity; all those things will quickly be taken away, XXV, 290.

**ST. AUGUSTINE.**—Humanity was so created that it had no necessity of dying; but through sin the state of nature was so changed that a human being must die, XLV, 1112. Humanity was thrust into the necessity of dying, XXXIII, 547. Death is appointed for all, XXXVIII, 1480; XXXIX, 1506, 1513. It is a debt which no one escapes, XXXVIII, 1192. My body does not belong to me, 1191. My prison is temporary; my chain is temporary, ibid. Every human being is born bound by the condition of death and the laws of hell, XXXVIII, 1105. The necessity of dying dates from sin’s very origin, 489; XLIV, 113. It accords with God’s judgment that the sinner die, yet death does not accord with His work, XLV, 1354–1355. Liability to death appears in the involuntary movement of the flesh, XXXIV, 422. Human beings are subject to death even though they are freed from sin through baptism, XLI, 379; XLIV, 181. The first death—that is, bodily death—passes to all human beings, XLV, 1170. The first death is common to all, but not the second, XLI, 398. The first must necessarily be undergone by all; the second is prepared for the wicked alone, XXXIX, 1513. Death of the flesh belongs to that fire by which each person’s work is tested, XLI, 745. We must die, and no one wishes to do so, XXXVI, 238. Death alone is certain here, XXXVIII, 590. All other things are uncertain, XXXVI, 428. In great mercy God has hidden from us the day of death, 332; XXXVIII, 241. God willed the day of death to be uncertain, XXXVII, 1301; XXXIX, 1876. The final day is hidden so that every day may be watched, XXXVIII, 241. The day of death is uncertain but near, 241, 839. The whole life of a human being lasts few days, XXXVI, 373. As long as the age revolves, understand it to be a point, 234. The longest human life is a morning breeze, 361. The whole life of mortals hastens on; even what seems longer is a vapor that lasts a little longer, 996. Life is more the shadow of life than life itself, XXXIX, 1538. Our life is death, XXXVII, 1889. Life is more truly death than life, XXXIX, 1522. Human life decreases as it increases, XXXVIII, 122, 237. What is living long except running toward the end? 633. From the moment a human being begins to live, he begins to die, XLI, 383. This life ought to be for you [Col. 0202] like a stable for a traveler, not like a house for a resident, XXXVI, 326. No one leaves life except through death, XLI, 553. Life’s end is uncertain, XXXVIII, 76, 1111. Let us give thanks to God because He willed this life’s final day to be both brief and uncertain, 688. When the master of the house wills, he says, “Move on”; he has not made a contract with you or bound himself by agreement to a fixed term, XXXVI, 429. That human beings must necessarily die in the body is no small benefit of Christ’s grace, XLIV, 113.

**CASSIAN.**—Death lies in wait for every age, XLIX, 1180.

**ANTONINUS HONORATUS, bishop of Constantina.**—The world and all things in the world are to be dissolved, L, 568. The life of your body is in the power of your God, who can immediately take your flesh from you if you abandon the faith, 569.

**ST. PROSPER OF AQUITAINE.**—Death comes to no one earlier or later than God wills, LI, 159. Human beings are subject to death at every moment, 708.

**ST. PETER CHRYSOLOGUS.**—Time abandons humanity; age changes it; childhood weakens it; youth hurls it headlong; old age breaks it, LII, 326. To die belongs to nature; to perish is necessary, 482. Whence, when, how, and through whom death will come is unknown, ibid. All the elements perish and are destined to perish, 483–484. It is not so much will as necessity that leads to death, 503. The end of life comes, the time of death; already the final summons binds you, already judgment calls, 544. Death is the queen of destruction, 523. With its own leaders or counsels it captures, lays waste, and kills all whom nature brings into the present life; it leads kings, drags peoples away. It has never been overcome by prayers, softened by tears, or subdued by force, 523.

**SALVIAN.**—“Behold, you will die,” departing from the house of your body, not knowing where you are going, whither you will be led, to what punishments and what dreadful things you will be carried off, L, III, 224.

S. PATRICK, bishop of Ireland.—Ridiculous is anyone who loves and seeks the fleeting frailty of this world and the pleasure of the flesh, which soon perishes, LIII, 833.

ST. LEO THE GREAT.—The most vigilant meditation ought to be that of the wise Christian: since the days of this life are brief and its duration uncertain, death must never find the dying person unprepared, LIV, 450.

MAXIMUS OF TURIN.—That we shall die has been established by the former decree, LVII, 568.

FAUSTUS OF RIEZ.—We cannot know when or at what hour we shall be snatched away from this world, LVIII, 877. When the last day comes upon us, we shall lay aside the tent of our body, ibid.

ST. CAESARIUS, bishop of Arles.—The soul dwells within fleshly and fragile walls, LXVI, 67.

CASSIODORUS.—Human life is a shadow which, when the body through which it exists departs, itself likewise vanishes and perishes, LXX, 1017. Man is carried away like dust when the wind blows, 1016.

Lives of the Holy Fathers.—There is no art by which we may escape death, LXXIII, 459. How can anyone await death with an untroubled mind, when its coming cannot be avoided and is uncertain? ibid. Will death then at some time seize me? ibid. When I have died, shall I be dissolved into nothing? ibid. Let each reckon, not the years of his life, but the years of a good death, 510.

ST. GREGORY THE GREAT.—All, righteous and wicked alike, are subject to death, LXXV, 880, 881; LXXVI, 178. At every moment of life, man proceeds toward death, LXXV, 984. This very living of ours is daily passing away from life, 984. The present life is uncertain, and death as it steals upon us ought to be feared all the more because it can never be foreseen, 1008, 1009. Daily scourges press upon us and sudden mishaps overwhelm us, LXXVI, 1080. At the very moment when it is not expected, sudden death arrives, 1081. Everything that passes is brief, even though it may seem to come to its end more slowly, LXXV, 1031. A storm will overwhelm the sinner at an hour when he does not expect it, LXXVI, 53. The day of death is unknown so that it may always be believed near at hand, 988. The time of death is unknown in order that one may hasten to do good, ibid. The days appointed for each person by God’s eternal foreknowledge can neither be increased nor diminished, LXXV, 1013. Our life is winter, 425. It is a passing wind, 440. So long as we live, it is dawn, not the perfect day, 478, 479. No one knows the beginning or the end of his life, 496, 497. Life in the flesh is a flower in the grass, 983, 984. The course of the present life is expressed by comparison with sea and river, 991. The whole of life is a point, 1105. The span of life, from which a person believes himself to grow, diminishes, 321, 322. Perfect life is an imitation of death, 1032. We cannot endure long together with our possessions, LXXVI, 52.

COLUMBANUS, abbot.—By death and setting, all things pass away and do not remain, LXXX, 236. Life deceives, misleads, and blinds many, 240. O life: while you flee, you are nothing; while you appear, you are a shadow; while you are exalted, you are smoke, 240! From moment to moment, amid the uncertainties of my age, I hasten [Col. 0203] toward death, 242. Life is a road: long for some, short for others; broad for some, narrow for others; irrevocable for all, ibid.

TAIO, bishop of Saragossa.—Moment by moment time fails away, LXXX, 756. By the very increases of his age, wretched man is driven toward loss, 756. He is always diminishing in that by which he believes himself to advance in the span of life, ibid.

ST. ISIDORE OF SEVILLE.—We must consider how brief and miserable life is, LXXXIII, 735. Life declines through its own growth, 735. While a person thinks he will not die, he is taken away, 736. The rich are suddenly snatched away by an unexpected end at an hour they do not know, 737. The learned and the unlearned die alike, 595.

ST. EUGENIUS, bishop of Toledo.—After death, only that which you have done well, rightly, and justly will remain, LXXXVII, 360. Life passes; the end presses on; behold the herald of death, 364. At death, a man is to be left by all, 364.

THE VENERABLE BEDE.—Sudden death, breaking into the dwelling-place of flesh, carries off its master, XCII, 105.

ST. JULIAN, bishop of Toledo.—Countless deaths threaten each individual, XCVI, 466.

ST. PAULINUS, patriarch of Aquileia.—All things are vain and fleeting, XCIX, 244. When death comes, everything will be recognized as vain, 221. At death’s arrival, all life’s pleasures pass away, ibid. No human being knows the day of his departure, 243. Not all die in old age, but at various ages, ibid. At every moment of day and night death is imminent, ibid.

JONAS, bishop of Orléans.—He who promised pardon to the penitent did not promise the sinner tomorrow, CVI, 256. We can never foresee the last day, ibid. Certain death awaits all, 256.

RABANUS MAURUS.—The very fact that we speak, dictate, and write flies past as a portion of life, CIX, 858. A man finds himself old before he wonders that he is no longer young, ibid. Flesh is grass and a passing flower, ibid. Human frailty cannot go beyond the limit of its course, 828. Consider that you live only a few days, even if you are destined to reach old age, CX, 107.

ST. LUPUS, abbot of Ferrières.—I hold it most certain that one newly born can quickly die and that an old man cannot live long, CXIX, 440. It is more useful to pass the very brevity of uncertain time in mourning than in joy, ibid. This life is brief and uncertain, and persons younger than ourselves die every day, 518. We hasten toward death without interruption, 375.

ST. PASCHASIUS RADBERTUS, abbot of Corbie.—To die belongs to all human beings, CXX, 962.

ATTO, bishop of Vercelli.—In every region of the world death heaps up funerals, CXXXIV, 176.

ST. PETER DAMIAN.—Whether powerful or poor, men will have the same end, CXLV, 818.

RADULPHUS ARDENS.—For everyone the day of his death stands ever nearer, CLV, 1669. One must not trust in the strength of youth, ibid. How many has sudden death overtaken! ibid. God willed the boundary of our death to be unknown, so that death may always be expected, 1669.

ST. ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury.—Nothing is more certain than death; nothing more uncertain than the hour of death, CLVIII, 741. Whatever the love of the world brings forth is unstable and transitory, ibid. The body whose health, comfort, and pleasure are a concern will dissolve into rottenness and the vilest dust, 720. The boastfulness of words, the adornment of clothing, and the variety of luxuries also perish, ibid. Man must die unwillingly, 370, 371. Death spares no human being—learned, rich, or lowly, 700, 701, 702. No force can expel anyone from this life until it pleases God, 911, 912. For each person, the end of the world is the hour of his departure, 620, 621. The longer anyone has lived, the more briefly he will live, 1065, 1066, 1090. The present life has an end, and man does not know when the last day—toward which he approaches unceasingly by day and night—will come, 159, 171.

ST. BRUNO, bishop of Asti and Segni.—Once one has died, one does not return from the path of death, CLXIV, 612. The wicked, with their thoughts, will be scattered in destruction, 612, 613. When the wicked hope that they are living, they will not survive, 300, 301. This can be said because it has been or will be, but not because it is, 832. The powerful, abounding in all things, fall and die, 1002, 1003.

RUPERT, abbot of Deutz.—No one escapes death, CLXVIII, 1473. The time of death hastens on, 998, 999. All are subject to death. Whoever you are, go to the graves of the dead: they themselves will answer and inform you, CLXX, 362. Every day the dead are buried by the living, who are certainly themselves to die, 362.

HILDEBERT, bishop of Le Mans.—We and all that is ours are owed to death, CLXXI, 1021. Man enters the world on this condition: that he may depart from it, 1028. By death we are all compelled [lacuna]; a destiny to depart sooner or later, [Col. 0204] 1044. Death holds whatever part of life lies behind us, 1047. The whole of life is one day, 733.

ST. BERNARD OF CLAIRVAUX.—Death demonstrates the vanity and brevity of all things, CLXXXII, 843. The goods of the world do not follow the dying person, ibid. The life which we live is rather death—not life simply, but mortal life, CLXXXIII, 250. Death does not spare youth, CLXXXII, 621. Death stands at the doors for the old and lies in ambush for the young, 843. From the moment we begin to live, we begin to die, CLXXXIII, 250. Why do you count days and years for yourself in uncertainty, 541?

PETER LOMBARD.—Human life is evening, CXCI, 294. Death is the human spirit’s going from this world and not returning to the body in this world, 736. Great is human misery: to be unwilling to die, and yet to die, 303.

ADAM OF PRÉMONTRÉ.—This life is a pilgrimage, CXCVIII, 234. He who was ceases to be, and devouring, consuming death swallows him, 267. Life runs swiftly toward death, 267. The body’s emptying after death, 308. I am certain that I must depart hence, but I do not know the time, manner, or place, 431. Man is a leaf snatched away by the wind, ibid. After death the body will be a worm; after the worm, dust, 435.

PETER OF CELLES.—Death is certain; the hour of death uncertain, CCII, 1131.

PHILIP OF HARVENG.—Death does not measure rank or wealth, CCIII, 1113. It assails the happy and the unhappy, 1114. To wish to live and be unable is death, ibid. To wish to die and be unable is death, ibid. The present life is full of deaths, 127.

PETER THE CHANTER.—We share with death this very day on which we live, CCV, 354. At every hour, set your house in order, 353. Although nothing is more certain, nothing is more uncertain than death, 356. Death is sudden, untimely, and uncertain, ibid. Everything is perishable and transitory, 352.

PETER OF BLOIS.—By an equal sentence death enfolds every age and condition, CCVII, 472. The law of death is not changed by power or favor, 473.

## CHAPTER III.—Means of Dying Well, Especially Those Drawn from Consideration of the Death of the Good or the Wicked

TERTULLIAN.—Death is to be feared because of the judgment which follows, I, 614. Fear of death is not so great as that of torments, 625. Through the image of death you are initiated into faith; you meditate upon hope; you learn to die and to live; you learn to keep watch while asleep, II, 724. Philosophy teaches contempt for death, I, 533. Grief at death ought to be absent when the resurrection of the dead is certain, 1263. You would not know death to be evil unless you knew that something after death was to be feared, 615. For the Christian, death is beneficial and sweet, as God disposes it, II, 133. The difference between the death of a Christian and that of a pagan, 745. The common people think that everything ends after death, or that nothing remains, 721, 795.

ST. CYPRIAN.—Death must be despised by the Christian, IV, 793. Death must be despised, for Christ was slain, ibid. The crowns gave an end amid the pains of death which tortures had not given, 246. Precious is the death that purchased immortality, 247. Blessed is the death that received a crown from the completion of virtue, ibid.; the servant of God is crowned in the contest of the promised struggle, ibid.; he passes to immortality through a glorious death, 329. It is perverse not immediately to obey when God summons, 596. Why, then, do we pray and ask for the kingdom of heaven to come if earthly captivity delights us? 595. It belongs to one who does not wish to go to Christ to fear death, 584. They are transgressors who mourn the dead as though lost, 596. We ought rather to rejoice than grieve when those dear to us depart from the world, 586. Having crossed out death, we come to immortality, 585. What greatness of heart it is to confront, with the virtues of an unshaken mind, so many assaults of death! 592. It is great sublimity to stand upright amid the ruins of humankind, and not lie prostrate with those who have no hope in God, ibid. Death takes away the world’s oppressions, punishments, and tears, 586. For one who dies well there is true peace, trustworthy tranquility, stable, firm, and everlasting security, 585. Death, therefore, is to be desired, not feared, 268. By death the righteous are called to refreshment, 592.

LACTANTIUS.—In accepting death lies the highest duty of virtue, VI, 768. Death does not extinguish a human being but admits him to the reward of virtue, ibid. No one undergoes death except in hope of a longer life, 381. Death is good or evil because it must be weighed by preceding actions, 410.

ST. HILARY.—Souls departing from the body are immediately received either by rest or by punishment, IX, 323, 675. The soul of the righteous, departing from the body, rests in God’s reception, 343. The end of human life and death is resurrection, and the most certain reward of our warfare is incorruptible eternity, X, 428. After the law of death, man will be eternal, IX, 650. Death was desired by many saints, ibid. They lamented the lingering dissolution of their bodies, ibid. The Prophet desired death, 840. It will not avail to have been heard unless, on departing from the body, one is to rest in blessed places, 841, [Col. 0205] 842. Death gains believers fellowship with Christ, 646, 647. After death, sinners will feel God as avenger, whom amid their works of iniquity they did not consider, 343. The lot of sinners after this life, 406. Faith removes the fear of death.

ST. ZENO.—Immediately after death, righteous and wicked alike will receive, according to their merits, either a reward—and indeed an eternal one—or eternal punishment, XI, 460. An end worthy of a glorious departure, 405. When death, thought fearful, is tasted, then the promised happiness is bestowed: the glory of the soul abiding forever in blessed dwellings, thereafter to feel none of the world’s miseries, 386. Those who will die in the Lord are those who, by upright conduct and through the stages of observance of the divine commandments, are daily borne to heaven by the glory of their spiritual journey, 432.

ST. AMBROSE.—Death is not to be feared, as Christ’s example shows, XV, 1487, 1488. Death is not terrible, since it is the end of nature, not a punishment, 1727. Death itself is not terrible, but rather fear and opinion about death, which each person altogether dreads in accordance with his conscience, XIV, 555. For we have nothing to fear in death if our life has committed nothing to be feared, ibid. If you are strong, despise death; if you are weak, flee it, and follow Christ, who is life, XV, 1699. If we wish not to fear Christ, let us stand where Christ is, ibid. Bodily death is not to be feared by the brave, is to be desired by the wise, and sought by the wretched, 1709. The righteous person is moved by no fear of death, XIV, 1174. Death alone is rest for a man, 546. Where there is faith in the resurrection, death has not the appearance of death but of rest, XV, 1684. The Lord turned death’s sleep into the grace of delight, 1639. He who dies in order to rise again is nearer to salvation than he who lives in order to die, XIV, 1036. To die in Christ is arduous and glorious, 1127. It is more glorious to die for Christ than to reign in this world, 543. After death, neither does the sinner escape punishment for his wickedness, nor is the righteous deprived of the rewards of his justice, XV, 1285, 1286. Death is neither perpetual for believers nor unforeseen by the wise, XVI, 1326. How many have preferred death to grief, how many to dread of death, judging fear of death more grievous than death itself, 1351. When the occasion for a praiseworthy death is given, it must immediately be seized, ibid. Death is not to be fled, since Christ did not disdain it, 1327. Let there be in us a certain daily practice and disposition of dying, 1325, 1326. Why should we groan over the dead, when the reconciliation of the world with God has now been accomplished through the Lord Jesus? 1101. That is not to be called death which, joining one who has died to Christ, makes death gain for the dying person, XVII, 714. But true death is that which binds even a living person in the death of sins, ibid.

SULPICIUS SEVERUS.—Blessed is the departure when Christ receives us into his abode, cleansed from the stain of sin by conduct of a better life, XX, 224. Martyrs and prophets will meet us; angels and archangels will rejoice; and Satan, though his mouth be bloody, will grow pale in defeat, ibid.

ST. JEROME.—The whole life of the wise is a meditation upon death, XXII, 598. We must keep in mind what we shall someday be, ibid. No one, fearless and uncertain of the judgment, awaits it without dread, XXV, 291. We view death as though far away, XXII, 1056. Let us prepare for ourselves provisions necessary for the long journey, 557. A man devoted to Christ can die, but cannot be conquered, XXIII, 60. Consider, O man, that your days are brief and that you will soon cease to exist when released from the flesh, 1060. The day of death is better than the day of birth, 1061. Wherever we fall, overthrown by the tempest of death, there we shall remain forever, 1102. The day of death is terrible, because what will be fulfilled for all on the day of judgment is fulfilled for each person after death, XXV, 965. The day of the Lord is the day of each person’s departure from the body, ibid. He who daily remembers that he will die despises present things and hastens toward things to come, XXX, 376. To avoid an evil death, one must turn to God with fasting, weeping, and lamentation, XXV, 967. Holy men fear death because of the uncertainty of judgment and sentence, XXIV, 390. You would understand that the righteous person does not die but emigrates, and changes friends rather than leaves them, XXII, 597. The righteous receives the crown of completed work, 468. Already secure and victorious, he looks down upon you as a friend from on high, favors you in your labor, and prepares a place beside himself, 686. Let the dead be mourned—but the one whom Gehenna receives, whom Tartarus devours, 468. One whom heaven has received is not to be mourned in death, 472. His glory is not to be begrudged with lamentations and tears, ibid. Against death’s harshness and most cruel necessity, we are raised by this consolation: that soon we shall see those whose absence grieves us, 686. We are rather the ones to be mourned, for daily we stand in the battle of sins, are defiled by vices, receive wounds, and must render an account for an idle word, ibid.

ST. AUGUSTINE.—It is not opinion but nature that recoils from death, XXXVIII, 936, 1360, 1374, 1375. There is a certain sweet bond of the body; man is bound and does not wish to be released, 1366. Nature’s first and greatest voice is that man should flee death, XLI, 630. All human beings, like animals, flee death, XLI, 630; XL, 676. Fear of death is inborn in Adam’s descendants, XLV, 1530. God made fear of death for the sake of discipline, XXXVII, 1162. Fear of death is a torment, XLV, 1570, 1571. Death is feared more than labors, 1571. How greatly man labors to avoid death, XXXVIII, 706. Fear of death stings most when things go well for us, 238. What must be done in order that we may not die, 881. Death is such that, if you wish, it will not exist, XXXIX, 1513. Death of the soul is more to be feared than death of the body, XXXVIII, 430, 880. Temporal death is not to be feared, but eternal death, 1280. Death is bitter to one whose life is sweet, XLI, 635. How vainly men are held by fear of death, XXXVIII, 881. Those who fear dying, and do nothing but seek to die later, do not act so as not to die, ibid. All strive to delay the day of death, XXXIII, 544. Accelerated death is useful to some, XXXIV, 780. The manner of death does nothing that can harm the good after death, XLI, 471. Do not concern yourself with what a man dies from, but with where he will go after death, XXXVII, 1945. You who do so much in order to die a little later, do something in order never to die, XXXVIII, 1387. Those troubled by imminent death should look upon Christ himself, troubled for the same reason, XXXV, 1798. All flee the death of the flesh; few care about the death of the soul, 1747. Fear of bodily death makes men guilty, XLV, 1603. A person’s whole life can be made fearless against death, XXXIII, 74. The wise man does not fear bodily death or pains, XXXII, 971. It is better to suffer one death by dying than to fear all deaths by living, XLI, 25. Nothing makes death evil except what follows death, 26. To overcome fear of death is no small virtue, XLIV, 183. Christ showed by his own death that neither death nor its manner is to be feared, XL, 664. We fear death though it ends infirmity, XXXVII, 1268. No one invokes death in words, but by an evil life, XXXVI, 473. Although we desire to cleave to Christ, we nevertheless do not wish to die, 842.

Death must be borne with equanimity, XXXV, 1402; patiently, after Christ’s example, XXXVI, 831. When God commands it, it is not to be refused at whatever time it comes, XXXIV, 361. This house has been leased to you, not given to you, XXXVII, 1945. Death is not to be avoided by sin, but endured for righteousness if the opportunity is given, XLI, 301. The wise person ought patiently to bear death that comes from another cause than himself, 630. Love of God makes death despised, indeed even desired, XXXII, 1338; XXXVII, 1843. It is to be desired that, when swift death comes, we may hasten more quickly to Christ, XLIV, 630. The more we enjoy God through a mirror or in an enigma, the more ardently we desire to end our pilgrimage, XXXIV, 30. Through God’s mercy, death is turned to good uses, XLIX, 613, 614. Death is evil for the wicked, XLI, 378. Nothing except what follows death makes or proves death evil, XXXVIII, 612; XLI, 25, 26. Whatever harms the dying arises from life, not death, XXXIII, 649. The dying person will have either life or punishment as companion, XXXVIII, 811. Death is not to be considered evil when a good life has preceded it, XLI, 25. It is not within human power by what end one finishes this life, but it is within human power how one lives, so as to finish life securely, XXXVIII, 1400. To die in sin is the supreme evil, XXXV, 1678. One who has lived well cannot die badly, XXXVIII, 1162; XL, 676. Live so that, in dying, instead of a judge you may find a father; instead of a cruel officer, an angel carrying you into Abraham’s bosom; instead of prison, paradise, XXXVIII, 638. In one dying immediately after true conversion, God does not note the capacity but crowns the will, 131. Death is good, but in those whose life has been chaste, devout, faithful, and innocent, XXXIII, 389. There is a great difference between the death of the righteous and that of sinners, XXVI, 321. The wicked do not see what death is, although they see even wise persons dying, XXXVI, 551. Death must be understood with reference to the soul as either utterly worst or utterly best, 322. Precious is the death of the saints, XLI, 381. As death is rendered as wages in consequence of sin, so eternal life is rendered as wages in consequence of righteousness, XXXIII, 881. In the world to come there will be no death, XLI, 683.

One must always think of the sole final departure of man, XXXIII, 74. Amid noisy and restless assemblies and comings and goings, no familiarity with death is acquired, ibid. Death should be contemplated whenever we lie down in bed, XL, 1061. Thought of death restrains desire, XXXIX, 2152. By this punishment the sinner is struck: in dying he forgets himself, because while living he forgot God, 2153, 2221. A prayer should be said for one who is dying, XL, 1152. For the dying, it is pleasant and salutary to speak of Christ’s humanity and be satisfied by it, 1153. Not to mourn a death common to all is philosophical, 1199. Not to fear death because of the serenity of conscience surpasses all the world’s pleasures, XXXII, 1471. Angels stand by and render aid at the death of the righteous; evil spirits hand over the wicked, torn from their bodies, to fires, 1472. Those devoted to devout works do not perish by an evil death, XL, 1319, 1320, 1321. Many inwardly dead persons walk about, and the living carry their own funerals, XXXIX, 1785. The saints migrating hence seek heaven, XL, 918, 954, 981.

CASSIAN.—A man ought to restrain the movements of his mind, forget injuries, reject griefs, and despise pains and losses, as one who is to die daily, XLIX, 266. Every day and at every moment the righteous person believes himself summoned, ibid.

FASTIDIUS, bishop of Britain.—One must beware every sin, since it is known that judgment is both present for sinners and reserved for the future, L, 389.

ST. PETER CHRYSOLOGUS.—Whenever anyone sees a dead person, so often he declares himself destined for death; thus a mortal cannot but grieve over death, LII, 380. He is rightly raised to friendship with God who, for God’s sake, despises human deaths, 481. Wretched mortality, hostile to itself, grieves that it dies and fights lest it be able to rise again, 411. We must pray that Christ, when he comes, may find us such as he wishes and commands the sharers of his kingdom to be, 390. Death is mistress of despair: “Behold,” she says, “your mistress, reducing your soul to nothing, consuming your flesh with decay and your bones with age,” 523. Give childhood to games; give adolescence to pleasures; give youth to sensual enjoyments; give old age to me, ibid. Death is the daughter of unbelief: as though you would not die, as though you would escape death, so you make arrangements for life; man, faith deceives you; you believe a faith which, in order to take away present things, promises future things, ibid. A man always began to do good when death had taken away his time for doing it, 545. A man fears the shame of the future judgment, in which there is no longer time for repentance, ibid. He blushes more before his conscience than before the fire of Gehenna, ibid. When danger of death presses, one must have recourse to counsel for the soul, compunction of heart, the aid of mercy, and the advocacy of confession, ibid. Even at the point of death there is room for repentance, LII, 637. In death, the righteous receives a kingdom for pains, glory for reproach, honor for insults, favor for contempt, and immortality for punishments, 388. But for the services rendered to pleasure, ministers of punishments stand ready for the unrighteous, ibid.

SALVIAN OF MARSEILLE.—On his deathbed the greedy man sighs, no longer concerning alms to be offered, but forgetful of himself, concerning an heir to be enriched, LIII, 224. Rather, he should see that no one is nearer or dearer to him than his own soul, ibid.

MAXIMUS OF TURIN.—In this brief life we must make provision for eternal life, LVII, 455, 456. Through good works—namely fasting, almsgiving, and prayer—each person ought to prepare himself for death, 456.

ST. FAUSTUS OF RIEZ.—If we wish to die in the Lord, let us diligently and continually think upon the day of our death and the terrible, fearful judgment, LVIII, 876. How useful it is for the sinner to think upon that hour when he will depart from this world, ibid. We must attend to how severe the examination before Christ’s tribunal will be, ibid. That we may die in the Lord, let us cleanse our consciences by almsgiving and prayers, and hasten to enter the harbor of repentance, 877. Let each person heal the corruptions of sins, uncover wounds, and overcome concupiscence, moved by fear of eternal death, 888, 889. While there is time, let us condemn ourselves and daily accuse ourselves before the Judge, 889.

ST. PAULINUS OF NOLA.—The present life must be despised in order that we may attain the future one, LXI, 670. The death of a righteous person must never be called untimely, because his soul is pleasing to God, 210, 211. It is devout to grieve at the separation of loved ones, but holy to rejoice in the hope and faith of God’s promises, 211, 212. Let us desire our own as those sent ahead, but not despair of receiving them again, 212. The death of children merits both tears and joy, 676, 677.

EUGYPPIUS, African abbot.—Before death, one must do what will be of benefit after death, LXII, 1020.

ST. FULGENTIUS OF RUSPE.—Upon the end of this life depends the beginning of that life in which whatever is rendered never ends, LXV, 557. Whoever ends this life in love of iniquity cannot attain life, ibid. Whoever has refused to seek pardon in this time will by no means be able to find it after death, ibid. No one ends the present life securely unless, before ending life, he departs from iniquity, 572. The time of death will be not for remission but for recompense, 555. There mercy will not justify the wicked; rather, justice will distinguish the righteous from the wicked, 556. He who perseveres in the seed of good work in the present time must come to the joy of the future harvest, 559. Whoever lives badly and does not change his life before he ends it is a most destructive enemy, 556. As good deeds cause flesh and soul to enjoy heavenly blessedness, [Col. 0208] so evil works cause soul and flesh to be tortured in eternal fire, ibid.

ST. BENEDICT, founder of monks.—Let us keep death daily before our eyes, LXVI, 296. So one must live as though one were to die today. Commentary, 325. I shall not remain in this world beyond this present day, ibid. God’s judgment must be feared, 266, 267. Eternal life ought to be desired with every spiritual longing, 296. Commentary, 325.

Lives of the Holy Fathers.—Let us keep the last day before our eyes, and at every moment fear the punishments of eternal pains, LXXIII, 265. Death is not to be feared by the righteous because they pursue the world and the things in the world with hatred, 450. It is to be feared by the wicked because they cannot be torn away from present things, ibid. There will be a time when iniquity shall cease, 265. Much concerning the soul’s departure must be committed to memory, 374. At that hour, none but our works will accompany us, ibid. What fear and trembling must seize us, when Hilary and other anchorites feared that awful hour! 375. “O humble soul, you have served Christ for eighty years, and do you fear to depart?” ibid. Meditation on death overcomes faintheartedness, 1019.

ST. GREGORY THE GREAT.—All its rewards follow the dying person, LXXV, 1040. He who considers what he will be like in death is always fearful in his actions, 1032. He considers himself almost dead because he does not at all fail to know that he will die, ibid. The dying person carries away the punishment for the things for which guilt was incurred, though all things for which the guilt was committed are left behind, LXXVI, 52. The time will come when the sinner awakes, and then he will know how empty was what he had held in sleep, ibid. Death opens the sinner’s eyes, 52, 53. Death restores the elect to light; it takes light away from the reprobate, 489. The death of the righteous aids the good and testifies against the wicked, 1261. He who is secure in his hope and conduct, when the time of approaching death comes, rejoices at the glory of recompense, 1124. The sinner, especially at life’s end, recognizes by how harsh bonds he is held, LXXV, 1046. The righteous daily look ahead to the day when the strict Judge will come, LXXVI, 305. The righteous fear death even on account of sins not committed, ibid. By fear of death they are cleansed from slight sins, 306. At the point of death, the soul of the righteous beholds the face of God, ibid. The nearer the righteous are to death, the more fervent they become, LXXV, 684, 685. From a brief and fleeting life the reprobate pass into eternal punishments, 783. The righteous person, dying, rejoices exceedingly with inward joy, LXXVI, 306. Having trampled underfoot every change and shadow of mutable things, he clings to the truth of eternity, ibid. When death, that last enemy, is destroyed, we shall then have no adversary and fear no enemy, LXXIX, 631. After death, God leaves nothing either unpunished or unrewarded, 76. The blindness of those who regard the present life as a homeland rather than a road, LXXV, 1157, 1158; LXXVI, 1079, 1080. Brief life is succeeded by an eternity blessed or miserable according to merits, 999. We should rejoice at the death of a righteous person because he has reached eternal joys, LXXVII, 1280. The wicked are removed from life suddenly and unexpectedly because, by reflection, they do not know how to foresee their end, LXXVI, 307. Those who now neglect to bend through humility of heart will be bent by the Judge’s sentence, 321.

COLUMBANUS, abbot.—The wise person sees not what is, but what will be, LXXX, 236. Everyone ought to live as though he died each day, ibid. What is yours, except your soul? 237. Death puts an end to pleasures, ibid. Before heaven is death; beyond heaven is eternal fire, 238. Human life, so fleeting, is to be feared, 240. In order to die well, we must desire what is above and set our minds on what is above, 244.

TAIO, bishop of Saragossa.—He who already sees the day of eternity bears with difficulty the day of his mortality, LXXX, 756. The Lord willed the last hour to be unknown, 910. Each person must prepare himself for it without interruption, ibid. A holy man trembles at approaching death and at the same time exults, 911. What is done for eternal life is preserved after death, 910. Death’s pain washes away sins, 909. It increases patience, ibid.

ST. ISIDORE, bishop of Seville.—A man must die in the flesh to the world, lest he die in the soul to Christ, LXXXIII, 736. Each person ought to consider the limit of his life, ibid. The wicked person, dying, draws many away from guilt through fear of punishment, 737. The departure of the wicked is dreadful, ibid. Apostate angels receive wicked men as they die, 738. After death, the wicked are led away to be tormented; but the righteous, after labor, sleep secure, 654. The righteous fears lest he be worthy of punishment, 738. Security is dangerous in this life for the wicked, while the grief of the good is tranquil, 653, 654.

ST. EUGENIUS, bishop of Toledo.—After death, only that which you have done well, rightly, and justly will remain, LXXXVII, 360.

VALERIUS, abbot.—After death, the souls of the righteous, received by an angel, will be borne to a most delightful place, [Col. 0209] LXXXVII, 431. Supported by faith in the Lord, the righteous does not fear death, 468.

THE VENERABLE BEDE.—One must live each day as though judgment were to come on another day, XCII, 104. The last day, which cannot be foreseen, must be feared, 107.

ST. JULIAN, bishop of Toledo.—The man who is going to die labors not to die, but the man who will live eternally does not labor not to sin, XCVI, 465. When the soul is separated from the body, we must acknowledge that angels are present there, ibid. Bodily death is not to be feared by Christians, 467. Let us embrace the day of death which restores us to paradise and the kingdom, 470. One must not be broken by despair when disturbed by approaching death, 472. If death had no hardship, or only slight hardship, there would be no glory of martyrs, ibid. At the end, the dying person must persist in prayer and commend himself to the prayers of the brethren, 472, 473. The devil strives to entangle the final stage of our life in his snares, ibid. But he flees from the place where he hears the Lord’s name, ibid. Many at the hour of their departure have been delivered from the devil lying in wait by the prayers of brethren, ibid. After their passage, the souls of saints go to heaven, but those of sinners are led into the lower world, 473.

ST. PAULINUS, patriarch of Aquileia.—Let the last day always turn before your eyes, XCIX, 243. A choir of angels meets the righteous person as he dies, and all the saints mingle in that person’s embraces, ibid.

ALCUIN.—As souls leave their bodies, the good have joy and the evil torments, C, 898. Prepare yourself, so that when that day which now approaches me comes to you, it may find you prepared, 690, 691.

ST. BENEDICT OF ANIANE.—Let the last day always turn before your eyes, CIII, 698. In good works, be such as you wish afterward to be, ibid.

JONAS, bishop of Orléans.—Death itself, when it comes, will be conquered if it is feared before it comes, CVI, 257. Punishment awaits those caught in their crimes, ibid. Trembling shakes them; pallor covers their faces, ibid.

ST. LUPUS, abbot of Ferrières.—After death, an account will be required of your years, months, hours, and moments, CXIX, 560. Do not purchase everlasting misery for yourself at the price of this most brief life, ibid.

HINCMAR, Archbishop of Rheims.—The righteous, when dying, are received into blessed rest, CXXV, 911. What each person hopes will be done for him by others after his death, let him do for himself while he lives, 912.

ST. BRUNO, Bishop of Würzburg.—The death of sinners is most evil, CXLII, 146. But the death of saints is precious, 422. Glorious is the passage which makes Christ’s members imitators of their Head, ibid.

ST. PETER DAMIAN.—Bodily death is the beginning of eternal life, CXLIV, 673. The righteous man shines forth after death among fiery spirits. The death of the condemned is most hideous, CXLV, 745. For them there is death without death, an end without end, and failing without failure, ibid. The soul departing from the body is hemmed in by great anxieties, 737–738. Recalling the forbidden acts it committed, it strives to remain but is compelled to depart, 738. It reckons the whole course of its past life as though it were one very brief step of a journey, ibid. It blushes because, for the sake of that substance subject to worms, it neglected that which was to be joined to the choirs of angels, ibid. A dreadful throng of demons attends that condemned soul, 738. It is shaken by intolerable terror, disturbed by the violence of their assault, and violently torn from the prison-house of flesh, ibid.

LANFRANC, Archbishop of Canterbury.—The sinner is found unprepared at death, CL, 341, 343, 344.

CANUTE I, King of England.—We command that every person should always reckon the end of his days to stand before him, CLI, 1177.

ST. BRUNO, founder of the Carthusians.—Death is most sweet to the good, most bitter to the evil, CLII, 1246.

GUIBERT, Abbot of Nogent.—Immediately after death the sentence of salvation or damnation is pronounced, CLVI, 610–611.

GOFFRID, Abbot of Vendôme.—A good death does not follow an evil life, CLVII, 246. The present life must be despised for the sake of the future, 184. Death, which produces a better fruit, is not to be postponed, 43.

THIOFRID, Abbot of Echternach.—Happy is the person who dies to the flesh before the death of the flesh, CLVII, 323. At death a human being is born into rest and glory, 324.

WERNER, Abbot of St. Blasien.—The soul of the dying impious person is shaken by bitter terror and lacerated by the stings of a gnawing conscience, CLVII, 1159. Meditation on death restrains the movements of concupiscence, ibid.

ST. ANSELM, Archbishop of Canterbury.—For the wretched, death is an object of desire, CLVIII, 795. Not to fear death because of the serenity of one’s conscience surpasses all the goods of this life, ibid. Three things remove the fear of death: serenity of conscience, firmness of faith, and certainty of hope, 792. To be released from the mortal body is blessedness, 810. The death of the elect is precious, 795. Angels [Col. 0210] attend the death of the elect and place themselves against their enemies, ibid. The soul of the righteous person, departing from the body, sees all its works, 732–733, and therefore rejoices, ibid. Immediately the angel who guarded it during life receives it, ibid, places it before God’s throne, ibid, and other angels come to meet it with congratulations, ibid. A righteous man prays concerning his last things, 641. How peacefully one falls asleep who falls asleep in the Lord, 995–996. The sinner’s soul, compelled to leave the body, is received by Satan’s angels, 735–736. They drag it in fiery chains to the torments of hell, ibid. Fear meets it upon fear, pain upon pain, 720. The hour of dreadful death is terrifying to all because of the horrible examination, the strict Judge, and insolent adversaries, 720–721.

SIGEBERT OF GEMBLOUX.—A life spent in labors is crowned at death with heavenly glory, CLX, 674.

ST. BRUNO, Bishop of Asti and Segni.—The departure of the righteous is joyful and happy, CLXIV, 899–900. They hold death in desire, 832. They long to be numbered among the angels in heaven, 450. The departure of the wicked is evil, 942. The spirit is taken from the good so that they may rest in peace, from the wicked so that they may be tormented, 1096–1097.

RUPERT, Abbot of Deutz.—Death is joyful for Christians, CLXVII, 539. The death of saints is more glorious than their life, 1484. Worldly people fear death, without considering the cause of death, CLXIX, 79. Death is rather to be desired than fled, 175–176. How dreadful is death’s arrival, 355–356. At human death most hideous spirits stand by, lying in wait, 355.

HILDEBERT, Bishop of Le Mans.—Each person’s death is the day of the Lord, CLXXI, 465. Every living thing dreads death; even saints fear it, and Christ himself also feared it, 1001–1002. The wicked person dies amid a heap of vices, the righteous amid a heap of merits, 542. As each person is found at death, so shall he be judged, 851–852.

GODEFRID, Abbot of Admont.—The remembrance of death purifies the soul, CLXXIV, 687. Demons lie in wait for a person dying, 920. The devil also alleges false crimes so that despair may prevail, 1101. In the hour of death one must enter into conflict with malignant enemies, 129. Therefore prayer should be offered without ceasing in order to overthrow the deceptions of unclean spirits, ibid. At death, whoever confesses his sins is to be saved, 22. One must have recourse to Christ’s mercy, ibid.—to him who gives the help of grace, 23, 703, 1101.

HONORIUS OF AUTUN.—Those who always consider themselves about to die do not die a sudden death, CLXXII, 1156. Wherever the evil die, they die an evil and sudden death, since they do not consider themselves about to die, ibid.

ST. BERNARD OF CLAIRVAUX.—Holy men hold death in desire, CLXXXIII, 91, 903–904, 1132–1133. To them it offers not loss but gain, 906. Three things make death precious: rest from labor, joy at what is new, and security concerning eternity, 687. The good death of the righteous is good because of rest, better because of newness, best because of security, CLXXXII, 241. For those beloved by the Lord, death is the gate of life and the beginning of refreshment, CLXXXIII, 619. Terror awaits them at their departure, pain in their passage, and shame before the glory of the great God, ibid. The death of sinners is most evil: they suffer three evils—fire, worms, and conscience, 747. The evil death of sinners lies in losing the world; it is worse in separation from the flesh; it is worst in the twofold torment of worm and fire, CLXXXII, 241. O soul, entering alone a wholly unknown region, you will see most hideous monsters rushing upon you in crowds! CLXXXIII, 619. Who will protect you from those roaring creatures prepared for prey? ibid. The hour of death is horrible, 216. “I dread Gehenna; I dread the face of the Judge,” 852. “I tremble at the wrath of the Mighty One, at the sight of fury,” ibid. “I shrink from the gnawing worm [lacuna] and the pouring fire,” ibid. The soul’s anxiety after separation from the body, 216. The remembrance of death must always be retained during life’s course, CLXXXII, 431. “While there is time, with tears I shall forestall the gnashing of teeth, harsh bonds, and the weight of chains that press, constrict, burn, and do not consume,” CLXXXIII, 852. Death is desirable to the saints of the New Law, but hateful to those of old, CLXXXII, 233–235. Separation from friends is harsher than death, 906.

PETER LOMBARD.—Those who live well die well, CXI, 304. The wicked fear death because of the soul’s separation from the body, 466. But at the hour of death only iniquity is to be feared, 467. Christ feared death, representing human weakness, 227. Swift death is a short-cut for evildoers, CXCI, 1575.

ADAM OF PRÉMONTRÉ.—A good death is the result of a good life, CXCVIII, 199. Foreknowledge of death induces fear, 307. The hour of departure is terrible, 308. “I fear the accusing enemy, the attesting conscience, the striking Judge,” ibid. At that hour Jesus Christ must be invoked for help, ibid.

PETER OF CELLE.—Before death one must prepare that by which one may live happily after death, [Col. 0211] CCII, 1132. Remedies that mitigate death are: confession of sins; penitence against the powers of the air; the defense of the holy cross; and the viaticum of the Lord’s body, ibid. In addition, the oil of anointing, to nourish the lamp of conscience and remove death’s darkness; God’s protection; the help of all the saints; and the prayer of the brethren, 1133. How useful the consideration of death is, 1133–1134.

PETER THE CHANTER.—Almsgiving must be prepared for death, CCV, 290. One must form one’s mind as if one had come to the end, 352.

GAUFRID, Subprior of St. Barbara.—Happy is the departure which is entrance into life and the reward of labor, CCV, 848. By prayers one must ask that a happy death be obtained from God, 848–849.

THOMAS THE CISTERCIAN.—The death of penitents and righteous persons, CCVI, 672–673. The death of the reprobate, ibid.

PETER OF BLOIS.—At the death of friends or parents one ought to feel consolation rather than grief, CCVII, 485, 488, 472–474.

ALAN OF LILLE.—At a friend’s death, one should grieve more for the danger to the soul than for exclusion from this temporal life, CCX, 138. When death is imminent, one should not grieve but prepare for its onset by steadfastness of mind, 138. Let the desire for eternal life invite you to death, ibid. Let us ensure that, as much as temporal life decreases, so much eternal life increases, 135. Fear of death must be driven away by contempt for earthly things and hope for heavenly things, 134–135. Death is bitter for worldly people, 258. Death is good for the righteous, 258.

INNOCENT III.—On the day of death the sinner sees Christ present for confusion; the righteous person sees him for exultation, CCXVII, 736.

## CHAPTER IV.—Examples of Good or Evil Deaths

LACTANTIUS.—The shameful death of the persecutor Decius is attributed to divine vengeance, VII, 201. The most cruel death of the persecutor Valerian, who died after his skin had been stripped off amid most severe torments, 203, 306, 482, 649. Galerius, a persecutor notable for ferocity and barbarity, is struck by God with an incurable wound, 420, 250. The miserable end of Maximinus the persecutor, 271, 374.

RUFINUS, Priest of Aquileia.—The disgraceful death of Arius, worthy of his blasphemies and foul mind, XXI, 485.

ST. AUGUSTINE.—A certain young man, adorned by gravity of character and modesty, desiring to be released, fell asleep in the Lord while psalms were being sung, [Col. 0212] XXXIII, 694, 697.

AUTHOR OF THE *Lives of the Fathers*.—A woman converted by reflection on death dies piously, LXXIII, 1048. A woman who entered a forbidden place in disguise fell dead, 337. A devout passage into life, 460–462. The miserable end of a certain rich man, 1012. The death of one bringing a calumny and of one enduring it, 1135, 1140.

ST. WARNAHARIUS.—The just punishment of the murderers of St. Desiderius, LXXX, 198.

AUDOENUS, Bishop of Noyon and Rouen.—Concerning a man who died miserably because he had perjured himself, LXXXVII, 580. Concerning the end of one who had seized a field belonging to the church: he is divinely struck down in the act of his crime, ibid. A young man accusing his father is seized and struck by a demon, 582–583.

ALCUIN.—Concerning a man who perished miserably because of a theft which he had committed in God’s Church, CI, 722.

ADSO, Abbot of Montier-en-Der.—A certain man who had distributed his goods receives among the saints the reward of blessed immortality, CXXXIV, 630.

BERNARD THE SCHOLIAST.—The lamentable death of a matron, CXLI, 162–163.

ARNOLD OF ST. EMMERAM.—Concerning twelve men who had sworn contrary to law and were consumed by manifold punishment, CXLI, 1010.
