PETER DAMIAN.—The terrible death of a certain count, CXLV, 433. A remarkable example of a man alienating the Lord’s chalice and removing it from a church, 573. Concerning one whom an evil spirit assailed after he had committed adultery, 616.

GUIBERT, Abbot of Nogent.—Because of their evil conduct, two monks are struck by lightning, CLVI, 886.

SIGEBERT OF GEMBLOUX.—A certain man, miserably deceived by a demon, perishes by sudden and eternal death because of the killing of an innocent person, CLX, 780.

HERBERT, Archbishop of Torres in Sardinia.—Concerning a certain convert who died happily, CLXXXV, 1301.—The happy death of a pious priest, 1348. A girl most diligent in assisting the sick was illustrious in death, 1353.

PETER THE VENERABLE.—Concerning the death of a man who made confession at the last, CLXXXIX, 856–857. Concerning another’s death after confession, 857.

HERBERT OF BOSHAM.—The punishment of certain sacrilegious knights, CXC, 1304–1306.

AELRED, Abbot of Rievaulx.—Concerning the miserable death of a traitor, CXCV, 762–763.

[Col. 0211]

## CXXVII. INDEX ON THE PARTICULAR AND PRIVATE JUDGMENT OF EACH HUMAN BEING AFTER DEATH, IN WHICH VARIOUS OPINIONS OF THE HOLY FATHERS CONCERNING ITS CIRCUMSTANCES ARE CONSIDERED

God’s judgment is described in Holy Scripture as manifold: one judgment of discernment and another of condemnation; one hidden and the other manifest. “The hidden judgment is the punishment by which each human being is now either exercised for purification or admonished to conversion; or, if he has despised God’s calling and discipline, is blinded unto condemnation. The manifest judgment is that by which the Lord who is to come will judge the living and the dead, all confessing him to be the one from whom rewards are granted to the good and punishments to the evil; but then that confession will avail not for the remedy of evils but for the increase of condemnation.” (St. Augustine, *On John*.)

The hidden judgment is carried out in this life; the manifest judgment will occur after death, when each person must come into the Lord’s presence, render an account of every thought, word, and deed, and finally receive the Judge’s sentence. This will occur at two distinct times: first, immediately after the death of each individual; second, at the end of the world. The first judgment is particular and private. For when each of us departs from this life, he is immediately brought before God’s tribunal, where a most just inquiry is held concerning everything that he did, said, or thought while living here this mortal life. The second will be general, when, on one day and in one place, all human beings together will stand before the tribunal of the supreme Judge; while all the people of every age look on and listen, each will receive the sentence pronounced upon him. Immediately the reprobate, standing on the Judge’s left upon the earth, will be cast into eternal fire with the devil and his angels; but the elect, caught up into the air to meet Christ, will hasten with him into the eternal kingdom prepared for them before the foundation of the world, and thus they will always be with the Lord in heaven.

Concerning the particular and private judgment, which is the subject here, since none of the Fathers has treated it expressly, and since it is also treated in the Indexes on the Creed and on the supreme Judgment, we refer the reader to those Indexes, where he will find what he seeks.

[Col. 0213]

## CXXVIII. INDEX ON HEAVEN, SET FORTH LOGICALLY, PRESENTING ALL THAT THE FATHERS WROTE CONCERNING ITS EXISTENCE AND LOCATION, AND CONCERNING HEAVENLY BLESSEDNESS

### Notice

In this Index, so that the reader may find what he seeks more easily, we have established fifteen chapters, arranged in logical order:

I. Definition of the name.  
II. Definition of the thing.  
III. The notion of blessedness in general.  
IV. Heavenly blessedness and what it consists in.  
V. How highly this heavenly blessedness is to be valued, desired, and sought.  
VI. To whom it is to be given and to whom denied.  
VII. The time of blessedness.  
VIII. The location of the kingdom of heaven.  
IX. The way to heaven.  
X. Sermons on heaven.  
XI. Homilies on heaven.  
XII. Expositions of psalms treating heaven.  
XIII. Explanations of the Gospels.  
XIV. Treatises on heaven.  
XV. Heaven considered physically.

Matters concerning the heavenly hierarchy will be found in the Index on Angels; matters concerning the intercession of saints, in the Index on the Veneration of Saints.

[INDEX ON HEAVEN.]

## CHAPTER I.—Definition of the Name

What is the origin of the name *caelum* (“heaven”), and why this name is received in different senses in Holy Scripture: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 263.—Why heaven is so called: Lactantius, VI, 182, 706; St. Ambrose, XIV, 135, 136, 137, 152.—What is signified by the name “heaven” in Genesis: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVII, 199.—How the word *caelum* is to be understood: St. Jerome, XXVI, 547; St. Augustine, XL, 1027.—What are the spiritual and material senses of this word: St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 981.—A fine literal and mystical meaning of Paradise: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 334.—The word *caelum* comes from *celare* (“to hide”): St. Augustine, XL, 1028; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 492.—Heaven is so called because it hides all things within itself: Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXX, 816.—Heaven is named from *cernere* (“to discern”): Rupert, Abbot, CLXVIII, 226.—Heaven is called, as it were, *casa ilios* (χάβας ἡλίου), that is, “house of the sun”; or like a chased vessel, because it is marked out with stars: Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 141.—According to the Hebrews, heaven derives its name from waters: St. Jerome, XXII, 659–660.—The word “heaven” is used in three ways: St. Jerome, XXVI, 300.—It is used variously: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVIII, 1516; Rupert, Abbot, CLXVIII, 55–56; CLXIX, 957; CLXX, 81; Garnerus, CXCIII, 35.—The apostles and prophets: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 708; St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 100, 153.—Preachers are called heavens: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 579, 863–864; LXXVI, 420, 550, 1225.—Every holy teacher is a heaven: Garnerus, CXCIII, 35.—The righteous are called heavens: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 1004, 1100; St. Bruno of Würzburg, bishop, CXLII, 77, 153, 444.—A person is called heaven who practices the life of angels by guarding integrity: St. Ambrose, CV, 1364.—The heaven of heaven is a pure mind made most harmoniously one with God: St. Augustine, XL, 915.—Heaven: the soul of the righteous: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 508, 955, 1282; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 917; Garnerus, CXCIII, 31.—The heavens are the priests, Pharisees, and teachers of the Law among the Jewish people: Garnerus, ibid., 33.—The heaven of the righteous is more excellent than visible heaven: St. Prosper, LI, 327.—Paul was a heaven; James and John were heavens: St. Ambrose, XVI, 1020.—Evangelical poor are called heavens: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 1100–1101.—The ornaments of the heavens are the virtues of preachers: ibid., LXXVI, 1224.—The Lord Jesus himself was the human being’s perpetual heaven: St. Ambrose, XIV, 1020.—The thunders of heaven are the perfect desires of the elect: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 89.—The heavens are the hearts of saints: Stephen of Tournai, CCXI, 736.—How the holy soul is called heaven: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 912.

Eternal life is denoted by the land of Canaan: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 1191.—It is expressed by God’s right hand: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 99.—Heavenly glory is signified by the name “cedar”: ibid., LXXVI, 1648.—It is denoted by “my garden”: Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXX, 1092.—By the Sabbath eternal rest is signified: St. Bruno, CLII, 791–792.—That Abraham’s bosom signifies Paradise is established by the opinions of many teachers: St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 476.—The dwellings of heaven are called caves: Rupert, CLXVIII, 562.

What is understood by the word “Paradise”: St. Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 876.

The general meaning of Paradise is every place where one lives happily: St. Augustine, XXXIII, 834; Alcuin, C, 969; Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXX, 987; St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 52.—Paradise: the blessed life: St. Augustine, XXXIV, 202, 214.—Paradise: possession of God’s kingdom: St. Hilary, IX, 255–256.—Paradise: the land of the living: St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 83, 209; Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXX, 192, 1006.—The Paradise of delight is the will of God: Guibert, Abbot, CLVI, 65.—The place of delight is God: Venerable Guibert, ibid.—Earthly Paradise was planted in likeness of the heavenly: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVII, 268.—On the difference between paradises: St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 474.—The names of the four rivers said to flow from Paradise and water the whole earth are interpreted mystically: St. Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 971.—Which Paradise is meant when the Savior says to the repentant thief, “Today you will be with me in Paradise”: Garnerus, CXCIII, 1250.—What the host of heaven is: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 214.—What the harmonies of heaven are: ibid., 532–534.

## CHAPTER II.—Definition of the Thing

Heaven, the dwelling-place of the living God: Tertullian, I, 377.—That heaven is God’s dwelling-place not which is seen, but Jerusalem which is built up in the glorification of holy angels and human beings: St. Prosper, LI, 367–368.—Heavenly blessedness is Christ’s dominion: Venerable Godefrid, CLXXIV, 658.—What the region of the saints is: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 1048; CXII, 1095.—The kingdom of heaven and place of the righteous: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1168.—Heaven, the true land of the living: St. Ambrose, XXII, 11–12.—Heaven, the Christian’s homeland: Tertullian, II, 260; St. Cyprian, IV, 601; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1118; Alcuin, CI, 1307.—Zion, the city of all the elect: Rupert, Abbot, CLXIX, 16–17.—Earth is humanity’s exercise; heaven, its crown: St. Ambrose, XVI, 1132.—Heaven, the reward of labor after this life: Rupert, CLXIX, 659–660.—By the kingdom of God we mean the greater blessedness: Eadmer the monk, CLIX, 633.—The true life to come is one consumed by no fear of death or grief, etc.: Columbanus, LXXX, 295.—The true life, spoken of without qualification, will be without end and without any misery: St. Prosper, LI, 349.—The life in which the eternal brightness of highest truth and the contemplation of the Creator will appear: Venerable Bede, XCIV, 161.—Eternal life: true honor without limit, true delight without weariness, true rest without end: Radulfus Ardens, CLV, 1434.—Joy whose fullness is diminished by no touch of any disturbance, eternity which is never dissolved by any limit: Venerable Bede, XCIV, 165.—The reward of those serving God is eternal life, eternal blessedness, eternal joy: Eadmer the monk, CLIX, 621.—God’s tabernacle, in which he reveals himself to his saints: St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 761.—God’s storehouses are eternal blessedness: Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXX, 1657 ff.—Eternal life is God himself: St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1388.—Eternal life is Christ: ibid., XLIV, 175.—Blessedness is compared to an inheritance: Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXX, 436.—Everlasting blessedness: St. Leo, LV, 92.—The heavenly reward of saints: ibid., 32.—The delights of completed blessedness: ibid., X, 370–371.—The eternal inheritance is called a lot: Peter Lombard, CXCII, 261.—An unceasing feast, the age to come: Rabanus Maurus, CX, 1031–1032.

Paradise is interpreted as a most pleasant place and the eternal security of most happy delight: Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXX, 987.—A garden of delights: Alcuin, C, 949.—Paradise is not a bodily place: Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 1157.—Paradise is a place of divine loveliness appointed for receiving the spirits of the saints: Tertullian, I, 520; II, 297.—Paradise, the eternal region of saints: St. Hilary, IX, 257–258.—The lot and kingdom of Christ’s inheritance: ibid., 835.—Paradise is eternal life: Alcuin, C, 1103.—Paradise, the mountain of God: St. Jerome, XXV, 273.—Paradise, the land of the living: Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXX, 192, 1106.—Paradise is our country: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1118.—A fine literal and mystical significance of Paradise: Rabanus, CXI, 334.—It signifies a garden, the Church, and the land of the living: ibid.—Paradise is the dwelling-place of saints in heaven, where they enjoy the vision of God: St. Bruno of Asti, ibid., 307.—The supercelestial Paradise: a blessed and glorious region, full of delight and the sweetness of glory and joy, grace and kindness: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 838.—The spiritual Paradise, the dwelling of the blessed, which eternal Wisdom made from the beginning, where the Godhead itself is beheld by them face to face: Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 1157.—There are three kinds of paradises: the pleasurable sweetness of visible things, the pure purity of spiritual things, and the delightful truth of supercelestial things: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 807.—Eternal life, the reward of labor: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 422.—It is a reward and yet grace: ibid., XXXIII, 881; XL, 282.—Length of days: eternal life: ibid., XXXVII, 1169.—The kingdom of God is the salvation of human beings: Werner, Abbot, CLVII, 1068.—The kingdom is God the Father, and he contains in himself such power of a kingdom: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 404.—Palms signify the victory of the elect: Alcuin, C, 1133.—The kingdom of heaven is compared to pearls: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 331.—To the ten virgins: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1118.—To a hidden treasure: ibid., 1120.—To spoils: St. Bruno, founder of the Carthusians, CLII, 1308.—By the Lord’s resurrection eternal life is signified: Eugyppius, Abbot, LXXII, 690.

## CHAPTER III.—On Perfect Blessedness in General
What blessedness is, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1401.---Wherein it consists, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 472.---What true blessedness is, St. Prosper, LI, 436, 536.---Wherein it consists, Alcuin, C, 629; CI, 850; Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, CLXXI, 176.---What the fullness of supreme happiness requires, St. Augustine, XLV, 1498; Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 923.---What true glory is, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 47.---What the blessed life is and where it is to be had, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 795.---The will to attain blessedness is one and the same in all; but concerning blessedness itself there is a great diversity of wills, idem, XLII, 1018.---A man cannot fail to will even blessedness, however great he understands it to be, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 344, 345.---He who wills something for the sake of blessedness wills nothing other than blessedness, ibid.---He wills to be blessed in proportion as he knows more fully that this is possible, ibid.---Why, although all desire blessedness, that is chosen by which one departs from it, St. Augustine, XLII, 1020.---The will for blessedness is not blessedness, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 541, 542.---Blessedness is not in the mind, as the Stoics maintained, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 439.---Blessedness is attaining the highest good, idem, XXXII, 1254, 1260.---The highest good is called that to which all things are referred, idem, XXXIII, 438.---Blessedness consists in enjoyment of the true and highest good, St. Augustine, XLI, 233, 703.---It is situated in the sole possession of truth and goodness, St. Ambrose, XIV, 611; XV, 1296.---The Academics placed it in the inquiry for truth alone, St. Augustine, XXXII, 908.---Blessedness is joy in truth, ibid., 793.---The perfect knowledge of truth which is to be enjoyed, ibid., 976.---Blessedness, the sum and accumulation of all goods, idem, XXXVI, 72.---Blessedness is adherence to the highest good, idem, XLII, 950.---Man’s blessedness is God, or the knowledge of God, idem, XXXIII, 840.---The end of blessedness is to know God, St. Jerome, XXII, 369.---No one can be blessed unless he has knowledge and imitation of God, St. Augustine, XLI, 233.---To know God is supreme blessedness, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 810, 811.---To know the Trinity is eternal life, idem, CLXXXII, 799, 800; LLXXXIV, 375, 376.---Truly blessed, and perfectly blessed, are those who truly and perfectly love God, CLXXXIV, 375, 376.---Nothing but God suffices for man, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 780, 781.---All blessedness is from God, St. Ambrose, XLV, 1262.---The blessedness of human beings and angels comes from God alone, St. Augustine, XLI, 217, 220, 269, 279, 280, 290, 349, 656.---The Platonists too acknowledged this, ibid., 279, 290.---Blessedness is God himself, idem, XXXII, 848, 965, 968; XXXIII, 503; XLII, 163, 554; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 333; St. Anselm, CLVIII, 711, 712.---The end is the eternal presence or possession of God, Hildebert, CLXXI, 662.---Man’s blessedness is the enjoyment of God, St. Augustine, XXXII, 787.---The attainment of God, ibid., 1315, 1319.---To cleave to God, ibid., 795.---To rejoice in God, toward God, and for God, ibid.---The summit of blessedness is to see God, Alcuin, C, 385, 386, 486.---The supreme reward is to enjoy God and others in him, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 32.---Man’s blessedness is to run from many things to one, and to remain with the one, idem, XXXVIII, 587.---Truth and knowledge of friends, without fear of deception, must be present in the blessed life, ibid., 1404.---Blessedness does not exist without justice, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 344, 345, 346.---Two conditions of blessedness: enjoyment of the immutable good, and security that it will not be lost, St. Augustine, XLI, 328.---The perfect privilege of blessedness cannot obtain its full measure unless it is enclosed by the infinity of eternity, St. Ambrose, XVII, 1002, 1003.---Eternity and security are required for blessedness, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1404; XLI, 327, 360, 370, 433.---Blessedness, eternity, truth, happiness, ibid., 369.---Eternal life alone is blessed, St. Prosper, LI, 448, 449.---Eternal life alone ought to be called life, Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXX, 857, 858.---A blessed life is not such unless it is eternal, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1402, 1403; XL, 23; XLII, 605.---True life is only that which is eternal and blessed, idem, XXXV, 1573; XXXVIII, 519, 1402, 1403.---Life without any qualification is eternal and blessed life alone, idem, XXXVII, 1555.---Although there are many goods, eternal life is one [Col. 0217], St. Ambrose, XV, 1621.---Immortality alone can fill the measure of perfect blessedness, idem, XLII, 607, 1022.---That blessedness is deceptive and false in which future misery is either unknown or feared, idem, XLI, 371.---He is not blessed who fears losing what he possesses, idem, XXXII, 965.---Nor is he who foreknows that he will fall into misery, idem, XLIV, 932, 933.---An insecure possession of blessedness destroys the love of God, idem, XLI, 371.---The perfect gift to be given to all in glorification, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 164.---That great and true blessedness which is promised to the saints in the age to come, Eugyppius, abbot, LXII, 861.---Only the glory awaited in heaven is secure, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 529.---Carnal thinking about future happiness, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1189.---Temporal life is in faith; eternal life will be in sight, idem, XXXV, 1727.---The blessed life is the fruit of present things, but eternal life the hope of future things, St. Ambrose, XVI, 107.---Blessed, and truly blessed, are those whose king is Christ, who deserve to enjoy his eternal vision and behold his glory, Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 193.---What kind of happiness is to be hoped for in the future age, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 34, 36, 135, 1384.---What the promised eternal reward is, St. Augustine, XLIV, 222.---May heaven’s mystery be taught to me by God himself, who made it, not by a man who has not known himself, St. Ambrose, XVI, 974.---Blessedness is not placed in riches, powers and honors, nobility of lineage, grace or beauty, nor in bodily health, idem, XIV, 927.---Blessedness is sufficiency in which there is no lack, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 395, 396.---A state made most perfect by the gathering of all goods, ibid., 597, 598.---Those are called blessed who have whatever they desire, ibid., 597.---Those who have what they will and will rightly, Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1368.---Eternal peace, final blessedness, St. Augustine, XLI, 636, 637.---Life is a good, but eternal life, St. Ambrose, XIV, 586.---This is eternal life: to live without punishment and possess glory, idem, XVII, 212.---Happiness is situated in eternity, truth, and charity, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 744.---To be released from the body and to be with Christ is blessedness, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 810–813.---For he is called blessed who lacks nothing; and the saints, being with Christ, will lack nothing, St. Bruno, CLIII, 431.---Future blessedness: the end of the righteous persons’ expectation, the end of prophecy and law, the end of all holiness, St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 809.

## CHAPTER IV.—On heavenly blessedness

Wherein heaven’s preparation consists, St. Hilary, X, 459, 460.---What chiefly constitutes the kingdom of heaven, *Lives of the Fathers*, LXXIII, 258.---The state of the blessed life, St. Hilary, IX, 500, 854.---The price of the kingdom of heaven, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1521.---The price of the eternal vision, idem, XXXVIII, 707; XXXIX, 1518.---The eternal kingdom in which God will reign with the saints reigning together with him, St. Hilary, IX, 855, 856.---What the state of the future age will be, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 109.---How great the dignity of the heavenly dwelling is, St. Hilary, IX, 299, 300.---On the happy state of the heavenly homeland, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 998.---What eternal life is, idem, CLXXXIV, 256, 257, 474 ff.---Praise of eternal life, St. Augustine, XXXV, 1647.---The state of the blessed, idem, XXXIV, 476; Rupert, CLXVIII, 1631.---The gifts and state of blessedness, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 252.---The eternal life of the blessed, Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 1029.---The exaltation of the saints is eternal life, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1589; St. Prosper, LI, 360.---Length of days, eternal life, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1169.---Eternal life is the contemplation of truth, idem, XXXIX, 1633.---The goods of God’s kingdom, St. Patrick, LIII, 831.---The abundance of eternal recompense, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1132, 1133.---Blessedness is to be inferred from the goods of this world, St. Augustine, XLI, 792.---From Christ’s death, ibid.---In blessedness: victory, truth; dignity, holiness; peace, happiness; life, eternity, ibid., 78.---The eternal reward, idem, XLIV, 222.---What eternal light is, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 307.---Our place is eternal light, idem, LXXV, 673, 908.---Our eternal homeland is our light, ibid., 1158.---The reward of the heavenly homeland, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 490.---Its price, idem, CLXXXV, 39.---How great heaven is and what dwellings are there, Rupert, CLXVII, 204.---The glorious heavenly seat in which the souls of the saints exult, St. Leo, LV, 136.---The health-giving and saving drinks of paradise, St. Cyprian, III, 1116.---The saints’ reward is certain, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 848.---Eulogies of the blessed souls, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 373, 374.---What it is to enjoy heavenly goods, and what those goods are, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 517.---Eternal life is nourished and preserved not by another, but by itself, St. Hilary, IX, 468, 469.---The recompense of glory incomparably exceeds every merit of the good will and work bestowed by God, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 159.---Christians will have greater things in the state of future glory than in the state of innocence, Richard of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 526.---Possession without defect, Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 1089, 1109.---On the reward of the heavenly homeland, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 492.---The saints’ reward: glory and splendor, Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 691, 1147; CXI, 1033–1042.---Christ promises magnificent rewards for small things, heavenly ones for earthly things, everlasting ones for temporal things, together with glory, St. Ambrose, XVII, 123, 124.---The righteous endure harsh labors here, but eternal rewards await them, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 940.---The righteous person despised here will shine with great power in the future life, ibid., 950.---A comparison of saints and stars, Walbero, abbot, CXCV, 1049.---One beauty of the saints belongs to their character, another to their rewards, ibid., 868.---The festival of the blessed in heaven, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 375, 952.

Heavenly blessedness, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 259, 260.---What the course or cycle of blessedness is, ibid., 31.---The happiness of the future life, St. Hilary, IX, 877; St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 135, 651, 660, 686, 813, 1090; XL (Appendix), 820, 917, 918, 993; XLII, 1018; Godfrey, abbot, CLVII, 184, 197; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 952.---Happiness and delight, idem, CLXXXIV, 493.---Of what kind and how great it is, St. Jerome, XXVI, 457; Venerable Hildebert, CLXXI, 167; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 616; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 165 ff., 664 ff.---It surpasses all understanding, St. Augustine, XLI, 796.---Ineffable, idem, XXXIV, 25; Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXX, 602.---Compared with earthly happiness, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 136.---Heavenly blessedness is perfect knowledge of God, Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 314, 315.---Blessedness in love, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1220.---Faith is succeeded by sight, which we shall see; and hope is succeeded by blessedness itself, to which we shall attain, Eugyppius, LXII, 942, 943.---Proclamation of eternal blessedness, ibid., 794.---The reward, St. Benedict, LXVI, 237.---Fullness, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 1172.---A most delightful description, Franco, abbot, CLXVI, 803–806.---The blessedness of the saints, Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXX, 260, 313, 621; Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 764.---After death, St. Hilary, IX, 840.---After the resurrection, ibid., 393.---The blessedness promised to the righteous will be likeness to God’s angels, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 524.---The blessedness which God possesses, such will the saints receive from him, St. Bruno, CLIII, 431.---The eternal happiness of the blessed, St. Patrick, LIII, 832, 837; Eugyppius, abbot, LXII, 625; Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXX, 1301; Alcuin, CI, 1307; Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 1147; Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1143; Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 1091, 1092.---Happiness and security, St. Hilary, IX, 876, 877.---Rejoicing over the happiness of the blessed, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 413.---Delight, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1108.---Pleasure, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 1171.---How great the happiness of heavenly blessedness is, and how great a fullness of joy will receive the souls of the righteous, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 273.---Fourfold blessedness, Thomas the Cistercian, CCVI, 134.---The twofold cause of blessedness, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 791.---The four rivers flooding the blessed, ibid., 835.---The blessedness of the soul in heaven, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 174; St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 459.---The blessedness of the body in heaven, ibid.---The blessedness of body and soul is expressed in a twofold state, Wolbero, abbot, CXCV, 1027, 1054.

The glory of paradise, St. Leo, LIV, 348, 349; St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 832; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 247; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 510; Henry, cardinal, CCIV, 304.---The glory and happiness of the heavenly kingdom, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2136; XL, 820, 822, 861, 915, 954, 958, 966, 993.---A description of heavenly glory, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 599.---The glory of God’s kingdom, completed in us by heavenly glory, St. Hilary, IX, 258, 259.---In blessedness there will be true glory, true honor, true peace, St. Augustine, XLI, 801.---Whence true, abiding glory comes to man, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 384.---The glory, power, and splendor of God’s kingdom, Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1262 ff.---In heaven there are glory, perpetual praise, and tireless proclamations, St. Jerome, XXII, 684.---The excellence of heavenly glory, its contemplation, and the manner of attaining it, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 178.---Future glory is truly great; present glory is deceptive and empty, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 249, 250.---Eternal glory consists in two things, Peter Cantor, CCV, 365.---The glory of the righteous, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 515.---The glory of the Lord and of the saints, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 604, 605.---Whence the saints’ glory and praise come, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 476.---The glory of the blessed is not material, Venerable Guibert, CLVI, 673.---God will be glorious in them, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 124.---On the crown of the blessed, Richard of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 478.---The glory and joys of heaven, St. Augustine, XL, 919; Alcuin, CI, 833; St. Anselm, CLVIII, 782, 783.---The immeasurable joys of blessedness, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 967.---What the chief joys are, Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1143.---Joy [Col. 0219] and peace in heaven, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 589.---The supreme delight of paradise, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1771.---The delight of eternal life, Eugyppius, LXII, 689.---Present life is full of labor; future life, of joy, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 740.---Every joy is communal, true, and eternal joy, Radulfus Ardens, CLV, 1522.---This joy will not enter into those who rejoice; rather, those who rejoice will enter into it, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 818, 819.---It will be full, ibid.---Human speech cannot explain, nor the mind conceive, what and how great the joys in heaven are, Haymo, CXVIII, 888.---Eternal delight consists in two things: knowledge and the joy of the saints in their homeland, Peter Cantor, CCV, 365.---Blessedness gladdens the elect, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 365.---Complete joy in heaven over the subjection of evil spirits, Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 492, 845, 846.---The joys of the blessed, St. Augustine, XL, 822; XLI, 691; Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 456–458; CXI, 1585; William, abbot, CLXXX, 222–227.---How great is the gladness of the saints, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1121, 1129.---Their joy is consummated, St. Hilary, IX, 743, 744.---They will rejoice as much as they will love; they will love as much as they will know, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 241, 242, 818.---The joy of the righteous when they hear, “Come, you blessed,” etc., ibid., 720, 721.---The Lord’s rest is the fullness of blessedness, Rupert, CLXIX, 152, 153.---Peace without disturbance, Alcuin, CI, 54; Smaragdus, CII, 679.---Peace and joy in heaven, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 589, 590.---Eternal life in rest before the resurrection, St. Augustine, XXXV, 1614.---On the repose of eternal blessedness, Guichard of Lyons, CXCIX, 1114.---On the peace in the heavenly Jerusalem, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI (Appendix), 1159.---Jerusalem is named as a city of peace, St. Hilary, IX, 876, 877.---The repose of the saints, Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 485, 497, 632.---The saints’ perfect repose and delight in all things, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 469, 470.---The blessed will pass from rest into rest, St. Augustine, XLI, 694.

On the hundredfold and eternal life, Geoffrey, abbot, CLXXXIV, 473.---On the name of the city of God, Henry, cardinal, ibid.---On the heavenly Jerusalem, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI (Appendix), 1159; Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 860, 875.---On the gates of the heavenly Jerusalem, ibid., 1162.---On the streets of the heavenly Jerusalem, ibid., 1164.---On its broad ways, ibid., 1166.---On its cloister, ibid., 1167.---On the silence of the heavenly cloister, ibid., 1174.---Description of the heavenly Jerusalem, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1169.---Its four gates, ibid., 1117.---The hope, beginning, and perfection of the heavenly kingdom are treated in Psalms CXLVII and CXLVIII, St. Hilary, IX, 878.

## Wherever the saints are, they are with God

Wherever the saints are, they are with God, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1366.---God alone is the blessedness of the blessed, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 491, 492.---The Lord alone is the saints’ inheritance, St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 739.---The saints in heaven reign with God, St. Paulinus, LXI (Appendix), 730.---God’s cohabitation is proper to Christ, and he shares it with the apostles, St. Hilary, IX, 415–417.---Through Christ as mediator, the blessed are assumed into the unity of the Father’s majesty, ibid., 467, 468.---Eternal life with God, from God, and in God, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 652.---In eternal life, love of God’s presence is neither diminished nor ended, St. Prosper, LI, 297.---How the saints are alike and unlike God, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 35.---How the saints will be like Christ, ibid., 915.---The blessed are gods, St. Hilary, IX, 770.---Each blessed person in the homeland is called Christ, Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, CLXXI, 480.---Eternal life is dwelling with Christ, St. Hilary, X, 320.---Paradise contains within itself Christ, the tree of life, idem, IX, 255.---The saints’ rest is situated in fellowship with Christ and the angels, ibid., 500.---The saints are joined to Christ, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1425, 1434, 1441.---After death the saints are with Christ in heaven, St. Hilary, IX, 646; St. Jerome, XXII, 608, 642, 684.---The kingdom of God consists solely in fellowship with Christ, St. Augustine, XLIV, 118.---The face of God, Christ, is present to each saint, St. Hilary, IX, 840, 841.---The souls of the saints already reign with Christ in heaven, St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 496.---The blessed, at rest with Christ, await the redemption of their body, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1420, 1454.---The saints’ life will then be in splendor, when they appear with Christ in glory, St. Prosper, LI, 319.---Our future life has already been completed in Christ, our head, St. Augustine, XLII, 249.---The righteous will judge with Christ, Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 681, 682; CXI, 755.---Angels and the souls of saints speak to God, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI (Appendix), 1176.---God speaks to souls, ibid., 1177.---After the resurrection God will speak to human beings, ibid., 1178.

## They see God

[Col. 0220]

The vision of God, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 34, 712.---The beatific vision, Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXX, 1303 ff.---Noonday is the blessed vision, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 953.---The vision of God in the form of God, St. Augustine, XXXV, 1572, 1573.---Eternal blessedness consists in the vision of God, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 629, 630; Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 385.---Blessedness is seeing God’s brightness, Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 761.---The vision of God is our end, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 366.---No end is more blessed than the vision and love of God itself, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 56.---Nothing is more sublime than the vision of God, St. Augustine, XLIV, 601.---The vision of God, and whether God can be seen, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 613.---Threefold vision: bodily, spiritual, and intellectual, Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 998.---Bodily and spiritual vision in the future, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 616.---What the future vision of God will be like, St. Augustine, XLI, 797.---The vision of God as he is, in the other life, St. Augustine, XXXV, 1779, 1662.---The face-to-face vision of God is reserved for the resurrection, idem, XXXVI, 485; St. Leo, LIV, 310.---The threefold vision of Christ: in exile, at judgment, and in the kingdom, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 360, 637.---The Father’s house is the vision of the Almighty, in which the righteous glory as in the Lord, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 1162.---The difference between the contemplation of the blessed and of wayfarers, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 259, 260.---The vision of Christ is our whole reward, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1176.---God himself is the spectacle of the blessed, ibid., 1901.---The saints see God, St. Cyprian, IV, 676.---They have come to the Lord’s presence and kiss, ibid., 267, 428.---They behold God and his Christ, ibid., 404, 405.---The blessed will call upon, see, love, and praise God, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1061, 1062, 1403; XXXVIII, 1235, 1147, 1176, 1185, 1186; XXXIX, 1632; XLI, 801, 804; XLII, 314, 315.---To see God and praise God: this will be the harbor of our labors, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 235.---We shall see what we believe, idem, XL, 343.---In glory the saints see whatever belongs to divine light, honor, and glory, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 663.---The blessed see God not merely in charity, but in his own nature, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 93.---God of gods will be seen in Zion—that is, in the mirror of perpetual rest, Alcuin, CI, 54; Smaragdus, CII, 679.

We shall see God without end, and he is the end of our desires, St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 524.---All saints will see God, Haymo, CXVIII, 877.---The food of the righteous is the present countenance of God, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 655.---God is seen by the blessed in himself and in creatures, ibid., 654, 655, 797.---The saints will glory in heaven and enjoy the vision of God, St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 60.---The blessed see and await God, Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 1631.---They do not see God as he beholds himself, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 94.---The vision of God is not apprehended by bodily senses, Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 1144.---Human sight cannot comprehend God, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 594.---We shall see God in that vision in which the angels now see him, St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 522.---The vision by which the saints will see God is like that of human beings seeing one another, Eugyppius, LXII, 813 ff.---In that brightness in which the disciples saw the Lord shining on the mountain, Haymo, CXVIII, 880.---The saints will see God in this body, St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 520; St. Augustine, XLI, 797.---Whether through the body, ibid.---Whether God can or cannot be seen by the outward person, it is certain that he will be seen by the inward person, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 628.---I can see God with the mind, or by the inward sharpness of the heart, idem, XXXVIII, 670.---The light of glory is necessary for the beatific vision, Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXX, 459 ff.---Ezekiel saw not glory, but the likeness of God’s glory, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 868.---Angels enjoy the vision of the Word, St. Augustine, XXXV, 1540.---God cannot be seen without joy, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 47.---The blessed’s joy in contemplating the Creator and creatures, ibid., 552.---So great will be the saints’ joy in contemplating God that it will allow no entrance to sorrow, CLXI, 1014.---Vision is supreme happiness, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 711.---How great is the happiness of seeing God’s face, ibid., 931.---Delight, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 940.---How great the joy will be in heaven for those who see God, St. Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 980.---How blessed and sweet the vision of God in heaven is, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 940.---In it, our whole intellect will be borne toward God without discursive movement, idem, CLXXXII, 803.---What makes the blessed in their homeland is the vision of genuine glory, namely, the humanity and divinity of Christ, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 863.---What repose and fulfillment of the will ought to be understood in the vision, St. Augustine, XLII, 992.---How angels and the blessed desire to look upon God whom they see, Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, CLXXI, 863.---The saints’ reward is the vision of God, which will provide us with ineffable joy, St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 519.---The vision of God alone is the true refreshment of our mind, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 627.---All receive glory and light from contemplation of God’s majesty, St. Hilary, IX, 555.---The beatific vision transforms us into God’s brightness, Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 834.---In the vision of God prophecy and knowledge will cease, for all things will be naked and open, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 333.---While God’s countenance is beheld unfailingly by the saints, the mind is satisfied without end with the food of life, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 655.---The saints are never sated with the vision of God, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 94.---The vision and love of God both satisfy and do not satisfy, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1100.---Without the vision of God, one endowed with every other good is most unhappy, St. Augustine, XLI, 294.---Everything that abounds without the vision of God is poverty, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 182.---The blessed vision is to be desired for detecting the devil’s deceits, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 954, 955.

## They love God

They will love God, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1061, 1062, 1403; XXXVIII, 235, 1147, 1176, 1185, 1136; XXXIX, 1632; XLI, 801, 804; XLII, 314, 315.---The blessed love God and one another through him, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 816.---Because they love others as themselves, ibid., 818, 819, 1172.---God loves the blessed more than they love themselves, ibid., 238, 816.---He loves himself and them through himself, ibid., 816.

## They praise God

The voice of eternal life is: “Let every spirit praise the Lord,” Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1296.---The praise of God is the food of the saints, Rupert, CLXVIII, 236.---The occupation of blessed spirits is to rejoice with the Lord and praise him, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 262.---Our whole occupation will be the praise of God, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1121.---Heaven resounds with the saints’ praise and thanksgiving, Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 899, 901.---The blessed sing judgment and mercy—the song of the blessed, Rupert, CLXIX, 1157, 1158.---The saints will praise God tirelessly, St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 523.

## They possess God

For the blessed, the enjoyment of God will take the place of all goods, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1189.---God himself is the saints’ satisfaction, Alcuin, CI, 54.---God is the food of the blessed mind, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 709.---The blessed’s repose and food will be truth, idem, XXXIX, 1633.---Christ gives himself to us as our reward in heaven, anonymous author, CLXXXIV, 789.---How great the blessed’s happiness is in possessing God, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 559.---For one who enjoys God, whatever he wills will be; and what he does not will shall not be, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 238, 785, 816, 1172.---Those who enjoy God will be called sons of God and gods, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 816, 818.

## They see and know one another

In heaven the blessed see one another, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1434.---All will see one another divinely when they are filled with God, ibid., 1146.---They will see one another’s thoughts, ibid., 1145; XL, 387.---In eternal life nothing in one’s neighbor will be hidden from one’s neighbor, idem, XXXIII, 318.---In their perception, the deepest feelings of their souls are discerned, idem, XLIII, 84.---In heaven each person will be visible to another as he is now to himself, Garnerus, abbot, CXCIII, 305.---The good know the good, Haymo, CXVIII, 882; Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 1161.---The Evangelist testifies to this, St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 486.---This knowledge gives them joy, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 373.---They also know good persons whom they have never seen, ibid., 376.

## Equal joy amid unequal brightness

Eternal life is equal for all, but honor is not equal, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 533; XXXIX, 1507.---Heaven is shared by the saints, but their brightness differs, idem, XXXVIII, 736.---Blessedness is one, but recompense differs, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 381.---The blessedness which they receive there is one, but the recompense they obtain through diverse works differs, St. Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1001.---The degrees of glory are not identical for all, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 217; St. Augustine, XXXV, 1819; St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 703.---The kingdom of heaven has diverse rewards, St. Augustine, XL, 410; St. Ambrose, XIV, 926; XV, 1486.---The merits of the saints differ, Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 860; Alan of Lille, CCX, 537, 538.---The saints enjoy unequal glory because of the diversity of merits, St. Augustine, XXXV, 1812; Alcuin, C, 146, 147; CI, 53, 60.---On the difference of dwellings in heaven, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 957; Master Bandinus, ibid., 1112.---The glory and dwellings of the blessed differ, St. Hilary, IX, 415–417, 422 ff.---Dwellings differ according to the diversity of merits, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 1162.---The inequality of merits makes the vision differ, St. Salvian, LIII, 49, [Col. 0222] 50.---In blessedness there will be certain degrees of rewards without envy, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 533; XLI, 802.---The blessed rejoice no less in another’s good than in their own, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 431.---They rejoice more in God’s happiness than in their own and others’, St. Anselm, CXLVIII [probably CLVIII], 1172.---Whether and how inequality of love exists among the blessed, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 370 ff.---Who the greater and lesser among the blessed are, St. Augustine, XLIV, 225.---As, in musical instruments, varied distinctions of sounds are united through the octave, so in the heavenly kingdom the saints, though diverse in merits, through the harmony of charity resound as one and think as one, Othlo, CXLVI, 123.---If there will be a distinction of dwellings there, the highest equality of one perfection will nevertheless exist among those who possess the one happiness of the heavenly kingdom, Haymo, CXVIII, 877.---There will be equal joy amid unequal brightness, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 959; St. Prosper, LI, 486.---The life of blessedness is one, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 977, 1155, 1156; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 1080.---Eternal life is equal for all, St. Ambrose, XVII, 725.---The blessed life is the common possession of all, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1401.---The saints in heaven will be harmonious, not discordant, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1964.---As the number of possessors increases, the kingdom of God is not diminished, because it is not divided, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 549.---What is held harmoniously by many is entire for each, ibid., 549.---The kingdom of heaven is possessed jointly by all and wholly by each individual, ibid.---All the blessed possess God’s house, and each possesses the whole, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1061.---Yet all the saints receive the honor of heavenly glory, St. Hilary, LX, 415–417.

All the blessed will have one will, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 238, 816, 1172; Eadmer, monk, CLIX, 639.---The Lord’s kingdom consists in the peace and unanimity of the saints, St. Hilary, IX, 876, 877.---The saints will obtain supreme peace within themselves, among themselves, and with God, St. Augustine, XLI, 797.---To reign in heaven is, through love, to have one will with God, angels, and holy human beings, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 1171, 1172.---Peace and unity present to us the form of the heavenly city, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 450.---In true and supreme happiness, as delightful love cannot be lacking, so mutual love cannot be lacking, Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 917.

## What faculties the blessed possess
The endowments of souls in the blessed: Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 818; Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 1172.---The endowments of the souls of the blessed explained: Guigo the Carthusian, CLXXXIV, 358–363.---The inward and outward glory of the saints: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 875.---The saints stand firm in heaven in spirit: Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXX, 909, 910.---How holy souls will be without spot or wrinkle: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 468–482.---The saints will shine in heaven like gold and be transparent like glass: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 83.---The righteous and holy are so by participation in divine wisdom, not by comparison with it: ibid., 86.---Which virtues cease in heaven: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV.---Human beings in heaven will be such as good angels now are: St. Anselm, CLVIII, 395, 396.---Martyrs in heaven will show us their scar as a crown: St. Ambrose, XV, 1845, 1846.---The saints are praised securely in heaven: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 476.---On the activity and joy of the blessed: Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 1169.---What the free choice of the blessed will be like: St. Augustine, XLI, 802.---In the blessed there will be an inalienable will for godliness and justice, as there is for happiness: ibid.---Free choice will be set free from every evil: St. Anselm, CLVIII, 804, 805.---As their essence will in some fashion be unchangeable in the blessed: ibid.---The blessed will be all-powerful with respect to their own will, as God is with respect to his: ibid., 238, 816.---The bodies of the blessed are signified as bright with gold and transparent with glass: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 84.---Certainly, wherever the spirit has power, the body will immediately be: St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 520.---Bodily eyes will have their own function: St. Augustine, XLI, 798.---The knowledge of the blessed: St. Augustine, XL (Appendix), 996; St. Patrick, LIII, 832, 837.---What we shall know when established in glory: Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXX, 1303.---The saints now established in the light of truth: St. Augustine, XLIII, 188.---The knowledge and wisdom of the blessed will be full and perfect: id., XLI, 724.---The blessed are ignorant of nothing where they know the One who knows all things: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 376.---They will know that which is outside themselves: St. Augustine, XLI, 784.---They will see all things from which they are bodily absent: ibid., 797.---They will not need bodily eyes to see all things: ibid., 798.---With the eyes of their bodies now made spiritual they will see bodily things: ibid., 799.---The soul, greater in heaven, will see more than it hoped and believed: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 923.---The saints in heaven see what is done on earth: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 999.---Not the souls of the wicked, but only those of the saints, know what may be done by the living: St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 492.---The souls of the righteous rejoice in their own glory, [Col. 0223] but are concerned over our absence: Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 1162.---In heaven they await us: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 93.---The saints do not know the salvation or damnation of the living: Alan of Lille, 374.---They do not know the day of judgment: ibid.---Whether the good can behold the evil established in torment, or the evil the good established in rest: St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 520 ff.---The good will see the consciences of the evil, but not conversely: Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 1179.---The saints know what takes place in punishments: St. Augustine, XLI, 784; St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 520.---The sight of the punishment of the reprobate does not cloud the blessedness of the righteous: Peter Lombard, CXCII, 962.---They rejoice when they see the punishments of the evil: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 213.---The glory of the saints increases while the wicked are condemned to their deserved punishment: St. Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1014.---Why the saints in heaven do not pity the reprobate in hell: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 758, 855; LXXVI, 691.---Antitheses of the blessed and the damned: Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 1173.---On the state of the wretched and the blessed after judgment: Peter Lombard, CXCII, 1008.---It must be believed without hesitation that the blessed will have greater glory after judgment than before it: ibid., 959.

On the memory of the blessed, whether it then retains preceding evils: Peter Lombard, CXCII, 944.---The memory of sins does not affect blessedness: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 678.---The joy of the blessed over the labors endured on the way: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 981.---How the blessed will forget their evils: St. Augustine, XLI, 803.---There we shall have both forgetfulness and remembrance alike: St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 522.---Whether the blessed grieve: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1446.---They grieve that they did not labor more for the attainment of blessedness: Venerable Guibert, abbot, CLVI, 673, 674.---They rejoice in the assumption of a blessed soul: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 23, 24.---What the activity of the blessed will be: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1147.---What exercise the saints have in heavenly glory: Venerable Guibert, CLXVI, 675.---The blessed are not changed into God’s substance: St. Augustine, XLIV, 265.---That in glory the saints may perform pious offices, rendered to them here: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 529.---The souls of saints appear when and to whom they wish, whether to the waking or sleeping: Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 1162.---They appear in a human body formed from air: ibid.---What the saints will do after the resurrection: Eugippius, LXII, 813.

## In heaven there is no evil

Every evil is banished from heaven; every good abounds there: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 405.---The exclusion of all evils: Haymo, CXVIII, 881.---There is no sin in heaven: St. Jerome, XXII, 684.---Eternal joy is diminished by no mass of vices: ibid., 780.---The saints will have a nature by which, even if they wish to sin, they cannot: Eugippius, LXII, 637 ff.---The Pelagians vainly wish to introduce concupiscence into paradise: St. Augustine, XLIV, 803.---In the heavenly city there will be no calamity to endure, no desire to restrain, but only love of God and neighbor to retain: id., XXXIII, 525.---There will be neither anything to fight against nor anything to titillate; all will yield to peace: id., XXXVII, 1860.---Nothing will remain either in mind or body that rebels against the soul: ibid., 1862.---Neither burdensome activity nor idle rest: id., XL, 343.---Neither surfeit nor hunger: id., XXXV, 1405.---No sin, nor any conflict with the desire for sin: id., XLIV, 600.---No concupiscence: ibid., 153.---The blessed will not perform works of iniquity: id., XXXVII, 1062, 1099, 1108, 1941.---No place for sadness or guilt: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 630.---No envy: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1812; St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 525; St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 639.---The joy of the blessed is multiplied by the blessedness and joy of others: St. Anselm, CLVIII, 241, 818, 819.---The blessed will need nothing for the substance of body and soul: St. Hilary, IX, 876.---The elect have no need of another’s intercession or prayers: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 357.---In the homeland there will be no want or labor, but perfect rest and satisfaction: St. Fulgentius, LXV, 344.---In this life sadness and consolation are mingled; not so in the future life: ibid., 601.---God’s kingdom is fittingly compared to summer, because then the clouds of our sorrow pass away and the days of life shine with the brightness of the eternal sun: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1080.---Death, mourning, pain, and crying will not remain in the future eternity: Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 861.---How ineffable will be that happiness where there is no evil and where no good is lacking: Alcuin, CI, 54; Smaragdus, abbot, CII, 679.---The righteous will possess the land of the living, which is without end, pain, or groaning: St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 139.---That life in which all harmful things are removed and every good is supplied: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 494.

## In heaven there is every good

[Col. 0224]

The abundance of goods in heaven: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 595; CLXXXIV, 492; St. Ambrose, XIV, 562, 563; St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 707, 711; Haymo, CXVIII, 881; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1594; St. Anselm, CLVIII, 703, 795, 797, 798, 881, 882, 897.---There, in perfect peace and possession of every good, the blessed will rejoice without end with God their Creator: St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 761.---Everlasting life, the promise of every good: St. Jerome, XXIV, 531.---They are to be endowed with such great blessedness that none greater can exist: Alcuin, C, 954; Radulphus Ardens, CLV, 1310.---In heaven are delight, abundance, life, and truth: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 264.---Blessedness is light, peace, and a fountain: id., CLXXXIII, 104.---Noonday knowing no evening: ibid., 952.---In it is the threefold fruition of God: ibid., 472.---The knowledge of God, eternal life, perfect blessedness, consummate delight: id., CLXXXIV, 486.---Rest from labor, gladness from newness, security from eternity: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 838.---The souls of saints and righteous persons rest in heaven: St. Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 996.---There will be goods of body and soul: St. Anselm, CLVIII, 1172.---Goods with respect to the soul: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 473, 474, 826 ff.---Goods with respect to the body: ibid., 473, 474.---The goods of your blessedness: ibid., 526, 527, 529.---Threefold joy: ibid., 466, 467.---Three things will be granted to the elect in the future: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 862.---Three things await the elect in the future: id., CLXXVI, 617; CLXXVII, 860.---Inward satisfaction, eternal gladness, delightful pleasure: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1142–1144.---In the storehouse of the heavenly homeland are four oils of sweetness: the glorification of bodies, fellowship with angels, sitting at the Father’s right hand, and the vision of God: Thomas the Cistercian, CCVI, 57.---The seven goods of the heavenly banquet: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 634.---The two eternal felicities vainly introduced by the Pelagians: St. Augustine, XLV, 1188.

What food there will be in the kingdom of heaven: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 969.---At the heavenly table they feast with the choirs of angels: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 653.---The saints are mingled with the choirs of angels: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 906.---They always hear the heavenly symphony: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 219.---The blessedness of angels increases through ours: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1110, 1111.---Whether there is satisfaction in the blessed: id., CLXXXIV, 588, 589.---There is no surfeit in heaven: ibid., 735.---The blessed will have an insatiable satisfaction: St. Augustine, 1643.---The blessed who thirst are satisfied, and, though satisfied, thirst: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 91.

## Heavenly blessedness is eternal

The times of the Lord’s kingdom: blessedness: St. Hilary, IX, 693, 694.---The eternity of blessedness: St. Jerome, XXII, 820; XXVI, 190; St. Augustine, XXXIV, 1288; XXXVIII, 663, 1778; XLI, 342, 343, 347; St. Prosper, LI, 391; St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 396, 430, 436; St. Leo, LIV, 173, 174, 176, 201, 221, 262, 302, 318, 440, 441, 442, 448, 458, 1056; Eugippius, LXII, 882 ff.; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 381, 918; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 324; Haymo, CXVIII, 877; St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 86, 190, 287; St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 800; St. Anselm, CLVIII, 217, 733, 734; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 300; Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 961, 972; Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 470, 471, 484, 485.---Whatever comes to pass in the saints will be eternal and attended by the consciousness of blessedness: St. Hilary, IX, 255.---In heaven are eternity and truth: St. Augustine, XXXIV, 1070.---The day of eternal life is one day without sunset: id., XXXVI, 202.---All the blessed will be immortal: id., XLI, 751.---The immortality of the blessed cannot be taken away by sin: ibid., 403.---The longest human life is nothing compared with God’s eternity: id., XXXVIII, 1176.---Compared with eternity, the present life is like a point in time: Peter Cantor, CCV, 352.---In the other life death is neither anxiously avoided by nature, shamefully feared by cowardice, nor bravely endured by wisdom: St. Augustine, XXXIII, 464.---There all live; none dies: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 838.---The souls of the saints in heaven enjoy eternal joys: St. Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 996.---Saints and righteous persons will receive us into eternal dwellings: Eugippius, abbot, LXII, 840.---The punishments of hell and heavenly blessedness alike will endure without end: Othlo, monk, CXLVI, 72.

## CHAPTER V.—How highly heavenly blessedness ought to be valued and how greatly desired

The reward of present labor is to be considered: St. Jerome, XXII, 424.---Eternal life must always be set before the mind: St. Augustine, XXXV.---How greatly it should be loved: id., XXXVIII, 519, 706, 1385, 1387; XXXIX, 1513, 1515.---Eternal joys are to be meditated upon: id., XL, 822.---Eternal blessedness should be set before one’s eyes: St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 1119, 1121.---Contemplation of glory is commended: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, [Col. 0225] 312.---The soul dwells in heaven by thought and longing: ibid., 1075, 1076.---Meditation on heavenly glory: id., CLXXXIV, 124.---Consideration of the heavenly homeland: St. Anselm, CLVIII, 711, 742.

Eternal life is to be desired: St. Benedict, monk and father, LXVI, 324; Smaragdus, abbot, CII, 620; Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 1130, 1133, 1138; St. Anselm, CLVIII, 391, 392, 595 ff.; Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 995, 996; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 477, 479, 953; CLXXXIV, 236, 237, 505.---We should long for the heavenly homeland, where the saints await us: St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2160.---Christians should direct their attention to the future life: id., XXXVIII, 1196; XXXIX, 1650.---All apprehend the blessed life: St. Benedict, LXVI, 228.---All wish to attain it: Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXX, 856.---Aspiration toward the heavenly homeland: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 163, 591 ff.---Toward the blessed vision: id., CLXXXIV, 235.---The threefold desire of the elect: to dwell unanimously in the Lord, to gain victory over the world, and to enjoy God in his presence: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 860; St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1142.---The three origins of monastic tears: desire for the heavenly homeland: Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 886.---The delay of blessedness increases both its desire and its merit: ibid., 701.---When the light of the heavenly homeland is contemplated, the mind is caught up into ecstasy: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 417.---The remembrance of the future life melts the soul: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 217.---The soul thirsts to see God; the flesh thirsts to rise again: St. Gregory the Great, LXXXI, 1030.---The desire for eternal life may be called the virginal son of the converted soul: Venerable Godfrey, LXXIV, 767.---Desire for the heavenly homeland belongs especially to the new law: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1049.---Eternal life is the satisfaction of desires: id., CLXXXIV, 588.---Who ought to thirst for heavenly goods: Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 862.

Eternity must be sought: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1658.---Every person seeks eternity, truth, and blessedness: id., XLII, 887.---What we seek is not here: ibid.---The glory of the heavenly reward must be sought: St. Leo, LV, 139.---Eternal life must be more diligently investigated: Eugippius, LXII, 562.---Seek the kingdom of God and his righteousness: Venerable Bede, XCIV, 171.

Let us raise our eyes to heaven; let us judge that we must strive toward it, and deem that seat preferable to all earthly things: St. Ambrose, XVI, 1135.---Let there be a step toward higher things: ibid., 1053.---If life is loved, let it be acquired where it enjoys no death: St. Augustine, XXXIII, 486.---Let us not cease to seek eternal life until we reach it: id., XXXVI, 206.---To that one life in which one lives with God and from God, all other things that are usefully and properly desired must without doubt be referred: id., XXXIII, 499.---Our life is now hope; afterwards it will be eternity: id., XXXVII, 1372.---The life of mortal life is the hope of immortal life: ibid., 1389.---The glorification of saints is the most perfect of gifts: St. Fulgentius, LXV, 164.---If love does not draw one toward the kingdom, fear remains: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1117.---The kingdom of heaven is worth as much as you possess: Radulphus, CLV, 1307; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1090.---How many causes for mourning belong to the soul that sighs for its heavenly homeland: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 75, 76.---An explanation of the beatitudes to which every Christian ought to aspire: St. Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 97.---Three books on love of the heavenly homeland: Haymo, bishop of Halberstadt, CXVIII, 875–958.---The Apostle teaches that we should fly up to heaven on spiritual wings: St. Ambrose, XVI, 286; St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 524.---By the labors of this life the saints are urged to desire their eternal homeland: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 756.---An exhortation to desire the heavenly and eternal blessedness: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 264 ff.---The hope of blessedness makes people better: Tertullian, I, 529.---It makes them worthy of heaven: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 787, 788.---Holy hope is the hope of attaining the kingdom of God and his righteousness: St. Anselm, CLXIII, 592.---How useful the remembrance of the heavenly homeland is to sinners: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 414.---How sweetly the remembrance of heavenly joy assists those who pray: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 591.---Vicious affections are to be driven out by its remembrance: ibid., 626.---Tears shed from desire for the heavenly homeland: St. Beatus; St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 890; LXXVI, 291.---Carnal imagining of the heavenly kingdom: St. Augustine, XL, 1007.---Eternal goods are not to be conceived carnally: id., XXXVI, 488.---Those awaiting the rewards of eternity draw strength from adversities: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 36.---Out of love for the heavenly homeland, we love the penalties of exile: id., LXXV, 775.---When love of the heavenly homeland calls, the sufferings of this way impel: id., LXXVI, 359, 360.---He desires eternal rest who bears the burden of the day in this life: id., LXXV, 809.---The present life is not to be loved for its own sake, but endured for the sake of the future: id., LXXVI, 562.

[Col. 0226] Through hope of attaining blessedness, the devout bravely endure the evils of this life: St. Augustine, XXXIII, 668.---Many saints lamented the length of this life out of longing for heaven: St. Hilary, IX, 650.---Everything must be cast aside in order to attain eternal life: St. Augustine, XXXIII, 499.---In comparison with eternal life, the present life is to be reckoned not life but death: ibid., 223; XXXVII, 1555; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1274.---The present life is to be despised in hope of the future: St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1517; Godfrey, abbot, CLVII, 184.---The rich, looking toward heaven, trample earthly things underfoot: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 348 ff.---For the hope of eternal things, the loss of temporal things must be reckoned most slight: St. Leo, LIV, 310.---The heart, despising earthly things, sighs only for heavenly things: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 417, 479.---Whoever loves blessedness thinks all earthly things of little worth: Venerable Guibert, abbot, CLVI, 219.---Heavenly things must be sought after earthly things have been despised: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 91.---Earthly prosperity ought not to hinder heavenly joys: St. Leo, LV, 68.---One who considers eternal recompenses despises temporal evils: Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXX, 460.---The more the soul is affected by heavenly desires, the more it dies to earthly things: ibid., 1082, 1083 ff.---Temporal things, compared with eternal things, are narrow and contemptible: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 673, 795, 983.---One desiring eternal things grows weary of the love of temporal things: ibid., 673, 829, 987, 1115, 1116; LXXVI, 559, 905.---To the wise, earthly things become tasteless in comparison with heavenly things: ibid., 1114; St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 255; CLXXXIV, 929, 1020; Alan of Lille, CCX, 591, 592.---Monks ought to forget earthly things and long for heavenly ones: Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 876.---After the great dangers of the sea, let us hasten to enter the safest harbor of heaven: St. Jerome, XXII, 793.

For eternal glory we must struggle: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 524 ff.---Let us labor to possess eternal glory: ibid., 540.---With all desire and all strength let us sigh and strive toward the heavenly homeland: Radulphus, CLV, 1521.---Having been invited there, let us hasten to enter: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1129.---On entering the heavenly rest, toward which we must hasten: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 732.---Those tending toward heaven do not turn aside from God’s way: Rupert, CLXVII, 1082.---The hope of future blessedness is the courage of martyrs: St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1678; XXXVIII, 1425.---Martyrs perish with cheerful mind, to be restored to something better: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 703.---The saints have hope of eternal joy and gladness: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 348.---Devout persons aspire to the heavenly homeland: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1220.---Though saints are bodily on earth, in spirit they nevertheless fly beyond heaven itself: St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 569, 570.---It belongs to one who does not wish to go to Christ to fear death: St. Cyprian, IV, 584.---It is inconsistent for us to ask to live long in this world while asking for God’s kingdom to come swiftly: ibid., 533.---The sure promise of future goods ought to inflame us to meet death bravely: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 326.---The present life must be despised so that we may attain the future one: St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 670.---Eternal happiness is far superior to the present life: Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXX, 434.---Wearied by this life, the saints always long for eternal rest: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 986.---On the groans of the soul sighing for its heavenly homeland: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1062.---Every day we die, every day we are changed, and yet we believe ourselves eternal: St. Jerome, XXII, 601.---What punishments the prophet invokes upon forgetfulness of heaven: St. Hilary, IX, 780, 781.---How greatly people neglect eternal life in favor of temporal life: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1747.---He who does not long for the promised kingdom is slothful: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 404.---Those who neglect the rewards of the heavenly homeland fall here into their own pleasures: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 964.---Those who feign righteousness have no hope of eternal recompense: St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 636.---The present life, placed between heaven and hell, has citizens of both enrolled in it: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1284.---How the hope of eternal life is nourished: St. Hilary, IX, 570.---It is nourished by the sense and understanding of Holy Scripture: Venerable Godfrey, 767.---By the praises of martyrs, peoples are inflamed toward the heavenly reward: St. Zeno, XI, 451.---Gratuitous love of God does not remove hope of reward: St. Augustine, XXXIII, 1482.---Our treasure laid up in heaven is preserved: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 205.---The temporal is loved more before it is possessed; the eternal is loved more ardently once attained than when desired: Eugippius, LXII, 943.

The eternal is the most excellent of all things: ibid., 1083, 1084.---He who asks with his mouth but does not desire eternal life in his heart is silent while crying aloud: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 237, 238.---A foretaste of heavenly rewards: ibid., 903, 904.---Love of temporal and eternal things: Hugh, CLXXVI, 955 ff.---Everyone should rejoice exceedingly to be even the least in God’s kingdom: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1156.---Through love of [Col. 0227] heavenly glory, sins that have been committed are felt more grievously: LXXVI, 382.---Death is desired by one touched by longing for heavenly life: id., LXXV, 775.---What has one who possesses heaven to do with earth? St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 269.

## CHAPTER VI.—To whom it is to be given and to whom denied

Those nations that seize the kingdom of heaven from the Jews: St. Hilary, IX, 980, 981.---Who sees God: St. Ambrose, XIV, 977.---Who is the man who clears paths for himself and sets up steps by which he may ascend to the royal palace of heaven: id., XVI, 1132, 1133.---Who is happy and worthy of every blessedness: St. Jerome, XXII, 965.---Within whom the kingdom of God is: id., XXIV, 300.---Who are possessors of God’s kingdom: St. Augustine, XXXII, 612.---Who is great and who least in the kingdom of heaven: id., XXXVIII, 1168.---Who will be eternally happy: St. Fulgentius, LXV, 350.---Who will enter the heavenly city: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 777, 859.---Who is worthy of this ascent: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 628.---To whom, and when, heaven is opened: Robert Pullus, CLXXXVI, 850.---God is the lawful possessor of paradise; man is its stranger: Rupert, CLXVII, 268.---The heavens stand open to martyrs: St. Cyprian, IV, 352.---Martyrs hasten to divine dwellings: ibid., 419.---Leaving the world, they seek heaven: ibid., 292.---They stand among angels: ibid.---The apostles and martyrs are in paradise: ibid., 601.---Martyrs immediately see God: ibid., 674.---Martyrs succeed dead kings in the honor of the everlasting kingdom of heavenly grace: St. Ambrose, XV, 1807, 1808.---The crown of martyrs is woven of roses and violets, that of confessors of lilies: St. Jerome, XXII, 905.---Martyrs are honored with heavenly rewards even before judgment: St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2155.---The more bravely martyrs fight, the fuller their crown of martyrdom: id., XLI, 299, 678.---The greatest rewards of martyrs: id., XXXVIII, 1281.---The reward of martyrs is prepared for those who follow Christ and keep the faith: ibid., 1379, 1394.---The glory of martyrs is hidden from the foolish: ibid., 1400.---The glory of martyrs is sought by the shedding of blood: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 512 ff.---One who does not shrink from the endurance of martyrs will attain their glory: Rabanus Maurus, CX, 68.---Those who pour out their life in defense of Christians will obtain the kingdoms of heaven: St. Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 719.

Virgins in heaven: St. Cyprian, IV, 602.---Virgins will cleave more intimately to God in heaven: St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 472.---On the three benefits of the future life which virgins will obtain: anonymous author, CLXXXIV, 699.

Those who have not consented to sacrilegious edicts will reign with Christ: St. Cyprian, IV, 674.---Through the confession of a single voice, the kingdoms stand open: ibid., 800.---God’s paradise flourishes with witnesses: ibid., 793.

Heavenly blessedness awaits the sexually continent: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1112.

God will be seen only by peacemakers: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 162.---The vision of God is specifically promised only to the pure in heart: ibid., 368.---When the eyes of the heart are cleansed, the joy of the heavenly homeland is opened: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 292.---The wage of sin is death; that of righteousness, eternal life: St. Augustine, XXXIII, 881.---The righteous are called to refreshment: St. Cyprian, IV, 592.---The righteous are rightly called inhabitants of heaven: St. Ambrose, XVII, 853.---When this life is over, the righteous seek the heavens and God: St. Augustine, XXXV, 2371; XL, 1165.---Christ will give the righteous life, kingdom, and glory; in death the righteous mock death and pass over to life: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 512 ff.---The righteous themselves will be sacrifices in the kingdom of heaven: St. Augustine, XLI, 706.---Leaving behind the lowly things of the world, the righteous have raised to higher things the summit of their faith in heavenly life: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 618.---One who has endeavored to live rightly here will be able to enter the kingdom of heaven: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1117.---Only the good person will enter into the joy of his Lord: Venerable Bede, XCVI, 100; St. Anselm, CLVIII, 607, 608, 733, 734; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 759; St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1141.---This is the true and sole reward of those who sorrow according to God: to rejoice in his perpetual vision: ibid., 158.---The reward of the righteous is the vision of Christ: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 719.---The souls of saints and righteous persons are in heaven with Christ: Ratherius, CXXXIV, 710.---The blessed possess the land of the living: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1420.---The righteous will enter Christ’s house, that is, the Church or the heavenly Jerusalem: St. Bruno, bishop of Würzburg, CXLII, 59.---A reward is rendered to saints and righteous persons for unjust curses inflicted upon them: St. Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 829.---Catholics who live well will have eternal life: ibid., 76; St. Augustine, XL, 677.---In the other life are the righteous and penitents: Venerable Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 1114, 1143.---Paradise is open only to the unstained, and how: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 616.---Heaven is closed to no one [Col. 0228] except the person whom the profession of his own utterance has excluded: St. Ambrose, XIV, 334; XV, 1752.---No age is too weak for God’s kingdom: id., XIV, 348; XV, 1756.---Nor is any sex excluded: id., XV, 927, 928; Tertullian, I, 307.---The marriage-feast of the Lamb is adorned by the bruises of confessors, the blood of martyrs, the lilies of virgins, and also the crowns of priests: St. Ambrose, XVI, 173, 1354.---To whom God’s kingdom is promised: St. Augustine, XXXII, 619, 674.---The crown is reserved for the victor: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 552 ff.---It is promised to faithful combatants: ibid., 259.---Heavenly crowns are given to those who serve as soldiers on earth: ibid., 585.---Blessedness is promised not to the idle but to those who labor: St. Leo, LIV, 252.---The kingdoms of heaven seek inhabitants unencumbered and supported by the lightness of wings: St. Jerome, XXII, 953.---It is certain that all the good will enter the kingdom of heaven by grace’s gift, and none of the evil through the merit of wickedness: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 87.---Human beings will receive eternal life together: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1751.---All who die in the Lord are blessed, because after the merit of virtue they attain the reward of blessedness: Werner, abbot, CLVII, 1155.---The kingdom of heaven is given without distinction to those whom faith commends and taken from the wicked: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 562.---The kingdom of heaven is the reward of those who receive and preach the Gospel: ibid., 1434.---It awaits baptized penitents, martyrs, and confessors: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 983, 1118.---Some seize the kingdom of heaven by force, others purchase it, others steal it, and others are compelled to enter it: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 864; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 726.---Blessed here and in heaven is one loved by God and human beings: St. Bernard, CLXXXV, 106, 107.---Capable of eternal life: the true penitent, the good obedient person, the lovable companion, the faithful servant: id., CLXXXIV, 493.---The penitent flies up to heaven: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 636.---Only those will reign eternally in the land of the living who here have subjected to themselves every earthly thing and every vanity: Rodulphus, CLV, 1517.---To those seeking eternal life God will give glory, that is, brightness of body and illumination of soul: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLIII, 785.---To those who fear him the Lord gives the health of incorruption, the life of immortality, and the blessing of perpetual inheritance: Rabanus, CIX, 1009.---The heavenly court stands equally open to all: St. Jerome, XXII, 581; St. Anselm, CLVIII, 918, 919.---No condition is excluded from it: id., XXVI, 584.---All are invited to the kingdom of God: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 540.---We all move toward eternal life: id., XXXV, 1574.---Not all who wish attain blessedness: id., XXXIII, 393;
