St. Anselm, CLVIII, 535–538.---The weak are called to the kingdom of heaven together with the strong: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 777, 859.---The heavenly kingdom is opened equally to Jews and Gentiles, to righteous and unrighteous persons converted to the faith: ibid., 1018.---The kingdom of God is denied to no one as a gift of knowledge: Rupert, CLXIX, 271, 272.---Why so few attain blessedness: St. Augustine, XXXII, 1237.---On those who immediately receive their reward and are crowned: St. Cyprian, III, 786.---Not all are chosen for dwelling with God: St. Hilary, IX, 415, 417.---Who desires the kingdom of heaven wrongly and who rightly: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 489.---No one can be fit for the future life who has not exercised himself for it: id., XXXVII, 1937.---No one is secure concerning eternal life in this life: id., XLV, 1031.---One who will reign should leave behind what is his own: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 263.---Let him cast away worthless things: ibid., 269.---Being sure of the kingdom, let him despise worldly things: ibid.---Those who will reign should send their goods ahead through the hands of the poor: ibid.---God magnifies the saints: St. Leo, LV, 91.---Those considered contemptible in this life will appear in the other clothed in glory and majesty: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 328, 329.---The souls of the devout, stripped of their bodies, go immediately to paradise, to God: Gennadius of Marseilles, LVIII, 1049, 1050.

No one has true righteousness unless justified, nor true glory unless glorified: St. Fulgentius, LXV, 164.---We shall receive the blessed life if we reckon ourselves dead to this life: ibid., 349.---The person who does God’s will will enter the kingdom of heaven: Victor of Capua, LXVIII, 273.---Whoever humbles himself will be greater in the kingdom of heaven: ibid., 301.---Some lay claim to the heavenly homeland, though they do not love it: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 418.---Whether the kingdom of heaven can be given to murmurers: ibid., 1155.---Who possess blessedness in hope in this life: St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 554.---One who diligently strives, while living here, to ascend by good character and good works will be placed in heaven: St. Anselm, CLIX, 171.---Which souls will someday be blessed and which someday wretched cannot be comprehended by a human being: id., CLVIII, 216, 217.---No soul is unjustly deprived of the highest good: ibid., 218.---All people, even the unjust, desire blessedness: ibid., 344, 345.---No one can be blessed who does not desire blessedness: ibid.---As many human beings will be assumed to blessedness [Col. 0229] as angels remained in it: ibid., 389.---No one can attain blessedness with sin: ibid., 392, 394, 398, 524.---One who has not paid God what he owes cannot be blessed: ibid., 394–398.---It is necessary that some human beings attain blessedness: ibid., 398.

What those who desire to see the Lord’s glory ought to be like: St. Anselm, CLIX, 601, 605.---No one will enter the heavenly homeland without good works: St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 526.---Not all to whom God has spoken are blessed and elect: Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 1336.---Why heaven is open to the baptized: Robert Pullus, CLXXXIV, 848.---What it means for heaven to be open to the baptized: ibid., 849.---On the twofold order of those to be saved and damned: ibid., 1005.---Lazarus exchanges the misery of a laborious life for the honor of blessed rest: St. Hilary, IX, 624, 635.---Christ led with him to the heavenly homeland those whom he freed from hell: St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2195; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1484.---Mary’s body was assumed into heaven: Alan of Lille, CCX, 64.---Paradise promised to the thief: St. Augustine, XXXIX, 712.---How the thief was in paradise with Christ himself on the day of Christ’s death: id., XXXIV, 833.---Heaven honored by the thief’s entrance: id., XXXIX, 2049.---Caecilia led herself and her husband to heavenly things: St. Leo, LV, 139.---The heavenly dwelling receives St. Clement: ibid., 141.---Paradise is opened daily to penitents: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1065.---God promises heavenly glory to persons almost despairing: ibid., 414.

The kingdom of heaven: to whom it will be denied, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1156.---Not heretics alone, but also those who live wickedly, do not belong to the kingdom of God, St. Augustine, XLIII, 170.---Whoever has lost the wedding garment cannot enter the kingdom of heaven, St. Zeno, XI, 1062; Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, CXXV, 362.---Those rebaptized cannot possess the kingdom of God, because they have lost the wedding garment, St. Zeno, XI, 1043.---Those who merely say, “Lord, Lord,” will not enter the kingdom of heaven, Victor of Capua, LXVIII, 273; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 387.---Wicked persons, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 534.---The lustful and the proud, Smaragdus, abbot, CII, 546.---The depraved and criminal, Beleth, CCII, 786.---Catechumens, even if they die in good works, Alcuin, C, 519.---Unless one has been born anew, he cannot see the kingdom of God, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 844.---The righteousness of a Christian must exceed that of the Scribes and Pharisees if he is to enter the kingdom of heaven, Rabanus Maurus, CX, 359; Beleth, CCII, 403.

What things draw people away from the vision of the Word, St. Augustine, XXXV, 1540.---Nothing but sins separates a person from eternal life, idem, XLIV, 129, 141.---Even a single crime excludes one from the kingdom of God, idem, XLIII, 171.---Had the first human being not sinned, heaven would have stood open to him and to his descendants, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 176, 177.---Through our sins heaven has become a far-off country, Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 773.---By the gusts of evil habits people are driven back from their homeland, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 23.---Sin turned the path owed to heaven toward hell, Robert Pullus, CLXXXVI, 763.---Original and personal sin exclude from the kingdom of God, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 454, 455.---Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1619.---Spiritual wickednesses cannot inhabit the kingdom of heaven, where eternal wisdom dwells, Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 470.---Pleasure alone strips us of paradise, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1195.---Humanity was expelled from paradise by the devil’s counsels, St. Jerome, XXIII, 214.---The devil, in order to remove the kingdom of God far from us, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 401.---Some reject second marriages from the kingdom of God, St. Jerome, XXVI, 259.---We departed from it through unlawful delights; we return to it through repentance, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1113.

## CHAPTER VII.—When heavenly blessedness is given

A person will be recalled to paradise in the condition in which he was driven from it, Tertullian, II, 833.---The return to paradise from which Adam departed: a figure, St. Hilary, IX, 961.---Christ, inviter not merely to a long life but to eternal life, Tertullian, II, 424.---Immortality and eternity are promised to those departing from this world, St. Cyprian, IV, 586.---Promises of eternal blessedness in the prophets, St. Augustine, XLI, 753.---Through Jeremiah the eternal reward was foretold, idem, XLIV, 224.---The kingdom of heaven was not promised in the Old Testament, St. Jerome, XXIII, 525; St. Augustine, XLII, 129, 130.---The name “kingdom of heaven” is not found in the ancient books, but in the new ones, ibid., 368.---It is first proclaimed in the Gospel, St. Jerome, XXIII, 525.---John the Baptist was the first expressly to proclaim the kingdom of heaven, Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 1351, 1352 and following.---The kingdom of God promised, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 641.---He who hangs upon the wood promises paradise, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 210, [Col. 0230] 211.---The Gospel promises eternal goods, Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 101.---The promise of eternal life is firm, Alan of Lille, CCX, 246.---The length of days promised here is eternal life, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 249, 250.---A special hope and promise of eternal life made by God to Othlo, Othlo, CXLVI, 343.---The eternal reward belongs to the New Testament, St. Augustine, XLIV, 225, 226.---Certainty of the reward promised by God, idem, XXXVIII, 237.---The kingdom of Christ is reserved for the times of the heavenly Jerusalem, St. Hilary, IX, 258, 259.---By it we are advanced into the kingdom of God the Father, ibid., 583.---The reward due to the saints is laid up for another life, Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1475.---Full and perfect peace is reserved for another life, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 102, 317.---The full peace of the heart is reserved for the future life, ibid., 317.---Eternity succeeds this brief life, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 908, 999.---After the narrowness of the present life comes eternal spaciousness, idem, LXXVI, 972.---After this life, blessedness and rest follow, St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 298.---“Tomorrow” signifies the future life; “today,” the present life, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII.---The present life is evening; the future, morning, Venerable Guibert, CLVI, 39, 40.---Our life is twofold: eternal and temporal, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 725; XL, 513.---The happiness of souls is one thing before, another after, the resurrection, idem, XXXVIII, 1282.---According to the merit of their past will, those departing from the body are received either by rest or by punishment, St. Hilary, IX, 322.---Between blessedness and misery there is no middle state in which a rational creature can exist, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 832, 1337; XLI, 266.---Every human soul is either always miserable or at some time blessed, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 218.---A rational nature either is blessed in the contemplation of God or will be so, ibid., 381, 382.---There are two lives of a human being in the body: one before death, the other after the resurrection, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 561.

The Church knows that two lives have been divinely proclaimed to her, one in time and the other in eternity, etc., Haymo, CXVIII, 885.---There are three states of holy souls: the first in a corruptible body, the second without a body, the third in a now-glorified body, etc., Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 841.---Three receptacles for souls after death, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1057, 1058.---There are three places—heaven, earth, and hell—and each has its own inhabitants, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1141.---With death blotted out, to come to immortality, St. Cyprian, IV, 585.---Death restores Christians to paradise and the kingdom, ibid., 601.---Through death we pass over to immortality, ibid., 597.---We come to the seat of the kingdom, ibid., 498.---God has prepared refreshment, ibid., 314.---The blessed life is prepared for us through God’s mercy, St. Hilary, IX, 403, 404.---God created humanity as a participant in his blessedness, ibid., 269, 270.---Faithful persons dying are kept in Abraham’s bosom until they attain the kingdom of heaven, ibid., 660, 661.---Life after this life in Abraham’s bosom, in which the name of God is blessed, ibid., 404.---Privileges after this life, St. Hilary, IX, 887 and following.---Unless life is undertaken for the gain of eternity, it will be the source of miseries, not life, ibid., 390.---May God grant eternal things for enjoyment and temporal things for use, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 413.---Faith does not bear the troubles of life resentfully, but regards them as rudiments of blessedness, ibid., 36.---David desired the future life, ibid., 576.---Hereby he is shown to hope for it: he aspires to a life which he does not yet possess, ibid., 510, 511.---Knowing that he cannot obtain true life here, David hopes for eternal life, ibid., 602, 603.---Another life, more blessed, St. Hilary, IX, 404.---True blessedness is not found here, St. Ambrose, XV, 1404.---The doctrine of Aristotle, the Peripatetics, and the Pythagoreans concerning blessedness was recognized earlier by Abraham, St. Ambrose, XIV, 490.---The life of the saints is not here on earth but in heaven, idem, XVI, 1372.---Many are blessed not because of what is present, but because of what will be present, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1504.---Here the righteous weep; in the future they will laugh, St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 209.---The saints have been with Christ since the Lord’s resurrection, St. Jerome, XXIII, 1086.---How great a reward is with God, if no recompense were hoped for in the present, St. Jerome, XXII, 532.---We have learned that future blessedness is truly everlasting not by human arguments but by the assistance of faith, St. Augustine, XLII, 1023.---The immortality of blessedness is made credible by the incarnation of the Son of God, ibid., 1023.---All souls of the saints must be believed to be in heaven, St. Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 996.---Eternal life must be believed by faith, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1196.---Faith in eternal life is established from the death of the Son of God, idem, XXXVII, 1942.---It is more incredible that he who is eternal died than that he who is immortal should live eternally, ibid., 1942.---Testimonies to eternal life from the ancient books, idem, XLII, 363.---The blessedness of all the righteous is not uncertain, St. Bruno, CXLII, 162.---Nothing is truer than that every rational soul, striving through love to desire supreme blessedness, will at some time receive it for enjoyment, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 216; Ratherius, on the words, “These shall go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life,” CXXXVI, 262.---The temporal prosperity of the wicked is for the elect a testimony to eternal happiness, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 609.---A devout physician is taught by a twofold vision that life remains after death, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 699, 700.---The punishments of the damned and those being purified, and likewise the joys of the blessed, shown to a certain man, Othlo, CXLVI, 380.---The vision of a certain monk concerning the state of souls after death, John the monk, CLXXX, 177.---The eternity of punishments and rewards established, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 737.---The martyrs would never have steadfastly spent this life unless they had believed another to be happier, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 703.---While they unhesitatingly undergo the endurance of death, the hope of immortality is plainly affirmed, ibid., 708.---If eternal life comes to an end, all Christian labor is useless, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 250.---Against those who doubt the other life, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1381; XXXIX, 1601.---The doubt of some concerning the blessedness of the saints before the day of judgment is reproved, Alcuin, C, 342.---Against those who assert that earthly bodies cannot become incorruptible and eternal, idem, 389, 390.---The struggles of martyrs are proofs of the future life, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 1238.

The time of the kingdom of heaven, St. Hilary, IX, 660.---When the kingdom of God is, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 391.---When the good and the evil will see God, Robert Pullus, CLXXXVI, 1003.---The time of the elect is not the present life but the future one, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 766.---No soul could enter heavenly paradise before Christ’s death, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 416, 417.---Paul in paradise before his martyrdom, St. Hilary, X, 172.---The righteous are often caught up into paradise, and how this occurs, St. Ambrose, XIV, 300.---How the city of the blessed kingdom, begun here, is to be completed hereafter, St. Hilary, IX, 876.---The heavenly Jerusalem is built before it is gathered together, ibid., 870, 871.---The beatific vision is impossible in this life, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 658, 940.---No one participates in it in this life, Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1111, 1114.---The blessedness for which humanity was made cannot be possessed in this life, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 375, 376.---No one is perfectly blessed before attaining future blessedness, Haymo, CXVIII, 879, 886; St. Benedict of Aniane, CIII, 590.---When freed from the mass of flesh, the soul will behold the divine essence more fully, St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLIII, 126.---Heaven was opened to Stephen as he was about to enter it, St. Hilary, IX, 365, 376.---Whether blessedness is obtained immediately after this life, or only at the end of the age, St. Augustine, XXXV, 1351.---When the burden of earthliness is laid aside, we shall rejoice in the lightness of heavenly glory, St. Bruno, CLIII, 212.---The vision of God after this life, ibid., 1654.---Death is the beginning of happiness for the righteous, St. Augustine, XXXII, 1471; St. Hilary, IX, 84; St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 585; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 298.---Saints taken from earth inhabit heaven, Alan, CCX, 537, 538.---The recompense for all works will be made after death, Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 568, 569, 574.---The glory of the saints is greater after death, Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1485, 1486.---The death-day of the saints is their birthday, Philip of Harvengt, CCIII.---Martyrs possess the heavenly kingdom without any delay, St. Cyprian, IV, 292.---They see God immediately, ibid., 676.---Blessedness is given to saints departing from this world, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 666, 868, 869, 1037, 1038; LXXVI, 761, 1156, 1157; LXXVII, 357; St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 478, 493; St. Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 997; Haymo, CXVIII, 883; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 467, 702, 791; Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 1157; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 487.---Not all who are saved are received into blessedness as soon as they die, St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 467.---Then the heart and soul of all the elect will be perfectly one, when God shall be all in all, Haymo, CXVIII, 886.---The blessedness of the saints is single before the resurrection, but twofold afterward, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 527, 328; LXXVI, 762.---In receiving the blessedness of souls and bodies, the Church of the elect will receive a double blessedness at the end of time, idem, LXXV, 527.---The saints will not be made complete without us, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 183.---Are the saints fully blessed before the general resurrection? ibid., 463–469.---The saints will not obtain complete blessedness until, after judgment, bodies are joined with souls, St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 686, 687; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 307, 308; St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 993; CCXXXVIII, 92, 463–468 and following, 659.---Now the elect enjoy only the blessedness of their souls; after the resurrection, that of souls and bodies together, Haymo, CXVIII, 883.---How Christ will come to judge in human form and appear gracious to the elect, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1134.

## On the resurrection

[Col. 0232]

As blessedness is promised to the soul, so resurrection is promised to the flesh, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 751.---On the state of the saints before the resurrection, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 462.---Before the resurrection they lack something of glory, but have nothing of misery, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 1006.---They do not possess the perfection of contemplation, idem, CLXXXIII, 699, 700.---The souls of the blessed desire to receive their bodies again, idem, CLXXXII, 993.---Without bodies they neither wish nor are able to be made complete, ibid.---There are two lives of a human being in the body: one before death, the other after the resurrection, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 561.---The resurrection of bodies is certain, St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 141–145, 504; Alcuin, CI, 52, 80, 1073; St. Bruno, CLIII, 408; St. Anselm, CLVIII, 401, 402, 538, 539, 643.---The resurrection is twofold: one from vices, the other into eternal life, St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII.---On our twofold resurrection, Guerric, abbot, CLXXXIV, 144.---The future resurrection commended, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 167.---Our resurrection is certain, whether unto life or unto damnation, Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 606.---It is proved by the law of nature, St. Bruno, CLXII, 209.---The doctrine of the resurrection is most fully affirmed by Job’s testimony, St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 617, 618, 621; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1080.---The Sadducees, who deny the resurrection of the flesh, are refuted by Christ the Lord, St. Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 256.---The resurrection of bodies with transformation and immortality, Rupert, CLXX, 174, 175.---Both good and evil will rise again, St. Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 74, 972.---Resurrection concerns all human beings, but transformation only the saints, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 1080; St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 504; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 248; St. Anselm, CLVIII, 384, 385.---The manner of resurrection, Godfrey, abbot, CLVII, 257; Werner, abbot, ibid., 939; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 603.---On the order of rising again, and how or what sort of bodies will rise, Werner, abbot, CLVII, 953; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 601.---An image of our resurrection displayed in the Lord’s transfiguration, Godfrey, abbot, CLVII, 212, 213.---Whether miscarried fetuses and monsters will rise, and in what condition, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 602.---The condition of bodies after the resurrection, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 1077.---The body will be spiritual not by nature but by power, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 238, 239, 816, 817.

What human bodies will be like after the resurrection, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 1178 (Appendix).---We shall all rise into a perfect man, St. Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1012, 1013.---On the age and stature of resurrected bodies, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 943.---Master Bandinus, ibid., 1110.---We shall rise at the age at which Christ died and rose again, ibid., 201.---Whatever belonged to the substance and nature of the body will rise again, ibid., 946.---All will be of the same stature, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 605.---Our flesh will rise whole, with all its parts, St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 510; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 596.---There those now eaten by beasts or mutilated by diverse dismemberments will rise again and receive the integrity of their bodies, St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 510.---All will rise as large in body as they were, or would have been, at youthful age, ibid., 505.---Against those who assert that earthly bodies cannot become incorruptible and eternal, St. Augustine, XLI, 389, 390.---The glory of those rising again will differ, Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1684.---On the endowments of bodies in the blessed, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 1168, 1169; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 475; Guigo the Carthusian, CLXXXIX, 355.---The body of the blessed will be fully subject to the spirit, St. Augustine, XLI, 802.---Endowed with beauty, ibid., 781.---With incorruption, idem, XXXIII, 439.---The bodies of all saints will rise conspicuous in every happiness of the glory of immortality, etc., St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 507; Haymo, CXVIII, 881.---In the glory of resurrection they receive an incorruptible body, Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 494.---In their homeland the bodies of the blessed will shine like the sun, Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, CLXXI, 818.---Blessedness is completed by resurrection through the strengthening of God’s glory, St. Hilary, IX, 876, 877.---The blessedness even of bodies is a reward of good works, St. Augustine, XLIV, 239.---After the resurrection the ascent to heaven in the flesh is promised to the saints, St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 520; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1014.---The state of glory after the resurrection, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 544, 545.---The glory of martyrs is greater after the resurrection, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1282, 1454.---The body will share in blessedness, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 918; Jonas of Orléans, CVI, 276; Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, CLXXI, 707.---Complete joy in heaven will follow the resurrection, Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 293, 294, 314, 315.---How earthly bodies remain in heaven, Werner, abbot, CLVII, 979; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 1178.---In that [Col. 0233] resurrection the soul will give life to the body in such a way that it will live perpetually without needing any food, St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLIII, 212.---Whether saints will see God through the body, St. Augustine, XLI, 797.---Saints will see God in the body itself, ibid., 797; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 125, 126.---Some say that God will be seen through the spiritual body, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 719, 623.---When we have a spiritual body, we shall see the Trinity, whether with the mind or, in a wondrous manner, even with the body, ibid., 460.---Evodius and Augustine affirm that God’s substance cannot be seen by any glorified body whatever, even that of the Lord himself, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 703, 704, 707.---The blessed will have tongues and voices with which to utter divine praises, ibid., 350.---All the members and inward parts of the incorruptible body will serve the praises of God, Alcuin, CI, 54; Smaragdus, CII, 679.

On the resurrection of the flesh, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 52.---On the state of human beings after the resurrection, Robert Pullus, CLXXXVI, 988.---A poem on the resurrection of bodies, Venerable Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, CLXXI, 1715.

## CHAPTER VIII.—The abode of the kingdom of heaven

The abode of the kingdom of heaven, St. Hilary, IX, 882, 883.---What are the dwelling places of souls after death until the final day of judgment, idem, XIV, 135, 936; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 1179.---On the different receptacles of souls, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 948.---Visible heaven is not a dwelling worthy of God, St. Hilary, IX, 668.---Yet the common opinion concerning God’s seat is not excluded, namely, that the heaven of heavens is his throne, ibid., 669.---The eternal region of the blessed, ibid., 257.---What is beyond heaven: the God of heaven, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1131, 1132.---Where the kingdom of God is to be understood to be, St. Augustine, XLIV, 518.---Where paradise is, in which the souls of the blessed, stripped of their bodies, rest, St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 475.---Paradise is where Christ is; and to be with Christ is to be in paradise, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 935.---Heaven is where sin has ceased; where crimes are punished; where there is no wound of death, St. Ambrose, XVI, 450, 451.---True blessedness does not belong to this life, St. Augustine, XXXII, 701; XLI, 433, 628, 631, 1106, 1363; XLII, 887.---Where the good life is to be sought, idem, XXXVIII, 1106.---The blessedness of those who behold God is possessed in this life, idem, XLI, 631, 648.---The kingdom of heaven is beyond this bodily heaven, indeed beyond every place, idem, XL, 1012, 1020.---Nor will the bodies of the saints be supported by a bodily heaven, ibid., 1029.---The righteous have a heaven more excellent than the visible one, St. Prosper, LI, 327.---The kingdom of God is within us in hope, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 308.---The heaven into which Paul was caught up, St. Augustine, XLI, 1028; XXXIV, 482; St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 832, 925.---Stephen looked upon Christ, St. Augustine, XL, 1028.---On Christ’s ascension, with the apostles and Mary standing by, Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1482.

## CHAPTER IX.—The way to heaven

The way to glory, St. Leo, LIV, 379, 393, 438.---Heaven’s gate, closed by Adam, now stands open, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2085.---The way to the blessed life was hidden from philosophers, and would be hidden from us also unless it itself had come to us, idem, XXXVIII, 814.---No certain way to blessedness is found without divine authority, idem, XLI, 600.---How eternal life is acquired, idem, XLIV, 301, 302; St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 397; St. Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 483; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 332, 332.---How a person is made blessed, Smaragdus, CII, 680; St. Augustine, XLII, 903.---He speaks at length concerning that which conveys us to heaven, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 520.---The way of the elect person journeying to heaven is described, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 949.---Sacred Scripture is the way of going to heaven, Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 365.---The monastic life is a short way to heaven, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 595.---At what price the kingdom of heaven is bought, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2136.---At how different a price it is bought, idem, XXXVII, 1468.---The way to heaven is narrow, Marcus of Cassino, LXXX, 183; Alan of Lille, CCX, 529, 530.---The way to heaven is narrow for the wicked, Rupert, CLXVIII, 1457, 1458; St. Benedict, LXVI, 232; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 415, 416, 1274.

By his own merit, without God’s help, a human being cannot attain eternal life, St. Hilary, IX, 569, 570.---Without excluding the duty of meriting, ibid., 770.---How blessedness, as a reward, is said to be given in measure, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 261.---No one can attain perpetual life except by grace, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 720, 721; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 817.---The blessed life is prepared for us through God’s mercy, St. Hilary, IX, 403, 404.---Although the merit of faith is a cause of blessedness, God’s mercy is nevertheless its greatest cause, ibid., 770.---It is built up from God’s mercy through the grace of justification, ibid., 870, 871.---Eternal life can be obtained from God alone, St. Augustine, XLI, 193, 194.---It is sought in vain from gods, ibid., 175, 183, 187, 189.---When God gives eternal life, he completes what he began by justifying, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 159.---The merit of eternal life is not attained except by God’s gift, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 419.---The blessedness of the saints comes both from the gift of mercy and from the recompense of justice, St. Prosper, LI, 359, 431.---Eternal life is possessed through God’s grace, St. Bruno, CLIII, 61.---It is called grace, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 881.---The recompense of glory is called mercy in the Scriptures, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 159.---In glorifying the saints God foreknew the works of his grace, ibid., 161.---Election to glory wholly rests in God’s will, St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 373, 374.---Eternal life is grace for grace, Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, CLXXI, 797; St. Augustine, XLIV, 893.---By the Lord’s blessing the saints receive eternal rest, Angelomus of Luxeuil, monk, CXV, 126.---The glory of the saints is owed to God, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 837.---How God brings persons to glory, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 157.---God brings about the salvation of the elect in three ways through created things, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 1024, 1025.---Whence we have merit for perfect blessedness, St. Hilary, IX, 322.---No one can enter heaven except through Christ, Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 679, 680.---Both the good life and the blessed life are in Christ and from Christ, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 159 and following.---Christ is the way to blessedness, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 813; XLIV, 747.---Heavenly blessing is in Christ, Rufinus of Aquileia, XXI, 330.---Before Christ’s ascension, a flaming sword stood at the gate of paradise, so that access to it might not be open to humanity, Tertullian, II, 747; St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 536.---The heavenly barriers were closed before Christ opened the gates of paradise with the thief, St. Jerome, XXIII, 1041.---Christ opened paradise’s gate by the shedding of his blood, St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 508.

The fiery way to paradise was tempered by the water from Christ’s side, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 648.---Our return to paradise was restored through Christ, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1259.---Expelled from heaven through Adam, we are brought back to it through Christ, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 619.---The acquisition of the beatific vision of God by human beings was the end and aim of Christ’s whole dispensation in the world, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 628.---Christ came to make us heavenly, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 917.---No one will attain eternal life unless reborn in Christ, St. Augustine, XLIV, 121, 122.---Unless he clings to Christ, Venerable Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 381, 631.---Unless he hears and follows Christ’s voice, Venerable Bede, XCIV, 246.---Unless he is in Christ’s body, that is, in the Church, ibid., 200.---One God must be worshipped in order to obtain blessedness, St. Augustine, XLI, 280.---Through the kingdom of the Lord we ascend to the kingdom of God the Father, St. Hilary, IX, 882, 883.---We shall be nearest to the Father’s kingdom when we are in the Son’s kingdom, ibid., 862, 863.---Only one who is reborn can have eternal life, St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 158.---Those coming to heaven must cross a river: that of baptism, repentance, or suffering, Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 1018.---Regeneration is given for the hope of future blessedness, St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 159.---The apostles, bishops, and priests have been given the power to open not only the Church but also heaven to others, St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 214.---Eternal glory is prepared here, and how, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 585.---Temporal life does not possess true blessedness, St. Augustine, XLI, 433.---The present life is the way by which we strive toward our homeland, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 279, 280, 1114; St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 839; Werner, abbot, CLVII, 1106; Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1483.---One must live in time in such a way as to live in eternity, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 499.---Earthly happiness must be used for eternal gains, ibid., 356.---How this temporal life should be conducted so that one may attain eternal life, ibid., 354.---One must devote oneself wholly to acquiring heavenly glory, St. Bernard, LXXXIII, 599.---Merit for glory, St. Hilary, IX, 770.---There are many ways to the promised land, ibid., 775, 776; Alan of Lille, CCX, 591.---Five steps to blessedness, ibid., 250, 251.---Steps to the kingdom of heaven, St. Chromatius, bishop, XX, 324–328.---By what steps the heavenly kingdom is brought to completion, St. Hilary, IX, 879.---Three things prescribed by Christ for recovering blessedness, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 688.---Three steps of heaven: poverty, humility, charity, Alan of Lille, CCX, 246, 247.---The three horses by which we are carried to heaven: sorrow from repentance, fervor from religion, desire from love, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1152.---How a person ascends to heaven by various distinctions, St. Ambrose, XIV, 1025.---The progress of the elect is distinguished by four steps, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 228.---On the eight ascents of the soul, Werner, abbot, CLVII, 978.---What the character of those awaiting blessedness ought to be, St. Hilary, IX, 500.

The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1168; St. Jerome, XXII, 424.---The kingdom [Col. 0235] of heaven must be stormed, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 355.---How only the violent seize the kingdom of heaven, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1666; XVII, 605, 606, 820.---How it is within us and suffers violence, Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1516.---One must fly to heaven with spiritual wings, St. Ambrose, XVI, 286.---One ascends to blessedness not by the frailty of the flesh but by eagerness of mind, St. Leo, LV, 92.---The beatific vision requires ardent desire, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 942.---Chaste looks, ibid., 774, 940.---One must continually sigh for eternal life, St. Augustine, XXXV, 1474.---With what desire the Prophet sighed for it, ibid., 1404, 1405.

Everything must be cast aside for the attainment of eternal life, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 499.---Labor is necessary for meriting it, St. Hilary, IX, 299, 300.---Through labor and hardships, Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 810, 946, 949, 950.---The cross alone is the way to heaven, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 739, 760.---The cross is the way to glory, idem, CLXXXIII, 254.---For the thief, the cross was a short passage from the mire of dregs to the paradise of delight, idem, CLXXXII, 105.---Present tribulation is the way to glory, idem, CLXXXIII, 254; St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 474.---Tribulation is a sign and pledge of heavenly glory, ibid., 489, 490.---God mixes bitterness with earthly felicities so that another happiness may be sought, whose sweetness is not deceptive, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 621.---How blessed eternity is to be merited by us, St. Hilary, IX, 952, 955.---An exhortation to bring force against heaven, St. Bernard, CLXXXV, 168, 169.---One must go through the midst of battle-lines, idem, CLXXXIII, 204.---Here one must fight for the heavenly crown, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 585.---Great rewards must be reached through great labors, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1275.---Those about to undergo the gravest contests are first promised crowns, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 223.---It seems difficult for them to purchase hope with dangers and, at the cost of present things, merit the gain of the future age, St. Ambrose, XV, 1710, 1711.---The grace of paradise is not sought for one day, or two, or a few months; it is always sought and sought through all things, ibid., 1257, 1258.---Temporal merit may be worthy, but not commensurately worthy, of an eternal reward, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 890.---For the merit of temporal military service, the reward of eternal glory, Werner, abbot, CLVII, 1098; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 826.---Why eternal recompense is made for temporal merits, Alger, Scholasticus, LXXX, 825.---No saint attains heavenly glory except by preserving patience, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 846, 847.---For eternal life people do not endure what the Israelites endured for an idol, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 644.---Blessedness is accessible only through virtues, Alan, CCX, 519.---Blessedness is the reward of faith, St. Augustine, XXXV, 1830.---No one can attain true blessedness except through the Catholic faith, Alcuin, CI; St. Augustine, XLIII, 1020, 1033.---Faith cleanses and prepares the eye of the mind to see God, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 986, 987.

Hearts are cleansed by faith so that they may be fit to see God, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1640.---Eternal glory is rendered from the merit of faith, though God’s mercy is nevertheless its greatest cause, St. Hilary, IX, 770.---The heavenly Jerusalem will be built in us through the work of faith and hope, ibid., 870, 871.---The defense of faith merits paradise, Godfrey, abbot, CLVII, 117, 218.---By faith, hope, and charity one lives that life which is lived in the Lord, Werner, abbot, CLVII, 1154.---Eternal life must be promised only to that faith which works through love, St. Augustine, XL, 230.---Love is required for it, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 1171, 1172.---It is acquired through the merit of love and service, St. Hilary, IX, 270.---From charity toward God comes steadfastness and the firmest hope of eternal happiness, Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1143.---The greater the lack of rest here through love for the Creator, the greater will be rest in blessedness, St. Gregory, LXXVII, 705.---The disposition by which one becomes capable of meriting heavenly things, idem, LXXV, 665.---There are as many keys of the kingdom of heaven as there are virtues, St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 562.---There are two keys to paradise’s gate: patience and charity, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 755.---Your blood is the key of paradise, Tertullian, II, 747.---The martyrs came to the Lord by a glorious road, St. Cyprian, IV, 249.---The martyrs’ fetters were changed into a crown, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1306.---The virtues possessed in the present are rays of future joy, St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLIII, 108.---Marriage fills the earth; virginity fills paradise, St. Jerome, XXIII, 226.---Humility opens heaven’s gate, Venerable Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 1041.---Without the way of humility, the heavenly gate cannot be found, Venerable Bede, XCIV, 199.---If you desire to become greater in the kingdom of heaven, be more humble here, Radulphus Ardens, CLV, 1460.---The vision of God is specially promised to purity of heart, St. Anselm, CLIX, 60.---On purity of heart, Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1282–1304.---Poverty [Col. 0236] merits blessedness by the help of divine grace, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 595, 596.---All on earth who have wished to ascend to the heavenly homeland have loved the virtue of counsel, Smaragdus, abbot, CII, 645.---One must press on by the way of holiness toward the vision of majesty, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 107.---The heavenly marriage has been prepared through baptismal regeneration and through good conduct in the spiritual life, Venerable Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 614.

The joys of eternal blessedness which we cannot obtain through perfection of life, may we be able to attain through true and humble repentance, Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 616.---What we deserve here, we shall receive in the future, Robert Pullen, CLXXXVI, 702.---God has given the time for acquiring eternal life only in this present life, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 689.---As you leave this life, so shall you be restored to that life, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 361.---Upon the end of this life depends the beginning of eternal life, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 557, 562.---Let us walk by the path of righteousness, that we may reach the dwelling-place of the heavenly homeland, Theofrid, CLVII, 416.---Righteousness alone makes blessed, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 473, 474.---A blessed life follows a good life, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 707, 708.---A righteous life will profit in the life to come, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 550.---Those who are to ascend to the heavenly kingdom shall be made white beyond snow, St. Hilary, IX, 452, 453.---Nothing defiled shall enter that inheritance, St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 826.---It cannot be reached except by the forgiveness of sins, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 373, 376, 395, 396.---We must fly hither naked, St. Jerome, XXII, 1080.---Let us transfer all earthly things that we possess into the dwellings to come, St. Paulinus, patriarch, XCIX, 243.---He who strives toward the heavenly kingdom must restrain himself from present things, Rabanus, CX, 117.---By the desirable things of the world even heavenly things are purchased, Theofrid, CLVII, 330.---He who disdains earthly things merits eternal things, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 252.---That eternal things may be seen, temporal things must be passed over, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 523, 524.---Miracles do not make a person holy, but virtues do, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 496.---A sober manner of life, a righteous action, and a devout disposition make one holy, ibid., 683.---Holy fear and love, id., CLXXXII, 806.---The condition of blessed life is secure if there are also devotion toward God, patience in adversities, and contempt for wealth, St. Hilary, IX, 395.---Nothing makes a human being blessed except him who made the human being, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 667, 669, 670.---Apart from baptism and participation in the Lord’s table, no one attains eternal life, St. Augustine, XLIV, 128.---Eternal life is the fruit of the Eucharist, St. Augustine, XXXV, 1613.---The fruit of the Lord’s vineyard, Walbero, abbot, CXCV, 1262.---The Holy Spirit is the pledge of eternal life, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1673.

Works necessary for entrance into the heavenly land, Peter Lombard, CXCI, 214, 1051.---One reaches the vision of God only through good works, St. Hilary, IX, 933; St. Augustine, XXXII, 976, 1321; XXXVIII, 103, 367, 571; St. Benedict, LXVI, 236.---The kingdom of heaven is not obtained by verbal services alone, St. Hilary, IX, 952.---It will be granted not for miracles but for good works, ibid.---Christ’s kingdom is acquired not by hereditary succession but by labours, Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1094.---The reward of good works is most just, Rabanus, CVIII, 551, 552; CIX, 869.---Human works are seeds of eternity, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 843.---Good things must be sent ahead into heaven before death, St. Jerome, XXII, 557.---That we may rest eternally in the most blessed state, let us labour temporarily in God’s service, Eadmer, monk, CLIX, 678.---The works of God can bestow eternal life upon those who do them, St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 1130.---How is eternal life given freely when the price consists in good works? St. Ambrose, XVII, 575.---God cries out that he has the kingdom of heaven for sale, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 1171, 1172.---The martyrs stormed heaven by force, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1425.---Heaven is often acquired by a small thing and a good will, Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 682.---Yet only by leaving the world, ibid., 722.---It is received for a cup of cold water, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 574.---Whatever labour you undertake for the advancement of others shall be repaid to you in eternal life, Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 682.---Treasure is to be stored in heaven, St. Chromatius, XX, 365, 366; Alcuin, C, 644.---The poor are the bearers of our treasure into heaven, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 205, 208.---The rich purchase heaven from the poor, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 725.---Perseverance leads to the heavenly nuptials, Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 109.---To heaven’s joys, ibid., 920.---Remembrance of the promised reward makes one persevere in the work, St. Augustine, XXXV, 2003.

Blessedness is to be sought by prayers and works, St. Hilary, IX, 416, 417.---Prayer shuts and opens heaven, Peter Cantor, CCV, 319.---Let us not cease to ask for eternal life until we attain it, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 206.---All the righteous who have merited the kingdoms of blessed life obtained them by praying, Werner, abbot, CLVII, 968.

The Lord preserves participants in the eternal kingdom, St. Hilary, IX, 864.---Angels lead the souls of the righteous into heaven, Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 712.---The devil, unwitting and unwilling, serves the salvation of the elect, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 359.---Saints who perish in this world are preserved for eternal glory, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 697, 698.---Let one who wishes to ponder eternal years rest from every outward disturbance, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 976.---The fruits of eternity are so great, Salvian of Marseilles, LIII, 225.---It is worth as much as you possess, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 574.---Why ascent to the third heaven is necessary for a human being to be caught up into paradise, St. Ambrose, XIV, 300.---To see God, the eye of the mind must be cleansed from a threefold defilement, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 459, 460.---One leaps into heaven more fittingly from a hut than from a palace, Peter Cantor, CCV, 257.---Against those who, through love of temporal life, lose eternal life, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1515.

Aelred, abbot, CXCV, 283, 303, 309, 336, 339, 348, 352; Peter of Celle, CCII, 770–785, 785–794, 843–848, 848–869; Peter Cantor, CCV, 700; Peter of Blois, CCVIII, 627, 660, 703; St. Martin of León, CCVIII, 1085–1204; ## CHAPTER XI.—Homilies concerning Heaven

St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 325, 363, 367, 377, 446, 507, 511; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1114–1118, 1118–1123, 1274–1284; Venerable Bede, XCIV, 181–189, 189–197, 202, 224–228 (among the spurious homilies), 447–450, 450–454, 452–455, 481–489; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 16, 42, 70, 198, 231, 270, 358, 370; Remigius of Auxerre, CXXXI, 878; Radulphus Ardens, CLV, 1156, 1305, 1410, 1430, 1459, 1470, 1475, 1598, 1609, 1621, 1762, 1911, 1917, 1922, 1962, 1979, 1996; St. Anselm, CLVIII, 617, 630; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 625, 665, 709, 770, 858, 2017; Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 471, 621, 719, 897, 1010, 1040.

## CHAPTER XII.—Exposition of Psalms Treating of Heaven

[Col. 0238]

The verse of Psalm 8 is explained: “For I shall see your heavens, the works of your fingers,” Cassiodorus, LXX, 75; Haimo, CXVI, 220; Theodoric of Paderborn, CXLVII, 665; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 720.

Explanation of this verse in Psalm 17: “And he bowed the heavens and came down,” St. Jerome, XXI, 704; Haimo, CXVI, 247; Theodoric of Paderborn, CXLVII, 768; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 748.

Psalm 18 is explained: “The heavens declare the glory of God,” St. Jerome, XXI, 712; St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 348; Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXX, 138; Venerable Bede, XCIII, 579; Theodoric of Paderborn, CXLVII, 768; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 757; Garnerus, CXCIII, 895.

Verse 5 of Psalm 49 is explained: “He shall call heaven from above, etc., and the earth, to judge his people,” St. Jerome, XXI, 844; Cassiodorus, LXX, 350; Haimo, CXVI, 365; Remigius of Auxerre, CXXXI, 392; Theodoric of Paderborn, CXLVII, 853; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 874.

The verse of Psalm 67 is explained: “Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God; sing psalms to the Lord; sing psalms to God, who ascended above the heaven of heaven toward the east,” Remigius of Auxerre, CXXXI, 479; Theodoric of Paderborn, CXLVII, 821.

On verse 39 of Psalm 148: “Let the heavens and earth praise him,” etc., Theodoric, CXLVII, 824; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 961.

On verse 9 of Psalm 72: “They have set their mouth against heaven,” Remigius of Auxerre, CXXXI, 516; Theodoric of Paderborn, CXLVII, 102; Garnerus, CXCIV, 342.

On verse 24 of Psalm 72: “For what have I in heaven?”, St. Jerome, XXI, 946; Remigius of Auxerre, CXXXI, 516; Theodoric of Paderborn, CXLVII, 1005; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 875; Garnerus, CXCIV, 334.

On verse 7 of Psalm 77: “And he commanded the clouds above and opened the gates of heaven. And he rained manna upon them to eat, and gave them the bread of heaven,” Remigius of Auxerre, CXXXI, 545; Theodoric, CXLVII, 1039; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 998.

On Psalm 83: “How beloved are your tabernacles, O Lord of hosts,” Remigius of Auxerre, CXXXI, 582; Theodoric of Paderborn, CXLVII, 1081; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 1025; Garnerus, CXCIV, 514.

Longing for the heavenly homeland: Psalm 133, “Upon the rivers of Babylon,” etc., Remigius of Auxerre, CXXXI, 798; Theodoric of Paderborn, CXLVII, 1335; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 1335.

On the words of Psalm 72: “Full days shall be found in them,” St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 975.

Sermon on these words: “And in the morning you shall see his glory,” St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 94–109.---On Job, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 1074–1080.

## CHAPTER XIII.—The Gospels Treating of Heaven Are Explained

On the words: “The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who went out early in the morning to hire workers for his vineyard,” Victor of Capua, LXVIII, 309; Smaragdus, abbot, CII, 102; Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 674; Radulphus Ardens, CLV, 1762; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1417; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 797.

On the parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who wished to settle accounts with his servants,” Victor of Capua, LXVIII, 304; Venerable Bede, XCV, 1442; Smaragdus, abbot, CII, 498; Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 628; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 796; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 390.

On the parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like ten virgins,” etc., Venerable Bede, XCII, 106; Smaragdus, abbot, CII, 549; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 1084; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 192; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 799.

On the parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who made a wedding for his son,” Victor of Capua, LXVIII, 318; Venerable Bede, XCV, 1444; Smaragdus, abbot, CII, 487; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 498; Zacharias Chrysopolitanus, bishop, CLXXXVI, 390.

On the parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his field,” Victor of Capua, LXVIII, 286; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 190; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 791.

On the parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed,” etc., St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 507; Victor of Capua, LXVIII, 287; Venerable Bede, XCII, 67; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 793.

On the parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven,” etc., St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 511; Victor of Capua, LXVIII, 287; Venerable Bede, XCII, 68; Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 497; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 191; Zacharias Chrysopolitanus, CLXXXVI, 228.

[Col. 0239] On the parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field,” Victor of Capua, LXVIII, 288; Venerable Bede, XCII, 69; Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 502; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 794.

On the parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea and gathering fish of every kind,” Venerable Bede, XCII, 69; Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 506; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 192; St. Bernard, CLXXXV, 794; Zacharias Chrysopolitanus, bishop, CLXXXXI [probably CLXXXVI], 235.

On the parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking fine pearls,” Venerable Bede, XCII, 69; Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 504; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 194, 1067.

On the parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings out of his treasure things new and old,” Victor of Capua, LXVIII, 268; Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 508; Zacharias Chrysopolitanus, bishop, CLXXXVI, 235.

The meaning of the parable of the man who made a great supper and invited many, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 819.

Explanation of these words of Matthew: “Permit the little children to come to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven,” Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 1413.

How these words are to be interpreted: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven,” St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 525; Eugyppius, abbot, LXII, 844; St. Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 1414.

Explanation of the Gospel words of St. Mark: “And immediately, coming up out of the land, he saw the heavens opened,” Venerable Bede, XCII, 138, 358.

What these words of Jesus Christ, choosing Peter as his vicar, mean: “And I shall give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven,” Rabanus Maurus, CX, 353; Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 562.

These words of the Holy Gospel are explained: “Not everyone who says, ‘Lord, Lord,’ shall enter the kingdom of heaven,” etc., Smaragdus, abbot, CII, 413; Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 325; Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 517.

These words of the Holy Gospel are explained: “Who do you think will be greater in the kingdom of heaven?”, Smaragdus, abbot, CII, 477; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 263.

On the words of the Gospel according to John: “And no one ascends into heaven except he who came down from heaven,” Eugyppius, abbot, LXII, 1045; Venerable Bede, XCIV, 424; Smaragdus, abbot, CII, 341; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 265.

What these words mean: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away,” Smaragdus, CII, 825. And these other words: “The heavens shall pass away with a great rushing sound,” etc., ibid., 829.

On the words of the Gospel according to Matthew: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near,” St. Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 85; Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1545.

On the words of St. Matthew: “Good teacher, what shall I do that I may have eternal life?”, St. Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 233.

On the words: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven,” Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 226.

On the words: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven,” Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 226.

On the words: “Go and preach the Gospel to every creature, saying that the kingdom of heaven has drawn near,” Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 410.

On the words: “From the days of John until now the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it,” Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 440.

On the words: “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless you are converted and become like little children, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven,” Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 604.

On the words: “Blessed are those servants whom the Lord, when he comes, shall find watching,” Werner, abbot, CLVII, 733.

On the words: “The sower went out to sow,” etc., Werner, abbot, CLVII, 843, 850.

On the words: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes [lacuna] you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven,” Werner, abbot, CLVII, 1053.

On the words: “For whoever wishes to save his life shall lose it,” etc., St. Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 216.

On the words: “There are three who bear witness in heaven,” Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 778.

Other passages of sacred Scripture treating of heaven are explained.

On the words of the prophet Isaiah: “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet,” Haimo, CXVI, 1075.---“And I saw heaven opened, and behold, a white horse,” id., CXVII, 1171.

On the words: “And I saw a new heaven and a new earth,” Haimo, CXVII, 1191.---“And the holy city Jerusalem descending from heaven, from God,” ibid., 1192.

[Col. 0240] On the words: “Behold, I create new heavens and a new earth; former things shall not be remembered, nor shall they come upon the heart,” Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXX, 574.

Alcuin, CI, 977.---Who denied that it revolved, Lactantius, VI, 426, 953.---Who believed that the revolution of the heavens produces an inexpressible harmony, St. Ambrose, XIV, 480, 922.---Because of the name “firmament,” one should not suppose that the heavens stand still, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 272.---Heaven, strengthened throughout by air, bears the waters and is not borne, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 481.---The heavens’ stability is unchangeable, St. Hilary, IX, 757, 758.---Heaven is many times greater than earth, St. Ambrose, XIV, 948.---How much broader heavenly spaces are than terrestrial ones is obscure, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1262.---The aerial heaven denotes sterility, St. Ambrose, XVI, 12.---According to Aristotle, heaven is not composed of the four elements, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 387.---Plato assigns the place of heaven to fire, St. Augustine, XLI, 236.---Heaven is the beginning of the work of the world, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1131, 1132.---By the heaven that God created first, all invisible things are signified, St. Augustine, XXXV, 2218.---What the heaven created with the world was like, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 444.---Whether the heaven of heavens was empty, ibid., 445.

Alan of Lille, CCX, 327.---How the powers of heaven are to be moved, Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 52.---Whether they shall perish in the conflagration of the final Judgment, St. Augustine, XLI.---Scholars dispute which heavens shall perish by fire, id., XXXVII, 1313.---Some falsely claim that collapses occur daily in heaven, St. Jerome, XXVI, 43.---Heaven and earth shall not perish, id., XXIV, 486, 644.---God does not say that the heavens perish, but that they are folded up, ibid., 370.---The heavens and earth shall grow old and perish, not so as not to exist, but so as to exist otherwise, St. Prosper, LI, 283, 284.---So that they may exist in a better state, Venerable Bede, XCII, 26, 104, 265; # CXXIX. INDEX OF HELL, LOGICALLY SETTING FORTH EVERYTHING THE FATHERS HAVE SAID CONCERNING ITS EXISTENCE, THE PUNISHMENTS OF THE DAMNED, AND THEIR ETERNITY

## NOTICE

The hell of the damned is the lowest region of the earth, or a most foul and dark prison, where the souls of the reprobate, eternally deprived of the vision of God, are tortured with the devil and his angels in perpetual and inextinguishable fire; this is a matter of divine and Catholic faith. Accordingly, in this Index we treat in turn: I. the existence of hell; II. the various punishments of the damned; III. the eternity of those punishments; IV. the location and names of hell; V. the avoidance of the lower world—recalling the opinions of the Holy Fathers concerning these matters.

# [INDEX OF HELL]

## I.—THE EXISTENCE OF HELL

### 1. It is proved by Sacred Scripture

Fire is prepared for the devil and his angels, St. Ambrose, XV, 1228.---Hell is affirmed by the text of Isaiah, St. Jerome, XXIV, 634.---The existence of hell is affirmed from the Gospel text, St. Caesarius of Arles, LXVII, 1080.---The punishments of hell are affirmed from the Gospel, St. Paulinus, LXXI, 685 ff.---The existence of hell is derived from Scripture, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 1126.---Christ threatens Gehenna in the Gospel, Venerable Bede, XCII, 778.---Isaiah teaches the existence of hell, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 279.---Hell is proved by two passages from Deuteronomy, Robert Pullen, CLXXXVI, 820.---The doctrine of hell rests upon the text of St. Matthew, ibid., 999.---Testimonies of the prophets concerning the condemnation of the ungodly, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 869.---The truth about hell is contained in Scripture, Helinand, CCXII, 530.

### 2. It is proved by the Holy Fathers

Christians promise everlasting punishment to the unjust, Minucius Felix, III, 268.---Christians proclaim and fear fires, ibid., 272.---God prepared heaven, but he also prepared Tartarus, St. Cyprian, IV, 314.---A twofold way: to heaven and to hell, Lactantius, VI, 644.---In teaching hell, Zeno agrees with the sacred books, ibid., 761.---The blessed are so in this life; the miserable, in the future, ibid., 769.---Divine fire will burn and restore the ungodly, ibid., 802.---Avenging hell receives us immediately after death, St. Hilary, IX, 290.---The ungodly rise again for punishment, ibid., 491.---Some shall rise to confusion, others to glory, ibid., 492.---The rest of the wicked is in hell, St. Ambrose, XVI, 40, 41.---The rewards of righteousness; Gehenna for crime, Aquilius Juvencus, XIX, 142.---Hell was made manifest in a vision, Rufinus, XXI, 429.---The punishment of the ungodly in the present and in the future, ibid., 875.---Let him who denies hell experience what he has denied, St. Jerome, XXXIII, 428.---Hell is the place of the ungodly after death, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 93.---Those excluded from heaven receive the punishment of Gehenna, id., XXXVIII, 962.---Those who sinned willingly shall be tortured unwillingly, id., XXXIII, 562.---God punishes evildoers with eternal darkness, id., XXXVI, 998.---On the three dwellings: the world, the kingdom of God, and hell, St. Patrick, LIII, 831.---There are certain punishments after death that are not purgatorial, Eugyppius, LXII, 789.---Hell has sinners to burn, St. Caesarius of Arles, LXVII, 1080.---An argument for the existence of hell, Cassiodorus, LXX, 85.---The existence of hell, St. Gregory the Great, LXXI, 542.---The house of the condemned person is hell, id., LXXIX, 177.---God repays punishments to sinners, Paul the Deacon, XCV, 1215.---On the sheep and the goats, ibid., 1215, 1216, 1217.---The wicked shall be cast into a furnace of fire, ibid., 1333.---Profession of belief in infernal flames, Hincmar, CXXV, 542.---The souls of the elect are in heaven, those of the wicked in hell, Burchard, CXL, 1039.---Hell is a place of torments, Werner, CLVII, 1013.---On the twofold city, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 1093.---On the twofold order of those to be saved and condemned, Robert Pullen, CLXXXVI, 1005.

### 3. It is proved by pagan testimonies

Gehenna existed even among pagans, Tertullian, I, 520.---Plato taught hell, Arnobius, V, 831.---The vulture of Tityus is testimony to hell, Lactantius, VI, 802.---The punishments of hell are represented in poets’ fables, St. Paulinus, LXXI, 685 ff.---Whatever poets have invented about hell is fable, Helinand, CCXII, 530.

3. Distribution of the punishments of hell.—A person will be punished in that wherein he sinned: St. Cyprian, III, 800, 801.—Various punishments for various sins: St. Jerome, XXIV, 481, 482, 1280.—There are different degrees in damnation: St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1406; XXXVIII, 879; XL, 275, 284; XLI, 731; XLIII, 171; XLIV, 117, 230.—Those alike in guilt are alike in punishment: St. Caesarius of Arles, LXVII, 1080.—They are punished more severely in proportion as they sinned more grievously: ibid.—Hell is harsher for some, milder for others: Primasius, LXVIII, 647.—Unequal punishment binds the impious: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1302.—The damned are punished according to the measure of their crime: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 913.—The same sins receive the same torments: ibid.—Those who devised novelties for sin are punished by novel inventions: ibid., 1092.—Equal in crime, they shall be bound equally in punishment: id., LXXVII, 380, 381.—The more they shone, the more severely they shall be punished: id., LXXV, 1098, 1101.—There is one fire of Gehenna, but it will not torment all in one manner: id., LXXVII, 401.—Like sheaves for burning, the damned are bound together with those like themselves: St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 598.—There are many dwelling places in hell: ibid.—The lesser the wickedness, the more tolerable the damnation: St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 144, 145; ## III.—THE ETERNITY OF HELL

### 1. Proven from Sacred Scripture

The eternity of punishments is established through Solomon’s text: St. Jerome, XXV, 653.—The eternity of hell maintained from a text of St. Matthew: St. Caesarius of Arles, LXVII, 1080.—The Gospel openly teaches the eternity of punishments: Venerable Bede, XCII, 110; Paul the Deacon, XCV, 1218, 1219; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 98.—The eternity of infernal punishments is proved through a text from Revelation: Haymo, CXVII, 1110, 1188.—The eternity of hell confirmed through a text of St. Matthew: St. Paschasius, CXX, 870.—A terrible statement of Sacred Scripture: Venerable Hildebert, CLXXI, 429.—Proof of the eternity of punishments drawn from the Gospel: Hervaeus, CLXXX, 590.—“The tree remains where it falls”: Robert Pullus, CLXXXVI, 945.—The eternity of the underworld maintained from Revelation: St. Martin of León, CCIX, 374, 392.

### 2. Proven by the Holy Fathers

There is no end to torments: Minucius Felix, III, 348, 349; St. Cyprian, IV, 561, 562.—Hell is not extinguished, but punishes forever: Lactantius, VI, 320, 321.—The impious will be eternal fuel for eternal fire: St. Hilary, IX, 949.—Punishments without end for the impious: St. Ambrose, XVII, 264.—The impious are assigned to eternal fires: St. Gaudentius, XX, 940.—Sins are handed over to eternal punishment: St. Jerome, XXIV, 354, 481, 609; XXV, 245; XXVI, 190.—In hell, everlasting burning: St. Augustine, XLI, 214, 682.—It is absurd to suppose that the punishment of hell will end: ibid., 723, 750.—The subject is eternal punishments: id., XXXVIII, 196, 218; XL, 103, 342, 343.—In hell there is no satisfaction: St. Leo the Great, LIV, 252.—An argument for the eternity of punishments: Eugippius, LXII, 625, 792.—The damned will be tormented unto ages of ages: id., LXII, 793, 801.—The damned have no remedy of repentance: St. Caesarius of Arles, LXVII, 1080.—Eternal punishment holds the impious in torment: Cassiodorus, LXX, 213.—The damned will never come to God’s grace: ibid., 463.—In hell there is no repentance: id., LXXIII, 745.—For the damned there is no return to pardon: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 820.—The punishments of the reprobate are without end: ibid., 856.—The damned die, but are never consumed by death: ibid., 916.—The eternity of punishments is maintained: id., LXXVI, 738.—The flame of Gehenna is eternal: ibid., 1285.—Those assigned to Gehenna will burn forever: id., LXXVII, 401.—The righteous will not pray for the damned: ibid., 404.—The repentance of the eternal punishments: St. Boniface the Great, LXXXIX, 863.—Perpetual fire will devour the damned: Venerable Bede, XCIII, 589.—The fire of Gehenna is inextinguishable for a twofold reason: id., XCIV, reprobate are immortal: ibid., 1189.—Hell never says, “Enough”: ibid., 1191.—The torments of the wicked are without end: id., CXVIII, 947.—Angels or demons hold souls without change: ibid., 948.—No ### 3. Errors Refuted and Questions Resolved

Eternal fire according to Origen: St. Jerome, XXIII, 428, 429.—Those denying the eternity of punishments refuted: id., XXV, 246.—Whether at some time the punishments of the damned will be mitigated: St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1406.—The punishment of certain damned persons mitigated by prayers of the Church: id., XL, 283, note.—How the pain of the damned will not end: id., XLI, 658.—The error of the Priscillianists concerning the eternity of punishments: id., XLII, 668, 672.—Infernal fire is not eternal as God is: ibid., 563.—Eternal fire is not evil: ibid.—Several errors concerning the eternity of punishments refuted: id., XLI, 732, 733.—Why eternal punishment seems harsh and unjust: ibid., 726.—How just eternal punishments are: id., XL, 1128.—Origen’s delirium concerning the eternity of punishments: Gennadius of Marseille, LVIII, 983.—Whether bodies can remain perpetually in burning: Eugippius, LXII, 783, 784.—Those maintaining that all Catholics will be saved through fire refuted: ibid., 790.—Is it just that the periods of punishment should not be longer than the sins were? ibid., 787, 788.—In what respect does eternal punishment seem unjust? ibid., 788.—An objection drawn from Scripture answered: ibid., 790 ff.—The eternity of punishments explained by various examples: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1302.—How just eternal punishment is: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 738.—A transitory fault can be punished without end: ibid., 738; LXXVII, 404.—To what end will the reprobate always burn? id., LXXVII, 404.—Whether God threatened eternity only to restrain sinners: ibid., 401; Haymo, CXVIII, 941, 947.—Punishment is eternal because guilt is eternal insofar as possible: Venerable Bede, XCIII, 464; Paul the Deacon, XCV, 1219.—Why eternal fire? ## IV.—ON THE PLACE AND NAMES OF HELL

### 1. The Place of Hell

Hell is beneath the earth: St. Jerome, XXIV, 163; XXVI, 498; XXX, 832.—From Scripture, hell is in the middle of the earth: id., XXV, 1133.—No one knows the location of hell: St. Augustine, XLI, 682.—The infernal regions are beneath the earth: id., XXXII, 640.—A twofold hell, higher and lower: id., XXXVII, 1093, 1094.—On the manifold hell: Eugippius, LXII, 710, 711.—The account of the rich man shows that hell is beneath the earth: ibid., 711.—Hell beneath the earth: Cassiodorus, LXX, 615.—Where should hell be believed to be? St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 400.—On the place of the infernal regions: Taio, LXXX, 974; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 946.—Scripture proves that hell is situated beneath the earth: St. Julian of Toledo, XCVI, 478.—The place of hell escapes everyone’s knowledge: ibid., 517.—Hell is in the middle of the earth: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 728.—Hell is in the lower air: John Scotus, CXXII, 649.—Hell has no place: ibid., 971.—Subtle questions concerning the location of hell: ibid., 964 ff.—The souls of the impious are tormented beneath the earth: Radulphus Ardens, CLV, 1553; Werner, CLVII, 1008.—On the place of punishments: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 586.

### 2. Names of Hell

[Col. 0249]

# CXXX. INDEX ON PURGATORY, SETTING FORTH IN LOGICAL ORDER THE JUDGMENTS OF THE HOLY FATHERS CONCERNING ITS EXISTENCE AND PUNISHMENTS, AND THUS SHOWING THE PERPETUAL CONSENT OF THE CATHOLIC CHURCH ON THIS DOGMA

## Notice

Purgatory is a place of suffering in which the souls of the righteous pay the penalties due for their sins, until, wholly cleansed of them, they pass into the fellowship of the blessed. By divine and Catholic faith we believe that purgatory exists, and that souls detained there can be assisted by the suffrages of the faithful, especially by the sacrifice of the altar. Accordingly, this Index treats in turn: I. The existence of purgatory. II. Its punishments. III. What sins are to be removed in purgatory. IV. Whether, and how, souls detained in Purgatory can be relieved. V. The relations between the Church suffering and the Church triumphant. VI. The condition of the dead with respect to the living, etc.

[INDEX ON PURGATORY.]

## CHAPTER I.—ON THE EXISTENCE OF PURGATORY

Direct proof drawn by the Holy Fathers from Sacred Scripture: St. Ambrose, XLV, 980; XVII, 200; St. Jerome, XXIV, 217, 677; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 947; Julian, bishop of Toledo, XCVI, 483; Alcuin, C, 575, 579; CI, 53; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 357, 773, 930; Walafrid of Fulda, CXIV, 762; Haymo, CXVI, 214, 1081; CXVIII, 933; Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 165; St. Odo, CXXXIII, 545; Gerard, CXLII, 1299; Anselm of Laon, CLXII, 1363; Rupert, abbot, CLIX, 1200; Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 741.—The existence of purgatory established by various arguments: St. Cyprian, III, 889, 931; St. Jerome, XXIV, 678; St. Augustine, XXXIII, 1127, 1128; XLI, 728; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 393; Alcuin, CI, 1074; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 37; Haymo, CXVIII, 933, 936; Othlo, CXLVI, 368; Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 656, 1307; Radulphus Ardens, CLV, 1485; Anselm of Laon, CLXII, 1363; Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 741; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1100; CLXXXIV, 1058; Robert Pullus, CLXXVI, 1059, 1060; Egbert, CXCV, 15; Bernard, abbot, CCIV, 828.—Treatise on purgatory: Henry of Saltrey, CLXXX, 977–1004.—The existence of purgatory is indirectly proved from the matters stated below concerning prayers offered in the Church for the dead.

## CHAPTER II.—ON THE PUNISHMENTS OF PURGATORY

### I.—Punishments in General

Description of the punishments of purgatory: Alcuin, CI, 831.—The punishments of the damned and of those being purified shown to someone in a vision: Othlo, CXLVI, 380.—What the suffering of purgatory is like: id., CLXXXII, 1158; CLXXXIII, 663; Robert Pullus, CLXXXVI, 590.

### II.—The Fire of Purgatory

The souls in purgatory, long afflicted with pain for their sins, are purified for a long time by fire: St. Cyprian, III, 786.—Like gold, souls too will be purified through fire: St. Ambrose, XVII, 951.—The severity of purgatorial fire: Rufinus, XXI, 172.—St. Augustine, XXXVI, 92, 397; XXXVII, 1363; XXXIX, [Col. 0250] 1772, 2212; XL, 156, 217, 264; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII; Julian of Toledo, XCVI, 484; Haymo, CXVIII, 934, 935; Gerard, CXLII, 1299; St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLIII, 138; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXVII, 319; St. Bernard, CLXXXV, 76; Robert Pullus, CLXXXVI, 705.

### III.—The Severity of the Punishments of Purgatory

St. Augustine, XXXVI, 397; XXXIX, 756, 1947; XLI, 1328; XL, 800; St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 123; St. Boniface the Great, ibid., 756; Julian, XCVI, 486; Haymo, CXVII, 938, 939; Remigius of Auxerre, CXXXI, 341; St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 837; St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 854; St. Bruno, bishop of Segni, 18; St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXIII, 518; CLXXXIV, 124; CLXXXV, 89; Robert Pullus, CLXXXVI, 326; Peter the Chanter, CCV, 350; Alan of Lille, CCX, 174; Absalon, abbot, CCXI, 243.

### IV.—The Duration of the Punishments of Purgatory

It is greater in proportion as the sins are greater.

For perhaps months or even years our purification will endure, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1948.---We shall remain in purgatory as long as our sins are being consumed, ibid., 1947, 2212.---The purgatorial fire exceeds all human imagining in duration, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII; Julian of Toledo, XCVI, 485. The punishment of purgatory is prolonged to a lesser or greater extent according as temporal goods were loved less or more on earth. Those who are saved through purgatorial fire will not endure the torment of fire for one and the same period. Haymo, CXVIII, 935.---This transitory fire purifies some more slowly and others more quickly, according to the diversity of their sins, id., CXVII, 330, 321.---Souls remain in purgatory until full satisfaction has been made. On the day of the Last Judgment purgatorial fire will be ended. The souls in purgatory will be released before the Judgment, St. Ambrose, XVII, 931.---There is no purgatorial punishment after the Last Judgment, St. Augustine, XLI, 730, 734.---On the day of Judgment refreshment will be granted to souls detained in purgatory, St. Boniface of Mainz, LXXXIX, 717.---Souls will undergo purgatorial fire not after but before the Last Judgment, Julian of Toledo, XCVI, 485.---At the judgment of the Last Day purgatorial fire will disappear, Alcuin, CI, 53.---Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 1157.

Purgatorial fire is not eternal but transitory, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1946.---Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 38.---After purification by fire, the elect will pass into the kingdom of life, Haymo, CXVI, 1081.---Those who are in purgatory await redemption, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 663.---Those punished by purgatorial fire know beforehand that they will be saved, Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 1178.

## CHAPTER III.—WHAT SINS ARE TO BE REMOVED IN PURGATORY

### I.—Minor sins

What sins will furnish the material for the torments of purgatory? St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 949.---An enumeration of the sins to be removed in purgatory, Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 38; Gerard, CXLII, 1299.---Remigius of Auxerre, CXXXI. Sins which lead to purgatory are represented in Scripture by wood, hay, and stubble.---Only minor sins will be purged by this fire, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1946, 2214.---Light sins require to be purged by temporal correction, St. Fulgentius, LXV.---According to Scripture, only the smallest sins are removed by purgatorial fire, Taio of Saragossa, LXXX, 975.---Light sins are washed away in the torments of purgatory, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 396.---Those who have sinned lightly, once purified by fire, will be led to the repose of blessedness, St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 553.---Souls liable to minor sins will undergo purgatorial fire, Alcuin, CI, 53.---Light sins will be purged by transitory fire, Haymo, CXVIII, 933.---Purgatorial punishments after death are appointed not for criminal sins but for lighter sins, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 702. Venial sin is punished by a temporal penalty, Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 1177.---In what way minor sins are purged here or after this life, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1947.---The minor sins of the righteous must be purged by the tribulations of this life, so that they may escape the fire of the life to come, ibid., 1771.---Purgatory is appointed for souls that have lived not wickedly, but not perfectly, St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 144.

### II.—The remnants of sin

Whatever remains from more grievous sins will be abolished by purgatorial punishment, St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 123.---In this life sin is forgiven to those who are to be saved, but not the temporal punishment of sin, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 835.---Purgatorial fire completes penances begun but not completed in this life (CLXXXVI), Robert Pullus, CLXXXVI, 556.---Penitents overtaken by death and lacking time to make satisfaction are refined in purgatorial fire, Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 1177.---Who will undergo the fire of purgatory, Haymo, CXVIII, 934.---Many sins are discharged after this life by purgatorial fire, St. Bruno of Segni, CXXV, 180.---In what form those detained in purgatory exist, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 1158, 1159.---Few escape the fire of purgatory, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXV, 89.---Those baptized at the end of life do not undergo purgatory, St. Augustine, XL, 1127.

## CHAPTER IV.—HOW SOULS DETAINED IN PURGATORY MAY BE RELIEVED

How souls in purgatory are to be assisted, St. Augustine, XL, 1324.---In what ways we can aid the dead, id., XXXIX, 2101.---The suffrages of the living benefit the souls of the dead, *The Passion of the Holy Martyrs Perpetua and Felicity*, III, 44, 45. Souls of the dead are released in four ways, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 948.
