The Platonists and Pythagoreans, while asserting the immortality of souls, nevertheless did not know the manner and character of that immortality, 796. Epicurus and other pagan philosophers maintained that all things end after [Col. 0279] death, 795. Hymenaeus and Philetus affirmed that the resurrection had already occurred, 820. The Marcionites indirectly denied our resurrection by asserting that Christ’s flesh was not true flesh, 796, 797. Apelles and Valentinus acknowledged true flesh, but not human flesh—rather, flesh of the stars and of heaven—ibid. Some heretics say that the resurrection is destined for the soul alone, 848.

LACTANTIUS. — According to Lactantius, there will be a twofold resurrection of the dead: the first, of the faithful—that is, those who have lived in God’s religion—and the other, of the impious—that is, unbelievers—VI, 801, 802. In the first, the souls of the faithful will be raised to receive their own bodies, 801. Those whose sins prevail either in number or in weight will be condemned to punishment and burned by fire, 802, 803. But the righteous will not endure that fire, ibid. Then God will establish a holy city in the midst of the earth, where he will reign for a thousand years with those righteous persons who will preside over the living as judges, 808, 809, 810. After a thousand years the other resurrection will occur, namely, of the impious who either did not know the true God or denied him; all will be sent into eternal torments with the prince of demons, 813, 814, 815. When the world has been renewed, the righteous, happy and blessed in the likeness of angels, will always dwell before the Most High and will serve him forever, ibid.

The poets and philosophers affirm the resurrection, but in a mocking manner, according to Lactantius, 806. According to the Millenarians, the prophecies of the Sibyl attest that kingdom of the righteous, 807, 808. On the signs that will precede that resurrection, 812.

ST. ZENO. — To the Gentiles the resurrection seemed implausible, XI, 372. Here St. Zeno seems to defend the resurrection against heretics, probably the Seleucians, Hermians, or at least the Marcionites, 370, note I. The Priscillianists, who were also living in that age, could have been attacked by Zeno, 371, note I. Pythagoras and other philosophers and poets, discussing the transmigration of souls, did not know the manner of the resurrection, 373. Epicurus and Democritus abolished it, since they denied that the soul was immortal, ibid.

ST. PHILASTRIUS, bishop of Brescia. — Dositheus, a Jew by origin, said that one must live according to the flesh alone in the law of the Lord, not hoping for a future resurrection from it, XII, 1118. The Sadducees, following Epicurean madness rather than the ordinances of divine law, denied it, 1118, 1119.

ST. AMBROSE. — There are heretics who falsely assert that either the Lord’s body or ours will be aerial or phantasmal, or who teach metempsychosis, XVII, 535. They affirm that this body of ours is gradually to be dissolved into thin air after the resurrection, 546. The Gentiles denied the resurrection, 546. The Gentiles denied the resurrection of bodies, though they believed that human beings could be born from the sown teeth of the Hydra, XVI, 1335.

ST. JEROME. — Marcion’s error and blasphemies concerning the resurrection, XXIII, 387. The opinion of Origen, who asserts that our body in the resurrection will be aerial, clothed in no flesh proper to itself, 375, 376. The opinion of heretics among whom are Marcion, Apelles, Valentinus, and Mani, who utterly denied both the resurrection of flesh and that of bodies, since they ascribed salvation only to the soul, 376. They maintained that we shall rise in vain after the example of the Lord, since the Lord himself rose in a phantom, ibid. The opinion of John of Jerusalem, who distinguishes body from flesh, 379. They acknowledged the resurrection of the flesh in word only but denied it in mind, XXII, 747, 748.

S. AUGUSTINE.—The Platonists wrongly deny the resurrection, XLI, 392, 393. The Sadducees did not believe in the resurrection, XLII, 368. Hymenaeus and Philetus, mentioned by Paul, thought that the resurrection had already taken place, XXXIII, 206. The Seleucians do not think the resurrection will occur, but that it takes place daily in the begetting of children, XLII, 41. The Manichaeans denied that there would be a resurrection of bodies, XLII, 820, 247; though in a different way from the Sadducees, 331. The Manichaeans promised their hearers not resurrection but a return to this mortality, 826. The Origenists reject the resurrection, 33. One should not consult philosophers concerning the resurrection, not even those who excelled among the ancients, 903. Even among Christians there is sometimes found someone who contradicts the resurrection, XXXVI, 944. Pagans deceitfully deny the resurrection of the dead, XXXV, 2345. Philosophers attack it on the basis of the weight of the elements, XL, 643. That earthly bodies cannot be in heaven is a dogma of the philosophers, XLI, 390, 773. That a body could be immortal and eternal after death seemed absurd to philosophers, 389.

S. NICETAS, bishop of Aquileia.—There are many heretics who distort faith in the resurrection, claiming salvation for the soul alone while denying the resurrection of the flesh, LII, 872.

[Col. 0280] GENNADIUS OF MARSEILLES.—There is an opinion of the Millenarians, Stephen, and Gobar that there will be a twofold resurrection of the dead: the first of the righteous and the second of sinners, LVIII, 982 note, 1016. Origen thought that bodily substances would utterly fall away in the resurrection, note 1016.

S. GREGORY THE GREAT.—Eutychius, bishop of the city of Constantinople, maintained that the body in the resurrection would be intangible and aerial, LXXV, 1077.

HAYMO, bishop of Halberstadt.—Philosophers and pagans did not believe that the resurrection would take place, CXVII, 770. Many believers among the Macedonians and Thessalonians were involved in the same error, ibid.

S. BRUNO, founder of the Carthusians.—Certain heretics maintained that bodies still whole at the end of the world could rise again, but that bodies dissolved into ashes could never rise, CLIII, 408.

ALAN OF LILLE.—The Waldensian heretics tried, by many arguments, to overthrow this article of faith concerning the resurrection, CCX, 326.

II.—The resurrection of the dead is a dogma of faith.

TERTULLIAN.—The restoration of the flesh is easier than its original institution, II, 810. It is shown to be supremely possible for God, I, 522. “What new thing will happen to you? You who did not exist were made; when once more you shall not exist, you shall be made.” 524. In this matter there should be no greater doubt of God's power, since He composed into a living whole this vast body of the world out of what had not existed, ibid. “Give, if you can, an account of how you were made, and then ask how you will be made.” The cause and necessity of resurrection are the judgment appointed in the manner most fitting for God, II, 813. It was fitting that the human being, made from the union of both substances, should be presented and judged in both, ibid. The resurrection is proved by the whole recurring order of things, II, 810; I, 524, 525; by both the words and deeds of the New and Old Testaments, II, 835, 841, 842 ff.; especially by passages from Ezekiel, 836; Isaiah, 839; St. Matthew, 846, 847; and the Apostle, 851, 852, 853 ff. It is confirmed by the examples of the rising and setting light and stars, the seasons and fruits, I, 524, 525; II, 812; by Pythagoras’s opinion concerning the transmigration of souls, I, 521; and Plato’s, ibid.; by the eastern bird, the phoenix, which buries itself and is renewed, II, 811; and by Mithras, II, 55. The mortal soul will attain resurrection, 819. The word “resurrection” claims no other thing than that which has fallen, 491. Resurrection is the gate of the heavenly kingdom and the confidence of Christians, 795. Hope of resurrection is contempt for death, I, 585. The resurrection of the flesh is believed with greater difficulty than the one Godhead, II, 797. Yet the world does not fail to know it, even when it errs, 796. It ought not to be disapproved by pagans, 583. The resurrection of the flesh was received by the Jews in a simple and already familiar faith, without any question concerning its quality, 849. Platonists affirm that the soul can return into bodies, though not into the same bodies and not only into human ones, 796. The whole human race will be restored, to receive the due recompense for what it deserved in this age, whether good or evil, I, 527.

S. CYPRIAN.—We believe that the dead will rise, IV, 434. We mourn the dead: what would we do if God commanded only death without resurrection? Ibid. Hope of resurrection ought not to feel any loss whatever, ibid.

S. HILARY, bishop of Poitiers.—When these bodies have been dissolved and shattered by the fall of death, restoration will be granted at the will of their Maker, IX, 285. The renewal of the bodies of those who rise will take place according to God’s will, ibid. We know that salvation has been given by God both to soul and body, 402. The possibility of resurrection, 317, 318. Resurrection is not difficult for Him for whom the first beginning was easy, 411. We contemplate the hope of our resurrection in the risen Christ, 489. We behold ourselves rising from the dead in Christ rising, 415. We contemplate our resurrection in the resurrection in Christ of our body, 681. When we proclaim resurrection, the dead bodies of unbelievers, together with their vices, protest, 672. The hope of eternity is implanted in us: as there will be eternity for the soul, so too for the flesh, 401, 402. Resurrection must be hoped for with firm faith, 945. When Jesus raised Lazarus from the dead, He did not thereby indicate that there is no resurrection, 477. Faith in the resurrection to be hoped for is contained in the Law, 1046, 1047. Moses was seen with Christ at the Transfiguration so that it might be taught that the resurrection was decreed, 1014, 1015. Resurrection is the perfect gift of divine magnificence, 468. All flesh redeemed in Christ must rise, 360.

S. ZENO.—The Fathers frequently defended the doctrine of the resurrection, because certain Christians were being brought by pagan arguments into doubt, XI, 370, Note I. The Christian both hears and hopes for the future resurrection, 371, 372. Pythagoras and other philosophers in some manner admitted the resurrection of bodies, 373. If the soul is immortal, it must therefore be brought again into the body, 378. The Christian [Col. 0281] ought not doubt that the dead will be raised to their former state, 370. It is easier to restore what existed than to establish what previously did not exist, ibid. Resurrection is supported by the example of the setting and rising of the sun and stars, 380, 381; and of the moon, which gradually wanes and dies in order to live again, ibid.; of the phoenix, ibid.; and of a grain of wheat, which, buried in the earth, perishes so as to flower, 381, 382.

S. AMBROSE.—It belongs to divine power alone to command the dead to rise, XV, 1630. This is far more divine than forgiving sins, 1339. It is natural to all living creatures to be born and to die; but God bestowed especially upon humanity the grace of resurrection, so that one who has died may live again, XIV, 1076. Resurrection cannot easily be grasped except by the more perfected and firmly grounded, XV, 1846. Resurrection is no more incredible than Moses’s miracles and the other things recorded in the Gospel, XVI, 1335. Why should we wonder that what has existed can be born again, when we see that what had not existed has been born? 1333. The future resurrection of our body is proved by reason, by the example of the universe, and by testimony of accomplished fact, 1328. Reason shows that the body, like the soul, must receive reward or punishment for its deeds, 1328, 1329. The example of the universe is drawn from all the products of the earth, which die in order to rise again, 1329. It is natural for all things that are born to rise again; it is against nature to perish, 1330. We are taught to believe in resurrection by the examples of the Indian worm, the chameleon, and the phoenix, XIV, 258. If this is so for animals, God does not allow His saints to perish eternally, and He willed that the risen human being should be restored, ibid. Divine providence cares for the renewal of the crops and trees of the earth; does it then have no concern for human beings? XVI, 1330. Therefore let no one wonder how resurrection will occur or how decayed things will be made solid, 1329. If the elements rise at God’s word, why should not the dead rise at His word? Ibid. Accomplished fact proves it, for the dead have actually risen, ibid. Christ raised several persons, so that we might believe through more abundant examples, XVI, 1338, 1339.

Resurrection must be accepted, as is shown by the testimonies of the Old Testament, 1335 ff., and of the New Testament, 1337, 1338. Christ promised resurrection, and we must believe Him, 1340. The flesh must rise, since it is to receive the recompense for its deeds, 356. This is the order and rationale of justice: because the action belongs jointly to body and soul, both must come to judgment, and both must either be handed over to punishment or renewed in glory, 1340. If the transgressor is preserved for punishment, why should the righteous not be perpetuated for glory? If the worm of sinners does not die, why should the flesh of the righteous die? Ibid. All who are joined to the most holy Church and enrolled under the name of the divine Name will receive the prerogative of resurrection and eternal delight, XVI, 1349. The saints hoped for resurrection, 1354. It is pleasing to believe this; it is delightful to hope; not to have believed is punishment, to have hoped is grace, ibid. What sorrow does the grace of resurrection not console? What grief does it not banish, if you believe that nothing perishes through death? 1315. How weary we would become of this life if we saw that the labors of this body were to last for us without end! 1351. The resurrection of the dead was given so that guilt might cease while nature nevertheless endured, XIV, 547. It is a grave sacrilege not to believe in the resurrection, XVI, 1344. For by denying our resurrection, Christ’s resurrection too is denied, ibid.

ZACCHAEUS THE CHRISTIAN.—When the time of judgment arrives, every departed soul will receive its body, XX, 1091. Resurrection is possible for God: He who created all things can restore all things, ibid. It is demonstrated by comparison with trees and growing things, which each year either change or perish in order to live again, ibid. That human beings are easily raised is inferred from Ezekiel, 1163; and from other testimonies of Holy Scripture, 1164.

S. JEROME.—The flesh that has been reborn in Christ cannot perish, XXIII, 389. I confess that true, incorrupt, and immortal bodies will rise, XXIV, 628. Jerome does not doubt the general resurrection, 349. A powerful argument drawn from Holy Scripture proves it, ibid.; XXVI, 164. The resurrection was believed by Jews and Christians, XXIV, 346, 347.

S. AUGUSTINE.—The possibility of the resurrection of the flesh is commended, XXXVI, 751; XL, 194, 195, 342, 346, 347, 659. Creation ought to induce faith in resurrection, XXXVIII, 713; as also should what Christ accomplished, 727. Christ raised certain persons so that we might be prepared for the general resurrection, XXXV, 1746. The production of a tree from a tiny seed is no less, nor more, wonderful than the earth’s bosom returning whole bodies for the future resurrection, XXXIII, 372. It is just as easy for God’s omnipotence to raise newly dead persons as corpses long dissolved by time, ibid. Resurrection belongs only to rational creatures, XL, 650. The promise of resurrection is confirmed by so many other promises of God already fulfilled, XXXVIII, 1145. Faith in resurrection [Col. 0282] was commended when Job’s sons were restored not doubled, but in the same number as he had possessed, XXXIII, 549. Elijah and Elisha raised the dead, 521. The impossibility of resurrection objected by unbelievers is refuted by their own philosophers, XLI, 794. From the opinions of Plato and Porphyry the truth of the resurrection of the flesh is elicited, 793. It is more marvelous for incorporeal minds to be bound to earthly bodies than for earthly bodies to be raised to heavenly ones, 755. That resurrection can occur, and will in fact occur, is proved, XL, 627, 1163; both from God’s promises and from the eternity of souls, 1027. In no matter is the Christian faith so opposed as in the resurrection of the flesh, XXXVII, 1134. Resurrection is asserted against heretics, XXXII, 601, 1077, 1170; XXXV, 1554, 1580; XXXVIII, 712, 713, 1131; XXXIX, 1600, 1603, 1609, 1626, 1629; XLI, 754, 771, 795, 796. It is asserted against the Manichaeans, XLII, 847. We have already risen in mind, faith, hope, and charity; it remains for us to rise in body, XXXVI, 899. Resurrection of bodies is promised, XXXV, 1332. The promised resurrection is contrary to bodily death, XLIV, 112. Resurrection of the spirit precedes resurrection of the flesh, 232. The flesh will rise through the death of the soul, XXXVIII, 427. The future resurrection of the flesh will be for all human beings, XL, 272. Resurrection is shown from the omnipotence and truth of God, XXXIX, 1961; from creation and the quickening of seeds, ibid. He who gives life to grains of seed that die and decay, by which you live in this age, will much more raise you yourself so that you may live eternally, 1662. Created things bear witness to the future resurrection, ibid. As a plant which once lived, dies, and lives again from dust, so our body too lives again from dust, 1962. Christ’s resurrection is the pledge of ours, ibid. The Lord willed to rise so that we, encouraged by such an example, might most certainly believe in resurrection from the dead, ibid. Whoever does not believe that it will occur does not believe that Christ rose either, ibid. One must not doubt what Christ promised, ibid. Resurrection is a benefit and a matter of grace, XL, 660. It is a more wonderful power of grace that the righteous should live again from death to eternal blessedness than that they should not undergo death, 160.

CASSIAN.—Resurrection is called generation, since it regenerates unto life, L, 113.

S. PROSPER OF AQUITAINE.—Christ rose so that the hope of all believers might not doubt that what had gone before in the Head would be fulfilled, LI, 377, 402. This hope of resurrection must not be frightened by adversities, nor obscured by terrors, but must be steadfastly preserved to the end of life, 577.

S. PETER CHRYSOLOGUS.—One departed is raised by God more quickly than a sleeper is awakened by a human being, LII, 298. You rightly believe if you believe that, through God, you can rise from that death from which the elements always rise, 360. Flesh which has decayed and perished will rise through God, 375. Resurrection is the whole hope of the Christian faith, 522. And who doubts that slain martyrs rise, live, and reign? 314. The sheep which followed unto death must necessarily follow unto life. Human being, let faith not disturb you; let a hope so far-reaching not weary you, ibid. What is buried in death will rise in glory, 666.

S. NICETAS, bishop of Aquileia.—It is called resurrection because God will raise all bodies from the graves, LII, 865. If you fear the setting of the body, remember that there is resurrection, 866. If you do not believe in resurrection, you believe in God in vain, 871. Heretics who claim salvation for the soul alone are refuted, ibid.

S. MAXIMUS OF TURIN.—The resurrection of the dead was the chief purpose for which the Son of God assumed flesh: that He might endow flesh with perpetuity, LVII, 439, 440. The resurrection of the flesh must be believed, since it is the end of our religion and the sum of what must be believed, ibid. The whole hope of Christians rests in faith in resurrection, 776, 777. This ought to be fixed more firmly in us: when we depart from here, we shall one day return to our bodies, 943.

AURELIUS PRUDENTIUS.—The resurrection of the dead is shown from the care owed to graves, LX, 698.

S. PAULINUS OF NOLA.—The resurrection of the dead is proved by the example of Christ restored to life, LXI, 222. The Word of God both promised and taught the resurrection of the flesh unto eternal life, and proved it by rising again, ibid., 440, 441. By dying to this world through faith, may we be made alive to God, 204.

PRIMASIUS OF ADRUMETUM.—If the Head has risen, the other members too must follow, since Christ first rose in incorruptibility, LXVIII, 544.

GREGORY OF TOURS.—We believe that after death we shall live through the future resurrection, LXXI, 865. Gregory proves this against a presbyter infected with the venom of Sadducean malignity, 540, 541, 542. All things have been made manifest to the world in support of faith in resurrection, ibid. If there is to be no resurrection, what benefit will it be for the righteous to do good, [Col. 0283] and what harm for sinners to do evil? 543. “Let all fall into their own desires . . . if there is to be no resurrection,” 543. It is confirmed by a miracle, 788, 789.

S. GREGORY THE GREAT.—Beyond doubt, everyone knows that creating what did not exist is greater than repairing what did exist, LXXV, 738, 739. What difficulty is there in dust returning through resurrection to limbs, when we daily behold the Creator’s power, who wonderfully creates wood from a grain and, still more wonderfully, fruit from wood? 739, 740. Since we have been created rational, we ought from the very appearance and contemplation of things to gather hope for our resurrection, 1077. What wonder if, when God wills, He reforms into a human being the finest dust, reduced in the elements beyond our sight, He who restores huge shrubs from exceedingly small seeds? Ibid. Both Testaments proclaim the future resurrection, LXXXVI, 1031, 1032. Faith in resurrection is asserted most clearly and excellently, LXXV, 1076. The resurrection of many dead persons at Christ’s resurrection strengthens our confidence, LXXV, 1076; LXXVI, 1528, 1529. Many things in nature are no less hidden from us than resurrection, LXXVI, 1032, 1033. Human generation is a greater miracle than resurrection, 1033. The only reason in miracles is the power of the one who performs them, 1034. Christ showed in an example what He promised us as a reward, 1172. We shall answer God when He calls, when at the command to supreme incorruption we rise incorruptible, LXXV, 995. Who can weigh the abundance of divine mercy in this, that after sin it brings a human being to such glory? 996. Without faith in resurrection, all other beliefs are in vain, LXXVI, 1034.

TAIO, bishop of Saragossa.—Our flesh will be subtle but tangible, because it will not lose the essence of its true nature, 985. It will be the same by nature, different by power, ibid.

S. ISIDORE OF SEVILLE.—There will not be a first resurrection of the righteous and a second of sinners, as the fable of dreamers holds, but one resurrection of all, LXXXIII, 1230. The same corruptible flesh which falls will rise incorruptible, both that of righteous and of unrighteous, ibid. Those found alive at the end of the world will, according to many learned men, be suddenly changed into immortality without prior death, ibid. Resurrection will be at the age of youth, which needs no further growth, 594. Resurrection will take place at the measure of the age of Christ’s fullness, ibid.

S. HILDEFONSUS, bishop of Toledo.—In the resurrection nothing of human flesh will perish, XCVI, 142. Almighty God will wonderfully and ineffably restore in the resurrection, with marvelous swiftness, everything of which flesh consists, ibid. The bodies of the saints will rise spiritual, yet they will not be spirits, 143.

S. JULIAN, bishop of Toledo.—No human being knows the day of resurrection, XCVI, 497. The resurrection of the dead will occur in the twinkling of an eye, 503. Those who say that there will be two resurrections follow an error, 504. Resurrection will concern all human beings, but transformation only the saints, ibid. It is not an aerial body, but the flesh we wear, without any corruption, that will rise, ibid. Human beings will rise at the age or stature which they had in youth, or would have had if they had lived, 505. Men and women will rise in their own sex. No concern for food, drink, or clothing will trouble those who rise, 508. From the moment a human being begins to live in the mother’s womb, that person is believed to belong to the final resurrection, 509. Humans born as monsters will receive resurrection, but with the monstrous form removed, 510. Bodies dispersed in any manner or mutilated by various tearing will recover wholeness, ibid. Whether the bodies of the wicked rise with defects and deformities ought not to be investigated, 513.

ALCUIN.—The resurrection of the saints follows the Antichristian persecution, C, 1149. At the end of the age there will be a resurrection not of souls but of bodies, CI, 50.

RABANUS MAURUS.—The order and times when the resurrection of the dead will occur are expounded, CX, 287, 288.

HAYMO, bishop of Halberstadt.—God will raise bodies animated by their own spirits, CXVII, 600. Every human being will rise in his or her own body, ibid. Those found alive at the end of the age will die suddenly and rise suddenly, 773. The swiftness of resurrection, 772.

REGINO OF PRÜM.—Human beings will rise in their own proper flesh, CXXXII, 228, 248.

S. ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury.—A human being will be restored with the body in which he or she lives in this life, CLVIII, 401, 402. Such a person must be restored as he or she would have been if he or she had not sinned, 402.

S. BRUNO, bishop of Segni.—The dogma of the resurrection is most fully established by the testimony of Job, who says that his hope is laid up in his bosom, CLXIV, 618, 619. This truth is also argued from the fact that the wicked will be tormented eternally in their own flesh; Job says of the condemned: A fire that is not extinguished will devour him; he that is left in his tent will be afflicted, 622. For once the soul has been separated from the body, it never returns to it again except, by divine decree, at the time appointed for all, 1000.

RUPERT, abbot of Deutz.—The resurrection is twofold, of soul and body, CLXX, 175. That resurrection already accomplished in Christ must be accomplished in all, CLXVII, 629. Resurrection is necessary, 1667, and was wrongly denied by the Sadducees, CLXIX, 99, 100.

GODEFRID, abbot of Admont.—As each person's body was a partner in merit during life, so it will be a partner in reward in heaven, CLXXIV, 801, 802. Our resurrection is certain to all, either unto life or unto damnation, 606.

HERVAEUS, monk of Bourg-Dieu.—All the hope of believers lies in this: that the dead will rise, CLXXXI, 972.

S. BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux.—The faith of bodily resurrection is established, CLXXXIII, 210.

PETER LOMBARD.—Christ's resurrection is our general resurrection, CXCI, 1314, 1315. Commendation of the resurrection, 1678, 1679, 1680.

BONACURSUS, a Catholic converted from heresy.—The resurrection is proved from the testimonies of both the Old and New Testaments, CCIV, 782, 783.

ERMENGAUDUS.—The Waldensians, who destroy the doctrine of bodily resurrection, are refuted by many authorities, CCIV, 1266, 1267.

III.—When and how will the resurrection of the dead take place?

TERTULLIAN.—For a dead person to be raised is nothing other than to be made whole, II, 878. To rise is proper only to that which has fallen, 491. The flesh will rise—indeed all of it, indeed the very same flesh, indeed whole, 885. What is it to believe in resurrection except to believe it whole? 878. However a body has been dissolved, it will rise, I, 525. Wherever you have been dissolved, whatever matter has destroyed, swallowed, obliterated, or reduced you to nothing, will restore you, 525. We shall rise without defects, II, 878. If flesh is repaired after dissolution, much more will it be recalled after injury, ibid. Bodily injury is accidental; wholeness is proper to it, ibid. All flesh and blood rise alike in their own condition, 868. In the resurrection souls will receive the same bodies in which they departed, 746. The resurrection will take place after the destruction of Antichrist, II, 835. It will occur at the last time and on the first threshold of eternity, I, 526. There will be a resurrection only once, because God so willed, 525. There will be neither death any longer nor resurrection again and again; rather, we shall be the same persons we now are, and not others thereafter, 527.

S. HILARY, bishop of Poitiers.—The same body will rise, IX, 361. It will not rise as another body, although it will rise into another condition, 286. The body has not lost its origin, but has advanced to honor, ibid. It will be new by transformation rather than creation, 285, 286. In the resurrection of bodies, substance will not be abolished, but earthly weight will be, 974. The nature of the glorified body in resurrection will be solid and thence mutable, 659. Bodies will be formed into the shape and solidity of their members, 467. Women will rise in their own form, 1046, without allurements, ibid. Bodies are to be raised to the stature of the perfect man, 947. It is useless to ask what bodily appearance or nourishment will then be, 944, 945, 946. The common opinion is that the prophetic Scriptures contain nothing concerning the conditions of resurrection, 1045. The time of resurrection will come when the fullness of the Gentiles who are to believe is completed, 700. The time of resurrection is the mercy of morning, 841. The apostles will precede the rest in the glory and time of resurrection, 1038.

S. AMBROSE, bishop of Milan.—While the reality of the body remains, the body will be changed into incorruption, XIV, 949. An angelic likeness is promised us; the substance of flesh is not denied, XVII, 535. It is Catholic and right to confess that both sexes will remain in the resurrection of the flesh, without the functions of sex, ibid. There will be a true resurrection of flesh without the functions of flesh, ibid. We shall rise into the perfect man, who is Christ, 536. After the resurrection we shall neither eat nor drink, nor perform other such necessities, 537, 538, 539. The opinion of philosophers who say that our souls pass into the bodies of beasts and various living creatures is refuted, 1352, 1353. It is contrary to reason that a human being, to whom the kinds of other living creatures are subject, should pass, in the better part of himself, into an animal subject to him, 1335. Bodily wholeness will be restored to those swallowed by the sea or devoured by beasts, XVI, 1330, 1331. The resurrection will be deferred as long as all who are predestined to life believe, XVII, 468.

S. JEROME.—That which dies in a human being is also what is made alive, XXIII, 385. The truth of resurrection cannot be understood without flesh and bones, blood and members, 282. One must either be crowned in the body which acted chastely and justly, or condemned in the body which served pleasures and iniquity, 385. In the resurrection the substance of bodies will be the same as that which we now use, although with greater glory, 261. The word resurrection signifies not that one body dies and another is raised, 385. Elijah and Enoch were taken into heaven in the same flesh of their own, 380, 381. We shall rise into the perfect man and to the measure of the age of Christ's fullness, XXII, 902.

S. AUGUSTINE.—The very flesh which is buried will rise, XXXVIII, 1192, 1217. We shall all rise in our own bodies, XXXIX, 1965, 2175, 2181, 2182, 2192, 2193. In the resurrection flesh will be spiritual, and yet flesh, XLI, 783. Then bodies will be spiritual, while all their members nevertheless remain, XXXIII, 350. Some members of the body are for use, others for appearance, XXXVIII, 1145, 1146. Neither the inward members nor the hearts themselves will be hidden after the resurrection, 1145. All will rise in their own bodies and sex, XL, 1185, changing not sex but frailty, XXXIX, 2191. Flesh will rise without defect, XXXVIII, 1131. The bodies of the godly will rise without every blemish, yet the same in the substance of flesh, XL, 274. Nothing in bodily stature or appearance will be unbecoming, 293. How will an earthly body be in heaven? XXXVIII, 1140. The body will easily be lifted into heaven if the burden of sins does not weigh down the spirit, 1211. After the resurrection the body will be able to take food, but will not need it, XXXIII, 372. It will have the power of eating, as Christ did, but not the necessity, XXXVIII, 1139.

Human flesh that has passed into another person's food and flesh will be restored to the one to whom it first belonged, XL, 273. How superfluous matter will return to the body, ibid. Various difficulties concerning the size of resurrected bodies, XLI, 776, 777. At what size each person will rise, 783. The bodies of all the dead will rise according to the measure of the Lord's body, 777. Aborted fetuses will rise; what was not yet whole will be made whole, and what had been damaged will be restored, XL, 272, 273. A two-membered human being will not rise as one human being but as two human beings, ibid. Bodies scattered in whatever ways will be restored whole in the resurrection, XLI, 782. Children who died before or after baptism will rise, but at full age, XXXIII, 730; XXXVIII, 1140.

S. MAXIMUS OF TURIN.—This body, which is perishable in its nature, is to be renewed into the complete solidity of its members and into a state of beauty and comeliness, LVII, 943. When the saints rise, they will obtain their original wholeness and fullness of glory; we have been confirmed in this hope because in Christ we know that there is a true human being, 944, 945.

GENNADIUS OF MARSEILLES.—The resurrection is of all human beings, but one, simultaneous, and once for all, LVIII, 982. It will not, according to Origen, be a transformation—that is, a different new body in place of flesh, 982 note, 1016. In the resurrection the form of sex will not be changed, 998. A man will rise in the form of a man, a woman in the form of a woman, ibid. Even malformed aborted fetuses will rise, note 1015. Resuscitated bodies, free from corruption, will not lose their proper nature, note 1016. Learned men say that those found alive at the resurrection, while the soul remains in the body, will be changed to incorruption and immortality, 983.

S. FULGENTIUS OF RUSPE.—Male or female sex, as it was in creation, will remain in the resurrection, LXV, 688, 508. The flesh and soul of the righteous will be changed, but will remain the same, 702.

S. GREGORY THE GREAT.—After the resurrection our flesh will be the same in nature and different in glory, LXXV, 1079. Job believed that our flesh would be restored to a whole condition, ibid. By adhering to the spirit, flesh is preserved forever; by adhering to flesh, the spirit is preserved unto God, LXXVII, 321. The time of resurrection was foreseen and foretold by Job, LXXVI, 354. Christ's resurrection occurred on the third day; ours is deferred until the end of the world, LXXV, 1075.

[Col. 0286] TAIO, bishop of Saragossa.—Our flesh will be subtle but tangible, because it will not lose the essence of its true nature, 985. It will be the same by nature, different by power, ibid.

S. ISIDORE OF SEVILLE.—There will not be a first resurrection of the righteous and a second of sinners, as the fable of dreamers holds, but one resurrection of all, LXXXIII, 1230. The same corruptible flesh which falls will rise incorruptible, both that of righteous and of unrighteous, ibid. Those found alive at the end of the world will, according to many learned men, be suddenly changed into immortality without prior death, ibid. Resurrection will be at the age of youth, which needs no further growth, 594. Resurrection will take place at the measure of the age of Christ’s fullness, ibid.

S. HILDEFONSUS, bishop of Toledo.—In the resurrection nothing of human flesh will perish, XCVI, 142. Almighty God will wonderfully and ineffably restore in the resurrection, with marvelous swiftness, everything of which flesh consists, ibid. The bodies of the saints will rise spiritual, yet they will not be spirits, 143.

S. JULIAN, bishop of Toledo.—No human being knows the day of resurrection, XCVI, 497. The resurrection of the dead will occur in the twinkling of an eye, 503. Those who say that there will be two resurrections follow an error, 504. Resurrection will concern all human beings, but transformation only the saints, ibid. It is not an aerial body, but the flesh we wear, without any corruption, that will rise, ibid. Human beings will rise at the age or stature which they had in youth, or would have had if they had lived, 505. Men and women will rise in their own sex. No concern for food, drink, or clothing will trouble those who rise, 508. From the moment a human being begins to live in the mother’s womb, that person is believed to belong to the final resurrection, 509. Humans born as monsters will receive resurrection, but with the monstrous form removed, 510. Bodies dispersed in any manner or mutilated by various tearing will recover wholeness, ibid. Whether the bodies of the wicked rise with defects and deformities ought not to be investigated, 513.

ALCUIN.—The resurrection of the saints follows the Antichristian persecution, C, 1149. At the end of the age there will be a resurrection not of souls but of bodies, CI, 50.

RABANUS MAURUS.—The order and times when the resurrection of the dead will occur are expounded, CX, 287, 288.

HAYMO, bishop of Halberstadt.—God will raise bodies animated by their own spirits, CXVII, 600. Every human being will rise in his or her own body, ibid. Those found alive at the end of the age will die suddenly and rise suddenly, 773. The swiftness of resurrection, 772.

REGINO OF PRÜM.—Human beings will rise in their own proper flesh, CXXXII, 228, 248.

S. ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury.—A human being will be restored with the body in which he or she lives in this life, CLVIII, 401, 402. Such a person must be restored as he or she would have been if he or she had not sinned, 402.

S. BRUNO, bishop of Segni.—In the general resurrection, the bodies of all human beings will rise from their tombs at the trumpet’s sound, perfect and whole in every part, CLXIV, 595, 596. He maintains this against heretics who deny that bodies will be whole, 595.

HUGH OF ST. VICTOR.—The saints who are found alive at Christ’s coming will pass with wondrous swiftness through death into immortality, CLXXVI, 601. The resurrection will be in true flesh, 602. Because Christ showed his doubting disciples that his flesh was the same as before, ibid. If I rise in an airy body, I shall no longer be the one who rises, 601. The restoration of all limbs, however they may have been scattered, is promised, 603. All will rise in bodies as great as they either were, or would have been, in youthful age, 605.

ROBERT PULLUS.—The resurrection will assuredly do two things: it will supply what was lacking to the living, and restore what after death has been dispersed in any manner whatever, CLXXXVI, 983. At the resurrection some things are to be taken up again, others left behind, 987. Each person who is to rise will have neither less nor more than is fitting, ibid. Human beings will rise at that bodily stature which each had at the thirtieth year of life, or would have had if he had lived, 988.

PETER LOMBARD.—The Jews believed in the future resurrection, but in such a way that they would marry and beget children there, CXCI, 1689. The resurrection will occur with the utmost swiftness, ibid. Those alive at the end of the world will not rise unless death has preceded, ibid. We shall rise unto a perfect man, so that nothing will be lacking to anyone and nothing further need be added, CXCII, 202; and at the age at which Christ rose, 201.

ALAN OF LILLE.—Our bodies, from which souls will be separated, will be the same bodies that are raised, CCX, 325.

IV.—What qualities or transformations bodies will have, and how these will bring glory to the righteous but shame to the damned.

[Col. 0287]

TERTULLIAN.—At the resurrection the saints will be clothed over with the proper substance of eternity; the profane, however, and those not whole before God, [will be] in the punishment of an equally unceasing fire, I, 527. In God’s kingdom the flesh will be restored and made angelic, II, 632. After the resurrection flesh will assume an angelic condition, 854. The dead will rise according to the order of their merits, I, 864. All who have died from the beginning will be raised, reviewed, and restored according to the merits of each, 378. The limbs will be delivered from their functions and necessities, II, 882, 883, 884. We shall rise without lusts and disordered motions, 879. The flesh will remain incapable of suffering, 880; incorruptible, ibid.

LACTANTIUS.—After the resurrection the flesh will be indissoluble and enduring, failing neither under torments nor under fire, VI, 801.

ST. HILARY, bishop of Poitiers.—There will be a resurrection of all, but it will not be glorious for all, IX, 468. Christ will make the saints conformable to the glory of his body, 469. All flesh will rise, but not all will be transformed, 481. All flesh redeemed in Christ must rise; nevertheless, glory and honour in rising are not promised indiscriminately to all, 360. Only those who have died with Christ through faith will be transformed by resurrection, 355. The resurrection of the ungodly will be for punishment, IX, 258. Their body is compared to dust and mud, 258, and is reserved only for the nature of a penal substance, ibid. Their bone remains wandering, crushed, winnowed, scattered, and restless, ibid. Then every ungodly person will be put to shame, both by the disgrace of his own condition and by comparison with another’s honour, 334. They are to be shamed, not running to heavenly things but returning to their own earthly and original things, 715. The earthly will rise in a body of disgrace, 744, 745. Their resurrection is compared to foul water and liquefied earth, 370. The resurrection of the ungodly is without transformation; salvation is unto nothingness, 360. The holy people, with every corruption and weakness driven away, will be clothed over with heavenly honour, 469. No longer will human life’s transformation be subject to bodily growth, nourishment by foods, and the accidents of weakness; rather, eternity will be bestowed on all—a condition which, by the power of its own nature, contains itself, that is, feeds and preserves itself—465. When Christ is again in us through fellowship of the flesh, he will swallow up death and restore immortal and eternal life, ibid. We shall inhabit the heavenly city and the Church of spirits founded in the Lord, 682. The resurrection of corruptible bodies will be into the glory of incorruption, 286. Therefore the resurrection of the righteous is not to be doubted, since they will be like the substance of angels, 948. The bodies of the righteous are lilies breathing forth life, a flower ever blooming, 948, 949. A glorious resurrection; nuptials, 1061. Whatever takes place in us will be eternal, with the consciousness of blessedness, 258. Wherein that transformation of bodies consists, 361. Bodily weakness, falls, and tears will be removed, ibid. Incorruption will devour corruption; immortal power will swallow up death, ibid. Those granted resurrection will lack nothing for the substance of body and soul, 876, 877. After the resurrection there is perfect blessedness: without desire, fear of enemies, or troubles, 393, 394, 876. The reward of those living rightly and perfectly is that they be transferred from the matter of this corruptible body into a new and heavenly substance, 949. Therefore let us be reborn through the progress of a new birth and be refashioned into that blessed, God-pleasing form of our renewed restoration, 286.

ST. ZENO.—There is a twofold mode of rising: the first, of the saints, who under Christ as leader will be brought into blessedness; the second, of the ungodly, who are appointed to punishment, XI, 382. The flesh will rise now pure, now free, now superior to death, now breathing heavenly things, seeking truth, and desiring spiritual things, 383.

ST. AMBROSE.—We shall be raised according to the order of our merits, XVI, 1349. All shall rise, but the grace of coming to life and the condition thereof will differ, 1341. The flower of resurrection is immortality; the flower of resurrection is incorruption, 1329. That rest is to be sought, to which the perpetual delight of the future resurrection will succeed, where there is no succession of sins and no enticement to transgression, 1351. All the righteous will be transformed unto brightness at the resurrection, XVII, 534. Death is from the earth, whereas resurrection is from heaven—provided, however, that one is transformed unto glory, 295. The ungodly will rise, but in order to perish, 271; the saints, however, will be transformed in brightness, ibid. They will rightly differ in glory, 268. At the time of resurrection every bond of the devil will be loosed, and all his triumph will no longer exist, XIV, 1082. Let us now be renewed in grace, so that renewed flesh may receive the radiance of eternal light, XVI, 1349.

[Col. 0288]

ZACCHAEUS THE CHRISTIAN.—It pleased divine mercy to restore appearances, so that splendour might adorn the bodies of the good, while the shame of deformity might darken the wicked, XX, 1092. The righteous will rise into eternal joys; light, multiplied beyond the sun from the sight of God, will be poured in upon them, 1094. According to the differing degrees of righteousness, they will possess the brightness of the sun, ibid. Thus each will enjoy the honours of attained happiness, so that neither the higher is exalted nor the lower despised, ibid. A gentle, perpetual temperateness and the inestimable joys of that blessedness will remain; no recollection of things past will torment them, 1095. Even if the coming abolition did not remove the use of this present world, the righteous would nevertheless rejoice rather at having passed beyond it than grieve, ibid. What is the splendour of heavenly dignities to them, what the grace of eternal riches which they will possess? 1164, 1165. Take this as certain: nothing necessary will be lacking to them; but God will bring forth for all all things in the newness of inestimable joys that may be judged worthy of possessing his presence, 1165.

ST. JEROME.—The resurrection of the dead will be incorruptible and perpetually enduring, XXII, 827. Likeness to angels is not a transformation of human beings into angels, but an advance into immortality and glory, XXIII, 382. Saint and sinner will be perfected in a like resurrection, nor will they differ from one another in time; but one will be drawn to rewards, the other to punishments, XXIV, 616. In this the sinner will be accursed: with an incorrupt body he will suffer eternal punishments, 646.

ST. AUGUSTINE.—The rising flesh will be changed and itself become a heavenly and angelic body, XXXVIII, 1217; and a spiritual body, 1142. How our body will be spiritual after the resurrection, XXXIII, 628; XXXV, 2061, 2062; XL, 674. Some think that the body is to be changed into spirit, XXXIII, 618. Those who think that the body then becomes spiritual when it is changed into spirit are refuted, 945. The inconveniences consequent upon this opinion, 619.—Augustine thinks, though without complete confidence, that the body may then be called spiritual because of a certain ineffable facility, 629. This mortal body, raised again, is transferred into an angelic condition and a heavenly quality, XXXVII, 1682. The qualities of spiritual bodies, regarded by Augustine as virtually beyond doubt: mortality, corruption, and the weight of heaviness are taken away from them, XXXIII, 623.

The body of the saints after resurrection will be immortal, XLIV, 113. All will rise incorrupt, but among them the righteous also will be transformed into that incorruption to which corruption could do no harm at all, XXXIII, 947. The body of the saints after resurrection will be wholly incorruptible, wholly immortal, wholly agile and easy to move, XXXVIII, 1137. The stability of bodies after resurrection, XXXII, 603. In the bodies of the blessed there will be brightness, and differing degrees of brightness because the merits of love differ, XXXVIII, 1138. In the bodies of the blessed there will be beauty, complete in all, 1146. By resurrection our life will be like that of angels, free from the operations of corruption and need, 1623, 1631. Nothing will resist our spirit, XXXVII, 1688. The heavenly body, after Christ’s example, will be able to enter a house with doors closed, XXXVIII, 1264. We must believe that we shall have bodies such that we may be wherever we wish, whenever we wish, 1140, 1143. The resurrection will accomplish the transformation of the whole human being for the better, XL, 193, 194. The body after resurrection will be better than that of the first parents in paradise, XXXII, 601.

The resurrection of the body will be for good to some, for evil to others: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 709; XXXVII, 1672; XXXIV, 144. We shall rise neither to sufferings of pain, like the ungodly, nor to the delights of fleshly desires, XXXVIII, 1059. The wicked will rise incorrupt in the integrity of their limbs, but subject to corruption through the pain of punishments, XXXIII, 947. There will be a certain firmness of bodies, but a corruptible firmness, ibid. How will they be incorruptible if they suffer pain, or corruptible if they cannot die? XL, 275. At the resurrection the glory of merits will differ, XXXIII, 947. After resurrection the whole human being, made divine, will cleave to immutable truth, 909. He will enjoy first this happiness: that he will begin neither to will to sin further, nor be able to do so, XXXIX, 1964. When every misery and sorrow have ceased, innocence wholly and happiness wholly will possess him, ibid. In human breasts, the charity of angels—among whom human beings, having received heavenly flesh, are joined—will shine without the weakness of flesh, ibid. They will suffer no further weariness from the everlasting power of their Lord, nor any failure amid the perpetual exultation of their praises, ibid.

ST. PROSPER OF AQUITANIA.—Resurrection is called a generation which creates the saints unto the incorruption of blessed eternity, LI, 414.

ST. PETER CHRYSOLOGUS.—The character of our resurrection is indicated by an angel’s glory, [Col. 0289] LII, 411. Humanity will be restored in the very brightness of the angelic body, 419. There the flesh will be possessed by the spirit, not the flesh possess the spirit, where corruption, fault, and crime perish, 522. When the innocent rise, terror and death will take possession of the ungodly, 419. In the resurrection the saints will see all that belongs to divine light, honour, and glory, 664, 665. Then the labouring reaper will see in harvest what he does not see in seed, and he who weeps in the furrow will rejoice in the fruit, 314. Let resurrection, therefore, always sound in our mouth; let resurrection always be conveyed to the hearing of our mind, 522. We must pray that we may die to vices and be buried to temporal pomp, so that we may rise in Christ unto eternity, 431, 432.

ST. NICETAS, bishop of Aquileia.—The raised bodies of the saints no longer fear death, LII, 872. They will live with Christ in heaven: this is the hope for which we are born, believe, and are reborn, 873. Let the mind always be in heaven, hope in the resurrection, and desire in the promise, 874.

PATRICK, apostle of the Irish.—After resurrection the elect have a threefold vision: bodily, by which bodies are seen; spiritual, by which they behold likenesses of bodies in the spirit and not in deceptive fantasy; intellectual, by which with the pure eye of the mind they will see God in the Spirit, as well as their own souls, their inmost powers, and angelic spirits, LIII, 838.

ST. MAXIMUS OF TURIN.—The righteous possessed flesh without earth, body without the sensation of pain, soul without fear, life without end, age without time, light without death, and blessedness without end, LVII, 945. Resurrection is a reward to the righteous, 596. But unbelievers, sinners, and those who do not fulfil God’s commandments must rise in order that their flesh, made immortal, may be committed to eternal fires, 777, 778.

GENNADIUS OF MARSEILLES.—The same corruptible flesh of both righteous and unrighteous will rise incorruptible, LVIII, 982: able either to endure punishment for sins or to remain in eternal glory for merits, 983.

JULIANUS POMERIUS.—Incorruption and immortality will be given to the bodies of the wretched; immortal punishment will not consume them but punish them, LIX, 420. The bodies of the righteous will be endowed with blessed incorruption and immortality, so that eternal glory may remain both in them and they in glory, 420. After resurrection no visible creature will be hidden from bodily eyes, because the sight of incorruptible bodies will certainly be incorruptible, ibid. When human substance has been exalted to the likeness of its Creator, all goods naturally corrupted by sin will be restored for the better, 422. When bodies have been endowed with immortality, slowness is to be removed, not integrity; necessity, not will, so that they may be without delay of time or weight of themselves wherever they wish to be, 427. The life to come is believed to be blessedly everlasting and everlastingly blessed, where there is sure security, secure tranquillity, happy eternity, and eternal happiness, 420. Human nature, perfectly made blessed, will behold the glory of its Creator and its own glory, 427.

ST. FULGENTIUS OF RUSPE.—At the resurrection the righteous, but not the unrighteous, will be transformed, LXV, 688. Corruption, ignobility, and weakness, in which the bodies of the ungodly are sown, will not be removed from them, 688. There are different degrees of glory in the bodies of those rising, 807. The first degree is shown to belong to virgins, the second to the continent, the third to married persons, 507, 508. The righteous in recompense will become equal to angels, 283. The body will be spiritual, not because body itself will be spirit, but because, enlivened by the Spirit, it will remain immortal and incorruptible, 702.

ST. GREGORY THE GREAT.—At the resurrection our body will be subtle through the effect of spiritual power, yet tangible through the truth of nature, LXXV, 1077. We must hasten with entire purpose toward the glory of resurrection, LXXVI, 1204.

TAIO, bishop of Saragossa.—At the resurrection all the elect, separated from the reprobate, will rejoice, LXXX, 987. All the wicked, struck by final vengeance, will be put to shame, 987.

ST. ILDEFONSUS, bishop of Toledo.—The bodies of the reprobate will indeed rise, but with their defects and deformities, to be punished perpetually, XCVI, 143. Holy bodies in their diversity will possess only what is fitting, ibid.

JULIAN, bishop of Toledo.—How much subtler the movements of the body will be at the resurrection, XCVI, 520. After resurrection we shall see God by the vision by which angels now see him, 522. We shall have both forgetfulness and remembrance, ibid. All the saints will enjoy a liberty much firmer than that of this life, ibid. There will be diversity of merits and rewards, yet none will envy another, 523.

ALCUIN.—The body will rise clothed in incorruption and immortality, CI, 52. Although flesh is not spirit, it will nevertheless not be subject to fleshly defects, ibid.

[Col. 0290]

JONAH, bishop of Orléans.—Righteous and unrighteous alike will rise; but the righteous in order to be transformed, while the unrighteous pass from corruption to perpetual and ineffable corruption, CVI, 268. Everyone must strive that resurrection may come to us for glory, not reproach, 269.

RABANUS MAURUS, archbishop of Mainz.—Those renewed by the glory of resurrection will enjoy the perpetual vision of God, without any fear of death or stain of corruption, CX, 289. In the resurrection the saints will know more fully what good God’s grace has bestowed, 144. The ungodly also will rise, each in his own flesh, so that they may be punished with the devil and his angels, CX, 144. The diversity and qualities of bodies to come in the resurrection, 410, 411, 412. If the consolation of resurrection is so great, let mourning for the dead perish, 131.

HAYMO, bishop of Halberstadt.—The endowments of the righteous will be more glorious; those of the damned, a most shameful deformity, CXVII. After resurrection human creation will be so perfected that it can no longer be changed for better or worse, CXVIII, 881. No secret thing will be hidden from the perfectly blessed, CXVIII, 881. The incorruptibility, freedom, and blessedness of the elect, 882. The glory of incorrupt bodies will shine forth most brightly, 881. The splendour of the future light will be such as bodily sight could not endure, ibid. The elect will recognize all the good, ibid. The glorious elect will be raised with the Lord to things above, whereas the reprobate will remain in the lowest regions of hell, CXVII, 772.

ATTO, bishop of Vercelli.—The glorious qualities of bodies, CXXXIV, 404, 405. The merits of those rising will vary, 405.

LANFRANC, archbishop of Canterbury.—At the resurrection of the dead the glory of merits will differ, CL, 211. The righteous will be transformed into incorruption, because the kingdom of God is incorruption, 213. The unrighteous will indeed be incorrupt in the integrity of their limbs, but subject to corruption through the pain of punishments, 213.

ST. BRUNO, founder of the Carthusians.—At the resurrection the trumpet will invite the saints to the palm and terrify the ungodly toward punishment, CLIII, 409. We shall truly rise incapable of suffering, ibid. Although all rise, they will nevertheless differ in the glory of resurrection, 211. The endowments of the saints’ bodies are wonderful, 211, 212.

ST. ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury.—That bodies will possess great swiftness at resurrection is clear from the Apostle’s words, “in the twinkling of an eye,” CLIX, 589. Bodies will not make minds slower or heavier, 590. The freedom and incapacity for suffering of the elect, 590, 591.

GODEFRID, abbot of Admont.—After resurrection the body will be glorified, CLXXIV, 663, 955. If the Lord restored the body that we now bear, its recovery could bring us no joy, but rather grief, 955. The soul will be rewarded with such freedom and glory that, wherever it wishes, the body will immediately be present without impediment, 294, 315.

HUGH OF ST. VICTOR.—The bodies of the saints will rise without any defect, corruption, burden, or difficulty, CLXXVI, 604. How great their swiftness and facility will be, 604. The harmony of flesh and spirit after resurrection, 605. It should not be investigated how the body of the reprobate will be incorruptible if it can suffer pain, or corruptible if it cannot, 605. The philosophers’ arguments about bodily agility are futile, because they will never explain how great is the difference between the body’s present state and future immortality, 606. Moreover, they contradict God’s omnipotence, ibid.

HERVAEUS, monk of Bourg-Dieu.—There are different glories of the saints at resurrection, CLXXXI, 987, 988. For virginity will shine there in one way, married chastity in another, and holy widowhood in another, ibid. Thus each will appear according to the character of his or her merit, 987. The unrighteous will have incorruption of flesh in which they suffer, not in which they die, 994. But the righteous will be incorrupt and transformed, 994, 995.

ST. BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux.—Flesh sown in death will bloom again in resurrection, CLXXXII, 979. The bodies of the saints will possess seven endowments: beauty, swiftness, strength, freedom, health, delight, and duration, CLXXXIV, 355. These are explained at length, 356, 357, 358. The damned will have defects opposed to these endowments, 363, 364.

ROBERT PULLUS.—In the Transfiguration Christ showed an example of our future brightness, CLXXXVI, 988. Some saints will surpass others in the resurrection, 989. Their qualities, 989, 990. The great lightness of bodies that will ascend in the cloud, coming from different parts of the world, 990.

PETER OF BLOIS.—At the resurrection the mortal, animate, ignoble, earthly, and muddy body will be conformed to Christ’s body of glory.

[Col. 0291]

CXXXIV. INDEX CONCERNING THE UNIVERSAL AND FINAL JUDGMENT.

DIVISION.

I. On judgment in general and its certainty.—II. On the names and figures of judgment.—III. Errors concerning the final judgment.—IV. On the time and place of judgment.—V. On the circumstances preceding judgment.—VI. On the Judge and the qualities of his coming.—VII. On the different orders that will be present at judgment; or, in other words, those who will judge, be judged, and not be judged.—VIII. On the manner and qualities of judgment, the Judge’s sentence, and the matters that will follow it.—IX. Appendix, or certain questions pertaining to judgment.

[INDEX CONCERNING THE UNIVERSAL AND FINAL JUDGMENT.]

I.—On judgment in general and its certainty.

Tertullian’s *On the Spectacles*, I, 661. His *Apology*, ibid., 523. His books *Against Marcion*, II, 523.—Poems by an uncertain author, ibid., 1090.—St. Hilary’s Treatises on the Psalms, IX, 362.—Tyconius the African’s *Book of Seven Rules*, XVIII, 17, 18.—C. Vettius Aquilinus Juvencus, Book IV of the *Gospel History*, XIX, 302.—Sulpicius Severus, Letter I to his sister, XX, 223.—Rufinus of Aquileia, priest, *Commentary on the Creed*, XXI, 369 and following.—St. Jerome’s Commentary on Ecclesiastes, XXIII, 1040, 1041. Supplement to his works: *Rule of Monks*, XXX, 417.—St. Augustine’s Tractates on the Gospel of John, XXXV, 1771. His Expositions on the Psalms, XXXVI, 117, 944, 945; XXXVII, 1235. His Sermon XXII, XXXVIII, 151; XXXIX, 1846, 2153, 2207, 2209, 2210; XL, 189, 305, 774; XLI, 342, 346, 657, 662, 683, 699.—St. Peter Chrysologus’s Sermons, LII, 364.—Salvian, priest of Marseilles, *On the Government of God*, Book I, LIII, 35.—St. Patrick’s *Confession*, ibid., 802.—St. Maximus of Turin, homily on Christ’s Second Coming, LVII, 225.—The treasury compiled by St. Eugyppius from St. Augustine’s works, LXII, 132.—Vigilius of Tapsus, *On the Trinity*, Book XI, ibid., 302.—Sermons of St. Eleutherius, bishop of Tournai, LXXV, 85.—St. Fulgentius, *On the Power of Predestination*, Book III, ibid., 667. His single book *On Faith*, ibid., 702. His fragments *Against Fabianus*, ibid., 750.—Letter of Bishop Facundus, LXVII, 872.—The letters and short works of Fulgentius Ferrandus, ibid., 941.—A homily of St. Caesarius, ibid., 1075.—Victor, bishop, *Interpretation of Gospel Harmonies*, LXVIII, 334. His commentaries, ibid., 692.—St. Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, LXXI, 193.—*On the Lives of the Fathers*, Book I, LXXIII, 472, 860.—The books of Morals of Pope St. Gregory, LXXV, 585; LXXVI, 202, 698, 1205, 1148.—Alulf’s exposition of the Old and New Testament, LXXIX, 1173.—St. Columbanus’s Instructions, LXXX, 246.—Venantius Fortunatus’s *Miscellanies*, LXXXVIII, 322.—St. Aldhelm, fragment on the Day of Judgment, LXXXIX, 298.—Sermons of St. Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, ibid., 843, 854.—The Venerable Bede, *On the Day of Judgment*, XC, 575. His Doubtful and Spurious Works, XCIII, 530, 534. His hymns on the Day of Judgment, XCIV, 557, 633.—Peter the Deacon’s homiliary, XCV, 1474.—St. Ildefonsus, *On Virginity*, XCVI, 85.—The exegetical works of Blessed Abbot Alcuin, C, 1151.—Theodulf, *On the Order of Baptism*, CV, 227.—Candidus, short work on the Passion of the Lord, CVI, 80, 81.—Rabanus Maurus, vol. CVII, 809, 995, 1096.—Rabanus Maurus’s Commentary on Ecclesiastes, CIX, 1049. His homilies, CX, 329. His description of the final judgment, CXII, 720. His poem on Christ’s coming, ibid., 1618.—Haymo’s Exposition on the Epistles of St. Paul, CXVII, 694. His exposition of Zechariah, ibid., 292. His homilies, CXVIII, 18, 203.—John Scotus, *On the Division of Nature*, CXXII, 873, 980.—Ratramnus of Corbie, *On the Faith of the Pharisees concerning Judgment*, CXXI, 310.—Remigius of Auxerre’s Expositions on the Psalms, CXXXI, 172. His homily, ibid., 865.—Ratherius, *Phrenesis*, CXXXVI, 390.—St. Odilo’s *Belief*, CXLII, 1036.—St. Peter Damian’s poems and prayers, CXLV, 979. His scriptural sayings concerning the Day of Judgment, ibid., 739.—Othlo’s verses on the Day of Judgment, CXLVI, 298.—Samuel the Moroccan, book on the past coming of the Messiah, CXLIX, 347.—Guitmund’s confession concerning the Holy Trinity, ibid., 1499.—Radulf [Col. 0292] Ardens’s homily on the Second Coming, CLV, 1572, 1678.—Abbot Werner, *On the Coming of the Lord*, CLVII, 756, 761.—St. Ivo’s Decree, Part I, on faith, CLXI, 74.—William of Champeaux, *On the Catholic Faith*, CLXIII, 1072.—The works of Rupert, CLXVII, 1298.—Sermons of the Venerable Hildebert, CLXXI, 348.—Honorius of Autun’s *Elucidarium*, CLXXII, 1165, 1166.—Homilies for Sundays by the Venerable Godefrid, CLXXIV, 66.—Hugh of St. Victor’s notes on Joel, CLXXV, 366, 799.—St. Bernard’s letters, *On Judgment*, CLXXXII, 74, 101.—Zacharias, bishop of Chrysopolis, CLXXXVI, 378.—Ernald’s book on the principal works of Christ, CLXXXIX, 1667.—Peter the Venerable’s sermons, ibid., 964. His poem on Christ’s coming, ibid., 1015.—Gerhoh’s Commentary on the Psalms, CXCIV, 405.—Richard of St. Victor’s exegetical works, CXCVI, 815.—Garnerius of Langres’s sermons, CCV, 770.—The commentary on the Song of Songs by Thomas the Cistercian and John Algrin, CCVI, 524.—Peter of Blois’s sermons, CCVII, 868. His verses of the Sibyl-prophet concerning Christ’s final coming, ibid., 870.—Pope Innocent III’s sermons, CCXVII, 511 and 742.

II.—On the names and figures of judgment.

The severity of judgment signified by a bow, St. Hilary, IX, 371.—God’s judgment is signified in the face, ibid., 803.—The Day of Judgment is called an evil day, St. Jerome, XXIV, 791; XXVI, 179.—The Day of Judgment, an incurable day, id., XXV, 959.—Why judgment is called a stretched bow, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 717.—The day of judgment expressed by a furnace, id., XXXVII, 1362.—A burning and smoking oven, a figure of judgment, id., XXXIX, 1746.—The cry of clamorous birds shortly before light flashes forth is a figure of our Judge, Aurelius Prudentius, LIX, 778.—The Day of Judgment, the day of greatness, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 312.—The Day of Judgment likened to the times of Noah and Lot, Victor, bishop of Capua, LXVIII, 334.—Why does the Psalmist so often call the day of the Judge an evil day? Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXX, 296.—Why is judgment called a storm? ibid., 350.—The Day of Judgment compared to a storm, ibid., 599.—The day of judgment is called the gate of the kingdom, Pope St. Gregory, LXXV, 734.—Morning signifies the Day of Judgment, ibid., 836, 1155; LXXVI, 37.—Judgment called the day of the Lord’s wrath, LXXV, 1101.—Why called night, LXXVI, 54.—Why the final judgment is signified by the name “bow,” ibid., 133.—Judgment is called lightning, ibid., 723.—The Day of Judgment is designated by the number eight, ibid., 1030.—On the various names of judgment, ibid., 1121.—The terror of judgment is expressed in fire, id., LXXIX, 143.—Midnight, when the cry was made, signifies the Day of Judgment, Anonymous writer of the seventh century, LXXXVIII, 1074.—Judgment designated by the Flood, the Venerable Bede, XCI, 86.—What is signified by the darkness and furnace of fire that appeared after sunset? III.—Errors concerning the final judgment.

Dosithaeus, a Jew by birth, did not expect a future judgment from the Law and the Prophets, St. Philastrius, XII, 1118.—The Samaritans do not expect a future judgment, ibid., 1120.—Marcion, a native of Pontus, denied that Christ is judge of all, ibid., 1162.—The Proclianites, who deny that Christ came in the flesh, do not believe in resurrection or judgment, ibid., 1171.—The Floriani, or Carpocratians, deny judgment, ibid., 1172.—The Manichaeans do not hope for judgment, ibid., 1176.—The Symmachians likewise deny it, ibid., 1177.—The Arians deny that the Holy Spirit knows the Day of Judgment, St. Ambrose, XVI, 690.—On those who suppose that, at the final judgment, no human being will be condemned because of the intercessions of the saints, St. Augustine, XLI, 732.—The heresy of the Gnoitae, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 376.—Errors concerning the place of judgment, John Scotus, CXXII, 996.—On the Felician heresy, St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 826.

IV.—On the time and place of judgment.

Christ’s coming: why at the end of the ages? Arnobius, V, 932.—When will the judgment take place? Arius and Eunomius refuted, id., XXVI, 181.—What is the reason why Christ is said to be ignorant of the day of judgment? ibid., 181, 182.—St. Augustine does not venture to calculate the times of the Savior’s coming, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 890.—No one knows the time, day, or hour of judgment, ibid., 899, 900, 901, 902, 903.—The end of the age will not come before the Gospel is preached throughout the whole world, ibid., 900.—It cannot be known when Christ’s coming will take place, ibid., 907, 908.—He who says that the Lord’s coming will be sooner, and he who says that it will be later, are both mistaken, ibid., 924, 925.—Explanation of the words, “But concerning that day,” etc., id., XXXVI, 90.—Some believe that the Lord’s coming for judgment, reckoning the years from Adam, will occur after seven thousand years. Refutation of this opinion, ibid.—Why is Christ said not to know the day of judgment? id., XXXVI, 355 and XL, 48.—Why did God wish that day to remain hidden? ibid., 354.—Answer to those who say, “Judgment is far off,” id., XXXVIII, 128.—The day of judgment is hidden, ibid., 271.—The disciples’ inquiry concerning the time of Christ’s future coming and Christ’s answer, ibid., 1219.—Let him be anathema who says that what is written, “But concerning that day and hour neither the angels nor the Son know,” is true in accordance with the blasphemy of the Arians and not because of the economy of assumed flesh, M. ### VI.—The Judge and the Characteristics of His Coming

On Christ’s second coming, Tertullian, II, 330.—God, a just and severe judge, ibid., 302.—Christ alone received from the Father all judgment, St. Cyprian, IV, 480.—Christ himself will come as Judge, ibid., 719, 722.—Christ comes manifest in power, ibid., 637.—On Christ the Judge, ibid., 1029, 1031.—On the day of judgment Christ will come in the clouds of heaven as the Son of Man, Lactantius, VI, 481.—All judgment has been given to the Son, ibid., 798.—On Christ the Judge, St. Hilary, IX, 926.—What will Christ’s coming be like? ibid., 1056.—On the day of judgment all will see Christ in the flesh, id., X, 85.—Why will the Lord come in fire? St. Ambrose, XV, 1733, 1734.—On the day of judgment all tribes of the earth will see the Son of Man coming with great power and exalted majesty, id., XVII, 651.—How will Christ appear on the day of judgment? ibid., 768.—Christ, the exalted Judge, Aquilinus Juvencus, XIX, 126.—Christ’s second coming will be in glory, St. Jerome, XXVI, 179.—All persons of every rank must render account to Christ, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 1028.—How will Christ come for judgment? ibid., 1406, 1624, 1675.—The Father will not come for judgment, id., XXXV, 1571.—In what form Christ will appear, ibid., 1553, 1580; XXXVIII, 711, 1070, 1219.—Christ as man received authority to exercise judgment, id., XXXV, 691, 1580.—Christ, judged with great humility, will judge with great authority, id., XXXVI, 408.—He who came hidden to be judged will come manifest to judge, ibid., 568.—Christ will come in human form to judge, id., XXXVII, 1096.—How severe [Col. 0297] the Judge will be, ibid., 1197, 1198.—Christ will judge the whole world, because he gave the price for the whole world, ibid., 1236.—On the day of judgment he who is now witness to your life will be the judge of your case, id., XXXVIII, 75.—When Christ comes to judge, he will be manifest, ibid., 124, 128.—At the last judgment God is an incorruptible Judge, ibid., 75, 299, 649.—What Christ will be like when he comes, ibid., 1369.—Our Judge cannot be deceived by the devil, ibid., 568.—He will come to human beings; a man will come; but God-man will come. True man and God will come, that he may make human beings gods, id., ibid., 1219.—Christ will come with his angels and will appear in glory to all, including those risen from the dead, ibid., 1453.—God gave the Son authority to exercise judgment, id., XXXIX, 1629, 1925.—Christ’s second coming will not be hidden, ibid., 2051.—Christ will come to judge the living and the dead, ibid., 2182.—In what form Christ will come for judgment, id., XL, 647.—He who first came hidden will come manifest in power, ibid., 658, 666.—Christ the Judge who is to come is declared not only in the Old but also in the New Testament, id., XLI, 705.—Christ as man received authority to exercise judgment, id., XLII, 222.—Christ will come in human form for judgment, ibid., 691.—The wicked will see Christ in the form of a servant, the righteous in the form of God, id., XLIV, 223.—If anyone does not say that Christ sits at the Father’s right hand in the flesh which he assumed, and that in this flesh he will come to judge the living and the dead, let him be anathema, Arnobius the Younger, LIII, 321.—Christ will be the Judge of the holy Fathers, ibid., 802.—On the majesty of the Judge, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 315.—Why will a multitude of angels be present at Christ’s coming? ibid., 161.—Christ will come for judgment in the same flesh in which he ascended, ibid., 398, 399.—A scrutiny of all human beings is to be carried out by Christ at the final judgment, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 436.—How great is the Judge’s majesty, Julianus Pomerius, LIX, 491.—Why was authority to judge given to the Son?
