which he took from the Virgin to judge the living and the dead, St. Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia, XCIX, 295.—In what form Christ will be seen in judgment, Alcuin, C, 814.—No one will judge more justly than he who was judged unjustly, ibid., 864.—The Lord will come for judgment with the elders of the people, ibid., 1094.—Christ will come for judgment in the form of a servant, not in the form of divinity, ibid.—That form will be Judge in which he stood before a judge, id., CI, 51.—Who indeed is he who will judge the world: a solitary human being only, or God, the Son of Man? ibid., 179.—The Judge of human beings, Christ, is true God, not God merely by name, ibid., 197.—How Christ will appear at the end of the age, ibid.—Christ will appear to all the elect, noble and exalted, sitting with the senators of the earth, Abbot Smaragdus, CII, 428.—Christ will come to judge in the same form of flesh and substance in which he came to be judged, ibid., 310.—The Son of God who came gentle in order to save will come strict in order to judge, ibid., 316.—On Christ’s coming with great power and majesty, ibid., 518.—On the day of judgment he who appeared despised in his passion to the wicked will appear glorified in his saints, ibid., 559.—The time will come when Christ himself will judge, bringing the hidden things of darkness to light, Candidus, monk of Fulda, CVI, 81.—Christ himself will come with angels for judgment in the glory of his Father, ibid., 86.—Human beings will see with power and majesty him whom they refused to hear when he was in humility, Christian Druthmar, CVI, 1459.—We know what judgment the Father gave to the Son, ibid., 1469.—The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 774, 810.—How will Christ appear at the very time of judgment? ibid., 997.—Christ will come for judgment in the very body in which he ascended into heaven, id., CX, 28.—In judgment God will appear gentle to the righteous and terrible to the unrighteous, ibid., 142.—On the day of judgment Christ will come to confound the impiety of the proud by displaying the tokens of his passion and the cross itself as well, ibid., 149, 178.—The Savior’s second coming will be not in humility as before, but in glory and majesty, ibid., 424.—The reprobate will not be permitted to behold the only-begotten Son of God in the form of divinity, ibid., 504.—On the day of judgment our Redeemer will be seen in his terror, ibid., 505.—God will appear gentle to the righteous and terrible to the wicked, Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 113, 223.—How Christ will come for judgment, id., CXIV, 234, 321.—Christ will come for judgment in the glory of his Father, Angelomus, monk of Luxeuil, CXV, 268.—When the Lord comes for judgment, the Jews will see in him the wounds which they inflicted, Amulo, bishop of Lyons, CXVI, 150.—God, once hidden because divinity was concealed in humanity, will come manifestly in judgment, Haymo, bishop of Halberstadt, ibid., 365.

All judgment has been given to the Son, Haymo, bishop of Halberstadt, CXVI, 434; CXVII, 14, 155, 381, 828.—The Lord will come for judgment with the patriarchs and prophets and with his princes, ibid., 272, 740.—Christ will come manifestly for judgment so that he may be seen by all, id., CXVII, 772.—On Christ’s second coming in power, ibid., 779.—On the day of judgment all alike, elect and reprobate, will see Christ, id., CXVIII, 41.—No reprobate person should be thought to see at judgment the glorified majesty of the Lord’s body or the brightness of the bodies of the saints, ibid., 223.—At judgment only that form of the Son which was unjustly judged will be seen, ibid., 312.—It is just and fitting that the Son of God should appear as Judge of the living and the dead at the universal judgment, ibid., 331.—On Christ’s exceedingly fearful coming for judgment, ibid., 939.—That the second coming will be shown not in humility as before but in glory, ibid., 940.—At the last judgment Christ will appear gentle to the elect and terrible to the reprobate, ibid., 942.—How strictly the eternal Judge will come on the day of judgment, ibid., 944.—How and by whom Christ will be seen, St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 820.—How justly and fittingly the mighty Son of Man will come for judgment, ibid., 859.—On the coming of the Son of Man, ibid., 860.—At Christ’s coming there will be manifestation only according to his humanity, ibid., 861.—The Catholic faith unhesitatingly believes that our Lord Jesus Christ will come to judge the living and the dead, John Scotus, CXXII, 980.—Storm and fire will accompany the terrible Judge coming for judgment, Hincmar, [Col. 0299] CXXVI, 163.—Only the pure in heart will see the Judge in the form of God, Remigius of Auxerre, CXXXI, 598.—Why is judgment attributed to the Lord’s manhood? ibid., 190.—When Christ comes in the Father’s majesty, he will be terrible to the wicked and gentle to the righteous, ibid., 538.—He willed to be judged gently in order to come to judge terribly, ibid.—How and through whom will God judge? Atto, bishop of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 150.—He who here was judged in humility will come there to judge in majesty, St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 70.—Judgment was given to Christ according to his human nature, ibid., 270.—Christ will come with the same body with which he ascended into heaven to judge the living and the dead, ibid., 560.—He will come in the same form in which he was crucified, died, was buried, and rose: and why? ibid., 568.—What will Christ’s coming for judgment be like? St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 477.—What place will there be for hope when the Judge comes—he who stood before a judge—with trumpets sounding beforehand, angels crying aloud, and the elements burning? ibid., 818.—Christ’s glory and majesty will be manifest at his second coming, Samuel of Morocco, CXLIX, 345.—On the day of judgment Christ will come with great power and majesty—St. Bruno, founder of the Carthusians, CLIII, 480.—Christ will come with power and majesty to judge the world by fire, John, monk of the Charterhouse of Portes, ibid., 901.—On the Judge, Radulfus Ardens, CLV, 1337.—What Christ will be like when he comes for judgment, and with what insignia, ibid., 1372.—The person of the Son alone will appear at judgment, ibid., 1488.—Will the scars of Christ’s wounds appear on the day of judgment? Venerable Guibert, CLVI, 66.—Christ’s office and authority of judging, Godfrey, CLVII, 252, 260.—At judgment the form of man which is in the Son of God will be seen, and the Son of God will judge in it, ibid., 261.—Christ will come in the flesh for judgment, ibid., 268.—In what form will Christ appear at judgment? Abbot Werner of St. Blasien, ibid., 750, 756.—On the nature of the Judge’s person, ibid., 761.—God will judge . . . through Jesus Christ, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 621.—The strict Judge will come for judgment, St. Ivo, CLXI, 1013.—What was Christ like when he came, and what will he be like when he comes? id., CLXII, 567, 568.—The Son of Man and Son of God will come for judgment, Anselm of Laon, ibid., 1463.—It is fitting that he who was judged should judge, St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 774.—At the second coming Christ will come manifest, not to be judged but to judge, ibid., 874.—On Christ’s coming in glory and majesty, id., CLXV, 217.—Christ’s coming will be mercy to the elect and wrath to the wicked, Rupert, CLXVII, 403.—Christ’s second coming will be terrible, ibid., 862.—On the coming of the dreadful Judge: how he himself will sit on the throne of his majesty, ibid., 1811.—On the day of judgment Christ, the Son of God, will appear as Judge, ibid., 1018.—Description of Christ’s second coming, ibid., 1298.—At judgment Christ will appear, and it will be evident that he was a human being, ibid., 1431.—To exercise judgment belongs to the Son, id., 169, 420.—Christ’s second coming, like a thief in the night, id., CLXX, 196.—That coming will make earthly persons tremble as the angel made the soldiers by the tomb tremble, ibid., 197.

The Lord will come in fire, Venerable Hildebert, CLXXI, 352.—On the day of judgment the wicked will see Christ in a crown of power, but the righteous will see him in a crown of glory, ibid., 367.—God the Father gave the Son, according to his human nature, authority also to exercise judgment, Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 978.—Christ the Judge will come in human flesh, ibid., 44.—The Judge’s appearance will be one thing to the righteous and another to the reprobate, ibid., 55.—On the day of judgment the Lord will judge the righteous and the wicked, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 243.—The question is asked: what does it mean that the Father does not judge, but has given all judgment to the Son? ibid., 848.—On the nature of the Judge’s person, id., CLXXVI, 598.—The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, id., CLXXVII, 561.—Why is Christ said to have received all judgment from the Father? ibid., 563.—The third coming in lightning, ibid., 852.—At the final coming God must be seen as terrible, ibid., 656.—Christ received from the Father authority to judge, ibid., 811.—On the Lord’s coming, when he will render his fury to the wicked with great indignation, Hervaeus, monk of Bourg-Dieu, CLXXXI, 584.—On the coming of the Son of Man with great power and majesty, ibid., 370.—We shall all stand before Christ the Judge, ibid., 789.—On Christ’s terrible coming, ibid., 53, 82.—Christ as Judge and witness on the Last Day, ibid., 507.—On the Judge who cleanses his threshing floor with a winnowing fan, ibid., 81.—At the final coming Christ will come in glory and majesty, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 50, 503.—At the final coming Christ will come in wrath and indignation, as though enraged, ibid., 155.—Christ will come to judge in human form so that he may appear gracious to the elect, ibid., 1136.—God gave the Son authority to judge as man: and why? ibid., 1136.—On Christ’s second [Col. 0300] coming, Guerric, abbot of Igny, CLXXXV, 12.—Christ’s final coming will be manifest and wonderful, ibid., 16.—Christ, God and man, the Judge, Peter Lombard, CXCI, 699.—How Christ will come for judgment, ibid., 476.—How Christ will appear to believers and how to unbelievers, id., CXCII, 315.—On the form of the Judge, ibid., 955.—On the day of judgment Christ will appear in the form of a servant, ibid., 956.—Why is Christ said, according to the form of a servant, to raise bodies? ibid., 956.—He who came in humility to be judged for us will come to judge all in majesty, Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, CXCII, 1326.—At the final judgment God will appear calm to the righteous and angry to the unrighteous, Garnerius, CXCIII, 71.—The exercise of judgment belongs principally and especially to the Son, Gerhoh, ibid., 735, 844.—And he who was judged unjustly will judge the world by manifest judgment, ibid., 759.—God will become man and will come visible to all, ibid., 1596, 1597.—On Christ’s coming with great power, ibid., 1754.—All judgment has been given to the Son: and why? id., CXCIV, 313, 314.—How Christ will come at the second coming, ibid., 323, 324.—Christ, unjustly judged, will judge in human form, ibid., 382, 383.—Christ, God and man, will condemn earthly persons in judgment, ibid., 506.—Christ, the avenger and just Judge, will punish the wicked in judgment, ibid., 576.—The Lord will judge the earth, ibid., 1016.—In what form Christ will come at judgment, Blessed Aelred, CXCV, 219.—On the day of judgment Christ will be seen with the bodily and spiritual eye, Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 699.—On Christ judging, ibid., 850.—On judicial authority in the final and universal judgment, ibid., 1177.—At the end of the age the Son of God will come to judge the living and the dead, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1078.—At his third coming Christ will come to save, Thomas the Cistercian and John Ailgrin, CCVI, 230.—On Christ’s final coming, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 622.—On the day of judgment Christ will go forth not humble to be judged, but strong to judge, St. Martin of León, CCVIII, 40, 41.—In what form he will appear, ibid., 53, 54.—God and man, Jesus Christ, will come for judgment, not like rain upon fleece, but like a downfall dragging an unavoidable weight, ibid., 1197.—Christ will sit for judgment with the senators of the earth, id., CCXIX, 63.—The Lord will come for judgment with sound, fire, and tongue, Dom Garnerius, bishop of Langres, CCXII, 625.—Christ the King will come visibly on the day of judgment and will not keep silence, Sicardus, CCXIII, 282.—Christ will visibly come from heaven in the Lord’s manhood to judge the living and the dead, Anonymous, twelfth century, CCXIII, 722.—By what authority will the Son of God judge? ibid., 747.—On the Judge’s power, wisdom, and justice, CCXVII, 744.—At judgment Christ will be Judge and advocate, accuser and witness, Pope Innocent III, CCXVII, 988.—The Son of God alone will appear at judgment, ibid., 1120.

VII.—On the different orders of persons who will be at the judgment; or, in other words: On those who will judge, those who will be judged, and also those who will not be judged.

On the day of judgment not all will be judged by God, but only those who have lived within God’s religion, Lactantius, VI, 978.—Who are those to be judged and not judged on that day? St. Hilary, IX, 259, 373.—The power of judging is granted to the saints, ibid., 887.—Explanation of Christ’s words: “He who believes in me shall not be judged; but he who does not believe has already been judged,” St. Zeno, XI, 457.—He who does not believe in Christ has already been judged, St. Ambrose, XIV, 949.—Why the ungodly and faithless, who have not believed in Christ, are not to be judged at the last judgment, ibid., 949.—On the threefold order of persons who must be present at Christ’s final judgment, ibid.—Why the saint comes to judgment and the ungodly does not come, id., XV, 1491.—The ungodly do not rise in the judgment, but are punished as though judgment had already been held, ibid., 1701.—Not only the twelve apostles will judge, nor only the twelve tribes be judged, St. Augustine, XLI, 663.—He who does not believe has already been judged: why judged? id., XXXV, 1490. On the day of judgment a separation will take place [lacuna], so that some may stand to be judged, while others stand with the Lord to judge, id., XXXVI, 570.—At the judgment all the perfect will judge, ibid., 572; XXXVII, 1156 and 1407.—Who are living and who dead on the day of judgment, id., XXXIX, 1085.—Among the reprobate, some are judged and others are not judged, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 378.—Who at the final judgment will not be judged but will be judges, ibid., 379.—On the day of judgment all saints who have left the world perfected will come as judges, ibid., 803.—Who will be judged and who will not be judged, id., LXXIX, 666.—At the judgment there are two orders of the elect, ibid., 1170.—At the end of the age, those who are now unjustly judged for God’s sake will come as judges with God, Taio, bishop of Caesaraugusta, LXXX, 806.—On the day of judgment there will be two orders of persons [Col. 0301], which will nevertheless be divided into four, the Venerable Bede, XCII, 109.—Of those coming to judgment, some will judge and others will be judged, id., XCIII, 488.—There will be two orders of the elect, and likewise two orders of the reprobate, Paul Warnefrid the deacon, XCV, 1216.—On the seats of those judging, St. Julian, bishop of Toledo, XCVI, 502.—On those who will sit with the Lord to judge, ibid.—That not merely the twelve apostles will sit upon the twelve seats, but the entire number of the perfect, who are apportioned under the number twelve, ibid.—On the order of the future judgment, ibid., 513.—Those who are now following perfect works according to the Gospel precepts will appear as judges with Christ, Smaragdus, CII, 1075.—On those who will judge with the Son of Man, ibid., 397.—On the four orders which will exist on the day of the fearful assize, Jonas, bishop of Orléans, CVI, 271, 272.—Who, besides the Son of God, will sit in judgment in order to judge, ibid., 271, 272.—There are two orders of the elect and two of the reprobate, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 1024.—May you deserve to find God himself, when he comes to judgment with the others who judge the world in equity, gentle and merciful, CX, 33.—How these words are to be understood: “He who believes in me shall not be judged,” Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 1317.—Who will be judged on the day of judgment, CXII, 37.—The Lord appoints rulers who decide lesser cases, but any matter that is more serious they are to refer to him, Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 246.—At the judgment there will be four orders, ibid., 845.—On those who will judge with Christ and on those who will be judged, CXIV, 149.—Why is he who does not believe judged? ibid., 368.

The apostles, judges of the Jews, Angelomus, monk of Luxeuil, CXV, 270.—On those who will not be judged and those who will judge, Haymo, bishop of Halberstadt, CXVI, 200.—That in the future judgment there will be two orders of the elect and two of the reprobate, id., CXVIII, 942.—How the two orders of the elect at the judgment differ from one another, likewise the two orders of the reprobate, and what is opposed to each order, ibid., 943.—The saints will judge with the Lord at the future judgment, Hincmar, CXXVI, 15.—Of those rising again, some will rise to judgment and others will rise not to judgment, Remigius of Auxerre, CXXXI, 153.—There will be four orders at the judgment, Ratherius, bishop of Verona, CXXXVI, 260, 701.—On the day of judgment two orders will be divided into four, Burchard, bishop of Worms, CXL, 1056.—The ungodly rise, but not for judgment; the just person rises in order to judge, the sinner in order to be judged, St. Bruno, bishop of Würzburg, CXLII, 51.—The saints will judge this world, Blessed Lanfranc, CL, 172.—Who will judge and who will be judged, St. Bruno, founder of the Carthusians, CLII, 642.—Whom Christ will gather with himself for judgment, Radulphus Ardens, CLV, 1337.—There will be four orders at the judgment, ibid., 1683.—On the day of judgment two orders will be divided into four, Ivo, bishop of Chartres, CLXI, 1013.—There will be two orders at the judgment, of the elect and of the reprobate, id., CLXII, 1464.—The ungodly and sinners will rise, but not at the judgment, for they have already been judged, St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 699.—For not all who are to be saved will also judge; rather, few judges will sit upon thrones, Rupert, abbot of Deutz, CLXVII, 910.—The elders of the people who come with Christ to judgment will have judicial swords in their hands, ibid., 1018.—At the judgment there will be a fourfold class of persons, id., CLXVIII, 1579.—Who will be condemned at the final judgment, ibid., 656.—The saints will exercise judgment universally on the day of judgment, id., CLXIX, 115.—At the judgment there will be three orders of persons: namely, those to be judged, those judging, and those already judged, the Venerable Hildebert, CLXXI, 411.—How the statement that the saints will judge the wicked is to be understood, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 447, 523.—If the saints will sit at the hour of judgment, how will they stand? Or, if they stand, how will they sit? ibid., 509.—It is asked how the saints are to judge at the judgment, ibid., 523.—There are four kinds of persons who will come to judgment, ibid., 589.—It is asked whether children who die, or perfect righteous persons, are to be judged on the day of judgment, Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 631.—On the day of judgment the apostles will be judges, Hervaeus of Bourg-Dieu, CLXXXI, 475.—The saints will come with Christ to judgment, ibid., 865.—The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people and its princes, ibid., 62.—Explanation of these words: “He who believes is not judged, but he who does not believe has already been judged,” Zacharias, bishop of Chrysopolis, CLXVIII, 378.—On the twofold order of those to be saved and those to be damned, Robert Pullen, CLXXXVI, 1005.—On the judgment of the Lord and of the saints, ibid., 1007.—There will be four orders at the judgment, Peter Lombard, CXCI, 65.—Who will judge and who will be judged, ibid., 476.—On the day of judgment those who have left their own possessions will judge, ibid., 1143.—That the saints will judge, and how, id., CXCII, 951.—On the order of judgment [Col. 0302] and the ministry of the angels, ibid., 955.—On the order of those to be judged, Master Bandinus, ibid., 1111.—At the judgment, whom Christ will call to sit beside him, Garnerius, CXCIII, 247.—The most perfect saints will judge with the Lord, Gerhoh, ibid., 740, 1610, 1754.—On the day of judgment the apostles will be judges of the Jews, ibid., 663.—Only lovers of the faith will be judges of this world, ibid., 1597.—On those who will even judge angels, id., CXCIV, 263.—At the end, the most perfect will judge the world with God, Eckbert, CXCV, 59.—The perfect will sit with God and judge those to be judged, Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 747.—On the orders of those to be judged and those judging, those to be saved and those to be damned, ibid., 1177.—Who are to be judged by apostolic men, ibid., 1179.—The sons of men will be fellow judges with the Son of Man, Garnerius, CCV, 771.—On the day of judgment, those now judged lowly and contemptible will judge the rich, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 693.

VIII.—On the manner and characteristics of the judgment.—On the judge’s sentence and also on what will follow it.

According to Tertullian, the merits of each individual person will be carefully examined at Christ’s final judgment, Tertullian, I, 415.—On the day of judgment the whole human race will be restored, ibid., 527.—The more delayed the judgment is, the more just it will be, Marcus Minucius Felix, III, 348.—Why God’s just judgment is delayed, St. Cyprian, IV, 625.—On the day of judgment the final wrath of God will come upon the nations and will defeat them to the last one, Firmianus Lactantius, VI, 814.—No one will be exempt from judgment, id., VII, 151.—What sort of body the ungodly will have after judgment, St. Hilary, IX, 258.—Division of the future judgment, ibid., 387.—No one will be exempt from the final judgment, ibid., 523.—If even the Virgin capable of containing God is to come before the severity of judgment, who would dare desire to be judged by God? ibid., 523.—On the severity of judgment, ibid., 1056.—At Christ’s coming, another person’s merits will help no one, ibid., 1060.—The separation of evil persons from good persons at the judgment, ibid., 1063.—What Christ’s final judgment will be like, St. Ambrose, XIV, 950.—How terrible divine judgments are, id., XV, 1286.—At the judgment no innocent person will be endangered and no criminal will escape, ibid., 1427, 1430.

At God’s judgment the righteous person alone will rejoice; all others will tremble, St. Jerome, XXII, 354.—No one goes fearlessly to the Lord’s judgment, XXIII, 559.—On the primordial restoration which will occur on the last day, ibid., 1017.—The day of judgment is dreadful and terrible, XXIV, 209, 210.—On the day of judgment every creature will perceive itself to be nothing, ibid., 50.—God’s judgment will permit no one to depart unpunished, ibid., 352.—All hidden things will be disclosed and secret things made manifest, ibid., 305.—The day of judgment is fearful, XXV, 290, 985, 1052, 1236.—How great is the severity of the day of judgment, ibid., 959, 965.—The day of the Lord is a day of darkness and not light, and exceedingly terrible, ibid., 966.—On the day of judgment there will be no place for repentance, XXVI, 161.—After the day of judgment there will be no opportunity for good works and righteousness, ibid., 185.—On the dread of the final day of judgment, XXX, 374.—On the horror of the day of judgment, St. Augustine, XXXII, 1472.—On the effects of fear of judgment, ibid., 372.—How the judgment will take place, XXXIII, 906, 907.—A person will be judged only according to what he or she has done through the body, not according to what he or she would have done if he or she had lived longer, ibid., 984, 986.—On the effects of fear of Christ’s coming, XXXIV, 25.—How judgment will be carried out, XXXV, 1554.—If we believe that judgment is to come, let us live well: now is the time of mercy; then will be the time of judgment, XXXVI, 569.—God will judge the world in equity, ibid., 121.—When the time of judgment comes, there will be repentance, but fruitless because late, ibid., 608.—Almsgiving is the subject matter of judgment, XXXVII, 1235.—Against whom the Lord will execute judgment without mercy, ibid., 1236.—On the day of judgment there will be repentance, but a torturing repentance, not a healing one, XXXVIII, 131.—Only works of mercy are to be mentioned at the judgment, ibid., 406.—Why only almsgiving is treated at the judgment, ibid., 407.—On Christ’s final sentence on the day of judgment, XXXIX, 1543.—Only almsgivings are mentioned at the final judgment, ibid., 1700.—The threefold lot of persons at the judgment, ibid., 1949.—What we shall be like on the day of judgment, ibid., 1963.—The future judgment, a great punishment for sin, ibid., 2045.—What account must be rendered on the day of judgment concerning God’s benefits, ibid., 2207.—Whether one who has not taken another’s goods will be secure at the judgment, ibid., 2232.—At the judgment, one who has acquired piety through almsgivings will incur no ruin, ibid., 2232.—God’s judgments will appear most just on the final day, XLI, 660.—God will judge the deeds of angels, 659.—At the judgment there is a separation of good and evil, ibid., 702.—The order of events to be accomplished at the final judgment, 709.—How judgment will occur can scarcely be comprehended in the Holy Scriptures, XLIV, 325.—A person will be judged [Col. 0303] according to his or her works, ibid., 877, 878. At God’s judgment there are compassion and mercy, ibid., 239.

At the final judgment God, passing over other matters in silence, will call out concerning mercy toward the poor, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 233, 234.—When Christ comes, he discusses mercy before judging guilt, ibid., 319.—On the heavenly separation which will be carried out by angels, ibid., 332, 333.—The time of judgment is no longer a time for repentance, ibid., 545.—God will judge the world in equity, Salvian, LIII, 56.—Whether heretics will be punished more severely on the day of judgment than sinful Catholics, ibid., 96.—On the day of judgment an account must be rendered even for the smallest sins, St. Patrick, apostle of the Irish, ibid., 802.—On the judge’s sentence, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 290.—On the subject matter of the final examination, ibid., 165, 167.—On fearing God’s judgment, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 528.—Separation of the good from the evil, Julianus Pomerius, LIX, 420. On fearing God’s judgment, St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 460.—Judgment is a time for vengeance, not for pardon, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 555.—The judgment will be fearful and terrible, St. Benedict, LXVI, 267.—On the fearful judgment of God, ibid., 324.—God’s judgment is horrible and greatly to be feared, Primasius, bishop of Hadrumetum, LXVIII, 756.—On the day of judgment God will judge people’s secrets, ibid., 424.—At the judgment nothing will remain hidden that is not revealed, ibid., 669.—The day of judgment is a day of wrath, a day of tribulation and distress, LXX, 61.—How will the judgment take place? ibid., 42, 259.—God will judge the world in equity, ibid., 82.—Those to be condemned on the day of judgment, ibid., 88.—On fearing God’s judgment, ibid., 60, 599.—The terror of the reprobate, St. Gregory, pope, LXXV, 793.—On the judge’s sentence, St. Gregory, ibid., 734.—At the judgment God will acknowledge those who have despised him here, ibid., 821.—The greater his mercy is now, the greater will be the severity at judgment, ibid., 46, 592.—Why the reprobate will be ashamed on the day of judgment, ibid., 857.—How great is the severity of the final judgment, ibid., 876.—On the fearful day of judgment, ibid., 1082.—At the judgment the wicked will experience righteous and unrighteous accusers, ibid., 1100.—At the judgment evils hidden within will be revealed, ibid., 1101.—At the judgment even the least evils will be punished, ibid.—On the day of judgment the repentance of the ungodly is futile, LXXVI, 690, 1121.—On the day of judgment every sharp reproof and correction is wrath and anger, because after correction there is no pardon, ibid., 973.—On the joy of the righteous on the day of judgment, ibid., 1120.—On the day of judgment there will be repentance, but it will no longer be fruitful, ibid., 1121.—At the strictness of the final rebuke every argument of excuse ceases, ibid., 1289.—At the final judgment a new increase of glory will be given to the saints, LXXVII, 357.—As each person departs from here, so is that person presented at the judgment, ibid., 396.—The strict Judge will approve each person not because of the prerogative of a higher rank, but according to the merits of works, ibid., 531.—At the judgment God will console us with the greater grace insofar as he now sees that our sins are being punished by us, ibid., 627.—Who will stand secure at the judgment? ibid., 640.—At the judgment God will leave nothing either unpunished or unrewarded, LXXIX, 76.—Not only words but also thoughts will be judged by God, ibid., 81.—What will demons bring against us as accusations at the judgment? ibid., 343.

At the judgment we shall render an account not only for harmful speech but also for idle speech, St. Columbanus, LXXX, 251.—On the judge’s sentence, Taio, bishop of Caesaraugusta, id., 730.—On the fruitless repentance of the reprobate, ibid., 987.—The final day of judgment must be dreaded, St. Gall, abbot and confessor, LXXXVII, 26.—On the judge’s sentence, St. Valerius, abbot, id., 428, 429.—On the terror and examination of the day of judgment, anonymous author of an uncertain year in the seventh century, LXXXVIII, 1074, 1075.—Those who give alms to their brethren will hear a merciful sentence on the day of judgment, St. Boniface, LXXXIX, 757.—What will happen at the final examination, the Venerable Bede, XCI, 149.—The day of judgment, on which the virtue of the good and the wickedness of the evil will be displayed, id., XCII, 54.—On the day of judgment God will judge people’s secrets, ibid., 487, 547.—At God’s judgment the condemned person will grieve and the rewarded person rejoice, id., XCIII, 20, 21.—Where a work of mercy is found, the fire of sin will be extinguished, ibid., 21.—On the judge’s sentence, Paul the Deacon, XCV, 1216.—On the separation of ## FIFTEENTH SERIES

[Col. 0307]

### [PREFACE.]

In this Series we present all the works, and also shorter writings, of the Holy Fathers concerning the moral virtues and evangelical perfection. Hence there are eight indexes—alphabetical, chronological, and analogical—of authors and works, furnishing a concise analysis of each and affording the reader the greatest and best assistance. To these is further appended an Index on Conscience, which is the judgment of reason and the inward rule of moral actions.

[Col. 0307]

[Col. 0309]

## CXXXVI. MORAL LIBRARY OF THE FATHERS, OR ALL THE WORKS AND SHORTER WRITINGS OF THE ANCIENT FATHERS OF THE LATIN CHURCH ON CHRISTIAN ETHICS, ARRANGED ALPHABETICALLY BY AUTHOR

**St. AGOBARD, Bishop of Lyons.**---A short treatise *On Hope and Fear*, in which he shows that fear, if it is without hope, should more properly be called despair; while hope, if it is without fear, is vain presumption, CIV, 323.

**St. AILERAN, Scoto-Irish abbot.**---A mystical interpretation of Christ’s forebears, LXXX, 327.---A moral interpretation of the same names, ibid., 333.---In these two short works the author expounds the names in the Lord’s genealogy according to their mystical and moral sense, and thereby teaches us what must be done if we are to be made worthy of Christ’s promises.

**ALAN OF LILLE.**---*The Complaint of Nature*, a work in which he sharply inveighs against many vices, CCX, 431.

**St. AMBROSE, Bishop of Milan, Doctor of the Church.**---*On Paradise*, in which he shows what Paradise was, of what sort, and where it was; what the first parents did there; and by what deceit, order, and art they were tempted by the devil and finally fell into sin. It contains very much useful material for the formation of Christian morals, XIV, 375.---*On Noah and the Ark*, in which he describes Noah’s life, character, deeds, and loftiness of mind, and proposes this righteous man for the imitation of all, ibid., 361.---Two books *On Abraham*: in the first he sets forth Abraham’s life and virtues and the moral sense; in the latter he turns to allegory and explains how the soul is commanded to leave its own land and kindred, and from what things it must withdraw in order to attain complete purification, ibid., 419.---Two books *On Jacob and the Blessed Life*: here he treats the history of the patriarch Jacob and matters pertaining to the blessed life. He teaches that passions must be restrained and virtues cultivated from the examples of Jacob and others, in order that blessedness may be attained; he places it in the possession of the one supreme good, namely God, ibid., 595.---*On Joseph the Patriarch*: he teaches that Joseph is proposed to us as a mirror of chastity, since in his character and every deed that virtue, together with the certain radiance of grace which accompanies chastity, shines forth most perfectly, ibid., 641.---*On Naboth the Israelite*, where he sets before our eyes the cruelty of the avaricious rich man and the calamity of the poor man suffering every extremity; thereafter he exhorts the rich to almsgiving, ibid., 731.---*On Tobit*: here the author inveighs against usury. He proves it to be evil and accursed—being forbidden by the divine law—and no less serious than idolatry or homicide. He describes and rebukes [Col. 0310] the criminal devices of moneylenders by which they compel needy persons to receive their money on condition of paying interest, ibid., 759.---Three books *On Virgins*: in the first he considers the dignity of virginity; in the second, undertaking to form the conduct of virgins, he declares that he can do this most fittingly by examples, the first and foremost of which he takes from the Mother of God, the standard-bearer of all virgins; in the third he prescribes what virgins ought to follow and what they ought to avoid, XVI, 187.---*On Widows*: he maintains that the profession of widowhood stands next to virginity and greatly surpasses marriage. He adduces in support not only apostolic testimony but also examples from the Old Testament; finally, with all the force of his eloquence, he urges widows to persevere in the unmarried life, whose holiness, benefits, and proper virtues he there describes, ibid., 233.---*On Virginity*: defending the virginal state, he chiefly vindicates his own action by the example of the Forerunner; he extols the virgin state from the fact that Christ chose virgins to whom He would appear after His resurrection; then he gives a fine response to the objections raised, ibid., 365.---*On Penance*: he recounts the duties and merits of penance, XVII, 971, in the Appendix.---*On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*, addressed to Simplicianus: here the author briefly displays the strongholds of our enemy, with which he never ceases to attack those who live piously in Christ, ibid., 1057, in the Appendix. All these short writings of St. Ambrose, especially useful for the formation of morals, breathe great piety. There are many others which the kindly reader will find in the ascetical library.

**ANONYMOUS.**---Explanation of the Lord’s Prayer, CCXIII, 719.---Explanation of the Apostolic and Athanasian Creeds, ibid., 723, 735.---Book on the various orders and professions in the Church, ibid., 807.---Dialogue on the conflict of the love of God and the deceitful tongue, ibid., 851.---Book on penance and the temptations of religious, ibid., 865.---Short treatise on conscience, ibid., 903.---Book on the steadfastness of the soul, ibid., 911.

**ATTO, Bishop of Vercelli.**---Capitulary, namely admonitions to priests, CXXXIV, 27.

**VARIOUS AUTHORS.**---The *Lives of the Holy Fathers*, where much moral instruction is found, especially on cultivating virtues and avoiding vices. Those who read these lives of the Holy Fathers will derive much fruit for the formation of their morals, LXXIII, LXXIV, passim.

**St. AUGUSTINE, Bishop of Hippo, Doctor of the Church.**---*On the Blessed Life*, where it is proved that the blessed life consists only in the perfect knowledge of God, XXXII, 959.---*On the Good of Marriage*: he teaches that marriage is honourable for many persons, good not merely by comparison with fornication but by its own kind, and in itself free from every sin; continence, however, is far more excellent, XL, 373.---*On the Good of Widowhood*: here he teaches and exhorts widows to prefer the profession of holy widowhood to marriage; nevertheless, he proves that second marriages—even third and however many more—are lawful and never evil, ibid., 429.---Two books *On Adulterous Marriages*, where it is proved: (1) that wives cannot depart from their husbands except on account of fornication; (2) that faithful spouses ought not use the permission granted them to leave unbelieving spouses, ibid., 451.---*On Care to Be Taken for the Dead*, in which it is proved: (1) that burial altogether denied to dead bodies harms the dead themselves in no way; (2) that the place of burial is of no benefit in itself, but only incidentally; (3) that care for burial, since it makes no difference to happiness or misery, was rightly despised by the saints; (4) he speaks of dead persons who are reported to have appeared to the living in order that burial might be provided for their bodies; (5) whether the dead take part in human concerns and affairs, ibid., 591.---*On Friendship*, where a threefold friendship is discussed: carnal, worldly, and spiritual, ibid., 831.---*On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*: here virtue and the contrary of virtue alternately address the Christian, that he may pass over to their respective camps, ibid., 1091, in the Appendix.---Twenty-two books *On the City of God*, in which much moral as well as dogmatic material may be found, XLI, 13.---Three books *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins and on the Baptism of Infants*: here he discusses (1) original sin and its transmission; (2) proves that no one has ever been, is, or will be wholly free from sin, except the Mediator; (3) treats infant baptism, XLIV, 109.---*On the Perfection of Human Righteousness*, in which he teaches that that perfection and fullness of righteousness by which a human being is without any sin whatsoever is neither possible through the powers of nature, especially fallen nature, apart from grace, nor ever belongs to this present life, ibid., 291.---Two books *On Marriage and Concupiscence*: he sets forth the proper and natural goods of marriage and proves that concupiscence of the flesh is not to be reckoned among those goods, ibid., 413.---*On the Gift of Perseverance*, in which he proves that perseverance, by which one perseveres in Christ to the end, is a gift of God; for it would be mockingly requested from God if it were not believed to be given by God, XLV, 993.---For St. Augustine’s other moral works and short writings, see the Ascetical Library.

**BACHIARIUS, monk.**---*On the Restoration of One Who Has Fallen*, or *On Receiving Back the Fallen*, in which he teaches that sinners are to be received to penance with the greatest charity, XX, 1037.

**BALDWIN, Archbishop of Canterbury.**---Treatise *On the Corrupt Morals of Clergy and People*, CCIV, 415.---*On the Twofold Resurrection, Which Is Attained through Perseverance in Obedience*, ibid., 429.---Treatise *On the Rest Which Christ Sought and Prepared for Himself and Us*, ibid., 441.---The author wrote several other works which will be found in the ascetical library.

**St. BERNARD, Abbot of Clairvaux.**---Five books *On Consideration*, in which he discusses the dignity, authority, and virtues of the pontiff, etc., CLXXXII, 727.---Treatise *On the Conduct and Office of Bishops*, ibid., 809.---*Sentences*, CLXXXIII, 747, 751.---*Parables*, ibid., 757.---*Flowers*, or sayings, drawn from the works of St. Bernard, ibid., 1197.---These three short works especially treat various vices and virtues.---Many works and short writings of this author are moral and ascetical; they are listed in the ascetical library.

**BOETHIUS SEVERINUS.**---Five books *On the Consolation of Philosophy*: this work, small in bulk but great in learning, consists of a sequence of arguments known by the natural light of reason. By these, the human mind, raised up in adverse circumstances, is directed in attention to the first cause and ultimate end, so that, divested of prejudices, it is made more fit to attain truth and cultivate virtue, LXIII, 581.

**BURCHARD, Bishop of Worms.**---Twenty books of *Decrees*, in which the author embraces, with brilliant brevity, the entire ecclesiastical office and the ancient observances of the churches. Whoever reads them will find that in a short time he can gain no ordinary profit, CXL, 537.

**St. CAESARIUS, Bishop of Arles.**---Short work *On Preserving Widowhood*, LXVII, 1094.---Exhortation *On Maintaining or Guarding Charity*, ibid., 1151.---Letter to certain brethren, in which he especially discusses chastity and incidentally other virtues pertaining to virginity, ibid., 1154.---Exhortation *On the Ten Virgins*, concerning chastity, ibid., 1160.---For other works, see the ascetical library.

**CASSIODORUS the Senator, Abbot of Vivarium.**---*On the Soul*: this short work, which should be classified among dogmatic writings, is mentioned here because many moral teachings flow from it; in particular it discusses the virtues and the nature of the soul, LXX, 1279.

**St. CHROMATIUS, bishop.**---A single treatise *On the Eight Beatitudes*, concerning the spiritual marketplace and the acquisition of various virtues, XX, 323.

**St. COLUMBANUS, abbot and confessor.**---*On Establishing the Measure of Penances*, in which the duration of penances is fixed according to the gravity of offences, LXXX, 223.

**St. CUMMIAN, abbot.**---*On the Measure of Penances*, treating various sins and the penances to be imposed, LXXXVII, 981.

**St. CYPRIAN, Bishop of Carthage.**---*On Mortality*, by which Christians of excessively tender feeling over the loss of their own, or, what is more serious, of deficient faith, might be consoled through hope in things to come, IV, 581.---*On Works and Alms*, in which he shows how great the power of mercy is and with what rewards it is to be rewarded, ibid., 601.---Letter to Fortunatus, *On the Exhortation to Martyrdom*, in which he exhorts and encourages Christ’s soldiers to the heavenly and spiritual contest, ibid., 651.---*On Discipline and the Good of Modesty*: the author proves that modesty holds the first place among virgins, the second among the continent, the third in marriages, and is glorious in all these according to their respective grades, ibid., 819; a doubtful work.---*On Gamblers*: the author addresses priests, proves gambling harmful and a mortal crime, and exhorts them to avoid it, ibid., 827; a spurious work.---There are many other works of St. Cyprian classed among ascetical writings; see the Ascetical Library.

**DIONYSIUS EXIGUUS, monk.**---*On the Creation of Man*, a work of St. Gregory of Nyssa translated from Greek into Latin, in which many moral matters are intermingled with dogmatic ones, especially concerning the soul, LXVII, 347.

**St. EGBERT, Bishop of York.**---*Selections Compiled from the Sayings and Canons of the Holy Fathers*, in which many rules are found conducive to the ordering of ecclesiastical polity, LXXXIX, 379.---*Penitential*, or four penitential books, in which the author sets forth the discipline of the Church and invites to weeping and compunction, ibid., 401.

**EUGYPPIUS, African abbot.**---*Treasury from the Works of St. Augustine*: this work contains much that is both moral and dogmatic, especially concerning the virtues—charity, prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice—and the vices to be avoided in attaining eternal life, LXII, 561.

**EVAGRIUS, monk.**---Sayings for those living in monasteries and hostels: namely, what should be done and what avoided, XX, 1181.---Sayings for virgins, on cultivating virtues and avoiding vices, ibid., 1186.

**St. FULGENTIUS of Ruspe.**---Letter I, discussing the marital debt and the vow of continence made by spouses, LXV, 303.---Letter II, to Galla, a widow, concerning consolation for a deceased husband and the condition of widows, ibid., 311.---Two books *On the Forgiveness of Sins*, in which the author shows to whom, where, and when God forgives sins, ibid., 527.---There are many other moral works of St. Fulgentius; see the Ascetical Library.

**GERBERT, or POPE SYLVESTER II.**---*On the Formation of Bishops*, CXXXIX, 169.

**GERHOH, Provost of Reichersberg.**---*On the Building of God*, concerning the conduct of priests and ecclesiastical discipline, CXCIV, 1187.

**GODFREY, Abbot of Admont.**---*On the Ten Burdens of Isaiah*, which the author explains figuratively by referring them to human sins, and thereby teaches sinners true repentance, CLXXIV, 1157.

**St. GREGORY THE GREAT, Doctor of the Church.**---Twenty-five books of *Morals*, in which he expounds the Book of Job in its historical, allegorical, and moral sense; humility and patience amid tribulations especially shine forth here, LXXV, 527, and LXXVI, 9–780. Those who read these will receive great consolation in their patience.---Four books of *Dialogues*, or *On the Life and Miracles of the Italian Fathers*: here there is discussion of virtues and vices; those who read these books diligently will find an unfailing treasure, LXXVII, 149.

**GUNTHER THE CISTERCIAN.**---Thirteen books *On Prayer, Fasting, and Almsgiving*, CCXII, 97.---A short work *On Self-Knowledge*, ibid., 721.---*On the Good Government of a Prince*: he teaches what a king must do and avoid in order to obtain God’s kingdom, ibid., 735.---*On the Restoration of One Who Has Fallen*, namely, an exhortation to penance, in which he teaches ways of rising again to grace, ibid., 745.

**HERBERT OF BOSHAM.**---*Book of Melodies*, in which: (1) on the correspondence of the visible contest of the soldier, that is, St. Thomas, with the visible contest of the emperor, that is, Christ; (2) on the correspondence of the visible palm of the soldier with the visible palm of the emperor; (3) on the correspondence of the invisible palm of the soldier with the invisible palm of the emperor, CXC, 1293.

**St. JEROME, priest and Doctor of the Church.**---Letters, many of which contain material most useful for forming morals; see the Ascetical Library and the index of subjects at the end of volume XXII.---*Breviary on the Psalms*, where much moral material is found, especially concerning virtues and vices, XXVI, 823.

**St. HILARY, Bishop of Poitiers, Doctor of the Church.**---Letter to his daughter Abra: he exhorts her to wear modest garments and promises her a garment and a pearl of inestimable price, X, 549.

**HILDEBERT, Archbishop of Tours.**---*On the Complaint and Conflict of Flesh and Soul*, where he shows that the flesh lusts against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh, CLXXI, 989.---*On the Honourable and the Useful*, in which: (1) what is honourable; (2) the comparison of honourable things; (3) what is useful; (4) the comparison of useful things; (5) when that which seems honourable appears to conflict with that which seems useful, ibid., 1007.

**St. ILDEFONSUS, Bishop of Toledo.**---*On the Journey through the Desert*, in which it is indicated how, after baptism, a person hastens to arrive at the dwelling of eternal life—as after crossing the sea toward the promised land—through keeping the divine commandments, XCVI, 171.

**HINCMAR, Archbishop of Rheims.**---A short work *On the Person of the King and the Royal Ministry*, in which he furnishes from Scripture and the Holy Fathers suitable and highly useful teachings for forming the king’s character, CXXV, 833.---Instruction for Louis the Stammerer, ibid., 983.---*On Royal Institution*, ibid., 989.---To the magnates of the realm, *For the Instruction of King Carloman*, ibid., 993. These three short works are useful for the formation of a prince or king.---Synodal chapters, ibid., 1069.---*On the Offices of Bishops*, ibid., 1087.---*On Criminal Priests*, ibid., 1091. In these three short works he teaches bishops and priests, showing what must be done and avoided if they are to work for their own salvation and that of others, and attain the heavenly crown.

**HUGH OF ST. VICTOR.**---A short work *On the Five Sevens, or Septenaries*, concerning the seven vices, the seven petitions of the Lord’s Prayer, and the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, CLXXV, 405.---Two books *On Marriage*: the first on avoiding carnal marriages, the second on embracing spiritual marriages, CLXXVI, 1202.---Three books *On Beasts and Other Things*, CLXXVII, 15, in the Appendix.---*Miscellanies*, ibid., 469, in the Appendix. These two short works contain much useful for the formation of morals, especially concerning virtues and vices. Moreover, see the Ascetical Library.

**POPE INNOCENT III.**---Dialogue between God and the sinner, CCXVII, 691.---*On Contempt of the World, or On the Misery of the Human Condition*, ibid., 701.---A short treatise *On Almsgiving*, ibid., 746.---*Encomium of Charity*, ibid., 761.---Six books *On the Sacred Mystery of the Altar*, ibid., 774.---Commentary on the Seven Penitential Psalms, ibid., 967.

**St. ISIDORE, Bishop of Seville.**---The second and third books of *Sentences*, discussing vices and virtues, LXXXIII, 599, 736.---Two books of *Synonyms*, or rather *On the Lamentation of the Sinful Soul*. Whoever endeavours to proceed through this work with attentive mind will undoubtedly discover how to avoid vices, lament sins committed, and, restored through the laments of repentance, be endowed with eternal rewards, ibid., 827. For other works of St. Isidore, see the Ascetical Library.

**JOHN OF SALISBURY, Bishop of Chartres.**---Eight books of *Polycraticus, or On the Trifles of Courtiers and the Footprints of Philosophers*, in which the author proves that all things which are said or done yield to the wise person’s use and furnish matter for the exercise of virtue, CXCIX, 379.

**JONAS, Bishop of Orléans.**---A short work *On Royal Institution*, in which the author gives precepts for the formation of a king, CVI, 279.

**LACTANTIUS FIRMIANUS.**---Seven books of the *Divine Institutes*: (1) On false religion; (2) on the origin of error; (3) on the false wisdom of philosophers; (4) on true wisdom; (5) on justice; (6) on true worship; (7) on the blessed life. Here the author records many matters among dogmatic subjects, and very many useful for forming Christian morals; consequently this [Col. 0314] work has been given a place among moral writings and will be read with profit, VI, 110.

**St. LAURENCE, Bishop of Novara.**---*On Penance, Almsgiving, and the Canaanite Woman*, concerning perseverance and efficacy in prayer, together with several other matters for the formation of morals, LXVI, 89, 105, 116.

**POPE LIBERIUS.**---Prayer addressed to Marcellina, sister of St. Ambrose, on the giving of the veil of virginity, concerning virginity, silence, and religious life, VIII, 1345.

**LUCIFER, Bishop of Cagliari.**---*That One Must Die for the Son of God*, a book addressed to Emperor Constantius: the author reproaches the emperor for cruelty, threatens him with eternal punishment, and promises an incorruptible kingdom to suffering Christians, XIII, 1007.

**St. MAXIMUS, Bishop of Turin.**---Three treatises *On Baptism*, in which he shows against the Jews that Jesus Christ, true God and true man, our Redeemer, must be heard and adored; and he exhorts them, through the promise of eternal life, to abandon hardness of heart and behold in Christ the light of truth, LVII, 775.---Two letters on enduring illness and on the perfect man, ibid., 921, 933.

**OTHLO, priest and monk.**---Dialogue on Three Questions: the knowledge of divine goodness, the diversity of divine judgments, and the varied capacity for doing good, CXLVI, 59.---*On the Spiritual Course*, or alternatively *On the Manner of Running in This Life So as to Attain Eternal Life*, addressed to all Christians but especially to sinners that they may live again, ibid., 139.---*On the Admonition of Clergy and Laity*: admonitions through which all may turn their minds from carnal to spiritual things, from visible to invisible things, and behold things above, ibid., 243.

**St. PACIAN, Bishop of Barcelona.**---Letter to Sympronianus the Novatian, containing much on the name “Christian” and “Catholic,” XIII, 1050.

**St. PAULINUS, Patriarch of Aquileia.**---*Exhortation to Henry of Friuli*, or *On Saving Counsels*. This work concerns morals and is highly useful to preachers, especially priests upon whom rests the burden of speaking words to the people, XCIX, 197.

**PETER OF BLOIS, archdeacon.**---Compendium on Job, addressed to Henry II, King of the English: here the Christian is instructed in patience and various virtues, CCVIII, 795.

**PETER THE CHANTER, canon of Paris.**---*The Abbreviated Word*: this work is salutary and fruitful for the avoidance and protection from sin, the formation of morals, the acquisition of virtues, and the instilling in the mind of love of God and contempt for the world, CCV, 23.

**CARDINAL PETER DAMIAN.**---*The Book of Gomorrah*: here he laments the shameful and detestable crime into which persons consecrated to God in his time were falling, and contends that, as unworthy, they must be removed from holy orders, CXLV, 160.---*Against Love of Money and the Desire for Gifts*: he most gravely condemns the vice of avarice, especially in accepting gifts, and exhorts bishops to endeavour to uproot and banish it from the Church, ibid., 529.

**PHILIP OF HARVENG, Abbot of Bonne-Espérance.**---Moral interpretations of the *Song of Songs*, where much moral teaching is found, specifically concerning the virtues to cultivate and the vices to avoid, CCIII, 489.

**St. PIRMIN, abbot.**---*Scarapsus, or Collection, on the Individual Canonical Books*: here the author enumerates all virtues Christians must cultivate and vices they must flee, LXXXIX, 1029.

**St. PROSPER OF AQUITAINE.**---Book of sayings selected from the works of St. Augustine, especially concerning virtues and vices, LI, 427.---Poem *On Divine Providence*, ibid., 617.

**RABANUS MAURUS, Abbot of Fulda.**---*On the Oblation of Children*: the author proves that the world must be fled and praises those who, leaving all things, live in solitude in order to gain heaven, CVII, 419.---*Penitential*, in which he briefly indicates what the sacred canons decree concerning various crimes and how those who have committed them must perform penance, CX, 471. For other moral works of this author, see the Ascetical Library.

**RATHERIUS, Bishop of Verona.**---Three books of *Preliminary Discourses*, forming all persons of every rank, condition, sex, and age in the Christian life, CXXXVI, 145.

**REGINO, Abbot of Prüm.**---Two books *On Ecclesiastical Disciplines and the Christian Religion*: here bishops, priests, and clerics will find substantial instruction for the formation of morals and the rule of life, CXXXII, 185.

**RODULPHUS, Bishop of Bourges.**---*Chapters*, a work excerpted from the sayings of the Holy Fathers and the canons, and especially suitable for forming the character of priests, CXIX, 703.

**RUFINUS, priest of Aquileia.**---*History of the Monks*, or *Book on the Lives of the Fathers*, in which he shows forth great wonders profitable for the memory of posterity, so that those who learn their deeds and infer a perfect life from the testimony of the reading may be invited to imitate holy work and seek the palm of perfect wisdom or patience, XXI, 391.

**RUPERT, Abbot of Deutz.**---*On the Violation of Virginity, and Whether a Defiled Woman May Be Consecrated*, CLXX, 545. For Rupert’s other moral writings, see the Ascetical Library.

**St. SALVIAN, priest of Marseilles.**---Two books *On the Governance of God*, in which divine Providence in all things and above all things is splendidly maintained, LIII, 25.---Four books *Against Avarice*, in which the author inveighs against this bondage of idolatry and proves that mercy and generosity are the special good of Christians, ibid., 173.

**SEDULIUS SCOTUS.**---*On Christian Rulers and the Appropriate Rules by Which the Commonwealth Is Rightly Governed*, a work highly useful for forming a prince or king, CIII, 291.

**SICARD, Bishop of Cremona.**---*Mitrale*, or a compendium on ecclesiastical offices, CCXIII, 14, and especially the third book, which chiefly treats the duties of ministers.

**SULPICIUS SEVERUS.**---Three *Dialogues*: the author describes monasteries of the East, recounts various miracles, and incidentally discusses vices and virtues, XX, 183.---Two letters to his sister, concerning the last judgment and virginity, ibid., 223, 227.

**TAIO, Bishop of Saragossa.**---Five books of *Sentences*: beginning from the Trinity, the unchangeable essence of the almighty Lord, and from the origin of the world and the creation of humankind, the author surveys almost all the teachings of the Christian religion and expounds them elegantly in dogmatic and moral terms. There the reader will find to what he ought to cling more firmly and from what he should endeavour to withdraw as swiftly as possible, LXXX, 731.

**TERTULLIAN, priest.**---Two books *To His Wife*: he exhorts his wife to refrain from a second marriage or, if she wishes to marry, to be joined only to a Christian husband, I, 1273.---Two books *On Women’s Dress*, concerning the vanity of gold, gems, and clothing, and the avoidance of cosmetics and pigments, ibid., 1303.---*On the Veiling of Virgins*: he proves from Scripture, the Church’s discipline, examples of the saints, and the dangers to un-veiled virgins themselves, that virgins must be veiled, II, 887.---*On the Exhortation to Chastity*: he dissuades a certain widowed brother from a second marriage, which at one point he expressly permits and asserts is not forbidden by St. Paul, but at another condemns and describes as adultery. This treatise was written by Tertullian as a Montanist, ibid., 913.---*On Monogamy*: he claims to hold a middle way between those who deny marriage and others who introduce repeated marriages; he therefore defends monogamy and teaches that this discipline is not new, but ancient and proper to Christians. This work was rightly censured and condemned by the Church, ibid., 929.---*On Modesty*: having first praised modesty, the author follows the error of Montanus in treating the non-reception of penitents, at least adulterers and fornicators, ibid., 979.

THEODORE, Archbishop of Canterbury.—*Penitential*, in which may be found, as it were, an outstanding compendium of the whole of Christian doctrine and ecclesiastical discipline for the formation of morals, XCIX, 901.

THEODULF, Bishop of Orléans.—*Chapters for the Priests of His Church*: by reading them he exhorts them to order their conduct and amend their lives, so that they may strive with the peoples subject to them toward the heavenly kingdoms, CV, 191.—His *Capitulary to the Same*: here he prescribes to priests a prudent manner of conducting themselves in their ministry, ibid., 207.

VALERIUS (St.), Abbot.—*On the Vain Wisdom of the World*: this author, briefly reviewing the history of the Christian religion and both its struggles and its triumphs, shows how insignificant the wisdom of the world is in comparison with it, LXXXVII, 425.

VERANUS (St.), Bishop of Cavaillon.—*Judgment concerning the Chastity of Priests*, LXXII, 701.

VICTORINUS, rhetorician.—Two books *On Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians*, especially the second, which contains precepts of living suitable for Christians individually and collectively: what a master ought to do toward a servant, a son toward a father, and a husband toward a wife, VIII, 1235.

VICTRICIUS (St.), Bishop of Rouen.—*Book on the Praise of the Saints*: he exhorts readers to imitate the saints and discusses the virtues by which they shone, XX, 443.

WALAFRID STRABO, monk of Fulda.—*Treatise on the Destruction of Jerusalem*: the author expounds it anagogically, morally, and mystically, and applies it to the sinful soul; it contains likewise many things useful for the conversion of the sinner, CXIV, 965.

ZACCHAEUS THE CHRISTIAN.—Three books of *Consultations*, especially the third, in which there is much concerning Christian and monastic life, virginity, and continence, XX, 1071.

ZENO (St.), Bishop of Verona.—First book of *Treatises*: on faith, hope, and charity; justice, modesty, continence, patience, fear, and avarice; likewise on spirit and body, circumcision, the spiritual building of God’s house, and the resurrection, XI, 252.

[Col. 0315]

## CXXXVII. THE SAME LIBRARY OF THE LATIN FATHERS, MORALLY ARRANGED BY ANALOGY, WHILE PRESERVING IN THE ANALOGY BOTH ALPHABETICAL AND CHRONOLOGICAL ORDER

**Friendship.**—*Book on Friendship*, St. Augustine, XL, 831.

**Soul.**—Two books *On Abraham*, St. Ambrose, XIV, 419.—*Book on the Creation of Man*, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 347.—*Book on the Soul*, Cassiodorus, LXX, 1279.—*Book on the Stability of the Soul*, Anonymous, CCXIII, 911.

**Avarice.**—First book of *Treatises*, St. Zeno, XI, 253.—*On Naboth the Jezreelite*, St. Ambrose, XIV, 731.—*Book on Tobias*, ibid., 759.—Four books *Against Avarice*, St. Salvian, LIII, 173.—*Against Love of Money and Desire for Gifts*, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 529.

**Chastity, Modesty, Virginity.**—*Book on the Veiling of Virgins*, Tertullian, II, 887.—*Exhortation to Chastity*, ibid., 913.—*Book on Modesty*, ibid., 979.—*Book on Discipline and the Good of Modesty*, St. Cyprian, IV, 819.—Address to Marcellina, sister of St. Ambrose, Pope Liberius, VIII, 1345.—First book of *Treatises*, St. Zeno, XI, 253.—*Book on the Patriarch Joseph*, St. Ambrose, XIV, 641.—Three books *On Virgins*, [Col. 0316] the same author, XVI, 187.—*Book on Virginity*, ibid., 265.—Two letters to his sister, Sulpicius Severus, XX, 223, 227.—Three books of *Consultations*, Zacchaeus the Christian, ibid., 1071.—*Maxims for Virgins*, Evagrius, ibid., 1186.—Letter to certain brethren, St. Caesarius of Arles, LXVII, 1154.—*Exhortation concerning the Ten Virgins*, ibid., 1160.—*Judgment concerning the Chastity of Priests*, St. Veranus, LXXII, 701.—*The Book of Gomorrah*, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 160.—*On the Violation of Virginity*, Rupert, CLXX, 545.

**Charity.**—*On Maintaining or Preserving Charity*, St. Caesarius of Arles, LXXII, 1151.—*On the Conflict between Love of God and the Deceitful Tongue*, Anonymous, CCXIII, 851.—*Encomium of Charity*, Innocent III, CCXVII, 761.

**The Christian: what he is and what he must do.**—Two books *On Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians*, Victorinus, VIII, 1235.—Letter to Sympronianus the Novatian, St. Pacian, XIII, 1051.—*Book on Paradise*, St. Ambrose, XIV, 275.—*Book on Noah and the Ark*, ibid., 361.—[Col. 0317] Three books of *Consultations*, Zacchaeus the Christian, XX, 1071.—*Book on the City of God*, St. Augustine, XLI, 13.—Two letters *On the Perfect Man*, St. Maximus, LVII, 921, 933.—Five books *On the Consolation of Philosophy*, Boethius, LXIII, 581.—Twenty-five books of *Morals*, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 527; LXXVI, 9.—Mystical interpretation of Christ’s first ancestors, St. Aileran, LXXX, 327.—Moral interpretation of their names, ibid., 333.—Five books of *Sentences*, Taio, LXXX, 731.—*Book on the Journey through the Desert*, St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 171.—*On Saving Instructions*, St. Paulinus, XCIX, 197.—*Book on the Offering of Children*, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 419.—Three books of *Preliminary Discourses*, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 145.—*Dialogue on Three Questions*, Othlo, CXLVI, 59.—*Book on the Spiritual Course*, ibid., 139.—*Book on the Admonition of Laypeople*, ibid., 243.—*Book on What Is Honourable and Useful*, Hildebert, CLXXI, 1007.—*On the Corrupt Morals of the People*, Baldwin, CCIV, 415.—*On the Rest Which Christ Sought and Prepared for Himself and for Us*, ibid., 441.—*Compendium on Job*, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 795.—*On the Misery of the Human Condition*, Innocent III, CCXVII, 701.

**Knowledge of oneself.**—*Short Work on Self-Knowledge*, Gunther, CCXII, 721.

Berengosus, abbot of St. Maximin of Trier, CLX, 981. Bernard, prior of the Carthusian house of Portes, CLIII, 885, 892. Bernard (St.), abbot of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, throughout the letters; 833, 859, 941, 973, 1133; CLXXXIII, 794, 815, 819, 843, 848, 867, 878–1195. Bruno (St.) of Asti, bishop of Segni, CLXV, 875. Caesarius (St.), bishop of Arles, LXVII, 1097, 1107, 1121, 1125, 1135. Cassian, priest of Marseilles, XLIX, 53, 477. Chrodegang (St.), bishop of Metz, LXXXIX, 1057. Chromatius (St.), bishop of Aquileia, XX, 323. Columbanus (St.), abbot and confessor, LXXX, 209, 229. Cyprian (St.), bishop of Carthage, IV, throughout the letters; 441, 467, 493, 543, 581, 621, 637, 723, 787, 869–881. Defensor, monk of Locociag. [as printed], LXXXVIII, 597. Donatus (St.), bishop of Besançon, LXXXVII, 273. Drogo, cardinal and bishop of Ostia, CLXVI, 1557. Durand, abbot of Troarn, CXLIX, 1375. Eadmer, monk of Canterbury, CLIX, 587, 605. Eckbert, abbot of Schönau, CXCV, 103, 105, 114. Ernald, abbot of Bonneval, CLXXXIX, 1677, 1733. Eucherius (St.), bishop of Lyons, L, 701, 711, 833, 867, 877. Eulogius (St.), bishop of Toledo, CXV, 821. Eutropius (St.), abbot and bishop, LXXX, 9. Eutychian (St.), pope, V, 163. Fastidius, bishop of Britain, L, 383. Florus, deacon of Lyons, CXIX, 15. Gregory the Great, Doctor of the Church, LXXVII, 13; LXXIX, 550. Guibert, abbot of Nogent, CLVI, 31, 579. Guigo I, prior of the Grande Chartreuse, CLIII, 601. Guigo II, prior of the Grande Chartreuse, CLIII, 885, 892. William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, CLXXX, 205, 206, 249, 365, 397. Guitmund, archbishop of Aversa, CXLIX, 1427. Halitgar, bishop of Cambrai, CV, 651. Haymo, bishop of Halberstadt, CXVIII, 875. Henry, archdeacon of Huntingdon, CXCV, 979. Henry of Château-Marçay, cardinal, CCIV, 251. Jerome (St.), priest and Doctor of the Church, XXII, throughout the letters; XXX, throughout the letters, and 311, 319–391. Hildebert, archbishop of Tours, CLXXI, 1413, 1149, 1153, 1195. Hildebrand the Younger, CLXXXI, 1691. Hildegard (St.), abbess, CXCVII, 1053, 1065. Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, CXXV, 857, 1087. Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 1229, 1239, 1242, 1247, 1249. Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, CXCII, 1323. Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 618, 677, 703, 881, 925, 951, 969, 977, 993, 997, 1017, 1183; CLXXVII, 165. Isaac, abbot of Stella, CXCIV, 1889. Isidore (St.), bishop of Seville, LXXXIII, 867, 1131, 1153, 1201, 1243, 1247. John the Carthusian, monk of Portes, CLIII, 900. John of Michelsberg, CLXVI, 857. John of Salisbury, bishop of Chartres, CXCIX, 945. Jonas, bishop of Orléans, CVI, 121. Joscelin, bishop of Soissons, CLXXXVI, 1479. Julianus Pomerius, LIX, 415. Julian (St.), bishop of Toledo, XCVI, 453. Lactantius Firmianus, VI, 347, 545, 633. Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, CL, 443. Lawrence (St.) of Novara, LXVI, 89. Leander (St.) of Seville, LXXII, 873. Leo (St.) the Great, LV, 161. Leo (St.) IX, pope, CXLIII, 559. “Master,” an author of uncertain name, LXXXVIII, 943. Martin, bishop of Dumio, LXXII, 21, 29, 31, 35, 39, 41. Maximus (St.), bishop of Turin, LVII, 921. Nicetas (St.), bishop of Aquileia, LII, 865. Nicetius (St.), bishop of Trier, LXVIII, 365, 371. Peter of Blois, archdeacon, CCVII, 871, 895, 989, 1077. Peter of Celle, bishop of Chartres, CCII, 927, 1047, 1083, 1101.
