Smaragdus, abbot, CII, 593, 691, 935.

[Col. 0326]

Stephen (St.), abbot of Cîteaux, CLXVI, 1384. Stephen of Baugé, CLXXII, 1273. Stephen (St.) of Muret, CCIV, 1085, 1135. Sulpicius Severus, XX, 223, 227. Taio, bishop of Saragossa, LXXX, 727. Tertullian, priest, I, 619, 1143, 1223, 1249; II, 101, 121, 953. Theodoric, canon of Paderborn, CXLVII, 333. Vigilius, deacon, L, 373. William (St.), abbot of Hirsau, CL, 927.

[Note: [Col. 0325] **NOTE.** This index presents only authors who wrote on Christian and religious perfection; but since ascetical works are very often assimilated to moral works, the kindly reader should consult the moral index.]

[Col. 0325]

## CXL. ASCETICAL LIBRARY OF THE FATHERS, OR ALL THE WORKS AND SHORT TREATISES OF THE ANCIENT FATHERS OF THE LATIN CHURCH ON CHRISTIAN AND RELIGIOUS PERFECTION, ARRANGED IN ALPHABETICAL ORDER OF AUTHORS

**PETER ABAELARD.**—*Explanation of the Lord’s Prayer*, CLXXVIII, 611.—*Explanation of the Apostles’ Creed*, ibid., 618.—*Exposition of the Faith in the Athanasian Creed*, ibid., 629.—*Ethics, or the Book Called “Know Yourself”* (*Scito teipsum*), ibid., 633.—Heloise’s *Problems*, with the solutions of Peter Abaelard, ibid., 677.

**ADALGER, bishop of the Order of St. Benedict.**—*Book on the Study of Virtues, or Admonition to Nonsuinda the Recluse*, CXXXIV, 917.

**ADAM THE SCOT, Premonstratensian canon.**—*Book on the Order, Habit, and Profession of Premonstratensian Canons*, CXCVIII, 439.—*On the Threefold Tabernacle*, especially Part Three, ibid., 609.—*On the Threefold Kind of Contemplation*, ibid., 795.—Two books of *Soliloquies on the Instruction of the Soul*, ibid., 843.

**AELRED, abbot of Rievaulx.**—*Mirror of Charity*, CXCV, 505.—*Compendium of the Mirror of Charity*, ibid., 621.—*Book on Spiritual Friendship*, ibid., 659.—*Rule, or Instruction, for Recluses*, ibid., 701.

**ALAN OF LILLE.**—*On the Six Wings of the Cherubim*, CCX, 269.—*Penitential Book*, ibid., 281.

ALCUIN (Blessed).—Book on the Use of the Psalms, or on various forms of prayer, CI, 465.—Book on Virtues and Vices, ibid., 613.—Book on the Nature of the Soul, ibid., 639.—Book on the Confession of Sins, ibid., 650.—A Devout and Brief Exposition of the Penitential and Gradual Psalms, C, 569.—Among the letters of the same Alcuin, many are to be found which may be classed as ascetic and read with great profit, C, passim.

ALDHELM (St), bishop of Sherborne.—Treatise in Praise of Virginity, LXXXIX, 103.—Poem in Praise of Virgins, ibid., 237.—Poem on the Eight Principal Vices, ibid., 281.

ALGER (St), canon of Liège.—Book on Mercy and Justice, CLXXX, 857.

AMALARIUS SYMPHOSIUS, priest of Metz.—Books on the Rule of Canons and Nuns, CV, 816.

AMBROSE (St), bishop of Milan, Doctor of the Church.—First Book on Cain and Abel; from the fourth chapter onward, it contains outstanding material on pleasure, which ensnares human minds; likewise, that temptations must be resisted courageously; that virtue is acquired only through toil; and that vows must be discharged without delay, XIV, 315.—Book on Isaac and the Soul, or on the spiritual progress of the soul striving toward virtue, ibid., 502.—Book on the Good of Death; here it is demonstrated by cogent Christian arguments that death is not to be feared, ibid., 539.—Book on Flight from the World; it proves, by the examples set forth of the patriarchs, prophets, the Apostle, and Christ the Lord himself, wherein this flight consists and how glorious, useful, and necessary it is, ibid., 569.—Book on Elijah and Fasting; [Col. 0326] an exceedingly elegant treatise on the power and efficacy of fasting, ibid., 697.—The Earlier and Later Apologies of David: a portrayal, that is, of David as sinner and penitent, ibid., 851, 887.—Books on the Interpretation of Job and David; concerning the bodily and spiritual infirmity of man, and also endurance in adversity, ibid., 798.—Two Books on Penance, particularly to be read by novices and recent converts, XVI, 465.—Expositions on the Psalms, moral in character and adorned with exceptional elegance, XIV, 921.—Three Books on the Duties of Ministers; they contain a most excellent Christian ethics, XVI, 23.—Book on the Instruction of a Virgin, ibid., 305.—Book of Exhortation to Virginity, ibid., 335.—Book on the Fall of a Consecrated Virginity, ibid., 367.—Book to a Devout Virgin, XVII, 579. These last four works may be read profitably by monks and by those who have vowed virginity.—Book on Priestly Dignity, XVII, 567.—Among St Ambrose’s various letters, see especially Letter 38, to Simplicianus, on the riches of Christian life, XVI, 1095;—Letter 49, to Sabinus, on the solitary and humble life, where he explains the saying, “I am never less alone than when I am alone,” ibid., 1153;—Letter 58, to the same person, on the same life, ibid., 1178;—Letter 77, to Horontianus, on what is the inheritance of Christians, ibid., 1263.—You will also find very many letters to bishops in which he admirably describes the duties of prelates.

ANONYMOUS AUTHORS OF THE TWELFTH CENTURY.—Explanation of the Lord’s Prayer, CCXIII, 719.—Explanation of the Creed, ibid., 725.—Dialogue on the Conflict between Love of God and a Deceitful Tongue, ibid., 851.—Book on the Penance and Temptations of Religious Persons, ibid., 865.—Little Book on Conscience, ibid., 903.—Book on the Steadfastness of the Soul, ibid., 911.

ANSELM (St), archbishop of Canterbury.—On Contempt for Temporal Things and Desire for Eternal Things, CLVIII, 677.—Poem on Contempt for the World, ibid., 687.—Book of Meditations, ibid., 709.—Meditation on the *Miserere*, ibid., 821.—Prayers, ibid., 855.—Treatise on Peace and Concord, ibid., 1015.—Ascetic Treatise, ibid., 1021.—Letter 2, Book I, ibid., 1063, where he prescribes the standard of a perfect life.—Letter 8, Book I, 1072, on hatred of the world.—Letter 29, Book I, 1093, on vigilance.—Letter 43, Book I, 1113, on religious progress.—Letter 64, Book I, 1135, on patiently rendering obedience.—Letter 12, Book II, 1160, on Satan’s snare against monks.—Many others are also to be found in Book III, CLIX, passim.

ANSELM, bishop of Havelberg.—Book on the Order of Regular Canons, CLXXXVIII, 1091.—Apologetic Letter for the Order of Regular Canons, ibid., 1117.

ANTONINUS HONORATUS.—Consolatory Letter to Arcadius, driven into exile by Genseric, king of the Vandals. [Col. 0327] He exhorts him to undergo labours for Christ with equanimity and to overcome death. This letter has almost the ring of apostolic style and should be read with much profit by the afflicted and patient, L, 567.

ARNO, provost of Reichersberg.—Shield of Canons, CXCIV, 1493.

ANONYMOUS AUTHOR.—Exhortation to Monks, XVIII, 71.—Exhortation to the Bride of Christ, ibid., 77.—Another author: Rule for Virgins, LXXXVIII, 1053.

AUGUSTINE (St), bishop of Hippo, Doctor of the Church.—Eighth Book of the *Confessions*, on his conversion; especially to be read by the fallen and penitents, XXXII, 747.—Two Books on Order, on God’s providence over good and evil persons, for beginners in matters of faith, ibid., 977.—Two Books of Soliloquies, ibid., 869.—Book on the Morals of the Catholic Church; it embraces the whole of Christian ethics and is therefore most useful to novices, ibid., 1309.—Rule for the Servants of God, ibid., 1377.—Book on the Hermit Life, to a Sister, ibid., 1451. This work is falsely attributed to Augustine.

Among the letters, many are moral; but the following should especially be noted: Letter 243, to Laetus, in which he seeks to commend contempt for secular and temporal things, XXXIII, 1054.—Letter 26, to Licentius, on the same subject, ibid., 103.—Letter 127, to Armentarius and Paulina, on the same subject, urging them to fulfil the vow of continence which they had made, ibid., 483.—Letter 155, to Macedonius, on true happiness, ibid., 666.—Letter 118, to Dioscorus, on not investigating vain and curious matters, ibid., 432.—Letter 192, to Caelestinus, on true charity and friendship, ibid., 868.—Letter 22, to Bishop Aurelius, on strife and deceit, and on contempt for human praise, ibid., 90.—Letter 48, to Abbot Eudoxius and his monks, that they should not misuse leisure and solitude for idleness, ibid., 187.—Letter 210, to Felicitas and Rusticus, on patiently bearing evils and fraternal correction, ibid., 957.—Letter 211, to nuns: he exhorts them to submission and peace, and lays down rules for religious living, ibid., 958.—Letter 140, to Honoratus, on how great is the grace of the New Testament, and that we must not place our hope in the prosperity of this age but rather amid tribulations, ibid., 538.—Letter 130, to the widow Proba, on how God should be prayed to, ibid., 493.—Letter 111, to the priest Victorianus, an exhortation to patience in adversity, ibid., 421.—Letter 101, to Bishop Memorium: he condemns liberal studies unless a concern for piety is present, ibid., 367.—Letter 77, to Bishops Felix and Hilary: he exhorts them patiently to endure people’s curses and not to judge rashly, ibid., 268.—Letter 188, to Juliana: he teaches a virgin that she has received virtues, especially continence, only from God and therefore ought to refer them back to him, ibid., 848.—Letter 145, to Anastasius: he elegantly shows that servile fear is insufficient for conquering or expiating sin, ibid., 592.—Letter 21, to Bishop Valerius, on the retirement necessary for prelates and superiors, so that they may be suited to their imposed office, ibid., 88.—Letter 38, to Profuturus, on enduring ill health and restraining anger, ibid., 152.—Letter 3, to Nebridius, on true blessedness, ibid., 63.—Letter 189, to Boniface, on what Christian life consists in, ibid., 854.—Letter 218, to Palatinus, that, having already begun, he may despise earthly things and exercise himself in Christ’s wisdom, ibid., 989.—Letter 263, to the virgin Sapida: consolation over the death of her brother, ibid., 1080.—Letter 95, to Paulinus and Therasia, on how this present life must be lived in order to attain the eternal life, ibid., 351.—Letter 231, to Darius, on love of human praise, ibid., 1022.—Four Books on Christian Doctrine, XXXIV, 15, especially to be read by learned persons and teachers of the Christian religion.—Books on the Literal Interpretation of Genesis, ibid., 245, a work most useful to those devoted to understanding Holy Scripture.—The *Mirror from Sacred Scripture*, suitable for the same persons, ibid., 887.—Books on the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount, ibid., 1229. If anyone considers this work devoutly, I think that he will find in it, so far as the highest moral conduct is concerned, a perfect pattern of Christian life.—Book on Faith and Works, XL, 197, for beginners in matters of faith and for teachers.—*Enchiridion* to Laurentius, or Book on Faith, Hope, and Charity, on how God is to be worshipped; for the same persons, ibid., 231.—Book on the Christian Contest, in which he exhorts and instructs readers to fight the Christian battle with the devil, ibid., 289. This book is especially necessary for those who, having trampled underfoot the world, labour in the Christian contest.—Book on Instructing Beginners; there he sets forth precepts so that this duty may be performed not only by a sound method, but also without tedium and with cheerfulness; most useful for catechists, ibid., 309.—Book on Continence; he teaches that the virtue of continence has the duty [Col. 0328] of restraining the lusts both of body and soul; to be read by monks, ibid., 349.—Book on Holy Virginity, namely, on the excellence of sacred virginity consecrated to God, ibid., 395; for virgins of Christ.—Book on Lying, in which it is investigated, through examples and arguments weighed on either side, what a lie is and whether it may ever be permitted, ibid., 487.—Book against Lying, in which it is proved that one must never lie, especially in matters pertaining to religious teaching, ibid., 517.—Book on the Work of Monks, ibid., 547.—Book on Patience, for the afflicted and penitents, ibid., 612.—Book on Christian Discipline, on what it is to live well; what is the reward of a good life; who are true Christians; and who is the true teacher: for novices and beginners in matters of faith, ibid., 669.—On the New Song, or on Return to the Heavenly Homeland and the Perils of Life, ibid., 677.—On Cultivating the Lord’s Field, ibid., 685.—On the Deluge, ibid., 693.—On the Barbarian Age, ibid., 700.—On the Benefit of Fasting, ibid., 707.—On the Destruction of the City, ibid., 715. These six short works should be presented especially to recent converts, novices, and also the afflicted.

Among the spurious short works in the Appendix to volume XX, the following seemed to us worthy of inclusion as ascetic works: Book on the Substance of Love, 843.—On Loving God, 847.—Soliloquies, 863.—Meditations, 901.—On Contrition of Heart, 943.—Handbook, 951.—Mirror, 967.—Mirror of the Sinner, 983.—On the Threefold Dwelling-Place, 991.—On the Ladder of Paradise, 997.—On Knowledge of the True Life, 1005.—On Christian Life, 1031.—On Saving Counsels, 1047.—On the Twelve Degrees of Abuses, 1079.—On Sobriety and Chastity, 1105.—On True and False Penance, 1113.—On Visiting the Sick, 1147.—On the Uprightness of Catholic Conduct, 1169.—Sermons to Brothers Dwelling in the Desert, 1235.—On Rebuke and Grace, concerning the necessity and usefulness of correction, XLIV, 915. Many other ascetic works are to be found among the homilies and sermons of the same St Augustine, which the kindly reader may examine for himself.

AURELIAN (St), bishop of Arles.—Rule for Monks, LXVIII, 385.—Rule for Virgins, ibid., 399.

BACHIARIUS, monk.—Book to Januarius on the Restoration of One Who Has Fallen, XX, 1037; to be read by recent converts and penitents.

BALDWIN, archbishop of Canterbury.—Various treatises, among which especially: On Love of God, CCIV, 417.—On the Twofold Resurrection, obtained through perseverance in obedience, ibid., 429.—On the Angelic Salutation, on the threefold grace of God, namely grace of beauty, favour, and honour, ibid., 467.—On the Wound of Charity Inflicted by the Bride upon the Bridegroom, ibid., 477.—On the Evangelical Beatitudes, ibid., 483.—Exhortation to Priests, ibid., 529.—On the Cenobitic, or Common, Life, ibid., 545.

BEDE THE VENERABLE.—Little Book on the Offices, XCIV, 531.—Extracts from the Holy Fathers, ibid., 540.—On Meditation upon the Passion, ibid., 561.—On Remedies for Sins, ibid., 568.

BENEDICT (St), abbot of Aniane.—On the Harmony of Rules, CIII, 717.

BENEDICT (St), abbot and founder of monks.—Commentary on the Rule, LXVI, 215.—Monastic Order: how brothers in a monastery ought to conduct themselves religiously and diligently and serve as soldiers of the Lord, ibid., 937.—Various Rules for Monks are found in the Appendix to the works of St Benedict; we exhort monks to peruse them, ibid., 949 and following.

BERENGOSUS, abbot of St Maximinus at Trier.—Distinguished Little Book on the Mystery of the Lord’s Wood, CLX, 981.

BERNARD, prior of the Carthusian monastery of Portes.—Letters, on flight from the world, CLIII, 885, and on how one ought to live before the Lord, ibid., 892.

BERNARD (St), abbot of Clairvaux.—All the works of St Bernard breathe the greatest piety; nevertheless, the following seem to us especially suitable for presentation as ascetic works:

1. Letters, in which the author treats of vocation, religious status, and the virtues of religious persons; namely: exhortatory letters, that care for the soul be preferred to concern for the body, and that the world be renounced, CLXXII, Letter 440.—Admonitory letters, on entering religion, Letters 104, 108, 411, 412.—On progress, Letters 254, 345, 385.—On devotion to regular discipline, Letter 273.—On the conduct of the first Cistercians, Letters 488, 492.—On choosing the religious life, Letters 31, 34, 109, 131, 322.—On reforming a monastery, Letter 489.—To recall those who had defected to other communities, Letter 1.—To recall apostates, Letters 2, 112, 415.—To recall those who have gone astray, Letters 4, 7.—Against those who draw others away from religious life, Letter 292.—On love of solitude and silence, [Col. 0329] Letters 21, 48, 52, 69.—On monks’ avoidance of travel, Letters 57, 399.—On the use of medicines, Letter 345.—On avoiding the company of women, for monks, Letters 79, 405.—For peace between Cistercians and Cluniacs, Letter 229.—On the brevity and economy of letters, Letters 88, 90.—On a religious who had married, Letter 76.—On transfer to another religious order, Letters 94, 313, 443.—On admitting religious persons from elsewhere, Letters 3, 32, 33, 65, 68, 253, 293, 382, 395.—On the prerogative of virginity, Letter 113.—To a nun who had turned herself toward better fruit, Letter 114.

2. Various treatises: Book on Conversion, to Clerics, CLXXXII, 833.—Book on Precept and Dispensation, ibid., 859.—Treatise on the Degrees of Humility and Pride, ibid., 941.—Book on Loving God, ibid., 973.—Book on the Passion of Christ and the Sorrows of His Mother, ibid., 1133.

Almost all St Bernard’s sermons contained in volume CXLXXIII should be counted among ascetic works, especially the Sermons on Various Subjects and the following among the Sermons on the Song of Songs: Sermons 3 and 4, on the kiss of foot, hand, and mouth, and on the soul’s threefold progress, ibid., 794.—Sermon 9, on love of God, 815.—Sermon 15, on the efficacy and sweetness of the name of Jesus, 843.—Sermon 16, on contrition of heart and the three kinds of true confession, 848.—Sermon 20, on the threefold mode of love, 867.—Sermon 22, on the four cardinal virtues, 878.—Sermon 23, on the three modes of contemplation, 884; and Sermon 52, 1029.—Sermon 27, on the adornment of the Bride, by which she is made altogether heavenly, 912.—Sermon 33, on the four kinds of temptations to be avoided, 951.—Sermon 34, on humility and patience, 959.—Sermon 42, on twofold humility, 987.—Sermon 43, on how the soul remains unharmed amid prosperity and adversity by contemplation of Christ’s Passion, 993.—Sermon 46, that the active life is the way to contemplation, 1004.—Sermon 47, on virginity and martyrdom, 1008.—Sermon 49, on twofold charity, 1016.—Sermon 55, on true penance, 1044.—Sermons 57 and 74, on the Lord’s various visitations, 1050, 1139.—Sermon 62, on perfect purity of mind, 1075.—Sermon 70, on the virtues among which, as among lilies, the Bridegroom feeds, 1116.—Sermon 75, on seeking God at the proper time, in the proper manner, and in the proper place, 1144.—Sermon 79, on the soul’s perfect union with God through love, 1163.—Sermon 86, on the caution and modesty of the Bride seeking the Word, 1195.—Among the works spuriously attributed to St Bernard, the following especially deserve notice: Treatise to the Brothers of Mont-Dieu, CLXXXIV, 307.—Treatise on Contemplating God, ibid., 363.—Treatise on the Nature and Dignity of Love, ibid., 379.—The Ladder of the Cloistered, ibid., 475.—Most Devout Meditations on Knowledge of the Human Condition, ibid., 485.—Treatise on the Interior House, ibid., 507.—On the Ordering of Life and Formation of Character, especially for novices, ibid., 559.—Book on Charity, ibid., 583.—The Mystical Vine, or Treatise on the Lord’s Passion, ibid., 635.—Meditation on the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection, ibid., 741.—Instruction of a Priest, or Treatise on the Principal Mysteries of Our Religion, ibid., 771.—Treatise on the State of the Virtues, ibid., 791.—Book of Sentences, ibid., 1135.—Mirror of Monks, ibid., 1175.—Short Work on These Words: “Why have you come?” ibid., 1189.—Book on the Way of Living Well, ibid., 1200.

BRUNO (St) of Asti, bishop of Segni.—Three Books of Sentences, especially the second book, on the ornaments of the Church, where he treats of various virtues, CLXV, 875.

CAESARIUS (St), bishop of Arles.—Rule for Monks, LXVII, 1097.—Rule for Virgins, ibid., 1107.—Sermon to Nuns, ibid., 1121.—Two Letters to an Abbess and Her Community, ibid., 1125.—Exhortatory Letter to a Virgin Dedicated to God, ibid., 1135.

CASSIAN, priest of Marseilles.—Twelve Books on the Institutions of Cenobia, in which he discusses the virtues monks ought to cultivate and the vices they ought to avoid, XLIX, 53.—Collection of Twenty-Four Conferences, ibid., 477.—In St Benedict’s judgment, cenobites should continually peruse these above other books.

CHRODEGANG (St), bishop of Metz.—Rule of Canons, LXXXIX, 1057.

CHROMATIUS (St), bishop of Aquileia.—Unique Treatise on the Eight Beatitudes, especially to be read through by novices and monks, XX, 323.

COLUMBANUS (St), abbot and confessor.—Cenobitic Rule, LXXX, 209.—Various Instructions to Monks, ibid., 229.

CYPRIAN (St), bishop of Carthage.—Almost all his works are moral in character; yet the following appear more ascetic: Letter 1, to Donatus, the most elegant of all, shows from his own experience the wonderful efficacy of divine grace in changing human hearts, IV, 192.—Letter [Col. 0330] 8, to the martyrs, 245.—Letter 15, to Moses, 264.—Letter 26, from Moses to Cyprian, 290.—Letter 36, to the Thibaritans, on exhortation to martyrdom, 349.—Letter 77, to Nemesianus and the others … condemned to the mines, 414.—Letter 81, to Sergius and Rogatianus, imprisoned, 424.—Letter to Fortunatus, on exhortation to martyrdom, 651.—Book in Praise of Martyrdom, 787.—Book on the Twofold Martyrdom, 881.—In all these are found outstanding exhortations to suffer for Christ.—Book on the Good of Patience, in imitation of Tertullian, IV, 621.—Letter 69, to Florentinus, on bearing the slanders of detractors with equanimity, 400.—Book to Demetrianus, proving that calamities should be attributed not to Christians but to idolaters, ibid., 543.—Book on Zeal and Envy, ibid., 637.—Book on Mortality, ibid., 581.—Letters 4, 5, and 36, on care for the poor, 230, 231, 326.—Letters 37 and 40, on showing charity to the afflicted, 327, 359.—Letter 6, to Rogatianus, on observing discipline, 235.—Letter 7, to clergy and people, on imploring God for sins, 240.—Letter 65, to Rogatianus, on an arrogant deacon, 393.—Letters 9, 10, 11, 13, and 31, on not too readily granting pardon to the fallen, 250, 253, 256, 260, 307.—Book on the Fallen, IV, 467.—Book on the Unity of the Church, concerning peace and concord, ibid., 493.—Letter 33, on Aurelius ordained reader, 319.—Letter 34, on Celerinus ordained reader, 322.—Letter 35, on Numidicus ordained priest, 326.—Book on the Singularity of Clerics, ibid., 835. Those to be promoted to holy orders will read these four with profit.—Book on the Dress of Virgins, IV, 441.—Third Book to Quirinus, containing doctrines for Christian life, ibid., 723.—Treatise on the Twelve Abuses of the World, ibid., 869. These last two should especially be offered to beginners in matters of faith.

DEFENSOR, monk of Locojeac.—Book of Sparks, on virtues and vices drawn from Holy Scripture and the Holy Fathers, LXXXVIII, 597.

DONATUS (St), bishop of Besançon.—Rule for Virgins, LXXXVII, 273.

DROGO, cardinal-bishop of Ostia.—Book on the Divine Offices, or on the Canonical Hours, CLXVI, 1557.

DURANDUS, abbot of Troarn.—Book on the Body and Blood of Christ, CXLIX, 1375.

EADMER, monk of Canterbury.—Book on the Blessedness of the Heavenly Homeland, CLIX, 587.—Book on St Anselm’s Similitudes, ibid., 605.

ECKBERT, abbot of Schönau.—Short Work in Praise of the Cross, CXCV, 103.—Soliloquy, or Meditations, ibid., 105.—Goad of Love, ibid., 114.

ERNALDUS, abbot of Bonneval.—Treatise on the Seven Words of the Lord on the Cross, CLXXXIX, 1677.—Meditations, ibid., 1733.

EUCHERIUS (St), bishop of Lyon.—Little Book in Praise of the Desert, to Hilary, priest of Lérins, L, 701.—Admonitory Letter to his kinsman Valerius, on contempt for the world and secular philosophy, ibid., 711.—Certain Homilies to Monks, ibid., 833.—Book on the Canonical Institutions of Cenobia, ibid., 867.—Book on the Eight Evil Thoughts, ibid., 877. These various short works of St Eucherius should especially be presented to novices, monks, and those aspiring to perfection.

EULOGIUS (St), bishop of Toledo.—Instruction on Martyrdom, or Exhortation to Virgins Held in Prison for the Faith, that they may undergo martyrdom cheerfully, CXV, 821.

EUTROPIUS (St), abbot and bishop.—On the Eight Vices, LXXX, 9.

EUTYCHIAN (St), pope.—Exhortation to Priests, from an ancient Vatican manuscript, in which he briefly expounds everything to which priests are bound, V, 163.

FASTIDIUS, British bishop.—Book on Christian Life, setting forth what it is fitting for a Christian to do, L, 383. A work to be perused by beginners in matters of faith.

FLORUS, deacon of Lyon.—Short Work on the Exposition of the Mass, CXIX, 15.

FRUCTUOSUS (St), bishop of Braga.—Rule for Monks, LXXXVII, 1097.

FULGENTIUS (St), bishop of Ruspe.—Letter to Proba, on virginity and humility, LXV, 324.—Letter to the same woman, on prayer to God and contrition of heart, ibid., 339.—Letter to Abbot Eugyppius, on charity and love, ibid., 344.—Letter to Venantia, on right penance and future recompense, ibid., 352.—Two Books on the Remission of Sins, ibid., 527.

GREGORY (St), bishop of Tours.—Two Books of Miracles, LXXI, 705.—Book on the Glory of Confessors, ibid., 828.—Four Books on the Miracles of St Martin, ibid., 913.—Book on the Life of the Fathers, ibid., 1009. Although these various short works cannot be placed among ascetic writings, they nevertheless seem worth mentioning here, for the kindly reader will gather much profit from them.

GREGORY THE GREAT, Doctor of the Church.—Book of Pastoral Rule, LXXVII, 13.—Exposition of the Seven Penitential Psalms, ibid., 550.

GUIBERT, abbot of Nogent.—Books of Moral Reflections on Genesis, CLVI, 31.—Short Work on Virginity, ibid., 579.

GUIGO I, prior of the Grande Chartreuse.—Meditations, CLIII, 601.

GUIGO II, prior of the Grande Chartreuse.—Book on the Exercise of the Cell, CLIII, 787.

WILLIAM, abbot of St Thierry.—On the Solitary Life, CLXXX, 205.—Meditative Prayers, ibid., 206.—Book on Contemplating God, ibid., 249.—On the Nature and Dignity of Divine Love, ibid., 249.—Mirror of Faith, ibid., 366.—Enigma of Faith, ibid., 397.

GUITMUND, archbishop of Aversa.—Three Books on the Truth of Christ’s Body and Blood in the Eucharist, CXLIX, 1427.

HALITGARIUS, bishop of Cambrai.—Five Books on Vices and Virtues, CV, 651.

HAYMO, bishop of Halberstadt.—Three Books on the Variety of Books, or on Love of the Heavenly Homeland, dealing with the nature of the heavenly homeland, the works by which it is acquired, and the nature of punishment and everlasting penalties, CXVIII, 875.

HENRY, archdeacon of Huntingdon.—Little Book, or Letter, on Contempt for the World, CXCV, 979.

HENRY OF CASTRO MARCIAC, cardinal.—Treatise on the Pilgrim City of God, CCIV, 251.

JEROME (St), priest, Doctor of the Church.—Among St Jerome’s letters you will find many which breathe great piety, especially the following: Letter 14, in praise of the solitary life, XXII, 347.—Letter 22, on guarding virginity, ibid., 394.—Letter 52, on the life of clerics and priests, ibid., 527.—Letter 53, exhortation to study Holy Scripture, ibid., 540.—Letter 58, on the training of a monk, ibid., 579.—Letter 125, a pattern of life, ibid., 1072.—Letter 130, on preserving virginity, ibid., 1105.—Among the doubtful letters: Letter 2, on despising an inheritance, XXX, 45.—Letter 3, exhortation to endure adversity, ibid., 50.—Letter 4, consolation to a virgin sent into exile, ibid., 55.—Letters 5 and 6, to a sick friend, ibid., 61, 75.—Letter 12, on the seven orders of the Church, ibid., 148.—Letter 13, praise of virginity, ibid., 163.—Letter 19, on true circumcision, ibid., 188.—Letter 41, on bearing reproaches, 282.—Letter 42, on the life of clerics, ibid., 288.—Homily to Monks, ibid., 311.—Rule for Monks, ibid., 319, 391.

HILDEBERT, archbishop of Tours.—Brief Treatise on the Sacrament of the Altar, CLXXI, 1149.—Book on the Exposition of the Mass, ibid., 1153.—Book on the Holy Eucharist, ibid., 1195.—First Book of Letters; namely, the letters written to various persons are ascetic and moral, ibid., 141.

HILDEBRAND THE YOUNGER.—Little Book on Contemplation, CLXXXI, 1691.

HILDEGARD (St), abbess.—Explanation of the Rule of St Benedict, CXCVII, 1053.—Explanation of the Creed of St Athanasius, ibid., 1065.

HINCMAR, archbishop of Reims.—On Avoiding Vices and Practising Virtues, CXXV, 857.—On the Duties of Bishops, ibid., 1087.

HONORIUS OF AUTUN.—The Greater Ladder of God, CLXXII, 1229.—The Lesser Ladder of God, ibid., 1239.—On the Soul’s Exile and Homeland, ibid., 1242.—On the Cloistered Life, ibid., 1247.—*Eucharistion*, or Book on the Body and Blood of Christ, ibid., 1249.

HUGH OF AMIENS, archbishop of Rouen.—Book on the Catholic Faith and the Lord’s Prayer, CLCII, 1323.

HUGH OF ST VICTOR.—Four Books on the Vanity of the World, CLXXVI, 703.—Exposition of the Rule of St Augustine, ibid., 881.—Book on the Instruction of Novices, ibid., 925.—Soliloquy on the Soul’s Pledge, ibid., 951.—Book in Praise of Charity, ibid., 969.—On the Manner of Prayer, 977.—On the Love of the Bridegroom for the Bride, ibid., 987.—Golden Short Work on Meditation, or the Art of Meditating, ibid., 993.—On the Fruits of Flesh and Spirit, ibid., 997.—Four Books on the Cloister of the Soul, ibid., 1017.—Four Books on Noah’s Ark in Its Moral Sense, ibid., 618.—Book on Noah’s Ark in Its Mystical Sense, ibid., 677.—On Spiritual Medicine Compared with Bodily Medicine, ibid., 1183.—On the Soul and Its Formation toward Knowledge of Itself and of God, and toward True Piety, CLXXVII, 165.

ISAAC, abbot of Stella.—On the Office of the Mass, CXCIV, 1889.

ISIDORE (St), bishop of Seville.—Rule for Monks, [Col. 0332] LXXXIII, 867.—Book on the Conflict of Vices and Virtues, ibid., 1131.—Book of Sentences, ibid., 1153.—Exhortation to Humility, ibid., 1201.—Sentences of Distinctions on the Active and Contemplative Life, ibid., 1243.—Rule of Life, ibid., 1247.

JOHN, Carthusian monk of Portes.—Five Letters, on flight from the world, the manner of prayer, custody of the heart, and constancy in one’s resolve, CLIII, 900.

JOHN OF MICHAELSBERG.—Rule of the Templars, CLXVI, 857.

JOHN OF SALISBURY, bishop of Chartres.—On the Seven Sevens, CXCIX, 945.

JONAS, bishop of Orléans.—Three Books on the Instruction of Laypersons, CVI, 121.

JOSCELIN, bishop of Soissons.—Letter on the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer, CLXXXVI, 1479.

JULIAN (St), bishop of Toledo.—Three Books, *Prognosticon*.—In these is discussed the condition of our souls both at the time of death, after death before the Last Judgment, and finally in the Judgment itself, XCVI, 453.

JULIANUS POMERIUS.—Three Books on the Contemplative Life, LIX, 415.

LACTANTIUS FIRMIANUS.—Book on the False Wisdom of Philosophers, VI, 347.—Book on Justice, ibid., 545.—Book on True Worship, ibid., 633. This author often has the outlook of a Platonic philosopher; therefore these works are to be read only by the learned.

LANFRANC, archbishop of Canterbury.—Decrees or Statutes for the Order of St Benedict, CL, 443.

LAURENTIUS (St) of Novara.—Homily on Penance, LXVI, 89.

LEANDER (St) of Seville.—Rule, or Book on the Instruction of Virgins and Contempt for the World, LXXII, 873.

LEO (St) THE GREAT.—Letter to Demetrias, or Treatise on Humility; a doubtful work attributed to Leo the Great by Quesnel. The author commends humility with great praise, LV, 161.

LEO (St) IX, Roman pontiff.—Little Book on the Conflict of Vices and Virtues, CXLIII, 559.

THE MASTER, author of uncertain name.—Rule for Monks, LXXXVIII, 943.

MARTIN, bishop of Dumium.—Pattern of the Honourable Life, LXXII, 21.—Little Book on Morals, ibid., 29.—On Repelling Boastfulness, ibid., 31.—On Pride, ibid., 35.—Exhortation to Humility, ibid., 39.—On Anger, ibid., 41.

MAXIMUS (St), bishop of Turin.—Two Letters to a Sick Friend: the first is a consolation; the second treats of the perfect man. They are listed among the doubtful works of St Maximus, LVII, 921.

NICETAS (St), bishop of Aquileia.—Explanation of the Apostles’ Creed, for beginners in matters of faith, LII, 865.

NICETIUS (St), bishop of Trier.—Short Work on the Vigils of God’s Servants, LXVIII, 365.—On the Good of Psalmody, ibid., 371.

NOVATUS THE CATHOLIC.—A Saying on Humility and Obedience, and on Trampling Down Pride, for Monks, XVIII, 67.

ODO (St), abbot of Cluny.—Epitome of St Gregory’s Moral Reflections on Job, CXXXIII, 105.—Three Books of Conferences: in the first, on the various afflictions of this life and against those who despise ecclesiastical censures; in the second, on those who lapse into vices by the example of the wicked and approach the sacraments unworthily, or abstain from them in order to sin more freely; in the third, on the virtues and vices of superiors and inferiors, ibid., 517.

ODO (St), archbishop of Cambrai.—Exposition of the Canon of the Mass, CLX, 1053.

OTHLONUS, priest and monk.—Book on the Spiritual Course, CXLVI, 141.

PACIAN (St), bishop of Barcelona.—*Paraenesis*, or Exhortatory Little Book on Penance, XIII, 1018.

PASCHASIUS RADBERTUS (St).—Treatise on the Body and Blood of Christ the Lord, CXX, 1267, a devout and learned work.—Three Books on Faith, Hope, and Charity, ibid., 1387.—Letter to Frudegard, on the Lord’s Body and Blood, ibid., 1351.—Exposition of Psalm XLIV, to the Virgins of Soissons, ibid., 993.

PATRICK (St), bishop of Ireland.—Book on the Three Dwelling-Places, namely the kingdom of God, the world, and hell, LIII, 831.

PAULINUS (St), patriarch of Aquileia.—Book of Exhortation, or on Saving Counsels, XCIX, 197.

PETER OF BLOIS, archdeacon.—Book on Christian Friendship, CCVII, 871.—Book on Love of God and Neighbour, ibid., 895.—Book on the Twelve Benefits of Tribulation, ibid., 989.—Book on Sacramental Confession, ibid., 1077.

PETER OF CELLE, bishop of Chartres.—Book on Breads, [Col. 0333] CCII, 927.—Mystical Exposition of the Mosaic Tabernacle, ibid., 1047.—Book on Conscience, ibid., 1083.—Treatise on Cloister Discipline, ibid., 1101.

PETER (St) DAMIAN.—All St Peter Damian’s letters are full of most salutary instruction, but the following should especially be noted.—Letter 15, Book I, on the crimes of that age, CXLIV, 225.—Letter 1, Book II, on the pastoral office, ibid., 253.—Letter 5, Book II, on the Sabbath-rest, or the true rest and peace of the righteous in this life, ibid., 260.—Letters 11 and 12, Book II, on the office of abbot, 275.—Letter 5, Book IV, on the Last Judgment, ibid., 300.—Letter 15, Book IV, on the pastoral office, ibid., 325.—Letter 3, Book V, on what happens to sinners in death, ibid., 342.—Letter 4, Book V, on the vices of clerics, ibid., 344.—Book VI, throughout, on the hermit life, the virtues and vices of monks, and the office of abbots, ibid., 371.—Letter 6, Book VII, exhortation to bear labours with equanimity, ibid., 443.—Letter 1, Book VIII, on the office of the preacher, ibid., 461.—Letter 6, Book VIII, on enduring adversity with equanimity, ibid., 473.—Letter 8, Book VIII, on the vanity of temporal things and the Day of Judgment, ibid., 476.—Letter 12, Book VIII, against pride, ibid., 485.

Among the Works and Minor Works. — Sermon on the vice of the tongue, CXLIV, 912. — Sermon on spiritual combat, ibid., 919. — Treatise on almsgiving, CXLV, 207. — On the canonical hours, ibid., 221. — The book called *The Lord Be with You*, in which there is discussion of the praise of the eremitical life, ibid., 231. — Apologetic treatise on contempt for the world, against monks who make light of regular observance, ibid., 251. — On the perfection of monks, ibid., 291. — On the institutions of his own congregation, in which he sets forth the precepts of the eremitical life and conversion for a certain Stephen, who had migrated from a monastery to the hermitage and desired them, ibid., 335. — Against intemperate clerics, ibid., 387. — On fleeing ecclesiastical dignities, ibid., 455. — Against courtly clerics seeking advancement to dignities, ibid., 463. — On the shortness of the lives of the Roman pontiffs, including discussion of God’s goodness and providence, ibid. — Against regular clerics who possess private property, ibid., 479. — On the dignity of the priesthood, ibid., 491. — On the common life of canons, ibid., 503. — On the humble dress of ecclesiastics, ibid., 517. — On restraining anger and uprooting quarrels, ibid., 649. — On not breaking one’s pledge to God, ibid., 667. — On preferring holy simplicity to knowledge that puffs up, ibid., 695. — On bearing correction with equanimity, ibid., 703. — On chastity and the means of safeguarding it, ibid., 710. — On spiritual delights, ibid., 715. — On the complete formation of a monk, ibid., 721. — On the eremitical life and approved hermits, ibid., 749. — On patience amid the harassment of wicked persons, ibid., 791. — On the fleeting glory of the world and contempt for the age, ibid., 807. — On true happiness and wisdom, ibid., 831.

**PETER DE HONESTIS**, cleric of Ravenna. — Rule for clerics, CLXIII, 703.

**PHILIP**, abbot of Good Hope. — Six treatises on the formation of clerics, CCIII, 665.

**RABANUS MAURUS.** — Treatise on the soul, including moral virtues, CX, 1109. — Book on the Christian contest, CXII, 1229. — Three books on seeing God, purity of heart, and the manner of penance, ibid., 1261. — On virtues and vices and satisfaction for sins, ibid., 1335. — On the Passion of Christ, ibid., 1425.

**REINERUS**, monk of Liège. — Mirror of Penitence, CCIV, 51. — The Virgin’s Palm, ibid., 61. — Flower of the Desert, ibid., 69. — Three little books of tears, ibid., 133. — Books on the progress of death, ibid., 181.

**RICHARD OF ST VICTOR.** — Book on the preparation [Col. 0334] of the mind for contemplation, CXCVI, 1. — Five books on the grace of contemplation, ibid., 63. — Little book on meditation upon the last things, ibid., 201. — Mystical and devout expositions of certain psalms, ibid., 265. — Treatise on the destruction of evil and the advancement of good, ibid., 1073. — Three books on the state of the interior human being, ibid., 1115. — Book on the degrees of charity, ibid., 1207. — On the instruction of the interior human being, ibid., 1229.

**ROBERT OF ARBRISSEL**, monk. — Rules for nuns and precepts for right living, CLXII, 1079.

**RUFINUS**, priest of Aquileia. — History of the Monks, XXI, 387. — This little work is indeed improperly classified here among ascetic writings; nevertheless, because monks may read it with great profit, we have thought it worth noting.

**RUFINUS**, bishop of an uncertain see. — Two books on the good of peace, CL, 1593.

**RUPERT**, abbot of Deutz. — Books on the works of the Holy Spirit, especially Book II, CLXVII, 1571. — Seven books on the divine offices, in which ecclesiastical rites are explained tropologically, CLXX, 13. — Two books on meditation upon death, ibid., 357. — Three books on certain chapters of the Rule of St Benedict, ibid., 477.

**SALVIANUS**, priest of Marseilles. — Eight books on the governance of God, LIII, 25. There the divine Providence in all things and above all things is set forth excellently. — Four books against avarice, ibid., 173.

**SMARAGDUS**, abbot. — Diadem of Monks, on avoiding vices and acquiring virtues, CII, 593. — Commentary on the Rule of St Benedict, ibid., 691. — The Royal Way, ibid., 935.

**STEPHEN**, abbot of Cîteaux. — The Earlier Usages of the Cistercian Order, CLXVI, 1384.

**STEPHEN OF BALGIACO.** — Treatise on the sacrament of the altar, CLXXII, 1273.

**ST STEPHEN OF MURET.** — Book of Sayings or Reasons, CCIV, 1085. — Rule of St Stephen, ibid., 1135.

**SULPICIUS SEVERUS.** — Letter to his sister Claudia, on the Last Judgment, XX, 223. — Letter to the same woman, on virginity, ibid., 227.

**TAIO**, bishop of Saragossa. — Five books of sayings, LXXX, 727.

**TERTULLIAN**, priest. — On Patience, an ascetic and paraenetic work, I, 1259. — To the Martyrs: he consoles Christians imprisoned for the faith and exhorts them to martyrdom, ibid., 619. — On Penance: the formerly customary ecclesial rite of public penance must be properly understood, lest anyone doubt the possibility of a second pardon after a fall, ibid., 1223; especially for the afflicted. — *Scorpiace* against the Gnostics: on the praise of martyrdom, and how glorious and beneficial it is to suffer for God and Christ, II, 191. — On Prayer: a brief exposition of the Lord’s Prayer, I, 1143. — You will find much moral teaching on bearing persecutions for Christ with equanimity in the book *On Flight in Persecution*, II, 101. — Likewise, remarkable material on fasting and abstinence occurs in the book *On Fasts*, II, 953. But beware the doctrines of the heretic Montanus which he defends there: in the former he teaches that flight in persecution is unlawful; in the latter he attempts to establish an excessively rigorous rule of fasting binding upon all.

**THEODORIC**, canon of Paderborn. — Commentary on the Lord’s Prayer, CXLVII, 333.

**VIGILIUS**, deacon. — Rule of Monks, commonly called the Eastern Rule, L, 373.

**ST WILLIAM**, abbot of Hirsau. — Constitutions of Hirsau, or Gengenbach, CL, 927.

[Col. 0333]

## CXLI. THE SAME ASCETIC LIBRARY OF THE FATHERS, ANALOGICALLY ARRANGED, BUT IN THIS ANALOGY PRESERVING ALPHABETICAL AS WELL AS CHRONOLOGICAL ORDER

**Friendship.** — On Friendship, St Augustine, XXXII, Epistle 92, col. 868. — On Spiritual Friendship, Abbot Aelred, CXCV, 659. — Book on Christian Friendship, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 871.

[Col. 0334]

**Love; Charity toward God.** — Book on the substance of love, St Augustine, XL, 843. — On Loving God, ibid., 847. — On charity and love, St Fulgentius, LXV, 344. — The Lesser Ladder of God, or On the Degrees of Charity, Honorius, CLXXII, [Col. 0335] 1239. — Book in Praise of Charity, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 969. — On the Bridegroom’s Love for the Bride, ibid., 897. — On the nature and dignity of divine love, Abbot William, CLXXX, 249. — On Loving God, St Bernard, CLXXXII, 973. — On the Love of God, the same, CLXXXIII, 815. — On the Threefold Mode of Love, ibid., 867. — On Twofold Charity, ibid., 1016. — On the Perfect Union of the Soul with God through Love, ibid., 1195. — On the Nature and Dignity of Love, the same, CLXXXIV, 379. — Book on Charity, ibid., 583. — Spur of Love, Abbot Eckbert, CXCV, 114. — Mirror of Charity, Abbot Aelred, ibid., 505. — Compendium of the Mirror of Charity, ibid., 621. — On the Degrees of Charity, Richard of St Victor, CXCVI, 1195. — On the Four Degrees of Violent Charity, ibid., 1207. — On the Love of God, Baldwin, CCIV, 417. — On the Wound of Charity which the Bride inflicts upon the Bridegroom, ibid., 477. — On Charity toward God and Neighbor, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 895. — Dialogue on the Conflict between the Love of God and a Deceitful Tongue, anonymous, CCXIII, 851.

**Love; Charity toward One’s Neighbor.** — Charity to be shown to the afflicted, St Cyprian, IV, Epistles 37, 60, cols. 327, 359. — On the care of the poor, ibid., Epistles 4, 5, 36, cols. 230, 231, 326. — On true charity, St Augustine, XXXII, Epistle 92, col. 868. — On visiting the sick, the same, XL, 1147. — Treatise on almsgiving, Peter Damian, CXLV, 207.

**Soul, Spirit, Mind.** — Three books of the *Prognosticon*, St Julian, XCVI, 453. — Book on the rationality of the soul, Alcuin, CI, 639. — Treatise on the soul, Rabanus, CX, 1109. — On the soul’s exile and homeland, Honorius, CLXXII, 1242. — Soliloquy on the soul’s pledge, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 951. — Four books on the cloister of the soul, ibid., 1017. — On spiritual medicine for the soul compared with bodily medicine, ibid., 1183. — On the soul and its formation for true piety, the same, CLXXVII, 165. — On the soul’s threefold progress, St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 794. — On complete purity of mind, ibid., 1075. — Two books on the instruction of the soul, Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 843. — On the tripartite tabernacle, Part Three, ibid., 795. — On the Seven Sevens, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 945. — On the stability of the soul, anonymous, CCXIII, 911.

**Avarice.** — Four books against avarice, St Salvianus, LIII, 173.

**Blessedness, Happiness, Felicity.** — Treatise on the eight beatitudes, St Chromatius, XX, 323. — On true blessedness, St Augustine, XXXIII, Epistle 3, col. 63. — On true happiness, ibid., Epistle 155, col. 666. — Books on the Sermon on the Mount, the same, XXXIV, 1229. — On true happiness, Peter Damian, CXLV, 831. — Book on the blessedness of the heavenly homeland, Eadmer, CLIX, 587. — On the evangelical beatitudes, Baldwin, CCIV, 483.

**Canonry; Canons.** — Rule of Canons, St Chrodegang, LXXXIX, 1057. — On the Rule of Canons, Amalarius, CV, 816. — Book on the Order of Regular Canons, Anselm, CLXXXVIII, 1091. — Apologetic letter for the Order of Regular Canons, ibid., 1117. — Shield of Canons, Arno, CXCIV, 1493. — On the order, habit, and profession of canons, Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 439.

**Clerical State; Clerics.** — On an appointed reader, St Cyprian, IV, Epistles 33, 34, cols. 319, 322. — On the distinctiveness of clerics, ibid., 835. — On the life of clerics, St Jerome, XXII, Epistle 52, col. 527. — On the seven orders of the Church, the same, XXX, Epistle 12, col. 148. — On the life of clerics, ibid., Epistle 42, col. 288. — On the vices of clerics, Peter Damian, CXLIV, 344. — Against intemperate clerics, ibid., 387. — Against courtly clerics, ibid., 463. — Against regular clerics who possess private property, ibid., 479. — Rule for Clerics, Peter de Honestis, CLXIII, 703. — On conversion addressed to clerics, St Bernard, CLXXXII, 833. — On the formation of clerics, Philip of Good Hope, CCIII, 665.

**Conscience.** — Book on Conscience, Peter of Celle, CCII, 1083. — Little book on conscience, Anonymous, CCXIII, 903.

**Contempt for and Flight from the World or the Age.** — Book on Flight from the World, St Ambrose, XIV, 569. — On despising an inheritance, St Jerome, XXX, Epistle 2, col. 45. — On contempt for worldly things, St Augustine, XXXIII, Epistles 22, 26, 77, 218, 253. — On contempt for the world, St Eucherius, L, 711. — On conversion from the world, St Fulgentius, LXV, 348. — Treatise on contempt for the world, Peter Damian, CXLV, 251. — On the fleeting glory of the world and contempt for the age, ibid., 807. — On flight from the world, John the Monk, CLIII, 900. — On contempt for temporal things, St Anselm, CLVIII, 677. — Poem on contempt for the world, ibid., 687. — On hatred of the world, ibid., 1072. — Four books on the vanity of the world, Hugh of St Victor, [Col. 0336] CLXXVI, 703. — Little book on contempt for the world, Henry, CXCV, 979.

**Correction.** — On correction and grace, St Augustine, XLIV, 915. — On bearing correction with equanimity, Peter Damian, CXLV, 703.

**Worship.** — Book on true worship, Lactantius, VI, 633.

[Col. 0351]

CXLIII. INDEX ON CONSCIENCE, REPORTING VARIOUS SAYINGS OF THE HOLY FATHERS ON THIS DICTATE OF REASON, BY WHICH THE INTERNAL RULE OF MORAL ACTIONS IS COMMONLY ESTABLISHED, ETC.

[Col. 0351] TERTULLIAN.—Do you wish us to demonstrate God from the testimony of the soul itself? Although it is oppressed by the prison of the body, hemmed in by corrupt training, enervated by lusts and desires, enslaved to false gods, nevertheless, when it comes to itself—as from drunkenness, sleep, or some illness—and recovers its health, it names God by this name alone, because it is the proper name of the true God: “Great God! Good God! May God grant it!” This is everyone’s utterance, I, 376, 377.—It also calls Him to witness as judge: “God sees; I commend it to God; God will repay me.” O testimony of a soul naturally Christian! Finally, in uttering these things it looks not toward the Capitol but toward heaven, ibid.—We are a body by the consciousness of religion, the divine character of discipline, and the covenant of hope, ibid., 468.—Stand forth in the midst, O soul, whether divine or human: whence and how do you make man a rational living being, most capable of perception and knowledge? ibid., 610.—I address you as simple and untaught; I require from you the things which you bring into man, things that you have learned either from yourself or from whatever author you possess, ibid.—For you confirm God alone when you name God alone. Nor is the nature of God which we proclaim unknown to you: “God is good; God does good”—this is your own voice. “May God bless you!” You utter this as readily as a Christian must, ibid., 612.—These testimonies of the soul are as true as they are simple; as simple as they are common; as common as they are universal; as universal as they are natural; as natural as they are divine, ibid., 615.—This being so, it matters little whether the soul’s consciousness was formed by God or by the writings of God, ibid., 617.—By the testimony of the soul naturally Christian it is demonstrated that there is one God; for when it comes to itself or returns to itself, it cries out not “gods,” but one God, and invokes one Judge, ibid., 376, 377.—Certainly we ought to live so holy a life, and with the whole substance of faith, that we may be confessedly secure in our conscience, desiring that this may persevere in us, yet not presuming upon it, ibid., 1317.—Every soul is immortal; I shall also employ the conscience of the people, which attests the God of gods; I shall employ the remaining common perceptions which proclaim God as Judge: “God sees,” and “I commend it to God,” ibid.

ARNOBIUS.—For since, through His teachings and laws, we have received this great benefit among humankind—that evil ought not to be repaid with evil, that it is more excellent to endure an injury than to inflict one, to shed one’s own blood rather than stain one’s hands and conscience with another’s blood—the ungrateful world has long possessed from Christ this benefit, through which the frenzy of savagery has been softened, and hostile hands have begun to refrain from the blood of a kindred living creature, V, 750.—We all naturally know that God exists, whether when we cry out, “O God!” or when we appoint Him witness against wicked persons and, as though He saw us, raise our faces toward heaven, ibid., 815.—The idea and recognition of the one God are innate in all human beings, as is the inmost consciousness of all. For this notion has been implanted by God in the minds of individuals: they readily acknowledge that from the true God they have received not only their humanity, but also that all things were created by Him and are governed by His providence, Book II, 43.

LACTANTIUS.—God deferred the punishments of tyrants in order to produce in them great and wonderful examples, from which posterity might learn both that God is one and the same avenger and that He inflicts fitting punishments upon the impious and persecutors, VII, 192.—The consciousness of a good work is the light of souls, XI, 795.—Before witnesses, the upright conscience is confident; the corrupt conscience trembles, ibid., 287.

ST. HILARY, bishop of Poitiers.—The brightness of the inward conscience must be obtained, so that outward things may be washed away, IX, 795.—He also compared them to tombs which, though resplendent through human workmanship and adornment, are defiled with the bones of the dead and the uncleanness of corpses: that is, let them prefer the beauty of righteousness to empty words, but possess within themselves the brightness of their conscience and mind, ibid., 1050.—The Prophet does not fear witnesses of his life, and welcomes the examination of those who observe and behold his conscience; for the fear of a defiled conscience trembles at every intercession. But where there is the steadfast confidence of an innocent life, the intervention of many witnesses is pleasant, ibid., 515.

ST. AMBROSE.—The consciousness of a good deed is a reward to the devout mind, XIV, 476.—No pleasure is better than the favor of a cleansed conscience, XIV, 497.—The purpose of a devout mind does not seek a reward, but counts as its reward the consciousness of having done good and the accomplishment of a just work, 1127.—A good conscience is one which, when examined, is approved, XIV, 1255.—An innocent conscience does not fear the arbiter of justice and rewarder of merits, XV, 1211.—Each person’s conscience reveals itself before God, and a person’s thought either condemns or clears itself before it, XIV, 1127.—Another’s words cannot fasten a charge which one’s own conscience does not receive, ibid., 1045.—Eloquence itself falls silent if conscience is sick; a conscience rich in testimony for itself abounds, XVI, 881; XV, 1277.—Do not fear the sound of words if your conscience is clean, XVI, 361.—For a wise person, not so much the public exposure of disgrace as conscience is shameful, ibid., 153.—What punishment is heavier than the wound of the inward conscience? What judgment is more severe than the domestic tribunal in which each person is accused to himself and himself reproaches himself because he has grievously wronged a brother? Is this not more to be fled than death, exile, or the pain of physical incapacity? For who would not judge bodily defect or loss of property lighter than a defect of soul and a loss of reputation? ibid., 152.—The wise person intends nothing except what is sincere and without deceit; nor will he do anything by which he binds himself under any charge, even if he could remain hidden; for he is guilty before himself before he is guilty before others, ibid., 154, 155.—Even if he could remain hidden, the wise person will not offend; he will flee the contagion of sins no less than if concealment were impossible. For the wise person’s hope of impunity is not hiding, but innocence, because the just person has the law of his own mind and the norm of his own equity and justice. Therefore he is recalled from fault not by terror of punishment but by the rule of honor, ibid., 154, 155.—A guilt of conscience is grievous, so that it punishes itself without a judge and seeks to cover itself, while nevertheless it is naked before God, XVI, 522.—Conscience always convicts and judges its guilty person silently and without contradiction, XVII, 710.—Though it has no faculty of speech, it nevertheless does not know how to keep silence, XVII, 975.—A mind conscious of evil trembles to speak, loses its meaning, and errs in its words, XVII, 301.—The worm of conscience, ibid., 546.—An accomplice may be removed by death, but the consciousness of your crime is always with you and does not exist apart from you; it clings to your breast and never leaves you. It holds you guilty and always captive under its own power. If at some time the more cheerful breath of prosperity distracts your mind, it suddenly goads you, strikes you to the marrow, and interrupts you. An accomplice may be corrupted with gold or bought with money; conscience admits no corruption. Its testimony remains unimpaired, defended by the full firmness of faith, XVII, 977.

ST. JEROME.—Let sinners be tormented by their own conscience and burned with the fire which they have kindled for themselves, XXIV, 210.—Happy is the conscience which bears reproach for God! ibid., 772.—Happy is the conscience which, in time of affliction, recalls good works! ibid., 390.—If anyone is overcome by suffering, he will grieve over his wound and endure the torments of conscience because he has lost the free countenance and the purity of his unstained mind, XXVI, 506.—A good conscience escapes no one’s eyes, XXI, 789.—Let us fear the true judgment of conscience, ibid., 611.—A good conscience prevents tortures from raging around it, ibid.

ST. AUGUSTINE.—Conscience is like an altar upon which sacrifice is offered to God, XXXVI, 578.—Whoever blushes before his conscience sets a limit to wickedness, XXXVIII, 1457.—An erroneous conscience binds, XXXII, 1360.—If anyone thinks that what is evil is good and does it under that belief, he certainly sins in so thinking, XXXIII, 186.—Conscience is the *neuter* of the inward person [reading uncertain], XXXV, 1643.—The conscience of the godly is God’s dwelling-place, XXXVI, 520.—As the conscience of the ungodly is a great punishment, so the conscience of the godly is a great joy, ibid., 625.—As an evil conscience lies wholly in despair, so a good conscience rests wholly in hope, ibid., 261.—In tribulation, a sound conscience is a refuge in which a person finds God, ibid., 515.—The dwelling and rest of conscience in the wilderness, XXXVIII, 311.—Conscience: the desert where rest and consolation are found, XXXVI, 635.—A good conscience does not always suffice, XXXVII, 475, 480.—When it suffices, XXXVIII, 302.—A good conscience does not suffice if one’s conduct before people is negligent, ibid., 301.—An evil conscience is the pit into which the wicked fall, XXXVI, 670.—An evil conscience does not flee itself, XXXV, 1694.—Examination of conscience, XXXVIII, 110.—The abyss of conscience lies bare before God’s eyes, XXXII, 779.—Conscience must be cleansed quickly, XXXVIII, 300.—How this is done, ibid., 312.—The conscience of evildoers is not healed except by forgiveness, ibid., 516.—The joy of a good conscience is paradise, XXXIV, 482.—Virtue is better content with the testimony of conscience, XLI, 156.—Care for one’s reputation must accompany a good conscience, XXXIX, 1508, 1568.—For human esteem a great multitude of people is necessary; but for God’s sight conscience alone is required, XLIII, 545.—There is no greater tribulation than the consciousness of sins, XXXVI, 515.—The conscience of criminals overcomes the most dreadful prisons, the most terrible tortures of executioners, and hell itself, XXXIII, 651.—You may flee whatever you wish, O human being, except your own conscience, XXXVI, 234.—An evil conscience is compared to an evil wife and an evil inconvenience, ibid., 312, 344, 515; XXXVII, 1286.

CASSIAN.—Conscience is a thousand witnesses, judge, and avenger of crimes, XXXIX, 856.

ST. PETER CHRYSOLOGUS.—There is no punishment of a condemned person where there is guilt in nothing; conscience alone is guilty, LII, 566.

ST. LEO THE GREAT, POPE.—Let every Christian soul examine itself and scrutinize its inward parts with the severe inquiry of its conscience. Let it see whether any discord has clung there, whether any desire has settled there. Let chastity drive lust far away; let the light of truth drive the darkness of pretence far away. Let pride subside; let anger come to its senses; let the darts of injuries be broken; let the tongue’s detraction be restrained. Let acts of vengeance cease, and let injuries be consigned to oblivion, LIV, 265.—Let each person search his conscience and see whether in the secret of his heart he finds the peace which Christ gives: whether he does not despise the lowly, take pleasure in unjust gain, or burn with envy at another’s prosperity, ibid., 273, 283.—Therefore let minds examine themselves and judge the affections of their inmost heart by a true estimate; and if they find in their consciences anything laid up from the fruits of charity, let them not doubt that God dwells within them. And, that they may become ever more capable of so great a guest, let them become more generous in works of persevering mercy. For if love is God, charity ought to have no limit, because divinity can be confined by no end, LIV, 519.

BOETHIUS.—How often have I employed the freedom of conscience to defend justice, despising the offense of the powerful? LIII, 517.—What could those add to the praises of a wise person’s conscience, who measures his good not by popular rumor but by the truth of conscience? ibid., 743.—Seeing here a conscience defiled with disgraces, and comparing himself with his fortune, perhaps he fears that the loss of that whose enjoyment is pleasant to him will be painful, ibid., 819.

CASSIODORUS.—A good and clean conscience alone is a royal palace and the dwelling of the Holy Spirit, LXX, 129.—For the fear of a good conscience is more grave: after pardon, to err, so that one who owes gratitude may incur offense again, ibid., 279.

ST. GREGORY THE GREAT.—One who acts wickedly makes his conscience a prison for himself, LV, 958.—Therefore let the wicked flee human eyes: assuredly they cannot flee themselves. For, since they know the evil which they do, they have conscience as witness; they have their own reason as judge, LVI, 427.—Certainly they are witnesses to themselves in conscience, because they are not without excuse. For by the very fact that God made the human being a rational creature, He sets a seal in every person’s hand, so that each may know his own works, LVI, 427.—In everything said about us, we ought always silently to return to the mind and seek the inward witness and judge. For what harm is it if everyone reviles us and conscience alone defends us? ibid., 876.

[Col. 0354] ST. ISIDORE OF SEVILLE.—No one can escape himself; and even if public report does not condemn you, your own conscience condemns you. Do you wish not to be sad? Live well. A secure mind bears sadness lightly; a good life always has joy; but the conscience of the guilty person is always in punishment, tormented by its own goads, LXXXIII, 859.—A conscience mixed with evils is not good, CXXX, 962.

ST. PETER DAMIAN.—A conscience secure in itself possesses the most steadfast joy, CXLV, 148.

GUIBERT, abbot.—A mind conscious of evil is always tormented by its own goads.—But what is sweeter than a good conscience, what happier reward in the present life? CLVI, 605.

VENERABLE HILDEBERT.—The testimony of a good conscience is the safest consolation in adversity, CLXXI, 191.—Nothing is happier, nothing more delightful than a good conscience, ibid., 303, 304.—Conscience is a soft bed for the good but a hard one for the evil, CLXXI, 616.

HUGH OF ST. VICTOR.—Conscience and reputation: conscience is oil in the vessel; reputation, oil in the lamp. For conscience we go in; for reputation we go out. Conscience is the upper stream; reputation, the lower stream. Meditation belongs to conscience; preaching, to reputation. Silence belongs to conscience; speech, to reputation. By silence you sow your own field; by speech you sow your neighbor’s field, LXXVII, 524.—Let the purity of its conscience be the mattress of the blessed soul; let tranquility be its pillow or headrest, security its covering; and upon this bed may it sleep happily and rest happily, ibid., 747.—For this reason God did not will human consciences to be manifest to one another in the present life: lest, seeing them, people should be provoked to evil, and, possessing them, should be put to shame. For if the many evils which circulate in human hearts lay exposed, they would both incite those looking upon them to fault and furnish those possessing them with testimony to disgrace. Therefore the hidden things of hearts are veiled, so that there may be a place for judgment in the future, LXXVII, 506.

ST. BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux.—Treatise on building up conscience, CLXXXIV, 507.—Conscience must first be cleansed. But who will cleanse it? God and the human being: the human being through thoughts and affections; God through mercy and grace, CLXXXIV, 507.—Happy is the conscience in which mercy and truth have met each other, righteousness and peace have kissed, ibid.—Conscience is a house to be built upon seven pillars: first, good will; 2. remembrance of God’s benefits; 3. a clean heart; 4. a free spirit; 5. an upright spirit; 6. a devout mind; 7. an enlightened reason, CLXXXIV, 511 ff.—A pure conscience gladdens the soul, shows itself pleasing to God and worthy of reverence by human beings and angels, and remains reconciled and at rest within itself, ibid., 516.—Conscience is the heart’s knowledge. Nothing is more pleasant, sweeter, safer, or richer than a good conscience. Though the body oppress, the world drag away, and the devil terrify, it will be secure, ibid.—When the body dies, a good conscience will be secure when it stands before the tribunal of the supreme Judge. There is no more certain testimony of future blessedness than a good conscience, ibid.—One conscience is good and tranquil; another good and troubled; another evil and tranquil; another evil and troubled, ibid., 554. (One may consult the treatise *On Conscience* attributed to St. Bernard, ibid., 551.)

ADAM THE SCOT, canon.—The reproach of our heart is twofold: when we are convicted of evil, it judges us worthy not only of temporal tribulation but, when we persist in evil, of eternal condemnation, CXCVIII, 786.—Likewise the consolation of our heart is twofold. For when we ardently love and practise the good, we not only rest sweetly in the chamber of the mind, but confidently hope that we shall come to the eternal security of heavenly rest, ibid.

PETER OF CELLE.—A good conscience is whatever can be called or conceived more delightful, more beautiful, more useful, more pleasant, better, or more salutary; a good conscience is the pledge of future blessedness, CCII, 1086.—Conscience is nothing other than the heart’s knowledge. When the heart knows what is within itself, it is called conscience; but when it knows what is outside itself, it is called knowledge, ibid., 1090. (The present author’s book *On Conscience* may usefully be consulted, ibid., 1084.)

THOMAS THE CISTERCIAN.—One does not rest who feels the worm of a corrupt conscience, from which no guilty person is absolved, CCVI, 136.—But a good conscience has glory, does not fear disgrace, and awaits a crown, ibid.—Our conscience is opened four times: 1. to the priest; 2. to one’s neighbor; 3. to God; 4. to God, human being, and angel. First, in confession; second, in contact; third, in thanksgiving; fourth, in judgment, when an account is rendered. The first opening makes peace; the second builds up; the third obtains favor; the fourth examines, CCVI, 507.

ALAN OF LILLE.—Conscience must be cleansed before receiving Christ’s body, CCX, 591, 592.—How conscience is to be examined, ibid., 171, 196.—Purity of conscience brings perpetual joy, ibid., 16, [Col. 0356] 138, 139.—The effective testimony of conscience, ibid., 315.—The effects of an erroneous conscience, ibid.—The misery of a corrupted conscience, ibid.—An evil conscience is the devil’s book, CCX, 138, 139.

SIXTEENTH SERIES.

[Col. 0355]

[PREFACE.]

The law of God is the principle and measure of actions, according to which we are led to do good and recalled from evil. Hence, in this sixteenth Series, we gather together whatever concerns the law, the Decalogue, or the precepts of the Church. Yet, lest our Indexes increase too greatly in number, we discuss in the same place the Decalogue in general and each individual precept of the Decalogue separately, carefully distinguishing one from another, so that confusion may be avoided and the reader more usefully aided. The same method is observed concerning the precepts of the Church. Certain matters of greater importance, however, are treated separately; hence the Indexes on Love of Enemies and Forgiveness of Injuries; Almsgiving; Fraternal Correction; Feasts; Fasting and Abstinence; and Mortification of the Senses, Heart, and Mind, which we append.

[Col. 0355]

CXLIV. INDEX ON THE DECALOGUE, LOGICALLY COLLECTING WHATEVER THE FATHERS WROTE ON THE TEN COMMANDMENTS OF GOD AND ON FULFILLING THEIR OBSERVANCE, AND THEN EXPOSING IN ORDER THE VARIOUS OBLIGATIONS OF EACH COMMANDMENT.

NOTICE.

In this Index on the Decalogue are contained, collectively, all human duties toward God, neighbor, and oneself—or the rules of all human actions—in the Christian order.

We divide it into two sections. In the first, we shall treat of the Decalogue considered generally: that is, insofar as it explains the natural law, its promulgation, and so forth; in the second, of each commandment insofar as it is affirmative and negative, or of those things which it commands and forbids, and so forth.

[INDEX ON THE DECALOGUE.]

[Col. 0355]

FIRST SECTION.—The commandments of the Decalogue and their division.

I. “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. You shall have no strange gods before me. You shall not make for yourself a carved image, nor any likeness of what is in heaven above, or on earth below, or in the waters beneath the earth. You shall not worship them or serve them. I am the Lord your God, strong and jealous, visiting the iniquity of fathers upon children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, and showing mercy unto thousands to those who love me and keep my commandments.

II. “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain. For the Lord will not hold guiltless one who has taken the name of his God frivolously.

III. “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day. For six days you shall labor and do all your work. But the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord your God; you shall do no work on it—you, your son, your daughter, your male servant, your female servant, your beast of burden, and the stranger who is within your gates. For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested on the seventh day; therefore the Lord blessed the Sabbath day and sanctified it.

[Col. 0356] IV. “Honor your father and your mother, that you may live long upon the land which the Lord your God will give you.

V. “You shall not kill.

VI. “You shall not commit adultery.

VII. “You shall not steal.

VIII. “You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor.

IX. “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife.

X. “You shall not desire your neighbor’s house, male servant, female servant, ox, donkey, or anything that belongs to him.” (Exod. 20:2–17.)

[Note: [Col. 0356] NOTE. Most of the Fathers follow this method of numbering the commandments, in accordance with the version of the Seventy Interpreters [the Septuagint]. But others, adhering to the Hebrew and St. Jerome’s versions, find two commandments in the first commandment mentioned above and one only in the final two [lacuna]. This difference in numbering has been retained for each Father. It is merely noted that the Fathers follow the aforesaid method of counting the commandments unless otherwise indicated; this will be sufficiently apparent when, from the numbering indicated by us, others who follow another method depart.]

II.—On the Decalogue in general: its name; the appropriateness and manner of its promulgation; and the commendation of its observance in the evangelical law.

[Col. 0357] ALAN OF LILLE.—The enemies of the Christian religion maintain that the Mosaic law was given by the prince of darkness, that is, the evil god; but that the evangelical law was given by the prince of light, that is, the good God—so that, as there are two principles of things, two Testaments have likewise been handed down by them. They seek in many ways to maintain that the giver of the Old Testament was evil; for example: he was evil who ordered a man gathering wood on the Sabbath to be stoned without any mercy. Again, how could he be good who exercised killing in many cases? Again, what justice was it that spared David, a murderer, perjurer, adulterer, and proud man, but rejected Saul because he had preserved alive the king of the Amalekites? Again, the Mosaic law is called the law of death and the law of sin; therefore it was evil. Again, the Apostle says, “The law entered in so that the offense might abound,” and elsewhere that “the law brings no one to perfection.” Again, as to the Mosaic law: why was it abolished? etc., CCX, 337 [lacuna]

The foregoing objections are most aptly answered, CCX, 337–340; and the conclusion is admirably added: How can it be denied that the law is good, when the commandments contained in it are good and holy, such as the commandments of the Decalogue: “Honor your father and your mother; You shall not kill; You shall not commit adultery; You shall not steal,” and the like [lacuna], CCX, 341.

ATTO, bishop of Vercelli.—Moses appropriately fasted forty days when receiving the law of the Decalogue, in order to show thereby that no perfection exists in the Decalogue unless it is illumined by the grace of the holy Gospel [lacuna]. This fast was also granted to the prophet Elijah, because he was preacher and witness of the Old Testament and, still preserved, will also come in connection with the New [Testament]. But our Lord Jesus Christ likewise deigned to observe this fast because, as He Himself says, He came not to abolish the law but to fulfill it; or in order to show Himself to be the same author of the Old and New Testaments. For the holy four Gospels do not destroy the Decalogue, but rather endeavor to establish it; or because the same Lord would loose the Decalogue previously sealed and enclosed among the Jews and preach it through the four regions of the world [lacuna]. For by these forty days is signified the whole period of the active life, which requires continence, so that we may fast from this world’s enticements, meditating only upon the things of God and chewing over divine food, in order that by prayer we may deserve to attain the contemplative life, which is signified by paschal joy, CXXXIV, 840, 841.

AUGUSTINE (ST.), bishop of Hippo.—Certainly Moses received on the mountain the law to be administered to the people, written upon tablets of stone by the finger of God. It is bound up in ten commandments [lacuna], in which nothing is commanded concerning circumcision or the sacrifices of animals, which Christians do not offer. Therefore, among those ten commandments, apart from Sabbath observance, tell me what is not to be observed by a Christian: whether concerning the prohibition of making and worshipping idols or any gods besides the one true God; or not taking God’s name in vain; or giving honor to parents; or avoiding fornications, murders, thefts, false testimonies, adulteries, and coveting another’s property. Who among all persons could say that a Christian ought not to keep any of these?

In this wonderful correspondence, there is certainly a very great difference: there, the people were prohibited in terrifying dread from approaching the place where the law was given; but here, the Holy Spirit came upon those who, awaiting the promised One, had gathered together as one. There, the finger of God worked upon tablets of stone; here, in human hearts. There, therefore, the law was set forth outwardly, so that the unjust might be terrified; here, it was given inwardly, so that they might be justified. For, “You shall not commit adultery, you shall not murder, you shall not covet, and if there be any other commandment”—which was of course written upon those tablets—“is summed up,” he says, “in this saying: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ Love does no evil to a neighbor. Therefore love is the fulfillment of the law.” This has not been written upon tablets of stone, but has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us. Therefore the law of God is love [lacuna], XLIV, 215, 218.

At first, the law ought not to have been given in written form, because it had in some manner been implanted in nature itself, and knowledge of the Creator was not hidden by propagation. For who does not know what accords with a good life, or is ignorant that one ought by no means to do to another what one does not wish done to oneself? But when the natural law had vanished, overwhelmed by the habit of sinning, then the law had to be made manifest, so that all humanity might hear it in the Jews. Not that it had been entirely erased, but because it lacked its greatest authority and idolatry was being pursued. There was no fear of God on earth; fornication was practised; greedy desire was directed toward a neighbor’s property. The law therefore had to be given, so that things already known might possess authority and things which had begun to be hidden might be made manifest. For before Moses, we find that sins were not merely known but were also punished.

[Col. 0358] Hence many righteous persons are found who, knowing God to be an avenger, feared to sin. When this had begun to be neglected, the natural law had to be revealed, so that all might know by plain reasoning that God would call human actions to account. Although punishment is recorded in the Flood and in Sodom and Gomorrah, forgetfulness due to antiquity had covered these matters. Therefore through Moses they were recalled, to correct discipline by fear and restore faith in God. Thus the Apostle also says: “The law is not laid down for the just, but for the unjust [lacuna],” XXXV, 2219, 2220.

He called the ten propositions “ten words,” because the Savior also signified a meaning by the term “word,” saying among other things to the Jews, “I will ask you one word [lacuna].” He called this meaning a “word.” Similarly, the ten words written upon the two tablets are said to be ten meanings. Finally, He says: “You shall have no other gods besides me”—this is the first word; and He added the second: “You shall not make for yourself any likeness.” The third is: “You shall not take the name of your God [lacuna].” The fourth: “You shall keep the Sabbath of your God [lacuna].” These four words properly concern God and are contained on the first tablet. The remaining ones are these [lacuna]. The Apostle proves that these were written on the second tablet, saying: “Honor your father and mother, which is the first commandment with a promise.” For how could it be first unless the second tablet began with it? He says “with a promise” because he immediately added, “That you may live long upon the earth [lacuna].” This is the promise made to those who keep the commandments [lacuna], XXXV, 2221, 2222.

Having received authority over sinners, Moses came down from the mountain in honor, his face glorious. For the law was given against sinners. Therefore Moses, because he had not sinned, appeared glorious—so glorious that sinners could not see him. For it was shown in him that sinners do not deserve to behold the glory of God. After the image of the molten calf and the breaking of the tablets upon which the law had been given, Moses ascended the mountain again with tablets. Having received the law, he came down, and his face was made glorious, so that the children of Israel could not look upon his face, nor could Aaron, because he too had sinned. But he spoke to them with a veil placed between them, so that they would remain unworthy of God’s glory as long as they continued in sins [lacuna], XXXV, 2222.

“On the day when the third month had gone out after the children of Israel left the land of Egypt, they came into the wilderness of Sinai [lacuna], and Israel encamped there opposite the mountain [lacuna]. On the third day the Lord came down upon Mount Sinai before all the people” [lacuna]. On this day the law written on tablets of stone by the finger of God is found to have been given. This third day is evidently in the third month after Israel’s departure from Egypt. Therefore, from the day on which they celebrated Passover—that is, sacrificed and ate the lamb, which was the fourteenth day of the first month—to this day on which the law was given, fifty days are counted [lacuna], XXXIV, 620.

The question is asked how the ten commandments of the law should be divided: whether there are four up to the commandment concerning the Sabbath, which concern God Himself, and the other six, the first of which is “Honor your father,” etc., concern humanity; or rather whether the former are three and the latter seven. Those who say that the former are four separate the statement, “You shall have no other gods besides me,” so that “You shall not make yourself an idol,” etc., in which the worship of images is forbidden, is another commandment.
