But they wish these to be one: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife; you shall not covet your neighbor’s house.” Those, however, who say that the former are three and the latter seven wish all that is commanded concerning worship of the one God to be one commandment: that nothing else besides Him should be worshipped as God. But they divide the final commandments into two: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife” is one, and “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house” another. Yet neither party doubts that there are ten commandments, because Scripture attests this.

But it seems to me more fitting to take the former as three and the latter as seven, because those which concern God appear, to those who examine them closely, to indicate the Trinity more carefully. And indeed, the saying, “You shall have no other gods besides me,” is explained more perfectly when the worship of images is forbidden. Moreover, desire for another’s wife and desire for another’s house differ so greatly in sinful character that to the statement, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house,” other things are added. For Scripture says: “Neither his field, nor his male servant, nor his female servant, nor his ox, nor his beast of burden, nor any of his livestock, nor anything that belongs to your neighbor.” But it appears to have distinguished desire for another’s wife from desire for any other thing belonging to another when it began each commandment in this way: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife; you shall not covet your neighbor’s house,” and then began to add the remaining things to the latter.

[Col. 0359] It did not, after saying “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife,” connect to it the words, “nor his house, nor his field, nor his male servant,” etc. Rather, those things evidently belong together which appear to be contained in one commandment, and are distinct from the commandment in which the wife is named. But the statement, “You shall have no other gods besides me,” plainly receives a more detailed application in the matters added afterward. For what does “You shall not make yourself an idol,” etc., concern except what was said: “You shall have no other gods besides me”?

But again the question is asked: how does “You shall not steal” differ from the command given shortly afterward not to covet a neighbor’s possessions? Certainly not everyone who covets a neighbor’s property steals it; but if everyone who steals covets a neighbor’s property, then that precept concerning theft could have been included within the general prohibition of coveting a neighbor’s property.

Likewise the question is asked how “You shall not commit adultery” differs from the later statement, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife.” For that latter commandment could have been understood in the statement, “You shall not commit adultery.” Unless perhaps in those two commandments—against adultery and theft—the acts themselves are specified, whereas in the final commandments desire itself is specified. They differ so much that someone may at times commit adultery without coveting a neighbor’s wife, when he has intercourse with her for some other reason; and at times he may covet her but not have intercourse with her, fearing punishment. Perhaps the law intended to show that both are sins.

It is also customary to ask whether fornication is included under the name of adultery (*moechia*). For this is a Greek word which Scripture now uses in place of the Latin term. Yet the Greeks call only adulterers *moechi*. But certainly this law was given not only to the men among the people, but also to the women. For because it is said, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife,” a woman ought not to think that nothing is here commanded to her, and that she may, as it were lawfully, covet her female neighbor’s husband. Therefore, if it is understood here, from what was said to the man, though not expressly stated, that it also applies to the woman, how much more are both sexes bound by the words, “You shall not commit adultery,” since this command itself can be referred to both, like “You shall not kill,” “You shall not steal,” and other such commands which, though one sex is not expressly named, appear to speak commonly to both.

Yet when one sex is named, the more honorable is of course named—that is, the male—so that from this the woman may understand what is commanded to her. Accordingly, if a woman who has a husband is an adulteress by lying with a man who is not her husband, even if that man has no wife, then certainly a man who has a wife is an adulterer by lying with a woman who is not his wife, even if she has no husband. But it is rightly asked whether, if a man without a wife acts with a woman without a husband, both are guilty of transgressing this command. For if they are not, then fornication is not forbidden in the Decalogue, but adultery alone—that is, marital unfaithfulness—although every adultery is also understood to be fornication, as the Scriptures speak. [Lacuna.] For the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever dismisses his wife, except on account of fornication, causes her to commit adultery.” Here he certainly called fornication the sin committed with another by one who has a husband, which is adultery—that is, marital unfaithfulness. Therefore every adultery is also called fornication in the Scriptures. But whether every fornication can likewise be called adultery, no example of such usage occurs to me at present in those same Scriptures.

But if not every fornication can also be called adultery, I do not know whether it can be discovered where, in the Decalogue, that fornication is forbidden which is committed by men who have no wives with women who have no husbands. But if under the name of theft every unlawful appropriation of another’s property is rightly understood—for he who prohibited theft did not permit robbery; rather, he intended the whole to be understood from the part, whatever is unlawfully taken from a neighbor’s goods—then certainly under the name of adultery every unlawful sexual union, and every illegitimate use of those bodily members, ought to be understood as prohibited. XXXIV, 621–622.

BEDA, the Venerable.—Thus the people came to Mount Sinai on the forty-seventh day after departing from Egypt; there Moses went up to the Lord, and the Lord came down to him. But what does it mean morally that Moses went up the mountain and the Lord came down upon the mountain? The mountain is the height of our contemplation, to which we ascend in order to be raised to behold things beyond our weakness. But the Lord comes down upon it, because to saints making great progress he reveals a little of himself to their understanding. XCIII, 373.

Then, on the fiftieth day after the Passover had been celebrated, the Law was given to Moses. [Lacuna.] The written Law is said to have been written by the finger of God, and the Lord says of the Holy Spirit: “By the finger of God I cast out demons.” There all the people behold voices and lamps, the smoking mountain, thunders and lightnings, and the resounding blast of the trumpet. In the voices and thunders is understood the cry of the preachers; in the lamps, [Col. 0360] the brightness of miracles; in the sound of the trumpet, the powerful preaching of the saints—all of which at the coming of Christ [lacuna]. Therefore the Lord there gives Moses the Law of our innocence and of the knowledge of himself; he sets it forth in ten words and writes it with his finger upon stone tablets. These commandments are so arranged that three concern love of the divine Trinity, while seven concern brotherly love, by which human society is not harmed. XCIII, 373–374.

EUCHERIUS (St.), bishop of Lyons.—What should be said to those who inquire why God gave the Law through Moses to one nation alone, and only after so many ages of the world had already elapsed? Answer: that Law was not set forth for the Jews alone; it is implanted in all nations by the constitution of the natural law. The Apostle also confirms this, saying: “For when the Gentiles, who do not have the Law, naturally do the things of the Law, these, though they do not have the Law, are a law to themselves; they show the work of the Law written in their hearts.”

And therefore the Lord did not late in time gather the law of innocence into ten words, since its origin, already implanted in human hearts, had preceded it. He wrote it again late upon stone tablets only because he had already inscribed it earlier upon the pages of the heart. For before this Mosaic Law nature had its own law, by which it was readily possible both to acknowledge—and therefore to love—God as the Creator of the world and of life, and to observe justice and love toward one’s neighbor. “On these two commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets.” Thus they already knew beforehand: “All things whatsoever you would have men do to you, do also to them.”

And, to establish this by examples: before this written Law, by that law of nature, righteous Abel is recognized; Enoch is taken away; Noah is chosen; Abraham is called the father of nations. Therefore the preceding law of nature proves that this Mosaic Law was not promulgated late, through which many persons proved acceptable to God. What is that finger of God by which the two tablets of the Law are said to have been written? Answer: the finger of God here is to be understood as the Holy Spirit. L, 779–780.

HIERONYMUS (St.), priest.—“The Lord spoke all these words:

“[Commandment 1.] I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.

“[Commandment 2.] You shall have no foreign gods before me. You shall not make for yourself a carved image, nor any likeness which is in heaven above, or on earth beneath, nor of those things which are in the waters under the earth. You shall not worship them or serve them; for I am the Lord your God, mighty and jealous, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, unto the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, and showing mercy unto thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments.

“[Commandment 3.] You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain; for the Lord will not hold guiltless the one who has taken the name of his God vainly.

“[Commandment 4.] Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day. For six days you shall labor and do all your work. But the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord your God: you shall not do any work on it—you, your son, your daughter, your servant, your maidservant, your beast, and the stranger who is within your gates. For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, the sea, and all things which are in them, and rested on the seventh day; therefore the Lord blessed the Sabbath day and sanctified it.

“[Commandment 5.] Honor your father and your mother, that you may live long upon the land which the Lord your God will give you.

“[Commandment 6.] You shall not kill.

“[Commandment 7.] You shall not commit adultery.

“[Commandment 8.] You shall not steal.

“[Commandment 9.] You shall not speak false testimony against your neighbor.

“[Commandment 10.] You shall not covet your neighbor’s house; nor desire his wife, nor servant, nor maidservant, nor ox, nor ass, nor anything that is his.

“Now all the people saw the voices, the lamps, the sound of the trumpet, and the smoking mountain; and, terrified and shaken with fear, they stood at a distance, saying to Moses: ‘Speak to us, and we shall hear; let not the Lord speak to us, lest perhaps we die.’ And Moses said to the people: ‘Do not fear; for God has come to test you, and that his fear may be in you, so that you may not sin.’ And the people stood at a distance [lacuna].” XXVIII, 265–266.

HILDEBERT, the Venerable, bishop of Le Mans.—Concerning the written Law, these matters are to be considered: why it was given, to whom, when, and where. The written Law was given in order to restore the natural law and make it live again, since it had become obsolete through sin; and in order to prepare a rude people, through legal figures, for the truth to come. It accomplished the first through the ten natural commandments. [Lacuna.] To whom was it given? To Abraham’s seed, in the twelve tribes descended from the twelve sons of Israel.

Here one may ask: why to these alone? It may be said in answer that it was given to that people, and not another, because it was set forth as a figure. Hence the Apostle says: “All things happened to them in a figure”; and it was enough to show in one people what God set forth for the sake of figure and example. But the new Law is commanded to all, for it is not the figure but the very reality figured. And since in that people there were some perfect, some middling, and some very wicked, it was given to the perfect as a sign; to the middling as a pedagogue, to teach what should be done, forbid what should be avoided, and correct faults by punishing them; to the very wicked it was given by the angry Judge as vengeance, “that he who is filthy may become filthier still”; conversely, it was provided by the merciful Father for the good, “that he who is righteous may be justified still more.”

When was it given? On the fiftieth day from the departure out of Egypt and the sacrifice of the Paschal lamb. So too the new Law was given to the apostles—that is, the Spirit writing in the heart—on the fiftieth day after the sacrifice of the true Lamb, Christ. Where? On Mount Sinai, just as the discourse containing the perfection of the New Testament which Christ delivered on the mountain. In the Old Testament, as in the New, three things are contained. [Lacuna.] The commandments include natural and figurative precepts. The natural are called those ten which flow from the natural law; they were not begun in the written Law but renewed, because they had been erased through sins. These are the ten commandments also called moral; they were not brought to an end in the new Law, but rather fulfilled more perfectly. [Lacuna.] CLXXI, 1148–1150.

HUGH OF ST VICTOR.—The written Law was given in order to restore the natural law and make live again what had been abolished through sin, and to prepare a rude people, by legal figures, for the truth to come. It accomplishes the first through the ten natural commandments, with which alone the Decalogue deals. To whom was it given? To Abraham’s seed, that is, to the twelve tribes descended from the twelve sons of Israel. [Lacuna.] When was it given? On the fiftieth day from the departure out of Egypt and the sacrifice of the Paschal lamb. Where? On Mount Sinai. [Lacuna.]

The natural precepts are called those ten which flow from the natural law; they are also called moral, and were not terminated by the new Law but fulfilled more perfectly. In those ten commandments love of God and neighbor is commanded. The three on the first tablet concern love of God; the other seven on the second tablet concern love of neighbor. CLXXVI, 420.

MARTIN (St.) of León, regular canon.—On the forty-seventh day after departing from Egypt, the people came to Mount Sinai; there Moses went up to the Lord, and the Lord came down to him. [Lacuna.] Then, on the fiftieth day after the Passover had been completed, the Law was given to Moses. [Lacuna.] There the Law is said to have been written by God’s finger, which casts out demons. All the people behold voices and lamps, the smoking mountain, thunders and lightnings, and the resounding blast of the trumpet. [Lacuna.] Then God gives Moses the Law of innocence and of the knowledge of himself, establishes it in ten words, and writes it with his finger on stone tablets. These commandments are so arranged that three concern love of the divine Trinity, and seven brotherly love, by which human society is not harmed.

In these commandments he condemns worldly ambition and restrains the coveting of possessions. Thus the first prohibits superstition; the second, error; the third destroys love of the world; the fourth, impiety; the fifth strikes down fornication; the sixth, cruelty; the seventh, rapacity; the eighth destroys falsehood; the ninth, the thought of adultery; and the tenth, worldly covetousness. CCVIII, 781–783.

And it should be noted that, just as the Egyptians are struck with ten plagues, so the tablets by which God’s peoples are governed are inscribed with ten commandments. Why was the Law written upon two tablets, unless either to signify the two Testaments or because of those two commandments of love, namely love of God and neighbor, on which the whole Law and the Prophets hang? These are to be explained in the individual tablets. One contains three commandments concerning love of God; the other seven concerning fellowship with one’s neighbor. [Lacuna.] But why were the tablets made of stone, except to signify the stony heart of the Jews? [Lacuna.] Therefore, when Moses came down from the mountain with the tablets and heard that the people had consecrated themselves to idols, judging them unworthy to receive the Law, he threw the tablets from his hands. After breaking them, he burned the calf which they had made, ground it into small pieces, sprinkled it into the waters, and gave the mixture to the people to drink. [Lacuna.] Moses went up the mountain again, and God again gave him the Law on other tablets cut after the pattern of the former. CCVIII, 783–784.

PETER COMESTOR.—Therefore in the third month after the departure from Egypt—that is, June—on this day, on the Kalends of June, the Hebrews came to Mount Sinai and pitched their tents opposite the mountain, namely on the forty-seventh day [Col. 0362] after the Passover. For in expounding the Scriptures we count thirty days to a month, choosing, as it were, a middle path between lunar and solar months. Lunar months are indeed found to be under thirty days, but never above it; solar months, however, exceed that number more often. Sixteen days of the first month remained from the Passover; afterward thirty days of the second month elapsed. It follows, therefore, that the first day of June was the forty-seventh.

At dawn on the following day Moses went up the mountain to God, who said to him: “You shall say to the house of Jacob: ‘You have seen what I have done for you; now I shall add this also, that I may speak to you: if, therefore, you keep my covenant, you shall be my special possession among all peoples.’” When Moses reported this to the people, they answered: “All that the Lord has spoken we will do.” When Moses reported this to the Lord, the Lord said to him: “I shall come to you in darkness, so that the people may hear me speaking to you. Go and sanctify the people today and tomorrow; that is, let them wash themselves and their garments. Let them abstain from embraces and be ready for the third day. Set boundaries around the mountain; whoever then crosses them and touches it shall die. No hand shall touch him, but he shall be stoned or pierced with darts, whether beast or man.” In these two days, Josephus says, they made lavish use of feasts and fitting adornments. CXCVIII, 1162–1163.

“The third day had now come, and before sunrise thunders began to be heard and lightnings to flash; a dense cloud covered the mountain, and the trumpet-blast sounded loudly. The mountain smoked because the Lord had descended in fire, and the smoke rose like smoke from a furnace”; and, as the Hebrews say, the mountain shook. The people were afraid; indeed, they thought that Moses had perished by God’s wrath. At last Moses appeared, joyful, and calm air returned with him among them. He said to them: “Today you shall not hear Moses, son of Amram and Jochebed, but him who struck Egypt for you, made a way through the sea, sent food from heaven, granted drink from the rock, through whom Adam ate from the fruits of the earth; through whom Noah was rescued, or received, from the rains; Abraham gained Canaan; Isaac was born from aged parents; Jacob was enriched with offspring; and Joseph was exalted. Therefore let these words be dearer to you than sons or wives.”

And he led the people out to meet the Lord at the foot of the mountain. At the Lord’s command Moses and Aaron ascended beyond the boundaries; the priests—that is, the elders—and the people did not cross them. The Lord spoke to them in such a way that the voice escaped no one; and so on the fiftieth day he gave them the Law, only in word, as a figure of what he would give through the Holy Spirit on the fiftieth day.

“You shall not have foreign gods before me.” All the saints maintain that the Lord gave only ten commandments, but they differ in distinguishing them. Origen divides into two the first commandment, which Augustine regards as one; and Augustine combines into one the final two, which Origen treats as two—an arrangement with which Josephus agrees. Further, Augustine says that three were on one tablet and seven on the other; but Josephus and the Hebrews place five on each. Perhaps, because Augustine wished three to concern love of God and seven love of neighbor, he said that they belonged to the first and second tablet by a pious ordering rather than according to Scripture, as we are accustomed to speak of persons of the first and second rank. Yet however they may be distinguished, the meaning is the same. Josephus says that he saw the two stone tablets of the Law, each containing two and a half commandments, both the outer tablet and the inner. CXCVIII, 1164.

“And the Lord said to Moses: ‘Cut for yourself two tablets like the former, and I will write on them the words which the tablets that you broke contained.’” Deuteronomy likewise says that God wrote them. But in what follows he says: “Write these things for yourself,” and a little later: “Moses was with the Lord forty days, and he wrote upon the tablets the words of the covenant, the ten words.” It may be said that the authority for writing belonged to the Lord, the ministry to Moses.

When Moses had broken the tablets, he rose by night and went up the mountain; and when the Lord passed before him in the whirlwind, Moses lay prostrate on the ground in worship and said: “I beseech you, go with us, take away our iniquities, and possess us.” The Lord briefly reminded him of certain things which he had also previously commanded concerning the three festivals, the offering of firstfruits and firstborn; and he added that they should have no fellowship with the nations of the promised land.

“Moses was a second time with the Lord forty days and forty nights. He ate no bread and drank no water. When he came down from the mountain with the tablets, his face appeared horned, though he himself did not know it”—that is, rays of wondrous splendor streamed from his face and dazzled the eyes of those looking upon him; these are what the Apostle Paul calls the glory of Moses’ face. He placed a veil over [Col. 0363] his face when he spoke to the children of Israel. He also told them everything that had been commanded him. How long this glory lasted, and whether this happened once or more than once, we do not know.

The Hebrews also relate that he still went up to the Lord a third time, to obtain certainty of pardon for the people, and again remained with the Lord forty days and forty nights, fasting. When he returned with assurance of pardon, it was the ninth day of the seventh month; on the following day, celebrating because pardon had been granted, they afflicted their souls with fasting. From that time the tenth day of this month was called the Day of Atonement. CXCVIII, 1192–1193.

PETER LOMBARD, bishop of Paris.—The Decalogue has ten commandments, which are the ten-stringed psaltery. They are arranged so that the three on the first tablet concern God, namely knowledge and love of the Trinity; while the seven on the second tablet concern love of neighbor. CXCII, 830.

RUPERT, abbot of Deutz.—There are ten commandments, which a more accurate translation distinguishes thus: “You shall not have foreign gods before me. You shall not make for yourself a carved image, nor any likeness which is in heaven above, or on earth beneath, nor of those things which are in the waters under the earth; you shall not worship them or serve them. You shall not take the name of your God in vain. Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day. Honor your father and mother. You shall not kill. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not steal. You shall not speak false testimony against your neighbor. You shall not covet your neighbor’s house, nor desire his wife, nor servant, nor maidservant, nor ox, nor ass, nor anything that is his.” CLXVII, 1720.

God spoke all these words: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. You shall have no foreign gods before me. You shall not make for yourself a carved image, nor any likeness which is in heaven above or on earth beneath, nor of those things which are in the waters beneath the earth. You shall not worship them or serve them. [Lacuna.]” This Decalogue is set at the head of the Law, that is, the number of ten commandments, of which the first is: “You shall not have foreign gods before me,” and the last: “You shall not covet.” But the Apostle said: “Covetousness is the root of all evils.” Why, then, is “You shall not covet” not placed first?

It should be understood that, as the upper branches of an evil tree are first cut off and then one gradually reaches the roots, so evil works—the nearer they are to covetousness—are first gradually cut off, and finally covetousness itself, or desire, is cut away by the voice of prohibition. It should be noted that nearly all these commandments are stated as prohibitions. Hence the Apostle speaks most truly: “The Law is not laid down for a righteous person, but for the unrighteous, ungodly, and sinners, wicked and defiled persons.” God had undertaken to heal unjust persons wholly given over to covetousness; therefore, like a diligent farmer, he first devoted this care to them: that the tilling-up of ground occupied by evil roots might prepare it for a better planting, namely charity, which alone is appointed for the righteous.

For the same Apostle, before saying that the Law was laid down for the unrighteous and disobedient, not for the righteous—that is, before telling Timothy this—had said: “The end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith.” For where charity is, there is no need to say, “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery. [Lacuna.]” Accordingly, when the Lord was asked by a lawyer, “Teacher, what is the great commandment in the Law?” he answered: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart. [Lacuna.] On these two commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets. [Lacuna.]” Therefore at this beginning charity is not yet commanded, but what is contrary to charity is prohibited, so that, when those things have been rooted out, charity itself, the root of all good things, may finally be planted. CLXVII, 679–680.

Four of these serve love of God, six love of neighbor: “You shall have no foreign gods before me; you shall not make for yourself a carved image or any likeness; you shall not take the name of your God in vain; remember to sanctify the Sabbath day.” By forbidding the four things opposed to love of God, the word of God intends to prepare a place for that same love of God. For you cannot at once have foreign gods and love the true God. Therefore he says: “You shall have no foreign gods before me,” that is, you shall think no one God except the one Creator of heaven and earth.

Likewise, to make a carved image or any likeness of those things in heaven, on earth, or in the waters, and to suppose that God resembles any of these, is wickedness and opposed to the love of God. “To whom,” says the prophet, “have you made God like? Or what image will you set before him?” This applies against the anthropomorphites, who suppose that God is composed of human bodily members. In this way they fabricate for themselves a great image, which sits in heaven and touches the earth with its feet, though God himself says: “Heaven is my seat, but the earth is the footstool [Col. 0364] of my feet.” He therefore says: “You shall not make for yourself a carved image. [Lacuna.]”

Certainly, when God says: “I am the Lord your God, mighty and jealous, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, unto the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, and showing mercy unto thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments,” this is to be understood in every commandment: namely, that the transgressor may fear punishment and the fulfiller of the commandment may hope for a reward. At a fitting time, moreover, he here declared himself mighty and one who repays the fathers’ iniquity upon the children unto the third and fourth generation: namely, when all Mount Sinai was smoking and wholly terrible because the Lord had come down, which was a sign of power; and when he had now repaid, in the third and fourth generation, the iniquity of the fathers who had sold their brother Joseph. Yet this was not without mercy: after their captivity was released, they were returning from Egypt in the fourth generation.

Likewise, to take the name of God in vain—as poets do—or not to consider worthy of reverence the name of the Lord wherever it is invoked, is wholly contrary to love of God. Therefore he says: “You shall not take the name of your God in vain; for the Lord will not hold guiltless the one who has taken the name of his God in vain.” Likewise, to do something good not for praise of God or in hope of eternal recompense, but in order to be seen by human beings, is contrary to love of God. Therefore he says: “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day,” that is, in all your works attend to God’s recompense; or prepare rest in God for yourself as your reward. This is truly to sanctify the Sabbath day. [Lacuna.]

“Honor your father,” etc.; “You shall not kill,” etc. All these uproot the things hostile to love of neighbor and aid the natural law, which says: “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another.” This could in some measure be observed by Gentiles, or by the more honorable among the Gentiles; but without love of God it did not benefit them toward life. Since they had foreign gods and did the other things forbidden in the four commandments, they did not attain blessedness.

The distinction of the ten commandments is now found in our codices, according to the translation of blessed Jerome.

Yet elsewhere we read that the four commandments concerning love of God were reduced to three; and conversely, that the last of those concerning love of neighbor—namely, “You shall not covet”—was divided into two, so that one commandment is heard as “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife,” and another, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property.” Thus three commandments concern love of God and seven concern love of neighbor. We suppose that this arrangement was taken from the Septuagint translators. CLXVII, 680–681.

Truth therefore spoke truth, and Christ spoke with both complete truthfulness and solemn gravity: “Do not think that I came to abolish the Law or the Prophets. I did not come to abolish, but to fulfill.” I say, he spoke a true word, weighted with mature gravity, being conscious in himself of this Holy Spirit, the Spirit of counsel, whom he was to give, and through whom he was to fulfill the Law far better and more abundantly than we can say.

But to whom, and why, did he say and speak thus? He spoke, with his disciples present, to adversaries—scribes and Pharisees—who would soon hear him and lay snares and calumnies for him as an adversary of the Law. His disciples believed and rejoiced that Christ, or in their language the Messiah, had come; those others expected Christ’s carnal kingdom in a carnal sense, while they themselves were tormented by envy on account of that king and vainly sought how they might seemingly justly slander his teaching.

Concerning the latter it is clear how truly and firmly they were forestalled by that assurance, especially because he fulfilled what he said in actual deed: he taught no one to abolish the Law or the Prophets, but rather taught them, by the voluntary choice of their own counsel, to add what the weak Law had commanded less fully. But what shall we say of his disciples, who thought that his kingdom would be carnal, except that they supposed he intended to abolish the Law and the Prophets? For when they thought that in his kingdom it would be permissible to kill and strip the nations of their spoils, and to build a Jerusalem of gold and gems, what did they expect except to live without law and, under the name of God’s kingdom, to have a kingdom of covetousness?

He found them such and called them such, but, when the Holy Spirit was given, made them very different. Moreover, to every commandment he added a special counsel, because according to evangelical teaching the bare fulfillment of a commandment belongs to servants and deserves no great favor. CLXVII, 1729–1730.

WALAFRID STRABO, monk of Fulda.—“In the third month after the children of Israel departed from the land of Egypt, on this day they came into the wilderness of Sinai. They departed from Rephidim and came into the wilderness of Sinai; there [Col. 0365] Israel encamped opposite the mountain, and Moses went up the mountain of God, and the Lord called him. [Lacuna.] For on the third day the Lord will come down upon Mount Sinai before all the people. On this day the Law is found to have been given, written on stone tablets by the finger of God. [Lacuna.]

This third day appears to have been the third day of the third month from the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt. From the day on which they celebrated the Passover—that is, sacrificed and ate the lamb—which was the fourteenth day of the first month, fifty days are counted to the day on which the Law was given: seventeen days of the first month remained from the fourteenth; then all thirty days of the second month, making forty-seven; and the third day of the third month, which from the festival of the slain lamb is the fiftieth. Thus in this shadow of the future, according to the feast-day of the sacrificed lamb, because the Law was given on the fiftieth day, it was written by the finger of God. [Lacuna.]” CXIII, 247–248.

In enumerating the commandments of the Decalogue, Origen and Augustine seem to follow contrary opinions. Origen believes that ten commandments cannot be counted unless the second is: “You shall not make for yourself an idol nor any likeness,” etc. Augustine, however, although he does not reject Origen’s enumeration, judges another, different arrangement more fitting: he regards the prohibition concerning idols and images made for worship as an explanation of the first commandment, and then establishes two commandments for restraining forbidden desires—one concerning coveting another’s wife, the other concerning coveting all the other things belonging to one’s neighbor.

Athanasius, Gregory Nazianzen, Chrysostom, Jerome, and Ambrose follow Origen. The scholastic doctors follow Augustine’s enumeration in the sense held by Augustine himself: that is, they prefer it to the former, while nevertheless not judging the former unsuitable. Indeed, the opposition which a depraved inclination encounters in subduing those two desires seems rather to demand two distinct commandments. For there are people who covet another’s wife while disdaining to covet another’s wealth or slaves, and conversely; but there is no worshipper of the true God who finds difficulty in despising idols.

Yet this difference of enumeration produces no difference in the thing itself. Augustine does not set down any commandment denied by Origen, nor vice versa. Rather, one joins commandments by a principle of subordination which the other separates, and conversely, by a principle of verbal connection. Augustine joins the commandment not to make idols to the commandment to worship only one God, because the former is subordinate to the latter and is its more explicit extension to the prohibition of Gentile rites. Origen divides these into two commandments because, in the very context of the discourse, they seem distinguishable without any mark of connection, like the subsequent statements: “You shall have no foreign gods; you shall not make for yourself a carved image; you shall not take [the name],” etc.

Again, Origen combines the two prohibitions of the twofold desire into one commandment because the sequence of the text seems to concern a single statement: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house, nor desire his wife, nor,” etc. Augustine divides them into two commandments because, as I have said, the commandment not to covet a wife is not subordinate to the commandment not to covet wealth. Nor is the desire for forbidden pleasure ordered toward desire for possessions; they produce vices of different kinds and therefore must be prohibited by different laws. Hence this whole difference rightly agrees in substance: whether certain things are forbidden by one law or two distinct laws makes no difference, provided one acknowledges that the same things are forbidden by the same words, although the words make it uncertain whether they constitute one law or two. CXIII, 255–258.

ZACCHAEUS, Christian.—Moses is summoned to the mountain to receive the Law; held in converse with God for forty days and nights, he brings back the commandments written on stone tablets. Alas for the crime! He finds those whom he had left corrupted by sacrilege, although they were still being sustained with manna and heavenly delight. For when the same people complained of Moses’ delay as though he would not return, quickly forgetting the God by whom they had been led out of Egypt, though satisfied with the aforesaid abundance, they began in their indulgence to demand gods to worship. Throwing women’s ornaments into the fire, they professed themselves willing to give themselves to the religion which would reproduce the form of the idol worshipped in Egypt.

Moses, having returned, faithfully rages against the crime; after reducing to powder the head of the bull which had been made in the likeness of Egypt’s abomination, he breaks in indignation the tablets of the Law which he had brought, judging them unworthy of God’s written words because such an accursed deed had defiled them. Nor did he cease from the force of his anger until, by sending executioners through the camp, the crime was atoned for by the death of many; and, after the offense against God had been appeased, the commandments were brought back renewed upon tablets. Their restoration showed that God does not hate those whom he allows to be corrected, nor wishes those whom he thus chastises to be destroyed. [Col. 0366] [Lacuna.]

Then the Law was divinely promulgated, which by its publication brought not a novelty of commandments but the restoration of original justice, so that what previously only a very few wise persons knew, all might now behold and read. Ignorance can therefore have no place as an excuse, since what one does not perceive to be innate in oneself may be sought not by mental faculties alone but recognized by sight. XX, 1087–1088.

## SECOND SECTION

## First Commandment
> “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. You shall have no foreign gods before me. You shall not make for yourself a carved image, nor any likeness of what is in heaven above, what is on earth below, or of those things that are in the waters beneath the earth. You shall not worship them or serve them. I am the Lord your God, strong and jealous, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, and showing mercy unto thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments.”

ADAM, Premonstratensian.—What commandments seem to you the greatest? The greatest commandment appears to be that by which we are commanded to love our God, and the rest in this manner. The greatest prohibitions, however, as I judge, are those by which we are forbidden to commit adultery, steal, bear false witness, and whatever other similar things there may be, CXCVIII, 852.

AGOBARD (St.), bishop of Lyons.—Faith is that by which we believe in one almighty God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: true Trinity, true unity. O what a true Trinity, where none is born from himself, none proceeds from himself, but one is from another! The Son is born from the Father; the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and from the Son. Therefore it clearly appears beyond doubt that one is he who begot, another he who was begotten, and another he who proceeds from both. O what a true unity, where there is not one Spirit of the Father and another of the Son, but one Spirit of both; nor does he first proceed from the Father into the Son, and then from the Son in order to pour the gift of charity into the hearts of the faithful, but simultaneously from both. There is not one divinity of the Father, another of the Son, and another of the Holy Spirit, but one divinity of the three, and therefore truly one God . . . CIV, 269–287.

The first commandment of the Decalogue is this, God saying: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage. You shall have no foreign gods in my sight; you shall not make for yourself a carved image, nor a likeness of all things which are in heaven above and which move in the waters beneath the earth. You shall not worship them and you shall not serve them.” To these words St. Augustine very briefly adds: “In the first commandment, some likeness of God is forbidden among the inventions of men; not because God has no image, but because no image of him ought to be worshipped except that which is itself what he is—not in its stead, but with him.” In saying this, he briefly teaches us how we ought to understand the other commandments of this kind as well. For when it is distinctly said that no likeness is to be made of all things in heaven or on earth, this is not said only of likenesses of foreign gods, but also of heavenly creatures, or of those things which human thought could devise in honor of the Creator . . . CIV, 199.

But that images of the apostles and of the Lord himself were produced or preserved by the ancients for love and remembrance rather than for religious honor or some veneration in the manner of the Gentiles, let Eusebius be heard. He says:

> Since we have mentioned Caesarea Philippi, it seems right also to recall an event there which we judged worthy of history. The Gospels relate that the woman healed by the Savior while suffering from a flow of blood was a citizen of this city; and her house in it is still shown even now. Before the doors of her house, moreover, a certain base is displayed in a more elevated place, upon which there appears to be an image of the woman herself, as if fallen upon her knees and stretching out her hands in supplication . . . And it is no wonder if those who had believed from among the Gentiles seemed to offer such things as a gift in return for benefits received from the Savior, when even now we see images of the apostles Peter and Paul and of the Savior himself represented, paintings made, and ancient images of them preserved by certain persons. This seems to me to have been observed indiscriminately from Gentile custom, because they were accustomed thus to honor those whom they judged worthy of honor. For the preservation of memorials of the ancients for the remembrance of posterity is a sign of the honor paid to the former and of the affection of the latter . . .

CIV, 215.

“It should indeed be noted,” says the Venerable Bede, “that there are persons who think that God’s law forbids us to carve or paint likenesses either of human beings, animals of any kind, or things, in a church or anywhere else, because in the Decalogue of the law it says: ‘You shall not make for yourself a carved image . . .’ They would by no means think this if they recalled Solomon’s work, in which he made, inside the temple, palms and cherubim with various carvings; and on its columns embossed pomegranates and nets; likewise, in the bronze sea, twelve oxen and carved figures; and on the side-vessels lions with oxen, palms, axes, and wheels, with cherubim and a varied kind of paintings. Or if, at least, they had considered the works of Moses himself, who, at the Lord’s command, first made cherubim upon the mercy-seat and later a bronze serpent in the wilderness, at the sight of which the people might be saved from the poison of venomous serpents.

“For if it was lawful for the bronze serpent to be raised upon wood, so that the children of Israel who looked upon it might live, why is it not lawful to recall to the faithful, by painting, the exaltation of the Lord and Savior upon the cross, by which he conquered death; or his other miracles and healings, through which he wonderfully triumphed over that same author of death? The sight of these frequently brings great compunction to those who behold them, and it unfolds to those also who do not know letters a kind of living reading of the Lord’s history . . . If it was lawful to make twelve bronze oxen bearing the sea above them and facing the four regions of the world, what forbids us to paint the twelve apostles as they go forth, baptizing all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit . . .?

“The words of the law plainly declare that those likenesses are forbidden to be made by men which the impious are accustomed to make for the veneration of foreign gods, and which wandering Gentile error devised for worship and adoration. But, in my judgment, no letter of the divine law forbids such things simply as such. Otherwise, when the Pharisees tested the Lord about paying tribute to Caesar, concerning a coin on which, they said, Caesar’s name and image were impressed, he would by no means have answered: ‘Render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and unto God the things that are God’s.’ Rather, he would have corrected their error, saying: ‘It is not lawful for you to make Caesar’s image in the striking of your gold, because the divine law forbids such a carving.’ For there would have been occasion for him to say this when the tribute coin was shown him, if Caesar’s image had been made on it for idolatry rather than to signify royal authority for legal judgment . . .”

CIV, 216–217.

On this question there is a very extensive treatment in CIV, cols. 199–227.

ALAN OF LILLE.—On the love of God, CCX, 151.

AMBROSE (St.), bishop of Milan.—How the love of God speaks, XVII, 1069.

ANTONIUS.—A poem against the Gentiles, V, 262.

ARNOBIUS OF AFRICA, apologist.—Disputation against the Gentiles, V, 718 and following.

ARNOBIUS THE YOUNGER.—When you hear, “God is one; seek absolutely no other god. The Father with the Son and the Holy Spirit is altogether one God . . .,” LIII, 245–322.

AUGUSTINE (St.), bishop of Hippo.—All Catholic interpreters of the divine books who have written concerning the Trinity, which is God, have aimed, according to the Scriptures, to teach that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit reveal the divine unity by an inseparable equality of one and the same substance; and therefore they are not three gods, but one God. Yet the Father has begotten the Son, and therefore the Son is not he who is the Father; the Son has been begotten of the Father, and therefore the Father is not he who is the Son; and the Holy Spirit is neither Father nor Son, but only the Spirit of the Father and the Son, himself also equal to the Father and the Son and belonging to the unity of the Trinity . . .

Nevertheless, the same Trinity was not born of the Virgin Mary . . . but the Son alone; nor did the same Trinity descend in the form of a dove upon Jesus when baptized, but the Holy Spirit alone; nor did the same Trinity say from heaven, “You are my Son,” but it was the voice of the Father alone addressed to the Son, although Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, just as they are inseparable, also work inseparably. This is the Catholic faith.

But some are troubled by this when they hear of God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit, and yet that this Trinity is not three gods but one God; and they ask how this is to be understood. Especially when it is said that the Trinity works inseparably in everything God does, and nevertheless a certain voice of the Father sounded—a voice which was not the Son’s—they wish to understand how the Trinity made that voice, which was the Father’s alone; how that flesh in which the Son alone was born of the Virgin was created by the same Trinity; and how that form of a dove, in which the Holy Spirit alone appeared, was produced by the Trinity itself. Otherwise, the Trinity does not work inseparably: the Father does some things, the Son others, the Holy Spirit others; or, if they do some things together and some separately or in turn, then the Trinity is no longer inseparable . . . They are also troubled by how the Holy Spirit is in the Trinity, since neither the Father nor the Son nor both begot him, though he is the Spirit of both Father and Son, XLII, 824.

God alone is to be loved, XXXII, 1319; on charity as the union of hearts, ibid., 1378; on the love of God, ibid., 1463; on fostering love of God through meditation on God’s mysteries, ibid., 1465; on the origin of idolatry, XXXIV, 152; on loving God with the whole heart, ibid., 160, 948; on idolatry, ibid., 749, 890, 1060, 1066; God alone is to be worshipped, ibid., 1055; on the love of God, XXXV, 1831, 2059; “Serve the Lord in gladness,” XXXVII, 1275; on idolatry, ibid., 1483; “You shall have no foreign gods besides me,” on the ten strings, XXXVIII, 67, 75; on idols, ibid., 102, 165; XL, 89; the folly of those who worship idols, XXXVIII, 777; XL, 653–654; on the love of God, XXXIX, 1512; God is to be praised with the heart, ibid., 1643; on loving God, XL, 848; on rejecting the worship of gods, XLI, 77, 121, 132 . . .; God alone is to be worshipped, XLVI, 948.

BALDWIN, archbishop of Canterbury.—On the love of God, CCIV, 418.

BEDE THE VENERABLE.—The second commandment pertains to the Son, when it says: “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain”—that is, do not suppose the Son of Man to be a creature, because every creature is subject to vanity; but believe him to be equal to the Father, God of gods, the Word with God, through whom all things were made, XCIII, 374.

BEDE THE VENERABLE, priest.—“Love the Lord,” XCI, 384; XCIV, 214.

BERNARD (St.), abbot of Clairvaux.—Book on Loving God, CLXXXII, 974; on the threefold love of God, CLXXXIII, 620, 806; on the love of God, CLXXXIV, 1220.

BRUNO (St.), founder of the Carthusians.—On the worship of idols, CLIII, 175.

BRUNO (St.), abbot of Asti.—“You shall have no foreign gods before me,” CLXIV, 278.

CANUTE I, king of the English.—Come, let us also be diligent always to be obedient and faithful to our Lord, steadfastly to uphold his worship with all our strength, and to do his will. For whatever we have ever faithfully done for the true Lord, we do all this for ourselves, to our greater advantage. For God is assuredly gracious to him who is truly obedient to his Lord. It is also a great benefit to every lord to govern his servants justly, CLI, 1176.

CANUTE I, king of the English.—We also direct that every Christian should learn, so that he may at least be able rightly to understand the true faith, and should learn the *Our Father* and the *Creed*, since by the one every Christian ought to implore God, and by the other to declare the true faith. Christ himself first prayed, “Our Father,” and taught this prayer to his disciples. In this prayer of the Church there are seven petitions; whoever prays it from the heart always sends a message to God himself concerning every good thing necessary to him, whether in this life or in the life to come. But how can anyone ever pray to God from the heart unless he has inward charity and true faith in God? For he who refuses to learn this thereafter does not die in the communion of Christians or rest in consecrated burial ground; nor does he receive the holy Eucharist during his life; nor is he a good Christian. Nor can he duly sponsor another at baptism or confirmation unless he learns these things so as to know them well, CLI, 1176.

COMMODIAN.—Instructions against the gods of the Gentiles, V, 202 and following.

Is it not shameful—is it not shameful, I say—that faithful people who claim for themselves the authority of the Christian name should defend the empty superstitions of the Gentiles, mixed with spectacles, on the authority of the heavenly Scriptures, and confer divine authority upon idolatry? . . . What did Scripture forbid? It forbade viewing what it forbade doing. I say that it condemned all these kinds of spectacles when it abolished idolatry, the mother of all games, from which these monsters of vanity and frivolity came . . . Therefore, to pass over whatever else idolatry more broadly sanctions, how vain are the contests themselves: quarrels over colors, rivalries in races, partisanship in honors . . . How wholly idle a business this is—indeed, how shameful and disgraceful! . . . But, now that I have moved on from this shameless pollution of the stage, I am ashamed to recount what is said; I am ashamed also to accuse what is done: the twists of plots, adulterers’ deceptions, women’s immodesty, buffoonish jokes, filthy parasites, even householders in their togas—at one time foolish, at another obscene; in all things [Col. 0369] stupid, in all things shameless . . . A common disgrace delights them: to see it, to recognize it in leisure, or to learn it. People crowd there to the public shame of a brothel, to a school of obscenity, lest anything be done more privately than what is learned publicly, and whatever the laws forbid is taught amid the laws themselves. What is a faithful Christian doing among these things, when he may not even think of vices? Why does he take pleasure in images of lust, so that, having cast aside shame in them, he may become bolder for crimes? He learns to do them while becoming accustomed to see them . . . etc., in the book *On Spectacles*, IV, 779–788.

The Gospel commandments are nothing other than divine teachings: foundations for building hope, supports for strengthening faith, nourishment for cherishing the heart, rudders for directing one’s course, defenses for obtaining salvation. While they instruct the teachable minds of believers on earth, they lead them to heavenly kingdoms. God willed many things to be spoken and heard through the prophets, his servants; but how much greater are the things spoken by the Son, which the Word of God, who was in the prophets, testifies in his own voice—not now commanding that a way be prepared for one who is coming, but himself coming and opening and showing us the way, so that we who had formerly wandered in the darkness of death, heedless and blind, enlightened by the light of grace, might keep to the way of life under the Lord as guide and ruler . . .

Among his other saving counsels and divine commandments, by which he provides for his people’s salvation, he himself also gave a form of prayer; he himself instructed and taught what should be asked. He who made us live also taught us to pray, by that very kindness through which he deigned to give and bestow other things as well, so that, when we speak to the Father in the petition and prayer which the Son taught, we may be more easily heard. He had already foretold that the hour would come when true worshippers would worship the Father in spirit and truth, IV, 519.

Moreover, when worshipping, let him not be ignorant how the tax collector prayed in the temple with the Pharisee: not rashly lifting his eyes to heaven, nor insolently raising his hands, but beating his breast and confessing the sins enclosed within, he implored the aid of divine mercy. “Thus,” says the Lord, “you shall pray: Our Father who art in heaven,” etc. . . , IV, 522–544.

CYPRIAN (St.), bishop of Carthage.—On the Vanity of Idols, IV, 563 and following; idols are not gods, ibid., 655; on God’s threat against idolaters, ibid., 657 and following; nothing is to be preferred to love for God and Christ, ibid., 746.

DODANA.—On loving God, CVI, 111.

DRUTHMAR, Christian.—What it is to worship God, CVI, 1299.

FASTIDIUS, bishop of the Britons.—Who loves God, I, 392.

FIRMICUS MATERNUS.—On the Error of Profane Religions, XII, 982 and following.

FULGENTIUS (St.), bishop of Ruspe.—The faith concerning God which the holy patriarchs and prophets received divinely before the incarnation of the Son of God, which the holy apostles also heard from the Lord himself while he was in the flesh, and which, instructed by the teaching of the Holy Spirit, they not only preached by word but also left set down in their writings for the most salutary instruction of posterity, proclaims one God, the Trinity: namely, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

But the Trinity would not be true if Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were said to be one and the same person. For if, just as the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one substance, they also had one person, there would be nothing at all in which a Trinity could truthfully be said to exist. Again, the Trinity would indeed be true, but the Trinity itself would not be one God if, just as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinguished from one another by the proper character of their persons, they were also separate by diversity of natures. But because, in that one true God who is Trinity, not only his being one God but also his being Trinity is naturally true, therefore he who is true God is Trinity in persons and one in nature. Through this natural unity, the whole Father is in the Son and the Holy Spirit; the whole Son is in the Father and the Holy Spirit; and the whole Holy Spirit is in the Father and the Son. None of them is outside any other, because none precedes another in eternity, exceeds another in greatness, or surpasses another in power. For, as regards the unity of the divine nature, the Father is neither earlier nor greater than the Son or the Holy Spirit; nor can the Son’s immensity and eternity, as though earlier or greater, naturally surpass, precede, or surpass the eternity and immensity of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, just as the Son is neither later nor less than the Father, so the Holy Spirit is neither later nor less than the Son. For it is eternal and without beginning that the Son exists as born from the Father’s nature; and it is eternal and without beginning that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the nature of the Father and the Son. Therefore we rightly believe and say that the three are one God [Col. 0370], because the three persons have altogether one eternity, one immensity, and one divinity by nature.

Let us therefore hold that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are naturally one God; yet that the Father himself is not he who is the Son, the Son himself is not he who is the Father, and the Holy Spirit himself is not he who is Father or Son. For there is one essence of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, in which the Father is not one thing, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another—although personally the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another . . . LXV, 673–674.

GARNIER, bishop of Langres.—To prove the Trinity, the Prophet says: “By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power.” By “Word” we must understand the Son; by “Lord,” the Father; and by “the Spirit of his mouth,” the Holy Spirit. But since through the Son and the Holy Spirit, as through the Father, the heavens and all their power were established, equality in the persons is evident. The Lord himself proves the singularity of substance: “Hear, Israel: your God, God is one.” These things pertain to the First Testament. Concerning the Second, Truth itself proves the same plurality, commanding the disciples and saying: “Go, baptizing in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” He says “in the name,” not “in the names,” to show that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one name. The plurality of persons is shown yet more openly where, when the Lord was baptized, the Holy Spirit descended upon him in the likeness of a dove and the Father’s voice was heard: “This is my beloved Son.” Truth itself also proves the singularity of substance, saying: “I and the Father are one,” etc., CCV, 715–718.

GILLEBERT OF HOOILAND, Cistercian abbot.—Nothing is to be loved above God, CLXXXIV, 373. On the nature and dignity of love, CLXXXIV, 379.

GREGORY THE GREAT (St.), pope.—What it is to fear God, LXXV, 530.

JEROME (St.), priest of Stridon.—On idolatry, XXV, 519. “You shall love the Lord your God,” XXVI, 277.

HILARY (St.), bishop of Poitiers.—Against idolaters, IX, 765. Reasons why God should be praised, IX, 837. What unbelief is, IX, 950. What unbelief is, IX, 998.

HILDEBERT THE VENERABLE, bishop of Le Mans.—On the love of God, CLXXI, 458.

HONORIUS OF AUTUN.—The first commandment is: “Worship one God,” and it pertains to the Father.

HUGH OF ST. VICTOR.—The first commandment of the first table is: “The Lord is your God; you shall worship him and serve him alone.” It must therefore be observed that one kind of service is to be rendered to God alone, called in Greek *latria*; another may also be rendered to human beings, called in Greek *dulia*. We ought to show reverence to human beings as well, as the Apostle commands, but not as to God. Hence: “I will give my honor to no one.” This honor is that reverence which we render to God alone: to lay the whole mind at his feet through humility and devotion, and to believe him to be the beginning and end of every good. In this way God alone is to be worshipped. This service is called *latria*, as we have said.

Thus idolaters are called those who assign this worship to a creature, serving the creature rather than the Creator—that is, attributing to an idol what belongs to God. Of this the Apostle says that “an idol is nothing.” This is not said of the material, such as stone or wood, since these are God’s creatures; rather, it seems to be said of the form, which is not God’s work but the work of a human being imitating God; and for this reason it is nothing, CLXXVI, 121, 352–354.

Zoroaster, king of the Bactrians, is believed to have been the first discoverer of magic; some assert that he was Ham himself, Noah’s son, under a changed name. Ninus, king of the Assyrians, afterward conquered and killed him in war, and had his books, full of malicious arts, burned in fire. Aristotle writes of this very man that his books handed down to the memory of posterity as many as two million two hundred thousand verses dictated by him concerning magic. Democritus later enlarged this art, in the time when Hippocrates was renowned in medicine. Magic is not admitted in philosophy, but is an external false profession, the teacher of all iniquity and wickedness. It lies about truth and truly harms minds; it seduces away from divine religion, recommends the worship of demons, introduces corruption of morals, and drives the minds of its followers toward every crime and impiety.

Taken generally, it comprises five kinds of evil arts: *mantice*, meaning divination; vain astrology; sorcery; malicious magic; and illusions. *Mantice* itself contains five species: first, necromancy, from which comes divination performed through the sacrifice of human blood, for which demons thirst, CLXXVI, 810–812, [Col. 0371] 1246–1247.—On the love of God, ibid., 126–535; that God’s love is the life of the heart, CLXXVII, 563; what it is to love God, ibid., 766; sermon on the fear of God, ibid., 920; on the commandment of love, ibid., 1177.

IVO (St.), bishop of Chartres.—If anyone consults soothsayers, diviners from sacrificial victims, or enchanters, or uses amulets, let him be anathema, CLXI, 745.

Those who seek divinations and follow Gentile custom, or introduce such persons into their houses in order to inquire into something by magical art or for the sake of expiation, shall be subject, according to the defined grades of penance, to the rule of five years, CLXI, 747.

Some clerics or laypersons devote themselves to auguries and, under the name of a counterfeit religion, profess divinatory knowledge through what they call “the lots of the saints”; or they promise future events by consulting writings of any kind whatsoever. Any cleric or layperson discovered either to consult or to teach these things shall be held outside the Church, CLXI, 747.

This is the spirit of the world, by which godless fanatics are possessed. For among worldly spirits it is the more powerful; hence it is accustomed to divine through worldly conjectures, and is called Python. This is the spirit which is deceived and deceives through plausible things; this is the one that spoke through the Sibyl, following our senses and desiring to have a place among heavenly beings, CLXI, 747.

Concerning the Kalends of January and other auguries . . . we judge this to be detestable and pernicious both to us and to all Christians . . . We decree that the lots by which you make determinations in all matters in your respective provinces are nothing other than the divinations and magic condemned by the other Fathers. Therefore we will that they be wholly condemned, and we do not wish them to be named any further among Christians; we forbid them to continue, under the prohibition of anathema, so that they may be cut off, CLXI, 747.

Those who, though Christians, celebrate Gentile solemnities bring anathema into the Church. Those who investigate human lives and actions from the courses of the stars, or who inquire into the flight of birds and other such things formerly observed in the world, bring into the Church the anathema of Jericho; they defile the Lord’s camp and cause God’s people to be conquered, CLXI, 748.

The Apostle rebukes those who say: “I shall not set out today because it is a later day,” or “because the moon is in such a position”; or: “I shall set out so that matters may go favorably, because the position of the stars is thus.” Or: “I shall not conduct this business in this month because that star governs my month”; or, “I shall do so because it has taken charge of the month”; “I shall not plant a vineyard this year because it is a leap year.” No wise person, however, thinks that observers of times should be rebuked when they say: “I shall not set out because a storm has arisen,” or “I shall not sail because wintry conditions remain,” or “It is time for sowing because autumn rains have saturated the ground”; or if perhaps other natural effects relating to movements of air and moisture, affecting the changing qualities of the seasons, have been observed in the most orderly revolutions of the stars, CLXI, 751.

An explanation of these and other incantations is given in vol. CLXI, 751–780.

JOHN OF SALISBURY, bishop of Chartres.—What shall I say about necromancers, whose impiety, with God as its author, has now everywhere become contemptible of itself, except that those are worthy of death who attempt to borrow knowledge from death? As for auspices, augurs, leapers, diviners, Pythonists, diviners from victims, and others—whose enumeration would be tedious because of their multitude—it is superfluous to weave a longer discourse, since none of these now comes forth openly, but, if any such person exists, practises works of darkness in hiding. Yet certain of them should be touched upon to some extent for definite reasons. Even if they hide, diviners from sacrificial victims still survive to their own harm. It has been said that these divine in part from the entrails of animals. Under the name of entrails, indeed, are reckoned all things covered by the outer boundary of skin. Hence it is plain that those who prophesy from the shoulder-blades of rams, or from the bones of any animals whatsoever, are to be counted among them.

Palm-readers also boast that they know truths hidden in the wrinkles of hands. Since their error rests upon no reasoning, there is no need to attack it with arguments, although reason itself defeats them by this very fact: they fail through lack of reason. Yet there is one thing I ask you most earnestly, if you will listen to me patiently. What do these triflers—whom I do not doubt you know—produce when questioned about doubtful matters? . . . What did a hand-diviner, summoned and consulted, contribute? . . . Consultation of Pythonists, however, is more pernicious inasmuch as the deception of malicious spirits is clearer in them; whether they lie or do not lie, they always intend to harm. At times they deceive from eagerness to deceive, and at times because they themselves are deceived by the error of their blindness; but they continually strive to appear fully aware of future things. Hence they try to cloud their oracles in ambiguity of words, so that, when found false or deceptive, they may seek to defend their deception with some veil of reason. Thus, indeed, they do not cease deceiving until they have hurled their hearers into ruin.

For whose benefit have the answers of seers ever been from the beginning? For Croesus, or Pyrrhus, or anyone among those before or after them? While the Theban leader hopes for victory from an oracle, he is pierced by his brother’s sword. Yet his grandfather Laius had seemed to promise success in war . . . Croesus is confident, on the faith of oracles, that if he crosses the Halys, great kingdoms will be subjected to him; but when events turned out otherwise, deceitful Apollo cleared himself of the charge of lying by the equivocation of one little word. And Pyrrhus? . . . . . .

But lest the charge of deceit should be cast back upon oracles only in secular histories, let canonical history be examined, to whose sound faith one assents. Saul, changed from prince into tyrant, when he had been abandoned by the Lord because his sins demanded it and the hostile hand was gaining strength against the people of the Lord under his leadership, anxiously sought an outcome amid ruined circumstances. He therefore consulted the Lord, but the Lord did not answer him, either through dreams, priests, or prophets. Samuel had nevertheless foretold this to him: that the Lord regretted having made him king . . . CXCIX, 461–466.

Saul therefore changed his clothing, put on other garments, went with two men, and they came by night to a woman. Saul said to the woman—for women are more frequently possessed by the Pythonic spirit—“Divine for me by Python, and bring up for me the one whom I shall name to you.” Read the books, turn over the histories, search every corner of Scripture: you will scarcely ever find divination in a good sense . . . This man, first negligent, then disobedient, afterward obstinate, thereafter hardened, finally fell into such blindness that he did not preserve intact even the article of faith previously announced to him. For he did not altogether believe God to be just, supposing that even over saints after their departure from this life authority had been granted to malicious spirits . . .

Scripture does not say that Samuel was raised up by the power of Python, but wisely expresses the blindness of the impious understanding. For it says that, when he heard of the man’s appearance and clothing, “Saul understood that it was Samuel.” He understood this while deceived; as is proved by what follows: “and he bowed down and worshipped him.” For if he had been Samuel, he would by no means have allowed himself to be worshipped by a man who had believed and taught, according to the law, that one God and Lord alone is to be worshipped. Furthermore, holy souls are exempt from the power of malicious spirits . . . Though Saul believed that the speaker was Samuel, in truth he was an angel of Satan . . .

For when he says that the Lord will fulfill what he spoke “by my hand,” he undoubtedly pretends to be Samuel, through whom the Lord had spoken to Saul the things he announces. But when he adds, “Tomorrow you and your sons will be with me,” he speaks truly, but deceitfully. For on the next day Saul would lay hands upon himself in despair and pass down to hell, where he would have his portion with him . . . But he falsely flatters Saul, instilling hope of rest, while by gesture and words he pretends to be Samuel, to whom, it is certain, the Lord had granted a place of rest among those who call upon his name . . . What benefit, then, did the answers of Saul’s Samuel—or rather, of his Python—bring him? Had he not been forewarned, he might perhaps have hoped for better things, and at least, while being pierced by another’s sword, could have waited. But, rendered certain by the vanity of the oracle, he fell upon his own sword; and at the end, while seeking to provide for his own glory, as one who might have died more bravely in battle, he feared the mere breath of words and, by the counsel of a weak and prostrate mind, incurred the death of both body and soul, CXCIX, 466–470.

Let the Gentiles glory in their own strength . . . Let Cato drink poison at their prompting. Let Vulteius arm the hands and minds of his companions for voluntary death. Let Cleopatra send the incurable venom of asps through her breasts to her heart. Let Lucretia condemn another’s unchastity by shedding her own blood. I judge that it cannot occur that, under any circumstance of difficulty whatsoever, a human being may lawfully inflict death upon himself on his own authority; not even where chastity is endangered, although St. Augustine seems to make an exception for this case, CXCIX, 470–472.

There is still much on similar matters in this volume, CXCIX, cols. 472–479.

JONAS, bishop of Orléans.—It is true, and wholly consonant with sound faith, that absolutely no likeness of any things that are in heaven, or on earth, or beneath the earth, should be made to which the worship or adoration due to God alone is in any manner rendered. Since, therefore, God is everywhere, contains all things, and is contained nowhere, and is invisible to every creature, as the Apostle testifies, we are forbidden to make for ourselves a likeness of the things mentioned, lest He be believed to be corporeal. But since the meaning of this statement is plain—and has indeed been most fully expounded for us by the holy Fathers—and does not [Col. 0373] sufficiently concern the matter at hand, it must be considered whether perhaps, under the name of “likeness,” you intend to include images of saints and accounts of deeds done, painted in churches for beauty and remembrance. If that is so, I ask you why, at the Lord’s command, Moses made the two golden cherubim and the other things read of in Exodus in the tabernacle of the Lord, and why Solomon represented likenesses of oxen and lions in the house of the Lord. When you answer that these went before as figures of mysteries, you will nevertheless be unable to deny that likenesses of heavenly and earthly creatures existed. And if those things were made in the tabernacle and in the house of the Lord, not to be adored, but to prefigure types of things to come, then permit images of saints and accounts of the saints, not to be adored, but rather to provide a certain beauty and to impress upon the minds of the unlearned a memory of certain past events, to be painted in churches. But we hold it unlawful for a creature to be adored or for any service proper to God to be bestowed upon it; and with free voice we proclaim the perpetrator of this crime to be detestable and subject to anathema. CVI, 318.

One kind of adoration is due only to God alone; another is rendered by mortals to fellow mortals as an expression of humility and submission. Again, one kind of worship is that by which divine power alone must be served; another is that rendered, according to its proper measure, not only to rational but also to irrational creatures. On the diversity of worship, see St. Augustine (*City of God*, X.1) . . . CVI, 318–320.

It is one thing to worship, another to adore. At times a person may adore even unwillingly, as certain men flattering kings, when they see them devoted to such pursuits, pretend to adore idols, although they are certain in their hearts that an idol is nothing. To worship, however, is to devote oneself wholly to it with affection and zeal. CVI, 321, 322.

Some thought that the honor due to God should be paid to angels, whether by adoration or sacrifice; they were forbidden by the angels’ admonition and commanded to render these things to Him alone, to whom they knew it was lawful to render them. Holy men of God likewise imitated the holy angels. For Paul and Barnabas, after a certain miracle of healing had occurred in Lycaonia, were thought to be gods, and the Lycaonians wished to sacrifice victims to them; humbly rejecting this in piety, they proclaimed to them the God in whom they should believe . . . But we do not build temples to our martyrs as to gods, but memorials as to dead human beings, whose spirits live with God. Nor do we erect altars there upon which we sacrifice to martyrs; rather, we offer sacrifice to the one God, both theirs and ours. In that sacrifice they are named, according to their place and rank, as men of God who conquered the world in confessing Him; yet they are not invoked by the priest who offers sacrifice. For he sacrifices to God, not to them, although he sacrifices in their memory, because he is God’s priest, not theirs. The sacrifice itself is Christ’s body, which is not offered to them, because they themselves are that body . . . But observe holy human beings, who are like angels. When you find some holy servant of God, if you wish to worship and adore him in God’s place, he forbids you; he does not wish to claim God’s honor for himself; he does not wish to be God to you, but to be with you under God . . . Let no one say, “I fear that an angel will be angry with me if I do not worship him as my God.” For he is angry with you precisely when you wish to worship him; for he is good and loves God. As demons are angry if they are not worshipped, so angels are indignant if they are worshipped in God’s place. CVI, 322–325.

Therefore, that the holy Church, in remembrance of its redemption, reveres, adores, and worships the cross of Christ by tradition from the Fathers—not with the worship and adoration belonging to divinity alone, but rather in the manner of humility and remembrance mentioned above—is known to everyone except one who dissents from ecclesiastical tradition. Hence, in remembrance of the saving passion of the Lord, every year on the most holy day of Preparation, according to ecclesiastical tradition, the Church adores—that is, greets in supplication—the cross of Christ. Spread throughout the whole world, it bursts forth joyfully in Christ’s praise and sings: “We adore your cross, O Lord; behold the wood of the cross, on which the salvation of the world hung. Come, let us adore.” CVI, 331–334.

The bodies of the martyrs are precious, because they received wounds for the Lord, and because they bear in their limbs the marks impressed for Christ’s sake. As a royal crown, adorned on every side, emits varied splendors, so also the bodies of the holy martyrs, distinguished by wounds received for Christ as by precious stones, are made more precious and more splendid than every kingly diadem. For it is manifest to all the faithful that the bodies of these saints are divinely honored by many great miracles, and not without reason.
