It is fitting that those who usefully presented their bodies as members of righteousness and triumphed over the devil in them should shine with such evident miracles, so that the glorious signs of divine recompense may show how precious is death in the sight of the Lord and how great their power is with the Most High. “The bodies of the dead,” says St. Augustine, “especially of the righteous and faithful, must not be despised and cast away; for the Holy Spirit used them as instruments and vessels for every good work. For if a father’s garment or ring, or anything of that sort, is all the dearer to descendants in proportion as affection toward parents is greater, then bodies must by no means be despised—bodies which we certainly wear far more intimately and closely joined to ourselves than any garments.” Blessed Jerome writes that the bodies of the saints are to be honored by the faithful: “We honor the relics of martyrs, that we may adore Him whose martyrs they are. We honor servants, that the honor of the servants may redound to the Lord . . .” CVI, 328, 329.

“At the ashes of the saints,” says St. Jerome, “demons roar and flee from possessed bodies; and many other innumerable things take place through their intercession, with Christ’s grace cooperating.” CVI, 327.

Finally, in that treatise on the worship of images, from which we have excerpted these passages, there is much to be consulted concerning the present question. CVI, 305–394.

LACTANTIUS FIRMICUS.—Astrology, divination from entrails, augury, the things called oracles, necromancy, magical art, and whatever other evils people practice openly or secretly, are inventions of demons. By a pretended divinity they deceive human credulity, because it is not expedient for them to disclose the truth. These are they who taught people to fashion images and statues; in order to turn human minds away from the worship of the true God, they caused the fictitious features of dead kings to be made, adorned with exquisite beauty, set up, and consecrated . . . VI, 336, 337.

LACTANTIUS, rhetorician and apologist.—*Divine Institutions*, VI, 111 ff. On God and His unity, VII, 110.

LEO THE GREAT, St., pope.—On the worship of God, LIV, 187.

MARTIN, St., regular canon of León.—How old and young men ought to serve God, CCIX, 119.

The first commandment of the Decalogue pertains to God the Father, when it says: “The Lord your God is one,” so that, hearing this, you may worship one God the Father and may not defile your fornication among many fictitious gods. CCVIII, 782.

We must believe before all things in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—namely, the one true God; having found Him, we must believe faithfully in Him, love Him in all things and above all things. By His gratuitous goodness He first deigned to create us from nothing and, after the most grievous fault of the first parent’s transgression, mercifully to restore us to the first—indeed, to a better—state. We believe that no one can attain true blessedness except through true faith. Blessed is the person who both lives well by believing rightly and, by living well, preserves right faith. CCVIII, 1325.

MAXIMUS, St., bishop of Turin.—On superstitious festivals, LVII, 255. The evil of idolatry, LVII, 733.

NOVATIAN, presbyter.—The rule of truth requires that first of all we believe in God the Father and Lord Almighty, that is, the most perfect creator of all things: He suspended heaven in lofty height, made earth firm in its lowly mass, spread out the seas in their flowing liquid, and arranged all these things, adorned and full, with their proper and fitting instruments. In the firmament of heaven He caused the shining risings of the sun; for the night’s comfort, He filled out the bright globe of the moon through the monthly increase of its orb; He kindled the rays of the stars with varied gleams of flashing light, and willed all these to traverse the whole expanse of the world in ordained courses, bringing days, months, years, signs, seasons, and benefits to the human race. On earth likewise He raised the highest mountains into peaks, cast valleys down into the depths, spread plains levelly, and established herds of animals for the various useful services of humankind. He made the strength of forests firm for human uses, produced crops for food, opened the mouths of springs, and poured them into descending rivers . . . After this, lest He should not also have provided for the delight of the eyes themselves, He clothed all things in the varied colors of flowers for the pleasure of those who behold them. In the sea itself, though it was marvelous both in magnitude and usefulness, He fashioned animals of many kinds, now of moderate, now of enormous size, bearing witness through their variety of formation to their maker’s skill. Not content with these, lest the roar and rush of waters should perhaps seize a foreign element to the loss of the human possessor, He enclosed them within the bounds of shores, so that when the raging wave and foaming billow had come from the deep gulf, it might return again into itself and not exceed the limits granted to it, keeping the laws prescribed—so that humankind might observe divine laws all the more because even the elements observed them. After this He also set humankind over the world . . . III, 886, 887.

Thus we acknowledge and know God, the creator [Col. 0375] of all things. The Church knows and venerates this God; to Him both invisible and visible nature, always and wholly, bears witness; angels adore Him, stars marvel at Him, seas bless Him, lands reverence Him, and all things in the depths look up to Him . . . III, 891–899.

The same rule of truth teaches us to believe, after the Father, also in the Son of God as true God, and in the Holy Spirit as equally God, so that they are one God in substance, though three persons, etc. . . . There is a treatise on this, *On the Trinity*, III, 885–952.

PAULINUS, St., patriarch of Aquileia.—On the love of God, XCIX, 197–214.

PETER THE CHANTER.—The number of the cardinal virtues is four: prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice. Prudence is a wise and most discerning choice by which we prefer eternal things to transitory things, virtues to vices, homeland to exile, and freedom to slavery. Of this choice St. Augustine says to Macedonius: “Virtue is nothing other than loving what ought to be loved. To choose what ought to be chosen is prudence; not to be turned away from it by any hardships is fortitude; not to be turned away from it by any allurements is temperance; not to be turned away from it by any pride is justice . . .”

In these few words, therefore, the perfection of the Christian life is shown. This is the four-horse chariot by which those who have no abiding city here seek the city to come, etc. CCV, 305–309.

PETER CHRYSOLOGUS, St., archbishop of Ravenna.—On God’s fatherly love for us, LII, 352.

PETER COMESTOR.—FIRST COMMANDMENT. “You shall have no foreign gods before me,” that is, you shall have me alone as God. “You shall not have” is put for “Do not have,” imperatively, according to Hebrew idiom. For God does not assert this, since at times they did have them: “You shall not make for yourself a graven image,” or idol. Another reading: “which is nothing in the world,” that is, representative of no natural thing—as Ammon was made with a ram’s head, and Anubis, that is Mercury, with a beardless dog’s head. “Nor any likeness that is in heaven, or earth, or waters, or beneath the earth”—that is, do not make for yourself as God an image of the sun, moon, and such things; or of a human being, a beast, and such things; or of a dragon or any reptile, which the differing error of humankind worshipped. “You shall not worship or even adore them.” For to worship is to adore with the mind; but to adore is, if not in spirit, at least through fear or by flattering kings, to adore.

Afterward, to impress the observance of what had been said and what was to be said, He added incidentally: “I am the Lord your God, strong and jealous, visiting the sins of fathers upon children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, and showing mercy unto thousands to those who love me and keep my commandments.” Jealousy means envy; it also means love, but properly a husband’s love for his wife, by which he cannot endure another’s approach to her. In this sense the Lord says, “I am jealous,” that is, I shall not permit you to commit fornication after foreign gods. Heretics say of His addition that He visits the sins of fathers upon children: “This is not a good saying, that someone should be punished for another’s sin.” And they say that the Old Testament was not given by God. Yet God is not so cruel; rather, He appears gentle even in this, as is suggested by the very term “visiting.” For we visit the sick out of compassion; and He in gentleness does not punish the sinner immediately, but waits even until the fourth generation, as long as fathers are accustomed to live. If the father is corrected, or the children do not imitate him, He spares them; otherwise, as after a long waiting, He punishes more justly. This must be understood only of temporal punishment, as we read that vengeance was exacted upon the descendants of Ahab and Jehu. Or it may express the severity of a just judge: for sinners are punished more severely if they see even their children punished on their account, and more justly after a delay. Origen, however, understands fathers here as demons, descendants as accomplices whom we sometimes join to ourselves in sinning: “For example, first the devil entered Judas’s heart—behold, the father; then he came to the rulers, that they too might sin in this—behold, the children; then he received from them a cohort and attendants—behold, the third and fourth generation.” But the Lord does not here visit the sins of the fathers, who are reserved for eternal fire; nevertheless, He often now punishes human beings. CXCVIII, 1164, 1165.

PETER DAMIAN, St., cardinal.—There are three stages in the love of God, CXLIV, 647. God alone is to be adored, CXLV, 1016.

PETER LOMBARD, bishop of Paris.—The first commandment on the first tablet is: “You shall have no foreign gods; you shall not make for yourself a graven image, nor any likeness,” etc. Origen calls these two commandments; but Augustine (*On the Ten Strings*) calls them one. For what He had said—“You shall have no foreign gods”—He explains more fully when He forbids the worship of fabricated things: namely, an idol or [Col. 0376] the likeness of some thing. Origen says that these two differ thus: an idol is that which has nothing like itself, whereas a likeness has the appearance of some thing. For example, if someone makes in gold, wood, or another material the form of a serpent, bird, or other thing and sets it up for adoration, he makes not an idol but a likeness. But whoever makes a form which the eye has not seen but the mind has imagined—if someone fashions a dog’s or ram’s head upon human limbs, or two faces upon one human figure—makes not a likeness but an idol, because he makes that which has nothing like itself. Therefore the Apostle says, “An idol is nothing in the world.” For no form is taken from any existing thing, but rather from what an idle and curious mind has devised. A likeness, however, is made when something is fashioned from things that are in heaven, on earth, or in the waters.

Augustine, however, explains “An idol is nothing in the world” thus: among the creatures of the world there is no form of an idol. God made the material, but human folly gave it its form. Whatever was made was made naturally through the Word; but the human form in an idol was not made through the Word, just as sin was not made through the Word, but is nothing, and human beings become nothing when they sin. But the question is raised: how can the form of an idol here be said not to have been made through the Word, when elsewhere we read, “Every form, every joining, every harmony of parts was made through the Word”? This is resolved differently by different people. Some say that every form and everything that is, insofar as it is, is from God; and that the form of an idol, insofar as it exists or is a form, is from God—but not insofar as it is an idol, that is, insofar as it is set up for adoration. In this respect it is not a creature but a perversion of creation. Thus, what is sin, insofar as it is sin, is nothing; and when people sin, they become nothing because they are separated from Him who truly is. Hence Jerome says: “What is not from God, who alone is true, is said not to be.” Therefore sin, which leads us away from true being, is said to be nothing or not to be. Others say that every form that is natural, and everything that is natural, is from God; but the form of an idol is not natural, because it does not observe the justice of nature. For that is called natural which serves—and does not resist—the justice of the simple nature which is God, and does not corrupt created nature. CXCII, 831.

PROSPER, St., of Aquitaine.—On idols, LI, 457, 489, 491–501.

RUPERT, abbot of Deutz.—“For the Lord says, ‘You shall not have foreign gods before me.’” According to this commandment, all the righteousness of a servant consists in not having worshipped Baal, not having served Astarte, not having been initiated into Baal-peor, or anyone of that kind contrary to true divinity, and not having placed such a thing in God’s temple. But one who strives to exceed the condition of a servant attends not merely to the meaning of these words, namely “foreign gods,” but also to the etymology of this name “God”; so that he not only has no foreign gods before God according to the commandment, but fears no other for the sake of God alone, the true God. For God is called *Theos* in Greek, which is interpreted “fear.” The Creator is called by such a name because He must be feared, and it is rightly required of every rational creature that He be feared. Thus counsel beyond the commandment is accepted when the good servant, worthy of love or grace, sets before himself God alone as to be feared, considering no other God or Lord worthy of his fear. Even if he is compelled by the penalty of death to fear another, he is not bent from righteousness, standing firm for the sake of the true God and Lord, out of friendship—whereby He speaks to His own thus: “But I say to you, my friends: Do not be afraid of those who kill the body and afterward have nothing more that they can do. Fear Him who, after He has killed, has power to cast into Gehenna. Yes, I say to you, fear Him.” CLXVII, 1720, 1721.

“You shall not have foreign gods before me,” that is, you shall adore no one as God except the one creator of heaven and earth. Likewise, to make a graven image or any likeness of things that are in heaven, on earth, or in the waters, and to think any of them like God, is wickedness and opposed to the love of God . . . CLXVIII, 680.

SMARAGDUS, abbot.—On the love of God, CII, 598–648.

TAIO, bishop of Zaragoza.—The spiritual Fathers of the Old Testament believed God Almighty to be Trinity, just as the Fathers of the New Testament spoke openly of the same Trinity. Moses said: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth, and the Spirit of God was moving over the waters . . .” Without doubt, under the name “God” the Father is to be understood; under the name “Beginning,” the Son; and under “Spirit of God,” the same Holy Spirit. God is Trinity in the begetting one, the begotten one, and the proceeding one—that is, in Father, Son, and [Col. 0377] Holy Spirit—namely, in appellative or relative names . . . LXXX, 738, 739.

RABANUS MAURUS.—In the Council of Agde it is written concerning diviners by lots or those who observe auguries: “Lest it perhaps seem that something has been omitted concerning that which most especially presses upon the faith of the Catholic religion: certain persons, whether clerics or laypeople, give themselves to auguries; and under the fictitious name of religion, they profess a knowledge of divination by what they call the lots of saints, or promise future events through the examination of any writings whatever. Any cleric or layperson discovered either consulting or teaching these things shall be held outside the Church.” CX, 492. There is also a complete treatise on magical arts, CX, 1095–1110.

On not making idols, CVIII, 550. On loving God, CVIII, 865. On the error of idolatry, CIX, 720. Love of God, CX, 348. On the punishments of idolatry, CX, 603–741. Rebuke of idolatry, CXI, 877.

RODULPHUS, bishop of Bourges.—Any of the faithful who observe auguries and omens, dreams, or any divinations in the manner of the pagans; or the lots which they falsely claim are those of saints—whether clerics or laypeople found either consulting or teaching them; or who bring into their houses persons of this kind to discover something by magical art; or who purify their houses—shall be kept outside the Church for five years, performing penance according to the established ancient rules. For Christians may not observe the traditions of the pagans, worship the elements, the moons, the courses of the stars, or the empty deception of signs, whether for building a house, sowing grain, planting trees, or contracting marriages. For it is written: “Whatever you do, do everything in the name of the Lord.” Nor is it lawful, in gathering herbs, to observe any rites or incantations, except only with the divine Creed and the Lord’s Prayer . . . CXIX, 722.

TERTULLIAN, presbyter of Carthage.—A recent act of generosity by the most excellent emperors had taken place: in the camps, soldiers were being registered wearing laurel crowns. There was present a certain soldier of God, more steadfast than the other brethren, who had presumed that he could serve two masters; he alone had his head uncovered, with his crown idly in his hand . . . The murmuring was brought to the tribune, and the man had already come forward from the ranks. At once the tribune said, “Why are you so different in dress?” He replied that, unlike the others, it was not lawful for him. Asked for the reason, he answered, “I am a Christian.” O soldier glorious in God! He was made an accused man and sent to the prefects; there he laid aside his heavy military cloak, beginning to be relieved of its burden; he removed from his feet the most troublesome military boots . . . he surrendered the sword, unnecessary even for the Lord’s defense; the laurel also fell from his hand . . . and he awaits Christ’s bounty in prison . . . “Where,” some say, “are we forbidden to be crowned?” . . . And those who call themselves true Christians ask, “Where is it written that we are to be crowned?” II, 76–78.

And as long as [we proceed] along this line . . . If no Scripture has determined this, certainly custom has confirmed it, a custom which without doubt flowed from tradition. For how can anything be employed if it was not first handed down? “Even under the pretext of tradition,” you say, “written authority must be required.” Then let us inquire whether tradition too ought to be received. Surely we shall deny that it should be received if the examples of other observances do not establish a precedent—observances which we maintain without any written instrument, by the title of tradition alone and then by the support of custom. II, 78, 79.

But why is the case for Christian observances made stronger when nature also defends them? Thus he first writes that a crown is not fitting for the head . . . II, 82. So too the crown becomes a thing sacrificed to idols (*idolothytum*). Therefore the Apostle cries out: “Flee from idolatry” . . . Blessed John says: “Little children, keep yourselves from idols.” II, 90–99.

*To the Nations*, I, 559 ff. *On Idolatry*, I, 661 ff. On gratitude toward God, I, 1255. On the worship of idols, II, 90, 91.

VENANTIUS FORTUNATUS.—A copy of the Athanasian Creed: “Whoever wishes to be saved must above all hold the catholic faith . . . so that we worship one God in Trinity and Trinity in unity, neither confusing the persons nor dividing the substance. For the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another; but the divinity is one, the glory equal, the majesty coeternal. Such as the Father is, such is the Son, and such also the Holy Spirit. The Father uncreated, the Son uncreated, the Holy Spirit uncreated. The Father immeasurable, the Son immeasurable . . . The Father eternal . . . and yet not three eternals, nor three uncreateds, nor three immeasurables, but one eternal, one uncreated,” etc. . . . “Likewise the Father almighty, the Son almighty, the Holy Spirit almighty; and yet not three almighties, but one almighty . . . Thus the Father is God, the Son God, the Holy Spirit God; and yet not [Col. 0378] three gods, but one God . . .” LXXXVIII, 585.

Brief exposition of this creed, LXXXVIII, 586–592.

ZENO, St.—The foundations of Christian excellence consist in three things: hope, faith, and charity; and these seem so joined together that each is necessary to the others. For unless hope comes first, for what does faith labor? If faith is absent, how can hope itself be born? If you withhold charity from these, both cease, because neither faith without charity nor hope without faith can operate. Thus, if the Christian wishes to be perfect, he must be built upon these three things; for if any one of them is lacking, he will not possess the perfection of his work. Therefore, first of all, hope in future things must be set before us; without it, we see that even present things cannot stand. So completely is this so that, take away hope, and all humanity grows numb. Take away hope, and every art and all virtues cease. Take away hope, and all things are destroyed . . .

But hope arises from faith. Although hope is placed in the future, it is rightly subject to faith; for where faith is not, neither is hope. Faith is the substance of hope, and hope the glory of faith, because faith earns the reward which hope possesses. Faith indeed fights for hope, but wins for itself . . . For faith itself is the immovable foundation of our life, an unconquered fortress against the devil’s attacks, and likewise a weapon, an impenetrable breastplate for our soul, the brief and true knowledge of the law, terror to demons, the strength of martyrs, the beauty—or wall—of the Church, God’s handmaid, Christ’s friend, the Holy Spirit’s guest . . .

Let faith triumph, if it will, with whatever virtues; let hope propose many and great things; yet without charity neither will stand: faith, first of all, if it does not love itself; hope, if it is not loved. Add that faith benefits itself alone, whereas charity benefits all. Add that faith does not fight without reward, whereas charity is accustomed to confer benefits even on the ungrateful. Add that faith does not pass into another, whereas it is too little to say that charity passes into another—it passes into a people. Add that faith belongs to few, charity to all. Add that hope and faith have their time, whereas charity has no end: it increases at every moment, and the more those who love one another entrust themselves to it, the more they owe one another, etc. XI, 269–275.

WALAFRID STRABO, monk of Fulda.—“I am the Lord your God.” Of one who despises the present age, namely Egypt, and is translated through God’s Word so as not to be found, because he hastens toward the age to come, God says: “I am . . .” This is said not only to those who departed from Egypt, but also to those who no longer serve Egyptians, having been led out of Egypt, from the house of slavery. The business of the age and acts of the flesh are the house of slavery, just as abandoning worldly matters and living according to God is the house of freedom. Hence John says: “If you remain in my word, you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.” Therefore Egypt is the house of slavery; Judea and Jerusalem, the house of freedom. Hence Galatians: “The Jerusalem above is free.” Therefore, as earthly Egypt is called a house of slavery for the children of Israel in comparison with Judea and Jerusalem, which are for them a house of freedom, so in comparison with heavenly Jerusalem, which is the mother of freedom, the whole world and the things in it are called a house of slavery. Since by sin one came from the paradise of freedom into the slavery of the world, the first statement of the Decalogue concerns freedom: “I am . . . who brought you out of the land of Egypt.” You cannot hear this voice in Egypt. Even if you are commanded to keep Passover, gird your loins, put sandals on your feet, hold a staff in your hand, and eat unleavened bread with bitterness; not in the first station, nor the second, nor the third; not when you have crossed the Red Sea, even if you have come to the sea and its bitterness has been turned to sweetness for you; not in Elim, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees; even if you have passed Rephidim and ascended the remaining stages—still you are not judged worthy. But when you have come to Mount Sinai, only then will you scarcely at last deserve to receive the commandments of freedom and hear: “I am . . . who brought you out of the land . . .” Yet here this is not the wording of a command, but indicates who it is that commands. The first commandment, therefore, is: “You shall have no other gods besides me.” This first commandment pertains to God the Father: “The Lord your God is one God,” so that, hearing this, you may worship one God, the Father, and may not pour out fornication among many fictitious gods. “You shall not make for yourself an idol or any likeness.” Some think all these are one commandment. But if counted thus, the number of ten commandments will not be completed. Therefore the first commandment is: “You shall have no other gods besides me,” etc.; the second: “You shall not make for yourself an idol or any likeness,” etc.

[Col. 0379]

Let us begin, therefore, with the first commandment: “You shall have no other gods besides me.” If He had said, “There are no [other gods],” the statement would seem more absolute; but because He said, “There shall not be,” He did not deny that they exist, but forbade their being gods to the person to whom these commandments are given. I think Paul took this from here: “For indeed there are those called gods, whether in heaven or on earth.” In other passages also you will find gods named, as in: “A great king over all gods,” and, “God spoke to God.” The same Apostle says of lords: “Whether thrones, or dominions,” etc. Dominions are nothing other than a certain order and multitude of lords. In this the Apostle seems to open the meaning of the law, as if saying: Although there are many lords ruling over other nations, and many gods worshipped by them, yet for us there is one God and one Lord. Hence: “When the Most High divided the nations and separated the children of Adam, He established the bounds of the nations according to the number of the angels of God.” Scripture therefore calls the angels to whom the Most High entrusted the nations “lords” or “gods”: gods as given by God, and lords as having received authority from the Lord. Hence it is said to them: “I said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High . . .” Therefore to you, O Israel, who are God’s portion and His measuring-line, He says: “There shall be no other gods for you besides me,” because the true God is one God, and the true Lord is one Lord. To the others, created by Him, He granted this name not by nature but by grace. These words are spoken not only to Israel according to the flesh, but indeed to you who have become Israel by seeing God with the mind and are circumcised in heart, not flesh—provided, however, that you act so as to be worthy to be God’s portion and to be measured in the line of His inheritance. Otherwise, let those who were called to be God’s portion be an example to you: because of the demands of their sins, they were scattered among all nations; and, having been led out of the house of slavery, they now serve not Egyptians alone but all nations. “For whoever sins is the slave of sin.” CXIII, 249–251.

“Thou shalt not make for thyself an idol, nor any likeness . . .” Idols are one thing; gods another. For concerning gods the Apostle says: “Indeed, there are many gods and many lords.” But concerning idols: “An idol is nothing in the world.” He did not add that likenesses are nothing. Here, however, it is said: “Thou shalt not make for thyself an idol . . .” Therefore making an idol is one thing, making a likeness another. For example, if someone makes in gold or silver, wood or stone, the form of a quadruped, serpent, or bird, and sets it up for worship, he makes not an idol but a likeness. But one who makes that which does not exist—that is, a form which the eye does not see but the mind imagines for itself—such as one who gives a human body the head of a dog or ram, or two faces in one human figure, or the hindquarters of a horse or fish to a human breast: one who does this makes not a likeness but an idol, for he makes what does not exist and has nothing like itself. Therefore the Apostle says: “An idol is nothing in the world.” For its form is not taken from any existing thing, but is what an idle and curious mind devises. A likeness, however, is made when something is fashioned from things that are in heaven, on earth, or in the waters.

But although it is easy to make a pronouncement concerning likenesses of things on earth or in the sea, it is not so with heavenly things, unless perhaps one says that this can be understood of the sun, moon, and stars, whose forms the Gentiles reproduce. Yet Moses, instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, wished also to forbid things among them which were hidden, such as Hecate and other forms of demons, which the Apostle calls “spiritual wickednesses in the heavenly places.” By these forms and likenesses they invoked demons to drive away or avoid evils.

Nevertheless, it must be understood that, when you resolve to keep this commandment and to have only one God and Lord, you thereby declare war on all the others whom you renounced in baptism, confessing God alone—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Yet, unless in making this confession we love the Lord our God with our whole heart, whole soul, and whole strength, and cleave to him, we have not become the Lord’s portion; instead, set on the borderland, we suffer those whom we flee to be offended, while we do not make propitious the one to whom we flee. To such persons the prophet says: “Woe to the double-minded” . . . Therefore there is no fellowship between the temple of God and idols. If we are God’s disciples, we ought to be such temples in which God may dwell and walk . . . CXIII, 251–252.

“Thou shalt not worship them, etc.” To cultivate is one thing; to worship is another. A person may worship unwillingly, either by flattering idolatrous kings or by being overcome by tortures, while knowing that an idol is nothing. But to cultivate is to devote oneself to such things with one’s whole affection and zeal. Therefore he cuts off both, so that you may not worship even in affection, CXIII, 252.

“I am the Lord, etc.” Thus God’s kindness, in order to teach us and make us perfect, does not reject the weakness of human affections; he does and suffers all things for our sake, speaking to us through affections familiar and customary to us.

“Jealous.” Every woman is either under a husband and subject to her husband’s laws, or she is a prostitute and uses the freedom to sin. He who enters a prostitute knows that he has entered one who is public and open to all; therefore he cannot be indignant about others. But he who lives in lawful marriage does not allow his wife to sin; rather, he is kindled with zeal to preserve the chastity of marriage, so that he may become the lawful father. Thus every soul is either prostituted to demons and has many lovers entering her: now the spirit of fornication, now of avarice; after this will come the spirit of pride, and many others. Yet one does not envy another, nor is jealousy aroused, but they invite one another . . . Thus the soul prostituted to demons experiences no jealousy from her lovers. But if she has been joined to a lawful husband, that is, Christ, then, even if she has at some time been sinful, he no longer permits her to sin, nor can he endure her sporting with adulterers. His zeal is stirred on her behalf, and he defends the chastity of the marriage. But if he sees her violating the laws of marriage and seeking an occasion for sin, he gives her a bill of divorce; hence Isaiah: “Because of your iniquities he dismissed your mother.” He who says this is both jealous and moved by zeal.

This too is a new kind of his goodness: even after adultery he receives her when she returns and repents with her whole heart . . . Therefore, if this jealous God seeks and desires your soul to cleave to him, if he guards, corrects, and is indignant toward you, recognize in this, as it were, a certain jealousy toward you, that there is hope of salvation. But if you despise correction, his zeal departs from you, according to that saying: “Therefore my zeal departs from thee.” Behold God’s mercy and loving-kindness: when he wishes to show mercy, he says that he is indignant and angry . . . But this is terrible, this is the end: if we are not corrected for our sins. For when we exceed the measure of provoking zeal, even God’s zeal will be taken away from us, and he will no longer be angry, CXIII, 252–253.

“Visiting the iniquity of the fathers, etc.” The heretics say that this cannot be the utterance of a good God, because he says that one person is punished for another’s sins. Yet they call the God of the Law just, and cannot show how he is unjust if, when one person sins, he punishes another. But our inward person is said either to have God as Father, if he lives according to God, or the devil, if he does the devil’s will. Hence: “You are of your father the devil,” etc. . . .

Let us therefore see how God repays the sins of fathers upon sons to the third and fourth generation, and not upon the father himself. Nothing, indeed, is said of the fathers. The devil, therefore, because he has already exceeded the measure of sinning, like a garment clotted with blood, will not be cleansed in this age; he is not scourged for sin, for all things are reserved for him in the future. Hence: “Why hast thou come before the time to destroy us?” But sins are repaid upon the sons whom he has begotten through sin, who, being in the flesh, are scourged. “For God wills not the death of the sinner, but rather that he be converted and live.” Therefore in mercy he repays the sins of fathers upon sons, because the devil and his angels, who also become fathers of sin, are unworthy to be corrected in the present life; their sons, and those whom they have drawn through themselves into fellowship in sin, receive in the present life what they have done, so that, being purified, they may not become companions of the devil in punishment. Hence: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod, etc.” For God is jealous and does not wish the soul which he has espoused to himself in faith to remain in the defilement of sin, but wishes it quickly purified. But if it refuses to be purified, he will laugh at their destruction, saying to them: “Depart from me . . .” Let us therefore know that we are corrected in the present, so that we may rest in the future. Hence: “When we are chastened, we are corrected by the Lord, lest we be condemned with this world,” CXIII, 253, etc.

WERNER, abbot.—On the measure of loving God, CLVII, 834–861.

## Second commandment

“Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain. For the Lord will not hold guiltless him who has taken the name of the Lord his God in vain.”

ALGER OF LIÈGE, scholastic.—That a shameful promise should not be made, CLXXX, 864.

AUGUSTINE (Saint), bishop of Hippo.—On oaths, XXXIII, 184; On fulfilling an oath, XXXIII, 475; On a vow, XXXIV, 744; On oaths, XXXIV, 890; On a vow, XXXVI, 967; What a vow is, XXXVII, 1717; Thou shalt not take the name of thy God in vain, XXXVIII, 68; On the ten strings, XXXVIII, 75; Blasphemy must be avoided, XXXVIII, 457; On avoiding swearing, XXXVIII, 972; What swearing is, XXXVIII, 975; On swearing, XXXVIII, 1408; On a vow, XLV, 1860; Thou shalt not take the name of thy God in vain, XLVI, 948.

AUXILIUS, Frankish priest.—That an oath concerning an evil matter is not to be observed, CXXIX, 1085; That an oath, even one exacted by force, must be inviolably observed unless it entails sinning, ibid., 1101.

[Col. 0381] BEDE, the Venerable, priest.—On Herod’s oath, XCIV, 239.

BRUNO (Saint), abbot of Asti.—Thou shalt not take the name of God in vain, CLXIV, 278; on a vow, ibid., 459.

BURCHARD, bishop of Worms.—That the manifold confusion of oaths and perjuries, through which many souls of the faithful are known to have been lost, ought to be declared to all with care, as detestable and hateful to God. For this evil is so great that at the shrines of martyrs, where various infirmities are healed, perjurers, although they may not sometimes appear visibly tormented, are, by God’s just judgment, seized by demons. And, as St. Gregory says, the sick come to their bodies and are healed, while perjurers are tormented by demons, CXL, 875.

Just as one who does not speak cannot lie, so one who does not desire to swear cannot commit perjury. An oath must therefore be guarded against and used only in sheer necessity. To swear is not contrary to God’s commandment; but when we make a practice of swearing, we incur the crime of perjury. Therefore one who fears perjury never swears. Many, while speaking, always delight in swearing, although this alone ought to be in their mouths: “Yes, yes; no, no.” For whatever is beyond “yes” and “no” is from evil. Many commit perjury in order to deceive, so that by the credibility of the oath they may establish the credibility of their words; thus, while deceiving, they commit perjury and lie, and deceive an unwary person. Sometimes we are deceived by false tears and believe those who wept but ought not to have been believed.

Frequently we intend to speak without an oath, but are compelled to swear by the unbelief of those who do not believe what we say; and through such necessity we make swearing habitual. Many are slow to believe, and are not moved to faith by words. Those who compel persons speaking to them to swear commit a grave offence. By whatever verbal artifice a person swears, God, who is witness of conscience, nevertheless understands it as the person to whom the oath is sworn understands it. He will be guilty in two ways: both because he takes God’s name in vain and because he ensnares his neighbour by deceit. An oath by which evil is rashly promised is not to be kept—for example, if someone promises an adulteress a perpetual pledge of remaining with her. For it is more tolerable not to fulfil the oath than to remain in the shamefulness of fornication. To swear is that providence of God which has established that what is established should not be overturned . . . , etc., CXL, 877–884.

CHROMATIUS (Saint), bishop of Aquileia.—On oaths, XX, 352.

CYPRIAN (Saint), bishop of Carthage.—One must not swear, IV, 741; one must not curse, ibid.; One must never murmur, but must bless God in all that happens, IV, 742; What one has vowed to God must be promptly rendered, ibid., 752; The devil can do nothing to a human being unless God permits it, ibid., 772.

DEFENSOR, monk of Locociacum.—On oaths, LXXXVIII, 665.

DONATUS (Saint), bishop of Besançon.—That swearing is altogether unlawful, LXXXVIII, 285.

ERMENGAUD.—On oaths, CCIV, 1269.

GERHOH, the Venerable.—On oaths, CXCIII, 825.

GREGORY VII (Saint), pope.—Treatise on the discharge of oaths, CXLVIII, 1250.

HERVAEUS, archbishop of Reims.—On restraining perjuries, CXXXII, 704.

JEROME (Saint), priest.—On a vow, XXIII, 1052; One must not curse, ibid., 1100; One must swear only by God, XXVI, 40; On Herod’s oath, ibid., 97; He who swears and does not deceive, ibid., 855; On forbidding oaths, XXX, 369.

HILARY (Saint), bishop of Poitiers.—The practice of swearing removed from Christians, IX, 940.

HINCMAR, archbishop of Reims.—On oaths and perjuries, CXXV, 882.

GREGORY (Saint), bishop of Tours.—On perjurers, LXXI, 823.

HUGH OF ST VICTOR.—The second commandment is: “Thou shalt not take the name of thy God in vain.” And just as the first commandment pertains to the Father, so this one pertains to the Son. He takes the name of God in vain who believes that the Son of God is merely human. He takes it in vain who does not worship him, though he was made by him and redeemed by him. Hence he himself said: “You believe in God; believe also in me,” so that we may understand that he must be worshipped by us not only in the divinity through which he created, but also in the humanity through which he redeemed. Hence the prophet: “Worship his footstool.” For he who thus worships the humanity of Christ Jesus—that is, him who redeemed us in humanity—worships not a creature but the Creator, CLXXVI, 121.

HUGH OF ST VICTOR.—A vow is a certain attestation of a voluntary promise, more properly referred to God alone and to things belonging to God. For to vow is, by the attestation of a voluntary promise, to bind oneself to God and establish oneself as his debtor. One who promises simply pledges himself to do something; but one who vows calls witnesses to his promise and confirms that promise itself. Insofar as it is a promise, he is bound; insofar as it is an attestation, he is obligated. One kind of vow is hidden, directed to God and made before God; another is manifest, directed to God but made before human beings. A hidden vow broken is a sin. A manifest vow broken is both sin and scandal. In the first God is offended; in the second one also sins against one’s neighbour. But if you ask which vows must in every case be kept . . . , etc. . . ., CLXXVI, 521–524.—On vows, ibid., 519; On rendering vows, ibid., 1054.

HUMBERT, cardinal.—On rendering a vow, CXLIII, 1070.

INNOCENT III, pope.—On lawful and unlawful oaths, CCXVI, 1225; On a vow, ibid., 1257.

IVO (Saint), bishop of Chartres.—Everything that enters into covenants of peace then stands more firmly when the interposition of an oath strengthens it; and everything that unites the minds of friends then endures more faithfully when the bonds of an oath bind them. For whatever a witness confirms is established more truly when the addition of an oath affirms it. And if a witness is lacking, the mere pronouncement of an oath makes the good faith of the innocent person manifest, CLXI, 781.

An oath is not contrary to God’s commandment when it arises from the evil not of the swearer but of the unbelief of the person by whom he is compelled to swear. Hence it is understood that the Lord prohibited swearing in such a way that, insofar as a person can avoid it, he should not swear. Many do otherwise, keeping oaths in their mouths as though they were something great and sweet. Yet certainly the Apostle knew the Lord’s commandment and nevertheless swore. For those who do not regard these utterances as oaths are not to be heard. What, indeed, will they do with this: “I die daily, by your glory, brethren, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord”? The Greek copies prove that this is clearly an oath. Therefore the Apostle does not swear insofar as it lies in him, for he does not seek an oath through desire or delight in swearing. For whatever exceeds “yes, yes; no, no” is from evil, and thus arises from the weakness or unbelief of those who are otherwise moved to belief, CLXI, 781.

In the New Testament it was said that we should not swear at all. This, I think, was said not because swearing is a sin, but because perjury is a dreadful sin. He wished us to be far from it when he warned us not to swear at all. Although it was said, “Do not swear,” I do not remember reading anywhere in the Holy Scriptures, “Do not accept an oath from another,” CLXI, 781.

You do not do evil when you make good use of an oath, because—even though it is not good—it is necessary in order to persuade another of what you beneficially urge; but it is from the evil of the person through whose weakness you are compelled to swear, CLXI, 782.

Consider that the Saviour did not forbid swearing by God, but by heaven, earth, Jerusalem, and your head. And this had been allowed by the law, as it were, to little children: just as they sacrificed victims to God lest they sacrifice them to idols, so they were permitted to swear by God—not because they did this rightly, but because it was better to render this to God than to demons.

To swear is not contrary to God’s commandment; but when we make a practice of swearing, we incur the crime of perjury, CLXI, 782.

If swearing were a sin, neither would it have been said in the old law: “Thou shalt not commit perjury, but shalt render unto the Lord thy oath.” For sin would not be commanded to us . . . We do not tell you that we do not swear; for if we said so, we should lie. So far as concerns me, I swear, but, as it seems to me, compelled by great necessity. When I see that, unless I do so, I shall not be believed, and that what he does not believe is not beneficial to the person who does not believe me, then, weighing this rationale and considering it, I say with great fear: “Before God,” or “God is witness,” or “Christ knows that this is so in my mind.” And I see that this is more—that is, more than “yes, yes; no, no”—and, although it is not from the evil of the swearer, it is from the evil of the unbeliever, CLXI, 782.—And further matters, ibid., cols. 782–802. On oaths, ibid., 801.

JONAS, bishop of Orléans.—Since, as the Apostle James testifies, we all offend in many things, careless swearing is committed very grievously and pitiably among both orders, namely clerical and lay, indeed among both sexes, CVI, 221. On avoiding swearing, CVI, 221. On false witness, CVI, 225.

MARTIN (Saint), regular canon of León.—The second commandment pertains to the Son when it says: “Thou shalt not take the name of thy God in vain”; that is, do not think Christ, the Son of God, to be a creature, since every creature is subject to vanity; but believe him equal to the Father, God from God, the true Word with God, through whom all things were made, CCVIII, 782.

[Col. 0383] NICHOLAS I, pope.—You Bulgarians report that you had the custom, whenever you decided to bind someone by an oath in any matter, of bringing a sword into the midst, and that the oath was made upon it. But now you ask us to prescribe by whom you ought to swear. Before all else, we judge it unworthy to swear not only by a sword but by any created object whatsoever. For that by whom a person swears he surely both loves and venerates, and also entrusts his confidence to it with firm stability. Therefore one must swear by God, who is to be loved and venerated by human beings; in whom all hope and confidence must be placed; and from whom help, above all creatures, must always be expected. For when the Lord commands that one not swear by heaven, earth, one’s head, or Jerusalem, he undoubtedly forbids swearing by a creature.

But that we are commanded to swear by God’s name, we have learned from his own command. We may indeed swear only by those creatures which are assigned to divine worship, such as the temple and altar: one who swears by them swears by them and by him who dwells in them, and likewise with other things of that kind. Therefore it is right to swear by the Gospel, in which whatever is contained is recognized as nothing other than belonging to God, who is written and read therein. For it is our law, our testament, which the Lord and Redeemer, as lawgiver and testator, established for his elect. And if we love it, we also swear by it; for everyone who speaks truth swears by the one whom he loves. Therefore, if we swear by the Gospel, we show that we love both the testator and the testament itself, and undoubtedly signify that we do not wish to depart from its commandments . . ., CXIX, 1005.

OTHLONUS, monk.—What punishment awaits perjury, CXLVI, 366.

PASCHASIUS RADBERTUS, abbot of Corbie.—On oaths, CXIX, 253.

PETER, the Chanter.—On avoiding oaths, CCV, 322.

PETER COMESTOR.—“Thou shalt not take the name of thy God in vain”; that is, you shall not swear falsely, superfluously, or deceitfully by God’s name, nor, so far as lies in you, cause his honour to vanish by thinking wrongly of him, CXCVIII, 1165.

PETER DAMIAN (Saint), cardinal.—He who despises fulfilling a vow perishes unhappily, CXLV, 656, 1667. God’s name must not be taken in vain, CXLV, 1017.

PETER LOMBARD, archbishop of Paris.—Perjury is a lie confirmed by an oath. Here it is asked whether there is perjury where there is no lie. Some think so on the authority of St. Jerome, who says: “It must be observed that an oath has three companions: truth, judgment, and justice. If these are lacking, there will be not an oath but perjury. But where what is false is sworn, truth is lacking.” Therefore, if something false is sworn, even if there is no intention to deceive, it seems to be perjury because truth is lacking.

Others hold that there is no perjury where there is no lie; and just as a false statement is sometimes made without lying, so something false may be sworn without perjury. Perhaps the Apostle said something false when he promised that he would come to the Corinthians; nevertheless, he did not incur, as was alleged against him, the guilt of lying, because that was his intention. Even if he had confirmed it by an oath, he would not have incurred perjury, because, so far as depended upon him, he spoke truth; and, had he added an oath, so far as depended upon himself, he would have sworn truth, even though things turned out otherwise than he had said. Therefore, just as no one is a liar unless he thinks differently in his mind from what he says, whether the matter is so or not, so some hold that no one commits perjury unless he thinks differently in his mind from what he says, whether the matter is so or not, CXCII, 835.

He is also believed to commit perjury who swears falsely with intent to deceive; who swears what is true while thinking it false; and who swears what is false while thinking it true. Hence St. Augustine: “People swear falsely either when they deceive or when they are deceived. Either a person thinks that something false is true and swears rashly; or he knows or thinks it false and nevertheless swears it to be true, and thus swears wickedly.” The two perjuries he mentions differ. Suppose a man swears to what he thinks true; what he swears to he thinks true, yet it is false. This man does not commit perjury in his mind, but is deceived. He considers falsehood truth; he does not knowingly introduce an oath concerning something false. Give us another who knows something is false and swears it to be true when he knows it false—for example, to make this clear: it rains in that place; you ask a man, and he says that it has rained; and it is then raining there, but he thinks that it has not rained: he is a perjurer. It matters how the word proceeds from the mind; the tongue is not guilty unless the mind is guilty.

These points plainly teach that a person commits perjury in three ways, as we have said: either by knowingly swearing what is false, or by swearing what is true while thinking it false, or by swearing what is false while judging it true. But this last does not seem to be perjury, even though no perjury is incurred; because what is false is sworn, it does not seem to be perjury in the one who swears thus, since his mind is not guilty and therefore neither is his tongue. On the contrary, his mind is guilty when he presumes to swear to what he does not plainly perceive to be true. Therefore not every perjury is a lie, nor does everyone who commits perjury lie; but everyone who, while lying, swears commits perjury, and everyone who swears what is false, whether lying or not, commits perjury.

But when someone swears what is true while thinking it false, it is asked what the perjury there is. For the signification of his speech is true, since he unknowingly speaks the truth. Therefore the signification itself is neither false nor a lie, because it is true; and what is true does not seem to be perjury. To this we reply that to speak thus—that is, contrary to one’s mind, under the attestation of an oath—is perjury . . . , CXCII, 835–836.

If it is asked whether swearing is evil, we say that it is sometimes evil and sometimes not. To swear voluntarily and without necessity, or to swear falsely, is a grave sin. But to swear from necessity—for example, to establish one’s innocence, confirm covenants of peace, or persuade hearers of what is beneficial to them—is not evil, because it is necessary for them. Hence Augustine: An oath should be made in necessary matters, since people are slow to believe what is beneficial to them. An oath is not good; yet it is not evil when necessary. That is, it is not to be sought as good, nor is it to be avoided as evil when it is necessary.

For an oath is not contrary to God’s commandment; rather, it is understood that the Lord prohibited swearing in such a way that each person, insofar as it lies in him, should not swear. Many do otherwise, keeping an oath in their mouths as something evil yet sweet. The Apostle knew the Lord’s commandment and nevertheless swore. We are forbidden to swear from desire or delight in swearing. Therefore Christ’s saying in the Gospel, “I say unto you, do not swear at all,” is understood as commanding that no one seek an oath as a good thing and, through frequent swearing, slip into perjury.

But what he added, “Let your speech be, Yes, yes; No, no,” is good and to be desired. “Whatever is more is from evil”; that is, if you are compelled to swear, know that it comes from the necessity arising from the weakness of those whom you seek to persuade. That weakness is certainly evil. Hence we pray daily to be delivered, saying: “Deliver us from evil.” Therefore he did not say, “What is more is evil.” You do not do evil when you make good use of an oath; rather, it is from the evil of one who otherwise does not believe—from weakness, which is sometimes punishment, sometimes both punishment and fault. There the Lord forbade evil, commended good, and permitted what is necessary, CXCII, 836.

It is asked whether it is lawful to swear by creatures. This seems not to be so, since it is written in the Law: “Thou shalt render unto the Lord thy oaths,” and Christ commands in the Gospel, “Do not swear at all, neither by heaven, nor by earth, nor by Jerusalem, nor by thy head.” The Jews, as though little children, were permitted to swear by the Creator, and commanded that, if it happened that they swore, they should swear only by the Creator and not by a creature, because those swearing by angels and elements venerated creatures with honour; and it was better for this to be rendered to God than to creatures. Therefore he prohibited it to the weak; but he did not prohibit it to the saints, who venerated only the Creator in creatures. Hence Joseph swore by Pharaoh’s welfare, venerating God’s judgment in him who had been placed in the lowest place. But Christ prohibited swearing by creatures in order that either something divine should not be believed to exist in them, for which reverence would be owed them, or that people swearing falsely by them should not think themselves bound by an oath, CXCII, 836.

It is asked what it means to say, “I swear by God.” It means to call God as witness. For the Apostle swore when he said: “God is my witness,” as if he had said, “By God, it is so.” Hence Augustine: “It is ridiculous to think this: if you say ‘By God,’ you swear; if you say ‘God is my witness,’ you do not swear. For what is ‘By God’ except ‘God is my witness’? Or what is ‘God is my witness’ except ‘By God’?” What is swearing, moreover, except rendering right to God when you swear by God—the right, namely, of truth and not of falsehood?

Likewise: behold, I say to your charity that one who swears falsely by a stone is a perjurer, because he calls as witness not the stone, which does not hear, but its Creator. Therefore, to swear by any creature is to call its Creator as witness. There is also a most serious kind of oath, made by imprecation, as when someone says: “If I did that, may I suffer this,” or “may this happen to my children.” In this way we understand also what is sometimes meant when someone swearing says: “By my health,” or “By my children,” and the like. For he binds this to God, CXCII, 837.

On those who swear by false gods, CXCII, 837.

It must be considered whether every oath must be fulfilled. For if someone has sworn something to another contrary to faith and charity, whose observance leads to a worse outcome, it should be changed rather than fulfilled. Hence Ambrose: “It is sometimes contrary to one’s duty to God to fulfil a promised oath,” as Herod did. Likewise Isidore: “In evil promises, break faith; in a shameful vow, change your resolution. Do not do what you have vowed rashly; a promise fulfilled through wickedness is impious.” The same: “An oath by which evil is rashly promised is not to be kept—for example, if someone promises an adulteress a perpetual pledge of remaining with her. For it is more tolerable not to fulfil the oath than to remain in fornication.” Likewise Bede: “If we happen to have sworn something incautiously whose observance leads to a worse outcome, let us know that it may freely be changed for a more salutary course of action” . . . , CXCII, 837–838.

“Thou shalt not take the name of thy God in vain,” which literally means: You shall not swear God’s name for nothing. Allegorically, however, it commands that you should not think Christ, the Son of God, a creature, since every creature is subject to vanity, but equal to the Father, CXCII, 831.

On perjury, CXCII, 835.—On a vow, CXCII, 932.

PETER OF POITIERS.—On perjury and the kinds of oaths, CCXI, 1157.

PROSPER (Saint) OF AQUITAINE.—On making a vow to God, LI, 429, 435, 503.

RABANUS MAURUS, abbot of Fulda.—On fulfilling a vow, CVIII, 568, 791. Oaths must be guarded against, CIX, 917.

RODULF, bishop of Bourges.—On perjury, CXIX, 721.

RUFINUS, priest of Aquileia.—On the good of an oath observed, XXI, 696. On a vow, XXI, 958.

RUPERT, abbot of Deutz.—To take God’s name in vain—as poets do—or not to consider it worthy of reverence wherever the Lord’s name is invoked, is altogether contrary to the love of God, CLXVII, 681.

On a vow, CLXVIII, 1243.

Thus stands the second commandment: “Thou shalt not make a graven image, nor any likeness which is in heaven above, or which is on the earth below, or of those things which are in the waters beneath the earth; thou shalt not worship or serve them.” Through this commandment the following is required of the servant: that he should suppose no likeness whatsoever to exist, in heaven, on earth, or in the sea, of that one and only God before whom he ought to have no strange gods.

This, I say, is required of him: that he should know that the true God is circumscribed by no form. Those who held God to be human-shaped imagined him as bounded or defined, like a human being, by limbs according to human form, painting in their minds a great idol, or, in accordance with Daniel’s vision, a venerable old man or the Ancient of Days. What an image, do you suppose, was fashioned in their hearts or error when they heard him say: “Heaven is my throne, and the earth my footstool”? If they were asked about what is written—“Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand and weighed the heavens with his palm?”—what could they answer or conceive in their minds according to the same fantasy?

Therefore, as has been said, this is required of the servant by the commandment: that he confess God to be without place and uncircumscribed, and suppose that no creature is or can become like God, lest he experience against himself the following saying: “For I am the Lord thy God, strong, jealous, visiting the iniquities of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation.” For one who has painted such an idol for himself stores up great wrath from the strong and jealous God, since he consequently thinks wrongly of the Son of God . . . But if a person desires to be a friend, after this commandment he extends his whole mind also toward counsel: namely, that he should not be content merely not to think thus concerning God, but should strive as far as possible for the salvation of others, showing by sound doctrine that not according to bodily . . . , CLXVII, 1721–1722.

TERTULLIAN, priest of Carthage.—On blasphemy, I, 681. On reverence for God’s name, I, 691.

VALERIAN, bishop of Cimiez.—On promises made and not fulfilled, LII, 702.

VICTOR, bishop of Capua.—On oaths, LXVIII, 269.

ZACHARIAS, bishop of Chrysopolis.—On oaths, CLXXXVI, 132.

WALTER, bishop of Orléans.—On avoiding oaths, CXIX, 736.

## Third commandment

“Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day. Six days shalt thou labour and do all thy works. But the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord thy God; thou shalt do no work therein, thou and thy son and thy daughter, thy manservant and thy maidservant, thy beast and the stranger who is within thy gates. For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth and sea and all things that are in them, and rested on the seventh day. Therefore the Lord blessed the Sabbath day and sanctified it.”

ALCUIN, abbot.—On the Lord’s Day, CI, 1226.

AMBROSE (Saint), bishop of Milan.—Rebuke of the people for not attending church, XVII, 689.

AUGUSTINE (Saint), bishop of Hippo.—On Sabbath rest, XXXIII, 212. On Sabbath observance, XXXIV, 305. On praising God, XXXVI, 309. Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day, XXXVIII, 69, 75. On those who attend church rarely, XXXIX, 1755. On the Lord’s Day, XXXIX, 2274; XLI, 355; XLV, 1868. On the true Sabbath, XLV, 1882; XLIV, 950.

AUNARIUS (Saint), bishop.—On observance of the Lord’s Day, LXXII, 764.

BEDE, the Venerable.—The third commandment concerning the Sabbath pertains to the Holy Spirit, by whose gift eternal rest is promised to us. For because the Spirit is called holy, he likewise sanctified the seventh day. For in the other days no sanctification of works is mentioned except on the Sabbath, where it is said: “God rested.” Therefore this commandment pertains to the Holy Spirit, both because of the name of sanctification and because of eternal rest, which belongs to the gift of the Holy Spirit. For it says there: “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day. Six days shalt thou labour and do all thy works; but the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord thy God.”

In the work of the six days is contained the activity of six thousand years; but in the seventh is shown the rest of that blessed time of the kingdom, which the Jews sinfully observe in a carnal manner. We do not fit this to faith in the deception of a lie. God cries through the prophet: “My soul has hated your new moons and Sabbaths.” How, then, were those Sabbaths sanctified which the Lord hated? Therefore that is the sanctified Sabbath in which, after the good works of this life, eternal rest is promised to us. Consequently, whatever we do, if we do it for the rest of the age to come, we truly observe the Sabbath, XCIII, 374.

On the Sabbath, XCIV, 85.

BERNARD (Saint), abbot of Clairvaux.—On the reverence owed to holy places, CLXXXIII, 535.

BRUNO (Saint), abbot of Asti.—Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day, CLXIV, 279.

CANUTE I, king of the English.—On Sunday we strictly forbid commerce, every gathering of the people unless there is the greatest necessity, and hunting; and on this holy day all worldly works must diligently cease, CLI, 1175.

EUGYPPIUS, abbot.—On the rest of the Sabbath, LXII, 685.

GAUDENTIUS (St.), bishop of Brescia.—On the Sabbath, XX, 920.

JEROME (St.), presbyter.—On the benefits of fulfilling the Sabbath, XXIV, 540. On the manner of observing the Sabbath, XXIV, 573. “My house [shall be] a house of prayer,” XXVI, 150.

HUGH OF ST VICTOR.—The third commandment pertains to the Holy Spirit. “To observe the Sabbath day” means: await rest through the goodness of God, that is, through the Holy Spirit, CLXXXVI, 122, 354.

JONAS, bishop of Orléans.—For this reason we earnestly beseech you that, in observing the Lord’s Day—on which God created the light of the world, on which the Author of life rose from the dead, and on which he also sent the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, from heaven to the apostles—you give the due care which we formerly begged you to give when admonishing your father, and render to so great a day the honour owed to it: namely, that you free yourselves, as far as possible, from cares and worldly anxieties; that you yourselves do what is fitting for reverence toward so great a day; and that, by your example, you instruct and teach your people both to do this and to put it into practice, CVI, 303.—On observing the Lord’s Day, ibid., 304.

MARTIN (St.), regular canon of León.—The third commandment concerns the Sabbath and pertains to the Holy Spirit, by whose gift everlasting rest in heaven is promised to us. For because he is called Spirit, the Lord also sanctified the seventh day. For sanctification is not named in connection with works on the other days, but only on the Sabbath, where it says: “God rested from all his work.” Therefore this commandment pertains to the Holy Spirit both because of the name of sanctification and because of the eternal rest belonging to the gift of the Holy Spirit. For it says there: “Remember the Sabbath day,” etc. The work of six thousand years is contained in the six days of work. But in the seventh is shown the rest and time of that blessed kingdom, which the Jews sinfully celebrate in a carnal manner, CCVIII, 782.

HUMBERT, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church.—The Church, sharing the suffering of the Lord who suffered and was buried, rejoices with him in his resurrection on the Lord’s Day; whereas overwhelming sorrow seized the Jews, and the guards of the tomb attempted to corrupt [others] with money. Therefore, retaining to this day the apostolic tradition concerning the Sabbath, and wishing to retain it until the end, we have taken care to set down here what our ancient and venerable Fathers thought and confirmed on this matter. Among their number the most blessed Pope Sylvester, spiritual father of the Emperor Constantine the Great, said among other things:

> “If every Lord’s Day is to be observed in the joy of Christians because of the Resurrection, then every Sabbath day must be assigned to the execration of the Jews because of the burial. For all the Lord’s disciples mourned on the Sabbath, sighing for their buried Lord, while the Jews rejoiced in gladness. But sorrow ruled while the apostles fasted. Therefore let us grieve with those who grieve at the Lord’s burial, if we wish to rejoice with them at his resurrection. For it is not lawful for us to observe, in the Jewish manner, the abstinence from food and ceremonies of the Jews.”

In agreement with this judgment, St Pope Innocent says:

> “The clearest reasoning shows that one must fast on the Sabbath. For if we observe the Lord’s Day not only at Easter because of reverence for the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, but also, more frequently, in every week as an image of that day, and if we fast on Friday because of the Lord’s Passion, we must not pass over the Sabbath, which appears enclosed between the sorrow and joy of that time. It is certainly established that during those two days the apostles were in mourning and hid themselves out of fear of the Jews. Nor is there any doubt of it; and it is reported that they fasted so strictly on those two days that the Church’s tradition has it that the sacraments are not celebrated at all during that two-day period. This pattern must certainly be observed every week, for which reason the remembrance of that day is always to be kept.
>
> “But if you think that one must fast once only, on a single Sabbath, then the Lord’s Day and Friday likewise are surely to be observed only once at Easter. But if the image of the Lord’s Day and Friday is to be renewed in every week, it is madness to maintain the customary observance of the two days while omitting the Sabbath, since it has a cause no different from Friday: namely, the day on which the Lord suffered, when he was among the dead below, so that, rising on the third day, he might restore joy after the preceding sorrow of two days. Thus we do not deny that one must fast on Friday; but we say that this must be done on the Sabbath, since both days imposed sorrow upon the apostles and those who followed Christ. Refreshed on the Lord’s Day, they wished not only that day itself to be most festive, but also judged that it should be observed throughout all the weeks . . .”

CXLIII, 936–937.

You pitiable Jews observe the Sabbath carnally, and yet are wholly ignorant of what the Sabbath is. You would observe it well if you understood it spiritually. Thus you appropriate the name of Sabbath because you observe it not spiritually but carnally. You delight in keeping the Law carnally, though you ought to understand it spiritually, as the Lord testifies through the prophet: “I will open my mouth in parables . . .” and “Our fathers have told us . . .” The fathers of the Old Testament—that is, the patriarchs and prophets—have therefore narrated these things to us. If, then, the Law and the Prophets consist in parables and enigmas, as you cannot at all deny, the observance of the Sabbath must be understood not carnally but spiritually. For its carnal periods of rest have been entirely annulled both by the Lord and by the Fathers.

We read in Genesis that God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because on it he had ceased from all the work that he had done. Yet he is not said to have created anything new on that day, unless one should say that he completed the work on the seventh day, which he blessed and sanctified. For, as Master Peter says, blessing and sanctification are a work; Solomon too performed a work when he dedicated the Temple. Thus God is said to have sanctified and blessed the seventh day because he granted it a mystical blessing and sanctification above the others. Hence the Law says: “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day.”

Again, if it is a crime not to observe Sabbath rest, tell us why Joshua, Moses’ disciple and successor, at the Lord’s command led forth the army and its arms for seven successive days—among which, of course, the Sabbath was included—and, while the ark went round and trumpets sounded, overthrew the walls of Jericho. What again shall I say concerning the Maccabees, of whom it is written: “The Jews were unwilling on the Sabbath day to avenge themselves upon the foreigners; but afterward, having received counsel, they fought on the Sabbath day and triumphed over their enemies”? By these testimonies we are taught that this elementary Sabbath day does not pertain to faith, but another, spiritual Sabbath does.

Know, therefore, O Jews, that this carnal Sabbath was given not for purification but for testing, as the Lord says in Deuteronomy: “I shall give them commandments, that I may test them whether they will walk [Col. 0388] in my ways or not.” Hence the Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, saying: “I gave them commandments that were not good, and judgments by which they would not live.” Certainly this is because certain carnal things were permitted to you, O Jews, living carnally; yet these ceased with the coming of the Gospel, as the prophet Ezekiel says: “I will make all her joy and her Sabbaths cease”—that is, those of the Israelite people.

I ask you, O Jews: if your Sabbaths are eternal, why did the Lord command that they cease? And if they are good, why did he hate them? But because you can make no answer at all to so evident and subtle a judgment, by God’s grace preceding, accompanying, and following me, I shall explain it to you briefly and carefully, CCVIII, 1335–1336.

These are the Apostle’s words: “That which is spiritual is not first, but that which is animal.” The first man begot us according to the flesh; the second man—namely Jesus Christ, God and man—made us spiritual children of God through the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit. Therefore, O Jews, while you were unformed in knowledge and living carnally, God first gave you carnal commandments; yet they were not to remain forever, because he foreknew that you would sin and worship idols. You needed milk, not solid food; for you were not yet able—and indeed even now you are not able. Thus it was not fitting, while you were still unformed and infants in the knowledge of God, to set pearls before you—that is, to deliver spiritual sacraments—but rather to test or try you through the burdens of the Law.

Had you persevered in those commandments according to his good pleasure, he would have transferred you, together with the other children of the Church, to the spiritual sacraments of the Gospel and adopted you as spiritual children. Thus God’s good commandments became condemnatory to you because of your sins demanding it, and hateful to God. God’s commandment saves those who obey it and condemns those who disobey it. For *Sabbath* means “rest.” But you spend this idle Sabbath festival in feasting and drunkenness.

But perhaps someone says: If the Sabbath is not to be kept, why was it said among God’s commandments: “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day? . . .” The answer is that the works of the six days signify the works of six thousand years. For a thousand years are compared with one day before God . . . The Sabbath of these days, therefore, is the time of the seventh thousandth year and the rest of the kingdom and age to come, where there will no longer be any activity of affairs, but only the rest of the saints; for the Lord hates these temporal Sabbaths . . . He rightly said “your Sabbaths,” because they are no longer those which the Lord himself commanded, but those which you devised for yourselves, in which you might devote yourselves more abundantly to feasting and drunkenness . . .

The Lord’s Day, says Isidore, doctor of the Spaniards, was decreed by the holy apostles to be celebrated with religious solemnity because on that day our Redeemer rose from the dead. It is called the Lord’s Day so that, abstaining on it from earthly works and the enticements of the world, we may serve God alone in worship, giving this day honour and reverence because of the hope of our resurrection which we have in it. For just as our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ rose from the dead on the third day, so we hope that we too shall rise on the last day. Hence on the Lord’s Day we pray standing, which is a sign of the life to come. This is done by the whole Church, which is established in this pilgrimage of mortality, awaiting at the end of the age that which was prefigured in the body of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the firstborn of the dead, CCVIII, 1336–1338.

MAXIMUS (St.), bishop of Turin.—On the Sabbath, LVII, 516, 527, 717.

NICHOLAS I, pope.—You wish to know whether anyone may perform any labour on the Sabbath or the Lord’s Day. On this matter St Pope Gregory, addressing the Romans, says:

> “It has come to me that certain men of perverse spirit have sown among you some erroneous doctrines contrary to the holy faith, so that they forbid work of any kind on the Sabbath day. What else should I call them but preachers of Antichrist, who, when he comes, will cause both the Sabbath day and the Lord’s Day to be observed free from all work? For, because he will pretend to die and rise again, he wishes the Lord’s Day to be held in reverence; and because he compels the people to Judaize, in order to restore the outward rite of the Law and subject them to the faithlessness of the Jews, he wishes the Sabbath to be observed.
>
> “For the command spoken through the prophet, ‘Do not bring burdens through your gates on the Sabbath day,’ could be maintained as long as it was lawful to keep the Law according to the letter. But after the grace of almighty God, our Lord Jesus Christ, appeared, the commandments of the Law which were spoken figuratively cannot be kept according to the letter. For whoever says that this must be observed regarding the Sabbath must also say that carnal sacrifices must still be offered; he must say that the command concerning circumcision of the body must still be retained. But let him hear the Apostle Paul speaking against him: ‘If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing.’
>
> “Therefore, what was said of the Sabbath we have understood spiritually and keep spiritually. For Sabbath means rest; and we have as the true Sabbath our Redeemer himself, the Lord Jesus Christ. Whoever knows the light of his faith, if the sin of lust draws his mind through the eyes, brings burdens through the gates on the Sabbath day. Therefore we do not bring burdens through the gates on the Sabbath day if, established in the grace of our Redeemer, we do not draw the weights of sin into the soul through the bodily senses. For the same Lord and our Redeemer is read to have done many things on the Sabbath day, so that he rebuked the Jews, saying: ‘Which of you does not untie his ox or ass on the Sabbath day and lead it to water?’ If Truth itself commanded that the Sabbath not be kept according to the letter, whoever observes Sabbath rest according to the letter of the Law contradicts none other than Truth itself.”

But on the Lord’s Day one must abstain from earthly work and apply oneself altogether to prayer, so that what is negligently done during the six days may be expiated through the day of the Lord’s resurrection, CXIX, 984–985.

PETER COMESTOR.—“You shall not commit adultery,” that is, you shall not have sexual relations with anyone apart from the bond of marriage, CXCVIII, 1165.

“Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day,” that is, hold it sacred and as a holiday. “You shall not do any work on it, you and your son and your daughter, nor your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your beast, nor the stranger who is near your gates”—that is, serving with you in your household—because “God rested on the seventh day”; and we observe the seventh day, though not this one which they observe. For Josephus likewise says: “The fourth discourse concerns the keeping of the weeks, when they were to refrain from all work”; therefore we say that this must be understood of servile work, CXCVIII, 1165.

PETER DAMIAN (St.), cardinal.—“Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day,” CXLV, 1017.

PETER LOMBARD, bishop of Paris.—The third commandment is: “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day,” where, according to the letter, observance of the Sabbath is commanded. Allegorically, however, it commands that you await rest—here from vices, and hereafter in the contemplation of God—from the Holy Spirit, that is, from charity and God’s gift. This does not mean that the Holy Spirit accomplishes this without the Father and the Son. The Church has indeed received this gift: that remission of sins should occur in the Holy Spirit. Although the Trinity accomplishes this remission, it is nevertheless said properly to belong to the Holy Spirit because he is the Spirit of the adoption of children, the love and bond, or communion, of the Father and the Son. Therefore our justification and rest are quite often attributed to him, CXCII, 831.
