PROSPER (St.) of Aquitaine.—On the Sabbath, LI, 442, 468, 477, 524.

RABANUS MAURUS, abbot of Fulda.—On the Lord’s Day, CVII, 108, 335, 443. Homily on the days of the Lord, CX, 76.

RODULPHUS, bishop of Bourges.—The apostles decreed that the Lord’s Day be observed with religious solemnity because on that day our Redeemer rose from the dead. It is therefore called the Lord’s Day, so that, abstaining on it from earthly works and from the enticements of the world, we may serve God alone in worship. For just as our Lord Jesus Christ and Saviour rose from the dead on the third day, so we hope that we too shall rise in the final age. Hence we also pray standing on the Lord’s Day; this is a sign of the resurrection to come . . .

The Lord’s Day, moreover, has been celebrated by Christians since the Lord’s resurrection, and from then began to have its festal character. Therefore the observance of this day ought to be so great that, apart from prayers, the solemnities of the Mass, and things pertaining to eating, nothing else should be done: that is, neither servile works should be performed on it, nor should men engage in country labour, cultivate vineyards, plough fields, reap harvests, cut hay, set hedges, clear woods, cut down trees, work in stone, build houses, make a garden, move earth, attend judicial assemblies, or hunt, except only from necessity of food or cold.

Likewise women should not perform textile work, make garments, sew, wash clothing, anoint [them], beat flax, presume to card wool, or shear sheep, so that in every way the rest of good people may be rendered on the Lord’s Day. For it is the first day of the world. On it the elements of the world were formed; on it the angels were created; on it manna was given from heaven; on it the Redeemer of humankind rose from the dead; on it the Holy Spirit descended upon the disciples . . . , CXIX, 716.

RUPERT, abbot of Deutz.—“Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day.” This commandment is lawful, and it is lawfully observed when a servant, in doing good work, seeks not his own glory but that of his Lord; seeks neither present praise for himself from the mouths of his fellow servants [Col. 0390] nor proposes to establish vain glory for his own name, but attends to Scripture, which says: “Let them see your good works,” not that you may be seen, but “that they may glorify your Father who is in heaven.” This indeed is to remember to sanctify the Sabbath: that is, for the servant to direct his purpose toward deserving, through good works, to enter into his Lord’s rest.

But we no longer regard the remembrance of that Sabbath which the Jew still remembers today as a commandment; indeed, we confess it to be contrary to the commandment and to the Lord’s will, because that Sabbath was defiled by wicked servants with the blood of their Lord from that great Sabbath day on which, as it approached, they crucified the Lord; and from then the Lord’s soul hates every Sabbath and every feast of theirs with profound hatred. Thus this is the commandment, “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day”: that is, in working well, establish the entire end of your work there where rest is holy and true.

But this is counsel: that even now you “keep Sabbath” (*sabbatizes*), that is, rising beyond the active life, devote yourself to contemplation. This part is so much better as sweet friendship surpasses the relation of a faithful servant, as the Lord himself testifies when he says: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious . . .” He did not rebuke Martha’s service, but preferred Mary’s part as that which is best to what is good . . . , CLXVII, 1223–1224.

The Law of the carnal Sabbath was also holy, just, and good. For just as the sign of circumcision foretold the Incarnation, and the sacrifice of the paschal Lamb the future Passion of the same only-begotten Son of God, so that Sabbath observance proclaimed the rest laid up after this life for the saints and elect, where God rests in the light of his wisdom; and he has prepared that rest itself for them as a reward.

But the spiritual person strives to keep Sabbath not on one day of the week but at all times, always attentive to the Word of God, in accordance with the Psalmist, who speaks of this Sabbath—or rather, through whom speaks the Lord of Sabbaths himself: “Be still,” he says, “and see that I am God.” Be still, therefore, from the actions of the world, and in holy and quiet study see that the Lord is God: this is the beginning of that Sabbath which we call the contemplative life, and which Truth itself testifies to be the best part: “Mary,” he says, “has chosen the best part, which shall not be taken from her.” Knowing that its sweetness already breathes gently upon those who love it in the present life, the same Lord elsewhere says: “Come to me, all,” etc., CLXVII, 263–264.

To do something good not for the praise of God or in hope of eternal recompense, but in order to be seen by people, is contrary to the love of God. He therefore says: “Remember to sanctify the day of Sabbaths,” that is, in all your works attend to God’s recompense, or prepare rest for yourself in God as a reward. This truly is to sanctify the Sabbath day; for these things were said concerning the carnal Sabbath observance of the Jews, namely that these . . .

“You shall not take the name of your God in vain.” A servant necessarily hears and obeys this, if he does not wish to be cruelly tortured with servile blows or killed. For what is it to take the name of the Lord his God, except to swear falsely by the name of his God, or to make a display of the name reverenced by heaven and earth in trivial or playful matters? Therefore not to take the name of one’s God in vain is a necessary and lawful commandment; if a servant keeps it, he escapes punishment, so far as this can be understood under that intention: “For the Lord will not hold guiltless him who takes the name of his God in vain.”

But if he desires the free status of a friend, it is counsel not to swear at all. For that Lord and Angel of Great Counsel says in the Gospel: “You have heard that . . . You shall not swear falsely . . . but I say to you, do not swear at all . . .” We are compelled to acknowledge that this is not a commandment but counsel grounded upon the commandment stated above, because we do not suppose that the holy, good, and just Law is contrary to the Gospel, or the Gospel to the Law; indeed, we avoid even suspecting this as impiety . . . , CLVII, 1722–1723.

THEODULF, bishop of Orléans.—On observing the Lord’s Day, CV, 198.

## Fourth Commandment

“Honour your father and your mother, that you may be long-lived upon the land which the Lord your God will give you.”

ABSALON, abbot.—On obedience, CCXI, 175, 232.

ADALGER, monk.—On obedience, CXXXIV, 918.

ADAM THE SCOT, monk.—On obedience, CXCVIII, 251.

ALAN OF LILLE, doctor.—On obedience, CCX, 144.

ALGER, scholastic of Liège.—One must not obey in evil, CLXXX, 869.

AMBROSE (St.), bishop of Milan.—Parental affection and filial gratitude ought to be equal, XIV, [Col. 0391] 645. “Honour your father and mother,” XV, 1787. Exhortation to parents to encourage their children toward virginity, XVII, 198. On the disobedience of children, XVII, 62. On obedience toward authorities, XVII, 162. On the obedience of servants, XVII, 407. The response of submission in the book *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*, XVII, 1061.

ANSELM (St.), archbishop of Canterbury.—On obedience, CLVIII, 1017, 1135; CLIX, 606, 658.

ATTO, bishop of Vercelli.—“Render to Caesar,” etc., CXXXIV, 260. “Children, obey,” etc., CXXXIV, 581.

It is no slight matter to assail royal majesty, even if it appears unjust in some respect. For it is God’s ordinance; it is God’s dispensation. It is profane to violate what God ordains. For the Lord says through Moses: “You shall not curse the ruler of your people.” Since it is not even lawful to curse him, it is plainly evident that it is not lawful to persecute him either. And through blessed David: “Do not touch my anointed ones.” How gently David himself observed this is clear.

Certainly Saul had already been rejected by God himself because of his arrogance; David himself had already been anointed king by divine grace. Yet when Saul came into David’s power in the cave, David’s servants said to him: “Behold, the day of which the Lord spoke to you: ‘I shall give your enemy into your hand, that you may do to him as seems good in your eyes.’” David therefore arose and silently cut off the hem of Saul’s cloak [lacuna]. Although he did not at all doubt Saul’s rejection or his own election, and although Saul pursued him until he was confined in the innermost part of the cave, he nevertheless refused to stretch out his hand against him, but waited for divine judgment. And afterward he repented even that he had cut off merely the hem of Saul’s cloak [lacuna].

“Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s.” This must be understood as referring not only to payment of tribute, but to the reverence of all honour due. Even when he himself was pressed by tax collectors to pay, he did not deign to make payment, but said to Peter: “Go to the sea,” etc. Thus Peter himself, instructed by so great a Master’s teaching, exhorts the Church in every way to preserve obedience toward kings. For he says: “Fear God, honour the king,” [lacuna], CXXXIV, 96–97.

AUGUSTINE (St.), bishop of Hippo.—Obedience and disobedience, XXXIV, 377. On reverence toward parents, XXXIV, 704, 809, 950, 969. On parents’ duties toward children, XXXIV, 964. Higher authorities must be obeyed, XXXV, 2083; XXXVIII, 109. “Honour your father,” XXXVIII, 69, 75, 603; XL, 1248, 1262, 1344. Jesus’ obedience, XXXVIII, 343. Mary’s obedience, XXXIX, 2104. On love for parents, XXXIX, 2264; XL, 1054, 1080. “Honour your father,” XLXI, 950.

BEDE the Venerable.—After the first three commandments comes the sevenfold number of commandments pertaining to love of neighbour, and it begins with honouring parents, although this is fourth in order: “Honour your father and your mother.” For a person opens his eyes through his parents, and this life takes its beginning from love for them; therefore this commandment is first among the seven, just as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Honour your father . . . This is the first commandment.” But how is it first when it is fourth, except because it was spoken of in the sevenfold number? For, since it pertains to the love of neighbour, it is first on the second tablet. For this is why the two tablets of the Law were given.

Therefore, in this commandment children are ordered to honour their parents, not to behave contemptuously toward them, but to render them the reverence due through the duty of filial devotion. For one who does not know how to show honour to parents—whom will he be able to spare, if he hates his own people? XCIII, 374. On obedience, XCIV, 67.

BENEDICT (St.), father of monks.—On obedience, LXVI, 221, 349.

BERNARD (St.), abbot of Clairvaux.—On obedience, CLXXXII, 868; CLXXXIII, 60, 542. On the virtue of obedience and its seven degrees, CLXXXIII, 653.

BRUNO (St.), founder of the Carthusians.—On obedience toward authorities, CLIII, 105, 153, 563. On obedience toward parents, CLIII, 347.

BRUNO (St.), abbot of Asti.—“Honour your father,” CLXIV, 280. On obedience, CLXV, 933.

CASSIAN, presbyter of Marseilles.—On obedience, XLIX, 162, 183.

CASSIODORUS, senator and abbot.—Faith is to be kept with the king, LXIX, 807.

COLUMBANUS (St.), abbot.—On obedience, LXXX, 888.

CYPRIAN (St.), bishop of Carthage.—Parents must be obeyed, IV, 770. Fathers ought not to be harsh toward their children, IV, 771. On servants toward masters, and conversely, IV, 771.

DEFENSOR, monk.—On honouring parents, LXXXVIII, 685. On children, ibid., 687.

GILBERT OF HOILAND, abbot.—Readiness in obedience is commended, CLXXXIV, [Col. 0392] 570. On obedience, CLXXXIV, 799.

GREGORY THE GREAT (St.), pope.—On obedience, LXXVI, 765. On the obedience owed to a tribune, LXXVII, 565. On the obedience owed to a bishop, LXXVII,

HAYMO, bishop of Halberstadt.—On honouring parents, CXIX, 717.

HERVEUS, monk.—On obedience, CLXXXI, 774.

JEROME (St.), presbyter of Stridon.—“Honour your father and mother,” XXV, 105. Obedience toward parents, XXVI, 537. Servants toward masters, XXVI, 541. A good example must be set for children by parents, XXXVI, 582. Higher authorities must be obeyed, XXVI, 590. On honouring parents, XXX, 145. On obedience, ibid., 321. On obedience toward prelates, 398.

HILDEGARD (St.), abbess.—On obedience, CXCVII, 339.

HUGH OF ST VICTOR.—The first commandment of the second tablet concerns the earthly father, just as the first commandment of the first tablet concerns the heavenly Father. It is this: “Honour your father and your mother, that you may be long-lived upon the land.” Honour them in matters that are not contrary to God Most High, obeying them and assisting them, as far as you can, in their needs. “That you may be long-lived upon the land,” namely, the land of the living, CLXXVI, 122, 352–353.

On obedience, CLXXVI, 919. To whom obedience should be rendered, CLXXVII, 581. On fivefold obedience, ibid., 841.

INNOCENT III, pope.—On obedience, CCXVII, 1150.

JOHN OF SALISBURY, bishop of Chartres.—The reverence that is rendered bodily consists either in persons or in things. The consideration of persons, however, arises from nature, office, character, condition, or fortune. By nature we venerate parents and children, and those whom flesh has joined to us—for example, a wife, blood relatives, and relatives by marriage. Hence this has been accepted also by the law of the Gentiles, because it occurs equally among all peoples. We are compelled to it also by divine law, since we know what is written: “Honour your father,” etc. . . . It was not necessary to commend children very much, because “no one ever hated his own flesh”; nor wife either, on account of whom a man leaves father and mother, cleaving to “his wife,” so that “the two are one flesh.” Yet the commands of the divine Law are not lacking in this respect. Although they are more rarely introduced because the prompting of nature, which presses sufficiently, requires them, they nevertheless extend to blood relatives and relations by marriage, whom nature itself commends. Office is the obligation to perform what each person must do by institutions or customs. For from this, acts proper to each individual are fitting . . .

But we, upon whom truth has shone from heaven, believe that great reverence must be shown not to gods, who do not exist, but to the ministers and friends of the true God; and at times also to his enemies, because he himself commanded this, who often granted great power over his own people to very wicked men for their instruction. Hence: “Be subject,” etc., CXCIX, 514–551.

JONAS, bishop of Orléans.—There are many who love their children more spiritually than carnally, and others who love them more carnally than spiritually. Likewise, some urge them to learn the law of heaven more than that of the world, while others, to the contrary, urge them to learn the laws of the world more than those of heaven. There are also some who teach them to aspire more to heavenly than to earthly things, and, to the contrary, others who teach them to aspire more to earthly than to heavenly things. Therefore let those who love their children carnally and strive to instruct them in the laws of the world rather than in heavenly laws hear what the Lord says in Deuteronomy: [lacuna] “Let them therefore imitate blessed Job, whose diligence in educating his children was such that he not only made them outwardly perfect in deed and speech, but even cleansed their hearts by the offering of sacrifice [lacuna] Let them also attend to David instructing his son Solomon [lacuna] Let them attend also to Tobit, [lacuna] CVI, 192–194.

St Ambrose says: We are taught what the affection of parents and the gratitude of children ought to be; but paternal love itself often harms children unless it maintains moderation, whether by excessive indulgence it relaxes discipline for wrongdoing, or by preferring one child it turns the others away from brotherly affection. More is gained for the child for whom love of brothers is gained. This is the more illustrious generosity of fathers; this is the richer inheritance of children. Let equal favour unite children whom equal nature has joined. Filial affection knows no monetary gain where there is loss of filial affection. Why are you surprised if quarrels arise between brothers over an estate or a house, when envy flared among the holy sons of Jacob over a tunic? What then? Is Jacob to be reproved because he preferred one to the others? Yet we cannot take away from parents the freedom to love more those whom they believe deserve more, nor should we cut off from children the effort to please more. In short, Jacob loved him more in whom he foresaw greater marks of virtue.

Some parents exhort their children only with gentle words and are not deterred by the example of the priest Eli, who restrained his children only in words and shrank from striking them with the strictest severity. But many parents neglect to correct their children with blows toward good conduct while they are still at a slippery age. Once they have reached an age of understanding and begun to devote themselves to evil works, they cannot easily be restrained from evil by parental discipline. There can be no doubt that their sins are imputed to those parents who were unwilling to discipline them in their tender age, CVI, 194–195.

Now just as there are those who render honour to their parents worthily and reverently, so, to the contrary, there are those who neglect to do so, not considering—or at least unwilling to consider—that those who dishonour parents do injury to God, who is the Creator and true Father of all; and that the Lord by no means permits injuries to parents to go unpunished unless worthy repentance follows. Therefore it must be shown how great is the condemnation, and how far removed from human dignity, not reverently to acknowledge parents; and how great is the recompense for obediently rendering them due honour [lacuna].

God says in the Law: “Honour your father,” etc. St Ambrose says in the book *On Joseph*: “First of all, how great a reverence we learn to render to parents when we read that he who was blessed by his father was blessed, and he who was cursed was cursed. Therefore God granted this grace to parents so that filial devotion might be encouraged. The prerogative of parents is the discipline of children. Honour your father, then, that he may bless you. Let the devout person honour his father for gratitude; the ungrateful, out of fear. Even if a father is poor and does not possess abundance of riches to leave to his children, he nevertheless has the inheritance of a final blessing, by which he may bestow upon his successors the riches of sanctification. And rightly it is greater to become blessed than rich.”

There are indeed children of perverse will who, wrongly understanding the honour to be rendered to parents, pretend that it consists only in acknowledging their parents, humbling themselves to them in body but not in mind, and refusing to provide them with what they need. Let them therefore observe that in the Scriptures honour is understood not so much in the rendering of respectful greetings as in alms and the offering of gifts. Considering the infirmities, age, and poverty of parents, the Lord commanded children to honour their parents also by supplying the necessities of life, CVI, 195–196.

LEO THE GREAT (St.), pope.—Exhortation to obedience, LIV, 645.

LEO IX (St.), pope.—On obedience, CXLIII, 563.

MARTIN (Saint), regular canon of León.—After the three precepts of the first table, there follows the number seven of commandments pertaining to love of neighbor. The first is on the second table, and begins with honoring parents. Yet it is fourth in order: “Honor your father and your mother.” What then is the first commandment, if not the fourth? This is because, among the seven commandments that pertain to love of neighbor, it is first on the second table; for two tables of the Law were given by God. In this commandment, therefore, children are ordered to honor their parents and not to behave insolently toward them, but to render due reverence through the duty of filial devotion. For one who does not know how to show honor to parents—to whom will he be able to show forbearance or kindness? Or how can he love others when he hates his own? CCVIII, 783.—Sermon on obedience, CCIX, 101.

MAXIMUS (Saint), bishop of Turin.—On love toward parents, LVII, 903.

NOVATUS, Catholic.—Saying on obedience, XVIII, 67.

ODO, prior of Saint-Victor.—On obedience, CXCVI, 1402, 1404.

OTLOH, monk.—On obedience, CXLVI, 285.

PETER THE CHANTER.—On obedience, CCV, 314.

PETER CHRYSOLOGUS (Saint), archbishop of Ravenna.—The love of fathers toward their children, LII, 352.

PETER COMESTOR.—“Honor your father and your mother” with a twofold honor: namely, reverence and the provision of necessities. For in the matters that follow, almost everywhere, the whole is understood from a part. Thus the Lord, teaching that these things must be understood in their entirety, fulfilled the Law, CXCVIII, 1165.

PETER DAMIAN (Saint), cardinal.—On obedience, CXLIV, 680. What the power of obedience is, CXLV, 570. On obedience toward parents, CXLV, 1018.

PETER LOMBARD, bishop of Paris.—On the second table, however, were seven commandments pertaining to love of neighbor, the first of which concerns one’s earthly father, just as the first commandment of the first table concerns the heavenly Father. It is: “Honor your father and mother, that you may be long-lived upon the land,” namely, the land of the living. Parents, moreover, are to be honored in such a way that due reverence is shown them and necessities are provided for them, CXCII, 832.

On obedience, CXCI, 1503; CXCII, 217. On reverence toward masters, CXCII, 359, 391.

PHILIP OF HARVENG, abbot.—On obedience, CCIII, 839.

PROSPER (Saint) OF AQUITANIA.—On obedience, LI, 452, 461.

RABANUS MAURUS, abbot of Fulda.—Parents are to be honored by their children, CIX, 777, 808. On obedience, CXI, 1560.

RALPH ARDENS.—On obedience, CLV, 1828.

RATHERIUS, bishop of Verona.—On masters, CXXXVI, 174. On servants, ibid., 175. On father, mother, and children, ibid., 201.

RUPERT, abbot of Deutz.—“The fifth commandment: ‘Honor your father and your mother’: a great commandment, worthy of great observance and to be repaid with a great and beautiful reward, which the discourse immediately proposes to the attentive hearer: ‘That you may be long-lived,’ it says, ‘upon the land.’ Higher and more excellent than this commandment is the counsel not to have father or mother besides God. This counsel the majesty of the Gospel openly proclaims; yet even the humility of the Law did not altogether keep silent about it. For it says: ‘He who said to his father: I do not know you . . .’ Therefore it is a commandment to honor father and mother; but it is a counsel not to know father and mother—not in the contrary manner by which father and mother are dishonored, but in a reasonable and just manner by which God, surpassing all affections, is rightly preferred to father and mother. For parents are not dishonored where the Creator alone is preferred to them . . .,” CLXVII, 1724–1726.

SMARAGDUS, abbot.—On obedience, CIII, 519, 649.

STEPHEN OF MURET, monk.—On obedience, CCIV, 1139.

TERTULLIAN, presbyter of Carthage.—On honor toward authority established by God, I, 700. On obedience in general, ibid., 1234.

THEODULF, bishop of Orléans.—On the duty of children toward parents and vice versa, CV, 202.

Fifth commandment.

“You shall not kill.”

ADALGER, monk.—On charity, CXXXIV, 917.

ADAM THE SCOT, Premonstratensian.—On the virtue of charity, CXCVIII, 265.

ADAM, abbot of Persenia.—On charity, CCXI, 1095.

AELRED, abbot of Rievaulx.—Mirror of Charity, CXCV, 505. On spiritual friendship, ibid., 661.

ALAN OF LILLE.—Here are authorities that provide a remedy against detractions. Jerome says: “When some deed is invented by a slanderer, another person’s reputation is assailed.” The same says: “You cannot rightly rebuke in others what you yourself do, nor can you accuse hypocrisy when you are yourself found guilty.” Likewise: “Take care not to have either an itching tongue or itching ears; that is, neither slander others yourself nor listen to others slandering. Slander no one, nor think yourself holy if you tear others to pieces, if you wound others with your slanders. This is not correction, but satisfying your own vice.” Likewise: “It is incongruous to hide the body while the tongue wanders through the whole world. Take care, while rebuking vices, not to incur the vice of slander.” Likewise: “The race of servants is given to complaining; however much it is afflicted, it is too little for them. For they consider not what is given, but how much; and they console their sorrow only by slanders.” The same: “He who frequently slanders others offends very many people. It is shameful to tear apart the absent and to describe another’s life; he is less eloquent who excuses himself by another’s fault. The slanderer bears the image of the scorpion, because, just as the scorpion presents the face of a maiden and then emits its sting, inflicting a sharp wound from above, so the slanderer presents flattering words before people’s faces, conceals the sting of slander in secret, and, as though wounding from above, slanders those who are better. O human being, what do you think of yourself while you brandish the dart of slander? The first arrow returns upon you, and the wound is inflicted upon you before it is inflicted on others. You badly conceal the enormity of your own deed when you wish to cloak it through the slander of another. While you slander people, you make yourself suspect, make yourself hateful to everyone, and endeavor to make enemies, by the poison of slander, of those whom you ought to make friends through honorable speech. While you strive to defame others, you infect yourself more deeply; and what falsehood you devise against others, you find true in yourself. Of slanderers it is said: ‘Their throat is an open sepulcher’ [Col. 0395]. A whitewashed tomb is outwardly fair but holds within the stench of a corpse; so the slanderer, wishing to color his inward malice, breaks out into bites of slander. But by this very act the tomb is opened all the more, and the stench of inward malice comes forth. Slanderers bear the image of dogs, who indiscriminately devote themselves to barking and inflict bites upon everyone. These are they who find a knot in a reed, a stain in what is spotless, a corner in what is round, darkness in what is bright. This is the plague of hypocrites, the bite of the envious; that plague spares no one, increases guilt, diminishes grace, goes astray against one’s neighbor, sins against the Holy Spirit. Struck by this malignant plague, the scribes and Pharisees said: ‘By Beelzebub, the prince . . .’; and elsewhere they cried: ‘You are a Samaritan . . . [lacuna].’ O human being, what advantage is there in slander? What usefulness in the malicious tooth? While you think to harm your neighbor, you rather add to his honor, because good people are commonly slandered, and the disease of envy rages against virtue. Slander is the enemy of the mother of virtues, namely charity. Whoever wounds a neighbor with slander drives charity away from himself, because the Holy Spirit will flee the fabrication of slander and abhors the lie of reproach, the sin of slander. He who offends the Holy Spirit scarcely finds a place of forgiveness either here or in the future. O human being, ash and dust that you are, with what face, with what brow marked by shame, do you dare to vomit out the poison of slander against one better than yourself, or to render judgment upon one less evil, or only a little evil? If you judge your neighbor unjustly, you will be judged justly by one greater; for the judgment of slander you will experience the judgment of eternal condemnation,” CCX, 164–167.

IVO (Saint), bishop of Chartres.—“I do not approve the counsel that persons should be killed in order that no one may be killed by them, unless perhaps he is a soldier or holds public office, so that he acts in this way not for himself but for others, or for the city in which he too resides, having received lawful authority, if it is appropriate to his office. Those who are kept, by some error, from doing evil may perhaps themselves receive some benefit. This is why it was said, ‘Let us not resist evil’: not that we may neglect the correction of people, but lest vengeance delight us, since it feeds the mind on another’s evil. Hence a Christian is not guilty of another’s death if, after he has enclosed his property with a circuit of walls, someone is struck and dies through the use of those walls. For neither is he guilty if his ox at some time kills someone by goring, or his horse by kicking; otherwise Christians ought not to have horned oxen, hoofed horses, or toothed dogs. Or again, since the Apostle Paul took sufficient care to report to the tribunes that traps had been laid for him by certain wicked men, and on this account received armed escorts: if criminal persons had encountered them, would Paul have acknowledged his own guilt in their shedding of blood? Far be it that, if by means of things which we do or possess for a good or lawful purpose, some evil should happen to anyone apart from our will, this should be imputed to us. Otherwise household and farm implements must not be kept either, lest anyone kill himself or another with them. And why mention more, when I cannot finish mentioning all the things in human use that are good or lawful and from which harm can be inflicted, if even killing itself is permitted by no authority of law?” CLXI, 1304–1305.

“If a person may not, by private authority, kill even an innocent human being, whose killing no law permits, then certainly one who kills himself is also a murderer; and he becomes all the more guilty when he kills himself, the more innocent he was in the matter for which he judged himself deserving of death [lacuna] A human being may not kill himself, since in the words written, ‘You shall not kill,’ nothing further is added, and certainly the person to whom the command is addressed is not excepted. ‘You shall not kill’—neither yourself nor another. For one who kills himself kills nothing other than a human being [lacuna] Yet the same divine authority has made certain exceptions. Apart from those whom God commands to be killed by an explicit command for a particular person and time, given without a law—or where the person who kills renders the service due to the commander, as a sword is the instrument of its user—those who, with God as author, waged wars, or who, holding public authority, put criminals to death according to his laws, that is, at the command of the most just reason, have in no way acted against the commandment, ‘You shall not kill.’ Abraham was not merely acquitted of the charge of cruelty, but was even praised with the name of devotion because he wished to kill his son not wickedly but obediently. And it is rightly asked whether what Jephthah did—killing the daughter who met her father—should be regarded as done by God’s command, since he had vowed to sacrifice to God whatever first met him as he returned victorious from battle. Nor is Samson otherwise excused for crushing himself with his enemies beneath the collapse of the house, except because the Spirit, who worked miracles through him, secretly commanded this. With these exceptions, therefore—those whom either a just law commands generally to be killed, or God himself, the fountain of justice, commands to be killed—whoever kills a human being, himself or anyone else, is bound by the guilt of homicide [lacuna],” CLXI, 1305–1306.

JOHN, bishop of Chartres.—For what will a son do except what he sees his father doing? CXCIX, 400.

Tender age must be kept more diligently from lusts and from pleasure, the parent of vices; and great care must be taken lest anything too licentious be done by adults in the presence of children. Eleazar nobly, when he was urged to transgress the Law of the Lord in order to save his life, set before them the danger of example, saying: “Who am I, Eleazar, ninety years old, that I should pass over to the life of foreigners and lead religious young men astray?” CXCIX, 40.

“We always strive toward what is forbidden, and desire what is denied.” (Ovid)

“And stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread more pleasant,” CXCIX, 403.

JULIANUS POMERIUS.—Holy Scripture has delivered an unshakable judgment, saying: “Pride is the beginning of every sin.” What could be said more plainly or more convincingly? “The beginning,” it says, not of some sin but of every sin, is pride, so that it might clearly show that pride itself is the cause of all sins; for not only is it itself sin, but no sin could have been, can be, or will be committed without it. For every sin is nothing other than contempt for God, whereby his commands are trampled underfoot. Nothing else persuades human beings to this contempt for God [Col. 0398] except pride, which was also the cause of eternal ruin in the devil himself, causing him to become a devil from an angel, etc. [lacuna], LIX, 476.

Let us now see by what marks a proud person may be detected, so that the signs by which he may be recognized as one to be avoided may appear clearly. I pass over those whom even their dress and gait show to be proud: their raised necks, grim faces, fierce eyes, and terrible speech proclaim naked pride. Possessed by a lust for domination, they violently subject to themselves those whom they can; they confound human and divine laws, swell with honors, plunder everything everywhere, rejoice in their crimes, and, corrupted by the disease of pride, do not comprehend themselves. I pass over, therefore, those in whom pride reigns so openly that it neither deigns to hide itself nor is able to do so [lacuna] Pride itself makes a place in the hearts of such people for the devil; it opens its undefended breast familiarly to his arrival; it welcomes him as he enters; it establishes for him the dominion of a life lived in ruin; it strips of all virtues everyone whom it has once invaded; it destroys whatever remains in them that might resist the vices, lest it perhaps gain strength against itself.

Hence those whom the festering corruption of a proud mind has ruined do not observe but judge the commands of their elders; when rebuked for their negligence, they either rebel insolently or murmur; they contend for a higher place; they shamelessly desire to be preferred even to better persons, etc. [lacuna]; they preserve neither reverence in service, nor moderation in speech, nor discipline in conduct. They have stubbornness in intention, hardness in heart, boastfulness in talk; they are deceitful in humility, obstinate in hatred, impatient of subjection, seekers of power, hateful to all good people, sluggish in good work, etc. [lacuna] These are the signs of raging pride, by which God is offended, departs, and abandons proud hearts. Nourished by these evils, the devil exults and is invited to come [lacuna], etc., LIX, 484–486. On envy, LIX, 486. On the praise of charity, LIX, 843.

PETER LOMBARD, bishop of Paris.—The second commandment of the second table is: “You shall not kill.” Here, according to the letter, the act of homicide is forbidden; according to the spirit, even the will to kill. Hence, to this commandment according to the letter an addition is made in the Gospel, because the letter of the Gospel expresses what the letter of the Law did not express. The letter of the Gospel expresses the spiritual understanding, that is, the understanding which spiritual persons have and according to which one lives spiritually; the letter of the Law expresses the carnal sense, that is, the understanding which carnal persons have and according to which one lives carnally, and to that there has been made an addition, CXCII, 832. RUPERT, abbot of Deutz.—“You shall not kill.” The commandment requires an implicit qualification, so that a judge or authority who bears the sword is not considered a transgressor when he kills one who was lawfully to be killed, or when a relative of the slain avenges him with the law’s permission. Thus, when it is said, “You shall not kill,” it must be understood: by taking up a sword that has not been given to you. For the Lord Christ said: “All who take up the sword shall perish by the sword”—that sword, surely, of which the Psalmist says: “Deliver me from the evil sword.” Beyond this commandment, moreover, there is the counsel of perfection: “Do not resist evil; but if anyone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the other also” [lacuna]

What was said, “You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy; an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth [lacuna],” is neither a commandment nor a counsel, but only a permission. But true and genuinely Christian innocence so abhors blood that it hears and proclaims as a commandment both not to resist evil and to love even one’s enemy, CLXVII, 1726.

Sixth commandment.

“You shall not commit adultery.”

ADALGER, monk.—On continence and its varieties, CXXXIV, 920.

ADAM, Premonstratensian.—“Whence, then, are you tempted?”

“I think of the multitude of well-dressed and beautiful women.”

“What do you think of them? How do you depict them to yourself, and how do they appear to you in thought?”

“Very beautiful, very pleasant, and very sweet.”

“For what are they beautiful and pleasant, and for what are they sweet?”

“Beautiful to look at, pleasant to embrace, and sweet to kiss.”

“What happens within you when you think such things?”

“My mind sighs, my body is stimulated, my heart desires to attain the fulfillment of pleasure, and my flesh exults.”

“Such exultation must be deeply lamented and mourned. Why do not your heart and flesh rather exult in the living God? You ought not to be like a raven but like a dove at your windows, lest death enter through them; so that, when perhaps by a movement of mind or body you go forth from the ark of your repose into the flood of this world, you may not find where to set the foot of your heart in love. But now, on the contrary, outward beauty deceives you; and while it rashly invites the inner eye of your flesh to behold it, it also ruinously exercises your gaze. Thus it happens miserably that, the more vigorously the bodily eye within you is active in looking upon what appears outwardly, the more dangerously the spiritual sight within you is darkened in discerning what lies hidden within. And therefore what shines outwardly draws you to desire itself, because you do not behold what stinks inwardly. Do you not know that when you look at a woman with a loving and sensual eye, you seek to possess a painted latrine? And when what appears outwardly beautiful pleases you unlawfully, do you not see what lies within, ugly? When you desire lustfully to embrace a woman who has been seized, you also desire to hold in your arms a silken sack full of dung. The sack may indeed be pleasant to touch, but what it contains, or what is contained within it, is foul to smell. What shines outwardly ought not to please when it contains within itself what stinks.

“For what is an indecent woman to you, when you love her indecently—beautiful indeed in body, but full in many ways of filth that ought not even to be named—except a kind of tomb full of the foul impurities and filthy stenches of the dead? When you desire lustfully to kiss in her such beauty as a small mouth, soft lips, ruddy cheeks, a pleasing face, eyes laughing, caressing, beckoning, speaking, offering, seeking, drawing, capturing, and so forth; when you admire with impure love a slender or graceful body and well-formed, pleasing limbs: you desire, and in desiring behold, a tomb whitewashed without, but within full of the stinking bones of the dead and of most savage serpents. For what is an indecent woman to you except a kind of monument full of filthy stenches? What are her deadly words, her seducing eyes, her alluring tender limbs unlawfully desired by you, except creeping things that bite and, by biting, kill? Therefore you must take every precaution lest, while you love too much what you see outwardly as shining, beautiful, and pleasant, you fall ruinously into that which inwardly defiles and kills.

“Finally, when you greedily and desirously propose to fulfill with her the pleasure of your flesh, you hunger for deadly bait that conceals a hook. And when you desire to taste what is sweet, the sting hidden beneath the sweetness pierces your throat lethally. Behold what the women of whom you think are like; so are they beautiful, so pleasant, so sweet. What do you think? Are they not such?”

“Entirely such.”

“Indeed they are such—if not in themselves, yet in you who desire them unlawfully. For I do not condemn either them, if they are respectable women, or their form or beauty, created in them by God, even if they themselves are not respectable; rather, I condemn the disordered concupiscence or complacency of your mind, by which you look upon them, because of their appearance, with the impure eye of unlawful desire. I do not, I say, blame in them either the beauty or sweetness of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; rather, in you I accuse Eve’s wanton gaze and gluttonous taste.”

“You speak well.”

“Therefore guard yourself against ‘the root of the serpent, from which comes forth the basilisk, lest its seed swallow the bird.’”

“I have often heard these words in Isaiah, but I do not know how they should be understood.”

“The serpent is the ancient serpent; its pestilential root is suggestion; the basilisk is the movement of the mind; the basilisk’s seed is an evil act; the bird is the soul, light by purity and lofty by contemplation. Therefore from the serpent’s root comes forth the basilisk, and its seed swallows the bird: because through the devil’s suggestion the mind is shaken, and unlawful action destroys the soul, since ‘sin, when it is consummated, brings forth death.’ Therefore purify yourself from impure thoughts by frequent meditation on Scripture, continual rumination upon the Psalms, and pure, humble confession. Mortify your members which are upon the earth, together with their vices and concupiscences, so that, holding the little ones of Babylon, you may dash them against the rock, and the moderation of drink and food may wear away the pride of your flesh [lacuna].”

“Your words both make me, though sorrowful, greatly glad; they instruct one who does not know and strengthen one who is weak. You have now shown me that, when this vice tempts me, I ought not to grieve too greatly; and that by despising what shines and is sweet, by seeing fully what it is and to what destruction it draws, I can overcome it through God’s grace—so that I may know how to scrape the discharge from my ulcer with a potsherd,” CXCVIII, 845–847.

ADAM THE SCOT, Premonstratensian.—On purity, CXCVIII, 203.

ALANUS OF LILLE.—If a preacher wishes to instruct his hearers to flee lust, he may begin from this authority: “Flee fornication.” The Lord says in the Gospel: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands.” Paul says: “God will judge fornicators and adulterers.” Solomon: “A harlot is a deep pit; she lies in wait on the road like a robber; those whom she sees unwary she kills.” Jesus son of Sirach: “Do not give a woman power over your soul, lest she enter by means of your strength and you be put to shame.” Jerome: “Woe to him whose limit of lust comes only with the end of life. For chastity is difficult to preserve amid riches. He who lives luxuriously is dead while living [Col. 0401], and he who is drunken is dead and buried.” Gregory: “While the belly is stretched by satiety, the sting of lust is aroused.” He who restrains the pleasure of a lustful suggestion does not proceed to consent to lust. If the pleasure of fornication delights more than the love of chastity, sin still reigns in the person. Every unclean defilement is called fornication; it is better to die than to commit fornication; it is better to die than to be stained by lust. Lust plunges a person into hell. Lust burns more severely the one whom it finds idle; draw nearer to a burning fire than to a young woman, when you yourself are young. [lacuna] What monster is more monstrous than lust? [lacuna] This is that plague in which what delights passes quickly, while what torments remains without end. [lacuna] This is the plague that hates light, seeks darkness, looks for a covering, sets a doorkeeper at the gate. [lacuna] CCX, 121, 122.

If a preacher wishes to invite his hearers to flee gluttony, he may use this authority: “I chastise my body,” etc.; and, “Let us live soberly, righteously, and devoutly in this world.” The body, I say, must be disciplined so that it serves us; it is to be indulged, not served. For he who serves the body must serve many things; he fears too much for its sake who refers everything to it. [lacuna] Isidore says: “Wherever satiety and drunkenness are found, lust holds dominion.” Therefore, O man, you ought to conduct yourself in such a way that you seem not to live for the body, but are able to live as though without a body. Make use of yourself, and of the best part of yourself; regard flesh as a necessary thing rather than a great thing. [lacuna] Therefore discipline the flesh, which resembles a dog, a servant, and a beast of burden.

The more a servant is indulged, the more he is dissolved in idleness; the more a dog is beaten, the more he gives himself to barking; the more a beast of burden is fed, the more it kicks against its master. How diligently, then, must gluttony be fled, since it turns the body’s dwelling-place, the receptacle of spirit and soul, into a dung-heap, and reduces the mass of our flesh to mud! [lacuna] CCX, 119, 120.

Consider, O man, how Adam lost paradise through gluttony; Elijah ascended to heaven through abstinence; Noah uncovered his thighs through gluttony; Moses deserved converse with God through abstinence; Lot fell into incest through drunkenness; David obtained the remedy of penitence through abstinence. O man, consult nature: it will tell you what ought to be the rule of life. The law of nature is that you should drive away hunger and thirst; for this there is no need to cross seas or to follow armies: that which nature desires is obtainable and close at hand. [lacuna] Take up the medicines of fasting against the assaults of so great a disease: fast from food, lest the flesh grow wanton; fast from temporal pleasure, lest the mind languish; fast from sin, lest the soul grow numb. CCX, 121. Against lust, ibid.; to virgins, CCX, 194. Gifts of chastity, CCX, 551.

ALCUIN, abbot.—Exhortation to chastity, C, 469, 626. On fornication, CI, 633.

ALDELMUS, Saint, bishop of Sherborne.—On the praises of virgins, LXXXIX, 238.

AMBROSE, Saint, bishop of Milan.—How to resist temptations of pleasure, XIV, 324. The crime of adultery shown by the example of Pharaoh, XIV, 423. The crime of adultery shown by the example of Abimelech, IV, 442. Joseph, a mirror of chastity, XIV, 641. Isaiah’s prophecy shows destruction to the lustful, XIV, 721. Feasting parties to be avoided, XIV, 726. What kind of leisure should be indulged in to preserve modesty, XVI, 50. The example of Mary set before virgins, XVI, 208. Remedies against temptations from women, XVI, 312. The unhappiness of one who has lost the benefit of virginity, XVI, 369. One should not live in low-lying places in the manner of the luxurious, XVI, 1061. Why the Law forbids men to use women’s clothing and women men’s clothing, XVI, 1232. On fornication, XVII, 207. Words concerning chastity, XVII, 1072. On spiritual fornication, ibid.

ANSELM, Saint, archbishop of Canterbury.—On lost virginity, CXVIII, 725. On purity of heart, CLVIII, 1019. On the concupiscence of flesh and spirit, CLVIII, 1026. On chastity, CLVIII, 1029. How thoughts are to be feared, CLIX, 167.

ATHANASIUS, Saint.—On chastity, XVIII, 84.

ATTO, bishop of Vercelli.—On fornication, CXXXIV, 345.

AUGUSTINE, Saint, bishop of Hippo.—In the Book of Wisdom we have it written that no one can be continent unless God grants it. [lacuna] But the Lord himself says concerning that greater and more glorious continence by which one abstains from the marriage bond: “Not all receive this saying, but those to whom it has been given.” XL, 350, 532.

Now, so long as the flesh desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh, it is enough for us not to consent to the evil things that we feel within ourselves. But when there is such consent, that which defiles a person proceeds from the mouth of the heart. When, through continence, consent is withheld, the evil of carnal concupiscence, against which spiritual concupiscence fights, is not permitted to do harm. XL, 553. Within us is the concupiscence of sin, which must not be permitted to reign; there are its desires, which must not be obeyed, lest it reign over those who obey. Therefore concupiscence must not claim our members for itself, but continence must claim them for itself, so that they may be weapons of righteousness for God and not weapons of unrighteousness for sin; for thus sin will not rule over us. The Apostle exhorts us not to live according to the flesh, lest we die, but by the Spirit to put to death the deeds of the flesh, that we may live. So that we may know what these works of the flesh are, he says: “Now the works of the flesh are manifest: fornications, uncleannesses, lusts . . .” XL, 354.

There are evil desires within us; by not consenting to them, we do not live badly. There are within us concupiscences of sins; by not obeying them, we do not accomplish evil, but by having them we do not yet accomplish good. The Apostle shows both: neither is good perfected here where evil is thus desired, nor is evil accomplished here when such concupiscence is not obeyed. Evil concupiscences therefore arise in us when we take pleasure in what is unlawful; but they are not completed when, while the mind serves the law of God, lusts are restrained. And good is done when that which gives wrongful pleasure is not done because a good delight prevails; but the perfection of good is not fulfilled so long as, while the flesh serves the law of sin, lust desires what is unlawful, and though it is restrained, it nevertheless moves. For it would not need to be restrained unless it moved. Therefore flesh is not evil if it is free from evil—that is, from the vice by which man has been corrupted: man was not made evil, but made himself so. [lacuna] XL, 361, 362.

My speech is addressed to you, O young men, flower of age, peril of the mind. No time indeed, and no age in which this corruptible flesh is borne, can be free from temptations. And so long as any good person wrestles in the contest lest he be overcome by the adversary, he lives amid dangers, so long as he contends with him in this mortality, as though in a sandy arena. [lacuna] But if even the infancy of mortal man is not free from temptations because of the bond of corruption, what shall I say of the other ages? Is old age perhaps excepted? Has blood in flesh already near to a corpse, together with the members of unlawful concupiscence, grown cold, and has the material of temptation withered away from a body weary and nearly dead? [lacuna] If, then, neither childhood nor old age is free from temptations—of which the one, childhood, has scarcely yet entered this life, while the other is already leaving it; one was not here a little before, the other will not be here a little after—what must be thought, what said, about the ardour of youthful age? Established between both, it has already departed from the weakness of childhood and has not yet reached the torpor of old age. It is shaken by more numerous and greater storms of temptation; it is overwhelmed by the more frequent surge of the overflowing world. It presumes on its strength, boasts in the dignity of beauty, and either desires or delights to shine with the display of temporal things. [lacuna]

Nor, young women, should you suppose this discourse unrelated to yourselves. For I say these things to you, not to shame you, but to admonish you as my dearest daughters: flee youthful desires. Married women, think of Susanna; widows, of Anna; virgins, of Mary. Nor should you therefore go out in public wishing to display the flower of your hay—your youthful bloom—to human eyes, and seek death in the house of life. [lacuna] XXXIX, 1706–1709.

“You have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.” The lesser righteousness, therefore, is not to commit adultery by union of bodies; the greater righteousness of the kingdom of God is not to commit adultery in the heart. Whoever does not commit adultery in the heart more easily keeps from committing adultery in the body. Thus he who gave this command confirmed the former command; for he came not to abolish the Law but to fulfil it. It should certainly be considered that he did not say, “Everyone who has desired a woman,” but, “who looks at a woman in order to desire her”: that is, who regards her with this end and this intention, namely to desire her. This is no longer merely to be titillated by the pleasure of the flesh, but to consent fully to lust, so that unlawful appetite is not restrained but, if an opportunity is given, satisfied.

For there are three stages by which the command is violated: suggestion, pleasure, and consent. Suggestion occurs either through memory or through the bodily senses, when we see, hear, smell, taste, or touch something. If it becomes pleasant to enjoy it, unlawful delight must be restrained—for example, when we fast and, on seeing food, the appetite of the palate rises: this happens only through pleasure. [lacuna] Yet before habit is formed, pleasure is either nonexistent or so slight as to be nearly nothing; and to consent to it, when it is unlawful, is a great sin. But once a person has consented, he commits sin in the heart. If he proceeds even to deed, desire seems to be satisfied and extinguished; but afterward, when suggestion returns, a greater pleasure is kindled [Col. 0403]. Yet this is still much less than that which comes through repeated acts into habit. It is exceedingly difficult to overcome this; nevertheless, if one does not abandon oneself and does not shrink from Christian warfare, under that leader and helper one will overcome even habit itself. [lacuna]

Therefore, just as sin is reached by three steps—suggestion, pleasure, and consent—so there are three kinds of sin itself: in the heart, in deed, and in habit, as though three deaths. [lacuna] Whoever reads the Gospel recognizes that the Lord raised the three kinds of dead. [lacuna]

Accordingly, under the name of adulterers one must understand every carnal and lustful concupiscence. [lacuna] And who would doubt that every evil concupiscence is rightly called fornication, when the soul, neglecting the higher law by which it rules lower natures, is corrupted by being prostituted, as it were for a fee, to shameful pleasure? Therefore, whoever feels carnal delight rebelling against his right will through a habit of sins, by whose untamed violence he is dragged captive, should recall as far as possible what peace he lost by sinning, and cry out: “Wretched man that I am,” etc. [lacuna] XXXIV, 1246, 1247.

The act of lust itself—not only in certain acts of sexual violation, where hiding places are sought in order to evade human judgments, but even in the use of prostitutes, a shamefulness which the earthly city has made lawful—though it is done in a manner punished by no law of that city, yet lust, even where permitted and unpunished, avoids public sight. (Saint Jerome says: “The laws of the Caesars are one thing, those of Christ another; Papinian commands one thing, our Paul another. Among them the reins of unchastity are loosened for men, and, once rape and adultery alone have been condemned, lust is freely permitted through brothels and female slaves, as though rank, rather than will, made guilt.”) Even brothels themselves, by natural shame, have been provided with secrecy; and unchastity could more easily lack the bonds of prohibition than shamelessness could remove the hiding places of that foulness. Yet even those who are themselves foul call it foulness; though lovers of it, they do not dare to be its displayers.

What of marital intercourse, undertaken according to the prescriptions of marriage documents for the begetting of children? Does not even this, though lawful and honourable, require a chamber removed from witnesses? Does not the husband send outside all servants, even the attendants of the marriage, and any persons whom whatever relationship had allowed to enter, before he begins even to caress his wife? And since, as Cicero, the greatest authority in Roman eloquence, says, all rightly done things wish to place themselves in the light—that is, they seek to be known—this rightly done act seeks to be known and yet is ashamed to be seen. For who does not know what spouses do with one another in order that children may be begotten, since wives are married with such public ceremony precisely that this may take place? Yet when that from which children are born is being done, even the children themselves, if any have already been born from it, are not allowed to be witnesses. Thus this rightly done thing seeks the light of minds so that it may be known, yet flees the eyes. Why is this, unless what is fitting by nature is so performed that shame, arising from punishment, accompanies even it? XLI, 426, 427.

Though there are lusts for many things, when “lust” is mentioned without stating the object of lust, the mind almost always thinks only of that by which the obscene parts of the body are aroused. This lust claims for itself not merely the entire body, and not merely outwardly, but inwardly also; it moves the whole person, with the emotion of the soul joined and mingled with the appetite of the flesh. Thus there follows a pleasure than which none is greater among bodily pleasures, so that at the very moment when its climax is reached, nearly all keenness and, as it were, wakefulness of thought is overwhelmed.

Who, however, being a friend of wisdom and of holy joys, while living married life and, as the Apostle advises, “knowing how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honour, not in the passion of desire, like the Gentiles who do not know God,” would not prefer, if possible, to beget children without this lust? Then, even in this duty of sowing offspring, the parts created for this work would serve the mind’s command, just as all the other members assigned to their respective functions do, moved by the nod of the will and not aroused by the heat of lust. Yet even lovers of this pleasure, whether for marital intercourse or for the uncleannesses of shameful acts, are not aroused whenever they wish. Sometimes that movement is troublesome when no one calls for it; at other times it deserts one who longs for it, and while concupiscence burns in the mind, the body is cold. Thus, in a wonderful manner, lust serves neither the will to beget nor even the lust to indulge in wantonness. And although it commonly resists the whole mind when the mind restrains it, sometimes it is divided even against itself: when it has stirred the mind to stir the body, it does not itself follow through. XLI, 424, 425.

[Col. 0404] Let a virgin who continually reflects upon the most precious treasure of virginity—possessed with so much benefit and lost so irreparably—guard it with the utmost diligence and earnestness. Let her think without ceasing for whose bridal chamber she is appointed, for whose embrace she is being prepared. Let her set before herself the Lamb whom she must follow wherever he goes. Let her contemplate most blessed Mary leading the choirs of virgins and singing before them, with the timbrel of virginity, that sweet song which no one can sing except virgins of either sex: “These are they,” it is written, “who have not been defiled with women; for they are virgins.” Do not judge this to have been said as though a man could not be defiled without a woman, or a woman without a man, when that detestable crime by which man with man, or woman with woman, is judged more damnable than all other shameful acts. But virginity is often corrupted and chastity violated without intercourse with another’s flesh. [lacuna] If a more vehement heat, shaking the flesh, subdues the will to itself and carries off the members, let the virgin think above all of what in her has been sanctified to God, kept incorrupt for Christ, dedicated to the Holy Spirit. Let her judge it unworthy to hand over to Satan what belongs to Christ; and let her be ashamed that her virginal members should be stained even by a mere movement. XXXII, 1439.

Let no one flatter himself, let no one soothe himself, let no one deceive himself. Chastity is never acquired or preserved by young people without great contrition of heart and affliction of flesh; it is frequently endangered even among the sick and the aged. For although continence is a gift of God, [lacuna] he nevertheless judges unworthy of so great a gift those who refuse to undergo any labour for it, wishing to be chaste amid pleasures, continent amid banquets, to associate with boys and girls and not be tempted, to swell with foul humours amid feasting and drunkenness and not be defiled, to bind their sight to flames and not be burned. [lacuna] XXXII, 1459, 1460.

AVITUS, Saint, bishop of Vienne.—On the praise of chastity, LIX, 369.

BALDWIN, archbishop of Canterbury.—On the carnal man, CCIV, 524.

BEDE THE VENERABLE.—“You shall not commit adultery”; that is, let no one, because of the bond of marriage, have relations with other women to satisfy lust. For adultery is committed in the strict sense by one who approaches another woman besides his own. XCIII, 374.

BENEDICT, Saint, abbot of Aniane.—What uncleanness and immodesty are, CIII, 549. On avoiding drunken excess, CIII, 634.

BENEDICT, Saint, father of Western monks.—Temptation of the flesh overcome, LXVI, 132.

BERNARD, Saint, abbot of Clairvaux.—Vanity of carnal pleasures, CLXXXII, 841. On the adulterous woman, CLXXXIII, 392. Blessed are the pure in heart, CLXXXIII, 460. On the corruption of men, CLXXXIII, 695. On lust, CLXXXIII, 977.

BRUNO, Saint, founder of the Carthusians.—On fornication, CLIII, 152.

BRUNO, Saint, monk of Asti.—“You shall not commit adultery,” CLXV, 106. On chastity, CLXV, 929.

[Col. 0405] CAESARIUS, Saint, bishop of Arles.—On adultery, LXVII, 1085. On the concupiscence of the eyes, LXVII, 1010. On fleeing fornication, LXVII, 1123.

CANUTE I, king of the English.—We teach also that people should always be admonished to abstain from shameful sexual violation, unlawful intercourse, and every adultery. CLI, 1177.

CASSIAN, John, priest of Marseilles.—According to the tradition of the Fathers, our conflict against the spirit of fornication is longer and more enduring than the others, conquered completely by very few: an immense war which, beginning to assail humankind from its earliest time of disturbance, is not extinguished unless the other vices are first overcome. [lacuna] Saint Gregory the Great, pope, describes well the nature of this vice and how it is to be conquered, explaining what was said concerning Amalek to the people of Israel: “Do not spare him, and do not desire anything belonging to him; but kill from man to woman, child and nursing infant, ox and ass, sheep and camel.” “Who,” he says, “spares Amalek except one who retains something of wantonness either in thought, in speech, or in the flesh? For many do not perform shameful deeds, but do not restrain their tongue from shameful speech; many avoid lust in deed but do not avoid it in thought; some do nothing shameful, but desire in their heart what they flee in action. Therefore he spares Amalek who entertains the allurements of wantonness in speech, intention, or thought. He said, ‘Do not spare him,’ because nothing from such a wicked vice should be kindled in the mind, nothing allowed to burn in deed. ‘Do not desire anything belonging to him,’ so that it may be wholly uprooted from thought. Who are the men to be killed except the persuasive impulses of shamefulness? For they are men because they urge violently and pour the seeds of wickedness into corrupted minds,” etc. XLIX, 266, 267.

Saint Jerome expressed in these words how difficult, protracted, and dangerous is the contest which we must wage continually against the spirit of fornication—that is, lust or the concupiscence of the flesh: “Avarice is trampled down by many and laid aside with the purse. A commanded silence corrects a cursed tongue. Care of the body and the fashion of clothing are changed within an hour. All other sins are external, and what is outside is easily cast away. Lust alone, implanted by God for the procreation of children, exceeds its bounds, overflows into vice, and by a certain law of nature breaks forth into crime. It is a work of great virtue and vigilant diligence to overcome what you were born with, to live in the flesh but not carnally, to fight daily with yourself, and to watch the enclosed enemy, as they say Argus did, with a hundred eyes. This is what the Apostle said: ‘Every sin that a man commits is outside the body; but he who fornicates sins against his own body.’ And elsewhere: Avarice does not shake us thus, pride does not puff us up thus, ambition does not delight us thus; we easily dispense with other vices. This enemy is enclosed within us: wherever we go, we carry the enemy with us.” XLIX, 267.

Again in the same place, heightening this same difficulty by his own example and experience, and recalling how much distress he had experienced from this domestic enemy even amid the greatest austerity of life: “O how often,” he says, “when I was in the desert, in that vast solitude burned by the sun’s heat, which affords monks a dreadful dwelling, did I think myself amid Roman delights! I sat alone because I was filled with bitterness; my limbs, disfigured by sackcloth, were horrifying, and my squalid skin had taken on the condition of Ethiopian flesh. Daily there were tears, daily groans; and if ever approaching sleep overcame my resistance, I dashed my bones, scarcely clinging together, against the bare ground. Thus I, who through fear of Gehenna had condemned myself to such a prison, companion only of scorpions and wild beasts, was often present among choirs of girls. My face was pale from fasting, yet my mind burned with desires in a cold body; before a man already almost dead in his flesh, only the fires of lusts bubbled up. Therefore, deprived of every aid, I cast myself at Jesus’ feet, watered them with tears, wiped them with my hair, and overcame the resisting flesh by weeks of hunger. [lacuna] etc.”

Agreeing with Saint Jerome, Saint Augustine says: “Among all the contests of Christians, the battles for chastity alone are hard, where the struggle is daily and victory rare. For chastity has received a grievous enemy, whom it resists daily and always fears.” XLIX, 267.

Book on the spirit of fornication, XLIX, 265. On the concupiscence of flesh and spirit, XLIX, 583. On chastity, XLIX, 869, 1145. The general rule of continence, XLIX, 307.

CASSIODORUS, senator and abbot.—Against adulterers, LXIX, 784.

CHROMATIUS, Saint, bishop of Aquileia.—“You shall not commit adultery,” XX, 348.

[Col. 0406] COLUMBANUS, Saint, abbot.—On chastity, LXXX, 211. On lust, LXXX, 284.

CUMMIANUS, Saint, abbot.—On fornication, adultery, etc., LXXXVII, 983.

CYPRIAN, Saint, bishop and martyr of Carthage.—Chastity is the honour of bodies, the adornment of morals, the sanctity of the sexes, the bond of modesty, the fountain of purity, the peace of the household, the head of concord. Chastity is not anxious about pleasing anyone except itself; chastity is always modest, since it is the mother of innocence; chastity is always adorned by modesty alone, then well conscious of its beauty if it displeases the wicked; chastity seeks no ornaments, for it is itself its own beauty. It commends us to the Lord and joins us to Christ; it overcomes every unlawful battle of desire arising from the members and brings peace to our bodies. Blessed in itself and making blessed those among whom it deigns to dwell, it can never be accused even by those who lack it; it is venerable even to its enemies, since those who cannot overcome it admire it all the more. IV, 821.

Nothing so delights the faithful mind as the unbroken consciousness of unstained modesty. To have conquered pleasure is the greatest pleasure, and no victory is greater than that won over desires. One who conquered an enemy was stronger than another; one who restrained lust was stronger than himself. One who cast down an enemy struck an external foe; one who subdued desire overcame a domestic enemy. Every evil is more easily conquered than pleasure, because whatever that evil is, it is harsh and not alluring. Nothing is more difficult to crush than that by which the one who removes desires also removes fears is armed; for fears arise from desires. Whoever conquers desires triumphs over sin; whoever conquers desires shows that the evil of humankind lies beneath his feet; whoever has conquered desires has given himself lasting peace. [lacuna]

Against the snares of the flesh, through which the devil presents himself as both companion and leader, one must struggle with every kind of virtue. According to the Apostle, the works of Christ must be taken up, and the mind must be withdrawn as far as possible from fellowship with the flesh; consent must be separated from the body; vices must always be chastised so as to be hated; before the eyes there must stand this ugly and abject shame of sin. IV, 825, 826.

The example of chastity begins with Joseph. A noble young Hebrew, noble by birth from his father and nobler by innocence, was sold by his Israelite brothers because of envy over his revelations. He came into the house of an Egyptian man and, through service, innocence, and complete faithfulness in slavery, readily won his master’s favourable and kindly disposition. His appearance had commended him to all, as much by his freeborn speech as by his age. But the master’s wife interpreted this nobility otherwise than was fitting. In a secluded and unwitnessed part of the house, remote and suited to crimes, the incontinent woman thought that by promises now, now by threats, she could overcome the young man’s chastity by her own immodesty. When he was held by his clothing while trying to flee, he left the very garments because of the audacity of so great a crime; and, though the innocence of his naked body would bear witness to his integrity, the reckless woman did not hesitate to cast upon him the slander of her own unchastity. Dishevelled and inflamed, and distressed at the rejection of her desire, she complained to the others and to her husband, with feigned grief, that the Hebrew youth had attempted to inflict upon her the violence which she herself had tried to inflict. Her husband, ignorant of the facts and grievously inflamed by his wife’s accusation, was enraged. But the chaste youth, because he had not joined his conscience to wrongdoing, was cast into the depths of prison. Yet chastity was not alone in prison: God was with Joseph, and the guilty were given into his hand, because he had been innocent. [lacuna] IV, 823.

But, from the other sex, another like example of chastity arises for us from women’s continence. There was, as we read, Susanna, wife of Joachim, most beautiful, and more beautiful in character. [lacuna] Two elders had begun to burn with desire for her, mindful neither of divine fear nor of their own age, now withering in years. Thus the flame of returning lust recalled them into the fires of the passion of youth now past. These robbers of chastity professed love, but hated it. They threatened slanders against her resistance; themselves adulterers in desire, they said that they would accuse her of adultery. Amid these rocks of lust she sought help from the Lord, because she could not resist with bodily strength. And the Lord heard from heaven chastity crying to him; and, though she was being led away to punishment, crushed by injustice, she saw vengeance upon her enemies after being delivered. Twice victorious, surrounded so many times by such deadly dangers, she escaped both lust and death. IV, 824. And on these matters, the book *On the Discipline and Good of Chastity*, IV, 819–828.

HILARY, Saint, bishop of Poitiers.—What is pleasure? IX, 998.

HILDEBERT, bishop of Le Mans.—If anything is pleasant through use, one is naturally drawn to it freely; hence the flesh yearns after carnal delights, and the more pleasing experience is, the more intemperate is its appetite. Neither baptism erases this law of the members, nor time destroys it, nor the will scrapes it away. [lacuna] Paul, caught up to the third heaven and hearing secret words that no human being may utter, nevertheless complains that he feels this law in his members, resisting the law of his mind and dragging him captive under the law of sin. CLXXI, 998.

The whole book *On the Conflict of Flesh and Soul* consists of this question, CLXXI, 989–1003.

HILDEBERT THE VENERABLE, bishop of Le Mans.—On virginity, CLXXI, 193. What is concupiscence of the eyes? CLXXI, 469.

HINCMAR, archbishop of Reims.—On fleeing lust, CXXV, 868. On evil thoughts, CXXV, 908.

HONORIUS OF AUTUN.—What concupiscence is, CLXXII, 1143.

HUGH OF SAINT VICTOR.—The third commandment is: “You shall not commit adultery.” Fornication is twofold: spiritual, of which it is said, “You have destroyed all who commit fornication away from you”; and bodily, of which this passage treats. In the Gospel Christ forbids every unlawful concupiscence, saying: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.” For these commandments were begun in the Law and brought to completion in the Gospel. CLXXVI, 122, 356.

The Law prohibited bodily adultery; it prohibited concupiscence. What further provision did the Gospel have to make? Yet it must be understood that the old Law, although it restrained a person's desire for another’s property, did not at all moderate desire in what was one’s own. For he who said, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife or property,” did not forbid a woman or property to be desired altogether, but showed only that desire must be restrained from what belongs to another. The new Law, however, taught that one must be self-restrained even in one’s own possessions, so as to exclude every unlawful desire.

It may also suitably be said, in another interpretation, that the old Law, in speaking of desire for another’s wife or property, meant not that desire which is exercised in the will alone, but ambition and contrivance which, with a certain exertion and striving to fulfill desire and obtain its object, is exercised outwardly in action [Col. 0408]. The new Law, however, not only condemned unlawful desire outwardly in the pursuit of action, but also showed it to be condemnable inwardly in the desire of the will, CLXXVI, 358, 369.

On the lust of the flesh, CLXXV, 121. “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife,” CLXXVI, 124. On lust and its retinue, CLXXVI, 1002. Condemnation of lust, CLXXVII, 607. On threefold virginity, CLXXVII, 843.

INNOCENT III, pope.—On lust, CCXVII, 725. On intercourse against nature, CCXVII, 726. On the uncleanness of the heart, CCXVII, 724.

IVO (Saint), bishop of Chartres.—On virginity, CLXII, 22. On adulterous dress, CLXII, 607.

JOHN OF SALISBURY, bishop of Chartres.—On lust and lechery, CXCIX, 723.

JONAS, bishop of Orléans.—Just as there are many who occupy themselves with obscene speech, buffoonery, insults, and idle talk, so there are very many who, while delighting in vain and unclean thoughts, believe that they have committed no sin. Thus they bring upon themselves the stain of sin not only by speaking, but also by willingly lending an ear. Unclean thoughts, moreover, commonly draw people into wicked acts. … It is evident that, just as holy thoughts guard one, so, conversely, unclean thoughts, while they delight, defile. Whatever, as the Venerable Priest Bede says, we are accustomed frequently to do, say, or hear, must necessarily return frequently to the soul as though to its familiar and proper abode. And just as wallowing swine frequent marshes, while doves frequent clear streams, so unclean thoughts disturb an impure mind, while spiritual thoughts sanctify a chaste one.

Saint Isidore also writes: “Even though a person does not engage in an evil deed, he will nevertheless not be innocent because of the wickedness of a perverse thought alone. … We sin not only by deeds but also by thoughts, if we delight in them when they unlawfully arise.” … CVI, 154, 155. On guarding against unclean thoughts, CVI, 154. On obscene speech, CVI, 250.

JULIANUS POMERIUS.—Having treated very many matters pertaining to the sixth commandment, LIX, 480–482, he adds: “And lest anyone judge that I, who truthfully condemn these things, ought myself to be condemned, let him know that perhaps for this reason it was decreed by the ancients that no young persons should read the Book of Genesis, or likewise part of the prophet Ezekiel, or the Song of Songs, and other such writings in which are written the births, deeds, and names of certain women. Although we believe that these women existed according to history, we understand virtues to be figuratively represented by their names. For just as those women pleased not only their husbands through holy conduct, but also strangers, without loss of their modesty, because of their exceptional beauty, so holy virtues render their own possessors admirable to all and strike strangers with a certain admiration of themselves.

“Hence even those who live viciously place virtues above vices, because what they do through disease is one thing, and what they are compelled to approve by judgment is another. But lest those still carnal should receive these spiritual matters according to the flesh, and should not think of the virtues signified by those women but, by thinking carnally of the women themselves, should perish, younger persons were deliberately forbidden to read those writings which, received spiritually, give life, but which, for those who understand carnally, by that very carnal understanding furnish occasions of carnal desire. Each person frequently has upon his lips the names of those women whose desires he bears in his wounded heart; and the obscenity which he is ashamed to enact in deed he retains in his mind—guilty not before human judgment, but before divine judgment,” LIX, 483. Mournful description of a priest living carnally, LIX, 435.
