PETER DAMIAN (Saint).—It is likewise worthwhile continually to contemplate the rewards promised to chastity. Drawn by their sweetness, you will pass with the free step of faith beyond whatever craft the cunning tempter sets in your way. For if one considers the happiness which is attained only by passing through, that through which one labors becomes light; and the hired digger eases the weariness of his labor while eagerly awaiting the wage due for his work.

Consider, then, what is said through the prophet concerning the soldiers of chastity: “Thus says the Lord to the eunuchs who have kept my Sabbaths, chosen what I willed, and held fast my covenant: I will give them, in my house and within my walls, a place and a name better than sons and daughters.” For eunuchs are those who restrain the insolent impulses of the flesh and cut off from themselves the effect of wicked action. Yet many of those who serve the pleasure of fleshly enticement desire to leave behind them the remembrance of their name through the succession of offspring; and with their whole affection of mind they desire this because they by no means reckon themselves to die wholly to this world if they extend the title of their name through the surviving shoot of remaining progeny.

But those who are celibate receive this same gift far more clearly and happily—the gift for which those with offspring are inflamed with the heats of such ardent ambition—because their memory always lives with him who, in the state of eternity, does not pass away under any law of time. Therefore a name better than sons and daughters is promised by the divine voice to eunuchs, because the remembrance of a name which the posterity of children might have extended for a brief span of time, these persons deserve to possess forever without any obstacle of oblivion: “For the righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance.” And again, in the Apocalypse through John, it is said: “They shall walk with me in white, because they are worthy; and I shall not blot their names from the book of life.” Again it is said: “These are those who have not been defiled with women; for they are virgins, who follow the Lamb wherever he goes.” And they sing a song which no one can sing except those one hundred and forty-four thousand.

Virgins, indeed, sing a singular song to the Lamb because, together with him and above all the faithful, they rejoice forever even in the incorruption of the flesh. Other righteous persons cannot sing this, although, placed in the same blessedness, they deserve to hear it; for through love they gladly contemplate the height of those persons, but do not rise to their rewards. Therefore it must be pondered and turned over in our minds with every effort: how great is the dignity and excellence of becoming highest there, where the greatest happiness is to be even lowest; of ascending there to the height of privilege, where it is most blessed to observe the laws of the country of equity. Certainly, as Truth testifies, “not all receive this saying in this age”; so not all attain in the age to come to the glory of that outstanding company.

Whoever you are, consider these and many other such matters in the secret places of your mind, and hasten with all your strength to preserve your flesh immune from every plague of lust, so that, according to the teaching of the Apostle, you may know how to possess your vessel in sanctification and honor, not in the passion of desire, as do the nations that do not know God. If you are still standing, beware of the precipice; but if you have fallen, confidently stretch out your hand to the hook of repentance, which is everywhere ready, so that, if you could not dwell with Abraham far from Sodom, you may at least be permitted to depart with Lot when the ruin of the nearby conflagration is already pressing. [lacuna], CXLV, 186, 187.

PETER DAMIAN (Saint).—Before all else, strive with watchful diligence to preserve chastity and exclude every crime of deadly defilement, so that, according to the Apostle, you may know how to possess your vessel in sanctification and honor. For this is holiness, without which no one shall see God. Let the garment of your body be kept clean, and let no stain of wanton lust be found defiling it at the nuptials of so great a king.

Let chastity therefore always be in your body and always in your mind, so that the lilies of undisciplined flesh may grow white under cultivation as from ploughed soil, and so that the root too may remain unshaken in the grace of its freshness. When the enticement of the flesh tickles you and incentives to lust arise, immediately rush to the apostolic weapons and, as a fervent warrior, seize also the Gospel sword. With Christ as your leader, you will readily strike down the raging ranks and barbarity of the enemy. [lacuna]

Therefore, lest endangered chastity suffer shipwreck amid the hazards of this fluctuating life, let sobriety, the mistress of your body, hold the helm. Be always watchfully diligent also in driving away thoughts, because it is no more necessary [Col. 0410] to restrain the flesh from seductive stimulation than to guard the mind from the phantasm of shameful thoughts. I knew a brother in Christ who observed this strict rule for his mind with constant and wakeful attention: whenever a suggestion of lust crept in, he would immediately say to his thought, as if ready to set out on a journey: “Let us go about the cemetery.”

At once, in imagination, he surveyed all cemeteries and tombs, and with curious scrutiny examined the poison and pus of decaying corpses, the swarming worms, and the foul juices of rotting flesh. When he considered that those bodies, once flourishing in their vigor, had become subject to these miseries, he did not doubt that his own body too would shortly become what he now saw those bodies to be. He gives pleasure to lust who offers his eye to corruption; nor does lust find lodging in a mind occupied with a grave. Oh, how often that brother pressed a glowing knife and ploughshare, like a kind of cautery, upon his genitals, so that, as the fire of the seared flesh crackled, smoke seemed by some force to rise even to his nostrils.

When, therefore, some necessity requires that you cannot refuse conversation with a woman, always look with sidelong eyes; as though intent elsewhere, make your presence absent from yourself; speak from afar; withdraw even while conversing; and, with your gaze fixed upon the ground, conduct yourself so that you cannot judge whether her face is pale or flushed. Once, when the blessed Romuald was returning from a conversation with Countess Sibylla, he is said to have cunningly remarked to the disciple accompanying him: “What an elegant and handsome-faced woman—were it not, alas, that she suffered the loss of one eye!” The disciple replied: “Far be it, master: just as her face is certainly beautiful, so too, as I observed attentively, her eyes are both equally sound.” The master immediately rebuked him with the sharpest correction: “And who,” he said, “taught you to look upon women’s faces?” Then the disciple, seeing that he had been caught, blushed in repentance. [lacuna], CXLV, 722, 723, 724.

RUPERT, abbot of Deutz.—“You shall not commit adultery.” The permission of the Law once made this commandment more lax; now the severity of the Gospel binds it more firmly and tightly. For Moses commanded that a bill of divorce be given. But Christ … Therefore, not to commit adultery is a commandment; but above this commandment, to abstain entirely from marriage is counsel. [lacuna], CLXVII, 1726, 1727. Book on the violation of virginity, CLXX, 545.

SMARAGDUS, abbot.—On continence, CII, 623. What the impulse of the flesh is, CII, 685.

TAIO, bishop of Saragossa.—The evil of lust is committed either in thought [Col. 0411] or in deed. For when our crafty adversary is driven from the effect of action, he endeavors to pollute the secret recesses of thought. The Lord says to the serpent: “You shall crawl upon your breast and belly.” The serpent crawls on its belly when the slippery enemy exercises lust through human members subjected to him, even to the completion of the act; but the serpent crawls on its breast when it pollutes in thought those whom it cannot overcome in the act of lust. Whoever performs lust in action: for him the serpent crawls from the belly; but whoever turns it over in his mind as something to be performed: for him the serpent crawls from the breast. To flee burning Sodom is to shun the unlawful fires of the flesh. Whoever, lifted up by the successes of this world, feels himself tempted by the stings of lust through the flattering joy of the heart, should call Joseph’s deed to mind and keep himself in the citadel of chastity (*Morals*, XXX, 10), LXXX, 945.

We must understand very carefully that what the mind suffers from the temptation of the flesh is one thing, and what occurs when it is bound to pleasures through consent is another. Often it is struck by an evil thought but resists; often, however, when it conceives something perverse, it turns it over within itself even in desire. Certainly, an unclean thought does not defile the mind when it knocks, but when it subjugates the mind to itself through delight. Paul, the outstanding preacher, says: “Let no temptation overtake you except what is human.” Human temptation is that by which we are often touched in thought even unwillingly, because it belongs to the burden of corruptible human nature in ourselves that unlawful things may sometimes enter the mind. Demonic, rather than human, temptation occurs when the mind binds itself by consent to what the corruption of the flesh suggests.

The same Paul says: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body.” He forbade sin not to exist but to reign in the mortal body, because in corruptible flesh temptation by sin cannot fail to exist for the human race, but it can fail to reign. To be tempted by sin is sin from which, while we live, we are never wholly and perfectly free; since holy preaching could not expel this, it took its kingship from the dwelling-place of our heart, so that unlawful desire, although it often secretly inserts itself like a thief into our good thoughts, may at least not rule if it enters.

It is written in Genesis: “The Lord rained sulphur and fire upon Sodom and Gomorrah.” What is signified by sulphur but the stench of the flesh, and by fire but the heat of carnal desire? Therefore, when the Lord decided to punish the crimes of the flesh of the inhabitants of Sodom and Gomorrah, he marked the stain of their crime in the very character of the punishment: sulphur has stench, fire heat. Thus it was fitting that those who had burned toward perverse desires from the stench of the flesh should perish together by sulphur and fire, so that through a just punishment they might learn what they had done through an unjust desire, LXXX, 946, 947. On virgins and the continent, ibid., 858. On the concupiscence of the eyes, ibid., 939. On lust, ibid., 945.

TERTULLIAN, priest of Carthage.—Adultery, which is also a matter of fornication, is shown by the first Law of God itself to be reckoned among crimes of the greatest wickedness according to the nature of the deed. For after forbidding the worship of other gods and the making of idols; after commending reverence for the Sabbath; after commanding the duty toward parents, second only to that toward God, the Law set down no other commandment for establishing and enjoining such duties than: “You shall not commit adultery.” … Understand now what kind of offense it is whose prohibition was placed after idolatry. Nothing is further from the first than the second; nothing is as close to the first as the second; that which becomes another thing from the first is, in some manner, first. Therefore adultery is akin to idolatry. For idolatry, often reproached to the people under the name of adultery and fornication, will be joined to it in fate, as also in sequence; it will cling to it also in condemnation, as it does in arrangement. Moreover, after first saying, “You shall not commit adultery,” it adds, “You shall not kill”; it surely aggravated adultery by putting it before homicide.

Therefore, on the very front of the most holy Law, in the first headings of the heavenly edict, where the proscription of the principal offenses is marked, discern from its place its measure, from its order its standing, and from its adjacency the merit of each. Evil too has its rank, when it is placed at the top or in the middle of the worst offenses. I see a certain procession and tribunal for adultery: on one side the leadership of preceding idolatry, on the other the accompaniment of following homicide. Between the two most eminent summits of crimes it has doubtless taken its worthy seat, and has filled the place between them, as though vacant, with an equal authority of crime. Who will tear it, enclosed by such flanks and buttressed by such ribs, from the body of its companions—from the bond of neighboring crimes and the embrace of kindred wickedness? Idolatry and homicide cry aloud: “Adultery is our wedge, our joint. … Divine Scripture has made us one body [Col. 0412]. … I, idolatry, very often furnish occasions for adultery. My groves and mountains, my living waters, and the temples themselves in cities know how much we contrive to overthrow chastity. I too, homicide, sometimes labor for adultery. To pass over tragedies: poisoners and magicians today know how many adulterous affairs I avenge, how many rivalries I defend, how many guards, informers, and accomplices I remove. Midwives also know how many adulterous conceptions are murdered.

“Even among Christians adultery is not without us: there is idolatry where there is the work of unclean spirits; and there too is homicide, where a human being, when defiled, is slain. Therefore, either not even for them … You condemn an idolater and a murderer once for all, yet do you extract the adulterer from between them—the successor of idolatry, the predecessor of homicide, the colleague of both?” … II, 987–989. On public spectacles, I, 627. On women’s dress, ibid., 1303. On the veiling of virgins, II, 887. On the exhortation to chastity, ibid., 913. On modesty, ibid., 979. On Sodom, ibid., 1101.

## SECOND SECTION

### Seventh Commandment

> “You shall not steal.”

HUGH OF SAINT-VICTOR.—The fourth commandment is: “You shall not steal.” Sacrilege is included under theft, namely, taking either a sacred thing from a sacred place, a non-sacred thing from a sacred place, or a sacred thing from a non-sacred place. Sacred is called whatever is assigned to divine worship, whether it is a temple or property of a temple. Robbery also is included under theft; for he who prohibited theft did not permit robbery. Saint Augustine says of this: “So long as the thing on account of which the sin was committed is not restored, repentance is not performed but feigned.” Usury is included under robbery. Jerome: “There is no difference between seeking usury, defrauding, and robbing. Lend to your brother, receive what you gave, and seek nothing additional.” Augustine: “Usury is receiving more than one gives.” What the children of Israel did to the Egyptians was not theft, because they did it by a familiar command. For if he who makes the law commands otherwise, one who obeys him does not transgress the law, CLXXVI, 122, 356.

INNOCENT III, pope.—On the crime of usury, CCXVI, 1237. On restitution, CCXVI, 1238.

IVO (Saint), bishop of Chartres.—In the ancient statutes of the Church there is a decree that one who takes another’s property shall not go unpunished, but shall restore everything with an additional amount. Hence it is written also in the Gospel: “If I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold”; and the laws of the world provide: “Whoever steals another’s property shall restore elevenfold to the person whose property was plundered, restoring what was taken.” [lacuna], CLXI, 803.

“The Lord said to Moses: ‘Let a man ask from his neighbor, and a woman from her neighbor, gold and silver vessels and clothing.’” No one should think that an example is here provided for despoiling one’s neighbor in this way. For God commanded this, knowing what each person ought to suffer; and the Israelites did not commit theft, but rendered service at God’s command, just as when an officer of a judge kills someone whom the judge has ordered killed: if he does it on his own initiative, he is undoubtedly a murderer, even if he kills someone whom he knows ought to have been killed by the judge, CLXI, 803.

It is punishable to take secretly; it is punishable much more severely to seize openly. Therefore the commandment forbids taking from an unwilling person, whether secretly or openly. For under the name of theft every unlawful appropriation of another’s property is rightly understood. He did not permit robbery who prohibited theft, but certainly intended robbery too to be understood under the name of theft in the Law of the Old Testament. For by the part he signified the whole: whatever is unlawfully taken from the possessions of one’s neighbor, ibid.

If another’s property, on account of which sin has been committed, is not restored when it can be restored, repentance is not performed but feigned. But if repentance is truly performed, the sin will not be forgiven unless what was taken is restored—provided, as I have said, that it can be restored. For often someone who takes loses it, either by suffering other wicked persons or by himself living wickedly, and has nothing else with which to make restitution. To such a person we certainly cannot say, “Restore what you took,” unless we believe that he has it and is denying it. In that case, if he suddenly endures torments because he is thought to possess what he should restore, there is no injustice; for, even if he lacks the means to repay the stolen money, nevertheless, while he is compelled to repay it through bodily hardships, he pays the penalties for the sin by which it was wickedly taken. Yet it is not inhumane to intercede even for such people—not in order that another’s property should not be restored, but lest one person rage fruitlessly against another, CLXI, 803, 804.

Many more matters on these subjects remain, CLXI, 804–808.

PETER LOMBARD, bishop of Paris.—The fourth commandment is: “You shall not steal,” under which sacrilege and every robbery are forbidden. For he who prohibited theft did not permit robbery, but intended every unlawful appropriation of another’s property rightly to be understood under the name of theft. Sacrilege is committed in three ways: namely, when either a sacred thing is taken from a sacred place, a non-sacred thing from a sacred place, or a sacred thing from a non-sacred place. Sacred, however, is called whatever has been dedicated to divine worship, such as a church or church property. Hence usury also is forbidden, being included under robbery.

Jerome says: “There is no difference between seeking usury, defrauding, and robbing. Lend to your brother and receive what you gave, and seek nothing additional, because surplus is reckoned as usury.” For, as Saint Augustine says, “Usury occurs when someone exacts more, by injury or in any kind of thing, than he has received.” Jerome again: “Some think that usury exists only in money; but let them understand that usury means excess—namely, whatever exceeds what has been given. Thus, if in winter we give ten bushels and at harvest receive fifteen.”

But if the question is asked concerning the children of Israel, who, at the Lord’s command, borrowed gold and silver vessels and precious clothing from the Egyptians and carried them away, whether they committed theft, we say that those who did this at God’s command in order to obey did not commit theft and did not sin at all. Hence Augustine: “The Israelites did not commit theft, but rendered service at God’s command. For this was commanded by God, who gave the law. Just as an officer of a judge kills without sin one whom the law commands to be killed; but if he does it of his own will, he is a murderer, even if he kills someone whom he knows is to be killed by a judge. But the weak persons who deceived the Egyptians from greed were permitted, rather than commanded, to do this to those who justly suffered such things. …” CXCII, 833.

RABANUS MAURUS, abbot.—On not receiving usury, CVIII, 543, 934. On interest, CIX, 973. Against fraud, CX, 117.

RODULPHUS, bishop of Bourges.—On usury and interest, CXIX, 720. On theft and robbery, CXIX, 721.

RUPERT, abbot of Deutz.—“You shall not steal.” In accordance with this commandment, when the Apostle had said, “Let him who stole steal no more,” he immediately added the counsel: “Rather,” he says, “let him labor, working with his hands at what is good, so that he may have something to give to one who suffers need.” Nevertheless, this counsel differs little from the force of a commandment. For when he says, “Let him labor, working with his hands at what is good,” he wishes it to be understood: if he wishes to eat. For elsewhere too he says: “If anyone is unwilling to work, neither let him eat.” Likewise, by saying, “Let him give to one who suffers need,” he wishes it to be understood: if he wishes to be helped himself in necessities. [lacuna], CLXVII, 1727.

STEPHEN OF MURET (Saint), abbot of Grandmont.—On usury, CCIV, 1111.

TERTULLIAN, priest of Carthage.—On usury, II, 398.

### Eighth Commandment

> “You shall not speak false testimony against your neighbor.”

ADALGERUS, monk of Saint Benedict.—On restraint of the tongue, CXXXIV, 922.

ALAN OF LILLE.—Whoever wishes to avoid the destruction caused by lying should shape himself by these maxims. We read in the Gospel: “You shall not bear false testimony”; and Paul says: “Putting away falsehood, speak truth, each one with his neighbor.” Solomon says: “He who lies is a deceitful witness. …” Isidore says: “Everything that departs from truth is iniquity. O man, how far you depart from the highest truth while you devote yourself to fabricated lies! How do you think you will come to the True One if, in your words, you disagree with truth? I do not know with what conscience one asks God by the tongue that has belched forth a lie. No sin brands the conscience as does the mark of lying. Although every mortal sin alienates a person from truth, no evil does so more than lying, which detracts from the nature of truth.

“This is what devises false testimony, fabricates flatteries, invents frauds, and completes detractions. Through this vice one speaks with heart and mouth and becomes divided against oneself: one denies with the mouth what one holds in the heart. Through this vice heart contradicts heart and mouth opposes heart. This vice begets heresy, produces schisms, breeds suspicions, devises unheard-of rumors, colors reproaches, conceals what should be exposed, and exposes what should be concealed. It attends perjuries, sits beside dishonorable actions, and opposes all things which by natural law tend toward the advantage of one’s neighbor, since it even attacks truth itself. It contains in itself a rust of such great wickedness that it can be excused on no grounds. Natural affection did not free the midwives from its guilt; rational fear did not free the Gibeonites; error of mind did not free Peter; nor did the provision of necessity free Ananias.

“No sin so breathes toward trickery, reaches for fraud, looks to deception, and pants for betrayal as the vice of lying, the disgrace of falsehood. O children of men, how long, heavy of heart, [lacuna] do you so greatly wish to pursue the vanity of our nature, you who alter truth even in speech? But if there is guilt now in falsehood, there will not be lacking punishment in truth hereafter; and one who is now false through lying will hereafter be true in Gehenna. You know that through lying you imitate the devil, the father of lies, who did not stand in truth but fell through the vanity of pride. His children are those who depart from truth; his accomplices are those who indulge falsehoods. O man, if there is falsehood in your lie, there will be truth in your guilt,” CCX, 164–166. Against verbosity, CCX, 162. Against detractions, CCX, 166. Against lying, CCX, 164.

AMBROSE (Saint), bishop of Milan.—Guard must be set upon the tongue, XIV, 1040. On fleeing lying, XVII, 666. On avoiding detraction, XVII, 1062. How truth speaks, XVII, 1070. On excessive talk, XVII, 1071.

ANSELM (Saint), archbishop of Canterbury.—On lying, CLIX, 680. On detraction, CLIX, 685.

ANSELM (Saint), canon of Laon.—“Do not judge,” CLXII, 1313.

ATHANASIUS (Saint), priest.—Guard must be set upon the mouth, XVIII, 83.

AUGUSTINE (Saint), bishop of Hippo.—One must consider what lying is. But here a most difficult and intricate question arises: whether it belongs to the duty of a just person ever to lie. For some go so far as to maintain that even to commit perjury, and to say something false concerning matters pertaining to the worship of God or concerning the very nature of God, is sometimes a good and pious act. To me, however, it seems that every lie is indeed a sin; but it makes a great difference with what intention and about what matters each person lies. For the person who lies with a view to helping does not sin in the same way as the person who lies with a view to harming; nor does one who, by lying, sends a traveller onto the wrong road do as much harm as one who corrupts the way of life by deceptive falsehood. Certainly, no one who says what is false while believing it to be true is to be judged a liar; for, so far as he is concerned, he does not deceive, but is himself deceived. Therefore, one who holds falsehoods, carelessly believed, to be true is to be blamed not for lying but sometimes for rashness. Conversely, so far as he is concerned, that person lies who says what is true while believing it false. For, as regards his intention, because he does not say what he thinks, he does not speak truth, although what he says is found to be true; nor is one in any way free from lying who unknowingly speaks the truth with his mouth while knowingly lying in his will, XL, 240.

For not everyone who says what is false lies, if he believes or supposes that what he says is true. The difference between believing and supposing is this: sometimes one who believes recognizes that he does not know what he believes, although he has no doubt whatever concerning the thing which he knows himself not to know, if he believes it most firmly; but one who supposes thinks that he knows what he does not know. Whoever asserts what he holds in his mind either as a belief or as an opinion does not lie, even if it is false. For he owes this fidelity to his assertion: that through it he should utter what he holds in his mind and possess it as he utters it. Yet he is not therefore without fault, even though he does not lie, if he either believes what should not be believed or thinks himself to know what he does not know, even if it is true; for he treats as known what is unknown. Consequently, the liar is one who has one thing in his mind and states another in words or by any other means of expression. Thus the liar is also said to have a double heart: that is, a double thought—one concerning the thing that he either knows or thinks to be true and does not state; the other concerning the thing he puts forward instead of it, knowing or thinking it to be false. Hence it follows that one may say what is false without lying, if one thinks it is as one says, though it is not so; and that one may say what is true while lying, if one thinks it false and asserts it as true, though in reality it is as one asserts. For a person is to be judged a liar or not a liar by the judgment of his own mind, not by the truth or falsehood of the things themselves. . . . But the liar’s fault is, in making a statement, the desire to deceive: whether he deceives when someone believes his false statement; or does not deceive, either when he is not believed or when, intending to deceive, he states as true something he does not think true. . . . , XL, 188–189.

Is it ever useful to assert something false with the intention of deceiving? Those who think so bring forward testimonies for their opinion, recalling that Sarah, after laughing, denied to the angels that she had laughed; that Jacob, questioned by his father, answered that he was Esau, his elder son; that the Egyptian midwives, so that the newborn Hebrew children might not be killed, also lied, and were approved and rewarded by God; and, selecting many examples of the same kind, they recall the lies of persons whom one would not dare to blame, and thus confess that a lie can sometimes be not merely undeserving of reproof but even worthy of praise. . . .

Against them, those who hold that one must never lie argue much more strongly. They first employ divine authority, since it is written in the Decalogue itself: “You shall not bear false witness”; and this category embraces every lie, for whoever asserts anything bears witness to his own mind. Likewise: “A lying mouth kills the soul,” etc. . . . They say that they are not alarmed by those examples of lies brought forward from the ancient books, where whatever was done may be taken figuratively, even though it really occurred; but whatever is done or said figuratively is not a lie. For every assertion must be referred to that which it asserts. But everything done or said figuratively asserts what it signifies to those for whose understanding it is presented. Hence it must be believed that those persons who are recorded as having possessed authority worthy of prophetic times did and said prophetically all things written concerning them; and that no less prophetically there happened to them whatever happened in such a way that it was judged worthy to be committed to memory and writing by the same prophetic Spirit.

But concerning the midwives, since they cannot say that, for the sake of signifying a future truth by a prophetic spirit, they reported one thing to Pharaoh in place of another, they say that, though something done through them may have signified something without their knowing it, they were approved and rewarded by God according to their own degree. . . . , XL, 491–492.

Therefore, from the books of the New Testament, apart from the Lord’s figurative sayings, if one considers the lives and morals of the saints and their deeds and sayings, nothing of this kind can be produced that invites imitation in lying, XL, 492, 540, 543. Since eternal life is lost through lying, according to Sacred Scripture, one must never lie for anyone’s temporal life. . . , XL, 495–500. The various kinds of lying having been condemned without any doubt, there follows another kind, as though for those rising step by step toward better things, which is commonly attributed to kindly and good persons: when the liar not only does no harm to another, but also benefits someone. The entire dispute concerns this kind: whether one who thus benefits another by acting against truth harms himself; or whether the truth that alone must be spoken is that which illuminates minds themselves by an inner and immutable light. Certainly, he acts against some truth, because—even if the bodily senses are deceived—one acts against truth who says that something is so, or not so, when neither his mind nor his senses nor his opinion or belief reports this to him. Whether, then, one who benefits another in this way does not harm himself, or whether he does not harm himself by that compensation through which he benefits another, is a great question. If so, it should consequently also be permissible to benefit oneself by a lie that harms no one. But these points are connected, and, once granted, they necessarily draw along consequences that are highly troubling. For if one asks what harm is done to a person overflowing with superfluous wealth if, out of countless thousands of measures of grain, he loses one bushel—which bushel could nevertheless help the thief toward necessary sustenance—it will follow that theft too can be committed without blame, and false witness spoken without sin. What could be said more perverse than this? . . . XL, 501, 510, 546, 547.

Passages of the Gospel that seem to support lying are examined; likewise passages from the Acts of the Apostles and the Epistles of the blessed Apostle Paul. . . XC, 536–540.

It is also written: “But I say to you, do not swear at all.” Yet the Apostle himself swore in his Epistles. . . . Thus he shows how these words are to be understood: namely, lest by swearing one come to readiness to swear, from readiness to habit, and thus from habit fall into perjury. Therefore, he is not found to have sworn except in writing, where more careful reflection does not permit a hasty tongue. . . ; the word “at all” is included so that, as far as lies in you, you do not seek, love, or desire an oath as though it were a good thing, with any delight. . . , XL, 507–509.

And concerning false witness, which is placed among the ten commandments of the Law, it cannot at all be disputed that love of truth must be kept in the heart, and falsehood uttered to the person before whom testimony is given. For when one speaks to God alone, then truth need only be embraced in the heart; but when one speaks to a human being, truth must also be spoken by the bodily mouth, because a human being is not an inspector of the heart. Yet it is reasonably asked, concerning testimony itself, before whom each person is a witness. For we are not witnesses before all persons to whom we speak, but before those for whom it is fitting and due to know or believe the truth through us: for example, a judge, lest he err in judging; or a person instructed in religious teaching, lest he err in faith or waver in doubt through uncertainty about the teacher’s authority. But when one questions you, or wishes to learn something from you, who seeks a matter that does not concern him or which it is not advantageous for him to know, he seeks not a witness but a betrayer. Therefore, if you lie to him, perhaps you will be free from false witness, but you certainly will not be free from lying, CL, 511–513.

AUGUSTINE (Saint), bishop of Hippo.—With regard to the saying, “You shall not bear false witness against your neighbour,” it is customary to ask whether this commandment is directed against those who say that one ought to lie when that lie benefits someone and does no harm to the person to whom one lies. For such a lie is not “against your neighbour,” so that Scripture might seem to have added this phrase for that reason, though it could have said briefly, “You shall not bear false witness,” just as it said, “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal.” But this is a great question and cannot suitably be explained by those in haste: how such sayings as “You will destroy all who speak falsehood” and “Not to wish to lie [is] every lie,” and others of this kind, are to be understood, XXXIV, 622–623.

FULGENTIUS (Saint), bishop of Ruspe.—Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that every creature of God is good and that nothing is to be rejected which is received with thanksgiving; and that servants of God who abstain from meat or wine do so not because they reject as unclean things made by God, but abstain from stronger food and drink solely for the chastening of the body, LXV, 704. GREGORY THE GREAT (Saint), pope.—One must not judge rashly, LXXV, 533. On deceit, LXXV, 586. On much speaking, LXXV, 800. On detractors, LXXV, 1070. On lying, LXXVI, 40. To be silent is often to be wise, LXXVI, 258. On an idle word, LXXVI, 634.

HERVAEUS, archbishop of Rheims.—On liars, CXXXII, 706.

JEROME (Saint), priest of Stridon.—One must withdraw from slander, XXIV, 526. On an idle word, XXVI, 82. “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth,” XXVI, 513. One must not be deceived by the empty words of the insolent, XXVI, 522. “Who speaks truth in his heart,” XXVI, 854. “Set a guard over your mouth,” XXVI, 1235. On avoiding detraction, XXX, 369. On restraining the tongue, XXX, 411.

HILARY (Saint), bishop of Poitiers.—On the helpful lie, IX, 304. What is calumny? IX, 618. Slips of the tongue and remedies, IX, 826.

HILDEBERT, bishop of Le Mans.—On the tongue, CLXXI, 516.

HUGH OF SAINT VICTOR.—The eighth commandment is: “You shall not bear false witness.” Here perjury is forbidden; but because every perjury is a lie, it must be said what a lie is and how a lie is perjury. Augustine: To lie is to speak contrary to what is felt in the mind. An objection is raised from Jacob, who said to his father, “I am Esau,” at his mother’s counsel; for he said contrary to his conscience, since he truly knew that he was not Esau. Augustine nevertheless says: “What Jacob did at his mother’s direction, so that he might seem to deceive his father, was not a lie but a mystery.” Again, an objection is raised from Joseph, who said to his brothers, “By Pharaoh’s life, you are spies,” and said that he divined by means of a cup—though this was not true. Some say that this was a lie, but not such a lie as is sinful. For they say that not every lie is a sin, but only that which is spoken with the intention to deceive. Jacob’s intention, however, was to obey his mother. Similarly, Joseph did not intend to deceive, but did not wish to reveal himself so soon. But Augustine does not seem to hold this view, since he says that one must not lie even for someone’s life. Therefore it seems better to say that they did not lie, but said this by a familiar command, just as the Hebrews too are excused from theft by a familiar command. For when Jacob’s mother commanded this to him through the Holy Spirit, in obeying his mother he obeyed the Holy Spirit. . . . Augustine: Certainly, no one who says what is false while thinking it true is to be judged a liar; for, so far as he is concerned, he does not deceive but is himself deceived. Conversely, that person lies who says what is true while thinking it false. A lie is a false signification by speech with the intention of deceiving. When you lie from a motive of humility, if you were not a sinner before lying, you become guilty through the lie. For if you call yourself a sinner and do not believe it, truth is not in you. It is permissible to conceal the truth, so as not to betray one sought for killing; but one ought not deny the truth. An objection is raised against this: if the intention is good, the action is good; and the person who denies having seen him, though he has seen him, acts with a good intention in order to save him from death. The reply is that an intention which is not according to knowledge, though pious, must not be called good. For a good intention must possess both piety and rectitude, because mercy without justice is not a virtue. An objection is raised from the midwives and Rahab, who were rewarded for such a lie. But, as Saint Augustine says, they were rewarded not for lying but for piety. For two things are considered in lies of this kind: the affection of piety from which these statements are made, and the lie itself. Let the affection be rewarded, not the lie. Playful lies and lies of irony are not lies.

Now it must be considered what perjury is. Perjury is a lie confirmed by an oath. If anyone happens to have sworn to do some evil to another, it is better to break the oath than fulfill it. Yet he ought to repent because he swore rashly. Isidore: “An oath by which evil is heedlessly promised must not be kept.” For example, if someone pledges perpetual fidelity to an adulteress, it is more tolerable not to fulfill the oath than to remain in fornication. Bede: “David indeed swore by the Lord to kill the foolish man Nabal; but at the first intercession of the prudent woman Abigail he withdrew his threats, recalled the sword to its sheath, and did not grieve that he had incurred any guilt through such perjury.” Isidore likewise says: “He who swears by verbal trickery—God, who is the examiner of thoughts, understands it as the person to whom the oath is sworn understands it.” This must be explained thus: “by verbal trickery,” that is, one who swears in order to defraud another. God, however, truly understands it in the way the person unjustly deceived understands it. That is, if a person, in order to avoid danger—not in order to harm his neighbour, but to free himself or another from necessity—speaks the truth and nevertheless conceals by that truth something which, if disclosed, would bring danger, he does not sin; as Abraham, in saying of Sarah, “She is my sister,” did not lie, since she was his sister, that is, his kinswoman; and even if he had sworn this, he would not have sinned, CLXXVI, 121–124.

HUGH OF SAINT VICTOR, canon regular.—On lying, CLXXVI, 122. On the tongue, CLXXVI, 943.

ISIDORE MERCATOR.—Detraction must be avoided, CXXX, 99.

IVO, bishop of Chartres.—Description of lying, CLXI, 793.

JOHN OF SALISBURY, bishop of Chartres.—On detractors, CXCIX, 701.

JONAS, bishop of Orléans.—Among the ten commandments which the Lord gave on Mount Sinai through his servant Moses to the Israelite people, he expressly forbade false witness: “You shall not bear false witness.” Thus the just Lord admonished them to love justice and forbade them to utter falsehood. Consider who set before mortals such an edict to be observed: namely, the King of kings, Lord of lords, and creator of all things. Amid flames of fire and flashing lightning, the crash of thunder and the blast of the trumpet, he promulgated this law with terror: by it evil is forbidden and good commanded; truth is held to be pursued and falsehood avoided. And what is very dreadful and fearful, it is despised, since transgression of this divine commandment has become so customary for some that they almost practice it as though it were a law; and when they utter it, they believe that they commit no sin, or almost none, unless they confirm by an oath that what they have falsely uttered is true. Such persons deceive themselves with vain hope. . . . False witnesses are commanded in Deuteronomy to be examined with the greatest care. . . . Saint Isidore says: “A false-speaking witness is answerable to three persons: first, to God, whom he despises by his oath; second, to the judge, whom he deceives by lying; finally, to the innocent person, whom he harms by false witness.” When false witnesses have been convicted, the falsehood of the lie is discovered slowly; but if they are separated, it is quickly made manifest by the examination of the judge, CVI, 225–227.

First, Saint Augustine says in *Against Lying*, chapter 14, is the capital lie that must be fled far from: that committed in religious teaching. No one should be brought to this lie under any circumstances. Second is that which unjustly harms someone: such a lie benefits no one and harms someone. Third is that which so benefits one person as to harm another, though not by bodily impurity. Fourth is lying merely from the lust of lying and deceiving; this is the true lie. Fifth is that done from a desire to please, by agreeable speech. Once all these have been entirely avoided and rejected, there follows the sixth kind: that which harms no one and benefits someone, as when a person, knowing where another’s money is, lies that he does not know, lest it be unjustly taken. Seventh is that which harms no one and benefits someone, as when a person unwilling to betray one sought for death lies—not only concerning a just and innocent person but even concerning a guilty one—because Christian discipline requires that one neither despair of anyone’s correction nor close to anyone the way of repentance. . . . Therefore, one must not lie to a person seeking where one is who has entrusted himself to one’s protection; rather one should answer, “I shall neither betray nor lie.” . . . The eighth kind of lie is that which harms no one and benefits someone by preserving him from bodily impurity. Therefore one must not lie in the teaching of piety: it is a great crime and the first kind of detestable lie. One must not lie in the second kind, because injustice must be done to no one. One must not lie in the third kind, because one person must not be helped to another’s injury. One must not lie in the fourth kind, because of the lust for lying, which is vicious in itself. One must not lie in the fifth kind, because even truth itself should not be stated for the purpose of pleasing human beings; how much less a lie, which is disgraceful in itself precisely because it is a lie! One must not lie in the sixth kind; for not even the truth of testimony is rightly corrupted for anyone’s temporal advantage and safety. No one is to be led to eternal salvation by the aid of a lie; for no one is to be converted from bad conduct to good conduct by conduct which, once converted, he himself must practice toward others. Thus he will be converted not to good but to bad conduct, when, on becoming converted, he is offered for imitation the very thing that was done to convert him. Nor must one lie in the seventh kind; for someone’s temporal advantage or safety must not be preferred to the fulfillment of faithfulness. Nor, if anyone is so perversely affected by our rightly performed actions that he becomes worse in mind and further removed from piety, are right actions therefore to be abandoned; for we must chiefly refer ourselves to that goal to which we ought to call and invite those whom we love as ourselves. . . . Nor must one lie in the eighth kind, because in good persons there is chastity of mind and purity of body; and among evils, what we ourselves do is greater than what we allow to be done. Among these eight kinds, the less one sins in lying, the nearer one rises to the eighth; the more one sins, the nearer one rises to the first. But whoever thinks there is any kind of lie which is not a sin will shamefully deceive himself while imagining himself an honourable deceiver of others, CVI, 227–228.

PETER LOMBARD, bishop of Paris.—The eighth commandment is: “You shall not speak false witness against your neighbour,” where the crime of lying and perjury is forbidden. For such a lie is not against one’s neighbour; this, they say, is why Scripture seems to have added the phrase, CXCII, 833.
