RICHARD OF SAINT VICTOR.—On the usefulness of discernment, CXCVI, 48. On guarding the tongue, CXCVI, 461. On the vice of fraudulence, CXCVI, 1358.

RUFINUS, priest of Aquileia.—On lying, XXI, 660. On the good of truth, XXI, 695.

RUPERT, abbot of Deutz.—“You shall not speak false witness against your neighbour.” Concerning this commandment, it is a great and praiseworthy thing, according to time and circumstance, to endure falsehood when one is able to refute the testimony, following the example of our Lord: “At last two false witnesses came and said, ‘This man said: I am able to destroy [Col. 0420] the temple of God, and after three days to rebuild it.’” When they said this, and the chief priest also rose and pressed him, saying, “Do you answer nothing to what these men testify against you?” Jesus, however, says the Evangelist, remained silent. Likewise, “when he was accused by the chief priests and elders,” and Pilate pressed him, saying, “Do you not hear how many things they testify against you?” “He did not answer him one word, so that the governor marvelled greatly.” Why? Because, he says, “If I tell you, you will not believe me; but if I ask you, you will not answer me nor let me go.” Therefore, let whoever approves this example of enduring the rashness of false testimony also approve its rational basis: namely, that if there is hope that falsehood can be corrected by a true answer, one should answer and, by answering, gain the souls of those who speak against one—if not all of them, at least some of those who would otherwise be led to shed blood, not knowingly or deliberately but through false witness. Thus Jeremiah, when priests and prophets testified against him before the princes and all the people, saying, “This man deserves the judgment of death . . . ,” did not remain silent, but said, “The Lord sent me to prophesy . . . .” Conversely Naboth the Jezreelite, because he was accused and judged not through error or sudden agitation of mind, but through the malicious deliberation of Jezebel and the nobles or elders, with diabolical men planted as witnesses, is recorded to have remained silent and given no answer—rightly, indeed, and wisely. For he would have poured out speech in vain where there was no hearing. . . , CLXVII, 1727–1728. On detraction, CLXVIII, 1292. On rash judgment, CLXVIII, 1450.

SMARAGDUS, abbot.—On much speaking, CII, 634.

STEPHEN OF MURET, abbot of Grandmont.—On speaking truth, CCIV, 1101.

TAIO, bishop of Saragossa.—The way of truth is altogether plain, and the road of lying is hard. . . . Whoever, abandoning truth, resolves to lie in order to deceive the hearer’s mind, how great his labour is in carefully guarding against the discovery of his very deceit! For he sets before his eyes what may be answered him by those who know the truth, and with much thought considers how, by arguments of falsehood, he may overcome the evidence of truth. The laborious deceit of lying covers itself on every side, and against the point at which it may be detected seeks an answer resembling truth; whereas, if he wished to speak truth, he could certainly do so without effort. Every lie is iniquity, and every iniquity a lie, because whatever disagrees with truth undoubtedly departs from equity. Sometimes it is worse to devise a lie than to speak one. For speaking is often due to precipitancy, but devising to deliberate wickedness; and who does not know how greatly the guilt differs according as one lies through precipitancy or design? Every lie must be avoided with the utmost care, although sometimes a kind of lie may involve lighter guilt, when someone lies in order to assist another. . . . Perfect persons also carefully avoid even this kind of lie, so that neither may anyone’s life be defended by their deceit nor may they harm their own souls while striving to benefit another’s flesh—although we believe this very kind of sin to be most easily forgiven. For if any fault is customarily cleansed by a subsequent pious action, how much more easily is this one wiped away, since piety itself, the mother of good action, accompanies it? Some attempt to maintain from the midwives’ deceit that this kind of lie is not a sin. Etc. On avoiding detraction, LXXX, 690. On much speaking, LXXX, 942. On lying, LXXX, 949.

TERTULLIAN, priest of Carthage.—On rash judgment, II, 400.

VALERIAN (Saint), bishop of Cimiez.—On the insolence of the mouth, LII, 706. On idle words, LII, 709.

WERNER, abbot.—On lying, CLVII, 1075.

WIBALD, abbot of Stavelot.—The distinction between lying and saying what is false, CLXXXIX, 1240.

ZACHARIAS, bishop of Chrysopolis.—One must neither judge nor condemn, CLXXXVI, 147.

## Ninth Commandment

“You shall not covet your neighbour’s wife.”

BEDE THE VENERABLE.—“You shall not covet your neighbour’s wife.” In this commandment he forbids the intention of adulterous thought. For it is one thing to do such a deed regarding a wife; another not to desire another man’s wife. Therefore there are two commandments: “You shall not commit adultery,” and “You shall not covet your neighbour’s wife,” XCIII, 375.

HUGH OF SAINT VICTOR.—The sixth commandment is: “You shall not covet your neighbour’s wife.” An objection is raised from the fact that the Lord, in the Gospel, when he completed the commandment “You shall not commit adultery,” says: “But I say to you: whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire [Col. 0421] her has already committed adultery with her.” But this was not an addition, since the same thing is prohibited in the Law in this commandment: “You shall not covet your neighbour’s wife.” For here concupiscence seems to be prohibited, as there. To this one may reply that this commandment, rightly understood, truly forbids both the act and the will; and those who, understanding it thus, abstained from evil in both deed and will were to be called not people of the Old Testament but of the New, and the Law thus understood was for them not old but new. Accordingly, no addition was made in the Gospel, but what had been hidden there is explained. But while the Law, rightly understood—not according to the letter but according to the spirit—prohibited both, carnal persons understood only one thing, namely the prohibition of the act, and this according to the letter of the Law. Hence: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life.” In this sense an addition was made, CLXXVI, 124, 358–359.

PETER COMESTOR.—“You shall not desire his wife, nor male slave, nor female slave, nor ox, nor ass, nor anything that is his.” Here he forbids covetousness of movable property. According to Origen, it is one commandment, CXCVIII, 1166.

(For completion, see the sixth commandment above in this index.)

RUPERT, abbot of Deutz.—“You shall not covet your neighbour’s house; nor desire his wife, nor male slave, nor female slave, nor ox, nor ass, nor anything that is his.” By the iron axe, as it were, of this tenth commandment, the root of every transgression is cut off or uprooted. “For covetousness is the root of all evils.” And it should be observed that universal covetousness is struck, as it were, by seven blows—a number commonly signifying totality—when it is forbidden by a sevenfold prohibition. For though it could have sufficed to say, “You shall not covet,” even if nothing had been added, he chose rather to make the prohibition sevenfold. First: “You shall not covet your neighbour’s house.” Second: “You shall not desire his wife.” Third: “Nor male slave.” Fourth: “Nor female slave . . . .” And seventh: “Nor anything that is his.” Therefore love of all things in the world is condemned, “because everything that is in the world,” says the Apostle James, “is the lust of the flesh . . . .” A transgressor of this commandment is already guilty as soon as he has the will to commit adultery, theft, or any such transgression, even if he cannot fulfill that will in act. And what shall we say concerning the addition of a counsel, when scarcely—or almost not at all—does anyone perfect appear in fulfilling this commandment? “For who shall boast that he has a chaste heart?” I boldly say that more persons are or have been found who accepted the counsel than who perfectly fulfilled this commandment. For we do not doubt that more persons—that is, some—have said or could say, “I desire to depart and be with Christ”; but no one, or very few, can boast of having a chaste heart. Let it therefore suffice to say this: not to covet is a commandment; to desire to depart and be with Christ is a counsel, CLXVII, 1728.

## Tenth Commandment

“You shall not covet your neighbour’s house, nor male slave, nor female slave, nor ox, nor ass, nor anything that is his.”

BEDE THE VENERABLE.—“You shall not covet your neighbour’s property.” In this commandment he condemns worldly ambition and restrains covetousness of possessions and desire for the world, XCIII, 375.

[Col. 0422] HUGH OF SAINT VICTOR.—The seventh commandment is: “You shall not covet your neighbour’s property”; there will and act are forbidden. Will, according to the literal sense . . . , CLXXVI, 124.

JOHN OF SALISBURY, bishop of Chartres.—Those who take care only to heap up riches wish nothing in life to be thought a better way than that which they have preferred to all others. In order that their need may be satisfied, different things are tested by different persons. No grave danger appears if hope in deceitful money shines forth. Love of money almost conquers nature itself and reduces things almost impossible to the capacity of the possible. To the miser nothing seems cheap or base; and while the crowd hisses, he consoles himself—indeed, applauds himself—as soon as he beholds coins in his chest. . . . So long as he makes profit, no part of the world seems inaccessible, and a greater fire of avarice overcomes even the heat of the torrid zone. . . . , CXCIX, 673.

PETER COMESTOR.—“You shall not covet your neighbour’s house.” According to Saint Augustine, here he forbids covetousness of another’s immovable property, CXCVIII, 1165.

(For completion, see the seventh commandment above in this index.)

PETER DAMIAN (St).—These are the ordinances of the divine law. From them proceed all the instruments of sacred Scripture; upon them rests the whole discipline of holy religion. These indeed are the bandages for flowing wounds; this is the wholesome medicine of languishing souls. All the plagues which we endured in Egypt—or rather, all the diseases of our inward sicknesses which we contracted upon the plain of worldly life—we must heal at Mount Sinai, that is, in the height of our sacred resolution. Therefore, O man, always be occupied with these things. Meditate diligently upon them; and, so to speak, continually grind these spices or ingredients in the mortar of your mind. Do not depart from this storehouse of aromatics; rather, here examine more carefully every hiding-place of your soul; search out all the secrets of your inward parts; apply medicines to wounds according as you perceive each to be suitable; and, once health has been attained, strive with sleepless diligence to preserve it. For a relapse is worse than a fever; and, as physicians maintain, diet is to be observed no less than treatment: that is, you must avoid foods which are harmful, and disdain as deadly poison whatever is noxious or found contrary to the antidotes you have received.

This, indeed, is that ten-stringed psaltery which we are commanded to strike with the frequent stroke of the plectrum. This is to set vibrating, by holy works, as many strings as there are commandments. When these have been rightly tuned, climb the mountain with Moses; embrace the arduousness of a stricter life, that you may deserve with him to hear: “Go and say to them, ‘Return to your tents’; but you, stand here with me, and I will speak to you all the commandments, ordinances, and judgments.” You too, having renounced the world, remain continually with the Lord and stand ready in his presence. For he does not say, “Sit here,” or “Recline with me,” but “Stand here with me,” so that you may understand that spiritual repose itself consists in the exercise of labour. Stand, then, with the Lord on the mountain, that you may continually wage an unyielding battle against the spirits of wickedness, and vigorously break the alluring impetuosities of carnal passions. Thus fight against the barbarian host of encroaching vices, so that, victor with Joshua, you may overcome rebellious kings; and that he himself may command you to tread upon their necks with victorious feet, so that, enriched with the spoils of your enemies and distinguished by the trophies of your victories, you may attain as a conqueror the land of promise—or rather, with the true Israelites, may always possess by hereditary gift the land of the living. CXLV, 694.

[Col. 0421]

CXLV. INDEX ON THE LOVE OF ENEMIES AND THE FORGIVENESS OF INJURIES, SHOWING FROM THE FATHERS THE EXTENT OF THE EFFECTS OF THIS OBLIGATION UPON US.

We divide this index into two parts: the first part treats the question in the chronological order of the Fathers, and the second in alphabetical order, etc.

FIRST PART. The question is here treated according to the chronological order of the Fathers.

[Col. 0421]

TERTULLIAN, presbyter and apologist of Carthage.—“Love [Col. 0422] your enemies and bless those who hate you, and pray for those who slander you”; say, “You are our brothers,” to those who hate you. For if those who are enemies, hate, and slander are to be called brothers, then he who commands that they be regarded as brothers has surely commanded that those who hate be blessed and that prayer be offered for slanderers, II, 395 ff. What could more wisely prohibit wrongdoing or evil speech? What could more thoroughly teach that injury should not be inflicted—or even retaliation for injury permitted? I, 499. Know that, in an overflowing abundance of kindness, we are commanded by the sacred books even to pray to God for our enemies and to wish good things for our persecutors, ibid., 446. For by divine discipline we are commanded also to love enemies and pray for those who persecute us, so that our goodness may be perfect and distinctive rather than common. For loving friends belongs to everyone; loving enemies belongs to Christians alone, ibid., 696.

CYPRIAN (St), bishop and martyr of Carthage.—Because one who is asked ought to relent and not imitate the offender; divine censure ought also to be applied, and, as it is written, “I forgave you your debt because you asked me.” Since God is forgiving, we too ought to be forgiving, IV, 314. By Christ’s examples, enemies are to be loved and patiently endured, ibid., 626.

ARNOBIUS, rhetorician and apologist.—For, since we have received Christ’s teaching that evil ought not to be repaid with evil, that enduring an injury is preferable to inflicting one, and that it is better to shed one’s own blood than to stain one’s hands and conscience with another’s blood, the ungrateful whole world has long possessed this benefit of Christ, by which the fury of savagery has been softened, V, 728.

LACTANTIUS, apologist.—Great is the reward of mercy, to which God promises that he will forgive every sin: “If,” he says, “you hear the prayers of your suppliant, I too will hear yours,” VI, 676 ff. Therefore, let us strive to be clothed with the garment of righteousness and piety, of which no one may strip us and which may furnish us everlasting adornment, ibid., 686.

HILARY (St), bishop of Poitiers.—The Lord commanded that we should be good to all, considering all things common to all, IX, 932.—For the merciful he prepares the gifts of mercy, so that he will bestow his mercy upon the merciful alone, ibid. Binding all persons together in mutual charity, he permits no prayer marked by enmity; but when those offering gifts at the altar remember that they have some dispute with their brethren, he commands them, once reconciled in human peace, to return to divine peace, passing into God’s charity through charity toward men, ibid., 938. Faith does not permit any injury to cause such grievous pain that it seeks revenge or that anyone becomes the avenger of an insult inflicted upon himself; for in God’s judgment there is greater consolation for those who have endured injury and a harsher punishment for those who injure others, ibid., 941. He summed up all things in perfect goodness: faith commands enemies to be loved and breaks the wanton impulses of human minds by the affection of common charity. Thus he calls us to imitate God, who grants sun and rain to good and evil alike, so that we too may be perfect as our heavenly Father is perfect, ibid., 942. Our enemies must always be forgiven, because the Lord always forgives us, ibid., 1022. Christ taught that all enemies should be loved, not rejecting Judas’s kiss, ibid., 804. Where malice is not evident, it is safer to judge others well than ill (by the same author). By love of enemies we are called to God both as an inheritance and as an object of imitation, ibid., 688.

FELIX (St), pope.—We who suffer unjust things ought to reserve them for the judgment of God, who will render to each according to his works, who thundered through his ministers: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay,” XIII, 26. We have not been taught to conquer in this way, but through the patience of long-suffering and humility . . . so that we may at least gradually be able to imitate him who deigned to humble himself for our sake, ibid., 27.

AMBROSE (St), bishop of Milan.—Hospitality is good: first, it has its reward in the gift of grace; then, what is greater, in the divine resurrection. In this dwelling-place we are all strangers, XIV, 435. Therefore let our soul put on charity, and a charity strong as death; for as death is the end of sins, so too is charity, ibid., 530. Let us recognize that the perfect man is not moved by the injury of a desire for revenge and does not return evil for evil. Joseph is rightly admirable, for before the Gospel he was such a man as to spare those who injured him, not repay injury when sold, but return kindness for insults, ibid., 642. How broad is the commandment of charity: “Love,” he says, “your enemies.” He surely included all within the effect of charity who did not exclude enemies, XV, 1379. A Christian is not permitted not to love enemies; for hear the broad commandment: “Bless those who persecute you, and do not curse,” ibid. The just man is silent and prays for those who curse him, ibid., 845. Injury is to be endured with equanimity, XV, 1525. A Christian ought to petition for enemies and pray also for persecutors, just as the Lord prayed, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing,” XVI, 1370. A merciful man is good: while helping others, he provides for himself and heals his own wounds by another’s remedy; for in forgiving he recognizes himself to be human, ibid., [Col. 0424] 1391. Therefore forgive injuries yourselves. Prayer is a good shield, by which insult is excluded, cursing driven away, and often turned back upon those who cursed, ibid., 1217. Christians are taught not to return evil for evil, so that they may be perfect, XVII, 160. God wills that benefits also be given to our enemies, so that we may win them to life and overcome them by good, ibid.

CAIUS VETTIUS AQUILINUS, poet.—But I shall command that no one dare rise in anger or be stirred amid the burning hatred of a brother; and that, hastening first to seek peace and then reconciled to brotherly love, he offer pleasing gifts to God with tranquil heart, ibid., 125.

COELIUS SEDULIUS, poet.—Let us who ask that all debts be remitted to us remit them ourselves also; and we are bound more grievously against salvation if we refuse to loose another’s bonds, XVII, 420.

SULPICIUS SEVERUS, historian and poet.—Saint Martin had assumed such patience against every injury that, so far as lay in him, he repelled from his charity no one by whom he had been injured, XX, 176.

CHROMATIUS (St), bishop of Aquileia.—Does not the Gospel command us to love enemies, love those who hate us, and pray for slanderers, that we may truly deserve to be children of God? XX, 355. There is no enemy if you grant forgiveness of sins, ibid. Forgive offences, and no wars will trouble you, if you spare enemies who lie in wait, ibid., 448.

EVAGRIUS, monk.—Put resentment and anger far from you, and let the memory of malice not remain with you, XX, 1085.

JEROME (St), presbyter of Stridon.—It must be known that Christ commands not impossible things but perfect things. Stephen also, the martyr, prayed for enemies who were stoning him, and Paul wishes himself to be accursed for his persecutors. Jesus both taught and did this, saying: “Father, forgive them,” XXVI, 41. For without that love by which we are commanded to love enemies and persecutors, we cannot fulfil the Lord’s law in which he said: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you,” XXXI, 1264.

AUGUSTINE (St), bishop of Hippo.—Therefore be merciful as merciful persons, because in loving your enemies, you love your brothers, XXXV, 2041. A remarkable description of justice by Saint Augustine: “Justice knows not brother, knows not mother, knows not father; it knows truth, accepts no person, imitates the Lord,” XXXVII, 1967. Pray for your enemy, that he may be a son of his Father and thus a son of the Most High; think of the Father and recognize the inheritance, XXXVIII, 120. Do you wish to be forgiven? Forgive, ibid., 515. If you do not love your enemies, do not pray; do not say in the Lord’s Prayer, “Forgive us our debts,” ibid., 384. Exercise yourselves, as far as you can, in showing gentleness even toward your enemies, ibid., 1430. Charity must extend even to enemies. We must forgive in order that we may be forgiven. You ask mercy of me; do not be sluggish in showing mercy, XXXIX, 1695 ff. Enemies must be loved; God loved us even when we were enemies, ibid., 2256. It is not without reason that one who forgives others hopes that his own sins will be spared, XXXV, 1862. Blessed is the person who loves an enemy for God’s sake, ibid., 1874. We must pray for our enemies, either that their conversion may be obtained or that the imitation of divine goodness may be found in us, XLV, 1876. A condition so gracious must indeed be embraced by a human being: that by forgiving another’s offences, he may wash away his own, ibid., 1892. God likewise commands us to be reconciled to our brother, whether we know that he has something against us justly or unjustly, XLIX, 343.

CASSIAN, monk.—If he has attained the imitation of God, then, clothed in the compassion of the Lord’s long-suffering, he will pray even for sinners, saying: “Father, forgive them,” XLIX, 861.

PROSPER (St), poet.—A righteous disposition is extended even toward the unrighteous, although they may scorn the kindly prayers of men, LI, 507.

PETER CHRYSOLOGUS (St), bishop of Ravenna.—Envy, an ancient evil, the first ruin, the poison of the ages, cast the angel himself down from heaven, LII, 195.

VALERIAN (St), bishop of Cimiez.—Let each person therefore forgive his brother from his whole heart; let no one recall an injury, let no one seek revenge. Let your conversation with an enemy be gentle and pure, LII, 731. This is to love enemies: not to answer hatred with hatred, to endure insults patiently, and to forgive an injury committed by hand or word, ibid., 733. Let us obey Christ by enduring the injuries of enraged brethren, ibid., 309. Therefore forgive completely those who sin against you, if you yourself wish to owe the Lord nothing of your debts, ibid., 400.

LEO THE GREAT (St), pope.—Alms-deeds afflict sins, destroy death, and extinguish the punishment of everlasting fire. [Col. 0425] This virtue makes all virtues useful. In what will those standing at the right hand be praised, except in works of benevolence and offices of charity which the Lord Jesus will account as rendered to himself? And what will be objected against those on the left, except neglect of love, harsh inhumanity, and mercy denied to the poor? LIV, 165. For one who relieves the temporal misery of a sufferer escapes the eternal punishment of a sinner, ibid. And deservedly the Lord commands that enemies be loved and prayers offered for sinners, ibid., 170. Let us take the model for loving our neighbour from the love of God, who is good even to the evil and cherishes even those who deny him with his gifts, ibid., 190. Let no one despair that brightness may be restored to him even after many sins, if he has sought to be cleansed through the purification of alms, ibid. All works are weighed in the balance of charity, ibid., 169.

MAXIMUS (St), bishop of Turin.—See, then, what is the grace of mercy: it alone is the virtue that redeems every sin. Thus almsgiving extinguishes sins as the water of baptism extinguishes the fire of Gehenna. Almsgiving is more forgiving, since the washing of baptism is given only once; but as often as you give alms, so often you obtain pardon, LVII, 482. He does not prepare the way for the Lord who burns with the deadly hatred of envy against his brethren, ibid., 386.

SALVIAN, presbyter of Marseilles.—Christ commands us to love enemies and do good to persecutors, LIII, 65.

PAULINUS (St), bishop of Nola.—To return injury for injury is human revenge; but to love an enemy is heavenly vengeance, LXI, 296.

FULGENTIUS (St), bishop of Ruspe.—The Lord commands charity to be extended even to enemies and goodwill to be enlarged even toward sinners. For those who love their enemies will be children of God, LV, 739.

BENEDICT (St), abbot.—If you remember that anyone has done evil to you, rise quickly and pray for him, that God may spare him, LVI, 347.

CASSIODORUS, abbot.—Perfect hatred is to love our enemies because they are human beings, and always to abhor their vices, LVI, 992.

GREGORY (St), bishop of Tours.—Always offer good counsel to friend and enemy alike, LXXI, 399. Let no word of malice dwell in your heart against one who injures you, so that you may be able to say, “Forgive us our debts,” LXXIII, 975.

GREGORY THE GREAT (St), pope.—Enduring injuries is the gate of heaven, LXXIII, 659. To endure an injury and not return like for like is to lay down one’s life for one’s neighbour, ibid., 681. Therefore let us forgive what is owed to us, so that what we owe may be forgiven, LXXIV, 1210. Charity is broad, therefore, because it includes the love of enemies, ibid., 840. The Lord commands that friends be loved in him and enemies for his sake: he bears the gibbet of the cross and yet bestows the effect of love upon his persecutors, LXXIV, 1204.

TAIO, bishop of Saragossa.—He truly possesses charity who loves a friend in God and an enemy for God’s sake, LXXX, 896.

DEFENSOR, monk of Logogniac.—He loves for God’s sake who also loves those by whom he is not loved, LXXX, 607. As God forgave us our sins, so we too should forgive those who sin against us, ibid., 611. If your enemy falls, do not rejoice, ibid., 698.

BONIFACE (St), archbishop of Mainz.—Because sacred Scripture instructs us not to return evil for evil, but even good for evil, LXXXIX, 628.

BEDE THE VENERABLE.—By love of enemies we become children of God; therefore imitate your Lord and intercede for enemies, LXXXIX, 616.

ALCUIN, abbot.—A sinner who does not show mercy to those sinning against him cannot ask and hope for mercy from God, CI, 617. Each person will receive from God the kind of forgiveness which he himself has granted his neighbour, ibid.

SMARAGDUS, abbot.—Friend and enemy alike should be loved for God’s sake, CI, 936.

JONAS, bishop of Orléans.—Moreover, it is characteristic of Christians to love a friend in God and an enemy for God’s sake, CVI, 233.

DRUTHMAR, monk of Corbie.—Lord, forgive us whatever we have sinned against you, because we too, according to your commandment, forgive those who sin against us, CVI, 1315.

RABANUS MAURUS, archbishop of Mainz.—We must love enemies not in order that they may remain enemies, but that they may become brothers and that we may attain, insofar as it lies in us, the perfection of our Father, CVII, 832 ff. Therefore, brethren, I ask you to forgive from the heart one who offends you, that your sins may be forgiven, CX, 41.

[Col. 0426]

WALAFRID STRABO, monk of Fulda.—We must love not only brethren, since the Lord says that we must pray even for enemies, CXIV, 98. We make this covenant with the Lord: if we forgive, it shall be forgiven us, ibid., 876. “Forgive them these things, I pray, and do not repay, O Judge, what they have done to me; . . . you who command such things, mercifully hear such things.” (Thus Saint Mammas prayed while being tortured by his tormentors), CXIV, 1061.

HAYMO, bishop of Halberstadt.—That is, in such charity as knows how, in imitation of divine goodness, to do good even to enemies and to love them, CXVIII, 588. Forgive your neighbour who wrongs you, and then, when you pray, your sins are remitted, ibid., 912.

RODULPH, bishop of Bourges.—It was decreed that those who have separated from one another in hatred should be expelled from the fellowship of the Church until they come to the charity which covers a multitude of sins, CXIX, 716.

PASCHASIUS RADBERTUS (St), abbot of Corbie.—The love of children is acquired by charity alone; charity, moreover, is strengthened by the love of enemies, CXX, 263 ff. We can be his children only by imitating the heavenly Father. “Love your enemies mercifully, and by this love alone fulfil all that I have commanded you, that you may be children of your Father,” ibid. No human being is excepted from mercy, since we must love even enemies, ibid., 1470.

ABBO, monk of Saint-Germain.—You ought to forgive, that you may be forgiven; and do not deceive other people through corrupt falsehoods, CXXXII, 768.

HUCBALD, monk.—Without charity, other virtues can be of no benefit whatever to a human being, CXXXIV, 917.

ADALGER (St), bishop.—It is fitting that, after pardon for an offence, we restore our enemies to the fullness of former friendship, CXLIV, 379.

PETER DAMIAN (St), cardinal of the Holy Roman Church.—Forgive us, Lord, because we forgive our debtors in your name, CXLVII, 338.

THEODORIC, canon of Paderborn.—Show yourself more affable toward one who has injured you, CLIII, 626.

ANSELM (St), archbishop of Canterbury.—In prayer for enemies, let him pray to God thus: “Hear, Lord, and grant not only to friends but also to enemies those things which you know to be expedient for each, and mercy to all living and dead,” CLVIII, 910. God commands us wholly to forgive those who sin against us, ibid., 79. We must forgive those who sin against us if we wish the sins we have committed against God to be forgiven, ibid., 167.

ANSELM, canon of Laon.—Love your enemies so that you may imitate him who, being always your Father, is kindly disposed toward evil and good alike, CLXII, 1303. Love your enemies, not friends only; for if you love only those who love you, you will have no reward, ibid. You must love enemies, so that as you are children of God by creation, you may also be so by imitation, CLXIII.

BRUNO (St), monk of Signy.—You shall therefore forgive one who confesses voluntarily, CLXVII, 949.

RUPERT, abbot of Deutz.—As Christ loved you when you were enemies, in order to make you friends, so you too love enemies, that they may become friends, imitating Saint Stephen, who prayed for those who stoned him, CLXIII, 1421 ff.

HILDEBERT, bishop of Le Mans.—If you forgive, it will be forgiven you; if you do not forgive, you lie to God. You can lie to God, but you cannot deceive him, CLXXI, 1170. One who deceitfully kisses an enemy will be Judas’s companion. Love is the limit of perfection, ibid., 834.

GODEFRID, abbot of Admont.—Let them exalt mercy above judgment, that they too may obtain mercy, CLXXIV, 442 ff.

HUGH OF SAINT VICTOR, abbot.—It belongs to the perfect to forgive all debtors with a pure heart and to grant them the services of charity, CLXXV, 772. Let us so love human beings that we do not love their errors; let us love nature, not fault. Charity is the source of all virtues; through charity God remains in us, for God is charity, CLXXVI, 975 ff.

ALGER, canon of Liège.—Let goodwill accomplish more toward those to be corrected than severity, charity more than power; and rightly the Psalmist exalts mercy above judgment, CLXXX, 866. The prince of the apostles fell in order that he might forgive the offences of the fallen, ibid., 159. An enemy must be loved so that he may love God, CLXXXIII, 1024.

BERNARD (St), abbot of Clairvaux.—Through love of enemies, a human being becomes a child of God; by it the image of divine goodness is most fully restored. Thus one who forgives is forgiven; thus one becomes a child of God and an heir, indeed a co-heir of Christ, CLXXXIV, 612. Through charity a human being is in God and God in the human being, ibid., 587. Love of enemies made the Son of God man, CLXXXIII, 410. To love enemies is more divine [Col. 0427] than human, CLXXXIII, 443. Be perfect according to your ability, so that you seek to benefit even enemies, which God plainly does, CLXXXVI, 137.

ZACHARIAS, bishop of Chrysopolis.—Christ himself, judge of all, commanding the sword to be returned to its sheath, prays and seeks pardon on the cross for those who kill him, CLXXXIX, 1765.

ERNALD, abbot of Bonneval.—The sweet yoke of Christ is charity, and the light burden is brotherly love, CXCV, 531.

AELRED (Blessed), abbot of Rievaulx.—Who, hearing that voice full of sweetness and charity, “Father, forgive them,” does not immediately embrace his enemies with all affection? CXCV, 582. That he may rest more perfectly and sweetly in brotherly charity, let him embrace even enemies in the arms of true love, ibid.

RICHARD OF SAINT VICTOR, abbot.—Great is the enlargement of charity which extends itself to enemies and includes all in its bosom, CXCVI, 526.

ADAM, Premonstratensian regular canon.—We are commanded to love both a friend in God and an enemy for God’s sake, CXCVIII, 782.

STEPHEN (St), abbot of Grandmont.—One who returns good for evil to an enemy takes full revenge upon his malice, because he destroys it, CCIV, 1112.

PETER COMESTOR.—The Lord’s sweet yoke is love of God, and the light burden is love of neighbour, CCVII, 904. Therefore, if you are an imitator of Christ, you will always forgive one who injures you, CCV, 280.

PETER OF BLOIS.—How will Christ give himself to you if you close the bowels of mercy to the needy? CCVIII, 728.

GUATHERUS, Cistercian monk.—Observe the condition: if we desire the debts of our offences to be released by the heavenly Father, it is necessary that we too forgive, CCXIII, 192.

INNOCENT III, pope.—The breadth of charity extends even to an enemy, CCXVII, 763.—You must wholly forgive an offence, since by divine command you are bound to love enemies, ibid., 758. Love enemies in heart, pray for them with the mouth, and do good to them in deed, ibid., 756. Almsgiving cleanses, frees, redeems, protects, pleads, obtains, perfects, blesses, justifies, raises again, and saves, ibid., 747.

SECOND PART. The question of love of enemies; in this part the question is treated according to the alphabetical order of the Fathers.

AMBROSE (St), bishop of Milan.—Joseph as an example of forgetting injuries, XIV, 642. On patience toward revilers, XIV, 1033. On the good of bearing abuse and not returning it, XV, 1272. Enemies must not only be forgiven, but also treated kindly, XVII, 161. “Let not the sun go down upon your anger,” XVII, 392. The example of charity given by Christ, XV, 1637.

AUGUSTINE (St), bishop of Hippo.—“With what measure you have measured, it shall be measured again to you,” XXXIII, 379. “Love your enemies,” XXXV, 1089, 2035, 2083. One who hates a brother is in darkness, XXXV, 2016, 2053. Enemies must be loved, XXXVII, 1273, 1433. Offences must be forgiven to enemies, XXXVIII, 53, 324, 366, 383, 391, 401. On forgiving injuries, XXXVIII, 514, 652, 806. On brotherly concord and forgiving offences, XXXVIII, 1054, 1274. The commandment concerning love of enemies, XXXIX, 1684, 1695, 1859, 1870, 1907, 1957, 2137. On avoiding hatred, XXXIX, 1973. The manner of loving friends and enemies, XXXIX, 2156, 2160, 2250, 2253, 2256. In what respect the wicked are to be hated, XLV, 1863.

BENEDICT (St), abbot of Aniane.—How we should love enemies, CIII, 540.

BRUNO (St), abbot of Asti.—One must forgive one’s neighbour, CLXV, 226.

CASSIAN, presbyter of Marseilles.—Debts must be forgiven, XLIX, 796.

CYPRIAN (St), bishop of Carthage.—On the good of patience, IV, 621. An injury received must be remitted and forgiven, IV, 750, 777.

DRUTHMAR, Christian abbot of Corbie.—Brethren must be forgiven, CVI, 1308.

GREGORY THE GREAT (St), pope.—The power of prayer for enemies, LXXV, 873.

JEROME (St), presbyter.—“Love your enemies,” XXV, 41. Forgetfulness of injuries, XXVI, 133. An exhortation to bear reproaches, XXX, 282. On forbidding revenge, XXX, 369.

HILARY (St), bishop of Poitiers.—On patience, IX, 398. Loving enemies is a commandment, IX, 599. Vengeance must be left to God, IX, 791. The desire for revenge must be restrained, [Col. 0428] IX, 941. Love of enemies, IX, 942. On forgetting injuries, IX, 1022.

LEO THE GREAT (St), pope.—Enemies must be loved, LIV, 167, 291.

PASCHASIUS RADBERTUS, abbot of Corbie.—Enemies must be loved, CXX, 262, 631.

PAUL THE DEACON WINFRID.—A brother must be forgiven, XCV, 1264, 1443. “Love your enemies,” XCV, 1538, 1545.

PETER CHRYSOLOGUS (St), archbishop of Ravenna.—“Forgive us our debts,” etc., LII, 392, 395, 400, 406. On forgiving a brother’s offence, LII, 572.

PETER OF BLOIS.—Among neighbours we are commanded to love an enemy, and the preceding command, “hate an enemy,” appears contrary to this; but divine dispensation decreed by the wondrous artifice of charity that the human will, which is ready to hate an enemy, should be restrained by the command of love, while the same will, too headlong in loving a friend, should be moderated by the censure of the divine law which enjoins hatred toward an enemy. We have counsel from the Lord concerning virginity, almsgiving, humility, abandoning possessions and giving them to the poor, visiting the sick, and other works of mercy; and concerning these, although they do not always carry an imposed necessity, we expect eternal recompense. But concerning love of an enemy, the Lord binds us in the Gospel by a sure and explicit decree, so that whoever does not love his enemy is a transgressor of the divine law.

“Love,” he says, “your enemies, and do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you”; and, adding the measure of the reward, he says: “That you may be children of your Father who is in heaven.” God is supreme goodness; in love for him you must compel your will, so that, as he makes his sun rise upon good and evil, you may likewise look with the same eye of grace upon friend and enemy for Christ’s sake. If you love a friend because he loves you, the law of friendship demands this; if you love a friend for Christ’s sake, this adds to your merit. But you merit God’s grace with far greater distinction and excellence if, commanding your will for Christ’s sake, you love an enemy for God’s sake.

Hear further what Truth says in the Gospel: “If you love those who love you, what reward will you have? Do not even the tax collectors do this?” Bears, lions, and lamiae likewise obey nature in love for their own. But if you are a disciple or professed follower of Christ, you must do good to evildoers, bless those who curse, and pray for those persecuting you. For the order of heavenly justice and the divine rule of equity require that those already illumined by the Sun of righteousness pray for the illumination of their adversaries, and that those who are darkness may become light in the Lord, according to the Prophet’s prayer: “For you enlighten my lamp, Lord; enlighten my darkness.” Paul says: “Returning evil to no one for evil, nor cursing for cursing.” Christ, as blessed Peter testifies, suffered for us and left us an example that we should follow in his steps. He himself prayed for those crucifying him: “Father,” he said, “forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”

James and Stephen, and very many others besides, followed these footsteps: amid the straits of death they embraced their murderers with all the depths of their heart and soul in the embraces of intimate charity. For the man whom you regard as your enemy is an enemy to himself, not to you. He harms himself, not you. You think that he injures you, but he advances you toward innocence. For it is written that Abel cannot exist unless Cain’s malice exercises him. If you repay evil for evil and cursing for cursing, you pronounce judgment in your own cause; and, making yourself judge in your own case, you deprive, so far as lies in you, him to whom God the Father gave all judgment—and who says, “Vengeance is mine; I will repay”—of the power of judging and repaying.

Therefore show to your enemies for Christ’s sake the love which you would show to those who love you. Although this may at first seem burdensome to you, you will nevertheless gather from this love the sweetest fruits of life. This love proceeds indeed from a new commandment. For whereas the ordinance of the old law commands us to love a friend and hate an enemy, the censure of the new law binds us to love an enemy, not shadowily or hypocritically, but in deed and truth. Therefore the lawgiver, not content merely to say, “Love your enemies,” plainly showing that they must be loved in will and deed, added: “Do good to those who hate you”; and again: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; and if he thirsts, give him drink. For in doing this you will heap coals upon his head.” The head of the inward person is reason; and, in my opinion, no one is so cruel that he is not softened by benefits bestowed, that he does not abandon hatred in response to a neighbour’s goodwill, and that he does not kindle thoughts of charity as coals of fire once the heat of anger has been removed.

Therefore, in one who harasses you more grievously, [Col. 0429] love the image of God, sharing your nature; and hate his sin in such a manner that you love the sinner. For this is the hatred of the perfect: “With perfect hatred I hated them.” Recall Joseph’s love for his wicked brothers; Moses’ love for the rebellious people; and David mourning his most grievous persecutors, Saul and his parricidal son. Although Christ, the Gospel lawgiver, first promulgated the decree of this love, many Fathers of old, inspired by his grace, had nevertheless humbly practised its observance, CCVII, 936–938.

Above all, let our love flow in its natural order toward those of our own blood, whom we are bound to love by the necessity of nature itself; for it is exceedingly inhuman that they should be excluded from the sanctuary of our love. For, as the Apostle testifies, “Whoever does not provide for his own, and especially for members of his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.” Hence this love proceeding from nature is first established by God’s command among the commandments pertaining to love of neighbour: “Honour,” he says, “your father and your mother.” From there our love advances toward those especially joined to us by mutual friendship or duty, spreading more broadly in a kind of fuller embrace.

Yet this love does not surpass the righteousness of the Pharisees, to whom it was said: “You shall love your friend and hate your enemy.” Certainly affection for parents and friends, even though faithfully maintained, receives little reward, since natural law prompts us to the former and reciprocal services urge us to the latter; nevertheless, if either is neglected, it brings an accumulation of condemnation.

Truth says in the Gospel: “If you love those who love you, what reward will you have? Do not the Gentiles do this? And if you greet your brethren, what more are you doing?” Therefore, that our love may extend to a wider range, let it embrace also those who serve God alongside us and who are joined to us by the profession of the same life, in the bond of peace and unity of spirit. God, indeed, is the efficient cause of this love, while the spiritual anointing flows from the head down Aaron’s beard [Col. 0430] and to the hem of his garment, so that those who, being anointed by the Anointed One, are called Christians from Christ, may all embrace one another in participation in the name of Jesus through the common bond of mutual charity.

There still remain two classes of persons: namely, those who are outside—the Gentiles and Jews, and also schismatics and heretics [lacuna]. Charity further enlarges its tent and so broadens and stretches its cloak—which in the time of the old Law was short—that it suffices to cover two persons, while by the new anointing of the Holy Spirit it binds its enemy to its own soul. By this love a human being becomes a son of God, and the image of divine goodness is most fully restored. “Love,” says the Lord, “your enemies; do good to those who hate you; and pray for those who slander you, that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven.” Thus one who forgives is forgiven. This love, when it beholds an enemy with a single eye, can say in utter security: “Forgive us, as we also forgive.” Thus one becomes a son of God, an heir of God, and a co-heir with Christ. Consider, O human being, how safe, sweet, and delightful it is to have compassion on enemies; not to be stirred by injuries; to love for Christ’s sake one by whom I perceive myself not to be loved; and to bear toward that person the affection which a most indulgent father bears toward his dearest son afflicted by madness—so that, the greater the injuries inflicted by him, the more fervently charity may burn toward him. CCVII, 912–913.

**PROSPER (Saint), bishop of Aquitaine.**—On loving enemies, LI, 427, 433, 450, 452, 466.

**STEPHEN OF MURET (Saint), monk of Grandmont.**—On avenging enemies, CCIV, 1124.

**STEPHEN, bishop of Tournai.**—On forgetting injuries, CCXI, 410.

**TERTULLIAN, presbyter.**—On charity toward enemies, I, 697. On forgetting injuries, I, 1264.

**ZACHARIAS, bishop of Chrysopolis.**—On forgiving brethren from the whole heart, CLXXXVI, 310.

[Col. 0429]

## CXLVI. INDEX ON ALMSGIVING, SETTING FORTH IN LOGICAL ORDER VARIOUS SAYINGS OF SCRIPTURE AND THE FATHERS CONCERNING ITS NATURE AND NECESSITY, ITS CONDITIONS, RECIPIENTS, ETC.

This index is divided into two parts: the first contains certain special matters relating to almsgiving; the second treats the subject solely in alphabetical order.

## PART ONE. CERTAIN SPECIAL MATTERS CONCERNING ALMSGIVING

[Col. 0429]

### The nature and necessity of almsgiving

**HILARY (Saint).**—The command to ward off the thirst of the needy with drink, their hunger with food, and their nakedness with clothing, IX, 941.

**ZENO (Saint).**—To deny alms to a person dying in want is to kill that person, XI, 287.

**AMBROSE (Saint).**—The rich person owes alms to the poor, XIV, 740, 746, 749, 753. Whoever gives alms pays a debt; he does not bestow what is not owed, 743. How just it is to sprinkle something of your goods upon the poor, XV, 1303. Everyone ought, according to what he possesses, to give to those in need, XVII, 655. This is justice: because God gives, a human being should in return give from it to one who lacks, 313. How wrongly some excuse themselves from distributing alms, 683. Do not display yourself as merciful with another’s plunder, 750.

**JUVENCUS.**—Almsgiving commended, XIX, 129.

**JEROME (Saint).**—Whatever we can possess beyond food and clothing should be spent in feeding the poor and in generosity toward the needy, XXIII, 360.

**AUGUSTINE (Saint).**—The Greek word *eleemosyna* means mercy, XXXVIII, 1043; XI, 268. Almsgiving commended, XXXV, 2023; XXXVI, 423; XLI, 25. God commands that alms be given, XXXIV, 1092. Gifts of almsgiving are those by which the King is worshipped, XXXVI, 1511. God’s counsel concerning giving alms is to be embraced, XXXVIII, 530. Christ is needy in the poor person, 240, 615, 524, 253, 1129. Christ asks nothing from you except what he gave you: the Giver himself wishes to become a debtor, 686, 326. We entrust to God what we give to the poor, XXXIII, 1092. In almsgiving, see what you buy, when you buy it, and at what price you buy it, XXXVII, 1326. Avarice excuses itself under the appearance of devotion toward children, XXXVIII, 89. How poor people may give alms, XXXVII, 1664–1665. Set something aside as a debt, as though it were to be repaid to the treasury, XXXVII, 1911.

**CASSIAN.**—The necessity of distributing alms, XLIX, 1159.

**VALERIAN.**—The necessity of almsgiving, LII, 739. Mercy is necessary if the kingdom of heaven is to stand open to us, 711. It should be practiced frequently, 718.

**LEO THE GREAT (Saint).**—One who does not provide for another’s necessities differs in no respect from beasts, LIV, 189. Its omission is a ground of condemnation, ibid., 164, 184.

**EUGYPPIUS.**—Those who neglect almsgiving are to be punished with eternal punishment, LXII, 793.

**FULGENTIUS (Saint).**—Riches should be sent beforehand to Christ, LXV, 321. Something should be withheld from luxuries in order to be spent on the needy, ibid. If not all can fulfil what the Lord said, “Sell what you possess,” yet what he added in saying, “Give alms,” is possible for all; it ought to be common to all, 723.

**LIVES OF THE SAINTS.**—Almsgiving, in the guise of a virgin crowned with an olive branch, appears to Saint John the Almsgiver, LXXIII, 344.

**GREGORY THE GREAT (Saint).**—The poor are to be supported both with gentle speech and with the service of generosity, LXXVI, 206. Alms should be given even from necessities, 1165. Almsgiving is a work of justice, not of mercy, LXXVII, 86. What is surplus must be distributed as alms, 1186.

**ALCUIN.**—Almsgiving is commended to all, C, 224. It is to be performed by all who possess earthly goods, CI, 625.

**RABANUS.**—One gives alms who does not cease to share temporal goods with his brethren; who supplies food and clothing to the needy; who receives people with hospitality; who visits the sick; and who does not cease to rescue those destined for death and punishments, CVII, 340. God must be propitiated for past sins by alms, CIX, 783. One’s eyes must not be turned away from the poor, 784. An exhortation that the Corinthians send alms to the poor in Jerusalem, CXII, 207; and that they should be given swiftly and abundantly, 211. The gift of almsgiving must not be delayed, CIX, 783.

**REGINO.**—Sins are to be redeemed by alms, CXXXII, 212, 246.

**RATHERIUS.**—Almsgiving to be distributed, CXXXVI, 179–180; to be given by the rich while they live, 179.

**PETER DAMIAN (Saint).**—Almsgiving is strong armour, CXLIV, 775.

**BRUNO (Saint), founder of the Carthusians.**—Almsgiving called “substance,” CLIII, 258.

**ZACHARIAS.**—Whoever can help a person dying in any necessity and does not do so, kills that person, CLXXXVI, 135.

**PETER LOMBARD.**—Almsgiving is an odour of sweetness and God’s incense, CXCII, 255.

**PETER THE CHANTER.**—Almsgiving is the daughter of mercy, CCV, 265.

### Conditions of almsgiving

**CYPRIAN (Saint).**—Almsgiving must not be done for display, IV, 756.

**AMBROSE (Saint).**—By giving to the poor, let us obtain the favour of angels and of the other saints, XV, 1765. Many who have given their goods to the poor and have become wealthy ought not to demand such a reward from the Lord of the ages, 1297. The Lord does not wish riches to be poured out all at once, but administered, XVI, 66. One must give in such a way that it does not bring want upon the giver, XVII, 308. Not only how much is given is asked, but also from what and with what disposition, 313. What it means to give “in simplicity,” 156.

**JUVENCUS.**—Almsgiving should be done secretly, XIX, 131.

**CHROMATIUS (Saint).**—Those giving alms must not sound a trumpet, XX, 70–71.

**JEROME (Saint).**—Christ’s substance must not be poured out imprudently, XXII, 583. Prudence in giving alms ensures that no poor person is sent away empty, 891. Whenever you stretch out your hand, think of Christ, 556. When you give alms, let God alone see it, 412. Many give them for the sake of vanity, 417. Each person should be given what is needed, not what serves luxury, 583. Give what sustains necessity, not what increases riches, 642. In almsgiving we seek empty glory, XXIII, 546. Rare is the person who does not do it with that intention, ibid. Not every alms pleases God, XXVI, 242.

**AUGUSTINE (Saint).**—Almsgiving should be done not from plunder but from just labours, XXXVIII, 648, 962. The measure and end with which alms should be given, 243, 253. It should be done from the heart, XXXVI, 482; distributed with humility and cheerfulness, XXXVIII, 1200; neither proudly nor stingily, 89. One who helps the poor should not exalt himself over him, 1128. “If you have given bread while sad, you have lost both the bread and the merit,” XXXVI, 482. Almsgiving proceeds from the heart, XXXVII, 1660. Let it be done in secret, XXXVI, 512.

**VALERIAN.**—Almsgiving should be voluntary, LII, 716.

**PETER CHRYSOLOGUS (Saint).**—Almsgiving should accompany fasting, and the great blessings arising from this, LII, 208. It should be secret, out of regard for the poor person’s shame. In it, the right hand should not know the left, and how this is so, 226 ff. It should always accompany prayer and fasting, 349. It is harmful to its giver when made from fraud or another’s goods, ibid. Whoever does not give alms from his own goods is guilty of a crime, 537.

**LEO THE GREAT (Saint).**—Although not all have equal means for almsgiving, they should have equal devotion, LIV, 159, 168, 173, 175. Those whose wealth is unequal can have equal intention, 442. It should be joined with fasting, 439. The alms of those unable to fast should be more abundant, ibid. The generosity of almsgiving should be so moderated [Col. 0432] that the refreshment of the poor may rejoice in it while the sufficiency of one’s household does not suffer, 443.

**PRUDENTIUS.**—Secret almsgiving and the praise that arises from it, LIX, 855. Those chiefly give alms who devote riches to churches, 634.

**EUGYPPIUS.**—Worthy alms, LXII, 796.

**FULGENTIUS (Saint).**—One who gives should not think himself superior to the person to whom he gives, LXV, 321.

**VICTOR OF CAPUA.**—On secret almsgiving, LXVIII, 270.

**CASSIODORUS.**—What perfect almsgiving is, LXX, 265. How it should be given, 295. It must not be given with delay, 1092.

**LIFE OF THE FATHERS.**—Almsgiving should be given without measure, LXXIII, 1945; cheerfully, 1187. It should be given to the poor not from natural affection but from piety, LXXIV, 33.

**GREGORY THE GREAT (Saint).**—The end and manner of almsgiving, LXXV, 923. It is to be evaluated chiefly from the disposition of the mind, LXXVI, 178. Alms from plunder are evil, LXXV, 1012. What perfect almsgiving is, LXXVI, 178. It should proceed from a clean heart, 229. What caution ought to be used in almsgiving, LXXVII, 84. It must not be made from theft, 87. What almsgiving pleases the Redeemer’s eyes, 1029. Alms should be distributed wisely, 1146. Those who give alms should not be lifted up by pride but weighed down by fear, 84.

**PAULINUS (Saint) OF AQUILEIA.**—How almsgiving should be given, XCIX, 201; from one’s own goods, not another’s, 225, 258.

**RABANUS.**—Almsgiving should be performed with a simple heart, CIX, 845.

**PASCHASIUS (Saint).**—Almsgiving should be done so secretly that not even the left hand may know it, CXX, 272.

**HINCMAR.**—The almsgiving pleasing in God’s eyes is not amassed from unlawful means and injustice, but expended from permitted goods rightly acquired, CXXV, 863.

**ISIDORE MERCATOR.**—Almsgiving must not be made from another’s goods, CXXX, 269.

**RATHERIUS.**—Almsgiving must not be made from another’s property, CXXXVI, 150, 272, 698; nor from something given by another for a different—even pious—purpose, 631 ff. Empty glory must be avoided, 698; for almsgiving done for empty glory is defective, 276.

**ANSELM (Saint).**—We ought not to acquire by plunder, usury, and fraud the means from which to give alms, CLVIII, 657. The almsgiving due to the poor must not be diminished, CLIX, 57.

**RUPERT.**—Almsgiving should come from abundance, CLXVIII, 814.

**HILDEBERT.**—Alms should be given cheerfully, CLXXI, 1569; and without reproach, 1016–1017.

**ZACHARIAS.**—When you give alms or do any good thing, do not mingle human praise with it, CLXXXVI, 137.

**ROBERT PULLUS.**—If we intend to visit those confined by illness or prison; if we comfort, or give actual aid to, the naked, thirsty, hungry, travellers, or those oppressed by any necessity or bereft of counsel, CLXXXVI, 917.

**GRATIAN.**—Do not wish to give alms from interest and usury, CLXXXVII, 961. An offering from plunder is rejected by God, ibid. Nothing should be seized from the rich in order to give it to the needy, ibid.

**PETER THE CHANTER.**—How and in what order almsgiving should be performed, CCV, 148, 182, 183, 492. Almsgiving should be given solely with God in view, 288. Abbot Stephen rejected almsgiving made by a simoniacal priest, 144. Alms must not be made from unlawfully acquired goods, 146.

**ALAN OF LILLE.**—Alms should be bestowed from one’s own goods, CCX, 316.

**GUNTHER.**—Almsgiving ought to be done secretly, CCXII, 212. Purity of mind, simplicity, humility, liberality, and cheerfulness befit one giving alms, 211.

**INNOCENT III.**—Almsgiving should be done from charity, for blessedness, cheerfully, and according to rule, CCXVII, 753 ff.

### Praise of almsgiving

**CYPRIAN (Saint).**—The good of almsgiving, IV, 728. He warns against neglecting widows, the sick, the poor, or travellers, 326.

**AMBROSE (Saint).**—Money is worthless when stored up, precious when scattered abroad, XIV, 1020. Make of an instrument of avarice a support of mercy, and of the enticement of corruption a grace of sincerity, 724. What good is pitying the needy unless you also grant them sustenance? XV, 1376.

**JEROME (Saint).**—To have practiced almsgiving is a great thing, XXII, 726. It is preferred to the building of churches, [Col. 0433] 1119. Almsgiving and humility, if genuine, are counted in place of sacrifices, XXVI, 64.

**LEO THE GREAT (Saint).**—The merit and usefulness of almsgiving, LIV, 157, 289, 439. Whoever gives alms is a minister of divine mercy, 304.

**MAXIMUS (Saint).**—The merit of almsgiving commended, LVII, 297, 478, 739.

**ISIDORE (Saint) OF SEVILLE.**—It is good to distribute one’s resources to the poor with prudent administration, LXXXIII, 1241.

**INNOCENT III.**—Almsgiving is better than fasting and prayer, CCXVII, 752.

### Spiritual almsgiving

**BENEDICT (Saint).**—One who ministers instruction to the foolish and the word of knowledge to the ignorant deserves to be praised with the commendations due to an almsgiver, LXVI, 314.

**AUGUSTINE (Saint).**—One kind of almsgiving is made from the heart, XXXVIII, 398. The twofold kind of almsgiving: forgiving and giving, 252, 1199. Another kind of almsgiving is to spare enemies, 1042, 1045, 1053. Nothing is greater than that alms by which we forgive from the heart whatever anyone has sinned against us, XL, 266.

**GREGORY THE GREAT (Saint).**—Sinful poor persons must be corrected, LXXVI, 1309.

**ALCUIN.**—Let your almsgiving consist in saving souls, C, 224. It is spiritual almsgiving to forgive the person by whom you have been injured, CI, 626.

**RABANUS.**—One gives alms who corrects a sinner persevering in wicked deeds; leads the erring person into the way of truth; teaches the ignorant; or preaches God’s word to neighbours, CVII, 340. Whoever grants forgiveness of sin, or corrects by the rod, gives alms, CIX, 783.

**HAYMO.**—Whoever grants forgiveness of sin, corrects with a rod, or restrains by some discipline gives alms, CXVIII, 903.

**RATHERIUS.**—A form of almsgiving is to direct one’s neighbour into the Lord’s way by sound counsel, rebuke, entreaty, or reproof, CXXXVI, 698.

**HILDEBERT (Saint).**—Almsgiving is twofold: giving one’s own goods and forgiving others their wrongs, CLXXI, 448.

**ROBERT PULLUS.**—Let us strive to benefit our neighbour, so that, if he is evil, he may be recalled from error; but if good, he may be advanced in his purpose, CLXXXVI, 916.

**PETER THE CHANTER.**—A person’s almsgiving toward a neighbour is manifold: in correcting a brother so that he may amend; in prayer for him; in compassion; and in giving holy counsel, CCV, 290.

**ALAN OF LILLE.**—It is almsgiving to forgive those who have injured us, CCX, 301.

**GUNTHER THE CISTERCIAN.**—We show mercy to our neighbour by prayer, correction, and counsel, CCXII, 210.

### Recipients

**CYPRIAN (Saint).**—Almsgiving should be denied to no one, IV, 730.

**JEROME (Saint).**—To whom almsgiving should be given, XXII, 555, 962; XXV, 174. To whom it should especially be given, XXIII, 350. One should not choose the person to whom one will do good, 418. Whoever considers whom he will benefit and does not give to everyone who asks often passes over the person who deserves to receive, 417.

**AUGUSTINE (Saint).**—Those to whom we give alms should be sought out, XXXVII, 1366–1367. Almsgiving to poor persons who are also pretenders, XXXVIII, 1251. How we are commanded to give to everyone who asks and forbidden to give to a sinner, XXXVII, 1327. Alms for the dead, XL, 158.

**LEO THE GREAT (Saint).**—To whom alms should chiefly be given, LIV, 62. They should be given even to unbelievers, 274; believers are to be preferred, ibid. They should be given to the modest in a manner attentive both to poverty and shame, 162. They should be given to the needy before they ask, 490.

**CASSIODORUS.**—Almsgiving should be given to the needy, but especially to holy persons, LXX, 295.

**LIFE OF THE FATHERS.**—Almsgiving bestowed on the poor is received by Christ as given to himself, LXXIII, 499. It is most rightly expended on the poor, 920, 922. It should rather be given to those not related by blood, 930. An inheritance is profitably given to the poor under the name of almsgiving, 1053.

**GREGORY THE GREAT (Saint).**—The poor are to be sought as intercessors with God, LXXVI, 1309. Alms should be distributed even to strangers, 207. They must not be supplied equally in every case, LXXVII, 1147. Whether they should be supplied to a poor sinner, 85. They should first be given to believers, then to the enemies of the Church, 585.

**ALCUIN.**—Alms should be given to everyone who asks, without distinction, C, 712.

[Col. 0434] **BENEDICT (Saint) OF ANIANE.**—Almsgiving should be given to everyone who asks, CIII, 1049.

**RATHERIUS.**—To whom almsgiving should be given, CXXXVI, 272. Especially to saints and the poor in spirit, 633. It should rather be bestowed on those who blush while receiving it, 607. Let us give rather to the good than to the evil, if they can be distinguished, 698.

**PETER DAMIAN.**—To whom alms should be given, CXLIV, 297.

**BERNARD (Saint).**—Almsgiving should especially be bestowed on one who asks unwillingly, receives modestly, and glorifies God upon receiving, CLXXXII, 373.

**ZACHARIAS.**—Let us simply give without distinction to all who are in need, asking not to whom, but why, we give, CLXXXVI, 135.

**PETER LOMBARD.**—Alms should be given even to evil persons and sinners, CXCII, 163.

### Fruits

**CYPRIAN (Saint).**—Almsgiving cleanses sins, IV, 603.

**LACTANTIUS.**—God grants forgiveness of sins through almsgiving, VI, 686.

**HILARY (Saint).**—The fruits of almsgiving, IX, 1061. Alms are indeed ambitious embassies of human treasures before God, 320.

**AMBROSE (Saint).**—It advances merit when a person gives from his own goods to the needy, XVII, 391. Almsgiving benefits the giver himself, 683, and thus he becomes richer, ibid. Almsgiving is such a welcome work that it cleanses every stain and defilement of a person, 419. Almsgiving is a good gift, cleansing every stain and squalor, 583, 656.

**JEROME (Saint).**—How great are the powers and rewards of almsgiving, XXII, 642. In it there is no diminution of substance, but an exchange, ibid. Whatever you take from your own resources for expenditure, count it as profit, 549.

**AUGUSTINE (Saint).**—Those who give alms engage in trade, XXXVIII, 410. Those who do not cease giving alms give the price of their soul’s redemption, XXXVI, 549. Alms greatly assist prayer, XXXIII, 503. Their power to redeem sins, XXXVIII, 407. Alms benefit those who have changed their life, ibid., 243; XL, 265, 267, 268. They do not benefit those who have not abstained from lusts and crimes, XXXIII, 675.

**PROSPER (Saint).**—The fruit of almsgiving is eternal, LI, 371.

**PETER CHRYSOLOGUS (Saint).**—Almsgiving makes one blessed; it is help against the evils of the world; it enriches, and how it does so, LII, 260. It heals the withered hand, 291. The virtues and goods it brings with fasting, 315; where its effects are stated. How the almsgiver may believe that he will live after death, 351. It pleads for sins, 499.

**LEO THE GREAT (Saint).**—Almsgiving is a kind of baptism, a second washing from sins, LIV, 158, 190. Sins are cleansed by its purification, 165, 190, 302. How pleasing mercy toward the poor is to God, 300. Works of mercy save people, 161. Alms bring refreshment to the dead, LV, 1143.

**MAXIMUS (Saint).**—The fruits of almsgiving enumerated, LVII, 424. A small alms can have great recompense with God, 818. How pleasing mercy toward the poor is to God, and how useful it is for obtaining forgiveness of sins, 266.

**EUGYPPIUS.**—Alms have power to blot out former sins, LXII, 795.

**LAURENTIUS (Saint).**—Almsgiving not only cleanses sins and heals the wounds of conscience, but also recalls the soul itself from death and makes it a partaker of heavenly kingdoms, LXVI, 105. If almsgiving finds a just person, it heaps up merits for him; if a sinner, it absolves him from sins; if a sick person, it relieves his pains, 106.

**CASSIODORUS.**—The reward of one giving alms, LXX, 295. It is most acceptable to God, 286. It reconciles the human race, 295. Through it sins are cleansed, ibid.

**ALCUIN.**—The most effective entreaty for sins lies in almsgiving, CI, 625.

### Remarkable examples of charity and almsgiving

**TERTULLIAN.**—How great Christians’ charity toward one another was, I, 471. They called one another brethren, ibid. Through charity they had all things in common, 472. How great their charity was toward the needy, and especially toward martyrs, 470, 475, 619. They could not suffice to bring assistance to begging human beings and gods of the Gentiles, 494. The mutual charity of Christians was greatly astonishing even to the Gentiles, 704. Among brethren and fellow-servants there are common hope, fear, joy, sorrow, and suffering, because there is a common Spirit, 1245.

**EUSEBIUS.**—Constantine’s beneficence toward the poor, VIII, 27. No one ever approached him without carrying away the fruit of some kindness. To strangers who came to him, he showed himself humane and generous, ibid. When his own forces had gained victory, he ordered them to spare the conquered, 40.

**PAULINUS OF NOLA.**—The duty of assisting the poor is shown by the example of Lazarus and the rich man feasting in the Gospel, LXI, 216, 217, 686. Pammachius provided a feast in the basilica of Saint Peter at Rome for all the poor, for the soul of his deceased wife, 213–214. How well Saint Felix distributed alms, 482. Martinianus is received kindly by the brethren, 620. Paulinus, fellow-guest of Theridius, gives him clothing, 621. Felix commends Bishop Maximus, carried on shoulders, to a certain holy woman, 474.

**BENEDICT (Saint).**—The lavish alms of Egyptian monks, LXVI, 310; of Benedictines, 311–312. How disposed Saint Benedict was toward the poor, 310. Hostels raised in monasteries for the poor, 312. Sacred vessels sold, 313. Monasteries’ tithes given to the poor, 310–311; likewise a fifth part of monastic revenues, ibid., and also a third part, ibid. Leftover food given to the poor, ibid. Old clothes to be distributed to them, 788. The feet of three poor persons to be washed daily, and alms given to them, 763. Amator sends Sylverius small gifts to relieve the want of exile, 86.

**SYLVERIUS.**—Sylverius praises Amator because he not only takes care to inquire after and visit him, but also does not cease to support and sustain him with his goods.

**GREGORY OF TOURS (Saint).**—A multitude of poor people came together to Aridius like bees to a hive, and none departed from him empty, LXXI, 1122. Whatever he possessed [Col. 0436] he distributed entirely among the poor, cenobitic communities, various churches, and his own monastery, ibid. He was a foot to the lame, an eye to the blind, a father of orphans, and a comforter of widows, 1129. Quintianus was magnificent in almsgiving, 1025. Senoch gave away what he received for the various needs of the indigent, so that in his lifetime he released more than two hundred persons from the bond of slavery and the burden of debt, 1072. Saint Martin aids an innocent man, 366; provides wine to a poor person, 947. The emperor Tiberius was an almsgiver, an excellent defender of the poor, and redeemer of captives, 339. Saint Paulinus of Nola sold everything he had and distributed it to the poor. Guntram bestows treasures on the poor, 444, 450. Perpetuus makes, declares, and appoints the needy, beggars, sick, widows, and orphans as his heirs, 1152. Benedict Agricola builds a hostel for lepers, 893.

**RADEGUND (Saint), queen of France.**—Besides the daily table at which she refreshed the needy, she washed their heads, did not shrink from festering scabies, and sometimes even extracted worms; she combed individually the heads she herself had washed. She soothed ulcerated scars by pouring oil upon them, despite the contagion of disease. She did not cease to offer food with a spoon to the sick and blind, LXXII, 657–658.

**DOMNOLUS (Saint).**—He wonderfully enlarged the monastic establishment to receive monks, pilgrims, and visitors. He built another hostel for the poor, pilgrims, and needy, LXXII, 631.

**GERMANUS (Saint).**—He brings captives out of prison, LXXII, 73. Content with a chasuble or tunic, he clothed a naked poor person with whatever remained, 76.

**COGITOSUS.**—Saint Brigid never allowed the needy to depart from her with an empty fold of the garment, LXXII, 786.

**LIFE OF THE FATHERS.**—John the Almsgiver received and comforted those whom he welcomed as guests, not as captives but as brethren truly by nature, LXXIII, 344. He ordered the wounded and sick to lie in hostels and hospitals, with care and medicine supplied to them without payment, ibid. ff. He visits the sick twice or three times a week, 283. The charity of Abraham, interceding for unbelievers who afflicted him, LXXIV, 76; of Achilles, doing good to one less worthy, 913; of Anastasius, caring for a leper in his house, LXXIII, 306.

The charity of Apollonius, who considered Christ in his neighbour, 1038; of Apollonius the patriarch, who aided a modest young man with remarkable skill, LXXIV, 220, 222; of Apollonius, who acted as physician and pharmacist for the brethren, LXXIII, 1105; LXXIV, 263; of Christians toward soldiers, LXXIII, 231; of a certain hermit, who released brigands apprehended on his account, ibid., 1031; of Eulogius, who cared for an elephantiasis sufferer and mutilated man, ibid., 1040, 1123; of a certain brother, who saved his father from a fall, ibid., 880; of a certain brother, who brought warm bread from Egypt to a sick man, ibid., 975; of a certain brother, who, so as to continue serving an elder bedridden from a wound, drank the wash-water of the wound, ibid., 977; of a certain brother who afflicted himself for a brother guilty of fornication, LXXIV, 166; of brethren when firewood failed in the monastery, LXXIII, 830; of brethren working for a sick man and compelling him to receive their wages, ibid., 975; of John the Almsgiver, who called the poor his lords, ibid., 342; of the same, who did good to his insulting nephew, ibid., 352; of the same, who had a more valuable coverlet given to him sold repeatedly, ibid., 355; of Abbot John, concealing a brother’s error, ibid., 974; of monks sending grapes to their neighbours, ibid., 764; of Egyptian monks working in order to aid the poor, ibid., 838; of Moses filling the monks’ water-jars at night, ibid., 1120; of Pachomius performing the office of absent brethren, ibid., 244; of Pambo yielding his camel to another, ibid., 788; of Polychronius, accustomed to fast seven days, who took some food in order to induce a sick man to do so, LXXIV, 83; of a certain elder giving another the straps of his baskets, LXXIII, 790, 975; of a certain elder teaching that a debt ought not be exacted anxiously from brethren, ibid., 797; of a certain elder whose charity toward the living and dead was admirable, LXXIV, 129; of Serapion, who gave away everything, even his book of the Gospels, LXXIII, 772, 888; of Serapion Sindonites, who distributed to the poor the wages of his subordinate brethren’s labours, ibid., 1176; of the same, selling himself to mime-actors and to a certain Manichaean in order to win them for God, ibid., 1178, 1180; of Symeon Stylites, giving his food to the poor, ibid., 326; of Sisoes, who ate with a departing guest during a fast, ibid., 907; of Theodore, who disapproved of exceptional food within the community, ibid., 767.

Onuphrius’s almsgiving, LXXIII, 217; John’s, ibid., 236; Eleemon’s, who sold books to assist the poor, ibid., 1197; that of an old woman who distributed in church whatever she earned by her hands, LXXIV, 183. Almsgiving frees Zeno from an impious punishment [Col. 0437], ibid., 208. Help given to an unhappy woman frees Moschus from prison, ibid., 215. Peter the Toll-collector throws a loaf of rye bread to a poor person, LXXIII, 355; he becomes a notable almsgiver, ibid.; gives his inner garment to a poor person, orders himself sold, and has the price distributed to the poor, ibid., 357. Serapion hires out his labour with monks in harvest time in order to assist the poor, ibid., 1176; sells the Gospel book, ibid., 359; sells himself to gain them, ibid., 359, 1178. Josaphat’s alms toward the poor, ibid., 579, 586, 591. The lavish alms of Olympias, ibid., 1209.

**GREGORY THE GREAT (Saint).**—He grants freedom to the slaves of the Roman Church, LXXV, 838. He provided support for those abandoning schism or heresy, ibid. He aided three thousand nuns, ibid., 839. He writes to Maurice on behalf of peoples oppressed by exactions, 794. If bishops’ revenues were wholly insufficient to feed the poor, he himself supplied what was enough, ibid., 838. He devoted himself entirely to the gain of souls, ibid., 742. Gregory’s zeal in giving alms, ibid., 452. After founding monasteries, he sold his property and gave it to the poor, ibid., 242, 252. Four times yearly he distributed alms from his patrimony to the poor, ibid., 96. He personally and locally arranged alms, ibid., 111 ff. Having nothing from which to give alms, he orders a silver dish to be given to a poor person, ibid., 65. The care he took of the poor, ibid., 106, 124, 294; even after death, ibid., 232, 23 [as printed]. He wished the goods of deceased bishops to be reserved for the poor, ibid., 391. He mourns for a poor man who died in want as though he had killed him with his own hands, ibid., 96. He founded a hostel at Jerusalem, ibid., 110. He appointed governors over hostels to administer the goods of the poor energetically, ibid. Saint Desiderius was a nourisher of little children, guardian of old persons, protector of widows, and defender of wards, ibid., 87, 239.

**ELIGIUS (Saint).**—He constantly went about surrounded by crowds of poor people, to whom he gave both food and alms. Everything he had, except clothing and food, he scattered entirely among the needy and monasteries, LXXXVII, 489. He always had the greatest love for the poor and, among other things, served old persons, widows, and orphans, ibid., 507–508. With exceptional kindness he supported pilgrims, ibid., 508.

**VENANTIUS.**—Saint Menardus, whatever he was due to receive as food, if he saw a poor person, offered that food to the needy and himself endured want, LXXXVIII, 535. Saint Maurilius visited the sick as a most faithful steward of God’s word, ibid., 567.

**WALAFRID STRABO.**—How great was Saint Othmar’s mercy toward the poor, CXIV, 1034–1035.
