## Part Two: On Almsgiving

The question is treated as a supplement according to the alphabetical order of the Fathers.

### Alan of Lille

> “Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the needy and wandering into your house.”

And elsewhere:

> “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you.”

Likewise:

> “Give to everyone who asks of you.”

Likewise: Blessed is he who forestalls the hand of one perishing. Likewise: If you see a person dying of hunger and do not help, you have killed him.

[Col. 0438] O man, almsgiving is the seasoning of fasting, the ornament of prayer, the glory of vigils, the badge of generosity, and a special remedy for sin. Christ invites you to it: by example, giving away all things as a poor man; by word, preaching works of mercy. Let no poverty excuse you from it. If you cannot give money, give a piece of bread; if you cannot do that, at least give a drink of cold water. If you cannot help your neighbour by deed, help by word, either interceding for him or instructing him.

For almsgiving is manifold: it proceeds from the hand, in giving generously to the poor; from service, in ministering to the giver; from the tongue, in instructing one’s neighbour or interceding for him; from the mind, in compassionating the sinner or forgiving injuries. Some alms are ordered, others disordered. Ordered alms are those shaped by their proper circumstances; disordered alms are deprived of them. These are the circumstances of almsgiving: who, what, how much, to whom, where, when, why.

“Who”: whether he is rich or poor; for the alms of the poor person are more pleasing than those of the rich. Thus the Lord says in the Gospel that the poor woman who put two small coins into the treasury gave more than the rich who had put in great sums. By “who” is also meant whether he is just or unjust. For if a just person gives alms, it avails for both purposes; but if an unjust person gives alms, it avails him for escape from punishment, not for the merit of glory.

By “what” is indicated that almsgiving ought to be made from one’s own goods, not another’s. For it is not right to make alms from theft or robbery; because, as Scripture says, to make alms from the substance of the poor is to slaughter a son in his father’s sight.

By “how much” is shown that one ought not to give everything to one person, but distribute portions among many. By “to whom” it is suggested that alms should be given rather to the poor than to the rich; rather to a kinsman or relation than to a stranger; rather to members of the household of faith than to the troublesome. Thus, to indicate “how much” and “to whom,” it is said: “He scattered abroad; he gave to the poor.”

“Where”: namely, openly for the instruction of others, but with every human praise set far aside. Hence the Lord says: “So let your works shine . . .” “When”: at a time of need. “Why”: for God’s sake, not for earthly gain or human favour.

Almsgiving is heavenly dew, quenching the furnace of sin; it alone pleads for you before God; it alone will plead for you before the strict Judge. For what will Christ praise in the blessed at the judgment? Because they kept silence? No. Because they were continent? Not at all. Because they devoted themselves to vigils? By no means; but because they practised almsgiving.

Almsgiving bears the likeness of oil, fasting that of light. For as a lamp is extinguished when its oil is removed, so fasting without almsgiving is deprived of the power of merit. Whoever refuses alms to one in need violates that special and natural precept: “What you wish people to do to you, do also to them.”

Almsgiving is threefold: cold, lukewarm, and hot. Cold almsgiving is not done from the prompting of natural compassion or the ardour of charity, but only for human favour. Lukewarm almsgiving is done from the prompting of natural compassion, as that which is done for unbelievers through natural affection. Hot almsgiving is done in the heat of charity. The first deserves punishment; the second avoids it; the third obtains grace.

Almsgiving ought to be made not only from superfluities but also from necessities. Thus it is said: “He who has two tunics, let him give to one who has none.” He names a tunic, not a cloak, because a tunic is more necessary: thereby indicating that we are bound to give not merely superfluities but necessities also. This was made plain in blessed Martin, who, in severe weather, gave to a poor person part of the cloak with which alone he was clothed.

There are indeed some who give to the poor things scarcely fit to set before swine, believing that by these they redeem their sins. This is, as it were, blasphemy against God: it is to honour the gods with unworthy things and to offer to heavenly pearls things that ought to be trampled by swine, CCX, 175–176.

> “Do not forget hospitality . . .”

O man, Christ cries at your door in his members and asks for lodging. Receive the pilgrim on earth, that he may receive you rejoicing in your homeland. Abraham, because he received angels in the guise of guests, deserved to be granted a son. Lot, because he received angels as guests, deserved to be delivered from the conflagration of Sodom. The widow who honoured Elijah with the kindness of hospitality deserved the restoration of her son to life. The disciples going to Emmaus were enlightened through Christ’s teaching; but through the service of hospitality they deserved to be enlightened by him more fully and perfectly.

O man, if you know that you are a stranger and pilgrim in this world, if you recognize the condition of your pilgrimage, you will not deny lodging to a stranger. For if you exclude Christ’s poor person from your roof, you exclude Christ himself from the hospitality of your heart. [lacuna] Hear what he himself says: “What you did to one of the least of mine . . .”

Hospitality itself ought to be cheerful, generous, displaying humility and embracing liberality. For a great part of honourable hospitality is serenity of countenance. [Col. 0439] Generosity, too, is part of hospitality: we should not receive a petitioner only when overcome by annoyance, but should even anticipate him with a prior act of service. For, after the example of those going to Emmaus, guests are not merely to be invited but drawn in. Humility must also be shown to guests, so that, through the grace of humility—which indeed completes the whole of hospitality—the service rendered may be more welcome.

Let us therefore receive in the pilgrim him who for us journeyed upon earth from heaven, who for us left his homeland and became a beggar on the road. O happy hospitality offered to Christ in the poor! O happy bed on which Christ rests in the body! Happy table at which the God-man sits in a human being! O man, among the Gentiles the laws of hospitality are observed; among the faithful they are broken. Brute animals rejoice at the arrival of their like and in some fashion offer them the right of companionship; but human beings withhold the office of humanity.

> “Blush, O Sidon, says the sea.”

Let the sea blush to be aided by rivers. Let the rational blush to be instructed by the irrational. Let the sun blush to be warmed by a furnace and torches [lacuna], CCX, 181–182. On almsgiving, CCX, 175.

### Ambrose, Bishop of Milan

On the duty of almsgiving, XIV, 724. On the benefits of almsgiving, XIV, 1069. The example of generosity toward the poor set forth by the Gospel widow, XVI, 242.

### Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury

On almsgiving, CLIX, 56.

### Augustine, Bishop of Hippo

Certainly one must beware lest anyone suppose that those unspeakable crimes, committed by persons who “shall not possess the kingdom of God,” may be perpetrated daily and redeemed by daily alms. Rather, one’s life must be changed for the better, and God must be propitiated through alms for past sins—not, as it were, bought off so that it may always be lawful to commit such acts with impunity, XL, 265.

Certainly, those who live most wickedly, take no care to correct such a life and character, and do not cease amid their very crimes and shameful deeds frequently to give alms, flatter themselves in vain because the Lord says: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you.” [lacuna], XL, 267.

For the person who wishes to give alms rightly must begin with himself and give it first to himself:

> “Have mercy on your own soul, pleasing God.”

[lacuna] For this order of love it was said: “You shall love your neighbour as yourself.” Therefore, when the Lord rebuked the Pharisees because they washed themselves outwardly but within were full of robbery and iniquity, he admonished them that the inner things must be cleansed by a certain alms which a person ought first to give to himself: “But nevertheless,” he says, “give alms . . .” XL, 268.

When you hear that all evil deeds are redeemed by alms, do not understand it as certain perverse people do. Alms can indeed profit you to blot out past sins, if you change your character. But if you persist in the same evils, you do not corrupt the Judge by your alms. I speak of those wicked deeds and crimes which all who receive the body and blood of the Lord must now avoid.

Moreover, I do not deny that this mortal life, established in corruptible flesh, cannot be without sins; but those daily and slight sins have their own daily washings [lacuna]. What God established—that alms should aid with slight sins—that person thinks can help him with those grave sins from which he is unwilling to depart, but in which he desires to remain forever. Let him make alms for them, but let his life be changed; let him depart from there and come here. But if he says in his heart: “If I commit daily robberies, if I defile myself with daily adulterous corruptions [lacuna], and do not depart at all from such a life, yet by making daily alms I extinguish all sins”—indeed you extinguish them, but once you have extinguished them [lacuna], the sins therefore perish, but with you. If, however, you change your life, they perish and you will be found [alive], XXXIX, 1701, 1901, 2343.

But do not think that adulteries are to be committed daily and cleansed by daily alms. Daily alms are insufficient to cleanse those greater crimes. It is one thing to change one’s life, another to endure life. The former must be changed: if you were adulterous, do not be adulterous; if you were a fornicator, do not fornicate; if a murderer, do not be a murderer [lacuna]. Do you suppose that these deeds, unless they cease to be done, can be cleansed by daily alms? [lacuna] XXXVIII, 88.

### Cyprian, Bishop of Carthage and Martyr

The Holy Spirit speaks in the divine Scriptures:

> “By alms and faith sins are cleansed.”

And:

> “But give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you,”

etc. [lacuna] Remembering these precepts, Daniel, when King Nebuchadnezzar was distressed by an ominous dream, prescribed a remedy for averting evils and obtaining divine help, saying:

> “Therefore, O king, let my counsel please you: redeem your sins by alms and your injustices by mercies to the poor.”

The king did not obey him and suffered the adversities and calamities he had seen; he could have escaped and avoided them if he had redeemed his sins by alms.

The angel Raphael likewise testifies to the same things and urges that almsgiving be done gladly and liberally:

> “Prayer with fasting and almsgiving is good, because almsgiving delivers from death and itself cleanses sins.”

He shows that our prayers and fasts are of less force unless assisted by alms, and that prayers alone have little power to obtain what is sought unless helped by the addition of deeds and works, IV, 605–606.

Nor do we advance these things without confirming by the witness of truth what the angel Raphael said. In the Acts of the Apostles faith is placed in the event itself, and it has been established by the proof of an accomplished deed that souls are delivered by alms not merely from the second death but from the first. Tabitha, greatly devoted to righteous works and giving alms, fell ill and died. Peter was summoned to the lifeless corpse. When he came promptly in apostolic compassion, the weeping widows stood around him, begging and showing the cloaks, tunics, and all the garments they had previously received. They pleaded not for the dead woman by their voices, but by her works.

Peter perceived that what was thus requested could be obtained, and that Christ’s help would not fail the pleading widows, when Christ himself was clothed in the widows. Therefore, having prayed on his knees, this effective advocate of widows and the poor carried their delegated prayers to the Lord. Turning to the body, which already lay washed upon its bier, he said: “Tabitha, arise in the name of Christ.” Thus death is suspended and the spirit restored; and, while all marvel and are amazed, the body, restored to life, is animated anew for this world’s light [lacuna], IV, 606–607.

More on this question is read in the work. On alms, IV, 601, 622.

On almsgiving, IV, 601. On the benefit of work and mercy, IV, 723.

### Gunther, Cistercian Monk

We show mercy to our neighbour in several ways: namely, by compassion, prayer, correction, counsel, assistance, and beneficence. We show mercy by compassion when we mercifully grieve either over his sins or over his miseries. David grieved over the sins of his son Absalom when he pursued his father, and he grieved over his miseries when he lamented his pitiable death.

Likewise, we show mercy by prayer in two ways: when we humbly implore God in prayer either for a neighbour’s sins or for his miseries. Stephen prayed for his neighbours’ sins when he prayed for those stoning him. Paul prayed for miseries when he raised by prayer the young man [Col. 0441] Eutychus, slain by a wretched fate.

We also show mercy by correction in two ways: when, rebuking him, we correct him for evil deeds already done; or when we mercifully draw him away from committing them [lacuna]. We show mercy to our neighbour by counsel when we assist with sound advice one who is in error and wholly ignorant of himself. We show mercy to the same neighbour by assistance when we mercifully procure or provide help for him to do or obtain a good which he cannot do or obtain by himself. We show mercy by beneficence when, from compassionate purpose, we give a needy person material support, such as food, drink, clothing, or money.

In providing such beneficence, these points are clear: it must not be made from another’s property; it must not be without measure; it must not be given to one unworthy. It must not be made from another’s property [lacuna]; it must not be without measure—for example, if you gave to one person what might have helped many; it must not be given to one unworthy if an equally needy worthy person can be found. As it is written: “Let your alms sweat in your hand until you find the righteous person to whom you may give.” Although elsewhere it is written, “Give to everyone who asks of you,” yet these benefits of ours ought to be extended more abundantly and more frequently to members of the household of faith and to our neighbours or intimates, CCXII, 210–211.

These qualities are fitting for one who gives alms: purity of mind, simplicity, humility, generosity, and cheerfulness. Purity of mind is very necessary, without which whatever he might do would not be almsgiving; for, since almsgiving is nothing other than mercy, no one can be merciful to another who is shown by the impurity of his heart to be ungodly and merciless toward himself. Therefore, if you intend to give alms, you must begin with yourself and proceed to your neighbour [lacuna].

Simplicity is also fitting: because almsgiving ought to be done solely for compassion’s sake, one should not seek human favour, as the Pharisees do [lacuna]. Humility too is greatly necessary, lest what ought humbly to be done out of love for God and neighbour be done arrogantly and proudly, as certain most depraved people do, who give to jesters and actors what should be bestowed upon the poor [lacuna]. Generosity should likewise accompany the giver of alms, so that he may not be bloodless and dry in giving, but gladly share with his brother according to his means, fearing not so much his own future want as considering the other’s present poverty. For he ought to remember that he who supplied the present gift can, after these things have been distributed, provide others more abundantly [lacuna]. Cheerfulness must always accompany the giver of alms, so that he gives the very thing he gives with a glad heart [lacuna].

These five things result from almsgiving: forgiveness of sins, increase of charity, spiritual joy, certain hope of the promises, and reception of rewards. That forgiveness of sins proceeds from almsgiving ought to be doubtful to no one [lacuna]. An increase of charity proceeds from almsgiving both toward God and toward one’s neighbour [lacuna], and other things, CCXII, 209–222.

### Innocent III, Pope

> “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you.”

No one could commend almsgiving more worthily than Truth itself has commended it, declaring that all things are cleansed through almsgiving. Thus the name fittingly accords with the effect and with an interpretation of truth. For *eleemosyna* is said to derive from *elimino* (“I remove”), or from *eli*, which is “God,” and *Moys*, which is “water,” because through almsgiving God removes the stains of sins and washes away the filth of vices.

Almsgiving is assistance given to one in need out of compassionate regard. Sacred Scripture shows how great its fruit is. For almsgiving cleanses; almsgiving delivers; almsgiving redeems; almsgiving protects; almsgiving pleads; almsgiving obtains; almsgiving perfects; almsgiving blesses; almsgiving justifies; almsgiving raises to life; almsgiving saves.

Hear examples of each in order. The Lord says: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you”: behold how almsgiving cleanses. The angel Raphael says to Tobias: “Prayer with fasting and almsgiving is good, better than laying up treasures of gold; for almsgiving delivers from death, and it is what cleanses sins and causes one to find eternal life”: behold how almsgiving delivers.

Daniel said to Nebuchadnezzar:

> “Let my counsel please you, O king: redeem your sins by alms and your iniquities by mercies [Col. 0442] to the poor; perhaps God will forgive your offenses.”

Behold how almsgiving redeems.

Tobias, while travelling “through all his kindred, distributed to each according to his ability from his possessions; he fed the hungry, gave clothing to the naked, and carefully provided burial for the dead. When the king ordered him killed, he fled and hid naked, because many loved him”: behold how almsgiving protects.

> “Hide almsgiving in the bosom of the poor, and it will pray for you,”

because water extinguishes burning fire and almsgiving resists sins: behold how almsgiving pleads.

Cornelius the centurion, making many alms to the people and praying to God always, clearly saw in a vision an angel of God saying to him: “Your prayers and your alms have risen in remembrance before God”: behold how almsgiving obtains.

The Lord also says: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, give to the poor, and you will have great treasure in heaven”: behold how almsgiving perfects.

The Lord says: “In the third year you shall set apart another tithe from all that is born to you at that time and lay it up within your gates. Then the Levite, who has no other possession with you, and the stranger, the orphan, and the widow who are within your gates, shall come and eat and be satisfied, that the Lord your God may bless you in every work of your hands that you do”: behold how almsgiving blesses.

> “He scattered abroad; he gave to the poor; his righteousness remains for ever and ever; his horn shall be exalted in glory”:

behold how almsgiving justifies.

When Tabitha, who was full of good works and alms, died, “all the widows stood around Peter weeping and showing the tunics and garments which she made for them. He knelt and prayed, and said: ‘Tabitha, arise’; and she opened her eyes, and seeing Peter sat up”: behold how almsgiving raises to life.

Zacchaeus, standing, said to the Lord: “Behold, I give half my goods to the poor, and if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.” Jesus said to him: “Today salvation has come to this house, because he too is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man came to seek and save what was lost”: behold how almsgiving saves, CCXVII, 745–748.

There are also many other effects of almsgiving, which you can learn from the testimonies set below. At judgment the Lord commended works of mercy, for which he will grant the merciful an eternal kingdom, while declaring that he will punish the wicked:

> “Come, blessed of my Father . . . for I was hungry and you gave me food . . . Blessed are the merciful . . . With the measure with which you have measured, it shall be measured back to you . . .”

That rich man clothed in purple and fine linen, who feasted splendidly every day, because he did not have mercy on the beggar named Lazarus, [lacuna] “died and was buried in hell” [lacuna]. That servant who refused mercy to his fellow servant as his master had shown mercy to him was handed over to the torturers [lacuna], etc., CCXVII, 748–750. On alms, CCXVII, 432, 747, 1145.

“That almsgiving has no merit in sins actually committed and does not attain its effect, but is nevertheless preparatory toward obtaining God’s grace [lacuna].”

But if almsgiving is of such power—or rather, if the power of almsgiving is so great—let people do whatever they please and merely persist in almsgiving, confident in Truth, which says: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you.” Are all things, then, clean for those who give alms—for drunkards, adulterers, murderers, and people entangled in the remaining filth of vices? May they therefore freely practise their shameful acts and pursue their pleasures, if almsgiving is sufficient to redeem sins. Far be it! For, as Scripture testifies, “Whatever the unclean touches shall be unclean.” Offerers are not pleasing because of their gifts; rather, gifts are pleasing because of their offerers [lacuna].

Consider carefully what the Apostle says: “If I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor [lacuna], but do not have charity, it profits me nothing [lacuna].” True almsgiving therefore proceeds from true charity. For this is the commandment of charity: “You shall love your neighbour as yourself.” To this belongs: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do also to them.” Therefore, as we wish to be helped by others in our necessities, so we ought to help others in theirs, so that we may love our neighbour as ourselves.

Unless the branch of almsgiving springs from the root of charity, it has no richness or moisture by which to produce sweet or ripe fruit. For almsgiving is truly the fruit of charity. “Charity covers a multitude of sins.” Of it Truth says: “Many sins are forgiven her, because she loved much.” The almsgiving that proceeds from charity certainly cleanses from vices and redeems from sins [lacuna].

Thus almsgiving bestowed apart from charity—or, rather, before charity—does profit, though it does not suffice. It is preparatory, though not [Col. 0443] meritorious, for grace or salvation; yet through it one arrives at grace and salvation. For it makes a person capable, fit, and suitable—like one thirsting, panting, and approaching the fountain of saving grace—by which he is delivered from death, cleansed from guilt, and redeemed from sin, CCXVII, 750–752.

Among works of mercy which, according to the Apostle, have the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come, divine Scripture especially and frequently commends hospitality to us. For it embraces all those things on account of which the Lord declares that in the examination of the final judgment he will reward the good and punish the wicked. It feeds the hungry, gives drink to the thirsty, gathers in guests, clothes the naked; and it not only visits the sick but, taking their infirmities upon itself, cares for those who are ill. It helps those in prison, and, as it shares with the living in their sickness, so it shares in the burial of the dead.

Through hospitality some pleased God by receiving angels as guests: Abraham and Lot, devoted to hospitality, deserved to lodge angels. Through them Abraham, though now old, received the promise of future offspring, and Lot was delivered from the fire of Sodom. The two disciples who constrained Jesus to stay as their guest, whom they had not known in the exposition of Scripture, knew him in the breaking of bread.

Through hospitality, the superfluities of the rich, perhaps otherwise stored up for death, are spent for the needs of the poor unto life. Through it earthly things are exchanged for heavenly and transient things for eternal in a blessed commerce, while through the hands of the poor we store treasure in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys and where thieves do not break in or steal; and we make friends for ourselves from the mammon of unrighteousness, so that when we fail, they may receive us into eternal dwellings [lacuna], CCXV, 77.

Fasting is good, but almsgiving is better, because what fasting takes away, almsgiving bestows. Otherwise, what fasting takes away from pleasure, it restores to desire. But the person who gives alms spends wholly on another whatever he withdraws from himself. Through fasting one’s own flesh is afflicted; through almsgiving another’s is refreshed. The former produces hunger; the latter provides satiety.

Again, prayer is good, but giving is better, because almsgiving does both, descending to one’s neighbour and ascending to God. Hear the saying of the Wise Man on this point: “Shut up almsgiving in the heart of the poor, and it will pray to the Lord for you.” For one who does not cease to do good does not cease to pray, since it is better to pray by deed than by speech.

But you will say: “I am poor, needy, and destitute. I have no bread, no clothing, no means from which I can give anything.” Yet consider that with God a good will suffices where the suitable means are lacking. He considers not so much the quantity of the gift as the devotion in the deed, weighing more from how much than how much. For Jesus, looking up, saw rich people putting their offerings into the treasury. He also saw a certain poor widow putting in two small copper coins, and said: “Amen, I say to you, this poor widow has put in more than all of them. For all these gave out of their abundance into God’s offerings; but she, from what she lacked, put in all the livelihood she had” [lacuna], CCXVII, 752.

Moreover, diligently observe that unless you give the alms of the heart, God does not accept the alms of outward work. He himself says: “If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will forgive your offenses. But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father forgive [lacuna].” You see plainly that God does not approve the gift of outward work unless you first offer the gift of the heart.

You prudently give the alms of the heart when either you forgive one who has offended you or you make satisfaction to one whom you have offended, so that neither he may retain resentment or hatred against you in his heart, nor you retain resentment or hatred against him in your heart [lacuna], CCXVII, 753–757.

That perseverance is required in almsgiving, as in any and every good work, see CCXVII, 759, 762.

It remains to say from what goods alms should be made. Surely it seems that they should be made from what you possess justly and have acquired reasonably, according to the saying of the Wise Man: “Do not offer wicked gifts, for God will not receive them.” [lacuna] There are many such passages in Scripture [lacuna].

Yet the Lord seems to teach the contrary in the Gospel: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of unrighteousness, so that when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings.” But among things acquired unjustly, there are some in which ownership is transferred and others in which it is not transferred. From those in which ownership is transferred—for example, in commerce, military service, and the like—almsgiving may lawfully be made. For although you sinned by acquiring them unlawfully, once they have become yours you may nevertheless lawfully give from them as from your own goods.

But from things in which ownership is not transferred, such as theft, robbery, sacrilege, and usury, it is not lawful to make alms. Since they are another’s property, not yours, you are bound to restore them to those [Col. 0444] to whom they belong, not to handle them against their owners’ will [lacuna]. The Gospel’s phrase “mammon of unrighteousness” therefore refers to those unjust acquisitions in which ownership is transferred, from which almsgiving may lawfully be made.

But because it is not hearers of the law but doers who are righteous before God, I ask, exhort, entreat, and admonish you, whoever you are, Christian, if you wish to be what you are called: strive to do what you have heard, holding firmly that almsgiving given “from a pure heart, a good conscience, and sincere faith” gives great confidence before the Most High and is itself a saving remedy against every danger, CCXVII, 758–759. Encomium of charity, CCXVII, 761–764.

Concerning almsgiving, attend carefully to four things: namely, its cause, end, manner, and order. Its cause: that it be done from charity; its end: that it be done for blessedness; its manner: that it be done cheerfully; its order: that it be done according to rule.

Almsgiving must be given from charity; for as a tree stands in relation to its fruit, so charity stands in relation to almsgiving. “For a good tree cannot produce bad fruits, nor a bad tree good fruits.” Therefore the Apostle says: “If I distribute all my possessions,” etc. [lacuna] Let no one, then, deceive himself in vain by supposing that almsgiving without charity can suffice for his salvation, although almsgiving distributed apart from charity has force for three things: either for making one capable of receiving grace, or for mitigation of eternal punishment, or for obtaining some temporal good.

Therefore, when anyone gives alms, he ought to give them for the sake of eternal blessedness, not for worldly favor or human recompense. Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “When you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before yourself, as hypocrites do in synagogues and streets, that they may be honored by men. Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward. But when you give alms, let not your left hand know what your right hand does, so that your alms may be in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.” This is not contrary to what the Lord says elsewhere: “Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” First, because one’s intention may remain hidden while one’s action is open, so that, on account of the hidden intention, the left hand does not know what the right hand does; and on account of the manifest action, those seeing the good works may glorify the Father. Secondly, because no one ought to do a good work in order that he himself may be glorified by men, but in order that men may glorify God. Thus the former is forbidden and the latter commanded. Again Truth says elsewhere: “When you make a dinner or supper, do not invite your friends or brothers, relatives, or rich neighbors, lest perhaps they invite you in return and you receive recompense. But when you make a feast, invite the poor, the weak, the lame, and the blind; and you shall be blessed, because they have nothing with which to repay you. For you shall be repaid at the resurrection of the just.” This is the end, this the reward, this the prize for which almsgiving must be performed.

Moreover, alms should be given not sorrowfully but cheerfully; not slowly but promptly. Thus the Apostle teaches, saying: “Each one [should give] as he has determined in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion. For God loves a cheerful giver.”

Furthermore, observe an ordered rule in giving alms. For almsgiving is threefold: that of the heart, the mouth, and the deed. It is given from the heart through compassion; from the mouth through correction; from the deed through generosity. Of the first the Apostle says: “Who is weak,” etc.; of the second the Lord says: “If your brother sins against you,” …; of the third the prophet says: “Break your bread for the hungry …” But this threefold almsgiving must be given in due order: first to ourselves, secondly to our neighbor. For cruel and foolish is the person who has compassion on another and does not pity himself; who chastises another and does not amend himself; who assists another and despises himself. On the contrary, it is commanded: “Have mercy on your own soul, pleasing God …” Therefore almsgiving must first be given to yourself. After yourself, give alms to your neighbors, and among them also keep an order, preferring believers, members of the household, and relatives. For this reason the Apostle says: “Let us do good to all, especially to those of the household of faith.” For ordered charity requires this … Yet among these the just ought to be preferred, if the other circumstances are equal … Since every human being, both good and bad, is our neighbor by reason of shared nature, and since by divine command we are bound to love our neighbors as ourselves, it plainly seems that we are bound, when able, to assist every needy person indiscriminately; and since doing good to enemies seems more meritorious than doing good to friends … On the other hand, Truth itself testifies: “Whoever [Col. 0445] receives a just man in the name of a just man shall receive a just man’s reward …”

Almsgiving would therefore often be delayed if it were always necessary to distinguish between the good and the bad. Yet why should you not prefer a just person to an unjust one in giving alms, when by his merits and prayers he can obtain more for you from the Lord? Certainly good should be done to good and bad alike, to just and impious persons, to friends and enemies, when necessity requires it and means allow it; but in such matters the circumstances must be weighed, so that one may discern when, how, where, and to whom assistance should rather be given. For it can happen that at some time a bad person should be assisted more than a good one, if he is oppressed by greater need—especially when assistance cannot be postponed without danger. And although it is more meritorious to do good to enemies, because then the mind most forcibly acts for God’s sake—hence: “From the days of John the Baptist, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it”—nevertheless, if one’s parents are in need, I believe they should rather be helped, because of that special commandment: “Honor your father and your mother.” … Although, therefore, good ought generally to be done to all neighbors, it should be done more abundantly to the good than to the bad, to the just than to the impious, unless some special exception, after the circumstances have been weighed, qualifies the general rule.

**LAURENTIUS (St.), bishop of Novara.**—Among the many useful and salutary precepts written in the divine Scriptures, there is no other medicine for our wounds so effective, so powerful, and so swift as the commandment concerning almsgiving. For almsgiving not only cleanses sins and heals the wounds of conscience, but also recalls the soul itself from death and makes it a sharer in the heavenly kingdoms. The author of this precept and work is the most just Tobias: blind in body but illustrious in deed; tried for a time yet not put to death; deprived briefly of temporal sight but full of the everlasting light of good works. With such admonitions he instructed his son: “My son, give alms from your substance, and do not turn your face away from any poor person; so it shall come to pass that God’s face shall not be turned away from you.” He also removed the scruple from the mind of one who gives timidly or doubtfully, so that no one may cease giving, whether from much or from little. “My son, do according to what you have; if your substance is abundant, give more generously; if it is scanty, offer a little.” And do not doubt while giving; do not distrust, saying, “Perhaps there will not be enough for us.” Rather be glad while giving, because God loves a cheerful giver.

Since we are human beings, often sinning in our slippery nature, let the soul abound without ceasing in the water of righteousness. What is the root of all evils? Avarice. What is the root of all goods? Almsgiving. And you who are now wounded through avarice, heal yourself through almsgiving. Have you died through avarice? Give yourself life through almsgiving. Is your soul ulcerated by sins? Anoint it with the work of piety and righteousness. You have heard the admonition of the just man: “Almsgiving delivers from death and does not permit one to enter into darkness.” Has covetousness entangled you? You have many offenses. Do you lie ruined by avarice, corrupted by lust? Have you slandered, blasphemed, because you have often lied to many people and frequently sworn falsely? Is the mind buried beneath these forms of wickedness and others like them; is conscience convulsed? What then? Must one despair amid these things? The Lord does not command so. But what does he command? “Give alms,” he says, “and all things shall be clean for you …” LXVI, 105, 116.

**MAXIMUS (St.), bishop of Turin.**—Mercy toward the needy, LVII, 473, 478, 480, 531, 739.

**NICOLAS I, pope.**—You Bulgarians have inquired to whom alms should be distributed. The Lord clearly shows this in the Gospel, saying: “Give to everyone who asks,” etc. … Nevertheless, in giving alms a certain order of discernment must be observed, which we shall now omit to explain fully in the interest of brevity. But let us first indicate what this name signifies: *eleemosyna* is Greek, and in Latin means mercy; and certainly it is written: “Have mercy on your own soul, pleasing God.” Therefore a person ought first, before all others, to give alms to himself; for one ought to begin every rule of right action with oneself, namely by pleasing God through purity of mind and body, and thereby giving oneself that living bread which came down from heaven. Then alms must be given [Col. 0446] to relatives suffering need, as it is written: “Do not despise your own flesh.” Nature itself teaches us this; and what I do not provide for my relative, when will a stranger provide it? Then mercy ought especially to be shown to those who are ashamed to ask. Certainly it must be noted that there are some to whom nothing ought to be given, as it is written: “Give to the good man, and do not receive the sinner …” etc., CXIX, 1013, 1014.

**PASCHASIUS RADBERTUS (St.), abbot of Corbie.**—On the manner of practicing almsgiving, CXX, 270.

**PAULINUS (St.), patriarch of Aquileia.**—On alms and pious works, XCIX, 200, 227.

**PAULUS WINFRIDUS, deacon.**—On almsgiving, XCV, 1216, 1346.

**PETER THE CHANTER.**—On almsgiving, CCV, 286.

**PETER CHRYSOLOGUS (St.), archbishop of Ravenna.**—On almsgiving, LII, 208, 231, 314, 320.

**PETER DAMIAN (St.).**—**PRAISE OF ALMSGIVING:** O power of almsgiving, which, like the flow of a watering spring, both washes away the defilements of sins and extinguishes the flames of burning vices! O blessed almsgiving, which draws the children of darkness from the abyss of hell and introduces them, adopted into everlasting light, into the heavenly kingdoms! You fly to heaven from the hands of the poor, and there prepare lodging for those who love you. If you are wine, you do not turn sour; if bread, you do not grow moldy; if flesh or fish, you do not decay into putrefaction; if, moreover, clothing, you acquire no age or wear. You are always preserved fresh and new; and as soon as your giver has died, you immediately return to him multiplied. You make those lying beneath the filth of crimes conspicuous; you make saints out of those condemned; you make Christians out of Gentiles. Cornelius clearly demonstrates this, for his alms had ascended to the height of the divine presence.

O rich almsgiving, which grants your lovers an unfading inheritance and the dignity of the heavenly court! O wondrous power of mercy, which cleanses away the rust of every sin, mortifies the fuel and incitements of vices, and illumines the dark minds of human beings with the splendor of heavenly grace! This makes God a debtor to human beings, so that they seek the kingdom of heaven no longer as something foreign, but boldly take possession of it as something belonging to them by right. O blessed mercy, born indeed from misery, yet producing true blessedness for those who perform it! You are a merchant more prudent than every trader, purchasing heavenly things with earthly merchandise and exchanging eternal things for transitory ones! Blessed are your markets, in which lodging is given and a dwelling received; a small loaf is offered and a kingdom received; a coin is extended and the palace of heaven purchased …, CXLV, 222.

This holy Father has a little work on almsgiving, in which excellent things are read, CXLV, 207–227.

Although every saint must necessarily flourish in all virtues—for no individual quality is truly a virtue if it is not joined with other virtues—nevertheless one virtue should be chosen by each person above the rest, to which the mind, clinging more familiarly, may devote itself, and from whose service, so to speak, it may not depart. For we cannot exercise ourselves equally in all virtues; but while we guard one more closely, in it we supply what is lacking from the rest; and while we embrace this one without ceasing, we possess, as it were, the whole body of virtues through participation in one member.

What virtue, then, do I urge you to pursue particularly? Fasting? But you will immediately answer: “If I wear down my body with excessive fasts, I shall soon collapse under the pressures of so many affairs and journeys.” If I prescribe meditation upon psalmody, you will say: “I am hindered from constancy in prayer, because every day I am compelled to answer friends’ greetings and engage in conversation.” If I urge you, according to the custom of the apostles, to walk barefoot; if I urge you, in imitation of John, to tame your limbs with harsh haircloth; if finally I bid you go into exile, or command you to be shut up in prison custody after the manner of penitents, you will promptly plead impending illness—or rather, that you cannot endure so grievous a burden of bodily hardship. Therefore, since you still fear to afflict the members of your body—indeed, since you are not yet able to offer yourself to God as a sacrifice through the severity of penitence—stretch out your hand, I beg you, to the things around you; and because you cannot give yourself, at least distribute what is yours, CXLV, 209, 210.

“That fruit is obtained from riches when they are distributed to the poor.” Certainly no putrefaction of a wound stinks more intolerably in God’s nostrils than the dung of avarice. And every covetous person, while he heaps up the gain of filthy money, turning a hall into a latrine, piles up, as it were, a mass of dung. Hence it is said through Ezekiel: “Their silver shall be cast outside, and their gold shall be [Col. 0447] in the dung heap; their silver and gold shall not be able to deliver them on the day of the Lord’s wrath.” And elsewhere: “Woe to him who multiplies what is not his—how long?—and heaps upon himself thick mud!” For the greedy person to heap thick mud upon himself is to accumulate earthly gains together with the weight of sin. [lacuna] Let anyone, then, be chaste, sober, intent on feeding the needy, devoted to hospitality; let him fast, keep vigil, and join day to night in psalmody: if nevertheless he is greedy, he loses everything, so that among all those guilty of crimes he cannot find anyone worse than himself. For nothing is more wicked than a greedy person; nothing more unjust than to love money. What then will it profit you not to kill, not to commit adultery, not to rob, nor finally to commit perjury, and to preserve yourself wholly free from every crime, if avarice is not driven out of you? Nothing more wicked, nothing more criminal than you can be found. CXLV, 532, 533.

On the benefits and effects of almsgiving, CXLV, 207. On [Col. 0448] charity, CXLV, 326. On restraining anger, CXLV [printed CXLX], 649. “You shall not kill,” CXLV, 1019.

**RABANUS MAURUS, abbot of Fulda.**—On the giving of alms, CVII, 814. On alms and the poor, CIX, 783, 845. On the generosity of almsgiving, CX, 23, 97, 112, 205.

**RATHERIUS, bishop of Verona.** On almsgiving, CXXXVI, 698.

**TAIO, bishop of Saragossa.**—He who gives outward substance to a needy neighbor, but does not guard his own life from wickedness, gives his property to God and himself to sin. He has offered the lesser thing to the Creator and reserved the greater thing for iniquity. Sometimes arrogant rich persons oppress their inferiors and seize what belongs to others, yet distribute certain things as though generously to others …, LXXX, 891–893.

On almsgiving, LXXX, 939.

# CXLVII. INDEX ON FRATERNAL CORRECTION, EXPOUNDING THE CIRCUMSTANCES AND CONDITIONS REQUIRED FOR EACH PERSON TO BE OBLIGED BY THIS PRECEPT TOWARD HIS NEIGHBOR, AND THE FRUITS TO BE DERIVED FROM IT

## NOTICE

This index is divided into two parts. The first contains certain general notions in alphabetical order; the second contains the resolutions of questions, as an appendix to Index CXLV on the love of enemies, in chronological order.

## [INDEX ON FRATERNAL CORRECTION]

### PART ONE. Special notions concerning fraternal correction, in alphabetical order

**AUGUSTINE (St.), bishop of Hippo.**—Take heed lest you so remove the speck from another’s eye that you do not see the beam in your own eye; nor wish so to relieve another’s fall that you do not see your own downfall. Nor ought you so to heal another’s disease that you neglect yourselves as sick persons, lest it be said to any of you: “Physician, heal yourself.” Therefore heal yourself first, so that, once healed, you may be able to heal another’s wounds. Hear what the Lord said to the Pharisees accusing the adulteress: “He among you who is without sin, let him first cast a stone at her.” With what face can we accuse others of what we find more gravely in ourselves? It belongs to us, therefore, to be clean and holy; and if we then see our brother sinning, we ought to rebuke him with all gentleness, lest through our negligence he perish. But charity must draw the sword of correction not from hatred or resentment, but from zeal for justice. Let mercy always then be bound in your hearts, lest the one who sinned, like Judas, despairingly go to hanging, XL, 1258.

**PETER DAMIAN.**—Among the other marks of holy conduct, take care above all not to bear corrections harshly at any time, lest upon any occasion you be ashamed to be reproved even by your juniors. This is so familiar and natural to this condition, namely, that the person reproved flees … For a person leaves the world and submits himself to the instruction of regular discipline in order that the file of harsh correction may remove the rust he acquired from the seductive world. Hence Wisdom speaks in Proverbs: “Turn yourselves to my correction, and I will pour out my Spirit to you.” … Correction is rightly called not that of a human being but of the Lord when any severity is imposed from neighbor to neighbor in the love of Christ; and he departs far from wisdom who does not bow his proud heart beneath divine reproofs. Thus Solomon says: “He who loves discipline loves wisdom; but he who hates reproofs is foolish.” Therefore he also says: “Why did I hate discipline, and why did my heart not yield to reproofs? Why did I not hear the voice of those teaching me and incline my ear to my masters? …” CXLV, 704, 705, 706.

Now there comes to mind that Paul, as he writes to the Galatians, reproved his fellow apostle blessed Peter; but inwardly he agreed in purpose with the man whom he outwardly rebuked as though in disagreement. “When Peter,” he says, “came to Antioch, I resisted him to his face …” O words harsh on the surface, and, if considered only in their syllables, utterly foreign to the dignity of the apostolic eminence! Peter is reproachable—the man to whom all the kingdoms of the earth were entrusted for rebuking and correction. He is withstood to his face, at whose command the gate of Christ’s heavenly kingdom is opened to the faithful; he is called the author of dissimulation, he who is first among the preachers of truth. “But when I saw that they were not walking uprightly according to the truth of the Gospel, I said to Cephas before them all …” What is this, blessed Paul? Why do you tear your superior with reproofs and exasperate him with rebukes? How do you not fear to put him to shame before human eyes, he to whom it was granted by a special right to preside over the universal Church of the whole world? Or have you perhaps forgotten what the common Teacher of you both instructed? “If your brother,” he says, “sins against you, rebuke him between yourself and him alone; but if he will not hear you, bring two or three witnesses.” But you do not address him privately, nor secretly before witnesses; instead, you accuse him openly before all, and moreover write down for the knowledge of future posterity—which is more serious—that you did this. Have you also forgotten what you yourself commanded Timothy: “Do not rebuke an elder, but entreat him as a father”?

But in this, that Paul openly rebuked blessed Peter before all, he appeared outwardly as an opponent, yet fulfilled the desires of Peter’s heart. For Peter did not dare, in the presence of those who believed from the circumcision, to receive Gentiles coming to the faith into fellowship at table, lest those persons be scandalized and immediately fall back from a faith still tender under this pretext. Thus he who was accustomed to eat with Gentiles withdrew himself from their fellowship when certain persons came from James, fearing those believers from the circumcision, lest, if they saw him eating with Gentiles, they run the risk of unfaithfulness. For that Peter agreed in every respect with Paul—that the Gentiles ought not to observe Jewish rites—no one who has read the Acts of the Apostles can doubt; indeed, Peter is undoubtedly found as the first author of this opinion among the apostles, though he is now accused by Paul as though a transgressor. For he says: “Now therefore why do you test God by placing a yoke upon the necks of the disciples, etc. …?” Peter therefore very much wished to be publicly rebuked; he rejoiced to be confounded by the rebuker’s contrivance, so that, once reproved, he might cease doing what he was doing unwillingly, and might find a companion in what he had feared to undertake alone. Paul therefore opposed Peter and undoubtedly inwardly agreed with the man whom he rebuked inwardly; otherwise, how could Paul condemn in another what he himself, compelled by a similar necessity, had done? For because of the Jews who asserted that observance of the Law and the old rites must be maintained, he circumcised Timothy, the son, that is, of a Gentile man; and, dissolving the old law itself, he shaved his own head and offered sacrifice according to the ceremonies of the old Law, CXLV, 708, 709, 710.

**PETER OF BLOIS.**—A friend should so respect the face of a friend that he does not offend his ears or eyes by word, gesture, or deed. Modesty is the best companion and most precious ornament of friendship. Conversely, shamelessness and the folly of brazen-facedness destroy it. It often happens that, when the fire of anger conceived in people’s hearts was already coming out in public, or when a word of insult had already reached their lips, the sight of an arriving friend soothed the motion of their burning spirit and suddenly made the disturbed countenance of the mind serene by a certain gentleness of expression and venerable authority.

Here too the great strength of friendship appears: it has much power in persuading or dissuading one concerning something, since neither its loyalty is doubtful nor its gentle admonition suspect. Therefore openly, freely, and confidently urge upon a friend what is honorable; and if his advantage requires it, do not fear to rebuke him. But since truth is often troublesome and friendship is sometimes thereby disturbed, that service is indeed condemnable which makes a friend more indulgent toward vices. Let admonition, therefore, not be bitter, nor rebuke insulting; let honorable and pleasant affability be present. But let all flattery, alien to the nature of friendship, be far away.

It is a saying of blessed Ambrose: If you discover something faulty in a friend, first reprove him secretly; if he does not hear you, reprove him openly; if indeed he thinks himself injured, nevertheless reprove him; and if bitter correction wounds his spirit, nevertheless reprove him. For the wounds of a friend are more tolerable than the kisses of flatterers. As the author of Roman eloquence writes, rebukes are sometimes necessary; they should be made with greater force of voice and sharper gravity of words, so that we seem angry. Yet, as in cauterizing and cutting, we should come unwillingly and very rarely to this kind of chastisement, especially when no other medicine remains. But anger itself must be far away, for with it nothing can be done thoughtfully or rightly. Let chastisement, therefore, be tempered with gravity and gentleness, so that insult may be excluded and the person rebuked may recognize that he himself is the cause of this severity. In all things, then, let the restraint of moderation be maintained, lest one seem to satisfy one’s own anger more than love.

For there are some who boil inwardly and cloak and color the heat of madness under the name of zeal; but those who follow the impulse of their own mind rather than reason scarcely, or never, make progress in correction. Therefore, I beg, let one’s speech in correction be sadder, one’s face cast down; let sobs and tears interrupt the words, so that the person reproved may perceive that all this proceeds from love, not resentment. If perhaps he rejects the first correction, he will receive the second. Meanwhile pray, weep, sigh, and let the voice of groaning break off your speech. Let a friend act in truth in whatever way can soften the other’s mind; yet let nothing in word, lament, or sob be contrived through any dissimulation. For dissimulation and flattery are two most poisonous plagues, which must always be banished far from friendship. …

Therefore let correction of a friend proceed wholly from the marrow of the soul and from the deepest compassion, so that one may be toward the friend’s improvement as the Prophet desires for himself, saying: “May the just man correct me in mercy and rebuke me; but let not the oil of the sinner make my head fat …” But just as dissimulation and flattery poison the purity of friendship, so concealment among friends sometimes begets and nourishes purity of affection. For there is a certain simulated but prudent postponement of correction according to place, time, and person. For if a friend must be rebuked publicly, insofar as it can be done without violating the law of friendship, it becomes us to overlook or excuse his error and to seek an appropriate time and familiar privacy for his correction. While the sick mind is still unsettled from recent disturbance, such concealment is needed until, the cloud of the mind having cleared, it more peacefully admits the words of gentle admonition. Certainly when King David had added betrayal and murder to adultery, the prophet Nathan, about to rebuke him, nevertheless deferring to royal majesty, did not at once or with a disturbed mind charge him with so great a crime. Rather, after suitable concealment and by presenting an appropriate riddle, he drew from him a judgment against himself, CCVII, 891–893.

[Col. 0450]

**SMARAGDUS, abbot.**—The apostle Paul says: “If anyone does not obey our word through this Epistle, mark that person, and do not associate with him, that he may be ashamed; yet do not regard him as an enemy, but reprove him as a brother.” As though he said: If the authority of our Epistle does not correct him, inform us by your letters who he is, so that he may be reproved by us, or even excommunicated through our Epistle. And do not associate with the excommunicated person until he obeys and assents to the apostolic commands. In this passage the Apostle plainly indicates that we should have no fellowship with an excommunicated person, neither in action, counsel, nor any association.

In one and the same person we can love brotherhood and hate vices at once. For being a brother is one thing; being a vicious person is another. Let us therefore love in him our brotherhood and hate his viciousness. Let us pursue the vice in him and, once amended, love him as ourselves. Hence blessed Gregory says: We must indeed show to our neighbors such discrimination in hatred that in them we love what they are as human beings and hate what opposes us on the path to God.

An elder said: A human being ought to mortify himself from every evil thing before leaving the body, and should injure no one. Unless a person has in his heart that he is a sinner, God will not hear him. What does it mean to have in one’s heart that one is a sinner? It means that one bears one’s own sins and does not see one’s neighbor’s sins. For when a person has abandoned his own will, then God is reconciled to him and receives his prayer. For if we behold our own sins, we do not see our neighbor’s sins. It is foolishness for a person who has his own dead body, to leave it and go away to weep over his neighbor’s dead body … Therefore each person ought to lament his own dead body, that is, his own sin … For the Prophet calls sin a dead body when he says: “He who washes himself after touching a dead body, and again touches a dead body”—that is, he who laments sin and again commits sin—“his washing profits him nothing.” CII, 672, 673.

[Col. 0455]

## CXLVIII. INDEX OF THE SIX PRECEPTS OF THE CHURCH, LOGICALLY REFERRING THE JUDGMENTS OF THE FATHERS CONCERNING THE NECESSITY OF FULFILLING THEM, AND SETTING OUT IN ORDER THE DUTIES OF CHRISTIANS CONCERNING EACH ONE

The Church sets before us these six precepts in French:

1. “On Sundays you shall hear Mass,  
   And on holy days of obligation.
2. You shall sanctify the feast days  
   That are commanded for you.
3. You shall confess all your sins  
   At least once a year.
4. You shall receive your Creator  
   Humbly, at least at Easter.
5. You shall fast the Ember Days and vigils,  
   And the whole of Lent.
6. On Friday you shall not eat meat,  
   Nor likewise on Saturday.”

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE AUTHORITY OF THE CHURCH

[Col. 0455]

After our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, who before the ages was true God, had deigned, for our redemption, to appear at the end of the ages as true man from the womb of the Virgin, he granted to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, the power of binding and loosing in heaven and on earth, and allowed him to open the gates of the kingdom of heaven. Upon the firmness of his faith he deigned to establish his holy Church, according to his truthful utterance: “You are Peter,” etc. By the cement of that promise of holy apostolic institution, its foundations began to rise from precious stones; and, with divine mercy consenting, through the labor of its builders and the solicitude of apostolic authority, they were brought unbreakably to the summit, so as to stand perpetually in due measure without the assault of a hostile wind. Blessed Peter deservedly obtained its primacy.

After him, his vicars also, serving God most faithfully and free from the density of mists that commonly obstruct the straight path, received this office worthily and persevered diligently in the care of government which they undertook for the Lord’s sheep . . . . . For it is established that the holy Roman Church, through blessed Peter, prince of the apostles—who deserved to receive from the Lord’s own mouth the primacy of the Churches—is the head of all Churches, and that from her they must seek and follow rectitude and order in all beneficial matters and ecclesiastical institutions, which she maintains inviolably and incontrovertibly according to the canonical and synodal decrees and the ordinances of the holy Fathers.—And therefore it follows that what is decreed with full authority by the rulers of this See must not be set aside upon the pretext of any custom, by following merely private wishes, but must be held more firmly and without disturbance. Pope Nicholas II, CXIX, 785, 786.

He says in his letter to Ado, archbishop of Vienne: “We have often received letters from Your Holiness, warning and earnestly requesting us to instruct your Church how it ought to proceed in ecclesiastical matters. Therefore nothing seemed better to us than to teach Your Holiness from the decrees and institutions of our predecessors, who have left us most clearly in their writings what we must maintain concerning the order in which we know that the Church presides through God as author, whether other Churches founded from her far and wide are concerned.

“Most blessed Pope Innocent, giving instruction in this matter, laid down the following: If the priests of the Lord wished to observe intact the ecclesiastical institutions as they were handed down by the blessed apostles, no variety or diversity would occur in those orders and consecrations. But while each person thinks that what he himself considers proper, rather than what has been handed down, ought to be maintained, they appear to retain or celebrate different practices in different Churches. Thus a scandal arises for the peoples, who, not knowing that ancient traditions have been corrupted by human presumption, think either that the Churches are not in harmony with one another or that this very opposition was instituted by the apostles.

“For who does not know, or fail to notice, that what was handed down to the Roman Church by Peter, prince of the apostles, and has been preserved until now, ought to be observed by all; and that nothing should be added or introduced which either lacks authority or appears to take its precedent from elsewhere? . . . . . They must follow what the Roman Church preserves, from which they undoubtedly received their beginning, lest, while pursuing foreign inclinations, they seem to lose the head of their institutions . . . . . If your predecessors maintained something deficient or different, we answer now not because we think you do not know it, but so that with greater authority you may either instruct your own people or admonish—or not delay to judge—those who depart from the institutions of the Roman Church, so that we may know who they are that introduce novelties or judge that the custom of another Church rather than that of Rome must be observed.” Nicholas, CXIX, 889, 890.

## [INDEX OF THE SIX PRECEPTS OF THE CHURCH]

## FIRST PRECEPT

“On Sundays you shall hear Mass,  
And on holy days of obligation.”

**FLORUS, deacon of Lyons.**—Formerly the sacrifices of the Jews according to Aaron consisted in animal victims, and in this mystery there was not yet the sacrifice of the Lord’s body and blood, which is now spread throughout the whole world . . . . . For it is written: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: you are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek.” . . . . . For the sacrifice of Aaron has been removed, and the sacrifice according to the order of Melchizedek has begun. Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ willed to be our salvation in his body and blood . . . . .

He, then, our priest sent by the Lord God, took from us what he might offer to God: the holy firstfruits of flesh from the Virgin’s womb he offered to God as a whole burnt offering . . . . . You are priest, you are victim, you are offerer, you are offering. He himself is the priest who has now entered within the veil . . . . .

The holy Fathers in the Old Testament offered victims to the one God and Creator of all things—victims which he himself willed should be offered to him—promising through their likeness the true victim by which he reconciled us to himself in Christ Jesus our Lord through forgiveness of sins. Thus a likeness was offered to him, promising the truth of the sacrifice; and that truth itself, once rendered, was to be offered in the passion of Christ’s body and blood. Before Christ’s coming, the flesh and blood of this sacrifice were promised through victims in likeness; in Christ’s passion they were rendered through the reality itself; after Christ’s ascension they are celebrated in remembrance through the sacrament.

Accordingly, the former sacraments observed and celebrated under the Law were announcements beforehand of Christ to come. When Christ had fulfilled them by his coming, they were abolished; and they were abolished because they had been fulfilled. For he did not come to dissolve the Law but to fulfill it. Other rites have been instituted, greater in power, better in usefulness, easier in practice, and fewer in number . . . . . so that in the priest himself and in the sacrifice there might be forgiveness of sins . . . . . CXIX, 11–21.

This grace, therefore, of our cleansing and redemption, which the Lord and Savior commended to us in the sacrament of his body and blood, he proclaimed to the peoples long before he suffered; but on the day before he suffered—that is, on the night when he was betrayed—he delivered it to his disciples at the Supper . . . . . CXIX, 11–24.

This is why, at that Paschal Supper when the Lord was betrayed, John himself says nothing about this mystery of the body and blood: he had plainly explained it more fully and more sublimely in preceding portions of his Gospel, and knew well that the other three evangelists had carefully set forth what had been handed down at that same Supper, in remembrance of the Lord’s passion and for the salvation of the faithful. For Matthew’s words are these, etc. . . . . . CXIX, 21–24.

Thus, when they first assemble together and the faithful stand in the house of God, the chanting of divine praises comes first; then the reading of the apostles and Gospels; then sometimes also the sermon and address of teachers; then the confession of the Creed, the offerings of the people, and the beginning of the consecration of the sacraments, by which the minds of those present are prepared to think upon and desire divine and heavenly things. The priest then stands at the altar and, about to celebrate the divine mysteries, prays while greeting the Church and greets it while praying, saying: “The Lord be with you . . . Lift up your hearts,” etc. CXIX, 25–72.

**IVO, bishop of Chartres.**—On Sundays or feast days, after the sermon customarily delivered during the solemnities of Mass, the priest ought to exhort the people to pour out common prayers to the Lord, according to apostolic institution, for various needs: for the king; bishops and rulers of the Churches; peace; plague; the sick who lie in bed in that parish; and those recently deceased. In each of these petitions he should say the Lord’s Prayer silently. The priest, however, should solemnly complete the prayers proper to each petition. After this, the sacred offering should be celebrated. For the Apostle says: “I urge, first of all, that prayers be made,” etc. . . . . . CLXI, 193.

Priests ought to exhort the peoples subject to them to make, or permit, cattle-herdsmen, swineherds, and other shepherds or ploughmen who remain continually in the fields or woods, and therefore live like beasts, to come at least to Mass on Sundays and other feast days. For Christ redeemed these also with his precious blood . . . . . CLXI, 194.

On Sundays or feast days, before priests celebrate Mass, they should ask the people whether a parishioner of another parish is in church and wishes to hear Mass there after disregarding his own priest. If they find such a person, they should immediately expel him from the church and compel him to return to his own parish . . . . . CLXI, 194.

**IVO [OF CHARTRES].**—In the old Scriptures, no time is commanded for observing Easter except from the fourteenth moon of the month of New Things to the twenty-first. Yet because the Gospel plainly reveals also the day on which the Lord was crucified, lay in the tomb, and rose again, the observance of those days was added by the councils of the Fathers, and the whole Christian world was persuaded that Easter should be celebrated in that manner.

The forty-day fast has authority both in the ancient Books—from the fast of Moses and Elijah—and in the Gospel, because the Lord fasted for the same number of days, demonstrating that the Gospel does not disagree with the Law and the prophets. For the Law is understood in the person of Moses and the prophets in the person of Elijah. Between them the Lord appeared glorious on the mountain, so that what the Apostle says of him might stand out more clearly: “Having testimony from the Law and the prophets.” In what part of the year, then, could the observance of Lent be more suitably appointed than that adjoining and contiguous to the Lord’s Passion? For it signifies this laborious life, which requires this self-restraint, so that we may fast from friendship with this world, which certainly never ceases deceitfully to flatter us and to scatter and cast about the juices of its enticements. CLXI, 190. (See the third precept of the Decalogue, in the index, 144, and the index concerning feast days, 149.)

## SECOND PRECEPT

[Col. 0458]

“You shall sanctify the feast days  
That are commanded for you.”

**POPE NICHOLAS I.**—You ask on what feast days of apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins you ought to cease from earthly work. Certainly, on the solemnities of the blessed Virgin Mary; the holy twelve apostles; the evangelists; John, the Lord’s forerunner; St Stephen the first martyr; and likewise on the anniversaries of those saints whose commemoration is celebrated and whose day is observed as a feast among you, God granting it.

It should indeed be understood that worldly work is to cease on feast days so that the Christian may more freely go to church; apply himself to psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs; devote himself to prayer; present offerings; share in commemorations of the saints; rise to imitate them; attend to the divine utterances; and distribute alms to the needy. If anyone neglects these things, is unwilling even to devote himself to prayer, and instead turns to the other vanities of the world and to permitted occupations, it would have been better for him on that day, obeying the precepts of the blessed apostle Paul, to labor with his hands so that he might have something to give those suffering need. Paul himself, although he says that the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel, did not use that authority; rather, he worked with his hands so as not to burden any of those to whom he preached the Gospel.

As to your question whether judgment may be conducted on saints’ feast days, and whether on such a day a person, if deserving it, ought to be sentenced to death: you should know that, on those feasts on which we showed above that all worldly work must cease, we decree still more emphatically that secular business, and especially executions, must be avoided. For although perhaps either may be carried out without sin, nevertheless, when one ought to cling more closely to the things of God, it is fitting wholly to cut off from oneself the things of the world. Above all, a person entering on divine service on that day should not become entangled in secular affairs; and, out of reverence for so great a solemnity, nothing should be brought forward except that from which joy, peace, and spiritual gladness may arise for all. CXIX, 985, 986.

**RODULFUS, bishop of Bourges.**—We have decreed that feast days be celebrated during the year: that is, that Easter Sunday be honored with all reverence and sobriety; likewise, we have decreed that the entire week be observed; and that the Lord’s Ascension Day be fully celebrated. Pentecost is to be observed in the same manner as Easter. Likewise, the Nativity of St John the Baptist; the single feast day of Peter and Paul; St Lawrence; the Assumption of St Mary; the dedication feast of St Michael; the feast of St Martin; St Andrew; and all the apostles . . . . . .

We have also decreed that those saints’ feasts be observed whose holy bodies rest, or whose relics are venerated, in each parish. We have said that on the aforesaid days work must cease. We judge that the other feasts of holy apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins ought to be celebrated with fitting honor. CXIX, 717. (For this precept, see the very extensive index concerning feast days below, 149.)

## THIRD PRECEPT

“You shall confess all your sins  
At least once a year.”

**CANUTE I, king of the English.**—We also beseech, for the love of God, that every Christian diligently understand his own advantage . . . . . But we must act so as to turn back from sins most diligently, and each of us must carefully confess our offences to our confessor, so that we may continually abstain and diligently make recompense. CLI, 1175.

**REGINO, abbot of Prüm** (from Burchard).—Priests ought to admonish the people subject to them that every person who knows himself wounded by the deadly wound of sin should, with all haste, flee on the Wednesday before Lent to the life-giving mother Church. There, after simply confessing with all humility and contrition of heart what he has wickedly committed, he should receive the remedies of penance according to the measure laid down by canonical authorities, and be delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that his spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord.

Nor only he who has committed some mortal sin, but every person who recognizes that he has stained with the blot of sin the spotless robe of Christ which he received in baptism, should hasten to come to his own priest . . . . . CXXXII, 245. (See the following precept.)

## FOURTH PRECEPT

[Col. 0459]

“You shall receive your Creator  
Humbly, at least at Easter.”

**FLORUS, deacon of Lyons.**—“Give us this day our daily bread.” In this petition we ask for a sufficiency of daily nourishment, signifying the whole by the name “bread.” For the entire sacrament of the faithful is called bread; and it is necessary in this present time, yet not for attaining the happiness of this present time, but that eternal happiness. For Christ is the bread of life, whom we ask may be given to us daily, lest we who are in Christ and receive the Eucharist daily should be separated from Christ’s body through the intervention of some graver offense . . . . . Therefore we ask that our bread, that is, Christ, be given to us daily, so that we who remain and live in him may not depart from his sanctification and body, without which we cannot live eternally. CXIX, 67.

**GEZO, abbot of Tortona.**—We strictly command that confessions be made, especially concerning disturbances of the mind, before one goes to Mass, lest anyone perhaps approach the altar unworthily—that is, if he does not have a pure heart. For it is better to wait until one is sound and free from scandal and envy than rashly to approach the judgment of the tribunal. For Christ’s tribunal is the altar, and there he judges those who approach unworthily by his body together with his blood.

Therefore, just as one must refrain from carnal and capital sins before communicating, so one must abstain from interior vices and the diseases of the languishing soul before union with true peace and the bond of eternal salvation. When, therefore, a suitable time invites us to the dreadful table, every precaution must be taken that no Judas may be found there, that no evil person may approach, that the tongue may utter no feigned words, and that no snares may be hidden in the mind; rather, let speech declare what the will possesses.

And now Christ is present—the same Christ who furnished that table also consecrates this one. For it is not a human being who makes the elements set forth into Christ’s body and blood, but Christ who was crucified for us. The words are uttered through the priest’s mouth, but they are consecrated by God’s power and grace: “This,” he says, “is my body.” By this word the elements set forth are consecrated. And just as the utterance, “Increase and multiply and fill the earth,” was spoken once, yet in every age has its effect through nature working in generation, so that utterance also was made once, yet gives firmness to the sacrifice at all the tables of the Church, up to the present day and until his coming.

Let no hypocrite, then, approach; let no one with a feigned heart dare to draw near to such great mysteries, lest he be condemned, incur sentence, and suffer what Judas suffered. For after Judas’s participation in the table, the devil entered him—not because he had despised the Lord’s body, but because the shamelessness and wickedness of his mind enabled the adversary to dwell in him. From this learn that snares are prepared by the devil for those unworthy persons who celebrate the secrets of the mysteries deceitfully, and are attempted ever more forcefully against those who hasten to communicate without a right disposition.

And I say these things not to frighten you, but to make you more cautious. Let no one be Judas at the table. This sacrifice is spiritual food. For just as bodily food, when it finds the stomach occupied by harmful humors, injures it more, harms rather than helps, so this spiritual food, if it finds anyone polluted by wickedness, destroys him more—not by its own nature, but through the fault of the recipient. Therefore, a pure mind, etc. . . . . . CXXXVII, 391, 392.

**IVO, bishop of Chartres.**—It is plainly apparent that, when the disciples first received the Lord’s body and blood, they did not receive them fasting. Is the universal Church, then, to be criticized because it is always received by those who are fasting? For the Holy Spirit determined that, in honor of so great a sacrament, the Lord’s body should enter the mouth of a Christian before other foods. This practice is therefore observed throughout the world.

Nor, because the Lord gave it after food, should brethren who have dined or supped assemble to receive that sacrament; nor should they mingle it with their own meals, as did those whom the Apostle rebukes and corrects. The Savior wished to impress this upon the hearts and memories of the disciples as his last act before departing to his Passion, in order to commend the depth of that mystery more strongly. Therefore he did not command in what order it should subsequently be received, reserving this matter for the apostles through whom he was to order the Churches. For if he had instructed that it must always be received after other food, I think no one would have changed that custom.
