But when the Apostle, speaking of this sacrament, says: “Therefore, brethren, when you come together to eat, wait for one another; if anyone is hungry, let him eat at home, so that you may not come together for judgment,” he immediately adds: “The remaining matters I will arrange when I come.” From this he makes us understand that it was a great matter to set before them the entire order of practice which the Church throughout the world observes, and that this order was established precisely so that it should not vary with any difference of hours. CLXI, 190, 191.

**JONAS, bishop of Orléans.**—We likewise admonish you concerning the reception of the sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, as is fitting for Christian religion, you should beneficially prepare yourselves at suitable times, attending to that Gospel saying: “Whoever eats . . . ,” etc. CVI, 304.

NICHOLAS I, pope . . .—You ask whether you ought to communicate daily with the body and blood of the Lord during the greater Lent. We humbly beseech the almighty Lord that this may be done, and we most earnestly exhort you all to do so, provided, however, that the mind is not disposed toward sinning; or that an unrepentant conscience does not perhaps accuse it of grave sins, or of not being reconciled; or that any one of you remains unreconciled through his own fault with a brother with whom he is at variance. For one whose conscience reproaches him concerning any of these matters, we judge that he is burdened by so great a gift rather than receiving any remedy from it. But concerning this, and concerning those who indeed enter the church yet do not communicate after the offering has been made, the sacred canons perhaps sufficiently declare what is to be imparted to your bishop, who, God being the author, is to be appointed for you through our humble agency; and by him to the priests, who hold only the keys of opening knowledge, and likewise to you, wherever this is necessary and in no way forbidden. Meanwhile, throughout that Lent which the custom of the Church calls the greater, communion is to be received every day, while observing the foregoing rule; for one must always devote oneself to prayer and attend the sacrifices of the faithful . . . [CXIX, 983–984.]

Then it is rightly unlawful for anyone to receive Christ’s communion when, given over to gluttony, he is found not to be fasting—so that, making little of the mystical table, he appears first to have broken his fast by taking ordinary food, and, failing to distinguish Christ’s venerable body and precious blood from other foods, is known not to have preferred them to every human meal but to have put them afterward. For Christ’s body is a saving remedy against sin; and one who does not reverently receive it before every food . . . Certainly, every day we see physicians administer their draughts to empty stomachs; and if this is done for bodily health, how much more ought it to be done for the salvation of the soul? Moreover, no rule teaches why one from whose mouth or hands blood has flowed should not receive Christ’s body and blood. For what a person suffers unwillingly ought not to be imputed to him as guilt, and therefore he ought not to be restrained from partaking of so great a remedy. For we know that the woman who suffered a flow of blood came humbly behind the Lord, touched the fringe of his garment, and was immediately freed from her infirmity. If, therefore, this woman, afflicted with a flow of blood, was not judged unworthy by touching the Lord’s garment—indeed, by the Lord himself, for he said, “Someone touched me”—why should one who endures a flow of blood from the mouth or nostrils not be permitted to receive Christ’s saving sacraments? [CXIX, 1004–1005.]

TAIO, bishop of Saragossa.—Every sinner, receiving the price of redemption through the cross, confesses and praises God . . . In order that the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion may not be idle in us, we ought to imitate what we receive and preach to others what we venerate . . . [LXXX, 795.]

## FIFTH COMMANDMENT

You shall fast the Ember Days and Vigils,  
And the whole of Lent.

ABSALON, abbot of Springiersbach.—You might see people, forgetful of God’s commandments, turning even the fast-days themselves more to mockery than to profit; for, even if they sometimes fast, they fast neither wholly, nor devoutly, nor soberly. They do not fast wholly, because, fasting once or twice in the week, on the other days they devote themselves to feasting and drinking cups dry, although all persons from their fifteenth year upward are bound to the entire fast, unless excused by illness or another definite and reasonable cause. They do not fast devoutly, because, though they abstain from food, they never abstain from vices; yet abstinence from food is fruitless when abstinence from vices is not its companion. They also fail to fast devoutly because what they withdraw from the body by fasting they put into their chest, to offer again to their belly. As Gregory testifies, this ought to be called not God’s fast but the belly’s, since what we can deprive ourselves of through abstinence ought to be bestowed upon another’s poverty. They do not fast soberly, because they break their fast with food and drink more greedily, more splendidly, earlier, or more abundantly than is proper. Esau is reproved for eating greedily, since through his greedy eating of lentils he lost the dignity of his birthright. So also, excessively sumptuous eating is reproved in the rich man of the Gospel, of whom it is said: “He feasted sumptuously every day.” [Col. 0461] To break the fast earlier than is proper is likewise held sinful by ecclesiastical ordinance, which established that fasting should continue until the ninth hour. Hence blessed Jerome says: “There is no one who does not know the third, sixth, and ninth hours, as well as evening and dawn; nor is food to be taken before these prayers are offered to God.” This can rightly be understood of the season of fasts. Reason itself also proves that breaking the fast with more food or drink than is fitting is sinful, since this is not abstinence but service to pleasure . . . [CCXI, 105–108.]

ALAN OF LILLE.—On vigils, [CCX, 178.]

ATTO, bishop of Vercelli.—On the Lenten fast, [CXXXIV, 40.]

AMBROSE, saint, bishop of Milan.—Lent has six weeks; Telesphorus added a seventh week, and this period was called Quinquagesima. Lent is observed because Moses, Elijah, and the Savior are read to have fasted forty days and nights. [XVII, 833.]

AUGUSTINE, saint, bishop of Hippo.—You ought to know that this solemn fast, which our gracious mother the Church commands to be observed on this present day, God commanded Adam and Eve at the very beginning of the world’s creation in Paradise, that they should abstain from the fruit of the tree. Holy Moses also observed this before the Law and received the Law. Elijah observed it under the Law and flew in his course to heaven. As long as Eve abstained, she was a virgin and remained in Paradise; but when she violated the fast, she fell into misery, experienced the corruption of lust, remained placed under a lord, and was expelled from Paradise. Moses too, after fasting, spoke with God face to face; before fasting he had neither dared to see God nor to approach him. Jerusalem, in the time of King Hezekiah and Isaiah, was delivered from Sennacherib by fasting; and one hundred and eighty-five thousand were slain from heaven in one night, and, lest their bodies should stink, they were burned to ashes and reduced to dust. Likewise, when Jonah preached fasting, pardon was obtained in ashes and sackcloth. Did Joshua son of Nun not fast before he regulated the course of the sun and moon through the day and overcame his enemies? . . . But know that of old our faithful fathers were accustomed to fast on the vigils of great solemnities until night; and this was praiseworthy and good . . . Yet I do not wish you to fast on Sundays . . . [XL, 1275–1276.] On the Benefit of Fasting, [XL, 707–716.] On the Lenten Fast, [XXXII, 1456.] On the Fast of the Bridegroom’s Sons, [XXXV, 1339.] On the Forty-Day Fast, [XXXV, 2170.] The Number Forty in Fasting, [XXXVIII, 695, 811.]

BENEDICT, saint, founder of the monastic order.—On the observance of Lent, [LXVI, 731.]

BERNO, abbot of Reichenau.—As may be understood from the sermons of the ancients, especially of Saint Augustine, it is necessary for our religion to celebrate four fasts annually. For the year revolves through four seasons: spring, summer, autumn, and winter. These four seasons are accustomed, through their pleasures, to call us back from love of the Creator; and therefore we must fast in each season, so that our four elements may be chastised and not be stolen away by delight in the world . . . [CXLII, 1090.]

BERNO, abbot of Reichenau the Rich.—On the Fast of the Ember Days, [CXLII, 1073.] Dialogue on the Fast of the Ember Days, [CXLII, 1087.]

BERNARD, saint, abbot of Clairvaux.—On the Fast of Lent, [CLXXXIII, 173.] On celebrating saints’ vigils by fasting, [CLXXXIII, 501.]

BERTARIUS, saint, abbot of Monte Cassino.—How one ought to fast through the year, [CXXVI, 987.]

BONIFACE, saint, bishop of Mainz.—Exhortation on the Fast of Lent, [LXXXIX, 854.]

BURCHARD, bishop of Worms.—Lent must be observed with the utmost care, so that the fast in it may in no way be broken, except on Sundays, which are exempted from abstinence, unless someone is prevented by illness; for these days are the tithe of the year. Thus, from the first Sunday of Lent to the Lord’s Easter six weeks are counted, amounting to forty-two days. When the six Sundays are subtracted from abstinence, no more than thirty-six days remain in abstinence. For example, if the year is reckoned at 365 days and we afflict ourselves for thirty-six days, we give God, as it were, the tithe of the year. And in order to complete the sacred number of forty days, which our Savior consecrated by his holy fast, the four days of the preceding week are to be added to make up the forty days: namely, Wednesday, which is marked as the beginning of the fast, and the following Thursday, Friday, and Saturday. [Col. 0462] Unless we join these four days to the preceding thirty-six, we shall not have forty days of abstinence. We are commanded by almighty God to give the tithes of all our goods. Therefore, that every tithe may rightly be paid by us to God, let us take the tithe of the year, and in it, by confessing our sins, correcting ourselves, fasting, keeping vigil, praying, giving alms generously, cleanse ourselves; and let us tithe our flesh, so that we may reach holy Easter in security. [CXL, 884–885.]

We decree that the Ember Days of the year are to be observed by all with fasting: that is, in March, the first week; in June, the second; in September, the third; and in December, the fourth—the full week before the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity—namely Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday.

When, because of sins, the peoples of Gaul were being fiercely destroyed by the ravages of wolves, and no remedy for this scourge could be found, the bishops of Gaul are said to have assembled at the city of Vienne and jointly decreed that they should keep a three-day fast. When the Lord mercifully removed the plague, these days entered into the custom of annual observance, to be celebrated throughout the provinces of Gaul before the day of the Lord’s Ascension. Let us also observe these days with the utmost reverence and devotion, with abstinence of the flesh and humility of heart—not in order to escape the ravages of visible wolves, but in order to overcome the temptations of invisible wolves, that is, unclean spirits. Let no one, moreover, wear costly garments on these days, when we ought to mourn in sackcloth and ashes. Drunkenness and feasting are to be forbidden. [CXL, 886.] When priests announce the sacred festivals to the people, they should also exhort them by every means to observe the fast of the vigils. [CXL, 887.]

CALLISTUS, pope.—Thus he addresses Benedict, his fellow bishop: “We are bound by the love of brotherhood and compelled by apostolic governance to answer the inquiries of our brethren as the Lord gives us power, and to instruct them by the authority of the Apostolic See.” The fast which you have learned to celebrate three times yearly, we now decree should more fittingly be observed at the four seasons, so that, just as the year turns through four seasons, we too may keep the solemn fast four times through the year’s four seasons; and just as we are filled with grain, wine, and oil to nourish our bodies, so may we be filled with fasting to nourish our souls . . . [CXXX, 129.]

CANUTE, king of the English.—On one who violates a fast, [CLI, 1179.]

CHRODEGANG, saint, bishop of Metz.—On the observances of Lent, [LXXXIX, 1073.]

ERNALD, abbot of Bonneval.—On Christ’s fast, [CLXXXIX, 1163.]

GUIDO, abbot of Farfa.—On the Fast of the Ember Days, [CL, 1237.]

HONORIUS OF AUTUN.—On Lent, [CLXXII, 655.] On the Lord’s fast, and why we do not fast at the time when he fasted, [CLXXII, 656.] On the Fast of the Ember Days, [CLXXII, 684.]

HUGH OF SAINT-VICTOR.—On the beginning of the fast and on penance to be begun on the same day, [CLXXVII, 881.]

IVO, bishop of Chartres.—On the beginning of the fast, [CLXII, 578.]

JOHN BELETH, theologian of Paris.—On the institution of Lent and the remaining forms of fasting, [CCII, 22.] Why we do not fast at the time when Christ fasted, [CCII, 90.] On the fasts of the Ember Days and their institution, [CCII, 137.] On the vigil of Saint John, [CCII, 141.]

LEO THE GREAT, saint, pope.—Why the Ember fasts were instituted, [LIV, 185.] On the Lenten fast, [LIV, 263.] On the institution of the Pentecost fast, [LIV, 418.] On the manner of fulfilling a fast, [LIV, 453.] Treatise on the Saturday fast, [LV, 627.]

MARTIN, saint, regular canon of León.—But what does it mean that Moses fasted forty days? His fast is a kind of figure, considered in relation to this number. For Moses, Elijah, and the Lord himself fasted for the forty-day number. For we are commanded by the Law and the Prophets—among whom the Savior also shone forth in the middle on the mountain—that, restraining our appetite from all the enticements of the world as by the fast of temperance, while the perfection of the Decalogue of the Law is preached throughout the four parts of that same world, that is, in the whole world, ten multiplied by four may signify the number forty. [CCVIII, 785.]

It should further be noted that the number of days in holy Lent was instituted not only by the holy Fathers, but also consecrated by the Lord Jesus Christ. Moses fasted on Mount Sinai for forty days and an equal number of nights, not by his own strength but by the grace of divine dispensation. Elijah likewise could not have walked forty days and forty nights by the strength or refreshment of one ash-baked loaf, [Col. 0463] unless God’s mercy had granted this to him. The Son of God also consecrated this number by fasting himself, and commanded that it be observed for the remission of sins throughout his whole Church. Therefore, these sacred fasts are not to be despised by the faithful, nor passed over idly or negligently, because they were established not by human will or wisdom but by divine dispensation. Therefore no one should neglect to do for the remission of his sins what the Son of God and of man—who committed no sin and in whose mouth no deceit was found—is known to have done in order to give us an example of abstinence . . . [CCVIII, 785.]

MAXIMUS, saint, bishop of Turin.—We have often set forth the rationale of holy Lent, whose beginning we celebrate today, and often taught why we fast for such a number of days. For we have said that the Lord Jesus Christ consecrated this same number of fasting days, and, taking no food through continuous days and nights, made one body of fasting: that is, although the course of day was interrupted by the coming of night, the course of the fast was not interrupted . . . [LVII, 311.]

Consider how many lessons of spiritual life arise for us, and by what magnificent examples we are summoned to the purpose of holiness, since blessed Moses and the Son of God are reported to have fasted forty days. Clearly observe this: as far as a servant is from his lord, so far must their fasting differ. Moses is the promulgator of the old Law; Christ, the founder of the New Testament. Moses fasts in order to train one people in the discipline of legal precepts; Christ fasts in order to redeem all nations . . . [LVII, 325.] But we, for whom the unconquered champion dedicated this venerable Lent, rejecting fleshly desires, should so chastise our members by fasting that we may fatten our souls with virtues. Let destructive luxury fast in us; let every iniquity fast; let hateful contention fast. Let us abstain from banquets; still more, let us abstain from vices. Let us so restrain ourselves, let us be so sober with respect to wine, that no drunkenness of pleasures may rule us. For what benefit is there in keeping the times of the forty days’ fast by outward observance and not keeping the law of fasting? What benefit is it to refrain from banquets and occupy the day with lawsuits? What benefit is it not to eat one’s own bread and to plunder the food of the poor? The fasting of the Christian ought to be the refreshment of one in need . . . [LVII, 326, 328, 361, 388.]

On the Lenten Fast, [LVII, 303.] On the General Fast, [LVII, 558.] On the Lord’s Fast on a Feast-Day, [LVII, 561.]

NICHOLAS I, pope.—To the Bulgarians who ask whether it is permissible, apart from a time of fasting, to eat even a very small amount very early in the morning, we reply that we remember, and find in no records whatever, that any of our fathers ate before the third hour, or that holy Church received a tradition of taking food before that hour. On the contrary, we find that some fasted until evening, others until the ninth hour of the day, and others again until the sixth; but we find none who took even a small amount in the morning, especially since we read that “Woe” was pronounced upon those who eat in the morning. Therefore, desiring that you should be free from this curse, we exhort you not to take any bodily food whatsoever before the third hour of the day, even on the most distinguished solemnities. For what solemnity can be more exalted than Pentecost, at which the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles, and through this men merited to receive the Lord within themselves? At this feast the holy apostles, with certain others, are found fasting at the third hour of the day, when, filled with the Holy Spirit and speaking in the languages of all nations, they were heard and marvelled at by certain unbelievers, who falsely said to those present together that they were full of new wine. Peter, prince of the apostles, answered: “For these are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is the third hour of the day.” Here it should be noted that not only the apostles, but all who were with them—that is, the one hundred and twenty men upon whom the Holy Spirit fell—are found fasting at the third hour of the day. It should also be noted that blessed Peter did not say simply . . . But he added, “since it is the third hour of the day,” as though he were plainly saying: “You yourselves clearly know that these men do not customarily break their fast before the third hour of the day; therefore you wrongly suppose them drunk.” Imitate them, therefore, so that the Holy Spirit, finding you fasting, if not later, at least at the third hour of the day, may fill you also, as he did them, with the inspiration of his grace. [CXIX, 1002–1003.]

PETER CHRYSOLOGUS, archbishop of Ravenna.—On the Lenten fast, [LII, 634, 678.]

PETER DAMIAN, saint, cardinal.—On the fast of vigils, [CXLV, 800.] On the three-day fast, [CXLV, 962.]

[Col. 0464] PETER DE HONESTIS, cleric of Ravenna.—On the Fast of the Ember Days and vigils, [CLXIII, 722.]

PRUDENTIUS, poet:

While we offer the sacrifice of fasts,  
Nothing is surely purer than this mystery,  
By which the living fibre of the heart is cleansed,  
By which unbridled entrails are subdued.  
Thus, if, dissolving freely in drink and food,  
You do not duly restrain your fasting limbs,  
It follows that, through frequent languid delight,  
The noble spark of the mind grows cold,  
And the soul snores in its sluggish breast.  
Therefore let the desires of the body be bridled . . . etc.  
([LIX, 812–814.])

RABANUS MAURUS, abbot of Fulda.—On the fast of Lent and Pentecost, [CVII, 335.] On the fast of the tenth month, [CX, 13.] On the Lenten fast, [CX, 20.] On the fast of the fourth month, [CX, 45.] On the fast of the seventh month, [CX, 56.] On vigils, [CX, 90.] On fasting, [CXI, 136.]

REMIGIUS, bishop of Chur.—On the fast of the seven weeks before Easter, [CII, 1103.]

REGINO, abbot of Prüm (from the Council of Mainz).—We decree that the Ember Days of the year be observed by all with fasting: namely, in March, the first week; in June, the second; in September, the third; and in December, the fourth, being the full week before the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity—that is, Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday. Let all come to church at the ninth hour with litanies for the solemn celebration of Mass. [CXXXII, 243.]

(From Burchard.)—When priests announce the sacred festivals to the people, they should also exhort them by every means to observe the fast of the vigils. [CXXXII, 244.]

(From the Council of Mainz.)—If anyone, in pride, despises an appointed fast and refuses to observe it with the other Christians, the Council of Gangra commands that he be anathematized. Whoever violates an appointed fast without grave necessity should remember Jonathan, son of King Saul, who made light of his father’s curse, ate a little honey from the tip of a rod, and thereby incurred sentence of death. [CXXXII, 244.]

REGINO, abbot of Prüm.—On the fast of the Rogation Days, [CXXXII, 243.] On the Fast of the Ember Days, [CXXXII, 243.] On saints’ vigils, [CXXXII, 244.]

RODULFUS, bishop of Bourges.—The Lenten days must be observed with the utmost care, so that the fast may in no way be broken in them, except on Sundays, which are exempt from abstinence, because these days are the tithe of our year, which we ought to spend in all devotion and holiness. For no occasion to relax the fast is permitted during them, since at another time a fast is customarily relaxed for the sake of charity. During this time, however, it must never be relaxed; and to fast at another time is to gain a reward. But during this time, apart from the sick or little children, whoever does not fast gains punishment for himself, because the Lord consecrated these same days by the sacred fasting of Moses, Elijah, and himself . . . [CXIX, 718.]

Concerning the observance of fasting at the four seasons of the year, when the twelve lessons are read on Saturday: the holy Fathers decreed that, in the first month in the first week, in June in the second week, in September in the third week, and in December in the fourth week, for three days—that is, Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday—all except infants and the sick should fast until the ninth hour and abstain from meat. In the same way one must fast on the Rogation Days and abstain from meat for three days. Fasts appointed by priests are not to be broken without reasonable necessity. Therefore, on fast-days alms should be given, and each person should distribute to the poor the food and drink which he would have used had he not fasted; for to fast and save the food of dinner for supper is not an increase of merit but of food. [CXIX, 718.]

RUPERT, abbot of Deutz.—On the Fast of the Ember Days, [CLXX, 62.]

SIGEBERT OF GEMBLOUX.—On the distinction of the Ember Days, [CLX, 814.]

STEPHEN, Cistercian abbot.—In which week the Ember fasts are to be held in the month of September, [CLXVI, 1412.]

STEPHEN OF MURET, saint, founder of Grandmont.—On the times of fasting, [CCIV, 1158.]

UDALRIC, monk of Cluny.—On the Fast of the Ember Days in the month of June, [CXLIX, 673.] On the week of the Ember-Day fast, [CXLIX, 691.] On the beginning of the fast and on Lent, [CXLIX, 696.] On the Fast of the Ember Days in the month of March, [CXLIX, 697.]

URBAN III, pope.—On observing fasting, [CCII, 1339.]

[Col. 0465] UNKNOWN AUTHOR.—On the spring fast, [CLI, 995.] On the summer fast, [CLI, 997.] On the autumn fast, [CLI, 1000.] On the winter fast, ibid. On the beginning of the fast and on Lent, [CLI, 1013.]

TERTULLIAN, priest of Carthage.—They likewise accuse our stations—fasts, according to Pamelius—as unworthy, and some of them as established too late, under the charge of novelty; saying also that this duty is to be performed at one’s discretion and ought not to be prolonged beyond the ninth hour, in accordance, of course, with their own practice. But as regards the question of prohibition, I shall answer once for all causes . . . If, because Peter and those with him are read to have entered the temple at the ninth hour of prayer, who will prove to me that on that day they had performed a station, so as to interpret the ninth hour as the close and discharge of a station? . . . On the contrary, you would more easily find that Peter, at the sixth hour, went up into the upper rooms to pray before taking food, so that the sixth hour of the day could more suitably serve this observance, since after prayer it seemed likely to bring it to its conclusion. Furthermore, since in the same account of Luke the third hour is shown as the hour at which those initiated by the Holy Spirit were thought drunk; the sixth, at which Peter went up into the upper rooms; and the ninth, at which they entered the temple: why should we not understand that, with the time plainly left indifferent, one should pray always and everywhere and at every time? [II, 966–967.]

Therefore, in observing these times, days, months, and years, are we becoming Galatians? Certainly, if we observe Jewish ceremonies and legal solemnities; for the Apostle dissuades from those, checking persistence in the Old Testament buried in Christ and establishing the New. But if there is a new condition in Christ, there must now also be new solemnities; or if the Apostle wiped out entirely every devotional observance of times, days, months, and years, why do we celebrate Easter in an annual cycle in the first month? Why do we pass fifty days thereafter in every kind of rejoicing? Why do we designate Wednesday and Friday for stations, and Good Friday for fasting? . . . [II, 973–974.]

We have proceeded, then, to examples . . . Israel had sinned by the water at Mizpah, having been gathered by Samuel; but the fast immediately washed away the sin so thoroughly that the peril of battle also fled. When Samuel was offering the burnt offering, we hear of God’s mercy being secured by nothing more than the people’s abstinence . . . [II, 962–963.]

Let us return and hasten on to new proofs. At the threshold of the Gospel, Anna the prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, both recognized the infant Lord . . . Her testimony of fasts is also added. The Lord himself soon consecrated his own baptism—and in his own, that of all men—by fasts . . . He also taught that more terrible demons must be fought by fasting. Finally, in order that the favor of the Holy Spirit, together with the further gift of prophecy, might hasten upon the centurion Cornelius while still unbaptized, we read that his fasts were heard. I think, too, that the Apostle, among his labors, dangers, and hardships, after hunger and thirst, also lists very many fasts. [II, 963–964.]

THEODULF, bishop of Amiens.—On the Lenten fast, [CV, 203.]

(See the INDEXES: “On fasting and abstinence,” CL; and “On the mortification of the senses,” CLI, below.)

## SIXTH COMMANDMENT

On Friday you shall not eat meat,  
Nor on Saturday either.

NICHOLAS I, pope.—At what times or on what days throughout the circuit of the year one ought to abstain from meat . . . Meanwhile, on fast-days, on which one ought especially to entreat the Lord through abstinence and penitential mourning, one must by every means abstain from meat. For although prayer and abstinence are fitting for all, still, at times of fasting one ought to apply oneself more fully to abstinence: namely, so that one who knows he has committed unlawful acts may, in accordance with the sacred decrees, also abstain during these times from certain lawful things—namely, during the Lenten season before Easter; the fast after Pentecost; the fast before the solemnity of the Assumption of the holy Mother of God and ever-virgin, our Lady Mary; and likewise the fast before the festival of the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ. These fasts the holy Roman Church received in ancient times and maintains. On Friday of every week, and on all vigils of distinguished festivals, one must refrain from eating meat and devote oneself to fasting, so that it may truly be possible to say with the Psalmist: “Weeping will linger at evening, and joy in the morning.” If, however, any of you should perhaps wish to abstain from meat on other days, he is not to be forbidden; for the more anyone sows here in tears, the more abundantly he will reap in joy in eternal life . . . [CXIX, 980–981.]

Although on Wednesday, more than on other days except Friday, one ought to give oneself to mourning, because on that very day the Lord was in a manner already buried in the heart of the earth—that is, in the heart of Judas the traitor—while Judas himself was devising to hand him over to death: nevertheless, if any of you wishes to do so on that day, he may certainly eat meat, unless this has perhaps been forbidden him by a priest or unless the day happens to fall among fast-days; for it is written, “Obedience is better than sacrifice” . . .

But on Friday, remembering the Lord’s Passion and the sorrow of the apostles, our taste must be restrained from the feasts of all flesh and from rich foods—unless the Nativity of the Lord, his Epiphany, the feast of the blessed Mother of the Lord and immaculate Virgin Mary, of the chief apostles Peter and Paul, of Saint John the Baptist, of blessed John the Evangelist, likewise of Andrew the Apostle, blood-brother of the keeper of heaven’s keys, or indeed of blessed Stephen the first martyr, should perhaps occur on that day. For the Lord testifies in the Gospel that holy Church, as a faithful soul, ought to break fasts or abstinences on their feast-days when these have not been undertaken by a perpetual vow, saying: “A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow; but when she has borne the child, she no longer remembers the anguish because of joy that a human being has been born into the world.” By “woman” he means holy Church. For as a woman rejoices when a human being is born into this world, so the Church is filled with worthy exultation when one of the faithful people passes into the life to come; for that person’s birth, while the Church labors and groans much in the present as though in childbirth, causes her pain. Nor should it seem strange to anyone if one who has departed this life is said to be born; for just as, in customary speech, a person is said to be born when he comes forth from his mother’s womb and enters this light, so anyone who reaches the light of the living from the darkness of this age may rightly be called born. For this reason, ecclesiastical custom fittingly holds that the solemn days of blessed martyrs and confessors of Christ, on which they passed from this world into the region of the living, are called their birthdays; and that their solemnities are called not funeral observances, as though for the dead, but natal celebrations, as of those being born into true life . . . [CXIX, 980–982.]

(See Indexes CXLIX and CL, in which this commandment is more frequently treated incidentally.)

[Col. 0465]

# CXLIX. INDEX OF FEASTS, WHICH TREATS IN TURN AND SYSTEMATICALLY OF FEASTS IN GENERAL, AND OF THEIR ORIGIN, NUMBER, AND ANTIQUITY; OF VIGILS AND OCTAVES; OF THE FEASTS OF THE LORD, OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY, OF MALE AND FEMALE SAINTS; AND OF SUNDAY, ETC.

## NOTICE

This analytical index, “On feasts in general and in particular,” contains five parts: the first, on feasts in general, Vigils, and Octaves; the second, on the feasts of the Lord; the third, on the feasts of the Blessed Mary; the fourth, on feasts of saints, considered both generally and individually; and finally the fifth, on Sunday in general [Col. 0467] and on each Sunday throughout the year. Each part is divided and repeatedly subdivided into chapters. Matters pertaining to any feast or to any Sunday, most carefully excerpted from the holy Fathers, collected into one body, and arranged according to logical order, are included under a single chapter or article. Each feast is given a literal and logical definition and a mystical interpretation; its institution, antiquity, excellence, the manner in which it is to be observed, and the reasons for doing so are set forth. At the end of each article, in the manner of an appendix, are indicated the office, Mass, liturgical prayers, sermons, homilies, hymns, poems, and so forth that belong to that feast. All who are about to undertake this subject as preachers or writers may consult this particularly complete and carefully composed index of feasts with no little profit.

# INDEX OF FEASTS

## PART ONE. ON FEASTS IN GENERAL

### CHAPTER ONE.—On the definition, institution, and number of feasts

Days are called *fasti* because law is spoken (*fatur*) on them; and *nefasti* because law is not spoken on them. *Feriae* are named from speaking (*fando*): Rabanus Maurus, [CX, 361.]—A festival (*festivitas*) derives from feast-days (*festi dies*), as it were “festive divinity,” because on them only divine business is done: the same author, [CXI, 307]; Saint Isidore, [LXXXII, 250.]—Festival as though “divine fasti”: Honorius of Autun, [CLXXII, 644.]—Mystically, a feast-day is the communion of the faithful: Abbot Godefrid, [CLXXXIV, 102.]—A feast-day means passing from evil to good: ibid., 170.—What is understood by a festival but inward joy, and by the Sabbath but rest of mind? Hugh of Saint-Victor, [CLXXV, 587.]—An unceasing festival will be celebrated in heaven: Rabanus Maurus, [CX, 1032.]—Those things which were notably done on specified days are celebrated annually in the Church: Saint Augustine, [XLII, 503.]—Days made notable by some miracle or mystery are honored yearly by a more solemn festival: Saint Paulinus of Nola, [LXI, 649.]—A feast-day is a solemn day consecrated in honor of God and by the confession of saints: Aurelius Cassiodorus, [LXX, 822.]—The Church calls solemn feasts those that are established by a fixed observance: Beleth, [CCII, 17.]—God grants us a feast-day from heaven: Saint Peter Chrysologus, [LII, 472.]—God instituted feast-days: John, archbishop of Rouen, [CXLVII, 253.]—An ecclesiastical festival is not fruitless: Saint Peter Chrysologus, [LII, 467–468.]—They are not to be consecrated according to our wishes but according to their own merits: ibid., 471–472.—The feasts of the Lord declare their own causes by their names: ibid., 613.—They agree under diverse names: Anonymous, [XIII, 652.]—They are customarily expressed by several names: *Festivitas* (festival), *Festum* (feast), *Celebritas* (celebration), *Exitus* (departure), *Obitus* (death), *Transitus* (passing), *Assumptio* (assumption), *Depositio* (laying to rest), *Dormitio* (falling asleep), *Passio* (passion), *Dedicatio* (dedication), *Nativitas* (birth), *Natalis* or *Natale* (birthday, nativity), and *Natalitium* (birthday celebration): Beleth, [CCII, 17.]—Some feasts are general, others particular: ibid., 18.—There is a threefold solemnity: the solemnity of sinners, the solemnity of the righteous, and the solemnity of the blessed. The flesh celebrates the first outwardly, the spirit the second, and angels together with glorified humanity the third: Thomas the Cistercian, [CCVI, 220.]

Christians abstained from the festivals of the heathen, Tertullian, I, 492. One must abstain from the holidays of the Gentiles, and why, St. Ambrose, XVII, 617–618.---Christians celebrated festivals wholly distinct from the festivals of Jews and heathens, Tertullian, I, 682.---If we observe Jewish ceremonies, we become Galatianized, the same author, II, 973.---One must avoid association not only with Gentiles but also with Jews, St. Ambrose, XVII, 617–618.---Jewish feast-days are not to be observed after the Gospel, St. Jerome, XXII, 1220–1221.---Jewish festivals are figures of Christian festivals, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 359.---Jewish festivals had earthly causes, Rupert, CLXVII, 1756.---Ours, however, are spiritual, ibid., 1647.---The Israelite people chiefly observed four solemnities: Passover, Pentecost, the Feast of Tabernacles, and the Dedication; we, however, observe only two of these, Passover and Pentecost, but for quite different reasons, Beleth, CCII, 135; Sicard, CCXIII, 378.---The Church anathematizes those who decree that, together with the Jews, the fourteenth day and the Sabbaths are to be observed at the Paschal festival, St. Jerome, XXII, 1222.---The pomp of festivals made the Jews obstinate, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 219–220.---Christian feast-days and pagan solemn days, St. Augustine, XL, 343.---Christian feast-days are not the same everywhere, Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXIX, 1045, 1055.---The Apostle and the Gospels declared that the festival of Passover and other celebrations ought to be honoured, Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXIX, 1053, 1153.---Origin of the assemblies (synaxes) of the saints, Walafrid Strabo, CXLV, 921; Arnobius, V, 1076.---Banquets on feast-days, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 542.

Christians observed the Lord’s Day, Tertullian, II, 79.---The birthdays of martyrs, ibid.; St. Augustine, XL, 676; St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 572–573.---They offered oblations for the dead, Tertullian, II, 79.---The Catholic Church maintains eight festivals: the Sabbath, the Nativity of the Lord, the day of [Col. 0468] Epiphany, the fast of Lent, the Fourth Day of the Sabbath [Wednesday], Parasceve [Good Friday], the festival of Passover, and Pentecost, St. Philastrius, XII, 1273–1274.---The feasts of the Lord’s Ascension and of the coming of the Holy Spirit were received by tradition, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 200.---St. Paulinus of Nola enumerates Christian solemnities, LXI, 649, 828.---The feasts of Christ’s Nativity, Epiphany, and Ascension were established in ancient times, ibid., 648.---They are celebrated at distinct times in the Church, ibid., 649–650.---The feasts of saints were received in Gaul from ancient times, Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 169–171.---The solemnity of the Circumcision was numbered among the principal festivals about the middle of the seventh century, St. Isidore, LXXXI, 478 (note).---In the age of Paulinus of Aquileia, feasts were to be kept as sabbatical days, like Sunday, St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 339 (note).---Feasts received in Gaul in the middle of the twelfth century, Adalhard, *Statutes for Monks*, CV, 537–538.---Days on which monks must obey the Lord’s command concerning work, ibid.---Festivals on which extra portions were given, ibid., 544.---Times of holiday throughout the year, Hetto, CV, 764; Rodulf, CXIX, 717; Walter, ibid., 740; Grimald, CXXI, 768; Regino, CXXXII, 265; Ecclesiastical Capitularies of Louis II, CXXXVIII, 624–625; St. Ivo, CLXI, 266–267; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1781.---Feasts must be observed without any legal or market work, Flodoard, CXXXV, 498.---On which feasts the use of the pallium was granted to the bishop of the Beneventan see, John XIII, CXXXV, 677; John XIX, CXLI, 1138.---The remarkable concord between the eight solemnities of the Old Law and the eight festivals of the New Law, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 331–334.---Four grades of festivals in the monastery of Cluny, Uldaric, CXLIX, 654–656.---In the Rule of St. Benedict, Lanfranc, CL, 473.---Among the Carthusians, Guigo, CLIII, 651–654.---The Holy Roman Church has nine prefaces, and the festivals on which they are used, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 7511.---What a station or procession is, Beleth, CCII, 18.---Stations seem to have passed to us from the Old Law, ibid.---There are two processions: one on Palm branches, and the other on Sundays, in memory of that which the disciples rendered to Christ on the day of the Ascension, ibid., 20.

Litany means supplication or rogation; it is twofold, major and minor. Why this is so, Beleth, CCII, 28.---The Major Litany is celebrated on the feast of Blessed Mark; the Minor Litanies are celebrated with fasting and processions during the three days before the Ascension, Sicard, CCXIII, 367.

The primitive Church observed Thursday in memory of the Ascension, just as it observed Sunday in memory of the Resurrection, Sicard, CCXIII, 374.---Baptism belongs to Sunday and to the third hour, but is placed on Saturday, and why.

Those who come to church only on feast-days and solely out of regard for the solemnity are rebuked by Origen, in St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1755, 1757.---Festivals at Tours, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 565.---A double or triple feast falling on a Sunday is celebrated, John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 39.---New feasts are not to be instituted rashly and without consulting the Apostolic See, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 335.

## CHAPTER II.—Things to Be Done or Avoided in the Celebration of Festivals

How shall we celebrate Sunday solemnities? Certainly as did the Apostles: secure through faith, not money, Tertullian, I, 119.---The pious and holy synaxes of Christians, ibid., 468.---It is unlawful for Christians to attend the shameful banquets of the heathen in an association, St. Cyprian, III, 1030.---Feast-days are not to be observed with Jews or heretics, nor with pagans, St. Ambrose, XVII, 617–618; St. Leo the Great, LVI, 718.---Christians are not to gather at idolatrous assemblies, St. Isidore, Council of Laodicea, LXXXIV, 132–133.---Feasts are not to be celebrated with pagans, ibid.---Jewish banquets are forbidden to Christians, ibid.; Council of Orléans, II, 281.---It is forbidden to celebrate feasts with heretics, Jews, or pagans, or to receive festive gifts from them, Fulgentius Ferrandus, LXXXVIII, 187, 872; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1417–1418; Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 289.---To celebrate festivals spiritually is to refrain from evil works, Rupert the abbot, CLXVIII, 679.---We sanctify ourselves, that we may celebrate the holy day in holiness, St. Jerome, XXIII, [Col. 0469] 99.---He knows nothing of the joys of solemnities who has neither a pure heart nor a chaste body, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2169.---Chastity must be observed through all festivals, St. Ambrose, XVII, 605.---Feasts are to be observed religiously, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 274.---Certain feasts were celebrated with the joy of diners at public tables, ibid.; St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 542; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 518.---On feast-days secular persons prepare banquets for themselves; religious persons, delights of the heart, St. Bernard, LXXXIII, 452.---At first the Church was permitted to celebrate the feast-days of martyrs with luxury, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 118.---In various places, on Sundays, the fifty days after Easter, martyrs’ solemnities, and every feast, people take their meal, ibid., 146.---Certain Christians affront the solemnities of martyrs by their excesses, the same author, XXXVI, 867.---It is unworthy that feasts should be turned into vanity and pleasures, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 44.---Abuses at saints’ feasts, ibid., 480.---At Easter festivals, ibid., 282.---The festivals of saints are celebrated not by more lavish banquets but by imitating them, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 555.---Festivals ought to be preceded for many days by good works, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1974, 1976.---Observance of the Sabbath means applying oneself to good works, St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 467.---True Sabbath observance is abstinence from sin, ibid., 477.---He celebrates the Sabbath badly who abstains from good works, ibid., 467.---Let the joy of a festival include mercy toward the needy, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 489.---The Jew honoured heavenly festivals with tithes; let the Christian honour them even with hundredths, ibid., 219–220.---Let the joys of festivals be guarded, ibid., 549–550.---At festivals care must be taken that all have recourse to God’s grace, ibid., 214.

On feast-days clothing is more splendid, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 272.---Churches are more richly adorned, ibid.; St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 464, 908–909; with flowers, ibid., 467, 909; with veils, ibid., 909.---The soul must above all be cleansed, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 272.---Feast-days are to be celebrated with both outward and inward joy, ibid.---One must cease from sins and cease from labour, ibid., 506.---On feast-days the portions of food are to be increased, St. Benedict the abbot, CIII, 1222–1223.---At the solemnities of the Lord’s Nativity and Easter, monks’ portions were increased, Anonymous, CV, 749.---On feast-days ancient Christians devoted themselves wholly to prayer, St. Agobard, CIV, 75.---To keep a feast-day is to abstain from harmful works and be restrained from every superfluity, Godefrid the abbot, CLXXIV, 96.---Solemn feast-days are exempt from fasting, Tertullian, II, 79; St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 331.

On Sunday or other greater festivals the divine mysteries must be heard in their entirety, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2276, 2278.---At Masses one must stand for the space of one or two hours, ibid., 2277–2279.---Solemnities of Mass, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 820–821.---At festivals, if one celebration is insufficient, there should be no doubt about repeating the sacrifice, St. Isidore, *Epistle of Leo*, LXXXIV, 119.---Masses are to be celebrated at the third hour only on the principal solemnities, ibid.; Council of Orléans, II, 281.---On which days the distributions of *eulogiae* [blessed bread] were made, St. Eutychian, V, 166; Udalric, CXXXV, 1073; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 682.---At the solemnities of the Blessed Virgin Mary and of the twelve Apostles and Evangelists, etc., one must cease from worldly work and devote oneself to divine things, Pope Nicholas, CXIX, 986.---On Sunday or other feast-days, even when war presses, it is more fitting to cease from arms than from prayer, ibid.---Lamps were appointed in churches for sacred readings on Sundays and feast-days, Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVIII, 1227, 1243.---On feast-days people ought to pray standing, Regino, CXXXII, 388.---On which feasts one does not kneel, St. Ivo, CLXI, 261, 267.---Shepherds and oxherds are to come to Mass on Sundays and feast-days, Regino, CXXXII, 279, 363, 457, 459, 461; Burchard, CXL, 638.---The solemnities of Mass are not to be celebrated before the third hour, Regino, CXXXII, 188.---Pope Telesphorus decreed that no one should celebrate Mass before the third hour, Gilbert, CXXXIX, 537.---Sunday and festivals approved for priests are to be observed, Atto, CXXXIV, 106.---They are to be proclaimed by one’s own bishop, Assembly of Louis, King of Germany, CXXXVIII, 614.---It is not customary for a king to appear crowned on feast-days, Atto, CXXXIV, 982.---Blessed Remigius asks that an offering be made by an *atio* [reading uncertain] on all feast-days and Sundays in commemoration of him, Flodoard, CXXXV, 65.---Every Sunday feast is to be observed from the afternoon hour of Saturday until daybreak on Monday, Anonymous, CXXXVIII, 514.---The whole Easter week is to be celebrated festively, and on Pentecost Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday are to be honoured as solemnly as Sunday, Constitutions of Otto the Great, ibid., 832.---Days on which legal work is forbidden, ibid.; Edict of Otto III, CXXXVIII, 854.---The people are not to be drawn away from public Masses by private Masses, Burchard, CXL, 635.---When priests announce sacred festivals to the people, they should also admonish them in every way to observe the fast of the vigils, ibid.; Council of Orléans, CXL, 887.---At the beginning of the Church’s birth the solemnities of Mass were not celebrated with the manner or order now used, Berno the abbot, CXLII, 1055–1056.---Something must always be offered at the solemnities of Mass, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1720.---Celebration of solemn Masses in the Church of Lyons according to ancient statutes, Statutes of the Church of Lyons, CXCIX, 1094–1095.

Four times in the year—that is, at the Lord’s Nativity, the Lord’s Supper, Easter, and Pentecost—all the faithful ought to communicate, Udalric, CXXXV, 1073; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 562 (note); Burchard, CXL, 963.---Each of the faithful should communicate three times a year, namely at Easter, Pentecost, and the Lord’s Nativity, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 562 (note); Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1738.

Among the Saxons, the people were required to pay plough-alms fifteen days after Easter; tithes of young animals at Pentecost; tithes of the fruits of the earth at the feast of All Saints; St. Peter’s penny at St. Peter’s feast; and church dues at St. Martin’s feast, Anonymous Works, CXXXVIII, 458; Eleventh-Century Liturgical Monuments, CLI, 1174, 1193.

Something from the Gospel or Epistle is to be proclaimed to the faithful every Sunday or feast-day, Pope Leo IV, CXV, 679.---A sermon to the people is to be given on feast-days, Flodoard, CXXXV, 409.---There is to be one manner of prayer for all priests, Canons of King Edgar, CXXXVIII, 502.---Every priest is to admonish the people on feast-days as to what prayers they ought to pour out to God, Burchard, CXL, 658; St. Ivo, CLXI, 193.---Those absent from divine offices on Sundays and feast-days are to be observed and noted in the parish, John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 254.---What sort of sermons are fitting on feast-days, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 44.---A prelate ought not to be absent from his church, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 179.---The feasts on which the Archbishops of Rouen made distributions to the chapter and offered bread and wine, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 1179.---On feast-days wine was distributed to the people in the church courtyard, Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 1021.---The festivals of apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins must be observed with fitting honour, Rodulf, CXIX, 717.

Feasts on which it was formerly permitted to eat meat even if they fell on Friday, Pope Nicholas, CXIX, 981.---Certain festivals are not celebrated at their own time: why, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 243.---Such are the festival of Easter, the Ascension of the Lord, Pentecost, the Beheading of St. John the Baptist, the feast of St. James, and also that of St. Peter in Chains, ibid.---On more solemn feasts all bells are to be rung, John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 32, 40, 33, 57–59, 73, 84, 103, 160–161, 178, 181, 187, 189.---Feasts on which the *Credo* (“I believe”) is sung, ibid., 38.---On which feasts the *Credo* (“I believe”) was said in the Order of St. Benedict, Lanfranc, CL, 481.---At feasts during Advent and Lent, *Gloria in excelsis* (“Glory in the highest”) was not sung, John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 38, 81, 165.---If feasts fall in Lent, they are celebrated like Sundays, Udalric, CXLIX, 656.---Times and feasts on which the peace of God and of Holy Church was granted throughout the kingdom, Laws of Edward III, CLI, 1191.---The solemnities of church dedications are to be celebrated for eight days every year, St. Ivo, CLXI, 203.---The royal court is held at Christmas, Easter, and Pentecost; in Spain, at four solemnities, namely Christmas, Easter, Pentecost, and St. James’s day, the same author, CLXII, 328.---On all feast-days when the great bells are rung, the canons sing Vespers, Matins, and the Sunday Mass throughout the year, Guichard, CXCIX, 1094.---Any feast, whether of apostles or martyrs, if it falls on privileged Sundays, is to be transferred to Monday, Beleth, CCLI, 73.---The Feast of Fools, customarily held every year on the feast of the Innocents, St. Stephen, or the Circumcision, is forbidden, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 1168, 1173.---On solemn days such as Sundays and others, we divide the office into three nocturns, Sicard, CCXIII, 154.---At the solemnities of saints likewise, we celebrate three nocturns or Vigils, ibid., 158.

At the feasts of the Lord and St. Mary, or of the twelve Apostles and of other saints whose observance is customary in the province, the divine office is to be performed each year by day and night, St. Chrodegang, LXXXIX, 1074.---Feasts on which the bishop gave a meal to his clergy, ibid.---At principal solemnities the full office is to be celebrated and meals are to be taken twice, ibid., 1089.---Feasts whose Vigils Carthusians observe on bread and water, Guigo, CLIII, 646.---The feasts and octaves on which Carthusians do not celebrate the office for the dead, ibid., 656.---At Christmas, Easter, and Pentecost also, when some brother is about to make profession, he sings the greater Mass, LXXXIX, [Col. 0471] 666.---At the feasts of the Purification and Annunciation, *Gloria in excelsis* (“Glory in the highest”) is said whenever they occur, ibid., 1146.---Feasts on which Carthusian brothers have wine twice, ibid., 733.---Feasts to be celebrated annually with chapter, ibid., 1149.---On feast-days monks stand in white garments, Rupert the abbot, CLXX, 53.

Sunday and other festivals are to be celebrated without servile work, from evening to evening, Pope St. Eutychian, V, 166; St. Jerome, XXII, 1222; Regino, CXXXII, 190, 285, 356; Udalric, CXXXV, 1073; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 455, 562 (note).---The Fathers decreed rest on feasts and on Sunday, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2274.---On holiday days, when divine service is performed, people must abstain from lawsuits, St. Isidore, LXXXIII, 965.---Sunday and other feasts are to be observed by ceasing from the works of servitude and the flesh, by devoting oneself to holy works, and by hearing the sacred word, St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 336–337.---First one must abstain from every sin and every earthly work, all the clamour of lawsuits ceasing, ibid., 338 (note).---God forbids labour on a feast-day, Haymo, CXVIII, 1006.---Feasts on which one must rest from work, Rodulf, CXIX, 717; Nicholas, ibid., 986.---At these festivals there are to be no judicial proceedings, ibid.---Above all, let us take care to keep Sunday and the festivals of saints most carefully from every secular work, St. Odo the abbot, CXXXIII, 950.---On feast-days one must sometimes abstain even from lawful things, when the Church’s command so requires, St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 279.---It is sometimes permitted to work on feast-days, Regino, CXXXII, 438.---Times during which a public court or assembly is forbidden, Adrevald, CXXIV, 1077; Assembly of Louis, King of Germany, CXXXVIII, 595; Burchard, CXL, 888; St. Ivo, CLXI, 274.---Feasts and fasts to be observed, Edicts of King Canute, CLI, 1175.---Feasts and times on which ordeals and oaths are forbidden, ibid.---Violators of festivals are to be punished, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 1159.---God punishes transgressors, Haymo, CXVIII, 1006.---Ratherius prohibited, under pain of excommunication, servile work on Sunday; and he enforced this by force, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 682.

If a freeman works on feast-days, he loses his freedom; if a slave does so, he loses his skin or pays *hidgild* [a compensatory fine], Ecclesiastical Laws of Alfred the Great, CXXXVIII, 458.---Laws of Edward the Elder, ibid., 461.---If a lord compels his slaves to work on a feast-day, he is to be punished, ibid., 461.---Among the Danes he loses the slave and pays the penalty for breaking the law; among the English, he pays a fine, Edicts of King Canute, CLI, 1179.---First one must abstain from sin, St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 477; St. Leo the Great, LIV, 506; St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 336.---Gorging oneself with meat on Sunday is condemned, Gregory of Tours, LXXVII, 1551–1552.---Times at which one must abstain from wives and from marriages, Pope St. Eutychian, V, 166–167; St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 338; Burchard, CXL, 960, 100, 1013; Beleth, CCII, 72.---Likewise, for three weeks before the feast of St. John the Baptist, St. Ivo, CLXI, 616.---And also at solemnities of saints, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1645.---Those who violate Lent, Sunday night, or any notable festival are to do penance for forty days, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 573.---Christians must abstain from wedding festivities, dances, and clamorous hunts, St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 729.---Public spectacles are by no means to be held on feast-days, Fulgentius Ferrandus, LXXXVIII, 931; Atto, CXXXIV, 43.---Dancing and revelry are forbidden at solemn feasts, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 455.---Whoever goes to spectacles on a solemn day is to be excommunicated, St. Ivo, CLXI, 265.---No one is to celebrate greater feasts in a country village, ibid., 266.---On feast-days, at least during the time of divine office, the bells are to be closed off [silenced], John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 43.---Markets are not to be held on feast-days, ibid., 233.

## CHAPTER III.—On Vigils in General

The day preceding a feast is called a Vigil, or instead of it a fast, established in place of Vigils, Beleth, CCII, 141.---Devotion to Vigils is very ancient, Tertullian, I, 1294; Alcuin, CI, 1275.---The devotion of Vigils is ancient, a familiar good of all saints, St. Jerome, XXX, 234; St. Isidore of Spain, LXXXIII, 759; St. Chrodegang, LXXXIX.---Vigils are ancient and founded upon authority, St. Jerome, XXX, 237.---The grace of Vigils is attested in both the Old and New Testament, ibid., 235.---It is established by examples and admonitions, ibid.---Vigils began with the shepherds who, at Christ’s birth, kept watch over their flocks by night, Honorius, CLXXII, 644; Sicard, CCXIII, 216.---They may have been instituted to correct pagan vigils, St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 251 (note).---The heretics called Nyctages considered Vigils superfluous, St. Chrodegang, LXXXIX, 1067.

Vigils are called nocturns, Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXX, 547.---Night Vigils, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 428; Regino, CXXXII, 356.---Formerly there were three Vigils by night in the Church, John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 83–84.---Night Vigils are divided into three nocturns, Rupert the abbot, CLXX, 14; Sicard, CCXIII, 158.---Morning Vigils, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 294.---Vigils are twofold, spiritual and material, Alan of Lille, CCX, 178–179.---Spiritual Vigils are to be preferred to material ones, ibid.---Some Vigils belong to carnal persons, others to spiritual persons, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 403.

Sunday Vigils, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 807, 978.---Vigils of St. Mary, St. Eutychian, V, 166.---Vigils of saints, St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 660; Sicard, CCXIII, 158.---Vigils of the Apostles, Pope Leo IV, CXV, 681.---Vigils of martyrs, Flodoard, CXXXV, 41.---Solemn Vigils for the dead, Atto, CXXXIV, 974.

Vigils are beneficial, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 678.---Benefits of Vigils, Alan of Lille, CCX, 178–179.---Fruitful, St. Augustine, XLII, 1117.---The place and necessity of Vigils, Rabanus Maurus, CX, 90.---Observance of Vigils, Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXIX, 962, 985, 1189.---Vigils are to be attended, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1977, 2019, 2022, 2029.---People should assemble in church for Vigils before dawn, ibid., 2275, 2280.---During Lent, women came to Vigils with children to be baptized, ibid., 1751.---It is suggested that poor people and artisans attended Vigils even on non-feast-days, ibid., 2284.---Sunday Vigils were attended by the faithful, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 807, 978.---Vigils are to be celebrated devoutly, ibid., 782.---Vigils are to be kept with fasting, so that, purified through abstinence, we may celebrate more worthily the joy of the following feast, Alcuin, CI, 1214; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 501.---At saints’ Vigils, a spiritual person who wishes to celebrate the solemnity in spirit and truth must also keep watch, ibid., 403.---Sanctification is required at the Vigils of solemnities, Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 209.---The people made a point of attending Vigils at saints’ festivals, Alcuin, CI, 712.---The solemnities of saints were celebrated from ancient times by privilege, St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 660.---Vigils of the Apostles are to be observed, Leo IV, CXV, 681.---Vigils of martyrs were observed most religiously, Flodoard, CXXXV, 41.---Vigils were held at martyrs’ tombs outside churches, Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXXIX, 1008.---How Vigils were observed at the festivals of saints or at all solemnities, St. Benedict, CIII, 897.---At the Vigils of all feasts one must abstain from wives, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 566.---At Vigils the celebrant must afflict himself so that at the solemnity he may be able to rejoice, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 548.---That peace may prevail everywhere at all Vigils, Eleventh-Century Liturgical Monuments, CLI, 1191, 1134.---Clerics are not to be absent from Vigils, Atto, CXXXIV, 38.---At the Vigil of St. Mary, St. John, and the prescribed Vigils of other saints, *eulogiae* are to be distributed to the people after Mass, St. Eutychian, V, 166.---Night Vigils on feasts were observed by all, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 821, 898, 978.---Vigils were celebrated every week from the evening when Saturday was dawning, Cassian, XLIX, 141.---They were both more numerous and stricter in monasteries, ibid., 134.---They were longer on Saturday, ibid., 145.---People fasted at Vigils, Regino, CXXXXII [perhaps CXXXII], 244; St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 610.---At Vigils of saints, fasting is to be on Lenten food, St. Augustine, XXXII, 1458.---Fasts were established on certain saints’ Vigils, the same author, XL, 1276; Alcuin, CI, 1213.---The fast before the Assumption and before the Lord’s Nativity was received and observed by the Roman Church in ancient times, Pope Nicholas, CXIX, 931.

Practice of Vigils, St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 327.---From the beginning, Paschal Vigil was customarily celebrated on Saturday in the basilica of St. Peter, Anastasius the Librarian, CXXXVIII, 1263.---On the existence and celebration of sacred Vigils in the Church of Aquileia in the age of St. Nicetas, St. Nicetas, LII, 1091.---Vigil stations at principal solemnities were instituted in the Church of Tours by Perpetuus, bishop of Tours, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 567.---On which Vigils a fast was prescribed in the age of St. Paulinus, St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 235.---Gregory III restored and enlarged the rules for celebrating the solemnities of Vigils, Anastasius the Librarian, CXXXVIII, 1029–1030.---The practice of Vigils in the Church of Auxerre, prescribed by Bishop Aunarius, Anonymous, ibid., 233.---Among Cluniac monks, Lanfranc, CL, 573.---Among Carthusians, Guigo, CLIII, 646.---When a Vigil falls on Sunday, the fast and commemoration are to be held on Saturday, ibid., 1145.---Priests should admonish the faithful to observe the fast of Vigils, Burchard, CXL, 887.

[Col. 0473] The practice of Vigils was changed into a fast, St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 251; John of Rouen, CXLVII, 84; Beleth, CCII, 141.

In ancient custom, two nocturnal offices were held on principal festivals: one at the beginning of the night by the bishop with his chaplains, the other in the middle of the night, at which the people were present, Sicard, CCXIII, 216.---Later, Vigils were prohibited, while the fast retained their place and name, ibid., 375.---On Vigils, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 223, 476.

## CHAPTER IV.—On Particular Vigils

### § I.—On the Vigils of the Lord

On the Vigil of the Lord’s Nativity.—Practice of the Church, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 29; St. Protadius, LXXX, 422; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 112; Christian Druthmar, CVI, 1261; Grimald, CXXI, 859, 884, 886; Usuard, CXXIII, 833; Ado, ibid., 177, 201; King Robert, CXLI, 945; Udalric, CXLIX, 691; CLI, 951; Stephen, CLXVI, 1385; Honorius, CLXXII, 729, 733; Beleth, CCII, 75.---The Vigil of the Nativity is to be celebrated with fasting, Pope Nicholas, CXIX, 981; St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 800–801.---Among the chief Vigils, it has its own nocturnal and diurnal office, Sicard, CCXIII, 375; sermons of St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 87, 90, 94, 100, 105; Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 200, 203, 208, 213; Peter of Celle, CCII, 654.---Homilies: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1103; the Venerable Bede, XCIV, 31; Paul the Deacon, XCV, 1162; Haymo, CXVIII, 47; Godefrid, CLXXIV, 639, 642, 645, 648, 651, 655.

On the Vigil of Epiphany.—Practice of the Church, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 38; St. Protadius, LXXX, 412; St. Isidore, LXXXV, 626; LXXXVI, 150; Rabanus, CX, 1124; Grimald, CXXI, 859, 884, 886; Eleventh-Century Liturgical Monuments, CLI, 952; Stephen, CLXVI, 1391.---The Vigil of Epiphany has no fast, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 293 (note); Helperich, CXXXVII, 487.---Yet a fast was formerly observed on it, John of Rouen, CXLVII, 43, 90.---Homily: Paul the Deacon, XCV, 1186.

On the Vigil of Easter.—It is called the “night of Vigils” in part, St. Gaudentius, XX, 843.---The Easter Vigil is, as it were, the mother of all holy Vigils, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1088.---Christians kept watch through the night of Easter; they held this Vigil as a solemn observance, Tertullian, I, 1294.---Most celebrated, Aurelius Prudentius, LIX, 818.---Let us celebrate the Easter Vigil outwardly and inwardly, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1088.---At the Easter Vigil, *Gloria in excelsis Deo* (“Glory to God in the highest”) is sung for those to be baptized, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 804.---Mass in the night, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 231–232.---On the Easter Vigil, Alcuin, CI, 1215.---The pure proclamations of the Paschal night, Rupert, CLXX, 168.---Homilies: the Venerable Bede, XCIV, 133; Paul the Deacon, XCV, 1326; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 135, 137; Haymo, CXVIII, 444. (See **HOLY SATURDAY**.)

On the Vigil of the Ascension.—Practice of the Church, Amalarius, CV, 1300; Grimald, CXXI, 898; Honorius, CLXXII, 700; Einhard, CIV, 418; Sicard, CCXIII, 375.---Formerly there was a fast on the Vigil of the Ascension, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 688.---Homilies, St. Augustine, XXXV, 1901; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 226, 228.

On the Vigil of Pentecost.—Practice of the Church, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 110; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXV, 609; LXXXVI, 685; Alcuin, CI, 1225–1226; Amalarius, CV, 1068, 1215; Grimald, CXXI, 868, 898; John of Rouen, CXLVII, 57; Udalric, CXLIX, 671; Stephen, CLXVI, 1407; Honorius, CLXXII, 701, 735, 756; Sicard, CCXIII, 375.---Fasting on the Vigil of Pentecost, Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 206–207.---Lessons are read on the Vigil of Pentecost, Alcuin, CI, 1225–1226.---Baptism on the Vigil of Pentecost, Alcuin, CI, 1225–1226; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 455; Sicard, CCXIII, 375.---Homilies: the Venerable Bede, XCIV, 189; Godefrid, CLXXIV, 876; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 247, 249, 252, 253. (See **PENTECOST**.)

### § II.—On the Vigils of the Blessed Virgin Mary

The Vigil of the Nativity of the Blessed Mary was celebrated, and a miracle was obtained on it, John XIII, CXXXV, 1066.---Formerly there was a fast before the Purification of Blessed Mary, John of Rouen, CXLVII, 90.

On the Vigil of the Assumption.—Practice of the Church, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 130, 132; St. Protadius, LXXX, 418; Amalarius, CV, 1306; Grimald, CXXI, 912; Eleventh-Century Liturgical Monuments, CLI, 897, 967.---The Vigil of the Assumption is to be celebrated with fasting, St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 235 (note); Nicholas, CXIX, 981; Peter Damian, CXLV, 800–801.---Homilies: Godefrid, CLXXIV, 957.

### § III.—On the Vigils of Saints

On Vigils of saints, Stephen, CLXV, 1415; Honorius, [Col. 0474] CLXXII, 644.---Mass at the Vigil of the Apostles, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 150; Eleventh-Century Liturgical Monuments, CLI, 943.---Mass at the Vigil of one martyr, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 163.---Mass at the Vigil of several martyrs, ibid., 165.---Mass at the Vigil of confessors, ibid., 167, 169.---Mass at the Vigil of virgins, ibid., 171.

On the Vigil of St. John the Baptist.—Practice of the Church, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 120; St. Protadius, LXXX, 417; Grimald, CXXI, 909; Guido the abbot, CL, 1219; CLI, 892; Honorius, CLXXII, 700; Einhard, CIV, 589.---Mass at the Vigil of St. John the Baptist after sunset, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 394, 695.---Homilies: the Venerable Bede, XCIV, 202; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 336–337.

On the Vigils of the Apostles Peter and Paul.—Practice of the Church, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 123; St. Protadius, LXXX, 417; Amalarius, CV, 1306; Guido the abbot, CL, 1221; Eleventh-Century Liturgical Monuments, CLI, 892; sermon of St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 403; Odilo, CXLII, 1020.---Homilies: the Venerable Bede, XCIV, 214; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 343, 348; Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 823.

On the Vigil of All Saints.—Practice of the Church, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 146; St. Protadius, LXXX, 420; Guido the abbot, CL, 1240.---The Vigil of All Saints is a day of affliction, Sicard, CCXIII, 424.

## CHAPTER V.—On Octaves

Christian feasts, but not pagan ones, were celebrated with an octave, Tertullian, I, 682.---The Book of Leviticus indicates that the eighth day is to be celebrated, saying: “The eighth day shall be most celebrated and most holy,” Sicard, CCXIII, 226.---By the octave Christ’s second coming was signified, Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXX, 58.---The octave pertains to eternal rest, ibid., 94.---The days of octaves are holy, St. Augustine, XL, 581.---Some octaves are of institution, some of devotion, and some also of veneration, Beleth, CCII, 78.

Octaves are celebrated for diverse and special reasons, Sicard, CCXIII, 226.---For a similar reason the octave of Epiphany is celebrated, ibid.---The octave of the Passion is not celebrated, because the succeeding feast of joy overshadows and abolishes the commemoration of sorrow, ibid.

Why the octaves of saints are celebrated, Rupert, CLXX, 218.---The solemnity of the Easter octave, ibid.---Why the sacred Paschal solemnity has octaves, ibid., 198.---Octaves of those regenerated, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 1235.---The eight days of the newly baptized are distinguished, the same author, XXXIII, 220.---By some, the third day of the octave, or even the octave day itself, was chosen for the washing of feet, ibid.

Offerings of bread and wine made to the chapter of Rouen during the octaves of Easter and Pentecost, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 1179.---On the octaves of the Lord and of saints, Stephen, CLXVI, 1415.

## PART TWO. ON THE FEASTS OF THE LORD

## CHAPTER ONE.—On the Nativity of the Lord
The day on which Christ was born, St. Philastrius, XII, 1273.---“Nativity” is so called because Christ was born in it, Alcuin, CI, 1173.---Christ was conceived and crucified on Friday; he was born and rose again on Sunday, Sicard, CCXIII, 218.---The Nativity of the Lord was established by the Fathers as a votive solemnity, because on it Christ willed to be born bodily for the redemption of the world, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 761; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 343.---It is celebrated annually in order to recall the memory of the twofold coming, Godfrey, CLXXIV, 21, 36, 42.---It is celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of January [25 December], St. Protadius, LXXX, 422; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 441; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 1186.---It is not the same as the day of the Epiphany, St. Jerome, XXXI, 18, 19.---Although in Egypt it was celebrated in the same solemnity, Cassian, XLIX, 820, 821.---It does not recur on the same day, because it is not celebrated sacramentally, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 205; Alcuin, CI, 1175.---The feast of the Lord’s Nativity, Lanfranc, CL, 448; Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 265. Its ceremonial splendour and solemnity, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 126.---The feasts of the Lord declare their own causes by their names: by being born, he gave the day its name of Nativity, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 613.---In the Church only the birthdays of Christ and John are celebrated, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1301, 1309; Godfrey, CLXXIV, 45.---And that of Mary, ibid.---The great, new, and glorious solemnity of the Lord’s Nativity: the coming of God to humankind, St. Isidore, LXXXIII, 762.---The birthday is rightly called a new sun, St. Ambrose, XVII, 613.---On it the sun of righteousness rises for us, God being its author, ibid., 614, 615.---Light entered into the darkness of the age, St. Jerome, XXX, 220.---The Nativity of the Lord is recalled from the sun, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 471, 472.---A most longed-for season, Godfrey, CLXXIV, 21, 36, 42.---The wondrous ordering of this mystery, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 190.---In a new [Col. 0475] order, by a new birth, the Son of God was begotten, I. IV, 195.---While the Church venerates Christ’s birth, it celebrates its own, ibid., 213.---Christ’s Nativity is the wedding of the Church, Hildebert, CLXXI, 388.---The Nativity is of peace, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 215.---It may be called a visitation, Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXX, 75.---The night of the Lord’s Nativity is full of grace, Godfrey the abbot, CLXXIV, 44.---Wonderful and rare matters in Christ’s Nativity, Nicholas of Clairvaux, CLXXXIV, 827.---Christ’s Nativity is to be wondered at, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 86.---The day of new redemption, ancient restoration, and eternal blessedness, ibid., 96.---It ought always to seem new, ibid., 111.---The marvels and signs which preceded the Nativity, Alcuin, CI, 1173.---The mysteries of Christ’s Nativity and infancy are never sufficiently to be recollected, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 212.---The Incarnation of the Son of God is God’s greatest work, Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 245.---Its sublimity and incomprehensibility, ibid., 219.---The twofold coming of Christ, Rabbi Samuel, CXLIX, 345.---Christ’s true birth is described, Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 190; explained, ibid., 200.---The three births of Christ, Thomas the Cistercian, CCVI, 128.---The place of the Nativity, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 112; Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 235; its fruit, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 87; St. Thomas the Cistercian, CCVI, 358.---Its circumstances, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 122; Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 235.---Its wonderful effects, Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXIX, 123, 446, 450, 663; LXX, 136.---God became man so that man might become God, St. Jerome, XXX, 220.---He was born in the flesh so that we might be reborn of the Spirit, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 198.---The Incarnation of the Son of God made us his brothers and adopted sons of God the Father, Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 116.---He willed to be born at the end of the year, in order to show that he came in the last age of the world, Sicard, CCXIII, 218.---The birth of Jesus is an example of humility and gentleness, Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 244.---Born at night, he teaches that display is to be avoided; born in troublesome winter, he teaches that hardships are to be chosen, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 123.---The remedies brought by the Nativity, ibid., 100.---What does Christ’s Nativity require of us? Aelred, CLXXXIV, 856.---All who sleep lose Christ; those who watch find him, St. Ambrose, XVII, 606, 608, 615.---Since human speech is inadequate to magnify God in so great a festival, one must have recourse to the proclamations of the angels, St. Ambrose, XVII, 612.---It is to be celebrated with joy, Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXX, 832.---No one ought to be excluded from the joy of the Nativity, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 190.---The Nativity is to be celebrated with spiritual, not carnal, joy, ibid., 199.---With what great joy the mystery of the Christ being born should be received, ibid., 221.---Christ’s Nativity from the Virgin is the cause of our exultation, Rupert the abbot, CLXVIII, 233.

The feast of the Nativity was established in antiquity, St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 648, 649, 922; Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 567; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 1686.---It was received in Gaul in antiquity, Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 169.

The Nativity of the Lord is to be kept as a holiday, Adalhard, CV, 544; Hetto, ibid., 764; Rodulf, CXIX, 717; Regino, CXXXII, 265; Flodoard, CXXXV, 409; Anonymous, CXXXVIII, 624; St. Ivo, CLXI, 266, 267. Four days are to be kept as holidays at the Nativity, Rodulf, CXIX, 717; Walter, ibid., 740; Guigo, CLIII, 733. Eight days, eleventh-century diplomas, CLI, 1194.---Christmas, a universal feast, Beleth, CCII, 18.---It is reckoned among the principal feasts, Udalric, CXLIX, 691; Lanfranc, CL, 473.---It has a Vigil, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 567; St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 235 (n.); John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 83, 84; Rupert, CLXX, 68; Udalric, CXLIX, 691.---It is to be celebrated with fasting, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 800.---Prostration at the reading of the Martyrology on the Vigil of the Nativity, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 110; Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 201.---It has a fast, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 567; St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 235 (n.).---A fast before the Nativity is prescribed, Rabanus Maurus, CCVII, 334.---It was received and observed by the Roman Church in antiquity, Pope Nicholas, CXIX, 981.---It has an Octave, St. Protadius, LXXX, 422; St. Chrodegang, LXXXIX, 1074.---Fasting is excluded in the Octave of the Nativity, Peter de Honestis, CLXIII, 721.---The Octave of the Nativity is one of veneration, Beleth, CCII, 78.---During the Octave of the Nativity the Carthusians do not perform the office of the dead unless the body is present, Guigo, CLIII, 656.

The Nativity of the Lord is to be celebrated only in cities and parishes, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 411; St. Ivo, CLXI, 266; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1783.---Abstinence from meat for four weeks before Christmas is prescribed, Rather, CXXXVI, 565.---If the Lord’s Nativity falls on Friday, it is permitted to eat meat, Pope Nicholas, CXIX, 981.---To fast on Christmas Day smacks of heresy, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 894.---Whoever does not truly honour Christ’s birth according to the flesh is a heretic, ibid., 410.---The Priscillianists, who fast at the Lord’s Nativity, are condemned, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 160.---From Christmas to the Circumcision, fasting was relaxed by the holy Fathers, St. Benedict, CIII, [Col. 0476] 1146.---Before Christmas, abstinence from wives is required, Regino, CXXXII, 249.---Baptism was once celebrated on Christmas, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 390 (n.); Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 314.---A miracle at the baptistery of St. Marcellinus, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 390 (n.).---No baptisms are to be performed at Christmas, Pope Siricius, XIII, 1134.---All the faithful ought to communicate, ibid.; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 266; Pope Leo IV, CXV, 681; Regino, CXXXII, 189, 227; Atto, CXXXIV, 42; Udalric, CXXXV, 1073; Rather, CXXXVI, 562; St. Ivo, CLXI, 168; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1738.---One who does not communicate is not to be regarded as Catholic, Egbert, Bishop of York, LXXXIX, 385.---He must do penance for twenty days on bread and water, Burchard, CXL, 963.---Incense is to be burned before the altar for nine days before the Lord’s Nativity, John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 41, 86, 160.---Antiphons eight days before the Lord’s Nativity, ibid., 123, 159, 184.---Formerly there was one Mass on Christmas in the Gallican order, Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 170.---The Masses at the Nativity, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 29, 30, 31;
