Alcuin, CI, 1175; Anonymous, CLI, 836; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 441, 877; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1217; Peter Cantor, CCV, 100; Sicard, CCXIII, 221.---The three Masses were not celebrated in the same church or by the same priest, Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 173, 174.---By three different priests, John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 41, 86, 160.---Formerly, in the Church of Lyons, all three Masses belonged to the archbishop, Ancient Statutes, CXCIX, 1094.---Three Masses are offered to God as Creator, Redeemer, and Rewarder, Godfrey the abbot, CLXXIV, 45.---The three Masses signify three times:

> The preceding night, the following dawn, the highest daylight . . .  
> Night, dawn, day; shadow, figure, God,

Sicard, CCXIII, 221–225.---The mystery in the order of the Masses, Peter Lombard, CXCI, 401.---In the first, the eternal generation is sung; in the second, the promise of the coming; in the third, the fulfilment of the promise, ibid.---Two Masses are celebrated at night because of the two Nativities, Rupert, CLXX, 75, 76.---The Night Mass was instituted by Pope Telesphorus, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 29; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 344; Ado, CXXIII, 209; Anastasius, CXXVII, 1175; Gilbert, CXXXIX, 537; ninth-century liturgical monument, CLI, 836; Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 200; Sicard, CCXIII, 221–223.---At other times Mass is not to be celebrated before the third hour of the day, St. Ivo, CLXI, 175; Gratian, CLXXVII, 1721.---On the night of the Nativity, *Gloria in Excelsis* was sung solemnly, John the Archbishop, CXLVII, 161.---On the Lord’s night, hymns and sacred mysteries, Anonymous, LXXIII, 611.---The Christmas Matins were celebrated, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 333.---At the first Nativity all bells are rung, John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 40, 53, 58, 161.---A procession after Terce, ibid., 41, 162.---The episcopal blessing at Mass, ibid., 154. At the Nativity the *Credo* is sung, ibid., 38.---On the first day of the Lord’s Nativity, Lanfranc, CL, 481.---The solemnity of the Nativity among the Carthusians, Guigo, CLIII, 651, 656, 666, 733.---Within the Octave the full office is to be celebrated and there are two meals, St. Chrodegang, LXXXIX, 1089.---At the Nativity the bishop is to provide a meal for the clergy in his own house, ibid., 1074.---The Archbishops of Rouen made certain distributions, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 1179.---At Christmas the bishops of Gaul sent *eulogiae* [blessed gifts] to one another or to the king himself, St. Protadius, LXXX, 594; Marculf the monk, LXXXVII, 752, 753.---At Christmas the king’s peace lasts eight days, eleventh-century diplomas, CLI, 1194.---The court of kings, St. Ivo, CLXII, 328.---Permission to use the pallium, Heribert, CXLI, 1138.---Ordeals and oaths prohibited, Adrevald, CXXIV, 1077; eleventh-century diplomas, CLI, 1175. The year begun from the Lord’s Nativity, Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 347.---The Lord’s birthday is celebrated in military camps, Einhard, CIV, 421, 422; even during war, ibid., 429, 435, 437, 440, 441, 444, 445, 448, 449, 452, 453, 457, 465, 469.---Baldwin celebrates Christmas at Jerusalem, William, CLXXIX, 1328.---He is crowned at Bethlehem on Christmas Day, ibid., 1332.---Charlemagne was crowned by Pope Leo on Christmas Day, Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 225.---The Lord’s Nativity: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 29, 30, 31; St. Protadius, LXXX, 422; Taio, ibid., 775; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXV, 183; LXXXVI, 114; Alcuin, CI, 1173; Einhard, CIV, 958; Adalhard, CV, 537; Hetto, ibid., 1159, 1221; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 754; CX, 1186; Wandalbert, CXXI, 62; Ratramnus, ibid., 81; Ado, CXXIII, 177, 203; Usuard, CXXIV, 835; Calendars and Martyrologies, CXXXVIII, 1188, 1194, 1204, 1210, 1257, 1264, 1279; John the Archbishop, CXLVII, 40; Udalric, CXLIX, 691; Lanfranc, CL, 448; eleventh-century liturgical monuments, CLI, 1004; Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 984; Stephen the abbot, CLXVII, 1387; Rupert the abbot, CLXX, 68, 75; Honorius, CLXXII, 644, 729, 733, 780, 797, 807, 815; Godfrey the abbot, CLXXIV, 656, 659, 663; Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 17; Ernald the abbot, CLXXXIX, 1615; Peter [Col. 0477] Comestor, CXCVIII, 1537; Beleth, CCII, 75; Ermengand, CCIV, 1243; Alan of Lille, CCX, 232, 234; St. Sicard, CCXIII, 218, 226.

## CHAPTER II.—On the Circumcision of the Lord

The Kalends of January were polluted by various superstitions of the nations, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 609; Alcuin, CI, 1176.---Formerly Christians were subject to the superstitions of pagans, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 291 (n.).---The Feast of Fools, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 1168, 1173.---A public fast on the Kalends of January was prescribed throughout all churches, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2002, 2004; St. Benedict, CIII, 1141.---Because of the error of the gentiles, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 774.---And their profanation, St. Alcuin, CI, 1177.---Whoever wishes to make sport with the devil will not be able to rejoice with Christ, St. Ambrose, XVII, 617, 618; St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 610, 611.---So that no one may presume to observe the Kalends of January or lead dances, Atto, CXXXIV, 43.---On this day a Mass is assigned to prohibit idolatry, St. Gregory the Great, LXXXVIII, 291 (n.).

The feast of the Circumcision coincides with the eighth day of the Lord’s Nativity, St. Gregory the Great, LXXXVIII, 291 (n.); Rabanus Maurus, CX, 1121, 1122.---At the Circumcision two feasts coincide: that of the Mother who gave birth and that of the Birth, on account of the Octave, Beleth, CCII, 78.---The mystery of the Circumcision, Alan of Lille, CCX, 236.---Christ did not reject circumcision so that we might be circumcised in spirit, Alcuin, CI, 1176.---He accepted the legal observances in order to free us from them, Hildebert, CLXXI, 399.---Christ’s Circumcision explained, St. Ivo, CLXII, 571.---Christ’s Circumcision proves the reality of his assumed humanity, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 132.---Christ’s humility in the Circumcision, ibid., 131.---In it he teaches us something to love, something to admire, and something to imitate, ibid., 136.---Circumcision of the heart is better than circumcision [Col. 0478] of the flesh, Godfrey the abbot, CLXXIV, 444.---Baptism succeeded circumcision, Alan of Lille, CCX, 348.---The ancient celebration of the Circumcision, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 291.---About the middle of the seventh century it was included, under the laws of the Visigoths, among the feasts on which legal business ceased, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXI, 478.

The solemnity of the Circumcision among the Carthusians, Guigo, CLIII, 733.---Among the monks of Cluny, when Mass is finished, all the bells are rung, Udalric, CXLIX, 655.---The *Credo* is said at the principal Mass, Lanfranc, CL, 481.---On the day of the Circumcision, the Archbishops of Rouen made certain distributions, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 1179.---The Circumcision is to be kept as a holiday, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1781.---On the Kalends of January in the Octave of the Lord: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 36; Alcuin, CI, 1176, 1177; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 1121, 1122; Wandalbert, CXXI, 585; the Martyrologies of Ado, CXXIII, 145, 205; of Usuard, ibid., 601; of Notker, CXXXI, 1029; ancient calendars and martyrologies, CXXXVIII, 1185, 1193, 1203, 1209, 1257, 1265; Udalric, CXLIX, 693; eleventh-century liturgical monuments, CLI, 1007; Stephen, CLXVI, 1388; Honorius, CLXXII, 647, 839.

On the Circumcision: St. Jerome, XXX, 437; Flodoard, CXXXV, 442; St. Protadius, LXXX, 411; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXV, 217; LXXXVI, 139; Alcuin, CI, 1176; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 1121, 1122; Lanfranc, CL, 451; Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 987; Honorius, CLXXII, 797; Ernald the abbot, CLXXXIX, 1621; Beleth, CCII, 78.

## CHAPTER III.—On the Epiphany of the Lord

Epiphany is so called, that is, appearance or manifestation, Hildebert, CLXXI, 401; Alcuin, CI, 1178.---Theophany, ibid., 413.---The day of lights, Guerric the abbot, CLXXXV, 51.---The day of manifestations, which are read to have occurred on the same day, though in different years, Beleth, CCII, 79.---Epiphany, the appearance of God; the sacred day of the Epiphany, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 292 (n.).---Christ’s first Epiphany, his manifestation in the world, St. Ambrose, XVII, 619, 620; St. Philastrius, XII, 1273.---He appears not so much to human eyes as for salvation, St. Ambrose, XVII, 619, 620.---The Epiphany is observed annually for human remembrance, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 614, 615.---It is celebrated in January according to ancient custom, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 293 (n.), 649.---The day of the Epiphany and that of the Nativity are not the same, St. Jerome, XXXI, 18, 19.---Although in Egypt it is celebrated on the same day, Cassian, XLIX, 820, 821.---The feast of the Epiphany is greater than that of Christ’s Nativity, Hildebert, CLXXI, 415.---This most sacred solemnity contains many mysteries within itself, Alcuin, CI, 1178.

Apostolic men marked the day of the Epiphany with festal solemnity, because on it the Saviour was revealed by a star, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 762; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 344.---A day renowned for three reasons, St. Ivo, CLXII, 573.---Adorned by three miracles, Sicard, CCXIII, 235.---It is one solemnity of Christ’s threefold manifestation, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 620; Guerric the abbot, CLXXXV, 58.---It reveals in three ways God made man, ibid., 611, 620.---There are four feasts on one day, Beleth, CCII, 79.---On it the Magi confess God by their gifts; on it Christ changes water into wine and is baptized in the Jordan, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 620 and following; St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 407, 707; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXII, 250.---Christ appeared to the Magi a few days after his birth, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 149.---A threefold manifestation on one day, ibid., 147, 148.---In the first he became known as true man, in the second as Son of God, in the third as true God, ibid., 147, 151.---Christ was baptized on the same day on which he was adored by the Magi, ibid., 145.---There are three Gospels of this feast: one concerning baptism, the second concerning the Magi, the third concerning the Wedding, Beleth, CCII, 80.---Christ, being born, wishes to be acknowledged by all, [Col. 0479] St. Leo, LIV, 234.---The star represents Grace, the Magi all nations, Herod the pagans, and the slain infants the martyrs; this feast is present in all times, ibid., 260.---Christ’s baptism is the Christian’s Nativity, Hildebert, CLXXI, 415.---The Epiphany is the Nativity of Christians, Guerric the abbot, CLXXXV, 58.---By changing water into wine Christ showed the mystery and pattern of the future resurrection, St. Ambrose, XVII, 619, 620.---The manifestation of the Trinity in Christ’s baptism, ibid., 623, 624.

The three Magi were inwardly illumined, Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 394.---By their gifts they attest their faith, St. Leo, LIV, 234.---The calling of the Magi is the beginning of our calling, ibid., 237, 240; Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 394.---Each person ought to emulate the gifts of the Magi, St. Leo, LIV, 237.---This feast is to be celebrated with thanksgiving, ibid., 240.

The feast of the Epiphany was established in antiquity, St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 648.---It was received in Gaul in antiquity, Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 169, 170.---It is to be kept as a holiday: St. Philastrius, XII, 1273; St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 339 (n.); Adalhard, CV, 537, 538; Hetto, ibid., 764; Rodulf, CXIX, 717; Walter, ibid., 740; Regino, CXXXII, 265; Flodoard, CXXXV, 408; John XIII, ibid., 977; St. Chrodegang, LXXXIX, 1074, 1089; Anonymous, CXXXVIII, 624, 625; St. Ivo, CLXI, 266.---It is to be celebrated only in cities and parishes, ibid.---It is reckoned among the principal solemnities, Lanfranc, CL, 475.---And is celebrated, Udalric, CXLIX, 655.---It lacks an invitatory, John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 42, 89, 164.---“Come, let us exult” (*Venite, exsultemus*) was sung in the third nocturn, ibid., 42, 189.---The *Credo* is sung at the principal Mass, Lanfranc, CL, 481.---A procession is held, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 319, 325; John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 135.---On Epiphany the beginning of Lent is announced, Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 178.---Easter is announced, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 947; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 367.---Water was blessed, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 293 (n.).---A veil was imposed upon virgins, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 943.---On the Vigil of Epiphany, a sermon concerning the Innocents slain by Herod, Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 432.---Herod announces to the world that Christ is born and tries to take him away, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 237.---No baptisms are to be performed on Epiphany, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 281; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 165; Alcuin, CI, 1178, 1236; St. Ivo, CLXI, 79, 81; Rupert, CLXX, 84.---In some places solemn baptism was conferred, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 389, 723.---At Epiphany the baptistery in the city of the Coeanenses sweats, Anonymous, LXXIV, 237.---Fasting is not permitted on Epiphany, St. Benedict, CIII, 1146.---Within the Octave of Epiphany, Peter de Honestis, CLXIII, 721.---If Epiphany falls on Friday, it is permitted to eat meat, Pope Nicholas, CXIX, 981.---Abstinence from wives and from marriage celebrations, Pope St. Eutychian, V, 166.---Abstinence from judicial proceedings, Anonymous, CXXXVIII, 854.---How the Carthusians celebrate Epiphany, Guigo, CLIII, 733, 1145.---Evagrius communicated on the feast of Epiphany, from the *Lives of the Fathers*, LXXIII, 1184.---The Archbishops of Rouen made certain distributions, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 1179.

On Epiphany: Ancient Calendar, XIII, 676; St. Jerome, XXX, 437; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 38, 40; St. Protadius, LXXX, 412; Isidore Mercator, LXXXV, 230; LXXXVI, 175; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 18, 1124; Alcuin, CI, 1178; Amalarius, CV, 1226, 1275, 1278; Christian Druthmar, CVI, 1279; Wandalbert, CXXI, 585; Ado, CXXIII, 145, 211; Usuard, ibid., 619; Notker, CXXXI, 1032; ancient calendars and martyrologies, CXXXVIII, 1185, 1193, 1203, 1210, 1257, 1265; Udalric, CXLIX, 654, 693; Lanfranc, CL, 191; eleventh-century liturgical monuments, CLI, 1008; St. Ivo, CLXII, 584; Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 989, 992; Rupert the abbot, CLXX, 84; Honorius, CLXXII, 647, 731, 781, 797, 843; Sicard, CCXIII, 235.

## CHAPTER VI.—On the Resurrection of the Lord

*Pascha* is a Hebrew, not a Greek, name, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 842; XXXVII, 1609, 1709; Eugyppius, LXII, 752; Alcuin, C, 923; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 351; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1399.---It took its name from *Phase*, St. Jerome, XXV, 1229; XXVI, 190; Beleth, CCII, 118.---It is called a passing-over, St. Ambrose, XVII, 672; St. Augustine, XXXVI, 785; St. Leo, LIV, 608; St. Fulgentius, LXV, 741; Alcuin, C, 923; St. Paschasius Ratbertus, CXX, 1345; St. Bruno, CLIII, 147; Godfrey the abbot, CLXXIV, 170; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 280; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1572; Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 1060.---Because Christ passed from death to life, Candidus, CVI, 60, 61; Rather, CXXXVI, 555.---Because through this mystery we pass from worse things to better, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 515; Bede the Venerable, XCIII, 370.---*Pascha* is Hebrew *Phase*, Greek *Pascha*, and Latin *transitus* [“passing-over”], Honorius, CLXXII, 676.---*Pascha* signifies not suffering but passing-over, St. Jerome, XXIV, 356; Bede the Venerable, XCIV, 536; Beleth, CCII, 117.---This name *Pascha* was formed by divine design from Greek πάσχειν (*paschein*, “to suffer”) and Hebrew *Phase* (“passing-over”), since in the Lord’s Passion there was his passing-over, Beleth, CCII, 118; Sicard, CCXIII, 343.---Passover is the passage of souls from vices to virtue, St. Ambrose, XIV, 129; XVI, 907.---The very day of the Resurrection is called Easter, St. Philastrius, XII, 1278; Beleth, CCII, 117, 118; Sicard, CCXIII, 310.

It was prefigured by the Passover of the Jews, Tertullian, I, 1294; II, 460; St. Ambrose, XVI, 1034, 1035; St. Augustine, XXXV, 1758; XLI, 322; St. Isidore, LXXXIII, 766; Bede the Venerable, XCIV, 535; Alcuin, C, 904; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 350.---The handing down of Passover from the ancient Jews is noted, Rupert, CLXVIII, 1531.---The observance of the Jewish Passover is full of spiritual types, St. Gaudentius, XX, 867.---A type of Pentecost in the old law, Cassian, XLIX, 1194.---The Jewish Passover, Pentecost, and Feast of Tabernacles (*Scenopegia*) signified the threefold state of the Christian religion: namely, repentance, righteousness, and glory, Peter Lombard, CXCI, 970.---The final Jewish Passover, Rupert, CXLIX, 647.---That ancient feast of the Jewish people was changed by the solemnity of this day, St. Jerome, XXX, 225.---The mystical Passover was abolished by the immolation of Christ, the true Paschal Lamb, Gezo the abbot, CXXXVII, 398.---When Christ rose from the dead, the solemnities of the Jews were fulfilled, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 627.---Christ ate the Passover by which his coming Passion was signified before he suffered voluntarily, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 431.---At the same supper Christ ate the Jewish Passover and instituted ours, ibid.

Our Passover is distinguished from the Jewish Passover, Eugyppius [Col. 0481] the abbot, LXII, 757.---The old Passover was celebrated with unleavened bread, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 541, 543; Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 264.---It is a figure of ours, ibid.; Godfrey, CLXXIV, 269.---The new Passover is to be celebrated with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth, Julius Hilarianus, XIII, 1106; St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 650; Rupert, CLXX, 207; Richard, CXCVI, 264.---The Passover of the Jews is in shadow; ours is in light, Alcuin, C, 904.---At Passover the Jews celebrated their own deliverance, Christians their own Redemption, Beleth, CCII, 135.---The Paschal solemnity does not join old things to new, but delights in the infancy of new regeneration, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 406, 407.---The Paschal solemnity is not joined to Jewish antiquity, ibid., 650.---On it the Lamb is sacrificed; on it Christ is born and transformed into complete joy and glory, ibid., 651.---The true Passover of Christians, Eugyppius the abbot, LXII, 830.---The most true Passover celebrated in Christ, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 844.---The true Passover: Christ’s immolation, ibid., XXXV, 1785.---The Paschal Lamb is eaten in one Church, ibid., XL, 1196, 1201.---Christ is our Passover, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1177.---Out of so many Jewish feasts Christ chose the day of Passover; Christ, the destroyer of the law, also desired to observe Passover, Tertullian, II, 460.---The Jewish Paschal rite compared with the Christian Passover, Hildebert, CLXXI, 475.---The rationale for celebrating Passover, Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 501.---The agreement of the Old and New Testaments concerning the celebration of Passover, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 217, 218; Ceolfrid, LXXXIX, 350.---Paschal time is prescribed in four ways in the Old Testament, Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 639–643.---In what month and on what day of the month Christ is believed to have been crucified, and where his resurrection was first celebrated: this was variously reported by the Fathers, ibid., CVII, 704, 721.---The apostles could establish nothing concerning how Passover ought to be observed; they celebrated Passover on the fourteenth moon of March, Bede the Venerable, XC, 607.---Doubt concerning the celebration of Passover, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 564.---The question of the day of Passover, St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 565.---It was debated long and extensively, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 946.---It was not celebrated at the same time by everyone, St. Cyprian, III, 1159; Eusebius Pamphilus, VIII, 50; Julius Hilarianus, XIII, 1106; St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 403; Peter Lombard, CXCII, 505.---When it is celebrated by Greeks and Latins, Alcuin, CI, 984.---The bishops of Asia celebrated with the Jews on the fourteenth moon, St. Jerome, XXIII, 657; the Tessaracaedecatites, St. Augustine, XLII, 31; the Quartodecimans, St. Leo, LVI, 715.---In determining the day of Passover, the Scots differed from the Church, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 951–953.---St. Leo writes to St. Cyril and Paschasius concerning the determination of Easter Day, St. Leo, LIV, 606.---The controversy, ibid., 601, 602.---The Gallican churches adopted the Paschal cycle of Anatolius, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 952.

Pascha ought to be celebrated by all on the same day: Council of Arles, St. Augustine, XLIII, 787; Council of Antioch, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 125; First Council of Orléans, ibid., 238; Fourth Council of Carthage, ibid., 204; St. Leo, LIV, 1079; LVI, 886; Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 372; St. Ivo, CLXI, 265, 267.—The Council of Nicaea decreed that all Christians should observe Easter at one and the same time: St. Ambrose, XVI, 1027; Gennadius, LVIII, 1000, 1053; Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 277.—This Nicene rule concerning the celebration of Easter was established by the illumination of the Holy Spirit: Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 19.

Easter is to be celebrated in the first month: Tertullian, II, 973; St. Ambrose, XVI, 1032; Gaudentius, bishop, XX, 834, 844; Ceolfrid, LXXXIX, 350; Bede the Venerable, XC, 512; Theodore, archbishop, XCIX, 952; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 714, 722, 725; CVIII, 895; St. Abbo, CXXXIX, 538; St. Ivo, CLXI, 190.—Because it signifies newness of life: St. Augustine, XXXIII, 206, 208.

There is authority for its sometimes being deferred to the second month: St. Ambrose, XVI, 1033; Gaudentius, XX, 846, 847; St. Augustine, XXXIV, 722; Ratbert, CXX, 1342.—Six years before, Easter was celebrated on 21 April: St. Ambrose, XVI, 1033; on 23 April: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 600; on 24 April through error: ibid., 605.—In the year 444, on 26 March: St. Leo, LIV, 601, 602.—In the year 457, on 29 March: Victor, LXVIII, 943.

After the vernal equinox: St. Augustine, XLII, 1221; Gennadius of Marseilles, LVIII, 1000, 1053; Dionysius, LXVII, 142, 148; St. Fulgentius, LXXXVIII, 840; Ceolfrid, LXXXIX, 350; Bede the Venerable, XC, 512; Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 15, 121, 838; St. Ivo, CLXI, 190.—Not before the full moon which first occurs after the vernal equinox: St. Augustine, XLII, 1221; Rupert, CLXX, 169.

The third week of the first month: Ceolfrid, LXXXIX, 350; Bede the Venerable, XC, 512; St. Ivo, CLXI, 190.—Christians celebrate Easter according to the computation of sun and moon: St. Augustine, XXXIII, 209. [Col. 0482]

Neither on the fourteenth lunar day nor after the twenty-first: Julius Hilarianus, XIII, 1106, 1114; St. Ambrose, XVI, 510, 1032, 1398; Gaudentius, XX, 847; Eugyppius, LXXII, 757; Bede the Venerable, XC, 510, 607, 609, 610; XCIV, 675, 676, 682; Theodore, archbishop, XCIX, 952; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 713, 714, 720, 722, 725; CVIII, 501; Anonymous, CXXIX, 1299; Abbo, CXXXIX, 538; Humbert, CXLIII, 935; St. Ivo, CLXI, 190; Rupert, CLXVIII, 1533.

It must not be celebrated with the Jews: Tertullian, II, 72; St. Jerome, XXII, 1222; St. Ivo, LVI, 706; Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 22, 142, 148, 458, 459; St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 564; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 125; Fulgentius Ferrandus, LXXXVIII, 822; Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 15, 121, 838.—Our Easter does not coincide with the Jews’ day: St. Augustine, XLII, 503.—Pope Victor prohibited Easter from being celebrated with the Jews: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 952.—Pope John IV reproved certain Christians of Scotland for celebrating Easter with the Jews: St. Protadius, LXXX, 601.—The Church anathematizes those who violate this law: St. Jerome, XXII, 1222; excommunicates them: Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 22, 458, 459; rejects them: ibid., 142, 148; St. Leo the Great, LVI, 706.

The Easter feast must be celebrated only on Sunday: St. Ambrose, XVI, 1029, 1030; St. Augustine, XXXIII, 209, 211; Ceolfrid, LXXXIX, 350; Bede the Venerable, XC, 510, 512; Theodore, archbishop, XCIX, 952; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 713, 720; Helperich, CXXXVII, 43; St. Ivo, CLXI, 190, 265, 267.—The Lord’s resurrection occurred on the first day of the week: St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 172, 572; St. Anselm, CLVIII, 62; Rupert, CLXX, 198.—Christ rose on the same day on which he had created the world: St. Gaudentius, XX, 845.—The day of the resurrection must be observed: St. Ambrose, XVI, 996, 1029, 1030.—Pope Victor decreed that Easter be celebrated on Sunday: St. Abbo, CXXXIX, 538; likewise Pope Pius: Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVII, 141, 1214; St. Abbo, CXXXIX, 537; Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 200; likewise Eleutherius: Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVII, 1279.

The Easter day is to be announced by a council: Dionysius Exiguus, LXXVII, 205.—Notice of the Paschal celebration and of the convoking of a council must be given: Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 354.—It is to be determined by provincial councils: ibid., 571.—Before Epiphany, the announcement of Easter is to be considered among bishops: Fourth Council of Toledo, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 367.—The day of Easter is to be communicated to all by a subscribed formal letter: Fifth Council of Carthage, ibid., 210.—Each year Easter is to be announced beforehand by the metropolitan bishop: Second Council of Braga, ibid., 575.—Among the Spaniards, metropolitan bishops announce it to the clergy: Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 465.—The Paschal day was determined through letters of the bishop of Alexandria: Cassian, XLIX, 820, 821; St. Leo, LIV, 1055, 1071.—The announcement was entrusted to the Roman pontiff: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 947.—This announcement was made on Epiphany: ibid.—The Paschal day was proclaimed to all Western Christians by the supreme pontiff: St. Leo, LIV, 1110.—In Sardinia the announcement belonged to the metropolitan: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 946, 947.—The Easter day is to be received from the Church of Carthage: St. Leo the Great, LVI, 420; Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 196; Fulgentius Ferrandus, LXXXVIII, 830.—Among Africans, the Paschal day was determined by a synod and publicized through envoys sent by the council: Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 336.—The Easter day of the year 417 was declared by a miracle: St. Leo, LIV, 609.—Constantine wrote a letter to Eusebius concerning the Paschal feast: Eusebius, VIII, 79.—After the Council of Nicaea, he congratulated the Church on its agreement in celebrating Easter: ibid., 501.—Three Paschal letters of Theophilus of Alexandria, for the years 401, 402, and 403, translated by Jerome: St. Jerome, XXII, 773, 792, 813.—Victor, bishop of the city of Rome, Narcissus of Jerusalem, Polycrates, Irenaeus, and Bacchylus wrote on this question: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 566.—The Paschal cycle, first composed by Hippolytus and finally perfected by the most blessed Cyril: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 125.—Authors on the Paschal computation: Hippolytus, Eusebius, Theophilus, and Prosper; after them Victorinus treated the matter more diligently: St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 632.—Under Pope Benedict, Dionysius the abbot composed the Paschal calculation by remarkable reasoning: Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 215.—By the Paschal limit the other limits are found: Helperich, CXXXVII, 45.

Praise of the Easter day: St. Augustine, XXXV, 2368.—The Apostle and the Gospels said that the feast of Easter ought to be honoured: Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXIX, 1053.—A day foretold by the prophet Jeremiah: Tertullian, I, 1222.—A day bearing the image of the Lord’s sacrament and discharging the obligations of the four seasons: Zeno, XI, 503, 506, 507, 508. [Col. 0483]—The day on which Christ rose: St. Philastrius, XII, 1273.—As it were the crown of feasts and a figure of attaining and bringing to completion perfection and blessedness: ibid., 1275.—The solemnities of Easter were held to be exceedingly great: St. Cyprian, IV, 348.—The Lord’s feasts express their causes through their own names: by rising, he gave the day its name of resurrection: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 613.—Easter alone should be called the great day: St. Leo the Great, LIV, 498.—The greatest of feasts: ibid., 294, 297, 300, 305, 944, 1100.—The solemnity of solemnities: St. Gregory the Great, 1177; St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2068; Rupert, abbot, CLXX, 193.—The shadow of the coming solemnity: ibid., 1203.—The first of all feasts: St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXII, 250.—A day loftier than all others, brighter than all, rightly called the solemnity of solemnities: Rabanus Maurus, CX, 34, 35.—The solemnities of Easter and Pentecost are the greatest of all feasts: ibid., CXI, 307.—A feast reaching the superlative degree: Udalric, CXLIX, 656; Lanfranc, CL, 473.—A most celebrated day: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 29.—It is the greatest of feasts and full of consolation: Godefrid, CLXXIV, 186.—This solemnity is so great that, by antonomasia and excellence, it is called “the solemnity of solemnities”: Beleth, CCII, 119.—Honorific epithets of Easter: St. Benedict, CIII, 1196.—The feast of Easter: St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 387, 395, 406, 549, 602, 963, 981.—Holy: ibid., 709, 1095.—The feast of the Resurrection: ibid., 302, 502, 566.—A magnificent and desirable feast: ibid., 916.—Sunday is named from the Lord’s resurrection: ibid., 173; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 476 note.—The Easter feast-day is universal among Christians: *From the Lives of the Fathers*, LXXIII, 233.—The solemnity of the Easter day: Alcuin, CI, 1221; Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 501.—A venerable feast: Einhard, CIV, 958.—Christ’s resurrection made it illustrious: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 1694, 1696.—The day of resurrection is the eighth day, in which are our Sabbath and rest: ibid., 1712.—Peter teaches Christ’s resurrection from the Psalms: ibid., 1673.—The apostles’ fear and silence from Easter until Pentecost: CLXX, 15.—The apostles saw Christ on the eighth day of Easter at Nazareth, in Mary’s house: ibid., 232.—The day of the Lord’s resurrection rejoices in a twofold gift: it is a solemnity of ineffable, inestimable, and infinite dignity: ibid., 154.—The mystery of Easter, at the full moon: ibid., 166.

The three chief reasons for the Easter solemnity: redemption of souls, resurrection of bodies, and the solemnity of baptism: ibid., 169.—Easter is understood in two senses: Alan of Lille, CCX, 367.—Mystical interpretation of Easter: ibid., 337.—The time before Easter signifies the tribulation in which we now are: St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1937.—Easter signifies the future life: ibid., 1938.—Eternal blessedness: Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 651.—The Easter season signifies the future time of rejoicing; the six weeks of Lent are the six ages of the world: ibid., 658.—From this solemnity comes an example of the future resurrection: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1177.—No one rightly celebrates Easter who still remains seated through negligence and sloth: St. Paschasius Ratbertus, CXX, 1345.—Those who celebrate Mass daily make Easter daily, that is, they eat the flesh of the Lamb: Ratherius, CXXXVI, 557.—Everyone keeps a solemn Easter for the Lord who strives to do what God commanded: ibid., 726.—Easter is a sacrifice: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1572.—This lawful Easter should be eaten very frequently with reverence: Gezo, abbot, CXXXVII, 398.—We celebrate the true Easter if we always maintain in life and conduct what is expressed by the mysteries of things and times: St. Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 590.—Easter, when *Alleluia* is sung, indicates the passage from toil to blessedness: Honorius, CLXXII, 651.—God’s pleasing Easter is the conversion of a human being: Godefrid, CLXXIV, 170.

How ancient the Easter feast is: St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 95, 649, 828.—Christians kept vigil throughout the night of Easter: Tertullian, I, 1294.—We celebrate the Lord’s resurrection in the morning: St. Cyprian, IV, 387.—Anciently received in Gaul: Gallican Liturgy, 169, 170.—The Paschal celebration is annual: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 171.—Easter is observed both sacramentally and in remembrance of the event that was done: XXXIII, 205.—The annual Paschal day does not return on the same date of the year, because of Sunday and the moon: St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 768; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 351; Honorius, CLXXII, 651.—It is to be celebrated only in cities and parishes: St. Ivo, CLXI, 266; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1783; Regino, CXXXII, 396.—How Christ’s resurrection benefited us: Peter Lombard, CXCII, 245.—It is our justification: ibid.—The Paschal feast makes people more fervent: St. Augustine, XLIII, 330.—When the Lord rose, his members received hope of resurrection: Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXX, 653.—Christ’s resurrection and ascension confirm within us hope of heavenly things: Godefrid, CLXXIV, 561.—Christ’s resurrection manifests his divinity: ibid., 879.—It excludes every doubt and distrust: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1314.—Christ’s resurrection prepares for the soul the grace of a twofold resurrection: Guerric, abbot, CLXXXV, 148.—The joy of the Lord’s resurrection: ibid., CLXXXIV, 736.—Pure faith in the resurrection belongs not to Gentiles or Jews, but to Christians: ibid., 168.—By whom Easter is to be celebrated: Alan of Lille, CCX, 337.

Sanctification of Easter: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 148, 149, 696.—The Easter day should be observed with the observance of a devout mind: St. Ambrose, XVI, 1027.—Whoever has celebrated the Lord’s Easter well here will be in everlasting light: ibid., 1398.—It must be celebrated in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth: Julius Hilarianus, XIII, 1106, 1144; St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 650.—The Lord’s Easter must be celebrated by those who are chaste and sanctified: St. Ambrose, XIV, 129; XVI, 907; St. Jerome, XXIII, 99.—Sins are to be abandoned and the practice of virtues begun, so that hearts may be prepared to celebrate Easter: St. Jerome, XXII, 789.—Hearts must be prepared by charity and purity to celebrate the Easter feast: St. Leo, LIV, 322.—Whoever desires to celebrate the solemnity of Paschal joy should eat the flesh of the Lamb roasted by fire, so as to understand that all things are dispensed through the patience of the Holy Spirit: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1179.—Virgins are veiled at Easter: St. Ambrose, XIV, 708; XVI, 348; XVII, 674.—On Low Sunday the veil was placed upon virgins: Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 943.—Consecration of a virgin on Easter Monday: Anonymous, CXXXVIII, 1094, 1104.

On the Easter day, those formerly bound in chains were customarily released: St. Ambrose, XVI, 996.—Persons accused were released by emperors: St. Leo, LIV, 271, 297, 539.

Nothing bloody is to be prescribed: St. Ambrose, XVI, 1027.—From Septuagesima until the Octave of Easter, marriages must be abstained from: St. Eutychian, V, 167; St. Ivo, CLXI, 616.—Intercourse with wives must be abstained from from Septuagesima until the Octaves of Easter have passed: St. Eutychian, V, 167.—On the octave of Easter: Ratherius, CXXXVI, 566.—During the solemnity: Beleth, CCII, 72.—Litigation must cease for fifteen days: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1201.—At Easter the king’s peace lasts eight days: eleventh-century diplomas, CLI, 1194.—At Easter they observed a solemn fast: St. Philastrius, XII, 1286; St. Augustine, XXXIII, 222; Rupert, CLXX, 169.—It is decreed for all priests that Lent be observed before the solemnity of Easter: Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1783. (See Lent.)—Paschal joy is enlarged also by the preceding fast: ibid.—Fasts are suspended from Easter to Pentecost: Tertullian, II, 79; St. Ambrose, XIV, 866; St. Augustine, XXXIII, 218; Cassian, XLIX, 1184, 1193, 1194; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 386; St. Benedict, abbot, CIII, 1037, 1146; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 734; Peter de Honestis, CLXIII, 721.—The Church prohibited fasting for forty days, because for forty days after the resurrection Christ associated with human beings: Hildebert, CLXXI, 579.—During Eastertide knees are not bent: Cassian, XLIX, 110, 111, 1184, 1193; St. Leo, LVI, 925; Burchard, CXL, 641; Rupert, CLXX, 211.—The Paschal days are a time of remission and indulgence: St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2075.—A season of joy: Tertullian, II, 80, 873; St. Ambrose, XIV, 866; XVI, 1034, 1035; St. Augustine, XXXIII, 218; Venantius Fortunatus, LXXXVIII, 130; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 720.—They celebrated fifty days of Easter: St. Ambrose, XV, 1773.—In accordance with the ordinances of their elders, the faithful celebrated the feast of Easter, the festival of public salvation, joyfully and exultantly: ibid., XVI, 1034, 1035.—Easter is a sign of exultation and joy in heaven and on earth: St. Jerome, XXX, 215.—The season of the Resurrection is a time of joy for the heart of Jesus: Wolbero, CXCV, 1146.—From Easter to Pentecost is a forty-day season of joy: Beleth, CCII, 84.—The Sundays from Easter to the Ascension belong to the joy of the resurrection which the Lord promised would follow the sorrow of the Passion: Sicard, CCXIII, 364.—From Easter to Pentecost praise is offered to God and *Alleluia* is sung: St. Ambrose, XIV, 866; St. Benedict, LXVI, 452, 453, 454.—*Alleluia* must be sung by day and by night: Ratherius, CXXXVI, 734.—The responsory is not sung: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 454.—Easter week is celebrated *in albis*, “in white garments”: ibid., 453.—At the Easter solemnity the bishops of Gaul sent eulogiae, blessed gifts, to one another and to the king himself: St. Protadius, LXXX, 594; Marculf, monk, LXXXVII, 752, 753.—The court of kings at Easter: St. Ivo, CLXII, 328.

The faithful should prepare themselves for the Paschal solemnity: St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1801.—Easter must be prepared for the Lord on high, not below: Hildebert, CLXXI, 357.—As Easter approaches, temptations are accustomed to become more severe: St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1775.—At the conclusion of the Paschal solemnity, neophytes change their attire: ibid., 2075.—We must die with Christ in order to rise with Christ: St. Leo the Great, LIV, 382, 384, 392. [Col. 0485]—To neglect the Paschal feast is a very great evil: ibid., 383.—We ought to remain such as it is fitting to be found on the feast day: ibid., 275.—Christ’s resurrection requires from us a passage to a better life: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 383.—Confession is to be made at Easter: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 281.—One must approach a confessor at Easter even if one is conscious of no sin: Alan of Lille, CCX, 107, 298.—Communion is to be received: St. Eutychian, V, 167; St. Leo the Great, LIV, 305; St. Isidore, LXXXIV, 266; St. Egbert, LXXXIX, 350; St. Leo, CXV, 681; Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 189, 227; Udalric, CXXXV, 1073; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 719, 720, 722, 724; St. Ivo, CLXI, 167, 168; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1738; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 281.—Those who have not communicated are not to be reckoned among Catholics: St. Egbert, LXXXIX, 350; Atto, CXXXIV, 42.—They must do penance for twenty days on bread and water: Burchard, CXL, 963.—Baptized infants must receive communion on every day of the week: Anonymous, CXXXVIII, 1076.

Ceremonies of Easter: Alcuin, CI, 1221.—Rites: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 148, 149, 696.—The festival and order of prayers: Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 1077.

The Creed is to be recited publicly in all churches eight days before Easter: St. Ivo, CLXI, 114.—During the Paschal season the sacraments of the Creed were explained: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 358.

In celebrating Easter, the three days of the crucified, buried, and raised Christ must be observed: St. Augustine, XXXIII, 215.—On the vigil of Easter solemn baptism takes place: Tertullian, I, 1222; St. Eutychian, V, 166; Pope St. Siricius, XIII, 1188; St. Ambrose, XIV, 708; XVI, 348; XVII, 674; Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 284; St. Isidore, LXXXIV, 167, 183, 314; Fulgentius Ferrandus, LXXXVIII, 906; Hetto, CV, 764; Leo IV, CXV, 679; Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 328; Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 240, 241; Udalric, CXXXV, 1072; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 555, 556; Anonymous, CXXXVIII, 624; Burchard, CXL, 725, 729; John of Rouen, CXLVII, 272; St. Ivo, CLXI, 81, 82, 110; Rupert, CLXX, 84, 169; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1798, 1799.—In Thessaly baptism was performed only on the days of Easter: Ratramnus of Corbie, CXXI, 308.—At Rome the Easter baptism was formerly celebrated in the Basilica of St. Agnes: Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVIII, 185.—At the monastery of Blessed Martial, baptism is performed at Easter, and there slaves are granted freedom by their masters: Jordan, bishop of Limoges, CXLII, 1594.

Easter was formerly begun after Saturday evening: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 380 note.—Formerly there were three Masses at Easter: Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 173.—Rogations or processions everywhere at Easter: St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 1034, 1175.—Litanies at Mass: *Acts of Emperor St. Henry*, CXL, 54.—The Easter procession was fourfold: John, archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 54, 104.—At Lauds, before the crucifix, on the octave of Easter: ibid. Formerly, on Easter Day, the archbishop of Rouen gave the clergy the kiss of peace at Lauds: ibid., 104.—From the day of resurrection until Saturday in White, only three psalms at the nocturns and three lessons are read, according to ancient custom: Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1859.—Three nocturns during Eastertide: John of Rouen, CXLVII, 55, 107, 180.—During Eastertide the Office of the Dead is not to be celebrated except at a burial or anniversary: ibid., 37, 56, 191.—During the eight days of Easter the Creed is sung: ibid., 38.—At the principal Mass on the first day of the Lord’s resurrection: Lanfranc, CL, 481.—The Easter station at Rome is at St. Mary’s: Rupert, CLXX, 53, 204.—At Easter one *Alleluia* is sung, but two on Saturday: Alan of Lille, CCX, 209, 210.—The Easter solemnity among the Carthusians: Guigo, CLIII, 646, 653, 656, 666, 733.

The octave of Easter is the octave of reverence for Christ: Beleth, CCII, 78.—The Paschal days were formerly called eight holy solemn days, on which sermons were given daily to the people: St. Gaudentius, XX, 828, 829 note.—Easter week is to be kept as a holiday: Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 201, 283, 377, 378; St. Benedict, abbot, CIII, 1196; Ratramnus of Corbie, CXXI, 770; Anonymous, CXXXVIII, 832; Berno, abbot, CXLII, 1061; St. Ivo, CLXI, 266, 267.—During the Paschal days, the Lord’s resurrection was customarily recited according to the four Evangelists: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1107, 1126.—The Resurrection according to all the Evangelists is read in church during the seven days of the Easter octave: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 315, 546.—The solemnity of the Paschal octave: Rupert, CLXX, 218.—Why this sacred Paschal solemnity has an octave: ibid., 198.—At Pentecost there were two readings, one from the Apostle and the other from the Gospels, as on Sundays and Saturdays: Cassian, XLIX, 90.—The alms of prayer is to be paid on the fifteenth day after Easter: eleventh-century diplomas, CLI, 1174.

[Col. 0486] The Easter feast was celebrated most devoutly by Constantine the Great: Eusebius Pamphilus, VIII, 74.—With the greatest solemnity by monks: St. Jerome, XXIII, 92.—Attended with the greatest lukewarmness by a few Manichaeans: St. Augustine, XLII, 178.—Most devoutly by Louis I: Einhard, CIV, 967; St. Eulogius, CXV, 1377, 1378, 1381, 1390.—Celebration of Easter during a military expedition: Heribert, CXLI, 596, 598.—Sisinnius was baptized at Easter by Pope Clement together with 323 persons: Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 198.—At Easter the archbishops of Rouen made certain distributions to the chapter of Rouen: Peter of Blois, CCVII, 1179.—Markets held on Easter Day: Martin of León, CCIX, 899.

The year began at Easter: Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 405.—“Closed Easter,” or “the closing of Easter”: ibid., 200, 201.

The *anniversary Easter* appears to have been celebrated after Low Sunday: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 381 note, 775.—*Pascha annotinum* is the anniversary of the preceding Easter: Bede the Venerable, XCIV, 536.—It is called *Pascha annotinum* when someone annually celebrates the day on which he received baptism: Beleth, CCII, 88.

## CHAPTER VII.—On the Ascension

The Lord’s Ascension is celebrated on the fortieth day after the Resurrection: Anonymous, CXXXVIII, 624; St. Anselm, CLVIII, 729. It is celebrated because Christ is remembered to have ascended into heaven: St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 768; Alcuin, CI, 1225; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 353, 357.—Before he ascended, Christ accomplished all things: St. Leo the Great, LV, 38.—In the Ascension was completed the revelation of the sacraments written in the Law and the Prophets: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 628.—Christ ascended into heaven while the disciples looked on: ibid., 371; St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 173, 484, 1025.—Christ’s Ascension completes the other solemnities, manifests their fruit, and increases grace: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 309.—The Ascension was beneficial to the apostles and the whole Church: Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXX, 1104.—Christ’s Ascension is a pledge of ours: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1210.—Our security and earnest: ibid., XXXIX, 2081, 2082.—Our glorification: ibid., 2083; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 383.—It was delayed forty days in order to strengthen our faith: St. Leo the Great, LIV, 394, 395.—A cause of joy for us: ibid., 398; LV, 37; Rupert, CLXIX, 734; Guerric, abbot, CLXXXIV, 736.—It ought not to have been delayed: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1151.—Faith in it: ibid., 1163.—The effect of the Lord’s Ascension is desire for heaven: St. Leo the Great, LIV, 500.—We must ascend after Christ, namely in heart: St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2082.—Whoever wishes to share in Christ’s feasts should strive also to do what Christ does: Ratherius, CXXXVI, 743.—Christ’s resurrection and ascension confirm within us hope of heavenly things: Godefrid, abbot, CLXXIV, 561.—The Lord’s ascent is triumphant: St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 231; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 735.—The Ascension of the Son and the Assumption of the Mother are described in a similar style: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 713.—A twofold ascension commended by the Apostle: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 317. [Col. 0488]—The four stages of the Ascension: ibid., 740.—The Lord’s ascent is threefold: Guerric, abbot, CLXXXIV, 1146.—He ascended onto the gibbet of the cross, ascended to the triumph of resurrection, and ascended into heaven: Alan of Lille, CCX, 242.—The effects of this threefold ascent: ibid.—Christ ascended bodily into heaven: ibid., 321.—He ascended in order to teach the future life: Pope St. Damasus, XIII, 377.—In order to lead captivity captive: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 371; Alan of Lille, CCX, 242.—The feast of the Ascension is received by tradition: St. Augustine, XXXIII, 200.—Instituted in ancient times: St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 648.—And received in Gaul: Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 169, 170.—Ascension Day is to be kept as a holiday: Anonymous, CXXXVIII, 624; Udalric, CXLIX, 655; Lanfranc, CL, 475; St. Ivo, CLXI, 266.—It is to be celebrated only in cities and parishes: ibid.—The disciples offered Christ a procession on Ascension Day: Beleth, CCII, 20.—A procession at the Ascension in which an accused person is released: John, archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 110, 122.—Judicial proceedings are forbidden: Anonymous, CXXXVIII, 854.—At Mass the Creed is sung: Lanfranc, CL, 481.—The feast of the Ascension and the deposition of St. Leontius are celebrated on the same day: St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1208.—On Ascension Day in the Basilica of Lord Martin: St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 566.—The celebration of the Lord’s Ascension in the cathedral church of Rouen: John, archbishop, CXLVII, 57, 110.—Among the Cluniac monks: Udalric, CXLIX, 654.—Among the Carthusians: Guido, CLIII, 646, 733, 1145.—At the Ascension the archbishops of Rouen made certain distributions: Peter of Blois, CCVII, 1179.—St. Elizabeth sees the mysteries of the Ascension: Egbert, CXCV, 147.—The primitive Church observed Thursday in memory of the Ascension: Sicard, CCXIII, 374.—The octave of the Ascension extends to Pentecost: ibid., 375.

On the Lord’s Ascension: Tertullian, I, 1222; St. Philastrius, XII, 1273, 1286; St. Jerome, XXX, 508; St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 172, 325, 707; *From the Lives of the Fathers*, LXXIII, 467; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 108; St. Isidore, LXXXV, 598; LXXXVI, 651; Alcuin, CI, 1225; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 353; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 736; John, archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 57, 125; Samuel the Moroccan, CXLIX, 347; Guido, abbot, CL, 1213; eleventh-century liturgical monuments, CLI, 849; Goffrid, abbot, CLVII, 258; Stephen, CLXVI, 1407; Rupert, abbot, CLXX, 255; Honorius, CLXXII, 683, 700, 955; Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 60; Ernald, abbot, CLXXXIX, 1667; Sicard, CCXIII, 372; Innocent III, CCXVII, 409.—On the Lord’s threefold ascent: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 806.—On the joy and wonder of Blessed Mary at the Ascension of her Son: Amadeus, bishop of Lausanne, CLXXXVIII, 1331.

Sermons on the Ascension of the Lord: St Peter Chrysologus, LII, 432; St Leo the Great, LIV, 394, 396, 499; St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 623, 625, 627, 853; St Fulgentius, LXV, 914, 915; Atto, CXXXIV, 845; Rather, CXXXVI, 734, 740; Odilo, CXLII, 1011; Abbot Werner, CLVII, 952, 969, 972; St Ivo, CLXXII, 591; Bruno of Asti, CXLV, 1012, 1014; Heribert, CLXXI, 580, 583; Honorius, CLXXII, 1127; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 1200, 1114; Abelard, CLXXVIII, 495; St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 299, 301, 304, 309, 316; Abbot Guerric, CLXXXV, 153; Isaac, CXCIV, 1829; Abbot Aelred, CXCV, 283; Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1778; Peter of Celle, CCII, 785, 788, 791; Garnerius of Langres, CCV, 700; Peter of Blois, CCVII, 627; St Martin of León, CCVIII, 1085, 1197; Absalon, CCXI, 182, 187, 193; Helinand, CCXII, CCII, 591, 595.

## CHAPTER VIII.—On Pentecost

Pentecost is so called from πεντήκοντα (*pentēkonta*, “fifty”), because this day is fifty days distant from the Lord’s Resurrection: Beleth, CCII, 137.—Pentecost is one thing, Quinquagesima another: [Col. 0489] ibid., 135.—Pentecost is interpreted “Fiftieth”; but not every Fiftieth is called Pentecost: Sicard, CCXIII, 378.—Pentecost marks the beginning of the eighth week: St Ambrose, XV, 1773.—The feast on the fiftieth day is called Pentecost: St Gregory the Great, LXVIII, 381 (note).—Among the Hebrews Pentecost was a celebrated day, observed after five decades: St Isidore of Seville, LXXXII, 250.—On the fiftieth day after the slaughter of the lamb the Law is given on Sinai; on the fiftieth day after Christ’s resurrection the Holy Spirit is sent to the apostles: Rather, CXXXVI, 746; St Cyprian, III, 1189, 1202.—The day of Pentecost, that is, the period of the Paschal Fifty Days: Archbishop John of Rouen, CXLVII, 81.—The harmony of the Old and New Testaments concerning the celebration of Easter and Pentecost: St Augustine, XXXIII, 217, 218.—The festival day of Pentecost is derived from “Weeks”: ibid., XXXVIII, 73.—The Pentecost of the Jews is a figure of the Pentecost of Christians: ibid., XLII, 503.—The reason for the festivity of Pentecost: the Law given on Sinai and the coming of the Holy Spirit: St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 768; the Venerable Bede, XCIV, 537; Alcuin, CI, 1226; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 354.—The Jewish Passover, Pentecost, and Feast of Tabernacles (*Coenopegia*) prefigured the threefold state of Christian religion, namely penitence, righteousness, and glory: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 970.—The feast of Pentecost had a holier cause than the other Jewish festivals: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1756.—The Jews celebrate Pentecost because they then received the Law; we, because we received the Holy Spirit: Beleth, CCII, 135.—The solemnity of the Holy Spirit’s coming is to be venerated both on account of the Person and on account of the cause: Sicard, CCXIII, 375.—On the day of Pentecost God glorified Christ as greatly as the Jews had dishonoured him on Preparation Day: Baldwin, CCIV, 1132.—At Pentecost the apostles received the mystery of perfect baptism and of every kind of consecration: St Peter Damian, CXV, 103.—They received the second grace of the Holy Spirit: Rupert, CLXVII, 1647.—Baptism now instituted on Saturday prefigures the coming of the Holy Spirit: Sicard, CCXIII, 375.

A feast-day signified by Jeremiah, a day properly called a feast: Tertullian, I, 1222.—A day more solemn than all others in every age: St Augustine, XXXIX, 2094.—The feast of Pentecost is compared with the feast of the Incarnation: St Gregory the Great, LXLVI [perhaps LXXVI], 1225.—How honourable is the solemnity of Pentecost: ibid.—The joys of Pentecost: St Philastrius, XII, 1273; Pope Nicholas, CXIX, 1210.—To be celebrated joyfully: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 354.—Through the Pentecostal Fifty Days eternal joy is shown forth: Haymo, CXVIII, 883.—The solemnities of Easter and Pentecost are the greatest of all festivals: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 307.

The feast of Pentecost is ancient: St Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 95, 649, 828.—Received by tradition: St Augustine, XXXIII, 200.—Anciently received in Gaul: Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 169, 170.—Universal: Beleth, CCII, 18.—To be celebrated only in cities and parishes: St Ivo, CLXI, 266.—It reaches the highest rank: Udalric, XLIX, 656; Lanfranc, CL, 473.—The feast of Pentecost must always be observed on Sunday: St Augustine, XXXV, 2289; Egbert, bishop of York, LXXXIX, 384.—Many think that Christ ascended to heaven on the day of Pentecost: St Augustine, XLV, 2093.—They thought fasting from Easter to Pentecost unlawful: Tertullian, II, 79; St Ambrose, XV, 1773; St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 372; St Benedict, abbot, CIII, 1137, 1146; Peter de Honestis, CLX, 111, 721.—The reason for joy, and also Christ’s intercourse with the apostles: St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 372.—When the feast of Pentecost is ended, fasts are relaxed: Eugyppius, LXII, 760.—During the days of Pentecost knees are not bent: Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 152; St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 768; Fulgentius Ferrandus, LXXXVIII, 828, 829, 887; St Ivo, CLXI, 267; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1784.—The Pentecostal Fifty Days signify the future life: St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 326.—The holy days of Pentecost are days of rest: Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1781.—They are all like Sundays: St Ambrose, XV, 1773.—During Pentecost the gradual is not sung: Rupert, CLXX, 29.—From Easter to Pentecost the responsory is not sung: Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 454.—From Rogation Days until the Octaves of Pentecost have passed, abstinence from wives and marriage is required: St Eutychian, V, 167.—Abstinence from wives before Pentecost: Regino, CXXXII, 249.—At Pentecost: Beleth, CCII, 72.—At the Octave: Rather, CXXXVI, 566.—The Saturday of Pentecost is to be equated with Holy Saturday: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 355.—It is to be celebrated in the same manner: Anonymous, CXXXVIII, 1076; Beleth, CCII, 137.—Pentecost affords the broadest opportunity for baptisms to be ordained: Tertullian, I, 1222.—The vigil of Easter and of Pentecost are the two lawful seasons for baptism: St Eutychian, V, 166; Pope St Siricius, XIII, 1134; Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 232, 284; Isidore of Seville, [Col. 0490] LXXXIV, 167, 183; Hetto, CV, 764; Leo IV, CXV, 679; Regino, CXXXII, 240, 241; Rather, CXXXVI, 555, 556; Anonymous, CXXXVIII, 624; Burchard, CXL, 725; Jordan, CXLII, 1394; St Ivo, CLXI, 81, 82, 110; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 455; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1798, 1799.—In the monastery of St Martial, baptism is administered at Pentecost and slaves are granted freedom by their masters: Jordan, bishop of Limoges, CXLII, 1394.—On the Saturday of Pentecost, the three litanies may on no account be omitted: ibid., 1395; John of Rouen, CXLVII, 52, 103, 176.—All the bells are rung at the *Gloria in excelsis* on the Saturday of Pentecost: ibid., 42, 105, 177, 181.—On the Saturday of Pentecost the Creed is not sung: ibid., 38.—Water was blessed: Ratramnus, CXXI, 768.—The vigil of Pentecost was celebrated with readings: ibid., 770.—Fasting on it: Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 206, 207.—Formerly the day of Pentecost began to be celebrated after Saturday Vespers: St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 380 (note).—Formerly flowers were cast down at the third hour on the day of Pentecost: John of Rouen, CXVII, 58, 112.—The altar is incensed by seven priests wearing chasubles: ibid., 111.—During the Octave, only by the celebrant and deacon: ibid.—Formerly there were three Masses at Pentecost: Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 173.—At Pentecost all the faithful must communicate: St Eutychian, V, 166; St Isidore, LXXXIV, 266; Egbert, bishop of York, LXXXIX, 385; Regino, CXXXII, 189, 227; Atto, CXXXVI, 42; Udalric, CXXXV, 1073; Rather, CXXXVI, 542 (note); St Ivo, CLXI, 163; Gratian, CLXXXVIII, 1738.—One who does not communicate is not to be reckoned a Catholic: Egbert, LXXXIX, 385; Atto, CXXXIV, 42.—He must do penance for twenty days on bread and water: Burchard, CXL, 963.—Louis I celebrated Pentecost with piety: Eginhard, CIV, 967.—At Pentecost it is utterly forbidden to conduct judicial proceedings: Anonymous, CXXXVIII, 854.—Among the Saxons the people paid tithes of offspring: ibid., 503, 514; eleventh-century diplomatic documents, CLI, 1174.—At Pentecost the king’s peace lasts eight days: ibid., 1191, 1194.—The royal court: St Ivo, CLXII, 328.—St Elizabeth sees the mysteries of Pentecost: Abbot Egbert, CXCV, 147.—On Pentecost day through Saturday, according to ancient custom, three psalms at nocturns and three lessons are said: Gratian, CLXXCVII [perhaps CLXXXVII], 1859.—During the eight days the Creed is sung: John of Rouen, CXLVII, 38.—The Octave of Pentecost is one of veneration: Beleth, CCII, 78.—The Octaves of Easter and Pentecost were formerly observed as holidays: Ratramnus, CXXI, 770; Berno, CXLII, 1061.—On the second, third, and fourth weekdays of Pentecost they were honoured no less solemnly than Sunday: Anonymous, CXXXVIII, 832.—Litanies after Pentecost were celebrated from Thursday to Saturday: St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 314.—The solemnity of Pentecost among the Carthusians: Guigo, CLIII, 646, 656, 666, 733.—In the Order of St Benedict: Lanfranc, CL, 471.—On Pentecost day the archbishops of Rouen made certain distributions: Peter of Blois, CCVII, 1179.—The fast celebrated at Pentecost: St Philastrius, XII, 1686; Rupert, CLXX, 29.—By apostolic tradition and the institution of the Holy Spirit: St Leo the Great, LIV, 415.—Lent after Pentecost: Egbert, LXXXIX, 425, 426.—Fasting does not sadden the solemnity of the Holy Spirit: Rupert, CLXX, 96.

## CHAPTER IX.—On the Feast of the Body of Christ

## CHAPTER X.—On the Transfiguration of the Lord

On the eighth day before the Ides of August, the Transfiguration of the Lord on Mount Tabor is celebrated: John of Würzburg, CLV, 1089; Alanus of Lille, CCX, 322.—It is celebrated on this day not because it occurred on this day, but because it was manifested by the apostles on this day: Sicard, CCXIII, 419.—The white garments of the transfigured Christ signify the saints: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 486.—Offerings of bread and wine were made to the chapter of Rouen on the Transfiguration: Peter of Blois, CCVII, 1179.—Formerly there were three Masses on the Transfiguration: Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 173.

On the Transfiguration: St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 408; St Anselm, CLVIII, 315, 602, 604, 607; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1084; Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1581; Beleth, CCII, 147; Peter of Blois, CCVII, 777; Sicard, CCXIII, 419.

Sermons on the Transfiguration: St Leo, LIV, 520; Peter the Venerable, CLXXXIX, 953; Peter of Celle, CCII, 840, 843.—Homily: St Ambrose Autpert, LXXXIX, 1305.—Office: St Isidore of Seville, LXXXV, 806.

# PART THREE. ON THE FEASTS OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY

## CHAPTER ONE.—On the Feasts of the Blessed Mary in General

All the disciples venerated Mary and served her with the affection of love: [Col. 0492] St Jerome, XXX, 124.—Those who celebrate the feasts of the Blessed Mary are made worthy through her intercession: Abbot Godefrid, CLXXIV, 374.—On four feasts of the Blessed Mary, John XIX permitted Poppo, patriarch of Aquileia, the use of the pallium: John XIX, CXLI, 1138.—At the feasts of the Blessed Mary, except the Annunciation, the Creed is said: Archbishop John of Rouen, CXLVII, 38.—At all feasts of the Blessed Mary the Creed is to be said at the principal Mass: Lanfranc, CL, 481.—On the vigils and feasts of St Mary, the peace of God and of holy Church extends throughout the whole kingdom: ecclesiastical laws of Edward III, CLI, 1191.—The feasts of the Blessed Mary are general: Beleth, CCII, 18.—Five feasts of the Blessed Mary are authentic and approved: ibid., 149, 150.—The feast of the Assumption; the feast of the Woman Giving Birth at the Nativity of the Lord; the feast of the Nativity; of the Annunciation; and the feast of Mary at the Martyrs, now called the feast of All Saints: ibid.; Sicard, CCXIII, 414.—A feast of the Blessed Mary: Abbot Goffrid, CLVII, 149.—On every feast of the Mother of the Lord: ibid., 266.—Saturday dedicated to the Blessed Virgin: St Peter Damian, CXLV, 566.—A pious devotion: reciting the office of the Blessed Virgin and celebrating the solemnities of Mass in her honour every Saturday: ibid., 564.—The Saturday fast was celebrated by a heavenly vision: ibid., 804.—The Mass of Blessed Mary on Saturdays, on feasts of the chapter, and on candle feasts is to be said privately, except on the days of the Lord’s Nativity, Holy Saturday, and the four feasts of the Blessed Mary: Guigo, CLIII, 1144, 1145.—Saturday is a day consecrated to the Virgin Mary: Abbot Guerric, CLXXXIV, 638.—Sermon in praise of Mary on account of the Saviour’s birth: St Fulgentius, LXV, 898.—Homily on the solemnity of Mary, perpetual Virgin: Haymo, CXVIII, 765.—Sermon on the feast of the Blessed Mary: Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 770.—Sermon on Blessed Mary: Abbot Aelred, CLXXXVIII, 353.

Hymns on St Mary: Bishop Ennodius, LXIII, 332; Venantius Fortunatus, LXXXVIII, 265; Walafrid Strabo, CXIV, 1089; Abelard, CLXXVIII, 1803.—Prose sequence on the Blessed Virgin: Fulbert, CXLI, 345.—Verses on the church of the Blessed Virgin Mary: Flodoard, CXXXV, 493.—Poem on the Virgin Mary: Hildebert, CLXXI, 1407.—Praises of the Virgin Mary: St Peter Damian, CXLIV, 933, 934.—A metrical prayer to her: ibid., 937.—On the praises of Blessed Mary, ever Virgin: Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 770.—Treatise in praise of the glorious Virgin: St Bernard, CLXXXII, 1141.—Sentences on St Mary: Alanus of Lille, CCX, 246.—*Mariale*: Adam the Scot, CCXI, 733.—On the Virgin’s childbirth: ibid., 699, 711.—Marian fragments: ibid., 743, 753.—Mass in honour of St Mary: eleventh-century liturgical monuments, CLI, 907.—Blessings for the feast of the Blessed Mary: Grimald, CXXI, 876.

## CHAPTER II.—On the Individual Feasts of the Blessed Mary

### § I.—On the Conception

Office for the Conception of the Blessed Mary: St Isidore of Seville, LXXXV, 932.—The feast of the Conception of Blessed Mary was first instituted in England by St Anselm. In the same author, ibid. (note).—In Greece, from the year 1166, it was among those feasts on which commercial activity ceases: ibid., 933 (note).—The immaculate conception of Blessed Mary is intimated: Hildebert, CLXXI, 629.—It is affirmed as immaculate: Abbot Oger, CLXXXIV, 940.—It is shown by miracles that it should be celebrated: St Anselm, CLIX, 319, 323; Sicard, CCXII, 421.—Mary is free from original and actual sin: Abbot Guerric, CLXXXV, 192; CLXXXIV, 1074.—The feast of the Conception has long been celebrated by some, but is not yet authentic and approved: Beleth, CCII, 149, 150.—At the Conception of Blessed Mary the archbishops of Rouen made certain distributions to the chapter of Rouen: Peter of Blois, CCVII, 1179.—The Conception of the Blessed Virgin was celebrated because of a revelation made to a certain abbot: Sicard, CCXII, 421.—Treatise on the Conception of Blessed Mary: St Anselm, CLIX, 311.—Sermon on the Conception of Blessed Mary: ibid., 319.—Sermon on the Conception of Blessed Mary: Abbot Oger, CLXXVII, 918.

### § II.—On the Nativity of the Blessed Mary

The feast of the Nativity: St Jerome, XXX, 437; Adalhard, CV, 544; Flodoard, CXXXV, 408; John XIII, ibid., 977; John XIX, CXLI, 1138; Udalric, CXLIX, 655; Lanfranc, CL, 475.—The Nativity of St Mary is to be kept as a holiday: St Ivo, CLXI, 266, 267; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1781; St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 136, 137.—The Nativity of Blessed Mary noted by the martyr Boniface, from the Gallican Liturgy: LXXII, 171, 172.—Likewise by the Council of Narbonne and Gregory of Tours: ibid.—The feast of the Nativity of Blessed Mary is authentic and approved: Beleth, CCII, 149, 150.—The feast of the Nativity instituted through revelation: ibid., 152.—It has [Col. 0493] an octave, not by institution but by devotion: ibid.—The Nativity of Blessed Mary is declared to be celebrated through revelation: Sicard, CCXII, 421.—In St Anselm’s time the Octaves of the Nativity of Blessed Mary were already observed in many churches: St Anselm, CLIX, 224.—Many asked that they be observed in the church of Canterbury: ibid.—The Nativity of Mary is holy: St Bernard, CLXXXII, 332, 334.—The feast of the Nativity received: ibid.—With what zeal the Church of God observes the birthday of Blessed Mary: St Peter Damian, CXLIV, 741; Abbot Godefrid, CLXXIV, 1010.—On the day of the Nativity of Blessed Mary a demoniac was delivered: Flodoard, CXXXV, 486.—At the Nativity of Blessed Mary the Carthusian brothers receive wine twice: Guigo, CLIII, 733.—At the Nativity, the archbishops of Rouen made certain distributions to the chapter of Rouen: Peter of Blois, CCVII, 1179.—During the octave of the Nativity of Blessed Mary, the ferial *Kyrie eleison* is to be said without the *Gloria in excelsis*, unless it is Saturday or a feast of twelve lessons: Guigo, CLIII, 1145.

Sermons on the Nativity: authors uncertain, XCVI, 277, 279, 280; Odilo, CXLII, 1028, 1029; St Peter Damian, CXLIV, 736, 740; CXLV, 1038, 1119, 1150, 1161, 1171; Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 1022; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 907, 979, 1102; St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 437; Abbot Odo, CLXXXVIII, 1653; Blessed Father Isaac, CXCIV, 1872; Aelred, CXCV, 316, 322, 326; Garnerius of Langres, CCV, 759, 763, 774; Peter of Blois, CCVII, 672; St Martin of León, CCIX, 25; Abbot Absalon, CCXI, 265; Helinand, CCXII, 652, 661; Innocent III, CCXVII, 497, 585.

Homilies on the Nativity: Paul the Deacon, XCV, 1514; the Venerable Bede, XCIV, 413; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 54; Radulphus Ardens, CLV, 1439, 1443; Godefrid, CLXXIV, 1003, 1006, 1010, 1012.

Office for the Nativity of the glorious Virgin: St Isidore, LXXXV, 844.—Preface for the Nativity: Grimald, CXXI, 913.—Sequence for the Nativity: Notker, CXXXI, 1015.—Responsory: King Robert, CXLI, 946; eleventh-century liturgical monuments, CLI, 853, 875.—On the Nativity of the Virgin Mary: Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 689, 769, 1000.—Poem on the Nativity: the Venerable Bede, XCIV, 631.—The Nativity of Blessed Mary is treated in the Martyrology: St Protadius the Martyr, LXXX, 419; Rabanus’s Martyrology, CX, 1167; Wandalbert, CXXI, 610; Ado, CXXIII, 167, 201, 348; Usuard, ibid., 449; Notker, CXXXI, 1148; ancient calendars and martyrologies, CXXXVIII, 1188, 1191, 1200, 1206, 1241, 1262, 1275.

### § III.—On the Presentation of the Blessed Mary in the Temple

On the eleventh day before the Kalends of December: the Presentation of the Blessed Virgin in the Temple: John of Würzburg, CLV, 1090.—The Presentation of Mary in the Temple: St Anselm, CLVIII, 748.

### § IV.—On the Annunciation

The feast of the Annunciation: Calendar of St Jerome, XXX, 437; St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 52; Martyrology of St Protadius, LXXX, 414; Adalhard, CV, 544; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 1137; Wandalbert, CXXI, 593; Ado, CXXIII, 151, 242; Usuard, ibid., 871; Notker, CXXXI, 1058; Flodoard, CXXXV, 408; John XIII, ibid., 977; ancient calendars and martyrologies, CXXXVIII, 1187, 1195, 1205, 1220, 1260, 1267; John XIX, CXLI, 1138; St Anselm, CLVIII, 962; CLIX, 560; St Ivo, CLLII, 583; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 699, 700; Alanus of Lille, CCX, 200.—The Annunciation of Christ is reckoned among the chief feasts of the second class: Lanfranc, CL, 475.—Miracles at the solemnity of the Annunciation of the Lord: Flodoard, CXXXV, 446.—Christ’s descent from heaven is more wonderful than Mary’s Assumption: St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 425.—The circumstances of the Annunciation are expounded: ibid., 395.—The solemnity of the Mother of the Lord on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January is to be celebrated in every way: St Isidore, Tenth Council of Toledo, LXXXIV, 441.—The Annunciation of Blessed Mary was celebrated on 18 December and called the feast of St Mary the Virgin: LXXXV, 170.—On the feast of the Annunciation, the Greeks, according to ancient custom, consecrate during Lent and do not fast: St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 324.—At the Annunciation the Creed is not sung: Archbishop John of Rouen, CXLVII, 38.—At the Annunciation nothing more is done than on any Sunday: Udalric, CXLIX, 654.—If the Annunciation falls on Sunday, the Carthusian brothers receive wine twice: Guigo, CLIII, 733.—The *Gloria in excelsis* is said whenever it occurs: ibid., 1145.—When the Annunciation is celebrated after Easter, the responsory *Prope est Dominus, alleluia* (“The Lord is near, alleluia”) is said: ibid.—The feast of the Annunciation is suitably celebrated in Lent: Abbot Guerric, CLXXXV, 115.—The joy and effect of the Lord’s Annunciation: ibid.—If the feast of the Annunciation should fall within [Col. 0494] Septuagesima, the chants of joy are not omitted except the *Alleluia*: Beleth, CCII, 87; Sicard, CCXIII, 410.—At the feast of the Annunciation, certain distributions were made to the chapter of Rouen by the archbishops of Rouen: Peter of Blois, CCVII, 1179.

Sermons on the Annunciation: St Peter Chrysologus, LII, 517, 575, 579, 582, 585; St Leo the Great, LIV, 501, 508, 509; LVI, 1140; Eleutherius, LXV, 96; Odilo, CLLII, 1001; St Ivo, CLXII, 583; Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 1028; Hildebert, CLXXI, 605; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 933, 975; Abelard, CLXXVIII, 379; St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 55, 109; Abbot Guerric, CLXXXV, 115, 120, 124; Abbot Aelred, CXCV, 251; Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1537; Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, CCI, 167; Peter of Celle, CCII, 705, 708, 711, 715, 718, 722; Alanus of Lille, CCX, 200; Abbot Absalon, CCXI, 118, 124, 130; Innocent III, CCXVII, 521.

### § VII.—On the Purification of the Blessed Virgin and the Presentation of the Lord

The Purification: Calendar of St Jerome, XXX, 437; St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 46, 297 (note); Martyrology of St Protadius, LXXX, 413; St Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 339; Adalhard, CV, 537, 538; Hetto, ibid., 764; Rabanus’s Martyrology, CX, 1130; Wandalbert, CXXI, 588; Rodulphus, CXIX, 717; Walter, ibid., 740; Grimald, CXXI, 768; Ado’s Martyrology, CXXIII, 149, 225; Usuard, ibid., 721; Notker, CXXXI, 1042; Regino, CXXXII, 265; John XIII, 977; in the ecclesiastical capitularies of Louis, CXXXVIII, 624; in the capitularies of Charles II, ibid., 714; ancient martyrologies, ibid., 1168, 1194, 1204, 1214, 1259, 1265; John XIX, CXLI, 1138; eleventh-century liturgical monuments, CLI, 889; St Anselm, CLVIII, 620, 624; St Ivo, CLXII, 575.—It is called either the Purification, Candlemas, or ὑπαντή (*Hypantē*, “Meeting”): Purification because of the precept of the Law; Candlemas because candles are customarily carried in procession; *Hypantē* because Simeon and Anna the prophetess went to meet Christ: Beleth, CCII, 87.—Mary was not bound by the law of Purification: St Bernard, CLXXXII, 369.—The Purification of Blessed Mary teaches humility: Abbot Guerric, CLXXXV, 75.—Mary fulfilled purification in order at once to signify the virtue of most obedient humility and the truth of Gospel Purification: ibid., 63.—Preparation for worthily celebrating the Purification of Blessed Mary: Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 445.—The feast of the Purification is to be kept as a holiday: St Ivo, CLXI, 266, 267; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1781.—Authentic and approved: Beleth, CCII, 149, 150.—Celebrated with greater solemnity: Udalric, CXLIX, 655.—Assigned among the chief festivals of the second class: Lanfranc, CL, 475.—Very devoutly performed: St Eulogius, CXV, 1390.—The day of the Purification of Holy Mary is to be celebrated festively as the Assumption, except for vigils and octaves: Archbishop John of Rouen, CXLVII, 43, 44.—The Presentation of the Lord is compared to the carrying of a confessor’s soul into heaven by angels: St Peter Damian, CXLIV, 522.—A twofold solemnity, namely of the Woman Giving Birth and of the Birth: with regard to the Mother it is called Purification; with regard to the Son it is called *hypapante*, or Meeting: Sicard, CCXIII, 243.—Those meeting at the Purification of Mary in the Temple: Joseph, Anna, Simeon: Thomas the Cistercian, CCVI, 130.—It is also called the feast of Simeon: St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 297 (note).—By ancient custom, processions with lighted candles take place on this feast: St Gregory the Great, ibid., 297, 298 (note); St Isidore, LXXX, 693; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 345; Helperich, CXXXVII, 787, 788; Archbishop John of Rouen, CXLVII, 43, 44; St Anselm, CLVIII, 625; Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 87; Sicard, CCXIII, 243.—The origin of the candles at the feast of the Purification comes from the pagan [Col. 0495] February festivals: Alcuin, CI, 1181.—Pope Sergius ordered litanies to be made on it: ibid.—Theophanes assigns the institution of this feast to the year 542: St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 298.—According to some, it was instituted because of the city-purification ceremony conducted at Rome: ibid., 299.—The Purification of Holy Mary falls on the fortieth day from the Lord’s Nativity: CXXXVIII, 714.—Blessing over candles at the Purification of Holy Mary: eleventh-century liturgical monuments, CLI, 838.—It is the Church’s custom that the faithful carry tapers or candles on the feast of the Purification: St Anselm, CLXVIII [perhaps CLVIII], 625.—At the Purification of St Mary we carry candles in order that we may in some measure share the happy joy of righteous Simeon: Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 87.—At Reims, miracles were twice obtained in the church of Blessed Mary on the day of the Purification: Flodoard, CXXXV, 441, 442.—If the Purification falls within Septuagesima, nothing in it, according to Roman custom, is to be changed from the usual celebration except the *Alleluia*: eleventh-century liturgical monuments, CLI, 1012; Sicard, CCXIII, 410.—At the feast of the Purification the *Gloria in excelsis* is to be said whenever it occurs: Guigo, CLIII, 1145.—At the Purification, the Carthusian brothers receive wine twice: ibid., 733.—At the Purification, the archbishops of Rouen made certain distributions to the chapter of Rouen: Peter of Blois, CCVII, 1179.

Sermons on the Purification: Anonymous, XCVI, 272; Odilo, CXLII, 999; St Anselm, CLVIII, 621; St Ivo, CLXII, 575; Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 865, 1025; Hildebert, CLXXI, 611, 615, 625; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 1006, 1009, 1181; Abelard, CLXXVIII, 417; St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 365, 368, 369, 373; Abbot Guerric, CLXXXV, 63, 67, 71, 75, 79; Aelred, CXCV, 234; Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1544; Peter of Celle, CCII, 674; Garnerius of Langres, CCV, 633, 636, 645; Peter of Blois, CCVII, 592, 596; Abbot Absalon, CCXI, 87, 92, 97; Helinand, CCXII, 529, 535; Innocent III, CCXVII, 505.
