Sequences: Notker, CXXXI, 1008; Adam, CXCVI, 1481.

Hymns: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1658; Walafrid Strabo, CXCIV, 1083; Abelard, CLXXVIII, 1792.—On the Purification: Alcuin, CI, 1181.—On the Purification and the procession of candles: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 345.—On the Purification: Lanfranc, CXLIX, 695; Abbot Goffrid, CLVII, 262; Stephen, CLXVI, 1417; Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 649, 734, 782, 798, 819; Adam, CCXI, 726.—On the Lord’s *Hypapante* (“Meeting”): Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1542; Sicard, CCXIII, 242.—Verses on the Lord’s *Hypapante*: Marbod, CLXXI, 1663.

### § VIII.—On the Compassion of the Blessed Mary

On the compassion of Blessed Mary for her crucified Son: St Anselm, CLIX, 566.—Book on the sorrows of the Mother of the Lord: St Bernard, CLXXXII, 1134.—Homily on the strength of mind, or martyrdom, of the Blessed Virgin: Amadeus, bishop of Lausanne, CLXXXVIII, 1325.

### § IX.—On the Assumption of Blessed Mary
Assumption feast: Calendar of St. Jerome, XXX, 437; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 132, 134; Martyrology of St. Protadius, LXXX, 418; Einhard, CIV, 585; Rabanus’s Martyrology, CX, 1163; Wandalbert’s, CXXI, 607; Ado’s, CXXIII, 165, 331; Usuard’s, CXXIV, 365; Notker’s, CXXXI, 1141; ancient calendars and martyrologies, CXXXVIII, 1188, 1190, 1199, 1206, 1238, 1262, 1273; Adalhard, CV, 544; Hetto, ibid., 764; Rodulf, CXIX, 717; Walter, ibid., 740; Grimald, CXXI, 768; Regino, CXXXII, 265; Flodoard, CXXXV, 408; John XIII, ibid., 977; in the ecclesiastical capitularies of Louis II, CXXXVIII, 624; John XIX, CXLI, 1138; St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 321; Udalric, CXLIX, 473; Abbot Godfrey, CLVII, 65; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 807, 808; Gratian, CLXXXVIII, 1781.

“Today the glorious ever-Virgin Mary ascended into heaven,” St. Jerome, XXX, 126. — “With good reason Blessed Mary is exalted by our praise, she who offered the world a singular exchange,” ibid., 143. — The solemnity of the Assumption of Blessed Mary is to be preferred to the solemnities of martyrs, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2130. — She is believed to have been assumed into heaven, ibid. — “Holy Scripture [Col. 0496] records nothing,” id., XL, 1144. — We truly confess Mary to be Queen of Heaven, id., XXXIX, 2130. — On the Assumption of Blessed Mary’s body into heaven: St. Gregory of Tours, ibid. He was the first of all to commit it to writing, id., LXXI, 707. — The Assumption and Nativity of Blessed Mary noted by the martyr Boniface, Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 171, 172. — Likewise by the Council of Narbonne and Gregory of Tours, ibid. — The Son’s Ascension and the Mother’s Assumption are described in similar language, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 713. — Mary, assumed into heaven, sits at the right hand of her Son, ibid., 717. — Mary is said to have been assumed, while Christ is said to have ascended, because the Savior descended by the command of sovereign power, whereas Mary was assumed by the help of uplifting grace, ibid. — Celebration and encomium of Mary’s Assumption, Rabanus Maurus, CX, 433, 455. — The glory and blessedness of Mary’s Assumption, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 964. — At Blessed Mary’s Assumption the angels were struck with wonder, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 425. — Christ’s generation and Mary’s Assumption are beyond narration, ibid., 415. — Christ’s descent from heaven is more wondrous than Mary’s Assumption, ibid., 425. — Galler of St. Victor’s opinion on Mary’s Assumption, Robert Pullen, CLXXXVI, 1061, 1062. — The Church believes Blessed Mary already glorified in the flesh; Pullen does not dissent, ibid. — “Mary was assumed,” Thomas of Cîteaux and John Algrin, CCVI, 763. — Threefold assumption, ibid. — Mary’s body assumed, Alan of Lille, CCX, 64. — Mary finds Christ in her Assumption, ibid., 72. — The passing of Blessed Mary is pre-eminently called the Assumption, because she was first assumed in soul and afterward, as is piously believed, assumed in body, Sicard, CCXIII, 420. — The day of Blessed Mary’s Assumption is to be kept as a feast, St. Ivo, CLXI, 266, 267; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1781. — The Assumption of Blessed Mary is foremost among her feasts, John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 59. — The day of the Assumption is celebrated festively, ibid., 43, 44. — The Assumption of St. Mary reaches the superlative rank, Udalric, CXLIX, 656. — It is reckoned among the chief feasts, Lanfranc, CL, 473. — Hildebert urges that Blessed Mary’s Assumption be celebrated more solemnly, CLXXI, 266. — The feast of the Assumption received, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 333. — All priests celebrate on this feast, id., CLXXXIII, 713. — Five authentic and approved feasts of Blessed Mary, Beleth, CCII, 149, 150: the feast of the Mother who bore on the Nativity of the Lord; the feasts of the Nativity and Annunciation; the feast of St. Mary at the Martyrs; and the feast of the Assumption, ibid. — Constantine dedicated a basilica to Blessed Mary, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 713. — Festival of Blessed Mary in the eleventh month, ibid. — Formerly in Gaul the Assumption was celebrated in January, ibid.; Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 179, 180. — The Assumption of the Blessed Virgin was at one time celebrated on 18 January, St. Isidore, LXXXV, 819; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 401, note. — On 15 August, solemn rites for the Repose of St. Mary, ibid., 132. — The Dormition of the most holy Mother of God, ibid., 401. — The departure of the most glorious holy Mother of God, ibid. — Ceremonies of the Assumption of Blessed Mary, Abbot Guido, CL, 1226. — Octave of St. Mary, ibid., 1229. — St. Leo ordered the octave day of the Assumption to be celebrated, Anastasius, CXXVIII, 1311. — Within the octave of the Assumption, the weekday “Lord, have mercy” (*Kyrie eleison*) is to be said without “Glory in the highest” (*Gloria in excelsis*), except on Saturday or on a feast of twelve lessons, Guigo, CLIII, 1145. — At the Assumption, the Gospel reading is *Intravit Jesus* (“Jesus entered”), Abbot Guibert, CLVI, 557. — The Creed is sung at the principal Mass, Lanfranc, CL, 481. — During the octave of the Assumption of St. Mary, a sequence is sung, Udalric, CXLIX, 655. — Octave day of the Assumption, Lanfranc, CL, 475. — At the Assumption, prayers and litanies were customarily performed at night, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 586. — Formerly, at the *Magnificat* (“My soul magnifies”), the antiphon *Ascendit Christus* (“Christ ascended”) was sung with a threefold repetition, John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 155. — Formerly, at the Assumption the Church said a prayer different from the present one, Hildebert, CLXXI, 629. — If the Assumption falls on Friday, it is lawful to eat meat, Pope Nicholas, CXIX, 981. — Celebration of the Assumption even on military expedition, Heribert, CXLI, 598. — On the feast of her Assumption Mary frees innumerable persons from the punishments of purgatory, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 586. — At the Assumption the Carthusian brethren receive wine twice, Guigo, CLIII, 737. — On the feast of the Assumption, the Archbishops of Rouen made certain distributions to the chapter of Rouen, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 1179.

Office for the feast of the Assumption: St. Isidore, LXXXV, 819; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 701, 703, 798, 801. — Fragments of the Office at the Assumption: John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 129; eleventh-century *Liturgical Monuments*, CLI, 968, 669. — Mass of the Assumption: St. Isidore, LXXXV, 819; Abbot Guibert, CLVI, 888. — Sequences for the Assumption: Notker, CXXXI, 1015; Anonymous, CLI, 807; Adam of St. Victor, CXCVI, 1501. — Preface on the day [Col. 0497] of the Assumption, Grimald, CXXI, 912. — Hymns: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1758; Walafrid Strabo, CXIV, 1084. — Poem on the Assumption, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 934.

Treatise on the Assumption, St. Augustine, XL, 1141. — On the Assumption, Udalric, CXLIX, 683. — On the day of the Assumption of St. Mary, eleventh-century *Liturgical Monuments*, CLI, 852, 897. — On the Assumption, Honorius, CLXXII, 991. — On the Assumption of Blessed Mary and her praises, Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 522. — On the Assumption of Blessed Mary, Beleth, CCII, 148. — *Mariale*, on the Assumption, Adam, CCXI, 733.

Sermons on the Assumption: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 865, 867; anonymous author, XCVI, 239, 250, 254, 258, 259, 264, 267, 269, 271; Atto, CXXXIV, 856; Odilo, CXLII, 1028, 1029; St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 717; St. Anselm, CLVIII, 644; Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 1032; Hildebert, CLXXI, 627, 631, 636; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 979, 1024, 1025, 1207; Abelard, CLXXVIII, 539; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 415, 417, 421, 425; Abbot Oger, CLXXXIV, 1001; Abbot Guerric, CLXXXV, 187, 190, 193, 197; Blessed Father Isaac, CXCIV, 1862, 1866, 1870; Abbot Aelred, CXCV, 303, 309; Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1784; Peter of Celle, CCII, 848, 850, 851, 860, 861, 863, 864, 867; Garner of Langres, CCV, 741, 750; Peter of Blois, CCVII, 660, 663, 665, 667; St. Martin of León, CCIX, 19; Abbot Absalon, CCXI, 245, 250; Helinand, CCXII, 636, 646; Innocent III, CCXVII, 575, 581. — Homilies: St. Jerome, XXX, 122; St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 613; the Venerable Bede, XCIV, 420, 421, 422; Paul the Deacon, XCV, 1494, 1505, 1565; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 55, 433, 435; Haymo, CXVIII, 767; Radulfus Ardens, CLV, 1421, 1425; Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 839; Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 959, 964, 971, 974, 977, 979, 985, 988; Amadeus, Bishop of Lausanne, CLXXXVIII, 1336.

# PART FOUR. ON THE FEASTS OF THE SAINTS.

## CHAPTER ONE. — On the Feasts of Saints in General.

Christians celebrated birthday anniversaries, Tertullian, II, 79. — The merits of martyrs avail greatly if they ask nothing contrary to the Judge and contrary to the law of the Lord, St. Cyprian, IV, 480. — Feast of All Saints, St. Jerome, XXX, 437. — The examples of the saints benefit us, St. Leo the Great, LV, 198; as does their commemoration, ibid., 23; and likewise their well-attended solemnities, ibid., 28. — Commemorations of the holy Fathers were celebrated in the devout assemblies of Christians, recalling their virtues to mind, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 415. — Feast days in honor of saints were instituted in ancient times, St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 572, 573. — Feasts of saints instituted at Rome by Gregory III, Anastasius, CXXVIII, 1025, 1029. — Ancient veneration of saints, St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 529; Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 169. — Invocation of saints, St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 463, 464, 468; St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 800; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1605; St. Anselm, CLVIII, 732. — Intercession and invocation, Alcuin, CI, 1258. — The invocation of saints defended, Hildebert, CLXXI, 239. — Saints are to be honored, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 991; invoked, from the *Lives of the Fathers*, id., LXXIV, 87. — The solemnities of saints were anciently celebrated by an all-night vigil, St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 166; St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 566, 815. — The merits of saints are celebrated perpetually, St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 670. — One who disparages saints is punished by divine judgment, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 281. — Invocation of saints in the Mass, ibid., 1361. — It is most useful to write the lives and deeds of saints, ibid., 1117, 1119; Arevald, CXXIV, 106. — Innumerable miracles of saints, Einhard, ibid., 594. — God works miracles through the intercession of saints, Priest Joseph, CVI, 898. — Saints are our powerful intercessors, Alcuin, C, 296. — Our advocates before Christ the Judge, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 815; our counselors, ibid. — The patronage of saints must be highly valued, ibid., 591. — It is glorious to match the triumphs of saints who have gone before, ibid., 453. — The death of saints is the beginning of life, ibid., 585. — The days of the saints’ passage from this world are called their birthdays, Alcuin, C, 955. — They are called birthdays because they are born into glory, id., CI, 1213; CLXXXIV, 995; Pope Nicholas, CXIX, 982. — The Church celebrates the death of saints because it is an entrance into life, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 410. — Feasts of saints are to be celebrated, John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 43. — Those who celebrate the feasts of Blessed Mary and the saints are made worthy through their intercession, Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 374. — The feasts of saints are to be commemorated, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 34, 540, 541. — Feasts of virgins, confessors, and martyrs, ibid., 540. — Feasts of saints are celebrated with a threefold benefit, St. Bernard, [Col. 0498] CLXXIII, 462. — The feasts of saints awaken a threefold desire in us, ibid., 477. — Three things are to be considered in saints’ feasts: the saint’s aid, the saint’s example, and our own shame, ibid., 404. — We trust that through the prayers of saints sins are forgiven in the Church, Alcuin, C, 409. — The prayers of saints are a most mighty wall, Rabanus Maurus, CX, 651. — On the saints’ part, they keep the feast in this world, id., CVIII, 788. — They devote themselves peacefully to God, id., CIX, 640. — The suffrages of saints are to be implored and hoped for by us for four reasons, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 480. — Why octaves of saints are celebrated, Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 218. — The examples of saints spur us to three things, Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 749. — Relics of saints are to be honored, from the *Lives of the Fathers*, LXXII, 531; Alcuin, CI, 773. — Dedication of an altar with saints’ relics; relics placed upon the altar, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 734, 735; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 285, 540, 619, 812, 832, 834, 908, 964. — It is an ancient institution of the Church to dedicate basilicas by bringing in and placing holy relics, id., LXXVIII, 422, note. — Rite for bringing relics into a new basilica, ibid. — Relics are solemnly transferred to the new church in procession, ibid. — Solemnity of the translation of saints’ relics, Einhard, CIV, 450. — Power and efficacy of relics against demons, Alcuin, CI, 821. — Alcuin seeks the patronage of relics of the Holy Cross and others, C, 202. — Great crowds gather at saints’ relics, id., CI, 708.

Gregory III restored and enlarged the rules for celebrating the solemnities of all saints, Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVIII, 1029, 1030. — Sergius II placed beneath the altar together the bodies of saints whose names are known to God alone, with other saints whose names are known, ibid., 1299.

Martial built two oratories, one in honor of St. Stephen the Protomartyr and the other in honor of St. Peter the Apostle, Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 193; and solemnly dedicated them, ibid., 195. — Hilary the Sardinian supplied many precious ornaments in basilicas of saints, ibid., 209. — Symmachus the Sardinian adorned saints’ basilicas with ornaments of many kinds, ibid., 210. — In the primitive Church, when the apostles did not yet have particular solemnities, it was ordained that on the Kalends of May a solemnity in honor of all the apostles should be celebrated, Beleth, CCII, 131.

Boniface IV, having obtained the Pantheon from Phocas, dedicated it in honor of Blessed Mary and all martyrs—for feasts were not yet held for confessors—and decreed that every year on that day the feast of the martyrs should be celebrated, just as the feast of the apostles was held on the Kalends of May, ibid., 133. — Gregory IV transferred these two feasts to the Kalends of November, ibid., 133, 134. — Why we do not celebrate the feasts of saints who rose with Christ, ibid. — The glory of all saints, Thomas of Cîteaux, CCV, 562.

Feasts of saints anciently received in Gaul, Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 199, 170, 171. — Feasts of St. Stephen, St. John the Evangelist, and the Innocents; of St. Geneviève and St. Mary; the Chair of St. Peter; the feast of St. John the Baptist; the feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul; the Passion of St. John the Baptist; then the Common of Martyrs and Confessors, ibid.

Commemorations of confessors are celebrated among the memorials of martyrs, St. Cyprian, IV, 328. — Those who endured evils for Christ ought also to have glory with Christ: “As you are partners in the sufferings, so you shall be in the resurrection,” St. Ambrose, XVII, 713, 718. — The blood of martyrs was held in veneration by Christians, St. Augustine, XLI, 612. — Memorials of martyrs, id., XXXVII, 1782. — Martyrs’ birthdays are celebrated, id., XL, 676; Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 281, 299, 300; Fulgentius Ferrandus, LXXXVIII, 830; St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 578. — Christians honor the memorials of martyrs, St. Augustine, XLI, 255; XLII, 384. — Memorials of martyrs are to be celebrated in church, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 871. — Martyrs must be honored with special honor, ibid., 709. — Their memorials are not to be despised, Fulgentius Ferrandus, LXXXVIII, 826. — Basilica of eight martyrs, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1578. — Birthday anniversary of twenty martyrs, ibid., 1447. — Temples, altars, sacrifices, and priesthoods are not established for martyrs, ibid., 1251, 1437; XLI, 255, 772. — We construct for martyrs not temples but memorials, Jonas, Bishop of Orléans. — Yet we establish altars to the God of martyrs, though in the memorials of martyrs themselves, St. Augustine, XLII, 384, 385; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 356. — Martyrs are not honored with worship (*latria*), St. Augustine, XLII, 384, 385.

In ancient times only holy martyrs were honored in the Church, by an appointed feast day with a special Office and Mass; only after some time had passed were confessors introduced, and only a few and the more celebrated ones, St. Nicetas, LII, 1076, 1077. — The feast [Col. 0499] of all apostles was celebrated within the octave of SS. Peter and Paul, St. Leo the Great, LV, 58. — A multitude flocked to the feasts of martyrs, ibid., 33.

The death of martyrs is honored in the Church of God as their true birthday, Maximus of Turin, LVII, 684; St. Bruno, CLII, 1252. — The suffrages of martyrs are to be sought, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 1151. — Martyrs are to be loved and venerated as disciples of the Lord, St. Agobard, CIV, 214. — Blessed Pope Gregory decreed that Masses be celebrated over the bodies of martyrs, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 357; CXXVII, 142, 1435. — It is the custom of the faithful to visit churches and seek out the courtyards of venerable martyrs in the affection of devotion, St. Eulogius, CXV, 789. — The solemn days of the blessed martyrs of Christ are called birthdays, Pope Nicholas, CXIX, 982. — Pope Symmachus decreed that “Glory in the highest” (*Gloria in excelsis*) be said on every Sunday and on martyrs’ birthdays, Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVII, 143. — Boniface obtained from Phocas the Pantheon, in which he made the church of St. Mary and All Martyrs, ibid.

Martyrs honored, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 1009. — Patronage of martyrs, ibid., 826; encomia, ibid., 799. — Mass in honor of martyrs, ibid., 748. — Basilica of forty-eight martyrs, ibid., 555. — In ancient times baptism was solemnly administered on martyrs’ solemnities, a practice afterward prohibited, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 391. — Offerings on martyrs’ feast days are to be divided equally among the clergy, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 568. — The examples of saints fortify us against evils that rush upon us, St. Bruno, CLIII, 555. — Martyrs are the wall of the Church, Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 954. — The Catholic Church alone possesses true martyrs, ibid., 1077. — The Church does not distinguish feast days for Old Testament martyrs, because they did not attain the same form of martyrdom, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 231.

From the beginning, the Church recognized no veneration or worship except that of martyrs, St. Nicetas, LII, 1076, 1077. — The canonization of somewhat earlier non-martyred saints began from the discovery of their bodies, ibid., 1079. — Memorials of confessors are celebrated in the Church; encomium of confessors, Rabanus Maurus, CX, 70. — The solemn days of Christ’s confessors are called birthdays, Pope Nicholas, CXIX, 982.

Feasts of martyrs were instituted so that we may be admonished to imitate them, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 52, 1293, 1252, 1364, 1414, 1447. — So that we may be kindled to imitate them, id., XXXV, 1248. — Martyrs’ solemnities are exhortations to martyrdom, id., XXXIX, 2160. — Saints’ annual feasts are celebrated for our remembrance, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 356. — We celebrate the triumph of martyrs so that we may imitate their constancy, St. Leo the Great, LV, 26. — No memorial of martyrs is to be approved at all unless it is where a body or relics are present, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 170. — The commemoration of saints is a path to virtue, from the *Lives of the Fathers*, LXXII, 531. — Why feasts of apostles, or solemnities in honor of martyrs, were instituted, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 770; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 356.

Saints’ solemnities are to be celebrated most devoutly, St. Leo the Great, LV, 84. — One should rejoice at the commemoration of saints, id., LIV, 426. — When about to celebrate saints’ solemnities, let us have purity of mind, id., LV, 84. — The days of their death are to be celebrated with joy, for the glory and blessedness of our brethren, Alcuin, CI, 1211–1214. — At saints’ birthdays we rejoice in their glory, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 384. — The Church rejoices in the Nativity of her Son, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 556. — Martyrs’ birthdays are celebrated with annual joy in remembrance of the event, ibid., 565. — It is not so much death as faith and devotion that makes a martyr, ibid., 552, 553. — A crowd stands at a martyr’s death as also at the annual feast, but in a different manner, ibid., 555. — Their feasts are celebrated by fervent prayer and faithful imitation, ibid., 602. — Martyrs’ solemnities must be celebrated through imitation of their virtues, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1414. — To honor martyrs’ feasts without imitating them is nothing other than to flatter falsely, ibid., 1447. — Certain Christians insult the solemnities of martyrs by their extravagances, id., XXXVI, 867. — Whoever wishes rightly to celebrate martyrs’ birthdays should desire to imitate the martyrs, ibid., 869. — They truly honor them who imitate them, id., XXXIX, 2160. — The Savior is praised by the honoring of martyrs, ibid., 2154. — Feasts of saints are to be honored with divine praise and almsgiving, Alcuin, C, 472. — We ought to celebrate their memorials solely in order that posterity may be stirred to imitate them, St. Agobard, CIV, 214. — It is blameworthy to honor saints’ memorials ostentatiously in pursuit of popular glory, ibid., 213. — One must especially abstain from vices and sins on feast days, John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 263. — Superfluous things are not to be done, ibid., 59. — Fast days precede the principal saints’ feasts [Col. 0500], so that through purification by abstinence we may be found worthier and more capable of spiritual joys, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 501. — On the vigil of Holy Mary, St. John, and the apostles, on the appointed vigils of other saints, and on their feasts, blessed breads (*eulogiae*) are to be distributed to the people after Mass, Pope St. Eutychian, V, 166. — In various places, banquets are held on martyrs’ solemnities and on every feast, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 146. — At first the Church permitted martyrs’ feast days to be celebrated with luxury, ibid., 118. — Banquets on martyrs’ birthdays, ibid., 115. — Feasts at martyrs’ tombs, St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 601. — Abuse, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 480. — Saints’ feasts are not celebrated in lavish banquets but in imitation of them, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 555. — We rightly admire saints’ virtues when we ascribe them to the goodness of the Creator, St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 302. — The faithful are to be exhorted to virtue by saints’ examples, ibid., 339. — On saints’ solemnities one must abstain from marital intercourse, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1645. — The people should devote themselves to divine offices, not dances or songs, ibid., 1782. — Public entertainments are by no means to be held, Fulgentius Ferrandus, LXXXVIII, 931. — The passions of martyrs are read in churches on their anniversary day, St. Leo the Great, LVI, 429; Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 196; St. Gregory of Tours, XXXI, 781, 1119; Fulgentius Ferrandus, LXXXVIII, 830; St. Benedict, Abbot, CIII, 898. — The lives of saints are to be heard gladly, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 747.

That birthday feasts are not to be held during Lent: Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 170; Fulgentius Ferrandus, LXXXVIII, 828; Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 371; John of Rouen, CLVII, 46, 94. — Except on Saturday and Sunday: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 324, note; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 134; Atto, CXXXIV, 44; John of Rouen, CXLVII, 46, 94. — Memorials of martyrs are not to be held on fast days, Fulgentius Ferrandus, LXXXVIII, 899. — Nor on Sundays after Easter, John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 56. — The bodies of martyrs are rightly placed beneath the altar, upon which Christ is placed above, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 689. — Transferred bodies are buried beside the altar, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 888. — Martyrs overshadow with the branches of their protection the places where they suffered, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 879. — How great is the love for visiting saints’ tombs, ibid., 835. — Lights at saints’ tombs, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 872. — Lamps are to be set up in cemeteries around Rome on birthday anniversaries, Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVIII, 1929. Lamps are to be supplied from the Lateran for martyrs’ cemeteries on every Sunday, ibid., 623. The solemnities of Masses were celebrated in cemeteries even in the seventh century, ibid., 891.

The multitude and devotion of those celebrating the birthday of St. Felix, St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 405. — Songs at martyrs’ feasts, Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXIX, 1114. Praises of saints whose relics are laid in the basilica at Naumetum, Venantius Fortunatus, LXXXVIII, 126. — The annual feast day of SS. Juventius and Maximinus, Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXIX, 1054. Feasts of saints celebrated with chapter among the Carthusians, Guigo, CLIII, 1149. — New feasts are not to be instituted rashly or without consideration, except by the Apostolic See, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 335. On the observance of saints’ feasts: Prudentius, CV, 486; Amalarius, ibid., 1300; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 356; John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 184. — On the feasts of various apostles and saints, Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1659. — January feast days, id., CX, 1122. — Full enumeration of April’s feasts and saints, ibid., 1138. — Description of June’s feasts, ibid., 1148; July’s, 1154; August’s, 1160. — On appointing and observing saints’ feasts, Rodulf, CXIX, 740. — On transferring them, John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLIX, 272.

On saints’ feasts in the monastery of Cluny, Udalric, CXLIX, 674.

On the veneration of saints, Thiafrid, CLVII, 507. — On saints’ birthday feasts and their octaves, Amalarius, CV, 1228. — Memorial of saints, St. Eulogius, CXV, 739. — Martyrological record, ibid., 821. — History of the translation of saints’ bodies, Priest Joseph, CVI, 891. — Rite for bringing relics into a new basilica, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 422. On the dedication of a church by saints’ relics and the miracles which the Lord displayed on that day through his servants, Priest Joseph, CVI, 898.

## CHAPTER II. — The Common of Saints.

### § I. — The Common of Apostles.

Calendar of Jerome, XXX, 437. — The birthday feasts of the apostles are to be kept: St. Ivo, CLXI, 266, 267; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1781. Feasts of the apostles are general feasts, Beleth, CCII, 18. — Feast [Col. 0501] of all the apostles celebrated within the octave of SS. § IV.—27 December: St. John the Evangelist.

He was apostle, evangelist, and prophet, ibid., 868.—John was more intimate with Christ than the other disciples, Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 265, 303, 304.—He was honoured by Christ threefoldly in life: by intimacy, virginity, and keenness of understanding, ibid., 299.—He is to be honoured threefoldly in death, ibid., 306.—The day of his nativity is to be observed as a feast, St. Ivo, CLXI, [Col. 0504] 266, 267; Gratian, CLXXXII, 1781.—His feast, Calendar of St. Jerome, XXX, 437; St. Protadius, LXXX, 422; Martyrology of Ado, CXXIII, 177, 187, 204; Usuard, CXXIV, 843; ancient calendars and martyrologies, CXXXVIII, 1188, 1194, 1204, 1210, 1257, 1264, 1279; St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 193; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 33, 34; St. Isidore, LXXXV, 199; LXXXVI, 127; Amalarius, CV, 1273; Grimald, CXXL [probably CXXI], 860, 885; St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 857; Honorius, CLXXII, 646; Beleth, CCII, 77, 133; Sicard, CCXIII, 408.—A solemn assembly for his feast, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 866.—His feast has an octave, St. Protadius, LXXX, 422.—It is celebrated with a chapter among the Carthusians, Guigo, CLIII, 1149.—When Mass is finished, all the bells are rung, Udalric, CXLIX, 655.—Procession of priests wearing chasubles, John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 41.

§ VI.—18 January: Feast of the Chair of St. Peter at Rome.

§ VII.—22 February: Feast of the Chair of St. Peter at Antioch.

We read that three chairs are especially commended in Scripture: those of Moses, Elisha, and Peter, by which are signified the teaching of the Law, prophetic teaching, and apostolic teaching, Cardinal Henry, CCIV, 320.—Peter’s chair ought rather to be called Christ’s than Peter’s, ibid., 516, 519.

[Col. 0505] Feast of the Chair of St. Peter, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2101; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 50, 654 (note); Martyrology of St. Protadius, LXXX, 414.—Ancient calendars and martyrologies, CXXXVIII, 1199, 1236, 1262, 1273; Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 649, 783, 898.—The anniversary of the Chair is celebrated everywhere, St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 855.—The double feast of Peter’s Chair, Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 181, 182, 251, 256; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 50, 654 (note); Rabanus Maurus, CX, 1127, 1133; Martyrology of Ado, CXXIII, 147, 149, 217, 331; Beleth, CCII, 87.—Formerly the feast of both Chairs was celebrated on 22 February, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 303 (note). Later, the observance of the Antiochene Chair alone remained, ibid.; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 1133.—Martyrology of Ado, CXXXII, 149, 331; Usuard, ibid., 785; Notker, CXXXI, 1048.—We celebrate this because St. Peter was appointed bishop in the Antiochene see, Sicard, CCXIII, 411.

The feast of the Chair of St. Peter at Rome seems later, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 50 (note), 303 (note); Beleth, CCII, 87; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 1127; Martyrology of Ado, CXXIII, 147, 217; Usuard, 665; Notker, CXXXI, 1037.—It was not instituted by Gregory III, but perhaps restored by him, St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 480 (note).—The Chair of St. Peter at Rome in January is very ancient in Gaul, Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 181, 182, 251, 256; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 588.—In Spain, ibid.—Formerly it was customarily celebrated in January in Gaul and in February at Rome, ibid., 651 (note).—Hence arose the occasion for celebrating the feast twice, ibid.—How the feast of St. Peter’s Chair is celebrated if it falls outside Lent, Udalric, CXLIX, 655.—How it is celebrated if it falls within Lent, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2101; Guigo, CLIII, 1143, 1146; Sicard, CCXIII, 410.

Sermons on the feast, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 505; St. Ivo, CLXXII, 595; Peter of Celle, CCII, 817; Abbot Odo, CXXXVIII, 709.

Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1781.—Classed among the general feasts, Beleth, CCII, 18.—To be celebrated only in cities and parishes, St. Ivo, CLXI, 266.—It has a fast, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 120; Beleth, CCII, 73.—A vigil, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 120; § XVIII.—1 August: St. Peter in Chains.

This solemnity is celebrated on the Kalends of August, St. Jerome, XXX, 226.—Instituted by Pope St. Sylvester, ibid., 228.—So that the fisherman’s solemnity might overshadow the emperor’s solemnity, Beleth, CCII, 146; Sicard, CCXIII, 418, 419.—It received its name from the chains, St. Jerome, XXX, 228.—The chains are venerated on the feast-day itself, St. Gregory the Great, 391 (note).—The feast is not celebrated at its proper time, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 243.—It was observed with the greatest solemnity, Udalric, CXLIX, 656.—Celebrated by John of Würzburg in the little church at the prison itself, John of Würzburg, CLV, 1086.

The twofold feast of St. Michael—namely, his apparition and the dedication—Beleth, CCII, 134, 154.—This is called the feast of all angels, ibid.—We owe angels reverence, devotion, and trust, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII.

Dedication of St. Michael: Martyrology of St. Protadius, LXXX, 419; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 1171; Wandalbert, CXXI, 612; Ancient calendars and martyrologies, CXXXVIII, 1188, 1191, 1201, 1207, 1263, 1275.

Festival: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 143; Lanfranc, CL, 475; St. Anselm, CLIX, 215, 222; Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 1075; Honorius, CLXXII, 690, 1007; Beleth, CCII, 134, 154; Sicard, CCXIII, 414, 422.—To be kept as a holiday: St. Ivo, CLXI, 266, 267; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1781.—The feast has a vigil: eleventh-century charters, CLI, 1191.—And a three-day fast, ibid., 1167.—On it, the Peace of God applies, ibid., 1191.—The *Credo* is sung: John, archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 38.—When Mass is finished, the bells are rung: Udalric, CXLIX, 655.—The Carthusian brothers receive wine twice: Guigo, CLIII, 737.

Sermons on St. Michael: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 794; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 1169, 1172, 1175; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 447, 451; Peter of Blois, CCVII, 677, 681; Martin of León, CCIX, 37.

Homilies: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 445; Venerable Bede, XCIV, 441, 502; Paul the Deacon, XCV, 1522, 1525; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 58, 60; Haymo, CXVIII, 770; Radulphus Ardens, CLV, 1456, 1459; Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1040.

Mass: St. Isidore, LXXXV, 875.—Mass for Monday in honour of the holy angels: eleventh-century liturgical monuments, CLI, 937.

Sequences: Notker, CXXXI, 1018; eleventh-century liturgical monuments, CLI, 854, 907; Adam of St. Victor, CXCVI, 1523.

Preface: Grimald, CXXI, 914.

Hymns: St. Ambrose, XVII, 1218; Drepanius Florus, LXI, 1086; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1659.

Verses for the altar of St. Michael: Alcuin, CI, 737, 740, 770, 774.

§ XXV.—18 October: St. Luke the Evangelist.

Life of St. Luke: Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 185.—Feast day: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 144; Martyrology of Rabanus, CX, 1173; Wandalbert, CXXI, 615; Ancient calendars and martyrologies, CXXXVIII, 1188, 1201, 1207, 1247, 1263, 1275; Honorius, CLXXII, 1013; Beleth, CCII, 155; Sicard, CCXIII, 422.—At the feast the sequence is sung: Udalric, CXLIX, 655.

Sermons: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 644; St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 800; CXLV, 1010, 1069, 1070, 1159.

Homilies: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1138; Venerable Bede, XCIV, 443; Paul the Deacon, XCV, 1530; Radulphus Ardens, CLV, 1465.

Preface: Grimald, CXXI, 914.

§ XXVI.—28 October: Saints Simon and Jude.

Feast day of Saints Simon and Jude: Martyrology of St. Protadius, LXXX, 420; Rabanus, CX, 1176; Wandalbert, CXXI, 616; Ado, CXXIII, 171, 185, 385; Usuard, CXXIV, 629; Ancient calendars and martyrologies, CXXXVIII, 1188, 1202, 1208, 1248, 1263, 1277.—Festival: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 145; Lanfranc, CL, 479; Honorius, CLXXII, 1013; Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 177; Beleth, CCII, 155; Sicard, CCXIII, 423.—It is celebrated with chapter: Guigo, CLIII, 1149.—At Mass the sequence is sung: Udalric, CXLIX, 655.

Mass: St. Isidore, LXXXV, 888.

Homily: Venerable Bede, XCIV, 489.

Preface: Grimald, CXXI, 914.

Poems: Alcuin, CI, 768, 769; Flodoard, CXXXV, 499.

§ XXVII.—1 November: Feast of All Saints.

The feast of all saints was instituted by Pope Gregory III: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 409.—The Pantheon was dedicated by Boniface in honour of all saints: [Col. 0512] Alcuin, CI, 1230; Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVIII, 143; Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 216; Beleth, CCII, 133.—Feast day of all saints: St. Protadius, LXXX, 415, 420; Martyrology of Rabanus, CX, 1177; Wandalbert, CXXI, 617; Ado, CXXIII, 173, 587; Usuard, CXXIV, 641; Calendars and martyrologies, CXXXVIII, 1249, 1263, 1277; St. Jerome, XXX, 437; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 146; Alcuin, C, 294; CI, 1230; Udalric, CXLIX, 688; Lanfranc, CL, 475; Abbot Guido, ibid., 1242; Abbot Godfrey, CLVII, 46, 71, 76; Honorius, CLXXII, 690, 1013; Beleth, CCII, 133, 156; Sicard, CCXIII, 423.—To be kept as a holiday: St. Ivo, CLXI, 266, 267; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1781.—To be celebrated on the Kalends of November: Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 265; eleventh-century charters, CLI, 1191.—It has litanies: St. Isidore, LXXXIV.—A vigil: XCII, 401.—A fast: Alcuin, C, 496; Beleth, CCII, 156 [probably “156,” not “1561”].—A solemnity, ibid.—An octave, ibid.—This feast is very ancient in Gaul and Germany: Alcuin, C, 296.—It is celebrated in the same manner as the Assumption: CXLVII, 60, 114.—With the greatest solemnity: Udalric, CXLIX, 656.—It embraces saints from the earth: St. Bernard, CLXXXVII, 475.—The *Credo* is sung on it: John, archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 38; Lanfranc, CL, 481.—The first fruits of the earth are rendered: eleventh-century charters, CLI, 1174.—Communion is held: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 453.—The archbishops of Rouen made distributions: St. Peter of Blois, CCVII, 1179.—Sermons on the feast of all saints: Hildebert, CLXXI, 695, 701, 705; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 960, 1082, 1160, 1163; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 453, 462, 468, 471, 475; Abbot Guerric, CLXXXV, 205, 210; Isaac, CXCIV, 1689, 1693, 1701, 1704, 1708; Aelred, CXCV, 336, 339; Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1800, 1806; Peter of Celle, CCI, 880; Garnerius of Langres, CCIV, 798; Peter of Blois, CCVII, 685, 688, 693, 695, 697, 698, 700, 701, 703; St. Martin of León, CCIX, 45; Abbot Absalon, CCXI, 270, 277, 287; Helinand, CCXII, 668, 678, 687; Innocent III, CCXVII, 587, 589.

Homilies: St. Leo the Great, LIV, 461; Venerable Bede, XCII, 401; XCIV, 447, 450; St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 811; Radulphus Ardens, CLV, 1470, 1475; Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1043.

Mass: St. Isidore, LXXXV, 893.

Sequences: Notker, CXXXI, 1019; eleventh-century liturgical monuments, CLI, 854, 875, 899, 900; Adam of St. Victor, CXCVI, 1526.

Blessings: Grimald, CXXI, 876.

Hymns: Rabanus, CXII, 1668; Ratramnus, CXXI, 624; Heribert, CXLI, 1371.—Verses on all saints: St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 960.

§ XXVIII.—2 November: Commemoration of All the Faithful Departed. (Martyrology of St. Protadius, LXXX, 420.)

Offerings for the dead were made: Tertullian, II, 79; St. Cyprian, IV, 399.—In the time of St. Jerome, the same lessons as today were read: St. Jerome, XXX, 532.—Sacrifices of the altar and almsgiving for the departed: St. Augustine, XL, 158, 283; St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 507, 875.—Sacrifice for the departed: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 936.—Celebrated in cemeteries: ibid., 777; St. Leo the Great, LVI, 506.

Mass for the departed was customarily held on designated days: Cassian, XLIX, 530.—The third, seventh, and thirtieth days after death are observed: Alcuin, 1278, 1280; Hincmar, CXXV, 775.—And likewise the anniversary day, ibid.—An anniversary for the dead should be anticipated rather than deferred: Beleth, CCII, 75.—Various Masses for the departed: St. Isidore, LXXXV, 1010, 1027.—At every solemn celebration of Mass, prayer should be made for the departed: Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1730.—Solemn vigils for the dead: Rabanus Maurus, CX, 128; Atto, CXXXIV, 974.—The commemoration of the faithful departed follows the Feast of All Saints: Guigo, CLIII, 655; Hildebert, CLXXI; Sicard, CCXIII, 424.—Formerly there was a fast on it: Hildebert, CLXXI, 612.—A proper Compline was recited: John, archbishop of Rouen, CXXVII, 60.—The high altar and the celebrant are incensed: ibid., 126.—The Hours of the day precede the Office of the Dead: ibid., 60, 114.

Homilies for the day of souls: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1746; XXXVIII, 935; XXXIX, 1961.

Office: St. Isidore, LXXXVI, 977; John, archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 126.—Beleth, CCII, 156, 159, 161.—On the commemoration of all the faithful: Udalric, CXLIX, 688.—On the celebration of the departed and the resurrection of the dead: Rabanus Maurus, CX, 130.

Hymn for the funeral rites of a deceased person: Aurelius Prudentius, LIX, 875.

§ XXIX.—11 November: St. Martin.

[Col. 0513]

Feast day of St. Martin: Martyrology of St. Protadius, LXXX, 420; Rabanus, CX, 1178; Wandalbert, CXXI, 618.—Festival: Heribert, CLXI, 609; Lanfranc, CL, 475; Beleth, CCII, 164; Sicard, CCXIII, 431.—The first fruits of seed were rendered on it: eleventh-century charters, CLI, 1174.—At Tours it has an octave: St. Protadius, LXXX, 420.

Sermons on St. Martin: Abbot Odo, CXXXIII, 749; Alphanus, CXLVII, 1145.

Sequence: Notker, CXXXI, 1020.

Hymns: St. Ambrose, XVII, 1217, 1218; Ermodus, bishop, LXIII, 333; Walafrid Strabo, CXIV, 1086; Abbot Odo, CXXXIII, 515.

PART FIVE. ON SUNDAY.

CHAPTER ONE.—On Sunday in General.

Under the old law, three times of Sabbath rest were consecrated: Aelred, CXCV, 575, 628.—“Sabbath” means freedom from work or rest: Ratherius, CXXXVI, 557; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 308; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 587. One must not abstain from work on the Sabbath with the Jews: St. Jerome, XXII, 1221, 1222; St. Leo the Great, LVI, 718; St. Fulgentius Ferrandus, LXXXVIII, 827; Humbert, CXLIII, 937; St. Ivo, CLXI, 1121; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1784.—Sabbath rest prescribed: Eugyppius, LXII, 725.—The Sabbath was abolished together with the Law: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 394, 512.—Sunday is preferred to the Jewish Sabbath: St. Isidore, LXXXIII, 761.—It is preferred by faith in the Resurrection, not by the custom of eating: St. Augustine, XXX, 146.—Sunday is called the first day of the Sabbath: idem, XXXVI, 532; XXXVII, 1192, 1960; Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXX, 170; St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 337 (note).—Sunday took the place of the Sabbath: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 507.—Holier than the Sabbath: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 197, 198.—Most holy and most celebrated: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 507.—Declared holy by God: St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 279.—Sunday, the perfect Sabbath, was devoutly observed by the apostles: St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 239.—It signifies a greater rest: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 197.—Honour must be paid to it: Jonas, bishop of Orléans, CVI, 304; Abbot Regino, CXXXII, 396.—The Sabbath is illuminated by Christ, so that it may shine in the Church on Sunday: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 411.—Sunday is the primary Sabbath; the Jewish Sabbath is secondary: ibid., 417.—The Jewish Sabbath is the memorial of creation; the first day of the Sabbath is the memorial of restoration: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 197.—The many names and privileges of Sunday: St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 333, 336.—It is endowed with great privilege by both divine and human law: ibid.—Praises of Sunday: Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 64.—Sunday is the day of our salvation and joy: St. Leo the Great, LIV, 279, 280.—It was revealed not to Jews but to Christians by the Resurrection: Eugyppius, LXII, 760; St. Isidore, LXXXIII, 761.

Sunday is called the Lord’s Day by the Lord: Eugyppius, LXII, 685; St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 173.—It is called the day of the Lord’s Resurrection: St. Leo the Great, LIV, 625, 682; St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 808; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 476 (note); St. Isidore, LXXXII, 231; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 308.—The apostles established the Lord’s Day as a religious solemnity because on that same day the Redeemer rose from the dead: St. Isidore, LXXXIII, 760; Venerable Bede, XCIV, 551; Alcuin, CI, 1226; Rodulphus, CXXX, 716; Humbert, CXLIII, 937.

Sunday is an image of the Resurrection: Atto, CXXXIV, 105.—It is called the eighth day: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 532; LXXVI, 972.—The eighth day signifies regeneration: Eugyppius, LXII, 685.—Sunday is the third day from the Passion, but the eighth from creation: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1027.—It is called the day of the sun: St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 336 (note); eleventh-century liturgical monuments, CLI, 514, 1175.—It is called the Lord’s Day because it belongs to the Lord: Ratherius, CXXXVI, 156.—It is to be honoured as the day of the Lord: ibid.—Every Sunday is Easter: ibid., 557.—God made the other days by his command; he consecrated this one by his blood: ibid.—On Sunday both the world was created and Christ was born: Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 73.—Christ sanctified Sunday by his Resurrection; for Sunday is the first day of the age, the day of the Resurrection, and the day of Pentecost, and is therefore holy: St. Egbert, bishop of York, LXXXIX, 384.—Sunday is observed both because of the Resurrection, because of the sending of the Holy Spirit from heaven, and because John so named it: Beleth, CCII, 17.—Through Sunday the glory of the Resurrection is displayed: Haymo, CXVIII, 884.

Christians observed Sunday: Tertullian, II, 79; Philastrius, XII, 1273.—Its sanctification was instituted by the apostles: [Col. 0514] Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 356; CX, 76.—It is founded upon Sacred Scripture.—God blessed and sanctified this day: St. Victor, martyr, V, 307.

Constantine commands the observance of Sunday: Eusebius Pamphilus, VIII, 224.—The Sabbath of Christians is in the tranquillity of a good conscience: St. Augustine, XXXNII [sic; reading uncertain], 1172.—One must rest from the laborious desire for temporal things: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 332.—To sanctify the Sabbath is to devote oneself to good works: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 467.—And not to cease from them: St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 277.—He who works well on the holy Sabbath is holy: ibid.—By the true sanctification of the Sabbath, love of the world is slain: LXII, 725.

Privileged Sundays: Beleth, CCII, 94.

Sunday is to be observed from evening to evening: St. Eutychian, V, 166; St. Benedict, abbot, CII, 1144; Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 190, 260; Udalric, XXXV, 1073; CXXXVIII, 497; Burchard, CXL, 644.—From Saturday afternoon until daybreak on Monday: Anonymous works (*Opera adespotica*), CXXXVIII, 497; CLI, 1175.—From morning until evening: idem, CXXXVIII, 624, 625.

On Sundays the Office is divided into three nocturns: Sicard, CCXIII, 154.—All attend the morning vigils: St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 807, 978; Aunarius, CXXXVIII, 253.—Eating before Mass is forbidden: ibid., 255.—Sunday night: hymns and sacred mysteries: *From the Lives of the Fathers*, LXXIII, 611.—Communion on Saturday and Sunday under Pachomius: ibid., 1110.

On Sunday, water is to be blessed before Mass: Pope St. Leo IV, CXV, 679; Udalric, CXXXV, 1072; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 560; Richard, CXL, 634; St. Ivo, CLXI, 193.—Sprinkling of the altars and choir: John, archbishop, CXLVII, 158.

On Sunday a procession is to be held: Hartmann, LXXXVII, 32; John, archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 40, 43; Udalric, CXLIX, 654.—The Sunday procession represents Christ’s Resurrection: Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 130.—It is celebrated in memory of that which the disciples offered Christ as he ascended into heaven: Beleth, CCII, 20.

The solemnities of Mass are to be celebrated: St. Augustine, XLI, 829; Theodulf, CV, 198; Burchard, CXL, 749; Udalric, monk of Cluny, CXLIX, 654.—They are solemnly celebrated about the seventh hour: St. Augustine, XLI, 829.—In the monastery of Cluny there are two Masses, the morning Mass and the principal Mass: Udalric, CXLIX, 654.

Every Sunday, something from the Gospel or Epistle is to be proclaimed to the people: Pope St. Leo IV, CXV, 679.—Read: Udalric, bishop of Augsburg, CXXXV, 1072.—Preached: Anonymous works (*Opera adespotica*), CXXXVIII, 502.

“Glory to God in the highest” is to be sung: Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVII, 143; Abbot Berno, CXLII, 1059; Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 210.

In every church, the Creed is to be recited every Sunday: St. Isidore, LXXXIV, 351.—Sung: John, archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 38; Lanfranc, CL, 481.—The *eulogiae* are to be distributed to the people after Mass: St. Eutychian, V, 166.

This day is to be observed: Eusebius Pamphilus, VIII, 73; St. Isidore, LXXXIV, 255; St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 335, 336 (note); Abbot Odo, CXXXIII, 950; Atto, CXXXIV, 106.—It is to be sanctified: St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 959, 1159.—Worldly cares must be avoided: Jonas, bishop of Orléans, CVI, 304.—The whole day is to be devoted to God alone: Rodulphus, bishop of Bourges, CXIX, 716.—St. Martin always celebrated the Sunday solemnities without blemish: St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 917.

Attendance at Mass: St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2275; St. Maximus, bishop of Turin, LVII, 719; Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 405; Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 279, 363, 457, 459, 461; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 563; Burchard, CXL, 638; Anonymous works (*Opera adespotica*), CXXXVIII, 587, 595; eleventh-century liturgical monuments, CLI, 1246.—Swineherds and oxherds are to come to Mass on Sundays and feast days: Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 279, 363, 457, 459, 461; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 563; Burchard, CXL, 638.—On Sundays clerics must attend the solemnities of Mass: Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 586.—A bishop must not be absent from church on Sundays: Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1783.—No one may leave the church until the divine mysteries are completed: St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2276, 2278.—The people must not be diverted from public Masses by private Masses: Theodulf, CV, 205.—Parishioners absent from the divine offices on Sundays are to be noted: John, archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 254.

Hearing of the sacred word: St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 335, 336 (note).

Communion on every day of Lent: Rodulphus, CXIX, 718, 719; Burchard, CXL, 749; St. Ivo, CLXI, 193.—The Greeks communicate every Sunday, whether laypeople [Col. 0515] or clerics; and those who have not communicated for three Sundays are excommunicated: Theodore, archbishop, XCIX, 955.

Devotion to good works: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 467; St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 572; St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 335, 336 (note); Ratherius, CXXXVI, 557; St. Ivo, CLXI, 266.

Abstention from servile work: St. Eutychian, V, 166; St. Jerome, XXII, 1221, 1222; St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 572; St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 980, 988; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 255, 610; St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 335, 336, 338 (note); Theodore, archbishop, ibid., 954; Alcuin, CI, 1247; St. Benedict, abbot, CIII, 1182; Theodulf, CV, 198; Pope Nicholas, CXIX, 985; Abbot Regino, CXXXII, 251; Abbot Odo, CXXXIII, 950; Atto, CXXXIV, 37; Udalric, bishop of Augsburg, CXXXV, 1072; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 557; Anonymous works (*Opera adespotica*), CXXXVIII, 587, 595; Burchard, CXL, 641; eleventh-century liturgical monuments, CLI, 1175, 1179, 1246; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 279.—Servile works are not to be performed on Sundays: men are neither to undertake rural work nor hunting, and women are not to perform textile work: Anonymous works (*Opera adespotica*), CXXXVIII, 587, 595.—No cleric may presume to prosecute any secular business on Sunday: Atto, CXXXIV, 37.

Abstention from sins: St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 335, 336, 338 (note); St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 279.—Those must be rebuked who, for the sake of a worldly banquet, despise the heavenly meal, and abandon Christ’s table while taking delight in a human table: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 719.—It is reprehensible to gorge oneself with meat on Sunday: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1551, 1552.

Abstention from marital intercourse: St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 952; St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 338 (note); Abbot Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 249; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 566; Burchard, CXL, 960, 1000, 1013.—The person who consummates a marriage on Sunday night is reproved: Ratherius, CXXXVI, 570.—Let him do penance for four days: Theodore, XCIX, 947.—Abstention from hunting: Anonymous works (*Opera adespotica*), CXXXVIII, 587, 595; ecclesiastical laws of Cnut, CLI, 1175.

On it, *agapae* are not to be held: Fulgentius Ferrandus, LXXXVIII, 829.—Carting: Walter, bishop, CXIX, 737.—Judgements and lawsuits: Eusebius Pamphilus, VIII, 224; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 719; St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 338 (note); Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 420; Anonymous works (*Opera adespotica*), CXXXVIII, 854; Burchard, CXL, 888.—Markets: St. Agobard, CLV, 75; Walter, bishop, CXIX, 737; Anonymous works (*Opera adespotica*), CXXXVIII, 706.—Trade: ecclesiastical laws of King Cnut, CLI, 1175.—Market-days: St. Ivo, CLXI, 267, 274.—Commercial dealing: Anonymous works (*Opera adespotica*), CXXXVIII, 458, 461.—No legal assembly is to be held: Regino, CXXXII, 346; Anonymous works (*Opera adespotica*), CXXXVIII, 587, 595; ecclesiastical laws of Cnut, CLI, 1175; St. Ivo, CLXI, 267, 274.—No oath is to be sworn: Regino, CXXXII, 346.—No spectacles are to be held: Fulgentius Ferrandus, LXXXVIII, 931; Atto, CXXXIV, 43.—No one is ever to be put to death judicially on it: laws of Alfred the Great, CXXXVIII, 458; laws of King Cnut, CLI, 1179.—Bathing is not to be forbidden: Pope Nicholas, CXIX, 981; Gratian, CLXXXVIII, 1784.

Things permitted and forbidden on Sunday: St. Ivo, CLXI, 267, 268.

One who violates Sunday is punished by God: St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 562, 808, 971, 972, 979, 986, 987, 1073.—Or who works on it: ibid., 1007, 1040.—By human law: laws of Edgar, CXXXVIII, 497, 624.

Those who work on Sunday: the Greeks rebuke them the first time, take something from them the second time, and the third time take a third part of their goods; moreover, they are beaten or must do penance for seven days: Theodore, archbishop, XCIX, 934.—If anyone presumes to engage in commerce on Sunday, he forfeits his capital: laws of Alfred the Great, CXXXVIII, 458; for holding a market, laws of Edgar, ibid., 461.—If a free person works, he is to suffer a fine; if a slave, he is to be beaten: laws of Cnut, CLI, 1179.—The obstinate offender is to be beaten and shorn: laws of Stephen, ibid., 1246.

The many privileges of Sunday: St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 335, 336 (note).—They gave themselves to joy on Sunday: Tertullian, I, 375.—The Church customarily spends Sunday always in joy: St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 335, 336 (note).—Therefore let us feast every Sunday: Ratherius, CXXXVI, 557.—There is to be no fasting on it: St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 239; St. Leo the Great, LVI, 886; Dionysius Exiguus, LVII, 160; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 204, 615, 634; Fulgentius Ferrandus, LXXXVIII, 826, 887; Venerable Bede, XCIV, 533; St. Benedict, abbot, CIII, 1140, 1144, 1353; Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVII, 143; Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 269, 347, 424; Regino, CXXXII, 371; Atto, CXXXIV, 44, 45; Burchard, CXL, 888; St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 330; St. Ivo, CLXI, 265, 269, 271; Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 96, 98; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1784, 1785; CLXXXVIII, 205.—Because of the joy of the Sunday Resurrection: Venerable Bede, XCIV, 533; St. Benedict [Col. 0516], abbot, CIII, 1353; Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 96.—Anyone who deliberately fasts on Sunday is not to be regarded as Catholic: St. Leo the Great, LVI, 886; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 204.—The Manichaeans fasted on Sunday and Monday in honour of the sun and moon: St. Leo the Great, LIV, 274.

No kneeling: St. Hilary, IX, 249; Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 152; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 97, 624; Fulgentius Ferrandus, LXXXVIII, 887; St. Benedict, abbot, CIII, 1144; Atto, CXXXIV, 42; Burchard, CXL, 641; St. Ivo, CLXI, 261, 267.

The consecration of bishops takes place: St. Leo the Great, LIV, 634; St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 298; Abbot Regino, CXXXII, 378; John, archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 59.—The Office of the Dead is not to be celebrated except at a burial or anniversary: ibid., 37, 56, 191.—Lamps were established in churches for sacred readings on Sundays and feast days: Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVIII, 1227, 1243.—Faustinianus was baptized by St. Peter on Sunday: Orderic, CLXXXVIII, 122.—Sundays are counted from the feast day of St. Cyprian: Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 299.

On Sunday: Alcuin, CI, 1226; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 355; John, archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 61.—Litanies for the procession on Sundays: Hartmann, LXXXVII, 32.—Sunday procession after Easter: John, archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 55.—Homily on Sundays: Rabanus Maurus, CX, 76.

CHAPTER II.—On Particular Sundays.

On Sundays from Advent to Septuagesima: Lanfranc, CL, 448.

§ I.—On the Advent of the Lord.

The Advent of the Lord is not celebrated without cause: St. Ambrose, XVII, 604, 605.—We celebrate the Advent of the Lord for a twofold reason: Sicard, bishop, CCXIII, 192; Godfrey, CLXXIII, 21, 36, 42.—For a threefold reason: Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 641.—Christ’s Advent was foretold by the prophets: ibid., 643.—It is preached through Isaiah: Alan of Lille, CCX, 232.—It began at the beginning of the world in holy men, prophets, and sacrifices: Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 131, 132.—Christ’s Advent is incomprehensible: Alan of Lille, CCX, 237.—The various advents of Christ into the world: Hildebert, CLXXI, 351.—The name “Advent” is known to the whole world, but the reason for the name is not equally known: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 33.—Christ’s Advent is necessary: ibid., 53.

Christ’s Advent is twofold: St. Ivo, CLXII, 565; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 46; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 252; Sicard, bishop, CCXIII, 192.—Christ’s first Advent was like the whisper of a gentle breeze: Abbot Rupert, CLXXVIII, 24.—This one was peaceful, breaking bow and sword: ibid., 50.—Mercy and truth: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 252.—Comparison of the second Advent with the first: Abbot Godfrey, CLXXVIII, 21, 36, 42.—The distinction: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 302.—The first concerns the soul; the second, the body: ibid., 52.—The first was in humility; the second will be in majesty: Sicard, bishop, CCXIII, 192.—Christ’s carnal Advent is called both “going out” and “coming in”: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 965.—The Church now awaits Christ’s second Advent: Abbot Guerric, CLXXV, 11.

Christ’s Advent is threefold: one in the flesh, one in the spirit, one in glory: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 587.—In flesh and weakness; in spirit and power; in glory and majesty: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 49.—To human beings, into human beings, against human beings: ibid., 44.—Of grace, of glory, and of both together: Abbot Guerric, CLXXXX, 16.—In charity, in flesh, in glory: Alan of Lille, CCX, 214, 237.

The circumstances of Christ’s Advent: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 34.—Its effects: Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXX, 663; St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 62.—Christ came to help and teach us: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 676.—Not only for instruction but also for deliverance: idem, CLXXXII, 1070.—Through Christ’s Advent the calling of the Gentiles is manifested: Honorius, CLXXII, 643.—The wounds of the world were healed: Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXX, 416.—The human race was healed: ibid.—The devil was bound; humankind set free: ibid., 136.—At the Lord’s Advent the earth was moved: ibid., 123.—Eternal rewards are prepared for those who await and love Christ’s Advent: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 485.—The pious desires of the Church awaiting the Bridegroom’s Advent: ibid., 477, 537.—Christ coming is to be met with exultation: Abbot Guerric, ibid., 15; Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 97, 98.—The Savior’s Advent is to be awaited as that of a bridegroom: ibid., 108.—The season of Advent is a time for singing mercy and judgement to the Lord: Aelred, CLXXXIV, 817.—A time of sanctification: St. Ambrose, XVII, 604, 605, 607, 608.—Sermons are to be delivered to the people: ibid., [Col. 0517] 604, 605.—Evening sacrifices three times a week: Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 168, 169, 170.—Songs of joy are silent: John, archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 40, 165; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 441, 442; Beleth, CCII, 71.—Except for the *Alleluia*, ibid.—For nine days before the Nativity the altars are incensed: John, archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 176.—For eight days before the Nativity, antiphons: ibid., 123, 159, 184.—On Advent Sundays at Rouen, the deacon and subdeacon wore chasubles: ibid., 38, 75, 159, 165, 168, 208.—No procession is held on Saturdays from Advent until Easter: ibid., 40, 83.

Fasting is to be observed in Advent: St. Philastrius, XII, 1286; Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 168, 169, 170; Beleth, CCII, 73.—Formerly a fast of forty days was prescribed: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 433 (note).—It varied according to the diversity of times and places: ibid., 434 (note).—How it was observed by monks in Gaul: ibid., 434, 531.—By Romans: ibid.—By penitents: St. Egbert, bishop of York, LXXXIX, 425, 426.

Abstinence from meat: Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 168, 169, 170; Ratherius, CXXXXI, 564, 565; Dunstan, CXXXVII, 486.—From marriage from Advent until after the octave of Epiphany: St. Eutychian, V, 167; St. Ambrose, XVII, 605; St. Ivo, CLXI, 616; Beleth, CCII, 71.—From wives: St. Eutychian, V, 167; St. Ambrose, XVII, 605; Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 168, 169, 170; Regino, CXXXII, 249; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 565.—For twenty days after Christmas: ibid.; Burchard, CXL, 960, 1000, 1013.

From Advent until the next Monday after Epiphany, peace is to prevail everywhere: eleventh-century liturgical monuments, CLI, 1134.—Ordeals and oaths are entirely forbidden: ibid., 1175.

The Advent of the Lord is celebrated from the fifth day before the Kalends of December until the third day before the Nones of the same month: John, archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 157.—It ought to contain twenty-one days apart from the vigil of the Nativity: Beleth, CCII, 72.—Various ways of counting the Sundays in Advent: Abbot Berno, CXLII, 1065.—Six are counted in Ambrosian Masses: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 733 (note).—In the Mozarabic Missal and Breviary: St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXV, 139.—Elsewhere five are counted: St. Gregory, LXXXVIII, 144, 190, 191, 192, 433.—Four: ibid., 189, 433.—Three complete weeks: Beleth, CCII, 74.

The history of the second week is taken partly from prophetic books and partly from Gospel books: Sicard, bishop, CCXIII, 206.—The history of the third is compiled partly from the prophets and partly from the Gospel: ibid., 207.—In the fourth week, the common texts of both Advents are sung: ibid., 214.

The week immediately before the Nativity of the Lord is called the Preparation: Honorius, CLXII, 644.

On the Advent of the Messiah: Amalarius, CV, 1158, 1218; Samuel the Moroccan, CXLIX, 345; Udalric, ibid., 690; eleventh-century liturgical monuments, CLI, 1003; Odo of Cambrai, CLX, 1103; St. Ivo, CLXII, 565; Abbot Stephen, CLXVI, 1385; Rupert, CLXX, 55; Honorius, CLXXII, 641, 732, 796, 1077.—On fasting in the Advent of the Lord: Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 66.—On the diversity of those observing the four fasts: Abbot Berno, CXLII, 1087.—On the seven solemn antiphons of the Advent of the Lord: Cardinal Henry, CCIV, 260.—Blessings in Advent: Grimald, CXXI, 857.—Responsory: King Robert, CXLI, 944.—Sermons: St. Ambrose, XVII, 603, 607, 608, 665; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 531, 533, 843, 845, 847; Atto, CXXXIV, 833; Abbot Werner, CLVII, 733, 751; St. Ivo, CLXXII, 527; Hildebert, CLXXI, 343, 347, 351, 352, 364, 370, 376; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 911; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 35, 40, 43, 47, 50, 52, 54; Aelred of Rievaulx, CLXXXIV, 817; CXCV, 209, 363; Abbot Guerric, CLXXXV, 11, 14, 18, 21, 26; Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1721, 1725, 1732, 1735; Peter of Celle, CCII, 637, 641, 644, 647, 648, 649; Garnerius of Langres, CCV, 559, 570, 583, 591; Peter of Blois, CCVII, 559, 564, 568; St. Martin of León, CCVIII, 31, 37; Alan of Lille, CCX, 214; Abbot Absalon, 15, 20, 26, 31, 38; Helinand, CCXII, 481.—Homilies: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 221, 225, 227, 233, 235; Venerable Bede, XCIV, 22; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 10.

Practice of the Church: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXXVII, 875.

On the first Sunday of Advent: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 190; St. Isidore, LXXXV, 109; LXXXVI, 47; Grimald, CXXI, 905; John, archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 123; eleventh-century liturgical monuments, CLI, 857, 949; Rupert, CLXX, 56; Honorius, CLXXII, 728; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 876; Innocent III, CCXVII, 313, 319, 323.

Sermons: Abbot Werner, CLVII, 729, 1217; Abbot Odo, CLXXXVIII, 1645; Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 102, 106, 111, 119, 127.

[Col. 0518] Homilies: St. Maximus, bishop, LVII, 226; Venerable Bede, XCIV, 318; Paul the Deacon, XCV, 1459; Haymo, CXVIII, 11; Radulphus Ardens, CLV, 1667, 1671; Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 747, 749; Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 21, 25, 32, 36, 42, 46.

On the second Sunday of Advent: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 190; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXV, 121; LXXXVI, 68; Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 58; Honorius, CLXXII, 643, 728; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 876; Innocent III, CCXVII, 327, 333.—Sermons: Abbot Werner, CLVII, 739; Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 135, 141, 146, 151, 157, 162, 168, 174, 181, 186, 190, 194.—Homilies: St. Maximus, bishop, LVII, 227; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1077; Venerable Bede, XCIV, 320; Haymo, CXVIII, 17; Radulphus, CLV, 1675, 1678; Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 752; Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 51, 55, 60.

On the Fourth Sunday of Advent: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 192; St. Isidore of Spain, LXXXV, 130; LXXXVI, 87; Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 66; Honorius, CLXXII, 643, 729, 731; Homilies: St. Maximus, bishop, LVII, 221; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1099; the Venerable Bede, XCIV, 332; Haymo, CXVIII, 41; Radulph Ardens, CLV, 1688, 1691; Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 753; Godefrid, CLXXIV, 82.

On the Sunday immediately before the Nativity of the Lord: St. Isidore, LXXXV, 139; LXXXVI, 107; Honorius, CLXXII, 644.—Sermon: Abbot Werner, CLVII, 757.—Homily: the Venerable Bede, XCII, 133.—Sermon on the Vigil of the Nativity: Werner, CLVII, 763, 767.

§ III.—On the Sundays from the Nativity of the Lord to Septuagesima.

On the Sunday within the Octave of the Nativity, or on the First Sunday after the Nativity: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 37; Amalarius, CV, 1275; Grimald, CXXI, 802, 861, 886; Honorius, CLXXII, 647.—Sermons: Abbot Werner, CLVII, 793; Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 334, 342, 352, 363.—Homilies: Paul Winfrid (from Origen), XCV, 1179; the Venerable Bede, XCIV, 339; Haymo, CXVIII, 83; Radulph Ardens, CLV, 1719, 1721; Godefrid, CLXXIV, 89.

On the First Sunday after Epiphany: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 50; Amalarius, CV, 1278; Grimald, CXXI, 803, 862, 887; Honorius, CLXXII, 648; Innocent III, CCXVIII, 345.—Sermons: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 499, 501, 503; the Venerable Bede, XCIV, 63; Abbot Werner, CLVII, 813, 818; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 155, 157; Blessed Father Isaac, CXCIV, 1713, 1716; Peter of Blois, CCVIII, 590.—Homilies: Haymo, CXVIII, 120; Radulph Ardens, CLV, 1734, 1737; Bruno of Asti, CXLV, 767; Abbot Godefrid, CLXXIV, 95, 102.

On the Fourth Sunday after Epiphany: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 48; St. Isidore, LXXV [probably LXXXV], 252; LXXXVI, 220; Grimald, CXXI, 803, 863, 887.—Sermons: Abbot Werner, CLVII, 833; Abbot Isaac, CXCIV, 1732, 1735, 1738.—Homilies: the Venerable Bede, XCIV, 343; Paul Winfrid (from Origen), XCV, 1196; Haymo, CXVIII, 147; Radulph, LLV [probably CLV], 1753, 1753, 1756; Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 768; Godefrid, CLXXIV, 125.

[Col. 0519] On the Fifth Sunday after Epiphany: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 48; St. Isidore, LXXXV, 256; LXXXVI, 224; Grimald, CXXI, 804, 863, 887.—Sermons: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 253, 257; Abbot Werner, CLVII, 837.—Homilies: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 433; Godefrid, CLXXIV, 125.
