§ IV.—On the Sundays from Septuagesima to Easter.

On Septuagesima.—On the Sundays from Septuagesima to Passion Sunday: Lanfranc, CL, 452; Honorius, CLXXII, 755.—Septuagesima is called the beginning of Lent: St. Rupert, abbot, CLXX, 508.—It is reckoned among the five principal Sundays: Lanfranc, CL, 475.—It is celebrated differently in different places: Alcuin, C, 259, 263; CI, 1183.—Various interpretations of Septuagesima: Amalarius, CV, 993, 994; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 346; Pope Nicholas, CXIX, 1207, 1208; St. Ivo, CLXII, 577.—It is called Septuagesima from “seventy”: Honorius, CLXXII, 652; Beleth, CCII, 82; Sicard, CCXIII, 244.—It is so called not from seventy days but from seven Sundays: Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 87.—It is calculated as nine weeks before the Lord’s Easter and ends after Easter on the Saturday of the seventh week: the Venerable Bede, XCIV, 534; Amalarius, CV, 993, 994; Alanus, CCX, 210.—It consists of ten weeks from that day until the close of Easter: Alcuin, C, 261.—The number seven is perfect in Scripture: ibid., 571.—It is sacred and mystical: St. Benedict, abbot, CIII, 899.—Septuagesima corresponds to the first age of the world: Cardinal Henry, CCIV, 361, 362, 395.—It bears the type and figure of the present life: Alanus of Lille, CCX, 210.—It recalls the past and signifies the present: Sicard, CCXIII, 244.

It is a season of weeping and penitence: Anonymous, XIII, 641.—Of mourning: Beleth, CCII, 71.—One must cease from excessive rejoicing: Anonymous, XLI, 641.—During it life is to be renewed: St. Ambrose, XVII, 631, 632.—Songs of joy fall silent: Anonymous, XIII, 641; John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 40, 165; Eleventh-Century Diplomatic Monuments, CLI, 1012; Honorius, CLXXII, 651; Beleth, CCII, 71.—Organs are not played: John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 165.—If the Feast of the Purification falls within Septuagesima, nothing is changed in its observance except the Alleluia: Eleventh-Century Liturgical Monuments, CLI, 1012; Sicard, CCXIII, 410.—The same applies to the feasts of St. Matthias and of the Annunciation: Beleth, CCII, 87; Sicard, CCXIII, 410.—Also to the Chair of St. Peter, the Dedication, the special patronal feast, and Easter in its anniversary observance: ibid.—The celebration of Septuagesima at Rouen: John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 38, 75, 159, 165, 168, 208.—At the monastery of Cluny: Udalric, CXLIX, 655.—During it rich food is omitted: Dunstan, CXXXVII, 488.—The beginning of the ecclesiastics’ fast: St. Gregory, LXXVIII, 305.—It was added to complete the Lenten fasts: the Venerable Bede, XCIV, 533; Alcuin, C, 259, 262; CI, 1184; St. Benedict, abbot, CIII, 1200; Beleth, CCII, 84.—From Septuagesima until the Octaves of Easter have passed, marriages are forbidden: St. Eutychian, V, 166; St. Ivo, CLXI, 616; Beleth, CCII, 72.—So too marital intercourse: St. Eutychian, V, 166.—Oaths and ordeals are prohibited until the fifteenth day after Easter: Eleventh-Century Diploma, CLI, 1175.—The Peace of God is maintained until after the Octaves of Pentecost: ibid., 1134.—Until the Octaves of Easter have passed: ibid., 1193.

On Septuagesima: St. Ambrose, XVII, 631, 632; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 53; Alcuin, CI, 1182, 1184; St. Benedict, abbot, CIII, 1198; Amalarius, CV, 993, 1281; Udalric, CXLIX, 696; Eleventh-Century Liturgical Monuments, CLIV, 1012; Stephen, CLXVI, 1395; Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 88; Honorius, CLXXII, 651, 689, 737, 783, 851; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 443; Beleth, CCII, 81; Cardinal Henry, CCI, 361; Sicard, CCXIII, 243; Innocent III, CCXVII, 351, 355.—On the rationale of Septuagesima: Alcuin, C, 259, 263; CI, 1182; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 878.

Sermons: Anonymous, XIII, 611; St. Ambrose, XVII, 630, 632; St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 524; Abbot Werner, CLVII, 843, 849; St. Ivo, CLXII, 577; Hildebert, CLXXI, 419; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 1043, 1046; Abelard, CLXXVIII, 425; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 161, 166; Abbot Odo, CLXXXVIII, 1649; Abbot Isaac, CXCIV, 1741, 1945; Garner of Langres, CCV, 657; Peter of Blois, CCVII, 599; [Col. 0520] St. Martin of León, CCVIII, 554, 559.—Homilies: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1153; Paulinus Winfrid, XCV, 1205; Haymo, CXVIII, 154; Radulph Ardens, CLV, 1759, 1762; Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 770; Abbot Godefrid, CLXXIV, 131, 139, 144.

Office: John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 124. Blessings: Grimald, CXXI, 863.

Preface: ibid., 887.

Responsory: King Robert, CXLI, 943.—Hymn: Walafrid Strabo, CLIV, 1083.

On Sexagesima.—The name and mystical significance of Sexagesima: Hildebert, CLXXI, 421.—The sixth Sunday from the last is called Sexagesima: Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 88.—Sexagesima derives its name from sixty: Alcuin, C, 259, 263; John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 45, 206.—It extends from that very day to mid-Easter: the Venerable Bede, XCIV, 534; Alcuin, CI, 1187; Amalarius, CV, 998; Beleth, CCII, 82.—Typical interpretations of Sexagesima: Amalarius, CV, 998; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 346; Pope Nicholas, CXIX, 1207, 1208.—The number six signifies perfection: St. Ambrose, XVII, 633.—Affliction and penitence: John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 46.—Widowhood: Sicard, CCXIII, 250.—It corresponds to the second age of the world: Cardinal Henry, CCIV, 361, 362, 395.—Sexagesima is the beginning of the Greek fast: the Venerable Bede, XCIV, 553; Alcuin, CI, 1182.—It was added to make up for Saturdays and Sundays: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 305.—By Pope Miltiades, to make up for Sundays and Thursdays: the Venerable Bede, XCIV, 533; Alcuin, C, 259; Beleth, CCII, 84.

On Sexagesima: St. Ambrose, XVII, 631, 632, 633; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 53; Alcuin, CI, 1182, 1184, 1187; St. Benedict, CIII, 1198; Amalarius, CV, 998, 1283; Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 93; Honorius, CLXXII, 653, 691, 739, 784; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 444, 878; Beleth, CCII, 81; Cardinal Henry, CCIV, 371, 395; Sicard, CCXIII, 250.—On the rationale of Sexagesima: Alcuin, C, 263; CI, 1182.

Sermons: Abbot Werner, CLVII; Abbot Isaac, CXCIV, 1749, 1752, 1756, 1758, 1761, 1765, 1768, 1772, 1774; St. Martin of León, CCVIII, 607.

Homilies: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1131; the Venerable Bede, XCIV, 345; Paul Winfrid, XCV, 1208; Haymo, CXVIII, 163; Radulph Ardens, CLV, 1765, 1768; Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 772; Abbot Godefrid, CLXXIV, 157.

Blessing: Grimald, CXXI, 863.—Preface: ibid., 887.

On Quinquagesima.—The Sunday which is fifth from the last is called Quinquagesima: Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 88.—Quinquagesima precedes Lent: St. Benedict, abbot, CIII, 1198.—Interpretations of Quinquagesima: Amalarius, CV, 999; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 346; Pope Nicholas, CXIX, 1207, 1208.—Pentecost is one thing, Quinquagesima another: Beleth, CCII, 135, 136; Sicard, CCXIII, 378. The period of fifty days is threefold: one is of penitence and affliction, another of joy, and the third of typology: ibid.—It is named from fifty days: St. Ambrose, XVII, 633; Alcuin, C, 259, 264.—It reaches to Easter Day itself: the Venerable Bede, XCIV, 534; Alcuin, C, 259; CI, 1189; Honorius, CLXXII, 654, 557; Beleth, CCII, 82.—The seven weeks of penitence are assigned for this reason: sins are remitted in seven ways: Honorius, CLXXII, 657.—The number fifty is that of remission: St. Ambrose, XIV, 866; Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 693; Sicard, CCXIII, 252. It expresses penitence: Honorius, CLXXII, 654.—Quinquagesima corresponds to the third age of the world: Cardinal Henry, CCIV, 361, 362, 395.—The beginning of the clerics’ fast: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1350; Alcuin, CI, 1182.—Observed by some: St. Ambrose, XVII, 633.—From it monks are to keep Lenten abstinence: Dunstan, CXXXVII, 488.—Why and how it is celebrated: Alcuin, C, 264; CI, 1189, 1230.

On Quinquagesima: St. Ambrose, XVII, 631, 632; Eugyppius, LXII, 979; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 54; St. Isidore of Spain, LXXXV, 282; LXXXVI, 243; Alcuin, C, 259, 263, 264; CI, 1182, 1189; Amalarius, CV, 999, 1285; Rupert, CLXX, 94; Honorius, CLXXII, 654, 691, 740, 784, 870; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 445, 879; Beleth, CCII, 81; Cardinal Henry, CCIV, 380, 395; Sicard, CCXIII, 251.

Sermons: Abbot Werner, CLVII, 849, 855, 859; Abbot Isaac, CXCIV, 1778, 1780, 1784; St. Martin of León, CCVIII, 621.

Homilies: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1081; the Venerable Bede, XCIV, 347; Paul Winfrid, XCV, 1210; Haymo, CXVIII, 172; Radulph Ardens, CLV, 1770, 1775; Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 775; Godefrid, CLXXIV, 158.

[Col. 0521] Blessings: Grimald, CXXI, 864; preface, ibid., 888.

On Ash Wednesday.—The ancient beginning of Lent in the Church was Wednesday before the First Sunday: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 301.—Something must be added to the days of Lent: St. Ambrose, XVI, 225.—The beginning of the Lenten fast, namely the Wednesday of Quinquagesima, began in the Church after the age of Gregory the Great: LXXVIII, 306 (note).

Wednesday is the beginning of Lent: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 949; Alcuin, CI, 1192; Adrevald, CXXIV, 1077; Anonymous, CXXXVIII, 595; Eleventh-Century Liturgical Monuments, XLI, 1013; Abbot Goffrid, CLVII, 143; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 445, 880; Sicard, CCXIII, 253.—On it penance was imposed: Alcuin, CI, 1192; John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 46; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 881.—The people are to be urged to confession: St. Eutychian, V, 166.—From Wednesday at the beginning of the fast until after the Octaves of Easter, public courts or assemblies are forbidden: Adrevald, CXXIV, 1077; Anonymous, CXXXVIII, 595.—The expulsion of penitents before the procession: John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 47, 94, 131.—Prostration: ibid., 131.—Penitential psalms: ibid., 96, 131, 132, 165.

At the beginning of the fast, Mass is at None, and everything follows the Lenten order: Eleventh-Century Liturgical Monuments, CLI, 1013.—Carthusians shave themselves: Guigo, CLIII, 653.—They alter the night and day offices and the prayers: ibid., 641.—They veil the crosses, to be uncovered on Good Friday: ibid.—On Wednesday at the beginning of the fast: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 55, 949; St. Isidore of Spain, LXXXV, 288; LXXXVI, 246; John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 125; Udalric, CXLIX, 696; Lanfranc, CL, 258, 452; Eleventh-Century Liturgical Monuments, CLI, 879, 955, 1013; Stephen, CLXVI, 1393; Honorius, CLXXII, 654, 656, 734, 741, 785, 875; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 445, 880; Sicard, CCXIII, 253; Innocent III, CCXVII, 357; Alcuin, CI, 1192.—Ceremonies of the Lenten beginning: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 432.

Sermons: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 205, 208, 212, 259, 634, 234, 484; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 301; Atto, CXXXIV, 839, 889; St. Ivo, CLXII, 579; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 167, 171, 173, 176, 178, 181, 183; Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1749; Peter of Celle, CCII, 677, 680; St. Martin, CCVIII, 631.

Homilies: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1287; XXXVIII, 243; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 301; the Venerable Bede, XCIV, 349, 500; Radulph Ardens, CLV, 1778, 1782; Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 777.

On Lent.—The First Sunday of Lent is called “Lent” because it begins here and ends on the Lord’s Supper: Beleth, CCII, 82; Sicard, CCXIII, 253.—Lent is to be observed before the Easter solemnity: St. Isidore, First Council of Orléans, LXXXIV, 277; Pseudo-Isidore, CXXX, 410.—There is one Lent according to apostolic tradition: St. Jerome, XXII, 475.—In certain monasteries there are two: St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 330.—Three: Thomas the Cistercian, CCVI, 130.—The Lenten fast before Easter was anciently adopted and observed by the Roman Church: Pope Nicholas, CXIX, 981.—It is ancient and holy: St. Ambrose, XIV, 699.—It was not instituted by human beings but consecrated by God: the same author, XVII, 661; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 309.—It is observed not superstitiously but by divine law: St. Augustine, XL, 492.—It is strengthened by the authority of both Testaments: Eugyppius, LXII, 761.—It is consecrated: the Venerable Bede, XCIV, 533.—It arises from divine and apostolic institution: St. Leo the Great, LIV, 275, 286, 294.—It has great authority from the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospel: Anonymous, XIII, 646; Alcuin, CI, 530.—Telesphorus did not so much institute the Lenten fast: Ado, CXXIII, 209; Gilbert, CXXXIX, 537; John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 212; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 36.—As ratify it: Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVII, 1175, 1177.—For the Fathers recognized that the Lenten fast had been instituted by the Lord: ibid.—It began from the fast of Moses and Elijah and from Christ’s forty-day fast: St. Ambrose, XVII, 635; St. Jerome, XXVI, 31; Cassian, XLIX, 1204; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1137; St. Isidore of Spain, LXXXIII, 771; Alcuin, CI, 1190, 1191.—The Lenten fast was prefigured by Moses and Elijah: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 335, 779; Hildebert, CLXXI, 466.—Consecrated by Christ: ibid.; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 310; Beleth, CCII, 84; St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2025, 2031.—And by the examples of the saints: ibid.—It is as it were the tithe of the year that we pay to God: Anonymous, XIII, 646; Cassian, XLIX, 1200; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1137; the Venerable Bede, XCIV, 534; Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 96; Honorius, CLXXII, 657; Beleth, CCII, 22, 84.—Lent is called from forty days: Honorius, 655.—Mystical interpretation of Lent: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 335, 779; Pope Nicholas [Col. 0522], CXIX, 1207, 1208; St. Ivo, CLXII, 580.—Various opinions on its etymology: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 346.—Septuagesima is called the beginning of Lent: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 430.—The beginning of Lent is regulated and observed according to the moon of March: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 715.—The beginning of Lent on the Wednesday before the First Sunday is most ancient in the Church: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 309.—The beginning of Lent is to be reckoned not from Ash Day but from the following Sunday: Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 183; Alcuin, CI, 1190.—Holy Lent: St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 1071.—Most holy: St. Leo the Great, LIV, 275, 301.—Consecrated days: Einhard, CIV, 958; Anonymous, XIII, 646.—Most sacred throughout the whole world: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1046, 1051.—Not to be defiled by lustful desires: Anonymous, XIII, 646.—But to be venerated with great devotion and religious reverence: ibid.—To be kept with every observance: St. Ambrose, XVII, 646; St. Donatus, LXXXVII, 285; Theodulf, CV, 203; Rodulf, CXIX, 718; St. Odo, abbot, CXXXIII, 950; Burchard, CXL, 884; St. Ivo, CLXI, 271; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1860.

The Lenten season is a season of remission: St. Ambrose, XIV, 381.—Of redemption and, as it were, heavenly medicine: the same author, XVII, 637.—Of reconciliation: ibid., 639.—Of remission through fasting and almsgiving: Hildebert, CLXXI, 466.—Of salvation: CLXXIV, 834.

The observance of Lenten fasts is pre-eminent: St. Augustine, XXXIV, 594; XLIII, 700.—Holy: St. Jerome, XXII, 813.—The Lenten fast: Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 258, 259.—Mystical and most sacred: St. Ambrose, XVII, 649.—Greatest and holiest: St. Leo the Great, LIV, 275, 301.—Useful and necessary to Christians: ibid., 283, 301.—It is called the Paschal fast: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 306 (note).—It is a preparation for Easter: St. Leo the Great, LIV, 291, 298; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 309.—The Church’s custom is that we prepare for the Lord’s passion and resurrection by fasting in body, as for spiritual nourishment: St. Jerome, XXVI, 57.—The season of the year and the number of days must be observed: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1047.—The fast is stricter than at other times: St. Jerome, XXII, 420.—It is good to fast at all times, and better to fast Lent with Christ: St. Ambrose, XVII, 647, 648, 649.—When we are preparing for the immolation of the Lamb: St. Jerome, XXX, 323.—Christ gave us the example of fasting: St. Maximus, LVII, 310.—We ought to follow him in fasting: the same author, LVII, 307.—Through these fasts of forty days God is reconciled, heaven is opened, and hell is unlocked: St. Ambrose, XVII, 639, 650, 654.—Carnal desires are restrained and the devil conquered: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 515; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 691.—It should be burdensome to no one: St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2027.—It is to be observed not only by those to be baptized but by all who have been reborn: St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2033.—It was formerly observed even by infants: Hildebert, CLXXI, 503.—Not to observe Lent altogether is sacrilege: St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2022.—To violate it in part is sin: St. Ambrose, XVII, 644, 647, 648; St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2022.—Unless illness excuses one: ibid.—Whoever violates it on one day is charged as a violator of the whole: St. Ambrose, XVII, 661.—Days of Lent: Rufinus of Aquileia, XXI, 313.—The number and nature of fast-days among Easterners, Greeks, and Latins: Alcuin, C, 259.—The fast of the primitive Church was longer: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 430.—No more than thirty-six days of the same abstinence are found: Anonymous, XIII, 646; Cassian, XLIX, 1204; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 306 (note); John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 46, 91; Hildebert, CLXXI, 466; Beleth, CCII, 84; Sicard, CCXIII, 253.—Four days were added afterwards: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 306 (note); St. Benedict, abbot, CIII, 1146; John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 46, 206; Beleth, CCII, 84.—Nevertheless, Christians were said to fast “Lent”: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 306 (note).—Forty days of fasting: St. Ambrose, XIV, 381; XVII, 639, 650, 654; St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 695, 1048, 1049, 1052, 1147, 1178, 1184; St. Leo the Great, LVI, 719; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 515; St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 1072; Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 258, 259; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 305 (note); LXXVI, 1137; Theodorus, XCIX, 932; Rabanus Maurus, XCII, 743; Atto, CXXXIV, 44, 45; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 565; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1783; Beleth, CCII, 84.—We fast forty days so that we may not exceed, in the forty days from Easter until the Ascension which we are to spend in joy: ibid.—Through these forty days we recall the forty years in which we know that the people returned from Egypt to their homeland: Sicard, CCXIII, 256.

The mystery of the number forty: St. Jerome, XXII, 416, 420, 428; St. Augustine, XXXIV, 48; XXXVIII, 352, [Col. 0523] 695, 1039, 1051, 1177, 1178, 1216, 1239; XL, 40, 96; St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 415.—It signifies the present Church: St. Augustine, XL, 40, 97.—It suggests the mystery of perfection: the same author, XLII, 895.—The number of affliction and sorrow: St. Jerome, XXV, 1010.—A type of penitence: Alcuin, C, 261, 530; Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 430.—It is suitably adapted to temporal life: Amalarius, CV, 1002.

It signifies the course of the present life: St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 1068.—Labor: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1041; Eugyppius, LXII, 979.—Humility: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1041.—Mourning: the same author, XXXVII, 1463.—Affliction: Haymo, CXVIII, 885; Honorius, CLXXII, 658; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 326.

It suits sinners, prayer, and sackcloth: St. Jerome, XXV, 1140.—Fasting: ibid.; Alanus of Lille, CCX, 205.

Various ways of observing Lent: St. Ambrose, XVII, 632.—Some abstain for six weeks: Alcuin, C, 251; Burchard, CXL, 885; Honorius, CLXXII, 657.—Others for seven: Alcuin, C, 251; CI, 1182; Gilbert, CXXXIX, 537; John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 212; St. Ivo, CLXI, 267; Honorius, CLXXXI [probably CLXXII], 657; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 36; CLXXXVIII, 200.—Pope Telesphorus decreed that clerics should abstain from meat and other luxuries for seven weeks before Easter: St. Ivo, CLXI, 267; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 36; CLXXXVIII, 200.—Seven weeks of abstinence are assigned for this reason: sins are remitted in seven ways: Honorius, CLXXII, 657.—These forty-two days are compared with the stations of the Israelites: St. Ambrose, XVII, 640, 641, 642, 643; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 311.—We fast six weeks because we sin in the six ages, and now hasten to make satisfaction through the six works of the Gospel: Honorius, CLXXII, 657.—Others abstain for eight weeks: Alcuin, C, 251.—At present there are forty days of fasting and forty-five of abstinence: John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 45, 46, 206.—Because through desires of the flesh we have despised the commandments of the Decalogue, it is fitting that we afflict that same flesh four times ten: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1137.—Easter concludes the fast: St. Ambrose, XIV, 708; St. Jerome, XXII, 790.

The observance of Lent: Cassian, XLIX, 669, 820.—It varies according to places and times: ibid., 1200; Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXIX, 1155; Anonymous Author, LXXIII, 1115; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 306, 307; Alcuin, CI, 1190.—How it was observed by monks: Anonymous Author, LXXIII, 1111.—Observed differently by the same persons: ibid., 1115.—Some sought solitude: ibid., 674.—How it was observed by St. Paulinus: St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 226.—By Louis I: Einhard, CIV, 967.—The Greeks use the Presanctified throughout Lent: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 324 (note).—On Saturdays, Sundays, and the feast of the Annunciation, they consecrate and do not fast: ibid.—The Greek fast begins at Sexagesima; the clerical fast at Quinquagesima: Alcuin, CI, 1182.—Sexagesima was added to make up for Saturdays and Sundays: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 305 (note).

One must fast every day, eating dry food: St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 194.—On every day except Sundays, the clergy are to take refreshment after Vespers: St. Chrodegang, LXXXIX, 1073.—Formerly, fasting was relaxed on Saturdays: Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 185; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 305, 324 (note).—Sundays are excepted from the Lenten fast: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1136; Radulph, CXIX, 718; Pseudo-Isidore, CXXX, 239; Atto, CXXXIV, 44, 45; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 565; St. Ivo, CLXI, 271; Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 98; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1784, 1860; Sicard, CCXIII, 253.—The fast is not to be relaxed even on the Lord’s Supper: Burchard, CXL, 886; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1783.—Gregory established that, during Lent, fasting and the celebration of Mass should take place on Thursday: St. Abbo, CXXXIX, 570.—Penitents fasted Lent on bread and water: St. Egbert, abbot, LXXXIX, 425, 426.—Readers who did not fast on Wednesday or Good Friday in Lent are to be deposed: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 314 (note).—Those who feast for seven days and fast for seven are rebuked: St. Ambrose, XVII, 649.—Some falsely pretend to observe Lent: St. Ambrose, XVII, 647; St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1044, 1045.—No one is to eat or drink before None during it: St. Ambrose, XXII, 655.—Before the evening hour: John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 272.—One must abstain from meat: Anonymous, XIII, 646; St. Jerome, XXII, 818; St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1040, 1043; XLII, 491, 493; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 1194; St. Ivo, CLXI, 267; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 36.—From certain fruits: St. Augustine, XLII, 491, 493.—Those who keep the precepts of the laws do without wine in fasts and reject the eating of meat: St. Jerome, XXII, 818; St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1040, 1143.—They restrain insatiable greed [Col. 0524]: St. Jerome, XXII, 818.—The fare of the poor is to be imitated by all: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1053.—The body is to be sustained on cheaper food: ibid., 1044, 1045.

Above all, one must fast from vices: the same author, XXXIX, 2025.—From works of the flesh and other luxuries: Anonymous, XIII, 646; St. Ivo, CLXI, 267; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 36.—From wives: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1040, 1043, 1045, 1047, 1052; Theodorus, archbishop, XCIX, 932.—From marriages: St. Leo the Great, LVI, 719; Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 170; Fulgentius Ferrandus, LXXXVIII, 828; Ratramnus, CXXI, 772; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 36.—From lawsuits: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1040.—From oaths and ordeals: Eleventh-Century Diplomatic Documents, CLI, 1175.—From courts and legal assemblies: *Opera adespota* (“anonymous works”), CXXXVIII, 595.—Let the Peace of God prevail everywhere: Eleventh-Century Diplomatic Documents, CLI, 1134.

Pious works are to be undertaken more fervently: St. Ambrose, XIV, 381; St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1040, 1041, 1052.—God is to be served more diligently and life lived more holily: St. Leo the Great, LIV, 264, 268, 272, 276, 286, 290, 295, 300, 302, 507.—Let fervor be greater: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 175.—On each Sunday of Lent the faithful ought to receive communion: Rodulf, CXIX, 718, 719; Burchard, CXL, 749; St. Ivo, CLXI, 167.—In Lent the sails of continence are to be spread: St. Jerome, XXII, 876.—Luxuries are to be curtailed, not exchanged for others: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1043, 1044.—More generous alms are to be distributed: ibid., 1040, 1042, 1045, 1046, 1047, 1052, 1053.—Enmities are to be ended: ibid., 1042, 1045, 1046, 1054.—Food for our soul for the whole year is to be provided: St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2019.—Spiritual losses are to be repaired: ibid.—A sermon is to be preached in the Lenten season: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 1057, 1179.—For the six days of Easter nothing besides bread, salt, and water is to be taken: St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 194 (note).—No one ought to celebrate the Lenten solemnity in a village: Pseudo-Isidore, CXXX, 411; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1783.—No baptism takes place in Lent: Fulgentius Ferrandus, LXXXVIII, 828.—At the beginning of Lent, infants to be baptized are to be presented: St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1751.

The Lenten veil is hung between us and the Holy of Holies: the same author, XXXII, 1457.—During these days all are to assemble for Vigils, Terce, Sext, and None: the same author, XXXIX, 2019.—The perfect go beyond the rule of Lent: Cassian, XLIX, 1207, 1208.—Monks are especially tempted in the Lenten season: ibid., 1204.—Snares are prepared by the devil: St. Leo the Great, LIV, 263.

Rogations held in Lent: St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 273, 278.—Songs of joy fall silent in Lent: St. Benedict, LXVI, 452, 453, 454; John, Archbishop, CXLVII, 38, 81, 165.—Bread is not to be offered except on Saturday and Sunday: St. Leo the Great, LVI, 719; Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 169; St. Isidore of Spain, LXXXIV, 134.—*Opera adespota* (“anonymous works”), CXXXIV, 589.—The anniversaries of martyrs are not to be celebrated; rather, their commemoration is to be made on Saturdays and Sundays: St. Leo the Great, LVI, 719; Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 170; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 324 (note); St. Isidore of Spain, LXXXIV, 134; Fulgentius Ferrandus, LXXXVIII, 828; Atto, CXXXIV, 44.—*Opera adespota* (“anonymous works”), CXXXVIII, 589; Burchard, CXL, 886; John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 46, 94.—From Septuagesima until Easter organs are not played: John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 165.—Celebration of the First Sunday among the monks of Cluny: Udalric, CXLIX, 654.—Celebration of the Chair of St. Peter among the Carthusians: Guigo, CLIII, 1143.—Whatever feast is celebrated in Lent receives in no way any greater observance than a single Sunday: Udalric, CXLIX, 656.—The celebration of the Feast of Dedication in Lent is forbidden: Lanfranc, CL, 657.—The feast of the Annunciation is suitably celebrated in Lent: Abbot Guerric, CLXXXV, 115.—Lent borders on Passion Sunday because this laborious life is signified: Eugyppius, LXII, 761.—So that we may understand that the affliction of the present life brings forth future immortality: Alcuin, CI, 1281.—It is most suitably adjoining and contiguous to the Passion: Amalarius, CV, 1002.

The Creed is to be publicly recited in all churches eight days before Easter: Burchard, CXL, 726.

On Lent: Eugyppius, LXII, 761; St. Philastrius, XII, 1273; St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 273, 278, 375, 429, 547, 602, 677, 956, 1033; the Venerable Bede, XCIV, 534, 535; Alcuin, CI, 1182, 1190; Amalarius, CV, 1001, 1286; Udalric, CXLIX, 696; Lanfranc, CL, 452; Eleventh-Century Liturgical Monuments, CLI, 1013; Honorius, CLXXII, 657, 685, 693, 742; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 445, 446, 880, 1057; Beleth, CCII, 81; Cardinal Henry, CCIV, 385, 395.—The end of Lent: CXXIX, 1282.—Method for finding the beginning of Lent: ibid., 1299.—Explanation of Lent: St. Ivo, CLXII, 580.—On the Sundays of Lent: Stephen, CLXVI, 1395.—On the two weeks before Easter: ibid., 1396.—On the seven weeks: [Col. 0525] Honorius, 657.—On the Sundays from Septuagesima to Easter: ibid., 755.

Sermons: St. Ambrose, XVII, 636, 637, 639, 642, 644, 646, 648, 651, 654, 657, 660, 662, 664, 665, 667, 668, 669; Peter Chrysologus, LII, 219, 222, 226, 287, 314, 317, 320, 634; St. Valerian, bishop, LII, 749; St. Leo the Great, LIV, 263, 267, 272, 274, 281, 285, 288, 291, 294, 297, 301, 305, 488, 490.—Sermons on fasting: the same author, LIV, 168, 172, 173, 174, 176, 180, 182, 185, 188, 437, 438, 441, 444, 447, 450, 453, 456, 458; LVI, 1131; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 558, 561, 563, 565, 567, 569, 573, 575, 577, 579, 583, 585, 587; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 689; St. Ivo, CLXII, 581; Hildebert, CLXXI, 428, 432, 440, 451, 456, 463, 467, 471; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 167, 171, 173, 176, 178, 181, 183; Abbot Guerric, CLXXXV, 91, 96; Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1752; Garner of Langres, CCV, 662; Peter of Blois, CCVII, 600, 603, 605, 607; St. Martin of León, CCVIII, 633; Absalon, abbot, CCXI, 102, 108, 115.

Homilies: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 303, 307, 311, 313, 318, 319, 323, 325; St. Eligius, LXXXVII, 603.

Hymns: St. Ambrose, XVII, 1202, 1211; Aurelius Prudentius, LIX, 842, 856; Walafrid Strabo, CXIV, 1083.

Responsory: King Robert, CXLI, 943.

On the Sunday and first week of Lent: St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 57; St Isidore, LXXXV, 296; LXXXVI, 258; Grimald, CXXI, 864, 888; eleventh-century liturgical monuments, CLI, 841; Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 96; Honorius, CLXXII, 691, 785, 879; Sicard, CCXIII, 256; Innocent III, CCXVII, 371.---Sermons: St Peter Chrysologus, LII, 219, 222, 226, 231, 275, 479; St Leo the Great, LIV, 308; Abbot Werner, CLVII, 860, 863, 872; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 1179; Abbot Isaac, CXCIV, 1787, 1790, 1793; Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1754, 1757; Peter of Celle, CCII, 682; St Martin of León, CCVIII, 675.---Homilies: St Leo the Great, LIV, 268; St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1134, 1135; the Venerable Bede, XCIV, 83, 110, 356, 364; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 20; Haymo, CXVIII, 190, 208, 217; Radulphus Ardens, CLV, 1785, 1788, 1795; Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 782; Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 165.

On the Sunday and second week of Lent: St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 62; St Isidore, LXXXV, 316; LXXXVI, 322; Grimald, CXXI, 864, 889; Rupert, CLXX, 98; Honorius, CLXXII, 691, 785, 886; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 881; Sicard, CCXIII, 265.---Sermons: St Peter Chrysologus, LII, 183, 187, 190, 194, 365, 529, 533, 536, 540; Abbot Werner, CLVII, 873; Abbot Isaac, CXCIV, 1797, 1800, 1809, 1812; St Martin of León, CCVIII, 741.---Homilies: St Leo the Great, LIV, 272; the Venerable Bede, XCIV, 96, 102; Paul the Deacon, XCV, 1233, 1248, 1252; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 22; Haymo, CXVIII, 226, 238, 244; Radulphus Ardens, CLV, 1797, 1800; Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 789; Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 191.

On the Sunday and third week of Lent: St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 65; St Isidore, LXXXV, 333; LXXXVI, 379; Grimald, CXXI, 865, 890; Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 99; Honorius, CLXXII, 692, 786, 889; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 881; Sicard, CCXIII, 268; Innocent III, CCXVII, 381.---Sermons: St Peter Chrysologus, LII, 246, 572, 647; Abbot Werner, CLVII, 877; Abbot Isaac, CXCIV, 1817; St Martin of León, CCVIII, 755.---Homilies: St Leo the Great, LIV, 275; the Venerable Bede, XCIV, 106, 380; Paul the Deacon, XCV, 1267, 1272; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 24; Haymo, CXVIII, 253, 268, 272; Radulphus, CLV, 1803, 1805; Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 794; Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 210.

On the Sunday and fourth week of Lent: St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 69; St Isidore, LXXXV, 353; LXXXVI, 438; Grimald, CXXI, 865, 891; Honorius, CLXXII, 692, 786, 894; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 882; Sicard, CCXIII, 272; Innocent III, CCXVII, 380, 393.---Sermons: St Peter Chrysologus, LII, 379, 382, 487; Abbot Werner, CLVII, 887; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 1015; Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1761; Peter of Celle, CCII, 694, 695, 699; St Martin of León, CCVIII, 769.---Homilies: St Leo the Great, LIV, 281; the Venerable Bede, XCIV, 110; Paul the Deacon, XCV, 1293, 1299; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 25; Haymo, CXVII, 284, 305, 315; Radulphus, CLV, 1815; Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 800; Godfrey, CLXXIV, 235.

On the Sunday and fifth week of Lent: St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 72; St Isidore, LXXXV, 370; LXXXVI, 500; Grimald, CXXI, 865; Honorius, CLXXII, 787.---Sermons: St Peter Chrysologus, LII, 460, 467.---Homilies: Rabanus Maurus, CX, 27; Haymo, CXVIII, 327, 342, 347; Radulphus Ardens, CLV, 1820, 1823; Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 244.

On Passion Sunday.---The days of the Lord’s Passion are reckoned from two weeks before the Lord’s Easter: Amalarius, CV, 1199.---Most fittingly, for two weeks [Col. 0526] the memorial of the Passion is recalled, a Passion which is written and prefigured through the two ages of the world: ibid.

The Carthusians changed the chapters, omitting the customary suffrages until the Monday after the octave of Easter: Guigo, CLIII, 646.---“Glory to God in the highest” is kept silent: Rupert, CLXX, 122.

After the most orderly arrangement of seven Sundays, by which the seven ages of the world—all redeemed by the Passion—are represented, the celebration of Passion Sunday itself begins: Sicard, CCXIII, 287.

Passion Sunday: St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 73; Amalarius, CV, 1199, 1291; Udalric, CXLIX, 698; Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 119; Honorius, CLXXII, 734, 908; Sicard, CCXIII, 287.

Sermons: St Peter Chrysologus, LII, 557; Abbot Werner, CLVII, 895; Peter of Celle, CCII, 725, 728, 731, 734; St Martin of León, CCVIII, 791, 799; Abbot Absalon, CCXI, 137, 148.

Homilies: Blessed Pope Leo, LIV, 313; St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1149, 1150; Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 802.---Homilies for Passion Week: Paul the Deacon, XCV, 1317, 1322.

Office: Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 883.

Responsories: King Robert, CXLI, 943.

Preface: Grimald, CXXI, 893.

Hymns: St Ambrose, XVIII, 1197, 1203.

On Palm Sunday.---The practice of the Church on Palm Sunday: St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 956; St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 76; St Isidore, LXXXV, 388; LXXXVI, 565; Alcuin, CI, 1200; Amalarius, CV, 1008; Udalric, CXLIX, 698; Abbot Guido, CL, 1195; eleventh-century liturgical monuments, CLI, 879; St Ivo, CLXII, 584; Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 129; Honorius, CLXXII, 658, 662, 734, 744, 913; Sicard, CCXIII, 292.

Various names for this Sunday: Hildebert, CLXXI, 502; Alcuin, CI, 1200.---The feast is called that of Palms or of Olives: St Ambrose, XVII, 667.---“The day of head-washing” (*Capitilavium*): Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 127.---Called the Sunday “in Palms” at the handing over of the Creed: ibid., 263.---“Flowering Easter”: Sicard, CCXIII, 343.

“We call it the feast of Palms or of Olives because, while singing psalms, we carry branches of palms or olives in our hands”: St Ambrose, XVII, 667; St Isidore of Seville, LXXXII, 251.---“It is called Palm Sunday because on this day the crowds came out to meet the Lord with palms and received him in triumph with praises”: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 347; Honorius, CLXXII, 662; Sicard, CCXIII, 293.---The palm signifies Christ’s triumph: Alcuin, CI, 650.---It signifies the cross: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 946.---“In vain does he carry an olive branch whom the devil overcomes by deceiving him”: St Ambrose, XVII, 669.

It is celebrated on the fifth day before the Passion: St Ambrose, XVII, 608.---It is a most ancient solemnity: St Gregory the Great, 309 (n.).---At it a procession is made with blessed branches: ibid.; John XIX, CXLI, 1129, 1130; Archbishop John of Rouen, CXLVII, 95, 111, 117, 118; Hildebert, CLXXI, 502; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 473; Beleth, CCII, 20.---“The Church celebrates a procession with branches and flowers, carrying olives and palms in its hands”: Sicard, CCXIII, 293.---This procession is not to be counted among the other Sunday processions: ibid.

Palm Sunday has two processions: Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 129; Dunstan, CXXXVII, 489.---On that same day the Lord came down from Bethany to Jerusalem: Anonymous, XIII, 652; Amalarius, CV, 1008.---In it Christ is presented glorious and humiliated: Abbot Guerric, CLXXXV, 135.---Ceremonies of this feast among the monks of Cluny: Udalric, CXLIX, 654.---In the church of St Peter, before John XIX, no procession with palms was held: John XIX, CXLI, 1129.---Blessing of palm and olive: edict of Otto III, CXXXVIII, 1057; eleventh-century liturgical monuments, CLI, 843; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 473.

Office: Archbishop John of Rouen, CXLVII, 125; Stephen, CLXVI, 1397; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 884.

Mass: eleventh-century liturgical monuments, CLI, 843.

Sermons: Atto, CXXXIV, 842; Abbot Werner, CLVII, 899, 903; St Ivo, CLXII, 586; Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 997; Hildebert, CLXXI, 476, 481, 485, 491, 502; Abelard, CLXXVIII, 429, 435, 443, 448; St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 253, 256, 259; Aelred, CLXXXIV, 869; CXCV, 258, 264; Abbot Guerric, CLXXXV, 127, 130, 134, 137; Richard of St Victor, CXCVI, 1059; Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1764; Peter of Celle, CCII, 735; Garnerius of Langres, CCV, 669; St Martin of León, CCVIII, 811, 827, 831; Abbot Absalon, CCXI, 143; Helinand, CCXII, 544, 554, 561, 572, 580.

Homilies: St Augustine, XXXVI, 172; St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 327; the Venerable Bede, XCIV, 120, 121; Rabanus Maurus, [Col. 0527] CX, 29; Haymo, CXVIII, 353, 355; St Peter Damian, CXLIV, 543; Radulphus Ardens, CLV, 1827, 1830; Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 805; Godfrey, CLXXIV, 258, 269, 271, 275, 288, 292.

Preface: Grimald, CXXI, 894.

Hymn: Walafrid Strabo, CXII, 1083.

Verses to be sung by boys on Palm Day: Theodulf, CV, 304.

On the three days before Easter.---On the offices in the nights from the Lord’s Supper until Easter: St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 959.---During the three days before Easter, the nocturnal office was celebrated at night: Archbishop John of Rouen, CXLVII, 168.---Bells are not to be rung: ibid., 50, 170, 206.---The kiss of peace is not given: ibid., 49, 53, 170, 175, 177, 296.---Private Masses are forbidden: ibid., 99.---A general communion of people and clergy takes place: Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 193; St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 324, 338 (n.); Bishop Rodulfus of Bourges, CXIX, 718, 719; Archbishop John of Rouen, CXLVII, 50, 52, 98, 100, 101, 128, 131, 132, 175, 206.---In the Rule of St Benedict, a deceased person is buried without light or incense: Lanfranc, CL, 1143.

For the two days before Easter there is no consecration: St Leo, LIV, 515; St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 379 (n.); Archbishop John of Rouen, CXLVII, 49, 206.

On the Lord’s Supper.---Thursday at the Lord’s Supper: Archbishop John of Rouen, CXLVII, 127.---The Lord’s Supper is the Thursday of the final week of Lent, when he first handed over to the apostles the mystery of his body and blood: St Isidore, LXXXIII, 764; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 347; Honorius, CLXXII, 662.---It is called the Supper because the Lord is said to have supped with his disciples today: ibid., 665.---It is called Great Thursday: St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 81.---“The birthday of the chalice”: Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 187.---Celebrated for four reasons: Honorius, CLXXII, 662.---The mystical Lord’s Supper is prepared with fear and love: Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 60.---Christ ate the Passover by which his coming Passion was signified, before he suffered: St Fulgentius, bishop, LXV, 431.---At the same Supper he ate the Jews’ Passover and instituted ours: ibid.

At the Lord’s Supper there are three Masses: St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 318 (n.).---Two in Africa: ibid.---The hour of Mass is moved earlier: ibid., 314 (n.).---On the final Thursday, the offering is made in some places only at evening, but elsewhere both in the morning and at evening: St Augustine, XXXIII, 202.---The Mass is performed in gladness and the Hours in sadness: Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 136.---Penitential psalms are recited: Archbishop John of Rouen, CXLVII, 96, 131, 172, 165.---At the church of St Peter, before John XIX, “Glory to God in the highest” was not said at the Lord’s Supper: John, CXLI, 1129, 1130.---At the Lord’s Supper, “Glory to God in the highest” is to be sung: ibid.---On this day penitents are to be reconciled: Rabanus Maurus, CX, 482; Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 696; Archbishop John of Rouen, CXLVII, 132; Hildebert, CLXXI, 520; Honorius, CLXXII, 662; Gratian, CLXXXVIII, 1786.---Chrism is consecrated: St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 316 (n.); John XIX, CXLI, 1129; Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 140; Honorius, CLXXII, 662.---Oil is blessed: St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 316 (n.); edict of Otto III, CXXXVIII, 1063; Honorius, CLXXII, 662.---A communion of clergy and people takes place: Ratherius, CXXXVI, 562 (n.), 694; Burchard, CXL, 749, 763; Archbishop John of Rouen, CXLVII, 50, 98, 103, 177; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1738.---“While the fast was observed until None, on the other days the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood was received”: Ratherius, CXXXVI, 697.---A procession takes place to carry away Christ’s body: Archbishop John of Rouen, CXLVII, 50, 127, 128.---Formerly all the bells were rung at Vespers: ibid., 50.---The altars are stripped: St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 335 (n.); Archbishop John of Rouen, CXLVII, 49, 50, 99, 171.---They are incensed: ibid.---Altars, walls, floors, and sacred vessels are washed: St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 333, 334 (n.); St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 764.---Some do not wash on Thursday or relax the fast, while others do otherwise: St Augustine, XXXIII, 202.---The washing of feet takes place: St Isidore, LXXXIV, 556; St Benedict, CIII, 1201; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 694, 718; Rupert, CLXX, 143.---Formerly some relaxed the fast: St Gregory, LXXVIII, 318 (n.).---At the Supper it must not be relaxed: Ecclesiastical Rules, LXVII, 169; St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 134; Fulgentius Ferrandus, LXXXVIII, 828; Alcuin, CI, 559; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 694; Burchard, CXL, 886; St Ivo, CLXI, 273; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1783.

A miracle concerning the baptistery built at Embrun by St Marcellinus was formerly accustomed to occur annually on Christmas Day and at the Lord’s Supper: St Gregory the Great, LXXXVIII, 390 (n.).---How the Lord’s Supper is performed among the monks of Farfa: Abbot Guido, CL, 1197.---Among the Carthusians: Guigo, CLIII, 643.---Pope Victor II was ordained on the Lord’s Supper [Col. 0528]: Berthold, CXLVII, 343.

On the Lord’s Supper: St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 81, 951, 1009; Alcuin, CI, 1203; Amalarius, CV, 1009, 1200; Candidus, CVI, 61, 62, 63, 64, etc.; Udalric, CXLIX, 656; eleventh-century liturgical monuments, CLI, 843, 880; St Ivo, CLXII, 586; Stephen, CLXVI, 1398, 1399; Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 138; Honorius, CLXXII, 735, 745, 787, 921; Abbot Ernald, CLXXXIX, 1641, 1650; Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1615; Beleth, CCII, 95; Sicard, CCXIII, 301; Innocent III, CCXVII, 397.

Office for Thursday at the Lord’s Supper: St Isidore, LXXXV, 406; LXXXVI, 596; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 449, 886, 887, 889.

Blessing: Grimald, CXXI, 865.

Preface: ibid., 895.

Verses and prayers at the Lord’s Supper: Ratherius, CXXXVI, 1077.

Sermons: Ratherius, CXXXVI, 714; St Peter Damian, CXLV, 1033; Abbot Werner, CLVII, 907, 909, 911; St Ivo, CLXII, 588; Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 1001; Hildebert, CLXXI, 505, 510, 524, 531, 534, 538, 543; St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 271; Ogerius, CLXXXIV, 880, 883, 889, 895, 898, 902, 905, 910, 912, 920, 929, 935, 940, 944, 946, 949; Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1768, 1769; Peter of Celle, CCII, 738, 742, 748, 751, 757, 761, 766, 769; Garnerius of Langres, CCV, 673; Peter of Blois, CCVII, 611, 614; St Martin of León, CCVIII, 837, 843, 865.

Homilies: St Augustine, XXXVI, 761; St Eligius, LXXXVII, 607, 611, 612, 614, 628, 630, 638, 639; the Venerable Bede, XCIV; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 30; Haymo, CXVIII, 440; St Peter Damian, CXIV, 553; Radulphus Ardens, CLV, 1833, 1838; Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 780.

Friday in *Parasceve* (Preparation Day).---The day on which Christ suffered: St Philastrius, XII, 1273; St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 707, 833; From the *Lives of the Fathers*, LXXXII, 467.---Friday in Easter itself: St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 365, 366.---A privileged day: Beleth, CCII, 99.---The sequence of the Old Testament shows that the day of the Passion and that of the Resurrection must be celebrated separately: St Ambrose, XVI, 1033.---“On the former we fast; on the latter we are refreshed”: ibid., 1029.---The feast of the Passion: From the *Lives of the Fathers*, LXXIV, 32.---The solemnity of the Preparation Day: Alcuin, CI, 1207.---The time of Christ’s Passion is now the most festive season of the whole world: St Augustine, XLII, 179.

The day of Christ’s Passion and Resurrection, by which we were freed from the devil’s slavery, is most celebrated: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 29.---*Parasceve* means “preparation”: Alcuin, CI, 1207; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 557; Rupert, CLXX, 153; Honorius, CLXXII, 666; Beleth, CCII, 99.---Why? Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 450.---Because on this day the Lord offered for us and on our behalf that manna of sweetness which may suffice us for the Sabbath of eternity: Sicard, CCXIII, 311.---It is called the pure supper and the Sabbath of rest: Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 153.---*Phase* [Passover]: Sicard, CCXIII, 343.

The Preparation Day is held in solemn observance because on that day Christ fulfilled the mystery of the cross: St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 764; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 348.---On Friday the first human being was created, on the same day deceived, and on the same day reconciled through Christ: Hildebert, CLXXI, 504.---On the same day humanity was formed, deformed, and re-formed: Sicard, CCXIII, 311.---The Savior’s Passion is the salvation of human life: St Ambrose, XVII, 674.---In what month and on what day of the month Christ is believed to have been crucified has been variously reported by the Fathers: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 704, 721.---The memorial of Christ’s Passion was held once a year: Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVII, 1147.---These things were committed to writing and confirmed by decree by Alexander rather than recently established: ibid., 1149.---On this day the faithful of the primitive Church either made a station before God or fasted: St Victor, martyr, V, 307.---Constantine commanded both ordinary people and soldiers themselves to observe Friday: Eusebius Pamphilus, VIII, 73.---Christ was dishonoured by the Jews on Preparation Day: Baldwin, CCIV, 1132.

It is fitting that he who deigned to suffer for the salvation of all should be publicly praised: Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXX, 833.---In Christ’s Passion the divinity was not absent: ibid., 153.---The Lord’s death is described: ibid., 400.---Various circumstances of the Lord’s Passion: Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 888, 897.---The mystery of the Cross and Redemption was prefigured in ancient times: St Leo the Great, LIV, 318.---On Christ’s crucifixion, in which the distinction between the elect and the reprobate is figured through the thieves: ibid., 322.---Our salvation is set upon the cross: ibid., 325.---The power of the Lord’s cross: Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 455, 456.---Christ’s cross joins heaven and earth: St Peter Damian, CXLIV, 762.---Three matters are to be considered in Christ’s Passion: the work, the manner, and the cause: St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 262.---Christ, exalted on the cross, drew all creatures into communion with his Passion: St Leo [Col. 0529] the Great, LIV, 325.---At the Paschal solemnity Christ chose to suffer: ibid., 331.---We must live not for ourselves but for Christ, who died for us: ibid., 337.---The Paschal feasts, which brought forth true redemption for us, are not to be celebrated mournfully: ibid., 341.---Easter is not rightly celebrated except by believers: ibid., 358.---The cross must be borne continually: ibid., 380.---The Lord’s Passion is brought to completion until the end of the world through the mortification of his members: ibid.

Preparation Day is celebrated in sorrow: Alcuin, CI, 1210.---Not with joy, as are the passions of martyrs: Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 52.---It is to be celebrated rather with grief than joy: Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 490.---With abstinence and compunction of sorrow, in commemoration of the Lord’s Passion: Atto, CXXXIV, 105.---“From morning until None let us maintain deep silence, befitting sorrow, recalling the combat and reproaches of the Savior”: Sicard, CCXIII, 312.

The fast on Preparation Day must not be relaxed: St Isidore, LXXXIV, 368.---The fast of Preparation Day without food: Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 137; St Benedict, CIII, 1202.---On bread and water: Archbishop John of Rouen, CXLVII, 52, 101, 131, 175.---The fast is devoutly and strictly observed in memory of Christ’s spiritual fast: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 352.---The date of the Passion does not always fall on the same day: Eugyppius, LXII, 752.---On the anniversary day Psalm XXI is sung: St Augustine, XXXVI, 170, 171, 172, 178, 179.---The Lord’s Passion is solemnly read: id., XXXVIII, 1084.---But only according to Matthew: ibid., 1107.---Later it was read from the four Evangelists, but at different hours: Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 187.---Prostration on the Passion: Archbishop John of Rouen, CXLVII, 129.

Ceremonies of Preparation Day: Beleth, CCII, 105, 108, 109.---Public prayers customarily held on Friday of Holy Week throughout the whole world by apostolic tradition: St Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 209, 210; Alcuin, CI, 1210.---Offerings: John XIX, CXLI, 1129.---Hymns used to be sung and nocturnal prayers recited: Flodoard, CXXXV, 51.---Formerly the whole Psalter was recited: Archbishop John of Rouen, CXLVII, 51, 99, 175.---The tract is sung by four canons: ibid., 129, 173.---Those carrying the cross are answered in Latin and Greek, but not in Hebrew: Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 163.---Mass is not sung: ibid., 153.---The cross was unveiled: Guigo, CLIII, 641.---The cross is to be adored: Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXX, 949.---On Preparation Day the adoration of the cross takes place: St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 85; Alcuin, CI, 1210; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 349; Archbishop John of Rouen, CLVII [probably CXLVII], 51, 100, 129, 174.---At Vespers: St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 85.---At the ninth hour: Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 157.---It is an ancient custom: St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 332 (n.).

Procession: Archbishop John of Rouen, CXLVII, 51, 130, 174.---The final elevation of the Host: ibid., 130.---The celebrant communicates under the single species of bread: St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 332 (n.); Alcuin, CI, 1211 (n.).---With the presanctified gifts: Guigo, CLIII, 644.---For four reasons Christ’s body is not consecrated on this day: Beleth, CCII, 99.---Lights are not kindled: St Benedict, CIII, 1203; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 349.---The altars are stripped: ibid.; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 450.---The altars, walls, and floors of the church, and the sacred vessels, are washed: St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 333, 334 (n.); St Benedict, CIII, 1203.---Feet are washed: Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 450.---In the church of St Peter, before John XIX, Preparation Day was observed irreverently: CXLI, 1129.---How it is performed in the monastery of Farfa: Guido, CL, 1201.

On Preparation Day: St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 85, 1013; Alcuin, CI, 1207; Amalarius, CV, 1024; Archbishop John of Rouen, CXLVII, 129; Udalric, CXLIX, 661; eleventh-century liturgical monuments, CLI, 844, 882; Stephen, CLXVI, 1398, 1401; Rupert, CLXX, 153; Beleth, CCII, 99; Sicard, CCXIII, 311; Innocent III, CCXVII, 525.---Office of Preparation Day: St Isidore of Seville, LXXXV, 422; LXXXVI, 604; Dunstan, CXXXVII, 492; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 450, 889.---Office of the dry Mass: Archbishop John of Rouen, CXLVII, 51, 129.---On the Office of Tenebrae: Beleth, CCII, 105.---On the number of candles: ibid.---On washing the floor: ibid., 108.---On stripping the altar: ibid., 109.---Blessings on Preparation Day: edict of Otto III, CXXXVIII, 1070.---Verses and prayers on Preparation Day: Anonymous, 1077.

On the Passion of Christ: Bishop Taio, LXXX, 780; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 1125; CX, 1117; Wandalbert, CXXI, 593; Honorius, CLXXII, 661, 666, 735, 746, 787; Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 51–58; Abbot Ernald, CLXXXIX, 1656; Ermengand, CCIV, 1243.---Book on the Passion of Christ: St Bernard, CLXXXII, 1134.---Short work on the Lord’s Passion: Candidus, CVI, 57–103.---Commentary on the Lord’s Passion: Christian Druthmar, ibid., 1471.---Meditation on the Passion of Christ: St Anselm, bishop of Lucca, [Col. 0530] CXLIX, 601; St Anselm, CLVIII, 761.---Blessing concerning the Passion: Grimald, CXXI, 866.

Hymns on the Passion: Sedulius, CI, 609; Walafrid Strabo, CXIV, 1083.---Verses on the Lord’s Passion: Theodulf, CV, 379.---On Christ Crucified: John Scotus, CXXII, 1222.---To the image of the Crucified: Froumund, CXLI, 345.---Rhythmical poem on Christ’s Passion: Einhard, CIV, 593.---Rhythmical prayer to each individual member of the suffering Christ hanging from the cross: Abbot Ogeric, CLXXXII, 1319.

On the Holy Cross: Alan of Lille, CCX, 223, 224; Sicard, CCXIII, 413.---On the power of the Lord’s cross: Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 455.---On the praise of the Holy Cross: St Peter Damian, CXLIV, 406, 601, 602; Abbot Egbert, CXCV, 103.---Two books on the praises of the Holy Cross: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 135.---On the adoration of the Holy Cross: Amalarius, CV, 1028, 1200.

Mass of the Holy Cross: Alcuin, CI, 454; eleventh-century liturgical monuments, CLI, 907.

Hymns of the Holy Cross: St Fortunatus, CI, 562; Fulbert, CXLI, 345; Heribert, ibid., 1369; St Peter Damian, CXLV, 930, 931.

Verses on the cross: Venantius Fortunatus, LXXXVIII, 87, 89, 95; John Scotus, CXXII, 1223.---To the cross: Bernowin, CV, 446.---At the altar of the Holy Cross: CI, 761, 770.

Sermons on the Passion: St Leo the Great, LIV, 313, 317, 318, 322, 325, 328, 331, 537, 342, 346, 349, 353, 357, 361, 364, 368, 372, 375, 380, 491, 492; LVI, 1133; Abbot Werner, CLVII, 952; St Anselm, CLVIII, 675; Hildebert, CLXXI, 547, 551; Abbot Ogerius, CLXXXIV, 953.

Homilies on the Passion: St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 331, 333, 335, 339, 341; St Faustinus, LIX, 408.

Sermons on the Holy Cross: Odilo, CXLII, 1031; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 1205; Abelard, CLXXVIII, 453.---Sermon on Preparation Day: Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 1007.---Homilies on Preparation Day: St Leo the Great, LIV, 337; Radulphus Ardens, CLV, 1842; Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 788.

Holy Saturday.---Saturday in Easter itself: St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 365, 366; Alcuin, CI, 1215.---The Easter vigil was celebrated among the ancient Christians: Aurelius Prudentius, LIX, 818.---The veneration of Easter Saturday is celebrated because on that day the Lord rested in the tomb: St Isidore, LXXXIII, 766; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 350; Beleth, CCII, 110; Sicard, CCXIII, 322.---The Sabbath *par excellence*, because it signifies Christ’s rest from the work of re-creation: Beleth, CCII, 110; Sicard, CCXIII, 322.---For three reasons it shines brightly, illumined in our delights: because of the redemption of souls, the resurrection of bodies, and the sacrament of baptism: ibid.---The commandment concerning the Sabbath properly applies to it: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 862.---A great feast and joyful celebration through the night: id., CVII, 550.---The solemnity begins at the second hour after noon: St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 86.---On Holy Saturday joy is restored and the angelic hymn is sung: Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 190.---All bells are rung at “Glory to God in the highest”: Archbishop John of Rouen, CXLVII, 52, 105, 177, 181.---The Paschal office, the Paschal season, begins: Beleth, CCII, 117.

The sacred veneration and rite of Easter Saturday: Alcuin, CI, 1215–1217.---Various ceremonies: Amalarius, CV, 1032.---Holy Saturday is free from the station: Hildebert, CLXXI, 499.---The sacrament of Christ’s body and blood is not celebrated: St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 279 (n.).---The Mass is to be celebrated by night: Archbishop John of Rouen, CXLVII, 49, 52, 97, 101, 175.---Certain things are absent from the solemn Mass: Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 90.---The Introit is not sung: Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 453.---The Creed: Archbishop John of Rouen, CXLVII, 38.---The *Agnus Dei*: St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 87.---On Holy Saturday the fast was relaxed by some: Alcuin, C, 263.---In the evening among the Alexandrians: St Leo the Great, LIV, 1087.---Observed not only by Romans but also by Eastern Christians: Cassian, XLIX, 1201.---Even by little children: John the Deacon, LXXV, 65.---It must be observed as on the other days of Lent: Alcuin, C, 287.---It must not be relaxed before the beginning of night: Burchard, CXL, 886; St Ivo, CXLI, 271.---Before the cockcrow of Sunday among Eastern Christians: St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 306 (n.).

On Holy Saturday the blessing of fire and incense takes place: eleventh-century liturgical monuments, CLI, 845, 846; Sicard, CCXIII, 324, 325.---Of lamps: Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 196, 197; St Benedict, CIII, 1203.---Of the Paschal candle: Alcuin, CI, 1215; Grimald, CXXI, 800; Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 467; Sicard, CCXIII, 324, 325.

Formerly at Rome wax lambs, in place of the Paschal candle, were blessed by the archdeacon for distribution to the people: St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 357, 530 (n.).---Water was blessed: Ratramnus, CXXI, 768.---In some places an unauthorized and disorderly sprinkling with blessed water took place: Berthold, CXLVII, 386.---The blessing of the fonts takes place: St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 87, 338 (n.); Archbishop John of Rouen, CXLVII, 48, 176.---Solemn baptism is celebrated: Gratian, CLXXXVII, 374; Sicard, CCXIII, 322. (See Vigils.)---A procession for blessing the new fire and the fonts: Archbishop John of Rouen, CXLVII, 48, 176.---A sevenfold litany is sung at the fonts: St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 87, 338 (n.); St Eulogius, CXV, 1445.---Litanies are said on Holy Saturday: Alcuin, CI, 1477.---Milk is blessed at Mass because of those newly baptized: St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 379 (n.).---Feet are washed after baptism: Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 220, 275.---Compline on Holy Saturday: Archbishop John of Rouen, CXLVII, 53, 178.---After the hour of baptism on Holy Saturday, a bishop may be ordained: Gratian, CLXXXVII, 374.---How it is performed on Holy Saturday among the monks of Farfa: Abbot Guido, CL, 1203.

On Holy Saturday: St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 87, 1014; Alcuin, CI, 1215; Amalarius, CV, 1032, 1200; Dunstan, CXXXVII, 494; ancient calendars and martyrologies, CXXXVIII, 1187, 1205, 1260; Udalric, CXLIX, 663; eleventh-century liturgical monuments, CLI, 1016; Stephen, CLXVI, 1398, 1403; Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 168; Honorius, CLXXII, 668, 735, 747, 787; Beleth, CCII, 109; Sicard, CCXIII, 321.

Office on Holy Saturday: St Isidore, LXXXV, 436; LXXXVI, 614; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 889; Beleth, CCII, 110.---On the Paschal candle: ibid.

Blessings on Holy Saturday: Anonymous Works (*Opera adespota*, “works without an attributed author”), CXXXVIII, 1072; Grimald, CXXI, 866.

Preface: Grimald, CXXI, 895.---Holy readings for Holy Saturday: Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVIII, 1354.

Hymns on the Paschal candle: Aurelius Prudentius, LIX, 818; Drepanius Florus, LXI, 1087.

Verses and prayers on Holy Saturday: Anonymous, CXXXVIII, 1077.

Sermon on the Vigil of Easter: St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 853.

Homilies on the Vigil of Easter: the Venerable Bede, XCIV, 133, 139; Paul the Deacon, XCV, 1326; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 33, 135, 137; Haymo, CXVIII, 444; Radulphus Ardens, CLV, 1844; Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 807.

§ V.---On the Sundays from Easter until Pentecost.

On the fourth Sunday after Easter: St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 105; St Isidore, LXXXV, 579; LXXXVI, 645; Grimald, CXXI, 805, 897; Rupert, CLXX, 241; Honorius, CLXXII, 699, 799; Sicard, CCXIII, 365.---Sermon: Abbot Werner, CLVII, 947.---Homilies: the Venerable Bede, XCIV, 158; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 207, 209; Haymo, CXVIII, 514, 516; Radulphus, CLV, 1884, 1888; Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 813; Godfrey, CLXXIV, 338, 347.

On the fifth Sunday after Easter: St Gregory the Great, CLXXVIII, 105; St Isidore, LXXXV, 585; LXXXVI, 647; Grimald, CXXI, 897; Rupert, CLXX, 247; Honorius, CLXXII, 690, 799; Sicard, CCXIII, 366.---Sermon: Abbot Werner, CLVII, 955.---Homilies: the Venerable Bede, XCIV, 163, 165; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 219, 222; Haymo, CXVIII, 520, 522; Radulphus, CLV, 1892, 1894; Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 816; Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 355, 359.

On the three Rogation Days.---A litany is called a supplication or petition; hence “Rogations”: Alcuin, CI, 1224.---They are named from the litanies: Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 203; Ratherius, [Col. 0532] CXXXVI, 735 (n.).---The Rogations, or processions, are three principal ones: Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 817.---Public processions: St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 886; Archbishop John of Rouen, CXLVII, 120, 122.---Solemn processions: St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 785, 842.---The litanies are not Roman but Gallican: eleventh-century liturgical monuments, CLI, 1018.---Supplications of the Rogations and of other days in Gaul: Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 203, 204, 205.

The Rogations were instituted by St Mamertus, bishop of Vienne: St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 223, 231; St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 384 (n.); the Venerable Bede, XCIV, 537; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 735 (n.); Anonymous, CXLIX, 32; Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 248.---To implore God’s mercy and avert the scourges of his wrath: Rabanus Maurus, CX, 37, 38; Hildebert, CLXXI, 571.---To allay plague and restrain the madness of wolves: Heribert, CLXXI, 577.---They are celebrated before the Ascension: St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 223, 231; the Venerable Bede, XCIV, 537; Alcuin, CI, 1225; Burchard, CXL, 886; Anonymous, CXLIX, 32; eleventh-century liturgical monuments, CLI, 1018; Honorius, CLXXII, 681, 699, 755; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1783.

Before St Mamertus there were litanies, Rogations, and processions, but they were not fixed on a particular day: St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 385 (n.).---Processions at Rome commanded by St Gregory: St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 528.---Leo III established that litanies should be celebrated before the Ascension: Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVIII, 144, 1223.

The three Rogation Days are to be observed as holidays, S. Ivo, CLXI, 266, 267; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1781.---Days not so much festive as penitential, *Liturg. Gall.*, LXXII, 170.---In the celebration of the Rogations, the same authority and dress were prescribed to the faithful as were imposed upon public penitents, Hildebert, CLXXI, 576, 577, 579.---The penitential psalms are recited, John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 121, 122, 180.---Days of abstinence, Burchard, CXL, 886.---Formerly there was a fast during the three Rogation Days, *Liturg.*, LXXII, 380; St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 384, 386 (note); Amalarius, CV, 1066, 1207.---Works without a master (*opera adespotica*, ἀδεσποτικὰ), CXXXVIII, 832; John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 56, 110; Anonymous, CXLIX, 32.---The Rogation fast was introduced in Gaul in the tenth century, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 561 (note).

On Rogations and litanies, St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 106; Alcuin, CI, 1224, 1225; Amalarius, CV, 1066, 1207; Udalric, CXLIX, 669; Abbot Guido, CL, 1210, 1212; Stephen, CLXVI, 1406; Honorius, CLXXII, 681, 699, 755; Sicard, CCXIII, 367.---On the vigil of the Ascension, Honorius, CLXXII, 700, 749.---On the Mass at the vigil, Rupert, CLXX, 250.---The limit for Rogations, Anonymous, CXXIX, 1283.---A method of finding the Rogation Days, ibid., 1299.---Preface on the weekdays of the Rogations, Grimald, CXXI, 897, 898.

§ VI.—On the Sundays after Pentecost.

On Sundays after Pentecost in general, Honorius, CLXXII, 704.

On the Sunday in the Octave of Pentecost, which is also the first Sunday after Pentecost, St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 116; St Isidore of Seville, LXXXV, 621; LXXXVI, 695; Grimald, CXXI, 806, 869, 873, 900; Rupert, CLXX, 315; Honorius, CLXXII, 704, 1037.---Sermon, Abbot Werner, CLVII, 1003, 1007.---Homilies, Venerable Bede, XCIV, 197; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 279, 282; Haymo, CXVIII, 578; Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 818; Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 387, 401. (See Trinity.)---From the Octave of Pentecost until the first Sunday of the Lord’s Advent there are twenty-eight weeks when the interval is longer, but when it is shorter there are twenty-three, Stephen, CLXVI, 1408.

Sunday of the Holy Trinity.---The feast of the Holy Trinity, [Col. 0533] Abbot Godfrey, CLVII, 141, 159, 173.---The feast of the Trinity is a general feast, Beleth, CCII, 18.---On the octave day of Pentecost the Mass of the Holy Trinity is sung, Udalric, CXLIX, 673.---The Sunday in the Octave of Pentecost, St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 116; Isidore, LXXXV, 621; LXXXVI, 695; Grimald, CXXI, 806; Lanfranc, CL, 475; Abbot Guido, ibid., 1217; Stephen, CLXVI, 1407; Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 293, 314; Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 686, 703, 736; Master Bandinus, CXCII, 971; Richard of St Victor, CXCVI, 987.---The Sunday in the Octave of Pentecost, which is the first after Pentecost. Concerning this Sunday there is a threefold variation: some sing of the Trinity, others of the octave, while others of the first Sunday after Pentecost, Sicard, CCXIII, 385.---The Office of the Trinity is approved by Alexander and by Gregory the Great, ibid., 387.---An ancient solemnity of the Holy Trinity in the Church, ibid.

On the feast of the Dedication of churches.

The dedication of a church took its beginning from the Old Testament, [Col. 0536] Rabanus Maurus, CX, 73.---We read in the Gospel that the annual feasts of the dedication of churches were celebrated according to ancient custom, St Isidore, LXXXIII, 771.---The mystical meaning of what is done at the dedication of a church, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 439, 440.---Historical and tropological exposition, the same author, CLXXVII, 903.---Anagogical exposition, ibid., 907.---The dedication of a church, or the dedication of any oratory whatsoever, is to be observed as a holiday, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1781.---The solemnities of the dedications of churches are to be celebrated each year, ibid., 1711; St Ivo, CLXI, 203.---Formerly the feast of the Dedication was celebrated for eight days, St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 160, 426 (note); St Ivo, CLXI, 203.---It is an ancient institution of the Church to dedicate basilicas by the bringing in and deposition of saints’ relics, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 285, 540, 812, 832, 834, 908, 964; LXXVIII, 422 (note).---Dedication of St Mary of the Martyrs, ibid., 687.---At Rome, the dedication of the first church built and consecrated by the blessed apostle Peter, ibid., 399 (note).---Celebrated on the Kalends of August, Rabanus Maurus, CX, 1160.---Innocent of Albano dedicated the basilica of Saints Protasius and Gervasius, Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 207.---When celebrating the solemnities of a church’s Dedication, we ought to be worthy of the solemnity: just as temples are adorned with lights and song, so we should adorn the inner chambers of our hearts with the necessary ornaments of good works, St Hilary, X, 879.---The dedications of churches are to be celebrated in purity of mind, St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 870, 880.---Very many miracles are recorded as having occurred at them, ibid., 898.---Feasts were formerly customarily held at a Dedication, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 518.

At the feast of the Dedication the *Credo* is sung, John of Rouen, CXLVII, 38.---At the principal Mass, Lanfranc, CL, 481.---If the Dedication falls outside Lent, it is celebrated with the greatest solemnity, Udalric, CXLIX, 656.---Celebration of the feast of the Dedication during Lent is forbidden, Lanfranc, CL, 657.---If the feast of the Dedication happens to be celebrated between Septuagesima and Easter, songs of praise other than the *Alleluia* are not suppressed, Sicard, CCXIII, 410.---The Archbishops of Rouen made certain distributions to the chapter on the feast of the Dedication, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 1179.---At the feast of the Dedication, Carthusian brothers have wine twice, Guigo, CLIII, 733.

# CL. INDEX OF FASTING AND ABSTINENCE, LOGICALLY REFERRING TO VARIOUS SAYINGS OF THE HOLY FATHERS ON ITS NATURE AND NECESSITY, CONDITIONS, POWER, ETC.

This index is divided into three parts: in the first part are particular teachings arranged by propositions; in the second an index of questions is given in the chronological order of the Fathers; and in the third there is a fuller treatment in alphabetical order.

## NOTICE

Although in Index CXLVIII, *On the Precepts of the Church*, under the fifth and sixth precepts, we have noted certain matters—though few—concerning fasting and abstinence, while chiefly directing the reader to this index, here the question is treated especially and expressly, as will be evident to the reader.

# [INDEX OF FASTING AND ABSTINENCE]

## PART ONE. PROPOSITIONS EXTRACTED FROM THE FATHERS ON FASTING AND ABSTINENCE

[Col. 0537]

### I.—What fasting consists in

What Christian fasting is, St Augustine, XXXV, 1339; XL, 711.---Fasting is essentially voluntary, the same author, XXXVI, 476; St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 258.---Etymology of *fasting* (*jejunium*), Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 337.---Fasting is abstinence from food, ibid.; Radulphus Ardens, CLV, 1795.---Discrimination among foods in fasting, St Jerome, XXII, 620; St Leo, LIV, 444; St Agobard, CV, 204.---On taking food on fasting days, Cassian, XLIX, 1198; John of Rouen, CXLVII, 92; Ivo, CLXI, 275.---On the hour at which food may be taken during a fast, St Agobard, CV, 204; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 566, note; Hildebert, CLXXI, 449; St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 174; Robert Pullen, CLXXVI, 1144.---One meal on fasting days, St Bernard, CLXXXVI, 1143, 1144; Peter Cantor, CCV, 103.

### II.—The excellence of fasting

The evils of gluttony and the goods of fasting contrasted, St Ambrose, XIV, 700, 701, 1068; St Jerome, XXXIII, 305, 307; St Peter Chrysologus, LII, 225; St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 561; Julius Pomerius, LIX, 463; St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 315, 316; Alcuin, CI, 625, 1191; Halitgar, CV, 677.---The wondrous power of fasting is described, St Ambrose, XIV, 698, 704, 710; XVII, 644, 645; St Jerome, XXII, 1116; XXIII, 305, 307, 308; St Augustine, XXXII, 1358, 1360; XXXVII, 1108; St Peter Chrysologus, LII, 209, 225; St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 577; Julius Pomerius, LIX, 462; Cassiodorus, LXIX, 827, 829; St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 776, 848; St Paulinus, XCIX, 235, note; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 333; CXXXVIII, 434; St Bernard, CLXXXV, 1243.---Fasting is commendable through the example of Christ and the saints, St Ambrose, XIV, 698, 999; XVI, 1191, 1193, 1194; XVII, 639; XVIII, 72; St Jerome, XXIII, 310; St Augustine, XXXIII, 723; St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 575, 576; St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 321, 322; LXXVI, 556; St Eligius, LXXXVII, 605, 606; Haymo, LXVIII, 194; St Remigius of Auxerre, CXXXI, 882; Rupert, CLXVIII, 1369, 1436; St Bernard, CLXXXVIII, 167; CLXXXIV, 776.---Fasting, the bulwark of chastity, St Ambrose, XV, 1618; XVI, 1193; XVII, 529; XVIII, 72; Zacchaeus, XX, 1187; St Jerome, XXII, 817, 897; St Augustine, XL, 706; XXXVIII, 1049; St Leo, LIV, 416; St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 571; Julius Pomerius, LIX, 467; Eugippius, LXI, 627; St Benedict, LXVII, 335; St Martin of Dume, LXXII, 25; St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 30; LXXIX, 322, 323, 324, 325, 364, 397; Taio, LXXX, 942; St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 648, 649, 651, 848; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 21, 90; Peter Cantor, CCV, 332.---Weakness resulting from fasting need not be feared, St Ambrose, XVI, 359; St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 317.---Fasts are camps for Christians, [Col. 0538] St Ambrose, XVII, 644.---The swift feet of the soul are faith and fasting, ibid., 978, 979.---An objection against the excellence of fasting answered, St Jerome, XXIII, 312.---One should fast in both tribulation and joy, St Augustine, XXXVI, 1339.---On the reason and usefulness of fasting, Cassian, XLIX, 1192; St Leo, LV, 39; Julius Pomerius, LIX, 502; St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 325; St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 176; Innocent III, CCXVII, 357.---Various sermons on fasting, St Peter Chrysologus, LII, 314, 208, 219; St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 559.---Fasting as satisfaction for sin, Salvian, LIII, 185; St Eligius, LXXXVI, 605; Venerable Bede, XCIV, 24; St Paulinus, XCIX, 235, note; Alcuin, CII, 120; Burchard, CXL, 888.---On the repression of gluttony, Cassian, XLIX, 229; Eugippius, LXII, 837; St Paulinus, XCIX, 233; Burchard, CXL, 888; St Anselm, CLVIII, 680; Hildebert, CLXXI, 1040.---Fasting is to be loved, St Benedict, LXVI, 319.---Fasting makes the flesh a handmaid, St Leander, LXXII, 884; St Benedict, CIII, 694; St Peter Damian, CXLIV, 320.---Abstinence is good, St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 555.---Abstinence approved by a miracle, the same author, LXXVII, 153, 155.---Feasts fatten the body; fasting fattens the soul, the same author, LXXIX, 314.---Fasting is a condition of virtue, St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 649; Valerius, LXXXVII, 424; Haymo, CXVIII, 192, 194.---Through fasting prayer more readily penetrates heaven, St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 65; St Boniface of Mainz, LXXXIX, 866; St Benedict, CIII, 524; CLIV, 1249; CLX, 876.---The flesh extinguished by fasting thirsts for the Lord, St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 651.---Fasting is pleasing to God, Haymo, CXVIII, 114.---Fasts confer the remedy of everlasting life, ibid., 901; Rupert, CLXVIII, 760, 761.---Temptation is overcome by fasting, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 691; St Anselm, CLVIII, 680.---Fasting is useful to the living and the dead, Ratherius, CXXXVIII, 434.---In public calamities, God’s wrath is to be appeased by fasting, Burchard, CXL, 888.---The excellence of fasting from Scripture, Radulphus Ardens, CLV, 1793, 1794; St Anselm, CLVIII, 89.---Three degrees of abstinence, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 548; Alan of Lille, CCX, 121.---The precept of self-denial is fulfilled by fasting, Godfrey, CLXXIV, 715.---Fasting is refreshment of the heart, St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 171.---Fasting fattens, ibid.---Praise of fasting, Ernald, CLXXXIX, 1364.---Exhortation to fasting, Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 422; CCX, 176, 177.---Fasting is efficacious, the same author, CXCVIII, 422; Alan of Lille, CCX, 176, 177.

### III.—The precept of fasting

The precept of fasting was instituted at the creation of the world, St Ambrose, XIV, 700.---Christ fasted lest you should evade the precept, the same author, XV, 1556.---We are bound by the precept of fasting, Rufinus, XXI, 1040; St Leo, LIV, 473; St Benedict, LXVI, 639; St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 114; Regino, CXXXII, 244.---The precept of fasting is enjoined from [Col. 0539] Scripture, St Augustine, XXXIII, 147; St Leo, LIV, 447; Venerable Bede, XCI, 714; XCIII, 434; XCIX, 235, note.---Under the new law, the precept of fasting was not abolished but confirmed, St Leo, LIV, 175.---The precept of fasting derives from the authority of the Church and of the Apostles, St Leo, LIV, 416, 421; St Benedict, LXVI, 303; St Paulinus, XCIV, 194, 195; Burchard, CXL, 885; Rupert, CLXX, 97.---The precept of fasting before the law, under the law, and under grace, Alcuin, C, 531.---Fasting is a matter of divine authority, Rupert, CLXVIII, 1436.---The precept of fasting is enjoined by threefold authority, Garnerius, CCV, 660.

### IV.—Dispensation from fasting

How wrongly some excuse themselves from fasting, St Ambrose, XVII, 681; Salvian, LIII, 32.---Tender age is a reason for dispensation from fasting, St Jerome, XXII, 874, 875; St Benedict, CIII, 366.---How fasting is made up for when a dispensation has been granted, St Augustine, XXXVIII, 811; XXXIX, 2022; St Leo, LIV, 440; St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 451; St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 1219; Theodore of Canterbury, XCIX, 938, 939; Halitgar, CV, 705, 706; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 22; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 567.---Old age is a reason for dispensation from fasting, Cassian, XLIX, 210; St Benedict, CIII, 566.---Illness is a reason for dispensation from fasting, St Leo, LIV, 286, 489; St Leander of Seville, LXXII, 884; St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 1219; Theodulf, CV, 204; John Scotus, CXLVII, 56.---Who is the dispenser of fasting, St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 425.

### V.—The conditions of fasting

The first condition of fasting: almsgiving.---Fasting and almsgiving joined in Scripture, St Ambrose, XVI, 1194.---Fasting sanctified by good works, St Jerome, XXIII, 312; St Gregory the Great, LXXXII, 82; Haymo, CXVIII, 195; Rupert, CLXVIII, 223; see Hildebert, CLXXI, 1448.---Let fasting not be idle with respect to good works, St Jerome, XXIV, 35.---Almsgiving should be joined to fasting, St Augustine, XXXVI, 482; XXVIII, 88, 398, 811, 1041, 1042, 1046; Taio, LXXX, 861; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 22; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 273.---The food which fasting takes away from us should be distributed to the poor, St Augustine, XXXIX, 2027; Taio, LXXX, 861; St Eligius, LXXXVII, 536; Smaragdus, CII, 683; Theodulf, CV, 204; Halitgar, CV, 668; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 695; Burchard, CXL, 887; Radulphus Ardens, CLV, 1795; St Anselm, CLVIII, 1116.---Fasting with almsgiving is pleasing to God, St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 428; LXXVII, 83; Alcuin, CI, 1191; Haymo, CXVIII, 194, 195, 902.---Fasting without almsgiving is nothing, St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 1220; Ratherius, CXXXVIII, 434; see Hildebert, CLXXI, 443.

The second condition of fasting: prayer.---During a fast let us devote ourselves to prayer, St Jerome, XXIV, 563.---Fasting and prayer are joined, St Fulgentius, LXV, 321.---Those who fast need spiritual food, St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 305; LXXIX, 364.---Fasting is perfected in prayer, Alcuin, CI, 624; Haymo, CXVIII, 901; St Bernard, CLXXXIV, 180; Innocent III, CCXVII, 364.---Devotion is to be joined to fasting, St Bernard, CIII, 524.---The power of fasting joined with prayer is affirmed from the Gospel, Rabanus Maurus, CX, 90.---By prayer fasting ascends to heaven, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 696.

The third condition of fasting: absence of sin.---Fasting is useless without avoidance of sin, St Augustine, XXXIX, 2029; St Eucherius, L, 842, 843; St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1161 ff.; Haymo, CXVIII, 901; Radulphus Ardens, CLV, 1795.---Above all, one must fast from vices, St Augustine, XXXIX, 2025.---The fasting of the soul from vices must be joined to the fasting of the body from food, Cassian, L, 307; St Eucherius, L, 482; St Leo, LIV, 187; LV, 106, 108; St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 569, 578, 580; St Columban, LXXX, 234; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 339; Haymo, CXVIII, 901; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 567; St Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 93; St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 171.---What does it profit not to drink wine and yet to be intoxicated by the poison of anger? St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 569.---Impatience and pride lie in wait for fasting, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 30; Taio, LXXX, 861, 862; Haymo, CXVIII, 195; St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 171.---Sins injuring one’s neighbour are to be avoided in fasting, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 89; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 695.---Fasting must be sanctified by the wearing away of vices, Alcuin, CI, 1192; Smaragdus, CII, 682, 683.---Those who fast while indulging sin imitate demons, Alcuin, CI, 625.---Those who fast should preserve purity in conscience, Radulphus Ardens, CLV, 1784, 1789.

The fourth condition of fasting: concealment of it.---Fasting should be cheerful, [Col. 0540] St Leo, LIV, 443.---Through vain glory those who fast do not fast for God but for human beings, St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1234; St Paschasius, CXX, 303; Rupert, CLXVIII, 751, 752.---Fasts should be in secret, St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 651.---Those who fast should not wear a sad countenance, St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 1211; St Eligius, LXXXVII, 536; Haymo, CXVIII, 182; St Paschasius, CXX, 302.---One should fast for sins, not for glory, St Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 777 ff.---Four ways in which we appear to people as fasting, Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1750.
