The fifth condition of fasting: prudence in fasting.---One should not fast to the point of excessive bodily weakness, St Jerome, XXII, 1116.---Fasting is more perfect in moderate food than in total abstinence, ibid., 404, 555; St Jerome, LXXIII, 1026; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 696; Radulphus Ardens, CLV, 1796; St Bernard, CLXXXIX, 716.---Discretion must be observed in fasts, St Jerome, XXII, 537; St Augustine, XXXIII, 960; St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 185; St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1095.---Scripture is opposed to prolonged fasting, Cassian, XLIX, 1192.---The flesh is to be disciplined by fasts, not killed, St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 558; St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 652; Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 256.

### VI.—Various seasons of fasting

1. **Advent.**---The fast before the Nativity of the Lord is discussed, St Augustine, XXXIII, 234.---The Advent fast was observed in various ways in antiquity, St Germanus of Paris, LXXII, 169, 170; St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 434.---During the Advent fast abstinence from meat and marital intercourse prevailed, St Germanus of Paris, LXXII, 169, 170; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 566.---The Advent fast is reckoned among the penitential seasons, Venerable Bede, XCIV, 534; Alan of Lille, CCX, 208.---Various testimonies concerning the Advent fast, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 565, note.---Sermon on the feasts and fasts of Advent, Beleth, CCII, 72.

2. **Vigils.**---On vigils of saints in general, St Augustine, XL, 1276; Alcuin, CI, 1214, 1215; St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 501.---On the vigils of certain apostles, St Leo, LIV, 144; LXXIV, 1178; St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 503; Robert Pullen, CLXXXVI, 1143.---On the vigil of Pentecost, St Leo, LV, 643, note; St Germanus of Paris, LXXII, 206; LXXXV, 612.---On vigils in general, Alcuin, CI, 1275; Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 244; Burchard, CXL, 887; Innocent III, CCXVII, 359, 362.---On the vigils of Epiphany and Purification, John of Rouen, CLVXII [sic], 43.---On the vigil of the Ascension, Guido, CL, 1212.

3. Ember Days.—Fasting in the Ember Days: St. Augustine, XXXII, 1458; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 394; Venerable Bede, XCIV, 538, 539.—Why the Ember-Day fasts were instituted: St. Leo, LIV, 185, 186; Alcuin, CI, 1227; Berno, CXLII, 1090, 1091; Garnerius, CCV, 661; Innocent III, CCXVII, 360.—Origin of the Ember-Day fast: St. Leo, LIV, 418, 519; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 394; Garnerius, CCV, 661.—On the Ember Days considered separately: St. Germanus of Paris, LXXII, 165, 170; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 308; CLI, 995, 997, 1000; Rupert, CLXX, 289.—Various usages in the Ember-Day fast: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 61, 62; Udalricus, CXLIX, 673, 674, 690, 697.—The Ember-Day fasts to be announced: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 394; Regino, CXXXII, 189; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 562.—How the Ember-Day fast was distributed: St. Paulinus, XCIX, 235, 236, note; Alcuin, CI, 1229; Berno, CXLII, 1087.—Decree of the Council of Mainz concerning the Ember-Day fast: Regino, CXXXII, 242.

4. Rogation Days.—During the Rogation Days fasting and mortification are to be embraced: St. Germanus of Paris, LXXII, 287; Regino, CXXXII, 243; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 562; Guido, CL, 1212; John Mich., CLXV, 1407.—On the institution of the Rogation Days: Regino, CXXXII, 243; Venerable Bede, XCIV, 537; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 561, note; Burchard, CXL, 886.—Sermons for the Rogation Days: Wernerus, CLVII, 561; Abelard, CLXXVIII, 485; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 297; St. Martin of León, CCVIII, 1009, 1035.

5. Lent.—Various sermons for the season of the Lenten fast: St. Ambrose, XVII, 636; St. Augustine, XL, 1314; St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 634; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 565 ff.; St. Leo, LIV, 263; St. Germanus of Paris, LXXII, 185; St. Boniface of Mainz, LXXXIX, 865; Henry the Cardinal, CCIV, 385; St. Martin of León, CCVIII, 631 ff.; Isaac of Stella, CXCIV, 1749.—The gravity of the Lenten precept expressed in various ways: St. Ambrose, XVII, 645; St. Augustine, XXXIX, 594, 2022, 2031; XLII, 492; XXXII, 1456; St. Leo, LIV, 301; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 368, 583; Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 76; St. Germanus of Paris, LXXII, 185; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 307; St. Isidore of Spain, LXXXIV, 266, 425; St. Paulinus, XCIX, 194; Theodulf, CV, 204; Regino of Prüm, CXXX, 250; Burchard, CXL, [Col. 0541] 884; Innocent III, CCXVII, 825.

—The antiquity of Lent is noted: St. Ambrose, XVII, 648, 649; St. Jerome, XXII, 475; XXIII, 311, 386; St. Augustine, XXXII, 1456; XXXIII, 217; XLII, 492; St. Leo, LIV, 275; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 568; Eugyppius, LXII, 761; Cassiodorus, LXX, 246; St. Germanus of Paris, LXXII, 259; St. Isidore of Spain, LXXXIII, 258, 359, 771; LXXXV, 287; Venerable Bede, XCII, 18, 366; XCV, 128; XCIX, 804; St. Paulinus, XCIX, 194; Alcuin, CI, 1179, 1183; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 22; Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIX, 840; Ivo, CLXI, 270; St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXIII, 175.—The observance of Lent is universal in the Church: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1096, 1054; St. Leo, LIV, 269; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 258; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 185.—Various practices in Lenten observance: St. Augustine, XXXII, 1456; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 307, 316; Udalricus, CXLIX, 696 ff.

—On the number of days composing Lent: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 695; Cassian, XLIX, 1204, 1208; Eugyppius, LXII, 761, 762; St. Germanus of Paris, LXXII, 184; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 307, 308; St. Boniface of Mainz, LXXXIX, 865; Alcuin, C, 264; Burchard, CXL, 885; John of Rouen, CXLVIII, 46; Lanfranc, CL, 453; CLI, 1013.—Origin of Lent, Quinquagesima, Sexagesima, and Septuagesima: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1051; St. Leo, LIV, 488, note; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 584; St. Benedict, LXVI, 737; Venerable Bede, XCIV, 804; Alcuin, CI, 1182, 1183; Amalarius, CV, 1002; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 346; Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 839; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 445, 446.—Mystical significance of the number forty: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1051, 1216; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 772; St. Boniface of Mainz, LXXXIX, 867; Alcuin, C, 261, 262, 263, 531; Smaragdus, CII, 124; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 219, 220, 346; Haymo, CXVIII, 193, 194; St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 545; John of Rouen, CXLVII, 46; Goffridus, CLXII, 863; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 93; Alanus of Lille, CCX, 203.

—Usefulness of Lent: St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2019, 2027; St. Leo, LIV, 283; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 569, 573, 575.—During Lent fasting is to be embraced: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1040, 1043, 1044, 1047; XXXII, 1261, 1262; St. Leo, LV, 633; LVI, 720; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 583; St. Benedict, LXVI, 473; LXXIV, 1066; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 297, 306; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 369; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 565, note, 566; Burchard, CXL, 886; Ivo, CLXI, 270; Venerable Hildebert, CLXXI, 503.—During Lent, abstinence from meat and wine: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1040, 1043; XLII, 491, 492; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 569; St. Germanus of Paris, LXXII, 184; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 134; St. Fructuosus, LXXXVII, 1108; St. Chrodegang, LXXXIX, 1073; Ivo, CLXI, 882; Robert Pullus, CLXXXVI, 426.

—During Lent continence is to be observed: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1040; XXXIX, 2031; Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 76; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 1220; LXXXIV, 134, 581; St. Donatus, LXXXVII, 285; St. Boniface of Mainz, LXXXIX, 867; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 22; Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 290; Burchard, CXL, 887.—During Lent every kind of mortification is to be embraced: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1039, 1040 ff.; St. Benedict, LXVI, 741; St. Paulinus, XCIX, 235; Alcuin, CI, 1213; Smaragdus, CII, 124; Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 841; Ivo, CLXI, 274; St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 220; CLXXXIII, 184.—Hunting is forbidden during Lent: St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2029; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 581; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 24, 25.—During Lent war must be waged upon vices: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 226; St. Leo, LIV, 276; St. Boniface of Mainz, LXXXIX, 867.—During Lent alms are to be distributed: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1040; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 22; Venerable Hildebert, CLXXI, 466.—During Lent injuries are to be forgiven to enemies: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1041 ff.; Theodulf, CV, 203.—During Lent God is to be served more fervently: St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2019, 2021; St. Leo, LIV, 276, 291; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 569, 577.—Marriages are not to be celebrated during Lent: St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 134; Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 290; Ivo, CLXI, 894, 895.

6. Other times of fasting.—On the fast of the Kalends of January or November: St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 774; LXXXV, 226, 653, 1051; Venerable Bede, XCIV, 538.—On the Wednesday fast: St. Augustine, XXXIII, 140, 150; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 458; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 258.—On the Saturday fast: St. Augustine, XXXIII, 137, 138, 139, 140, 150, 281; St. Leo, LV, 627, 628, 630; LVI, 516; Paul the Deacon, XCV, 1377; Regino, CXXXII, 372.—On fasting in various months: St. Leo, LIV, 175, 189, 458; LV, 41, 105, 107; LXXIV, 1133, 1178; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 391; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 57.—On the fast of Pentecost: St. Isidore of Seville, [Col. 0542] LXXXIII, 773; Venerable Bede, XCIV, 538; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 45.—By decree of the Council of Elvira, fasting is to be observed every month: St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 304.

## VII.—On abstinence from meat and wine

Abstinence from meat and wine on fast-days: St. Jerome, XXII, 620, 818.—Abstinence from meat and wine during Lent: St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2025, 2029; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 567, 578; St. Germanus of Paris, LXXII, 184; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 425; Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 40; Ivo, CLXI, 694.—The true rationale for abstinence from these foods is explained: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1047, 1052; St. Leo, LIV, 279; LVI, 439; Julius Pomerius, LIX, 469; Eugyppius, LXII, 702, 703; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 325, 778, 1241; LXXXIV, 582; LXXXV, 113; Alcuin, C, 1079; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1096.—Abstinence from meat is extremely ancient, before and after the law of grace: Salvian, LIII, 193; St. Benedict, LXVI, 654; St. Leander of Seville, LXXII, 389; St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 718, 719; Robert Pullus, CLXXXVI, 1144.—Abstinence from meat and wine is good and approved by Scripture: Gennadius, LVIII, 996; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 777; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 339; Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 189; Ivo, CLXI, 77.—Various statements concerning abstinence from meat among monks: St. Benedict, LXVI, 391, 475, 588, 596, 640, 760; St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 387; Innocent III, CCXVII, 1141.—Abstinence from meat during Advent: St. Germanus of Paris, LXXII, 169, 170; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 566.—On abstinence from meat on Friday: St. Bernard, CLXXXVI, 975, 1144.

## Part Two. On fasting and abstinence, in chronological order of the Fathers

**TERTULLIAN.**—In nothing is God’s mercy more effectually obtained than through the abstinence of the people, II, 962.

**AMBROSE.**—Fasting is contrition and humiliation of the soul, XVII, 11.

**ST. AUGUSTINE.**—Fasting: a great work, a Christian work, XXXVII, 1108. What Christian fasting is, XXXV, 1339. Our fasting differs in purpose from the fasting of pagans, Jews, and heretics, XL, 611. Fasting is the humiliation of the soul, XXXIX, 2080. It is the fitting satisfaction of all the members, XL, 1274. There is a twofold fasting and a twofold food, 1064. Fasting on dry foods, XLI, 811, 812. The chief fasting is from vices, XXXIX, 2025, 2079. Two kinds of abstinence, XXXIX, 2112. Abstinence from wine, meat, oil, and bathing, XXXIII, 1111; XL, 768, 777.

**CASSIAN.**—One fasting is spiritual, another bodily, XLIX, 238.

**ST. PETER CHRYSOLOGUS.**—Fasting is a school of merits, the master of teaching, the discipline of disciplines, LII, 209. It is the salutary provision for the Church’s life. It is the unconquered command of Christian warfare, ibid.

**ST. LEO THE GREAT.**—A twofold fasting, of flesh and spirit, LIV, 458. In what spiritual fasting consists, ibid. Bodily fasting without spiritual fasting is of no benefit, ibid. The Church’s fasts were instituted by the Holy Spirit, 415. The Lenten fast, 305. The fast of the Ember Days prescribed by the Church throughout the whole year, 186. On the Saturday fast of the Ember Days, LX, 631; of the Saturdays in Lent, 632; the Lenten fast, 633; the fast of the fourth month, 41; of the seventh month, 105; of the tenth month, 106.

**ST. MARTIN OF LEÓN.**—Abstinence from eating meat during the Lenten fast is most ancient in the Church, LVII, 570. The Lenten fast was not established by men but commanded by heavenly majesty, 308. Its beginning on Wednesday before the first Sunday in Lent is very ancient in the Church, 303.

**EUGYPPIUS.**—Fasting is the chastisement of the whole body, LXXII, 1013.

**CASSIODORUS.**—*Jejunium* (“fasting”) is so called, as though from *inedium* (“lack of food”), because it leads those who abstain, for a longer time, as far as want of food, LXX, 246.

**Life of the Fathers.**—Abstinence from drink, LXXIII, 824; from wine, from bread, from water, from bread and water, from bread and wine, from meat, from cooked foods, 1103.

**ST. ISIDORE OF SEVILLE.**—Fasting is a holy thing, a heavenly work, the gate of the kingdom, an image of the future; whoever performs it in holiness is joined to God, estranged from the world, and made spiritual, LXXXIII, 776.

**ST. ELIGIUS.**—Fasts are the beginnings of God’s grace, sacrifices of reconciliation, remedies of salvation, foundations of chastity, LXXXVII, 605.

**ST. PAULINUS.**—A twofold fasting, of body and soul, XCIX, 252.

**SMARAGDUS.**—On abstinence, CII, 622.

**ST. BENEDICT OF ANIANE.**—On fasting, CIII, 807. The Wednesday and Friday fast, 1138; the Kalends of January, 1141; Lent, 1137, 1198; Holy Week, 1202; Good Friday (*Parasceve*), 1202.

**RODULPHUS.**—On the Lenten fast and other appointed fasts, CXIX, 718.

**REGINO.**—The Ember-Day fast, CXXXII, 456; the fast of vigils, 244; of Rogation Days, 243.

**GOFFRIDUS.**—This is spiritual fasting, through which fellowship with the citizens above is undoubtedly gained. He laudably keeps this fast whom no slander exasperates, whom neither fury nor immoderate anger disturbs, whom pride does not strip of God’s grace, whom the tongue does not stain with curses, and whom resentment does not torment, CLVII, 171.

**HONORIUS.**—For three reasons the Church instituted fasting before Easter. First, because Christ’s Passion is celebrated before Easter, so that through affliction of the flesh she may suffer with him and thereby deserve to reign with him. Second, because at springtime all things are stirred by natural impulse toward lust, they may be restrained from the onset of sensuality by fasts. Third, because at that season the children of Israel entered the promised land, or those people returned from Babylon, CLXXII, 656.

**HILDEBERT.**—Fasting is twofold, bodily and spiritual. Bodily fasting is that by which we restrain ourselves from foods; spiritual fasting, that by which we abstain from vices, CLXXI, 447.

**ST. BERNARD.**—The Lenten fast, CLXXXIII, 174.

**BELETHUS.**—Fasting is the common satisfaction of all the members: that is, the members make satisfaction for the sins which they have committed, CCII, 20. One fasting is of the flesh, another of the mind: that of the flesh is when someone abstains from food; that of the mind, when someone fasts from vices, 22. There is also fasting of obligation, of devotion, of parity [equal observance], and of dispensation.

**PETER OF CELLES.**—Abstinence is twofold: abstinence from food and abstinence from evil, CII, 681.

**GARNERIUS.**—On the various kinds of fasting, CV, 660.

**ALANUS OF LILLE.**—Fasting is manifold: fasting from habit, from avarice and covetousness, from infirmity, from excess and gluttony, from praise and outward appearance, CCX, 177. On the various circumstances of fasting. Fasting is abstinence from food and drink, 822. It is called abstinence from temporal goods; it is also called freedom from sin, ibid.

**GUNTHERUS.**—To fast is to abstain; hence *jejunium*, that is, abstinence, is derived. Fasting is spiritual and bodily. Spiritual fasting is humbly to abstain from all wicked pleasures of mind and body, CCXII, 207. Bodily fasting is rationally to abstain from bodily food and drink for the salvation of the soul, 208.

**INNOCENT III.**—On the threefold solemn fast: namely, that of the Ember Days, of Lent, and of vigils, CCXVII, 360.

## I.—On the conditions of fasting and abstinence

**TERTULLIAN.**—That a person might be more easily formed for fasting, he was accustomed to few and unglorious foods, and was not to hunger after more luxurious fare, II, 306.

**ST. AMBROSE.**—What fasting ought to be, XIV, 709 ff. Boasting in fasting is to be avoided, 710. To fast and abstain from foods is of little benefit unless piety is added, 473. Those who fast from food but do not abstain from evil are like the devil, who does not eat and yet does not cease from evil, XVII, 664. Our fasts should not be occupied with worldly business, but exercised in the sacred Scriptures, 662. What you deprive yourselves of by fasting, you ought to send to heaven through the poor, 663.

**ST. HILARY.**—Those who fast should have a pure conscience and good works, IX, 943.

**JUVENCUS.**—One must fast, but not in order to seek vain fame, XIX, 133.

**ST. CHROMATIUS.**—Let us fast for God alone, not for human glory but for future hope, XX, 363. Those who fast in such a way as to please people more than God do indeed undergo bodily affliction, but through vain glory cannot have from God the reward of their labor, ibid. Let us veil the work of fasting and the affliction itself of body and soul with a cheerful countenance, 364.

**ST. JEROME.**—During fasting one must abstain from wine and meat, XXIII, 610. What the strongest fasting is and what it is like, 234. Fasts should be moderate, 575. Superstitious fasts should be avoided, 234. It is no great thing to feign [Col. 0544] fasting, to abound in the revenues of possessions, and to parade a cheap little cloak, 281. It profits nothing to keep one’s stomach empty for two or three days if fasting is compensated by satiety, 255. Let fasts be daily and refreshment avoid fullness, ibid. Fasts then bear fruit when we withdraw from vices and weep for former sins, XXIV, 772. Let our fasting not be profit for the money-bag, 566. When you fast, let your face be cheerful, XXII, 412. You ought to fast in such a way that you do not tremble and can scarcely breathe, 1117. How those who fast are worse than those who do not fast, 421.

**ST. AUGUSTINE.**—Those who fast in order to dine more sumptuously engage in the business of the belly, not of religion, XXXVII, 1108. What fasts are acceptable to God, XXXVIII, 1042. Fasting with prayer and almsgiving, 811. Fasting without prayer and almsgiving is insufficient, XXXVI, 482. Let the fasting person’s prayer be free from covetousness and hatred, XXXVIII, 1044. Fasting without mercy is nothing to one who fasts, 1043. The meal omitted through fasting must be distributed to the poor, XXXVI, 482. Let the hungry Christ receive what the fasting Christian receives less, XXXVIII, 1053. Let the voluntary poverty of the well-supplied become the necessary abundance of the needy, ibid. What you remit from yourselves by fasting, add to almsgiving by generous distribution, 1040, 1047. Fasting is useless for those who do not withdraw from injustice or devote themselves to pious exercises, XXXIX, 2029. Whatever you do apart from God’s command, though you abstain, you do not fast, 2030. Fasts acceptable to God, 2080. They are acceptable to God if those who fast through necessity are refreshed by us, 2026. Fast in such a way that you rejoice to have dined in another person who is eating, 2027. That our fasts may be full, let them be enriched with the fatness of almsgiving, ibid. Prayer is the refreshment of fasting, 1887. Let prayer with mercy be fasting’s companion, XXXV, 2364. Fasting with almsgiving is a twofold good; without almsgiving, no good at all, 2023. Without almsgiving it is like a lamp without oil, 2024. Fasting without almsgiving is a kind of business transaction, 2029.

**CASSIAN.**—What abstinence ought to be in order to overcome the spirit of fornication, XLIX, 274. The measure of abstinence is not uniform for all, 158.

**ST. PETER CHRYSOLOGUS.**—Fasting hungers and thirsts when it is not nourished with the food of piety or given the drink of mercy, LII, 209. Fasting is cold and fails when its face is not covered by almsgiving and it is not clothed with the garment of compassion. Piety makes fasting shine and radiate with the whole brightness of continence. As the sun’s splendor makes the day brighter and scatters all the darkness of clouds, so almsgiving sanctifies the holiness of fasting. Mercy and piety are fasting’s wings, by which it is lifted and carried to heaven; without them it lies and wallows on the ground. Fasting without mercy is an image of hunger; without piety, fasting is an occasion for avarice, not a purpose of frugality, 210. Fasting without mercy is not truth but a figure. Whoever does not fast for the poor deceives God; whoever, while fasting, does not distribute his meal but stores it away, is shown to fast for covetousness, not for Christ, ibid.

—When a prudent helmsman puts out a ship from shore and is about to cross the sea amid the waves, he lays aside concern for house, homeland, wife, and children; thus he is wholly occupied in mind, body, and feeling with the labors of seamanship, so that he may overcome the dangers of the waves and, victorious over peril, enter the harbor of profitable anchorage, 208. So we, having entered upon the journey of abstinence, the sea of fasting, the road of Lent, should cast off the ship of our body from the worldly shore; renounce concerns for our earthly homeland; spread all the sails of our mind upon the tree of the cross; secure the course of our vessel with the ropes of virtues, the oars of wisdom, and the rudders of discipline. Withdrawn from the land, let us watch the sky, so that under the guidance of the heavenly signs we may keep an unimpeded course among the clear heights of the hidden way; and, with Christ steering and the Holy Spirit blowing, after conquering the foam of pleasures, surmounting the waves of vices, passing through the storms of crimes, crossing the rocks of sins, and avoiding the shipwrecks of all offences, may we enter the harbor of Easter, the gain of life, and the joys of resurrection, 208 ff.

**ST. SALVIAN.**—What useless fasting is and what it is like, LIII, 233. Fasting with almsgiving is good, 185. Long fasts are necessary for one who has lost the time for making satisfaction, 233.

**ST. LEO THE GREAT.**—Fasting without almsgiving is not so much purification of the soul as affliction of the flesh, and should be assigned more to avarice than to continence when a person abstains from food in such a manner that he also fasts from piety, LIV, 175. Let our fasts abound in the fruits of generosity and be fruitful in kindly gifts to Christ’s poor, ibid. Almsgiving must be added to fasting, 172; and prayer, 173. How fasting is to be observed, LV, 106. One must fast not only from fleshly foods [Col. 0545] but also from harmful delights of the mind, 110.

**ST. MAXIMUS.**—That person sanctifies fasting whose heart is not turned from the path of righteousness by the flattery of powerful persons, the favor of friends and relatives, or the small and great gifts of clients. He sanctifies his fasting whose heart does not grow cheap in justice. He sanctifies fasting who quenches the flames of raging anger by the calmness of a gentle mind; who turns lustful eyes from shameful sight with the reins of chastity; who scatters the darts of insults by repelling them with the shield of patience; who restrains the tumults of litigants by the health-giving speech of a peacemaker and the skill of a wiser tongue; who, like a farmer of his own breast, cuts out with the Gospel ploughshare the thorns of vain thoughts rising within himself; who relieves the want of the needy, according to the measure of his substance, with the humanity of a compassionate hand; who, intent upon the commands of divine law, rejects diabolical temptations from his heart, LVII, 307, 308.

—If we wish to offer fasts pleasing to God, let us be strong in heart, just in judgments, faithful in friendship, patient in injuries, moderate in disputes; let us flee shameful speech, be steadfast against wrongdoing, sober at banquets, simple in charity, cautious among the deceitful, compassionate toward the sorrowful, resistant toward the obstinate; sparing in suspicions, silent among evil-speakers, and equal among the humble, ibid.

**ST. FULGENTIUS.**—Let voluntary fasting relieve the hunger of those who fast from necessity, so that the fruitfulness of your fasts may appear in the fruit of mercy, LXV, 321. Moderation must be applied to fasts, so that neither fullness may inflame our body nor immoderate hunger weaken it, 332.

**ST. BENEDICT.**—Fasting on bread and water as a penalty for drunkenness, LXVI, 320.—For violated abstinence, 640; for violated silence, 365.

**VICTOR OF CAPUA.**—Let fasting be hidden, LXVIII, 271.

**Life of the Fathers.**—What abstinence from food and drink ought to be and what it ought to be like, LXXIII, 1090.—Moderate fasts are better, LXXIV, 29.—The best measure of fasting, LXXIII, 920.

**ST. ISIDORE OF SEVILLE.**—This is perfect and reasonable fasting: when our outer person fasts and the inner person prays, LXXXIII, 651. Abstinence is often feigned and fasts are practiced hypocritically. Some abstain unbelievably, in order to appear holy to inquisitive people. Fasting and almsgiving love to be hidden, so that God alone, who beholds all things, may repay the merit of good works, 652. Fasts with good works are acceptable to God. But those who abstain from food and act wickedly imitate demons, who have no food and yet always possess wickedness. Those who deprive themselves of meat from a zeal for abomination rather than by a vow of abstinence are themselves rather to be abominated. A fast that is refreshed in the evening by a filling of food is despised. A fast that is compensated in the evening by delicacies is despised.

**SMARAGDUS.**—Whoever supports his own hunger by the satisfaction of a poor person whom he has fed fasts well, CII, 683. He fasts well who, restraining himself by remembrance of divine judgment, withdraws himself from every pleasure of enticements. He fasts well who chastises his flesh, budding with the shoots of vices, by meditation on holy virtues and love of sobriety. He fasts well who forgives injuries done by brothers with the gentleness of a peaceful breast. He offers to God a most welcome fast who guards his mind from wicked thoughts, his eyes from desire, and his tongue and hands from conflict. Thus let chastity sanctify our fasting, patience adorn it, kindness cherish it, mercy gladden it, and humility commend it, ibid. How fasting is sanctified, ibid.

**THEODULF.**—The Lenten fast must be observed with the utmost care, CV, 203. Almsgiving must be joined with fasting, 204. From what one should abstain while fasting, ibid. Fasting is of no value when defiled by marital intercourse and not commended by prayers, vigils, and almsgiving, 205.

**HAYMO.**—We must fast not only from desire for foods, but from every delight in temporal pleasures, CXVIII, 901.—If, while fasting bodily, we are entangled in the most destructive vices of the soul, bodily affliction will profit us nothing when the more precious part is defiled, ibid. Since almsgiving is fasting’s companion, it is fitting that what we withdraw from our body through abstinence we distribute to the poor through mercy, 194. Whoever fasts for himself and not for God withdraws something from his body through abstinence but does not distribute it to the poor, reserving it for himself for later, 195. But whoever fasts and gives alms must necessarily guard his heart from all anger, hatred, and impatience, ibid. To sanctify fasting is, together with abstinence of the flesh, to give alms and perform the other works of piety, ibid.

[Col. 0546] **ST. PASCHASIUS.**—A person fasts for people if, captivated by their favor, he seeks vain glory. But he fasts for God the Father if, for love of him, he mortifies himself and generously gives to another what he withdraws from himself, CXX, 303. On the days of our fasts, it is not enough for the head to be anointed with works of mercy without a pure conscience; nor is it enough for the conscience to be washed from works of sin if we do not earnestly perform the good works that we can, ibid. In order that the head, flooded with the grace of the Holy Spirit, may shine, let the conscience be cleansed from every stain of sin and washed in the fountain of tears, so that fasting may become acceptable and the grace of the Holy Spirit, poured upon us, may commend us as brighter and whiter, ibid.

**RATHERIUS.**—Unless our abstinence is threefold, it is wholly useless for perfection: first, that we cease from evil thought; second, from harmful speech; third, from perverse action, out of fear or love of God, CXXXVI, 692. One must fast by abstaining from vices, 691. Those fast badly who do not give to the poor what they withdraw from their stomach, but save it for either their stomach or Mammon, 695. Those are reproved who, on days of abstinence, do not abstain from sins, ibid. No solemnity delights God more than that fast in which one abstains from food and from vices, 567. Prayer and almsgiving must be joined with fasting.

**RADULPHUS.**—In fasting one must have right intention; in the mind, compassion of mercy; in the conscience, purity; and in heaven, the laying up of treasure, CLV, 1782.

**RUPERT.**—There is a threefold difference among those who fast: some fast for God’s kingdom; others because of the unhappy remembrance of adverse events; others from desire for human praise, so that they may be glorified by people as righteous, because they are filled with miserable ambition, CLXVIII, 1438. Those who, while fasting, did not anoint their heads or wash their faces are those whose treasures stored on earth have been destroyed by moth or rust, because the head is very moth-eaten and the face rusty when all the fruit of fasting consists in being seen and glorified by people, while wicked hypocrites are thought holy because of their sadness and the mournful gauntness of their faces, ibid.

**HILDEBERT.**—To sanctify fasting, let us restrain ourselves not only from foods but from vices; forgive those who sin against us; and bestow good things upon those in need, CLXXI, 448. Fasting is to be sanctified by prayer and mercy, 450.

**ST. BERNARD.**—You should nourish your body in such a way that it does not become proud; and again you should restrain it in such a way that it does not collapse. You should refresh your flesh in such a way that it serves, CLXXXIV, 1244. With every effort we must despise the gluttony of foods; the craving for fare must be scorned; concern for the belly must be avoided. We ought not to eat in order that the belly may be filled, but that the body may be sustained, ibid. Fasting must be undertaken with devotion and fervor, CLXXXIII, 175.

**PETER LOMBARD.**—Fasting must be joined with almsgiving, CXCI, 1622.

**PETER COMESTOR.**—It belongs to a fasting person to seek dirt, sit in ashes and sackcloth, wear dirty clothes, live in mortification of the flesh, moderation of diet, sadness and pallor of countenance, not wash his face, and not sit at rich tables with an anointed head, CXCXVIII, 1749. Let the fasting person choose the wilderness: that is, let his members abandon the customary workshops of fleshly desires; let the eyes abandon the sight of vanity; let the ears cease to attend to fabulous trifles; let the tongue cease to gorge itself with food and become drunk with wine, in which is dissipation; let the hands cease to shed innocent blood; let the feet cease to run after other men’s children, 1760. The fasting person’s action is threefold: fasting, almsgiving, and prayer, ibid.

**PETER OF BLOIS.**—To sanctify fasting is to fast in holiness and righteousness before God, not before people, like the sad hypocrites, CCVII, 601. The form and manner of fasting, ibid.

**ST. MARTIN OF LEÓN.**—One must fast not for human favor but for eternal glory; not for the praise of men but for hope of heavenly goods; not for the world but for God; not as pleasing people but as serving God, CCVIII, 673. Hypocrites disfigure their faces because they do not fast devoutly for God, but so as to receive a temporal reward from people. They do not fast in order to obtain remission of sins, but in order to be honored by mortals. They fast sadly not to redeem sins, but to please flatterers, 674.

**ALANUS OF LILLE.**—Bodily fasting profits nothing without fasting of the mind. For what does it avail if the mouth fasts from food while the tongue is loosened to lying, the eye feasts upon vain things, the ear delights in tales, and the nostrils luxuriate in perfumes? CCX, 177.

**GUNTHERUS.**—These things befit a fasting person: constancy of mind, purity of body, spiritual joy, cheerfulness [Col. 0547] of face, maturity in words and deeds, sobriety in food and drink, CCXII, 209.

**INNOCENT III.**—On the manner of fasting, CCXVII, 364.

## II.—On the power and efficacy of fasting

**TERTULLIAN.**—Fasts obtain not only changes in nature, the averting of dangers, and the blotting out of offences, but also knowledge of the sacraments, II, 963. Droughts were driven away by fasts, I, 703. Israel immediately erased its offence by fasting, II, 962.

**ST. AMBROSE.**—Elijah, while fasting, raised the widow’s son from the dead; while fasting, he stopped the rains by his word; while fasting, he brought down fire from heaven; while fasting, he was carried to heaven in a chariot; and by a fast of forty days he gained the divine presence, XIV, 698, 699.—By fasting he halted the streams of the Jordan’s mouth and suddenly crossed the dried channel of the overflowing river with dusty footstep, ibid.

Fasting is refreshment of the soul, food of the mind, life of angels, death of guilt, destruction of offences, remedy of salvation, root of grace, foundation of chastity, 699. Fasting is a good covering, which shields the soul lest it be caught by the tempter; a good veil, which covers guilt. Fasting frees from sin, 701. Fasting extinguished the power of fire, shut the mouths of lions, solidified the waters of the sea, and melted the rock into springs of water, 704. Fasting is the mastery of continence, the discipline of chastity, humility of mind, chastisement of flesh, pattern of sobriety, rule of virtue, purification of soul, expenditure of compassion, instruction in gentleness, attraction of charity, grace of old age, safeguard of youth. It is the relief of weakness, the nourishment of salvation. No one suffers indigestion by fasting; no one has felt a stroke of blood through continence. It is good provision for a journey, good for the whole of life, good at sea: it calms shipwrecks and preserves food, 705. The drink of abstinence and the food of frugality teach one to know no vices, because they teach one to know no causes of vices, XVI, 203. Abstinence even causes the years of youth to grow old, 1196. The soul grows fat with the spiritual fat of fasting. The saints themselves become more excellent when they fast: Moses received the Law while fasting; Peter was taught the grace of the New Testament; Daniel shut the mouths of lions and saw the affairs of times to come, 1193. A belly contracted by abstinence raises human senses on high, XVII, 759. There is no sin so grave that it is not cleansed by abstinence and extinguished by almsgiving, 605. Fasting is a wall for the Christian, impregnable to the devil and uncrossable by the enemy, 644.

**ST. JEROME.**—Through fasting we can return to Paradise, from which we were expelled through satiety, XXIII, 307. Elijah, prepared by a fast of forty days, saw God on Mount Horeb, 308. Samuel gathered the people at Mizpah, strengthened them by proclaiming a fast, and made them stronger than their enemies. King Ahab, though most impious, obtained through fasting an escape from God’s sentence. Hannah, the wife of Elkanah, deserved to fill with a son the womb that fasting had left empty of food. Daniel and the three youths deserved revelation by fasting. Cornelius the centurion, in order to receive the Holy Spirit before baptism, deserved it through alms and frequent fasts.

**ST. AUGUSTINE.**—Fasting is deprivation of the flesh and gain of the mind, XL, 706. The power of fasting, XXXII, 1456; its fruits, XXXIX, 1887. The usefulness of fasting is shown by many examples, 2025, 2026.

**CASSIAN.**—The power and usefulness of fasting, XLIX, 553.

S. PETER CHRYSOLOGUS.—Fasting is the singular plough of holiness: it tills hearts, uproots crimes, tears out offences, overthrows vices, sows charity, nourishes abundance, and prepares the harvest of innocence, LII, 288. Fasting is the death of vices, the life of virtues, the peace of the body, the glory of the members, the adornment of life, the strength of minds, the vigor of souls. It is the wall of chastity, the bulwark of modesty, the city of holiness, 209.

ST. LEO THE GREAT.—Abstinence prepares the way for the Lord and raises the mind to heavenly things, LIV, 186. When one abstains from what is permitted, one more easily resists what is forbidden, 450. Through abstinence the incentives to vice are cut off, 416. Fasts make us stronger against sins, overcome desires, repel temptations, bend down pride, soften anger, and nourish all the dispositions of good will unto the full maturity of virtue, 175.

ST. MAXIMUS.—Fasting sanctifies a person and bestows great grace upon him, LVII, 314. The fasting of Christians is compared with the forty-two encampments, after completing which the Israelites came from Egypt to the promised land, 311. By a fast of forty days and forty nights Moses merited to receive the tablets written by the finger of God, 577.

ST. PAULINUS.—Fasting, by which we abstain from everything forbidden, is the soul’s garment, LXI, 313. It nourishes the soul of the body, 208. It fosters chastity, 626.

[Col. 0548] ST. BENEDICT.—Fasting serves the preservation of chastity, LXVI, 334.

ST. GREGORY OF TOURS.—The efficacy of fasting, LXXI, 193.

Lives of the Fathers.—By abstinence the domestic enemy is weakened, LXXIII, 866. The demon is driven away, 436. Fasting overcomes passions, 768. It weakens the domestic enemy, 866. It is the bridle of sin, 868. It is the monk’s seasoning; it dries up the channels of pleasures and raises the mind, ibid. Fasting and vigils humble the soul, 1014.

ST. GREGORY THE GREAT.—The fruits and dignity of holy abstinence, LXXIX, 323. By abstinence many impulses of the flesh are enfeebled, 324. Abstinence together with humility can overcome fornication, 397.

ST. ISIDORE OF SPAIN.—Through fasting the hidden mysteries of heavenly things are revealed and the secrets of the divine sacrament are disclosed, LXXXIII, 651. Fasts are mighty weapons against demonic temptations. These temptations are quickly conquered through abstinence, ibid. By fasting lust is restrained and luxury overcome; when satiety is set aside, luxury does not rule, 848. Abstinence overcomes the flesh, checks luxury, breaks the assault of lust; thirst and hunger destroy the flesh’s luxury, ibid. Through fasting vices are overthrown, the flesh is humbled, and the devil’s temptations are conquered, 776.

ST. ELIGIUS.—Fasts imitate the angelic life; by them the minds of the faithful are stirred, by them souls are refreshed, through them offences die and sins are erased; by these steps one comes to heavenly things, and with these arms we fight against the devil, LXXXVII, 605.

ST. PAULINUS.—Fasting is good for soul and body, XCIX, 234.

HAYMO.—As gluttony is the fomentation of all vices, so abstinence is the nurse of all virtues, CXVIII, 194. So long as the first parents remained in paradise, they abstained from the forbidden food. After they satisfied the desires of gluttony, they immediately lost paradise’s pleasantness. Daniel and the three youths, who displayed remarkable abstinence in the king’s court, not only escaped the lions’ teeth and felt not the fiery furnace, but also received knowledge for interpreting sacred mysteries. John, because he practised remarkable abstinence, merited not only to see but also to baptize the Redeemer, ibid.

GODEFRIDUS.—Fasting together with humility overcomes the temptations of demons, CLXXIV, 166. It prepares us for Christ’s coming, 66.

ST. BERNARD.—Through fasting fornication is overcome and luxury restrained, CLXXXIV, 1243. Abstinence overcomes the flesh, breaks the movement of lust, and dissolves the power of fornication. Through hunger and thirst luxury is destroyed. Abstinence builds virtues in the soul and destroys bodily vices, 1244. The youths did not burn in the fiery furnace because they were abstinent. Daniel was delivered from the lions’ mouth because he preserved in himself abstinence from food. Fasting is the refreshment of the heart, 171. It heals wounds and soothes exasperated consciences, ibid. Fasting is not merely the abolition of sins, but the uprooting of vices; it not only obtains pardon, but also merits grace; it not only erases past sins that we have committed, but also repels future sins that we might have committed, CLXXXIII, 176. Fasting gives devotion and confidence to prayer and merits the grace of praying, ibid.

BELETHUS.—Eve, so long as she abstained, was an uncorrupted virgin. Moses spoke with God after fasting. Elijah, after fasting, was borne to heaven in a fiery chariot. Jerusalem was delivered from Sennacherib in the time of King Hezekiah and Isaiah, after one hundred and eighty-five thousand citizens had been killed in a single night; and, lest they should stink amid the ashes, Sennacherib alone fled with only ten men to Nineveh, where on the sixtieth day afterwards he was killed by his own sons. Likewise, when Jonah preached God’s wrath, the Ninevites, performing a penitential fast in sackcloth and ashes, obtained pardon. Joshua son of Nun, fasting while he kept it throughout the whole day at Gibeon, held back the course of sun and moon and overcame his enemies, CCII, 21.

PETER OF BLOIS.—By fasting the wantonness of the flesh is restrained; by weeping and lamentation the soul, mortifying itself in these things and, as though planted together in the likeness of Christ’s death, is purified. It is converted in its affliction, and its affliction is turned into grace and glory, CCVII, 601.

ST. MARTIN OF LEÓN.—Moses, through a fast of forty days and nights, merited to receive the Law from the Lord, CCVIII, 673. Elijah, fasting forty days, withdrew into the wilderness, and standing at the entrance of the cave saw a great vision of God. Daniel, with an angel revealing it, merited to know the sacraments of the mysteries.

ALANUS OF LILLE.—Fasting emaciates the flesh, raises the soul, restrains the fuel of desire, and awakens reason. By fasting Moses merited converse with God, [Col. 0549] Daniel the interpretation of dreams, Elijah assistance, and the Ninevites remission of sins, CCX, 177. Fasting avails for the healing of body and soul: it preserves the body from sickness and the soul from sin, 178.

GUNTHERUS.—The effects of fasts are: the expulsion of demons, the exclusion of evil thoughts, remission of sins, mortification of vices, expectation of future goods, and the attainment of heavenly joys, CCXII, 210.

INNOCENT III.—Fasting avails to appease God’s wrath and obtain pardon; to avoid punishment and uproot wickedness; to retain purity and repel ignorance; to gain victory and obtain grace, CCXVII, 357 ff.

### III.—On the Necessity of Fasting

ST. AMBROSE.—Just as man had lost grace through the desire for the forbidden fruit, so his strength had to be restored through fasting, XIV, 1067. Fast, if you wish to overcome the enticement of the flesh, XV, 1618. By the number of forty days, and by more frequent fasts and prayers, let us lighten the punishments due for our sins, XIV, 360. Whoever does not fast is unprotected, naked, and exposed to a wound, XVI, 1127. What salvation can there be for us unless we wash away our sins by fasting? 1193. The arms of abstinence and sobriety must be taken up against the spiritual powers of wickedness, XVII, 401.

ST. AUGUSTINE.—Fasting is necessary for subduing the flesh, XL, 709. We must fast when we contend with the enemy in a sharper struggle, XXXVIII, 1049.

CASSIAN.—Abstinence from flesh-meat is necessary for restraining lust, LIX, 225. Its necessity, 551.

ST. LEO THE GREAT.—Fasting must be observed by all, LIV, 301. A penitential fast is necessary, 447. Through fasting all vices must be expelled, 1438.

ST. FULGENTIUS.—One must persist in fasts, LXV, 321.

ST. LEANDER.—Fasts must be imposed upon the strong body; and those whom the rebellious flesh attacks under the law of vices must be made lean by continual fasting, LXXII, 884. The stubborn flesh must be subdued by fasts and restrained so far that, as a handmaid, it may be subject to the law of the mind and the commands of the soul, 882–883.

ST. ISIDORE.—If you feel the pains of the flesh; if you are touched by the flesh’s goads; if you are assailed by the suggestion of lust; if the memory of fornication tickles your mind; if the flesh attacks you; if luxury tempts you; if lust invites you: take away from yourself satiety of bread; chastise your body by frugality; devote yourself to fasts and abstinence. Hunger and thirst; abstain and grow dry. You cannot overcome temptations unless you are trained by fasting, LXXXIII, 848. Lust increases through foods; fullness of food awakens the flesh’s luxury; through the vice of greediness the temptation of the flesh grows, ibid.

ST. ELIGIUS.—Just as medicines are necessary to a wounded body, so fasting is necessary—and much more so—to a soul wounded by the injuries of sins. Especially because we know that our first parents were expelled from the joys of paradise on account of gluttony, we must ensure, if we desire to return there, that through abstinence we prepare for ourselves the road of return, LXXXVII, 605.

HAYMO.—Fasting is necessary for overcoming the devil’s temptations, CXVIII, 192. Let us mortify our flesh by abstinence, 194. We must receive the power of abstinence with our whole heart, so that we may both extinguish future evils and wash away past sins, ibid.

ADALGERUS.—The body must be afflicted through abstinence, CXXXIV, 924. It must always be chastised and afflicted, lest it draw the soul toward an evil work, and so that it may always be fit for accomplishing good, ibid.

RATHERIUS.—One must fast so that the devil may be expelled from the heart, CXXXVI, 692.

GOFFRIDUS.—For attaining eternal salvation bodily abstinence alone is insufficient, unless the fasting of the soul, by abstinence from vices, is joined to it, CLVII, 171.

ST. ANSELM.—Take away from yourself satiety of bread; chastise your body through frugality; intent upon fasts and abstinence, keep your face pale and bear a dry body. Unless you are trained by fasts, you cannot overcome temptations, CLVIII, 680.

HUGH OF ST. VICTOR.—The mortification of the flesh must be made lean by fasts, lest it fly back to a voluptuous life with a new itching, CLXXVII, 857.

ST. BERNARD.—No one can receive the perfection of virtues unless he has first subdued in himself the gluttony of the belly, CLXXXIV, 1244. As all spiritual virtues shine forth and are built up in the soul through abstinence, so through the sweetness of foods all vices are nourished and strengthened in the body. No one can drive demonic temptations from himself unless he restrains in himself the appetite of gluttony, ibid. One must fast and abstain from foods. A dry body must be borne. Luxury increases through food and drink. If we have sinned through gluttony and greed, what [Col. 0550] remains except that we be restored through abstinence? CLXXXIII, 678. Let the eye that plundered the soul fast; let the ear fast; let the tongue fast; let the hand fast; let the soul itself fast, 176. Let the eye fast from curious looks and every wantonness; let the ear fast from tales and rumours; let the tongue fast from detraction, murmuring, useless, empty, and buffoonish words; let the hand fast from idle signs and from every kind of work; but much more let the soul itself fast from vices and from its own will, ibid.

ST. MARTIN OF LEÓN.—Let harmful luxury fast within us; let the costly greediness of the belly fast; let every perverse iniquity fast; let hateful contention fast. Let us fast from feasts, and especially from vices, CCVIII, 731.

### IV.—On the Time of Fasting

ST. AMBROSE.—We cannot fast on the Lord’s Day, XVI, 1029. To appoint a law of fasting on the day of the Resurrection is to disbelieve in Christ’s resurrection, ibid. Some have decreed that meat must not be eaten on the fourth feria [Wednesday]; some do so on Saturdays; others again eat from Easter until Pentecost, XVII, 167.

ST. AUGUSTINE.—Fasting before the solemnity of Christ’s Passion is especially suitable, XXXVIII, 1050. Why it was instituted according to the number forty, 1051. The Lenten fast has authority in both the old books and the books of the Gospel, XXXIII, 217. The Manichees did not observe the fast before Easter, XLII, 178. The fasts of Christians during the days of Easter and other solemnities in Christ, and their fasts for pagans during the latter’s profane festivals, XXXVII, 1261. The fast of the Nativity of the Lord, XXXIII, 234. Wednesday is fasted because on that day the Jews are found plotting to kill the Lord, 150. The Roman people customarily fast on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday, 140. The Romans do not think that one ought to fast on the fifth feria [Thursday], ibid. Even those who dine on other Saturdays fast on the Saturday preceding Easter, 150. Some fast on Saturday because of the humility of the Lord’s death; others relax the fast because of God’s rest, ibid. A sermon of a certain Urbicus, in which he proves that one must fast on Saturday, is extremely injurious to the universal Church, 137. Some Romans suppose, while others consider it false, that the Saturday fast arose because Peter fasted on the preceding day when he was about to contend with Simon on the Lord’s Day, 146. In observing the Saturday fast, the custom of the bishops must be followed, 156. For certain causes the Church forbids fasting for several days, XXXVIII, 1052. Fasting is especially not practised on feast days, XXXIII, 145. Christians relax fasts at Eastertide, pray standing, and sing Alleluia, which is a sign of the Resurrection, 218. Fasting on the Lord’s Day is not unlawful, but no one should prescribe fasting on that day without just scandal, XXXVIII, 144, 150. The Apostles were not accustomed solemnly to fast on the Lord’s Day, 249. The days on which one must or must not fast are not defined, 158. Arians do not wish fixed fasts to be solemnly celebrated; rather, they hold that one should fast whenever one wishes, XLII, 40. Daily fasting is recommended, except on those days on which the Church forbids fasting, XXXVIII, 1052. Except for Saturday and Sunday, many fast throughout their lives, especially those established in monasteries, XXXIII, 140. Frequent, daily, or even incredibly continuous fasts in Catholic communion, XLII, 225. A publicly proclaimed fast, XXXIX, 1865, 1948. A public fast on the Kalends of January, 2002. Fasts before Easter, XXXV, 2364. Why they were also instituted on certain vigils of saints, XL, 1276. At the fasts of the four seasons, on the vigils of saints, and likewise on Wednesday and Friday, one should fast on Lenten fare, XXII, 1458.

CASSIAN.—Why the Saturday fast was instituted at Rome and in the Western Church, XLIX, 147. The fast must be relaxed on Sundays and at Pentecost, III.

ST. LEO THE GREAT.—To what extent one must not fast on the Lord’s Day, LVI, 886.

ST. BENEDICT.—The fast of the fourth and sixth feria [Wednesday and Friday], LXVI, 662. The fast on the sixth feria [Friday] even during Eastertide, ibid. Relaxation of fasting at Eastertide on Sundays, 669. Also on principal feasts, 668.

ST. GERMANUS.—The Lenten fast, LXXII, 257. The three-day fast of the Rogation Days, 286. The fast on the vigil of Pentecost, 206.

Lives of the Fathers.—The Wednesday and Friday fast, LXXIII, 1161. The weekly fast in Scythia, 931. The martyrs Epictetus and Astion are tortured by a thirty-day fast, 402. Weekly fasts, 897.

ST. ISIDORE OF SPAIN.—On the fast of Lent, of the seventh month, of Pentecost, of the Kalends of November and January, the three-day fast, and various days, LXXXIII, 771.

Mozarabic Liturgy.—The Epiphany fast, LXXXV, 224. The fast of the Kalends of January, ibid. The Saturday fast.

ST. FRUCTUOSUS.—From Easter until Pentecost fasts are to be observed; from Pentecost until the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October, and from the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October until Easter, fasting must be diligently observed; and in Lent one must altogether abstain from wine and oil, LXXXVII, 1107–1108.

ST. BONIFACE.—On the fasts of Lent, LXXXIX, 867.

ST. BERTORIUS.—In the first week of the first month one must fast on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday until evening, CXXVI, 987. In the second week of the fourth month, that is June, one must fast on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday until None [the ninth hour]. On the remaining fasts, 988.

ANASTASIUS.—St. Callixtus commanded the observance of the fast of the four seasons, CXXVII, 1317. St. Innocent I commanded the Saturday fast, CXXVIII, 147. Telesphorus instituted the fast of seven weeks before Easter, CXXVII, 1175. Under no circumstance should a fast be performed on the Lord’s Day or the fifth feria [Thursday], 1499.

ST. ISIDORE.—One must not fast on Sundays, CXXX, 271; nor on the fifth feria, called the Lord’s Supper, 563. One must not fast in the months of July and August, 420. To fast on the Nativity of the Lord savours of heresy, 894. One who fasts on Sunday must be considered a heretic, 583.

ATTO.—On the Lenten fast and that of the four seasons, CXXXIV, 44–45.

RATHERIUS.—The fast of the four seasons and of the Rogation Days, CXXXVI, 560. Fasting should be prolonged until None [the ninth hour], 565. During Lent one must fast daily, except on Sundays, ibid.

Ancient Collection of Canons.—That one must not fast on the Lord’s Day, CXXXVIII, 134. That one must fast on Wednesday and Friday, ibid.

BURCHARD.—On fasting, CXL, 883.

JOHN OF ROUEN.—The Lenten fast, CXLVII, 212. That of the four seasons, 207.

PETER DE HONESTIS.—One must fast from the Kalends of November until the Nativity of the Lord, and from Septuagesima until holy Easter, CLXIII, 723. One must fast on Wednesday and Friday, on the Saturday of the four seasons, and on vigils, ibid.

GRATIAN.—On the times at which fasts are to be celebrated, CLXXXVII, 369 ff.

ST. BERNARD.—The fast on the vigil of St. Andrew, CLXXXIII, 503. The Saturday fast observed at Rome but not at Milan, CLXXXII, 402. Regular fasts until None [the ninth hour], CLXXXIII, 174.

ST. MARTIN OF LEÓN.—There is a fourfold reason why we continue our fast until Easter. We fast before Easter so that the Resurrection may immediately follow the Passion. The second reason is that by this we may imitate the children of Israel, who celebrated Passover immediately after their departure; the third is that the heat of lust is more apt to inflame us in springtime; the fourth, that immediately after the fast we ought to receive the Lord’s body.

### V.—On Remarkable Examples of Fasting and Abstinence

ST. AMBROSE.—Elijah found at his head a small cake and a vessel of water, and therefore in the strength of that food he fasted for forty days, XVI, 1197. Our fathers, when they crossed the sea on foot, drank water, not wine. Daniel and the Hebrew youths, by their native food and their drink of water, restrained the fury of lions, 1197. Nineveh freed itself from death by fasting, 1128.

JUVENCUS.—Christ’s fast, XIX, 113. That of the disciples of John and Christ, 176.

RUFINUS.—The abstinence of the monks living with Evagrius, who used only bread, salt, and water, XXI, 449.

CASSIAN.—The abstinence of the ancient Fathers, XLIX, 164. The abstinence of a certain elder who ate six times and was still hungry, 244. That of Abbot Paesius until sunset, 245. An example of exceptional abstinence, 958.

ST. PAULINUS OF NOLA.—How Paulinus observed the Lenten fast, LXI, 226.

Lives of the Fathers.—The abstinence of Abban from water, LXXIV, 41. Of Abraamis, who lived on lettuces, chicory, and celery, and in autumn on fruits, 77. Of Aaepsimas, who lived on lentils soaked in water, ibid. Likewise of Damian, disciple of Polychronius, 95. Of Adolius, who ate only every other day, but in Lent refreshed himself after the fifth day, LXXIII, 1191. Of Ammonius, who never tasted anything cooked, 1103; likewise of his followers, 1175. Of Ammoy, who even in illness was indifferent to food, 865. Of Anaxamontes, satisfied with the very smallest amount of food, LXXIV, 139. Of Antony, using only bread, salt, and water, LXXIII, 132; likewise of Palaemon, 221; likewise of the monks dwelling with Evagrius. Of Arsenius, satisfied with very scant food, 865. Of Barlaam, living on water and vegetables, 564. Of Benjamin, who did not taste oil for three years, 895. Of Candida, abstaining from meat, 1211. Of Conon, who for thirty years ate bread and drank water only once a week, [Col. 0552] LXXIV, 120. Of Elijah, later a bishop, abstaining from wine, 134. Of Elpidius, eating only on Saturday and Sunday, LXXIII, 1192. Of Esius, taking no food before sunset, 819. Of another Evagrius, living only on water and vegetables, 1183. Of Eusebius, sustaining himself on chickpeas and beans soaked in water, LXXIV, 79; of the same man, spending Lent on fifteen figs, ibid. Of Hilarion, who in monastic life ate nothing slaughtered, 865.

Of John, who for ten years deprived himself of every bodily food, 1152. Of John, abstaining from viaticum because the elder had not blessed it for him, LXXIV, 146. Of Macarius the Roman, living on herbs for three years, LXXIII, 424. Of Macarius the Alexandrian and his companions, abstaining from grapes, 1112; for seven years he ate only raw food, ibid. Of Macedonius, sustaining himself on soaked barley, LXXIV, 65. Of Marcian, never eating or drinking to satiety, 27. Of Mary of Egypt, living in the wilderness for seventeen years on three loaves, LXXIII, 683; thereafter content with herbs, 684. Of a monk abstaining from every drink, 824; likewise of another elder who abstained from drink for eleven days, 872. Of another monk, abstaining from all drink even in a raging fever, reaping in the field, and not eating even an ear of grain without permission, 867. Of monks living about the Jordan during Lent, 675; of the same not eating bread, LXXIII, 1195. Of seven monks living on herbs, fruit, and dew, 804. Of monks in Scythia abstaining from every broth, 865. Of Moses, living on twelve single pieces of dry bread, 1120. Of Onuphrius, living on dates and leaves of herbs, 215. Of Pachomius, who throughout the whole time of his conversion was never sated by any creature, 262. Of Palaemon, living only on bread, salt, and water, 233. Of Paul the Galatian, spending Lent on a sextarius of lentils and a small vessel of water, 1028. Of Paul of Nazareth, living for fifty years on bread given as alms by the Church’s minister, LXXIV, 139. Of Peter Pyonius, using lukewarm water instead of wine, 868. Of Philoromus, abstaining from cooked foods, 1194. Of Pior, living on salt water, one biscuit, and five olives, 757. Of Pityrion, eating only twice a week, 1177. Of Polychronius, accustomed to fast seven days. Of Posidonius, abstaining from bread for forty years, LXXIII, 1178. Of Posthumius, eating only water and vegetables, 432. Of Publius, eating bread by weight, LXXIV, 142. Of Romanus, content only with bread, salt, and water, 62. Of the ancient Scythians, who never took food except for hospitality’s sake, 147. Of a certain elder, LXXIII, 740. Of another refusing food even in illness, 872; likewise of another sick man, forgetful of all food, ibid. Of an elder abstaining from drink for forty days, ibid. Of Symeon Stylites, taking food only on the seventh day, 325. Of Sisvius, abstaining from wine, ibid. The remarkable abstinence of the boy Theodore, 250. Of a certain virgin, eating only on Saturday and Sunday, 1122. Of Macarius, chastising cups of wine even by abstinence from water, 767.

The five-day fast of Adolius, 1192. That of Conon, who for thirty years ate only once in the week, LXXIV, 129. That of Cyra, worker of miracles, 112. The two-day fast of David, disciple of Eusebius, 140. The weekly fast of Elijah in youth, LXXIII, 1155. That of Elpidius, eating only on Saturdays and Sundays, 1192. The three-month fast of Heron, except for communion and occasionally a wild herb, 1133. The three- and four-day fast of Euphrosia, 630. The remarkable fast of Macarius, 1115. That of Mark, fasting for entire weeks, LXXIV, 126. That of the layman Theodore, until evening for twenty-two years, apart from Saturdays and Sundays, 198.

ST. GREGORY THE GREAT.—His abstinence from food was so great that, his stomach having become weak and being tormented, he would doubtless have seemed scarcely able to survive, LXXV, 65. Moses, that he might merit to receive the Law, fasted twice for forty days, LXXIX, 321. Elijah, that he might escape Jezebel’s hands, came in the strength of one meal over forty days to Horeb, God’s mountain. Jesus Christ, fasting forty days in the wilderness, took no food, ibid.

ST. ELIGIUS.—Moses fasted forty days; Daniel continued a fast of three weeks and merited angelic conversations. Elijah the prophet, in the strength of one hearth-baked loaf and a small cup of water, journeyed forty days and nights. John the Baptist’s food was locusts and wild honey, LXXXVII, 606.

RABANUS MAURUS.—We read that some saints extended fasting for two days, three days, or even a whole week; that very many drank neither wine nor strong drink and ate nothing besides dry bread and vegetables; that some abstained from every kind of meat; and that others practised abstinence so greatly that they did not even use bread as food, but sustained their bodies upon a few figs, CVII, 338.

HAYMO.—Christ fasted forty days and nights. Moses and Elijah likewise, CXVIII, 193. The remarkable abstinence of Daniel and John, 194. Likewise that of the Ninevites, ibid.

[Col. 0553] ST. PETER DAMIAN.—The abstinence of Rodulphus, CXLIV, 1011. St. Venerius did not eat bread, drink wine, or taste anything cooked at all; but he lived on the fruits of trees alone and roots of herbs, 975. For an entire year Romuald had no other food, but lived each day only on a single handful of boiled chickpeas, 961. How great was the abstinence of Caesar Augustus, CXLV, 565. The abstinence of certain hermit brothers is commended, 543.

HONORIUS.—The Lord fasted forty days without food; Moses abstained from all food twice for forty days; Elijah remained fasting forty days; Daniel went three weeks without food, CLXXII, 650.

ST. BERNARD.—Christ fasts before preaching; Elijah fasts so that he may be raised in a fiery chariot; the Ninevites redeem their destruction by fasting; Esther preserves her people by fasting and calms Ahasuerus’s indignation; John the Baptist spends his whole life in fasting to prepare the way for the Gospel, CLXXXII, 705. The remarkable abstinence of a certain novice, ibid.

PETER THE CHANTER.—Paul the First Hermit always fasted until bread was sent to him from heaven, CV, 328. Hilarion was content with five figs a day for fifteen years. The holy Egyptian woman lived forty years on two loaves and roots. Jerome was content with a cheap little vegetable dish, bran bread, and water, ibid.

## PART THREE. THE QUESTION IS EXPOUNDED IN A DIFFERENT WAY, IN ALPHABETICAL ORDER

ADALGERUS, monk.—On abstinence, CXXXIV, 924.

ALANUS OF LILLE.—On fasting, CCX, 176.

ALCUIN, abbot.—On fasting, CI, 624.

ANSELM (St.), Archbishop of Canterbury.—On fasting, CLIX, 88.

ANSELM, Bishop of Havelberg.—On the manner of fasting and abstinence from meats, CLXXXVIII, 1104.—On fasting, ibid., 1108.

AUGUSTINE (St.), Bishop of Hippo.—Therefore, let it not seem to you a light or superfluous matter, lest perhaps anyone who does this according to the Church’s custom should think within himself and say to himself—or hear the tempter prompting him inwardly—“What are you doing by fasting? You defraud your soul; you do not give it what delights it. You inflict punishment upon yourself; you yourself become your own torturer and executioner. Does God then take pleasure because you torment yourself? Then he is cruel, since he delights in your punishments.”

Answer such a tempter: “Indeed I torment myself, so that he may spare me; I exact punishment from myself, so that he may aid me; so that I may please his eyes and delight his sweetness. For a victim too is tormented in order that it may be laid upon the altar.” My flesh will press less heavily upon my mind.

And answer this evil dissuader, this slave of the belly, by the following comparison, and say: “If perhaps you were riding a beast of burden, or using a horse that could throw you headlong while carrying you, would you not, in order to travel safely, withhold fodder from the raging animal and tame by hunger one whom you could not tame by the bridle? My flesh is my beast of burden; I am travelling to Jerusalem. It often carries me away and attempts to turn me from the road; but my road is Christ. Shall I then not restrain it when it is exulting, by fasting?” Whoever understands this also proves by experience itself how beneficial fasting is. For will this flesh, which is now being subdued, always be subdued? While it is subject to temporal change, while it is weighed down by the condition of mortality, it has its own manifest impulses, dangerous to our mind. For the flesh is still corruptible; it has not yet risen. It will not always be thus; it does not yet possess the proper state of heavenly blessedness. For we have not yet been made equal to God’s angels, XC, 709.

The end of our fasts is directed to our journey. We must consider what that journey itself is and whither we are tending. For pagans too sometimes fast, yet they do not know the country to which we are tending; Jews too sometimes fast, yet they have not found the road on which we walk. It is as though someone were taming a horse on which he might go astray. Heretics fast: I see what kind of people they are; I ask where they are going. “You fast,” I say, “to please whom?” “God,” they reply. Do you think that he accepts a gift? But first see what he says: “Leave your gift, and first go and be reconciled with your brother.” Do you rightly tame your members when you tear Christ’s members apart? Your fast would therefore be condemned if you were immoderately severe toward your servant. Will your fast be approved when you do not acknowledge your brother? I do not ask from what food you abstain, but what food you love. Tell me what food you love, so that I may approve your abstinence from that food. Do you love righteousness? “Perhaps,” you say, “I love it.” Let your righteousness then appear . . ., XL, 711–712.

On fasting, XXXVIII, 811; On fasting and abstinence, [Col. 0554] XXXVIII, 1043; Sermon on the usefulness of fasting, XL, 707; On fasting and where it was instituted, XL, 1275.

BENEDICT (St.), Abbot of Aniane.—How the order of fasts is to be observed, CIII, 438; On the manner of fasting, CIII, 524; On fasts, CIII, 566, 694.

BERNARD (St.), Abbot of Clairvaux.—On fasting, CLXXXIII, 176; On the double vice to be feared by those fasting, CLXXXIII, 743; On abstinence, CLXXXIV, 716.

BRUNO (St.), Bishop of Segni.—On abstinence, CLXV, 936.

BURCHARD, Bishop of Worms.—On fasting, CXL, 884.

CANUTE, King of the English.—On fasts, CLI, 1175.

ELIGIUS (St.), Bishop of Noyon.—On the praises of fasting, LXXXVII, 605.

EUGYPPIUS, African abbot.—On fasting, LXII, 1035.

FRUCTUOSUS (St.), Bishop of Braga.—On fasts, LXXXVII, 1107.

GARNERIUS, Bishop of Langres.—On fasting, CCV, 660.

GUIGO I, Prior of the Carthusians.—On fasts, CLIII, 705.

GUNTHERUS, Cistercian monk.—Let us consider fasting: what it is, how many kinds there are, to whom it is suitable to fast, and what the usefulness or effect of fasts is. To fast, as they say, is to abstain; from this, *jejunium*, that is, abstinence, is derived both in sense and in word. There are, however, various kinds of it. For there is a spiritual fast and a bodily fast. The spiritual fast is humbly to abstain from all depraved pleasures of mind and body. The bodily fast is reasonably to abstain from bodily food and drink for the salvation of the soul. Of the spiritual fast, I think nothing truer can be said than that it must be observed and maintained at every time by every person. But concerning bodily fasting, a definite teaching can be arranged according to its various kinds . . . . The fasts received in the Church in the time of grace are either of Catholic institution, monastic observance, voluntary devotion, or necessary correction. Those of Catholic institution are the fasts proposed for observance by all whom age or sickness does not prevent: such as the fast of the Lord’s Advent, of Lent, of the Four Seasons, or of the holy Vigils. Those of monastic observance are . . . Among these fasts, since that which precedes Easter is more famous, it is said of the Saviour: “When he had fasted forty days and forty nights, etc. . . .”

The following things are appropriate to one fasting: steadfastness of mind, purity of body, spiritual joy, cheerfulness of countenance, maturity in words and deeds, and sobriety in food and drink. Steadfastness of mind is that which tramples down and restrains the snares of tempting gluttony; purity of body, lest lust and impurity of the flesh harm the person fasting more than fasting benefits him; spiritual joy, by which he may already exult and rejoice in certainty of the reward of future blessedness. Cheerfulness should be in the countenance, so that one may not be sad like the hypocrites . . .; maturity in words and deeds . . . . . . There are five ways in which people customarily act against sobriety: by craving food impatiently, anticipating the proper time, seeking more luxurious foods, preparing them with excessive refinement, and taking them in excessive quantity. Esau sinned in food in the first manner, when he exchanged his birthright for a dish of lentils. David sinned in drink in the same manner, when he desired water from the cistern that was in Bethlehem, . . . In the second manner Jonathan sinned . . . . . . In the third manner are those for whom things purchased at greater expense taste better . . . . . CCXII, 207–209.

The usefulness or effect of fasts is the expulsion of demons, the exclusion of evil thoughts, the remission of sins, the mortification of vices, the sure expectation of future goods, and the enjoyment of heavenly joys. The expulsion of demons is effected not so much by others as by ourselves: for when the malign spirit sees a person afflicting himself for his sins and sees itself despised, it no longer dares to remain with him; although demons are also frequently driven out from the bodies of others who are possessed, through the power of fasting, as the Saviour says: “This kind of demon is not cast out except by prayer and fasting.” The exclusion of evil thoughts follows because, for one fasting on account of sins, it is hateful to think of committing sin. There is remission of sins, because the Lord was appeased toward the fasting Ninevites—which assuredly would not have been so had their sins not been forgiven. There is mortification of vices because, when the flesh has been mortified by continual fasting, the very hunger for sin is extinguished within it. There is a sure expectation of future goods because one who devoutly and purely afflicts himself for sins cannot fail to hope for the rewards promised to penitents. There is the enjoyment of heavenly joys because all who afflict their bodies by prolonged fasts for eternal life are brought, as soon as they depart from the flesh, to the banquets of eternal satiety, CCXII, 210.

Book on Fasting, CCXII, 207.

PETER, the Chanter.—In a general fast one abstains from every mortal sin; in the particular fast discussed here, from food and drink. This the Lord consecrated when he fasted in the wilderness forty days and forty nights; it was prefigured by the fast of Moses and the fast of Elijah. Of this the Prophet says in the person of the Lord: “I humbled my soul in fasting.” And the Lord says in the Gospel: “This kind of demon cannot be cast out except by prayer and fasting.” And the Apostle: “Let us present ourselves as ministers of God, in much patience, in fastings,” etc. And the Lord: “But when you fast, do not become sad like the hypocrites,” etc.

The fasting of the miser is detestable; the fasting of the physician is indifferent; and the fasting of the hypocrite and the proud person is an abomination . . . And the fasting of the Christian consists in the mortification of the flesh: dry and sober . . .

This was the path of pale and bloodless saints hastening toward their homeland. For, as St Jerome testifies in the *Life of St Paul*, Paul the first hermit always fasted until bread was sent to him from heaven. It was doubled when Antony came to him. Paul said to him: “Come, brother, let us eat; our ration has been doubled for us.” And, what seems incredible to you, St Hilary was content with five figs a day for fifteen years. Yet in old age and weakness he was refreshed with a morsel of barley bread. Saint Mary of Egypt lived forty years on two loaves and roots. St Jerome was content with cheap vegetables, coarse bread, and water. But we cannot attain this most severe fast because of our sloth and corruption. Let us therefore have a strict fast of bread and water, yet such as makes our service reasonable . . ., CCV, 527–528.

CLI. INDEX ON THE MORTIFICATION OF THE SENSES, OR OF MIND AND HEART, GATHERING IN LOGICAL ORDER VARIOUS SAYINGS OF THE HOLY FATHERS.

This index is divided into two parts. The first, following the chronological order of the Fathers, gives a summary statement; the second, in alphabetical order, sets out various sayings of the Fathers at length, so that the question may be understood most fully by all.

[INDEX ON THE MORTIFICATION OF THE SENSES.]

PART ONE. PASSAGES OF THE FATHERS IN CHRONOLOGICAL ORDER, WITH THE PARTICULAR PROPOSITION NOTED, ARE ONLY INDICATED.

[Col. 0555]

I.—On the mortification of the senses in general.

Mortification of the senses established by Christ’s example: St Hilary, IX, 923; St Ambrose, XV, 1765; St Augustine, XXXVIII, 275; St Gregory the Great, LXXV, 628, 666; Smaragdus, CII, 284; Rupert, CLXVII, 1036; Hildebert, CLXXI, 842; St Bernard, CLXXXII, 663.

The senses must be put to death by mortification: St Ambrose, XIV, 828; XVI, 251, 485; XVII, 24; St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 85, 86.—Self-denial is urged: St Ambrose, XVI, 65.—The soul’s strength is increased by the flesh’s weakness: St Ambrose, XVI, 485; St Jerome, XXII, 555; St Eucherius, LIII, 166; St Leo, LIV, 421; St Paulinus, LXI, 204; St Bernard, LXXXIII, 932.—The body must be reduced to servitude: St Ambrose, XVI, 1093; XVII, 233; St Augustine, XL, 294; Cassiodorus, LXX, 1083; Bede, XCIV, 113.—By mortification the flesh is crucified with Christ: St Ambrose, XVII, 123; Bede, XCII, 137; St Peter Damian, CXLIV, 350; John of Rouen, CXLVII, 46; Lanfranc, CL, 283, 284; Ralph Ardent, CLV, 1536, 1538.—On the cup of mortification: St Jerome, XXII, 480.—Mortification is a great merit of virtue: ibid., 554; St Eucherius, L, 836.—Abstinence is easier than temperate use: St Augustine, XL, 390.—The senses are to be used only for the necessities of life: the same author, XXXII, 1327.—Love of sensible things is harmful: the same author, XXXVIII, 646, 1415.—The flesh must be tamed by mortification: the same author, XL, 691, 709; XXXVIII, 107, 854; XLIV, 183; XXXVII, 1826; XLII, 391; Eugyppius, LXII, 962.—On mortification: Cassian, XLIX, 1279; Adalger, CXXXIV, 924; Alan of Lille, CCX, 149.—The body must be chastised in order to overcome the devil and the world: St Augustine, XL, 294; XLI, 283.—By not sparing the body, one provides for it: the same author, XXXVIII, 1258, 1261.—Luxuries must be despised: the same author, XXXIII, 296.—One must not yield to satiety: Cassian, XLIX, 240.—Mortification of the senses is an instrument of perfection: the same author, L, 306.—One must refrain even from lawful things: ibid., 311; St Gregory the Great, LXXV, 666; LXXVI, 1256; Theodore of Canterbury, XCIX, 935; Halitgar, CV, 678; St Remigius of Auxerre, CXXXI, 885; Ralph Ardent, CLV, 1795.—Interior mortification is softened by grace: St Benedict, LXVI, 239.—God visits those who are mortified: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1075.

Myrrh is a symbol of mortification in the Church: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1075; St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1113; Haymo, CXVIII, 114; Rupert, CLXVII, 915.—Thought of hell lightens the labor of mortification; those who do not care to subdue gluttony rashly rise to spiritual battles: St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 555, 556.—Mortification is a treasure: the same author, LXXV, 688.—Effects of mortification: ibid., 683; LXXVI, 1137.—Mortification of the flesh must never be abandoned: the same author, LXXIX, 520.—Mortification constitutes the greater part of the monastic rule: St Columbanus, LXXX, 215.

Mortification is the companion of humility: St Columbanus, LXXX, 215.—Mortification is threefold: ibid., 266.—What does reclining upon grass mean? Venerable Bede, XCII, 72.—Christ offers our mortifications to God the Father: ibid., XCIII, 53.—The righteous conquered amid thirst, cold, and nakedness: St Paulinus, CXIV, 251.—According to Paul’s word, by mortification let us become a living sacrifice: Alcuin, CI, 1191.—What mortification consists in: Smaragdus, CII, 618.—Let us drink the bitter cup of mortification, so that we may rejoice in the salvation which follows: St Odo, CXXXIII, 631; Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 841.—The dreadful devastation caused by un-mortified flesh: St Peter Damian, CXLIV, 229.—Mortification beneficial for penitents: ibid., 231, 351, 609; John of Rouen, CXLVII, 45.—Flesh not mortified is regarded as the field of a slothful man: St Peter Damian, CXLIV, 427.—Let us bear the insignia of mortification: ibid., 912.—Mortification restrains vices: ibid., 758; Venerable Hildebert, CLXXI, 511.—One must not live carnally: Lanfranc, CL, 213, 232.—God is praised in mortification: St Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 819.—Our members must be mortified: Rupert, CLXVIII, 999.

Praise of the mortification of the outward senses: ibid., 1103.—How necessary mortification of the flesh is for Christians: Venerable Hildebert, CLXXI, 588.—Mortification grows gentler through practice: ibid., 941; St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 308.—Mortification gives life to the soul: Godfrey, CLXXIV, 328, 682.—By chastisement we are prepared for death: ibid., [lacuna], 25.—Mortification is a sweet dish for God: ibid., 612.—What is troublesome to the flesh should rather be chosen: St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 123.—Mortification of the flesh benefits the flesh itself: ibid., 223, 347.

II.—On the mortification of gluttony.

(See above, the complete Index CL, On fasting and abstinence.)

III.—On the mortification of sight.
