Various statements of St Augustine are cited on guarding against the pleasure of sight: St Augustine, XXXII, 799, 800.—In the evangelical law, mortification of the eyes is commanded: Salvian, LIII, 193.—Guarding the eyes is commended: St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 810; St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 1172.—On mortification of the eyes among monks: St Benedict, LXVI, 407.—On restraining the eyes’ concupiscence: St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 89; Taio, LXXX, 939; Venerable Bede, XCIV, 57.—Vices enter through eyes that are not mortified: St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 849; Venerable Bede, XCII, 68; St Anselm, CLVIII, 679; Venerable Hildebert, CLXXI, 306.

IV.—On the mortification of hearing.

The pleasure of the flesh must be guarded against even in song: St Augustine, XXXII, 799; St Agobard, CIV, 335.—The allurements of singing must be repressed: Eugyppius, LXII, 581.—In monasteries, musical instruments are forbidden: St Benedict, LXVI, 475.—Melodious music softens the soul and disposes it toward vice: Blessed Bede, XCIII, 68.—The ears must be fenced with thorns: the same author, XCIV, 57; St Agobard, CIV, 335, 336.

V.—On the mortification of touch by haircloth.

Haircloth is a very ancient instrument of penance: St Pacian, XIII, 1088; St Paulinus, LXI, 312, 313, 871, 900; Venerable Bede, XCII, 15; XCIII, 682.—The use of haircloth is urged: St Jerome, XXIII, 97; St Paulinus, LXI, 52.—Haircloth must be worn by penitents: Salvian, LIII, 185; St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 438; St Fructuosus, LXXXVI, 1126; Venerable Bede, XCII, 15; John of Rouen, CXLVIII, 94; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 881; Peter the Chanter, CCV, 349.—What haircloth is, is defined: St Benedict, LXVI, 777; Cassiodorus, LXX, 245; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 881.—Haircloth is placed upon the dying: St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 340, 341; Alcuin, CI, 1277.—Haircloth is called the garment of the Church: Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 434.—Saints are continually clothed in haircloth: Marbod, CLXXI, 1557.

VI.—On the mortification of the tongue.

The un-mortified tongue is a source of sins: St Ambrose, XVI, 27, 28; St Jerome, XXII, 954; Arnobius the Younger, LIII, 550; St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 73; Taio, LXXX, 942, 943; Jonas of Orléans, CVI, 250; Haymo, CXVIII, 292; Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 130; St Bernard, CLXXXIV, 537, 1229; Alan of Lille, CCX, 163.—Exhortations to tame the tongue: Zacchaeus, XX, 1186; St Augustine, XXXVIII, 935, 978; XLIV, 254; XL, 1239; Salvian, LIII, 65; St Benedict, LXVI, 350; St Gregory the Great, LXXV, 802; St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 1174; St Peter Damian, CXLIV, 912 and following; St Anselm, CLVIII, 679; Venerable Hildebert, CLXXX, 1569; St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 597.—Various benefits of silence: St Jerome, XXII, 554; St Augustine, XXXVI, 414; XXXVIII, 1146; XL, 1102; St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 907; LXXVII, 72; St Donatus, LXXXVII, 288; St Odo, CXXXIII, 149; Adalger, CXXXIV, 923; St Peter Damian, CXLIV, 913; St Bernard, CLXXXII, 589; CLXXXIII, 435, 445; CLXXXIV, 369, 569, 568, 688, 682; Adam Scotus, CXCVIII, 324, 422; St Stephen of Grandmont, CCIV, 1154.—Examples of silence: St Jerome, XXIII, 1037; St Augustine, XXXII, 1450, 1453; St Benedict, LXVI, 360, 365, 368; St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 256; LXXIX, 321, 322; St Columbanus, LXXX, 240; St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 878; St Donatus, LXXXVII, 281; St Bernard, CLXXXIV, 687.—Nature teaches humankind silence: St Benedict, LXVI, 406, 47.—A discourse on the benefits of silence: Cassiodorus, LXX, 280, 285, 286.—On idle words: St Paulinus, XCIX, 244; St Benedict, CCII, 513; Jonas of Orléans, CVI, 249; Adalger, CXXXIV, 922.—The monk has a crucified tongue which Christ did not have: St Hildebert, CLXXI, 569.

PART TWO. CERTAIN SAYINGS OF THE FATHERS, GIVEN AT LENGTH IN ALPHABETICAL ORDER, SO THAT THE QUESTION MAY BE MORE CONVENIENTLY UNDERSTOOD.

ADALGER, bishop.—“I admonish your charity,” he says in his letter to Nonsuida, a recluse, “not to seek delicate foods, nor to wish to eat before the appropriate hour, nor to say in your heart: ‘See, other women do this or that.’ Know for certain that, in proportion as each person labors more in God’s service in this life, so will that person receive from the Lord a greater reward after death. Therefore, lest the virtue of continence seem so burdensome, I shall insert here a miracle.

“Dorotheus undertook to live in such a way that every day he gathered stones from the sea and every year built a lodging-house; and he gave these lodgings to persons who had none. At night he made baskets for their food. His food consisted of six ounces of bread, one small bundle of chopped vegetables, and water to drink. Living thus from his youth, he did not fail even in old age. He was never seen asleep in a bed, stretching out his feet for rest, or sleeping at will . . . A certain man said to him as he labored: ‘Why do you destroy your body in this way?’ He replied: ‘Because it destroys me.’” . . . , CXXXIV, 920–922. There are various examples concerning continence of the eyes, speech, and dress; abstinence; compunction; and the character of prayer . . ., ibid., 921–928.

There is a great contest of vices against virtues. You will be able to conquer every vice, through resistance aided by divine help, if you set the corresponding virtues against each vice. For the conflict of vices against virtues usually contributes to human advancement, because through that contest the mind is stirred and cleansed of the vice of pride. Virtues must likewise be applied against particular vices: against lust, purity of heart; against anger, patience; against fear, confidence; against tepidity, zeal; against evil sadness, spiritual joy; against acedia, courage; against avarice, generosity; against pride, humility; against hatred, the virtue of charity . . . If drowsiness weighs upon you, strive to overcome it by loving wakefulness . . . If the use of baths delights you, let blessed James, the brother of the Lord, come to mind—he who first governed the Church of Jerusalem after the apostles. Josephus relates of him that he never ate meat, never used a bath, was never clothed in linen garments, and did not anoint his head with oil according to his nation’s custom. If luxuries become a delight to you, set before your eyes John the Baptist, who was sanctified in his mother’s womb and of whom the Lord Jesus said that no one greater than he had arisen among those born of women. For the holy Gospel relates of him that he ate wild honey and locusts. If you cannot forgive wholeheartedly, as you wish to do, someone who sins against you, slanders or curses you, or harms you in any way, remember how much and what Christ suffered for you: for you he became human—mortal, corruptible, and passible—though he was immortal and impassible. For you he assumed flesh from the Virgin, in which he might suffer and die; for you he was also scourged, struck with blows, smeared with spittle, crowned with thorns, and finally crucified. Christ endured all these things for you, in order to free you from the devil’s power. And hanging for you upon the cross, what did he say? “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.” Therefore he who was put to death without sin prayed for his enemies; and you, if you suffer some annoyance from anyone, cannot forgive from your whole heart? . . . If the desire to wander comes upon you, remember that you are already dead, that you are crucified. The desire to wander never comes to a crucified person, because he thinks of nothing except his death . . . Therefore, if you wish to live, mortify every vice through virtues. By charity mortify hatred; by joy kill sadness; by peace extinguish discord; by patience mortify impatience; by goodness kill malice; by gentleness extinguish fierceness; by continence mortify intemperance; by chastity kill impurity. If you take care to mortify the deeds of the flesh in this way, you will without doubt enjoy everlasting joy with the angels, CXXXIV, 929–931.

AELRED, abbot of Rievaulx.—“To wear down the body by continual vigils, afflict the flesh by daily labors, and weaken the strength of one’s limbs by the meanest food is not only no slight labor, but is also so contrary to that charity which you strive so earnestly to commend that, emptying the mind of all sweetness, it renders it barren of every spiritual delight. This is the ridiculous opinion of certain persons who place spiritual sweetness, in some fashion, in the pleasantness of the flesh, asserting that bodily affliction is contrary to the spirit and that the sufferings of the outer person diminish the holiness of the inner person. For, they say, since flesh and spirit are joined by their natural affection, they must mutually share each other’s sufferings. Thus it is impossible that the gladness of one should not be disturbed by the oppression of the other, so that the spirit, cast down by an anxious sorrow, can in no way breathe freely into that spiritual joy. These views seem to be investigated or demonstrated shrewdly. What a shameful thing! Spiritual grace is sought according to the rules of Hippocrates. Thus indeed, thus do those err who rely more on medical arguments than on apostolic precepts. These arguments belong to him who crawls upon his belly, eats earth, sleeps in the shade in damp places, and carries on the business of belly and lust under the guise of holiness. For in this way he thinks more easily to frighten simple people away from apostolic poverty and angelic purity, if they suppose that the greater grace of divine sweetness is reserved for them in a more relaxed life to come.

“Certainly this is wisdom not descending from above but altogether earthly, animal, diabolical. This is the prudence of the word, the wisdom of the flesh: while it teaches the sweetness of the flesh, it strives to make void the cross of Christ. Yet, as regards the flesh, in that cross there is nothing sweet, nothing soft, nothing tender, nothing at all delicate. But the cross is not made void; rather, it overthrows this delicate teaching—a teaching which the nails driven into the sacred limbs assault, which that lance, thrust with saving point into the sweet entrails, defeats. I hold precisely the contrary, and boldly declare that bodily affliction, provided sound intention precedes it and discretion is observed—a discretion which must be learned not by one’s own conjecture but from the examples of the elders, lest perhaps laxity and dissipation disguise themselves under the pallor of discretion—I say that bodily affliction is not contrary to the spirit, but necessary to it. Nor does it lessen divine consolation; rather, I judge that it calls it forth, so that in this life at least these two are always equal: outward tribulation and inward consolation. What? Does God perhaps impart the sweetness of his consolation to someone overflowing with riches and luxuries, while withholding it by strict judgment from his poor person, daily dying for his sake? Far be it from us to think or believe such a thing concerning one so sweet, so gracious, so compassionate! But if I say it, perhaps one may doubt. Yet if Christ says it, it is heretical not to believe. ‘What then?’ you ask. ‘Should I believe your opinion rather than my own experience?’ And what if someone else testifies to having experienced something quite different? Certainly, the more that person is afflicted, the greater the grace of divine sweetness that person experiences. Indeed, he has mercy on whom he wills,” CXCV, 654–655.

Let therefore that most valiant athlete, most faithful witness, excellent disputant—in whom Christ speaks—come forward: he who dies daily for Christ, endures every tribulation, has battles without and fears within, chastises his body and reduces it to slavery; who does not eat his bread for nothing, but labors in toil night and day; whose hands supply necessities both for himself and for those with him; who, finally, labors as Christ’s most resolute soldier under the standard of Jesus amid hardship and distress, many vigils, hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness. Let him, I say, decide this question and show whether so great a tribulation and so extraordinary a weariness have taken spiritual consolation away from him. Let Paul therefore say whether, in present tribulation, that surpassing Comforter leaves his own without consolation . . . Therefore, let those who place a greater consolation of divine sweetness in the pleasures of the flesh than in tribulation listen to Paul saying: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies,” etc., “the God of all consolation, who consoles us in all our tribulation.” Whether, therefore, we are worn down by fasts, afflicted by fasts, or crushed by labors: “Blessed be God who consoles us in all our tribulation.” Though we are overwhelmed with stones, bound in chains, beaten with rods, or endure the constrictions of prison: “Blessed be God, who consoles us in all our tribulation.” Let the devil rage, the world be cruel, pursue us with hatred, attack us with curses, plunder our possessions, soil our reputation: “Blessed,” etc. Here he promises his consolation not to those who live amid riches and pleasures, but to those who are in every affliction. And, leaving no room for dispute, he added: “For as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our consolation also abounds.” What could be clearer? This plainly means that these two are equal: outward sufferings and inward consolations.

Finally, Solomon declares in mystical words to whom divine consolation is to be poured out, saying: “Give strong drink to those who mourn, and wine to those whose heart is bitter. Let them drink and forget their poverty, and remember their sorrow no more.” In these words he plainly promises that wine which gladdens the human heart not to those relaxed in idleness, not to those who spend the day in laughter and gossip, but to those whose heart is bitter. And he declares that this strong drink, made from new and old fruits and preserved by the bride among the delights of the bridegroom, is to be given not to those feasting and drinking, but to those mourning because of the straits of this life and suffering from poverty and pain: “Let them drink,” he says, “and forget their poverty”—affirming, that is, that the greatness of their labor is lessened by divine consolation. The Psalmist most plainly agrees with this statement: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have made my soul glad.” O consolation that heals the weak, strengthens the feeble, and relieves the despairing! It is consolation to those who groan, rest to those who labor, protection to those tempted, and provision for travelers. But those deprive themselves of this consolation who, recoiling as soon as the first sweat appears, either fall back into their former sluggishness or seek worthless consolations in frequent conversation, visits from friends, or, certainly, the freedom of their own will. Despising such filth of consolations, the holy Prophet says: “My soul refused to be consoled.” What then? Was it left without all consolation? Far from it: “I remembered God, and was delighted.” Therefore let no one shrink from that arduous way which leads to life. Let no one, with cowardly unhappiness, return to the laxity once rejected; but, as St Bernard says, let the one who endures not grow weary or depart, knowing that in proportion to the multitude of labors endured for Christ, God’s consolations will make that person’s soul glad. But, having tasted spiritual sweetness, do not immediately dissolve into idleness; for spiritual Amalek will soon rise up to lie in wait, and he must be conquered not by weapons but by prayers. Since in temptations the mind is exhausted beyond measure, one must hasten with attentive devotion in prayer to the maternal breasts of Jesus. Drawing from their abundance the milk of wondrous consolation, say with the Apostle: “Blessed be God, who consoles,” etc. . . ., CXCV, 656–657.

Thus one who has experienced it will prove that to be suffused with the sweetness of chastity is not merely devoid of labor, but is indeed of the highest pleasantness—although it is burdensome to restrain by the bridle of temperance the natural incentives and unclean desires that arise from the concupiscence of the flesh. Likewise, when the concupiscence of gluttony has been overcome, it is not merely pleasant but even glorious to see oneself not as the slave of one’s own belly but as its master, rejoicing in that wondrous exultation: “But I have learned to be content in whatever circumstances I am. I know how to be humbled, and I know also how to abound; everywhere and in all things I have learned both to be hungry and to be filled, both to abound and to suffer want.” But if the love of the flesh has been perfectly put to sleep, or indeed absorbed by the fire of divine love, there will be no labor in outward things; for that mind cannot be disturbed by affliction when it cannot be dissolved by love. Therefore the pleasantness of the Lord’s yoke and the lightness of his burden consist in contempt for pleasures. Let no one, then, suppose that there is greater delight in vices than in virtues, CXCV, 657–658.

ALAN OF LILLE.—The Prophet admonishes penitents to be in fasting, weeping, and mourning. Yet the Lord says: “When you fast, do not become sad like the hypocrites.” Gregory also says that the sinner ought even to devote himself to fasting, so that God may at some time turn his heart to repentance. Fasting weakens the flesh, raises the soul, restrains the fuel of concupiscence, and awakens reason. By fasting Moses earned converse with God; Daniel, the interpretation of dreams; Elijah, aid; and the Ninevites, remission of sins. Christ gave us an example of fasting when he fasted in the wilderness forty days and forty nights. Yet bodily fasting is of no benefit without the fasting of the mind; otherwise it is deceitful and deceptive. For what does it avail if the mouth fasts from food while the tongue is loosened for lying, the eye feasts on vanities, the ear is delighted by tales, the nostrils idle among perfumes, touch roams over smooth things, the hand engages in plunder, and the foot goes outside the ordinary path? Let the other senses fast together with taste, so that those which were companions in pleasures may be partners in sufferings.

There are, however, many kinds of fasting. There is fasting from custom, performed not from charity but from custom alone, lest a person seem to sail against the public current. This profits only by avoiding a bad example, so that no occasion of scandal is given. There is the fasting of avarice and greed, in which the stomach is emptied so that the purse may be filled; this is ruinous. There is fasting due to illness, undertaken to obtain health; this is indifferent, since it is neither good nor bad. There is also the fasting of excess and gluttony, so that food may be taken more eagerly; this is the worst. There is the fasting of praise and appearance, used by hypocrites to gain human praise; this is evil.

There is fasting of need and necessity, by which the poor fast; this is indifferent. There is fasting by compulsion, which many cloistered persons practice; this is insufficient. Setting aside all other fasts, then, one must aspire to that fasting which belongs to charity, by which the body is chastised, the spirit rules, and the person thus lives as an angel. For by fasting a person becomes spirit; by moderate food, a person; by superfluous food, a beast.

There are many circumstances which give form to fasting itself: namely, from what, where, when, and why. From what: one should abstain from delicious foods. For what use is it to fast from food if one recovers, in pleasure or quantity, what one has lost in time? At the hour of the meal, the faster ought to use moderate food, so as to assist his neighbor with bread and thus afflict himself while refreshing his neighbor. One must also consider where: the custom of one’s country must be kept, so that, if you are at Rome, live according to the Roman manner. Hence Augustine says: “When I am at Rome, I do not fast on Saturday; when I am at Milan, I fast.” When: fasting should be practiced on appointed days. For there are certain days on which one must not fast, [Col. 0562] such as Sundays and certain great feasts, because of scandal. Why: it should be done with God in view, from charity. As many as are the abstinences from carnal things, so many are the different kinds of fasting. There is fasting in continence, abstinence, humility, gentleness, and rejoicing. Augustine says concerning fasting: “Let fasts praise you, not belching entrails.”

Fasting is beneficial as a medicine for body and soul. It preserves the body from illness and the soul from sin. In this medicine heavenly philosophy agrees with natural philosophy. For this medicine cleanses both the stomach from the vice of excess and the soul from indignation. If Adam had fasted in paradise from the forbidden food, he would not have been condemned to exile. If Esau had fasted from the lentil dish, he would not have lost his birthright. If Noah had fasted from wine, he would not have exposed his thighs or private parts. Therefore by fasting the body is cleansed so as to receive the Eucharist sacramentally, and the spirit so as to receive it spiritually. This ought to be the preliminary to receiving the Eucharist. Let a person, therefore, despise present material food, lest in the future he feel the fire of Gehenna. Let these three things be present which give form to fasting: good intention, the generous giving of alms, and the kindling of charity. If the flesh desires the pleasures of food, let a person consider that it makes no difference from what material excrement is produced. If the flesh wishes to anticipate the hour of the meal, let it flee to the refuge of work, lest idleness awaken gluttony and increase appetite. O human being, if you considered the ancient Fathers, who used scant food only twice or once in a week, your fasts would seem to you nonexistent or slight. But if the examples of the ancients do not move you, at least let the infancy of blessed Nicholas move you: on Wednesday or Friday he nursed at the breast only once.

It should shame an adult not to have fasted when he saw a little child fast. The example of a child redounds to our confusion, when infants and boys correct us, CCX, 176–178.

If a preacher wishes to incline the minds of his hearers toward fleeing avarice and covetousness, let him begin his sermon with that authority which says that avarice is the service of idols; or with that which says that there are three things insatiable, and a fourth which never says, “Enough” [lacuna]. While other things are bounded by fixed limits, avarice is bounded by none. The earth is delimited by its own boundaries; heaven is confined by its own bounds; avarice alone is not stayed by any measure [lacuna].

Hear what nature says against you! “O man, I begot you without honours; return to me without honours. I bore you without riches; come to me without riches. You entered without worldly glory; depart without it! O man, you seek to make your own what belongs to another! Surely those things which were not born with you are alien to you; they cannot be yours for long, or forever.” Consider the saying of the philosopher: “Cheerful poverty is an honourable thing [lacuna].” If you live according to nature, you will never be poor; if according to opinion, you will never be rich. Nature desires little; opinion, boundless amounts [lacuna]. CCX, 123, 124.

Hear what charity says against you: “O man, why do you enrich yourself with things of which your neighbour is in need? Why do you appropriate to yourself what ought to be shared with the poor? Why do you feed moths and worms with what ought to feed the poor?” [lacuna]

Hear what your neighbour says against you: “O man, why do you wrong me? Why do you contrive death for me by means of what is mine? Why do you bring false accusations and invent charges, in order to empty my purse and squeeze money from me? If you wrong me, vengeance will be taken on you at once; if you rob me of money, you will first have robbed yourself in soul; if you wound me in body, you will first be wounded in mind.” CCX, 124.

AUGUSTINE (St.), bishop of Hippo.—How he conducts himself amid the temptations of gluttony.—We repair the daily ruins of the body by eating and drinking, until, Lord, you destroy both food and stomach, when you kill my need by a wonderful fullness and clothe this corruptible thing with everlasting incorruption. But now this necessity is sweet to me; and I fight against this sweetness, lest I be captured by it. I wage a daily war by fasting, often bringing my body into bondage; and my pains are driven away by pleasure. For hunger and thirst are pains of a kind: they burn, and, like a fever, kill, unless the remedy of food comes to the rescue. And since this remedy is at hand through the consolation of your gifts, in which earth, water, and heaven serve our weakness, calamity is called delight.

You have taught me that I should approach food as I would medicines, intending to take it. But while I pass from the annoyance of want to the rest of satiety, in that very passage the snare of concupiscence lies in wait for me. For the passage itself is pleasurable, and there is no other way to the place to which necessity compels one to pass. And although health is the reason for eating and drinking, dangerous pleasure joins itself to it as a handmaid, and often tries to go first, so that what I say or wish to do for the sake of health may be done for its sake. Nor is the measure of the two the same: what is enough for health is too little for pleasure. And often it becomes uncertain whether the necessary care of the body still seeks the aid it needs, or whether the deceptive, pleasure-seeking appetite is furnishing an occasion for service. At this uncertainty the unhappy soul rejoices, and in it prepares a defence of excuse, glad that it does not appear what is enough for moderation in health, so that, under the pretext of health, it may cloak the business of pleasure. Against these temptations I try daily to resist, and I invoke your right hand for my salvation; and I refer my perplexities to you, because my decision in this matter is not yet settled [lacuna]. You have taught me, good Father, that “all things are clean to the clean” [lacuna], and that every creature of yours is good, and that nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving [lacuna]. I have learned these things; thanks to you, praise to you, O my God, my teacher, who strikes upon my ears and enlightens my heart. Deliver me from every temptation. I do not fear the uncleanness of food, but the uncleanness of desire. I know that Noah was permitted to eat every kind of flesh useful for food; that John, endowed with wonderful abstinence, was not defiled by animals—that is, locusts—being used as food; and that Esau was deceived by desire for lentils; that David reproached himself for desiring water; and that our King was tempted not by meat, but by bread. Therefore, too, the people in the wilderness deserved reproof, not because they desired meat, but because in desiring food they murmured against the Lord.

Placed amid these temptations, then, I struggle daily against the desire to eat and drink; for this is not something which I can decide to cut off once for all and never touch again, as I was able to do concerning sexual intercourse. Therefore the reins of the throat must be held by a measured loosening and tightening. And who is there, Lord, who is not carried at least a little beyond the bounds of necessity? Whoever he is, he is great; let him magnify your name [lacuna]. XXXII, 797–799.

He confesses how he fares with the temptations of carnal lust.—You certainly command, Lord, that I refrain from the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and worldly ambition [lacuna]. Yet images of such things still live in my memory, where habit fixed them; and they meet me when I am awake, indeed without force, but in dreams not only so as to produce pleasure, but even consent and an act very like the real thing. Such is the power of the illusion of images in my soul and flesh that, while asleep, false visions persuade me to what true things cannot persuade me while awake. Am I then not myself, O Lord my God? Yet how great is the difference between myself and myself in the instant when I pass from here into sleep, or return hither from there! Where then is reason, which when awake resists such suggestions and remains unmoved even if the things themselves are presented? Is it shut up with the eyes? Is it put to sleep with the bodily senses? And whence is it that we often resist even in dreams, mindful of our resolve and remaining therein most chastely, giving no assent to such enticements? Yet the difference is so great that, when it happens otherwise, on waking we return to the repose of conscience and discover by that very difference that we did not do it—though we grieve that in some manner it was done in us.

Is your hand not able, almighty God, to heal every weakness of my soul and, by your more abundant grace, extinguish even the wanton motions of my sleep? You will increase your gifts in me more and more, Lord, so that my soul, freed from the glue of concupiscence, may follow me to you, may not rebel against you, and may not even in dreams commit these shameful corruptions through animal images unto the emission of the flesh—nay, may not even consent to them. For to make nothing of this sort, not even so little as can be restrained by a nod, pleasing to the chaste affection of one asleep—not only in this life, but even at this age—is no great matter for the Almighty, who can do beyond what we ask or understand. Yet I have told my good Lord what I still am in this kind of evil, rejoicing with trembling over what you have granted me and grieving over what remains unfinished, hoping that you will bring your mercies to completion in me unto that full peace which my inward and outward parts shall have with you, when death has been swallowed up in victory. XXXII, 796, 797.

How he conducts himself amid the enticements of smells.—I do not trouble myself greatly about the enticement of smells. When they are absent, I do not seek them; when present, I do not reject them, being prepared always to do without them. So it seems to me; perhaps I am deceived. For these too are lamentable darknesses, in which my own capacity, which is within me, is hidden from me; so that when my mind questions itself concerning its own powers, it judges that it cannot easily be trusted, because what is within is generally hidden unless experience reveals it. And no one ought to feel secure in this life, which is called wholly a temptation, whether one who could become better from worse may not also become worse from better. One hope, one confidence, one firm promise: your mercy. [Col. 0564] XXXII, 799.

How he conducts himself amid the enticements of the eyes.—The eyes love beautiful forms and varied, bright, pleasing colours. Let these not hold my soul captive; rather, let God, who made them, hold it. They are indeed very good, but he is my good, not they. They affect me throughout my waking days, and I am given no rest from them, as I am sometimes given rest from musical sounds, from all of them, in silence. For this light, the queen of colours, bathing everything that we see, wherever I may be during the day, flatters me by its manifold approaches while I am doing something else and do not attend to it. Yet it insinuates itself so strongly that, if it is suddenly withdrawn, it is sought with longing; and if it is absent for long, it saddens the mind.

“O light which Tobias saw, when, with these eyes closed, he taught his son the way of life” [lacuna]. I resist the seductions of the eyes, lest my feet, with which I walk in your way, become entangled [lacuna]. How countless are the things which human beings have added to the enticements of the eyes—by diverse arts and crafts in clothing, shoes, vessels, and objects of every kind, even paintings and varied fashioned images—things far exceeding necessary and moderate use and pious signification. Following outwardly what they make, they abandon inwardly him by whom they were made, and destroy what they were made to be. But I, my God and my glory, sing a hymn to you even over these things, and offer a sacrifice of praise to my Sacrificer; for beautiful things passing through souls into skilful hands come from that Beauty which is above souls, for which my soul sighs day and night. Yet makers and followers of external beauties draw from that Beauty the standard by which they approve, but do not draw from it the standard by which they use. It is there, and they do not see it, lest they go farther away and keep their strength for you rather than scatter it in enervating delights. As for me, although I say and discern these things, I still fasten my steps upon these beauties; but you pluck me out, Lord—you pluck me out—for your mercy is before my eyes. For I too am pitifully caught, and you mercifully pluck me out: sometimes without my feeling it, because I had fallen more lightly; at other times with pain, because I had already clung fast. XXXII, 800, 801.

How he conducts himself amid the pleasures of hearing.—The pleasures of hearing had more tenaciously entangled and subdued me; but you have loosed and freed me. Now, in sounds by which your words are given life, when they are sung in a sweet and artistic voice, I confess that I find some repose—not so as to cling to them, but so as to rise when I wish. Yet, together with the very sayings by which they live, in order to gain admission to me, they seek in my heart a place of no small dignity; and I scarcely grant them a fitting place. For sometimes I seem to myself to pay them more honour than is proper, when I perceive that our minds are moved more religiously and ardently into the flame of piety by these holy sayings when they are sung in this way than if they were not so sung; and that all the affections of our spirit, according to their diversity, have their own proper modes in voice and song, stirred by some hidden affinity I cannot explain. But the pleasure of my flesh, to which my mind ought not to be surrendered and weakened, often deceives me. Sensation does not follow reason so as patiently to remain behind; merely because it has deserved admission for reason’s sake, it tries also to run ahead and lead. Thus I sin in these things without perceiving it, though afterwards I perceive it.

At other times, guarding against this very deception too excessively, I err through excessive strictness; indeed, at times I could wish that every sweet melody of songs by which the Davidic Psalter is commonly accompanied were removed from my ears, and from the Church itself. The safer course seems to me to be what I often remember being said of Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria: with so slight an inflection of voice did he cause the reader of the Psalm to sound, that he was nearer to speaking than to singing. Yet when I recall the tears which I poured forth at the chants of your Church in the beginning of my restored faith, and how I am moved even now, not by the singing but by the things sung, when they are sung with a clear voice and most fitting modulation, I again acknowledge the great usefulness of this practice. Thus I fluctuate between the danger of pleasure and the experience of benefit; and, though without pronouncing an irrevocable judgment, I am more inclined to approve the custom of singing in church, so that through the delight of the ears a weaker mind may rise into an affection of piety. Yet whenever it happens that the singing moves me more than the thing that is sung, I confess that I sin deserving punishment; and then I would prefer not to hear the singer. Behold where I am. Weep with me, and weep for me, you who inwardly do with me something good, from which deeds proceed. For you who do not do so are not moved by these things [lacuna]. XXXII, 800.

CASSIAN, priest of Marseilles.—Although the vices assail the whole human race, they do not attack all persons in one way. In one person the spirit of fornication occupies the chief place; in another anger rides roughshod; in another [Col. 0565] vainglory claims tyranny; in another pride holds the citadel. And though it is certain that all are attacked by all, each of us suffers in a different manner and order.

Therefore we must take up battle against these vices in such a way that each person, having discovered the vice by which he is most severely harassed, takes up the principal contest against it: directing every care and concern of mind to combating and watching against it; sending daily arrows of fasts against it; hurling against it at every moment the sighs of his heart and frequent weapons of groans; devoting to it the labours of vigils and meditations upon his own heart; and continually pouring out to God tears of prayer, specially and unceasingly asking him to extinguish that assault. For it is impossible for anyone to gain triumph over any passion until he understands that he cannot once and for all obtain victory in the contest by his own industry or labour, though, if he is to be purified, he must remain day and night in every care and vigilance. And when he feels himself released from that vice, let him again search the hiding places of his heart with like attention, discover which of the remaining vices he sees to be more grievous for him, and set all the weapons of the spirit in motion more particularly against it. Thus, by always overcoming the stronger, he will gain a swift and easy victory over those that remain; for his mind will become stronger by the progress of its triumphs, while the successive battle against the weaker will make the course and outcome of the conflicts more ready—just as happens with those who are accustomed, before the kings of this world, to fight beasts of every kind in the spectacle commonly called *pancarpum*, with the prizes in view. Such men, when they see beasts more terrible because stronger in force or fiercer in rage, take up the contest of the first encounter against them; once these have been slain, they bring down the rest, which are less fearful and less violent, with an easier result. So too, once the stronger vices have always been overcome and the weaker follow, perfect victory will be prepared for us without any danger.

Yet one must not suppose that a person chiefly fighting against one vice, and, as though heedless, looking out for the missiles of the others, can more easily be wounded by an unexpected blow. That will by no means happen. For it is impossible that one who, solicitous for cleansing his heart, has armed the attention of his mind against an assault from any vice should not also have a general dread of, and similar guard against, the other vices. But when the chief attention of our heart has, as it were, undertaken a particular battle against one passion, it will pray more attentively concerning that passion, pleading with special care and effort so that it may watch it more diligently and thereby deserve to gain a swift victory. XLIX, 630, 631.

PATRICK (St.), bishop of the Irish.—One must therefore resist carnal pleasure vigorously, fight vigorously against the deceitful blandishments of this world, and keep watch against Satan’s manifold suggestions. With every effort the broad way of the world, which leads to death, must be avoided; but with every desire of the heart the narrow way which leads to life must be approached and sought. This narrow way is the way of abstinence, chastity, humility, and all religious devotion: the way which Christ trod out before us, and by which he passed into his kingdom. Let us too follow both his way and his footsteps, until after him we arrive at the royal city in which he reigns [lacuna]. LIII, 833.

PAULINUS (St.), patriarch of Aquileia.—Let us crush the pride of our flesh, because it is the flesh that destroys the soul and brings in all pride. “He who sows in the flesh shall also reap corruption from the flesh.” It is the flesh that receives the devil; for the devil sows in our flesh his own seeds—that is, murder, fornication, covetousness, lust, anger, quarrelling, drunkenness, pride, theft, and every evil suggestion. As the Apostle says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the spirits of this air, against spiritual forces in the heavenly places” [lacuna]. The flesh is a miserable beast which weighs down the soul, as the Apostle says: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God” [lacuna]. For our flesh always wishes to be strong in wickedness; but in abstinence—that is, in fasting, vigils, prayers, and good works—it pretends to be weak [lacuna].

Therefore let us mortify our flesh by abstinence, fasting, vigils, and prayers, lest it bring the devil upon you with evil desires. The flesh, moreover, has been given to us as a kind of warfare for the soul: if it is mortified, it brings life; if it is nourished, it prepares itself for war against the soul. I praise the person who can have mastery over his own flesh. While we fear the weakness of our flesh, we neglect the salvation of our soul [lacuna]. Woe, woe to the miserable soul persecuted by the flesh! Our flesh fights daily against the soul, and we must fight daily against the flesh. [Col. 0566] The flesh desires and displays every evil suggestion; the flesh desires every evil; the flesh urges wicked deeds; the flesh provokes anger, murder, adultery, and quarrelling; the flesh introduces drunkenness and carries every evil desire of this age; the flesh desires all evils. O flesh, cruel beast, what have you to do with burdening the soul, which would have desired nothing except to serve God had it not joined itself to you, its enemy? But you, miserable flesh, kill not only yourself but also the soul. Your own destruction does not suffice you: you still wish to plunge the soul into hell. Woe to you, soul, who have received a hostile flesh, which neither itself enters nor permits you to enter the kingdom of heaven! O evil flesh, what do you seek, what do you desire? You do not wish to endure labour; you do not wish to rest from unrest; you suffocate the soul so that, with roles reversed, you may be mistress and it a handmaid [lacuna]. Nor will you escape punishment while the soul itself suffers Gehenna; for without you it cannot be judged on the day of judgment. XCIX, 274–278.

There is yet another accumulation of evils of the flesh. XCIX, 278, 279.

Prayer of the soul to God against the evils of the flesh.—Let there not be in me, I beseech you, Lord, the desire of lust, but love of most beautiful chastity. Let me be slow to hear evil, quick for your word, swift to carry it out. Let me be watchful in your fear, perfect in love, steadfast in faith, in no way doubting in hope. Let me burn with love of my neighbour; let me not be consumed by love of hatred or waste away with the sickness of envy. Always breathe a holy work into me, that I may think it; compel me, that I may do it. Persuade me to love you; strengthen me to hold fast to you; guard me lest I lose you. Let neither the foot of pride nor the desire of gluttony, fornication, avarice, envy, anger, sadness, or vain glory enter or rest in my dwelling, where your habitation ought to be. But I ask for deep humility [lacuna]. Grant a measured abstinence, by which the excessive greediness of the belly that destroys me may be checked. Grant purity of heart, which may make me undefiled. Grant cleanness of spirit, because unclean fleshly lust plunges me down. Grant hands lavish in giving alms, that grasping avarice may be rejected. Grant the love of charity, by which the zeal of envy may be extinguished. Grant the patience of endurance, by which anger, that cruel beast, may fail when overcome. Bestow hope of eternal joy, by which the bitterness of sadness may be soothed. Make my mind inwardly glory in you over a good work, so that the boasting of vain glory may not proceed outwardly from me. Give me also to maintain in all things justice, magnanimity, and temperance; and make me prudently simple, so that I may sincerely live the blessed life and prudently flee evil; so that I may understand the devil’s fraudulent and deceptive cunning, lest he deceive me under the appearance of good; and may rationally discern and foresee what good I should do and what evil I should flee. Make me thereafter gentle, kind, peaceable, meek, without pretence, at peace with all good persons, and steadily diligent in vigils, fasts, and prayers. Grant also moderation of speech in meekness and the attainment of silence, so that I may say what is fitting and be silent about what ought not to be said; and grant me whatever you deign to bestow from the fruit of virtues. Grant that I may keep faith in you without any error and that my works may be worthy of my faith, so that I may not defile right faith by wrong action; so that I may not deny by evil living the one whom I confess by believing; and so that I may not offend by works of negligence the one whom I follow in deed with steadfast faith.

Make me, living in a holy resolve, pursue justice, love mercy, cherish truth, reject falsehood, devise or speak nothing false, fear you without ceasing, love you, cherish you, keep your commandments, retain peace with all without deceit, call those at discord to concord without pretence, offer unfeigned charity to all, give scandal to no one, prefer myself to no one but judge myself inferior to all, show reverence and fear not out of fear of the powerful but for the sake of the Most High; offer obedience to elders and charity to equals; show younger persons the favour of timely affection; bear with equanimity the burdens and dangers of my brethren; benefit all together and harm none; injure no one, oppose no one, slander no one, set a stumbling-block before no one, judge no one, speak ill of no one, be injurious to no one, criticize no one’s life, investigate no one’s path; but be concerned only for myself; never repay evil for evil; be in no way either mindful or avenging of wrongs done me; overcome malice by every goodness; prepare a blessing for one who curses; love enemy and friend; endure without repayment the abuse and insults of angry persons; quickly forget injuries; forgive one who offends me; always be ready to grant pardon; covet nothing belonging to another or seize it under any pretext; but mercifully distribute what is mine to those who lack it; receive for your sake, you who redeemed me, the stranger and traveller; refresh the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, take in the guest, clothe the naked, visit the sick, seek out the prisoner, console the sorrowful, sympathize with the afflicted and mourning, provide necessities for the needy, share food and clothing with the destitute, embrace the indigent, cherish the member of my household, love the foreigner, ransom the captive, receive the newcomer, protect the fatherless and orphan, support the widow, aid the oppressed, give help to the desolate [lacuna]; and diligently believe and hear whatever teachings set forth your commandments, eagerly investigate them, wisely understand them, speedily practise them, desirefully fulfil them, and always stand humble before you, so that I may rise and not be cast down, be lifted up and not fall, ascend and not descend. For the flesh with which I dwell always wishes to lead me to sin; it wishes to be crowned with me, but not to fight with me.

I endure no worse enemy than my body, in which I dwell. It is like a destructive lion in my house, consuming me by tearing me apart on every side with its deadly bite. Therefore, drawing long sighs, I shall cry out: “Wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God.” Through whom? “Through Jesus Christ our Lord.” These things I desire, O good Jesus, Saviour and most excellent Redeemer; these things I desire, for which I have thus far now pleaded in supplication; these and these I ask, because I have been redeemed by your most precious blood: that through the corruption of the flesh I may not perish eternally, may not come to the second death, nor to the land of forgetfulness. Let this my voice sound in the ears of your mercy, so that I may do your will, not the flesh’s; and let all my mind meditate upon you, delight in you, follow you, confess you. For in redeeming me, your mercy is eternal; and in your mercy I, lost through the sins of my youth, came to life again and did penance before you, because you preserved for me a time of conversion; considering my sins, I was pierced with compunction and, through your inspiration, did penance before you.

Now therefore, joyful, I give you countless thanks, now and always: because, that I might find you, you first sought me; that I might return to you, you compelled me; that I might be chastised, you looked upon me as a loving Father; that I might confess, you worked within me; that, recognizing myself, I might weep, you gave this to me. Set, Lord, my tears before you, and let my prayer reach you in heaven. Be present, I beseech you, and help; and receive me, commended to you, into your hands, delivering me from the mouth of the most savage dragon and from the hand of the most dreadful hell. When you receive me, take me away from amid the shadow of death; indeed, lead me into the path of light, into the most bright land of the living. Place me in the safest sheepfolds of your flocks, for you are the good shepherd who seeks and brings back the lost sheep, protects and saves it when found, heals and cherishes it when sick. And you are the merciful Lord, who do not put to shame those hoping in you, do not forsake those seeking you, do not reject those returning to you; but receive them with rejoicing and praise, and grant them to reign eternally in eternal blessedness together with your saints and elect. For with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit you possess one Godhead, glory, strength, dominion, and power unto ages of ages. Amen. XCIX, 279–282.

PETER THE CHANTER.—On the vice of the tongue.—There are four causes of evil talkativeness or garrulity: flattery, boasting, covetousness, and unguarded speech. Talkativeness is therefore contrary to good silence, against which the Prophet cries: “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips. Do not incline my heart toward words of malice.” Hence Abbot Serapion says: “There is no member of my body that I fear as much as my tongue.” “If anyone thinks himself religious, while not restraining his tongue from evil but deceiving his heart, that person’s religion is vain.” The same Serapion says: “I wept for a long time, endured many labours, and lived long in the desert; yet I could never attain the measure of humility and silence possessed by my son Zacharias.” Likewise: “Never, when an elder was present, did I utter a word; rather, I approved what he said.” Again, the same man, replying to someone who asked, “How shall I live in quiet?”: “Among those with whom you live, live as a stranger, not as a master; and never let your word have power before you.” Again he says: “If you wish to be loved and to live quietly, keep much silence. For in much speaking sin will not be lacking.” Lanfranc, lest he be proud of his learning, remained always silent until a matter of faith came into danger.

One of the Fathers, in order not to sin with his tongue, almost always carried in his mouth, as though a bridle, a little stone. Likewise, just as it is safer to err through excessive mercy than through the rigour of justice, so it is safer in silence than in talkativeness. Likewise: “Who is the man who desires life,” etc. [lacuna]. CCV, 195, 196.

Gluttony has four attendants: what, how much, of what kind, and when. “What” consists in, and is considered according to, the kind of food; [Col. 0568] “how much,” in quantity; “of what kind,” in the seasoning of food, sauce, or even nutritional value; “when,” in the appropriateness and frequency of the time.

Because of gluttony, a person searches the seas and the land; he pursues some creatures with hooks, others with snares, others with various kinds of nets, at great labour. No animal enjoys peace, except through being disdained. How little, from these banquets procured through so many hands, do you drink with a mouth wearied by pleasures? How little does the sickly, nauseated master taste from this dangerously caught food? How little from so many shellfish, brought from so far away, slips through this insatiable stomach? I say that you are unhappy because you do not understand that you have a hunger greater than your stomach. CCV, 330.

St Jerome says: “Some, fattened and swollen from the inheritance of the Crucified One, disgrace and distend their belly with banquets and wine, turning a stomach unaccustomed to its office into a sack; they put in and put out decayed and rotten foods, and soothe and relieve the burning stomach with drink, as Saul, drinking waters, was drunk on successive nights” [lacuna]. “But if the Apostle, O daughter, chastises his body and brings it into bondage, lest, after preaching to others, he himself should become reprobate, how can you, still a young woman in the heat of youth, filled with banquets and wine, be secure concerning chastity? If burning Vesuvius, fire-belching Olympus, and Aetna full of vapours burn with heat, how much more do youthful marrow-bones, full and inflamed with wine and banquets!” [lacuna]. CCV, 331.

It is therefore clear from the authorities of the saints that abstinence and sobriety are the companions and nurses of continence, while gluttony is the companion of lust. For a belly inflamed with strong wine easily slips into lechery. Beware lest you be cast down at the banquet among the dishes with the daughters of Job. Satan overwhelmed Job’s children at their elder brother’s banquet, not because they were given over to the belly, but because amid banquets the good intention of the mind is less fervent and less watchful. Samson overthrew the Philistines amid feasting; Nebuchadnezzar, abusing the banquets and vessels of the Lord, heard terrible voices [lacuna]. The devil tempted our first parents through gluttony [lacuna]. CCV, 332.

We join gluttony and drunkenness, because drunkenness, like gluttony, distends the belly, inflames the flesh, fosters and nourishes lust. Hence Lot, whom Sodom did not conquer, was conquered by wine, so that he committed incest with his daughter; Noah also, etc. [lacuna]. CCV, 330.

Against the slothful.—To those who weaken the sacred Scripture and are the most wicked evaluators of sins, accumulated sloth is also joined; through it they neither read nor search the sacred Scripture. Sloth is a very great sin. Rebuking it, Solomon says: “How long, sluggard, will you sleep? When will you arise from your sleep [lacuna]?” CCV, 246–249.

And although sloth can be rebuked and found in almost every kind of human being, it is found especially among the clergy, because clerics have great leisure. There is nothing for them to do, although the Apostle says: “Command these persons to eat their own bread,” that is, the bread of their own labour. Thus too that saying is explained: “In labour and the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread.” By “bread” is understood every necessity of the body; understand the whole body from one part. For human labour consists not only in acquiring food, but in clothing oneself and preparing the building in which one dwells. Labour is manifold: of nature, of grace, and of fault. Natural labour is twofold, namely bodily and spiritual: spiritual in thought, bodily in many forms. Nor does the Lord prohibit the labour of nature—that is, labour for necessity—when he says, “Do not be anxious about tomorrow,” speaking of vicious anxiety, not necessary foresight. The labour of grace is for grace and because of grace. It too is twofold, bodily and spiritual, and each is threefold. For there is penitential labour, as: “I have laboured in my groaning [lacuna].” CCV, 249, 250.

### Commendation of the Solitude of the Place

St. Jerome, flying from the schools of the liberal arts to the desert, writes thus to someone, inviting him to the desert and to contempt for the world:

“O desert, flourishing with Christ’s flowers! O solitude, in which are born those stones from which, in the Apocalypse, the city of the great King is built! O wilderness, enjoying God’s more familiar presence! What are you doing, brother, in the world—you who are greater than the world? How long will the shadows of roofs press upon you? How long will the prison of famous cities confine you? Believe me: in the desert I behold I know not what greater light. There one may, having cast off the burden of the flesh, fly to the pure radiance of heaven. Do you fear poverty? But Christ calls the poor blessed. Are you frightened by labor? No athlete is crowned without sweat. Do you think about food? But faith does not fear hunger. Do you fear that limbs worn away by fasting will strike the bare ground? But the Lord lies with you. Does the unkempt hair of a neglected head horrify you? But Christ is your head. Does the boundless vastness of the desert terrify you? Yet walk in paradise with your mind. [Col. 0569] Whenever you pass there in thought, so often you will not be in the desert. Does rough skin, drawn tight without baths, distress you? But one who has once been washed in Christ has no need to be washed again. And, briefly, hear the Apostle answering all these things: ‘The sufferings of this present time are not worthy . . . .’ You are a soft soldier if you wish to rejoice here in the world and afterward to reign with Christ.” CCV, 213–214.

“. . . . Let us enter,” he says likewise, “the solitude, as it were certain hidden places of the countryside, where bread for our food, vegetables watered by our own hands, milk—the rustic luxury—provide cheap indeed but innocent fare. Living thus, neither sleep will call us back from prayer nor fullness from reading. If it is hot, the shelter of a tree will provide shade. If it is autumn, the very mildness of the air and leaves spread beneath us will show a place of rest. In spring the field is painted with flowers, and among the singing birds psalms will be sung more sweetly. If there is cold and winter snow, I shall not buy firewood: I shall keep warm while awake, or at least while sleeping; and, what I know to be more useful, I shall not be cold. Let Rome keep her tumults, let the arena rage, the circus go mad, the theatres luxuriate, and people occupy themselves with rumors and delight in paying calls: ‘But it is good for us to cling to God . . . .’” CCV, 214.

He says likewise: “Whenever I was situated in the desert—that is, in the grim dwelling-place of monks—and imagined myself present amid Roman pleasures, I sat alone, because I was filled with bitterness. My limbs recoiled at the sackcloth; my skin was ugly and foul, as though it were clothed in Ethiopian flesh. Daily there were tears, daily groans; and whenever threatening sleep overcame me despite my resistance, I dashed my bones, scarcely clinging together, upon the bare ground. Thus, through fear of Gehenna, I had condemned myself to such a prison; and, made companion to scorpions and wild beasts, I was often among choirs of girls. My face grew pale through fasting, but my mind burned with desires. I lay at Jesus’ feet, watered them with tears, wiped them with my hair; and I subdued the resisting flesh by vigils and fasts, using raw food and cold water—for there is some luxury in cooked food.” CCV, 215.

### St. Peter Damian, Cardinal

“Come now, man: what is this flesh that you cover with such watchful care in garments and nourish tenderly as though it were royal offspring? Is it not a mass of rottenness? Is it not worm, dust, and ashes? Nor does the wise man attend to what it is now; rather, it is fitting to consider the pus, poison, stench, and filthy overflow of obscene corruption which it will afterward become. What thanks, then, will the worms render you—the worms that are to devour the flesh you have nourished softly and pleasantly?

“Come now, I say: why did Christ suffer? Was it in order to wash away his own guilt and blot out the offenses he himself had committed? But hear Peter speaking of him: ‘He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth.’ Why then did he suffer? Peter himself again answers: ‘Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his footsteps.’ Therefore Christ suffered first; the apostles immediately followed him, and we too are commanded to imitate their footsteps, as one of them says: ‘Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ.’ Why, then, do we read that Christ suffered, except that we may follow the example he left in his footsteps?

“I beseech you therefore, beloved: close your ears to the serpentine hissing of those who speak perversely, and preserve them as virgins in the simplicity of poor and crucified Christ Jesus. Drive from your mouth the golden cup of Babylon and the cup of God’s wrath, which is offered to you enticingly; avoid the deadly poisons of those who are proud and adulterate the word of God. Of them the Apostle says to Timothy: ‘Avoid profane and empty talk; for they advance greatly in impiety, and their speech spreads like a cancer.’ May the twofold dread which the Apostle sets forth in different places never befall you or me—God forbid: ‘I fear for you, lest, as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted and fall away from the simplicity that is in Christ Jesus’; and, for myself, ‘I fear lest I may have labored among you in vain . . . .’

“Therefore let not the holy mind fear to share Christ’s cross, nor blush at his reproach in bodily nakedness . . . . Certainly, one who contemplates with the clear eye of the mind the future rewards of recompense is never ashamed of the nakedness of his body; nor does one shrink from the harshness of blows, which flies by in a moment, when he prudently considers the sweetness of eternal delight that is to compensate him.

“O how pleasant, how splendid a spectacle it is when the heavenly Judge looks down from heaven and a man casts himself down below for his own offenses! There the accused person himself, presiding in the tribunal of his own breast, holds a threefold office: in his heart he appoints himself judge; in his body, defendant; and with his hands he gladly offers himself as torturer—as though the holy penitent said to God: ‘Lord, there is no need for you to command that I be punished by your office; it is not fitting that you yourself strike me with the vengeance of just judgment. I lay hands upon myself; I exact vengeance from myself and repay my sins in kind.’ And this is indeed what the Apostle Peter admonishes when he says: ‘Let none of you suffer as a murderer, or a thief, or an evildoer, or one who covets another’s goods; but if as a Christian, let him not be ashamed.’

“Indeed, where this takes place, demons flee, and they shudder to behold what is done for Christ’s glory and their own disgrace. Conversely, angels stand by this spectacle; they rejoice over the converted sinner and joyfully announce this to God, while the invisible Judge already sees the same thing with delight. This is the victim that is sacrificed alive and carried to God through angels as an offering; and thus the sacrifice of the human body is invisibly united with that one sacrifice offered upon the altar of the cross. Thus every sacrifice is laid up in one treasury: namely, that which each member has offered, and that which the Head of all the elect has offered.” CXLV, 684–686.

### Smaragdus, Abbot

“Let us sanctify our fasts by the observances of religion. What else is it to ‘sanctify a fast’ than, on account of fasting, to will holy things, do just things, and avoid wicked things? He sanctifies a fast who extinguishes the flames of raging anger by the placable gentleness of his mind.

“He sanctifies a fast who turns wandering eyes away from shameful sights by the reins of chastity.

“He sanctifies a fast who scatters the darts of insults by repelling them with the shield of patience. He sanctifies a fast who restrains the uproar of disputants by the skill of peaceful speech and a wiser tongue. He sanctifies a fast who, like a farmer of his own breast, cuts away the thorns of vain thoughts rising within himself with the ploughshare of the Gospel. He sanctifies a fast who comforts the need of the poor, in proportion to his own resources, by the kindness of a compassionate hand. Above all, he sanctifies a fast who, intent in everything upon the commandments of the divine law, drives diabolical temptations from his heart.

“And therefore, if we wish to offer fasts pleasing to God, let us be strong in faith, just in judgments, faithful in friendship, patient under injuries, moderate in disputes, avoiding shameful speech, steadfast against wrongdoing, restrained amid insults, continent in pleasures, simple in charity, cautious among the deceitful, compassionate toward the sorrowful, resistant to the obstinate, sparing in suspicions, silent among slanderers, and equals among the humble. If we wish to sanctify our fasts by virtues of this kind, then, through the Lord’s gift, we shall come to the feast of Paschal grace and to the joys of heavenly promises with unhesitating confidence and a more joyful conscience.

“He fasts well, whoever sustains his own hunger by the satisfaction of a poor person who has been fed. He fasts well who, restraining himself through remembrance of the divine judgment, abstains from every pleasure of enticements. He fasts well who chastises his flesh, sprouting seeds of vices, by meditation upon holy virtues and love of sobriety. He fasts well who forgives his brothers’ injuries with the gentleness of a peaceful heart. He offers a fast most pleasing to God who guards his mind from wicked thoughts, his eyes from lust, and his tongue and hands from strife. Thus let chastity sanctify our fast, patience adorn it, kindness cherish it, mercy gladden it, and humility commend it, so that by a kind of twofold fast of body and soul we may always commend ourselves to divine grace.” CII, 682–683.

### Taio, Bishop of Saragossa

“Let those who are ignorant of sins of the flesh fear a headlong fall all the more carefully because they stand on higher ground. Let them know that, the more conspicuously they stand in an elevated position, the more frequent are the arrows by which they are attacked by the ambusher, who is accustomed to rise up all the more fiercely the more robustly he sees himself being defeated; and he disdains defeat all the more intolerably when he sees himself being fought against by the whole ranks of weak flesh. Those who preserve chastity must be admonished to look continually to the rewards . . . . For eunuchs are those who, having restrained the movements of the flesh, cut off within themselves the inclination to a wicked act. These follow the Lamb wherever he goes; these sing the song which no one can sing except those one hundred and forty-four thousand . . . .” LXXX, 858–860.

“Let those who abstain always look carefully lest, while they flee the vice of gluttony, sharper vices should arise in them from their virtue; lest, while they mortify the flesh, they burst forth into impatience of spirit, and the conquest of the flesh should no longer be any virtue if the spirit is overcome by anger. One must consider how slight is the virtue of abstinence, which is commended only by other virtues . . . . For to sanctify a fast is to show God a bodily abstinence made worthy by other accompanying goods. Those who abstain must be admonished to know that they offer an abstinence pleasing to God when they distribute to the needy what they withhold from themselves in food . . . .” LXXX, 861–862.

## Seventeenth Series

[Col. 0571]

## [Index on Faith]

In the preceding Series we treated of the commandments both of God and of the Church; and since virtues arise from their observance, this seventeenth Series will in turn present indices concerning the theological virtues—Faith, Hope, and Charity; concerning the moral virtues, which are manifold; concerning the offices or functions of both regular and secular clergy; concerning Continence and Celibacy; concerning Virginity and Virgins; concerning nuns consecrated to God; concerning Widows; concerning Kings; and so forth. We furthermore append three indices: the first, an Anecdotal Index, sets before the reader the most outstanding deeds reported in the Patrologia; the second recalls memorable sayings excerpted from the Holy Fathers, especially those bearing upon virtues and the formation of the Christian life; the third records particular virtues of the pagans which the Fathers extolled in praise.

[Col. 0571]

## CLII. INDEX ON FAITH, CONSIDERED AS A THEOLOGICAL VIRTUE, PRESENTING THE TEACHING OF THE FATHERS ON ITS NATURE AND EXCELLENCE, ITS NECESSITY AND EFFECTS, ITS QUALITIES, OBJECT, AND REWARD

### I.—On the Nature of Faith

[Col. 0571]

The gift of faith, St. Hilary, X, 258.—Faith is an office of the soul and heart, same author, IX, 434.—Faith is a gift of God’s mercy, St. Ambrose, XVI, 83.—Faith is from God, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 83.—It is God’s work, same author, XXXV, 1602.—A gift of God, same author, XXXII, 622; XXXVII, 1116; XXXVIII, 254, 730, 911, 913, 915; XLIII, 247; XLIV, 552, 897, 976.—An altogether gratuitous gift, same author, XLVI, 399, 616.—The beginning of faith is God’s gift, same author, XXXVIII, 979; XLIV, 961.—Not only the beginning of faith but also its increase is God’s gift, same place, 992, 995.—The derivation of the word *fides*, same author, XXXV, 1760; XL, 515.—Faith is so called because what is said is done, XXXIII, 285; XXXVIII, 320.—Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen, same author, XXXVIII, 699.—Catholic faith, collected from the testimony of reading and founded upon apostolic truth, same place, 355.—Faith wavers if the authority of the divine Scriptures wavers, same author, XXXIV, 35.—Faith has a certain light of its own in the Scriptures, same author, XXXVIII, 698.—Faith is believing what one does not see, same author, XXXV, 1690.—Faith properly concerns things not seen, same author, XL, 235.—Faith is removed if assent is removed, same place, 243.—Where reason fails, there is the building of faith, same author, XXXVIII, 1157.—Faith is right belief, from which proceeds everything that is not sin, and without which it is impossible to please God, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 570.—Faith is given by God, same place, 159, 448, 473.—The derivation of the word *fides*, Cassiodorus, LXX, 563.—Faith is evidence for things not apparent, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1202.—Faith is evidence for those things that cannot appear, Taio of Saragossa, LXXX, 816.

Faith is that by which we believe that what we are not yet able to see will come to pass, St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 108.—Faith is certainty regarding an unknown and wondrous thing, Alcuin, CI, 972.—It is believing what one does not see, C, 867.—Faith is the substance of things hoped for because it bears within itself all things that are not seen, St. Paschasius, CXX, 1394.—Faith is God’s greatest gift, same place, 1436.—Faith is the origin of righteousness, the head of holiness, the beginning of devotion, and the foundation of religion, same place, 1389.—Faith is that by which we truly believe and confess even though we do not yet understand, [Col. 0572] same place, 1399.—Faith is the foundation both of the present and of the future life, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 27.—Faith is belief in God accepted without distinction, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 594.—What faith is, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 708.—What faith is, Guibert, CLVI, 657.—Faith is a virtue through which we believe with fullest certainty, and do not doubt will come to pass, those things told us, although they do not yet appear, St. Bruno of Segni, CLXV, 903.—Definition of faith according to the Apostle, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 1068.—It is a true virtue if it works through love, same place, 1069.—The derivation of the word *fides*: namely, because what is said is done, same author, 1022.—Faith, the first of all virtues, same author, 1213.—Faith is the greatest of all virtues, Godefridus, CLXXIV, 342.—A compendium of the Old and New Testaments, same author, 515.—What faith is, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 43.—He refutes Abelard’s definition of faith as an opinion, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 1061.—How faith differs from understanding, same author, 790.—Faith does not arise from merit but is God’s gift, Robert Pullus, CLXXXVI, 837.—What faith is, Peter Lombard, CXCI, 883.—Faith is given to us by grace alone, Baldwin, CCIV, 587.—God is the perfecter of faith, same author, 592.—Faith is from God alone, Peter Cantor, CCV, 266.

### II.—On the Various Kinds of Faith

Dormant and almost sleeping faith, St. Cyprian, IV, 468.—Rough faith, same author, III, 1194.—Certain faith concerning future things, same author, IV, 676.—Faith of the heart, St. Hilary, IX, 338; St. Philastrius, XII, 1297.—Faith of baptism, same place, 1181.—Historical and temporal faith; spiritual and eternal faith, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 166.—Twofold faith: the faith by which we believe and faith in promises, same author, XLIV, 235.—One faith is common, another higher faith, from which believers are called faithful, same author, XXXVIII, 145.—One faith concerns human agreements, another is that by which the baptized are called faithful, same author, XXXIII, 184.—Living faith is that which believes in what ought to be believed, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 221.—Dead faith, however, is that which merely believes in what ought to be believed, same place.—Faith is said to be twofold, Rupert of Deutz, CLXIX, 435.—Threefold faith: of commandments, signs, and promises, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 668.—What lively and victorious faith is, same author, 293.—What dead and feigned faith is, same author, 668.—Faith is divided three ways, and what is called feigned, dead, and proven faith, Wolbero, CXCV, 1019.

### III.—On the Excellence of Faith

Nothing is more precious than faith, St. Ambrose, XIV, 1020.—It is your price, by which divine mysteries are purchased, same author, 660.—It is our price, by which all people have been acquired for Christ, same author, 1175.—For faith is an eternal inheritance; money is temporal, same author, 420.—Nothing is more sublime than faith, same author, 1258.—Faith is richer than all treasures, same author, 580.—O faith, richer than all treasures! O faith, stronger than all bodily powers! same author, 292.—Faith gives dignity and merit, same author, XVII, 81.—Faith is beautiful in all things, same author, XVI, 164.—Faith is greater than the Law, same place, 78.—Faith is to be preferred to gold, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 218.—Faith is gold, the bridle of carnal desire, same author, XXXVII, 1242.—How great is the excellence of Christian faith, St. Maximus of Turin, LIII, 348.—Faith is the first of all virtues, St. Gregory the Great, LXXIV, 588.—Faith is the first mother and origin of virtues, Peter Cantor, CCV, 270.—Faith is the foundation of other virtues, Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 1090.

### IV.—On the Necessity of Faith

God does not desire our blood but seeks faith, St. Cyprian, IV, 594.—At the end of the world, only one who is found in the blood and sign of Christ will escape, same author, III, 1120.—The necessity of faith in matters concerning God, St. Hilary, X, 37.—The authority of the Lord’s utterance alone establishes the necessity of believing, same author, 275.—Faith is a prerequisite for meriting salvation, same author, 195.—It is likewise required for the salvation of the soul, same place.—Once the foundation of faith has been dug out, hope does not remain, same author, IX, 783.—Catholic salvation principally consists in it at the end, same author, X, 718.—Without faith, good works are done in vain, same author, IX, 304.—Virtues without faith are leaves: they seem green but cannot be useful, St. Ambrose, XIV, 943.—Works too are vain, same author, XV, 1725.—Faith is necessary here, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 236.—Necessary for salvation, same place, 784.—Without faith no one has ever been, or will be, righteous, same author, XL, 621.—How long faith is necessary, same author, XXXII, 877.—Without faith it is impossible to please God, XLIV, 755.—Faith is the first commandment and beginning of religion, same author, XXXVIII, 237.—The beginning of salvation, same place, 912.—Faith is necessary for living devoutly, same author, XLI, 610.—All righteousness takes its beginning from faith, same author, XXXIII, 877.—Faith without works profits nothing, just as works without faith do not, same author, XXXVI, 258.—The necessity of faith, same author, XXXIX, 1950; XL, 753, 775.—Without faith no good work is ever begun and completed, same author, XXXIX, 2234; XLV, 1791.—Integrity of faith in all articles is necessary for salvation, St. Nicetas, LII, 1081.—Without faith nothing is holy, nothing chaste, nothing alive, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 207.

How necessary faith is, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 671.—Without faith by which we believe in God, it is impossible to please God, same place, 622.—Faith and baptism are necessary for salvation, same place, 702.—Purity of heart cannot exist where faith is absent, same place, 171.—Unbelievers are called dead, Cassiodorus, LXX, 625.—The necessity of faith, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 320.—As branches without the strength of their root wither, so good works separated from faith are nothing, same author, 711.—No one can attain true blessedness except through faith, Haymo, CXVIII, 896.—We cannot please God unless we follow the right rule of faith, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 21.—Faith is the origin of virtues, the foundation of good works, and the beginning of all human salvation, same place.—Without faith it is impossible to please God, Lanfranc, CL, 400.—The necessity of faith, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 221.—Faith is necessary so that the soul may tend toward the supreme essence by believing in it, same author, 263.—No human being possessing understanding can merit the kingdom of God without faith, 531.—The necessity of faith for salvation is supreme, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 482.—They do not enter the palace of the heavenly kingdom without faith, St. Bruno of Segni, CLXV, 902.—Holy Church receives no one coming to her unless first clothed with the adornment of faith, same place.—Faith is necessary: by it things unseen are believed, and things not yet present to us in vision subsist in us through faith, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 983.—Faith is in us the origin and foundation of virtues and good works, same place.—No one can be righteous without faith, Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 290.

### V.—On the Effects of Faith
