Faith that is whole is secure concerning salvation, Tertullian, I, 1222.—Christians are safe by faith, same author, II, 119.—Where faith is, even beasts themselves cannot harm, same place, [Col. 0574] 421.—If faith can move mountains, much more can it move a soldier, same author, 119.—Hearts are cleansed by faith, St. Cyprian, III, 1204.—Faith greatly profits, same place, 735.—The strength of faith is immovable, same place, 798.—Our faith terrifies the wicked and renews the righteous, St. Hilary, IX, 412.—The power of faith against magical arts, same author, 369.—To ward off pain, same author, X, 378.—Through faith the mind has that by which it is settled, same author, IX, 193.—It possesses in itself the power of general aid against every disease, same author, X, 64.—Faith is the immovable foundation of our life, St. Zeno, XI, 270.—It cleanses the conscience to the marrow, and how, same author, 258.—Where faith is, there is no pain, same author, 420.—Faith commends one to God, St. Optatus, XI, 883.—Where faith is true, there is the grace of true light, St. Ambrose, XV, 1316.—Christ illumines by the brightness of faith, by the glory of his resurrection, and by the power of divine works, same author, XV, 1442.—Faith makes people wise, same place, 1432.

Christ is touched by faith; Christ is seen by faith, St. Ambrose, XV, 1638.—Faith presents us to God, same author, XIV, 977.—Faith is what obtains gifts, same author, 753.—Faith justifies those who flee to it, same author, 117.—God’s grace has appointed faith alone for salvation, same author, 82.—Whoever believes in Christ receives by faith alone, freely, the remission of sins, same author, 183.—Faith makes God favorable, if it is approved by good works, same author, 220.—Christian faith cuts off all pride, same author, XVI, 506.—Faith’s victory occurs when all vices and crimes are subdued, same place, 482.—Whoever joins himself to Christian faith becomes a fellow citizen of the saints and a member of God’s household, same place, 379.—Where faith is, there is freedom; where freedom is, there is grace; where grace is, there is inheritance, same author, XVII, 1258.—By faith we received power to become children of God, St. Augustine, XLV, 1614.—Faith draws us to Christ, same author, XXXIII, 878.—By faith one truly approaches Jesus, same author, XXXIV, 1101.—If faith in Christ is present, no sins will remain, same author, XXXVIII, 788.—Faith is life, same author, XXXV, 1577, 1727, 1815.—Faith makes us capable of receiving divine things, same author, XLII, 822.—Hearts are purified by faith, same author, XXXIV, 447; XXXVII, 1550.—Through faith in temporal things a human being comes to eternal truth, same author, XXXIV, 1070.—Faith leads to vision, same author, XXXVIII, 103.—Faith will make joyful in the homeland one whom it does not console on the journey, same author, XXXIV, 541.—Faith admits us into the divine commonwealth, XXXIII, 533.—Faith prepares the saints for God’s kingdom, same author, XXXV, 1815.—By faith the mind is cleansed so that it may be able to see God, same author, XXXVIII, 36, 368, 541.

Through faith comes the salvation of the nations, St. Peter Chrysologus, LI, 18.—Faith suddenly cures what art does not cure for a long time, same place, 33.—It gives salvation, same place, 34.—By faith we approach God, same place, 100.—Faith both recalls the impious to righteousness and the dead to life, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 309.—Faith pulls out the roots of sin, St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 299.—Faith is renewal of life, Eugyppius, LXII, 587.—Faith offers fruits so sweet that it even wins the hearts of rulers, Cassiodorus, LXIX, 522.—On the efficacy of faith, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 933, 1020.—Through faith joined to works, darkness is illumined, serpents flee, idols are overthrown, and so forth, same author, 741.—By faith and works one reaches eternal glory, same author, LXXIII, 470.—Faith joined to works saves a human being, St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 189.—Faith cleanses us from all sins, illumines our minds, reconciles us to God, and so forth, Halitgarius, CV, 671.—The fruits of faith in the centurion, St. Paschasius, CXX, 349.—Sinners are justified through faith, Lanfranc, CL, 117.—By faith we are cleansed from original sin, Guibert, CLVI, 490.—Graces are given according to the measure of faith, same author, 422.—How great faith’s efficacy is appears from various examples, St. Bruno of Segni, CLXV, 903–904.—Faith makes a person merit rightly, Rupert, CLXIX, 43.—It exalts human beings to the rank of angels, same author, 18.—By faith the elect are joined to God as a wife to her husband, same author, 200.—Faith begets us for Christ, Godefridus, CLXXIV, 760.—It wins for Peter the key of the heavenly kingdom, same author, 124.—Faith makes and preserves the righteous, St. Bernard, CLXXXV, 115.—It conquers prosperity and adversity, same author, 114.—Likewise the world and death, same author, CLXXXIV, 274.—It ennobles all equally, same author, 140.—By faith we conquer enemies, same author, CLXXXIII, 293.—Only faith working through love produces the good man, Robert Pullus, CLXXXVI, 839.—Faith fulfills the will and obtains salvation, same place.—Through faith we are changed into a new creature, Baldwin, CCIV, 592.—We become children of God, same author, 593.

### VI.—On the Qualities of Faith

Let curiosity yield to faith, Tertullian, II, 27.—Faith is praiseworthy when it believes first that something must be observed before it has learned it, same author, 78.—It is a perversion of faith not to believe what has been proven, and to presume what has not been proven, same author, 146.—The quality of faith can be assessed from one’s manner of life, same author, 56.—Faith has temptation and testing, same author, 112.—It does not fear hunger, I, 678.—It is indebted to martyrdom, same author, II, 138.—Our faith ought to be simple, St. Cyprian, IV, 760.—Faith is one, same author, 1136.—There can be no fellowship between faith and unbelief, same author, III, 829.—Faith ought to be joined to mouth and heart, St. Hilary, X, 397.—Knowledge is in faith; reason is in God’s power, same place.—Faith is in simplicity; righteousness is in faith, same author, 398.—Fear belonging to faith is demonstrated by keeping God’s commandments, same author, 559.—Faith’s warfare is to keep the commandments, same author, 626.—Humility is the greatest work of our faith, same author, 725.—The unity of faith, same author, 267.—The nature of faith does not permit itself to be subjected to the devices of loquacity, same author, 259.—How presumptuous is that faith which prefers its own novel tradition to be believed rather than antiquity, same author, 265.—Where faith is small, there is disturbance, St. Ambrose, XV, 1633.—It ought not be divided but remain whole, same author, 1834.—Good faith shines with the beautiful adornment of works, same author, XVII, 562.—If faith has no works, it is dead, St. Jerome, XXIII, 227.—It is perfect to believe God from God, same author, 171.—Pure faith suffers no delay, same author, 1040.—It should not be idle, same author, XXIV, 660.—Faith does not belong to the proud, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 650, 874.—It possesses humility, same author, XXXV, 1670.—While we are little children, we ought to be nourished with the milk of faith’s simplicity, same author, XL, 309.—Faith without hope and charity is not devout, same author, XXXIII, 436.—What faith ought to be, same author, XXXIX, 1959.—The faith of a Christian and that of the devil, same author, XL, 1190.—Interior and exterior faith, same place, 1189.—Faith alone, without works, does not commend one before God, same author, XXXV, 2412.—Faith is nourished by hope as the body by food, and enlivened by love as the body by the soul, same author, XL, 1025.—Our faith ought not depend upon people’s conduct, same author, XXXVII, 1592.—One who does not love believes and hopes in vain, same author, XLI, 286.—Faith without charity is death, same author, XXXV, 1578.—Faith does not require arbiters, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 9.—Faith stands by prayer, fasting, and almsgiving, same place, 43.—It must be placed in the heart, not on paper, same place, 57.—Whoever seeks faith does not seek reason, same place, 58.—Faith must be committed to memory, not to a book, same place, 61.—What a Christian’s faith is and what it ought to be, St. Salvian, LIII, 69.—Charity is the strength of faith; faith is the strength of charity, same author, 289.

True salvation will not exist where true faith has not existed, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 573.—There is no good conscience except where there is unfeigned faith, same author, 543.—The Apostle calls feigned faith “faith,” not according to the truth of the matter but according to common opinion, same place.—Let not the tongue conceal what the mind believes, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 1029.—Faith precedes charity, same author, LXXVI, 98.—What signs ought to accompany true faith, same author, 1374.—Faith adorned by no works is found not merely unbeautiful, but dead, St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 189.—The faith of all Christians ought to be one, Alcuin, CI, 1346.—Faith everywhere weakens without confidence and courage, St. Paschasius, CXX, 360.—Every Christian must reflect that his faith ought to be whole, and not merely of any sort, same author, 717.—Faith stripped of human powers: victory has never failed anyone except the one lacking such faith, same author, 1425.—Right faith is truer than sight, same author, 1395.—How faith is true, Lanfranc, CL, 115.—Faith is dead without the love of God, Goffridus, CLVII, 232.—Without charity faith is of no use, Rupert, CLXIX, 869.—Faith without work is a star without light, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 403.—Only perfect faith pleases God, St. Bernard, CLXXIV, 728.—Feigned faith is worse and more dangerous than none, same author, CLXXXV, 111.—Idle faith is useless, same author, CLXXXII, 216.—What kind of faith is required of us, Peter Lombard, CXCI, 127.

### VII.—On the Object and Merit of Faith

The first and greatest duty of faith is to believe in the true God, St. Augustine, XLI, 127.—Faith in God the Creator does not suffice for salvation, same author, XLIV, 249.—Not even one of the righteous, including the ancients, could be saved from the condemnation of the whole mass of perdition except through faith in Christ, same author, XXXV, 1918.—Whatever is contrary to Catholic faith must be believed, without any doubt, to be utterly false, same author, XXXIV, 262.—What Catholic faith holds, same author, 221.—An exposition of Catholic faith, same author, XXXIX, 2180.—Nothing can be added to or taken away from faith, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 1062.—Wherever you may be situated, hold first and without doubt with all your heart that the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 673.—This is the Catholic faith: that we believe, etc., St. Boniface, LXXXIX, 857.—One must equally believe in the Father, the Son, and their Spirit, etc., St. Anselm, CLVIII, 220.—To will to believe what ought to be believed is to will rightly, same author, 529.—Those things that must be believed concerning Christ are set forth distinctly, same author, CLXIV, 425.

According to the merits of faith, each person receives only as much as he believes he will receive, St. Cyprian, IV, 665.—The merit of faith, St. Hilary, X, 184, 195, 627.—Faith is not to be expected from salvation, but salvation from faith, same author, IX, 965.—What is asked must be merited by faith, same place.—Blessedness is reserved for faith’s merits, same author, 599.—How mercy is bestowed in view of preceding merit of faith, St. Augustine, XXXV, 2061.—Faith begins merit, but even faith’s merit is God’s gift, same author, XLIV, 965.—Faith is the beginning of merit, St. Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 736.—Faith does not arise from merit, but is God’s gift, Robert Pullus, CLXXXVI, 837.—Faith is not bestowed because of the merit of preceding works, Baldwin, CCIV, 587.

### VIII.—On the Faith of the Ancients

Faith did not exist on earth before Christ, Tertullian, I, 1260.—Before the Lord’s Passion salvation came through bare faith, same author, 1215.—The faith of the Old and New Testaments is the same, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 319, 354.—The ancients lived and pleased God in faith in Christ, same author, 314, 319, 454, 365, 377.—On the faith of the ancients and on the perfection and imperfection of charity, Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 1115.

### Books Treating of Faith

Treatise on Faith, St. Zeno, XI, 269.—Five books on Faith, St. Ambrose, XVI, 523.—Book on Faith, Rufinus, XXI, 1124.—One book, *On Faith in Things Not Seen*, St. Augustine, XL, 172.—One book, *On Faith and the Creed*, same author, 181.—One book, *On Faith and Works*, same author, 197.—*On Faith, Hope, and Charity*, same author, 231.—One book, *On Faith, or the Rule of True Faith*, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 672.—*On Faith*, Taio of Saragossa, LXXX, 816; St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 188.—Homily on Faith, Hope, and Charity, Rabanus Maurus, CX, 83.—*On Faith*, Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVIII, 896.—*On Faith, Hope, and Charity*, St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 1388.—*On Catholic Faith*, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 19.—*On Faith*, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 327; Abelard, CLXXVIII, 1695.—*On Faith*, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1200; CLXXXIII, 770.—*On Faith*, Robert Pullus, CLXXXVI, 816.—*On Faith*, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 805, 1082.—Book on the Commendation of Faith, Baldwin, CCIV, 571.—On the Commendation of Faith; the Failure of Faith, Peter Cantor, CCV, 266.—Testimonies of the Gentiles concerning Faith, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 869.—*On Faith*, Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 1089.

[Col. 0577]

### CLIII. INDEX OF HOPE, AS A THEOLOGICAL VIRTUE, BY WHICH THE MIND IS RAISED TO HOPE FOR ETERNAL BLESSEDNESS FROM GOD, TO BE OBTAINED WITH HIS HELP; TREATING OF ITS NATURE AND CERTAINTY, ITS NECESSITY, EXCELLENCE, OBJECT, AND EFFECTS, AND OF PRESUMPTION AND DESPAIR, WHICH ARE OPPOSED TO IT.

#### I.—On the nature of hope.

[Col. 0577]

The nature of hope, St. Hilary, X, 628.—Hope should not be a presumption concerning uncertain things, but an expectation of things known, ibid., IX, 417.—What is hope except expectation of future things? St. Ambrose, XVI, 1081.—Hope concerns only good things, only future things, and things pertaining to the person who hopes, St. Augustine, XL, 235.—What hope is, Haymo, CXVIII, 875; St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 1435.—What the difference is between hope and faith, ibid., 1438.—“Hope which is seen is not hope,” Lanfranc, CL, 132.—What hope is, St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLIII, 47, 74, 427.—What hope is, St. Bruno of Segni, CLXV, 906; Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 1069; Hugh of Saint-Victor, CLXXV, 464.—How hope and faith differ, ibid., CLXXI, 1069.—On hope: what it is, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 811.—What the difference is between faith and hope, ibid.—What hope is, Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 1094.

#### II.—On the various kinds of hope.

One hope belongs to the Gentiles, another to Christians, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1024.—Carnal hope, ibid., 34.—How vain and uncertain is hope in temporal goods, ibid., 861.—Vain hope in money, honour, and a powerful friend, ibid., XXXVI, 237, 600.—Perverse hope deceives, just as good and right hope liberates, ibid., XXXVIII, 535.—One hope concerns eternal rewards, another divine assistance, ibid., XXXVII, 1541.—The varieties of hope, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 668.

#### III.—On the certainty of our hope.

Our hope rests upon God’s promises, St. Hilary, IX, 548.—It rests especially upon God’s mercy, ibid., 322.—By how many titles of pardon God has invited us to hope for forgiveness, St. Ambrose, XV, 1442.—The certainty of our hope, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 861.—How firm the hope of Christians is, ibid., XXXVII, 1074.—Our hope is founded upon God’s promise, XXXV, 1656.—By what pledges of salvation God raises up our hope, XXXVII, 1941, 1942.—Because the hope of salvation given to us is certain, the Apostle speaks of that salvation as though it had already been given, XLII, 251, 252.—Our hope is in Christ, because that which we hope has been promised to us has already been fulfilled in him, XLII, 251.—The certainty of hope is why that which must be done is spoken of as done, ibid., XXXVIII, 180.—How certain hope is, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 200.—Hope arises from the knowledge of God and of oneself, ibid., CLXXXIII, 973.—“I consider three things in which my whole hope consists: the love of adoption, the truth of the promise, and the power of fulfilment,” St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 344.—Our hope rests upon God’s gratuitous election and goodness, Adam of Prémontré, CXCVIII, 820.

#### IV.—On the necessity and excellence of hope.

Hope must be shown in deeds, St. Hilary, IX, 548.—Hope for eternal goods is contained in the lives and deeds of the ancient Fathers, ibid., 631.—Through hope for the future age, worldly things must be despised, ibid., 941.—Hope appears to be so joined with faith and charity that each is necessary to the others, St. Zeno, XI, 269.—One must not distrust the Lord’s mercy, and why, St. Ambrose, XIV, 1035.—Hope is necessary here, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 369.—It is faith’s companion, ibid.—Hope cannot exist without faith, but faith can exist without hope, ibid., XL, 234.—All hope must be placed in God’s mercy, St. Fulgentius, XLV, 3.—How necessary hope is to sinners for repentance, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1021.—Hope is necessary to the soul, Alcuin, CI, 616.—Besides love of God, hope is necessary, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 219.—The excellence of hope, St. Hilary, X, 627.—Wherein the merit and excellence of hope consist, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 397.—As nothing is worse than despair, so nothing is better than firm hope, CLXIV, 794.

#### V.—On the qualities of hope.

Our hope ought to be patient, St. Cyprian, IV, 758.—Steadfast hope, ibid., IX, 672.—What the hope of the faithful is, St. Hilary, IX, 661.—“Even if you are crushed, even if afflicted,” etc., nevertheless wait for the Lord, and hope will not put you to shame, St. Ambrose, XIV, 1005.—Faith excludes fear, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 311.—Let fear rather than security accompany our hope, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 493, 670, 686.—How hope grows amid adversities, Haymo, CXVIII, 896.—At present neither is hope altogether exercised without fear, nor is fear raised to higher things without hope, St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 1455.

#### VI.—On the object of hope.

Christ, the one hope of the whole world, Tertullian, II, 760.—The hope of Christians is in heaven, ibid., I, 260.—What we hope for, we behold in the glorious body of Christ, St. Hilary, IX, 715.—All our hope is in God, ibid., 320.—Christ our hope, ibid., 392, 417.—All hope must be placed in God, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 165.—The hope of those who hope for anything from God other than God himself is mad, ibid., XXXVI, 437, 438.—We hope for equality with the angels, ibid., XXXVIII, 834.—Our hope ought to be in God, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 154.—On not placing hope in man, Haymo, CXVIII, 896.—Holy hope is the hope of attaining the kingdom of God and his righteousness, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 594.—His goods are beyond conception, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 221.—We hope not only in God, but for God himself, CLXXXIII, 220.

#### VII.—On the effects of hope.

Hope consoles the afflicted, St. Hilary, IX, 548.—Hope is the safest defence against the devil, ibid., 392.—Hope at hand gives strength, St. Ambrose, XV, 1349.—In the time of our humiliation, hope is consoling, ibid., 1282.—When we are anxious and troubled, let hope strengthen us by expectation of future things, ibid., XIV, 816.—Hope is accustomed to kindle love, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1487.—

Faith, hope, and charity enroll us in the commonwealth of God, ibid., XXXIII, 533.—Hope obtains salvation and blessedness for us in this life, ibid., XLI, 631.—Hope is consolation in this pilgrimage, ibid., XXXVIII, 866.—Hope nurses us, nourishes us, strengthens us, and consoles us here, ibid., 1188.—The certain hope of our return consoles and exhorts us even while we are sorrowful pilgrims, ibid., XXXVII, 1884, 1889.—God’s sweetness is revealed to those who hope, ibid., XXXVIII, 791.—Hope cannot exist without joy, ibid., XXXVII, 1885.—The saints are always rejoicing, both here and in heaven: here in hope, there in possession, ibid., XXXVIII, 1498, 1659, 1679, 1703, 1889.—Hope in the Lord changes all things for the better, Cassiodorus, LXX, 303.—Hope in heavenly things strengthens the mind, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 994.—Those who firmly hope in God, although they suffer persecutions, tortures, and death itself at the hands of enemies, cannot be torn away from steadfast faith and their purpose of righteousness, because God never abandons those who hope in him, ibid., CLXIV, 716.—Saints who place their hope in God alone will never be deprived of his help and consolation, CLXIV, 762.—The wonderful effects of hope, St. Bruno of Segni, CLXV, 907.—It makes us capable of mercy, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 394.—It makes a human being omnipotent, ibid., CXXXIII, 1190.

#### VIII.—On despair and presumption.

Hope and despair must be feared in sins, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1876, 1877.—By hoping and despairing people are endangered: how this occurs, ibid., XXXV, 1651.—How God provides for those who hope and those who despair, ibid.—So that people might not live worse in hope of pardon, God made the day of death uncertain, ibid., XXXVII, 1301.—On despair, St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 1450.—One must never despair of God’s mercy, ibid., CLVIII, 737, 873.—Whoever sins in hope of remission does not deserve remission, CLVIII, 1162.—Temptation against hope is the most grievous of all, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 240.

Treatise on Hope, St. Zeno, XI, 269. Treatise on Hope, Taio of Zaragoza, LXXX, 817. Treatise on Hope, Alcuin, CI, 616. Treatise on Hope, Halitgar of Cambrai, CV, 672. Treatise on Hope, Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVIII, 895. Treatise on Hope, Faith, and Charity, St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 1387. Treatise on Heavenly Hope, Othlo, monk, CXLVI, 267. Treatise on Hope, St. Bruno of Segni, CLXV, 904. Treatise on Hope and Charity, Hugh of Saint-Victor, CLXXVI, 43. Treatise on Hope, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1201; CLXXXIII, 770. ### CLIV. INDEX OF CHARITY: HOW GREAT A THEOLOGICAL VIRTUE IT IS; SETTING FORTH ITS EXCELLENCE, NECESSITY, EFFECTS, AND OBJECT—NAMELY TOWARD GOD, NEIGHBOUR, AND ONESELF; AND ALSO ENUMERATING BOOKS TREATING OF CHARITY.

#### I.—On the nature and excellence of charity.

[Col. 0579]

The nature of charity, St. Hilary, X, 628.—The excellence of charity, ibid., 627.—Charity belongs to all, St. Zeno, XI, 272.—Charity has no end, ibid., 273.—It is evident that love is the substance and natural teacher of all divine virtues, ibid., 274.—Its praises, ibid., 278.—Since hope and faith are in charity, there is no doubt that charity is greater, St. Ambrose, XV, 1439.—Charity is greater than all things, ibid., 1848.—How good is the fire of charity, ibid., 1380.—Although charity is called by one name, it nevertheless consists of many things, XVII, 226.—It is, as it were, the mother of souls, ibid., 167.—Charity cannot exist without the other virtues, nor the other virtues without charity, ibid., 821.—Charity is the mother of all virtues, St. Jerome, XXII, 742.—Charity cannot be compared, nor has it a price, ibid., 335.—The dignity of charity, XXIII, 425.—It holds primacy among the virtues, XXVI.—What charity is, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 143; XL, 25.—Charity is the virtue by which that which ought to be loved is loved, XXXIII, 739.—The Pelagians deny that charity is a gift of God, XLV, 1292.—Charity is God’s gift, XXXIII, 576, 595; XXXVIII, 210, 577, 620, 715, 793, 1323, 1241, 1462; XLIV, 237, 240, 290, 904.—No gift of God is more excellent than charity, XLII, 864, 865.—We cannot possess charity from ourselves, but from God through the Holy Spirit, XLV, 1105.—How great a good charity is, XXXIX, 764.—The greatest of all goods, XXXIII, 811.

The praise of charity, XXXIII, 854; XXXIX, 1533, 1534.—Charity is God himself, ibid., 818.—Charity is so truly God’s gift that it is called God, XXXVIII, 852.—Charity is a great and true virtue, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 737; XXXVIII, 1397.—A virtue of the soul, XXXVII, 1353.—Charity is greater than faith and hope because, when their object arrives, these cease, whereas charity increases, ibid., 1171.—Charity must be possessed in all things and above all things, XXXII, 1340.—Charity is the grace of the New Testament, XXXIV, 755.—Charity is called love of God and neighbour, XXXVI, 260.—Charity is the bond by which human beings are joined to one another and to God, XXXV, 878.—Charity is the movement of the mind to enjoy God for his own sake, and oneself and one’s neighbour for God’s sake, XXXIV, 72.—Charity is love of God, of one’s neighbour, and of oneself according to God, XLI, 410.—Charity is the root of all goods, XLIV, 370, 374.—What is more precious, more luminous, firmer, or more useful than charity? XXXVIII, 764.—That nothing ought to be preferred to charity, Cassian, XLIX, 1023.—Nothing is more sublime than charity, which surpasses all God’s gifts, St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 288.—Charity is the mother of all virtues, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 262.—On the praise of charity, Julianus Pomerius, LIX, 493.—Charity is the first fruit of spiritual gifts, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 344.—Charity is the fountain and origin of all goods, ibid., 732.—God is charity, and charity is from God, ibid., 353, 512, 634.—The excellence of charity is such that whoever possesses it in the heart can never adequately express it in words, CLXV, 345.—Charity is God’s gift; covetousness, the devil’s snare, LXV, 739, 740.—Charity is the Holy Spirit’s principal gift, Fulgentius, LXV, 187.—Wherein true charity consists, Cassiodorus, LXX, 100.—What true charity is, Theodulf of Orléans, CV, 202.—On the praise of charity and the fact that it is the mother of all virtues, Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVIII, 887.—What charity is, St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 1461.—Charity is the teacher of all goods, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 221.—Charity is the mother of all virtues, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 866.—Charity is more excellent than all gifts, Lanfranc, CL, 199.—Charity is the distinction between good and evil, St. Bruno of Segni, CLXV, 624.—Charity is the chief good, Rupert of Deutz, CLXIX, 867.—Charity is the perfection of virtues, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 771.—Charity is the root of all virtues, ibid., 900.—Queen of virtues, 544.—Charity surpasses all virtues, ibid., 834.—Its excellence, ibid., 241.—What charity is, and whether God is charity according to Augustine, Hugh of Saint-Victor, CLXXV, [Col. 0581] 900.—Whether charity alone should be called virtue, and not—, Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 1570.—The nature of true charity, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 188, 300, 508.—The excellence of charity demonstrated, Aelred, abbot, CXCV, 505.—The excellence of charity, ibid., 1078.—Nothing is better or more delightful than charity, Richard of Saint-Victor, CXCVI, 917.—On charity and the excellence of charity, St. Stephen of Grandmont, CCIX, 1098.—That charity is the most excellent of all virtues, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 895.

#### II.—On the necessity of charity.

Whoever does not have charity does not have God, St. Cyprian, IV, 511; St. Zeno, XI, 275.—Without it, no martyrdom can either be called or be martyrdom; without it, the greatest and most commanding virtue lacks effect; without it, all knowledge of languages is of no value, etc., St. Optatus, XI, 1019.—Love of God is the greatest commandment in the law, St. Ambrose, XV, 1280.—The Lord requires charity; the servant, fear, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1257.—Whoever does not have charity should know that he does not have God, XVII, 252.—Charity cannot exist without the other virtues, nor the other virtues without charity, ibid., 821.—The two commandments of charity must always be considered and meditated upon, St. Augustine, XXXV, 1531.—Augustine finds the two commandments of charity in every utterance of Scripture, XXXIII, 223.—Without charity a human being is nothing, whatever else he may possess, XXXV, 1539.—What is done without charity is by no means done well, XLIV, 993.—The law is not fulfilled without charity, XXXVIII, 267, 696, 1241.—Where charity is, what can be lacking? But where it is not, what can be of use? XXXV, 1141, 1151; XXXV, 1845.—With charity all things are possessed; without it, nothing whatever that can be possessed is useful, XXXV, 1646; XXXVII, 1627.—Add charity, and all things are beneficial; take charity away, and the rest are of no benefit, XXXVIII, 44, 562, 575, 764, 783.—Without charity all good things are of no benefit, XXXIII, 229, 755.—Neither truth, nor sacraments, knowledge, prophecy, or faith [is of benefit], XLIII, 312, 314, 601.—Other gifts are removed from one who does not have charity, XXXVII, 1905.—Whoever refuses to serve charity must necessarily serve iniquity, XXXVI, 163.—Without charity the other virtues do not benefit, St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 697.—Without it they perish, ibid.—According to the Apostle, without charity the other things are of no benefit, ibid., 83.—Without charity the other things have the appearance of piety, not its reality, ibid.—The commandment of charity is above all books; every tongue and every teaching of the saints serves it, ibid., 383.—The two commandments of charity are two wings by which souls strive toward God, ibid., 289.—The necessity of charity, ibid., 478.—Without charity virtues are bare and fruitless, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 299.—Without charity the other virtues contribute nothing to salvation, ibid., 299, 400, 419.—Christ’s charity must be preferred to the world, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 711.—Charity toward one’s neighbour is necessary for every virtue, ibid.—Charity is indeed necessary here: it separates us from the devil, purifies us from sin, and reconciles us to God, Julianus Pomerius, LIX, 495.—Without charity one may make a sound, but cannot possess life, St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 187.—O good debt of charity, holy debt, debt filled with heavenly advantages! ibid., 737.—On the commandment of charity, St. Columbanus, abbot, LXXX, 250.—That no good things profit without charity, Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVIII, 892.—For whom charity is necessary, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 66, 521.—Its power and necessity, St. Bruno of Segni, CLXV, 907.—Charity is the eye of the heart; whoever lacks it is blind, Rupert of Deutz, CLXX, 95.—Why there are not three commandments of charity, Hugh of Saint-Victor, CLXXVI, 531.—Without charity the remaining virtues are of no benefit, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 817.—The two commandments of charity, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 1083.—Without charity the other virtues fail, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 272.

#### III.—On the effects of charity.

By it anger, jealousy, ambition, iniquity, extravagance, and covetousness are restrained, St. Hilary, X, 628.—Charity restrains countryside, cities, and peoples, and preserves peace, St. Zeno, XI, 273.—It checks wars, removes disputes, annuls legal claims, restrains courts, uproots hatreds, and extinguishes angers, ibid.—The wonderful effects of charity, ibid., 278.—Charity mortifies guilt and all sins, St. Ambrose, XV, 1423.—Great charity remits sins, XIV, 870.—It excludes every disturbance, XV, 1321.—It binds us to the beings above and implants us in heaven, XIV, 177.—Liberty makes a human being free; charity makes him God’s friend, XVI, 1090.—It can do all things, St. Jerome, XXII, 527.—Charity makes us capable of receiving divine things, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 705.—Charity enrolls us in the commonwealth of God, XXXIII, 533.—By charity the faithful are one in the one unchangeable One, XLIV, 109.—Charity makes one heart out of many human hearts, XXXV, 1538.—Charity kills what we were, so that we may be what we were not, XXXVII, 1628.—Charity conquers the lusts of the flesh, XXXV, 2061, 2062.—The power of charity, XXXVI, 541.—Persecutions are resisted by charity alone, XXXVI, 424.—The more God’s charity reigns in anyone, the less iniquity rules that person, XXVII, 1058.—Charity makes citizens of Jerusalem, XXXVII, 773.—Charity not only makes sons from slaves, but also bears the image and likeness of God, Cassian, XLIX, 855.—God’s charity conquered the world of the ungodly, St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 702.—By charity a multitude of sins is covered, LIV, 189.—Nothing is more effective against the devil than the generosity of charity, through which every sin is either avoided or overcome, ibid., 400.—Charity gives life to faith and the other virtues and makes them useful, ibid., 166.—How much perfection charity bestows on those founded in it, Julianus Pomerius, LIX, 496.—The effect of charity is remission of sins, St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 737.—The effects of charity enumerated, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 782, 847, 935.—What and how great are the goods which charity has wrought in the holy Fathers, Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVIII, 891.—That charity is of such great power that in it we can fulfil the whole law and all God’s commandments, ibid., 894.—Its effects and properties, Lanfranc, CL, 199.—Charity makes human beings come to God’s likeness, Rupert of Deutz, CLXX, 313.—The two fruits of charity: affection and effect, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 544.—Charity makes even those far removed present to us and more intimate, CLXXI, 217.—It makes heaven and earth one commonwealth, ibid.—The effects of true charity, St. Bernard, CLXXII, 93.—It is the mother of friendships, ibid., 109.

#### IV.—Things to which charity is compared.

Why charity is compared to water, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1353.—Charity is signified by the upper regions of heaven, ibid., 1342.—The symbol of charity is scarlet, XXXIV, 734.—The tabernacle of ten curtains, ibid., 634.—Charity is the law of the City of God, XXXVII, 1261.—Charity is light, XXXIII, 561; XXXV, 1598.—The precious pearl of the Gospel, XL, 670.—Charity is like a ship, XXXVII, 1699.—Charity is oil, XXXV, 1435; XXXVIII, 575.—Bread, XXXV, 1342.—Our root, XXXVI, 557, 607.—Charity is the wisdom of God, XXXIII, 557, 607.—The seamless garment of Christ, XXXVII, 176.—Charity is the wedding garment, XXXVIII, 563; XLIII, 669.—Charity is called a nail, Cassiodorus, LXX, 878.—By wine is understood the fervour of charity, ibid., 1100.—Charity is compared to spring rain, ibid., 100.—By coals are understood prayers kindled by the fire of charity, ibid., 903.—Oil is a type of charity, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 595.—Charity is called the law of Christ, ibid., 922.—Charity is compared to heat, ibid., 1160.—Charity is denoted by the name gold, LXXVI, 732.—Charity is called the breadth of the spiritual building, ibid., 955.—By scarlet dyed twice are signified charity toward God and neighbour, ibid., 975, 1288.—Charity is called fire, ibid., 1241.—Why charity is signified by the wedding garment, ibid., 1287.—How charity resembles scarlet dyed twice, LXXVII, 29, 471.—Charity is signified by gold, St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 832.—It is called a house, ibid., 1083.—Charity is signified by the radiance of the sun, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXIII, 711.—It is compared to wine, ibid., 1043.—How it is called the law of the Lord, CLXXXII, 111.—Charity is gold, Garnerius, Regular Canon, CXCIII, 305.—Fire, ibid., 331.—Charity toward God and neighbour shown by scarlet dyed twice, ibid., 439.

#### V.—On the object of charity.

It follows that we should also love our neighbours with the affection with which we love ourselves, St. Zeno, XI, 276.—Whoever retains awareness of his nobility loves his brother, ibid., 276.—Let us consider whence true charity comes, where it abides, and to whom it is especially owed, ibid., 278.—If we love our parents, how much more ought we to love the Creator of our parents and our own Author? St. Ambrose, XIV, 574.—In what sense Christ commands us to hate parents and love enemies, ibid., XV, 1415.—The things with which charity ought to concern itself, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1599.—Charity toward God consists in three things; charity toward one’s neighbour in seven, XXXVI, 281.—Charity must extend to enemies, XXXVIII, 564.—Charity embraces not only brothers who are present, but also those scattered throughout the world, XXXV, 2048.—We must show charity not only to brothers, but also to those outside, XXXVI, 299.—Charity is called love of God and neighbour, ibid., 260.—By charity we love God, and are loved mutually, XXXV, [Col. 0583] 1852.—Charity is the bond by which human beings are joined to one another and to God, ibid., 878.—That the perfection of charity is to pray for enemies, Cassian, XLIX, 857.—Charity extends even to unbelievers and enemies, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 251, 262.—God must be loved with the whole heart, ibid., 169.—When one’s neighbour is loved, God is loved, ibid., 460.—To whom charity is owed, St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 739.—Charity must also extend to enemies, ibid., 739.

Charity begins from two commandments and extends to innumerable matters, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 922.—Charity toward one’s neighbour consists in two things, ibid., LXXVI, 226, 1205.—A person must begin charity with himself, ibid., 122.—He inculcates love of neighbour and zeal for concord, St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 216.—How one who loves his brother according to the commandment appears, and how one who does not love is reproved, St. Benedict, CIII, 540.—Who are the enemies whom we are commanded to love, ibid.—How through charity a friend is loved in God and an enemy for God’s sake, Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVIII, 895.—That charity is twofold, ibid., CXX, 1466.—That there are four things to be loved, ibid., 1467.—Who the neighbour is whom we are commanded to love, ibid., 1469.—Charity extends to the love of enemies, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 224.—Not only friends, but our very enemies, must be loved in obedience to Christ’s commandment, St. Bruno of Segni, CLXV, 110.—There are four things to be loved by us: God, who is above us; ourselves, who are within us; our neighbour, who is beside us; and our body, which is beneath us, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 520.—Charity is twofold, namely toward God and neighbour, Hugh of Saint-Victor, CLXXVI, 528, 529 and following.—Whether love embraces every human being, and not—, Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 1569.—Charity begins with itself, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 735.—Charity toward one’s neighbour is practised in three ways, ibid., 723.—Whether, by that commandment, we are commanded to love the whole neighbour and our whole selves, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 814.—Whether it is better to love friends than enemies, or conversely, ibid., 818, 1084.—That in the present time God is not loved perfectly, ibid., CCIV, 419.—That God must be loved with the whole heart in his benefits, ibid., 420.—That he must be loved with the whole soul in his benefits, ibid.—That God must be loved with all one’s strength in his judgments, ibid., 423.—On human love toward God, St. Stephen of Grandmont, CCIV, 1099.—Charity ought to be begun with oneself and perfected in one’s neighbour, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 278.

#### VI.—On the qualities of charity and its order.

The endowments of charity, St. Cyprian, IV, 510, 632; St. Zeno, XI, 373.—A person truly loves who keeps the commandments without sadness, without fear, by willing zeal rather than compelled obligation, St. Ambrose, XV, 1380.—Charity cannot exist without faith, ibid., XVI, 280; XVII, 252.—Perfect charity has all faith, ibid., XVII, 1268.—Whoever follows charity is humble toward all, ibid., 492.—No tortures overcome it, ibid., 430.—Charity has no measure, St. Jerome, XXII, 483.—It should be inclined to mercy, not insulting those who sin, ibid., 789.—Charity cannot exist without faith, ibid., XXXVIII, 564.—Where love is, faith and hope are necessarily present, XXXV, 1826.—What charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith is, ibid., XXXIV, 36.—Charity alone remains always, ibid., XXXVIII, 867.—Charity is greater than faith and hope because, when their object arrives, these cease, whereas charity increases, ibid., XXXVII, 1171.—The breadth, length, height, and depth of charity, ibid., XXXIII, 564, 365, 611.—Charity is twofold: severity and gentleness, ibid., XLIII, 85.—Serving charity, ibid., XXXVII, 1733.—It should not fear sometimes to be troublesome to friends, ibid., XXXVIII, 539.

Love of God should be gratuitous; love of neighbour beneficent, St. Jerome, XXXVIII, 571.—Charity casts out fear, but servile fear, ibid., XXXIII, 560.—Charity drives away one fear and introduces another, ibid., XXXVII, 888.—Charity can always increase, ibid., XXXIII, 739.—On the perpetuity of charity, Cassian, XLIX, 496.—On the degrees of charity, ibid., 1028.—By what degrees one may ascend to the sublimity of charity, and what stability it has, ibid., 853.—Perfect and imperfect charity, St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 696.—Charity has no limit, because the Godhead can be enclosed by no boundary, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 300.—The endowments of charity, Julianus Pomerius, LIX, 495.—The praises of charity, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 195.—The nature of charity’s breadth, ibid., LXXVI, 987, 993.—The offices of charity explained, ibid., 925.—Charity is patient against evils and kind, so that it loves those whom it bears, ibid., LXXVI, 1262.—A description of charity, St. Agobard of Lyons, CIV, 261.—What the beginning of charity is, and what its perfection, St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 1474.—What charity is like, St. Bruno of Segni, CLXV, 909.—The marks of charity assigned by St. Paul are exceptionally explained, CLXV, 910.—An encomium of charity, Hildebert, CLXXI, 521.—Whether charity, once possessed, is lost, Hugh of Saint-Victor, CLXXVI, 539; CLXXVIII, 1574; Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 1125.

The order of charity, St. Augustine, XLI, 643.—To order charity, ibid., XXXVIII, 603.—He places weaker persons before stronger ones not in the order of loving, but in the order of assistance, ibid., XXXIII, 537.—The order of charity, Julianus Pomerius, LIX, 497.—Charity is commanded to be ordered in order that sin may be avoided, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 167.—On the order of charity, Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 1472; Hugh of Saint-Victor, CLXXVI, 125.—What the ordering of charity is, Hugh of Saint-Victor, CLXXVI, 15.—Charity begins with oneself, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 734.—How it ought rightly to be ordered in a prelate, ibid., CLXXXIII, 1018.—On the order of loving: what comes first and what afterward, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 816.—On the manner and order of charity, where many doubtful points are discussed, Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 1095.

### CLV. INDEX OF VIRTUES.

#### [Preface.]

In this Index we shall treat analogically of virtues: namely, virtues in general; the theological virtues—that is, faith considered in itself, and the foundations of faith, or Sacred Scripture, tradition, and the authority of the Fathers and councils in matters of faith; and faith put into action, or religion and piety; then hope; afterward charity, or the love owed to God, to one’s neighbour, and to ourselves. These topics are further enlarged by references drawn from the Fathers, which are merely noted alphabetically and should be consulted.

Then we shall treat of the moral virtues, the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and the principal evangelical counsels, observing the same rules; afterward, alphabetically, certain particular virtues; and finally, the evangelical beatitudes.

Here are the virtues treated in this Index:

[Col. 0585] Self-denial. Abstinence. Equity. Love. Kindness. Goodness. Chastity. Charity. Clemency. Compassion. Compunction. Confession. Constancy. Continence. Contrition. Discernment. Almsgiving. Faithfulness. Faith. Weeping. Fortitude. Joy. Gratitude. Cheerfulness. Hospitality. Humility. Forgiveness. Innocence. Understanding. Fasting. [Col. 0586] Generosity. Meekness. Mercy. Purity. Mortification. Obedience. Prayer. Frugality. Patience. Poverty. Peace. Perseverance. Piety. Repentance. Uprightness. Foresight. Prudence. Modesty. Religion. Wisdom. Simplicity. Sobriety. Solicitude. Hope. Silence. Temperance. Fear. Vigilance. Virginity. Zeal.

#### [Index of Virtues.]

[Col. 0585]

#### I.—ON VIRTUE IN GENERAL.

By the name of virtue is understood God’s gift, by which a person has both facility and inclination for knowing and fulfilling the duties of the Christian life. This inclination and capacity come from God. No one can acquire them by his own powers. “And when I knew,” says Holy Scripture, “that otherwise I could not be continent unless God granted it—and this itself was wisdom, to know whose gift it was—I went to the Lord and besought him.” And elsewhere: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights.”

There are other definitions of virtue which almost all reduce to this one: Virtue is a good quality of the mind, by which one lives rightly, which no one uses badly, and which God works in us without us; or: Virtue is a disposition of the soul which makes its possessor good and renders his work good; or finally: Virtue is a disposition consonant with nature, moderation, and reason, which makes the soul excellent.

BONIFACE, Archbishop of Mainz.—We ought to consider the condition of the present life: both what actions we must avoid with every effort and what actions we must pursue with the full exertion of our powers. Among all that can be done here, we must always consider how we may resist the devil, our deceiver, and how we may please God Jesus, our Redeemer. We please him when we do what he commanded and reject what he forbade. He forbids us to commit sins and iniquities, and commands us quickly to heal those already committed with the medicine of repentance. Therefore he commanded us to live rightly and devoutly, to seek eternal things, and diligently to discharge each one’s own place and condition, lest anyone appear idle or less useful in his station.

For our body has one soul, in which its life consists, but many members distinguished by different functions. So too in the Church there is one faith, which must work everywhere through charity, but there are diverse ranks having their own ministries. For one is the order of those set over others, another that of those subject to them; one that of the rich, another that of the poor; one that of the old, another that of the young. Each person has his own particular commands, just as each member has its own proper office in the body. For it is the office of bishops to forbid wrongdoing, console the faint-hearted, and rebuke the insolent. Then royal dignity ought to be an object of fear and reverence to peoples, [Col. 0586] because there is no authority except from God. Likewise, all powerful persons and judges attached to the king ought to be faithful, humble, and merciful; to judge in equity and not for gifts; to defend widows, orphans, and the poor; to be subject to their bishops; to oppress no one by force; not to covet unjust riches; and rather to give their own goods to those in need than seize another’s.

Likewise, among God’s people some are wise and others foolish. It belongs to the wise both to carry out in deed the good things they know and to preach them to others. What profit is it to a traveler to know the road if he does not wish to enter upon it? But one who knows and enters the way of God and brings others into it is like the firmament, which shines with many stars. He who edifies many glories in the reward of many. Therefore the powerful ought always to have God present before them; although they may not fear a human being, they should nevertheless fear God, and use the authority granted to them for God’s honor and for the salvation of their own souls. Those who are foolish and unlearned should humbly learn from the wise, because whoever does not know will be unknown; nor should they suppose that ignorance can excuse them before the strict Judge, who considers each person’s hidden things.

There are three degrees among humankind. Some know what is good and do what they know; these are the best of human beings and nearest to God. The second rank consists of people who do not themselves know good things but wish to learn from those who know them well and fulfill what they have learned; their life is useful in the Church. Whoever scorns to learn the good which he does not know has a life useless to all and harmful to very many. Therefore let one who knows do what is good, and one who does not know learn, so that the former may rejoice in his knowledge and the latter may advance through his diligence.

In the Church some are rich and others poor. The poor are commanded to be humble and to hope in God, who said, “Blessed are the poor in spirit,” and to love better riches all the more eagerly because they are empty of these earthly goods. The rich are commanded to give what is their own, not seize what belongs to others, and to clothe and cover others, because through their abundance the rich make many things superfluous, whether in food or clothing. Therefore let the refreshment of the poor wash away the sins which excess has incurred, because “as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin.” The rich man who spares his riches does not spare his soul; or to whom is he generous who is miserly toward himself? Let each person consider for what price he would wish to ransom himself from a present fire if compelled to burn even for one day: how much fiercer is the fire of judgment? [Col. 0587] Moreover, the fire of Gehenna is eternal. Therefore one who possesses riches should anticipate the Judge’s countenance and have mercy upon the wretched, so that God may have mercy upon him; whoever has mercy upon the poor lends at interest to the Lord, and he will repay him.

It befits old men to be religious, to have well-ordered conduct, to adorn their gray hair with sobriety, and always to think of their entrance into the other life. Young people ought to devote themselves to obedience and submission to their elders, that they may always advance in God’s household and become better and better. They should not permit evil spirits to enslave them through vain amusements and harmful desires, but should strive to bring themselves, chaste and undefiled, to mature age.

Parents also are commanded to instruct their children in the fear of God. For what profit is it to a parent if he has a son assigned to everlasting torments? Therefore fathers should train their children more diligently in the discipline of godliness, so that they may possess them here and in the age to come through the blessing of inheritance. Children, too, should obey their parents, for Christ himself is read to have been subject to his parents. Husbands should love their wives in pure chastity and continence, and, as toward a more fragile vessel, show them the honor due in the fear of God. Wives should be subject to their husbands in fear and faith, knowing that a wife’s subjection to her husband has been established by God.

There are also other commands in the Church common to every rank, age, and sex: to love the Lord God with one’s whole heart, whole mind, and whole strength, and one’s neighbor as oneself; and that no one should do to another what he would not wish done to himself. Patience is also necessary for all, as are the disposition of compassion, generosity in mercy, equity in justice, purity of faith, steadfastness of hope, perseverance in prayers, and gentleness of conduct. By these and such sacrifices divine clemency is won. These commands of salvation suit all and are known to be necessary for everyone. By these steps the heavenly way is traveled, and by these keys the gate of the heavenly homeland is opened. By these footprints all the saints completed the course of the present life, and those who now reign with Christ came to him by these paths. This way is not laborious but exceedingly glorious: it is traversed in a short span, yet crowned with everlasting joy and glory. Whoever does not cease to proceed by it becomes a participant in angelic blessedness and enjoys the eternal vision of the Lord God Almighty himself. LXXXIX, 860–862.

Virtues in general are right faith and an undefiled life. Right faith is belief in God the Father Almighty, in Jesus Christ his Son, and in the Holy Spirit—one almighty God in perfect Trinity. But because it is written, “Faith without works is dead,” one must love God [lacuna]; then one’s neighbor [lacuna]; fear of the Lord, peace, kindness, patience, humility, continence, modesty, justice, mercy [lacuna]. Boniface, bishop, LXXXIX, 856.

JULIANUS POMERIUS.—Every holy virtue is a divine, wholly incorporeal, and utterly pure reality. Defiled minds do not defile it; rather, it cleanses the defiled. By participation in it, what is formless is formed, what is dead is raised, what is weak is healed, what is crooked is corrected, and what is hostile is reconciled. No one possesses it except God and the person to whom God has given it. It dwells in the soul, but sanctifies both soul and body. No one approaches it unwillingly, and no one loses it except when deceived by his own will. No one can bestow it upon himself, though he can take it away; nor can he either bestow it upon or take it away from another.

Accordingly, when virtue so great and such as this has shone upon someone still languishing among his pleasures and stirred in him a salutary desire to long for it, immediately a conflict of two contrary delights arises in his mind. His will, divided against itself by a twofold delight, draws and draws back his mind in opposite directions: now reproving what it had chosen, now choosing what it had reproved. Thus, as he turns himself now to one side and now to the other by the variety of his thoughts, a certain lukewarm middle state between virtue and vice itself vexes and tears him. For any person, until he confirms himself by a settled decision in what he has chosen, is torn apart by the very diversity of his wills, so long as he now does not want what he wanted, now begins to want what he did not want—set, as it were, at a crossroads of uncertain deliberation.

On one side virtue reminds him of his salvation and calls him; on the other, vicious habit delays and recalls one wishing to leave it. When he has turned away from it for a little while but has not yet fully turned toward virtue, it flatters him with the recollection of accustomed pleasure and displays every allurement in which he once recklessly indulged. It also sends in shameful desires by which he may be conquered; and to one already almost disgusted it softly whispers some seductive, I know not what, and begs him not to prefer hard things to soft, sad things to joyful, uncertain things to certain, future things to present pleasure. It urges him to consider how painful and difficult it is to go without sweet delights, [Col. 0588] renounce carnal allurements, be burdened by the continual labors of abstinence, be tortured by an unbroken succession of fasts and vigils, seek the reward of uncertain recompense by definite affliction of the flesh, take up arms in resistance against the devil, skilled in deception, and avoid his snares and frauds by the watchful caution of the mind. Finally, it tells him how wretched it would be, after being overcome by the enormity of such harshness and deceived by diabolical fraud, to return to what he had rejected, enjoy the pleasures he had cast aside, and delight in all the things he had despised when he heedlessly undertook a laborious purpose. LIX, 498, 499, 500.
