## II.—ON THE THEOLOGICAL VIRTUES

The theological virtues are those which refer immediately to God, which are known only by divine revelation, and which are faith, hope, and charity. It is clear that they refer immediately to God, since through faith we believe in God; through hope we hope in him; and through charity we love him. Therefore God is the proper, primary, and immediate object of the theological virtues.

The moral virtues are very numerous. But all are reduced to four principal ones, called cardinal because they are, as it were, the hinges and foundations of the rest: namely prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice. These refer not immediately to God, but first, directly, and immediately to the right ordering of conduct; that conduct must subsequently be referred to God. For God is the final end to which all things pertaining to conduct ought to be referred. Conduct is not wholly pure unless its holiness is referred to God.

“If you wish to know,” says St Jerome, “what adornments the Lord seeks: I possess prudence, justice, temperance, fortitude. With these wounds enclose heaven; may this four-horse chariot swiftly bear you, as Christ’s charioteer, to the goal. Nothing is more precious than this necklace, nothing more distinguished than this variety of gems; let them be for you beauty and adornment on every side, and a defense.” The philosophers hold that the virtues adhere to one another; and the Apostle James holds that whoever lacks one lacks all.

PETER LOMBARD, Master of the *Sentences*.—Faith, hope, charity, and action are in one respect equal in the present life. Hence St Gregory says: “While we live in this life, we find faith, hope, charity, and action to be equal among us, because we love as much as we believe; and we presume from hope as much as we love. For every faithful person believes as much as he hopes and loves; and acts as much as he believes, loves, and hopes. Yet charity is called greater than hope and faith because, when one comes to the vision of God, hope and faith pass away, but charity remains; and because charity is the mother of all virtues. It is not placed after faith and hope because it arises from them, but because it will remain afterward, increased. ‘Charity never fails.’”

The equality just stated must properly be understood with respect to the intention of interior acts. Yet the assertion that charity does not arise from faith and hope, but rather the reverse, appears to conflict with what the Apostle says: “The end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, and a good conscience, and faith unfeigned.” Explaining this, St Augustine says: “He takes heart for intellect and conscience for hope. What kind of charity,” he says, “is the end of the commandment, proceeding from a pure heart—that is, from a pure intellect, so that nothing but God is loved—and conscience—that is, from good hope—and faith unfeigned—that is, not feigned? Therefore charity does not seem to precede faith and hope; rather, faith and hope seem to precede charity.”

Understand this to have been taught on the ground not that faith and hope precede charity, the mother of all good things, either causally or in time, but that charity cannot exist in anyone without them, whereas they can exist without charity—although faith or hope is not steadfast without charity. Charity is therefore said to proceed from faith and hope because it comes to no one without them. CXCII, 510, 511.

The same St Augustine: “Faith working through love certainly cannot exist without hope; nor can love exist without hope, nor hope without love, nor either of them without faith. And faith without love profits nothing. Yet something may be believed which is not hoped for; nothing, however, can be hoped for which is not believed. Therefore believing, which is an act of faith, naturally precedes hoping, which is an act of hope, because unless something is believed it cannot be hoped for. For something is believed which is not hoped for. Hence Scripture frequently states that faith precedes hope and hope follows faith—not because the virtue of faith precedes the virtue of hope in excellence or causality, but because the act of faith naturally precedes the act of hope. Some also concede this concerning the very virtue of faith: that it naturally precedes hope, though not in time. Thus faith alone is rightly called the foundation of all virtues and good works; but it is not the foundation of charity, because it is not the cause of charity; rather, charity is the cause of the very virtue of faith.

“For charity is the cause and mother of all virtues. If it is lacking, the rest are possessed in vain; but if it is present, all are possessed. Charity, moreover, is the Holy Spirit. Therefore it is the cause of all virtues, and no virtue is its cause, because it surpasses all gifts. Hence St Augustine says: ‘Look at the gifts of the Church, and you will recognize that the gift of charity excels them all. Like oil, it cannot be pressed down to the bottom, but springs upward.’ Faith, then, is not its cause or foundation.”

St Gregory says that unless faith is first held, one cannot in any way attain spiritual love. For charity does not precede faith, but faith charity, because no one can love what he has not believed, any more than he can hope for it. But this may be understood as said of faith which is not a virtue. For such faith frequently precedes hope and charity; or of the act of faith, which perhaps naturally precedes the act of charity, as it precedes the act of hope. The carefully noted preceding words indicate this, as do those which he adds: “Unless,” he says, “you believe the things which you hear, you will not be inflamed to love the things which you hear”; this applies only to things not seen [lacuna]. Hence St Chrysostom says: “Faith causes the things not seen, with which faith is properly concerned, to subsist in our soul; for faith does not concern things seen, but recognition.” CXCII, 807.

### On Faith

Here we shall treat: 1. faith considered in itself; 2. the foundations of our faith; 3. faith put into practice, or religion and piety; 4. faith put into practice through prayer.

#### 1.—Faith Considered in Itself

Faith is a supernatural light infused by God into our minds, by which we firmly believe in God and fully assent to all things which God has revealed, even if they surpass our understanding. This is explained as follows. It is a light because by it our mind is illuminated and knows the things revealed by God. Through this light we firmly—that is, without doubt, with full assent, and with absolute certainty—believe that God exists, and we place complete trust in him.

Among the things revealed by God, some we grasp by understanding; others surpass the reach of our intelligence; and we believe both by faith. We understand, for example, that heaven and earth were created by God. We do not fully understand how one God can subsist in three persons. We nevertheless believe both with the surest faith because God revealed both, since the sole foundation of this faith is the Word of God. For by theological faith we believe nothing other than what God has said and revealed. We believe God who reveals, because God, being most wise, cannot be deceived, and, being most good, cannot deceive; for it is impossible for God to lie.

We know the things revealed by God through the ministry of Christ’s Church, to which God entrusted the deposit of his word. The Church derives this from Holy Scripture and tradition. Whatever God has revealed to humankind, whatever the Church proposes for belief in matters of faith, is wholly contained in Scripture or tradition. By Scripture we understand the written Word of God in those books which we call canonical; by tradition we understand the Word of God not written in canonical books, but transmitted orally from the apostles down to us in continuous succession and, as it were, handed down from hand to hand.

We call Scripture and tradition the deposit of God’s word, entrusted by Christ to the Church, because by Christ’s institution it belongs to the Catholic Church alone to distinguish true and genuine Scriptures and traditions from false ones, and to interpret and declare the meaning of Scripture and tradition.

St Augustine says, *Against Faustus*, book XIII, chapters 4–5: “Will Faustus call our apostles as witnesses on his behalf? I do not think so. He will produce not people but books; yet he will find them opened not for him but against him. If he says that they have been falsified, he will assail the credibility of his own witnesses. But if he produces other codices which he claims are those of our apostles, how will he give them the authority which he did not receive through the Churches of Christ established by the apostles themselves, so that it might pass down to posterity with confirmed attestation? The authority of our books, strengthened by the agreement of so many peoples and by the succession of apostles, bishops, and councils, is opposed to the Manichaeans. Yours, however, has none, because it is produced by very few and by people who worship God and Christ as liars.”

And in book XXVIII, chapters 2 and 4: “You will say that the account is not Matthew’s which the whole Church, conveyed in certain succession from apostolic sees down to present bishops, says is Matthew’s [lacuna] Believe this book to be Matthew’s: the Church has brought it down, through an uninterrupted succession of times and a certain connected sequence, from the time when Matthew himself lived in the flesh to the present age. But perhaps you will produce another book bearing the name of some apostle whom Christ is known to have chosen, and in it you will read that Christ was not born of the Virgin Mary. Since one of these books must be false, to which do you think we ought rather to give credence? To that which the Church, begun by Christ himself and advanced through the apostles in a certain series of successions down to our own times, spread throughout the whole world, recognizes and approves as handed down and preserved from the beginning—or to that which the same Church rejects as unknown?

“For if any letters were produced which, without any other person reporting it, were said to belong properly to Christ himself [lacuna] even if those letters were produced, one would certainly have to consider by whom they were produced. If by Christ himself, they could undoubtedly first have been produced to those who then adhered to him, and through them also have reached others. If that had happened, they would have become evident by the most firmly confirmed authority of the succession of leaders and peoples. Who, then, is so mad as today to believe that a letter is Christ’s because a Manichaean has produced it, yet not believe that what Matthew wrote was done or said by Christ? Or, if he doubts concerning Matthew himself whether he wrote these things, why should he not rather believe of Matthew himself what he finds in the Church, which is shown by a certain series of successions from Matthew’s own time down to this time, rather than believe some unknown person coming sideways from Persia?

“Even the Apostle Paul, called from heaven after the Lord’s Ascension, would not have been believed by the Church at all if he had not found the apostles in the flesh, so that, by communicating and conferring the Gospel with them, he might show that he belonged to the same fellowship. But because he knew that he was proclaiming what they too proclaimed, and lived in their communion and unity, he deserved authority with the Lord’s commendation, so that his words today are heard in the Church as though Christ were heard speaking in him. And does the Manichaean think that the Church of Christ ought to believe him when he speaks against Scriptures established by such great and so well-ordered authority, Scriptures through which it was especially enjoined upon him that whoever proclaims anything other than what it has received should be anathema?”

Therefore, since we see such great help of God, continues the same St Augustine in *On the Usefulness of Belief*, chapter 17, no. 35, and such progress and fruit, shall we hesitate to cast ourselves into the bosom of that Church which has obtained the summit of authority, from the apostolic see through successions of bishops down to the confession of the human race, while heretics bark around it in vain and are condemned partly by the judgment of the people itself, partly by the weight of councils, and partly even by the majesty of miracles? Not to grant it primacy is surely either the height of impiety or headlong arrogance. For if there is no sure path to wisdom and salvation for minds except when faith goes before and prepares them for reason, what else is it to be ungrateful for divine aid and assistance than to wish to resist an authority foretold with such force? [lacuna] We hold to the truth of the Scriptures when we do what has now pleased the universal Church, which the authority of Scripture itself commends; so that, since Holy Scripture cannot deceive, whoever fears being deceived should consult concerning this obscurity of question the same Church which Holy Scripture itself shows without any ambiguity.

Vincent of Lérins says in his *Commonitory*: “Therefore, having often inquired with great care and the utmost attention from very many men eminent in holiness and learning how I might distinguish, by some sure and as it were general and regular method, the truth of Catholic faith from the falsehood of heretical depravity, I always received from almost all of them this answer: that if I, or anyone else, wished to detect the frauds of heretics who arise, avoid their snares, and remain sound and whole in sound faith, he ought, with the Lord’s help, to fortify his faith in a twofold way: first by the authority of divine law, and then by the tradition of the Catholic Church.

“Perhaps someone may ask here: Since the canon of Scripture is perfect and more than sufficiently adequate for all things in itself, why is it necessary to join to it the authority of ecclesiastical interpretation? Because, owing to Scripture’s very profundity, not everyone receives it in one and the same sense; rather, one person interprets its utterances one way and another another way, so that nearly as many meanings as persons seem capable of being drawn from it. Novatian expounds it in one way, Sabellius in another, Donatus in another; Arius, Eunomius, and Macedonius differently; Photinus, Apollinaris, and Priscillianus differently; Jovinian, Pelagius, and Caelestius differently; and finally Nestorius differently. Therefore, amid so many windings of such diverse error, it is exceedingly necessary that the line of prophetic and apostolic interpretation be directed according to the rule of ecclesiastical and Catholic understanding.”

The holy Council of Trent decrees concerning this question of tradition, in order to restrain insolent intellects, that no one, relying upon his own judgment, shall dare in matters of faith and morals pertaining to the edification of Christian doctrine to twist Holy Scripture to his own senses against that sense which Holy Mother Church has held and does hold—she whose office it is to judge the true sense and interpretation of the Holy Scriptures—or even against the unanimous consent of the Fathers, even if interpretations of this kind were never to be published at any time. Compare Matthew 11:25; 16:18; 18:17; 28:20; Luke 10:16; Romans 1:14; 1 Corinthians 1:26; Ephesians 4:14; 1 Timothy 3:15.

Faith is altogether necessary for salvation. There is no salvation for those who do not firmly believe everything which the Church believes and teaches. Hence it is wholly necessary that every individual believe in general everything which the Church believes, and distinctly know certain principal articles among these: namely, the mysteries of the Most Holy Trinity, of the Incarnation of the Word, and of humanity’s Redemption through Christ; everything contained in the Apostles’ Creed; the commandments of God and of the Church; and many matters pertaining to the sacraments, especially baptism, the Eucharist, and penance.

This we explain as follows. Each person is bound to have a greater or lesser distinct knowledge of the articles of faith according to his state, condition, abilities, time, and other such circumstances. It is difficult to determine certainly what distinct knowledge is necessary for each person. The question here is not what had necessarily to be believed before Christ. We speak only of baptized persons who possess the free use of reason. No one among them can be saved unless he knows the mysteries of the Most Holy Trinity, the Incarnation, and the Redemption. Every individual is bound at least to learn the commandments of God and the Church, the Apostles’ Creed, the effect of baptism, and many other things which pertain [Col. 0593] to the sacraments of confirmation, the Eucharist, penance, and extreme unction, and to the requirements and duties of his own state and condition.

Let these statements be understood concerning the less educated among Christians. For ignorance is more dangerous to those who are able thoroughly to investigate and know religion but do not care to do so. Nothing is of greater importance to us, nothing concerns us more, than knowing individually the things which the Church believes and investigating the reasons for all the Church’s observances and rites. If this is so, it is astonishing that most Christians lie inert in careless and abject ignorance, whose outcome for them is greatly to be feared at God’s dreadful judgment. If they devoted to the study of religion the time which they spend on games, trifles, empty conversation, and pleasures, this occupation would be easy, pleasant, and useful to them. They have no basis for excusing their ignorance.

PETER LOMBARD.—We must speak of the sufficiency of faith for salvation. For those who preceded Christ’s coming and those who followed it, faith seems to have advanced with the progress of time, just as knowledge advanced. Faith is called great either because of knowledge and the number of articles, or because of steadfastness and devotion. Yet there is a certain measure of faith without which salvation could never exist. Hence the Apostle: “Whoever approaches God must believe that He exists, and that He rewards those who hope in Him.” But it is asked whether this belief was sufficient for salvation before the coming [of Christ] and before the Law. For in the time of grace it is certainly clear that this is not sufficient: all things contained in the creeds must be believed. But neither before the coming nor before the Law does this seem to have been sufficient, because the authorities of the saints testify that no human being, whether before or after, was saved without faith in the Mediator. Hence St. Augustine: “That faith is sacred by which we believe that no human being, whether of greater or lesser age, is delivered from the contagion of death and the obligation of sin contracted at first birth, except through the one mediator between God and men, Jesus Christ.”

By the most saving faith in this man, who is also God, those righteous persons too were made safe who, before He came in the flesh, believed that He would come in the flesh. For their faith and ours are the same. Accordingly, since all the righteous, whether before the Incarnation or after it, neither lived nor live except by faith in Christ’s Incarnation, surely the written declaration that “there is no other name under heaven in which we must be saved” has been effective for saving the human race from the time when it was corrupted in Adam.

The same St. Augustine says: “No one is freed from the condemnation brought about through Adam except through faith in Jesus Christ. The same faith in the Mediator which saves us made the righteous of old—little ones together with great—safe; for as we believe Christ to have come in the flesh, so they believed that He would come; and as we believe Him to have died, so they [believed] that He would die; and as we believe Him to have risen, so they [believed] that He would rise; and [we and they believed] that He would come for the judgment of the living and the dead …” CXCII, 809–811.

Faith is the virtue by which things not seen are believed. Yet this must not be understood of all things not seen, but only of those things which it pertains to religion to believe. For there are many matters whose ignorance by a Christian entails nothing to fear, since he does not thereby depart from religion.

Faith is understood in three ways: namely, as that by which one believes, and it is a virtue; as that which is believed, and it is not a virtue; and as that in which one believes, which is different from that by which one believes. Hence St. Augustine says: the things which are believed are one thing, and the faith by which they are believed another. For the former are things believed to be, to have been, or to be future; whereas the latter is in the believer’s mind, visible only to the person whose it is. Yet both are designated by the name faith: namely, that which is believed and that by which one believes.

That which is believed is called faith, as in St. Athanasius’s Creed: “This is the Catholic faith …” But the faith by which one believes, if it is joined with charity, is a virtue, because charity is the mother of all virtues and gives form to them all; without it there is no true virtue. Therefore faith working through love is the virtue by which things unseen are believed. This is the foundation which cannot be changed; when laid as a foundation, it permits no one to perish. Hence St. Augustine says: “The foundation is Christ Jesus, that is, faith in Christ—namely, the faith which works through love, through which Christ dwells in hearts, and which permits no one to perish. For faith without love is empty. Faith with love is the Christian’s; another is the demon’s. For demons too believe and tremble. But it matters greatly whether one believes that Christ is [the Christ], believes Christ, or believes in Christ. The demons believed Him to be Christ, but nevertheless did not believe in Christ.

“For it is one thing to believe in God, another to believe God, and another to believe that God exists. To believe God is to believe that what He says is true; even the wicked do this, and we believe a man, but not in a man. To believe that God exists is to believe that He is God; the wicked do this also. To believe in God [Col. 0594] is, by believing, to love; by believing, to go to Him; by believing, to cleave to Him and to be incorporated into His members. By this faith the ungodly person is justified, so that thereafter faith itself may begin to work through love. For only those works are to be called good which are done through love of God. Love itself is called the work of faith. Therefore the faith possessed by demons and false Christians is a quality of mind, but unformed, because it is without charity. For the Apostle shows that the wicked too have faith though they lack charity, saying: ‘If I have all faith, but do not have charity,’ etc. This faith may also be called a gift of God, because even in the wicked there are certain gifts of God.” CXCII, 805.

## 2. On the foundations of faith: Holy Scripture, tradition, and the authority of councils and Fathers

Although faith is spoken of in different ways, we must nevertheless confess one faith, as the Apostle says: “One Lord, one faith.” Whether faith is understood as that which is believed or as that by which one believes, faith is rightly called one. If it is understood as that which is believed, it is called one faith in this sense: we are commanded to believe the same thing, and the one same thing is believed by all the faithful. Hence it is called the Catholic faith, that is, the universal faith.

But if faith is understood as that by which one believes, it is called one faith not because it is numerically one in all persons, but in kind—that is, in likeness. Hence St. Augustine: “Faith (those who have it being called faithful, and those who lack it unbelieving) is common to all the faithful, just as a face is said to be common to many persons, though each has his own. For faith is not numerically one, but one in kind; when it is in one person, it is also in others—not the same faith, but a similar one. Because of this similarity, we say it is one rather than many, just as those who will the same thing are said to have one will, though each has his own will, and two very similar persons are said to have one face.”

It should be noted that faith properly concerns only things not apparent. Hence St. Gregory: “Things apparent do not have faith, but recognition.” Thus when Paul says, “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not apparent,” what is not customarily seen is truly said to be believed. For what can be seen can no longer be believed. Thomas saw one thing and believed another: he saw the man and confessed God … Each person sees faith itself to be in his own heart if he believes, or not to be there if he does not believe … Therefore, since we are commanded to believe because we cannot see what we are commanded to believe, nevertheless we see faith itself in ourselves when it is in us: for faith is present concerning absent things; faith concerning external things is inward; faith concerning things not seen is itself seen; and it itself comes into being temporally in human hearts, and if unbelievers become believers, it passes away from them … Faith therefore is conviction concerning things not apparent, because through faith the things still hoped for have existence in us even now, and in the future they will have existence through experience. It is also proof and conviction concerning things not apparent, because if anyone doubts them, they are proved through faith, as the future resurrection is still proved because the patriarchs and other saints so believed. Or it is proof and certainty that certain things not apparent exist. Properly, however, faith is called the substance of things hoped for, because it underlies the things hoped for and is the foundation of good things, which no one can suppose [otherwise].” CXCII, 805–807.

Since, from the testimonies already quoted, faith is the first virtue which subjects the soul to God, because knowledge of divinity and truth must be learned by Catholic faith, because “without faith it is impossible to please God,” truly blessed is the person who both lives well by believing rightly and preserves right faith by living well. Therefore, just as faith without good works is idle, so good works profit nothing without right faith. This is the Catholic faith, etc.
