## On the first foundation of faith, which is Holy Scripture

Holy Scripture is the written word of God in those books which we call canonical: that is, books containing the rule of our faith and whose sequence is contained in several canons of the Church. Thus we call rules laid down by the Church.

The canonical books are those contained among us in our Bibles, etc. … concerning which the Council of Trent thus decrees:

“The most holy, ecumenical, and general Council of Trent, lawfully assembled in the Holy Spirit, … keeping this perpetually before its eyes, that, errors having been removed, the very purity of the Gospel may be preserved in the Church—the Gospel which our Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, first proclaimed with His own mouth, having been promised beforehand through the prophets in the Holy Scriptures, and afterwards commanded to be preached to every creature by His Apostles as the source of all saving truth and moral discipline—and perceiving that this truth and discipline are contained in the sacred books and in unwritten traditions which, received by the Apostles from Christ’s own mouth or transmitted, as it were, from hand to hand by the Apostles themselves at the dictation of the Holy Spirit, have come down to us: following the examples of the orthodox Fathers, it receives and venerates, with equal devotion and reverence, all the books both of the Old and New Testament, since one God is the author of both, and likewise the traditions themselves pertaining both to faith and morals, as dictated either orally by Christ or by the Holy Spirit and preserved in the Catholic Church in continuous succession.” [Col. 0596]

But should Christians read Holy Scripture? Certainly they should. For the reading of the divine Scriptures—especially of the New Testament, the Psalms, and the moral books of the Old Testament—ought to be the chaste delight and daily exercise of Christians who seek to nourish piety rather than vanity or curiosity. The Church especially approves and earnestly desires this.

Yet it must be admitted that there are very many Christians for whom, because of cruder ignorance or slowness of mind, reading the Scriptures would be of little benefit; and others for whom, because of a proud and unteachable disposition, such reading would be harmful. Alas, they are exceedingly sick people for whom even the remedy of their sickness is deadly. Therefore Holy Scripture must be read with a reverent, humble, teachable mind. What is understood must be held fast; what exceeds one’s capacity must be believed and accepted. In all things one must obey the judgment of the Church. God must be prayed to before and after reading, that He may open our understanding for the comprehension of the Scriptures and Himself impress His words upon our hearts. Whatever is read must be deeply fixed in the mind and continually expressed in conduct as occasion offers, lest we be like “a man who looks at his natural face in a mirror; for he considered himself and went away, and immediately forgot what kind of man he was.”

These points must be explained by the authority of the Fathers … Let St. Chrysostom be heard first. “I beg you,” he says in Homily 2 on Matthew, chapter 1, “to turn over in your minds these things sown from the Scriptures. For from such study and care a certain immense good and salvation are gained for souls. By attending to these things we can please God, and, while we are exercised in spiritual utterances, we shall preserve mouths clean from abusive, obscene speech and insults; we shall be able to terrify demons by fortifying our tongue with the weapons of such words; and then we shall be able to merit greater grace from God. From this the keenness and light of your mind are increased …

“‘I am not a monk; I have a wife and children, and manage a household.’ This is what corrupts all things as though by one plague: you think that reading the divine Scriptures belongs only to monks, whereas it is much more necessary for you than for them. Those who live in public and receive wounds daily have greater need of medicine. Therefore it is much graver and worse to think the law of God superfluous than not to read it at all … For discourse drawn from the divine Scriptures kindles the soul of the hearer more vehemently than fire itself and prepares it for every use of good things. Thus Paul also made the Corinthians, whom he found puffed up and swollen, more gentle through the correction of his discourse; and David, after his sin, because he heard God’s word, hastened to that saving repentance … Therefore let us not despise hearing the divine Scriptures. It is the mind of the devil that prevents us from looking upon the treasure lest we acquire riches. That is why he urges that there is no benefit whatever in hearing the divine laws, lest he see that action also follows from hearing …”

The same author, in Homily 3 on Lazarus, says: “This I always urge and will never cease to urge: that you attend not only here to what is said, but also, when you are at home, that you devote yourselves continually to the reading of the divine Scriptures. Let no one say to me: ‘Those are cold words; much in them ought to be despised. I am tied to legal cases, conduct public business, exercise a trade, have a wife, support children, manage a household; I am a worldly person. Reading the Scriptures is not for me, but for those who have said farewell to the world, occupied mountain peaks, and continually live such a life.’

“What are you saying, man? It is not your business to search the Scriptures because you are distracted by innumerable cares? On the contrary, it is more your business than theirs. For they do not need the protection of the Scriptures as much as you who are tossed amid the waves of business. Monks, indeed, are free from the law court and legal affairs; they have set their little dwellings in the desert and have no dealings with anyone, but in that quiet calm philosophize with complete security and, as though seated in a harbor, enjoy extremely safe conditions. We, on the other hand, are tossed as if in the midst of the sea and, willing or unwilling, are continually bound by innumerable sins; we always need the constant, unbroken consolation of the Scriptures … Because you continually stand in battle line and receive frequent blows, you need remedies all the more … We must incessantly draw armor from the Scriptures … Let us ward off the devil’s missiles coming from afar, extinguishing and repelling them through constant reading of the Scriptures. For it cannot happen—it cannot, I say, happen—that anyone attains salvation unless he continually occupies himself with spiritual reading …

“For us the instruments of our craft are the books of the Apostles and prophets, and every Scripture inspired by God and useful … By them we fashion our own soul, correct it when depraved, and renew it when grown old … Therefore let us not neglect to provide ourselves with books, lest we receive a wound in vital matters … Let us store up in ourselves the treasure of spiritual books … Wherever spiritual books are found, all the force of the devil is expelled from there, and much consolation comes to those who dwell there … From sacred books we are made safer and stronger. For as soon as anyone touches the Gospel, he immediately puts his own mind in order and draws it away from worldly things, and this comes from the sight alone. But if careful reading is added, the soul is purified and made better, just as one initiated in sacred sanctuaries into divine things, God conversing with it through those Scriptures.

“But what, they ask, if we do not understand what is contained in the books? Even if you do not understand the things stored up there, much holiness is born from the reading itself. Yet it cannot be that you should be equally ignorant of everything. For the grace of the Spirit arranged and tempered the Scriptures so that tax collectors, fishermen, tent-makers, shepherds, and apostles—uneducated and illiterate persons—might be saved through these books; so that none of the unlearned might resort to this excuse of difficulty; so that what is said might be plainly accessible to all, and that the craftsman, servant, widow, and least educated of all persons might gain some profit and benefit from hearing the reading …

“For to whom are not all things written in the Gospel clear? Who, on hearing that the meek are blessed, the merciful blessed, the pure in heart blessed, and the rest of the same kind, will require a teacher in order to learn any of the things said? Even the signs, miracles, and histories—are they not known and plain to everyone? This is a pretext and an excuse, a covering for sloth. You do not understand what is contained in them? How will you ever be able to understand what you are unwilling even to inspect lightly? Take the book in hand; read the whole history; retain in memory what is known; and repeatedly go through what is obscure and less plain. If you cannot find what is said through persistence in reading, go to someone wiser, seek out a teacher, discuss with them what is written, and show earnest zeal. If God sees that you bring such readiness of mind, He will not despise your watchfulness and care. But even if no human being teaches you what you seek, He Himself will undoubtedly disclose it …

“Reading the Scriptures is a great defense against sin; ignorance of the Scriptures is a great precipice, a deep abyss. To know nothing of the divine laws is a great loss of salvation; it has produced heresies and introduced a corrupt life. For it cannot happen—it cannot, I say, happen—that one who delights in continual and attentive reading of the Scriptures should depart without fruit …”

“What, then,” he continues in Homily 10 on chapter 1 of John, “do we ask of you? That on one day of the week, or at least on the Sabbath, you make it your care to read the Gospel lessons: to have them in your hands before these sermons, repeat them frequently at home, carefully investigate their meaning, note what in them is clear and what obscure, what seems contradictory although it is not. Thus, when you have examined all things thoroughly, you will show yourselves most attentive at these sermons. By this means no small benefit will come to both of us …

“If there are any who allege business, occupations, and concerns of public and private affairs, first, they err greatly in this, that they are involved in so many affairs and so constantly attached to worldly business that they spend not even the smallest effort upon matters which are most necessary. Then they offer a frivolous excuse of no weight; for their associations with friends, their lingering in theaters, and their gatherings to watch horse races—in which they very often consume an entire day—could rather be charged against them in this regard …

“Those who are negligent also have the foolish excuse of a lack of books. It is ridiculous to make this answer to the wealthy. But since I think many poor persons often use this excuse, I would like to jest a little with them and ask whether they possess all the instruments of their trade, and whether poverty greatly prevents their acquiring them … Some are so ignorant of Paul that they do not even clearly know the number of his Epistles. This is not caused by ignorance, however, but because they are unwilling continually to keep this man’s writings in their hands. For we know what we know not because of natural goodness or sharpness of intellect, but because, loving that man intensely, we never leave off reading him … Therefore, if you too resolve to devote zealous and diligent effort to this reading, there will certainly be nothing else for you to seek.”

Now, to bring forward some of our holy Latin Fathers, let us hear Jerome and Augustine.

[Col. 0598] The former says, in his Letter to Laeta: “Instead of jewels and silk, let your daughter love the divine codices, in which she may delight not in the worm-woven picture of gold and Babylonian embroidery, but in an accurate and learned arrangement conducive to faith. Let her first learn the Psalter and divert herself with these songs; and let her be instructed for life in Solomon’s Proverbs. In Ecclesiastes let her become accustomed to trample underfoot worldly things. In Job let her follow examples of virtue and patience.

“Let her proceed to the Gospels, never laying them down. Let her drink in the Acts and Epistles of the Apostles with all her heart. And when she has enriched the storeroom of her breast with these treasures, let her commit to memory the Prophets, the Heptateuch, and the books of Kings and Chronicles, as well as the volumes of Ezra and Esther. Finally, without danger, let her learn the Song of Songs, lest, if she reads it at the beginning and does not understand under its carnal words the wedding-song of spiritual marriage, she be wounded …”

St. Augustine says, *Confessions*, book III, chapter 5, §9: “And so I set my mind to attend to the holy Scriptures, that I might see what they were like. And behold, I see a thing not accessible to the proud nor disclosed to children, but humble in its approach, exalted in its progress, and veiled in mysteries. My pride recoiled from its manner, and my sharpness did not penetrate its interior. Yet it was such as would grow with little ones; but I disdained to be a little one, and, swollen with arrogance, seemed great to myself.”

Accordingly, in *Confessions*, book VI, chapter 5, §8: “Since we were weak for finding truth by clear reason, and therefore had need of the authority of the holy writings, I had already begun to believe that You would by no means have bestowed upon that Scripture such excellent authority throughout all lands unless You had wished both to be believed through it and to be sought through it … And its authority appeared to me more venerable and more worthy of holy faith because it was readily available for all to read, while preserving the dignity of its secret in a deeper understanding; it offered itself to all in the clearest words and humblest manner of speech, while exercising the attention of those who are light of heart, in order that it might receive all into its popular bosom.”

The same author, in *Tractates on John*, 18.1: “For heresies and certain doctrines of perversity which entangle souls and plunge them into the deep have arisen only because good Scriptures are not well understood, and what is not well understood in them is rashly and boldly asserted. Therefore we must hear these things very cautiously, since we are little ones for grasping them; and, holding with a devout heart and with trembling this rule of soundness, we must rejoice as over food in what we are able to understand according to the faith with which we have been imbued. But regarding what we cannot yet understand according to the sound rule of faith, we must remove doubt and postpone understanding; that is, even if we do not know something, we must never doubt that it is good and true.”

The same author, in his Letter to Volusianus, chapter 1, §3: “So great is the depth of the Christian Scriptures that I should make progress in them daily if, from early childhood to decrepit old age, with the greatest leisure, the highest diligence, and better ability, I attempted to learn only them. This is not because one reaches the things necessary for salvation in them with such difficulty; but when one has held the faith without which one cannot live rightly and piously, there remain for those making progress so many things to be understood, obscured beneath so many and such varied shadows of mysteries; and so great a depth of wisdom lies hidden not only in the words by which these things are said, but also in the matters which must be understood, that even those most advanced in years, most acute, and most ardently desirous of learning experience what the same Scripture says: ‘When a man has finished, then he begins.’”

But the very manner of expression itself (chapter 5, §18) in which Holy Scripture is woven—how accessible it is to all, though penetrable by very few! What it contains openly speaks to the hearts of unlearned and learned alike as an intimate friend, without disguise. What it conceals in mysteries does not raise itself in proud speech, so that a slow and unlearned mind might not dare approach it as a poor man approaches a rich one; rather, in humble speech it invites all, nourishing them not only with things plain but also exercising them with the truth of things hidden, having in the manifest what it has in the concealed. But lest the plain things should be despised, they are in a way renewed when desired, and, renewed, sweetly made inward. By these things crooked minds are wholesomely corrected, small minds nourished, and great minds delighted. The mind hostile to this teaching is one which either, through error, does not know it to be most wholesome, or, through sickness, hates the medicine.

Therefore, as *On True Religion*, chapter 51, §100, says, setting aside theatrical and poetic things, let us feed the mind through the contemplation and treatment of the divine Scriptures; let us give drink to it when wearied and fevered by the hunger and thirst of empty curiosity, and when it vainly desires to be refreshed and satisfied by empty phantasms as though by painted banquets. By this truly liberal and noble recreation we shall be beneficially instructed. If the marvels and beauty of spectacles delight us, let us desire to see that Wisdom “which reaches from end to end and orders all things sweetly.” [Col. 0599]

St. Bernard, in Sermon 5 on the Advent of the Lord, says: “Keep the word of God, for it too is living bread and food for the mind … Keep the Word of God; for blessed are those who keep it. Let it therefore pass into the innermost parts of your soul, and pass into your affections and your conduct. Eat what is good, and your soul shall delight in abundance. Do not forget to eat your bread, lest your heart wither; rather let your soul be filled with fatness and richness.”

## On the second foundation of faith, which is the authority of tradition in matters of faith

Those who think that every individual has the right and capacity, apart from the authority of the Church, to interpret and determine the legitimate sense of Scripture are wholly mistaken. For this perverse opinion opens the way to every kind of error, fraud, and license. There has never been a heretic who has not publicly brought forward Holy Scripture, adapted by his own private interpretation to his own opinions and inventions.

Furthermore, those who think in this way oppose Holy Scripture and reason. They oppose Scripture because “no prophecy of Scripture,” says the Apostle Peter, “comes by private interpretation.” Certainly individual Jews were never permitted to interpret the holy Scriptures according to their own fashion; rather, in obscure matters they were obliged to go to the priests: “For the lips of the priest shall keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts.”

Nor do those who hold such views less oppose reason. It is utterly contrary to reason to establish as certain something that cannot in any way be put into practice. Yet this is the kind of proposition they maintain concerning private interpretation of Scripture. How, indeed, will unskilled and unlearned persons, called to faith no differently from the learned and constituting the greater part of the Church, interpret the Scriptures? How, I ask, will those interpret the Scriptures who neither know how to read nor understand Hebrew or Greek, the languages in which the sacred text consists?

Nor does it matter if one replies that, even though the unlearned do not know how to speak Greek or Hebrew, nothing prevents them from understanding from vernacular translations of Scripture what the legitimate sense of the Scriptures is. For before they can judge from vernacular versions concerning the legitimate sense of Scripture, they must first determine which Scriptures are canonical and which apocryphal. But who of sound mind does not see that the unlearned cannot make this distinction?

Suppose they are certain about the authority of the books: how can they be certain of the fidelity of translations? Those translations were made by persons liable to error. How will the unlearned know whether the translators have in fact erred? Many translations of Scripture are daily criticized and condemned as departing from the twofold sense of the sacred text; and it is certain that this is especially the case with even the most learned Protestant translations. Remove the authority of the Church, which, supported by Christ’s promise, gives us both the sacred sources and their faithful translation without any fear of error, and everything will lie open to doubts.

Suppose that the rude and unlearned, apart from the authority of the Church, are certain of the reliability of translations: they will not for that reason attain the legitimate sense of Scripture. To do so, it is necessary to compare testimony with testimony, book with book, and to connect what precedes with what follows—something which the unlearned cannot even attempt.

At this point the further objection is raised: “I grant that it is impossible for every Christian, even one rude and unlearned, to attain the legitimate sense of Scripture by his own powers. But if they are enlightened by the supreme light of the Holy Spirit, if God opens each person’s understanding to comprehend the Scriptures, nothing will prevent them too from understanding the Scriptures.”

But I remember having heard or read somewhere that this is the Protestants’ opinion: that they maintain that the Holy Spirit is present to each of the faithful, whether reading or hearing the Scriptures, in order to suggest to them their legitimate sense, according to Christ’s promise: “The Spirit of truth will teach you all truth.” They also maintain that this is confirmed by the Apostle when he reports this prophecy of Jeremiah: “This is the covenant which I shall make with the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord: I shall give my laws into their minds, and I shall write them upon their hearts; and I shall be their God, and they shall be my people. And no one shall teach his neighbor, nor anyone his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord’; for all shall know me, from the least [Col. 0600] to the greatest.” By these words it seems to be indicated not obscurely that this is the Church’s prerogative: that absolutely all Christians are enlightened by the supreme inspiration of the Holy Spirit so as to understand the law of God and therefore the Scriptures and their genuine meaning …

The answer is: this is not the meaning of these testimonies of Holy Scripture. For the first testimony you have offered concerns the Apostles and the body of the Church; and, if its meaning is extended to individuals, it means that no one can possess knowledge of all truth except through the Holy Spirit. For by no means do all Christians know all truth, as everyday experience itself plainly shows.

With respect to the second testimony adduced from Jeremiah and from the Apostle, it is likewise certain that its meaning is not that each individual Christian will understand the law of God and the hidden sense of the Scriptures without a teacher. For this interpretation is refuted both by evident experience and by other clear passages of Scripture. “Faith,” says the Apostle, “comes by hearing. And how shall they hear without a preacher?” Therefore, only this is to be inferred from the testimony of Jeremiah cited by the Apostle: that this is the prerogative of the New Testament—that the law of God is to be written in the minds and hearts of men by the Holy Spirit in such a way that Christians may be taught this law without great difficulty. That is, God himself, by his grace, instils into the minds and hearts of individuals what they are taught by their teachers.

And certainly, if the meaning of testimonies of this kind, which are found in no small number in the New Testament, were that all individual Christians were to be illuminated by a heavenly inspiration of the Holy Spirit in order to perceive the more hidden sense of Scripture, there would now be no way to restrain the inventions of sects springing up on every side. Calvin would claim divine illumination against Luther, and Luther against Calvin. The Anabaptists would make the same claim, as would all the fanatics whom the world may produce; every fanatic, I say, would maintain that the sense of Scripture on which his sect rests had been divinely infused into him. Thus everything would lie open to fables, errors, and deceits. For can the Holy Spirit—the Spirit, indeed, of truth—contradict himself? He cannot reveal to Luther that Christ is truly present in the Eucharist, and to Zwingli that Christ is in fact absent from the Eucharist. From this conclude that men must absolutely acknowledge a supreme authority which may decide controversies concerning religion as they arise, without fear of error. Otherwise everything will lie open to disputes; nothing but doubt will occur in matters of faith, nor can it be prevented that we should all “be children tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the wickedness of men, by craftiness unto the circumvention of error.”

God, most good and great, meets this difficulty by his ineffable wisdom. For he commanded that the Church be heard and consulted by all; and he promised that the Church would remain to the end of the ages, certainly unstained and incorrupt, and that the gates of hell would never prevail against it.

The necessity of tradition is further proved from the heterodox themselves, who profess to make little account of tradition.

Protestants themselves believe many things and observe many things which we know only by tradition. They believe that baptism administered to infants, administered by infusion, and administered by heretics, is valid; and we too believe this. Yet this is established not by Scripture, but by tradition alone. They sanctify the Lord’s Day in place of the Sabbath; they celebrate several feast days; and in Great Britain this observance of feast days is more frequent. Tradition alone teaches that these things should be done, as St Augustine says.

Moreover, there are many commands in Scripture from whose observance they refrain, yet they do not suppose that they sin in doing so. That these commands are not necessarily to be observed is evident only by tradition. It will suffice to give two examples.

First example. Protestants wholly omit the washing of feet, although Christ commanded it in such terms that, if one considers the literal sense of the words, he seems to institute a sacrament by that rite. For Christ says to Peter: “If I wash thee not, thou shalt have no part with me”; and afterwards: “Ye call me Master and Lord, and ye say well; for so I am. If then I, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet, ye also ought to wash one another’s feet. For I have given you an example, that as I have done to you, so ye also should do.” Who would not understand from these words that a sacrament is instituted, unless the most certain tradition established that they are not to be understood in this way?

Second example. There is the solemn law enacted by the Apostles in the Council of Jerusalem, which commands abstinence from things strangled and from blood; yet we by no means abstain from these, nor do Protestants themselves abstain. It is useful to cite the very words of the council: “It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us, to lay upon you no further burden than [Col. 0601] these necessary things: that ye abstain from things sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from things strangled.” We know only by tradition that this was commanded by the Apostles for a time.

Thus Protestants cannot escape the authority of tradition. Even unwillingly, they are bound to follow it, whatever they may babble to the contrary.

We shall now set forth testimonies of certain Fathers concerning the authority of tradition.

Ignatius, Eusebius says in *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chapter 36, having received the Church of Antioch second after Peter, was conducted through Asia under the most exact guard of soldiers; nevertheless, confirming by his discourses and exhortations the Churches of the several cities which he entered, he especially warned them above all to beware of the corrupt opinions of heretics, which, having then first begun to emerge into the light, were multiplying more abundantly. He exhorted them to cling firmly to the traditions of the Apostles; and, in order that these might be known more certainly by posterity, he judged it necessary to commit them to writing, confirmed by his own testimony.

“For when,” says Irenaeus, book III, *Against Heresies*, chapter 2, “we appeal to that tradition which is from the Apostles and is preserved in the Churches through the successions of presbyters, they oppose tradition, saying that they are wiser not only than the presbyters but even than the Apostles, and that they have discovered the pure truth . . . It follows, therefore, that they agree neither with Scripture nor with Tradition.”

Therefore, in chapter 3: “The tradition of the Apostles, manifested throughout the whole world, is available for all to behold in every Church who wish to see the truth; and we are able to enumerate those whom the Apostles instituted as bishops in the Churches, and their successors down to our own time—men who taught and knew nothing resembling what these persons rave about. For if the Apostles had known hidden mysteries which they taught the perfect separately and secretly from the rest, they would especially have delivered them to those to whom they entrusted the Churches themselves. For they desired those whom they left as successors, handing over to them their own office of teaching, to be altogether perfect and irreproachable in all things; and, if these administered rightly, great benefit would result . . . By pointing out the tradition which the greatest, most ancient, and universally known Church, founded and established at Rome by the two most glorious Apostles Peter and Paul, has from the Apostles, and the faith proclaimed to men which has come down to us through the succession of bishops, we confound all those who, in whatever way—whether through self-pleasing, vain glory, blindness, or evil judgment—assemble otherwise than they ought . . . [lacuna]”

“Since, therefore, there are such demonstrations, one ought no longer to seek the truth from others when it is easy to receive it from the Church. For the Apostles, like a rich man placing money in a treasury, most fully deposited in her all things belonging to the truth, so that everyone who wishes may draw from her the drink of life . . . One ought with the utmost diligence to love the things that belong to the Church and to grasp the tradition of truth. For even if there should be a dispute about some minor question, ought one not to have recourse to the most ancient Churches, in which the Apostles conversed, and receive from them what is certain and clear concerning the present question? But if the Apostles had not even left us Scriptures, ought we not to follow the order of tradition which they handed down to those to whom they entrusted the Churches? Many barbarian peoples who believe in Christ assent to this order: without paper or ink, they have salvation written in their hearts by the Spirit and preserve the ancient tradition.”

Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, book I, says: “Those who preserved the true tradition of the blessed teaching—received from Peter, James, John, and Paul, the holy Apostles, as a son receives from his father—have, by God’s will, come down even to us, to deposit among us those seeds given by their forebears and apostolic in origin. Now he did not reveal to many what was not for many, but to the few whom he knew to be suited to it, who could both receive these things and be formed by them. Mysteries, however, are entrusted as God is entrusted—by word, not by writing . . . Let him who hears secretly hear also from us that what is hidden will be made manifest to him; and that what is covered will be opened to him who can secretly preserve the things handed down, so that truth, and what is hidden from many, may be made manifest to the few.”

Tertullian, *On the Soldier’s Crown*, chapter 3, says: “If no Scripture has determined this, certainly custom has strengthened it; and custom undoubtedly has flowed from tradition. For how can anything be practised unless it has first been handed down? Even under the pretext of tradition, it is said, written authority must be demanded. Let us therefore ask whether tradition should not be received unless it is written. Certainly we shall deny that it should be received, if there are no precedents of other observances which, [Col. 0602] without the written instrument of Scripture, we maintain on the title of tradition alone and, thence, under the protection of custom. Finally, to begin with baptism: when we are about to enter the water . . . But somewhat earlier in the Church, under the hand of the bishop, we solemnly profess that we renounce the devil, his pomp, and his angels. Then we are immersed three times, answering something more than the Lord prescribed in the Gospel. Having come forth, we taste the concord of milk and honey; and from that day we abstain from the daily bath for the whole week. We receive the sacrament of the Eucharist, commanded by the Lord for all, at mealtimes and also in assemblies before daylight, from no hand other than those of the presiding ministers. We make offerings for the dead, on the annual day of their birth. On the Lord’s Day we declare fasting, or worship on bended knees, unlawful. We enjoy the same exemption from Easter Day until Pentecost. We anxiously suffer no part even of our cup or bread to be knocked upon the ground. At every movement and advance, every entrance and departure, in putting on clothes and shoes, at baths, at meals, at lights, in bed, on seats—in every activity that occupies us—we mark our foreheads with the sign of the cross. If you demand from Scripture a law for these and other disciplines of this kind, you will find none. Tradition is put forward to you as their author, custom as their confirmer, and faith as their observer. Either you yourself will perceive, or learn from someone who has perceived, the reason which supports tradition, custom, and faith. Meanwhile, you will believe that there is no small authority to which obedience is due.”

“Therefore one must not appeal to the Scriptures, nor establish the contest in matters in which victory is either nonexistent, uncertain, or equally uncertain. For even if the comparison of the Scriptures did not turn out so as to leave both sides standing, the order of things required that the point now alone to be debated should first be proposed: to whom faith itself belongs; whose the Scriptures are; by whom, through whom, when, and to whom the teaching by which men become Christians was delivered. For wherever the truth of Christian teaching and faith shall appear, there shall be the truth of the Scriptures, their expositions, and all Christian traditions.”

Christ, says *On Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 20, while he lived on earth, himself declared what man was to do, whether openly to the people or privately to his disciples. From these he had chosen twelve especially, destined to be teachers of the nations. Therefore, when one of them had been removed, he commanded the remaining eleven, on departing to the Father after the resurrection, to go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The Apostles immediately . . . having chosen Matthias by lot as the twelfth in Judas’s place . . . and having received the promised power of the Holy Spirit for miracles and speech, first through Judaea, after bearing witness to faith in Jesus Christ and establishing Churches, and then setting out into the world, proclaimed to the nations the same teaching of the same faith. Accordingly, they founded Churches in every city, from which the other Churches thereafter borrowed—and daily borrow—the offshoot of faith and the seeds of doctrine, in order that they too may become Churches. For this reason they too are reckoned apostolic, as offspring of apostolic Churches. Thus the many and great Churches are that one first Church from the Apostles, from which they all descend. Thus all are first and apostolic, while all demonstrate their unity in the one Church, and while they have communion of peace, the name of brotherhood, and the exchange of hospitality—rights governed by no other principle than the one tradition of the same sacrament.

Hence, in chapter 21, we direct our prescription: If the Lord Jesus Christ sent the Apostles to preach, no preachers other than those appointed by Christ are to be received, because no one knows the Father except the Son and him to whom the Son has revealed him . . . But what they preached—that is, what Christ revealed to them—I here prescribe cannot be proved otherwise than through the very Churches founded by the Apostles themselves, whom they instructed both by living voice, as the saying is, and afterwards by letters. If these things are so, it follows that every doctrine which agrees with those apostolic Churches, the mother Churches and original sources of the faith, must be reckoned true, since it undoubtedly holds what the Churches received from the Apostles, the Apostles from Christ, and Christ from God. Every other doctrine, however, must be prejudged false if it savours against the truth of the Churches, the Apostles, Christ, and God. It remains, then, for us to show whether this doctrine of ours is reckoned to belong to the Apostolic tradition, and thereby whether the rest derive from falsehood. We communicate with the Apostolic Churches because no doctrine differs among us; this is the testimony of truth.

St Basil says, *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 27: “Of the doctrines and observances proclaimed in the Church, some we possess from written teaching, while others we have received from the tradition of the Apostles, handed down in mystery—that is, in secret. Both have equal force with respect to piety, and no one disputes this who has even [Col. 0603] slight experience of ecclesiastical usages. For if we attempt to reject unwritten customs as having little force, we shall unknowingly inflict grave injury upon the Gospel; or rather, we shall reduce the very preaching of the faith to a bare name. To mention first what is first and most common: who taught in writing that we should mark with the sign of the cross those who have placed their hope in Christ? What Scripture taught us to pray turned toward the East? Which of the saints left us in writing the words of invocation used when the bread of the Eucharist and the cup of blessing are consecrated? For we are not content with what the Apostle or the Gospel records; rather, before and after, we say other things, as having great force for the mystery, which we received from unwritten tradition. By what writings do we consecrate the water of baptism, the oil of anointing, and, moreover, the person who receives baptism? Is it not by a silent and secret tradition? What written word has taught the anointing with oil itself? Again, whence from Scripture comes the triple immersion of a man? And the remaining acts performed in baptism, such as renouncing Satan and his angels—from what Scripture do we have them? Is it not from this least public and secret tradition? Is it not from the teaching which our Fathers preserved in calm and uncurious silence? They acted well, being learned men who knew that reverence for mysteries is preserved by silence. For since it is unlawful for the uninitiated even to behold these things, how fitting was it that their teaching should be publicly circulated in writing? . . . The Apostles and Fathers who prescribed definite rites at the beginning of the Church preserved the dignity of the mysteries in secrecy and silence. For that which is carried to popular and common ears is not at all a mystery. This is why certain things were handed down without writing: lest knowledge of doctrines, through familiarity, come into contempt among the multitude. Dogma is one thing, proclamation another: dogmas are kept silent, whereas proclamations are published. A kind of silence is also the obscurity employed by Scripture, which makes the meaning of doctrines difficult to understand, and this for the benefit of those engaged with Scripture . . . The day would fail me if I continued to enumerate the mysteries of the Church handed down without writing. I omit the rest: from what writings do we have the profession of faith itself, by which we believe in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit?”

“It is sufficient,” says St Gregory of Nyssa, *Against Eunomius*, “for the demonstration of our argument that we possess a tradition coming down to us from the Fathers, like an inheritance transmitted in succession from the Apostles through the saints.”

“Even if,” says St Jerome, *Against the Luciferians*, chapter 4, “the authority of Scripture were lacking, the consensus of the whole world . . . would have the force of a command. For many other things also, observed in the Churches through tradition, have claimed for themselves the authority of written law: for example, to immerse the head three times in washing; then, on coming forth, to taste a mixture of milk and honey, as a sign of infancy; on the Lord’s Day and throughout the whole Pentecost, neither to worship on bended knee nor to fast; and many other things, not written, which reasonable observance has established for itself.”

St Augustine, book 10 of *Against Julian*, no. 34, says: “What the holy Fathers found in the Church they maintained; what they learned they taught; what they received from their fathers they handed on to their children.”

“The Church maintained a most salutary custom,” *On Baptism*, book I, chapter 7, no. 12, “even in schismatics and heretics: to correct what is wrong, not to repeat what has been given; to heal what has been wounded, not to treat what is sound. I believe this custom comes from Apostolic tradition, like many things which are found neither in their writings nor in the councils of later times, and yet, because they are maintained throughout the universal Church, are believed to have been handed down and commended by the Apostles themselves.” “What the universal Church holds,” book IV, chapter 24, no. 31, “and was instituted not by councils but has always been retained, is most rightly believed to have been handed down by Apostolic authority alone.”

Vincent of Lérins, *Commonitorium* I, chapter 3, says: “In the Catholic Church itself, every care must be taken to hold that which has been believed everywhere, always, and by all. For this is truly and properly Catholic, as the force and meaning of the name itself declares, which embraces almost all things universally. But this will be so only if we follow universality, antiquity, and consensus. We shall follow universality in this way: if we confess that one faith to be true which the Church throughout the whole world confesses; antiquity, if we depart in no respect from those meanings which our holy elders and Fathers are manifestly known to have upheld; and likewise consensus, if, in antiquity itself, we follow the definitions and judgments of all, or at least almost all, priests and teachers alike.” A Christian, chapter 4, if some portion of the Church cuts itself off from universal communion, or if a contagion attempts to defile the whole Church . . . will take care to cling to antiquity, which can no longer be deceived by any fraud of novelty. He will make every effort to prefer, to the rashness or ignorance of a few, any decrees of a universal council universally established in antiquity. He will strive to consult and inquire into the compared judgments of the elders—only those, however, who, though in different times and places, remained masters approved in the communion and faith of the one Catholic Church. Whatever he discovers that not merely one or two, but all together, have openly, frequently, perseveringly held, written, and taught with one and the same consensus, he should understand that he too must believe without any doubt.

“Nothing is to be innovated,” chapter 9, “except what has been handed down.”

“Therefore it has never been lawful, is never lawful, and never will be lawful to proclaim to Catholic Christians anything beyond what they have received; and it has never not been necessary, is never not necessary, and never will not be necessary to anathematize those who proclaim anything beyond what has once been received.”

“But the Church of Christ,” chapter 32, “the diligent and cautious guardian of the dogmas entrusted to her, never changes anything in them, diminishes nothing, adds nothing; she does not cut away necessities, add superfluities, lose what is her own, or usurp what belongs to another. With every effort she studies this one thing: faithfully and wisely handling ancient matters, to refine and polish whatever was formerly shaped and begun; to strengthen and confirm whatever has already been stated clearly and explained; and to preserve whatever has already been confirmed and defined. Finally, what else has she ever accomplished by decrees of councils except that what was formerly believed simply should afterwards be believed more carefully; that what was formerly preached more slowly should afterwards be preached more urgently?” The ancient consensus of the holy Fathers, chapter 39, “must especially be sought out and followed by us with great diligence in the rule of faith . . . But the judgments only of those Fathers are to be compared who, living, teaching, and abiding holily, wisely, and steadfastly in the Catholic faith and communion, deserved either faithfully to die in Christ or happily to be slain for Christ. Yet they must be believed according to this rule: whatever all, or the greater number, have plainly, frequently, and perseveringly established in one and the same sense, as though by some harmonious council of teachers, by receiving, holding, and handing it down, must be regarded as undoubted, certain, and settled. But whatever anyone, however holy and learned, however bishop, confessor, or martyr, has thought apart from all or even against all, is to be set apart among his own private, hidden opinions, from the authority of the common, public, and general judgment.”

Therefore, not everything necessarily proposed to us for belief in God is contained in the canonical books. For many things are not written in them, and we cannot attain the genuine sense of what is written except through tradition. Moreover, the necessity of tradition is evident from Scripture, from all the Fathers of the Church, indeed from the very heretics who profess to despise it.

1. From Scripture, this is proved by the Epistles of Paul: 2 Thessalonians 2:14; 1 Corinthians 11:2; 2 Timothy 2:2; Hebrews 5:11.

2. From the Fathers: St Ignatius, disciple of the Apostle Peter; St Irenaeus, who flourished in the second century; St Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian, Eusebius, St Basil, St Gregory of Nyssa, St Epiphanius, St Jerome, St Augustine, Vincent of Lérins, and others who flourished either in the first five centuries of the Church or thereafter down to our own times. All speak with one voice on this subject. Not one among them failed to acknowledge the necessity of tradition. Before citing certain of their testimonies, some points must be noted.

The authority of tradition is altogether the same as the authority of Scripture: whether the divine word is written or not makes no difference; in each case it is the divine word. This is evident from all the holy Fathers cited above. By this means the unwritten word has reached us—a word taught by the Apostles, who had been instructed by Christ and who appointed bishops in the cities. These in turn taught others who would succeed them, and from them still others were taught and ordained. Thus the deposit of God’s word has been preserved in the Church down to our own times.

But it is said: Who knows with certainty that the word of God was not corrupted while it passed down to us through so many mouths and through the succession of so many ages? The answer is that this could not have happened:

1. Because the Church is guided by the Spirit of God, and it cannot ever err in matters of faith.

2. Because it is wholly contrary to human reason and custom for a doctrine and practice received everywhere throughout the world to be overthrown without anyone noticing or contradicting it. Everyone knows what tumults and contradictions an attempt at novelty is accustomed to excite.

3. Because the experience of every age teaches that, if anyone has ever attempted to introduce a new dogma or new customs into the Church, he was immediately detected, refuted, and condemned, as is evident from the heresies which arose in almost every century.

4. Because whatever has come down from the Apostles to us by tradition has repeatedly been written by the holy Fathers who flourished in each age. Each reports what the Church believes and observes in his own time. Traces, or certain evidences, of this are also found in councils, liturgical books, and other monuments of ecclesiastical antiquity; these books were long ago spread throughout the whole world. A false tradition cannot be put forward as true in matters of customs or dogmas unless all those writings from which true and genuine traditions are drawn are at the same time falsified and corrupted. Anyone who could persuade himself that this was possible would seem, indeed, to be mad. It is therefore certain, and most certain, that whatever the Church now believes, it has believed from the times of the Apostles.

And concerning ecclesiastical observances: whatever is observed throughout the whole Church in such a manner that the beginning of the observance is unknown—for example, the Lenten fast, the sign of the cross, infant baptism, and so forth—has most certainly come down to us from the Apostles by tradition . . . [lacuna]

The Church makes use of tradition in precisely two ways:

1. To determine which books are truly canonical.

2. To possess the legitimate sense of Scripture.

For the Church receives no books into the number of canonical Scriptures except those which it knows by certain tradition to have descended from the Apostles. Nor does it expound Scripture except in the sense always held by the Church.

On the third foundation of faith, namely, the authority of councils and of the holy Fathers in matters of faith.

The Supreme Pontiff preserves the deposit of faith, and the bishops preserve it also. They settle controversies that arise by their judgment, whether alone or in councils. Councils are ordinarily convened either when a controversy concerning faith must be resolved, or when something must be established concerning discipline, where one bishop could not decide the matter with equal success. Councils are general, national, provincial, or diocesan. General councils, also called in Greek *ecumenical*, are assembled from the bishops of the whole Church; national councils, from the bishops of one kingdom or nation; provincial councils, from the bishops of one or several provinces; diocesan councils, from the bishop and clergy of one diocese.

In councils bishops sit: some as judges; others as defenders and guardians of the canons; others sit or stand as experts in divine and ecclesiastical matters, in order to examine and debate the controversies on both sides.

By right, bishops alone sit as judges. Yet there are others to whom the Church has granted the right of voting by ancient custom: for example, the general superiors of religious orders and abbots. Emperors, kings, princes, and envoys or magistrates sent by them sit as defenders and guardians of the canons and of public tranquillity . . . [lacuna] Presbyters sit; deacons and other experts in ecclesiastical matters stand, in order to examine and debate controversies on both sides, so that, after matters have been thoroughly discussed and the opinions of advisers heard, the judges may determine what they judge ought to be [Col. 0606] decided.

The custom of convening councils in the Church is ancient; for it already prevailed from Apostolic times. The Apostles themselves resolved grave questions which had arisen among believers converted from Jews or Gentiles by holding a council at Jerusalem, with these solemn words: “It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us.” The Apostles used these words so that we might understand that the Holy Spirit presides over sacred councils and himself speaks through the Fathers assembled there.

A definition concerning faith by a general council is certain and free from error, because these councils represent the universal Church, to which Christ promised eternal stability in the true faith: “The gates of hell shall not,” etc. The definition of other councils has the same authority if the consent of the whole Church is added. For when the faith of the whole Church is certain—whether the Church is assembled in general councils or, spread over the whole world, gives its consent to particular councils—it makes no difference. It is enough that the faith of the whole Church be certain. For the faith held by the Church spread throughout the world is certainly in accordance with tradition, the unshaken rule of our faith.

To understand this, it must be recalled that the deposit of faith is contained in sacred Scripture and tradition, and that this twofold source is the surest norm of our faith. Therefore, when questions of faith arise, the Church consults Scripture and tradition. If the question concerns the genuine interpretation of Scripture—as almost always happens, for heretics have always abused obscure statements of Scripture to their own and others’ destruction, as the Apostle Peter says—the Church receives the genuine sense of Scripture from tradition. That is, tradition, older than the controversies which arise and extending by continuous succession to Apostolic times, is the one certain means of understanding what sense of Scripture the Church received from the Apostles.

We have already said that only what the Church spread throughout the whole world holds and has always held is considered divine and Apostolic tradition. There are various ways to know certainly whether all Churches agree in a single dogma or practice. First, all bishops of every Church, to whom the deposit of faith has been entrusted, may be summoned, so that each may state the tradition of his Church concerning the controversy which has arisen. This occurs in general councils. But because councils of this kind are not assembled so easily, another way is both more expedient and more common for certainly determining the Church’s tradition. The Supreme Pontiff renders his judgment on the question proposed; the consent of the individual Churches throughout the world is added. Sometimes bishops assembled in provincial or national councils render a judgment; these judgments are referred to Rome and to the other Churches, are confirmed by the Roman Pontiff, and the consent of all the Churches is added. Each Church recognizes in that judgment the faith which it professes. Such consent of the Churches to a matter defined by one particular council is a most certain proof of tradition and has the same authority as a general council.

There are very many examples of heresies proscribed by this multiple procedure: through ecumenical councils, through supreme pontiffs, through bishops, or through particular councils, with the consent of the whole Church added. Indeed, certain councils not ecumenical by convocation have, with the consent of the Church, been regarded as ecumenical. Such was the First Council of Constantinople, in which the heresy of Macedonius was condemned. It is counted second among ecumenical councils, and by convocation was only a national council of the entire East; but, with the consent of the West added, it became ecumenical. Conversely, the Council of Sardica was ecumenical by convocation but not in result, as most theologians maintain, because the consent of the whole Church was not added.

What we have said of faith should be understood also of the discipline and morals of the Church. There are many canons concerning discipline and morals enacted by provincial councils which, because they have been received by the universal Church, possess ecumenical authority and are deservedly called “canons framed by the Holy Spirit and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world.”

We all know that the Church regards as heretics and expels from her bosom those who do not hear her when she defines matters of faith, according to the saying: “If anyone will not hear the Church, let him be,” etc.

It is further asked what weight should be assigned to the opinions of the holy Fathers in matters of faith. To this it is answered that the Church venerates the Fathers as witnesses to tradition, each in his own age. If one of them differs from the others, his opinion in this matter is not to be valued highly. The opinion of all, or of the greater number, who hold the same view is to be valued most highly. Where some holy Fathers think one thing and others another, the Church for the most part defines nothing, because, when tradition on that matter is neither certain nor one, it is not regarded as divine or [Col. 0607] apostolic tradition. Hence among Catholic theologians arises a diversity of opinions concerning matters not pertaining to faith.

But in such matters, which do not pertain to faith, in which the Church has defined nothing and there is no single opinion among theologians, what opinion is to be embraced?

It is answered that one may then, with the Church’s permission, take either side. Each person is bound to embrace the opinion which he judges truer. But a twofold caution must be observed: first, we must be so disposed that we abandon our opinion and wholeheartedly submit ourselves to the Church if the Church should eventually define otherwise than we think; secondly, peace and charity must be maintained with those who think differently from us. For nothing ought to be more important than peace and charity: “In necessary matters let unity be preserved; in doubtful matters, liberty; in all things, charity.”

And Saint Augustine further says concerning matters not pertaining to faith: “For what is proved to be neither contrary to faith nor to good morals is to be held indifferent, and, for the sake of the society of those among whom one lives, is to be observed.”

There are further testimonies which follow.

St Ambrose, Letter 32: “I follow the teaching of the Council of Nicaea, from which neither death nor sword shall be able to separate me.”

St Gregory the Great, Letter 24, Book I, says that he venerates the first four councils as he venerates the four Gospels.

St Jerome, Dialogue against the Luciferians: “How,” he says, “could Athanasius and Hilary act against the Synod of Nicaea, for which they endured exile?”

St Augustine, Letter to Januarius, chapter 1, no. 1, says: “Those things which are not written but are handed down we keep; and because they are observed throughout the whole world, it is understood that they have been commended and established for observance either by the Apostles themselves or by plenary councils, whose authority in the Church is most salutary.”

Cardinal Bellarmine, *Controversies*, vol. II, Book I, chapter 2, maintains the necessity of councils for resolving controversies of faith in these words:

“Although general councils are not absolutely necessary, nevertheless I scarcely doubt that some councils, whether general or particular, are altogether necessary for the good government of the Church. For if scandals must come, as the Lord says, and heresies must exist, as the Apostle says, then surely there must also be in the Church some certain judgment by which scandals may be removed and heresies condemned; otherwise the whole Church would in a short time be torn into parties and perish; for every kingdom divided against itself shall be laid waste. And although the Supreme Pontiff is judge . . . yet in deciding controversies concerning God he ought neither to trust solely to his own judgment nor to await a divine revelation, but to employ the diligence which so great a matter requires, and the ordinary means, and only then await the assistance of the Holy Spirit and divine direction. Moreover, that a council—great or small, one or several, as he himself judges—is an ordinary and therefore necessary means can easily be proved.

“First, from that divine promise: ‘Where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in their midst.’ For the Synod of Chalcedon and other synods understand this passage of councils.

“Secondly, from the action of the Apostles, who, although they could each separately have settled controversies, nevertheless, lest they seem to neglect the ordinary means shown by Christ himself, chose not to decide without a council the controversy concerning legal observances which had arisen at Antioch.

“Thirdly, from the practice of the whole Church and of every age. For this practice has always existed in the Church: councils of bishops were held in order to explain doubtful matters. Even the Roman Pontiffs themselves never condemned any new heresy without a new council, as anyone may discover who chooses to consult either the volumes of councils or ecclesiastical histories. And who would dare deny that what has always been done by all may be called—and truly is—ordinary?

“But let confirmation be added from the Fathers. St Cyprian, Book II, Letter I, to Stephen: ‘We found it necessary,’ he says, ‘when several priests had assembled in one place, to convene and celebrate a council.’ Gelasius says: ‘If,’ in vol. *On the Bonds of Anathema*, ‘the consent of the pontiff preceded, let it be shown by whom and where it was given; whether it was celebrated according to the rule of the Church, whether it proceeded from paternal tradition, whether it was issued according to the custom of the elders, whether it was brought forth after a proper examination. Here, beyond doubt, it must be asked whether it was celebrated by a synodal gathering; which, in the reception of one condemned and the expulsion of one who is Catholic, since the case is new, is most certainly to be done.’ Therefore, although God could by his absolute power preserve the Church without councils, nevertheless, according to his ordinary providence, councils are necessary for the good government of the Church.”

[Col. 0608] Holden, Book I, *On the Analysis of Faith*, chapter 9, says:

“Now that the certainty of Catholic tradition has been established, and especially established in its unity, it remains to investigate by what way and means those things are to be known which are divinely revealed and instituted, and which rest upon this tradition. Since, however, what we seek is something universal or Catholic—namely, universal tradition—it is most evident that it must not be sought in this respect from any particular and individual person. For whatever any individual person, whoever he may be, can declare or announce, cannot have the character of universal tradition under the restricted title of a particular declaration, although perhaps this character may belong to it because the judgment of the one and of the whole body is universally and Catholicly the same. Indeed, even though it is the testimony of a very great number assembled in council, unless it is universal and Catholic, it does not possess the perfect certainty of tradition.

“From these things it clearly follows that the pastors and rulers of Christ’s Church, whatever authority they otherwise possess, are only guardians and witnesses of revealed truths: indeed most faithful and invincible ones, whether teaching and governing their flocks separately throughout the whole world in their several dioceses and parishes, or assembled and agreeing universally under due circumstances and conditions. But no truly Catholic and discerning person should dare maintain that they are creators of the articles of faith. For every article of revealed faith necessarily rests upon the authority of God who reveals; and no Catholic has acknowledged that new revelations are communicated to the Church which establish a dogma of Catholic faith. Therefore, to say that the number of articles of revealed and Catholic faith can be increased is the language either of ignorance or of calumny.

“We presuppose, therefore, as an unquestioned axiom among all Catholics, that Christ alone was the one and only founder and author of revealed truths and divine institutions. Another truth follows this, which St Augustine has in Letter 118 to Januarius: ‘No one dares alter what Christ prescribed.’ Thus, just as the Church cannot hand down, establish, or impose upon the faithful any new divinely revealed or instituted article of Catholic faith, so neither does it lie within the power and authority of the whole Church to alter or change in any degree a truth revealed by Christ or an institution issued by God—under this anathema, I say: ‘Not one iota or one stroke shall pass from the law.’”

It must therefore be established that a general council can most certainly and without any danger of error announce and declare—what others call decreeing and defining—whatever has been directly and expressly divinely revealed or instituted. This is nothing other than that all these bishops together, and each one separately, can testify what is believed or practised in each and all of their provinces as an article of revealed doctrine or as a divinely instituted religious observance . . . Bishops and rulers of the Church judge in a general council as instructors and teachers; the people, however, are bound to learn and obey as disciples.

## General Councils

### General Councils of the Greeks

In the year 325: First General Council of Nicaea, under Pope Sylvester.

In 381: First Council of Constantinople, under Damasus.

In 431: Council of Ephesus, under Celestine I.

In 451: Council of Chalcedon, under Leo I.

In 553: Second Council of Constantinople, under Vigilius.

In 680: Third Council of Constantinople, under Agatho.

In 787: Second Council of Nicaea, under Adrian I.

In 869: Fourth Council of Constantinople, under Adrian II.

I. In the year 325: Nicaea I, the ecumenical council convened by Emperor Constantine, at which Hosius, bishop of Corduba, presided in the name of Sylvester, Roman pontiff. There three hundred and eighteen Fathers proscribed Arius and his impious doctrine; on the other hand, they established the consubstantiality of the divine Word with the eternal Father and settled the question, so long debated in the Church, of the celebration of Easter.

II. In the year 381: the Second Ecumenical Council of Constantinople, convened by Theodosius to confirm the Council of Nicaea, so that St Gregory Nazianzen might be restored to his see at Constantinople and the faith concerning the divinity of the Holy Spirit, attacked by Macedonius, might be established. One hundred and fifty bishops assembled there, and unanimously decreed that the bishop of Constantinople should hold the first place after the Roman Pontiff.

[Col. 0609] III. In the year 431: the Third Ecumenical Council of Ephesus, convened by Theodosius and presided over by the legates of Celestine, Roman pontiff, was a most celebrated council of two hundred bishops. By them Nestorius, who admitted two persons in Christ, was struck with anathema; he denied that the Virgin Mary should be called Mother of God, maintaining that she was only mother of Christ. It began on the twenty-second day of June in 431, and in it the heresy of Pelagius was again proscribed.

IV. In the year 451: the Fourth Ecumenical Council of Chalcedon was celebrated, with six hundred and thirty bishops and four legates of the most holy Father Leo. Emperor Marcian was present with Empress Pulcheria, attended by a great company of senators and magistrates. It began on the eighth day of October and was concluded at the beginning of November after thirteen Acts or sessions. In it the Council of Ephesus held in 449, together with Dioscorus and Eutyches, who confused the natures in Christ or divided the persons, was condemned.

V. In the year 553: Constantinople II, the Fifth Ecumenical Council, convened by Justinian despite Pope Vigilius, the Roman pontiff, who nevertheless afterwards approved it. It was therefore numbered among the ecumenical councils. In it the errors of Origen and also the Three Chapters were condemned.

VI. In the year 680: Constantinople III, the Sixth Ecumenical Council, convened and completed in the following year. In it the five preceding councils were approved; against the Monothelites it was defined that there are two wills in Christ; Pope Honorius also was condemned.

VII. In the year 787: Nicaea II, the Seventh Ecumenical Council, convened jointly by Emperor Constantine, son of Leo and Irene, and by Supreme Pontiff Adrian. It began at Constantinople in 786, but was transferred to Nicaea in 787; [it consisted] of three hundred and fifty [representatives of] churches, who established the veneration of sacred images against the Iconoclasts.

VIII. In the year 869: Constantinople IV, the Eighth Ecumenical Council, convened by Emperor Basil under Pope Adrian II, concerning the schismatic Photius, who was made an exile, and the restoration of St Ignatius, patriarch of Constantinople, to his patriarchal see.

### General Councils of the Latins

In 1122: Lateran I, under Calixtus II.

In 1139: Lateran II, under Innocent II.

In 1179: Lateran III, under Alexander III.

In 1215: Lateran IV, under Innocent III.

In 1245: Lyons I, under Innocent IV.

In 1274: Lyons II, under Gregory X.

In 1311: Vienne, under Clement V.

In 1409: Pisa, under Alexander V.

In 1414: Constance, under John XXIII.

In 1431: Basel, under Eugenius IV.

In 1439: Florence, under Eugenius IV.

In 1512: Lateran V, under Julius [II] and Leo X.

In 1545: Trent, under Paul III, Julius III, and Pius IV.

IX. In the year 1122: Lateran I, the Ninth Ecumenical Council, was assembled while Pope Calixtus was seated, concerning the recovery of the Holy Land from the Saracens.

X. In the year 1139: Lateran II, the Tenth Ecumenical Council, convened by Innocent II against the antipope Peter, son of Leo, and concerning the preservation of ecclesiastical property.

XI. In the year 1179: Lateran III, the Eleventh Ecumenical Council, convened by Pope Alexander III against the Waldensians, Albigensians, and schismatics ordained by the antipope Victor IV.

XII. In the year 1215 Lateran IV, the Twelfth Ecumenical Council, was convened while Supreme Pontiff Innocent III was seated, against the Albigensians; in it Abbot Joachim was condemned. It is the first council in which the word “transubstantiation” is found, though it is read in authors who lived a hundred years earlier. More than one thousand two hundred and eighty-three Fathers were present, among whom six hundred and seventy-three were bishops.

XIII. In the year 1245: Lyons I, the Thirteenth Ecumenical Council, convened by Innocent IV concerning an expedition against the Saracens for recovery of the Holy Land. Moreover, that council attempted to depose Emperor Frederick; yet such power over Christian princes belongs neither to the Supreme Pontiff nor to the Church.

XIV. In the year 1274: Lyons II, the Fourteenth Ecumenical Council, under Gregory X, concerning recovery of the Holy Land; against Greek errors; and for receiving those who wished to return to peace and to the bosom of the Church.

XV. In the year 1311: Vienne, the Fifteenth Ecumenical Council, presided over by Clement V. The kings of France, England, and Aragon attended, as did the patriarchs of Alexandria and Antioch and more than three hundred bishops. [Col. 0610] In it the Order of the Templars was abolished; the heresies of the Fraticelli, Dulcinists, Beghards, and Beguines were condemned; and the recovery of the Holy Land was discussed.

XVI. In the year 1409: Pisa, regarded in France as the Sixteenth Ecumenical Council, because it was convened by the College of Cardinals with all legal forms observed, the see being vacant because two simultaneously elected pontiffs were competing for the Roman See. Both Benedict XIII and Gregory XII were then deposed, and Alexander V was appointed in their place; he approved that council and convoked the subsequent Synod of Constance.

XVII. In the year 1414: the Council of Constance, regarded in France as the Seventeenth Ecumenical Council, because it was convened by John XXIII, the legitimate successor of Alexander V, as an appendix and continuation of the Council of Pisa. In it John XXIII voluntarily abdicated the pontificate in order to quiet the schism, and Martin V was elected in his place; he approved everything done in the council. The heresies of Wyclif and John Hus were proscribed. It began in 1414 and was concluded in 1418.

XVIII. In the year 1429: Basel, begun in the territory of Ticino, afterwards continued at Siena, and then convened at Basel by Eugenius IV. He approved its first sixteen sessions and annulled the others from the twenty-sixth inclusive. The Gallican Church likewise retained for approval the first twenty-six sessions, which concern almost solely the condemnation of the Bohemians; to these the Faculty of Sacred Theology of Paris added the decree concerning the Immaculate Conception of the Virgin Mary from the thirty-sixth session. Eugenius IV transferred that synod to Ferrara, and afterwards to Florence.

XIX. In the year 1439: Florence, begun at Ferrara by Eugenius IV in the year of salvation 1438, to remove the schism between Greeks and Latins. John Palaeologus, emperor of the East, attended with the patriarch of Constantinople. Very many theological doctors of the fifteenth century did not recognize that council as ecumenical; now, however, it is received by all.

XX. In the year 1512: Lateran V, begun under Julius II and concluded under Leo X in 1517, against the Synod of Pisa; concerning recovery of the Holy Land, ecclesiastical discipline, and the abolition of the Pragmatic Sanction. Theologians dispute among themselves concerning the ecumenicity of this council; and ultramontane doctors, such as Bellarmine, allowed freedom to dissent on this matter, because Leo X defended the rights of the Roman Church too vehemently.

XXI. In the year 1545: Trent, regarded by some as the Nineteenth and by others as the Twenty-first Ecumenical Council and the last; begun in 1545 and completed in 1563, against Luther, Zwingli, and Calvin, and concerning reform of ecclesiastical discipline. It was transferred to Bologna in 1547 and only eight months later recalled to Trent. There it was interrupted three times and resumed in its entirety. In France its canons concerning doctrine are finally revered, but those concerning discipline are rejected.

## Faith Put into Practice through the Virtues of Religion and Piety

### On religion

The good to which religion is ordered is the rendering to God of the honour due to him. Honour is owed to someone by reason of excellence; and God possesses singular excellence, inasmuch as he infinitely transcends all things in every respect. Therefore a special honour is owed to him, just as in human affairs we see that different honour is owed to different excellences of persons: one honour to a father, another to a king, and so with the rest.

We render reverence and honour to God not for his own sake, since of himself he is full of glory and nothing can be added to him by a creature, but for our own sake: because, namely, by revering and honouring God our mind is subjected to him, and its perfection consists in this. For everything is perfected by being subjected to its superior . . . . . The human mind, however, needs the guidance of sensible things in order to be united with God, because “the invisible things of God are perceived through the things that have been made.”

Therefore in divine worship it is necessary to employ certain bodily things, so that, as by certain signs, the human mind may be stirred to spiritual acts by which it is united to God. Religion therefore has interior acts as its principal acts and those belonging to religion in themselves; but exterior acts are secondary, and ordered to interior acts.

### On piety

A human being becomes indebted to others in different ways, according to their different excellence and the different benefits received from them. In both respects God holds the highest place, for he is most excellent and is the first principle of our being and governance. The secondary principles of our being and governance are parents and country, from whom and in which we are born and nourished. Therefore, after God, a human being is most indebted to parents and country; and thus, just as it belongs to religion to render worship to God, so in a secondary degree it belongs to piety to render worship to parents and country.

But since God is the principle of being and governance in a far more excellent manner than father or country, piety is another virtue by which worship is rendered to God; and the attributes of creatures are transferred to God by a certain supereminence and causality. Hence, by excellence, the worship of God is called piety, since God is pre-eminently our Father.

## 4.—Faith Put into Practice through Prayer

### On prayer

Prayer is also an external bodily posture by which we signify to God the inward disposition of our soul and heart; this is external adoration. Since we belong to God not only in respect of soul but also in respect of body, we owe him external and bodily worship, which worship is especially rendered through the virtue of prayer.

For those who pray do with the members of their body what is fitting for suppliants: they bend the knee, extend their hands, or even prostrate themselves on the ground, and perform whatever else is visible. Yet their invisible will and the intention of their heart are known to God, nor does he need such signs in order that the human mind may be disclosed to him. But by these means a person more readily stirs himself to pray and groan more humbly and fervently.

Because we are composed of a twofold nature, namely intellectual and sensible . . . . . we offer God a twofold adoration: spiritual adoration, which consists in the inward devotion of the mind—that is, in faith—and bodily humiliation outwardly—that is, in prayer. External adoration or prayer itself is made for the sake of inward adoration: namely, so that through the signs of humility which we display bodily, our affection may be aroused to submit itself to God, since it is natural to us to proceed from sensible things to intelligible things.
