## III.—ON HOPE

**On hope.**—Hope is the gift of God by which we confidently await whatever God has promised us. It is called a gift of God because God gives it, and we cannot have it from ourselves, according to Paul’s saying: “What have you that you did not receive?” It is said to be that by which we confidently await, for our hope rests upon God’s own promises—God, I say, who can neither be deceived nor deceive—and upon Christ’s merits, for he came for this sole purpose, to procure eternal life for us.

Yet this confidence is moderated by a certain fear. For our sins very often hinder us from attaining eternal life, which God has promised us; and no one knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred, or whether he will persevere to the end. It is said, “whatever God has promised us”; under this general designation are understood both eternal life and the means necessary to attain life—namely, the graces and divine aids granted through Christ, which are necessary both for justification and for the perfecting of good works. Even temporal goods are understood under this general designation, since they too are promised and given by God, and contribute to eternal life if one uses them lawfully. Thus it is permissible to desire or ask for them, but only insofar as they contribute to salvation, and not otherwise.

One must hope wholly in God. For whoever hopes in him shall never be put to shame. But cursed is the person who hopes and trusts in anything else—for example, in himself, in any human being, in riches, or in his own authority or that of his own people. One must hope in God alone because God alone is supremely good, great, and powerful. He alone can make us truly blessed. Apart from God, there is nothing but what is fragile, perishable, and deceptive.

Hope is not the same in all Christians. For what we have said of faith may also be said of hope. In some there is living hope, as the apostle Peter calls it: that is, when it is perfected by charity; and then the apostle Paul calls it a firm anchor, which never puts one to shame. There is also imperfect, dead hope, insufficient for salvation: namely, when it is devoid of charity.

**PETER LOMBARD, Master of the *Sentences*.**—Hope is the virtue by which spiritual and eternal goods are hoped for, that is, confidently awaited. For hope is the certain expectation of future blessedness, arising from God’s grace and preceding merits—either merits preceding hope itself, which charity by nature precedes, or merits preceding the thing hoped for, namely eternal blessedness. For to hope for something without merits may be called not hope but presumption.

But it may be asked whether the description of faith applies [also to hope]. Certainly, this may either be granted or denied. If it is said to apply, there are nevertheless many other points in which faith and hope differ; yet it may reasonably be said to belong to faith alone, not to hope, because faith alone is called the foundation—not because faith can be a virtue without hope and charity—CXCII, 887.

And just as faith concerns invisible things, so also does hope. Hence St Augustine: “We call faith [belief] in those things which are not seen.” Concerning hope also it is said: “Hope that is seen is not hope. For what a man sees, why does he hope for it?” With regard to not seeing either what is believed or what is hoped for, faith and hope have this in common. Nevertheless, faith is distinguished from hope both in name and by a rational difference. For faith concerns evil things as well as good, because both good and evil are believed—and this by good, not evil, faith . . . . But hope concerns only good things, only future things, and only things belonging to the person who is said to entertain hope for them, CXCII, 811.

Concerning this virtue, namely theological hope, consult the Fathers cited below.

## IV.—ON CHARITY

### 1.—Charity considered in itself, or love of God

Although, speaking theologically, the terms “love of God” and “charity” signify one thing, we follow the language of the Fathers, distinguish them, and set them forth under two articles.

[Col. 0617] Charity, or the love of God, is the gift of God by which we love God for his own sake above all things, and our neighbour for God’s sake as ourselves.

This is explained as follows: it is a gift of God. For God alone bestows it; no one can possess it from himself. “The charity of God,” says the Apostle, “has been poured forth in our hearts through the Holy Spirit.” And St Augustine says that one who thinks that his goodness is produced not by God but by himself must necessarily love God little.

We say, “by which we love God for his own sake”; that is, we love God without seeking any other reward of love or possessing any other ground of love than God himself.

We continue, “above all things”; that is, we prefer nothing to the love of God—not ourselves and not anything else.

And further, we love our neighbour for God’s sake as ourselves. This is the second part of the commandment of charity, concerning the love owed to ourselves and our neighbour.

Now we love God above all things when we love him in such a way that we are ready to suffer anything whatever rather than sin, so that we prefer the loss of possessions, parents, friends, reputation, and even life itself to any sin whatsoever. And we are bound to this love by the divine command: “He who loves father or mother,” says Christ, “above me is not worthy of me; and he who loves son or daughter above me is not worthy of me.” And elsewhere: “He who loves his life shall lose it; and he who hates his life in this world shall keep it unto eternal life.” The apostle Paul says: “Who shall separate us from the charity of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or persecution, or the sword . . . ? In all these things we overcome through him who loved us. For I am certain that neither death nor life, nor principalities nor powers, nor things present nor things to come, nor strength, nor height nor depth, nor any other creature shall be able to separate us from the charity of God.”

Nor should this commandment be thought new. It is first of all in antiquity, dignity, and necessity. It is grounded in human nature itself. By the law of nature, we are bound to offer supreme worship and honour to God as Creator. “God is not worshipped except by loving,” says St Augustine; that is, God cannot be worshipped with perfect worship except through charity. “God must be worshipped,” he says, “by faith, hope, and charity,” because, as the holy Doctor says elsewhere, the house of God is founded by believing, raised by hoping, and perfected by loving. These statements can have no other meaning than that God is not worshipped except by loving.

This commandment was already known to the Jews. For it is the first and greatest commandment in the Law, whose words are: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength. And these words which I command you today shall be in your heart; and you shall relate them to your children, and meditate on them while sitting in your house and walking on the way, while sleeping and rising. And you shall bind them as a sign upon your hand,” etc.

Christ gave this same commandment to Christians and said that no one can enter life unless he has kept it. “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments. You know the commandments: You shall love . . . and your neighbour as yourself.” And when asked which was the great commandment in the Law, he said: “You shall love the Lord your God . . . . This is the greatest and first commandment.” But what is the meaning of the words, “You shall love the Lord,” etc.? Their meaning is that all the desires of the heart, all free thoughts of the mind, and every act of life must be offered to God—as the pleasure-seeker refers everything to pleasure and the miser everything to riches. God does not wish our heart to be divided into two parts, so that God possesses one part and a creature the other. He claims the whole heart as his due: “No one can serve two masters.”

And what further is the meaning of Moses’ words, “These words shall be . . . and you shall bind them as a sign upon your hand”? Answer: By these words Moses plainly intimates that the Jews, no less than Christians, were commanded to act in all things from an inward disposition of love toward God, and to refer all things to God, even those actions which we daily perform by the natural inclination toward the necessary support of life.

The apostle Paul commands Christians the same thing: “Whether you eat,” he says, “or drink, or do anything else, do all to the glory of God.” Do not suppose, however, that the Apostle said this in the sense that whatever is done without habitual or even actual charity, properly and strictly so called, is thereby truly sin and deserves no praise in the order of salvation. For acts of faith, hope, supernatural fear, and other moral virtues—by which a sinful person, through heavenly grace inspiring and assisting him, [Col. 0618] prepares for himself the way to righteousness—are neither truly sins nor can be called such. Although, in the absence of charity, they do not possess full and perfect worth sufficient for attaining salvation, they nevertheless possess some worth even in the order of salvation, namely from the divine grace through which they are elicited. St Augustine sometimes calls this grace good will and love of what is right.

The commandment of love, being affirmative, does not oblige at every moment and for every moment. Therefore the Apostle’s meaning seems to be that a person should never do anything contrary to charity and the law of God; that he should prefer nothing to God; that his heart should not be divided into two parts, one for God and the other for the creature; and that he should refer all things to God at least indirectly and interpretatively. Whatever good exists in a human being falls back, by its own weight as it were, wholly into God, the source and author of every good. In this sense all theologians after St Thomas affirm that the commandment of the love of God includes something negative and does not oblige always and at every time. St Thomas says: “A person places his whole heart in God in such a way, namely, that he thinks or wills nothing contrary to divine love.”

### 2.—Charity considered with regard to ourselves, or self-love

By the commandment of charity we are bound to love ourselves: “You shall love your neighbour as yourself.” This cannot in any way be fulfilled unless we love ourselves as is fitting. And we ought to love ourselves for God’s sake; that is, the love with which we love ourselves must be referred to God. Now this love is referred to God if we place our happiness in God; if we tend toward God alone, because God alone is the highest good—from whom are all things, in whom are all things, for whose sake are all things, and toward whom are all things. He alone is the supreme happiness of human beings.

But to love oneself is nothing other than to wish to be happy, to tend toward true happiness, and therefore toward God. Thus we do not love ourselves as we ought unless we love God above all things. This is true love of ourselves; the other is evil and forbidden. We love ourselves wrongly when that love tends only to our abounding in bodily pleasures, riches, and honours; when we follow only the concupiscence of the flesh, the concupiscence of the eyes, and the pride of life. Since human nature, corrupted by original sin, tends only toward this, we are bound continually to do violence to ourselves in order to overcome this threefold concupiscence.

Therefore, when Christ commands us to deny ourselves and to die to ourselves, he commands nothing other than that we guard against that disordered self-love. Because this perverse love daily puts down new roots, follows the tendency of corrupted nature, and is especially adapted to prejudices drawn from bad upbringing and from the example and habits of other people, Christ teaches that we must constantly do violence to ourselves, carry the cross daily, take care lest the heat of custom sweep us away, enter through the narrow gate, and walk the confined path which very few indeed follow. Otherwise, we shall never die to ourselves and so attain life.

All this seems arduous and difficult; but the reward is infinite and eternal. Indeed, Christ promised that he himself would greatly lighten the labour: “Come to me, etc.; for my yoke is sweet, etc. . . .” All who sincerely worship God and follow the evangelical commandments daily experience the trustworthiness and truth of the divine promise. Since charity has been poured into their hearts through the Holy Spirit, they experience more sweetness and consolation in bearing the cross than sinners experience in satisfying their desires.

This love by which we love ourselves as we should is also called charity, for it is a part of charity; charity has reference either to God, to ourselves, or to our neighbour.

**INNOCENT III, pope.**—The following authorities set forth the form of charity: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart . . . and your neighbour as yourself . . . etc.” Augustine says: “Whatever we do without charity profits us nothing; we expend foolish and empty effort if we do not possess charity, which is God.” Likewise St Gregory: “The rust of sins is consumed more fully as the heart of the sinner is burned by the fire of charity . . .”

Thus, from these points we should proceed as follows: What person endowed with Ciceronian eloquence, what person furnished with every kind of wisdom, is sufficient to express the praises of charity and to set forth its virtues in every detail? This is charity: it teaches us to flee allurements, to trample pleasures underfoot, to restrain the desires of the flesh, to break unlawful desires, to despise honours, and finally to reject every seduction. “Love is strong as death.” For as death punishes bodily sensation, so charity punishes the inclination of fleshly desire. “Jealousy is hard as hell,” because it compels those whom the desire for eternal things draws inwardly not only to reject pleasant things but also to endure adversities for the sake of obtaining that which they love.

This is the charity that made Abel a martyr and led Abraham out of his country. This preserved Joseph in Egypt. This is the flame that extinguished the flame in the furnace for the three youths. This is charity, the greatest of all good things: nothing alien, harsh, or confused is pleasing to it; it strengthens the other virtues with the protection of its perfection. Whoever is grafted into its root neither loses greenness nor withers away from its fruits, because he does not effectively lose the work of fruitfulness. Isidore says of it: “No reward is weighed out without the love of charity. Though someone believes rightly, yet without charity he cannot attain blessedness, because such is the power of charity that even prophecy and martyrdom are believed to be nothing without it. Charity holds the primacy among all virtues.”

This is the charity which so prevailed over God that it brought him down from the throne of supreme majesty to the weakness of our humanity; it wounded the impassible, bound the unconquerable, drew the immutable, and made the eternal mortal. If charity could do so much in God, how much ought a human being to be able to do in himself? If God endured so much for humankind, what will a human being refuse to endure for God? Be ashamed, O human being, not to submit to charity, which subjected to itself the Creator of the world; do not be ashamed that clay submits to charity, when charity subjected to itself even the potter.

Charity is the origin of all virtues. Charity enlightens the human mind, cleanses the conscience, gladdens the soul, and reveals God. In a soul in which charity dwells, pride does not inflate, envy does not ravage, anger does not vex, avarice does not blind, evil sadness does not scatter, gluttony does not inflame, and lust does not defile. It is always pure, always tranquil, always chaste, always joyful, always peaceful, always kind, always modest; secure in adversities and not elated in prosperity . . . , CCXVII, 761–764.

**JULIANUS POMERIUS.**—Charity is a right will wholly turned away from all earthly and present things, inseparably joined and united to God, kindled by a certain fire of the Holy Spirit—from whom it comes and to whom it is referred—free from every defilement, incapable of corruption, subject to no defect of mutability; exalted above all things loved carnally; most powerful of all affections; eager for divine contemplation; always unconquered in all things; the sum of good actions, the salvation of character, the end of heavenly commands, the death of crimes, the life of virtues, the strength of those who fight, the palm of victories, the soul of holy minds, the cause of good merits, and the reward of the perfect.

It raises those dead in their sins, heals the sick, restores the ruined, inspires hope in the despairing, and dwells in peaceful minds; fruitful in penitents, joyful in those making progress, glorious in those persevering, victorious in martyrs, and active in all the faithful without exception. Faith conceives it, hope runs toward it, the progress of all serves it, and whatever work is good lives from it. Under it obedience grows; through it patience conquers; for its sake religious devotion despises fleshly allurements. Without it no one has pleased God; with it no one could sin, nor will be able to sin. This is true, genuine, perfect charity, which the Apostle calls a more excellent way . . . , LIX, 493–497.

**PETER LOMBARD, Bishop of Paris.**—Charity is the love by which God is loved for his own sake and one’s neighbour for God’s sake, or in God. It has two commandments: one concerning love of God, which is the greatest commandment in the Law; the other concerning love of one’s neighbour, like the first: “You shall love the Lord your God, etc., and your neighbour as yourself.” By one and the same charity we love God and neighbour. Charity is one and the commandments are two, because with the charity by which we love God—that is, for God’s sake—we love our neighbour by that same charity—that is, for God’s sake. The commandments are two because two movements take place in the mind when God and neighbour are loved: the mind is moved to love God and is moved to love neighbour, and much more toward God than toward neighbour.

Let us consequently consider the measure of each love. This rule of love has been divinely established: that you love God for his own sake with your whole heart, and your neighbour as yourself—that is, according to that for which and for whose sake you ought to love yourself. For you must love yourself in the good and for God’s sake; therefore your neighbour must be loved in the good, not in evil, and for God’s sake. By “neighbour” every human being must be understood, since there is no one with whom one should act wickedly.

Therefore, whoever loves people must love them either because they are righteous or in order that they may be righteous; that is, in God or for God’s sake. Thus he must also love himself: in God or for God’s sake, that is, because he is righteous or in order that he may be righteous. For one who loves himself otherwise loves himself unjustly, because he loves himself in order to be unjust; therefore, if he loves himself in order to be evil, he no longer loves himself . . . The measure of love for God is that you devote to him all your thoughts, your entire life, and all your understanding, since you have from him the things that you devote to him. Thus no part of our life should be idle; whatever enters the mind should be carried to that toward which the impulse of love runs . . . CXCII, 812, 814.

### 3.—On charity toward one’s neighbor, considered in itself, or on love of neighbor

Among God’s commandments charity holds the first place. It must therefore be loved and maintained; for, as the Apostle Paul testifies, without its perfection nothing can please God. Hence the Lord Himself, when asked by a certain scribe which was the greatest commandment, replied: “You shall love . . . ,” etc. [lacuna] If anyone should perhaps ask who his neighbor is, let him know that every Christian is rightly called a neighbor, because in baptism we are all sanctified as children of God, so that we may be brothers spiritually in perfect charity. Spiritual generation is nobler than carnal generation. [lacuna]

Therefore, just as the blessedness of God’s kingdom has been preached equally to all, so entrance into the kingdom of God is open equally to every sex, age, and person, according to the worthiness of their merits. There is no distinction there based on what one was in this world—layperson or cleric, rich or poor, younger or older, slave or master—but each shall be crowned with everlasting glory according to the merit of a good work. [lacuna]

By the law of charity we are commanded also to love our neighbor as ourselves. By “neighbor” are understood absolutely all human beings: Christians, heretics, Jews, gentiles, and indeed enemies themselves, whoever they may be. The meaning of the words, “You shall love your neighbor,” etc., is that, by the law of charity, every person is bound to seek and provide, in intention and, so far as possible, in deed, for his neighbor’s salvation no less than for his own. This applies also to temporal goods, but always with due regard for God and salvation; otherwise, what we wish or seek, whether for our neighbor or for ourselves, is not charity but covetousness.

The foundation of this love is charity toward God, since the charity of God consists in our loving God supremely. But we cannot love God supremely without desiring that God be known, loved, and cherished by absolutely everyone; and if we truly desire this, we do all that lies within us to bring it about. If anyone does all in his power that God may be known, loved, worshipped, and adored by all people, that person certainly seeks his neighbors’ salvation and therefore loves his neighbor. Thus the commandment to love one’s neighbor necessarily depends upon and follows from the commandment to love God.

Accordingly, by the law of charity we are bound to desire for our neighbor, no less than for ourselves, salvation and whatever contributes to salvation, directly or indirectly. We are not, however, bound to desire for our neighbor the same means of salvation as for ourselves, unless all circumstances are entirely equal. Since God requires one thing from one person and another from another, and since their duties differ according to their state and condition, we are certainly not bound by the law of charity to desire precisely the same means contributing to salvation for every individual. It is fitting, necessary, and sufficient to desire this one thing for all and each: that God grant to us, and likewise to all others without exception, whatever He knows to be necessary for each person’s salvation, and remove everything else altogether.

Since the condition of human beings is not such that they can help all people in the same way—for God’s providence alone extends to every individual—it is sufficient, according to the modest measure of our strength and resources, if we observe the established and necessary order of charity in these matters. This order of charity is that we should first help those nearer to us, and then others, insofar as human resources permit, always preserving, as is proper, the order of greater or lesser closeness. Thus parents, children, [Col. 0624] brothers, and others joined to us by kinship or affinity must be helped before other people; Christians before unbelievers; pastors and others regarded as standing in a parent’s place before the general body of Christians; subjects before strangers; and so forth. [lacuna] The signs by which it may truly be known whether we love our neighbor are as follows:

1. If we neither wish, do, nor seek any evil for him; indeed, if we desire for him every kind of good, with regard to his condition and duties; and if we help him in all things according to our ability, while preserving the order of charity.

2. If, in accordance with the Apostle’s commandment, we bear one another’s burdens; if we patiently and kindly endure the faults and infirmities of our neighbor, accepting them as far as possible.

3. In a word, if in everything we do for another what is both fair and what we wish to be done in return for ourselves.

4. If we perform toward our neighbor the works of mercy, whether spiritual:

   1. to teach the ignorant and uneducated what pertains to religion;
   2. to correct and rebuke sinners;
   3. to give counsel to those needing counsel;
   4. to console the afflicted;
   5. patiently to bear injuries received and the faults of neighbors;
   6. gladly to pardon and remit offenses;
   7. to pray for the living, the dead, and those who persecute us.

Or corporal works of mercy:

1. to provide food for the hungry and drink for the thirsty;
2. to receive travelers into lodging;
3. to clothe the naked;
4. to visit the sick;
5. to visit and console those in prison;
6. to ransom captives;
7. to bury the dead.

These matters are explained more or less fully in the following material on charity.

AMBROSE (Saint), bishop of Milan.—Tobit incurred an edict forbidding anyone to give burial to any of the children of the captivity who had died. Yet he was not deterred by the prohibition, but rather incited by it, lest fear of death seem to make him abandon the duty of piety. The reward was mercy; the punishment was death. When caught guilty of such an offense, he was scarcely at last able, through a friend, to be restored to his own people, impoverished and exiled after his property had been plundered.

Again he occupied himself with these duties; and, if he had any food, he looked for a stranger with whom to share it. Thus, when weary from the duty of burial, he returned and provisions had been set before him for eating, he sent his son to look for a companion at table. While the guest was being summoned, news was brought of the remains of an unburied body. He left the meal, for he did not consider it pious that he should take food while a lifeless body lay in public.

This was his daily work, and a great work indeed. For if the law commands us to cover the naked who are alive, how much more ought we to cover the dead! If we are accustomed to accompany travelers on a long journey, how much more those departing for that eternal home from which they will not return! Nothing is more excellent than this duty: to give to one who can no longer repay you; to rescue a companion in nature from birds, to rescue him from beasts. [lacuna]

Wearied by so holy a duty, the prophet rested in his chamber; and when a white discharge fell from a sparrow’s nest, he was struck with blindness. He did not complain or groan, nor say, “This is the reward of my labors.” He was more grieved to be deprived of the service he rendered than of the use of his eyes; he regarded blindness not as a punishment but as an impediment, XIV, 760–761.

LACTANTIUS FIRMICUS.—The greatest duty of piety is the burial of strangers and the poor, a duty which ancient philosophers, teachers of virtue and justice, did not address. For they could not perceive it, because they measured all duties by usefulness. In other matters, although they did not hold to the true boundary, still, because they discerned some advantage in them, held as it were by a certain scent of truth, they wandered closer to it. But this matter, because they could see no advantage in it, they abandoned.

Indeed, there were those who regarded burial as superfluous and said that there was no evil in lying unburied and cast aside. Every class rejects their impious wisdom, as do the divine utterances which command burial. Yet they do not dare to say that burial ought not to be performed; rather, they say that if it should not occur, no harm results. Thus in this matter they undertake not so much the office of those who command as of those who console, so that if this should happen to a wise person, he may not think himself miserable for that reason.

We, however, are not saying what a wise person must endure, but what he himself ought to do. We are not now asking whether the whole practice of burial is useful or not; rather, even if it is empty—as they suppose—it must nevertheless be done, if only because it appears good and humane among people. For the disposition is sought and the intention weighed. Therefore we shall not allow the form and handiwork of God to lie as prey for beasts and birds, but shall return to the earth that from which it arose. Even in the case of an unknown person, we shall perform the duty of relatives; in their place, because they are absent, humanity shall succeed. Wherever a human being is lacking, there we shall think our duty demanded.

In what does the principle of justice consist more than in this: that what we provide for our own through affection, we provide for strangers through humanity—which is far more certain and just? When this is done, the service is no longer rendered to a human being, who feels nothing, but to God alone, to whom a righteous work is a most dear sacrifice. [lacuna] VI, 681–682.

The redemption of captives is a great and distinguished service of justice. Cicero himself approves it: “And this generosity,” he says, “is also useful to the commonwealth: to ransom captives from slavery, to enrich those of lesser means. I greatly prefer this custom of generosity to the lavish distribution of gifts. This is the mark of serious and great men.” It is therefore the proper work of the righteous to ransom captives, since among the unrighteous, if any do these things, they are called serious and great. For it is a matter of the highest praise for them to benefit persons from whom no one expected it. One who does good to a relative, neighbor, or friend earns either no praise or certainly no great praise, because he ought to do it; and he is impious and detestable if he fails to do what both nature and relationship require of him. If he does it, he acts not so much to gain glory as to avoid blame. But one who acts for a stranger and unknown person is truly worthy of praise, because humanity alone has moved him to act. Justice is therefore found where there is no bond of necessity compelling one to do good, VI, 679.

It is a great work of justice to protect and defend abandoned or needy orphans and widows. The divine law prescribes this so fully to everyone that all good judges consider it part of their office to cherish them by natural humanity and strive to benefit them. Yet these works are properly ours, who have received the law and the words of God Himself commanding them. Others indeed perceive by nature that it is just to protect those who lack protection, but they do not see why this is so.

God, whose mercy is everlasting, commands that widows and orphans be defended and cared for, lest anyone be held back, by concern and pity for dependents, from accepting death for justice and faith. Rather, such a person may face it without hesitation and courageously, knowing that he leaves his loved ones to God and that protection will never fail them. It is likewise the highest humanity and a great work to undertake the care and support of sick people lacking anyone to attend them. [lacuna] VI, 680.

AUGUSTINE (Saint), bishop of Hippo.—The care of funerals, the condition of burial, and the pomp of obsequies are consolations for the living rather than assistance for the dead. [lacuna] Philosophers have despised concern for burial; and often whole armies, while dying for their earthly country, did not care where they would afterward lie or to what beasts they might become food. [lacuna]

Nevertheless, the bodies of the dead, especially of the righteous and faithful, are not therefore to be despised and cast aside. The Holy Spirit used them as instruments and vessels for every good work. For if a father’s garment, ring, or anything of that kind is so much dearer to descendants according as their affection for their parents is greater, then the bodies themselves must by no means be despised. We wear them much more intimately and closely united to ourselves than any clothing whatever. For these belong not to an ornament or an aid applied externally, but to human nature itself.

Accordingly, the funerals of the righteous of old were cared for with dutiful piety; their obsequies were celebrated and their burial provided. While they were still alive, they gave their children instructions concerning the burial or even the removal of their bodies. Tobit is commended, on the angel’s testimony, as having deserved God’s favor by burying the dead. The Lord Himself, who was to rise on the third day, praises and commends for proclamation the good work of the devout woman who poured costly ointment upon His limbs and did this for His burial. The Gospel also commendably recalls those who took His body down from the cross and carefully and honorably provided for its covering and burial.

But these authorities do not teach that corpses possess any sensation. Rather, they signify that even the bodies of the dead pertain to God’s providence, to whom such offices of piety are pleasing, for the purpose of establishing faith in the resurrection. From this we also beneficially learn how great may be the reward for alms which we give to the living and sentient, if even the careful performance of a duty toward the lifeless limbs of human beings does not go unrewarded before God, XLI, 26–27.

### 4.—On charity put into practice toward one’s neighbor, or on almsgiving

By the name *almsgiving* is understood whatever charity may be exercised toward one’s neighbor. Thus almsgiving is either spiritual or corporal: spiritual if spiritual works are performed, and corporal if corporal works are performed.

Almsgiving follows from the commandment of charity, 1 John . . . III, 14, 17, 18, and from Christ’s saying, Matthew XXV, 41 et seq. If anyone is not terrified by these pronouncements of Christ and not moved to exercise mercy toward the poor, he may deservedly be called hard in heart and almost reprobate.

Almsgiving is more useful to the giver than to the recipient. The gift that you give a poor person is slight and passing; the reward that you receive from God is eternal. To fulfill this commandment, one must give whatever is superfluous after what is necessary has been set aside. Necessity, however, is twofold: necessity of nature and necessity of status. Necessity of nature is what is required for food and clothing; necessity of status is what is required, with all luxury excluded, for the decency appropriate to one’s rank and condition.

Again, the needs of the poor differ. The poor suffer either ordinary need, serious need, or extreme need. Ordinary need is that which all poor people commonly suffer. Serious need is that suffered by a person who, unless a friendly hand is present, comes into danger of life. Extreme need is suffered by those who are in the utmost danger of death.

These points being granted, in order to fulfill the commandment of almsgiving, where the poor suffer only ordinary need, one must give altogether whatever remains after the necessities of one’s status are set aside. Where they suffer serious need, one must prudently take something from what is necessary to one’s status, more or less according to the greater or lesser need of the poor. But where extreme need presses, one must give altogether—if relief cannot otherwise be provided—whatever remains after the necessities of nature have been set aside. Whoever acts otherwise incurs the danger of eternal condemnation. For one sins more or less according to the greater or lesser amount of what is superfluous, and likewise according to the greater or lesser need of the poor. “You did not feed the poor man; you killed him,” says Saint Ambrose.

### 5.—On charity put into practice toward one’s neighbor, or on hospitality

LACTANTIUS FIRMICUS.—Hospitality is the chief virtue of beneficence, as philosophers also say; but they twist it away from true justice and drag it toward advantage. “Hospitality,” says Cicero, “has rightly been praised by Theophrastus. For it seems to me very becoming that the houses of distinguished men should stand open to distinguished guests.” In the same way he erred again as when he said that generosity should be bestowed on suitable persons. For those distinguished and powerful persons can lack nothing: their own wealth both protects and honors them.

But nothing ought to be done by a just man unless it is a benefit. A benefit, however, if repaid, perishes and comes to an end; for we cannot retain intact something whose price has been paid to us. The principle of justice therefore concerns those benefits which remain whole and uncorrupted.

They remain so only if they are bestowed on persons who can in no way be of use in return. But in receiving distinguished guests, Cicero looked to nothing but utility, nor did that clever man conceal what advantage he expected from it. For he says that anyone who does this will, through the favor of princes whom he has bound to himself by the right of hospitality and friendship, become influential among foreigners. [lacuna] How, then, could he defend himself against the charge that such ambitious hospitality was malice?

“You,” the same man adds, “run about through every gate, so that the princes of peoples and cities who arrive may visit your house, and so that through them you may acquire influence among their fellow citizens; and you wish to appear just, humane, and hospitable, though you are pursuing your own advantage.” Behold how openly he testifies that he gives instructions not for true justice, which he does not possess, but for a shadow and image of justice. We must therefore pardon this teacher of shadows and images, and must not demand truth from one who confesses that he does not know it, VI, 678–679.

### 6.—On charity put into practice toward one’s neighbor, or on mercy

“Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy,” and many other Gospel texts might be cited. [lacuna] The Apostle Paul also says: “Be kind to one another, merciful, forgiving one another, as God also in Christ forgave you. [lacuna] Put on, as God’s elect, bowels of mercy, kindness . . . bearing with one another and forgiving one another, if anyone has a complaint against another . . .”

“Man,” says Saint Ambrose, “how broad you are, if you expand the bosom of your mind to the breadth of the heavenly commandments! How broad is the commandment of charity: ‘Love your enemies!’ He surely included all in the affection of charity who did not exclude enemies. [lacuna] It cannot be said to Jews or gentiles that they should be at peace with all. They scarcely love their own people. [Col. 0629] But Christians are not permitted not to love even their enemies. When I say ‘Christian,’ I mean a perfect Christian. Hear the broad commandment: ‘Bless those who persecute you . . . and do not curse.’ The very one who says that the commandment is broad proved it by saying: ‘They indeed slandered me, but I prayed.’”

The various works of mercy toward one’s neighbor are discussed in the references indicated below.

LACTANTIUS FIRMICUS.—One must by every means hold fast to this: that the hope of receiving anything in return must be entirely absent from the duty of mercy. The reward for this work and duty must be expected from God alone. For if you expect it from a human being, it will no longer be humanity but the lending of a benefit at interest. Nor can one seem to have deserved well who does what he does not for another but for himself. Yet the matter comes to the same result: anyone who gives something to another while hoping for no advantage from that person truly gives it to himself, since he will receive his reward from God.

God Himself commanded that whenever we prepare a dinner, we should invite to the meal persons who cannot invite us back or return the favor, so that no action of our life may lack the service of mercy. Yet no one should suppose that fellowship with friends or affection toward neighbors is forbidden him. But God has made known to us what a true and just work is; we ought to live with our neighbors in such a way that we know the former belongs to human beings, the latter to God, VI, 676–677.

VALERIANUS (Saint), bishop of Cimiez.—“Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.” The chief work of mercy is indeed to give a hand to one who has fallen, show the way of salvation to one who errs, visit the sick, and remain close with consolations to those in tribulation. But above all one should expect this: to feed the hungry, clothe the naked, ransom the captive, and lend necessities for a time to one who lacks them. [lacuna] Let no one avoid a lame person; let no one pretend not to have heard a deaf person; let no one withhold his hand from one who is weak. [lacuna]

For our Lord’s concern for the wretched is so great that He counts as done to Himself whatever merciful generosity has bestowed upon the needy. If we consider the fruit of our labor and the mercy of heavenly forgiveness, we receive far more than we give. Behold: for feeding the poor, the kingdom of heaven is promised to us in the Gospels; for giving broken bread, providing shelter, or clothing an unclothed body, the Lord promises us His help when we call upon Him through the prophets. Behold, we give earthly things; He gives heavenly things. Temporal things are offered by us; everlasting things are bestowed by Him, LII, 713–722.

Concerning these aforementioned theological virtues, although they are treated here more abundantly, much has already been said of them, over and over again, in the Index on the Decalogue, under the first commandment; and in the indexes, *On Love of Enemies*, *On Almsgiving*, *On Fraternal Correction*, and others, as the reader will readily observe. But since the subject of these virtues is exceedingly extensive and of the greatest importance, they can never be praised too much; and concerning them one might deservedly say, “Things repeated give pleasure.”

## ON THE FOUR CARDINAL VIRTUES
One goes to the counsel of the ungodly in four ways. Some are dragged there unwillingly; others are drawn by enticement; others are led astray through ignorance; others follow of their own accord. For these, four virtues are necessary, by which, armed, they may resist lest they go into that counsel. Those who are unwilling need fortitude, by which they resist threats, tortures, and losses even unto death. Those drawn by enticement need temperance, which restrains unlawful desires, yields neither to promises nor is softened by flattery. Those who are led astray through ignorance need prudence, which distinguishes the useful from the useless and teaches what ought to be retained and what rejected. Those who follow voluntarily need justice: justice is rectitude of will, which neither loves to sin nor consents to sin. Justice is ordered in this way: rejecting evils and preferring better things to good ones.

For prudence is reason instructed—namely, by grace—to avoid the contagions of injustice for the sake of justice [lacuna]; justice is the perfection of the rational soul. The other virtues, fortitude, temperance, and prudence, serve to acquire or preserve it: they preserve justice lest it be lost or diminished. But once justice is perfect and passes into the heart’s affection, it is the same as those three, because it is strong, prudent, and temperate.

What have this age’s wise men to do with virtues, when they are ignorant of Christ, the power of God? Where, I ask, is true prudence except in Christ’s teaching? Whence comes true justice except from Christ’s mercy? Where is true temperance except in Christ’s life? Where is true fortitude except in Christ’s Passion? Therefore only those imbued with his teaching are to be called prudent; only those are just who have obtained forgiveness of sins from his mercy; only those are temperate who strive to imitate his life; only those are strong who steadfastly hold to the examples of his patience amid adversities. Accordingly, one labors in vain to acquire virtues if one thinks they are to be hoped for from any source other than the Lord of virtues: his teaching is the seedbed of prudence; his mercy, the work of justice; his life, the mirror of temperance; and his death, the emblem of fortitude. —St Bernard, Sermon 73, *On Various Subjects*.

And the same writer continues in the book *On Consideration*: Here too you must observe a most delightful harmony and interweaving of virtues, and how one depends upon another. As you see here, prudence is the mother of fortitude; and any daring not brought forth by prudence is not fortitude but rashness. Prudence likewise sits as a kind of arbiter between pleasures and necessities, marking out their boundaries on each side by fixed limits, assigning and supplying to the latter what is sufficient, and declaring the former, when excessive, to be madness. Thus from both it forms a third virtue, called temperance. Consideration itself judges intemperate both the person who obstinately takes away what is necessary and the one who indulges in what is superfluous. Temperance, therefore, does not consist only in cutting away superfluities; it also consists in admitting necessities [lacuna]. The Apostle seems not merely a supporter but the author of this judgment, since he teaches that provision for our flesh is not to be made “for desire.” In the first words he restrains superfluities, while in the words “for desire” he does not exclude necessities. Thus one does not seem altogether absurd in defining temperance as that which neither precedes necessity nor exceeds it, according to the philosopher’s saying: “Nothing in excess.”

Now, concerning justice, one of the four: is it not clear that the mind is anticipated by consideration, so that it may form itself according to justice? For it must first consider itself, in order to derive from itself the norm of justice: it will neither do to another what it does not wish done to itself, nor deny to another what it wishes done to itself. In these two points, clearly, the whole condition of justice consists. Yet justice is not solitary either. Consider with me now its beautiful connection and coherence with temperance, and likewise that of both with the two higher virtues, prudence and fortitude. For since it is said to be part of justice not to do to another what one does not wish done to oneself, while its perfection is what the Lord says: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do also to them,” neither of these will occur unless the will—from which the whole pattern is drawn—is so ordered that it neither desires anything superfluous nor superstitiously refuses anything necessary. This belongs to temperance. Finally, temperance imposes a measure even upon justice itself, if justice is to be just: “Do not be excessively just,” says the Wise Man, showing thereby that justice which is not restrained by temperance’s moderation is by no means to be approved. Indeed, wisdom itself does not reject this bridle, Paul saying: “Do not think more highly than you ought to think, but think soberly [lacuna].” Therefore, to keep measure is justice, temperance, and fortitude [lacuna]. Thus justice seeks, prudence finds, fortitude vindicates, and temperance possesses.

Fortitude is needed against the temptations of sin, so that we may resist the roaring lion, steadfast in faith, and courageously repel his fiery darts with this very shield. Justice is needed, that we may do good. Prudence is needed, lest we be rejected with the foolish virgins. Finally, temperance is needed, lest, indulging pleasures, we someday hear what that wretched man, when the splendor alike of feasts and garments had ended and he begged for mercy, heard: “Remember, son, that you received your good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now he is comforted here, while you are tormented.”

Let temperance be love keeping itself whole for that which is loved; fortitude, love readily enduring everything for the sake of that which is loved; justice, love serving the beloved alone and therefore ruling rightly; prudence, love wisely choosing between the things by which it is helped and those by which it is hindered [lacuna].

For if God is the highest good of the human being, it surely follows, since to seek the highest good is to live well, that to live well is nothing other than to love God with one’s whole heart, whole soul, and whole mind. From him comes the preservation of that love in him, uncorrupted and whole: this is temperance. That it be broken by no hardships is fortitude. That it serve no other is justice. That it watch in discerning things, lest deception or fraud gradually creep in, is prudence. This is the human being’s one perfection [lacuna].

That saying of the philosophers is true which defines the four virtues as certain fountains of all virtues [lacuna]. Not only philosophers, but our own authorities as well agree that there are four principal virtues. But why four, and what are the particular works of each? [lacuna] Almost no one is ignorant that the number four is consecrated to perfection. For the whole world is found to be bounded by four regions or corners—East and West, North and South—and Adam himself, who is the father of the human race, or the general name *homo* (“human being”), is expressed in four letters. The body, moreover, constructed from four elements, contains in itself the mystery of the number four [lacuna]. The four rivers issuing from the fountain of paradise, the four Gospels, the four wheels of the divine chariot, and the living creatures—their four wings and faces—abundantly commend the dignity of this number. Therefore we must diligently consider how much holiness these virtues, containing so much perfection in their number, confer upon the Christian soul, and how there is no perfection anywhere that is not contained in these virtues. For though temperance makes a person temperate, prudence prudent, justice just, and fortitude strong, I do not know what can be more perfect than one who acts temperately, justly, prudently, and courageously. It is indeed difficult to display the names of the virtues that arise from those four; but when their properties and actions begin to be unfolded, they will become apparent from the distinct dispositions of each. Above all, however, we must know and maintain that these four virtues, and all those arising from them, are gifts of God; and that no one has them, has had them, or will have them except one to whom God, who is the source and proper possession of all virtues, grants them. For all who, at any time and among any people, have lived by faith as believers in God could indeed become temperate and prudent, just and strong, through his gift. But those who, ignorant of God or even blaspheming him, have lived without faith must be believed incapable of receiving or possessing any of these virtues from God. LIX, 501–502.

## The Cardinal Virtues Considered Separately

### On Prudence

Christian prudence, or the moral virtue, is defined by St Augustine: “Love rightly discerning the things by which it is helped toward God from those by which it may be hindered”; or, “Knowledge of the things to be sought or avoided.”

After Aristotle, St Thomas defines it as “right reason concerning things to be done.”

These definitions come to the same thing. Their collective meaning is that prudence is the virtue by which we distinguish the things that lead to God from those that draw us away from God; we flee the latter and wisely choose the former [lacuna]. Hence St Augustine says: “Does not that disposition or movement of the soul by which it understands eternal things, knows that temporal things are lower than they—even within itself—and knows that the higher things ought rather to be desired than the lower, seem to you to be prudence?”

### On Justice

St Augustine gives many definitions of Christian justice: “Justice,” he says, “is the virtue by which each person receives what is his own”; or, what is the same thing, “Justice is a disposition of the soul which, preserving the common advantage, gives each person his due dignity”; or, “It is the ordering of the soul by which we serve no one except the one God; make ourselves equal to no one except the most pure souls; and seek dominion over no one except the beastly and bodily nature”; or, “Justice is love serving God alone, and therefore ruling well over the other things subject to the human being.”

From all these definitions of justice, which come to the same thing, justice may be defined: “The virtue by which the soul gives to God, neighbor, and itself what is due to each.”

Justice may be taken as the aggregate of all Christian virtues; in that sense, “Justice is love of God and neighbor.”

And for this reason, through justice we give what we owe to God, to ourselves, and to our neighbor, when we love God above all things, ourselves for God’s sake, and our neighbor as ourselves; and consequently when we render to every being—whether superior, equal, or inferior—what belongs to it [lacuna].

“Justice,” says St Ambrose, *On Duties*, chapter 28, “is referred to the fellowship of the human race and to community.” How great justice is may be understood from the fact that it is excepted neither by places, persons, nor times, and is preserved even toward enemies. Thus, if a place or a day has been agreed with an enemy for battle, it is considered contrary to justice either to anticipate him in place or in time. If justice therefore has force even in war, how much more must it be kept in peace. Justice alone belongs to every time, born rather for others than for itself; in daily practice and public benefit, it safeguards others’ interests to its own loss. It has no utility of its own, but the highest praise. Justice is the fountain of the other virtues, illuminating the other virtues. Prudence without justice harms; fortitude also, unless justice restrains it, is intolerable insolence, nearer to fury than reason, to domination than liberty [lacuna]. Justice alone embraces all virtues and commends them all [lacuna].

These matters will appear more clearly from the references noted below.

If in this life we strive to fulfill justice, whose proper work is to render to each what belongs to each, let us return ourselves to God, by whom we were made; and let us not permit the things over which we are naturally set to rule us. Let reason rule the vices; let the body be subject to the soul, and the soul to God: then the entire perfection of the human being is fulfilled. And in this way justice makes us participants in itself: we give each thing its due if we subject lower things to better things, and bodily pleasures to virtues. Just as in reasoning we set living things above lifeless things, sentient things above living things, intellectual things above sentient things, and immortal things above mortal things, so in living well let us prefer useful things to pleasurable ones, honorable things to useful ones, holy things to honorable ones, and all perfect things to holy ones. Nevertheless, neither the body will be able to obey the spirit nor appetite reason, unless God—who created both spirit and body—delighted by our thoughts, rests in us and, like the true farmer in his own field, causes our heart to prosper. Thus, whatever faith plants in it and devotion waters, he may bring to the increase of complete maturity; and so, as we voluntarily submit to him, he may subject evil desires to us, so that from our very acts it may appear who is our indweller and whose will is done in us. ### On Fortitude

Christian fortitude, or the cardinal virtue, is defined by St Augustine: “Love readily enduring everything for God’s sake”; or, “That disposition of the soul by which we despise all hardships and losses of things not subject to our power”; or, “Firmness of mind against things that are temporally troublesome.”

From the meaning of these definitions it may be described as the virtue by which nothing—not persecution, not the sword—can separate us from the love of God, but by which we stand ready to suffer everything rather than forsake God’s law and the duties prescribed to us.

From this we come to practice. Why, says Origen, *On Various Heresies*, book VI, do you not have fortitude? Why do you not have confidence and trust in me? Even if death were to rush upon you, ought you not to endure it with the greatest constancy? For fortitude is necessary for everything whatsoever that may happen; for every danger or tribulation, even to the soul’s departure. Likewise, in relation to riches, pleasures, and earthly honors, firmness of mind must be maintained, so that you may neither be exalted, O human being, nor raised into pride; so that you may not despise enemies or scorn the humble, forget the Lord, abandon the Creator, or become ungrateful. If, therefore, fortitude is necessary in need and dangers, in order that you may manfully endure all things with faith, it is much more necessary amid pleasures and luxuries, lest you fall into the devil’s snare.

On fortitude, St Augustine says in *On the Morals of the Church*: Not much need be said. That love, which ought to burn with entire holiness toward God, is called temperate in not desiring these things and strong in losing them. Yet among everything possessed in this life, the body is the human being’s most grievous bond, by God’s most just laws, on account of the ancient sin—a sin than which nothing is more widely proclaimed or more hidden to understand. To prevent this bond from being shaken and afflicted, the soul fears labor and pain; to prevent it from being taken away and destroyed, it fears death. For by force of habit it loves the body, not understanding that, if it uses it well and knowingly, its resurrection and restoration will be subject to its rightful order by divine help and law without any trouble. But when, knowing these things, it has wholly turned itself toward God in this love, it will not merely despise death but will even desire it. Therefore, since fortitude is needed, it must be sought from him who commanded us to be strong; unless he himself makes us strong, we shall not be what he commanded. It must be sought from him who said, “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved,” lest the soul weaken itself by arrogating fortitude to itself.

Thus, says St Ambrose, *On Duties*, chapter 35, no. 176, fortitude is a virtue as though loftier than the rest, yet never unaccompanied; for it does not entrust itself to itself. Otherwise, fortitude without justice is the material of injustice. The stronger it is, the readier it is to oppress the weaker.

David never made war unless provoked. Therefore he had prudence as fortitude’s companion in battle. When he was about to fight in single combat against Goliath, a man of enormous bodily bulk, he refused the arms by which he would have been burdened; for strength relies more on its own arms than on another’s covering. Then, striking from a distance in order to hit more severely, he killed the enemy with a stone’s blow [lacuna]. Afterwards he never undertook war without consulting the Lord. Hence he was victorious in all battles; until extreme old age, ready of hand, he entered upon war against the Titans, mingling as a warrior with fierce battle lines, eager for glory and careless of safety.

But this alone is not distinguished fortitude. We also recognize the glorious fortitude of those “who through faith, by greatness of spirit, shut lions’ mouths, quenched the power of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, became strong from weakness,” who, not equipped with retinues and legions and winning a common victory with many, but by the naked strength of mind gained a singular triumph over the faithless [lacuna].

Therefore, the glory of fortitude does not lie only in bodily strength and arms, but rather in strength of mind; nor is the law of virtue to inflict injury but to repel it. For one who does not, when able, repel injury from a companion is as much at fault as one who inflicts it [lacuna].

And truly, with good reason that is called fortitude when each person conquers himself, restrains anger, is softened or bent by no enticements, is not disturbed by adversities, is not elated by prosperity, and is not carried about, as though by some wind, by the changing variation of circumstances. What could be loftier or more magnificent than to exercise the mind, afflict the flesh, and reduce it to servitude, so that it obeys command and follows counsel, and so that in undertaking labors it vigorously carries out the purpose and will of the mind?

This, therefore, is the first force of fortitude, since fortitude of mind is considered in two kinds. First, that it regard outward bodily things as of the least importance and as superfluities to be despised rather than desired. Second, that it pursue to completion, with noble concentration of mind, the highest things and all matters in which moral goodness is perceived. For what is so noble as to shape your mind so that you neither regard riches, pleasures, or honors as the greatest goods nor devote all your effort to them? Once your mind is disposed in this way, you must judge that moral goodness and beauty are to be preferred; and you must direct your mind to them in such a way that whatever happens by which minds are normally broken—loss of property, diminution of honor, or the slander of unbelievers—you do not feel, as one superior to it. Then the dangers to your very life undertaken for justice’s sake must not move you [lacuna]. Fortitude of mind, then, is neither mediocre nor separate from the other virtues: it wages war with the vices; alone it defends the ornaments of all virtues and preserves judgments; it fights an unremitting battle against every vice, unconquered in labors, strong in dangers, more rigid against pleasures, and hard against enticements, to which it does not know how to lend an ear [lacuna].

All these things are unfolded and discussed in the indicated references [lacuna].

Fortitude of mind must be understood as that which not only remains unmoved when struck by various afflictions, but also does not collapse, dissolved by any enticements of pleasure. Otherwise, if it indeed breaks the assaults of raging evils, withstands whatever calamities strike, persists untiring amid the cruelties of injuries, storms of distressing oppressions, enmities or present losses, and manifold persecutions, yet boasts of its endurance of adversaries, rejoices not in God’s gift by which it is enlightened, but carnally delights in popular favor by which it is praised, and takes greater joy in being praised than in having that for which it is praised—thus preferring human praise to divine gifts—who would doubt that such a disposition of mind cannot be called virtue? If it were virtue, it would also strongly resist such flatteries and would not yield to soft things when, with the Lord’s help, it had overcome hard and harsh things. For love of the world makes some people insuperable amid harsh sufferings; in them, not patience but astonishing hardness is to be observed.

But those whom God’s love makes strong for bearing sufferings are corrupted by no bodily delight and no deceptively pleasing pleasure. For it matters greatly not what we suffer but for what reason we suffer it. Patience is not found in those who bear distressing things with equanimity, but only in those whom justice makes strong to endure them [lacuna].

Therefore, one for whom the Lord is the fortitude of the mind should yield to no carnal desires, acquiesce in no pleasures, and overcome ambition and popular glory. Let not love of money enslave such a person, nor the bitterness of sufferings and losses cast him down. Let God be to that person total praise, perfect glory, pure delight, certain hope, firm security, sound power, and incorruptible health; so that whatever pleases carnal persons in this world may displease that person; whatever appears precious may become cheap; whatever appears splendid may grow sordid in contemplation of future things. Nor should the person permit himself to be conquered by things already overcome through God’s grace. For it seems still more disgraceful that the mind should be conquered by vices it has conquered; and it profits nothing to have overcome some, if it remains subject to some vice it neglected to overcome. For one is not ordinarily considered strong merely because one has shone in undertaking labors and dangers, or has persistently checked and subdued pleasures; rather, that person is to be judged great and exalted, powerful and worthy of the name of fortitude, who has permitted no vice to rebel against or rule over him. Yet let cowardice be absent, lest we despair of being able to do what we can; and let sinful presumption be absent, lest we ascribe to ourselves what we can do through God’s grace. For whether we despair of God’s gift, by which we are made strong, or boast of our own ability, we cannot be fit to resist vices. And fortitude of mind must surely shake off the cowardice of despair just as much as it must oppose boastfulness. LIX, 505.

### On Temperance

Temperance is defined by St Augustine: “Love keeping itself whole and incorrupt for God”; or, “A disposition restraining and checking appetite from those things which are shamefully desired”; or, “A curbing of desire from things that give temporal delight.”

From these definitions, which come to the same thing, temperance may be described as the virtue by which we love none of the things that are sought and enjoyed temporally, but take from them only as much as is sufficient for the necessities of this life and its duties—using them with moderation, not with the affection of one who loves them [lacuna]. By things that are sought and enjoyed temporally are understood riches, pleasures, honors, and whatever desire can seek.

Therefore, as Origen says in Homily VII on Leviticus, the divine word requires the Lord’s priests to be sober in all things, since, approaching God’s altar, they ought to pray for the people and intercede for others’ sins, and since they have no portion in the land, but the Lord himself is their portion [lacuna]. In the sickness of drunkenness body and soul alike are corrupted; the spirit is corrupted together with the flesh. It weakens every limb: it disables the foot, hand, and tongue; darkens the eyes; and forgetfulness veils the mind, so that a person neither knows nor feels that he exists. Drunkenness, therefore, first brings this bodily disgrace. But if we investigate in how many ways the human mind becomes drunk, we shall find drunk even those who think themselves sober. Anger intoxicates the soul; fury makes it more than drunk, if indeed anything can be more than drunkenness. Desire and greed make a human being not merely drunk but mad. Obscene lusts intoxicate the soul; and, conversely, holy desires intoxicate it as well—but with that holy drunkenness of which one of the saints said: “How excellent is the cup that intoxicates [lacuna].” See how many things intoxicate the soul: fear intoxicates it, and vain suspicion; envy and malice, moreover, waste it beyond every drunkenness.

But temperance contains tranquillity of mind, a pursuit of gentleness, the grace of moderation, care for what is honorable, and consideration and pursuit of what is fitting.

Temperance is the companion and intimate of a peaceful mind, fleeing insolence and all foreign excess. It loves sobriety, cherishes honorableness, seeks that which is fitting; temperance cuts off desires.

Yet not only that temperance which is sparing in food is praiseworthy, but also that which concerns lust [lacuna]. Hence Paul teaches temperance even in marriage itself; for one who is unrestrained in marriage is like a certain adulterer, transgressing the apostolic law [lacuna]. “You command us continence [lacuna]. Give what you command, and command what you will [lacuna]. You know concerning this matter the groaning of my heart and the streams of my eyes.” —St Augustine, *On the Morals of the Church*.

Temperance makes one temperate, self-restrained, sparing, sober, moderate, chaste, silent, serious, and modest. If this virtue dwells in the soul, it checks lust, moderates the passions, multiplies holy desires, chastises vicious ones, orders everything confused within us, strengthens what has been ordered, removes evil thoughts, implants holy ones, extinguishes the fire of lustful pleasure, kindles the soul’s lukewarmness with desire for future reward, composes the mind in peaceful tranquillity, and continually defends the whole person from every storm of vices. Temperance brings our intemperance in eating and drinking back to a decent measure, so that we are content with what is set before us; lest we shamelessly ask for what perhaps the person asked does not have, or offend others by what pleases our desire, or make evident the unrestrained appetite of our gluttony. Nor should we judge those who wish to abstain from foods that we ourselves take; nor should we shame those who perhaps take what we ourselves abstain from, and give thanks to God—being certain that it is quite wretched to condemn some persons for partaking of food or drink, or to arrogate holiness to ourselves through abstinence. LIX, 502.

It belongs to temperance that we show reverence to elders, honour equals with brotherly affection, and extend to younger persons the favour of paternal love; that we grant silence to an elder who is speaking, await his command before speaking ourselves, do not raise an excessive voice in conversation, do not allow laughter to burst forth into loud guffaws, neither disparage anyone nor calmly tolerate those who disparage others. For we know that both those who disparage and those who assent to disparagers are corrupted by the disease of vanity: they wish others to appear contemptible in order to commend themselves by comparison with those whom they criticize, and to seem free of the vices which they maliciously reprove in others. Temperance removes this evil. Whoever wishes to serve temperance attends, not to what he may criticize in his brethren, but to that for which he may praise God. Accordingly, it also belongs to temperance that we are not merely temperate in the functions of all our members, but willingly observe everything that makes us moderate and sober. LIX, 503.

THOMAS THE CISTERCIAN and Cardinal JOHN ALGRINUS, CCVI, 117.

## On the Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit

EADMER, monk of Canterbury.—There are seven gifts of the Holy Spirit: namely, fear, piety, knowledge, fortitude, counsel, understanding, and wisdom. Of these gifts, fear is the first and, as it were, the foundation of the others. For the Holy Spirit lays it as a foundation in the field of the mind and places the other gifts upon it in their order, as in a building. First he makes the mind afraid, lest for its sins it be separated from God and tormented with the devil in the punishments of hell. Then, upon this fear, he places piety, when he inspires the mind thus fearful with compassion for itself and makes it devoutly consider how miserable it will be if separated from God and tortured in hell with the devil. Next he places knowledge upon piety, when the mind which thus fears and has compassion on itself seeks how it may be saved, and the Holy Spirit grants it knowledge of this matter. Thereupon he places fortitude upon knowledge, when the fearful mind, compassionate toward itself and now knowing what it ought to do, is made strong by the Holy Spirit’s gift to do what it has learned, through which it trusts that it can be saved. After this he builds counsel upon fortitude, when the mind, now strong to do what it knows through devout fear must be done, has learned by the grace of the Holy Spirit, from its own experience in these matters, what counsel it ought to give others. CLIX, 680.

But these five gifts of the Holy Spirit pertain to the active life; the two which follow—understanding and wisdom—pertain to the contemplative life. Yet the Holy Spirit places them upon the first five, so that the building of his gifts may be wholly completed. For after the Holy Spirit has made the mind fearful and compassionate toward itself, courageously doing what it knows must be done, and counselling others by its own example concerning these things, he kindles that same mind to understand why God commands this or that, and why a person, though doing good to another, ought to demand no reward from him. Once the Holy Spirit inspires the mind with understanding of these matters, he finally adds wisdom also, when what it understands becomes savoury and exceedingly sweet to it, and it follows, solely from love of rectitude, what it understands ought to be followed. Yet the Holy Spirit begins, through the Prophet, to enumerate his gifts from this wisdom, which we have placed last, and descends by enumeration as far as fear, from which we began to ascend. Hence it should be observed that by descending he indicates to us how, by ascending, he constructs in us a building from these same gifts. Therefore, when this building has been so constructed, the Holy Spirit dwells in it and governs and disposes for service the whole household of the inner house—that is, all the faculties of the soul. CLIX, 681.

## On Fear

Fear, when it comes, prepares a place for charity; for while we fear the Judge’s punishments, we avoid faults, the cause of those punishments. But when this is done by fear alone, vices are no longer committed outwardly in deed, yet they have not been driven out inwardly from the mind. And because we abandon evil acts but love them in our mind, the beginning of wisdom is now present, but wisdom itself is still absent. It will come, however, when you do not wish to act wickedly, even though you could do so with impunity. But this heavenly will serves charity. Whoever, through the Holy Spirit’s generosity, is anticipated by fear and preserves that purpose for which fear came first, will at length be enriched with charity, having become wise through the beginning of wisdom; for truly, rightly to love is at last to be wise. Thus fear is deservedly called the beginning of wisdom. Accordingly, as though the seed had been sown, charity—which is wisdom—may spring up. But while charity grows, it diminishes fear; once it is perfected, fear is immediately absent, because, as John testifies, “the one who fears is not perfect in charity.” Therefore you can fear and love at the same time; but while you fear, you cannot be perfect in love. Hence, servant of God, because while you live you fear, while you live you are not perfect. You fear God while you live; therefore you continually say to him: “My heart rejoices that it may fear your name.” In the future you will rejoice without fear; now you rejoice in order to fear, because by charity you enjoy the hope of blessedness in such a way that, through frailty, you fear being deprived of the hoped-for reality. Hence the Apostle says: “Let the one who stands take heed lest he fall.” Charity, kindled by the desire for heaven, draws one toward righteousness; fear, pricked by the horror of hell, draws one back from unrighteousness. Since you are not a good person unless you turn aside from evil and do good, fear and charity rightly accompany one another in you: by the former you overcome the assault of wicked impulses, and by the latter you attain, through zeal, the practice of good arts. Therefore, while you are mortal, you love and fear without ceasing—unless perhaps at last, through God’s revelation, you become certain of your salvation, so that you who formerly chastised your body and reduced it to slavery lest perhaps you should become reprobate may finally know whom you have believed and be certain, saying with the Apostle: “Henceforth there is laid up for me,” etc.

And because you now fear nothing but only love, charity is now perfected in you: “For perfect charity casts out fear.” Therefore, while charity advances through its degrees, fear declines through corresponding degrees in this life, until after death charity, having advanced to its height, no longer permits fear to remain with it. For charity and fear have such a nature that one whom you fear excessively you do not love at all, and one whom you love perfectly you do not fear at all. But once you have loved anyone even in part, you immediately cease to fear him excessively; for charity, when it comes, moderates fear, and as it advances, cuts it away. Accordingly, because he fears, he is not perfect in charity. Christ could not possess this fear, because he excelled in perfection of charity. [lacuna] CLXXXVI, 815–816.

JULIANUS POMERIUS.—Before the mind sins, let it look to the punishment owed to sins; let it set against carnal inducements the tortures and pains which are accustomed to follow the sinner. Then no pleasure of sin will delight it, nor will any bodily delight incline it to sin. For we yield to our enticements and pleasures not because we cannot resist, but because we ourselves promise ourselves security in concealing the crime; and while we believe that what we do can be glossed over or redeemed, enticed by the hope of presumed impunity, we allow our pleasure to exercise dominion over us. But if, at the time when anyone resolves to sin, he should with a sound mind consider what punishment awaits those caught in their crimes and shameful deeds, what penalty tortures those convicted, what trembling shakes their limbs, what pallor spreads over their faces, and finally how greatly it humiliates them and renders them hateful to all, I do not know whether even the disgrace of a shameful reputation itself could permit assent to any vices whatsoever. For what evil deed can be done at which not even those whom their own shameful acts delight blush? Hence those who vainly and disgracefully boast of their good qualities conceal the disgraces by which they are stung and humbled. [lacuna] LIX, 490.
