## On the Evangelical Counsels, and Especially on Chastity, Poverty, and Obedience

The evangelical counsels concern the perfection of the Christian life. Although that perfection consists in the perfection of charity, it is more easily acquired by observance of the evangelical counsels. It is known that the more anyone is estranged from the world’s concupiscence and clings more closely to God, the more perfect he is; and that the more anyone clings to the world and is more estranged from God, the worse he is and the further he is from perfection. For everything pertaining to religion is referred to charity.

Therefore all divine commandments are referred to charity, of which the Apostle says: “The end of the commandment is charity, from a pure heart and a good conscience and unfeigned faith.” Thus the end of every commandment is charity; that is, every commandment is directed to charity. But whatever is done through fear of punishment or some carnal intention, in such a way that it is not directed to that charity which the Holy Spirit pours out in our hearts, is not yet done as it ought to be done, although it may appear to be done. For this charity is love of God and neighbour; and indeed on these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets. Add the Gospel; add also the Apostles. For the saying does not come from elsewhere: “The end of the commandment is charity, and God is charity.” Therefore whatever God commands, one example being, “You shall not commit adultery,” and whatever is not commanded but urged by spiritual counsel, one example being, “It is good for a man not to touch a woman,” are then rightly done when they are directed to loving God and one’s neighbour for God’s sake, both in this age and in the age to come: now God through faith, then through sight; and one’s neighbour now through faith …

But perfection of Christian life and perfect charity are attained through the evangelical counsels. Hence it may be said that the perfection of charity consists principally and essentially in the commandments, and secondarily and instrumentally in the counsels. For love of God and neighbor does not fall under a commandment according to any fixed measure; and this is so because the end of the commandment is charity. Now no measure is applied to an end, but only to things directed toward the end. Thus it is clear that perfection consists essentially in the commandments; but secondarily and instrumentally perfection consists in the counsels, which, like the commandments, are all ordered toward charity, though in different ways. For commandments other than the commandments of charity are ordered toward removing things contrary to charity, with which charity cannot coexist; but the counsels are ordered toward removing obstacles to the act of charity which are nevertheless not contrary to charity, such as [Col. 0647] marriage, involvement in secular affairs [lacuna]. Therefore Abbot Moses says in the *Conferences*: “Fasts, vigils, meditation upon the Scriptures, nakedness, and the deprivation of all possessions are not perfection, but instruments of perfection, because the end of that discipline does not consist in them, but through them the end is reached.”

Therefore the evangelical counsels are certain excellent things which Christ urged Christians to do, but did not command. The difference between counsels and commandments is that commandments are necessary for salvation for everyone; counsels are not, unless perhaps someone has bound himself by a vow to observe the counsels.

The principal evangelical counsels are chastity, poverty, and obedience. Evangelical chastity is the resolve of perpetual virginity or continence; evangelical poverty is the voluntary renunciation of riches, so that we may follow Christ’s footsteps more perfectly; and obedience is the renunciation of one’s own will and the resolve to submit oneself in all things to the will of some superior.

Although these counsels are not necessary for salvation, Christ set them forth as things excellent by their nature, which lead to perfection and make the observance of the commandments easier. That the evangelical counsels are something excellent is evident in itself. Everyone understands that nothing can be done more pleasing to God than the offering, as it were the sacrifice, of one’s body, one’s will, one’s money, and one’s property. This is accomplished through evangelical chastity, obedience, and poverty.

The evangelical counsels lead to perfection. For Christian perfection consists, as we have said, in being free from every sin and cleaving to God alone in perfect charity. But nothing leads us more happily to this disposition of mind than evangelical chastity, obedience, and poverty. For through evangelical chastity we are made free from the lust of the flesh; through evangelical poverty, from the lust of the eyes; and through evangelical obedience, from the pride of life. This threefold lust, the fountain and origin of all sins, is the sole reason why we do not cleave to God as we ought.

Finally, the evangelical counsels make the observance of the commandments easier. All are commanded to serve God alone and not to limp between two sides, so that God possesses one part of the heart and a creature the other. God must be loved with the whole heart. Yet it is far easier to serve God alone for one who leads a celibate life, who has no wife, than for one entangled in marriage.

All are commanded to keep their heart free from riches. Yet this is easier when riches are entirely cast away than when they are retained.

All are commanded to deny themselves, restrain pride, and die to themselves. Yet this is far easier for one who submits in all things to the will of some superior than for one who, left to his own discretion, does what he pleases.

For those who follow the evangelical counsels, three things are altogether necessary; otherwise embracing the evangelical counsels contributes nothing toward salvation:

1. A right end: one must propose to oneself nothing else in one’s heart than to please God and serve His glory.
2. Great humility: one must not therefore think oneself better or more perfect than those who do not embrace the evangelical counsels.
3. Great fidelity in observing the commandments: a commandment must be observed before a counsel; otherwise the observance of a counsel is wholly useless. For it may happen that those who follow the commandments but not the counsels are more perfect than those who have embraced the evangelical counsels, if they are more free from every desire, more united to God through charity, and more solicitous about observing the commandments—those who are their own masters and joined in marriage—than those who profess to follow the evangelical counsels. This does not rarely occur. Then those who follow not the counsels but the evangelical commandments are more perfect than those who, having embraced the evangelical counsels, neglect the commandments. For perfection does not consist in carrying out the evangelical counsels, but in the perfection of charity, which we may attain, though more difficultly, even without the evangelical counsels.

All these matters are explained in the references noted below.

## On Continence

If perhaps anyone thinks it harsh and hard that we speak confidently of a thing almost contrary to nature, let him now cease to be troubled, understanding that this is the greatest glory of Christian virtue: to tread nature itself underfoot. But since virtue always casts pleasures into shadow, and nothing is right for anyone except what he loves, especially when all peoples cultivate it with one desire, there is no doubt that whoever dissuades people from marriage is judged either a public enemy or certainly insane. Yet I shall not fear the envy of public talk that invents tales about me; for I do not condemn marriage, but I set better things before marriage, and this with the Apostle Paul himself urging it: “But I say to the unmarried and to widows: it is good for them if they remain as I am. But if they are not continent, let them marry; for it is better to marry than to burn.” And marriage is better for this reason: because burning is worse.

Finally, if it seems good, let us compare what distinction there is between a virgin and a married woman. The married woman thinks how she may please her husband; the virgin, how she may please God [lacuna], XI, 301–311.

## On the Eight Evangelical Beatitudes

“Blessed are the poor.” Here you have temperance, which abstains from sin, tramples the world underfoot, and does not seek alluring things.

“Blessed are those who hunger [lacuna].” For whoever hungers has compassion on the hungry; through compassion he gives, through giving he becomes righteous, because “his righteousness remains forever.” Therefore we understand hunger and thirst there spiritually: the desire for the food or drink of righteousness. For virtue itself is, as it were, the material of virtues, so that the righteous person may show himself equal to his inferiors, exclude deceit, and seek truth.

“Blessed are you who weep now, etc.” Here you have prudence, whose task is to weep for perishable things and seek those which are eternal, to mourn ages that fight against themselves, to seek the God of peace, who chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, and who destroys the things that are not, so that you may attain the things that are.

“Blessed will you be when they hate you [lacuna].” Here you have fortitude, but not the kind that deserves hatred because of wrongdoing: rather, it suffers persecution because of faith. Thus one comes to the crown of suffering, if one disregards human favor and follows divine favor. Finally, that you may know suffering to be the consummation of fortitude: “Thus,” he says, “their fathers did to the prophets,” because the Jews persecuted the prophets even to bodily death. It is also fortitude to conquer anger, restrain indignation, and thereby fortitude strengthens the soul along with the body and does not permit it to be disturbed by any fear or pain, by which we are often struck down as by perverse interpreters.

Augustine, *Exposition on Luke*, Book V, 62.

[Col. 0653] When the Lord Jesus was preaching in a certain place and healing many sick persons, great crowds gathered to Him. He went up to a higher place and began to teach them, saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth. Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled. Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy. Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God. Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” The Lord promised the blessedness of the kingdom of heaven to those who keep His commandments, and first He speaks of humility, saying:

1. “Blessed are the poor in spirit, etc.” Let us not think that those are blessed whom necessity and want make poor. Rather, those are truly blessed who are humbled in spirit and, although they possess riches, are not lifted up in pride, but glorify God in humility, who always does good to those who hope in Him. For humility is the foundation of every good thing, because theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Through pride and disobedience man lost the kingdom of heaven; therefore through humility and obedience we must gain the kingdom of God.

2. “Blessed are the meek, etc.” God is gentle toward us and grants us all necessary things. He does this so that we may be meek and kind toward our neighbors, and gladly perform always whatever good works we can, as the Lord Himself admonishes elsewhere, saying: “Learn from me, because I am meek, etc.” The meek shall possess the earth—not this corruptible earth, full of the bodies of the dead, which is often oppressed through pride and polluted by bloody wars—but the meek shall possess that earth of which a certain saint says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.” That is the land where angels and the souls of saints dwell, where joy is eternal and happiness without end.

3. “Blessed are those who mourn, etc.” Blessed are those who lament their sins in this world, lest they mourn with the devil in eternal punishments. It is better to repent here for a short time for one’s offenses and rejoice eternally with the saints than to indulge without restraint the brief joys of this world and, after this life, be punished by eternal torments [lacuna].

4. “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, etc.” Not all who hunger and thirst are blessed, but only those are blessed who always hunger for righteousness. We must hunger for righteousness in such a way that we never think ourselves sufficiently righteous, but always beseech God to increase our merits in goodness. For whoever thinks that he has enough righteousness does not hunger for righteousness, but is lifted up in pride and will immediately fall. The humble person, however, will always go from virtue to virtue and always delights in making progress toward what is better.

5. “Blessed are the merciful, etc.” We greatly desire that God forgive us our offenses when we repent. So too we ought to forgive the debts of our neighbors when they ask us, as the Lord Himself said: “Be merciful, as your heavenly Father is merciful.” The merciful shall also obtain mercy, because if we forgive people their sins, our heavenly Father will forgive us our offenses as well.

6. “Blessed are the pure in heart, etc.” Those will be pure in heart who drive every malice, deceit, envy, and lust from their hearts, and cleanse their consciences through charity, chastity, righteousness, and the other holy virtues, so that they may see God in the heavenly kingdom. For God does not wish to dwell in a body polluted by sins; therefore let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and mind, so that God may dwell in our hearts and direct us to every good work. For if we confess our sins, amend ourselves, and do not return to them, God will cleanse us from our sins, fill us with heavenly virtues, and make us worthy of heavenly blessedness with all the saints. But if we conceal them, God will reveal them, whether we wish it or not. And it is better to confess sins to one person than, at that dreadful judgment, to be exposed and put to shame for sins before the three households—of heaven, earth, and the underworld—not for amendment, but for everlasting punishment.

7. “Blessed are the peacemakers, etc.” We ought to pursue peace in such a way that we first make peace between God and ourselves, following what He has commanded and fleeing the evils hateful to God. Then we ought to make peace among any of our neighbors whom we see in discord with one another. Through peace we shall be called children of God. Great is God’s goodness and ineffable the Creator’s mercy: we are not worthy even to be God’s servants, and yet we are called children. Let us therefore strive to deserve through good works to be worthy of so great an inheritance [Col. 0654] and not separate ourselves from so loving a Father, who has deigned to number us among the lot of His children.

8. “Blessed are those who suffer persecution, etc.” Christ, the Son of God, endured scourges and reproaches for us and finally underwent death itself for us. Therefore we too must patiently endure every adversity for His name, because through many tribulations we shall enter the kingdom of God, if we endure them for righteousness’ sake. Thus blessedness has been prepared for us in heaven; let us prepare ourselves for it by good works, and let us run toward it with all our desire. All the angels and saints in heaven await us and rejoice that we are willing to come to them. Let us therefore praise God’s mercy, give Him thanks in all things, and always beseech Him that He who deigned to redeem us may Himself cleanse us from all sins and make us sharers in His kingdom with all the saints [lacuna]. Boniface of Mainz, LXXXIX, 850–852.

## On Repentance

Yet let no one lose heart or despair of himself if, overcome by greed, driven by lust, deceived by error, or compelled by force, he has fallen into the way of injustice. For he can be brought back and freed, if he repents of his deeds and, turning to better things, makes satisfaction to God. Cicero did not think this possible, for he says: “If it were permitted to those who had gone astray on a journey to correct their error by repenting, just as they correct the error of having followed a wrong road, the amendment of rashness would be easier.” But it is indeed permitted. For if, when we see our children repent of their offenses, we judge them to have reformed, and though disowned and cast out, nevertheless receive them back, cherish and embrace them, why should we despair that the mercy of God the Father may be appeased by repentance? Therefore the same Lord and most merciful Father promises that He will forgive sins to those who repent, and blot out all the iniquities of one who has begun anew to practice righteousness. For just as the uprightness of one’s former life benefits nothing to a person living wickedly, because subsequent wickedness has erased works of righteousness, so old sins harm nothing to a reformed person, because subsequent righteousness has obliterated the stain of the former life.

For one who repents of his deed recognizes his former error; therefore the Greeks call it more aptly and expressively *metanoia* (μετάνοια), which we Latins may call *resipiscentia*, “coming to one’s senses.” For one comes to his senses and recovers his mind from madness when he is sorry for his error; he corrects himself for his folly and strengthens his mind to live more rightly. Then he takes the greatest care not to be led again into the same snares. Even dumb animals, when caught by deceit, if they manage somehow to escape in flight, afterward become more cautious and always avoid all those things in which they have perceived tricks and snares. Thus repentance makes a person cautious and diligent in avoiding the sins into which he has once fallen through deceit.

For no one can be so prudent or so watchful that he does not sometimes fall. Therefore God, knowing our weakness, in His mercy opened for humankind a harbor of salvation, so that the remedy of repentance might meet this necessity to which our frailty is subject. Therefore whoever has strayed, let him turn back, recover himself as soon as possible, and be reformed. —VI, 722–723.

## On Patience

Although the blessed life is sought through diverse virtues, all are nevertheless, by one and the same agreement, brought as it were into a certain harbor of patience. Without it nothing can be heard, understood, said, or taught [lacuna]. For patience is always mature, humble, cautious, wise, provident, content with every necessity, tranquil amid every storm of disturbances. It does not know how to let its serenity be clouded by storms; it knows no repentance; it is ignorant of what wrangling is; it either avoids or endures every injury. It is uncertain whether it should be judged incapable of suffering, since, after it has suffered something, it is found as though it had suffered nothing. Finally, it is impossible to assess the virtue whose victory may be conquered.

No force dislodges it from its place: not labor, hunger, nakedness, persecution, fear, danger, death, torments more grievous than death itself, power, ambition, or prosperity. It remains always immovable, firmly poised by a certain lofty and divine self-control, restraining all disturbances of the soul with tranquil moderation; and, lest it conquer all things too greatly, it first conquers itself [lacuna]. —XI, 311–314.

Jacob, through patience, gained both his brother and his blessing; he gives way to wrath, confident that he may return home; he commends himself to his father, and departs slowly and gently, in order to show that he both deserved, and had not coveted, what he had gained. And lest anyone should obscure this patience by calling it timidity, the same character appears also in his taking of wives. He gladly receives the condition, observes the long periods of time, and willingly endures all his father-in-law’s commands. Had he been impatient, and outwitted by guile, he would afterwards have served for Rachel at a time which could never be recovered. Joseph is likewise found patient: patient when he is carried off from the pasture by his brothers; patient when he is lowered into the pit; patient when he is sold under the harsh spear; patient in prison; more patient in the kingdom; most patient when he recognizes his longed-for brothers; and, though boastfulness cannot restrain itself, he restrained himself when placed in honour. This assuredly is heavenly patience, which neither misery, nor prosperity, nor affection could move from its station. — XI, 315.

Against Job the devil—who cannot be supposed to assess matters gently—may be judged capable, once provoked, of every possible design, especially when he had received from God the power to test an ancient cruelty against a righteous man, employing whatever weapons and strength he could. Thus a new and almost incredible battle is undertaken. The devil fights beyond his usual manner; but Job fights more powerfully by disregarding him. The former destroys in a single moment his great and exceedingly rich estate; and, by a most terrible blow, hastily buries beneath the ruin of collapsing roofs the flourishing company of his dear children, with excessive cruelty, before he has slain them. Finally, he clothes the man himself, whom he had stripped of great riches, with great sores; and moreover introduces devouring worms into them, so that, in the torments of the dying man, the accidental wound joined to the human body might be completed by an indwelling wound. But Job, having overthrown with calm expectation all the forces of the adverse party, was exceedingly strong in himself; and, when all that war had destroyed was restored to him in a better form, he did not, through his disregard, lose the condition of his former prosperity, but transformed it.

Here I do not dare compare him with the patience of the Lord, lest God, reckoned among human beings, should suffer some injury; for praise is not fitting when comparison removes pre-eminence. … — XI, 316–317.

But, O Patience, queen of all things, how I wish, if I could, to celebrate you more worthily in conduct! For I know that you rest more willingly in your own practices, your own foundations, and your own counsels than in the bare words of others; and that you place not so great a glory in multiplying virtues as in bringing them to completion. You preserve virginity, so that its flower may not fade through any sickness or any time. You are the most faithful harbour of widowhood, set amid the frequent storms of changing tempests. You guide those who submit their untrained necks to the most holy yoke of marriage, harmonizing them, like a skilled charioteer, with gentle reins into equal exertion of labour or love. You taught friendship to will and not to will the same things. You, the sole and strongest consolation of slavery, often bring forth freedom. You ensure that poverty, when it bears everything, possesses everything by being content with itself. You raised up the prophets; you bound the apostles to Christ. You are both the daily mother and the crown of martyrs. You are the wall of faith, the fruit of hope, the friend of charity. You especially gather the whole people and the divine virtues, like flowing hair, into the knot of one head, into honour and beauty. Happy, and eternally happy, is the person who has always possessed you within. — XI, 317–318.

Cicero says: “If anyone wishes to unfold a compact conception of the mind, let him now teach himself that a good man is one who benefits those whom he can, unless provoked by injury.” O how that philosopher corrupted a simple and true proposition by the addition of two words! For what need was there to add “unless provoked by injury”? Was it so that he might attach vice to the good man as a most shameful tail, and deprive him of patience, the greatest of all virtues? He said that a good man would do harm if provoked; yet by that very fact he must lose the name of good man if he does harm. For it is no less evil to return an injury than to inflict one.

For whence do conflicts, battles, and disputes arise among human beings, except because impatience, set against wickedness, often raises great storms? But if you set patience—than which no virtue is truer or more worthy of a human being—against wickedness, it will immediately be extinguished, as when water is poured upon fire. But if that provoking wickedness has found impatience as its equal, then, as though oil had been poured over it, it will kindle so great a conflagration that not a river but an outpouring of blood will extinguish it. Great, therefore, is the principle of patience which the wise man took away from the good man. For it alone ensures that no evils are done; if it were granted to all, there would be no crime and no fraud in human affairs. What, then, could be more disastrous or more contrary to the good man than to let loose the reins of anger, which strips him not only of the title of good but even of that of human being? For to harm another is not in accordance with human nature. …

For even cattle, if you provoke them, resist either with hoof or horn; and serpents and wild beasts cause no trouble unless you pursue them in order to kill them; and ignorant and foolish people, when they suffer injury, are driven by blind and irrational fury and try to return the like to those who harm them. In what, then, does the wise and good man differ from evil and foolish persons, except that he possesses the unconquered patience which fools lack, and knows how to govern himself and moderate his anger, whereas they, lacking virtue, cannot restrain it? …

Thus by two words he took from the good and wise man the two greatest virtues, innocence and patience. But because he practiced a dog-like eloquence, he also wished a human being to live in a dog-like manner, so as to bite back when provoked. How destructive such repayment of insult is, and what slaughter it commonly produces, from what source could a more suitable example be sought than from the most grievous fate of that teacher himself? While he eagerly wished to obey these precepts of the philosophers, he destroyed himself. If, when provoked by injury, he had maintained patience; if he had learned that it belongs to a good man to overlook and bear an insult, impatience, frivolity, and madness would not have poured forth those famous speeches written under another’s title; he would never have stained with his own blood the rostra in which he had once flourished; nor would that proscription have utterly destroyed the commonwealth.

Therefore it is not the part of the wise and good man to wish to contend or expose himself to danger, since victory is not in our power and every contest is uncertain. Rather, it is the part of the wise and excellent man not to wish to remove his adversary—which cannot be done without crime and danger—but to remove the contest itself, which can be done both beneficially and justly. Patience, therefore, must be held the highest virtue. …

Since it is impossible and useless to struggle against nature so that people are never stirred at all, nevertheless, before that agitation bursts forth to cause harm—which can be prevented—it should be put to sleep more promptly. God commanded that the sun should not go down upon our anger, lest it depart as witness of our fury. … — VI, 700–703.

## On Humility

The men of Greece who wish to appear wise, more curious than all others, raised their hearts beyond what is lawful by arrogant arguments, in an idle occupation. When they ascend to heaven in words, persuade God that He is what they wish Him to be, pretend to know the secrets of the nature of things, and impose names upon the stars and labours upon the sun, … they thus destroyed both themselves and others. …

David, humble, rejected, and obscure, lay low in his father’s house, continually tending sheep, almost like a stranger, innocent and counted among the innocent. He pleased God; he was anointed king and inspired as a prophet. Yet, though exalted in the kingdom, he overawes no one with prophetic terror; he does not prosecute his wrongs by royal power; he loves those who hate him, spares his enemies, forgives his parricidal sons; and his persecutor—indeed, more than that, a king repeatedly delivered by God into his hands—he always prefers to fear rather than kill, wishing, by a reversed but grateful service, to please God by retaining God’s gift. A gentle king, a loving father, a modest prophet: he can do everything, disregards everything; he is not changed by the great and wonderful things of the age, and everywhere retains the mild and humble shepherd. …

The Pharisee and the tax collector stand in God’s temple. The Pharisee foolishly stretches toward heaven hands that are often agents of slaughter and plunder; he shamelessly raises eyes whose seduction makes the world unhappy. His tongue thunders, though it is never without a serpent’s venom; and, what is greater madness than all else, he praises himself before God. But the tax collector beseeches God not merely with individual members but wholly, because wholly humble in fear; confessing his sins, frequently striking his breast, in some fashion modestly chastising his own heart with his hand; and seeking forgiveness of sins by silence alone, not by speech. Hear what each obtained: he who had promised everything to himself departed empty; he who presumed nothing departed from the temple justified. — XI, 321–322.

EADMER, monk of Canterbury. — Humility is a great mountain, upon whose summit is no small light and a most beautiful multitude of honourable persons, that is, holy virtues. But whoever desires to reach it must necessarily ascend by certain steps, if he wishes to know and inhabit this mountain. (There follows an account and explanation of the seven degrees of humility.) CLIX, 665–669.

BERNARD (Saint), abbot of Clairvaux. — Humility is the virtue by which a person, through the truest knowledge of himself, becomes contemptible in his own eyes. This belongs to those who, having set ascents in their heart, advance from virtue to virtue—that is, from degree to degree—until they reach the summit of humility, where, as though placed in Zion, that is, in contemplation, they behold the truth. … CLXXXII, 942 (followed by the twelve degrees of humility, CLXXXII, 942–957), and 599–600.

## On Liberality

JULIAN POMERIUS. — Liberality proceeds from the fountain of justice and overflows even toward those who seem to lack nothing. … There are many works of beneficence by which the needs of those who suffer are compassionately relieved and, from earthly wealth, the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom is obtained—provided that the work of beneficence is done without any display, and that a shameful love of popular glory does not impel us to exercise mercy. Some have been found who assist the diverse needs of diverse people, but are moved either by the desire to acquire a reputation, by carnal affection, by hope of receiving what they give, or by the obligation to repay what they have received.

There are others whom sheer cunning greed alone moves to give something to the poor: they distribute things for the purpose of receiving greater things here. Whatever is entrusted to them for distribution as though they were shepherds of the poor, while those whom they undertake to support are hungry, they spend all or almost all that they have received upon their own pleasures; and, what is worse, they shamefully desire to be regarded among the generous and merciful, or even to be praised above them. Far different from all these and such like are those who desire God, not themselves, to be praised in their works; whom hope for future reward has brought to good work; and who wish Him alone to be witness of their work, from whom they believe, with the full firmness of faith, that they will receive their recompense. LIX, 506–507.

# CLVI. INDEX OF PRIESTLY VIRTUES, SYSTEMATICALLY RELATING ALL THE OBLIGATIONS, DUTIES, OR FUNCTIONS OF GOD’S MINISTERS DISCUSSED BY THE HOLY FATHERS

Since we have already treated, in the **Index on the Priesthood**, the dignity of priests, the virtues appropriate to a priest, the vices he must avoid, and also his offices and knowledge, that Index is mentioned here only, lest repetition prove wearisome. Let the kindly reader consult Index LXXXIV in the preceding volume, and there he will find what he seeks.

[Col. 0673]

# CLVII. INDEX ON THE CONTINENCE OF CLERICS AND MONKS, AND ON PRIESTLY CELIBACY, PRESENTING THE TEACHING AND TRADITION OF THE HOLY FATHERS CONCERNING THIS LAW IN THE CATHOLIC CHURCH

## Notice

The Index which we publish today on the celibacy of God’s ministers will surely, it seems, benefit all who wish to have this most serious question resolved for them. But it will be particularly useful:

I. To those who wish to learn how rash, how unjust, how wicked—in a word, how incontinent—was the attack made by Luther and other heretics of the same stamp upon this venerable law of the Church, always and everywhere plainly visible to all.

II. To all—both professors and sacred orators, and perhaps advocates as well (as occurred quite recently)—for whom law and duty will require the production of the Fathers’ testimonies on the present subject.

III. Finally, to all those holy priests who, if the carnal enemy makes an assault, will gain a glorious victory when, amid the struggle, they hear the voice of Mother Church.

We have established two parts:

I. On continence.

II. On celibacy.

[INDEX ON THE CONTINENCE OF CLERICS AND MONKS.]

## PART ONE. ON CONTINENCE IN GENERAL

[Col. 0673]

(Years 160–245.) TERTULLIAN, presbyter of Carthage, I, 1285: “Continence has been shown to us by the Lord of salvation as an instrument of eternity, as a testimony of faith, as a recommendation of the flesh” (and other passages).—I, 1286: “The altar of God ought to be kept clean.”—I, 1316: “Since we are the temple of God, into which the Holy Spirit has been brought and consecrated, modesty is the custodian and high priest of that temple.” [Col. 0674]—I, 1325: “Where God is, there is modesty.”—I, 1332: “For Christian modesty it is not enough to exist; it must also be visible. For its fullness ought to be so great that it flows from the mind into one’s bearing and bursts forth from the conscience onto the surface.”—II, 903: “Virginity rests upon grace, but continence upon virtue.”—II, 922: “We shall be foolish if we suppose that what is not permitted to priests is permitted to laypeople. Are not we laypeople also priests?”—II, 925: “Let us renounce carnal things, so that at some time we may consider spiritual things.”—926: “We ought to enter into the discipline of the Lord as is fitting, not according to the heated desires of the flesh.”—980: “Modesty is the flower of morals, [Col. 0675] the honor of bodies, the adornment of the sexes, the integrity of blood, the fidelity of lineage, the foundation of holiness.”

(Year 258.) ST. CYPRIAN, bishop of Carthage and martyr, IV, 599: “Everything which is in the world is the lust of the flesh. The world will pass away, and its lust.”

(Years 308–328.) LACTANTIUS, VI, 716: In human beings there is found a desire greater and more vehement than in other animals, because God gave virtue to humankind alone, so that there might be praise and glory in restraining pleasures and in self-denial.

(Year 333.) ST. SYLVESTER, pope, VIII, 835: We direct that none of the subdeacons proceed to marriage, lest he presume by some transgression.

(Years 340–397.) ST. AMBROSE, bishop of Milan, XVI, 257: He says that those who have turned their own hands against themselves are to be condemned, showing that this is neither useful, since it does not in the least remove the desire of the mind, nor honorable, since the occasion for struggle is not sought in the thing itself. Only those who have conquered themselves through continence are to be commended. But no one is to be compelled to this, since neither the Apostle nor Christ himself imposed the law of continence upon anyone by command.

(Appendix to the fourth century.) ANONYMOUS AUTHOR, whose works appeared under the name of St. Athanasius, XVIII, 77: Beyond the testimonies of Scripture, we are also taught by the practice of the Church how great a blessedness holy virginity possesses in heaven.—Ibid.: It is a great and immortal thing, and almost beyond bodily nature, to put luxury to sleep, to extinguish by strength of mind the flame of desire kindled by the torches of youth, and by spiritual effort to exclude the force of natural pleasure. (Many other passages.)

(Years 358–420.) ST. JEROME, presbyter of Stridon, XXII, 258: “Let chastity be your armor when you go to battle.”—243: “Clerics devoted to licentiousness opened their mouths against him and despised him.”—876: During Lent the sails of continence must be spread, and all the reins of the charioteer must be loosened for the hurrying horses; although the condition of secular persons differs from that of virgins and monks.—XXIII, 228: Nature makes some eunuchs, and human violence makes others. I approve those eunuchs whom not necessity but will has castrated. I gladly receive into my bosom those who have castrated themselves for the kingdoms of heaven and, for the sake of worshipping me, refused to remain what they were born. (And many other passages.)

(Years 387–430.) ST. AUGUSTINE, bishop of Hippo, XXXVIII, 736: But you who have already vowed continence, discipline your body more strictly, and do not allow the reins of desire to be loosened even for things themselves permitted; so that you may turn away not only from unlawful intercourse, but may also despise even a lawful look. Remember that, whatever your sex, whether male or female, you lead the life of angels upon earth.—1052: I think it is no great matter for virginity to be preserved throughout the entire Paschal solemnity.—XL, 380: Marriage is good, but it is to be sought only for the sake of something else. The saints ought to have used marriage in the earliest times; now continence is to be preferred. At col. 349 and following is found one book *On Continence*, followed by treatises *On Holy Virginity* and *On the Good of Widowhood*. XLIV, 742: Married persons make good use of that which continent persons make better use of by not using. Therefore, the thing of which married persons make good use, and which is present in married persons for them to use well, is also present in continent persons for them to use better by not using it.

(Years 450–460.) ST. SALVIAN, presbyter of Marseilles, LIII, 197: It remains to say something about ministers and priests, although perhaps some things said may be superfluous. For whatever has been said about all others undoubtedly applies still more to those who ought to be an example to all.—198: In the Gospel the Savior himself enjoins upon presbyters not a voluntary but an imperative duty of perfection, unlike that imposed upon others. (And other passages.)

(Years 447–461.) WORKS ATTRIBUTED TO ST. LEO THE GREAT, LV, 129: God, the gracious indweller of chaste bodies.

(Years 447–461.) APPENDIX TO THE WORKS OF ST. LEO THE GREAT, *Code of Canons*, LVI, 389: If anyone in sound health mutilates himself, he ought to cease, even if he is in the clergy; and henceforth no such person ought to be ordained.—426: Clerics or continent persons are not to approach widows or virgins except by the command or permission of bishops or presbyters. Nor are bishops or presbyters themselves to have access to women of this sort alone.—523: The Church must altogether maintain what is worthy, modest, and honorable: priests and Levites are not to have intercourse with their wives, because they are occupied with the daily necessities of ministry; for it is written: “Be holy, because I am holy.”—524: Monks who have long remained in monasteries and afterward seek to attain clerical rank ought not to depart from their earlier resolution, and they cannot have wives.—558: Christ wished the Church, of which he is the bridegroom, to shine forth in the beauty of chastity, [Col. 0676] so that, on the day of judgment, when he comes again, he may find her—as he established through his Apostle—without spot or wrinkle.—726: A man who, while a layman, married a widow is not to be admitted to the clergy.—Ibid.: Moreover, we advise what is worthy, modest, and honorable: that priests and Levites not have intercourse with their wives, because ministers engaged in ministry are occupied by daily necessities.—864: At the council held at Carthage in the year 419, Bishop Aurelius said: “When the preceding council discussed continence and the regulation of chastity, it was decided, as is fitting, that these three ranks—bishops, presbyters, and deacons—who are bound by a certain obligation of chastity through their consecrations, namely sacred bishops and priests of God, likewise Levites, or those who serve the divine sacraments, should be continent in all things.” (And other passages.)—871: It was decided, as has also been confirmed in various councils, that subdeacons who handle the sacred ministries, deacons, presbyters, and likewise bishops, according to the earlier statutes, should refrain even from their wives, so that they may appear as though they had none.

(Year 466.) ST. MAXIMUS, bishop of Turin, LVII, 250: Let us love chastity above all things, because Christ showed that it was pleasing to him when he chose the purity of a virgin womb.

(Years 492–500.) JULIAN POMERIUS, LIX, 435: Here may be read a mournful description of a priest living carnally.

(Poets of the fifth century.) ST. PAULINUS, bishop of Nola, LXI, 634: Let the priest’s daughter-in-law be holy.

(Years 521–525.) POPE HORMISDAS, LXIII, 424: Those whom it is necessary to preside over persons needing correction ought to be beyond reproach. Ibid.: With what conscience can one absolve a guilty person when he knows that, before the people as witnesses, he himself has confessed his sins? For who will venerate as a bishop one whom he saw lying fallen a little before?

(Year 543.) ST. BENEDICT, head of all Western monks, LXVI, 306: Let all members of the order avoid and flee visits from relatives and carnal affections; otherwise let them be punished according to the measure of their fault.—307: According to the saying of a certain Father, many monks, entangled in secular affairs and legal business, have lost their souls while wishing to benefit their relatives.—308: Self-denial is a complete forgetting of the past and a withdrawal from our own desires. To deny oneself is for one who was luxurious to become chaste.—337: For the safeguarding of life and the avoidance of the devil’s snares, we judge that familiarity with all women, whether relatives or strangers, should be forbidden; nor may any woman dare enter the inner court of the monastery. (There too much may be read on the same subject.)—379: Let him hasten to cut off the desires of the flesh.—394: Women ought in every respect to flee monks and bishops.

(Year 540.) DIONYSIUS EXIGUUS, LXVII, 39: (*Code of Canons of the Universal Church; Canons XX of the First Ecumenical Council of Nicaea, year 325.*) If anyone in health mutilates himself, it is fitting that he abstain, even if he is established in the clergy; and henceforth no such person ought to be promoted.—42: The great Synod absolutely forbade any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or indeed anyone at all in the clergy to have a woman introduced into his household, except perhaps his mother, sister, aunt, or only such persons as escape every suspicion.—LXVII, 50: (*From the Council of Ancyra.*) Any deacons who, at their very ordination, declared and said that they ought to take wives, because they could not remain thus, may remain in the ministry if they subsequently take wives. But those who were silent at ordination and afterward proceed to marriage must cease from the diaconate.—55 (*From the Council of Neocaesarea*): If a presbyter takes a wife, let him be removed from his rank. But if he commits fornication or adultery, let him be expelled altogether and reduced to penance.—56: A presbyter is not to attend a banquet for the marriage of a twice-married person.—Ibid.: If it has been clearly proved that the wife of any man was adulterous while he was a layman, such a man cannot enter the ministry.—58: If anyone separates himself from a married presbyter, as though he ought not to receive communion from his offering while he ministers, let him be anathema. (*From the Council of Gangra.*)—72 (*Council of Laodicea*): Priests, clerics, and monks ought not to bathe with women.—94 (*Fourth Ecumenical Council of Chalcedon*): The holy synod decreed that those who seize women under the name of marriage, or provide assistance to, or consent with those who seize them, if they are clerics, shall fall from their own rank.—142: A bishop, presbyter, or deacon is by no means to undertake secular concerns; otherwise let him be deposed.—144: If anyone mutilates himself—that is, if anyone cuts off his genitalia—let him not become a cleric, because he is his own murderer and an enemy of God’s creation.—144: If anyone, being a cleric, mutilates himself, let him be utterly condemned.—147 (*Canons XX of the Council of Nicaea*): If anyone is cut by physicians because of illness, or mutilated by barbarians, let him remain in the clergy. But if anyone in health mutilates himself, it is fitting that he abstain even if established in the clergy, and henceforth none such ought to be promoted.—Ibid.: The great Synod absolutely prohibited any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone whatsoever in the clergy from keeping an introduced woman, except perhaps his mother, sister, aunt, or only such persons as escape suspicions.—155 (*Rules of the Council of Ancyra*): All who promise virginity and break their promise are to be reckoned among the twice-married. We forbid virgins who live with certain persons as sisters to do so.—191 (*Synod held at Carthage*): Aurelius said: “It was decided, as has been confirmed in various councils, that subdeacons who handle the sacred mysteries, deacons, presbyters, and likewise bishops, according to their proper statutes, should refrain even from their wives, so that they may appear as though they had none. If they do not do so, they are to be removed from ecclesiastical office.”—194: Clerics or continent persons are not to approach widows or virgins except by command or permission.—205: Bishops, presbyters, and deacons ought to refrain from their wives.—234 (*Decretal Letter of Pope Siricius*): Monks and nuns are to be punished most severely if they violate the continence of those vowed to continence.—Ibid.: Pope Siricius rebukes incontinent clerics and refutes their arguments drawn from the fact that, in the Old Testament, priests had been allowed to take wives and beget children. (And other passages.)—236: A cleric who takes a second wife is to be deposed.—237: If through ignorance or as penitents, twice-married persons, or husbands of widows have been made clerics, they are not to be promoted.—242 (*Collection: Decrees of Pope Innocent*): A cleric is not to take a widow as wife, because one aspiring to the priesthood would be barred by this impediment.—Ibid.: A layman who has married a widow cannot become a cleric.—243: One who has had a second wife cannot become a cleric.—245: The incontinence of priests is discussed more fully.—248: Whoever willingly amputates a part of his body cannot be a cleric; one who does so unwillingly may be.—249: Twice-married persons cannot be admitted to the clergy.—Ibid.: A layman who, after baptism, has known neither a concubine nor a prostitute may be admitted to the clerical rank.—250: Those who beget children while in the presbyterate ought to be removed from office.—258: If a catechumen has had a wife, and after she dies takes another after baptism, he cannot be a cleric.—307 (*Decrees of Pope Gelasius*): Concerning those who have mutilated themselves, the canons of the Fathers have plainly laid down what must be followed. They say that persons committing such acts, as soon as they are recognized, must be excluded from clerical office.—308: Second marriages are not denied to laypeople, but for this very reason they are by no means permitted to enter the clergy.

(Year 542.) ST. CAESARIUS, bishop of Arles, LXVII, 1100 (*Rule for Monks*): Women are never to enter the monastery.

(Year 555.) PRIMASIUS, bishop of Hadrumetum, LXVII, 665 (*Commentary on the First Epistle to Timothy*): It is asked why he made no mention of presbyters. But under bishops he includes presbyters also, because theirs is the second and almost the same rank. Likewise: modest, continent.—680 (*Commentary on the Epistle to Titus*): Just, holy, continent. Such a person is to be chosen as can both exhort and rebuke those who contradict. (And many other passages.)

(Year 555.) MAGNUS AURELIUS CASSIODORUS, senator and abbot of Vivarium, LXIX, 933 (*Tripartite History*): Seeking to correct the life of human beings and of those living in the churches, the Synod established laws which we call canons. In their discussion, some seemed to introduce a law that bishops, presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons should not sleep with the wives whom they had married before consecration. But Paphnutius the confessor rose in the midst of the assembly and opposed this, declaring marriage honorable and saying that intercourse with one’s own wife is chastity. (And other passages.)

(Year 595.) ST. GREGORY, bishop of Tours, LXXI, 183: Here is recounted the story of continence maintained between two spouses by mutual consent.—461: After relating the story of an incontinent abbot, Gregory adds: “Therefore let this case be a warning to clerics not to enjoy the company of strange women contrary to the statutes of the canons, since both the canonical law itself and all Holy Scriptures forbid it.”—883: A story is recounted in which shines forth the chastity of the wife of Bishop Simplicius, and also the continence of the bishop himself.—884: There is likewise an account of another bishop who, after ordination, courageously resisted his wife in accordance with the rules of the canons.

(Sixth century.) *Lives of the Fathers*, LXXIV, 174: Here [Col. 0678] is related the life of a virgin presbyter and of his wife, likewise a virgin.

(Years 595–604.) ST. GREGORY THE GREAT, LXXVII, 672: In a letter to Bishop Boniface, Gregory urges him to attend to the morals and reputation of his clergy. Concerning his subdeacons, he decrees what was stated above concerning the Sicilians.—691: In a letter to Bishop Constantius, he urges him to assist Venantius, bishop of Luni, in reforming his clergy and the other religious persons.—996: Women are not to live with bishops or clerics constituted in sacred orders, under the rule that they are not to abandon their wives but are to govern them chastely.—1069: Letter to Savinus, regional subdeacon. He orders the most diligent inquiry into Sisinnius, accused of sodomy.—1286: The priests of Nursia who live with strange women ought to be restrained.

(Year 615.) COLUMBANUS, abbot and confessor, LXXX, 211: A monk’s chastity is judged in thought. What profit is it to be a virgin in body if one is not a virgin in mind?

(Uncertain year of the eighth century.) CRISCONIUS, African bishop, LXXXVIII, 826: (*From the Council of Nicaea.*) Those who mutilate themselves are to be excluded from the clergy.—848: If anyone has taken a widow, a woman who has been put away, or a prostitute, he is not to be admitted to the clergy.—Ibid.: A man who has had two sisters is not to be admitted to the clergy.—Ibid.: One who has made himself a eunuch is not to become a cleric.—Ibid.: A cleric who has made himself a eunuch is to be cast out of the clergy.—850 (*From the decrees of Pope Innocent to Victricius, bishop of Rouen, title XXI*): “You have proposed what ought to be observed concerning those whom you have found incontinent while placed in the ministry of the diaconate or in the office of the presbyterate.” And the rest.—880: Concerning monks and virgins who do not keep their profession.—883: With whom women ought to live when there is a bishop, presbyter, or deacon.—Ibid.: Concerning presbyters who have had marriages. “Whoever separates himself from a presbyter who has had a wife, as though one ought not to receive from the offering while he ministers, let him be anathema.”—884: A presbyter ought not to pray at the marriage of a twice-married person.—916: If anyone willingly amputates a part of his body, he cannot be a cleric.—918: Concerning the catechumen who loses his wife before baptism and afterward takes another: he cannot be a cleric.—923: Second marriages are not denied to laypeople, but for this very reason it is by no means fitting for them to aspire to the clergy.—928: Clerics or continent persons are not to approach virgins and widows.—387 (*Canon of Orléans*): If an abbot is not chaste, let him be removed from his dignity.—Ibid.: A monk who incestuously assaults little boys or adolescents is to be publicly whipped; he is to lose the crown of the head which he wears, and, shaved bald, suffer shameful reproaches; or, bound tightly in iron chains, he is to be worn down by the confinement of prison.—388 (*Canon of Agde*): If a monk commits adultery or theft . . . and the rest.—389 (*Canon of Carthage*): A presbyter ought not to attend a banquet for a second marriage.—403 (*Penitential of St. Egbert*): If a bishop commits adultery, according to canonical law he shall fast for twelve winters. (And other passages.)—Ibid.: If a presbyter commits fornication, he shall fast for three winters . . . and the rest.—405: If a monk commits fornication, he shall fast for seven winters.—421: Ministers of God ought always to preserve chastity.—Ibid.: Women are to be kept away from living with ministers, lest perhaps, through the devil’s temptation, sin be committed with them.—424: If a bishop commits any fornication or adultery, he shall fast for twelve years; a presbyter and monk for ten years; a deacon for seven; and a cleric for six.—425: If an ordained bishop, presbyter, monk, or deacon had a spouse before ordination, leaves her for the love of God, receives orders, and afterward they unite with each other through fornication, each shall fast according to his rank, as was stated above concerning homicide.—432: If any cleric is wanton, insolent, or foul-mouthed, he must do penance for three days.—433: If any cleric presumes to speak alone with a woman alone without two or three witnesses, which the ancient statutes of the canons prohibit, let him be rebuked most severely.—445: Under the heading “On Fornication” one reads: “If a monk violates a laywoman, let him do penance for three years.”—449: Under the heading “On the Penance of Clerics,” much is read that pertains to the matter treated in the present table.

(Year 766.) ST. CHRODEGANG, bishop of Metz, LXXXIX, 1083: The first temptations are the frequent visits of women, and these expose clerics to blame. What indeed have you to do with women, you who converse with the Lord at the altar?—Ibid.: Were women present in the choir of the apostles?—Ibid.: No one walks safely among serpents and scorpions.—Ibid.: If women live with men, the devil’s deputy will not be absent. (And many other passages.)—1087: Clerics should flee very frequent [Col. 0679] visits to widows and virgins. They should also strive to preserve forever the chastity of an undefiled body. (And other passages.)—1105: If any cleric of canonical rank commits graver sins—that is, adultery, etc.—let him first be subjected to corporal punishment. (And other passages.)

(Year 858.) POPE BENEDICT III, XCV, 691: Here is read a letter to the bishops established in Charles’s kingdom against Hubert the cleric, ordering him to come to Rome within thirty days to answer for innumerable adulteries, fornications, and other crimes.

(Years 800–814.) CHARLEMAGNE, emperor, XCVII, 275: (*From the Chapters Given to Presbyters.*) No priest is to permit women to live with him, except his mother, sister, or aunt.—512: Clerics and monks are to remain in their vow.—517: (*On Ministers of the Altar and the School.*) We also entreat your holiness that ministers of God’s altar adorn their ministry with good morals. (And other passages.)—524: (*On Presbyters Who Have Women in Their Houses.*) The bishops have decreed concerning presbyters who indiscriminately permit women to live with them, and who are thereby marked by the suspicion of bad repute, that if, after being admonished, they do not correct themselves, they are to be struck with canonical censure as despisers of the sacred canons.—620: Since we have also learned that certain canons and monks, setting aside the modesty of their religious profession, shamelessly and irreverently visit monasteries of holy women, both monastic and canonical, without consulting their bishop, we strictly forbid this practice.—706: If ecclesiastical persons commit the crimes mentioned above, an honorable person shall lose his rank; persons of lower condition shall be beaten or sent to prison.—723: Presbyters are not to obtain permission to keep women with them.—Ibid.: The bishops have decreed concerning presbyters who indiscriminately permit women to live with them, and who are thereby marked by the suspicion of bad repute, that if, after being admonished, they do not correct themselves, they are to be struck with canonical censure as despisers of the sacred canons.—743: Here is read the same prohibition issued to presbyters. Moreover, bishops who neglect to act as correctors are declared accomplices and therefore are to be punished.—764: If a reader, subdeacon, deacon, or presbyter despises the honor of clerical status, let him be subjected, with his possessions, to the condition of the curial class.—821: It has been decreed concerning presbyters who indiscriminately permit women to live with them and are thereby noted for suspicion of bad repute, that if, after being admonished, they do not correct themselves, they are to be struck with canonical censure as despisers of the sacred canons.—845: Clerics ought to be admonished and instructed that they themselves should first be free from every fornication, uncleanness, luxury, and every defilement of the flesh. (And other passages.)—857: By the law of the Fathers clerics are admonished to abstain from the pleasures of the world. (And many other passages.)—899: Women are not to enter a monastery of monks.—XCVIII, 1384: Concerning a bishop violating a woman.

(Years 804–825.) THEODORE, archbishop of Canterbury, XCIX, 931: Women are not to sit at a meal among priests.—946: If any cleric speaks abusively of a girl’s or woman’s breast or private parts, let him do penance for five days. If a monk or priest does anything of the kind, let him do penance for twenty days.—948: A bishop, presbyter, or deacon who has fallen into fornication is to be deposed, but not deprived of communion.—957: Likewise, if a presbyter commits fornication, let him be deposed.—958: If anyone amputates his own genitalia, he absolutely cannot be a cleric. If anyone amputates his genitalia after receiving rank, let him be utterly condemned. If anyone mutilates himself, let him be deprived of communion for three years.—960: A monk who commits fornication and does not find [the intended object is uncertain] shall do penance for one year and a half. Likewise, a monk who does so with a girl shall do penance for six years.—Ibid.: If anyone commits fornication as the Sodomites did, then, if he is a bishop, let him do penance for twenty-five years; a presbyter, fifteen years; a deacon or monk, twelve years.—Ibid.: If anyone desires to commit fornication but cannot, or if a woman does not receive him, then, if he is a bishop, let him do penance for seven years; a presbyter, five; a deacon or monk, three.—970: (*From the Roman penitential, of Bishop Theodore, and of the presbyter Bede.*) If they are canons and commit fornication, let them do penance for one year. He who is in holy rank shall do penance for three years. (And many other matters on the same subject.)—972: If a presbyter kisses a woman out of impure desire, let him do penance for twenty days.—Ibid.: If a cleric commits fornication with a four-footed animal, let him do penance for two years; a subdeacon, three; a deacon, five, as also a monk; a presbyter, seven; and a bishop, ten years.—Ibid.: Concerning the penance to be imposed upon sodomitical clerics.—976: (*From Burchard.*) Here is treated the case of a bishop who committed fornication according to nature, and of others.—979: (*Headings of the chapters [Col. 0680] of Theodore’s penitential book.*) Concerning the fornication of clerics.—900: Concerning sodomites, effeminate persons, and unclean pollutions.—985: No woman is to stand among those ordained in church, nor sit among priests at a meal.—996: (*Selected Canons.*) None of those who have mutilated themselves through impatience of lust may enter the clergy.—997: If anyone’s wife has committed adultery, he absolutely ought not to be admitted to ecclesiastical ministry.—998: If anyone has joined himself to a female slave, he cannot approach the ranks known in the clergy.—1004: A man about to be ordained bishop must first be examined as to whether his life is chaste. (And many other passages.)—1012: If any cleric has confessed adultery or has been convicted of it, let him be confined in a monastery for the whole time of his life.—1046: (*Canon of Agde.*) No cleric is to enter into familiarity with strange women for any reason whatever.—Ibid.: (*Canon of the Apostles.*) A cleric who mutilates himself is to be utterly condemned.—Ibid.: Only clerics, readers, and singers are permitted to have wives.—1054: (*Canon of Autun.*) A monk is not to have familiarity with strange women.—Ibid.: Women are in no way permitted to enter a monastery of men.—1054: In this column and also the following one may be read rules for girls consecrated to God.—1077: (*Replies of Blessed Pope Gregory to Augustine, whom he sent in his stead to Saxony to preach; on the stipends of clerics who take wives.*) But if there are any who, being constituted in holy orders, cannot remain continent, they ought to take wives, because it is written: “It was distributed to each according as anyone had need.”

(Year 804.) ALBINUS, or ALCUIN, abbot and teacher of Charlemagne, CI, 1079: I call marriages good, since they are granted by God’s authority for the sake of children. But I maintain that continence is better than these, if it is chosen for the purpose of being free for God, with all pleasures despised.—1080: Therefore I think that the husband of two married women after baptism ought not to be ordained a cleric; nor should one who had only one woman, but a concubine rather than a wife.

(Year 820.) SMARAGDUS, abbot of the monastery of St. Michael of Verdun, CII, 623 ff.: Isaiah testifies that virgins are happier in eternal life. Chastity is security of the mind and health of the body.

(Year 820.) SEDULIUS SCOTTUS, CIII, 233: Read what the Epistle of St. Paul to Timothy says after these words: “the husband of one wife.”

(Year 821.) ST. BENEDICT, abbot of Aniane, CIII, 445: If any woman enters a monastery or cells of monks with the counsel or consent of the abbot, the abbot himself should deservedly lay aside both his office and the name of abbot.—460: (*From the Treatise of Orsiesius.*) Preserve the purity of your body, that you may be a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed.—488: (*From the Rule of St. Basil, bishop of Cappadocia, for monks.*) Here is to be read the answer to the following question: whether one who has devoted himself to a pious and devout life ought also to observe continence.—538: Defilement of the flesh is to mingle with those who commit unlawful and abominable acts.—579: (*From the Rule for Solitaries by the presbyter Grimlaicus.*) Read chapter II, “On the Higher Precepts of Monks.”—689: (*From St. Basil’s Admonition to a Spiritual Son.*) If a cleric or monk improperly visits the houses of women, and a virgin permits such a person to enter to her, they immediately forfeit their former dignity and by their own will lose what they promised to the Lord.

(Year 831.) HALITGARIUS, bishop of Cambrai, CV, 687: If a presbyter takes a wife, let him be deposed from his rank. But if he commits fornication or adultery, he must be expelled more completely.—Ibid.: Likewise, if a deacon falls into the same sin, let him be removed from the rank of ministry.—Ibid.: (*On the Canon of the Apostles.*) A presbyter or deacon caught in fornication, perjury, etc. . . . . is to be deposed, but not deprived of communion. For Scripture says: “The Lord will not judge twice concerning the same thing.”—688: The great Synod absolutely forbids any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone at all in the clergy to have an introduced woman.—Thereafter, in the same place, monks and virgins abandoning their resolution are discussed.—706: (*From the Great Council under King Louis.*) If a presbyter neglects his manner of life, . . . . and the rest.

(Year 836.) AHYTO, or HETTO, bishop of Basel, CV, 764: (*From Hetto’s capitulary.*) The same priests are commanded not to permit strange women to live with them, in accordance with the Council of Nicaea.

(Year 836.) SYMPHOSIUS AMALARIUS, presbyter of Metz and chorepiscopus, CV, 863: Those who teach well and live badly are discussed.—864: Presbyters who live badly are discussed.—Ibid.: Concerning carnal superiors.—865: Here is read a mournful description of presbyters [Col. 0681] who live badly.—874: Concerning introduced women.—881: Concerning clerics and monks who do not remain in their resolution.

(Year 856.) RABANUS MAURUS, abbot of Fulda and archbishop of Mainz, CXII, 1419: The continence of clerics is discussed.—112: That a bishop ought to be the husband of one wife.

(Year 866.) RODULPHUS, bishop of Bourges, CIX, 711: Concerning women not to be received by presbyters.

(Year 867.) WALTERIUS, bishop of Orléans, CXIX, 732: (*Council of Nicaea; Theodulf’s letter to the clergy.*) In accordance with the prohibitions of the holy Fathers, no priest is to permit any woman whatsoever to live in his house; nor is he to presume to speak alone with any woman without arbiters or suitable witnesses. And the rest.

(Year 865.) ST. PASCHASIUS RADBERTUS, abbot of Corbie, CXX, 654: “There are eunuchs who were born so from their mother’s womb; there are eunuchs who were made so by human beings; and there are eunuchs who have castrated themselves for the kingdoms of heaven. Let the one who can receive this, receive it.”

(Appendix to the Ninth Century. Date uncertain.) ISIDORE MERCATOR, CXXX, 256: (Collection of Decretals; canons of the Council of Nicaea.) If anyone has been operated on in illness by physicians, or castrated by barbarians, it has been decided that he may remain among the clergy. But if anyone in sound health cuts himself off, even if he is in the clergy, he ought to cease; and henceforth no such person ought to be ordained.---379: (Second Council of Arles.) No deacon, presbyter, or bishop shall introduce into the private quarters of the cellarer a girl, whether freeborn or slave.---381: (Third Council of Arles.) No one shall dare to ordain a man twice married.---380: (Second Council of Orléans.) Those who, unable to resist the vice of the flesh, mutilate themselves cannot enter the clergy.---383: (Council of Valence.) It is fitting that no one of those twice married be ordained.---393: (Council of Orange.) With respect to those who have fallen into this condition before being ordained, the judgment of the Synod of Turin is to be followed, by which they are commanded not to be promoted further.---401: (Council of Agde.) It has been decided that female slaves or freedwomen are to be removed from the cellarer’s or private service, and from the same dwelling in which a cleric resides.---403: Monasteries of girls should be situated at a distance from monasteries of monks, whether because of the snares of the devil or because of human slander.---404: Clerics ought to shun marriage because of the most serious inconveniences found in gatherings of this kind.---412: (Council of Orléans.) Regarding intimacy with unrelated women, bishops, presbyters, and deacons shall observe the decrees of the earlier canons.---416: (Councils of Spain; Council of Elvira.) If bishops, presbyters, or deacons, placed in ministry, are discovered to have committed adultery, it has been decided that, both because of scandal and because of the unspeakable crime, they ought not to receive communion even at the end [of life].---Ibid.: A bishop, or any other cleric, may have with him only a sister or a virgin daughter dedicated to God.---428: (Council of Lleida.) If those who serve at the altar should suddenly fall through a weakness of the flesh that must be kept hidden, and, under the Lord’s regard, should worthily repent . . . . (And much else.)---429: Although the holy Fathers, by ancient admonitions, commanded that intimacy with unrelated women be wholly avoided in the churches, it has nevertheless now seemed good to us that anyone proved guilty of such conduct, if after a first and second warning he neglects to amend himself, be deprived of the dignity of his office. (And other matters.)---475: (Fourth Council of Toledo.) Either paternal devotion or personal profession makes a monk; . . . We bar these from access to the world.---Ibid.: Some monks, leaving the monastery, not only return to the secular world but even take wives. (And the rest.)---499: (Eighth Council of Toledo.) More fully treated: 1. concerning incontinent bishops; 2. concerning incontinent presbyters and deacons, and the women joined to such men; 3. concerning incontinent deacons.---568: If any clerics retain with themselves, and live with, certain other women as though adopted—on account of a mother, a sister, or even women joined by close blood relationship—as the sect of Priscillian taught, let them be anathema. (From the First Council of Braga.)---581: (From the book, chapter, of matters collected from Greek synods.) Concerning eunuchs made by others, or those who cut off their own sexual organs.---582: If any presbyter or deacon has committed fornication or adultery, let him be expelled and do penance.---Ibid.: If the widow of a bishop, presbyter, or deacon takes a husband, no cleric and no religious person shall share a meal with her. And the rest.---583: Concerning adopted women introduced into the household.---584: A presbyter ought not to attend a second marriage as a guest at its banquet. How can that man be a presbyter who, for the sake of a banquet, takes part in such a marriage?---597: At the fourth session it was reported to us that certain unlawful ordinations had recently occurred in the church of Astigi, such that certain husbands of widows [Col. 0682] were consecrated to the ministry of levites; these men ought to be recalled from the rank received as null and void, and those found to have been instituted contrary to divine and ecclesiastical law should not thereafter be advanced to the ministry of deacon. (From the Second Council of Seville.)---678: There will there be found in full the decrees of Pope Siricius: 1. concerning monks and virgins not keeping their profession; 2. concerning incontinent ministers; 3. what sort of persons ought to attain the office of the clergy; 4. concerning clerics who enter second marriages, that they are to be deposed; 5. concerning women who ought to live with clerics.---698: (Chapters of Pope Innocent.) 1. Concerning wives of clerics, that they be joined to virgins; 2. that if a layman has married a widow, he shall not become a cleric; 3. that one who has taken a second wife shall not be a cleric; 4. that priests and levites ought not to cohabit with women.---702: (Letter of Innocent to Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse.) You have asked what ought to be observed concerning those who, placed in the ministry of the diaconate or in the office of the presbyterate, have been revealed by the begetting of children to be, or to have been, incontinent . . . . that they are not to be admitted to such ministry, which can be fulfilled by continence alone. (And much else.)---706: (Letter of Innocent to Felix, bishop of Nuceria.) It is decreed that men twice married cannot be admitted to the clergy.---709: (Innocent to bishops Aurelius and Augustine.) That no one be made bishop contrary to the ordinance of the canons.---720: (To the synod assembled in the city of Toulouse.) Concerning one who had a wife before baptism and another after baptism: he shall not become a cleric.

(Year 902.) RICULPHUS, bishop of Soissons, CXXXI, 16: Know, therefore, that it was said to you: “Be cleansed, you who bear the vessels of the Lord.”---20: We also admonish that it be observed that presbyters or clerics do not cohabit with women, nor give occasion for slander against themselves. (And much else.)

(Year 915.) REGINO, abbot of Prüm, CXXXII, 192: Let such a bishop be found that disreputable morals and blameworthy conduct do not render him contemptible.---210: (From the words of St Augustine.) Therefore I do not wish my sister to be with me, because those who are with my sister are not my sisters. (And much else, above and below, on the same subject.)---255: That clerics shall not attend weddings.---316: (Council of Carthage.) Clerics or continent persons shall not enter the dwellings of virgins.---331: If they are canons and commit fornication, let them do penance for one year; if frequently, for two.---Ibid.: If a monk without rank, or a canon holding rank, has committed fornication with a lay girl, let them do penance for three years.---Ibid.: If a bishop has committed fornication, let him do penance for eight years. (And much else extracted from the canons.)---333: If any cleric has committed fornication with a four-footed animal, let him do penance for two years; a subdeacon for three; a deacon and monk for five; a presbyter for seven; a bishop for ten. (And other matters.)---334: A cleric or monk who pursues youths or little children, or who has been reproved for an indecent kiss or any shameful occasion, shall be publicly whipped and lose his tonsure; having his head shamefully shaved, he shall be smeared on the face with spittle; and, bound tightly with iron chains . . . . and the rest.---395: The guilt belongs to the bishop, or to the presbyter who presides over a parish, if younger widows or consecrated women are placed under the domestic intimacy of clerics for the support of their present life.

(Year 922.) HERVAEUS, archbishop of Rheims, CXXXII, 698: (Acts of the Council of Trosly.) It deals with the access, association, and cohabitation of presbyters and clerics with women.

(Year 961.) ST ODO, archbishop of Canterbury, CXXXIII, 946: Let Odo’s constitutions concerning the office of bishops, likewise of presbyters, likewise of clerics, be read.

(Year 960.) ATTO, bishop of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 36: That no cleric shall have a woman in the companionship of household intimacy.---Ibid.: That a cleric shall have no association with a woman after designation [to clerical office].---39: It is not fitting for a presbyter to dine at the wedding of a twice-married man; for since the twice-married man requires penance, what presbyter could, for the sake of a banquet, give assent to such a marriage?

(Years 966–973.) Continuation of Flodoard; Appendix to the History of the Church of Rheims; Synodal Statutes, CXXXV, 408: Let clerics shine like stars.---Ibid.: Nor shall they speak with women or keep them in their homes.

(Years 974–977.) RATHERIUS, bishop of Verona, CXXXVI, 496: It treats of the endowments to be found in ministers of God.---499: On the same subject.---568: Concerning a certain unlawful marriage.---585: These words of the Council of Neocaesarea are mentioned: “If any presbyter takes a wife, let him be deposed.”

(Appendix to the Tenth Century.) Works *adespota* [anonymous works]. Ancient Collection of Canons, CXXXVIII, 599: He who has had a concubine shall not approach sacred orders.---401: That men twice married are not to be admitted to the clergy.---Ibid.: He who took two wives while still a layman before baptism shall not be promoted to the clergy [Col. 0683].---Ibid.: Likewise, he who took a second wife.---Ibid.: But if anyone has taken a widow, a repudiated woman, or a prostitute, let him not be admitted to the clergy.---Ibid.: That one who has made himself a eunuch shall not become a cleric.---Ibid.: If anyone has deliberately amputated a part of his body, he cannot be a cleric.---Ibid.: That if a twice-married man, or the husband of a widow, has become a cleric, he shall not be promoted. (And other matters of the same kind.)---415: Concerning the punishment of a monk who has begotten a son.---416: Concerning monks who do not remain in their profession.---Ibid.: Concerning an adulterous monk.---Ibid.: Women ought not to enter a monastery, nor become spiritual co-mothers.---479: In the ecclesiastical laws of Edmund, king of the English, one reads: First, those initiated into sacred things, from whom the people of God ought to seek an example of virtue for imitation, whether men or women, shall live chastely, as the rule of their order requires; but if they do not do so, let them be punished.---624: (Ecclesiastical capitularies of Emperor Louis II.) Ninth: the same priests are to be commanded not to permit unrelated women to be with them. (And the rest.)

(Year 1004.) ST ABBO, abbot of Fleury, CXXXIX, 488: Concerning monks who do not keep their profession. The words of Siricius to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona, are mentioned.

(Years 1024–1027.) ST HENRY, August Emperor, CXL, 227: (Laws of St Henry at Pavia.) No presbyter, no deacon, no subdeacon, no one in the clergy shall admit a wife or concubine. If he does so, let him be deposed according to ecclesiastical rule.---Ibid.: Just as a bishop shall have no woman, so he shall by no means live with any woman. If he does so, let him be cast out from the honour of which he has made himself unworthy.

(Year 1026.) BURCHARD, bishop of Worms, CXL, 628: That sons of concubines are no longer to be ordained.---646: (From the Council of Tours.) Since no place ought to be given to the devil, we have decreed that this especially be observed: no clerics shall have familiarity with unrelated women or provide persons with any opening for evil speech or thought; for through this improper occasion it frequently happens that the devil, who lies in wait like a lion in his den, exults over the ruin of God’s servants. But if any cleric, after his bishop’s prohibition, presumes to persist in these practices, let him be held alien from communion. (And much else on the same subject.)---643: That those to whom it is not lawful to take wives should avoid the weddings of others.---803: (From the Council of Seville.)
