Let this precaution be observed concerning all: laymen, kept away from the private quarters of virgins, are not even to have customary permission to enter as far as the vestibule. And other matters.---605: That monks and nuns are not to be permitted to live together in one monastery.---812: (From the Council of Urbicus.) If an abbot permits a woman to enter his monastery, or to watch any festivities there, let him be confined for three months in another monastery.---797: The letter of Pope Siricius concerning monks and nuns who have mingled in sacrilegious intercourse is mentioned.---1068 and following: let the Statutes of the Canons concerning the office of priests be read; their compiler has remained unknown.

(Year 1068.) ST STEPHEN, cardinal of the Roman Church, CXLIII, 1410: (Council of Tours.) Concerning bishops, presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons who, held in carnal intercourse with a woman, have not ceased from office.

(Year 1064.) ST PETER DAMIAN, cardinal and bishop of Ostia, CXLIV, 290: He exhorts Gebehard, archbishop of Ravenna, to contend courageously against the bishops of Pesaro and Fano, whom he calls ministers of the devil.---344: In this fragment of a letter, from a passage of Jeremiah, he shows how detestable are the impurity and intemperance of clerics.---358: (Letter to the chaplains of Duke Godfrey.) At length he proves against them that clerics cannot take wives.---CXLV, 503: Therefore, that the pen may return to the point from which it has digressed, it seems to us—if it please you—that bishops ought to use this counsel: that they suspend from administration the unworthy and those who have fallen disgracefully.

(Year 1073.) ALEXANDER II, pope, CXLVI, 1402: Letter of Alexander II to Landulf. He replies that a man cannot enter monastic life and take a vow of continence otherwise than with his wife’s consent.

(Year 1079.) JOHN of Avranches, first bishop and afterwards archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 223: (On the pastoral office.) Priests ought to be chaste; here many matters occur written concerning the priest and addressed to the priest.

(Year 1085.) ST GREGORY VII, pope, CXLVIII, 786: (Roman Council.) If there are any presbyters, deacons, or subdeacons lying in the crime of fornication, we forbid them, on behalf of Almighty God and by the authority of St Peter, entry [into church] until they repent and amend. (And other matters.)

(Year 1085.) ST ANSELM, bishop of Lucca, [Col. 0684], CXLIX, 506: (Canonical Collection.) That no women may live with priests except those permitted by the canons.---509: That a twice-married man or one who has a concubine cannot be a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or any other [minister].---511: That one who has taken a widow as wife, whether before or after baptism, shall not become a cleric.---Ibid.: That a cleric shall take neither a widow nor a repudiated woman as wife.---Ibid.: That one who has taken a non-virgin wife shall not aspire to sacred orders.---513: Concerning eunuchs who have cut themselves off.---516: That presbyters and levites shall not have intercourse with their wives.---Ibid.: That clerics’ concubines shall be sold, while penance is imposed upon the clerics.---519: That presbyters unable to clear themselves of fornication shall be removed from ministry. (And other matters of the same family.)

(Year 1115.) LORD IVO, bishop of Chartres, CLCI, 453: That sons of concubines ought no longer to be ordained.---455: Concerning incontinent clerics.---456: That a cleric who has taken a second wife shall be deposed.---Ibid.: What women may live with clerics.---Ibid.: That if a layman has taken a widow, he shall not become a cleric . . . . . . Nor shall one who has taken a second wife become a cleric, because it is written: “The husband of one wife”; and again: “My priests shall marry once.”---Ibid.: What ought to be observed concerning the incontinence of priests or levites.---457: A man cannot be a cleric who has voluntarily cut off a part of his body.---461: Concerning incontinent ministers. Gregory to the citizens of Rome. After other matters he adds this: “Nor ought I to pass over in silence this thing—which I say with great sorrow of heart: I see priests living with women, a thing monstrous to say and hear, and contrary to the enactments of the canons . . . . Brothers, it is necessary to beware unlawful things, so that we may be able to lift pure hands to the Lord.” (And other matters.)---462: Concerning avoiding intimacy with women.---465: What is to be done concerning incontinent clerics.---That an incontinent presbyter shall not minister.---478: That twice-married men or husbands of repudiated women shall not be promoted to the priesthood.---479: If any layman, after his wife, has known another woman of any condition, he shall by no means be admitted to the clergy.---487: Here are reported the often-cited words of: 1. the Council of Nicaea; 2. likewise, of Neocaesarea; 3. likewise, of Pope Siricius; 4. likewise, of the Council of Agde; 5. likewise, of the Council of Tours; 6. likewise, of the Council of Nantes.---537: (From the Council of Toledo.) Concerning the condemnation of priests’ sons. These words are read: “Although many pronouncements of the Fathers concerning the incontinence of the clerical order have thus far been issued, and the correction of their morals has by no means been able to be secured, the offences they committed carried the sentence of the judges so far that punishment struck not only the perpetrators of crimes but also the offspring of the condemned. Therefore, if anyone from bishop down to subdeacon, established in office, should henceforth beget children by a detestable union either with a slave-woman or with a freeborn woman, those by whom they are proved to have been begotten shall be condemned by canonical censure; while offspring born from this defilement shall not only receive no inheritance from their parents anywhere, but shall also remain in perpetual servitude to the church from the disgrace of whose priest or minister they were born.”---548: Concerning monks who do not keep their profession. (Letter of Siricius.)---549: By what penance a monk who, abandoning his profession, takes a wife is to be purified.---551: That there be no double monastery. These and other things are read: “Monks and nuns shall not live in one monastery. For cohabitation leads to adultery, if a monk has access to a nun, or a nun to a monk, for private conversation.”---564: (From the Register of St Gregory.) “In no place do we permit monks and nuns to have one monastery, nor those which they call double.”---565: Monks begetting children shall be thrown into prison, lamenting so great a crime in continual mourning.---1142: Sons of presbyters are prohibited from sacred offices.---Ibid.: Those born from priests who presided over the Apostolic See.---Ibid.: Priests’ sons are not prohibited from the episcopate if other virtues are found in them.---1143: Those castrated by physicians, barbarians, or their masters are not excluded from the clergy.---Ibid.: A twice-married man is not to be ordained.---1149: The heading “On the Continence of Those to Be Ordained” is read.---1151: Priests are always commanded to observe chastity.---Ibid.: Those who serve the divine sacraments ought to be continent.---Ibid.: Priests and levites ought not to have intercourse with their wives.---1161: Presbyters, deacons, or subdeacons lying in the crime of fornication shall not enter the church.---Ibid.: The Mass of a presbyter who has a concubine shall not be heard.---Ibid.: He whose crime has become manifest cannot be restored to the priesthood.---Ibid.: He who has preferred pleasure to office must by all means be removed.

(Year 1135.) VENERABLE HILDEBERT, bishop of Le Mans, CLXXI, 709: For us established in sacred orders the necessity of continence has been imposed [Col. 0685]. There is no middle course: we shall be either on the mountain or in Sodom. The angels wished to lead Lot, after he had departed from Sodom, to the mountain.---931: How can laypeople abhor the uncleanness of the flesh when they hear that certain clerics or priests are stained by the disgrace of fornication?

(Year 1142.) VENERABLE GODEFRID, abbot of Admont, CLXXIV, 994: Deceived by love of this spiritual Herodias—that is, worldly desire—priests take her as a wife; placing her delightfully in the chamber of their hearts, they unlawfully engage in unlawful marriage with her.

(Year 1142.) HUGH OF ST VICTOR, CLXXV, 666: Concerning priests to be reproved, from the book *Pastoral Care* of blessed Gregory.

(Year 1153.) ST BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 853: (Sermon on Conversion, addressed to Clerics.) He rebukes incontinent men who do not fear shamelessly to profane sacred orders.---1074: We sought an excellent man, a liberator of many; and behold, we labour to find one capable of saving himself. The best man today is he who is not excessively bad.---CLXXXIII, 685: From the valley of crimes one ascends to the mountain of chastity by a threefold continence: of limbs, senses, and thoughts.---1005: Therefore a man taken up for the adornment and beauty of the household ought to be adorned with good morals. (Much else.)---1092: Does not the fraud seem openly exposed to you, and the fox caught? If he does not remove the woman, he does not remove the scandal. (And the rest.)---CLXXXIV, 1239: (Book on the Way of Living Well.) The chapter “On Continence” is read.

(Twelfth Century.) GRATIAN’S DECRETUM, CLXXXVII, 194: Presbyters ought not to attend wedding banquets.---Ibid.: One who marries a widow may, if necessity requires, become a subdeacon.---270: A deacon or presbyter caught in adultery cannot be restored.---302: Those who cut themselves off are not to be admitted to the clergy.---303: One cut by physicians because of illness may be admitted to the clergy.---A bishop castrated through the plotting of men may lawfully be ordained.---304: Those castrated by physicians, barbarians, or their masters are not excluded from the clergy.---306: Sons of presbyters are prohibited from sacred offices.---311: (Pope Urban II.) Priests’ sons are not barred from the episcopate if other virtues are found in them.---388: A cleric convicted or confessing adultery shall be confined in a monastery.---389: A presbyter or deacon caught in crime shall be deposed, but not deprived of communion.---390: A bishop, presbyter, or deacon taking a woman, or retaining one whom he has taken, shall be deprived of office and benefice.---391: A cleric who frequents the homes of married women shall be deposed.---392: Priests may not live together with women.---394: Women shall not live with clerics, except those excused by kinship.---395: Unless ordered by their superiors, clerics shall not enter women’s homes.---396: Bishops shall take care that virgins are not attached to the household intimacy of clerics under the pretext of temporal support.---398: What penance is to be imposed on a priest convicted of fornication.---399: A bishop consenting to the fornication of his clerics shall be suspended from office.---1375: A cleric shall be deposed if he has committed adultery with a consecrated woman.

(Years 1166–1169.) GERHOH of Reichersberg, provost, CXCIV, 1257: Clerics sunk in the mire of vices must be reformed to the apostolic life; Gerhoh rejoices that this has already been done at Rome.

(Year 1179.) PETER COMESTOR, CXCVIII, 1809: Let the sermons delivered in synods be read.

(Year 1186.) PHILIP OF HARVENG, abbot of Bonne-Espérance, CCIII, 728: Let the treatise on clerical continence be read.

(Year 1197.) PETER THE CHANTER, CCV, 184: Only a man perfect in morals is to be chosen as priest and levite.

(Year 1203.) HUGH V, abbot of Cluny, CCIX, 884: It is plain to all how much destruction of souls and ruin of places have resulted from women’s proximity and companionship. Therefore we decree that no woman shall ever be received in another place as a nun, convert, or prebendary except for relief [of need]. But in places where they have already been received, they shall be removed from the table and every shared life or association with monks. Exceptions are outlying places where women must be kept from necessity; yet they must be women of such character and age as to give rise to no suspicion, and only one in each grange.

## SECOND PART. ON MARRIAGE AND CELIBACY, INSOFAR AS THIS QUESTION CONCERNS MINISTERS OF GOD AND MONKS OF EVERY ORDER

(Years 160–245.) TERTULLIAN, presbyter of Carthage, [Col. 0686], I, 1286: The apostle’s prescription does not allow twice-married men to preside. II, 922: In the old law I observe that the freedom of marrying repeatedly was curtailed: “My priests shall not marry more than once.” But, as in other things, so also in this, the fullness of the law was reserved for Christ. Therefore among us it is prescribed more fully and more expressly that those chosen for the priestly order must be men of one marriage.---Ibid.: If you have the right of a priest in yourself where it is necessary, you ought also to have the discipline of a priest where it is necessary to have the right of a priest.

(Year 333.) ST SYLVESTER, pope, VIII, 835: We command that none of the subdeacons proceed to marriage, lest he presume upon any transgression.

(Years 340–397.) ST AMBROSE, bishop of Milan, XVI, 260: Those who venerate the adulteries and debaucheries of the gods establish penalties for celibacy and widowhood.---1206: Our author, on the words “the husband of one wife,” says: “He who is without fault and the husband of one wife is bound by the law for receiving the priesthood; but he who has repeated marriage indeed bears no guilt of defilement, yet is deprived of the priestly prerogative.”---Ibid.: The Apostle not only laid this down concerning a bishop and presbyter, but the Fathers also added in the Council of Nicaea that no cleric ought to be one who has entered into second marriages.

(Appendix to the Fourth Century.) ANONYMOUS AUTHOR, whose works were published under the name of St Athanasius, XVIII, 72; on the words, “It is good to marry; it is better not to marry,” says: “To avoid forbidden things is the yoke of necessity; to overcome permitted things is the gift of free choice. To abstain from evils is the reward of discipline; to go beyond good things is the freedom of merit, not the end of authority.”

(Year 417.) POPE INNOCENT I, XX, 605: That those who have begotten children while in the presbyterate ought to be removed from office.

(Years 358–420.) ST JEROME, presbyter of Stridon, XXII, 656: Whether bishops or presbyters—although among the ancients bishops and presbyters were the same, since the former is a title of dignity and the latter of age—they are commanded to be chosen for the clergy as men of one marriage.---XXIII, 230: And why do we not offer to God, in hope of rewards, that which must be exacted from unwilling persons? “He who is without a wife is concerned for the things of the Lord, how he may please God.” (And other matters.)---340, on clerical celibacy: “Oh, wickedness! Vigilantius is said to have bishops as accomplices in his crime—if indeed they ought to be called bishops, who do not ordain deacons unless they have first taken wives, trusting chastity to no unmarried man.” (And much else.)---XXV, 441: The priest’s office is to teach the people what is holy and what is polluted, what is clean and what is unclean; let us refer the first distinction to doctrines, the second to deeds performed through the flesh.---XXVI, 259: For just as ecclesiastical dignities exclude not only fornication but also marriage—for neither bishop, presbyter, nor deacon can be twice married—so perhaps a twice-married man will also be cast out from the assembly of the Church’s firstborn and undefiled, which has neither spot nor wrinkle.---568: Let the bishop be chaste, whom the Greeks call *sōphrona* (σώφρονα, “self-controlled”). But if laypeople are commanded to abstain from intercourse with their wives for prayer, what should be thought of a bishop, who is daily to offer to God unblemished victims for his own sins and those of the people?

(Years 387–430.) AUGUSTINE, bishop of Hippo, XXXIII, 1078: When persons joined in marriage have, by equal consent before God, vowed continence and agreed to the same compact of continence, they must faithfully render what was promised until the end.---XXXIV, 711: Certainly, if the high priests were then not forbidden to take wives or beget children, a great question arises. For the law says that a man is unclean until evening even through marital intercourse, even when he has washed his body with water.---712: It follows that the high priest was either continent or refrained from offering incense on certain days.---713: Every doubt is removed: none of the priests, whether chief or secondary, ought to approach the holy things if his uncleanness was upon him. The priest’s continence was therefore a consequence.

(Years 440–461.) ST LEO THE GREAT, pope, LIV, 610: St Leo writes to bishops established throughout Campania, Picenum, Tuscany, and all the provinces that whoever has been promoted to the priesthood as either the husband of a widow or a man having multiple marriages is to be excluded from ecclesiastical offices.---612: The husband of a widow and one who has been the husband of more than one wife are to be kept from sacred ministry.---615: In a letter to metropolitan bishops established throughout Illyricum, St Leo commands that twice-married men, husbands of widows, or husbands of repudiated women be excluded from the priesthood according to the canons.---617: In a letter to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica, he commends observance of the canons, especially in ordinations [Col. 0687], from which husbands of widows and twice-married men are excluded.---672: On this question, “Who are to be excluded from the priesthood?”, Leo the Great writes as follows: “The election of priests is so exalted that matters which are not counted as blameworthy in other members of the Church are nevertheless held unlawful in them.”---Ibid.: “For although those outside the clerical order are free to devote themselves to marital union and the begetting of children, nevertheless, for displaying the perfect purity of continence, not even subdeacons are permitted carnal marriage: so that those who have [wives] may be as though they had none, and those who do not have [wives] may remain unmarried. If this is worthy of observance in this order, the fourth from the head, how much more must it be observed in the first, second, and third?” (And other matters.)---1204: It is asked concerning those who minister at the altar and have wives whether they may lawfully have intercourse with them. Response: The law of continence for ministers of the altar is the same as for bishops and presbyters . . . . When they reached the aforesaid ranks, what had been lawful for them ceased to be lawful.---1207: It is written concerning a monk that he transgresses, abandoning the better choice, when he enters marriage.

(Years 447–461.) Appendix to the Works of St Leo the Great, Code of Canons, LVI, 443: A presbyter who takes a wife ought to be deposed from his order.---500: From the Letter of Pope Innocent to Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse, it is evident that incontinent deacons and presbyters are to be deprived of every ecclesiastical honour.---502: If anyone has been defiled by carnal desire, with what shamefacedness will he presume to sacrifice?---Ibid.: Let no one believe this permitted because it is written, “the husband of one wife.” For he who said this also said more openly: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God.” (And other matters.)---890: That no presbyter, deacon, or subdeacon shall presume to live or associate with women; and if he is found doing so, let him be expelled from his rank.---895: But if, after ordination, it should happen that a minister of the altar enters his wife’s own bed, let him not cross the threshold of the sanctuary, let him not be a sharer in the sacrifice, nor touch the altar.

(Year 540.) DIONYSIUS EXIGUUS, LXVII, 54: (Code of Canons; from the Council of Neocaesarea.) If a presbyter takes a wife, let him be removed from his order.---90: (From the Fourth Ecumenical Council of Chalcedon.) Since in certain provinces readers and singers have been permitted to take wives, the holy synod decrees that none of them may take a wife from another sect.---141: A bishop or presbyter shall by no pretext of religion cast off his own wife; but if he repudiates her, let him be excommunicated, and if he persists, let him also be deposed.---143: If anyone after baptism has entered a second marriage or has had a concubine, he cannot be a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or at all among those who serve in ministry.---Ibid.: He who has taken a widow, repudiated woman, or prostitute shall not be admitted to the clergy.---Ibid.: He who has taken in marriage two sisters, or his brother’s daughter, cannot be a cleric.---144: We direct that unmarried men who have been promoted to the clergy may, if they wish, take wives—but readers and singers only.---155: (Rule issued at the Synod of Neocaesarea, XIV.) If a presbyter takes a wife, let him be deposed from his order.---174: (Ecclesiastical rules promulgated by the holy Council of Chalcedon.) Since in certain provinces readers and singers have been permitted to take wives, the holy synod decrees that none of them may take a wife from another sect.---Ibid.: A virgin who has consecrated herself to God the Lord, and likewise a monk, may not contract matrimonial bonds; if they are found to have committed this, let them be excommunicated.---186: (Synod at Carthage.) Let the words of Bishop Aurelius be read.---187: Faustinus, bishop of the Church of Potentia, said: “It is fitting that bishop, presbyter, and deacon, or those who handle the sacraments, as guardians of chastity, abstain from their wives.” All the bishops said: “It is fitting.”---191: Concerning bishops and the succeeding orders who handle the most holy mysteries: it has been decided that they should refrain from their wives.---243: (Decrees of Pope Innocent.) That priests and levites ought not to have intercourse with women.---244: That a monk, if made a cleric, may not take a wife.---245: The incontinence of priests is treated more fully.---250: That those who have begotten children while in the presbyterate ought to be removed from office.---279: (Decrees of Pope Leo.) That whoever has been promoted to the priesthood as either the husband of a widow or a man having multiple marriages be excluded from all ecclesiastical offices.---288: That deacons, like bishop and presbyter, ought to abstain from every marital act; yet they are not to repudiate their marriages.---290: A monk’s profession, voluntarily and by his own choice undertaken, cannot be abandoned without sin; for what one vows to God one ought to render. Therefore one who, abandoning [Col. 0688] the profession of singleness, has fallen into marriage must be purified by the satisfaction of public penance, because, though marriage may be honourable, abandoning the better choice is a transgression.---293: That bishops be ordained by metropolitans not from laymen, not from twice-married men, not from husbands of widows, but from irreproachable persons.---Ibid.: That carnal marriage be denied to subdeacons.

(Year 542.) ST CAESARIUS, bishop of Arles, LXVII, 1090: No one shall dare to ordain to the aforesaid offices a twice-married man or the husband of a woman previously married.

(Years 548–556.) ST. AURELIANUS, bishop of Arles, LXVIII, 390: (Rule for monks.) No women at all, whether religious or secular—not even the mother of the abbot or of any monk, nor any relative or acquaintance—are to be allowed to enter for greeting or prayer.

(Year 595.) ST. GREGORY, bishop of Tours, LXXI, 181: (History of the Franks.) Among the Arverni, after Stremonius, bishop and preacher, the first bishop was Urbicus, a convert from the senatorial class. He had a wife who, in accordance with ecclesiastical custom, having withdrawn from the society of the priest, lived devoutly.

(Years 595–604.) ST. GREGORY THE GREAT, LXXVII, 336: A story is told of a priest who was near death and forbade his wife, or *presbytera*, to put her ear to his nostrils, crying out: “Go away from me, woman; a little spark still lives—take away the straw.”---506: The subdeacons of all the churches of Sicily had been forbidden, according to the custom of the Roman Church, to have intercourse in any way with their wives. This seems harsh and unsuitable to me: that a man who has not attained the practice of continence should be compelled to separate from his wife.---Ibid.: But we do not wish those who, after the prohibition was issued, have refused to abstain from their wives to advance to sacred order.---515: Furthermore, we wish that priests dwelling in Corsica should be forbidden to associate with women, except only their mother, sister, or wife, who is to be governed chastely.---996: Women are not to live with bishops or clerics established in sacred orders, on the condition that they do not abandon their wives but govern them chastely.---1033: Nor may other women live with priests, except those whom, as stated above, the sacred canons permit.---1185: (Gregory’s reply.) If there are clerics not established in sacred orders who cannot remain continent, they ought to take wives.---LXXIX, 95: The new priesthood shines with the splendors of chastity.

(Year uncertain, eighth century.) CRISCONIUS, African bishop, LXXXVIII, 823: (Abridgment of the Canons of Fulgentius Ferrandus, deacon of the Church of Carthage.) If a priest takes a wife, he is to be deposed. But if he has committed fornication, he is also to be compelled to do penance.---825: (Council of Carthage.) Readers, when they reach the years of puberty, are to be compelled either to take wives or to profess continence.---Ibid.: (Council of Zellae, from the Epistle of Siricius.) A cleric is not to take a woman as wife; and one who, while a layman, has taken a widow is not to be admitted to the clergy.---Ibid.: (Council of Carthage.) Clerics, even those who are continent, are not to approach widows or virgins without the command or permission of a bishop or priest.---840: (Canonical Breviary.) A bishop or priest is not to abandon his wife, whom he ought to govern chastely.---846: Men married twice are not to be admitted to the clergy. Note well: here are mentioned the Canons of the Apostles; the Council of Laodicea; the decrees of Pope Siricius; likewise of Innocent; likewise of Pope Leo.---149: (From the decrees of Pope Siricius to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona, title 7.) “For we have learned that very many priests of Christ and Levites, after long periods of their consecration, have begotten offspring both from their own wives and even from shameful intercourse, and defend their crime by this prescription.” And what follows.---852: We command that unmarried men who have advanced to the clergy may, if they wish, take wives—but readers and singers only.---877: Concerning deacons who, at the time of ordination, testified concerning marriage.---882: Concerning priests who have taken wives or committed fornication.---Ibid.: That priests and Levites ought not to have intercourse with women.---922: That carnal marriage is denied to subdeacons.

(Year 729.) ST. EGBERT, archbishop of York, LXXXIX, 382: (Extracts from the canons.) No priest is to have familiarity with unrelated women, nor ever permit any woman to live in the house in which he himself resides.---383: (From the Council of Nicaea.) The great synod altogether forbids a bishop, priest, deacon, or anyone at all who belongs to the clergy to have a woman introduced into his household.---Ibid.: The canons also teach that if anyone has taken a widow or a divorced woman, or has married twice, he is never to become a deacon or priest.---384: A bishop, [Col. 0689] priest, or deacon caught in fornication is to be deposed.---421: If a priest or deacon takes a wife, he loses his order. And what follows.---Ibid.: Priests of God, deacons, and the other ministers of God must always preserve chastity.---Ibid.: Priests, deacons, and ministers of God who themselves neither wish nor are able before God to preserve the chastity imposed upon them are to be driven from their ministry.

(Year 766.) ST. CHRODEGANG, bishop of Metz, LXXXIX, 1088: Priests, deacons, subdeacons, and thereafter those who are not permitted to take wives are to avoid the wedding-feasts of others . . . (And what follows.)---Those priests who have begotten children while in their priesthood ought to be removed from their office.---1095: And a subdeacon, exorcist, doorkeeper, reader, or acolyte who has children and a wife, and nevertheless preaches Christ, is not to be condemned.

(Years 800, 814.) CHARLEMAGNE, emperor, LXLVII, 275: (From the Capitularies issued to priests.) No priest is to permit women to live with him, except his mother, sister, or paternal aunt.---509: Likewise, in the same synod it was forbidden to priests, deacons, and all who are in the clergy to have a woman in their house, on account of suspicion, except a mother or sister, or only such persons as avoid suspicion.---641: Concerning women living with priests: it was decided that they should be expelled altogether and no longer associate with them in any manner; and if, after the first admonition of his bishop, a cleric is convicted by three to seven suitable witnesses of having transgressed, he is to be liable to the loss of his rank. (And other matters.)

(Years 804–825.) THEODORE, archbishop of Canterbury, LXLIX, 949: The law of continence is the same for ministers of the altar as for bishops and priests. While they were laymen or readers, they could lawfully both take wives and beget children; but when they have reached the aforesaid ranks, what was lawful for them ceases to be lawful. Thus carnal marriage becomes spiritual marriage. They ought neither to dismiss their wives nor, as it were, to have them, but to have them as though they had them not; so that the charity of marriage may be preserved and marital intercourse may cease.---956: A priest defiled by touching a woman is to do penance for forty days.---1012: (Selected canons.) No cleric from subdeacon upward is to have intercourse with the wife whom he formerly had. If he does so, he is to be deposed from office. If anyone knowingly admits him to office, he is to be suspended from his office for three months with penance.---Ibid.: Clerics who, having received the blessing, suppose that marriages ought to be chosen, though they were willingly ordained at lawful age without any objection, are to be expelled from communion together with the women whom they have taken. (And other matters.)---1013: (Caesarean canon.) A priest who takes a wife is to be deposed. If he has committed fornication or adultery, he is to be cast out of the Church among the laity to perform penance.---Ibid.: A bishop is to be degraded if he knowingly ordains a cleric who has had a widow, a divorced woman, or a second wife.---1014: (Letter of Pope Hormisdas throughout all the provinces.) If any deacon or priest, after receiving the Levitical blessing, is found incontinent with his wife, he is to be removed from office. (And very many other matters.)---1041: (Canon of Agde.) Priests and the other ministers who are not permitted to have wives are to avoid the wedding-feasts of others, lest hearing or sight, devoted to the sacred mysteries, be polluted by disgraceful spectacles and the contagion of suggestive speech.---Ibid.: (Canon of the Africans.) A buffoonish cleric, making jokes in obscene words, is to be removed from office.---1043: (Nicene canon.) No bishop or other cleric is to live with women, except his mother or persons of that kind.---Ibid.: (Canon of the Africans.) A cleric is not to live with unrelated women.---Ibid.: (Canon of Arles.) No bishop, priest, or deacon is to admit a woman into the private store-room.---Ibid.: (Canon of Agde.) It was decided that women are to be removed from the store-room, from confidential service, and from the dwelling in which a cleric resides.---Ibid.: (Canon of Mâcon.) No woman is to be allowed to enter a bishop’s bedchamber except with two priests, or at least deacons.---Ibid.: (Canon of Orléans.) We decree that no bishop or cleric of any kind has permission to keep any woman in his house, except those of whom the canons speak. (And other matters.)---1044: (Canon of the Apostles.) Let no bishop, priest, or deacon whatsoever put away his own wife under a pretext of religion; if he puts her away, let him be excommunicated; if he persists, let him be deposed.---1046: Only clerics, readers, and singers may have wives.---Ibid.: (Canon of Carthage.) Let readers read until the years of puberty. Thereafter, unless they have either preserved chastity or taken wives, they are not to be allowed to read.---1047: Readers, when they reach the years of puberty, [Col. 0690] are to be compelled either to take wives or to profess continence.

(Year 804.) ALBINUS, or ALCUIN, abbot and teacher of Charlemagne, CI, 1090: Therefore I think that a man who has been husband to two wives after baptism ought not to be ordained a cleric.

Year 540. ST. AGOBARD, bishop of Lyons, CIV, 232: Hence the Fathers teach that no one can be advanced to the priesthood if he has married a widow, etc.

(Year 821.) THEODULPH, bishop of Orléans, CV, 195: No woman is to live in one house with a priest. Although the canons permit his mother, sister, and persons of that kind, in whose case there is no suspicion, to live with him, we abolish this altogether because, in their service or on their occasion, other women come who are not connected with him by kinship and entice him into sin.

(Year 831.) HALITGARIUS, bishop of Cambrai, CV, 687: A priest who takes a wife is to be deposed from his order.---Ibid.: Likewise a deacon, if he falls into the same sin, is to be removed from the order of ministry.---Ibid.: Priests of God and deacons, or those who handle the sacraments, as guardians of chastity are to abstain from wives.---Ibid.: Furthermore, what is worthy, modest, and honorable the Church ought absolutely to maintain: namely, that priests and Levites do not have intercourse with women.

(Year 849.) WALAFRID STRABO, monk of Fulda, CXIV, 628: “The husband of one wife” . . . that is, monogamous after baptism. For if he also had a wife before, who died, this is not imputed to him, who is altogether new, and to whom neither sexual sins nor other things that existed before now do harm.

(Year uncertain; Appendix to the ninth century.) ISIDORE MERCATOR, CXXX, 257: (Council of Nicaea.) The holy synod forbade in every way that a bishop, priest, deacon, or any cleric whatsoever should be permitted to keep with him an unrelated woman, unless perhaps she is his mother, sister, grandmother, paternal aunt, or maternal aunt. And what follows.---267: (Council of Neocaesarea.) A priest who takes a wife ought to be deposed from his order. But if he has committed fornication or adultery, he must be cast outside the Church and reduced to penance among the laity.---Ibid.: A priest ought not to attend secular weddings.---Ibid.: The husband of an adulterous wife ought not to become a cleric.---322: (First Council of Carthage.) Gratus said: “Therefore, if it pleases you, no man or woman devoted to holiness and virginity ought ever to dwell in one house with unrelated persons, because of blasphemy against the Church.” (And other matters.)---333: (Third Council of Carthage.) That unrelated women are not to cohabit with any clerics whatsoever, but only mothers, grandmothers . . . (And what follows.)---347: (Fourth Council of Carthage.) A bishop is to be subject to the same sentence if he knowingly ordains a cleric who has had a widow, a divorced wife, or a second wife.---350: (Fifth Council of Carthage.) Since the incontinence of certain clerics, even toward their own wives, had been reported, it was decided that bishops, priests, and deacons should abstain even from their wives according to their proper regulations; unless they do so, they are to be removed from ecclesiastical office. Other clerics, however, are not to be compelled to this.---379: (Second Council of Arles.) No one bound in the bond of marriage can be admitted to the priesthood unless conversion has been promised.---Ibid.: If any cleric from the rank of deacon upward presumes to keep with him as a companion a woman other than his grandmother, mother, sister, daughter, niece, or a converted wife, he is to be held excluded from communion.---392: (Council of Orange.) It was further decreed that henceforth married deacons are not to be ordained unless they have first professed chastity by a purpose of conversion.---Ibid.: If anyone, after receiving the Levitical blessing, is found incontinent with his wife, he is to be barred from office.---393: The character of life itself requires, with regard to worthy and approved men bound to the clergy, that if they happen to enter second marriages, they may not receive the subdiaconate or ecclesiastical dignities beyond it.---399: (Council of Agde.) It was decided concerning men married twice . . . and what follows.---401: It was likewise decided that, if married priests or deacons wish to return to their wives’ beds, the ordinance of Pope Innocent or the authority of Bishop Siricius is to be observed. (And many other matters of the greatest importance which you should read.)---Ibid.: But no cleric is to live with unrelated women.---411: (Council of Orléans.) If a monk has joined himself to a wife, being guilty of so great a transgression, he is never to obtain an ecclesiastical rank or office.---417: (Council of Spain; Council of Elvira.) It was decided that bishops, priests, deacons, and subdeacons engaged in ministry must entirely abstain from their wives and not beget children. Whoever does this is to be expelled from the honor of the clergy.---423: [Col. 0691] (Council of Tarragona.) If any reader wishes to have intercourse with, or cleave to the companionship of, an adulterous woman, let him either leave the adulteress or be considered outside the clergy. The licentiousness of doorkeepers is to be punished by the same sentence.---424: (Council of Girona.) Those ordained without wives are not to keep unrelated women in their house.---433: Concerning priests and deacons, if they have begotten children after ordination. (From the First Council of Toledo.)---434: (The same, First Council of Toledo.) The holy synod further decreed that if a faithful reader takes as wife another man’s widow, he is to be nothing more, but always remain a reader, or perhaps a subdeacon.---Ibid.: But if, after his wife’s death, a subdeacon takes another wife, he is to be removed from the office to which he had been ordained. (And many other matters.)---439: (Second Council of Toledo.) No one from the subdiaconate upward is to have an unrelated woman.---434: (Third Council of Toledo.) The holy council has learned that bishops, priests, and deacons coming from heresy are still joined to wives by carnal desire. Therefore it commands that this not happen in future. (And many other matters.)---471: (Fourth Council of Toledo.) Whoever is established in the priesthood of God ought to be blameless, as Paul testifies.---474: Unrelated women are in no way to live with clerics, except only a mother, sister, daughter, paternal aunt—persons in whom the bond of nature permits no wrongdoing to be suspected; for this too the ordinance of the ancient Fathers decreed.---Ibid.: Concerning clerics who, having no lawful marriage, seek prohibited unions with unrelated women or their own maidservants.---Ibid.: Clerics who, without consulting their bishop, take wives, or take in marriage a widow, a divorced woman, or a prostitute, ought to be separated by their own bishop.---475: Certain monks, leaving the monastery, not only return to the world but even take wives; therefore, when recalled, they are to be assigned to penance in the same monastery from which they departed, and there lament their sins.---584: (Book of Capitula collected from Greek synods.) A reader who takes another man’s widow as wife is to remain in the rank of reader; or, should necessity arise, he may become a deacon, and nothing higher.---592: (Third Council of Braga.) Priests, or anyone of the clergy, are not to live with any women without witnesses. This canon begins: “Although the ancient institution of the canons has laid down clear and manifold disciplines concerning such presumption, . . .” and what follows.

(Year 915.) REGINO, abbot of Prüm, CXXXII, 190: No cleric is to go to weddings.---203: The words of the Council of Neocaesarea concerning priestly continence are mentioned.---209: Priests of the Lord and deacons, or anyone handling the sacraments, as guardians of chastity are to abstain from wives.---Ibid.: (Burchard, book II.) Furthermore, what is worthy, modest, and honorable the Church ought absolutely to maintain: that priests and Levites do not have intercourse with women. And what follows.---Ibid.: (You will find reported the words of the Council of Nicaea, of Pope Siricius, and of the Council of Carthage.)---210: (Council of Worms.) It was decided that bishops, priests, deacons, and subdeacons should abstain from wives, so as not to beget children. If they violate this decree, they are to be expelled from the honor of the clergy.---Ibid.: (From the sayings of Saint Pope Gregory.) Those who devote their bodies to chastity are not to permit women to live with them. (And many other matters.)---392: (Council of Tribur.) If a cleric, having left his wife, receives the tonsure, and is permitted to have a wife, he is to be compelled to be tonsured again.

(Years 974–977.) RATHERIUS, bishop of Verona, CXXXVI, 619: At the end of the column one reads: “What a ruined whole body of tonsured men, if there is no one among them who is not either an adulterer or an *arsenocoetes* [one who lies with males]! For among us an adulterer is one who lives as a husband contrary to the canons.” (And many other matters.)

(Appendix to the tenth century.) *Opera Adespota* [Anonymous Works], CXXXVIII, 401: Which clerics ought to be joined to wives.---415: Concerning the punishment of a monk who begets a son.---Ibid.: Concerning a monk who takes a wife.---443: (Canonical epistle.) No priest, deacon, or subdeacon is to be permitted to live or associate with women.---503: (Canons published under King Edgar.) We also teach that no priest should love the companionship of women too much, but should love his lawful wife, that is, his church.---514: (Prayer of King Edgar to Dunstan, archbishop of Canterbury.) He enumerates the vices of married clerics, decrees that they are to be expelled, and that monks are to be introduced.---520: (Charter of King Edgar made for Malmesbury monastery, in the year 974.) He states that he expelled secular clerics and introduced monks of regular life.---830: (Ecclesiastical Constitutions of the Three Ottos.) We absolutely forbid the sons of deacons, priests, and bishops from becoming notaries, *sculdasii*, counts, or judges.

(Years 1024–1027.) HENRY, emperor Augustus, CXL, 227: (Laws of St. Henry of Pavia.) No priest, deacon, subdeacon, or anyone in the clergy is to admit a wife or concubine.---Ibid.: Just as a bishop is to have no woman, so he is to live with absolutely none.---Ibid.: Sons and daughters begotten by all clerics from any free woman, in whatever way she may have been joined to them, are to be serfs of their church. (And many other similar matters.)

(Years 1024–1027.) BURCHARD, bishop of Worms, CXL, 645: Concerning a priest who, if he takes a wife, must be deposed; and here are mentioned various canons already noted in the present table, as well as the decrees of Siricius, Leo, and others.---650: Carnal marriage is granted to none of the clerics, not even to a subdeacon.

(Year 1064.) ST. PETER DAMIAN, cardinal and bishop of Ostia, CXLIV, 358: (Letter to the chaplains of Duke Godfrey.) He argues at greater length against those who maintain that clerics can take wives.---CXLV, 391: “Let the effeminate and incestuous clerics therefore go, degenerate from the true nobility of their order; let them seize arms with Abimelech. Yet all their conflict ends in this result: after the blow of the stone, they too are killed by their own armor-bearer’s sword.”---392: But wicked clerics say: “Does not the Apostle say: ‘Because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband? Let the husband render to the wife her due, and likewise the wife to the husband’?” To this I reply: (And what follows, which you should read.)---414: Such men, indeed, while they fall as impure men, while they strive to defend themselves, are rightly judged heretics. Hence married clerics are called Nicolaitans, because they derive this designation from a certain Nicolas who taught this heresy.---492: Here you may read Damian’s treatise on the dignity of the priesthood, in which you will find much pertaining to the present subject.

(Year 1085.) ST. ANSELM, bishop of Lucca, CXLIX, 516: (Canonical Collection.) That priests and Levites are not to have intercourse with their wives.---Ibid.: Concerning women introduced into the household.---That priests are not to live with women, except those whom the authority of the canons permits.---That the law of continence is the same for ministers of the altar as for bishops and priests.---Ibid.: That deacons also ought not to live with women.---Ibid.: That subdeacons ought not to have carnal marriage.---Ibid.: That clerics are not to go alone to women’s dwellings or speak with them alone.---519: From which offices ministers of the altar are to abstain if, after ordination, they have intercourse with their wives.---Ibid.: That priests and Levites are not to have intercourse with their wives, because they are occupied in daily ministry. (And other matters of the same kind.)

(Years 1089–1098.) BLESSED LANFRANC, archbishop of Canterbury, CL, 352: After the words, “A bishop must be the husband of one wife,” and certain others, our author adds: “Likewise, deacons must be chaste.”

(Eleventh century.) Ecclesiastical laws of King CANUTE, CLI, 1173: We exhort and teach all ministers of God, especially priests, to obey God and love chastity. Let them know most carefully that they ought absolutely not to have intercourse with a woman for the sake of sexual union.

(Year 1100.) ST. BRUNO, founder of the Carthusians, CLIII, 156: Where the Apostle says, “his own wife,” he excludes those to whom it is not lawful to take a wife in legitimate marriage, such as those who minister at the altar.

(Year 1104.) VENERABLE GUITBERT, abbot of St. Mary of Nogent, CLVI, 848: The paragraph “On married priests” is read.

(Year 1115.) LORD IVO, bishop of Chartres, CLXI, 465: (Clement, in the second epistle.) “But if after ordination it happens that a minister enters his wife’s own bed, let him not cross the thresholds of the sanctuary, touch the altar, or approach the carrying of the Lord’s body; but let him only hand water to the priests for their hands.” (And other matters.)---467: Concerning the chastity of priests and Levites. Innocent to Victricius.---474: Concerning a subdeacon who took a wife after ordination. (Stephen to Adon, archbishop of Vienne.) One reads: “Concerning that cleric named Alvicus, whom you say had lived through ecclesiastical orders up to the subdiaconate, we wonder why he took a wife by your authority, since we have never given permission to anyone to take a wife except those whom ecclesiastical rule permits to have one.”---572: (Gregory to the subdeacon Anthony.) What is to be done concerning monks who take wives. One reads: “Since we have learned that some monks have proceeded to such great wickedness as publicly to acquire wives, seek them out with every vigilance.” (And other matters.)---573: If monks or nuns have fallen, what is to be done? (Pelagius to Secundinus, defender.)---646: Concerning clerics who take wives without consulting [their] bishop.---Ibid.: (Gregory to Bishop Etherius.) “You asked concerning a certain man married twice, whether he could advance to sacred order; and according to the canonical rule, we forbade it.”---1135: When priests or deacons are appointed in parishes, they ought to make a profession to their bishop that they will live chastely and purely in the fear of God; and once he has bound them by such a profession, they are to maintain holy discipline.---1149: Priests, deacons, and subdeacons of the Eastern Church are joined in marriage, but not those of the holy Roman Church.---Ibid.: At Paphnutius’s dissuasion, the Synod of Nicaea did not decree that priests should not sleep with their wives.---Ibid.: Priests are to abstain from the embrace of their wives, not permanently, but at the time of offering.---1150: Deacons are not to be prohibited from ministry because of marriage if, at ordination, they say that they cannot remain continent.---Ibid.: It was decided that deacons, if they are whole or chaste, may be appointed to ministry even if they have wives.---1150: One who has not promised chastity is not to be compelled to separate from his wife.---1151: No one is to become a subdeacon who has not promised to live chastely.---Ibid.: A priest who takes a wife is to be deposed from his order.---1152: Those who abstain from their wives are admitted to sacrifices.---Ibid.: A priest, for whom prayer must be continual, must always abstain from marriage.---Ibid.: A deacon with his wife, or an incontinent priest, is to be removed from office.---Ibid.: A subdeacon must observe continence.---Ibid.: Carnal marriage is forbidden to subdeacons.---Ibid.: Those who devote themselves to wives after the diaconate are to lose benefice and office.---1153: Those wishing to take a wife must do so before the order of subdeacon.---Ibid.: No one is to approach sacred orders unless a virgin or of proven chastity.---Ibid.: Those established in the three ranks are to abstain even from wives.---Ibid.: The same law of continence applies to ministers of the altar as to bishops and priests.---Ibid.: Those established in minor orders are to take wives, unless prohibited by a vow or religious habit.---1154: Those outside sacred orders are to take wives and receive their stipends from the Church.---Ibid.: Readers are either to take wives or profess continence.---Ibid.: Women are not to live with clerics except those whose natural bond excludes every suspicion.---Ibid.: A priest is to love his wife as a sister and flee from her as an enemy.---1162: A bishop, priest, or deacon who takes a wife or retains one already taken is to be deprived of office and benefice.---Ibid.: A cleric convicted of or confessing adultery is to be confined in a monastery.---CLXII, 222: Clerics are told by their ordainers on the day of ordination: “This is the generation of those who seek the Lord,” not “of those who seek marriage.”

(Year 1124.) POPE CALIXTUS II, CLXIII, 1363: (Lateran Council.) We altogether forbid priests, deacons, and subdeacons the cohabitation of concubines and wives, and cohabitation with other women except those specified by the Synod of Nicaea. (And what follows.)

(Year 1135.) VENERABLE HILDEBERT, bishop of Le Mans, CLXXI, 770: “Fornication, dearest brothers, is forbidden us because, since we are ministers of God, we are his members. How shameful it is for a cleric to be led captive by a prostitute, so as to become a member of a prostitute! For if marriage is forbidden to us, how great a crime will fornication be judged in us!” (And many other matters.)

(Year 1142.) HUGH OF ST. VICTOR, CLXXV, 598: It is asked whether a man should be called monogamous, and can be ordained, if he had a wife before baptism, put her away, was reborn in Christ, and afterward took a believing wife.---Solution.---Jerome says that such a man is not a bigamist and can be ordained. But Augustine says that he is not monogamous and ought not to be ordained. (Many other matters.)

(Year 1153.) ROBERT PULLUS, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, CLXXXVI, 923: Marriage may be contracted below the rank of subdeacon; afterward ecclesiastical discipline forbids it. For this reason the last three orders are called sacred: the nearer they approach the altar, the more bindingly they oblige themselves to a continent life. (Many other matters.)---956: You may read the chapter entitled: “What good or evil marriage brings.”

(Twelfth century.) Decree of Gratian, CLXXXVII, 149: One who is to be ordained bishop must be monogamous after baptism.---Ibid.: One who had one wife before baptism and another after baptism is not to be ordained. Augustine, however, testifies to the contrary, writing in the Epistle to Titus. (See what follows.)---150: A man is proved a bigamist if he had another wife before baptism.---153: A bigamist does not sin, but is deprived of the prerogative of the priesthood.---Ibid.: No one is to be ordained deacon unless he has professed chastity.---Ibid.: Those marrying after a vow are not to be separated from one another.---154: It is damnable for those who have vowed virginity to wish to marry.---155: No one is to become a subdeacon who has not promised to live chastely.---Subdeacons and those above them who are incontinent and take a wife or concubines are to lose ecclesiastical benefice and office.---156: Those established in sacred orders are not to take wives; and if they take them, they are to be separated.---CLVII: Those who are to enter the subdiaconate are to profess continence.---158: A man established in marriage ought not to be admitted to the priesthood.---Ibid.: Deacons who do not profess chastity are not to be ordained.---Ibid.: Deacons are not to be prohibited from ministry if, at ordination, they say that they cannot remain continent.---159: A priest who takes a wife is to be deposed from his order.---160: The ordination of a certain bishop is delayed because he has a wife and children.---162: A priest is not to despise his own wife on account of religion.---162: A priest bound in an unlawful marriage is to abstain from office.---170: Priests are commanded always to observe chastity.---Ibid.: Those who serve the divine sacraments ought to be continent.---Ibid.: Priests and Levites ought not to have intercourse with their wives.---171: Those who abstain from their wives are to be admitted to sacrifices.---A priest, for whom prayer must be continual, must always abstain from marriage.---172: The same law of continence applies to ministers of the altar as to bishops and priests.---173: A bishop or priest is not to put away his own wife from his care.---Ibid.: Here is mentioned Paphnutius’s dissuasion at the Synod of Nicaea.---174: Priests are to abstain from the embrace of their wives, not permanently, but at the time of offering.---175: The Western Church, not the Eastern, imposed the vow of chastity.---Ibid.: Nor is marriage granted even to subdeacons.---177: Those outside sacred orders are to take wives and receive stipends from the Church.---Ibid.: A subdeacon is not permitted to take a wife.---Ibid.: The Mass of a priest who has a concubine is not to be heard.---178: The same matter is treated.---180: One who wishes to take a wife must do so before the order of subdeacon.---171: Readers are either to take wives or profess continence.---Ibid.: Subdeacons must preserve continence.---Ibid.: Subdeacons and those thereafter are to be excluded from the dignity of their ranks if they refuse to be continent.---182: No one is to approach sacred orders unless a virgin or of proven chastity.---183: Women are not to live with clerics unless their natural bond excludes every suspicion.---187: Concerning a certain bishop who had a concubine before attaining the summit of his episcopate.---191: A man who has children by a maidservant after his wife’s death may be allowed to become a deacon.---Ibid.: No one who has known another woman besides his wife is to be admitted to the clergy.---194: A subdeacon taking a second wife is to be assigned among readers or doorkeepers.---1378: A monk and a virgin consecrated to the Lord, if they marry, are to be excommunicated.---1382: A monk and a virgin who dedicate themselves to God cannot be joined in marriage.---1385: A monk who takes a wife is never to obtain an office of sacred rank.---1387: Monks joined to wives are to be confined in a monastery.---Ibid.: Whoever, after professing continence, takes a wife is to be separated from her.---1388: The marriages of those who have taken vows are not to be dissolved. (FROM AUGUSTINE.)

[Col. 0695]

CLVIII. INDEX OF THE OFFICES OR DUTIES OF MONKS.

This Index treats of: I. The name, titles, and various kinds of monks; the origin and praise of monastic life.---II. The life of monks and their virtues.---III. Things to be avoided by monks.---IV. Things to be fulfilled by monks.---V. The faults of monks.---VI. The clothing of monks.---VII. The food and drink of monks.---VIII. The sleeping of monks.---IX. Novices.---X. The principal offices of the monastery.---XI. The monastery.---XII. Rules and constitutions of monasteries; homilies and sermons addressed to monks.

[INDEX OF THE OFFICES OR DUTIES OF MONKS.]

I.—On the name, titles, and various kinds of monks.—The origin and praise of monastic life.

[Col. 0695]

The name and calling of a monk, St. Jerome, XXII, 582, 583.---What the name signifies, ibid., 350.---Why monks are so called, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1732.---Heretics insult Catholics concerning the name “monks,” ibid., 1730.---Why monks are called thus, St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 50.---Concerning the name of monks, id., XCVI, 1296.---Why monks are so called, Rabanus Maurus, CII, 93.---The meaning of “monks” and “canons,” St. Peter Damian, CXL, 506.---Etymology of “monk,” St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 705.---Why monks are thus named, Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 770.---What the term “monk” signifies, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 366; Alan of Lille, CCX, 191, 199.

Monks are simply called servants of God, St Augustine, XXXIII, 993; XXXVIII, 1070.---Soldiers of Christ fighting in silence, etc., the same author, XXXIII, 997.---The Christian soldiery of monks, the same, XLII, 226.---Monks are called Fathers, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 341.---This title of monks is found among Greek and Latin writers, ibid., 719, 720.---Monks as followers of the apostolic life, St Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXIII, 595.---Members of God’s household, the same, CLXXXII, 169.---Monks called saints, ibid., 278.---The name of holiness bestowed upon them, ibid., 236.---Likewise, that of blessedness, ibid., 449.

Three kinds of monks in Egypt, St Jerome, XXII, 419; XXX, 324.---The kind of monks called Remboth, ibid.---On the three kinds of monks found within Egypt, Cassian, XLIX, 1093.---On the kinds or manner of life of monks, St Benedict, [lacuna]LXVI, 246; St Valerius, abbot, LXXXVII, 437.---On the four kinds of monks, the same, LXXXVIII, 951; CIII, 729, 735, 745.---Their various kinds, Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 93.---Three kinds of monks in Egypt, Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 795.

The renown of the monastic institution, St Ambrose, XVI, 1107.---There were no monks in Syria before Hilarion, St Jerome, XXIII, 34.---Countless monasteries are built throughout all Palestine, ibid., 41.---Monks established at Alexandria by St Mark, Cassian, XLIX, 79.---Their origin from the apostles, ibid., 1094.---Monks established by St Eusebius of Vercelli, so as to perform the offices of clerics in the Church. Further material concerning their establishment is found in St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 887.---Elijah, the first founder of monks, Rupert of Deutz, CLXVIII, 885.---The first monks were the prophets and their sons, the same, CLXX, 527.---Origin of monks, ibid., 534.---The monastic order was the first in the Church, from which the Church began, St Bernard, CLXXXII, 912.---The source and origin of monks, Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 769, 770.---Christ instituted the solitary life of monks; John the Baptist commended it, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 216.

Monks and virgins, flowers and ornaments of the Church, St Jerome, XXII, 489.---The institution of monks, anchorites, and cenobites commended, ibid., 1338.---Praise of the cenobitic life, ibid., 1077.---The monastic manner of life most widely known throughout the whole world, St Augustine, XLIII, 372.---Its brief commendation, the same, XXXVII, 1277.---The Christian soldiery of monks, the same, XLII, 226.---“Though still placed upon earth, you display the life of angels,” St Eucherius of Lyons, L, 865.---Praise of monastic life, Cassiodorus, LXX, 734.---The cenobitic and eremitic life commended, ibid., 955.---For many, monastic profession and life are necessary for salvation, Gregory the Great, LXVII, 663.---“O how happy is the life of monks, pleasing to God, beloved by angels!” [Col. 0696] etc., Alcuin, C, 298.---On the praises of the solitary life, St Peter Damian, CXLV, 336.---Monastic institution and flight from the world, the best remedy for preserving virginity, Guibert of Nogent, CLVI, 604.---Monastic profession, like baptism, wipes away all sins, Lanfranc, CL, 607.---Monastic life extolled in praise, ibid., 558.---Eulogy of monastic life, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 542, 669, 750.---How great, already in this life, is the happiness of cenobites or monks, ibid., 873.---The monastic order resembles the angelic orders, St Bernard, CLXXXII, 912.---Eulogy of monastic profession, the same, CLXXXIII, 716.---It is a second baptism, ibid., 569.---It is an apostolic life, ibid., 641.---Likewise an angelic life, and in a certain manner a prophetic one, ibid.---Monastic life, a short road to heaven, ibid., 595.---An excellent description of monastic life, ibid., 663.---How exalted their profession is, Guigo the Carthusian, CLXXXIV, 311.

II.---On the life monks ought to lead and their virtues.

Description of true monks, St Jerome, XXII, 1075.---The rule and exercises of that life, ibid., 1080 ff.---False monks, ibid., 1081.---A monk is commanded to live so as to deserve to be a cleric, ibid., 1082.---Let him not defile his youth with any stain, ibid.---Let him go forth to Christ’s altar as a virgin from the bridal chamber, having a good testimony from those outside, ibid.---Their life is called harsh, ibid., 595.---It is the height of folly to renounce the world, leave one’s country, and live just as one would have lived in one’s native country, ibid., 489.---The life and condition of a true monk, the same, XXIII, 351.---How a monk ought to order his life from the beginning, Cassian, XLIX, 265.---What should be a monk’s end, ibid., 773.---Some monks are such only in dress and name, ibid., 608.---To come to the desert is the highest perfection; not to live perfectly in the desert is the highest condemnation, St Eucherius of Lyons, L, 855.---Who are true monks, St Leo the Great, LIV, 1015.---A monk ought to live in a monastery as in a safe harbour, St Gregory the Great, LXXV, 511.---A monk takes the religious habit in vain unless he abandons his vices, the same, LXXVI, 889.---Monks rise to the consummation of the perfection they have begun, the same, LXXVII, 864, 865.---The holiness and duties of monastic life, the same, LXXIX, 516, 517.---The virtues and pursuits of monks, Alcuin, C, 298.---What is the life of monks, if not charity, humility, and obedience? ibid., 288.---A moderately perfect monk is better than a secular man, even a devout one, St Peter Damian, CXLV, 747.---What monks ought to be, the same, CXLIV, 901; Ratherius of Verona, CXXXVI, 586.---What evils the unhappy soul of a monk suffers when it returns to lower things, the same, CXLV, 263.---What monastic conduct ought to be, St Anselm of Canterbury, CLIX, 183.---Cloistered life in the monastic vocation is, in a sense, a paradise of this life, ibid., 169.---Character of a true monk, the same, CLIII, 688.---Not tonsure but virtue makes the monk, ibid., 689.---The virtues of monks, ibid., 703 ff.---The distinct life of monks and clerics, Rupert of Deutz, CLXX, 526.---The gifts of monks, St Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 550.---An excellent description of monastic life, the same, CLXXXIII, 663.---In community they must live in an orderly manner for themselves, sociably toward their neighbour, humbly toward God, ibid., 407.---Virtues peculiar to monks, Alan of Lille, CCX, 262.

On the humility of monks.---“However much you abase yourself, you will not be humbler than Christ,” St Jerome, XXII, 646.---On humility, the same, XXX, 376.---Humility, mistress of all virtues, Cassian, XLIX, 1015, 1128.---The humility of Abbot John, ibid., 1128.---On the humility of Abbot Pynuphius, ibid., 190, 1149.---Necessary for acquiring perfection, ibid., 460, 473.---What true humility consists in, ibid., 198.---How it is to be acquired, ibid., 473.---Those devoted to humility, St Eucherius of Lyons, L, 848.---“Blessed before God is that soul whose humility shames another’s pride,” ibid., 850.---Monks should endeavour to plant humility, ibid.---“For this lamp to have a most brilliant light, it must always be filled with the oil of mercy, humility, etc.; but humility must especially be cultivated, for it makes us equal to the righteous, joins us to angels, and makes us draw near to God,” ibid., 865, 866.---The profession of monks, a purpose of humility, St Leo the Great, LIV, 793.---“If any of us lacks the richest grace of humility, let him go to those in whom he sees it more abundantly present,” St Faustus of Riez, LVIII, 871.---“How can the soul be healed? Surely by praying, fasting, and cultivating true humility,” ibid., 873.---“Again I ask and exhort you: strive continually to show obedience and humility not only to elders and equals but also to juniors,” ibid., 875.---“It must be known that, in proportion as we are humbler and more obedient to our superiors and Fathers, so the Lord will obey our prayers,” ibid., 886.---The more we advance, the more we should humble ourselves, ibid.---Humility and obedience are still a necessity in juniors, but already a dignity in elders, ibid.---On humility, St Benedict, LXVI, 371 ff.---Humility is especially fitting for monks, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 574.---On what the humility of brothers ought to be, by what means it is acquired, and how, once acquired, it is preserved, the same, LXXXVIII, 966.---“Love humility, and do not rest content with your own counsel,” St Benedict of Aniane, CIII, 429.---On humility, ibid., 648, 833 ff.---The twelve degrees of humility, ibid., 838 ff.---On humility, Bernard the Carthusian, CLIII, 898.---Humility adorns monks, Rupert of Deutz, CLXX, 526.---Humility, signified by clothing, is necessary to us, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 872.---On humility, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 887.---“Pursue humility before all things,” St Bernard, CLXXXII, 549.---The draught of humility to be sought, ibid., 551.

On the obedience of monks.---“If anyone is disobedient, he shall be admonished ten times,” St Jerome, XXIII, 82.---On obedience, the same, XXX, 321.---How great is the obedience of juniors, even in matters subject to natural necessity, Cassian, XLIX, 162.---On the obedience of Abbot John, through which he advanced as far as the grace of prophecy, XLIX, 183 ff.---The obedience of Abbot Musius, ibid., XLIX, 186.---On the obedience of the brother who, carrying ten baskets about, publicly sold them at the abbot’s command, XLIX, 189.---Not to obey and to wish to depart is to do the devil’s will in two ways, St Eucherius of Lyons, L, 837.---Disobedience hardens the mind once it has seized it, so that it cannot be bent to receive commands either by authority or by reason, ibid., 838.---On the effects of obedience, ibid., 839.---Whoever wishes his works to be safe or right in God’s sight should prefer nothing to obedience, ibid.---In what obedience compunction is shown, ibid., 860.---Our Saviour especially impressed this obedience upon us, ibid., 867.---“Blessed before God is that soul whose obedience silently rebukes another’s sloth,” St Faustus of Riez, LVIII, 871.---One should rejoice over a monk displaying obedience in the monastery … and conversely mourn over a disobedient monk, ibid., 874.---Neither the works nor the fasts of those who obey their own wills rather than those of their elders are acceptable to the Lord, ibid., 886.---On obedience, St Benedict, LXVI, 349; St Ferreolus of Uzès, ibid., 959; St Columbanus, LXXX, 209; St Fructuosus of Braga, LXXXVII, 1103.---On the obedience a disciple ought to show, the same, LXXXVIII, 959.---How we ought to obey one another, St Benedict of Aniane, CIII, 517.---On obedience, ibid., 815.---That brothers should be obedient to one another, ibid., 1367.---On obedience, Adalger, CXXXIV, 918.---“First impose obedience upon yourself,” Ratherius of Verona, CXXXVI, 314.---On most ready obedience, so that whatever is commanded may be carried out with the greatest zeal, St Peter Damian, CXLV, 332.---Obedience commended among monastic virtues, Lanfranc, CL, 445.---Either obedient, we shall obtain rewards; or disobedient, we shall pay eternal penalties, John the Carthusian, CLIII, 905.---He is not a monk who does not practise obedience, Geoffrey of Vendôme, CLVII, 175.---Without a superior’s permission he may not do even good deeds, ibid., 170, 279.---Indeed, a monk’s highest virtue is to obey his prior, ibid., 706.---Description of monastic obedience, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 589.---Nothing is greater than obedience: for as disobedience harms, so obedience prevails, ibid., 882.---Four orders before God … the fourth, those who for God’s sake are subject in obedience to the Fathers, ibid., 883.---Obedience, understood through subjection, is necessary to us, ibid., 892.---There are some who bear the cross of obedience in likeness of Christ, obedient to God and to their prelates, ibid., 897.---Above all, four virtues are necessary to this order: charity, humility, obedience, and discipline, ibid., 900.---Obedience is the inciter of virtue, ibid., 901.---On obedience, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 919.---“Our order is abasement, humility, obedience,” etc., St Bernard, CLXXXII, 297.---Degrees of obedience, the same, CLXXXIII, 656.---He does not consider what sort of thing is commanded, being content with this alone: that it is commanded, the same, CLXXXII, 100.---The degrees of obedience, and how the gravity of disobedience is to be known according to the distinctions set forth above, ibid., 868.---Obedience is burdensome and troublesome only to the imperfect, unwilling, and carnal; to others it is sweet and easy, ibid., 874.---What obedience is like among the monks of Clairvaux, ibid., 712.---An example of perfect obedience in Peter and Andrew, St Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXIII, 509.---What rule St Benedict requires, Aelred, Abbot of Rievaulx, CXCV, 610.---On the virtue of perfect obedience, Adam of Prémontré, CXCVIII, 580.---On obedience, St Stephen of Grandmont, CCIV, 1139 ff.; St Martin of León, CCIX, 101; Alan of Lille, CCX, 143.

On the charity of monks.---“Let each one of you be more gracious in charity,” St Eucherius of Lyons, L, 856.---Among all brothers this shall be observed: let them possess patience, humility, and charity, Fastidius, L, 379.---The profession of monks consists chiefly in faith and charity, St Leo the Great, LIV, 845.---“If any of us lacks the oil of charity, let him go to those in whom he sees it more abundantly present,” St Faustus of Riez, LVIII, 871.---“Again and again I ask and exhort you, brothers, continually to strive to show obedience, humility, and charity not only to elders and equals but also to juniors,” ibid., 875.---The remarkable charity of monks toward the poor, St Benedict, LXVI, 310.---On charity, St Ferreolus, ibid., 961.---Let all that we do be done with charity, St Benedict, ibid., 990.---On charity, the same, LXXIII, 973.---On love of God and neighbour, St Fructuosus of Braga, LXXXVII, 1099.---On charity, St Benedict of Aniane, CIII, 441, 488, 512, 647, 686 ff.---Where he exhorts all in common to devotion to charity, St Peter Damian, CXLV, 326.---Four virtues necessary to the monastic order: charity, humility, obedience, discipline, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 900.---On love of God and neighbour, and on unity of hearts, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 881.---The Rule of St Benedict is subject to charity, St Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 408.

On the poverty of monks.---On poverty, St Jerome, XXX, 330.---Religious poverty, Cassian, XLIX, 167.---Let no one have in his cell, beyond what is prescribed by the monastery’s rule, either a few coins or anything of his own, the same, L, 287.---Deacon Vigilius, ibid., 375.---“But this especially belongs to our profession: to seek poverty deliberately,” St Eucherius of Lyons, ibid., 842.---“Is it not already a great part of the reward to possess, with the fear of the Lord, sufficiency amid glorious poverty?” ibid., 844.---It is especially characteristic of a monk to seek poverty deliberately, St Faustus of Riez, LVIII, 870.---Poor monks and clerics living holy lives are to be preferred to rich laypersons endowed with whatever rank, St Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 649.---Nothing is to be possessed as one’s own, especially among monks, St Benedict, LXVI, 991.---He is not a monk who seeks a possession on earth, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 245.---Monks may not possess anything as their own, the same, LXXVI, 420.---On poverty and the trampling-down of covetousness, St Columbanus, LXXX, 211.---Let monks have all things in common, St Benedict of Aniane, CIII, 482.---A monk ought to have nothing of his own, Ratherius of Verona, CXXXVI, 412.---Poverty in clothing, and by what considerations it is commended, St Peter Damian, CXLV, 553.---Monks must relinquish everything, the same, CXLIV, 552.---Monks possessing money are excommunicated, John of Rouen, CXLVII, 146.---Poverty provides monks with a pretext for relaxing regular discipline, Guibert of Nogent, CLVI, 1053.---Hildebert frequently calls monastic poverty “communion,” because monks ought to hold everything in common, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 892.---Voluntary poverty, for which without doubt your reward is abundant in heaven, St Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 530.---On the property of monks, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 366.

On the chastity of monks.---Description of a good monk, St Jerome, XXII, 1075.---The continence and gentleness of the monks of Nitria, ibid., 756.---On chastity, the same, XXX, [Col. 0699] 325.---On the spirit of fornication, John Cassian, XLIX, 265.---On chastity, ibid., 869.---The exceptional chastity of Abbot Serenus, XLIX, 669.---Of Abbot Theonas, ibid., 1179.---An example of chastity teaching that not all practices should be emulated by everyone, ibid., 960.---“For what benefit is it if someone is chaste in body and polluted in mind?” St Eucherius of Lyons, L, 843.---“Let each one of you be purer in chastity,” ibid., 856.---The vow of chastity is included in Benedictine profession, St Benedict, LXVI, 824.---Do not suppose you have modest eyes if you harbour immodest minds, ibid., 984.---Yet it is a crime both to desire women and to wish to be desired by them, ibid.---On chastity, St Columbanus, abbot, LXXX, 211.---“You who fear the Lord, arm yourselves with chastity,” St Benedict of Aniane, CIII, 460.---On chastity and the means of preserving it, St Peter Damian, CXLV, 710.---What care must be taken to preserve chastity, ibid., 721.---That sobriety is chastity’s safeguard, ibid., 722.---Virtues proper to monks, Alan of Lille, CCX, 262.---Chastity, the ornament of virtues, ibid.

On the mortification of monks.---Moderate and temperate food is useful both to body and soul, St Jerome, XXII, 1075.---“Do you think that you can pass without falling and without injury unless you guard your heart with every vigilance?” ibid., 1076.---On abstinence, especially from meat, the same, XXX, 345.---On mortification, Cassian, XLIX, 1279 ff.---“Recognize that bodily abstinence alone does not suffice for attaining eternal salvation,” St Eucherius of Lyons, L, 843.---“Let us so exercise the body by fasts that we cleanse the mind of vices,” ibid.---“Let each one of you be more restrained in sobriety,” ibid., 856.---Mortification of the flesh serves the preservation of chastity, St Benedict, LXVI, 335.---Mortification necessary for prayer, ibid., 330.---On mortification, St Columbanus, abbot, LXXX, 215.---Threefold mortification, St Benedict of Aniane, CIII, 836.---On fasting, ibid., 694.---Why monks were appointed to fast three days a week, St Peter Damian, CXLV, 797.---On bodily affliction, Bernard the Carthusian, CLIII, 897.---“Subdue your flesh by fasts and abstinence from food and drink, insofar as health permits,” Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 892.

III.---Things monks must avoid.

The vices of certain persons living in monasteries censured, St Ambrose, XVII, 814.---What monks must flee, St Jerome, XXII, 583.---How monks’ vices are to be corrected, Cassian, XLIX, 1142.---The conduct of lax monks elegantly described, St Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 254.---Monastic failings described, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 668.---What a monk ought to avoid, Ratherius of Verona, CXXXVI, 313.---“We have seen some leave monasteries, give themselves over to the service of certain powerful men, and then return to monasteries,” St Ambrose, XVII, 857.---Wandering monks, St Augustine, XL, 575.---Gyrovague monks excellently portrayed by Paulinus, St Paulinus, LXI, 918.---On wandering or fugitive monks, the same, LXVI, 966.---The manner and penalties under which returnees are to be received, St Benedict, LXVI, 526 ff.---They shall remain separated from the community, ibid., 530.---Deprived of the monastic habit, ibid.---Fugitive monks are to be sought out and brought back to the monastery, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 503, 760, 895.---Monks who escaped by flight from the monastery are discovered by miracle, ibid., 1155 ff.---Description of wandering monks, St Benedict of Aniane, CIII, 1211.---On monks constantly roaming about, St Peter Damian, CXLV, 260.---Travel abroad forbidden, Geoffrey of Vendôme, CLVII, 162.---How often fleeing monks are to be received, Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 446.---Nothing is more disgraceful than roaming through cities, St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 716.---On gyrovagues, Hugh of Cluny, CCIX, 889.---He who has deserted a monastery must return altogether, Ratherius of Verona, CXXXVI, 417 ff.---Why it is unfitting for a monk to live with his mother, St Jerome, XXII, 1078.---He ought to avoid looking upon women, the same, XXIII, 352.---Association with women condemned by the elders, Cassian, XLIX, 418.---That no woman should enter the monastery, the same, LXVI, 961.---Conversations with women without witnesses prohibited, ibid., 979.---Let women not frequent your dwelling, ibid., 985.---Women must never be seen at all, not even in the reception-room, the same, LXVIII, 390.---Abbot Equitius kept monks from conversation with nuns, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 168.---Monks who take wives are to be excommunicated, ibid., 487.---A monk’s marriage is invalid, ibid.---Monks must not introduce women into the monastery, ibid., 717.---Nor make them their spiritual co-mothers, ibid.---On women, Guido I the Carthusian, CLIII, 681.
