Monks greedy for riches are proved unworthy even of necessities, [Col. 0700] St Jerome, XXII, 1118.---Under the title of religion monks practised unjust gain, ibid., 1082.---The rich die with full money-bags, though they lived as if poor, ibid.---The wealth of Croesus disclosed at one man’s death, ibid., 1077.---Avaricious monks hunt after matrons’ wealth through their attentions, ibid., 596.---Those who become wealthier than they were as secular persons are condemned, ibid.---A monk who frequently talks about money is a trader, not a monk, ibid., 584.---Among monks, *philargyria*, or the vice of private ownership, is especially to be detested, Cassian, XLIX, 296.---Avarice and prodigality are equally to be avoided, St Benedict, LXVI, 542.---On avoiding avarice, the same, CIII, 691.---That Ananias and Sapphira sinned less than monks who possess money, St Peter Damian, CXLV, 253.---That a monk cannot possess Christ and money at the same time, ibid., 254.

Monks seeking offices of authority or the role of teacher censured, Cassian, XLIX, 353, 412 ff.---The ambition of monks, Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 33.---Ambitious monks rebuked, St Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 832, 833.

A monk should flee secular concerns, Cassian, XLIX, 775.---That no one should involve himself in outside affairs, the same, LXVI, 952.---On monks entangling themselves in worldly cares, Taio of Saragossa, LXXX, 849.---No one is to be sent alone on any business, the same, CIII, 480.---Monks must not attend secular courts, Burchard, CXL, 809.---Monks are forbidden to be at the king’s court, St Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 1155.---Monks must not attend secular courts, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 568.

Idle monks, St Augustine, XL, 575.---The idleness of monks, ibid., 560.---Against idleness, Regino of Prüm, CLIII, 893.---The sluggish and languid are censured, St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 525.---One must abstain from excessive joking and laughter, the same, LXVI, 957.---That a monk should laugh rarely, ibid., 967.---That a monk should cease swearing, ibid., 967.---Lying, swearing, and idle speech are to be condemned throughout the whole brotherhood, ibid., 989.---No oath is to be sworn at all, the same, LXVIII, 389.

Those who are lukewarm in monasteries are not to be cast out as dead but treated as sick, St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 246.---On the lukewarmness of monks, Taio of Saragossa, LXXX, 850.

Monks must avoid singularity within the community, Cassian, XLIX, 64.---Monks who love singularity censured, St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 852.---On the singularity of monks, Ivo of Chartres, CLXV, 544.

IV.---Things monks must fulfil.

On prayers, St Fructuosus of Braga, LXXXVII, 1099.---On reverence in prayer, the same, LXXXVIII, 1009.---On those who come late to the work of God, St Benedict of Aniane, LXXXVIII, 1009.---On those who come late to the work of God, the same, CIII, 445, 1151.---On reverence in prayer, ibid., 927.---On brothers working far from the oratory or travelling, ibid., 1204.---On common prayer, Bernard the Carthusian, CLIII, 896.---Obstacles to prayer, ibid., 897.---On prayer, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 681.---That the Psalms be sung in order every day, the same, LXVI, 964.---While psalmody is being sung, no one may speak or work with his hands, the same, LXVIII, 388.---On the course of Psalms, St Columbanus, LXXX, 212.---On the divine offices at night, the same, LXXXVIII, 1002.---On the divine offices by day, ibid., 1004 ff.---On discipline in psalmody, ibid., 1008.---On the duty of psalm-singing, the same, CIII, 555.---On the governance of monks, St Dunstan of Canterbury, CXXXVII, 479.---How a brother should rise for Nocturns, Udalric of Cluny, CXLIX, 705.---How he should conduct himself at the regular hours, ibid., 705.---How he should carry a wooden lantern to Nocturns, ibid., 706.---The annual customary of the monks of St Benedict, Lanfranc, CL, 446 ff.---On the divine office, Guigo I the Carthusian, CLIII, 639, 651, 723, 895.---On the ceremonies to be observed both at the canonical hours and in the celebration of Masses, the same, CLXVI, 1422.---At all times monks shall devote two hours a day to spiritual meditation, the same, LXVI, 981.---On various matters concerning meditation, the same, CLIII, 810, 830 ff., 836, 838, 840, 845, 855.---A monk’s meditation is fourfold, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 681.

On manual labour, St Jerome, XXX, 362.---Manual work prescribed for Egyptian monks, Cassian, XLIX, 389, 390.---On daily manual labour, St Benedict, LXVI, 704.---On the craftsmen of the monastery, ibid., 801.---That no one may presumptuously dare to enter the workshops of the craftsmen without being ordered, ibid., 955.---On those who wish to learn any craft, ibid., 756.---That each should promptly undertake work in the mill or any work of the ground, ibid., 956.---On the safekeeping of tools in work, [Col. 0701] ibid., 957.---That a monk should do some work every day, ibid., 969.---On Sunday night, in reverence for the Lord’s resurrection, manual labour should cease, ibid., 980.---When they make bread, or in every bodily ministry, they should mutually lighten one another’s labour, ibid., 981.---While they work with their hands, holy meditation should not cease in the heart, the same, LXVIII, 391.---It is not alien to monks to cultivate gardens and work fields, Cassiodorus, LXX, 1142.---Manual labour, St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 1059.---On work, St Fructuosus of Braga, LXXXVII, 1102.---On tools and implements, ibid., 1103; LXXXVIII, 985.---How brothers ought to work, St Benedict of Aniane, CIII, 438.---On the work of monks, ibid., 445.---While working, let them say nothing secular, ibid., 478.---On monks’ work, ibid., 555, 1175.---On the craftsmen of the monastery, ibid., 1259.---Monks perform daily agricultural work, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 260.---On manual labour, Udalric of Cluny, CXLIX, 675.---On how manual work is regularly to be performed, St William, CL, 1105.---On manual labour, Guido of Farfa, CL, 1255; CLIII, 880.---Monks are bound to manual work for only two reasons, Guibert of Nogent, CLVI, 1055.---That a monk should always work, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 544.---On labour, CLXVI, 1450.---It is clear that manual labour is not a command of blessed Benedict but merely permitted, Rupert of Deutz, CLXX, 514.---On regular discipline, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 682.---It belongs to them to live by the labour of their hands, St Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 607.---The life of monks is in labour, ibid., 589.---That monks should read daily until Terce, the same, LXVI, 968.---That a monk should have frequent reading in his hands, ibid., 966.---That no monk should be ignorant of letters, ibid., 963.---From the sixth hour to the ninth they should give themselves to rest or reading, ibid., 981.---Books of the gentiles are to be read more rarely by monks, ibid., 328.---Let monks learn all letters, the same, LXVIII, 391.---Monks who do not devote themselves to sacred reading rebuked, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 605.---Let there always be either work or a little book in the hands, Alcuin, C, 216.---Study of Holy Scripture commended to them because of the spread of heresies, ibid., 298.---On monks’ reading, the same, CIII, 445.---All shall have permission to read until the third hour, ibid., 480.---On monks eager to study grammar, St Peter Damian, CXLV, 306.---On reading, Bernard the Carthusian, CLIII, 897.---A monk should not spend his life on the pursuit of schools, St Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 1102.---How brothers should conduct themselves during reading-time, St Stephen of Aster, CLXVI, 1446.

Professed monks may not return to the world, St Benedict, LXVI, 819.---Monks who willingly leave the enclosure of the monastery harm themselves and others, St Anselm of Canterbury, CLIX, 57.---An abbot ought not grant monks permission to leave the enclosure, ibid.---A monk ought to remain in the monastery in which he first made profession, St Anselm of Canterbury, CLIX, 123.---He who freely made a monk’s vow in one monastery and then in another is bound to remain in the first, the same, CLVIII, 1173.---Stability in a monastery is required unless it is such that the monk is unwillingly compelled there to do evil, ibid., 1096.---He who has publicly worn the monastic habit, even if he has not read the profession, is bound before God always to live in the holy resolve and habit, the same, CLIX, 191.

Hospitality to be practised by monks, Cassian, XLIX, 556.---On receiving guests, St Benedict, LXVI, 750.---How clerical guests ought to be received in a monastery, the same, CIII, 440.---On receiving guests, ibid., 483, 571, 1215; Guido of Farfa, CL, 1278; CXIII, 712; CLXVI, 1462.

How the sick ought to be cared for in a monastery, St Fructuosus of Braga, LXXXVII, 1116.---How bodily illnesses ought to be recognized by the Father who presides, the same, CIII, 239.---On sick brothers, ibid., 571, 1083.---On one who wishes to visit a sick brother, St William, CL, 989.---On servants who attend the sick person, ibid., 1127.---What is to be done when the community enters to visit a sick person, ibid., 1288.---On care for the dead, the same, CLIII, 660.---On care for the sick, ibid., 714, 715; CLXVI, 1465.

V.---On the faults of monks.

On the diversity of faults, St Columbanus, LXXX, 216.---On the offences of monks, St Fructuosus of Braga, LXXXVII, 1105.---On the guilty, ibid., 1107.---What is to be observed concerning monks who fall away from their own monastery through vices, ibid., 1127.---On excommunication for faults, the same, LXXXVIII, 976.---How an excommunicated brother ought to be treated, ibid., 976.---How an excommunicated person ought to do penance, ibid., 978.---On a monk’s offences, St Egbert of York, LXXXIX, 422.---How each person’s faults are to be corrected, St Benedict of Aniane, CIII, 440.---On offenders, ibid., 577.---On offences, ibid., 568.---On excommunication for faults, ibid., 973.---On graver faults, ibid., 999.---On those who offend in any other matters, ibid., 1026.---How boys of younger age are to be corrected, ibid., 1039.---A disobedient monk is like Adam, St Peter Damian, CXLIV, 424.---On a lighter fault, Udalric of Cluny, CXLIX, 708.---On a graver fault and other kinds of faults, ibid., 724.---On faults and satisfactions, Lanfranc, CL, 497.---On a lighter fault, ibid., 387.---On a graver fault, St William, CL, 1043.---Let a light fault be restrained by such a procedure, ibid., 1259.---A monk ought to reveal his own sins and those of others to the abbot, Geoffrey of Vendôme, CLVII, 179.---How he ought to behave in chapter, ibid., 228, 229.---A comparison between a monk who sins and a layperson, the same, CLIX, 654.---On monks who do not keep their profession, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 548.

VI.---On the clothing of monks.

Monastic clothing, St Ambrose, XVI, 957.---What colour garment monks used, ibid., 48.---On clothing, St Jerome, XXX, 361.---On the habit of a monk, Cassian, XLIX, 59.---On the monk’s belt, ibid., XI.---On the monastery.

On its various names.---The monastery, the house of God, St Benedict, LXVI, 546.---The Lord’s sheepfold, ibid., 256.---A snare, ibid., 388.---A fulling workshop, ibid., 550.---Compared to Noah’s ark, ibid., 228.---Monasteries are fishponds of souls, St Peter Damian, CXLV, 766.---The monastery, paradise, St Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXIII, 1083.---Jerusalem, the holy city, the same author, CLXXXII, 169 and following.---God’s tabernacle, ibid., 116.---A place of penitence, ibid., 667.---The flowering little bed of the bride, the same author, CLXXXIII, 1004.---A prison, ibid., 519.---Monasteries compared to ponds, ibid., 506.

On the foundation and exemptions of monasteries.---What must be observed in founding or constructing monasteries, St Benedict, LXVI, 906.---Monasteries should not be built without the bishop’s permission, ibid., 909.---Monasteries ought to be remote from the courts of princes, from places of devotion or pilgrimage, and from cities, ibid., 907.---Where monasteries, as regular places, should be situated, ibid., 909.---Before a monastery is built, a cross must first be placed, especially where the altar is to stand, ibid.---A monastery cannot be founded on another’s property against the owner’s will, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 684.---A monastery should not be consecrated unless a lawful endowment has first been assigned, ibid., 1117, 1271.

The principal cause of monasteries’ exemptions was oppression of subjects, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 458, 1341.---Or the avarice of prelates, ibid., 723.---Monastic exemptions far more ancient than Gregory the Great, ibid., 458.---Monasteries should in no way be subject to any secular services, ibid., 580, 1342.---A monastery’s exemption from the bishop’s jurisdiction should favour regular discipline, not impunity for vices, ibid., 580.---When an abbot dies, bishops should neither inventory nor administer the monastery’s property, ibid., 578, 1341 and following.---If any disputes arise, let them be referred to elected abbots and Fathers who fear God, the same author, LXXIII, 579.---On monastic privileges, ibid.---A bishop should not celebrate public Masses in a monastery, the same author, LXXVII, 579, 1342.---Why this is forbidden to him, ibid., 832.---A bishop may not place his cathedra in a monastery, ibid.---A bishop is to have no authority to command or to make even the slightest regulation in monasteries, unless requested by the abbot, ibid., 580, 1342.---A bishop should not visit monasteries too often, lest they be burdened, ibid., 919, 920.---Monasteries should not be burdened by clerics, ibid., 820, 821.---The exemption of abbots from diocesan bishops disapproved, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 139.

The goods of monasteries.---The common goods of monasteries, St Jerome, XXIII, 57.---Monasteries ought to be endowed with sufficient income, but not abound in riches, St Benedict, LXVI, 908.---By common law, the goods of converts are acquired by the monastery in the very act of a monk’s profession, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 673, 1061.---Monks’ property passed to the monastery, and consequently their debts as well, ibid., 663.---What has once been joined to a monastery’s ownership escapes the right of another acquisition, ibid., 1067, 1077.---Goods common to a monastery and a hospice are ordered to be divided, ibid., 1076.---What the abbot acquires, he acquires not for himself but for the monastery, ibid., 1067.---For what purpose the goods of monasteries were bestowed, Guibert, CLVI, 1062.

CLIX. INDEX ON VIRGINS.

In which are discussed: I. The nature and excellence of virginity.---II. Things to which virgins are compared.---III. Virginity among the pagans.---IV. The consecration of virgins.---V. The duties of virgins.---VI. The virtues of virgins.---VII. The prerogatives and reward of virginity.---VIII. The preservation and loss of virginity.---IX. Whether virginity is a precept.---X. Objections against virginity answered.---XI. Rules, treatises, and homilies on virginity.

[INDEX ON VIRGINS.]

I.---On the nature and excellence of virginity.

Virginity consists in grace, Tertullian, I, 1287; II, 903, 915.---Already on earth, by not marrying, they are assigned to the angelic household, the same author, I, 1281.---Chastity is the flower of morals, the honour of bodies, the beauty of the sexes, integrity of blood, etc., the same author, II, 980.---The more sublime glory of virginity, St Cyprian, IV, 443.---Virginity is that flower of the Church’s seed, the glory and ornament of spiritual grace, etc., ibid.---The image of God corresponding to the Lord’s holiness, the more illustrious portion of Christ’s flock, ibid.---Virginity depicted under the form of a garment and a pearl, St Hilary, X, 549.---Its advantages and endowments, 550.---Virginity is a spiritual kind of marriage, St Optatus, XI, 1074.---The name “virgin” is a title of modesty, St Ambrose, XVI, 190.---What is virginal chastity but integrity free from defilement? ibid., 194.---Merit is produced not by virginity of the flesh alone, but also by integrity of mind, ibid., 270.---Virginity displays the life of angels, ibid., 342.---It is no wonder if virgins are compared with angels, since they are joined to the Lord of angels, ibid., 191.---Marriage is honourable, but integrity more honourable, ibid., 256.---Marriage is good, through which posterity for the succession of humankind has been found; but virginity is better, through which a heavenly inheritance is acquired, ibid., 1124.---Would you know how great is the beauty of her who is loved by the King and approved by the Judge? etc., ibid., 199.---Nothing is so excellent and useful as virginity, the same author, XVII, 221.---Virginity is the praise of age: it befits adolescence, adorns youth, and enhances old age, XVI, 242.---The excellence of virginity, anonymous author, XVIII, 77.---The good of virginity demonstrated, Sulpicius Severus, XX, 228.---On the comparison of virginity and marriage, St Jerome, XXIII, 203, 229.---Virginity is against nature and beyond nature, the same author, XXII, 1116.---Wherein the virginal privilege consists, the same author, XXV, 442.---Praise of virginity, the same author, XXX, 163.---Virginity received its name from abstinence from unlawful acts, St Augustine, XXXVIII, 574, 575.---Virginity is an imitation of heavenly life, the same author, XL, 398.---It is an angelic portion, and, in corruptible flesh, a continual meditation upon incorruption, ibid., 401.---Even bodily virginity is spiritual, ibid., 400.---Virginity is honoured because it is dedicated to God, ibid.---Virginity is to be preferred to marriage, the same author, XLIV, 142.---No marital fruitfulness can be compared with it, the same author, XL, 399, 400.---Virginity should be preferred in such a way that marriage is not condemned, ibid., 404.---Virginity is set before marriage not as good before evil, but as better before good, XLV, 1418.---Virginity of the flesh: an untouched body; virginity of the heart: incorrupt faith, the same author, XXXVII, 1920.---Virginity of mind, the same author, XXXIX, 1495.---Virginity of mind is faith, hope, and charity, the same author, XXXV, 1499.---Encomium of virginity, XXXIV, 112.---“Virgin” is a name of integrity, not of age, ibid., 492.---Virgins, a more honourable member of Christ, the same author, XXXV, 1499.---Everyone is counted among virgins who has not admitted corruption through the senses, XXXVII, 1920.---Virginity consists in integrity of heart and body, Cassian, XLIX, 1229, 1230.---What true and incorrupt virgins of Christ are like, etc., ibid., 1230.---Virginity of the flesh: an untouched body; virginity of the soul: incorrupt faith, St Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 438, 521.---Virginity is ever akin to angels, St Peter Chrysologus, LII, 583.---To live in the flesh beyond the flesh is not an earthly life but a heavenly one, ibid.---To acquire angelic glory is greater than to possess it, ibid.---Virginity rivals angelic integrity, St Leo the Great, LV, 130.---Virginity is loftier than either good, Gennadius of Marseilles, LVIII, 996, 1037.---Virginity of mind and body is better than other gifts, St Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 328.---A manifold comparison between virginity and marriage, ibid., 329.---Virginity far superior to carnal marriage, ibid., 330.---A twofold virginity, ibid., 333.---What use is bodily virginity if one is not a virgin in mind? St Columbanus, LXXX, 211.---The pre-eminence of virginity over marriage, Taio of Saragossa, ibid., 859.---From what virginity is named, St Isidore of Seville, LXXXII, 417.---Virginity is loftier than either good, the same author, LXXXIII, 1241.---Let virginity be praised, lest marriage be condemned, ibid., 805.---The twofold good of virginity, ibid., 643.---The dignity of virginity, Alcuin, C, 468.---Virginity of mind, virginity of body, St Agobard, CIV, 206.---It is beyond the use of nature, Rabanus Maurus, CX, 72.---For it becomes the true image of God, corresponding to the Lord’s holiness, the more illustrious portion of Christ’s flock, ibid.---What a virgin signifies typologically, the same author, CXII, 1080.---The origin of virginity, St Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 1000 and following.---Virginity is a virtue more than natural, Guibert, CLVI, 137.---Nothing can be more pleasing, nothing sweeter to a good mind, than true virginity, ibid., 497.---How excellent and arduous virginity is, ibid., 580.---Virginity of the flesh joined with virginity of mind, Rupert of Deutz, CLXIX, 1091.---What virginity is, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 629.---Virginity is a certain freedom of the flesh, ibid., 195.---On the threefold virginity, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 843.---Virginity is Christ’s offering, whose mind no thought and whose flesh no lust has defiled, Hervaeus, CLXXXI, 887.---On the beauty and excellence of true virginity, St Bernard, CLXXXIV, 690.---What virginity of heart is, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 70.---What virginity of flesh is, ibid.---Commendation of virginity, CXCI, 1595 and following.---Virginity surpasses human nature, ibid.---Virgins are Christ’s forms, Richard of St Victor, CXCVI, 516.---Virgins are close to the angelic manner of life, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 245.

II.---Things to which virgins are compared.

The flower of that ecclesiastical offspring, St. Cyprian, IV, 443.---The image of God corresponding to the holiness of the Lord, ibid.---Virgins are Christ’s lilies, St. Ambrose, XVI, 327; XV, 1732.---Those women who do not marry, and those men who do not take wives, are like angels on earth, ibid., 342.---Virgins are compared to bees, ibid., 200.---Enclosed gardens, ibid., 201.---They are like lilies full of myrrh, displaying the whiteness of integrity and the glory of bodily allurements put to death, ibid., 1361; St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 476.---Virgins of both sexes are signified by the chariot-team of white horses, Rupert of Deutz, CLXVIII, 740.---As, amid an abundance of dew or of the early and latter rain, the growth of a well-cultivated garden gladdens the eye with blooming roses and gleaming lilies, so virgins are seen throughout the whole world, 775.---Virginity is the flower of a garden, to which modest reserve is kindred, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1000.---Virginity is compared to Lebanon, id., CLXXXIV, 89, 90.---What beauty can be compared with your flowering virginity, which is your true and distinctive lily? ibid., 690.

## On the establishment and origin of virginity

Virginity has the authority of antiquity from the beginning of the age, and the fullness of its profession from Christ, St. Ambrose, XVI, 192.---We do not readily find virgins on earth until God descended into these limbs of an earthly body, ibid.---Virginity flowed down from heaven, ibid.---Its author is the immaculate Son of God, ibid., 194.---Christ is the source of integrity: he taught virgins to dedicate integrity of mind and body more to the Holy Spirit than to a husband, ibid., 600.---Virginity is dedicated by the virgin Savior, St. Jerome, XXII, 406, 510.---Whence the gift of virginity flowed more richly to women, ibid., 408.---How virginal dignity began from the Mother of the Lord, XXXVIII, 348.---The Virgin’s Son, author and bridegroom of virginity, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 326.---It summoned from heaven what it might imitate on earth, Rabanus Maurus, CX, 72.---Before the incarnation of the Savior, few vowed and consecrated their virginity to God, Godfrey of Deutz, CLXXIV, 978.---Blessed Mary was the first of all to vow virginity, Alan of Lille, CCX, 65.

## III.—On virginity among the heathen

There are also virgins among the heathen: among the Romans, and in the town of Aegium in Africa, Tertullian, I, 1284.---We know virgins of Vesta, Juno, Apollo, and Minerva, Tertullian, II, 928.---They were forced into the profession of virginity, Zeno, XI, 289.---Among the Gentiles, virginity is customarily held venerable amid altars and hearths. St. Ambrose, XVI, 269.---It is sought by the nations, but when consecrated it is violated; it is attacked by barbarians and unrecognized by the rest, ibid., 192 ff.---The Gentiles do not possess a holy virgin, ibid., 193.---The perpetual chastity of the virgins of Vesta, Apollo, Juno, etc., St. Jerome, XXIII, 270.---Virgins were always held in honor among the Romans, ibid., 271.---Among the twelve signs of heaven, the Gentiles placed a virgin, ibid.---Virginity commended among heathen priests, id., XXII, 1051.---Among the heathen it always held first place, id., XXIII, 270.---Fables concerning persons begotten by virgins, ibid., 273.

## IV.—On the consecration of virgins

Those who have once professed virginity ought not to be compelled again to profess it anew, St. Optatus, XI, 1071 ff.---Young girls may profess virginity, St. Ambrose, XVI, 276.---It ought to be a matter of priestly caution that a girl not be veiled rashly, ibid.---Mothers who prevent their daughters from professing virginity are reproved, ibid., 205.---It is more glorious if virgins embrace virginity despite resisting parents, ibid., 206.---A memorable deed of a certain noble and devout virgin wishing to profess virginity despite her parents’ resistance, ibid., 206.---A virgin publicly professing chastity, ibid., 382.---Offering her hair to be consecrated by the sacred veil, ibid., 331.---Virgins were veiled on Easter Day, ibid., 348.---The words with which Ambrose offers a sacred virgin to God at the altar, ibid., 372.---The people affirm the virgin’s profession, saying, “Amen,” ibid.---She who has pledged herself to Christ and received the holy veil is now married, now joined to an immortal husband, ibid., 373.---A virgin consecrated by profession who wishes to marry under the common law of matrimony commits adultery and becomes a slave of death, ibid.---Virgins to be consecrated come from the district of Piacenza, from that of Bologna, and from Mauretania, that they may be veiled at Milan, ibid., 204 ff.---How many virgins the Church of Alexandria, and the whole Church of the East and of Africa, customarily consecrated, ibid., 275.---So great is the number of virgins that they constitute a community of modesty, a people of integrity, an assembly of virginity, ibid., 975.---Virginity is honored because dedicated to God, St. Augustine, XL, 400.---The vow of virginity, ibid., 412.---The sealing of virginity, id., XXXIII, 229.---Some vow virginity from their earliest age, XXXVI, 967.---The more eminent rank in the Church of those who vow virginity, XXXV, 1459.---Praise of the virginal profession, XXXIII, 645.---With what care girls were examined before being admitted to dedicate virginity to God, St. Nicetas, LII, 1086.---What age was required of girls for admission to make their resolution of virginity, ibid., 1094.---In solemn veiling consisted the public and full profession of the virginal resolution, ibid., 1097.---What the veiling of virgins signified, and whence this ceremony of veiling virgins was derived, ibid.---Evidence for the veiling of virgins in the first and second centuries in the Roman Church, ibid., 1098, 1099.---Antiquity called the veil of virgins sacred and holy, and the source of its holiness, ibid., 1099.---Further matters concerning this virginal veil, relating to its form, material, quality, and use, are transmitted chiefly from a certain passage of Tertullian, ibid., 1099, 1100.---The veiling of virgins was called *consecration* in antiquity, and was always so called, ibid., 1100.---This was performed at the divine altar, especially on the holy day of the Lord’s Resurrection, ibid., 1000, 1001.---This solemnity was also held on the Nativity of our Savior; finally, other feasts too were appointed for it, ibid.---Offerings of virgins at the sacred altar, St. Leo the Great, LV, 49, 50.---Their names recited at the altar itself, ibid.---Their blessing, ibid., 129.---The days on which virgins are to be veiled, LVI, 697.---The age at which they are to be consecrated, ibid., 868.---The profession of virginity, and the treatment of those who violate it, ibid., 441, 544, 700.---Those not yet veiled who have pretended to remain in the resolution of virginity, if afterward they wish to marry, are to be subjected to penance, ibid., 526.---It is an ancient custom of Christians for virgins to be consecrated to God, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 428.---It belongs to the bishop to consecrate virgins, ibid., 173.---A priest is not to consecrate virgins without consulting the bishop, ibid.---The days on which virgins are commanded to be consecrated, ibid.---Formerly virgins consecrated to God wore dark clothing, ibid., 173.---The age at which a virgin’s veiling is to take place, LXXVIII, 429.---The year of age in which a profession of virginity is to be made, ibid.---Formerly virgins sacred to God were veiled with a solemn rite, ibid., 174.---In parts of Egypt and Syria, religious women—that is, virgins and widows—were formerly tonsured, ibid., 431.---Subsequently the tonsure of religious women came into use among Latins and Greeks, ibid.---The age required for consecrating virgins, [Col. 0711] St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 373.---The sacred veil is not to be placed on virgins to be veiled except at Epiphany, or at other Paschal feasts, or at the feasts of the apostles’ nativities, and not before twenty-five years of age, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1175.---Virgins who have spent many years of their life in monasteries are forbidden to marry, 1178.

## V.—The duties of virgins

Virgins who have dedicated themselves to Christ in faith are to persevere in chastity, St. Cyprian, IV, 366.---Virgins ought not to live with men, ibid., 365.---It belongs to virgins to tremble and to fear every entrance of men, to dread every male enticement, St. Ambrose, XV, 1555.---She ought to know Christ whom she loves, and to recognize in him the whole mystery both of his unbegotten divinity and of his assumed incarnation, id., XVI, 201.---Let her persist in prayers, and let her face grow pale through continual supplication, ibid., 357.---Let her mouth resound with praise of the Lord, gratitude to the Bridegroom, and confession of the cross, as she recites the Creed and sings psalms in her chamber, ibid., 353.---Although many profess devotion to chastity, they seek aids to beauty beyond what befits those consecrated to the Lord, ibid., 360.---Let her seriousness be the first thing to announce a virgin: modest reserve in meeting others, sober gait, modest expression, ibid., 223.---Not even a freer sort of merriment is fitting in virgins, ibid., 358.---I wish visits to younger virgins to be less frequent, ibid., 222.---Celebrations of banquets are to be avoided, greetings shunned, ibid.---Virgins are prepared to die for the preservation of integrity, ibid., 272.---A vowed virgin who has publicly professed virginity is kept from the company and familiarity of secular people, id., XVII, 881.---Virgins ought to refuse the small gifts of men offered under a pretext of piety, ibid., 703.---A virgin ought to flee the company of married women, St. Jerome, XXII, 403.---Let going out in public be rare, ibid., 404.---Virgins who strive to please men by more elegant dress are reproved, St. Augustine, XL, 415.---Let virgins love the Bridegroom with their whole heart, ibid., 427, 428.---A virgin must turn neither to the right nor to the left, St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 331.---A virgin who has vowed virginity, if she marries, will incur condemnation, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1175.---Virgins and widows who depart from their resolution of virginity and widowhood are condemned, ibid., 1178.---Virgins who have spent many years of their life in monasteries are forbidden to marry, ibid., 1179.---Sacred virgins ought not to attend weddings, Rupert of Deutz, CLXIX, 278.

## VI.—The virtues of virgins

The virtues a virgin ought to possess, St. Ambrose, XVI, 330.---Let there be simplicity in her heart, moderation in her words, modesty toward all, devotion toward relatives, and mercy toward the needy and poor, ibid., 332.---She ought to be gentle, humble, and meek, ibid., 327.---A virgin’s manifest modesty confirms her integrity, ibid., 893.---Let modesty, sobriety, and self-restraint gird the hair of sacred virginity, ibid., 332.---Foremost among all excels the pursuit of sobriety, and its proper character, ibid., 360.---Let her seriousness be the first thing to announce a virgin: modest reserve in meeting others, sober gait, modest expression, ibid., 223.---In virgins, modest reserve adorns their age, and silence commends their modesty, ibid., 222.---Nothing is holier in a virgin than shamefastness, ibid., 893.---Ambrose shows what sort of virgins those already vowed ought to be, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 113.---Virginity is shameful without virtues, XXXVI, 968.---Love of sacred virgins, id., XXXVIII, 884.---Fear is necessary even for virgins—not worldly or servile fear, but the chaste fear of God, id., XL, 418.---What a virgin ought to consider, so that she may truly not dare to prefer herself to a married woman, ibid., 422.---Virginity must be guarded by humility, ibid., 396.---Humility is especially commended to virgins, ibid., 412, 413, 414 ff., 426, 427.---However great virgins are, let them humble themselves in all things, id., XXXVIII, 1020.---The holier they are, the humbler let them be, id., XL, 427.---A humble marriage is better than a proud virginity, id., XXXVI, 968; XXXVI, 1280.---The manner in which humility should be practiced by virgins, id., XL, 426, 427.---Charity is the guardian of virginity; humility is the dwelling-place of this guardian, ibid.---She who is corrupt in heart is a virgin in body in vain, id., XXXVII, 1168.---All virgins ought to be in the faith, XXXVIII, 1064.---The holy virgin’s pursuit is justice, piety, faith, charity, patience, and meekness, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 335.---The union of virginity with humility is the highest perfection in this life, ibid., 325.---Bodily virginity cannot attain Christ without humility, ibid., 338.---True humility is virginity’s inner virginity, ibid.---Humility in preserving virginity, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 106.

## VII.—The prerogatives and reward of virginity

[Col. 0712]

Virginity is destined for the kingdom of God, St. Cyprian, IV, 444.---A great reward awaits you: a great prize of virtue, a supreme gift of chastity, ibid., 461.---Angels fell from heaven into the world because of their intemperance; virgins have passed from the world into heaven because of their chastity, St. Ambrose, XVI, 203.---Virginal chastity merits the protection of the angels, whose life it merits, ibid., 202.---Through a man and a woman flesh was expelled from paradise; through the Virgin it was joined to God, ibid., 1198.---Christ has assigned no fuller gifts to any than to virginity, ibid., 317.---Virgins have rewards in heaven surpassing those of others, ibid., 341.---The nature of virginity’s reward, Sulpicius Severus, XX, 228.---The recompense of virgins and chastity, St. Jerome, XXII, 424.---Virginity begins to be crowned after death, id., XXIII, 241.---Marriage fills the earth; virginity fills paradise, ibid., 235.---The future glory of virgins is greater, with joys in heaven peculiarly their own, St. Augustine, XL, 410.---To follow the Lamb wherever he goes belongs especially to virgins, ibid., 411.---The song of virgins, which no one else can sing, ibid., 410.---Virgins yield the sixtyfold fruit, id., XXXV, 1325.---Holy virginity is adorned by Christ so that it may remain beautiful, and crowned so that it may reign gloriously, St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 326.---Christ is the fruit, beauty, and gift of holy virginity, ibid.---Virginity’s future reward will be great, ibid., 331.---Virgins sing the song to the Lamb in a distinctive manner, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 106; Taio of Saragossa, LXXX, 859.---How great the heavenly blessedness possessed by holy virginity, Amalarius of Metz, CV, 954.---Virginity is a holy thing, possessing a special crown in God’s kingdom, Rabanus Maurus, CX, 72.---The three prerogatives of virgins, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 629.---The prerogatives of virginity in the present and in the future, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 257.

## VIII.—On preserving and losing virginity

The holiness of virginity is violated by the very act of looking, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1199.---How uncertainly trustworthy the inspection and visitation of virgins are, ibid., 893, 894.---Other proofs and testimonies are required for examining virginity, ibid., 895.---The fall of a consecrated virgin is mourned most bitterly, ibid., 367.---How great and what kind of penance is necessary for a fallen virgin, ibid., 376.---He who corrupts a sacred virgin has certainly committed adultery and sacrilege, ibid., 379.---The penance which he must undergo, ibid., 380.---Rules for preserving the integrity of virginity are given, St. Jerome, XXII, 410.---How difficult it is to preserve it intact, ibid., 401.---Virginity once lost is not compensated by any fruitfulness of the flesh, St. Augustine, XL, 410.---Virgins who, through their own fault, have been violated by force ought not to dare compare themselves with those uncontaminated, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 653.---A virgin’s adornment is to preserve the good of virginity no less in mind than in body, St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 331.---To preserve chastity one must remain continually vigilant, Guibert of Nogent, CLVI, 582.---The means by which the virtue of chastity ought to be defended, ibid., 591.---The ways in which virginity is defiled, ibid., 602.---Monastic observances and flight from secular persons are the best remedy for safeguarding virginity, ibid., 604.---Virginity is lost irrecoverably and must be preserved without end, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 726.---She who has lost virginity through fornication is faithless to God, perjured against God, and an adulteress of Christ, ibid., 726.---Lamentation for lost virginity, 725 ff.---After losing virginity, more persons have pleased God more by penitent chastity than many others, though holy in virginity, id., CLIX, 192.---Bodily virginity is lost through defilement, but spiritual virginity can be recovered, Rupert of Deutz, CLXVIII, 53.---Virginity is lost through sodomy, id., CLXX, 546 ff.---Virginity is judged preserved so long as bodily integrity remains, ibid., 547.---It is endangered in a proud mind, ibid., 550.---Virginity of mind is lost through desire for a man or a woman, 549 ff.---Whether a woman whose defilement is unproved and who is not of ill repute may be consecrated in a monastery, ibid., 558.

## IX.—Whether virginity is a commandment

The first decree commanded increase and procreation; the second commended continence, St. Cyprian, IV, 463.---Virginity is a matter of will, not necessity, St. Optatus, XI, 1073 ff.---Virginity, being above the law, is not commanded, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1199.---It cannot be commanded, but may be desired, ibid., 195.---It alone can be urged, not commanded, ibid., 341.---It is more a matter of vow than of precept, ibid.---Why it is urged and not commanded, ibid., 255, 259.---The Apostle gives counsel, not a command, for attaining virginity, [Col. 0713] Sulpicius Severus, XX, 229.---Why no command is given concerning virginity, St. Jerome, XXII, 507.---Virginity is a work of supererogation, not of commandment, St. Augustine, XL, 412.---Christ intended virginity to be free, ibid., 398.---Virginity is commended not by command but by counsel, for winning singular glory in the future life, ibid., 402 ff.---Virginity is a matter of will, not necessity, St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 193.---Paul offers not a command but counsel concerning virginity, ibid.---Why virginity was not commanded, id., LXXV.---The first decree of God commanded increase and procreation; the second commended continence, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 805.---The old commandment required that the earth be filled with offspring, but the new that heaven be filled with continence and virginity, ibid.---Whether virginity is commanded, St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLIII, 159.

## X.—Answers to objections against virginity

It is proved that the state of virginity is neither evil nor new, St. Ambrose, XVI, 273.---Nor is it useless, ibid., 275.---Those who excluded virginity from the Church of God are reproved, ibid., 269.---Against those who think continence useful only for the present life, St. Augustine, XL, 401.---Two contrary errors concerning virginity and marriage, ibid., 405.---The objection from the denarius paid to all, against diversity of rewards, ibid., 410.---Answers to the customary petty objections against the virtue of chastity, Guibert of Nogent, CLVI, 600.

*Sermon on Virgins*, St. Bruno of Segni, CLXV, 1073.

*On the Violation of Virginity, and Whether a Defiled Woman May Be Consecrated*, Rupert of Deutz, CLXX, 544.

*Letter on Virginity*, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 193.

*On the Threefold Virginity*, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 843.

*On the Connection of Virginity and Humility*, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 669.

*On Virginity*, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1238.

*On the Three Disadvantages of the Present Life Which Virgins Escape, and the Corresponding Advantages of the Future Life Which Await Them*, CLXXXIV, 696, 699.

*On the Beauty and Excellence of True Virginity*, CLXXXIV, 690.

*On the Devout and Fruitful Words of Virgins*, CLXXXIV, 682.

*To Virgins*, Alan of Lille, CCX, 194.

[Col. 0713]

# CLX. INDEX ON NUNS

The following questions are discussed in this Index: I. On the profession and consecration of nuns.---II. On the obligations of nuns.---III. On the life of nuns, what it ought to be, and on their virtues.---IV. On matters to be avoided by nuns.---V. On the various superiors of nuns.---VI. On the faults and confession of nuns.---VII. On the meals, bathing, and sleeping of nuns.---VIII. On the convent of nuns; enclosure.---IX. Rules, books, sermons, and letters addressed to nuns.

## [INDEX ON NUNS]

### I.—On the profession and consecration of nuns

Young girls may profess virginity. St. Ambrose, XVI, 276.---It ought to be a matter of priestly caution that a girl not be veiled rashly, ibid. Mothers who prevent their daughters from professing virginity are reproved, ibid., 205. A memorable deed of a certain noble and devout virgin wishing to profess virginity despite her parents’ resistance, id., 206. A virgin publicly professing chastity, id., 382. Offering her hair to be consecrated by the sacred veil, id., 331. Virgins were veiled on Easter Day, id., 348. The words with which Ambrose offers a sacred virgin to God at the altar, ibid., 372.---The people affirm the virgin’s profession, saying, “Amen,” ibid.---Virgins to be consecrated come from the district of Piacenza, from that of Bologna, and from Mauretania, that they may be veiled at Milan, ibid., 204, 205.---How many virgins the Church of Alexandria, and the entire Church of the East and of Africa, customarily consecrated, ibid., 275.---So great is the number of virgins that they constitute a community of modesty, a people of integrity, an assembly [Col. 0714] of virginity, ibid., 975.---The profession and dwelling of monks, St. Augustine, XXXII, 1339.---Praise of the virginal profession, id., XXXIII, 645.---That sacred virgins be veiled on appointed days, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 306.---Concerning girls, at what time they are to be veiled, Charlemagne, XCVII, 526, 729.---That little children are not to be veiled, ibid., 777.---Concerning virgin girls not to be veiled by priests, ibid., 864.---Concerning abbesses and religious women who, contrary to the canons, impose the veil upon widows and girls, ibid.---According to the Greeks, a priest may consecrate a virgin with the sacred veil, id., XCIX, 1128.---That virgins are not to be consecrated before twenty-five years of age. Pseudo-Isidore, CXXX, 334.---How religious virgins are to be ordained, ibid., 339.---Concerning virgins who, under necessity, are veiled below twenty-five years of age, ibid., 374; CXXXII, 396.---Concerning the time when sacred virgins are to be veiled, ibid., 943.---At what time the sacred veil should be placed upon sacred virgins, Burchard, CXL, 795.---Concerning religious women who presume to veil others, CXL, 795.---Concerning the age at which virgins ought to be veiled, ibid.---The clothing in which virgins ought to come for consecration, ibid., 796.---Concerning girls who, before the lawful years, have of their own accord dedicated themselves to sacred religion, ibid., 812.---Concerning virgins who, before the age of twelve, have placed a veil upon themselves without the knowledge of their guardians, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 553.---At what time the veil ought to be placed upon sacred virgins, ibid.---Concerning religious women who presume to veil others, ibid., 554.---Concerning the age at which virgins ought to be veiled, ibid.---The clothing in which virgins ought to come for consecration, ibid., 555.---Women whose husbands have died are not to veil themselves quickly, ibid., 559.---The veil is to be imposed upon virgins only on specified days, ibid., 1175.---Virgins are not to be consecrated before their twenty-fifth year, ibid.; CLXXXVII, 1102.---They are not to be consecrated before their sixtieth year of age.

### II.—On the obligations of nuns

Concerning nuns who do not keep their resolution of chastity, Pope Siricius, XIII, 1137.---Concerning a veiled virgin who has changed her resolution, and the judgment on her, ibid., 1182.---She who has pledged herself to Christ and received the holy veil is now married, now joined to an immortal husband, St. Ambrose, XVI, 273.---A virgin consecrated by profession who wishes to marry under the common law of matrimony commits adultery and becomes a slave of death, ibid. That veiled handmaids of God, if by public marriage or secretly by defilement they have given themselves over to corruption, are not to be admitted to penance unless the man to whom they had joined themselves has departed from the world, St. Innocent I, XX, 480.---If a nun marries, she will be reckoned an adulteress, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1058.---That virgins professing continence are not to marry, Pope Symmachus, LXVI, 55.---Concerning virgins entering into the legal bonds of marriage, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 174.---Concerning veiled virgins, if they go astray, ibid., 244.---Nuns are not to marry, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1340. Nuns who marry are to be punished, ibid., 752.---Concerning veiled virgins, if they go astray, Pope St. Zachary, LXXXIX, 936.---Penalties against religious women committing adultery, Charlemagne, XCVII, 452; XCVIII, 91.---Concerning virgins who do not keep their resolution, Halitgar, CV, 689. Concerning religious women, if they depart from their sacred resolution, Burchard, CXL, 794.---That those consecrated to God may not enter into the legal bonds of marriage, ibid., 797.---Concerning nuns who have joined themselves to sacrilegious contamination, ibid., 797.---Concerning virgins who have violated their commitment, ibid.---Concerning virgins who do not keep their resolution, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 548.---Concerning consecrated virgins, if they have fallen, ibid., 549.---The offense committed by girls who abandon their voluntary resolution of virginity, ibid.---Concerning sacred virgins who have violated their commitment, ibid., 556.---How nuns who have fallen into adultery ought to do penance, ibid., 572.---Concerning virgins found with men in the same bed who do not confess defilement, ibid., 573.---That the incest of religious women is greater than adultery, ibid., 574.---Concerning widows and virgins who depart from their religious resolution, ibid., 1178.---Girls who of their own free will have undertaken the resolution of virginity may not choose marriage, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1101.

She ought to know Christ whom she loves, and to recognize in him the whole mystery both of his unbegotten divinity and of his assumed incarnation, St. Ambrose, XVI, 201.---Let her persist in prayers, and let her face grow pale through continual observance, XVI, 357.---The various exercises of a virgin, St. Jerome, XXII, 1119.---Let her mouth resound with praise of the Lord, gratitude to the Bridegroom, and confession of the cross, XVI, 353.---On Matins and the manner of reciting the divine office, St. Jerome, XXX, 419.---On the order for saying the hours of Prime, Terce, Sext, and None, ibid. Persist in prayers at the appointed hours and times, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 960.---Let nuns work in common, ibid., 963.---Let them request books at a fixed hour each day, ibid.---Let her work with her hands and be adorned with modest reserve, ibid., 1455.---Let a virgin always fearful guard herself by meditation on the word of God, ibid., 1461.---That at all times they devote two hours to reading, St. Caesarius of Arles, LXVII, 1109.---You ought so to devote yourselves to reading and prayer that, above all, you may also be able to perform something with your hands, St. Caesarius of Arles, ibid., 1124.---That, while seated at work, they either meditate on holy things or keep silence, ibid., 1109.---That a virgin pray and read continually, St. Leander, LXXII, 883.---How one is to hasten to the divine office, St. Donatus of Besançon, LXXXVII, 280.---On the discipline of psalmody in the Oratory, ibid., 281.---How sisters ought to cultivate silence, ibid.---How they should devote themselves to reading, ibid. How work ought to be done with the hands on ordinary days, id., LXXXVIII, 1063.---On nourishing and educating children, ibid., 1070; CV, 969.---What religious women ought to do, CXXXII, 316.---On the character of prayer, Adalger, CXXXIV, 928.

### III.—On the life of nuns, what it ought to be, and on their virtues

[Col. 0716]

The virtues a virgin ought to possess. St. Ambrose, XVI, 329, 330.---Let her be holy in body and spirit, XVIII, 84.---Examine the character of your Bridegroom, ibid., 85.---A virgin ought to adorn and compose herself, ibid. Let her indeed be adorned, but with inward ornaments, so that she may be arrayed spiritually, not carnally, ibid., 86.---Let her shine with the gold of righteousness and gleam with the jewels of holiness, ibid., 86.---Do all things as a daughter of God, ibid.---Present yourself so that heavenly birth may be apparent in you and divine nobility shine forth, ibid.---You must live by Christ’s example, ibid.---Strive more to be holy than to appear so, ibid., 88.---Ambrose shows what sort of virgins those already vowed ought to be, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 113.---Those who have vowed virginity lead the life of angels on earth, XXXVIII, 736.---The common life of religious women is praised, XXXVII, 1058.---The common life of religious women is more excellent, XL, 423.---On preferring the ornaments of virtues, XXXII, 1462.---Let life be held in common, ibid., 960.---Live all of you in unanimity and harmony, ibid.---Do not seek to please by clothing, but by character, ibid., 961.---In your walking, standing, dress, and every movement, let nothing be done that may entice anyone’s lust, but rather what befits your holiness, ibid.---What a virgin ought to be like, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 338.---As secure as you are concerning the past, so anxious be concerning the future, St. Caesarius of Arles, LXVII, 1122.---It is not enough to lay aside secular clothing and continually maintain good behavior; rather, against the evil and sweet pleasures of this world, while we live, we must labor with Christ’s help, ibid.---Hold firmly to the plow and do not look back, ibid., 1123.---Follow Christ by holding steadfastly what you have ardently willed, ibid., 1124.---In this life one must never cease to contend with vices, if one wishes to bear away triumph over the enemy, ibid., 1136.---Consider without interruption that you have been appointed a lamp of this Church, ibid., 1136.---What the life of a virgin dedicated to God ought to be, ibid., 1137.---How private life is to be avoided, St. Leander of Seville, LXXII, 890.---What are the instruments of good works, St. Donatus of Besançon, LXXXVII, 276.---Wise virgins and foolish virgins, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 903.---Let not the vanities of this world move you. They will lay those things aside even in death; your holiness will not abandon you, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 259.---The title of virginity will be obscured by depravity of character, ibid., 260.---From that point you will bear a false name and an empty veil, ibid.

She ought to be gentle, humble, and meek, St. Ambrose, XVI, 327.---On preserving community and kindness, St. Jerome, XXX, 396.---Let true humility be present, St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 338.---Meekness, that you may possess that land of the living in which David, in full faith, trusts that he will see the good things of the Lord, ibid. Having cast aside pride, which God resists, let her lay the foundation of profound humility, St. Caesarius of Arles, LXVII, 1122.---Let us preserve true humility as far as we can, ibid., 1123.---Above all, fleeing feigned humility, pursue that humility which is true, which Christ taught, and in which no pride is enclosed, ibid., 1127.---How many are the degrees of humility, St. Donatus of Besançon, LXXXVII, 285 ff.---On humility, Adalger, CXXXIV, 917.---Christ chose to have a humble mother, and he also wishes to have humble daughters, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 903.---Let the mind be chaste, the expression humble, and speech gentle, ibid., 905.

Nothing is so contrary to God, nothing so detestable, as to hate anyone or wish to harm anyone; nothing so commendable as to love all, Hildebert, XVIII, 87.---On preserving charity and unity, St. Jerome, XXX, 393.---On the love of God and neighbour, and first on how it is to be practised toward one’s neighbour by nuns, St. Augustine, XXXII, 1463.---On stirring up the love of God through meditation upon the mysteries of Christ, ibid., 1465.---But the love among you ought not to be carnal but spiritual, id., XXXIII, 964.---Preserve among yourselves the sweetness of charity, so that through holy conversations you may prepare spiritual remedies for one another, St. Caesarius of Arles, LXVII, 1123.---Love equally; do not love one woman more and another less, ibid., 1137.---What is to be preferred to love, ibid.---On loving one another, id., LXXXVIII, 1058.---I do not wish you to think those souls Christian who hate—not to say brothers or sisters—but who do not love their neighbours with their whole heart, St. Benedict of Aniane, CIII, 681.---On charity, Adalger, CXXXIV, 917.---This is the will of God: that there be no envy or detraction among you, but love alone, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 904.

On rendering obedience to superiors, St. Jerome, XXX, 398.---On reverence and submission toward the abbess, ibid., 399.---On readiness in carrying out commands, [Col. 0717] ibid., 402.---The prioress is to be obeyed as a mother, with honour preserved, lest God be offended in her, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 964.---Still more the presbyter who has charge of you all, ibid.---On changing one’s dress and rendering obedience, St. Caesarius of Arles, LXVII, 1107.---On loving one another or obeying one another, id., LXXXVIII, 1058.---On obedience, Adalger, CXXXIV, 918.

On seeking austerity in bedding, St. Jerome, XXX, 418.---On sobriety, ibid., 421.---On the quality and quantity of food and drink, St. Augustine, XXXII, 1457.---Subdue your flesh by fasts and abstinence from food and drink, insofar as health permits, id., XXXIII, 960.---On the observance of Lent, St. Donatus of Besançon, LXXXVII, 285.---On the manner in which the table is to be administered or observed, id., LXXXVIII, 1062.---On abstinence, Adalger, CXXXIV, 924.

On possessing nothing as one’s own, St. Jerome, XXX, 394.---Do not call anything your own, but let all things be common to you, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 960.---You know how much poverty of spirit ought to be present in a sacred virgin, St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 338.---Let no one consider anything her own property, St. Caesarius of Arles, LXVII, 1109.---Let all things be common to you, and let no one presume to call or claim anything as her own, St. Aurelian of Arles, LXVIII, 402.---That no one may be permitted to possess private property, St. Donatus of Besançon, LXXXVII, 278.---If poverty constrains you, endure it in common, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 904.

The modesty of a virgin is open to all, St. Ambrose, XVI, 893.---Let modesty bind up the hair of sacred virginity, ibid., 332.---Let a virgin first be announced by her own gravity, with modesty meeting the eye, a sober step, and a modest countenance, id., XVI, 223.---Let her possess the rosy colour of reserve and the purple hue of blushing and modesty, id., XVIII, 86.---Let there be in you a new gravity, admirable honourableness, astonishing reserve, a virginal bearing, the manner of true chastity, and speech always modest, ibid., 86.---In walking, standing, and dress, let nothing be done that may entice anyone’s lust, but only what befits your holiness, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 961.---And do not say that you have chaste minds if you have unchaste eyes, ibid.---Whenever you are together in church, and wherever men are present, guard one another’s chastity, ibid., 962.---On guarding the eyes, St. Caesarius of Arles, LXVII, 1110; St. Donatus of Besançon, LXXXVII, 288.---On restraint of the eyes, Adalger, CXXXIV, 921.---Beware of the temptation of the eyes, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 904.

IV.---Things to be avoided by nuns.

See that you do not in any respect love human glory, XVIII, 87.---Let them not hold their heads high because they are associated with women whom they would not have dared to approach outside, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 940.---Nor let them be exalted if they have contributed something from their own resources to the common life, ibid.---Pride even lies in wait for good works in order that they may perish, ibid.---A proud virgin is not Christ’s bride, St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 335.---Integrity of the flesh is not long preserved where the mind is corrupted by the swelling of pride, St. Caesarius of Arles, LXVII, 1123.---Above all, one must fight bravely against the sickness of pride; why this is so, ibid., 1126.---Pride raises up the minds of some women, either because they are more learned, more noble, or more prudent, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 903.---Let women noble by birth not prefer themselves to those of humbler birth, id., CV, 963.---Restrain your tongue from evil speech, and put upon your mouth the bridle of the law, id., XVIII, 88.---By the authority of Scripture frighten off slanderers of the absent as malicious persons, ibid.---On avoiding feigned and harmful speech, St. Jerome, XXX, 409.---On restraining the tongue in speaking, ibid., 411.---Whoever injures another by insult, curse, or even accusation of a crime, should remember to remedy as speedily as possible by satisfaction what she has done, id., XXXIII, 964.---Let her restrain her tongue, reject detraction as poison, utter no idle words, etc., St. Caesarius of Arles, LXVII, 1122.---Set a sufficiently watchful guard over your mouth, ibid., 1127.---That they ought not to quarrel among themselves or utter insults, St. Donatus of Besançon, LXXXVII, 289.---On restraint in speech, Adalger, CXXXIV, 922.---There are other virgins who delight in empty talk, slanders, and laughter, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 903.

Before all else I admonish you to flee the evil of rivalry as though it were viper’s poison, St. Caesarius of Arles, LXVII, 1123.---Let envy find no place in your soul, ibid., 1127.---A virgin ought to avoid the company of married women and secular men, St. Jerome, XXII, 403, 1121.

For preserving the reward of virginity I give this counsel: strive with all your strength to repel from yourselves, and from your hearts, unsuitable familiarity, [Col. 0718] St. Caesarius of Arles, LXVII, 1124.---The harmful effects of familiarity are enumerated, ibid.---Let her have associations with men as seldom as possible, ibid., 1130.---Young men, indeed, should either never, or only with difficulty, be seen, ibid.---In habitual familiarity, neither laymen nor religious men are ever to be admitted, ibid.---That laywomen are to be avoided, St. Leander of Seville, LXII, 881.---On avoiding even holy men, ibid., 882.---That a virgin ought to avoid young men, ibid.---Men, id., CV, 968.

That a nun should not secretly receive letters or any little gifts from anyone, St. Augustine, XXXII, 962.---Nothing is to be received secretly, St. Caesarius of Arles, LXVII, 1111.---Letters from no persons, not even parents, are to be received secretly, ibid., 1118.---Letters are neither to be given nor received without the knowledge or permission of the abbess, St. Aurelian of Arles, LXVIII, 401.

On detesting costly clothing, St. Jerome, XXX, 415.---On the danger of ambition in clothing, ibid., 416.---On seeking lowliness in dress, ibid., 417.---Their dress should not be conspicuous, nor should hairnets appear beneath their head-coverings, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 961.---On restraint in dress, Adalger, CXXXIV, 923.

Have no quarrels at all, or end them as swiftly as possible, lest anger grow into hatred, make a beam out of a speck, and make the soul a murderer, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 964.---Have no quarrels, St. Aurelian of Arles, LXVIII, 402.---Avoid occasions of discord and quarrels, St. Benedict of Aniane, CIII, 682.

V.---On the various officers of nuns.

Abbess.---On the governance of the abbess, St. Jerome, XXX, 399.---On reverence and submission toward the abbess, ibid.---On the office and authority of the abbess, ibid., 403.---On the order and works of the abbess, ibid., 405.---The prioress is to be obeyed as a mother, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 964.---How an abbess ought to act, St. Caesarius of Arles, LXVII, 1113.---How an abbess ought to proceed to the visitors’ room, ibid., 1114.---That an abbess should never eat outside the community except on account of illness, ibid.---On the election of an abbess, ibid., 1118. A holy abbess is to remain within the community, St. Aurelian of Arles, LXVIII, 402.---A holy abbess may not sell or give away any of the monastery’s possessions, nor act in any respect contrary to the institutions of the Rule, ibid., 402.---A holy abbess is not to take refreshment outside the community, ibid., 403.---That the holy abbess should supply whatever is necessary in sufficient measure, ibid., 404.---What sort of woman ought to be chosen as abbess, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 681.---What sort of woman an abbess ought to be, St. Donatus of Besançon, LXXXVII, 273, 277.---How the abbess should go out to the visitors’ room to exchange greetings, and how the handmaids of the Lord ought to greet their parents, ibid., 291.---On the election of an abbess, ibid., 297.---What sort of woman the abbess of a monastery ought to be, id., LXXXVIII, 1053.---On abbesses, Amalarius of Metz, id., CV, 961, 963 and following.

Cellarer.---How the cellarer ought to attend to the sick, St. Caesarius of Arles, LXVII, 1115.---On the election of a cellarer, and what sort of woman she should be, ibid., 1121.---She should take charge, with every care, of the sick, infants, guests, and poor, ibid.---Let her regard all the vessels and all the property of the monastery as if they were consecrated vessels of the altar, ibid.---On what the monastery cellarer ought to be like, St. Donatus of Besançon, LXXXVII, 292; LXXXVIII, 1057.

Portress.---What sort of woman the portress ought to be, St. Caesarius of Arles, LXVII, 1121.---She ought to have a cell near the gate, ibid.---What kind of women ought to be chosen for the wicket gate, St. Donatus of Besançon, ibid., 292.---On the monastery gatehouse, id., LXXXVIII, 1055; CV, 971.

Prioress.---The prioress is to be obeyed as a mother, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 964.---What sort of woman the prioress in the infirmary ought to be, St. Caesarius of Arles, LXVII, 1113.---Admonition or instruction concerning how the prioress ought to attend to the sick, ibid., 1115.---Let no one choose work to do according to her own pleasure, but do what has been commanded by the abbess or prioress, St. Aurelian of Arles, LXVIII, 402.---On the prioress of the monastery, St. Donatus of Besançon, LXXXVIII, 277.---What sort of woman the monastery prioress ought to be, id., LXXXVIII, 1054.

Superior, steward; including the bishop.---On the bishop’s jurisdiction over the sisters, St. Jerome, XXX, 406.---On the order to be maintained between the bishop and the sisters, ibid., 407.---On appointing for the sisters, after the bishop, a superior who is a presbyter, ibid.---On the authority of the bishop and superior with respect to observances of the order, id., XXX, 424.---An offender is to be corrected more severely, according to the judgment of the prioress, presbyter, or bishop, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 962.---How the monastery stewards ought to enter the monastery, St. Caesarius of Arles, [Col. 0719] LXVII, 1114.---But if, for the needs of the monastery, you must speak privately with a steward, do so in the presence of two, or at least three, chosen sisters, ibid., 1138.---On the stewards of the monastery, St. Donatus of Besançon, LXXXVII, 290.

VI.---On the faults and confession of nuns.

The fall of a consecrated virgin is mourned most bitterly, St. Ambrose, XVI, 367.---The fall of a consecrated virgin has stained the Church, and from it every Christian soul has received a grave wound, ibid.---How great and what kind of penance is necessary for a fallen virgin, ibid., 376.---On admonishing and rebuking offenders, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 962.---That another’s sin should not be concealed, St. Caesarius of Arles, LXXII [probably LXVII], 1110.---How those who have either committed theft or struck one another are to be dealt with differently, ibid., 1111.---What the manner of excommunication ought to be, St. Donatus of Besançon, LXXXVII, 294.---On graver faults, ibid., 295.---On those who have not amended after repeated correction, ibid.---On excommunication for faults, id., LXXXVIII, 1067.---What excommunication ought to be like, ibid.---On those who, though repeatedly corrected through diligent care of reproof, have refused to amend, ibid.---The method of correction with respect to offenders, id., CV, 966.

How they should come to confession every day, St. Donatus of Besançon, LXXXVII, 282.---On confession to be made continually, id., LXXXVIII, 1059.---On not revealing the confessions of sisters, ibid., 1060.---Love confession, if you seek beauty: to confession are joined comeliness and beauty, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 258.---If there are sins, they are washed away in confession; if there are good works, they are commended by confession, ibid.---Confession is a good ornament of the soul: it both cleanses the sinner and makes the righteous purer, ibid.

VII.---On the meals, baths, and sleeping arrangements of nuns.

On foods and the order of eating, St. Jerome, XXX, 420.---On fasting, ibid., 421.---On readings at table, ibid., 422.---On the quality and quantity of food and drink, St. Augustine, XXXII, 1457.---Let her take no food outside the hour of the meal, unless she is ill, id., XXXIII, 960.---When you come to table, listen without disturbance or dispute, until you rise from it, to what is customarily read to you, ibid.---The sick are treated differently in their diet, ibid., 961.---Order at meals, St. Caesarius of Arles, LXVII, 1120.---Let no one store beside her bed anything that can be eaten or drunk, St. Aurelian of Arles, LXVIII, 401.---While seated at table, let them keep silence, ibid., 403.---Let them never take meat as food, ibid.---Chickens and other fattened fowl are to be served only to the sick and infirm; fish, however, on specified feasts, ibid.---No one may taste any food or drink outside the common table, except the sick and infants, ibid.---On the manner of fasting, St. Leander of Seville, LXXII, 884.---On the use of wine, ibid., 885.---On those who have presumed to hide something near their beds, St. Donatus of Besançon, LXXXVII, 282.---On those who have not observed the blessing at table, and other similar matters, ibid., 283.---On those who have spilled something in the kitchen, ibid.---That those seated at table should keep silence, ibid., 284.---At what hours the sisters should take their meals, ibid., 296.---On the manner in which the table is to be administered or observed, id., LXXXVIII, 1062.---At what suitable hours in winter or in summer the meal should be taken, id., LXXXVIII, 1063.---On feeding infants, ibid., 1070.---All are to take their daily meal together in the refectory, id., CV, 963.---On the quantity and quality of food, id., CV, 964.

Let washing of the body and use of baths not be frequent, but be allowed at the interval customarily observed, that is, once a month, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 963.---Unless necessity caused by illness compels it, the body is not to be washed more frequently, ibid.---Nor may they go to the baths, or wherever it is necessary to go, fewer than three together, ibid.---How they ought to use the bath, St. Caesarius of Arles, LXVII, 1112.---To what extent a virgin ought to use bathing, St. Leander of Seville, LXXII, 885.

[Col. 0720] Before sleep one must examine one’s conscience and grieve for sins, St. Augustine, XXXI, 1459.---At vigils care must be taken that no one sleep, St. Caesarius of Arles, LXVII, 1109; St. Aurelian of Arles, LXVIII, 402.---How they ought to sleep, St. Donatus of Besançon, LXXXVII, 293.---How they ought to sleep in the dormitory, LXXXVIII, 1065.---All are to sleep in the dormitory, each, namely, in a separate bed, id., CV, 963.

VIII.---On the monastery of nuns.---Enclosure.

On enclosure of the house, St. Jerome, XXX, 414.---Above all, it must be observed that no one leave the monastery until her death, St. Caesarius of Arles, LXVII, 1107; St. Aurelian of Arles, LXVIII, 399.---Neither men nor women may enter the monastery, ibid., 401.---That not even the stewards themselves may enter the monastery, except for those purposes established in this Rule, ibid.---How monastery stewards or other men ought to enter the monastery, St. Donatus of Besançon, LXXXVII, 290.---That neither secular matrons nor girls are to be permitted to enter, ibid.---On the enclosure of nuns, Robert of Arbrissel, CLXII, 1081. Amalarius of Metz, id., CV, 963.
