CLXI. INDEX CONCERNING WIDOWS.

This Index treats: I. Of the praise and commendation of widowhood.---II. Of the care and honour due to widows.---III. Of the profession of widowhood and the life of widows.---IV. Of the duties of widows.---V. Of the dress of widows.---VI. Books and homilies treating of widowhood.

[INDEX CONCERNING WIDOWS.]

I.---On the praise and commendation of widowhood.

The priesthood of widowhood, Tertullian, I, 1286.---Widowhood is praised, ibid., 1287; II, 806, 1928, 1932.---Widowhood is commended, St. Zeno, XI, 803.---The turtledove is praised for its widowhood and on this account is preferred even to Christian women, St. Ambrose, XIV, 232.---Learn, women, how great is the grace of widowhood, ibid., 232.---The various benefits of widowhood, id., XVI, 249 and following.---How glorious it is for widows that Elijah was sent to a widow, ibid., 235.---The dignity of widows is explained: because divine wrath is most gravely stirred by injuries inflicted on them, ibid., 236.---It is vain for widows to think that marriage should be renewed for the sake of having children, ibid., 261.---Nor does a widow receive a command, but counsel, ibid., 260.---Good is that widowhood which is so often extolled by apostolic judgment; for it is a teacher of faith and a teacher of chastity, ibid.---Honour is bestowed so generously upon widows that they are honoured even by bishops, ibid., 237.---What her treasures are, ibid., 244.---On preserving widowhood, St. Jerome, XXII, 550.---Widowhood is commended because of the troubles of marriage, ibid., 551, 558.---The good of widowhood is more excellent than the good of marriage, St. Augustine, XL, 432.---Exhortation to the good of widowhood, ibid., 445.---Comparison among three kinds of widows, ibid., 440.---The good of widowhood is not diminished by praise of the good of marriage, but increased, ibid., 435.---The good of widowhood is greater than that of marriage, which nevertheless is truly good, ibid., 432.---The good of widowhood is called honourable because it is more honourable, not because marriage is regarded as shameful, ibid., 434.---He exhorts to the good of widowhood, ibid., 445.---Let a widow not enter into a second marriage, Alanus of Lille, CCX, 194.---The benefits of widowhood, ibid.

II.---On the care and honour of widows.

See how fairly he who has done good to a widow is regarded, Tertullian, I, 1287.---Care for widows is commended, St. Cyprian, IV, 327.---Every approved widow is to be honoured, ibid., 771.---Widows are to be protected, ibid., 778.---Defend widows and orphans, Lactantius, VI, 680.---To whom this care especially pertains, ibid.---Which ecclesiastics ought to visit the homes of widows and virgins, and how, ibid., 49, 50.---Widows supported by the alms of the Church, St. Jerome, XXXIII, 232.---God guards widows and orphans, id., XXXIV, 1896, 1897.---Care for widows pertains to bishops, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 459.---Emperors and kings have granted bishops the right to defend their causes, ibid., 607.---The Church supported widows and virgins at its own expense, St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 327.---Fathers of widows and orphans, Alcuin, C, 157.---Young and weak widows are supported by their own Church, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 348.---On widows maintained by Church stipends, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 395.---That younger widows or consecrated women are not to be neglected by the bishop, id., CXL, 804; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 563.---He ought to care for widows’ causes before those of others, St. Bernard, CLXXII, 741.---If she is truly a widow and destitute, then let her be supported from the Church’s resources, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 149.---Honour widows by providing necessities and sustaining them with consolations, ibid., 148.

III.---On the profession of widowhood and the life of widows.

What sort of widow ought to be chosen for the profession of widowhood, St. Ambrose, XVI, 237.---The Apostle did not think younger women should be recalled from the desire for widowhood, ibid., 238.---The widow’s strength is not chastity of body alone, but a great and abundant discipline of virtue, ibid., 238.---It is not defined by bodily abstinence alone, but marked by virtue, ibid., 235.---What her life ought to be like, ibid., 241.---How merciful and generous a widow ought to be toward the poor, ibid., 243.---She must first be chaste from wine, in order that she may be chaste from adultery, [Col. 0722] ibid., 247.---What widow ought to be admitted to the Church’s support, id., XVII, 476.---What kind of life a widow ought to lead, St. Jerome, XXII, 728.---How a widow left without children ought to live, ibid., 980.---The holy profession of widowhood, St. Augustine, XL, 431.---Second marriages are not condemned by the profession of widowhood, ibid., 433.---A widow should take care to be holy both in body and spirit, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 313.---Examples of the widows Judith and Anna, ibid., 319.---What sort of women widows admitted to ecclesiastical ministries ought to be, Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 619.---Their virtues, ibid.---On the profession and dress of consecrated widows, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 526.---On widows who have professed widowhood before a bishop, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 395.---That widows should not put on a veil without consulting their bishop, Burchard, CXL, 397.---That widows are not to be veiled under any blessing, ibid., 798.---On widows: that no one may presume to veil them, ibid.---On widows who have violated professed continence, ibid., 799.---That the profession of widowhood is to be made before a bishop, ibid., 800.---On widows abandoning their resolution, ibid., 801.---On widows and girls who have assumed the religious habit in their own homes, ibid., 802.---Widows are to follow the Lamb, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 490.---What true widows are, St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLIII, 449.---No one may violate a profession of widowhood made before a bishop, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 201.---That widows should not put on a veil without consulting their bishop, ibid., 556.---That no one may presume to veil widows, ibid., 557.---On widows who have violated professed continence, ibid., 558.---That the profession of widowhood is to be made before a bishop, ibid., 559.---That widows who depart from their resolution of widowhood are to be excommunicated, ibid.---That veiled widows are not to proceed to marriage, ibid., 560.---On a widow who, under the pretext of religion, has put on a veil for a time, ibid.---On widows who have assumed the religious habit in their own homes, ibid., 561.---Those who intend to preserve chastity are to make the profession of widowhood and assume the religious habit, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1103.---No one is permitted to violate a profession of widowhood made before a bishop after the habit has been assumed, ibid., 1386.---How a widow may be judged good, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 495.---How she ought to live, ibid.---What kind of widow the Apostle commands to be chosen, Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 754.

IV.---Duties of widows, and things to be avoided by them.

That a widow should raise her children, honour her parents, desire to please God, etc., St. Ambrose, XVI, 236.---The first duty is piety, the second the practice of hospitality and service of humility, the third the ministry of mercy, ibid., 238.---Widows ought to instruct their daughters-in-law, so that in mature age they may have support in old age from them, ibid., 244.---They should be especially careful not to leave room for an unfavourable reputation, and why, ibid., 242.---When a widow should honour her parents, St. Jerome, XXII, 551.---Let divine reading and frequent prayers always be in your hands, ibid., 730, 731.---Nurses and servants must be avoided, ibid., 551.---Adornment of clothing, ibid., 553.---Conversations with young men must be avoided, ibid., 556.---What works widows ought to undertake, id., 347.---More diligent care of prayers seems imposed upon widows, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 506.---Let widows beware of avarice, id., XL, 447, 448.---The true widow perseveres in prayers, St. Salvian of Marseilles, LIII, 195.---The widow’s duty is to cling to God and persevere in prayers, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 318.---How a widow should conduct herself in food and banquets, ibid., 318.---The canons forbid clerics’ widows, after their husbands’ deaths, to marry again, id., LXXVII, 710.---Widows supported by the Church’s stipends ought to assist the Church with their prayers, Isidore Mercator, [Col. 0723] CXXX, 348.---Widows must avoid carnal conversations, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 493.

V.---On the dress of widows.

Widows’ dress is distinct from matrons’ dress, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 1081.---They are indicated as wearing dark clothing, ibid.---Widows had particular garments in the time of the patriarchs, id., XXXIV, 583.---The adornment and dress of widows, St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 317.---The colour of veil worn by Spanish widows, St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 329.---Those who have received the veil, even unwillingly, are not to lay it aside thereafter, ibid.---Whether widows may be veiled, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 374.

VI.---Books, homilies, and sermons treating of widowhood.

One book On Widows, St. Ambrose, XVI, 234.

[Col. 0724] Letter On Preserving Widowhood, St. Jerome, XXII, 550.

Letter to a Widow, teaching how she should raise surviving little children and what kind of life she herself ought to lead, ibid., 724.

How a widow left without children ought to live, ibid., 982 and following.

Letter On Monogamy, ibid., 1046.

Book On the Good of Widowhood, or Letter to Juliana the Widow, St. Augustine, XL, 429.

Short work On Preserving Widowhood, St. Caesarius of Arles, LXVII, 1094.

The Apostle instructs Timothy concerning widows, Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 615.

Various decrees concerning widows, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 379.

On Widows, Alanus of Lille, CCX, 194.

On Widows, Ratherius of Verona, CXXXVI, 202.

CLXII. INDEX CONCERNING KINGS.

This Index discusses: I. Royal power considered in itself and in relation to ecclesiastical affairs.---II. The anointing and titles of kings.---III. The duties of kings.---IV. The virtues of kings.---V. Our duties toward kings.---VI. Books treating of kings.

[INDEX CONCERNING KINGS.]

I.---On royal power in itself and in relation to ecclesiastical affairs.

The king is on his own throne up to God, yet beneath God, Tertullian, II, 251.---The emperor is inferior to God alone, id., I, 448.---Second after God, id., I, 700.---This is a great name, and why, id., I, 449.---The emperor’s power derives from the same source as spirit and life, id., I, 441.---He has been established by God, id., I, 448.---Christians believed that emperors had been chosen by God, ibid.---The power of kings is from God through Jesus Christ, St. Hilary, X, 700.---There is no one above the emperor except God, St. Optatus, XI, 1001.---The ordering of authorities is from God, St. Ambrose, XV, 1621.---The emperor makes laws, which he himself must be the first to observe, id., XVI, 1005.---The emperor is within the Church, not above the Church, ibid., 1018.---Things divine are not subject to imperial rank, ibid., 996, 999.---The emperor has been entrusted with authority over public walls, not sacred things, ibid., 999.---Palaces belong to the emperor; churches to the priest, ibid.---By ancient law, imperial powers were bestowed by priests, not usurped by them, ibid., 1001.---They see divine law made subject to human authorities, id., XVII, 163.---A king may impose new commands upon his subjects, St. Augustine, XXXII, 690.---A human king rules humans in human affairs; but another King rules in divine affairs, id., XXXVI, 647.---All power of rulers and laws is from God, id., XL, 76.---Kings are better said to be named from ruling (*regere*) than from reigning (*regnare*), id., XLI, 154.---The emperor’s care extends not merely to earthly affairs, but also to preventing anyone from sinning against divine matters with impunity, id., XLIII, 749.---The power of kings comes from God’s bounty, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 226.---A king is called from ruling (*regere*), Alcuin, C, 159.---Imperial power has been bestowed by God especially for the protection of the Church, ibid., 428.---That a kingdom is given not by men but by God, in whose hand all kingdoms stand, Jonas of Orléans, CVI, 295.---On imperial law, Burchard, CXL, 896.---That kings are bound by laws, ibid., 907.---On the discipline of kings in the Church, ibid.---That emperors may not introduce bishops into the Church, Placidus, CLXIII, 633.---On the king’s power concerning investitures, ibid., 637.---In what matter earthly rulers ought to have power in the Church, id., CLXIII, 666.---How Pope Adrian anathematized rulers who involved themselves in the election of prelates, ibid., 667.---Why emperors were permitted to invest churches, ibid.---The respective duties of ecclesiastical and secular power are distinct, Robert Pullen, CLXXXI, 906.---Why and how authorities are established by God, ibid., 919.---On earthly authorities, ibid., 921.---The laws of rulers ought not to prevail over natural law, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 48.---In ecclesiastical causes, the royal will must yield to priests, ibid., 53.---The tribunals of kings are subject to priestly authority, [Col. 0724] ibid., 54.---Kings need pontiffs for eternal things, and pontiffs need kings for temporal things, ibid.---All power is from God, Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1504.---On the difference between a ruler and a tyrant, and on what a ruler is, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 513.---That a ruler is the minister of priests, ibid., 513.

II.---On the anointing and titles of kings.

The law commands that royal chrismal anointing not be performed in captivity, Tertullian, II, 634.---Threefold anointing: priestly, royal, and prophetic, St. Jerome, XXV, 1325.---In former times kings and priests were anointed, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1952.---The anointing of kings is a type of Christ, id., XLI, 543.---Sacred anointing especially pertained to the royal and priestly person, XXXII, 627.---Kings and priests were anointed only in that kingdom in which Christ was prophesied, id., XXXVI, 505.---In earlier times it pertained only to the two persons of king and priest, ibid., 200.---Through sacred anointing in the Old Testament priests and kings were appointed; prophets conferred this, St. Maximus of Turin, XLVII, 778.---Why the kings of the Jews were anointed, St. Agobard of Lyon, CIV, 171.---Kings were chosen in former times as they are now, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 899.---The custom of creating and anointing them, ibid.---Kings and priests were anointed under the old law as figures of Christ, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 797.---Why kings and priests were formerly anointed, Peter Lombard, CXCI, 267.

Emperors are called “lords,” Lactantius, VII, 573.---When the Latin people first bestowed upon them the royal title, ibid., 648, 762.---The designations “emperor” and “prince” are used interchangeably, ibid., 650.---Emperors receive the titles “Serenity” and “Majesty,” Pope St. Boniface, XX, 770.---The designation “father” befits kings, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1108.---The title “Highness” given to a king, Alcuin, C, 355.---“Excellency,” ibid., 366.---The title “Loftiness” given to a king, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 385, 512, 668.---“Excellency,” ibid., 463.---“Majesty,” ibid., 329.---“Serenity,” ibid., 390.---“Sublimity,” ibid., 462.

III.---On the duties of kings.

The duty of kings is to watch over the liberty of their subjects, St. Hilary, X, 557.---Although a king has laws in his power, he is nevertheless more subject to God, St. Ambrose, XV, 1435.---It is the duty of emperors to protect religion, the same author, XVI, 961.---Rulers are given so that evil may not occur, the same author, XVII, 163.---The office of kings set forth, St. Jerome, XXIV, 811.---The duties of Christian kings, St. Augustine, XLIII, 527.---Kings serve the Lord both as men and as kings, [Col. 0725] the same author, XXXIII, 801.---It belongs to devout kings of the earth not only to restrain with suitable severity adulteries, homicides, and other such crimes, but sacrileges as well, ibid., 910.---Emperors are raised to sovereignty chiefly for the purpose of bringing aid to the faith and to the Church, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 975, 1149.---Heretics are to be restrained by them, ibid., 1117, 1133.---It is their duty to cut away scandals against faith and discipline, ibid., 1020, 1023.---Kings ought not to meddle in priestly causes, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 689.---The correction of the wicked belongs to kings, ibid., 955, 1041.---Those whom they govern outwardly by counsel, they do not permit to perish inwardly, ibid., 1037.---The highest good in kings is to preserve for each person what is his own undefiled, ibid., 1047.---The reins of government must be moderated toward subjects, ibid., 1055.---The office of kings, Alcuin, C, 159; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 1146.---What a king is, what he ought to be, and what he ought to avoid, Jonas of Orléans, CVI, 287.---What, properly speaking, the ministry of a king is, ibid., 290.---At the reception of the diadem a prince ought to swear that he will not become a supporter of heretics, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 488.---It is the part of a good prince to protect the Churches, ibid., 222.---It belongs to kings not merely not to seize the property of others, but also to restore what has been fraudulently taken from others, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 460.---Emperors, defenders of the Church, ibid., 438.---That to punish the unjust is a sacrifice to God, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 821.---What the office of a prince is, ibid., 825.---Princes are not lords of the Church but its advocates, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLIX, 92, 101.---Princes are especially bound to correct the evils of their subjects, ibid., 174.---A king ought to restrain thefts, punish adulteries, remove the impious from the land, and not permit parricides and perjurers to live, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1312.---The office of a good and just king, Hildebert, CLXXI, 145.---The office of a Christian and most excellent prince, ibid., 182.---He ought to punish rapacious officials, ibid.---Kings, defenders of the Church, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 150.---Their glory is God’s work, ibid., 293.---The office of a prince, ibid., 281.---The duty of an emperor is to defend the Church, ibid., 442.---The king must restrain thefts and crimes, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1229.---To restore ruined churches, not persecute bishops, belongs to a good prince, ibid., 466.

### IV.---On the virtues of kings.

Emperors ought to be stricter in establishing laws, but merciful in exacting punishments, St. Ambrose, XIV, 1018.---Amid honors kings should not forget that they are men, St. Augustine, XLI, 171.---The greater their earthly exaltation, the more they ought to humble themselves before God, the same author, XXXVII, 1779.---Kings serve the Lord in fear by religiously forbidding and punishing those things which are done contrary to the Lord’s commands, the same author, XXXIII, 801.---Kings reign with Christ when they believe in him, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 734.---An emperor is a vessel unto honor if he lives holily in the true faith and subjects the summit of royal dignity to holy religion, ibid., 648.---The endowments of kings: zeal and gentleness, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1289.---Royal virtues, Alcuin, C, 354.---What a king ought to be, Jonas of Orléans, CVI, 287.---That equity in judgment is the support of a kingdom, while injustice is its overthrow, ibid., 294.---What princes ought to be like, Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1129.---The virtues of kings, Ratherius of Verona, CXXXVI, 222, 272, 284.---Let them give alms more than others, [Col. 0726] ibid., 272.---On the patience of kings, Burchard of Worms, CXL, 906.---The piety of kings toward God preserves kingdoms, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 439.---That the strength of justice preserves kingdoms, the same author, CXLV, 819.---A prince possesses clemency together with justice, Rupert of Deutz, CLXVII, 523.---Clemency is especially fitting for kings, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 144.---The example of a king flows down to his subjects, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 150.---What evils or goods come to subjects from the character of princes, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 554.

### V.---On our duties toward kings.

What the Roman faithfulness toward emperors was, Tertullian, I, 583.---How they rendered them the loyalty due, ibid., 460.---They honored them sincerely, and how, ibid., 448, 700.---The highest reverence must be shown to a king, St. Hilary, X, 630.---Prayers for the king’s safety, ibid., 701.---How great is the honor due to the emperor, St. Optatus, XI, 1000.---Christians ought to be subject to higher powers, lest anyone think that the ordinance of an earthly king may be dissolved, St. Ambrose, XV, 1634.---They are to be subject not only because of present punishment, but also because of the future judgment, XVII, 163.---He commands that the things first due to royal authority be paid, ibid., 164.---Prayer must be offered for kings and emperors, St. Jerome, XXII, 827.---Honor and obedience are owed by Christians even to unjust and unbelieving kings, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1653, 1654.---Christ and his disciples commanded, even by their own example, that obedience be shown to kings, ibid., 1591.---Subjects ought to pray for kings and their families, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 859, 862.---The emperor or king must be obeyed as God, St. Benedict of Aniane, CIII, 816.---That all ought humbly and faithfully to obey royal authority, which is ordained only by God, Jonas of Orléans, CVI, 296.---A prince must not be cursed, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 482.---That opponents of kings be excommunicated, Burchard of Worms, CXL, 900.---That no one presume, while a prince lives, to choose another king, ibid., 901.---That no one plot the destruction of a king, ibid.---A king is especially to be honored when he obeys his Creator, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 441.---Exhortation that service be rendered to the emperor in such a way that God is not offended, the same author, CLXIII, 682.

# CLXIII. INDEX ON POVERTY.

In which are treated: I. The nature of poverty and its kinds.---II. The prerogatives of the poor and the excellence of poverty.---III. The duties of the poor and their vices.---IV. The duties of Christians toward the poor.---V. The poverty of Christ and the Apostles, to be imitated by us.---VI. The historical section on poverty.---VII. Sermons, treatises, etc., on poverty.

[INDEX ON POVERTY.]

### I.---On the nature of poverty and its kinds.

No one is poor in spirit except the humble, Tertullian, I, 1267.---Voluntary poor persons, St. Hilary, IX, 743.---Poverty is a middle condition: both good and evil persons can be poor, [Col. 0726] St. Ambrose, XV, 1650.---Not every poverty is holy, nor are riches criminal, ibid., 1769.---Poverty is not the punishment of sin, the same author, XIV, 844.---What poverty is good and not to be avoided, ibid., 910.---Who the mystical poor person is, ibid., 988.---Poverty is not a matter of nature but of opinion, [Col. 0727] the same author, XVI, 1213.---Where there is hunger for desires, where there is insatiable appetite, there certainly is poverty, ibid., 1098.---For to holy men poverty itself is always rich, the same author, XVII, 734.---Who are poor in spirit, St. Chromatius of Aquileia, XX, 325.---He who is poor with Christ is rich, St. Jerome, XXII, 348.---Who are to be called poor, St. Augustine, XLI, 204.---The true poor person, the same author, XXXVIII, 115.---God’s poor person is poor in mind, not in the world, the same author, XXXVII, 1727, 1814.---If a poor person has God, what does he lack? the same author, XXXVIII, 492, 521.---In what thing the truly poor are rich, the same author, XXXVI, 170; XXXVII, 1649.---He has left much behind who has left not merely all that he had, but also all that he desired to have, the same author, XXXVII, 1371.---The poor, established as bearers for the rich, the same author, XXXVIII, 130, 240, 406.---The poor are hidden channels through which our possessions go before us into heaven, the same author, XXXVI, 424.---Who are poor in spirit, ibid., 943; XXXVIII, 364.---Poverty in itself is neither blessedness nor misery, the same author, XXXVIII, 327.---Voluntary poverty pertains to Christian perfection, the same author, XLIII, 341.---Five kinds of poverty, the same author, XL, 1313.---The poor and the rich share one nature, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 167.---The Christian poor person is always rich, ibid., 276.---Who are the true and evangelical poor, ibid., 462.---Poverty of spirit, or humility, is the first step toward blessedness, ibid., 461.---“Poor” signifies the humble person, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 750, 1151; LXXVI, 205, 378.---Who are truly poor, the same author, LXXVI, 205.---He who lacks clothing is less needy than he who lacks humility, the same author, LXXVII, 208.---Twofold poverty, St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 216.---Who is poor in spirit, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 484.---There are three classes of poor: the compelled, the spontaneous, and the voluntary, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 475.---Voluntary poverty, Christ’s fortress, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXIII, 671.---Poverty is martyrdom, ibid., 462.---Not poverty, but the love of poverty, is reckoned a virtue, ibid., 671.---Voluntary poverty cuts off every superfluity, ibid., 134.---Who is truly poor, Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 739.---What voluntary and honorable poverty is, Adam of Prémontré, CXCVII, 379.---Poor in possessions and in spirit, Thomas of Cîteaux, CCVI, 767.---Fourfold poverty, Alan of Lille, CCX, 248.---Wherein poverty of spirit consists, ibid., 140.

### II.---On the prerogatives of the poor and the excellence of poverty.

The Lord always justifies the poor and condemns the rich beforehand, Tertullian, I, 1260.---Poverty benefits a person: it exercises the body but does not oppress it, St. Ambrose, XIV, 263.---It is good if undertaken from piety and the practice of virtues, ibid., 1132.---If blessed poverty, to which heaven lies open, is ours, let us disregard these earthly riches and avoid bodily excess, ibid.---There is a glorious poverty, and why, the same author, XV, 1713.---How the poor surpass the rich, the same author, XIV, 263.---There is a good poverty in moral character, ibid., 1069.---Be poor in spirit, and you will be rich in whatever estate, ibid., 328.---How much chaste poverty surpasses dowry-gains, the same author, XVI, 206.---Poverty in priests is glorious, ibid., 940.---Christ does not despise the poor person in his kingdom, but hears him and delivers him from all straits and troubles, ibid., 1275.---The tears of the poor are redeeming tears, ibid., 1292.---The gifts of the poor bind God, ibid., 1017.---The poor are truly the treasures of the Church, ibid., 141.---The poor are the feet of the Lord, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 1760.---The poor are blessed throughout the Scriptures, the same author, XXXIX, 2310.---Heaven is promised only to the poor in spirit, the same author, XL, 1084.---The riches of the poor person, the same author, XXXIX, 1936.---The value of evangelical poverty, ibid., 1934, 1935.---The poor, gems of great price, *Lausiac History*, LXXIII, 1097; LXXIV, 257.---Poverty is the monk’s treasure, *Lives of the Fathers*, LXXIII, 891.---The poor will judge the world on the day of judgment, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 950.---The rejected and despised poor person is a pearl in a dung-heap, the same author, LXXVI, 1312.---On the road to the homeland, poverty is a faithful companion, ibid., 1024.---Who the blessed poor are, St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 216.---The poor and the elderly in the Church are more honorable than others, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 348.---The fruits of evangelical poverty, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 258.---Poverty is rightly placed first among virtues, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 595.---The poor are prefigured in the Lord’s feet, anointed by Mary with ointment, Rupert, abbot, CLXX, 129.---The poor are blessed, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXIII, 456.---The same promise has been made to the poor and to martyrs, ibid., 462.---The poor are secure in the future judgment, ibid., 216.---Evangelical poverty possesses both heavenly and earthly things, ibid., 875.---A certain blessed poverty, Philip of Harvengt, [Col. 0728] CCIII, 24.---The kingdom of God is purchased with poverty, ibid., 411.---The reward of voluntary poverty, ibid., 720.---Praise of poverty, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 396.---Voluntary poverty, guardian of virtues, ibid., 65.---Poverty, nurse of humility, ibid., 181.---Commendation of poverty, Alan of Lille, CCX, 184.---The benefits of poverty, ibid., 124.

### III.---On the duties of the poor and their vices.

Prayer sustains the poor, Tertullian, I, 1196.---Those who are supported by the Church should be content with simpler foods, St. Cyprian, IV, 363.---No one ought to complain about poverty; the example is cited of the swallow, which abounds in industry, St. Ambrose, XIV, 230.---There are trials in poverty and in riches, ibid., 264; CCXV, 1309.---The ugliness of want often breaks saints whom fear of death had not broken, the same author, XV, 1405.---Want does not make a poor person more commendable if, amid filth and destitution, he does not avoid sins, St. Jerome, XXII, 724.---What vices the poor ought to avoid, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 521.---They must beware of desire for riches, ibid., 522, 956.---A peaceful poor person is to be preferred to a covetous rich person, the same author, XLI, 114.---Many poor are rich in covetousness, the same author, XXVII, 1371.---The poor person possessed by covetousness is worse than the rich person, the same author, XXXVIII, 114.---It profits a poor person nothing to lack resources while burning with covetousness, the same author, XXXVI, 609.---The poor person who desires riches and is puffed up is numbered among the reprobate rich, ibid., 545; XXXVII, 1727.---A true poor person is scarcely found in the crowd of the poor, the same author, XXXVIII, 114.---A proud poor person is intolerable, the same author, XXXVII, 112, 218.---The poor are bound to curb their desires, the same author, XXXVIII, 522.---Want does not help many poor people, since they are rich in vices and bad habits, the same author, XXXIX, 2311.---Nothing is more foolish than a proud poor person, the same author, XL, 1084.---The poor are not excluded from giving alms, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 160, 190, 277.---The poor are to be crowned for patience, ibid., 177.---The poor person anxiously seeks the goods which the rich person possesses with fear, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 1114.---The poor and weak, but not the poor and proud, are invited to the banquet, the same author, LXXVI, 1269.---God knows the poor but does not know proud rich persons, ibid., 1305.---It often happens that the rich person is humble but the poor person proud, the same author, LXXVII, 574.---How far poor persons may give alms, Ratherius of Verona, CXXXVI, 187.---Against idle poor persons, ibid., 188.---Let them earn their food by work, ibid., 186.---Poverty is a great instrument by which the creature is subjected to the Creator, Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 1384.---Poverty is corrupted by attachment even to the smallest things, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXIII, 636.---Poverty is free from envy, both its own and that of others, ibid., 671.---Three kinds of people feign poverty, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 152.---Poverty finds no flattery, ibid., 141.

### IV.---On the duties of Christians toward the poor, and on this question: Why God has permitted the poor.

It is gain to incur expense in the name of piety if the poor are helped, Tertullian, I, 474.---The poor must be fed, St. Cyprian, IV, 541.---Care for the poor commended, ibid., 230, 232, 240, 327, 329.---Greater care and love should be shown to poor persons steadfast in the faith, ibid., 329.---It is good that the poor should not hunger in the Church, St. Hilary, IX, 743.---Let no one mock the poor person, and why, St. Ambrose, XV, 1783.---He who mocks the poor provokes the one who made him, ibid., 1340.---Which poor persons are to be helped before others, the same author, XVI, 123 and following.---That poor person who does not see you must be visited; that one who is ashamed to be seen must be sought out, ibid., 124.---If you feed the poor, wash their wounds, and cleanse away their filth, you have indeed wiped Christ’s feet, ibid., 1117.---Would that they might always charge this crime against me: that gold is distributed to the poor, ibid., XVI, 1017. “The poor of Christ are my treasury; this is the treasure I know how to gather,” ibid.---Do not despise the poor person: he made you rich, ibid., XVI, 1213.---No one pretends in dealing with a poor person, ibid., 182.---The friendships of the poor are generally better than those of the rich, ibid.---Giving generously to the poor benefits oneself and one’s own, St. Gaudentius, XX, 942.---Give to the poor, not to the wealthy, not to the proud, St. Jerome, XXII, 643.---Some give a little to the poor in order to receive more, the same author, 535.---How poor and rich persons can share and lessen one another’s burdens, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 899.---The poor are clothed, the same author, XXXIV, 471.---Care of the poor, the same author, XXXVIII, 433.---The Church feeds the poor, the same author, XLIII, 94.---The bishop administers the care of the poor, the same author, XXXIII, 809.---Faithfulness to a friend must be maintained in his poverty, the same author, XXXVIII, 247.---The poor must not be despised, the same author, XXXIX, 1842.---But honored, the same author, [Col. 0729] XL, 1065.---Interchange between the poor and the rich, the same author, XXXIX, 2335.---Whether neglect of the poor is venial, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 165.---The poor must be helped, especially those who are modest and ashamed, ibid., 162.---In the poor we feed Christ, ibid., 163.---Without mercy toward the poor, no virtue profits, ibid., 165.---To whom the distribution of alms to the poor belongs, St. Benedict, LXVI, 313; St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 909.---The poor are patrons whom we ought to entreat, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1310.---Vicious poor persons are to be reproved and fed, ibid.---The honor due to the poor is demonstrated by an example, ibid.---Exhortation to honor and relieve the poor, ibid., 1372.---Which poor persons should be admonished, the same author, LXXVII, 52.---The poor must be comforted, ibid. Whether alms should be given to a poor sinner, ibid., 85.---The bishop has the poor’s goods to administer, the same author, 1274.---How do we dismiss the poor who come to the door and ask? And whether each person ought to offer bread or whatever else, etc., St. Benedict of Aniane, CIII, 525.---Care of the poor commended, St. Agobard of Lyons, CIV, 184.---Let each person feed a poor member of his own household, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 363.---Excellent sayings on relieving the miseries of the poor, Guibert, abbot, CLVI, 776.---How one should give to a poor person or to a rich person, Arnulf of Lisieux, CCI, 199.---The poverty of widows must be relieved, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 148.---On seeking out the poor, Pope Innocent III, CCXVII, 1208.---On service to the poor, ibid., 1146.

God often makes his servants needy, though he can feed them, in order that he may find persons at work, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1128.---Why God made the poor person and the rich person, the same author, XXXVII, 1649, 1650; XXXIX, 1980, 2230, 2336, 2341; XL, 1176; St. Leo the Great, LIV, 176; St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 484.

### V.---On the poverty of Christ, the apostles, and the saints.

Christ’s poverty, St. Ambrose, XIV, 954.---Christ redeemed the world in poverty and contempt, the same author, XV, 1464.---He came here poor so that the devil might have nothing to take away, ibid., 1624.---How he was rich in poverty, the same author, XIV, 1070.---“His poverty is my inheritance, and the Lord’s weakness is my strength,” the same author, XV, 1568.---The supreme poverty of Christ, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 844.---Christ, who became poor, came to fill the poor, ibid., 455.---Christ’s poverty is our riches, ibid., 454.---Who is said to be filled by Christ’s poverty, the same author, XXXIII, 567.---Christ’s poverty and riches, the same author, XXXVIII, 215.---The magnanimous poverty of Christ, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 462.---Christ became poor in order to enrich us, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 179.---Christ chose poor parents, ibid., 1085.---Christ uniquely poor, St. Bruno of Würzburg, CLXVIII, 262, 319.---How greatly Christ loved poverty in his actions, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 611.---How poor Christ was, ibid., 732.---Christ’s poverty, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXIII, 289.---Christ taught poverty by word and example, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 68.---Christ’s poverty appeared most fully on the cross, ibid., 77.

The apostles first offered us in themselves an example of blessed poverty, St. Chromatius, XX, 333.---As strangers and poor throughout the whole world, what could they have said? St. Jerome, XXII, 1057.---Not weighed down by the burden of riches, they were able to pass through the eye of the needle, ibid.---As to riches, they left nothing; as to will, they left the whole world, ibid., 646.---No one was poorer than the apostles, and no one left so much for the Lord, ibid., 1192.---The magnanimous poverty of the apostles, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 462.---The apostles’ care for the poor, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 217.

[Col. 0730] The love of a certain woman for the poor, St. Jerome, XXII, 880.---Caesarius publicly accuses himself because he sometimes neglected to give his small garments to the poor, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2024.---Guntram distributes treasures to the poor, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 444, 451.---Perpetuus appoints the poor as his heirs, ibid., 1151.---The poverty of John the Almsgiver appears from his will, *Lausiac History*, LXXIII, 379.---The poverty of Agatho, refusing to receive anything, ibid., 773.---A certain abbess’s pursuit of poverty, rejecting greater things, ibid., 627.---The poverty of Arsenius, refusing clothing, *Lives of the Fathers*, LXXIII, 888.---The poverty of Julian, who possessed nothing except a hair-shirt, a cloak, a little wooden vessel, and a book, the same work, LXXIV, 145.---The poverty of Messima, who used one tunic, ibid., 72.---The poverty of Paul in Pherme, who accepted nothing except what he could eat that same day, the same work, LXXIII, 1122.---The poverty of Serapion the Sindonite, who sold the Gospel and himself in order to assist the poor, ibid., 772, 889.---Perfect poverty taught by Antony through outstanding doctrine and example, ibid., 771.---The poverty of St. Malachy, bishop, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 1098.

### VI.---Historical section on the poor.

How charitably Christians assisted the poor, Tertullian, I, 470.---Collections for the poor established by the apostles, St. Hilary, IX, 743.---The poor ought to stand at the doors of churches, St. Gaudentius, XX, 938.---The custom of dismissing the poor with the words, “Go in peace; may God give to you,” St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2305.---In former times the Church fed the poor, St. Prudentius, LX, note 306.---They were present before the doors of the Church, ibid., 41.---They lived in upper rooms, ibid., 168.---The reception of the poor in monasteries, St. Benedict, LXVI, 765.---Guesthouses in monasteries erected for the benefit of the poor, ibid., 312.---Monastic tithes given to the poor, ibid., 310.---A fifth part of a monastery’s revenues, ibid., 311.---Likewise a third part, ibid.---Old clothes are to be distributed to the poor, ibid., 788.---The feet of three poor persons are to be washed daily and alms given to them, ibid., 763.---Poor people kiss the hands of rich persons when they receive something from them, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXIII, 797.

### VII.---Sermons, treatises, etc., on poverty.

Sermons on the poor, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 111, 247; XXXIX, 1934.

The eternal reward of the patience of Christ’s poor, St. Augustine, XL, 625.

The proud poor person, the poor in spirit, the humble poor person, the noble poor person, ibid., 1084.

Let them pursue poverty; the happiness of poverty, ibid., XL, 1218.

Sermons on the rich man and Lazarus, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 529 and following.

On the poverty of clothing and the love of plain dress, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 553.

On voluntary poverty, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXIII, 671.

On pursuing poverty, the same author, CLXXXIV, 1193.

On the rich man and Lazarus, Zacharias Chrysopolitanus, CLXXXVI, 337.

On Christ’s poor, St. Stephen of Grandmont, CCIV, 1104.

On assistance to the poor, ibid., 1108.

That God is a provident steward for the poor, ibid., 1145.

On the benefit to be bestowed upon the poor, ibid., 1152.

On poverty, Peter the Chanter, 64.

ERACLIUS, bishop.—On the faith of Eraclius, bishop of Lyons, which was so great that he experienced in himself a remarkable miracle, CXXXV, 944.

[Col. 0733] EUGYPPIUS, abbot.—That, if anyone cavils about the time of the world’s origin, they may be refuted from the place of the world, LXII, 619.

EUSEBIUS, bishop of Vercelli.—On his exhorting the people to work for salvation, XII, 949.

FALCO of Benevento.—On Cardinal Matthew, who from his earliest years happily joined mastery of learning with piety, CLXXIII, 1261.

FIRMICUS MATERNUS.—On demons: that he himself saw them nourished in idols by continual sacrifices and the blood of victims, LXXI, 1011.

FULGENTIUS (Saint), bishop.—That, upon seeing earthly Rome so splendid, he himself exclaimed: “How much more splendid will the City of God be!” LXV, 103.—That Moses, David, and the Apostle Paul had the same spirit of faith, ibid., 201.

GEBUINUS, archbishop of Lyons.—On his commendation of humility, CXLVII, 1210.

GENNADIUS, priest of Marseilles.—On Patriarch Photius, who refused to admit the Emperor Basil, a murderer, to the sacred rites, LVIII, 1032.

GERHOHUS of Reichersberg.—On his withdrawing from communion with a schismatic bishop, CXCIII, 482.

GERMANUS (Saint), bishop of Paris.—On those who formerly were not going to receive Communion at Mass and departed without waiting for it, LXXII, 130.

GESO, abbot of Tortona.—On a monk who escaped punishment through the saving Host, CXXXVII, 399.

GODEFRIDUS BULLONIUS [Godfrey of Bouillon].—That he was distinguished by humility and other virtues, CLV, 369.

GODEFRIDUS, abbot of Admont.—On his prudence, religious devotion, and learning, CLXXIV, 9.

GRATIAN.—On the decrees of the canons incorporated into a body, CLXXXVII, 10.

GREGORIUS MAGNUS (Saint Gregory the Great), pope.—That zeal for souls is a sacrifice most pleasing to God, LXXIX, 593.—How Saint Audolinus devoted himself to captivity in order to free the son of a certain widow, LXXV, 804.—On the Herulian monk to whom there appeared a crown of white flowers descending from heaven onto his head, ibid., 70.—On the pope’s three mitres, LXXVIII, 1114.

GREGORIUS (Saint Gregory), bishop of Tours.—On Blessed Portianus, who miraculously healed his master, LXXI, 1027.—On Aredius, who healed the sick by laying upon them the banner of the Cross, ibid., 561.—On Saint Hospitius opening the eyes of the blind through the power of the Holy Cross, ibid., 378.—On the same saint driving demons out of a woman, placing the Holy Cross, with oil, upon her forehead, ibid.—On the singular power of the relics of Saint Sergius the martyr, ibid., 435.—On Saint Martin’s power on behalf of a boy, after the sign of the Holy Cross, ibid., 444.—On Bishop Veranus, who received Theodoric from the baptismal font and often restored the sick to health through the sign of the Cross, ibid., 483.—On Ratherius, Childebert’s envoy, and his conduct toward the bishop of Marseilles, ibid., 455.—On God’s vengeance upon a robber and arsonist after he had sworn a false oath, ibid., 460.—On the death of Terentiolus, count of the city of Limoges, and the vengeance of his adversaries against him, ibid., 467.—On Bishop Praetextatus, struck by a murderer, ibid., 470.—On the circumstances that enabled the bodies of Merovech and Chlodovech to be found and identified after their deaths, ibid., 453.—That the history of a certain martyr was true, although falsehoods concerning it had been believed by a bishop, ibid., 763.—On Eberulf plotting to kill Gregory, and on the clerics gathered in the basilica of Saint Martin, ibid., 429.—On Gundovald’s pride and presumption, ibid., 440.—On the necromantic art of Desiderius of Tours, ibid., 484.—On Abbot Buciovald in the election of the bishop of Verdun, ibid., 504.—On Boso’s arrogance in the affairs of Carcassonne, ibid., 509.—On Chrodield’s boastfulness and Basina’s repentance, ibid., 547.—On Rancingus, who despised his dependents and committed wicked deeds against them, ibid., 318.—On Riccolemus, who threatened that, unless Guntram were taken from the holy basilica, he would immediately burn the city with fire, ibid., 319.—On Felix, bishop of the city of Nantes: his boastfulness and greed, ibid., 320.—On the fugitive Leudast and Queen Marcovefa, ibid., 364.—On the priest Riculf, who sought the episcopate and was so inflated by promises that he equalled the pride of Simon Magus, ibid., 364.—On Palladius provoking Bishop Parthenius with insults and, by divine vengeance, killing himself with his own sword, ibid., 303.—On King Guntram’s devotion during the calamity of the plague at Marseilles, ibid., 503.—On King Childebert demanding through envoys the sorceress Fredegund, ibid., 424.—On a certain heretic despoiling the church of Agde and being brought before the bishop of the place, ibid., 776.—On a priest-bishop dying and Nicetius succeeding him, ibid., 299.—On the whole cell of Saint Friard being shaken as Bishop Felix passed by, ibid., 300.—On Saint Germanus’s words to his brother Sigibert, who was laying siege, ibid., 313.—On the heaviness and lightness of the body of Saint Germanus of Paris when it was to be buried, ibid., 324.—On the repentance of the monk Patroclus, ibid., 325.—On Saint Martin removing a storm from a certain field, ibid., 937.—On clerics plotting perversely against Bishop Aetherius, ibid., 404.—On gifts offered to King Guntram by priests in order that he might grant them the episcopate, ibid., 406.—On Sagittarius following Gundovald’s party, ibid., 432, 442.—On the priest Cato having himself elected bishop after the death of Saint Gallus, ibid., 273.—On Bishop Cautinus’s wicked conduct toward the priest Anastasius, ibid., 277.—On Rachingus demanding his servants, ibid., 318.—On the priest Senocho shutting himself up in a cell, ibid., 324.—On Prince Merovech being tonsured and made a monk, ibid., 327.—On Nantin dying unhappily because of injuries inflicted on priests, ibid., 352.—On Bishop Salvius’s prediction of the death of the two sons of a certain man who had plundered the king’s house, ibid., 370.

On a heretic addressing a Catholic: “Do not blaspheme the Arian law which you do not observe; as for us, although we do not believe what you believe, nevertheless we do not blaspheme it,” LXXI, 360.—On the priest Transobad, mocked and insulted by many because he sought the episcopate, ibid., 363.—On famine oppressing Burgundy, ibid., 220.—On the army of King Theuderic devastating the city of Auvergne, ibid., 250.—On King Chilperic compelling Gundovald to flee, ibid., 310.—On Saint Gallus fleeing worldly nobility, ibid., 1029.—On Leudast attempting to undermine Gregory by unjust and wicked calumnies, ibid., 365.—On Riquuthe, Chilperic’s daughter, troubling her mother, ibid., 511.—On Chrodield violently hurling calumnies against the abbess of the monastery at Poitiers, ibid., 546.—On the inappropriate prayer of Bonulf, prostrate before Saint Martin’s altar, ibid., 952.—On Abbot Mummolus succeeding Bishop Pappolus in the Church of Langres, ibid., 323.—On a young girl cutting off Amalo’s head, ibid., 506.—On Richard sending envoys to Kings Guntram and Childebert so that, through the intervention of charity, they might unite with one another by treaty, ibid., 481, 494.—On Childebert making peace with Richard, ibid., 494.—On Guntram’s clemency toward Garacharius, count of Bordeaux, ibid., 453.—On the flood sent by God against the iniquities of humankind, ibid., 164, 572, 598, 676.—On the overflowing of the river Tiber, so great that it covered the city of Rome, ibid., 527, 551.—On Sedulius’s love of learning, ibid., 442.—On Berthefled, a lazy and self-indulgent religious woman, ibid., 510.—On Tiberius ordering four crosses laid one upon another to be removed, and afterwards finding treasure in their places, ibid., 339.

On Queen Fredegund’s words to the king: “For a long time the divine mercy has sustained us while we act wickedly [lacuna]; often it has chastised us with fevers and other evils, and we have not amended our ways. Why do you delay?” LXXI, 350.—On Gundovald praying to God, ibid., 443.—On Genesius of Béziers punishing a lie uttered in an oath, ibid., 770.—On a church consecrated in the name of the Virgin Saint Mary, in which divine vengeance appeared against perjurers in the city of Tours, ibid., 722.—On Abbot Mommolus, elected to the episcopate of the city of Langres, ibid., 323.—On Chilperic and a certain bishop discussing justice, ibid., 335.—On the chastity of Simplicius being recognized when a charge of lust had been brought against him, ibid., 883.—On Gratian, first bishop of the city of Tours, ibid., 563.—On peoples so terrified by hail, rain, and thunder that on account of these things they were converted, ibid., 806.—On divine vengeance against Gundovald’s soldiers, who were seized by a demon, ibid., 440.—On Bishop Magnulf’s address while Gundovald was besieging Toulouse, ibid., 432.—On Bishop Ennius, excessively devoted to wine, ibid., 557.—On Eberulf’s continual drunkenness, ibid., 428.—On a Breton priest who, shortly after drinking wine, was seen to be drunk, ibid., 474.—On King Chlothar attempting to take a third part of the produce from the churches, ibid., 271.—On Merovech, tonsured and fleeing to the basilica of Saint Martin, ibid., 329.—On the alms of Caesar Tiberius from the treasures of his predecessor Justin, ibid., 339.—On hidden money revealed by a recluse in confinement who knew of it, ibid., 340.—On miracles that appeared at the tomb of Blessed Martin, ibid., 323.

On a Jewish father, hostile to Christ the Lord and to His laws, who threw his own son into a burning furnace because the boy had approached, with other children, to partake of the Lord’s body and blood, ibid., 714.—On a certain Jew striking with a weapon a holy image fastened to the wall in a church [lacuna], ibid., 724.—On Chlodovech, hearing the reading of the Passion, exclaiming: “If I had been there in the praetorium with my Franks, I would have avenged the injuries done to Christ,” [Col. 0735] ibid., 586.—On Cyrola, bishop of the heretics, persecuting Catholics, ibid., 193.—On Gregory’s own dispute with Oppila, a Spanish envoy, ibid., 407.—On the image of Diana worshipped by the people on the mountain where Wulfilaicus built a basilica, ibid., 458.—On an image of the Crucified at Narbonne, ibid., 725.—On Chilperic’s vices, although he claimed to be the wisest of all men, ibid., 413.—On the intemperance of many people of Tournai when they had been invited by Fredegund, ibid., 558.—On the lust of Emperor Avitus, ibid., 578.—On Childeric’s excesses, ibid., 579.—On the intemperance and lust of King Dagobert, ibid., 644.—On Albinus, governor of the province of Marseilles, ibid., 306.—That Gundebard wished to convert and secretly asked to be anointed with chrism, ibid., 230.—On Bishop Avitus converting very many Jews, ibid., 326.—On the conversion of King Richard, ibid., 493.—On a certain Chuno violently seizing the crown from Saint Martin’s tomb, ibid., 915.—On a crown, as if natural, upon Nicetius’s head, ibid., 1098.

On Charegisilus, chamberlain of King Sigibert, who was as frivolous in conduct as he was weighty in greed, LXXI, 314.—On Chilperic rebuking his flatterer Aetius, ibid., 335.—On Chilperic flattering a certain bishop, ibid.—On Count Nantin, excommunicated and absolved, ibid., 352.—On a certain cleric plotting to kill Bishop Aetherius, ibid., 403.—On the alliance of Guntram, Childebert, Brunhild, and Audelai, ibid., 497, 501.—On everyone’s indifference toward King Chilperic, ibid., 414.—On the concord of Justinian and Aetherius, ibid.—On a man shut up in a tower who, when soldiers were driving him from it, truly foretold the outcome, ibid., 377.—On a certain citizen of Bourges made mad through the devil’s snares, ibid., 556.—On a demon that, out of envy, inflicts sores upon human bodies, ibid., 459.—On visions granted to the abbot of Saint Avitus and to King Chilperic, ibid., 452.—On Saint Martin’s appearance to a certain deacon, ibid., 459.—On signs shown for two nights to Guntram’s envoys, ibid., 460.—On blood appearing on an islet near the city of Venice, ibid., 465.—On the appearance of Blessed Germanus, saving certain persons during a fire spreading through Paris, ibid., 473.—On prodigies around the time of Childebert, ibid., 483.—On an apparition announcing the destruction of Antioch, ibid., 555.—On Arvatius, bishop of Tongeren, receiving an answer from heaven concerning the invasion of Gaul by the Huns, ibid., 577.—On various miraculous apparitions in heaven under King Theuderic, ibid., 617.—On Bishop Cautinus’s avarice, ibid., 276.—On Aetherius returning to the episcopate, ibid., 404.—On a Jew wickedly killed by an injurious man, ibid., 430.—On Claudius’s greed in approaching Queen Fredegund in order to obtain gifts from her, ibid., 440.—On Chlodovech receiving baptism from Saint Remigius, ibid., 226.

On the unbelieving Jew Priscus, LXXI, 373.—On Saint Martin’s relics, ibid., 311.—On Maroveus, bishop of Poitiers, sending clerics to the eastern regions to seek relics of the wood of the Lord’s Cross, of the holy Apostles, and of other martyrs, ibid., 518.—On relics of the saints brought from the city of Rome by a certain deacon in the time of King Childebert, ibid., 527.—On Deacon Gregory, who after the theft of relics was consecrated to the office of pontifical grace and made pope of the City, ibid., 529.—On Queen Radegund’s devotion to relics of the Lord’s Cross and of the holy martyrs, ibid., 709.—On miracles through the power of relics of the Virgin Saint Mary and others from the monastery at Jerusalem, ibid., 715.—On the tomb of John the Apostle and Evangelist, exuding manna like flour, from which blessed relics grant health to the sick, ibid., 730.—On the man Aridius, who through the relics of Saint Clement, bishop and martyr, obtained the return of waters to a certain spring, ibid., 738.—On the forty-eight martyrs who asked for their relics to be gathered, because, as they say, not one of them perished, ibid., 751.—On one of Chrodield’s soldiers, who, when he was just about to kill the abbess with his sword, was himself struck by another blade, ibid., 544.—On the lead sarcophagus of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle, cast into the sea and carried to the island of Lipari, ibid., 734.—On Felix, bishop of Nola, divinely saved from death by spiders’ webs, ibid., 796.—On Guntram ordering restored what Chilperic had unjustly taken away, ibid., 427.—On the referendary Marc, who, after amassing treasures through plunder, was suddenly seized with pain in his side, had his head tonsured, accepted penitence, and gave up his spirit, ibid., 395.

On the repentance of Bishop Praetextatus, LXXI, 426.—On a certain enclosed girl of the monastery at Poitiers who escaped through the wall, greatly enraged against the abbess, but soon returned wholly converted and performed penance, ibid., 520.—On Deacon Gregory’s exhortation to the people [Col. 0736] to repent, ibid., 528.—On the repentance of the Ninevites, ibid.—On the penance imposed on Chrodield and the nuns of her party, ibid., 549.—On the reconciliation of Justinian and Tiberius, ibid., 347.—On Aega, who acted more prudently than the other magnates and surpassed them all, ibid., 657.—On Sigismund killing his son Sigiric, ibid., 244.—On the wicked conduct of Siagrius and Sirivald, ibid., 267.—On Count Leudast setting snares for Fredegund in order to slaughter her sons with the sword, ibid., 328.—On Guntram killing with the sword the two sons of Magnacharius, ibid., 332.—On the massacres, murders, and sacrileges of the priests Salomius and Sagittarius, ibid., 340.—On Maracharius, cruelly killed by enemies because of his distinguished deeds, ibid., 351.—On Nantin avenging Maracharius’s death upon a priest accused of this crime, ibid., 352.—On Salvius’s constancy in the exercise of prayer, ibid., 418.—On the strength and efficacy of the prayer of Eupheonius and his other companions, ibid., 436.—On the holiness of Bishop Theodorus, ibid., 455.—On a man and woman praying and unafraid of flames while their cell was burning, fortified by their most firm hope in the power of Blessed Martin, who would save them, ibid., 473.—On the churches in Paris being saved from fire, together with their neighboring houses, ibid., 473.—On the bishop of Marseilles who, while a plague was raging, obtained an end to the disaster through the intercession of Saint Victor, bishop of Marseilles, ibid., 503.

On Queen Ingoberga’s immense exercises of charity and piety, ibid., 505.—On the sermons of Deacon Gregory, ibid., 529.—On Queen Chrotechilde continually passing the nights in prayers and vigils at the shrine of Saint Martin of Tours, ibid., 588.—On Blessed Columbanus, bishop, and King Theuderic, ibid., 624.—On a certain priest who, when the city of Bazas was under siege, exhorted everyone to prayer, ibid., 717.—On Aetius fighting among the enemy, and on his wife beseeching the Lord for him, ibid., 199.—On Saint Modestus, bound in chains in the stocks, who, after prayer to the Lord, was miraculously brought into the basilica of Saint Medard, ibid., 367.—On King Chilperic and the Jew Priscus, ibid., 375.—On the peaceful death of Saint Hospitius, ibid., 378.—On Eulalius reproved by his mother, ibid., 535.—On the hatreds of Chilperic and the Franks, ibid., 665.—On Guntram Boso seeking pardon from the queen through bishops, ibid., 487.—On Bishop Fronimius of Vence and King Leuvichild, ibid., 504.—On Fredegund’s hatred for her daughter, ibid., 512.—On Wado, his wife, and son, ibid., 513.—On Adalulf the Lombard and Queen Gundeberga, ibid., 638.—On Saint Ambrose sleeping upon the altar and, when awakened, answering: “Do not be troubled; Martin has died, and I am going to perform the offices of his funeral,” ibid., 919.—On Bishop Maroveus, who, made captive by Guntram, converted one sacred golden chalice into coin and redeemed himself and the people, ibid., 431.—On offerings in Saint Martin’s honour made by a little child, whenever he had any coin in his hand, ibid., 457.—On the prediction of Childebert’s birth, ibid., 451.—On Childebert being baptized on the holy day of Pentecost and raised to the throne on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, ibid., 452.—On a blessed death on the feast of the Lord’s Saint Martin, bishop of Tours, ibid., 184.

On Clodovech’s death at Paris, LXXI, 240.—On the misfortunes of the concubine Marcatrude, ibid., 288.—On the patrician Amatus engaging the Lombards in battle and turning his back in flight, ibid., 304.—On the miserable end of King Chrodobert, ibid., 312.—On the monk Julian using neither wine nor broth, ibid., 295.—On the simplicity and charity of Sunniulf, abbot of monks, ibid., 296.—On a monk who, after obtaining a miracle through his prayers, was beaten by order of his superior to remove vain glory from him, ibid., 297.—On Guntram visiting holy places and the basilica of Saint Avitus the abbot, ibid., 450.—On Chrodield’s skill and deceits, ibid., 515.—On a monk severely rebuked by his abbot lest he glory too much, though he was distinguished and powerful in prayer, ibid., 857.—On Abbot Augustus governing two monasteries, ibid., 887.—On the holiness of Aridius, ibid., 1122.—On a Spanish envoy saying that he was Catholic, but at Mass neither exchanging the peace with Catholics nor communicating with them in the sacrifice, ibid., 406.—On Masses celebrated in the city of Orléans with King Guntram present, ibid., 449, 453.—On Rachingus’s wife, who, after he had been killed, mounted a horse and hastened to the basilica of Saints Crispin and Crispinian, ibid., 488.—On the funeral of Blessed Radegund in the city of Poitiers, ibid., 906.—On the remarkable abstinence and unheard-of fasts of Deacon Gregory, such that, his stomach weakened, he could scarcely stand, ibid., 527.—On John, son of Eulalius, who by his penitence filled everyone with amazement, ibid., 536.—On the penance of the Breton Winnoch, [Col. 0737] ibid., 342.—On the iron chains and hair-shirt worn by the monk Hospitius, ibid., 376.—On the recluse Marianus, found dead beneath a tree, ibid., 889.—On Bishop Aegidius, Sigibald, and others, ibid., 424.—What King Guntram thought of the acclamations of the Jews when he entered the city of Orléans, ibid., 449.

GUIBERTUS VENERABILIS, abbot of Nogent.—On the military achievements of Christians, which surpass the achievements of pagans, CLVI, 679.

GUIBERTUS, abbot of Gembloux.—On Guibert himself, surnamed Martin because of a special devotion and service toward Saint Martin, archbishop of Tours, CCXI, 1281.—On Guibert Martin, who shows himself mindful toward Philip, archbishop of Cologne, of benefits received from him, CCXI, 1287.

GUICHARDUS, archbishop of Lyons.—On concord restored between the Church of Lyons and Count Guigo, CXCIX, 1089.—On Rachingus and Guntram meeting one another, LXXI, 487.—On a certain woman unjustly accused of adultery by her husband, whom God’s mercy sustained beneath the water after she had been thrown into a river, LXXI, 767.

GUILLELMUS, abbot of Saint Arnulf at Metz.—On his remarkable humility, CL, 876.

GUILLELMUS DANDINA.—On Hugh de Lacerta, a knight mindful of Christ’s poor, who supplied hoes and the other necessities of labor to those who lacked them, CCIV, 1182.

HALINARDUS, bishop of Lyons.—On his practice of the virtue of humility, which he maintained as long as he lived, while also multiplying works of charity, CXLII, 1333.

HAYMO, bishop of Halberstadt.—On the Holy Innocents killed by order of King Herod, CXVII, 75.

HELINANDUS, monk of Froidmont.—On his abandoning worldly habits, CCXII, 477.

HENRICUS, emperor.—On his principal deeds from the beginning of his reign until the foundation of the church of Bamberg, CXL, 60.

HENRICUS DE CASTRO, bishop of Albano.—How Henry, count of Champagne, set out for the holy war, CCIV, 215.

HERVEUS, monk of Bordeaux.—On Abbot Rainald, who was outwardly marked by such sweetness that he surpassed the pleasantness of honey, CLXXXI, 1723.

HIERONYMUS (Saint Jerome), priest.—That the only good which we possess in the present age is to eat Christ’s flesh and drink His blood, not only in the mystery but also in the reading of the Scriptures, XXIII, 1039.—On Roman rulers passing over to the faith of Christ, XXIV, 589.

HILARIUS (Saint Hilary), bishop of Poitiers.—That the prophet David and Christ provided examples of humility, IX, 632.—The misery of drunkenness vividly depicted, ibid., 687.—On the teaching of the new impiety of Hosius, X, 522.—On the adoration rendered by the Magi to Christ the infant in the cradle, ibid., 68.—On the distinction between fear of God and fear of men, IX, 704.—Who the authors of the Arian heresy are, X, 716.—How widely the devil spread the poison of the Arian heresy, ibid., 479 ff.—That Ursacius and Valens do not cease to spread the Arian and Eusebian heresy, ibid., 641.—That heretics are men of blood, IX, 814.—That heretics are incapable of the Holy Spirit and of understanding the Scriptures, X, 307.—That many feign peace while in fellowship with heretics, IX, 453.—That the Lord of the saints is the crown of the sanctified earth, IX, 422.—On the overthrow of idolatry through the spread of God’s name among the nations, ibid., 789.—That the Son of God washed away the first crimes of the world by the flood, ibid., 412.—That heresies arise from Scripture wrongly understood, X, 52, 202.—That the birth of the Son of God is made illustrious by human birth, ibid., 224.

HILARIUS.—On the blasphemy composed at Sirmium by Hosius and Potamius, X, 487.

HILARIUS (Saint), confessor.—That through the power of the Cross, making a threefold sign over the waters, he checked a flood, XXXI, 1233.

HILARIUS (Saint), bishop of Arles.—On the efficacy of Christ’s grace in himself, as he was converted through Honoratus’s exhortations, L, 1262.

HILDEGARDIS (Saint Hildegard).—That, among the other virgins of the monastery on Mount Saint Disibod, she was an example of radiant piety and subtle learning, CXCVII, 139.

HINCMARUS, archbishop of Reims.—On spells cast upon betrothals and removed by an ecclesiastical blessing, CXXV, 717.—On the reply he gave to Gunthar, archbishop of Cologne, concerning Boso’s wife, who had left her husband, CXXVI, 154.

HUGO, abbot of Flavigny.—On Saint Peter and Clement III, who exercised the priesthood for twenty years and held the episcopal chair of the city of Rome for the same number of years, CLIV, 24, 26.

[Col. 0738] HUGO (Saint), bishop of Lincoln.—On his education under a certain aged religious man, in secular, pagan, and ecclesiastical disciplines, CLIII, 945.

HUGO DE SAINT-VICTOR.—On gluttony, sloth, avarice, and lust, as avengers of injuries inflicted by us upon God, CLXXV, 776.—That spiritual men converse with one another concerning spiritual matters in order to uproot the evils of hell, CLXXVII, 186.

INNOCENT II, pope.—On the letters, lies, and deceits with which Antipope Anacletus was filled, CLXXIX, 699.

INNOCENT III, pope.—On the permission which he himself granted to the archbishop of Milan, allowing him in his church to promote to the diaconate and priesthood those who had received orders from the supreme pontiff, CCXIV, 18.—He grants the people of Treviso, since they are prepared to make satisfaction to the Church for the murder of the bishop of Belluno, that they may be released from the sentence of interdict by the bishop of Ferrara, ibid., 922.—How he himself exhorts the people of Treviso to return to the Church and amend their crimes, ibid., 555.—That he confirms the treaty concluded between Philip, king of France, and the count of Flanders, ibid., 117.—That he confirms a certain constitution concerning the revenues of Ivo’s benefice, ibid., 138.—That he confirms the election of the abbot of Saint-Denis, ibid., 162.—That he confirms certain revenues of the chapter of Segunto, ibid., 943.—Likewise, on the endowments of the church of Saint Mary of Palenzano, ibid., 1087.—Likewise, on the concord concluded between the bishop of Paris and the abbot of Saint Geneviève, CCXV, 33.—On the admonition he gave to the abbot and convent of the monastery of Abola, that they ought to show obedience and reverence to the bishop of Luni, CCXIV, 38.—On the protracted dispute concerning precedence and obedience between the monasteries of Monte Sacro and Calano, decided by himself, ibid., 401.—On the admonition addressed to the archbishop of Arles that he should restore the abbot of Saint Gervais to obedience and duty, ibid., 435.—On Frederick, king of Sicily, who exhorts the people of Montefiascone to be obedient to the Supreme Pontiff, ibid., 734.—On the illustrious king of Hungary, whom the pope exhorts to devotion or service toward the Apostolic See, ibid., 971.—On the admonition to Meganippanus, a nobleman of Serbia, that he return to the Catholic faith and render obedience to the archbishop of Colossae, CCXV, 28.—On the admonition addressed to the nobleman Peter and the people of Venice, that they return to obedience, CCXVI, 88.—On what must be done for the correction of the monastery of Cluny, its abbot, and monks, ibid., 86.—On the warning given to certain persons to effect correction in the monastery of Vaugaditia, ibid., 801.—On the correction of clerics and others, ibid., 1143.

ISAAC OF STELLA.—On Alcher: that he cultivated the liberal arts with piety in the abbey of Clairvaux and was highly learned, CXCIV, 1687.

ISIDORUS (Saint Isidore), bishop of Seville.—On the cleric Redemptus performing penance, LXXXI, 30.—On the remarkable spread of the Catholic faith, the madness of the Arians being defeated with the help of the venerable teacher Leander, LXXXII, 29.

IVO (Saint), bishop of Chartres.—On his liberality toward the abbey of Saint-Quentin, CLXI, 10.

JOANNES BELETH, theologian of Paris.—It is reported of him that he was a jewel among theologians, CCII, 9.

JOANNES DE BELMEIS, archbishop of Lyons.—That, freely resigning the episcopate, he embraced monastic life in the abbey of Clairvaux, CCIX, 877.

JONAS, abbot of Elnone.—On Herchantrude, who in tender age endured such great scourges that her patience in suffering might be compared with Job’s patience, LXXXVII, 1073.

JONAS, bishop of Orléans.—On avoiding falsehood, CVI, 227.

LACTANTIUS FIRMICUS.—That in the rite of adoration it was customary to bring the hand to the mouth, VI, 135.—That not only images but also statues of conquered peoples and cities were carried before and displayed at the funerals of emperors, ibid., 559.—That among angels some are guardians and others destroyers of human beings, ibid., 332.—On the sacrileges and jocular sayings against the gods of Dionysius, tyrant of Sicily, ibid., 273.—That the piety of pagans could only be false, ibid., 581.—That the celebrations of games are festivals of the gods, and that dedications of temples are made on their birthdays, ibid., 712.—On the two virtues, innocence and patience, which are the chief and greatest virtues in a good and wise man, ibid., 701.—That a certain soldier, recently slain, was restored to life at Pompey’s request, ibid., 778.—On baptism formerly administered on the Great Saturday before Easter or on the Saturday before Pentecost, VII, 617.—That crowns are prepared for Christ’s soldiers after victory, ibid., 704, 705.

LAMBERTUS, bishop of Arras.—On the acts of the people of Arras [Col. 0739] under Pope Urban, when they shook off the yoke of subjection to Cambrai and recovered their ancient dignity, CLXII, 627.

LUCIFERUS, bishop of Cagliari.—On Emperor Constantius, who committed sacrilege even against Christ by making sport of Him, VI, 273.

MAMERTINUS.—On his flattery toward Julian Augustus, XVIII, 415.

MARTIN I (Saint), pope.—On Bishop Theodore, who had restrained the fury of heretics, LXXXVI, 63.

MARTINUS (Saint), priest of León.—On his elevation to the priesthood and his life in a monastery under the Rule of Blessed Augustine, CCVIII, 15.

MAXIMUS (Saint), bishop of Turin.—On kindling the love of God through faith and longing for the Saviour, LVII, 676.

MILO, monk.—That the people of Ghent were brought to the faith by Saint Amandus, CXXI, 945.

NOTKERUS, monk of Saint Gall.—On the feast of the Apostles Philip and James and on their life, CXXXI, 1074.

NOVATUS, Catholic.—That one does not regard another as superior to oneself unless one possesses perfect humility, XVIII, 67.

ODALRICUS, archbishop of Reims.—On anathema and excommunication against sacrilegious thieves, CXXXIII, 965.

ODO DE SOLIACO, bishop of Paris.—On Peter the precentor and deacon, who held erroneous opinions concerning the manner of consecrating bread and wine in the Eucharist, CCXII, 48.—On the Feast of Fools at the Kalends of January, ibid., 49.—On donations made to the Church of Paris, ibid.—On his own generosity, so that there might be a greater gathering at the feast of Saint Stephen, ibid., 50.

OPTATUS (Saint), bishop.—On the threefold rank of the priesthood: deacons are placed in the third rank, priests in the second, and bishops hold the summit of the priesthood, XI, 910.

ORDERICUS VITALIS.—On Herod’s crimes against Christians, especially against John the Baptist, James, and Peter, CLXXXVIII, 112.—On the piety and praiseworthy conduct of King William, especially toward God’s ministers, ibid., 322.—On the cleric Ranulf, who obtained the friendship of King Rufus and, above all royal officials, won office from the king through ingenious accusations and manifold flatteries, ibid., 380.—On various events in England, Normandy, and Burgundy, ibid., 94.—On other various events among the French and Normans, especially Robert, who rebelled against William, duke of the Normans, and died after being killed with poison, ibid., 261.—On lightning striking down people in a church, ibid., 377.—On Duke William of Normandy crossing the sea to the English and making himself king, ibid., 451.—On various events in diverse places, ibid., 579, 647, 789.

PALLADIUS (Saint), bishop of Auxerre.—On three basilicas built through his own care, LXXXVII, 215.

PASCHASIUS RADBERTUS (Saint), abbot of Corbie.—On the passion of Rufinus and Valerius, CXX, 1490.

PATRICIUS (Saint Patrick), apostle of the Irish.—On the confession of Catholic truth made by himself in a foreign land, after the Lord had opened to him an understanding of unbelief and he had turned to the Lord with his whole heart, LIII, 801 ff.

PAULINUS (Saint), bishop of Nola.—That by the term *confessio* is understood the place in which the bodies of the Apostles are laid, LXI, 848.

PAULUS OROSIUS.—On the parricide of the Danaids and Perseus devastating Asia, XXXI, 718.—On the comparison and vicissitudes of different kingdoms, XXXI, 745.

PAULUS, bishop of Verdun.—On the Church of Verdun, which was so destitute of resources that it could not provide for the clerics necessary for divine worship, LXXXVII, 213.

PETRUS, bishop of Blois.—That the custom of mourning those who have died is an act of piety, if it is moderate, CCVII, 3.—He himself consoles his nephew over the death of his uncle in a fire, and demonstrates that the afflictions of this life are signs of divine love toward us, ibid., 36.—On the nun Anselma: that, having embraced the monastic rule, she should overcome every temptation of flesh and world and courageously guard the treasure of chastity, ibid., 113.—He praises a certain nun because she preserved the chastity consecrated to God in religious life, etc., ibid., 114.—On his own entreaty for the monks’ prayers, that he might be worthily initiated into the priesthood, and on the reasons why he had hitherto avoided it, ibid., 413.

PETER THE CHANTER.—On himself, that by integrity of character he lent weight and gravity to his teaching, being like a lily among thorns, a rose among nettles, fragrant incense in summer days, and as it were a heavenly trumpet and the Lord’s harpist, CCV, 11.

[Col. 0740] ST. PETER CHRYSOLOGUS.—That flattery is the devil’s final temptation, LII, 276.—On satisfaction enduring unto death, ibid., 544.

PETER DAMIAN, cardinal.—On fraternal correction, which must not be omitted, CXLIV, 276.—On love of neighbour, ibid., 278.

PETER LOMBARD.—On the humility of Philip, son of Louis the Fat, CXCI, 9.

PETER THE VENERABLE, abbot of Cluny.—On Peter Maurice, distinguished by knowledge of human and divine learning, CLXXXIX, 9.

PETER OF RIGA.—On his own old age and the dawn, CCXII, 13.

PETER BERNARD OF CORILLO, abbot of Grandmont.—On himself: first a married soldier, then a monk, and afterwards ordained priest, CCIV, 1163.

PHILIP OF HARVENG, abbot of Bonne-Espérance.—On Amandus, ordained bishop to the office of preaching, CCIII, 1246.

PHOEBADIUS, bishop of Agen.—On the blasphemies of the Arians, XX, 16.

PIBO, bishop of Toul.—On his instruction in letters by Anno, archbishop of Cologne, CLVII, 413.

ST. PROSPER, bishop of Aquitaine.—On how to recognize ecstasy when fear accompanies it, LI, 331.

RABANUS MAURUS, archbishop of Mainz.—On Paulinus’s birth and on the birth of Rabanus himself, CVII, 9.—On the nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary, CX, 54.—On the prophet Jeremiah cursing the day of his birth, CXI, 962.—On Solomon’s judgment concerning the women disputing over infants, CIX, 126.—On the Lord’s Supper, CXII, 31.—On Blessed Martha, who saw her sister’s soul borne to heaven by angels, CXII, 1503.

RATHERIUS, bishop of Verona.—On the Paschal dishes and the Paschal lamb, which was their figure, CXXXVI, 720.

REGINO, abbot of Prüm.—King Guntram, having gone one day to hunt in a forest, fell asleep overcome by a heavy sleep. A little later, awakened from sleep, he testified that he had seen a remarkable vision, declaring that he had crossed a certain river over an iron bridge, etc., CXXXII, 31.

REINERUS, monk.—On his hatred of flatterers, CCIV, 9.

RICHARD OF ST. VICTOR.—On Achard, bishop of Avranches, flourishing in integrity of life and manifold learning: he devoted his adolescence to humane letters, his youth to philosophy, and his more mature age to theology, making exceptional progress in each, CXCVI, 1371.—On Lord Hervisius, abbot of St. Victor, in whose honour Pope Alexander III issued a directive to the monks, ibid., 1375.

ROBERT, king of the Franks.—On three responsories composed by himself for the Office of the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary, CXLI, 901.

RUFINUS, priest of Aquileia.—On a venerable man named Hor: when demons came to him in the Thebaid in the guise of angels, the one who seemed to be regarded as king over the others said to him: “You have fulfilled everything; it remains for you to worship me,” XXI, 406.

RUPERT, abbot of Deutz.—On the burning of the town of Deutz, seen in his own lifetime, CLXX, 333.—On the blasphemy of Arius, the heretical priest, against Pope Alexander, CXVI, 1122.—On God’s zeal for his Church, so that the elect may ask God with greater urgency, CLXVIII, 230.

HUGH OF ST. VICTOR.—On Judea insofar as it is interpreted “confession,” just as Jerusalem is “vision of peace,” CLXXVI, 1132.

SIGEBERT, abbot of Gembloux.—On the deeds or acts of the abbots of Gembloux, CLX, 595.—On the liberality and generosity of Wicbert, who bestowed all his goods upon churches and the poor, CLX, 666.

STEPHEN, abbot and bishop.—On himself, trained from earliest youth in exercises of piety, CCXI, 205.—On a certain man ordained simoniacally, ibid., 344.—On himself pledging his service concerning Cardinal Vivian, ibid., 354.—On the murder of John the dean, over which there was great mourning in the Church of Orléans, ibid., 309.—On the abbot of St. Germain-des-Prés, acquitted of the killing of a certain scholar, ibid., 471.—On the bishop of Soissons granting him authority to administer the sacrament of confirmation in his diocese, ibid., 473.

STEPHEN, bishop of Tournai.—That he requested from the bishop of Soissons authority to administer the sacrament of confirmation at Marisy, CCXI, 473.

SULPICIUS SEVERUS.—How he rejected the evil pleasures of the present life and embraced a new life, XX, 81.

SYMMACHUS.—On his immense love for his paternal uncle, XVIII, 312.
