[Col. 0741] TERTULLIAN, priest of Carthage.—That no one ought to take offence if a believer, even a martyr, has fallen from the rule; for faith is not proved by persons, but persons are proved by faith, II, 14 ff.—On crowns customarily used among pagans, which Christians must not adopt, ibid., 85.—By what numerous, various, and horrible tortures Christians were tortured and slaughtered by pagans, I, 964.—That the blood of martyrs possessed greater persuasive power than the eloquence of pagan orators, ibid., 966.—On the martyrdom of St. Boniface, I, 619.—On those who killed themselves by the sword at their own prompting, such as Lucretia, Mucius, Regulus, etc., I, 625, 626.—On the charge of idolatry imputed to the origin of public games, with the testimonies of subsequent posterity, I, 636, 637.—On idolatry, I, 666.—That the names of angels and demons were known to pagan poets, philosophers, and the common multitude of uneducated people, I, 867.—On the giants desiring the daughters of men, I, 870.—How far pagans were from Christian fasts, I, 939.—On the sacred assemblies (*synaxes*) of Christians, I, 948.—With what absurdity the Romans boasted that by piety toward the gods they had deserved dominion over the whole world, I, 1121, 1123.—That for one hundred and seventy years and more the Romans worshipped their gods without images, I, 1129.—How absurdly images of beasts were propitiated for Liber, Cybele, etc., I, 1131.—On certain pagan rites in which initiates were admitted through washing, I, 1204 ff.—On the necessity of penitence for salvation for those who had fallen after baptism, I, 1242.—On patience, demonstrated by the examples of the prophets, apostles, Isaiah, and St. Stephen, I, 1270.

ST. THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury.—On his supreme humility when approaching the lord king, CXC, 26.

THOMAS, Cistercian cardinal.—On John Algrin, who, because of his learning, became a doctor of theology and, his upright character being added, became dean of the Church of Amiens, CCVI, 11.

[Col. 0742] POPE URBAN II.—On Bishop Gebehard: that he was especially praiseworthy because amid episcopal cares he never abandoned the fervour and zeal for the regular life which he had imbibed under William, abbot of Hirsau, CLI, 52.

ST. VALERIUS, abbot.—On the monk Maximus, who recounts a vision of the delights of paradise and the lamentations of hell, LXXXVII, 431.—On the monk Bonellus, to whom a revelation of hell was made, ibid., 433.

VENANTIUS FORTUNATUS.—On Leontius, bishop of Bordeaux, who showed such liberality in building and adorning the basilica of St. Vincent the martyr, LXXXVIII, 72.

VICTOR OF TOURS.—On Eutychetes, priest and archimandrite, preaching heresy, LXVIII, 941.

POPE VICTOR II.—On the sacrilege committed by a certain subdeacon who put poison into the sacred chalice of Pope Victor himself, CXLIII, 802.

ZACHARIAS CHRYSOPOLITANUS.—On himself, never having left the monastery of Prémontré, where he devoted himself constantly to study, CLXXXVI, 10.

ST. ZENO.—On the honour accorded to images of rulers and punishments imposed upon their violators, XI, 276.—That a denarius was given during the ceremonies of baptism, ibid., 360.—That Epicurus, Democritus, etc. argued against the immortality of the soul, ibid., 373.—That the nations, by pouring libations at the tombs of the dead, signified belief in the immortality of souls, ibid., 372.—On the calling up of Samuel’s soul, ibid., 376.—On the midwife who found the Mother of God to be a virgin, X, 415.

WALAFRID STRABO, monk of Fulda.—On Abbot Gallus expelling demonic apparitions appearing in the form of women, CXIV, 988.

[Col. 0741]

CLXV. INDEX OF MEMORABLE SAYINGS EXCERPTED FROM THE HOLY FATHERS, RELATING ESPECIALLY TO THE VIRTUES AND TO THE FORMATION OF CHRISTIAN LIFE, ARRANGED ALPHABETICALLY BY SUBJECT.  
(The reader is sometimes referred to bold-faced numbers inserted in the text.)

NOTICE.

It seemed highly useful to us to prepare a special index in which the choicest and shorter sayings of the Holy Fathers might be set out for Christian readers, for edification and the formation of life. We are pleased to offer this synoptic work, as it were a moral handbook. Hence preachers of the divine word, and all who have undertaken the governance of souls, will be able to draw forth, in few and distinguished words, counsels of most salutary doctrine, faith, and piety. We present this index in alphabetical order of the words.

[INDEX OF MEMORABLE SAYINGS.]

## A

[Col. 0741] **SELF-DENIAL.**—Self-denial is necessary for pleasing God, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 285.—Let us deny ourselves as we have made ourselves by sinning, and remain what we have been made by grace, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1567.—He who denies himself is himself righteous and himself worthy of Christ, St. Ambrose, XVI, 38.

**ABSENCE.**—He loses little through absence who is joined by constant letters, St. Jerome, XXII, 937.—The absence of bodies does no harm where hearts have been united through faith, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 32.—Those are not counted absent whose mind does not differ from the other in mutual charity, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 659.—One should not speak ill of those absent, but rebuke them to their face, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 75.

**ABSOLUTION.**—Who can be absolved who is not innocent even in his own eyes? St. Ambrose, XVI, 38.—God does not acquit the guilty person, but forgives sins to one who has turned back, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 152.—Each person is absolved all the more swiftly the more vigorously he condemns himself, Cassiodorus, LXX, 359.—The sinner who adds sins to sins in hope of forgiveness does not deserve absolution of sins, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 346.

**ABSTINENCE.**—In nothing is God’s mercy obtained more effectively than in the abstinence of the people, Tertullian, II, 962.—It is much better to take a little every day than enough rarely, St. Jerome, XXII, 289.—In abstinence one must not fear the uncleanness of food, but the uncleanness of desire, St. Augustine, XXXII, 798.—Abstinence from earthly things is often easier than their moderate use, ibid., XXXVII, 390, 392.—Abstinence is the first medicine of a human being, if it is accompanied by almsgiving, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 41.—By abstinence, the vices of the flesh—not the flesh itself—must be extinguished, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 675.—The abstinence of hypocrites is empty, ibid., 277.—The proof of abstinence is perfect chastity, id., [Col. 0743] LXXIX, 266.—He cannot have bodily abstinence who does not fill his mind with spiritual foods, ibid., 303.—Abstinence from vices is better than abstinence from foods, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 834.—That abstinence is pleasing to God which not only avoids evils, but also uses some lawful things in moderation and, in contemplation of God, entirely relinquishes others, Robert Pullen, CLXXXVI, 84.—When one abstains from lawful things, one more easily resists unlawful ones, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 355.

**ABUNDANCE.**—Abundance is where there is satiety, St. Ambrose, XVI, 10.—Abundance in paradise was true abundance; what is abundance after sin? Misery and calamity, St. Augustine, XXXV, 224.—The abundance of earthly things weighs down the eyes of minds, Ven. Gerhoh, CXCIII, 207.

**ABYSS.**—There is an abyss in a good heart and in an evil heart, but these are laid bare before God, St. Augustine, XXXV, 1749.

**APPROACH.**—We approach God or depart from him not by place but by conscience, not by a vehicle but by the mind, not by feet but by affections, St. Augustine, XXXV, 1871.

**ACCUSATION.**—To accuse an innocent person is to commit crimes, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 175.—Joyful accusation of one’s own wrongdoing after a sin has been committed is a great sign of salvation, Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 179.—He who accuses himself and rages against his own injustice is righteous, St. Gregory the Great, CLXXVI, 1234.

**ACTION, DEED.**—The whole good action of a human being is to turn to God, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 382.—In every movement of action, both the beginning and the end must be considered, ibid., XXXVIII, 200.—What is done by you, God does in you; nothing is ever done by you which God himself does not do in you; yet sometimes he does in you what is not done by you, ibid., XXXVI, 390.—The active life is first and more abundantly fruitful, ibid., XXXIX, 640.—No one orders better what he should do than one who is more ready not to do what divine power forbids than eager to do what human thought has devised, ibid., XXXVII, 316.—Whatever you do, do it well, and you have praised God, ibid., XXXV, 341.—Good deeds have their own cry, Cassiodorus, LXX, 22.—He praises the Lord who commends himself by an approved action, ibid., 385.—For a good action to be more worthy, it ought to seem unworthy to the doer himself, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 146.—The devil more wickedly besieges the end of an action if he has not deceived at its beginning, Ven. Gerhoh, CXCIII, 207.—All our deeds must be done with Christ as companion or witness, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 297.

**ADHERENCE.**—How good it is to cling to God: most blessed through affection, love, and charity, St. Augustine, XXXII, 1322.—He clings to the Lord who always strives to do the commands of his will, St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 178.—To cling to God and place one’s hope in him is always good, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 622.—He who clings to God is one spirit with him, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 181.—How great is the happiness of one who clings to God, ibid., 411, 412.—By clinging to him who always exists blessedly, we can always exist and exist blessedly, id., CLXXXIII, 36.

**HELPER, HELP.**—When God ceases to help, you can labour but cannot conquer, St. Augustine, XXXV, 1424.—God helps us to do his commands, from whom we hope for his promises, ibid., XXXVI, 1669.—What he commands is neither hard nor burdensome, since he helps bring about what he commands, ibid., 584.—To help the weak is charity; to help the powerful is pride, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 545.—He seeks outside help who has an enemy within, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 171.

**ADOLESCENCE.**—The path of adolescence is slippery, St. Jerome, XXII, 19.—Foolishness is bound up with adolescence, ibid., XXIV, 484.—Very few young people, from their earliest age, commit no condemnable sins, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 730.

**FLATTERY, FLATTERER.**—Flatterers are gentle as milk in prosperity, bitter as curd in adversity, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 333.—A severe rebuker is to be loved more than a flatterer who anoints the head, St. Jerome, XXII, 304.—To flatter the wicked because of their power and despise the good because of their poverty is a common vice, ibid., XXVI, 82.—Flattery is seduction by deceitful praise, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 1561.—It is the companion of all evils, ibid., XXXV, 142.—Flattery is the oil of the sinner, ibid., 1824.—The tongues of flatterers bind souls in sins; for it is pleasant to do those things in which one not only fears no reprover, but also hears a praiser, ibid., 126.—A rebuker who heals loves more than a flatterer who anoints the head, ibid., XXXIII, 114.—Flatterers are hidden rocks, ibid., XXXVI, 1835.—All sell oil, ibid., 2350.—Flatterers are said to bury their dead, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 225.—They are sellers of oil, ibid., 1478.—Flatteries blind the inner eyes, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 76.—One who despises gifts does not know how to flatter, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 58.—Flattery is both oil and a curse, ibid., 114.—Flattery flees the poor and follows the rich, ibid., 115.—Every flatterer is a traitor, ibid., 117.—Flatterers often turn virtues into vices and vices into virtues, Alan of Lille, CCX, 311.—The severe mercy of a righteous person is better than the bland flattery of a sinner, St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 507.

**ADVERSITY.**—In adversities, thanks must be given to God, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 331.—Without an adversary there is no crown of victory, St. Ambrose, XVI, 840.—A hidden adversary is a great evil, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 20.—The word of God is an adversary to your will until it becomes the author of your salvation, ibid., XXXVI, 636.—In adversity, lovers of this world think more of escaping what afflicts them than of receiving the means by which they may be cured, ibid., XXXIII, 938.—Adversity is the gift of a God who admonishes, ibid., 957.—Any temporal adversity is easily borne in order that eternal punishment may be avoided and eternal rest gained, ibid., XXXVI, 444.—No adversity breaks one whom no prosperity corrupts, ibid., XXXV, 1058.—Both adversity and prosperity must be guarded against: the latter lest it corrupt, the former lest it break us, ibid., 1824.—It is more to be feared if we suffer no adversities or only slight ones, ibid., XXXVI, 1813.—Adversities either correct or test, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 40.—Adversity becomes prosperity for the righteous, by which they are made safe from vanity, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 251, 851.—He who does what is right and endures adversity labours in adversity, but will be perfected in glory, ibid., 531.—Adversities must be borne bravely outwardly and gently inwardly, ibid., 710.—He who seeks no prosperity fears no adversity, ibid., 717.—Adversity is sometimes useful, like a storm, id., LXXVII, 519.—Let adversity itself increase the zeal for good works, ibid., 876.—Instructed by adversities, we discover God’s understanding more subtly, ibid., 895.—Let those humbled by adversity rejoice in hope of the eternal inheritance, ibid., 78.—We ought neither to be broken by adversities nor lifted up by prosperities, ibid., 662.—We who have sinned much through the flesh’s blandishments are cleansed through its affliction, ibid., 1114.—Those who love heavenly things alone powerfully endure the adversities of the world, id., LXXIX, 233.—God touches with the goads of adversity those unwilling to correct themselves by their own resolve, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 264.—In adversities, we await a more merciful Judge in proportion as we now patiently endure him while he is more severe, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 318.—Adversities compel us toward God and separate the mind from earthly things, ibid., 181.—If God strikes, we cry out that he may spare us; if he spares, we provoke him again to strike us, ibid., 251.—Adversity and prosperity urge us on in the course of love, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 393.—Love yields neither to adversity nor to nature’s weakness, ibid., 6.—No adversity will harm where no iniquity rules, id., CLXXXIII, 496, 843, 866.—Adversity purifies the soul, Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 181.—Adversity is difficult to resist unless prudence is joined to courage, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 275.—Adversity is night, Ven. Guibert, CXLIV, 73.—God directs adversity and prosperity toward good, ibid., 83.—Adversities do not cast down the strong, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 124.

**EDIFICATION.**—We build as though we were always going to live, St. Jerome, XXII, 965.—To hear and not do is to build on sand; to hear and do is to build on rock; neither to hear nor to do is to build nothing, St. Augustine, XXXV, 1335.—Those loving nothing besides Christ build gold, silver, etc., ibid., 413.

**SICK PERSON, SICKNESS.**—The sick reject wholesome foods, St. Cyprian, IV, 39, 41.—As with desperate sick persons, so the reprobate are not denied what they desire, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 681.—Sickness wounds the flesh and heals the mind, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 503.—A sick person does not seek an eloquent physician but a wise one, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 20.

**ENVY.**—It is characteristic of patience not to envy, Tertullian, II, 1268.

**EQUALS, EQUALITY.**—Equality itself, true and first unity itself, is perceived not by sense but by the mind, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 146.—To an equal we owe counsel and assistance, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 725.

**EQUITY.**—Equity without goodness, in the judgment of heaven, is cruelty, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 145.

**MISERIES.**—Where misery is reckoned human, there blessedness begins in the divine judgment, St. Ambrose, XVII, 59.—Misery points to the affliction of penitence, St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 145.

**HEAT.**—He who is protected by the shade of divine power knows no heat of body, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 142.—One heat belongs to the body, another to the heart, Wolbero, CXCV, 39.

**AGE.**—No age is too late for learning, St. Ambrose, XVI, 837.—Age is perfect where virtue is perfect, ibid., 1200.—Faith increases age, ibid., 7.—To warn a slippery age is an act of piety, St. Jerome, XXII, 504.—Mature age despises the errors of adolescence, [Col. 0745] ibid., 457.—Though it seems long, age is proved short when it arrives at its end, because it ends, St. Augustine, XXXV, 1613.—It is not years but morals that make a person younger in age, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 5.

**ETERNAL THINGS, ETERNITY.**—Nothing is eternal except after the resurrection, Tertullian, II, 880.—God has one time: eternity, St. Jerome, XXVIII, 691.—Every time is brief compared with eternity, ibid., XXVI, 359.—Eternity has become our refuge, so that we may flee to it from this mutability of time, St. Augustine, XXXV, 1142.—God gives eternal things for enjoyment, temporal things for use, ibid., XXXVI, 413.—Meditation upon eternal things exercises the mind’s instability, ibid., XXXVII, 824.—One who desires eternal things grows weary of love for temporal things, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 134, 393, 496, 985.—Our place is eternal light, ibid., 134.—One who yearns for eternal things fears nothing from the world, ibid., 356.—Eternity ought to be our intention, temporality our use, ibid., 489.—He who asks with his mouth but does not desire eternal life in his heart is silent while crying out, ibid., 718.—Eternal things lie before us; temporal things are behind us, ibid., 1198.—Things passing away become cheap to a mind that knows eternal things, ibid., LXXIX, 33.—Eternity is compared to a point, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 48, 61.—It contains all times, ibid., 125.—Love of eternal things makes earthly things cheap, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 632.—Insofar as we know eternal things, we despise transitory things, Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 431.—The present life compared with eternity is like a point of time, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 320.—He despises temporal evils who considers eternal recompenses, Cassiodorus, LXX, 217.

**AFFECTION, DISPOSITION.**—Your disposition gives its name to your work: as it proceeds from you, so it is judged, St. Ambrose, XVI, 39.—All affections are right in a right life and perverse in a perverse life, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 416.—If there are no affections, one does not then live rightly, ibid., 415.—Affections belong to this life, not to the future life that is hoped for, ibid.—Our affections are our feet on the journey to God, id., XXXV, 1217.—Let us run to God by affections, not by steps, ibid., XXXVIII, 681.—A pious affection entering the mind appears to be milk, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 89.—Meditation forms the disposition if it is discerning, reforms it if it is frequent, ibid., 95.—Human affections are transformed in the homeland into divine ones, id., CLXXXIII, 602.—Affection supplies what nature cannot do, Alan of Lille, CCX, 328.

**AFFLICTION, AFFLICTIONS.**—By temporal affliction, penitents not only escape eternal punishments but also blot them out, Tertullian, I, 1244.—Affliction in this world is material for rewards, St. Jerome, XXII, 711.—People are afflicted so that they may seek God, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 1163.—Affliction is punishment for sin to the wicked, a crown of virtue to the good, St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 821.—When a believer afflicts himself, being chastised he escapes God’s wrath, Cassiodorus, LXX, 298.—Affliction received from neighbours is grievous, ibid., 148.—Here we are afflicted by God’s best counsel, lest we love the road instead of the homeland, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 752.—In affliction, let Christ’s commandments console us, id., LXXVII, 895.—The affliction of penitence is the path of life, id., LXXIX, 95.—There is no greater affliction than that arising from consciousness of sins, ibid., 556.—The affection of love is better than affliction of the flesh, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 104.—It is characteristic of the afflicted to regard release from troubles as the highest happiness, id., CLXXXIII, 854.—How miserably he lives who does not devote himself to affliction of the flesh, Guibert, CLVI, 457.

**FIELD.**—One field belongs to God, another to man, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 2325.—He who cultivates a field badly causes evil for himself, not for the earth, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 7.

**WINGS.**—The two wings by which we are raised to heaven are the two commandments of charity, or else charity and humility, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 2312.—God’s wings are mercy and charity, St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, Psalm XVIII.—To lose wings is to lose the lofty flights of contemplation, Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 1353.

**ALTAR, SHRINE.**—There is a heavenly altar, which no unworthy person touches, and a visible altar, which many unworthy persons touch, St. Augustine, XXXV, 193.—The altar of the Lord is the heart of the righteous, St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 176.—Christ is the altar of the temple; the Church is the temple, Rupert, CLXIX, 412.—Our heart is figured in the altar, Wolbero, CXCV, 12.

**TO LOVE, LOVE.**—We ought to love God as sons and fear him as servants, Lactantius, VI, 322.—God demands to be loved by us, since that love benefits not himself but us, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 39.—Nothing is so useful as to be loved; nothing so useless as not to be loved, St. Ambrose, XVI, 77.—The judgments of lovers are blind, St. Jerome, XXVII, 109.—A lover of himself leads himself astray, ibid., XXVIII, 522.—Holy love has no impatience, [Col. 0746] ibid., XXII, 290.—No one can be possessed by two loves: if you are a lover of the flesh, you do not receive the love of the spirit, ibid., XXIV, 505.—We love only something beautiful, St. Augustine, XXXII, 701, 1183.—A person loves that from which he thinks he will be happy, ibid., XXXVII, 672.—He who loves does not labour, ibid., XXXIV, 1741.—What you love for a time will either be taken away from you, or you will be taken away from it, ibid., XXXVI, 1653.—Things possessed with love do not perish without grief, ibid., XXXVII, 156.—Love God: you will find nothing better, ibid., XXXVI, 1531.—To love God freely is piety, ibid., 1469.—You love by charity whatever you love rightly, ibid., XXXVI, 160.—By loving God we are called gods; by loving the world we are called world, ibid., 678.—Love is the weight by which the mind is borne wherever it is borne, ibid., XXXII, 848.—Love cannot be idle, ibid., XXXV, 19.—In what is loved, either one does not labour, or the labour itself is loved, ibid., XXXVII, 448.—When anyone seems to possess what he loves, he is called happy; but he is truly happy not if he has what he loves, but if he loves what ought to be loved, ibid., XXXV, 202.—Each person lives from his love, whether well or badly, ibid., XXXVIII, 228.—He who loves rightly believes and hopes rightly; but one who does not love believes or hopes in vain, ibid., XXXVII, 285.—The measure in loving God is to love him without measure, ibid., XXXIII, 419.—To love God is justice and blessedness, ibid., XXXVII, 1047.—He cannot love another who does not love God, ibid., 843.—The love of God is a burden, but it removes the burden of sins, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 3.—He cannot love who fears excessively, ibid., 7.—Love directed toward God ought neither to grow proud amid prosperity nor fail amid adversity, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 42.—Without love of the good, no one is good, ibid., 349.—To love God is natural to humanity, St. Benedict, LXVI, 106.—No one can be excused from loving God, ibid.—Where love is, there is not labour but delight, ibid., 36, 244.—No one can love what he does not believe, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1348.—Love often stirs sluggish minds to work, ibid., 208.—Love is never idle, ibid., 1576.—The more we are strengthened in God’s love, the more we fail in our own strength, ibid., 134.—Love of God produces weariness of life, ibid., 318.—He who loves God already has him, ibid., 1575.—The measure of loving God is to love without measure, ibid., 1639.—Those sin against love of neighbour who, doing good deeds secretly, permit bad opinions of themselves, id., LXXVII, 95.—God’s commandments are light to one who loves, id., LXXIX, 273.—Earthly love soils the eye of the heart, ibid., 457.—Nothing is difficult to one who loves, St. Peter Damian, CXIV, 152.—Love of neighbour is the ladder to the love of God, ibid., CXLIV, 76.—Divine love in us ought to be extinguished neither by adversity nor prosperity, ibid., 301.—Nothing is loved unless it is known, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 21, 91.—He who loves something other than God has not the charity of God in him, ibid., 259.—To love God above all things is just and rational, ibid., 191, 267.—God alone is to be loved, and without end, ibid., 224.—He who loves God more than himself already begins to hold what he wishes perfectly to possess in the kingdom of heaven, ibid., 349.—If you wish to be king in heaven, love God and human beings for his sake, ibid., 341.—He loses the life he lives who does not love God, ibid., 228.—He who loves God becomes God himself, ibid., 201.—A reward is owed to one who loves, not to one who is loved, ibid., 418.—The love of God is the life of the heart, Rupert, CLXXVII, 563.—God is to be loved without measure, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 58.—When God loves, he desires nothing other than to be loved, ibid., 401.—Nothing is to be loved above God, ibid., 238.—We are forbidden to think more highly than we ought, but commanded to love even more than we can, ibid., 396.—To love God is to eat, ibid., 934.—Nothing is difficult to one who loves, ibid., 1050.—Love is an eye; to love is to see, ibid., 396.—Love cannot exist without being sweet, ibid., 104.—Love cannot be satisfied by itself, and yet cannot be fed except by itself, ibid., 58.—God is love; whoever loves him loves love, ibid., 394.—Loving love makes a circle, so that love has no end, ibid.—Christ is the incitement of love, ibid., 66.—True love does not seek a reward, but deserves one, id., CLXXXIII, 591.—For one who loves God, all things are held in common with God, ibid., 1427.—The love of God and of the world are two feet, Ven. Gerhoh, CXCIII, 311.—Where love is, there is the eye, Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 10.—The force of love is not restrained by reason and is checked by no impossibility, ibid., 1196.—A visitation of love delights; its alternation troubles, ibid., 1198.—Love is the gate of death or life; it is good or evil: evil love is called cupidity, good love charity, Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 459.—Love and fear are two wings for seeking eternal things, Ven. Guibert, CLVI, 45.

**BITTERNESS.**—God, who by his nature is sweet and kind, is made bitter by our vices, St. Jerome, XXVI, 30.—He to whom God is sweet becomes bitter to himself, St. [Col. 0747] Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1280.—Bitterness of heart exercises virtues; it does not overthrow them, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 130; Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 460.—God mingles bitter things with pleasures even for the innocent, so that we may have no love except for eternal life, St. Augustine, XXXV, 458.

**FRIENDSHIP, FRIENDS.**—To love friends belongs to everyone, but to love enemies belongs to Christians alone, Tertullian, I, 698.—There is no true friendship where flattering deception exists, St. Ambrose, XVI, 140.—The friendships of the poor are for the most part better than those of the rich, ibid., 140.—Friendship is a virtue, not a source of gain; an aid to life, ibid., 139.—What is a friend but a partner in love, so that you wish two persons to become one? ibid., 140.—Another self, ibid., 664.—A friendship which can cease was never true, St. Jerome, XXII, 13.—That friendship is true which is formed not by the advantage of household resources nor merely by bodily presence, but by fear of God and devotion to the Scriptures, ibid., 270.—It is better to undergo lasting enmities than provoke God’s offence through harmful friendships, ibid., 719.—Friends are rare and faithful, ibid., 756.—A friend is sought for a long time, scarcely found, and difficult to keep, ibid., 13.—Friendship is formed by similar characters, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 243.—True friendship flows from the charity of eternity and truth, ibid., XXXIII, 667.—There is no true friendship unless God binds it together among those who cling to him in charity, ibid., XXXII, 696.—Friendship is never faithful except in Christ, ibid., XXXVI, 555.—There is no friend among the wicked, ibid., XXXV, 1177.—Those who agree only in merely human matters are not friends, ibid., XXXIII, 1072.—Not everyone who spares is a friend, nor is everyone who strikes an enemy, ibid., 323.—The death of a friend is bitter; change is more bitter, ibid., XXXVIII, 635.—True friendship is eternal and cannot cease, ibid., XXXVII, 833, 837, 839, 1040. It begins here and is perfected in heaven, ibid., 841.—Those among whom there is agreement in vices falsely assume the name of friendship, ibid., 833, 836.—A friend is, as it were, the guardian of the soul, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1562.—He is God’s friend who strives to make others his friends, id., LXXIX, 226.—Friends are many in prosperity, few in adversity, Blessed Alcuin, C, 224.—True friendship does not exist unless it has a firm foundation in God, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 402.—Mutual knowledge of conscience and the same will make friendship, ibid., 278.—True friendship sometimes contains rebuke, but never flattery, id., CLXXXIII, 242.—Spiritual friendship is always and everywhere consistent with itself, ibid., 66.—He is unworthy of love who serves a friend against God, ibid., 265.—A friend is another self, ibid., 59.—God nourishes friends by grace and refreshes those most dear, Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 500.—Do not prefer riches and honours to friendship, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 62.—Quarrels between friends renew love, Alan of Lille, CCX, 422.—A friendship wholly dissolved was never true, ibid., 428.

## SOUL, MIND

The soul is the whole of what we are, Tertullian, II, 775. — The soul can be overshadowed, but cannot be extinguished, ibid., 720. — Every good of the mind is either innate, taught, or compelled, ibid., 980. — What is so much the human being as his soul? St. Ambrose, XVI, 923. — Christ found the soul exiled from paradise and, retracing the winding course of error, called it back to paradise, ibid., 1069. Where the soul has cleansed the heart, it finds the Word and sees God, ibid., 236. — Faith, grace, mercy: the redemption of the soul, ibid., 770. — Enter wholly into your own soul; gather yourself within it; dwell in it and abide with it; let all your intercourse be within it, so that you may be not in the flesh but in the spirit, ibid., 917. — Disturbance of soul removes constancy; abandonment reveals cowardice and indicts sloth, ibid., 61. — The soul of the believer is the true temple of Christ, St. Jerome, XXII, 324. — What is more beautiful than a soul called God's daughter and seeking no outward adornments? ibid., 283. — The Lord seeks the souls of believers more than riches, ibid., 433. — As a body is called healthy if it is afflicted by no sickness, so a soul is healthy, without fault, if it is shaken by no disturbance, ibid., 794. — Wherever the soul turns, it finds bitterness in earthly things; it has nothing by which it may be sweetened unless it lifts itself to God, St. Augustine, XXXV, 1085–1086. — Just as the soul cannot illuminate itself from itself, so it cannot satisfy itself from itself, id., XXXII, 853. — A soul bound by earthly love has, as it were, birdlime on its wings and cannot fly, id., XXXV, 1618. — By loving the body the mind becomes weak, id., XXXIV, 27. — He whose mind does not die to this age shall rise not to life but to punishment, ibid., 25. — Truth is the food of the mind, id., XXXVIII, 62. — No good except the highest is sufficient for the soul, id., XXXVII, 962. — Nothing fills it except God, ibid., 887. — Great is the misery of the soul that does not love Christ, ibid., 953. — The soul lies in the body as in a bed of pain, St. Peter Chrysologus, [Col. 0748] LII, 14. — It must not be cast down from the heights of heaven into a tomb of gold, ibid., 22. — The more afflicted the substance of the flesh, the more purified the soul becomes, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 314. — The faithful soul is corrected by fear and rejoices in correction, St. Maximus of Turin, LIV, 29. — The mind languishes with the love of God when it sets nothing above love for him, Cassiodorus, LXX, 509. — We may be bent in body, but not in mind, ibid., 129. — The pious soul is the City of God, ibid., 334. — Without God the soul is always captive, ibid., 390. — The soul is the life of the body; God is the life of the soul, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 135. — The more contemptible the soul makes itself to itself, the more precious it becomes to God, ibid., 583. — The soul exults when, despising all things, it loves God alone, id., LXXIX, 53. — A soul separated from God cannot perceive God, ibid., 471. — Luxuries kill the soul as hard things wound the flesh, ibid., 490. — The governance of souls is greater than imperial rule, St. Agobard, CIV, 299. — The soul in vices is called a desert, St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, Psalm XXVIII. — A holy soul is a garden of delights, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 66. — The soul has been made so that it may always live, if it always wishes to do that for which it was made, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 25. — Idleness of the soul is contrary to God's order, St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 9. — The mind or thought is the head of the soul, ibid., 176. — The soul is immortal, yet while it sins it dies and is separated from true life, which is Christ, id., CLXV, 55. — A good mind is a garden of delight, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 506. — The present time is assigned to souls, not bodies, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 299. — For the salvation of souls, sweet leisure must be set aside, ibid., 145. — By virtue the soul becomes nearer to God, ibid., 364. — The true love of the soul is that by which truth is loved, ibid., 401. — Though corrupt, the soul is capable of great grace and blessedness, ibid., 155. — The rational soul has two regions: the lower, governed by the flesh; and the higher, in which God rests, ibid., 552. — God is the soul’s true life, ibid. — How difficult it is for the soul to gather itself from itself back to itself, Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 152. — With how great a fullness of shame will the soul which, living here, has defiled in itself God’s likeness return to God? ibid., 211. — The soul that labours more severely under temptation will be rewarded more fully in perfection, ibid., 494. — The soul that loves God is not sated with love, ibid., 1200. — In this life the soul continually needs correction, Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 91. — The soul of the righteous is the house of wisdom, Alan of Lille, CCX, 166.

## YEARS

Eternal years, years without years, one day, St. Augustine, XXXV, 976.

## APOSTLES

The apostles, like salt, are sowers of eternity, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 682. — The apostles still groan, because there is labour on account of the many who are still tossed by the waves, St. Ambrose, XVI, 927. — The virtues of the apostles are to be imitated before the simplicity of their words, St. Jerome, XXII, 318.

## TREE

A storm does not overthrow a sturdy tree, St. Cyprian, IV, 197. — A tree does not bear fruit when, in the spring season, it all burns with blossom, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 162. — We cut branches from trees for ourselves by imitating the examples of better people, St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 296.

## ARROGANCE

Arrogance is to be avoided even more than ignorance, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 585.

## ART

No art is learned without a master, St. Jerome, XXII, 942. — The art of the world has vigorous lovers; the art of divine fear has languid ones, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 204.

## ASCENT

The ascent to great things is not easy, St. Cyprian, IV, 180. — Ascent is in labour; descent is in pleasure, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 224.

## SIGHT

Sight is darkened by smoke; the sight of a tree stained the woman’s eyes; the sight of Christ’s tomb cleanses them, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 77.

## INSPIRATION

God’s inspiration is understood as signifying eternal happiness, and the inclination of the shadows as signifying the unending night of this mortality, Wolbero, CXCV, 39.

## EARS

Tribulation opens the ear, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 843. — The ears must be carefully fenced about, Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 972.

## GOLD

God made gold, and made you above gold, so that you might be its master, not its slave, St. Augustine, XXXV, 1646. — Many lose faith in order to acquire gold, ibid., 1645. — Gold ought to follow you, not you gold, id., XXXVI, 1417. — It ought to be led, not to lead; possessed, not to possess, ibid. Gold properly belongs to the person who uses it well; thus it is God’s truth, ibid., 327. Gold and silver are good, not because they make you good, but because they provide the means of doing good, ibid., 410. — Gold is an evil master and a treacherous servant, ibid., 1933. — It is more useful when despised, ibid. — Gold benefits the giver, not the possessor, Bl. Alcuin, C, 127. — The gold of wisdom is born from the travail of new life, Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 333. — To place the blessed life in gold and silver is most shameful, Peter the Chanter, [Col. 0749] CCV, 45. — Not everything that shines is gold, Alan of Lille, CCX, 426.

## HELP

Supported by the Lord’s help, one shall not fall, Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 1131–1132. — God’s help is twofold: correction and consolation, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 585.

## THE AVARICIOUS

All the avaricious are leprous within, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 1832. — The avaricious person is like a sick man, id., XXXVII, 1058. — The avaricious person reckons as lost whatever another possesses, Peter Chrysologus, LII, 7. — The avaricious person reduces himself to his own moneybag, ibid., 54. — The avaricious deceive when they say that they bestow benefits, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 53. — The avaricious person, like a bird, after devouring the bait of earthly things, is strangled in the snare of sin, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 65. — Riches are ruinous to the avaricious and envious, Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 856. — By living stingily, the avaricious person heaps up wealth for another to devour, ibid., 843. — The more the avaricious person increases money, the more he burns with thirst for money, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 188.

## TURNING AWAY

By turning away from God, man is darkened; by turning to God, he is enlightened, St. Augustine, XXXV, 193.

## B

## STAFF

The staff of the good shepherd is the Blessed Virgin Mary, Adam of Perseigne, CCXI, 23. — The staff of support, ibid., 173.

## BEARER

Christ is our bearer, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 15.

## BAPTISM

Those who receive baptism and renounce the world in words but not in deeds have true baptism, but are not made alive by it, St. Augustine, XL, 189. — Baptism, like an impressed mark, adorns the soldier and convicts the deserter, id., XXXV, 433. — Since in baptism I died with Christ, I received from Christ the light of life, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1098. — Let the baptized person not be slothful, but make his way by the path of God’s commandments toward the heavenly homeland, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 176.

## THE BLESSED; BLESSEDNESS

The hope of blessedness belongs to all nations, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 187. — Innocence and knowledge make one blessed, St. Ambrose, XVI, 72. — The blessed life is the fruit of present things, but eternal life is the hope of future things, ibid., 74. — The end of blessedness is to know God, St. Jerome, XXVI, 460. — Those who are called blessed not because of virtue but because of gifts will be hurled into death, id., XXII, 141. — Blessedness is attaining the highest good, and not living as each person wishes, St. Augustine, XXXII, 1254. — The blessed life is not blessed unless it is eternal, id., XXXVI, 1403. — Blessedness is deceptive and false when future misery is either unknown or feared, id., XXXVIII, 371. — Blessedness is not to be sought here, ibid., 1106. — The blessed life, if it is not loved, is not possessed, ibid., 433. — No one is blessed except the righteous, ibid. — Two things make one blessed: to will well, and to be able to do what one wills, id., XXXIX, 1020. — Blessed is the person who lives as God wills, id., XXXVI, 2159; XXXVII, 725. — The blessedness of the righteous begins in fear and advances into desire for God’s commandments, St. Prosper, LI, 461. — Blessed is the person who watches and forestalls the enemy’s snares, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 27. — Blessedness is promised not to the idle but to those who labour, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 130. — Whoever seeks blessedness here rises before dawn, Cassiodorus, LXX, 442. — An upright life with faith makes one blessed, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 191. — The delay of blessedness gives believers cause for groaning, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 218. — In blessedness, repose will be greater in proportion as there has been no repose here in love of the Creator, id., LXXVII, 712. — No one can be perfectly and laudably blessed who wills what he can neither be nor ought to be, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLIX, 68. — Blessedness is sufficiency in which there is no need, id., CLVIII, 85. — Nothing but God, who himself is the blessed life, is sufficient for humanity, ibid., 203, 228. — There is no blessedness if there is no righteousness, ibid., 69. — Blessedness is to see God’s brightness, St. Rupert, CLXIX, 322. — Blessed here and in heaven is the one beloved by God and human beings, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 974. — Truly and perfectly blessed are those who truly and perfectly love God, ibid., 240. — Blessed is the person troubled lest he be overwhelmed both by benefits and by sins, id., CLXXXIII, 870. — Whoever loves blessedness regards all earthly things as of little value, Ven. Guibert, CLVI, 1151. — The height of blessedness is to see God, Bl. Alcuin, C, 158.

## WAR

No war is more grievous and bitter than that of will and passion, in which no one wins, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 658. — It is a great war for us to see no enemies and yet conquer them, id., XXXV, 1854. — Better is war with hope of eternal peace than captivity without any thought of deliverance, id., XXXVIII, 729. — Those proceeding to war under Christ as their leader should show by their work what they proclaim by their mouth, St. Gregory the Great, [Col. 0750] LXXVI, 991.

## BLESSING

God’s blessing is eternal life, St. Augustine, XXXV, 1442. — When God blesses, he does what he says, ibid., 1444. — The wicked bless in prosperity; the good bless even in adversity, Cassiodorus, LXX, 163.

## GOODWILL

No food is sweeter than goodwill and affection, St. Ambrose, XVI, 412. — There is no beneficence where there is no goodwill, ibid., 38. — Everyone trusts the counsel of one well-disposed toward him more than that of a wise person, ibid., 167. — Remove goodwill from human life, and you will have removed the sun from the world, ibid.

## GOODS, THE GOOD, GOODNESS

Goodness, unless it is governed by justice so as to be just, will not be goodness if it is injustice, Tertullian, II, 298. — Everything just is good, ibid. — Nothing is good except knowledge and enjoyment of God, ibid. — The good labour more; imitate them, St. Cyprian, IV, 261, 305. — By sharing our goods with the needy, we shall be worthy of the things that we need from God, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 688. — Many things are good but not pleasant, and pleasant things are not good, ibid., 517. — The good is to be done rather than merely thought about, ibid., 72. — More beautiful is the good done not from necessity but willingly, St. Ambrose, XVI, 932. — What is good is not to be avoided; what is better is to be chosen, ibid., 205. — Habit in goodness has lost the practice of its former perversity, ibid., 227. — The highest good is the fountain of life, from which the substance of life is supplied to all, ibid., 908. — Every good which we possess is the Lord’s gift, St. Jerome, XXII, 1034. — To know is the work of judgment; to do is the work of labour, ibid., 106. — Only with toil and sweat can we scarcely change evils into goods, ibid., 613. — Unless we hate evil, we cannot love good, ibid., 941. — Every good is either God or from God, St. Augustine, XXXII, 1265. — God is the highest good; the soul a great good; the body a small good, id., XXXVI, 853. — Only inward goods are to be loved; other things are to be used for necessity, not enjoyed for delight, id., XXXV, 81. — When the good delights us, it is a great gift of God, ibid., 1547. — No one has anything good unless he has received it from him who alone is good, ibid., 1670. — God will not take away spiritual goods unless you abandon them; but he himself takes away fleshly and temporal goods, ibid., 201. — Do you wish to possess goods and not wish to be good? Your life is contrary to your desires, id., XXXVI, 521. — Temporal goods, when desired, burn us; when obtained, grow cheap; when lost, vanish, ibid., 861. — They never cease to inflame before they come, corrupt when they come, and torment as they pass away, ibid. — A good person is one who, when able to do evil, does not do it, id., XXXV, 1190. — Do not praise yourself even when you are good; for by praising yourself you become bad instead of good: humility had made you good; pride makes you bad, ibid., 1193. — The good person labours for a time; the wicked person flourishes for a time, ibid., 1191. — Earthly prosperity does not make one good, id., XXXVI, 135. — Some goods make a person good; others are means by which one acts well, id., XXXVII, 2153. — Eternal goods are loved more ardently once obtained than when desired; temporal goods are otherwise, id., XLV, 1876. — God instructs the good through the wicked, St. Prosper, LI, 577. — Every good is from God, ibid., 876, 879. — Good is to be done with joy, ibid., 559. — The person seeking future rather than present goods is not troubled by the prosperity of the wicked, ibid., 422. — Goods of every kind can perish without charity; without charity they cannot profit, ibid., 951. — Temporal goods are provisions for the journey, not enticements to remain, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 352. — He is not good who becomes good only for himself, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 587. — Under the appearance of good, evil sometimes lies hidden, St. Benedict, LXVI, 207. — There is no satiety in good things, Cassiodorus, LXX, 408. — The wicked rest upon fleeting goods, despising true goods, and perish with those goods, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 662. — Good works ought to proceed from a pure heart, ibid., 112. — The truly good are those who are good among the wicked, ibid., 17, 673. — The good are never alone except in heaven, ibid., 1637. — Our good deeds are God’s works, ibid. — It is blameworthy not to imitate a good thing that pleases, id., LXXVII, 797. — The person who despises vain goods is rescued from real evils, ibid., 276. — Temporal goods are our evils, St. Valerian, LII, 3. — Strictly speaking, nothing is good except what is eternal, St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 91. — We desire only those things which we think good, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLIX, 4. — Nothing whatever is good through which the highest good is changed or corrupted, ibid., 10. — What is the highest good is the highest greatness, id., CLVIII, 25. — The goods and evils of this age are neither truly good nor truly evil, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 296. — God alone does not wish to be better than himself, because he cannot be, id., CLXXXIII, 98. — To know and to will the good is perfect religion and religious perfection, ibid., 915. — Temporal goods, if loved, are unlawful; if not loved, lawful, but in every case dangerous, [Col. 0751] ibid., 370. — At times one should rejoice more in another’s good than in one’s own, ibid., 1437. — Good works cannot exist without faith, hope, and charity, Wolbero, CXCV, 157. — The good which leads to the highest good is apprehended by few, ibid., 116. — A person becomes good in proportion as he loves good people, Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 429. — Goods mixed with evils do not please God, ibid., 446. — Good things are first lost; then evil deeds are committed, ibid., 1327. — Temporal goods are acquired with labour, possessed with love, and lost with grief, Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 406. — Earthly goods are not true goods, Alan of Lille, CCX, 156. — To be good among the wicked is the greatest crown, John of Rouen, CXLVII, 471. — There is no good where God is absent, Ven. Guibert, CLVI, 1151.

## BREVITY

The brevity of this present life should always remain in our memory, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 32.

## C

## CORPSE

A corpse buried in mud does not know the bites of worms, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 121.

## BLINDNESS

Blindness of the inner eyes is failure to understand, St. Augustine, XXXV, 1552. — Blindness of heart is at once a grievous punishment and a sin, id., XLI, 258.

## HEAT

The heat of earthly love gives way when a flame of the divine will has kindled the Christian mind, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 628.

## CALUMNY

Those who seek to devise knotty calumnies become entangled before those whom they strive to entangle, St. Augustine, XXXV, 654.

## GREY HAIR

Grey hair deserving reverence is the grey hair of the soul, shining forth in grey thoughts and deeds, St. Ambrose, XVI, 823. — It is not the grey hair of years but of character that is praised, ibid., 7.

## SINGING

No one sings anything worthy of God unless he has received from God what he can sing, St. Augustine, XXXV, 323. — Whoever desires, though the tongue is silent, sings with the heart, ibid., 1101. — One must sing with the heart, not with the flesh, ibid., 774. — Let us sing with the voice so that we may stir ourselves; let us sing with the heart so that we may please God, ibid., 1917. — Whoever lives for God sings to God, ibid., 814.

## CAPTIVITY

Captivity of the body is grievous; captivity of the soul is far more grievous, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 458. — This is true captivity: souls captive to sin are led to death, St. Ambrose, XVI, 306. — The captivity of a people for God’s word is more glorious than the freedom of nations, St. Rupert, CLXIX, 597.

## HEAD

Christ is the head of the saints; the devil, of the wicked, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 590. — A sickly head is a teacher committing sin, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 326.

## FLESH, FLESHLY, FLESHLY THINGS

Affliction of the flesh is an acceptable sacrifice to the Lord through the sacrifice of humiliation, Tertullian, I, 1269. — The torments of the flesh are the Lord’s arrows, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 420. — If you care for the flesh, your soul is brutish, St. Zeno, XI, 103. — Our flesh cannot be everlasting and enduring; it must die, rise again, be dissolved, and rest, St. Ambrose, XVI, 5. — Whoever is held by no pleasure of the flesh does not fear weapons or barbarians, since he does not even fear death, ibid., 865. — Let the flesh sleep and faith keep watch; let the bodily enticements sleep and prudence of heart keep watch; let your limbs smell of Christ’s cross and of burial, ibid., 293. — What is fleshly is servile, ibid., 1163. — The fleshly person is not in Christ; but if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creature, ibid., 945. — While it sins, it is called flesh, just as a rightly governed body is called spiritual, id., XVII, 127. — Unless one buries the desires of the flesh, one cannot attain eternal blessedness, ibid., 11. — Not to live fleshly while in the flesh is a great virtue, St. Jerome, XXII, 287. — Frail flesh, destined to become ashes, fights alone against many, id., XXIV, 89. — Love of the flesh is overcome by love of the spirit, ibid., 100. — Let the strength of the soul be stronger than the weakness of the flesh, ibid., 288. — What the frailty of the flesh cannot endure, the mind overcomes through faith speaking with God, ibid., 260. — It is one thing to be in the flesh and another to live according to the flesh, ibid., 415. — How many are prepared to endure martyrdoms, exiles, and poverty, yet are nevertheless overcome by passion of the flesh, ibid., 684. — A person devoted to the flesh forgets glory, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 114. — Whoever conquers the desires of the flesh will easily conquer a torturer’s torments, St. Valerian, ibid., 23. — Whereby the flesh is refreshed, thereby the spirit fails, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 358. — Not to be in the flesh is not to love fleshly things, ibid., 483. — The flesh plunges down those whom proud knowledge raises up, ibid., 824. — The desires of the flesh, not the flesh itself, are to be killed, ibid., 984. — Whoever grants the flesh more than is fitting nourishes the enemy, ibid., 1388. — Fleshly people have grievous labour; spiritual people have none, [Col. 0752] ibid., 188. — The Spirit, entering a fleshly person, changes him into another man, id., LXXIX, 243. — When fleshly people speak of heavenly things, they use realities which they are forbidden to perceive, like sick persons, ibid., 206. — The king of his own flesh is adorned with hope of immortality, ibid., 209. — Spiritual love ought to be preferred to fleshly love, St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 68. — Blooming flesh quickly loses its bloom and decays, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 106. — It is more to hate the flesh than the world, ibid., 301. — Mortification of the flesh is the mark of Christ’s soldier, ibid., 991. — No enemy is nearer than the flesh, id., CLXXXIII, 758. — Mortification of the flesh benefits the flesh itself no less than the spirit, ibid., 945. — Pleasure of the flesh is evil; affliction is good, ibid., 782. — Those living carnally are dead, ibid., 899. — The beginning of the carnal life is sweet, like good wine; its end is wretched, like inferior wine, Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 217. — Let our flesh sleep so that the mind may keep watch in Christ, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 218. — Our flesh is a wall hindering the vision of God, Alan of Lille, CCX, 15. — Flesh by itself brings ruin upon itself, Ven. Guibert, CLVI, 311.

## CHASTISEMENT

Religious chastisement is sweeter than indulgent remission, St. Ambrose, XVII, 449.

## CHASTITY

Chastity is not restrained by punishment, but increased by religion and preserved by faith, St. Ambrose, XVI, 222. — Chastity seeks solitude; its first victory is to conquer the desires of possessions, ibid., 836. — The homeland of chastity and virginity is in heaven, ibid., 151. — Chastity’s reward is beyond labour, its grace beyond ordinary use, its recompense beyond work, ibid., 208. — Chastity cuts off lust, and a woman conquers men, St. Jerome, XXII, 293. — Chastity is to be loved above all things, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 36. — It is the adornment of our soul, ibid., 679. — Chastity without love of neighbour is vain, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 205. — There is no chastity of the flesh which the sweetness of the mind does not commend, ibid. — Proud chastity profits nothing, ibid., 680, 697. — By chastity a human being is made equal to angels, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 846. — Chastity is to be judged more by purity of heart than by continence of the flesh, ibid., 55. — Proud chastity is not chastity but a brothel adorned for the devil, ibid., 279. — Chastity without charity is a lamp without oil, id., CLXXXIII, 465. — Whoever cultivates chastity imitates God, Ven. Guibert, CLVI, 311.

## FALL

You fall by loving the world; you rise by loving God, St. Augustine, XXXV, 546. — Since, when healthy, he did not listen lest he fall to the physician’s command, let him listen even when ill, so that he may rise, ibid., 458, 951.

## CHARITY

The master requires charity; the servant, fear, St. Ambrose, XVI, 83. — Freedom makes a person free among human beings; charity makes him God’s friend, ibid., 936. — Charity is the head and foundation of religion, id., XVII, 155. — If charity is lacking, whatever goods we may seem to possess are dead, ibid., 509. — Those whom charity joins are not separated by distance of lands, St. Jerome, XXII, 435. — Charity makes those absent present, ibid., 347. — It alone exists without labour, ibid., 498. — True charity, violated by no one, grows both in strength and in number as it increases, ibid., 422. — Charity is the life of the heart, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 564. — If through charity Christ is with us on earth, through it we are with him in heaven, id., XXXV, 1630. — When charity is expended, it does not fail, id., XXXIX, 272. — Take away charity, and there is nothing that moves you to a good work; or, if you do act, you act as a slave, id., XXXVI, 369. — By charity you love whatever you love well, ibid. — Add charity: everything is profitable; remove charity: the rest profits nothing, ibid., 44, 562. — Charity is loved, yet not felt, ibid., 166. — Whoever has charity should attend to his own conscience, and there sees God, id., XXXV, 1951. — Fleshly desire reigns where God’s charity does not reign, id., XXXVII, 287. — The greater charity is, the better is the person in whom it is found, ibid., 286. — We are carried by charity, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 81. — Whoever does not have charity is without God, ibid., 53. — Charity has no limit; by charity the human being is distinguished from beasts, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 62–63. — In love of God nothing is excessive; in love of the world all things are harmful, ibid., 352. — Nothing other than the love of righteousness ought to be loved, ibid., 370. — Christ’s charity is to be preferred to the world, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 628. — One runs to God on the feet of charity, St. Benedict, LXVI, 14. — A blessed conscience is tested in charity’s fire, Cassiodorus, LXX, 216. — Those who love God above all things serve him gladly, ibid., 331. — We ought tirelessly to do everything that can help another, ibid., 383. — Charity is not true if it measures less than two cubits, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1340. — Charity melts diverse minds into one, ibid., 1343. — Placed between faith and hope, we stretch toward charity, ibid., 1421. — For charity’s sake all things are to be despised, id., LXXIX, 457. — When charity burns in the heart, it sends forth a cry, ibid., 486. — Charity is unity of souls, Bl. Alcuin, C, 191. — Charity moves the foot toward perfection; pride, toward falling, ibid., 377. — It is better not to have charity than to feign it, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV [printed “LXLIV”], 191. — Whoever burns with charity need not be commanded, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 180. — Charity nourishes, advances, and adorns all virtues, St. Bruno of Asti, CLIV, 81. — Those who possess charity, place their hope not in the uncertainty of riches but in God, and devote themselves to virtue, are not lovers of the world even if they are rich in this world, id., CLXV, 273. — Charity is true knowledge, St. Rupert, CLXIX, 308; and perfect and true thanksgiving, ibid., 760. — Charity is not so much a powerful virtue as the power of virtues, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 392. — Charity is the way and life of virtues, ibid., 403. — Wherever charity is, it shows itself in works, ibid., 475. — God is held by charity alone, ibid., 392. — Without charity the other virtues are empty and tasteless, ibid., 107–108. — Charity is stronger than death, ibid., 391. — The glory of charity is to humble oneself for friends, ibid., 1006. — Charity robs no one and yet seizes all things, ibid., 391. — That charity is imperfect which needs fear’s goad, ibid., 60–61. — Charity is offered to everyone and taken from no one except the willing, ibid., 392. — Charity is the life of faith, id., CLXXXIII, 899. — There is no place for vanity to enter where charity occupies the whole, ibid., 1322. — Charity begins with oneself, ibid., 411. — Charity is a fountain in which a stranger does not share, Robert Pullen, CLXXXVI, 168, 353. — Charity is the virtue, centre, and fullness of virtues, Wolbero, CXCV, 171, 186. — Where charity is, there too is fullness, Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 730. — Nothing is better or more pleasant than charity, ibid., 917. — Charity ought to begin with yourself and be completed in your neighbour, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 248. — Detraction harms charity more sharply than other vices, ibid., 33. — All virtues are daughters of charity, ibid., 245. — Mercy is charity’s special daughter, ibid., 247. — Charity is the form of all virtues, Alan of Lille, CCX, 89. — The charity of the perfect is to prefer the neighbour’s spiritual salvation to the welfare of one’s own body, Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 218.

## CHRISTIANS

The one who does what Christians do not do is excluded from the Christian name, Tertullian, I, 278. — Christians are made, not born, ibid. — A Christian is a disciple of heaven, a trader in life, a builder of realities, an enemy of error, a restorer, expresser, and guardian of truth, ibid., 514. — For a Christian, the world is a prison, ibid., 622. — Christians do not dislike thinness, for God did not give the flesh for weight, id., II, 978. — Christians do not speak great things but live them, St. Cyprian, IV, 326. — Christians will receive God’s promises only when they have come to God, ibid., 223. — A Christian who sins becomes a servant of the world and a labourer of the devil, St. Hilary of Poitiers, X, 392. — Christians are made, not born, St. Jerome, XXII, 678. — To be a Christian is great; to seem one is not, ibid., 325. — A Christian ought not to have a criminal charge, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 1697. — A Christian is one who knows himself to be a pilgrim here, id., XXXVI, 642. — For good Christians, their whole life is a holy desire, id., XXXIV, 2008. — To a Christian who loves, the law is not a burden but an honour, not torment but an ornament, id., XXXVI, 207. — A Christian assured of life, kingdom, and immortality is not anxious about clothing, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 163. — The Christian renounces the devil so that he may return to heaven by another way, ibid., 159. — They are not Christians unless they imitate Christ, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 87. — Christian life is a perpetual cross, ibid., 173. — The readier Christians are to imitate Christ, the nearer they will be to grace, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 637. — The Christian who does not possess the world possesses Christ wholly here, ibid., 130. — Many desire to appear Christians, but not to be Christians, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 614. — Bad Christians have eyes open in faith and closed in works, ibid., 801, 863. — Pretended Christians are more grievous enemies of the Church, ibid., 1000. — All Christians are one Christ, St. Agobard, CIV, 116. — Christians are here like sheep in a desert, St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, Psalm LXXVII. — True Christians possess royal dignity; therefore it is shameful for a Christian to live under slavery to vices, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 49. — Christians who do not conform themselves to the Christian religion by good morals and right faith seem in mind to have departed from Christ, St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 74. — Christians ought to be full of eyes, St. Rupert, CLXIX, 390. — Christians are many in name, few in reality, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 942. — Among all Christians’ contests, the battles of chastity alone are harder, where the conflict is daily and victory rare, ibid., 345. — The life of false Christians is night, ibid., 583. — The whole life of a Christian is cross and martyrdom, [Col. 0754] ibid., 480. — A Christian separated from Christ becomes a monster, id., CLXXXIII, 815. — The Christian life ought to be cross and martyrdom, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 72. — Christians living uprightly are stars of heaven, Guibert, CLVI, 17.

CHRIST. — Christ, the sole hope of the whole world, Tertullian, II, 760. — Healer of sicknesses, ibid., 373. — Christ, illuminator and savior of the human race, St. Cyprian, IV, 213, 258, 287. — He is ignorant of Christ as God who is ignorant that God was born, St. Hilary of Poitiers, X, 381. — Christ’s resurrection brought hope of conquering death and admitted humanity to the rewards of immortality, St. Zeno, XI, 94. — Christ was accursed because he took upon himself our curses; he wept, lest you, O human being, should weep long; he suffered wrongs, lest you should grieve over your own injury, St. Ambrose, XVI, 94. — While I am on the way, I belong to Christ; when I have arrived, I belong to the Father; but everywhere through Christ, and everywhere with Christ. There is the safeguard of our salvation where Christ is, ibid., 169. — Christ is everything: if you desire to heal a wound, he is the physician; if you burn with fevers, he is the spring; if you are weighed down by injustice, he is righteousness; if you need help, he is strength; if you fear death, he is life; if you desire heaven, he is the way; if you flee darkness, he is light; if you seek food, he is nourishment, ibid., 237. — Christ is our rest and the source of our strength, ibid., 979. — For small things Christ promises magnificent rewards; for earthly things, heavenly rewards; for temporal things, everlasting rewards with glory, id., XVII, 74. — Christ is the one voice of the whole world, St. Jerome, XXII, 334. — The perfect servant of Christ possesses nothing besides Christ, ibid., 33. — Whoever belongs to Christ is the more our own, ibid., 782. — Christ alone heals every ailment and infirmity, id., XXIV, 53. — Christ is our physician and our health, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 1397; XXXV, 481. — Christ is both our example and our help, id., XXXVI, 608. — Christ becomes our heir: he need not be sought far from us; he is among the poor, St. Valerian, LII, 10. — Christ is known to all and is the cause of joy, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 64. — By being born Christ became our flesh; by being reborn we become his body, ibid., 77. — Christ’s life is the rule for living, ibid., 136. — Christ came to us so that we might return to him, Cassiodorus, LXX, 234. — He hates peace who does not love Christ, ibid., 430. — In order to reach Christ, one must pass beyond all human beings, St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 423, 467. — To know Christ is useless unless he is loved, ibid., 309. — To die for Christ is to rest, ibid., 436. — Christ is fed by human good works, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 230. — Christ’s wounds are remedies for our senses, ibid., 309. — In Christ crucified is all the Christian’s glory, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 217. — Christ does not dwell in those who live softly and are given over to pleasures, St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 269. — Christ alone was fit to perform penance on our behalf, St. Rupert, CLXIX, 107. — Christ showed himself to human beings in his humanity because he could not be comprehended in his divinity, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 519. — The name of Christ shines when preached, nourishes when pondered, anoints when invoked, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 564. — When you read, you are instructed concerning Christ; when you pray, you enter into familiar conversation with him, ibid., 22. — Christ labored for us, not for himself; Christ is conceived by faith, born through preaching, nourished by devotion, held fast by love, ibid., 342. — Christ is like bread twice baked, necessary for those sailing in this world, ibid., 489. — Christ is the way in example, truth in promise, life in reward, id., CLXXXIII, 914. — Christ’s death freed us from death, his life from error, his grace from sin, ibid., 555. — The more lowly Christ became for us, the dearer he becomes to us, ibid., 796. — To bear Christ is not a burden but an honor, ibid., 840. — The follower of Christ has nothing to fear, ibid., 110. — Christ is the book of humankind, always to be read, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 87. — One ascends to Christ by three steps: servitude, lowliness, and hardship, Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 387. — Christ, the true day, Alan of Lille, CCX, 24.

CIBUS [FOOD]. — The necessity of food is a calamity, though it is called a delight, St. Augustine, XXXII, 797. — God is our food: he alone refreshes and does not fail, id., XXXV, 1742. — If you do not wish to be the serpent’s food, do not be earth, ibid., 1386.

CIVITAS [CITY]. — The king of the heavenly city is truth, its law charity, its measure eternity, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 533.

CLERICATUS, CLERICI [THE CLERICAL OFFICE; CLERICS]. — The clerical office is a burden, not an honor, St. Jerome, XXII, 937. — Clerics ought to shine through good works, John of Rouen, CXLVII, 483. — The shapeless life of clerics has no saint as its teacher, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 362. — It is unworthy of clerics to be occupied in serving the courts of princes, id., CLXXXIII, 445.

COELUM, COELESTIA [HEAVEN; HEAVENLY THINGS]. — Heaven will be granted not by miracles but by good works, [Col. 0755] St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 698. — Heaven is where guilt has ceased; heaven is where crimes are struck down; heaven is where there is no wound of death, St. Ambrose, XVI, 377. — Earth is humanity’s exercise-ground; heaven, its crown, ibid., 972. — The course upward is safe; descent to lower things is dangerous, ibid., 96. — Let there be a step upward, for it is better to ascend, ibid., 904. — The kingdoms of heaven seek inhabitants unencumbered and supported by the lightness of wings, St. Jerome, XXII, 795. — After the great perils of the sea, let us hasten to enter the safest harbor of heaven, ibid., 584. — Here we must fly naked, ibid., 1080. — Heaven is closed to no one except one who has excluded himself; people are driven back from the heavenly homeland by the winds of evil habits, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 23. — The kingdom of heaven is bought for as much as each person is able to possess, id., XXXV, 1470. — Snares of earthly things cannot entangle those who desire heavenly things, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 129. — What has one who possesses heaven to do with earth? ibid., 90. — Earth must be exchanged for heaven, ibid., 124. — The clouds of earth darken heaven, ibid., 41. — For love of the heavenly homeland, we love the penalties of exile, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 219. — The harmony of heaven is not heard by the wicked, ibid., 965. — It is hard for an earthly human being to climb to the heights of heaven, ibid., 866. — Those who live rightly in this world are neighbors of the citizens of heaven, id., LXXIX, 152. — Heaven is the healed and holy soul, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1363. — It is better to leap into heaven from a hut than from a palace, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 227. — It is dreadful to gather dust and rubbish from heavenly things, ibid., 10.

COGITARE, COGITATIO [THINKING; THOUGHT]. — Bodily and earthly thoughts will perish with the earthly body, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 631. — To think evil is wicked; more wicked still is to wish to carry out evil thoughts, St. Jerome, XXII, 943. — Thinking what is good is less than desiring it, St. Augustine, XLI, 584. — Good thoughts are a voice to God, St. Prosper, LI, 555. — Thought is the mouth of the heart, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 473. — What the root is to a tree, one’s thought is to a human being, ibid., 412, 444. — A mind that does not think on divine things is in exile, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 445. — To think of the saints is to see them, ibid., 1040. — Evil thought is the seed of sin, Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 227.

COGNITIO, COGNOSCERE [KNOWLEDGE; TO KNOW]. — The more we advance in the knowledge of God, the more we tend toward living, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 1965. — To know God and not glorify him as God is impiety and folly, id., XLI, 212. — Already, by fearing God, you know what wisdom is in yourself, though you cannot yet know what it is in itself, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 610. — In knowing God, we recognize ourselves and judge ourselves more severely, ibid., 875. — God cannot be known except by a tranquil heart, ibid., 1113. — The more anyone knows himself, the more he displeases himself, ibid., 1145. — Knowledge of oneself leads to the knowledge of God, Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 51. — Knowledge of God grows fruitlessly in us unless love grows, ibid., 1206. — Knowledge of God is eternal life, perfect blessedness, consummate delight, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 320.

COLUMBA [DOVE]. — Let us possess the dove’s simplicity, so that we may devise deceit against no one, St. Jerome, XXII, 324. — The dove’s wings must be taken up to avoid the powers of the air, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 98. — Noah’s dove announces that the flood has departed, and the dove of the Holy Spirit that the shipwreck of the world has ceased, ibid., 160.

COMMODUM [ADVANTAGE]. — No one wills anything except what at some time he judges advantageous to himself, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 68. — The desire for advantage, if it exists alone, makes one only miserable, ibid., 116.

COMMUNIO [COMMUNION]. — Communion with a brother in the present will also exist in the future, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 4. — Those fast from the power of the sacrament of communion because, before receiving the Eucharist, they do not examine themselves, St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 59.

COMPASSIO [COMPASSION]. — Through compassion we water the Lord’s feet—and therefore his members—with tears, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1596. — True justice has compassion; false justice despises and disdains, ibid., 1600. — How necessary compassion is for priests, ibid., 1594.

COMPUNCTIO [COMPUNCTION]. — The mind visited by God is pierced with compunction, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 328. — A heart kindled by the fire of compunction is an altar, ibid., 1427. — Those whom God wounds through compunction, he heals through the assurance of pardon, id., LXXIX, 146. — A mind pierced by love is fed with the food of angels, ibid., 417. — Compunction is born from the love of God, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 302.

CONCORDIA [HARMONY]. — Harmony joined together cannot be conquered, St. Cyprian, IV, 95. — Harmony makes grow what rivalry has scattered, St. Jerome, XXII, 465. — Without harmony, no offering is acceptable to God, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1239. — Whoever is in harmony with God and with righteous people already begins to reign, [Col. 0756] St. Anselm, CLVIII, 349.

CONCUPISCENTIA [CONCUPISCENCE]. — Concupiscences do not wish to follow you; do not follow them. They rebel: rebel in turn; they fight: fight; they attack: attack in return. Only see to it that they do not conquer, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 816. — Concupiscence is conquered by those who assail it, not by those who praise it, id., XLI, 1343. — That concupiscence may not reign, keep control of your members, and do not yourself arm your adversary against yourself, id., XXXVI, 719. — From him who grants victory over concupiscence and pleasure comes also the strength of patience, St. Prosper, LI, 456. — With concupiscence there should be not peace but war, ibid., 556. — He treats concupiscence badly who thinks to cure it by satisfying it, St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 304. — Holy and chaste concupiscence is love of God, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 259. — Pleasure, or concupiscence of the flesh, is evil above all evils, ibid. — Since the world’s concupiscence passes away, together with everything the world possesses, we must delight in the Lord, since he himself is now the good, St. Bruno of Asti, 369. — Concupiscence can be restrained but cannot be extinguished, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 730.

CONFESSIO, CONFITERI [CONFESSION; TO CONFESS]. — Confession relieves sin as much as concealment aggravates it, Tertullian, I, 1243. — Confession of fault is the second plank after shipwreck, St. Jerome, XXII, 528. — Confess that you are in captivity, that you may be worthy to be freed, St. Augustine, XXXV, 1071. — Confess now what you have done against God, and forever you will confess what God has done for you, ibid., 226. — Let one who wishes to attain divinity confess his weakness, ibid., 1907. — You fear to confess, though by not confessing you cannot remain hidden; silent, you will be condemned, though by confessing you could be set free, ibid., 808. — Confession of evil deeds is the beginning of good deeds, id., XXXIV, 1491. — Confession of sins praises God, St. Prosper, LI, 397. — Those descend into the pit of eternal misery who, through obstinate pride, have lost the remedies of confession and penance, ibid., 513. — Confession is the entrance into saving life, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 56. — One confessing his sins gives glory to God, Cassiodorus, LXX, 188. — A sinner’s confession is life; a righteous person’s confession, glory, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 120. — Where there is confession, there is beauty, ibid., 122. — Let it have mortification and prayer as companions, ibid., 1212.

CONFUSIO [SHAME]. — Let not a Christian fear temporal shame; if he does not have this, he will have eternal shame, St. Augustine, XXXV, 232.

CONSCIENTIA [CONSCIENCE]. — Conscience is crowned in peace, St. Cyprian, IV, 219, 274. — The conscience of a good work is the light of souls, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 795. — For the wise person, it is not so much the public exposure of a disgraceful deed as conscience that causes shame, St. Ambrose, XVI, 29. — Conscience always silently convicts and judges its guilty person without contradiction, id., XVII, 462. — Though it has no faculty of speech, it nevertheless does not know how to keep silence, ibid., 592. — Conscience is like an altar upon which sacrifice is offered to God, St. Augustine, XXXV, 578. — The joy of a good conscience is paradise, id., XXXIV, 842. — An evil conscience is the pit into which the wicked fall, id., XXXV, 670. — There is no greater tribulation than conscience of sins, ibid., 515. — You may flee whatever you wish, O human being, except your conscience, ibid., 234. — Nothing heals the consciences of the wicked except forgiveness, ibid., 516. — From the tree of knowledge conscience is cold; from the mustard tree it becomes warm, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 99. — A deceitful conscience dares nothing openly, ibid., 158. — While a person lives, no one ought to be despaired of with regard to conscience, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 1423. — Whoever acts wrongly makes his conscience a prison for himself, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 370. — Conscience is the mirror of the soul, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 342. — A gnawing conscience follows the sinner everywhere, ibid., 332. — The stings of conscience compel sinners to beg outside themselves for consolations, ibid., 307. — It is more useful to run to conscience than to wisdom, unless wisdom itself builds conscience, ibid., 341. — A conscience full of good works is a flower-strewn bed, id., CLXXXIII, 1429. — A guilty conscience is the soul’s prison and hell, ibid., 1004. — A good conscience has a twofold consolation: present merit and future reward, Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 443. — The voice of preaching follows a conscience made serene, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 13. — Purity of conscience causes enduring joy of mind, Alan of Lille, CCX, 73.

CONSILIUM [COUNSEL]. — Where there is counsel, there is grace; where there is command, there is law, St. Ambrose, XVI, 205. — How can you judge as superior in counsel one whom you see inferior in conduct? ibid., 84. — To give counsel to a fool is an act of charity, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 545. — No counsel is better than example, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 725. — One’s own counsel is leprosy, ibid., 904.
