CONSOLATIO, CONSOLARI [CONSOLATION; TO CONSOLE]. — The consolation of the afflicted is eternal hope, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 320. — It is a great consolation to one who suffers if he has even one person who suffers with him, [Col. 0757] St. Ambrose, XVII, 188. — The best consoler is not one overcome by his own groans, St. Jerome, XXII, 177. — Many consolations are false, id., XXV, 682. — God consoles a good heart and torments an evil heart, St. Augustine, XXXV, 1748, 1749. — Our consolation is in hope; our groaning is in the reality, ibid., 165. — That consolation is true by which what cannot be lost will be given, id., XXXVI, 365. — The saints admit no consolation from the miseries of this exile, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 587. — Divine consolation is not granted to those who accept another consolation, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 309, 310. — God’s consolation and correction are a twofold help, id., CLXXXIII, 1333. — Whoever does not know desolation cannot recognize consolation either, ibid., 796.

CONSUETUDO [HABIT]. — The pestilential sweetness of habit, St. Augustine, XXXII, 1307. — Habit becomes necessity when it is not resisted, ibid., 753. — Evil habit is the house in which the sinner rests, St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 372. — The habit of sinning is a very narrow well from which grace alone can draw us out, id., LXXVI, 843. — Through habit all things grow soft, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 7.

CONTEMPLATIO [CONTEMPLATION]. — Contemplation is the holy intoxication of a mind estranged from the temporal things flowing away below, and holding fast the eternal light of wisdom, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 276. — In contemplation, love of truth seeks holy leisure, id., XXXVIII, 647. — One does not attain contemplation unless carnal desires have been put to sleep, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 162. — The repose of contemplation removes temptations, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 186. — The reward of contemplation is to see God, St. Anselm, CLI, 109. — Contemplation is the prelude to blessedness, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 16. — We do not attain the summit of contemplation unless we cease from outward things, Venerable Gerhoh, CXCIII, 368.

CONTEMPTUS, CONTEMNERE [CONTEMPT; TO DESPISE]. — Where there is contempt, injury is frequent, St. Jerome, XXII, 33. — Contempt of God makes times evil for us, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 43. — To despise the world is to gain Christ, and it is a profitable exchange, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 1001. — Contempt of all things for Christ is a work of divine power, id., CLXXXIII, 117. — Pride is driven away by self-contempt, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 25.

CONTINENS, CONTINENTIA [THE CONTINENT PERSON; CONTINENCE]. — Will makes a person continent, not weakness, St. Ambrose, XVI, 206. — Let the continent person consider what is lacking to him, not what is present, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 1565. — A humble married person is better than a proud continent person, ibid., 1564. — Continence and abstinence are sisters born of the same womb, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 71.

CONVERSATIO [CONDUCT]. — Blessed is the conduct that becomes for others an occasion of salvation, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 191.

CONVERSIO, CONVERTI [CONVERSION; TO TURN]. — Conversion is found in few, error in many, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1178. — There is no shame in passing to better things, ibid., 834. — Anticipate your accuser: if you yourself accuse your sins, you will fear no accuser, ibid., 428. — It is grievous to be changed for the worse, ibid., 782. — A human being turns to him by whom he was created in order to become something, St. Augustine, XXXV, 896. — Fleeing, you have a judge; returning, have a father, id., XXXVI, 780. — No one can turn to God unless he turns away from this world, id., XXXIX, 102. — It is impious to refuse one’s hand to converts, id., XXXIII, 784. — Conversion of heart is God’s gift, St. Prosper, LI, 881. — Conversion is not received in the mouth but in the heart, St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 93. — First one must rise from sin; then one must hasten toward heavenly things, ibid., 420. — The love of God alone converts souls, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 598. — To be unwilling to convert is to be ignorant of God, ibid., 1404. — Those converted once and again perverted rarely come to their senses, ibid., 994.

COR [HEART]. — Let the heart keep watch while the flesh sleeps, lest the flesh begin to keep watch wickedly in sins, St. Ambrose, XVI, 274. — Christ loves to be in the heart, ibid., 244. — A man’s heart is deep where there is nothing shallow, ibid., 243. — God loves those whose hearts and lips agree, St. Jerome, XXV, 873. — Each person sails in his own heart and suffers no shipwreck if he thinks good thoughts, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 424. — For the heart to stand, it must be fixed in God, id., XXXII, 814. — Our heart is restless, O God, until it rests in you, ibid., 661. — Whatever a human being is, he is in the heart, ibid., 781. — God is the light of hearts; Christ, life, id., XXXIII, 560, 564. — Tears are the blood of a wounded heart, ibid., 1081, 1082. — When our heart is wholly in God, it is not lost to us, id., XXXVI, 212. — One is upright in heart who praises the father’s lash, ibid., 146. — The heart’s cry is intense concentration of thought, St. Prosper, LI, 459. — Love and fear are the two principal impulses of the human heart; by this pair it is either opened or closed to God, ibid., 509. — One migrates in heart who changes one’s affection, ibid., 596. — A pure heart is a fitting place for prayer [Col. 0758] and God’s temple, ibid., 594. — The heart is penetrated by God alone, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 50. — The matter of salvation lies between heart and tongue, ibid., 56. — The heart is heaven where Christ reigns, ibid., 75. — We are joined to God by heart, not by body, ibid., 102. — If we think of God in the heart, we shall find him there, Cassiodorus, LXX, 110. — The heart is lofty when it thinks heavenly things and avoids earthly ones, ibid., 209. — Those who zealously desire to protect earthly possessions lose the heart’s peace, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 230. — The heart is an altar on which fire is commanded always to burn, ibid., 794. — The human heart is a boiling sea that God alone can restrain, ibid., 915. — The heart’s cry is fervent devotion, id., LXXIX, 168, 486. — Through evil thoughts the devil rests in the heart, ibid., 164. — The reprobate person does not possess his own heart, for the devil possesses it, ibid., 54. — Lust produces blindness of heart, ibid., 357. — God does not inhabit an envious heart, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 299. — Guarding the heart and weighing thoughts are useful, id., CXLV, 345. — Nothing is more sublime than the human heart, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 328. — The whole world is insufficient for the heart, ibid., 361. — A heart not full of God is subject to vices, ibid., 329. — The heart’s speech is affection, ibid., 294. — The whole heart consists in four affections: love and fear, joy and sorrow, id., CLXXXIII, 817. — It is shameful for a human being to have the heart downward and the head upward, ibid., 1109. — The heart is crooked when it seeks low things, upright when it seeks those above, Venerable Gerhoh, CXCIII, 201. — The hearts of the wicked are hard and insensible bronze, ibid., 436. — A most evil heart wastes away through malice, ibid., 498. — To lift hearts together with hands to God is to believe and to work, Wolbero, CXCV, 24. — A heart that cannot be softened by benefits God softens and teaches by scourges, Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 1201. — The human heart is deep and inscrutable, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 194. — Faith begins a pure heart; hope and charity bring it to completion, ibid., 262.

CORONA [CROWN]. — Grace is given to the unworthy so that a crown may be rendered to the worthy, St. Augustine, XLI, 341. — We receive as many crowns as the vices we overcome, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 128. — The crown of thorns is placed upon Christ not by bloodstained hands, as by the Jews, but by wicked thoughts and the perversity of deeds, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 598.

CORPUS [BODY]. — The body is not abolished by glory but changed, St. Hilary of Poitiers, X, 399. — Let us be away from the body, lest we be away from Christ; though we are in the body, let us not nevertheless follow what belongs to the body, nor abandon the laws of nature, but choose beforehand the gifts of grace, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1144. — The bodies of believers are God’s temple, St. Jerome, XXV, 1040. — Our body was an ornament to us; we sinned and received fetters from it, St. Augustine, XXXV, 1896. — It is more marvelous for incorporeal souls to be bound to earthly bodies than for earthly bodies to be raised to heavenly things, id., XXXVIII, 755. — The body, once our ornament, afterwards became our fetters, St. Prosper, LI, 554. — There is no one in this life whose soul is not weighed down by a corruptible body, ibid., 456. — The body is absent by place; the soul is a pilgrim by affection, ibid., 466. — Our body is a mystical ship, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 8. — The body is the bed of our pain, ibid., 14. — The body’s presence is of no use while the mind is absent, ibid., 32. — Those who refresh the body without the mind are dead in mind but alive in flesh, St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 218. — Our body is an estate, whose steward is the inner human being, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 696. — The body is our burden and prison; we owe it health, not pleasure, id., CLXXXIII, 847, 1115. — One who has a beautiful body and an ugly soul is more to be mourned than if he had an ugly body, Guibert, CLVI, 458. — Provision should not be made for the body in such a way that we forget the spirit, Alan of Lille, CCX, 432. — Afflict your body as though dying daily, that by dying you may return to life, St. Ambrose, XVI, 201.

CORREPTIO, CORRIPERE, CORRIPI [CORRECTION; TO CORRECT; TO BE CORRECTED]. — Take as much care to correct your own way as you take to observe another’s, St. Ambrose, XVII, 489. — The one loved by God is corrected; the one neglected is abandoned to his sins, St. Jerome, XXVII, 42. — Everything corrected is imperfect, ibid., 693. — It is better that a person be corrected while small than broken when hard, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 873. — Whoever does not correct does not rule, id., XXXV, 504. — One who strikes is merciful; one who spares is cruel, id., XXXVI, 111. — To correct belongs to the true shepherd, ibid., 762. — Correction is not made in order to insult, but to heal by shame, ibid. — To be corrected and instructed by God are recalled to the same gentleness, ibid., 510. — Fraternal correction is to correct as a judge and forgive as a brother, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 139. — Those whom we cannot correct by admonition we ought to tolerate patiently, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 417. — One who cannot endure correction cannot be perfect, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 194. — It belongs to the wise to love correction [Col. 0759], but to the foolish to hate it, id., CXLV, 755. — No one can correct himself without God, St. Anselm, CLIX, 263. — Let one correcting others be blameless, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 76. — Correction is a sure testimony of God’s love, id., CLXXXIII, 1100.

CREATOR, CREATURAE [CREATOR; CREATURES]. — The lowliness of creatures is shown so that the sublimity of God may appear, St. Jerome, XXII, 601. — When the Creator is neglected, every creature rises against sinners, id., XXXVII, 944. — The salvation of a creature is the Creator’s gain, ibid., 947. — Nothing but God suffices to fulfill the needs of creatures, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 349. — God is the true food of the rational creature, id., XLI, 255. — The creature is in continual flux; to stand belongs to the Creator alone, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 167. — There is no truth in the creature, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 161. — The rational creature was made to avoid evil, ibid., 65. — When a creature does not will what it ought, it dishonors God, id., CLIX, 80. — Creatures, as inferior to humanity, are to be despised by humanity, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 415. — Created, we become our own; God’s through a good will, the devil’s through an evil will, yet in either case our own, id., CLXXXIII, 610. — One must not cling to creatures, but ascend from them to the Creator, St. Prosper, LI, 554.

CREDERE [TO BELIEVE]. — To the believer the whole world is riches, St. Jerome, XXII, 281. — In religion it is not shameful to believe before knowing, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 183. — Believe what you do not yet see, lest you be ashamed when you do see, id., XXXV, 1208. — To believe quickly is to fall quickly, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 83. — In peace many believe in Christ, but in persecution few are martyrs, ibid., 32. — To will to believe what must be believed is to will rightly, St. Anselm, CLIX, 130. — To believe in the highest essence is, through believing, to tend toward it, ibid., 27. — It profits no one to believe in it unless he tends toward it, ibid.

CRIMINA [CRIMES]. — Lovers of crimes accuse the virtues, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 32. — The birds of crimes must be driven away by the spear of the cross, ibid., 171.

CRUCIATUS [TORMENT]. — God does not delight in torments but in our righteousness; nor is the question what each person suffers, but why, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 1293. — One who is tormented, if he gains no good from it, grieves at the loss of salvation, id., XXXVIII, 641.

CRUX [CROSS]. — By the power of the cross Christ now winnows through the cross; later he will winnow through judgment, Tertullian, II, 98. — Christ’s cross was set in the midst of the earth, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 807. — Following the bare cross while naked, one climbs Jacob’s ladder more freely and lightly, St. Jerome, XXII, 319. — Let us ponder Christ’s cross, and we shall regard riches as mud, ibid., 265. — An impious voice empties Christ’s cross of its force, ibid., 186. — Christ’s cross is the ship by which we cross the sea of this age, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 1389, 1390. — The cross is the trap in which the devil was caught, id., XXXVI, 726. — We must be borne by the Lord’s cross in order to cross over to our homeland, ibid., 47. — A Christian ought perpetually to hang upon the cross, ibid., 1039. — The cross must be borne after God, not before him, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 54. — Christ’s cross is the sacrament of the true altar, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 1109. — The cross is the cause of our hope, ibid., 212. — In the Church the cross is what a tree is in a ship, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 155. — It does not suffice to bear the cross unless we follow Christ, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1629. — The cross is a refuge from the storms of this age, Isidore of Seville, LXXXII, 309. — One who bears the cross ought to die to the world, ibid., 193. — The cross joins heaven in covenant with earth, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 15. — The sign of the cross foreshadows all virtues, ibid., 199. — Those who bear the cross are borne by Christ, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 507. — The wood of the cross is the sign of life, id., CLXXXIII, 327. — Christ’s cross makes the law sweet, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 204.

CULPA [FAULT]. — When a guilty person is killed, not the fault but the person is punished; but when fault is put away, the acquittal of the person is the punishment of sin, St. Ambrose, XVI, 897. — The greater the fault, the greater the aids that must be sought, ibid., 401. — Not rank but will makes fault, St. Jerome, XXII, 459. — Through fault we lose confidence of countenance, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 93. — Faults are more serious when they imitate virtues, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1207. — Nothing is worse than to recognize fault and not weep over it, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 209. — Fault is the more insensible the more praiseworthy it is held to be by those who commit it, Venerable Gerhoh, CXCIII, 273.

CUPIDITAS [COVETOUSNESS]. — To break the desires of mind and body is the greatest gain of heavenly hope, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 697. — One who cannot cure desires is like a person dragged by unbroken horses: he is rolled about, trampled, torn, and afflicted, St. Ambrose, XVI, 175. — Covetousness does not know where necessity ends, St. Augustine, XLI, 773. — Frustrated covetousness turns into grief, [Col. 0760] id., XXXVIII, 711. — There is not so much satiety in the fulfillment of desires as oppression, id., XXXV, 238. — Covetousness excessively hinders the way to heaven, St. Valerian, LII, 4. — Covetousness sold Christ, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 249. — The depth of human covetousness is a place of misery, St. Anselm, CLIX, 205, 206. — Covetousness oppresses with labor, fear, and pain, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 556. — Covetousness arises from the heart’s hunger; necessity, from the flesh’s weakness, id., CLXXXIII, 857.

CURA [CARE]. — All our concern should be not with present things but with future ones, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 688, 694. — Not to care about what you have done is the greatest cruelty, St. Ambrose, XVI, 48. — Care for the flesh should serve and not rule, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 336. — Greater cares open an easier road to vices, ibid., 546. — One occupied with worldly concerns carries dust in his eyes, by which he cannot see what he desires to see, id., LXXIX, 32. — Pastors are required to give care, not cure, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 435. — Human life in this world is governed by no less care than a ship on the sea, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 17.

D

DAEMONES [DEMONS]. — Demons are the magistrates of this world, Tertullian, I, 168. — The devil’s one work is always to test what is in you—whether you are willing, id., II, 916. — This is always the devil’s work: to tear apart God’s servants by lies, St. Cyprian, IV, 69. — The devil gains possession only of those whom God abandons, St. Hilary of Poitiers, X, 428. — To the strong the devil is small, St. Ambrose, XVI, 11. — Friendship with the devil is unhappy, id., XVII, 548. — The devil’s city is the whole body of the reprobate, ibid., 503. — Demons are worshipped through vices, St. Jerome, XXII, 505. — Whatever sins we commit is the dominion of demons, ibid., 953. — Demons conquer no one except through partnership in sin, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 300. — The devil must be fled, not followed, St. Prosper, LI, 561. — It is better to have him as an enemy than as a ruler, ibid. — Those devoted to earthly desires are his food, ibid., 390. — The devil is ruler of the wicked; Christ, of the faithful, ibid., 609. — The devil is filled with faults; he promises heavenly things in order to drag people down to hell; he uproots peace and rejoices in our evils; when he is conquered, vices have no power, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 11, 13, 19, 53, 97. — It is the demons’ sport to roll human minds from vice to vice, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1076. — As many demons rest in hearts as there are unclean desires, id., LXXIX, 164. — Demons receive those whom God abandons, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 213. — The knowledge of demons is folly, St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 95. — Sin is the devil’s food and refreshment; whoever sins more prepares greater banquets for him, St. Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 522. — The devil does not wound the person who resists him, but crowns him, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 372. — He beats us with our own staff, id., CLXXXIII, 822. — In cold minds the devil sleeps securely, Venerable Gerhoh, CXCIII, 601.

DELICIAE [DELIGHTS]. — Miseries are exchanged for delights, and delights for miseries, St. Jerome, XXIII, 234. — Let not those be thought blessed who enjoy the prosperity and delights of this age, ibid., 335. — Life amid temporal delights, in comparison with eternal life, must be called not life but death, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 223. — Delights are not taken away from the converted person but changed, id., XXXV, 946. — Pleasures of the senses do not make people happy and hinder future joys, St. Bernard, CLXXII, 355.

DELICTUM [TRANSGRESSION]. — Cessation from sin is the root of pardon, Tertullian, II, 1001. — Whoever walks in transgressions has the devil upon his head, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 105.

DESIDERIUM [DESIRE]. — Desire is the thirst of the soul, St. Augustine, XXXV, 750. — Things long desired are obtained more sweetly, id., XXXVI, 411. — Whoever does not groan as an exile will not rejoice as a citizen, because desire is not in him, id., XXXV, 1940. — Your desire is your prayer; if desire is continual, prayer is continual, ibid., 404. — Let punishments draw those to good desires whom rewards do not invite, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 839. — To be left by God to one’s own desire is a grave punishment, St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, Psalm LXXX. — Desire is the soul’s hunger, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 394. — Desire is a cry to God, ibid. — Desires of the age become shadows of death and destruction, ibid., 1028. — God is sought by desires, not by the steps of feet, id., CLXXXIII, 1559. — Desire for the Lord is not in the flesh but in the soul, St. Jerome, XXV, 347.

DESPAIR, DESPERATION.—No one ought to despair, whatever his age, if he is willing to turn to the Lord, St. Ambrose, XVII, 410.—Nothing concerning God is to be despaired of, St. Augustine, XXXV, 597.—Lest men live worse through despair, God promised a harbor of forgiveness; again, lest they live worse in hope of pardon, He made the day of death uncertain, ibid., 1876.—God can restore to one in despair what He promises, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 90.—Let him who considers past gifts not despair of those to come, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 839.—In this life we must not despair of the salvation of sinners, Robert Pullus, CLXXXVI, 54.

DETRACTION, DETRACTOR, TO DETRACT.—Let the detractor learn, when he sees you, neither willingly to listen nor readily to speak ill, St. Jerome, XXII, 266.—To listen to a detractor is harmful, Cassian, I, 29.—Detractors, after the manner of beasts, devour human beings, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 459.—To speak ill of one present is less serious than to speak ill of one absent, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 40.—A detractor harms himself more than another, Alan of Lille, CCX, 94.

GOD.—God is the hearer not of the voice but of the heart, as He is its beholder, Tertullian, I, 1175.—To search out God’s secrets is devout, but things unsearchable must be confessed to be so, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 491.—If God reigns in us, virtue reigns, chastity reigns, devotion reigns, St. Ambrose, XVI, 385.—He who utterly casts God out of his heart is dead, ibid., 309.—When God is defined, He grows by His own definition, ibid., XVII, 352.—God, the physician, heals by striking and gives life by putting to death, ibid., 404.—God is good by nature; by communion with Himself He makes persons holy, St. Jerome, XXII, 546.—God begins amid sorrows and ends amid joys, ibid., 756.—The soul renders to God what it owes, whether by suffering or by doing, St. Augustine, XXXII, 1293.—To dwell in God is to live, ibid., 870.—God preserves Himself for the good, id., XXXV, 918.—God is sufficient for us, but without God there is nothing, id., XXXVI, 492.—The more subject one is to God, the more perfect one is, St. Prosper, LI, 952.—God is the life of the soul, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 19.—The servants of God stand; they do not lie down, ibid., 15.—Where God is, there is no sin, ibid., 44.—God attends to hearts, not words, ibid., 142.—He for whom God is life cannot die, ibid., 166.—God tolerates the wicked for the sake of the good, St. Leo the Great, LV, 223.—By chastising He heals; by restoring, He graciously instructs, ibid., 58.—The whole ordering of our life must be referred to God, St. Maximus, LVII, 62.—The sweeter God becomes to us, the dearer we become to Him, Cassiodorus, LXX, 353.—Where God is not present by grace, He is present by vengeance, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1241.—God changes times, not purposes, St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, Psalm LXVII.—To deny God by one’s deeds is to perish, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 32.—To serve God is to reign, ibid., 317.—God’s speech is His will, St. Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 2.—God sometimes visits with scourges, in order to turn from us the spirit of self-exaltation and confirm us in humility, ibid., 233.—God does not delight in the punishments of the wretched, St. Rupert, CLXIX, 537.—To hunger for God is always to seek Him, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 170.—A person divided from God is rebellious against himself, ibid., 329.—God loves, and is Love itself, id., CLXXXIII.—God is never more praiseworthy than when He is more merciful, Venerable Guibert, CLVI, 307.—He who lends to God receives a hundredfold, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 109.—God’s throne is eternity, Alan of Lille, CCX, 173.

DEVOTION.—Lively devotion is prompt faith and tireless hope, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1046.—Our devotion ought not trust in its own powers, but should commend the affection of its good purpose to divine grace, St. Leo the Great, LVII, 571.—The fervor of devotion is the tongue of the soul, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 461.—Devotion raises the mind so that grace may meet it; it opens the heart so that grace may enter; it enlarges the affection so that it may receive as much of grace as possible, ibid., 409.

DAY.—Those do not prolong their days who live a long time, but those who make them great by the magnitude of good works, St. Jerome, XXIV, 455.—Evil days are always in the world; good days are always in God, St. Augustine, XXXV, 317.—Days are evil because one passes away for another to come; the good days of eternity will be one day, id., XXXVI, 1084.—Christ’s day is without night and without end, St. Maximus, LVII, 180.—The day will come when no darkness of sin remains, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 919.—A day is a thought of the mind, id., LXXIX, 322.—The true day, which knows no setting, is eternal truth, true eternity, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 875.—The Day of the Lord is eternity itself, Venerable Gerhoh, CXCIII, 524.

DIGNITY.—To have lost dignity is a more grievous evil than never to have possessed it, St. Ambrose, XVII, 79.—To seek dignities is wicked, especially for unsuitable persons, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 155.—Let one who presides by dignity also preside by integrity of conduct, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 98.

LOVE, TO LOVE.—It is difficult to be loved by those whom one surpasses in rank, St. Jerome, XXIV, 502.—Each person worships what he loves, id., XXV, 953.—Love your enemies, lest unawares you hate even your friends, St. Augustine, [Col. 0762] XXXVI, 1404.—Love is light; hatred, darkness, id., XXXV, 633.—He truly loves himself who, in order to love God, does not love himself, St. Prosper, LI, 605.—There is no love without justice, St. Rupert, CLXIX, 140.—The more love drinks, the more it thirsts, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 640.—To love enemies is more divine than human, ibid., 443.—Nothing is sweeter than the sweetness of love, Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 916.—However great love may be on the way, it cannot equal love of God in the homeland, Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 210.

LEARNING, DISCIPLE.—Learn over a long time what you are to teach, St. Jerome, XXV, 945.—Let us learn on earth those things whose knowledge will endure for us in heaven, ibid., 281.—The salvation of disciples is the reward of teachers, id., XXVI, 560.—Things more useful, rather than more marvelous, ought to be learned, St. Augustine, XXXII, 1054.—Those who learn are happier than those who teach, id., XXXV, 594.—To learn is safer than to teach, St. Prosper, LI, 599.

DISCIPLINE.—Those who deny punishment despise discipline, Tertullian, II, 808.—Discipline is the guardian of faith, St. Cyprian, IV, 173.—The entire sum of our discipline lies in mercy and godliness, St. Ambrose, XVII, 297.—One who despises discipline is an enemy of his own soul, St. Valerian, LII, 2.

RICH PERSON, RICHES.—Riches are not merely to be despised, but are dangerous, St. Cyprian, IV, 210.—God knows as rich only the person who is rich in eternity, who stores up not the fruits of wealth but of virtues, St. Ambrose, XVI, 941.—Every wise person is rich, ibid., 941.—The righteous person is rich even if he seems poor to others, ibid., 109.—Riches are a burden if you do not know how to use them, ibid., 959.—One who does not know how to govern his own estate is sunk by his own burden, ibid., 1044.—It is exceedingly rare that one who possesses riches tends toward rest, id., XVII, 490.—To possess riches is not praiseworthy, but to despise them for Christ’s sake is, St. Jerome, XXII, 692.—Truth produces poverty; falsehood, riches, ibid., 509.—You have riches: your need has increased, not your power, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 956.—One is not to be judged rich unless one uses riches well, ibid., 327.—A person rich in conscience sleeps more securely on the ground than one rich in purple, ibid., 216.—The more a rich person has, the more he owes, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 26.—One who closes granaries to the poor closes them to himself, ibid., 121.—No rich person was made for himself alone, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 29, 52, 61.—The peace of rich sinners is always at strife with conscience, Cassiodorus, LXX, 353.—However great the prosperity of the rich, it ends in eternal misery, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 487.—The consolation received from riches is misery, id., LXXIX, 557.—Our riches are virtues, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 863.—Riches without virtue are of no use, Venerable Guibert, CLVI, 457.—The rich person who is not content with necessities is a wolf, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 45.—No one tells the truth to the rich, ibid., 43, 116.—To give to the rich is to lose, ibid., 122.

TEACHING, TEACHER, DOCTRINE.—To teach what you do is the chief point of the art, St. Jerome, XXII, 423.—It is most foolish to teach what the person whom you teach already knows, id., XXV, 109.—It is one thing to speak sound doctrine, and another to teach the things that accord with sound doctrine, ibid., 713.—A bad person is not a teacher, St. Augustine, XXXII, 1223.—One who does not do what he teaches others, if he is sometimes useful, does not do so himself but God does it, id., XXXIV, 1305.—It is a teacher’s grave incompetence to wish to teach someone better than himself, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 212.—Teachers who do not do what they teach are destroyers of themselves and cultivators of others, ibid., 1411.—When hearing a proud teacher, gather the roses and avoid the thorns, ibid., 853.—Teaching that savors of filth is called mud, ibid., 1129.

GRIEVING, GRIEF.—What hurts enough is driven out by a greater pain, St. Jerome, XXII, 783.—The pain of this life passes away, but that of the other life will not end, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 658.—Grief issues from conscience when it speaks calmly; when it remains silent too much, it torments more, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 240.—The heart does not grieve over what the eye does not see, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1040.

HOUSE.—Let no one remain in a house in which he must every day either perish or conquer, St. Jerome, XXII, 783.—You enter your house in order to inhabit it; enter God’s house in order to be inhabited, St. Augustine, XXXV, 1721.—The house of the mind is that which it inhabits by loving, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 257.

GIFTS.—Gifts strip the giver and kill the recipient, St. Jerome, XXVII, 514.—We ought not delight in God’s gifts so as to prefer what is given to the Giver, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 109.

SWEETNESS.—Feigned sweetness conceals the worst poison, St. Jerome, XXIII, 463.—Sweetness is more effective than harshness, [Col. 0763] St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 103, 104.—Sweetness is not a virtue without justice, id., CLXXXIII, 309.

## E

CHURCH.—God purifies and exercises the Church by certain medicinal troubles, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 25.—Tyrants exercise the Church’s patience; heretics, its wisdom; enemies, its goodwill, or even its beneficence, id., XLI, 613.—The Church knows how to say only what is fitting to be believed, Cassiodorus, LXX, 8.—The Church can be troubled by waves, but it cannot be sunk, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 160.—The Church’s chant is a great voice from heaven, St. Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 446.—Nothing so destroys the Church as for clerics to see laypeople better than themselves, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 39, 151.

NEEDY.—You will not become needy by giving, because the heavenly treasure is possessed more securely, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 1469.

EXALTATION.—All self-exaltation has nothing but ruin, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 668.

ALMSGIVING.—Almsgiving is sold, not given, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 33.—By almsgiving a golden house is built for us in heaven, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 433, 436.—Almsgiving is forgiving those who have injured us, Alan of Lille, CCX, 196.

ELOQUENCE.—It is better to possess holy rusticity than sinful eloquence, St. Jerome, XXIV, 264.

BISHOPS.—It belongs to bishops and priests daily to make themselves better, St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 137.—The episcopal chair is a burden, not an honor; a work, not a title; one of virtues, not of riches, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 374.

FEASTS.—The abundance of feasts breaks body and soul, St. Jerome, XXIII, 341.—The feasts of this earth are daily medicines, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 489.

TO ERR, ERROR.—To err is human; to remain in error through obstinacy is diabolical, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 901.—It is no small error to prefer a lesser good to a greater, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 216.

TO BLUSH.—If blushing is a crime, it belongs to the one who makes a false accusation, not to the one accused, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 856.

BEING.—To be able to exist is one thing; to exist is another, St. Jerome, XXIII, 701.

EUCHARIST.—The Eucharist is medicine, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1909.—The Eucharist is consolation for soul and body, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1390.

GOSPEL.—The Gospel of Christ is a little book of perfection, Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 266.

TO EXCUSE, EXCUSE.—In order to excuse themselves, the ungodly accuse God, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1172, 1691.—An excuse does not remove punishment but pardon, id., XL, 357.

EXAMPLE.—To teach by example is better than by words, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 696.—By examples of the good God calls us back to Himself, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 329, 768.—One ought to teach by example rather than speech, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXIII, 1469.

EXERCISE.—The exercise of labor strengthens the mind, Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 506.

EXPERIENCES.—Experiences correct the person whom words do not correct, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 405.

EXILE.—A Christian is nowhere an exile, id., XLI, 209.

OUTWARDLY.—There is no benefit in being fortified outwardly if there is hunger within, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 85.

## F

FACE.—One must not turn one’s face away from a neighbor, Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 1061.

DEEDS.—Deeds are proved by words; without deeds, words are of no use, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 64.

ELOQUENCE.—Eloquence is struck dumb where a diseased conscience lies beneath, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 14.

REPUTATION.—No one believes a report except an unreflective person, Tertullian, I, 310.—Our reputation is necessary for others, and our life for ourselves, St. Augustine, XL, 448.—A good reputation is a kind of reward for virtue, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXIII, 128.—The stability of reputation arises from perseverance in virtue, Alan the Scot, CXCVIII, 419.—One who neglects his reputation is cruel to himself and his neighbor, ibid., 418.

FRIENDS.—Let your intimate friends be few, Alan of Lille, CCX, 90.

HUNGER.—This life is a day of hunger, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 79.

HAPPINESS.—God is our happiness and blessedness, St. [Col. 0764] Augustine, XXXVII, 898.—The happier one seems to oneself, the more greatly unhappy one is, id., XXXVIII, 1165.—No misfortune breaks the person whom no prosperity corrupts, id., XXXVII, 1058.—It is great happiness not to be conquered by happiness, id., XXXVIII, 483.—The first happiness is not to have sinned; the second, to have found pardon for sin, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 34.—It is a great part of happiness to despise the world, Rufinus, XXI, 192.—Neither the prosperity of this world makes us blessed nor adversity wretched, if we love true goods, St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 581.—Happy is the person whose present happiness, if it has smiled upon him, has not mocked him, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXIII, 425.

FAITH.—Faith is the harbor of our religion, St. Hilary of Poitiers, X, 368.—Faith is a matter of the heart, not of the body, St. Augustine, XLII, 1016.—Faith is the eye of the heart, id., XXXVII, 1069.—Faith joined with love is Christian faith; without love, faith is demonic, id., XXXV, 2055.—For the faithful, earth is foul and heaven lies open, St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LII, 777.—The time of faith is laborious, Valerian, LII, 38.—Faith is proven by deed, not speech; not by the tongue, but by the heart, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 72.—Where faith is, there is freedom; where freedom, grace; where grace, there is inheritance: faith is richer than all treasures, St. Ambrose, XVI, 488.

CONFIDENCE.—Those who think little of themselves have confidence in God, St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 478.

END.—Whatever is ended is small, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 1310.

TO BE SCOURGED.—Do not fear being scourged, but being disinherited, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1793.—God’s scourges are benefits and remedies, id., XXXIX, 1851.—God’s scourges do not take away hope but increase it, St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 443.—God’s scourges will cease if we turn to God, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 20.—Through the scourge we are turned to God when we are recalled to peace, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 80.

TO WEEP.—In this life there is a time for weeping, not laughing, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 882.

WEEPING.—Weeping over present things is the reward of future things, St. Ambrose, XVI, 179.

FORTITUDE.—The fortitude of a believer is not to yield to the persecutor who destroys him, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 572.—It belongs to fortitude to endure adversities patiently, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 284.

FOUNDATION.—The foundation of preaching is holiness of life and good conduct, Peter the Chanter, CCXV, 13.

## G

TO REJOICE, JOYS.—No one can rejoice here with the world and reign there with the Lord, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1415.—Tribulation is the entrance to heavenly joy, id., LXXIX, 286.—All our joy is in hope, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 51.—Joy in tribulation frees us from the snares of the devil, id., CLXXXIII, 1060.

TO GROAN.—The wretched are wont to groan at the recollection of past goods, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 549.—Those who groan wrongly or rejoice wrongly make themselves objects of lamentation, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1298.—He groans rightly who sighs for his homeland, not he who is oppressed by miseries, id., XXXV, 1435.—The good groan even in times of peace, while the wicked prevail, St. Prosper, LI, 787.—One who knows himself to be an exile does not cease groaning here, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 213.—The groans of those who rightly mourn in this world are indeed great, but sweet, Rupert, CLXIX, 22.

SWORD.—It is more tolerable to perish by another’s sword than by one’s own, St. Ambrose, XVI, 615.—God’s sword cuts away corruption and heals Christ’s members, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1866.

GLORY.—Through desire for glory the mind does not feel pain, St. Hilary of Poitiers, X, 353.—Glory deferred escapes and is not easily grasped, St. Ambrose, XVI, 107.—Solid glory before God is in the conscience, Rufinus, XXI, 36.—The freer a person is from desire for glory, the more like God he is, St. Augustine, XLI, 159.—Virtue is the road to glory, ibid., 156.—To glory in God is God’s blessing, id., XXXVI, 89.—One must glory in God and not in merits, St. Prosper, LI, 38.—Humility is the straight road to glory, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 1019.—The highest glory is to yield to God and the Church, id., CCXXXIII, 179.—One must glory in God alone, not in the mouth of men, ibid., 1304.—The happiness of heavenly glory is a day without evening, Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 81.

GRACE.—He who hopes in God’s grace conquers, not he who presumes upon his own strength, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1204.—Grace and mercy are God’s ears, Rufinus, XXI, [Col. 0765] 70.—Grace is the kingdom of God, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1908.—Virginity is the first grace, and penitence the second, Rupert, CCXIX, 378.—Grace does not fail us so much as we fail grace, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1118.

ACCEPTABLE.—As often as we humble ourselves for God’s sake, we offer God an acceptable sacrifice, Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 424.

## H

TO HAVE.—Recognize that you have, and that from yourself you have nothing, so that you may be neither proud nor ungrateful, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1084.

INHERITANCE.—That alone is an inheritance in which God is one’s portion, St. Ambrose, XVI, 899.

HUMAN BEING.—Nothing is more necessary to a human being than care for the true God, Tertullian, II, 285.—The end of humanity is eternal life, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 144.—The new human being changes vices into virtues, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 114.—The restoration of humanity is more wonderful than its creation, St. Leo the Great, LV, 151.—A human being fails precisely where he thinks himself to advance, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 391.—A human being left to himself is carried off by every breeze of temptation, ibid., 323.—A human being is born through sin, lives through labor, and dies through pain, Alcuin, CI, 142.—Virtue and wisdom make a human being perfect, Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 279.

HONESTY.—Integrity is like good health, St. Ambrose, XVI, 229.

HONOR.—Honor ought to seek you, not you it, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 242.—One who loves honor imitates God, id., XLII, 593.—The greater the honor, the more laborious it is, St. Isidore of Seville, ibid.—Honor that does not come from love is not honor but flattery, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 400.

ENEMY.—An earthly enemy does not prevail over heavenly things, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 12.

HUMAN.—Human nature is transformed through glory into an eternal substance, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 613.

HUMANITY.—Humanity often bends those whom neither virtue nor reason could overcome, St. Ambrose, XVI, 89.

HUMBLE, HUMILITY.—Let us be humble in heart, exalted in understanding and soul, St. Hilary, IX, 498.—The humbler one is, the more exalted one is, St. Jerome, XXII, 396.—The way of humility is the way of life, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 145.—The pretense of humility is greater pride, id., XL, 421.—One who performs good works without humility carries dust into the wind, id., XXXIX, 2314.—At the highest honor let there be the highest humility, ibid.—It is more to be feared to be received into glory than to be trampled in humility, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 455.—Even rich people can be adorned with humility, id., LV, 264.—By everything that we see we are admonished to be humble, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 829.—Humility seeks glory from God; pride, from human beings, Alcuin, CI, 517.—Humility ascends; self-exaltation descends, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 73.—By humility the kingdom of heaven is purchased and divine grace acquired, id., CLXXXIII, 767.—Humility minimizes the faults of others and accuses its own, Adam the Scot, CXCVIIII, 200.

## I

FIRE.—Divine fire does not know how to burn the merciful, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 42.—Fire is cold in stone and concealed in iron; by their collision it bursts into flame, ibid., 109.

IGNORANCE, TO BE IGNORANT.—To be ignorant of what one should believe has not so much pardon as reward, St. Hilary of Poitiers, X, 2191.

TO FORGIVE.—God, forgiving us without measure, also wills that we forgive others without measure, St. Hilary, IX, 760.—God forgives better than He is known, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 947.—By forgiving a person loses nothing; enlarged by charity, he returns home, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 252.—Forgive when you have suffered wrong, lest there be two evil persons, id., XXXVI, 638.

IMAGE.—One’s own image must be rendered back to God, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1379.—One truly preserves God’s image who always cleaves to Him, id., XXXVI, 896.—God’s image seeks truth, not vanity, id., XXXVIII, 566.

TO SACRIFICE.—The life of virtues is sacrificed to God by the death of vices, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 109.

IMMORTALITY.—God created us for immortality and eternity, not for death, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 412.—Immortality is more a burden than a benefit unless grace breathes upon it, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1146.—God’s immortality is truly immortality, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 128, 1059.—True immortality is health, St. Valerian, bishop, LII, 15.

[Col. 0766] IGNORANCE.—Ignorance is no small punishment of this life, St. Augustine, XLI, 728.—It is the fault of ignorance not to understand rightly what is right, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 897.

UNGODLY PERSON.—The ungodly person is his own punishment, St. Ambrose, XVI, 14, 16.—The ungodly dread death in sickness, but the righteous rejoice, since they hope for a perpetual inheritance, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 631.

IMPENITENCE.—Impenitence is the only crime that cannot obtain pardon, St. Jerome, XXII, 1087.

INCENSE.—Arabian incense is not as willingly smelled by God as is the holiness of a sincere heart, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 87.

TO BEGIN.—To one who does not finish, beginning is of no benefit, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 132.

THE NEEDY.—We are needy, all the more truly the more inwardly so, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 693.—No one lacks anything that he does not wish for, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 116.

INDUSTRY.—Let industry correct whatever defect there is in nature, St. Ambrose, XVI, 21.

INFAMY.—It is foolish to bear infamy to no purpose, St. Jerome, XXIII, 409.

MISFORTUNE.—No misfortune breaks the person whom no prosperity corrupts, St. Augustine, XLV, 1679.

INFERIOR.—An inferior readily does what he sees done by a superior, St. Ambrose, XVII, 29.

HELL.—Those who know that the evil they do is evil descend alive into hell, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 639.

WEAK.—One who considers his hidden weaknesses presses himself down in humility, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1008.—More weak is the person unable to consider his own weakness, id., LXXVII, 852.—No one is more incurable than the sick person who thinks himself healthy, id., LXXIX, 494.

NATURAL ABILITY.—Natures liberally educated are more readily overcome by shame than by fear, St. Jerome, XXVII, 397.

ENEMIES.—We are commanded to love our enemies, not God’s enemies, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 583.—It is easier to beware of an avowed enemy than to endure a foe concealed under a friend’s name, St. Jerome, XXIII, 529.—One who hates another is certainly his own enemy, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 283.—Enemies are to be loved, so that we may be superior to Gentiles and beasts, id., XXXIX, 2258.—One who does not spare his enemy is first an enemy to himself, ibid., 1882.—When an enemy is loved for God’s sake and a friend in God, charity is true, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1466.—Charity knows no enemies, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 391.

INIQUITY.—Iniquity is so much less worthy of pardon insofar as justice was not unknown to it, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 786.—Nothing is more laborious than iniquity and impiety, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 127.—The iniquitous person is no small punishment to himself, id., XXXVI, 605.—It is better to suffer iniquity than to commit it, id., XXXIX, 1881.—The joy of the wicked passes into punishment; the punishment of the innocent, into joy, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 494.

INJURY.—One who despises an injury is better than one who grieves over it, St. Ambrose, XVI, 7, 22.—Forgetting injuries is a great virtue, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 183.—One who does not repel an injury when able incurs a like guilt, Guibert, CLVI, 2.

INJUSTICE, UNJUST PERSON.—It is better to endure injustice than to commit it, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1655.—Whether gentle or fierce, an unjust person is harmful both to himself and to others, id., XXXVII, 1805.—Injuries are to be embraced with love, St. Benedict, abbot, LXVI, 215.

INNOCENT, INNOCENCE.—To strike an innocent person is homicide; to strike the guilty is justice, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1018.—It is difficult for innocence, oppressed by evils, not to grieve, St. Jerome, XXIV, 793.—Innocence would perish if power were always joined to wickedness, id., XXIII, 418.—He is not innocent, although he does no harm, who wishes to do harm, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1190.—That innocence alone is true which harms not even an enemy, id., XXXVI, 102.—Your innocence, even while you sleep, is the voice of your soul, id., XXXVII, 1317.—No innocent person exists on earth apart from Christ, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 30.—Innocence of life is the foundation of all knowledge, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 13.

UNDERSTANDING, INTELLIGENCE.—The fruit of understanding is to put into practice what has been learned, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 358.—Unclean hearts do not bear the light of spiritual understanding, id., 470.—To understand is more excellent than to be or to live, St. Augustine, XXXII, 1244.—Always to remember and love God—this is to be in His image, St. Anselm, CLIX, 203.

[Col. 0767] INTENTION.—Intention makes a work good, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 259.—The intention of a good conscience is the oil by which lamps—that is, good works—are kept burning, id., XXXIII, 571.—From a perverse intention nothing follows but a depraved work, even though it appears right, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 196.

ENVY, ENVIOUS PERSON.—An envious person must be cut away like a wasting disease of the body, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1950.—Envy devours every good, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLIX, 192.—Envy belongs only to the small-minded, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 956.—Not to envy and to rejoice in another’s virtue is a rare virtue, id., CLXXXIII, 1437.

TO INVOKE.—It is not fitting to invoke God without purity of heart, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 249.

ANGER.—Let not this sun set upon anger, lest the Sun of righteousness abandon the very mind, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1045.—God’s anger passes over the righteous; it does not remain, id., XXXVI, 1119.—To conquer anger is greater than to subject a city to oneself, Peter the Chanter, CC, 250.

## J

FASTING.—He fasts long enough who refreshes himself in accordance with Christ’s will, St. Ambrose, XVII, 422.—Those who fast receive much more than they offer, St. Jerome, XXII, 1020.—Fasting is the deprivation of the flesh and the light of the mind, St. Augustine, XL, 706.—One ought to fast from this world, id., XXXVIII, 695.

JESUS.—The name of Jesus is the sinner’s confidence, St. Augustine, XL, 946.—The name of Jesus is salvation, anointing, and glory; medicine for the soul, honey in the mouth, melody in the ear, jubilation in the heart, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 130.

JUDGE, JUDGMENT.—No one is more severely condemned by another’s judgment than the fool who is himself the author of his evils, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1043.—God’s judgments benefit the good and harm the wicked, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 603.—That the Judge’s sentence may not be bitter, let the Father’s scourges be sweet to us, St. Augustine, XLIII, 1793.—A strong man scorns popular judgment in the light of conscience, id., XLV, 1863.—Lest we be judged, let us be our own judges, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 173.—At judgment severity will be so much greater as mercy is now greater, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 563.—One who judges himself does not await judgment, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 129.

YOKE.—Christ’s yoke is for the Christian what wings are for a bird, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 719.—Christ’s yoke is sweet to one who loves, hard to one who does not love, id., XXXVIII, 1507.—Christ’s yoke does not weigh down but lifts up, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 405.

JUSTICE, RIGHTEOUS PERSON.—The righteous person sometimes judges another fairer than himself, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1100.—Justice is sparing toward itself, wholly outward-looking; whatever it has, it pours out upon its neighbors, ibid., 1129.—A righteous person is never alone who is always with God, id., XVI, 109.—These are the arms of the righteous: to conquer by yielding, id., XVI, 720.—Unhappy is the place where peace is lost and justice absent, St. Jerome, XXV, 729.—Human justice needs God’s mercy, id., XXII, 1068.—Wisdom befits justice, and still more folly injustice, St. Zeno, XI, 33.—He who made you without you does not justify you without you, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 923.—Whoever is righteous is immediately good, ibid., XXXVII, 1577.—No one is righteous except the humble and devout person, id., XXXVI, 585.—Justice is nothing other than not sinning, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1863.—No righteous person in this life is without labors and troubles, St. Peter Chrysologus, LI, 526.—Justice delights more than iniquity, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 362.—To uphold justice for love of reward is unjust, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 35.—One is not righteous who abandons justice in suffering, ibid., 449.—The righteous person begins in fear and is perfected in charity, ibid., 29.—It is one thing to retain justice, another to love it, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 429.

## L

LABOR.—A change of labor is a truce of rest, St. Ambrose, XVI, 178.—The labor of this present world will receive its end, and everlasting joy will succeed it, St. Jerome, XXVII, 622.—By all the labor of a brief day one reaches the desired reward, St. Jerome, XXV, 219.—People must labor, so that the devil may always find us occupied, id., XXII, 939.—If you wish to endure labor, attend to the reward, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 372.—Rest is purchased by labor, id., XXXVII, 1211.—Labor will have no end unless that which cannot be taken away is loved, id., XLV, 1870.—Where there is no labor, there is no fruit, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 14.—Things acquired by labor please more, id., LII, 101.—The remedy for labor is the beginning of another labor, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 420.—The good turn the labor [Col. 0768] of nature into the labor of grace, but the wicked into the labor of guilt, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 220.

TEARS.—Tears often nourish and lift up the mind, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1185.—The tears of the guilty are sweeter than the pleasures of theatres, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1683.—The Lord’s tears are the world’s joys, id., XXXIX, 1928.—Tears are the baptisms of sinners, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 103.—Tears wash away the sores of guilt, id., LII, 167.—Tears are the blood of the penitent, St. Valerian, LII, 8.—In tears there is always spiritual sowing, Cassiodorus, LXX, 440.—The grace of tears is given by God, Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 47.—Tears are signs of a wounded heart, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 98.—Tears are seeds of justice, id., CLXXXIII, 1402.—The tears of penitents are the wine of angels, ibid., 1376.—Tears of penitence make the chalice of the altar sweeter, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 84.

LASCIVIOUSNESS.—Lasciviousness often lies hidden beneath the sad garb of the mind, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1138.

LAUD, PRAISE.---Let the sacrifice of praise proceed from the holiness of works, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 175.---To be mute regarding God’s praises is a great misery, ibid., 552.---No one is more praiseworthy than the person whom everyone can praise, id., XVI, 147.---Whoever sees that he is being praised should deliberately strive to ensure that what is said is true, St. Ambrose, XVII, 106.---The praise of God is truly continuous if one lives well without ceasing, St. Prosper, LI, 382.---Praise is then pleasing to the Lord when voice and life have come together as one, Cassiodorus, LXX, 492.---To praise people’s evil deeds is to increase them, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 559.---One ought to be praised in God, not in oneself, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 310.---The vanity of human praise torments the good and makes the wicked happy, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 389.---No one should be praised before death, ibid., 1016.---To wish to add to heavenly praises is to detract from them, id., CLXXXIII, 357.---No praise is secure where life itself is not secure, ibid., 1030.---True praise arises from a right will made known through a good work, Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 21.---To be praised by disgraceful persons is as disgraceful as to be praised for disgraceful things, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 129.

LAW.---The remembrance of the Law does not allow sins to be generated or to grow, St. Jerome, XXVII, 901.

FREEDOM, FREE.---Innocence makes one free; guilt makes one a slave, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1163.---We are born in freedom: how miserable it is to die in slavery, ibid., 938.---To be free from God is the greatest crime, id., XVII, 135.---True freedom is to serve Christ, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 128.---The law of freedom is the law of charity, ibid., 740.

LUST.---Lust is like a straw: it is quickly kindled and swiftly consumed, St. Ambrose, XVI, 896.---If lust has exceeded its bounds, it spills over into vice, St. Jerome, XXII, 287.---When lust is conquered, the devil is conquered, St. Augustine, XLIV, 801.---Lust conceives pain, gives birth to sin, and produces death, id., XLV, 1644.---Lust must be conquered by flight, id., XXXIX, 2301.---Unless the flame of lust is extinguished by purity of heart, whatever virtues arise are in vain, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 688.---Lust destroys all good works, id., LXXIX, 371.---Our desire comes to rest in God’s illumination; it does not fail, Guibert, CLVI, 45.---Rather than be stained by lust, it is better to die, St. Anselm, CLIX, 191.---The more lust is exercised, the more it grows, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 247.

LILIES.---Lilies grow better in a valley than on a mountain, Alan of Lille, CCX, 87.

TONGUE.---Let your tongue be subject to your mind, St. Ambrose, XVI, 513.---Let the tongue know nothing except Christ, St. Jerome, XXII, 991.---Whoever does not bridle the tongue destroys concord, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 55.---The vice of the tongue is equivalent to the gravest crimes, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 388.---His tongue preaches without effort whose life preaches by its conduct, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 17.

PLACE.---A place does not make saints, St. Augustine, XL, 1282.

SPEECH, SPEAKING.---Fault is more readily avoided by not speaking, or rather by keeping silence, Cassiodorus, CXX, 132.---Silence from divine speech is hunger of the mind, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 201.---He knows how to speak well who has first learned to do good, ibid., 1282.---He speaks well who lives perfectly, id., LXXVII, 873.---Rather than speak, it is safer to be silent, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 380.

LAMP.---A lamp exposes a thief, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 54.

WRESTLE.---To wrestle while the world is present is more difficult, but more glorious, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 107.

PLAY.---No one plays safely with a serpent, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 159.

[Col. 0769] LIGHT.---A human being cannot be light to himself, St. Valerian, LII, 182.

LIGHT.---The light of reason shines even amid the darkness of an evil conscience, Rupert, CLXIX, 93.

LUXURY, LUXURIOUS LIVING.---Once a person begins to live luxuriously, he begins to stray from the true faith, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1818.---Luxury is a fire devouring unto destruction, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 688.

M

TEACHER.---He who has not been a disciple ought not to become a teacher, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 156.

GREAT THINGS.---A great thing requires great strength, St. Augustine, XXXII, 909.

GREATNESS OF SOUL.---Greatness of soul does not make people arrogant, nor does humility make them faint-hearted, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXIII, 100.

GREATNESS.---Greatness is proved in moderation, Tertullian, II, 261.

GREAT.---Great is the person who desires eternal things, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 180.

EVILS, EVIL PEOPLE, WICKEDNESS, EVIL.---Evil is nothing in itself, but arises from human vice, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 249.---Nothing is evil to a person except through his own fault, ibid., 789.---Our weakness causes us to judge as evil that which we suffer, ibid., 363.---Wickedness acts against itself, St. Ambrose, XVII, 98.---Once the seed of wickedness has been removed, the fruits of depravity will wither, ibid., 35.---It is better to hate evil persons than to associate with them, ibid., 488.---Our wickedness makes God drunk, St. Jerome, XXVI, 679.---An evil is judged brief when a better end follows it, id., XXII, 179.---It is a lesser evil to sin openly than to feign and pretend holiness, id., XXV, 277.---However powerful the wicked may be, they are objects of contempt to holy people, Rufinus, XXI, 65.---Those who live badly, even if their tongue is silent, curse the Lord by their life, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1335.---It belongs to Christians to endure temporal evils and hope for eternal goods, id., XXXVIII, 1356.---An evil work is done only by evil persons, id., XLI, 421.---Evils must not be done so that good things may result, id., XLIV, 808.---The wicked person is himself his own punishment, id., XXXVIII, 1364.---Even if he reigns, a wicked person is a slave, id., XLI, 114.---The wicked are to be tolerated for the sake of the good, not the good abandoned for the sake of the wicked, id., XXXIII, 329.---The wicked are preserved here so that the good may arise from them, id., XXXVIII, 1383.---Evil Christians are to be guarded against more than Jews and pagans, id., XL, 343.---We can overcome evils here, but not flee them, id., XXXIX, 2272.---It is not enough to avoid evils unless good also is done, id., XL, 1040.---Every time of evils is brief, St. Prosper, LI, 556.---Wickedness turns people into vipers, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 137.---The grievous evils of this life do not seem grievous to one who thinks of eternal goods, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 354.---Let us neither despair of the wicked nor imitate them, id., 1514.---One who seeks an answer wrongly does not deserve one, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 727.---In Scripture, evil means not only sin but also the punishment of the sinner, Hincmar of Reims, CXXV, 56.---Our evils are ours alone; our goods are both God’s and ours, ibid., 126.---The sum of all evils is that we live according to the examples of the wicked, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 210.

COMMANDMENTS.---God’s commandments are to be held not so much in memory as in conduct, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 621.---God’s commandments are bitter to the wicked but sweet to the good, Rufinus, XXI, 87.

REMAIN.---We must remain in him who remains for ever, St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 540.

MEEKNESS.---He who is dear has meekness and not harshness, St. Ambrose, XVI, 415.

SEA.---The sea represents this age: bitter through saltness, turbulent through waves, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 780.

MARTYR, MARTYRDOM.---The blood of martyrs is the seed of Christians, Tertullian, 535.---Christ’s martyr is the Church’s treasure, St. Ambrose, XVI, 242.---The death of martyrs is itself a reward, ibid., 1074.---Wherever martyrs are, they are with God, where all is well, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1366.---Peace has its martyrs, id., XXXIX, 2301, 2302, 2307.---Martyrs are born through death, begin at their end, and shine in heaven, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 152.---Martyrdom is a hard road for the flesh, but a blessed way for the soul, Cassiodorus, LXX, 223.---The blood of martyrs cries for vengeance; Christ’s blood cries for pardon, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 419.

MEDICINE.---The rich person is medicine for the poor person, and conversely, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 124.

PHYSICIAN.---A physician’s praise is to cure many, St. Ambrose, [Col. 0770] XVII, 233.---The physician whom the sick man deceives heals with difficulty, St. Valerian, LII, 6.

MEDITATION.---Meditation must not be abandoned amid temptations and hardships, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 22.---Daily meditation removes sleepiness and produces watchfulness, St. Ambrose, XVII, 96.---By constant meditation a person is enlightened to know himself, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLIX, 214.---Meditation produces knowledge; knowledge, compunction; compunction, devotion, ibid.---Meditation is medicine for a sick conscience, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 660.---Meditation is, as it were, the material of fire; love, its flame, ibid., 176.---By meditation and prayer we ascend, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1063.

LIE, LYING.---A lie in speech is shameful, much more so in conduct, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1061.---To lie about one’s religion is the greatest impiety, Tertullian, I, 403.---To lie is sacrilege, St. Jerome, XXII, 688.---To lie is to kill the soul, ibid., 118.---Lies deceive their own lovers, Rufinus, XXI, 69.---It is worse to lie than to be deceived, St. Valerian, LII, 133.---The throat of a liar is a grave of the dead, Cassiodorus, LXX, 26.

BEGGAR.---A beggar is one who does not have God, even though he abounds in every other good thing, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1883.---We are all God’s beggars, id., XXXVIII, 366, 380.

MIND.---A good mind is a good possession, St. Ambrose, XVI, 11.---Blindness of mind is healed only by Christ’s teaching, St. Jerome, XXV, 120.---A mind joined to God draws forth his mercy, id., XXVI, 523.---A mind excluded from the light of truth finds in itself nothing but darkness, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 386.---A mind conscious of no evil in itself laughs at everything, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 941.

REWARD.---Let the reward raise you up if the work distresses you, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1517.

MERITS.---Merits are acquired here; rewards are rendered in heaven, St. Augustine, XLV, 1182.---All merits begin from faith, id., XLV, 1850.---Our merits are God’s gifts, and for them we receive eternal rewards, St. Prosper, LI, 276.

CRUMB.---One who gives a crumb to the poor receives the whole, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 8.

MIRACLE.---The conversion of a sinner is the greatest miracle, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1919.---It is a singular miracle to fail to see what has been seen, to fail to know what has been known, and not to believe what has been believed, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 81.

WRETCHED PEOPLE.---Wretched are those who either do not have what they want or have what they do not rightly want, St. Augustine, XLV, 1864.---Under a just God, no one is wretched unless he deserves it, ibid., 1865.---True misery is false happiness, id., XXXVII, 1099.---Whoever recognizes himself to be in true misery will be in true happiness, ibid.---All this misery of the human race is a medicinal pain, not a punitive sentence, ibid., 1793.

MERCY.---If we grant pardon to unlawful acts, we retain mercy but not the justice of mercy, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 596.---For mercy’s sake it is better to endure ill will than to display cruelty, St. Ambrose, XVI, 102.---Mercy itself is justice, ibid., 1205.---Mercy is the redemption of the soul, ibid., 777.---At times, not to deserve mercy for the present is a great happiness, St. Jerome, XXVI, 92.---Hypocrites sell mercy; they do not give it, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 9.---Mercy is the greatest of God’s works, ibid., 62.---Without the rain of mercy, our hearts are like land without water, Cassiodorus, LXX, 319.---Mercy is a name of God, St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 522.---Mercy is imprudent when it benefits a few and harms many, Alcuin, C, 148.---To ask mercy from God is the best defence for the accused, St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 205.---God takes the material for showing mercy from himself, but the material for punishing from us, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXIII, 186.---Mercy fastened Christ to the cross, Alan of Lille, CCX, 137.

MEASURE.---Measure is a virtue; excess is a vice, St. Jerome, XXII, 937.---The measure of the mind is indeed wisdom, St. Augustine, XXXII, 975.

MORALS.---Bad morals are more grievous enemies than hostile foes, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 312.---Good morals are like wings that raise us to the heights of heaven, ibid., 438.

DYING, DEATH.---All things die in order to live again, Tertullian, I, 524.---Death is not the destruction of the soul but its departure from the body, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 329.---Death is not an evil, since it restores freedom and excludes pain, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1140.---We die daily, we change daily, and yet we believe ourselves eternal, St. Jerome, XXII, 346.---The death of the saints is sleep, [Col. 0771] St. Jerome, XXV, 356.---The death of one whose life is sweet is bitter to us, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 611.---Do not concern yourself with the manner in which a person dies, but with where he is going after death, id., XXXVII, 1945.---Death is the beginning of blessedness, id., XXXII, 1471.---Meditation on death is useful for repressing all boasting, St. Prosper, LI, 610.---The death of the soul is God’s departure from it, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 19.---He to whom God is life cannot die, ibid., 166.---To die for Christ is to reign with Christ, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 556.---Live as though you were to die today, St. Benedict, abbot, LXVI, 139.---The death of martyrs flourishes in the faith of those who live, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1637.---We must die to the world in order to be made alive, id., LXXIX, 60, 61.---The image of death is a strong shield against the world, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 774.---Three things remove the fear of death: serenity of conscience, firmness of faith, and certainty of hope, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLIX, 233.---We begin to die when we begin to live, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 875.---Those who live according to the flesh are dead, ibid., 899.---A good death is the result of a good life, Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 69.

WORLD.---The world’s vice is the desire of acquiring, Tertullian, I, 1283.---The world is God’s temple, St. Cyprian, IV, 227.---What is the world but a field full of contests? St. Ambrose, XVI, 971.---Those who displease Christ please the world more, St. Jerome, XXII, 324.---Why is the world the seat of God? St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 368.---The world is a great sea in which the larger fish devour the smaller, id., XXXVI, 422.---The world is like a flood, upon which faith floats, id., XL, 847.---The world is a battlefield with the devil and vices, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 94.---For one to whom the world is wearisome, life a burden, and flesh a pain, death is a desire, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLIX, 234.---The world has gold on its horn, but hay at its tail, ibid., 312.---The world’s glory is not glory but a devouring fire, ibid., 338.---This world is empty like dreams, and all its desire is more bitter than vinegar, id., 220.---The world’s three vices must be trampled underfoot: pleasure, curiosity, and pride, Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 230, 231.

N

BE BORN.---It is not a great thing to be born from men most famous in the world, but it is wonderful to despise this, St. Jerome, XXII, 692.---We are born for pains, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 87.

NATURE, NATURAL.---The good of nature is not enough for righteousness, St. Jerome, XXII, 692.---Grace alone gives expression to nature, St. Prosper, LI, 853.---It is natural to avoid all inconveniences, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 240.

SHIP.---Whenever Christ sleeps in our ship, a storm rushes in, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 129.---The soul is like a ship sailing upstream, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 94.

BUSINESS.---The affairs of this life afflict the mind, Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 505.

NO ONE.---No one lives without sin, Rabanus Maurus, CX, 702.---No one ought to be protected by his own deceit, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 125.

NOT KNOWING.---To be safely ignorant of something is better than to learn it at risk, St. Jerome, XXII, 113.---Not to be known by God is the same as to perish, Rufinus, XXI, 11.---Not knowing is a lesser punishment than failing to fulfil what one knows, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 289.

NAME.---A name is of no use where the reality is absent, St. Augustine, XXXV, 2007.

NIGHT.---Night is the time of temptation, Guibert, CLVI, 75.---Night is the life of sinners, Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 445.

O

OBEDIENCE, OBEYING.---Not to obey God is unjust and ungrateful, Tertullian, I, 1255.---Obedience alone holds the palm; disobedience alone finds punishment, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 897.---Where disobedience is, there is pride, id., XL, 1221.---It is always useful to a person to obey God when he commands, and always ruinous not to obey, St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 185.---The reward of obedience is eternal life, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 205.---To obey willingly is easier than to command with discernment, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 268.---It is one thing to obey according to the letter, another according to the intention, ibid., 422.---The vow of obedience is medicine for vices, Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 320.

OFFERINGS.---Our dispositions and good will render our offerings acceptable to God, St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 86 [lacuna].

BE KILLED, KILLING.---Sinners are killed when, darkened in understanding, they are alienated from the life of God, St. Augustine, [Col. 0772] XXXVI, 1800.---God wishes to kill in a human being what the human being made, and to save what he himself made, id., 1692.

EYE.---An immodest eye is the messenger of an immodest heart, St. Augustine, XXXII, 1391.---The eyes of parents and relatives are lamps to their children, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 1.---Human eyes are deceived in God’s works without God’s light, ibid., 51.---Eyes are not dulled by the greatness of the light but by their own weakness, ibid., 112.---To imperfect eyes shapes grow large, appearances are disturbed, and they are deceived, id., 176.---The soul has two eyes: one by which it understands, the other by which it inquires, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 396.---Two things make the eye simple: love of the good and knowledge of the true; blindness and perversity make the evil eye, ibid., 183, 515.

HATRED.---It is not the part of a saint to have furnished a cause for hatreds, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 488.---Hatred is darkness; love is light, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 633.---Hatred is death; love is our life, ibid.---Perfect hatred is to love people while always abhorring their vices, Cassiodorus, LXX, 472.

OFFENCE.---It is a great offence not to wish to appease those whom you have offended, St. Jerome, XXV, 856.

OFFER.---God regards not the gifts of those who offer, but their will, id., XXVII, 305.

OIL.---The oil of the sinner is flattery, St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 594.

ALL THINGS.---All things are subject to us if we are subject to God, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 134.---Everything that charity does has a certain force and efficacy of unwearied prayer, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 30.---For everyone, bodily necessity is a kind of speech, ibid., 183, 595.

WORKS, WORK.---Let our work shine forth to others while we ourselves conceal it, St. Hilary, IX, 683.---It is not enough for a work to be good in the integrity of the deed, unless the will also is good, ibid., 456.---Works that are compelled rightly require the fullness of grace, ibid., 356.---Let your works shine, so that they may bear the image of God, in whose image you were made, St. Ambrose, XVI, 336.---A work without faith is perishable and weak, St. Jerome, XXII, 604.---Good works are like the children of our life, St. Augustine, XLII, 1004.---Let no one be exalted by his good works; let no one despair because of evil ones, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 935.---We labour at a good work in vain if we do not persevere to the end, id., LXXVI, 38.---In works, he who does not despise small things advances not merely gradually but effectively, id., CLIX, 20.---For the negligent in the work of salvation a threefold evil remains: terror at departure, pain in passage, and shame in the sight of the glory of the great God, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1144.---A tranquil mind amid work and in the midst of affairs is a rare bird on earth, ibid., 334.---A work without a good intention is a body without life, Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 1120.

REPROACH.---The good are a reproach to the wicked, St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 256.

PRAYER, PRAYING.---Whoever prays is near heaven, Tertullian, II, 926.---Prayer nourishes the poor, Tertullian, I, 1196.---To weep in prayer belongs to virtue, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1134.---For our prayer to ascend to him, God bends himself down toward us, ibid., 1204.---The best prayer is a righteous life, St. Augustine, XLI, 653.---Desire prays even if the tongue is silent, id., XXXVIII, 498, 821.---Let action be supported by prayer, and prayer by action, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 560.---In prayer God hears not words but the desires of the heart, id., 718.---Prayer is empty where action is evil, id., LXXVII, 1138.---It is better to pray than to read, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 288.---Prayer is of the heart, not of the lips, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 356.---At the time of prayer, the whole soul is beautiful, ibid., 94.---In prayer God often does not grant many people what they want, in order to grant what leads to salvation, ibid., 357.---Prayer should be trusted more than one’s own industry, id., CLXXXIII, 440.---The prayer of a wise person ought to accord with his life, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 19.

ORDER.---Order is a guide to God, Tertullian, I, 990.---The order of things must be preserved if the soul is to act well, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 539.---Human affairs are strengthened by order, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 109.---The reward is rendered not to the highest rank but to the greatest labour, St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 221.---Things not done in charity have no order, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 403.

MOUTH.---Our mouth is our gate, St. Ambrose, XVI, 233.---Trifles in a priest’s mouth are blasphemies, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXIII, 425.

LEISURE.---Leisure and rest make the mind small, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 286.

P

PEACEMAKERS, PEACE.---Whoever is at peace with God fears no one’s enmity, St. Ambrose, XVII, 231.---Perfect peace does not exist as long as one struggles against vices, St. Augustine, [Col. 0773] XLI, 657.---Here we possess peace in hope, id., XXXVII, 1582.---The order of peace with other people here is this: first, that one harm no one; then, that one benefit anyone one can, id., XLI, 643.---God is peace; Christ is peace, id., XXXVII, 1656.---That which does not rise from the root of charity must not be called peace, id., XXXIX, 1916.---Not to preserve peace is to despise Christ, id., XXXIX, 1838.---Nothing is better than peace, Guibert, CLVI, 606.

PALM.---The palm of the conqueror is a reward, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1192.

BREAD.---The bread of the heart is righteousness, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 562.

PARADISE.---Your blood is the key of paradise, Tertullian, II, 747.---Paradise contains within itself Christ, the tree of life, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 24.---Paradise is the land of the living, Cassiodorus, LXX, 90, 479.

PARENTS.---Everyone loves to follow the life of his parents, St. Ambrose, XVI, 58.---Let parents learn that children can be taught more by examples than by speech, St. Jerome, XXII, 686.

PASSOVER.---Passover occurs when the soul puts off an irrational passion and takes on good compassion, St. Ambrose, XVI, 179.---The Passover of eternal life begins here through faith, Rufinus, XXI, 102.

PASSION, SUFFERING.---The consolation of sufferings is that through them we are made like the Lord, St. Hilary of Poitiers, X, 715.---Suffering is life for Christians and a defence against persecutors, St. Ambrose, XVII, 312.---Sufferings are what demonstrate one’s merit for the future life, ibid., 180.---Suffering finds medicine for itself in grievous illnesses, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 35.

SHEPHERD.---The fault of shepherds and the vice of teachers is the vexation of the sheep, St. Jerome, XXVIII, 55.---A shepherd should be loved, a hired hand tolerated, and a robber avoided, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 756.---The panting shepherd goes after the lost sheep, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 54.---Good shepherds, like skilled physicians, first feel the pulse and then strike, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 780.
