PATIENCE.---Patience enables us to persevere, St. Cyprian, IV, 252.---Where patience is absent, wisdom finds no place, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 825.---Patience is greater in proportion as charity is greater, id., XL, 619.---Adversities are always softened by patience, Cassiodorus, LXX, 316.---Patience is the guardian of our condition, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 43.---Patience is superior to strength, id., LXXIX, 268.

HOMELAND.---He does not love his homeland for whom exile is sweet, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1089.---The faithful pass from the world into their homeland; the unfaithful pass away with the world, St. Augustine, XXXV, 1785.---The homeland is the life of Christ; the way is the death of Christ, id., XXXVII, 1089.---The heaven of the homeland is approached by two feet: meditation and desire, Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 248.

POVERTY, POOR PERSON.---The tears of the poor are redeeming tears, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1115.---Do not despise a poor person: he makes you rich, ibid., 1003.---Poverty is everywhere where there is hunger of desires, where there is an insatiable appetite, ibid., 943.---He who is poor with Christ is rich, St. Jerome, XXII, 29.---A poor person possessed by greed is worse than a rich person, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1019.---Whoever defrauds the poor is a man of blood, Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 1011.---The poor are a trustworthy storehouse for riches, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 299.---Nothing is more detestable or more miserable than a proud poor person, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 1043.---A poor person laughs more sincerely than a rich person, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 42.---Let a cleric be poor in money and rich in conscience, ibid.

SINNING, SIN.---By sinning, one undoubtedly admits idolatry, Tertullian, I, 644.---The day of sin is called a day of confusion, St. Ambrose, XVI, 425.---The death of sin is gain, and its life is punishment, ibid., 1144.---A sinner’s conscience stinks more than every grave, ibid., 13.---Take sins away from the midst, and you have made God near to yourself, id., XVII, 420.---To sin belongs to a human being; to lay snares belongs to the devil, St. Jerome, XXIII, 560.---Let neither the sinner despair of salvation nor the righteous person be secure in his own virtue, id., XXII, 912.---When God is not angry with sinners, it is great anger, id., XXIII, 412.---The multitude of sinners does not diminish the crime, ibid., 542, 565.---Nothing offends God so much as a raised neck after sins, id., XXII, 223.---Sin speaks of death, id., XXVI, 725.---Our sins come from us; our goodness from God, ibid., 805.---Sin is the sole death of the soul, St. Augustine, XLII, 95.---If you wish to sin, seek a place where God does not see you, and do what you wish, id., XXXVIII, 736.---A neglected sin grows; none is small in God’s sight, id., XL, 1119.---God will permit no sins to go unpunished, ibid., 1351.---Sins are conquered by love, St. Peter Chrysologus, [Col. 0774] LII, 94.---The sinner departs from himself before departing from God, ibid., 2.---The sinner becomes a beast, ibid.---Great is the person who does not sin in the flesh; greatest is the one who does not sin even in the heart, ibid., 89.---Sins become cheap through habit and are no longer felt, St. Valerian, LXI, 45.---The pleasure of sin is brief; its punishment eternal, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 225.---The sinner’s present prosperity is compared to smoke and a wheel, id., LXXVII, 492.---Sins that are light for beginners are reckoned grievous for the perfect, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 217.---Whoever defends sin sins more than the one who commits it, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 90.---No sin remains unpunished, ibid., 593.---Every sin dishonours God, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLIX, 208.---There ought to be no punishment of sin where there is no will to sin, St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 150.---The bodies of sinners are graves of the dead, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 1044.---The sinner is his own murderer, ibid., 507.---Sin is to be guarded against more than its punishment, ibid., 855.---To sin is grave; not to repent is more grave; most grave of all is to undergo eternal torments for sin and impenitence, Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 826.---One who does not correct when able consents to sin, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 189.

BREAST.---That breast is the tomb in which Christ is held dead and buried, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 75.

MONEY.---Money is poison to right hope, St. Augustine, XXXII, 1006.---Put your hand to money in such a way that you free your heart from it, id., XXXVIII, 955.---Money is a cruel weight: it corrupts hearts, purchases falsehood, and removes truth, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 37.

WINGS.---There are two wings with respect to future things, love and hope; with respect to past things, fear and repentance, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1203.

TO BE A PILGRIM, PILGRIMAGE.---Our pilgrimage is to be endured, not loved, St. Augustine, XL, 679.

PERFECTION, PERFECTING.---All perfection is in truth, St. Ambrose, XVI, 63.---Not to wish to be perfect is to sin, St. Jerome, XXII, 34.---That we may merit perfection, let us confess imperfection, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 784.---Perfect is the person who is not impatient with his neighbour’s imperfection, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 153.---One must always fear for the perfect person, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 468.---Where someone ceases to make progress, there he begins to fail, ibid., 305, 243.---Whoever strives to make progress always finds room to grow, ibid., 303.---It belongs to the perfect to glory in tribulation, id., CLXXXIII, 45.

DANGER, DANGEROUS THINGS.---Nothing is more burdensome to a person than awareness of danger, St. Augustine, XLIV, 176.---He who strives for the kingdom despises danger, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 22.

PERSEVERANCE, PERSEVERE.---God’s mercy is necessary for perseverance, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 381.---He has no perseverance for whom his own progress is already sufficient, St. Augustine, XLV, 1878.---To persevere is not to be conquered by temptation, St. Leo the Great, LV, 206.---Perseverance is not in human power but in God’s, Archbishop Hincmar, CXXV, 74.---Perseverance is an image of eternity, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXIII, 458.

PHILOSOPHY, PHILOSOPHER.---The philosopher is an animal of glory, Tertullian, II, 647.---The philosopher is a worker in words, a destroyer of things, a friend and advocate of error, id., I, 1233.---Philosophy is neither parent nor rule of life, Lactantius, VI, 382.

PIETY.---True piety is that which places divine things before human, and eternal things before temporal, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1055.---Piety toward God is the summit and crown of virtues, St. Jerome, XXII, 580.---Piety and true religion are the royal road, id., XXV, 674.---The beginning of piety is to think most rightly about God, St. Augustine, XXXII, 1224.---Piety suffices for true happiness, id., XLI, 114.

PLEASE.---We ought to please God even with our body, St. Hilary, IX, 196.---We should please people as far as possible, ibid., 197.---To wish to please people only is to displease God, ibid., 102.---Whoever wishes now to please God must necessarily displease the ungodly, ibid., 400.

REPENTANCE.---Repentance does not perish because it finds patience, Tertullian, I, 1228.---Let repentance not be less than the offence, St. Cyprian, IV, 192.---The voice of repentance is to pray with tears, St. Hilary, IX, 391.---Never to repent belongs to God alone, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1043.---No one can do penance well unless he has hoped for pardon, ibid., 390.---Such is the medicine of repentance that God seems to change his sentence, ibid., 427.---The punishment of sin is greater in proportion as forgetfulness of God is longer, St. Jerome, XXV, 855.---The punishment of sinners is God’s sanctification, id., XXVI, 337.---After shipwreck, repentance is the second plank for the wretched, [Col. 0775] St. Jerome, XXII, 985.---The crown of repentance is woven from the flowers of Scripture, id., XXII, 899.---True repentance is measured not by years but by contrition of heart, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2216.---The penitent rises more through pardon than he fell through guilt, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 4.---Perfect repentance is to avoid future sins and mourn past ones, Cassiodorus, LXX, 170.---From the mourning of penitents arise the virtues of saints, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1274.---Through repentance let us seize the inheritance of the righteous which we did not hold through life, id., LXXVI, 1525.---Fervent repentance is preferred to sluggish innocence, id., LXXVII, 83.---Repentance paves the road to heaven, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 228.---Repentance is reckoned in place of innocence, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXIII, 1151.---Whoever postpones repentance until the day of death rarely truly repents, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 317.

POSSESSION.---A pure human being is a precious possession, St. Ambrose, XVI, 5.---Everyone praises what he possesses more highly, St. Jerome, XXII, 207.---What you possess is not yours, but a stewardship entrusted to you, ibid., 324.---He is possessed, rather than possessing, who is held by desire for things, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 544.---What is lost without grief is possessed without love, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1006.

PRECEPTS.---God’s precepts must not only be done but also loved, St. Hilary, IX, 394.---Those who despise divine precepts are not content to err in one way, Rufinus, XXI, 421.---God’s precepts must be obeyed through love, not fear; willingly, not from necessity, ibid., 7.---Those who despise God’s precepts are like grass that grows on roofs, St. Prosper, LI, 478.---Those who despise God’s precepts ask him in vain, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 510.---To observe precepts is a sacrifice, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 271.

PREACH, PREACHING.---A preacher is a dispenser of spiritual jewels, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2319.---A good preacher is a chariot and charioteer, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1412.---Let the preacher return to his own heart, id., LXXVII, 73.---Let the preacher teach first by work rather than by voice, id., LXXVII, 100.---Let the preacher fulfil in work what he teaches, id., LXXIX, 243, 306.---A preacher who does not burn does not kindle, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 14.

REWARDS.---One must reach great rewards through great labours, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1627.---Rewards gained by labours are more welcome, Alan of Lille, CCX, 291.

MAKE PROGRESS.---One must always make progress on the way to God, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1798.---Those who make progress ascend; those who fail descend, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLIX, 175.

GO FORWARD.---In going forward one always either ascends to heaven by living well or descends into hell by living badly, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLIX, 415.

PROSPERITY. — Prosperity is not happiness for those whom an evil conscience torments, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1180. — Prosperity is more to be feared than adversity, id., XLI, 43, 44. — By prosperity a man becomes defiled, so that he may be ensnared, Guibert, CLVI, 643. — Prosperity should be used in such a way that it is not an occasion of sin but an aid to virtue, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 965. — Prosperity exalts far more people, although adversity breaks many, id., CLXXXIII, 766.

PROVIDING. — Nothing is more foolish than not to provide for one’s last things, St. Jerome, XXV, 694. — Let the provident and good God himself be your granary, your storehouse, your purse, your riches, etc., St. Augustine, XXXII, 1471.

PRUDENCE. — It is great prudence to seek gold in mud, St. Jerome, XXII, 688. — Prudence, by sharing itself with others, increases the more, Alan of Lille, CCX, 340.

CHASTITY. — A stain upon chastity can be washed away by no nitre and by no fuller’s herb, St. Jerome, XXII, 789.

FIGHTING. — He who does not live justly does not fight, but is dragged along, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 821. — You labor in fighting, but you will rejoice in triumphing, ibid.

BEAUTY. — Beauty is a good of God, St. Augustine, XLI, 467. — He whose body is beautiful but whose soul is deformed is more to be pitied than if he had a deformed body, id., XXXIV, 119. — Beauty without virtue is of no use, Guibert, CLVI, 456.

Q

SEEKING. — True wisdom is sought in love, St. Augustine, XXXII, 1324. — Those who seek God no longer seek things passing away and destined to die, id., XXXVI, 122. — God must be sought without end, because he must be loved without end, id., XXXVII, 1392. — God must be sought within us, not [Col. 0776] outside, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 233, 320. — To seek Jesus is sweet; to hold him is sweeter, ibid., 1. — No one seeks God who has not first found him, id., 593.

REST. — The rest of the righteous is rest in Christ and therefore in God, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 269. — Rest without resources is like exile from life, id., X, 1. — Where there is no rest, there the mind is often drawn away from its purpose, St. Jerome, XXIII, 34. — With God there is mighty rest and undisturbed life, St. Augustine, XXXII, 682. — God made us for himself, and our heart is restless until it rests in God, ibid., 661. — Where there is rest, there is sanctification, id., XXXIII, 219. — There is no rest where gold is kept, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 22. — Love does not know how to rest, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 7.

R

RARE. — What is rare is dear, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 455.

REASON. — Reason is a thing of God, Tertullian, I, 1227. — Reason without goodness is not reason, ibid., 291. — The things which seem to us to have no reason are full of justice and reason, St. Jerome, XXV, 910. — Virtue is superior to reason, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 147. — Reason and love are the two eyes for seeing God, St. Bernard, CLXXXI, 182. — Reason is the eye of the mind, Alan of Lille, CCX, 331.

CUSHION. — A pure conscience is the cushion upon which Christ reclines and rests, Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 444.

RIGHTEOUS RULER, MORE RIGHTLY, RIGHT. — The heart is right with God when God is sought for God’s sake, St. Augustine, XLV, 1879. — Those are not upright who fear here to suffer evils for the sake of eternal goods, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 154. — It is more right and safer to do good works while we live, which we hope may be done for us by others after death, id., LXXVII, 472. — A ruler of souls should be pre-eminent in works, ibid., 508.

REDEMPTION, REDEEMED. — Although human redemption could have been accomplished otherwise, it nevertheless ought not to have been accomplished otherwise than through the cross, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 495. — Christ is to be loved more for the work of redemption than for that of creation, id., CLXXXIII, 869. — He who trusts in his own strength cannot be redeemed, Peter Lombard, CXCV, 104.

GOVERNMENT. — The governance of souls is the art of arts, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 3.

RELIGION. — Nothing is greater than religion, nothing more sublime than faith, St. Ambrose, XVI, 826. — The sum of religion is to imitate the one whom you worship, St. Augustine, XLI, 242. — The Christian religion is the royal road to the kingdom, ibid., 342. — One who professes the Christian religion and nevertheless detracts from its honor is abominable, Guibert, CLVI, 264. — Religion is founded upon humility, preserved by poverty, and adorned by purity, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 769.

LEAVING. — Those have left all things even while possessing them who, in this world, possess nothing by loving nothing, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1633. — He has left much who has retained nothing for himself, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 825. — It is more expedient to leave the world than to be left by it, ibid., 285.

REPROVING. — What we reprove in others, far be it from us to do ourselves, St. Jerome, XXIII, 552. — He who reproves is a friend, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 617, 618.

THE REPROBATE. — The reprobate now rise up like ears of grain, but the elect lie hidden like kernels, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 540. — The reprobate will always persecute the righteous, but they cannot wound the soul, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 62.

REST. — Our rest is in heaven, not on earth, St. Ambrose, XVI, 979. — God loves us so greatly that, because we rest, he says that he himself rests, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1725. — Rest is bought with labor, id., XXXVI, 1212. — A good conscience is the rest of the soul, St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 418. — Rest is the Lord’s fullness and blessedness, Rupert, CLXIX, 68.

ANSWERING. — If answering back is evil, having provoked it is much worse, St. Jerome, XXII, 538. — In answering, let us so govern everything that we refute the charges made and refrain from injury, ibid. — It is not always easy to answer a fool wisely, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLIX, 73.

RESURRECTION. — Immortality is the flower of the resurrection, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1148.

LAUGHTER. — Laughter makes the one laughing lax; it scarcely corrects and reforms him, St. Jerome, XXIV, 437. — Brief laughter, everlasting sorrow, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 144.

ASKING. — He alone must be asked whose protection is true and eternal, St. Jerome, XXV, 201. — He who despises one who asks may perhaps hear one who rebukes, id., XXII, 209.

[Col. 0777] RUIN. — Ruin from a height strikes with a heavier fall, St. Ambrose, XVI, 230. — The downfall of others is an example for the righteous, St. Jerome, XXII, 301.

S

SABBATH. — It is better to spend the Sabbath digging all day than dancing, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 281. — He truly keeps the Sabbath who does not sin, ibid., 1242.

PRIESTS. — For priests, the losses rather than the gains of this world are better, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1161. — Great is the dignity of priests, but great too is their ruin if they sin, St. Jerome, XXVI, 585. — To hold the priesthood is less than to deserve it, id., XXII, 235. — The priesthood’s weapons are words which destroy iniquity, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1815. — Let the priest fear to sin, but fear despair even more, id., XL, 1118. — Priests are compared to bees, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 371. — Priests are the seasoning of souls, and souls are the Lord’s food, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1504. — Let the priest teach by word and example, id., LXXVII, 508. — A priest must mourn the sins of the people as though they were his own, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 334. — The office of an unworthy priest is the ruin of the people, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 168. — A priest stands between God and the people, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 298.

SACRIFICES. — God seeks not sacrifices but the disposition of those who offer them, St. Jerome, XXV, 784. — He offers sacrifice to God who punishes himself, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1824. — The sacrifice most acceptable to God is to offer and sacrifice oneself to him, Cassiodorus, LXX, 93.

THE WORLD. — The world belongs to God; worldly things belong to the devil, Tertullian, I, 585. — The peace of this world is a storm, St. Jerome, XXII, 32. — Every good of the present world is confusion; that of the world to come is perpetual, id., XXIV, 477. — He who trusts in worldly affairs forgets God, id., XXV, 936. — The world knows how to devour its lovers, not to carry them, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 694. — Once love of the world is weakened, love of God alone must necessarily grow strong within us, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1346.

SALVATION. — It is better for one’s property to be diminished than for the salvation of one’s soul to perish, St. Jerome, XXII, 912. — Make the salvation of others gain for your own soul, ibid., 322. — Our salvation is Christ himself, our physician, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1499. — Bodily infirmity is the health of the mind, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 50. — The beginning of salvation is knowledge of sin, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 331.

SAINTS. — The life of the saints is a long martyrdom, St. Jerome, XXII, 723. — No saint has been crowned without struggle, ibid., 124. — The saints now have one robe; after judgment they will have a double one, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 215. — The saints have one life but diverse rewards, id., XXXIX, 2182. — The victory of the saints is the work of God dwelling in heaven, St. Prosper, LI, 884, 885. — Holiness of conduct, when preserved, is the Lord’s proclamation, Cassiodorus, LXX, 76. — Holiness before human beings is not always holiness before God, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1129. — The virtues of the saints become more clearly known through tribulations, ibid., 9. — The more truly saints know the highest things, the more loftily they despise earthly things, ibid., 264. — The more saints know God, the more worthless they become in their own eyes, ibid., 596. — The rule of life must be taken from the saints, ibid., 905. — The death of the saints is the beginning of life, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 1177. — The virtue of the saints gives forth fragrance like spices in fire, id., CXLV, 78. — The life of the saints is more fruitful than miracles, ibid., 495. — The life of the saints is contempt for earthly things and eager pursuit of heavenly things, St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 47.

WISE PERSON, WISDOM. — Wisdom grows cold without grace, St. Ambrose, XVI, 361. — Every wise person is free, but every fool is a slave, ibid., 931. — It belongs to the wise person neither to be compelled nor restrained, ibid., 935. — Whatever human beings may think without God is foolish, id., XVII, 123. — A wise person can never be alone, St. Jerome, XXIII, 315. — It belongs to the wise to follow wisdom going before them and not to heed empty rumors, ibid., 446. — Wisdom is the tree of life which, unless it is planted in the midst of the virtues, the other trees will wither, ibid., 398. — A wise person is one who lives justly and prudently, Tertullian, I, 1256. — It belongs to the wise always to keep the end of life before their eyes, St. Prosper, LI, 675. — Wisdom is found only among tranquil minds, Cassiodorus, LXX, 368. — It belongs to the wise to love correction, and to the fool to hate it, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 735. — To be wise without God is to be foolish, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 245. — Even if you are wise, you lack wisdom if you do not belong to yourself, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 417. — Wisdom, when shut up, perishes; when scattered abroad, it increases, Peter the Chanter, CCX, 394.

[Col. 0778] BEING SATISFIED. — To be satisfied is a great art, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1388.

KNOWLEDGE. — Knowledge is imperfect, just as this life is, St. Ambrose, XVII, 155. — The best knowledge is to abandon vices and turn to God with one’s whole mind, ibid., 514. — Knowledge without works is weak and fleeting, St. Jerome, XXII, 604. — It is part of knowledge to know what you do not know, id., XXIV, 510. — The truth of knowledge must be sought from the fountain rather than from the streams, id., XXVII, 850. — The more we desire to know, the more we display our vanity and superfluous words, ibid., 435. — Useful knowledge is that which is the companion of charity and the teacher of humility, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1848. — Knowledge of the good is not true unless it is known for the purpose of being done, id., XLIV, 166. — The worst knowledge of evil is to know that evil exists; and the worst ignorance of good is to know that good does not exist, St. Prosper, LI, 359. — Through human knowledge we are blinded by ourselves, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 76. — He deserves to know who fears to know, ibid., 143. — The first degree of knowledge is to understand that we know ourselves least of all, Cassiodorus, LXX, 246. — Knowledge without piety is harmful, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 32. — The first pursuit of knowledge is to seek God, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 690. — Knowledge is seasoned with charity, lest it puff one up, Guibert, CLVI, 286. — Knowledge which love does not accompany is condemnable, Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 48. — Let justice in action attend knowledge of the truth, lest it become an occasion of ruin, ibid., 49.

DIVISIONS. — Cracks in walls are accustomed to precede the ruin of buildings, Rufinus, XXI, 541.

SCRIPTURE. — All sacred Scripture tends to this one end: that faith, hope, and charity may be built up in the mind, St. Augustine, XLII, 951.

SECURITY, SECURE. — Security produces negligence, and negligence contempt, St. Jerome, XXVII, 354, 1089. — No one proceeds securely among serpents and scorpions, id., XXII, 89. — Security, if God be present, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 391. — Security in death, fear in life, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 367. — The highest security is never to be secure, ibid., 914. — Excessive security is harmful to the soul, Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 183.

SOWING. — To sow in tears belongs to all Christians, St. Valerian, LII, 31.

OLD AGE. — The reward of good old age is an unstained life, St. Ambrose, XVI, 94. — Old age which has trained its youth in honorable disciplines reaps the sweetest fruits, St. Jerome, XXII, 256. — Let him serve in old age who did not serve in youth, Alan of Lille, CCX, 65.

SENSE. — Our sense is drawn toward the desire of that thing by whose pleasure it is captivated, St. Jerome, XXIII, 338. — A person following sensuality is like brute beasts, Guibert, CLVI, 643. — The pleasure of the senses does not make one happier, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 405. — Five senses, five loves, ibid., 250.

SEPARATING. — One is separated from God if one despairs of God, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLIX, 300.

TOMB. — A human being is the tomb of a human being, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 120.

SPEECH. — Good speech does not seek concealment; rather, it delights in its own praises and in the testimony of very many people, St. Jerome, XXII, 964. — Speech, reason, knowledge, and faith without works are empty and unstable, ibid., 614. — To range through the whole world in speech and tongue, while hiding in body, is incongruous, St. Jerome, XXII, 782. — Speech that often pleases the hearer displeases the speaker, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 1745. — Vain speech is the mark of a vain conscience, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 354. — The word of God is not to be preserved in memory, but in conduct, id., CLXXXIII, 129.

SERVING, SERVITUDE. — There is no dignity greater than serving Christ, St. Ambrose, XVI, 278. — He who serves from the heart is outwardly such as he is inwardly, id., XVII, 274. — Servitude to righteousness is true liberty, St. Augustine, XL, 247. — Whoever refuses to serve charity must necessarily serve iniquity, ibid., 163. — Service is free where not necessity but charity serves, id., XXXVII, 1275. — To be a servant of God is great dignity and blessedness, St. Prosper, LI, 514. — The servant of God stands; the servant of man lies prostrate, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 19. — Serving God is not a burden but an honor, St. Peter of Clairvaux, CLXXXIII, 364. — The service of God is sweeter than every sweetness, ibid., 1139. — To serve God is to reign, Alan of Lille, CCX, 435.

SEVERITY. — Severity is good if it is just, and if the judge is good, that is, just, Tertullian, II, 302. — The severity of a ruler is inwardly seasoned with charity and humility, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1306.

SILENCE, BEING SILENT. — Christ is silent before judgment, and yet he is not silent, St. Augustine, XLIII, 718. — One must be silent [Col. 0779] unless, by speaking, we can benefit others, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 716. — To be silent is often to be wise, ibid., 736. — One must learn not silence by speaking, but speech by being silent, ibid., 282. — Silence is not greatest when there is much eloquence of the heart, ibid., 240. — He who by silence restrains his tongue but not his mind sins all the more dangerously because he sins more securely, id., LXXVII, 153. — To know how to be silent is more difficult than to speak, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 300.

LIKENESS. — The likeness of God is the perfection and end of the human being, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 228.

SIMPLE PERSON. — A simple person thinks himself rich if he has enough for food, St. Ambrose, XVI, 295.

DISSIMULATION. — Dissimulation is the patronage of falsehood, St. Jerome, XXXIII, 301. — Unless the veil of dissimulation is taken away from you, Jesus will not turn to you, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 155.

SINGULARITY. — Singularity must be avoided by those living devoutly, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1045.

FELLOWSHIP. — It profits fellowship nothing for persons to be near one another in body if they differ in mind, St. Cyprian, IV, 143. — A fellowship is just when it serves God, St. Augustine, XXXII, 691. — Association with an innocent person teaches innocence; that with a perverse person leads toward perversity, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 647.

HOPING, HOPE. — By hoping we shall fear; by fearing we shall beware; by being watchful we shall be saved, Tertullian, I, 1318. — Hope of the resurrection is contempt for death, ibid., 585. — Perverse hope deceives, just as good and right hope sets free, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 535. — Each person’s hope lies in his own conscience, id., XXXIV, 71. — Hope cannot exist without love, nor love without hope, id., XL, 235. — Hope nurses us, nourishes us, strengthens us, etc., id., XXXVIII, 1188. — Those who have no hope in God soon have their defenses scattered, St. Jerome, XXV, 873. — To hope with certainty for what often proves uncertain is ridiculous, id., XXII, 230. — Hope in the Lord changes all things for the better, Cassiodorus, LXX, 142. — Hope of the future resurrection softens every evil, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1614. — To wish to establish hope upon falling things is to lay a foundation in flowing waters, ibid., 698. — The hope of those who perish becomes the recovery of the lost, ibid., 1090. — The hope of the world is dry, ibid., 1322. — Hope is the third wing of the human being, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 279. — There is no hope where there are no merits, Guibert, CLVI, 287. — Hope for mercy in such a way that you fear justice, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLIX, 191. — To hope without merits is not hope but presumption, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 598. — He hopes in vain who does not cease to sin, ibid., 816. — We hope not only in God, but for God himself, ibid., 853. — Human beings are endangered both by hoping and by despairing, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 11.

SPIRIT. — The animal spirit is the driver of the body, Tertullian, II, 740. — Those not led by the Spirit consequently are led by the flesh, St. Augustine, XXXV, 2139. — The Holy Spirit makes spiritual persons out of animal persons, id., XXXVIII, 1328. — The spirit of the flesh urges softness, the spirit of the world vanity, and the spirit of evil bitter things, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1131.

STARS. — The stars are saints shining with heavenly grace, St. Ambrose, XVI, 286.

FOLLY. — To be free from folly is the first wisdom; but no one can be free from folly unless he has understood it, St. Jerome, XXIV, 395. — Fools judge everyone according to their own judgment, ibid., 469. — There is no misery like folly, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 64. — Call yourself foolish, but say it inwardly, and you will be wise, id., XXXVIII, 436.

PRIDE, THE PROUD. — Nothing hinders perfection here as pride does, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 709. — Humility had made you good; pride makes you evil, ibid., 193. — Whomever the devil has made proud, he conquers, id., XXXV, 2031. — The proud person is raised up; God plunges him down, id., XXXVI, 1205. — The proud are compared to smoke, id., XXXVIII, 440. — Pride is a swelling, not greatness and not health, id., XXXIX, 1996. — The proud person is mute even if he chants psalms, Cassiodorus, LXX, 253. — To ascend to the summit of pride is ruinous, ibid., 449. — Human pride ends in rottenness, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 381. — Pride turns a human being into a beast, id., LXXVII, 6. — Pride brings ruin upon itself, not upon others, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 124. — Through pride, there is nothing more miserable than the person who exalts himself because of a good work, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLIX, 248. — Pride lies in hell; humility remains in heaven, ibid., 249. — The Lord passes by the proud and visits the humble, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1433. — Pride is the ruin of the whole spiritual edifice, Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 163, 164.

[Col. 0780] T

TABERNACLE. — Our tabernacle is the secret place of the heart, which requires the gold of serenity of heart, the silver of purity of speech, and the bronze of strength in action, Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 417.

KEEPING SILENT. — To keep sins silent is evil, St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 137.

WEARINESS. — Intense weariness and bitterness of heart exercise the virtues; they do not overthrow them, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 130.

TEMPERANCE. — Temperance is the royal road of our entire life, Alcuin, C, 77.

STORM. — For each person, his own desire is a storm, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 161.

TEMPLE. — A pure mind is a holy temple for God, St. Augustine, XLIV, 205. — The heart of the faithful person is God’s spacious temple, id., XXXVIII, 158. — We build the temple of God by living well, id., XLI, 546.

TEMPORAL THINGS, TIME. — Time reveals all things, Tertullian, I, 310. — Since we are the temple of God, let us renounce material anxieties, St. Ambrose, XVI, 240. — We are the times: let us live well, and the times are good, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 498. — A temporal thing is loved more before it is obtained, but becomes cheap when it has arrived, id., XXXIV, 35. — Temporal things, when desired, burn fiercely; when acquired, become cheap; when lost, vanish, id., XXXVIII, 861. — Contempt for God makes times evil for us, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 43. — With respect to time, one must repent concerning the past, rejoice concerning the present, and fear concerning the future, ibid., 46. — Time seems short to one arranging matters, long to one who loves, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 435. — Temporal prosperity is tribulation in the world, ibid., 946. — Nothing is more precious than time, and among human beings nothing is cheaper, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 304.

BEING TEMPTED, TEMPTATIONS. — God tempts in order to teach; the devil tempts in order to deceive, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 29. — Temptations are like fire to hay, but to the good they are like fire to gold, id., XXXVII, 1375. — He who conquers temptations does not conquer himself, but God who is in him, ibid., 1643. — To be delivered from the temptations of this life is a great benefit of God, St. Prosper, LI, 39. — An unclean temptation consumes a person’s flesh as a moth consumes a garment, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 389. — Temptations cleanse vices and increase merits, ibid., 516. — He who is broken by temptation does not seriously consider God’s providence, ibid., 822. — To suffer temptation in the heart is human; to be overcome by temptations in battle is demonic, LXXVII, 12. — In temptation one must keep watch under God’s protection, ibid., 328. — Amid temptations no one stands firm unless the grace of the Creator continually helps him, Guibert, CLVII, 190. — Temptation lays hold only of the will, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 119, 121, 126. — No temptation, even an inward one, can overcome the soul which God defends, ibid., 256.

EARTH, EARTHLY THINGS. — Earth leads onward to heaven, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 124. — Envy burns the earth, id., LII, 172. — If we despise earthly things, we are always joyful from God, Cassiodorus, LXX, 278. — I who do not care for earthly things rarely envy, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 180. — Our light falls to earth when we desire earthly things, ibid., 637. — Because he seeks goods in the land of the living, a human being must bear evils in a foreign land, id., LXXVII, 1175. — Earthly things are for use; eternal things are for desire, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 823. — To cling to the earth is unworthy of a human being, id., CLXXXIII, 1348. — Earthly things possessed burden us, loved defile us, and lost torment us, id., 107.

WITNESS. — No one can be a witness concerning himself, St. Cyprian, IV, 721.

TREASURE. — A good will is the treasure of the poor, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 371.

FEARING, FEAR. — The fear of man is the honor of God, Tertullian, I, 1241. — Fear leads to liberty, liberty to faith, faith to charity, charity obtains adoption, and adoption inheritance, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1084. — The fear of God enables us to despise all other fears, St. Jerome, XXII, 199. — He who fears God is neither uplifted by prosperity nor crushed by adversity, id., XXII, 445. — Let a person not fear what he has no power to avoid, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 547. — Not the north wind nor the seas must be feared, but God their creator, ibid., 1127. — Do you wish to be feared by one lower than you? Fear one greater than you, id., XXXVII, 1762. — The faith of one who fears Christ but does not love him is the faith of a demon, id., XL, 1190. — That fear is useful which hope raises up, not that which despair sinks, St. Prosper, LI, 526. — The weight of fear is unhappiness of heart, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 208. — Fear in a person without piety has no value before God, id., LXXVI, 1380. — By fearing God we avoid evils, and by serving him we do good, id., LXXIX, 277. — Fear is the fourth wing of the human being, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 279. — The fear of God is the gate to God and to the city of the heart, Guibert, CLVI, 89.

PATIENCE. — He who has lost patience has fallen from heaven, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1194. — He who does not tolerate others shows that he has not made progress, St. Prosper, LI, 560.

TRIBULATIONS. — The soul is purified by continual tribulations, St. Ambrose, XVII, 186. — A Christian suffers tribulation throughout the whole time of life, even when all goes well for him, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1089. — God sends tribulations so that faith may grow fervent and be exercised, id., XXXVII, 1118. — In tribulation, that which is brief in time is not great, id., XXXVIII, 402. — The soul suffers tribulation as it stands between God’s commands and the soul’s passions, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 45. — In tribulation it is good to pray, fast, chant psalms, and show mercy, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 291. — God cleanses by tribulations those whom he scourges, so that he may receive them once purified, Cassiodorus, LXX, 304. — Tribulations become sweeter through our tears, ibid., 339. — One sows in tribulation, in order that afterward the fruit of joy may be gathered, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 356. — Tribulation is a sign and pledge of heavenly glory, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 296. — Tribulations demand a spirit of piety, St. Rupert, CLXIX, 369. — Present tribulation is the medicine of the merciful one, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 964, 966. — Tribulation is the way of glory, id., CLXXXIII, 878. — In tribulation, hope of glory is like a harvest in seed, ibid., 876.

WHEAT. — The wind does not carry off wheat, Tertullian, XXXVI, 197.

SORROW. — The sorrow of one suffering injustice is better than the joy of one committing injustice, St. Augustine, XLIV, 1876. — Sorrow often follows heaviness of heart, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 35.

BASE PERSON. — A base person defames base persons, St. Cyprian, IV, 4.

U

SHADOW. — The shadow of death is the way of sin, St. Valerian, LII, 366. — The shadow of death is death of the flesh, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1078.

ONE. — All the faithful are one in Christ, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 477.

USEFUL, USEFULNESS. — Nothing useful is pleasant unless it benefits the common good, St. Ambrose, XVI, 114. — He who is useless to everyone cannot be useful to himself, St. Ambrose, XVI, 114.

V

VANITY. — A human being is subjected to vanity because he was unwilling to be subjected to truth, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1532, 1549. — Vanity clouds the mind; iniquity blinds it, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 349. — Whatever the love of this world produces is deceptive vanity, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 214.

WILLING. — Willing alone, without action, does not attain perfect blessedness, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 22. — To will and not to will belong to us; yet even that which belongs to us is not ours without God’s mercy, St. Jerome, XXII, 989. — To will to sin is evil; to sin is worse; to persevere in sin is worst; not to will to repent is deadly, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 342.

POISON. — Poison is death to a human being, life to a serpent, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 79.

BELLY. — A belly seething with wine quickly foams over into lusts, St. Jerome, XXII, 423.

WORD. — The word of God is our bread; let us sweat in hearing it, lest we die in fasting, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 206. — He eats well and digests badly who hears the word of God and does not do it, id., XXXVIII, 183. — Idle words wound the mind, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 387. — With words one gives grace to the countenance and adorns the mind, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 80.

TRUTH. — Truth blushes at nothing except concealment alone, Tertullian, II, 345. — Truth is always hated, Tertullian, I, 354. — Truth does not deceive, justice does not ensnare, virtue does not mislead, St. Ambrose, XVI, 162. — It is the nature of things that truth is bitter and vices are thought pleasant, St. Jerome, XXII, 186. — Truth can be troubled; it cannot be conquered, id., XXIII, 821. — Truth is found only with great labor, St. Augustine, XLII, 174. — Truth alone is possessed securely, ibid., 1261. — Truth can be concealed for a time; it cannot be conquered, id., XXXVI, 740. — The true day that knows no setting is eternal truth and true eternity, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXIII, 875. — The nearer anyone comes to truth, the more remote from it he considers himself, id., CLXXXII, 389. — Truth is disclosed by purity of heart, id., CLXXXIII, 17. — Many suppress truth by knowing it, but do not touch it by living it, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 657.

WAY. — Whoever is not on God’s way is on the way of sin, St. Hilary of Poitiers, X, 299. — We ought to follow the Lord’s ways and guard our own, St. Ambrose, XVI, 4. — Let our way be narrower, our virtue more abundant, our path more confined, etc., St. Ambrose, XVI, 914. — Our ways are made straight not by our own labor, but by God’s help and mercy, St. Jerome, XXV, 791. — On the way, do not remain behind, do not turn back, do not stray, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 926. — It is better to limp on the way than to walk vigorously off the way, id., XXXVIII, 778. — The way is narrow to one laboring, but becomes broad to one loving, id., XXXVII, 1531. — The happiness of the wicked is a passing way; when the way is ended, that happiness is finished, id., XXXVI, 360. — It is a beautiful way to walk from virtue to virtue until one comes to the highest virtue, St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 709. — Necessity and desire are the ways of human beings, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXIII, 855.

CHANGE. — Change alone is pleasing in created things, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXIII, 1109.

VICTORY. — No victory is certain in this life, St. Jerome, XXV, 90. — One eager for victory does not know how to fear, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 22.

SEEING. — Seeing and being seen belong to the same lust, Tertullian, II, 891.

WATCHFULNESS, KEEPING WATCH. — Watchfulness and self-guarding are necessary for everyone at every age, St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 179. — To keep watch more is to live more, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 24.

CONQUERING. — To conquer anger is better than to capture a city, Rufinus, XXI, 35. — You will conquer him who is accustomed to conquer if he who cannot be conquered dwells in you, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 2006. — For victory, the love of God endures all things and overcomes all things, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 112.

VIRGINITY. — Virginity in the flesh belongs to few; it ought to be in the heart of all, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1920.

VIRTUE. — Virtue is built up by hardness and destroyed by softness, Tertullian, I, 624. — The likeness of virtue is not likeness of nature, St. Hilary, X, 375. — Virtues make good days for one living rightly; vices make bad days, St. Jerome, XXII, 572. — Virtue is the art of attaining immortal happiness, St. Augustine, XLI, 128, 258, 789. — Virtue is the order of love, ibid., 467. — Every virtue flows from God, St. Prosper, LI, 854. — All virtues falter without mercy, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 53. — To avoid virtues as though they were vices is affliction, ibid., 132. — Virtue kills those who become proud because of it, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 223, 1033. — One virtue without another is either no virtue or very slight, ibid., 680. — The first virtue is to avoid sins; the second, to correct those committed, ibid., 199. — Unless virtue increases, it must decrease, id., LXXVII, 94. — Virtue and pleasure are the two wives of a human being, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 155. — There is no virtue without a good will, Guibert, CLVI, 69. — Virtues acquired by labor are lost through idleness, St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 178. — Virtue and truth wish to be together, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 181, 182. — The reward of virtue is a good reputation, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXIII, 907. — Virtue is acquired in peace, tested in distress, and approved in victory, ibid., 131. — Virtue wishes to be taught with humility, sought with labor, and possessed with love, id., CLXXXII, 208.

LIFE, LIVING. — An evil life corrupts the whole person, St. Ambrose, XVII, 128. — It is fitting for this life that we weep and groan, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 165. — From the moment a human being begins to live, he begins to die, id., XLI, 383. — To live well is to love with one’s whole heart, whole mind, and whole soul, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 1330. — He certainly knows how to live who rightly knows how to pray, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1849. — Eternal life is God; present life is vapor, St. Valerian, LII, 302. — The soul lives by faith; the body by the soul, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 55.

VICES.—Vices are no more easily endured than demons, St Ambrose, XVII, 550.—Vices deceive only under the shadow and appearance of virtues, St Jerome, XXII, 684.—External vices are easily cast off, but pleasure is not so, ibid., XXII, 287.—Vices end and perish in themselves; virtues abound in fruits, ibid., XXVI, 505. Do not love a vice because of a person, nor hate a person because of a vice, St Augustine, XXXVIII, 323.—Vices are diseases of the soul, Cassian, L, 1008.—Vices of the flesh, while they are beginning, are easily crushed in Christ, but not once they have taken root, Cassiodorus, LXX, 466.—Vices make an alliance against us, St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, [Col. 0783] 99.—Vices are born from vices, and whoever neglects small matters gradually falls, ibid., 348, 349.—Those who do not abstain from vices surrender themselves to the devil, id., LXXVII, 49.—Vices must first be uprooted before virtues are planted, ibid., 93, 94.

WILL.—He who is unclean in will is not cleansed by action, St Augustine, XXXVII, 1528.—The works of the human will are like spiders’ webs, St Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 168.—Nothing is happier than a good will, Guibert, CLVI, 3.—The will is not right because it wills rightly; rather, it wills rightly because it is right, St Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 128.—The will alone is capable of misery or blessedness, St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 605.—When the will is joined to truth, it is love; when it is nourished by [Col. 0784] grace, it is affectionate love; when it enjoys, it is charity, St Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 226.

PLEASURE.—There is no pleasure greater than disgust with pleasure itself, Tertullian, I, 659.—The more pleasures and riches increase, the more wisdom is lacking among men, St Jerome, XXIV, 297.—At the price of pleasure, each person by sinning sells his soul to the devil, St Augustine, XXXV, 2071.—In pleasure lies every descent, St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 224.—Few escape the pit and destruction of pleasures, ibid., 669.

WOUNDS.—The wounds of Christ: signs of victory, St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1016.—Contemplation of Christ’s wounds heals the wounds of the soul, ibid., 1480.

[Col. 0783]

CLXVI. INDEX OF SPECIAL VIRTUES OF THE PAGANS WHICH THE FATHERS HAVE EXALTED WITH PRAISE, ARRANGED ALPHABETICALLY BY SUBJECT.

[Col. 0783]

FLATTERER.—Portrayed from Terence, John of Salisbury, CXCIX.

AFFECTIONS.—The sound opinion of the Peripatetics concerning the affections, Lactantius, VI, 688.—The sound opinion of the Academics concerning these same affections of the soul, St Jerome, XXII, 1148.—Cicero’s opinion concerning the affections, ibid., XXIII, 542.—Horace concerning the affections or passions, ibid., XXII, 1148.—Plato’s sound opinion concerning the affections, in agreement with the Gospels, ibid., XXVI, 91.—The sound opinion of the Peripatetics concerning the affections, ibid., XXIII, 542.

FRIENDSHIP.—Pythagoras’s sound opinion concerning friendship, St Jerome, XXIII, 485, 486.—Cicero on friendship, St Augustine, XXXIII, 1071, 1072.—Cicero concerning friendship, Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 666.—Seneca concerning friendship, ibid., 183.—What Cicero says concerning friendship, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 570.

ANGEL.—The Epicureans, Platonists, Pythagoreans, Peripatetics, Stoics, and Academics acknowledge angels, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 414.—Plato on angels, John Scotus, CXXII, 762.

SOUL.—The unity of the soul defended by Heraclitus and Aenesidemus, Tertullian, II, 669.—Plato, Strato, Epicurus, Democritus, Empedocles, Socrates, Aristotle, Herophilus, Erasistratus, Diocles, Hippocrates, Soranus stand for a principal faculty of the soul, ibid., 670 ff.—The immortality of the soul according to Plato, Arnobius, V, 865, 893.—Xenocrates’s sound opinion on the incorporeality of the soul, Lactantius, VII, 66.—St Augustine sets forth Plato’s teaching concerning the illumination and blessedness of the soul, and says that this teaching accords with the Gospel, St Augustine, XLI, 281.—Pythagoras acknowledges the immortality of the soul, ibid., XXXII, 954; XXXIII, 721.

FREE WILL.—Plato is cited concerning free will, Arnobius, V, 910.—Peter Abelard cites Aristotle to prove free will, Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 1213.

ATHEISM.—The sound opinion of the Stoics concerning atheism, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 975.

COURT.—The court is to be fled, according to Isocrates, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 400.—“Let him leave the court,” says Lucan, “who wishes to be devout,” John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 586.

AVARICE.—Juvenal concerning avarice, Peter Abelard, CLXXXVIII, 883.—Ovid on avarice, Helinand of Froidmont, CCXII, 689.

GOOD AND EVIL.—The Stoics agree with the Gospels concerning the definition of good and evil, St Jerome, XXIV, 147.—Plato places the end of the good in divine wisdom, St Augustine, XXXIII, 441.

SUPREME GOOD.—Euclides’ sound opinion concerning the supreme good, Lactantius, XI, 380.

CHARITY.—Charity toward the poor: Seneca, Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 593.

CHRISTIANITY.—Plato agrees with Christians in many matters, St Augustine, XXXIII, 442.

[Col. 0784]

CLEMENCY.—According to Ovid, a ruler ought to be merciful, Helinand of Froidmont, monk, CCXII, 737.

KNOWLEDGE OF GOD.—The incapacity in which man finds himself, by the help of natural light alone, to attain to the knowledge of God, Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 1151, 1152.

CONTEMPT FOR RICHES.—Antisthenes despises riches, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 582.—Plato despises riches and pleasures, ibid., 739.

CONFESSION OF FAULT.—Cicero concerning confession of fault, Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 443.

CUSTOM.—The dominion of custom according to Horace, John of Salisbury … CXCIX, 489.

CONTINENCE.—Seneca, a follower of poverty and continence, Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 297.

CORRECTION.—How correction should be administered, according to Plutarch, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 531.

CREATION.—The sound opinion of the Stoics concerning the creation of all things, Lactantius, VII, 115.—Plato’s sound opinion concerning the creation of the world, consonant with Genesis, St Augustine, XLI, 236.—Plato concerning the creation of the world, Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 766.—Anaxagoras’s sound opinion concerning creation, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 643.—Plato’s sound opinion concerning creation, ibid., 646.

WORSHIP OF GOD.—Hermes Trismegistus’s sound opinion concerning the worship to be rendered to God, Lactantius, VI, 728, 729.

ECLIPSES OF THE SUN AND MOON.—Thales of Miletus discovered and predicted eclipses of the sun and moon, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 643.

DESPAIR.—The sound opinion of the Stoics concerning despair, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 975.

GOD.—The agreement of Plato and Christians concerning God, Arnobius, V, 830.—Antisthenes admitted one God, the maker of things, Lactantius, VI, 134.—Aristotle admitted one God, ibid., 135.—Cicero’s sound opinion concerning God, ibid., 135, 136.—Epicurus’s sound opinion concerning God is noted, ibid., 380.—Hermes Trismegistus’s sound opinion concerning God, ibid., 139.—Orpheus’s sound opinion concerning God, ibid., 131.—Ovid’s sound opinion concerning God the Creator, ibid., 133.—Plato’s sound opinion concerning God the Creator, ibid., 135.—The same author’s sound opinion concerning the majesty of God, ibid., 153, 154.—The poets’ sound opinion concerning God, ibid., 131, 132.—Pythagoras acknowledged one God, ibid., VII, 113.—The same confesses God to be maker and creator, ibid., VI, 302.—Seneca’s sound opinion concerning God, ibid., 137.—Zeno acknowledged the unity of God, ibid., VII, 114.—Cicero mocks the pagan gods, St Augustine, XLI, 136, 137.—Truths which philosophers discovered concerning God, St Augustine, XXXVIII, 776.—Plato concerning the pagan gods, ibid., XLI, 229.—Varro holds that one God ought to be worshipped, ibid., 138.—The Platonists, Epicureans, Pythagoreans, Peripatetics, Stoics, and Academics admit God the Creator, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 414.—The Platonists say that God is guardian, judge, and arbiter, ibid., 415.—The Platonists affirm that God is incorporeal, ibid.—The Platonists held sound views concerning the [Col. 0785] unity of God, Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 1005.—Plato is cited on God the founder, ibid., 1175.—Plato admits God as creator and governor, ibid., 1317.—Virgil on the immensity of God, ibid., 1127.—Antisthenes taught omniscience in God, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 990.

PAGAN GODS, MOCKED.—Mocked by Seneca, Tertullian, I, 343.—Homer and other poets likewise.

RICHES.—Crates despises riches, St Jerome, XXII, 580.—Philosophers, and especially Diogenes, despised riches, St Jerome, XXIII, 304, 305; XXII, 964.—Seneca despises riches, Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 590.—Riches despised by Diogenes, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 583.

DEMONS.—On their existence: Plato, philosophers, poets, Socrates, Tertullian, I, 404.—Hermes Trismegistus concerning freedom from the assaults of demons, Lactantius, VI, 335.

PAINS AND DISTRESSES.—Clitomachus concerning pains and distresses, St Jerome, XXII, 592.—The philosophers’ moderation in pains, ibid.—Sorrow is to be cast off according to Pythagoras, ibid., XXIII, 485, 486.

ELOQUENCE.—A passage of Cicero on bad orators, St Jerome, XXIII, 535.

ERRORS OF THE MULTITUDE.—The errors of the multitude are to be avoided according to Pythagoras, St Jerome, XXIII, 485, 486.

EXAMPLES.—Quintilian concerning the authority of examples, Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 798.—The efficacy of examples, from Juvenal, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 581.—The force of examples, from Claudian, Helinand of Froidmont, monk, CCXII, 517.—Horace on the same subject, ibid.—Juvenal on the same subject, ibid., 741.

HAPPINESS.—The Stoics place happiness in virtue, Lactantius, VI, 380.—The same, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 414.

SON OF GOD.—Philosophers bore witness to the Father and the Son, St Augustine, XXXIV, 604, 1390.—Hermes Trismegistus concerning the Son of God, Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 1060.—Plato on the Son of God, ibid., 1013.

FRUGALITY AND MODESTY.—The frugality and modesty of Pythagoras, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 642, 643.—Praise of frugality by Quintilian, ibid., 764.

GRACE.—Virgil concerning the working of grace in souls, Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 1025.

EIGHTEENTH SERIES.

[Col. 0787]

[PREFACE.]

Having set forth in the preceding Series the various virtues and duties arising from the observance of God’s commandments, we now take up the various sins and vices opposed to them. Accordingly, in this eighteenth Series we present indexes concerning sins in general, original sin, and the capital sins; vices arranged alphabetically; homicide, duelling, and suicide; simony and usury among clerics; profane and unlawful pleasures, games, dances, and spectacles; errors and vices of pagans assailed by the Holy Fathers; and so forth.

[Col. 0787]

CLXVII. INDEX CONCERNING SINS, IN WHICH THE NATURE, GRAVITY, EFFECTS, AND PUNISHMENTS OF SIN; ORIGINAL SIN AND ITS CONSEQUENCES; AND THE CAPITAL SINS ARE TREATED LOGICALLY.

NOTICE.

If our purpose had been to include in this compendium everything which the title of this Index appears at first sight to embrace, the material before us would certainly have been much more extensive than it is here. But since several sins have already been discussed elsewhere, especially in the Decalogue, we judged it superfluous to speak again of the same matters. Therefore, after considering sins in general, we have spoken of the seven capital sins or vices.—But first of all, in order better to provide for clarity, we divided the present material into various parts. Thus, in the first section we have said: I. On the nature, species, and gravity of sins.—II. On their subject and cause.—III. On their effects and the punishment by which they are visited.—IV. On the necessity of avoiding sin and the means of rising from it. In the second section, we deal with original sin, and especially with its existence and consequences. As for the third section—that is, sins in particular—we discuss them according to the theological order of the Holy Fathers: I. The exposition is on pride.—II. On avarice.—III. On lust.—IV. On envy.—V. On gluttony.—VI. On anger.—VII. On acedia, or sadness.

It should further be noted that only a few matters concerning remedies for sins have here been touched upon; fuller explanations will be found in the analytical Index of Virtues.

With these points thus set forth and understood, it remains to say that, in reporting the various opinions of various Fathers, we have arranged everything in such a manner as gives us reason to hope that sacred orators, theologians, and children being catechized will, by the Lord’s gift, derive abundant benefit from this Index.

[INDEX CONCERNING SINS.]

[Col. 0787]

SECTION ONE. ON SINS IN GENERAL.

I.—On the definition and gravity of sins.

Theologians give various definitions of sin, chiefly following the thought of St Augustine.

For sin is defined as turning away from God and turning toward the creature. It is also defined—nearly amounting to the same thing—as the disordered love of oneself and of created things.

For St Augustine says, *Against Faustus*, book XXII, chapter 27: “Sin, therefore, is any deed, word, or desire contrary to the eternal law. But the eternal law is either divine reason or the will of God, commanding the preservation and forbidding the disturbance of the natural order. If nothing unlawful gave pleasure, no one would sin. Therefore, one sins who yields rather than restrains pleasure in what is unlawful. Now what is unlawful is that which the law forbids by which the natural order is preserved.”

I pass over the other definitions of sin. Among them, this single definition is especially pleasing: sin is, in one word, “transgression of the law of God.” It is called “transgression,” a general term encompassing every kind of violation; for we transgress the law when we think, say, do, or omit anything contrary to the law’s command. It is called “of the law of God,” another general expression encompassing whatever God commands, whether directly or through others. Thus “the law of God” means the eternal, natural, and positive law.

“The eternal law”: this law is nothing other than uncreated divine reason, or the will of God, commanding the preservation and forbidding the disturbance of the natural order. By this law we are bound to turn our love away from temporal things and, once purified, to direct it toward eternal things. This is explained as follows:

That law which is called the highest reason, according to Augustine, *On Free Choice of the Will*, book I, chapter 6, no. 15, which must be obeyed, and through which the wicked deserve a miserable life and the good a blessed life; through which, finally, that law called temporal is rightly enacted and rightly changed—this law appears to everyone to be immutable and eternal. For can it ever be unjust that the wicked should be miserable and the good blessed, or that a self-controlled and serious people should create magistrates for itself, while a disorderly and depraved people should lack that liberty? At the same time, in this mortal life, nothing appears just and lawful that men have not derived for themselves from this eternal law … Therefore, to explain briefly in words, as far as I can, the notion of the eternal law impressed upon us: it is the law by which it is just that all things should be in the most perfect order.

Since, therefore, this is the one law from which all those temporal laws for governing human beings vary, it itself can in no way vary; nor can any force, accident, or ruin of things ever make it not just that all things should be in the most perfect order. For what ought temporal law to command except that these things which may be called ours for a time, when people cling to them through desire, should be possessed by the right through which peace and human society may be preserved, insofar as it can be preserved in such matters? Such things are, first, this body and its so-called goods: sound health, keenness of the senses, strength, beauty, and whatever other things there are—some necessary for useful arts and therefore more highly valued, others less valuable. Next comes liberty: not indeed any true liberty, except that of the blessed and of those adhering to the eternal law; but I now mean that liberty by which those who have no human masters think themselves free, and which those who wish to be manumitted from masters desire. Next are parents, brothers, wife, children, relatives, connections by marriage, household members, and all who are joined to us by some bond of obligation. Finally, there is the state itself, commonly regarded as standing in the place of a parent; there are also honors and praises, and what is called popular glory. Last of all is money, a single name comprehending everything of which we are justly owners, or over the sale or gift of which we appear to have power. It would be difficult and lengthy to explain how that law distributes all these things to each person, and it is plainly unnecessary for the purpose we have proposed. It is enough to see that this law’s power in exacting punishment extends no further than to deprive and take away from the person it punishes these things, or some of them. It therefore restrains through fear and bends and turns back to its own purpose the souls of the wretched, to whose governance it is suited. For while they fear losing these things, they observe in using them a certain moderation appropriate to the bond of civic society, such as can be established among people of this sort. Yet the law does not punish sin when these things are loved, but when they are wickedly taken from others.

Natural law is a certain reason inborn in the hearts of all human beings, by which they are moved toward good and called away from evil. The Apostle speaks of this law in these words: “When the Gentiles, who do not have the law [of Moses], do by nature—that is, without written law—the things of the law, such persons, though not having the law, are a law to themselves; because they show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness to them, and their thoughts among themselves accusing or even defending one another.” By this law we know that we ought not do to another what we do not wish done to ourselves. This law can be obscured in human hearts, but it cannot be utterly erased, in accordance with Augustine’s saying: “Your law is written in the hearts of human beings, and not even iniquity itself will erase it.”

This is explained as follows: namely, we understand either the natural law (St Augustine, *Letter to Hilary*, no. 15), which appears at those ages in persons already able to use reason, or the written law, which was given through Moses. For it too could neither give life nor free from the law of sin and death derived from Adam, but instead added increase to transgression. “For where there is no law,” says the same Apostle, “there is no transgression.” Therefore, because there is also a law in the reason of a person who already exercises freedom of choice, naturally written in the heart, by which one is admonished not to do to another what one does not wish to suffer oneself, all are transgressors according to this law, even those who have not received the law given through Moses.

Augustine, *On Psalm* LVII, no. 1: Since truth, by the hand of our Maker, has written in our very hearts: “What you do not wish done to you, do not do to another.” Even before the law was given, no one was allowed to be ignorant of this, so that there might be grounds on which even those to whom the law had not been given might be judged. But lest people complain that anything had been lacking to them, what they did not read in their hearts was written on tablets. For it was not that they did not possess it in writing, but that they were unwilling to read it. What they were compelled to see in conscience was placed before their eyes; and, as if by a voice of God applied from without, a human being was driven inward to his own interior … But because people, desiring what lies outside, have become exiles even from themselves, the written law was also given—not because it had not been written in their hearts, but because you were a fugitive from your own heart: you were apprehended by him who is everywhere, and recalled within yourself to yourself. Therefore the written law cries out to those who have abandoned the law written in their hearts: “Return to the heart, you transgressors.”

For who taught you not to wish another person to approach your wife? Who taught you not to wish theft to be committed against you? Who taught you not to wish to suffer injury, and whatever else may be said generally or particularly? For there are many matters about which, when asked individually, people answer clearly that they do not wish to suffer them. Come then: if you do not wish to suffer these things, are you the only human being? Do you not live in the fellowship of humankind? Whoever was made with you is your companion; and all were made in the image of God, unless by earthly desires they wear away what he formed. Therefore, what you do not wish done to you, do not do to another. For you judge that to be evil which you do not wish to suffer; and the inward law, written in your own heart, compels you to know this. You were doing it, and the cry was raised amid your very actions. How are you compelled to return to your heart when you suffer this at the hands of others? Is theft good? No. I ask: is adultery good? All cry out, “No.” Is homicide good? All cry out that they detest it. Is coveting your neighbor’s property good? No: that is everyone’s answer. Or if you do not yet confess it, someone comes who covets your property. Let that please you, and answer as you wish. Therefore, when questioned about these things, all cry out that they are not good. Thus all sinners on earth are not without reason judged transgressors. For no one inflicts injury on another without being unwilling that it be inflicted upon himself; and in this he transgresses the law of nature, which he is not permitted to ignore, since he does not wish to suffer what he does. [lacuna] Positive law is that which is handed down by a legislator either orally or in writing. This is either divine or human. Divine law is established by God; human law by human beings. [lacuna]

Divine law is divided into old and new. The old law was delivered in writing to the Jews through Moses; the new law was promulgated through Christ and written by the Holy Spirit “not on tablets of stone, but on tablets of fleshly hearts.”

Human law is either ecclesiastical or civil. Ecclesiastical law is that enacted by the Church; civil law is that promulgated by temporal rulers.

By divine law it is commanded that we obey the Church, indeed also temporal rulers who command what is just, and that not only because of wrath but also because of conscience; for, according to the Apostle, whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance. Therefore transgression of human law is rightly included under the general notion of transgression of God’s law.

There are two kinds of sins: original and actual.

Original sin is that which, transmitted from Adam to his descendants, is contracted by each human being through birth itself. We shall shortly discuss it in particular.

Actual sin is that which is freely committed by one’s own act and will by persons possessing the use of reason. There are many kinds of these. For they are: 1. either mortal or venial; 2. either of omission or commission, and these are committed either in heart, mouth, or deed; 3. either spiritual or carnal; 4. either directly injurious to God, to one’s neighbor, or to the sinner himself; 5. either of weakness, ignorance, or malice; 6. either one’s own, or both one’s own and another’s. Finally, there is the customary division by which all actual sins are referred back to the seven heads called the capital sins. We shall treat separately each of those seven sins, from knowledge of which the various kinds of sins now indicated will be understood, after the exposition of matters pertaining to original sin, concerning which we shall speak shortly after certain further matters relevant to the question of sin in general.

CXII, 1394.—In thought and speech, ibid.—Its various kinds, ibid., 1395.—Sin is twofold, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 81.—Original and actual sin, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 308.—Daily and lighter sins, ibid., 273.—The gravity of sin because God’s presence is offended, ibid., 482.—There are three ways of sinning: thought, word, and deed, St Bruno, CXLII, 49.—Hidden and another’s sin differ, ibid., 100.—Sin is transgression of the law, CXLIV, 950.—How many kinds it has, ibid., 519.—The difference between sin and iniquity, St Gregory the Great, LXXV, 978.—Sin is called a sour grape, ibid., 973.—It is called blood, ibid., 1027.—Sins are compared to nets, ibid., 1046.—Likewise to a fire of sulphur, ibid., 1051.—Sin is signified by juniper, id., LXXVI, 149.—The difference between sin and crime, ibid., 201.—Sin is called a pit into which the sinner is plunged, ibid., 387.—Sin is perpetrated either through ignorance, weakness, or deliberate purpose, ibid., 339.—To sin precipitately is one thing; Sin is called the devil, Lanfranc, CL, 128.—What is meant by hidden and open sins, ibid., 634.—Sin is called a thorn, St Bruno, CLII, 760.—Iniquity, ibid., 861.—It is committed in two ways, ibid., 1068.—It is called a dead work, id., CLIII, 538.—Sins are called works of darkness for three reasons, Radulphus Ardens, CLV, 1670.—Four ways of sinning, Guibert, CLVI, 467.—How harmful the habit of sinning is, ibid., 30.—To sin from weakness or ignorance is one thing; from proud deliberation another, ibid., 167.—Sin is transgression of the law, St Anselm, CLVIII, [Col. 0793] 635.—To sin is nothing other than not to render God what is due to him, ibid., 375.—To sin is an evil and bitter thing, ibid., 870.—Every sin is injustice, ibid., 514.—Sin can be called a certain corruption of virtue, ibid., 463.—Each person’s sin is in nature and in the person, ibid., 431.—The sin which each person draws with nature in his very origin is called original; it may also be called natural, ibid.—The actions performed by an unjust will are called sins, because sin is in the will by which they are done, ibid., 438.—Every sin dishonours God, 723.—No sin ought to be regarded as small, ibid.—We sin wickedly whenever we knowingly do anything, however small, contrary to God’s will, ibid., 392.

Sin is drawn in through the eyes and heart, Rupert, CLXVIII, 32.—Sin is committed because we do not keep watch over ourselves, id., CLXIX, 75.—Inveterate sins are punished more severely, ibid., 148.—Sin with deceit is worse, ibid., 155.—It is threefold: through ignorance, through pride, and through weakness, ibid., 459.—Sin of heart and deed is perpetrated in four ways, ibid., 978.—Sin is understood to be irremissible, or unto death, unless one does penance, ibid., 816.—To rejoice in most evil things is a most grave sin, ibid., 1030.—What the stages of sin’s growth are, ibid., 1235.—Blasphemy is defending sin, ibid., 1119.—Sin is from nothing, id., CLXX, 456.—The first sin, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXV, 41.—Sin at the door, ibid., 44.—What sin against the Holy Spirit is, and whether it is irremissible, ibid., 447.—How sinning against God is graver than sinning against one’s neighbour, ibid., 524.—What actual sin is, id., CLXXVI, 110.—In general, ibid., 111.—What its nature is, ibid., 112.—What is properly called sin, Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 636 ff.—On spiritual and carnal sins, ibid., 648.—Sin is only against conscience, ibid., 653.
