## II.—On the subject and cause of sin

St Augustine teaches most clearly in *Against Lying*, book 1, chapter 7, that all acts are to be judged good or bad according to their intention and cause, except certain acts which are so evil that they can never be good, even if they seem to have a good cause. “It matters greatly,” he says, “for what cause, to what end, and with what intention anything is done. But things which are acknowledged to be sins must not be done under the pretext of any good cause, any supposedly good end, or any seemingly good intention. Human actions, indeed, if they have good or bad causes, are now good and now bad—those, that is, which are not sins in themselves. Thus, providing food for the poor is good if it is done from mercy with right faith; and marital intercourse, when it is for the sake of procreation, if it is done with the end that those born may be regenerated. But these same things [Col. 0794] are evil if they have bad causes: for example, if a poor person is fed for the sake of boasting; or if intercourse with one’s wife is for the sake of lust; or if children are begotten so that they may be reared not for God but for the devil. But when the works themselves are sins in themselves, such as thefts, fornications, and blasphemies, who would say that they should be done for good causes, or that sins are not evil in themselves—or, what is more absurd, that sins are just? Who would say: ‘Let us steal from the rich, so that we may have something to give to the poor’; or, ‘Let us give false testimony, not so that innocent persons may thereby be harmed, but rather saved’? For here there are two good things: that the innocent person should not be punished, and that the needy person should be fed. Or who would say that adultery must be committed so that, by means of the woman with whom it is committed, a man may be delivered from death? Why, indeed, do we not suppress true wills and substitute false ones, so that inheritances may not go to those who do no good, but rather to those who help the needy? Why should those evils not be done for the sake of these goods, if, because of these goods, those acts are not evil? Why should not a good man seize riches from impure prostitutes, whom fornicators enrich, in order to distribute them to the needy, if there is no evil when something is done for a good purpose? Who could say this except someone trying to overthrow human affairs, morals, and laws? For if we once agree that in evil acts the question to be asked is not what is done but why it is done, so that whatever is done for good causes is not itself judged evil, then what we do may rightly be said capable not merely of being done without punishment, but even gloriously: in it punishment is not feared, but reward expected. Yet justice rightly punishes the man who says that he took surplus goods from a rich man in order to provide for a poor one; and the forger who corrupts another’s will so that the heir might be the person who would give abundant alms rather than one who would give none; and the man who admits that he committed adultery in order to rescue from death the person through the woman with whom he committed it.”

From this one discerns which act is sin: namely, one having an evil cause. Yet not that alone, since there are some acts which, even if they have a good cause, are nevertheless sins, as we have shown. It consequently seems that an evil will or action is not always judged from its end, as in cases which are sins in themselves. For when anyone performs such acts for some good cause, he seems to have a good end; nor is the will evil because of its end, nor does the action become evil from the will, but the will becomes perverse from the action. Among such cases some place the act of the Jews who, in crucifying Christ, thought that they were rendering service to God, because they say that they could have had a good end—namely, service to God—yet they nevertheless maintain that their will and action were perverse [lacuna].

Therefore all human works are judged good or evil according to intention and cause, except those which are evil in themselves; that is, those which cannot be performed without transgression. Thus, simply and truly good are those acts which have a good cause and intention—that is, which are accompanied by a good will and tend toward a good end. Those which have a perverse cause and intention, however, should simply be called evil. Hence St Ambrose says: “Your disposition gives your work its name.” And St Augustine, on Psalm 31: “Let no one count his good works before faith. For they seem to me like great strength and a very rapid course taken off the road; for where faith itself was absent, good work was absent. For intention makes a work good; faith directs intention. Do not pay much attention to what a person does, but to what he attends to when doing it, toward what goal he directs the oars of his good steering” [lacuna].

But you will say: from these statements it seems that where there is no faith, there is neither good intention nor good work. On this question there are various opinions [lacuna]. St Augustine says: “The life of all unbelievers is sin, and nothing is good without the highest good; where knowledge of eternal truth is lacking, virtue is false, even amid the finest morals.” And James says in his Epistle: “Whoever offends in one point”—namely, charity—“has become guilty of all.” Therefore whoever does not possess faith and charity, every action of his is sin, because it is not referred to charity; for whatever is not referred to charity is not done as it ought to be done, and is therefore evil. Thus a person lacking charity does not keep the commandments, because without charity none of the commandments is kept. Hence St Augustine says: “The Apostle calls keeping the law not getting drunk, not killing, not committing adultery, and other such things pertaining to good morals; these cannot be fulfilled without charity, faith, and hope. Therefore one who does not have faith and charity fulfils no commandment and does no good work” [lacuna], CXCII, 747–749. These matters are made clear by the following references.

Every sin is to be ascribed to impatience, Tertullian, I, 1258.—How sin came to humankind, Lactantius, VII, 123, 134.—The rulers of the air are authors of sin for us, St Hilary, IX, 460.—Demons supply incentives to sin and accuse us concerning what we have done through them, ibid., 608.—The practice of sin derives from the desire of the will and the pleasure of vices, ibid., 475.—Whoever [Col. 0795] has committed graver sins easily falls into the rest, St Ambrose, XIV, 353.—You yourself are the cause of your wickedness and the instigator of your crimes, ibid., 140.—Even a small spark of sin, if stirred by some fuel of vice, kindles a serious conflagration, ibid., 934.—The author of sin is not the flesh but the disposition, ibid., 604.—The law is absent from those who sin; if it were present, they would not transgress, ibid., 322.—While we are in the desire of sinning, the eyes of the mind are darkened by a sort of smoke of iniquity, lest they see the ugliness of the things they desire, ibid., 461.

God is not the cause of sins, St Augustine, XXXII, 830, 1269; XLIV, 731.—Although sinners are accustomed to cast their sins back upon him, id., XXXIV, 209.—A human being has sin only from himself, not from God, id., XXXVII, 1318, 1848.—Sins arise not from God but from the will of sinners, id., XXXII, 1271; XLII, 560.—Unless the will is the cause of sinning, nothing remains of justice in laws, institutions, and praises, id., XXXIII, 1061.—The cause of sinning is from the soul, not the flesh, id., XLI, 405.—For whoever sins, sins willingly, id., XXXII, 1294.—Sin is altogether voluntary, id., XXXIV, 133.—Nor would sin be sin if it were not voluntary, id., XXXII, 603.—The first and sole cause of sin is the will, id., XXXIII, 773.—Sin arises only from the will, id., XLII, 103; XLV, 1312.—Sin has its origin in the will, ibid., 1477.—Although sin can exist without a will to sin, it cannot exist without a will to perform the act, id., XXXII, 609.—The Manicheans attribute the origin of sins not to free choice but to the necessity of a contrary nature, id., XLII, 566.—There is a certain necessity of sinning, id., XXXII, 753, 759; XLIV, 286, 295.—Sin arises only from free choice, id., XLII, 537, 538.—What cannot in any way be avoided is not sin, id., XXXII, 1295.—All who sin with delight and love of sin sin especially through free choice, id., XLV, 1110.—Actual sin has a twofold origin, id., XXXII, 1285.—A twofold cause, id., XLIV, 554.—The twofold cause of sin: ignorance and concupiscence, ibid., 565.—Ignorance and weakness, id., XL, 271; XLIV, 152, 167.—The cause of sins is either ignorance, frailty, or contempt, id., XXXIV, 729.—Sins from weakness arise from the transmitted condition of Adam’s first sin and from evil habit, id., XLII, 541.—We all contract daily sins from the weakness of the flesh, id., XXXIX, 1541.—Two things cause all sins in a human being: desire and fear, id., XXXVI, 413.—Sin is not committed without a cause, id., XXXII, 679.—It is committed only for advantage or pleasure, id., XL, 513.—The Jovinian heresy: that a person after baptism cannot sin, id., XLV, 1114, 1116.—The Pelagians taught that the whole Church is without sin, id., XXXVIII, 980.—They are refuted, ibid.—Pelagius’s teaching that a person can, if he wishes, be without sin, id., XLIV, 350.—And the doctrine of Celestius, ibid., 234.—No one in this life is without sin, id., XXXIII, 674; XXXV, 1697, 1780, 1790; XXXVIII, 132, 893, 979; XL, 228, 720.—However righteous he may be, id., XLI, 657, 748, 788; XLII, 632; XLV, 1115, 1235.—Except for the one Mediator, no one in this life is without any sin, id., XLIV, 155, 245, 631, 726, 753.—He alone came without sin who found us sinners, id., XXXVI, 233.—No one here can live without sin, id., XXXVIII, 401.—Not sinning is one thing; not having sin is another, id., XXXV, 2140.—No one lives so justly in this flesh as to have no sin, id., XLIV, 316.—Many are without crime; no one is without sin, id., XLI, 415.—Why no one is without sin in this life, id., XLIV, 167.—Scriptural testimonies and examples proving that a human being is not without sin, ibid., 268.—Although people are sometimes found in Scripture to have been called blameless, none is found called without sin except Christ, ibid., 253.—God is not the author of sin, id., XLV, 1833, 1841, 1848.—Sin does not occur without the devil’s operation, id., XL, 1177.—Even the Manichean was compelled to confess that sin belongs to one’s own will, id., XLII, 1141.—All sins have two origins: error and pride, id., XXXIX, 2003.

Sins arise from the will of sinners, Eugyppius, LXII, 1067.—Let no one suppose or boast that he is without sin, ibid., 865.—Sin is not from God’s predestination, St Fulgentius, LXV, 174.—Every sin takes its beginning from the heart, ibid., 233.—As sin is not in God, so it is not from God, ibid., 156.—Death and sin are not God’s work, ibid.—Excepting infants recently baptized, not even saints can live here without sin, ibid., 704.—The absurd consequences of the opinion of those who deny sin in infants, ibid., 469.—We are all bound by the law of sin, Cassiodorus, LXX, 490.—This life is not lived without light sin, ibid., 1074.—The devil [Col. 0796] does not lead us into sin except willingly, St Gregory the Great, LXXV, 1026.—By our own will we consent to be drawn by the devil into sin, ibid., 1096.—God does not impel anyone to sin, id., LXXVI, 915.—Sin is born from sin, id., LXXV, 783.—Many can live without crime, but cannot live without sin, St Isidore, LXXXIII, 620.—Sin is not to be attributed to God but to the human being created by God with free choice, with commandments set before him which he could keep, Rabanus, CIX, 663, 665.—Its cause, id., CXII, 1545.—Nowhere in human nature is sin found apart from the will, St Anselm, CLVIII, 451.—Adam’s descendants sin by a natural necessity, ibid., 454.—Sin arises from two causes: ignorance and weakness, Blessed Ivo, CLXI, 1021.—A person sometimes sins by a movement of the mind, sometimes through the frailty of the flesh, ibid., 870.—No saint or righteous person is free of sin, ibid., 881.

Lust is the most shameful of all vices and supplies both impulse and fuel for many sins, St Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 266.—Not only a perverse understanding of the law, but every corruption and every depravity of mind, can be called leaven, which causes very many sins, ibid., 257.—Gifts, too, are causes of sins, because they blind and overthrow minds, ibid., 295.—The soul’s impurity can arise from three sources: from the deception and suggestion of heretics and of all evil people; from itself, when a person by his own will rushes into some heresy or grave sin, ibid., 394.—God is not the author of sin, Rupert, CLXX, 212.—Three things compel us to sin: the flesh, one’s neighbour, and the devil or the world, Hildebert, CLXXI, 364.—Three deaths come upon the soul: through thought, deed, and persistence, ibid., 474.—How heavy a burden sin is, ibid., 525.—There are two ways of sinning: through desire and fear, ibid., 1142.—God is not the author of sin, Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 134.—Pride is the cause of sins, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 44.

## III.—On the effects of sin, and also the punishment by which it is chastised

Although the human soul is truly said to be immortal, it nevertheless has a kind of death of its own. For it is called immortal because, in some measure, however slight, it does not cease to live and feel; whereas the body is called mortal because it can be abandoned by all life and does not in any way live through itself. Therefore the soul’s death occurs when God abandons it, just as the body’s death occurs when the soul abandons it. The death of both, that is, of the whole human being, occurs when the soul, abandoned by God, abandons the body. For then the soul itself lives neither from God, nor does the body live from it [lacuna]. For in that final and everlasting punishment [lacuna], the death of the soul is rightly so called because it does not live from God; but the death of the body is in some way death although it lives from the soul [lacuna]. Thus the soul lives from God when it lives well; for it cannot live well unless God works in it what is good. St Augustine, *The City of God*, book III, chapter 27.

“What, do you think, are God’s wonders? What is more wonderful among God’s wonders than raising the dead? ‘Am I dead, then?’ you ask. If you were not dead, it would not be said to you: ‘Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will give you light.’ All unbelievers, all wicked persons, are dead: they live in body but are extinguished in heart. But one who raises a body from the dead restores it to behold this light and breathe this air; yet the one raising it is not himself its light and air. It begins to see as it saw before. The soul is not raised in this way. The soul is raised by God—though the body also is raised by God—but when God raises the body, he restores it to the world; when he raises the soul, he restores it to himself. If the air of this world withdraws, the body dies; if God withdraws, the soul dies. Therefore, when God raises the soul, the raised soul does not live unless the one who raised it is present. For he does not raise it and leave it to live by itself [lacuna]. God raises it; it dies if God departs. For I shall say boldly, brothers, yet truly: there are two lives, one of the body and the other of the soul. As the soul is the life of the body, so God is the life of the soul. Just as the body dies if the soul leaves it, so the soul dies if God leaves it. When you are with me, I live, and you are the life of my soul, which will die if left to itself.” St Augustine, *Exposition on Psalm 70*, sermon 2, no. 3.

“Whoever,” says St Jerome on Jeremiah chapter 2, “is stained by the filth of lighter sins is cleansed by milder admonitions. But grave sins, which draw one to death, can be washed away neither with nitre nor with the herb Borith, but require harsher torments [lacuna]. There are light sins and grave sins. To owe ten thousand talents is one thing; to owe a quadrans is another. We shall be held accountable both for an idle word and for adultery; but to be put to shame is not the same as to be tortured; to blush is not the same as to be tormented for a long time. Hear the apostle John: ‘Whoever knows [Col. 0797] that his brother is committing a sin not unto death—let him ask, and he shall give him forgiveness, to one committing a sin not unto death. But whoever has sinned unto death, who shall pray for him?’ You see that if we pray for lesser sins, we obtain forgiveness; but for greater sins obtaining it is difficult, and there is a great difference between sins and sins [lacuna].”

Since sin is a kind of sickness of the soul, a particular sin is called mortal by analogy with a disease called mortal, because it brings about an irreparable failure through the loss of some principle. . . . . . . Now the principle of spiritual life, which is life according to virtue, is orientation toward the last end; . . . . and if this is lost, it cannot be restored by any intrinsic principle, but only by divine power. . . . . . Therefore sins of this kind are called mortal, as being virtually irreparable. But sins which involve disorder concerning the means to the end, while the orientation toward the last end is preserved, are reparable; and these are called venial. For sin has pardon when the liability to punishment is removed; and this ceases when sin ceases. It must further be said that one who sins venially clings to a temporal good, not as one enjoying it—that is, not establishing one’s end in it—but as one using it, referring it to God, not actually but habitually. . . . Venial sin is so called from *venia*, “pardon.” . . . It does not deserve eternal punishment, but temporal punishment. . . . For when the will is directed toward something which in itself conflicts with charity, by which a human being is ordered to the last end, that sin, by reason of its object, is mortal. Hence it is mortal by its kind, whether it is against the love of God, as blasphemy, perjury, and the like; or against love of neighbour, as homicide, adultery, and similar acts. But sometimes the will of the sinner is directed toward that which in itself contains a certain disorder, yet does not conflict with love of God and neighbour, such as an idle word, excessive laughter, and the like; and such things are venial sins by their kind. . . . Although we should not think that these venial sins kill the soul, yet they make it ugly, as it were, with certain pustules and with a kind of dreadful scab, so that they allow it to come to the embraces of the heavenly Bridegroom either only with difficulty or with great shame. Therefore they must continually be redeemed by constant prayers, more frequent fasts, more generous almsgiving, and above all by forgiving those who sin against us, lest perhaps, gathered together, they make a heap and sink the soul. For whatever of these sins has not been redeemed by us must be purged in that fire of which the Apostle says: “For it shall be revealed in fire; and if any man’s work is burned, he shall suffer loss.” Either, while we live in this world, we ourselves weary ourselves by penitence; or else, by God’s will or permission, we are afflicted with many tribulations for these sins; and if we give thanks to God, we are delivered. . . . . . . Thus the sins themselves are purged in this world, so that in the world to come that purgatorial fire may find nothing—or at least little—to burn. But if we neither give thanks to God in tribulation nor redeem our sins by good works, we ourselves shall remain in that purgatorial fire as long as the aforesaid small sins are consumed like wood, hay, and stubble.

“But someone says,” says St Caesarius, Sermon 37, “It does not concern me how long I remain there, provided that I go on to eternal life.” Let no one say this, because that purgatorial fire will be harsher than anything that can be thought, seen, or felt as punishment in this world. Therefore let each person labour with all his strength to escape capital crimes, and to redeem small sins by good works in such a way that nothing of them may seem to remain which that fire can consume. But those who commit capital crimes, if during their lifetime they refuse to redeem them by the remedies of penitence, will not go to that fire of which the Apostle says, “He himself shall be saved, yet so as through fire”; rather, they will enter that fire under that severe and irrevocable sentence of which Christ says: “Depart from me, you accursed, into eternal fire.”

These matters are explained in the following indications drawn from the Fathers.

We lose through sins things blessed, greatest, and nearest to God, St Hilary, IX, 788.---The face of the Lord is turned away from everyone who remains in sins, ibid., 429.---There are certain sins which remove from the mouth the word of truth, ibid., 544.---Sins deserve reproach, ibid., 525.---Our sin always confronts us like an evil tax-collector, or like a wicked moneylender meeting his debtor, St Ambrose, XIV, 1070.---We are guilty without an accuser; we are tortured without a torturer; we are bound without chains; we are sold without a seller, ibid., 1022.---How sins are punished, ibid., 348.---The unjust are winnowed like chaff, ibid., 834.---The day of sin is called the day of confusion, [Col. 0798] id., XVI, 506.---No pain is greater than that which wounds the conscience with the point of sin; nor is any burden heavier than the load of sins and the weight of shameful deeds, ibid., 1235.---Nothing causes such great sorrow as for a person held captive to remember from where he fell and from where he was cast down, ibid., 523.---Internal sins defile a human being, Juvencus, XIX, 647.---Sin is our death, St Jerome, XXII, 339.---Sins generate negligence, ibid., 654.---Sin is a wall separating God and human beings, id., XXIV, 576.---It speaks of death, id., XXV, 575.---Our sins are the cause of all evils, LVII, ibid., 57.---Sin is the death of the soul, id., XXVI, 465.---Everyone who sins loves darkness, id., XXIV, 356.---Everyone who sins is born of the devil, ibid., 659.---He who has sinned and done evil is dead, ibid., XXIII, 1077.

Sin is the death of the soul, St Augustine, XXXV, 1748.---It is the sole death of the soul, id., XLII, 95.---Iniquity alone places one far from God, id., XXXVII, 1775.---By sinning a human being departs from God, id., XXXIII, 838.---Sins alone separate from God, id., XLI, 300.---And from salvation and eternal life, id., XLIV, 129.---In sin are darkness and cold, id., XXXV, 1579.---Sins are the darkness of souls, id., XLIII, 118.---Sin cannot go unpunished, id., XXXVI, 505, 701; XL, 358.---Sin must be punished either by God or by man, id., XXXVI, 505.---By the desert of sin vengeance is eternal, id., XXXIII, 381.---The punishment and outcome of sins are that persons are first devastated by the fire of their lusts; then, by the stench of their evil deeds, they are cast out from the company of the blessed; finally, carried away and submerged, they pay unspeakable penalties, id., XXXVI, 137.---The punishments of sin are diverse, id., XXXII, 674.---God does not bring forth from himself that by which sins are punished; rather, he orders sins themselves so that what had been pleasures to the person sinning become instruments for the Lord punishing, ibid., 107, 108.---Effects of sin, id., XXXIX, 1974, 2224, 2225.---God will permit no sin to remain unavenged, id., XL, 1350.---None can remain unpunished, id., XLV, 1876.

Sin is the death of the soul, Gennadius, LVIII, 990.---Nature is corrupted by sin, Eugyppius, LXII, 1017.---The good is lost, ibid., 996.---Sins are the darkness of souls, ibid., 872.---Sin generates death, ibid., 118.---Human sin caused days now to be reckoned from darkness, ibid., 155.---It drove humankind out of Paradise, ibid., 158.---Through sin a human being lost the capacity for good thought and good will, Fulgentius, LXV, 467.---The greater sins are, the farther they drive one from God, Cassiodorus, LXX, 56.---Whoever sins loses the grace of the Holy Spirit, ibid., 367.---Sin is a disease of souls, ibid., 298.---Sins are bonds, ibid., 856.---Sin is the death of the soul, *Vita Patrum*, LXXIII, 509.---God leaves no sin unavenged, St Gregory the Great, LXXV, 653.---By those things which a person preferred to his Creator in sinning, God punishes him, ibid., 606.---No sin is hidden from divine wrath, id., LXXVI, 27.---Those entangled in sins cannot see the light, id., 336.---Those living wickedly within the bosom of the Church are struck by divine vengeance as ungodly persons, ibid.---He suffers the darkness of vengeance who here voluntarily endured the darkness of pleasure, ibid., 1108.---While the soul feeds upon sin, it cannot eat the bread of righteousness, id., LXXV, 973.---The punishment of sin in hell is eternal, id., LXXVII, 401.---Why is a sin which is finite in itself punished with an eternal punishment? ibid.---Sin kills the soul, Rabanus, CVII, 481; CVIII, 227.---Those infected by its stain are excluded from access to heaven, id., CIX, 654.---Those polluted by it vainly place confidence in the temple, id., CXI, 859.---Sinners shall be destroyed like mud, St Bruno, CXLII, 197.---They are cast away like dust, ibid., 147.---They vanish like smoke, 249.---They have no peace in conscience, ibid., 274.---On the effects of sins, St Peter Damian, CXLV, 223.---No sin remains unpunished, ibid., 578.---Bodies subject to sins are dead, Lanfranc, CL, 700.---A sacrifice benefits nothing one enveloped in sins, ibid., 398.---Sin is a weight, ibid., 402.---Sins inwardly blind the mind, Radulfus, CLV, 1670.---They draw it into outer darkness, ibid.---Those who voluntarily persist in deadly sins are like drunken and dead persons: they see nothing and perceive nothing, whether good or evil, Guibert, CLVI, 34.---All sins injure the soul, St Anselm, CLVIII, 559.---The righteousness of a just person who falls is abolished, ibid., 877.---The more freely someone sins, the more gravely he is sick, ibid., 665.---While sins attract, they promise sweetness; while they drag away, they inundate with bitterness. While they persuade, they anoint; after they have persuaded, they prick the soul even to death, ibid., 1010.---Sins tear the conscience apart, ibid., 950.---Through sin a human being dies, though in some measure he lives, ibid., 873.---The abyss of sins calls upon the abyss of judgments and punishments, [Col. 0799] ibid., 1001.---When human nature first sinned, it was scourged with this punishment: that it should never naturally produce offspring except such as we see infants born, ibid., 534.---And after this life it should be exiled for ever in hell from the kingdom of God for which it was made, ibid.---The punishment of sin is the necessity of sinning, ibid., 463.---Illnesses, death, and so forth are punishments of sin, ibid., 464.---Death is from sin and is the punishment of sin, ibid., 394.---Sins are ropes, Rupert, CLXVII, 1048.---Sin in the human being brought us death of soul and body, ibid., 1330.---Sin subjects the soul to the devil, Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 447.---It binds a human being, ibid., 744.---Sin destroys in us the dwelling-place of God, Godefridus, CLXXIV, 27.---And binds the soul like a cord, ibid.---It makes us slaves, ibid., 483.---Sin is the death of the soul, Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 1157.

## IV.—On the necessity of avoiding sin, and the means of rising from it

From what was said in the preceding paragraph concerning the penalties reserved for capital and venial sins, we infer that those who desire to be freed from everlasting punishment and from purgatorial fire should not commit capital crimes; or, if they have already committed them, they should perform fruitful penitence and should not cease to redeem those small or daily sins by good works.

Yet I wish, says St Caesarius, to make clearer to you by what works small sins are redeemed. Whenever we visit the sick, seek out those shut up in prison and placed in bonds, call the discordant back to concord, fast when a fast has been proclaimed in the Church, wash the feet of guests . . ., give alms to poor persons passing before our door, and grant pardon to our enemies whenever they ask it of us, by these and similar works we redeem small sins daily.

For capital crimes, however, this alone is insufficient. Tears, groanings, and sighs must be added; fasts continuously practised and prolonged for a long time; more abundant alms must be distributed; we must voluntarily remove ourselves from communion with the Church, remain for a long time in mourning and sadness, and even perform penitence publicly. For it is just that one who has destroyed himself together with the ruin of many should redeem himself together with the edification of many.

“There is a penitence,” says St Augustine, Sermon 351, chapter 3, no. 3, *On the Benefits of Performing Penitence*, “whose practice must be undertaken throughout this whole life in which we dwell in mortal flesh, with perpetual humility of supplication. For no one desires eternal, incorruptible, and immortal life unless he repents of this temporal, corruptible, mortal life. . . . Who can doubt that, whatever temporal prosperity we enjoy, we must nevertheless repent of this life, so that we may run with all eagerness toward that incorruption? . . . . . . Who then hastens and desires to return to his homeland and to contemplate that form which is face to face, unless he has repented of his pilgrimage? From this grief of the penitent there also bursts forth and is heard that pitiable cry: ‘Alas for me, for my pilgrimage has been made long!’”

Therefore, even though someone has been justified from previous sins through baptism, let no one dare to be proud if he commits nothing for which he must be separated from communion at the altar, as though already boasting of complete security. Rather, let him preserve humility, which is almost the sole discipline of Christianity. . . . . . . Let not earth and ashes be proud until this whole night has passed. . . . . . . Who, then, of sound mind would not groan? To whom would this condition not be displeasing through penitence? Who, supplicating in all humility, would not make himself fit to be heard by divine help, until all this substance of temptations and earthly shadow pass away? . . . Then, as one crucified to the world, each person disciplines his members away from every evil work, so that sin may no longer reign in his mortal body, to obey its desires. Let him worship the one true God alone; be devoted to no rite of idols; be entangled in no worship of demons; not take the name of the Lord his God in vain; confidently await everlasting rest; render due honour to parents; be neither bloodstained by homicide, dishonoured by fornication, fraudulent in theft, double in falsehood, nor defiled by coveting another’s property or wife. Let him neither overflow with luxury even in his own possessions nor wither through avarice; let him not be contentious, abusive, or reviling. Finally, let him sell all his goods, give to the poor, follow Christ, and fix the root of his heart in heavenly treasure. . . . Let him provide for his neighbour as he has felt provision made for himself. Such a person, then, will live amid human affairs bound not by carnal but by spiritual acquisition’s duty; not indeed occupied with secular business, but, because he serves as a soldier of God, neither sluggish nor cast down in idle indolence. Let him give all his alms, if he can, with every cheerfulness; let him not be broken by weariness amid the difficulties of circumstances, which must necessarily arise in order to show [Col. 0800] a human being that he is human. Let anger not creep into him against one who attacks him hatefully, asks inopportunely through compulsion of poverty, or [concerning] his own business. . . . Let him give nothing more or less than is fitting. . . . Let him not speak more than is necessary. . . . Yet they gather dust from dry ground. . . . . Therefore we must have daily penitence, not only because of the mortality and ignorance of this life itself, and because of the evil of the day . . . which we are commanded to bear and carry . . . and to endure, acting manfully with God, that we may bear fruit with patience; but also because of that very dust of this world . . . which clings to the feet of those who give counsel as they go about caring for others, and because of the losses which occur in the very busy activity of administration—losses which the Lord may grant to be compensated by greater gains.

Whoever carefully examines himself and deceives himself by no self-flattery understands well enough with how great a danger of eternal death, and with how great a lack of perfect righteousness, he lives as a pilgrim away from the Lord. . . . “You must hate in yourself your own work,” says St Augustine, *Tractates on John* XII, no. 13, “and love God’s work. But when what you have done begins to displease you, then your good works begin, because you accuse your evil works; confession of evil works is the beginning of good works. He who does the truth accuses his own evils; he does not spare himself; he does not forgive himself, so that God may forgive him; for what he wishes God to forgive, he himself acknowledges.”

Christ is ready to forgive, but those who acknowledge [their sins]. Yet one who walks in his love and mercy, even when freed from those deadly and great sins—such as crimes, homicides, thefts, and adulteries—makes the truth of confession on account of those sins which seem small, whether sins of tongue, thought, or immoderation in permitted things, and comes to the light in good works; for many small sins, if neglected, kill. . . . The journey of this world is burdensome and full of temptations: in prosperity, let a person not be puffed up; in adversity, let him not be broken. He who gave you this world’s prosperity gave it for your consolation, not your corruption. Conversely, he who scourges you in this world does so for correction, not condemnation. Bear the Father who instructs you, lest you experience the Judge who punishes you.

Finally, all saints who faithfully serve God strive to devote themselves to reading and prayer and to persevere in good works. Building upon the foundation of Christ neither capital crimes nor small sins—that is, wood, hay, and stubble—but good works—that is, gold, silver, and precious stones—they shall pass through that fire of which the Apostle says, “For it shall be revealed in fire,” without any injury. But those who, though they commit no capital crimes, are ready to perpetrate small sins and negligent in redeeming them, will come to eternal life because they have believed in Christ and have not committed capital sins. Yet first they must either be purified in this world by the justice or mercy of God, as has already been said, through most bitter tribulations—and themselves be delivered through God’s mercy by many alms, especially when they mercifully forgive their enemies—or else be tormented for a long time in that fire of which the Apostle speaks, so that they may reach eternal life without spot or wrinkle. But those who have committed homicide, sacrilege, adultery, or other such acts, unless worthy penitence comes to their aid, as has likewise already been said, will not deserve to pass through purgatorial fire into life; rather, they will be cast down through everlasting fire into death.

Through these foregoing statements, the matters concerning the necessity of avoiding sin and the fitting means of rising from it appear sufficiently demonstrated for us. They are further demonstrated by what follows.

Not only sins of deed, but also sins of will, must be avoided and purged by penitence, Tertullian, I, 1232.---Occupations which lead to sin must be wholly abandoned, ibid., 667.---To all sins committed in flesh, spirit, or will, he who appointed punishment through judgment also promised pardon through penitence, ibid., 1233.---Fasts merit the blotting out of sins, id., II, 65.---Prayer washes away offences, raises the fallen, supports those who are falling, and sustains those standing, id., I, 1196.---To obtain pardon for sins we need daily sanctification, St Cyprian, IV, 523.

How God overlooks our sins, St Hilary, IX, 860.---Pardon for sins, ibid., 783.---The Law and the Gospel promise pardon for sins through penitence, ibid., 789.---God grants pardon for absolutely all sins through faith, after a return in confession, by his own gift rather than our merit, ibid., 1022.---Sins are corrected by humiliation, ibid., 567.

A great remedy removes great sins, St Ambrose, XIV, 724.---How their cords and bonds are loosed, [Col. 0801] id., XV, 1311.---When bent by involuntary vices, let us make God propitious to us; let us follow what he commands, avoid what he forbids; let there be zeal to propitiate the Godhead, obedience in following the command, and caution against transgressing the prohibition, id., XIV, 575.---Let the sinner confess his fault, the ungodly groan, and the righteous not exalt himself, ibid., 805.---He who confesses his own sin is justified, ibid., 533.---Sin is forgiven through grace, blotted out through the blood of the cross, covered through charity, ibid., 876.---Let righteousness remit iniquities, fortitude fear, and temperance impurities, so that forgiveness of sins may be perpetual, id., XV, 1248.---How remission of lighter sins may be obtained, ibid., 479.---Sin must not be concealed if we wish our guilt to be forgiven, Rufinus, XXI, 803.

The necessity of forgiving sins, St Jerome, XXVI, 132.---For sin one’s own blood is worthily offered, id., XXV, 1210.---Our sins are not loosed unless we receive them from the hand of the Lord, id., XXIV, 400.---By what remedies light and grave sins are purged, ibid., 693.---However grave sin may be, if one turns back, it can be healed, ibid., 100.---The beginning of salvation is to understand and weep for one’s sins, ibid., 1231.---Different sins must be treated with different remedies, id., XXV, 677.

Sins are dissolved and abolished in Christ’s glorification, St Augustine, XXXIV, 595.---Christ alone can take away sins, 638.---He alone who came without sin can free from sin, id., XXXV, 1694.---Sins are taken away when Christ’s death is contemplated, id., XXXIV, 489.---No one is freed from sins except by the grace of God through Jesus Christ, id., XXXIII, 885; XLI, 1119.---The sin of one’s own will is also loosed and healed through Christ, id., XLIV, 120.---Christ takes away sin in three ways, XLV, 1176.---A human being is not made free from sin by law but by grace, ibid., 896.---Sin is removed by grace alone, id., XXXV, 2065.---By what means sins are cleansed, id., XLIII, 475.---They are forgiven in three ways, XL, 636.---The remedies for sins are almsgiving, fasting, and prayer, id., XLIII, 63.---Sins are expiated by prayer and God is made propitious, id., XXXIII, 665, 675.---Sins must be drained away daily by good works lest they sink the ship, id., XXXVI, 819.---Alms do not redeem sins unless life is changed, id., XL, 265, 267.---Graver sins are blotted out through the Lord’s Prayer if, in repentance, life has been changed for the better, ibid., 265.---However great sins may be, they are forgiven in the Church through penitence, ibid., 262.---Only penitence practised in true religion obtains pardon and purges what has been committed, XXXIII, 391.---Sins are not forgiven by God to one who does not forgive, id., XL, 193, 1273.---The remedy for sins, id., XXXVII, 1698; XLIII, 213.---All sins are blotted out when from a true heart and full confidence we say: “Forgive us,” id., XXXVII, 1361.---Venial sins are blotted out in the Lord’s Prayer, id., XL, 636.---Small sins must not be despised, id., XXXVIII, 88, 382.---They must not be neglected, ibid., 650.---If neglected, they kill, id., XXXV, 1492.---If you despise light sins when you weigh them, be afraid when you count them, ibid., 1982.---Light sins gathered together, like scab, either kill or destroy our beauty, ibid., 1541.---Everyone ought to avoid even the lighter sin, id., XL, 499.---Grave sins must be avoided; smaller ones must be treated by a threefold remedy, id., XXXVIII, 88.---Daily cleansing and daily medicine for sins, ibid., 127, 299, 382, 983, 1207.---If you wish to sin, seek where God does not see you, and do what you wish, ibid., 736.---Confession of sins before God arouses hope, id., XXXII, 675, 787.---Sins are better accused so that they may perish than excused so that they may remain, id., XXXVII, 1410.---Sins are added to sins when sins already committed are covered by other sins, id., XXXV, 1469.---Excusing and perversely defending sin, id., XXXVIII, 138, 183, 186.---Those who do not confess sins but defend them are compared with vanishing smoke, ibid., 153.---When we excuse sins, the devil triumphs; when we accuse them, he groans and suffers pain, ibid., 186.---How swiftly the burden of sins must be laid down, XXXV, 1474.---Sins, like illnesses, are avoided in two ways, id., XLIV, 287.---Sins of three kinds must be healed by a threefold remedy, id., XL, 287.---To sin is human; to cease from sin is Christian; to persevere is diabolical, ibid., 1155.---No sin is so great that it has no pardon through repentance, ibid., 1179, 1182, 1187, 1199.---Sins must be redeemed daily, XXXIX, 2221, 2224.---Whenever they creep in, a remedy must be provided for them without delay, ibid., 1788.---God has provided remedies for sins which rich and poor alike can employ, ibid., 2259.---Remedies for sins, ibid., 1877; XL, 1348.---Three remedies, XXXIX, 1859.---We can redeem them through charity, ibid., 1066.---Forgiveness by brethren hastens pardon for sins, [Col. 0802] id., XXXIX, 1869.---The small sins of the righteous must be consumed by the fire of tribulation, ibid., 1771.---Capital sins must be expiated by true confessions and worthy fruits of penitence, id., XL, 1066.

Eternal salvation is promised not merely under the simple name of penitence; the mass of sins is also overwhelmed by the affection of charity, Cassian, XLIX, 1160.---Through the fruit of alms healing is given to our wounds, ibid.---Through the outpouring of tears the washing away of sins is sought. Likewise, through confession of crimes their abolition is granted, ibid.---Also through affliction of heart and body, and through amendment of life, ibid., 1161.---Sometimes also through the intercession of saints and the merit of mercy and faith; often through conversion and the salvation of those whom our admonitions save, ibid., 1162; through our own forgiveness and remission, ibid. and following.

All sins, however great, are forgiven in baptism, St Prosper, LI, 454.---Those who forgive sins to their neighbours loose their own sins, ibid., 510.---Sins must be confessed, not excused, ibid., 402.

Sins are overcome by fasting, St Peter Chrysologus, LII, 254.---They are forgiven through Christ, ibid., 360.---One must not despair because of the magnitude of sins, ibid., 437.---They are forgiven to people through people, ibid., 437.---The sin of a city is abolished by Christ alone, ibid., 462.---Manifold mercy so assists human falls that hope of eternal life is restored not only through the grace of baptism but also through the remedy of penitence, St Leo the Great, LIV, 1012.---Sins must be removed in order to make God propitious to us, St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 566.---If sinners are silent about their sins in confession, they become more criminal, ibid., 522.---A remedy for human sins prepared by God, LX, 819.---God bestows gifts on sinners so that they may be converted, ibid., 831.---Sins are overcome by alms, St Paulinus, LXI, 76.---We must now die to them, lest later we live in punishments, ibid., 377.---Even the smallest must be avoided, lest we gradually fall, ibid., 725.---They are blotted out by baptism and penitence, ibid., 332.---It is exceedingly dangerous not to resist their beginnings, ibid., 452.---Sins are not forgiven without charity, Eugyppius, LXII, 984.---Charity covers sins, ibid., 998.---Prompt remedies must be applied to sins, ibid., 662.---God will punish both original and actual sin in the wicked, St Fulgentius, LXV, 655.---The requital of eternal punishment begins when the wicked person receives in himself the due reward of his error, ibid., 564.---Certain things in human nature are harmful because of guilt, ibid., 592.---To obtain remission is nothing other than to be freed from the condemnation of sin, ibid., 539.---Three things—faith, good works, and time—are so necessary for the remission of sins that salvation cannot be obtained if any one of them is lacking, ibid., 531.---Remission of sins belongs to this life alone, ibid., 571.

The first remission of sins is that by which we are baptized in water, St Caesarius of Arles, LXVII, 1075; the second, the affection of charity; the third, the fruit of alms; the fourth, the outpouring of tears; the fifth, confession of crimes; the sixth, affliction of heart and body; the seventh, amendment of life; the eighth, the intercession of saints; the ninth, the merit of mercy and faith; the tenth, the salvation of others; the eleventh, our forgiveness and remission; the twelfth, the suffering of martyrdom, ibid.---How sins are blotted out, Cassiodorus, LXX, 364.---They are forgiven in many ways: through baptism, martyrdom, almsgiving, forgiving our brethren’s sins, and when someone turns a sinner from the error of his way, ibid., 60.---The singular remedy by which sins are avoided is the presence of God, ibid., 114.---One never abandons sin who loves what he sins in, ibid., 374.---We must always remember our sins, ibid., 269.---Sins must be hated, *Vita Patrum*, LXXIII, 940.---Our own sins must be weighed more than those of others, ibid., 969.---One who mixes sins with good works does the same as one who pours water into a perforated vessel, ibid., 762.---The first virtue is to avoid sins, St Gregory the Great, LXXV, 751.---The perfect should always weep for past sins, id., LXXVI, 1038.---Sins must be confessed, and not excused lest they be doubled, id., LXXV, 655.---Confession of sins is the opening of wounds, id., LXXVI, 1302.---The medicine for sin is the humility of mourning, id., LXXV, 621.---How those subject to small but frequent faults ought to be admonished, id., LXXVII, 115.---Whoever neglects to avoid the smallest sins falls wholly from the state of righteousness, id., 116.---Sins redeemed by alms must not be repeated, id., 85.---How sins of deeds must be lamented, ibid.---It profits nothing to forsake sin unless it is cleansed by tears, id., 110.---The sins of others must be forgiven so that our own may be forgiven, id., 428.---Manifest sins must not be purged by secret correction, [Col. 0803] id., 1326.---Sin must be considered in the mind so that we may be kindled toward penitence, id., LXXIX, 184.---How one must guard against falling back into sin, id., 199.---Sins must not only be confessed but also erased by the austerity of penitence, id., 429.---We cover sins by uncovering them through confession, id., 559.

To admit sin is to fall into a pit; to make a habit of sinning is to narrow the mouth of the pit, so that one who has fallen cannot get out, St Isidore, LXXXIV, 624.---Frequent sinning must be avoided, ibid., 625.---A wicked thought produces delight; delight, consent; consent, action; action, habit; habit, necessity, ibid., 624.---Daily and light sins are purged by the Lord’s Prayer, Halitgarius, CV, 656.---How the rest are forgiven, ibid.---On the seven remissions of sins, Jonas, CVI, 130, 131.---Sins must be redeemed by alms, Regino, CXXXII, 212.---Confession is the best remedy against future falls, Guibert, CLVI, 604.---Memories of sins are the nails of righteousness, ibid., 1153.---One who by no means abandons sin for God’s sake, not from the gift of grace, ibid. [reading incomplete].

Our sins require confession and penitence, Goffridus, CLVII, 200.---They must be anticipated, lest we be anticipated by them, ibid., 209.---Sins are not forgiven unless one forgives from the heart the person sinning against oneself, St Ivo, CXLI, 1017.---As often as a sinner falls, so often he must rise again, ibid., 877.---Sins are not remitted without worthy penitence, ibid., 880.---How we should correct our sin through discipline, Rupert, CLXVII, 834.---God never abandons one who truly acknowledges his sin, ibid., 1204.---Sin which is not through malice is forgiven more readily, ibid., 919.---Confession of sin merits pardon, ibid., 760.---To defend one’s sin when the sinner is reproved displeases God, ibid., 1082.---For the hidden sinner, the oil of mercy is applied; for the public sinner, the cautery of penitence, id., CLXX, 107.---Confession of sins is the torment of demons, Hildebert, CLXXI, 425.---Sin must not be repeated after penitence, St Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1249.---Sins must be lamented in two ways, ibid.---Knowledge of sin is the beginning of salvation, ibid., 529.---The remedy for sins is sincere confession, ibid., 530.---No work blots out sins without the humility of penitence, id., CLXXXV, 61.---How great an evil is the defence of sin, id., CLXXXIV, 987.---The death of sinners is evil in the loss of the world, worse in separation from the flesh, worst in the double crushing of worm and fire, id., CLXXXII, 240.---By the habit of sinning a human being rushes into the abyss of evils, ibid., 969.---To persevere in sin is diabolical, id., CLXXXIII, 40.---The occasion of sin must be fled, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 199.

## SECOND SECTION. ORIGINAL SIN

### On its existence and consequences

The name of the first parent of humankind was Adam, and that of his wife Eve. God placed them in the Paradise of delight, a most pleasant garden in which “the Lord God caused to grow from the ground every tree beautiful to look upon and pleasant for food; also the tree of life in the midst of Paradise, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.” The tree of life, St Augustine says, was so called because they were to taste of it so that death or old age might not creep upon humankind; the tree of the knowledge of good and evil was so called from its effects.

To understand this more clearly, one must know what God commanded the human being placed in Paradise. “Eat of every tree of Paradise,” he said; “but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil do not eat; for on whatever day you eat of it, you shall die by death.” Thus the tree of the knowledge of good and evil was so called because it was to come about that, on its account, human beings would know by experience either good or evil: good, that is, the blessed life, if they obeyed the divine command; but evil, that is, every kind of misery, if they did not fear to eat the forbidden fruit. Hence this tree was not evil by its nature; indeed, it was good by its nature, like all the rest. . . . But obedience, says St Augustine, was commended in the command: that is, God decreed abstinence from that tree so that he might test human obedience by an easy command. . . .

But alas! our first parents lost their original innocence by sinning against God’s command, when they were not ashamed to eat of the forbidden fruit. This happened thus: Eve, the woman, deceived by the devil, ate and gave to Adam, who also ate. And immediately our first parents, because they had sinned in this matter, knew that they were naked [lacuna]; and hence punishments were imposed upon them, and others were transmitted to their descendants.

[Col. 0804] We shall speak only of these latter punishments. They were precisely the same as those which they themselves transmitted. Hence we are born subject to every kind of infirmity, to death, ignorance, threefold concupiscence, slavery to sin and the devil, enmity toward God, and sonship of wrath and Gehenna. Thus, by God’s most just, though incomprehensible, justice, absolutely all human beings are held guilty of sin. All are born corrupted by an inborn stain, and it is just that they should suffer its penalties [lacuna].

On these matters let the Council of Trent be heard, Session 5, Decree on Original Sin:

1. If anyone does not confess that the first man Adam, when he had transgressed God’s command in paradise, immediately lost the holiness and justice in which he had been constituted, and incurred, through the offense of such transgression, the wrath and indignation of God, and consequently the death with which God had previously threatened him, and, together with death, captivity under the power of him who thereafter held the dominion of death—that is, the devil—and that the whole Adam, in body and soul, was changed for the worse through the offense of that transgression: let him be anathema.

2. If anyone asserts that Adam’s transgression injured himself alone and not his posterity, and that the holiness and justice received from God, which he lost, he lost for himself alone and not also for us; or that, being defiled by the sin of disobedience, he transmitted death and bodily punishments only to the whole human race, but not sin also, which is the death of the soul: let him be anathema. For he contradicts the Apostle who says: “Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death; and thus death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned.”

3. If anyone asserts that this sin of Adam—which is one in origin and, transmitted by propagation rather than imitation, is proper to each individual—is removed either by the powers of human nature or by any remedy other than the merit of the one Mediator, our Lord Jesus Christ, who reconciled us to God in his blood, etc.: let him be anathema.

Thus, in a word, since we were all enclosed in our first parent in an ineffable manner: “In him,” says the Apostle, “all sinned [lacuna]”; and behold original sin. Yet it cannot at all be comprehended how the soul of each human being, which is certainly created pure and immaculate by God, contracts, through its conjunction with its own corrupted body, the body’s defect and the stain of a sin committed so many ages ago. This sin of origin is a mystery. It exceeds the grasp of the human mind [lacuna]. Therefore we believe the truth of original sin by faith, infer it by reason, and experience its inborn misery. God has plainly revealed this in the Scriptures. The Church has always taught it; upon it, as upon a foundation, the entire order of religion rests, as will clearly appear from the following references.

Original sin is affirmed by Tertullian, I, 813.—Original sin: St Cyprian, IV, 363.—Sin of origin: St Hilary, IX, 599, 601, 976.—By Adam’s sin we lost the dignity of our first and blessed creation, ibid., 644.—Man is born under the origin of sin and under the law of sin, ibid.—Human beings are held in sins by bodily weakness and their condition of origin, ibid., 754.—The law of sin, ibid., 404.—From one, the sentence of death and the toil of punishment went out to all, ibid., 385.—The soul contracted some stain of sin from its association with the flesh, ibid., 527.—Both the law and the origin of sin remain in us, ibid., 376.—Original sin: St Zeno, II, 352.—The effects of original sin are toil, groaning, impiety, pain, illness, and misery, ibid., 340.—Sin of origin: Philastrius, XII, 1243.—“Before we are born, we are stained by contagion; and before we enjoy the light, we receive the injury of origin itself”: St Ambrose, XIV, 872.—Unless the Lord forgives, no one whom the inheritance of a harmful condition itself has bound over to guilt can be saved, ibid., 1053.—Through the succession of nature, a succession of guilt too has been transmitted from one to all, ibid., 914.—Adam transmitted to us the inheritance of vice, ibid., 1125.—One iniquity is ours;
