## THIRD SECTION. ON SINS IN PARTICULAR, OR ON THE CAPITAL SINS

By the seven capital sins are understood the seven heads to which all the other sins that can be committed by human beings are customarily reduced. The explanation is given because, as Gregory the Great says, *Morals*, Book III, chapter 17, “evil is often born from good things through the vice of negligence. The righteous person carefully considers how arrogance may arise from learning, cruelty from justice, laxity from piety, anger from zeal, sluggishness from meekness [lacuna]. For when he labors to acquire learned studies, he diligently prepares his mind against the conflict of arrogance. When he desires justly to punish the faults of offenders, he most shrewdly avoids allowing the cruelty of vengeance to exceed the measure of justice [lacuna]. When he stirs himself by the impulses of righteous zeal, he takes the greatest care not to kindle himself with the flame of anger beyond what is necessary. When he restrains himself with the great tranquility of meekness, he watchfully observes that he may not grow cold in body [lacuna]. For not all faults seize the heart with equal onset. But while the greater and fewer faults first overcome the neglected mind, the lesser and innumerable ones pour upon it in troops. For pride itself, the queen of vices, when it has fully taken possession of a conquered heart, immediately hands it over to be devastated by seven principal vices as by certain commanders of its own. An army follows these commanders, because from them undoubtedly arise troublesome multitudes of vices [lacuna]. Pride is the root of every evil [lacuna]. Its first offspring, namely the seven principal vices, spring from this poisonous root: vainglory, envy, anger, sadness, avarice, gluttony, and lust [lacuna]. From vainglory arise disobedience, boasting, hypocrisy, quarrels, obstinacy, discords, and presumptuous innovations. From envy arise hatred, whispering, detraction, exultation in a neighbor’s adversities, and distress at a neighbor’s prosperity. From anger proceed quarrels, swelling of mind, insults, shouting, indignation, and blasphemies. From sadness arise malice, rancor, faint-heartedness, despair, sluggishness in regard to commands, and wandering of mind toward unlawful things. From avarice arise betrayal, fraud, deceit, perjuries, restlessness, acts of violence, and hardenings of heart against mercy. From gluttony are propagated foolish merriment, buffoonery, uncleannesses, much speaking, and dullness of understanding.

“From lust are generated blindness of mind, thoughtlessness, instability, rashness, self-love, hatred of God, attachment to this present age, and dread or despair concerning the age to come [lacuna]. Of these seven, five are spiritual and two carnal. But each is joined to another by such close kinship that one is produced only from another. For the first offspring of pride is vainglory; when it has corrupted an oppressed mind, it immediately produces envy, because, while it craves the power of an empty name, it languishes lest another should obtain it. Envy in turn generates anger, because the more the mind is wounded by the inward injury of envy, the more it loses the meekness of tranquility [lacuna]. Sadness too arises from anger, because the more a disturbed mind shakes itself in disorder, the more it confuses itself by binding itself [to that disorder] [lacuna]. Sadness, moreover, is led into avarice [lacuna]. After these, however, two carnal vices remain—namely gluttony [Col. 0809] and lust—but it is clear to all that lust is born from gluttony.”

“Capital vices,” says St Thomas, *First Part of the Second Part*, question 84, article 84, in the body of the article, “are called those from which others arise, especially according to the character of final cause. Such origin may be considered in two ways. One is according to the condition of the sinner, who is so disposed as to be chiefly inclined toward one end, from which he commonly proceeds to other sins. But this kind of origin cannot fall under an art, because particular human dispositions are infinite. The other is according to the natural relation of the ends themselves to one another; and in this way, in most cases one vice arises from another. Therefore this mode of origin can fall under an art. Accordingly, those vices are called capital whose ends have certain primary reasons for moving the appetite; and the capital vices are distinguished according to the distinction among those reasons.”

The capital sins, however, are pride, avarice, lust, envy, gluttony, anger, and sloth, which theologians commonly call *acedia*. From these, as from a fountain, all other sins flow; hence they are called “capital.” Yet capital sins are not all mortal; for they are sometimes mortal and sometimes venial. That is, pride, avarice, lust, and the other capital sins may be committed either mortally or venially. They are committed mortally when the matter is grave and there is full consent of the will. They are committed venially when the matter is slight or consent of the will is imperfect [lacuna].

These matters will become clearer to anyone who reads through the following references, each pertaining to one particular capital sin.

The order of the capital sins is as follows:

1. Pride.—2. Avarice.—3. Lust.—4. Envy.—5. Gluttony.—6. Anger.—7. Sloth (*acedia*).

### I.—On Pride

Pride is the appetite for perverse exaltation. Perverse exaltation consists in the mind’s abandoning the principle to which it ought to adhere and making itself, in a certain fashion, its own principle and source of being. This happens when it pleases itself excessively. But it so pleases itself when it falls away from that immutable good which ought to please it more than it itself does.

Pride is at once the first, gravest, and most dangerous of all sins. It is “first” because, as Tobit says, “every destruction took its beginning from pride.” For the angel’s sin and that of the first human being were through pride. It is “greatest” both because it is the fountain and origin of all the others, and because no other sin is more opposed to God or more injurious to his supreme dominion. It is “most dangerous” both because it lies in wait even for good works, that they may perish—hence even in right actions it must be feared, lest things laudably done be lost through the desire for praise, as St Augustine says—and because we have the fountain and root of that sin within ourselves, and nothing lives in us earlier or dies later than pride; and because, if pride happens to rule in a person, it is for the most part a sign of reprobation.

“Flee pride,” says St Bernard, *Sermon* 1, no. 3, *On the Lord’s Advent*, “my brothers, flee it greatly. Pride, the beginning of every sin, so swiftly darkened with eternal gloom Lucifer himself, who shone more brightly than all the stars; it transformed not merely an angel, but the first of angels, into a devil [lacuna].” “I judge pride to be a great sin,” says St Augustine, *Exposition on Psalm XVIII*, no. 15. “Do you ask how great this sin is—the sin which casts down an angel, which made a devil out of an angel, and shut against him the kingdom of heaven forever? It is a great sin, the head and cause of all sins. For it is written: ‘Pride is the beginning of every sin’; and lest you despise it as something slight: ‘The beginning,’ it says, ‘of a human being’s pride is apostasy from God.’ This vice is no slight evil, my brothers: Christian humility is displeasing to this vice in those eminent persons whom you see [lacuna]. From this vice, which is the head of all vices because the other vices are born from it, came apostasy from God, as the soul went into darkness and made evil use of free choice, with sins following as well [lacuna]. Because of this vice, because of this great sin of pride, humble God came. This cause, this great sin, this vast disease of souls brought the omnipotent physician down from heaven, humbled him to the form of a servant, subjected him to insults, and hung him upon the wood, that this swelling might be cured through the health of so great a remedy. At last, then, let the human being be ashamed to be proud, for whose sake God became humble.”

Four forms of pride are commonly enumerated:

1. When someone glories in himself on account of goods of soul, body, nature, or grace.
2. When someone who admits that something was given him from above thinks that he received it through his own merits, or behaves as though he thought that God owed him something.
3. When someone claims for himself what he does not possess and lies that he possesses it.
4. When someone despises others.

The sins that proceed from pride as from a root are vainglory, disobedience, boasting, hypocrisy, contention, obstinacy in one’s own opinion, discord, dissensions, rivalries, angers, quarrels, presumption of vanities in matters concerning faith or morals, and finally ambition, the vice so often denounced by Christ [lacuna].

Examples of pride and of the punishments God inflicts upon the proud occur throughout the Scriptures: namely, Exodus XIV, 4 and following; II Kings XXIV, 1 and following; IV Kings XIX, 28 and following; Daniel IV, 1 and following; V, 17 and following; Esther III, 1 and following; V, 8 and following; II Maccabees IX, 4 and following; Acts XII, 21 and following [lacuna], etc.

All these matters are developed at length in the references that follow [lacuna].

Pride is condemned among Christians: St Cyprian, IV, 536.—Human pride despises, St Hilary, III, 529.—It renders good works vain, ibid., 523.—By no sin is God’s wrath more provoked against us than by pride, ibid.—The remedy for pride that trusts itself and is insolent toward others, ibid., 308.—What pride is and how great a vice it contains: St Ambrose, XV, 1234.—Pride is the greatest sin in man, and why, ibid., 1283.—It does not know how to stand; and if it falls, it does not know how to rise again, id., XIV, 966.—Description of the proud, ibid., 386.—Why everyone proud is unclean in the sight of the Lord, id., XV, 1421.—Pride is thinking lofty thoughts, id., XVII, 160.—Pride and self-exaltation are sin, ibid.—It is the greatest evil, dreadful and fearsome, ibid., 756.—Seven vices arisen from it are listed, ibid.—It is regarded as a kind of madness, ibid., 206.—All the proud are children of the devil, ibid., 676.—The mind of the proud bears no fruit worthy of God, ibid., 195.—When vainglory has fully seized the mind, it immediately generates within it sevenfold wickedness: disobedience, boasting, hypocrisy, contention, obstinacy, discord, and presumptuous innovations, id., XVII, 756.—But if true humility is opposed to it, all its wickedness is emptied, ibid.—No one ought to boast, id., XIV, 252.—Let there be no boasting because of precedence, id., XV, 1619.—If boasting must be avoided, how much more ought no one to boast falsely of things as true, id., XIV, 324.—Pride is the beginning of every sin: Rufinus, XXI, 669.—It is called a great offense, ibid., 715.—Always hateful to God, ibid., 1085.—Pride has God as its adversary: St Jerome, XXII, 546.—A swollen mind and an erect neck provoke God’s hatred against themselves, ibid., 688.—Nothing in this world is worse or emptier than pride and the self-pleasing person to whom nothing pleases except what he himself has made, id., XXIII, 1076.—What the voice of pride is, id., XXIV, 160.—Every proud person is ready to inflict injury, ibid., 212.

Pride: what it is, St Augustine, XLI, 356, 420.—It is the love of one’s own excellence, id., XXXIV, 436; XXXIX, 1565.—Pride is wishing to seem what one is not, XXXIV, 199.—All pride takes delight in what is its own and, as it were, private, id., XXXIII, 564, 568.—Pride: swelling, id., XXXIX, 1676.—No one is proud unless he is empty; if he were full, he would not be puffed up, id., XXXVII, 1233.—Pride does not wish to have a superior, not even God, ibid., 1470.—It approaches nothingness, id., XLI, 421.—The origin of pride, id., XXXIV, 203.—From earthly prosperity, id., XXXVIII, 206.—Riches most especially bring pride, id., XXXVII, 1769.—Pride builds its nest out of riches, id., XXXVIII, 957.—Pride, the worm of riches, ibid., 112, 215, 412.—An excellent description of pride, id., XXXII, 1184.—Pride, chief of all sins, ibid., 1286.—The head of all evils, id., XXXV, 1603, 1604.—The fountain of evils, id., XXXIV, 436.—The first sin, id., XXXVI, 156, 687.—A great transgression, and the head and cause of all transgressions, ibid., 163.—Pride, the cause of all vices, id., XLIV, 168.—How great an evil it is, id., XXXVI, 709.—No vice is more monstrous, id., XXXII, 929.—How dangerous is the disease of pride, id., XXXVIII, 945.—By the cup of pride death was offered and imparted to us, id., XL, 416.—It is the deceptive greatness of the weak: once it has taken possession of the mind, it casts down by raising up, empties by puffing up, and scatters by stretching out, id., XXXIX, 1561.—Pride, the serpent’s head, id., XXXVI, 354.—Above all, one must keep watch against pride, id., XLIV, 171. Every other iniquity is exercised in evil works so that they may be done; but pride lies in wait even for good works, so that they may perish, id., XXXIII, 960.—Pride must be avoided by overcoming the desire to please people, id., XL, 26.—The danger of pride, id., [Col. 0811] XLIV, 753.—The proud person is one in whom his own spirit lives, St Aug., XXXVII, 1852.—And one who follows his own spirit, id., 1856.—The proud, who please themselves, are so called in Scripture, id., XLI, 421.—The proud soul wishes to please in the sight of men, id., XXXVI, 163.—A proud person is one who wishes to be praised in himself, id., 310.—By praising yourself as good, you become evil: humility had made you good, but pride makes you evil, ibid., 193.—A proud person is one who either does not confess his sins, or attributes to himself such goods as he seems to possess, id., XXXVII, 1203.—The proud person loves to defend his own opinion, not because it is true, but because it is his own, id., XXXII, 839.—The proud have their hearts raised on high, but against the Lord, id., XXXVIII, 168.—Whence the fall of the proud arises, id., XXXII, 701.—Where you pride yourself on God’s gift, there you lose what you had received, id., XXXVIII, 751.—Whomever the devil has made proud, he conquers, id., XXXV, 2030.—God will be higher above you by as much as you are more exalted, id., XXXVIII, 1780.—The proud are compared to smoke, id., XXXVIII, 440.—They are called the body of the devil, id., XXXVII, 1807.—Though proud persons are high, they vanish like smoke, ibid., 1184.—They are compared to lions, id., XXXIV, 361.—Like snow, they freeze and fall, ibid., 875.—They are represented by mountains, id., XXXVII, 1243, 1865.—They are darkness, id., XXXV, 874.—How God resists the proud, id., XXXVII, 1426.—It is a rule of law that one who exalts himself shall be humbled, id., XXXVI, 266.—Christ treads upon the heads of the proud, id., XXXVII, 1210.—The proud person loses what the humble person obtains, id., XXXVIII, 108.—The proud are weakened so that they may be perfected, id., XXXIV, 1414.—What pride is, id., XL, 1089; XLV, 1884.—Its various kinds, id., XXXII, 1462.

The characteristics of arrogance, insolence, pride, and obstinacy, St Augustine, XL, 1256.—The disposition and evils of pride, ibid., 1058.—The worst of all sins, ibid., 1223.—By what medicine the swelling of pride is healed, id., XXXVII, 1523.—Not even the humility inherent in mortality subdued the exaltation of the proud, ibid., 1542.—The divine medicine against pride, id., XLIV, 168.—Christ heals our pride by his humility, id., XXXV, 1604.—Because of the great sin of pride, God came humble, id., XXXVI, 163.—God made man is a great medicine against pride, id., XXXVIII, 487.—At last let man blush to be proud, for whose sake God was made humble, id., XXXVI, 163.—Pride is a poison which is not cured except by poison, id., XXXVIII, 893.—The effects of pride, id., XXXII, 1190; XXXIX, 1561.—By this vice apostasy from God occurred, id., XXXVI, 163.—Pride cast out the devil, id., XLIV, 263.—Man would not have perished had he not swelled with pride, id., XXXVIII, 684.—By pride we fell, id., XXXVI, 353.—Through pride man perishes from the righteous way, id., XLIV, 265.—Pride, the cause of the Jews’ blindness, id., XXXV, 1778, 1780.—The fountain of idolatry and other sins, id., XXXVIII, 1022.—Pride is the mother of envy, XXXIII, 561; XXXVIII, 1290; XXXIX, 783; XL, 413.—By pride there is a departure from God, id., XLIV, 206.—Nothing moves the foot toward ruin except pride, id., XXXVII, 1608.—It prevents faith in Christ, id., XXXVIII, 656, 874.—By pride man is driven into his own darkness, id., XLIV, 206.—It stops up the ears of the heart, ibid., 618.—It extinguishes charity, id., XXXV, 1982.—Pride, presumptuously relying on empty greatness, does not allow a person to walk by the narrow way or enter through the narrow gate, id., XXXVII, 1471.—What *cenodoxia* [vain glory] is, Cassian, XLIX, 399.—It is manifold and multiform, ibid., 402.—It lies in wait for every virtue, ibid., 622.—The two kinds of vain glory, ibid., 624.—How it is to be purged, ibid., 399.—The tinder of all vices springs from pride, ibid., 431.—Pride is such a great evil that it deserves to have God himself as its adversary, ibid., 434.—How it is to be overcome, ibid., 437.—Pride is twofold: carnal and spiritual, ibid., 424.—The ugliness and destructiveness of pride described, ibid., 462.—It removes all virtues alike, ibid., 424, 425.—Because of pride Lucifer was made from an archangel into the devil, ibid., 426.—Pride always hateful to God, St Prosper, LI, 419.—The first and last vice of man, ibid., 444.—The several degrees of pride, ibid., 470.—The proud do not seek grace, and wish to please themselves, not in God but in themselves, ibid., 360.—What the flame of pride causes, St Peter Chrysologus, LII, 465.—Pride destroys what labour had acquired, ibid., 623.—Pride, the origin of all sins, St Leo the Great, LIV, 287.—Its twofold kind, id., LV, 167.—Its beginning from the devil, ibid., 168.—Which kind is more harmful, ibid., 175.—It is excluded by humility and charity, ibid.—Pride is the cause of all evils, Julianus Pomerius, LIX, 476 ff.—It is conquered by the virtue of humility, ibid., 478.—By what signs pride may be shown, ibid., 484, 485.—Vanity is a certain inflated disposition of a languishing soul concerning its various pleasures: greedy for obtaining honour, puffed up by the disease of empty excellence; hollow, diseased, turbulent; mistress of fickle minds, soul of vices, tinder of carnal pleasures, and corruption of morals, ibid., 488 ff.

Pride is the destroyer of all good works, St Paulinus, LXI, 411.—What pride is, Eugyppius, LXII, 640.—The beginning of every sin, ibid., 630.—The gate of salvation is shut to the proud, ibid., 678.—Whence pride took its beginning, St Fulgentius, LXV, 164.—The beginning of sin, ibid.—It is called the beginning of every sin in order to show that every sin springs from it as from a root, ibid., 334.—The devil instils pride if he cannot command virginity, ibid., 333.—Those who set themselves above the poor to whom they give alms, or congratulate themselves upon riches which they have despised, sin more gravely than those who preserve some boastfulness in their heart concerning the possession of such riches, ibid., 321.—Pride is the desire for perverse exaltation, St Benedict, LXVI, 320.—There is pride of heart, speech, deed, and bearing, ibid., 376.—God permits the proud to fall into some shameful sin, ibid.—Who are to be called proud, Cassiodorus, LXX, 665.—Pride is the mother of vices, ibid., 842.—It is the greatest transgression, ibid., 143.—The Lord especially abominates it, ibid., 534.—God turns his face away from the proud and withdraws grace, ibid., 739.—The more arrogantly people thought they had attained heights, the deeper they descend into the abyss of Tartarus, ibid., 139.—All wish to be praised, Martin of Dume, LXXII, 33.—In pride lies the first ruin of all the wicked, ibid., 36.—Vain glory generates from itself presumption in every novelty, inventions of false doctrines, tortures of disputation, contentions, and heresies. Pride gives birth to indignation, envy, contempt, detraction, and murmuring, ibid., 38.—Pride hinders entrance into heaven, *Vita Patrum*, LXXIII, 1034.—If it ascends into heaven, it is brought down into hell, ibid., 1035.—Nothing is more destructive than pride and haughtiness, ibid., 1090.—Pride is the beginning of heresy, St Gregory the Great, LXXV, 621.—How it torments a person, ibid., 668.—The devil ravages and crushes one who exalts himself because of his virtues, ibid., 776.—It is commonly signified by the neck, ibid., 961.—Human pride ends in rottenness, ibid., 972.—Pride and vain glory are two principal vices, ibid., 1072.—Pride of heart is like a certain fatty thickness, ibid., 1113.—It destroys every virtue, ibid., 1134.—The first manifestation of pride is commonly in the eyes, ibid.—Four kinds of pride, id., LXXVI, 257.—The Lord represses movements of self-exaltation among the disciples, ibid., 258.—One who claims good for himself alone comes nearer to likeness with the devil, ibid.—A remedy against pride, ibid., 747.—It is the seedbed of lust, ibid., 743.—The mind must be guarded against pride with every vigilance, ibid., 364.—Pride is the commander of the devil’s army, ibid., 620.—The queen of vices, ibid.—Corruption of the flesh commonly follows the spirit of pride, ibid., 648.—Pride comes through the eyes as through certain windows, ibid., 743.—It attacks not only one virtue but all of them, ibid., 744.—How great is the slaughter wrought by pride in the soul, ibid.—Its effects, ibid., 746.—The condition of the proud, ibid., 300, 301.—Their life and end, ibid., 971.—Their glory is compared to mud and ashes, ibid.—They are not enriched with virtues, ibid., 1012.—They have no root in this world, ibid.—The proud attribute to themselves whatever they know, id., LXXVI, 147.—The more they see, the more they grow dark and half-blind, ibid., 316.—They measure their teaching by their much speaking, ibid., 372.—While displaying themselves, they pretend to speak for God, ibid.—Pride turns a person into a beast, id., LXXVII, 18.—It feigns love for uprightness, ibid., 78.—Let the abasement of humble life cure what the exaltation of pride wounded, ibid., 111.—Vanity must be trampled underfoot, St Columbanus, LXXX, 211.—Vain glory, unclean exaltation, and pride are conquered by true humility and contrition of heart through the fear of God, ibid., 260.

On pride and vain glory, LXXX, 928 ff.—Pride is threefold, LXXXIII, 97.—On boasting, ibid., 697.—Those inflated by pride feed upon wind, ibid., 639.—As pride is the origin of all crimes, so it is the ruin of every virtue. It is the greatest of sins, because it destroys the human mind both through virtues and through vices, ibid., 640.—Pride is a great evil: it cast the devil down from heaven and drove man out of paradise; daily it presses wretched people down from the state of uprightness to the depths, and after death is plunged into hell, Smaragdus, CII, 961.—First it raises a person in thought, and afterwards lifts him up, once raised, in deed, ibid.—Pride must be avoided, St Benedict, CIII, 695.—On the vice of pride, Halitgarius, CV, 659.—By what signs it may be detected, ibid., 660.—Its remedy: humility, [Col. 0813] ibid., 661.—Pride is the beginning of every sin, Jonas, CVI, 239.—It is a great sin. Its effects, ibid., 240.—Pride is crushed by Christ’s humility, Rabanus, CVIII, 1150.—Mortals scarcely escape it, id., CIX, 45.—Still more rarely do those who rule or excel others escape it, ibid.—How it is to be avoided, ibid.—Its gravity and detestability, ibid., 827; CX, 110, 689; CXII, 1210, 1581.—Pride is worse than every vice, id., CX, 110.—Whatever good a person does, he must seek praise from God, not for himself, ibid., 112.—Pride, which God resists, must be avoided; boasting, which displeases God, must be shunned; arrogance, which is an abomination before God, must be abhorred, ibid.—A remedy against pride, id., CXII, 1382.—Its nature and origin, ibid., 1351.—Its two kinds, hateful to God, ibid.—The fall of the first parents is to be ascribed more to it than to the serpent’s cunning, id., CVII, 486, 487.—How the Prophet calls it the root of all evils, id., 829.—The various effects of each kind, ibid., 831, 834.—The proud person always despises the works of others and always admires what he himself does, Hincmar, CXXV, 872.—Self-exaltation raises the spirit, ibid., 873.—Pride is the greatest transgression, St Bruno, CXLII, 102.—The effects of pride upon the human mind, St Peter Damian, CXLIV, 389.—It brings ruin upon itself, not upon others, ibid., 138.—Pride does not tolerate an equal, St Bruno of Chartres, CLIII, 307.—It is the greatest transgression, id., CLII, 713.—It is signified by the horn, ibid., 1017.—The queen of all vices, ibid.—Pride brings the blindness of a reprobate mind, Guibert, CLVI, 164.—It does not bear right intention, ibid.—The proud overflow through outward things, ibid., 155.

A lover of vain glory never ceases acting so as to be continually praised, Werner, CLVII, 1106.—As the eye’s sight is dulled when it looks upon the sun’s ray, so one who immoderately searches into things too high for himself is blunted from attention to truth, ibid., 1107.—As an eagle is cast down from on high to the *secas* [reading uncertain], so a person is plunged from the height of good conduct to lower things through carnal desire, ibid.—Through pride the heart is inflated, ibid., 1068.—Envy follows pride, ibid.—The three kinds of pride: in estimation, in will, and in deed, Lanfranc, CL, 111, 112.—That which exists in will alone is more damnable; that which exists in estimation is more incurable, ibid.—Pride seeks praise, id., CLVIII, 868.—Or, while fleeing praise, it takes glory precisely from that, ibid.—The daughters of pride: anger, impatience, discord, indignation, rancour of spirit, weariness of mind, gluttony, murmuring, avarice, and rapacity, ibid., 869.—Vain glory not only stains a person through evil works, but also slays him on account of good works. Certain condemnation awaits the proud, ibid.—Every vice derives its origin from pride. God first punished the sin of pride: 1. in the transgressing angels; 2. in Adam, who believed the serpent’s delusions; 3. in those who presumptuously undertook to raise a tower to heaven, St Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 185.—Pride makes a sinner both dead and stinking, Rupert, CLXVIII, 231.—The sin of pride causes us to lose both the heavenly and earthly gift, ibid., 287.—Pride is confidence in one’s own works, ibid., 535.—Pride, the fountain of original sin, Godefridus, CLXXIV, 181.—It opens the human heart to the devil, ibid., 281.—It is the mother of uncleanness and anger, ibid., 354.—Pride denies God, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXV, 776.—Its origin, ibid., 775.—Pride is the desire for one’s own excellence, St Bernard, CLXXXII, 821.—Its first degree is curiosity, ibid., 957 ff.; the second, frivolity of mind; the third, foolish merriment, ibid., 965; the fourth, boasting, ibid., 964; the fifth, singularity; the sixth, arrogance, ibid., 965; the seventh, presumption; the eighth, defence of sins; the ninth, feigned confession, ibid., 966; the tenth, rebellion; the eleventh, freedom to sin, ibid., 968; the habit of sinning, ibid., 969.—This is pride: when you are greater in your own eyes than before God and in truth, id., CLXXXIII, 946.—The first sin in heaven, ibid., 689.—It changed the prince of the angels into the devil, ibid., 36.—The Lord passes by the proud, ibid., 1041.—Pride is detestable, ibid., 104.—Beware boasting; flee the desire for vain glory; presume nothing about yourself; do not insolently exalt yourself; attribute no good to yourself; do not glory in a good work; do not be inflated by the wind of favour, id., CLXXXIV, 1259.—Whoever wishes to increase and not lose all his virtues should hide them because of self-exaltation and flee being seen for what he has deserved, ibid.—Pride made philosophers foolish and blind, Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1528.—It is the cause of all vices, id., CXCII, 268.—Pride, the beginning of every sin, Garnerius, CXCIII, 148.—Pride is the ruin of the entire spiritual building, Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 349.—It lies in wait for good works, ibid., 455.—Pride inflates, produces injustice, snatches a person above himself, Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1828.

Pride is the cause of all sins and evils, [Col. 0814] Peter the Chanter, CCV, 44.—It is the last sin for penitents and the first for those beginning to sin, ibid.—God detests this vice above all other vices, ibid., 45.—Christ’s Passion does not benefit the proud, ibid., 46.—All evils arise from pride, St Martin of León, CCV, 721.—It has four kinds: the first is when someone attributes to himself the good which he possesses; the second, when he believes it has been given by God, yet on account of his own merits; the third, when he boasts that he possesses what he does not possess; the fourth, when, others having been despised, singularly, ibid.—Pride effeminates one’s bearing, destroys the obstinate, casts down the exalted, and delivered philosophers over to a reprobate mind, Alanus, CCX, 135.—It is signified by the north wind; it is hostile to good things, destroys the fruit of work, and binds the mind with the frost of perversity, ibid.—It is the mother of every wickedness. It is a wind which casts dust from the face of the earth; it is a swelling which expels medicines that have been poured in, ibid.—Pride, unbearable to all and hateful to everyone, is always first and always last among all vices, CCXVII, 729.—How detestable it is, ibid., 730. On the characteristics of arrogant persons, ibid., 731.

## II.—On avarice

Avarice is the lust of possessing, or the disordered love of temporal things. Avarice exists when temporal goods are desired or possessed with covetousness. This may be discerned: first, if we either rejoice immoderately in possessing riches or grieve at their loss or deprivation; secondly, if we either acquire or retain them wickedly, against God’s commandment; thirdly, if we desire, possess, and keep them too greedily; fourthly, if we use them beyond or below the measure of necessity, to satisfy either pride, the lust of the eyes, or the lust of the flesh; fifthly, if we do not spend upon the poor whatever is superfluous.

It can be known that a person’s mind is free from the desire for riches: first, if he thinks himself neither happy through their possession nor wretched and unfortunate through their deprivation; if he neither rejoices too much over possessing them nor grieves too much at lacking them; secondly, if he prefers poverty to riches wickedly acquired and retained contrary to right; thirdly, if he uses lawfully acquired riches not for covetousness but only for necessity; fourthly, if he spends in pious works whatever remains over for himself and his own . . . . These points will be made most evident by the indications concerning avarice which follow; but before we set them out, it seems appropriate to provide some examples of this vice drawn from Scripture. They are as follows:

Joshua 7:11 ff.: “Israel has sinned and transgressed my covenant, says the Lord; they have taken of what was devoted to destruction, stolen it, lied, and hidden it among their goods . . . . . I shall no longer be with you until you destroy the one guilty of this crime. And whoever is discovered in this offence shall be burned with fire, together with all his property. For he has done wickedly in Israel.” And Joshua said to Achan: “My son, give glory to the Lord God of Israel, confess, and tell me what you have done; do not hide it.” Achan answered Joshua and said to him: “Truly I have sinned against the Lord, the God of Israel, and this is what I did. For I saw among the spoils a very fine scarlet cloak, two hundred shekels of silver, and a bar of gold weighing fifty shekels; and desiring them, I took them and hid them in the ground in the middle of my tent, having buried the silver in a pit . . . .” Joshua said: “Because you have troubled us, may the Lord trouble you this day.” And all Israel stoned him, Achan, and all that belonged to him was consumed with fire.

There is still, in the Old Law, a memorable example of avarice and its punishment in the person of Nabal, the husband of Abigail. See 1 Kings 25:2 ff.

There are also very many examples in the Gospel. Matthew 26:14 ff.: “One of the twelve, named Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests and said to them: ‘What will you give me if I hand him over to you?’ And they agreed upon thirty pieces of silver for him. And from then on he sought an opportunity to hand him over . . . . When evening came, Jesus was reclining at table with his twelve disciples. And while they were eating, he said: ‘Amen, I say to you, one of you is about to betray me.’ Greatly distressed, they began one by one to say: ‘Surely it is not I, Lord?’ He answered: ‘The one who dips his hand with me in the dish will betray me.’ Judas, who betrayed him, answered and said: ‘Surely it is not I, Rabbi?’ He said to him: ‘You have said it’ . . . . While he, Jesus, was still speaking, behold, Judas, one of the twelve, arrived, and with him a great crowd with swords and clubs, sent by the chief priests and elders of the people. His betrayer had given them a sign, saying: ‘Whomever I shall kiss, he is the one; seize him.’ And immediately approaching Jesus, he said: ‘Hail, Rabbi.’ And he kissed him. Jesus said to him: ‘Friend [*Amice*, OCR: “Amlee”], for what purpose have you come?’ Then [Col. 0815] they came up, laid hands on Jesus, and seized him . . . . . And they led him, Jesus, bound, and handed him over to Pontius Pilate the governor. Then Judas, who had betrayed him, seeing that he had been condemned, moved by repentance returned the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders, saying: ‘I have sinned in betraying innocent blood’ . . . . And throwing the silver pieces into the temple, he withdrew; and going away, he hanged himself with a rope . . . .”

Luke 16:19 ff.: “There was a certain rich man, who clothed himself in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day. And there was a certain beggar, named Lazarus, who lay at his gate, covered with sores, desiring to be fed from the crumbs which fell from the rich man’s table; and no one gave him anything. But even the dogs came and licked his wounds. It came about that the beggar died and was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom. The rich man also died and was buried in hell. Raising his eyes while he was in torments, he saw Abraham from afar, and Lazarus in his bosom. And he cried out: ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, because I am tortured in this flame.’ Abraham said to him: ‘Son, remember that you received good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now he is comforted here, while you are tortured . . . .’”

Acts of the Apostles 5:1 ff.: “A certain man named Ananias, with Sapphira his wife, sold a field. With his wife’s knowledge, he withheld part of the price of the field, and bringing a certain portion, laid it at the apostles’ feet. But Peter said: ‘Ananias, why has Satan tempted your heart for you to lie to the Holy Spirit and withhold part of the price of the field? While it remained unsold, did it not remain yours? And when sold, was it not in your power? Why have you conceived this thing in your heart? You have not lied to men but to God.’ Hearing these words, Ananias fell down and died. The young men arose, removed him, carried him out, and buried him. After an interval of about three hours, his wife entered, not knowing what had happened. Peter said to her: ‘Tell me, woman, whether you sold the field for so much?’ She said: ‘Yes, for so much.’ Peter said to her: ‘Why then have you agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord? Behold, the feet of those who buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out.’ Immediately she fell before his feet and died. The young men came in, found her dead, carried her out, and buried her beside her husband. And great fear came upon the whole Church and upon all who heard these things.”

The avarice of the heathen, who set money above the soul, Tertullian, I, 1261.—The darkness of avarice, St Cyprian, IV, 612.—The avaricious person, about to lose himself, fears losing his money: busy, sad, anxious, without any rest, he is always held fast by fear of loss; forgetful of honour, disregarding friendships, hostile to humane feeling, ignorant of religion, wholly hating goodness, IX, 687.—Avarice is the enemy of justice, XI, 385.—Whoever labours to have more than he had acts the part of avarice, ibid., 286.—The avaricious person is one who seeks what he does not have, and who thinks he does not possess what he does have, ibid., 529.—Avarice breaks faith, neglects charity, denies justice; it recognizes no affection, despises divine laws, excludes the claims of human ingenuity, and, if it could, would seize the whole world, ibid., 337.—It instils in those without riches the desire to possess them; from those who possess them it takes away satiety, ibid., 331 ff.—How great an evil avarice is, St Ambrose, XVII, 381.—Every miser is impious, harmful both to himself and to others, ibid., 442.—How old and ancient avarice is, id., XVI, 158.—How deadly and alluring it is, ibid.—How vain it is to gather wealth, ibid., XCIV.—Miser, do not hoard, lest you become a Christian in bare name but a Jew in deed, ibid., 1356.—Let possessions of treasure not possess a man who is pre-eminent; let one who rules free people not serve money, ibid., 120.—Avarice distributes as private property the rights of possessions which God had wished to be common to all, ibid., XVI, 1804.—Abundance of prosperous things is a great enticement to sin: it raises people into pride and infuses forgetfulness of their Creator, id., XIV, 834.

How great human avarice is, ibid., 217.—The insatiable avarice of merchants rebuked, ibid., 722.—Avarice is inflamed by profit, not extinguished, ibid., 733.—The more it has taken away, the more it believes itself poor, ibid., 527.—The goods of the avaricious are not true goods, ibid., 1162.—Barrenness alone is profitable to it, ibid., 740.—For the avaricious every gain is a loss to virtue and fuel for desire, ibid., 216.—Every miser is a slave and a beggar, ibid., 649.—What else is the mind of a miser but metal? ibid., 857.—From avarice, certainly, seven wickednesses are produced: betrayal, fraud, deceit, perjury, restlessness, violence, and hardness against mercy, id., XVII, 758.—Opposed to this is contempt for the world, [Col. 0816] ibid.—Avarice is the nurse of lust, id., XIV, 752.—What vices it generates, ibid., 653.—It is the first to weaken justice, ibid., 62.—Nothing is so contrary to courage as being conquered by gain, ibid., 87.—Avarice commonly takes hold of human senses and perverts opinions, ibid., 885.—Desire for gold is the material of faithlessness, and sacrileges commonly arise through devotion to avarice, ibid., 858.—It breaks faith and does not preserve simplicity of speech, ibid., 941.—It even holds its own soul for sale, ibid.

Avarice is the root of all evils, St Jerome, XXII, 418.—It is lust, fraud, and idolatry, ibid., 549.—No works can satisfy it, ibid., 897.—The more it has, the more it demands, ibid.—It despises laws and scorns the flames of Gehenna, ibid., 826.—It imitates hell. At feasts it devours not food but injustice; in courts it stirs up quarrels and discords. It has one measure: always to seek beyond measure, ibid.—We burn with avarice, and while discoursing against money, we open our breast to gold, and nothing is enough for us, ibid., 1057.—The root of avarice is the concern of the heathen, ibid., 417.—For many, the name of good works is an occasion for avarice, id., XXIII, 36.—Luxuries and varieties of banquets are incentives to avarice, ibid., 301.—Avarice is condemned among idols, id., XXIV, 48.—The avaricious are robbers and slaves of Mammon, ibid., 476.—The evil of avarice must be avoided, id., XXII, 417.—Fear of God restrains insatiable avarice, ibid., 818.—Let us shun it as the worst moneylender, ibid., 211.

What avarice is, St Augustine, XLI, 356.—General avarice: when one desires more than is enough, id., XXXVII, 1530.—Avarice is insatiable, id., XXXVI, 530, 422, 458; XXXIX, 1651.—More money does not close the jaws of avarice but widens them; it does not moisten but inflames them, ibid.—Avarice is a grave sin, id., XLIII, 89.—It is the work of an evil person, not of God, XXXVII, 1691.—The crime of avarice is its punishment, id., XXXVIII, 958.—It is a burden, ibid., 897.—Avarice is a chain upon the feet, id., XXXV, 2057.—The losses of those who sin for profit, XXXVII, 1645.—There is a certain avarice in lust and in idolatry, ibid., 650.—Every form of avarice must be cut off, ibid., 627, 630.—A remedy for avarice, ibid., 1636.—A person serves avarice, not God, id., XXXIX, 1205.—Christ frees from the yoke of avarice, id., XXXVIII, 526.—Love of wisdom cleanses from the filth of avarice, id., XLI, 204.—The proverb of the avaricious: “As much as you have, so great are you; break the moon and make your fortune,” id., XXXVI, 610; XL, 674.—A miser is not only one who steals another’s property, but also one who greedily keeps his own, id., XXXVIII, 628.—The miser is like a martyr for gold, id., XXXIX, 1461.—He does not so much possess as think himself to possess, id., XL, 674.—What *philargyria* [love of money] is, and whence it arises, Cassian, XLIX, 300.—It is made not by money but by love of money, ibid., 313.—Its three kinds, ibid., 303.—A shameful and dishonourable vice, ibid., 293.—It hinders every virtue, ibid., 298.—It produces many evils, ibid., 296.—How it is to be overcome, ibid., 315.—It can be conquered only by dispossession, ibid., 515.—Avarice is the root of all evils, St Peter Chrysologus, LII, 626.—It is the school of impiety, ibid., 285.—It generates poverty and is recognized by gold, ibid., 518.—The miser is envious, ibid., 194.—From the tinder of avarice we see causes of hatreds spring up; from it arise conflicts of crimes; from it fraternal battle-lines are marshalled; by it covenants of friendship are destroyed, St Valerian, LII, 752.—Contentions, quarrels, rage, and murder, ibid., 753 ff.—Avarice, the handmaid of idolatry, St Salvian, LIII, 188.—A disease, ibid., 175.—Those devoted to avarice place their riches in hell, ibid., 177.—Nothing is more wicked than a miser, ibid., 182.—Avarice is destructive, St Leo the Great, LIV, 544.—Avarice is a great evil, St Maximus, LIV, 476. Whoever seeks money loses faith; whoever gathers gold squanders grace, id., LVII, 476.—How many troubles the miser vainly endures in accumulating riches, ibid., 711.—A denunciation of avarice, Victor of Vita, LVIII, 405.—Desire is so mixed with pride that no sin occurs which does not proceed from both, Julianus Pomerius, LIX, 499.—A rebuke of the avaricious, Dracontius, LX, 834.—General avarice, Eugyppius, LXXII, 642.—Special avarice, ibid.—The devil fell through avarice, ibid., 645.—Avarice is called love and hunger for possessing, Arator, LXVIII, 131.—The root of all evils, ibid., 132.—Avarice is punished with such a lot that, though it seizes much, it is always needy, Cassiodorus, LXIX, 631.—The sword is despised where gold is received, id., 708.—The miser’s hand closes the harbour; when it draws in its fingers, it simultaneously closes the sails of ships, ibid., 714.—Flee that queen of shameless vices, avarice, to which all crimes slavishly minister with detestable devotion, ibid., 854.—Once it has entered the human breast, it admits treacherous cohorts in troops, ibid.—The vice of avarice, St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 308.—Hunger, ibid., 1029.—Its denunciation, ibid., 935.—The avaricious are [Col. 0817] always poor, *Vita Patrum*, LXXIII, 513.—They are like springs containing frogs, ibid., 1186.—The miser is described by a beautiful comparison drawn from singing and hunting birds, ibid., 531.—Avarice owes what almsgiving had prepared, ibid., 364.—Macarius teaches and converts a virgin by a good stratagem as a remedy for avarice, ibid., 1095.

Avarice is the head of all evils. St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 1074.—Compared to fire, ibid., 1093.—Signified by the name of lead, ibid., 1071.—It is heightened by pride and vainglory, ibid., 1073.—It steals in either through fear or through self-exaltation, 1096.—What the daughters of avarice are, id., LXXVI, 621.—What its temptations are like, ibid., 622.—How avarice torments the miser, LXXV, 666.—Those who burn here in the fire of avarice shall also burn in the flesh in the fires of Gehenna, ibid., 1016.—The miseries of the avaricious, ibid., 1094.—They are miserable here and eternally, ibid., 1095.—He whose mind is ravaged by avarice has an eruption upon his body, id., LXXVII, 25.—When it is not checked in small matters, it expands without measure, ibid.—It is shameful to care more for money than for souls, 821.—Like a bird, the miser, having devoured the bait of earthly things, is strangled in the snare of sin, ibid., 85.—How many crimes avarice is the root of, id., LXXIX, 233.—Covetousness is overcome by possessing nothing as one’s own and by holding all things in common, St. Columbanus, LXXX, 260.—On avarice, Taio, LXXX, 931, 932.—Avarice is divided into a twofold punishment, St. Isidore, LXXXIII, 96.—Almsgiving and hope of eternal recompense subdue avarice, ibid., 98.—Discourse on covetousness, St. Ambrose Autpert, LXXXIX, 1277 ff.—Avarice is an excessive desire to acquire, possess, or retain riches, CI, 634.—Its offshoots are envy, thefts, robbery, murders, lies, perjuries, plundering, violence, restlessness, unjust judgments, contempt for truth, forgetfulness of future blessedness, and hardness of heart, ibid.—Description of the miser, id., C, 690.—His misery, ibid., 691, 692.

Avarice knows no moderation, recognizes no restraint, and puts off any end to acquisition, Smaragdus, CII, 965.—It produces many evils: from it, expelled from the forehead [that is, from open shame], forgers are found in the assembly; from it, assassins in the midst of the city; from it, poisoners in public; from it, crime is openly admitted; from it, wickedness is publicly committed, ibid.—One eager for money has his soul up for sale, St. Benedict, CIII, 691.—Because of avarice Achan was stoned together with all his household; Saul was made an alien from the Lord, ibid.—On avarice and its remedy, Halitgar, CV, 665, 666.—On the vice of avarice and its effects, Jonas, CVI, 245.—Why avarice is called idolatry, Rabanus, CXII, 446.—Condemnation of it, ibid., 1244, 1245.—It is compared to dropsy, ibid.—The remedy against it, ibid., 1364, 1367.—Its nature and origin. Notes, id., CVII, 834; CIX, 244.—Avarice, the root of sin, Haimo, CXVII, 796.—On avoiding the vice of avarice, Hincmar, CXXV, 870.—On avarice, Regino, CXXXV, 464.—Avarice, the root of all evils, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 234.—As smoke issues from the fire of a steaming furnace, so the darkness of all vices is produced from the hearth of boiling avarice, ibid.—The miser’s difficulty in giving alms, id., CXLV, 213.—The threefold class of misers, ibid.—Avarice surpasses every wickedness, ibid., 533.—Its nature, ibid.; its effects, ibid., 534.—Its end and intention, ibid., 531.—Exhortation against avarice, ibid.

Avarice is the root of all evils, Lanfranc, CL, 359.—Avarice arose after the Flood, Guibert, CLVI, 147.—The propagator of all wickedness, ibid., 154.—On avarice and its remedy, Werner, CLVII, 1164, 1165.—Avarice is the god of the Jews, Rupert, CLXVIII, 155.—The cause of evils, ibid., 554.—It was evil to trade in the Temple and to sell Christ, ibid., 616.—The miser who gathers riches brings shame upon his house, ibid.—Avarice, which is an immoderate desire of having, compels a mind lacking inward good and not sufficient to itself to seek outward things, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 776.—The avaricious man is like hell, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1266.—Covetousness is a grave sin, the material of all crimes, ibid.—Through covetousness Judas sold Christ, ibid.—Avarice hinders pure worship of God, Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1059.—It is equated with idolatry, id., CXCII, 280.—What avarice is, and how it is the root of all sins, ibid., 350.—Avarice is like a jar which keeps the mouth of the heart opened wide by its circumference, Garnerius, CXCIII, 141.—The fruits of avarice, ibid., 153.—Avarice torments and draws a man outside himself by wandering, because it makes him embrace dung in place of crocuses, Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1828.—No vice is more vile than avarice, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 719.

What avarice is, Peter Cantor, CCV, 72, 75.—It is the service of idols, ibid., 75.—It is more difficult to cure than the vice of lust, ibid., 76.—No one can invoke upon another anything more grievous than avarice, ibid., 75.—Misers are called leeches, ibid., 94.—The miser lacks even the things which he possesses, ibid., 74.—Every miser is unclean, ibid., 75.—The covetousness of priests gave birth to the sale of Masses, ibid., 102.—The wheels, chariots, and drivers of avarice, Thomas of Cîteaux, CCVI, 116.—The earth is bounded by its limits; water is confined by its borders; air is enclosed by its boundary; heaven is restricted by its bounds: avarice alone is not stopped by measure, Alanus, CCX, 123.—Fortune, nature, charity, one’s neighbor, the elements, the sea, and God accuse avarice, ibid., 124, 125.—On the malice of avarice, ibid., 464.—Where coin speaks, the trumpet of Tullian eloquence grows hoarse; where coin goes to war, the thunderbolts of Hector’s warfare fall silent; where money fights, Hercules, once victor, is conquered, ibid.—Money conquers; money rules the world; money commands all things, ibid.—What advantage is it to pursue, with Ptolemy, the flights of the fugitive science of astronomy by the course of subtlety; with Euclid, to investigate the hidden things of geometrical riddles; with Milerius [reading uncertain], to discover the harmonious friendships of musical proportions; with Pythagoras, to examine the conflicts of numbers through the power of multiplication; with Tully, to adorn the stars with the constellations of rhetorical colors; and so forth, when in our times wisdom is rewarded by the pay of no profit, no favorable breeze of fame exalts it, while money itself buys titles of honor and the proclamations of praise? Ibid.—Avarice relaxes friendships, generates hatred, gives birth to angers, sows wars, nourishes quarrels, breaks treaties, and incites children against parents, ibid., 465 ff.—The war of avarice, ibid., 573.—It is to be overcome by generosity, ibid.—It is called an infernal fury, ibid., 564.—It attacks man with all its retinue, ibid., and 565.—The miserable condition of misers, ibid., 585.

The desire of the covetous is insatiable, Innocent III, CCXVII, 719.—The miser and hell both consume and do not digest, ibid., 721.—The miser neither has compassion on sufferers nor aids the wretched, but offends God, offends himself, and offends his neighbor, ibid.—As an idolater serves an image, so the miser serves treasure. On other characteristics of avarice, ibid., 722.—How many avarice has destroyed: the people stoned Achan because he took gold and silver from what was devoted to destruction; Naboth was slain so that Ahab might possess his vineyard; Judas hanged himself with a noose because he sold and betrayed Christ; sudden death destroyed Ananias and Sapphira because they defrauded the apostles of part of the price of the field, ibid.

III.—On lust.

Lust is the sin by which sexual pleasure is either sought or received contrary to the law of God. “Lust,” says St. Augustine, “is the vice . . . of a soul perversely loving bodily pleasures, while neglecting the temperance by which we are fitted for things spiritually more beautiful and incorruptibly more delightful.”

There are seven species of this sin: namely, simple fornication, adultery, defilement, sacrilege, incest, rape, and the vice against nature. Under this general name are understood effeminacy, the sodomitical crime, bestiality, and other abominations of this kind . . . We include all these under the name of Lust.

In the matter of this sin, not only those persons sin who actually commit the evil acts stated above, whether they sin alone or with others in the sexual act itself; but also: 1. those who without necessity speak, sing, read, write, paint, invent, or willingly hear sexual and indecent matters; 2. those who without necessity and with a sense of pleasure look with their eyes upon persons, pictures, statues, or other things of that kind from which an appetite for lust arises; 3. those who consent to perverse thoughts concerning lust; and 4. those who willingly and pleasurably occupy themselves with such perverse thoughts, even though they do not consent to them.

One may ask what things usually provoke a human being to lust. To this question [Scripture] answers: “This was the iniquity of Sodom,”—these are God’s words in Ezekiel—“pride, fullness of bread, abundance, and idleness of herself and of her daughters; and they did not stretch out a hand to the needy and poor.” Besides these, there are other incentives to lust: namely, association and familiarity with persons of the other sex, profane spectacles, dances and dancing, the reading of books in which love affairs are described—for example, comedies, chivalric romances, or other such works excessively widespread in the public sheets of our times.

St. Gregory the Great enumerates eight daughters of lust: blindness of mind, thoughtlessness, rashness, inconstancy, self-love, hatred of God, attachment to the present age, and dread or despair of the future. One may add that lust most often entails hardness of heart, loss of health, the confusion and dissipation of household property, buffoonery, obscene speech, slowness and dullness of intellect, and, finally, death in sin without prior repentance.

[Col. 0819] The antidotes or remedies for lust, which either draw one away from that sin or bring one back from it, are: first, avoidance of all the things which we have just said usually provoke lust; second, devotion to prayer and groaning of heart; third, withdrawal from frequent association with people; fourth, continual labor; fifth, mortification of the flesh; sixth, diligent custody of the senses and a mind free from all curiosity; seventh, frequent use of the sacrament of penance; eighth, unceasing meditation on death and eternity. It remains for us to say that lust is a grave sin, a sin mortal and most grievous by its very kind . . . It rarely happens that a sin in the class of lust is venial.

An elucidation of all these matters is found in the following notices.

He to whom lust is mistress rolls in what mire of disgrace, St. Hilary, IX, 687.—He hangs upon opportunities for adulteries; anxious about the stealthy deeds of his lewdness, in eyes, mind, and body he is wholly among prostitutes, ibid.—Seeing and hearing daily the human laws against adulterers, he devises adultery in the very forum; he fears what he does, and does not flee what he fears, ibid.—How great is the lust of men, St. Ambrose, XIV, 218.—It has neither faith nor observance of discipline; it is the seedbed and origin of vices, ibid., 720.—Lust is the mother of sexual desire, id., XVI, 1197.—How bitter is the fruit of lust, ibid., 381.—The lustful add house to house, estate to estate, and dig up the earth, ibid., 1061.—The lustful man detests the work of virtues; the glutton recoils from it, ibid., 1947.—When a person begins to indulge lust, he begins to depart from the true faith, ibid., 1181.—Lust produces blindness of mind, thoughtlessness, inconstancy, rashness, self-love, hatred of God, attachment to the present age, and dread or despair of the future, id., XVII, 760, 1072.—Lust is insatiable, St. Jerome, XXII, 826.—The waves of lust swell more and more frequently against us, ibid., 774.—Those who are captivated by its delight cannot accept correction, ibid., 818.—In wine is lust; in lust, pleasure; in pleasure, indecency, ibid., 663.

Lust. St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 526, 529.—What it is, XLI, 356.—Julian says that lust is an evil, but not concupiscence, id., XLV, 1349, 1350.—The evil of lust is committed by consenting to concupiscence, ibid., 1349.—Lust is signified by slipperiness, id., XXXVI, 328.—Fornication is twofold: of flesh and of spirit, id., XL, 469.—Of heart and flesh, id., XXXVIII, 1063.—Fornication is condemned in Scripture by divine law, id., XLII, 439.—A great evil, id., XXXIV, 743.—It bears deadly guilt, id., XL, 378.—It excludes from the kingdom of God, id., XXXVIII, 879.—It is a crime injurious to God, ibid., LXXXV, 878.—By the vice of fornication the image and temple of God in man are corrupted, ibid., LXXXVI, 1271.—And an injury is done to the grace of God, ibid., 85.—How great is the perversity of the human race in committing fornications and adulteries, ibid., 84.—Fornication of heart was in all; fornication of flesh in few; in all, [fornication] of heart, id., XXXVIII, 1063.—Sexual desire absorbs the mind, id., XLIV, 773.—It does not permit holy thoughts, ibid., 808.—It stirs and claims the whole human being for itself, id., XLI, 424.—It prevents the soul from raising itself toward eternal things, ibid., 227.—Spiritual fornication, Cassian, XLIX, 973.—On the principal remedy against the spirit of fornication, ibid., 269.—Purity of flesh cannot be attained without cleanliness of heart, ibid., 281.—Lust is called a contagion, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 363.—Like despair, ibid., 197.—It profanes all holiness, ibid., 304.—Lust seeks the destruction of chastity, the death of modesty, the death of holiness, ibid., 654.—Lust is restrained by plain and austere food, ibid., 227.—Lust hinders the way to heaven, St. Valerian, ibid., 698.—By lust the devil subjected the whole world to himself, St. Maximus, LVII, 305.—It is the companion of drunkenness, ibid., 582.—Lust is not a vice of beautiful and pleasant bodies, but of a soul perversely loving bodily pleasures, Eugyppius, LXII, 633.

Lust of the flesh; lust of the heart, St. Benedict, LXVI, 230.—That lust must be overcome by labor is aptly taught through a potter who made for himself a wife and offspring, *Lives of the Fathers*, LXXIII, 746.—A demon kindles lust, ibid., 302.—Fornication of the mind, ibid., 874.—Lust is denoted by damp places, St. Gregory, LXXVI, 674.—It is signified by the name “caterpillar,” ibid., 714.—Sins of the flesh are rightly compared with foul-smelling and burning sulphur, id., LXXV, 1051.—Lust is a fire devouring unto destruction, id., LXXVI, 201.—Through the temptation of lust, demons disturb the chaste movements of the soul, id., LXXV, 112.—Lust extinguishes all good works, ibid., 201.—What the daughters of lust are, ibid., 622.—How lust must be restrained, ibid., 190.—Stench and mist signify carnal concupiscence, id., LXXVII, 388.—Lust arises from gluttony, ibid., [Col. 0820] 80.—Through lust the virtues of the soul are destroyed, ibid.—Why the greater part of humankind rush headlong into fornication, id., LXXIX, 358.—The vice of lust must not only be struck but rooted out, ibid., 407.—It must especially be plucked out from the heart, ibid., 408.—God’s hatred of lust is severe, ibid.—What must be done in order that it may be completely subdued in the flesh and utterly eradicated from the mind, ibid., 401.—The examples of the saints must be brought forward to overcome it, ibid.

Lust is overcome by watchful chastity and continence that always fears, St. Columbanus, LXXX, 260.—On lust, Taio, id., 945, 946.—Fornications must first be removed from the heart, and they will not break forth in deed, St. Isidore, LXXXIII, 642.—Fornication of the flesh is adultery; fornication of the soul is slavery to idols, ibid.—It is the greatest crime because it violates God’s temple and, taking away Christ’s members, makes them members of a prostitute, ibid.—To be defiled by fornication is worse than every sin. Lust leads a human being to the punishments of hell, ibid.—Lust (*luxuria*) takes its name from extravagance (*luxus*), Alcuin, CI, 1194.—It is a bodily vice, ibid.—From fornication are born blindness of mind, inconstancy of the eyes, danger to life, hatred of God’s commandments, weakening of the mind, unjust desires, neglect of the future life, and love of the present, ibid., 634.—Lust is bodily uncleanness, ordinarily arising from the intemperance of sexual desire and the softness of a soul which consents for its flesh to sin, Halitgar, CV, 668.—When the mind begins to incline toward delight in the flesh, it is necessary to bring the fear of judgment back to mind and carefully to consider the punishments of hell, ibid., 670.—On the vice of lust, Jonas, CVI, 244, 245.—Condemnation and malice of lust, Rabanus, CXII, 1371.—A remedy against it, ibid., 1372.—Its nature and origin, ibid., 1370.—Its marks, ibid.—A body polluted by carnal works, unless washed by tears and cleansed through the worthy fruits of repentance, shall burn in the conflagration of eternal fire, Hincmar, CXXV, 874.

Lust gains strength through feasts, blazes up through excessive fullness of the belly, and pierces the soul with the sting of drunkenness, Hervaeus, CXXXII, 703.—It kills the life of the soul, takes away the heart, brings blindness upon the mind, quickly weakens the very body, hurls its broken frame swiftly into wretched old age, and, unless God has mercy, plunges man into hell and drags him to the torments of Tartarus, ibid., 704.—Lust, the tinder of avarice, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 232.—On lust, St. Bruno, CLIII, 312.—Fornication and every uncleanness must be avoided, Radulf, CLV, 1804.—One ensnared by the pleasure of the flesh is hemmed in by many evils, Guibert, CLVI, 603.—Occasions of lust must be fled, ibid., 66.—Lust subjects to slavery the person seduced by gluttony, Werner, CLVII, 1068.—Fornication is twofold, of both soul and body, Rupert, CLXVIII, 75.—To commit fornication is to depart from God, ibid., 36.—Lust and avarice are insatiable, ibid., 75.—It is signified by mud, and how it is punished, ibid., 578.—The remedy for lust must be sought from God, ibid., 776.—Lust is the vice of a beast, Hildebert, CLXXI, 708.—Humility and study preserve one from it, ibid., 709.—Lust is a most shameful vice, Godfrey, CLXXIV, 80.—It is like horses, ibid., 78.—Most evil beasts, ibid., 201.—Flesh inflamed through excess of food immediately boils over into sexual desire, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 776.—Lust is a slippery and unbridled prostitution of mind or body, descending from impure desires, id., CLXXVI, 1002.—Its companions are pleasure, wantonness, idleness, insolence, staggering, flattery, and luxury, ibid.—Among the other seven vices, fornication is the greatest crime, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1241.—It not only stains the body but also the conscience.

Fornication is overcome by flight alone, Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1584.—A most great and powerful disgrace, ibid.—The evil of lust committed in two ways, Garnerius, CXCIII, 220.—Thought of lust signified by the breast, ibid.—Lust enervates, brings forth uncleanness, and lowers man beneath himself, because, though made in God’s image, he lives as a pig, Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1828.—On lust and sexual desire, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 123.—Through lust man loses his dignity and God’s image, so that he is wholly swallowed up, becomes earth, and is changed from a rational being into a reptile and a beast of burden, Peter Cantor, CCV, 332.—Abstinence subdues sexual desire; for as the body is weakened by hunger, so the mind is recalled from unlawful desire, St. Martin of León, CCVIII, 723.—Lust is a plague more harmful than every monster: it empties the purse, weakens the body, intoxicates the soul, effeminates the condition of the mind, defiles the spirit, ruins reputation, offends one’s neighbor, and loses God, Alanus, CCX, 122.—It hates the light, seeks darkness, looks for a covering, and sets a doorkeeper at the entrance, ibid.—Chastity is an ointment; lust corrupts it, ibid.—To avoid lust, one must beware of [Col. 0821] gluttony, which is the foment of lust, the prologue to incest, the bridge to impurity, and the preface to incontinence, ibid., 123.

Lust is always preceded by ardor and wantonness; stench and uncleanness always accompany it; pain and repentance always follow it, Innocent III, CCXVII, 725.—It corrupts every age, confounds every sex, dissolves every order, and perverts every rank, ibid.—It overthrew the Pentapolis and the adjoining region, destroyed the Sodomites and Shechem with its people, struck down Dinah’s ravishers, slew Amnon at a banquet, killed Uriah, stoned the elders, cursed Reuben, seduced Samson, and perverted Solomon, ibid., 726.

IV.—On envy and its retinue.

Envy is grief at a neighbor’s good, as though it were our own evil, because we think that our own glory or excellence is diminished by that good.

For understanding this definition, observe that not every grief over a neighbor’s good is envy. From charity we may sometimes be grieved when someone abounds in goods of which he is wholly unworthy; from this arises not envy but indignation.—We may be grieved through fear at another’s good—namely, because we fear that he may abuse those goods to our ruin—and that grief is not called envy.

Thus the character of envy is properly found in this: that we are grieved at our neighbor’s goods as at our own evils, especially because we think that those goods tend to the detriment of our glory or excellence. For example, a man skilled in some art grieves at the reputation of another skilled in the same art because he thinks that his neighbor’s reputation tends to his own disadvantage. This we call envy. A man influential with a prince grieves that another is influential; for he thinks that this will diminish his own authority. This is envy. The same judgment applies to eloquence, virtue, and knowledge, which we wish to be so exclusively our own that they are shared with no one else, lest, if they be found in many persons, they diminish the renown of our name. Likewise, it is envy if, being miserable ourselves, we are grieved that others are happy and wish to draw them into the same misery with ourselves.

The causes of envy are always pride, and sometimes the concupiscence of the flesh or the concupiscence of the eyes . . . Pride indeed: for we grieve at our neighbor’s goods as though they were our own evils because we place ourselves above our neighbor and love our own excellence excessively; and this is pride. Concupiscence, whether of the flesh or of the eyes, is also a cause, because through excessive desire for temporal things the envious person grieves that his neighbor possesses riches which he himself would wish to possess alone.

St. Gregory the Great enumerates five daughters of envy: hatred of one’s neighbor, by which we come to wish evil to him; whispering, detraction, exultation in adversity, and grief in prosperity.

We may keep the mind free from all envy if we attentively consider that there is no vice which makes us more like the devil. For he harms us through envy alone: he is grieved that we are happier than he and therefore endeavors by every means to draw us with himself into ruin.

Envy is a grave sin, and mortal by its kind, according to the Apostle, Galatians 5:19 ff., and according to the Fathers cited below. Yet envy can be a venial fault if it concerns a slight matter and if the movement of envy is neither vehement nor fully deliberate. The remedies for envy are to keep the soul free from concupiscence of the flesh, concupiscence of the eyes, and pride of life. For one who is neither proud nor highly values perishable things—honors, rank, renown, pleasures, riches, and all other possessions of that sort—envies no one.

The following treat of these matters:

Envy quickly follows prosperity, St. Ambrose, XIV, 444.—How it may be appeased, ibid., 461.—How great is the Lord’s abhorrence of the envious, id., XV, 1625.—From envy arise hatred, whispering, detraction, exultation at a neighbor’s adversities, and grief at his prosperities, id., XVII, 756.—Charity is opposed to it: charity does not envy but rejoices together; does not hate but loves; does not whisper but rebukes; does not detract but reproves; does not rejoice at a neighbor’s adversities but grieves; does not feel grief at prosperities but receives consolation, ibid., 757.—Through envy death entered into the world, St. Jerome, XXII, 585.—Envy bites its own possessor, ibid., 482.—It always follows virtues, ibid.—The envious person is tormented by another’s happiness, and the glorious man lies open to snares, id., XXIII, 1045.—The more a person envies his brother, the more he himself wastes away and perishes, ibid.—The nature of envy, id., XXVI, 416.—It is divided into a twofold passion, ibid.—An elegiac poem on envy, ibid., 417.—Envy is like rust and vipers, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1769.—It is a devilish vice, ibid., 725.—A sin unto death, ibid., 1970.—It has its origin in pride, id., XLV, 1884.—What it is, id., XL, 1089.—The misery of envy, id., XXXIX, 1769.—Its remedy, XL, 1095.—The envious person must be cut away like a wasting disease of the body, id., XXXIX, 1950.—Or like a harmful limb, ibid.—Discourse on envy, id., XL, 1264.—Envy and emulation: how they differ, id., XXXV, 2142.—Envy, hatred of another’s happiness, id., XXXIV, 436; XXXVI, 180, 632; XXXVIII, 324, 397.

Envy, hatred of another’s happiness, St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 470.—It is born from pride, ibid., 471.—Envy is never other than malignant and is not satisfied with others’ evils, ibid., 278.—The envy of the Hebrews toward Christians, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 194 ff.—It admits neither piety nor charity. It drives away joy. It suffers no companion, ibid., 197.—It grieves at another’s good, not at its own loss, ibid.—It is accustomed to separate in order to join, ibid., 287.—Another’s good is punishment to the envious person, ibid., 574.—It is a disease. The torch of envy is an evil eye, ibid.—Envy is the disease of a deadly pestilence, St. Salvian, LIII, 175.—By what torment of mind envy afflicts the envious, Julianus Pomerius, LIX, 480.—By what signs the envy of the envious is shown, ibid., 486.—Envy, seed of many sins, St. Paulinus, LXI, 725.—What envy is, Eugyppius, LXII, 640.—The vice of envy, ibid., 601.—Whatever is said from envy is not thought true, Cassiodorus, LXIX, 512.—It seeks no measure, ibid., 549.—It oppresses those who are superior, ibid., 634.—Punishment of the envious, St. Gregory, LXXV, 228.—The evils of envy, ibid., 232.—The envious person testifies that he is inferior to the one whom he envies, ibid.—In envy the ancient serpent shakes out and vomits all its venom, ibid., 233.—Description of the envious person, ibid., 234.—Envy prepares a way to the gravest crimes, id., LXXVII, 63.—It kills all virtues; how great is the blindness of the envious, ibid.—Envy, Taio, LXXX, 935 ff.

Envy is afflicted with a twofold flame, St. Isidore, LXXXIII, 96.—The envious person is a limb of the devil, ibid., 700.—Envy burns up every shoot of virtue and devours every good thing with its pestilential heat, ibid., 853.—It is the moth of the soul: it consumes the understanding, burns the breast, and, like a plague, feeds upon the human heart, ibid., 854.—Against envy charity must be prepared; one must not grieve over another’s good, ibid.—To be jealous and envious is a great and serious sin, Smaragdus, CII, 961.—Cain, through the rancor of jealousy, killed his righteous brother Abel; Esau became hostile to his brother Jacob; Joseph was sold by his brothers, ibid.—Through the unjust jealousy of rancor, fear of God is cast aside and Christ’s teaching is neglected, ibid.—Hence every bond of peace is broken, brotherly charity is violated, truth is adulterated, and unity is divided, ibid., 962.—Envy is a torment, St. Benedict, CIII, 732.—The disposition of the envious, ibid., 977.—On the vice of envy and its remedy, Halitgar, CV, 662.—As small things grow through concord, so great things diminish through hatred and envy, Jonas, CVI, 241.—The divine oracles teach that these vices must be diligently avoided, ibid., 242.—In what ways envy is committed, Rabanus, CXII, 1243.—Its various species; its nature and origin, ibid., 1360.—What torments the envious; its marks, condemnation, and remedy, ibid.—On avoiding the vice of envy, Hincmar, CXXV, 876, 877.—On envy, Regino, CXXXII, 463.—The nature of envy, Lanfranc, CL, 295.—One must not envy another’s good but take it as an example, ibid., 398.—On envy, Werner, CLVII, 1036, 1037.—Effects of envy, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 682.—Hatred separates a man from God’s kingdom, removes him from heaven, and expels him from paradise. V.—On gluttony.

Gluttony is an inordinate appetite for food or drink. It is termed “inordinate” because we may lawfully desire food and drink.

We desire them lawfully when we seek them solely for necessity and the preservation of health. We desire them unlawfully and inordinately when the appetite extends beyond necessity and toward pleasure alone.

One sins through gluttony: first, when one eats or drinks too much—that is, beyond necessity or to the detriment of health; second, when one eats or drinks too eagerly; third, too lavishly; fourth, too fastidiously—that is, when foods prepared with excessive refinement are sought; fifth, when abstinence or fasting is broken on days on which, by the precept of the Church, one must fast or abstain from meat or from other foods.

Those sin in this vice who gorge themselves with food and drink until vomiting or drunkenness. Drunkenness is the sin by which someone is deprived of the use of reason through excessive drinking. It is a most grave and dangerous sin. It also causes grave harm both to health and to household resources. Drunkards cannot live long; they become the reproach of humankind and the scorn of the people . . . The daughters of gluttony are foolish merriment, buffoonery, uncleanness, much talking, and dullness of mind . . . The remedies for gluttony are temperance, fasting, affliction of the flesh, and meditation on death.

These points will appear most clearly from the following notices.

From the beginning gluttony was a murderer in Adam, Tertullian, II, 958.—The companions of gluttony are sexual desire and lust, ibid., 953.—The evil of drunkenness must be avoided, Caius, V, 179.—What is more wretched than the dominion of drunkenness? To pour into the belly beyond its capacity, to begrudge the body its proper function, to take reason from the senses, neither to speak nor remember, and to impose a kind of death while nature remains sound, St. Hilary, IX, 687.—Gluttony expelled the ruler [Adam] from paradise, St. Ambrose, XIV, 700.—What disturbances it commonly brings into a household, ibid., 705.—Those who serve gluttony and the belly walk in the womb, ibid., 312.—How ridiculous and hateful drunkenness is among common people is set forth in an elegant description, ibid., 712, 718.—And especially among military men, ibid., 713.—Likewise among women, ibid., 719.—The effects of drunkenness; how great are the evils of drunkenness and wine, ibid., 701, 705, 718, 721.—Gluttony soon brings forth foolish merriment, buffoonery, uncleanness, much talking, and dullness of the faculties of understanding, id., XVII, 759.—Adam lost paradise through food; Esau lost the honor of primogeniture through lentils; Judas cast down the lofty dignity of the apostolate through a morsel, ibid., 661.

Drunkenness and overindulgence exhaust the treasure of souls, St. Jerome, XXII, 818.—Through wine a man’s senses are overthrown, his feet stumble, his mind wavers, and sexual desire is inflamed, id., XXVI, 417.—Drunkenness arises from various causes, 416 ff.—Lust is always joined to it, ibid.—Its effects, 566, 667.—A drunkard is never chaste, ibid.
