Drunkenness entangles words, distorts the sight, produces torments of the stomach; it drives out modesty itself from the mind and the guard of the mouth, and breaks the seal of chastity, ibid.---For gluttons, the fruits of trees are not enough, nor the roots of plants, nor fish of the sea, nor beasts of the earth, nor birds of heaven; spices are sought and aromatics are purchased, Innocent III, CCXVII, 723.---What is more shameful than a drunkard, whose mouth stinks, whose body trembles, who promises much and betrays secrets, whose mind is estranged and face transformed? ibid., 724.---Gluttony closed paradise, sold Esau’s birthright, hanged the baker, beheaded the Baptist, ibid.---Drunkenness laid bare shameful things, committed incest, killed the king’s son, and slaughtered the commander of an army, ibid.

## VI.—On Anger

Anger is an immoderate movement of the mind by which someone violently repels things displeasing to him. “Immoderate movement”: for there is also a movement of the mind moderated by reason, by which someone, with an impulse tempered by reason, violently repels things that rightly displease him; this anger is praiseworthy. “Be angry, and do not sin,” says the royal Prophet. One must know, says St Gregory the Great, that anger stirred by impatience is one thing, while anger formed by zeal for justice is another. The former is generated by vice, the latter by virtue.

Anger is just and reasonable when it is aroused for a just cause consistent with reason—for example, to repel evil or accomplish some good—and does not grow hot too immoderately. Phinehas, kindled by this anger, appeased the Lord. Christ himself stirred it up in himself when he drove sellers and buyers from the Temple. This anger is called zeal.

Anger is sin when it is aroused in a person by wicked affections and desires: the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life. From this threefold source, as is known, flows every kind of sin, and therefore anger also, since a person is thus disposed that he is ready violently to repel whatever opposes his desires. Even when anger is moved by a just cause, it can be sin—for instance, if it boils up too violently, or if it is stirred without necessity, or through pride. For even in just matters pride can excite anger: the proud cannot endure any contradiction and are therefore more quickly moved to anger. Anger should be stirred only when there is hope that by this means evil may be driven away or good accomplished. Nor should you think such necessity imaginary; for some people have such a disposition that they are never either turned away from evil or effectively stirred toward good unless you move against them with vehement incitement and salutary anger. This salutary impulse is sometimes more effective both to awaken the sinner and to give courage to the righteous. But much prudence is necessary here; for unless zeal is tempered by prudence, it does much harm rather than good.

The daughters of anger are contentions, quarrels, enmities, lawsuits, insults, outcries, acts of revenge, killings, mental fear, indignation, and blasphemy.

Anger can be either mortal or venial sin. It is mortal if it is more violent, if it has become entrenched, if it is accompanied by hatred of one’s neighbour or a deliberate desire for revenge, if it gives grave scandal—in short, if it extinguishes charity in the heart. But it is venial sin if it is slight, not long-lasting, and does not extinguish charity in the heart.

The remedies for anger are to follow reason and faith as one’s guides in all things; to do nothing from desire, nothing from headlong impulse, but everything with serious deliberation; and to keep the mind trained in prayer, silence, and patience.

These matters are indicated in the following references.

Anger arising from impatience, Tertullian, I, 1258.---Whether anger is evil, Lactantius, VI, 693.---It strips us of the name of human beings, ibid., 701.---For what use it was given by God, ibid., 704.---The stages and effects of anger, St Hilary, IX, 374.---One should not be angry with those from whom one suffers anything, but pity their wretched lot, ibid., 712.---In the Gospel, causeless anger incurs the same punishment as murder does in the Law, ibid., 639.

How grave a passion anger is, St Ambrose, XIV, 975.---It is excellent to temper emotion with counsel; and it is judged no lesser virtue to restrain irascibility than never to be angry at all, the same, XV, 1650.---If we are angry, let our emotion receive a movement according to nature, not sin contrary to nature, ibid., 1204.---It is better to find the praise of clemency in indignation than to rouse anger for revenge, ibid., 1590.---Irascibility must be avoided, and how, ibid., 50.---At every time, as far as possible, the Christian man ought to restrain irascibility, especially when he approaches prayer, ibid., 457.---Anger is a natural movement, which usually tends to the correction of the offender, the same, XVII, 390.---A mind in anger necessarily thinks evil thoughts, ibid., 391.---In anger nobody recognizes what is useful, ibid., 399.---What anger toward offenders ought to be like, ibid., 593.---When it has boiled beyond measure, it cruelly wounds the mind, dulls the understanding, changes the tongue, darkens the eyes, and throws the whole body into disorder, ibid., 757.---From it immediately arise quarrels, insults, shouting, indignation, swelling of mind, and blasphemies, ibid.---Anger puts the face of a lion upon us, St Jerome, XXII, 478.---The anger of a man proceeds from a disturbed mind, the same, XXIII, 540.---It is justice to mitigate anger by swift repentance, ibid.---It is safer to endure the rage of a lion than that of a human being, ibid., 58.---Anger appointed for the correction and instruction of inferiors, ibid., 1062.---Anger is always joined to pride; and if a wise man is irascible, he is convicted of foolishness, ibid.---The nature of anger, the same, XXV, 953; XXVI, 516.---What anger is, St Augustine, XL, 140.---It is a turbulent desire to remove obstacles to ease of action, the same, XXXIII, 73.---It is a movement of the mind urging the infliction of punishment, the same, XXXVI, 92.---It is the desire for revenge, the same, XXXVIII, 396; XLI, 424.---Anger is used to mean vengeance, the same, XLII, 410.---The empty pretexts of anger, the same, XL, 1096.---Its stages, ibid.---Its effects, ibid.---How much harm anger does, the same, XXXIX, 1131.---The true light is justice and wisdom; XXXVI, 189; XXXVIII, 324, 397.---Anger is a shoot which, unless quickly uprooted, grows into a beam, the same, XXXVI, 632, 397.---One who harbours anger avoids an enemy outside himself, while retaining a far worse one in his heart, the same, XXXVIII, 1045.---As vinegar corrupts a vessel if it remains there too long, so anger corrupts the heart if it lasts into another day, the same, XXXIII, 958.---Description of an angry person and another who bears patiently, the same, XXXVII, 1241.---Even brief anger must be avoided, Cassian, XLIX, 341, 342.---How many evils it produces, ibid., 342 ff.---How it is cured, ibid., 339.---Its three kinds, ibid., 626.---The poison and nature of irascibility, ibid., 323.---How the sin of irascibility is expiated, ibid., 342, 1030.---It is most pestilential to retain anger in the breast and conceal it, ibid., 340.

## VII.—On Acedia, or Sadness

*Acedia*, or sloth, is distaste for the good commanded us by God, whereby a dejected mind does not raise itself to fulfil it.

Those guilty of the sin of acedia are:

1. Those who do not perform their duty according to the state to which they have been called by God; those who will not learn what is necessary to salvation; those who obstinately refuse the offices to which God calls them.
2. Those who live sluggishly in idleness.
3. Those who waste time in empty conversations, walks, visits, games and pleasures, and other trifles and follies of that kind.
4. Those who neglect the things of God and those things absolutely necessary for attaining salvation; for example, those who are sluggish in prayer and in other matters to which they are bound by office.
5. Those who postpone their repentance; who do not labour continually to uproot their vices; who do not strive to make new progress daily and to grow, as the Apostle says, “in the grace and knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

The sources of acedia are the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life; for people give themselves to acedia because they do not wish to constrain themselves and their desires. The daughters of acedia are:

1. Malice, by which spiritual goods are attacked, since acedia induces hatred of them.
2. Rancour or indignation against those who impel one toward God.
3. Faint-heartedness, or abjection of mind, by which commandments are neglected as though too arduous.
4. Despair, by which someone casts aside all care for salvation through excessive distrust, judging attainment of salvation impossible.
5. Torpor, or a certain slackness of mind in observing commandments, so that they are either wholly omitted or performed negligently.
6. Wandering of mind, by which the soul, through weariness of spiritual things, turns itself outward in order to take pleasure in external things.

To these may be added the avoidance of every labour, excessive sleep, carousing, hatred of truth, hardness of heart, and other things of this kind.

Acedia is a deadly sin if it is grave and extinguishes charity. “Cast the useless servant into the outer darkness,” says Christ. To drive out acedia, one must diligently investigate and carefully examine by meditation what God requires of all Christians without exception, and what he requires differently of others in view of their state, condition, disposition, and temperament; and, once all these things have been discovered, one must make every effort and employ all diligence to fulfil them carefully and faithfully. To understand this more perfectly, note that, besides what God requires of all Christians generally, and besides what is proper to each person’s state and condition, there are duties proper to each individual. For example, God requires one thing from a sinful person and another from someone of the same condition who does not need severe repentance; one thing from the fervent, another from the more lukewarm; one thing from the sick, another from the healthy; one thing amid adversity, another amid prosperity. Thus duties vary according to the diverse dispositions, states, and circumstances of individuals. As each person is disposed, as each stands in relation to others, as condition allows, and as occasion requires, so each must serve God. Therefore one must diligently investigate what God wills and what he requires from all and from individuals, and must do all this with no less diligence. Whoever takes little care either to know or to accomplish these things sins through acedia.

The remedies for acedia are prayer, continuous and tireless labour, repentance, mortification of the flesh, and reading pious books. Above all, continual meditation on death and eternity, and on other things that are accustomed to move people more effectively to pursue the business of salvation, is conducive to fleeing acedia. This meditation is especially helpful for avoiding every other sin as well. . . .

A fuller understanding of all these matters will be possessed by one who chooses to apply himself diligently to the following references.

Acedia described, Cassian, XLIX, 360.---Closely related to sadness, it especially attacks solitaries about noon, ibid.---It blinds the mind to every contemplation of virtues, ibid., 369.---How pestilential its effects are, ibid., 370.---How acedia is overcome, ibid., 396.---Whence it arises, ibid., 620.---Sloth must be avoided, St Benedict, LXVI, 322.---Acedia is the beginning of departure from God, *Lives of the Fathers*, LXXIII, 924.---How it is overcome, ibid., 900.---Even the guarding of one’s cell for God’s sake drives acedia away, ibid.---Likewise, thought of future things, ibid., 780.---The vice of acedia is driven away if heavenly goods are always contemplated, St Gregory, LXXIII, 364.---The instability of acedia must be corrected by steadfast gentleness and residence in one place, St Columbanus, LXXX, 260.---On torpor of mind and sloth, Taio, the same, 947, 948.---Acedia is a pest by which the idle person, languishing in carnal desires, neither rejoices in spiritual work nor delights in the salvation of his soul, Alcuin, CI, 635.---It infects the mind with many miseries. which, with Lot’s wife, looks back toward Sodom; which causes the monk’s vow to grow lukewarm; which desires to use more delicate foods and recline on softer beds; which fears undertaking great things and grows weary of what it has begun, Alanus of Lille, CCX, 126.---This is what keeps the cleric from study, nourishes vices, excludes virtues, gives birth to lust, sows detractions, and produces quarrels, ibid. O human being! Why is it that other creatures devote themselves to the duties assigned them? The sun completes its yearly course; the moon moves through its monthly changes; brute animals do not languish in the exercises of their nature; but you alone, lulled by sloth, depart from your duty, deform the image of God within you, live while dying, and die while living. Let at least the industry of the ant move you to shame, ibid., 127.---How ruinous sluggishness is, ibid., 128.---When David sat idle in the palace, he fell into adultery. This is the cowardice that offers a man unarmed to the devil, exposes him naked to suggestion, and weak to temptation, ibid.---It calls the devil to battle, the flesh to wantonness, the mouth to gluttony, and the mind to negligence, ibid.

There is a threefold sleep: of negligence, ignorance, and concupiscence, [Col. 0830] Innocent III, CCXVII, 322. One must rise from this threefold sleep, ibid.---Nothing is more friendly to iniquity than negligence. From ignorance arise error, heresy, unbelief, and excuse in sins, ibid.---What do we think or do all day? ibid., 323.---We weave spiders’ webs; we consume our days; we squander our time on vain pursuits, wicked works, and pleasures of the flesh, ibid. and following.

## NOTICE

This index, which could more easily than any other have been extended without limit, has deliberately been abbreviated and reduced. Very many things are omitted, either because they have already been treated in the preceding indices—for example, On the Decalogue, On Love of Enemies, On the Virtues, where contraries cure contraries, On the Vices, etc. Thus, for example, here also we refer to the preceding index on matters relating to the seven capital vices: pride, avarice, lust, envy, gluttony, anger, and acedia; and so often concerning other vices and human defects, although we pass over many things which might seem to belong specifically to this index. . . . The reader, noticing the omissions, will from his own mind be led to the indices that explain them, and will readily grant us pardon.

## [INDEX OF VICES]

### FLATTERY

Flattery is praise that is either false or excessive. Whoever ingratiates himself with his neighbour by false praises, or exceeds the proper measure in true praises, flatters.

Flattery is a kind of lie especially harmful to one’s neighbour, and is therefore a sin.

Flattery, says St Jerome, in Book *Against the Pelagians*, is always treacherous, crafty, and ingratiating. The flatterer is aptly defined among philosophers as a “friendly enemy.” Truth is bitter, severe of countenance, and sad, and it offends those who are corrected. Hence the Apostle says: “Have I become your enemy because I tell you the truth?” And the comic poet says: “Compliance produces friends; truth, hatred.”

“The tongues of flatterers,” says St Augustine, on Psalm X, no. 21, “bind souls in sins. For it pleases people to do those things in which they not only do not fear a reprover, but are even praised by a hearer.”

“He who justifies the wicked and he who condemns the just,” says St Gregory the Great, Book XVIII of the *Moralia*, no. 4, “are both abominable before God. For there are some who, while extolling people’s evil deeds with praises, increase the very things which they ought to have reproved. Thus it is said through the prophet: ‘Woe to those who sew cushions beneath every elbow of the hand, and make pillows beneath the head of every age.’ A cushion is placed in order that one may rest more comfortably. Whoever flatters those doing evil therefore places a cushion beneath the head or elbow of one lying down, so that one who ought to have been corrected for his fault may rest softly in it, supported by praises. Hence again it is written: ‘He builds a wall, but they plaster it.’ For the wall signifies the hardness of sin. To build a wall, therefore, is to construct for oneself obstacles of sin. But those flatter people who commit sins plaster the wall, so that what the others build by acting perversely, they themselves by flattery render, as it were, bright. But the holy man, just as he does not esteem evil things to be good, so refuses to judge good things of evil people.”

### ADULTERY

“A woman,” says the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 7:4, “does not have authority over her own body, but her husband does; and likewise a husband does not have authority over his own body, but his wife does.” The violation of this fidelity is called adultery, when, whether prompted by one’s own lust or by another’s consent, one lies with another man or woman contrary to the marriage covenant. Thus the fidelity is broken which, even in bodily and lowly matters, is a great good of the soul; and it is therefore certain that it ought to be preferred even to bodily safety, by which our very life is sustained.

Married persons therefore owe one another not only the fidelity of sexual union for the sake of begetting children, which is the first fellowship of the human race in this mortality, but also the mutual bearing of weakness. To avoid unlawful sexual intercourse, there is, in a sense, mutual servitude: thus, if perpetual continence pleases one of them, it cannot be practised without the other’s consent. For this is why a wife does not have authority over her own body, but her husband does; likewise, a husband does not have authority over his own body, but his wife does: so that, when either seeks something not for the begetting of children but because of weakness and incontinence, whether the wife from her husband or the husband from his wife, neither may deny the other, lest through this they fall into condemnable corruptions through Satan’s temptation, because of the incontinence of both or of either one. Marital intercourse for the purpose of generation has no fault; intercourse to satisfy concupiscence, though with one’s spouse, has a venial fault on account of fidelity to the marriage-bed; but adultery or fornication has a deadly fault. . . .

On adultery, see the Index *On the Decalogue*, under the article on the sixth commandment; the preceding index, under the article *On Lust*; and this index, under *On Fornication*.

### AMBITION

The ambitious person is always fearful, always attentive lest he say or do anything displeasing in people’s eyes. He feigns humility, pretends respectability, displays affability, shows kindness, follows and serves, honours everyone, bows to all, frequents courts, visits great men, rises to greet them and embraces them, applauds and flatters, Innocent III, CCXVII, 727.

Ambition, says St Bernard, Sermon 6 on the Psalm, no. 4: “A subtle evil, a secret poison, a hidden plague, an artificer of deceit, mother of hypocrisy, parent of envy, origin of vices, tinder of crimes, rust upon virtues, moth of holiness, blinder of hearts; out of remedies creating diseases, out of medicine producing languor, stripping away the wedding garment, and depriving the exercises of virtues of the fruit of piety. How many has this plague wickedly overthrown and shamefully cast down! . . . And what nourishes this worm but alienation of mind and forgetfulness of truth? . . .”

## EXAMPLES OF AMBITION

Matthew 20:20 ff.: “Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee came to him [Jesus] with her sons, worshipping and asking something of him. And he said to her, ‘What do you wish?’ She said to him, ‘Say that these two sons of mine may sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your kingdom.’ But Jesus answered and said, ‘You do not know what you ask.’ And when the ten heard it, they were indignant with the two brothers. But Jesus called them to himself and said, ‘You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them . . . ,’ etc.”

Luke 22:24 ff.: “And there arose also a dispute among them, which of them seemed to be the greater. And he said to them: ‘The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who exercise authority over them are called benefactors; but you are not so . . .’”

As is apparent from these passages, ambition is the sin by which someone desires honour in a disordered way—either honour which he does not deserve, or honour which he refers not to God but solely to his own advantage. Honour entails a certain reverence shown to someone as testimony to that person’s excellence.

But two points must be considered concerning a human being’s excellence. First, that by which a person excels does not come from himself, but is something, as it were, divine within him. Therefore honour is due chiefly, not to him, but to God. Secondly, that in which a person excels is given him by God so that he may benefit others by it. Hence a person should take pleasure in the testimony to his excellence shown by others only insofar as it opens a way for him to benefit others.

The desire for honour may be disordered in three ways. First, when someone desires testimony to an excellence which he does not possess: this is to desire honour beyond one’s proper measure. Secondly, when one desires honour for oneself without referring it to God. Thirdly, when one’s desire rests in honour itself, without referring that honour to the benefit of others. Ambition, therefore, signifies a disordered desire for honour. Hence it is clear that ambition is always a sin. St Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, II–II, question 131, article 3, conclusion.

## ARROGANCE

It is an inward evil by which those who please themselves concerning themselves become vain, though they please no one else, or displease others, and do not even seek to please others. But those who please themselves greatly displease God: not merely because they treat things not good as though they were good, but also because they treat God’s goods as their own; or because, although rejoicing in them as from your grace, they do not rejoice in fellowship with others, but envy others for them. St Augustine, *Confessions*, book X, chapter 39, no. 64.

For it is no slight ground of condemnation to glory privately in a good that is given in common: to know from whom one received the good, yet not know how one ought to use what one has received. There are, indeed, four forms in which all the swelling pride of the arrogant is displayed: when they think that they possess a good from themselves; or, if they believe it was given them from above, think they received it because of their own merits; or when they boast of possessing what they do not possess.

For one who boasted that he had a good from himself is addressed through the Apostle: “What have you that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” Again, lest we should believe that the good of grace is given us for our preceding merits, the same Apostle warns us: “By grace you have been saved through faith; and this is not from yourselves, but is the gift of God—not from works, lest anyone should boast.” . . . Again, some boast that they possess what they do not possess, as the divine voice says through the prophet concerning Moab: “I know his pride and his arrogance, and that his strength is not commensurate with it.” And as it is said to the angel of the Church of Laodicea: “Because you say, ‘I am rich, I have become wealthy, and I need nothing,’ and do not know that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked.”

Again, some, despising others, seek to appear to possess in a singular fashion the good which they have. Hence the Pharisee went down from the temple without justification because, assigning to himself, as though uniquely, the merit of good works, he preferred himself to the praying publican. In this fourth form of arrogance, therefore, the human mind frequently falls: it glories in possessing, in a singular fashion, what it possesses. Yet in this it approaches more closely to diabolical likeness; for whoever rejoices in possessing a good uniquely, whoever seeks to appear higher than others, imitates him who, despising the good of fellowship with the angels, proudly desired likeness to the Most High and, by an unrighteous desire, strove to break forth, as it were, to a certain pinnacle of singularity.

A question concerning these matters is treated below.

## AUDACITY

One sins through audacity when one trusts in one’s own powers, without any help from God, believing that one can attain salvation or do some good.

Anyone who begins, says St Bernard, Sermon 85 on the *Song of Songs*, continuation, no. 5, to strive toward perfection of virtue will surely know how steep the ascent is, and how vain the endeavour without the Word’s help. . . . What a voice of confidence: “I can do all things in him who strengthens me.” Thus, supported by the Word and clothed with power from on high, no force, no fraud, no allurement will thereafter be able either to cast him down while he stands or to subdue him as ruler. . . . Finally, he who did not stand in the truth was not supported by the Word; he trusted in his own strength. For he said: “I will sit upon the mountain of the covenant”; but, God judging otherwise, he fell, as the Lord says: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven.”

If the human mind, says St Augustine, Sermon 2 on Psalm 31, no. 1, should wholly surrender itself to its own weakness and incline itself to this thought, saying that God’s mercy is so prepared at the end for all sinners who persist in any sins whatsoever, provided only that they believe God delivers and forgives, that none of the wicked faithful will perish—that is, none of those who say to themselves: “What do you want me to do? Though I defile myself by whatever crimes and shameful deeds, though I sin ever so much, God in his mercy delivers me, because I have believed in him”—then the person who says none such will perish is inclined by an evil thought toward impunity for sins. And that righteous God . . . finds a person who presumes wrongly concerning him and abuses God’s mercy for his own destruction, and he must condemn him. Such a thought, therefore, hurls a person down. . . . What, then, were you saying, you who sin in hope? “Whenever I convert, God will forgive me everything; I shall do whatever I please.” . . . You always wait, and promise yourself very much from God’s mercy. He who says, “God is good and merciful; I shall do what pleases me; I shall let loose the reins to my pleasures and desires; I shall fulfil the desires of my soul,” is deceived by hoping. Why this? Because God is merciful, good, and gentle. . . . It must be feared that hope may kill you, and that, while you hope greatly in mercy, you may fall into judgment.

Here is the audacity treated in the following references.

## AUGURIES

Augury, which belongs to the magical art, is named from birds: when someone attempts to foreknow future events by birds’ cries or movements, or by those of any animals whatsoever, or by human sneezes or the twitching of limbs. This generally belongs either to *angurium*, so called from the chattering of birds, or to auspice, so called from the observation of birds. Hence what pertains in these matters to the ears is called augury, from birds’ chattering; and what pertains to the eyes is called auspice, from the observation of birds.

To divine by auguries, says St Thomas, contrary to the order of nature or of divine Providence, is superstitious and unlawful. The movements or cries of birds, or any dispositions whatsoever observed in such matters, plainly are not causes of future events; hence future things cannot be known from them as from causes. . . .

“Do not practise divination, nor seek auguries,” says Scripture.

And the Council of Ancyra, I, A.D. 314, chapter 23, says: “Those who observe auguries or auspices . . . according to the custom of the Gentiles, or bring persons of this sort into their houses . . . having confessed, shall perform penance for five years, according to the rules established of old. . . .”

To the class of *anguria* belong all bindings and remedies which even the medical art condemns: whether charms, certain signs called characters, certain things to be hung up or tied on, or things somehow fitted, not for the regulation of bodies but for certain hidden or even manifest signs, which people call by the milder name of “physical,” so that they may seem to confer benefit by nature rather than entangle people in superstition.

To these are joined, says St Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, book II, chapter 20, no. 31, thousands of utterly vain observances: for example, if some limb twitches; if, when friends are walking together, a stone, dog, or child comes between them. And the fact that they tread on the stone, as though it severed friendship, is less offensive than that they strike an innocent child with a blow if he crosses between people walking side by side. Yet dogs sometimes avenge this injury on children; for some people are so superstitious that they dare even strike a dog that has come between them, not without punishment. For sometimes that dog quickly sends the person who struck it, from a vain remedy, to a true physician. So also with such practices as these: treading on a threshold when one passes before one’s house; returning to bed if one sneezes while putting on one’s shoes; returning home if one stumbles while setting out; trembling more at the suspicion of coming evil when clothes have been gnawed by mice than grieving at the present damage.

Hence Cato’s elegant saying. When a man consulted him because mice had gnawed through his shoes, he replied that this was no portent; but it would truly have been a portent if the mice had been gnawed by the shoes.

See in this Index, “SUPERSTITIONS.”

## CALUMNY

Calumny, which is a branch of detraction and denotes whatever is said against a neighbour’s reputation, occurs when what is said against one’s neighbour is false; for if it were true, it would be reviling. But we shall treat these matters under the name of detraction or calumny.

Calumny exists in greater or lesser degree: first, when a false crime is imputed to a neighbour; secondly, when a true crime is magnified in speech; thirdly, when something hidden is publicized; fourthly, when another’s deeds or words are rashly interpreted in a bad sense, if this is done in speech; fifthly, when outstanding deeds are minimized in speech or praised coldly where an occasion for praise presents itself; sixthly, even silence sometimes takes the place of calumny, if someone, for example, remains completely silent when he ought by all means to praise another’s outstanding act, and the bystanders may take that silence as an offence against the neighbour.

Calumny is altogether a grave sin, for by it a neighbour’s reputation is injured and thus wrong is done to one’s neighbour: “Revilers shall not possess the kingdom of God,” says the Apostle.

## BLASPHEMY

Blasphemy is an insulting and contumelious word directed against God or the saints; that is, a word by which some defects are attributed to God or some perfections are denied him. For example, a person would be blasphemous who denied that God is just, almighty, or truthful; he would be blasphemous who said that God is the author of sin or subject to change, and so forth. Indeed, insulting words against the saints are counted among blasphemies, because the injury inflicted on the saints rebounds upon God himself, just as honour shown to the saints is referred to God.

There is scarcely any sin more serious than blasphemy. [Col. 0835] This is clear from the penalties imposed upon blasphemers at every period. Under the Mosaic law blasphemers were overwhelmed with stones, Numbers 24:10 ff. God consigned one hundred and twenty-seven thousand Syrians to death in punishment for the blasphemous word spoken by Ben-hadad, king of Syria, 3 Kings 20:19 ff. Because of the blasphemy uttered by Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, one hundred and eighty-five thousand of his army perished in a single night, destroyed by an angel, 4 Kings 19:22 ff. The Apostle delivered Hymenaeus and Alexander to Satan, that they might learn not to blaspheme, 1 Timothy 1:20.

According to the ancient ordinances of the kings of France, blasphemers ought to be disgraced by an exemplary public punishment, which they call an honourable amends; moreover, after their tongues have been pierced and their lips slit, they are to be punished by exile. According to the canon of the last Council of Narbonne, they are to be struck with excommunication. We append certain provisions concerning them, namely an ordinance of the year 1617:

“And if any adventurers be found who have used . . . execrable blasphemies, we will that they be punished by justice with such and similar penalties . . . at the discretion of justice; and the said execrable blasphemers, before suffering death, shall have their throat opened with a hot iron, and their tongue drawn out and cut beneath; and this done, they shall be hanged and fastened to the gibbet or gallows, and strangled according to their deserts. Given at Lyons, 25 September 1525, and the ninth year of our reign” (Francis I).

Henry II, in the year 1550: “The soldier who blasphemes the name of God in vain shall be placed in the public square in the pillory on three separate days, for three hours each time; and at the end of these, bareheaded, he shall ask God’s forgiveness.”

The Council of Narbonne says: “By what penalty those who with sacrilegious mouth blaspheme the holy name of God, and of our Saviour Jesus Christ, and of the Virgin Mary, Mother of God, or of other saints, ought to be punished, is plainly established by God’s own words, when he commands that the blasphemer, cast outside the camp, be stoned. Therefore we decree that if anyone with impure mouth shall blaspheme . . . he shall be punished . . . and, expelled from the assembly of Catholics, be publicly declared excommunicated by the parish priest.”

On these matters see the Index on the Decalogue, article “On the Second Commandment of God.”

## CUPIDITY

“Covetousness is the root of all evils.” No one can undertake spiritual battles perfectly unless he has first subdued the pleasures of the flesh. A mind that desires the earthly and transitory things of this world cannot be free to contemplate God. The eye of the mind cannot see lofty things if the dust of earthly covetousness closes it. Cupidity is a grave sin; it is the material of all crimes. It is no wonder that those dying are assigned to the fires of hell, when, while living, they did not extinguish the flame of their cupidity.

He who has a desire of possessing, even if he possesses nothing, gains nothing by it. Bodily nakedness profits us nothing if we have a desire for clothing. Judas sold Christ through cupidity. We are born naked into this life, and naked we shall depart from it. Why, then, do we desire earthly and transitory things? If we believe that this world’s goods will perish, why do we love them with so great an affection? If we love this world’s earthly and transitory things more than we ought, we sin. Therefore, if cupidity is the root of all evils, we must expel it from our hearts, so that the other offspring of vices may not sprout and perverse cupidity may not be in us. . . .

## CURIOSITY

The holy Fathers identified curiosity with “the desire of the eyes,” for they judged it to belong not only to the outer but also to the inner person.

Every superfluous beauty that the eyes love in varied forms, bright and pleasing colours, various works of craftsmanship, garments, shoes, vessels, paintings, sculptures, and diverse fabrications exceeding necessary and moderate use belongs to outward curiosity. Lovers of the world seek all these things for the eyes’ enticements, following outwardly what they themselves make, abandoning inwardly him by whom they were made, and destroying what they were made to be.

Inward curiosity chiefly consists in three things: namely, the desire for harmful or vain knowledge; investigation of another’s life, not in order to imitate it, but to envy it if it is good or to mock it if it is evil; or merely from curiosity in order to know whether it is evil or good; and lastly a restless curiosity concerning knowledge of worldly matters or actions.

From all these things, when minds are taken captive, no slight trouble is born—whether such pursuits are exercised without restraint, or whether those who delight in exercising them are forbidden. Hence it is that many who have given their minds to vain philosophy, and who are also accustomed to meditate on the *Eclogues* alongside the Gospels, to read Horace with the prophets, Cicero with Paul, to play with verse and weave amorous material in wanton songs, or challenge each other in readings . . .

Hence too, after we have in some manner gone out from ourselves by devoting the whole day to vain spectacles or attentively listening to rumours, when we return to ourselves we introduce again the images of vanities. Carrying a heart full of images even to the place of our rest, we spend sleepless nights on the most foolish vanity: with utterly foolish presumption we depict before our eyes the battles of kings and victories of commanders, and arrange idle wanderings even during our prayers.

There is yet another, most evil, kind of curiosity, by which only those conscious to themselves of great virtues are tempted: namely, an examination of one’s own holiness by displaying miracles. This is to tempt God. . . . etc.

Look first to your own faults rather than those of others. . . . Do not seek what anyone says or does. Beware of curiosity. Abandon concern with another’s life. Let no curiosity deceive your mind; let no desire for detestable curiosity steal upon you; let there be no concern in you to know hidden things. Beware of investigating things which you ought not to know; pass over as a secret whatever you have not learned on the authority of Holy Scripture; seek nothing beyond what is written; investigate nothing further than the divine writings show. Never desire to know what you ought not to know. . . .

## DRUNKENNESS

Let us flee drunkenness, lest we incur the crime of lust. . . . For God gave us wine for gladness of heart, not for drunkenness. Therefore let us drink not as much as gluttony demands, but as much as the weakness of nature requires. Let us not, then, turn to destruction what has been granted for the healing of our bodies.

I ask you, tell those subject to you in your household that many have committed murders and fornications and have not even refused death; others, through wine, have been seized by demons. Drunkenness is nothing other than a most manifest demon. The drunkard thinks he is doing something excellent when he has been hurled into precipices. Through drunkenness he is armed for curses and insults against his neighbours; his mind is changed and his tongue stammers. Such a man, while thinking that he drinks wine, is drunk by wine. Very many people have contracted the greatest weakness through wine and have been unable to regain their former strength, because they did not restrain the burning of gluttony.

For as a fish hastens with greedy jaws to swallow bait and suddenly finds the hook within its jaws, so the drunkard receives into himself wine, his enemy, which immediately drives him toward every most shameful deed; and so a rational human being is captured like an irrational animal.

Plutarch relates this concerning Pyrrhus: “Pyrrhus had heard that certain young men, while drinking, had fiercely abused him with many insults. On the following day he ordered them all brought before him, and first asked one of them whether they had said such things about him. He replied without hesitation: ‘Such things indeed; and we would have said more, if we had had more wine.’ . . .”

Drunkenness and its consequences are treated in the preceding Index, in the article “On Gluttony.”

## FEAR

A human being willingly entangles himself in love of bodies and vanity; but, willing or unwilling, he is tormented by fear and pain over their loss—whether the bodies themselves are taken away or he himself is blamed. For love of perishable things is, as it were, a source of useless fears, pains, and every anxiety. . . . Either completely extinguish desire, or prepare yourself to be troubled—that is, to fear and grieve over what you ought not. . . . The human soul is tormented within itself as long as it can be tormented—that is, as long as it loves anything besides God. . . .

As cold comes from ice, so useless fear and other miseries invade the soul from love of temporal things. Remove from yourself everything that gives you cause for fear. . . . For nothing should be feared except what can and ought to be avoided, namely sin.

Whatever suffering you experience, whether through fear or anger, . . . attribute it solely to yourself—that is, to your own desire, ignorance, or sluggishness. There are four fears: two good and two evil. . . . Evil fear is a kind of passion or disturbance of mind, arising neither from faith nor from the Spirit of God. That fear is evil because it disturbs the mind over what ought not to disturb it: namely, the loss of worldly wealth or approaching adversities which ought to have been endured courageously for the sake of usefulness.

Likewise, another evil fear comes indeed from faith, but not from the Spirit of God. By it the mind is sometimes disturbed, but does not amend itself. . . . All demons have this fear, described in James 2, always and without exception, because “they believe and tremble.” But not all evil human beings have it; many who are desperate do. In Acts 24, Felix trembled, but did not amend himself. . . . The first man feared with this fear. . . . For he did not fear rightly when he hid himself and refused to confess his fault.

Good and evil fears differ because evil fear is passion and disturbance, whereas good fear is peace and rest of mind. . . . Good fear—but not yet the perfect and highest fear which perfect charity casts out—is that which comes from faith and from the Spirit of God; the others are not so. . . . Finally, concerning every sort of fear—this fear, servile fear, and the others—a question is treated in the following references.

## FORNICATION

St John Chrysostom, Homily 18 on Matthew, chapter 5: [lacuna] Christ not only said that the adulterer must be punished [lacuna] but also restrains the unchaste gaze: “For whoever,” he says, “looks at a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.” That is to say: whoever makes it his business to gaze too curiously upon beautiful bodies, to hunt after attractive faces, to feed his soul with such a spectacle, and to fix impure eyes even upon lovely countenances. For the Lord was not content to come merely to turn the body away from evil acts, but first to turn the soul also away from thoughts of this kind. [lacuna]

“How,” you ask, “can we be freed from lust?” Indeed, if we wish, it is possible even to mortify it itself, and to restrain it from breaking forth into action. [lacuna] For the person who strives to look upon elegant faces especially kindles for himself the furnace of this passion; making his soul captive, he quickly leads it also into action. [lacuna] For he did not simply say, “Whoever has lusted”; for someone may lust even while remaining within the secret places of the mind. Rather: “Whoever,” he says, “looks at a woman in order to lust after her,” that is, whoever has summoned lust to himself, and, although nothing at all compels him, has suddenly unleashed a wild beast upon a thought at rest. For this is no longer a matter of nature, but wholly of one’s own indolence; and it was certainly forbidden long ago even by the old Law: “Do not,” it says, “learn another’s beauty.”

Then, lest anyone should say, “But what if I look and yet am not captured?” he restrained the gaze, lest, trusting in such licence, one should at some time fall even into sin. “But what,” you ask, “if I see and do lust, yet do nothing at that moment?” Even so you are already numbered among adulterers. For the Lawgiver has pronounced judgment, and there is no need to dispute the matter further with scruple and anxiety. For if you look thus once, twice, or three times, perhaps you can restrain your mind; but if you do it frequently, willingly kindling this furnace, you will be captured, though protected. For it does not lie outside human nature and human hazard.

Just as, when we see a sword held by a child, even if we do not yet see anyone wounded by it, we nevertheless strike the child and forbid him ever again to touch it, so God also restrains the shameless gaze before the deed itself, lest you should at some point fall into the action itself. For whoever has once kindled the flame of desire, even when the woman he saw is absent, continually paints within himself images of shameful things, and from these often proceeds to the act itself. Christ also destroyed those embraces that occur in the heart alone. What, then, will those answer here who have dared rashly to live with virgins?

Every unclean defilement is called fornication, although each person may take pleasure in a different kind of shamefulness. For various crimes are born from the delight of fornication, by which the kingdom of God is closed. [lacuna] Fornication defiles not only the body but also the conscience. One who lives dissolutely, though he seems alive, is nevertheless dead. Fornication is a grave sin. [lacuna] The eyes are the messengers of fornication. [lacuna] Dinah, etc.; David, etc.; Samson, etc. [lacuna]

## THEFT

Those are guilty of theft who either unjustly take or retain the property of others, and inflict injury or loss upon their neighbour’s goods. This is done either secretly, while one’s neighbour is unaware; or by fraud, while one’s neighbour is deceived; or against the neighbour’s will, while he suffers violence. It is astonishing how widely this sin spreads! In scarcely any rank of life are persons found who are free from it. And, what is more lamentable, scarcely anyone regards it as a religious obligation not to seize what belongs to another: wives, children, slaves, merchants, magistrates, and other administrators of public offices, litigants, advocates, legal procurators, craftsmen, labourers, rich and poor alike—all these repeatedly fall into theft, whether through ignorance, insufficient caution, or less moral seriousness than is fitting.

For example, merchants and traders are guilty of theft:

1. When they use false weights and measures;
2. When they sell counterfeit and deceptive, or defective, merchandise as good and genuine;
3. When they exploit either their neighbour’s need or ignorance in order to sell at too high a price or buy at too low a price;
4. When they practise fraudulent monopolies;
5. When, in buying or selling, they employ bad faith or fraud in any other way. [lacuna]

On these matters and similar matters proper to each rank, see the Index on the Decalogue, under the article on the seventh commandment.

## HYPOCRISY

What is hypocrisy? It is an appearance artfully composed, which does one thing in fact and promises another in its countenance. This flourished among the Pharisees through knowledge that puffed them up. [lacuna] Hypocrisy was in their faces; dropsy of envy was in their minds; in their breast was a thirsty spring, a burning wave, which was ever more and more inflamed by its own streams, so that it did not extinguish the thirst of the drinker but increased the burning. [lacuna]

See Envy. ## IGNORANCE

The Wise Man’s precept concerning ignorance is this: “Do not lean upon your own prudence.” For a human being does not know what is advantageous to him in his life, during the number of days of his pilgrimage and the time that passes like a shadow. For unless the inward eye were darkened, he would doubtless never so often err in the judgment of truth. Whence, I ask, come contrary counsels, so frequent and such diverse opinions—not, I say, from different persons, but from one and the same heart, and almost at the same time? Whence, I say, except from the darkness of the heart and the uncertainty of truth?

We sin in two ways in the examination of our judgment, while we still frequently make our way beneath the cloud of so great an uncertainty. For we err sometimes in discerning quality, sometimes in examining quantity. Whoever calls good evil, or evil good, errs in the quality of things; and whoever calls what is greater lesser, and what is lesser greater, sins in quantity. Certainly the quality of works had deceived those whom the prophet rebuked when he said: “Woe to those who call good evil and evil good, putting darkness for light and light for darkness, putting bitter for sweet and sweet for bitter.” The error in the examination of quantity is found in that which is rebuked through the prophet: “The sons of men are deceitful in the scales, so that they may deceive, they are vanity upon vanity.” Something is indeed placed on a scale so that its quantity may not be unknown. Thus we inquire into the weight of gold and silver in order to appraise their value correctly. But no one would be deceitful in the scale if no one deceived another, if no one had been deceived by another. Hence that saying: “A deceitful scale, weight and weight, both are abominable to God.” The Law, by contrast, commands: “Let there be a just measure and an equal sextary.”

Hence it is that, when the children of Israel receive the promised inheritance among themselves, they divide it with a measuring line, so that each virtue in its action may maintain the measure of just equity and not exceed the bounds of right discernment. Who can find me a person who never errs in estimating quality or quantity, who is never deceived by the business that walks in darkness? The best merchant would be one who can never be deceived in estimating the quality or quantity of things, and who never wishes to deceive. But when can such a person exist, wrapped in darkness and dwelling in the region of the shadow of death? This is surely impossible for every human being while darkness is upon the face of the abyss, until he who said that light should shine out of darkness, sending forth his light and his truth, begins to divide light from darkness, and evening and morning come to be.

For once understanding of truth has been sent forth and received, a person immediately begins to see light from darkness, and to discern first good from evil and evil from good; then goods from better goods and evils from worse evils; and finally better things from the best, and worse things from the worst. In this manner, according to the saying of the Wise Man, the path of the righteous advances like light and grows until the perfect day. The received light gradually advances and increases until the perfect day, when what has been received makes progress and at times reaches full discernment. [lacuna] Therefore we must ascend by certain stages of knowledge if we wish to attain, from this lowest point, that highest summit of ascent.

## IMPIETY

Since virtue is ordered to the good, where there is a special character of good, there must be a special virtue. But the good to which piety is ordered is the rendering to God of the honour due to him. Honour is owed to someone on account of excellence; but singular excellence belongs to God, insofar as he infinitely transcends all things in every respect. Therefore special honour is due to him. [lacuna] And impiety is the obstinate denial to God of this honour. [lacuna]

## SHAMELESSNESS

Consider, I beg you, how beastly, indeed more than beastly, is the life which, casting off human shame, rushes headlong into everything; which does not blush even at things deserving shame, either before the divine sight or the faces of men; and which finally at some point gives itself unbridled rein to every evil. [Col. 0842] For what else is shamelessness but headlong and unbridled malice? Shamelessness removes from a person moderation and watchfulness over himself. Those who are such often patiently, indeed willingly, endure many labours and many pains in order to afflict others; and they prefer to suffer misery themselves rather than not inflict it upon others. Shamelessness crushes everything in one’s neighbour: it attacks, condemns, and annihilates not only others’ weak points but also their strengths. Therefore it tears everything to pieces by defamation, and what it cannot defame it tramples through contempt. To pass over other things: in this wretched sin the wicked mind does not know how to blush, and loses that sensitivity of heart which it ought to possess.

Shamelessness is the unbridling of the mind, when, without any hesitation or reconsideration, shame is trampled down; the soul exposes itself to every transgression, casts off the bridle of shame and the curb of fear, rushes headlong into everything, and thereafter becomes like horse and mule, which have no understanding. And the soul thus corrupted, when after every evil it has reached the depth of evils, loses even hope of recovery and falls into despair.

But if we have heard how the mind, always falling from bad to worse, is finally cast down into the depth of evils, let us hear how and whence that same mind is sometimes re-formed, after many and ultimate evils, into the wholeness of rectitude. We read in the Apostle: “Where iniquity abounded, grace abounded still more.” From this place of Scripture it is easy to perceive that none of our malice can conquer divine mercy. [lacuna]

## INCONSTANCY

Inconstancy implies a certain withdrawal from a determined good purpose. [lacuna] For just as every rectitude of practical reason pertains in some manner to prudence, so every defect of it pertains to imprudence. Therefore inconstancy, in its complete form, pertains to imprudence. And just as rashness arises from a defect concerning the act of counsel, and inconsiderateness from a defect concerning the act of judgment, so inconstancy arises concerning the act of command; for a person is called inconstant because reason fails in commanding the things that have been deliberated and judged.

## DISOBEDIENCE

A disobedient will, or disobedience, is also called self-will. For self-will is that which cannot have the will of God as its advocate, as if it should be asked [lacuna] such a will, arising from the devil’s suggestion [lacuna] and, properly speaking, disobedience is arrogance, boastfulness, pride. Therefore have recourse to these vices if you wish to have a more complete notion of disobedience.

## MADNESS

Madness, or insanity, as it is understood here, has its seat in anger, or is anger itself; for certain wise men have said that anger is a brief madness. Hence madness, or the anger specially treated in the preceding Index, consists in a bold and threatening expression, a sad brow, and a grim look; either pallor or redness of the face; blood boiling from the depths of the breast; eyes blazing and flashing; lips trembling; teeth clenched; the chest shaken by frequent and ever more violent sighing; anxious groaning; a rabid outburst of voice; the neck strained; restless hands; teeth grinding; hurried steps; the ground beaten with the feet; limbs trembling; and the whole excited body tossed in unstable agitation. Horrible madness, displaying great angers from itself, deforms and swells itself up, so that one does not know whether the vice is more detestable [Col. 0843] or more ugly. [lacuna] Nothing, therefore, is less fitting for a wise person than anger.

## INTEMPERANCE

Intemperance is the vice opposed to temperance, which was discussed in the preceding Index. [lacuna]

Intemperance exists in riches, pleasures, honours, and in those things which desire can seek. [lacuna] Consideration itself judges as intemperate both the person who stubbornly withholds necessities and the person who indulges in superfluities. [lacuna] Therefore temperance does not consist only in cutting away superfluities, but also in admitting necessities. [lacuna] In the sickness of drunkenness, body and soul alike are corrupted; the spirit is vitiated together with the flesh. It weakens all the limbs, etc. [lacuna] And so with the other actions in which we exceed the measure of temperance. [lacuna]

On these matters see the preceding Index, the Index on Virtues, and the Index on Mortification of the Senses. [lacuna]

## LUXURY

For the first parents God made garments of skins after sin; and Christ says to Christians: “Do not have two tunics.” But the proud person, in order to seem magnificent, strives to be clothed in double garments, dressed in soft clothing, and adorned with costly things.

Consider what the Lord threatens against excessive adornment through the prophet: “Because the daughters of Zion have been haughty and walked with outstretched necks, and went with beckoning eyes [lacuna], on that day the Lord will take away the ornament of their footwear, crescents, necklaces, pendants, bracelets, turbans, hair-bands, anklets, little chains, perfume bottles, earrings, rings, jewels hanging upon the forehead, changes of clothing, cloaks, linen garments, pins and mirrors, fine linen, headbands, and veils. And instead of a sweet fragrance there shall be stench; instead of a belt, [Col. 0844] a rope; instead of curled hair, baldness; instead of a breast-band, sackcloth.”

Why, then, do you proudly enlarge your phylacteries and make your fringes magnificent? That rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen was buried in hell. Dinah, the daughter of the patriarch Jacob, remained a virgin before she went out to buy the adornment of the women of the region; but when she went out, Shechem violently violated her. Holofernes, who sat in a canopy woven of purple, fine linen, gold, emerald, and precious stones, was beheaded by Judith. [lacuna]

This worldly luxury is treated in the following entries.

MENDACITY.—A lie is a false signification of speech with the intention of deceiving; to lie is to speak contrary to what one thinks in one’s mind. It is therefore clear that whoever tells a lie lies, but not conversely; for someone may lie while speaking the truth, just as one may not lie while speaking falsehood. Accordingly, there is no doubt that a Jew lies when he says that Christ is God and man, though he does not tell a lie. There are three kinds of lies: one committed for someone’s safety or advantage, as the midwives lied; a second uttered in jest; a third proceeding from malice and duplicity of mind, in order to deceive. Yet St. Augustine distinguishes eight kinds of lies: first, that which is made under the guise of religious teaching; second, that which harms no one and benefits someone. This is divided into three, not because it has three species, but because there are three reasons for which such a lie is usually told: first, if someone possesses money liable to unjust seizure, he says that he does not know where it is, though he knows; second, if someone does not wish to betray to death a person being sought, and lies by saying that he does not know where he is, though he knows; third, if someone by lying defends some man or woman from bodily uncleanness. Every kind of lying is a sin. For speech was devised as a kind of vehicle by which understanding may be conveyed from one person to another and our thought may come to another’s knowledge. If anyone abuses words in order to deceive, so that he causes something other than what he thinks to be understood, he abuses words, which are God’s gifts, and thus sins.

But which lie is a venial sin, which a mortal sin, and in what respect it is venial or mortal, must be distinguished according to the aforesaid kinds. That third kind of lie which proceeds from duplicity of mind is a mortal sin, both in the perfect and in the imperfect. That first kind, committed for another’s safety, and the second, committed in jest, are venial in the imperfect. Hence the midwives sinned venially when they lied to Pharaoh. The same must be said of Rahab: this is said on the authority of St. Augustine, though St. Gregory thinks otherwise; see *Patrologia*, CCXI, 1153–1154 . . . There is also much concerning jocular and well-intentioned lying; consult the same place likewise . . .

For each of these matters, see the Index on the Decalogue, under the eighth commandment.

PERJURIES.—Perjury is either a false or unjust oath, or the violation of a lawful oath.

But if anyone swore either falsely, without necessity, or unjustly, he is not bound to fulfill the matter thus sworn; for if what he promised with an oath is unjust or evil, he sinned in swearing and would sin more gravely in fulfilling it. But if someone, without necessity, swore to confirm something true, he swore rashly and therefore sinned in swearing, yet he is bound to keep the oath. By the same reasoning, if someone swore neither without necessity nor concerning an unjust thing, but nevertheless swore falsely—because, having used an oath, he promised something while intending not to fulfill the promise—he has bound himself by the gravest crime of perjury and is bound to perform what he promised.

Those perjuries are more grievous than others which injure God, one’s neighbor, or the perjurer himself more severely; which carry an imprecation or curse imposed upon oneself, when, for example, a person devotes himself or others to dire curses; or which involve blasphemy, concerning which some things have been said above, although they are not specially noted in this Index.

“Who swears to his neighbor and does not deceive”: what, then, is this? Here an oath seems to be permitted to the perfect man among the virtues fitting him; but in the Gospel it is altogether prohibited. What then shall we say? That the Lord everywhere, in both the Old and New Law, has the same purpose in His commandment. For He wishes to prevent the effects of sins and to cut out wickedness from its earliest beginnings. Thus the old Law says, “You shall not commit adultery”; but the Lord says, “You shall not lust . . . .” So here the Prophet is content with an oath that is just and right; but the Lord cuts off even the very occasion of perjury . . . . —St. Basil, *Homily on Psalm XIV*.

Men, says St. Augustine, *Sermon* 180, or 28 *On the Words of the Apostle*, ch. 2, no. 2, swear falsely either when they deceive or when they are deceived. For a man either thinks true what is false and swears rashly; or he knows or thinks it false, yet swears that it is true, and nonetheless swears wickedly. These perjuries differ. Suppose a man swears to what he thinks true; he thinks it true, yet it is false. He does not perjure himself from his heart: he is deceived and takes as true what is false; he does not knowingly introduce an oath concerning something false. Take another man who knows that it is false, says that it is true, and swears as though true what he knows to be false. You see what a detestable beast this is, one to be banished from human affairs. For who would wish this to happen? All men detest such things. Take another: he thinks it false and swears as though it were true, and perhaps it is true . . . . He is perjured. It matters in what way the word proceeds from the mind. The tongue is not made guilty unless the mind is guilty. Yet who is there that is not deceived, even though he did not wish to deceive? What person is not overtaken by error? And nevertheless oaths do not leave the mouth; they are frequent; there are often more oaths than words . . . .

Read on these matters in what follows.

SIMONY.—Not only is he a simoniac who gives or receives a price for sacred things, services, or orders, but also he who sells a synod, votes in papal elections, for example, or who traffics in priestly judgment. “He shall execute justice rightly,” says Scripture; but he executes just things unjustly who is stirred to defend justice not by zeal for virtue but by love of temporal reward. For one is rightly said to execute just things unjustly if he does not hesitate to sell the justice he professes; whereas the contrary is said of him who, in defending justice, seeks nothing other than justice itself.

Two authors of the simoniacal heresy are plainly found in Scripture, one in the Old Testament and the other in the New; they likewise established the two kinds of simoniacs, namely sellers and buyers. Gehazi, indeed, sold the gift of the Holy Spirit; Simon Magus attempted to purchase it. Gehazi, after Naaman had been cured and was already returning, dared to demand money for the gift of the Holy Spirit. “But Elisha said to him: You have received silver and garments, that you may buy olive groves and vineyards, sheep and oxen, male and female servants; but Naaman’s leprosy shall also cleave to you and to your seed forever.” Concerning Simon Magus, what is read of him in the Acts of the Apostles is known: “May your money perish with you,” etc. . . .

This abominable crime is discussed in the following entries.

SIMULATION.—Minds given to feigning and serving hypocrisy are accustomed not only to boast of what they possess, but even to pretend that they possess goods which they do not possess at all. Conversely, they are accustomed craftily to excuse manifest evils and cunningly to conceal hidden evils . . . We know that the fraud of hypocrites, in everything it does, yearns for the advancement of its own honor. For everything it does, or intends in doing, serves ambition.

What is said about ambition may be said about dissimulation and hypocrisy; therefore consult that heading, and, friendly reader, you will find what these are under the article “On Hypocrisy.”

SUPERSTITIONS.—Superstition is worship that is improper or excessive, or an observance that is useless, vain, or dangerous.

One sins by superstition in four ways: first, when vain, superfluous practices, prohibited by God and not approved by the Church, are observed in the worship of God; second, when outward idolatry is committed—that is, when the supreme worship of *latria*, owed to God alone, is rendered to a creature; third, when, in contempt of God’s or the Church’s prohibition, means are employed which have no natural connection with the effect expected from them; fourth, when, by force of some pact, express or tacit, made with the devil—or indeed even without a pact—future or hidden things are curiously investigated. This is called divination and has many species: first, diabolical magic; second, divination by lots; third, sorcery; fourth, the art of knowing the future by inspection of some object, [Col. 0847] for example by the appearance of the dead, called necromancy; by inspection of the hand, called chiromancy; by inspection of water, called hydromancy; by inspection of fire, a stone, or another such object, called geomancy; by inspection of birds, called augury or auspicy; by inspection of the entrails of a slaughtered animal, especially one sacrificed to demons, called haruspicy; and so forth; fifth, judicial astrology, by which future contingencies are predicted from consideration of the position and movement of the stars; sixth, use of a wooden or iron rod to investigate hidden things, for example veins of gold, silver, and other metals, springs of water, hidden treasures, thefts, murders, adulteries, fornications, and other things of that kind; seventh, investigation of hidden things by cold water, by fire, by lots, and so forth.

Nor are only those who practise such superstitions guilty of their crime, but also those who consult their practitioners, even if they give no credence to their answers; and those who take part in another’s superstition by helping, advising, praising, consenting, or sometimes even by remaining silent. For in matters of this kind, one who keeps silent seems to consent, especially if he is bound by office to prevent the superstition, or if he is placed in circumstances in which silence seems to be taken as tacit approval of the acts.

Superstition, therefore—whether magical, lying falsely through a counterfeit profession of truth while truly causing harm—seduces men away from divine religion, commends the worship of demons, and drives its followers to every wickedness. It contains five kinds of evil arts: *mantice* (divination), *mathematica* (astrology), sorceries, lot-divinations, and magical deceptions . . . Horoscopic divination consists in constellations; sorceries are performed by incantations; lot-divinations by lots; magical deceptions by phantasmal illusions. Zoroaster, king of the Bactrians, invented magic, and after a long time Democritus enlarged it; the Persians are said to have invented hydromancy; the Phrygians, auguries; Mercury, magical deceptions . . .

USURY.—Usury is profit from a loan. By “profit” here is meant money or any other temporal thing assessable in price, whether a service or any other burden assessable in price is imposed, or anything else. Usury exists where more is demanded than is given; for example, if you give ten solidi and demand more, or give one measure of grain and exact something in addition.

“If you lend to a man,” says St. Augustine on Psalm XXXVI, Sermon 3, no. 6, “that is, if you give him your money as a loan and expect to receive something more than you gave—not money alone, but something more than you gave, whether it be wheat, wine, oil, or anything else—if you expect to receive more than you gave, you are a moneylender, and in this are to be disapproved, not praised.”

It is certain that usury is unlawful. For it is by its nature unlawful and contrary to commutative justice, in exchanging one thing for another, to demand or receive more than the thing given is worth, unless something else intervenes on account of which that additional amount may justly be received. But to receive anything above the principal for a loan is, in exchange for the thing lent, to receive more than it is worth, unless something else intervenes on account of which it may justly be received. Therefore, by the force of the loan alone, it is wicked by its nature and contrary to commutative justice to receive anything above the principal; consequently usury is unlawful, contrary to commutative justice, and subject to restitution . . .

FORCE.—See VIOLENCE.

VICES.—Certainly, just as disease is one thing and a wound another, so without doubt vice is one thing and sin another. As we see in the body, so we ought to understand concerning the heart: one thing is an inward corruption emerging from what is hidden, another a manifest injury inflicted from without. Thus one thing is when evil is felt in thought alone, even at its beginning; another is what is committed by voluntary assent after deliberation. The former is, as it were, born from within; the latter is, as it were, inflicted from without.

[Col. 0850] Vice, therefore, is the very infirmity of natural corruption; sin is the wrongful assent to tempting infirmity. Vice is, as it were, a passion of nature; sin is a voluntary act of deliberate agency. Vice is the very appetite for evil, which usually precedes or provokes consent; sin is the consent to evil itself, which often follows or accompanies appetite. Certainly, it is one thing to feel a wrongful movement in the heart, another to consent to that wrongful movement. What we feel as a wrongful movement is vice; what we consent to as a wrongful movement is sin. Vice is therefore in perception and affection; sin, however, is in consent alone, or also in affection. When what is true appears false to us and what is false appears true, there is vice in perception. When what is just appears bitter to us and what is unjust appears pleasant, there is vice in affection. But when we give credence to a false opinion, the vice of our perception already passes into sin. Likewise, when we yield to wrongful pleasure, the vice of our affection similarly passes into guilt. In this way vices pass into sins and make the one who consents guilty. Vice in the perceptions becomes the origin of errors; vice in the affections, the root of iniquities. By perception here we mean not that of the body but that of the heart, and therefore do not hesitate to call it judgment. Dull perception and disordered affection are therefore the origin of all evils. In this way vice rules perception and affection, and when it entices consent—or even passes into outward effect—it becomes the cause of sin. Yet consent is not always followed by the act; but when action is prevented by necessity, the guilt of sin is consummated by consent alone. Vice is threefold: disgust for good, desire for evil, and uncertainty in distinguishing the two. That is: a person is sluggish toward good, ardent and restless toward evil, and dull and dim-sighted in distinguishing either. Behold the three vices: weakness, ignorance, and concupiscence . . .

The struggle of vices against virtues is great. You will then be able to overcome all vices through resistance aided by God if you set the corresponding virtues against each vice. For the conflict of vices with virtues is accustomed to promote a person’s progress, because through that contest the mind is aroused and purified from the vice of pride. Virtues must likewise be applied against individual vices: against lust, purity of heart; against anger, patience; against fear, confidence; against lukewarmness, zeal; against evil sadness, spiritual joy; against sloth, fortitude; against avarice, generosity; against pride, humility; against hatred, charity; and so with the rest . . . These too are mentioned in what follows.

## CLXIX. INDEX ON HOMICIDE, LOGICALLY SETTING FORTH THE SAYINGS OF THE FATHERS CONCERNING HOMICIDE, SUICIDE, DUELLING, INFANTICIDE, ABORTION, ETC.; ALSO PRESENTING THE LEGISLATION AND JURISPRUDENCE PREVAILING IN THE MIDDLE AGES CONCERNING THESE MATTERS, AND THE PENALTIES INFLICTED FOR THESE CRIMES

### Preliminary Notice

How useful—perhaps necessary—how advantageous, and consequently how agreeable, this synoptic and analytical table of the Latin Fathers of the Church concerning homicide and all questions more or less connected with it may be: this you yourself, excellent reader, will see by fixing your eyes upon this table and visiting and following, one by one with slow and attentive step, all its streams:

1. To the theologian who applies himself diligently and keenly not only to examining and understanding the principal features of Catholic tradition, but also its smallest details—in which the greatest matters not infrequently shine forth wonderfully—in order to make himself, those entrusted to him, and the pupils whom his office requires him to instruct, more certain of Catholic dogma and morality; or to raise for some public good an edifice of teaching founded upon the firm rock of tradition; or still to investigate more deeply, historically or dogmatically, certain particular points, such as duelling, suicide, and so forth.

2. To the Christian teacher and preacher in the chair of truth, whose strongest support there, after Holy Scripture, is surely the continuous and universal tradition of the Christian centuries, for enlightening minds and also for inclining the hearts of the faithful toward the word of truth and soothing them.

3. Finally, to every Christian who takes even the slightest care to act rightly and safely before God; indeed, to the wise person who stands outside [the Church] yet obeys mere natural reason: for unravelling so many questions of justice, in which many of the ancients erred no less than they laboured; for questioning abysses of life and death so deep, so obscure, and consequently impervious to the uncertain light of human reason.

### How to Use It

In it you will find—not, I say, every word of the Holy Fathers bearing upon homicide, which perhaps would not have been for the best either for you or for me—but certainly all the principal ideas and very often also the more remote ones expressed over twelve centuries in the Western Church. These are generally indicated in a twofold manner: first, by giving the general title, then the chapter and sometimes the chapter number of the work of a given Father; second, by referring the reader to the volume of the entire *Patrology* and to the column of that volume, as both volume and column occur in our edition. This method of indication will make this table very useful even to those who do not yet possess our edition of the Fathers, provided they adhere to the first notation.

One point remains for me to say. No work in the *Patrologia Latina* occurs which is wholly concerned with the present subject. Few works—three or four, and these mostly brief—treat of it to any great extent, so that most often there occur only passages of greater or lesser length, or incidental texts. Yet we have diligently collected all such material, the more precious indeed because rarer and expressed with almost aphoristic brevity; we often reproduce such shorter texts, while clothing the longer ones in a more condensed form. Thus our table presents itself to your eyes and mind as a pleasant field luxuriant with a varied and astonishing number of ideas, breathing forth everything found in the Latin Fathers. It therefore rightly bears the title we have given it: a synoptic, universal table, sounding in a single opening of the mouth the whole tradition of the Western Church over twelve centuries concerning homicide and its consequences.

This does not prevent you from consulting the original text, should we through human frailty have omitted something, failed to express it clearly enough, or—even, being too hasty in the work—understood something incorrectly. As for the theological division of the material, which is necessary for order and clarity, think of it whatever you please. It is wholly ours; if it is defective, we alone are at fault.

## Order of Matters Concerning Homicide

**Preliminary Chapter.**—Question 1: What is homicide?—Question 2: How many kinds of homicide are there?

**Chapter I.**

I. On the illegitimacy of homicide.—Assertion 1: Homicide considered in general is gravely unlawful.—Assertion 2: Direct private homicide, perpetrated for any cause either against oneself or another, is gravely unlawful; this includes suicide, duelling, parricide, sacrilegious homicide, and abortion.

II. On the legitimacy of homicide.—Assertion 3: Public homicide, whether direct or indirect, perpetrated against oneself, is not sufficiently shown to be lawful.—Assertion 4: Public homicide, whether direct or indirect, perpetrated against others for a just cause, is entirely lawful.—Assertion 5: Indirect private homicide (that is, homicide not intended and primarily willed in itself), whether perpetrated against ourselves or others under pressure of a reasonable and sufficiently grave cause, is lawful.

1. Defence of endangered reputation and honour.
