2. Defence of possessions of great value.
3. Defence of one’s own life against an unjust assailant.
4. Defence of violated chastity.
5. Defence of the marital right injured by adultery.

Assertion 6: Mediate homicide—homicide in which we only cooperate—takes the respective character of homicide considered under the preceding several aspects. This includes commanding, advising, consenting to, or participating in homicide.

To each assertion will be appended [Col. 0855]:

1. The penalties enacted by canon law or even civil law against the particular prohibited crime, insofar as they occur in the *Patrologia*.
2. Various facts concerning the subject that either elucidate or confirm it.

**Chapter II.**—On public law concerning homicide, as it occurs in Latin patrology.

**Chapter III.**—On mutilation, or imperfect homicide.

A few further remarks.—Since, in this highly difficult and abstruse matter, the Holy Fathers do not always agree among themselves when compared with one another, and sometimes even appear to contradict themselves in their different works, we have taken care, where such disagreement occurs, to separate the discordant texts and distinguish the opinions, setting them forth one after another. With everything thus settled, then, we begin with the first question of the preliminary chapter.

# [INDEX ON HOMICIDE]

## PRELIMINARY CHAPTER

### QUESTION ONE.—What is homicide?

“To kill is to take the soul from the flesh”: Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, II, 835.---“Homicide” (*homicidium*) is composed from “man” (*homo*) and “killing” (*caedes*): Hervaeus, monk of Bourges, on Romans, ch. 1, CLXXXI, 616.---Homicide is the daughter of envy: envy is the mother of homicide and fratricide. For driven by it, Cain deceitfully said to his brother, “Let us go into the field.” Driven by it, Joab killed Amasa with a dagger. Peter the Chanter, *The Word Abbreviated*, ch. 11, CCV, 53.---Homicide is the killing of a human being; parricide is the killing of a parent: St Isidore, bishop of Seville, *Etymologies*, bk. IV, ch. 26, LXXXII, 210.---“Homicide” is compounded from “man” and “killing”; a parricide is one who kills a parent: Alcuin, *On the Divine Offices*, ch. 13, C, 1195.

### QUESTION TWO.—How many kinds of homicide are there?

For a correct understanding of what follows, we append here certain distinctions of our own, and shall add several others from the Holy Fathers.

Homicide is:

1. Begun under public or private authority, and thus public or private.
2. Direct or indirect: direct when it is primarily intended in itself; indirect when it is not primarily intended in itself, but is procured as a means toward some end which we intend.
3. Immediate or mediate: according as it is committed not simply by ourselves, but through the intervention of some cause distinct from ourselves which we ourselves move to kill.
4. Perpetrated against ourselves or against others.

Presupposing these and several other distinctions, the Holy Fathers speak particularly of spiritual homicide.

Spiritual murderers are worse than murderers of bodies: St Augustine, *Expositions on Psalm 104*, XXXVI, 645.---There is a twofold homicide: one of the body, the other, much worse, of the soul: St Benedict, commentary on the *Rule*, ch. 4, LXVI, 312.---Blessed Peter said that there are three kinds of homicide and taught that their punishment would be alike. For just as he declared those who kill their brothers to be murderers, so also their detractors and those who hate them. Gratian’s *Decree*, pt. II, cause 33, question 3, on penance, ch. 24, CLXXXVII, 1526; Ivo of Chartres has the same, *Decree*, pt. X, ch. 157, CLXI, 737; and Pope Clement, epistle 4 to the people of Jerusalem, ch. 16.

A murderer is one who persuades his brother to evil, ibid., ch. 27. St Augustine says the same in tractate 42 on John, ch. VIII.

The homicide forbidden by the Law was thought to mean only the killing of a body. But the Lord revealed that every wicked impulse to harm one’s brother is to be reckoned among kinds of homicide: Gratian’s *Decree*, pt. II, cause 23, ch. 28. St Augustine has the same in bk. XIX, ch. 23 of *Against Faustus*. Every iniquity, oppression, and injustice is a judgment of blood; and though it does not kill with the sword, it nevertheless kills by the will: Gratian’s *Decree*, pt. II, cause 23, question 3, ch. 25. St Jerome has the same in his commentary on Isaiah, ch. XXXIII.---There are homicides of deed and of will: Peter Lombard, on the Epistle of Blessed Peter to the Romans, ch. I, CXCI, 1335.

The second commandment is: “You shall not kill.” According to the letter, the act of homicide is forbidden; according to the spirit, the very will to kill: Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, bk. III, distinction 37, CXCII, col. 852.---Master Bandinus says the same in his *Sentences*, bk. III, *On the Incarnate Word*, distinction 37, CXCII, 1088.---On the different ways in which someone may be guilty before God when committing homicide: Pope Innocent III, CCXVI, 125.---The spiritual murderer: St Gregory the Great, *Morals*, bk. XVI, on Job ch. XXIV, ch. 59, LXXV, 1155.

A confessor should question a murderer about the circumstances of his crime: whether he killed in a sudden movement of anger . . . or in hope of money, or while repelling force with force, or while avenging or warding off injuries inflicted: Alanus of Lille, *Penitential Book*, CCX, 289.---No one fulfils this commandment, “You shall not kill,” unless he has the intention not to kill even when provoked; nor do all who do not kill fulfil this commandment: Peter of Poitiers, *Sentences*, bk. IV, CCXI, 1150.---The crime of homicide consists in sinning against a human being’s safety: Aurelius Cassiodorus, *Variae*, LXXIX, 701.---The spiritual murderer nourishes his flesh with necessary food and kills his soul by evil deeds: St Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, *On the Forgiveness of Sins*, bk. II, ch. 6, LXV, 556.---The first material of homicide is envy: Primasius, bishop of Hadrumetum, on Romans ch. 6, LXVIII, 421.---The first homicide, both that of the devil and that of Cain, arose from envy; and even now homicides sometimes occur through envy: Hervaeus, monk of Bourges, on Romans ch. 1, CLXXXI, 616.---Intention itself in a just war, according to St Bernard, can change the nature of an act: under the impulse of one intention or another, it becomes theologically blameworthy though outwardly irreproachable. Consider the Doctor’s words in ch. 1, no. 2, of the book *To the Knights Templar*, CLXXXII, 922, 923. He says: “For the Christian’s peril or victory is assessed from the disposition of the heart, not from the outcome of the war. If, in willing to kill another, it should happen that you are killed instead, you die a murderer; but if you prevail and perhaps, with the will to overcome or avenge yourself, kill a man, you live as a murderer.”---Certainly, from the rancour of envy, anger, lust, and also avarice, homicides arise: Halitgar, bishop of Cambrai, *On Penance*, bk. IV, CV, 681.

St Clement, presiding in a council, asserted that there are three kinds of murderers, and taught us that their punishment would be alike. For just as he called the killers of brothers murderers, so too their detractors and those who hate them: Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, epistle 22, bk. IV, CLVII, 166.---Again, on intention. When an officer of a judge kills one whom the judge ordered to be killed, certainly, if he does it voluntarily, he is a murderer—understand, in disposition, not in the deed—even if he kills someone whom he knows ought to have been killed by the judge: Gratian’s *Decree*, pt. II, cause 23, question 5, ch. 14, CLXXXVII, 1222. Ivo of Chartres has the same, *Decree*, pt. X, ch. 103, CLXI, 724; as does St Augustine, *Questions on Exodus*, question 39.---Bishops, priests, and deacons should beware of spiritual homicide: St Jerome, commentary on Jeremiah, bk. IV, ch. XXIV, 811.---That there are many kinds of murderers: Burchard of Worms, *Decree*, pt. II, bk. VI, ch. 28, CXL, 771.

The Holy Fathers, and especially canon law, apply to homicide several other distinctions of the greatest importance: namely voluntary and involuntary homicide, homicide committed willingly or unwillingly, by accident or by human action, as will appear in the course of the Index.

Anger is the seedbed of homicide: Rabanus Maurus, archbishop of Mainz, *Homilies on the Principal Feasts*, homily 60, CX, 112.

St Salvian indicates the manifold ways in which homicide occurs, bk. III, ch. 2, LIII, 59.---Adam’s third sin was homicide, because by sinning he killed himself: Venerable Bede, XCIV, 556.

## CHAPTER I

### I.—ON THE ILLEGITIMACY OF HOMICIDE

Homicide considered in general is gravely unlawful.

**Nature of the precept.**—The commandment “You shall not kill” is such that it can neither be called altogether unchangeable nor be found [to be so].

**ASSERTION I.**—It is specially assigned neither to any class of persons nor to any condition of times; rather, from the beginning it has been imposed generally upon all, such that it is lawful to change it only for Him who imposed it: Philip of Harvengt, abbot of Bonne-Espérance, *On the Obedience of Clerics*, ch. 37, CCIII, 922.---That no one may kill anyone is proved by the commandment in which the Lord forbade homicide in the Law, saying, “You shall not kill”; likewise in the Gospel: “All who take the sword shall perish by the sword”: Gratian’s *Decree*, pt. II, cause 24, question 5, CLXXXVII.---Jesus forbade homicide, for He said to Peter, “He who takes the sword shall perish by the sword”: Ivo of Chartres, *Decree*, pt. X, ch. 78, CLXI, 717, 718.---All laws, both ecclesiastical and civil, forbid the shedding of human blood: Ivo of Chartres, *Decree*, pt. X, ch. 1, CLXI, 489.---Whoever kills a human being shall be sent into exile for whatever length of time seems fitting to us: Isaac of Langres, ch. 11, CXXIV, 1085.---It is forbidden lest certain persons, unsupported by any public office, should perpetrate against many persons out of their own hatreds what the king ought at least to do against one person for the terror of many: idem, ch. 7, CXXIV, 1086.---Let no one lay violent hands upon a sinful cleric: Pope St Sylvester, Roman Council, act 2, ch. 17, VIII, 839.

What shall we say of those who destroy God’s work, who shed human blood, who say, “Let us remove the righteous man, for he is useless to us”? St Ambrose, *Hexaemeron*, bk. VI, ch. 48, XIV, 261.---The gravity of homicide: “If beasts harm human beings, they harm, as it were, strangers; therefore a human being sins more grievously when he lies in wait for a brother”: St Ambrose, *On Noah and the Ark*, ch. 26, XIV, 405.---God Most High does not know how to prepare an injury for anyone: “My Lord is He who forbids murders and does not provoke wars.” Words of a certain Brachman: idem, *On the Customs of the Brachmans*, XVII, 1138.

> You have heard the command, moderated by the ancient Law:  
> If anyone stains his hands with human blood,  
> he, guilty, will pay the penalty under the avenging sword.

Juvencus, *Gospel History*, bk. I, vv. 532–534, XIX, 124.

Homicide is the worst of all deaths: St Jerome, XX, 534.---Every kind of homicide is forbidden in the single saying, “You shall not kill”: Tertullian, I, 632.---Every homicide outside the woods is brigandage: idem, II, 986.---How great is the human punishment for homicide, ibid., 706.

No murderer has eternal life abiding in him: St Augustine, on the Epistle of John to the Parthians, tractate 5, ch. 3, no. 10, XXXV, 2018.---The voluntary murderer is deserving of punishment: idem, *Questions on the Heptateuch*, bk. II, ch. 73, XXXIV, 626.---Everyone who kills a human being without any authority of legitimate power is a murderer: idem, epistle 204, XXXIII, 940.---Scripture sufficiently indicates that it is not lawful to kill another who wishes and asks to die and is now unable to live: idem, XXXIII, 940.---Homicide committed from fear is not free from guilt: idem, *On Free Will*, bk. I, XXXII, 1226.---It is not lawful for anyone except a judge to kill another with the sword: idem, XXXV, 2314.---See a fuller and more particular treatment in *The City of God*, bk. I, chs. 16–20, XLI.---The murderer is described: idem, sermon 8, ch. 6, XXXVIII, 70.

John, once slain, condemned homicide: St Peter Chrysologus, sermon 174, LII, 654, 655.---The murderer is greatly hated: Eugyppius, abbot of Africa, *Treasury*, ch. 115, LXII, 726.---The positive divine law forbids us to kill: Rabanus Maurus, archbishop of Mainz, *Homilies on the Principal Feasts*, homily 60, CX, 112.---Murderers shall not possess the kingdom of God: idem, homily 60, CX, 114.---The books of the Old and New Testaments make it entirely manifest how abominable homicides are: idem, *Penitential*, preface, CX, 468.---Murderers must be rebuked under severe discipline and correction: *Collection of Capitularies of Benedict*, bk. I, no. 241, XCVII, 731.---There is a grave judgment in Holy Scripture concerning those who commit voluntary homicide, the Apostle saying: “If anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him”: Nicholas I, CXIX.---The guilty person is one who inhumanely kills contrary to the commandment: Philip of Harvengt, abbot of Bonne-Espérance, *On the Obedience of Clerics*, ch. 38, CCIII, 924.---For how homicide is committed against the secondary natural law, profitably consult Philip of Harvengt’s *On the Obedience of Clerics*, chapters 38, 39, and 40 of the fifth treatise. It is an excellent work, written almost as a teaching manual.---The commandment “You shall not kill” is treated by Peter of Poitiers, *Sentences*, bk. IV, CCXI, 1150.---Whoever has no legal authority to kill and knowingly kills, sins: Alanus of Lille, *Against the Heretics*, bk. II, ch. 22, CCX.---It is not lawful to kill: Peter of Poitiers, *Sentences*, bk. IV, CCX, 1150.---How God wills that we not kill: Ermengard, *Against the Waldensians*, ch. 19, CCIV, 1272.---Those who have presumed to disregard the commandment “You shall not kill” have been punished more strictly, as you know, because the Lord severely rebuked Cain, and consequent vengeance overtook both him and other killers: Philip of Harvengt, *On the Obedience of Clerics*, ch. 38, CCIII, 924.---No one except a judge may kill anyone with the sword: Ivo of Chartres, bishop, *Panormia*, bk. VIII, ch. 23; likewise St Augustine, XXXV, 2314.---A person who maliciously hands over an innocent person to authority to be killed sins more grievously than the authority itself, if it kills him through fear of another and greater power: Ivo of Chartres, bishop, *Decree*, pt. X, ch. 100, CLXI, 722.

**ASSERTION II.**—Direct private homicide, committed for any cause either against oneself or another, is gravely unlawful.

#### I.—Private homicide in general

[Col. 0858]

Although texts for both assertions—some supporting one, some the other—may lawfully and truthfully be advanced and affirmed, we nevertheless append the following general texts with some selection, as they seem more pertinent here.

Gladiators, murderers, are cursed by Christ: Tertullian, *On Patience*, ch. 3, I, 1254.---How great is the folly of pagans who approve homicides in the circus, though elsewhere they would punish them: idem, *On the Shows*, ibid., 653.---Heathen murderers immersed themselves in water to obtain impunity for their crime: idem, I, 1205.---Human vengeance for homicide is as great as the nature itself which is avenged: idem, *On the Soul*, ch. 33, II, 705, 706.

Alcuin treats of homicide, LIX, 106, 533.---“Who uses the sword shall fall by the sword.” Now the person who uses the sword is one who arms himself to shed another’s blood without any superior and legitimate authority either commanding or compelling him: Ivo of Chartres, *Panormia*, bk. VIII, ch. 44, CLXI, 1314.---A human being must not be put to death unless the law commands it: idem, *Decree*, pt. X, ch. 41, CLXI, 702.---Those who have voluntarily and by ambush killed a human being should submit themselves to continual penance: idem, *Decree*, pt. X, chs. 141–143, CLXI, 734.---That Christians may never lawfully kill anyone—and the contrary: Peter Abelard, *Theological and Philosophical Works: Yes and No*, ch. 156, vol. CLXXVIII. There see this most illustrious man’s sophistries concerning the present question.---The Jews themselves must not be killed: St Bernard, epistle 363, CLXXXII, 564.---It is not expedient, whether dead or alive, victor or vanquished, to be a murderer; wretched the victory in which, by conquering a human being, you are conquered by vice: idem, *To the Knights Templar*, ch. 1, CLXXXII, 923.---Whoever, without any public office, wrongly kills a wrongdoer, thief, or any criminal whatever, shall be judged as a murderer; and this all the more severely because he did not fear abusively to usurp a power not granted to him by God: Gratian’s *Decree*, pt. II, cause 23, question 8, CLXXXVII, 1262.

Join these texts of the latter assertion to the texts of the former, and a sufficiently abundant light concerning the unlawfulness of homicide will shine forth for you. Here, therefore, excellent reader, we could pause if our task concerned nothing other than proving the general thesis of theology. But our charge extends further. Since we are to report complete texts of the Holy Fathers concerning homicide, and since the excessive reward of the work has induced us [to go further], we shall here arrange alongside them the remaining matters concerning homicide in particular, certainly far more numerous than the foregoing. Hence, in a few words:

Homicide considered generally is gravely unlawful; therefore it is so also in particular. Immediate, direct, private homicide, perpetrated for any cause either against ourselves or others, is gravely unlawful. In ourselves, therefore, it is suicide. In others it may occur in two ways. Either a contest is undertaken by agreement between two persons, with danger of death, mutilation, or grave wounds, whether a place and time are designated or not. In the former case it is duelling; in the latter case [the contrasting case is omitted in the supplied text], it is, in addition to general homicide, especially:

1. Sacrilegious homicide;
2. Parricide;
3. Fratricide;
4. Regicide;
5. Infanticide.

Therefore duelling, sacrilegious homicide, parricide, regicide, fratricide, and infanticide are gravely unlawful. This has certainly been sufficiently proved. But let us return, to disclose the pronouncements of the Holy Fathers concerning each of these crimes individually; and first:

To strike even a condemned person is homicide. Why do you rage? What authority have you received? If it is homicide for a condemned person to perish without due order, what is it to strike one unheard, to strike one untried, to strike an evil man without having received any authority? St Augustine, sermon 302, ch. 14, XXXVIII, 1390.

#### II.—On suicide.

Suicides were called by Christians *biothanati* (“self-killers”), John Cassian, *Conferences*, Conference 2, *On Discernment*, ch. 5, XLIX, 530.---The meaning and etymology of this word *biothanati*, ibid., 304.---Judas ended his life by the death of a *biothanatus*, id., *Institutes*, bk. VII, ch. 14, ibid.---By the institution of the ancient Fathers and ecclesiastical discipline, it was forbidden to commemorate in the sacred rites, or to make an offering for, those who had voluntarily taken their own lives, id., Conference 2, *On Discernment*, ch. 5, ibid., 530.---The Council of Braga and the Council of Orléans decree that Mass is not to be offered for them, nor their bodies borne to burial with the singing of psalms, ibid., 529, 530.---Lactantius relates that many of the ancient philosophers laid hands upon themselves, VI, 406.---Nothing more criminal can be done, ibid., 407.---Suicide is to be considered a greater crime than homicide, ibid.---The doctrine of suicide is execrable and to be wholly shunned, ibid., 408.---What were Cato’s reasons for a voluntary death? Lactantius, VI, 408.---The Pythagoreans and Stoics vainly recommend voluntary death. Nothing can be more criminal than this; for if a murderer is wicked because he destroys a human being, he who kills himself is bound by the same crime, because he kills a human being; indeed, this deed must be judged a greater crime, since its punishment belongs to God alone. (See this point developed more fully in the author himself.) Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, bk. III, ch. 8, ibid., 406, 407, 408.---All those philosophers, and Cato himself, the foremost representative of Roman wisdom, who pierced themselves through, were murderers, id., *Divine Institutes*, bk. III, ch. 18, ibid., 407, 408.

In Africa, the *Circuitores* compel those whom they find on the road to be killed by them [lacuna]. But some die by casting themselves down a precipice, and undergo a different ruinous death. Since they hasten thus to perish without cause, they suffer the loss of an honourable death and involve themselves rather than free themselves in the coming judgment of God, St Philaster, *On Heresies*, XII, 1197, 1198.---We must wait; nor can we abandon and despise what the king commands, St Ambrose, XIV, 542.---“I receive no soul which is separated from the body against my will,” St Jerome, XXII, 468.---Let foolish philosophy have such martyrs as Zeno, Cleombrotus, or Cato.---Judas’s homicide was worse than every other homicide, Jerome, XXV, 1052.---It is unlawful for us to lay hands upon ourselves, as is clear from the example of the Lord saying: “Destroy the temple of my body—you, not I,” id., XXVI, 202.---The unlawfulness of suicide is proved by the example of Jonah saying, “Take me and throw me”; it is not ours to seize death, but to receive it when inflicted; hence it is not permissible to perish by one’s own hand in persecutions, id., XXV, 1129.---Judas’s suicide is condemned, St Augustine, XLI, 31.---Suicide is unlawful and a graver sin, ibid., 30, 31.---Why is suicide unlawful? “You shall not kill”: neither another nor yourself, ibid., 35.---Suicide is not a mark of greatness of soul but rather of weakness, ibid., 35, 36.---Whatever examples the nations may adduce, it is manifest that this is not permitted; the example of Cato is subjected to examination and rejected, ibid. (Seek many other matters concerning suicide in this distinguished work of this doctor, *The City of God*, ibid.: “This is what we say, affirm, and approve in every way: that no one ought to inflict voluntary death upon himself—whether in fleeing temporal troubles lest he fall into eternal ones; or because of another’s sins, lest by this very act he begin to possess a most grievous sin of his own; or because of his past sins, for which he has greater need of this life, so that he may be healed by repentance; or, as though from desire for the better life hoped for after death, because the better life after death does not receive those guilty of their own death.” St Augustine, *City of God*, bk. I, ch. 17.---Ivo, bishop of Chartres, reproduces the words and judgment of this holy doctor many centuries later, *Panormia*, bk. VIII, ch. 41.---We cannot make an agreement concerning ourselves by our own right: for we have a Lord, and we do not belong to ourselves, St Prosper of Aquitaine, in his *Confession*, LI, 610.---A human being ought not to kill a guilty person, much less himself when innocent, St Augustine, XXXIII, 666, 940.---No innocent person is killed by himself, id., XLIII, 712.---This is shown by the example of Job, ibid., 727.---He who inflicts death upon himself, even when compelled to evil, perishes eternally, id., XXXIII, 755.---He who takes his own life is a worse parricide, id., XI, 617.---The two most base and customary deaths are those of persons who kill themselves by a noose or by a precipice, id., XLIII, 299.---The Donatists are rebuked because they kill themselves, id., XXXIII, 797, 798.---St Augustine refutes the objection to the foregoing drawn from the example of Razis in the books of Maccabees. The act is to be judged rather than imitated: great, but not good, ibid., 941.

Spiritual suicide, Eugyppius, African abbot, LXII, 1081.---By various forms of death the Circumcellions were accustomed to kill themselves, and to seduce into this madness, so far as they could, persons of both sexes, at times threatening them with death at the hands of others unless they did so, St Augustine, *On Heresies*, bk. I, ch. 69, XLII, 43.---No authority of law permits anyone to kill himself, Gratian, *Decree*, pt. 2, cause 23, question 5, CLXXXVII, 1218.---No one may lay violent hands upon himself, ibid., chs. 10, 11, 12, CLXXXVII, 1219; the same in Ivo of Chartres, *Decree*, pt. II, ch. 4, CLXI, 691.---We do not venerate as martyrs those who tied a noose around their necks; those who killed or cast themselves down were false martyrs, St Optatus, XI, 1010, note 61; ibid., ch. 7, CLXI, 693.---If a person is tormented by the devil and, not knowing what he is doing, kills himself, it is beneficial that prayers be said for him, Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury, *On Penance*, XCIX, 932.---The offering of one who has attempted his own life is not to be received, ibid., 945.---He condemns himself to death who pierces himself through by his own hand, as is clear from Pilate’s example, Haymo, bishop of Halberstadt, CXVIII, 827.---He who kills himself is a murderer, [Col. 0860] because it was said, “You shall not kill,” id., CLXI, 691, 692.---A weak mind is disclosed when it cannot bear either the harsh severity of its own body or the foolish opinion of the crowd, Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 1604.---On the suicides of Cleombrotus, Cato, and Lucretia, ibid.---Plato himself teaches that one must await nature and forbids a person to inflict death upon himself; Plotinus pursues more deeply the same seeds of the Platonic school, ibid.---Pythagoras forbids one, without God’s command, to depart from the guard-post and station of life, St Augustine, XLVII, 1044. (Likewise Cicero, *On Old Age*, no. 73.)---Inquiry is to be made, as concerning a great crime, whether anyone, impelled by the devil, killed himself, St Regino, abbot of Prüm, CXXXII, 282.---It is not lawful to perish by one’s own hand, except where chastity is endangered, Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 1603.---In suicide the mind is found to be far more weak than great, Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 1255.

Various events.---The Patricians held the flesh to be so contemptible and to be rejected by every means that some of them did not hesitate even voluntarily to inflict death upon themselves. They say that only the person able steadfastly to kill himself is perfect, St Philaster, XII, 1177.---In Africa the Circuitores compel those whom they find on the road to be killed by them, saying that they desire to suffer martyrdom, ibid., 1197.---The same account occurs in the *Lives of the Fathers*, bk. IV, ch. 43, LXXIII, 841.---Hero, after he had grown old in every virtue, always living in the desert, was shamefully deceived by Satan and cast himself down into a well. Drawn out from it, he died three days later in his obstinacy and was judged unworthy of commemoration in the sacrifice, John Cassian, *Conferences*, Conference 2, *On Discernment*, ch. 5, XLIX, 529, 530, 531.---How great a crime was Judas’s suicide! Even in dying he sinned; so perverse was his conversion that he sinned even in repenting. He rose against himself, not with the judgment of one repenting, but with the frenzy of one perishing, id., LIV, 328, 352.

Lucretia’s suicide is discussed, St Augustine, *City of God*, XLVII, 1042.---The Donatists killed themselves, id., XXXIII, 797.---Razis is excused for having inflicted death upon himself, id., XLVII, 1044–1046.---The deed of Razis is elucidated by Rabanus Maurus, archbishop of Mainz, *Commentary on the Books of Maccabees*, bk. II, ch. 14, CIX, 1254.---The crimes of Herod, who slaughtered not only his three sons but also himself, Haymo of Halberstadt, *Epitome of Sacred History*, bk. I, ch. 8, CXVIII, 820.---The utterly frenzied deaths which some Donatists inflict upon themselves, St Augustine, *Letters*, XXXIII, 204, 940.---Samson, by God’s will, killed himself, Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 1604.---The prophet Jonah did not wish to lay violent hands upon himself, ibid.---In his death Samson is a figure of Christ, who while living indeed killed few, but after the temple had been destroyed killed innumerable enemies as he died, Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1197, 1198.---Saul and his armour-bearer slaughter themselves, id., *Commentary on the Book of Kings*, CIX, 70.---A certain brother, refusing all food, by foolish presumption inflicted upon himself the death which the Lord wished to avert from him, *Lives of the Fathers*, bk. IV, ch. 44, LXXIII, 841, 842.---A certain wicked servant killed himself, ibid.; *Spiritual Meadow*, bk. X, ch. 75, LXXIV, 154.---A certain young woman, fleeing the hands of unchaste pursuers, fell headlong into a river; she is ordered to be given ecclesiastical burial because, says Innocent III, she did not cast herself down voluntarily but fell by accident, Innocent, *Letters*, bk. IX, letter 11, CCXV, 816.---Samson’s suicide is excused because the Spirit had secretly commanded it, St Augustine, *City of God*, XLI, 35.---Samson killed himself and thus obeyed a command not formerly written upon tablets, but newly inspired inwardly, Philip of Harveng, *On Clerical Obedience*, ch. 38, CCIII, 926.---Saul, who inflicted death upon himself, is not easily excused, notwithstanding David’s praises, St Augustine, XLVII, 1045.---After he had killed Saul’s daughters, he himself rushed upon the sword in order to die, Venerable Bede, *Exposition on Samuel*, ch. 10, XCI, 709.---The punishment of those who inflict death upon themselves: they are deprived of ecclesiastical burial, Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury, *Penitential*, CXCIX, 945.---It is not ours to seize death, but willingly to receive it when inflicted by others. Therefore, even in persecutions it is not permissible to perish by one’s own hand except where chastity is endangered, but one must submit one’s neck to the striker, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1306.

Unusual acts of certain Christians.---The wife of the prefect of Rome, who had become a Christian, killed herself lest she be violated by Maxentius, tyrant of Rome, and proclaimed more clearly than any voice to all mortals now living and those who should live thereafter that chastity among Christians alone is unconquered, impregnable, and not subject to death, Eusebius Pamphilus, *Life of Constantine*, bk. I, ch. 34, VIII, 24.---The virgin Apollonia voluntarily leaped into the fire and thus inflicted death upon herself, Peter Abelard, [Col. 0861] CLXXVIII, 1603.---Certain holy women, in the time of persecution, voluntarily cast themselves into a river or fire that would kill them in order to escape persecutors of their chastity; probably they were not deceived by human impulse, but sent and obedient by divine command, ibid., 1604.---The example of certain Christian virgins who killed themselves to preserve chastity is illustrated: they did this not as persons deceived by human impulse, but as persons commanded by God, St Augustine, *City of God*, XLI, 39.---Elsewhere, as will be seen, several admitted it lawful to kill oneself in order to guard against lapses arising from the weakness of the flesh: “It is not lawful,” says St Jerome, “to kill oneself except where chastity is endangered,” St Jerome, XXV, 1129.---The same judgment of this holy doctor is made clear by examples of pagan virgins who killed themselves to preserve virginity, of whom he speaks with praise and admiration, id., XXX, 270, 271, 272, 273.---On the contrary, it is not lawful to kill oneself in order to preserve chastity, St Augustine, XLI, 30.---The judgment of the holy doctor, which became the more common view, is supported by the reason that chastity has its seat in the mind and not in the body. Therefore no external act can of itself overcome it in any way. Why then kill oneself? ibid.

General principle.---Excepting those whom either a just law commands in general, or God himself, the fountain of justice, commands in particular, to be killed, whoever kills a human being or himself is implicated in the crime of homicide; and all who have committed this act upon themselves may perhaps be admired for greatness of soul, but not praised for soundness of wisdom, Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 1254.

Punishments of suicides.---Since, in the preservation of justice, punishment ought always to be proportioned to the crime, here and everywhere in this table where punishments are considered, after having perceived, as it were in theory only, the gravity of the offence, you will also, excellent reader, so to speak, touch it most clearly in action and in a perceptible manner. You will see with your own eyes how both the Church and the civil authority treated offenders. This addition, therefore, and similar additions on the following pages, new both in itself and in relation to what precedes, will be, especially for beginners, a treatment of the subject under discussion and an outstanding confirmation of the statements made.

No commemoration is to be made in the offering for those who lay violent hands upon themselves, nor are their corpses to be borne to burial with psalms. Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury, *Penitential*, ch. 26, XCIX, 345.---For one who has killed himself of his own will it is not lawful to perform Masses; only prayers may be said and alms distributed, ibid., 932.---The offering of one who has attempted his own life is not to be received, ch. 26, ibid., 945.---Precisely the same punishment for suicide is reported in Halitgar, bishop of Cambrai, CV, 681, 682.---Likewise in Rodolph, bishop of Bourges, in these words: “Let it also be decreed that for those who violently inflict death upon themselves, whether by iron, poison, precipice, hanging, or any other manner, no commemoration be made in the offering, nor their corpses borne to burial with psalms,” Rodolph, bishop of Bourges, CXIX, 723; CXXXIII, 506.---He who kills himself is to be deprived of Mass and offerings, Ivo, bishop of Chartres, CLXI, 693.---The Council of Auxerre decrees the same, CLXI, 693.---The First Council of Braga decrees the same, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 746; the Council of Orléans, XLIX. The same punishment is reported in St Isidore of Seville, CLXXXIV, 567.---If anyone kills himself at the devil’s instigation, it is not permitted that Mass be sung for such a person, or that his body be committed to earth with any psalmody, St Egbert, archbishop of York, LXXXIX, 416.

Books to consult.---St Augustine treats the question of suicide extensively in his celebrated work *The City of God*, bk. I, XLI, 30, 35, 40.---Peter Abelard cites many testimonies from antiquity and disputes concerning suicide, for and against, ch. 155 of *Theological and Philosophical: Yes and No*, CLXXVIII, 1603, 1604, 1605.---You will also profitably consult Rabanus Maurus, *Commentary on II Maccabees*, CIX, 1254.

## III.—On Duel

From what has already been said, a duel is a contest entered into by agreement between two persons, involving danger of death, mutilation, or severe wounds, at an appointed place and time. The testimonies of the holy Fathers concerning it are rarer.

Reasons for avoiding duels.---Injury is often the lot of the good, St Hilary, IX, 444. The saint, while being struck, grieves not for himself but for the one striking him, ibid., 321.---One who inflicts injuries deserves compassion, not anger, ibid., 484.---The Gospels demand forgetfulness of injury, not vengeance, ibid., 687, 688.---*Duellum* is used for war, which it signifies in its original sense, Aquilinus Juvencus, Spanish priest, XIX, 198.---A duel was called “God’s judgment,” St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 424, 419, 638.---A duel is proposed, [Col. 0862] ibid.---A duel was admitted in order to discover whether someone was innocent or perhaps guilty of a particular charge, ibid., 638.---The duel was instituted by Gundobad, king of Burgundy, to settle disputes, St Agobard, bishop of Lyons, *Against the Law of Gundobad*, CIV, 117, 118. The disastrous consequences of duelling, ibid., 117.---The duel was instituted by Gundobad at the beginning of the sixth century, ibid.---How greatly the duel conflicts with law and Christian charity, St Agobard, CIV, 118, 119.---Reasons urgently requiring the avoidance of duelling, ibid.---To the objection for the lawfulness of duelling—“God will provide that the just man does not succumb”—St Agobard replies that God, in his providence, is not bound to grant victory to the innocent; for the recompense of merits is not in the present but in the future. Justice must be sought not in combat but in the examination of cases and in the subtlety of investigations, ibid., 119.---The objection of duellists drawn from the example of the Jews, who, by God’s will, ran to arms rather than to the law to avenge a shameful outrage, is refuted, ibid., 120, 121, 122.---St Avitus, bishop of Vienne, severely condemns such contests; he most wisely and laudably restrained and rebuked Gundobad’s madness, and refuted the arguments for instituting and approving it, ibid., 124, 125, 254.---St Agobard vigorously attacks duelling, ibid., 117, 118, 119 [lacuna] 126.---Among the Burgundians, in the time of St Agobard, single combats were rather frequent, ibid.---Before Louis I, about the year 820, St Agobard treats of duelling and presses arguments for its abolition drawn from benevolence and unity in charity under the new law, ibid. Duels are contrary to the reconciliation of humankind and to Christ the reconciler, ibid., 249, 250.---The designation “judgment of God,” falsely attributed to the duel, is rejected, ibid., 251.---That most evil custom of duelling is contrary to six hundred sayings of Sacred Scripture, *Against the Judgment of God*, ibid., 254–268.---These contests are vehemently contrary to Christian simplicity and piety, ibid., 119.---These contests are forbidden by decrees of princes and canons of councils, ibid., 258.---It accords with their honour and is the duty of princes to oppose with all their strength, by persuasion or force, the holding of duels, St Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 581.---According to St Bernard, to expose oneself to the danger of a duel is madness, not virtue; it is not courage but rather insanity, id., CLXXXII, 566.---St Bernard prays that that wickedness of duelling, that dreadful passion for duelling, may cease, ibid., 566.---At the beginning and in the middle of the twelfth century, the practice of duelling to ascertain the truth or falsity of an alleged fact flourished in the West, Wibald, abbot of Stavelot, CLXXXIX.---That contest was then very honourable, ibid.---The procedure is described where an accused person was to be cleared by proof through duel, CLXXXIX.---Duels ought not to be tolerated in any case, Clement III, CCIV, 1501.---A consultation is sent to Rome on whether a duel ought to be tolerated, ibid., 1501.

Those who practise single combat appear merely to tempt God, Ivo, bishop of Chartres, CLXI, 633.---Divine authority has nowhere sanctioned single combat as law, ibid.---A most beautiful figure of the duel between Christ and Antichrist, between death and life, Rupert, abbot of Deutz, CLXVII, 1099, 1103.---On the cross Christ entered into a hard battle with that mighty ancient adversary, Venerable Godfrey, abbot of Admont, CLXXIV, 854, 855.---At Rome, in the time of Constantine the Great, exhibitions of single combatants were then forbidden for the first time, Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXIX, 892.---King Theodoric commands that people resort not to a duel but to a judge to settle disputes, ibid., 589.---*Variae*, bk. III, letter 24. In the time of Theodoric, king of the Goths, the practice of duelling to settle cases flourished among the barbarians of Pannonia, ibid., 589.---The meaning and etymology of the word *duellum*, St Isidore, bishop of Seville, LXXXII, 640.---It is so called because in every war there are two sides of combatants: “You shall not kill,” neither yourself nor another, Peter Cantor, abbot, *Textus alter*, chs. 79, 80, CCV.

On those cooperating in a duel.---He sins most grievously who supplies armour, fighting equipment, and many such things to men about to fight in single combat, without which it would not take place, ibid.---St Bernard entreats Suger, the greatest prince in the kingdom, to oppose by every means the holding of the fairs (*tournois*) where single combats occurred: “Oppose such great evils,” letter 376, CLXXXII, 581.---It is not advantageous, whether dead or alive, victor or vanquished, to be a murderer. Unhappy is the victory in which, while overcoming a person, you are overcome by vice, id., *To the Knights Templar*, ch. I, ibid., 923.---Innocent III calls duels a perverse custom, id., bk. XI, letter 64, CCXV, 1381.---Again concerning duelling in the same pontiff, ibid.---“We utterly forbid those detestable fairs at which knights customarily gather by agreement and rashly engage one another in display of their strength and boldness, from which dangers to human lives and souls often arise. If any of them dies there, he is to be deprived of ecclesiastical burial; nevertheless, viaticum is not to be denied him,” Ivo, bishop of Chartres, *Panormia*, bk. VIII, ch. 148, CLXI, 1344.---“We do not accept single combat as law, since we do not find that it was commanded; although we read that some entered upon it, as sacred history relates of holy David and Goliath, yet divine authority nowhere sanctions that it be held as law,” Regino, abbot of Prüm, *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*, bk. III, ch. 77, CXXXIII, 300.---Likewise Nicholas I, letter 501; Burchard, bk. IX, ch. 51.---Concerning the duel which King Lothair proposed to use in order to establish the innocence of his wife Theutberga, it is said: “Every prudent person now recognizes how contrary such things are to every divine law,” Regino, abbot of Prüm, *On the Description of the Church*, bk. II, ch. 78, CXXXIII, 300.---Duelling is discouraged, LXIX, 589.---In single combat there is death of soul and body, Peter of Poitiers, *Book of Sentences*, bk. IV, CCX, 1151.---Decree of King Rudolph that all who may have jurisdiction in his kingdom may, if they judge it expedient, postpone a day appointed for a duel. See this quite remarkable letter, in which the well-known evil of duelling is not merely touched upon, but it even seems to be approved by the bishop of Liège himself, *Codex Carolinus*, bk. III, letter 23, A.D. 1279, XCVIII, 815, 816.---When someone abuses us, provokes us, incites us to violence, or calls us to quarrelling, then let us practise silence; then let us not blush to become mute. For he who provokes us and does us injury is a sinner and desires us to become like himself, St Ambrose, *On the Duties of Ministers*, bk. I, ch. 5, XVI, 28, 29, 30.---How one ought to conduct oneself when provoked to a duel by injuries or in another way.

To strike even a condemned person is homicide: why do you rage, what authority have you received? If it is homicide disorderly to strike a condemned person, what is it to strike one unheard, to strike one untried, to strike an evil person without having received any authority? St Augustine, Sermon 302, ch. 14, XXXVIII, 1390.

Various events.---On the single combat of David and Goliath, Rabanus Maurus, archbishop of Mainz, *Commentary on I Kings*, CIX, 51.---Mystically explained, St Augustine, Sermon 32, XXXVIII, 196.---St Bernard intercedes for Humbert, defeated in a duel, CLXXXII, 145.---St Bernard pleads for another man made unhappy in a duel, ibid., 147.---A notable example of a duel, CLVI, 1197.---A most beautiful exposition of the single contest between Goliath and David the shepherd, Rupert, abbot of Deutz, CLXVII, 1099, 1101, 1102, 1103.---A duel entered upon between an Alamannian and a Vandal on behalf of their respective peoples, LXXI, 712.---Likewise between Chosroes and Heraclius, ibid., 638.---St Gregory, bishop of Tours, *History of the Franks*.

A public single combat was undertaken between two representatives, one appointed by the Lombards and the other by the Assipitti, Paul the Deacon, *Deeds of the Lombards*, bk. I, ch. 43, XCV, 450.---A notable duel and other judgments of God are related, CLVI, 1197, 1198, 1199.

If any of them dies, he is to be deprived of ecclesiastical burial; nevertheless, viaticum is not to be denied him, Ivo, bishop of Chartres, *Panormia*, bk. VIII, ch. 148, CLXI, 1344.---Ecclesiastical judges of duels were advanced to some dignity only by dispensation, Innocent III, *Letters*, bk. XI, letter 64, CCXV, 1381.

If, applying contemporary French jurisprudence to those more ancient times, you confine yourself to the general legal rules concerning homicide, as may rightly be done and as we have elsewhere already indicated, you will have, excellent witnesses indeed, material sufficiently abundant for judging, arguing, pressing the case, and entreating.

## IV.—On Sacrilegious Homicide, Whether in Respect of the Agent, the Victim, or Both

The archbishop of Canterbury urges bishops to remove an abuse that had become established in England: namely, that killers of laypersons were punished by capital sentence, whereas killers of clerics and bishops suffered only the penalty of excommunication, letter 73, CCVII, 334.---A bishop caught in homicide is torn away from the priesthood (Apostolic Canon 25), St Agobard, note, CIV, 304.---The crime of Herod in the killing of St John the Baptist is described, St Maximus of Turin, *On the Chapters of the Gospels*, ch. 4, LVII, 811.---Evildoers who drew the sword against Abbot Conon had their hands raised aloft and remained motionless, *Lives of the Fathers*, bk. X; *Spiritual Meadow*, ch. 15, LXXIV, 127.---A Saracen who had killed an anchorite was lifted aloft by a bird and then dropped to the ground, dying from the fall, ibid., 129.---Another Saracen, about to kill a certain monk, was swallowed up by the earth when it split open before he could perpetrate the crime, [Col. 0864] ibid., 198.---Certain monks were wicked enough to slaughter their own abbots, *Commentary on the Rule of St Benedict*, ch. 4, LXVI, 312.---Punishment of homicidal priests and monks, ibid.

Demons seized and tormented the killers of Nunetus, a wonderful abbot, until they shook their souls from their bodies by a cruel death, Paul, deacon of Mérida, *Lives of the Fathers of Mérida*, ch. 3, LXXX, 128.---Let one who kills a sacred person fast for seven winters, St Egbert, archbishop of York, *Penitential*, bk. I, ch. 23, LXXXIX, 407.---If a priest or deacon commits homicide, let him be degraded and do penance until the end of his life, id., *Extracts from the Decrees and Canons of the Holy Fathers*, canon 162, ibid.---If a cleric consents to a homicide and it is committed, let him do penance for seven years, ibid., 400.---If a bishop or priest kills a person, let him lose his order, id., *Penitential*, bk. II, ch. 1, ibid., 415, 416; likewise St Nicholas, *Letters and Decrees*, ch. 144, CXIX, 1134.---See the penance imposed upon one who had killed a priest-monk, ch. 147, ibid., 1122.---Let wergild for a slain priest be paid to the bishop, Isaac, bishop of Langres, *Canons*, title II, *On Homicides*, CXXIV, 1084.---On payment of wergild and completion of penance for homicide committed in churches or their precincts, ibid., 1085.---Whoever kills a subdeacon shall pay 300 solidi; a deacon, 400 solidi; a priest, 600 solidi; a monk, 400 solidi, ibid., 1085.---Whoever kills a monk or cleric shall lay aside arms forever and serve God in a monastery, ibid., 1086.---A homicidal cleric shall be exiled for seven years, Regino, abbot of Prüm, *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*, bk. II, ch. 52, CXXXIII, 296.---On those who have killed a person consecrated to God, Ivo, bishop of Chartres, *Decree*, pt. X, chs. 8, 9, 10, CLXI, 693.---A certain person convicted of having been privy to the murder of his bishop is punished with the penalty of murderers, ch. 12, ibid., 693.---On the penance of a priest who had killed a priest, Isaac, bishop of Langres, CXXIV, 694.---See also Ivo, bishop of Chartres, *Decree*, pt. X, ch. 13, CLXI, 694; likewise ch. 16, ibid., 695.---On certain persons who killed their two bishops, so that henceforth they should be without a bishop, ch. 18, ibid., 696.---On an abbot who struck a servant once with a stick and the servant died after six months, ch. 21, ibid., 697.---On the punishment of a priest who struck a deacon, ch. 24, ibid., 698.---A homicidal priest shall be deprived of priestly office, ch. 29, ibid., 699. The same occurs in ch. 36, ibid., 701.---On the killings of bishops and persons of other orders, chs. 134 through 140, ibid., 731, 734.---A homicidal cleric, even though excessively compelled, must be forced to cease from his order, ch. 17, ibid., 741.---The most atrocious death of a certain archdeacon and his companions, Albert of Aachen, *History of Jerusalem*, bk. III, ch. 53, CLXVI, 468.---The impious killing of Thomas, prior of St Victor at Paris, Stephen, bishop of Paris, letter 9, CLXXIII, 1416, 1417.---A sentence of excommunication is thundered forth against the author and abettors of Thomas’s death, letter 8, ibid., CLXXIII, 1415.---Whoever kills a bishop, priest, or deacon shall suffer capital punishment, Capitularies of Charlemagne, XCVII, 145.---If anyone kills a minister of the altar, let him be an outlaw before God and before men, unless through exile and still more fully among the kindred he makes compensation or clears himself by capital purgation, Cnut I, king of England, CLI, 1178.---If a minister of the altar becomes a murderer, then let him lose both order and honour. He may, however, clear himself; but if he does not, let him be an outlaw, ibid., 1178, 1179.---On the slaughter of the Holy Innocents understood in its natural and spiritual sense, Ralph Ardens, Homily 8, CLV, 1328, 1329, 1330.---St Bernard treats of the killing of Archembold, subdeacon of Orléans, letters 161, 162, 163, CLXXXII, 320, 321.---“I wonder at your learned wisdom, in thinking that a priest, after perpetrating homicide, may minister in the priesthood—indeed, what is more absurd, in wishing to persuade us that we ourselves should assent to such presumption,” Gratian, *Decree*, pt. I, distinction 50, ch. 4, CLXXXVII, 256.---The different penances imposed by canon law upon homicidal clerics, whether voluntarily or involuntarily guilty, chs. 37, 38, 39, 40, 41, ibid., 276, 277.---On the absolution of those who lay violent hands upon clerics, Innocent III, letter 310, CCXIV, 269.---On the same matter, id., letters 129 and 161, CCXVI, 645, 950.---A priest who, having fallen again into the same fault, had for a second time laid violent hands upon a cleric, is declared by Innocent III able to return to his office after three years’ penance, letter 79, ibid., 83.---Innocent III’s lament and letter concerning the procured death of the bishop of Würzburg, letter 155, CCXIV, 1167, 1168, 1169.---A certain homicidal cleric is deposed from the exercise of his order, letter 385, ibid., 364.---The punishment imposed for homicide of a cleric committed by another cleric, Alexander II, *Letters and Diplomas*, letter 115, CXLVI, 1404.---An evil prelate is to be judged a murderer of souls, [Col. 0865] St Benedict, abbot of Aniane, *Concordance of Rules*, ch. 15, §19, CIII, 788.

Whoever kills a priest shall do penance for twelve years; if free, he shall fast for seventy days; but if a slave, he shall clear himself by walking over twelve burning ploughshares, Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury, *Penitential*, chs. 36, 37, XCIX, 947.---On the punishment of a priest who struck a deacon, Nicholas I, *Letters and Decrees*, CXIX, 1131, 1132.---A cleric who has killed a pagan is a murderer and ought not to be promoted to a higher rank; he must also be deprived of the rank already acquired, ibid., 1129.---Roger Tokellus and Guy, who had laid violent hands upon clerics, are excommunicated, Alexander III, letter 885, CC, 792.---With how great severity Alexander III deals not only with those who had killed Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, but also with those who had merely participated in that homicide, id., letter 1014, CC, 894.---Letter of King Louis of France to Alexander III concerning the killing of St Thomas, letter 20, ibid., 1378.---What obligations bind those who kill a priest, Ivo of Chartres, CLVI, 1306.---On those who kill a cleric, deacon, subdeacon, or monk, id., *Panormia*, bk. VIII, chs. 6, 7, 8, CLX, 1396, 1397.---Celestine III commands the chapter of Tarragona to declare William Raimund, who had cruelly killed Archbishop Berengar in the city of Gerona, anathematized, and to place his land under interdict, letter 164, CCVI, 1045.---On a subdeacon who unwillingly killed a boy, Clement III, letter 54, CCIV, 1503.---On the killing of St Thomas of Canterbury, Peter Bernard, prior of Grandmont, letters 3, 4, 5, 6, CCIV, 1167, 1168, 1169.---On clerics caught in homicide, CCVI, 1259.

## V.—On Parricide.—Punishments Imposed and Various Events

How detestable a crime parricide is, the Lord himself shows in the judgment rendered between Cain and Abel; he himself pronounced the sentence: “Cursed is the earth [lacuna] cursed [lacuna],” Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1410.---Ibid.---See very much further material on parricide, again in the *Penitential*, ch. 2.

Concerning the parricide of Romulus, which the gods did not avenge, St. Augustine, *City of God*, book III, ch. 6, XLI, 82.---Envious of his brother’s offering, Cain thirsts for his brother’s destruction; unhappy, he exults, and, because there is no witness, thinks himself free of the crime—though God saw him, conscience rebuked him, and his brother’s blood accused him, St. Zeno, book I, tract 7, XI, 314 and 315.---Abel is killed by Cain in the field of Damascus, according to Hebrew traditions, St. Jerome, XXIV, 316.---Cain, at once most impious and most foolish, when about to perpetrate the greatest wickedness, believed it sufficient, in committing fratricide with God as witness, to avoid human eyes, Salvian, priest of Marseilles, *On the Governance of God*, book I, ch. 6, LIII, 38.---How Cain, who committed fratricide, is punished, Peter the Chanter, *Verbum abbreviatum*, ch. 11, CCV, 53.---All crimes are contained in parricide against one’s father, St. Augustine, *Against the Academics*, book III, ch. 36, XXXII, 953.---A fratricide or parricide shall fast in a foreign land for ten winters, St. Egbert, archbishop of York, *Penitential*, book I, ch. 24, LXXXIX, 407.---Parricide is the killing of one’s parents, St. Isidore, bishop of Seville, *Etymologies*, book IV, ch. 26, LXXXII, 210.---Punishment of parricides. Formerly parricides, enclosed in a leather sack with an ape, a cock, and a serpent, were thrown headlong into the sea, book V, ch. 27, ibid., 214.---Parricide differs greatly from homicide, Tertullian, I, 316.---If anyone has shed the blood of a killing within his own kindred, the sacred canons have decreed that he is to be cast out until death and reckoned among rebels, Nicholas I, *Letters and Decrees*, CXIX, 921.---On the punishment of a certain man who had killed his mother, ibid., 1120.---On the penance of certain parricides and fratricides: they are forbidden to enter into bodily union, ibid., CXIX, 1128.---The same pope concerning another fratricide, ibid., 1119.---Penitent fratricides must not thereafter take up the military belt or make use of marriage and conjugal union, Rabanus Maurus, *Penitential*, ch. 7, CX, 473 and 474.---On the same matter, see Isaac, bishop of Langres, *Canons*, title 4, ch. 5, CXXIV, 1690.

Some canons assign parricides seven years of penance, others fourteen years, and still others their whole life, Regino, abbot of Prüm, CXXXIII, 296.---A parricide, all other forms of torment being set aside, is to be placed in a sack made of hides, with serpents enclosed therein with him, and thus cast headlong into the nearby sea, ibid., 296, 300.---Penance imposed on one who, though unwillingly, had caused his brother’s death, Alexander II, *Letters*, CXLVI, 1386.---A king must not allow parricides and perjurers to live, Ivo, bishop of Chartres, *Panormia*, book VIII, ch. 33, CLXI.---The manifold penance of parricides and fratricides is reported, idem, *Decree*, part X, ch. 163, CLXI, 738.---Again it is reported how [Col. 0866] detestable the crime of parricide is, chs. 164, 177, ibid., 742.---On the same subject, chs. 178, 179, 180, 185, ibid., 743, 745.---Cain condemned on account of homicide, Philip of Harvengt, abbot of Bonne-Espérance, *On the Obedience of Clerics*, ch. 37, CCIII, 922.---A notable example of fratricide and of the punishment due to such a crime, Freculph, *Chronicles*, book I, ch. 6, CVI, 921.---Cain’s homicide was to be punished by the Flood, Rabanus Maurus, CVI, 509.---Regicide is to be reckoned among the crimes of parricide; of it St. Optatus says: “We ought to learn from David, the child of God, that regicide is not to be committed,” St. Optatus, *On the Donatist Schism*, book II, ch. 25, XI, 980, 981.---How a matricide ought to be punished, Ivo of Chartres, *Decree*, part X, ch. 173, CLXI, 741.---On parricides and fratricides, Burchard, bishop of Worms, CXL, 1089.

VI.---On infanticide and abortion.

On those who procure abortion, St. Jerome, XX, 97.---The law did not intend the expulsion of an unformed fetus to count as homicide, because a living soul cannot yet be said to exist in a body lacking sensation, St. Augustine, *Questions on the Heptateuch*, book II, ch. 80, XXXV, 626.---It is a hastening of homicide to prevent birth, Tertullian, I, 319.---Infants slaughtered in the womb, idem, II, 691.---Infants injured in the womb by their mothers, ibid., 909.---A certain woman who had miserably killed her two children is, by a heavenly command, submerged in the depths of the sea, *Lives of the Fathers*, book X, *Spiritual Meadow*, ch. 77, CXXIV, 155.---How grave a crime infanticide is, ibid., 155.---By what punishment she is visited through God’s miraculous intervention and command, ibid., 155.---Women who act upon themselves to expel what they have conceived in the womb were indeed formerly excluded from the Church until the end of life; but we now decide more humanely that they should be assigned a period of ten years’ penance, *Code of Ecclesiastical Canons and Constitutions of the Apostolic See*, ch. 21, LVI, 441.

What punishment is to be imposed upon one procuring abortion, Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 112.---Who is mystically “abortive,” ibid.---The penance of those who kill offspring, CXII, 1410.---King Herod, being exceedingly angry, killed all the boys who were in Bethlehem, St. Maximus of Turin, homily 28, LVII, 286.---If a woman procures an abortion and that which was conceived from seed is killed within forty days, she shall fast for three years as for homicide, St. Egbert, archbishop of York, *Penitential*, book I, ch. 30, LXXXIX, 408.---Fornicating women who kill their little children or expel them by abortion shall do penance for ten years, Fulgentius Ferrandus, *Abridgment of the Canons*, can. 152, LXXXVIII, 826.---Cresconius, an African priest, has the same, *Breviary of Canons*, 113, LXXXVIII, 881.---If a mother kills her child, she shall fast for fifteen winters without interruption, except on Sundays, St. Egbert, archbishop of York, *Penitential*, book I, ch. 31, LXXXIX, 407.---Those who have attempted to kill ill-conceived children or children already born shall do penance for seven years, Council of Ancyra, LXXXIV, 108.---If any woman kills a child conceived in fornication; if she attempts to procure an abortion or to kill what has been conceived; or if she strives not to conceive, she shall do penance for ten years, St. Isidore of Seville, *Collection of Canons*, can. 77, LXXXIV, 584 and 585.---Women who kill children born of adultery are not to be granted communion even at the end, Council of Elvira, can. 63, CXXXIV, 308.---Such women are to be treated more leniently than in earlier centuries: they shall do penance for only ten years, St. Radulphus, bishop of Bourges, ch. 41, CXIX, 723.---On the manifold penance imposed on Wimar, who had miserably killed his three children, Nicholas I, *Letters and Decrees*, ch. 136, CXIX, 1130.---Women who kill children born of fornication shall do penance for ten years, St. Angilram, bishop of Metz, *Collection of Canons*, ch. 20, XCVI, 1037.---The enactments of the councils of Ancyra and Elvira concerning women seeking abortion are reported, Rabanus Maurus, *Penitential*, ch. 9, CX, 474.---Whoever strikes a pregnant woman and her child comes forth not yet formed shall suffer the penalty which the woman’s husband shall impose; but if it is formed, he shall give life for life, Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, *On the Divorce of Lothair and Theutberga*, question 12, CXXV, 694.---The putrid, lifeless abortion of Theutberga, ibid., 689.---A certain priest, having procured an abortion, is declared by Innocent III able to minister if the conceived child had not yet been quickened; otherwise he must abstain from the service of the altar, letter 107, CCXVI, 469.---If anyone kills an infant, he is to be held guilty as a homicide, Isaac, bishop of Langres, *Canons*, ch. 11, CXXIV, 1087.---A woman or man who through negligence smothers in bed an infant sleeping with her or him shall do penance, ibid., ch. 14.---The same penance as above for women who kill their offspring is found in Isidore Mercator, *Collection of Decretals*, Council of Ancyra, can. 21, CXXX, 266; Council of Braga II, can. 78, ibid.---The same is found in Regino, abbot of Prüm, *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*, book II, [Col. 0867] canons 63, 64, 65, 66, 67, 68, CXXXIII, 297, 298.---Parents who killed their children in certain parts of Spain are severely rebuked by king and bishops, and it is forbidden that so atrocious a crime should spring up again, Isidore Mercator, *Collection of Decretals*, Third Council of Toledo, CXXX, 456.---Those who, either by a vow or by some act, arrange that children should not be born to them, though they are called spouses, are not spouses and retain none of the reality of marriage; rather, they hold out an honorable name as a veil for shamefulness, Ratherius, bishop of Verona, *Preloquia*, book II, title 3, CXXXVI, 193, 194.

On women who conceive while their husbands are absent and destroy the fetus, Burchard, bishop of Worms, *Decree*, book VI, ch. 51; on those who seek to kill children ill-conceived, ch. 52; on those who secretly kill their offspring, chs. 53, 54, 55; on men or women who expel offspring, ch. 57; on women who carelessly smother infants in bed, ch. 58; on those who have procured abortion, ch. 601 [perhaps ch. 60], CXL, 931, 932, 933, 934.---A cleric who sought herbs for a woman by which her husband might be killed, if the man died as a result, is never to be promoted to higher orders, St. Anselm, bishop of Canterbury, letter 23, CLIX, 52.---Penance imposed on Theodoric, who killed his son unintentionally, Alexander II, *Letters and Diplomas*, letter 117, CXLVI, 1405.---One who expels a fetus not yet formed and animated is not, according to the law, held to be a homicide, and therefore homicide does not occur, Ivo, bishop of Chartres, *Panormia*, book VIII, chs. 2, 12, 13, and 14, CLXI, 1307.---St. Augustine has the same in *Questions on Exodus* XXXII, question 2; *Questions on the Old and New Testament*, ch. 38; Jerome, *To Algasius*, question 4.

Parents must be admonished not to place little children with themselves in one bed, lest, through some negligence, they be suffocated or crushed, and the parents themselves thereby be found guilty of homicide, Ivo, bishop of Chartres, *Decree*, part X, ch. 27, CLXI, 699.---Whoever destroys a conception in the womb by abortion is a homicide, chs. 181, 182, 183, ibid., 744.---On a certain woman who had killed her children, ch. 186, ibid., col. 745.---On the punishment of one procuring abortion, Gratian, *Decree*, part I, distinction 50, chs. 48, 49, 50, CLXXXVII, 278, 279.---Alexander III orders that a woman who had killed her infant enter a monastery, CC, 84, letter 14.---Again, on those who kill offspring by various methods, Halitgar, bishop of Cambrai, *On Penance*, book IV, ch. 3, CV, 1681.---Herod’s killings of his children and wife, Freculph, *Chronicles*, book VII, ch. 18, CVI, 1110.---On Mary, who, driven by famine, ate her own child, CXCIX, 423.---On those procuring abortion, Ivo of Chartres, *Decree*, part X, ch. 55, CLXI, 706. (St. Augustine has the same in *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book I, ch. 15.)---Why the law did not intend an unformed fetus to count as homicide, ch. 56, ibid., 706. (St. Augustine has the same in *Questions on Exodus*, ch. XX.)---According to St. Peter Damian, the more frequent cause of abortions is the frenzied desire of betrothed persons to have intercourse, even while the bride is pregnant. Are such people not murderers before they are fathers? St. Peter Damian, book VIII, ch. 15, CXLV.---Abortion, a fruit of avarice: the unknown fetus is buried in a new frenzy of hatred before it is born, already not in its mother’s womb but in its grave, unable to experience either lawful death or life, St. Zeno, book I, tract 9, XI, 326.

VII.---A penitential concerning homicide in general when unlawful, with various cases.

“If anyone strikes another and he dies, he shall surely be put to death”: St. Augustine admirably explains these words, *Questions on the Heptateuch*, book II, ch. 29, XXXIV, 625.---A homicide perpetrated by dumb animals is punished by virtue of the divine law itself, ch. 76, ibid.---One guilty of involuntary homicide had a place of refuge, ch. 79, ibid.---If anyone knows himself guilty of homicide, let him declare penance to himself in his own heart and exact vengeance upon his own evils; let him set before God for himself the ordeal and duration of penance, and by no means presume to receive communion, idem, in the Appendix, sermon 117, XXXIX, 1979.---In the time of St. Salvian, homicides were rare among slaves, through terror and fear of death, but continual among the rich, through hope and confidence of impunity, Salvian, priest of Marseilles, *On the Governance of God*, book IV, ch. 5, LIII, 75.---A murderer has no feeling of mercy or love, as is evident from Herod, killer of the innocents, St. Peter Chrysologus, sermon 152, LII, 604.

Those who commit voluntary homicide are indeed to submit themselves continually to penance, but near the end of life are to be considered worthy of communion, *Code of Ecclesiastical Canons*, LVI, 441.---For involuntary homicide, a period of five years’ penance is established, LVI, 442.---It is your duty to prevent a murderer from receiving the Eucharist before he has performed penance, St. Ambrose, sermon 6.---One who has killed a human being is unworthy of the Lord’s table, Martialis, bishop, in his letter to Bordeaux, LVIII, 1032.---Those who commit voluntary homicide [Col. 0868] are indeed continually to submit themselves to penance, but they shall attain its completion near the end of life; canon of the Council of Ancyra, XLI, XLVII, 156.---For involuntary homicide, the earlier ruling establishes seven years of penance, the later five years, can. 42, Dionysius Exiguus, XLVII, 156.---The pagan wise are full of envy and homicide, Primasius, bishop of Hadrumetum, XLVIII, 421.---A fine saying concerning murderers, *Lives of the Fathers*, book X, ch. 71, LXXIV, 152.---On a most impious old murderer, ch. 72, ibid., 153.---If anyone kills another out of necessity, let him fast forty days, LXXXIX, 407.---For the penalties for homicide set forth again, see St. Egbert, archbishop of York, *Extracts from the Canons*, canons 62 and 63, LXXXIX, 400; St. Gregory, letter 6, LXXVII, 1340; again St. Egbert’s *Penitential*, book II, ch. 1; for other penalties for the same crime, ibid., 415, 416; Fulgentius Ferrandus, *Abridgment of the Canons*, canons 153 and 154, LXXXVIII, 826; and Cresconius, African priest, *Breviary of Canons*, canons 103, 104, ibid., 881.---Sorcerers are to be granted communion only at death, LXXXIV, 322 and 323.---Murderers are excluded from the communion of the Church, ibid., 268.---The ancient Nicene canons concerning murderers are to be observed, *Collection of Canons* attributed to St. Isidore of Seville, Councils of Agde and Epaone, LXXXIV, 289.---Again, on the penalties of murderers, whether intentional or not, ibid., 585.---If a mistress, from jealousy, kills her maidservant by beating her, she shall do penance for seven years, Council of Elvira, can. 6, ibid., 302, 303.---Again, on homicide, whether voluntary or involuntary, Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury, *Penitential*, ch. 43, XCIX, 948; Works of St. Charlemagne, or the Carolingian Code, XCVIII, 90.---Cain, the first murderer and the first fratricide, Tertullian, I, 1258.---Among human beings, the vengeance for homicide is as great as the very nature which is avenged, Tertullian, *On the Soul*, ch. 33, II, 909.---Whoever kills his slave, even if guilty, without the knowledge of a judge, shall purge the guilt of blood by excommunication or by two years’ penance. If a mistress flogs a maidservant and death follows, she shall do penance for seven years, Radulphus, bishop of Bourges, ch. 40, XCIX, 722.---See again the penalties set forth for homicide, ch. 39, ibid., 722.---John VIII decrees that minors who have killed someone are not to be delayed in being promoted to orders after completing their penance, John III, letter 188, CXXVI, 817.---All murderers shall strictly perform seven years’ penance under the rule of a monastery, CXVI, 1290.---Intentional murderers, after continuous penance, shall receive communion at the end of life, St. Angilram, bishop of Metz, *Collection of Canons*, can. 21, XCVI, 1037.---On seven or five years of penance for involuntary homicide, can. 22, ibid.---Rabanus Maurus reports in his *Penitential*, chs. 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5, CX, 468, the various cases of homicide and penalties established successively that have been reported thus far.

Whoever kills his own wife shall, having laid aside his arms, do public penance, Isaac, bishop of Langres, *Canons*, title 11, ch. 6, CXXIV.---A woman inflamed by rage who beats a maidservant with whips, if the latter dies within the third day, shall do penance for about seven years, Isidore Mercator, *Collection of Decretals*, Council of Elvira, can. 5, CXXX, 415.---One who kills someone by sorcery is not to be granted communion even at the end, can. 6, ibid., 415.

An intentional murderer shall always remain subject at the door of the Catholic Church; but if he kills by accident, the earlier canon establishes seven years and the later five years of penance. Isidore Mercator, *Collection of Decretals*, Second Council of Braga, can. 79, CXXX, 587.---For the repeatedly reported penalties of the two kinds of homicide, see the same author, canons 21, 22, 37, ibid., 404, 266.---If anyone kills a person in public war, he shall do penance for forty days, ibid., 295.---Again, on a mistress beating her maidservant, Regino, abbot of Prüm, *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*, book II, ch. 58, CXXXIII, 296.---If a slave corrected by his master should happen to die as a result, the master is free from the guilt of homicide, ch. 59, ibid., 297.---Again and again, various penalties for homicide are reported, canons 81, 98, ibid., 287, 288, through 303.---A remarkable example of the uselessness of prayers for murderers after their death, Gezo, abbot of Deutz, *On the Body and Blood of Christ*, ch. 59, CXXXVII, 402.---Murderers are like a leaning wall, Blessed Bruno, bishop of Würzburg, *Exposition on Psalm LXI*, CXLII, 234, 235.

Concerning the penance of murderers, you will again find abundant material in Burchard, bishop of Worms, *Decrees*, book VI, “On Homicide in General and Its Various Kinds,” CXL, 763–778.---In that book all the kinds of penance customary in that age are described with considerable detail and care; for knowledge of these you may therefore usefully have recourse to it. See also the appendix, “Statutes of the Canons concerning the Office of Priests,” ibid., 1079, 1081, 1082.---One guilty of homicide, whether public or private (secret), is not to be admitted to the clergy, St. Anselm, bishop, letter 163, CLIX, 198.---Those who bring about homicide are punished with penance, even though they did not perpetrate it by either will or action, Letters and Decrees of Pope Alexander, CXLVI, 1408.---All the often-repeated penalties for homicide reported thus far are again reported by Ivo, bishop of Chartres, in part X of his *Decree*; there you will find them, CLXI, 689–746.---Among other points, the following may be noted: a murderer must not accuse a bishop, ch. 36, ibid., 701.---Murderers and poisoners are not to be admitted to make an accusation, ch. 37, ibid.---They are to be excluded from communion, ch. 38, ibid., 702.---St. Ambrose forbade the emperor Theodosius entrance into the church on account of indiscriminate killing, ch. 48, ibid., 703.---On the diverse matters of killings and injuries thereby inflicted, whether willingly or unwillingly, and on making reparation for them, whether by a physician, a slave, a master, or any other person, Ivo of Chartres, *Decree*, part X, ch. 49, CLXI, 704, 705.---Again, on intentional homicides and the manner of penance, chs. 130–133, ibid., 730, 731.---If anyone kills his own slave without the knowledge of a judge, let him mourn it as voluntary homicide, ch. 147, ibid., 735.---On those who, while occupied in necessary work, commit homicide, chs. 150, 151, ibid., 735.---On a murderer by poison, ch. 151, ibid., 737.---Murderers are to be excluded from the communion of the Church, ch. 158, ibid., 738.---Whoever kills a person devoted to sacred service, or indeed a layperson, shall expiate the sin according to the ancient custom; finally, all are to abstain from slaughter, robbery, and violence, Ecclesiastical Constitutions of Andrew, king of the Hungarians, VI, CLI, 1258.---Again, various penalties corresponding to different kinds of homicide may be found in the Venerable Bede, XCIV, 570, 571.---If anyone sacrifices a human being to the devil and offers him as a victim to demons in pagan fashion, he shall surely be put to death, Capitularies of Charlemagne, XCVII, 146.---If anyone kills his lord or lady, he shall surely be put to death, ibid.---If anyone, after baptism, has been involved in homicide by deed, command, counsel, or defense, and by some deception has entered the clergy, he shall be deposed and shall receive only lay communion at the end of his life, Gratian, *Decree*, part I, distinction 50, ch. 8, CLXXXVII, 257, 258.---Again, manifold penance for homicide, idem, chs. 42, 43, 44, 45, 46, 51, ibid., 277, 278, 279.---The laws of Baldwin, count of Flanders and Hainaut, concerning homicide, CCIX, 916.---For persons who were neither knights nor sons of knights: a dead person for a dead person, a limb for a limb, ibid., 916.---Again, on homicides committed voluntarily or involuntarily, Innocent III, CCXVI, 1252, 1254, 1255.---See Halitgar, bishop of Cambrai, *Penitential Book*, CV, 697, 702, and book IV, *On Penance*, of the same author, chs. 1, 2, 3, and 4, ibid., 681. (There you will find a new collection of penalties and cases.)---On the same subject, see also Rabanus Maurus, chs. 11, 12, 13, 15, CXII, 1410, 1411.---“I shall require a human being’s blood from the hand of his brother; whoever sheds blood, his blood shall be shed,” St. Ambrose, *On Noah and the Ark*, ch. 26, part XIV, 406, 407.---An example of horrible homicide, Cosmas of Prague, *Chronicle*, CLXVI, 377, 376.---A twofold penitential canon concerning voluntary homicide, one milder and the other stricter, though both already obsolete and excessively severe in the author’s time, Alan of Lille, *Penitential Book*, CCX, 294.---In the time of St. Gregory, bishop of Tours, as he himself testifies, murders and wars were rampant, St. Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book VII, ch. 47, LXXI, 446, 447.---Did Moses sin in killing the Egyptian? He was a type of Christ, CVII, 16, 17.

## CHAPTER II

II.---ON THE LAWFULNESS OF HOMICIDE.

**ASSERTION III.**---Public homicide, whether direct or indirect, perpetrated upon oneself, is not sufficiently shown to be lawful in itself. Although nothing concerning its punishment occurs in the Latin Fathers, this is nevertheless the rather more common and sounder opinion, which we have considered not inappropriate to insert for the connection of the subject.

**ASSERTION IV.**---Homicide perpetrated upon others by public authority and for a just cause . . ., whether directly or indirectly, is altogether lawful. These, namely, follow from and are exceptions to the general law: “You shall not kill.”

The commandment, “You shall not kill,” requires an implicit qualification, so that a judge or authority bearing the sword may not be judged a transgressor when he kills one who ought lawfully to be killed, Rupert, abbot of Deutz, *On the Trinity and the Holy Spirit*, book V, ch. 22, CLXVII.---In many cases a judge may not refrain from the sword, because he serves the law, St. Ambrose, *On Psalm XXXVII*, 51, XIV, 1035.---To punish murderers, sacrilegious persons, and poisoners is not an effusion of blood but a service of the laws, St. Jerome, *Commentary on Jeremiah*, III, book IV, ch. 22, XXIV, 811.---The same occurs in Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1226.---Killing a person is not always criminal; rather, killing through malice and not by the laws is criminal, Rufinus, priest of Aquileia, *Commentary on the Apostles’ Creed*, no. 40, XXI, 377.---In killing his son, spontaneous impulse is abominable; but obedient service when God commands is found not merely blameless, but even praiseworthy. The holy teacher adds that, in the natural order, it makes all the difference what is done, by whom, and under whose authority each person acts, St. Augustine, *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, book XXII, ch. 73, XLII, 446.---If Abraham had sacrificed his son of his own accord, what would he have appeared but horrible and insane? But when God commanded, what did he appear but faithful and devout? Book 22, ch. 73, ibid., 446.---An evil man has his judges: the commonwealth has been ordered, for it does not bear the sword without cause, idem, sermon 32, no. 12, XXXVIII, 1389.---Elijah was righteous, although he killed many false prophets with his own hand, idem, XXXIII, 178.---They did not at all act against the commandment, “You shall not kill,” who waged wars under God’s authority, or who, bearing the office of public power, punished criminals with death according to His laws—that is, by the command of most just reason; such were Abraham, Samson, and Jephthah, idem, *City of God*, book I, ch. 21, XLI, 135.---The commandment not to kill is not violated when the law kills, or when God commands that someone be killed, idem, XXXIV, 622.
