A judge does not oppose the natural law when he commands a murderer to be killed, because it is not he but the law itself that does it, Alan of Lille, *Against Heretics*, book II, ch. 22, CCX, 397.---Many heretics, especially the Waldensians, asserted that a person must not be killed in any case, on any occasion, or for any reason, ibid., 394.---It is established irresistibly and with strict logical rigor that it is lawful in many cases to kill a person; difficulties are explained and objections resolved, ibid., 396, 397, 398.---You will usefully consult Alan’s work, learnedly and logically written, on this subject, especially chs. 20, 21, 22, and 23, ibid.

Without sin, a soldier kills an enemy; so too a judge or his officer; and likewise one whose weapon happens, against his will and without his knowledge, to strike a person from his hand, St. Augustine, *On Free Will*, ch. 4, XXXII, 1226.---A murderer is punished for his crime when he is killed by a judge, Salvian, priest of Marseilles, 157.---Killing a person is not always criminal, Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, *On the Person of the King and Royal Ministry*, CXXV, 845.---Holy men have lawfully punished criminals with death in order to instill fear, ibid., 849.---One who corrects the wicked out of love for justice, far from sinning, serves Christ, ibid., 845. (The same in Augustine, letter 48 to Vincentius.)---A king ought to correct the wicked, ch. 25, ibid., 850.---The sword was permitted by God to the prince for the punishment of wrongdoers, ch. 26, ibid., 851.---It is not always unjust to kill a person, Aurelius Constantius, *On the Conception of the Virgin*, ch. 4, LVIII, 437.---Earthly judges do not bear the sword without cause: they are especially appointed because of homicide, in order to condemn murderers and restrain others by their fear, Ivo, bishop of Chartres, *Panormia*, book VIII, ch. 5, CLXI, 1300.---When this person is killed, the law kills him, not you, ch. 40, ibid., 1313.---A judge is not the author of a crime, nor does he kill a person by convicting him, chs. 52 and 53, ibid., 1315.---When the authority of laws is exercised against the wicked, the dictator will be guiltless; the power of death has been granted to the ruler by God himself, idem, *Decree*, part X, ch. 94, CLXI, 721.---A judge punishes not from delight in another’s misery, which is evil for evil, but from love of justice, which is good against evil, ch. 102, ibid., 723, 724.---Not without purpose were instituted the authority of the king, the jurisdiction of the investigator, the claws of the executioner, the arms of the soldier, the discipline of the master, and even the severity of a good father; all these have their own limits, causes, reasons, and utilities, ch. 108, ibid., 725.---Gratian, *Decree*: to punish robbers and pirates on one’s own authority is not blameworthy, ch. 113, ibid., 726.---He is not cruel who slays cruelly, ch. 112, ibid., 726.---A judge is innocent even when he kills, chs. 115 and 117, cols. 726 and 727.---A king, minister of vengeance, must not allow evildoers to live, ch. 171, ibid., 740.---On whether it is lawful to kill people or not, Peter Abelard, theologian and philosopher, *Sic et Non*, ch. 157, CLXXXVIII, 1609.---One who strikes evil people insofar as they are evil, has cause for killing, and kills the worst, is a minister of the Lord, St. Jerome, *Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians*, XXVI, 317.---For the killers of excommunicated persons, as you know the custom of the Roman Church, impose an appropriate form of satisfaction according to their intention. For we do not judge them murderers if, burning with zeal for their Catholic mother against excommunicated persons, it happens that they kill any of them, Urban II, letter 122, CXV, 394.---One who exercises public authority kills evildoers by the command of the law itself and is held neither a transgressor of that commandment nor alien from the heavenly country, as is clear from the tradition of the Fathers, Gratian, *Decree*, part II, cause 23, question 5, CLXXXVII, 1218.---The offices [Col. 0871] of punishment may be performed with a good disposition: how the law does so, and how the judge, ch. 16, ibid., 1222.---Kings not only can, but must, restrain evildoers in whatever way they are able, ch. 23, ibid., 1224; and chs. 38, 39, 40, 41, ibid., 1229, 1230.

Just as one who kills inhumanly contrary to a command is guilty of wrongdoing, so also one who, commanded to kill, does not kill deserves censure, Philip of Harvengt, abbot of Bonne-Espérance, CCIII, 924.---Although killing is not permitted, divine authority has nevertheless made certain exceptions, so that it is lawful to kill a person without violating the rule of holiness, provided the killer prudently understands that this derives from the commandments, *On the Obedience of Clerics*, ch. 38, ibid., 924.---There is also a concession of divine authority: if any persons, acting under God’s authority, bear the office of public power and see the enactments of laws and rights of the state being corrupted, they may, after due consideration, inflict death upon criminals, lest by sparing evildoers they foster an increase of their evil, and the evil of a few, spreading like a serpent, bring harm upon the commonwealth, ibid., 925.---Divine authority has made certain exceptions to the law forbidding killing, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 692.

On war.

The use of this principle makes wars; its abuse makes persecutions. Therefore the question of war and persecutions belongs here. Since it will often be by no means useless to know what ought to be thought and said concerning war, we shall place here the passages we have excerpted from the Holy Fathers, intending perhaps to treat persecutions more suitably elsewhere.

Hence wars and quarrels, St. Jerome, XIX, 764.---Private wars are vehemently contrary to Christian simplicity and piety, St. Agobard, *Against the Law of Gundobad*, CIV, 119.---Constantine, a most powerful warrior, surpasses Cyrus and Alexander, Eusebius Pamphilus, *Life of Constantine*, book I, chs. 7 and 8, VIII, 12, 13.---Many and grievous evils are the lot of those who wage impious wars, *Decrees and Constitutions of Constantine the Great*, VIII, 237.---Whoever kills another in public combat shall fast forty days, St. Egbert, LXXIX, 407.---A soldier is punished if he does, uncommanded, what he will be punished for not doing when commanded—namely, if he kills, Alan of Lille, *Against Heretics*, book II, ch. 22, CCX, 397.---Octavian Caesar fought five civil wars, Paulus Orosius, XXXI, 1042.---Civil wars arose in the time of Valerian, ibid., 1117, 1118.---The Social War stirred all Italy, ibid., 959.---A dreadful war at the entrance to the Capitol, ibid., 957, 958.---Wars are concluded by strength, not by numbers, ibid., 785.---Civil war between Constantine and Maxentius, ibid., 1134.---In war justice must be observed even toward enemies. If a place or day has been appointed with an enemy for battle, it must be judged contrary to justice either to arrive before the place or to anticipate the time, St. Ambrose, *On the Duties of Ministers*, book I, ch. 39, XVI, 63.---This is shown by the examples of Elisha and Moses, ibid.---It matters for what causes and under what authorities men undertake wars that must be waged, St. Augustine, *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, book XXII, chs. 73–76, XLII, 447, 448, 449.---Only necessity impels good kings to wage war and extend their realm, Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, *On the Person of the King and Royal Ministry*, ch. 7, CXXV, 840. (St. Augustine has the same in *City of God*, book IV, ch. 15.)---That those who waged wars under God’s authority did not sin, Hincmar, ch. 9, ibid., 841; and CLXI, 1305.---That those who conduct wars and serve under arms are not displeasing to God, Hincmar, ch. 10, ibid., CXXV, 841. (St. Augustine has the same in letter 205 to Boniface.)---That a soldier obeying authority does not sin if he kills a person, ibid. (St. Augustine has the same in *City of God*, book I, ch. 26.)---One who corrects the wicked from love of justice, far from sinning, serves Christ, Hincmar, ibid., 845. (Hincmar’s entire work *On the Person of the King and Royal Ministry* may usefully be consulted on the present point.)---For more on the lawfulness of war, see Ivo of Chartres, *Panormia*, book VIII, chs. 45, 46, 47, CLXI, 1314, 1305. (There, concerning the circumstances in which war must be conducted for it to be lawful, he has the same as St. Augustine, *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, book XXII, ch. 74.)---A just war is one waged by public declaration, either to recover things taken or to repel enemies, ch. 54, ibid., 1316. (The same in Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XVIII, ch. 2.)---Let the king go forth with the sword to cut down what is pleasing to God, ch. 55, ibid., 1316.---Military service is not a crime, but to serve as a soldier for plunder is a sin, ch. 60, ibid., 1316, 1317. (St. Augustine has the same in *On the Word of the Lord*, sermon 19 on Matthew.)---Not all wars are to be condemned, *Decree*, part X, ch. 107, CLXI, 727; and chs. 109, 110, 125, ibid., 725, 728.---Soldiers themselves please God, although they kill, ch. 126, ibid., 729.

In war, the cause must be just and the combatant’s intention right; death in war is the more precious in proportion as it is more glorious, CLXXXII, 922, 923.---On soldiering and war, see much that is useful in this work of St. Bernard, *In Praise of the New Knighthood, Addressed to the Knights Templar*: “If to strike with the sword is altogether unlawful for a Christian, why then did the herald of the Savior command soldiers to be content with their pay, instead of forbidding them all military service?” St. Bernard, *To the Knights Templar*, ch. 2, CLXXXII, 924.

The purpose of war. — Military service was instituted either to repel injury or to inflict vengeance, Gratian, *Decretum*, part II, cause 23, CLXXXVII, 1159. — Is military service a sin? In the affirmative sense, many testimonies drawn from Holy Scripture appear to exist. Gratian enumerates ten and, drawing also upon tradition, opposes to them the general proposition, which he in turn supports by tradition: the precepts of patience are to be observed not so much in the outward display of the body as in the disposition of the heart, CLXXXVII, 1159, 1160, 1161, 1162, 1163. — Yet although war is lawful in itself, certain things in war are rightly condemned: the desire to injure, the cruelty of revenge, an unpacified and implacable spirit of savage rebellion, the lust for domination, and whatever similar things are rightly blamed in wars, Gratian, *Decretum*, part II, cause 23, question 1, chapter 4, CLXXXVII, 1163, 1164. — Conditions for a war to be just, question II, ibid., 1166. — It must be waged by edict, either for recovering what is due or for repelling enemies; objections are advanced from Christ’s conduct and words, question 3, ibid., 1167. — On the expediency of war, chapters 18, 24, 26, ibid. (Consult that entire work on every matter concerning war; questions are proposed and resolved according to the rule and words of Christian tradition.) Those who have waged wars with God as their author have by no means transgressed the commandment not to kill, Gratian, *Decretum*, part II, cause 23, question 5, chapters 9, 13, CLXXXVII, 1219, 1222. — What is to be thought of killings committed by peoples stirred by divine law: at one time the authors of such killings are guilty, at another innocent, chapter 49, ibid., 1235. — Killing is lawful in war; this is proved from several examples in the Old Testament, Philip of Harveng, abbot of Bonne-Espérance, *On the Obedience of Clerics*, chapter 38, CCIII, 924. — On the Truce of God. — The period of the Truces is established; penalties are decreed for violators; and the persons enjoying complete security in wartime are specified, Ivo, bishop of Chartres, *Panormia*, book VIII, chapter 147, CLXI. — On penalties for those who commit homicide during the Truce of God, *Decretum*, part X, chapter 31, ibid., 700. — On what the Truce of God is: cessation from arms from Wednesday evening until the following Monday; the sanction, approval, and commendation of this agreement, CXLIII, 1395, 1396.

On judgments of God. — The sacred canons do not judge that a confession may be extorted from anyone by the test of red-hot iron or boiling water; nor may what has been established by the teaching of the holy Fathers be presumed upon through superstitious invention, Ivo of Chartres, *Decretum*, part X, chapter 27, CLXI, 699. (Very little concerning judgments of God or the Truce of God occurs in the *Patrologia Latina*.)

Works to be consulted. — With regard to war, profitably consult Bernard’s work, *In Praise of the New Knighthood, to the Knights Templar*, CLXXXII, 922. — Secondly, Gratian, *Decretum*, part II, cause 23, questions 1, 2, 3, 4, CLXXXVII, 1159–1213. (There you will find very many things, indeed almost everything necessary to know concerning war, treated logically.)

Various occurrences. — The Marcionites extend the commandment not to kill even to livestock, St Augustine, *City of God*, book I, chapter 20, XLI, 34. — The Manichees extend it even to plants, ibid. — Although righteous Elijah slew many false prophets with his own hand, St Augustine, XXXIII, 940. — Constantine delivered Maximian and other wrongdoers, who had laid snares for his life, to death, Eusebius Pamphilus, *Life of Constantine*, book I, chapter 17, VIII, 29. — Abraham was commanded to sacrifice his son not in order to tempt faith but to prove it, Tertullian, I, 1164. — On the same subject see St Augustine, *Against Faustus the Manichee*, book XXII, chapter 73, XLII, 446. — Phinehas killed; Abraham killed; Peter committed a double homicide; and thus they performed a spiritual work. Therefore let us not consider works alone, but let us most carefully inquire into the time, cause, intention, difference of persons, and whatever other circumstances attach to the deeds themselves, Ivo, bishop of Chartres, *Decretum*, part X, chapter 65, CLXI, 711. (St Chrysostom says the same in his homilies on Matthew, chapter 18.) — On the deed of St Boniface, who with grief sent a certain person to death by his words, chapter 67, ibid., 711. — Therefore Phinehas deserved the covenant of an everlasting priesthood, because he roused himself in zeal for vengeance, Peter Damian, *On the Celibacy of Priests*, chapter 1, CXCV, 381. — Jephthah is read to have offered his daughter; yet he is not read to have received this command from God, nor is there found in Scripture clear testimony proving that God was pleased with him through such a sacrifice, Philip of Harveng, *On the Obedience of Clerics*, chapter 38, CCIII, 325. (There you will also find discussion of Abraham’s deed when he was about to sacrifice his son.)

[Col. 0873]

Abuse of this principle. — They committed a wicked killing who, in a certain rebellion and battle, perpetrated the murder of princes and, for favour with their temporal lords, despised the eternal Lord; scorning his commands, they committed homicide not by accident but deliberately, Rabanus Maurus, *Penitential*, chapter 4, CX, 471, 472. — King David was guilty of slaughter, Tertullian, II, 14. — Among the degenerate Romans a man was killed at spectacles for another man’s pleasure; and the ability to kill was skill, practice, an art, St Cyprian, epistle 1, no. 6, IV, 206. — Among the Romans, homicide, which was a crime when committed by individuals, was called virtue when carried out publicly, ibid., 205. — King Herod, greatly enraged, killed all boys under two years old who were in Bethlehem, St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 286. — Herod’s crime in the killing of John the Baptist is described, ibid., *Sermon on the Gospel Chapter*, chapter 4, ibid., 811.

**ASSERTION V.** — Indirect private homicide—that is, homicide not intended in the act itself or in the first intention of the mind—whether committed in ourselves or in others, is lawful when a reasonable and sufficiently grave pressing cause exists.

Although the Latin holy Fathers wrote very little on this point—not yet, at least in its initial form, equipped with the distinctions of our scholastics and of the frequently subtler theology—nevertheless they did not pass it over altogether. We have taken care to gather here those few passages diligently and carefully: they are indeed worthy of note and retention because of the importance and difficulty of the matter. — Thus a twofold question is proposed: one general, concerning which theologians are fairly unanimous in the affirmative; the other special and practical, concerning which a rather great disagreement prevailed—namely, whether a reasonable and sufficiently grave cause exists and is judged to exist for indirect private homicide: (1) endangered reputation and honour; (2) property of great value liable to be lost; (3) one’s own life unjustly attacked; (4) violated chastity; and (5) injury to marital right through adultery. We append the sayings of the Fathers to this fivefold question, noting that on the first and last point nothing sufficiently explicit and measured occurs.

1. On preserving reputation and honour through killing the assailant. — The Donatists stripped bishops and priests of honour, most evil murderers. For what good is it that men live, if they have been killed by you in their honour? Compared with your deed, the savagery of robbers seems lighter. You produce a living homicide, St Optatus, *On the Donatist Schism*, book II, chapters 21–25, 976, 977, 978. — He who neglects his reputation through indolence is cruel, St Augustine, CLXXI, 304. — Indeed, in my opinion, we do not even have a good conscience if through our negligence we incur disgrace, Hildebert of Le Mans, epistle 32, CLXXI, 304. — A good name is better than great riches, St Bernard, CLXXXII, 602 and 606.

As you see, these texts proclaim the great value of a good name. Would you then rightly conclude that, in defending so excellent—what do I say, the most excellent—of all natural goods, and in preventing its loss, you may commit homicide against an adversary? By no means, according to modern writers.

2. On property of great value. — In the sight of divine providence, those who have been stained with human blood for the sake of things that ought to be despised are by no means free from sin, St Augustine, *On Free Will*, book I, chapter 5, no. 13, XXXII, 1228. — When one person is killed by another, it makes a great difference whether it is done from a desire to harm or unjustly take something, or from the necessity of escape or assistance, as when a robber is killed by a traveller or an enemy by a soldier, Gratian, *Decretum*, part II, cause 23, question 5, chapter 19, CLXXXII, 1223. — As you see, nothing explicit occurs. — Yet Augustine explains his view in these words: “It does not count as homicide if a night-thief is killed; but if a daytime thief is killed, it does count. For it could be discerned that he had come to steal, not to kill, and therefore he ought not to be killed.” Thus he declares himself against those who kill a thief to preserve temporal goods; he seems to contradict himself by declaring elsewhere that it is not even lawful to kill—what he here excuses—in order to defend one’s own life against a thief or another person unjustly attacking us.

3. On one’s own life unjustly attacked and defended, also called lethal self-defence. Two explicitly expressed opinions occur: one affirmative, the other negative.

1. The affirmative opinion. — When one person is killed by another, it makes a great difference whether it is done from a desire to harm or unjustly take something, or from the necessity of escape or assistance, as when a robber is killed by a traveller or an enemy by a soldier, Gratian, *Decretum*, part II, cause 22 [probably OCR for 23], question 5, chapter 19, CLXXXII, 1223. — Beyond the commandment, “You shall not kill,” there is the counsel of perfection: “Do not resist evil; but if anyone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also.” [Col. 0874] Yet true and truly Christian innocence so abhors blood that it receives and preaches “not to resist evil” as though it were a commandment, Rupert, abbot of Deutz, *On the Holy Spirit*, book V, CLXVII, 1726. (The whole knot of the difficulty is certainly resolved here: “not to resist evil” is a counsel beyond the commandment—not a commandment, but as though a commandment.) — Courage, which either defends the fatherland in war even against barbarians, or at home defends the weak, or companions against robbers, is full of justice, Ivo of Chartres, *Panormia*, book VIII, chapter 31, CLXI, 1312. (The same is found in St Ambrose, *On Duties*, book I.) — When unavoidable necessity presses for defence both of oneself and of one’s country or ancestral laws, preparations for war must by no means be spared, lest a person seem to tempt God if he has something he can do and does not take care for his own safety and that of others, ibid., chapter 37, ibid., 1313. — The law of virtue is not to inflict but to repel injury: for one who does not repel injury from a companion when able is as much at fault as one who inflicts it, chapter 58, ibid., 1316. (St Ambrose says the same, *On Duties*, book I, chapter 36.) — A person is understood to kill unjustly when he kills without any right. Therefore one who kills a robber lying in wait is not liable, provided that he cannot otherwise escape danger; nor is one liable under this law who kills by accident, ibid., *Decretum*, part X, chapter 49, ibid., 704. — Lethal self-defence is declared just, chapter 118, ibid., 727. (The same is found in the *Pandects*, book I, title 3.) — To repel injury from a companion is the law of virtue, chapter 120, ibid. (St Ambrose, *On Duties*, book I, chapter 36.) — If anyone deliberately commits homicide, not resisting violence but using violence, let him do severe and perpetual penance, chapter 143, ibid., 754. — Two travellers attacked to the death by their host killed him in defending themselves, without fearing that they incurred the stain of sin, Gezo, abbot of Deutz, *On the Body and Blood of Christ*, chapter 59, CXXXVII, 402. — It is lawful to repel force by force. Objections, especially those drawn from Holy Scripture and the practice of the early Church, are refuted, Peter of Poitiers, *Sentences*, book IV, CCXI, 1150, 1151. — Many hold the opinion that a person may not kill another lest he himself be killed, according to Augustine … [lacuna]. But we also grant that it is lawful to repel force by force with the moderation of blameless defence; nor is it lawful, in repelling injuries, deliberately to kill a person. Yet if, with the intention of defending himself, he kills another without intending to kill him, he has not sinned mortally, Alan of Lille, *Against Heretics*, book II, chapter 22, CCX, 397, 398. — Human law gives even a traveller power to kill a robber, lest he be killed by him, St Augustine, *On Free Will*, book I, chapter 5, XXXII, 1227. — It does not count as homicide if a night-thief is killed; but if a daytime thief is killed, it does count: for it could be discerned that he had come to steal, not to kill, and therefore ought not to be killed. This too is found in the ancient secular laws: a night-thief may be killed with impunity in any manner; but a daytime thief may be killed if he defends himself with a weapon. For then he is more than a thief, St Augustine, *Questions on the Heptateuch*, book II, chapter 84, XXXIV, 627. — Thus perhaps divine Augustine is inconsistent with himself. When one person is killed by another, it makes a great difference whether it is done from a desire to harm or unjustly take something—as by an enemy, as by a robber—or by the order of revenge or obedience—as by a judge, as by an executioner—or from the necessity of escape or assistance—as when a robber is killed by a traveller or an enemy by a soldier. Not everyone who is the cause of another’s death is guilty, ibid., epistle 153, chapter 6, XXXIII, 660, 661. — If any man attacks another, and the man attacked kills the one who attacked him in defending his own body, he ought thereby to have firm peace with God and with the friends of the slain man, CCIX, 316. — If anyone, defending himself, his parents, or his household, kills someone, he shall not be guilty, Halitgar, bishop of Cambrai, *Penitential Book*, CV, 702. — If anyone kills someone while defending himself, he shall not be guilty, LXXVIII, 456. — Let us repel force and injury. For it is rightly held that whatever anyone does for the protection of his own body has been done lawfully, Ivo of Chartres, *Panormia*, book VIII, chapter 56, CLXI, 1316. — One who kills another while defending himself is judged at least less culpable, Isaac, bishop of Langres, *Canons*, title 2, chapter 2, CXXIV, 1085.

The other, negative opinion. — I do not approve the counsel that people should kill human beings lest they themselves be killed, unless perhaps one is a soldier or bound by public duty, so that he does this not for himself but for others, St Augustine, epistle 47, XXXIII, 183. — In the sight of divine providence, those who have been stained with human blood for the sake of things that ought to be despised are by no means free from sin, ibid., *On Free Will*, book I, chapter 5, no. 13, XXXII, 1228. — It does not seem that a Christian, just, and wise man ought to seek life for himself through another’s death; thus, even if he encounters an armed robber, he cannot strike back when struck, lest, while defending his safety, he contaminate piety, St Ambrose, *On Duties*, book III, chapter 4. — It is not lawful to kill one who kills; rather, it is necessary to be killed, St Cyprian, epistle 36. — It is not lawful for the innocent to kill even a wrongdoer, ibid., epistle 57. — It is not lawful for the righteous to kill the impious, St Augustine, epistle 44, chapters 4–5, XXXIII, 177, 178. — The entire question is discussed, namely whether we may kill another lest we ourselves be killed by him, ibid., *On Free Will*, book I, chapter 5, XXXII, 1227. — A cleric-priest who had killed a pagan in defending himself would do well to withdraw from priestly office, Nicholas I, *Letters and Decrees*, CXIX, 1131, 1132. — Let one who, in defending himself, kills an unjust aggressor do penance for seven years, Isaac, bishop of Langres, *Councils*, chapter 13, CXXIV, 1087. — One who kills a priest rushing upon him with arms, in self-defence, is said to have killed that presbyter by the instigation of the devil and is consequently subjected to canonical penance, Alexander II, epistle 116, CXLVI, 1404. — The opinion of divine Augustine concerning lethal self-defence and the preservation of chastity is reported, Ivo of Chartres, *Decretum*, part X, chapter 101, CLXI, 722, 723. (The author had nevertheless said beforehand that a person can sometimes be killed without sin.)

4. On violated chastity. — A twofold opinion still prevails, one negative and the other affirmative.

The negative opinion. — Chastity is in the soul; therefore it cannot be taken away by a violent rapist. Accordingly, I do not find how I can defend those who kill, St Augustine, *On Free Will*, book I, chapter 5, XXXII, 1228. (See this opinion developed more fully in divine Augustine, *City of God*, book I, chapters 16–20, XLI, 30–35. Although the holy Doctor speaks only of killing oneself, his words can nevertheless be extended to killing an assailant.)

The affirmative opinion. — Those who do not disapprove of someone killing himself to preserve chastity do not appear not to have extended this authority also to the assailant’s life. — Human law gives a man or woman the power to kill, if possible, a rapist violently attacking them before the rape is inflicted, St Augustine, *On Free Will*, book I, chapter 5, XXXII, 1227. — Freedom and courage are needed to defend chastity, ibid., XIX, 979. — To honourable minds chastity is of greater concern than life, St Jerome, XX, 309. — To chaste minds virginity is more than a kingdom, ibid., 307.

5. On an adulteress caught in the act. — It is not lawful for a Christian man to kill his adulterous wife, St Augustine, *On Adulterous Marriages*, book II, chapter 25, XL, 481. — King Theodoric writes to Crispianus that, for a man who catches someone in adultery with his wife and kills him, husbands’ taking up the sword out of love for chastity is not to violate laws but to establish them. See the whole of letter 37, Aurelius Cassiodorus, *Variae*, book LXIX, 533. — The first Christians placed chastity before life, Tertullian, *On Modesty*, II, 983.

**ASSERTION VI.** — Mediate homicide—that in which we merely cooperate—follows the respective character of immediate homicide, considered under the several preceding aspects.

A murderer is one who, being able to save a person from death, does not save him, St Jerome, XX, 789. — Those who order killings—that is, who command or persuade people to kill—are to be punished just like murderers, Regino, abbot of Prüm, *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*, book II, chapters 86–87, CXXXII, 301. — One who has the will to kill a person, even if he has not struck him, has killed, Blessed Bruno, bishop of Würzburg, *Exposition on Psalm XLI*, CXLII, 234, 235. — Homicides are committed not only by hands but by contrivance and consent, St Bruno the Carthusian, *Exposition on the Epistle to the Romans*, chapter 1, CLIII, 27. — There are some who do not consider themselves guilty if they do not do evil things, but consent to those who do them. To consent is for someone, when able to rebuke, to remain silent or flatter; but both those who act and those who consent deserve eternal death, Hervaeus, monk of Bourg-Dieu, *Exposition on the Epistle to the Romans*, chapter I, CLXXXI, 618. — Those dangerously deceive themselves who think that only those are murderers who kill a person with their hands, and not rather those through whose counsel, fraud, and exhortation people are destroyed. For the Jews did not kill the Lord with their own hands; nevertheless the Lord’s death is imputed to them, who have the greater sin, Ivo, bishop of Chartres, *Decretum*, part X, chapter 160, CLXI, 738. — Gratian reports the same, *Decretum*, part II, cause 33, question 3, *On Penance*, chapter 23, CLXXXVII, 1526. — Not only one who commits homicide by deed, but also one who does not aid a neighbour in grave necessity, is to be regarded as that neighbour’s murderer, Alcuin, *Brief Exposition of the Decalogue*, C, [Col. 0876] 569. — If a cleric consents to homicide and it is committed, let him do penance for seven years, St Egbert, archbishop of York, LXXXIX, 400. — If we fail to restrain vices and robberies that we are able to suppress, we shall not be held guiltless. For it is written: “He who can correct crimes and does not correct them, commits them himself,” Ivo of Chartres, *Panormia*, book VIII, chapter 20, CLXI, 1309, 1310. — Gratian has the same, *Decretum*, part II, cause 23, question 8, chapter 12, CLXXXVII. — If anyone after baptism has been implicated in homicide by deed, command, counsel, or defence, and has entered the clerical state through some concealment, let him be deposed and at the end of his life receive only lay communion, chapter 8, ibid., 257, 258. — One who has voluntarily wished to kill a person and has been unable to accomplish it is to be punished as a murderer, CLXI, 703. — Sometimes one who was the cause of death is more at fault than the one who killed, St Augustine, epistle 153, chapter 6, XXXIII, 661.

Having now set forth things as they are in themselves and as they have been regarded by the holy Fathers, there remains one point not wholly untouched in the *Patrologia Latina*: namely, the forensic aspect of homicide—how jurisprudence then dealt with it. Whatever occurs concerning it, we shall expound faithfully.

## CHAPTER II. PUBLIC LAW CONCERNING HOMICIDE

Sorcerers who have killed people by hateful arts, poisons, or magical whisperings are to be condemned to death, Ivo, bishop of Chartres, *Decretum*, part X, chapter 26, CLXI. — Murderers must submit and amend, or knowingly die in their sins, Cnut I, king of England, CLI, 1178. — If manifest homicide occurs, so that a person has been slain, let the murderer be handed over to the relatives; and if there is an accusation and the purgation turns out badly, let the bishop judge, ibid., *Ecclesiastical Laws*, chapter 25, CLI, 1180. — Concerning those accused of homicide: the archpriest is to enter their names in the council register of that city; the count is to summon them; and if they are rebellious, he is to commit them to prison until either they perform worthy penance or, if they deny the charge, are tested by red-hot iron or consecrated water, Laws of Břetislav, duke of Bohemia, CLI, 1258. — The archpriest is to hand over fratricides, parricides, killers of priests, and persons guilty of crimes of this kind, punishable by death, to the count or duke, who is to expel them from the realm by the iron hand or through the belly, so that like Cain they may wander the earth as perpetual fugitives, ibid.

If a woman has conspired with others for her husband’s death, and the husband, defending himself, kills one of those women, then, if he can prove that his wife was guilty of the conspiracy, he may dismiss his wife. But the plotting wife, subject to penance, shall remain without hope of marriage, Ivo of Chartres, *Decretum*, part X, chapter 169, CLXI, 740. — In the New Testament no one who kills ignorantly is punished by death; indeed, however he kills, if he takes refuge in a church he will be safe. — Yet the guilty are punished by the secular judge, so that the punishment of one may be the fear of many, Alan of Lille, book II, chapter 22, CCX, 397. — A particular case in which, after money was paid as compensation for a homicide, a safe-conduct frees the murderer: appendix to the *Formulae of Marculf*, 39, LXXXVII, 795. — Murderers or other defendants who by law ought to die are to be given no food if they take refuge in a church, Benedict, *Collection of Capitularies*, book II, chapter 193, XCVII, 724. — For provisions concerning homicides committed in a church or its courtyard, see the same author, chapter 230, ibid., 729.

Different penalties are to be imposed upon those who scourge or kill bishops: if they obstinately persist in their perversity, they may finally be cut off from the body of the Church under an anathema, Nicholas I, *Letters and Decrees*, chapter 141, CXIX, 1134. — Laws of Baldwin, count of Flanders and Hainaut, concerning homicide, ibid., 916. — If a fugitive who has killed a person, mutilated a person, or, being outlawed, has returned to his country, no free town, lord, or person may protect or guarantee him, ibid., 917. — On one who kills his own wife, Ivo of Chartres, *Decretum*, part X, chapters 166–168, CLXI, 739, 740. — “For killers of excommunicated persons, as you know the custom of the Roman Church, impose appropriate satisfactions according to the measure of their intention. For we do not judge them murderers if, burning with zeal for their Catholic mother against excommunicated persons, they have happened to slaughter any of them,” Urban II, epistle 122, CLI, 394. — According to the laws of Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius, a sentence of death is not to be carried out until after thirty days, Ivo, bishop of Chartres, *Panormia*, book VIII, chapter 10, CLXI, 1308. (Ibid., chapter 11: those who slaughter excommunicated persons from zeal for the Church are not murderers.) — On judgments to be given by a judge to a person before he is killed, ibid., *Decretum*, part X, chapter 47, CLXI, 703.

The Church should protect one guilty of blood, lest it become a participant in bloodshed. This principle of Pope St Gregory, cited by Gratian and developed much more extensively, is the summary of the Church’s jurisprudence throughout the Middle Ages; for the Church recoils from blood. Developing that principle, Gratian, as we have said, extends the commandment “You shall not kill” even to wrongdoers to be punished with death by secular authority. See Gratian, *Decretum*, part II, cause 23, question 5, CLXXVII, 1213–1217.

Besides homicide, the fifth commandment properly claims the sin of mutilation, since mutilation is a kind of incipient homicide. We therefore append it in its entirety. All the divisions and distinctions that we have given concerning completed homicide rightly apply to it; yet we omit them here, since we are supplied with insufficient and rather few texts of the Fathers.

## CHAPTER III. ON MUTILATION, WHETHER OF ONESELF OR ANOTHER, DIRECT OR INDIRECT

It is a grave thing to deface God’s work: we have a good craftsman and painter. Do not, O man, erase a good picture, Ambrose, *Hexaemeron*, book VI, XIV, 260. — If anyone voluntarily mutilates a limb of himself, let him do penance for three years, LXXVIII, 455. — If anyone cuts off his genitals, let him not become a cleric, because he is his own murderer and an enemy of God’s creation, Dionysius Exiguus, *Code of Ecclesiastical Canons*, XXII, LXVII, 144. — If a cleric cuts himself, let him be altogether condemned, ibid. — A layman cutting himself is to be deprived of communion for three years, canon 24, ibid. — On the same subject see the Council of Nicaea, canon 1, and Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 147. — Two monks who castrated themselves, supposedly for the kingdom of heaven, were condemned and successively excommunicated by many bishops whom they approached, and finally by the supreme pontiff himself whom they visited, *Lives of the Fathers*, book V, LXXIII, 968. — It is not lawful to castrate oneself for the kingdom of heaven, ibid., 969. — A monk, deceived by the devil, circumcised himself, book IV, chapter 46, ibid., 842. — A certain priest who had mutilated himself by cutting off his genitals in order to avoid leprosy may minister in the priesthood by permission, Innocent III, epistle 310, CCXIV, 15. — A steward who had cut off the nose and injured the tongue of a certain presbyter found engaging wantonly with the steward’s wife was struck with anathema and later absolved under certain conditions, Innocent III, epistle 156, CCV, 461. — Innocent III commands that a priest whose genitals had been amputated in addition to wounds inflicted upon him be granted permission to perform priestly office, and that a sentence of excommunication be pronounced against those who perpetrate such a crime, letter, book VIII, epistle 16. To a priest whose genitals a soldier, stirred by jealousy, had cut off while he was still a deacon, Innocent III kindly granted—despite this canonical impediment, after he had presented himself for ordination and had been ordained—that he might minister in his order, *Letters*, book XI, epistle 103, CCXV, 1423. — The Hebrews relate that Daniel and his companions were made eunuchs in captivity, Walafrid Strabo, monk of Fulda, *Ordinary Gloss*, chapter 39, CXIII, 1280. — Those who have cut themselves off are to be excluded from the clergy, Fulgentius Ferrandus, *Abridgment of the Canons*, canon 145, LXXXVIII, 826. — One who in a quarrel renders a person weak or deformed by a blow must pay the physician’s expenses and do penance for half a year, Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury, *Penitential*, chapter 23, XC, 915. — On a limb removed, CCIX, 917. — One who mutilates a criminal or cripples him in his limbs is to be judged an old murderer, Gratian, *Decretum*, part II, chapter 33, question 8, CLXXVII, 1262. — An example of horrible mutilation, Albert of Aachen, *History of Jerusalem*, book VII, chapter 9, CLXVI, 573. — A certain knight, insufficiently religious, castrated a monk and another priest; for this unheard-of and monstrous, as it is called, crime he was compelled to make expiation by long and harsh penance, Ivo, bishop of Chartres, epistle 135, *Decretum*, part XI, chapter 26, CLXI. — One who cripples a priest, Levite, or monk must serve God in a monastery under severe penance for ever, Isaac, bishop of Langres, *Canons*, chapter 9, CXXIV, 1086, 1087. — The suffering caused by cutting off is detestable: therefore both one who inflicts it on unwilling persons is to be punished by public laws, and one who castrates himself is to be held infamous, St Jerome, *Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians*, book III, chapter 5, XXVI, 405. — One who castrates himself is to be held infamous, ibid. — The Nicene canons rule that no one who has cut out his own genitals through impatience with lust may come to, or be admitted among, the clergy (St Jerome).

For the different types of mutilation, whether voluntary or involuntary, performed by one’s own hand or another’s, as well as their attached penalties, see Gratian, *Decretum*, part I, distinction 55, chapters 6–13, CLXXXVII, 303–306. — One who has amputated his genitals may not become a cleric, chapters 4–5, ibid., 302, 303. — A cleric who inflicts mutilations on any persons, or commands them to be inflicted, is to be deprived for ever of the honour of his conferred order, though he may be admitted to communion at the end of life, Regino, abbot of Prüm, *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*, book II, chapter 55, CXXXIII, 296. — One who castrates a man, or does anything else to him so that he cannot beget or conceive, is to be punished capitally as a murderer, as Roman law commands, chapters 88–89, CXXXII, 301.

Works of the Latin holy Fathers to be consulted and profitably read concerning homicide and its various kinds.

For homicide in general: Philip of Harveng, abbot of Bonne-Espérance, a man of great authority, *On the Obedience of Clerics*, verses, chapter 37, CCIII, 920, 927. — Peter Abelard, *Theological and Philosophical Works*, *Sic et Non*, chapters 155–156, CLXXVII, 1603–1609. This most celebrated man reports very many passages and sayings of the ancients.

For the lawfulness of homicide in the commonwealth: Alan of Lille, *Against Heretics*, book II, a work learnedly and logically composed, CXX, 396.

For trial by combat: St Agobard, bishop of Lyons, in his book *Against the Judgment of God*, against the Law of Gundobad.

For suicide: as already stated, St Augustine, in his eminent work *City of God*, book I, XLI.

For the forensic aspect of homicide, especially penalties to be inflicted: Regino, abbot of Prüm, *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*, book II. — Burchard, bishop of Worms, *Decrees*, book VI, CXL, 763–778. — Ivo, bishop of Chartres, *Decretum*, part X, CLXI. — Gratian, *Decretum*, part I, decree 50. — The *Penitential Book* of Halitgar, bishop of Cambrai, and his book IV, *On Penance*, CV. — Rabanus Maurus, CXI. — Isidore Mercator, CXXX.

For war: Gratian, *Decretum*, part II, cause 23. There you will find nearly everything worth knowing or necessary concerning war.

[Col. 0879]

## CLXX. INDEX ON SIMONY, USURY, AND AVARICE AMONG CLERICS, SETTING BEFORE THE READER THE VARIOUS OPINIONS OF THE HOLY FATHERS ON THESE MATTERS, THE LAWS AND DECREES ISSUED AGAINST OFFENDERS BY BOTH CIVIL AND ECCLESIASTICAL AUTHORITY, AND THE PENALTIES INFLICTED UPON THEM

### NOTICE

Our index, arranged according to chronological order and therefore according to the volumes of the *Patrologia*, contains references to all passages of the holy Fathers in which simony is discussed.

This index may especially be used by those upon whom the duty rests, or in whom there is a desire, in whatever circumstances, to speak or write of that all-devouring rust of souls called simony, whose sister is usury and whose mother is avarice.

Accordingly, when we have fully completed whatever observations on simony occur to us, we shall also add a few things on usury and avarice, so that every guise of this wicked and detestable family may become known to all. Thus our whole labour will be comprised under this threefold title: first and principally, simony; secondly, usury; thirdly, avarice.

[INDEX ON SIMONY.]

[Col. 0879]

## I. ON SIMONY

TERTULLIAN, presbyter of Carthage, I, 672: Simon Magus was expelled from the faith because, among the miracles of his profession, he also wished to make known the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands. — II, 46: The doctrine of Simonian magic, serving angels, was itself reckoned among idolatries and was condemned by the apostle Peter in Simon himself.

CONSTANTINE the Great, emperor, VIII, 95: He decrees against clerks who impose unjust burdens on the poor. — 96: Against his officials who harassed others. — 101: Nearly the same matter is treated. — 189: Another decree against tax collectors.

PHILASTRIUS (St), bishop of Brescia, XII, 1141: He speaks of Helen, whom he calls a prostitute from Tyre, and asserts that she followed Simon Magus. — 1195: The apostle Peter had said to Simon Magus: “Repent, if perhaps what you have done may be forgiven you.”

AMBROSE (St), bishop of Milan, XV, 1628: Leprosy swiftly follows shameful gain, and money wickedly acquired defiles body and soul. — 1797: Who are money-changers except those who seek profit from the Lord’s money and distinguish neither good nor evil? — XVII, 919: Such traders, therefore, will weep and mourn in hell, because no one will buy their wares any longer; for they will lose what they seemed to possess and fall into the evil which they neglected to foresee.

RUFINUS, presbyter of Aquileia, XXI, 475: That no cleric is to take usury, etc.

JEROME (St), presbyter of Stridon, XXIV, 527: Simon and Elymas, magicians, opposed Peter.

LEO THE GREAT (Saint), pope, LIV, 507: Simon Magus wished to acquire the chair of pestilence when he coveted buying the grace of the Holy Spirit.---LVI: Appendix to the works of St. Leo the Great, Code of Canons.---537: If any bishop performs an ordination for money and sells a thing which can be acquired only by grace, and under payment ordains a bishop, priest, or deacon, he shall incur danger to his rank. (And other matters.)---890 and following: What do bishops think is not for sale, when they have subjected the holy mysteries to commerce?

MAXIMUS (Saint) OF TURIN, LVII, 406: Simon Magus called himself Christ and maintained that he could ascend by flight to God his Father. But Peter, kneeling firmly, prayed to the Lord and by holy prayer overcame magical levity.

DIONYSIUS EXIGUUS, Code of Canons, LXVII, 144: That ecclesiastical offices ought not to be obtained by money.---171: That bishops, or anyone of the clergy, ought not to be ordained for money.---306: That clerics should pursue no dishonorable trades or shameful profits.

ARATOR (Saint), subdeacon of the Roman Church, LXVIII, 132: Here are read several poems concerning the love of gold.

M. AURELIUS CASSIODORUS, senator and abbot of Vivarium, [Col. 0880] LXIX, 778: King Athalaric promulgates most salutary decrees against simoniacs, in accordance with ancient decrees of the senate.---781: King Athalaric commands that his edict and the senate decrees concerning the expulsion of simony be engraved on marble tablets and placed before the atrium of the basilica of St. Peter.

GREGORY (Saint), bishop of Tours, LXXI, 173: Our author inveighs against Nero, who had Simon Magus with him.---220: He recalls Simon Magus falling from a lofty height onto a rock.---365: He recalls the pride of Simon Magus.---406: Shameful profit must be avoided, lest we become like Simon Magus.---728: Peter, after the Neronian and simoniacal wars, came to the cross.

GREGORY THE GREAT (Saint), pope, LXXV, 127: Where the gifts of heavenly grace are judged saleable, the glory of God is not sought.---LXXIX, 610: There are persons who seem to possess gentleness in their words, while bearing hostile fury in their heart. Such was that Simon Magus, baptized by the apostles but afterwards rejected by the prince of the apostles because of his ambition for abominable trafficking.

ANGELRAMNUS, bishop of Metz, XCVI, 1036, 1037, 1050: Simony is condemned.

CHARLEMAGNE, emperor, XCVII, 531: Concerning priests: how they are to obtain admission into the Church.---186: That no abbot may demand a reward for receiving a monk.---237: That no one may be ordained for money.---448: That the simoniacal heresy be guarded against in such a way that henceforth no one may make a grant not only because of the receipt of gifts, but also on account of kinship, familiarity, any friendship, or service.

PAULINUS (Saint), patriarch of Aquileia, XCIX, 296: “We have taken care to decree that no one shall presume to sell or buy the gift of the Holy Spirit.”

REMIGIUS, bishop of Chur, CII, 1097: Whoever steals money or property of the Church commits sacrilege.

SYMPHOSIUS AMALARIUS, priest of Metz, CV, 874: Simony is condemned.

RABANUS MAURUS, archbishop of Mainz, CVIII, 901: On not accepting gifts and on rendering just judgments.

LEO IV, pope, CXV, 667: He teaches that simoniacal bishops must be judged in a council.

SERVATUS LUPUS (Blessed), priest and abbot of Ferrières, CXIX, 669 and following: He desires that ecclesiastical honors, which belong only to holy and learned persons, should not be obtained for money.

PASCHASIUS RADBERTUS, abbot of Corbie, CXX, 709: Let the exposition on Matthew be read, on these words: “Do not make my Father’s house a house of trade.”

ISAAC, bishop of Langres, CXXIV, 1098: If anyone presumes to obtain from the king a dignity which he has not deserved, he is to be regarded as sacrilegious.

HINCMAR, archbishop of Rheims, CXXV, 802: Persons unfit for office are not to be admitted to an order in return for any gift.

ISIDORE MERCATOR, Collection of Decretals, CXXX, [Col. 0881] 17: If any bishop, priest, or deacon has obtained this dignity through money, let him be deposed. (And other matters.)---309: It has come to the holy synod’s notice that, among those enrolled in the clergy, certain persons, for the sake of shameful profit, and the rest.---423: We have also decreed that no priest or cleric should dare, in the manner of secular judges, to accept gifts for advocacy undertaken at others’ expense. (And the remainder.)---470: The pernicious custom of simony has disturbed the Church. (And much else besides.)---473: Avarice is the root of all evils, and its thirst lays hold even of priests’ minds.---581: If any priest or deacon is found to have sold anything belonging to the ministries of the Church, since he has committed sacrilege, it has been decided that he is not to be retained in ecclesiastical office.

REGINO, abbot of Prüm, CXXXII, 234: Concerning those ordained through money. They and those who ordained them ought to be deposed.---257: That priests should not obtain churches by payment. From the Council of Mainz.

RATHERIUS, bishop of Verona, CXXXVI, 429: Simon’s curse is recalled.---512: “He who does not enter through the door into the sheepfold is a thief and a robber.”---593: Whoever commits a simoniacal act will not be able to escape Simon’s condemnation.---676: In a letter, Ratherius urges Martin, his fellow bishop, not to lay hands hastily upon anyone, and to remember Peter’s words to Simon Magus.

Ancient Collection of Canons, CXXXVIII, 400: That sacred ordination must in no way be sold. (And other matters.)

ABBO (Saint), abbot of Fleury, CXXXIX, 483: Simony is condemned.

BURCHARD, bishop of the Church of Worms, CXL, 555: That bishops should not obtain a position of governance through the simoniacal heresy.---Ibid.: Concerning those who have bought sacred dignity for a price.

JOHN XIX, pope, CXLI, 1157: He inveighs against simoniacs, and among other things the following splendid words are read here: “Spare, I beg you, spare, you who are called the salt of the earth and the light of the world. Let it suffice mankind that Christ was once already sold for the common salvation of all.”

LEO IX (Saint), Roman pontiff, CXLIII, 621: St. Leo, in the Synod of Mainz of forty bishops, with Emperor Henry present, condemns the simoniacal heresy.

HUMBERT, cardinal and bishop of Silva Candida, CXLIII, cols. 1006–1211: There survive three books Against the Simoniacs.

PETER DAMIAN (Saint), cardinal and bishop of Ostia, CXLIV, 222: Simoniacs are anathematized.---CXLV, 105: Gehazi was the master of sellers, just as Simon Magus seems to have been the author of buyers. (And many other matters.)---Ibid.: That Balaam was a simoniac and yet did not lose the spirit of prophecy.---139: That the simoniacal heresy has flourished down to this time.---152: The writer inveighs against simoniacs.---526: Here may be read a little work concerning sacraments administered by wicked men.

ALEXANDER II, pope, CXLVI, 1296: Alexander II forbids Gervasius, archbishop of Rheims, to consecrate Josselin, bishop of Soissons, convicted of simony.---1297: Letter of Alexander II to Josselin, archdeacon of Paris, concerning one who acquired a bishopric through simony.---1298: On uprooting simoniacs.---1362: Alexander’s letter to the clergy of Milan concerning a simoniacal archbishop.---1383: To the clergy of Milan, concerning simoniacs.---Ibid.: To the people of Milan, concerning simoniacal priests.---1406: Concerning a simoniacal bishop.---1388: Letter of Alexander II to the clergy and people of Lucca against simoniacal sacred ordinations and grants of benefices.

JOHN GUALBERT (Saint), abbot and first founder of the Vallombrosan congregation, CXLVI, 792: He urges others to root out the simoniacal heresy.

JOHN, archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 223: On the pastoral office, addressed to the pastors of the Church.

GREGORY VII (Saint), pope, CXLVIII, 54: The decretal letters of Gregory against simoniacs are discussed.---83: A sedition stirred up by simoniacs.---147: On Gregory’s acts against simony.---293: Letter to Beatrice and her daughter Matilda. He urges them to avoid simoniacs.---296: To all Christ’s faithful in Lombardy. He announces that he has excommunicated Gotefred because he simoniacally occupied the Church of Milan. He warns them not to support him and to defend the faith.---310: To Albert, bishop of Acqui. He urges him to oppose simoniacs.---312: From Henry, king of the Romans, to Pope Gregory. He humbly asks pardon because he invaded ecclesiastical property and sold churches. He asks Gregory to uproot by his authority the stain of simony from all churches, and especially from that of Milan.---317: He inveighs against Philip, king of the Franks, as a seller of churches.---339: Excommunication [Col. 0882] and deposition of a certain simoniac.---343: To William, count of Die, concerning the eradication of the simoniacal heresy.---354: He declares excommunicated all who hold the goods of the monastery of Reichenau granted by Albert the simoniac.---384: To Henry, king of the Romans. He rejoices that Henry is taking pains to eradicate simony in his kingdom.---396: To Rudolf of Swabia and Berthold, dukes of Carinthia. He inveighs against bishops who were disobedient in carrying out the decrees of the Apostolic See concerning simoniacal clerics; therefore he warns the dukes never to receive any simoniacs whom they recognize.---407: To the people of Lodi. He rejoices that they and their bishop are rising against the simoniacal heresy.---415: To the monks of St. Denis. Their abbot, who is to clear himself of simony, is to come to him.---417: To Anno, archbishop of Cologne. He states that in a synod he confirmed enactments against simoniacs.---427: He reports that he himself deposed the simoniacal bishop of Bamberg.---431: To Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz. He commands him to inquire whether the bishop of Strasbourg is guilty of the stain of simony; he charges him to ensure that simony is uprooted.---446: To Richer, archbishop of Sens. He complains of injuries inflicted on his Church by the bishop of Orléans, of that bishop’s disobedience and simony.---464: To Robert, count of Flanders, that he may persecute simoniacs.---467: To the people of Chartres, that henceforth they should not receive as bishop Robert the perjurer and simoniac.---543: What should be thought concerning those who have been ordained by simoniacs unknowingly and without trafficking.---619: To the clergy and people of Chartres. He commands them to receive with due honor their bishop, cleared of the false charge of simony, and to obey him as their own pastor.---674: Letter to William, king of England, concerning the simony of John, bishop of Dol, and his deposition.---758: Roman Council. Simony is discussed more fully.---803: On Gregory VIII’s zeal against simoniacs.---(N.B. Some further matters concerning simony are also read in cols. 1112, 1114, 1115, 1116, and 1117 of the Appendix to the works of St. Gregory.)

BERNARD, count of Besalú, CXLIX, 420: Letter to Bernard, abbot of Marseilles, for eliminating simony from the monastery of Ripoll.

URBAN II (Blessed), Roman pontiff, CLI, 143: The Council of Piacenza, held under Urban, is mentioned; seven canons against simoniacs were enacted there.---169: At the Council of Clermont, Pope Urban confirms the enactments of the Council of Piacenza.---362: Urban writes to the clergy and people of Amiens and commands them to obey Bishop Gerewin, cleared of simony.---395: Urban writes to Berengar, abbot of St. Lawrence at Liège, an opponent of simoniacs.---528: Urban’s letter to Vitalis, a priest, in which it is read that mercy may be extended to simoniacs in retaining their rank if their life commends them.---551: Urban commands the clergy and people of Limoges to obey Bishop Humbald, cleared of simony.

GOFFRIDUS, abbot of Vendôme, CLVII, 154: Speaking of a certain person whose name he suppresses out of indignation, he says that this man, to increase his iniquities, used Simon Magus’s art against the holy Church.---159: Bernerius, abbot of Bonneval, could not restrain his spirit from rebuking simoniacal impiety.---218: He speaks of simony and explains why it is called heresy.---227: Simon Magus became a heretic because he thought that he could possess God’s gift through money.---Ibid.: The author speaks of the promises which abbots make to bishops for consecration under the name of profession.

IVO (Saint), bishop of Chartres, CLXI, 216: It is read that a priest who has given anything to anyone—priest or layman—for the investiture of a church must be deposed.---217: Estates which a priest purchases must belong to the church which he joined possessing nothing.---230: Nearly the same thing is read as at col. 216.---231: It is read that bishops ought not unjustly to appropriate anything for themselves from the goods of churches.---237: A bishop who has sold church property is deprived of his office.---Ibid.: What must be done concerning priests if they are found to have sold anything belonging to the ministries of the Church?---255: What must be done concerning a bishop who has sold church property?---351: That bishops should not obtain a position of governance through the simoniacal heresy.---Ibid.: Concerning those who have bought sacred dignity for a price.---352: Nicholas the Younger, presiding over a synod in the Church of Constantinople, said that no mercy must be of simony is by service, another by hand, another by tongue.---354: That those sell doves who dispense the laying on of hands for a price.---Ibid.: Concerning a bishop ordained simoniacally.---355: That no one may buy holy orders.---Ibid.: On uprooting simoniacal depravity.---Ibid.: That a bishop ordained simoniacally gave gold and lost his soul, while the ordainer received money and gave Rainald the archdeacon, swear in Ivo’s presence that they were in no way compelled in William’s election.---144: In Ivo’s letter to Bishop Richard it is read that some condemn simony for no other reason than that they cannot themselves be simoniacs.

PASCHAL II, Roman pontiff, CLXIII, 100: In a letter to Bishop Ivo and the canons of Chartres, Paschal forbids the acceptance of a gift for ecclesiastical benefices.---138: He writes to Manasses, archbishop of Rheims, concerning the abbot of St. Médard, accused of simony by a knight hostile to simony.---440: He writes to Conrad, archbishop of Salzburg, that he should investigate the case of the abbot of St. Emmeram, accused of simony.

PLACIDUS, monk of the monastery of Nonantola of the Order of St. Benedict, afterwards bishop of an unknown see, CLXIII, 653: A true and certain proof that, just as the person ordained through avarice for money is a simoniac, so too the person who, through avarice for exalted rank, is most certainly proved to be a simoniac.---657: A simoniac is one who receives ecclesiastical offices from laymen.---660: On ecclesiastical offices not being sold.---665: On the fact that simoniacs are worse than Arians.---669: That money must by no means be employed in acquiring ecclesiastical offices.---Ibid.: That those ordained through ambition are not true bishops.---Ibid.: How serious it is rashly to violate a sacred order by any fraud.---Ibid.: By what many testimonies it is clear that sacred dignities ought not to be sought through ambition.

CALIXTUS II, pope, CLXIII, 1137: Pope Calixtus confirms the decree issued against simony by Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres.

BRUNO (Saint), bishop of Segni, CLXIV, 295: Simon Magus deceived, violated, and corrupted the Roman people; from him the buying and selling of sacred things is called simony.---363: Simoniacs sell the sacraments of the Church.---485: Let simoniacs and invaders of churches be deterred from so great a crime by the example of the punishment of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram.---CLXV, 158: Since God gives only freely, those are therefore guilty of simony who do not confer sacraments freely and who do not receive them freely.---245: Those who sell and buy in the temple of God—in whom simoniacs are understood—are most vehemently rebuked by Christ and driven from the temple.

FREDERICK, archbishop of Cologne, CLXVI, 1535: Letter of Frederick to the Church of Liège. He commands them not to receive in the see of Liège one intruded through simony by royal nomination.

RUPERT, abbot of Deutz, CLXVII, 489 and following: Simoniacs steal Laban’s idols.---1020: Avarice in prelates and priests is condemned as though it were the root of simony.---CLXIX, 296: We must not make the house of God a house of trade.---1024: Peter could have sold Simon Magus what he requested; indeed, he could have pretended to be selling it.

HILDEBERT (V), bishop of Le Mans, CLXXI, [Col. 0884] 157: From St. Jerome: because they accepted money, the prophecy of priests became divination.---273: Hildebert suspends from the order improperly received a cleric who obtained the diaconate simoniacally, and forbids him to receive the priesthood.---769: He enters badly into the Church’s dignities who enters through money. Whoever buys the Church’s prelacies and promotions will be condemned with Simon Magus, to whom Peter said: “May your money be with you for destruction.” A simoniac is one who buys the gifts of the Holy Spirit and afterwards sells them. And since he has entered the house of the Lord like a thief, he must be driven from the house of the Lord like a thief.---783: There are certain people in the Church whom the leprosy of simony has seized. All those are called simoniacs after Simon Magus, who tried to purchase the gifts of the Holy Spirit with money.---933 and following: Hildebert’s sermon to pastors against simoniacs.

HUGH OF ST. VICTOR, CLXXVI, 477 and following: Five questions are discussed: first, whence simony takes its name and what it is; second, concerning the authors of simony; third, concerning those who sell or buy spiritual things; fourth, concerning those who, by buying bodily things in the Church, buy spiritual things with them and in them; fifth and lastly, concerning the case in which only bodily things are sold.

WILLIAM, monk of Malmesbury, CLXXIX, 1294: In William’s work entitled *Deeds of the Kings of the English* one reads: “The simoniacal serpent had raised its slippery head so high that it corrupted ecclesiastical honors throughout the whole world with its deadly hiss.”

ALGER (Saint), canon and schoolmaster of Liège, CLXXX, 945: That a simoniac departs from the faith.---Ibid.: That it is indeed a capital crime to sell and buy the Holy Spirit.---Ibid. and following: How the simoniacal heresy was punished in both Testaments.---946: It is altogether execrable and most grave that sacred orders should be conferred through the simoniacal heresy, which first arose against the Church.---947: What else is selling doves but receiving payment for the laying on of hands?---Ibid.: In how many ways the price of simony is paid.---948: It is absolutely decreed that whoever hereafter is discovered to have offered any reward for receiving the dignity of a divine gift is from that time to know himself condemned under the reproach of anathema.---Ibid.: That whoever has sold or bought, not merely orders, but even the administration of any ecclesiastical good is liable to the loss of his own rank.---Ibid.: That selling or buying a church or tithes is simoniacal heresy.---949: That simoniacs of this age strive to buy the Holy Spirit in the sacraments, as Simon Magus did in miracles.---Ibid.: That simoniacs have no authority from the Old Testament for selling or buying, although this may seem to be implied somewhere.---950: That no good fruit can arise from the beginning of simony.---951: That the Holy Spirit does not shine in the sacraments of simoniacs.---Ibid.: That the Holy Spirit can neither be sold nor bought.---952: That not even almsgiving can be made from the price of simony.---Ibid.: Where gold pleases priests, vice also pleases.---953: That one who permits himself to be ordained by someone whom he knows to be a simoniac must be deposed.---Ibid.: That one must burn with great zeal against simony.---954: That simoniacs are to be persecuted or avoided.---Ibid.: That simony must be fought.---967: Avarice gives birth to simony.---968: All ought to know that simony must be condemned.

BERNARD (Saint), abbot of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 739: He severely censures the abuses of judges and their frauds.---812: Simony, an old evil but ever new, is the daughter of avarice.

ROBERT PULLUS, cardinal and chancellor, CLXXXVI: Under the title, “What Must Be Done So That One May Live Well in One’s Rank,” Robert Pullus speaks at length concerning simony.

GRATIAN’S *Decree*, CLXXXVII, 479: It is proved by the authority of many that buying spiritual things is a sin.---Ibid.: A priest ordained simoniacally is called a priest in vain.---Ibid.: One who has obtained a church through money must be stripped of honor.---480: He will have a share with Simon who does not burn vehemently against simoniacs.---Ibid.: Simon’s condemnation equally encompasses giver and recipient.---Ibid.: One ordained simoniacally is condemned by a sentence of anathema.---481: A bishop who performs an ordination for money is condemned.---482: One who ordains or is ordained through money is excluded from the priesthood.---Ibid.: No one can be ordained or promoted in the Church of God through money.---483: Simoniacs cannot be priests.---484: One who ordains for a price confers leprosy, not office.---485: Those who do not possess the perfection of the Spirit cannot give it.---487: Simoniacs do not possess integrity of faith.---488: [Col. 0885] A simoniac is thereby proved faithless.---488: It is proved that the heresy of simoniacs is more condemnable than the others.---491: “Both he who gives and he who receives, so that holy orders may be bestowed, let him be sheep.---496: The sacraments of simoniacs lack effect.---502: Simoniacs are guilty of the faithlessness of those scandalized by them.---533: Concerning those ordained non-simoniacally by simoniacs.---Ibid.: Concerning one ordained by a person whom he knows to be a simoniac.---Ibid.: No mercy is to be extended to simoniacs in retaining their rank.---Ibid.: Concerning those unwillingly drawn to the ordination of heretics.---534: Ordinations performed simoniacally are judged false.---535: Concerning the manifold kinds of simoniacs.---Ibid.: Let one who approaches holy orders by any kind of gift receive eternal condemnation.---536: Let no one approach holy orders through payment, favor, prayer, or supplication.---Ibid.: Let no one approach episcopal dignity through canvassing.---537: Let no one be promoted to holy orders through either favor or sale.---538: When a price intervenes, priestly office is not restored.---541: Nothing is to be demanded for dedicating churches.---Ibid.: Nothing is to be demanded from those approaching conversion, nor is anyone to be invited to conversion for a price.---543: Nothing should be demanded from the person being ordained, but voluntary offerings ought not to be refused.---Ibid.: Those whose churches supply sufficient sustenance are not to be supported.---547: Concerning those who sell churches or ecclesiastical benefices.---Ibid.: A bishop selling benefices or ecclesiastical offices is to be suspended from office.---Ibid.: Bishops may sell neither altars nor prebends.---548: Whatever is acquired in holy orders through money given or promised is to be held void.---Ibid.: Whoever has bought ecclesiastical benefices is shown to have bought churches also.---551: Ministers of the Church are to be ordained by bishops without any sale whatsoever.---553: Those who sell or buy God’s gifts are alike condemned by God.---Ibid.: Those who do not exercise freely the grace they receive from God are sellers of
