to obtain ecclesiastical benefices for money be deprived of honor improperly acquired.---562: Concerning children who buy churches through their parents’ greed.---Ibid.: Mercy may be extended to simoniacs in retaining their rank if their life commends them.---564: Concerning those who ordain in return for gifts.---Ibid.: A simoniac is one who bestows rewards in order to be elected.---565: Concerning those who ordain for gifts, and those who return from heresy and are received in their orders.---571: Simoniacs cannot do penance while remaining in an order improperly received.---599: Concerning one who, enticed by a promise, abandons an accusation.---Ibid.: Concerning those who abandon an accusation in order to receive ecclesiastical orders.---904: Let one who sells ecclesiastical property not dare approach the altar.

GERHOH, provost of Reichersberg, CXCIV, 1241: Bishops, who are as it were columns and images in God’s house and building, should keep their hands from gifts of every kind.---1336: Here, from col. 1336 to 1372, is read a treatise on simony, or the letter of Brother Gerhoh to Abbot Bernard against simoniacs.

STEPHEN (Saint) OF MURET, institutor and founder of the Order of Grandmont, CCIV, 1154: On simony, which must be wholly avoided.

PETER THE CHANTER, CCV, 92: A monetary agreement, whether made at absolution, beforehand, or for absolution, produces simony.---99: He treats against simony existing in the substances of the sacraments, especially the Eucharist.---100: Peter burns against simoniacs with the same zeal as the Lord against sellers and buyers in the temple.---102: Against the sale and multiplication of Masses.---120: Against external simony, namely in the Church’s offices, dignities, and revenues.---128: In how many ways is simony committed?---132: On the punishment of simoniacs.---417: The contagion of the simoniacal heresy long ago sprouted in Balaam, who, with the reward for divination offered, went to curse the people of God.

PETER OF BLOIS, CCVII, 178: To a friend complaining that bishops enrich their nephews from Christ’s patrimony.---352: He asks the dean of Tours to correct his nephew, who simoniacally peddles many Church benefices.---381: He inveighs severely against R., archdeacon of Orléans, because he introduced the simoniacal plague into the Church, and he shows by many examples that it is execrable.

[Col. 0886] ALAN OF LILLE, CCX, 292: If an ordainer or person ordained acquires anything simoniacally, he is bound to restore it. But if a prelate extorts anything simoniacally from his subjects, he is bound to pay it back. (And other matters.)---591: Our author publishes certain poems against the crime of simony.---311: Authority acquired simoniacally is acquired in sin and through sin, yet it is from God. Similarly, money acquired through usury is possessed in sin and through sin.

INNOCENT III, pope, CCXIV, 657: Here is read the pontiff’s letter against simoniacs, written to the archbishop of Canterbury.---702: Letter of the same to the chapter of Bath, concerning the punishment of simoniacs.---711: To the bishop of Assisi, concerning a dispute that arose between the archpriest and Hermann the canon, the said Hermann accusing the archpriest of simony.---CCXV, 1260: He commits simony who bequeaths his goods to a church on the condition that he obtain a prebend there.---CCXVI, 31: Whether it is permissible to give one’s goods to the Church in order to obtain a benefice.

## II.—ON USURY

CONSTANTINE THE GREAT, emperor, VIII, 395: Here is read a decree against usurers.

HILARY (Saint), bishop of Poitiers, IX, 307: What is so intolerable as to confer a benefit upon a needy person in such a way that he becomes more needy? (And other matters.)

AMBROSE (Saint), bishop of Milan, XIV, 762: He sets before our eyes the inhumanity of moneylenders toward the poor, and the devices by which they enslave them.---775: Pursuing the etymology of *usura*, he shows it to be more fertile than any plants, and that every other form of gain is surpassed by the greed for lending at interest.---792: Beware of binding yourself by another’s debt, lest you too be said to have sold this.---998: Lending at interest is twofold: one kind concerns money, the other favor.---XV, 1792 and following: Usury is discussed.---XVI, 1291: Likewise, but in few words.

RUFINUS, priest of Aquileia, XXI, 475: Let no cleric either take interest, or receive an increase of grain or wine, such as is customarily taken upon a new loan, whether sixfold or even double; if he does so, he is to be expelled as guilty of shameful profit.

PETER CHRYSOLOGUS (Saint), archbishop of Ravenna, LII, 271: Miserly man, make purses for yourself—but make purses for yourself by giving away, because whatever the poor person receives, the heavenly Father receives.---272: A sermon on the faithful steward is read.

LEO THE GREAT (Saint), pope, LVI, 398: If any cleric is found taking interest or pursuing shameful gains from any such business, let him be cut off from the clergy and held alien from ecclesiastical rank.---426: Let none of the clergy receive more than he has lent to anyone, whether he gives money or any other thing.---715: Ministers of the altar may not lend at interest or receive interest.---868: If a cleric lends money, let him receive money.

GENNADIUS, priest of Marseilles, LVIII, 997: It is good to distribute one’s possessions to the poor. Better still is to give them all at once with the intention of following the Lord.

DIONYSIUS EXIGUUS, Code of Canons, LXVII, 46: Those who pursue avarice and shameful gain forget Scripture.---151: A decree is issued against clerics pursuing interest.

M. AURELIUS CASSIODORUS, senator and abbot of Vivarium, LX, 511 and following: Interest is so called from use, because it continually creates an increase of money lent.

GREGORY THE GREAT (Saint), pope, LXVII, 729: On the hunter and the snare of souls. The riches of this world are the devil’s snare. How few wish to be freed from this snare! How many grieve that they are too little entangled!

CUMMIANUS (Saint), LXXXVII, 991: Usury is condemned.

ANGELRAMNUS, bishop of Metz, XCVI, 1036: Let an usurious bishop, priest, or deacon either desist or be condemned.---1040: Clerics are not to be usurers in any way.---1049: Clerics are not to be contractors or agents, nor are they to seek their livelihood through any shameful trade.

CHARLEMAGNE, emperor, XCVII, 205: Let no priest or other member of the clergy demand interest.---296: Let a priest not be a trader, nor accumulate money through any shameful gain.---529: Interest exists where more is demanded than is given.---621: Against the usuries of priests and laypeople.

SYMPHOSIUS AMALARIUS, priest of Metz, CV, 874, 882 and following: Usury is condemned.

ATTO, bishop of Vercelli, LXXXIV, 38: That clerics, and laypeople also, should not take interest (Council of Carthage). Likewise, it has been resolved that if a cleric lends money, he should receive money; if a commodity, he should receive the same commodity in the same quantity as he gave. Likewise laypeople also are to abstain from usury; if they do not, they are to be excommunicated.

Capitularies of the Frankish Kings, CXXXVIII, 648: Those who seize what belongs to others are excluded from the kingdom of God, as the Apostle says: “The rapacious shall not possess the kingdom of God.”

BURCHARD, bishop of Worms, CXL, 647: Interest exists where more is demanded than is given. For example, if you give ten solidi and demand more; or if you give one measure of grain and exact something extra.---650: It is not lawful for any member of the clergy to become a private contractor.

BRUNO (Saint), bishop of Würzburg, CXLII, 84: Christ worked justice when he drove sellers and buyers from the temple.---215: An exposition is read on these words: “Usury and deceit do not depart from her streets.”

JOHN, first bishop of Avranches and afterwards bishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 224: He speaks truly concerning just things who is going to do just things.

Eleventh Century, CLI, 1196: Edward III, king of England, forbids any usurer to remain throughout his entire kingdom.

BRUNO (Saint), founder of the Carthusians, CLII, 996: Usury signifies eternal punishments.

IVO, bishop of Chartres, CLXI, 459: That not only clerics ought not exact usury, but neither should laypeople.---Ibid.: That a cleric should practice lending at interest neither in his own name nor in another’s.---1167: A cleric found to be taking usury is deposed.---Ibid.: A deacon, priest, or bishop exacting usury, unless he ceases, is to be deposed.---Ibid.: A cleric must not receive more than he lent.---1168: Whatever is demanded beyond what has been stated is usury.---Ibid.: When more than is owed is demanded, usury is taken.---Ibid.: He pursues shameful gain who, from greed, buys cheaply in order to sell at a higher price.

BRUNO (St.), bishop of Segni, CLXIV, 459: We have often seen a small sum of money lent swallow up at once the entire substance of the poor.

RUPERT, abbot of Deutz, CLXIX, 295: The Law commands that no one take usury, and money lent at interest cannot be beneficial.

HILDEBERT (V.), bishop of Le Mans, CLXXI, 817: Every robbery and every kind of usury is forbidden.

BERNARD (St.), abbot of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 739: He sharply censures the abuses of advocates, judges, and procurators, and their frauds.---741: Advocates and procurators who make gain from injustice are to be severely punished.---568: All who have received the sign of the cross ought to abstain from exacting usury.

PETER THE CHANTER, CCV, 156: Chapter 50 against moneylenders is read.---433: Money begets usury.---Ibid.: It is the custom of certain churches that, when someone is instituted in an ecclesiastical benefice, he swears that he has neither given, nor promised, nor lent—nor has anyone, to his knowledge, done so for him—money or service under an agreement, so that this benefice might the more readily be conferred. But it seems to me that this should be added: neither without an agreement nor with one.

PETER OF BLOIS, CCVII, 62: He shows that a cleric engaged in trade differs in no respect from a usurer, and that every pursuit of heaping up wealth is vain and pernicious.---122: He reproves the provost of Arques because, though elected bishop of Cambrai, he does not perform the office of bishop; he involves himself in secular business, conducts cases of bloodshed, tyrannically despoils his subjects, and permits no one to sway him.---285: He vehemently attacks the bishop of Lisieux for avarice and eagerness to lend at interest, especially because in time of dearth he did not open his granaries to the poor.

ALAN OF LILLE, CCX, 292: If anyone has confessed the sin of usury, the priest should advise him to restore what he has seized through usury, if he has the means of restitution; otherwise there would be no salvation for him.---311: Power acquired simoniacally is possessed in sin and through sin, and yet it is from God. Likewise, money acquired through usury is possessed in sin and through sin.

INNOCENT III, pope, CCXIV, 376: To the archbishops, bishops, and other prelates of churches established in the kingdom of France: that usurers are to be punished notwithstanding any appeal.

### III.—ON AVARICE

HILARY (St.), bishop of Poitiers, IX, 395: These words are cited: “Do not put your hope in iniquity; … if riches increase, do not set your heart upon them.”

AMBROSE (St.), bishop of Milan, XVI, 80: Fortitude must contend against every vice, especially against avarice.---137: By many examples from the Old Testament it is shown how ancient an evil avarice is; and from this it further appears how empty the possession of money is. [Col. 0888]---138: In contempt for money lies a form of justice.---139: The memorable story is related of Ambrose’s use of sacred vessels for the redemption of captives.---886: We must learn to seek the riches of good works.---983: It is written that whoever does not lend his money at usury shall dwell in the tabernacle of God.---1256: Do not, greedy man, store up wealth, lest you become a Christian only in name, but a Jew in deed.---XVII, 393: We ought to be kind toward one another.---434: Avarice can admit every evil; therefore it is called the root of all evils.---758: Avarice follows sorrow, which is marked with equal abhorrence in both Testaments.---919: Against greedy and commercial priests.

JEROME (St.), priest of Stridon, XXIII, 1055: The miser is described as never being filled with riches, and as desiring the more the more he possesses (and elsewhere).---XXIV, 48: The Lord commands in the Gospel that we should not lay up treasures on earth.---XXV, 1297: Avarice is called evil in order to distinguish it from good avarice. Therefore, woe to him who multiplies for himself evil avarice.---XXVI, 519: One who is found in avarice cannot be called holy.---521: Whoever is subject to avarice cannot have an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God.

PROSPER (St.) OF AQUITAINE, LI, 328: Silver and gold belong to the *diligentes* (“those who love” [or “the diligent”]).

JOHN CASSIAN, abbot, XLIX: A discussion of avarice occurs in cols. 300, 313, 316, and 322.

PETER CHRYSOLOGUS (St.), archbishop of Ravenna, LII, 259 ff.: A sermon on concern for earthly things and on the watchful servant is found.---281: A sermon on gold is found.---518: Gold is not avarice, but avarice is recognized only through gold.

SALVIAN (St.), priest of Marseille, LIII, 175, 177, 182, 188: You will encounter much to read concerning avarice.

LEO THE GREAT (St.), pope, LIV, 345: See, beloved, and wisely consider what shoots and what fruits spring from the stem of avarice, which the Apostle rightly defined as the root of all evils, because no sin is committed without covetousness.

MAXIMUS (St.), bishop of Turin, LVII, 322: He conquers the devil who restrains avarice in his heart.

JULIAN POMERIUS, LIX, 458, 459, 479: The reader will encounter much concerning avarice.

DIONYSIUS EXIGUUS, *Code of Canons*, LXVII, 46: Those who pursue avarice and shameful gain are to be removed from the clergy.---187: Under the title “On Avarice” is read what Bishop Aurelius said at the Council of Carthage.---306: Clerics are not to pursue dishonest trading or shameful gains.

GREGORY (St.), bishop of Tours, LXXI, 294: The story is told of thirty monks who perished because of avarice.---306: A certain theft is recounted.---758: On a girl who, prompted by avarice, uttered a false oath at the tomb of St. Eugenius.---798: A remarkable miracle concerning the avaricious is read.---909: On a merchant who gave no alms.---934: On a man who lost both gold unjustly acquired and his only son.---1029: Prudentius says:

> For the hunger for gold proceeds ever greater from gold.

*Lives of the Fathers*, LXXIII, 364: Here is read a story that leads to contempt for riches.---1096: On a certain virgin who was troubled by love of riches.

GREGORY THE GREAT (St.), pope, LXXV, 184: Avarice produces no good, because it is the mother of all evils.---LXXIX, 235: It should be noted that the heat of avarice causes the acceptance of gifts, and the acceptance of gifts causes the perversion of judgment.---364: The good of voluntary poverty is contrary to the vice of avarice; but one cannot be poor in spirit who does not yet know how to love eternal treasures (and elsewhere).

CHARLEMAGNE, emperor, XCVII, 512: On avarice.

PAULINUS (St.), patriarch of Aquileia, XCIX, 226: A covetous man has his own soul for sale (and elsewhere).

BENEDICT (St.), abbot of Aniane, CIII, 751: *Philargyria*—the love of money—is condemned.

JONAS, bishop of Orléans, CVI, 213: On those who, because of earthly and fleeting honours, are so puffed up that they do not recognize the poor, their equals by nature.

RABANUS MAURUS, abbot of Fulda and archbishop of Mainz, CX, 117: Here is read a homily against fraud and avarice.

EULOGIUS (St.), archbishop of Toledo and martyr, CV, 802: On the hatred of his people against King Muhammad, on his own avarice, and on the tributes imposed upon Christians.

[Col. 0889] ISIDORE MERCATOR, CXXX, 473: Avarice is the root of all evils, and its thirst takes possession even of the minds of priests. Then there is discussion of priests who took away gifts made to churches and turned them to their own use.

REGINO, abbot of Prüm, CXXXII, 464: I also confess that I am most grievously guilty of avarice … (and the rest).

RATHERIUS, bishop of Verona, CXXXVI, 182: There are two kinds of rich people: one of good persons, the other of evil persons (and elsewhere).---184: According to Jerome, the miser lacks as much what he has as what he does not have.

Ecclesiastical laws of the Anglo-Saxon kings, CXXXVIII, 500: We also teach that every priest should conduct himself decently and should not be an unjust buyer or a greedy merchant.

ABBO (St.), abbot of Fleury, CXXXIX, 493: Avarice is condemned.

BRUNO (St.), bishop of Würzburg, CXLII, 84: Those who work righteousness shall enter into heaven.

PETER DAMIAN (St.), cardinal and bishop of Ostia, CXLIV, 234: Avarice, the root of all evils.---424: On the same matter.---CXLV, 212: Do not despise your brother in his present need, if you desire God to aid you at the moment of your final necessity. “He lends to God who has mercy on the poor.”---213: Therefore, brother, send your riches ahead of you, from which you may afterward live; your resources will go before you, and you will possess them in that immortality forever.---256: That the covetous worshipper of money is more truly called a worshipper of coins than a worshipper of Christ.---532: That profit is gained from riches if they are distributed to the poor.---533: What is avarice? To be avaricious is nothing other than to love money. Avarice is, as it were, a two-headed serpent (and elsewhere).---534: How pernicious it is to desire riches.

JOHN, first bishop of Avranches and then archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 224: A priest must not be eager for shameful gain.---227: A hunchbacked priest is one weighed down by the burden of earthly greed.

LANFRANC (Blessed), archbishop of Canterbury and primate of England, CL, 300, 301: We ought to be merciful toward one another.---328: Avarice must be avoided.---359: Avarice is the root of all evils.

BRUNO (St.), founder of the Carthusians, CXLIII, 343: The miser makes money his god.

GUIBERT (V.), abbot of St. Mary of Nogent, CLVI, 156: Avarice is the propagator of wickedness.---1153: Avarice arose after the Flood.

IVO (D.), bishop of Chartres, CLXI, 239: It is read that the Church possesses gold not to keep it, but to distribute it and to provide aid in times of need.

BRUNO (St.), bishop of Segni, CLXV, 406: The man with dropsy in the Gospel signifies the avaricious. Avarice is defined as an insatiable love of possessing.

RUPERT, abbot of Deutz, CLXVII, 1020: Avarice in prelates and priests is condemned, as though it were the root of simony.---CLXVIII, 75: Once avarice has occupied the mind, nothing is enough: “The priests shall eat and not be satisfied.”---157: Avarice is the god of the Jews.---219: The avarice of the Romans.---355: Avarice is the cause of evils.---364: That avarice being in the head signifies its being in everyone’s intention.---507: Avarice is signified by fire.---615: It was an evil of avarice to trade in the Temple and to sell Christ.---1244: The miser is always in want.---CLXIX, 878: Under Balaam’s name he speaks of all who, anywhere on earth, under the name or office of the priesthood, pursue avarice and love the wages of iniquity.---1024: Peter could have sold to Simon Magus what he sought; indeed, he could have pretended to be selling it. Churchmen, despite their avarice, do not imitate this course of action.

HILDEBERT (V.), bishop of Le Mans, CLXXI, 156: A letter in which he deals with a friend recently established in an ecclesiastical dignity concerning the gravity and dangers of avarice; he elegantly commends him because, generously refusing gold, silver, and other gifts offered for God’s sake, he offered him a most welcome sacrifice.

GODEFRIDUS, abbot of Admont, CLXXIV, 1034: He who attends to the avarice of this age, like a tax collector, takes what belongs to others.

HUGH OF ST. VICTOR, CLXXV, 584: Avarice is compared with idolatry, because the wickedness is not dissimilar. For as the idolater worships a log, so the miser worships a coin.---CLXXVI, 1001: Avarice is an insatiable and dishonourable desire for glory, riches, or any other things whatever. Its companions are *philargyria* (love of money), perjury, violence, usury, fraud, robbery, and deceit.

ALGER (D.), canon and schoolmaster of Liège, CLXXX, 967: Avarice gives birth to simony.

BERNARD (St.), abbot of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 739: He sharply censures the abuses of advocates, judges, procurators, and their frauds.---741: Advocates [Col. 0890] and procurators who profit from injustice must be severely punished.---825: He attacks the ambition of churchmen, the promotion of the young, and plurality of benefices.---852: He sharply censures ambitious persons who rashly and unworthily usurp the sacred offices of the Church.---274: In his letter to the bishops of Aquitaine against Gerard of Angoulême, where he nobly defends the cause of Innocent as the lawful pope, Bernard speaks at greater length about ambition.---CLXXXIII, 198 ff.: Covetousness is the root of iniquity; ambition, a subtle evil, a hidden poison, an unseen plague, an artificer of deceit, mother of hypocrisy, parent of envy, origin of vices, fuel of crimes, rust of virtues, moth of holiness, blinder of hearts, creating diseases from remedies and producing languor from medicine. (This eloquent description of covetousness should be read in full.)---311: Ambition for power deprived an angel of angelic blessedness.---820: Bernard complains of the avarice of those who have undertaken the care of governing souls.---876: The miser hungers like a beggar.---979: Avarice has claimed the chief place among the parts of robbery and fraud.---1155: The shepherds of the Church cannot love Christ because they love gifts and have given their hands to Mammon. Bernard reproves them because they go about neat and adorned, wrapped in varied garments, like a bride proceeding from her chamber.

AELRED, abbot of Rievaulx, CLXXXIV, 1265 ff.: Under the title “On Avarice.”

ZACHARIAS, bishop of Chrysopolis, CLXXXVI, 143: We must not lay up treasures on earth.---337: On the rich man and Lazarus.

PETER LOMBARD, CXCI, 707: The avaricious are defined not as those possessing riches, but as those devoted to riches.---CXCII, 208: The miser has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God. Avarice is equated with idolatry.---280: Avarice contaminates not the body but the soul.---359: Avarice is the root of all evils, which properly means love of money.

GARNIER, regular canon and superior of St. Victor in Paris, CXCIII, 141: Avarice is like a jar that keeps the mouth of the heart open.---153: From avarice arise treachery, fraud, deceit, perjuries, restlessness, violence, and the closing of hearts against mercy.---318: In Sacred Scripture the sin of avarice is sometimes denoted by the name “lead.”

RICHARD OF ST. VICTOR, CXCVI, 481: Avarice is a mortal sin.

HENRY OF CASTRO MARSIACO, abbot of Clairvaux, afterward cardinal and bishop of Albano, CCIV, 222: A letter to Pope Alexander concerning the monks of Dol, who by armed force had extorted tithes from the monks of the House of God, of the Cistercian Order, and had wounded some of them as well.

STEPHEN (St.) OF MURET, founder and institutor of the Grandmontine Order, CCIV, 1140: On not possessing lands.---1143: On avoiding gain.---1148: What revenues it is permissible to possess.

PETER THE CHANTER, CCV, 72: Covetousness is the root of all evils.

> Love of money grows in proportion as money itself grows.  
> —Juvenal

---74: Avarice in churchmen is detestable. Nothing is more wicked than a miser; nothing more unjust than to love money.---73 ff.: Avarice frequently promotes the unworthy to dignities.---400: Avarice is

> A leech that will not leave the skin until full of blood.  
> —Horace

PETER OF BLOIS, CCVII, 122: He reproves the provost of Arras because, though elected bishop of Cambrai, he does not perform the office of bishop; he involves himself in secular business, conducts cases of bloodshed, tyrannically despoils his subjects, and allows no one to admonish him.---178: To a friend complaining that bishops enrich their nephews from Christ’s patrimony.---249: He urges Simon, a canon, who has abandoned literary study and is occupied with accumulating wealth, to pursue learning after cutting away his greed for riches, following the example of many philosophers.---285: He vehemently attacks the bishop of Lisieux for avarice and eagerness to lend at interest, especially because in time of dearth he did not open his granaries to the poor.

ALAN OF LILLE, CCX, 123: The earth is bounded by its limits, water by its boundaries, air is enclosed by its limit, heaven is confined by its bounds: avarice alone knows no measure. ## CLXXI. INDEX OF PROFANE AND ILLICIT PLEASURES, COMPRISING SENTENCES, SAYINGS, SERMONS, TREATISES, AND THE BOOKS THEMSELVES OF THE HOLY FATHERS AND OF ALL THE WRITERS OF THE *PATROLOGIA LATINA*

### NOTICE

At the outset we set before the reader’s eyes the principal subjects treated in this index, according to the order of the numbers given below:

I. Profane love arising from desire or lust.---II. Licentious singing, little songs, songs, shameful tales, erotic poems, obscene books.---III. Immoderate care of the body; luxury in clothing and ornaments; false and vain valuation of beauty and appearance.---IV. Drunkenness.---V. Immoderate feasting, or gluttony.---VI. Company and conversations of the licentious; flattery.---VII. Games in which gain is made by chance, such as gambling, dice, ball-games, etc.---VIII. Frequent association with women and the sins arising from it.---IX. The pomp of the world, domestic luxury, vain desire for glory and riches.---X. Worldly pleasures, pagan festivals, dances.---XI. Wantonness of the eyes and curiosity for less decent paintings and images.---XII. Spectacles, comedies, tragedies, theatres, actors.---XIII. Idle talk and buffoonery.---XIV. Noisy, costly, and unbecoming hunts, tournaments, etc.

## [INDEX OF PROFANE AND ILLICIT PLEASURES]

[Col. 0891]

### I.—Profane love arising from desire or lust

TERTULLIAN.—Nothing can be loved apart from that through which it is what it is, II, 759.---Perfect love puts demons to flight and gives life to confession, 147.---Beauty is naturally an incitement to lust, I, 1317.---The desire to please through beauty does not arise from an unblemished conscience, ibid.---The use and fruit of beauty is luxury, 1319.

ARNOBIUS.—Lust blinds the mind; examples are given, V, 1207.---Human beings are inclined toward lust and, by the weakness of nature, prone to the enticements of pleasures, 1044.

LACTANTIUS.—Young men are inflamed by lust, which is especially aroused by sight, VI, 711.---On the pleasure of touch and lust, 716.---The abominable lust of Maximian Herculius, VII, 207.---Many, thinking that we are of concern to no god, or that after death we shall be nothing, give themselves wholly to lusts, 354.---He cries out concerning Sodom: “This matter cannot be described in proportion to the greatness of its crime … the greatness of the crime surpasses the capacity of speech,” VI, 707.---Those who indulge pleasures and obey lust enslave their soul to the body and condemn it to death, 718.

EUSEBIUS PAMPHILUS.—On the insatiable lust of the tyrant Maxentius, VIII, 24.---A noble Christian woman delivered over to him kills herself with a sword, ibid.---The tragic death of this tyrant, 26.

HILARY (St.) OF POITIERS.—The corruption of human flesh cannot be wholly abolished in this life, IX, 842.---The struggle with concupiscence in the regenerate, 876, 877.---Our flesh is daughter of Babylon and confusion, 783.---The vices of the flesh must be crucified, 605.---They are restrained by remembrance of God, 405.---Bodily pleasure contaminates the soul, 402.

ZENO (St.) OF VERONA.—The nature of sincere love must necessarily be known by everyone … for there is another love altogether contrary to our salvation … it is depicted with a boyish form, a wanton expression, naked, winged, armed with arrows, and blind, XI, 276.---This love jokes, plays, sighs, complies, tempts, deceives, flatters, rages, 277.---The foulness of lust, ever seething, is perpetrated either in reality or in imagination, 292.

[Col. 0892] AMBROSE (St.).—The stirrings of lust are often aroused by the devil, XIV, 1025.---A person must turn away the eyes of the soul lest they see the sewer of lusts, XV, 1268.---Whoever is subject to lust is a slave, XIV, 650.---The nature of the flesh resists discipline because it obeys pleasure, XIV, 363.---The flesh is always seething, 368.---Its frailty is described, 167, 168, 825.---He who burns in heart will burn in body, 891.---Much on avoiding lust, ibid.---Lust is a savage spur to crimes: it never allows the passion to remain at rest; it is hot at night, pants by day, wakes one from sleep, draws one away from work, recalls one from reason, takes away counsel, troubles lovers, bends those who have fallen, lies in wait for the chaste, inflames by possession, and is kindled by use, 538.---The tickling of love is tender, awakening an unlooked-for affection, XVI, 1318.---No power to love is stronger than grace, 30.---What is so innate to nature as to love one who loves you? 113.---Wantonness often lies hidden under the sorrowful garb of the mind, 1318.---Our rust is wantonness; our rust is luxury, 742.---Lust, like straw, is quickly kindled and quickly consumed, 1045.---Youthful frivolity is subject to the desires of the world, 296.---Pleasure alone stripped us of Paradise, 1193.

JEROME (St.).—What shameful love does, XXII, 1195 ff.---It is necessary to love something, 405.---The sweet words of lovers, 532.---Holy love has no flattering and sweet little letters, ibid.---Loving and being loved often occur through magical arts, XXVI, 415.---Love is expelled by love, XXII, 1080.---Illicit loves are difficult to root out in an old man, 957.---A lustful mind pursues shameful things more ardently, ibid.---No one can be possessed by two loves: if you are a lover of the flesh, you do not receive the love of the Spirit, XXIII, 1121.---Fomentations of lust, 553.---The wretched condition of lovers, 1071.---What it is to serve idols, XXII, 350.---Each person’s idol is what he loves, 400.

AUGUSTINE (St.).—The slippery lovers, so that they may be beautiful deceivers, do not care for truthful reprovers, XXXVI, 282.---A human being always loves himself and his own body, XXXIV, 27, 29.---Love is the weight by which the mind is borne, XXXII, 858; XXXIII, 677; XLI, 342.---Love, but see what you love, XXXVI, 260.---Love either ascends or descends, [Col. 0893] XXXVII, 1629.---When love is perverse, it is called covetousness or lust, XXXVI, 124.---There is a love that leads to every right action, and a love that leads to every sin, 1026.---We must not love people as gluttons love thrushes, XXXV, 2038.---A creature, if loved by one who neglects God, becomes a punishment to its lover, XXXII, 138.---The vices found in love, XLI, 632.---It is disordered love of things, not the things themselves, that is at fault, 356.---Disordered love of a creature is sin, XXXVIII, 143.---Love of temporal things is birdlime for spiritual wings, 646, 1415.---Illicit love, XXXIX, 1530.---Infernal love, XXXVII, 1816.---Lust, foul and favouring vice, pretends that God is love, XLII, 374.---The force of impure love, XXXVIII, 584, 883.---How many troubles it has, XXXVII, 1331.---Impure love hurls one downward; holy love lifts one upward, 1618.---Whoever loves carnally must necessarily love with deadly jealousy, XXXVI, 310.

What lust is, XL, 496.---Pleasure belongs to the senses, XLIV, 770, 771.---By *libido* people commonly understand the obscene movements of the body, XLI, 624.---Lusts must be distinguished from the senses, XLV, 1367, 1368.---The devil is the author of lust, XLIV, 801.---The evil of original sin, 142.---Lust resisting the spirit is evil, XLV, 1161.---A disease, XLIV, 469, 765.---A wound of nature, 732.---A punishment for sin, 120, 287.---It seeks concealment, XLI, 426, 427.---It is more shameful than other desires, XLIV, 756.---Shame at it is deserved, XLI, 425, 428, 431.---Why this is so, 431; XLV, 1161.---Why the movement of lust is more shameful than others, XLI, 427, 430.---The disease of lust must be distinguished from the business of marriage, XLV, 1090.---Lust is not comparable to hunger and other afflictions, XLIV, 773.---It absorbs the mind, ibid.---It does not permit holy thoughts, 808.---It agitates and claims the whole person for itself, XLI, 424.---Lust must be restrained even between spouses, XLIV, 716, 717.---When it is conquered, the devil is conquered, 801.---The onset of lust is broken by the gravity of singing, 798.---Lust belongs to the nature of beasts and to the punishment of human beings, XLV, 1360, 1363, 1372.---The lustful are described, XXXIV, 97.

JOHN CASSIAN.—On the struggle of flesh and spirit, XLIX, 591, 600.---On lust, 870.---The memory of lust must be wholly excluded, 1146.

PROSPER (St.).—The maladies of the soul arising from evil desire, LI, 285.---The desire of the flesh against the spirit can be diminished or increased, 349.---There must be not peace but war with it, 656.---How people should be loved, 465.---On the diversity of human affection, 448.---Creatures are not to be clung to, 438.

PETER CHRYSOLOGUS (St.).—Bodily beauty is not concupiscence; rather, the beauty of form drew me into concupiscence and led me to a fall, LII, 518.---What evils luxury brings forth, 190, 190, 198, 549.---Luxury resembles despair, 199.---He who burns with luxury would rather perish with it than return, 550.---The luxurious are the devil’s swine, 190.---Luxury is called a contagion of the flesh, 362.---See sermons on the prodigal son, 183, 187, 190, 194; and on impious Herod, 549, 653.

SALVIAN.—Love is foolish when it remembers another and forgets itself (in matters of salvation), LIII, 215.---Those lingering in the abyss of lust bury themselves beneath their own ruins, 184.---How certain enticements were permitted under the Law but removed by the Gospel, 193.

LEO THE GREAT (St.).—When one abstains from what is permitted, one more easily resists what is forbidden, LIV, 450.---Let the mind give itself to no carnal pleasure and be captive to no lie, 451.---The devil’s snares do not rest amid our occupations, 449.---There are two loves from which all pleasures arise, 448.---Desires serve as soldiers for the devil, 400.---Let us abstain from the heat of earthly desire and from all the enticements of vices, 506.---Rebellious desires must be restrained by reasonable moderation and holy purpose, 439.---Let not the mind, forgetful of its sovereignty, consent to the desires of the flesh, 147.

MAXIMUS (St.) OF TURIN.—Whoever, after receiving grace, has tasted worldly wantonness receives the distinction between good and evil, LVII, 360.---Our Lord, the corrector of every shamefulness, … with swift force forestalls the incitements of slippery flesh, 750.---How far from the human heart he wishes luxury to be, since with such caution he restrains and chastises wanton looks, ibid.---The lust of the scorpion stings us, 340. See 810.

PRUDENTIUS (St.).—A description of mad love, LX, 55.

EUGYPPIUS, abbot.—What young people especially ought to avoid, LXII, 605.

BOETHIUS.—One who clings to transient goods is like a drunken person, LXIII, 724.

FULGENTIUS (St.) OF RUSPE.—Disordered love is the beginning of sin, LXVII, 167.---Departure from the highest good toward the lowest [Col. 0894] good is the sinner’s own and voluntary evil, ibid.---Why worldly love is vicious, ibid.

*LIVES OF THE FATHERS.*—Shameful love is conquered by divine love, LXXIII, 563.---Lust lives even in old people, 883.---The temptation of lust must be overcome by hardships, 810.---Demons kindle lust, 566.

GREGORY THE GREAT (St.).—The perfection of pleasure is sought in vain, LXXV, 667.---Every descent lies in pleasure, 782.---God teaches us to beware of pleasures of the flesh, LXXVI, 363.---He inveighs against worldly pleasures, 1113.---The devil watches for an opportunity to tempt, LXXV, 566.---How great is the devil’s cunning in deceiving, 1047.---His suggestions are various, 1063; LXXVI, 716.---Evil thoughts must be examined as to their origin and repelled, LXXV, 587, 628, 629.---No one is immune from them, 1146.---If reason, as a mistress, returns, the thoughts of the heart return to order and the unclean spirit is cast outside, 546.---Lust consumes the flesh and, through it, all good deeds, 201.---Luxury is a fire that devours unto destruction, ibid.---The poison of lust springs from the root of pride, 364.---Our consent opened the gates of concupiscence, whence innumerable evils, LXXV, 660.---The human heart is an abyss, LXXVI, 77.---The need to guard and watch over the heart, 118.---One must return from outward things to the heart, 330.---When human hearts desire earthly things, they lay themselves open to be crushed by the devil, 594.---How great is the blindness of the luxurious, LXXV, 1162.---The luxurious person bears within himself a tumultuous crowd of shameful thoughts, 667.---So long as we live, the fire of concupiscence must be feared, LXXVII, 336.---What those who sin through sudden concupiscence ought to do, 113.---Pleasure and youth are vain, 324.

TAIO, bishop of Zaragoza.—On luxury, LXXX, 945.

ISIDORE (St.) OF SEVILLE.—What vehement love is like, LXXXII, 417.---Lust was worshipped by pagans, 324.---How it must be avoided, LXXXIII, 640.---The motions of lust, 616.

BEDE (Venerable).—While the flesh is weakly subjected to flattering desires, the army of vices is already firmly armed against the mind, XCIII, 52.

PAULINUS (St.) OF AQUILEIA.—May carnal love never exclude heavenly love; may the sweetness of this changeful and wondrous age never deceive you, I pray, XCIX, 220.---Let no bodily beauty deceive you, lest death enter your soul through the windows of your eyes, ibid.---When death comes, tell me, how much beauty will remain in the body? 220.

ALCUIN (Blessed).—Be conscious of chastity, not of lust; of continence, not of luxury; of sobriety, not of drunkenness, C, 161.---Let no carnal desire block for you the path of blessedness, 146.---Where there is bodily uncleanness, there is the dwelling-place of a devilish spirit, CI, 626.---Let a person set against the desire of his flesh the everlasting flames of torments, ibid.

SMARAGDUS, abbot.—He inveighs against the desire of flesh and spirit, CII, 415.---When the devil seeks to deceive, he first observes each person’s nature; then he applies himself where he has perceived the person most suited to sinning, 628.

SEDULIUS SCOTTUS.—On the itching luxury of the ancient Romans, CIII, 20, 21.

AGOBARD (St.) OF LYONS.—On love of visible things, CIV, 211.---A life too much devoted to lust becomes little suited to perceiving truth, 220.

HALITGAR.—On luxury, CV, 668.---Remedies against luxury, 669.---Canons against followers of luxury, 682.---A mournful description of priests living carnally, 692, 693.---“We wish to be called shepherds, yet do not strive to be so; our hearing admits nothing by which we may improve … They feed themselves, not the sheep … We attend only to what fosters and increases our pleasures … Who would not rage at these things?” ibid.

JONAS OF ORLÉANS.—On avoiding unclean thoughts, CVI, 154.---As marsh-dwelling swine are wont to frequent wallows, while doves clear streams, so unclean thoughts disturb an impure mind, whereas spiritual thoughts sanctify a chaste one, 154 [uncertain punctuation in the source].

RABANUS MAURUS.—On the origin of concupiscence in the sin of the first parent, CVII, 491.---When the wicked neglect in heart to pass over to eternal things and do not perceive that all present things are fleeting, they fix their mind in love of the present life and, as if for a long dwelling, build in themselves its foundation, 508.---The company of the wicked must be avoided, as Lot’s example teaches, 536, 553.---How slippery pleasure should be driven out amid prosperity, 632.---For the pleasures of the flesh, many desire the toilsome paths of this life, even though full of tears, CVIII, 655.---The immoderate use of lawful pleasures is reproved by Christ himself, CX, 425.

EULOGIUS (St.) OF TOLEDO.—Concerning the impious teaching of Muhammad, he says: “Thus the patron of uncleanness, serving the pleasures of lusts, has devoted you all to the impurities of everlasting luxury,” CXV, 767.

HAYMO OF HALBERSTADT.—Those should be chosen for the guarding of the soul who have learned, through long exercises, to extinguish the incitement of lust or the fire of covetousness, CXVIII, 123.---Carnal things always strive to drag us to hell; we must resist them in every way and persist in good and righteous labours, in chastity and continence, 506.

PASCHASIUS RADBERTUS.—An undisciplined soldier is quickly conquered by the inciter of unchastity, CXX, 187, 188.

HINCMAR of Rheims.---Such is often a piety from which impiety is born more than once: when, as the affection of the flesh prevails, bodily affection is preferred to that charity which is God, CXXV, 855.---Some receive their soul in vain, when they give the care of the flesh precedence over it, 850.---The ancient enemy oppresses humankind either through pride or through lust, 873.---The more freely the reins of lust are loosened, the more harmfully it takes delight, ibid.---Let the lustful consider what an inhabitant they possess—namely, the devil—who, Scripture teaches, rests in moist places, that is, in hearts tepid with wantonness and lust, whom he prepares along with himself for eternal torments, 873, 874.---Those who once burned with perverse desires from the stench of the flesh perished with sulphur and fire, 874.---Thus Job defines the crime of lust (XX, 12): “A fire consuming unto destruction,” 875.

ODO (St.) of Cluny.---The time of this present life must be mourned, in which all things are confused, when everything is seen to be full of wickedness and lust, CXXXIII, 584.---Certainly the Lord will visit and will be a swift witness against adulterers, for whom, according to Amos, there will be no escape; but if they climb up to heaven, He will bring them down, and if they hide themselves in the depths of the sea, there He will command the serpent, and it shall bite them, 585.

ATTO of Vercelli.---Those who come over to the faith of Christ should be warned not only to reject evil deeds from themselves, but also to extinguish shameful thoughts, CXXXIV, 435.---The Apostle, seeing the Corinthians impatient and incontinent, allowed what was lawful lest they pass over to what was unlawful, 351.---Whoever serves lust bends the knee to the devil, 561.

RATHERIUS of Verona.---Lust pursues even judges themselves and the avengers of crime, CXXXVI, 164.---It belongs to a man, with God’s help, to subject the flesh to the soul and the soul to God, to proceed against the pleasures of the world and the enticements of the flesh, 190.---Let a woman strive, by the strong vigor of her mind, to overcome the mad tumults of vices and pleasures rising up against the spirit, 191.---Unless hidden pride comes first, manifest ruin through lust does not follow, 200.---As through pride one goes into the prostitution of lust, so from lust one arrives at hardness of heart, 201.---The hearts of the lustful: monuments of the devil, ibid.---Carnal desires are extinguished especially by abstinence, 691.

AIMOINUS of Fleury.---Wretched clerics led into many crimes because of lust: a terrible example of blindness and an ungrateful mind, CXXXIX, 728.---The enticements and crimes of the impious queen Fredegund are exposed, 730, 731.

Acts of St. Henry the Emperor and St. Cunegund, his wife.---The remarkable continence of both, CXL, 49, 207.

FULBERT (St.) of Chartres.---Whoever, through the softness of his own delight, falls into the mire of lust is without doubt seized by the devil, because, having taken away his freedom of chastity, he has made him captive in the slavery of lust, CXLI, 287.---The mournful effects of lust arranged in quatrains, 289, 290.

ODORAMNUS, monk.---“Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people” (Psalm XLIV): by resisting the ticklings of idolatry or of the flesh; “and your father’s house”: by fleeing the stain of original sin or the delights of the body, lest they reach the point of consent, CXLII, 818.

GOZECHINUS, Scholasticus.---Every day the ruinous loss of morals and discipline sprouts more grievously, so that in no governance of regular duty is it permitted to employ the customary correction or rod of the elders, CXLIII, 899.---Because concerning morals there is an extreme question—or none at all: having returned to their own ways, having shaken from their untamed neck the yoke of fear and broken the bridle of discipline, they rush headlong, living ruinously themselves and corrupting others with the leaven of malice, 900.

ANDREAS, monk of Vallombrosa.---The modesty of St. Ariald from his earliest years, CXLIII, 1440.---The dissolute morals of the clergy of this time, 1441.

PETER DAMIAN (St.).---Certainly it is fitting that spiritual affection should surpass love of the flesh, CXLIV, 346.---For that love is useless, dry, and tasteless which so occupies itself with the neighbor that it is not also extended to God, 278.---When they serve so greatly not demanding nature but impatient gluttony, whether they wish it or not, the free reins of lust are loosened, 231.---Those are reproved who in marriage serve not the procreation of offspring but innate pleasure; who are not so much husbands as fornicators, not spouses but rather lovers, [Col. 0896] 232.---Whoever hastens to construct a lofty court with the stones of virtues must first clear away the bristling thickets of carnal pleasures, 426.---If the briars of carnal desires and passions are allowed to spring up in the field of the flesh, while hunger for the good grows, the whole inward structure of virtues collapses, 427.---The field of the lazy and foolish man is filled with nettles and thorns when the flesh of someone living idly is not cultivated by the discipline of continual labor, but is softened and nourished in desire for pleasure and wantonness, ibid.---Men for whom the Son of the Virgin was born take delight in the slough of lust, 232.---The kindling-tinder of incitement to lust consists in avarice and the material of covetousness, 233.---My unhappy heart, which is not sufficient to retain the mysteries of the Gospel even after reading them a hundred times, does not lose the memory of a form seen only once, 458.

BERNOLDUS.---A useful disputation on the celibacy of priests, CXLVIII, 1079.

ANSELM (St.) of Lucca.---Canons concerning the continence of clerics and priests, CXLIX, 516, 519.---Canons concerning married persons, 523, 524, 527, 528.

LANFRANC (St.).---The longer the intervals of place between those who love one another carnally, the more intensely they separate them from mutual love; but those whom the sincere charity of Christian religion unites, bodily absence does not at all disjoin, CL, 518.---He professes this unfailing love for God’s sake, 520.---He is truly a friend who rebukes us in mercy, but an enemy who flatters, ibid.

BRUNO (St.), father of the Carthusians.---The soul walks by means of affections, as the body does by means of feet, CLII, 685, 705.---Likewise, hands are so called because through them the devil is conquered, ibid.---Concupiscence is called the tinder of sin because from it evil delight and occupation arise, 793.---The Apostle calls pure hands clean affections, so that they may wish nothing to be given them by God which it would be unlawful for God to give, CLIII, 438.

GUIGO, prior of the Carthusians.---On the pleasures and base delights of the five senses, CLIII, 605.---Either extinguish concupiscence utterly, or prepare yourself for disturbance—that is, for fearing and grieving over what you ought not, 607.---On covetousness, love, and glorying in earthly things, 609.---On remedies against temptations of the flesh, 840.

RADULPHUS ARDENS, theological doctor of Poitiers.---On the conversion of Blessed Mary Magdalene, to be imitated, CLV, 1398.---Earthly delights are thought great so long as they are desired; when possessed, they become cheap and turn into disgust, 1441.---The works of darkness are called works especially of the flesh, 1670.---The city of the lustful is lust, 1702.---For what prize one ought to run, 1761.

GUIBERT of Nogent.---Those inclined to their own lusts seek to know nothing except what is sweet to the flesh, CLVI, 35.---Where God is not, neither is there any good omen, 511.---Good Jesus! Although through You we may have deserved greater things, what purity, what tranquility we lost in our first parents! 497.---The burnings of the flesh can never be subdued except through the flame of heavenly desire, 498.---Pleasures instill contempt for virginity, 497.---Pleasure captivates even old men, 580, 581.---Carnal softness corrupts within and without, 87.---How those severe in life themselves sometimes fall into the vice of the flesh, 598.---With what great circumspection it must be avoided, ibid.

GOFFRIDUS, abbot of Vendôme.---The soul infected the flesh, not the flesh the soul, CLVII, 176.---Lust is not more serious than pride, but it is more shameful, 241.---The penitence of wanton youth does not allow God to remember its sins, ibid.

ANSELM (St.) of Canterbury.---Nothing is loved unless it is known, CLVIII, 200, 413.---A person loves those things which he does not lose without sadness, 1140.---If adversity in those things which the servant of God ought to despise makes you sad, you show that you love transient things more than is fitting and eternal things less than is proper, 1140.---There are two loves, one good and one evil; one sweet and one bitter, 897.---They do not occupy one breast together, ibid.---Concupiscence is covetousness, is will, 335.---There is good and evil concupiscence, just as there is good and evil will, ibid.---The pleasure, or concupiscence, of the flesh is evil beyond all evils, 870.---It is born with a person, grows, and leaves him only when he is dead, ibid.---It is not to feel appetites, but to consent to them, that is sin, 437.---Each person’s own covetousness is a storm, 601.---These lower things have their own delights and their own loves, 896.---How far even lawful carnal pleasure differs from the delight of Christ and chastity, CLIX, 190.---What is the mud of dregs except the stench of carnal pleasure? CLVIII, 718.---Let no earthly delight here please you, 678.---It is better to die than to be defiled by lust, 679.---Lust stirs wars; you yield at the first blows and offer your neck to be pressed beneath a foul yoke! [Col. 0897] 695, 696.---Lust holds the reins due to virtue, 700.

IVO of Chartres (Blessed).---The disordered morals of peoples are compared to hair requiring a comb, CLXII, 16.---In the sacrifice of the Mass one must strive that, just as the outward defilements of the hands are washed away, so the inward enticing desires of minds may be purified, 561.

ANSELM of Laon.---When the gate of concupiscence has been opened, CLXII, 1297.---Whoever directs his love toward some earthly thing lays up treasure upon earth, 1310.---Many, having found the way of truth, do not return because they are captured by the pleasures of the world, 1316.---Those subject to impurity and pleasure are compared to impious Jezebel, 1311.---Likewise, to Babylon the harlot, 1560 ff.---In sensuality man is like brute animals, 1589.

BRUNO (St.) of Asti.---Blessed are those who fight in such a way, who kill in themselves all vices, all pleasures, and the concupiscences of the flesh, CLXV, 754.---Wretched adolescents whom the devil blows about and tosses, 772.---Not all chaste persons are virgins, nor are all virgins chaste, 930.

RUPERT, abbot of Deutz.---Those deceived by the blandishments of shameful suggestions succumb through the fleeting things of lust, CLXVIII, 1180.---The various allurements of pleasure lie in the five senses, CLXIX, 1154.---The most wretched end of lustful Belshazzar, CLXIX, 1359.

HILDEBERT of Le Mans.---Lust, the vice of a beast, CLXXI, 708.---Whoever loosens the reins to lust undoubtedly incurs eternal death, 708, 709.---There are others whom the pleasure of the flesh holds fast: they care nothing for money, but are so frail that they can scarcely resist the temptation of gluttony and lust, 736.---If one believes Cicero, although lust is shameful at every age, it is especially foul in old age, 1038.---Whoever is driven by the goads of lust easily falls into fornication and adultery, 437.---The unclean spirit has very many offspring, 432.---What the works of darkness are, 466.---The pleasures of the flesh are said to be those which the flesh seeks through unlawful movement, 468.---Then lust burns when it is resisted, 470.---How destructive the vice of lust is, 708 ff.---Lust separates a person from God, joins him to the devil, and violates God’s temple, 306.

GODEFRIDUS of Admont.---Worldly love separates the human heart from God, CLXXIV, 1968.---But whence, merciful Lord, whence comes to us such an unheard-of delight in carnal enticement? 134.---To what may the carnal sense of a human being be compared? 592.---Concupiscence presses even the elect, 262.---In this life it cannot be entirely extinguished, 515.---It draws the mind back from heavenly things, 480.---Concupiscence is not merely lust, but also a labor of the soul, 132.---That most shameful vice, 80.---He compares men to horses, 78.

HUGH OF ST. VICTOR, Paris.---Whatever is loved through concupiscence, that very concupiscence must also draw downward, CLXXV, 195.---What it is to walk, to be, and to think according to the flesh, 478.---On concupiscence, 474.---On lust and its retinue, CLXXVI, 1002.---Music exists so that the flesh may be loved, but the spirit more; so that the body may be cherished, but virtue not destroyed, 757.---There are those who love certain things contrary to God, and in them the foundation is wholly destroyed, because the love of God cannot exist where He is not either the sole or the supreme object, CLXXVII, 495.---The flesh is a beast of burden and the spirit the rider who applies the spurs, ibid.---A shameful change: that one who, by meditation searching the heavens, used to penetrate and in mind traverse the heavenly dwellings … should now enslave himself to the shameful service of the body, 684.---The sweetness of man: worms, 695.

ABAELARD.---The beginnings, burning course, and end of the mad love with which he burned, CLXXVIII, 126 ff.---The pious end of the same man’s life at Cluny, 19, 66, 103.

WILLIAM, abbot of St. Thierry.---Bodily forms hold us fast by their love, CLXXX, 402.---The temptation of the flesh requires afflictions of the flesh, 378.---Disordered love disorders everything, 515.---Love natural to man, CLXXXIV, 379.

BERNARD (St.) of Clairvaux.---Love absorbs all the other affections, CLXXXIII, 1182.---Love is a great thing, provided only that it returns to its own source, 1183.---I mistrust a love which seems to be supported by the hope of obtaining something else, ibid.---Love and hatred corrupt judgment, CLXXXII, 947.---To one who loves, nothing is difficult, CLXXXIII, 255.---Love is impatient, 815.---Where love is, there is no labor, but savor, 1191.---Concupiscence is the origin of all vices and evils, 611.---It does not destroy freedom, CLXXXII, 1023.---But it diminishes voluntariness, 1174.---It does no harm without consent, 618.---Its unpremeditated movements are not sins, 1176.---Carnal concupiscences remove the affection of compassion, 698.---Pleasures must be fled, CLXXXII, 708.---How slight and vain they are, 841.---Pleasure gives little, and entails no small loss of piety, 589.---The pleasure [Col. 0898] of sin passes away; its foulness remains, 803.---Perverse and unclean thoughts separate from God, CLXXXIII, 332.---Those living carnally are dead, 284.---Carnal affection is like wine, 819.---A softer affection blinds a person, CLXXXII, 755.

GILLEBERT of Holland.---The various affections of lovers, because their situations are various, CLXXXIV, 11.---Affection speaks in love, but words interrupt it, ibid.---Evil is this day which laid bare the paths of vices, displayed enticing appearances, and presented to the eye of concupiscence material that provokes it, 15.---Faith is in harbor, but the assault of evil habit and the mass of temptations must still be broken, 67.

GUERRIC, Cistercian.---Is not lust a worm? I do not know whether there is another more harmful one! CLXXXV, 49.---The worm of lust enters by flattering, bites while laughing, pierces through by delighting, and kills by voluntary consent, ibid.

ROBERT PULLUS.---After the fault of the first parent, mutual boiling wantonness produced shame and, through the tickling of the flesh, sought hiding places, CLXXXVI, 752.---The movements of concupiscence must be restrained, 835.

PETER THE VENERABLE, abbot of Cluny.---Far be it from you, far from every understanding, to have so asinine a mind as to regard eternal things as like bodily things, CLXXXIX, 510.---Christ opposes not only the act but also the pleasurable thought, 593.

GARNERIUS OF ST. VICTOR.---From lust or libido arise blindness of mind, thoughtlessness, inconstancy, rashness, self-love, hatred of God, attachment to the present age, horror and despair of the future, CXCIII, 153.---How it is propagated, 154.---Lust is accustomed to arise from gluttony, ibid.---The pleasure of lust is in the loins, 231.---Vices are joined together by a certain kinship, as dissipation of spirit, appetite for gluttony, and the uncleanness of lust, 273.---To gird the loins is to restrain lust, 138.---Carnal delight is flesh, 208.---The slippery desires of the wicked are like waters, 282.---Lust is called a caterpillar, 134.---The desires of the flesh: a devouring fire, 358.

ECBERT, abbot.---The wretched chastity of heretics who destroy marriages, CXCV, 36.---Their religion proceeds from the counsel of the evil one, ibid.---What things defile a human being, 38.---Every person labors under the penalty which original sin brought upon the world, 49.---What should be thought concerning little children aged five or seven who sin against chastity, 177.

AELRED (Blessed), abbot.---How great are the weaknesses of the soul, how great the concupiscences, how great the temptations, CXCV, 211.---Foul sinners are compared to goats because of lust, 215.---Whither do those flee who strive to extinguish lust? 221.---The body must be reduced to servitude because of concupiscence that makes war, 250.---The corruption of the flesh is lust; the corruption of the mind is pride, 255.---What heights does love not bring down, or what depths does it not raise up, in order to make them one in itself? 361.---Love is the delight of the soul, the sweeter the chaster it is, 505.---How great is the joy in contempt for pleasures and in victory, 570.---On the twofold carnal affection, 590.

RICHARD OF ST. VICTOR.---On the vice of imagination and sensuality, CXCVI, 5.---How imagination serves reason and sensuality serves affection, 4.---What is proper to love, 8.---Where love is, there the eye is, 10.---True love and vain love sometimes caused at the same time, 38.---Love does not know the name of difficulty, 1202.---What love of earthly things does, 458.---What carnal sins are, 690, 691.---He approves whatever each person loves.---What the custom of lovers is, 508.---Carnal pleasures blind the soul, 441.---Concupiscence grew from contact with the weakness of the flesh, 662.---Let reason rule sensuality, pardon its movements, and govern thoughts, 501.---God heard Paul, asking that the thorn of his flesh be removed, better when He did not remove it, 506.---On the weakness of carnal desire, 1119.---On its restlessness, 1121.---On the disturbance of the carnal spirit, 1122.---On the various degrees of corruption, 1282.

HILDEGARD (St.).---She foretells that the hand of God will soon avenge the injury inflicted upon her by the depraved morals of priests, CXCVII, 271.---“Why do you keep and tolerate among yourselves those who pollute the whole earth with their filthy iniquities? For they are drunkards and lustful men,” 250.---She is commanded to resist her flesh and serve the spirit, 261.---Against certain perverse monks she thus inveighs: “Your mind is like a cloud carrying storms, now holding anger in negligence, now the filth of beasts in wantonness, while you neglect the peaceful sacrifice,” 370–371.---She grieves over the excess of fools, the garrulousness of morals, and the clamor of dishonesty, 374.---The pursuits of people who, wearied in their hearts and deeds, sleep in disgrace cannot be hidden from God, 388.

[Col. 0899] ADAM THE SCOT.---Love is the gate of death or life; it is good or evil: evil love is called covetousness, good love charity, CXCVIII, 809.---The harms of concupiscence, 373.---Potiphar’s wife and Delilah are its figures, 814.---Concupiscence and ignorance, the two bonds of Satan broken by Christ in the elect, 255.---Lust blinds the mind, 536.---The appetite for bodily pleasures is full of anxiety, 383.---Bitterness succeeds love, as happened in senseless Amnon, 384.---The beginning of the carnal life is sweet like good wine, but its end miserable like inferior wine, 436.---The flesh must be restrained, but not destroyed, 256.

JOHN OF SALISBURY.---Why the ancient followers of philosophy were handed over to passions of dishonor, CXCIX, 479.---Concupiscence, a universal leprosy which infects everyone, 480.---The pleasure of Venus seems to have the stench of a goat, 755.---Wantonness is the most abject of vices, ibid.---No one doubts that lust is shameful in itself, 762.

ARNULF of Lisieux.---He reproaches Gerard, bishop of Montpellier and supporter of an invader of the Apostolic See, for the shameful filth of his lusts, CCI, 182.---If someone is intemperate and wanton in greater matters, will he be temperate in lesser ones? 177.---One must spare obscenity in words, 179.

PETER OF CELLE.---You labor if you do not love, CCII, 428.---Superfluous pleasure of the flesh, much sought, much desired, and much embraced by many, 429.---The delight of the flesh is called the root of sin, the moth of all honesty, the pit of vices, the well of demons, the abyss of souls, a most evil beast, 430.---The devil’s wiles must be feared and guarded against, 634.---What the household of lust is, 686.---Virginity does not know the itch and onset of the flesh, 723.---What the remedies for lust are, 730.---Carnal pleasure is a fly which disturbs, contaminates, and destroys the sweetness of ointment, 758.---The devil inflames with lust both youthful marrow and the deadened senses of the decrepit, 821.---The furnace of lust, 1018.

PHILIP OF HARVENG, abbot.---The disordered love of certain people, CCIII, 292.---The wiles of wanton lovers, 983–984.---The eclipses of lovers in speaking, 334, 335.---Youth subject to lusts, 812.

REINERIUS, monk of St. Lawrence at Liège.---The book entitled *Mirror of Penitence, or the Life of St. Pelagia the Sinner*, CCIV, 51 ff.

BALDWIN, archbishop of Canterbury.---A human being who falls away from the unchangeable God also himself declines, by degrees growing old and aged, CCIV, 516.---In turn he hates and loves, treats and retracts, approves and condemns, ibid.---First the earthly person must be crucified in us, then the carnal, afterward the animal person, 521.---Natural love, social love, chaste love, divine love, 477, 478.---On the threefold state of our flesh, 403.---A shameful servitude in which the mistress—that is, the will—serves the handmaid, the flesh, 404.

PETER THE CHANTER.---What nourishes lust, CCV, 332.---Concupiscence, the first temptation of man, 331.---The more it is exercised, the more lust grows, 277.---It is more easily cured than avarice, 76, 277.---The lustful man is compared to a pig, 265.---Lust consumes what avarice has gathered, 403 note.---Each several pleasure will be turned into a corresponding human torment, 264.---Carnal affection must be rejected, 209.

PETER OF BLOIS.---He rebukes the vices of a certain prelate, CCVII, 66 ff.---A eunuch violates a virgin for no reason except to satisfy lust, 89.---Luxuries and blandishments are the emptying of virtues and the overthrow of integrity, 156.---When the spirit of dizziness, the spirit of abomination, and of nausea oppresses, 158.---It was said to Alexander when he came of age: “It now befits your age to rule; therefore let it shame you that the pleasure of lust should rule in a royal body,” 176.---Pleasure bought with pain harms, 179.---Do not speak shameful things, for little by little shame slips away through words, 233.---The Lord’s speech is not harsh, but you are harsh: earthly, carnal, animal man, 236.---He urges a friend to read the Sacred Scriptures often if he wishes to overcome temptations of the flesh, 334.---He commends the same reading to Bishop Walter in exile, 373.---With every diligence it must be observed that nothing evil be found in our wills, nothing harsh in our morals, or dark, slippery, or distorted, 563.---Two things draw me into the precipice: on this side a corrupted condition, on that a weak will, 591.---How many evils there are in pleasure of the flesh, 902.

MARTIN (St.) of León.---Understanding of divinity is separated from the love of lower things in proportion as it is raised up to eternal things alone, CCXIII, 346.---By abstinence the incentives of the loins and movements of lust are restrained, 356.---Why the thorn of one’s flesh is given to the elect, 371.---While the flesh is carried away into delight, the weakened spirit too is bent away from its own rectitude, [Col. 0900] 393.---A lustful life quickly weakens, 490.---Concupiscence is called a snare of the soul, 677.

ALAN OF LILLE.---An excellent description of erotic love, CCX, 455.---It is a cruel moth of the mind, ibid.---The crimes committed at its instigation, ibid.---It is conquered especially by flight, 456.---The greatest ardor of love, 280.---The inconstancy of love, ibid.---Wantonness, companion of youth, 551.---The malice of lust, 239.---Remedies against lust, 470, 471.---A description of lust, 121.---How many evils it brings, ibid.---It is fouler than a dung-heap, 203.---The weapons of lust: sight, conversation, touch, kisses, deed, 122.---It is better to die than to be defiled by lust, 121.---Whoever lives in lust is dead while living, ibid.---It is a plague that has a familial likeness to Gehenna, 122.---It empties the purse, enervates the body, intoxicates the mind, effeminates the state of mind, defiles the soul, destroys reputation, offends the neighbor, and loses God, ibid.---It hates the light, seeks darkness, and looks for a covering, ibid.---It is put to flight by fleeing; it is struck down by withdrawing, ibid.

ABSALO, abbot.---Every lover of chastity is attacked by concupiscence of the flesh, CCXI, 42.---The flesh daily plots against chastity through unlawful desires, 41–42.---Concupiscence is what teaches a person all things pertaining to pleasures of the flesh, 46.---Three rivers of Babylon run between heaven and earth, drawing downward those who wish to ascend. The first is the flood of carnal desires; the second, of spiritual temptations; the third, of impending troubles, 184.

STEPHEN of Tournai.---Holiness perfects and completes the inner person; integrity arranges and orders the outward person, CCXI, 572.---Those who have a continual scab, itching with the heat of lust, are excluded from orders, 573.

ADAM, abbot of Perseigne.---What can be harsher on the way that leads to God than to afflict one’s flesh with its vices and concupiscences? CCXI, 586.---The name of love is common to very different things, 589.---The morals and deeds of the righteous are certain fragrances of virtues, 590.---The pleasure of the slippery body must be put to death, 609.---No one can devote himself to the studies of wisdom unless he has first removed the madness of insane love and become sound of mind, 615.

HELINAND, monk.---As death separates the soul from the body, so love separates it from pleasure of the flesh, CCXII, 650.---What distinction there is between true and false chastity, 661.---True chastity must have teeth, 665.

SICARDUS of Cremona.---The poet’s saying is explained concerning concupiscence: “We always strive for what is forbidden, and desire what is denied,” CCXIII, 173.---Those acting manfully will be set at the right hand in judgment, but those living effeminately at the left, 279.

II.---Lewd songs and books, songs, love ballads, tales, and the invented dramas of poets.

TERTULLIAN.---What the songs of the early Christians were like, I, 273, 477.---How vain poets are, 609.---They love nothing other than singing, II, 707.---Nor should they be believed, ibid.---Plato judged that they should be expelled from the state, and why, I, 595.---Why tales were devised by philosophers and poets, 519.---Some were invented in order to weaken the authority of the Scriptures, I, 395, 399.

CYPRIAN (St.).---Love songs must not be sung, IV, 449.---Those Greek contests, whether in songs, lyres, or voices, have various demons as their presiding powers, 783.---Idolatry, mother of all games, in order that Christians may come to it, allures them through the pleasure of eyes and ears, ibid.---A tale of Greek lust, 782.---The sorrowful tale of a virgin who sinned, 459.

ARNOBIUS.---Symphonies and obscene songs at banquets incite to corruption, V, 881.---The pleasure of the ears is not to be sought in serious matters, 798.---The base and obscene tales of the pagans are everywhere refuted, V, 713, 1075 passim.

LACTANTIUS.---On the sense and pleasure of hearing, VI, 713.---On elegant and pleasing speech, ibid.---On those insufficiently educated who are ensnared by the false quibbles of heretics, 541.---In this philosophers, orators, and poets are harmful: they can easily entangle unwary minds by the sweetness of speech … honey concealing poison, 549.---On those who despise Sacred Scripture, 550.---Those are reproved who attack St. Cyprian as though he had resorted to old wives’ tales, 552.

HILARY (St.) of Poitiers.---Before Christ the whole world resounded with the profane singing of ceremonies, IX, 419.---The divine utterances of our hope are not sung more sweetly than the obscene tales of shameful spectacles, 540.---What the key of each book is, 247.---The art of philosophers is vain against faith, 411.---Philosophy is incapable of heavenly mysteries, X, 286.---The eloquence of philosophy once held the nations in error, IX, 415.

[Col. 0901] ZENO (St.) of Verona.---What benefits faith, and what brings it harm, XI, 887.---That is not true faith which prevails by factions, whose professed adherents tell tales of secret matters, which prefers its own novel tradition to be believed rather than antiquity, 265.

AMBROSE (St.).---The deadly songs and stage entertainments of actors soften the mind for loves, XIV, 157.---What Christian songs are like, XV, 1667 ff.---He who first discovered the name of philosophy used to order a flute-player, every day before he went to bed, to play soft music, XVI, 225.---Nor does the Apostle avoid poetic verses, in order to destroy the tales of poets, XV, 1698.---The tales of idle people are those by which detraction is sown and malice revealed, XVI, 1201.---What evils the authors of impious books perpetrate, XIV, 887 ff.

JEROME (St.).---Let a Christian virgin not understand shameful words; let her be ignorant of the songs of the world, XXII, 871.---The songs of those serving idols are not hymns to God, but howlings, XXV, 880.---This is the fault of singers among friends: when asked, they never sing; unbidden, they never stop, XXII, 338.---Let young people hear this: God must be sung to not with the voice but with the heart; nor should throat and jaws be smeared with sweet ointment in the manner of tragedians, so that theatrical melodies and songs … may be heard in church, and so that the evil spirit of Saul may not be introduced among those who have made of God’s house a theater for the people, XXVI, 528, 529.---The tales relate that sailors went headlong upon the rocks through the songs of the Sirens, XXII, 957.---Who an iniquitous reader is, 495.---What a prudent reader ought to do, 501.---He quickly discovers the tunnels and snares by which truth is overthrown, 357.---What must be read cautiously, XXVI, 419.---Almost all books are full of secular learning and instruction, XXII, 689.---From a book’s style and saliva we recognize its author, 830.---Many, because of ignorance, prefer Iberian nonsense to authentic books, 742.---The books of the unlearned find readers, XXIII, 412.---Books which men compose with the greatest labor they often hand over to the lazy and idle, 1032.

AUGUSTINE (St.).---Singing is lovers’ business, XXXVIII, 207.---Pay attention not so much to the voice of the singer as to the morals of the doer, XXXVII, 1950.---God taught us no song other than that of faith, hope, and charity, 1171.---A love song of the Manichaeans, XLII, 507.---The dangerous delight of vain songs, XXXVIII, 79.---People are more inclined to hear vain songs than saving admonitions, ibid.---Profane songs and dancing were driven from the church where St. Cyprian was buried, 1415.---Those who sing shameful things are rebuked, XXXVI.---He sings in us whose grace makes us sing, XXXIII, 558.---The delight of the flesh must be guarded against even in divine song, XXXII, 799.---It is sin when the song delights more than the thing sung, ibid.---The wantonness of raging youths was soothed by the gravity of song, XLIV, 797.---The Donatists sing psalms composed by human ingenuity and mingle them with drunkenness, XXXIII, 120, 220.---Harmony in music is naturally innate in us, XLII, 889.---Lovers of pleasurable music, XXXIV, 98.---David loved pious music, XXXIII, 369.---Consult St. Augustine’s little work *On Music*, 368.---Diabolical songs, XL, 1172.---It is not right that a lustful song should be uttered from a mouth into which Christ’s body enters, XXXIX, 2239, 2268.---Psalms must be sung in place of shameful songs, 2325.

A fable is a lie composed for usefulness or pleasure, XXXII, 894.---Pagans attempt to interpret their tales according to the nature of things or the morals of people, XLII, 374.---And to refer them to certain, I know not what, natural philosophies or theologies, 275.---Plato held that poets, as enemies of truth, should be expelled from the city, XLI, 58, 237.---Among the Romans they were excluded from every honor, 57.---By the law of the Twelve Tables poets are forbidden to injure the reputation of citizens, 54, 58.---The lies of poets, XXXII, 1014.---The tales of poets are less obscene than the sacred rites of the gods, XLI, 53.---They are no less worthy of infamy than actors, 58.---Stage poets inflame lust, 59, 60.

The threefold error of readers, XXXVIII, 72.---Perverse zeal in reading is rebuked, XL, 390.---A book sweet in the mouth, bitter in the belly, XXXVI, 492.---The books of unbelievers are waters not common to all, XXXVII, 1360, 1361.---In the books of foreigners the best precepts of morals are found, but not humility, XXXVI, 270.---For whom the reading of disapproved books may be harmless, XLIV, 510.---Pope Innocent’s censure against Pelagius’s book, XXXIII, 788.---Likewise that of John, patriarch of Jerusalem, 829, and of St. Jerome, 764, 781.

PETER CHRYSOLOGUS (St.).---Let luxury cease; let dissipation, the plague of dancing-girls, the enticements of singers, and the incentives of pleasures be driven away, LII, 552.---Chrysologus does not reject a little song composed in honorable words and suited to lighten labor, and offers instead one that is decent and pious, [Col. 0902] 215.---Accordingly, various songs are given for sailors, farmers, and soldiers, in which neither morals nor piety is offended, 214–215.---What the council of impiety did, 322, 333.---The profession of faith in a heretic’s mouth is poisoned, 525. Lying persons cannot recognize truth; a mind acting as judge cannot discover the true amid messengers of falsehood, 559.

PROSPER (St.).---Tales of vain opinions recounted by the wicked, LI, 350.---Nothing useful is found in them, ibid.

SALVIAN.---Nothing is more shameful for a philosopher than to pursue obscene vices, LIII, 84.---No place must be given to the devil, so that he who drove the standing into ruin may not cast the fallen headlong into death, 185.---Every error is punished by the destruction of the one who errs, 230.

LEO THE GREAT (Saint).—Let nothing discordant be detected in the voices, nothing incompatible be found in the conduct, LIV, 505.—At times the hearing is struck by soft blows through enervating sounds, so that firmness of mind is preserved by alluring melody, and hearts, charmed by the habit of deadly delights and insufficiently sober, are taken captive, 445.—While the unwary ear takes pleasure in fabulous tales, you fall into the devil’s snares, LIV, 179.

MAXIMUS OF TURIN (Saint).—He employs the fable of the Sirens in order to restrain the pleasures of concupiscence, LVIII, 339.

ISIDORE OF SEVILLE (Saint).—What is read must be tested by cautious reflection and prudent judgment, so that we may retain what is right and refute what proves contrary to truth, LXXXIII, 685.—For this reason a Christian is forbidden to read the inventions of poets: through the pleasure of empty fables they stir the mind toward incentives to lust, 685.—All secular learning, resounding with frothy words and exalting itself through the swelling of eloquence, has been emptied by simple teaching and Christian humility, 687.—In reading, not words but truth is to be loved, ibid.

PRUDENTIUS (Saint).—Did God add wide-open ears for a frivolous girl’s lyric tunes, the sounds of strings, and the banquet-song of heated wickedness? LIX, 1034.

NICETIUS OF TRIER (Saint).—Let sound or melody consonant with holy religion be sung—not that which cries out tragic complexities, but that which displays Christianity in you; not that which smells of anything theatrical, but that which produces compunction for sins, LXVIII, 374.

PAULINUS OF AQUILEIA (Saint).—Secular songs are to be disregarded, especially by clerics, XCIX, 297.

AGOBARD OF LYONS (Saint).—On things not fitting to be sung in Christian churches, and on the correction of the antiphonary, CIV, 327, 329.

PASCHASIUS RADBERTUS OF CORBIE.—From this secular men derived their dramas, so that at weddings, in honor of bridegroom and bride, they might alternately sing a song of praise before the bridal chamber, CXX, 1010.

REGINO OF PRÜM.—What age or sex does not delight in musical songs? . . . Even if there are some who cannot sing skillfully and sweetly to others, they nevertheless sing something unpleasantly sweet to themselves, CXXXII, 489.—Human character is recognized through music. For a wanton and impudent mind delights in more lascivious tunes, or, by hearing them frequently, is softened and effeminized. Conversely, a harder and fiercer disposition either delights in or is stirred by harsher strains, ibid.—According to Cicero, when drunken young men, enticed by the sound of pipes, broke down the doors of a chaste woman in order to violate her chastity, 490.
