RATHERIUS OF VERONA.—On the scandalous luxury of certain bishops of his own time, who admitted singers, actors, and even female dancers to their banquets, CXXXVI, 292.

HROTSVITHA (Venerable), nun of Gandersheim.—She composed sacred comedies and certain poems in order to turn Christian readers away from profane and dangerous books, as she herself acknowledges in the Preface, CXXXVII, 971.

GEOFFREY OF VENDÔME.—What is worse, the populace composed a song against the pope’s legate . . . What we have heard grieves us, CLVII, 63.—To Ivo of Chartres: “I have never said anything dishonorable or insulting concerning your person; . . . but since your clerics themselves sang badly to me, I cannot, nor could I, dance well,” 75.—To Hildebert of Le Mans: “We sang well to you, insofar as we could, and expected you to dance for us . . . you did not provide a dance in keeping with the song,” 123–124.

ANSELM OF CANTERBURY (Saint).—Pour forth tears while there is time, lest in another age you weep without profit. For here is mercy, there judgment; here pleasure, there torments; here laughter, but there weeping; here song, there eternal fire, CLVIII, 678.—At the lord’s nod the light-minded crowd stands ready: both sexes sing; zithers and lyres resound; and organs there render sweet melody, 701.

IVO OF CHARTRES (Blessed).—We utterly forbid the making of any base or lustful song around churches or in the church courts; [Col. 0903] this must be avoided everywhere. (Council of Carthage.) CLXI, 1092.—Mention is made of a certain song against a cleric of Tours whose morals were suspected, CLXII, 81.

BRUNO OF ASTI (Saint).—Courtesans of Venus and lovers of luxury lamenting and composing love songs, CLXV, 772.

RUPERT OF DEUTZ.—All the enticements of pleasures exercised through hearing are condemned, CLXIX, 1154.—What the song of the saints in heaven is, 1158.—Idolatry employed every kind of music to entice people, so that, intoxicated by the festive sweetness of sounds, they might fall before the statue of pride and pleasure, 1348.—From the beast’s mouth came a spirit which, by flattering men with poetic fictions, raised them to the rank of gods and sang of them, transferred to heaven, in fabulous dirges, 1124.

HUGH OF ST VICTOR.—The new song is the new life; the old song, the old life. Whoever lives well sings well; whoever lives badly sings badly, because he is out of harmony, CLXXVII, 926.—A voice whose life is displeasing does not please, 927.—The deadly songs of Sirens or courtesans, 78.

GERHOHUS, provost.—He rebukes clerics who sang in church as though with a divided and greatly discordant mouth, because of vocal elaborations varied with certain theatrical melodies, CXCIV, 1258.

AELRED, abbot.—On the vain pleasure of the ears, CXCV, 571.—To what end, I ask, is that dreadful blast of bellows, expressing rather the crash of thunder than the sweetness of the voice? ibid.—Now the voice is constrained, now broken, now driven forward, now expanded in a more diffuse sound. At times, shameful to say, it is forced into horses’ neighing, ibid.—The standing crowd, trembling and astonished, marvels at the sound of bellows, cymbals, and pipes; but it watches with loud laughter and mirth the wanton gesturing of singers and the harlot-like contests and breaks in their voices, so that you would suppose them gathered not for an oratory but for a theater, not to pray but to look on, 571.

JOHN OF SALISBURY.—The Phrygian mode in music, like the other enticements of corruption, has no use in sound instruction, but reveals the malice of its abuser, CXCIX, 402.—Music, which was accustomed to inflame manly minds toward virtue, has been given a harlot’s face, ibid.—Do not banquets rage sufficiently by themselves unless they are stirred up by songs? 403.—The frivolous vanity of the emperor Nero, who strove to be considered foremost in singing and instrumental skill, 404.

PETER OF BLOIS.—He dissuades a certain friend from love songs and other youthful frivolities, and composes for the person to whom he sends it a song fashioned in a more mature style, CCVII, 172.—See this song on the mourning of flesh and spirit, 1127.—Likewise, he dissuades a companion, himself called Peter of Blois and canon of Chartres, from vain and base songs, 231 ff.—“I too at one time gave attention to trifles and songs of Venus; but by God’s grace I cast off all these things at the first threshold of youth,” 234.—“Completely abandon useless songs, old women’s tales, and childish ditties,” 237.

ALAN OF LILLE.—Present joys are followed by everlasting lamentations, CCX, 136.—No one can rejoice here with the world and reign there with God, ibid.—Three things must always be lamented: the sin of the soul, the assault of misery, and the delay of the homeland, 137.—Nor should we resemble those who neither rejoice nor mourn except when fortune brings them either prosperity or adversity, 138.—God’s servants have one permitted joy: the happy delight of a pure conscience, 139.—The devil’s book is handwritten; the conscience aware of evil is defaced with most ugly marks, ibid.

ABSALO, abbot.—Those who study and teach poetic inventions and other writings of the pagans, while passing by the Lord’s law with a deaf ear, cast a golden hook into troubled water, CCXI, 47.—There are certain clerics whom you may see more often in the marketplace than in choir, and hear singing songs more often than lamenting their sins, 142.

III.—Disordered adornment of the body.—Luxury of clothing and ornaments; improper and indecent dress; the vanity of beauty and physical form.

TERTULLIAN.—Now among women no limb is unencumbered by gold, I, 304.—Purple and bronze-colored garments do not please God, 1312.—With the garment, its voice enters, II, 1039.—What women’s clothing was like in former times, 911.—The dress of matrons and courtesans was formerly different, but later became alike, I, 301.—The women of Carthage veiled themselves in such a way that they were neither naked nor covered, II, 912.—Pagan Arab women cover their whole face, leaving only one eye free, ibid.—What feminine adornment is, II, 80.—By law men may not clothe themselves in women’s garments, I, 655.—Adorned women draw after them the eyes and sighs of young men, 1320.

[Col. 0904] On the care of the hair, I, 1322, 1323.—Women sin against God who anoint their skin with cosmetics, stain their cheeks with rouge, and smear their eyes with soot, I, 1325.—Women’s eyes ornamented at the outer edges with black powder, 1306, 1321.

CYPRIAN (Saint).—The adornment of costly clothing is put on, IV, 489.—To receive precious ornaments and elaborately worked necklaces is done at the cost of divine adornment, 498.—Though you adorn yourself with gold, gems, and pearls, without Christ’s adornment you are deformed, ibid.—A woman ought not to adorn herself in a worldly fashion, 755.—Virgins adorned with gold and pearls have lost the ornaments of the heart, 462.—A virgin should seek ornaments not of garments but of morals, ibid.—Men and women who adulterate God’s image are rebuked, IV, 454, 436.

HILARY OF POITIERS (Saint).—Those dissolved in luxury are the dwelling-place of demons, IX, 980.—God must be pleased even in the body, 426.—Human beings are to be pleased insofar as is permitted, ibid.—To wish to please human beings alone is to displease God, 333.—Modesty in dress is commended, X, 550, 551.—Worldly adornment is an insult to nature, IX, 612, 613.

ZENO (Saint).—The wanton woman cultivates herself with marvelous arts and seeks upon herself a face that she does not possess, XI, 294 ff.

FIRMICUS MATERNUS.—He vehemently rebukes pagan priests dressed as women, XII, 989, 990.

AMBROSE (Saint).—Women’s luxury is rebuked, XIV, 738.—Whether girls ought to wear earrings, 453.—The vanity of women’s ornaments, XVI, 203, 204.—The expense of ornaments, 284.—Those who falsify their face are reproved, 196.—A woman is made more deformed by the very effort to please, 203.—How unbecoming women’s proud adornment is, XVII, 467.—What use of hair is fitting, especially for women, XV, 1673.—A woman effaces God’s painting if she covers her face with material coloring and pours over it an acquired blush, XIV, 260.—“You are painted, O human being, and painted by the Lord your God. You have a good craftsman and painter; do not erase the good painting,” ibid.

JEROME (Saint).—The enticements of clothing and ornaments, XXII, 957.—Dress and adornment, 553.—On monks and clerics who, beneath the habit of religion, retain worldly morals, 413, 414.—“Let your garment be neither excessively clean nor dirty, nor conspicuous through any distinction,” 412.—What matrons’ pursuits are, 1113.—Changes of dress and cloaks, women’s ornaments, XXIV, 70.—Likewise needles, *sidones* [possibly fine linen fabrics], mirrors, bands, veils, girdles, sashes, etc., ibid.—Worldly clothing must be left in the world, XXII, 963.—Letting down one’s hair is luxurious, or characteristic of barbarians and soldiers, XXV, 437.—“Avoid men with womanly locks, goats’ beards, black cloaks, and bare feet enduring cold; all these things are arguments of the devil,” XXII, 413.—“There are others whose whole concern is that their clothing should smell good and that the foot should not be enlarged by loose skin. Their hair is curled in the trace of the curling iron; their fingers shine with rings; and, lest a damp path splash their soles, they scarcely set down the tips of their feet,” 414.—“A face which I have repeatedly painted against God’s command with purple-red, white lead, and stibium ought to be disgraced,” 891, 1113.

GAUDENTIUS (Saint).—“Why do you purchase silk garments every day? Why do you buy costly necklaces of gold and gems, while you plead barrenness, allege necessities, and complain of narrow means? It is shameful to say, painful to remember,” XX, 939 [printed “i939”].—What guilt awaits those men and women who habitually use silken, purple, and gold-woven garments, if they do not cover the naked with some kind of clothing? 941.

AUGUSTINE (Saint).—Inner linen garments, XXXVIII, 224.—How it is now sinful to mix purple with linen garments and use a *linostina* garment, 237.—Those who display themselves in women’s clothing are rightly deemed infamous and unstable, XXXII, 898.—Ornaments inviting seduction are deservedly rebuked, XXXIII, 1080.—Yet in married women this is excused if done at the husband’s demand, 1060.—Women who come to God’s church in proud dress are rebuked, XXXVIII, 205.

How beautiful and admirable the structure of the human body is, XLI, 470, 790.—The structure and composition of the body indicate their maker, the true God, XLII, 392.—How it was made in God’s likeness, XL, 32.—The body cannot receive the image of God, XLIV, 537.—Every incorporeal nature, even if vicious and miserable, is better than the body, XXXIII, 561.—The most worthless soul is superior to the most excellent body, XXXVII, 1885.—How we sin by loving bodies, XLII, 109.—The bodies of believers are God’s temple, XLIV, 433.—Our bodies have been purchased by Christ’s blood, XXXVIII, 886.—The more eagerly the ornaments of the outward person are desired, the more they harm the inward person, 884.—The body is now a burden, after the resurrection an honor; now a load, then a relief, 1259.—The chief adornment of Christian men and women is good conduct, XXXIII, 1060.—The wearing of gold, the braiding of hair, and other such things commonly employed either for empty [Col. 0905] display or to entice by beauty are deservedly rebuked, 1080.—Wives compelled by their husbands seem excusable for proud adornment if they retain a humble heart, 1081.—Beauty is a good of God, XLI, 467.—True beauty is in the soul, XXXIII, 65.—Beauty deceives those who pursue it, XXXIV, 139.—Why it often deceives, 150.—When it is loved wrongly, XLI, 467.—Women deceive men by simulated whiteness and blush and by paint applied to the face, XL, 446.

PROSPER (Saint).—The body, formerly our ornament, has afterward become our fetters, LI, 438.—There is no one in this life whose soul is not weighed down by a corruptible body, 340.

PETER CHRYSOLOGUS (Saint).—Earthly garments shine when new and grow foul when old, LII, 432.—Those who are earthly are clothed in earthly garments, ibid.—The evil rich man was clothed in purple and fine linen. “What is this, rich man? Does fine linen protect you from heat? Does purple resist hell? Those things remained behind; they deserted you; and now you yourself, naked, sweat and burn, you who once mocked those suffering heat, clothed in an artful nakedness,” 335.—Against those who imitated the costume and face of idols in games, he inveighs thus: “If there is such condemnation for giving assent, who can sufficiently lament those who make themselves into idols? Have they not lost God’s image, forfeited the likeness, and stripped themselves of Christ’s garment? Do not say: ‘These are not pursuits of sacrilege; they are the observances of amusements, and this is the joy of novelty, not the error of antiquity.’ . . . You are mistaken, man: these are not entertainments; they are crimes,” LII, 611.—“If there is in us any feeling of compassion, any concern for a brother’s salvation, let us draw away those who thus run to destruction, are hurried to death, dragged to Tartarus, and hasten toward Gehenna. Let father draw away son, master servant, citizen fellow citizen, one human being another—those who have compared themselves to beasts, made themselves equal to beasts of burden, adapted themselves to cattle, and fashioned themselves after demons,” ibid.

MAXIMUS OF TURIN (Saint).—He rebukes men who, raging on the Kalends of January, put on women’s adornments, LVII, 255 ff.

PRUDENTIUS (Saint).—He rebukes women who practice certain paintings upon themselves, LIX, 1030, 1033.

PAULINUS (Saint).—What kind of hair is fitting for women, LXI, 733.

GREGORY THE GREAT (Saint).—What it means to be clothed in soft garments, LXVI, 1097.—Costly garments are condemned, 1305.—Cheap garments are attributed to virtue, ibid.—The impious person and the heretic, like adulterers, cover their faces so that they may more securely pour out wickedness, LXXV, 1157.

COLUMBANUS (Saint).—A bodily religious profession colored by gestures is vain, LXXX, 234.—Let us not be like whitewashed tombs, ibid.—See his sermon *On Not Serving the Body*, 242.—“I shall say one thing that I know: whoever is fed here, filled here, delighted here, laughs here, is intoxicated here, plays here—there he will hunger, there thirst, there mourn, there lament, there howl,” 244.

TAIO OF ZARAGOZA.—On the adornment of clothing, LXXX, 958.

PAULINUS OF AQUILEIA (Saint).—On frivolous bodily beauty, XCIX, 220.

ALCUIN (Blessed).—The empty pomp of clothing, which benefits not even secular persons and greatly harms those who serve God, C, 166, 168.—Modesty in clothing is commended, 158.—“Let not the vanity of clothing soften you,” 222.—The pomp of clothing is madness, 243.—The body which we cultivate with such care will afterward be food for worms, 227.

ADO OF VIENNE (Saint).—How Saint Agnes, though young and exceedingly beautiful, rejected proud clothing and precious ornaments so that she might remain a virgin, CXXIII, 197.

RATHERIUS OF VERONA.—He describes the ridiculous luxury of certain prelates of his own time, CXXXVI, 291, 294.

OTLOH, monk of St Emmeram.—How detestable the luxury of clothing is in clerics, CXLVI, 357.—Certain clerics, repeatedly warned by God concerning such abuse, were threatened with lightning while assembled in church, so that all of them remained ill afterward, 358.

GUIGO, prior of the Carthusians.—“Adorned with costly garments, wrapped in ermine and gray furs, refreshed with numerous and exquisite foods, not so much laid upon as immersed in soft feathers like Sardanapalus—how do you suppose that God’s indignation can be appeased by our prayers?” CLIII, 596.—“Therefore let neither the favor of princes, nor the brilliance of ornaments, nor the glory of pageantry, nor the delights of banquets, nor any abundance of offered gifts take from you the care of it,” namely, the soul, 597.

ANSELM OF CANTERBURY (Saint).—“Pour forth tears while there is time, lest in another age you weep without profit: for here is laughter, but there weeping; here adornment of clothing, there the torture of worms,” CLVIII, 678.—“What will you gain from care for costly [Col. 0906] clothing except eternal punishments?” 679.—“Always bear modesty in your countenance . . . shame in your face,” 680.—“Walk with your face cast down, your expression lowered, your mouth sorrowful, your heart stricken, and your garment mournful,” 681.—Despise temporal and passing things, so that, like an outstanding warrior, leaving the world’s pomp behind, you may deserve the prize after victory, 679.—Keep the body and its members in the dignity appropriate to them, 713.—Christ himself deigns to dwell in you; he clothes, defends, and adorns you with himself, ibid.—Verses against luxury of body and clothing, 701, 702.—Description of the body’s decay in old age, 694.

ANSELM OF LAON.—The clothing of John the Baptist teaches us to use rough garments for subduing the flesh, CLXII, 1263.—Those who have not defiled their garments, 1513.—The harlot Babylon is described in proud apparel, 1561.

RUPERT OF DEUTZ.—The example of the impious queen Jezebel, who, when she heard that Jehu was entering, painted her eyes with stibium, adorned her head, and looked out of the window to seduce him; as a result she was cast down, CLXIX, 885.—He expounds the woman of the Apocalypse clothed in purple, scarlet, gold, precious stones, and pearls, holding in her hand a cup full of abomination, 1132.

HILDEBERT OF LE MANS.—On John the Baptist: “When, he says, he is clothed with rough garments, he instructs us to subdue the flesh by labors; when he girds his loins with a leather belt, he invites us to chastity,” CLXXI, 657.—Costly garments do not please God, 838.

GODEFRIDUS OF ADMONT.—The body is a symbol of corruption, CLXXIV, 688.—Garments are symbols of the human body, 783.—Superfluous cares are to be avoided, 682.—The lamentable end of the richly dressed and feasting rich man, 388 ff.

HUGH OF ST VICTOR.—Garments ought not to be excessively clean; for each person is so much the more defiled within as he is outwardly made clean for empty glory, CLXXVI, 908.—There is indeed a great difference between necessity and desire, ibid.—On priestly vestments, CLXXVII, 927.

BERNARD OF CLAIRVAUX (Saint).—The delights of the flesh are corruptions of the spirit; soft and warm furs, fine and costly cloth, long sleeves, a broad hood, forest-green coverings, and soft woven material do not make a person holy, CLXXXII, 77.—What idleness produces as weariness, exercise renders pleasant, ibid.—Care for the flesh is contrary to penitence, 624.—The flesh must serve the spirit, not the spirit the flesh, CLXXXIII, 600.—The flesh, a domestic enemy, is greatly to be feared, 343.—What is troublesome to the flesh is especially to be chosen, 123.—Luxury of clothing among clerics is blameworthy, CLXXXII, 770, 812, 912.—Vanity in dress is the leprosy of luxury, CLXXXIII, 289.—The beauty of garments does not beautify the wearer, CLXXXII, 238.—Luxury in clothing is forbidden, especially among monks, CLXXXIII, 85.—Artificial beauty is condemned, CLXXXII, 238.—It is in no way comparable to inner beauty, CLXXXIII, 913.—“You do not receive from the altar so that you may live luxuriously, or buy yourself golden bridles, painted saddles, and various gray furs from it,” CLXXXII, 86.—“Let us therefore be content with clothing by which we may be covered, not by which we may be wanton, not by which we may be proud, not by which we may strive either to resemble or to please little women,” ibid.—Pride yields where affection grows strong, CLXXXIII, 999.—On seeking true beauty in the soul, ibid.—Many celebrate saints’ feasts only through the pride of clothing and the pleasures of the body, 44.

GILBERT OF HOLLAND.—These are good garments, one of which adorns, the other arms, CLXXXIV, 133.—What the garments of the soul are mystically, 181, 182.

GUERRIC OF IGNY, Cistercian (Venerable).—“Is this the appearance of piety that we see in them: a harlot-like habit and gait, clownish speech, an immodest eye, a belly cultivated as a god, and all that insult to life publicly inflicted upon piety?” CLXXXV, 59.—Virtue is not always to be judged from dress, ibid.—“Not one Naaman, but innumerable Naamans: O rich men—and lepers! Proud men—but miserable!” 61.—The mantle of divine love must be put on in the winter of this life, 50.—The gold of wisdom is the soul’s precious ornament, ibid.

GRATIAN.—Decretum on clerical dress: clerics who indulge in bright and shining garments are condemned, CLXXXVII, 1117.—Likewise those who wear secular clothing, 1118.

PETER THE VENERABLE, abbot of Cluny.—He rebukes certain customary practices in clothing among the men of Clairvaux, CCXXXIX, 113.—Difference of color in monks’ clothing ought not to be a cause of division, schism, or boasting, 333, 334.—It matters little whether you are white or black, 404.—Even in a filthy habit the devil seeks what is his own, and sometimes interweaves the fabric [Col. 0907] of pride into the garments of humility, 944.—What should be applied to Christ’s garment? 960.—Statutes of the Cluniac order concerning clothing, by which softness and pride especially are extirpated, 1030, 1031.

GERHOHUS, provost.—He rebukes nuns who receive costly garments or any other ornaments from outside, CXCIV, 1279, 1283.

AELRED, abbot.—Garments of haircloth, wool, linen, and purple are mystically interpreted concerning the state of the soul, CXCV, 358, 359.

RICHARD OF ST VICTOR.—As soon as the soul departs, the body loses voluntary movement and every sensation, CXCVI, 210.—At every hour a person ought to remember his last things, ibid.—“Oh, with how great a shame will he return to God . . . who has trampled down, defiled, and obliterated God’s likeness in himself!” 211.—He rebukes women adorned with braided hair, gold, and costly clothing, 336.

ADAM THE SCOT.—The dangers of bodily beauty, CXCVIII, 384.—It blinds the eyes of those who look upon it, 815.—Modesty in dress is commended, 533.

ARNULF OF LISIEUX.—The propriety of dress increases the dignity of words and countenance, CCI, 183.—The modesty of the face proves the chastity of the soul, ibid.

REINER OF ST LAURENT, monk of Liège.—The pomp and vanity both of the clothing and ornaments of Saint Pelagia while still a courtesan, CCIV, 53.—Her beauty, by which the wretched children of the world were attracted, ibid.—What clothing she wore once she had become penitent, 59.—Having extinguished the vain beauty of her body by fasts, she attained the far more precious beauty of the soul, 60.

BALDWIN, archbishop of Canterbury.—The eye provokes love by its beauty and announces love by secret signification, CCIV, 481.—A woman who paints her eyes with stibium feigns a beauty she does not possess, ibid.

PETER THE CHANTER.—The superfluous curiosity of dress is rebuked, CCV, 251.—Various makers of these vanities are disapproved, 253.—He inveighs against softness in clothing, 254.—A monk’s garment should not shine, 485 note.—A Christian ought not to wear a *sirmatic* garment, 252.

PETER OF BLOIS.—He attacks the pride and arrogance of a certain canon, CCV, 75.—Elijah and John are praised for the roughness of their clothing, 578.—Look upon the child Jesus wrapped in the poorest rags, ibid.—Christ’s disciples are ragged, 587.

MARTIN OF LEÓN (Saint).—The world is not abandoned unless the softness of clothing is rejected, CCVIII, 634.—Haircloth and ashes envelop the body of the penitent, ibid.—Beauty is not to be loved in creatures, but in him who distributes it to creatures, 678.—Let our glory be to reject bodily delights, despise earthly things, and desire heavenly ones, 720.

ALAN OF LILLE.—The body is not to be indulged, CCX, 119.—The body must not be provided for in such a way that we forget the spirit, 588.—Beauty is a fragile good, 117.—Its last end must often be remembered, ibid.—Death destroys it; a single scratch from a needle kills it; illness demolishes it; old age plunders it, ibid.—Do not boast of distinguished attire, 118.—The human being’s mirror is threefold: Scripture, nature, and creation, ibid.

ABSALO, abbot.—Consider what is the condition of our flesh: miserable, necessarily destined to die, to live briefly, a keeper of the grave, to be joined to worms, assigned to judgment, and—unless mercifully delivered—to perish forever, 24.—Consider the misery of this prison, that is, the body, 42.—How monks differently contract the stain of property through clothing, 174.—He rebukes the luxury of certain clerics, 142.

ADAM, abbot of Perseigne.—Divine purity does not seek long trains of garments, necessary for nothing but stirring up dust and delaying the steps of those who hurry, ibid.—The shameless women of our time are not ashamed to resemble a little fox dragging a long tail behind it, 610.—A Christian woman ought to have moderate dress and a modest countenance, 611.—“Have weight, keep number, preserve measure, and you cannot be separated from the Creator,” 617.—Superfluity knows no measure, ibid.—Curiosity in clothing, superfluity of expense, and the pomp of riders are blameworthy in a widow, 694.

HELINAND, abbot.—What cleric is ashamed to go out into public elegantly dressed? Who is ashamed to walk with a soft and womanly step—indeed, who is ashamed to be a woman? CCXII, 633.—And what still lacks for them, in beautifying their appearance at the injury of their order and body, when they spend the whole day attending to a mirror? 633–634.—On knowledge of the human body, 729.—On its misery, 730.

SICARD OF CREMONA.—On the clerics’ sacred and domestic habit, and its mystical meaning, CCXIII, 57 ff., 72, 84.—They do not bear arms, because they attack not men but demons, [Col. 0908] 60.—To gird the loins with a belt is to restrain impulses of lust, 74.—Subdeacons wear the ankle-length *poderes* (*l’aube*, “the alb”) in order to learn to clothe themselves with bodily purity and chastity. Then they gird their loins with a belt (*le cordon*, “the cord”), so that, under the fear of the Lord, they may learn to restrain fleshly desires, 85.

The Deeds of Innocent III.—Since he saw great excess reigning in the world, especially among prelates, he reduced his household to the utmost moderation so that he might rebuke them more freely, CCXIV, CCXXV.—He exchanged ermine and gray furs for lambskin, ibid.

IV.—Drunkenness.

TERTULLIAN.—The use of wine was formerly forbidden to women, I, 302, 303, 1288.—The two demons of drunkenness and lust conspired and entered into a league with one another, 643.

HILARY OF POITIERS (Saint).—The misery of drunkenness is vividly portrayed, IX, 687.—Wine gladdening the heart of man, and wine piercing the heart of man, 386.—In wine is wantonness, ibid.

AMBROSE (Saint).—Wine did not spare even its own author, XIV, 701.—Incest, the fruit of drunkenness, 702.—On abstinence from wine, ibid. ff.—Drunkenness from wine is the fuel of lust, 327.—How great wine’s power is, XVI, 203.—Where the flesh is intoxicated, the mind stumbles, the soul wavers, and the heart is tossed about, 410.—Gluttons and drunkards are slaves of the belly and lust, XVII, 529.

BACHIARIUS, book to Januarius.—Until you have escaped the mousetrap of fornication, do not entrust yourself to the snares of drunkenness, XX, 1050.—Luxury and drunkenness have a certain kinship with one another in the birth of vices, ibid.

JEROME (Saint).—Never smell of wine, lest you hear that philosopher’s remark: “This is not offering a kiss, but pouring out wine,” XXII, 536.—Neither the fires of Etna, nor the land of Vulcan, nor Vesuvius and Olympus boil with such heat as youthful marrow full of wine and inflamed by banquets, 554.—The comic poet said: “Without Ceres and Liber, Venus grows cold,” ibid.—Festivals are not to be celebrated with wine, XXV, 1243.—But God hates . . . those who celebrate not God’s festivals but their own festivals, 1053.—Unless the brain is sound, all the members will be diseased, XXII, 662.—A belly boiling with unmixed wine quickly foams over into lusts: in wine is luxury, in luxury pleasure, in pleasure immodesty, 663.

AUGUSTINE (Saint).—The sin of drunkenness has become cheap and contemptible through custom, XXXVIII, 125.—Nothing is more insane than a drunkard, XXXVII, 1370.—The struggle against drunkenness and bad habit, XXXVIII, 816.—Drunkenness must be avoided, 1098.—It was exceedingly common in Augustine’s time, XXXIII, 365.—Drunken bouts in honor of holy martyrs, 91.—This vice is rebuked, 116.—There is a very great difference between one who is habitually drunken and one who is drunk, XLII, 427.

PETER CHRYSOLOGUS (Saint).—The consequences of gluttony and drunkenness in Herod, LII, 650.—The excesses customary on the Kalends of January are rebuked, 609 ff.—Drunkenness is a flattering demon, sweet poison, voluntary madness, an invited enemy, an enticement to dishonor, and an injury to modesty, 273.—Drunkenness is the mother of slaughter, parent of quarrels, begetter of fury, and a shameful teacher of impudence. Whoever possesses it does not possess himself; he is not a human being, but is sin itself, ibid.—Drunkenness is a crime in a Christian and sacrilege in a priest: the one kills his own soul with wine; the priest extinguishes the spirit of holiness, 273.

SALVIAN.—Drunkenness is common to nobles and commoners, LIII, 142.—The drunkenness of Christians is more detestable than that of the Huns and other barbarians, 87.—In their drinking bouts drunkards appear to scorn God, 170.

MAXIMUS OF TURIN (Saint).—Luxury is the companion of drunkenness, LVII, 736.

PRUDENTIUS (Saint).—One must take care that gluttony not rage, LIX, 813.

ISIDORE OF SEVILLE (Saint).—Food produces gluttony; drink, drunkenness, LXXXIII, 649.—Drunkenness produces disturbance of mind, madness of heart, and the flame of lust, 649.—Drunkenness enslaves rational judgment, 650.—Isaiah rebukes those given to wine and luxury, ibid.—Many, held fast by a bestial habit, serve luxury and banquets all day long, ibid.—The person who prepares delicacies for himself in the evening to fill his belly chews over banquets in thought all day, 652.

ALCUIN (Blessed).—No one is unaware how many evils drunkenness produces, C, 166.—He commends sobriety in drinking, 175.—Especially avoid habitual drunkenness: from the heat of wine, the burning of fevers commonly comes upon the unwary, ibid.—Avoid those who pursue drunkenness as you would the pit of hell, 243.—The habitual luxury of drunkenness is madness, ibid.

HINCMAR OF RHEIMS.—Among many, drunkenness is not only maintained as a customary practice, [Col. 0909] but they even boast and glory in it as though it were a virtue, CXXV, 876.

PETER DAMIAN (Saint).—Wine is a luxurious thing and drunkenness tumultuous; for becoming accustomed to wine and banquets is nothing other than opening an entrance for the enemies of the soul to enter, 428.

RALPH ARDENS.—What drunkenness is, CLV, 1670.—What evils it produces, ibid.

ANSELM OF CANTERBURY (Saint).—Whoever desires drunkenness or the immoderate pleasure of drinking loses through his own fault the grace he has received, CLVIII, 525.—Hunger and thirst; abstain and grow dry: unless you are trained by fasts, you cannot overcome temptations, 680.—In verse he rebukes drunkards and those devoted to gluttony, 701.

BRUNO OF ASTI (Saint).—One must abstain from every drunken indulgence and drunkenness, CLXV, 939.—How many evils proceed from wine, ibid.—Both drunkenness from wine and drunkenness of concupiscence are evil; for there is no secrecy wherever either rules, ibid.—How the sacrilegious drunkenness of King Belshazzar is punished, 1359.

HILDEBERT OF LE MANS.—Babylon’s golden cup is suspect; it is better to thirst, CLXXI, 432.—Drunkenness is condemned, 449.—Drunkenness removes understanding and weakens the body, 468.

GODEFRIDUS OF ADMONT.—Drunkenness and gluttony are the mother of luxury, CLXXIV, 1121–1122.—Our body is a griddle upon which the wretched soul suffers the various fires of temptation, 956.

HUGH OF ST VICTOR, Paris.—Drunkenness is that by which a certain forgetfulness of itself is produced in the mind through indulgence in excessive drinking, CLXXVI, 1001.

BERNARD (St.), Abbot of Clairvaux.—Do I blame that drink whose colour smiled so pleasantly upon the eyes and whose taste answered sweetly on the palate, or the silver cups? CLXXXII, 708.—Drunkenness is the cup of demons, 85.—Christ does not deign to offer his wines, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb, where there is a curious variety of foods, 86.—The Cistercians drink wine rarely, because it serves the body rather than the mind, 77.—They will mix water, CLXXXIII, 515.—Spiced wines are likewise forbidden them, CLXXXII, 911.—When the veins have been gorged with wine, throbbing throughout the head, what else does one rising from table desire except to sleep? ibid.

GRATIAN.—One must not give oneself over to revelries and drunkenness, CLXXXVII, 229.

PETER THE VENERABLE, Abbot of Cluny.—The carnal man wishes to drink pleasurably, excessively, and to become drunk; Christ wholly opposes him, CLXXXIX, 593.

GARNERIUS OF ST. VICTOR.—The fruits of drunkenness and intoxication in Herod, CXCIII, 169.

ECBERT, Abbot.—Drinking wine is not evil in itself, provided it is done temperately and in due order, as is shown against the Cathars, CXCV, 39.

JOHN OF SALISBURY.—The gatherings of those who feast and drink together are commonly shameful, CXCIX, 403.

PETER OF CELLE.—When someone is buried in wine, lust is enfeebled and nature mourns, CCII, 430.—Let us not be devoted to wine, in which there is lust, 651.

PETER THE CHANTER.—Against drunkenness, CCV, 330.—Drunkenness makes one forgetful of oneself and of God, 332.—Blind drunkenness has disfigured the image and likeness of God which shines forth in man, 762.—In drunkenness all the organs rave, ibid.—If you gorge yourself with wine, however much your tongue may sound God’s praises, your life blasphemes, ibid.

MARTIN (St.) of León.—Adam fell through gluttony; Lot through drunkenness; Solomon through lust, CCVIII, 677.

ALAN OF LILLE.—Description of drunkenness, CCX, 120, 462.—Its effects and evil character, ibid.—It drives one to crimes, 253.—Drunkards must be avoided, 255.—It is familiar even to clerics, 463.—Secrets should not be entrusted to drunkards, 581.

V.—Excess of gluttony.—Revelries, the delights of banquets and feasts, and drunken excess.

TERTULLIAN.—Food either kills or wounds every discipline, II, 960.—What mankind’s food was like at the beginning, 958.—What the public banquets of the pagans are, and how abominable, I, 452.—Lust and luxury are gluttony’s companions, II, 953.

CYPRIAN (St.).—Licentious banquets must be avoided, IV, 457.—Shameful, filthy banquets within the association, III, 1030.—Banquets with evil people forbidden, 829.—More lavish feasts must be avoided, IV, 244.—To hanker after feasts and dinners, 391.

HILARY (St.) of Poitiers.—The book of the living is different from the book of the righteous, IX, 485.

AMBROSE (St.).—Gluttony drove reigning man from paradise [Col. 0910], XIV, 700.—One serves an evil mistress, gluttony, which always demands and is never satisfied, 706.—What dangers are not incurred for the belly? 705.—Those who serve their belly and gluttony walk in the belly, 312.—The devil stretched out the snare of gluttony, 325.—Gluttony has killed very many; frugality, no one, 326.—Lust is fed by banquets, nourished by luxuries, kindled by wine, and inflamed by drunkenness.

JEROME (St.).—On elaborate foods, XXII, 533.—Secular banquets must be avoided, 536.—What profit is there in not eating oil, while seeking certain troubles and difficulties in food? 537.—A fat belly has not produced a subtle mind, 537.—It is far better to rule the body than to serve it, 479.—What have we animals of the belly ever done like this? Even if someone finds us reading at the second hour, we yawn; rubbing our faces with our hands, we restrain our stomachs, 478.—The abundance of feasts ruins both body and soul, XXIII, 301.—Chastity is difficult to preserve amid feasts, XXII, 957.—A full belly readily argues about fasting, 580.

AUGUSTINE (St.).—The eternal law admits food and drink only for the sake of preserving health, XLII, 426.—Foods should be taken as medicines, XXXII, 797.—Great is the person who is not carried even a little beyond the bounds of necessity in eating, 799.—What is enough for health is too little for pleasure, 797.—Food is not taken without pleasure in order that one may live, XLI, 622.—The need for food is a calamity, and foods are called delights, XXXII, 797.—In food the snare of desire lies in wait, ibid.—Food which no longer tastes good in the belly seems to taste good in memory, 786.—The craving for food is greater amid anxieties, 924.—Cheap and choice foods provide nothing more, XXXVIII, 413.—Spiritual food is superior to bodily food, XXXVIII, 1481.—God is our food: he alone refreshes and does not fail, XXXVI, 597.—Gluttons described, XXXIV, 97.

JOHN CASSIAN.—The spirit must struggle against gastrimargia, or gluttony, XLIX, 205, 217, 223, 229, 236, 636 and following.—The luxuries of food and drink must be avoided, 625.

PETER CHRYSOLOGUS (St.).—Consult the sermons on the rich feaster, LII, 529, 536, 540; and on the prodigal son, 183 and following.—In Herod lay flesh oppressed by drunken excess, captive to drunkenness, 654.—Behold all that banquets prolonged through whole nights bring forth, ibid.

SALVIAN.—He praises the rustic food and sobriety of the ancient Romans in order to shame the excesses of his own time, LIII, 32, 33.—We cannot partake both of the table of demons and of the table of the Lord, 155.

LEO THE GREAT (St.).—Let us beware of our adversary’s snares not only in the enticements of gluttony but even in fasting itself, LIV, 278.—Through the enticement of food the first cause of sin crept in, 421.—Daily experience proves that the sharpness of the mind is blunted by the satiety of the flesh and the vigour of the heart dulled by excess of foods, 186.—Elsewhere, speaking against the Manichees about food: “But if it is taken with immoderate greed, excess disgraces gluttons and drunkards; it is not the nature of food or drink that defiles,” 279.

MAXIMUS (St.) of Turin.—The drunken banquets of the Kalends are condemned, LVII, 270.—The vice of gluttony: how many harms it brings, 564.—Lust is always joined to satiety, 575.

GREGORY THE GREAT (St.).—Banquets are scarcely celebrated without fault, LXXV, 532.—Even in moderate banquets the devil finds a place, 568.—The banquet of the reprobate is delight in temporal pleasures, LXXVI, 709.—It is not food but appetite that is at fault, 557.—Temptations of gluttony, 622.—Gluttony tempts us in five ways, 556.—By gluttony all virtues are overwhelmed, ibid.—Gluttony is an ancient weapon of the devil, LXXVIII, 22.—How much it is to be feared, 314.

EUTROPIUS (St.).—He counts gluttony, or gastrimargia, as the first of the eight principal vices, LXXX, 9.—From gastrimargia arises fornication, or lust, 11.—It is distinguished into three kinds, ibid.—From gastrimargia are born revelries and drunkennesses, 12.

TAIO of Saragossa.—On the desire of gluttony, LXXX, 940.

ISIDORE (St.) of Seville.—On gluttony—what it is and how many kinds it has, LXXXIII, 647.—Through it lust is kindled and nourished. Revelries and costly banquets are censured, 648.—Unclean spirits are not easily expelled except through the extinction of gluttony and abstinence, 649.—No tax-collector is so importunate to a man as his belly, ibid.

PAULINUS (St.) of Aquileia.—Drunken excess and drunkenness must especially be avoided, particularly by clerics, XCIX, 297.

ALCUIN (Blessed).—What of the frequency of banquets, which commonly turns the soul away from the religion of a better life? C, 166.—Moderation in food and drink is commended, 158. Let not the luxury of foods enervate you, 222.—On gluttony, CI, 633.—On the greed of the belly, 1194.

[Col. 0911] HALITGARIUS.—On the greed of the belly, CV, 667.—On the remedy for gluttony, ibid.

JONAS of Orléans.—He vehemently rebukes those who, with their bellies distended by delicate foods and irrigated with most varied drinks, loosen their mouths not to the praises of God but to guffaws, CVI, 164.—Those occupied with feasts and much talk should be frightened by the condemnation of that purple-clad rich man who refused to give crumbs to needy Lazarus, 165.—Now food is scarcely taken without detraction, hypocrisy, mockery, actors’ dancing, obscene joking, filthy speech, buffoonery, and countless other vanities which soften the Christian mind, ibid.

RABANUS MAURUS.—At Herod’s luxurious and impure banquet bloody dishes were served, CVII, 960.—The carnal people of the Jews, scorning heavenly food, desired the pleasure of fleshly things, CVIII, 661.—Another temptation of the flesh arises when the flesh is served too immoderately in refreshment, CX, 937.—On the nature, tyranny, and remedies of gluttony, CXII, 1367 and following.

PASCHASIUS RADBERTUS.—Through gluttony the tinder of desires is nourished, and the incentives of lust are more sharply inflamed within us, CXX, 188.

HINCMAR of Rheims.—Capitularies by which taverns and revelries are forbidden to clerics, CXXV, 780.—Those devoted to gluttony must be warned lest, in what they most devote themselves to pleasure, they pierce themselves with the sword of lust, 875.—Gluttony draws men into lust, because when the belly is stretched by satiety, the stings of desire are stirred, 876.

ODO (St.) of Cluny.—The Apostle calls worshippers of gluttony enemies of Christ’s cross, having their belly as their god, CXXXIII, 567; and in Job it is written: “Wisdom shall not be found in the land of the living,” 567.

ATTO of Vercelli.—Whoever frequently comes to another’s table, being devoted to idleness, must flatter the person feeding him … a practice utterly opposed to the Lord’s discipline; for the god of such people is their belly, as they provide so foully for their own necessities, 662.

RATHERIUS of Verona.—On the table and luxury-laden banquets of certain bishops of his time, CXXXVI, 291.—How will one who serves gluttony abstain from vices? 696.—Why gluttony is called threefold, ibid.

PETER DAMIAN.—How can we gain triumph over our enemies, when we always wish to lie amid feasts, always in the gorging of abundant cups? CXLIV, 428.—Let gluttony’s greed be restrained, so that we may appear as conspicuous conquerors of sincere chastity, 429.—Whoever venerates his belly as God is convicted of denying God in some sense, ibid.—Let the bridle of discipline restrain the itch of gluttony, 426.—The belly is rightly called the chief of cooks, since cooks serve it with laborious work, 427.—The savage inhumanity of the rich feaster, 418.—What shall I say of gluttony, when all the wealthy know nothing of hunger and never wait for appetite? Unless swollen bellies expel wind promptly through either opening, they fear a rupture of the intestines; thus the preservation of life rests in tubes held in the hands, 231.—Their flaming mouths revel, yet, because disgust prevents it, they should not be said to eat but rather to lick greedily, ibid.

GUIGO, Prior of the Carthusians.—One must strive with all one’s might that the pride of the mind be subdued by humility and the lust of the flesh by sobriety, CLIII, 595.—When we are refreshed with numerous and exquisite dishes, how do we suppose that divine indignation can be appeased by our prayers?

RADULPHUS ARDENS.—We love our soul foolishly and badly if we satisfy its sensuality in greed, luxury, and pleasure, CLV, 1527.—Revelries and drunkennesses are works of darkness, 1670.—A revelry is a frequent and luxurious feasting, excessive in measure, time, and manner, ibid.

ANSELM (St.) of Canterbury.—In verse he inveighs against the followers of gluttony and drunken excess, CLVIII, 701, 702.—“The prostitute, cook, and actor regard certain things as supreme goods; they prefer no good to these or judge any good their equal. Whatever sea, land, or air nourishes for sustenance, the luxurious hunger of men seeks and obtains. The vast world scarcely suffices for the small belly,” 701.

IVO (Blessed) of Chartres.—The filled mind grows sluggish, and the watered soil of this body puts forth thorns and thistles, CLXI, 1126.—He rebukes certain clerics of Beauvais who were more devoted to their bellies than was fitting, 118.—One who thirsts does not care about the quality of foods.

ANSELM of Laon.—Gluttony is the gate and beginning of other pleasures, CLXII, 1271.—Above all through it the devil tempts human beings, 1272.—In John the Baptist’s food we are taught to use harsh and natural foods, [Col. 0912] not being overly concerned with foreign and distant foods, 1263.—The soul is more than food, 1312.

BRUNO (St.) of Asti.—Drunken excess and drunkenness are sins which burden hearts, corrupt the body, provoke lust, overthrow the mind, and make the outward person weak, CLXV, 936.—It is greater to abstain from vices than from foods, 937.

RUPERT of Deutz.—The joy of satiety, a herald of tribulation, CLXVIII, 968.—The belly is a clamouring tax-collector, 1167.—The terrible end of Belshazzar’s banquet, 1359 and following.

HILDEBERT of Le Mans.—Those who pursue revelries, drunkennesses, and luxuries are citizens of the devil, CLXXI, 865.—From satiety man is inflamed toward lust, 427.—The food is harsh but health-giving; it is bitter to taste, but once swallowed it will become sweeter than honey and the honeycomb, 431.—In the first woman’s sin, she was first captured by sight and smell; the serpent’s words beguiled her hearing; then touch ministered, and taste completed the sin, 842.

HONORIUS of Autun.—Drunken excess is the sin by which someone serves the enticements of gluttony so completely that, like a pig, he devotes all his care to his belly, CLXXII, 1010.—Those whose hearts are weighed down by drunken excess will be tormented, parched in the flame with the rich man, ibid.

GODEFRIDUS of Admont.—The condemnation of the rich man who feasted daily, CLXXIV, 388 and following.—As imprudence is attributed to the soul, so intemperance is attributed to the body, 1121.

HUGH OF ST. VICTOR.—On the greed of the belly, or gluttony, and its retinue, CLXXVI, 1001.—Three points must be considered in taking food: what is taken, when, and how, 1054.—And three things must be observed: moderation, measure, and number, 1055.—The fivefold vice of gluttony, CLXXVII, 850.—It is not food but appetite that is the vice, ibid.

BERNARD (St.) of Clairvaux.—Do I rebuke daily festive dishes, such blameless little bowls? CLXXXII, 708.—How base and unworthy is the pleasure of gluttony, 842.—The many harms of gluttony, 985.—Drunken excess is the cup of demons, 85.—Just as fire and water cannot exist together, so spiritual and carnal delights cannot tolerate one another in the same person, 86.—Excessive seasonings of food are forbidden to monks as incentives to lust, 77.—The belly, when it does not know, is burdened; but variety removes disgust, 910.—He inveighs against luxuries, CLXXXIII, 589.

GUERRIC.—As a stomach corrupted by immoderate use of sweets is cleansed by a bitter drink, so those who have lived pleasurably are healed in the bitterness of conscience by an austere life and habit, CLXXXV, 48.

ROBERT PULLUS.—How foods ought to be taken, CLXXXVI, 969, 974.—Foods do not defile a person, but desire and abuse do, 975.

GRATIAN.—On foods, CLXXXVII, 217.—On food and appetite, 219.—One must not give oneself over to revelries, 229.

PETER THE VENERABLE, Monk of Cluny.—He rebukes monks of his order who, scorning abstinence, pant after meat, CLXXXIX, 419.—Forests must be scoured; hunters are needed; pheasants, partridges, and turtledoves must be caught by fowlers’ skill, lest the servant of God perish of hunger, ibid.—The horrible end of gluttonous monks, 421.—The carnal man wishes to feast pleasurably and excessively; Christ utterly opposes him, 593.

GARNERIUS.—From the greed of the belly arise foolish joy, buffoonery, impurity, much talk, and dullness of mind, CXCIII, 153.—How it is propagated, 154.—The appetite of gluttony proceeds from a dissolution of spirit, 273.—Greed is denoted by the name *bruchus*, 134.

ECBERT, Abbot.—Although it is good and praiseworthy to abstain from meat, nevertheless the sober eating of meat is not always forbidden by the Church, CXCV, 36, 39.—What things defile a person, 38.

AELRED, Abbot.—How that worst thief, namely the devil, seizes and deceives us unawares through the senses, and first through the desire of gluttony, CXCV, 223.—Diet greatly serves to curb the desires of the flesh, 243.—The Egyptians—that is, the proud—overwhelm with stones those who in the world despise riches, honours, and luxuries, and who live sparingly, soberly, chastely, and religiously; that is, they pursue them with harsh insults, 244.

RICHARD OF ST. VICTOR.—Gluttony is, as it were, the handmaid and servant of lust, CXCVI, 690.—How sinful is the pleasure of drink and food, 481.—The more one despises outward delights, the more one will be able to delight in God, 518.—Let reason rule sensuality, 501.

HILDEGARD (St.).—When a person nourishes his flesh moderately, he has cheerful and gentle manners; but [Col. 0913] when he lives amid excess of food and banquets, he causes every harmful vice to spring up, CXCVII, 336.

ADAM THE SCOT.—The dishonourable excess of gluttony must be restrained, CXCVIII, 256.—You exceed the measure of sobriety no less when you exclude necessities from your body than when you expend superfluities upon it, 256.—The pleasure and luxuries of food are to be avoided by the healthy and permitted to the sick, 532.

RADULPHUS of Lisieux.—He reproaches a certain bishop for the luxury and excessive expense of banquets, CCI, 181.—He likewise accuses the same man of transferring the fragrance of incense to his feasts, ibid.—The miserable fruits of such sensuality, 182.—He praises the sobriety in food and drink of Pope Alexander III, 183.

PETER OF CELLE.—Nature, content with little, rejoices to abstain from the excesses of gluttony, CCII, 430.—The face of this monster, namely gluttony, is pleasant in order to deceive, ibid.—When the sceptre of the kingdom is gained by the betrayal of the flesh, what peace is there over Israel? ibid.—Where meat is eaten without permission, is not Adam’s transgression renewed? ibid.—Gluttony, the gate and funnel of the belly, 643.—Abundance of feasts and fullness of food supply tinder for the ticklings and incentives of the flesh, 681.—What is the household of gluttony, 686.—The remedy for gluttony: diet, or abstinence, 730.—What is the devil’s food, 782.

PETER THE CHANTER.—What gluttony is, CCV, 73.—On gastrimargia, 328.—Against gluttony and drunkenness, 330.—It produces lust, 331.—Gluttony, the desire of the flesh, and libido are connected vices, 332.

PETER OF BLOIS.—He severely rebukes the gluttony of a certain man and explains by examples how great are the evils born from it, CCVII, 259 and following.—The hunger of the prodigal son: a salutary lesson for everyone living luxuriously, 603.—Whoever hungers in the present age shall be satisfied in the future, ibid.—Gastrimargia is among the things God hates, 759.—He inveighs against revelries and drunkennesses, 762.

MARTIN (St.) of León.—If you truly wish to leave the world, reject the luxuries of foods and softness of clothing, CCVIII, 634.—Let the flesh fast from foods and the mind from vices, ibid.—From gastrimargia arise disputes and drunkennesses, 721.—Abstinence tames lust, 723.—One should seek not more refined but ordinary foods, 739.

ALAN OF LILLE.—An outstanding exhortation against gluttony, CCX, 119.—Description of gluttony, 120.—Its ruinous effects, ibid.—The origin of diseases, ibid.—Insatiable gluttony, 591.—Gluttony is called sulphur and the seedbed of lust, 248.—On the superfluity of foods, 464.

ABSALON, Abbot.—Gluttony daily schemes against sobriety by excessively desiring food and drink, CCXI, 42.—Through the appetite of gluttony no less than through the outpouring of lust, bodily dignity is corrupted, 175.—The fruits of the banquet served to Adam by the serpent in paradise of delight were weakness of nature, affliction of spirit, evil desire, and the calamity of punishment, 194.—Spiritual life and all other goods, both of grace and of nature, are consumed by gluttony and lust, 136.

ADAM, Abbot of Perseigne.—The luxuries of foods and the belly’s excessive satiety are censured, CCXI, 610.—A sober diet befits a Christian woman, 611.—In a widow, excess of expenditure and a multitude of courses are blameworthy, 694.

HELINAND.—Blessed are those emptied of earthly dishes, that they may deserve to be filled with heavenly ones, CCXII, 501.—The iniquity of those who say that people live well when they feed themselves well and indulge their pleasures has lied, 545.—In how many ways sobriety should be practised and gluttony restrained, 560–561.—Hunger and thirst are the best seasoning for food and drink, 200–201.

GUNTHER, Cistercian.—He inveighs against gluttony, CCXII, 209, 210.—The wantonness of the flesh is restrained by fasting, 219.

SICARDUS of Cremona.—The pious emperor Theodosius utterly destroyed the temples of the pagans, established laws, and prohibited licentiousness at revelries, CCXIII, 474.

ANONYMOUS.—Dialogue on the eating of birds forbidden to monks, CCXIII, 931.

The Deeds of Innocent III.—He wished his own table to be content with three courses, and that of his chaplains with two, CCXIV, 226.

VI.—The company, conversations, and evil counsels of the licentious; flatteries.

TERTULLIAN.—Words hostile to modesty are rebuked on account of loquacity, I, 1288.

CYPRIAN (St.).—Conversations with evil people forbidden, III, 829.—Unchaste conversations, IV, 457.—The contagion of poisonous speech, III, 829.—Smooth defenders of vices, IV, 781.

[Col. 0914] HILARY (St.) of Poitiers.—Often what one is ashamed to say, one is not ashamed to think, IX, 325.—The dangerous and most ready slip of the tongue, 826.—The swords and arrows of a murderous tongue, 410.

AMBROSE (St.).—Loquacity is the shipwreck of innocence and virtue, and an incentive to falling and guilt, XIV, 981–982.—Beware lest you speak imprudently, 335.—“Honey will drip from the lips of the sexually immoral woman … but afterwards you will find it more bitter than gall,” 324.—The prostitute delights the eyes and caresses the ears, but defiles the mind; she lies much, adds falsehoods, and takes away discipline, ibid.—Conversations among equals often corrupt good character, XV, 1210.

JEROME (St.).—I consider foolish speech to be that of people who recount shameful things in order to provoke laughter and, by pretended silliness, mock more effectively those whom they desire to please, XXVI, 519.—Foolish speech is more particularly applied to silly and inept tales, 520.—Fraudulent persuasions and snares must be avoided, which seem to possess a certain flower of speech and flatter those who sin, 622.

AUGUSTINE (St.).—Evil people cannot speak good things, nor good people evil things, XXXVIII, 473.—What it is to speak deceit, 123.—When sinners speak both iniquity and justice, they speak falsehoods, XXXVI, 677.—Those who speak vanity do not listen to those who speak truth, XXXVII, 1866.—A person does not speak rightly except insofar as the Lord helps him, XXXIV, 355.—To flatter; flatterers, XXXIII, 571; XXXVII, 1921; XXXVIII, 579, 1229; XL, 46.

PETER CHRYSOLOGUS (St.).—The devil is betrayed through counsels, LII, 227.—What the counsel of impiety has done, 324, 490.—Flattery is the devil’s final temptation, 276.—Scandal is a most harmful and sudden enemy, 275 and following.

VALERIAN (St.).—The homily on the insolence of the mouth should be consulted carefully, LII, 706.

SALVIAN.—The most impious words of the impious: what they are and what kind, LIII, 80, 82.—Another’s wickedness ought by no means to make us wicked, 134.—By scandals we are dragged into hell, 64.

MAXIMUS (St.) of Turin.—The devil, transformed into a serpent, by deceitful tongues maliciously deceived the pious, unformed innocence of the first human beings, LVII, 798.—Remove the shameful mystery of soft lips, and no snare of flatterers will be spread for simple men, 751–752.—The habit of malicious speech is a most evil work, 752.

PAULINUS (St.).—Evil conversations corrupt good morals, LXI, 211.—He asks God’s forgiveness for sins of the tongue, 439.

GREGORY THE GREAT (St.).—How harmful the tongue of the wicked is to the good, LXXV, 754.—What it is to have sweetness beneath the tongue, 1087.—How harmful it is to flatter sinners, LXXVI, 41.—The tongues of flatterers, like locusts, devastate the fruits of good works, 600.—Flattering speech is fire, 1053.—It creeps subtly into the mind, ibid.—Flattery must be immediately extinguished, 911.—Those who give evil advice are called apostate angels, LXXV, 618.—The crafty counsels of the devil must especially be guarded against, LXXVI, 859.

ISIDORE (St.) of Seville.—The devil’s mouth is his words, or hidden inspirations by which he burns human hearts with desires, LXXXIII, 666.—Reject immodest speeches; flee shameful words; let no indecency of speech creep into your ears, 857.

BEDE (Venerable).—On the evils arising from the incontinence of the tongue, XCIII, 26 and following.

ALCUIN (Blessed).—If we shall render an account for every idle word, how much more for a harmful and deceitful one, C, 247.—One counsellor of truth is better than a thousand flatterers of falsehood, ibid.—Wicked lips are those which strive, by suggestion, to urge us toward iniquity. Likewise, the deceitful tongue is that which wishes to turn us away from the path of righteousness, C, 619.

JONAS of Orléans.—There are many who take greater pleasure in lending their ears to vain and obscene talk than to divine readings, CVI, 147.

RABANUS MAURUS.—A good purpose is overthrown by conversation with evil people, CXII, 149.

PASCHASIUS RADBERTUS.—If anyone repeats buffoonish words, words provoking laughter, or anything shameful, he will be held guilty not of an idle word but of a criminal one, CXX, 474.

HINCMAR of Rheims.—Pastoral necessity requires that, lest dire contagions spread among many, the diseased be separated from the healthy sheep, CXXV, 713.—Flattery is a most pernicious plague; it quickly steals into the mind unless it is removed at its very beginning, 862.—Flatterers are pleasant enemies, and at the Judge’s coming they will be counted among the foolish and stupid, 861.

ODO (St.) of Cluny.—There is no fear of God before the eyes [Col. 0915] of those whose throat is like an open grave, CXXXVIII, 568.

RATHERIUS of Verona.—It befits a young man to restrain himself from the talk of his contemporaries, so that he may become accustomed to speaking little, lest, while his age is still unformed, he easily slip into unlawful things through speech, CXXXVI, 210.

FULBERT (St.) of Chartres.—Every evil speech easily infects the hearer’s mind, since continual conversations and prolonged use commonly pour pestilence into souls, CXLI, 361.—Youth is open to deception and easily deceived when it is surrounded by the snares of fraudulent people, ibid.

PETER DAMIAN (St.).—Of false friends he says: “While they caress with the sweetness of their flattering speech, while they anoint the hearer’s head with the oil of flattery, they blind the inner eyes, so that they may not enjoy their accustomed light,” 279.—Let the vain-speaking tongue hear; let the idle tongue hear; let the scabrous tongue hear, which suffers, as it were, from a certain scab and itch unless it is continually scratched by the sharp nail, in some fashion, of superfluous speech, 916.—For evil thought the gate of perverse speech stands open, 842.—The tongue: a restless member, a deadly member, ibid.

ANSELM (St.) of Canterbury.—The Christian’s mouth is Christ’s mouth, CLVIII, 713.—The favour of one who flatters soothes the mind; but favour and praise of vices are utterly blameworthy, 657.—Beware boasting; beware the desire for display; beware pursuit of empty glory, 680.—Prepare the shield of patience against a harsh word; offer the buckler of patience against the sword of the tongue, 681.—Beware popular acclaim. Let neither favour deceive you nor reproach break you, 683.—Reject immodest speeches; flee shameful words; do not chatter empty words. For vain speech quickly defiles the mind, ibid.—The talkative person is unskilled; the wise person uses few words, ibid.

IVO (Blessed) of Chartres.—The conversations of the licentious must be avoided, CLXII, 22, 23.—He rebukes a certain priest who fostered suspicious conversations, 41, 42.

HILDEBERT of Le Mans.—How pernicious flattery is, CLXXI, 507, 527, 1012.—The impious rejoice to deceive their fellow citizens and themselves, 865.—Speeches intended to persuade evil or dissuade good are condemned, such as flatteries and filthy talk, 428.

HUGH OF ST. VICTOR.—The counsel of the impious consists in four things: malice, cunning, audacity, and imprudence, which lead the sinner to burial, CLXXVII, 537.—How pernicious flattery is, 687.—See what is said about the nature of sirens, 78.

WILLIAM, Abbot of St. Thierry.—Just as bad air continually drawn in by breathing infects the body, so perverse speech continually heard infects the mind, CLXXX, 447.

BERNARD (St.) of Clairvaux.—Long conversations are enemies of prayer, CLXXXIII, 585.—The tongue is a tender member, yet can scarcely be held, ibid.—Let us therefore keep watch over our words, lest by them we either offend God or harm our neighbour, 586.—Those giving counsel should not flatter rashly, CLXXXII, 518.—Those who follow human counsel lose divine counsel, CLXXXIII, 150.—The devil is the author of the counsel of the impious, 693.—One goes to him by four ways, opposed by an equal number of virtues, ibid.

GILBERT OF HOILAND.—The perverse tongue, a mobile corruption of depraved nature, of itself turns excessively toward evil, CLXXXIV, 128.—The evils of the tongue: what and how great they are, ibid.

ROBERT PULLUS.—Bad associations are not to be avoided in every place and at every time, CLXXXVI, 969.

GARNERIUS OF ST. VICTOR.—Flatterers are compared to dogs, CXCIII, 102.—The tongues of flatterers are represented by locusts, 421.

AELRED (Blessed), Abbot.—As adulterers seek the itch of lust, so some seek the itch of flattery, CXCV, 248.—Many wish to be flattered by prelates, 248.

JOHN OF SALISBURY.—What the flatterer, yes-man, and sycophant are, and that nothing is more harmful, CXCIX, 481.—How greatly flatterers have multiplied, and how they drive every honourable person from his own place, 485.—Their fraud must be avoided from the beginning, 487.—Do not doubt that flattery is joined with deceit, 496.—The flatterer’s end is to have deceived by sweet speech, 497.—Flatterers must be punished as enemies, 506.

PETER OF CELLE.—There are those who speak from the heart, who make their words smoother than oil, though they themselves are darts, CCII, 459.

PETER THE CHANTER.—Contempt for gifts does not know how to flatter, CCV, 82.—Flattery is both oil and a curse, 140.—It flees the poor and follows the rich, ibid.—A person is tested by flattery and detraction as gold in a furnace, ibid.—Every flatterer is blind, 141.—He is a traitor, 142.—The words of flatterers corrupt, 56.—To be praised by the shameful is as shameful as to be praised for shameful deeds, 155.—Words that are pleasing are dangerous, 43.

[Col. 0916] PETER OF BLOIS.—Many offer you the poisons of treacherous flattery from Babylon’s cup, CCXVII, 113.—There is no lack of chatterers and talkers in the houses of magnates, 178.—The deceitful tongue most grievously corrupts the heart, ibid.—Evil associations corrupt good morals, 228.—Against flatterers, 238.

ALAN OF LILLE.—An excellent description of flattery, CCX, 469, 470.—The malignity of flattery, ibid.—Flattery attacks a person, 573.—Who are especially apt to be infected by flattery, 469.—One must carefully consider what sort of company one frequents, 592.—Evil associations must be avoided, 582.—How dangerous evil associations are, 492.

ABSALON, Abbot.—Even if a criminal has much knowledge, silence is imposed on him, because, impelled by the inclination of a perverse will, he frequently speaks twisted and harmful things, 116.

STEPHEN OF TOURNAI.—That cup is suspect whose exterior is smeared with honey, while its interior tastes not of wine but of poison, CCXI, 519.—Use the counsel of better and greater persons, lest you follow Rehoboam’s footsteps, 539.

HELINAND, Monk.—Human beings know only three forms of speech: the speech of the world, of the flesh, and of the devil. The first suggests lofty things; the second sweet things; the third malicious things, CCXII, 503.

VII.—Desire for games, with harm to one’s reputation, one’s own and another’s fortune, and one’s time.

TERTULLIAN.—He counts gambling among the greater vices of his age: “I pass over the Neros, Apiciuses, and Rufuses. I shall give a purgative remedy to Scaurus’s impurity, Curius’s gambling, and Antony’s drunkenness,” II, 1049.

AMBROSE (St.).—The inexorable tyranny of gambling; gatherings of gamblers. Fortune plays varied outcomes. They stake for each individual throw. Victory often passes to different persons. Their life turns like a die. The game is played for danger, and danger comes from the game. The shouts of those applauding; the weeping of those stripped.—Meanwhile the creditor sits among them like a tyrant, etc., XIV, 772–773.

INNOCENT I (St.), Pope.—Some people provide pleasures at public shows, which there is no doubt were invented by the devil, and either preside over or attend the arrangements for games or spectacles, XX, 478.

JEROME (St.).—The prophet does not sit in the council of those at play, either because he feared God’s hand hanging over him, or rather because he gloried that he had no fellowship with evil people, XXIV, 779.

AUGUSTINE (St.).—Games were first instituted for Telxion, king of the Sicyonians, XLI, 562.—Games sacred to the gods below, 99.—Secular games instituted at Rome, 98.—They too must be despised, XXXVII, 1046.—Why they were instituted for the gods, XLI, 569.—There ought to be no games among human beings if Romans were honourable, 112.—Games condemned by Plato, 237.—Processional games, XXXVIII, 148.

SIDONIUS APOLLINARIS.—He reproaches the citizens of Ravenna, where old men devote themselves to ball-playing and young men to gambling, LVII, 468.—Description of those at play, 448, 449.—Gamblers were summoned by shaking dice, 548.—On ball-playing, ibid.

EUGYPPIUS, Abbot.—Games must especially be avoided by young people, LXII, 603.

ISIDORE (St.) of Seville.—What gambling is, LXXXII, 660.—On the figures of gambling, 661.—On the prohibition of this game, 662.—On dice-towers, 661.—On counters and their movement, 661, 662.—On dice and their casting, ibid.—On ball-playing, 662.

CRISCONIUS.—The canons strictly forbid a bishop, priest, or any cleric or layperson to be a gambler; if they are, they are to be deprived of communion, LXXXVIII, 860.

RATHERIUS, Bishop of Verona.—He vehemently rebukes certain bishops of his time devoted to various games, CXXXVI, 290, 291.

IVO (Blessed) of Chartres.—“Flee the game of tables, luxurious and contrary to the soul’s salvation, as a seedbed of sins, not only in these days but at every time” (Augustine, sermon on the Litanies), CLXI, 1170.—He denounces as illiterate, a gambler, and a pursuer of women—and therefore to be rejected—a certain cleric improperly elected bishop, CLXII, 110.

HILDEBERT OF LE MANS.—According to Cicero, one may indeed make use of play and jest, but as of sleep and rest, once one has satisfied the claims of serious affairs, CLXXI, 1037.—There are two kinds of joking: one vulgar and disgraceful, the other polished and witty, ibid.—Play breeds anxious contention and anger, 1037.

ACTS OF ST BERNARD, Abbot of Clairvaux.—The saint wins a cleric at dice; another man, having been given money with which to gamble for him, he rescues from execution for a crime and makes a monk, CLXXXV, 801, 802.

[Col. 0917] GILLEBERT OF HOILAND.—Suspect to me are gains whose outcome is uncertain, whose danger to one’s own salvation is close at hand, and whose loss of inward sweetness is certain, CLXXXIV, 154.

GERHOH, Provost.—Reproved are the degenerate offshoots among clerics, who, though they may not be found barred from their offices, are nevertheless wanton, gamblers, hunters, and slaves to buffoonery, CXCIV, 1418.

JOHN OF SALISBURY.—On gambling, and its use and abuse, CXCVIII, 398.—Gambling: quieter trifles, ibid.—The gambler does not so much live as perish through devotion to dice, 399.—It is indeed pleasant and profitable to know the contests of numbers—for those, namely, who are found liable to plunder, 399.—Who were once celebrated gamblers, ibid.—Various kinds of this game, ibid.—Gambling is rightly banished from a region of good morals, ibid.

PETER THE CHANTER.—How detestable is the example of clerics playing at dice, CCV, 98.—How many evils gambling produces, 416 note.—The spiritual game of Wibald, bishop of Cambrai, 416 note.

PETER OF BLOIS.—The game of dice is a nursery of every evil and must be avoided, CCVII, 228.—I do not wonder that a young man is vicious whose father dedicated his childhood to gambling, ibid.

STEPHEN OF TOURNAI.—Praising Queen Ingeborg, he adds: “She knows no gambling; she is ignorant of dice,” CCXI, 524.

ADAM, Abbot of Perseigne.—Writing to the Countess of Perche, he says: “God’s daughter is not concerned with games of chance; she has no liking for the idle diligence of chess; the buffoonery of actors does not suit her purity,” CCXI, 609.

SICARD OF CREMONA.—Games are counted among the pomps and works of the devil, CCXIII, 279.—If anyone suddenly dies while playing ball or hoop, dancing, or bathing, he may be buried in a cemetery; but some deny him psalms and the other funeral offices, 430.

VIII.—Frequent association with women.—Incontinence, fornication, forgetfulness of the laws of marriage, prostitution.

TERTULLIAN.—Continence is more laborious for women, II, 903.—Women’s modesty has collapsed, I, 301.—Today there is no distinction between matrons and prostitutes, II, 1044.—Churches are distasteful to wealthy matrons puffed up by their rank, I, 1301.—Woman is the devil’s gateway, the first deserter of the Law, 1305.—Woman is a difficult creature, II, 909.—The abduction of virgins among the Romans in Tertullian’s time was regarded as just and lawful, I, 637.—Continence is necessary to human beings at every moment, as prayer is, II, 926.—Continence is an instrument of eternity, I, 1285.—Well-groomed women draw after themselves the eyes and sighs of young men, 1320.

CYPRIAN, St.—Christian women who love worldly adornment are condemned, IV, 490.—A woman stronger than men who torture her, 446.—Very many virgins are corrupted through unlawful and dangerous associations (*fréquentations*), 366.—She is not a virgin who lives in such a way as to be capable of being loved, 448.—She is not chaste who draws after herself the sighs of young men, ibid.—Fornication is a grave offence, 768.—The brazen voice of a prostitute is for sale, 214.

LACTANTIUS.—Speaking of the devil, he says: “By these obscenities he has plunged souls born for holiness, as it were, into a gulf of filth; he has extinguished shame and overthrown chastity . . . the magnitude of this matter cannot be described,” VI, 717.—Against the prostitution of women, VIII, 574.

EUSEBIUS PAMPHILUS.—The Emperor Constantine ordered the temple of Venus at Heliopolis, in which pagans allowed both women and virgins freely to commit sexual debaucheries, to be razed to the ground; and he ordered a church to the true God to be built in the same place, so that the people might be recalled to good morals, VIII, 66.—A law of the same emperor against abductors and corrupters, VIII, 197.—On concubines, 233.

HILARY, St.—The slavery of the adulterer, IX, 687.—He does what he fears, and does not flee what he fears, ibid.—Adultery is punished by death and judicial torture, 860.—The encounters of wanton women are treacherous to the eyes of the continent, 556.—How the danger to continence may be avoided, 551.

ZENO, St, of Verona.—A worldly woman described, XI, 292 ff.—What distinction existed between a married woman and a virgin, 302.

AMBROSE, St.—On dangers arising from woman, XIV, 891.—The lewd forwardness of a prostitute is not idle, nor is wantonness without effect: it makes young men’s hearts fly, so that they are carried here and there by burning love, 892.—How great women’s modesty ought to be, 438.—How great human luxury is, 324.—For the luxurious person, deprivation of pleasures is punishment, XV, 1770.—The companionship of a young man and the appearance of youth are dangerous to women, 1838.—In every way one must beware an encounter with a wanton woman, XIV, 891.—Temptations arising through women are harsher, XVI, 999.—Nothing is more treacherous than woman, 987.—Against fornicators, XVII, 215.

GAUDENTIUS, St.—Frequent sexual intercourse does not restrain lust, but rather inflames it, XX, 941.

JEROME, St.—Let women’s feet tread your lodging either rarely or never, XXII, 531.—Either equally ignore all girls and virgins of Christ, or equally love them; do not remain under the same roof, nor put confidence in former chastity, ibid.—Do not sit alone with a woman alone, in private and without an arbiter or witness, 532.—The dangers in which a young woman frequently finds herself, 956 ff.—Conversations with matrons must be avoided, 584.—Cast away as certain plagues those virgins and widows who, idle and inquisitive, go about the houses of matrons, 415.—Women are the source of all evils, XXIII, 1070.—Samson, stronger than a lion and harder than a rock, softened in the tender embraces of Delilah, XXII, 401.—They follow the examples of David and Solomon, ibid.—How many virgins fall every day, ibid.

AUGUSTINE, St.—The sight of a woman must be avoided, XXXVI, 586.—Though woman be far away, lust is near, 587.—Woman was tempted before man because she was weaker, XLI, 419.—Women deceive men by simulated brightness and strength, and by cosmetics applied to the face, XL, 446.—Greater guard is set over woman because her weakness is greater, XXXVIII, 84.—Why the prostitution of women is forbidden, XLII, 432.—A woman is desired, and desires, not merely by touch but also by affection and sight, XXXIII, 961.—Nothing casts down a manly mind from its citadel more than feminine blandishments, 878.—Through woman, death; through woman, life, XL, 303.—Through woman, poison; through woman, salvation, XXXVIII, 334.—Fornication is a great evil, XXXIV, 743.—A deadly fault, XL, 378.—It excludes from the kingdom of God, XXXVIII, 779, 1462.—Through the vice of fornication, the image and temple of God in a human being are corrupted, 86.—Spare Christ in yourself; recognize Christ in yourself, 878.—The heart of the fornicator becomes a slave of the body, 887–888.—Why prostitutes are tolerated, XXXII, 1000.—The prostitute’s house bears the image of hell, XXXIX, 1642.

PETER CHRYSOLOGUS, St.—What warfare wanton women have waged, LII, 277.—A prostituted woman is a new beast that cuts off John’s head, 551.—Her frenzy, 658 ff.—The touch of an evil woman burns one conscious of evil, pollutes an equal, marks the suspect, and forms a person of evil will, 464.—Woman becomes the material of total ruin, though she was made for a singular consolation, 597.—The perils of women: if John did not escape them, who, living among them, will escape unharmed?—“Pray, brethren, that we too may die to vices, be buried to temporal pomps, and rise in Christ to eternity,” 632.

SALVIAN.—Women cause apostasy from God, LIII, 134.—Excesses of lust and fornication in the city of Rome, 144.—Who is not a fornicator, not an adulterer—and this without cessation, without end? 145.—One prostitute makes many fornicators, 147.

PRUDENTIUS, St.—Women’s enticements for deceiving the eyes, LIX, 1030 ff.

LIVES OF THE FATHERS.—A woman encircled by a dragon, LXXIII, 417.—The sight of a woman is to be feared, LXXIV, 129, 148.—Woman dangerous to man, LXXIII, 561.—Love for a woman surpasses love for other things, 611.—Demons often lie in ambush under the appearance of women, 876.

GREGORY THE GREAT, St.—Woman is called the server of iniquity, LXXV, 1003; LXXVI, 1194.—The devil commonly rules both sexes through lust, LXXVI, 548.—Let the lustful person consider what sort of corpse he loves while it is alive, LXXV, 1162.—Even most holy women must be separated from the company of holier men, LXXVII, 229, 1286.—The spirit of fornication is driven away by the virtue of continence, LXXVIII, 364.—Why the greater part of humanity rushes headlong into fornication, 358.—The great and difficult contest against fornication, 408.

EUTROPIUS, St.—Fornication arises from *gastrimargia*, that is, gluttony of the belly, LXXV, 11.—From fornication arise obscene speech, buffoonery, jesting, and foolish talk, 12.

COLUMBANUS, St.—The book *On Assessing Penance* should be consulted, LXXX, 225.

ISIDORE, St, of Seville.—The derivation of *mulier* (“woman”) and *femina* (“female”), LXXXII, 417.—Excessive or womanish love, ibid.

ALCUIN, Blessed.—A cunning woman snatches away the precious souls of men; once she has entered the mind of a wretched lover, she draws him headlong down, and like a snare and net entangles the heart of a young man, C, 698.—Let our members be dedicated to God, not to fornication, CI, 626.—On fornication, 633.—Fornication is greater than all sins, 1194.—From it arise blindness of mind, thoughtlessness, instability, rashness, self-love, hatred of God, attachment to the present age, and dread or despair of things to come, ibid.

SEDULIUS SCOTTUS.—An exposition of the Apostle’s words, “It is good for a man not to touch a woman,” CIII, 140.—He inveighs against fornication, ibid.—On the devil’s seduction of woman, 233.

JONAS OF ORLÉANS.—On the holiness of marriage, CVI, 167 ff.—He speaks against fornication, 188 ff.

RABANUS MAURUS.—On King Solomon’s blinding through desire for women, CIX, 198.—On David’s adultery, 98.—People are ashamed of lust because they know it to be shameful, 99.—See his *Penitential*, where canons concerning sins of diverse kinds of lust are read, CX, 485 ff.—All prostitutes customarily receive payment from their lovers, 684.—A man’s fury against an adulterous wife is full, and cannot be redeemed at any price, 686.—What things in choosing a wife commonly impel a man to love, CXI, 193.—Fornication condemned, CXII, 49.—Every carnal pleasure is from the devil, 50.—See further, 63 ff.; 1370 ff.—The example of Mary Magdalene converted from a sinner, 1434.

HAYMO OF HALBERSTADT.—To widows: “Let them learn,” he says, “to avoid the wantonness of the flesh; let widows be ashamed in old age to violate chastity,” CXVIII, 88.—The eyes must be circumcised from unlawful sight, lest they look upon a woman in order to desire her, 95.

PASCHASIUS RADBERTUS.—The detestable fruit of lust in the death of St John the Baptist, CXX, 512.

HINCMAR OF RHEIMS.—An example of holiness restored to married love, CXXV, 717.—On the unlawful ardour of clerics toward women, 780.
