ODO, St, of Cluny.—How great a fault lies in sexual violation or pollution committed solely to satisfy lust, CXXXIII, 569.—“This [fornication] alone conquered the strongest Samson; it did not pass by the holiest David; it utterly suffocated the wisest Solomon,” 569.—An example of a monk punished for uncleanness, 570.—And of a priest of the district of Abrigantinum, ibid.

ATTO OF VERCELLI.—The vice of fornication is such that it makes God’s children into children of the devil, CXXXIV, 345.—The devil did not seduce the man but the woman; the man, however, was deceived through the woman, 670.

RATHERIUS OF VERONA.—Let woman strive, with the strong vigour of her mind, to conquer the mad tumults of vices and pleasures, CXXXVI, 191.—On the reciprocal duties of spouses, 191 ff.—On wives, 197.—Of Mary the sinner he adds: “She burned with the fire of divine love, who had formerly burned with the fire of pleasure,” 207.—A household is a dangerous burden and burdensome even to its master if its family is corrupt in morals, 273.

ABBO OF FLEURY.—The marital relation is permitted only by indulgence, lest an age more inclined to decline through the frailty of the flesh fall into something worse, CXXXIX, 463.—How much more perfect is the order of the continent or widows than that of married persons, since, having experienced fleshly pleasure, they bear a heavier penalty in abstaining from it, 464.—No one is ignorant how great is the glory of a virgin: through the prerogative of grace they possess what an angel possesses by nature, ibid.—Decree of Pope Siricius ordering the expulsion of monks and nuns who are lax through depraved morals, 488.

AIMOIN OF FLEURY.—The debauchery of the impious Queen Fredegund exposed, CXXXIX, 730–731.

ACTS OF ST HENRY, EMPEROR, AND ST CUNEGUND, HIS WIFE.—The remarkable continence of both, CXL, 49, 207.

FULBERT, St, of CHARTRES.—He reports Bachiarius’s words expressing Solomon’s fall, captured by love of women, CXLI, 233.—Many fears follow the pleasure-seeker, 285.

PETER DAMIAN, St.—He rebukes women who love only men’s bodies and pay little or no attention to their souls, CXLIV, 448.—All those pleasures which wives now provide from their husbands, they must necessarily provide also to other men, 233.—“I certainly knew a man who, while attempting to avenge an injury inflicted upon his wife, was killed by swords; she, however, is said to have gone on to a second marriage before the year’s circuit was complete,” ibid.—“If a woman violates the marriage-bed, while the report already flies through the whole neighbourhood, her husband alone still remains ignorant; and he who first endured the disgrace of his own household scarcely discovers it last,” ibid.—“Unhappy is my heart: it is not sufficient to retain the mysteries of the Gospel when read a hundred times, yet it does not lose the memory of a form seen once,” 458.—The flesh itself teaches what flesh is: memorable examples of women once famous in the world and extinguished by a most disgraceful death, CXLV, 743–744.

URBAN II, Pope.—“May the alluring blandishments of women and of your possessions not caress you into refusing to go; nor may the labours to be endured deter you into remaining,” CLI, 568.—“Woe to us, who have descended into this misery of so perilous a time: priests and Levites are killed; virgins are forced either to fornicate or to perish by torture; nor does more mature age protect matrons,” 570.

BRUNO, St, Founder of the Carthusians.—Women, when praying, should cover their heads with a veil, CLIII, 180.—The devil tempted the woman because he perceived her to be more weighed down by sensuality than raised up by reason, 182.—What women’s ornaments are, CLIII, 438.—A widow who lives in fleshly pleasures, living to the world, is dead to God, 449.

GUIGO, Prior of the Carthusians.—On the shamelessness of the fornicating soul, CLIII, 616.

ANONYMOUS.—Of Blessed Ida, Countess of Bouillon, it is read that, while her children still lay in the cradle, she did not allow them to be suckled from another woman’s breasts but from her own, fearing that they might be contaminated by depraved morals, CLV, 440.—On her remarkable chastity in marriage, 439.

RADULPHUS ARDENS.—Lust is called defilement, CLV, 1327.—One who is already corrupt in mind is not a virgin, ibid.—“You too who are married will be blessed, if you preserve marital chastity unviolated,” 1328.—The Mother of purity and holiness—the Blessed Virgin—does not shrink from purification; and do you, adulterer or adulteress, unclean man or woman, flee being cleansed through the discipline of purification and penance? 1343.—Virgins who are truly virgins are accustomed always to be fearful and to tremble at the sudden encounter of unfamiliar men, 1360.—See the sermon on Blessed Mary Magdalene, 1397.—What the sins of unchastity are, 1671.

GOFFRIDUS OF VENDÔME.—The female sex is hostile even to friends, CLVII, 67.—This sex either excludes from life or shuts into death all whom it attracts, 126.—Woe to a sex in which there is neither fear, modesty, goodness, nor friendship, and which may be more feared when loved than when hated, 168.—That sex commonly makes even the most religious persons suspect, 178.

ANSELM, St, of CANTERBURY.—Woman, a sweet evil, CLVIII, 696.—Avoid feminine jokes; they contain poison, ibid.—“If woman brought down holy Lot, Samson, David, and Solomon, who now will be safe?” 697.—Woman is Satan’s torch, 686.—Women should not despair of belonging to the lot of the righteous, 406.—The beginning of condemnation came from woman, ibid.—Whoever fornicates offends God, defiles the soul, and disfigures all the beauty of the body, 559.—Continual penitence must repair fornication, 726–727.—Adultery is forbidden by natural law, 583.

IVO, Blessed, of CHARTRES.—On the holiness of marriage, CLXII, 28, 137, 153, 158.—On the holy conduct of nuns, 22–23.—Those who defend adulterers are rebuked, 15.—“How will you be able to preserve chastity when you labour every day to engage in conversation with unchaste people?” 22.—Woman seduced the first parent in Paradise, 27.—A priest must especially beware private conversations with women, 42.—On the depravity of the monastery of St Fara in the diocese of Meaux, 90.

RUPERT OF DEUTZ.—Whoever desires to commit adultery seeks darkness, CLXVIII, 1066.—On the harlot Babylon and her fornications, CLXIX, 1152.—The devil commonly deceives men through association with women, 1261.

HILDEBERT OF LE MANS.—How dangerous familiarity with women is, CLXXI, 1428.—How destructive the crime of adultery is, 427.—He inveighs against fornicators and adulterers, 473.

HONORIUS OF AUTUN.—The severe penance of St Thaïs, formerly a sinner, CLXXII, 893.—Women’s beauty is vain, 1037.—The outstanding and singular example of St Marina, 1052, 1054.—The dreadful crime of an adulteress and a dancer, 997.

GODEFRIDUS OF ADMONT.—Woman is a type of human frailty, CLXXIV, 152, 361.—Commonly, a type of the soft life, 835.—And of weakness, 960.—The continent lead a heavenly life on earth, 1112.

HUGH OF ST VICTOR, of PARIS.—Fornication is a most serious sin, and why, CLXXIV, 526.—It is of many kinds, 522.—Marriage contracted for lust, CLXXVI, 496.—How woman was tempted by the serpent, 25.—Why she was made from man, 284.—The denunciation, in Holy Scripture, of intercourse with women and carnal marriage, 1206.—All perverse souls are daughters of the devil; in Scripture they are called daughters of Tyre, Sidon, Babylon, and so forth, CLXXVII, 671.—The threefold nature of fornication, and its remedy, 764–765.

ABELARD.—How wildly the mind of a woman in love raves! CLXXVIII, 181 ff.—Women’s weakness described, 213.—How they should be admonished, 215.

ALGER OF LIÈGE.—From Augustine: chastity cannot be taken from a woman by a violent rapist, CLXXX, 891.—If a virgin is forcibly deflowered in persecution, she is received as a virgin in the Gospel, ibid.

BERNARD, St, Abbot of Clairvaux.—By the name “women,” carnal souls are also signified, CLXXXIII, 976.—Likewise, the spiritual soul is called beautiful among women, that is, among earthly souls and those unlike itself, ibid.—How harmful cohabitation with women is, CLXXXII, 199–200.—To be always with a woman and not know woman is greater than raising the dead, CLXXXIII, 1091.—Attending a woman is not equally open to suspicion as living with her, ibid.—“Every day I see you beside a young woman, before your eyes and in your conversation; and do you wish to be considered continent? Granted that you are; nevertheless I am not free from suspicion,” ibid.—“Come now, good sir: who is this woman, and where did you get her?” 1092.—“If you do not wish to scandalize the Church, put the woman out,” ibid.—He congratulates Abbot Guerrin because he completely bars women from the monastery, CLXXXII, 459.—He disapproves of the monastery of St Denis because it is sometimes open to women, 193.—The spirit of fornication overcome by insults, CLXXXIII, 576.—The habit of fornication is a heavy and destructive chain, 575.

ROBERT PULLUS.—On marriage and its duties, CLXXXVI, 845 ff.

GRATIAN.—Decrees concerning association with women and the sins flowing from it, CLXXXVII, 1475 ff.

PETER THE VENERABLE, Monk of Cluny.—What should be thought of a marriage in which one spouse serves chastity, the other lust; one holiness, the other impurity, CLXXXIX, 438.

GARNERIUS OF ST VICTOR.—By the name “woman,” weakness is expressed, CXCIII, 141.—Women are called the minds of carnal persons, ibid.—By the same name many vices are signified, 142.

GERHOH, Provost.—Woman is so called from softness, CXCIV, 1027.—The madness of those who, instead of the cross, serve fornication and sexual violations, 1061.—Their eyes are blinded, ibid.—The first woman failed and broke away from hope when the hammer of temptation struck her, 1194.—Woman is not fashioned but built, ibid.—Of certain houses of nuns: “It is shameful to say what they do in secret,” 1278.

EGBERT, Abbot.—On the goodness and lawfulness of marriage, CXCV, 27.

AELRED, Abbot.—By the woman requiring purification after childbirth is signified human nature, which, unclean through vices and sins, was cast out of Paradise, CXCV, 235.—If woman was so weak in Paradise, who can find her strong in this place of misery? 333.

RICHARD OF ST VICTOR.—Married persons who serve their own pleasure are not the possession of the Beloved but of the devil, CXCVI, 514.—The shamelessness of the harlot in the Apocalypse, 833 ff.—The prostituted Babylon as a figure of the world, 840 ff.

HILDEGARD, St.—Cunning seducers of women, CXCVII, 251.—Now the force of manly strength has bent toward feminine weakness: this is a womanish age, which began with a certain tyrant, when every evil arose, 254.—By flattering and playful words the serpent deceived woman, 326.—He first seduced Eve, so that she might flatter Adam and induce him to assent, 392.—Consequences of fornication and adultery, 394.—In these sins there is neither shame nor moderation of lust, 396.—Regard for God is cast away, 398.

ADAM THE SCOT.—With woman, even the strongest virtue is endangered, CXCVIII, 534, 815.

PETER OF CELLE.—Each person must endure an unceasing struggle with woman, or with pleasure, CCII, 684.—The conversion of holy Magdalene is an example given to women, 825 ff.—Fornication, adultery, and every kind of uncleanness must be avoided, 885.

REINER, Monk.—The enticements of a prostitute by which she seeks to seduce, CCIV, 53.—She is called a most voracious Siren, ibid.—Converted by God’s grace, she is changed into a pure white dove, 54.—She confesses herself a disciple of the devil, likewise a sea of sins and mire of uncleanness, 55, 57.—The practices by which she curbed the seductions of the flesh, 59.

BERNARD, Abbot of FONTENAY.—A woman full of the enticements of vices readily seduces and is seduced, CCIV, 821.—Various duties and virtues of women, 825–826.

PETER THE CHANTER.—A married woman receiving little gifts from a lover is suspected of corruption, CCV, 85.—A prostitute has all her members for sale, 161.—No woman under sixty years old should be admitted to the care of virgins, 185.—What adultery is and how grave a crime it is, 333.—On fornication, 332.—On sodomy, 333.—St Bernard, about to preach to nuns, was struck dumb at the outset because of their sins, 37.

PETER OF BLOIS.—He rebukes a certain deacon because he was falling into affection for women and seeking marriage itself; he describes to him its many disadvantages, CCVII, 243 ff.—Cicero’s answer, declaring that he could not devote himself both to philosophy and to a wife, 246.—A woman, however honourable and chaste, is accustomed to cast off honour as soon as she can cast off her garment, 245.—Such a marriage—or rather cohabitation—contracted by a deacon of the Church can have only unhappy consequences, 246.—“Today we see priests sitting with Belshazzar at banquets with wives and concubines,” 725.—Women, while they make provision for the flesh in its desires, lose eternal life for a momentary pleasure, 744.—Virginity without humility does not please God, 746.—Who the foolish virgins are, ibid.—“Egyptian music frequently whistles to you, and the hidden temptation of the enemy invites you to return to the world,” 749.

MARTIN, St, of LEÓN.—Through penance Rahab the prostitute became a type of Christ’s Church, CCVIII, 44.—Heretics who regard marriage as evil are refuted, 484.—A woman who is adulterous is not therefore not a wife, 487.—Woman is seduced by the serpent, and man through woman, 587–588.—From fornication arise obscene speech, buffoonery, jesting, and foolish talk, 721.

ALAN OF LILLE.—Women are not to be trusted, CCX, 581.—Exhortation to married persons, 193.—The violation of marriage is a great dishonour, ibid.—Fornication is twofold, 238.—If the pleasure of fornication occupies the mind more than love of chastity, sin still reigns in the person, 121.—It is a plague more harmful than every monster, 122.

ABSALON, Abbot.—Woman was made in Paradise, but man outside Paradise; nevertheless woman sinned sooner and more grievously than man, CCXI, 18.—Eve, sinner and gate of perdition, 21.

STEPHEN OF TOURNAI.—A wonderful encomium of Queen Ingeborg, recently repudiated by Philip, king of the Franks, CCXI, 524.

ADAM, Abbot of Perseigne.—Wholesome counsels given to a woman living under the law of marriage, CCXI, 608 ff.—The marital act must not be performed in the abominable lust of whoremongers, 679.—What is permitted in some manner is not immediately permitted in every manner, in every place, and at every time, ibid.—A sermon on the valiant woman, 733.

HELINAND, Monk.—Woman is always variable and changeable, CCXII, 648.—Iron hearts are softened by wanton arrows, ibid.

SICARD.—The madness of Queen Cleopatra, who wished to seduce Octavian by costly garments and her beauty and provoke him to lust; frustrated in her hope, she brought death upon herself by the venom of an asp, CCXIII, 445.

DEEDS OF INNOCENT III.—He praises those who arrange marriages for prostitutes in order to bring them back from the path of error, CCXIV, 102.

IX.—Love of the world and the age; vain pomps, domestic luxury, the pride of riches, vainglory, ambition.

TERTULLIAN.—The nature of Roman luxury, I, 298.—He inveighs against luxury, 1314, 1325.—Vestibules were illuminated with lamps of the greatest brilliance and height, 459.—Sumptuary laws restraining ambition and expenditure are scorned, I, 302.—The Lord is found in no riches, 1260.—A rich man is difficult in the house of God, just as a bachelor is difficult, 1301.—Churches are distasteful to wealthy matrons puffed up by their rank, ibid.—The disadvantages of the ambitious, 1246.—The power of ambition, 1314.

CYPRIAN, St.—The world is one house containing good and evil persons, IV, 558.—It is in no way lovable to Christians, 802.—God’s law: everything born in the world dies, and everything that has grown grows old, 547.—The world has grown old, 546.—It totters, 600.—It collapses, ibid.—One should glory in nothing, 734.—The lofty summit of glory, 415.—Virtue overcomes the waves foaming around it, 790.—The wisdom of the world is not the kingdom of God, 770.

LACTANTIUS.—Having set forth the various miseries and crimes of this world, he exclaims: “How blessed and how golden would the condition of human affairs be, if gentleness, piety, peace, innocence, equity, temperance, and faith dwelt throughout the whole world!” VII, 674.

HILARY, St, of POITIERS.—The enticements and vanity of riches, IX, 799, 1026.—Restless wealth lacks the fruit of riches, X, 25.—In leisure and abundance there is nothing but beastly happiness, ibid.—The dwelling-place of this world is not the land of the living, IX, 518.—The entire world is full of snares, 832.—Everything transient is vain, 847.—Who vain people are, 399.—The desire for riches must be cut off, ibid.

ZENO, St.—The whole world daily boils with its poisons—those of lust, XI, 277.—All flesh, so long as it is driven by the shameful enticements of this world and by deadly darkness, is certainly brutish and exists in a wretched, fragile, and detestable condition, 383.—In this world, the righteous person is always in tribulation and always in punishment, 386.

[Col. 0923] AMBROSE, St.—How often David spoke of the world’s vanity, XIV, 835.—Everything that it counts magnificent is empty, 582.—This earth is a land of captivity; another land is a land of liberty, 987.—The world and the age must be fled, 569.—What it is to flee the world, 578.—Why we ought to flee it, 582.—How to flee, 590.—Whither one must flee, 587.—You owe nothing further to the world which you have once renounced, 485.—If you escape this world, it too will escape you, 1007.—I avoid the world as foul-smelling, guard against it as a plague, and leave it as harmful, XV, 1698.—The world’s struggle and contest, XVI, 1130.—The luxurious add house to house and estate to estate, and dig up the earth so that the element may yield to their dwellings, XVI, 1072.—No one gives himself up to luxury unless he departs from the commands of the true God, 1182.—Consult the book *On Naboth*, XIV, 731; XV, 1768.

BACHIARIUS.—The way of this age is slippery, XX, 1045.—This world is a field . . . the saints, providing what is good not only before God but also before people, sow within it, 1051.

GAUDENTIUS, St.—“Why do you strive every day to gain fresh silver? Why build houses in marble and acquire silk garments? It is shameful to say it; grievous to recall it!” XX, 939.

JEROME, St.—Those who displease Christ please the world more, XXII, 584.—The devil constructed the world out of vices, founded it upon crimes, and filled it with iniquity, 487.—Examples of contempt for the world, 881–882.—All the glory of this world is unstable, XXV, 41.—Everything born in the world dies, and everything that has grown grows old, 75.—The world is called the devil, XXVI, 466.—There is no security in the age, and how this is so, XXII, 350–351.—Everything in this age is full of enemies, 393.—Whoever trusts in worldly things forgets God, XXIV, 769.—The vanity of the rich, XXVI, 540.—Like waves and billows, possessions are occupied by masters succeeding one another, XXII, 965.—“The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head, and you measure out broad colonnades and vast spaces of roofs: you cannot be a companion of Christ.”

AUGUSTINE, St.—The world rules through unlawful pleasures, through pomps, and through curiosity, XL, 294.—This world is a slave, ibid.—A Christian uses the world; he does not serve it, XXXVII, 1677.—To die to the world in order to live to God is a sacrifice, XLI, 283.—It is one thing to cast fire upon the world, another to cast the world into fire, XXXVI, 715.—The world is full of afflictions, XXXVII, 1189.—How will you gather the world’s flowers if you do not withdraw your hand from thorns? XXXVIII, 241.—The world persecuting the world, 587.—The world wishes to swallow you; swallow the world, XXXVI, 341.—The world may rage in its malice, but not beyond the limit fixed by its Creator, XXXVII, 1127.—The world flatters in order to deceive, or terrifies in order to break one down, XXXVIII, 1256.—Neither believe it nor yield to it, 235.—The sweetness of God must be set against the world’s sweetness, 866.—On contempt for the world, XXXVIII, 622; XXXIX, 1517.—How the world becomes worthless, whether promising or frightening, XXXV, 2004.—The emptiness and disadvantages of riches, XXXVII, 1727.—How much anxiety they bring, XXXIX, 1520.—They are a burden, XXXVIII, 899.—The load of riches prevents a person from following Christ, XXXV, 1655.—When a person seeks superfluities, he desires to burden his own fetters, XXXVI, 864.—Riches are rivers that carry away those whom they raise up, XXXVII, 1769.—Hope must not be placed in them, XXXVIII, 958.—Do you wish to possess land? See that you are not possessed by the land, 365.—How it is permissible to possess all things, 781.—It is one thing to possess what is God’s, another what is man’s, XXXVI, 576.—Superfluous is what neither benefits nor harms, XXXV, 2118.—If we seek empty things, nothing is enough, XXXVII, 1922.—What is to be counted among superfluities, XXXVIII, 421.—Superfluities weigh down rather than raise up; burden rather than honour, 523.—The superfluities of the rich are the necessities of the poor, XXXVII, 1922.—See to whom your surplus remains, lest perhaps, while preserving what will let you live, you gather what will cause you to die, XXXVIII, 629.

PETER CHRYSOLOGUS, St.—It is more difficult indeed, but more glorious, to struggle against the world when it is present, LII, 498.—Christ’s birth is grievous to worldly people, 592.—Let the whole mist of secular pomp be scattered by thorns, 521.—He whom God, in creating him, called “world,” the enemy, in defiling him, makes “unclean,” 470.—The devil made the wise of the age foolish; he taught observers of the world to see nothing, and professors of knowledge to have no knowledge, 470.—In the world the Creator’s good things come first; the devil’s evils follow after, 472.—The abundance of earthly luxury must not be sought, 223.—To leave great things and love lesser things belongs to God’s power, not to human covetousness, 640.—“Yield, man, your riches: divine poverty is enough for you. Lay down the burdens of your riches; the laden person cannot reach the narrow way,” 646.—See the sermon on the rich man and Lazarus, 529, 536, 540.

SALVIAN.—He sets the sobriety and simplicity of the ancient Romans against the luxury of his own age, LIII, 32–33.

[Col. 0924] LEO THE GREAT, St.—Frugal moderation is always happier than lavish luxury, LIV, 457.—Those are condemned who are splendid outwardly but dark within, rich in temporal things but poor in eternal ones, 165.—For worldly wise people, their wisdom became blindness, and through it they could not know God, LIV, 211.—The arguments of worldly wisdom, hateful to the Lord, must be cast away, 294.—How dangerous the peace of the world is, 383.

MAXIMUS (St.), of Turin.—Lovers of the world endure very many things to no purpose, LVII, 711, 712.—Worldly cares choke the word of God in the heart, 688.—Upon the sea of this world we must greatly fear lest either a stormy tempest carry off our ship, or a wave swallow it up, or a cruel pirate lead it away as eternal prey, 419, 420.—The rich enter upon the way of the heavenly kingdom with difficulty, LVIII, 325.—Many are rich in gold in their houses, yet in the Church they are beggars in righteousness, 475.—Riches are fuel for wickedness to the foolish, nourishment for salvation to the wise, 732.

SIDONIUS APOLLINARIS.—He describes domestic luxury, LVIII, 447 ff.

PAULINUS (St.), of Nola.—The world is man’s enemy, LXI, 295.—The world must be fled in order that we may attain heaven, 670.—It is praiseworthy not to be sullied by the vices of the world, 630, 631.

FULGENTIUS (St.), of Ruspe.—By the name “world” are signified men who love the world, LXVII, 168.—Love of the world is not evil except insofar as it turns one away from the love of God, ibid.—He truly triumphs who treads the world underfoot, 349.

*Lives of the Fathers.*—The world is deceitful in its promises, LXXIII, 492.—It is a tyrant, 497, 498.—It must be despised, 908.—The folly of the world’s lovers, 493.—Its deceptive blandishments, 617.

GREGORY THE GREAT (St.).—Those who, troubled by love of the world, do not feel the evils they suffer are drunk, LXXVI, 715.—Love of the world overturns the seat of judgment in the soul, LXXV, 743.—Some are ensnared in the nets of the age under the name of respectability, 789.—The world is worthless in God’s sight, LXXVI, 71.—The world’s foolish wisdom, 162.—The calamities by which the world is daily afflicted, 1090.—How dangerous it is to cling to that which is falling away, ibid.—The world itself deters us from love of itself, LXXVII, 317.—In this world nothing is stable, but all prosperity is thrown into confusion by adversity, 647.—We are recalled from worldly waves to the shore of Christian peace, 884, 885.—He who loves the pomps of the world sees a dream while awake, 1105.—Its pomps must be despised, 1275.—However great it may be, the happiness of the rich ends in everlasting misery, LXXV, 1104.—Their houses are secure and peaceful because they live in sin, ibid.—The source of the rich man’s vain rejoicing is the source of the poor man’s still more vain affliction, 1114.—God’s darts rain down upon the avaricious rich man, 1096.—Anxiety in acquiring and preserving riches foreshadows eternal punishments, 1095.—In abundance of possessions, the sin of the flesh commonly reigns, LXXVI, 1237.

COLUMBANUS (St.).—The present life ought rather to be called a way than life, LXXX, 240.—Life is like a shadow, 241.—Your life is a wheel: it runs daily and does not wait for you; go with it, 258.—This world passes away and diminishes daily, 283.—On contempt for the world, 235.

TAIO, of Saragossa.—On lovers of the world, LXXX, 957.—On earthly desires and the wisdom of the age, 959.

BEDE THE VENERABLE.—The world of perdition loves itself with a false love, certainly not a true one; therefore it falsely loves itself and truly hates itself, XCII, 845.—It hates its own nature and loves vice, ibid.—“World” is understood to mean those who live according to the world’s desire, 859.—All lovers of the world, all seekers after trifles, are enemies of God, XCVII, 32.

ALCUIN (Blessed).—All the delights of this age flee like a flying shadow, C, 157.—Whatever is loved in this age is lost, 158.—Let the ambition of the age not overthrow your heart, 241.—Let not the blandishments of the age deceive you; let passing honours not exalt you; let popular favour not overthrow you, 245.—He commends moderation to King Æthelred in every use of this age, 158.—This is the difference between temporal and eternal things: the temporal is loved more before it is possessed, but becomes cheap when it has arrived; the eternal, however, is loved more ardently when attained than when desired, 211.—In everything moderation must be preserved; it is the royal road of our life, 249.

JONAS, of Orléans.—Because of evil days which, deceived by love of the world, they suppose to be good, many lose eternal days, CVI, 164.

RABANUS MAURUS.—These are God’s elect, who wholly forsake with all their will all the pleasures of this world, CX, 434.—No one can love transitory and eternal things at the same time, 937.

HAYMO, of Halberstadt.—The body of Christ suffers from lovers of the world what it suffered from the murmurings of the Jews, CXVIII, 341.—“World” is used of evil men dispersed throughout the whole earth, 391.—A stranger, pilgrim, or guest does not think about what is in a house not his own; thus we too, insofar as we can, by the Lord’s bounty, ought wholly to despise these things, 506.

PASCHASIUS RADBERTUS.—Mary, Star of the Sea, or illuminatrix, must be followed amid the wave-tossed waters of the sea in faith and conduct, lest we be drowned in the waves of the flood, but be enlightened through her, CXX, 94.—The whole world is everywhere full of the snares of temptations, 184.—Christ sought solitude lest he be oppressed by the straits of the world, 185.—Whoever gives himself to the pleasures and cares of the age eats heavenly bread and true food only among thorns, and even then in sweat and excessive toil, 489.

RATHERIUS, of Verona.—He severely rebukes the scandalous luxury of certain bishops of his own time, CXXXVI, 291, 294.

PETER DAMIAN (St.).—When one falls from the height of contemplation to perform any earthly or unclean matters, it follows that he is bitten in the Church by the reproaches of shameful derision, CXLIV, 382.—Any soul which the world, at the devil’s urging, tries to draw to itself and blind with the darkness of secular affairs preserves the unharmed eye of contemplation if, wholly resisting, it perseveres in its purpose of quiet, ibid.—At this time the whole world is nothing but gluttony, avarice, and lust, 231.—It is wholly immersed in vices, ibid.—The world blinds its lovers, 381.—Despise all these things, because all must be despised; and of them all make your burden contempt for the world, 837.—The world is like the sea, 313.—The incitements and fuels of lust are avarice and the material of covetousness; for, since luxury undoubtedly requires the outlay of many expenses, it cannot flow into the pleasures of delight unless resources abound in many ways, CXLIV, 233.

LANFRANC (St.).—This earth in which we are is daily shaken by so many and such great tribulations, and polluted by so many adulteries and other impurities, that scarcely any class of men remains which either cares for its own soul or so much as desires to hear the saving teaching of progress toward God, CL, 539.

URBAN II, pope.—To Berengar, abbot of St. Lawrence at Liège. What wall would stand unmoved, what mind would remain immovable in its firmness, where fat swine are continually grunting, where a crowd of malicious persons besieges the simplicity of innocence? CLI, 395.—Rejoice, because the King of Israel wishes his children to sit and weep beside the rivers of Babylon and to sigh with the free affection of their hearts for return to the land of promise, not to perish entangled in those rivers themselves and in secular pursuits, 397.—Certainly this way is most evil, because it is wholly remote from God, 567.—You do not truly keep the way by which you are to go to salvation and life, ibid.—Granted that the path of travellers is narrow, full of deaths, and beset by dangers; yet this very path will lead you, though lost, to your homeland, for through many tribulations you must enter the kingdom of God, 573.

RADULFUS ARDENS.—On contempt for the world, CLV, 1335.—Although the flower of the grass seems beautiful, it is a small and lowly thing; so the glory of the world falls when God’s wrath burns hot, 1525.—There is no end to our covetousness and ambition, 1529.—Why do we love the world? Why do we fall with that which falls, and perish with that which perishes? 1679.

GOFFRIDUS, of Vendôme.—He who follows the world strays from Christ’s way, 192, 205.—The world must first be forsaken before it forsakes us, 209.

ANSELM (St.), of Canterbury.—The age must be renounced, CLXIII, 685.—The world’s happiness is brief, 681.—Legitimate hatred of the age, 1072, 1073.—Do not believe the world even when it smiles upon you, 1143.—It does not favour you in order to cherish you, but in order to choke you, ibid.—Those whom the sweetness of the age attracts are seized by eternal bitterness, 1072.—The world must be laughed at when it laughs, 1066.—The world’s glory is not glory but a devouring fire, 1143.—It is like a perpetual tempest, 598.—The vanity of the world, and likewise the vanity of honour and riches, is expounded in verse, 687.—This world is an empty sponge, and all its desire is more bitter than vinegar, 759.—The luxury of buildings and delights is described, 700, 701.—What is present life? Temptation, troublesome conflict: here is always a battle-line, and the enemy is at hand, 690.

IVO (Blessed), of Chartres.—Before God, the wisdom of the world and secular power are of no consequence, CLXII, 122.

ANSELM, of Laon.—The world, displaying present goods and ridiculing invisible things, draws men to itself, CLXII, 1284.—The poor and meek person alone does not love the world: he recognizes himself as wretched and therefore desires heaven, 1286.—How burdensome, how miserable, is this earthly dwelling, ibid.

RUPERT, of Deutz.—The world cannot comprehend Christ’s mysteries, [Col. 0926] CLXIX, 756 ff.—The final conflagration of the world is most miserable, 1153, 1154.—The world lies in the evil one, 1446.

HILDEBERT, of Le Mans.—The world is so called unworthily, because it does not make us clean (*mundi*) but unclean (*immundi*), CLXXI, 467.—The City of God and the city of the devil have gates opposite gates: the gates of Zion opposite the gates of Babylon, 497.—This world is a true dung-heap, 365, 696.—How vain is this world’s prosperity, 837.—There are three things in the world to be hated: the desire of the flesh, of the eyes, and the pride of life, 848.—Love of the world is sweet at the beginning, bitter at the end, 206.

HONORIUS, of Autun.—The world is figured in Babylon, which means “confusion,” CLXXII, 879.—How the world must be fled, ibid.—Sts. Paul, Cyprian, Theophilus, Mary Magdalene, Mary of Egypt, and Thais fled the world, 881.

GODEFRIDUS, of Admont.—The age must be fled by the justified man, CLXXIV, 145.—It is called a desert, 68.—The cares of the age are like a tomb, 391.—They deprive one of the sweetness of divine visitation, 546.—The affairs of the age are pursued with greater diligence than salvation, 527.—The world is like the sea and a swift river, 633, 638.—Everything in it fluctuates through instability, 674.—Everything is fleeting, 944.—The gain of this world is pleasure of the flesh, vanity of heart, and pride of mind, 715.—The rich have in the rich man [of the Gospel] something to learn and something to fear, 387.—Worldly honours draw us back from the heavenly marriage-feast, 615.—The age may be called a shroud, 777.—Lovers of the age are haters of humility, 698.

HUGH OF ST. VICTOR.—Why the world is said to lie in the evil one, CLXXV, 554.—What is the difference between love of God and love of the world? CLXXVI, 619 ff.—Why this world is called a place of penitence, 28.—The vanity or instability of this world, 711, 712.—Contempt for it provokes us to love what is eternal, 713.—The vain abundance, dangers, and accidents of a rich man’s house, 707.—The delights and pomps of this age must be fled, CLXXVII, 78.

WILLIAM, abbot of St. Thierry.—On the yoke of the world and of Christ, CLXXIX, 218.—Open, Lord, the door in the side of your ark, that all those of yours who are to be saved may enter from the face of this flood overflowing the earth, 226.—O homeland, homeland, how from afar I see and greet you, where there are no evils and every good, 234.—As long as we live here, we must continue along the way of the present age, mingled together [with others], 445.

BERNARD (St.), of Clairvaux.—The world is a valley of tears in which sensuality reigns, CLXXXII, 789.—It is full of thorns, CLXXXII, 1012.—The world’s nights are many, 1149.—There is no rest there, 463.—The goods of the world are vain and perishable, CLXXXII, 243.—Its miseries and dangers, CLXXXIII, 139, 636.—The world rightly deceives souls forgetful of their dignity, CLXXXII, 842.—The vanity of worldly glory, 256.—Let no delights of the world bend you, no adversities cast you down, CLXXXIII, 315.—The prudent merchant, seeing toil in riches, punishment in honours, and envy in glory, makes contempt for the world his burden and flees, 663.—The world’s fetters must be left behind, however golden they may be, 577.—A powerful stimulus to flee the world, CLXXXII, 238, 239.—It is impossible to serve the world and God, 259.—He who loves the world more than God is impious and an idolater, 248.—Who is dead to the world and crucified to the world, CLXXXIII, 183.—The unhappiness of the children of this world, CLXXXII, 244.—The age is a torrent, 335.—Its life is night, 106.—The corruption of the age, 383, 417.—The luxury and delights of men are reproved, CLXXXIII, 590.—Especially those of prelates, 1155, 1156.—And of clerics, 200.

GILLEBERT OF HOILAND.—Whatever we see here through a mirror and in an enigma is wholly in darkness, CLXXXIV, 14.—The pleasures of the age universally offer an appearance of refreshment, but immediately dry up; like a torrent, they pass swiftly away, 196.—Woe to the inhabitants of the earth, where peace is rare, security nonexistent, toil unceasing, and strife gives birth to poverty, 263.

GUERRIC (St.), abbot.—Whatever the world can give or promise is not only cheap and unworthy, but also harmful, CLXXXV, 34.—The Master of humility does not condemn this pride, but rewards it, if you are so high-minded in contempt for the world that you look down, as from on high, upon all its glory, 47.—Almost the whole world professes in words that it knows God, but in deeds denies him, 59.—However great the tempest of wars that comes upon you, however great the want of provisions that you suffer in the desert, do not return in the faintness of your spirit, in your mind, to Egypt, 22.

PETER THE VENERABLE, abbot of Cluny.—On the remarkable example of Henry, brother of King Louis VII, who trampled underfoot luxury and the world’s delights flowing from a full horn, CLXXXIX, 398.—On the brief and fleeting appearance of human things, [Col. 0927] 404.—The world is called a valley of tears, 411.—The world in which Satan, as prince, plays with mortals as with birds, 416.—The devil tempts, the world entices, sin kills, 957.

GARNERIUS OF ST. VICTOR.—Those who, confused by love of this world, no longer feel the evils which they suffer are called drunk, CXCIII, 134–135.—The present world is called Ethiopia, CXCIII, 354.—The fruit of the world is ruin, 388.

GERHOH, provost.—This world is called a horse, whose rider is the devil, CXCIV, 1019.—The ark of the heavenly building, which is constructed on earth, is in no way raised to higher things without the waters of the flood, 1196.—How important it is that bishops should not become entangled in secular affairs, 1266.—The clergy serve not the world but the altar, 1272.—It is a great thing to keep oneself unstained from this age, 1327.

AELRED (Blessed), abbot.—Those who love the world, which is to perish, will perish with the world, CXCV, 212.—Christ is the sign which the whole world has contradicted, 262.—Lovers of the world seek consolation in riches, honours, many curiosities, desires of the flesh, and pleasures. They are wretched when they are sad, but far more wretched when they are thus consoled, 341, 342.—Strong is the soul which leaves the age, tramples fleshly desires, and despises worldly glory, 333.—On the pride of life and vanity, 574.—On the desire to rule, ibid.

RICHARD OF ST. VICTOR.—Why the world is called a desert, CXCVI, 430.—The world is understood in three ways, 795.—How the world will be renewed, 859.—He who entangles himself in secular affairs alienates himself from inward things, 690.—In contempt for the world comes the first advance in virtue, 1076.—Then also the destruction of evil, 1077.

HILDEGARD (St.).—The world is called shadowy, CXCVII, 301.—He who loves the age is like a tempest in governing his own conduct, 315.—O grievous toil, O hard burden which I bear in the garment of this life, because it is too heavy for me to fight against the flesh, 733.

ADAM THE SCOT.—Absalom is a type of worldly persons, CXCVIII, 816.—The world’s deceit and sad end, 435, 438.—The world’s three vices to be trampled underfoot: pleasure, curiosity, and pride, 454.—Learn to use the world, but to enjoy God, 453.—The world is not worthy of your love, ibid.

JOHN OF SALISBURY.—If the prophetic spirit had conceived our times, it might excellently be said that human life upon earth is a comedy, in which each person, forgetful of himself, plays another’s part, CXCIX, 488.—For everyone in this life there is cause for grief, 491.—Creation is subjected to vanity even against its will, ibid.—The world has its own Elysian fields, 492.—Among the senseless, those who do not wish to share in another’s madness are held to be mad, 493.—Likewise, those who look down upon the theatre of the world from the lofty summit of virtues and despise fortune’s game, ibid.

PETER OF CELLES.—These days are brief for shining, but great and burdensome for occupying us, CCII, 421.—The world is full of cowled persons and almost empty of monks, 600.—These are days of cloud and darkness, 687.—This way is indeed stony and thorny, but the homeland is attained through tribulation, 755.—The more weary you come to bed, the more indulgently you rest, ibid.

BALDWIN, of Canterbury.—Covetousness is love of the world, just as charity is love of God, CCIV, 490.—It grows through love of using or possessing and through desire of ownership, ibid.—O earth, earth, with how great vanity you are loved by the children of men! 492.—How greatly the wisdom of this world and God’s wisdom differ from one another, 500.—On the causes of mourning in this world, 502 ff.

STEPHEN (St.), founder of Grandmont.—While the world is loved by a man, the enemy draws him after himself according to his own pleasure; but when the age is abandoned by anyone, the devil pursues him in many ways, CCIV, 1090.

PETER CANTOR.—The pomps of the world can scarcely be guarded against, CCV, 46.—Pride and envy conspired together for the world’s ruin, 53.—Humility alone escapes the snares of the world, 59.—Who will judge the world? 67.—Covetousness is the root of all evils, 72.—Love of money grows in proportion as money itself grows, 73.—The two blood-sucking daughters of the devil are incessantly crying, “Bring! Bring!”—lust without cease, and covetousness still more without cease, 73.—To the believer the whole world is riches; the unbeliever, however, needs even an obol, 74.—Ambition is overthrown, 165, 168.—Present life is a dream when compared with eternity, 352.—The superfluity of buildings is reproved, 255.

PETER OF BLOIS.—The world’s pomp and popular favour are smoke and a breeze suddenly vanishing, CCVII, 114.—If you were in the age, everything would abound for you according to your desire, provided only that every laugh, every wantonness, every pleasure of the age be banished from you, ibid.—He exhorts someone to lay down the burden of vain furnishings, 130.—The world’s wisdom is foolishness with God, 106.—Evening is already drawing on for you, [Col. 0928] and the days of your life are declining, 130.—The riches of this life are deceptive, and its wealth treacherous, 168.—He rebukes a certain monk for courting the friendships of princes and the applause of the world, 386.—It displeases me if, in order to please the world, you do not fear to displease God, ibid.—There is a struggle between us and the world, 624.—Let us conquer the world lest we be conquered by it, 733.

MARTIN (St.), of León.—We must sow while we are in this world, CCVIII, 62.—The faithful soul rejects carnal things, despises the world’s prosperity, scorns transitory things, and seeks eternal things, 81.—Those who are entangled in marriages walk upon the earth; but those do not walk on earth, rather they fly like clouds, who, while seeking heavenly things, touch none of earthly desires, 160.—Some are set over others to rule, labouring outwardly against the storms and whirlwinds of the age, 532.—There are those who seek delights in secret while wishing to appear abstinent in public, 786.

ALAN OF LILLE.—“World” is often used for lovers of the world, CCX, 310.—The vanity of worldly pleasures, 358, 584.—The world is subject to storms, 582.—The whole world lies in the evil one, 545, 546.—On contempt for the world, 114.—The manifold dangers of worldly persons, 466.—Pride must especially be avoided, 552.—On contempt for worldly fear, 133.

ABSALO, abbot.—He mourns the lot of monks who, mindful of their former way of life, begin to be lovers of the age and seek pleasures and honours, 19.—This life is perpetually assailed by the storms of the age, 67.—In a certain sense, the Word becomes flesh in those who, neglecting Christ’s law, seek the enticements of the flesh, 55.—Those who love riches and possess gold and silver walk through the flowering field of this world, but cannot reach God unless they cross the river, 90.—What are the four gates of love of the world? 103.—An exhortation to leave the world, 173.

STEPHEN, bishop of Tournai.—He congratulates a certain friend for having taken leave of the world, CCXI, 447.

ADAM, abbot of Perseigne.—Nothing is harsher than to show oneself crucified to the world and the world crucified to oneself, CCXI, 586.—The burdens of the age must be cast off; honours must be reckoned as nothing, 600.—How much happier it is to be bound by the bonds of chaste love than by the theatrical wantonness of the world, 603, 604.—See further Epistle XIII, 624.—The world is called wretched, 599.—Unhappy, 588.—An abyss, 625.

HELINAND, monk.—The difference between the sayings of the world and the sayings of Christ, CCXII, 502.—O foolish children of the age, who set Fortune’s table and think themselves fortunate, 682.—How great is the power of the prince of this world? 687.

SICARDUS, of Cremona.—The Church, which wars on earth, ought to govern itself with evenness of mind in prosperity and adversity, CCXIII, 17.—The present age is night, 24.

X.—Worldly and pagan festivals; dances.

ARNOBIUS.—The very ridiculous and impious rites of the heathen are vigorously censured in *Against the Nations*, V, 713.—Wanton dancing-girls at banquets, 881.—Theatrical dances, 1072, 1073, 1265, 1266.—Why do you delay, why hesitate, to say that the gods themselves play, behave wantonly, dance, and compose obscene songs? 1269.

AMBROSE (St.).—Hannibal himself long insulted the religious rites of the Romans, XVI, 873.—In Phrygian rites, unchastity is a religious discipline, 193.—In the orgies of Liber, the mystery of religion is an incentive to lust, ibid.—When the prophet invites to song and dancing, he did not mean actors’ loose movements of the body, nor did he command unseemly noises by men and applause by women; for the revealed mysteries of the resurrection do not accord with the infamous practices of dance, XV, 1670.—Wanton dancing is the companion of delights and the mockery of luxury, XVI, 1179.

LUCIUS DEXTER.—The tragic death of Herodias’s dancing daughter, XXXI, 83.

JEROME (St.).—God cast down the festivals of those who flee a lion and run into a bear, who celebrate not God’s festivals but their own festivals, XXV, 1053.—God judges not the multitude of sacrifices, but the merits and motives of those offering them, ibid.—He does not deign to hear the songs of the impious, 1054.—The contrived praise of heretics is an uproar to the Lord and, so to speak, the grunting of swine and the braying of asses, ibid.—The gravest burden of error among the nations was idolatry, which pressed its worshippers down to earth and could not save them; it made their souls captive to the devil and demons, XXIV, 451.—Dumb images are insensible, ibid.—Many worship demons so that they may not harm them, 747.—Demons are worshipped through vices, XXVI, 415.

AUGUSTINE (St.).—False religions were abolished by the passion of the martyrs, XLI, 136.—Error proceeds from worshipping the creature in place of God, XXXIV, 130.—Various kinds of false religion, [Col. 0929] 169.—True religion is not to be sought among pagans or among heretics, 163.—Various kinds of superstition, 50.—How superstition is harmful, XXXIII, 377.—To observe days for performing some act is a great sin, XL, 270.—Superstition is compared to rain, XXXV, 1308.—What is superstitious, XXXIV, 50.—Who were called superstitious, XLI, 137.—The games and ritual practices of pagan sacred observances are most shameful, XXXIII, 415; XLI, 50.—The custom of playing and dancing was accepted in pagan solemnities, XXXIV, 473.—Through imitation of their gods they become worse, XXXIII, 414.—The feast days of pagans consist in abundance of banquets and drunkenness, 118; XXXVIII, 272.—The practice of dancing where St. Cyprian had been buried was removed, through the bishop’s care, as though an abuse, 1415.—Dancing with dogs’ carcasses as a punishment, XLIII, 579.—The shameful dances of the Primianists, 106, 107.

PETER CHRYSOLOGUS (St.).—He inveighs most sharply against games customarily held on the Kalends of January.—Those who mock the gods whom they venerate and treat them with insults are mockers, not worshippers, LII, 609.—But someone will say: “These are not pursuits of sacrilege, but vows of amusement.” You are mistaken, man: these are not amusements; they are crimes, 611.—No one plays with impiety or jokes about sacrilege, ibid.—Let the plague of dancing-girls, the seductive arts of singers, and the fuels of pleasures be cut off, 552.—John, Christ’s forerunner, the Lord’s surveyor, God’s witness, is given to an incestuous woman, handed over to an adulteress, assigned to a dancing-girl, 547.—Description of a most shameful dancing-girl, 654.—She is no longer called a girl, but a new beast, 551.

SALVIAN.—By sacrilegious superstitions the divine majesty is violated, LIII, 120.—Which gods are worshipped in theatres, ibid.—Everywhere are all the monsters of demons, ibid.

LEO THE GREAT (St.).—Various superstitions are noted, LIV, 218.—Brief and perishable are the joys of earthly pleasures, which seek to turn those called to eternity away from the paths of life, LIV, 147.

MAXIMUS (St.), of Turin.—Various superstitions are condemned, LVII, 257, 258.—He inveighs against the festival of the Saturnalia, ibid., 491.

ISIDORE (St.), of Seville.—On dancers, LXXXII, 659.—Under what patrons dances were performed, ibid.—Why they must be detested, ibid.

FULGENTIUS FERRANDUS.—According to the Council of Laodicea, title 41: no Christian should dare to dance or sing at weddings, LXXXVIII, 827.

CRISCONIUS.—Christians attending weddings ought not to applaud or dance, but should dine or take their meal reverently, as befits Christians; Council of Laodicea, title 53, LXXXVIII, 897.

JONAS, of Orléans.—He condemns obscene dances customary at banquets, CVI, 164.

PASCHASIUS RADBERTUS.—On the bloody murder of St. John the Baptist, CXX, 512 ff.

ANSELM (St.), of Canterbury.—How the life of the luxurious becomes a perpetual festival, CLVIII, 701, 702.—What ought to be set against the world’s delights, 677 ff.—Prodigal luxury knows no moderation, 702.

GODEFRIDUS, of Admont.—It is a feast day to pass from evil to good, CLXXIV, 780.—To keep a feast day is, putting aside crowds of useless thoughts, to form the mind for the rest of spiritual discipline, 96.

HUGH OF ST. VICTOR.—There are certain Kalends and festivals which God abominates, CLXXVII, 926, 927.—Those who delight in the pleasures and pomps of this age, as if lulled by heavy sleep, become the prey of the adversary, 78.

BERNARD (St.), abbot of Clairvaux.—It is unworthy to turn festivals into vanity and delights, CLXXXIII, 44.—Why do you prepare garments with such ambition for the Nativity of the Lord? ibid.—Let a member be ashamed to become delicate beneath a thorn-crowned head, 480.—Abuses in celebrating festivals are reproved, 479, 480.—Lovers of the age, enemies of Christ’s cross, Christians in name received in vain, throughout this whole season of Lent eagerly await the approaching days of the resurrection—alas!—that they may indulge pleasure more freely, 282.—Alas for grief! The resurrection of the Saviour has become a limit for relapsing, a time for sinning, ibid.—It is the custom of secular persons to prepare festive banquets for themselves on feast days, 453.

GARNERIUS OF ST. VICTOR.—How wickedly the dance of Herodias’s daughter prevailed with the drunken king, CXCIII, 169.

AELRED (Blessed), abbot.—He rebukes the wanton gestures of singers, the harlot-like alternations and breaks in their voices, which the common crowd itself watches not without loud laughter and amusement, CXCV, 571.—Honourable gravity brings excessive disgust to ears itching for the recollection of theatrical trifles, 572.—Devoted to empty spectacles or intent on hearing rumours, we go out of ourselves and afterward introduce images of vanities, 573.

PETER OF CELLES.—By removing disordered jesting, vain joys, laughter, dissipation of mind, irreligion, and unbridled sensuality are excluded, [Col. 0930] CCII, 730.

PETER CANTOR.—He rebukes those who sing on feast days only for money or for food and refreshment, CCV, 98.—And those who give themselves to games on those days, ibid.

ABSALO, abbot.—The dancing girl at Herod’s banquet sinned greatly, yet less than Judas at the Lord’s Supper, CCXI, 18.—Pride whispers this to a religious: “When you were in the world, you walked where you wished; you ran freely to the ends of the streets, to the gatherings of dances; wherever the impulse of your spirit was, there you went,” 41.

SICARDUS, of Cremona.—The pomps of the devil are spectacles, dances, games, wantonnesses—in a word, all vain and superfluous honours, CCXIII, 279.

XI.—Immodesty of the eyes; less decorous paintings and images.

TERTULLIAN.—Well-adorned women draw after themselves the eyes and sighs of young men, I, 1320.—What are the special torments of the eyes in the abyss? II, 845.—The face of a virgin, so dangerous, ought to be veiled, 899.—To see and to be seen belong to the same lust, 891.

CYPRIAN (St.).—Adultery is admitted through the eyes, IV, 785.—Women who, with eyes inquisitive for lust, prostitute bodies dedicated to modesty and chastity, 458.—Desires for present things stir and invite toward corruption, ibid.

ARNOBIUS.—Artists play and behave wantonly in fashioning gods, V, 1192.—Description of a workshop for images, 1193.—What models Praxiteles and Phidias used in fabricating images, 1190 ff.—Obscene and ridiculous images, 1188.

LACTANTIUS.—It was demons who taught men to fashion images and statues, VI, 337.—What was the first cause of making images? 258.

HILARY (St.), of Poitiers.—To free the eye from a snare is rare, IX, 819.—The movement of an eye falling upon another is equated with adultery in the Gospels, 938, 939.—The eyes both of body and soul must be turned away from vanity, 510.—How can curiosity approach one whose eyes are fixed upon God? 831.—How many and how great are the snares of souls? 832.—What shall we bring to Christ when he comes: treasures of wealth, ambitious titles of rank, or ancestral portraits of refined nobility? IX, 1012.

AMBROSE (St.).—The eye is the window of the harlot; therefore beware every irreverent eye, lest love enter through the window and lust penetrate, XIV, 891.—Do you not wish to be captured by love? Do not fix your gaze upon a woman’s appearance, 892.—You are painted, O man, and painted by the Lord your God. You have a good craftsman and painter; do not efface the good image, XIV, 260.

JEROME (St.).—A woman whose face you often observe ministers to you dangerously, XXII, 532.—Observe that no gaze is safe, even within the home, 401.—The eyes confess the secrets of the heart, 556.—What is seen with the eyes is retained more strongly in the mind, XXIV, 796, 800.—Through the gates of the eyes the greatest vices slip in, XXV, 1348.—What it is to see with the eyes of the flesh, XXVI, 256.

AUGUSTINE (St.).—The eyes are the windows of the mind, XXXVI, 468.—The eyes are the rulers of the senses, XXXII, 801.—The immodest eye is the messenger of an immodest heart, 1391; XXXIII, 961.—The wantonness of the eyes must be restrained, XXXVI, 587.—A man’s eye must not be fixed upon a woman, XXXII, 1391.—The enticements of the eyes, XLI, 232, 813.—To entice with the eyes, XXXVIII, 1413.—The loss of bodily eyes is judged greater than that of the soul’s eyes—but only by the blind, XXXVI, 860.—Light is food for the eyes, XXXVII, 1114; XXXVIII, 183.—To cast one’s eyes upon someone means to love, XXXIV, 496.—The eyes of the flesh are greatly loved; the eyes of the heart are greatly neglected, XXXVIII, 542.—Blindness of the inward eyes is failure to understand, XXXVII, 1552.—After sin, nakedness causes shame, XXXVIII, 542.—Shame at nakedness is born with every human being, XLIV, 565.—Wanton paintings, XXXII, 671.—Worshippers of paintings and tombs, 1342.—Trismegistus maintains that images are, as it were, bodies of gods, XLI, 247.—The Romans consecrated images of bodily vices, XLII, 374.—The origin of the use of images, 409.—It is reproved by Seneca, XLI, 190.—Those who established images did not remove fear but added error, 119, 198.—In images, demons gave deceptive oracles, 581.—How far worshippers of images have strayed from truth, XL, 90.—Not only a human being but even a beast is better than the images of the nations, XXXVII, 1482.

PETER CHRYSOLOGUS.—An enticing gaze cast down the woman; a saving gaze raised her, LII, 409.—The gaze is obscured by smoke, [Col. 0931] 410.—When the devil closed the woman’s eyes, the sight of the forbidden tree defiled her, 419.—Hypocrisy, while it seeks to capture eyes, is itself made captive by eyes, 205.—The eye as author of transgression, and other evils of the eyes, 573.—The wandering eye, wanton glance, and wicked look do not see to their own ruin, ibid.—Blind to their own crimes, clear-sighted toward those of others, ibid.—What wrath, what vengeance could so exact from idols the offense against God that those whom antiquity, with altars, incense, victims, gems, and gold, falsely declared gods, posterity should judge to have been the most shameful of men through shameful worship, and should mark out their life, habits, and deeds upon their very faces, teaching that they should be fled rather than worshipped . . . those whose adulteries they fashion in statues, whose fornications they commit to images, whose incests they label in paintings, whose cruelties they commend in books, whose obscenities they enact, LII, 610.

SALVIAN.—The forward glances of the immodest are not free from the guilt of adultery, LIII, 64.—The eyes are the gates of desires, ibid.—The eyes are now commanded to observe restraint, 199.—In those images of fornications the entire populace commits fornication in mind, LIII, 112.

LEO THE GREAT (St.).—The enemy’s darts draw the eyes toward various desires, so that either the fires of concupiscence are kindled by the beauty of the world, or the errors of superstitions are generated, LIV, 444.

MAXIMUS (St.) OF TURIN.—Lascivious glances are highly culpable, LVII, 750.—Our Lord, the corrector of all shamefulness, restrains the wantonness of human looks, ibid.—“If your right eye causes you to stumble”: that is, if by an unlawful intention you delight in seeing what can destroy you, 810.—Sight must be subjected to the reins of divine strength, lest the soldier of Christ be overcome by the lax allurements of thoughts, and lest a chaste woman be held in serpentine bonds by roving eyes, ibid.—Let us look more cautiously, lest the undisciplined gaze of wandering eyes steal upon our idle heart, 751.

LIVES OF THE FATHERS.—The sight of a woman becomes a cause of temptation, LXXIV, 129.—At the sight of a holy virgin, a young man is inflamed, 148.—The exceptional watchfulness of certain Fathers over their eyes, LXXIII, 872, 897.

GREGORY THE GREAT (St.).—Eyes that seize lead to fault, LXXVI, 190.—It is not lawful to look upon what it is not lawful to desire, ibid.—Let the eye not serve a heart desiring what is unlawful, 197.—By self-love of the heart the eye is blinded, ibid.—How far the eyes of fools differ from the eyes of the wise, 14.—Eyes: how they are to be governed, 189, 197.—What are the eyes of the devil? 710.—We have no eye where we neglect certain things, 843.—Those whose eyes are darkened have their back bent, LXXVII, 15.

TAIO OF SARAGOSSA.—On the concupiscence of the eyes, LXXX, 939.

ALCUIN (Blessed).—How, and by whom, human eyes were corrupted, CI, 923.

AGOBARD (St.).—The same must not be said of images of saints as of images of gods, which the pagans worshipped, CIV, 225.

JONAS OF ORLÉANS.—If the devil sees us repeatedly looking at a beautiful woman, he understands that the heart has been wounded by the dart of love, CVI, 155.

RABANUS MAURUS.—In order that a pure mind may be preserved in thought from the wantonness of degrading pleasure, the eyes must be cast down, as though they were certain ravishers leading into fault, CVII, 490.—The eye is the lamp of the body, 835.

HAYMO OF HALBERSTADT.—The eyes must be circumcised from unlawful sight, lest they look upon a woman in order to desire her, CXVIII, 95.—He who closes his eyes lest they see evil shall dwell on high, 97.—It is the darkness of morals that must be feared, not that of the eyes; and if that of the eyes, not the outward but the inward eyes, 322.

HINCMAR OF RHEIMS.—To see and nevertheless maintain that one does not see is expressed in an old Gothic proverb: “The one-eyed she-goat sees the garden, but nowhere sees the fence,” XXXV, 505.

BERNO, ABBOT OF CLUNY.—We are accustomed to defile our house through our five senses: enticing forms enter through the eyes, evil suspicion through the ears, lustful odor through the nostrils, gluttony defiles through the mouth, cruelty through touch, CXLII, 1082.

PETER DAMIAN (St.).—From more beautiful and painted eyes I guard my own eyes as boys from fire, CXLIV, 458.—My unhappy heart does not lose the memory of a form once seen, ibid.—In contemplating riches, there are only the allurements of unhappy eyes, when we are unable to turn them toward the expenses of our necessity, 424.

ANSELM (St.) OF CANTERBURY.—For shame at sin, blush to lift up your eyes, CLVIII, 680.—Those who strive to restore their eyes with cosmetics are ridiculed, 696.—Your wanton laughter, the little eyes of your burning nod, and your chatter displeased me, [Col. 0932] 697.—Lust desires whatever soft thing delights, whatever is seen, and whatever is beautiful, 702.—If you desire what is beautiful, who is more beautiful than he, God? 708.—Your eyes are Christ’s eyes, 713.—At the point of death the eyes, turned back toward the interior of the head, will close—eyes in whose vain and harmful wanderings I often delighted, 620.—Restrain your eyes from wantonness; remove the occasion and take away the material for sinning, 684.

IVO OF CHARTRES.—On the circumcision of the five senses, CLXII, 573.

ANSELM OF LAON.—On the concupiscence of the eyes, CLXII, 1297.—The eyes especially signify understanding, ibid., 1311.

HILDEBERT OF LE MANS.—How pernicious is the concupiscence of the eyes, CLXXI, 469.—How diligently it must be guarded against, 710.—The woman in paradise was deceived through sight, 842.—How necessary the mortification of the eyes is for preserving chastity, 306.—There is one inner eye and another outer eye, 815.

HONORIUS OF AUTUN.—On the scandal of the eyes, CLXXII, 1044.—The eye that leads us is the priest who guides us from the darkness of the world to the light of life, ibid.

GODEFRID OF ADMONT.—There are two eyes of the mind, namely understanding and affection, CLXXIV, 163.—The eyes are raised through intention, 626.—The eye indicates the intention of an act, 925.—The evil eye has two edges: ignorance and malice, 928.

HUGH OF ST. VICTOR.—The eyes of fools are in darkness, CLXXV, 196.—Why the eye is not satisfied with seeing, 140.—The scandal of the eyes must be removed, CLXXVII, 755.

BERNARD (St.) OF CLAIRVAUX.—Curiosity, especially that of the eyes, is the first degree of pride, CLXXXII, 957.—The eye of the perverse man, ibid.—The eyes must not be raised except to seek help or to render it, ibid.—Why do you wish to look at what you may not eat? 858.—My eye, my memory, CLXXXIII, 478.—The fourfold eye of the heart, CLXXXII, 881.—It must be cleansed from sins, 851.—To use a single eye means to conduct oneself and act rightly, 406, 407.—The evil eye, that is, blindness and perversity, 882, 883.—The eye of the mind must be cleansed from a threefold defilement in order to see God, CLXXXIII, 460.

PETER THE VENERABLE.—From what the eye of the mind must be cleansed, CLXXXIX, 397.—One eye belongs to spiritual persons, another to carnal persons, 405.

GERHOH (V.), PROVOST.—In Scripture the eye expresses the intention of the heart, CXCIII, 157.—What are the single eye and the evil eye? 158.—The various meanings denoted by “eyes,” 168 and following.

AELRED, ABBOT.—On the concupiscence of the eyes as situated in curiosity, CXCV, 572.—In monastic cloisters, cranes and hares, does and stags, magpies and ravens: not indeed instruments of Antony or Macarius, but feminine amusements, 572.—Those are reproved who meditate on pastoral poetry along with the Gospels, read Horace with the prophets, and Cicero with Paul, ibid.—Having devoted the entire day to empty spectacles, we in some manner go out from ourselves; returning again to ourselves, we bring back images of vanities, ibid.

RICHARD OF ST. VICTOR.—Where love is, there is the eye, CXCVI, 10.

ADAM THE SCOT.—How carefully the concupiscence of the eyes must be restrained, CXCVIII, 814.—The gaze must be drawn back from curiosity, 256.—Especially, it must not be fixed upon a woman, 534.—Holy David rashly cast his eyes upon a woman and became both adulterer and murderer, ibid.—According to the poet, God gave man an uplifted face and commanded him to look upon heaven, 447.

PETER OF CELLE.—The end comes, death comes: take away the pride of your eyes, O man, for these windows will soon be shut and will not be opened until the day of judgment, CCII, 678.—Eyes are called unchaste merely because they admire beauty; therefore they should diligently be turned away from Babylonian theatres, 676.

REINER, MONK OF ST. LAWRENCE, LIÈGE.—A chaste eye shudders at the forms or guise of unchastity, CCIV, 53.—The eyes must be turned away lest they see vanity, ibid.

BALDWIN, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY.—What is the single and pure eye? CCIV, 480.—How easily the eye that sees earthly things is disturbed, 481.—Where love is, there is the eye, ibid.—This eye looks at earth and not heaven, the world and not God, transient things and not eternal ones: it is impure and dark, 480.—The eye can see and be seen; it is accustomed to be both an indication and an enticement of love, 481.—Christ, the true bridegroom, loves the eye that turns away from him and often returns, ibid.

STEPHEN (St.), FOUNDER OF GRANDMONT.—When a religious man has looked upon something desirable, let him keep his eyes in prison; let him not fix them there, but turn his sight away, CCIV, 1089.

[Col. 0933] PETER THE CHANTER.—Who ought to have eyes before and behind, CCV, 74, 117.—Loss of the eyes disfigures the body most greatly, 117.—The hour of death must always be kept before one’s eyes, 353.—The concupiscence of the eyes is man’s temptation, 331.

ABSALO, ABBOT.—The concupiscence of the eyes is an outer abyss in which carnal people toil miserably, CCXI, 230.

ADAM, ABBOT OF PERSENIA.—He who sincerely loves another scarcely turns back upon the beloved the eye of his regard, CCXI, 566.—Smoke is usually troublesome to the eyes and nostrils, 599.—How many admire you and grieve that, in God’s love, you smoke rather than flame, 599.

SICARD OF CREMONA.—Without the eye-salve of grace, the eye of both nature and the letter is bleary, CCXIII, 173.

XII.—Spectacles: theatres, comedies, tragedies, the circus, pantomimes, actors.

TERTULLIAN.—There is now no spectacle without a disturbance of the spirit, I, 647.—The origin of spectacles lies in idolatrous superstition, 466.—With how many crimes they are contaminated, ibid., 630.—Whether Christians may attend spectacles, I, 493, 655.—The theatre is properly a sanctuary of Venus, 642.—A gathering-place of unchastity, 649.—An art of every shamefulness, ibid.—Theatres arise for the violation of morals, 299.—How obscene and abominable they are, 301.—Their prohibition follows from the prohibition of unchastity itself, 650.—A woman who had gone to the theatre returned with a demon, 637.—Tragedies and comedies are authors of lusts and crimes: bloody and wanton, impious and prodigal, I, 650.—We are carried away from the circus, where frenzy properly presides, I, 648.—Gladiators, 620.—Cursed by Christ, 1254.—Innocent persons enter the games in order to become victims of public pleasure, 651.—Gladiators praised by the pagans, 584.—Unwillingly, they were compelled by whips and rods to commit murder, 654.—They devoured beasts fattened upon human blood and flesh, 322, 584.—They drank the blood of others whom they themselves had killed, 323.

CYPRIAN (St.).—The shamefulness of theatres, IV, 206 and following.—Romulus instituted circus games for the abduction of the Sabine women, IV, 783.—A gladiatorial show is prepared so that blood may delight the lust of cruel eyes, 206 and following.—The misery of gladiators, 618.—A book *On Spectacles*, vigorously attacking them, 779.

ARNOBIUS.—Who the theatrical actors and spectators were, and what things were handed down as fit to be seen by the eyes, V, 1071, 1072.—How disgraceful the Floralian games were, 1264.—Amphitheatres: places of blood and public impiety, 875.

HILARY OF POITIERS.—The eyes must be turned away from those who devote themselves to theatrical games and serve the contests of the Circus, IX, 540.—Eyes defiled by theatrical spectacles, 303.

LACTANTIUS.—On the pleasure of the eyes and spectacles, VI, 705 and following.—All spectacles must be avoided, lest some vice lie in wait in the heart; [lacuna] and turn it away from God and good works, 712.—If anyone attends spectacles at which people gather for religious reasons, he has departed from the worship of God and gone over to the gods, 713.

AMBROSE (St.).—The musical performances of stage actors soften the mind, XIV, 157.—The stage is a valley; the circus is a valley, where the deceitful horse runs toward salvation, 156.—Valentinian, who was at first said to take great delight in circus games, effaced this disposition so completely that he thought circuses ought not be celebrated even on the solemn birthdays of emperors, XVI, 1363, 1364.

JEROME (St.).—Let us remove our eyes from spectacles—arenas, circuses, theatres, and everything that contaminates the purity of the soul as it enters the mind through the senses, XXV, 189.—All refinements, witticisms, laughable urbanities, and the other foolishnesses of lovers: we blush at them in comedies and detest them in people of the world, XXI, 532.—A certain poet, to whom anachronisms counted for nothing, nevertheless had many equally ignorant fellow pupils in the theatre, 585.—As, on theatrical stages, one and the same actor, now a bear, displays sturdy Hercules, now softens into Venus, now trembles as Cybele, so we have as many likenesses of persons as we have sins, 479.

AUGUSTINE (St.).—Varro placed stage games among divine matters, XLI, 132, 137.—The Greeks did not judge stage games shameful, 135.—They also admitted stage actors to participation in the administration of the state, 55.—Why stage games were instituted at Rome at the command of the gods, 44, 53, 58, 73, 132.—How dangerous they are, 75, 76, 134.—How shameful, 50, 51.—Although shameful, the gods ordered them to be exhibited there, 158, 237.—What is shameful to say, 239.—Stage games: a plague of morals, 97.—Divine majesty is not appeased by stage games by which human dignity is defiled, 78.—To have gods who delight in stage games resembles madness, XLI, 187.—Trifling games of iniquity and empty spectacles, [Col. 0934] XXXVIII, 81, 83, 88.—The lies of poets, XXXII, 1014.—Comedies and tragedies among the liberal arts, XLI, 53.—The fables of poets are less obscene than the rites of the gods, ibid.—Poets are no less deserving of infamy than actors, 58.—Stage poets inflame lust, 59, 60.—The spectacles of theatres are unlawful, XXXVIII, 868.—How dangerous they are, XLI, 44, 45.—Pernicious both to those who sponsor and those who watch them, XXXVII, 1918.—Spectacles were prohibited through the persuasion of Scipio Nasica, XLI, 44, 45, 51.—Christians are deterred from spectacles, XXXVIII, 548.—Through devotion to spectacles people become like demons, XL, 329, 330.—To permit spectacles is not the act of a true shepherd, XXXVIII, 274.—What spectacles Christians have, XXXV, 1440; XXXVI, 439; XXXVII, 1851, 1919, 1923; XXXVIII, 333.—Gladiators, professors of public shamefulness, XL, 220.

PETER CHRYSOLOGUS (St.).—The crime of Herodias: after a comedy had been enacted in the foulest manner, she immediately sang an abominable tragedy, LII, 653.—A sermon against spectacles delivered at the beginning of the year, 600 and following.

SALVIAN.—How, O Christian, do you pursue spectacles after baptism, which you confess to be the work of the devil? LIII, 114.—Let us laugh, I pray; let us rejoice continually as much as we wish, provided it be innocently [lacuna]. But spectacles and processions, according to our profession, are works of the devil, ibid.—In spectacles there is not pleasure but death, 115.—God’s temple is despised so that people may run to the theatre, 116.—When inhabitants of any city come to Ravenna or Rome, some become part of the Roman people in the circus, others part of the Ravennate populace in the theatre, 118.—The Church of Carthage raved in the circuses and luxuriated in the theatres, 122.—Do we follow the Savior’s footsteps in circuses and theatres? Did Christ leave us such an example? We read that he wept; we do not read that he laughed, LIII, 114.—God’s temple is despised so that people may run to the theatre. The church is emptied; the circus is filled, 116.—While we play in theatres and circuses, we perish, 120.

LEO THE GREAT (St.).—It is shameful to say it: demons are more attended than apostles, and mad spectacles obtain a larger crowd than blessed martyr-shrines, LIV, 433.—Who restored this city to safety? Who rescued it from captivity? Who defended it from slaughter? The circus games or the care of priests? ibid.

MAXIMUS (St.) OF TURIN.—See the sermons customarily delivered against spectacles on the Kalends of January, 255, 491.

PRUDENTIUS (St.).—What is the meaning of the mournful pomp of amphitheatrical spectacles? LIX, 151.

ISIDORE (St.) OF SEVILLE.—On spectacles in general, LXXXII, 651.—On the various spectacles known among the Romans, 652 and following.—On circus games, 653, 654.—On charioteers, four-horse chariots, the chariot, and riding, 655, 656.—On the amphitheatre, 659.—On the equestrian game, retiarii, secutores, and laquearii, 639, 666.—On the deadly contest and the condemnation of these games, 660.

CRISCONIUS.—Canon of the Council of Laodicea, title 54.—Clerics may not attend spectacles of games, LXXXVII, 899.—Even if they take place at weddings, ibid.—Spectacles may not be given on Sundays, according to the Council of Carthage, title 28, LXXXVIII, 931.

ALCUIN (Blessed).—Spectacles are condemned, C, 462.—They are called devilish fictions, ibid.

RABANUS MAURUS.—Explanations of ancient spectacles, CXII, 547 and following.—On the deadly contest and the condemnation of these games, 553.—The theatre is called a brothel and house of prostitution, ibid.

ISIDORE MERCATOR.—Christians ought not to be present at shameful spectacles, CXXX, 404.

REGINO.—Spectacles are not to be watched by Christians, CXXXII, 255.

ATTO OF VERCELLI.—The spectacles of games and theatres are to be removed on Sunday and on the other feast-days of the Christian religion, CXXXIV, 43.

HROTSVITHA (Venerable), NUN OF GANDERSHEIM.—She elegantly composed sacred comedies in order to turn Christian readers away from profane and unlawful stages, as she herself declares in the Prologue, CXXXVII, 971.

HUGH OF ST. VICTOR.—Those who delight in the pleasures, pomp, and theatrical enjoyments of this age, dissolved by tragedies and comedies, as though lulled by heavy sleep, become the adversary’s prey, CLXXVII, 78.

BERNARD (St.) OF CLAIRVAUX.—But, I ask, what do empty spectacles contribute to the body, or what do they appear to confer upon the soul? CLXXXII, 842.—Spectacles are wholly frivolous, empty, and trifling consolation, ibid.—The theatre provokes lust through feminine and foul turns, representing sordid acts, 217.—What game is good, ibid.

AELRED, ABBOT.—When, having spent the entire day on empty spectacles, we have in a sense gone out from ourselves, we return again to ourselves [Col. 0935] bringing in images of vanities and pass sleepless nights, CXCV, 573.

JOHN OF SALISBURY.—The profession of actors is shameful, CXCIX, 404, 405.—Spectacles and innumerable initiations into vanity have been admitted, 406.—Various kinds of actors, ibid.—Those publicly practicing shameful things, ibid.—Not only actors sin, but also those who support them and establish them in such an art, ibid.

PETER OF CELLE.—Thus concerning the glory of the saints: “Solemn fairs are celebrated in the marketplace, and do you not run, O sinner? Most beautiful spectacles are prepared, and do you close your eyes?” CCII, 882.

ALAN OF LILLE.—A shameful spectacle shamefully inflames the mind toward pleasure, CCX, 255.

HELINAND, MONK.—A ruler ought not to tolerate in his kingdom actors, mimes, buffoons, pimps, or prostitutes, CCXII, 735.

SICARD.—Spectacles are called the devil’s pomps and works, CCXIII, 279.

XIII.—Foolish speech, empty speech, buffoonery.

HILARY (St.).—The tongue’s fall is dangerous and very ready, IX, 826.—A door and a bar must be set upon the mouth, ibid.—The tongue of the fool and the tongue of the wise, 313.—Display, boasting, and blandishments of speech are condemned, 952, 953.—Among sound-minded people it accomplishes nothing, 399.

AMBROSE (St.).—Much speaking went out; sin entered, XIV, 335.—He is to be praised who wishes first to know what ought to be said before uttering what he thinks, XV, 1210.—Philosophers rich in discourse, poor in faith, bereft of truth, XIV, 981.—I have seen very many fall into sin by speaking, scarcely anyone by keeping silence, XVI, 25.—Death enters through your door if you speak falsely, shamefully, insolently, or where you ought not to speak, 286.—Bind your speech lest it run riot, lest it become wanton, and by much speaking gather sins to itself, 27.

JEROME (St.).—I do not want you to be a declaimer . . . To roll words about and, by speed of speaking, make an impression upon an uneducated crowd is characteristic of unlearned people, XXII, 534.—There are some who do not know their own measure and are of such stupidity and folly that in movement, gait, dress, and ordinary speech they provoke laughter in those who see them, 662.—I consider foolish speech to be that of persons who tell shameful stories in order to provoke laughter and, under a feigned ease, more readily mock those whom they desire to please, XXVI, 519.—Buffoonery follows foolish speech, 820.

AUGUSTINE (St.).—Vanity is more talkative than truth, XLI, 174.—What is much speaking? XXXII, 583; XLIII, 447.—The tongue must be restrained, XXXVIII, 635, 978.—How difficult it is to tame the tongue, XXXVII.—Without the help of grace we cannot do so, XLIV, 254.—The misuse of words in all languages, XLII, 410.

PETER CHRYSOLOGUS (St.).—We ought to speak according to the time, LII, 357.—What the mind contemplates in its affection, it brings forth by the mouth, pours out through the lips, distinguishes by the tongue, and still cannot wholly evaporate in speech, 357.

VALERIAN (St.) OF CIMIEZ.—Homily on idle words, LII, 709.—On the insolence of the mouth, 706.

MAXIMUS (St.) OF TURIN.—The undisciplined license of speech is reproved and shown to be the cause of many evils, LVII, 751.
