GREGORY THE GREAT (St.).—How many evils are caused by much speaking, LXXV, 800.—The mind, scattered outward by much speaking, is dissipated, ibid.—Talkativeness is the companion of banquets, 532.—Much speaking exposes us naked to the enemy, LXXVII, 72.

TAIO, BISHOP OF SARAGOSSA.—On much speaking, LXXX, 942.—On perverse speech, 943.—On folly, 944.

ISIDORE (St.) OF SEVILLE.—Empty speech quickly defiles the mind, LXXXIII, 856.—Let nothing proceed from your mouth that can impede; let no sound of the voice break forth that is not expedient, ibid.—Some, through imprudent boasting of virtues, fall back into vices, 698.

BEDE (Venerable).—On guarding the tongue, XCIII, 16, 26.

SMARAGDUS, ABBOT.—Much speaking arises from curiosity, CII, 668, 669.—It is a great vice that leaves neither body at rest nor soul without sin while one anxiously goes about other people’s houses or investigates others’ actions, ibid.—The vice of curiosity is incessantly accompanied also by idleness, ibid.—On much speaking, 634.

JONAS OF ORLÉANS.—One must not devote oneself to idle or shameful conversation, especially in churches, CVI, 147.

EULOGIUS (St.) OF TOLEDO.—Every empty talker shall come condemned into judgment, CXV, 760.

HAYMO OF HALBERSTADT.—Let widows learn not to go around [Col. 0936] houses, nor to live luxuriously, nor to occupy their tongue with idle tales, CXVIII, 88.—The tongue must be circumcised from curses, perjuries, falsehoods, murmurings, and the habit of idle speech, 96.—The boy Jesus was not found idle or occupied with tales, but in the temple, listening to the teachers and questioning them, 123.

PASCHASIUS RADBERTUS.—Our words are idle if, neglecting serious matters, we speak of frivolous things and tell old tales, CXX, 474.

RATHERIUS OF VERONA.—Some persist at night in psalmody and prayer, but during the day devote themselves to detractions, evil speech, idleness, and sloth, CXXXVI, 697.

ANSELM (St.) OF CANTERBURY.—Restrain your tongue from idle speech; do not chatter empty words, for empty speech quickly defiles the mind, CLVIII, 683.—Let your words be few; much speaking does not avoid sin, ibid.

BERNARD (St.) OF CLAIRVAUX.—Buffooneries must be avoided, CLXXXIII, 584.—One must beware of idleness and trifles, CLXXXII, 756.

JOHN OF SALISBURY.—On the arrogance of the unlearned multitude and on frivolous books, CXCIX, 653.—What is more brutish than one who, through lack of reason and the impulse of desire, neglects his own affairs, attends to those of others, and is not continually occupied with other people’s leisure? 389.

PETER OF CELLE.—Silence excludes lies, foolish speech, buffooneries, and every idle word, CCII, 730.—The occasion for much speaking must be removed and the tongue restrained, 732.

PETER THE CHANTER.—He inveighs against talkativeness and idle words, especially among preachers, CCV, 197.

MARTIN (St.) OF LEÓN.—Constant and idle speech must be avoided, CCVIII, 656.

ALAN OF LILLE.—Against verbosity and the tongue’s wandering, CCX, 162.—Empty speech is the mark of an empty conscience, 163.—The mobility of the tongue bends the mind in youth toward joking, in mature age toward deceitful speech, and in old age toward detraction, 163.—How carefully verbosity must be avoided, 164.

ABSALO, ABBOT.—Venomous detractions, obscenity, foolish speech, and buffoonery irrelevant to the matter deter people from good conduct, CCXI, 181.

XIV.—The disordered pursuit of hunting, dogs, horses, and birds.

OPTATUS (St.).—An excellent description of bird-catchers who capture birds with birdlime, compared to heretics, XI, 1080.

AMBROSE (St.).—From the eulogy of Valentinian: some said that he was occupied with hunting wild beasts and that his attention was diverted from public affairs; he ordered all the beasts to be killed in a single moment, XVI, 1364.

JEROME (St.).—As far as I can remember, I have never read “hunter” in a favorable sense, XXV, 1201.—Royal hunts in Babylon, XXIV, 159.

AUGUSTINE (St.).—The devil, the worst hunter of the world, XXXVIII, 334.—Hunter, XXXVIII, 85, 136, 333, 718; XL, 560.—The labor of hunters, XXXVIII, 444.—Hunters fighting bears, XL, 639.—The Lord hunted the lovers of hunting and the hunters themselves, XXXVIII, 333.

MAXIMUS (St.) OF TURIN.—Hunting during Lent is condemned, LVII, 581.

PAULINUS (St.) OF AQUILEIA.—Hunting and wandering through the woods are forbidden to all servants of God, especially clerics, XCIX, 316.

JONAS OF ORLÉANS.—On those who, because of hunting and their love of dogs, neglect the cause of the poor, CVI, 215.

RATHERIUS OF VERONA.—He reproves certain bishops of his time who, in the German manner, pursued hunting, CXXXVI, 291.

ANDREAS, MONK OF VALLUMBROSA.—In the *Life of St. Ariald* he describes the dissolute morals of the clergy, many of whom were devoted to licentious hunting with dogs and hawks, CXLIII, 1441.

GERHOH, PROVOST.—Clerical hunters are reproved, CXCIV, 1418.

JOHN OF SALISBURY.—On hunting, its authors and kinds; on its lawful and unlawful exercise, CXCIX, 390.—Nimrod and Esau: hunters “before,” that is, against, the Lord, 394.—The exultation of hunters over the head of their prey is exceedingly vain and ridiculous; one might think that they had captured the king of Cappadocia, 391.—The affinity of hunting and lust in the thought of ancient poets, 390, 391.—Hunting is the portion of those who wander from God, 394, 395.—“Where,” says the prophet, “are those who play with the birds of heaven?” ibid.—Hunting produces a pleasure allied to feasts, drinking bouts, [Col. 0937] banquets, music-making, and games; to more laboriously refined adornments, fornications, and various impurities. How regard must be paid to places, times, manner, and persons for hunting to be lawful, 398.

PETER OF BLOIS.—He urges Walter, an eighty-year-old bishop, by many arguments to cease from the pursuit of hunting, CCVII, 169.—Likewise, he dissuades a certain archdeacon of Salisbury from the pleasure of bird-catching, 181.—Sackcloth and a hawk do not suit one another well; neither do mortification of the flesh and the exercise of pleasure, 182.—It does not become Christ’s disciple to run and shout after delightful birds, 183.

ABSALO, ABBOT.—Does it not seem to you that the Word has become flesh in those who, living from the patrimony of the Crucified, feed from it not the poor but dogs, hawks, and actors? CCXI, 55.

[Col. 0937]

CLXXII. INDEX OF PARTICULAR VICES AND ERRORS OF THE PAGANS WHICH THE HOLY FATHERS REBUKED AND ATTACKED, ARRANGED ALPHABETICALLY BY SUBJECT.

[Col. 0937] FLATTERY.—Aristotle and Plato: flatterers, Tertullian, I, 500.

ADULTERY.—Speusippus perished in adultery, Tertullian, I, 500.

EQUITY (*égalité*, “equality”).—Plato’s equality, which would abolish the family, Lactantius, VI, 417, 418.

PASSIONS.—The error of Chrysippus and the Stoics concerning the passions, St. Jerome, XXIII, 542.—The error of the Stoics concerning the passions, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1528; XLI, 259; XXXIV, 395, 396.—The error of the Academics concerning the passions, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 641.

SOUL.—The errors of the Epicureans concerning the soul, Tertullian, II, 19.—Aenesidemus, Anaximenes, Heraclitus, and Heraclides erred concerning the substance of the soul, ibid., 660.—Anaxagoras’s confused teaching concerning the soul, ibid., 666.—Archimedes’s error concerning the soul, ibid., 669.—Messenius, Dicaearchus, Andreas, and Asclepiades oppose the soul’s governing power, ibid., 670.—Chrysippus’s error concerning the soul, ibid., 653.—Cleanthes’s error concerning the soul, ibid., 693.—Errors concerning the substance of the soul: Hipparchus, Heraclitus, Hippo, Thales, Critias, Empedocles, Epicurus, Critolaus, the Peripatetics, the Stoics, Zeno, and Democritus, Tertullian, II, 653, 667.—Errors concerning the soul’s immortality: Epicurus, Seneca, Pythagoras, and Empedocles, Tertullian, II, 19.—Empedocles’s error concerning the location of the soul, ibid., 671.—Error concerning the condition of souls after death drawn from the *Acherontic Books*, Arnobius, V, 909.—Aristoxenus’s erroneous opinion concerning the soul, Lactantius, VI, 779.—Cicero taught the immortality of the soul without faithfulness, ibid., 410.—Dicaearchus’s error concerning the soul, which he says perishes with the body, ibid., 761.—Plato’s arguments are insufficient for proving the soul’s immortality, ibid., 762, 763, 764.—Epicurus says that the soul perishes with the body, St. Jerome, XXIII, 294.—Epicurus’s error concerning the soul’s immortality, St. Augustine, XXXII, 932.—The Epicureans’ error concerning the soul, which they say perishes with the body, id., XXVIII, 811.—Plato’s error concerning souls: Plato said that souls, having fallen from heaven, are thrust down into bodies, id., XXXII, 587; XXXIII, 718.—Pythagoras’s error concerning souls: Pythagoras said that souls, having fallen from heaven, are thrust down into bodies, id., XXIII, 718.—The Stoics’ error concerning the soul: the Stoics said that souls were from God’s own substance, XXXII, 718, 723.—Zeno’s error concerning the soul, which he said was mortal, ibid., 955.—The Stoics say that the soul is mortal, id., CXI, 414.—The Peripatetics’ error concerning the soul: they say that one part of the soul is eternal, but the rest mortal, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 415.—Epicurus says that the soul is nothing other than a body, ibid.—Varro says that the soul is the fire of the world, ibid.—Anaxagoras’s error concerning the soul, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 982.—Epicurus’s error concerning the soul, which he says is mortal, ibid., 977.—Pythagoras’s error concerning souls, ibid., 928.—Socrates’s error concerning the soul, which he believes to be God, ibid., 982.

ASTROLOGY.—The astrology of the mathematicians is reproved, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 442, 443.

[Col. 0938] ATOMS.—The doctrine of atoms defended by Epicurus, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 64.—According to Epicurus, chance masses minute particles together into an immense bulk, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 977.—The Peripatetics’ error concerning atoms, ibid., 858.

COURTIERS.—The flatteries of courtiers are reproved from Juvenal, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 482.

THE HIGHEST GOOD.—Aristippus’s error concerning the highest good, Lactantius, VI, 366, 760.—In what Aristotle placed the highest good, and what he understood by virtue, ibid., 370.—Dinomachus’s error concerning the highest good, ibid., 364.—Epicurus’s error concerning the highest good, ibid.—Herillus’s error concerning the highest good, ibid.—The error of the philosopher Hieronymus concerning the highest good, ibid.—The Peripatetics’ error concerning the highest good, ibid.—Zeno’s error concerning the highest good, ibid., 423.—The Academics’ error concerning the highest good, St. Augustine, XL, 625, 626, 627.

CERTAINTY.—Anaxagoras errs concerning certainty, Lactantius, VI, 424, 428.—Arcesilaus’s error concerning certainty, ibid., 359, 361.—According to Carneades, nothing is certain, just as there is no virtue, ibid., 595, 596.

CONCUPISCENCE.—The effects of concupiscence from Ovid, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 403.

BODY.—Zeno admitted nothing except the existence of bodies, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 955.

CORRECTION.—Archytas of Tarentum’s error concerning correction, Lactantius, VII, 132, 133.

CORRUPTION.—Socrates, corrupter of youth, Tertullian, I, 500.

CREATION.—Cicero’s error concerning the creation of the world, Lactantius, VI, 397.—Democritus’s error concerning creation, ibid., 760.—Epicurus’s error concerning the creation of animals, ibid., 316.—Homer’s errors concerning creation, Lactantius, VI, 131.

DRUNKENNESS.—Aristippus feasts and drinks to excess, Tertullian, I, 500.

WORSHIP DUE TO GOD.—Cicero’s error concerning the worship due to God, Lactantius, VI, 457.—Lucretius’s impiety, ibid., 265.—Philosophers eradicated the worship and honor due to God, id., VII, 113.—Plato impious, id., VI, 457.

CURIOSITY.—The curiosity of philosophers, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII.

GOD.—Errors concerning God. Socrates’s error concerning God, Tertullian, I, 500.—Thales errs concerning God, ibid.—Plato errs concerning God, ibid.—Errors of the Platonists concerning God, id., II, 19.—The Stoics erred concerning God, ibid.

Arnobius proves the falsity of the pagan gods from their historians, and cites Antias, Valerius, and Antiochus, Arnobius, V, 82.---From the disgraceful stories about the gods Arnobius proves the falsity of those gods, and mentions Apollodorus, ibid., 1050.---Arnobius refutes the false gods from the ridiculousness of their origin and number, and mentions Aristotle and Granius, ibid., 979; Caesius, ibid., 994; Cicero, ibid., 945; Censius, ibid., 991; Crates, ibid., 989.---The pagan gods were human beings according to Euhemerus, Ennius, Nicanor, Pellaeus, Leontes, Theodorus, Hippo, [Col. 0939] Diagoras, and Melius, ibid., 1062.---Disagreements among pagans concerning the number of the gods, from Ephorus, ibid., 989.---Plautus, Sophocles, and Euripides are mentioned concerning pagan errors in the worship of the gods, ibid., 1265.---The worship of the gods was forbidden also by Heraclitus, ibid., 1143.---Errors concerning the number and origin of the gods; on this matter Hesiod, Lucretius, Manilius, and the *Memorial Writings* are cited, ibid., 989, 951, 993, 1185.---Pagan disagreements concerning the gods’ origin and number; shameful things admitted in the worship of the gods; their ridiculous histories, vain occupations, and inconsistency, drawn from Mnaseas, Myrtilus, Varro, Nigidius, Homer, Epicharmus, Sophocles, Apollodorus, Panyassis, Polemon, Sosibius, Patroclus, Thurius, Plutarch, Philostephanus, Posidippus, Pindar, Timotheus the theologian, Valerius, Varro, and Constant., ibid., 988, 989, 991, 984, 1121, 1136, 1050, 1206, 1048, 1088, 1096, 995, 1009, 1019.---Anaxagoras’ error concerning God, Lactantius, VI, 134.---Anaximenes’ error concerning God, ibid.---Cleanthes’ error concerning God, ibid.---Diagoras’ error concerning the gods, ibid., 120.---Ennius’ ridiculous histories about the gods, ibid., 190.---Epicurus denies the gods, id., VII, 87.---Euhemerus’ ridiculous histories concerning the gods, id., VI, 174.---Homer’s ridiculous theology, ibid., 125.---Plato’s teaching concerning God is inadequate, ibid., 597.---The poets’ error concerning the gods, ibid., 159, 170, 171, 215.---Protagoras calls the gods into doubt, ibid., 120.---Pythagoras, a pantheist, ibid., 134.---The Stoics’ error concerning God’s anger, id., VII, 88.---The Stoics think that the stars are gods, id., VI, 278.---Thales’ error concerning God, ibid., 132.---Anaximenes thinks air to be God, St. Augustine, XXXII, 782; XXXIII, 743; or that gods are generated from air, id., XLI, 226. Anaxagoras thinks mind to be God, id., XXXIII, 442.---Democritus’ error concerning God, ibid., 445.---Diagoras, an atheist, id., XLIII, 360.---Epicurus denied the gods, id., XLI, 601.---Plato taught the worship of many gods, ibid., 225.---St. Augustine notes the ridiculous things Varro wrote about the gods, ibid., 178.---Zeno’s error concerning the gods, whom he said were born from fire, id., XXXIII, 955.---The theologians, among whom Dionysius the Stoic, said that the world is God, Rabanus Maurus, CXCI, 415.---Others, such as Thales of Miletus, maintained that mind is God, ibid.---Some, like Pythagoras, thought that the soul pervading all things and lucid was God, ibid.---Some thought that detached mind was God, ibid.---Some, including Maro, thought both spirit and mind to be God, ibid. The Epicureans admit a God who is idle and inactive, ibid.---The Stoics affirm that God is corporeal, ibid.---Epicurus said that God consists of atoms, ibid.---Pythagoras says that God consists of numbers, ibid.---The philosophers either did not know God, or knew him imperfectly, id., CLXXXIX, 812.---Cicero’s error concerning God, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 992.---Varro’s error concerning God, ibid., 990, 991. Varro thinks that there are as many gods as there are plagues, ibid.

**DISAGREEMENTS.**---The disagreements of philosophers, Lactantius, VI, 556, 357; St. Augustine, XXXIV, 122; XLI, 601.---Varro’s inconsistencies in his theology, id., XLI, 218.

**DIVINATIONS.**---The divinations of astrologers, St. Augustine, XXXII, 737; XL, 29.

**RICHES.**---Democritus’ error concerning riches, Lactantius, VI, 422.

**PAINS.**---Epicurus’ error concerning pains, St. Jerome, XXIV, 644.---Cicero’s error concerning pains, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 667, 668.

**UNIVERSAL DOUBT.**---The universal doubt of the Academics, St. Augustine, XLII, 1019, 1056.---The Academics’ universal doubt, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 414.---On universal doubt, Peter Abelard cites Aristotle, Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 1349.---The Academics’ universal doubt is refuted, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 1062.---The Academics doubted everything, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 638, 981.---Arcesilaus taught universal doubt, ibid., 990.---Cicero’s universal doubt, ibid., 992.---Zeno’s universal doubt, ibid., 981.

**HARSHNESS.**---Plato’s manner of dealing with Hermias, Tertullian, I, 500.

**EDUCATION.**---The Stoics’ error concerning the education of women and slaves, Lactantius, VI, 429.

**ERROR.**---Cicero did not turn peoples away from error, Lactantius, VI, 263, 264.---Homer is involved in many errors, ibid., 131.---The many errors found in Pythagoras, St. Augustine, XXXII, 589.

**FATE.**---The fate of the astrologers, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 1061.---Epicurus’ fate, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 977.---The Stoics introduce fated necessity, ibid., 976.

**HAPPINESS.**---Epicurus’ ridiculous overstatement concerning the happiness of the good, Lactantius, VI, 434.---The philosophers erred in locating happiness in this life, St. Augustine, XLI, 627, 628; XXXIII, 830, 667.---The Stoics’ error concerning happiness, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 812.---Zeno places supreme blessedness [Col. 0940] in the very practice of virtue, St. Augustine, XLII, 1019.

**GOOD FAITH (*bonne foi*).**---Anaxagoras, an unfaithful keeper of a deposit, Tertullian, I, 500.

**FORNICATION.**---Diogenes, a fornicator, Tertullian, I, 500.---Democritus, a fornicator, ibid.---Aristippus, a fornicator, Lactantius, VI, 393.

**FORTUNE.**---Cicero’s error concerning fortune, Lactantius, VI, 120.---Epicurus’ error concerning fortune, ibid.

**GLUTTONY.**---Tertullian reproaches the orator Hortensius, Ausidius Lurco, and Asinius Celer for gluttony, Tertullian, II, 1048.

**HERESIES.**---Pythagoras’ teaching, a source of heresies, St. Jerome, XXII, 1148.---Heresies also flowed from Zeno, ibid.---Heresies arise from philosophers, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 415, 416.

**MAN.**---Anaxagoras’ error concerning man’s end, Lactantius, VI, 371.---Dicaearchus’ error concerning man’s end, ibid., 404.

**HOSPITALITY.**---Cicero’s error concerning hospitality, Lactantius, VI, 663, 675.

**IDEAS.**---Innate ideas against Plato, Arnobius, V, 849.---Plato’s error concerning ideas, Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 1307.

**IGNORANCE.**---The ignorance of philosophers, Lactantius, VII, 736.---Philosophers fostered ignorance because, having found God, they did not make him known, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 415.

**IMPIETY.**---See *Worship Due to God*.

**THE IMPOTENCE OF PHILOSOPHERS.**---Plato, Cronius, and Numenius are cited, Arnobius, V, 825, 826.

**FOLLY.**---The cause of philosophers’ folly, Lactantius, VI, 664.

**INSOLENCE.**---Diogenes, insolent, Tertullian, I, 500.

**SHAMELESSNESS.**---The shamelessness of the Cynics, Lactantius, VI, 394; St. Augustine, XLI, 428.---The shamelessness of Diogenes the Cynic, St. Augustine, XLI, 428.---The Cynics’ shamelessness, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 415.---The shamelessness of the Gymnosophists, who philosophize naked throughout India, ibid.

**ANGER.**---The Stoics did not distinguish bad anger from good anger, Lactantius, VII, 129.

**FREEDOM.**---Cicero’s error concerning freedom, which he makes conformable to fate, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 992.

**EVILS.**---The Stoics’ error concerning evils, St. Augustine, XLI, 629, 630.

**MATTER.**---Zeno’s errors concerning matter, Tertullian, II, 19.---The Peripatetics’ error concerning the eternity of matter, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 858.

**THE WORLD.**---Aristotle taught the eternity of the world, Lactantius, VI, 315, 735, 736.---The philosophers’ errors concerning the world and the cause of those errors, ibid., 739.---Plato’s error concerning the eternity of the world, ibid., 780.---Anaximander’s error concerning infinite worlds, St. Augustine, XLI, 226.---Epicurus’ error concerning the constitution of the world. Epicurus says that the world consists of atoms, Severinus Boethius, LXIV [lacuna]. Plato’s error concerning the soul of the world, Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 1720.

**MUTILATION.**---The Stoics mutilated human beings in order to eliminate pleasures, Lactantius, VII, 689.

**NATURE.**---The Stoics’ error concerning nature, Lactantius, VI, 741.

**OCCUPATIONS.**---The vain occupations of philosophers, St. Jerome, XXVI, 504.

**OPTIMISM.**---Plato teaches optimism, Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 1326.

**PRAYER.**---The Peripatetics’ opinion concerning prayer, Severinus Boethius, LXIV, 406.

**SINS.**---Zeno maintained that all sins are equal, Lactantius, VI, 423.---The Academics’ error concerning the equality of all sins, St. Augustine, XL, 242.---The Stoics’ error concerning sins, ibid., 339.---The Stoics’ error concerning the equality of sins, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 414.---The Peripatetics said that all sins are equal, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 858.

**EXTERNAL PERCEPTION.**---Errors of the Academics, Heraclitus, Diocles, Empedocles, Plato, the Stoics, and the Epicureans concerning external perception, Tertullian, II, 674.---The Epicureans’ error concerning perception of truth, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 441.

**CYCLES.**---Epicurus’ error concerning cycles, St. Jerome, XXIII, 1020.

**PHANTASMS.**---The phantasms of the Stoics, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 641, 642.

**PHILOSOPHY.**---Philosophy, an insufficient rule for living well, Lactantius, VI, 117.---It does not impart true religion, ibid., 266.---The foolish thoughts of philosophy, ibid., 350.---Philosophy is not devoted to wisdom, ibid., 352, 353, 433.---Philosophy is useless for seeking truth and forming morals, ibid., 433, 520, 604.---Philosophy is destructive, ibid., 349.---Philosophy disturbs truth, id., VII, 77. No happiness is found in philosophy, id., VI, 383.---Philosophy’s incapacity to attain [Col. 0941] truth, ibid., 740.---Philosophy, an evil governor of states, ibid., 418.---Seneca’s error concerning philosophy’s authority, ibid., 390, 391.

**POETS.**---Poets are pernicious, Lactantius, VI, 549.

**THE PRINCIPLE OF THINGS.**---Errors concerning the principle of things: Heraclitus, Tertullian, II, 19.---Empedocles’ error concerning the principle of things, Lactantius, VI, 320.---Heraclitus’ error concerning the principle of things, ibid., 309.---Thales’ error concerning the principle of things, ibid., 132.---Anaximenes’ error concerning the principle of things, St. Augustine, XLI, 226.---Anaximander’s error concerning the principle of things, ibid.---Democritus’ error concerning the principle of things, id., XXXIII, 445.---Diogenes says that air is the principle of things, id., XLI, 226.---The Stoics’ error concerning the principle of things, ibid., 226, 582.

**TREACHERY.**---Hippias, a traitor, Tertullian, I, 500.

**PROVIDENCE.**---Errors concerning providence: first, those of Epicurus, Tertullian, II, 726; Lactantius, VI, 120, 401.---Epicurus denied providence, St. Augustine, XLI, 601.---The Epicureans’ error concerning providence, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 415.---Aristotle’s error concerning providence, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 932.---The Stoics deny providence, ibid., 447.

**THE STOICS’ PHYSICAL THEORY.**---Lactantius, VI, 185.

**RELIGION.**---Cicero’s error concerning the explanation of the word *religion*, Lactantius, VI, 536.---Epicurus abolishes all religion, id., VII, 96.---Socrates abolished all religion, ibid., 415, 416.---Philosophers erred concerning religion, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 126.

**RESURRECTION.**---The errors of all philosophers concerning the resurrection, Tertullian, II, 19.---The philosophers denied the resurrection of the flesh, St. Augustine, 1134; XLII, 902, 903.

**WISDOM.**---Cicero’s error concerning the origin of wisdom, Lactantius, VI, 387.---Lucretius’ error concerning the origin of wisdom, ibid., 386, 387.---Philosophy is neither wisdom nor the road to wisdom, ibid., 352, 353.---The Stoics’ error in saying that wisdom consists in knowledge, St. Augustine, XXXII, 874.---They also said that a person enjoys no wisdom unless perfect in it, id., XXXIII, 738.

**KNOWLEDGE.**---The Academics entirely abolished knowledge, Lactantius, VI, 355, 360, 604.---Socrates abolished knowledge, ibid., 355.---The Academics’ error concerning knowledge, St. Augustine, XXXII, 923.

[Col. 0942] **THE SENSES.**---The Epicureans’ error concerning the external senses, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 441.

**STARS.**---Plato maintains that the stars are animate, Severinus Boethius, LXIV, 123.

**SODOMY.**---Sodomitical philosophers, St. Jerome, XXIX, 47.

**THE SUPREME GOOD.**---What the supreme good consists in according to the Peripatetics, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 858.---Virtue is the supreme good according to the Stoics, ibid., 975.

**SOPHISTS.**---Sophistical philosophers, Lactantius, VI, 356.

**SUICIDE.**---The teaching of self-killing handed down by philosophers, Lactantius, VI, 407, 408.---Plato himself taught self-killing, ibid., 408, 409.

**PRIDE.**---The pride of philosophers, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 777; XXXII, 707.---Plato’s pride prevented him from indicating the way of salvation, id., XXXII, 747; XXXIII, 440.---Proud philosophers, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 559.

**TYRANNY.**---Pythagoras and Zeno seek tyranny, Tertullian, I, 500.---Lycurgus also seeks tyranny, ibid.---What the oppression of tyranny is according to Plato, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 554.

**VANITY.**---Cicero’s vanity, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 586.---The vanity of philosophers, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 559.

**TRUTH.**---Democritus’ error concerning truth, which he says is shut up in a well, Lactantius, VI, 439.---The Academics’ error concerning truth, St. Augustine, XXXII, 924.---The philosophers held truth captive in unrighteousness, ibid., 707.---The philosophers could not find the way of truth, id., XXXVIII, 776.---The philosophers’ subtle evasions for concealing the emptiness of their teaching, id., XXXIII, 431.

**VIRTUE.**---Plato, destroyer of all virtues, Lactantius, VI, 420.

**LIFE.**---Cicero’s error concerning life, Lactantius, VI, 412.

**THE LIFE TO COME.**---The Epicureans’ error concerning the future life, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 389; XXXIX, 1528; XXXIII, 668.

**PLEASURES.**---Epicurus’ teaching favors every pleasure, Lactantius, VI, 398, 404.---The Peripatetics were servants of pleasure, id., 370.---Epicurus’ teaching concerning all pleasures and supreme happiness, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 673, 977.

## NINETEENTH SERIES

[Col. 0941]

[PREFACE.]

Since no one can do good or turn away from evil unless supported by divine mercy, it is necessary to have recourse to God in prayer. Therefore, in this nineteenth Series we present indexes concerning prayer in general: namely, its necessity, excellence, effects, and various conditions; mental and vocal prayer; prayers customary in the Catholic Church; and especially the Lord’s Prayer.

[Col. 0941]

## CLXXIII. INDEX CONCERNING PRAYER IN GENERAL, IN WHICH THE NECESSITY AND CONDITIONS OF PRAYER, ITS EFFECTS, TIME AND PLACE, MENTAL AND VOCAL PRAYER, AND THE OBJECTS FOR WHICH ONE SHOULD PRAY, ETC., ARE DISCUSSED IN LOGICAL ORDER

### I. On the definition and division of prayer

**HILARY (St.).**---Prayer is a service suited to our weakness, IX, 538.---The various degrees of prayer, 639.---Three kinds of prayers, 348.

**AMBROSE (St.).**---What prayer, entreaty, petition, [Col. 0942] and thanksgiving are, XIV, 307.---Various kinds of prayers are enumerated, XVII, 843.

**JUVENCUS.**---On prayer, XIX, 64.

**JEROME (St.).**---Prayer is the movement of the mind, XXIII, 32.

**AUGUSTINE (St.).**---Prayer is a human being’s speech to [Col. 0943] God, XXXVI, 1028.---It is a sacrifice, 575.---Under the name of prayer are understood all the rules of holy desire, XLIV, 300.---Prayer is evidence of the necessity of grace, 314.---The clearest testimony to grace, XXXIII, 766.---When we pray, we say nothing other than: “Give what you command,” 154.---Prayer is twofold, inward and outward, XXXVI, 404.---How prayers differ from entreaties, XXXIII, 635.---Entreaties are made before what is upon the table begins to be blessed; prayers, while it is being blessed; petitions, when the people are blessed; and, after all these, thanksgivings, 636.---What prayer is, XXXIX, 1884; XL, 997.

**CASSIAN (St.).**---Prayers are those by which we offer or vow something to God, XLIX, 783, 784.---The four forms of prayer—entreaty, prayer, petition, thanksgiving—783 ff.

**PROSPER (St.).**---Right prayer is God’s gift, LI, 349.---To pray to God is a gift of spiritual grace, 79.

**EUGYPPIUS.**---Entreaties, prayers, petitions, thanksgivings, LXII, 867.

**FULGENTIUS (St.).**---The disposition to pray is God’s gift, LXV, 339.---No one can pray worthily or keep vigil unless the Holy Spirit has poured himself into that person, 185.---The very disposition for prayer cannot be possessed unless it has been divinely bestowed, 350.

**BENEDICT (St.).**---Prayer is the ascent of the soul from earthly things to heavenly things, the pursuit of things above, and desire for invisible things, LXVI, 329.---It is familiar conversation and union of a human being with God. It is the affection of a person cleaving to God, a certain familiar and devout colloquy, and the standing of an illuminated mind for enjoyment, as long as this is permitted, ibid.---It is the devotion of the mind—that is, its turning toward God through a devout and humble disposition: humble from consciousness of one’s own weakness, devout from consideration of divine mercy, ibid.

**CASSIODORUS.**---Prayer is the utterance of the mouth by which, bowed down, we set forth our vows, LXIX, 705.---Supplication is frequent and persistent entreaty brought forth from the secret depth of the heart, ibid.---There are two kinds of prayers, 706.

**GREGORY THE GREAT (St.).**---How prayer and supplication differ, LXXIX, 639.

**ALCUIN.**---Prayer is the soul’s sweet supplication, joined with compunction of heart, C, 587.

**RABANUS.**---Prayer is called a petition, CXI, 126.---It is the ascent of the soul from earthly to heavenly things, CX, 616.---Entreaty is a petition for sins, by which each person, compuncted over present or past offences, begs forgiveness, CXII, 590.---Prayers are those by which we offer something to God, ibid.---Petitions are those by which we plead for all human beings, for kings, and for all who are in high position. Thanksgivings are those which the mind offers to the Lord when it recalls God’s past benefits, when present benefits are fulfilled, or when it looks ahead to the future gifts, both what and how great they are, which he has prepared for those who love him, ibid.

**BRUNO (St.).**---Prayer is the utterance of the mouth by which, bowed down, we present our vows, CXLII, 169.---Supplication is frequent and persistent entreaty brought forth from the secret depth of the heart, ibid.

**JOHN THE CARTHUSIAN.**---One who prays has contrition and groaning, especially when sins are lamented; one who praises and gives thanks is filled with spiritual joy and gladness, CLIII, 721.

**BRUNO (St.) THE CARTHUSIAN.**---The meaning to be understood by entreaties, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings is shown, CLIII, 435.---Prayer is signified by incense, 374.

**RADULPHUS.**---Prayer is made only to obtain good things; entreaty, to remove evils, CLV, 1690.---Prayer is the devout disposition of the mind toward God, 1901.

**Life of the Fathers.**---Prayer is conversation with God, LXXIII, 520.

**HILDEBERT.**---Entreaties are made when, through adjurations, we ask to be delivered from evils, CLXXI, 573.---Prayers are made when we ask that certain good things be given to us; petitions, when we ask for others, 574.---Thanksgivings concern benefits bestowed, 161.

**GODEFRIDUS.**---We entreat when, for the necessary acquisition of virtues, we supplicate God with the continual sobs of prayers, CLXXIV, 72.---We pray when, in order to obtain forgiveness of sins, we implore God’s mercy, ibid.---We render thanksgivings when we preserve in true humility the gifts granted us, ibid.

**HUGH OF ST VICTOR.**---Prayer is the mind’s devotion—that is, its turning toward God through a humble and devout disposition, supported by faith, hope, and charity, CLXXVI, 979.---There are three forms of prayer: supplication, petition, and insinuation. [Col. 0944] Supplication is humble and devout prayer without a specified petition; petition is the uncertain statement of a specified request. Insinuation is the disclosure of one’s will by narration alone, without a request, ibid.---A petition is made in three ways: by entreating, by asking, or by simply petitioning, 980.---Prayer is threefold: speech without devotion; devotion without speech; speech with devotion, 751, 752.

**HERVAEUS.**---Entreaty is prayer accompanied by adjuration or solemn appeal; prayer in the simple sense is a request, CLXXXI, 1277.

**BERNARD (St.).**---Entreaty consists in a reverent disposition, CLXXXIII, 608; prayer, in a pure disposition; petition, in an expansive disposition and the breadth of confidence; thanksgiving, in sweetest devotion, ibid.

**THOMAS THE CISTERCIAN.**---Entreaties are made for the remission of sin; prayers for obtaining good; petitions for one’s neighbor; thanksgivings to God, CCVI, 306.

**GUNTHER.**---Catholic prayer is the regular and earnest imploring of divine mercy for the salvation of the soul or for those things that can benefit it, CCXII, 166.

### II. On the conditions of prayer

**TERTULLIAN.**---The attention of prayer must be free from every disturbance of mind, I, 1167.---What lawful prayer is, 1165, 1195.---Prayers must be nourished by fasts, 1244.---Some washed their entire body before every prayer, 1168.---The duties of prayer, 1164.

**CYPRIAN (St.).**---The conditions of prayer, IV, 240 ff.---Prayer should be peaceful and simple, 324.---When we call God Father, we ought to act as children of God, 526.---Prayer without works is ineffective, 589.---Let us consider that we stand under God’s gaze, 519.---Prayers are not to be shouted out during sacrifices, 522.---A petition should be commended to God modestly, ibid.---Prayer should, with discipline, contain quietness and modesty, 518.---Not the sound of the voice but mind and inward sense ought to pray, 538.---Prayers whose merits of works place them before God rise swiftly, 539.

**HILARY (St.).**---God hears prayers everywhere, but innocence alone merits being heard, IX, 348.---Those are reproved who, asking something of God, approach him as though from a duty owed, 544.---What contemptible prayers are, 348.---The good qualities of prayer, 391.---Let it not be unpeaceable, 938.---Pure prayer, 549.---One prays confidently who, while in the flesh, is a stranger to the flesh, 391.---With an outpouring of the heart, 395.

**AMBROSE (St.).**---How one should pray, XIV, 334; XV, 1509.---What virtues are required in prayer, XIV, 350.---What that illustrious prayer and groaning are which God does not despise, 1027.---Humility commends prayer, 328.---By praying, it draws divine aid to itself, XV, 1429.---With bent knees the Lord’s displeasure is softened and grace is invited, XIV, 271.---If we pray with speech, let us also pray compassionately in mind, XV, 1260.---A good life makes prayer fly and gives spiritual wings to petitions, by which the prayer of the saints is borne up to God, 1512.---The prayer of the faithful, nourished by apostolic food, grows rich, 351.---When you pray, pray for great things—that is, for eternal, divine, and heavenly things, XV, 1472.---God hears only what he judges worthy of his gifts, ibid.---Why God frequently does not grant what is requested, 1722.---The order of good prayer, XVI, 306.---The first prayer should contain praise of God, the second supplication, the third petition, the fourth thanksgiving, 459.---Prayer should begin with God’s praise and end in it, ibid.---That the mind may pray well, the Spirit goes before it and leads it in the right way, lest carnal matters, lesser matters, or matters even beyond its powers creep in, 1082.---If you wish your prayer to be effective, lift pure hands through innocence, 458.---Let your conduct speak what you pray; let faith help and works commend it, 358.---One should pray more in secret than with loud cries, 457.---In prayer, much modesty is pleasing and beneficial, 44.---To weep in prayer belongs to virtue, 1314.---Let not place commend prayer, but a devout mind, XVII, 51.---The mind should be peaceful in prayer, 469.

**CHROMATIUS (St.).**---In prayer to God there is no need of a cry of the voice, since we know that he beholds the secrets of the heart, but of the cry of faith and the devotion of a religious mind, XX, 358.---There should not be a multitude of words, ibid.---The prayer of the self-boasting Pharisee is reproved; the humble and submissive Publican went down justified, ibid.

**JEROME (St.).**---One should pray with the body bent and the mind raised to the Lord, XXII, 592.---One should pray in secret and with the chamber of the heart shut, XXIV, 564.---What prayer ought to be like, XXVI, 220.---Perseverance in prayer is commended, XXIV, 754.---The prophet’s persevering prayer is noted, 604.

[Col. 0945] **AUGUSTINE (St.).**---The best prayer is a just life, XLI, 653.---How quickly the prayers of those who do good works are received, XXXVI, 482.---Faith precedes prayer, XXXIII, 878.---If faith fails, prayer perishes, XXXVIII, 655.---Faith, hope, and charity lead the one praying to God, XXXIII, 504.---Let prayer always fast from hatred and always be nourished by love, XXXVIII, 1044.---Faith in Christ is the means of obtaining, XXXV, 1328.---A person does not ask in Christ’s name if he thinks of Christ what ought not to be thought, or asks for something not pertaining to salvation, 1896.---That which pertains to the order of salvation is asked in the Savior’s name, XXXV, 1852.---Prayer is not righteous except through Christ, XXXVII, 1436.---We pray to him, through him, in him, 1082.---Suitable postures for suppliants: to bend the knees, stretch out the hands, and lie prostrate on the ground, XL, 597.---To strike the earth with the forehead, XXXVIII, 1419.---One should pray perseveringly, XXXVI, 801.---Persistence in prayer is commended, XXXVII, 1539.---We ought to hunger for God and beg at the door of his presence in prayers, 1895, 1896.---The prayers of the righteous are with tears and groaning, XXXVIII, 195.---The groaning of one who prays, XXXVI, 224.---What pure prayer is, XLIV, 302, 304.---The two wings of prayer are fasting and almsgiving, XXXVI, 482.---By their prayer the humble reach God, XXXVIII, 267.---Let prayer be chaste, so that we desire not what cupidity seeks but what charity seeks, 1044.---A heart that rightly asks, knocks, and seeks must be devout, 568.---Life knocks; to life it is opened, ibid.---One should pray not with a resounding voice but with conscience crying to God, XXXIX, 2281.---It is more beneficial to pray briefly and frequently than once at excessive length, unless inspired devotion prolongs the prayer without the knowledge of the person praying, XXXII, 1456.---What prayer ought to be like, 1316.---Humility is necessary for one who prays, XLV, 1865.---How we ought to be disposed before and during prayer, XL, 1057.---Prayer should be persevering, XXXIX, 1909.---What must be observed in praying, XXXVII, 1351.---How one should pray, XXXIV, 1274.---We do not know what we ought to pray for, XLIV, 531.---The person praying must avoid two things: asking either what ought not to be asked or from one from whom it ought not to be asked, XXXVIII, 378.---One must pray as Christ taught, XXXVII, 1352.---Prayer ought to begin with the praise of God, 1882.---A multitude of words in prayer must be avoided, XXXVIII, 358.---What it means to pray in closed chambers, XXXII, 1195.---When you pray, close the door lest the tempter enter, XXXVII, 1834.---Great concentration in prayer expresses the great affection of the one praying, 1585.---One who grieves that his prayer is lukewarm, cold, and almost nonexistent already prays, XL, 127.---Whom God hears when they pray, XXXVII, 1390.---Who can confidently expect to receive what he asks, XLIV, 311.---Those who remain in Christ receive what they ask, XXXV, 1842.---God hears the poor alone, XXXVIII, 864.---Whoever wishes to be heard by God should first hear him, 126.---People do not receive what they ask because they ask wrongly, XXXV, 1824.---Sometimes God, in anger, gives what you ask, and God, in favor, denies what you ask, XXXVIII, 1567; XLIII, 429.---God in anger granted some impatient people what they asked, XXXIII, 173.---Many are heard, and in many ways—not only Christians, but also pagans, Jews, and heretics, XLIII, 429.---How the prayers of the wicked are heard, XXXV, 2024.---Many are heard by God with their mouths closed, and many are not heard amid great outcries, XXXVII, 1604.---God hears some and not others according as he knows it to be expedient for each, 1088.---One who asks superfluously is heard without God’s favor, XXXVIII, 203, 498.---God does not hear prayers for temporal things, so that we may understand that eternal things are to be desired from him, XXXVI, 438.---A person who would make bad use of what he wishes to receive does not receive it, through God’s merciful intervention, XXXV, 1824.---God is a Father and does not give his children what they wrongly desire, XXXVII, 1899.---One should not ask for anything as fixed, but for what God knows to be expedient for us, XXXVI, 624.---When we love what God wishes us to love, he will undoubtedly give it to us, 202.---God may perhaps delay giving something, but leaves no one hungry, XXXV, 1557.---If God does not give immediately, he exercises the seeker; he does not despise the petitioner, ibid.---He wishes our desire to be exercised through prayers, so that we may be able to receive what he prepares to give, XXXIII, 502.---The faithful person prays for many things according to this age and is not heard; but is always heard with respect to eternal life, XXXVI, 718.---Whose prayers God hears or rejects, XL, 1041.---God refuses Saul the forgiveness which he grants to David when the latter begs for it, because the disposition of heart is not the same in each, XXXV, 2325.

**CASSIAN (St.).**---How attention and devotion are attained in prayer, XLIX, 839.---Brief and frequent prayer is acceptable to God, 817, 818.---Prayer requires the deepest silence, 99.---How it should be made in secret and in hiding, 800.---What it ought to be like according to the judgment of St. Antony, [Col. 0946] 807.---Perseverance, or constancy, in prayer is required, 773.---Why our prayers are not always heard, 909.

**PROSPER (St.).**---Prayer not made through Christ cannot blot out sin, but itself becomes sin, LI, 303.---How we ask for what we have received, ibid.---That the Church’s prayers are not heard on behalf of all must be referred to God’s hidden judgments, 665.---Prayers that ask what the one petitioned wishes are promptly granted, 379.

**PETER CHRYSOLOGUS (St.).**---On perseverance in prayer, LII, 309, 310, 311.---The best prayer is joined with fasting and almsgiving. These three must be combined, 319 ff.

**SALVIAN.**---What prayer ought to be like, LIII, 65.

**LEO THE GREAT (St.).**---The condition of prayer, LIV, 294, 304.---Why God delays hearing those who pray, LV, 74.

**MAXIMUS OF TURIN (St.).**---By what qualities prayer excels, and with what virtues it should be joined, LVII, 499.---The example of the Canaanite woman teaches that one must persevere in prayer, 745.

**LAURENTIUS OF NOVARA (St.).**---One should not make noise in prayer, nor scatter words with confused and uncontrolled voice, LXVI, 122.---One must cry out, not with the voice but with the mind, for God hears even those who are silent, 123.---If you are in the public square, pray within yourself; if you are before a judge, pray; if you are in the bath, pray: there too is a temple. The sea is before you and Pharaoh follows behind you: pray, ibid.

**BENEDICT (St.).**---For praying well, sincere purity of heart is required, LXVI, 330.---One must flee worldly business and mortify passions and affections; a suitable place for prayer must be sought, remote and secluded from every disturbance, ibid.---The utmost attention is required, ibid.---Prayer should be brief and pure, 480.

**CASSIODORUS.**---Who truly invokes God, LXX, 102.---Who prays perfectly, 117.---How we always pray before God, 1078.---The cause cries out to God more than the tongue, 220.---When we ask wisely and unwisely, 153.---Prayer should proceed from a humble, gentle, and sincere heart, 1008.---It is one thing to ask by testing, another by confessing, 358.---The cry of the faithful is the disposition of a devout mind, 887.---No one cries to the Lord unless with the whole disposition of the heart that person directs his petition to him, ibid.---The voice of supplication is purity of prayer, 993.---If you invoke God without devotion, you ask for judgment, not forgiveness, 539.---A fault common and especially idle among those who pray, 274.---God rejects those who deceitfully ask contrary to his commands, 840.

**GREGORY OF TOURS (St.).**---Persistent prayer pleases God, LXXI, 528.---It should be made in retirement, 1068.

**GREGORY THE GREAT (St.).**---An unclean mind is unfit for prayer, LXXV, 935.---Whose prayer is accursed, 936.---In prayer the mind should wipe away the remembrance of its guilt with tears, ibid.---Before prayer, unclean and earthly thoughts must be banished, ibid.---Prayer obtains nothing unless injuries have been forgiven, 1107.---Prayer in which God is not sought is more quickly wearied of, ibid.---Action is supported by prayer, and prayer by action, LXXVI, 42.---What true prayer is, 1088.---When prayer may be called pleasing to God, LXXV, 915.---Before prayer one must consider what in prayer may be reproved, 936.---How greatly attention benefits prayer, LXXVI, 238.---Prayer must be joined with good action, ibid.---God wishes to be prayed to persistently, 1084.---The Lord placed the condition of mercy upon the ordinance of petition, LXXV, 360.---Bitter groans, not composed words, make true prayer, 702.---Prayer seasoned with love of one’s neighbor, especially of one’s enemy, is heard more quickly, 760.---The tears of prayer are sacrificial offerings, 816.---The compunction of prayer conceived from love of God is compared to smoke from aromatic spices, 1071.---How few pray as they ought, 1208.---Before prayer one must forgive one’s debtors, 1209.---For prayer to reach God, it must rise from the depths of humility, LXXIX, 632.---Prayer should be accompanied by good works, 513.---One must persevere in prayer, 633.---Those pure and simple in heart, devoted to silence, are readily heard by God, LXXVII, 260.---Why God hears prayers in small and insignificant matters, 197.---Our mouth is heard by God in prayer all the less as it is more defiled by foolish speech, 256.---Our prayers are raised more swiftly to the ear of the Lord’s mercy insofar as the ardor of charity sharpens those prayers which are in turn poured out for us, 811.

ISIDORE (Saint).—One must never pray without groaning, LXXXIII, 673.—Let the mind preserve after prayer the character in which it presents itself during prayer. Prayer profits nothing if one again commits the very thing for which pardon must again be sought, ibid.—Prayer is pure when, at its proper time, worldly cares do not intervene, [Col. 0947] ibid. A mind which, before prayer, being devoid of God, busies itself with unlawful thoughts will, when it comes to prayer, immediately encounter the images of things which it has just been thinking, ibid.—The soul must be cleansed and separated from thoughts of temporal things, so that the pure gaze of the heart may be directed truly and simply to God, 674.—Just as no medicine benefits a wound if the iron is still in it, so the prayer of one whose pain still remains in the mind, or hatred in the breast, profits nothing, ibid.—The prayers of some are answered more slowly, so that, being delayed, they may be stirred up more strongly and enriched with greater rewards, LXXXIII, 677.—Whenever we who pray are not quickly heard, let us set our own deeds before our eyes, ibid.—People are not heard because of much speaking, 678.

ALCUIN.—If prayer is to be effective, it must be offered to God through Christ the mediator, C, 1135.

AGOBARD (Saint).—Prayer must be made with complete confidence and hope, CIV, 286.—Without anger, dispute, or hesitation, ibid.

CHRISTIAN DRUTHMAR.—It is the Lord’s command that, with the thought enclosed in the breast and the lips compressed, we pray to him, CVI, 1313.—Christians need not speak much in their prayers, 1314.

RABANUS.—Let us not frame our prayers to the Lord in much speaking, but let us believe that we are heard by him through compunction of heart and the pouring forth of tears, CX, 13.—Prayer must be performed without ceasing and with preparation, ibid.

WALAFRID STRABO.—Let us know that we are heard, not in a clamorous voice, but in tears and the intention of the heart, CXIV, 932.—Whoever in prayer asks something other than what he ought, or prays in a manner other than that indicated by the teacher of humility, either does not know how to pray or makes less progress than he might, ibid.—Whoever, after prayer has been completed, immediately rushes without reflection either into an evil habit or into new crimes loses the fruit of prayer, ibid.—Some, while praying, beat their breasts with their fists, strike their heads, lower their voices with feminine thinness, and do not fear to disturb others nearby by words or deeds, and to show themselves blameworthy, I, 933.—In praying, one is forbidden to resemble hypocrites, 99.

HAYMO.—When we stand for prayer, we must keep watch and devote ourselves to prayers with our whole heart, CXVIII, 898.—Every carnal and worldly thought must depart; the breast must be closed against the adversary and opened only to God, and must not allow the enemy of God to approach it at the time of prayer, ibid.—If we wish to present some petition to powerful people, we do not presume to do so except with humility and reverence; how much more, then, must we make supplication to the Lord God of all things with every humility and the devotion of purity, 899.—Prayer poured forth without fraternal hatred is acceptable to God, ibid.

PASCHASIUS RADBERT (Saint).—Do not pray in order to be seen by people; rather, pray within, with the door shut, CXX, 277.—Let prayer be made, not merely with a noise of words, but so that what we seek may be obtained inwardly through faith, hope, and charity, 275.

ISIDORE MERCATOR.—One must pray with an upright countenance, CXXX, 583.

ADALGER.—Prayer ought to be brief, CXXXIV, 928.—Whoever in prayer beseeches the Lord for the healing of his own soul or for the sins of others undoubtedly ascends the mountain in order to pray, 929.—Just as it is impossible for anyone to see his face in troubled water, so a soul not cleansed from alien thoughts cannot contemplate God, ibid.

RATHERIUS.—He asks wrongly who asks not for what the Lord commands, but rather for what he forbids, CXXXVI, 697.—One must pray unceasingly, with confidence, and never without groaning, 689.—Wanderings of the mind in prayer are exceedingly harmful, 697.—Unless you help the poor person crying out to you, God will not hear you when you pray, 692.

BRUNO (Saint).—One must pray without anger—that is, without hatred of one’s neighbour—and without distrust, CLIII, 438.

RADULPHUS.—One must ask with faith, confidence, and simplicity, CLV, 1524.—Let us ask all things for God’s sake, 1691.—With faith, desire, perseverance, and humility, let us believe that God is able to give the eternal good which we ask, 1802.—Let us not pray with lips alone, not lukewarmly, and not with much speaking, ibid.—With perseverance: for God does not despise the prayers of the poor; with humility, reckoning ourselves unclean dogs, often returned to the vomit of our filth, ibid.—Prayer ought to be devout, 1901.—That which is made with the heart alone, even if not with the lips, is acceptable to God. Susanna, though silent, is said to have cried out because of the vehemence of her mind’s intention, and to have been heard by God, ibid.—Prayer made with lips alone is not acceptable before God, ibid. We keep watch well in prayers if we keep watch not only in body but also in mind and works, 1930.—Whoever keeps watch in prayer with the body alone, but sleeps in sin by deed or mind, [Col. 0948] must be said not to be watching but sleeping, ibid.

GUIBERT.—God weighs not the words of prayer but the mind, CLVI, 628.

GOFFRIDUS.—Whoever entreats God with the mouth while his heart thinks upon worldly things has his prayer rejected by God, CLVII, 196.

ANSELM OF LAON.—In praying, the false intention of the Gentiles must be removed, CLXII, 1304.—Much speaking must be avoided, ibid.

BRUNO OF SIGNI (Saint).—Wherever you pray, if you pray in order to be seen by people, your prayer is not received, CLXV, 114.—If you wish to pray well, enter into your chamber; return to the heart. This is the chamber in which prayer is contained and in which God himself rests, ibid.—Pray there; speak there, where both what you say and to whom you speak are present. Shut the door: for he to whom you pray has no need of the sound of the mouth or of the cry of the voice, ibid.—He looks upon the heart and sees in secret; he attends not to the composition of words but to compunction of heart, ibid.—A prayer is heard not because it is long, but because it is made with a devout affection of mind, from a contrite heart and an afflicted spirit, ibid.

RUPERT.—There are three modes of prayer: first, when prayer is extended from the affection of divine inspiration; second, that the Lord hears not in a clamorous voice or much speaking but in contrition of heart, and that prayer ought to be brief and pure; third, when one prays inwardly with closed prayer, not only without a clamorous voice but also without movement of the lips, CLXVIII, 1427.—God is not moved by ornate and polished prayer, 1423.—Long prayer, if made with affection, is praiseworthy, 1424.—Faithful prayer touches God’s heart powerfully, 420.

HILDEBERT.—True prayer is a bitter groan with compunction, CLXXI, 349.—One does not cease praying who does not cease loving, ibid.—Confession must precede prayer, 568.—Prayer without fasting and almsgiving is not true; for these are its two wings to heaven, ibid.—One must ask urgently and perseveringly, 571.—For prayer to obtain its request, it must have three things: asking, seeking, and knocking, 574.—He asks wrongly who asks for things not conducive to salvation, ibid.—To ask for an enemy’s death is a mad prayer, 576.—Forgiveness of injuries is the chief condition of prayer, ibid.—For prayer to obtain its request, three things are necessary: prayer, good life, and perseverance, 372.—Prayer ought to be modest, pure, ample, and devout, 681.—Let the heart be lifted up, lest it decay upon the earth, 1160.

GODEFRIDUS.—If, at the time of prayer, the heart scattered among many things has not departed from us—indeed, if the voice of the mouth agrees with the lips of the heart—then we shall truly deserve to be heard by the Lord and shall obtain the effect of our petition, CLXXIV, 72.—One must ask God with humility and patience, 356.—Prayer must be intent upon good works, 550.—It must be made with the mind recollected, 750.—And attentively, 944.—Reconciled with one’s brother, 945.—And above all for spiritual things, 838.—And heavenly things, 945.—And not for oneself alone who prays, 946.—Without interruption, which is accomplished through good intention, 725.

HUGH OF SAINT VICTOR.—Our miseries and divine mercy furnish us with the occasion and ground for praying to God, CLXXVI, 977.—Prayer is made in four ways: with a modest affection, CLXXVII, 760; with a pure affection, when the sinner now approaches on his own account and confesses with his own mouth; with an ample affection, when it is made not only for oneself but for others; with confidence of heart, when it is offered without hesitation, ibid.

HERVAEUS.—He prays in the flesh, not in the spirit, who prays with a polluted mind, CLXXXI, 1277.

BERNARD (Saint).—Every prayer is lukewarm which inspiration has not preceded, CLXXXII, 987.—Care must be taken lest prayer be too timid, rash, or lukewarm, CLXXXIII, 178.—A prayer that is faithful, humble, and fervent will undoubtedly penetrate heaven, ibid.—Purity of intention and continence are necessary for one who prays, 809.—Likewise, withdrawal and secrecy, 983.—Prayer especially requires watchfulness, 609.—The union of prayer and fasting, 177.—Persevering prayer is necessary for the grace of the Holy Spirit, 322.—One praying must consider three things: what he asks, him of whom he asks, and himself who asks, 734.—Before prayer, the soul must be prepared, CLXXXIV, 1271.—He prays truthfully who thinks of nothing else in his heart. The judge is more quickly bent toward prayer if the sinner is corrected from his wickedness, ibid.—It is better to pray with the silence of the heart than with words alone without intention of mind. Let prayer be humble, joined to reading and to work, 325, 1252, 176.—Fervour and constancy in prayer are necessary, 39.—Sorrow renders prayer fruitless, 1220.

ROBERT PULLUS.—Prayer must proceed from a contrite and humbled heart, CLXXXVI, 915.—It happens that, though we multiply prayers, God does not hear because our hands are full of blood, 916.

[Col. 0949] ADAM OF SCOTLAND.—It is necessary that, before the very time of prayer, the heart be prepared from every emptiness of phantasms, CXCVIII, 763.—If we wish our prayer to breathe a sweet fragrance to God, we must cast away vain or wicked thoughts, 764.—Let one who prays carefully attend in mind to who it is that prays, who he is to whom he prays, what it is for which he prays, and how he prays, ibid.—One must pardon those sinning against us, 765.

MARTIN (Saint) OF LEÓN.—Let prayer be so pure, so devout, and so removed from every worldly tumult that it may obtain salvation for those infirm in mind and body, remission for sinners, and eternal blessedness for all the faithful, CCIX, 313.—Whoever prays truthfully and devoutly speaks with God, ibid.

ALAN OF LILLE.—We pray vainly if we do not have confidence of hope, CCX, 168.—One must ask devoutly, so that prayer may be formed rightly; perseveringly, so that the intention may be firmly rooted; one must beware of rancour of mind, lest wicked thoughts mingle themselves in, ibid.

GUNTHER.—If the one who asks is not faithful, he is neither said to pray nor to be thought worthy of being heard, because apart from faith God can neither be prayed to nor hear one who prays, CCXII, 156.—If one praying asks anything other than good, he is neither praying nor worthy of being heard, because prayer concerns only good things, ibid.—Moderation is necessary for one praying, because a stuffed belly and swollen stomach cannot direct subtle and pure prayer, 206.—Chastity is necessary, so that prayer may be presented pure and clean to God, because nothing is more shameful than to pollute the purity of prayer with the foulness of lust. Humility must attend one who prays, ibid.

INNOCENT III.—How one ought to pray, CCXVII, 565, 566.

III.—On the Necessity of Prayer.

TERTULLIAN.—Prayer is necessary to human beings at every moment, II, 926.

CYPRIAN (Saint).—Continual prayer is necessary, IV, 522.

HILARY (Saint).—Prayer is necessary for endurance of passions, IX, 569.—For attaining knowledge of the heavenly commands, 568.—Against temptations, 409.

AMBROSE (Saint).—Prayer is greatly necessary, XVII, 159.

JUVENCUS.—One ought to pray, XIX, 139.

JEROME (Saint).—The necessity of prayer, XXV, 399.

AUGUSTINE (Saint).—The necessity of prayer, XLIV, 151, 317, 318.—It is asserted against the Pelagians, XL, 443.—Prayer is necessary for those not led by grace, XLIV, 918.—For a person, not only that he himself may be forgiven, but also that he may not sin, 256.—That we may not enter into temptation, XXXIII, 990.—Prayer reminds us that we need the Lord’s help, lest we place in ourselves the hope of living well, XXXIII, 990.—God’s help must be invoked, XXXVIII, 895.—Prayer is necessary not because of what we were, but because of what we shall be, XLIV, 531.—Prayer and thanksgiving are necessary, XXXIII, 851, 856.

PROSPER (Saint).—Although God knows what is necessary for us, we must not therefore refrain from praying, LI, 77.

LEO THE GREAT (Saint).—Prayer is necessary against the force of temptation, LIV, 327.—God commands that recourse be had to him, 458.—The necessity of prayer, LVI, 456.—Even saints need prayer in which they ask: “Forgive us our debts,” 488, 489.

EUGYPPIUS.—Why one should pray although God knows what is necessary for us, LXII, 1031.

BENEDICT (Saint).—Just as breath is always necessary for us for the life of the flesh, so continual prayer is altogether necessary for the health of the mind, LXVI, 329.—I would more readily believe a human being to subsist without a soul than a perfect religious person without prayer, ibid.

SMARAGDUS.—God’s help must be sought in prayer, CII, 770.

BENEDICT (Saint) OF ANIANE.—We need prayer to obtain God’s gifts, CIII, 724.

SEDULIUS SCOTUS.—Where human frailty is insufficient, God’s help must be implored by prayers, 113.

JONAS.—The more sharply we are shaken in prayer by the adversities of the world and suffer the heavier tumults of carnal thoughts, the more ardently and vigorously we must persist in prayer, CVI, 145.—It is shown how much we must persist in prayer, ibid.

HAYMO.—Just as it is not fitting for a soldier to go into battle without weapons, so it is not expedient for a Christian person to proceed anywhere without prayer, CXVIII, 900.—Whatever a Christian begins, let him first direct prayer to God; whatever he completes, let him also complete it with prayer, ibid.

ISIDORE MERCATOR.—One must keep watch in prayers, CXXX, 15.

[Col. 0950] PETER OF CELLE.—Prayer is necessary to blot out the past and guard against the future, CCII, 1129.

ALAN OF LILLE.—One must devote oneself to prayers, CCX, 168.—Just as it is not fitting for a soldier to go out to battle without weapons, so it is not expedient for any Christian to proceed without prayer, ibid.

IV.—On the Effects of Prayer.

TERTULLIAN.—Prayer leads the spirit to God, II, 926.—Whoever prays is near heaven, ibid.—Prayer alone conquers God, I, 1195.—It washes away sins, repels temptations, extinguishes persecutions, consoles the faint-hearted, delights the high-minded, guides travellers, and calms waves, 1196.—It is the wall of faith, our arms and weapons against the devil, who watches us from every side, ibid.

LACTANTIUS.—The efficacy of devout prayers, VII, 596, 599.

HILARY (Saint).—The power of prayer against ignorance, IX, 951.—God’s protection granted to the prayer of faith, 392.—Prayer to God in temptations is the chief part and hope of salvation, 646.—It is the teaching of our hope that God, when prayed to, both has mercy and saves, 544.

AMBROSE (Saint).—Where prayer is present, the Word is present; greed is put to flight and lust departs, XVI, 252.—Through the prayers and merits of prophets, heavenly aid often came to the fathers, 249.—Pardon for graver sins must be reserved for the prayers of the righteous, 482.—Simple prayer is a sacrifice, 1163.—Prayer, tears, and fasts are the wealth of a good debtor, 518.—What a good shield prayer is, 1217.—God bends himself down to us, so that our prayer may ascend to him, 1393.—The power of prayer is wondrous, XVII, 21.—The intention of God when threatening is tempered by the modesty of most humble prayer, 977.—Diligent prayers move the judge’s mind to grant mercy, 453.

SEDULIUS.—The power of prayer, XIX, 691.

JEROME (Saint).—Every prayer and supplication draws forth the Creator’s mercy, XXIII, 579.—The efficacy of prayer, XXVI, 616.

AUGUSTINE (Saint).—The fruit of prayer, XXXIX, 1889; XL, 1057.—The devil is fought and conquered by prayer, XXXIX, 1797.—The prayer of the righteous is the key of heaven, 1849.—Whoever knows how to pray rightly truly knows how to live rightly, ibid.

CASSIAN.—Understanding of the Scriptures is attained more through prayer than through study, XLIX, 247.

PROSPER (Saint).—We have confidence that God will hear us, because he did not spare his own Son for us, LI, 329.

PETER CHRYSOLOGUS (Saint).—The devil fears those who pray, LII, 226.

MAXIMUS (Saint).—How effective prayer to God is, LVII, 465.

PAULINUS OF NOLA (Saint).—The prayer of the poor penetrates the clouds, LXI, 215.

FULGENTIUS (Saint).—Prayer to God washes away the sins of the righteous, LXV, 596.—It asks for the remedy of healing, 339.—Humble prayer merits divine help, ibid.

BENEDICT (Saint).—Prayer is the preservation of the world, reconciliation with God, mother and again daughter of tears, propitiation for sins, etc., etc., LXVI, 329.

CASSIODORUS.—By prayer we are brought into God’s presence, LXX, 897.—The words of prayer enter into the Lord’s sight like a kind of person, 621.—A continual remedy against sins is to beseech the Lord without ceasing, 999.—The Lord receives holy prayer as a most sweet fragrance, 1000.—By prayer the Lord’s wrath is held back, pardon is procured, punishment is escaped, and an abundance of rewards is obtained, 643.—Prayer speaks with the Lord and converses with the Judge; it makes present to itself him whom it cannot see, and through it appeases him whom it greatly provokes by its deeds, ibid.—Thus he saves the devout so as to make them blessed, while receiving the guilty, ibid.—A human being cries out so that God may not be silent, 193.—God regards good prayers as something delightful, 1003.—Prayer frees us from faults, reconciles the Judge’s mind, cleanses sins, and mercy cannot fail one who prays, 999.

GREGORY OF TOURS (Saint).—Divine light appears to one who prays, LXXI, 841.

LIVES OF THE FATHERS.—Prayer is a foretaste of future blessedness, LXXIII, 520.—It avails against the devil, 290.—A remedy against temptations of the flesh, 579.—It extinguishes shameful thoughts as water extinguishes fire, 806.—It must be employed against phantasms, ibid.—It quickly corrects the mind, 942.—It is medicine for one infirm on God’s way, 1017.—It overcomes temptations, 1055.

GREGORY THE GREAT (Saint).—Whence the efficacy of our prayer is suspect to us, LXXVI, 42.—If we do what God commands, we shall obtain what we ask, ibid.—God hears not words but the desires of the heart, [Col. 0951] 238.—Prayer is called a little rod of smoke, 1071.—Through insistence in prayer God is fixed in the heart, and the lost light of the mind is restored, 1083.—The power of monks’ prayer, by which the youth Theodore, oppressed by a demon at the point of death, is set free, 1159.—Wonderful effects of prayer, LXXVII, 257.

ISIDORE (Saint).—Prayer is poured out for the healing of sins, LXIII, 679.—We are cleansed by prayers, ibid.

PAULINUS (Saint).—The evil and foul thoughts of this age are driven from the soul by pure prayers and holy vigils, XCIX, 225.—Prayer is the fortification of the soul. Through most pure prayers, everything useful is granted us by the Lord, and all harmful things are escaped, ibid.—Just as the flesh is nourished by bodily foods, so the inward person is nourished and fed by divine sayings and prayers, ibid.

BENEDICT (Saint) OF ANIANE.—Prayer is the help of our life, conversation with God, forgetfulness of earthly things, and the way to heaven, CIII, 803.—It is the mother of all virtues, ibid.

WALAFRID STRABO.—The power of the righteous person’s entreaty is demonstrated by the example of Elijah, who by one prayer withheld rain from the earth and denied its fruits to mortals, CXIV, 680.

HAYMO.—Prayer looses Peter’s chains, CXVIII, 898.—It enlarged the boldness of Paul’s preaching, extinguished the fiery furnace, shut the mouths of lions, restrained sedition, opened Paradise, unbarred the gates of heaven, made the barren woman fruitful, and justified the publican, ibid.—Frequent prayer removes the devil’s darts, overcomes his weapons, and extinguishes the flames of vices. It is a great fortification of the soul. Through most pure prayers everything useful is granted us by the Lord, and all harmful things are without doubt escaped, ibid.

PETER DAMIAN.—How great is the efficacy of prayer, CXLV, 230.

RADULPHUS.—Prayer obtains from God forgiveness of sins, the bestowal of graces, the turning away of adversities, and consolation amid prosperity, CLV, 1901.—It drives away the devil, appeases God’s wrath, directs our way, and leads us to God’s kingdom. Its power is shown by Elijah’s example, ibid.—Through prayer we drive away the assaults of demons or vices and obtain virtues, the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and eternal blessedness, 1929.

GUIBERT.—By prayer wandering sensuality is restrained, CLVI, 153.

SIGEBERT.—A spring is brought forth through the prayer of saints, CLX, 762.

IVO OF CHARTRES.—By prayer vices are restrained and virtues nourished, CLXI, 486.—Through the practice of prayer one will be able to benefit those to whom one is joined in charity, ibid.

RUPERT.—Prayer makes us conquer spiritual enemies, CLXVII, 669.—Prayer is a human being’s strongest fortress, CLXX, 344.—The prayer of the devout is effective with God, 353.

HILDEBERT.—Prayer is a sweet vehicle on the way, a faithful forerunner to God, CLXXI, 604.—By prayer enemies are conquered and salvation is gained, 573.

GODEFRIDUS.—Prayer makes all things sweet, CLXXIV, 368.—True prayer is never without fruit and, like an arrow, always strikes, 602.—The prayer shared by the Church allows no one to perish, 559.—Prayer frees from temptations, 1147.—Its sweetness makes a person near to heaven, 722.—And is offered to God by angels from a chaste mind, 770.—It is like incense, 746.—Like a fiery, swift stream, 1126.

BERNARD (Saint).—God is found more easily by prayer than by disputation, CLXXXII, 806.—Prayer is a remedy against wicked movements of concupiscence, CLXXXIII, 460.—Christ willingly stands by those devoted to prayer, 300.—No prayer is fruitless, 180.—Through prayer we are cleansed of sins, CLXXXIV, 1272.—Frequent prayer removes the devil’s darts; daily prayer overcomes the devil’s weapons. Prayer is the foremost virtue against assaults of temptations; it overcomes the enemy’s trials, conquers demons, and defeats unclean spirits. Demons are conquered through prayer, ibid.—Vehement and devout prayer has great sweetness, 186.—By prayer a person is renewed, 74.—The practice of prayer makes the mind clean and bright, 148.—At the time of prayer the soul is wholly beautiful, 149.

PHILIP OF HARVENG.—The effects of prayer, CCIII, 1185.

BALDWIN.—Prayer is powerful to bring about all things asked in faith, CCIV, 602.

PETER THE CHANTER.—How great the effect of prayer is must be seen in God’s more secret matters, which are disclosed and opened to us by prayer alone, CCV, 318, 319.

MARTIN (Saint) OF LEÓN.—The efficacy of prayer is shown, CCIX, 212.

ALAN OF LILLE.—Prayer is a sacrifice of sweet odour, CCX, 168.—It penetrates Paradise and ascends [Col. 0952] even to God’s throne, 169.—It is called a rod and “straight,” because just as a rod is directed straight upward, so prayer is not bent down toward earthly things but is inflexibly directed toward heavenly ones. It is compared with smoke because, just as smoke arising from fire rises upward, so fruitful prayer, arising from the furnace of charity, ascends upward. It is said to ascend through the desert because the mind through which such prayer is poured out is separated from every tumult of wicked thoughts, ibid.

GUNTHER.—It is apparent how useful and effective prayer is: in this life it receives remission of sins, confers assurance of future blessedness, and finally leads to eternal life, CCXII, 206.

V.—On the Time and Place of Prayer.

TERTULLIAN.—How rash it is to pass a day without prayer, I, 1196.—One must pray before food, 1193.—Before bathing, and at the coming of daylight and night, ibid.—One must rise for prayer at night, 1294, 1296.

CYPRIAN (Saint).—One must pray in the morning, IV, 540.—At the departure of day, likewise at night; throughout the whole day. One must pray in the morning in order that the Lord’s resurrection may be celebrated, ibid.

HILARY (Saint).—One must pray without ceasing, IX, 409.—One must always pray to God, that he may strengthen the wavering endeavours of our will in restraining sins and extinguishing their incentives, 785.—We are taught to pray in every place, 1942.—Daily prayer, X, 725.—The words by which perseverance in prayer is expressed, IX, 427.—Tribulations ought not to hinder us from constancy in prayer, 834.

AMBROSE (Saint).—When one should pray, XIV, 335.—How frequently we are commanded to pray, XV, 1720.—Prayer ought to be continual and unremitting, XIV, 351.—How one should pray always, XV, 1475.—The day is not enough for supplication; one must rise by night, even at midnight, 1312.—The greater part of it must be assigned to reading and prayers, 1291.—“Woe is me if I do not rise at midnight to confess God,” 1579.—Whoever prays is redeemed, if he gives devout attention to prayers, is constant in prayer, anticipates the day, and frequents the night, XIV, 1001.—Where the human mind is troubled and the harsh, rough contests weary us, the Lord’s help must be sought, 960.—Because you always receive from God, always call upon him, XVI, 1393.—To call upon God on fixed days but not on all days is the act of one who is weary, not hopeful, ibid.—The host of angels is always to be in God’s praises, to conciliate him with frequent prayers, and to entreat the Lord, 1211.—Prayers must be offered with thanksgiving when we rise from sleep, when we go out, when we prepare to take food, when we have taken it, at the hour of incense, and finally when we go to bed, 225.

JEROME (Saint).—On the Lord’s Day and at Pentecost let us pray standing, XXIII, 163.—The Apostle commands us to pray without ceasing, XXII, 409.—In what circumstances the weapons of prayer must be taken up, 421.—When leaving lodging, let prayer arm you; when returning from the street, let prayer meet you. One must rise two or three times at night for prayer, ibid.—Daily prayer, 347.

AUGUSTINE (Saint).—Prayer without ceasing is heard more surely, XXXIII, 500.—To pray without ceasing is to desire without ceasing from God alone the blessed life, 501.—The frequent but very brief prayers, swiftly cast forth, of the brothers who are in Egypt, ibid.—To pray long when one has leisure—that is, when one is not hindered by other duties of good and necessary actions—is neither wrong nor useless, ibid.—To pray frequently is not to pray with much speaking, 502.—The time of prayer is the time of God’s grace, XL, 234.—The time for prayer is after the cock’s crow, XXXVII, 1587.—On the place of prayer, XXXV, 1519.

PROSPER (Saint).—A clean heart is a fitting place for prayer, LI, 479.—God, who is helper and witness to the person praying, must be prayed to incessantly, 404.—One must always pray, even when God has not heard, 401.

PETER CHRYSOLOGUS (Saint).—One must pray in the morning, LII, 320.—God must be prayed to while he chastises, 326.—Let prayer be fervent on saints’ feast days, 566.

SALVIAN (Saint).—Prayers must be continually offered to God, LIII, 36.—God’s mercy must be sought with frequent prayers, ibid.

MAXIMUS (Saint).—Prayers must be made to God in the morning after rising and in the evening before going to bed, that he may deign to keep us safe by day and night, LVII, 457.

BENEDICT (Saint).—To pray well, prayer must be frequent and constant, LXVI, 331.

CASSIODORUS.—It is fitting that God be continually entreated, LXX, 879.—Whoever has sinned through punishable wickedness must never cease from prayers, 611.

GREGORY OF TOURS (Saint).—Prayer must precede meals, LXXI, 375.

[Col. 0953] ISIDORE OF SEVILLE (Saint).—Prayer is more fittingly poured out in private places and obtains a greater grant when it is expressed with God alone as witness, LXXXIII, 678.

ALCUIN.—When we suffer tribulations from false brethren, let us call upon him who urges us to call upon him, CII, 481.—Let the spirit keep watch for the Lord in the morning and pray at the rising of dawn, so that from first light until evening his eyes may be upon us and his ears attentive to our prayers; and may he direct our steps into the way of peace, so that, walking without every stumbling-block of errors, no unrighteousness may rule over us, ibid.—We must pray daily with tears for the various wounds which we suffer, 486.—Not only every day, but also in evening, morning, and noon—indeed, at every hour of the day—let us offer praise to the Lord with the whole intention of the heart, 485.—After the span of the whole day has run its course, when we go to our beds to sleep, let us pray with all our vows before sleeping, 490.

SMARAGDUS.—One must pray without ceasing, CII, 651.

BENEDICT OF ANIANE (Saint).—Prayer before and after food, CIII, 1153.—Before and after manual work, 1195.—When leaving the monastery, 1227.—Before sleep, 911.

AGOBARD (Saint).—One must pray in afflictions, CIV, 153.

LANFRANC.—What it is to pray without ceasing, CL, 338.

RADULPHUS.—Let us say praise to the Lord seven times; whatever we do, let us always arm ourselves with prayer, so that by long habit, even while sleeping or dying, we may be unable not to pray, CLV, 1930.

ANSELM (Saint).—Frequent prayer, CLVIII, 679.—Rising during the night for prayers, ibid.

IVO (Blessed).—Anyone who cannot do more should pray at least twice every day, morning and evening, CLXI, 484.

BERNARD (Saint).—One must pray unceasingly, CLXXXIV, 1271.—One must pray continually, entreating God by day and night, ibid.—Prayer should be without cessation and frequent; its weapons should be continual, ibid.—One must always groan and mourn; one must rise by night for prayers, 1272.—After a brief interval with the eyes closed, one must pray again, ibid.

PETER LOMBARD.—One should pray especially in the night-time, CXCI, 1071.—Prayer must be offered to God every day in the morning, as the firstfruits of voice and heart, 1115.

GUNTHER.—On the time and place of prayer, CCXII, 163 and following.

VI.—What Must Be Asked, and for Whom One Must Pray.

CYPRIAN (Saint).—One must pray for all, IV, 213.—For the salvation of all, 526.—For those who have fallen and those who stand, 312.—Prayers for heretics, III, 805.—One must pray that no one, being excluded, may remain far from salvation, IV, 532.

AMBROSE (Saint).—One must pray especially for the people, XIV, 336.—If you ask only for yourself, you alone will ask for yourself; but if you ask for all, all will ask for you, ibid.

RUFINUS.—One must pray that we may not be handed over together with sinners, corrupted by wicked habits, and destroyed with those who work iniquity, XXI, 743.

JEROME (Saint).—No one is worthy to pray for sinners, XXIV, 775.—It is foolish to pray for sinners unto death, 772.
