AUGUSTINE (Saint).—One must pray for the persecutors of the Church, XXXIII, 637.—For enemies and persecutors, XXXVIII, 120, 806.—If you have learned to pray for your enemy, you walk in the Lord’s way, XXXV, 1985.—Whoever prays to God that he may oppress his enemy wrongs God, XXXVI, 436.—Our prayer performs alms when it is poured out for enemies as for friends, XXXVIII, 1044.—Why the Church now prays for enemies but will not pray at the last judgment, XLI, 737.—Supplication for a brother is more pleasing to God where the sacrifice of charity is offered, XXXIII, 87.—Let all members pray for one another; the head intercedes for all, XXXV, 1985.—Prayer is made for unbelievers that they may believe, XXXVIII, 914, 915.—A priest standing at the altar should exhort the people to pray for unbelievers, catechumens, and the faithful, XXXIII, 978, 988.—At the altar the priest prays aloud to God that he may compel unbelieving nations to come to his faith, 988.—For whom and against whom prayer is to be offered, XXXVI, 248, 438.—It is not lawful to pray against anyone, XXXIV, 1265.—Prayer for the dead at the altar, XXXII, 780.—Prayer for the departed, XLI, 737, 738.—A formula of prayer to God through the merits of all the saints for oneself and all people, XL, 939.—Prayers everywhere in the world, uniformly celebrated for idolaters, Jews, etc., XLV, 1759.—One must pray for all, XXXIX, 2287.—One must pray that God may give what he commands us to possess, XL, 443.—That he may preserve what has been given [Col. 0954] and supply what has not yet been given, 444.—That God’s gifts may increase in you, XXXVII, 1048.—Let us trust that we shall receive what we have not yet received, XL, 444.—Do not ask anything from God except God, XXXVIII, 1481.—“What will anything be to me, whatever you give me apart from yourself?” 1469.—After the integrity of forgiveness, we have received prayer as a remedy against sins, 752.—One must pray to the Lord that we may not sin, XXXIII, 775.—One must pray for the blessed life, and for other things on account of it, 497, 499, 503, 505.—How eternal and temporal benefits should be asked for, XXXVIII, 497.—Those asking God for temporal things ask for nothing, 794.—Many cry to the Lord for temporal things; scarcely anyone does so for the Lord himself, XXXVI, 1974.—The necessities of the body must be sought from God alone, not from demons, 752, 753.—One must pray that health, friendship, and sufficiency may be obtained or, if already present, retained, XXXIII, 499.—Let us pray that we may be able to do what we shall will, once, by God’s gift, we have rightly understood, 990.—What evils should not be requested from God, XXXV, 1824.—With all heart and all mind one must seek forgiveness of sins and God’s grace, XXXIX, 2281.—That must be requested which it pleases God to hear and which is expedient for us, XL, 939.

PROSPER (Saint).—God wills that prayer be made for all, LI, 664.—The Church prays for all, ibid.

PETER CHRYSOLOGUS (Saint).—One must pray that we may be able to believe, see, and possess eternal goods, LII, 374.

SALVIAN (Saint).—One must pray for our enemies, LIII, 58.

LEO THE GREAT (Saint).—That we may obtain what we ask, we must always ask for things pleasing to God, LV, 86.—God wills prayer for all, 186.—The Church prays for all, ibid.

PAULINUS OF NOLA (Saint).—That one must pray for the departed is shown by the example of Paulinus, who requested from Delphinus and Amandus prayers for the soul of his deceased brother, LXI, 350.

FULGENTIUS (St).—We render mutual charity when we pray for those by whom we are instructed, LXV, 325.—Prayer is a debt to be rendered by all and required of all, ibid.—The faithful are aided by the prayers of the faithful, ibid.—We should ask that, by the same grace through which it came about that the Church became Christ’s body, all its members may persevere in the unity of the body, LXV, 190.—God should be asked to turn our eyes away lest they see vanity; to show the way, to direct our steps and the works of our hands, 322.

GREGORY (St) THE GREAT.—We must pray for enemies from the heart, LXXVI, 1209.—What should be asked of God, 1084.—Temporal things, if lacking, should be sought from God, but not excessively, 1208.—What things ought to be sought from God in prayer, 1107.

ISIDORE (St).—Whoever is injured should not cease to pray for those injuring him; otherwise, one who does not pray for enemies sins, LXXXIII, 674.

PAULINUS (St) OF AQUILEIA.—The soul asks God for profound humility, chastity of heart, purity of spirit, the love of charity, the patience of endurance, hope of eternal joy, righteousness, magnanimity, and temperance, XCVI, 279–280.—That it may be gentle, kindly, peaceful, meek, without pretense, in harmony with every good, and steadfastly zealous in vigils and prayers, ibid.

ALCUIN.—According to the apostle’s command, prayer should be made for all, CII, 487.—It is good to pray for faithful departed persons, 488.—Prayer for one’s father and mother, and for all one’s kindred, 493.—For an abbot or a congregation, 494.—When evils, rather than goods, delight us, we ought rather to ask God that good things may delight us than that evils may be granted us so that evil things may delight us, C, 955.

AGOBARD (St).—Each person ought to be concerned in prayer not only for himself or for the saints, but also for all people, CIV, 285.

WALAFRID STRABO.—We should pray for the brethren, that they may be joined to us by the bond of brotherhood, CXIII, 98.

BRUNO (St) OF WÜRZBURG.—Prayer should be made for enemies, CXLII, 63.

PETER DAMIAN (St).—Let us seek from God not what any poor people seek from the rich of this world: not money, not food, not clothing for the naked body, CXLIV, 621.—Let us urgently request that which is most necessary for us above all things, and which he more gladly gives to those who ask, 612.

LANFRANC.—To pray to the Lord for temporal things is not to pray to God, CL, 717.

JOHN CARTHUSIAN.—Forgiveness of sins should be sought, not only of those of which we are conscious, but also of those into which we have fallen unknowingly, CLIII, 914.—Knowledge and fulfillment of the divine will, eternal salvation, ibid.—Prayer should be made for all rulers of the Church, for all who live either in our own profession or in holy conduct, [Col. 0955] 918.—For all ranks of the Church; for those undergoing spiritual or bodily tribulation; for unbelievers, ibid.

BRUNO (St).—It is shown that prayer ought to be made for all, CLIII, 437.

RADULPHUS.—Prayer should be made for the brethren, CLV, 1901.—We are not bound to pray in the same manner for heretics and unbelievers, and for those who sin against the Holy Spirit, ibid.—Nothing should be sought except what pertains to the love of God and his commandments, 1505.—Those ask idly and wickedly who ask for temporal goods in which they already abound to be multiplied for them, and who seek things not necessary for them—indeed, useless to them—as well as honors and offices, 1523.—Wisdom should especially be sought, ibid.—Let us seek not transitory but eternal things, not earthly substance but only the salvation of our souls, 1801.—Whoever asks for vain things, and vainly, is vain. Whoever seeks the death, loss, or vengeance of an enemy is evil, ibid.—Let us ask neither evils nor vain things from the Lord, as some do when they seek riches, glory, honors, pleasures, and worldly joys; rather, let us seek the unchangeable good, that our joy may be full, 1895.—Whoever seeks temporal things without discerning the condition attached to them asks foolishly and does not deserve to be heard, 1896.

ANSELM (St).—Prayers for schismatics and heretics, Jews and Gentiles, are not improperly made in the Church, CLVIII, 581.

IVO (Blessed).—All should jointly pour forth prayers to the Lord for various needs: for the king, bishops, rulers of churches, peace, plague, the sick, and the recently deceased, CLXI, 193.

HILDEBERT.—Three things should be sought in prayer: bread, signifying charity; fish, faith; and egg, hope, CLXI, 57.—Heavenly things should be sought continually, indeed importunately; temporal things in necessity, but not continually, 576.

HERVAEUS.—Prayer should be made for unbelievers, CLXXXI, 1278.

BERNARD (St).—Prayer should be made for good people, that they may persevere in goodness, CLXXXIV, 1272.—For evil people, that they may turn from evil to good; for friends and enemies; for all the faithful, living and dead, ibid.—Temporal things and gratuitously given graces should be sought conditionally; sanctifying grace and glory absolutely, CLXXXIII, 608.

MARTIN (St) OF LEÓN.—Let us pray for one another, that we may be saved; let us devoutly pour forth prayers to the Lord for the salvation of our neighbors, not merely temporal but rather eternal, CCIX, 213.

ALANUS OF LILLE.—If God is to hear, worthy things must be worthily sought; some seek evils, others temporal things, CCX, 169.

VII.—On mental prayer and its conditions.—On meditation and contemplation.

HILARY (St).—Prayer consists not so much in words as in affection, IX, 401.—It is not in words: every deed surpasses utterances, 942.—The place of prayer is the heart, ibid.—In prayer, the cry of the mouth, not that of the heart, is forbidden. The cry of silent prayer, 824, 622.—The use and office of meditation, 312.—It must not be abandoned in temptations and afflictions, 378.—It ought to be continual, 46.

AMBROSE (St).—There is a cry of inward affection which is heard from heaven, XV, 1542.—With God, not words but thoughts speak, XIV, 334.—Let prayer not proceed merely from the lips: attend wholly with your mind; enter into the recess of your breast; enter wholly, 456.—To pray in spirit is to direct prayer to God with a pure conscience and an uncorrupted faith, XVII, 402.—We must cry to the Lord not so much with the mouth as with the heart, 684.—Meditation upon Scripture is especially necessary for priests, XV, 1344.—Let us exercise ourselves in its unfailing use, 1370.—For one who meditates on the law, day is always light without failure, 1579.—For one whose meditation is God’s law, mercies are at hand, that he may live forever, 1344.—Daily meditation removes sleep and produces watchfulness, XVII, 159.

AUGUSTINE (St).—Prayer should be made in the temple of the mind, XXXII, 1195.—One does not pray rightly except in the innermost places of the heart, XL, 144.—The prayer of many has sound but has no voice, XXXVII, 1809.—Desire prays, even if the tongue is silent, XXXVIII, 498, 820.—A worthier result will follow from prayer when a more fervent affection precedes it, XXXIII, 502.—Desire itself is prayer; and if desire is continual, prayer is continual, XXXVI, 404.—Meditation is, as it were, an expansion of the mind, XL, 987.—What it is, 802, 803, 816, 997.—The office of meditation, 997.—Its usefulness, 943.—Its effect, 816.—What we ought to meditate upon, 846, 943.—When free, let the faithful person meditate on the things of God, XLV, 1877.—Book of *Meditations*, XL, 901.—Comparison of contemplation with meditation and prayer, 998, 1002.—Many contemplations, [Col. 0956] 955, 984.—The varied affections of the contemplating mind, 1003.—Meanwhile the soul thirsting for God asks for the wings of contemplation, 935, 953.—By contemplation a person becomes wholly spiritual, 1000.—The merit of contemplation, XXXIX, 1941.—Its sweetness, XL, 791, 804, 826, 922.—Its taste is not perpetual, 1001.—Obstacles to contemplation, 1004.—Contemplation, XXXVIII, 925.—The excellence of contemplating heavenly things, XXXIII, 128.

PROSPER (St).—Whoever prays in the secret of the heart prays in God’s presence, LI, 404.

LEO THE GREAT (St).—One should frequently devote oneself to sacred meditations, LIV, 186.

BENEDICT (St).—Mental prayer, LXVI, 484.

*Lives of the Fathers.*—Meditation upon going to bed, LXXIII, 270.—The devil does not prevail over meditation, 993.—Meditations of the twelve anchorites, 1059.

CASSIODORUS.—Frequent meditation is the mother of understanding, LXX, 1107.—What it is to meditate with the heart, 548.—Contemplation of God is the food of spiritual substances, 864.

GREGORY THE GREAT (St).—What a Christian ought to meditate upon daily, LXXVI, 286.—A troubled mind is not suited to contemplation, LXXV, 723.—Divine contemplation is a tomb in which the mind, dead to the world, rests, 683.—One does not attain contemplation unless carnal desires have been quieted, 707.—A mind devoted to contemplation more carefully cuts away superfluous thoughts, 712.—Fear and love of God are required for contemplation, 763.—The power of contemplation raises the mind to God’s invisible realities, 928.—They do not attain the summit of contemplation unless free from outward cares, LXXVI, 554.—Contemplation is signified by heavenly dew, 831.—The sweetness of contemplation, 953.—Those who think too immoderately on outward things are unfit for contemplation, 995.—Contemplation ought to be frequent among pastors and preachers, LXXVII, 41.—One occupied by worldly cares bears dust in his eyes, by which he cannot see what he desires to see, 51.—How dust is to be cast out of the eyes, ibid.—In vain does one seek contemplation who has not only no custody of the heart, but not even custody of the body, 53.—The fruit of divine contemplation, 54.—The steps by which one ascends to contemplation, 55.—The more highly one ascends in contemplation, the more one should apply oneself to good works, ibid.—Let humility accompany contemplation, 62.—The mouth of the mind is filled when its reason is raised by grace infused into it to contemplation, ibid.—The mind, taken up into contemplation of the divinity of its Redeemer, receives greatness of wisdom and fullness of charity, 79.—Different modes of contemplation are explained, 433.—We are prepared for contemplation of heavenly things by repose from work, silence of mouth, and casting away superfluous thoughts, ibid.—Those nourished by contemplation are adorned with the splendor of virtues, 203.—The higher we are suspended in contemplation, the stronger and more useful to our neighbor we are found, 251.—What preparation of mind is necessary for contemplating higher things, 265.—God wishes us to be near him through contemplation and prayer, 282.—Contemplation as the chamber of a royal house, 483.

ISIDORE (St).—Prayer belongs to the heart, not the lips, LXXXIII, 652.—For God does not attend to the words of one making supplication, but looks upon the heart of the one praying; if the heart prays silently and the voice is quiet, although this is hidden from people, it cannot be hidden from God, ibid.

GUIDO.—If we particularly desire our prayer to be pleasing to God and fruitful for us, let us watch with every care against insolent and unstable, harmful and useless thoughts, both before the time of prayer and, above all, during prayer, CLIII, 863.—When we pray, we ought to possess within ourselves unity, tranquility, and clarity, 864.—When approaching prayer, one should diligently strive and exert all one’s powers to bring an entirely pure heart, 869.—Whatever stings the conscience, one should strive to amend and cast away from oneself through full repentance, pure, humble, and faithful confession, and worthy satisfaction, ibid.

ANSELM (St).—By continual meditation a person is enlightened to self-knowledge, CLVIII, 741.—Meditation produces knowledge, knowledge compunction, and compunction devotion, ibid.—Meditation on God is sweet food, 881.—Prayers or meditations written for the love and fear of God, and for self-examination, 709.—Contemplation of God, 899.—The soul is not led to contemplate inward things unless it diligently withdraws itself from things which entangle it outwardly, 612.—The reward of contemplation is to see God, 595.

HILDEBERT.—Contemplation and sacred Scripture are the wine-cellar from which souls are spiritually intoxicated, CLXXI, 862.—Contemplation is dangerous unless God guides it, 746.

[Col. 0957] HUGH OF ST VICTOR.—What meditation is, CLXXVI, 399.—Its three kinds, 993 ff.—The manifold contemplation of God, CLXXVII, 545–546.—Three orders of contemplatives, 649.

BERNARD (St).—Meditation on evangelical teaching is commended, CLXXXIII, 313.—By meditation and prayer we ascend, 509.—How delightful it is to meditate on heavenly things, CLXXXII, 792.—Meditation on Christ’s mysteries, CLXXXIII, 553.—What meditation is, CLXXXIV, 475.—It is medicine for an ailing conscience, 969.—How effective are the devout sighs of meditation before God, 975.—The office of meditation, 476.—What contemplation is, CLXXXII, 744.—Its power and nature, CLXXXIII, 1188.—Its object, 671.—What preparation for contemplation is necessary, 1006.—The two kinds of contemplation, 1076.—Its obstacles, what they are, and how they should be removed, CLXXXII, 950.—Its sweetness, CLXXXIII, 170.—Sleep and rest, 62.—Its effect, 550.—Its usefulness, 497.—Threefold contemplation, 229.—What turns us away from contemplation, 483.—It is hindered by the darkness of sins, their recollection, and concern for earthly things, 1005.—Their remedies, ibid.

WOLBERO.—Intellectual contemplation is incomparable with nature and with intelligible reality, CXCV, 1071.—Contemplation has three parts, ibid.

ADAM THE SCOT.—The kinds of meditation serve for the correction of the inner senses, CXCVIII, 437.—The secret of contemplation, 777.—Its threefold kind and effect, 838.

ALANUS OF LILLE.—Contemplation is signified by mountains, CCX, 78.—Encomium of contemplation, ibid.—Its fruit, ibid.

VIII.—On vocal prayer: notable examples of vocal prayer and its wonderful effects.

TERTULLIAN.—Christians prayed with hands outstretched, I, 442, 1171.—Turned toward the East, 370, 579.—Without a prompter, from the inmost breast, 443.—With uncovered head, 444.—With chaste flesh, innocent soul, and the Holy Spirit, 444.—How pleasing to God was the power of their prayers, 468.—At public assemblies they rose by night to pour forth prayers, 273, 381, 468, 477; II, 79.—They prayed to God for all, 468.—And for the postponement of the end of the world, ibid.

HILARY (St).—An example of prayer, IX, 338.

JUVENCUS.—Prayers by which the ancients asked God for pardon on the final day of judgment, XIX, 60.

CHROMATIUS (St).—Hannah, praying faithfully in the Lord’s presence, poured forth the prayers of her desire, XX, 358.—Daniel, praying with the three youths, was heard, ibid.—Cornelius prays secretly and faithfully in his chamber; Jonah, shut in the belly of a beast, prays so earnestly that he comes forth safe and alive from the depths of the sea and from the belly of so immense a beast, ibid.

AUGUSTINE (St).—Outstanding prayers of Augustine to God, XXXII, 869, 888.—Vocal prayer without intention directed toward God is empty, XXXVII, 1585.

AURELIUS PRUDENTIUS.—At sunrise, and facing east, Christians poured forth prayers, LIX, 102.—Their prayers before sleep, 142.—After food, ibid.

PAULINUS (St) OF NOLA.—Prayer concerning a person endangered by shipwreck, LXI, 402.—Paulinus’s morning prayers to God, 439.

FULGENTIUS (St).—Vocal prayer should not be cast forth tumultuously, but commended modestly to God, LXV, 262.

LAURENTIUS (St).—The perseverance in prayer of the Canaanite woman, who persisted more insistently when driven away and pleaded more importunately after being refused, nor ceased before finding what she sought, LXVI, 122.

*Lives of the Fathers.*—Posthumius prays continually, LXXIII, 429–430.—Josaphat prays with arms outstretched, 588.—Zosimus at fixed hours, 676.—Arsenius prays from sunset to sunrise, 806.—A certain man prays while eating, 941.—Christopher prays a hundred times at night with bent knees, LXXIV, 172.—Lucius and Macarius teach how to pray, LXXIII, 806.—Abraham’s prayer for the conversion of Gentiles, 285.—Prayer restores to health the stiffened hand of a barbarian attempting to kill him, LXXIV, 153.—It frees the nun of Adelphius, 185.—Apollo renders immobile idol-worshipers together with their god, LXXIII, 1158.—He releases the same persons, ibid.—Anthony overcomes the devil, 128.—The prayers of Astion and [Col. 0958] Epictetus, even for enemies, 404.—Barlaam’s prayer to God for Josaphat, 599.—Basil heals a leper, 306.—

Bessarion makes sea water fresh, 808.—Bessarion, praying continually for fourteen days with hands outstretched toward heaven, 941.—Cyriacus obtains a cloud for one weary and overcome by heat, LXXIV, 146.—He renders the same man invisible to friends from whom he flees, ibid.—David’s fire is extinguished, 213.—Jacob of Nisibis frustrates the enemies’ machinations, 184.—John frees an enchanted ship, 160.—Josaphat for his father’s soul, LXXIII, 584.—The same man’s prayer to God, 599.—Innocentius discovers a theft, 1190.—Julian drives away a fever, LXXIV, 817.—A certain soldier’s prayer, repeated seven times in a day, 154.—A certain devout sailor obtains miraculous rain, ibid.—Nicholas saves a man whom Saracens are attempting to kill, 1198.—Pachomius’s prayer for monks afflicting him, LXXIII, 252.—His remonstrance with God, 262.—His prayer heals a scorpion’s sting, 268.—Posthumius puts bands of demons to flight, 438.—Publius restrains Julian’s emissary devil, 1002.—An old man obtains rain, 1165.—The same prayer of Symeon Stylites, 330.—Syrus obtains a ship and a favorable wind, 1165.—The prayer of Theodore, a noble youth, to God, 248.—Theodosius obtains a spring in a rock, LXXIV, 156.—Theon renders thieves immobile, LXXIII, 1154.—Zacchaeus averts plague, LXXIV, 187.—The continual prayer of Zebinas, 94.—By Theodore’s prayer sea water becomes fresh, 207.

Prayers of Anthony, LXXIII, 130.—Symeon Stylites offers God very many prayers every day, LXXIV, 109.—A virgin offers seven hundred prayers daily, LXXIII, 1122.—Macarius makes twenty-four prayers while going, and as many on returning, 1110.—Paul of Pherne recites three hundred prayers and uses the same number of pebbles, 1122.—Josaphat devotes himself to prayer, 558.

ALCUIN.—Prayers of monks, CII, 502; of St Augustine, 543; of Aurelius Prudentius, ibid.; of St Ambrose, 545; of St Benedict, 552; of St Cyprian, 567; of St Eugenius of Toledo, 579; of Pope St Gregory, 585; of St Jerome, 605; of St Columban, 608; of Alcuin at night; of Solomon at the dedication of the Temple, C, 720.—The poet’s prayer to the twelve apostles, CII, 769.

RABANUS.—Judith prays to God prostrate on the ground, CX, 618.—Prayer of Jeremiah the prophet, III, 1262.

HAYMO.—The Lord Jesus Christ taught us to pray not only in words but also in deeds, CXVIII, 898.—He himself was frequently praying and making supplication; keeping vigil throughout the whole night, he prayed in unceasing prayers, ibid.

ADALGERUS.—Blessed Arsenius stood in prayer, CXXXIV, 928–929.—Dulos remained doing so continually for four days, with hands outstretched toward heaven. Of Sisoes it was said that he did not quickly lower his hands. What zeal Blessed Paul had for prayer is written in the *Ecclesiastical History*, ibid.

RADULPHUS.—A certain priest, while dying, had reached such a state that he understood nothing in this world; nevertheless, from the long habit which he had practiced while living, even while dying he did not cease frequently to perform divine praises, CLV, 1930.

ROBERT (St).—A certain man, prostrate on the ground, wetting his face with tears and praying to God not to regard his sins, obtained what he sought, CLVII, 1285.—The sick, blind, deaf, and withered, devoted to prayer, are restored to health, 1286.

RUPERT.—Rebecca’s barrenness was healed through Isaac’s prayer, CLXVII, 447.—While Moses prayed, Amalek was defeated, 669.

GODEFRIDUS.—The Blessed Virgin Mary is an example in prayer, CLXXIV, 770.

HARIULFUS.—Blessed Richarius obtained by prayer that a spring might issue forth, CLXXIV, 1225.

GUILLELMUS.—Christ offered an example of prayer: at times he prayed alone, at times in a crowd, at times in the exultation of the spirit, at times in a sweat of blood, at times lifted up upon the cross, CLXXX, 219.

BERNARD.—If it is good always to pray to God in the mind, it is also good to glorify him with the sound of the voice, CLXXXIV, 1274.

PETER THE VENERABLE.—Abraham praying for Ishmael; Isaac for Rebecca’s barrenness; Jacob for his grandsons; Moses for the Jews, CXC, 823.—David, Samuel, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Hezekiah, and Jonah turned away the Lord’s wrath from the Jewish people through their prayers, ibid.—Elijah prayed for the rain to be removed, and also prayed for it to be restored, and was heard; the apostles ask the Lord for the Canaanite woman and are heard; Martha and Mary pray that their dear brother Lazarus may rise, and, Christ hearing them, he rises, 825.

TERTULLIAN.—Jews prayed three times a day, I, 193.—Their literal prayers, 579.—Pagans prayed to their gods [Col. 0959] after a prompter had first spoken, 443.—They prayed with hands outstretched, 412.—Facing east, 371.—But polluted by idolatry and every sort of crime, 465.

JEROME (St).—Concerning Pelagius’s prayer, XXIII, 585.

AUGUSTINE (St).—The prayers which the Church makes for unbelievers, that they may be converted, or for believers, that faith may increase in them and that they may persevere, are destroyed by the Pelagians, XLII, 748.

EUGYPPIUS.—How the Pelagians interpret the Lord’s Prayer, LXII, 986.

BENEDICT (St).—The error of the Pelagians concerning the Lord’s Prayer, LXVI, 448.

ISIDORE (St).—The prayer of Jews, as of heretics, does not avail for the merit of purification, but is instead turned into sin, LXXXIII, 676.

BRUNO (St) OF ASTI.—Pagans, deceived by some error or other, thought that by wordiness and long prayer they would be heard, CLXV, 114.

RUPERT.—Pagans devoted no small attention to the arrangement of sounds and words, CLXVIII, 1424.—They think that they will be heard through much speaking, and that they can bend or overcome God the judge more by a long and elegant prayer than by the truth of things, ibid., 1425.

GUNTHERUS.—It is not permitted for Gentiles and Jews, indeed even for heretics who have torn themselves away from the unity of faith through the various plagues of heresies, to pray, CCXII, 155.

CLXXIV. INDEX ON THE LORD’S PRAYER, PRESENTING VARIOUS EXPLANATIONS OF IT BY THE HOLY FATHERS.

[Col. 0959] The Lord’s Prayer consists of three things: the discourse by which it is uttered, the Spirit by which it profits, and the reason by which it teaches, Tertullian, I, 1151.—Christ’s prayer is placed before private prayers, 1165.—*Book on Prayer*, Tertullian, I, 1149.—*Book on the Lord’s Prayer*, St Cyprian, IV, 519, 1123.—Through the mirror of its words, the Lord’s Prayer, in common use, shows the form of a hidden mystery, St Hilary, IX, 110.—The Lord’s Prayer is brief and full of every virtue, St Ambrose, XVI, 450.—Exposition of the Lord’s Prayer, ibid., 360.—The Lord’s Prayer rendered in verse, Juvencus, XIX, 132; Sedacilus, XX, 623.—The Lord’s Prayer explained part by part, St Chromatius of Aquileia, XX, 460.—From the Lord’s Prayer, St Jerome, XXIII, 585.—A clause formerly added to the Lord’s Prayer, XXVI, 198.—Sermons on the Lord’s Prayer, St Augustine, XXXIX, 377, 386, 393, 400.—The Lord’s Prayer: a rule for petition given to the apostles by the heavenly Jurist, St Augustine, XXXVI, 1849.—Its exposition, XXXIII, 503; XXXIV, 1277; XXXVIII, 377; XL, 285.—In it, three petitions concern eternal life and four temporal life, XXXIV, 1285.—The Lord’s Prayer is said daily at the altar, XXXVIII, 399.—It contains all that may fittingly be prayed for, and all other prayers are reduced to it, XXXIII, 503.—It is daily medicine, XXXVIII, 127.—As it were, a daily baptism, ibid., 1064.—Its exposition, XXXIX, 1907.—In Matthew, the Lord’s Prayer has seven petitions, St Augustine, XL, 285.—In Luke, only five, XL, 286.—On the Lord’s Prayer, Cassian, XLIX, 788 ff.—Sermons on the Lord’s Prayer, St Peter Chrysologus, LII, 390, 665 ff.—On the Lord’s Prayer, St Nicetas, LII, 1010.—On the petitions of the Lord’s Prayer, St Leo the Great, LIV, 449.—The daily prayer which Jesus himself taught removes daily sins, Eugyppius, LXII, 797.—The Lord’s Prayer is directed to the person of the Father, St Fulgentius, LXV, 799.—On the Lord’s Prayer, St Benedict, LXVI, 447 ff.—The Lord’s Prayer is called the daily prayer, Cassiodorus, LXX, 384.

The Lord’s Prayer is recited in the Mass by all the people among Greeks and Gauls, St Germanus, LXXII, 139.—Not among Romans, ibid., 140.—Its “captivity,” 353.—By the Lord’s Prayer we bind ourselves more firmly if we do not forgive, St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1210.

On the Lord’s Prayer, St Ildefonsus, XCVI, 166.—Exposition of the Lord’s [Col. 0960] Prayer, Alcuin, CI, 1135.—Its seven petitions, 1267.—The Lord’s Prayer at Vespers and Matins, St Benedict, CIII, 896.—On the Lord’s Prayer, Amalarius of Metz, CV, 1148.—Formula of the Lord’s Prayer, Christian Druthmarus, CVI, 1314.—On the distinction of the Lord’s Prayer, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 333.—St Matthew includes seven petitions in it; St Luke five; its explanation, 817, 886.—Explanation of the Lord’s Prayer, Walafrid Strabo, CXIV, 100 ff.—Sermon on the Lord’s Prayer, Haymo, CXVIII, 800 ff.—On the Lord’s Prayer, Radulfus of Bourges, CXIX, 714.—On the Lord’s Prayer, Paschasius, CXX, 280 ff.—The Lord’s Prayer is to be said every day, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 467.—It ought to be recited by priests after Vespers and Matins, 424.—The Lord’s Prayer is to be taught to Christians, Regulation of Prüm, CXXXII, 189.—The Lord’s Prayer should be recited every day, Atto, CXXXIV, 39.—Commentary on the Lord’s Prayer, St Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 557.—The Lord’s Prayer demonstrates the unity of our brotherhood, John of Rouen, CXLVII, 36.—We received its form from Christ, 198.—Its exposition, ibid.—Commentary on the Lord’s Prayer, Theodoricus, CXLVII, 331 ff.—Meditation on the Lord’s Prayer, St Anselm, CXLIX, 569 ff.—Exposition of the Lord’s Prayer, Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 599 ff.—Explanation of the Lord’s Prayer, St Anselm of Laon, CLXII, 1304.—The Lord’s Prayer is the model of all prayers, Rupert, CLXVIII, 1430.—Explanation of the Lord’s Prayer and its seven petitions, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXV, 767 ff.—On the Lord’s Prayer, which is the prayer of the third action, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 435.—The Lord’s Prayer is expounded, Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 492, 611 ff.—Sermon on the Lord’s Prayer, St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 181.—Explanation of the Lord’s Prayer, CLXXXIV, 811 ff.—Exposition on the Lord’s Prayer, Joslenus of Lieu, CLXXXVI, 1489.—On the Lord’s Prayer, Hugh of Rouen, CXCII, 1324.—On the Lord’s Prayer, Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1564.—On the Lord’s Prayer, Beleth of Paris, CCII, 54.—On the Lord’s Prayer, St Martin of León, CCVIII, 1074 ff.—A fuller explanation of the Lord’s Prayer, Guntherus, CCXII, 171 ff.—Explanation of the Lord’s Prayer, CCXIII, 719.

SERIES TWENTY.

[Col. 0961]

[PREFACE.]

Historical annals constitute a large part of the *Patrologia*; therefore, collecting everything relating to them, we present to readers in this twentieth Series indexes concerning historical authors and their various works; concerning sacred, Jewish, ecclesiastical, secular, universal, and particular history; chronicles, and so forth; and indexes of abbeys and monasteries, making known their foundations, laws, rules, privileges, and monks more distinguished for holiness and learning. Moreover, we arrange alphabetically dioceses, cities, and monasteries, now destroyed and surviving only in memory, with their names translated from Latin into French. After these, we append two biographical indexes, which alphabetically list the Lives included in the course of the *Patrologia* and their authors.

[Col. 0961]

CLXXV. ALPHABETICAL INDEX OF HISTORIOGRAPHERS AND CHRONOGRAPHERS CONTAINED IN THE *PATROLOGIA LATINA*, WITH A DESCRIPTION OF THEIR WORKS.

[Col. 0961] ABBO, monk of Saint-Germain (tenth century).—Three books *On the Parisian War*: an account of the Northmen’s invasion in the ninth century, CXXXII, 721.

ADAMNAN (St), abbot of Iona (seventh century).—Three books *On the Holy Places*, from the account of Arculf, a Gallic bishop, LXXXVIII, 780.

ADAM OF BREMEN (eleventh century).—1. *Ecclesiastical History*, or *Deeds of the Bishops of the Church of Hamburg*, from Charlemagne to Emperor Henry IV, CXLVI, 457.—2. *History and Description of the Islands of the North*, or of the Danish province, ibid., 619.—3. *History of Norway*, concerning its first bishops, ibid., 646 ff.

ADELBOLD, bishop of Utrecht (eleventh century).—1. Fragment *On the Deeds of St Henry, Emperor*, CXL, 88.

ADEMAR, monk of the monastery of St Cybard at Angoulême (eleventh century).—1. Three books of *Histories*, or a *Chronicle of Frankish History*, from the year 420 to 1027, CXLI, 19.—2. *Commemoration of the Abbots of Limoges*, ibid., 80.—3. *On the Apostleship of St Martial*, ibid., 88.

ADO (St), archbishop of Vienne (ninth century).—1. A *Chronicle* divided into six ages: namely, from the origin of the world to the Flood; from the Flood to Abraham’s birth; from Abraham to David; from David’s reign to the migration of the Hebrews into Babylon; from that migration to Christ our Savior; and from Christ to his own age, CXXIII, 23.—2. *Martyrology with Additions*, ibid., 181 ff.

AELRED, abbot of Rievaulx in England (twelfth century).—1. *On the Battle of the Standard in the Time of King Stephen*, CXCV, 701.—2. *Genealogy of the Kings of England*, ibid., 711.—3. *Life of St Edward, King and Confessor*, ibid., 737.

AGNELLUS, abbot of St Bartholomew’s at Ravenna (ninth century).—*Lives of the Bishops of Ravenna*, from St Apollinaris, believed to have been a disciple of St Peter, to George, the forty-seventh bishop and a contemporary of Louis the Pious, CVI, 476 ff.

ANONYMOUS AUTHORS

Fourth century.—Ancient documents pertaining to the history of the Donatists from the year of Christ 203 to the year 350, VIII, 673.—Ancient documents pertaining to the history of the Donatists from the liberty restored to them by Julian to, etc., XI, 1179.—Proceedings of the Conference of Carthage, XI, 1231.

Eighth century.—Deeds of the Kings of the Franks, partly drawn from the history of Gregory of Tours, whose name they bear in the most ancient manuscripts, and partly derived from elsewhere, and brought down to King Theodoric II; by an unknown author who nevertheless lived in the time of the same Theodoric, XCVI, 1421.—Chronicle of the Bishops of Metz, ibid., 1465.—Two Books on the Deeds of Blessed Charlemagne, written by a monk of St. Gall, XCVIII, 1369.—Ancient Annals of the Franks, ibid., 1409.—Five Books of Annals on the Deeds of Blessed Charlemagne, by the Saxon Poet, XCIX, 684.

Ninth century.—Life of Louis the Pious Augustus, Emperor, CIV, 927.—Roman consular and imperial [Col. 0969] chronology, and Jewish pontifical chronology, from fifty years immediately preceding the Christian era to St. Sylvester I, CXXVII, 395.—Chronology from St. Sylvester to St. Gregory the Great, CXXVII, 601.—Chronology from St. Gregory the Great to Stephen III, ibid., 829.

Tenth century.—Little Book on the Successors of St. Hidulf in the Vosges, CXXXVIII, 203.—On the Deeds of the Bishops of Auxerre, CXXXVIII, 219.—Capitularies of the Kings and Emperors of the Franks, after the division of the empire, from the year 840 to 921, CXXXVIII, 525.

Eleventh century.—Annals of St. Emmeram at Regensburg from the year 748 to the year 1062.—Chronicle of Hildesheim, CXLI, 1233.—Chronicle of Petershausen, CXLIII, 301.—Anonymous author of Heidenheim on the Bishops of Eichstätt, CXLVI, 1004.—Chronicle of Fécamp, CXLVII, 479.—Deeds of the Bishops of Cambrai (eleventh century), CXLIX, 21.—Abridged Deeds of the Bishops, by a canon of Cambrai, [Col. 0970] CXLIX, 203.—Chronicle of St. Andrew of the Castle of Cambrai, CXLIX, 239.—Chronicle of the Abbey of Bec from its very foundation to the year 1467, CL, 639.—Deeds of Trier, CLIV, 1091.—Chronicle of St. Hubert of Andain, CLIV, 1337.—Deeds of the Bishops of Toul, CLVII, 445.—Chronicle of the Poles, CLX, 833.—Chronicle of the venerable abbots and illustrious benefactors and founders of the monastery at Dijon of the most blessed athlete of Christ, Benignus, CLXII, 755.—Deeds of the Bishops of Metz, CLXIII, 575.—Lesser Chronicle of Aldenburg, CLXXIV, 1451.—Greater Chronicle of Aldenburg, CLXXIV, 1505.—Anonymous writer of Melk on ecclesiastical writers, flourishing in the twelfth century, CCXIII, 959.—History of the Roman Pontiffs from St. Peter to Celestine III, that is, to the year of the Lord 1191, CCXIII, 987.—Chronicle of St. Benignus at Dijon, CLXII, 755 ff.

[Col. 0969]

CLXXVI. HISTORICAL INDEX, OR FOURFOLD SYNOPSIS, SETTING FORTH IN TURN WHATEVER IN THE COURSE OF PATROLOGY RELATES TO SACRED HISTORY, ECCLESIASTICAL HISTORY, UNIVERSAL SECULAR HISTORY, AND THE PARTICULAR HISTORY OF INDIVIDUAL PEOPLES; THE LAST OF THESE ARRANGED ALPHABETICALLY BY NATIONS.

I.—On sacred history.

[Col. 0969]

Fragment on the Making of the World, St. Victorinus, martyr, V, 301.—Little Book on the Duration of the World, Julius Hilarianus, XIII, 1097.—Two Books of Sacred History, Sulpicius Severus, XX, 96 ff.—St. Eusebius Jerome’s translation of the Chronicle of Eusebius Pamphilus, XXVII, 61.—Chronicle, whose first part treats of the origin of things, St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 535.—Chronicle: its first five ages treat of sacred history, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 1019.—Chronicle divided into six ages, St. Ado of Vienne, CXXIII, 23.—Chronicle of Ekkehard of Aura, CLIV, 497.—Chronicle of Frechulf of Lisieux, CVI, 919.—Six Books of the *Hexameron*, St. Ambrose of Milan, XII, 124.—On the Earthly Paradise, ibid., 276.—On the Patriarchs, ibid., 316.—Book on Genesis, Juvencus, XIX, 315.—Virgilian Centos in Testimony to the Old and New Testaments, ibid., 803.—Five Books on the Deeds of Mosaic History, St. Avitus of Vienne, LIX, 324.—Little book by an anonymous author on the genealogies of the patriarchs, ibid., 523.—Questions on the Old and New Testaments, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 129.—Short Chronicle treating specifically of sacred history, Claudius of Turin, CIV, 917.—Scholastic History: the history of each book of the Old and New Testament, Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1053.—Four Books of Evangelical History, Juvencus, XIX, 53.—Two Books on the Acts of the Apostles, Arator, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, LXVIII, 81 ff.—Interpretation of Gospel Harmonies, Ammonius of Alexandria, LXVIII, 255.—Deeds of Christ written in verse, Florus the deacon, CXIX, 264.

II.—On ecclesiastical history.

1. General history of the Church.—Book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, Lactantius, VII, 189 ff.—Fifteen fragments from a historical work, St. Hilary of Poitiers, X, 627.—Ancient documents pertaining to the history of the Donatists, VIII, 673.—Proceedings of the Conference of Carthage, XI, 1231.—History of the Albigensians, XIII, 544.—Five Books on the Destruction of the City of Jerusalem, St. Ambrose, XV, 1961.—Two Books of Sacred History from the creation of the world to the fourth century, Sulpicius Severus, XX, 95.—Two Books of Ecclesiastical History, from the heresy of Arius to Arcadius and Honorius, Rufinus, priest of Aquileia, XXI, 463.—Chronicle from the year of Christ 1 to the year 430, Flavius Lucius Dexter, XXXI, 56 ff.—Excerpts and ancient writings pertaining to the history of the Donatists, XLIII, 773.—Complete Chronicle of St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 552 ff.—Five Books of the History of the Persecution in the Province of Africa, Victor of Vita, LVIII, 180.—Brief Account of the Case of the Nestorians and Eutychians, LXVIII, 969.—Ecclesiastical History called the *Tripartite History*, from the three Greek authors Sozomen, Socrates, and Theodoret, twelve books, Cassiodorus, LXIX, 880.—Book on Illustrious Men, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 1081.—Three Books on the Holy Places, from the report of Arculf, Gallic bishop, St. Adomnán, abbot, LXXXVIII, 779.—Ecclesiastical History of the English People, the Venerable Bede, XCV, 23.—Martyrologies according to the Cologne and Bollandist exemplars, XCIV, 797.—Capitularies of Charlemagne, Louis I, and Lothar, XCVII, 122 ff.—Survey of the Churches of the City of Rome, CI, 1359.—Chronicle of Frechulf, Bishop of Lisieux, CVI, 1117.—Martyrology, Rabanus Maurus, CX, 1121.—On the Beginnings and Growth of Ecclesiastical Institutions, Walafrid Strabo, CXIV, 919.—Three Books of the Memorial of the Saints, St. Eulogius of Toledo, CXV, 732.—Epitome of Sacred History, or Record of Christian Affairs from the time of Christ’s birth to Emperor Theodosius, Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVIII, 819.—Chronicle from Christ to the year 815, St. Ado of Vienne, CXXIII, 75.—Martyrology with additions, ibid., 140.—Martyrology of Usuard, ibid., 600; XXIV, 10.—Hincmar’s Annals, or the third part of the Annals of St-Bertin, from the year 861 to the year 882, CXXV, 1203.—On Ecclesiastical Disciplines and the Christian Religion, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 185.—Four Books of the History of the Church of Rheims, Flodoard, canon of Rheims, CXXXV, 23.—Three Books on the Triumphs of Christ and of the Saints in Palestine, Flodoard, ibid., 549.—Fourteen Books on Christ’s Triumphs throughout Italy, ibid., 596.—Ecclesiastical Constitutions of the Three Ottos, the same author, CXXXVIII, 821.—Ancient calendars and martyrologies, ibid., 1185.—Nine Books on the Persecution of the Church, Bonizo of Piacenza, CL, 803.—Constitutions of Emperor Henry III, CLI, 1081.—Constitutions of Emperor Henry IV, 821.—Ecclesiastical History, in which events from the Incarnation of the Savior to the year 1140 are briefly described through the succession of emperors, kings, and Roman pontiffs, Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 17 ff.

2. Particular History of Churches.---*Ecclesiastical History, or the Deeds of the Bishops of the Church of Hamburg*, from Charlemagne to Emperor Henry IV, Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 45.---On the earliest bishops of Norway, ibid., 646 ff.---*Lives of the Bishops of Ravenna*, from St. Apollinaris onward, Agnellus, CVI, 476.---A short work on the bishops of Metz, Alpert of Symphorianus, CXL, 445.---Two books *On the Diversity of Times*, containing much historical material, particularly concerning events in the diocese of Utrecht, Alpert of Metz, ibid., 452.---Two books of Traditions of St. Emmeram, Anamodus of Regensburg, CXXIX, 901.---History of the Bishops of Liège, Anselm of Liège, CXXXIX, 1068; CXLIII, 861.---History of the Dedication of the Church of St. Remigius at Rheims, Anselm of St. Remigius, CXLII, 1412.

*Deeds of the Archbishops of Milan*, from the year 925 to 1077, Arnulf of Milan, CXLVII, 286.---*Deeds of the Bishops of Verdun*, from 379 to 1047, Bertarius of Verdun, CXXXII, 501.---Five books of the *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, Bede the Venerable, XCV, 24.---*Recent History*, or History of the British Church, from 1066 to 1122, Eadmer of Canterbury, CLIX, 348.---Collections concerning the affairs of the Church of Rochester, from the first foundation of the see to the writer’s own time, Ernulf of Rochester, CLXIII, 1444.---Milanese Chronicle, from 1102 to 1140, Falco of Benevento, CLXXIII, 1145.---Four books of the *History of the Church of Rheims*, from the founding of the city of Rheims and its first bishops to 949, Flodoard of Rheims, CXXXV, 28.---A *Syntagma* on the condition of the Church under Emperors Henry IV and V, Pope Gregory VII, and certain subsequent pontiffs, Gerhoh of Reichersberg, CXCIV, 1445.---The *Eichstätt Book of the Popes*, Gundechar of Eichstätt, CXLVI, 986.---Four books of the Chronicle, or Deeds, of the Church of Centula, Hariulf, abbot of Haldensburg, CLXXIV, 1215.---History of the Afflictions of the Church of Salzburg, Henry of Salzburg, CXCVI, 1539.---*Deeds of the Bishops of Tongeren, Maastricht, and Liège*, CXXXIX, 957.---On the Primacy of the See of Arras, Lambert of Arras, CLXII, 627.---History of Milan from St. Ambrose to 1082, Landulf of Milan, CXLVII, 817.---*History of Compostela*, CLXX, 880.---Five books *On the Deeds of the English Bishops*, CLXXIX, 1442.---On the Antiquity of the Church of Glastonbury, CLXXIX, 1681.

III.---On Universal, Secular History.

Chronology, or a short work on the duration of the world, Julius Hilarianus, XIII, 1097.---St. Jerome of Stridon’s translation of the Chronicle of Eusebius Pamphilus, to which are appended consecutively the surviving fragments of the Greek work, from the creation of the world to A.D. 329.---Beginning of the book; the sons of Noah; the nations of Shem, the nations of Ham, the nations of Japheth; succession of kings and the length of each reign; comparison of kingdoms, XXVII, 33, 71, 77, 107 ff.---St. Jerome’s Chronicle, from A.D. 330 to A.D. 381, XXVII, 675.---Chronicle of Prosper of Aquitaine, from A.D. 382 to A.D. 449, XXVII, 703.---Abridgement of St. Jerome’s Chronicle, XXIX, 871.---Chronicle of Comprehensive History, from A.D. 1 to A.D. 430, F. L. Dexter, XXXI, 50 ff.

Seven books of the Histories of Paulus Orosius, from the beginning of the world to the fifth century [lacuna]: division of the world into three parts; Egyptians, Ethiopians, Athenians, Lapiths, Amazons, Scythians, Trojans, Assyrians, Medes and Persians; Romans from the founding of Rome; Gauls; various peoples of Greece; various peoples of Italy; concerning the Carthaginians and their disasters in conflict with the Romans; and so forth; concerning the Roman Empire down to the invasion and devastation of the Alans, Suebi, and Vandals; concerning the Goths, XXXI, 664 ff.---The complete Chronicle of St. Prosper of Aquitaine, divided into two parts.

The first part, from the origin of things to the death of Valens, treats of the patriarchs; the Hebrews and their kings; their illustrious men; the Romans and their kings; the kings of the Persians, Egyptians, and Syrians; poets, philosophers, and historians distinguished among these peoples. The consuls are recorded from the death of Christ; likewise noted are persecutions, bishops of various sees, various heresies and [Col. 0972] the councils by which they were condemned, and the supreme pontiffs.

In the second part the history is continued from the death of Emperor Valens to the death of Valentinian III and the capture of Rome by the Vandals, LI, 535 ff.

Chronicle of Idatius, bishop of Aquae Flaviae, in which are mentioned various Roman emperors from Theodosius onward, heretics, notable bishops, Alans, Vandals, Suebi, Goths and their devastations, Huns, and so forth, LI, 873 ff.

Chronicle of Count Marcellinus, from A.D. 379 to 558.---Roman emperors, supreme pontiffs, certain illustrious men of this period, Vandals, Parthians, Goths, and so forth, ibid., 917.

The twelve books of the Tripartite History of M. A. Cassiodorus: Assyrian kings, Latin kings, Roman kings, consuls, Roman emperors from Julius Caesar to Emperor Anastasius, XLVIII, LXIX, 1215 ff.---Chronicle of Victor of Tunnuna, continuing where Prosper ends, from 444 to 566: heretics, councils, bishops, supreme pontiffs, Roman emperors, Huns, Vandals, LXVIII, 941.---Chronicle of John, abbot of Biclar, continuing where Victor ends, from Emperor Justin in the year 430 [an apparent chronological error] to Emperor Maurice, 539–602: Roman emperors, Armenians, Persians, Iberians, Moors, Gepids, Lombards, Suebi, Franks, councils, and so forth, LXXII, 864.---Chronicle of Marius, bishop of Aventicum: notices of consuls from Emperor Majorian, A.D. 457, to 580; Roman emperors, Franks, Goths, Saxons, Lombards, and so forth, ibid., 793.---Chronicle of Maximus, bishop of Caesaraugusta, from 430 to 595: Roman emperors, Goths, Britons, Alans, Huns, Franks, Vandals, Lombards, synods, bishops, popes, and so forth, LXXX, 619.---Chronicle of Eutrandus, from 606 to 630: Muhammad, synods, bishops, popes, ibid., 633.

Chronicle of St. Isidore, bishop of Seville, divided into six ages: the first age of the world, from Adam to Shem, 2244 years from the creation of the world; the second, from the year 2244 to Abraham, 3284; the third, from 3284 to David, 4165; the fourth, from 4165 to the Babylonian captivity of the Hebrews, 4680; the fifth, from 4680 to Octavian Augustus, 5211; the sixth, from 5211 to 5814, that is, to Heraclius, A.D. 610, LXXXIII, 1017.

A short chronicle from the beginning of the world to A.D. 810, divided like the preceding one, XCIV, 1173 ff.---Chronicle of Isidore of Pacensis; an Epitome of the Emperors, Annals of the Arabs, and a Chronography of Spain collected in one volume, XCVI, 1252 ff.---The *Mixed History* of Paul the Deacon, in twenty-four books, from the first king of Italy to Leo V, successor of Michael, in 815, XCV, 744 ff.---Landulf the Wise’s addition to the *Mixed History*, ibid., 1144 ff.---Annals of Abbot Einhard, from 741 to 829, CIV, 368 ff.---Abridgement of the Chronicle (Appendix to Einhard), from the creation of the world to A.D. 809, ibid., 608 ff.---Two volumes of Chronicles by Freculf, bishop of Lisieux: the first contains, from the beginning of the world to Christ’s birth, the history of events among various peoples—Hebrews, Trojans, Scythians, Amazons, Assyrians, Medes and Persians, Romans, Greeks, and Gauls, etc., etc.---The second volume of Chronicles, from Octavian Augustus and Christ’s birth to the kingdoms of the Franks and Lombards: Roman emperors, apostles, martyrs, heresies, synods, doctors, persecutions, Iberians, Armenians, Goths, Huns, Vandals, Saxons, Britons, etc., CVI, 917 ff.

Chronicle of St. Ado of Vienne, divided into six ages, namely:---1. From the origin of the world to the Flood, 1657.---2. From the Flood to the birth of Abraham, 2185.---3. From Abraham to David, 3125.---4. From David’s reign to the Babylonian deportation of the Hebrews, 4271.---5. From that deportation to Christ our Savior, 4832.---6. From Christ to the end of the world, CXXIII, 23 ff.

Annals of St. Prudentius of Troyes, or the second part of the Annals of St. Bertin, from 835 to 861, ibid., CXV, 1376.---Annals of Hincmar of Rheims, or the third part of the Annals of St. Bertin, from 861 to 882, ibid., CXXV, 1203 ff.---Chronology of St. Nicephorus, bishop of Constantinople, translated by Anastasius the Librarian: patriarchs, Hebrews, Persians, Egyptians, Roman emperors, empresses, kings of the ten tribes of Israel in Samaria, high priests in Israel, names of the patriarchs of Jerusalem after the ascension of Christ Jesus into heaven; exposition of the names of the bishops of Rome after Christ and the Apostles; catalogue of the bishops of Byzantium after Christ and the Apostles; bishops of Alexandria in Egypt; bishops of Antioch, ibid., CXXIX, 512, 522, 523, 525, 537 ff.---Chronicle of Albelda, perhaps by Dulcidius, bishop of Salamanca, and continued by Vigila, monk of Albelda [Col. 0973]: succession of Roman kings; succession of the Gothic people; Saracens in Spain; Arab governors in Spain, ibid., 1224.---Chronicle of Regino, abbot of Prüm, from the birth of Christ to 967: Jews, Gospel events, Roman emperors, apostles, first bishops, martyrs, Goths, Vandals, Alans, Franks, Lombards, English, Persians, Saracens, Roman pontiffs, and so forth; kings of the Franks, ibid., CXXXII, 15 ff.---History of the Deeds of Kings and Emperors, or *Antapodosis*, Liutprand, CXXXVI, 787 ff.---Chronicle of Liutprand, ibid., 973 ff.---Continuation of Regino, from 907 to 967, ibid., 152 ff.---Annals of Hildesheim, Quedlinburg, Weissenburg, and Lambert: six ages of the world, Roman emperors, memorable events from 702 to 1147, CXLI, 443.---Annals of St. Benignus of Dijon, from 564 to 1285, ibid., 875.---Five books of Rodulfus Glaber, monk of Cluny, on the history of his own time, principally from the election of Hugh Capet as king to 1046, ibid., CXLII, 611.---Chronicle of Herman the Cripple to 1054, CXLIII, 56.---Continuation of Herman’s Chronicle from 1054 to 1066, ibid., 263.

Annals of Berthold, priest of Constance, from 1056 to 1080, ibid., CXLVII, 343 ff.---34. Chronicle of Marianus Scotus, from the birth of Christ to 1104, ibid., 633.---Chronicle of Bernold, ibid., CXLVIII, 1299.---Chronicle of Hugh, abbot of Flavigny, in two books, from the birth of Christ to 1099, ibid., CXLIV, 21 ff.---Würzburg Chronicle of Ekkehard of Aura, from Christ to 1057, ibid., 460.---Universal Chronicle of Ekkehard: patriarchs, Jews, Assyrians, Egyptians, Persians, Romans, Gauls, Greeks, Syrians, Roman emperors; the origin of the Franks; history of the Goths; concerning the Amazons; concerning the origin of the Huns; history of the Lombards; an account of the acts of Charlemagne; concerning the origin of the Saxons; etc., etc., ibid., 497.---Chronicle of St. Hubert of Andage, from 825 to 1106, ibid., 1337.---Chronicle of Lupus the Protospatharius and the Annals of Bari, from 782 to 1102, ibid., 121.---Chronicle of Sigebert of Gembloux, from 381 to 1112, CLX, 61 ff.---Continuation by Anselm of Gembloux, from 1112 to 1136, ibid.---Gembloux Continuation, from 1136 to 1148, ibid.---Gembloux Supplement, from 771 to 1104, ibid., 265.---Supplement of Anchin, from 651 to 1168, ibid., 269.---Supplement of Affligem, from 597 to 1162, ibid., 280.---Continuation of Anchin, from 1149 to 1222, ibid., 293.---Supplement of Hasnon, ibid., 253.---Continuation of Tournai, from 1114 to 1334, ibid., 357.---Supplement of Laon, from 928 to 1145, ibid., 359.---Supplement of Corbie, from 419 to 885, ibid., 361.---Premonstratensian Continuation, from 1114 to 1155, ibid., 364.---Continuation of Burburg, from 1114 to 1164, ibid., 379.---Supplement of Beauvais, from 649 to 1163, ibid., 387.

Chronicle of St. Benignus of Dijon by an anonymous author, containing much concerning the kings of the Franks from the Incarnation of the Lord, 195, to 1026, CLXII, 755.---*Book of Ecclesiastical History and of the Deeds of the Romans and Franks*, briefly compiled by Hugh of St. Mary, CLXIIII, 821 ff.---Summary of the Whole of Universal History from the year 726, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 187.---Annals of Bamberg, from 1137 to 1180.---Annals of Ensdorf, from 1184 to 1568.---Lesser Annals of Augsburg, from 1137 to 1457, CLXXIII, 1364.---Pantheon of Godfrey of Viterbo: the first fifteen parts are lacking; the empire is transferred to the Greeks, CXCVIII, 880.---The empire is transferred to the Franks, ibid., 920.---Concerning the English and Saxons, ibid., 997.---Catalogue of all Roman pontiffs, all Roman emperors, and all kings from the beginning of the world to Pope Urban III, Emperor Frederick I, and his son King Henry VI, ibid., 1011 ff.---Chronicle of Helinand, monk of Froidmont, from A.D. 634 to 1204: Saracens, English, Saxons, Franks, Northmen, Moors, etc., etc., CCXII, 772.---Chronicle of Sicard, from Emperor Octavian to Emperor Leo, ibid., 777.---From Emperor Charlemagne, in the year of the Lord 700, to 1221, CCXIII, 441.

IV.---Particular History, or History of Individual Peoples.

Egyptians.---The Egyptian kingdom is older than the Roman kingdom, Tertullian, I, 432.---The Egyptians consecrated animals, ibid., 418.---The Egyptian gods: the ibis and the crocodile, idem, II, 302.---Egyptian bull-priests, ibid., 928, 953.---Egyptian hierophants, ibid., 260.---All [Col. 0974] superstition comes from Egypt, idem, I, 640.---On the animals worshipped by the Egyptians, Lactantius, VI, 618.---Their priests shaved their entire bodies, ibid., 235.---What their year was like, ibid., 325, 647, 934.---The ancient name of their land, ibid., 327.---They were the first to begin to observe and worship the stars, ibid., 328.---Among them rains are absent or rare, ibid., 329, 533.---They were the first to transmit the doctrine of transmigration of souls, ibid., 405.---The drowning of them and Pharaoh in the Red Sea, ibid., 470, 471, 785.---On their worship of animals, ibid., 620, 786.---They worshipped the sun in the image of Jupiter, ibid., 621.---Whether the Jews received the custom of embalming bodies from them, ibid., 772.---Worship of water among the Egyptians, Firmicus Maternus, XII, 984.---Idol worship among the Egyptians, Rufinus of Aquileia, XXI, 413.---Egypt also has many monks, ibid.---Egyptian kings, St. Jerome, XXVII, 94.---Comparison of the Egyptian kingdom with others, ibid., 108.---The individual cities of Egypt venerate individual animals, idem, XXIII, 296.---In Egypt and Palestine beef is not eaten, ibid., 295.---In Jerome’s time the Egyptian language was called Ham, ibid., 950.---Egypt, low-lying and flat, is irrigated by waters coming from Ethiopia, ibid., 1026, 1027.---The things in which Egypt is especially fertile, idem, XXIV, 182.---The Egyptian wilderness is fertile in venomous creatures, ibid., 638.---What are the idols of the Egyptians? ibid., 151, 152.---No nation was so devoted to idolatry as Egypt, ibid., 447.---Egyptians are called flies and Assyrians bees, ibid., 111, 112.---An Egyptian is admitted once as a husband to the rites of the bull, idem, XXII, 1051.---Egyptian priests used linen garments, idem, XXV, 436, note.

The provinces comprising Upper and Lower Egypt, Paulus Orosius, XXXI, 679, 680.---It pays a fifth part of every harvest, ibid., 711.---On the barrenness and famine of Egypt, for which Joseph provided through his resourcefulness, and on the vanity of Egyptian priests, ibid., 709.---On God’s people afflicted in Egypt by the ten plagues of Egypt; on the crossing of the Arabian Gulf and its remains; and on a certain hostile heat of the sun, ibid., 713.

The Egyptians were descended from the seed of Ham, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1398.---The Egyptian kingdom flourished in Abraham’s time, idem, XLI, 497.---Isis gave letters to the Egyptians, ibid., 597, 599.---The fabricated antiquity of Egyptian wisdom is refuted, ibid. Egyptian wisdom, especially astronomy, ibid., 599.---Egyptians loved geometry, idem, XXXIV, 549.---Egyptian custom regarding dead bodies, idem, XXXIX, 1605.---Egyptians excel in embalming the bodies of the dead, idem, XXXIV, 502.---Trismegistus foretold that Egyptian religion would fall, idem; XLI, 248, 251.---And he received this from demons, ibid.---Shepherds are abominable to the Egyptians, idem, XXXIV, 605.---The sacrifices of the Israelites are abominations to the Egyptians, ibid.---The ten plagues of the Egyptians are expounded, idem, XXXVI, 1001; XXXVIII, 67.---Why the Egyptians were subdued by frogs and flies, idem, XXXV, 2039.---The despoiling of the Egyptians wrongly criticized by Faustus, idem, XLII, 445.---How God permitted the Egyptians to be deceived by the Israelites in the reciprocal receiving of gold and silver, idem, XL, 34.---The riches of the Egyptians which the Israelites carried off were owed to them, idem, XXXVII, 1409.---Egyptian days, idem, XXXV, 2130.---Location of Egypt, idem, XLIII, 423.---Egypt is divided into two parts, John Cassian, XLIX, 79, note.---It is watered by the overflow of the Nile, ibid., 997.---Egypt becomes a Roman province, St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 549.---The gods of the Egyptians are innumerable, St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 517.---Their proper name is Jupiter Ammon, ibid., 515.---Their superstition in the rites of Isis, ibid., 518.---Egyptians called inhabitants of the Nile, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 163.---Their drowning, ibid., 806.---Dynasties, ibid., 170.---Their kings were called Pharaohs, then Ptolemies, ibid., 292, note.---Egypt, ibid., 166, 167.---Upper and Lower Egypt devastated by the Saracens, ibid., 657.---Martin is celebrated there, ibid., 1008, 1009.---Its deserts and hermits, ibid., 1021.---Antioch of Egypt captured by the Persians, ibid., 302.---Papyrus and plants, ibid., 375, note.---The city of Memphis is founded in Egypt, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 1025.---Egyptian kings, the Ptolemies, ibid., 1035.---Under Heraclius, the Persians seized Egypt and many provinces, ibid., 1056.---The Egyptians invented geometry, idem, LXXXII, 161.---Astronomy, ibid., 169.---From the course of the sun they discovered the day of the month, ibid., 219.---When the Egyptian kingdom began, ibid., 224.---Egypt is subjected to the Romans, ibid., 226.

How Egypt provides pasture despite the lack of rain there, Alcuin, C, 557.---Egyptians introduced into the palace school, ibid., 266.---Their calculation is rejected, ibid., 267, 277.---On the acts performed by Moses in Egypt, Freculf of Lisieux, CVI, 949.---Cambyses, the second king of the Persians, gained Egypt by war, ibid., 994.---Egypt [Col. 0975] joined to the empire of Artaxerxes, ibid., 1008.---Egypt is subdued by Alexander the Great, ibid., 1015.---Alexandria in Egypt is founded, ibid., 1019.---Many captive Jews were led into Egypt under Ptolemy, Alexander’s successor, ibid., 1025.---Egypt occupied by Antiochus, ibid., 1046.---The kingdom of the Egyptians was destroyed, and Egypt thereafter became a Roman province, ibid., 1114.---On Egyptian months, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 684.---The Egyptian kingdom begins, St. Ado of Vienne, CXXIII, 28.---The city of Memphis is founded in Egypt, ibid., 34.---Egypt revolts from the Persians, ibid., 52.---The Ptolemies, ibid., 59 ff.---Egypt made into a province, ibid., 75. Universal Chronicle of Ekkehard, containing much concerning the Egyptians, idem, CLIV, 497 ff.---On Egypt: Euxia, later called Egypt; the Thebaid; Thebes; monks; Babel; Egyptian Alexandria, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 126.---On the kingdom of Egypt; on the kingdom of the Egyptians after Alexander the Great, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 232, 234.---Catalogue of the kings of Egypt and Antioch after the death of Alexander the Great; catalogue of Egyptian kings, Godfrey of Viterbo, CXCVIII, 1025, 1026.---On the plagues of Egypt, Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1149.---On Egyptian days, ibid., 1152.---On the Egyptian desert, ibid., 1156.---On the location of the Ptolemies, ibid., 1498 ff.---In the crusaders’ expedition: the Egyptians enter our territory with innumerable forces. The king meets them, fights them too rashly, and is defeated, William of Tyre, CCI, 473.---The Egyptians pour into the kingdom with enormous forces; the king meets them and, after capturing some and killing many more, puts the rest to flight, ibid., 486.---The Egyptians enter the kingdom with immense forces; but when our men meet them with a strong hand, they are miserably overthrown, ibid., 540.---The region of Egypt is described and its character set forth, ibid., 770.---Saladin obtains the kingdom of Egypt, ibid., 789.---The king goes down into Egypt with his expeditionary forces, while Greeks also follow him by sea and land, ibid., 791.---Siege of Damietta, ibid., 792.---See in the following chapters the section on Egypt in this expedition.

Alemanni.---Alemanni, St. Jerome, XXII, 1057.---Alamanni, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 201, 205, 206, 588, 674.---They fight with the Vandals, ibid., 704.---Defeated by Clovis, they are made subject to him, ibid., 225, 586.---They ravage Gaul, ibid., 177, 178.---And Italy, ibid., 700.---They drive out the Transjurane peoples, ibid., 629.---They are subjected by Pippin and Carloman, ibid., 682, 683.---Kings of the Alamanni, ibid., 177, 205.---Their dukes, ibid., 661, 613, 649.---On the deeds of St. Henry, emperor, Adelbold of Utrecht, CXL, 88.---Chronicle of St. Andrew’s Castle, CXLIX, 239.

English and Britons.---The Britons are shut within the circuit of the Ocean, Tertullian, II, 611.---Places of the Britons inaccessible to the Romans are subject to Christ, ibid., 610.---When Britain was open to the faith, and when to the Arians, St. Hilary of Poitiers, X, 479.---Its bishops are united with the Gallican bishops, ibid.---Britain, a fertile province of tyrants, St. Jerome, XXII, 1157.---Britain and Mauretania were Christian in Origen’s time, idem, XXV, 723.---Britain traversed by St. James, Dexter, XXXI, 135.---And by St. Peter the Apostle, ibid., 212, note.---Britain, Paulus Orosius, XXXI, 689, 690.---Caesar invades Britain, ibid., 1014.---Britain formerly subject to the prefect of Gaul, idem, XLVIII, 412.---When, and by whom, the English Church was infected with the Pelagian heresy, ibid., 367 ff.---The lamenting book *On the Ruin of Britain*, Gildas the Wise, LXIX, 329.---Description of the island of Britain, Cassiodorus, LXIX, 1252.---St. Gregory sends St. Augustine to England; beginning of the Christian faith in Britain; idolatrous English occupy this island, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 364.---In Diocletian’s persecution it is made purple with the blood of martyrs, ibid., 365.---It is infected with the Pelagian heresy, ibid.---The state of England at the beginning of Gregory’s pontificate, ibid., 290.---English and Saxons summoned from Germany invade Britain, ibid., 366.---The English are of very beautiful appearance, ibid., 50, 71.---English boys for sale in the city of Rome, ibid.---Gregory ordered that the shrines of the English should not be destroyed but dedicated as basilicas, ibid., 1120.---The Britons receive the doctrine and rites of the Roman Church, ibid., 387.---The extent and character of Gregory’s accounts of the conversion of the English, ibid., 101, 102, 103.---Persecution rages against the Christian English, ibid., 387.---Gallican bishops neglected the conversion of the English, idem, LXXVII, 842.---Before conversion, the English worshipped wood and stones, ibid., 932.---The English converted to the faith, ibid., 1138 ff.

Five books of the *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, from Julius Caesar, the first of the Romans to assail Britain in war, to 731, Bede the Venerable, XCV, 24 ff.---The fertility and pleasantness of Britain, Rabanus Maurus, [Col. 0976] CXI, 354.---The boundaries of the Britons defined at the beginning of the Frankish kingdom, St. Lupus of Ferrières, CXIX, 560.---

Severus transfers the war to Britain, St. Ado of Vienne, CXXIII, 85.---The Britons request Roman aid against the Picts, ibid., 99, 100.---The English people arrives in Britain in three long ships, ibid., 102.---The Pelagian heresy disturbs the faith of the Britons, ibid., 103.---Augustine, Mellitus, and John are sent to Britain by St. Gregory, ibid., 111, 112.---On the conversion of the English or Britons to the Catholic faith, Aimoin of Fleury, CXXXIX, 748.---The Danes devastate England, Osbern of Canterbury, CXLIX, 380.---On Rollo’s victory over the English, William of Jumièges, CXLIX, 790.---On Athelstan, the most Christian king of the English, with whom Rollo entered into an indissoluble treaty of friendship, ibid., 792.---How Ethelred, king of England, who had married Emma, the duke’s sister, sent an army to subject Normandy to himself, ibid., 825.---On the cruelty of Ethelred, king of the English, toward the Danes, ibid., 826.---On Henry I, king of the English, ibid., 879.

Five books *On the Deeds of the Kings of the English*, William of Malmesbury, CLXXIX, 959.---Three books of *Recent History*, ibid., 1392 ff.---Five books *On the Deeds of the Bishops of the English*, ibid., 1441.---Kings of the English, Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 79.---Pantheon of Godfrey of Viterbo: concerning the English and Saxons, CXCVIII, 997.---On the Battle of the Standard in the time of King Stephen, Aelred, CXCV, 701.---Genealogy of the kings of the English, ibid., 711.---Life of St. Edward, King and Confessor, ibid., 737.---Eight books of the *History of the English*, from the origin of the British kingdom to 1154, Henry of Huntingdon, CXCV, 799.---Invasions of the English, Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 77.---Kings of the English, ibid., 79.---Ethelred, king of the English; various events in England, ibid., 94, 283, 295, 303, 308, 311, 329, 578, 787, 798.---Gruffydd, king of the Welsh, invades England, ibid., 566.---Account of English and Norman affairs, ibid., 721.---Wars between the peoples of the kings of France and England. The two kings confer and make a treaty, ibid., 844.---Wars between Louis, king of the Franks, and Henry, king of England. Various prodigies, ibid., 849 ff.; 860 ff.---Peace is arranged between the kings of France and England, ibid., 884.---Death and funeral rites of Henry, king of the English. Disturbances in England, ibid., 943.---Various events in England and Normandy, ibid., 949.---Peace between the kings of England and Scotland, ibid., 971.---King Stephen is captured in England by the Angevins, ibid., 977, etc.

Amazons.---The kingdom of the Amazons is older than the Roman kingdom, Tertullian, I, 432.---The origin of the Amazons’ name, Lactantius, VI, 158.---The Amazons subjected all Asia, St. Ambrose, XVII, 436.---They made men so savage that they were initiated into eating human flesh, ibid.---Origin, customs, and deeds of the Amazons, Paulus Orosius, XXXI, 724.---Epilogue of the history of the Amazons, in which he attacks the present blindness of the Romans, ibid., 728.---Region of the Amazons, ibid., 685.---While their husbands are absent in battle, the Amazons resist the enemies’ repeated assaults and overcome diverse peoples of Asia in war, Jordanes, LXIX, 1257.---On the Amazons’ intercourse with neighboring peoples and their childbirths, ibid., 1258.---On the men of the Amazons and their king Telephus, and on his origin and deeds, ibid. Amazons: Fredegar, LXXI, 698; Ekkehard of Aura, CLIV, 729; Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 733 ff.; Freculf of Lisieux, CVI, 960; Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 171.

Arabs.---What are the gods of the Arabs? Tertullian, I, 418.---Frankincense was exported from Arabia, ibid., 493.---Arabian women cover not only their heads but also their whole faces, so that, with one eye left free, they are content to enjoy half the light rather than expose their whole face, idem, II, 912.---The Arabs worshipped a stone as God, Lactantius, VII, 494; Arnobius, VI, 1185.---We find in the history of the ancient Ethiopians, Arabs, and Phoenicians that some practiced circumcision for their own purposes, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1245.---The foods eaten by Arabs and Saracens, St. Jerome, XXIII, 294.---They deem it unlawful to eat pork, ibid.---Arabs given to robbery besieged the roads of Jericho, St. Jerome, XXIV, 699.---Arabian women, like those of Mesopotamia, covered with *theristra* [veils], ibid., 70.---Arabia abounds in flocks, St. Jerome, XXX, 258, 259.---Septimius Severus conquered the Arabs, Paulus Orosius, XXXI, 1103.---Trajan captures Arabia, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 1043.---Severus Pertinax acquires Arabia, ibid., 1045.

Argives.---Succession of Argive kings, St. Jerome, XXVII, 86.---The Argive kingdom compared with others, ibid., 130 ff.---Inachus was the first king of the Argives, St. Augustine, XLI, 597.---Why Argos or the Argives are so called, ibid., 564.---Succession of Argive kings, ibid., 562.---The Argive kingdom arose at the same time as Abraham’s grandsons, ibid.---Fall of the Argive kingdom, ibid., 572.---On the transfer of the Argive kingdom to Mycenae, Freculf of Lisieux, CVI, 958.---The Argive kingdom, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 170; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 235; Godfrey of Viterbo, CXCVIII, 1027.

Athenians.---The Athenians occupied Asia, Tertullian, II, 700.---Athens, a city of eloquence, ibid., 651.---Those most acute in thought and speech are born at Athens, Tertullian, II, 683.---Kings of the Athenians, St. Jerome, XXVII, 88.---The city of the Athenians devoted to idolatry, idem, XXIV, 805.---Inscription of the Athenian altar, idem, XXVI, 572.---The city of Athens was either rebuilt or founded under King Cecrops, St. Augustine, XLI, 566.---Whence Athens derived its name, on what occasion, and under what king, ibid.---Greece had nothing more famous than Athens, ibid., 567.---The Athenians flourished in Greece more in reputation than in reality, ibid., 561.---At Athens arose the most talkative sects of philosophers, idem, XLIII, 454.---The kingdom of the Athenians changed into a republic, ibid., 577.---Athenian women took part in public deliberations, ibid., 566.---Why they were expelled from public deliberations, ibid., 567.---Conflict between the Cretans and Athenians, Paulus Orosius, XXXI, 722.---War between the Peloponnesians and Athenians, ibid., 738.---War of the Athenians against the Lacedaemonians: of the Peloponnesians and Boeotians against the Athenians, ibid.---Darius attacks the Athenians at peril to his own life and the lives of many others, ibid., 762.---The Athenians are attacked in the war of the Lacedaemonians at the urging of Alcibiades, who avenges himself for his exile, ibid., 782.---Severe battles of the Athenians against the Lacedaemonians, and dreadful disasters and slaughter suffered on both sides, ibid., 783.---Peace is granted to the Athenians on specified laws and conditions, and thirty rulers are appointed, ibid., 786.---On the slave war among the Athenians, ibid., 936.---The Athenian kingdom, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 171; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 235; Ekkehard of Aura, CLIV, 514 ff.

Assyrians.---Ninus was the first king of the Assyrians, Tertullian, II, 1034.---That kingdom is older than the Roman kingdom, idem, I, 432.---Their gods did not protect it, ibid., 608.---Secular histories begin with the Assyrians, idem, II, 1035.---The Assyrian kingdom, St. Cyprian, IV, 571; St. Jerome, XXVII, 77, 107.---For 1,300 years the Assyrians possessed the kingdom of Asia, Egypt, and Libya, St. Jerome, XXIV, 112.---The Assyrian kingdom held Jerusalem for seventy years, ibid., 204.---Enumeration of the Assyrian kings who conquered the people of Israel, ibid., 381.---Greek authors described the wars of the Assyrian nation, ibid., 200.---The ancient Assyrians are called Syrians, ibid., 187.---The Hebrews relate that the Assyrians’ bodies were burned while their garments remained unharmed, ibid., 138.---The regions held by Assyrians and Babylonians, St. Jerome, XXV, 1110.---Assyrians and Babylonians occupy the land of the North, ibid., 1432.---On Ninus and Semiramis and their kingdoms, Paulus Orosius, XXXI, 669.---On Sardanapalus, king of the Assyrians, ibid., 733 ff.---The Assyrian kingdom lasted for 1,160 years under fifty kings, ibid., 721.---It is transferred to the Medes, ibid., 735.---The Assyrian kingdom, extended far and wide by Ninus, St. Augustine, XLI, 116.---The Assyrian kingdom ruled all Asia except India, ibid., 497.---The Assyrian kingdom was exceedingly flourishing, ibid., 560.---It flourished in Abraham’s time, ibid., 497.---The Assyrian kingdom endured 1,240 years, ibid., 117, 577.---When the Assyrian kingdom ended, ibid.---Succession of Assyrian kings, ibid., 561.---For how many years the monarchy of the Assyrian kings lasted, Cassiodorus, LXIX, 1225, 1218.---How many kings it had, and how many years each of them reigned, ibid.---Transfer of the Assyrian empire to the Medes, St. Ado of Vienne, CXXIII, 45.---Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, ibid.---Nebuchadnezzar rules the Assyrians, ibid., 46.---Assyrians, Ekkehard of Aura, CLIV, 497 ff.---On the Assyrian kingdom, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 227.---Catalogue of Assyrian kings, Godfrey of Viterbo, CXCVIII, 1021; Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 166.

Babylonians.—The Babylonian kingdom was older than the Roman, Tertullian, I, 432.—The Babylonians were the first to call a certain image of Bel, said to have exercised rule over them, a god, St Ambrose, XVII, 59.—Semiramis, wife of Ninus, built Babylon’s walls, St Jerome, XXV, 838.—It was overthrown by the attack of the Medes and Persians, [Col. 0978] id., XXIV, 155.—It was founded by the Chaldeans, ibid., 454.—It was the metropolis of the Chaldeans, ibid., 155.—The circumference of Babylon, the height of its citadel, and the magnificence of the things contained in it are described, ibid., 164.—Babylon and the region of the Chaldeans are called “shadowy mountains,” ibid., 766.—The Babylonians were cruel, ibid., 182.—There were royal hunts at Babylon, ibid., 159.—Cyrus destroyed Babylon, Paulus Orosius, XXXI, 759, 760.—Babylonia was founded by Nimrod and restored by Semiramis, ibid., 758, 759.—Description of Babylon, ibid., 758, 759.—Babylon was founded by Nimrod, St Augustine, XLI, 482.—Babylon was founded in the innermost regions of Persia, id., XXXVI, 773.—Babylon, capital of the Assyrian kingdom, XLI, 497.—Semiramis founded or rebuilt Babylon, ibid., 561.—Description of Babylonia, St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 165.—By whom the Tower of Babylon was built, and its height, St Isidore of Seville, LXXIII, 1022.—Who first of all sought to rule men and to extend his kingdom, Alcuin, C, 533.—Whether the tower and city of Babylon were one work, ibid.—On Nimrod the giant and the confusion of languages at the building of the tower, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 528.—The founder and destroyer of Babylon, id., CXI, 337, 1164.—Its size, ibid., 1164.—How its kingdom passed to the Medes, CIX, 520.—Why the Babylonians carry about on their foreheads the Decalogue written on little parchments and suspended there, CX, 755; CVIII, 866.—Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylonia captures Jerusalem and transfers part of the Temple vessels to Babylon, St Ado of Vienne, CXXIII, 46.—The Jews are led captive to Babylon, ibid.—Succession of the kings of Babylonia, ibid., 49.—Babylon was captured by Cyrus, king of the Persians, ibid.—Destroyed by Darius, ibid.—On the kings of Babylonia, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 237; Godfrey of Viterbo, CXCVIII, 1027; Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 175.

Bohemians.—Chronicle of the Bohemians, from the earliest times of the Bohemian monarchy to the year 1125, Cosmas of Prague, CLXVI, 58 ff.—Continuation of Cosmas by the canon of Vyšehrad, ibid., 245.—Continuation of Cosmas by the monk of Sázava, ibid., 273 ff.—Continuations of Cosmas by the canons of Prague, ibid., 299 ff.—War brought upon the Bohemians, id., CLX, 907.—Defeat of the Bohemians and Zbigniew, ibid., 910.—On the Bohemians, ibid., 923, 924.

Carthaginians.—The Carthaginians, noble by antiquity and fortunate by novelty, Tertullian, II, 1030.—Their former style of dress, ibid.—Carthaginian contests, ibid., 133.—Carthage, a city exceptionally devoted to the pursuits of war, ibid., 1032.—Carthage’s foundress gave herself to the pyre, id., I, 532.—Its walls were imposed upon it by Statilius Taurus, id., II, 1031.—The schools of rhetoric at Carthage, ibid., 553.—Fires hung over the walls of Carthage in Tertullian’s age, id., I, 701.—The Tyrians founded Carthage, St Ambrose, XIV, 723.—Carthage was founded by Dido, St Jerome, XXIII, 273.—It is burned, ibid.—Carthage is thought to be Tarshish, ibid., 926.—Carthage is a Tyrian colony, id., XXIV, 201.—The Romans’ treaty with the Carthaginians, a cause of many evils, Paulus Orosius, XXXI, 810.—On the Carthaginians’ origin and the changing fortunes they experienced before the First Punic War, ibid., 870.—Regulus, having killed an enormous serpent, wins a victory over the Carthaginians, ibid., 875.—When peace was denied them, the Carthaginians gathered aid from every quarter and captured Regulus, ibid., 878.—Because the Carthaginians, denied peace, cruelly killed Regulus, while the Romans, fighting once and again in Sicily with little success, finally prevailed, ibid., 881.—The Carthaginians obtained peace on stipulated terms and for a price, ibid., 883.—The Carthaginians obtain peace with difficulty, ibid., 884, 885.—On the Second Punic War: Hannibal inflicted immense slaughter upon the Romans, opening a route through Gaul, ibid., 890.—Many strange and wondrous prodigies then appeared in various places; Hannibal, by cunning, nearly annihilated the army of the consul Flaminius, ibid., 892.—On the pitiable Roman defeat at Cannae; on the plan to abandon Italy; on how the Romans recovered and restored their army;
