likewise on various battles, ibid., 893.—Hannibal terrifies the Romans at the Anio, yet no opportunity is given to overwhelm him, ibid., 896.—On various defeats sustained by Romans and Carthaginians on either side, as victory now inclined one way, now the other, ibid., 899.—Hannibal was recalled to Africa, defeated and put to flight by Scipio, and the Romans granted peace to the Carthaginians, ibid., 903.—On the Third Punic War: the consuls set out to destroy Carthage, but were driven back; meanwhile, on the site of the city, XXXI, [Col. 0979] 914.—On Carthage’s pitiable overthrow and destruction, ibid., 915.—On Carthage restored, ibid., 942.—Carthage founded by Dido, St Augustine, XXXVI, 537.—The dominion of the heavenly goddess, id., XXXVII, 1270.—The beginnings of the Carthaginian state surpassed other peoples in seafaring, id., XXXVI, 537.—Three wars were waged between the Carthaginians and Romans, id., XLI, 62, note.—Carthage destroyed by Scipio Africanus, ibid., 102.—Carthage and Rome, two cities skilled in Latin letters, id., XXXIII, 436.

Carthage founded by Dido, Freculph of Lisieux, CVI, 964.—On the various battles by land and sea between Romans and Carthaginians, and on the countless multitude of persons slain on both sides, in the unceasing and most wretched wars that lasted twenty-five years, ibid., 1033.—How Hannibal, called the Romans’ most formidable enemy, set out from Spain with a great army and came into Italy, where for thirteen uninterrupted years he waged very grave and immense wars with the Romans, reducing them almost to utter despair, ibid., 1039.—Carthage was wholly destroyed by fire and sword in the six-hundredth year after its foundation, ibid., 1048.—On the rebuilding of Carthage, ibid., 1060.—The Carthaginians’ most terrifying war begins, St Ado of Vienne, CXXIII, 53.—Its various events, ibid. ff.

Brachmans.—On the customs of the Brachmans, XVII, 1132.

Chaldeans.—A Chaldean seed is led into Egypt, Tertullian, II, 1035.—The Chaldeans’ fiction concerning the antiquity of the world, Lactantius, VI, 780, 781.—The Chaldeans’ opinion concerning the upper world, St Ambrose, XIV, 459.—We have learned that they devote themselves more than others to vain superstition, ibid., 420.—They investigate the courses of the stars with the empty zeal of superstition and sow the errors of impious paganism, ibid., 931.—The Chaldeans’—that is, astrologers’—knowledge concerning human birth is useless, harmful, impossible, and impious, ibid., 192.—They are regarded as more expert in numbers, XVI, 1570.—“Chaldeans” is interpreted as “demons,” St Jerome, XXII, 394.—Chaldea belonged to the Assyrian kingdom, St Augustine, XLI, 492.—The Chaldeans inferred the future from the stars, St Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 631.—The Chaldeans were the first inventors of geometry and said that it was suited to all arts, Cassiodorus, LXIX, 608.—The Chaldeans worshipped fire as a god, Alcuin, C, 272, 534.

Franks.—The Franks were of the same origin as the Carpi and Goths, Lactantius, VII, 306.—Whether their frontier lay around the Danube, ibid., 354, 528.—They were defeated by Constantine, 529.—In Galerius’s time they had not yet overrun the whole of Gaul, 766, 767.—Their name was older than the times of both Valentinians, 767.—The Franks claimed Germany for themselves, St Ambrose, XVII, 914.—The Franks were driven from Gaul by Aetius, St Prosper of Aquitaine, II, 594.—The Frankish people was unbelieving, St Salvian of Marseilles, LIII, 86.—The Franks were liars, but hospitable, ibid., 142.—The Franks, rushing down through mountain passes, always brought war upon peoples, Cassiodorus, LXIX, 825, 826.—Constans subjected them to Roman rule, ibid., 963.—Frankish annals from the year 255 to Charlemagne, LXXI, 137.—Ten books of the *History of the Franks*, St Gregory of Tours, ibid., 161 ff.—Abridged history of the Franks by Fredegar, ibid., 573 ff.—Chronicle of Fredegar with his continuators, ibid., 605 ff.—Fragments of Fredegar on Frankish history, ibid., 697 ff.—Chronicle of Marius, bishop of Avenches, ibid., 794 ff.—On what day the Franks gave names to infants, St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 342.—The rite formerly observed in anointing Frankish kings, ibid., 255.—The first of them, Clovis, was inaugurated and crowned by St Remigius, ibid., 569.—At their coronation they make a profession of faith, ibid.—The source of the ancient right of the kings of the Franks to the kingdom of England, ibid., 572.—The formula for the coronation of Frankish kings asserts their right over the Saxons, Mercians, and Northumbrians, ibid.—The holy oil sent down from heaven with which they are anointed is called chrism, ibid., 573.—The head, breast, shoulders between the shoulder-blades, joints of the arms, and hands of Frankish kings are anointed, ibid., 574.

War of the Franks with the Saxons, Paul the Deacon, XCV, 566.—How the Frankish kingdom in Gaul began to be under the mayors of the royal household, ibid., 634.

Deeds of the kings of the Franks, partly drawn from Gregory of Tours’s history and partly from elsewhere, brought down to King Theuderic II; by an unknown author who lived in the time of that same Theuderic, Gregory of Tours, XCVI, 1421.—Capitularies of Charlemagne, XCVII, 122 ff.—Ancient annals of the Franks, XCVIII, 1410.—The Frankish name illustrious throughout the world, St Agobard of Lyons, [Col. 0980] CIV, 310.—An immense kingdom enlarged under Charlemagne, ibid., 321.—It comprised Gaul and Germany, ibid., 303.—Law of the Franks, 117, 126.—Annals of Abbot Einhard compared with the Lorsch Annals, from the year 741 to the year 829, CIV, 368.—Fragment of Erchambert, from the *Breviary of the Kings of the Franks and Mayors of the Household*, CXVI, 34.—Four books on the dissensions of the sons of Louis the Pious, Nithard, son of Angilbert, ibid., 45.—On the division of the empire after the death of Louis the Pious, Florus the deacon, CXIX, 249.—Annals of Hincmar from the year 861 to the year 882, CXXV, 1203.—On the conversion of the Franks, Flodoard of Reims, CXXXV, 49, 50.—Capitularies of Frankish kings and emperors, CXXXVIII, 526 ff.—Four books of *Histories*, Richer, monk of St Remigius, ibid., 18 ff.—Chronicle of the monk Benedict, CXXXIX, 10 ff.—Four books of the *History of the Franks*, Aimoin, monk of Fleury, ibid., 627.

Deeds of the Franks from the origin of the people itself to the death of King Clovis I, Rorico the monk, CXXXIX, 589.—Venetian Chronicle, John the deacon, ibid., 875.—Chronicle of Odorannus, monk of St Peter the Living at Sens, CXLII, 770.—Chronicle of Hermann the Lame, monk of Reichenau, CXLIII, 56 ff.—Abridged History of the Franks, Peter the Librarian, CLI, 1279.—On the origin of the Franks, Ekkehard of Aura, CLIV, 713 ff.—*The Deeds of God through the Franks*, or *History of Jerusalem*, nine books, Abbot Guibert, CLVI, 680.—Chronicle of Sigebert of Gembloux, CLX, 58 ff.—Continuations and additions by Anselm of Gembloux, 240 ff.—Chronicle of the kings of the Franks, Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 611 ff.—Summary of all universal history, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 187.—On the people and kings of the Franks from their origin to Charlemagne, and thereafter from Charlemagne to the successors of Charles the Simple, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 275.—The empire passes to the Franks, Godfrey of Viterbo, CXCVIII, 919.—Catalogue of Frankish kings, ibid., 1027 ff.—Chronicle of Helinand, monk of Froidmont, from the year 635 to 1186, CCXII, 771 ff.—A book briefly comprising ecclesiastical history and the deeds of Romans and Franks, by Hugh of Sainte-Marie, CLXIII, 821.—History of the Franks of Sens, ibid., 854 ff.—Book containing the deeds of the modern kings of the Franks, ibid., 874 ff.—History of the kings of the Franks of the monastery of St Denis, ibid., 911 ff.—Ecclesiastical History of Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 77 ff.

Gauls.—The Gauls sacrificed to Mercury, Tertullian, I, 316.

Gallic and German women had saffron-coloured hair, ibid., 1322.—African women envied their beauty, ibid.—The Gauls, priests of Cybele, cut off their genitals and lacerated their arms, ibid., 413, 425 ff.—The various nations of Gaul, now subject to Christ, Tertullian, II, 610.—The Gauls propitiated Esus and Teutates with human blood, Lactantius, VI, 230.—When those rites were abolished, ibid.—The Gauls, priests of Cybele, Lactantius, VI, 206.—Whence they were called Gauls, ibid., 234.—Their position in the goddess’s rites, ibid.—The Gauls, free from persecution under Constantius Chlorus, Lactantius, VI, 217, 322, 504, 700.—Gaul, free from persecution under Constantius, St Optatus, XI, 930.—Judges from Gaul requested by Africans, ibid.

The Gauls lay waste everything, St Jerome, XXII, 1058.—The native soil of the Gauls is subjected to Roman rule, ibid.—The ranks of the Gauls are laid low, ibid., 1110.—The Gauls mutilated by the Romans as an indignity, St Jerome, XXV, 851.—The Gauls were called *Galatae* from the whiteness of their bodies, St Jerome, XXVI, 353.—The Gauls called unteachable by Hilary, ibid., 355.—Their orators are frivolous, ibid.—The Gauls, priests of the Mother of the Gods, XXV, 851.—Why they were especially emasculated, ibid.—The boundaries of Gaul, id., XXII, 1058.—The flourishing studies of Gaul, ibid., 1075.—Victors from East and West settled in Gaul, ibid., 1058.—St James the apostle evangelizes in Gaul, Dexter, XXXI, 135.—The Gauls enter the city and slaughter the senators, Paulus Orosius, ibid., 792.—After exterminating its people, they pursue the very name of Rome, ibid., 793.—A huge multitude of Gauls is slaughtered near the river Anio, ibid., 808.—A third incursion through the coastal regions, ibid., 809.—The Senonian Gauls wage war against the Romans, ibid., 845.—The Cisalpine Gauls are slaughtered by the Romans, 887, 888.—The Gauls are slaughtered by Caesar, ibid., 1015.—Transalpine, Cisalpine, and Long-haired Gaul, ibid., 1006.—The Gauls’ surrender, ibid., 1013.—The Gallic incursion into the city, St Augustine, XLI, 108.—They burn Rome, with the Capitol Hill alone remaining, XXXVIII, 1356.—Camillus rescues his country from the Gauls, XLI, 62.—The Gauls were mutilated, ibid., 185, 213, 214.—The mutilation of Gallic priests is condemned, ibid., 214, 215.—The Senonian Gauls occupy Rome, St Prosper of Aquitaine, [Col. 0981] LI, 544.—Forty thousand Gauls slain by the Romans, ibid., 545.—Gaul inhabited by Romans, St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 207.—Senators of Gaul, ibid., 217.—The Gallic provinces disturbed, ibid., 204.—Afflicted by various disasters, 410.—Devastated by Chrocus, 177, 704.—By the Vandals, 191.—By the Huns, 197 ff., 593.—Saved by Aetius, 702.—Harassed by the Alamanni, 700.—By the Danes, 243, 588.—By the Lombards and Saxons, 304, 305.—One part subjected to Alamanni or Alans, 216.—To the Goths, 467.—To Clovis, I, 567.—Frequented by Egyptian merchants, 376, note.—Suffering from famine, 445.—From famine and plague, 556.—The Gauls enlightened by the preaching of the Gospel, 175.—Bishops sent by disciples of the apostles, 886, 887.—Long-haired, Gown-clad (*Togata*), and Cisalpine Gaul, 700, 701.—Further Gaul, 1120.—Narbonensian Gaul, 678.

Book on the history of Gaul published in the time of Wamba, St Julian of Toledo, XCVI, 764.—Dress of the Gauls, Charlemagne, XCVIII, 1391.—The Gauls’ defection from the Roman Empire, ibid.—On the Gauls who burned, ravaged, and finally sold Rome, Freculph of Lisieux, CVI, 1005.—The Gauls conspiring against the Romans were defeated three times, ibid., 1009.—On the wars between Romans, Samnites, and Gauls waged at the time when Alexander was ravaging the East, and the manifold miseries inflicted in fighting on both sides, ibid., 1020.—The severe wars waged between Romans, Gauls, Histri, and Illyrians, ibid., 1037.—Marius killed 440,000 Gauls, apart from the women and children who killed themselves, ibid., 1062.—How the provinces of Gaul were allotted to Caesar by the Senate, and on the various battles fought in Gaul, ibid., 1081.—The subjection of the Gauls by Caesar, St Ado of Vienne, CXXIII, 69, 70, 71.—On Gaul, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 130.—Customs of the Gauls, Richer of St Remigius, CXXXVIII, 49.

Germans.—The Germans are not permitted to cross their boundaries, Tertullian, II, 611.—They were already subject to Christ, ibid.—First and Second Germany, St Hilary of Poitiers, X, 479.—Very many cities and peoples were transferred into Germany, St Jerome, XXII, 1058.—In Jerome’s time Germany possessed worshippers of the holy language, ibid., 838.—Germany now called France, St Jerome, XXXIII, 39.—The Germans devastate Gaul and Italy, Dexter, XXXI, 385.—Having crossed the Alps, the Germans reach Ravenna, Paulus Orosius, XXXI, 1118.—The Germans invaded by Domitian, ibid., 1087.—The farther Germans take possession of Spain, ibid., 1119.—Slaughter of Germans, ibid., 1008, 1009.—The Franks invade Germany, St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 203, 204.—Driven thence, ibid., 578.—Chrocus devastates it, ibid., 703.—Attila spares its cities, ibid., 701.—On the transfer of the Empire to the Germans, Charlemagne, XCVIII, 508.

Goths.—The places inhabited by the Goths, Lactantius, VII, 306, 364.—Under Diocletian they invaded part of the neighbouring Roman provinces, ibid., 364.—Ezekiel prophesied the wars of the Goths, St Ambrose, XVI, 587.—Ambrose promises Emperor Gratian victory over the Goths, St Ambrose, XVI, 587 ff.—Driven from Macedonia by the prayers of St Arhohi [reading uncertain], ibid., 957.—Distressed and terrified by savage famine and burning pestilence, they fled; later they returned and sought peace, ibid.—The Goths are believed to be a Scythian people dwelling in wagons, ibid., 997.

On the Gothic invasion through Thrace and the death of Valens, Rufinus of Aquileia, XXI, 522.—The Goths ravage the Empire, Dexter, XXXI, 435.—When they came into Spain, ibid., 557.—The Gothic kings in Spain before Leovigild, and how many there were, 570, note ff.—The Goths invade the city, Paulus Orosius, XXXI, 795.—The Goths request that Christian teachers be sent to them, ibid., 1148.—How the Goths were expelled; what their king Ataulf instituted; on the Gothic kings Sigeric and Wallia, ibid., 1171.—Destruction of the Goths by Constantine the Great, ibid., 1137.—The cheapness of Gothic captives, ibid., 1161.—How Rome was invaded, plundered, and burned by the Goths, while Christians alone remained safe and free, ibid., 1163.—Gothic power, St Augustine, XLI, 115.—The Goths, having assembled an army, devastate Italy, ibid.—The Gothic incursion into the city, ibid., 109.—Pagan Goths besieging Rome are defeated, id., XXXVIII, 624.—Gothic gladiators, ibid., 90.—The Donatists’ attempts to win over the Goths, id., XXXIII, 793.—When the Goths ravaged the city, Marius Mercator, id., XLVIII, 195, note.—Eight thousand Goths slain under the general Aetius, Idatius, LI, 881.—The Goths enter Spain, ibid., 885.—The Goths, or a part of the Goths, brought to the Christian faith, and how, St Nicetas, LII, 890.—Where the Gothic Church was located.—The Goths, Arians, ibid., 891.—In favour of the Goths, four Gospels were translated into the Gothic language in the fourth century, ibid., 1017.—Gothic military forces, tainted with Arianism, repeatedly occupied Aquileia and the territory of Aquileia in the fourth and fifth centuries, ibid., [Col. 0982] 1021.—The Goths honoured Catholic priests, St Salvian, LIII, 137.—The Gothic people treacherous but chaste, ibid., 142.—Among them it is not permitted to be a fornicator, ibid., 134.—The Goths, most loathsome of heretics, ibid., 97.—Passing from city to city, they devastated everything, ibid., 139.—On the Gothic army and its king, slain by the prayers of saints, St Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 674.—The Goths defeated in Italy in the year 405, ibid., 570, note.—On the origin and deeds of the Getae or Goths, Jordanes, bishop of Ravenna, LXIX, 1251 ff.—How the Goths migrated, and how the Arian plague came to the Goths, Cassiodorus, LXIX, 1118.—The Gothic king received the oaths of the Romans, ibid., 737, 738.—Their custom in choosing kings, ibid., 820.—The Goths capture Rome, ibid., 1243.—They enter Gaul, ibid.—The Goths in Spain, St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 837.—They fight against Attila, ibid., 701.—They drive out the Britons, ibid., 215.—And slaughter them, ibid., 582.—Defeated by Clovis, ibid., 568.—After his death, they recover what they had lost, ibid., 260.—They capture Arles, 261.—Driven out by Ecdicius, ibid., 221.—They subjugate Galicia and the Suebi, ibid., 602.—Defeated by the Franks, 587.—They subjugate Cantabria and several cities, ibid., 622.—Incursion into the province of Arles, ibid., 486.—King Pippin exacts vengeance for Goths killed by Waifar, 689, 690.—The Goths, Arians, ibid., 864.—They become Catholics, ibid., 613.—Their custom of killing kings, ibid., 263, 264, 590.—It is restrained, ibid., 658.—The end of their kingdom in Italy, ibid., 591.—Gothic kings, ibid., 196, 583, 652, 700, 701.—History of the kings of the Goths, St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 1057.—Chronology and succession of Gothic kings from the Royal Vatican codex, ibid., 1115.—The Goths ravage the churches of Italy, Alcuin, CI, 807.—An exhortatory poem to the Gothic people, ibid., 798.—The Goths at once pagans and heretics, St Agobard of Lyons, CIV, 119.—On the Goths who defeated Valens, the erring ruler, in war and finally burned him alive, Freculph of Lisieux, CVI, 1220.—On Alaric, king of the Goths, who devastated Rome, and another Gothic king who entered Italy with a great army and perished with all his forces, ibid., 1236.—On Theodoric, king of the Goths, how he obtained Italy by grant of Emperor Zeno, and on his deeds, ibid., 1249.—The Goths crushed in Italy, ibid., 1252.—Expelled from the kingdom of Gaul, 1254.—Destroyed in Italy, ibid., 1255.—On the martyrdom of Hermenegild, son of the king of the Goths, 1256.—On the killing of Gothic kings by their own people, Aimoin of Fleury, CXXXIX, 680.—On the origin of the Goths and where they first lived, William of Jumièges, CXLIX, 782.

History of the Goths, Ekkehard of Aura, CLIV, 725.—What part of Gaul they occupied, Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 611.—On the first arrival of the Goths in Italy, in the time of Leo, emperor of the Greeks; and when Charles Martel freed Italy from the Goths, Godfrey of Viterbo, CXCVIII, 923.—On the Goths from whom Pippin freed the Roman Church and all Italy, ibid., 925.—Catalogue of Gothic kings, ibid., 1029.

Greeks.—The Greeks seek their own wisdom, not God’s, Tertullian, II, 481.—Gods of the Greek philosophers, ibid., 260.—The Greeks’ talent for fashioning images, id., I, 430.—The elder Cato thought they should be expelled from the city, id., II, 1039.—The Greek kingdom, St Cyprian, IV, 571.—Among the Greeks philosophers stood in greater glory than orators, Lactantius, I, 114.—They gave human names to mountains and rivers, ibid., 181.—Idolatry originated from them, ibid., 181, 196.—Verses of the Sibyls concerning them, ibid.—They always regarded the most trivial matters as the greatest, ibid., 211.—Their wickedness in consecrating images of Cupid and love, 221.—Why they were called wearers of the pallium, ibid., 365.—Their frivolity often noted by Cicero, ibid., 388.—Why they invented philosophy, ibid., 397.—Greek frivolity and vanity, St Jerome, XXII, 344.—The Greeks occupied almost all islands, and the coasts and lands adjoining the sea throughout the world, id., XXIII, 952.—The whole of Greece subdued by Philip, Paulus Orosius, XXXI, 817.—It loses its freedom, ibid., 821.—Devastated by Brutus and Cassius, ibid., 1044.—Destroyed by an inundation of Goths, ibid., 1119.—After Troy’s destruction, the Greeks returning home were crushed by various disasters, St Augustine, XLI, 573.—The Greeks’ vain superstition and custom of enrolling the dead among the gods, ibid., 565.—The Greek language takes precedence among nations, ibid., 235.—Greek perjuries, Charlemagne, XCVIII, 1394.—On the customs of Greeks and Romans, Theodore of Canterbury, XCIX, 931.—On the emperors of Constantinople, William of Malmesbury, CLXXIX, 1309.—The Pantheon; the Empire passes to the Greeks, Godfrey of Viterbo, [Col. 0983] CXCVIII, 879 ff.—Catalogue of Greek kings, ibid., 1024.—The role of the Greeks in the crusading expedition, William of Tyre, CCI, 213 ff.—Chronicle of Helinand, monk of Froidmont, containing much concerning Greek emperors, id., CCXII, 771 ff.

Spaniards.—All the regions of the Spains already believed in Christ, Tertullian, II, 610.—Whence the Spaniards came and why they are called Iberians, St Jerome, XXV, 253.—The Spains daily tremble at enemy incursions, id., XXII, 1058.—Spain is called Iberia and Celtiberia, id., XXIV, 667.—From whom Spain first received the message concerning Christ, Dexter, XXXI, 96, 97.—They send envoys to the apostle Peter, and why, ibid., 97, note 7.—Spain, the first of the world’s provinces converted to Christ, ibid., 103.—Certain Spaniards were present at Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost, ibid., 93, note 3.—Spanish martyrs in the time of Diocletian, whose names are not extant, ibid., 436, note 40.—When the Catholic monarchy of the Spanish kings was established, ibid., 570, note 12.—How Caesar entered Spain and conquered the Cantabrians and Asturians, Paulus Orosius, XXXI, 1055.—Vices of the Spaniards, St Salvian of Marseilles, LIII, 135.—Spain devastated by Vandals and Suebi, St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 191.—Under Vandals, Alans, and Suebi, ibid., 704.—Occupied by Germans, ibid., 700.—By Saracens, ibid., 678.—Persecution there, ibid., 353, 601, 704.—Spain devastated by Franks, ibid., 590.—Expedition into it by Childebert I, ibid., 249, 891.—By Childebert and Chlothar, ibid., 263.—By Guntram, ibid., 465, 467.—By Childebert II, ibid., 409.—Kings of Spain, ibid., 242, 263, 300, 353, 469, 621.—Queens of Spain, ibid., 249, 200, 301, 353, 595, 602.—Whence Spain derived its name, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 350, 351.—Its riches, pleasantness, and division, ibid.—A chorography of Spain collected in one volume, Isidore of Beja, XCVI, 1254 ff.—On the origin, location, and antiquity of the city of Córdoba, id., CXV, 925 ff.—On the affairs of the kings of Spain, Aimoin of Fleury, CXXXIX, 704.—On the Spanish kings, ibid., 785.—On the persecution of Catholics in Spain, ibid., 718.

Huns.—The peoples of the Huns, or Chuns, obey only the laws of the dice-game, St Ambrose, XIV, 773.—They are subject to moneylenders, ibid.—They wage war by every means, ibid.—The Chuns rose against the Alans, the Alans against the Goths, and the Goths against the Taifali and Sarmatians, id., XV, 1806.—Peace of the Huns with the Romans, id., XVI, 1038.—The Huns claimed Pannonia for themselves, id., XVII, 914.—The Huns burst into the East, St Jerome, XXII, 695, 696.—According to Herodotus, they held the East captive for twenty years and exacted annual tribute from the Egyptians and Ethiopians, ibid.—They learn the Psalter, ibid., 870.—They eat half-raw meat, id., XXIII, 295.—The Hunnic people against the Goths, Paulus Orosius, XXXI, 1146.—The Hunnic people was unchaste, St Salvian of Marseilles, LIII, 87.—On the accursed origin of the Huns, namely, the intercourse of sorcerers with unclean spirits; and on the Huns’ expedition against the Scythian Ostrogoths, including their monstrous and terrifying appearance, Jordanes, LXIX, 1268.—They devastate Thrace, Cassiodorus, LXIX, 1181.—They are driven from Italy, ibid., 1244.—The Huns depart from Pannonia, St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 168.—They invade Gaul, ibid., 197, 287, 292, 575, 577, 700, 880.—They are expelled, ibid., 701.—By the Lombards, ibid., 596.—They drive off the Franks by magic, ibid., 292.—They make peace with Sigebert, ibid., 595.—They besiege Constantinople, ibid., 1174.—Kings of the Huns: Bleda, Attila, Gaucherius, Gaganus, etc., ibid., 205, note 198, 700, 701, 717, 718, 636, 1107, 1108.—The Hunnic people, St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 1065.—On the Huns, Charlemagne, XCVIII, 1392.—The Huns, also called Avars, who invaded Italy and Bulgaria, were defeated and dispersed, Alcuin, C, 142.—Subdued by Pippin, ibid., 197.—The Hunnic people, savage and formidable, ibid., 188.—Converted to Christ, ibid.—Nearly all Europe emptied by the swords of Huns or Goths, ibid., 151.—Gaul despoiled for nine years, Alcuin, CI, 807.—On the battles of the king of the Huns against Romans and other peoples, Freculph of Lisieux, CVI, 1245.—On the Hun invasion of Thuringia, Aimoin of Fleury, CXXXIX, 754.—On the Huns dispersed throughout the Empire, Heriger, CXXXIX, 1021.—On the origin of the Huns, Ekkehard of Aura, CLIV, 735; Hugh of Flavigny, CLIV, 80 ff.

History of Jerusalem.—Five books on the destruction of the city of Jerusalem, St Ambrose, XV, 1962 ff.—A summary history of the destruction of the city of Jerusalem, ibid., 2206 ff.—Treatise on the overthrow of Jerusalem, Walahfrid Strabo, CXIV, 966.—Three books on the holy places, based on the report of Arculf, a Gallic bishop, St Adamnan, [Col. 0984] abbot of Hy, LXXXVIII, 780 ff.—Bernard’s itinerary to the holy places, made in the year 870, Bernard, a Frankish monk, id., 569.—A little book entitled *The Oppression, Liberation, and Restoration of the Holy Church of Jerusalem*, Ekkehard of Aura, CLIV, 1060.—Documents concerning the holy war, CLV, 466.—The deeds of Tancred in the Jerusalem expedition, by Ralph of Caen, his associate, CLV, 490 ff.—History of the Franks who captured Jerusalem, Raymond of Aguilers, canon of Le Puy, CLV, 592.—*History of Jerusalem*, nine books, Robert, monk of St Remigius, ibid., 665 ff.—Five books of *History of the Journey to Jerusalem*, Tudebodus, priest of Sivray, ibid., 764.—*History of Jerusalem* from the year 1095 to 1127, three books, Fulcher of Chartres, ibid., 822.—Six books of the *History of the Deeds of Our Time on the Road to Jerusalem*, Guy of Paris, ibid., 912.—Book of the holy places of the land of Jerusalem, Fretellus, archdeacon, ibid., 1038.—Description of the Holy Land, John of Würzburg, ibid., 1054.—Brief account of the holy war, Anonymous, ibid., 1090.—On the beginnings and discovery of the sacred religion of the Jerusalemites, ibid., 1098.—*Cartulary of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre of Jerusalem, published from Vatican manuscripts by M. Eugène de Rozière*, CLV, 1106.—*The Deeds of God through the Franks*, or *History of Jerusalem*, nine books, Abbot Guibert, CLVI, 684.

History of the Jerusalem expedition, twelve books, Albert of Aachen, CLXVI, 390.—History of Jerusalem: how Christians from remote parts of the world, with the greatest labour, sought it out, stormed it, and held it, Baldric of Dol, CLXVI, 1064.—History of Jerusalem, Lisiard of Tours, CLXXIV, 1589.—Seven books on the journey into the East of Louis VII, king of the Franks, surnamed the Younger, in which the author himself took part, Odo of Deuil, CXCV, 999.—Twenty-three books of the *History of Deeds Done in the Regions beyond the Sea*, from the time of Muhammad’s successors to the year of the Lord 1184, William of Tyre, archbishop, CCI, 210 ff.—Continuation of William of Tyre’s history of the holy war, in the French language, written by an ancient author 1,500 years ago, ibid., 894.

Indians.—Indian naked philosophers, Tertullian, I, 260; St Ambrose, XVI, 1092.—On the captivity of Frumentius and Edesius, and the conversion of the Indians accomplished through them, Rufinus of Aquileia, XXI, 478.—The Indians have many wives, St Jerome, XXIII, 274.—Among them it is law that the most beloved wife be burned with her deceased husband, ibid.—The kingdoms of India most wealthy, ibid., XXII, 541.—India is scarcely reached over the Ocean in a full year, ibid., 1074.—Many spices come from India by way of the Red Sea, ibid., XXIV, 726.—The boundaries and peoples of India, Paulus Orosius, XXXI, 675, 676.—Semiramis brought war upon the Indians, ibid., 700.—Alexander subdues India, defeats King Porus, and subjects cities and peoples, ibid., 835.—On the conversion of the Indian people, Cassiodorus, LXIX, 943.—India has neither lead nor bronze, St Isidore of Seville, LXXXII, 589.—It produces elephants, ibid., 436.—India divided into three parts, Alcuin, 768.—Whence India takes its name, and its situation and fertility, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 335.—Its division, ibid.—St Thomas in India; mission to India, William of Malmesbury, CLXXIX, 1082.

Italians, or Latins.---Italy, first called Oenotria and afterwards Saturnia, Tertullian, I, 330, 602.---It was occupied by the Phrygians, idem, II, 700.---Italy was once called Greater Greece, St. Jerome, XXII, 510.---The people of Italy are called *Casei* by Ennius, ibid., 342.---What Cicero said concerning them, ibid.---Their custom in writing and sending letters, ibid.---Civil wars in Italy, ibid., 696.---The kingdom of the Latins, idem, XXVII, 271 ff.---Description of Italy, Paulus Orosius, XXXI, 687.---Attila devastates Italy, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 201.---The Saxons dwell there, ibid., 304.---They depart thence, ibid., 597.---The kingdom of Italy, ibid., 1153.---Italy disastrous to the Franks, ibid., 265.---Captured by them, ibid.---Childebert’s Italian expedition, ibid., 505.---The Lombards invade Italy, ibid., 303, 307.---Kings of the Latins, Cassiodorus, LXIX, 1215.---Catalogue of Italian kings, Godfrey of Viterbo, CXCVIII, 1019.---On the kingdom of the Latins, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 237.

Jews.---The Jews learned through Moses to worship God, Tertullian, I, 403.---Their kingdom flourished so long as they obeyed the divine precepts, ibid., 393.---From Tiberius until the time of Vespasian they had an opportunity for repentance, idem, II, 354.---Now they wander dispersed throughout the world, idem, I, 393.---The Jews departed from God, St. Cyprian, IV, 677, 679.---They killed the prophets, ibid., 680.---And Christ himself, ibid., 525, 549.---They lost the grace given to them, [Col. 0985] ibid., 578.---The Jews anoint and wash the dead, Lactantius, VI, 270.---Who wrote concerning their affairs, ibid., 459.---For how many years they lived under judges and kings, ibid., 956.---On their captivity in Egypt, ibid., 470.---Whence the Jews derive their name, ibid., 475, 958.---Their government down to Christ, ibid., 473.---On their custom in burying the dead, ibid., 512.---On the duration of their stay in Egypt and in the land of Canaan, ibid., 267.---After royal dignity, they served the Roman Empire in greater disgrace, St. Zeno, XI, 519, 521.---Conversion of the Jews, St. Philastrius, XII, 1295.---At what periods the Jewish people had kings, St. Ambrose, XV, 1595.---The ten tribes of the Jews were carried away to the Assyrians, idem, XIV, 941.---By whom the Jewish people were governed from Jehoiakim to Christ, St. Jerome, XXIV, 819.---The Jews earned the friendship of the Lacedaemonians, Athenians, and Romans, ibid., 29.---They have no judges of their own, but Roman ones, ibid., 58.---The final devastation occurred under Vespasian, Titus, and Hadrian, ibid., 361.---The Jews and their teachers bound the Decalogue around their heads, idem, XXV, 230.---After the Lord was offered up, kingship failed among the Jews, St. Jerome, XXV, 543.---Civil wars of the Jews, ibid., 1501.---Jewish rebellion in Libya, Dexter, XXXI, 303.---They are dispersed by Hadrian, ibid., 307.---Their rebellion in Palestine, ibid., 315.---The Jews subdued by Pompey, Orosius, XXXI, 1004.---By Hadrian, ibid., 1093.---Their slaughter in Alexandria and Mesopotamia, ibid.---Septimius Severus restrained them, ibid., 1102.---They are expelled from Rome, ibid., 1075.---How the rule of the Emperors Vespasian Augustus and Titus crushed the rebellious Jews and razed the city of Jerusalem together with its Temple to the ground, ibid., 1083.

At what time the Jews were led captive into Babylon, St. Augustine, XLI, 382.---After the Babylonian captivity the Jews had no kings, ibid., 596, 607.---The Jewish captivity ended by Cyrus, ibid., 582.---After the restoration of the Temple, the Jews had no prophets, ibid., 606.---The Jewish kingdom and priesthood were a prophecy of the coming king and priest, idem, XLII, 409, 417.---Why God allowed them to be subdued by the Romans, XXXIV, 1051.---Made tributaries of the Romans by Pompey, idem, XLI, 607.---In Augustine’s lifetime there was no Jew in Jerusalem, idem, XXXVI, 759, 1650.---Why the Jews were preserved and dispersed throughout the whole world, idem, XLIV, 594; XLI, 140, 221, 608, 610; XXXVIII, 268, 1032; XXXIV, 1061.---The Jews are permitted to repair their synagogue, and under what conditions, Cassiodorus, LXIX, 561.---The Jews accuse Christians before the Persians, ibid., 943.---They are driven from Alexandria, ibid., 1195.---On the Jew who, although often baptized, departed from the water of the font, ibid.---The Jews are to be converted to Christ at the end, idem, LXX, 413.---Jews converted in the East, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 715.---Chilperic compels the Jews to baptism, ibid., 388.

The Jews are oppressed by diverse calamities, and their kings, caught between the Egyptians and Babylonians, are afflicted by adverse fortune, Freculphus of Lisieux, CVI, 984.---The Jews were led captive into Babylon, ibid., 986.---The Jews are released from captivity, ibid., 990.---They return to Jerusalem under Ezra, ibid., 998.---The walls of Jerusalem are rebuilt under Nehemiah, ibid.---On the occasion on which the Temple on Mount Gerizim was built, ibid., 1015.---Ptolemy, Alexander’s successor, captures Jerusalem by deceit and leads many Jews with him captive into Egypt, ibid., 1025.---How Ptolemy Philadelphus honored Eleazar, high priest of the Jews, and the Temple with gifts. He also released more than one hundred thousand Jewish captives, ibid., 1029.---While Ptolemy Philopator was reigning, 60,000 Jews were killed by Antiochus, ibid., 1038.---How Mattathias, resisting Antiochus’s edicts, defended the ancestral laws, ibid., 1051.---How, when Jerusalem was captured, Antigonus was seized and killed, and Herod was made king, ibid., 1096.---How great were the evils suffered by the Jews under Tiberius as punishment for the Cross, ibid., 1126.---On the final ruin of Jerusalem and the multitude killed according to Josephus’s calculation, ibid., 1143.---How Herod destroyed the genealogy of the Jews, Haimo of Halberstadt, CXVIII, 820.---How many evils befell the Jews, ibid., 826, 829.---The overthrow of Jerusalem by Titus and Vespasian, ibid., 832.---The final destruction of the Jews, ibid., 839.---Why the Jews are under God’s wrath, Rabbi Samuel, CXLIX, 337.---He shows that the Jews are blind, ibid., 340.---That the Jews deceive others and themselves, ibid.---How, after the killing, the dispersion of the Jews occurred according to Daniel, ibid., 344.---Rejection of the Jews, ibid., 352, 353.---Slaughter of the Jews, ibid., 354.---Rejection of Jewish sacrifice, ibid., 358.---That the Jews wrongly condemn Christian chant, ibid., 363.---History [Col. 0986] from Hezekiah to the return from Babylon, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 221.---History from Cyrus to Judas Maccabaeus, ibid., 222.---History from Judas Maccabaeus to Christ, ibid., 224.---On Vespasian and the destruction of Jerusalem, ibid., 245.

Lacedaemonians.---The Lacedaemonians first devised the cloak (*paenula*) for games, Tertullian, I, 302.---The flogging of Lacedaemonian boys, ibid., 626.---The Lacedaemonians erected a temple to armed Venus, Lactantius, VI, 225.---Lacedaemonian frugality, St. Jerome, XXIII, 302.---Kings of the Lacedaemonians, idem, XXVII, 89.---The war of the Athenians against the Lacedaemonians, Paulus Orosius, XXXI, 738.---Lest their offspring fail, they permitted indiscriminate intercourse with all women, ibid., 710.---On the various wars of the Lacedaemonians with the Thebans, ibid., 797.---On the Lacedaemonians’ defeat in Arcadia, ibid., 803.---Lacedaemonian mothers urged their sons into military contests more ardently than the sound of the standards, so that they might shed their blood for their earthly fatherland, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 1057.---King Festus of the Lacedaemonians, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 170.---On the kingdom of the Lacedaemonians, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 235.

Lombards.---The Lombards claimed Italy for themselves, St. Ambrose, XVII, 914.---Whence the Lombards arose, and why they were so called, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 595.---Their god Wodan, ibid., 596.---They invade Italy, ibid., 303, 501, 596.---They break into Gaul and are driven out, ibid., 304, 306, 307, 596.---They crush the Franks, ibid., 505, 531, 532.---Tributaries of the Franks, ibid., 533, 635, 689.---They ransom themselves, ibid., 636.---They burn the church of St. Peter, ibid., 688.---They afflict the Romans, ibid., 686.---Driven out by the Franks, ibid., 687, 688.---Their dukes, ibid., 306, 597.---Kings of the Lombards, ibid., 271, 635, 637, 533, 637, 649, 689.---Catalogue of Lombard kings, Paul the Deacon, XCV, 427.---Six books on the deeds of the Lombards, ibid., 433 ff.---On the Lombards invading Italy, Freculphus of Lisieux, CVI, 1256.---History of the Lombards from the year 774 to the year 888, Erchembert of Monte Cassino, CXXIX, 745.---On the origin and deeds of the Lombards, Aimoinus of Fleury, CCXXIX, 675.---On the kings of the Lombards, ibid., 687.---On Alboin, king of the Lombards, ibid., 690.---On the first king of the Lombards, ibid., 718.---On the tribute which the Lombards paid to the Franks, ibid., 771.---On Adaloald, king of the Lombards, his successor, and Queen Gundeberga, ibid., 773.---On the deeds of Grimoald, king of the Lombards, ibid., 789.---Venetian Chronicle, John the Deacon, CXXXIX, 876.---History of the Lombards, Ekkehard of Aura, CLIV, 788.---History of the Lombards, who were formerly called Vinuli, Godfrey of Viterbo, CXCVIII, 931.---Catalogue of Lombard kings, ibid., 1030.

Lydians.---The Lydians made a compact by drinking blood, Tertullian, I, 381.---Immigrants from Asia, they settled in Etruria under the leadership of Tyrrhenus, ibid., 636.---Kings and kingdom of the Lydians, St. Jerome, XXVII, 88, 350.---The Lydians were reckoned among the strongest peoples, idem, XXV, 251.---Gyges, king of the Lydians, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 170.---Beginning of the Lydian kingdom, Freculphus of Lisieux, CVI, 978.---On the kingdom of the Lydians, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII.

Macedonians.---The Macedonians hearing the tragedy of Oedipus: concerning an incestuous affair [the printed reading is uncertain], Tertullian, I, 325.---Kings and kingdom of the Macedonians, St. Jerome, XXVII, 82, 341.---For how many years the Macedonian kingdom endured, idem, XXV, 557.---Description of Macedonia, Paulus Orosius, XXXI, 686.---Darius conquers Macedonia, ibid., 762.---The deeds of Philip, king of Macedonia, and the peoples or cities he subdued, ibid., 815, 821, 823.---Alexander, succeeding Philip, utterly subdues the Thebans, Illyrians, Thracians, and other cities, and defeats Darius, ibid., 827.---Alexander subdues India; overcomes King Porus; subjugates cities and peoples, ibid., 835.---All provinces, terrified by Alexander, send ambassadors seeking peace. Alexander dies by poison, ibid., 838.---Alexander’s commanders divide the whole world among themselves and consume one another in mutual wars, ibid., 845.---Macedonia is destroyed by an inundation of Goths, ibid., 1119.---How long the Macedonian kingdom lasted, St. Augustine, XLI, 358.---The Macedonians subject to no one, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 699.---Their origin, kings, Philip, and Alexander, ibid.---Macedonia possessed by the ancestors of the Franks, ibid., 577.---Darius, king of the Persians, subdues Asia and Macedonia, Freculphus of Lisieux, CVI, 995.---Philip, king of the Macedonians and father of Alexander the Great, waged many wars, destroyed cities, and utterly subdued countless nations, ibid., 1010.---Alexander the Great: how great and what deeds he performed among his own people; how he first overcame the Parthians in war, then, after subduing Egypt and Syria, came to Jerusalem, ibid., 1015.---After Alexandria was built in Egypt and the Persian Empire destroyed, Alexander held the monarchy of the world for five years, [Col. 0987] ibid., 1019.---Among whom he divided the kingdom cruelly acquired, ibid., 1022.---After Alexander’s death his commanders consumed one another in mutual wars, ibid., 1023.---The Parthians withdraw from the Macedonian yoke, ibid., 1037.---How Philip, king of the Macedonians, defeated by the Romans, gave his son Demetrius as a hostage, ibid., 1045.---On the kingdom of the Macedonians, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 229.

Medes.---The Median kingdom is older than the Roman, Tertullian, I, 432.---Kings and kingdom of the Medes, St. Jerome, XXVII, 84, 339.---Madai, founder of the Median people, idem, XXIV, 214.---The attack of the Medes and Persians upon Babylon, ibid., 158.---The Medes and Persians formed one kingdom under Darius and Cyrus, XXV, 536.---The Median kingdom is greater than the Persian, ibid., 522.---The kingdom of the Medes and Persians was destroyed by the Macedonians, ibid., 1454.---On Phraortes, Deioces, and Astyages, kings of the Medes, Paulus Orosius, XXXI, 733.---The end of the Median Empire, ibid., 736.---Kings of the Medes, Freculphus of Lisieux, CVI, 978 ff.---On the kingdom of the Medes, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 227.---Catalogue of Median kings, Godfrey of Viterbo, CXCVIII, 1022.

Milanese History.---History of Milan, Landulf the Elder, CXLVII, 809.---Milanese History, Landulf the Younger, CLXXIII, 1499.

Northmen.---War against the Northmen, Charlemagne, XCVIII, 1402.---Northmen as pirates, ibid., 1403.---The Northmen despise baptism, ibid., 1408.---Slaughters by the Northmen throughout Gaul under Charles the Bald, under Louis, under Charles the Simple, Odo, and Robert, etc., Aimoinus of Fleury, CXXXIX, 803.---On the customs and deeds of the dukes of Normandy, Dudo the Dean, CXLI, 607.---Eight books of the History of the Northmen, William of Jumièges, CXLIX, 779.---Historical poem on the deeds of the Northmen in Sicily, Apulia, and Calabria, William of Apulia, CXLIX, 1027.---Brief Norman Chronicle (A.D. 1041–1085), ibid., 1083.

Persians.---The Persians believed the sun to be a god and worshipped it, Tertullian, I, 369.---They had it depicted on their shields, ibid., 370.---Incest of the Persians with their mothers, ibid., 325.---Kings of the Persians from the time of Cyrus, Anonymous, III, 670.---The Persian kingdom, St. Cyprian, IV, 571.---When the Persians were defeated by Galerius, Lactantius, VII, 208.---On their custom of serving their kings, ibid., 228.---The Persians situated in the East, St. Jerome, XXIV, 470.---Obscure before Cyrus, ibid., 191.---They founded Seleucia and Ctesiphon in place of Babylon, ibid., 159.---The Persians, a very strong people, XXV, 251.---They use ointments in place of baths, ibid., 553.---The Persian kingdom: strict, and marked by a more frugal way of life, ibid., 529.---The sequence and succession of kings, ibid., 45, 528, 549.---Fourteen kings, ibid., 549, 550, 558.---One kingdom of Persians and Medes after Cyrus’s victory, ibid., 1428.---Kings and kingdom of the Persians, St. Jerome, XXVII, 84, 427.---On Cyrus, king of the Persians, Paulus Orosius, XXXI, 733, 757, 761.---Darius, king of the Persians, attacks the Scythians and is put to flight; he conquers Asia, Macedonia, and Ionia, ibid., 762.---Xerxes, king of the Persians, with a most numerous army suffers a great defeat at the hands of a few Spartans under Leonidas, and is defeated by stratagem, ibid., 765.---Themistocles, leader of the Athenians, meets Xerxes in battle, ibid., 768.---Mardonius, Xerxes’ commander, while carrying out the remainder of the war, loses his forces and flees. Xerxes, despised by his own people as unfortunate, is killed, ibid., 770.---The king of Persia carries the Jews away captive, ibid., 810.---The Persians worshipped only two gods, St. Augustine, XLI, 168.---The Persians prohibit marriage to some persons, XXXIV, 705.---The Persians and their god, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 165.---Countless persons become Christians, ibid., 614.---They harass the Empire, ibid., 645.---They are driven out, ibid., 646.---By Tiberius, ibid., 347, 601.---By Phocas, ibid., 618.---They ravage Armenia, ibid., 555.---They invade Antioch, ibid., 302.---Kings of the Persians, ibid., 676, 613.---On Persian ambassadors, Charlemagne, XCVIII, 1396.---Charlemagne’s gifts to the king of Persia, ibid., 1397.---Kings of the Persians and their history, Freculphus of Lisieux, CVI, 990, 994, 998, 1001, 1003, 1005, 1008, 1019.---On the kingdom of the Persians, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 228.---Heraclius defeats the Persians, Godfrey of Viterbo, CXCVIII, 914.---Catalogue of Persian kings, ibid., 1023.

Poles.---Three books of chronicles and deeds of the dukes or princes of the Poles, CLX, 844.

Romans.---The Romans derive their origin from Aeneas, Tertullian, I, 424.---The Phrygians beget them, idem, II, 1035.---Their empire begun and enlarged by crimes, idem, I, 430 ff.---How far their realm extends, idem, II, 611.---They occupied the world, idem, I, 439.---Yet they did not extend their kingdom beyond the Germans, Britons, Moors, and Gaetulians, idem, II, 610 ff.---Their entire religion was military, idem, I, 367.---At public games they washed Jupiter Latiaris in human blood, ibid., 317; II, 136.---Their empire was founded before any worship of the gods had been established at Rome, [Col. 0988] idem, I, 429.---Roman emperors, idem, III, 673.---On the Romans’ own gods and their sacred rites, Lactantius, VI, 216.---How great was the insolence and license of the Roman people, idem, VII, 326.---What the day was like among the Romans, and from what point they began it, ibid., 383 ff.---On their practice of committing their affairs to memory through paintings or engraved stones, ibid., 396, 477.---They bestowed honor even upon shapeless stones, ibid., 499.---Under the emperors they were far less superstitious, ibid., 802.---They worshipped Jupiter Latiaris with human blood, idem, VI, 230.---At what hour judicial proceedings were customarily conducted among them, ibid., 510.---The power of the Assyrian, Persian, and Macedonian kingdoms had passed to the Romans, St. Ambrose, XVII, 842.---The destruction of the Roman Empire foretold, ibid., 914.---Roman kings, consuls, and emperors, St. Jerome, XXVII, 99, 100, 703.---The Roman kingdom, ibid., 366 ff.---Chronicle of St. Jerome, ibid., 676 ff.---Chronicle of Prosper of Aquitaine, ibid., 704 ff.---In the Roman Empire all kingdoms became one, idem, XXIV, 187.---Civil and foreign wars among the Romans, idem, XXII, 601.---Roman blood shed for twenty years and more, ibid., 600.---Many thousands of Romans killed in various places, ibid., 1110.---The seven books of Orosius’s Histories, from the founding of Rome to the barbarian invasions, idem, XXXI, 749 ff.---Rome founded by the Trojans, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 505.---By the descendants of Aeneas, idem, XLI, 80.---By Romulus and Remus, idem, XXXVIII, 505; XLI, 82.---Authors disagree concerning the date of Rome’s foundation, idem, XLI, 80.---In what year of the kingdoms of Judah and Israel Rome was founded, ibid., 578.---And in what year of Numitor, ibid.---Rome captured, plundered, and burned by the Goths, ibid., 70, 96.---The first burning of Rome by the Gauls, and the second by Nero, idem, XXXVIII, 1356.---The public burning of Rome, idem, XLI, 99.---Camillus frees Rome from the Gauls, ibid., 117.---The destruction of Rome by the Goths, ibid., 469.---The calamity inflicted on the Roman people by Alaric’s first siege of the city at the end of A.D. 408, idem, XXXIII, 365 and note.---Rome was captured and plundered by Alaric, idem, XLI, 14, 15 and note, 19, 20.---Rome’s burning by the Goths was the third, idem, XXXVIII, 1336.---The Romans descended from the Trojans, idem, XLI, 79, 81.---The Romans were called the house of Aeneas and Assaracus, idem, XXXIV, 533; XLI, 462.---The life of the Romans under kings, idem, XLI, 92.---The beginnings of the Roman Empire under Numa Pompilius were peaceful for forty years, idem, XXXIV, 800, 801.---How dreadful were the ends of the Roman kings, idem, XLI, 92.---The Romans, intolerant of kings, created consuls, ibid., 154, 155.---How greatly the Roman Empire increased in a short time under the consuls, ibid., 154, 155.---The nature of Roman victories from the time of the consuls, ibid., 95.---The Romans’ shameful treaty with the Samnites, ibid., 97.---The Romans borrowed Solon’s laws from the Athenians, ibid., 60, 96.---Two splendid orders among them: the Equestrian and Senatorial, ibid., 108.---By what evils the Roman commonwealth was afflicted after the beginnings of consular rule, ibid., 95.---By what internal evils it was harassed, ibid., 104.---Cicero’s judgment concerning the Roman commonwealth, ibid., 66.---Sallust on the vices of the Roman commonwealth, ibid., 64.---The Sibyl sang of the fates of the Romans, idem, XXXIV, 1054.---The Romans did no harm to the peoples upon whom, after subduing them, they imposed their laws, idem, XLI, 160, 161.---They imposed not only their yoke but also their language upon conquered peoples, ibid., 634.---The Roman war with the Etruscans, ibid., 94.---Various conspiracies of enemies against the Romans, ibid., 97.---By what great disasters the Romans were worn down in the Punic Wars, ibid., 98.---And by Hannibal, ibid., 100.---The boundaries of the Roman Empire were altered under the emperors Hadrian and Julian, ibid., 135.---And under Jovian, ibid., 136.---The Roman nobility devoted to idolatry, idem, XXXII, 750.---The Romans’ gods innumerable, idem, XLI, 118.

Theodoric, king of the Visigoths, defeats in battle Rechiar, king of the Suebi, who had invaded Spain.---With Theodoric’s permission, the Suebi choose Remismund as their king, Jordanes, LXIX, 1283.---The Suebi crush the Saxons, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 331, 599.---They receive lands, ibid., 331.---Under King Chrocus, ibid., 704.---Under Trasamundus they cross into Spain, ibid.---Arians, ibid., 923.---They become Catholics, ibid., 925 note.---Subject to the Visigoths, ibid., 602.---History of the Suebi, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 1080.

Syrians.---Kings of Syria, St. Jerome, XXVII, 83.---Kings of Syria after Alexander the Great, idem, XXV, 559.---The provinces comprised by Syria, Paulus Orosius, XXXI, 678.---Antiochus, king of Syria, ibid., 905.---On Pompey’s deeds in Syria, ibid., 1004.---On the kingdoms of Syria, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 1031.

History of Trier.---Deeds of Trier, CLIV, [Col. 0989] 1064.---First supplement and continuation, ibid., 1178.---Appendix of Trier monuments, ibid., 1234.

Visigoths.---After the Ostrogoths had been defeated by the Vandals, the Visigoths sought and obtained Moesia as a place to dwell from Emperor Valens; and when they wished to become Christians, Valens, being an Arian, sent Arian preachers to them, Jordanes, LXIX, 1269.---Subject to the Romans, severely oppressed by famine and treated most cruelly by Roman commanders, the Visigoths claim their freedom and occupy Thrace and Riparian Dacia, ibid., 1270.---The Visigoths invade Italy, ibid., 1271.---Wallia, fourth king of the Visigoths, restores Placidia to the Romans, ibid., 1274.---Theodoric, fifth king of the Visigoths, ibid., 1275, 1283.---Euric, king of the Visigoths, ibid., 1281, 1285.---Kings of the Visigoths, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 199.---Chronicle of Visigothic kings, attributed to St. Julian, XCVI, 809.

[Col. 0989]

CLXXVII. INDEX CONCERNING THE JEWS, BRIEFLY COMPRISING FROM THE FATHERS THEIR HISTORY AND LAWS, HERESIES AND CRIMES, AS WELL AS PUNISHMENTS, DISPERSION AMONG THE PEOPLES, AND CONVERSION AT THE END OF THE AGE.

I.---History of the Jews.

[Col. 0989]

TERTULLIAN.---The Jewish nation was from the beginning divided according to tribes and families, II, 450.---The kingdom flourished so long as they obeyed the divine precepts, II, 1393.

LACTANTIUS.---For how many years the Jews lived under judges and kings, VI, 459.---On their captivity in Egypt, ibid., 470.---On the misfortunes of the Jews and their government down to Christ’s Passion, ibid., 478.---How the Jews conducted themselves in time of persecution, VII, 575.

ST. AMBROSE OF MILAN.---The Jews first lent money at interest to the Gentiles, XIV, 784.---At what periods the Jewish people had kings, XV, 1594.---The ten tribes of the Jews were led away to the Assyrians; but the other two, Judah and Benjamin, as guilty of a more grievous crime, passed into Babylon, XIV, 941.---At some point God’s goodwill toward the Jews ceased, ibid., 962.---Jews claiming that an inheritance is due to them because of the Old Testament are refuted, VI, 1257.---The Jews living at Rome in the time of the apostles did not hold a right belief concerning Christ, XVII, 45 ff.---From the time of Judas Maccabaeus they began to be called Jews, ibid., 55, 56.---The surname “Jews” is observed to signify a threefold lineage, ibid., 69.---Prerogatives of the Jews, ibid., 72 ff.---Those who killed the Lord and persecuted his apostles had already been devastated by the Romans at the time when the vision of John’s Apocalypse was revealed, ibid., 913 ff.

ST. GAUDENTIUS.---Jewish tradition concerning the duration of the world, XX, 916.

ZACCHAEUS.---Whence the Jews originate, XX, 1084.---Why, after leaving Egypt, they were led into the wilderness, or why the Law was given, ibid., 1087.

RUFINUS OF AQUILEIA.---On the Jews’ attempts to rebuild the Temple at Jerusalem, XXI, 505.---How, through an earthquake there and a fire kindled by God, the Jews were hindered in their unlawful undertakings, ibid., 506.---On the terrifying pieces of wood and powers which turned to the Jews’ destruction, ibid., 507.---God was known only to the Jews, ibid., 1067.

ST. JEROME.---No people more avaricious than the Jews, XXIV, 48.---The Jews have no judges of their own, no warrior prophet, and no authority to bear arms, ibid., 58, 59.---By whom the Jewish people were governed from Jehoiakim to Christ, ibid., 819.---After Christ’s death, they sent letters to all peoples urging them not to receive [Col. 0990] his Passion, ibid., 179.---Jerusalem alone in the whole world received the Law, ibid., 49.---Romans, Gauls, and Spaniards called by God to besiege Jerusalem, ibid., 90.---The sedition in Jerusalem was divided into three parts, ibid., 656; XXVI, 178.---Description of Jerusalem’s utter desolation, XXIV, 372.---The final devastation occurred under Vespasian, Titus, and Hadrian, ibid., 361; XXV, 227, 1063, 1355, 1079.---The Lord is shown to have fought for the Jews when the Romans were victorious, XXIV, 582.---Their desolation will endure to the end, ibid., 34, 36.---The description of incurable wounds expresses their everlasting captivity, ibid., 30.---They are forbidden by law to enter the holy city, XXIV, 797; XXV, 1354.---Compared with the former multitude, scarcely a tenth part remains, ibid., 101.---Antichrist lies hidden in Jewish traditions, ibid., 578.---Civil wars of the Jews, XXV, 1501.---Judaea became tributary after Augustus Caesar, XXVI, 161.---Having become subject to tribute, sedition arises, ibid., 162.---The Jews divided fourfold, ibid., 472.

PAULUS OROSIUS.---On the people of God afflicted in Egypt, XXXI, 713 ff.---The king of Persia carries the Jews away captive, ibid., 810.---The Jews subdued by Pompey, ibid., 1005.---Persecution: Jews expelled from Rome, ibid., 1075.---How Vespasian and Titus crushed the rebellious Jews and razed the city of Jerusalem, together with its Temple, to the ground, ibid., 1083.---The Jews attack different regions in war; their slaughter in Alexandria and Mesopotamia; finally massacred by Hadrian, ibid., 1092 ff.---Septimius Severus restrained them, ibid., 1102.

ST. AUGUSTINE.---Why God allowed the Jews to be subdued, XXXIV, 1051.---On the captivity of the Jewish people and Sennacherib’s coming into Judaea, XXXV, 2188.---On the Babylonian captivity, ibid.---On the principal wars carried out with the Lord’s help, ibid., 191.---Generations from Abraham to Christ, XXXVIII, 199.---The Jews before Pilate seeking to alter the inscription, ibid., 1085.---Jewish manuscripts support our faith. Why the Jewish sect was not wholly destroyed, XL, 178.---On the kingdom of the Jews, established and preserved by the one true God until they remained in true religion, XLI, 140.---At what time God’s promise concerning the land of Canaan, received as a possession even by carnal Israel, was fulfilled, ibid., 523.---On the Jewish priesthood and kingdom, which, though said to be established forever, do not remain, ibid., 536.---On the disruption of the Israelite kingdom, ibid., 537 [printed “37”].---On the kings after Solomon, whether in Judah or in Israel, [Col. 0991] ibid., 557.---On the changing condition of both kingdoms, until both peoples were led into captivity at different times; thereafter Judah was restored to its own kingdom, which finally passed into Roman power, ibid.---On the prophets who were either the last among the Jews, or whom Gospel history records around the time of Christ’s birth, ibid.---At what time Moses led the people out of Egypt, ibid., 568.---What fabrications of myths arose at the time when judges began to rule the Hebrews, ibid., 570.---Which philosophers flourished while Zedekiah was king among the Hebrews, when Jerusalem was captured and the Temple overthrown, ibid., 582.

Saint Leo the Great, Roman Pontiff.—Jewish festival food is not to be received from them, nor are festivals to be observed with them, LVI, 548.—Nor are unleavened breads to be received from them, nor is communion to be held with their impieties, ibid., 548.

Emperor Justinian.—Jews and Samaritans are not to be exempted from curial status on account of their religion and worship, but are to be subject to curial obligations and not enjoy the privileges thereof, LXXII, 986.—Decrees concerning the Samaritans, ibid., 1050.—Concerning Hebrews and how they ought to read the Scriptures, ibid., 1051.—Justinian’s constitutions concerning the Samaritans, ibid., 1085 ff.

Saint Gregory the Great.—Utmost solicitude for securing the salvation of the Jews, LXXV, 108, 109, 407.—Gregory forbids the unjust harassment of Jews, ibid., 406.—He orders the restoration to the Jews of a place taken from them, where they assembled to celebrate their solemnities, ibid., 305.—What dispositions he required for receiving baptism, ibid., 108.—He wished Jews to be burdened with taxes, ibid., 364.—He ordered the burdens of dues to be partially lightened for those converted to the Church, ibid.—He held it unlawful for Christians to be subjected to Jews, ibid., 204, 205, 332.—The laws prohibited this, ibid., 332.—Slaves of Jews who flee to the Church are granted freedom, ibid., 205.—Jewish slaves who precede their masters in coming to the faith are forbidden to be subjected to them thereafter, even if those masters become Christians, ibid., 206.—Gregory judged the gifts of Jews abominable, ibid., 206, 207.—On relocating a Jewish synagogue if it hinders church services, [Col. 1002] ibid., 457.—To Peter, Bishop of Terracina, that he should restore a place previously granted to the Jews, ibid., 489.—Jews are not to be compelled to baptism, ibid., 509.—Jewish slaves fleeing to the Church for the sake of faith are to be claimed for freedom, ibid., 675.—Jews are not permitted to retain a Christian slave, ibid., 690.—The burdens of dues are to be reduced for Jews converted to Christ, ibid., 729.—If a Jewish slave desires conversion to the Christian faith, he is to be claimed for freedom, ibid., 823.—To Fantinus the defensor, that he assist Jews approaching the Christian faith, ibid., 924.—It is to be established that Jews may not possess Christian slaves, ibid., 1037, 1039.—Jews are not to be excluded from their solemnities, but are to be stirred to conversion by admonitions and kindnesses, ibid., 1267.

Saint Isidore, Bishop of Seville.—That baptized Jews should celebrate feast days with bishops, LXXXIV, 439.—On marriages between Christians and Jews, ibid., 386.—Jews are not to be compelled by force to believe, ibid., 379.—On those who render service and favor to Jews against the faith of Christ, ibid., 380.—On Jews formerly Christian and afterward returned to their former rite, ibid.—On baptized Jews who associate with unbelieving Jews, ibid., 381.—On converted Jews who subsequently apostatize, that they are not to be admitted to give testimony, ibid.—Jews are not to hold public office, ibid.—Jews are not to possess a Christian slave, ibid.—On confirming laws promulgated against Jewish wickedness, ibid., 477.—At Passover, Jews may not go about among Christians from the Lord’s Supper until the second day after the Sabbath, nor mingle with Catholic peoples on any pretext, ibid., 285.—Christians are not to join Jews in marriage, ibid., 291.—Jews are not permitted to have Christian wives or concubines, nor to acquire Christian slaves for their own use, ibid., 354.—How Jews who desire conversion are to be received, ibid., 268.—Christians are to avoid Jewish banquets, ibid., 269.—Jews may not conduct a corpse with psalm-singing; rather, according to their ancient custom and practice, they are to conduct and bury the body, ibid., 611.

Crisconius, African bishop.—No bishop, priest, or deacon is to celebrate Passover with Jews, LXXXVIII, 822.—No one is to receive festival food from Jews, ibid., 827.—No one is to receive unleavened bread from Jews, ibid.—Jews are not to be admitted to make accusations, ibid., 828.

Blessed Charlemagne.—Capitularies concerning the Jews, XCVII, 369 ff.

Saint Agobard, Bishop of Lyons.—Consultation on the baptism of Jewish slaves, CIV, 100, 173.—Letter on avoiding association with Jews, ibid., 110.

Rabanus Maurus, Abbot of Fulda.—On those who joined themselves to Jews, CX, 490.—On those who eat with Jews, ibid.

Pope Stephen VI.—Complaint that Jews were granted the power to possess allodial estates, CXXIX, 857.

Isidore Mercator.—One must not participate in the unleavened bread of Jews, CXXX, 290.—Jewish blessings over fruits are not to be permitted, ibid., 418.—On Christians who eat with Jews, ibid.—On Jews not being compelled by force to believe, ibid., 476.—Jews are not permitted to have Christian wives, ibid., 455.—On baptized Jews who afterward apostatize from Christ, ibid., 477.—On Jews who have Christian women as wives in marriage, ibid., 477.—Jews, or those descended from Jews, are in no way to seek public offices, ibid.—Jews are not permitted to possess Christian slaves, ibid., 478.—Decrees concerning Jews, ibid., 515.—That baptized Jews should celebrate feast days with bishops, ibid., 526.—On confirming laws promulgated against Jewish wickedness, ibid., 551.—On Reccared’s constitution against the Jews, that it was not corrupted by a gift of gold, ibid., 1106.—On Jews coming to the faith, ibid., 404.

Regino, Abbot of Prüm.—Jews are not to circumcise slaves of another nation, CXXXII, 302.—A Jew is not to take a Christian wife, ibid., 311.—A Jew is not permitted to possess a Christian slave, ibid.

Gezo, Abbot of Derton.—Jews are to be excluded from every assembly of the faithful, especially where the Christian offering is celebrated, CXXXVII, 390.

Pope Alexander II.—Jews are not to be killed, but preserved, CXLVI, 1387.

Saint Edward, King of the English, Confessor.—Charters concerning the Jews, CLI, 1195.

Ivo, Bishop of Chartres.—Decree concerning Jews, CLXI, 76.—Public offices are not to be entrusted to Jews, ibid., 820.—Jews are not to presume to buy Christian slaves, ibid., 82.—Christians are not to attend Jewish banquets, ibid., 821, 826.—Jews are not to appear in public from the Lord’s Supper until [Col. 1003] the second day after the Sabbath, ibid.—Jews are to be called to the unity of faith through kindness, ibid., 82, 105, 123, 125.—On the slaves of Jews who flee to the Church, ibid., 82, 824.—Jews are not to be forcibly excluded from their solemnities, ibid., 822.—On Jewish slaves, should they wish to become Christians, ibid., 823.—Converted Jews are to be honored, ibid., 824.—With what care investigation should be made concerning Jewish slaves, ibid.—That Jews should be preserved, not killed, ibid.—Medicine is not to be received from a Jew, ibid., 825.—Jews are to be examined before baptism, ibid., 123.—After a fast of forty days, Jews are to be baptized on the Lord’s Day, ibid., 82.—Their baptized children are to be separated from their parents, ibid., 124.—On Christian Jews who have apostatized, ibid.—Christians ought not to be subordinated to or serve Jews, ibid., 125.—A Jew can baptize, ibid., 1052.—Jews about to receive baptism ought first to abstain for forty days, ibid., 1054.—For how many months Jews are to remain among the catechumens, ibid., 1061.—Just as Jews are not to be compelled to the faith, so converts are not to be permitted to depart from it, ibid., 1062.—Baptized children of Jews are not to live with them, ibid.—For Jews coming to the faith, there is to be no intercourse with an unbeliever, ibid.—On the many Jews who frequently return to Judaism, ibid.

Saint Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux.—He teaches that Jews are not to be persecuted, much less killed, CLXXXII, 567.—He rebukes the monk Rodolph, who was arming the faithful to kill Jews, ibid., 570.

Gratian.—Baptized Jews, CLXXXVII, 556.—Unless a Jew comes to the faith, he is to be separated from his believing wife, ibid., 1424.—Baptized children are to be separated from unbelieving parents, ibid., 1425.—One must neither eat nor dwell with Jews, nor receive medicine from them, ibid.—Clergy and laity alike are to avoid Jewish banquets and not receive Jews into their own associations, ibid.—Whoever joins himself in the bond of marriage to Jewish depravity is to be deprived of Christian communion, ibid., 1427.

Pope Clement III.—Decrees concerning Jews converted to the Christian faith, CCIV, 1482, 1493.

Pope Innocent III.—Goodwill toward recently baptized Jews is commended, CCXIV, 754.—Constitution for the Jews, ibid., 864.—Innocent writes to the king, urging him to restrain the insolence of Jews living in the kingdom, CCXV, 501–694.—To Master Peter, that he not permit the slaves of his parish to live with Jews, ibid., 507.—He rebukes the King of Castile for holding Jews in honor, ibid., 616.—That the sacrament of faith must not be denied to a Jew requesting it, ibid., 977.—On Jewish tithes, ibid., 1157.—Letter against the Jews, ibid., 1291.—To Philip, illustrious King of the Franks, that Jews remit interest owed by those marked with the cross, ibid., 1470.

VI.—Polemical writings against the Jews.

Tertullian, Priest of Carthage.—On the Jews, I, 400 ff.—Book against the Jews, II, 595 ff.

Saint Cyprian, Bishop of Carthage.—Three Books against the Jews, IV, 675 ff.

Anonymous.—Treatise against the Jews, IV, 919 ff.

Constantine the Great.—Constantine’s Letter against the Jews, VIII, 501.

Saint Sylvester, Pope.—Fragment of a lost work against the Jews, VIII, 814.

Saint Ambrose, Bishop of Milan.—The Jewish opinion concerning the mystical interpretation of the blessing of Simeon and Levi is refuted, XIV, 676.—Defense of David against the Jews, ibid., 897 ff.

Coelius Sedulius.—Poem against the Jews, XIX, 741–742.

Saint Augustine, Bishop of Hippo.—It is proved against the Jews that Christ is the Messiah, XXXVIII, 567.—A question put to the Jews concerning Christ, ibid., 572.—Treatise against the Jews, XLII, 52 ff.—Against the unbelief of the Jews, ibid., 1123, 1124.

Saint Maximus of Turin.—Treatise against the Jews, LVII, 793 ff.

Saint Agobard, Bishop of Lyons.—Letter on Jewish superstitions, CIV, 78 ff.—Consultation on the baptism of Jewish slaves, ibid., 100–173.

Amulo, Bishop of Lyons.—Book against the Jews, CXVI, 142 ff.

Saint Fulbert, Bishop of Chartres.—Treatise against the Jews, CXLI, 305 ff.

Saint Peter Damian, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church.—Antilogus against the Jews, CXLV, 42 ff.—The errors of the Jews are refuted, [Col. 1004] ibid., 51.—Dialogue between a Jew and a Christian, ibid., 57.—The manner in which one ought to dispute with Jews, ibid., 41.

Samuel of Morocco, a Jew converted to Christianity.—Book on the coming of the Messiah whom the Jews rashly await, CXLIX, 338 ff.

Radulphus Ardens.—On Christ’s coming against the Jews, CLV, 1701.—Against certain persons who thought that they possessed righteousness and salvation from the works of the Law, CLXXV, 2040.

Guibert, Abbot of Saint Mary of Nogent.—On the Incarnation against the Jews, CLVI, 489 ff.

Gislebert Crispin, Abbot of Westminster.—Disputation of a Jew with a Christian concerning the Christian faith, CLIX, 1005.

Odo, Bishop of Cambrai.—Disputation against a Jew named Leo concerning the coming of Christ, the Son of God, CLX, 1103.

William of Champeaux, Bishop of Châlons.—Dialogue between a Christian and a Jew concerning the Catholic faith, CLXIII, 1015.

Rupert, Abbot of Saint Heribert at Deutz.—Dialogue between a Christian and a Jew, CLXX, 559 ff.

Venerable Hildebert, Archbishop of Tours.—Against the Jews: On the Incarnation, CLXI, 811 ff.

Hugh of Saint Victor.—Defense of the Incarnate Word, CLXXVII, 315 ff.

Peter Abelard, Abbot of Rhuys.—Dialogue between a philosopher, a Jew, and a Christian.

Peter the Venerable, Abbot of Cluny.—Treatise against the Jews, CLXXXIX, 507 ff.

Richard of Saint Victor.—Two books on Emmanuel, in which are refuted the objections which Jews are accustomed to raise against us concerning our Emmanuel, CXCVI, 601 ff.

Walter of Châtillon.—Treatise against the Jews, CCVIII, 426 ff.

Alan of Lille.—Treatise against the Jews, CCX, 399 ff.

Anonymous.—Treatise against the Jews, CCXIII, 749 ff.

VII.—On the conversion of the Jews at the end of the world.

Saint Cyprian of Carthage.—Jews can receive pardon if they wash Christ’s blood away in his baptism and, entering the Church, obey its commands, IV, 694.

Saint Philastrius, Bishop of Brescia.—Conversion of the Jews, XII, 1295.

Saint Ambrose, Bishop of Milan.—Jews ought not to hope for pardon unless they are willing to do penance, XV, 1741.—God reserves pardon for them, even though they do not wish to be healed, XIV, 842.—It is certain that at the end of the world they will return to faith in Christ through the preaching of Elijah and Enoch, XVII, 869, 872.

Saint Jerome, Priest of Stridon.—The confusion of the Jews when they recognize Christ, XXIV, 298.—The conversion of the Jewish people at the consummation of the age, XXV, 1332.

Saint Augustine, Bishop of Hippo.—The conversion of Christ’s killers, XXXVIII, 947.—The Jews will have a time of salvation, ibid., 1427; XL, 339.—On Elijah’s coming before judgment, through whose preaching, revealing the hidden things of Scripture, the Jews will be converted to Christ, XLI, 703.

Cassiodorus.—The Jews are to be converted to Christ at the end, LXX, 411, 661, 941.

Saint Gregory the Great.—At the end of the world Christ is to return to the Jews from whom he came forth, LXXV, 585.—Conversion of the Jews at the end of the world, LXXVI, 763, 764, 768, 919, 1176.—The Synagogue’s repentance at the end for its former darkness, LXXIX, 532, 538.

Tajus, Bishop of Zaragoza.—On the conversion of the Jewish people near the end of the world, LXXX, 978.

Saint Isidore, Bishop of Seville.—At the end of the world the Jews will believe, LXXXIII, 508.

Alcuin, abbot.—With Elijah and Enoch preaching, they will come to worship at the feet of the Church, C, 1112.

Haymo, Bishop of Halberstadt.—On the conversion of the Jews at the end of the world, CXVI, 357, 393.

Saint Bruno, Bishop of Würzburg.—The Jews will be converted to Christ at the end of the world, CXLII, 227.

Blessed Lanfranc, Archbishop of Canterbury.—The Jews will be converted at the end of the world, CL, 334.

Venerable Godfrey, Abbot of Admont.—They will be converted at the end of the age, CLXXIV, 54, 56, 65, 104, 105, 143, 203, 268, 414, 875.

Saint Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux.—On the conversion [Col. 1005] of the Jews at the end of the world, CLXXXII, 567; CLXXXIII, 1163.

Peter Lombard, Master of the Sentences.—The Jews are to be converted through Elijah and Enoch, CXCI, 629, 1488.

Adam the Scot, Regular Canon of the Premonstratensian Order.—At [Col. 1006] the end, the Jews will be converted to Christ, CXCVIII, 140.

Philip of Harvengt, Abbot of Bonne-Espérance.—The Jews will be converted at the end of the world, CCIII, 473.

Triumphs of the Saints in Palestine, Flodoard of Reims, CXXXV, 492.---*Pantheon, or Memorial of the Ages*, Godfrey of Viterbo, CXCVIII, 880.---*On the Parisian War*, three metrical books, Abbo, CXXXII, 723.---History of Paul’s rebellion against Wamba, St. Julian, XCVI, 763.---Chronicle of the Poles, Anonymous, CLX, 833.---Pseudochronicle, Appendix to St. Prosper, LI, 859.

Quedlinburg Annals, CXLI, 443.

Lives of the bishops of Ravenna, Agnellus, CVI, 476.---History of the Church of Reims, Flodoard, CXXXV, 23.---Catalogue of the Roman pontiffs, Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVII, 133.---Epitome concerning the lives of ninety-six Roman pontiffs, St. Abbo, CXXXIX, 535.---Catalogue of the Roman pontiffs, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 239.---History of the Roman pontiffs, Anonymous, CCXIII, 987.---Deeds of the archbishops of Rouen, Appendix to John of Rouen, CXLVII, 271.

History of the calamities of the Church of Salzburg, Henry the archdeacon, CXCVI, 1540.---Chronicle of the Monastery of St. Lawrence at Liège, Rupert, CLXX, 669.---Deeds of the abbots of St. Vitonus, Laurence of Liège, CCIV, 915.---Deeds of the Saxons, Widukind, CXXXVII, 115.---*Book on the Saxon War*, Bruno of Magdeburg, CXLVII, 495.---*Book on Ecclesiastical Writers*, Gennadius, LVIII, 1053.---*Book on Ecclesiastical Writers*, Sigebert, CLX, 547.---*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, four books, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 197.---*Book on Ecclesiastical Writers*, Anonymous, CCXIII, 960.---*Book on the Birth and Death of the Fathers of Sacred Scripture*, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 129.---Sicilian History, Geoffrey Malaterra, CXLIX, 1101.---*Summary of the Whole of Universal History*, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 187.

Book of the places of the Holy Land, Fretellus the archdeacon, CLV, 1037.---Description of the Holy Land, John the priest, CLV, 1053.---Restoration of the Abbey of St. Martin of Tournai, Hermann, CLXXX, 39.---Deeds of the Church of Utrecht, Alpert the monk, CXL, 452.---*On the Triumphs of Christ Accomplished at Antioch*, two metrical books, Flodoard, CXXXV, 549.---Poem on the Trojan War, Berno the abbot, CXLII, 1205.---Deeds of the abbots of St. Trond, Rodulfus the abbot, CLXXXII, 11.---Deeds of the bishops of Toul, Appendix to Guy, CLVII, 445.---Deeds of the bishops of Tongeren, Heriger the abbot, CXXXIX, 957.

History of the Abbey of Vabres, Agio, CXXXII, 781.---Commentary on Vandal History, Appendix to Victor of Vita, LVIII, 359.---History of the Vandal Persecution, Victor of Vita, LVIII, 245.---Deeds of the bishops of Verdun, Bertarius, CXXXII, 501.---Deeds of the bishops and abbots of Verdun, Laurence of Liège, CCIV, 919.---History of the Monastery of Vézelay, Hugh of Poitiers, CXCIV, 1562.

Watten Chronicle, Ebrardus, CXLIX, 1513.---Weissenburg Annals, Guido, CXLI, 443.---Chronicle of Würzburg, Ekkehard, CLIV, 459.---Chronicle of the Visigoths, Appendix to St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 1113.---Chronicle of the Visigothic Kings, Appendix to St. Julian, XCVI, 809.

[Col. 1009]

**CLXXIX. INDEX OF ALL MONASTERIES, BOTH OF MEN AND OF WOMEN, MENTIONED IN THE *PATROLOGIA LATINA*, SETTING FORTH THE PLACE AND TIME OF EACH ONE’S FOUNDATION OR RESTORATION, TOGETHER WITH THE PRIVILEGES OF THE HOLY PONTIFFS, AND THE DIPLOMAS AND CHARTERS OF KINGS AND NOBLES.**

[Col. 1009] **ABENDENSIS, or MOUNT ROMARICUS** (the convent of Remiremont or Romarieberg, Vosges): a celebrated nunnery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded about the year 620 by St. Romaricus, monk of Luxeuil, and St. Radulf, bishop of Metz, LXXI, 644, note.---Charter of St. Romaricus, LXXX, 461.---Testament of St. Ansegisus, abbot of Fontenelle, CV, 747.---On the dispute between the abbess of Romaricus and the abbot of Chaumousey, CLXII, 1130 ff.---Letter of Paschal II to Gisela, abbess, in 1105, CLXIII, 139, 140, 182, 197, 206.---Privilege of Lucius II, 1114, CLXXIX, 839; of Eugenius III, 1146, CLXXX, 1170; of Adrian IV, 1157, CLXXXVIII, 1508; of Alexander III, 1170, CC, 625.---Letter of Innocent III, 1202, CCXIV, 1035.

**ABENTONENSE, or ABENDONENSE, OF ST. MARY** (St. Mary’s, Abingdon, county of Berkshire, in the diocese of Salisbury, England): monastery of St. Benedict founded about 950 by St. Æthelwold, bishop, CXXXVII, 88; later made illustrious by St. Ælfric, abbot, CX, 1006; CXXXIX, 1455.---Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1203, CCXV, 49.

**ABERBRUCHOTENSE** (Aberbruhot in Ireland): monastery, to whose prior Innocent III wrote concerning certain disputed tithes, 1207, CCXV, 1126.

**ABOLENSE** (Aboli, diocese of Luni in Etruria): monastery founded by a bishop and confirmed by Innocent III, 1198, CCXIV, 37, 38.

**ABUNDANCE, ST. MARY’S** (Notre-Dame de l’Abondance, diocese of Geneva): monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded in 1157.---Letter of Innocent III, 1211, CCXVI, 479.

**ACAPINENSE** (Acapui near Thessalonica in Turkey): monastery in which Mary, formerly empress, took refuge with her sons.---Privilege of Innocent III, 1210, CCXVI, 227.

**ACERITANUM, or ACERETENSE** (Acerra, Papal States): monastery mentioned in a letter of Celestine III to the bishop of Faenza, permitting the monastery of Gamundio not to be subject to it, 1195, CCVI, 1064.

**ACRE, ST. THOMAS’S** (St. Thomas of Acre, or Ptolemais in Syria): monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, built in the time of the crusaders; Innocent III confirmed its privileges and possessions, 1209, CCXV, 1525.

**HOSPITAL OF ACRE** (Hospitallers of St. John of Acre): Innocent forbade it to wear white publicly in the manner of the Knights Templar, 1210, CCXVI, 312.

**ACUENSIS, ST. MARY’S** (Notre-Dame de l’Aiguille near Marseilles): nunnery to which Innocent III granted a privilege, 1216, CCXVII, 263.

**ADESCANCASTRENSE, or EXONIENSE** (Exeter, England): monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in which Boniface, later made bishop of Mainz, was received as a boy, 700, LXXXIX, 605, 638.

**ADMONT, ST. BLAISE’S** (St. Blaise of Admont, diocese of Salzburg): monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by Bishop Gebhard at the end of the eleventh century; Paschal II granted it a privilege in 1104, CLXIII, 1290.---The venerable Abbot Godfrey flourished in 1142, CLXXIV, 9.---Privileges of Innocent II, 1139, CLXXIX, 433, 650; Lucius II, 1144, CLXXIX, 837; Alexander III, 1171, CC, 718; Lucius III, 1185, CCI, 1361.---Decree of Urban III concerning the observance of the Rule of St. Benedict, 1187, CCII, 1515.

**ADURANUM, ST. QUITERIA’S** (St. Quiteria on the Adour, diocese of Auch): monastery in Gascony apparently identical with St. Sever (St.-Séver), whose abbot is at the same time bishop; founded at an unknown date, but restored about 963 on the River Adour, LXXI, 907, note. See **ST. SEVER**.

**ST. GILES OF NÎMES.** See **ST. PETER**.

**ST. GILES.** See **SEMENSENSE**.

**ST.
