GILES OF TOULOUSE** (St.-Gilles of Toulouse): monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose possessions and rights Urban II confirmed, rejoicing also at the restitution made by Count Raymond, 1095, CLI, 399.---Privilege of the same pope, 1096, CLI, 477.---Letters of Paschal II concerning the abbot and monastery, CLXIII, 138, 139, 202, 203, 223, 242, 243, 416.---Privilege of Calixtus II, 1119, CLXIII, 1103, 1105.---Letters of the same pope for the monastery’s defense, ibid., 1212, 1213, 1214, 1306, 1307.---Letter by which he again subjects that monastery to Cluny, 1125, CLXVI, 1228.---Letter of Celestine III to the count of Toulouse concerning damage inflicted upon the monastery and its reparation, 1196, CCVI, 1155.---Privilege of Innocent III, 1208, CCXV, 1480.

Ancient Egyptian monasteries are described, XXI, throughout; XLIX, 53; LXXIII, 89.

**AERENSE** (probably Ayr or Aix in Scotland): monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, from which Celestine III removed the priory of Bromholm, 1194, CCVI, 1031.

**ST. AEMILIAN’S:** celebrated monastery in Aragon, founded by St. Aemilian in 574, LXXX, 703.

**AFFLIGHEM, ST. MARY’S** (Notre-Dame d’Afflighem in Brabant): monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded in 1083 by Henry, count of Louvain, and made illustrious in 1125, CLXIII, 1199.---Blessed Ida made gifts to this monastery about 1090, CLV, 457.---Privilege of Paschal II, 1105, CLXIII, 142.---Privilege by which Calixtus II assigns to it the church of Bornhem, 1121, ibid., 1199.---Privilege of Eugenius III, 1148, CLXXX, 1324.---A marvelous prodigy performed in an image of the Blessed Mary before St. Bernard, 1146, CLXXXV, 1827.---Letters of Innocent III, 1204, CCXV, 344.

**ST. AFRA OF AUGSBURG** (St. Afra, Augsburg): monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose goods and privileges Adrian IV confirmed, 1156, CLXXXVIII, 1465.

**AGALIENSE** (Agali near Toledo, Spain): monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in a suburb of Toledo while the Goths ruled; it is mentioned in the *Life of St. Maximus*, 644, LXXX, 612.---It was founded by King Athanagild and entrusted to St. Euphemius, abbot, 592, ibid., 626.---St. Ildephonsus, later bishop, professed monastic life there in 631, XCVI, 11.

**ST. AGATHA’S** (St. Agatha on the Ticino in Lombardy): monastery called New, built on the Ticino by Grimoald, king of the Lombards, 673, XCV, 613.

**AGDE, ST. TIBERIUS’S** (St. Thibéry of Agde, Hérault): monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, otherwise called Caesarionense or Cessoronense, believed to have been built in 770.---Privilege of Paschal II, by which he confirmed its rights and possessions, 1116, CLXIII, 401.---Privilege of Innocent III, 1216, CCXVIII, 266.

**AGDE, ST. ANDREW’S** (St. Andrew of Agde): monastery founded by St. Severus, abbot, about 502; later transferred to canons of St. Augustine, LXXI, 775, note.

**AGAUNE, ST. MAURICE’S OF MALTACENA, OTHERWISE OF BURGETO** (Agaune or St. Maurice-en-Valais): monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by King Sigismund in 545, [Col. 1011] LXXI, 589; LXXII, 209.---Pope Stephen II, fleeing to King Pippin, was honorably received there in 750, CXXVIII, 1091.---Privilege of Eugenius, 827, CXXIX, 987.---Almost destroyed, it was restored by Empress Adelaide and St. Odilo of Cluny in 1024, CXLII, 858.---Privilege of Pope St. Leo IX, 1050, CXLIII, 665.---Honorius, by privilege, confirms the canons established there, 1129, CLXVI, 1292.---Privilege of Alexander III, 1179, CC, 1212.---Of Celestine III, 1196, CCVI, 1159.---Privilege of Innocent III, 1207, CCXV, 1156; CCXVI, 615, 939.

**AGELLO, ST. MARTIN’S OF** (St. Martin of Agello, in the March of Treviso, Italy): nunnery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose possessions and rights Eugenius III confirmed by bull, 1148, CLXXX, 1375.

**AGENSI ISLAND, ST. MARTIN’S OF** (St. Martin of Ains or Ahun, former diocese of Saintes): monastery built by Boso, count of the Marche, about 997.---Privilege of Paschal II, 1107, CLXIII, 218.

**AGERENSE, ST. PETER’S** (St. Peter near St. Airy, diocese of Verdun): monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built on the Meuse beside the abbey of St. Agericus by the noble Arnold and his wife Arsendis; Pope Nicholas II confirmed its foundation by privilege in 1060, CXLIII, 1337.

**ST. AGERICUS, FORMERLY ST. MARTIN’S** (St. Airy, diocese of Verdun): monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, of the congregation of St. Vitonus at Verdun, where St. Agericus rests; founded in 639, LXXI, 504, note.---Privilege of Pope St. Leo IX, 1050, CXLII, 667.

**AGGERINENSIS** (Enger near Erfurt, diocese of Mainz): nunnery whose foundation is falsely attributed to St. Boniface and King Widukind by the author of the *Life of St. Matilda*, CLI, 1316; for it appears to be identical with the nunnery of Erfurt, founded by King Dagobert II in 677. See the **ERFURT NUNNERY**.

**AGNANENSE, ST. MARY’S** (St. Mary of Agnano, in the Terra di Lavoro, Naples): monastery of the Camaldolese Order, to which Urban III assigned the church of St. Christina of Clano, 1187, CCII, 1564.

**AHUSANUM, ST. MARTIN’S** (St. Martin of Ahus, in Swabia): monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built shortly before 1125 by Count Adelbert and his father Manegold; in that year Pope Honorius II confirmed it by privilege, CLXVI, 1237.---Privilege of Innocent II, 1136, CLXXIX, 256.---Of Celestine II, 1143, ibid., 772.---Of Eugenius III, 1149, CLXXX, 1409.

**AIENSE, AIENTENSE, or ANTIMONASTERIUM** (Eymoutiers, diocese of Limoges): monastery founded by Hildegarius and shortly afterward converted into a college of canons by Bishop Alduin, 1012, CXLI, 52.---Urban III confirms an agreement between these monks and the bishop of Saintes, 1186, CCII, 1367.

**AUMALE, ST. MARTIN’S OF** (St. Martin of Aumale, diocese of Rouen): monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built about 1130.---Privilege of Innocent III, 1203, CCXV, 263.

**ST. ALBAN’S** (St. Alban, diocese of Worcester, England): monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in the diocese of Worcester; St. Oswald, bishop, placed St. Ælfric over it as abbot to reform it, 980, CXLVII, 1194.---Privilege of Alexander III, 1259, CC, 134, 1053.---Letters of Innocent III to the abbot, 1203, CCXV, 228, 729, 734, 740.

**ST. ALBAN’S.** See **BASILEENSE**.

**ST. ROMAN’S OF ALBANIA** (St. Romain of Albane, diocese of Rouen): college of clerics in the Church of Rouen, founded in 1245 by Peter, formerly bishop of Albano, then archbishop and cardinal of Rouen, CXLVII, 211.---Pope Clement reduced the number of these clerics (canons) to sixteen in 1350, CXLVII, 215.

**ALBARENSE** (Albaro, Papal States): monastery whose abbot brought a complaint to Innocent III concerning the election of the abbot of Monte Albo.---Letter of Innocent III, 1205, CCXV, 703.

**AUBERIVE** (Auberive, diocese of Langres): Cistercian abbey, sprung from Clairvaux and founded by Willenco, bishop of Langres, in 1136 on the River Alb.---Abbot Garnerius made it illustrious in 1198, CCV, 555.---Privilege of Innocent II, 1138, CLXXIX, 353. Donations made by Guy of Saulx, 1179, CLXXXV, 1436. Gift of Godfrey, bishop of Langres, 1158, CLXXXV, 1476.

**AUBETERRE, ST. SAVIOR’S** (St. Savior of Aubeterre, diocese of Périgueux): monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by St. Maurus, or, according to others, in 785.---Letters of Innocent III to the abbot of Tenalia concerning its reform, 1203, CCXV, 245, 248, 276.

**ALBELDENSE** (Alveda, near Logroño, Spain): [Col. 1012] monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose monk Vigila was the continuator of the *Chronicle of Albelda*, eleventh century, CXXIX, 1123.

**ALBI, ST. SALVIUS’S** (St. Sauve of Albi): college of canons, concerning whose dispute Innocent III wrote, 1203, CCXVII, 101.

**ST. AUBIN’S** (St. Aubin of Angers): monastery founded by that holy bishop about 540 near Angers, according to the Rule of St. Benedict, and later made famous, LXXI, 899, note. Diploma of Charlemagne, 769, XCVII, 916.---Letter of Urban II to Abbot Geoffrey concerning his dispute with the abbot of Vendôme, CLI, 355.---Privilege of Urban II, 1096, CLI, 465.---Letters of Paschal II, 1111, CLXIII, 293, 382.

**AUBIGNY, ST. KILIAN’S** (Aubigny near Saint-Pol): monastery of the Order of St. Augustine near Arras, eleventh century, CXLIX, 131.

**ALBORENSE** (Albore, diocese of Montecalvo, kingdom of Naples): monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, which Pope Calixtus II twice ordered the bishop of Rossellano not to harass, 1124, CLXIII, 1307, 1313.

**ALCIACENSE** (Auchy-les-Moines, Pas-de-Calais): monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built—or rather restored and endowed—by Ingelram, count of Hesdin, 1072–1079, CLXVI, 911, note.---Letter of Innocent III concerning the election of the abbot, 1209, CCXVI, 40; CCXVII, 94.

**ALCOBAÇA, ST. MARY’S** (St. Mary of Alcobaça in Estremadura, Portugal): monastery of the Cistercian Order, built by King Alfonso I in 1148. Innocent III wrote to its abbot in 1198, CCXIV, 191, 192, 194, 302, 774.

**ALDAHENSE, or ALTAHENSE, ST. MAURICE’S** (St. Maurice of Altörich, diocese of Regensburg): monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, which, at the request of Abbot Godehard, Emperor St. Henry II received under his protection in 1004, CXL, 259.---Privileges of the same emperor, 265, 287, 288, 291, 349; of Honorius II, 1126, CLXVI, 1314; of Eugenius III, 1148, CLXXX, 1318, 1536; of Lucius III, 1184, CCI, 1273.

**ALDENBURG, ST. PETER’S** (St. Peter of Audembourg near Ostend, Netherlands): monastery of the Order of St. Benedict founded by St. Arnulf, bishop of Soissons, in 1083, CLXXIV, 1451. It had Arnulf as its third abbot in 1142, CLXXIV, 1211.---*Chronicle of Aldenburg*, by Hariulf, 1459.---Diplomas of St. Arnulf, 1565, 1567.---Diploma of Charles, count of Flanders, 1568; of Thierry, count of Flanders, 1569; of Simon, bishop of Tournai, 1570; of Walter of Heines, 1572; of Gerald, bishop of Tournai, 1573; privilege of Pope Adrian II, 1156, CLXXIV, 1574; of Count Philip, 1576, 1577, 1579; of Everard, 1580, 1582; privilege of Pope Celestine II, 1195, 1583; of Count Baldwin, 1197; privilege of Adrian IV, 1156, CLXXXVIII, 1488; of Celestine III, 1196, CCVI, 1150.

**ALDERSPACH** (Alderspach or Aldersbach, diocese of Passau in Bavaria): monastery of the Cistercian Order, built by a nobleman named Bernard about 1080, but transferred to the Cistercians only in 1147. Bishop Otto of Bamberg acquired it for himself about 1132, CLXXIII, 1279.---Privilege of Eugenius III, 1147, by which it was given to the Cistercians, CLXXX, 1265.

**ST. ALEXANDER’S** (St. Alexander of Lehr, near Wildeshausen, duchy of Bremen): abbey in the district of Leer near Wildeshausen, built and granted to canons of St. Augustine by the nobleman Walbert; Pope Stephen V confirmed this by privilege in 891, CXXIX, 816.

**ST. ALEXANDER’S.** See **BERGOMACENSE**.

**ST. ALEXIUS OF THE CITY.** See **BONIFACE AND ALEXIUS** among the **ROMAN MONASTERIES**.

**ALMENÈCHES, or ALMONACHES** (nuns of Almenèches, Orne): nunnery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by Roger of Montgomery in the eleventh century, CCII, 1317.

**ALNET, ST. MARY’S** (Notre-Dame d’Aulnay, diocese of Bayeux): monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded in 1131 by Jordan of Saget and his wife Lucy.---Letter of Innocent III, 1203, CCXV, 256.

**ALPIRSBACH, ST. BENEDICT’S** (St. Benedict of Alpirsbach, duchy of Württemberg): monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded in 1100 by the noblemen Rothmann of Husin, Adelbert of Zolro, and Alwic of Sulz.---Privilege of Pope Paschal II, 1110, CLXIII, 67.

**ALSIACENSE.** See above, **ALCIACENSE**.

**ALTA BRUGERIA.** See **BLANCA LANDA**.

**HAUTE-CRÊTE, ST. MARY’S** (Notre-Dame de Haute-Crête, near Palézieux, diocese of Lausanne): monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded by Guy, bishop of Lausanne, in 1134; St. Amadeus, Guy’s successor, confirmed its possessions by privilege, CLXXXVIII, 1291.

**HAUTECOMBE, ST. MARY’S** (St. Mary of Hautecombe, on Lake Bourget in Savoy): monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded by Amadeus III, duke of Savoy, in 1125; Amadeus, monk of Clairvaux, was its second abbot after Vivian and afterward bishop of Lausanne, CLXXXVIII, 1279, 1280.

**HAUTERIVE, ST. MARY’S** (Notre-Dame de Hauterive, one league from Fribourg): monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded in 1137 by the nobleman William of Glâne, to which Amadeus, bishop of Lausanne, made gifts, CLXXXVIII, 1291.

**ALTAHENSE.** See above, **ALDAHENSE**.

**ALTENENSIS** (Altena, Lower Saxony): nunnery whose abbess commends herself to the prayers of St. Hildegard, twelfth century, CXCVII, 320.

**ALTENBERG, ST. MARY’S** (St. Mary of Altenberg, diocese of Trier): nunnery of the Premonstratensian Order, founded before 1151; in that year Eugenius III confirmed its possessions and rights by privilege, CLXXX, 1480.---Privilege of Lucius III, 1185, CCI, 1327.

**AUTREY, ST. MARY’S** (Notre-Dame d’Autrey, Vosges): monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, founded by Stephen of Bar, bishop of Metz, in 1150.---Privilege of Lucius III, 1182, CCI, 1146.

**HAUTMONT, SS. PETER AND PAUL’S** (St. Peter of Hautmont, Ardennes): monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, founded near Maubeuge by Blessed Vincent, count and afterward abbot, in 640, CXLIX, 137. It is mentioned in the testament of St. Ansegisus, abbot of Fontenelle, CV, 746.---Privilege of Innocent III, confirming to this monastery the chapel of Grantreiny, 1199, CCXVII, 52.

**HOSPITAL OF ALTOPASSO** (Hospitallers of Altopasso, in the principality of Lucca): Pope Anastasius IV wrote to their rector Guy in 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1076.

**HAUTVILLERS** (Haut-Villiers, diocese of Reims): abbey of the Order of St. Benedict founded by Blessed Nivard, bishop of Reims, who entrusted it to St. Bercharius as abbot, 662.---Privilege of Nivard, LXXXVIII, 1181; CXXXV, 107.---The monk Almanus flourished in 868, CXXI, 385, 387.---The beginnings of its monastery, CXXXVII, 676.

**ALTDORF, SS. STEPHEN AND CYRIACUS’S** (St. Cyriacus of Altdorf, Swabia): monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded in Alsace by Hugh and Heilwig, father and mother of Pope St. Leo IX, and dedicated by the pope himself in 1049, CXLIII, 637, 689.---Privilege of Paschal II, CLXIII, 155; of Celestine III, 1192, CCVI, 950.

**ALTOVICENSIS** (Altuwich, diocese of Trier): nunnery whose abbess formerly commended herself to the prayers of St. Hildegard, abbess of St. Rupert’s, in the twelfth century, CXCVII, 321.

**ARVIÈRES CHARTERHOUSE** (Chartreuse d’Arvières, diocese of Belley): founded in the diocese of Belley by the Venerable Arthand, Carthusian monk, in 1164. The founder himself was its first prior; afterward he was bishop of Belley from 1184 to 1190, then returned to his monastery, where he died in old age in 1206, CLIII, 797. St. Hugh, bishop of Lincoln, visited this monastery in 1199, CLIII, 1088.

**ST. AMAND’S**, situated in the county of Trahesin: when it was falling into ruin, Emperor Lothair gave it to the monastery of Cluny in 960, CXXXVII, 779.

**ST. AMAND’S, or ELNONENSE** (St. Amand on the Elnon, diocese of Arras): monastery founded on the Elnon in the diocese of Arras by St. Amand and King Dagobert I in 637, LXXX, 548.---Charter of St. Amand, LXXXVII, 1273. Diploma of Louis the Pious, 822, CIV, 1113, 1117.---The monk Milo flourished there in 872, CXXI, 925.---Likewise Hucbald, monk and biographer, in 893, CXXXII, 815.---On the condition of this abbey in the ninth century under Abbot Ratherius, CXXXVI, 139, 140. The monk Guillebert, 1090, CL, 1434.---Privilege of Paschal II, 1107, CLXIII, 211; of Calixtus II, 1119, CLXIII, 1139.

**ST. AMANTIUS OF RODEZ** (St. Chamant of Rodez): abbey dependent on St. Vitonus of Verdun, 511, LXXI, 1023.---St. Desiderius of Cahors restored that monastery, LXXXVII, 219.

**AMBAZAC** (Ambazac, diocese of Limoges): abbey built in the Limousin before 593 and mentioned by Gregory of Tours in 590, LXXI, 1141.

**AMIENS, ST. JOHN’S** (St. Jean-les-Amiens): monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, founded in 1124 by Enwerrand, bishop of Amiens, and Milo, abbot of St. Josse of the Wood.---Privilege of Innocent II, 1137, CLXXIX, 308; of Alexander III, 1163, CC, 222.

**AMIENS, ST. MARTIN’S** (Convent of the Ladies of St. Martin at Amiens): nunnery built where the holy bishop clothed a poor man with his own garment in the sixth century, LXXI, 928.---Bull of Paschal II, 1109, CLXIII, 258.---Privilege of Eugenius III, 1148, CLXXX, 1331.

**EMBRUN, ST. JUSTUS’S** (St. Just of Embrun): monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose abbot was St. Barnard before he was chosen to govern the Church of Vienne, 817.---Letter of Pope Paschal I, CXXIX, 979.---Charter [Col. 1014] of Abbot Hision and Peter of Cluny, 1132, CLXXXIX, 1062.

**AMELUNGSBORN, or AMELUNXBORN, ST. MARY’S** (St. Mary of Amelungsborn, Hanover): monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded by Count Sigefrid of Bommelberg in 1129, when Honorius II honored it with a privilege, CLXVI, 1299.---Privilege of Celestine III, 1197, CCVI, 1226.

**AMIATINUM, or OF AMIATA.** See **MONTE**.

**ANAGRATENSE** (Annegray, diocese of Besançon): monastery founded by St. Columbanus about 570, LXXXVII, 1019; testament of St. Ansegisus, abbot of Fontenelle, 833, CV, 746.

**ST. ANASTASIUS’S** (St. Anastasius near Perugia): Pope St. Gregory VII wrote against the abbot of this monastery in 1074, CXLVIII, 376.

**ST. ANASTASIUS AT THE WATERS OF SALVIA.** See among the **ROMAN MONASTERIES**.

**ANDAGINENSE, ST. HUBERT’S** (St. Hubert of Chiny in the Ardennes): monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by Duke Pippin and his wife Plectrude in 702, LXXXVIII, 1215, note.---Emperor Henry II subjected it to the bishop of Liège in 1006, CXL, 269, note.---Privilege of St. Gregory VII, 1074, CXLVIII, 652.---Of Pope Urban II, 1098, CLI, 511.---Complaint of Abbot Theodoric to Urban II against Viredus, its oppressor, 555.---Chronicle of St. Hubert from its foundation, CLIV, 1342.---Privilege of Innocent II, 1139, CLXXIX, 448.

**ANGERS, ST. MAURUS’S** (St. Maur on the Loire, diocese of Angers). See **GLANFEUIL**.

**ANGERS, ST. NICHOLAS’S** (St. Nicholas of Angers): monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by Count Fulk, called Nerra, in 1020.---Privilege of Urban II, 1096, CLI, 447.---Charter of donation of Fulk, count of Anjou, CLV, 481, 482.---Privilege of Eugenius III, 1149, CLXXX, 1419.---Of Alexander III, 1178, CC, 1176, 1197.

**ANGERS, ST. JOHN OF ALMSGIVING** (St. John of the Alms at Angers): monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, built for the sick and pilgrims; Innocent III confirmed its goods and privileges in 1208, CCXV, 1379.

**ANGERS, ST. STEPHEN’S** (St. Stephen below Angers): monastery situated in a suburb of Angers, mentioned in a diploma of Charlemagne, XCVII, 918; no other reference to it exists anywhere, ibid., note.

**ANGERS, SS. SERGIUS AND MEDARDUS’S** (St. Medard of Angers): monastery which, under Abbot Theodebert, held a privilege from King Childebert III in 705, LXXXVIII, 1103.

**ANGERS, ST. VENANTIUS’S** (St. Venance-les-Angers): monastery founded by Bishop Licinius about 520, later transferred to canons of St. Augustine, LXXI, 568, note.

**ANGERS, ST. ALBIN’S.** See **ALBIN’S**.

**ANDELYS, ST. MARY’S** (Convent of St. Mary at Andelys-sur-Seine): ancient nunnery founded by St. Clotilde on the Seine at Andely in 526; it was destroyed by the Northmen in the tenth century, XCV, 128, note; CV, 745.

**ANDLAU, SS. FABIAN AND FELICITY’S** (nuns of St. Fabian at Andlau, diocese of Strasbourg): nunnery founded by Emperor Charles the Fat and his wife Richarda at a place called Heljon or Helgon, diocese of Strasbourg; Pope St. Leo IX granted it a privilege in 1049, CXLIII, 653.---Likewise Victor II, 1055, CXLIII, 815.

**ST. ANDOCHUS OF SAULIEU** (St. Andoche of Saulieu, diocese of Autun): monastery built in the diocese of Autun before 722 by Widerad, abbot of Flavigny, LXXXVIII, 1268.

**ST. ANDREW’S.** See **MOUNT SORACTE**.

**ST. ANDREW’S** (St. Andrew of Vulcano Island in Sicily): monastery mentioned by St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 779.

**ST. ANDREW’S OF ARCE, or ARDE** (St. Andrew of Arc or Ard in Ireland): monastery whose goods and privileges Innocent III confirmed in 1204, CCXV, 368.

**SS. ANDREW, MICHAEL, AND MARTIN AT MOUNT ANDAEON** (St. Andrew or St. Michael of Andan; otherwise St. Andrew of Villeneuve-lès-Avignon): monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in 999.---Privilege of Gregory V, CXXXVII, 937.---Of Urban II, 1096, CLI, 216, 480.---Privilege of Pope Gelasius II, 1118, CLXIII, 542.

**ST. ANDREW’S IN AUVERGNE** (St. Andrew of Clermont): this monastery is mentioned by Gregory of Tours about 563, LXXI, 204.---It later passed to the Premonstratensians by privilege of Alexander III, 1174, CC, 988.

**ST. ANDREW’S ABOVE MASCALAS** (St. Andrew of Mascala, diocese of Taormina in Sicily): monastery situated in the diocese of [Col. 1015] Taormina, mentioned by St. Gregory the Great in the sixth century, LXXVIII, 657.

**ST. ANDREW’S OF THE CASTLE OF ST. MARY** (St. Andrew or Our Lady of Le Cateau-Cambrésis): monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, begun by Bishop Gerard and completed by his successor St. Lietbert in 1050, CXLVI, 1447.---The monastery is mentioned in letters of Alexander III, 1166–1169, CC, 515, 619.

**ANDRES, ST. SAVIOR AND ST. ROTRUDE’S** (St. Savior or St. Rotrude of Andres, diocese of Boulogne): monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by Count Baldwin I in 1084.---Privilege of Paschal II, 1118, CLXIII, 433.---Of Calixtus II, 1124, CLXIII, 1301.---Of Alexander III, 1173, CC, 898.---Decrees and letters of Innocent III, 1208, CCXV, 1509, 1514, 1515, 1517, 1519; 1211, CCXVI, 402, 523.

ANGELI (St.) DE PLANO (Saint-Angel of the Plain, diocese of Fermo in the March of Ancona, Papal States), monastery whose abbot, expelled from his monastery by the bishop, was reinstated by Innocent III in 1212, CCXVI, 628.

ANGELI (St.) DE SPATA (Saint-Angel of the Sword at Viterbo), monastery to whose abbot Innocent III wrote in 1210, CCXVI, 472.

ANGELI (St.) IN CORNACULA (Convent of Saint-Angel, diocese of Chieti, in the Abruzzi, Naples), mentioned in a privilege of Innocent III, 1208, CCXVII, 180.

ANGELIACENSE or ANGERIACENSE OF ST. JOHN (Saint-Jean-d’Angély, Indre-et-Loire), monastery built in the diocese of Tours about 520, LXXI, 1085.—The monastery of St. Eparchius of Angoulême was subjected to Angériac by Urban II in 1096, CLI, 443; letter to Abbot Ansculf, 445. Letter of Innocent III in 1210 against the bishop of Poitiers, CCXVI, 285, 758.

ANGLIACENSE OF ST. JOHN (Saint-Jean-sur-Angle, diocese of Poitiers, Vienne), monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, built by William Tempier, bishop of Poitiers, in 1192. Letter of Innocent III to Abbot Peter concerning a certain abuse, 1202, CCXIV, 1165.—(It is also called “Of the Holy Cross”; see CRUCE.)

ANIANENSE OF THE HOLY SAVIOUR (Saint-Sauveur of Aniane, Hérault), monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by Abbot Benedict about 800 in the diocese of Montpellier, CII, 351.—Aniane charters of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious, CII, 1419.—Diploma of Lothair, 826, CIV, 1155.—Privilege of Pope John XV, 989, CXXXVII, 835.—Alexander II subjected it to the bishop of Maguelonne in 1072, CXLVI, 1385.—Letter of Urban II to the bishop of Maguelonne concerning the abbot of Aniane, CLI, 431.—Privilege of Paschal II, 1113, CLXIII, 320.—Of Adrian IV, 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1361.—Of Alexander III, 1162, CC, 142.—Letter of Innocent III concerning the relief of this monastery’s poverty, 1212, CCXVI, 770.

ANIANENSE (Saint-Aignan at Orléans), monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, later a college of canons, founded by Abbot Leodebod in 617, as is clear from his charter, LXXXVIII, 1186.—Diploma of Charlemagne, 800, XCVII, 993.—Leodebod’s testament, 623, CXLI, 908.—Privileges of Alexander III, 1162, CC, 159, 239, 1044, 1246.—Privilege of Innocent III, 1207, CCXV, 1190, 1191.

ANIANI AND LAURENTII (SS.) (Saint-Anien at Nevers), monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, rebuilt in 843. Privilege of Pope Urban II, 1089, CLI, 303.

ANICIENSE or PODIENSE OF ST. PETER (Saint-Pierre du Puy-en-Velay), monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, to whose prior Innocent III entrusted the case of the canons of Brioude in 1208, CCXV, 1514.

ANISOLANUM or ST. CARILEFUS (Saint-Calais, Sarthe).—This very distinguished abbey already existed in the territory of Le Mans in the time of Merovech, about 480, LXXI, 327.—Charters of King Dagobert, LXXX, 561, 571.—Diploma of Theuderic, 674, LXXXVII, 1320; of Clovis III, LXXXVIII, 1085; of Dagobert III, 1111, 1115; of Theuderic IV, 1133.—Precept of Charlemagne, 774, XCVII, 930; of Louis the Pious, 814, CIV, 986, 11146, 1278, 1290.—Charter of St. Aldric, bishop, CXV, 72, 77, 88 and following.—Privilege of Pope Nicholas, CXIX, 865 and following.

ANSIONENSE, see ENIXIONENSE.

ANTHYMI (St.) OF SIENA, Italy (Convent of Saint-Anthyme at Siena), whose rights and possessions Louis the Pious confirmed in 814, CIV, 1003.—Privilege of Anastasius IV, 994.—Adrian IV commends Abbot Wibald to the Roman emperor in favour of this monastery, CLXXXVIII, 1427.

ANTIMONASTERIUM, see AIENSE or AIENTENSE.

ANTISSIODORENSE OF ST. AMATOR (Saint-Amateur of Auxerre, Yonne), monastery founded by St. Ursus, bishop, and successor of St. Germanus, about 590, CXXXVIII, 229.—Privilege [Col. 1016] of Innocent II, 1131, CLXXIX, 101.—Charter of Alan, bishop of Auxerre, 1163, CCI, 1389.

ANTISSIODORENSE OF ST. GERMANUS (Saint-Germain of Auxerre, Yonne), monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded and endowed in the suburb of the city by St. Germanus, bishop, under the invocation of SS. Cosmas and Damian; it later passed to the Congregation of St. Maurice, 570, LXXI, 336; CXXXVIII, 226.—Diploma of Louis the Pious, 816, CIV, 1039.—Under Hugh, bishop and abbot, many religious houses of different orders were founded in this diocese in the eleventh century, CXXXVIII, 293.—Urban II entrusted the monastery of St. Germanus to Blessed Hugh of Cluny in 1098, CLI, 538.—Privilege of Paschal II, 1107, CLXIII, 221.—It was subjected to Cluny by the same Paschal, 235.—Decree of Lucius II concerning a dispute with the monastery of Vézelay, 1144, CLXXIX, 842.—Anastasius IV conferred on the bishop of Auxerre jurisdiction over the abbot of St. Germanus in 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1065; Urban III again subjected it to Cluny in 1187, CCII, 1483.—Letters and privileges of Innocent III, 1198, CCXIV, 164, 241; CCXV, 27; CCXVI, 59, 422, 632. Innocent protected that monastery against the bishop, CCXVI, 1243; CCXVII, 255.

ANTISSIODORENSE AT QUOTIACUM or COACUM (probably Couches, Saône-et-Loire), monastery founded by St. Germanus, but destroyed shortly afterward when the Huns broke forth, 570, CXXXVIII, 226, 233.

ANTISSIODORENSE OF ST. PETER (Saint-Pierre of Auxerre), monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built outside the city in the place called Brucrolense by the nobleman Ribal and his son Albert, and confirmed by King Henry in 1058, CLI, 1036.—Privilege of Alexander III, 1174, CC, 973.—Letter of Innocent III, 1213, CCXVI, 934.

ANTISSIODORENSE OF ST. JULIAN (Convent of Saint-Julien at Auxerre), nunnery mentioned under the episcopate of Tetricus, eighth century, CXXXVIII, 244.—Decree of Lucius III concerning a certain settlement between the abbot and the count of Joigny.—Privilege of Celestine III confirming its property, 1196, CCVI, 1187.

ANTISSIODORENSE CANONRY OF ST. EUSEBIUS, endowed by Bishop Alan and confirmed by Adrian IV in 1158, CLXXXVIII, 1547.—Privilege of Alexander III, 1162.

MONASTERIES OF THE DIOCESE OF AUXERRE, see DECIMIACENSE, FONTANENSE, MANUACENSE, SAFFIACENSE AND DE VARENAS, and ST. MARY OF THE ROUND.

ANTISSIODORENSE OF ST. MARY, outside the walls, to which Bishop Vigilius granted many things in 670, LXXXVIII, 1193.

ANTONINI (St.) (Saint-Antonin, diocese of Rodez), monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, to which King Pippin subjected the monastery of St. Peter of Mormac in 767, XCVI, 1562.—Henry the monk flourished there in 881, CXXIV, 1129.—Letter of Innocent III concerning a certain dispute, 1203, CCXVII, 101.

ANTURNACENSIS, a nunnery in Germany whose location we have not found specified, and whose abbess once wrote to St. Hildegard in the twelfth century, CXCVII, 336.

APOLLINARIS (St.), see CLASSENSE.

APOSELLANUM OF ST. THOMAS (Saint-Thomas of Aposilla, near Ravenna), monastery of the Camaldolese Order in the diocese of Ravenna, where Pope Clement II died.—Privilege of Nicholas II, 1060, CXLIII, 1339.

APPANIS (of), monastery situated in the valley of Susa. It was annexed under one abbot to Novalesa by Emperor Lothair in 825, CIV, 1151.

APRI (St.) OF TOUL (Saint-Èvre of Toul), monastery built in the suburb of Toul before the reign of Chlothar, 622, and later made illustrious by Abbot Frotharius in 844, LXXI, 640; CVI, 863.—It was restored by Leo IX while he exercised the episcopal office there, in 1030, CXLIII, 582.—Privilege of the same pope, 583.—Privilege of Bishop Pibo, 1072, CLVII, 419.—Letter of Paschal II concerning the dispute with Molesme, 1115, CLXIII, 380.—Privilege of Alexander III, 1179, CC, 1252.—Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1203, CCXV, 271.—Privilege of the same, 1074.

AQUA-BELLA OF ST. MARY (Our Lady of Aiguebelle, diocese of Saint-Jean-de-Maurienne in Savoy), monastery of the Cistercian Order, not to be confused with Aquabella in the diocese of Tricastin.—Letters of Innocent III, 1104, CCXV, 191, 815; CCXVII, 206.

AQUA FORMOSA (of) (Aiguebelle, former diocese of Castro in Apulia, Naples), monastery of the Cistercian Order, sprung from Clairvaux and built in 1200.—Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1203, CCXV, 250.

AQUENSE (Aix-en-Provence), monastery of canons regular of St. Augustine, of which Alberic, author of the *History of Jerusalem*, was a monk, 1125, CLXVI, 387.—Privilege of Celestine II, 1144, CLXXIX, 788.—Letter of Clement III, 1188, CCIV, 1378.

AQUENSE (Acqua, bishopric in the Papal States), college of canons [Col. 1017], whose possessions Adrian IV confirmed by privilege in 1156, CLXXXVIII, 1480.

AQUISCINCTIENSE or AQUICINENSE OF ST. ANDREW (Saint-André of Anchin, diocese of Arras), monastery founded in Flanders in 1079, while Gerard of Cambrai was bishop, by the distinguished men Siger of Looz and Walter, CXLIX, 270. The first abbot was Waldric; the Venerable Gerland also flourished there in 1117. Charter of Bishop Gerard II concerning the foundation of this monastery, 1092, CL, 1381.—Privilege of Paschal II, 1112, CLXIII, 302.—Letter of Innocent II to Abbot Alvisus, 1131, CLXXIX, 93.—Letter of Alexander III concerning injuries inflicted upon the monastery, 1171, CC, 147.—Letter of the same against the abbot, 899.

AQUILEIENSIS (Aquileia in Friuli, Italy), nunnery founded by St. Nicetas, bishop, in 458, LII, 960.

AQUILEIENSIS OF ST. MARY (Saint Mary of Aquileia), nunnery built by Engelbert, count of Gorizia, and the bishop of Trieste, whose property Innocent III confirmed in 1199, CCXIV, 664.

COLLEGE OF CANONS OF AQUILEIA (canons of the Church of Aquileia), congregation whose possessions and privileges Alexander III confirmed in 1176, CC, 1077.—Privilege of Lucius III, 1184, CCI, 1300.

AQUISGRANENSE OF ST. ADELBERT (Saint-Adalbert of Aachen), monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, founded by St. Emperor Henry II in 1018, CXL, 340.

AQUISGRANENSE OF ST. MARY (Our Lady of Aachen), monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, whose possessions Adrian IV confirmed by privilege in 1158, CLXXXVIII, 1574.

AQUISTRENSE OF ST. MARY (Our Lady of Guîtres, diocese of Bordeaux), monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded before 1108 near Libourne and subject to Cluny. Privilege of Alexander III, 1171, CC, 727.

ARCE (de), see ST. ANDREW.

ARCHANGELI DE MACHARI (Convent of the Holy Archangel at Machari, near Naples), monastery mentioned by St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1073.

ARCHANGELI DE MORFISA (the Holy Archangel of Morphisa, in Naples), monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built within Naples, whose goods and privileges Paschal II confirmed in 1116, CLXIII, 404.

ARDENA (in) OF ST. MARY (Our Lady of Ardennes, diocese of Bayeux), monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, founded by Ailulf of Falaise and his wife Asseline; Gilbert, disciple of St. Norbert, was its first abbot, 1138. Privilege of Pope Lucius II, 1144, CLXXIX, 869.—Letters of Innocent III, 1203, CCXV, 256, 594.

ARDURELLENSE (Ardorel, diocese of Albi, Tarn), monastery of the Cistercian Order, built by Viscountess Cecilia, daughter of Bernard Aton, in 1114; she granted it to the Cadouin monastery of Bonneval under Adrian IV in 1159, CLXXVII, 1599.

ARELATENSIS OF ST. MARY (Nuns of St. Mary at Arles), nunnery established by St. Aurelian, bishop, in 554, LXXI, 859.—Theodechild, widow of Charibert, brother of King Guntram, was confined there by Guntram’s order in 564, LXXI, 291.

ARELATENSIS OF ST. CAESARIUS (Saint-Césaire of Arles, also called the Great Monastery), nunnery founded by St. Caesarius, bishop; its first abbess was his sister Caesaria, about 501–542. Bull of Celestine III concerning reform of its monastery, 1194, CCVI, 1032.

ARELATENSE OF ST. HONORATUS (Saint-Honorat of Arles), monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, to whose abbot Innocent III wrote concerning a certain matrimonial case in 1209, CCXVI, 66.

AREMARENSE OF SS. PETER AND PAUL (Saint-Pierre of Moutier-Ramey, diocese of Troyes), monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded in 837 by Aremar, priest, and Aledran, count of Troyes. Charter of Hugh, count of Troyes, 1122, CLXXXV, 1477.—Nicholas was first a monk of Aremar before going to Clairvaux and becoming St. Bernard’s secretary; he flourished in 1175, CXVI, 1589.—Testimony of the abbot in the succession case between the counts of Champagne and Erard of Brienne, heard under Innocent III in 1213, CCXVI, 979.

ARENULENSE OF THE HOLY SPIRIT (Convent of the Holy Spirit at the Little Arenas), monastery whose location is not sufficiently known to us; but from the kind of tribute imposed upon it by Innocent III, it seems to be situated near Constantinople, 1198, CCXIV, 117.

ARETINENSE (Arezzo in the Florentine countryside), monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, whose goods and privileges Pope Stephen X confirmed in 1057, CXLIII.

ARETINENSE OF ST. MICHAEL (Saint-Michel of Arezzo), monastery of the Order of St. Benedict and of the Camaldolese, to which Clement III granted a privilege in 1188, CCIV, 1283.

[Col. 1018] ARETINENSE OF SS. FLORA AND LUCILLA (Saint-Flora of Arezzo, Tuscany), monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built before 1133, in which year Innocent II confirmed it by privilege, CLXXIX, 199. Privileges of Alexander III, 1179, CC, 1201; of Lucius III, 1183, CCI, 1208.

ARGENTINENSE OF ST. MARY (Our Lady of Strasbourg), monastery endowed by King Dagobert II in 675, LXXXVII, 1305.—Precept of Carloman, 769, XCVI, 1575.—Testament of Remigius of Strasbourg, 778, XCVI, 1582.

ARGENTOLIENSIS OF ST. MARY (Our Lady of Argenteuil), nunnery to which Gisela, wife of Charlemagne, and her daughter Theodrada withdrew in 814.—The Saviour’s tunic is believed to have been kept there. This monastery later passed to the Benedictines of St. Maurus, LXXI, 712.—Donation of Childebert III, 697, LXXXVIII, 1095.—Charter of Abbot Einhard, 824, CIV, 604.—It was restored to the monastery of St. Denis by Louis the Pious and Lothair in 825, CIV, 1142.—Letter of Honorius by which the monastery was restored to St. Denis, 1129, CLXVI, 1296.—Diploma of Cardinal Matthew on the same subject, 1129, CLXXIII, 1265.—Privilege of Innocent II on the same matter, 1130, CLXXIX, 64.

ARGONENSE OF ST. PAUL (Saint-Paul-en-Argonne), monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by Bishop Geoffrey, whose goods and privileges Pope Honorius II confirmed, year [not given], 1237.

ARGONA (in) OF ST. MARY (Our Lady in Argonne, Châlons-sur-Marne), monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, founded by Geoffrey, bishop of Châlons; charter of foundation, 1134, CLXXIII, 1395.

ARIDAGAMANTIA (of), or DE ARVASIA, otherwise called ARIENSE (Arouaise, diocese of Arras), monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, built in 1090. Letter of Alexander III concerning the return of the head of St. James, 1168, CC, 544.—Privilege of Urban III, 1186, CCII, 1399; of Celestine III, 1197, CCVI, 1211.

ARIMINENSE OF SS. ANDREW AND THOMAS (Saint-André of Rimini, Italy), monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, endowed with privileges by St. Gregory the Great at the end of the sixth century, LXXV, 321.—Letter of St. Gregory the Great to the abbot of St. Andrew, LXXVII, 580.

ARMETWAYTENSIS OF ST. MARY (St. Mary of Armathwaite, Cumberland, England), nunnery of the Order of St. Benedict, to which King William, called the Conqueror, made certain gifts about 1085, CXLIX, 1359.

ARNESBURGENSE (Arensberg, in the Westphalian district), monastery situated in Thuringia on the Weser, built in the eighth century; later restored about 1140 by the nephew of Frederick, count of Westphalia, and transferred to the Premonstratensian Order, LXXXIX, 742 note.

ARNOLDSTEINENSE (Arnoldstein, Carinthia, Bavaria), monastery of the Cistercian Order, built by Otto, bishop of Bamberg, about 1107, CLXXIII, 1279–1280.

ARNSTEINENSE or OF ST. MARY AND ST. NICHOLAS (Arnstein in the diocese of Trier), monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, founded by Count Louis in 1139, which foundation Archbishop Adalbero confirmed. Privilege of Innocent II, 1142, CLXXIX, 597.

ARNULFI-AUGIENSE (Schwarzach, former diocese of Strasbourg), monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, situated in Lower Alsace, to which Rothard made many donations in 718. Louis the Pious transferred the monastery to Ortenau in 826, LXXXVIII, 1314.

ARNULFI (St.) OF METZ (Saint-Arnould of Metz), monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by St. Arnulf, bishop of Metz, in honour of the Holy Apostles in 625, LXXI, 639, 644.—Charter of donation of Chilperic II, 717, LXXXVIII, 1128.—Charter of Pippin and his wife Plectrude, by which they cede Nugaretum, 691, 1219. Likewise of Duke Drogo, 1221; of Godfrey, 1222; of Hugh, son of Drogo and priest, 1262. Donation of Hildegard, wife of Charlemagne, 783, XCVIII, 971.—Diploma of Charlemagne, 973. Privilege of Bishop Robert, 916, CXXXII, 531.—Abbot John flourished here, CXXXVII, 211.—On this monastery’s foundation, by an anonymous tenth-century author, CXXXVIII, 189. Privilege of St. Leo IX, 1049, CXLIII, 781.—Abbot William, 1090, CL, 871.—Charter of Pibo, bishop of Toul, 1073, CLVII, 421.—Privilege of Pope Paschal II, 1107, CLXIII, 210.—CLXIII, 210.—Of Celestine III, 1192, CCVI, 935.

ARROASIA, see above ARIDAGAMANTIA.

ARULENSE OF ST. MARY (Arles-sur-Tech, Roussillon), monastery in the diocese of Elne, in the valley of Aperi-Monasterii (Apremont), founded in the eighth century. Louis the Pious took it under his protection in 820, CIV, 1097.—Privilege of Pope Sergius IV, 1011, CXXXIX, 1517.

ARZILLA (of) ST. MARY (Saint Mary of Arzilla, diocese of Fano in the duchy of Urbino), monastery of the Camaldolese Order, founded by the nobleman Valerius, count of Fano, shortly before 1197, when Celestine III confirmed it by privilege, CCVI, 1230.

[Col. 1019] ASCHOVIENSE OF ST. MARY (perhaps Aschbach near Wissembourg, Lower Alsace), monastery which Remigius, bishop of Strasbourg, subjected to the religious house of St. Mary in 778, XCVI, 1582.

ASINDENSIS OF THE HOLY TRINITY (Holy Trinity of Essen, diocese of Cologne), nunnery of the Order of St. Benedict, rebuilt by Abbess Hatwig under Emperor Odo in 946. Privilege of Pope Agapetus, CXXXIII, 893.

ASMANTIA (of) CELL, or priory (Amance, Meurthe), founded by Countess Sophia in the eleventh century. Privilege by which Pibo, bishop of Toul, confirmed its foundation, 1076, CLVII, 422, 426.

ASMIALDENSIS OF ST. MARGARET (Saint Margaret of Asmialde, Finland, Russia), nunnery of the Order of St. Augustine, whose goods Alexander III confirmed in 1178, CC, 1193.

ASMINGIENSIS CELL (Amelange in Lorraine), small monastery subject to the abbey of St. Michael at Verdun. Letter of Eugenius III to the bishop of Metz, that Count Henry of Salm should restore this cell, 1152, CLXXX, 1524.

ASPACENSIS CELL (small convent of Aspach, diocese of Regensburg), dependent on the bishop of Bamberg, CLXXIII, 1280.

ASPRENSE (Apremont, Haute-Saône), monastery to which relics were brought from the monastery of Jumièges, on which it depended, when the Northmen were ravaging everything with fire, CXLIX, 134.

ASTENSE OF ST. PERPETUUS (Saint-Perpétue of Asti, Montferrat, Italy), monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, especially made illustrious by St. Bruno, its abbot, later bishop of Segni in the Roman Campagna, in 1079 under Gregory VII, CLXIV, 99, 103.—Oddo, monk of Asti, flourished under Blessed Bruno, CLXV, 1141.—Privilege of Alexander III, 1169, CC, 599.—Of Lucius III, 1182, CCI, 1165.

ATHANASII (St.) MONASTERY, see MONTE SANCTO.

ATHANENSE OF ST. MARTIAL or ST. AREDIUS (Saint-Yrieix, diocese of Limoges), monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded in the seventh century by Aldeon, brother of St. Eligius, and restored by Alduin, bishop of Limoges, in 1012. Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1206, CCXV, 1099.

ATHENACENSE OF ST. MARTIN (Ainay near Lyons), monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in the sixth century on the very site where the holy martyrs of Lyons had suffered, LXXI, 751.—Privilege of Paschal II, 1107, CLXIII, 205.—Letter of Innocent III to the abbot concerning certain surreptitious letters, 1198, CCXIV, 190.

ATREBATENSE OF ST. VEDAST (Saint-Vaast of Arras), monastery of the Order of St. Benedict. It was first called Nobiliacense after the place where it had been built by St. Aubert in 534, CI, 678, 679; 131.—Privilege of Pope John VIII, CXXVI, 658.—Abbot Ledwin flourished in 1040, CXLI, 1333.—The same abbot restored this monastery from its foundations, ibid.—Letter of Paschal II concerning the dispute of this monastery with the clergy of Arras, to be settled, 1113, CLXIII, 335.—Letter of Innocent II to Abbot Walter concerning obedience due to the bishop, 1131, CLXXIX, 98.—Admonitory letter of Adrian IV to the abbot and brethren of St. Vedast, 1157, CLXXXVIII, 1545.—Alexander III, 1164, CC, 322, 623, 1095, 1245.—Privileges of Innocent III, 1198, CCXIV, 122, 143; 1206, CCXV, 934, 938, 1104, 1509; CCXVI, 64, 494, 717; CCXVII, 181, 102, 266.

ATREBATENSE OF ST. MARY (Our Lady of Arras), monastery of canons of the Order of St. Augustine, whose privileges and possessions were confirmed by Bishop Vindicianus in 680, LXXXVIII, 1200; CXLIX, 130.—Letter of Eugenius III concerning ecclesiastical offices, 1152, CLXXX, 1578.

AUBERTI or AUTBERTI (St.) OF ARRAS, monastery built within the city walls according to the Order of St. Augustine by St. Autbert, bishop, 580, CXLIX, 128.

AUBECHIENSE (Auchy-les-Moines), formerly a nunnery built by the nobleman Adalscarius in the diocese of Cambrai about 700; later restored as a Benedictine monastery by Bishop Gerard in 950. Privilege of Urban II, 1095, CLI, 434.

AUDARDI (St.) (Saint-Audard, near Montauban), monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose abbot complained to Eugenius III of injuries inflicted on him by the count of Toulouse. Letter of Eugenius, 1145, CLXXX, 1051.

AUDOENI (St.) OF ROUEN (Saint-Ouen of Rouen), formerly St. Peter’s monastery; it changed its name when it received the body of St. Audoenus, bishop. This celebrated abbey of the Order of St. Benedict produced many learned men, among whom John the deacon is numbered, 659, LXXI, 670; charter of King Dagobert, LXXX, 430; LXXXVII, 473.—Privilege of Pope Eugenius [Col. 1020] II, 827, CXXXIX, 985.—The monk Theodoric flourished in 1090, CL, 1187.—John the deacon, monk of St. Audoenus, CLXII, 1151.—Privilege of Alexander III, 1180, CC, 1277.—On the first abbots of this monastery after its restoration, CCII, 1314.

AUDOMARENSE (Saint-Omer, Pas-de-Calais), monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, whose possessions and rights St. Gregory VII confirmed in 1085, CXLVIII, 728.—Canon Lambert flourished in 1030, CLXIII, 1003.—Privilege of Innocent II, 1142, CLXXIX, 623; of Adrian IV, 1158, CLXXXVIII, 1589.

AUDOMARENSE, see SITHIVENSE.

AUGIENSE or AUGIAE DIVITIS (Reichenau, or Auge, diocese of Basel; *ow* or *au* means “meadow” in German), monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, called “Rich” because of its innumerable possessions. This abbey was also called Sint Leo Zesavia after the noble Swabian Sintlaus, governor of Germany, who gave land to St. Abbot Pirmin, its founder; it is situated in the diocese of Basel.—Diploma of Louis the Pious to Bishop Hetto, 816, CX, 767; Abbot Haito or Hotto, CXV, 10; the monk Ermanric, CXVI, 23; Purchard, 1003, CXXXIX, 350.—Berno was chosen abbot under the protection of Emperor Henry in 1014, CXLII, 1099.—Hermann the Lame flourished in 1054, CXLIII, 9.—Gregory VII excommunicated the despoilers of its monastery in 1074, CXLVII, 354.—Privilege of Innocent II, 1140, CLXXIX, 501.—Letter of Innocent III to the abbots, 1207, CCV, 1286.

AUGUSTINI (St.), see CANTUARIENSE.

AUGUSTENSE OF ST. URSUS (Saint-Urse of Aosta, in Tarentaise), monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, to which Innocent II, at Bishop Herbert’s request, granted a privilege in 1132, CLXXIX, 166, 248.—Privilege of Lucius II, 1144, CLXXIX, 834; of Eugenius III, 1146, CLXXX, 1133, 1496; of Adrian IV, 1158, CLXXXVIII, 1596; of Alexander III, 1162, CC, 131; of Lucius III, 1183, CCI, 1228, 1257, 1303; of Urban III, 1187, CCII, 1477.

AUGUSTENSE OF THE HOLY CROSS (Holy Cross of Augsburg, Bavaria), monastery whose provost Innocent III addressed concerning the establishment of a bishopric on the island of Chiemsee, 1213, CCXVI, 868.

AUGUSTENSE OF ST. MARY (Our Lady of Augsburg), monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, whose goods Celestine II confirmed by privilege in 1143, CLXXIX, 771.

AUGUSTODUNENSE OF ST. SYMPHORIAN (Saint-Symphorien of Autun), monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded in the fifth century by Bishop Euphronius. Its invaders were excommunicated by order of John XIII. It was given to Fleury for reform in 971, CXXXV, 987.

AUGUSTODUNENSE OF ST. MARTIN (Saint-Martin of Autun), monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, rebuilt by Emperor Charles; Pope Nicholas II granted many privileges to its abbot Gregory in 1059, CXLIII, 1327.—Privilege of Alexander III, 1165, CC, 346.

AUGUSTODUNENSE OF ST. JOHN (Saint-Jean-le-Grand of Autun), monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded about 589. Since it had fallen into the greatest decay, Innocent III wrote to the bishop and to certain neighbouring abbots concerning the restoration and reform of this monastery in 1198, CCXIV, 201.

AUGUSTODUNENSE OF ST. MARY (Saint Mary of Autun), nunnery founded by Bishop Siagrius, whose dissensions St. Gregory, bishop of Tours, recounts about 535, LXXII, 519.—Letter of St. Gregory the Great to the abbess, LXXVII, 1265.—Charter of Ansebert, 696, LXXXVIII, 1231.

AUREAVALLE (DE) OF ST. PETER (Saint-Pierre of Orval, diocese of Trier), monastery first of the Order of St. Benedict, then of St. Augustine, and finally of the Cistercian Order, founded in 1070 by Albert, count of Chiny. The origin of this monastery is described, XCVIII, 812, 816. Privilege of Innocent II, 1141, CLXXIX, 538.

AUREAVALLE OF ST. PETER (Saint-Pierre of Airvault, Poitou), monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, built by Viscountess Hildegard in 975.—Privileges of Paschal II, 1112, CLXIII, 308; of Innocent II, 1134, CLXXIX, 215; of Innocent III, 1198, CCXIV, 440.

CANONS OF THE HOLY CROSS OF ORLÉANS. Privilege of Adrian IV, 1159, CLXXXVIII, 1603.

AURELIANENSE, see ANIANENSE, SS. EVURTIUS, MAXIMINUS, and ST. SAMSON.

AURIENSIS OF ST. PETER (Saint-Pierre of Caldas de Orense, Galicia, Spain), monastery concerning which Innocent III wrote about the deposition of an intruded abbot, 1212, CCXVI, 607.

AURILIANENSIS (Origny-Sainte-Benoîte on the Aisne, Picardy), nunnery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded in 854 by the queen, wife of Charles the Bald. Innocent III’s letter to the abbess, given [Col. 1021], forbids the promising of benefices not vacant, 1210, CCXVI, 388, 413, 414.

AURILIACENSE OF ST. GERALD (Saint-Géraud of Aurillac, Cantal), monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded at the end of the ninth century by Blessed Gerald, count of Aurillac, CXXXIII, 971, note.—The illustrious Gerbert, later pope, was educated in this monastery. Letter of Alexander III, 1165, CC, 389, 390.—Privilege of Innocent III, 1198, CCXVII, 20.

AUTISSIODORENSE, see ANTISSIODORENSIS.

HOUSE OF THE TEMPLARS OF AUXIMENSIS, in Innocent III, 1211, CCXVI, 388, 414.

AVELLANENSE or OF THE FOUNTAIN OF AVELLANA (Fonte Avellana, Campania, Italy), monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded in the wilderness by Ludulf, formerly called St. Andrew’s and now Holy Cross, near Catria of Sitria in Italy, 1009, CLXIV, 22 and following.—Relationship of the Camaldolese and Avellanites, ibid., 27, 43.—Life of St. Rodulf, CXLIV, 1007.—Abbot Guido, called of Arezzo, flourished there in 1034, CXLI, 375.—Privileges of Innocent II, 1129, CLXXIX, 472; of Lucius II, 1144, ibid., 856; of Eugenius III, 1149, CLXXX, 1383; of Clement III, 1189, CCIV, 1435.

AVENACENSIS (Avenay, diocese of Reims, Marne), nunnery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in Aurea Vallis by the blessed Gombert and his wife Bertha, about 660; he is numbered among the saints. Letter of William, archbishop of Reims, concerning the election of abbesses, 1200, CCIX, 359.

AVENDI or ABENDI, see ABENDENSE.

AVENIONENSE, see SS. ANDREW or MICHAEL IN ANDAON.

AVENIONENSE OF ST. RUFUS (Saint-Ruf near Avignon), monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, founded about 1090 by Bishops Rostagnus and Ghibelline and Abbot Arbert. Privilege of Urban II issued at Troyes, 1095, CLI, 427. It was later transferred to Valence (see ST. RUFUS). Privilege of Pope Paschal II, 1113, CLXIII, 336.—Oldegarius, abbot, was elected archbishop of Barcelona, 111 [as printed], ibid., 405.

AVENIONENSIS CANONRY, established in the time of Urban II; the same pope confirmed its goods and possessions by privilege in 1095, CLI, 426.

AVERBODIENSE OF ST. MARY (St. Mary of Averbode, diocese of Augsburg), monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, built by Count Arnulf shortly before 1139; in that year Innocent II, granting Abbot Andrew’s request, confirmed its possessions, CLXXIX, 445.

AVERSANUM OF ST. LAWRENCE (Saint-Laurent of Aversa, between Naples and Capua), monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, dependent on the Apostolic See. On account of his praiseworthy administration, Urban II granted its abbot Guarin the use of mitre and ring in 1092, CLI, 346.—Privilege of Lucius III, 1183, CCI, 1188; of Celestine III, 1194, CCVI, 1029.—Letter of Innocent III, 1202, CCIV, 1181.

AVITI (St.) OF CHÂTEAUDUN (Saint-Avit, near Châteaudun, diocese of Chartres), monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by King Chlothar I in 521 and later destroyed by the Northmen. Wanelo, treasurer of St. Martin of Tours, rebuilt it and introduced nuns there. Letter of Innocent III concerning the election of an abbess, 1210, CCXVI, 263.

AVITI (St.) OF ORLÉANS (Saint-Avit of Orléans, Loiret), monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, which some wrongly confuse with Micy; it was built in 530, LXXI, 901 note, and is mentioned by St. Fortunatus of Poitiers in the *Life of Leobinus*, LXXXVIII, 549.

AZAICO (of) (Azay-le-Brûlé, near Saint-Maixent, Deux-Sèvres), priory dependent on St. Maixent, which, through the perverse will of abbots, fell into lay hands—an occurrence emphatically censured by Innocent III in 1198, CCXIV, 56.

BACKNANGENSE OF ST. PANCRAS (Saint-Pancras of Backnang, Württemberg), monastery endowed by Margrave Herman, in whose church the margraves of Baden were buried; privilege of Pope Paschal II, 1116, CLXIII, 415.

BAIENSI ISLAND (of) (convent of the island of Baya, on the coast of Sicily), monastery of the Order of St. Benedict near Sicily, whose abbot Stephen, formerly patriarch of Antioch, was appointed under Pope Agatho in 676, CXXVIII, 811.

BAINSONENSE OF ST. PETER (Saint-Pierre of Bagneaux or Bagneux, former diocese of Soissons), monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by the parents of Urban II and granted by him to the monastery of Cluny in 1096, CLI, 450.

BAJOCENSE, see ST. VIGOR.

BALGENTIACENSE OF ST. MARY AND ST. GENTIAN (Our Lady [Col. 1022] of Beaugency on the Loire, Loiret), monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded about the end of the seventh century and transferred to the canons of St. Augustine in 1104. Their abbot Joscelin obtained a privilege from Pope Innocent II in 1140, CLXXIX, 505.

BALMENSE (La Baume, diocese of Besançon), ancient monastery built in the sixth century, now entirely ruined, LXXI, 1015.—It was subject to Cluny; Berno, abbot of this monastery, was raised to the government of Cluny and became Odo’s instructor. Privilege of Pope Urban II, 1089, CLI, 311.—Decree of Eugenius III depriving the monastery of the title of abbey as punishment for a most serious crime committed against Abbot Osbert, 1147, CLXXX, 1227.—Likewise Clement III asserted the monastery’s subjection to Cluny in 1188, CCIV, 1299.—Letter of Innocent III revoking all alienations and confirming its subjection to the Cluniacs, 1198, CCIV, 103; 1205, CCXV, 632.

BALMENSIS NUNNERY (La Baume-les-Nonains, diocese of Besançon), of the Order of St. Benedict, situated between Besançon and Montbéliard, seventh century, LXXI, 1015 note.—The testament of St. Ansegisus mentions this nunnery, 833, CV, 747.

BALMENSE OF ST. ROMANUS (Saint-Romain of La Baume, otherwise La Baume-les-Moines, in the Jura, diocese of Lyons), monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose foundation is referred to the fifth century, rebuilt in 926 by St. Bermundus, abbot of Gigny. Letter of Innocent III concerning a dispute with the bishop of Autun, 1199, CCXIV, 619, 852.

BALNENSE OF ST. MARY (St. Mary of the Baths, diocese of Arezzo, Italy), monastery in Emilia, in the diocese of Arezzo, founded by John, bishop of Arezzo, and confirmed by Pope Adrian II in 871, CXXIX, 1015.—Privilege of Innocent II, 1136, CLXXIX, 283.

BALNEOLENSE OF ST. MARY OF CLAIRVAUX (Our Lady of Clairvaux at Bagnolo near Milan), monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded by Anselm Archynta in 1135; Innocent granted it the monastery of St. Peter of Cerreto in 1139, CLXXIX, 486.—Privilege of Eugenius, 1148, CLXXX, 1354.

BALNEOLENSE (perhaps Bagnaux near Donzy, Nièvre), monastery endowed and perhaps founded by Hervé, count of Nevers, and the noble Countess Matilda, whose goods Pope Innocent III confirmed in 1211, CCXVI, 548.

BALNEOLENSE OF ST. STEPHEN (Saint-Étienne of Bagnolles or Banyoles, near Bezaudun, diocese of Girona, Catalonia), monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by Abbot Bonitus; Louis the Pious later granted it to Abbot Mercoral at the request of Count Rampo, 815, CIV, 1024.—Privileges of Pope Benedict VIII, 1017, CXXXIX, 1608; of Urban II, 1096, CLI, 474; of Alexander III, 1175, CC, 1015.

BAMBERGENSE OF ST. MICHAEL (Saint-Michel of Bamberg, Franconia), monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, to which St. Emperor Henry II granted thirteen estates in 1015, CXL, 320; CLXXIII, 1280.—Charter of Otto, ibid., 1333.—On the donation of the chapel of St. Faith, ibid., 1347.—On a new donation, 1349.—Letter of the abbot to St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 284.—Privilege of Lucius III, 1184, CCI, 1275.

BAMBERG, ST. JAMES (Saint-Jacques of Bamberg), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, built outside the walls by Bishops Hermann and Otto, from 1071 to 1108, CLXXIII, 1280.

BAMBERG, SS. KILIAN AND GEORGE (Saint-Kilian or Saint-Georges of Bamberg), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, to which Emperor St. Henry, its founder, granted a large estate called Fürth, situated in the district of Nordgau, in 1087, CXL, 276.—Another gift by the same, 277, 278.—It is discussed, CLXXIII, 1281.

BANNOCHORENSE (Banchor or Bangor, in Wales), a British monastery which existed before the arrival of St. Augustine, and whose abbot Dinoth answered this arriving Augustine on behalf of the bishops, in 601, LXXX, 21.—This monastery flourished greatly in Bede’s time and supported 2,000 monks, XCV, 83.—There St. Malachy, the holy abbot whose life St. Bernard of Clairvaux wrote, had established an oratory, CLIX, 161 note.

BANT, ST. MARY (Banti or Bante, in Apulia, Naples), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by Duke Roger and his brother Bohemond near Acherontia (Cirenza) in Apulia; Ursio was its first abbot. Pope Urban II consecrated this monastery in 1088, CLI, 35.—Privilege of Paschal II, 1103, CLXIII, 114.

BANTH, ST. LAWRENCE (Saint-Laurent of Banthz or Banthen, in Bavaria), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by the distinguished woman Alberada in 1071 and granted to the church of Bamberg; it was later reformed by St. Otto, bishop, [Col. 1023] CLXXIII, 1284.—Charter concerning the foundation of this monastery, 1127, CLXXIII, 1340.

BANZA, ST. MARY, a certain Italian monastery whose possessions and privileges St. Gregory VII confirmed in 1075, CXLVIII, 650.

BARAL, ST. GEORGE (Saint-George of Baralles, diocese of Arras), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, founded about 535 by King Clovis and St. Vedastus, bishop of Arras, CXLIX, 129.—The Northmen destroyed it in the ninth century, ibid.

BARBARA ISLAND. See ISLAND.

ST. BARBARA (Sainte-Barbe, in the diocese of Parenzo, Istria), a monastery mentioned in Alexander III’s privilege of 1177, CC, 1101.

ST. BARBARA IN AUGE (Sainte-Barbe-en-Auge, diocese of Lisieux), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, founded in 1128; its subprior Geoffrey flourished near the end of the twelfth century, CCV, 827.

ST. BARBAT, a monastery (Saint-Barbat in the Sabine territory, Papal States), built in the territory of Pollutrium by Raynerius and his wife Engeltrude, and granted to monks of the Order of St. Benedict about 1043. Privilege of Pope Alexander II, by which he attached it to the monastery of Magellanum (Magliano), 1063, CXLVI, 1399.—It was finally made subject to the Vatican Church by Gregory XIII, ibid., note.

BARDESLERA. See BORDESLEJA.

BARCELONA, HOLY CROSS AND ST. EULALIA (Sainte-Croix or Sainte-Eulalie of Barcelona, Spain), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, whose provost Raymond obtained a privilege from Pope Paschal II in 1104, CLXIII, 125.

BARI, MOST HOLY TRINITY, a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose possessions and privileges Pope St. Leo IX confirmed in 1053, CXLIII, 733.

BARI, ALL SAINTS (All Saints Abbey at Bari, Naples), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, apparently founded by Ursus and Elias, bishops of that city, and taken under the protection of Pope Calixtus II in 1123, CLXIII, 1296.—Privilege of Lucius II, 1144, CLXXIX, 911.

BARI, ST. NICHOLAS (Saint-Nicolas of Bari), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by Dukes Roger and Bohemond on the occasion of the translation of St. Nicholas’s relics from the East, under Pope Victor II. Privilege of Paschal II, 1105, CLXIII, 178.

BARISIS, or PARISIS, or FAVEROLLES (Barisis-au-Bois, Pargny, or Faverolles, diocese of Laon), a monastery granted to St. Amand by Queen Innichild, wife of Sigebert, and Childeric, son of Grimoald, about 664, LXXXVII, 313, 1271.—Diploma of Childeric, 661, ibid., 1285.—Of Louis the Pious, 831, CIV, 1193.

BARNOET (Barnoett, diocese of Ely, county of Cambridge, England), a monastery to whose abbot Innocent III entrusted a certain matrimonial case in 1205, CCXV, 593.

ST. BARTHOLOMEW OF NOYON (Saint-Barthélemi of Noyon, Oise), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, built in 1064 by Baldwin, bishop of Noyon. Letter of Innocent III to its abbot, 1206, CCXV, 939.

ST. BARTHOLOMEW OF THE CHARBONNIÈRE (Saint-Barthélemi de la Charbonnière, Lombardy), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, subject to the abbey of St. Mary at Pulsano, mentioned in Alexander III’s privilege of 1177, CC, 1097.

ST. BARTHOLOMEW ON LIPARI ISLAND (Saint-Barthélemi of Lipari, off the coast of Sicily), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, situated near Sicily, to which Urban II granted a privilege in 1091, CLI, 329.

ST. BARTHOLOMEW IN PENNE (Saint-Barthélemi of the diocese of Penne, Naples), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose possessions and privileges Pope Paschal II confirmed in 1116, CLXIII, 412.—Privilege of Innocent II, 1139, CLXXIX, 413.—Of Eugenius III, 1150, CLXXX, 1437.

ST. BARTHOLOMEW IN THE STONE, OF LUCCA (Saint-Barthélemi de La Pierre, at Lucca), a hospital-house concerning whose rector Innocent III wrote in 1208, CCXV, 1464.

BARVENSE, a monastery founded in England by Winfrid, to which he withdrew after his deposition from the episcopate, in 675, XCV, 184.

BASENVILLE (Bassèneville, Calvados), a priory whose immunity Pope Lucius III confirmed in 1183, CCI, 1172.

BASEL, ST. ALBAN (Saint-Alban of Basel), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by the Venerable Bishop Burchard and later confirmed by a privilege of Eugenius III in 1147, CLXXX, 1297.—Privilege of Pope Celestine III, 1196, CCVI, 1148.

ST. BASLE (Saint-Basle of Verzy, diocese of Reims), a monastery founded by Bishop St. Basolus about 570, CXXXV, 97.—Ebbo, bishop of Reims, resided there, [Col. 1024] CXVI, 17.—The beginnings of this monastery are described, CXXXVII, 651.—It was rebuilt in 980, ibid., 659.—Privilege of Urban II to Abbot Burchard, 1090, CLI, 324.—Letter of Alexander III in favour of this monastery, 1172, CC, 832.

BASSEFONTAINE, ST. MARY (Notre-Dame de Bassefontaine, diocese of Troyes), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, built in the forest of Brienne in 1143 by Walter, count of Brienne. Privilege of Eugenius III, 1148, CLXXX, 1343.

BARTHONIENSE (Bath, or the Baths, county of Somerset, England), a monastery founded by St. Elphege near the end of the tenth century, before he became archbishop of Canterbury, CXLIX, 375.—Diploma of William the Conqueror, 1082, CXLIX, 1353.

BAUGÉ or BAUGERIACUM (Baugerais, diocese of Tours, three leagues from Villeloin), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded in 1153. Abbot John wrote to Geoffrey, subprior of St. Barbara, about 1180, CCV, 827, 835, 842.—Charter of gift by Henry II, king of the English, 1178, CCVII, 1161.

BAUMBURG, ST. MARGARET (Sainte-Marguerite of Baumbourg, diocese of Salzburg), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by Count Berengar before 1114, when Paschal II confirmed it by privilege, CLXIII, 363.—Privilege of Honorius II, 1130, CLXVI, 1308.—Of Innocent II, 1139, CLXXIX, 422.—Of Lucius II, 1144, ibid., 933.—Of Clement III, 1189, CCIV, 1447.—Of Celestine III, 1195, CCVI, 1079.

BAUMGARTEN, or BAUMGARTENBERG, or ST. MARY’S ORCHARD (Notre-Dame du Verger, or the abbey of Baumgartenberg, Upper Austria, formerly in the diocese of Strasbourg), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded in 1142 by Otto, count of Raugland. Privilege of Eugenius III, 1151, CLXXX, 1476.—Letter of the same concerning a dispute with the bishop of Passau, 1477. Privilege of Lucius III, 1182, CCI, 1163.—Of Celestine III, 1195, CCVI, 1137.—Letter of Innocent III concerning the church of Westhusen, 1205, CCXV, 564; CCXVI, 24.

ST. BAVO. See GHENT.

BASSAC, ST. STEPHEN (Saint-Etienne of Bassac, Charente), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in the diocese of Saintes, built in the eleventh century by the distinguished man Guardard of Lorich; according to others, by Wardrad, lord of Jarnac, and his wife Rixinde. Letter of Innocent III to the abbot concerning the granting of prebends, CCXVI, 832.

BEAMFLED (Beamfled, diocese of Worcester, England), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in the diocese of Worcester, whose reform St. Oswald, bishop, undertook in 980, CXLVII, 1194.

BEBRONNENSE. See JURA, ST. RAGUIBERT.

BEC, ST. MARY (Le Bec in Normandy), a distinguished monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in the diocese of Rouen, founded in 1042 by the nobleman Herluin, who was also its first abbot; it was especially renowned through his disciples Lanfranc and Anselm, who became archbishops of Canterbury, CL, 21, 31.—Chronicle of Bec, from the beginning to 1467, ibid., 639.—William, its third abbot, 713.—St. Anselm of Bec becomes a monk, 1060, CLVIII, 54.—Privilege of Paschal II, 1102, CLXIII, 90.—Letter of Innocent II to the monks of Bec, 1136, CLXXIX, 258, 633.—Privilege of Eugenius III concerning the church of the Holy Trinity of Beaumont, 1146, CLXXX, 1159, 1225.—Of Alexander III, 1170, CC, 618.—Of Celestine III, 1195, CCVI, 1120.—Privilege of Innocent III, 1203, CCXV, 46; CCXVII, 275.

BECKEREGIENSIS (Becskérek, Hungary), a house of Hospitallers founded by the nobleman of Baze and his wife in 1204, in which year Innocent III honoured it with a privilege, CCXV, 344.

BEDRICHSUERD (St. Edmundsbury, England), a monastery founded by the devout King Sigebert, into which he himself withdrew after renouncing royal power, in 630, XCV, 144.

ST. REMIGIUS OF BELGICA (Saint-Remy of Belge, former diocese of Arras), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, established in a village once very famous, from which, as they say, Belgica took its name, in the eleventh century, CXLIX, 132.

BELINO, ST. BENEDICT (Saint-Benoît of Beliné or Belino, diocese of Aquileia), a monastery in the diocese of Aquileia, built by Patriarch Maxentius in 834; but later it was abandoned because of the harshness of the climate and attached by Gregory XI to the monastery of SS. Gervasius and Protasius at Udine, CVI, 50.

BELLECOMBE, ST. MARY (Notre-Dame de Bellecombe, diocese of Le Puy), a monastery and nunnery of the Cistercian Order, built about 1148 by the lords of Calanson (Chalançon), CCIV, 89.—Letter of Henry, abbot of Clairvaux, 1188, ibid., 230.

BELLEVAUX, ST. PETER (Saint-Pierre of Bellevaux, [Col. 1025] diocese of Besançon), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded in 1119 and endowed by Archbishop Humbert in 1145. Privilege of Innocent II, 1138, CLXXIX, 387.—Likewise of Eugenius III, 1145, CLXXX, 1072.—Letter of Celestine III to its abbot concerning the canonization of St. Peter, bishop of Tarentaise, formerly abbot of Bellevaux, 1191, CCVI, 871.

BELLEVILLE (Belleville-sur-Saône, in the Beaujolais), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, built in 1159 by Humbert, lord of Beaujeu.—Letter of Innocent III permitting it to build oratories, 1198, CCXIV, 121.—The same exempts the monastery from annually providing procuration for the brethren of St. Irenaeus, ibid.—Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1213, CCXVI, 1203.

BELLELAY, ST. IMER (Belleley, diocese of Basel, Switzerland), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, founded in 1140 by Sigenand, provost of Grandval. Privilege of Innocent II, 1142, CLXXIX, 585.—Of Eugenius III, 1148, CLXXX, 1352.—Of Lucius III, 1182, CCI, 1127.

BELLEY (Belley, Ain), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, founded by Bishop William shortly before 1142, when Innocent II honoured it with a privilege, CLXXIX, 604.

BEAULIEU (Eure-et-Loir), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by Cluniac monks with Bishop Ivo’s consent about 1115.—Charter of Ivo, CLXII, 296.

BEAULIEU, ST. MARY (Notre-Dame de Beaulieu-lès-Mans), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, to which Pope Alexander II granted a privilege in 1070, CXLVI, 1355.

BEAULIEU, ST. MARY (Notre-Dame-de-Beaulieu-sur-Aube, Troyes), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, founded by the priests Osbert and Alard near the end of the eleventh century. Privilege of Innocent II, 1131, CLXXIX, 75.—Likewise of Eugenius III, 1147, CLXXX, 1215.

BEAULIEU, HOLY TRINITY (Beaulieu near Loches), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in 1010 by Fulk III, count of Anjou.—Privilege of John XVII, CXXXIX, 1491; likewise of Pope Sergius IV, 1525.—Letter of St. Gregory VII, 1074, CXLVIII, 378.—Privilege of Paschal II, CLXIII, 435.—Of Alexander III, 1173, CC, 911.—Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1198, CCIV, 207.

BEAULIEU (Beaulieu or Bellec, diocese of Bourges), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded on the Dordogne about 840 by Rodulf, bishop of Bourges. Privilege by which Pope Urban II granted it to the monastery of Cluny, 1096, CLI, 468.

NUNNERY OF BELLI LOCI. See PULCHRI LOCI.

BATTLE (Battle, county of Sussex, England), the name given to a monastery founded by William the Conqueror at Hastings in England, in Sussex, in honour of the Holy Trinity and St. Martin, in fulfilment of the vow he had made before the battle by which he obtained the kingdom of Britain, 1064, CXLIX, 1356, 1358.—Letter of Urban III, 1187, CCII, 1499, 1511, 1528.—Letter of Innocent III, 1208, CCXV, 1504.

BEAUMONT (Beaumont, diocese of Tours), a nunnery built near Tours by Hervaeus, treasurer, in the ninth century. It had previously existed under the name St. Mary of Scriniolum, because it was enclosed within the precincts of St. Martin, LXXI, 510.—Decree of Innocent III concerning the immunity of this monastery, 1212, CCXVI, 764.

BELLOVACENSE. See ST. QUINTIN, ST. LUCIAN, ST. JUSTUS, ST. LAWRENCE.

ST. BENEDICT ON THE LOIRE (Saint-Benoît-sur-Loire). See FLEURY.

ST. BENEDICT ON THE PO. See PADOLIRONE.

BENISSONS-DIEU (Bénissons-Dieu, diocese of Lyons, Loire), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, sprung from Clairvaux and built by Louis VII in 1138. It was later enlarged by Guy and Matilda of Forez. Letter of Henry, abbot of Clairvaux, 1188, CCIV, 230.

ST. BENEDICT (Saint-Benoît, diocese of Nepi, Papal States), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, which Innocent III subjected to the monastery of St. Paul Outside the Walls in 1211, CCXVI, 527.

ST. BENEDICT OF SCALOCLA, or SCALOCEHIA (Saint-Benoît of Scalocchia, diocese of Civita Castellana, Papal States), a monastery mentioned in Adrian IV’s privilege of 1158, CLXXXVIII, 1560.

BENEDICTOBURANUM. See BURENSE or BURONENSE.

BENEVENTO, ST. MARY (Notre-Dame of Benevento), a monastery whose church was built by Abbot Gardinone; it obtained a privilege from King Arichis in 769, LXXXVII, 1417.

BENEVENTO, ST. MODESTUS (Saint-Modeste of Benevento), [Col. 1026] a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict whose possessions and rights Celestine III confirmed in 1195, CCVI, 1243.

BENEVENTO, ST. SOPHIA (the convent of St. Sophia at Benevento), a monastery dependent on Monte Cassino, whose possessions and privileges Benedict VIII confirmed in 1022, CXXXIX, 1625.—Privilege of Emperor St. Henry II, CXI, 363.—Of St. Leo IX, 1052, CXLIII, 692.—Of Urban II, 1092, CLI, 341.—Of Paschal II, CLXIII, 75.—Of Calixtus II, 1120, CLXIII, 1186.—Antipope Anacletus’s privileges, 1130, CLXXIX, 719, 728, 729.

BENEVENTO, ST. VINCENT. See VINCENT.

BENEVENTO, ST. SOPHIA, a nunnery (the nuns of St. Sophia at Benevento), or women’s hospice, built by the devout King Ratchis in 774, LXXXVII, 1418.—He endowed it with many gifts, ibid.—Privilege of St. Gregory VII, 1084, CLXIII, 710.—Privilege of Gelasius II, 1118, CLXIII, 493.

BENEVENTO, ST. VICTORINUS NUNNERY (the convent of St. Victorinus at Benevento), of the Order of St. Benedict, whose possessions and privileges Alexander III confirmed in 1166, CC, 479.

ST. BENIGNUS OF DIJON (Saint-Bénigne of Dijon), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine; it is believed to have been founded by that holy bishop in the second century and entrusted to St. Eustasius as its first abbot, LXXI, 860 note.—Gift of the devout woman Goyla, 734, LXXXVIII, 1287.—The devout God-consecrated woman Ermenoara gave the estate of Ruffiacum in 715, when Bobolenus was abbot and Astoricus bishop of Langres, LXXXVIII, 1259.—Diploma of Louis the Pious, 828, CIV, 1171.—Privilege of Pope Benedict VIII, 1012, CXXXIX, 1581, 1629.—St. William becomes abbot, 1031, CXLI, 835.—Annals of St. Benignus of Dijon, CXLI, 875.—Privilege of St. Gregory VII, 1078, CXLVIII, 685.—Letter of Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, on behalf of this monastery, CLVII, 516.—Chronicle of the abbots of St. Benignus, CLXII, 755.—Privilege of Paschal II, 1102, CLXIII, 86.—Of Calixtus II, 1124, CLXIII, 1320.—Letter of Honorius II to Bishop Berard, 1126, CLXVI, 1275.—Charter of Stephen, bishop of Autun, twelfth century, CLXXII, 1309.—Letter of Innocent II, 1132, CLXXIX, 121.—Blessed Aleydis, mother of St. Bernard, was buried in the monastery of St. Benignus about 1106, CLXXXV, 1402.—Privilege of Alexander III, 1177, CC, 1102.—Of Lucius III, 1184, CCI, 1266.—Of Celestine III, 1193, CCVI, 989.—Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1207, 1207, CCXV, 1185.—Concerning the reform of this monastery, 1211, CCXVI, 495.

BERAC, ST. PETER (Saint-Pierre of Berac, canton of Vaud), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded in the diocese of Lausanne by the nobleman Rodulf in 998 and restored by Odilo, abbot of Cluny, in the eleventh century, CXLII, 858.

BERARDINGHO, ST. PETER (Saint-Pierre of Berardingho, in the territory of Siena), a monastery of the Camaldolese Order, whose possessions and rights Urban III took under his protection in 1186, CCII, 1375.

BERBORG (Bewrborg, Ireland), a monastery to whose abbot Innocent III wrote in 1208, CCXV, 1583.

BERCHERSGADONENSE. See BERGHDESGAMENSE.

BERCLAUSE, ST. SAVIOUR (Billy-Berclause on the Deûle), a monastery founded by Abbot Ledwinus not far from Arras and made subject to the monastery of St. Vedastus in the seventh century, CXLIX, 131.

BERCETO, ST. ABUNDIUS, LATER ST. REMIGIUS (Berzeta, duchy of Parma), a monastery on Monte Bardone in Lombardy, enlarged so greatly by King Liutprand in 718 that he may rightly be reckoned its founder, XCV, 668; CXXXV, 70.

BERCHTESGADEN, or BERGHTESGADEN, or BERCHTOLSGADEN, SS. JOHN AND MARTIN (Berchtolsgaden, diocese of Salzburg), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by Counts Berengar and Chuno shortly before 1115, when Paschal II confirmed it by privilege, CLXIII, 368.—Privilege of Calixtus II, 1121, CLXIII, 1206.—Of Innocent II, 1142, CLXXIX, 753.—Of Eugenius III, 1145, CLXXX, 1057.

BERG, ST. MICHAEL (Saint-Michel of Berg or Berghen, Westphalia), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose possessions and rights Eugenius III confirmed by privilege in 1146, CLXXX, 1092.

BERG, ST. MARY (Notre-Dame of Berg in Westphalia), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded by Adolf, count of Cologne, shortly before 1140, when Innocent II confirmed it by privilege, CLXXIX, 502.

BERGAMO, ST. ALEXANDER (St. Alexander of Bergamo, Lombardy), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, established before 1132, when Innocent II confirmed it by privilege, CLXXIX, 136.—Letter of the same concerning the resistance of these canons to their bishop, 1134, CLXXIX, 213, 395, 631.—Of Celestine II, 1143, CLXXIX, 775, [Col. 1027] 809.—Of Lucius II, 1144, 837, 859, 898.—Letter of Eugenius III concerning the disputes of this monastery, 1148, CLXXX, 1100.—Anastasius confirmed Eugenius’s decision, CLXXXVIII, 1058.—Privilege of the same, 1068.—Of Urban III, 1189, CCII, 1549.—Of Clement III, 1188, CCIV, 1414, 1465.

BERGAMO, ST. VINCENT (Saint-Vincent of Bergamo), a monastery of the Augustinian Order, to which Paschal II granted a privilege, CLXIII, 73.—Privilege of Henry II, 1125, CLXVI, 1217.—Of Innocent II, 1140, CLXXIX, 509.—Decree of Eugenius III concerning a dispute with the canons of St. Alexander, 1145, CLXXX, 1059.—Judgment of Pope Anastasius, ibid., CLXXXVII, 1058.—Privilege of Adrian IV, 1156, CLXXXVIII, 1566.—Of Alexander III, 1169, CC, 610.—Of Urban III, 1186, CCII, 1429, 1549, 1550.—Of Clement III, 1190, CCIV, 1465.

BERGAMO, ST. GRATA, a nunnery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded during the pontificate of St. Leo IX. Privileges of Urban III, 1186, CCII, 1440, 1517.

BERINENSIS, BERICINENSIS, or BERCINENSIS, an English nunnery founded by Erchonwald, bishop of London, for his sister Æthelburh; Hilda or Hildelina, and Queen Æthelburh, later retired there, in 675, XCV, 184.

BERNAY, or BERNAC, ST. MARY (Notre-Dame of Bernay, Eure), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded about 1025 by Judith, duchess of Normandy. In 1142 Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, reconciled its abbot with the abbot of Fécamp, to whom he had refused obedience, CCI, 9.—Letter of the same Arnulf, ibid., 92.—Concerning the foundation of this monastery, CCII, 1314.

BERNRIED, ST. MARTIN (Saint-Martin of Bernried, diocese of Augsburg), a monastery of the Augustinian Order, built by Emperor Otto and his wife Adelaide before 1122, when Pope Calixtus II confirmed its possessions, CLXIII, 1257.

SS. BERTHIER AND ATALEN (Saint-Berthier or Berthaire and Saint-Atalen at Bleurville, diocese of Toul), a nunnery built at Bleurville in the diocese of Toul in 1050; Pope St. Leo IX confirmed its possessions and privileges in the same year, CXLIII, 661.

BERTAUCOURT (Bertaucourt-les-Dames, Picardy), a nunnery founded in 1065 by St. Gualbert, abbot of Pontoise. Decree of Alexander III, 1165, CC, 325.

ST. BERTIN. See SITHIU.

BERTANCOURT (Bertancourt, diocese of Amiens), an oratory founded and consecrated with a privilege in 1036 by Bruno, bishop of Toul, later pope, CXLIII, 585.—Later transformed into an abbey: privilege of Eugenius III, 1147, CLXXX, 1268.

BERTANCOURT, ST. MARY (Notre-Dame of Bertancourt, diocese of Amiens), a nunnery built beside the preceding monastery in 1095 by the distinguished women Godelinde and Helewide. It is mentioned in Eugenius III’s privilege of 1147, CLXXX, 1268.

BESSE, ST. JAMES (Saint-Jacques of Besse or Bexia, diocese of Vercelli), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by Bishop Raynerius; Innocent II took its possessions and privileges under his protection in 114[?], CLXXIX, 521.

BETHLEHEM. See FERRARA.

BETHLEHEMITE MONASTERIES frequented by St. Jerome and John Cassian, XLIX, 9.

BÈZE (Bèze, diocese of Langres), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded in the diocese of Langres, on the river Bèze, by Amalaric, duke of Burgundy, who gave it his own son Waldalenus as abbot, LXXI, 643 note.—The possessions of Duke Adalric were conveyed to this monastery by King Theuderic in 677, LXXXVII, 1324.—Charter of Abbess Adalsinda, LXXXVIII, 1166.—It was ravaged in 763, LXXXVIII, 1167.—Diploma of Emperor Lothair, 830, LXXXVIII, 1186.—Charter of Bruno, bishop of Langres, 1008, CXXXIX, 1539.—Privilege of Pope St. Leo IX, CXLIII, 768.—Chronicle of Bèze, by the monk John, CLXII, 861.—Privilege of Paschal II, 1145, CLXIII, 142.—Letter of Innocent III concerning the restoration of this monastery, 1198, CCXIV, 189.

BEYRON, ST. MARY (St. Mary of Beyron or Baron, Swabia), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by the nobleman Peregrinus before 1130, when Honorius II confirmed this foundation, CLXVI, 1312.

BIBURG, ST. MARY (St. Mary of Biburg, diocese of Regensburg), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, acquired by Otto, bishop of Bamberg, about 1132, CLXXIII, 1279, 1309.—Privileges of Innocent II, 1139, CLXXIX, 397, 427.—Letter of Adrian IV, 1158, CLXXXVIII, 1601.

BIFURCO, ST. BENEDICT (St. Benedict of Bifurco, [Col. 1028] on the Italian side of the Alps), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, which Emperor Henry II gave to St. Romuald, founder of the Camaldolese, in 1022, CXL, 362.—Privilege of Calixtus II, 1124, CLXIII, 1318.

BISENSIS NUNNERY, in the diocese of Toledo, founded by St. Ildefonsus about 635, XCVI, 49.

BISULDUN, ST. PETER (St. Peter of Bezaudun, diocese of Girona, Catalonia), a monastery founded by Miro, bishop of Girona, and granted to the Roman Church by his successor Gausbert; privilege of Pope Benedict VII, 979, CXXXVII, 334.—Of Benedict VIII, CXXXIX, 1613.

BISULDUN, SS.
