MICHAEL AND GENESIUS (Saint-Michel or Saint-Giniès of Bezaudun), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in the diocese of Girona (Girona, on the borders of Catalonia), built in 998 by Bernard, count of Bisuldun, and confirmed by a privilege of Gregory V, CXXXVII, 924.—Likewise of Benedict VIII, CXXXIX, 1606.

BISULDUN, ST. STEPHEN. See above, BALNEOLENSE.

BITURICENSE. See ST. SULPICIUS.

BOURGES, ST. LAWRENCE (the nuns of St. Lawrence at Bourges), a nunnery of the Benedictine Order, probably to be assigned to the time of St. Sulpicius, although its foundation is attributed to Charlemagne, LXXX, 582 note.

BIVORENSE, a monastery whose location appears to be in Lombardy, to which Pope John XII granted a privilege in 963, CXXXIII, 1036.

BLACHERNAE, ST. MARY OF THE LITTLE PALACE (Sainte-Marie de Palatiole, near Ravenna), a monastery built in the old palace of King Odoacer by Abbot Agnellus in 842, CVI, 430.—In the tenth century it was attached to the monastery of St. Paul within the walls of Ravenna, CVI, 442.

WHITE LAUDE, ST. MARY (Notre-Dame de Laude or de la Bruyère, diocese of Coutances), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, founded by Richard de la Haye in 1137.—Charter of Richard, CCVII, 1165.—Diploma of confirmation by Henry II, king of England, 1157, CCVII, 1166.

BLANDIN, ST. PETER (Blandin or Blandenberg near Ghent), a monastery of the Benedictine Order, built by St. Amand in 653; Pope Alexander II threatens its invaders with excommunication in 1067, CXLVI, 1321.—Privilege of Pope Paschal II, 1103, CLXIII, 111.—Of Innocent II, 1135, CLXXIX, 237.—Of Eugenius III, CLXXX, 1087.

BLANGY, ST. BERTHA (Blangy-en-Ternois, Pas-de-Calais), at first a monastery of girls, later of men of the Order of St. Benedict, built in the district of Calais about 660 by St. Bertha, daughter of Count Rigobert.—It was afterward granted to the monastery of Fécamp by Roger, count of St. Pol; his charter, XCLIII, 475.—Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1202, CCXVII, 94.

ST. BLAISE IN THE BLACK FOREST, or HERCYNIA (Saint-Blaise in the Black Forest), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in the duchy of Baden in 963 by Emperor Otto and St. Regimbert the hermit. Urban II confirmed in 1094 a gift made to this monastery by Countess Matilda, CLI, 374, 541.—Abbot Werner flourished in 1126, CLIII, 719. Privilege of Calixtus II, 1119, CLXIII, 1100, 1336.—Of Honorius II, 1126, CLXVI, 1254.—Of Innocent II, 1130, CLXXIX, 62, 164, 336, 338, 499, 500.—Of Adrian IV, 1157, CLXXXVIII, 1500, 1514.—Privilege of Alexander III, 1179, CC, 1209.—Of Celestine III, 1197, CCVI, 1207.

ST. BLAISE HOSPITAL (Hospitallers of St. Blaise at Mondovì), whose master Adam received a privilege from Pope Eugenius III in 1150.—Privilege of Adrian IV, 1157, CLXXXVIII, 1527.

ST. BLAISE. See ADMONT.

BLASILIENSIS, ST. PETER (Saint-Pierre of Blesle, diocese of Saint-Flour), a nunnery built in 910 by Countess Ermengard, wife of Count Bomard.—Privilege of Pope Urban II, 557.

BLAUBEUREN, or ST. JOHN THE BAPTIST (Saint-Jean of Blaubeuren, diocese of Constance), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in 1095 by the brothers Counts Henry and Hugh; Urban II granted it a privilege in 1099, CLI, 540.—Privilege of Adrian IV, 1159, CLXXXVIII, 1639.

BLAYE, ST. ROMAN (Blaye on the Gironde), a monastery situated in the district of Bordeaux and made subject by Louis the Pious to the abbey of St. Andrew at Bordeaux in 828, CIV, 1171.

BLENDECQUES, ST. COLUMBA (Sainte-Colombe of Blendecques, Pas-de-Calais), a Cistercian nunnery built by Desiderius, bishop of Thérouanne, and Philip, count of Flanders, [Col. 1029] Privilege of Innocent III, 1207, CCXV, 1294.

BLESENSE. See ST. LAUNOMAR.

BLOIS, ST. MARY (Notre-Dame du Bourg-Moyen at Blois), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, at Blois in the place commonly called Bourg-Moyen, founded by Count Odo and his wife Bertha.—Privilege of Ivo, bishop of Chartres, 1105, CLXII, 290.—Privilege of Calixtus II, 1123, CLXIII, 1271.

BOBBIO, or BAUBIO (Saint-Columban of Bobbio, Milanese territory), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded in Lombardy by St. Columban in 600, LXXX, 201, 203.—Charter of King Agilulf, ibid., 321.—Privilege of St. Columban, by which he ceded his monastery to the Apostolic See, ibid., 322.—Charters of King Adiwald, ibid., 323.—Of King Ratchis, LXXXVII, 1376.—Diploma of Charlemagne, 774, XCVII, 1000.—Gerbert, later Pope Sylvester II, served there as abbot in 990, CXXXIX, 57.—Privilege of Innocent II, 1142, CLXXIX, 582.—Of Lucius II, 1144, ibid., 823.—Letters of Innocent III concerning the restoration of this monastery, 1199, CCXIV, 782, 783; 1207, CCXV, 1320.

BOCONIENSE, ST. SAVIOUR, a monastery built by St. Boniface, bishop of Mainz, apparently the same as Fulda, built in the forest of Buchonia. See FULDA.

BODON’S MONASTERY (Bon-Moûtier, former diocese of Strasbourg), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by Abbot Dodo near the White Mount (Blaumont), on the Vezouze in the diocese of Strasbourg. Diploma of Louis the Pious, 816, CIV, 1046.

BODUIMENSE (Bodinyn, Cornwall, England), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine. Privilege of Innocent III, 1203, CCXV, 132.

BOELTHUM, or BOLONICENSE (Boelthum, Lancashire, England), a monastery to whose prior Innocent III wrote in 1203, CCXV, 192.

BOICENSE HOSPITAL. See HOSPITAL OF THE CROSS-BEARERS.

BOULOGNE, ST. MARY (Notre-Dame of Boulogne-sur-Mer, Pas-de-Calais), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, founded in the twelfth century by Eustace III, count of Boulogne. Privilege of Innocent III, 1208, CCXV, 1429.

BONNE-ESPÉRANCE, ST. MARY (Notre-Dame de Bonne-Espérance, diocese of Cambrai), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, founded in 1126 by Reynald de la Croix and his wife Beatrice, at the exhortation of St. Norbert.—Privilege of Innocent II, 1143, CLXXIX, 622.—Philip of Harveng, its second abbot, flourished in 1186, CCIII, 9.—Privilege of Celestine III, 1194, CCVI, 1051.

BONNEVAUX, ST. MARY (Notre-Dame de Bonnevaux, diocese of Vienne), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded by Guy, archbishop of Vienne, later Pope Calixtus II; its first abbot was John, later bishop of Valence. Privilege of Calixtus II, 1120, CLXIII, 1157.—Privilege of Eugenius III, 1147, CLXXX, 1198.—Letter of recommendation from Innocent III, 1207, CCXV, 1304.

BONNEVAL, ST. FLORENTIN (Saint-Fiorentin of Bonneval, former diocese of Chartres, now of Blois), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by the knight Fulk in 841.—Ravaged by the Northmen, it was rebuilt by Odo I, count of Chartres, in 965. It was distinguished by Abbot Ernald in 1156, CLXXXIX, 1507.—Letter of Alexander III to Theobald, count of Blois, concerning the protection of this abbey, 1165, CC, 355.—Letter of Innocent III, 1210, CCXVI, 263.

BONNEVAUX, ST. MARY (Notre-Dame de Bonnevaux, near Vivonne, diocese of Poitiers), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, built in 1119 by Hugh, lord of Lusignan, and his wife Saracena. Decree of Adrian IV concerning a settlement with the monastery of Cadouin, 1158, CLXXXVIII, 1599.

ST. BONIFACE, a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in the Italian March, to whose abbot Pope Gregory VII wrote in 1075 concerning the restoration of certain goods to the Church of Pisa, CXLVIII, 397, 399.

ST. BONIFACE ON THE FULDA, a monastery—see FULDA—in which Ebbo, archbishop of Reims, was confined by Louis the Pious because he had followed Lothair’s party, in 835, CXVI, 17.

BONIFAY, ST. MARY (Notre-Dame de Bonfay, Vosges), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, founded in 1145 by William of Bernolio near Mirecourt. Privilege of Eugenius III, 1148, CLXXX, 1307.—Of Lucius III, 1181, CCI, 1094.

BONNEFONTAINE, ST. MARY (Notre-Dame de Bonnefontaine in Thiérache, diocese of Reims), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded in 1132 near Rumigny by Nicholas, lord of Rumigny. Privilege of Alexander III, 1165, CC, 386.

BONNEMONT (Bonnemont, otherwise Bernon, canton of Vaud, Switzerland), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded in 1131. Privilege of Alexander III, 1165, CC, 359.—Walcher and his brother Stephen built this monastery, note, ibid.—Letter of Innocent III to the abbot concerning the case of the bishop of Lausanne, 1198, CCXIV, 146, 305.

ST. MARY OF BONRAS (Sainte-Marie de Bonras, diocese of Auxerre), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, built in 1119 by Hugh de Tilly and monks of Pontigny. Privilege of Lucius III, 1184, CCI, 1272.—Letter of Pope Innocent III concerning a certain sale, 1211, CCXVI, 518.

BOLOGNA, ST. JOHN ON THE MOUNT (Saint-Jean du Mont, Bologna, Papal States), a monastery to whose prior Innocent III wrote against the abbot of St. Bartholomew of Ferrara in 1210, CCXVI, 325.

BOLOGNA, ST. FELIX (Saint-Félix of Bologna), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, greatly distinguished by the monk Gratian at the beginning of the twelfth century, CLXXXVII, 9.—Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1209, CCXVI, 84.

BONONIENSE. See ST. VULMAR, both WITHIN THE WALLS and IN THE WOOD.

BOLOGNESE NUNNERY, founded by St. Ambrose in the fourth century, XVI, 204.

BONONIENSE S. PETRI (Saint-Pierre of Bologna), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, to which Honorius II granted a privilege in 1129, CLXVI, 1292.---Privilege of Alexander III, 1166, CC, 504.---Of Urban III, 1187, CCII, 1500.

BONONIENSE S. PROCULI (Saint-Procule of Bologna), a monastery whose abbot Innocent III admonished concerning certain heretics called the Poor, in 1206, CCXV, 820.

BONONIENSE S. STEPHANI (Sainte-Étienne of Bologna), a monastery to whose abbot Innocent III wrote that he should restrain certain heretics called the Poor, in 1206, CCXV, 820; and further concerning the suspension of the bishop of Alexandria, in 1211, CCXVI, 472.

BONONIENSE HOSPITALE (the Brethren of the Holy Cross of the Hospital of Bologna), whose house and order Urban III approved in 1187, CCII, 1507.

BONO-SOLATIO (of) B. MARIAE (Notre-Dame de Bon-Secours, duchy of Lucca, Lombardy), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose possessions and rights Celestine II confirmed by privilege in 1144, CLXXIX, 810.

BORDELSLEJA (of) (Bordesley, diocese of Worcester, England), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, built in 1138 by the Empress Matilda, daughter of King Henry. Letter of Innocent III, 1205, CCXV, 776.

BORNETO (of) S. MARIAE (Notre-Dame du Bournet, diocese of Angoulême), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, later Cistercian, founded in 1113 by Gerald of Salles, or by the Lord of Montmoreau, shortly before the building of the monastery of La Couronne. Letter of Innocent III, 1202, to the abbot of this monastery, CCXIV, 1162.

BORNHEIMENSE (Bornhem, Belgium), a monastery first of the Order of St. Augustine and afterwards of the Order of St. Benedict, founded about 1100 by Wenemar, castellan of Ghent, and confirmed by a privilege of Odo, bishop of Cambrai, in 1112. It finally became a priory subject to the abbey of Afflighem, CLX, 1158.---Privilege of Paschal II, 1104, CLXIII, 129.

BOSCHETTO, or VALLELUCIDA (of). See VALLIS LUCENTIS.

BOSCIANI (S.) (San-Bosciano, diocese of Lodi), a monastery whose abbot Innocent III wrote to concerning the election of the abbot of St. Peter of Pado, in 1203, CCXV, 139.

BOSCODUNENSE S. MARIAE (Notre-Dame de Boscandon, diocese of Embrun), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in 1130. Its property and privileges were confirmed by Alexander III in 1176, CC, 1077.---Privilege of Innocent III, 1198, CCXIV, 504; 1204, CCXV, 366.---Letter of the same, 1207, ibid., 1180.

BOSONIS VILLA (of) S. CRUCIS, or S. MARIAE (Sainte-Croix or Notre-Dame of Bouzonville, diocese of Metz), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, established in 1033 by Judith, wife of Count Adalbert. Its abbot wrote to St. Hildegard about 1145, CXCVII, 289.---Privilege of Alexander III, 1179, CC, 1248.

BOTRANENSE S. MARIAE (Sainte-Marie of Botrano, diocese of Cosenza, in Lower Calabria), a monastery whose certain agreement with the bishop Innocent III confirmed in 1204, CCXV, 434.---Privilege of the same, ibid., 439.

BOVINGARTENPERGENS E. See BAUMGARTENSE.

[Col. 1031] BOXELENSE (Boxell, diocese of Canterbury), a monastery concerning which Alexander III directed Thomas, archbishop, that the monks should pay tithes to the Church of St. Mary, in 1170, CC, 613.

BOZOWIENSE S. MARIAE (Sainte-Marie of Bozowe, in Thuringia), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built before 1152, in which year Eugenius III confirmed it by privilege, CLXXX, 1551.

BRADIENSE S. GEORGII, a monastery in the diocese of Verona, whose prior Innocent III entrusted with the task of reforming the monastery of Vangadizza, given over to corrupt morals, in 1212, CCXVI, 801.

BRAJACUM (Brou, diocese of Chartres), a monastery situated in the district of Chartres, whose provost St. Leobinus was appointed by St. Aetherius in 535, LXXXVIII, 353.

BRAMENSE S. MARIAE, or EVODII (Saint-Yvod or Notre-Dame of Braine, diocese of Soissons), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, founded in 1130. Privilege of Eugenius III, 1157, CLXXX, 1231.---Likewise of Adrian IV, 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1378.---Of Alexander III, 1172, CC, 753, 754, 755.

BRANTOMENSE (Brantôme), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by Count Boson in the district of Limoges, and long violently attacked in the tenth century by Guy, viscount, CXLI, 53.

BREDA (of) S. SALVATORIS (Saint-Sauveur of La Brède, former diocese of Girona, Catalonia), a monastery whose abbot Innocent III entrusted with the reform of the monastery of Saint-Cucufa, in 1211, CCXVI, 511.

BREDLINGHAMENSE (Bredlingham, diocese of York, England), a monastery whose abbot Innocent III entrusted with the care of reforming certain monasteries, in 1207, CCXV, 1128.

BREMENSE S. ANSCHARII (Saint-Ansgar of Bremen, in Saxony), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, whose possessions and privileges Clement III confirmed in 1188, CCIV, 1373.

BREMENSE SS. STEPHANI et VILLEHARDI (Saint-Étienne of Bremen, Lower Saxony), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, built by Albero, archbishop of Bremen, before the time of Alexander III, whose privilege survives, 1179, CC, 1238.---Letter of Innocent III on behalf of the same canons, 1205, CCXVII, 104.

BREMETENSE S. PETRI (Saint-Pierre of Bremen), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by St. Emperor Henry II and Margrave Adalbert at Bremen, to receive the monks of Novalesa, driven from their monastery during the Saracen invasion.---Privilege of Benedict VIII, 1014, CXXXIX, 1591.---Of Eugenius III, 1152, CLXXX, 1504.

BREWNOWIENSE S. SALVATORIS SS. BENEDICTI et BONIFACII (Saint-Sauveur of Brewnow, diocese of Prague), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded about 980 by Adalbert, bishop of Prague.---Privilege of Pope John XV, 993, CXXXVII, 847.

BRIGANTINUM (Briançon in Dauphiné), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by the nobleman Udalric and his wife Bertha; its abbot Gebard obtained a privilege from Innocent II in 1139, CLXXIX, 418.

BRISACENSE S. MARIAE (Notre-Dame of Brisach, in the Black Forest of Swabia), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, restored in 1125 by Bruno, provost of Strasbourg, CLXVI, 239.

BRIVATENSE SS. MARTINI ET JULIANI (Saint-Julien of Brioude, Haute-Loire), a monastery mentioned by Gregory of Tours about 510; it had Augustus as abbot, LXXI, 887, 1104.---Diploma of Louis the Pious, 825, CIV, 1149.---It became a chapter of canons, whose possessions Calixtus II confirmed in 1099, CLXIII, 1094.---Letter of Innocent III concerning a certain lawsuit with the bishop of Clermont, 1213, CCXVI, 873.---Privilege of the same pope, ibid., 874.

BRIXELLENSE S. GENESII (Saint-Geniès of Bresello, in the duchy of Modena), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, belonging to the Roman Church, to which Anastasius IV granted a privilege in 1153, CLXXXVIII, 1004.

BRIXIENSE S. EUPHEMIAE (Sainte-Euphémie of Brescia, Lombardy), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by Landulf, bishop of Brescia, shortly before the time of Calixtus II, who adorned it with privileges in 1123, CLXIII, 1262.

BRIXIENSE SS. FAUSTINI et JOVITAE (Saint-Faustin, in one of the suburbs of Brescia, Venetian States), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by St. Rambert, bishop, shortly before 1132, when Pope Innocent II confirmed it by privilege, CLXXIX, 154.---Letter of Innocent III on behalf of the nunnery of St. Peter of Ripa, 1205, CCXV, 632.

BRIXIENSE S. MARIAE (Sainte-Marie of Brescia), a monastery [Col. 1032] of the Order of St. Augustine, founded under Pope Honorius II. Privilege of Eugenius III, 1148, CLXXX, 1306.---Of Alexander III, 1175, CC, 1132.

BRIXIENSIS S. SALVATORIS et S. JULIAE (nuns of Saint-Sauveur of Brescia), a royal nunnery whose rights and possessions, together with a certain exchange with the abbot of Nonantola, Louis the Pious confirmed in 814, CIV, 1007.---Privilege of Nicholas II, 1060, CXLII, 1341, 1343.---Likewise of Alexander II, 1063, CXLVI, 149.---Privilege of Paschal II, 1106, CLXIII, 189.---Of Calixtus II, 1123, ibid., 1283.---Of Innocent II, 1132, CLXXXIX, 156.---Of Eugenius III, 1148, CLXXX, 1363.---Of Lucius III, 1184, CCI, 1269.

BRIXIENSIS SS. MICHAELIS et PETRI (nuns of Saint-Michel of Brescia), a nunnery founded by the illustrious Queen Ansa, whose abbess was Ansilperga, in 758, LXXXVII, 1368.---Charter of Jobianus, subdeacon, for the same nunnery, ibid., 1339.---Likewise of Valerian and Leodoald, ibid., 1399.

BROBURGENSE. See BURBURGENSE.

BROCARIENSE. See STAMPENSE PARTHENON.

BROLIO (of) S. STEPHANI (Saint-Étienne of Broglio, in the Milanese), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, to which Innocent III commended a certain person to be received, 1199, CCXIV, 825; CCXV, 190.

BROMHOLMENSIS PRIORY (priory of Bromholm, near Ayr, Scotland), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, which Celestine III exempted from the jurisdiction of the monastery of Ayr in 1194, CCVI, 1031.

BROMIADENSE SS. PETRI, LAURENTII ET COLUMBANI (Saint-Pierre of Bormio, in the Grisons), a Lombard monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose possessions St. Emperor Henry II confirmed in 1014, CXL, 314.

BRONIENSE S. MARIAE, or S. GIRARDI (Saint-Gérard of Brogne, diocese of Namur), a monastery in the county of Namur, founded by Abbot Gerard in 931.---Privilege of Stephen VII, CXXXII, 1053.

BRUFENINGENSE. See PRUEFENINGENSE.

BRUGENSE S. DONATIANI (Saint-Donatien of Bruges, Belgium), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, whose goods and possessions Pope Paschal II confirmed in 1110, CLXIII, 279.---The canon Gualbert flourished in 1127, CLXVI, 873.---Privilege of Eugenius III, 1146, CLXXX, 1158; of Alexander III, 1173, CC, 913, 1144.---Of Celestine III, concerning the testament of Margaret, countess of Flanders, 1195, CCVI, 1069.

BRUGENSE S. ANDREAE (Saint-André near Bruges), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in 1098 by Robert the Frisian and his wife Clementia, CLXVI, 896, 891.---Privilege of Baldric, bishop of Noyon, in 1105, for the same monastery, ibid.---Donations of the nobleman Thangmar, 893.

BRUGENSIS S. MARIAE, collegiate church (Collegiate Church of Notre-Dame of Bruges), founded by Baldric, bishop of Noyon, under Pope Paschal II. Privilege of Lucius III, 1184, CCI, 1252.

BRUNDUSINUM S. ANDREAE (Saint-André of Brindisi, Naples). Innocent III rebuked the abbot of this monastery, as well as the archbishop, on a charge of rebellion and treason, in 1203, CCXV, 209.

BRUNDUSINUM S. MARIAE DE PARVO PONTE (Sainte-Marie du Petit-Pont of Brindisi, Naples), a monastery to which Innocent III confirmed a donation made to it by a nobleman of Saint-Omer, in 1212, CCXVI, 591.

BRUNETESHUSENSIS, a nunnery in Saxony, built in the tenth century by Duke Liutolf of Saxony and his wife Oda, with the consent of Altfrid, bishop of Gandersheim, CXLI, 1173.

BRUNSWICENSE S. AEGIDII (Saint Giles of Brunswick), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded in 1113 by Margravine Gertrude, widow of Count Henry of Northeim. Letter of Innocent III, 1205, CCXV, 645.

BRUNWILLARENSE (Brunwillers, near Cologne), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built on their own estate by Herman, archbishop of Cologne, and his sister Richeza, former queen of Poland, and endowed with privileges by Emperor Henry III in 1051, CLI, 1111, 1113.---Abbot Wolphelmus flourished about 1091, CLIV, 403.

BUCCA-LEONIS (OF) THE HOSPITAL OF ST. MICHAEL. See CONSTANTINOPOLIT.

BRUXELLENSE S. MICHAELIS ET GUDULAE (Saint-Michel of Brussels), a college of canons, whose possessions and privileges Alexander III confirmed in 1178, CC, 1189.

BUCHAVIENSIS, BUCHOVIENSIS, and BUCHANGIENSIS (Buchau, Swabia), a nunnery situated near Lake Federsee [Col. 1033], on the right bank of the Danube. Diploma of Louis the Pious, 818, CIV, 1093, 1106.---Letter of Innocent III concerning the election of an abbess, 1212, CCXVI, 803.

BUCILIENSE S. PETRI (Saint-Pierre of Bucilly, Aisne), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in 950 by Countess Hersindis, or Gertrude, wife of Count Ebbert. It was first entrusted to nuns, and later passed to the monks of Saint-Martin-des-Champs in the twelfth century. Privilege of Eugenius III, 1148, CLXXX, 1366.

BULIENSE S. MARIAE (Notre-Dame du Beuil, diocese of Limoges), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, built in 1123. Letter of Innocent III to its abbot, 1206, CCXV, 928.

BULLONIENSE S. PETRI (Saint-Pierre of Bouillon), a small monastery founded by Godfrey the Bearded, duke of Lorraine, before 1070, the year in which he died and was buried at Verdun.---Privilege of Godfrey, duke of Lorraine and afterwards king of Jerusalem, by which he more richly endowed this monastery, 1094, CLV, 394.

BUNNENSE (Bonn or Bunn, diocese of Cologne), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, built before 1131, in which year Innocent II confirmed its goods and privileges, CLXXIX, 83, 222, 495.

BURBURGENSIS S. MARIAE (Notre-Dame of Bourbourg, Nord), a nunnery built in 1099 by Clementia of Burgundy, countess of Flanders.---Privilege of Calixtus II, 1119, CLXIII, 1127; of Alexander III, 1163, CC, 227, 537, 539, 1005.

BURDIGALENSE S. CRUCIS (Sainte-Croix of Bordeaux), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by King Clovis II in 650. Pope Urban II confirmed the rights and possessions of this monastery at the request of Amatus, archbishop of Bordeaux, in 1099, CLI, 545.---Diploma of Archbishop Amatus, 1099, CLV, 1647.---Privilege of Calixtus II concerning the church of Saint-Macarius, which he assigns to this monastery, 1123, CLXIII, 1276.---Privilege of Alexander III, 1165, CC, 341.---Judgment of Cardinal Henry, formerly abbot of Clairvaux, against the abbot of Saint-Sever in favour of the abbot of Sainte-Croix, 1188, CCIV, 241.

BURDIGALENSE S. SEVERINI (Saint-Seurin of Bordeaux), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built upon the Garonne.---Diploma of Louis the Pious, 814, CIV, 984; of Emperor Lothair, 828, ibid., 1171.

BURENSE (Buren, canton of Bern, Switzerland), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, dependent upon imperial jurisdiction.---Letter of Innocent II to the bishop of Augsburg, that he should not molest it, 1137, CLXXIX, 236. (Perhaps the same as Buronense below.)

BURGO ACHARDI (OF) S. LAUDI (Saint-Lô of Bourg-Achard, Eure), a priory of the Order of St. Augustine, whose goods and privileges Alexander III protected in 1180, CC, 1315.

BURGO MEDIO (OF) S. MARIAE. See BLESENSE.

BURGULIENSE, or BURGIDOLENSE, SS. TRINITATIS ET S. PETRI (Bourgueil-en-Vallée, Indre-et-Loire), a monastery founded, at the urging of Abbot Gausbert, by Emma or Emmelina, countess of Poitou, and her son William, duke of Aquitaine, with a privilege of Sylvester II, 1003, CXXXIX, 285; CXLI, 824; CXLVI, 1255.---Privilege of Urban II, 1093, CLI, 370.---Baldric, formerly abbot, became archbishop of Dol, 1114, CLXVI, 1049.---Letter of the convent to Suger and of Suger to the bishop of Angers, CLXXXVI, 1349, 1350.---Letter and privilege of Innocent III, 1198, CCXIV, 182, 270. A rule of life was given by the same pope, 1207, CCXV, 1111, 1115, 1121, 1459, 1460.

BURIO (OF) (Burjo, diocese of Braga, Portugal), a monastery to whose abbot Innocent III wrote concerning the dispute between the Hospitallers and the Church of Saint Christina of Longos, 1198, CCXIV, 182, 704.

BURONENSE S. MARIAE (Sainte-Marie or Saint-Martin of Buron, diocese of Constance), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, built in 1097 on his own land by the nobleman Peregrinus, in the diocese of Constance, on the bank of the Danube. Privilege of Urban II, CLI, 498.---Privilege of Innocent II, 1131, CLXXIX, 82. Letter of the same pope, 650. Of Eugenius III, 1146, CLXXX, 1107, 1312; of Adrian IV, 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1403.

BURTHONENSE (Burton, county of Stafford, England), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded in the eleventh century by Wulfric Spot, courtier of King Æthelred.---Privilege of Lucius III, 1185, CCI, 1366.

BUSBRUNNENSE, a monastery whose abbot Fabigaudus attended the famous council of Attigny convened by Pippin in 765. We have been unable to determine its location, XCVI, 1516.

BUSIACENSE (Bousse or Bouessay, Mayenne), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by the priest Lonegisilus under the reign of Chlothar, in the district of Le Mans, Hadoind then being bishop. Charter, LXXX, 455.---Charter of Chlothar, 459.

BUTTENBURGENSE S. NICOLAI (Saint-Nicolas of [Col. 1034] Buttenburch, in German Flanders), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, whose possessions and privileges Calixtus II confirmed, at the request of John, bishop of Thérouanne, in 1124, CLXIII, 1334.

BUXARIIS (OF) (Buxières, former diocese of Angers or Le Mans), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict.---Diploma of Emperor Louis the Pious, 857.

BUXERIENSE S. MARIAE (Notre-Dame of Bussières, diocese of Dijon, Côte-d’Or), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded in 1131 at Auzerolle by Garnier of Sombernon. Charter of Walter, lord of Sombernon, 1188, CLXXXV, 1421.---Donation of Gerard le Broz, ibid., 1422.---Likewise of Hervé and Walter of Sombernon, 1424, 1427.---Charter of Blanche of Sombernon, 1427; of William of Montaigu, 1428; of Alexander of Montaigu, 1429.---Letter of Innocent III concerning an inheritance, 1198, CCXIV, 210.

BUXERIENSIS S. MARIAE (Nuns of Sainte-Marie of Bussières), a nunnery founded by Gauslin, bishop of Toul, to which Pope Stephen VIII granted immunities in 941, CXXXII, 1090.---Charter of Pibo, bishop of Toul, 1073, CLVII, 421.

BUZANGIA (OF). See BOZOWIENSE.

CABILONENSE S. MARCELLI. See MARCELLI.

CABILONENSE S. PETRI (Saint-Pierre of Châlons-sur-Saône), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded before the end of the sixth century by Flavius, referendary of King Guntram and later bishop, and restored in the ninth century by Bishop Girbold.---Privilege of Innocent III, 1205, CCXV, 590.

CABILONENSE NOVUM-MONASTERIUM (Le Moutier-Neuf at Châlons-sur-Saône), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, apparently built about 1100 by canons, formerly secular, who then professed the rule under Abbot Alberic.---Privilege of Pope Paschal II, CLXIII, 47.---Decree of Adrian IV ordering restitution to the monastery of Trinorc of a certain church, 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1402.

CABILONENSE XENODOCHIUM (Convent of the Hospitaller Brethren of Châlons), built by the pious Abbot Desiderius about 570 under St. Agricola, bishop, LXXXI, 893.

CABLASIO (OF) S. MAURICII. See AGAUNENSE.

CADOMENSE S. STEPHANI (Saint-Étienne of Caen), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, recently founded by William the Conqueror and entrusted to Abbot Lanfranc; Pope Alexander II took it under his protection in 1063. Privilege of the same pope, 1068, CXLVI, 1339.---Charter of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1366; charter of the barons, 1367.---Privilege of Pope Paschal II, 1102, CLXIII, 86.

CADOMENSIS S. THOMAE HOSPITALIS. See PORTA MILETI.

CADUNIENSE (Cadouin, former diocese of Sarlat), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, established about 1115 by Gerard of Salles, bishop.---Charter by which Blessed Robert of Arbrissel granted the site, CLXII, 1088. (See the canons of Périgueux.)---Decree of Adrian IV concerning a certain settlement with the monastery of Bonnes-Vallées, 1158, CLXXXVIII, 1599.

CADURCENSIS S. STEPHANI CANONIA (Saint-Étienne of Cahors), established in the time of Pope Urban II, who confirmed its possessions by privilege in 1095, CLI, 423.---Bull of Calixtus II, 1119, CLXIII, 1115.

CAESARAUGUSTANUM S. MARIAE (Sainte-Marie of Saragossa, Spain), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, built by Bishop Bernard and confirmed by Innocent II with a privilege in 1141, CLXXIX, 563.

CAESARAUGUSTANUM S. SALVATORIS (Saint-Sauveur of Saragossa), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by Alfonso V, king of Aragon.---Privilege of Eugenius III, 1147, CLXXX, 1252.

CAGIA (OF). See CRISPINI ET MARIAE.

CAINONENSE (Chinon in Touraine), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded and governed in the district of Tours by Blessed Abbot Maximus in the year 400, LXXI, 846, 847 note.

CAIRATHENSIS S. MARIAE (Sainte-Marie of Cairate in Lombardy), a nunnery founded on the Ticino by the illustrious woman Manegundis; her testament, 708, LXXXVII, 1397.

CALANENSE (Calane in Apulia, Naples), a monastery whose superior jurisdiction was disputed by the brethren of Monte-Sacro.---Letter of Innocent III, 1198, CCXIV, 401.

CALARITANUM S. SATURNINI (Saint-Saturnin of Cagliari in Sardinia), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose goods and privileges were confirmed in 1120, CLXIII, 1178.

CALATRAVA (of) (Calatrava in Spain), a military order instituted in Spain, whose possessions and privileges Urban III confirmed in 1187, CCII, 1548.---Privilege of Innocent III, 1199, CCXIV, 590; letter of the same, 1205, CCXV, 666.

CALAVENNENSE SS. PETRI et VITI (Saint-Pierre [Col. 1035] of Calavena, diocese of Verona), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, to which, at the request of Abbot Simeon, Lucius III granted a privilege in 1185, CCI, 1357.

CALDENBORNENSE. See KALTENBORNENSE.

CALENSIS S. MARIAE (Chelles, Seine-et-Oise), a nunnery, an illustrious abbey on the Marne, four leagues from Paris, founded about 680 by St. Bathildis, queen and wife of Clovis II, LXXI, 665; LXXXVII, 669.

CALETRICI (S.). See ANISOLANA.

CALMILIACENSE. See S. THEOTFRIDI.

CALMOSIACENSE S. SALVATORIS (Chaumouzey or Chamouzay, former diocese of Saint-Dié), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, in the former diocese of Saint-Dié, in the Vosges, built about 1099 by the illustrious Theodoric and his wife Hadwig; Seherus was its first abbot, 1118, CLXII, 1119.---History of this monastery, ibid.---Donations made to this monastery, 1142.---Rescript of Paschal II, CLXIII, 31, 72; privilege of the same, 354, 264.---Letter of Bishop Pibo to Paschal II, CLXIII, 447.---Letters of Abbot Seherus to Paschal II, 456, 458.

CALVENSE (Calve or Calbe in Holstein, former diocese of Lund), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, transferred from an earlier place called Wenga by Wolmar, king of the Danes, and Eskil, archbishop of Lund.---Privilege of Alexander III, 1169, CC, 612, 651.

CALVIMONTENSE S. MARIAE (Notre-Dame of Chaumont-la-Piscine, diocese of Reims), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, built in 1140 by Reginald of Rosto.---Privilege of Eugenius III, 1147, CLXXX, 1220.---Decree of Adrian IV forbidding the sale of the Church’s property, 1157, CLXXXVIII, 1533.

CAMALDULENSE S. PETRI DE PETRA PERTUSA (Camaldoli, near Arezzo in Tuscany), a monastery and congregation founded by St. Romuald about 1040, concerning which there is extensive discussion at CXLIV, 27 ff.---Blessed Peter Damian, disciple of St. Romuald, ibid., 50.---The relationship of the Avellanites and Camaldolese, ibid., 87.---Life of St. Romuald, by St. Damian, CXLIV, 953.---Approval of this order by Alexander II, 1072, CXLVI, 1373.---Privilege of Pope Gregory VII, 1074, CXLVIII, 646.---Of Paschal II, 1105, CLXIII, 152, 330.---Of Honorius II, 1125, CLXVI, 1223.---Of Innocent II, 1136, CLXXIX, 272.---Of Eugenius III, 1147, CLXXX, 1187, 1372, 1604.---Of Adrian IV, 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1396, 1521, 4576.---Of Alexander III, 1176, CC, 1045, 1064.---Of Lucius III, 1184, CCI, 1263.---Of Clement III, 1187, CCIV, 1275.---Of Celestine III, 1191, CCVI, 885, 985.---Letters and privileges of Innocent III, 1199, CCXIV, 546, 1173; CCXVI, 787, 908.

CAMBUSCHINENSE (Cambuschinel, diocese of Saint Andrews, Ireland), a monastery whose goods and privileges Innocent III confirmed in 1207, CCXV, 1134, 1583.

CAMBONENSE (Chambon, diocese of Limoges), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict situated in the district of Limoges, for whose defence a certain Aymericus, a false monk of the abbey of Saint Martial, took up arms and attacked a castle in the tenth century, CXLI, 45.

CAMERACENSE S. AUBERTI (Saint-Aubert of Cambrai), a monastery founded by Bishop Aubert and endowed by King Dagobert in 637, LXXX, 564.---St. Lietbert, bishop, introduced regular canons there in 1076, CXLIV, 1447; CXLIX, 128.---Privilege of Paschal II, 1103, CLXIII, 110.---Of Innocent II, 1136, CLXXIX, 280.---Of Eugenius III, 1148, CLXXX, 1521.---Letters of Innocent III to the abbot of this monastery, 1198, CCXIV, 139, 141; 1206, CCXV, 1022, 1105, 1175, 1549; 1211, CCXVI, 403.

CAMERACENSE S. SEPULCRI (Saint-Sépulcre of Cambrai), a monastery founded within the city walls by St. Lietbert, bishop, in 1064, CXLVI, 1447.---Letters of Alexander III concerning the abbot of this monastery, 1166–1169, CC, 515, 516, 619.

CAMERACENSE S. PRAEJECTI (Saint-Prix near Saint-Quentin, Oise), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built about 800 by Albert, count of Vermandois; it is mentioned at CLIX, 124.

CAMERACENSE S. MARIAE (Notre-Dame of Cambrai), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, mentioned at CLXIX, 133.

CAMERACENSE S. GANGERICI (Saint-Géry, near Cambrai), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, built in 600 by St. Gaugericus, bishop of Cambrai; St. Landon was its first abbot, CXLIX, 124.---Letters of Alexander III to the abbot of this monastery, 1166–1169, CC, 516, 619.

CAMERACENSE S. PETRI, or GISLENI (Saint-Ghislain in Hainaut), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, to which many donations were made in 691; see charter, LXXXVIII, 1224; CXLIX, 140.---St. Emperor Henry II confirmed its possessions and privileges in 1018, CXL, 341.---Charter of Bishop Odo [Col. 1036], 1172, CC, 785, 1088.---Of Lucius III, 1183, CCI, 1192, 1332.---Of Urban III, 1187, CCII, 1502.---Of Celestine III, 1191, CCVI, 887.---Letter of Innocent III to the abbot on behalf of the monastery of Saint-Vaast, 1198, CCXIV, 139, 141.

CAMERACENSE. See DUNENGENSE, HAMUMENSE, ASPRENSE, DUACENSE, LENENSE, LUCAVIENSE, DE MARACULO HAMALGIENSE, MARCENIENSE, BARALENSE, VILLA SANCTIS, etc.

CAMPELLIS (of). See LEODEGAR.

CAMPENSE S. MARIAE (Sainte-Marie of Campan, diocese of Cologne), a monastery of the Cistercian Order near Rheinberg, built in 1122 by Frederick, archbishop of Cologne.---Privilege of Innocent II, 1139, CLXXIX, 444.

CAMPESSENSIS (Campsey, county of Suffolk, England), a nunnery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in 1199 by Theobald de Malwinc for the benefit of his sisters Joan and Agnes.---Privilege of Innocent III, 1209, CCXVI, 153.

CAMPIDONENSE (Kempten, on the Upper Danube, Bavaria), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, for which Abbot Tatto obtained immunities and privileges from Emperor Louis the Pious in 834, CIV, 1248.---He effected an exchange with Count Wanning, 838, CIV, 1300, 1304.---Charter of Ulrich, bishop of Augsburg, 973, CXXXV, 999.---Letter of the abbot of Kempten to Hildegard, CXCVII, 206.

CAMPIS (of) S. MARTINI. See MARTINI.

CAMPO (of) S. MARIAE (Notre-Dame of Camp or Campin, diocese of Cologne), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, otherwise called Vetus Campus, “Old Field,” built in 1122.---Privilege of Innocent III, 1198, CCXVII, 16.

CAMPO ROTUNDO (of) S. PETRI. See BIZULDUNENSE.

CAMPO MARTIO (of) S. MARIAE (Sainte-Marie of the Field of Mars in the Roman Campagna), a nunnery to which Urban III granted a privilege in 1187, CCII, 1469.

CANAWELLA (of) S. AEGIDII (Saint-Gilles of Canawell, England), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose goods Eugenius III confirmed and which he took under his protection in 1148, CLXXX, 1336.

CAMBIDOBRENSE (Combronde in Auvergne), a monastery among the Arverni in which St. Quintian freed a demoniac in the sixth century, LXXI, 1025.

CANCELLATENSE S. MARIAE (Notre-Dame de la Chanceade, diocese of Périgueux), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, founded in 1135 by pious hermits, disciples of Fulk, abbot of Celle-Frouin.---Letter of Innocent III to its abbot, 1203, CCXV, 276.

CANIGONENSE S. MARTINI (Saint-Martin du Canigou, diocese of Perpignan), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded in 1001 by Wifred, count of Cerdanya, who himself became a monk.---Privilege of Alexander III, 1163, CC, 236.---The abbot was excommunicated by the same pope in 1176, CC, 1641.---Letter of Innocent III, 1212, CCXVI, 609.

CANNETO (of) S. MARIAE (Sainte-Marie of Caneto, diocese of Mantua, Italy), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose goods and privileges Innocent III confirmed in 1199, CCXIV, 650.

CANTAVENSE S. MARIAE (Sainte-Marie of Cantaben, Spain), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, to which Eugenius III secured possession of a certain estate in 1153, CLXXX, 1587.

CANTOBONENSE, or CATABENNENSE (Chantoin, diocese of Clermont), a monastery situated in the territory of Clermont, in which St. Urbicus, bishop, was buried about 380, LXXI, 181.

CANTUARIENSE S. AUGUSTINI (Saint-Augustin, or Saint-Pierre-et-Saint-Paul, of Canterbury), a celebrated monastery founded in honour of Saints Peter and Paul in 601 by St. Æthelberht and St. Augustine, bishop of Canterbury, LXXX, 95.---Privilege of Pope St. Deusdedit, 673, LXXXVII, 1143.---The title and name of this monastery were changed to that of St. Augustine, XCV, 74 note.---Blessed Peter, its first abbot, was sent as legate into Gaul, ibid.---Privilege of King Æthelred, 979–1016, CLI, 1170.---Of Cnut I concerning the translation of the body of St. Mildred, virgin, 1018, ibid., 1185.---The monk Goscelin flourished about 1100, CLV, 9.---Likewise, the monk Eadmer flourished in 1121, CLIX, 342.---Letter to Pope Paschal II, 1109, CLXIII, 462.---Privilege of Calixtus II, 1120, ibid., 1191.---Privilege of Innocent II, 1139, CLXXIX, 497, 532, 533.---Of Lucius II, 1144, ibid., 925, 926.---Of Eugenius III, 1149, CLXXX, 1382, 1391, 1539.---Of Adrian IV to Abbot Silvester, 1156, CLXXXVIII, 1443, 1490, 1491.---Letters of Alexander III concerning Abbot-elect Clerembald, 1165, CC, 383, 891, 1037, 1080, 1167, 1168, 1228, 1229.---Of Lucius III, 1181, CCI, 1090, 1091.---Letters of Urban III, 1187, CCII, 1499, 1511, 1527.---Letter of Clement III, 1188, CCIV, 1401.---Letters of Celestine III, 1191, CCVI, 874, 875, 884, 907, 1025, 1026.---Letters and privileges of Innocent [Col. 1037] III, 1198, CCXIV, 416, 1101, 1185; 1205, CCXV, 729, 734, 834, 1043, 1048.

CANTUMERULAE S. SERENI (Chantemerle, Marne), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, founded in 1135 by the counts of Champagne.---Privilege of Alexander III, 1165, CC, 351.

CANUSINUM (Canosa in Apulia), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, made illustrious in 1130 by the monk Donizo, author of the *Life of St. Matilda*, CLXVI, 1339.---Privilege of Adrian IV, 1157, CLXXXVIII, 1498.

CAPEIENSE S. MEDARDI (Saint-Médard of Cappy, near Péronne, diocese of Amiens), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by Peter, knight of Cappy, and Ralph, count of Vermandois.---Privilege of Lucius III, 1184, CCI, 1255.

CAPELLENSE (Capelle, former diocese of Trier, near Koblenz), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, whose goods and rights Celestine III confirmed by privilege in 1197, CCVI, 1196.

CAPELLENSE, or DE CAPELLA AD BLANCAS, S. MARIAE (Notre-Dame de la Capelle, near Calais, former diocese of Boulogne), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in 1090 by Blessed Countess Ida, CLV, 454.---Privilege of Eugenius III, 1147, CLXXX, 1214.

CAPPANULENSIS SS. MARTINI ET QUIRIACI (Saint-Martin of Cappanello, diocese of Lucca), a small abbey founded by a certain married priest and confirmed by Talesperianus, bishop of Lucca, in 725, LXXXVII, 1370.

CAPPENBERGENSE S. MARIAE (Sainte-Marie of Cappenberg, diocese of Münster), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, founded in 1112 by Godfrey, count of Cappenberg.---Privilege of Pope Honorius II, 1126, CLXVI, 1251.---Hermann, formerly a Jew, became a Christian Premonstratensian canon in 1135, CLXX, 803.---He is mentioned, ibid., 1305.---Privilege of Eugenius III, 1145, CLXXX, 1041, 1518.---Of Celestine III, 1197, CCVI, 1205.---Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, concerning the provostship of the Church of Cologne, 1203, CCXV, 36.

CAPUANUS S. MARIAE (Sainte-Marie of Capua), a nunnery built before 1120, in which year Pope Calixtus II wrote to Abbess Alpheranda that she should state why she retained the church of Saint Mary of Cinglini from the monastery of Monte Cassino, CLXIII, 1189.---The same abbess was excommunicated by Pope Calixtus in 1122, ibid., 1249.

CARACETO (of) S. MARIAE (Sainte-Marie of Caracedo, former diocese of Astorga, Spain), a monastery first of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by Bermudo II, king of León, in 990. It adopted the Cistercian rule in 1203, under Innocent III, CCXV, 189.

CARADIGUA (of) (a certain Benedictine convent at Burgos in Spain), a priory which Lucius II entrusted to the monastery of Cluny for reform in 1144, CLXXIX, 928.

CARA INSULA (of). See OMENSE.

CARALITANUM, and more correctly CALARITANUM, S. SATURNINI (Cagliari in Sardinia), a monastery whose goods and privileges Calixtus II confirmed in 1120, CLXIII, 1178.

CARALITANUM and CALARITANUM (Cagliari), a convent of girls founded by the most religious woman Theodosia in the time of St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 684, 723.

CARAMAGNENSIS S. MARIAE (Sainte-Marie of Carmagnola, Piedmont), a nunnery built in the time of Calixtus II, which Adrian IV granted to the bishop of Asti in 1157, CLXXXVIII, 1491.

CARANNI (S.) (Saint-Chéron-lès-Chartres, outside the city), a monastery of St. Augustine, founded in 599 in honour of St. Carannus, martyr.---Privilege of Eugenius III, 1151, CLXXX, 1463.

CARCADI (of) S. MARIAE (Sainte-Marie of Carcadi, diocese of Coimbra, Portugal), a monastery to whose prior, together with the dean of Lisbon, Innocent III wrote concerning the controversy between the bishop of Coimbra and the monks of Santa Cruz, in 1198, CCXIV, 302.

CARCASSONNENSE S. HILARII (Saint-Hilaire of Carcassonne), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose goods and privileges Louis the Pious confirmed in 815 at the request of Abbot Monnellus, CIV, 1037.---Privilege of Benedict VII, 982, CXXXVII, 344.---Likewise of Benedict VIII, 1024, CXXXIX, 1632.

CARCERE (of) S. MARIAE. See MARIAE.

CARDONENSE S. CASTORIS (Saint-Castor of Cardon in Saxony), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, whose rights and possessions Pope Urban III confirmed in 1186, CCII, 1457.

CARIACENSE (Saint-Céré, Lot), a small monastery which Amelius, abbot of Aurillac, granted to Hugh, abbot of Cluny, so that he might restore it to a better condition, about the year 1080, CLIX, 942.

CARICAMPENSE S. MARIAE (Notre-Dame de Chercamp, diocese of Arras), a monastery of the Cistercian Order near [Col. 1038] Hesdin, built in 1137 by Hugh de Faino, count of Saint-Pol, and his wife Beatrice.---Letter of Alexander III on behalf of that monastery, 1170, CC, 679.

CARILEFUS (Saint). See ANISOLANUM.

CARILOCUM, the same as the Place of Charles, or the monastery of Charles’s Castle.

CARINTHIA (in). See SAINT PAUL.

CARISIENSE S. CASSIANI (Saint-Cassien de Carisio, in Tuscany), a monastery of the Camaldolese Order, whose possessions and privileges Pope Lucius III confirmed in 1182, CCI, 1121.---Privilege of Clement III, 1188, CCIV, 1285.

CARITATE (de). See SAINT MARY.

CARMENSIS (Charmes, diocese of Soissons), a nunnery of the Order of Fontevraud, mentioned by Herbert, archbishop of Torres in Sardinia, in the twelfth century, CLXXXV, 1353.

CARNOTENSE S. PETRI (Saint-Pierre of Chartres), a celebrated monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, built in the Chartres suburb from the beginning of the monarchy. Yet, although it flourished, in the eleventh century the whole region was laid waste by the Northmen, and the monastery was razed to its foundations. Rebuilt by the surviving monks, it was unable to withstand the greed of a certain Bishop Elias. At last Bishop Agano came, and took care to restore this monastery to its former condition in 1030.---Charters of Hildegard and her son Richard; likewise of Ragenard, Gausfrid, and others, CXLI, 369 and following.---Paul, a monk of this monastery, described its beginnings and cartulary about the year 1100, CLV, 175, 179.---Letter of Bishop Ivo to Paschal II on behalf of the abbey of Saint Peter, CLXII, 287.---Privilege of Paschal II, CLXIII, 183.---Of Pope Honorius II, 1127, CLXVI, 1273.---Charter of Matthew, bishop and cardinal of Albano, concerning confirmation of Abbot Odo, 1128, CLXXIII, 1264.---Privileges of Alexander III, 1164, CC, 294, 339, 355, 369.---Letters and privileges of Innocent III, 1198, CCXIV, 461; CCXVII, 160, 224.

CARNOTENSE S. JOANNIS IN VALLE (Saint-Jean of Chartres-en-Vallée), a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine, founded by Blessed Ivo, who in 1099 introduced into the aforesaid monastery monks summoned from the monastery of Saint-Quentin.---Privileges of Pope Paschal II, CLXIII, 104, 209.---Of Eugenius III, 1151, CLXXX, 1462.---Privilege of Innocent III, 1216, CCXVII, 281.

CAROLI CASTRENSE S. PETRI (Saint-Pierre of Charlieu, diocese of Mâcon), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, built by Robert, bishop of Valence, in 876; it is mentioned in the Life of Peter the Venerable, 1145, CLXXXIX, 26.---Privilege of Lucius III, 1182, CCI, 1118.---Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1198, CCXIV, 200.

CAROLILOCI S. MARIAE (Notre-Dame of Charlis, former diocese of Senlis), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded about 1136. That priory passed from the monastery of Vézelay to that of Pontigny.---Charter of Abbot Gunther, by which he bound himself to the canons of Saint Mary of Paris, 1114, CCV, 907.---Letters of Innocent III, 1207, CCXV, 1260; 1210, CCXVI, 198.

CAROLILOCI S. MARIAE (Sainte-Marie of Charlieu, diocese of Mâcon), a nunnery built by Beatrice, countess of Chalon; Pope Adrian IV granted a privilege to its abbess Petronilla in 1157, CLXXXVIII, 1501.---Lucius III, 1182, CCI, 1118.

CARPENSE S. MARIAE (Sainte-Marie of Carpi, in the duchy of Modena), a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine, built by Astulf, king of the Lombards, in 750.---Privilege of Calixtus II, 1123, CLXIII, 1263.

CARRACETO or CARRAZETO S. SALVATORIS (Saint-Sauveur of Carracedo, former diocese of Astorga, Spain), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded by Bermudo II, king of León, in 990. Later, under Abbot Florentius, it adopted the Cistercian rule about 1126 and was dedicated to Blessed Mary.---Privilege of Innocent II, 1139, CLXXIX, 429.---Privilege of Innocent III concerning the union of this monastery with Cîteaux, 1203, CCXX, 189.---Concerning a certain grant made by the king of Spain, 1210, CCXVI, 345.

CARRARIENSE (Carrare, diocese of Padua), a monastery.---Letter of Innocent III to the abbot of this monastery concerning a surreptitiously obtained rescript, 1213, CCXVI, 856.

CARROFENSE (Carrou or Charrou, diocese of Arras), a monastery to which Innocent III granted a privilege in 1207, CCXV, 1264.---Confirmation of its privileges, ibid., 1517.

CARROFENSE S. SALVATORIS (Saint-Sauveur of Charroux, diocese of Poitiers), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded by Count Robert in 769; Charlemagne granted it immunities in 799, XCVII, 988.---Diplomas of Louis the Pious, 814, CIV, 1016; of Louis and Lothair, 830, CIV, 1188.---Reformed by William, duke of Aquitaine, about 1012, CXLI, 824.---Privilege of Pope Saint Leo IX, 1050, CXLIII, 648.---Privilege [Col. 1039] by which Innocent III confirmed to it certain properties in the dioceses of Beauvais and Arras, 1207, CCXV, 1264, 1517.---Privilege of the same pope for all its properties, 1211, CCXVI, 392.---Letter concerning the election of an abbot, ibid., 395.

CARRIONENSE S. ZOILI, a Spanish monastery granted to the Cluniacs for reform, to which they sent Abbot Arnulf in the time of Saint Odilo, eleventh century, CXLII, 868.

CARTHAGINIAN MONASTERIES were very numerous in the time of Saint Augustine, XXXII, 638.

CARTHUSIAE MAJORIS (La Grande-Chartreuse near Grenoble), a monastery and the head of a new order, founded by Saint Bruno and Saint Hugh, bishop, in 1084.---Privilege of Pope Urban II, 1092, CLI, 353.---Acts of Saint Bruno and history of the foundation of the Charterhouse, CLII, 9 and following.---Guigo I, first Carthusian prior general, ibid., 582.---Guigo II, Carthusian and second prior, ibid., 785.---Decree of Hugh of Grenoble forbidding women to approach the Charterhouse, 1084, CLXVI, 1572.---Privileges of Alexander III, 1164, CC, 293, 949, 1055, 1080, 1128; of Lucius III, 1184, CCI, 1305, 1306, 1331.---On the origin of the Carthusian Order, CCII, 1311.---Privileges of Urban III, 1187, CCII, 1476; Clement III, 1188, CCIV, 1338, 1462, 1464; Celestine III, 1192, CCVI, 924, 951, 957.

CARTHUSIAE ARVERIAE or ALBERIAE. See ALBERIA.

CARTHUSIA MAJOREVI. See MAJOREVUM.

CARTHUSIAE PORTARUM (Les Portes, diocese of Belley), founded in 1115 by Prior Bernard and several companions, CLIII, 790.---This Bernard is distinct from Bernard of Portes in Maurienne, bishop first of Maurienne and then of Belley, in the same period, ibid., 792.---Besides Saint Bernard the founder, it had celebrated priors, namely Nanthenolus, Stephen of Chalmeto, and the monk John, ibid., 886, 899, 931.

CARTHUSIAE SQUILLACENSIS monastery. See TURRITANA.

CASA AUREA. Monastery. See SAINT CLEMENT OF PESCARIA.

CASAURIENSE or DE CASA AUREA SS. TRINITATIS (La Casa d’Auro in Lombardy), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict in Lombardy, whose properties and privileges Emperor Henry III confirmed in 1047, CLI, 1105, 1106.

CASA DEI. See VICONIENSE.

CASA DEI SS. VITALIS ET AGRICOLAE (Chaise-Dieu, diocese of Clermont), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded in 1046 above the river Senoria among the Arverni by Blessed Robert the hermit, son of Gerard and Raimgard. Saint Leo IX confirmed its properties in 1052, CXLIII, 202, 232.---Privilege of Calixtus II, CLXIII, 1110.---Life of Saint Robert, by Marbod, bishop of Rennes, CLXXI, 1506.---Privileges of Eugenius III, 1146, CLXXX, 1102; Lucius III, 1183, CCI, 1245.

CASAE DEI (Case-Dieu, in Basilicata, kingdom of Naples), a monastery to whose prior Innocent III wrote in 1204, CCXV, 320, 373, 826.

CASALI S. PETRI (Saint-Pierre of Casal in Lombardy), a monastery of the Vallombrosian Order, founded by Abbot Andrew. Pope Urban II attempted to restore in it the original fervor of discipline in 1098, CLI, 544.---Privilege of Paschal II, 1113, CLXIII, 120.

CASALI. See EVASIUS and SAINT SAVIOR.

CASAMARII SS. JOANNIS ET PAULI (Saint-Jean of Casamario, diocese of Veroli, Papal States), a monastery first of the Order of Saint Benedict, which passed to Cîteaux in the time of Saint Bernard.---Privilege of Alexander III, 1170, CC, 671.---Letters of Innocent III to the abbot, 1203, CCXV, 181, 182, 329.

CASALIS BENEDICTI (Chezal-Benoît, diocese of Bourges), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded at the beginning of the twelfth century by Abbot Andrew, formerly a monk at Valle Brutiarum in Italy, CCII, 1312.

CASANOVA S. MARIAE (Sainte-Marie of Casa-Nova, diocese of Gran or Esztergom, Hungary), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, built in 1150 by Béla II, king of Hungary.---Privilege of Innocent III, 1199, CCXIV, 550.

CASEGONGUIDINENSE or CASAE CONGIDUNENSES (Cougnon, diocese of Trier), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict in the duchy of Luxembourg, on the river Desmarus (Sesmoy), between Chiny and Bouillon, founded by the blessed King Sigebert in 660, LXXXVII, 316.---Diploma of the same, ibid., 319.

CASINENSE (Monte Cassino, in the Terra di Lavoro, Naples), the renowned monastery situated on the summit of Monte Cassino among the Apennines, founded about 525 by Saint Benedict the Father after he voluntarily departed from Subiaco, [Col. 1040] LXVI, 152.---Visited by Totila himself, 542, ibid., 160.---Devastated by the Lombards, 573, ibid., 168.---After its rebuilding, enriched with gifts by the same Lombards, especially by Duke Gisulf, 768, LXXXVII, 1392.---Likewise, donation of King Desiderius, ibid., 1393.---Diplomas of Charlemagne, 810, XCXXII, 1040, 1041, 1044.---Privilege of John VIII, 882, CXXXVI, 950.---Saint Bertarius, abbot of Monte Cassino, crowned with martyrdom by the Saracens, 884, CXXVI, 975.---Privileges of Pope Marinus II, 994, CXXXIII, 867; Agapetus II, ibid., 929; Benedict VII, CXXXVII, 326; Benedict VIII, CXXXIX, 1592, 1627, 1636.---Precept of Emperor Saint Henry II, 1013, CXL, 300, 365.---Privileges of Benedict IX, 1037, CXLI, 1357; Saint Leo IX, 1049, CXLIII, 604, 605, 690, 731; Pope Victor II, 1057, ibid.; Pope Nicholas II, 1059, ibid., 1305; Alexander II, CXLVI, 1325, 1393, 1425.---Guaifer, monk and poet, 1084, CXLIII, 1282.---Privileges and letters of Gregory VII, 1078, CXLVIII, 688, 692.---Abbot Desiderius became pope in 1086 under the name Victor III.---Urban II consecrated the church of Saint Mary in 1093, CLI, 363.---Privileges of the same pope, ibid., 492, 512, 515, 549.---Privileges of Paschal II, 1101, CLXIII, 65, 77, 144, 291, 295.---Letter of Calixtus concerning Gunnarius’s donations, ibid., 1182.---Likewise, to Bishop Roger that he should protect the monastery of Monte Cassino, ibid.---Privilege of Calixtus II, 1122, ibid., 1250.---Leo of Marsica, monk, wrote the Chronicle of Monte Cassino, 1138, CLXXIII, 439.---Book on the illustrious men of Monte Cassino, by Peter the deacon and monk of Monte Cassino, ibid., 1003.---Book by the same author on the birth and death of the righteous men of Monte Cassino, ibid., 1063.---Catalogue of the abbots of Monte Cassino, ibid., 483.---Privileges of Innocent II, 1137, CLXXIX, 325; Anastasius IV, 1153, CLXXXVIII, 995; Alexander III, 1159, CC, 75, 882, 1158, 1161, 1267, 1303; Lucius III, 1182, CCI, 1155, 1225; Clement III, 1188, CCIV, 1337, 1395.---Letters and privileges of Innocent III, 1198, CCXIV, 365; 1208, CCXV, 1593, 1394; CCXVI, 22, 193; CCXVII, 152, 185, 249.

CASSANIA S. MARIAE (Notre-Dame de la Chassaigne, diocese of Lyon), a monastery of the Cistercian Order built by Stephen, lord of Villars, in 1145.---Letter of Innocent III concerning an accusation against the archbishop of Lyons, 1207, CCXV, 1299.

CASSIANENSIS (Cassan, Hérault), a priory of the Order of Saint Augustine, built about 1080 in the mountains of the diocese of Béziers.---Letter of Adrian IV concerning an agreement with the bishop of Béziers, 1158, CLXXXVIII, 1543.

CASSIANUS (Saint). See MONTIS-SCALARII.

CASTELBERGENSE (Castelberg in the Upper Palatinate, Bavaria), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, built by Count Frederick of Castelberg before 1103, CXLIII, 349.

CASTELLENSE (Cassel, in Hesse and the Upper Rhine district), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded by Counts Heringer and Frederick before 1139; in that year Innocent II confirmed it by privilege, CLXXIX, 427.

CASTELLIONE S. MARIAE (Sainte-Marie of Castiglione, in Lombardy), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, whose possessions Pope Lucius II confirmed by privilege in 1144, CLXXIX, 863.

CASTELLIONE S. PETRI (Saint-Pierre of Castiglione), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict near Lucca in Lombardy, founded by Aurinandus and Godefrid in 723, LXXXVII, 1368.

CASTELLIONENSE. See CONCHARUM.

CASTELLO-ABBATIALI (Château-l’Abbaye, diocese of Arras), a monastery first of the Order of Saint Augustine, built in 870.---Restored and reformed in 1153 by monks originating from Prémontré.---Privilege of Alexander III, 1173, CC, 924.

CASTELLO S. MATTHAEI (Saint-Matthieu of Castello, Papal States), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, to which Lucius III granted a privilege in 1183, CCI, 1229.---Privilege of Clement III, 1189, CCIV, 1440.

CASTELLO CAMERACENSI. See ANDREAE.

CASTILIONE S. MARIAE (Notre-Dame of Châtillon, former diocese of Langres, Côte-d’Or), a monastery founded by secular canons in 1137, whose first abbot was Aldo and which afterwards became of the regular Order of Saint Augustine.---Letter of Innocent II to Abbot Aldo, CLXXIX, 330, 650.---Of Eugenius III, 1145, CLXXX, 1050.---Letter of Innocent III, 1206, CCXV, 825.

CASTINIACENSES CELLAE (Les Chatenets, in Lorraine), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, built by Duke Thierry of Lorraine in 1115, CLXIII, 468.

CASTRI CENSORII. See POTENTIANI.

CASTRODUNENSIS CANONIA (a house of secular canons at Châteaudun, Eure-et-Loir), whose goods Innocent II assigned to regular canons in 1131, CLXXIX, 79.

CASTRILOCENSIS, a nunnery founded by Waldedrude, sister of Saint Aldegund, in the mountains of Hainaut about 610, CXXXII, 859.---This monastery is mentioned in the Testament of Saint Ansegisus, abbot of Fontenelle, 833, CV, 746.---Beginnings of this nunnery, CCIII, 1381.

CASTRO BRITTONUM. See MICHAELIS.

CASTROFORTE (Châteaufort, Indre-et-Loire), a priory of the Order of Saint Augustine dependent on Marmoutier.---Because of its excesses it incurred excommunication.---Letter of Alexander III, 1163, CC, 279.

CASTRO NOVO. See NUEMBERGENSE.

CASTRO S. MARTINI (Saint-Martin of Castro, diocese of Braga, Portugal).---Letter of Innocent III requiring obedience to be rendered to the archbishop of Braga, 1499 [probably 1199], CCXIV, 704.

CASTRO NAUTONIS S. SEVERINI (Saint-Séverin of Château-Landon, diocese of Sens), a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine, built in 1151 beside a church dedicated to Saint Severinus in the sixth century.---Letter of Alexander III to the abbot, 1163, CC, 194.

CATALAUNENSE S. PETRI or OMNIUM-SANCTORUM (Saint-Pierre of Châlons-sur-Marne), a monastery founded, or at least endowed, by King Sigebert and Saint Elaphius, bishop, who rested there in the sixth century, LXXI, 356 note.---Privilege of Bishop Gaufrid, 1138, CLXXIII, 1398.

CATANENSE S. AGATHAE (Saint-Agatha of Catania, Sicily), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, built by Count Roger in 1062, to which Urban II granted a privilege, CLI, 339.

CAUCIACENSE S. STEPHANI (Saint-Étienne of Choisy-le-Roi), formerly a celebrated monastery, later subject to Saint-Médard of Soissons, in which King Childebert was buried, 739, LXXI, 672.

CAULIANENSE, a monastery near Mérida in Spain, in which the monk Tarra seems to have lived, 600, LXXX, 19, 122.

CAUNENSE S. PETRI (Saint-Pierre of Caunes, Aude), which Abbot Anian made into a monastery from two older abbeys, and which Charlemagne subjected to the monastery of Saint-Laurent of Olibejio in 793, XCVII, 980.---Privilege of Gelasius II, 1118, CLXIII, 511.

CAURIENSE (Les Caureix or Chauray, in Poitou), a monastery whose properties Innocent III took under his protection in 1211, CCXVI, 416.

CAVEA or CAGIA. See MARY.

CAVENSE SS. TRINITATIS (La Cava, near Salerno), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict in Italy, built by the devout and noble Alferius, whose privileges Pope Gregory VII confirmed in 1085, CXLVIII, 720.---He also annexed certain other monasteries to it, ibid.---Diploma of Urban II, 1089, CLI, 57, 307.---Letter of the same pope to Abbot Peter, ibid., 347.---Privilege of Duke Roger, ibid., 350.---Of Alexander III, 1169, CC, 565.---Letter of Innocent III to the abbot concerning the election of the bishop of Policastro, 1211, CCXVI, 440.

CELLAE S. EUSITII (Celles-en-Berry, diocese of Blois, formerly of Bourges), a monastery founded by Abbot Eusitius and King Childebert in 532, LXXI, 890.

CELLAE NOVAE (Cella Nova, diocese of Caldas de Orense in Galicia, Spain), a monastery whose abbot refused to submit to the bishop; the controversy was brought before Innocent III in 1198, CCXIV, 52.

CELLAE PAULINAE (Celle-Sainte-Pauline, diocese of Mainz), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, built by Blessed Paulina, a distinguished matron, who introduced into it twelve monks from the monastery of Hirsau; among them were Wernher, the foundress’s son, and Geronzius, the first abbot, in 1107.---Privilege of Innocent II, 1136, CLXXIX, 278.

CELLAE S. SALVATORIS (Celle-Saint-Sauveur, near Arras), a monastery built in the place called Berclaus by Blessed Ledwin in 1040, CXLIX, 131.

CELLAE VILMARI (SEVEN MARCELLI) (Celle Vilmarcel, in Breisgau, diocese of Constance), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict dependent on Cluny.---Letter of Innocent III concerning this monastery, 1201, CCXVII, 81, 149.

CELLENSE SUPERIUS S. MICHAELIS (Saint-Michel, Upper Celle, near Würzburg), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, built by Provost John and his brother before 1133; in that year Innocent II adorned it with a privilege, CLXXIX, 170.

CELLENSE (Celles near Dinant), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded on the Meuse in Belgium by Saint Hadalin, abbot, in 664.---Saint Remaclus flourished at that time, CXXXIX, 1141.

CELLENSE S. PETRI (Moustier-la-Celle), a noble monastery founded in the suburb of Troyes, at the place called Germanic Island, by Saint Frodobert, its first abbot, in [Col. 1042] 650, CXXXVII, 599.---Peter of Celle flourished there as abbot; he afterwards presided over the monastery of Saint-Remigius at Rheims and finally became bishop of Chartres in 1187, CCII, 397.

CELLENSE SS. PETRI ET GISLENI. See CAMERACENSE.

CELSINIACENSE (Sauxillanges, Puy-de-Dôme), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict among the Arverni, which for some time was under Saint Odilo’s governance, later abbot of Cluny, in 1034, CXLII, 864.---Privilege of Urban II, 1095, CLI, 432.---Letter of Adrian IV concerning the monastery’s protection against Eustace, brother of Peter, abbot of Cluny, 1156, CLXXXVIII, 1477.

CENADIENSE DE AEGRIS (the Infirmary, diocese of Cenad, Hungary), a monastery to which Innocent III addressed a letter concerning the settlement of a dispute over tithes, 1213, CCXVI, 865.

CENETENSIS S. MARIAE (Saint Mary of Zénéda, Venetian territories), a monastery or hospice which Pope Honorius II took under his protection in 1289, CLXVI, 1129.

CENETENSE S. MARTINI DE COLLE (Saint-Martin of the Hill of Zénéda, in Venetia), a monastery whose abbot Innocent III wrote to on behalf of the archbishop of Durrës in 1209, CCXVI, 105.

CENOMANNENSE S. VINCENTII ET LAURENTII (Saint-Vincent or Saint-Laurent of Le Mans), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded by Saint Domnolus, bishop, and consecrated by Blessed Germanus of Paris in 570, LXXII, 630, 648.---Testament of Saint Domnolus in favor of this monastery, ibid., 650.---Charter of Saint Hadoind, LXXX, 567.---Diplomas of Louis the Pious, 832, CIV, 1217, 1218, 1219.---Privileges of Saint Domnolus, bishop, CXV, 40, 41.---What was done under Bishop Aldric, CXV, 103.---Privilege of Innocent III, 1204, CCXV, 494.

CENOMANNENSE S. VICTORIS (Saint-Victor-lès-le-Mans), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, ibid., 567.---Diploma of Charlemagne, 802, XCVII, 995.

CENOMANNENSE S. PETRI (Saint-Pierre of Le Mans), a monastery founded by Saint Bertramnus, bishop, through his testament in 623, LXXX, 386.---Bishop Hadoind favored it, ibid., 567.---Diploma of Charlemagne, 802, XCVII, 995.

CENOMANNENSE S. SALVATORIS (Saint-Sauveur of Le Mans), a monastery founded by Saint Aldric, bishop, in 837, CXV, 60.---Diploma of Louis the Pious, CIV, 1271.

MONASTERIES OF THE DISTRICT OF LE MANS. See Saint Martin at Pontlieue, Saint Victurius, Saint Richomer, Saint Scholastica, destroyed by the Northmen, Saint Carilefus or Anisola, Saint Julian, Saint Illidius, Tussiacense, Saints John and Trechius at Buxiolo, the canonry of Buxariae, Saint Martin in Diablenticum, Saint Mary at Aurionnum, the monastery of Buxedo of Semiliacum, of Caladon, and the canonry of Saints Gervasius and Protasius; their nomenclature is read in the diploma of Louis the Pious, year 83, CIV, 1220.---And in the Life of Saint Aldric, CXV, 41, 42 and following.

CENTULENSE S. RICHARII (Centule, called Saint-Riquier, diocese of Amiens), a celebrated monastery founded in Ponthieu, in the Forest of Cressy, on the Somme, about 625 by Saint Richarius, abbot, and King Dagobert; Charlemagne granted it a diploma in 798, XCVII, 986.---On the restoration of this abbey by Abbot Angilbert, XIX, 836, 841.---Diploma of Louis the Pious, 830, CIV, 1182.---Nithard, abbot, 853, CXVI, 35.---The Venerable Abbot Angilramnus flourished in 1045, CXLI, 1401.---This monastery, nearly ruined in the eleventh century, was rebuilt by Abbot Ingelard, to whom Ingelramnus succeeded, ibid., 1404.---History of Centule, by Hariulf, 1142, CLXXIV, 1211.---Letter of Alexander III to the bishop of Amiens concerning the obedience owed to him by the abbot, 1171, CC, 744.

CEPHALAEDIENSE (Cefeludi or Cefaledi, near Messina in Sicily), a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine which Antipope Anacletus made into a bishopric in 1130, CLXXIX, 721.

CERASIENSE S. VIGORIS (Saint-Vigor of Cérisy, Manche), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded by Saint Vigor in the sixth century and rebuilt in 1030 by Robert, duke of Normandy, CCII, 1315. See SAINT VIGOR.

CERISIERS HOSPITALLERS (a house of hospitallers at Cérisiers, diocese of Sens, Yonne).---Letter of Innocent III concerning their agreement with the monastery of Scarlais (Eschaalis), 1202, CCXIV, 1094.

CEROTENSE. See below, CERTESIENSE.

CERRETENSE S. PETRI (Saint-Pierre of Cerretti, diocese of Volterra, Tuscany), a monastery of the Camaldolese Order, whose properties and privileges Pope Lucius III confirmed in 1181, CCI, 1079.

[Col. 1043] CERRETO (Cerretti, in the diocese of Lodi, Liguria), a monastery whose prior Innocent III wrote to in 1203, CCXV, 139.

CERTESIENSE (Chertsey, county of Surrey, England), an ancient monastery on the Thames, built in 666 by Saint Erkenwald, son of King Offa and bishop of London, in 675, XCV, 184.---Privilege of Innocent III concerning confirmation of tithes, 1199, CCXIV, 609.

CERVIFRIGIDENSE SS. TRINITATIS (Holy Trinity of Cerfroid, diocese of Meaux), of the Order of the Redemption of Captives, founded by John of Matha and Felix of Valois in 1198.---Privilege of Innocent III, by which he confirmed the monastery and order in that same year, CCXIV, 216.---Decree of the same pontiff containing and confirming the rule of this order, 1198, ibid., 444; 1203, CCXV, 134.

CESTRENSIS S. WALBURGIS (Saint Walburga of Chester, England), a nunnery founded in England by the earl of Chester, according to Orderic Vitalis, ninth century, CXXIX, 895.

CHALOCHEIO S. MARIAE (Notre-Dame of Chaloché, diocese of Angers), a monastery of the Cistercian Order; Innocent III had entrusted its abbot with the case of the priory of Fontaine-Girard in the diocese of Le Mans in 1211, CCXVI, 449.

CHAALIS. See CAROLILOCUM.

CHANTILLIACENSE (Chalivoy, former diocese of Bourges, Cher), a monastery of the Cistercian Order built in the twelfth century; Innocent III wrote to its abbot concerning the disputed subjection of the abbey of Menat between the bishop of Clermont and Cluny in 1213, CCXVI, 965.

CHARITATE S. MARIAE. See MARY.

CHARITATE FULLENSI, the same as FULLENSE; see that entry.

CHAURIACENSE (Chauriac, Puy-de-Dôme), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict in Auvergne, built by Stephen, bishop of Clermont, and entrusted to Saint Odilo, abbot of Cluny, in 1034, CXLII, 864.

CHEMINONENSE (Cheminon, diocese of Châlons-sur-Marne), a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine, founded before 1102, in which year Paschal II confirmed it by privilege; later it passed to the Cistercians, CLXIII, 99.---Privilege of Calixtus II concerning this monastery’s suit with William, bishop of Châlons, CLXIII, 1152.---The canons adopted the institutions of the Cistercian Order in 1138.---Privilege of Innocent II, CLXXIX, 346.---Letter of Alexander III, 1172, CC, 782.

CHIEMSEENSE SS. SIXTI ET SEBASTIANI (Saint Sebastian and Saint Sixtus of Chiemsee, diocese of Salzburg), a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine, whose possessions and rights Innocent II confirmed in 1142, CLXXIX, 601.

CHIENSEENSIS B. MARIAE (the convent of Blessed Mary of Chiemsee, diocese of Salzburg), a nunnery ruled by Abbess Machildis in 1141; at her request Innocent II granted a privilege, CLXXIX, 540.

CHILIANUS (Saint). See PADERSBORNENSE.

CHORA S. MARTINI (Saint-Martin of Cure, diocese of Autun), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, so named from the river beside which it was built.---Privilege of Pope Alexander III, 1174, CC, 992.

CHORTATO S. MARIAE (Sainte-Marie of Chortato, diocese of Thessalonica), a monastery on whose behalf Innocent III wrote to the bishop of Albano in 1213, CCXVI, 851.

CHREMIFANENSE S. SALVATORIS (Saint-Sauveur of Kremsmünster, Bavaria), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, built by Tassilo, duke of Bavaria, and confirmed by a diploma of Charlemagne in 791, XCVII, 1065.---Diploma of Louis the Pious and his son Lothair, 828, CIV, 1173; CXLI, 1171.

CHREMNENSE, the same as the preceding.

CHRISTINAE S. DE OLONA (Saint Christina at the Sands of Olonne, Poitou), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict. Louis the Pious granted a privilege to its abbot Peter in 822, CIV, 1115.

CHRISTOPHORI S. DE MAGNO VICO (Saint Christopher of Grand-Vic, Aube), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, built by Widric the elder of Danobrium (or Brienne) and his wife Gepa. It was under Abbot Walter; with his consent, the same founders gave it to Blessed Hugh, abbot of Cluny, for governance in 1080, CLIX, 941.

CHRONONENSE. See CRONONENSE.

CHRYSOGONUS (Saint). See ROMANUM.

CHUCENSE S. OSITHAE (Saint Osith of Chuc, diocese of London, England), a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine, whose goods Innocent III confirmed in 1198, CCIV, 240.

CIBARDUS (Saint) (Saint-Cybard, diocese of Angoulême) appears to be the same monastery as Saint Eparchius (Saint-Eparèse or Eparche), founded about 570 and made illustrious by the monk Ademar in 1029, CXLI, 9.---Regular canons held it until 848, CXLI, 27, 79.---It was made subject to Angériac by Urban II in 1096, [Col. 1044] CLI, 443.---Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1198, CCXIV, 183, 209.

CICESTRENSE (Chichester, county of Sussex, England), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, whose abbot Innocent III wrote to concerning the church of Wdehord in 1205, CCXV, 591, 625.

CIKEDORENSE. See STEKEDORENSE.

CILENTIAN MONASTERIES, built in the district of Salerno and on Mount Cilento, which Saint Gregory VII annexed to the monastery of La Cava. These are: Saint Mary of Julia; Saint Nicholas; Saint Michael the Archangel; Saint Magnus; Saint Fabian; Saint George; Saint Matthew; Saint Angel of Mount Corase; Saint Blaise of Ratramnus; Saint John of Turesino; Saint Savior of Nuce; and Saint Zacharias of Lauris. This annexation was effected in 1085, CXLVIII, 720.

CIMOETERIO S. JOANNIS PAPIENSE (Saint John of the Cemetery, outside the gates of Pavia), a monastery which Innocent III took under his protection and whose certain properties he confirmed in 1198, CCXIV, 439.

CINCINNIACO (Cessières, diocese of Laon), a monastery founded near Laon by Saint Amand, bishop, and Duke Fulcoald in 664, LXXXVII, 1271.---It was annexed to the abbey of Barisis, ibid.

CIRICI S. DE BERCARIIS (Saint-Cyr of Perchères, Seine-et-Oise, former diocese of Paris), a nunnery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded by Robert III, bishop of Chartres, in 1156.---Charter of Abbess Soucelina, 1190, CCV, 912.

CISMARENSE S. MARIAE ET S. JOANNIS appears to be the same as LUBECENSE.

CISONIENSE S. CALIXTI (Saint-Calixte of Cisoing, diocese of Tournai), a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine, founded by Rainald, archbishop of Rheims, in 855.---Privilege of Alexander III, 1179, CC, 1265.---Of Celestine III, 1197, CCVI, 1236.---Privilege of William, archbishop of Rheims, 1190, CCIX, 850.---Letter of Innocent III, 1208, CCXV, 1381.

CISTERCIENSE S. MARIAE (Cîteaux, diocese of Châlons-sur-Saône), a celebrated monastery and the head of the new order instituted by Blessed Robert. It was founded in the diocese of Chalon by Odo I, duke of Burgundy, with the consent of Bishop Walter, in 1098. Robert, already abbot of Molesme, came there with certain chosen monks and laid the foundations of his order, CLVII, 1224.---Account of the foundation of Cîteaux, CLX, 1168.---Letter of Walter, bishop of Chalon, to Paschal II, CLXIII, 448.---Calixtus II confirmed the chapters of Cîteaux in 1119, CLXIII, 1147.---Stephen, bishop of Autun, twelfth century, CLXXII, 1309.---Privilege of Innocent II, 1132, CLXXIX, 122.---Of Eugenius III, 1152, CLXXX, 1541.---*Iter Cisterciense*, by James Meckler, parish priest in the Swiss March, 1667. *Description of the tombs of the Abbey of Cîteaux*, by two Benedictines.---Privileges of Alexander III, 1165, CC, 340, 390, 592, 594, 966, 979, 1269, 1287.---Of Lucius III, 1184, CC, 1301.---Of Urban III, 1187, CCII, 1472.---Of Clement III, 1190, CCIV, 1454.---Thomas, Cistercian monk, flourished about 1180, CCVI, 9.---On the foundation of the monastery of Schardeburg in England under Celestine III, 1192, CCVI, 961.---Letters and privileges of Innocent III, 1198, CCXIV, 158, 1031; 1204, CCXV, 355, 683, 1164, 1206, 1546, 1547, 1564; 1210, CCXVI, 283, 410, 411.---Decree of the same pope to all Cistercian abbots concerning the evangelization of Prussia, 1212, CCXVI, 668, 732.

CIVITACULA S. MARIAE (Notre-Dame of La Ciotat, diocese of Aix in Provence), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, whose properties and privileges Urban III confirmed in 1186, CCII, 1364.

CLARAVALLENSE S. MARIAE (Notre-Dame of Clairvaux, former diocese of Langres, Aube), an illustrious monastery and new head of the Cistercian Order, built in 1114 by Saint Bernard, abbot, with the assistance of Hugh, count of Champagne. Within a few years, and under Saint Bernard, this abbey produced more than seventy monasteries in different regions.---At Saint Bernard’s request, Innocent II confirmed the possessions and rights of that monastery in 1132, CLXXIX, 126.---Life and writings of Saint Bernard, CLXXXII–CLXXXV. Canonization of the holy doctor by Alexander III, 1103, CLXXXV, 610.---Charter of Joceran, bishop of Langres, 1121, ibid., 977.---Of Guy, abbot of Molesme, 979.---Of Alfonso, king of Spain, 981; of Queen Sancha, 982.---Of Thierry, count of Flanders, 983.---Of Miroslav, duke of Bohemia, 984.---Of Hato, bishop of Troyes, 985.---Of Theobald, count of Blois, and Jobert of La Ferté, 986.---Of Frederick Salvator of Sinaggio Gundrea, Spain, 987.---Charter of Garnier of Fontaines, 1230, CLXXXV, 1425.---Charter of foundation by Hugh, count of Troyes, 1097, ibid., 1447.---On the foundation of the abbey of Clairvaux, ibid., [Col. 1045] 1535.---Monuments of Clairvaux, 1550.---*Researches on the first site of Clairvaux*, 1698, 1737.---Charter of Robert de Brus, an Englishman, in favor of Clairvaux, 1273, ibid., 1759.---Bull of Honorius concerning relics given to Clairvaux by Cardinal Conrad, 1226, ibid., 1709.---Abbot Fastred flourished in 1163, CLXXXVIII, 1657.---Letters and privileges of Alexander III, 1165, CC, 348, 966.---Peter VIII flourished as abbot in 1186, CCI, 1391.---Henry of Château-Marsiac, abbot, 1188, CCIV, 211.---Letters of Innocent III to the abbot, 1206, CCXV, 1087, 1090; 1212, CCXVI, 635.

CLARETIS S. MARIAE (Notre-Dame des Clairets, diocese of Chartres), a nunnery of the Cistercian Order, built by Matilda, countess of Perche, in 1203.---Privilege of Innocent III in the same year, CCXV, 240.

CLARHOLTENSE S. LAURENTII (Saint-Laurent of Clarholten, diocese of Münster), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, founded before 1146, in which year Eugenius III confirmed it by privilege, CLXXX, 1139.

CLARIACENSE S. PETRI (Saint-Pierre of Clairac, diocese of Agen), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, whose founder is thought to have been Pippin near the end of the eighth century.---It was ravaged by the Albigensians in the thirteenth century.---Letter of Innocent III to the abbot against the archbishop of Auch, 1212, CCXVI, 789.

CLARIFONTIS S. NICOLAI (Claire-Fontaine), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, founded by Bishop Bartholomew and Blessed Norbert; its first abbot was Gerard, 1121, CLVI, 1001.

CLAROMARISCO (Clairmarais, diocese of Saint-Omer), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded in 1128 by Fulk, abbot of La Dune.---Letter of Alexander III to the abbot concerning the protection of the sister of Blessed Thomas of Canterbury, 1166, CC, 508.---Letter of Innocent III to the abbot concerning the reform of Saint-Josse, 1213, CCXVI, 957.

CLASSENSE SS. JOANNIS ET STEPHANI (Saint John of Classe, in the patriarchate of Ravenna), a monastery named from the city in which it is situated, a city formerly built by Julius Caesar on the Adriatic Sea, not far from Ravenna. Claudius, abbot of this monastery, was an intimate of Saint Gregory the Great in 600, LXXVII, 918 note.

CLASSENSE OF ST. SEVERUS (Saint-Sévère de Classe), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose goods and privileges were confirmed by Pope Alexander II in 1062, CXLVI, 1426.

CLASSENSE OF ST. APOLLINARIS (Saint-Apollinaire de Classe), a monastery mentioned in Agisellus, in 669, CVI, 681, 741.---St. Peter Damian writes to the abbot of this monastery, CLIV, 397.---The abbot of Classe takes an oath to Gerbert, then archbishop of Ravenna, in 998, CXXXIX, 269.---Charter of Emperor St. Henry II, 1009, CXL, 286.---Privileges of Lucius II, 1144, CLXXIX, 912; of Lucius III, 1183, CCI, 1244; of Urban III, 1186, CCII, 1371, 1555.

MONASTERY OF ST. CLAUDIUS. See CONDATESCENSE.

CLAUSTRO-NEOBURGENSE. See NIEWBURGENSE.

ST. CLEMENT’S, a monastery situated in the diocese of Genoa, mentioned in a letter of Adrian IV, 1155, CLXXXVIII, 1443.

ST. CLEMENT OF PISCARIA. See PISCARIENSE.

CLIVATENSE OF ST. PETER (Saint-Pierre de Clivati, in the Valtellina or the Grisons), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by Desiderius, king of the Lombards, in 755.---Mentioned at CLXXIII, 1472.

ST. CLODOALD. See NOVIENTENSE.

CLUNIACENSE OF SS. PETER AND PAUL (Saint-Pierre de Cluny, diocese of Mâcon, Saône-et-Loire), the most celebrated monastery, founded by the illustrious William, duke of Aquitaine, and entrusted to Berno as its first abbot, in 931.---Privilege of Pope John XI, CXXXII, 1055, 1058.---Likewise, privileges of Leo VII, 937, ibid., 1068, 1069, 1074, 1082.---St. Odo succeeded Berno, CXXXIII, 15.---Beginnings of this monastery, ibid., 94.---Privilege of Agapetus II under St. Aymard as abbot, 950, ibid., 900; of John XIII, CXXXV, 990; of Benedict VII, CXXXVII, 332.---Cartulary of Cluny under St. Aymard, ibid., 783.---St. Maiolus became abbot, 954, ibid., 707; St. Odilo, 778.---Privilege of Pope Gregory V, 932.---Letter of Peter Damian, CXLIV, 378.---Privileges of Sylvester II, 1003, CXXXIX, 283; of Benedict VIII, ibid., 1601.---[Privilege] of John XIX, by which he confirms all rights, goods, and privileges, 1027, ibid., 1135, 1145, 1146.---Rodulfus Glaber, monk, 1048, CXLII, 609.---St. Odilo, abbot, 1049, ibid., 831.---Charters of Odilo, 1039, 1041.---Charter of Count Amadeus, 1042.---Privileges of St. Leo IX, 1049, CXLIII, 607;
