of Victor II, ibid., 803.---Letter and privilege of Pope Stephen X, ibid., 879; of Alexander II, 1063, CXLVI, 1293.---Privileges of St. Gregory VII, 1075, CXLVIII, 661, 699.---Udalricus, monk, flourished in 1086, CXLIX, 633.---Pope Urban II, formerly a monk and prior of Cluny, 1076.---Privileges of Urban, [Col. 1046] CLI, 43, 291, 410, 441, 485, 493.---St. Hugh, abbot of Cluny, 1109, CLIX, 845.---Letter of Clementia, countess of Flanders, to Hugh concerning the reform of the monastery of St. Bertin, 939.---Charters and various donations made for the benefit of Cluny under St. Hugh as abbot, 955 and following.---Privileges and letters of Paschal II, CLXIII, 51, 53, 56, 81, 173, 204, 220, 225, 260, 262, 281, 338, 359, 442.---Privileges of Gelasius, 1118, ibid., 492, 509; of Calixtus II, 1120, ibid., 1164, 1189.---He congratulates Peter, abbot of Cluny, 1256.---Concerning Abbot Pons, deprived of office, 1314.---Privilege of Honorius II, CLXVI, 1225.---Brief of Honorius II against Pons, formerly abbot of Cluny, 1126, ibid., 1258, 1259.---Authority is affirmed for Abbot Peter, 1265.---Letter of Innocent [II] to Peter the Venerable concerning money granted by Henry, king of England, 1131, CLXXIX, 96.---An indulgence of forty days granted by the same Innocent II to penitents at Cluny, 1132, ibid., 127.---Privilege of Innocent II, 129.---Concerning the administration of the abbey of St. Bertin, 135.---Privileges of the same pope, 268, 444, 478, 636; of Celestine II, 1144, ibid., 810; of Lucius II, 1144, ibid., 887, 888; of Eugenius III, 1146, CLXXX, 1105, 1272; of Anastasius IV, 1153, CLXXXVIII, 1042, 1070; of Adrian IV, 1154, ibid., 1415, 1426.---Writings of Peter the Venerable, abbot, 1158, CLXXXIX, 9.---Charter of Adalbero, bishop of Liège, 1124, ibid., 1055.---[Charter] of Renaud, archbishop of Rheims, 1125, ibid., 1058, 1056.---[Charter] of King Louis VII, 1130, 1060, 1061.---Diploma of Stephen, king of England, 1133, ibid., 1063.---[Charter] of Hato, bishop of Troyes, 1138, ibid., 1066.---Charter of Count William concerning the monasteries of Mauziac and Celsiniac, 1153, ibid., 1067.---[Charter] of Emperor Frederick concerning the monastery of Balne, 1070; [of] Richard, bishop of Coutances, concerning the church of Morsalines, 1071.---Letters and privileges of Alexander III, 1159, CC, 113, 967, 1060, 1093, 1166, 1297, 1316; of Lucius III, 1185, CCI, 1326; of Urban III, 1186, CCII, 1365, 1379; of Clement III, 1188, CCIV, 1303, 1307, 1312, 1317; of Celestine III, 1191, CCVI, 890, 916, 918, 1179.---Hugh V, abbot of Cluny, flourished in 1203, CCIX, 881.---Letters and privileges of Innocent III, 1204, CCXV, 526, 1338, 1339; CCXVI, 791; CCXVII, 19, 230.---Concerning the right of correction granted to abbots, 234, 242.

CLUNICENSE (Gleinck, in the duchy of Nassau, Bavaria), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, which Otto, bishop of Bamberg, purchased from Margrave Leopold in 1132, CLXXIII, 1279.

CLUSANIENSE or CLUSINENSE (Chiuzi, in the territory of Siena), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, to whose monks Pope Celestine III wrote in 1191, CCVI, 898.

CLUSIENSE OF ST. MICHAEL (Saint-Michel de Cluse, in Savoy), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded in 966 by Hugh, count of Auvergne, whose first abbot was Benedict, CL, 1449, 1452.---Life of Benedict, abbot of Cluse, by William, his disciple, ibid., 1456.---St. Anselm lodged in this monastery, CLVIII, 98.---Privilege of Innocent III confirming a certain union, 1212, CCXVI, 682.

CLUSINCENSE (Les Clouzeaux, in the Vendée), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, to whose abbot Innocent wrote, directing him to refrain from usurpation to the detriment of the monastery, 1130, ibid., 72.

COACENSE or QUOTIACENSE. See THE MONASTERIES OF AUXERRE.

COLA (de). See ST. JOHN.

GOLDEN HEAVEN. See PAPIENSE.

COLLE BERTANNI (de), OF ST. JAMES (Saint-Jacques de Colle Bertanno, Italy), a hospital whose goods Innocent III took under his protection in 1204, CCXV, 509.

COLCESTRIENSE (Colchester, England), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, whose rights and possessions Paschal II confirmed, 1099–1118, CLXIII, 443.

COLDIZENSE (Colditz, in Saxony), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine which Innocent II, at the request of the bishops of Halberstadt and Bamberg, confirmed by privilege in 1142, CLXXIX, 599.---Privilege of Innocent III, 1208, CCXV, 1465.

COLIMBRIENSE. See OF THE CROSS.

COLONIENSE OF ST. CUNIBERT (Saint-Cunibert of Cologne), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, in which St. Bruno, founder of the Carthusians, was educated and made a canon, about 1076, CLII, 36.

COLONIENSE OF ST. PANTALEON (Saint-Pantaléon of Cologne), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose possessions and privileges Pope Benedict VII confirmed, in accordance with the wish of its imperial founder and foundress, in 976, CXXXVIII, 326.---Wolbero, abbot of St. Pantaleon, flourished in 1167, CXCV, 1001.

COLONIENSE OF ST. ANDREW (Saint-André of Cologne), [Col. 1047] a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, whose abbot commends himself to the prayers of St. Hildegard, abbess of St. Rupert’s, in the twelfth century, CXCVII, 310.

COLUDUNENSIS, a nunnery situated in England, whose abbess was Aebba, aunt of King Aelfrid, in 684, XCVI, 201.---It was destroyed by fire, 215.

ST. MARY OF COLUMBA (Sainte-Marie de Colomba, diocese of Piacenza), a monastery of the Cistercian Order and derived from Clairvaux; at the request of St. Bernard, Innocent II fortified it with a privilege in 1137, CLXXIX, 311.---Privilege of Eugenius III, 1145, CLXXX, 1041.---Letter of Innocent III, 1205, CCXVI, 735; CCXVI, 438.

SENONENSE OF ST. COLUMBA (Sainte-Colombe de Sens), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict.---Ordinance of Bishop Emmo concerning obedience owed to the abbot, 659, LXXXVIII, 1168. The same [bishop] confirmed the privileges of this monastery, 1171.---Letter of Celestine III concerning the priory of La Charité, 1196, CCVI, 1181.---Privileges of Innocent III, 1206, CCXV, 819; CCXVI, 422. Letter of the same, 718; CCXVII, 77, 100.

ST. COLUMBAN. See LUXOVIENSE.

COLUMBANIENSE OF ST. PATROCLUS (Colombiers in the former diocese of Bourges), a monastery built by St. Patroclus, abbot, near Mont Lucius (Mont-Luçon), about 541, LXXI, 1054.

COMENSE OF ST. ABUNDIUS (Saint-Abond of Como, in Lombardy), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, to which certain goods were confirmed by Louis the Pious in 818, CIV, 1087.---Diploma of 824, CIV, 1136, 1137.---Privilege of Urban II, 1095, CLI, 417.

COMENSE OF ST. FIDELIS (Saint-Fidèle of Como in the Milanese), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, built before 1116, in which year Paschal II granted it privileges, CLXIII, 393, 417.

COMODOLIACENSE OF ST. JUNIAN (Saint-Junien-les-Combles, diocese of Limoges), a monastery founded by St. Amandus and St. Junian beside the Vigenna (the Vienne), in the territory of Limoges, about 500. It began as a mere cell, gradually grew into a monastery, and later passed to secular canons, LXXI, 903 note.

COMPENDIENSE OF ST. MARY (Notre-Dame de Compiègne, Oise), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded near Verberie by Queen Constance, wife of King Robert.---Privilege of King Robert, 1029, CXLI, 968.---[Privilege] of Eugenius III, 1150, CLXXX, 1435.---[Of] Alexander III, 1162, CC, 180, 181, 314, 320, 659, 837, 842, 940, 947.---Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, appointing the bishop of Senlis as judge for him, 1198, CCXIV, 406, 435; 1204, CCXV, 504; CCXVII, 161.

COMPENDIENSE HOSPITAL (Brothers of the hospice of Compiègne), which Alexander III united to the preceding monastery in 1164, CC, 305, 314.

COMPLUTENSE. See ST. PETER OF THE MOUNTAINS.

CONA (de), OF ST. PETER (Saint-Pierre de Cône-sur-Loire, diocese of Nevers), a monastery of the Benedictine Order, whose goods and privileges Alexander III confirmed in 1172, CC, 889.

CONCHENSE OF CASTELLETO (Conches, diocese of Évreux), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by Roger the Englishman in 1035; Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, granted it the church of Castellato (Sainte-Foy de Châtillon-Largentière) in 1077, CLXVII, 509.---Concerning the foundation of this monastery, CCII, 1316.---Letter of Innocent III concerning the abbot of this monastery, 1198, CCXIV, 264, 573.

CONCHENSE or CONCHARUM (Conques, diocese of Cahors), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, in the diocese of Cahors, now that of Rodez, built, as it seems, by Bishop Ambrose in 755, LXXXIX, 1208.---It was subsequently converted into a priory, ibid.---Diploma of Louis the Pious, 818, CIV, 1090.---It was given by King Pippin to the monastery of Figeac about the same period, 755, CXLI, 23.---Likewise, this donation was confirmed by Pope Gregory VII in 1080, CXLVIII, 707.---Privilege of Eugenius III, 1153, CLXXX, 1601.

CONDAMINA OF ST. MARY (Notre-Dame de la Condamine, diocese of Geneva), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, built in the twelfth century; Innocent III wrote to its abbot concerning an accusation against the bishop of Besançon in 1211, CCXVI, 479.

CONDATENSE OF ST. MARY (Notre-Dame de Condé, former diocese of Cambrai), a very wealthy nunnery built on the Scheldt in the diocese of Cambrai, believed to have been founded by St. Amandus about 580.---Afterwards declining, it passed to certain secular canons, sixth century, CXLIX, 140.

CONDATENSE OF ST. MARTIN (Candé, diocese of Tours), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built at the confluence of the Loire and Vienne in the sixth century, LXXI, 184, 477.

CONDATESCENSE or OF ST. EUGENDUS IN THE JURA (Abbey of Saint-Oyand in the Jura), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, [Col. 1048] which later took the name of St. Claudius; it was founded in the Jura Mountains by Abbot Suspicius and his companion Romanus about 520, LXXI, 1042 note.---It took its name from Abbot Eugendus, ibid.---Privilege of St. Ado, bishop of Vienne, 870, CXXIII, 443.---Charter of Hugh, count of Troyes and Bar, 1101, CLXXV, 1460.

CONDOMENSE OF ST. PETER (Saint-Pierre de Condom, diocese of Bordeaux), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose possessions and rights Pope Gregory VII, at the request of Abbot Raymond, confirmed by privilege in 1076, CXLVIII, 668.

CONFLUENTENSE OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY, later OF ST. FLORIAN (Notre-Dame de Conflans near Trier), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, situated between the Rhine and the Moselle, which Emperor St. Henry II gave to Poppo, bishop of Trier, in 1018, CXL, 338.---Letter of the abbot commending himself to the prayers of St. Hildegard, twelfth century, CXCVII, 309.

CONFLUENTENSE OF ST. GEORGE (Conflans-en-Jarnisy, diocese of Metz), a monastery situated in Lorraine, to which King Childeric granted certain lands in 673, LXXXVII, 1298.

CONFLUENTENSE OF ST. HONORINA (Conflans-Sainte-Honorine), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded near Paris by Ivo of Beaumont, at the place where the Oise joins the Seine, and granted to the abbey of Bec in 1080, CLVIII, 1163.

CONSIACENSE OF ST. PETER (Saint-Pierre de Coincy, diocese of Soissons), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in 1072 by Theobald, count of Champagne, and later made subject to Cluny.---Privilege of Urban III, 1185, CCII, 1333.

CHAPTER OF ST. STEPHEN AT CONSTANCE (community or collegiate church of Saint-Étienne of Constance, Switzerland), whose goods and privileges Adrian IV confirmed in 1159, CLXXXVIII, 1611.

CONSTANTIENSE OF ST. SAVIOUR (Saint-Sauveur de Coutances), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by Nigel the viscount, eleventh century, CCII, 1318.

ST. CONSTANCE OF CIVITAVECCHIA (Saint-Constance de Civita-Vecchia, Italy), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, whose possessions and privileges Adrian IV confirmed in 1156, CLXXXVIII, 1477.

CONSTANTINOPOLITAN OF ST. MARY (Convent of St. Mary at Constantinople), a monastery which St. Peter Damian teaches us existed in the eleventh century for Latin monks, CXLIV, 396.

CONSTANTINOPOLITAN HOSPITAL CALLED “OF THE MOUTH OF THE LION” (*de Bucca Leonis*) (Hospitallers of Constantinople), in Innocent III, 1207, CCXV, 1364; CCXVI, 77.

CONSTANTINOPOLITAN STUDIENSE (Convent of Stoudios at Constantinople), a monastery which became very celebrated under Abbot Theodore, called the Studite, in 795; he vigorously assailed the Iconoclasts. St. Leo IX wrote to Abbot Nicetas concerning continence to be maintained by subdeacons, 1054, CXLIII, 781.

CONSTANTINOPOLITAN OF SS. JOHN AND SAMSON (Hospitallers of St. John of Constantinople). Alexander III commends a certain brother of this house to the Master at Jerusalem, 1163, CC, 273.---Privilege of Innocent III, 1208, CCXV, 1435; CCXVI, 217.

CONVENTRENSE (Coventry, diocese of Lincoln in Warwickshire), an ancient monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded and very frequently enriched by the kings of England, but long since destroyed. Celestine III wrote to the archbishop of Canterbury and the bishop of Lincoln concerning its restoration, 1197, CCVI, 1234.---Letter of Innocent III rebuking the bishop because he had expelled the monks from their monastery, 1198, CCXIV, 208; 1208, CCXV, 1528.

CONVENTRIENSE OF THE BLESSED MARY (Coventry, Warwickshire), a monastery founded in England by Earl Leofric, which Pope Alexander II endowed with privileges in 1063, CXLVI, 1299.---Privilege of Lucius II, 1144, CLXXIX, 862.

CORBEIENSE OF ST. PETER (Saint-Pierre de Corbie, diocese of Amiens), a distinguished monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built near the Somme by St. Clotilda and her son Clothar in 550, LXXI, 688 note.---Cartulary of this abbey under Adalhard, CV, 535.---Enlarged by St. Bathildis, LXXXVII, 670.---Diplomas of Clothar III, 1280, 1282; of Theodoric, 681, 1330; of Chilperic II, 716, LXXXVIII, 1123.---Charter of Berthefred, bishop of Amiens, 1178.---Diploma of Charlemagne, 769, XCVII, 915.---Privilege of Pope Nicholas I, CXIX, 815.---Paschasius Radbertus became master and then abbot, about 820, CXX, 11.---Privilege of the Council of Paris addressed to Paschasius Radbertus, 846, CXX, 27.---His predecessor Adalhard had been sent into exile at the monastery of Héri, CXX, 1528.---Ratramnus, monk, flourished in 868, CXXI, 9.---Privilege of Pope Nicholas V, [Col. 1049] 887, CXXIX, 794.---Likewise [that] of Benedict III, CXXIX, 1001; of Adrian II, 870, ibid., 1019; of the antipope Christopher, CXXXI, 45.---Widukind, monk, flourished in 983, CXXXVII, 114.---Privilege of Benedict VII, CXXXVII, 339.---Diploma of King Robert against the oppressor Elfled of Encre, 1016, CXLI, 955.---Privilege of Pope St. Leo IX, 1050, CXLIII, 641.---Letter of Alexander II to Gervase, archbishop of Rheims, for the defense of Corbie, CXLVI, 1283, 1321.---Charter of Guy, bishop of Amiens, 1066, CXLVI, 1507.---Privileges of Urban II, 1096, CLI, 456; of Paschal II, CLXIII, 215, 293.---Privileges of Eugenius III, 1147, CLXXX, 1260, 1332, 1491, 1493.---Wibald of Stavelot became abbot of Corbie, 1137, CLXXXIX, 1075.---Anastasius IV granted Wibald the use of a ring, 1153, CLXXXVIII, 1032.---Privilege granted by Adrian IV at Wibald’s request, 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1389.---The same [pope] subjects the monastery of Werben to Corbie, 1434.---[Privileges of] Alexander III, 1172, CC, 758, 847, 861, 1010; of Lucius III, 1184, CCI, 1294.---Privileges of Innocent III, 1198, CCXIV, 450, 455, 478; 1203, CCXV, 205, 1386, 1387; 1210, CCXVI, 193, 503.

CORBEIENSE-NEW (Corvey or New Corbie, diocese of Paderborn), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, endowed in Saxony and the diocese of Paderborn with many goods by Louis the Pious and St. Abbot Adalhard in 823, CIV, 1128, 1129, 1150, 1205, 1228, 1229, 1244, 1245.---Privilege of Emperor St. Henry II, 1002, CXL, 247.---Diploma of Emperor Conrad II, 1025, CLI, 1045, 1052; of Emperor Henry III, 1039, CLI, 1085, 1089.---Diploma of Frederick, archbishop of Cologne, 1120, CLXVI, 1352.---Privilege of Emperor Frederick, CLXXXIX, 1502.---Letter of Abbot Theodoric, 1337, CLXXXIX, 1506.

CORBINIACENSE OF ST. MARCULF (Corbeny), a monastery or priory in the diocese of Laon, subject to the abbey of St. Remigius, whose goods and privileges Pope St. Leo IX confirmed in 1049, CXLIII, 619.---Urban II commands Bishop Ingelram to restore that monastery to St. Remigius of Rheims, 1098, CLI, 539.---Paschal II exempts it from subjection to the monastery of Flavigny, 1107, CLXIII, 220.---Letter of Adrian IV concerning the reform of this monastery, 1155, CLXXXVIII, 1442.

CORBIONENSE or CURBIONENSE (Saint-Laumer de Corbion, diocese of Chartres), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict. Ansegisus, abbot of Fontenelle, 833, CV, 744; and in the Life of St. Bathildis, 590, LXXXVII, 669, note.

CORBOLIENSE OF ST. MARY (Notre-Dame de Corbeil, diocese of Versailles), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded in the time of Louis VI; Henry and Philip, brothers of Louis VII, were its abbots. Privilege of Alexander III, 1176, CC, 1043.

CORBOLIENSE OF ST. EXUPERIUS (Saint-Spire de Corbeil, former diocese of Paris), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded in 950.---Privilege of Celestine III, 1199, CCVI, 1199.

CORBOLIENSE OF ST. MARY OF THE FIELDS (Notre-Dame-des-Champs at Corbeil), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, built before 1125.---Privilege of Innocent III, 1214, CCXVII, 234.

MONASTERIES OF CORDOBA in the time of St. Eulogius:

1. Within the city: St. Acisclus, in whose church his body rested; St. Zoilus the martyr, with his tomb; SS. Faustus, Januarius, and Martialis, where their ashes were kept; St. Cyprian; St. Genesius; St. Eulalia the virgin.

2. Outside the city: St. Christopher beyond the river; the monastery of St. Mary of Cuteclara in the mountains neighboring Córdoba; the monastery of Tabanos, founded by St. Eulogius in the same mountains; St. Saviour of Pilemelar, built in the same period and places; Armilatense, on the bank of the river Armilata, founded by St. Zoilus; St. Felix, situated in the town of Froniano; St. Martin near the town of Royana; SS. Justus and Pastor at the village of Leinlense, 859, CXV, 919.

CORMELIENSE OF ST. MARY (Notre-Dame de Cormeille, between Lisieux and Pont-Audemer, Normandy), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in 1060 by the nobleman William, son of Osbern of Préaux.---Privilege of Alexander III, 1169, CL, 580.---This monastery is mentioned, CCII, 1316.

CORMERICENSE or CORMARICENSE OF ST. PAUL (Cormery-sur-Indre), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by Itherius, abbot of St. Martin of Tours, in 780 with Charlemagne’s assistance; it was thus dependent on Marmoutier. Privilege of Charlemagne, 800, XCVII, 992, 993.---Alcuin, Itherius’s successor, built three altars there, CI, 1430.---The first abbots were James and Odacer, 1431.---Diplomas of Louis the Pious, 807, CIV, 981, 1040, 1195, 1301.---Mention of the same, CXIX, 561.---Guy, formerly abbot, restored things unjustly taken away, 996, CXXXVII, 853.---Ordinance of King Robert, [Col. 1050] 1018, CXLI, 957, 959.---By a bull of Urban II, the abbots of Cormery are bound to receive the pastoral staff at the tomb of St. Martin, CLI, 456.---Agreement between the abbot of St. Paul and Robert of Arbrissel, 1109, CLXII, 1092.

CORONA (de) (La Couronne, diocese of Angoulême, Charente), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, founded in 1122 by Lambert, a cleric of Angoulême.---Letter of Innocent III, 1202, CCXIV, 1162; CCXV, 315.

CORSARUM. See ROMANUM.

CORSICENSE (island of Corsica), a monastery of men built by Sabina, a religious woman, in the time of St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 301.

CORTENBERGENSIS OF ST. MARY (Notre-Dame de Cortenberg, Belgium), a nunnery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded between Brussels and Louvain by Blessed Columban, abbot, and Duke Godfrey; by a charter Odo, bishop of Cambrai, granted it many things in 1110, CLX, 1155.

ST. COSMAS OF VICOVARO (Saint-Côme de Vicovaro, diocese of Pavia), a monastery whose goods Innocent III received under his protection in 1212, CCXCXVI, 633.

SS. COSMAS AND DAMIAN (Saint-Côme and Saint-Damien, Spain), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, mentioned in the Life of St. Maximus, 644, LXXX, 612.

SS. COSMAS AND DAMIAN OF THE MOUNTAIN (Saint-Cosmas and Damian of the Mountain, in Illyria), a monastery to which Innocent III granted a privilege in 1209, CCXVII, 194.

ST. COSMAS. See TURONENSE.

ST. COSMAS, a nunnery. See TALIACOTTIENSE.

COSTENSE (Costa, diocese of Braga, Portugal), a monastery to which Innocent III enjoins obedience to its bishop, 1199, CCXIV, 704.

COTUMENSIS (Nuns of Cotum, diocese of Lincoln, England), a nunnery for which Alexander III wrote to the bishops of York and Lincoln, 1177, CC, 1136.

COWENTRENSE. See CONVENTRENSE.

COXNAO (de). See CUXANENSE.

CRASSENSE OF ST. MARY (Notre-Dame de la Grasse, diocese of Carcassonne), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by Abbot Nimfridus and confirmed by diploma of Charlemagne in 779, XCVII, 962, C, 489 note.---Diploma of Louis the Pious, 814, CIV, 992, 963.---Privilege of Pope Agapetus II, 951, CXXXIII, 908.---Likewise, bull of Gelasius II, 1118, CLXIII, 504.---[Privilege] of Calixtus II, by which the church of Valeries is granted, ibid., 1114.---Letter of Eugenius III concerning observance of Urban II’s decree, 1153, CLXXX, 1593.

CREDONENSE. See below, CRONIENSE.

CREMELLENSE or CREMENSE OF ST. PETER (Saint-Pierre de Crême, Venetian States), a nunnery founded by Robald, bishop of Milan; a privilege of Urban III mentions its deed of foundation, 1187, CCII, 1490.

CREMENSE OF ST. BENEDICT (Saint-Benoît de Crême, Venetian States), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by Henry, count of Bergamo, and granted to the Apostolic See by Roger, bishop of Volterra and son of its founder, according to the tenor of a privilege of Pope Calixtus II, 1123, CLXIII, 1281.

CREMONENSE OF THE HOLY CROSS (Santa Croce of Cremona), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, which the monks of Nonantola claimed belonged to them before Pope Celestine III in 1196, CCVI, 1171.

CREMONENSE OF ST. LAWRENCE (Saint-Laurent of Cremona), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built before 1040; in that year Emperor Henry III, assenting to the bishop’s request, forbade the abbot to alienate the goods of this monastery, CLI, 1090.

CREMONENSE OF ST. GABRIEL (Saint-Gabriel of Cremona), a monastery to whose prior Innocent III wrote in 1203, CCXV, 139, 168.

CREMONENSE OF ST. MARY (Notre-Dame of Cremona), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, whose goods and privileges Calixtus II, after Urban II, confirmed in 1123, CLXIII, 1269.---Concerning its dispute with its bishop, ibid., 1316.

CREMONENSE OF ST. PETER (Saint-Pierre of Cremona), a monastery of St. Augustine. Decree of Calixtus II granting the election of the abbot to the bishop, 1120, CLXIII, 1177.

CREMONENSE OF ST. THOMAS (Saint-Thomas of Cremona), a monastery whose abbot wrote to Innocent III to ask whether, because of his infirmities, he might be permitted to resign his office, 1203, CCXV, 168.

CREMONENSE OF ST. JOHN (Saint-Jean of Cremona), a nunnery built by Count Bernard and his wife Bertha shortly before 1066, when he confirmed it by privilege, CLI, 484.

CREUZLINGENSE OF SS. UDALRIC AND AFRA (Saint-Udalric and Saint Afra of Kreuzlingen, at the gates of Constance, Switzerland), a monastery of regular canons whose goods Honorius II confirmed in 1125, CLXVI, 1270.

CRISENONENSIS OF ST. MARY (Crisenon, between Cravant [Col. 1051] and Vermenton on the Yonne, former diocese of Auxerre), at first a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict built in 1030 by Countess Adelaide, daughter of King Robert. It later became a nunnery, under Guy, abbot of Molesme, and was transformed into an abbey according to a privilege of Innocent II, 1140, CLXXIX, 519.---Privilege of Eugenius III, 1146, CLXXX, 1096; of Celestine III, 1196, CCVI, 1163.

CRISPIENSE OF ST. ARNULF (Saint-Arnoul de Crépy, diocese of Amiens), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in 1008 by Walter the White, count of Amiens.---It passed to Cluny in 1078.---Charter of Godfrey, bishop of Amiens, 1108, LXXII, 742.---Privilege by which Innocent II assigns it to the monastery of Cluny, 1130, CLXXIX, 67.---[Privilege] of Alexander III, 1162, CC, 147; of Lucius III, 1183, CCI, 1245.

CRISPINENSE OF ST. PETER (Saint-Pierre de Crespin, between Mons and Valenciennes), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by St. Landelin about 640, CXLIX, 140.---Privilege of Pope Urban II, 1099, CLI, 522.

ST. CRISPIN IN CAVEA or CAGIA (Saint-Crépin-en-Chaye, former diocese of Soissons), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in the fifth century, perhaps by the holy bishops Principius and Lupus. It was first ceded to canons of the Order of St. Augustine, but after its restoration in the eleventh century adopted the Rule of St. Benedict, LXXI, 350.---Privilege of Innocent II, 1142, CLXXIX, 619.---[Privilege] of Lucius III, 1181, CCI, 1086.

CRISPINIENSE (Religious of Crispino, in the countryside of Florence), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, which formerly had a suit with the monastery of St. Lawrence at Bifurco over a certain hospital; Innocent II settled it in 1230, CLXXIX, 625.

CRISTA (de) (La Crête, diocese of Langres), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded in 1121 by the counts of Champagne.---Letter of Innocent III, 1199, CCXIV, 793.

CRONIENSE, also CREDONENSE and CROVIENSE (Craon), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, situated in Anjou, LXXI, 900 note.---This monastery became the subject of litigation between the brethren of St. Albinus of Angers and those of Vendôme under Pope Nicholas in 1059; he assigned it to the men of Vendôme, CXLVI, 143; CXLVII, 1243.

CRONENSE, also CHRONONENSE (Cornon or Cournon), a monastery in Auvergne founded by St. Gallus, bishop of Clermont, about 554, LXXI, 303, 1030 note.

CRONCHTALLENSIS OF ST. GANGOLF, a German nunnery whose location is unknown to us. Its abbess once wrote to St. Hildegard, commending herself to her prayers, twelfth century, CXCVII, 329, 338.

CROYLANDENSE (Croyland, an island in Lincolnshire, England), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded in 716 by Æthelbald, king of the Mercians.---It was made illustrious by Roger, a monk and author of the Life of St. Thomas of Canterbury, CXC, 257.

CRUCENBERGENSIS-MONTIS (Mount Crucenberg, in Hesse), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose goods Pope Celestine III confirmed in 1191, CCVI, 898.

OF THE HOLY CROSS, ANGLIENSE (Sainte-Croix d’Angle, diocese of Poitiers), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, built in 1175 by William Tantpis, bishop of Poitiers.---Privilege of Innocent III, 1210, CCXVI, 381. (It seems to be the same as St. John of Angliac. See ANGLIACENSE.)

OF THE HOLY CROSS, BURIENSE (Sainte-Croix de Buris, near Metz), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, formerly called St. Eligius, founded in 1124 by Zacharias, abbot of Justemont, and endowed by certain pious and noble men.---Privilege of Alexander III, 1180, CC, 1312.

OF THE HOLY CROSS OF ST. LEUFREDUS (Croix-Saint-Leufroy, near Évreux, Eure), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by St. Leufredus himself in 692. In the ninth century its monks fled from the Northmen to St. Germanus of the Meadows, CCII, 1316.---Privilege of Innocent III, 1199, CCXIV, 645.

OF THE CROSS-BEARERS, ST. PETER’S (Hospice of St. Peter of the Cross-Bearers at Boica in Illyria), a monastery whose rector, Matthew, received a privilege from Urban III in 1186, CCII, 1387.

OF THE HOLY CROSS OF AVELLANA. See AVELLANENSE.

OF THE HOLY CROSS OF LEIRENA (Sainte-Croix de Leyrena, diocese of Coimbra, Portugal), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, which Innocent III recalls to obedience to the bishop, 1198, CCXIV, 191, 302, 773; CCXV, 232.

OF THE HOLY CROSS. See ENGESHEIMENSIS.

CRUDATENSE (Cruas, near Rochemaure, Ardèche), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded on the Rhône in the diocese of Viviers by Count Elpodorius; at the request of Abbot Bonald, Louis the Pious confirmed it by privilege in 817, CIV, 1063.

CRYPTA FERRATA (Monks of the Iron Crypt, near Rome), a monastery whose disputed case with the Knights Templar of Ovinento was decided by Innocent III in 1211, CCXVI, 456.

[Col. 1052] ST. CUCUFAS, also called OCTOVIENSE or VALLENSE (Convent of St. Cucufas or Octovio, in Catalonia), an equally celebrated and wealthy monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose possessions Urban II confirmed in 1098, CLI, 513.---Privilege of Calixtus II, 1120, CLXIII, 1159; letter of Innocent III concerning the correction of this monastery, 1211, CCXVI, 511.

CUISSIACENSE OF ST. MARY (Notre-Dame de Cuissy, diocese of Laon), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, built by Walter of Jumigny and Bishop Bartholomew in 1122, CLVI, 1001.---Privilege of Eugenius III, 1143, CLXXX, 1074.---Letter of Alexander III against the canons of St. Peter of Laon in favor of this monastery, 1174, CC, 932.---Letter of Innocent III concerning aid for the Holy Places, 1199, CCXIV, 934.

OF THE CULTURE, ST. PETER OF LE MANS (Saint-Pierre de la Couture, at Le Mans), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in the suburb of Le Mans by Bishop Bertrand in 589; Avesgot became its abbot in 1072, CXLIII, 1431.---Decree of Innocent III, 1205, CCXV, 740.

CUMENSE or OF THE ISLAND OF CUMAE (Cumes-en-l’Île, in Terra di Lavoro, Naples), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, dedicated to St. Euphemia.---Privilege of Alexander III, 1178, CC, 1171.

ST. CUNEGUND, or THE LOWER MONASTERY (St. Cunegund, or the lower convent at Paderborn), a nunnery to which, at the abbess’s request, Emperor St. Henry II granted a privilege in 1002, CLX, 242.

ST. CUNIBERT. See COLONIENSE.

CUPERSANUM OF ST. VINCENT (Saint-Vincent of Conversano, in Terra di Bari, Naples), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, once very flourishing. It was confirmed by privilege in 1110, CLXIII, 277.---But after discipline had grown lax, Celestine III wrote to the bishops of Polignano and Conversano concerning its reform and restoration in 1194, CCVI, 1034.

CUPRO (de) (Cupar, diocese of Brechin, county of Angus, Scotland), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded by King Malcolm III in 1160.---Privilege of Innocent III, 1206, CCXV, 870.

CURATIO OF ST. MARY (St. Mary of Corato, diocese of Reggio, Naples), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded by Roger of Marturano shortly before 1129, when Honorius honored it with a privilege, CLXVI, 1298.---Letter of Clement III, 1188, CCIV, 1357.---Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1203, CCXV, 250.

CURBA FOSSA OF THE HOLY TRINITY. See LUCERNENSE.

CURBIONENSE. See CORBIONENSE.

COURT-OF-GOD, ST. MARY’S (Notre-Dame de la Cour-Dieu, diocese of Orléans), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded in 1118 by John II, bishop of Orléans.---Privilege of Pope Alexander III, 1162, CC, 155.---Privilege of Lucius III, 1185, CCI, 1317.---Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1204, CCXV, 543, 1228, 1271, 1419.

CURIENSE OF ST. LUCIUS (Saint-Luce de Curlo, Italy), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, whose possessions and privileges Eugenius III confirmed in 1149, CLXXX, 1400.

CURTO RIVO, or MONASTERY OF THE RIVER OF NUNS (Conrupt or Montier-Rup-aux-Nonnains, on the Meuse, diocese of Toul), a nunnery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in 1060.---Privilege of Innocent III, 1198, CCXIV, 502.

CUSSANTIENSE OF ST. JOHN THE BAPTIST (Cusance, diocese of Besançon), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by St. Ermenfrid in the seventh century and subject to Luxeuil; later, made a priory, it was annexed to the abbey of St. Claudius by the testament of St. Ansegisus, abbot of Fontenelle, in 833, CV, 746.

CUSSIACENSE OF ST. MARY. See above, CUISSIACENSE.

ST. CUTHBERT OF RADEFORD (Saint-Cuthbert of Redford, England), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, founded by William of Suvelo before 1159, when Alexander III confirmed it by privilege, CC, 103.

CUXANENSE OF SS. MICHAEL AND GERMANUS (Saint-Michel de Cussan, diocese of Perpignan), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in the diocese of Elne by the brothers of Exalat, in 878.—Pope Agapetus II confirmed its possessions and rights, at the request of Abbot Gaudefred, in 950, CXXXIII, 903.—Privileges of John XIII, CXXXV, 969; of Sergius IV, 1011, CXXXIX, 1504.—The monk Garcius flourished there in 1045, CXLI, 1441.—Origins of this monastery, 1443. Privilege of Innocent II, 1130, CLXXIX, 69.

CYPRIAN (ST.). See PICTAVIENSE.

CYRIACUS (ST.), NUNNERY. See GERNRODENSIS.

CYRIACUS (ST.) (now Saint-Cirgues), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded in Auvergne before 560.—Once made illustrious by a miracle of St. Sidonius, bishop, LXXII, 157, 1021.

CZERWIŃSK OF ST. MARY (St. Mary of Czerwińsk near Płock in Poland), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, founded before 1154; in that year, at the request of Prior Guy, Adrian confirmed the rights and possessions of its monastery by privilege, CLXXXVIII, 1404.

PRIORY OF DAGUILIAC (Deuilly), founded in 1044 by the nobleman Walter and his wife Odila, and confirmed by Bruno, then bishop of Toul and afterwards Pope Leo IX, CXLIII, 587.

DALON OF ST. MARY (Notre-Dame de Dalon, diocese of Limoges), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, built by Gerald de Salis in 1114.—Letter of Innocent III to its abbot concerning the election of the abbot of Tulle, 1212, CCXVI, 643.

DAMIAN OF DONARIA (ST.) (Saint-Damien de Donari, in the Milanese), a nunnery subject to the same abbess as Farinata.—Privilege of Alexander III, 1169, CC, 602. See FARINATENSIS.

HERMITAGE OF ST. DAMIAN, OR SAXENA (Hermits of St. Damian at Ocri or Sassena in the province of Ravenna), a monastery whose prior was St. Damian; that he rebuked certain abuses there is shown by the letter of Pope St. Leo IX, CXLIII, 740; CXLV, 15.

DANIEL (ST.) OF VENICE. See VENETIARUM.

DAULEI OF ST. MARY (Notre-Dame de Tholey, diocese of Trier), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, which Celestine III took under his protection and whose property and privileges he confirmed in 1195, CCVI, 1133.

DEARNACENSE. See DURNACENSE.

DECIHANENSE (perhaps Dians-sur-Orvanne, Seine-et-Marne), a monastery whose abbot Innocent III wrote to in 1207, CCXV, 1216.

DECIMIAC OF ST. CYRIACUS (perhaps Dixmont near Joigny, Yonne), a monastery in the diocese of Auxerre, existing in the time of St. Aunarius, bishop—namely, in the seventh century, CXXXVIII, 233.

DEÉ OF ST. PHILIBERT (Saint-Philibert de Dée, or Grand-Lieu, diocese of Nantes), formerly a monastery and afterwards a priory, built in the diocese of Nantes in the district of Herbauge and on the island of Her; its abbot Arnulf obtained a privilege from Louis the Pious in 818, CIV, 1089, 1305.

DEGARENSE, or TEGERENSE, mentioned at CXLI, 1171: the same as Tegernsee.

DEMETRIUS (ST.). See THESSALONICENSE.

DENCKENDORF OF THE HOLY SEPULCHRE (Saint-Sépulcre de Denzdorf, in Swabia), a monastery of Canons of the Order of the Holy Sepulchre of Jerusalem, established by the illustrious Berthold shortly before 1130; in that year Pope Honorius II honored it with a privilege, CLXVI, 1309.

DEODATUS (ST.) (Saint-Dié-en-Vosges, otherwise called Les Jointures and Val-Galilée), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict founded by St. Deodatus in 667.—Charter of confirmation by Numerian, archbishop of Reims, LXXXVIII, 1191.—Privilege of Pope St. Leo IX, 1049, CXLIII, 632.—Life of St. Deodatus, by Walcand, CLI, 611.—Privilege of Paschal II, 1109, CLXIII, 256.—Of Calixtus II, 1223, CLXIII, 1281.—Of Innocent II, 1131, CLXXIX, 105, 255.

DEODATUS (ST.) OF BENEVENTO (Saint-Déodat, diocese of Benevento), a nunnery which Anastasius IV subjected, in 1153, to the monastery of St. Vincent at the Volturno, CLXXXVIII, 1021.

DERFORD OF ST. MARY (St. Mary of Derford or Depford, near London), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, built before 1199; in that year Innocent III confirmed its possessions by privilege, CCXIV, 564.

DERTONA OF ST. MARY (St. Mary of Tortona in the Milanese), a monastery to whose brethren Pope St. Gregory VII wrote in 1073, CXLVIII, 315.

DERTONA OF ST. MARTIAN (Saint-Martian of Tortona), a monastery founded by Bishop Giseprand.—Diploma of Emperor Otto IV, 950, CXXXVII, 369.

DERWENT NUNNERY in England, named from the river Derwent (now Ebchester), where Æbba, later abbess of Coldingham, lived for a time, 680, XCV, 201.

DER OF SS. PETER AND PAUL (Moutier-en-Der, Haute-Marne), a monastery built in the forest of Der in the diocese of Reims by Abbot St. Berchar and King Childeric, 673, LXXXVII, 1296.—Diploma of Theuderic, ibid., 1335.—Charter of Bertoend, bishop of Châlons, 692, LXXXVIII, 1225.—Diploma of Lothair I, 827, CIV, 1162, 1164, 1204.—The monk Adso flourished in 992, CXXXVII.—Life of St. Berchar, founder, 667.—Privilege of Pope St. Leo IX, 1049, CXLIII, 613, 644.—Of Pope Victor II, CXLIII, 818.—Of Alexander II, CXLVI, 1310.—Of Paschal II, 1100, CLXIII, 37.—Privilege of Calixtus II, [Col. 1054] 1124, CLXIII, 1320.—Letter of Alexander III concerning squandered monastic property, 1172, CC, 829, 932, 939.—Privilege of Innocent III, year unspecified.

DICKIRCHEN OF ST. PETER (St. Peter of Dirkirchen, Moselle), a nunnery whose property Innocent III confirmed by privilege in 1211, CCXVII, 214.

DIE AND DEÉ OF ST. MARCELLUS (St. Marcel of Die, in Dauphiné), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict and of the Cluniac congregation, eighth century, LXXI, 878 note.

DIESSEN OF ST. STEPHEN (St. Stephen of Diessen, Upper Bavaria), a monastery built by Counts Berctulf and Otto shortly before 1132; in that year Innocent II took it under his protection, CLXXIX, 119.

DIONYSIUS (ST.) OF PARIS (Saint-Denis near Paris), the most celebrated monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, begun by King Chlothar II and completed and endowed by his son Dagobert I in 632.—Charter of Chlothar, LXXX, 454.—Charters of King Dagobert, ibid., 514, 515, 533, 535, etc.—Charter of St. Landric, LXXXVII, 299.—Diploma of King Chlodovech II, 640, ibid., 681, 690.—Of Chlothar III, 658, ibid., 1277.—Of Theuderic, 681, ibid., 1329.—Of Chlodovech III, LXXXVIII, 1081, 1083, 1086.—Of Childebert III, ibid., 1089, 1091 and frequently.—Of Chilperic II, ibid., 1118 and following.—Of Theuderic IV, ibid., 1136.—Charter of Charles, mayor of the palace, concerning the donation of the estate of Clichy, 741, ibid., 1302.—Diploma of Pippin, ibid., 1308.—King Dagobert overlaid this with silver, XCVI, 1401.—Plea of King Pippin, 752, ibid., 1520, 1524, 1565, 1567.—Of King Carloman, 769, ibid., 1572, 1581.—Of Charlemagne, 769, XCVII, 943, 933, 939, 959, 966.—Charter of his sister Gisela, 798, ibid., 984.—Confirmed by Charlemagne, ibid., 985.—Diploma of Louis the Pious and Lothair, 825, CIV, 1141, 1142.—On the reform of its monastery under Abbot Hilduin, 832, ibid., 1206, 1211, 1224.—Privilege of Pope Nicholas I, CIX, 819.—Privilege of Leo III, 708, CXXIX, 967.—Of Nicholas I, ibid., 1013.—Of Pope St. Leo IX, 1049, CXLIII, 620, 791.—Of Nicholas II, 1061, ibid., 1351.—Of Alexander II, CXLVI, 1306, 1309.—Letter of St. Gregory VII to Abbot Hugh and the monks, 1075, CXLVIII, 415.—Privilege of William the Conqueror, king of the English, CXLIX, 1364.—Of Pope Paschal II, 1102, CLXIII, 88.—Of Calixtus II, 1119, ibid., 1126.—Letter of Pope Honorius II, 1129, CLXVI, 1296.—Diploma of Cardinal Matthew concerning restoration of the monastery of Argenteuil to the abbey of St. Denis, 1129, CLXXIII, 1265.—Privilege of Pope Innocent II, 1131, CLXXIX, 93, 111.—Privilege of Eugenius III, 1148, CLXXX, 1342.

Suger, abbot of St. Denis and regent of the kingdom, flourished in 1152, CLXXXVI, 1151.—Diplomas of Suger for the abbey of St. Denis, ibid., 1445 and following.—Privilege of Louis VII, 1124, ibid., 1461, 1463 and following.—William of Saint-Denis, monk and disciple of Suger, flourished in 1152.—Decree of Anastasius IV against the archbishop of Bourges concerning restoration of the church of Maison-Mère, CLXXXVIII, 1003.—Privilege of the same pope, ibid., 1004.—Of Adrian IV, 1156, ibid., 1485, 1593, 1594.—Odo of Deuil, abbot, flourished in 1168, CXCV, 991.—Privilege of Alexander III, 1170, CC, 629, 1196, 1258, 1288.—Of Lucius III, 1182, CCI, 1166, 1167, 1205, 1319, 1330, 1491.—Confirmation by Clement III, in 1189, of the church of Grand-Puits to St. Denis, CCIV, 1439.—Charter of Maurice de Sully, 1194, CCV, 905.—Of Celestine III, 1192, CCVI, 942, 1083, 1188, 1224.—Privileges and letters granted by Innocent III to Abbot Hugh, 1198, CCXIV, 154, 158, 162; CCXVII, 15, 63, 102, 145, 146, 226, 241, 254, 260.

DIONYSIUS (ST.). See REMENSE.

DIONYSIUS (ST.) OF MILAN (Saint-Denis of Milan), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built and endowed by the bishops of Milan, situated in the suburb; Eugenius III confirmed its property and privileges in 1147, CLXXX, 1194.

DIONYSIUS (ST.) OF THE PASS OF PARIS (Saint-Denis du Pas, Paris), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, whose property and privileges Lucius III confirmed in 1183, CCI, 1176.

DIONYSIUS (ST.) OF BROCARIUM (Broqueroy near Mons in Hainaut), a monastery founded by Richild, countess of Flanders, and granted by her to St. Gerald, abbot of La Sauve-Majeure, as the charter of that countess of 1082 states, CXLVII, 1013.

DIONYSIUS (ST.) OF AMIENS (Saint-Denis-sous-Amiens), a monastery formerly built by the priest Ingutio in the suburb of Amiens, later granted to the monks of Marmoutier and confirmed to them by Geoffrey, bishop of Amiens, in 1115, CLXII, 744.

DIONYSIUS (ST.), NUNNERY. See MONTMARTRE.

[Col. 1055] DIONYSIUS (ST.) OF THE PRISON (Saint-Denis-la-Châtre, Paris), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by the knight Ansold in 1122 and subject to St. Martin of the Fields.—Charter of Stephen, bishop of Paris, 1133, CLXXIII, 1423.

DIONYSIUS (ST.). See NOGENTENSE or NOVIGENTENSE.

DISIBOD OF THE MOUNT (Mont-Saint-Disibod, Disenberg, or Disibodenberg, in the diocese of Mainz), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict founded by St. Disibod in 674.—Privilege of Eugenius III, 1148, CLXXX, 1307.

DISIBOD OF THE MOUNT (Disenberg, diocese of Mainz), a nunnery founded by the same holy abbot, in which the holy virgin Hildegard, daughter of Count Palatine Hildebert and Mechthild, was consecrated in 1106, CXVII, 13.—Jutta, the count’s sister, was then abbess there, ibid., 14.—St. Hildegard succeeded her until she founded the nunnery of St. Rupert at Bingen. Origins of this monastery, by St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1100.

DIVE OF ST. PETER OR ST. MARY (Saint-Pierre-sur-Dive, diocese of Lisieux), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in the eleventh century by Lesceline, countess of Eu, and her sons Count Robert and Bishop Hugh, CCII, 1317.

DIJON OF ST. STEPHEN, a monastery subsequently held by Canons of the Order of St. Augustine and finally by secular canons, founded about 580, LXXI, 1038.—Letters of Innocent II on behalf of Abbot Herbert, 1131, CLXXIX, 114, 117, 125, 176.—Privilege of the same pope, 439 [as printed].—Privilege of Adrian IV, 1156, CLXXXVIII, 1456.—Of Alexander III, 1173, CC, 902.—Letter of Innocent III against a certain canon, 1210, CCXVI, 371, 550.

DIJON OF ST. BENIGNUS. See BENIGNI.

DODOSUM. See CICINENSE.

DÉOLS (Bourg-de-Déols, Indre), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in the territory of Châteauroux in the sixth century, LXXI, 215.—It is also called Penthole, CV, 744.—Letter of Gregory VII concerning the election of an abbot, 1079, CXLVIII, 533.—Letter of the same pope concerning restoration of monasteries, ibid., 560.—Decree of Innocent III confirming an agreement made with the lord of Châteauroux, 1202, CCXIV, 1048, 1137.

DOL OR RENNES OF ST. MELANIUS. See MELANII.

DOLOGI OF ST. MARY. See DAULEIENSE.

DOLOGI, OR THEOLOGI, OF ST. MAURICE (Tholey or Saint-Maurice-ès-Vosges, diocese of Trier), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict founded by King Dagobert in 623, under St. Modoald, bishop. St. Paul the hermit, later bishop of Verdun, withdrew there in 650, LXXXVII, 211.—Attached to the Church of St. Peter at Trier in 625, LXXX, 499.

DOMFERMELIN (Dunfermline, diocese of St. Andrews, Ireland [as printed]), a monastery mentioned in a letter of Innocent III, 1207, CCXV, 1194, 1583.

DOMMARTIN, OTHERWISE ST. JOSSE-IN-THE-WOOD (Dommartin, otherwise Saint-Josse-au-Bois, near Hesdin, Pas-de-Calais), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, founded in 1120 by Milo, a Premonstratensian monk and later bishop of Thérouanne, CLXX, 1269 note.—Rainald, archbishop of Reims, confirmed this foundation in 1130, CLXXII, 1343.

DONATUS (ST.) OF SCOZULA OR STROGULA (Saint-Donat de Scouzole, diocese of Milan), on whose behalf Innocent III wrote against the archbishop of Milan in 1198, CCXIV, 28, 337.

DONAWERD OF THE HOLY CROSS (Holy Cross of Donauwörth, Bavaria), a nunnery formerly built by the nobleman Mangold of Werde and consecrated by Pope Leo IX; later Gebhard, bishop of Constance, introduced monks into it.—Privilege of Innocent II, 1135, CLXXIX, 240; of Celestine III, 1194, CCVI, 1056.

DORNATIAC (Dornac or Dorny, Haut-Rhin), a nunnery built near Besançon; Adalsinda, daughter of Duke Amalgar, was its first abbess in 635, LXXI, 643 note.—She gave her abbey to the monastery of Bèze in 667, LXXXVIII, 1166.

DOROBERNIA OF SS. PETER AND PAUL. See CANTUARIENSE OF ST. AUGUSTINE.

DORTONA. See DERTONENSE.

DOVER (Dover, England), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, whose foundation is in question in 1136, CXCII, 1115.

DRIENCOURT OF NEW CASTLE (Hospitallers of Newcastle at Driencourt, England), a hospital house whose property Innocent III took under his protection in 1206, CCXV, 944.

DOUAI OF ST. MARY AND SS. MORANTIUS AND AMATUS (Saint-Morant of Douai), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, founded at an uncertain date, CXLIX, 132.—Privilege of Pope Paschal II, 1104, CLXIII, 136.

DOUAI OF ST. PETER (St. Peter of Douai, Pas-de-Calais), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine founded by Robert, bishop of Arras; Alexander III granted it a privilege in 1163, CC, 217.—Privilege of Clement III, 1189, CCIV, 1427.

TWO CHURCHES OF ST. MARY AND ST. PETER, a college of canons founded at Arras at an uncertain date, CXLVIII, 131.

DUDLEY OF ST. MARY (St. Mary of Dudley, county of Worcester, England), a monastery of the Cluniac Order, richly endowed, whose property and privileges Lucius III confirmed in 1182, CCI, 1144.

DUELLE OF THE MOUNTS (Hohenwiel, near Mons, Belgium), a monastery founded in its castle by Duke Burchard and his wife Hadwichild in 973, CXLIII, 319.—It was transferred by Emperor Henry from Mount Duelle to the bank of the Rhine at a place called Stein, ibid. See STEINENSE.

DUMIO OF ST. MARTIN (St. Martin of Dumio, diocese of Braga, Portugal), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict founded in 572 by St. Martin, abbot and later bishop, LXXII, 19.

DURHAM (county of Durham, England), a monastery whose bishop was also abbot.—Letters of Innocent III to the monks: in grave matters the abbot is to be consulted, 1198, CCXIV, 432; 1204, CCXV, 405, 874.—Privilege of the same pope, 1207, ibid., 1259.

DUNENGENSIS (Denain, between Douai and Valenciennes), a nunnery founded by Blessed Rainfred, who was also its abbess, in the eleventh century, CXLIX, 133.

DUNFERMELIN. See above, DOMFERMELIN.

DUNES, LATER BRUGES, OF ST. MARY (Notre-Dame des Dunes near Dunkirk, later transferred to Bruges), a monastery of the Cistercian Order founded by Count Theoderic of Flanders before 1165; Pope Alexander III confirmed it by privilege in 1165, CC, 343, 1233.—Elias of Koksijde, monk of Dunes, became seventh abbot of Cîteaux in 1203, CCIX, 991.—Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1208, CCXV, 1559.

DUNSTAN (ST.). See CANTUARIENSE.

TWELVE BRIDGES, a hospice built by Alcuin in the district of Troyes on the Seine about 780, CI, 1432.

TWO TWINS (Les Deux Jumeaux, near Bayeux), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded near Bayeux about 760 by St. Martin, abbot of Vertou.—Mentioned in the testament of St. Ansegisus, abbot of Fontenelle, 833, CV, 744.

DURBON CHARTERHOUSE (Durbon, diocese of Gap), built by some monks coming from the Greater Charterhouse; its first prior was Lazarus, 1116, mentioned in the statutes of that order, CLIII, 1123, 1125.—Letters of Prior Guigo I to the brethren of Durbon, CLIII, 584, 593.

DURMAC, also DEARMAC, a monastery in Ireland founded by St. Columba at the end of the sixth century, XCV, 122.

DUSER OF ST. MARY (Notre-Dame de Donzère), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict built on the Rhône by Abbot Norfrid with a privilege of Charlemagne, and confirmed by Louis the Pious at the request of Abbot Dexter in 814, CIV, 983.—Diploma of the same Louis, ibid., 1212.

DYNIAC, DENOCIAC, OR DENONIAC (Denain, diocese of Arras), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict founded in 764, later entrusted to nuns, to whom Eugenius III granted a privilege in 1153, CLXXX, 1580.

EADMUND (ST.). See below, EDMUNDI.

EBERBACH AND EBERAC (Eberbach in the Upper Rhenish Palatinate), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose abbot is mentioned in a letter of Celestine II, 1144, CLXXIX, 789.—These monks write to St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 369.—Privilege of Alexander III, 1178, CC, 1160.

EBERSBERG (Eberberg in the Upper Rhenish Palatinate), a monastery of canons, to whose abbot Celestine III wrote in a certain case concerning the monastery of Garsten, 1197, CCVI, 1188, 1221.

EBERBURD OR EBERDORF (Eberdorf in Meissen), a monastery whose abbot received a letter from St. Hildegard in the twelfth century, CXCVII, 295.

EBERSHEIM. See NOVIENTENSE.

EBLEHOLT OF ST. THOMAS OF THE PARACLETE (St. Thomas of the Paraclete at Ebelholten, Denmark), a monastery of Canons Regular of St. Augustine of the congregation of St. Victor of Paris; their first prior was William, to whom Alexander III granted a privilege in 1175, CC, 1039, 1186.—Privilege of Celestine III, 1197, CCVI, 1238.—Life of Abbot St. William, CCIX, 589.—Charter by which Absalon, bishop of Roskilde, [Col. 1057] took this monastery under his protection, 1171, ibid., 745.—The same man secured it to Abbot William in 1178, ibid.—Diplomas of Abbot William, ibid., 749, 750, 755.—Privilege of Walbert, abbot of Esrum, 752.—Diplomas of King Canute, 754.—Testament of Archbishop Absalon, 755.—Privilege of Innocent III, 1216, CCXVII, 265.

YORK OF ST. MARY (Our Lady of York), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, where Alcuin entered upon the first stages of learning under Master Ecgbert in 732, C, 22, 93.—Privilege of William the Conqueror, eleventh century, CXLIX, 1363.

YORK OF ST. PETER (St. Peter of York), a hospice mentioned in a charter of William the Conqueror, tenth century, CXLIV, 1370.

YORK OF THE HOLY TRINITY (Holy Trinity of York), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine.—Letter of Innocent III, 1203, CCXV, 95.

EBORIACENSE. See FARENSE.

EBRACH OF ST. MARY (Our Lady of Ebrach, diocese of Würzburg), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, built in 1126 by the noblemen Bruno and Richovius and by Emperor Conrad.—Privilege of Eugenius III, 1149, CLXXX, 1423.—Letter of the abbot of Ebrach to Geroh, provost of Reichersberg, concerning one Folmar preaching errors, about 1070, CXCIV, 1485.

ÉVREUX OF ST. SAVIOR (St. Savior of Évreux), a nunnery built by Count Richard, whose abbess Hilaria received a privilege from Eugenius III in 1153, CLXXX, 1572.—Mention of this monastery, CCII, 1318.

EBREUIL OF ST. LEODEGAR (St. Léger of Esbreville or Ebreuil in Auvergne), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict founded near Gannat in 971, under King Lothair.—Privilege of Paschal II, 1114, CLXIII, 344.

ÉVRON OF ST. MARY (Our Lady of Évron, diocese of Le Mans), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict founded by Hadoind, bishop of Le Mans, in 630.—Destroyed by the Northmen in the ninth century, it was restored by Hugh, archbishop of Tours, and the brethren of Marmoutier, in the time of Pope Lucius II, who confirmed it by privilege in 1144, CLXXIX, 906.

EBRULF (ST.). See UTICENSE.

ECHENBRUNN OF SS. PETER AND PAUL (Echenbronn, Bavaria), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose rights and possessions Pope Calixtus II confirmed in 1122, CLXIII, 1240.

EDER OF ST. BENEDICT (St. Benedict, perhaps of Herreruela near Burgos, Spain), a monastery whose abbot Innocent III wrote to in 1192, CCXIV, 92.

EDMUND (ST.) OF NORWICH (Edmundsbury, county of Suffolk, diocese of Norwich, England), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, formerly called *Badrices hurde* or Badricelmorde, and indeed most celebrated, founded by King Cnut I in 1020; later ravaged by Henry VIII, although his sister Mary, queen of France, was buried there.—Charter of Cnut I declaring it free from every burden, CLI, 1186.—Privilege of Alexander II, 1071, CXLVI, 1363.—Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1205, CCXV, 743.

EDMUND (ST.) OF LINCOLN, a monastery, perhaps that concerning which Gregory VII wrote to Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, that he should restrain a certain Arfast from troubling this monastery, 1073, CXLVIII, 314.—Letter of Innocent III concerning restitutions to be made by the bishop to the brethren of St. Edmund, 1198, CCXIV, 414.—Concerning the consecration of the church, 431, 608; 1204, CCXV, 298.

EENHAM. See below, EINHAMENSE.

EFTERNAC. See EPTERNACENSE.

EGMOND OF ST. ADELBERT (St. Adelbert of Egmond, North Holland), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict built by Count Henry II of Holland in 923, in the diocese of Utrecht.—Privilege of Innocent II, 1140, CLXXIX, 504.

EINHAM (Einham, near Oudenaarde, diocese of Mechelen), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine founded by Godfrey, count of Verdun, about 1000; later Count Baldwin of Flanders restored it and granted it in 1063 to brethren of the Order of St. Benedict, brought from the monastery of St. Vedast by St. Lietbert, bishop of Cambrai, CXLVI, 1467.—Privilege of Eugenius III, 1148, CLXXX, 1325.—Likewise of Clement III, 1190, CCIV, 1465.

EINSIEDELN (Einsiedeln, or Our Lady of the Hermits, Switzerland), also called the Cell of Meginrad and of the Solitaries, a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict among the Swiss. It began from the cell occupied by the pious hermit Meginrad in the ninth century, CXLII, 1179.—The abbot of this monastery was a prince of the Roman Empire in the time of Rudolf, [Col. 1058] 1274, XCVII, 826.—Thietland was its first royal abbot in 945, CXLIII, 45.

ELANT, OR SLANT, OF ST. MARY (Our Lady of Elant, diocese of Reims), a monastery of the Cistercian Order built by Witer of Rethel, count of Rethel, in 1154; Roger was its first abbot. Alexander III wrote against these monks as hostile to the brethren of St. Nicasius in 1174, CC, 960.

ELBORENSIS (Évora, Portugal), a monastery whose prior Innocent III wrote to in 1198 concerning the controversy between the monks of Holy Cross and the bishop of Coimbra, CCXIV, 193.

ALETH OF ST. MARY (Our Lady of Alet, Aude), a monastery at whose abbot’s request Pope Leo IX granted the monasteries of St. Paul of Valcabrère and St. Mary of Urbion in 1050, CXLIII, 639.—Privilege of Calixtus II, 1119, CLXIII, 1102.—Of Alexander III, 1159, CC, 140.

ALETH OF ST. POLYCARP (St. Polycarp of Alet, Aude), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict founded in 780 by Abbot Atal and his companions, subject to Alet and later to Lagrasse.—Decree of Paschal II granting it to Lagrasse, 1116, CLXIII, 410; of Calixtus II, ibid., 1108.—Letter of Innocent III, 1212, CCXVI, 609.

L’AUMÔNE OF ST. MARY (Our Lady of L’Aumône, called Little Cîteaux, at Marchenoir, diocese of Blois), a monastery of the Cistercian Order founded in 1121 by Theobald IV, count of Champagne and Blois, at the request of Stephen, abbot of Cîteaux, under Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres.—Privilege of Innocent II, 1137, CLXXIX, 316; of Alexander III, 1163, CC, 255.—Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1204, CCXV, 543; CCXVI, 263.

ELENFORDESMER OF ST. MARGARET (St. Margaret of Elenfordesmer, diocese of Salisbury, England), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict built by the nobleman Ralph of Chedeleswurd shortly before 1177; Alexander III confirmed it by privilege in that year, CC, 1156.

ELEVACENSE. See below, ELWANGENSE.

ELFSTAT (Ilfeld, county of Hohenstein), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order in Thuringia, mentioned among the notes to the letters of St. Boniface, LXXXIX, 742.—Also in the Life of St. Norbert, CLXX, 1306.

ELIGIUS (ST.). See NOVIOMENSE.

ELIGIUS (ST.) OF PARIS, a nunnery which Bishop Galo of Paris dissolved because of corrupt morals, at the command of Pope Paschal II, by a letter of 1105, CLXIII; and gave to the monastery of Fossatus to possess in 1107, 158 note.

ELNONENSE. See ST. AMAND.

ELY (county of Cambridge), a monastery in England situated in the diocese of Worcester; at the request of King Edward, Pope Victor II granted it privileges in 1055, CXLIII, 816.—St. Oswald, bishop, sent Brithnoth there as abbot to restore discipline in 982, CXLVII, 1194.

FOUNDATION OF THE MONASTERY OF ELTENHEIM by Heddon, bishop of Strasbourg, 763, XCVI, 1547.

ELLWANGEN (Ellwangen, Bavaria), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict built in the diocese of Augsburg by Hariculf, formerly bishop of Langres, in 764.—Privilege of Eugenius III, 1153, CLXXX, 1587.

EMMERAM, OR ST. EMMERAM OF REGENSBURG (St. Emmeram of Regensburg), a monastery first founded under the title of the Holy Savior by Count Ekkibert and Bishop Adalwin in 810; an imperial monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose bishops were also abbots. Louis the Pious conferred many gifts upon it; Bishop Ambricho carried out very numerous exchanges, as appears in Anamod’s book, *On the Transfers of St. Emmeram*. Others assign the beginning of this monastery to 697, under Theodo, duke of Bavaria, CXXIX, 897.—Emperor St. Henry confirmed all the rights and privileges of this monastery in 1021, CXL, 357, 358, 359.—Arnold, monk and later dean, lived about the middle of the eleventh century, CXLI, 985.—Description of the revenues and possessions of this abbey in the eleventh century, ibid., 1095.—The monk Othlo flourished in 1073, CXLVI, 9.—Letter of Paschal II concerning restoration of the abbot, CLXIII, 441.—Letter of Innocent II for the protection of the monastery, 1137, CLXXIX, 323.—Letter of Innocent III, 1210, CCXVI, 390; CCXVII, 39.

EMMERODIENSE. See HEMMERODIENSE.

ENGESHEIM OF THE HOLY CROSS, a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict built by St. Leo IX on his own inheritance on the Rhine; Gregory VII wrote concerning it to the bishops of Strasbourg and Basel in 1064, CXLVIII, 376.

ENGELBERG, OR MOUNT OF THE ANGELS, OF ST. MARY (Our Lady of Engelberg, canton of Unterwalden, Switzerland), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict founded by the nobleman Conrad, lord of Söldenbüren, [Col. 1059] in 1120, on the river Aa.—Privilege of Pope Calixtus II, 1124, CLXIII, 1317.—Abbot Frowin flourished in 1131, CLXIX, 1801.—Privilege of Adrian IV, 1157, CLXXXVIII, 1514.—Letter of Innocent III to the abbot concerning certain invaders of Church property, 1203, CCXVII, 99.

ENIXION, HENSION, AND ANSION, OF ST. JOVINUS OF THE MARAIS (commonly Saint-Jouin, diocese of Poitiers), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in the diocese of Poitiers near Thouars, to which St. Paternus withdrew about 482, LXXXVIII, 487.

ENSDORF (Ensdorf, diocese of Regensburg), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict founded by Otto, bishop of Rammelsberg, and accepted from Count Palatine Otto about 1139, CLXXIII, 1279.—Charter of St. Otto concerning the foundation of this monastery, 1139, ibid., 1350, 1351.—Of Celestine II, 1144, CLXXIX, 808.

EPARCHIUS (ST.) OF ANGOULÊME. See CIBARDI.

BISHOP’S TOWN (Ville-l’Évêque-sur-Marne, Aisne), a nunnery at a place called Gauchy, founded by Reolus, bishop of Reims, and Abbot St. Berchar in 686, LXXXVIII, 1212.

EPOSIUM (Ivoi, now Carignan, diocese of Trier), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built on a mountain summit near Trier by Abbot St. Ulfilas before 595, when it was visited by St. Gregory, bishop of Tours, LXXI, 457.

EPTERNAC (Epternac or Efternac, diocese of Trier), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict founded near Trier by St. Willibrord, bishop of Trier, and St. Irmina, abbess of Oeren, in 698, LXXXVII, 1309, 1310 and following.—Charter of Irmina, LXXXIX, 537.—Likewise of Heden, ibid., 535, 548; of Aengilbald, ibid., 538; of Pippin and Plectrude, ibid., 539, 541, 547; of Engelbert, ibid., 542, 546; of Abbess Bertilind, ibid., 543; of the monk Ansbald, ibid., 544, 545; of Charles, son of Pippin, ibid., 550; of Charles, mayor of the palace, ibid., 551, 552; of Rohing, ibid., 553.—Testament of St. Willibrord, ibid., 554.—Diploma of Charlemagne, 794, XCVII, 1067.—Of Emperor St. Henry, confirming to it the right of coinage, 1023, CXL, 367.—Abbot Thiofrid flourished in 1108, CLVII, 293.

EQUITIUS (ST.), a monastery situated in the province of Valeria in Italy, whose first abbot was Valentius in the time of St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 256; LXXVII, 165.

HERMITAGE OF TURRITANUM. See TURRITANUM.

ERASMUS AND MAXIMUS (SS.) (St. Erasmus or St. Maximus, Kingdom of Naples), a monastery near Naples whose abbot St. Gregory the Great writes to, LXXVII, 1075.—It had shortly before been founded by the illustrious woman Alexandra, ibid.

EREFORT, OR ERFURT (Erfurt in Saxony), a celebrated nunnery in Saxony made illustrious by St. Hthumoda, later abbess of Gandersheim, in 990, CXXXVII, 1170.—Privilege of Emperor St. Henry II, 1002, CXL, 246.

EREFORD, ERFURT, OR MOUNT ST. PETER (St. Peter of Erfurt, Saxony), a monastery founded in Thuringia by King Dagobert II in 677, LXXXVII, 313.—Falsely attributed to Dagobert III, LXXXVIII, 1104.—Diploma of Emperor Henry III, 1039, CLI, 1085, 1089, 1096.—Privilege of Adrian IV, 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1418.—Letter of the abbot to St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 311.—Letter of Innocent III, 1199, CCXIV, 854.

HERMITAGE OF ST. MEINRAD. See EINSIDLENSE.

ERMINIUS AND URSMAR (SS.) (Saint-Urmer, near Lobbes in Thiérache, Artois), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, perhaps founded by St. Ursmar himself, bishop, about 657, but certainly before 968, CXLIX, 139.—Excesses of the canons were restrained by Alexander III in 1174, CC, 1008.

ERPISFORD (Erpford in Thuringia), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict built in Thuringia by Countess Paulina under the rule of Henry IV; she established there monks brought from Hirsau under the governance of Abbot Gerung in 1107, CXLI, 1215.

ESLONZA OF ST. PETER (St. Peter of Exlonzo, Spain), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose property and possessions Urban III confirmed in 1186, CCII, 1407.

ESRUM OF ST. MARY (Our Lady of Esrum, diocese of Roskilde, Denmark), a monastery of the Cistercian Order founded by Eskil, bishop of Lund, in 1143.—Privilege of Eugenius III, 1151, CLXXX, 1482; of Clement III, 1189, CCIV, 1423; of Celestine III, 1192, CCVI, 980.

ESSEBY (Essby, diocese of Lincoln, England), a monastery whose prior Innocent III wrote to in 1204, CCXV, 368.

ESTERNAC, a monastery which some confuse with Epternac, was situated in the district of Trier. St. Willibrord, bishop, presided over it for a long time and was buried there, 740, [Col. 1060] CI, 705, 710.

EUCHARIUS (ST.) OF VERDUN, a monastery; it seems to be the same as that of Trier. See TREVIRENSE.

EUGENDUS (ST.) OF THE JURA. See CONDATESCENSE.

EUGENIUS (ST.) (Saint-Eugène, diocese of Siena, Tuscany), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict near Siena in Italy, founded by the nobleman Wanfred in 731, LXXXVII, 1403.—Privilege of Emperor Henry IV, 1081, CLI, 1150.—Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1206, CCXV, 973.

GUBBIO OF ST. MARY (Gubbio, Papal States), a monastery of St. Augustine, whose possessions Innocent II confirmed in 1138, CLXXIX, 351.—Privilege of Alexander III, 1170, CC, 712; of Lucius III, 1182, CCI, 1115.

GUBBIO OF ST. PETER (St. Peter of Gubbio), a monastery whose property and privileges Innocent III confirmed despite the bishop’s opposition in 1198, CCXIV, 624, 852.

EULALIA (ST.) OF BARCELONA (St. Eulalia of Barcelona, Spain), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict discussed in the Life of St. Maximus, 644, LXXX, 612.

ST. PETER OF THE ISLAND OF EUMORPHIANA (St. Peter, Isle Sainte-Marie), existed on the Tyrrhenian Sea from the sixth century, LXXVII, 513.

EUPHEMIA (ST.). See MUTINENSIS.

EUPHEMIA (ST.) OF MELITO (St. Euphemia of Melito, Calabria), a monastery mentioned in a letter of Paschal II, 1104, CLXIII, 124, 137 note.

EUSEBIUS (ST.) (St. Eusèbe, former diocese of Apt, Vaucluse), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict founded about the end of the eighth century by the holy hermit Martian.—Privilege of Anastasius IV confirming the possessions of this monastery, 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1071.

EUSITIUS (ST.). See CELLA.

EUSTACHIUS (ST.). See NERVESIA.

### St. Evasius of Casale

(St.-Evaux de Casal, Lombardy), a monastery of the Augustinian order, to which King Liutprand made many gifts in 743, LXXXVII, 1401.—Privilege of Pope Paschal II, 1108, CLXIII, 237, 350; of Calixtus II, 1120, ibid., 1176; of Innocent II, 1143, CLXXIX, 646; of Lucius III, 1184, CCI, 1278; of Urban III, 1185, CCII, 1331; of Innocent III, 1211, CCXVI, 496; CCXVII, 212.

### Evaux

(Evaux, diocese of Limoges), a monastery of the Augustinian order, situated in the Limousin territory, year uncertain, LXXI, 889.

### St. Mary of Evesham

(St. Mary’s, Evesham, diocese of Worcester, England), a monastery of the Benedictine order, built by St. Egwin, bishop, and Kings Cenred and Offa, in the place where the Blessed Virgin Mary appeared, 714, LXXXIX, 336, 340.—Charter of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1369.—Privilege of Innocent III, 1205, CCXV, 784, 1103.

### Evoriacense or Eboriacense

See **Farense**.

### St. Euvertus of Orléans

(St.-Euverte or Evurte of Orléans), a monastery of the Augustinian order. Its church was founded in the fourth century, and a monastery was attached to it in 783.—It passed to the canons of St. Victor of Paris in 1140.—Eugenius III confirmed this by privilege in 1146, CLXXX, 1109.—Abbot Roger flourished in 1180, CXCIX, 1125.—Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1208, CCXVII, 172.

### Holy Trinity of Essay

(Holy Trinity of Essay, Eure), a monastery of the Benedictine order, founded by Count Eudes in the eleventh century; its first abbot was Roger, a monk of Bec, CCII, 1318.—Privilege of Urban III, 1186, ibid., 1451.

### Charterhouse of Excubiae

(Could this be Escuyères, near Queyras in the Hautes-Alpes?), built about 1115 by Solfordus and certain monks who had come from the Greater Chartreuse; it is mentioned in the statutes of the Carthusians, CLIII, 1125.

### Cell of Excideuil

(Excideuil, diocese of Limoges), a monastery of the Benedictine order, founded by St. Aredius in the diocese of Limoges and given by him to the monastery of Attane (Saint-Yrieix), 572.

### Issoudun

(Issoudun, diocese of Bourges), a priory of the Benedictine order, built in 947 by Ralph, lord of Issoudun, and his wife Bathildis. Letter of Innocent III to the prior, 1203, CCXV, 222.

### Exeter

(Exeter, England), a monastery on whose behalf St. Leo IX wrote to Edward, king of the English, in 1049, CXLIII, 639.

### St. Mary of Pfäfers

(Pfäfers, otherwise Favières, diocese of Strasbourg), a monastery built about 731 in the Rhaetian Alps, above the Rhine and Marienfeld. Its abbot complained to Louis the Pious concerning the oppressions inflicted by a certain Count Roderic.—Diploma of Louis the Pious, 831, CIV, 1199.—Paschal II freed that monastery from the authority of the bishop of Basel in 1117, CLXIII, 397.—Privilege of Innocent II, 1139, CLXXIX, 468.

### St. Fabian

See below, **Farinatense**.

### St. Facundus

See **Sahagún**.

### Hospital of Falaise

(Hospitallers of Falaise, Normandy), a congregation founded by Count Geoffrey under Henry, king of England, shortly before 1131; in that year Innocent II received the same congregation under his protection, CLXXIX, 95.

### St. Lawrence of Fano

(St.-Lawrence of Fano, Papal States), a monastery of the Benedictine order. At the request of Abbot Albert, Pope Anastasius IV granted it a privilege in 1153, CLXXXVIII, 1001.

### St. Paternianus of Fano

(St.-Paternianus of Fano, States of the Church), a monastery of the Benedictine order, to which Adrian IV granted a privilege in 1156, CLXXXVIII, 1461.

### St. Mary of Fano

(St. Mary of Fano, duchy of Urbino, Italy), a monastery of the Augustinian order, to which Eugenius III granted a confirmatory bull in 1152, CLXXX, 1546.

### St. Stephen of Fano

(St. Stephen of Fano, duchy of Urbino, Italy), formerly a convent of nuns, who were removed by the bishop because of their misconduct; regular canons were substituted for them. Innocent III wrote to their prior in 1204, CCXV, 308, 315.

### Farense or Eboriacense: St. Fara’s Nunnery

(Faremoutiers, diocese of Meaux). This abbey of Benedictine nuns was founded in the district of Meaux by St. Fara, or Burgundofara, daughter of Agneric and sister of St. Faron, with St. Eustace, abbot of Luxeuil, about 625, LXXXVII, 1046, 1070.—St. Bathildis made many gifts to this celebrated nunnery in 670.—Charter of St. Faron, bishop, ibid., 1133.—Testament of St. Burgundofara, ibid., 1137.—Later, when that nunnery had forgotten discipline and morals, King Philip I entrusted it to Bernard, abbot of Marmoutier, for reform, CLIX, 837.—Innocent II settled a controversy between Bishop Manasses and Abbess Risinda in 1139, CLXXIX, 385.—Privilege of Lucius II, 1144, ibid., 892; of Eugenius III, 1145, CLXXX, 1089.

### St. Mary of Farfa

(St. Mary of Farfa, diocese of Sabina, Papal States), a celebrated Italian abbey, built in the sixth century by St. Lawrence, called the Illuminator, bishop of Sabina, and restored in 715 by Blessed Thomas of Maurienne.—It belonged to the Benedictine order.—Charlemagne sent Childeric there in 797 in order to be informed about the affairs of this monastery, XCVI, 1023.—He confirmed all its privileges in 803, XCVII, 1027.—Diplomas of Louis the Pious, 815, CIV, 1022, 1097, 1134, 1177.—Privilege of Stephen IV, 817, CXXIX, 973; of Paschal I, ibid., 978.—Letter of Sergius IV, CXXXIX, 1521.—Privileges of Benedict VIII, 1013, ibid., 1586, 1587, 1597, 1616.—Precept of Emperor St. Henry II, 1019, CXL, 347; of Gregory VI, 1045, CXLII, 573; of St. Leo IX, 1049, CXLIII, 591, 678, 740; of Nicholas II, ibid., 1845.—Abbot Guido, 1090, CL, 1191.—Diploma of Conrad II, 1027, CLI, 1047; of Emperor Henry IV, 1084, ibid., 1153.—Letter of Adrian IV, commending that monastery to Emperor Frederick, 1155, CLXXXVIII, 1127; privilege of Innocent III, 1208, CCXV, 1344; CCXVI, 101, 103, 933.

### St. Faron of Meaux

(St.-Faron near Meaux, Seine-et-Marne), a monastery of the Benedictine order, founded by St. Faron in 659.—Letter of Innocent III to its abbot concerning the Crusaders, 1212, CCXVI, 724; CCXVII, 229.

### Faversham

(Faversham, county of Kent, England), a monastery of the Benedictine order, of the Cluniac congregation, built in 1148 by King Stephen.—Letters of Urban III, 1187, CCII, 1499, 1511, 1528; of Clement III, 1188, CCIV, 1327.

### Sts. Fabian and Damian of Farinati

(Nuns of St. Fabian at Farinati, in the Milanese territory), a nunnery of the Benedictine order, whose possessions and privileges Alexander III confirmed in 1169, CC, 602.

### St. Hippolytus of Faenza

(St.-Hippolytus of Faenza, Papal States), a monastery to which Innocent III wrote concerning the exhumation of a certain heretic in 1206, CCXV, 1057.

### St. Peter of Faenza

(St. Peter of Faenza, Papal States), a monastery of the Augustinian order. Honorius II took it under protection and confirmed its property and privileges in 1128, CLXVI, 1277.—Privilege of Innocent II, 1143, CLXXIX, 651; of Lucius II, 1144, ibid., 884.—Letter of Alexander III, 1176, CC, 1050.

### St. Mary-at-the-Gate of Faenza

(Our Lady of the Gate at Faenza, Papal States), a monastery of the Benedictine order. Innocent III granted a privilege to its abbot Maccabaeus in 1202, CCXV, 26.

### Faverolles

See **Barisiacum**.

### St. Mary of Favernay

(Notre-Dame de Favernay), a monastery of the Benedictine order, founded about 747 in the diocese of Besançon, four leagues from Luxeuil. At first it belonged to nuns, but later passed to Benedictine monks, LXXI, 621.—Letter of Innocent III concerning the election of an abbot, 1198, CCXIV, 89.

### Felduar

(Felduar, diocese of Pécs, or Five Churches, Hungary), a monastery founded by St. Stephen, king of the Hungarians.—Decree of Innocent III concerning a controversy between the abbot and the bishop, 1198, CCXIV, 497.

### St. Felix

See **Bononiense**.

### St. Felix

(St.-Felix, diocese of Capodistria, suffragan of Venice), a monastery whose abbot Innocent III addressed concerning the parish church of Rialto in 1212, CCXVI, 730.

### St. Felicity

See **Florentinum**.

### Sts. Peter and Paul of Fenouillet

(St.-Paul-du-Fenouillet), a monastery in the diocese of Carcassonne, built by Bernard, count of Fenouillet, in 1011.—Privilege of Pope Sergius, CXXXIX, 1513.

### Ferraria of Teano

(Ferrara in the diocese of Teano, Capitanata, Naples), a monastery of the Benedictine order, founded by the nobleman Richard.—Privilege of Celestine III, 1192, CCVI, 978; likewise of Innocent III, 1201, CCXVII, 70.

### St. Bartholomew of Ferrara

(St.-Bartholomew of Ferrara, Romagna, Papal States), a monastery of the Augustinian order. Its possessions were confirmed by privilege by Alexander II, 1068, CXLVI, 1345; Innocent II, 1139, CLXXIX, 472; Adrian IV, 1158, CLXXXVIII, 1548; Alexander III, 1177, CC, 1152; and Innocent III, 1199, CCXIV, 837.—Letter of the latter concerning an accusation against the abbot, 1210, CCXVI, 325.

### St. Mary of Ferrières

(Ferrières-en-Gâtinais), a monastery of the Benedictine order, also called Bethlehem, built between Clairy and the Loing, in the district of the Gâtinais. It was founded by Clovis the Great under the name Bethlehem about 515 and later restored by Wandelbert.—The abbots Lupus, Aldricus, and Buchinus flourished there, CV, 797, CIX, 425.—Privilege of Paschal II, 1103, CLXIII, 118; of Eugenius III, 1147, CLXXX, 1207.—Letter of Adrian IV in favor of this monastery, 1156, CLXXXVIII, 1456; of Alexander III, 1161, CC, 129, 277.

### St. Ferreolus

(St.-Ferréol of Uzès), a monastery founded in 580 by the sainted bishop of that name, according to the rule which he himself had written, LXXI, 379 note.

### Sts. Ferreolus and Ferrucius

(St.-Ferjeux, near Besançon), a monastery from which Bishop Hugoninus, because of the monks’ excesses, transferred the bones of the holy martyrs to the episcopal church in 1053, LXXX, 426.

### St. Ferreolus

(St.-Ferréol in Burgundy), a monastery built in Burgundy by Widerad, abbot of Flavigny, in 721, LXXXVIII, 1268.

### St. Peter of La Ferté

A monastery whose location is unknown to us. Decree of Celestine III concerning obedience due to the abbot, about 1195, CCVI, 1250.

### Fussiaux

(Fussiaux, near Avesnes), a monastery of the Augustinian order, built in the diocese of Cambrai by Blessed Hetto, a Scottish abbot, year uncertain, CXLIX, 137.

### St. Bartholomew of Fiesole

(St.-Bartholomew of Fiesole, in the Florentine countryside), a monastery of the Benedictine order, whose possessions and rights Innocent II confirmed in 114[?], CLXXIX, 550; Celestine II, ibid., 815; Anastasius IV, 1153, CLXXXVIII, 1015.

### St. Hilary of Fiesole

(St.-Hilary of Fiesole, Florentine territory), a nunnery whose possessions and privileges Celestine II confirmed in 1144, CLXXIX, 797.—Privilege of Eugenius III, 1148, CLXXX, 1373; of Lucius III, 1181, CCI, 1083.—Decree of Clement III, 1188, CCIV, 1342.

### Feversham

See above, **Faversham**.

### St. Saviour of Fichecco

(St.-Saviour of Fichecco, at Lucca, Lombardy), a monastery of the Augustinian order, whose property and privileges Innocent III confirmed in 1208, CCXV, 1475, 1477.

### St. Fidelis

See **Comense**.

### St. Faith

See **Hershamense**.

### St. Saviour and St. Mary of Figeac

(Our Lady of Figeac), a monastery of the Benedictine order, built in 755 by St. Ambrose, bishop of Cahors, and King Pippin, LXXXIX, 1200 and following.—Consecrated by Pope Stephen himself, CXLI, 23.—Pope Gregory VII annexed this monastery to Conques in 1084, CXLVIII, 707; Urban II later separated it in 1096, CLI, 469.

[Col. 1063]

### St. Stephen of Fémy

(St.-Stephen of Fémy, diocese of Laon or Cambrai), a monastery of the Benedictine order, mentioned by Innocent III in 1213, CCXVI, 544.

### St. Firmus of Plorizano

(Convent of St. Firmus at Plorizano, diocese of Bergamo, Venetian States), a nunnery whose abbess Lucia received a privilege from Anastasius IV in 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1046.

### St. Mary of La Ferté-sur-Grosne

(Our Lady of La Ferté-sur-Grosne, diocese of Chalon-sur-Saône), a monastery of the Cistercian order, founded by Duke Savaric, Bishop Walter, and Stephen, third abbot of Cîteaux.—Charter of Walter, bishop of Chalon, year four [as printed], CLX, 1170.—Letters of Innocent III concerning the case of the monastery of Baume, 1199, CCXIV, 619, 852.

### Holy Trinity of Fécamp

(Holy Trinity of Fécamp), a monastery of the Benedictine order, founded in 952 by Richard, son of Duke William, who was later buried there, CXLI, 44.—St. William was abbot there from 1001, ibid., 843.—At first it was held by canons, but they were soon expelled because of their negligence. They were succeeded by Cluniacs introduced by St. Majolus, ibid., 952.—John, or Joannelin d’Alye, became abbot in 1028, CXLVII, 443.—Diploma of King Robert, 1006, CXLI, 952.—Catalogue of the abbots of Fécamp, CXLVII, 483.—Diploma of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1369.—On the foundation of this monastery, CCII, 1314.—Privilege of Urban III, 1187, ibid., 1479.—Of Celestine III, 1192, CCVI, 973, 977, 985, 1173, 1223.—Privilege of Innocent III, 1209, CCXVII, 194.

### Nunnery of Fécamp

(A convent of nuns at Fécamp), founded by the nobleman Wadingus in the seventh century, CXLI, 844.

### Fiteriense

(Perhaps Fistoles in Spain), a monastery of the Cistercian order, whose rights and possessions Eugenius III honored by privilege in 1152, CLXXX, 1522.

### St. Mary of Flabémont

(Our Lady of Flabémont, diocese of Toul, Vosges), a monastery of the Premonstratensian order, built in 1132 by Guy of Acrimont with the consent of Hugh, count of Vallimont.—Privilege of Eugenius III, 1148, CLXXX, 1332.—Of Clement III, 1188, CCIV, 1313.—Letter of Innocent III, 1209, CCXVI, 170.

### St. Geremarus of Flay

(St.-Germer-de-Fly, diocese of Beauvais), a monastery of the Benedictine order, built by St. Geremarus, abbot, in 860 and later confirmed by privileges from King Charlemagne in 807. For some time it had St. Ansegisus as abbot, CV, 735.—On the foundation of this monastery, CLVI, 1086, 1087.—Letter of Alexander III, ordering the abbot to obey the bishop, 1170, 628, 820.—Privilege of the same pope, ibid., 1178.

### St. Praejectus of Flavigny

(St.-Prix of Flavigny, Côte-d’Or), a celebrated monastery founded by Abbot Widerad in the district of Semur in 721, LXXXVIII, 1268.—Precept of Charlemagne, 775, XCVII, 948.—The same king sent to Manasses, abbot of Flavigny, a silver casket containing relics of St. James in 798, XCVIII, 910.—Privilege of King Robert, 1018, CXLI, 956.—The distinguished Hugh, abbot of Flavigny, flourished about 1104, CLIV, 9.—Privilege of Anastasius IV, 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1063.—Of Alexander III, 1161, CC, 127, 152.—Letters of Innocent III in favor of this monastery, 1198, CCXIV, 257.—Concerning the deposition of the abbot, 1207, CCXV, 1187.

### St. Flodoald

Appears to have been written in place of **Fuldense**, XCVI, 1516.

### St. Flora

See **Aretinense**.

### Sts. Peter and Dominica of Flore
