ISLE BARBE OF ST MARTIN (Saint-Martin de l’Île-Barbe), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict built on the Saône in the fourth century. Abbot Maximinus flourished there about 400, LXXI, 846 note, and Licinius in 640, ibid. — Diploma of Chlodovech II, LXXXVII, 688. — Of Louis the Pious, 815, CIV, 1026. — Privilege of Lucius III, 1183, CCI, 1202.

OF THE ISLAND IN THE DIOCESE OF BEAUVAIS (perhaps Saint-Germer de Fly), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict in the territory of Beauvais, founded by St Geremar. It is mentioned in Hincmar’s letter to the bishop of Laon and in the testament of St Ansegisus, abbot of Fontenelle, 833, CV, 745.

OF THE ISLAND IN THE DISTRICT OF TROYES (l’Île, near Troyes), a monastery founded in the district of Troyes; its abbot was Aventinus in 537, LXXI, 877.

OF THE ISLAND OF BARROIS, or BAR-LE-DUC (l’Île en Barrois, diocese of Toul), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, built in 1144. — Letter of Innocent III to its abbot, 1209, CCXVI, 170.

ISLAND OF MONTE CRISTO. See MONTE-CHRISTO.

INSULANUM OF ST PETER (Abbey of l’Île, in French Flanders), a monastery of the Order of St Augustine, built by the nobleman Count Theodoric of Flanders, with the counsel of the bishops of Noyon and Thérouanne, shortly before 1144, when Celestine II endowed it with a privilege, CLXXIX, 813.

IRINGI, OF THE CASTLE. See HERINGENSE.

ISSIODORENSE (Issoire), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict in which St Praejectus (St Prix) learned letters in 550, LXXI, 765.

IVREIO (Ivry-la-Bataille, Eure), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict founded by Roger of Ivry; Peter, a monk of Colombs, was its first abbot, CCII, 1320.

ST JAMES OF COMPOSTELLA (the military Order of St James of Compostela, Spain), an order founded by King Alfonso I and confirmed by Alexander III, whose first master was Pedro Fernández, in 1175, CC, 1024. — Decree of Lucius III, 1181–1185, CCI, 1378. — Privilege of Innocent III, 1210, CCXVI, 205.

ST JAMES OF NEUFCHÂTEAU (Saint-Jacques de Neufchâteau, Vosges), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, founded in 1097 by a monk named Ursus at the place called Sionna (Sionne) in the Vosges, and later enriched by many gifts, CLVII, 436.

ST JAMES. See MOGUNTINUM, RATISPONENSE.

JADRENSE, or JADERTINUM, OF ST CHRYSOGONUS (Saint-Chrysogone of Zara, on the Dalmatian coast), a monastery of the Order of St Augustine. Clement III assigned the church of St Martin to it in 1189, CCIV, 1444. — Privilege of Celestine III, 1195, CLVI, 1100.

JANDURIENSE OF ST MARY (Notre-Dame de Jandures, near Bar-le-Duc, Meuse), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, built by Gerard, castellan of Bar, in [Col. 1082] 1140. — Privilege of Eugenius III, 1147, CLXXX, 1233.

JANUENSE OF ST STEPHEN (Saint-Étienne of Genoa, Sardinian States), a monastery whose abbot Innocent III wrote to concerning the church of St Mary of the Castle, 1209, CCXV, 115.

JANUENSE OF ST THEODORIC (Saint-Théodoric of Genoa), a monastery whose abbot the same pope wrote to on the same matter, ibid.

JANUENSE OF ST LAWRENCE (Saint-Laurent de Jano, Sardinia), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, built by Marianus, judge of Cagliari, before 1120, when Calixtus II confirmed its possessions, CLXIII, 1194. — Privilege of Innocent II, CLXXIX, 299. — Privilege of Eugenius III, 1149, CLXXX, 1411, 1562.

JARUNTA OF ST MARY (Charron in the diocese of Poitiers), a monastery founded by Blessed Robert of Arbrissel and subject to the monastery of Fontevraud; it later passed to the Cistercians in the twelfth century, CLXII, 1087.

JERICHOENSE (Jericho, diocese of Hamburg), a Premonstratensian monastery built by Archbishop Hartwig and his mother Countess Richardis shortly before 1159, when, at his request, Adrian IV confirmed it, CLXXXVIII, 1618.

JESUS OF NAZARETH. See HUESCENSE.

JETTENSE OF ST MARY, later DILIGHEMIENSE (Notre-Dame de Jette or Dilighem, diocese of Mechelen), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, built shortly before 1106. In that year Odo, bishop of Cambrai, confirmed gifts made by Everard, Rodolf of Tournai, and his wife Helvide, CLX, 1151. — Privilege of the same Odo, ibid., 1156. — Privilege of Eugenius III, 1145, CLXXX, 1285. — Authentic charter of St Bernard of Clairvaux concerning the dispute between the abbots of Jette and Ninove, 1146, CLXXXV, 1825.

SS JOHN AND TRECHII AT BUXIDO (Saint-Jean-de-Bouis, Allier), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict in the district of Bourbonnais, subject to the bishops of Le Mans according to a diploma of Charlemagne, 802, XCVII, 995.

ST JOHN OF COLA (Saint-Jean-sur-Cole, diocese of Périgueux), a monastery whose prior is mentioned in a letter of Innocent III, 1207, CCXV, 1102.

ST JOHN AT ARCLANO (the convent of St John in the diocese of Chieti, Abruzzo, Naples); this monastery is mentioned in a privilege of Innocent III, 1208, CCXVII, 180.

ST JOHN IN EXSTORIO (Saint-Jean de Citou, diocese of Carcassonne), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, founded by Abbot Anianus, as Charlemagne’s ordinance teaches, 793, XCVII, 980.

ST JOHN IN LAMIS (Saint-Jean-aux-Lames, Capitanata, Naples), a monastery whose abbot Innocent III wrote to, ordering him to restore peace between the people of Foggia and Troia, 1204, CCXV, 442.

ST JOHN AT TITUS, or AT THE PINE, a monastery of the Order of St Benedict near the city of Classe in the diocese of Ravenna; its abbot John went to Constantinople in the seventh century, CVI, 696.

ST JOHN. See AUGUSTODUNENSE, GERBSTADENSE, HALBERSTATENSE, LUSITANUM, MONTIS-ST-JOHN, NICIENSE, PARMENSE, ROMANUM, etc.

ST JOHN OF PEÑA, a monastery of the Order of St Benedict in Spain, built by King Sancho and entrusted to St Odilo of Cluny so that regular observance might be renewed, eleventh century, CXLII, 868.

ST JOHN OF RIVIPULLUM (Saint-Jean de Rieux, near Aussone, Haute-Garonne), a monastery of the Order of St Augustine, founded by Berengar, bishop of Ausone, in 1089. — Privilege of Pope Urban II, CLI, 299.

ST JOHN IN THE VALLEY. See CARNOTENSE.

ST JOHN IN VENERE (Saint-Jean called “in Venere,” diocese of Chieti, Naples), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, built by Transmund, count of Chieti, already approved by Leo IX, Victor, Nicholas, and Urban II; it was confirmed anew by privilege of Alexander III in 1176, CC, 1073. — Privilege of Innocent III, 1204, CCXVII, 125.

ST JOHN IN THE VALLEY OF TURA (Saint-Jean de Thurtal, diocese of Constance, Switzerland), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, built by Wenceslaus, or Wezelo, of Ganderswilla in 1152. — Privilege granted in the same year by Pope Eugenius III, CLXXX, 1548.

ST JOHN OF THE VINES (Saint-Jean-des-Vignes, near Soissons), a monastery of the Order of St Augustine, founded by Hugh, count of Château-Thierry, and Bishop Theobald. Pope Urban II granted it a privilege in 1089, CLI, 295. — Privilege of Adrian IV, 1158, CLXXXVIII, 1585. — Letter of Alexander III on behalf of the abbot of this monastery, 1172, CC, 807, 813, 814, 1278, 1279. — Decree of Celestine III, 1197, CCVI, 1193. — Letter of Innocent III concerning the provostship of Calais, 1210, CCXVI, 260.

ST JODOCUS, or ST JUDOCUS (Saint-Josse-sur-Mer), an abbey [Col. 1083] situated among the Morini beside the sea, in the diocese of Amiens, over which Alcuin presided for some time in the eighth century, CI, 694; CXIX, 453. — Letter of Innocent III concerning the reform of this monastery, 1213, CCXVI, 936.

ST JODOCUS IN THE WOOD (Saint-Josse au Bois). See DOMMARTINENSE.

JOINVILLE. See URBANI.

JOSAPHAT (of) ST. MARY (Notre-Dame de Josaphat, diocese of Chartres), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, and his brother Goslin, in 1117. — Privilege of Calixtus II, 1119, CLXIII, 1136.

JOTRENSE (Jouarre-en-Brie, diocese of Meaux), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in the diocese of Meaux, founded by Ado, brother of St. Audoen, who withdrew there with other courtiers of King Dagobert’s palace about 630; for it consult the numbers of the following articles.

JOTRENSIS (Jouarre-en-Brie), a celebrated convent of nuns of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by the same Ado, brother of St. Audoen, in the forest of Jotrannes; St. Balthild gave it many gifts, in 684, LXXXVII, 670. — Privilege granted by Innocent III to Abbess Agnes in 1202, CCXIV, 1135. — Letter of the same pope to the abbess, 1208, CCXV, 1599, 1603. — Agreement between the bishop of Meaux and the church of Jouarre, CCXV, 1606.

JOVIACENSE or JOYACENSE, ST. MARY (Notre-Dame de Jouy, Seine-et-Marne), a Cistercian monastery in the territory of Brie, founded before 1124 by the noblemen Peter of Châtel and Milo, lord of Nanteuil. — Letter of Alexander III on behalf of a certain man who had left that monastery, 1174, CC, 1009.

JOVILLARENSE, ST. PETER (Saint-Pierre de Jovilliers, Meuse), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, founded in 1141 by Geoffrey of Joinville and his wife Felicity. — Privilege of Pope Lucius III, 1181, CCI, 1100.

JOVINUS (ST.). See ENIXIONENSE.

JOVINII, a Carthusian house in Bresse. See MAJOREVUM.

JOVISVILLA, ST. LAWRENCE (Saint-Laurent de Jouaville, Moselle), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, whose properties Innocent III confirmed by privilege in 1207, CCXV, 1122.

JUCELLENSE. See below, JUNCELLENSE.

JUDOCUS. See above, JODOCUS.

JUGO DEI, BLESSED MARY (Notre-Dame du Joug-Dieu, diocese of Lyon, Rhône), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by Wichard of Beaujeu and his wife Lucania in 1118. Innocent ordered its abbot not to accept money for marriages and burials, 1198, CCXIV, 191.

JULIACENSE, ST. MARY (Notre-Dame de Juilly, diocese of Meaux), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, founded by Foulques of Saint-Denis in 1182.

JULIACENSIS (Juilly, diocese of Langres, Côte-d'Or), a convent of nuns founded by Milo, count of Bar-sur-Seine; Blessed Peter, monk of Molesme, was formerly its prior. His life is described under 1178, CLXXXV, 1257. — Charter of Milo, 1408.

JULIA (ST.). See BRIXIENSIS.

JULIAN IN CALABRIA (Saint-Julien in Calabria), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, mentioned in letters of Pope Paschal II, 1103–1104, CLXIII, 125, 137. — Perhaps the same as St. Julian of Pereyo, a monastery to which Alexander III granted a privilege in 1176, CC, 1086. — Letter of Innocent III against heretics, 1204, CCXV, 329.

JULIAN OF LE MANS, a monastery mentioned by Charlemagne in a diploma of 802, XCVII, 995.

JULIAN OF TOURS. See TURONENSE.

JUMERIS (ST.), a cell whose location is unknown to us. For its church St. Radegund gave her ornaments and even her own garments about 545, LXXII, 655.

JUNANTENSE (Zunault, diocese of Rodez), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict founded by King Clovis; later, after being almost destroyed, it was given by King Pippin to the abbey of Figeac in 755, CXLI, 23.

JUNCELLENSE, ST. PETER (Joncels or Jaussalz near Lodève, Hérault), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose rights and possessions Pope Gregory VII confirmed in 1085, CXLIII, 717. — Privilege of Pope Innocent II, 1133, CLXXIX, 231, 471.

JUNTURAE (Abbey of Jointures). See DEODATI.

JUNGERIACO (Jonchéry-sur-Marne, near Chaumont in Bassigny), a monastery whose cause Alexander III defended against the count of Regiteste, 1174, CC, 956.

JUNQUARIA (Juncherias in Galicia, Spain), a Cistercian monastery originating from Monte Ramo and, on that very account, made subject to it by the king and by Innocent III, 1199, CCXIV, 720.

[Col. 1084] JUREDENSE, ST. ANDREW (Saint-André de Jau, diocese of Elne or Perpignan), founded by Abbot Miro and Count Gausselm on the River Tagidum; certain properties were granted to it by Louis the Pious in 829, CIV, 1179.

JURENSE, ST. RAGNIBERT or REGIMBERT (Saint-Rambert de Joux, diocese of Lyon), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, also called Bebronense because it was built on the stream Bebronna, at the foot of the Jura mountain, and was founded in the diocese of Lyons. Testament of St. Ansegisus, 833, CV, 748, note. — Privilege of Celestine III, 1191, CCVI, 893.

JURENSE, ST. ROMANUS (Saint-Romain de Joux), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by St. Romanus and his companions in 460, between the Helvetii and the Sequani, LXXI, 1011.

AT LAKE JURA, ST. MARY MAGDALENE (Sainte-Magdeleine du lac de Joux, Switzerland), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order in the diocese of Lausanne, built in 1133 by Seilger, lord of Oberoffen. — Privilege of Alexander III, 1177, CC, 1150.

ST. JUST OF BEAUVAIS (Saint-Just de Beauvais), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, first founded for women in 1107; under Bishop Odo it passed to the Premonstratensians in 1147. — Privilege of Henry I, archbishop of Rheims, 1163, CXCVI, 1577. — Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1208, CCXV, 1600, 1604.

ST. JUST, a monastery situated in the diocese of Chieti (Chieti, Abruzzi, Naples), mentioned by Innocent III, CCXVII, 180.

ST. JUSTINA. See the convent of nuns at LUCCA.

ST. JUSTINA OF ACQUI (Sainte-Justine d'Acqui, Piedmont), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, to which Celestine III granted a privilege in 1192, CCVI, 924.

JUSSANENSIS CONVENT OF NUNS (Joussan, diocese of Besançon), founded by Flavia, mother of St. Donatus, about 650, LXXXVII, 268; LXXX, 423.

JUVENACENSE, ST. MARY (Sainte-Marie de Giovenazzo, kingdom of Naples), a monastery mentioned in a privilege granted by the antipope Anacletus to the bishop of Giovenazzo in 1130, CLXXIX, 720.

JUVENAL (ST.). See ROMANUM.

JUVINIACENSIS, ST. SCHOLASTICA, convent of nuns (convent of Juvigny, Meuse), founded in the diocese of Trier by the Empress Richildis, wife of Charles the Bald, in 874. — Privilege of Urban II, 1096, CLI, 476. — Concerning the dispute between Abbess Hadwida and the abbot of St. Michael over the church of St. Tyriacus, CLXXIX, 452.

KALTENBORNENSE, ST. JOHN THE EVANGELIST (Saint-Jean de Kaltenbrunn, diocese of Halberstadt), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, built by the nobleman Wimann shortly before 1126, when Pope Honorius II endowed it with a privilege, CLXVI, 1152. — Privilege of Innocent II, 1139, CLXXIX, 494. — Privilege of Eugenius III, 1145, CLXXX, 1017, 1984. — Of Anastasius IV, 1153, CLXXXVIII, 1029. — Of Alexander III, 1162, 171, 178. — Of Lucius III, 1183, CCI, 1185.

KAMINATENSIS. See below, KEMINADENSIS.

KAROFENSE, ST. SAVIOR, or CARROSSENSE. See CARROFENSE.

KELCHOVIENSE (Kelchow, diocese of St. Andrews, Ireland), a monastery whose abbot Innocent III addressed concerning the election of the bishop of Aberdeen, 1207, CCXV, 1303.

KEMINADENSIS, ST. MARY (Sainte-Marie de Kaments, diocese of Bremen), a convent of nuns founded in the duchy of Brunswick by Count Gero, his wife Imma, and the Venerable Abbess Frederuna. Emperor St. Henry II took it under his protection in 1004, CXL, 255, 256. — Eugenius III wrote in its defense in 1148, CLXXX, 1331, 1421, 1491. — Letter of King Conrad to Eugenius, CLXXX, 1613. — Letter of Henry, duke of Saxony, to the same pope, 1621.

KEMPERLEGIENSE, HOLY CROSS (Sainte-Croix de Kimperley), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in Lower Brittany, founded about 550 by Duke Gurthian or Gunthern. The founder himself was also its first abbot. Pope St. Gregory VII confirmed the rights and possessions of this monastery in 1078, CXLVIII, 684. — Letters of Paschal II to the monks of Redon concerning the restitution of Belle-Île, 1117, CLXIII, 427. — Girard, bishop of Angoulême, threatens Duke Conan of Brittany with excommunication unless he makes satisfaction to the monastery of Holy Cross, CLXXII. — Gilbert’s letter to Conan on the same matter, ibid. Restoration of Belle-Île to the monks of Kemperley by Conan, 1327.

KENANENSE (Kénan, in the county of Tuam, Ireland), a monastery whose abbot Innocent III wrote to in 1205, entrusting a certain case to him, CCXV, 639.

KENINGENSE (Kenings, county of Lancaster, near [Col. 1085] Salford, England), a monastery whose properties and privileges Innocent III confirmed in 1206, CCXV, 1073.

KIRCHANENSE (Kirckcham, diocese of York, England), a monastery whose abbot Innocent III entrusted with responsibility for reforming certain monasteries in 1207, CCXV, 1128. — Privilege of the same pope, 1207, CCXV, 1183.

KITZINGENSE, SS. KILIAN AND GEORGE (Kissingen, diocese of Würzburg), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, which Emperor St. Henry II gave to the archbishop of Bamberg in 1007, CXL, 275.

KITZINGUNENSIS (Kitzingen, diocese of Würzburg), a convent of nuns whose Abbess Sophia wrote to St. Hildegard, commending herself to her prayers, twelfth century, CXCVII, 322.

KILIAN (ST.). See PADERBORNENSE.

KLUAYNARDENSIS, ST. MARY (Sainte-Marie de Kluaynard, England), a convent of nuns of the Order of St. Augustine, which Celestine III took under his protection and whose properties and privileges he confirmed in 1195, CCVI, 1152.

KNESTEDENSE (Knethstethde, diocese of Cologne), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order founded in the twelfth century; its abbot wrote to St. Hildegard, abbess of St. Rupert, CXCVII, 313.

LACENSE (Le Lac in the diocese of Trier), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by the noble Count Palatine Henry and his wife Adelheid and entrusted to Abbot Gislibert. At his request Innocent II confirmed its properties and privileges in 1139, CLXXIX, 409. — Privilege of Eugenius III, 1148, CLXXX, 1301.

AT LAKE JURA. See JURIENSE.

AT THE BLACK LAKE, or NEERLACENSE.

AT LAKE JUPITER, ST. MARY (Notre-Dame du Lac-de-Joux, canton of Vaud, Switzerland), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, built by Ebaldo, lord of Sarroz, in 1126. It was also called Locus Pontii (Lieu-Poncet), after a certain monk Pontius, who had previously built himself a small cell in the same place. — Blessed Amadeus of Lausanne negotiated for this monastery with the monks of St. Eugendus in 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1292. — Lucius III, 1185, CCI, 1325.

LAETIENSE, ST. LAMBERT (Saint-Lambert de Liessies or Liesses, diocese of Cambrai), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built near Avesnes by Count Wicbert and his wife Ada in 751. — Privilege of Innocent, 1131, CLXXIX, 81. — Privilege of Eugenius III, 1147, CLXXX, 1284. — Of Adrian IV, 1156, CLXXXVIII, 1461. — Letter of Alexander III, 1174, CC, 958, 1274. — Of Lucius III, 1184, CCI, 1254.

LAESTINGENSE, a monastery founded in England by Bishop Cedd and King Oswald; but the memory of this site has been lost, XCV, 154.

LAMBERT (ST.). See VALLE SEIN.

ST. LAMBERT OF STYRIA (Saint-Lambrecht in Upper Styria), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, which Pope Honorius II took under his protection and whose possessions and rights he confirmed in 1126, CLXVI, 1258.

AT LAMIS. See JOHN.

LANARIACENSIS (Lanneray, near Châteaudun, Eure-et-Loir), a priory whose cause Alexander III undertook against the monks of Quincy, 1174, CC, 1032.

LANCKEIMENSE (Lanckeim, diocese of Bamberg, Bavaria), a Cistercian monastery founded by St. Otto, bishop of Bamberg, in 1132, CLXXIII.

LANDELINENSE or WALLARENSE, ST. PETER (Wallers-en-Fagne), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by Blessed Landelin, bishop of Cambrai, and King Dagobert in 634. It was situated in the forest of Fagne and the diocese of Cambrai, LXXX, 533. — Charter of St. Autbert, bishop, ibid., 595.

LANDECURTENSIS (Landécourt, Meurthe), a priory built in 1100 by Lord Bencelin after his return from Jerusalem. — Privilege of Pibo, bishop of Toul, CLVII, 439.

LANGENHORSTENSIS (Langenhorst, diocese of Münster), a convent of nuns whose properties and privileges Clement III confirmed in 1189, CCIV, 1418.

LANSPRINGENSIS, ST. MARY, convent of nuns (Lansperg, Bavaria), whose rights and possessions Innocent III confirmed in 1138, CLXXIX, 373.

LANTHONIENSE (Lanthon, diocese of Lincoln, England), a monastery or priory founded by Robert, bishop of Lincoln, to which Innocent III granted a privilege in 1204, CCXV, 491.

AT THE ROCK, ST. MICHAEL (La Pierre Saint-Michel, Saxony). See MICHAELSTEINENSE.

LATTA, ST. MARTIN (Siran-la-Latte, near Sivré, diocese of Tours), a monastery not far from Severiacum and Nobiliacum (Neuilly), built in the territory of Tours; St. Gregory of Tours described its plundering, LXXI, 311.

LATERANENSE. See ROMANUM.

[Col. 1086] LATINIACENSE, ST. FURSEY (Lagny-sur-Marne, Seine-et-Marne), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict not far from Paris, founded about 654 by the devout Count Erchinoald, LXXI, 658, note; XCV, 149. — Diploma of King Robert for the restoration of that monastery, 1018, CXLI, 960. — Privilege of Pope Urban II, 1088, CLI, 523. — Letter of Innocent II to Abbot Radulf, 1143, CLXXIX, 621. — Letter of Alexander III, 1165, CC, 333. — Letter of Innocent III to the abbot concerning the election of the bishop of Meaux, 1207, CCXV, 1256, 1599; CCXVI, 193, 198, 729.

LAUBIENSE or LOBBIENSE (Lobbes, diocese of Liège), a celebrated monastery of the Order of St. Benedict on the Sambre, built by St. Ursmar, abbot, and Pippin the Elder after the defeat of Theuderic in 691, LXXXVIII, 1223, 1238. — Abbot Folcuin flourished there in 990, CXXXVII, 529. — On the deeds of the abbots of Lobbes, 541. — Abbot Heriger, 1008, CXXXIX, 955. — Mention and notice of that monastery, CXLIX, 138. — Abbot Folcard flourished in 1107, CLVII, 481. — Privilege of Pope Innocent II, 1131, CLXXIX, 90. — Of Eugenius III, 1150, CLXXX, 1431.

LAUCONENSE (Saint-Lupicin, in the Jura, former diocese of Lyon), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, mentioned in the Life of St. Lupicinus by Gregory of Tours, 520, LXXI, 1013.

OF LAUDE, ST. MARY. See below, LOSENSE.

LAUDENSE, ST. STEPHEN (Saint-Étienne de Lodi, in the Milanese), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by Queen Anselda and Blessed Lanfranc; Paschal II granted it a privilege in 1106, CLXIII, 199.

ST. LAUDUS (Saint-Lô, diocese of Coutances, Normandy), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine. Privilege of foundation granted by Innocent II to Bishop Algar, 1132, CXXIX, 126.

ST. LAUDUS OF ROUEN, discussed in a letter of Eugenius III, CLXXX, 1408. — It seems to be the same as the preceding.

LAUDUNENSE, ST. MARY or ST. PETER (Saint-Pierre de Laon), a very ancient college of canons, once enriched by St. Remigius, bishop of Rheims, CLVI, 993. — Later, in the twelfth century, Bishop Bartholomew enriched those same canons, who lived according to a rule, with many gifts, 1067. — Letter of Alexander III, 1172, CC, 816, 817.

LAUDUNENSE, ST. MICHAEL (Saint-Michel-en-Thiérache), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose abbot was Fulk in the eleventh century, CXLIX, 425. — Lord Gislebert became abbot of St. Michael and was later transferred to the abbey of St. Nicholas of Ribemont, CLVI, 1002.

LAUDUNENSE, ST. VINCENT. See VINCENTII.

LAUDUNENSE, ST. JOHN (Saint-Jean de Laon), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, established in the eleventh century by Blessed Bartholomew, bishop, from a once flourishing convent of nuns founded by Blessed Abbess Salaberga, but which had fallen into decline after her, CLXI, 1003. — On Abbot Baldwin, ibid., 1005, 1176. — On the replacement of the abbot, 1178. — List of abbots, 1180. — Life of St. Salaberga, CLVI, 1223. — Privilege of Innocent II, 1130, CLXXIX, 66. — Of Innocent III, 1205, CCVII, 140.

LAUDUNENSE, ST. MARTIN (Saint-Martin de Laon), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, established about 1124 by the Venerable Bishop Bartholomew with certain monks of St. Norbert, over whom he appointed Walter as abbot; it soon grew greatly, CLVI, 993, 1183. — List of abbots, 1184. — Privilege of Pope Innocent II, 1131, CXXIX, 89, 349. — Of Lucius II, 1144, ibid., 882. — Of Eugenius III, 1147, CLXXX, 1210. — Zacharias, monk and commentator, flourished in 1152, CLXXXVI, 9. — Letters of Alexander III, 1167–1169, CC, 517, 531, 989. — Letter of Innocent III, 1210, CCXVI, 198.

LAUNOMAR (ST.), Saint-Lomer of Clermont, a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict among the Arverni, devastated by the Northmen and restored by Count William in 928. — Privilege of Pope John X, CXXXII, 809.

LAUNOMAR (ST.) OF BLOIS (Saint-Lomer de Blois or Lomer-le-Moûtier, diocese of Blois), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by King Radulf and Count Louis of Blois in 924. — Privilege of Pope Paschal II, 1107, CLXIII, 208.

ST. LAWRENCE OF HESSE. See HESSENSIS.

ST. LAWRENCE OF BEAUVAIS (Saint-Laurent de Beauvais), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, on whose behalf Alexander III wrote to the bishop of Beauvais in 1174, CC, 941.

ST. LAWRENCE OF LIÈGE (Saint-Laurent de Liège), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by Bishop Eraclius in a suburb of Liège on Mont-Public about 968. — Abbot Wulpod, expelled from the monastery, appealed to the pope. Letter of Gregory VII, 1077, CXLVIII, 475. — Pope Urban II congratulates Abbot Berengar because he had risen against simoniacs and had been expelled from his own monastery, [Col. 1087] 1095, CLI, 395. — John, monk and author, flourished in 1147, CLXXX, 177. — Privilege of Eugenius III, 1147, CLXXX, 1213. — Reynerius, monk, flourished in 1188, CCIV, 9.

ST. LAWRENCE OF PARIS (Saint-Laurent-lès-Paris), a monastery built in a suburb of Paris in 591, of which St. Domnulus was at one time abbot, LXXI, 381.

ST. LAWRENCE AND HILARY OF THE ABBEY (Saint-Laurent-des-Aubats, diocese of Auxerre), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, founded by St. Ulfin in 578 and reformed in 1076–1084. — Privilege of Eugenius III, 1133, CLXXX, 1555.

ST. LAWRENCE OF OLIBEJO or MOUNT OLIVE (Mont Oléon, former diocese of Carcassonne), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in the diocese of Carcassonne, to which is subject the monastery of Caunes, built by Blessed Abbot Anianus. Precept of Charlemagne, 793, XCVII, 979. — Diploma of Louis the Pious, 815, CIV, 1031.

ST. LAWRENCE’S CELL in the district of Mâcon, founded by St. Odilo, abbot of Cluny, and Viscount Archimbald in 1039, CXLII, 866.

ST. LAWRENCE. See JANUENSE, SPELLENSE, VITERBIENSE.

LAURESHAMENSE, ST. NAZARIUS (Lauresheim, Laurisham, or Lorsch, diocese of Trier), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, defended by Charlemagne in the time of Abbot Gundelard against the claim of Count Eymeric Cancron’s son, in 770, XCVII, 1048. — Its properties were confirmed by him, 1049. — He granted a privilege of immunity, 1055, 1059. — Charter of Einhard, CIV, 601. — Of John XV, CXXXVII, 834. — Precept of Emperor St. Henry II, 1012, CXL, 297, 376. — Privilege of Pope St. Leo IX, 1049, CXLIII, 624. — Of Eugenius III, 1148, CLXXX, 1314, 1316. — Of Alexander III, 1179, CC, 1223, 1233.

LAURIACENSE (perhaps Lorch, in the duchy of Württemberg and diocese of Mainz), a monastery in Noricum on the Danube. — Privilege of Pope Eugenius II, 827, CXXIX, 989. — Of Innocent II, 1136, CLXXIX, 276. — Letter of Innocent III, 1199, CCXIV, 824, 873.

LAUSANNE COLLEGE OF CANONS (chapter of the church of Lausanne), whose possessions and privileges Alexander III confirmed in 1182, CCI, 1150.

LAUSIENSE or DE LAUSIA (Luze, diocese of Autun), a monastery built between Autun and the Loire, where St. Germanus, bishop of Paris, was educated under his kinsman St. Scopilio, the abbot, about 540, LXXII, 57.

LEBRAHENSIS PRIORY (Leber or Leberaw, former diocese of Strasbourg), a monastery founded about 774 by Fulrad, abbot of St. Denis, in the diocese of Strasbourg. — Diploma of Charlemagne, 791, XCVII, 1080, 1084. — Of Emperor Charles IV, 1348, XCVII, 1082.

LEGIONENSE, ST. ISIDORE (Saint-Isidore de León, Spain), a royal monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, where St. Martin, a distinguished preacher, flourished in 1200, CCVIII, 9.

LEHONNENSE or LEONENSE, ST. MAGLORIUS (Saint-Magloire at Saint-Pol-de-Léon, Finistère), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, founded in 849 and rebuilt about 1000. — Letter of Pope Lucius III concerning its dispute with the monastery of St. Maglorius in Paris, 1183, CCI, 1234.

LEHUNENSE (Lihons or Lihu, Somme), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, to which Count Robert of Flanders and Robert of Péronne gave an allod commonly called Harbonnières in 1104, as is shown by the charter of Geoffrey, bishop of Amiens, CLXII, 735.

LEMAUSENSE, ST. JOHN (Saint-Jean de Limours, near Étampes, diocese of Sens), a small women’s monastery in the district of Étampes, built by Gammon and his wife Adalgude. It was made subject to the monastery of St. Vincent, or St. Germain-des-Prés, under Childebert III in 703, LXXXVIII, 1099. — Charter of foundation, 697, LXXXVIII, 1235.

LEMOVICENSE. See ATHANENSE; ST. MARTIAL.

LEMOVICENSE, ST. AUGUSTINE (Saint-Augustin de Limoges), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict whose first foundation is attributed to the time of St. Martial. Atticus, the fourth bishop, enlarged it in 934; it was rebuilt by Bishop Turpio. — Privilege of Adrian IV, 1159, CLXXXVIII, 1613.

LEMOVICENSE, ST. PETER (Saint-Pierre de Limoges), a monastery built by Fulbert, abbot of St. Martial, in which he was later buried, at the beginning of the tenth century.

LENENSE (Leno in the Venetian States), a monastery taken under the protection of Calixtus II in 1123, CLXIII, 1271. — Privilege of Innocent II, 1132, CLXXIX, 152.

LENSENSE, ST. VULGAN (Lens in Artois), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, mentioned in CXLIX, 132; built about 1040 by St. [Col. 1088] Ida and her husband Eustace, CLV, 451. — It obtained many privileges from St. Lietbert, bishop of Cambrai, in 1072, CXLVI, 1447.

LEOBARD (ST.). See MAURI.

LEOBIN (ST.). See ST. AVITUS and BRAJACUM.

ST. LEOCADIA OF TOLEDO, a monastery mentioned in the Life of St. Maximus, 644, LXXX, 612.

LIÈGE, ST. JOHN (Saint-Jean de Liège), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, whose provost was Reimbald in 1115, CLXII, 749. — Privilege of Urban III, 1186, CCII, 1420.

LIÈGE, ST. JAMES (Saint-Jacques de Liège), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by Bishop Balderic about 1006, during the reign of Emperor Henry II, CXL, 281, note. — Privilege of Lucius III, 1185, CCI, 1323.

LIÈGE. See above, ST. LAWRENCE.

ST. LEODEGAR OF CAMPELLIS (Saint-Léger-sous-Beuvray), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine in the diocese of Autun, built by St. Leodegar; Ansebert made certain gifts to it in 696, LXXXVIII, 1231. — It later came within the diocese of Langres; Hugh and King Robert granted it a privilege in 994, CXLI, 945.

ST. LEODEGAR (Saint-Léger or Saint-Ligaire, near Niort, Deux-Sèvres), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in 961. — Letter of Innocent III to the abbot regarding a certain abuse in the church of St. Mary Major at Poitiers, 1202, CCXIV, 1165.

OF THE LEPER, ST. SILVANUS (Saint-Sylvain de Lairoux, near Luçon), a priory of the Order of St. Benedict. Letter of Innocent III to its prior, who is called the pope’s subdeacon, 1202, CCXIV, 1137, 1154; 1205, CCXV, 580.

LEPERS OF THE MOUNT. See MONTE.

LEPERS OF MISSINO (the Hospitallers of Missino, diocese of Faenza, Papal States), a monastery founded by the nobleman Missino shortly before 1210, when Innocent III confirmed it by privilege, CCXVI, 221.

LERINENSE (Abbey of Lérins, former diocese of Grasse, now of Fréjus), a monastery once distinguished, built on an island in the Mediterranean Sea, reportedly by St. Honoratus. Outstanding men flourished there: Faustus, Eucherius, Salonius, Honoratus, Hilary, Salvian, Vincent, and others. It was founded in the fourth century, L, 637; LIII, 967. — Letter of Calixtus II to the bishop of Fréjus concerning damage inflicted upon this monastery, 1123, CXIII, 1261. — Privilege of Pope Honorius II, 1135, CLXVI, 1245. — Letter of Adrian IV concerning protection of the monastery against the Saracens, 1158, CLXXXVIII, 1581. — Privilege of Celestine III, 1192, CCXI, 989. — Letter of Innocent III to the archbishop of Arles concerning reform of the monastery, 1198, CCXIV, 230. — The same pope confirms an agreement with the bishop of Antibes, 1210, CCXVI, 224, 226, 245, 969.

LESATENSE, ST. PETER (Saint-Pierre de Lézat, diocese of Pamiers, Ariège), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose foundation is attributed to Atto, count of Béziers, in 950. Letter of St. Ado, abbot, to Paschal II concerning the subjection of the small abbey of St. Peter of Courte, 1104, CLXIII, 456.

LESBURNENSE (Lesburn, diocese of Mons), a monastery whose abbot Innocent III wrote to concerning the translation of the bishop of Osnabrück in 1210, CCXVI, 334.

LETONENSE, ST. MARY, a monastery which seems to be located in the diocese of Girona, on the frontier of Spain; it is discussed in a bull of Calixtus II, 1124, CLXIII, 1314.

LEUBATIUS (ST.). See SENAPARIA.

ST. LEOCADIA (Sainte-Léocadie, diocese of Exeter, province of Canterbury, England). — Letter of Innocent III to the abbot of this monastery, CCXVI, 1250.

LEUFRED (ST.). See CRUCE.

LEUMENSE, a monastery whose abbot presented Innocent III with a complaint against the Hospitallers. It appears to have been situated in Denmark and the diocese of Lund, as may be inferred from the title appended to Innocent’s letter, CCXVI, 1208, 1209.

LEUTEVENSE or LUTEVENSE, ST. SAVIOR (Saint-Sauveur de Lodève), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict founded by Fulcran, bishop of Lodève, shortly before the time of Calixtus II, who endowed it with a privilege in 1122, CLXIII, 1254.

LEWENSE or LEWESENSE. See PANCRATII.

LEVENENSIS or QUIVENENSIS, a convent of nuns (Leven or Quiven, diocese of Verden in Westphalia), on whose behalf Clement III wrote to the abbot of Lune in 1188, CCIV, 1346.

LEXOVIENSIS, ST. PETER (Saint-Pierre de Lisieux), a convent of nuns built by Lezelina, countess of Eu, in the eleventh century, CCII, 1317.

LICHSFELDENSE (Lichfield, in Staffordshire, England), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, built and endowed shortly before 1144 by Roger, bishop of Coventry, [Col. 1089] CLXXIX, 862.

LIESBORNENSE (Leisborn, diocese of Münster), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in the district of Dreny and the county of Hermann of Dön, and belonging to the bishop of Mimigernaford. — Privilege of Emperor St. Henry II, 1019, CXL, 345. — Likewise of Pope Innocent II, 1132–1146, CLXXIX, 251. — Letter of Adrian IV concerning a controversy with the bishop of Paderborn, 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1375.

LIEVANENSE, ST. THURIBIUS IN SPAIN (Saint Turibius of Liébana), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in which St. Beatus, commonly called San Bieco, appears to have had his seat, 790, XCVI, 890.

LIGNIACENSIS, SS. VITUS AND MODESTUS (Lignière, Somme), a priory granted in 1103 by Geoffrey, bishop of Amiens, to the Parisian monastery of St. Martin-des-Champs and to Cluny, on which it depended, CLXII, 727.

LINCEIO (Lancay, former diocese of Le Mans, now of Blois), a priory of the Order of St. Benedict dependent on Marmoutier, mentioned in a privilege of Innocent III, 1211, CCXVI, 449.

LINCOLN, ST. ALBAN. See ALBANI.

LINDISFARNENSE (Lindisfarne or Holy Island, on the coast of Northumberland), a monastery situated on the island of the same name, over which Eata, abbot of Melrose among the Scots, was appointed by King Alhfrith in 662, XCV, 159. — It was distinguished by Æthelwold, XCVI, 1327.

LINGONENSE. See ST. MAMMETIS.

LINGRARICA, ST. PETER (Saint-Pierre de Lingraricca in Venetia), a monastery whose abbot Innocent III wrote to concerning the controversy between the archbishop of Durazzo and the nobleman Demetrius in 1209, CCXVI, 107.

LIPARENSE (Lipari, on the island of the same name), built by King Roger and endowed with a privilege by the antipope Anacletus in 1131, CLXXIX, 722.

LIRA. See LYRA.

LIRUMENSE, for LIRINENSE. See above, LERINENSE.

LISCKENSE, ST. MARY (Notre-Dame de Licques, Pas-de-Calais), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, built by Count Robert of Boulogne in 1132, when Milo was bishop of the Morini. — Privilege of Alexander III, 1164, CC, 315, 971.

LISSIENSE. See LAETIENSE.

LITOMIZLENSE (Lutomizl in Moravia), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, built by noblemen of that region and confirmed by privilege of Eugenius III at the request of Henry, bishop of Moravia, in 1145, CLXXX, 1045.

LIUBANENSIS, ST. MARY AND ST. ANDREW (convent of St. Mary of Leuben or Loiben, Upper Styria), a convent of nuns founded by Count Aribo from the county of Liuban at a place called Yoffia, and entrusted to the Venerable Abbess Hunegund. — Privilege of Pope Benedict VIII, 1020, CXXXIX, 1023.

LOBBIENSE. See above, LAUBIENSE.

LOCEDIENSE, ST. MARY or SS. MICHAEL AND JANUARY. See LUCEDIENSE.

LOECIS, ON THE ANGRE (Loches-sur-Cher, Indre-et-Loire), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict founded and governed by Blessed Abbot Ursus in 500; it later adopted the Rule of St. Benedict, LXXI, 1085.

LOCEDIENSE. See below, LUCEDIENSE.

LOCHEIENSE. See BELLOLOCO, OF THE HOLY TRINITY.

LOCUS DEI (Lieu-Dieu, diocese of Ribe, Jutland, Denmark), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order built by Omer, bishop of Ribe, with the assent of Absalon, archbishop of Lund; shortly afterward it adopted the Cistercian Rule. A privilege of Celestine III confirmed this foundation in 1197, CCVI, 1240. — Privilege of Innocent III, 1205, CCXVII, 134, 276.

LOCUS DEI, ST. MARY (Notre-Dame de Lieu-Dieu en Jard, Vendée), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, founded in 1145 by Louis the Younger, king of the Franks, and Richard, count of Anjou and king of England. — Privilege of Eugenius III, 1147, CLXXX, 1254.

LOCOCIACENSE or LOCOCEIACUM (Ligugé near Poitiers), a monastery founded by St. Martin near Poitiers in the fourth century, in the time of St. Hilary and before Martin was elevated to the see of Tours. It was later made a priory and finally passed to the Fathers of the Society of Jesus, IX, 164; LXXI, 185; LXXXVIII, 445.

LOCO PONTII (Lieu-Poncet). See LACU JOVIS.

LOCO-RESTAURATO (the Abbey of Lieu-Restauré, diocese of Soissons), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, built in 1138 by Count Ralph of Vermandois. Privilege of Eugenius III, 1145, CLXXX, 1067.

LOCO SANCTO, ST. MARY (Notre-Dame de Saint-Lien). See SEPTEM FONTIUM.

LOGIENSIS CONVENT OF NUNS, situated near Caudebec in [Col. 1090] Normandy, not far from the cell of Abbot Milo; it was endowed by Blessed Balthild in 680, LXXXVII, 670, 748.

LONDONIENSE. See below, LUNDONIENSE.

LONGISPONTIS, ST. MARY (Notre-Dame de Longpont, diocese of Versailles), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, given to the monastery of Cluny by the nobleman Guy of Trousseau, lord of Montlhéry, and his wife Hodierna, in 1061. — Privilege of Innocent, 1142, CLXXIX, 572. — Of Eugenius III, 1148, CLXXX, 1311. — Of Anastasius IV, 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1084. — Of Alexander III, 1170, CC, 617. — Of Lucius III, 1182, CCI, 1227. — Of Celestine III, 1195, CCVI, 1141. — Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1208, CCXV, 1518, 1600; 1213, CCXVI, 940.

LONGOGIONENSE, ST. AGATHA (Longuyon, diocese of Trier), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in the diocese of Trier, founded or substantially enlarged by Adalgisel under King Dagobert, in the seventh century, LXXXVII, 1343.

LONGOGILO (Longueil near Dieppe, diocese of Rouen), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in the district of Dieppe, mentioned in the testament of St. Ansegisus, abbot of Fontenelle, in 833, CV, 744.

LONGORETO. See MILEPECO.

LONGOVILLACENSE, ST. MARY (Notre-Dame de Longvilliers, Pas-de-Calais), a Cistercian monastery built by Stephen, count of Boulogne, in 1135. Letter of Innocent III to the abbot concerning reform of the monastery of St. Judoc, 1212, CCXVI, 936.

LONGOVILLANUM or GLANDERIENSE (Longueville, Glandières, or Saint-Martin-aux-Chênes), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in the diocese of Metz, formerly founded about 587 by Bodagisel, father of St. Arnulf. Many things were given to and taken from it by kings, and finally restored by Louis the Pious in 836, CIV, 1283.

LONNICENSE, ST. MARY (Sainte-Marie de Lonnecken, diocese of Trier), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, founded shortly before 1148, when Eugenius III confirmed it by privilege, CLXXX, 1304.

LONLEYENSE, ST. MARY (Notre-Dame de Lonlay-l'Abbaye, Orne), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in 1000 by William Talvas; William, monk of Fleury, was its first abbot, CCII, 1320.

LORSCH (Lorsch, diocese of Mainz), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine. Letter of Innocent III concerning a certain Hermann, canon of this monastery, 1199, CCXIV. See LAUREACENSE.

LOSENSE or DE LAUDE, BLESSED MARY (Loos-Notre-Dame, former diocese of Tournai), a Cistercian monastery built by Thierry, count of Flanders, in 1176. Privilege of Innocent III, 1204, CCXVII, 120, 198, 206, 210, 211.

LÜBECK, ST. MARY AND ST. JOHN (St. Mary or St. John of Lübeck, Denmark), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose properties and privileges Celestine III confirmed at the request of Abbot Arnold in 1191, CCVI, 872, 873.

LUBBOLDESBERGENSE, a German convent of nuns whose location is unknown to us. Its abbess wrote to St. Hildegard in the twelfth century, commending herself to her prayers, CXCVII, 327.

LUCAU, ST. MARY (Notre-Dame de Lucheul near Doullens), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, discussed in the *Deeds of the Bishops of Cambrai*, CXLIX, 131.

ST. LUKE (Saint Luke of Negroponte, Greece), a monastery whose abbot Innocent III wrote to in 1208, CCXV, 1492.

LUCELLENSE, ST. MARY (Notre-Dame de Lucel or Lutzel, diocese of Basel), a Cistercian monastery founded shortly before 1139, when Innocent II confirmed its rights and possessions by privilege, CLXXIX, 409. — Privilege of Urban III, 1189, CCII, 1543.

LUCEDIO OF SS. MICHAEL AND JANUARIUS (Saint-Michel de Locedio, diocese of Vercelli), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, situated near Vercelli, later transferred to the Cistercians. Blessed William, abbot of St. Benignus at Dijon, professed the monastic life there in 1031, CXLI, 835.---Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1199, CCXIV, 580.---Letter of Innocent III to the abbot while he was in the East, 1204, CCXV, 555.---Decree of the same pope, confirming to this monastery certain possessions and observance of the Cistercian Rule, in 1212, CCXVI, 594.

LUCEDIO OF ST. MARY (Sainte-Marie de Locedio), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by Rainerius, marquis of Montferrat, and granted by him to Bishop Anselm. Decree of Innocent II concerning a dispute that arose with the brethren of St. Michael, 1141, CLXXIX, 536.---Privilege of Celestine III, 1192, CCVI, 427.

LUCCA, ST. MICHAEL’S (Saint-Michel of Lucca), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded and endowed by the noble citizen Pertuald in 721, LXXXVII, 1365 [Col. 1091].---The election of its abbot was confirmed by King Liutprand in 728, ibid., 1371.

LUCCA. See ST. FRIGDIANUS.

LUCCA, ST. GEORGE’S (Saint-Georges of Lucca), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict. Letter of Eugenius III concerning a dispute with the canons of St. Frigdianus, 1145, CLXXX, 1089.---Letter and decree of Alexander III declaring void a simoniacal agreement entered into by the monks of this monastery in 1174, CC, 1017, 1018, 1066.

LUCCA, ST. ANGEL IN THE FORUM (Saint-Ange du Forum), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine. Innocent II commands the canons of this monastery not to harass the monks of St. Frigdianus, 1141, CLXXIX, 571.

LUCCA, ST. PETER’S (Saint-Pierre of Lucca), a monastery founded by Fortunatus and his son Romuald, both priests; they themselves entered there as monks under Talesperianus, abbot and bishop, in 713, LXXXVII, 1351.---Charter of Sichimund, 1373.---Privilege of Eugenius III, 1147, CLXXX, 1190; under him it had become a nunnery.

LUCCA, ST. MARTIN’S (Saint-Martin), a monastery of Canons Regular of St. Augustine, built before 1117. In that year Paschal wrote to these monks concerning a certain injury inflicted by them upon the canons of St. Frigdianus, CLXIII, 431.---Letter of Innocent II, 1137, CLXXIX, 335, 345.

LUCCA, ST. PONTIANUS’S (Saint-Pontien), an ancient monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, restored at the beginning of the eleventh century by the illustrious matron Willa, marchioness. At Abbot Ambrose’s request, it was honored with a privilege by King Conrad II in 1025, CLI, 1046.---Letter of Innocent III, 1206, CCXV, 972.

LUCCA, ST. REPARATA’S (Sainte-Réparate), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, whose prior received a privilege from Celestine III in 1194, CCVI, 1060.

LUCCA HOSPITAL, founded outside the walls, in the place called Apulia, by King Sichimund and certain magnates in 729, LXXXVII, 1372.---Charter of Bishop Walprand, 739, 1405.

LUCCA HOSPITAL OF ST. SYLVESTER, founded by the citizens of Lucca in 718, LXXXVII, 1361.

LUCCA, LITTLE MONASTERY. See CAPPANULAE.

LUCKA (Lucca or Lucka, diocese of Olomouc, Bohemia), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, founded by Otto, duke of Bohemia.---Privilege of Celestine VI, 1195, CCVI, 1091.

LUCCA, ST. JUSTINA’S (Convent of St. Justina, Lucca), a nunnery of the Order of St. Benedict, built within the city; Alexander III granted it a privilege in 1176, CC, 1072.

LUCCA, ST. SAVIOUR’S (Convent of Saint-Sauveur, Lucca), a nunnery, whose abbess Alperga received a privilege from Emperor St. Henry II in 1015, CXL, 332.---Diploma of King Conrad II, 1027, CLI, 1048.

LUCCA, ST. MARY’S (Convent of St. Mary, Lucca), a nunnery built by the cleric Ursus, in which his own daughter became abbess in 722, LXXXVII, 1566.

LA LUCERNE OF THE HOLY TRINITY (Sainte-Trinité de La Luzerne, Manche), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, built in 1143 by Hasculf of Suligny. Innocent III wrote to the abbot of this monastery in 1204, CCXV, 529.

LUCERNE, COURBE-FOSSE OF THE HOLY TRINITY (Sainte-Trinité de Courbe-Fosse at Lucerne, Switzerland), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose goods Eugenius III took under his protection in 1145, CLXXX, 1017.---Privilege of Urban III, 1185, CCII, 1347.

LUCERNE OF SS. MAURICE AND LEODEGAR (Saint-Maurice or Saint-Léger of Lucerne), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded in Switzerland in the eighth century. It was first subject to the monastery of Viviers, whose abbot Sigimar was then chosen by Emperor Lothair in 839, CIV, 1308; afterward it passed to Murbach.

ST. LUCIAN OF BEAUVAIS (Saint-Lucien de Beauvais), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by King Childebert in 540. It possessed the body of St. Lucian in the eighth century and was rebuilt by King Chilperic. Letter of Innocent on behalf of this monastery, 1131, CLXXIX, 74.---Privilege of Adrian IV, 1158, CLXXXVII, 1540.

LUCO OF ST. PETER, a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in the diocese of Florence, to which Pope Paschal II granted a privilege in 1107, CLXIII, 228.---Privilege of Urban III, 1186, CCII, 1370.

LUCULLANUM (Saint-Séverin of Lucullano, near Naples), an ancient monastery near Naples, whose abbot at the end of the fifth century was St. Eugyppius, an African by birth, LXII, 549.

LUCUSIANUM (Lucusio or Lucusiano, Palermo), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, one of the six monasteries founded by St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1167.

ST. LUDGER. See WERTHINENSE.

LUFFELD, a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in England, to which St. Hugh, bishop of Lincoln, confirmed possession of two churches at the end of the twelfth century, CLIII, 1122 [Col. 1092].---Privilege of Alexander III, 1174, CC, 989.

LYON, a nunnery at Lyons, mentioned by Gregory of Tours. It already existed in 570, LXXI, 536.---It was endowed by St. Anemundus, bishop of Lyons, LXXXVII, 473; LXXXVIII, 1164.

LUNÉLACKEN OF ST. MICHAEL (Saint-Michel de Lunélacken or Manauser, Bohemia), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by Count Conrad and his wife Matilda; its possessions and rights were confirmed by privilege of Innocent II in 1142, CLXXIX, 609.---Letter of Alexander III, 1175, CC, 1016.

LONDON, ST. MARY MAGDALENE’S (Sainte-Magdeleine of London, diocese of York, England), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded before 1186, in which year Urban III confirmed it by privilege, CCII, 1392.

LONDON, a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine built near the walls. At the request of Norman, its prior, Innocent II granted it a privilege in 1137, CLXXIX, 323.---Privilege of Eugenius III, 1147, CLXXX, 1289.

LONDON OF THE HOLY TRINITY (Sainte-Trinité of London), a college of canons whose possessions Innocent III confirmed in 1201, CCXVII, 69.

LUNDORF OF ST. MARY (Sainte-Marie of Londorf, Scotland), a monastery founded by King William, called the Lion, shortly before 1199, in which year Innocent III confirmed it by privilege, CCXIV, 540.

LÜNE (Lune or Luhne, Westphalia), a monastery whose abbot Clement III wrote to in 1188, CCIV, 1366.

LUPARA OF ST. THOMAS (Saint-Thomas-du-Louvre). See PARISIAN.

ST. LUPUS. See TRECENSE.

ST. LUPUS (Saint-Loup, diocese of Clermont), an ancient monastery apparently built in the diocese of Clermont. The canons of Billom had usurped it, to the detriment of Cluny, on which it depended. Urban II commanded them to restore it without delay in 1094, CLI, 392.---Letter of Innocent III to the abbot on behalf of the monks of Vézelay, 1211, CCXVI, 479.

LURE, OR LUTHRA, OF SS. MARTIN AND DEICOLA (Saint-Martin or Saint-Desle of Lure, diocese of Besançon), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict founded from 611 onward, rebuilt by the monks of Boscodon in 1176; it is mentioned in a privilege of Alexander III of the same year, CC, 1077.

LEUZE OF SS. PETER AND PAUL (Saint-Pierre de Leuze, diocese of Tournai), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, between Ath and Tournai, founded by St. Amand in 545, CXLXIX, 140.

LUXEUIL (Luxeuil, or rather Luxeu, former diocese of Besançon), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict founded by St. Columbanus, an Irishman by origin, about 590, LXXI, 626; LXXX, 203.---Angelomus became abbot in 856, CXV, 106.---St. Waldebert, its third abbot, CXXXVII, 687.---Letter of Honorius II to Matthew, cardinal of Albano, on behalf of this monastery, 1128, CLXVI, 1278.---Letter of Innocent III, 1198, CCXIV, 480.

LUZILAC (Lutzell, diocese of Basel, Switzerland), a monastery of the Cistercian Order built in 1124 by the counts of Montfaucon. See above, LUCELLENSE.

LYRE OF ST. MARY (Notre-Dame de Lyre, Eure), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded about 1050 by William, son of Osbern and steward of the duke of Normandy, CCII, 1316.---Letter to the abbot concerning the election of the provost of Coutances, 1210, CCXVI, 377.

MACENEIRA, in the diocese of Viseu (Viseu, Portugal), a monastery whose abbot Innocent [III] instructed to investigate the removal, by the bishop, of the abbot of St. Peter of Auriac, 1212, CCXVI, 607.

MAIZIÈRES OF ST. MARY (Notre-Dame de Maizières), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, built by Falcon of Reims in 1132. Innocent III wrote to its abbot concerning the case between the monastery of Flavigny and the monastery of Semur in 1198, CCXIV, 257.

MADALHARSTORF OF ST. JOHN (Madalharstorf, diocese of Regensburg, Bavaria), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by the distinguished Henry and his son Ernest shortly before 1139; at the request of Abbot Eppo, Innocent II confirmed it by privilege in that year, 396.

MADION OF ST. MARY (Notre-Dame de Madion, former diocese of Saintes), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded before 1203. In that year Innocent III wrote to its abbot concerning the reform of the monastery of Alba Terra, CCXV, 245.

MAGABRE OF ST. MARTIN (Saint-Martin de Mèvre, diocese of Autun), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict founded before 843 [Col. 1093]. Having later fallen into decay, it was given by Walter, bishop of Autun, to St. Odilo, abbot of Cluny, for reform in 996; he reformed it, CXLII, 856.

MAGUELONNE CANONRY (Maguelonne), formerly an episcopal city, now levelled to the ground. It stood in the territory of Montpellier; its clergy adopted the regular life in 1095, and Pope Urban II confirmed this, CLI, 408.

MAGDEBURG, ST. MARY’S (Sainte-Marie of Magdeburg), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, in which Archbishop Norbert substituted canons of the Premonstratensian Order, founded by himself, in 1129; it was confirmed in the same year by Honorius II, CLXVI, 1303.---Charter of St. Norbert, 1129, CLXX, 1358, 1359.---Privilege of Clement III, 1190, CCIV, 1471.---Privilege of Innocent III, 1206, CCXV, 1094, 1095.

MAGDEBURG, ST. JOHN OF THE MOUNT (Saint-Jean du Mont at Magdeburg), a monastery whose abbot Innocent III wrote to in 1207, CCXV, 1108.

MAGE, a monastery built on an island of Ireland by Colman, bishop of Lindisfarne, in 667, XCV, 180.---Perhaps the same as the following.

MAGY (Magy, diocese of Limerick, Ireland), a monastery whose abbot Innocent III wrote to concerning the annulment of the election of the bishop of Emly, 1210, CCXVI, 363.

MAGLIANO, ST. SAVIOUR’S (St. Saviour of Magliano), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in the Sabine country, to which Pope Alexander II secured various immunities in 1063, CXLVI, 1395.---Privilege of Alexander III, 1174, CC, 1019.

ST. MAGLOIRE OF PARIS (Saint-Magloire at Paris), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by Hugh Capet and his son Robert, who granted it many possessions by diploma in 1002, CXLI, 950.---Letter of Philip I concerning the reform of this monastery, CLIX, 840.---Privilege of Adrian IV, 1159, CLXXXVIII, 1621.---Letter of Alexander III on behalf of this monastery, 1176, CC, 1087.---Letter of Innocent III concerning the unpaid installation of an abbot, 1211, CCXVI, 504.

MAGNILOC OF ST. SEBASTIAN (Manlieu, near Clermont), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by St. Genesius, bishop of Clermont, in 656. Abbot Heymo obtained a privilege from Louis the Pious in 818, CIV, 1080.

ST. MAGNUS OF SALZBURG (Saint-Magne of Salzburg, Bavaria), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, otherwise called *Ad Ripas* (“At the Banks”); at the request of Gebehard, its steward, its possessions were confirmed in 1139, CLXXIX, 482.---Privilege of Lucius II, 1144, CLXXIX, 922.

MAGUZZANO ABBEY, otherwise called Maguzano, of the Order of St. Benedict, founded before the ninth century in the diocese of Verona. When it had been abandoned, Bishop Ratherius introduced clerics into it, that is, canons; his decree, 970, CXXXVI, 547.

MELROSE, an Irish monastery in which St. Cuthbert embraced the monastic life under the illustrious Abbot Eata, later bishop of Lindisfarne, in 660, in Venerable Bede, XCV, 220.

MAIMAC OF ST. MARY (Maimac, diocese of Limoges), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in 1088. Eugenius III confirmed in 1147 an agreement made by the bishop between that monastery and the brethren of Uzerche, CLXXX, 1242.

MAJELLANUM. See ST. PETER IN THE VALLEY.

MAJELLANUM OF ST. SAVIOUR (Saint-Sauveur of the Desert, or Magliano in the Abruzzi), a Carthusian house founded under Paschal II and confirmed by Adrian IV in 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1413.

MAJOREVI (Mairieux, in Franche-Comté), a Carthusian house built in 1116 in the county of Burgundy by certain hermits originating from the Great Chartreuse, CLIII, 800, 936.---St. Hugh of Lincoln visited this monastery after becoming bishop in 1199, CLIII, 1088.

MARMOUTIER, OR THE MONASTERY OF ST. MARTIN (Marmoutier or the Abbey of St. Martin of Tours), a most celebrated monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by St. Martin near Tours in the fourth century, later transferred to the Congregation of St. Maur, XX, 166; LXXI, 564, note.---Charter of Pope Adeodatus, 674, LXXXVIII, 1141.---Likewise of Bishop Ebbo, 720, LXXXVIII, 1264.---Precepts of Charlemagne, 774, XCVII, 931, 949, 970, 979, 990.---Charlemagne’s letter to Albinus (Alcuin), abbot of St. Martin’s, 803, XCVII, 921.---Diplomas of Louis the Pious, 814, CIV, 998, 1067, 1069.---From this time it appears to have passed to Canons Regular. Diplomas of the same [ruler], 1201, 1214, 1215.---Privilege of Leo III, CXXIX, 971.---Of Sergius III, CXXXI, 980.---Privilege of Leo VII, CXXXI, 1072.---Of Gregory V, CXXXVII, 907.---Charter of St. Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, 1024, CXLI, 353.---Privilege of St. Gregory VII, 1081, CXLVIII, 700 [Col. 1094].---In the eleventh century it was reformed by St. Maiolus, abbot of Cluny, and again became very flourishing under Abbot Bartholomew, CXLIX, 363.---Diploma of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1374.---Privilege of Urban II, 1090, CLI, 324.---His letter to the canons of St. Martin against simoniacs, CLI, 457.---His privilege, 518.---Charter of Ivo, bishop of Chartres, 1114, CLXII, 295.---Privilege of Paschal II, 1100, CLXIII, 51, 259.---Of Calixtus II, 1119, CLXIII, 1131.---Letter of Honorius II concerning the excommunication of Count Fulk, 1125, CLXVI, 1231.---Privilege of the same pope, 1129, CLXVI, 1300.---The chapel of St. Stephen was adjudged to it against the monks of Celles by Gerard, bishop of Angoulême, CLXX, 1319.---Privilege of Pope Innocent II, 1131, CLXIX, 106.---Innocent II granted this monastery the church of SS. Rufinus and Valerius at Basel, 238.---Privilege of Lucius II, 1144, CLXXIX, 878, 879.---Letter of Ulger, bishop of Angers, to Lucius II concerning Odo, dean of St. Martin’s, CLXXIX, 936.---Privilege of Eugenius III, 1145, CLXXX, 1022, 1337.---Letters of Ulger recommending Odo, dean of St. Martin’s, and Robert, prior, before 1148, CLXXX, 1655.---Letter of Alexander III, 1170, CC, 655, 915.---Privilege of the same pope, 1174, CC, 994, 1044, 1050, 1099, 1289.---Of Lucius III, 1184, CCI, 1260, 1296, 1321, 1350.---Decree of Celestine III, 1195, CCVI, 1110, 1233.---Letters of Innocent III, 1207, CCXV, 1121, 1297, 1459, 1575; 1211, CCXVI, 449.---Letter concerning its reform, CCXVII, 109.

MALA, perhaps for MALMUNDARIENSE. It is mentioned in the testament of St. Ansegisus, abbot of Fontenelle, 833, CV, 746.

MALENOUVE, OR MALNODA, AND FOOTEL OF ST. MARY (Sainte-Marie or Saint-Erasme of Malenoue, near Paris, Seine-et-Marne), a nunnery built in 1129, into which some of the nuns expelled from Argenteuil by authority of the Council of Paris in 1129 withdrew. Charter of Odo, bishop of Paris, concerning this nunnery, 1207.---Letter of Innocent III, 1203, CCXV, 791, 793.

MALARDI VALLEY, a monastery mentioned only in the testament of St. Ansegisus, abbot of Fontenelle, 823, CV, 745.

MAUBEUGE OF ST. MARY (Notre-Dame de Maubeuge), a nunnery founded and endowed by St. Aldegund, queen and nun, in 661, LXXXVIII, 1160; CXXXII, 817; CXLIX, 138.---Letter of Alexander III against nuns rebellious to their abbess, 1172, CC, 825.

MALBURG OF SS. PHILIP AND JAMES. See HOLY WOOD.

MALISNACENSE. See MECHLINIENSE.

MALLEONE. See MALO LEONE.

MALLERSDORF (Maelisdorf, diocese of Regensburg), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict acquired by Otto of Bamberg about 1132, CLXXIII, 1279, 1309.---Privilege of Pope Innocent II, 1131, CLXXIX, 110.

MAILLÉ OF ST. SOLEMNIS (Maillé, Lallier, Luynes, or Saint-Soûlein), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in the district of Tours, in which the body of St. Solemnis, bishop, long rested. It appears to have been founded by him under King Clovis, LXXI, 843.

MAILLEZAIS OF ST. PETER (Saint-Pierre de Maillezais, Vendée), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, formerly existing under the dedication of St. Rigomer. It was rebuilt by Duke William of Aquitaine and his wife Emma in 980, and greatly enlarged by their son William V in 1010, CXLI, 824.---The foundation of this monastery is described by Peter, monk of Maillezais, CXLVI, 1247.---Privilege of Pope Innocent II, 1135, CLXXIX, 233.

MALMESBURY, OR MELDUNENSE, a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in England, in Wiltshire, by St. Maidulf, an Irish abbot, in 680. King Edgar restored it and introduced monks there in place of the clerics by whom it had been occupied, in 974. Today only ruins remain, LXXXIX, 66, 309; CXXXVIII, 519.---Diploma of William the Conqueror, 1081, CXLIX, 1352.---It was granted to Abbot Edulf by Queen Matilda, while preserving the right of Archbishop Anselm, before 1142, CLIX, 156.

MALMEDY, a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by King Sigebert and Girmoald, mayor of the palace. St. Remaclus was its first abbot in 660, LXXXVII, 311, 315.---Diploma of Sigebert, 321.---Of Childeric, 1291.---Of Dagobert II, 1507.---Of Theoderic, 1331.---Of Clovis III, LXXXVIII, 1084.---Of Childeric III, ibid., 1152.---Of Carloman, 747, ibid., 1407, 1310.---Of Louis the Pious, 814, CIV, 991.---Privilege of Sylvester II, 1003, CXXXIII, 282.---Much is written concerning this monastery, CXLIX, 291 ff.---The monk William flourished in 1143, CLXXIX, 959 [Col. 1095].---Frederick, bishop of Cologne, subjected Malmedy to Stavelot in 1128, CLXXXIX, 1457.

MAULÉON OF THE HOLY TRINITY (La Sainte-Trinité de Mauléon, Deux-Sèvres), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, founded before 1079.---Letter of Innocent III to its abbot, 1207, CCXV, 1202; CCXVI, 64.

MALTACENA. See AGANENSE.

ST. MAMILIAN. See MONTE CHRISTI.

ST. MAMMES OF LANGRES (Saint-Mamme de Langres), a college of canons to which Alexander III granted a privilege in 1170, CC, 661.

MANDAN, MAUDAN, AND MALDUIN, OR MACLOVIENSE (Saint-Malo, diocese of Coutances), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in Neustria, built about 520, LXXXVIII, 496.

ST. MANDUS, a monastery situated in the diocese of Theate (Chieti, Abruzzi), mentioned in a privilege of Innocent III, 1208, CCXVII, 180.

MANNACENSE (perhaps Maincy, arrondissement of Melun), a monastery in the diocese of Auxerre, existing in the time of Aunarius, bishop, in the seventh century, CXXXVIII, 233, 234.

MAZAN (Manso Adae; Mazan, diocese of Viviers, Ardèche), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, built before 1137.---Letter of Innocent III concerning a monk formerly a physician, 1209, CCXVI, 66.

MANZANERA (Manzenera, diocese of Coimbra, Portugal), a monastery whose foundation seems to belong to the same period as those of Alcobaça and Seiça, namely the reign of King Afonso I.---Letter of Innocent III to the abbot concerning the right of the church of Coimbra, 1198, CCXIV, 195.

MARACULO (Mareuil, arrondissement of Abbeville), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, founded in the diocese of Arras by St. Bertilia and her son Fulbert in 935, CXLIX, 131.---See below, MAREOLENSE.

MARBACH OF ST. IRENAEUS (Marbach, Alsace), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine in the diocese of Strasbourg, founded by the noblewoman Guta in 1089; according to some, by Burchard, lord of Geblisweiler.---Privilege of Urban II, issued at Tours, 1096, CLI, 455.---Of Paschal II, 1103, CLXIII, 116.---Privilege of Calixtus, ibid., 1130.---Of Celestine III, 1192, CCVI, 911; another privilege of the same [pope], spurious, 1241.---Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1212, CCXVI, 812; CCXVII, 209, 217.

ST. MARCELLUS OF FELINES (Saint-Marcel de Felines, former diocese of Die), a monastery in the diocese of Die, built before 985. Do not confuse it with St. Marcellus of Salciac (Sauzet), in the county of Valentinois, as is done by the author of the *Eulogy of Odilo of Cluny*, CXLII, 865. See DIENSI.

ST. MARCELLUS OF CHALON (Saint-Marcel-les-Châlons or Obiliac), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded and endowed by King Guntram in 579, LXXX, 611.---Precept of Charlemagne, 779, XCVII, 964.---Of Louis the Pious, 835, CIV, 1261.---Privilege of Pope John VIII, 878, CXXVI, 805.---As discipline cooled, Count Theobald gave it to Cluny to be reformed about 960, CXXXVII, 780.---Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, came from it, CLVII, 487.

ST. MARCELLUS OF SALCIAC (Saint-Marcel-les-Sauzet, diocese of Valence), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in the county of Valentinois, near the village of Salciac (Sauzet), founded by Count Adhemar and his wife Rothild. But, because of certain abbots’ negligence, it was entrusted to the Cluniacs for administration under St. Odilo in 1037, CXLII, 865.---It was restored by Bishop Lambert, ibid.---Eugenius III confirmed to this monastery the gift of the church of Salvatia in 1146, CLXXX, 1106.---Concerning the claim of Hugh, duke of Burgundy, 1104, CLXXXV, 1400, 1401.

ST. MARCELLUS OF PARIS (Saint-Marcel or Marceau-les-Paris), a monastery that gave its name to the modern suburb; it belonged to the Order of St. Augustine, and its church was built by Roland, nephew of Charlemagne. Adrian IV took these canons under his protection in 1158, CLXXXVIII, 1571.---Settlement between Maurice, bishop of Paris, and the monastery concerning the children of a certain serf, 1163–1196, CCV, 906.---Letter of Innocent III, 1210, CCXVI, 351.

MARCHIENNES OF ST. RICTRUDE (Marchiennes, between Douai and Saint-Omer), a nunnery in Flanders on the Scarpe, founded by St. Amand, bishop; St. Rictrude was its first abbess in 647, CXXXII, 827.---At Count Baldwin’s request, Ledwin, bishop of Arras, introduced monks in place of the nuns in 1028, CXLI, 1334; CXLIX, 133.

MARCHTAL OF ST. PETER (Saint-Pierre de Marchtal, former diocese of Constance), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order [Col. 1096], established from an earlier college in 1170 by Count Hugh of Tübingen. Privilege of Celestine III, 1192, CCVI, 966.

ST. MARK (Saint-Marc, near Spoleto), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built near the walls of Spoleto from the time of St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 967.

ST. MARK (Saint-Mark of Zamora, Spain), a priory dependent upon the monastery of Novalesa, situated in the diocese of Zamora in Spain; Innocent III addressed a letter to its prior in 1198, CCXIV, 62.

MARCHIENNES, OR ST. PETER’S (Saint-Pierre de Marchiennes, Nord), a monastery founded by St. Amand not far from the nunnery of St. Rictrude; its first abbot was St. Jonatus in 647, CXXXII, 827, 893.---Privilege of Innocent II for this monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, 1141, CLXXIX, 554, 590.---Letter of the same, 555.

MARCIGNY, a nunnery founded in 1080 by Blessed Hugh, abbot of Cluny, and Geoffrey, Hugh’s brother, CLIX, 969.---Privilege of Urban II, 1095, CLI, 442.---St. Hugh’s exhortation and admonition for the nuns, CLIX, 947, 949.---Privilege of Calixtus II, CLXIII, 1192.

MARRE (Marre, near Verdun-sur-Meuse), a monastery on whose behalf Alexander III wrote to Henry, archbishop of Reims, in 1171, CC, 740.

MAREUIL-LES-ARRAS, a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine built by Fulbert, bishop of Cambrai, in 935.---Alexander III wrote to Henry, archbishop of Reims, on behalf of its abbot in 1172, CC, 809.

ST. MARGARET’S (Sainte-Marguerite de Beaune, diocese of Autun), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, whose abbot Innocent III entrusted with the task of reforming other monasteries in 1198, CCIV, 201.

ST. MARGARET. See OSTERHOVENSE.

MARIADURA (Mariadura, diocese of Piacenza), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, built shortly before 1199 by the nobleman Gandulf and his wife Gisla; in that year Innocent III honored it with a privilege, CCXIV, 858.

ST. MARIAN OF AUXERRE. See FONTANENSE.

ST. MARY’S, a small monastery or hospital at Le Mans, mentioned in a diploma of Charlemagne, 802, XCVII, 995.

ST. MARY-AT-THE-STEPS (Sainte-Marie-aux-Degrés, Cologne), a monastery of twenty canons at Cologne, founded by Archbishop Anno; Stephen X honored its goods and rights with a privilege in 1059, CXLIII, 1309.

ST. MARY AT THE END (Sainte-Marie, called Ad-Fineau-Bout, diocese of Pisa, Tuscany), a monastery of regular canons founded by Opitho, archbishop of Pisa, to which Alexander III granted a privilege in 1179, CC, 1241.

ST. MARY AT THE ORGAN. See VERONA (nunnery).

ST. MARY ON THE LOIRE (Sainte-Marie-sur-Loire), a monastery whose site is now almost unknown. Ageradus, bishop of Chartres, conferred many goods upon it in 686, LXXXVIII, 1228.---Perhaps it is the same monastery as St. Mary of Charity, below.

ST. MARY DEAURATA. See TOULOUSE.

ST. MARY IN THE WOOD. See below, ST. MARY OF ROTA.

ST. MARY OF CAGIA OR CAVEA (Notre-Dame de Cage in the suburb of Meaux), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, built in 1135 and honored by Innocent II with a privilege, CLXXIX, 244.---[Privilege] of Alexander III, 1174, CC, 1035.---Letter of Innocent III to the abbot concerning an accusation against the abbot of St. Dionysius of Reims, 1208, CCXV, 1587; CCXVII, 220.

ST. MARY OF THE FIELD (Sainte-Marie du Champ, diocese of Elne or Perpignan), a priory of the Order of St. Augustine, founded before 1164 by Bernard, bishop of Elne; in that year Alexander III granted it a privilege, CC, 284.

ST. MARY OF THE PRISON (Notre-Dame des Prisonniers, Padua), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, built by Bishop John. At his request Pope Adrian IV confirmed its possessions and rights in 1155, CLXXXVIII, 1428.---Privilege of Lucius III, 1184, CXI, 1309.---Of Urban III, 1186, CCII, 1449.

ST. MARY OF CHARITY (La Charité, Angers), a nunnery at Angers. Cathwallon, abbot of Redon, wrote to its abbess about 1035, CXLI, 1283.

ST. MARY OF CHARITY ON THE LOIRE (Notre-Dame de la Charité-sur-Loire, Nièvre), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose foundation is dated to 706. Twice destroyed, it was twice rebuilt; finally it passed to the monastery of Cluny and flourished greatly. Privilege of Paschal II, 1114, CLXII, 357 [Col. 1097].---Privilege of Innocent II, 1132, CLXXIX, 134.---Letter of William, prior, to Suger, 1119, CLXXVI, 1435.---Judgment of Adrian IV against the monks, 1156, CLXXXVIII, 1455.---Letter of Innocent III, 1214, CCXVII, 230, 242.

ST. MARY OF CHARITY (Sainte-Marie de la Charité at Rodrigo, diocese of Saragossa, Spain), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, to which Lucius III granted a privilege in 1185, CCI, 1343.

ST. MARY OF CHARITY (Notre-Dame de la Charité-les-Lésines, Yonne), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, built by William of Lesines in 1184; as a priory it was dependent upon the monastery of St. Columba at Sens.---Letter of Celestine III commanding that certain things be restored to it, 1196, CCVI, 1180.---Privilege of Innocent III, 1204, CCXV, 557.

ST. MARY OF CHARITY OF THE VENETIANS (Sainte-Marie de la Charité, Venice), a monastery whose visitors to the church Alexander III granted twenty days of indulgence in 1177, CC, 1116.

ST. MARY OF NEUBOURG, OR NEUENBURG (Notre-Dame de Newbourg, diocese of Worms), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by Count Anselm Conrad in 1134.---Privilege of Eugenius III, 1147, CLXXX, 1262.

ST. MARY OF JULIA. See CILENTIANA.

ST. MARY OF THE BED, a monastery in the diocese of Theate (Chieti in the Abruzzi, Naples), mentioned in a privilege of Innocent III, 1208, CCXVII, 180.

ST. MARY OF THE WOOD (Sainte-Marie de Ligno, diocese of Bisaccia or Cosenza in Calabria, Naples), a monastery dependent on the monastery of the Holy Spirit at Palermo; Innocent III wrote concerning its transfer in 1202, CCXIV, 1167.

ST. MARY OF MONTANO, a nunnery in the Milanese district, whose nuns Celestine II took under his protection against the canons of Rosate in 1143, CLXXIX, 768.

ST. MARY OF THE LITTLE BRIDGE. See BRINDISI.

ST. MARY OF THE MEADOW AT DONZY (Notre-Dame du Pré-les-Donzi, diocese of Nevers), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, formerly subject to Cluny; Pope Anastasius IV granted it a privilege in 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1055, 1071.

ST. MARY ON THE RENO (Sainte-Marie-sur-Reno, in the Bologna district, Papal States), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, built on the river Reno in the district of Bologna before 1136; in that year Innocent II confirmed it, CLXXIX, 288, 660.---Privilege of Lucius II, 1144, CLXXIX, 920.---Of Eugenius III, 1149, CLXXX, 1415.---Of Anastasius IV, 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1072.---Of Adrian IV, 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1399.---Of Alexander III, 1169, CC, 588, 1139.---Of Lucius III, 1182, CCI, 1138.---Of Urban III, 1185, CCII, 1355, 1466, 1467, 1480, 1485.---Of Clement III, 1188, CCIV, 1317, 1324.

ST. MARY OF ROTA (Notre-Dame de Rou or du Bocage, diocese of Angers), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, founded by Blessed Robert of Arbrissel in the very rugged forest of Craon in 1102, CLXII, 1049.---Grant of Paschal II, 1117, CLXIII, 419.---Privilege of Innocent II, 1136, CLXXIX, 265.

ST. MARY OF THE LITTLE SHRINE (Notre-Dame de l’Écrin, near Tours), a nunnery founded about 580 in the very precinct of St. Martin’s by Ingeltrude, maternal aunt of King Guntram, LXXI, 510.---This small monastery was later transferred near Beaumont in the eleventh century by Hervaeus the Treasurer, ibid., note. See BELLO MONTE.

ST. MARY OF SOULAC (Sainte-Marie de Soulac, near Lesparre, Gironde), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in the diocese of Bordeaux, subject to the abbot of Holy Cross by a privilege of Pope Benedict IX in 1036, CXLI, 1343.

ST. MARY OF THE VALLEY OF BESANÇON (Notre-Dame du Val, near Poligny, diocese of Besançon), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict founded, or notably enlarged, before 1119; in that year Calixtus II confirmed its possessions, CLXIII, 1098.

ST. MARY OF THE VOW (Notre-Dame-du-Vœu, diocese of Coutances, near Cherbourg), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, founded about 1050 by William, duke of Normandy, and restored by Empress Matilda in 1150.---Privilege of Urban III, 1189, CCII, 1512.---Charter of Henry II, king of England, 1178, CCVII, 1160, 1161.

ST. MARY IN THE SANDS OF WROCŁAW (Sainte-Marie des Arènes, Poland), a monastery whose goods Eugenius III confirmed by privilege in 1148, CLXXX, 1370.

ST. MARY IN AURIONNO, a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine from the district of Le Mans, assigned to the bishop by a diploma of Charlemagne in 802, XCVII, 995.---It is also called [the monastery] of SS. Gervasius and Protasius, and was founded by Bertramnus, bishop of Le Mans, about 620, LXXX, 385.

[Col. 1098] ST. MARY IN THE BASILICA, a monastery situated in the city of Luparello, diocese of Theate (Chieti, Naples), mentioned in a privilege of Innocent III, 1208, CCXVII, 180.

ST. MARY BELOW THE SARTHE. See CENOMANENSE.

ST. MARY NEW (Sainte-Marie-Neuve, in the Roman countryside), a monastery to which Alexander III granted the church of St. Sebastian in the Catacombs in 1161, CC, 126.

ST. MARY NEW OF VITERBO (Sainte-Marie-Neuve of Viterbo, Papal States), a monastery whose abbot Innocent III wrote to in 1210, CCXVI, 472.

ST. MARY IN REGULA (Sainte-Marie à la Règle, Ravenna), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose Abbot Rodulf received a privilege from Eugenius III in 1145, CLXXX, 1085.---Decree of Innocent III that secular persons may not judge concerning tithes, 1212, CCXVI, 590.

ST. MARY IN ROSSANO (Sainte-Marie of Rossano in Calabria, Naples), a monastery which Pope Anastasius IV granted to the Church of Fiesole by privilege in 1153, CLXXXVIII, 1016.

ST. MARY OF THE ROTUNDA (Sainte-Marie de la Rotonde, diocese of Ravenna), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, to which Innocent III adjudged certain estates in 1210, CCXVI, 293.

ST. MARY OF THE ROTUNDA (Notre-Dame de la Rotonde, Auxerre), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, whose Abbot Hervaeus obtained a privilege from Innocent II in 1143, CLXXIX, 627.---Privilege of Eugenius III, 1146, CLXXX, 1097.

ST. MARY’S HOSPITAL IN SAXIA (Hospitallers of Our Lady in Saxony), a house which Innocent III united in 1204 with the Hospitallers of the Holy Spirit established at Montpellier, CCXV, 377.

SAINT MARY. See Banza, Bono Solatio, Columba, Curatio, Eleemosyna, Flumine, Gardia, Gariberto, Jussanense, Losense, Moncellense, Novi Portus, Portus Suavis, Ravennatense, Rocca Majore, Veronense in Organo, etc., etc.

SAINT MARY MAGDALENE. See Lundense, Valle Fares, Vezuntionense.

SAINT PETER OF MAROILLES (Saint-Pierre de Maroilles, diocese of Laon), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, built in 671, over which Abbot Humbert presided and to which he made certain gifts, LXXXVIII, 1197. — This monastery is mentioned, CXLIX, 136. — Letter of Alexander III concerning the abbot, against a certain knight, 1172, CC, 892, 893, 923.

SAINT MARIUS. See CISTERCIAN.

SAINT RÉPARATE OF MARRATA (Sainte-Réparate de Marrata, diocese of Faenza, Papal States), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, whose possessions and privileges Pope Alexander III confirmed in 1166, CC, 501.

MARCHIENNES (Marchiennes, a town near Charleroi, Nord), a monastery first of Canons Regular of Saint Augustine and afterwards of the Order of Saint Benedict, granted by Alexander, bishop of Liège, to Saint Remigius of Rheims shortly before 1136; in that year Innocent III confirmed it by privilege to Odo, abbot of Saint Remigius, CLXXIX, 298.

SAINT MARTIAL OF LIMOGES (Saint-Martial de Limoges), a celebrated monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded at the beginning of the monarchy; but it adopted the Rule of the holy Father Benedict only about 848; in the eleventh century it passed to Cluny, and finally to secular canons, LXXI, 850 note; CXLI, 79. — Privilege of Urban II, 1096, CLI, 1162.

SAINT MARS IN AUVERGNE (Saint-Mars de Clermont), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded near Clermont by Saint Mars, bishop, in which he himself was buried in 525, LXXI, 1070.

SAINT MARTIN OF THE FIELDS AT PARIS (Saint-Martin-des-Champs, Paris), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, mentioned by Gregory of Tours in 567, LXXI, 384 note. — It was subject to Cluny and honoured by a privilege of Urban II, 1096, CLI, 470. — Restored by King Henry I and granted to Canons Regular in 1060, CLI, 1037. — Privilege of Pope Paschal II, 1107, CLXIII, 209; of Calixtus II, 1119, CLXIII, 1142. — Charter of Cardinal Matthew, 1129, CLXXIII, 1267. — Foundation of an anniversary observance by Geoffrey, bishop of Châlons, 1140, CLXXIII, 1398. — Privilege of Innocent II, 1138, CLXXIX, 357, 648; of Lucius II, 1144, CLXXIX, 918; of Eugenius III, 1146, CLXXX, 1107, 1239, 1250. — Alexander III granted it the priory of Saint Martin of Passo, 1164, CC, 318. — Charter of Maurice de Sully, bishop of Paris, 1164, CCV, 897. — Letter of Innocent III by which one half of the revenues of the church of Saint-Jacques de la Boucherie is awarded to Saint Martin, 1209, CCXVI, 166.

SAINT MARTIN OF LENIS (Saint-Martin-Lenne, Aveyron), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, to whose abbot Segarius Pope Agapetus II confirmed certain possessions, [Col. 1099] 955, CXXXIII, 928.

SAINT MARTIN OF THE MOUNT (Saint-Martin de Mont, diocese of Viterbo, Papal States), a monastery for which Innocent III issued a decree concerning the revocation of alienations, 1207, CCXV, 1243. — Privilege of the same pope, 1309.

SAINT MARTIN OF MONTE SACRO (Saint-Martin de Monte Sacro, near Sabaric, birthplace of the holy pontiff, in Pannonia), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, built by Saint Stephen, king of the Hungarians; Saint Ostricus, or Andrew, was its first abbot, 1001, CLI, 1254. — Privilege of Pope Paschal II, 1102, CLXIII, 105. — Letter of Innocent III settling its dispute with the bishop of Veszprém, 1211, CCXVI, 545.

SAINT MARTIN OF PONTLIEUE (Saint-Martin de Pontlieue, diocese of Le Mans), a monastery founded near Le Mans by Bishop Bertrichramnus about 620, LXXX, 386. — Diploma of Charlemagne, 802, XCVII, 995.

SAINT MARTIN IN AREIS (Saint-Martin des Aires, near Troyes), a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine, founded in 1104. — Letter of Innocent III, 1204, CCXV, 506.

SAINT MARTIN. See Henimense, Laudunense, Majus Monasterium, Murense, Santonense, Tornacense.

SAINT MARTIN ON BARBARA ISLAND. See ISLAND.

SAINT MARTIN IN DIABLENTICUM, a district in the diocese of Le Mans: a small monastery mentioned in a diploma of Charlemagne, 802, XCVII, 995.

SAINT MARTIN OF MAJANO (Saint-Martin de Majano, diocese of Fiesole, Tuscany), a monastery mentioned in the privilege of Anastasius IV for the Church of Fiesole, 1153, CLXXXVIII, 1016.

SAINT MARTIN OF FREISING (Saint-Martin de Frisingen, Swabia), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, built by monks of Tegernsee; at their request it was confirmed by privilege by Pope Paschal II in 1107, CLXIII, 232.
