SAINT MARTIN OF CHAMPAGNE, OR OF THE MEADOW (Saint-Martin des Champs or de la Prairie, near Dijon), a small monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine, built by Saint Stephen of Dijon in the tenth century, CLXXXV, 1635 note. — Jocerannus, bishop of Langres, confirmed it to the brethren of Saint Stephen in 1130, ibid.

SAINT MARTIN IN SICILY, a monastery founded in the sixth century, concerning which Saint Gregory the Great wrote to Cyprian, deacon, LXXVII, 760, 761.

SAINT MARTIN OF PALECTU (Convent of Saint-Martin, diocese of Chieti, Abruzzo, Kingdom of Naples), a monastery mentioned in a privilege of Innocent III, 1208, CCXVII, 180.

SAINT MARTIN IN THE VALLEY (Saint-Martin en Vallée, in the same diocese as the preceding). Innocent III, CCVII, 180.

SAINT MARTIN IN SPAIN, a monastery built between Saguntum and Carthago Spartaria before 583, LXXX, 837.

SAINT MARTIN OF THE MAJELLA VALLEY (Saint-Martin della Valle, Italy, between the Alps and the Apennines), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, whose location is obscurely indicated and to which Paschal II granted a privilege in 1112, CLXIII, 298.

SAINT MARTIN IN PANNONIA. See above, SAINT MARTIN OF MONTE SACRO.

SAINT MARY OF MARZAC (Marsac in Auvergne), a convent of nuns formerly subject to the monastery of Mausac, date uncertain, LXXI, 713.

MASCIACENSE. See below, MAUZIACENSE.

SAINT PETER OF MASSA DE MONTE NERONE (Saint-Pierre de la Masse, Monte Nerone, Italy), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, whose possessions Clement III confirmed by privilege in 1188, CCIV, 1412.

ALL SAINTS OF MASSA, OR SAINT ENGRATIA AT MASSA CANDIDA (Sainte-Engratie de la Masse-Blanche, that is, “of the Virgins,” Saragossa), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, mentioned in the Life of Saint Maximus, 644, LXXX, 611; LXXXVII, 347.

MARSEILLES (Saint-Cassien, Marseille), an ancient monastery founded for men by John Cassian about 425, which he governed according to the rules of the monks of Egypt and Palestine that he had learned, XLIX, 9. — It is later said to have been dedicated to Saint Victor, LXXI, 384 note. — See below.

SAINT MARY OF YVELINO, MARSEILLES (Sainte-Marie de Veaune, near Marseille), an ancient monastery for girls built by the same John Cassian, XLIX, 9. — Letter of Saint Gregory the Great to Respecta, abbess, LXXVII, 866.

SAINT SATURNIN OF MARSEILLES (Saint-Saturnin de Marseille), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict. After its monks had incurred excommunication for [Col. 1100] certain offences, they returned to better conduct and were absolved by Richard, at once abbot and cardinal, at the urging of Pope Saint Gregory VII, 1082, CXLVIII, 702.

SAINT VICTOR OF MARSEILLES (Saint-Victor de Marseille), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, apparently identical with the monastery founded outside the walls of Marseille by Blessed John Cassian in 425. After it received the relics of Saint Victor, it also assumed his name. It later became highly celebrated. It is mentioned by Saint Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 384. — Precept of Charlemagne, 790, XCVII, 978. — Diploma of Louis the Pious, 822, CIV, 1116. — Privilege of Pope John XVIII, 1009, CXXXIX, 1492; of Saint Leo IX, 1050, CXLIII, 654. — Charter of Raimbald, bishop of Arles, 551. — Letter of the same pope, by which he entrusts Abbot Richard with the care of certain monasteries, 1081, CXLVIII, 611, 629. — Concerning the excommunicated monks of Saint Saturnin, 701. — Privilege of Urban II, CLI, 48, 296, 425. — Charter of Raymond of Saint-Gilles, count of Toulouse, 1103, CLV, 483. — Privilege of Paschal II, 1113, CLXIII, 327; of Calixtus II, 1123, CLXIII, 1291; of Innocent II, 1136, CLXXIX, 287; of Lucius II, 1144, CLXXIX, 843, 844; of Anastasius IV, 1153, CLXXXVIII, 1007. — Letter of the latter to the bishop of Toulon, 1039.

SAINT STEPHEN OF MATINANTA (Saint-Étienne de Matinanta in the Capitanata, Kingdom of Naples), a monastery of the Camaldolese Order, dependent on the monks of Saint Mary in Pulsano; it is mentioned in a privilege of Alexander III, 1177, CC, 1097.

SAINT MATTHEW’S MONASTERY. See CILENTIANA.

SAINT PETER OF MÂCON (Saint-Pierre de Mâcon, Saône-et-Loire), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, built in 696 and later transferred to Canons of Saint Augustine, 1212, CCXVI, 734.

MAULBRUNN (Maulbrunn, diocese of Speyer, Württemberg), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded in 1138 by Walther of Lomesheim; Diether, monk of Neuburg, was its first abbot. — Privilege of Eugenius III, 1148, CLXXX, 1316.

SAINT MAURUS’ MONASTERY, OR MAURINIACENSE (Maurs-Munster near Saverne, Bas-Rhin), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, also called the cell of Saint Leobard (Saint-Liébard), in the diocese of Strasbourg. It was founded in 599 by Saints Maurus and Leobard, who presided over it. — Diploma of King Theuderic IV, 734, LXXXVIII, 1139. — Burned by fire, it was rebuilt by Abbot Celsus under Louis the Pious in 829 and subjected to Aniane. It is mentioned in the testament of Ansegisus, abbot of Saint Wandrille, 833, CV, 747. — Theulfus composed its chronicle in 1147, CLXXX, 131.

MONT MAURUS. See MORIMUNDENSE.

SAINT MAURUS OF ANGERS. See GLANNOFOLIENSE.

SAINT JOHN OF MAURIENNE (Saint-Jean de Maurienne), a college of canons whose donation from the nobleman Thomas, count of Maurienne, Celestine III confirmed in 1195, CCVI, 1065.

SAINT MAURICE. See AGAUNENSE, MEDIOLANENSE, DE TURRIBUS.

SAINT PETER OF MAUSAC (Saint-Pierre de Mausac, Corrèze), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, built in the sixth century by the senator Calmitus, or Calminus, and his wife Numada. Saint Austremonius was buried there, LXXI, 851, note. — Privilege of Alexander III, 1165, CC, 378. — Letter of Innocent III, 1206, CCXV, 903.

SAINT MAXENTIUS OF POITIERS (Saint-Maixent de Poitiers), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict. It was first built about 459 by Agapius and companions who had come from the monastery of Saint Hilary, under the invocation of Saint Saturninus. Later destroyed by Attila, it was rebuilt by Saint Maxentius, an eminent man, about 507, during the reign of Clovis. Saint Leodegarius flourished there as abbot, later bishop, in 678, XCVI, 371. — Diploma of Louis the Pious, 815, CIV, 1021. — Diploma of Emperor Lothair, 827, CIV, 1160. — Privilege of Paschal II, 1110, CLXIII, 274, 275.

SAINT RUMOLD, OR ROMUALD, OF MECHLIN, OR MALISNACENSE (Mécheln-sur-Maslines, Belgium), a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine, built in the sixth or seventh century and greatly enriched by royal gifts, CXLIX, 142. — Privilege of Eugenius III, 1153, CLXXX, 1559.

SAINT MÉDARD OF SOISSONS (Saint-Médard de Soissons), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded by King Chlothar in the suburb in 560, LXXI, 284. — Diploma of Louis the Pious, during the abbacy of Hilduin, 824, CIV, 1135. — Privilege of Pope John VIII, CXXVI, 660. — The monk Odilo flourished in 920, CXXXII, 575. — The dean Gerard flourished in the tenth century, CXXXVIII, 171. — Diploma of King Henry I, 1047, CLI, 1027. — Privilege of Pope Innocent II, [Col. 1101] 1131, CLXXIX, 102; of Eugenius III, 1146, CLXXX, 1118. — Letters of Alexander III on behalf of this monastery, 1172, CC, 756, 813, 904, 955. — Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1209, CCXVI, 35.

SAINT MÉDARD. See ANDEGAVENSE, TORNACENSE.

MEDHAMSTEDENSE (Burch, diocese of Girwon, Ireland), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, built by King Wulfhere in expiation for the murder of his own sons whom he had killed, under Bishop Sexwulf among the Irish in 675, in the district of Girwon, XCV, 184. — Reformed by Saint Æthelwold, bishop, in 950, CXXXVIII, 93. See HUNTINGDONIENSE.

MOYEN-MOÛTIER (Moyen-Moûtier, diocese of Saint-Dié, Vosges), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, situated in the Vosges, whose founder and first abbot was Saint Hidulf, companion of Saint Boniface, in 703, CXXXVIII, 303. — On Saint Hidulf’s successors, by an anonymous author, ibid. — Life of Saint Hidulf by Valcandus, CLI, 587. — Donations made to this monastery, ibid., 598. — Letter of Innocent II by which the estate of Berckeim is awarded to the bishop of Toul, 1132, CLXXIX, 123. — Privilege of the same pope, 1140, CLXXIX, 522.

MOYEN-MOÛTIER (Moyen-Moûtier, diocese of Bourges), a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine whose foundation is assigned to 624. — Letter of Innocent III, 1203, CCXV, 34.

SAINT MARTIN OF MILAN (Saint-Martin de Milan), founded by Martin himself before he finally set out for Gaul, fourth century, IX, 163; XX, 164. — He was expelled from it by the Arians, LXXI, 564.

SAINT DENIS OF MILAN (Saint-Denis de Milan), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded by Archbishop Otbert and entrusted to Abbot Arialdus; Eugenius III granted it a privilege in 1147, CLXXX, 1194. — It is mentioned in a decretal letter of Innocent III, 1207, 1275.

SAINT BARTHOLOMEW OF MILAN (Saint-Barthélemy de Milan), a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine, whose agreement with the monastery of Saint Denis Innocent III confirmed in 1207, CCXV, 1275.

SAINT MAURICE OF MILAN (Saint-Maurice called “the Greater,” Milan), a convent of nuns whose possessions Eugenius III confirmed and which he received under his protection by privilege in 1148, CLXXX, 1360.

HOLY TRINITY OF MILAN (Abbey of the Trinity, Milan), a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine, built by the priest Liprand in 1099 under Urban II, CLXXIII, 1458.

SAINTS GERVASIUS AND PROTASIUS, OR SAINT AMBROSE, OF MILAN (the convent of Saint Ambrose, Milan), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict. Hugh, still an infant and brother of the Empress Ermengard, was buried there; it was consequently enriched with many gifts by her and Louis the Pious in 835, CIV, 1268. — Privilege of Gregory V, CXXXVII, 920. — Privilege of Archbishop Angelbert, 829, CLI, 1263. — Paschal II, 1102, CLXIII, 82; Eugenius III, 1148, CLXXX, 1358; Alexander III, 1162, CC, 174. — Letter of Innocent III ordering the lifting of the interdict imposed on the church of Bergamo, 1210, CCXVI, 230.

SAINT SIMPLICIAN OF MILAN (convent of Saint Simplician, Milan), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, built in 700 near Milan, at the place where Saint Simplician had lived a solitary life. — Diploma of Saint Anselm, archbishop of Milan, 1099, CLV, 1657. — Privilege of Alexander III, 1179, CC, 1214.

SAINT THECLA OF MILAN (Sainte-Thecle de Milan), a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine, to which Pope Anastasius IV granted a privilege in 1153, CLXXXVIII, 996.

SAINT VICTOR OF MILAN (convent of Saint Victor), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded at an uncertain date, LXXI, 746 note.

SAINT EUSTORGIUS OF MILAN (Saint-Eustorgius hospice, in the suburb called the Pavia Gate), a hospital built by Galdinus, archbishop of Milan, shortly before 1173, in which year Alexander III confirmed it by privilege, CC, 907.

MEDIOLANENSE, of the Order of Clairvaux. See BALNEOLENSE.

SAINT SEPULCHRE OF MILAN (Canons of the Holy Sepulchre, Milan), a monastery founded by Anselm, archbishop of Milan, about 1100, according to the pattern of the Holy Sepulchre at Jerusalem, CLV, 1661.

MEDLICENSE. See below, MELLICENSE.

THE CELL OF MEINRAD, OR MEGINHARD. See MONASTERY OF THE HERMITS.

SAINT MÉLAINE OF REDON, OR DOLENSE (Saint-Mélaine de Redon, Brittany), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, built in Armorica shortly after the death of Saint Melaine in 530, LXXI, 868. — Bertulf, abbot of this [Col. 1102] monastery, attended the Council of Chalon in 650, ibid. — Letter of Gregory VII, 1076, CXLVIII, 458.

MELBODIENSE. See MALBODIENSE.

MELDUNENSE. See MALBEOBURIENSE.

MELITENSE (perhaps Millau), built on the border of Auvergne and made illustrious by Blessed Calupanus, abbot; mentioned by Gregory of Tours in 576, LXXI, 326, 1059. No other information concerning it survives.

SAINT PETER OF MELK (Saint-Pierre de Melk, Lower Austria), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, built by Leopold, margrave of Austria. He first introduced canons there, but his successor replaced them with Benedictine monks in 1089. — Privilege of Paschal II, 1110, CLXIII, 270; of Calixtus II, 1122, CLXIII, 1233; of Innocent II, 1137, CLXXIX, 305; CCXVII, 178.

MELLIO (Mellio, diocese of Passau, Lower Bavaria), a monastery whose abbot Innocent III addressed concerning the establishment of a bishopric on the island of Chiemsee, 1213, CCXVI, 868.

SAINT MARY OF MELLERAIE (Notre-Dame de Melleraie, Chablais, Switzerland), a priory of the Order of Saint Augustine dependent on the monastery of Greater Saint Bernard; for its benefit Blessed Amadeus settled a certain dispute in 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1292.

SAINT MELLON. See PONTISARENSE.

MELROSE (Melrose or Roxburgh, Scotland), a monastery of the Order of Saint Columba, founded in the seventh century by Abbot Aidan, later bishop of Lindisfarne. — Letter of Innocent III concerning this monastery’s controversy with a certain Alban, a nobleman, 1204, CCXV, 309.

MELUNDENSE. See MOLISMENSE.

MEMACUM. See NONNIACUM.

SAINT MEMMIUS (Saint-Menge, near Châlons-sur-Marne), a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine, built before 676 and mentioned by Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 876. — Privilege of Innocent II, 1131, CLXXIX, 79; likewise of Alexander III, 1165, CC, 335. — Letter of the same pope to the abbot of this monastery, 1168, CC, 549.

MENAT, OR MANAT (Menat, Puy-de-Dôme), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict in the diocese of Clermont, founded by Blessed Brachio, abbot, in the sixth century, LXXI, 326 note, 1063. — Letter of Innocent III concerning the disputed subjection of this monastery between the bishop of Clermont and Cluny, 1213, CCXVI, 965.

SAINT MARTIN OF MÉRY (Méry-sur-Cher), a monastery dedicated to Saint Martin, whose abbot was Saint Patroclus in 541, LXXI, 1052.

SAINT SAVIOUR OF MESSINA (Saint-Sauveur de Messine, Sicily), a monastery following the Rule of Saint Basil, built by William, king of Sicily; at his request Alexander III confirmed it by privilege in 1174, CC, 1033. — Celestine III secured for the same monastery certain tithes in 1197, CCVI, 1234.

SAINT THEODORE OF MESSINA (Saint-Théodore de Messine, Sicily), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, which kindly received monks of Turin expelled from their own monastery in the sixth century, LXXV, 300.

SAINT MARY AND SAINT THEOBALD OF METZ (Sainte-Marie de Metz), a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine, to whose church Celestine III granted indulgences in 1195, CCVI, 1106. — Privilege of Innocent III, 1212, CCXVI, 219.

SAINT MARTIN OF METZ (Saint-Martin de Metz), a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine, founded in the suburb of Metz by King Sigebert; he was subsequently buried there, 644, LXXI, 661; LXXXVII, 316.

SAINT STEPHEN OF METZ (Saint-Étienne de Metz), a monastery founded by Saint Chrodegang, bishop, in 740, LXXXIX, 1057.

SAINT VINCENT OF METZ (Saint-Vincent de Metz), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded by Bishop Theuderic in 968. — Privilege of John XIII, 970, CXXXV, 980; of Saint Leo IX, 1050, CXLIII, 659; likewise of Urban II, 1096, CLI, 452. — Diploma of Bishop Poppo, 1094, CLV, 1651. — Privilege of Celestine III, 1192, CCVI, 938.

METZ. See Arnulf, Cross of Buris, Symphorianus.

SAINT GLODESINDA OF METZ (Sainte-Glossinde de Metz), a convent of nuns founded by Saint Glodesinda, daughter of Quintrio, duke of Champagne, in 604, LXXI, 460. — Letter of Alexander III, 1165, CC, 354.

SAINT PETER OF METZ (convent of Saint Peter at Metz), a convent of nuns whose abbess Euphemia made certain exchanges with Fulrad, abbot of Saint Denis, according to the terms of a diploma of Charlemagne, 782, CXXXVII, 968.

SAINT MEVENNIUS, OR SAINT MACLOVIUS (Saint-Méen de [Col. 1103] Ghe, Brittany), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, formerly built in Armorica by Prince Judicael about 565. Saint Mevennius was buried there in 617. The pious King Judicael also rested in the same monastery shortly afterward, LXXI, 655 note. — Diploma of Louis the Pious, 816, CIV, 1042. — Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1206, CCXV, 1049.

SAINT MICHAEL OF CASTRO BRITTONUM (Saint-Michel de Castel de Britti, diocese of Bologna, Papal States), whose abbot Innocent III wrote on behalf of the monastery of Nonantola (Saint Silvester), 1213, CCXVII, 224.

SAINT MICHAEL IN THE CATHEDRAL OF BAMBERG (Saint-Michel du Dôme, Bamberg), a cell or small monastery in the episcopal city itself, founded by Bishop Otto about 1120–1132, CLXXIII, 1280.

SAINT MICHAEL IN PERIL OF THE SEA, OR OF MONT-TOMBE (Saint-Michel de Tombelaine sur mer, Manche), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded by Saint Aubert, bishop of Avranches, to whom, as they relate, Saint Michael the archangel had appeared, during the reign of Childebert, in 709, XCVI, 1387. — Privilege of Adrian IV, 1158, CLXXXVIII, 1589. — Abbot Robert of Torigni flourished there in 1186, CCII, 1306. — Chronicle of the same monastery by Robert, CCII, 1321. — Abbots of Saint Michael, 1325. — Letter of Innocent III concerning the reform of this monastery, 1208, CCXVII, 187.

SAINT MICHAEL AND SAINT PETER (Saint-Michel, Sicily), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded by Abbot Andrew in the time of Pope Saint Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 761.

SAINT MICHAEL IN PORCARIANA (Saint-Michel de Portzet or Boursette, near Aachen), of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded not far from Aachen by Empress Theophanu, wife of Otto II, in 974. It later passed to the Cistercians. Saint Henry II, emperor, confirmed its possessions and privileges in 1014, CXL, 305.

SAINT MICHAEL IN THIÉRACHE (Saint-Michel en Thiérache, diocese of Laon), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, built or rebuilt in 940 by Blessed Malcalenus, a Scot, and disciple of Saint Cadwin. — Letter of Innocent III, 1216, CCXVII, 277.

SAINT MICHAEL OF VERRUCA (Saint-Michel de Verruque, near Pisa). See PISANUM.

SAINT MICHAEL OF VERDUN (Saint-Michel de Verdun), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, built on the Meuse in 709 by Count Wulfoald and his wife Adalsinda, LXXXVIII, 1254. — Diploma of King Pippin, 755, XCVI, 1528. — Precept of Charlemagne, 772, XCVII, 921. — Made illustrious by Abbot Smaragdus in 820, CII, 9. — Privilege of Urban II, 1097, CLI, 500. — Decree of Innocent II concerning a dispute between the abbot of this monastery and Hadwida, abbess of Juvigny, CCXXIX, 452. — Privilege of Innocent III, 1200, CCXVII, 58.

SAINT MICHAEL. See Balneolense, Bambergense, Berghense, Clusiense, Cuxacense, Hildesheimense, Hugthowiense, de Lapide, de Pisino, de Subterra, de Valle, Orticariense, Romanum, Tornodorense, etc., etc.

MICHAELSTEIN, OR SAINT MICHAEL OF THE STONE (Michaelstein or La Pierre Saint-Michel, diocese of Halberstadt, Germany), founded in 1146 on Mount Wolckanannus. — Privilege of Eugenius III, 1151, CLXXX, 1460. — Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1205, CCXV, 603. — Letter of the same pope concerning the foundation of a hospital, CCXV, 1383; CCXVI, 558.

MICHELFELD (Michelfeld, diocese of Bamberg, Bavaria), a monastery for Black Monks founded by Bishop Otto in 1120, CLXXIII, 1279. — Charters of Otto, CLXXIII, 1328, 1329, 1330. — He likewise confirmed a certain donation in 1125, CLXXIII, 1338. — Privilege of Celestine II, 1144, CLXXIX, 812.

SAINT MAXIMINUS OF MICY (Saint-My or Saint-Mesmin, near Orléans), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded by King Clovis I in honour of Saints Maximinus and Euspicius about 507, LXXI, 1158. — Louis the Pious granted it use of ships on the Loire in 814, CIV, 1014. — Diplomas of Louis and his son Lothair, 825, CIV, 1145, 1165. — The monk Letaldus flourished there in 996, CXXXVI, 781. — Diploma of King Robert, 1022, CXLI, 261. — Privilege of Paschal II, 1117, CLXIII, 417. — Decree of Alexander III by which others are substituted for the abbot and monks, CCXVII, 57; 1163, CC, 248, 261, 318. — Privilege of Innocent III, 1199.

MIDDELBURG (Middelbourg, on the island of Walcheren in Zeeland), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, concerning whose translation Eugenius III wrote in 1149, CLXXX, 1417.

MILEPECO, OR OF LONGORETO (Longuay, diocese of Auxerre), a monastery originally of the Order of Saint Benedict and later of the Cistercian Order, founded by Abbot Sigirannus and King Dagobert I in 632 in the forest of Brionia, [Col. 1104] LXXX, 519; CXXXVIII, 244.

HOLY TRINITY AND SAINT MICHAEL OF MILETO (Saint-Michel de Mileto, Kingdom of Naples), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded by Count Roger before 1150, in which year Eugenius III honoured it with a privilege, CLXXX, 1452.

SAINT MARY OF MILETO (Sainte-Marie de Mileto, Naples), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, also called “of the Tower,” to which Paschal II granted a privilege in 1103, CLXIII, 124. — Letter of the same pope, 137, 438.

SAINT EUPHEMIA OF MILETO. See EUPHEMIA.

MILLY (Milly-en-Gâtinais), a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine, which formerly had a dispute with the abbess of Saint Mary of Beauvais over the church of Hanachia (Hanaches, Oise), settled by Cardinal Cono in 1115, CLXIII, 1434.

MILIDUNENSE. See SAINT PETER.

MILZE (Milze, Bavaria), a convent of nuns of the Order of Saint Benedict, subject to the monastery of Fulda under Abbess Einhild in 783, during the reign of Charlemagne, CV, 424.

SAINT SAVIOUR OF MILZE, OR MILSTADT (Saint-Sauveur de Milze, or Milstadt, Bavaria), a convent of nuns whose protection Calixtus II undertook in 1122, CLXIII, 1242.

SAINT MARTIN OF MINDEN (Saint-Martin de Minden, Westphalia), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, built by Bishop Sigebert with the assent of Emperor Conrad II in 1033, CLI, 1062.

SAINT PETER OF MINDEN (Saint-Pierre de Minden), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, built by Bishop Bruno and endowed with privileges by Emperor Henry III in 1043, CLI, 1094. — Diploma of Emperor Henry IV, 1059, CLI, 1141.

SAINT MINIATUS. See FLORENTINUM.

SAINT MARY OF THE MINERVA (Sainte-Marie de la Minerve, Rome). See among the ROMAN MONASTERIES.

SAINT MARY OF MIRABEL (Notre-Dame de Mirabel, diocese of Poitiers), a house of canons founded by Maurice, bishop of Poitiers, shortly before 1203, when Innocent III confirmed it, CCXVII, 103.

SAINT MARY OF MIRATOIRE (Notre-Dame du Miroir, diocese of Lyon), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded in 1131. Eugenius III wrote to Cluny on its behalf in 1152, CLXXX, 1517. — Privilege of Anastasius, CLXXXVIII, 1087. — Decree of the same pope confirming the sentence of excommunication pronounced by the bishop against the abbot and brethren, 1067.

SAINT NICHOLAS OF MISERAY (Saint-Nicolas de Miseray, diocese of Bourges), a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine, built by the nobleman Gisbert and others in 1112. — Privilege of Innocent II, 1140, CLXXIX, 507.

MIRAE-VALLIS (Mirevaux or Mureau, diocese of Toul), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, founded in 1157, whose possessions and privileges Pope Lucius III confirmed in 1183, CCI, 1173.

MISNENSE, OR MISINENSE (Saint John of Mionie or Meissen, Saxony), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, built on the river Elbe in the province of Talem, whose immunities John XIII confirmed in 968, CXXXV, 965. — Privilege of Innocent II, 1140, CLXXIX, 504.

MITRENSE, incorrectly for NIDRENSE.

SAINT BLAISE OF MONDOVÌ (Saint-Blaise de Mondovi, Piedmont), a monastery of a hospital order, founded by Arnold and his companions before 1141; Innocent II confirmed it by privilege in that year, CLXXIX, 553. — Celestine II, 1143, ibid., 768. — Alexander III, 1170, CC, 685.

SAINT JOHN OF MONDOVÌ (Saint-Jean de Mondovi), a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine, built by Queen Theodelinda in the eighth century. — Privilege of Calixtus II, 1120, CLXIII, 1173; of Innocent II, 1135, CLXXIX, 246.

MOUGINS (Mougins, formerly diocese of Antibes, Var), a monastery whose prior Innocent III addressed concerning a matrimonial case in 1210, CCXVI, 245.

SAINT ALBAN OF MAINZ (Saint-Alban de Mayence), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded by Saint Riculf, or Riculf, bishop, in 805, CVII, 101 note. — A synod was held there under Blessed Rabanus, bishop, and King Louis in 847, ibid., 98 note, 100. — It was transferred to a house of canons in 1419, ibid., 101 note.

SAINT JAMES OF MAINZ (Saint-Jacques de Mayence), a monastery formerly of the Order of Saint Benedict which passed to the Premonstratensians under Alexander III, after other monks were expelled because of suspicion of the murder of the archbishop of Mainz within the monastery. — Privilege of Alexander III, 1117, CC, 1142.

SAINT PETER OF MAINZ (Saint-Pierre de Mayence), a monastery of canons concerning which Celestine III wrote to the abbot of Hemmerode regarding a controversy between the brethren and their provost Sifrid in 1196, CCVI, 1188. — The same [Col. 1105] pope granted the same monastery the church of Altavilla, 1207.

SAINT GEORGE OF MAINZ. See VALLEY OF SAINT GEORGE.

SAINT VICTOR OF MAINZ (Saint-Victor de Mayence), a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine outside the walls, where Rabanus very often enjoyed the delights of solitude in 847, CVII, 102. — The abbot of this monastery commended himself to the prayers of Saint Hildegard, abbess of Saint Rupert, CXCVII, 308.

MAINZ: a convent of nuns outside the city, founded by the noblewoman Bilehild in 734, LXXXVIII, 1289.

MOISSAC (Moissac, diocese of Cahors), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, governed by Abbot Leotadius in 680. — He bought many things from a certain Nizetius of Toulouse, LXXXVIII, 1202. — The monk and historian Rorico flourished there in 1004, CXXXIX, 587. — Letter of Urban II against the expulsion of Abbot Ansquilinus, 1094, CLI, 392, 393. — Privilege of the same pope, ibid., 466. — Alexander III, 1170, CC, 626.

SAINT MARY OF MOGLIANO, OR MOLIANENSE/MULIANENSE (Sainte-Marie de Mogliano, in the Trevisan), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded in the diocese of Treviso by Emperor Henry and his wife Agnes. — Privilege of Pope Victor II, 1055, CXLIII, 810; of Clement III, 1188, CCIV, 1335.

SAINT MICHAEL OF MOLESME, OR MELUNDENSE, LATER SAINT MARTIN (Molesme, Yonne), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict in the diocese of Langres, built by Clovis the Great in the district of Tonnerre and the village of Melun at the beginning of the sixth century, CV, 747 note. — Privilege of Eugenius III, 1145, CLXXX, 1062.

SAINT MARY OF MOLESME (Notre-Dame de Molesmes), an illustrious monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded by Robert of Champagne about 1074 at Molesmes (Côte-d’Or), but sometimes confused with the preceding because of their similar names, CV, 747 note. — Charter of Bishop Pibo, 1096, CLVII, 435. — Letter of Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, to Robert the founder, CLVII, 523. — Life of Saint Robert, first abbot, ibid., 1255. — The village of Pauliac was purchased in 1113, CLXXXV, 1399. — Enlargement of this monastery by Count Hugh of Champagne, 1104, ibid., 1444. — Letter of Innocent III, 1204, CCXV, 269, 530, 1555.

SAINT MARY OF MOLOY (Notre-Dame de Moloy, diocese of Dijon, Côte-d’Or), a convent of nuns founded by Odo of Sombernon. — Charter of the same, 1143, CLXXXV, 1419. — Charter of Bartholomew of Sombernon, ibid., 1420.

MONASTERIENSE, OR MIMIGARDEFORDENSE (Münster, also Mons, Belgium), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded by Blessed Ludger, bishop, in the eighth century, 748. — Innocent II forbade alienation of the monastery’s goods, 1141, CLXXIX, 567, 578, 627. — Privilege of Lucius III, 1184, CCI, 1290.

MONASTERY OF THE VALLEY OF SAINT MARY. See HELMSTADENSE.

SAINT MARY OF MONASTERIOLO. See MARSHY PUTEOLI.

LOWER MONASTERY. See SAINT CUNEGUNDIS.

SAINT MARY OF MONCEL (Notre-Dame de Moncel, diocese of Châlons-sur-Marne), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order built near Vitry between 1133 and 1142, CCIV, 1318.

SAINT SALVIUS OF MONTREUIL (Saint-Sauve de Montreuil-sur-Mer, diocese of Arras, Pas-de-Calais), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, apparently built by Blessed Salvius himself, bishop of Amiens, 693–613 [dates uncertain]. According to others, it was founded by Hilgodus, count of Ponthieu, in 878. — Privilege of Anastasius IV, 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1060.

SAINT VERONICA OF MONTREUIL (Montreuil-les-Dames or Montreuil-sous-Laon), a convent of nuns built by Bartholomew, bishop of Laon, and Saint Bernard of Clairvaux in 1136; its first abbess was the virgin Guiburgis, CLVI, 1001.

SAINT SAVIOUR OF MONTE-ACUTO (Saint-Sauveur de Mont-Aigu or Monte-Acuto, in the territory of Perugia in Lombardy), a monastery of the Camaldolese Order, whose abbot Offredus Eugenius III granted a privilege in 1145, CLXXX, 1046.

SAINT MARY OF MONTE-AESTIVO (Notre-Dame de Montétif, diocese of Paris, now Seine-et-Marne), a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine, founded by Maurice de Sully, bishop of Paris, in 1164. — Privilege of Clement III, 1188, CCIV, 1284.

MONTE-ALBO, OR MONT-BLANC (Mont-Blanc, diocese of Viterbo, Papal States), a monastery dependent on Albarense. — Letter of Innocent III concerning the election of its abbot, 1205, CCXV, 703.

SAINT AUGUSTINE OF MONTE-ALTO (Saint Augustine of [Col. 1106] Montalto, in the March of Ancona), a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine, whose possessions and privileges Innocent III confirmed in 1204, CCXV, 341.

SAINT MICHAEL OF MONTE-ALTO (Saint-Michel de Haut-Mont, diocese of Aire or Auch), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, built before 1096 and subject to Cluny; Urban II granted it a privilege while travelling through those regions in 1096, CLI, 206, 465.

MONTE-AMIATO, OF THE HOLY SAVIOUR (Monte Amiata in Tuscany), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded in 747 by the Venerable Abbot Erpo and Rachis, king of the Lombards, LXXXVII, 1408.—Diploma of Louis the Pious, 816, CIV, 1049, 1051.—Privilege of Gregory V to Abbot Vinizon, 996, CXXXVII, 901.—Privilege of St. Leo IX, 1050, CXLIII, 650.—Diploma of King Conrad II, 1027, CLI, 1047.

MONTE-ANGELORUM. See ENGELBERGENSE.

MONTE-ARAGONUM, OF JESUS OF NAZARETH. See HUESCENSE.

MONTEBELLO, OF ST. MARY (Sainte-Marie de Montebello, diocese of Ravenna), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, to which Eugenius III granted a confirmatory privilege in 1150, CLXXX, 1428.

MONTEBOURG (Montebourg, diocese of Coutances), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded in 1080 by William I, king of the English, and Roger, monk of Holy Cross and first abbot of the same monastery, CCII, 1319.

MONTE-CASTRILOCENSIS, OF ST. WALDRUDE (Sainte-Waldrude of Mons), a convent of nuns founded by the Blessed Countess Waldetrude about 640, CXLIX, 139.—Privilege of Lucius III, 1182, CCI, 1116.

MONTE CASTRI LOCO, OF ST. GERMANUS (Saint-Germain of Mons, in Belgium), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, founded about 640 by the Blessed Viscount Vincent and his wife St. Waldetrude, CXLIX, 139.

MONTE CENISIO (Mont-Cenis, Savoy), a monastery or hospice founded for the benefit of pilgrims and endowed by Louis the Pious, CIV, 1151.—It was annexed, together with two other monasteries, by the Emperor Lothair in 825, ibid.

MONTE CHRISTI, OF ST. MAMILIANUS (Monte Cristo, in Corsica), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built on the island of Corsica before 595, and visited by command of St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 302.—Julius, abbot of this monastery, complains of the oppressions of Duke Roland, 719, LXXXVII, 1364.—Privilege of Gelasius II, 1118, CLXIII, 500.

MONTE CORASE, OF ST. ANGEL. See CILENTIANA MONASTERIA.

MONTE CORNELIO, OF ST. PETER (Saint-Pierre of Mont-Cornillon, near Liège), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, built by Bishop Adalbero about 1126, but later transferred to the Carthusians. In nearly the same place stood a convent of nuns in which flourished Blessed Juliana, who first requested the institution of the feast of the Most Holy Sacrament.—Privilege of Innocent II, 1143, CLXXIX, 655.—Of Eugenius III, 1168, CLXXX, 1309.

MONTE DEI (Mont-Dieu, between Rethel and Mouzon in Champagne), a celebrated Carthusian house founded in 1134 by Odo, abbot of St. Remigius of Rheims; its first prior was Godfrey, a disciple of St. Bruno. It is mentioned in CLIII, 590, 1125, where is published a manuscript of the statutes of this order preserved in that monastery.—Charter of foundation by Prior Odo, 1137, CLXX, 1333.—Privilege of Innocent II, 1136, CLXXIX, 296.—Of Eugenius III, 1145, CLXXX, 1072.

MONTE DESIDERIO, OF ST. MARY (Notre-Dame of Montdidier, diocese of Amiens), a priory of the Order of St. Benedict, founded in 1119 and subject to Cluny.—Privilege of Alexander III, 1174, CC, 969.—Likewise of Urban III, 1185, CII, 1338.

MONTE FALCONE, OF ST. GERMANUS, LATER OF ST. BALDRICUS (Saint-Bauldry of Mont-Faucon, diocese of Rheims), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by St. Baldric in the diocese of Rheims in the tenth century, CXXXV, 313.

MONTE FERREO, OF ST. BENEDICT (Saint-Benoît of Mont-Ferrier, in Pannonia), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by St. Astric, abbot of St. Martin of Monte Sacro, through the generosity of St. Stephen, king of the Hungarians, who had summoned him with his brethren to evangelize this kingdom, 1010, CLI, 1214.

MONTE FORTENSE, OF ST. JAMES (Saint-Jacques of Mont-Fort-la-Cannée, diocese of Rennes), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, built in 1151 by William, count of Montfort, and his wife Amicia.—Letter of Innocent III, 1206, CCXV, 1049.

MONTE FRIGIDO (Montefrio, diocese of Pamplona, Spain) [Col. 1107], a monastery whose abbot was entrusted by Innocent III with the case concerning the marriage of the king of Aragon, 1206, CCXV, 908, 916.

MONTE FERRANDO (Mont-Ferrand, diocese of Clermont), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, concerning which Innocent III wrote to the abbot of Mauziac, 1206, CCXV, 903.

MONTE GEROLDI (Mont-Geroult, Seine-et-Marne), a monastery whose abbot was written to by Innocent III in 1207, CCXV, 1216.

MONTE LAETO, OF ST. MARY (Sainte-Marie of Monte-Laeto, in Spain), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, whose possessions and privileges Alexander III confirmed in 1172, CC, 878.

MONTE JOVIS (Mont-Joux or Mont-Jeux, diocese of Besançon), a priory of the Order of St. Augustine.—Letter of Innocent III concerning its evil practices, 1212, CCXVI, 615.—The house of Valle-Sussionis was confirmed to it, 869.

MONTE LEPROSORUM (Mont-aux-Ladres, or Mont-aux-Malades, diocese of Rouen), a priory of the Order of St. Augustine, to whose prior Innocent III wrote concerning letters fraudulently obtained by a certain person, 1203, CCXV, 136.

MONTE MAJORE, OF ST. PETER (Saint-Pierre-de-Mont-Majour), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict. It seems to have been founded near Arles, about the middle of the tenth century, by a noblewoman named Theacinda; its possessions and privileges were confirmed by the antipope Leo VIII in 963, CXXXV, 994.—Privilege of Gregory V, CXXXVII, 927.—Of Sergius IV, 1012, CXXXIX, 1520.—Sergius rebukes Amalric, archbishop of Aix, for harassing this monastery, ibid., 1521.—Letter of the count of Arles to St. Gregory VII concerning the election of a new abbot, 1081, CXLVIII, 631.—Privilege of Innocent III, 1204, CCXV, 466.

MONTE MARTYRUM, PARISIAN, OF ST. DENIS (Saint-Denis of Montmartre near Paris), a royal convent of nuns built and endowed by Louis VI in 1140.—Privilege of Eugenius III, 1147, CLXXX, 1236.

MONTE MORELLO, OF ST. MARY (Notre-Dame of Mont-Morel, Manche), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, built between 1162 and 1171 by Ralph, canon of St. Victor at Paris. Innocent III wrote to the abbot of this monastery in 1204, CCXV, 529.

MONTENSE, OF ST. GERMANUS (Saint-Germain of Montfaucon, between Rheims and Verdun), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by the priest Baldric in 630.—Privilege of Pope Lucius III, 1184, CCI, 1313.

MONTENSE. See ST. QUINTINUS.

MONTE OLIVO. See ST. LAURENTIUS.

MONTE PILOSO, OF NEW ST. MARY (Sainte-Marie-Neuve of Monte Peloso, in Basilicata, Naples).—Letters of Innocent III to the prior, 1204, CCXV, 221, 373, 624.

MONTE-RAMI, OF ST. MARY (Sainte-Marie of Monte-Ramo, Galicia, Spain), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded in 1153 by Sancha, daughter of King Alfonso I.—Privilege of Alexander III, 1163, CC, 267.

MONTE REGALI, OF ST. MARY (Sainte-Marie of Montréal or Monte-Regali, Sicily), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded in 1174 by King William II, called the Good, and later annexed to Cassino.—Privilege of Alexander III, 1174, CC, 1000.—It was made a bishopric in 1183, CCI, 1178.—Innocent III compelled it to obey the bishop in 1203, CCXV, 97.

MONTE SACRO, OF THE MOST HOLY TRINITY (Sainte-Trinité of Monte Sacro, in the Capitanate, Naples), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose possessions Adrian IV confirmed in 1159, after Honorius and Eugenius, CLXXXVIII, 1608.

MONTE SACRO. See ST. MARTINUS.

MONTE SACRO IN APULIA (the convent of Monte Sacro, Apulia, Naples), a monastery built on an estate of the monastery of Calana, over which it later disputed superiority.—Letter of Innocent III, 1198, CCXIV, 401.

MONTE SANCTO (Monte Sancto, in the diocese of the same name, a suffragan of Thessalonica in Macedonia), a place called the Holy Mountain because it is occupied by three hundred monasteries. Among them shone the cenobium of St. Athanasius; Innocent III granted privileges to its abbot, as also to the others, in 1213, CCXVI, 956.

MONTE, OF ST. ROMARICUS (Remiremont, in the Vosges), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by St. Romaricus in the Vosges near a convent of nuns built in the same place, 680, LXXI, 644 note.—See ABENDENSE.

MONTE, OF ST. JOHN (Mont-Saint-Jean, near Vervins, Aisne), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, founded in 1136 by Walter of Gymmenich, dean of St. Gereon at Cologne, and his brother Hubert, in the former diocese of Liège; it is otherwise called Mosacum (Moussy-sur-Aisne).—Privilege of Celestine II, 1144, CLXXIX, 799.

[Col. 1108] MONTE, OF ST. MICHAEL (Mont-Saint-Michel, Normandy), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in 943 by Richard, son of Duke William, CXLI, 44.—Charter of John, archbishop of Rouen, pronouncing on its rights under Abbot Ranulf, 1061, CXLVII, 265.—Robert of Thorigny, abbot, flourished about 1150; he was the continuator of Sigebert’s Chronicle, CLX, 411.

MONTE SCALARIO, OF ST. CASSIAN (Saint-Cassien of Mont-Echelle, near Vallombrosa), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in Tuscany not far from the cenobium of Vallombrosa in the eleventh century, CXLVI, 790.

MONTE SERENO, OF ST. PETER (Saint-Pierre of Mont-Serein, diocese of Magdeburg), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, built by Margrave Conrad and his sons Otto, Theodoric, and Dedo.—Privilege of Innocent III, 1202, CCXIV, 959, 960.

MONTE-SERRATO, OF ST. CECILIA (Montserrat, Catalonia), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded about 888. It was granted at first to nuns, but passed in 964 to monks of St. Benedict; the rights and privileges of this monastery were confirmed in 972, CXXXV, 1090.

MONTE SION, OF ST. MARY (Notre-Dame of Mont-de-Sion, Jerusalem), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, founded shortly before 1179 by Godfrey, duke of Sicily; in that year Alexander III confirmed it by privilege, CC, 1214.

MONTE SORACTE (now Monte San Oreste), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, dedicated to St. Andrew and St. Sylvester, endowed by King Carloman in the eighth century, CII, 372.—St. Nonnosus lived there for a long time. He is mentioned by St. Gregory the Great in the *Dialogues*, sixth century, LXXVII, 181, 467 note, and by Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVIII, 1073.—Benedict, a monk of this monastery, flourished in 1001, CXXXIX, 9.

MONTE-SUAVI, OF ST. SYLVESTER (Saint-Sylvestre of Monte Soave, Italy), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict which, through the negligence of its abbot, had fallen into decay and was therefore entrusted by Eugenius III to the prior of Camaldoli in 1153, CLXXX, 1567.—Privilege of Adrian IV, 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1398.

MONTE THABOR, IN THE HOLY PLACES (Abbey of Mount Tabor, Holy Land), a monastery of the Cistercian Order.—Letter of Innocent III to its abbot, 1204, CCXV, 555.

MONTE TUMBA, OF ST. MICHAEL. See MICHAELIS.

MORANTIUS, ST. See DUACENSE.

MONTHERONE. See THELA.

KNIGHTS TEMPLAR OF MONTPELLIER (House of the Templars at Montpellier). Decree of Innocent III concerning an agreement with the chapter of Maguelone, 1198, CCXIV, 467.

MONTPELLIER, OF ST. MAURICE (Saint-Maurice of Sauret, near Montpellier), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by Bishop William in 1143 and confirmed in the same year by a privilege of Innocent II, whose letter survives, CLXXIX, 630.

MORBACENSE (Munsterthal, Alsace), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded in the Vosges by Count Eberhard and confirmed by Widegern, bishop of Strasbourg, in 728, LXXXVIII, 1281.—Sale of Theodo to the same monastery, 1285.—Precept of King Pippin, 753, XCVI, 1523, 1532.—Precept of Charlemagne, 772, XCVII, 923, 925, 947.—St. Simpert became abbot about 780, XCIX, 737.—Diploma of St. Emperor Henry II, 1023, CXL, 375.—Letter of Innocent II concerning the appointment of a prior in the monastery of Undendorf, CLXXIX, 325.—Privilege of the same, 426.

MOREROLA (Morérola, diocese of Zamora, kingdom of León, Spain), a monastery whose abbot Innocent III entrusted with the duty of detecting and correcting every transgression in monasteries, 1210, CCXVI, 248, 270, 333.

MORFISA. See ARCHANGELI.

MORIMOND, OF ST. MARY (Sainte-Marie of Morimond, on the Ticino, in the Milanese), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded about 1136 near Coronatum by monks from Morimond in France.—Privilege of Alexander III, 1171, CC, 734.

MORIMOND, OF ST. MARY (Notre-Dame of Morimond, diocese of Langres, Haute-Marne), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded in 1114 by Ulric of Agrimont, lord of Choiseul, and his wife Adeline, from which very many companies of monks went forth. Charter of foundation of Geoffrey, bishop of Châlons, 1142, CLXXIII, 1399.—Charter of Guilenc, bishop of Langres, from 1114, CLXXXV, 1441.—Gifts of Ulric or Odalric, 1148, CLXXXV, 1443.—Of Gerard, called “Without Land,” brother of Rayner of Acrimont, ibid.—Abbot Odo flourished in 1156, [Col. 1109] CLXXXVIII, 1643.—Alexander III, 1171, CC, 752, 757, 976.—Urban III, 1187, 1494.—Letters and privilege of Innocent III, 1199, CCXIV, 793; 1210, CCXVI, 356, 550, 866, 945.

MORINENSE, OF ST. AUGUSTINE (Saint-Augustin, diocese of Moringhen or Thérouanne, Pas-de-Calais), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, granted by Bishop Milo to monks of the congregation of St. Norbert before 1167, when Eugenius III confirmed it by privilege, CLXXX, 1295.—Privilege of Lucius III, 1181, by which he assigns to it the church of Quaquelles (Quesques), CCI, 1104.

MORINENSE, OF ST. JOHN. See YPRENSE.

MORRONA, OF ST. MARY (Sainte-Marie of Morrona, Tuscany), a monastery of the Camaldolese Order, whose rights and privileges Calixtus II confirmed at the request of Abbot Gerard in 1120, CLXIII, 1179.—Privilege of Innocent II, 1133, CLXXIX, 168.—Of Eugenius III, 1148, CLXXX, 1377.

MORTUI MARIS, OF ST. MARY (Sainte-Marie of Mortemer, diocese of Rouen), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, built by Abbot Alexander in 1134.—Privilege of Innocent II confirming its possessions, 1142, CLXXIX, 572.—Privilege of Eugenius III, 1146, CLXXX, 1104.

MOSACUM (Moussy-sur-Aisne). See MONTIS S. JOANNIS.

MOSACENSE, a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in the diocese of Aquileia, founded by Count Cancellinus about 1085 under Patriarch Frederick, XCIX, 641.

MOSOMENSE or MOSOMAGENSE, OF ST. MARY (Mouzon, diocese of Rheims), a celebrated monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, formerly a convent of nuns. Archbishop Adalbert rebuilt it and introduced Benedictine monks about 980, CXXXVII, 517.—Charter of Arnulf, archbishop of Rheims, 1015, CXXXIX, 1548, 1549.—Of St. Henry, 1023, CXL, 371.—Of Ebalus, archbishop of Rheims, 1024, CXLI, 1111.—Likewise of Archbishop Guy, 1043, CXLII, 1407.

MOXENSE, OF THE HOLY SAVIOUR (Saint-Sauveur of Moxi, Lombardy), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose goods and possessions Pope Paschal II confirmed in 1106, CLXIII, 195.

MOWENHEIMENSE, a convent of nuns situated in the diocese of Eichstätt, governed by St. Leubilus in the time of St. Walburga, abbess, 790, CXXIX, 872.

MULENBECHANUM (Mulenbach, diocese of Minden, Electorate of Brandenburg), a monastery of girls founded by the Venerable Hildiburga and Abbot Folchard. For it Abbess Bertheidis obtained a privilege from St. Henry in 1003, CXL, 251.

MULEBRUNN, OF ST. MARY (Maulbronn, diocese of Speyer), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded in 1138. Its abbot wrote to St. Hildegard, the illustrious abbess of St. Rupert, CXCVII, 283.—Likewise a monk of the same monastery to the same abbess, 357.

MUNSTERIENSE (Münster, diocese of Cologne), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, acquired by Henry, duke of Bavaria, and granted to Otto, bishop of Bamberg, to organize it about 1132, CLXXIII, 1279.—See MONASTERIENSE.

MURBACENSE. See MORBACENSE.

MURCEDO (Murcedo or Murdeco, diocese of Albano, Papal States), a convent of nuns built by the bishop of Albano, whose statutes Pope Innocent III confirmed in 1211, CCXVI, 416.

MURELENSE, OF ST. MARY (Notre-Dame of Moureille, near Luçon, Vendée), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded about 1169 by the lords of Triaze.—Privilege of Lucius III, 1182, etc., 1138.

MURENSE, OF ST. MARTIN (Saint-Martin of Muri, Aargau, Switzerland), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded in 1027 by Werner, bishop of Strasbourg.—Count Rotebodonus and his wife Itta adorned it with many gifts.—Privilege of Innocent II, 1139, CLXXIX.—Of Adrian IV, 1159, CLXXXVIII, 1626.—Privilege of Alexander III, 1179, CC, 1213.—Of Clement III, 1189, CCIV, 1421.—Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1203, CCXVII, 99.

MURIANO, OF ST. CYPRIAN OF VENICE (Saint-Cyprien of Muriano, Venice), a monastery whose complaint Lucius III heard concerning the construction of a new church by the clerics of Rovigo, 1185, CCI, 1364.

MUSCETANUM, OF ST. ANDREW (Saint-André of Musciano, diocese of Florence), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in the Florentine district. Its abbot Ralph entered the company of St. John Gualbert and later succeeded that holy founder in governing the holy congregation of Vallombrosa, 1073, CXLVI, 772.—Privilege of Alexander III, 1170, CC, 693.

MUTINENSE, OF ST. PETER (Saint-Pierre of Modena), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose goods and privileges Eugenius III confirmed in 1149, CLXXX, 1384.—Privilege of [Col. 1110] Alexander III, 1170, CC, 638, 912.—Of Urban III, 1187, CCII, 1476.

MUTINENSE, a college of canons to which Urban III granted a bull in 1187, CCII, 1474.

MUTINENSE, OF ST. EUPHEMIA (Sainte-Euphémie of Modena), a convent of nuns to which, at the request of Abbess Maria, Urban III granted a privilege in 1189, CCII, 1518.

NABORIS, ST., OF METZ (Saint-Avold of Metz), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by St. Fridolin, an Irishman by birth, under the invocation of St. Hilary, about 509; restored by Sigebert, bishop of Metz, in 765.—Bishop Angelianimus granted many things to this monastery in 787, XCVI, 1100.

NANTENSE, OF ST. MARCULF (Saint-Marculf or Marcou of Nanteuil, diocese of Coutances), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded in 526 by St. Marculf, its first abbot; Paschal II subjected it to Vabres in 1116, CLXIII, 405.

NANTENSE, OF ST. PETER (Saint-Pierre of Nant, Aveyron), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, originally a simple priory, raised to the rank of abbey by Pope Innocent IV in 1135, CLXXIX, 237.

NANTOLIENSE, OF ST. MARY (Notre-Dame of Nanteuil-en-Vallée, Charente), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by Charlemagne and subjected to the bishop of Bordeaux at the end of the eighth century.—Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1198, CCXIX, 209.

NANTUACENSE, OF ST. MARY (Notre-Dame of Nantua), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose foundation is placed before 757, when under Abbot Siagrius it obtained privileges from King Pippin. It later passed to Cluny, XCVI, 1529.—Privilege of Eugenius III.

NARNIENSE (Narni, Italy), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, endowed with privileges by Pope Alexander II in 1069, CXLVI, 1352.

NARBONNENSE, OF ST. PAUL. See PAULI.

NAVENSE, OF ST. SULPICIUS (Saint-Sulpice-les-Bourges or Notre-Dame de la Nef), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded near Bourges under King Clothar II in 628 by St. Sulpicius, called the Pious; he himself was buried there. It later passed to the Congregation of St. Maur, LXXX, 591.

NAZARIUS, ST. See LAURESHAMENSE, VERONENSE.

NEAPOLITAN, OF SS. ERASMUS, MAXIMUS, AND JULIAN (Convent of St. Erasmus, Naples), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by the noblewoman Alexandra and entrusted to Abbot Fuscus in the time of Gregory the Great, about 600, LXXVII, 1075.

NEAPOLITAN, OF ST. SEBASTIAN (Saint-Sébastien of Naples), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded at Naples in his own house by a nobleman named Romanus under Gregory the Great, who united it with Gratterense in Plaia, LXXVII, 1113, 1255.

NEAPOLITAN, OF SS. SEVERINUS AND SOSIUS (Saint-Séverin of Naples), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose abbot Pope Alexander III granted the use of the mitre in 1180, CC, 1290.—Privilege of Celestine III, 1194, CCVI, 1051.

NEAPOLITAN CONVENT OF GIRLS, founded by the noblewoman Rustica in the sixth century; Gratiosa was its first abbess, according to Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 660.

NEAS, a Jerusalemite monastery mentioned by St. Gregory the Great in the sixth century, LXXVII, 889.

NEMORE, OF ST. MARY (Notre-Dame du Bois, Pont-à-Mousson, Meurthe), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, built by Simon, duke of Lorraine, in 1126.—Privilege of Lucius III, 1182, CCI, 1110.

NEOCELLENSE, OF ST. PETER (Saint-Pierre of Newcell, near Freising, Saxony), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, founded by Otto, bishop of Freising, shortly before 1143, CLXXIX, 638.

NEOT, ST. (Abbey of St. Neot, Lincolnshire, England), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, on whose behalf Celestine III wrote to the bishop of Lincoln in 1194, CCVI, 1058.

NERANA, OF ST. MARY, a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in Tuscany which adopted the rule of Vallombrosa about 1074, CXLVI, 806.

NERIENSIS PRIORY (Néris, Bourbonnais), whose beginnings are uncertain; it is mentioned, LXXI, 1052 note.

NERITONENSE (Nardò, Terra d’Otranto, Naples), a monastery whose abbot Innocent III wrote to in 1212, CCXVI, 793.

NERLACENSE. See NIGRO LACU.

NERONIS VILLA, OF ST. PETER (Saint-Pierre of Néronville, Seine-et-Marne), a small monastery situated in the diocese of Sens, granted by the nobleman Disnon to the cenobium of La Sauve-Majeure in 1092, CXLVII, 1011.

NERVESIA, OF ST. EUSTACE (Saint-Eustache of Nervèze or Nervoie, bishopric of Treviso, Italy), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by Count Rambald and his mother [Col. 1111] Gisla; Calixtus II confirmed its rights and possessions in 1122, CLXIII, 1258.

NESSINUM, OF ST. PETER (Saint-Pierre of Nessio, diocese of Como, Lombardy), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, whose rights and privileges Pope Lucius III protected in 1184, CCI, 1268.

NEWBURGENSE, OF ST. BARTHOLOMEW (Saint-Barthélemy of Neubourg, diocese of Trier), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, endowed with a privilege by Pope Lucius II in 1144, CLXXIX, 873.

NEWBURGENSE, OF THE HOLY SAVIOUR AND ST. MARY (Klosterneuburg, Lower Austria), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, built in 1054.—Letter of Innocent III, 1203, CCXV, 174.—Perhaps identical with the monastery of Novo Castro (Neufchâtel).

NICHARDELSEHAUSEN. See below NITARSHAUSEN.

NICIENSE, OF ST. JOHN THE BAPTIST (Saint-Jean-Baptiste at Nice), an ancient monastery built in the time of St. Hospitius (now San-Sospir), of which only the church survives; it passed to the monks of St. Pons in the eleventh century, LXXI, 378 note.

NICHOLAS, ST., OF FRUTINO (Saint-Nicolas of Frottino, Tuscany), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict dependent on Monte Cassino, whose many possessions Clement III confirmed by privilege in 1188, CCIV, 1403.

NICHOLAS, ST., OF THE MOUNT (Saint-Nicolas du Mont, near Narni, Papal States), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, to which Innocent III granted a privilege in 1198, 317.

NICHOLAS, ST., OF TARASCON (Saint-Nicolas of Tarascon), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, consecrated shortly before the time of Calixtus II by the abbot of the monastery of St. Victor of Marseille, on which it depended.—Letter of Calixtus II, CLXIII, 1107.

NICHOLAS, ST., OF RIBODIMONTE (Saint-Nicolas of Ribemont, Aisne), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by Count Anselm in the former diocese of Laon and the forest of the Vosges in 1083. Concerning Simon, abbot of this monastery, CLVI, 1002.—Privilege of Innocent III, 1198, CCXVII, 10, 31.

NICHOLAS, ST. See MISERAYENSE, RIGENSE, STENDALENSE, TORNACENSE, VENETUM.

NIDI MERLI, OF THE WOOD, OF ST. MARY (Sainte-Marie of Nidoiseau, diocese of Angers), a convent of nuns founded by Blessed Robert of Arbrissel about 1108.—Privilege of Eugenius III, 1146, CLXXX, 1130.

NIDRENSE or NIEDER-ALTACENSE (Niederaltaich, or Lower Altaich, Bavaria, on the Danube), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by Duke Odilo and secured with privileges by Pope Benedict VII in 983, CXXXVII, 349.—Privilege of Pope St. Leo IX, 1054, CXLIII, 781.—Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1199, CCXIV, 560.

NIENZABAS, OF ST. MARY (Sainte-Marie of Nienzabas, Spain), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, whose possessions and rights Eugenius III confirmed by privilege in 1147, CLXXX, 1279.

NIEWBURGENSE, OF ST. MARY (Notre-Dame of Nieubourg, diocese of Passau), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, founded by Leopold, margrave of Austria, shortly before 1137, when Innocent II received it under his protection, CLXXIX, 339.—Of Eugenius III, 1146, CLXXX, 1172.

NIGRO LACU, or NERLACENSE, OF ST. MARY (Sainte-Marie of Nerlac or Noirlac, diocese of Bourges).

NINOVENSE, OF ST. CORNELIUS (Sainte-Corneille of Ninove or Ninive, diocese of Mechelen), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, built in 1137 by several noblemen of that place.—Privilege of Eugenius III, 1153, CLXXX, 1561.—Charter of Lord Bernard of Clairvaux concerning a dispute with the monastery of Jette, 1146, CLXXXV, 1825.—Privilege of Urban III, 1186, CCII, 1437.

NITARSHAUSEN, OF ST. MARY (Sainte-Marie of Nitarshusen, diocese of Mainz), a convent of nuns founded by Otto, bishop of Bamberg, in 1120 in the district of Tullefelt, CLXXIII, 1180.

NIVERNENSE. See OF THE HOLY SAVIOUR.

NIVERNENSE, OF ST. STEPHEN (Saint-Étienne of Nevers), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded in 600, rebuilt and reformed in 1063.—Privilege of Alexander III, 1159, CC, 145.

NIVERNENSE, OF ST. MARTIN (Saint-Martin of Nevers), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, founded before the eighth century; restored, it flourished in the twelfth century, when it was endowed by Hervé, lord of Donzy.—Privilege of Honorius II, 1129, CLXVI, 1297.—Privilege of Pope Innocent II, 1130, CLXXIX, 71.

NIVERNENSE, OF ST. VICTOR (Saint-Victor of Nevers), an ancient monastery of the Order of St. Benedict which, having fallen from a most flourishing condition into desolation and ruin, was restored by William, count of Nevers, [Col. 1112] and granted to the monastery of Blessed Mary of La Charité in 1055, CLI, 1032.

NIVIELLENSIS, or NIVIGELLAE (Nivelles in Brabant), a convent of canonesses built in 640 by the noblewomen Itta, wife of Pippin of Landen, and her daughter Gertrude; Pippin himself was buried there, LXXI, 659; LXXXVII, 309.—Privilege of Pope St. Leo IX, 1048, CXLIII, 611.—Charter of Odo, bishop of Cambrai, 1112, CLX, 1157.

NOBILIACENSE, OF ST. VEDASTUS (Neuilly in Artois), a monastery built by St. Vedastus, bishop of Arras.—Diploma, spurious, of King Theodoric, 680, LXXXVII, 1328; CI, 677. See ATREBATENSE.—Privilege of Pope Innocent II, 1135, CLXXIX, 227.

NOBILIACENSE. See below NOVALIACENSE.

NOCIATENSE, OF THE HOLY SEPULCHRE (Saint-Sépulcre of Noci, kingdom of Naples), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, to which Pope Benedict VII granted many things in 1013, CXXIX, 1589.

NOGARIENSE (Nogaro, Gers), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, in whose defence Innocent wrote to the worthy men of that place in 1141, CLXXIX, 566.

NOLANUM MONASTERIOLUM (Convent of St. Paulinus at Nola), established by St. Paulinus near the tomb of St. Felix the martyr, built about 400, LXI, 51.

NOLANUS (convent of nuns at Nola), a convent of the house of Obortius, mentioned by St. Gregory the Great in the sixth century, LXXVII, 467.

NONANTULANUM, OF SS. PETER AND PAUL (Saint-Pierre of Nonantola, diocese of Modena), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in 735 in the diocese of Modena by the Venerable Abbot Anselm and King Aistulf, LXXXVII, 1411.—The donation of Charlemagne called “Immanis,” 774, XCVII, 1002.—Donation of Countess Matilda, XCVIII, 646.—Louis the Pious, 814, CIV, 1007, 1103.—Lothair, 827, CIV, 1161, 1289.—Privilege of Sergius III, CXXXI, 977.—Of Paschal II, 1112, CLXIII, 306.

NONANTULANUM, OF ST. SYLVESTER (Saint-Silvestre of Nonantola, territory of Modena), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose possessions and privileges Pope Marinus II confirmed in 946 at the request of Abbot Theodoric, CXXXIII, 878.—Sergius IV allowed Abbot Ralph to build a parish church for St. Michael, CXXXIX, 1502.—It was granted to the bishop of Parma by Emperor Henry II, CXL, 250.—Privilege of Alexander II, 1067, CXLVI, 1333.—Of Innocent II, 1132, CLXXIX, 161, 446.—Letter of Anastasius IV concerning the election of a new abbot, 1153, CLXXXVIII, 1043.—Of Alexander III, 1166, CC, 493, 667, 668, 750, 867, 1041.—Of Pope Celestine III, 1191, CCVI, 878.—Privilege of Pope Innocent III, 1213, CCXVI, 861; CCXVII, 38, 78, 160, 221.

NONANTULANUM, COLLEGE OF CANONS OF ST. MICHAEL (Canons of Nonantola), a monastery whose abbot Alexander III ordered to restore certain things in 1178, CC, 1187, 1291.—Likewise Clement III, 1188, CCIV, 1398.—Admonition of Celestine III concerning certain matters requiring censure, 1197, CCVI, 1223.—Letter of Innocent III, 1212, CCXVI, 569.

NONNIACUM, or MEMACUM (Mémac, diocese of Limoges), a monastery founded by St. Aredius and granted by him to the brethren of St. Martin of Tours in 572, LXXI, 1144.

NONUM MONASTERIUM, on the island of Gades (Cádiz), Spain, built by St. Fructuosus, bishop, in 665, LXXXVIII, 1089.

NORTHAMPTONIENSE, OF ST. ANDREW (Saint-André of Northampton, England), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in England, whose possessions and rights St. Hugh, bishop of Lincoln, confirmed at the end of the twelfth century, CLIII, 1120.—Letter of Innocent III, 1206, CCV, 955.

NORTONIENSE, perhaps the same monastery as the preceding one.

NORTWICENSE, OF THE MOST HOLY TRINITY (Holy Trinity of Norwich, England), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by Bishop Herbert in 1096.—Privilege of Paschal II, 1117, CLIII, 432.

NOSTLATENSE (Nostlat, diocese of York, England), a monastery to which Innocent III granted a privilege in 1199, CCXIV, 637.

NOVA CELLA, or JUVINIACENSE (Juvignac, arrondissement of Montpellier), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by Benedict, abbot of Aniane, not far from his own monastery, and confirmed by a diploma of Charlemagne in 799, XCVII, 988.

NOVALIACENSE, or NOBILIACENSE, OF SS. JUNIANUS AND HILARY (Saint-Hilaire or Saint-Junien of Noailles, diocese of Poitiers), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, formerly dedicated to St. Junianus in 559.—Abbot Otto transferred it from Mariacum to Nobiliacum in 779.—Charlemagne and Louis the Pious bestowed various gifts upon it, [Col. 1113] 793, CIV, 979.—Privilege of Pope Gelasius II, 1118, CLXIII, 502.

NOVALICIACENSE, OF ST. PETER (Saint-Pierre of Novalesa, Piedmont), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded in the Susa valley by Abbo in 739, LXXXVIII, 1290.—Diploma of Charlemagne, 773, XCVII, 997.—Charlemagne’s renewal of Abbo’s testament, ibid., 1036.—Diploma of Louis the Pious, 814, CIV, 1009.—Diploma of Lothair, 825, CIV, 1151.

NOVALIIS, OF ST. MARY. See CRASSENSE.

NOVARIENSE (Novara, in the Milanese), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, whose possessions and rights Pope Innocent II confirmed in 1132, CLXXIX, 141.

NOVEIENSE (Novi or Novion, former diocese of Rheims, Ardennes), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in 548. Alexander III wrote to the archbishop of Rheims that property unjustly taken from it should be restored in 1170, CC, 622, 623.—Innocent III confirmed an agreement with the count of Regiteste in 1210, CCXVII, 200, 221.

NOVEM FONTIUM, OF ST. GILBERT (Saint-Gilbert of Neufonts, diocese of Clermont), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, founded about 1150 by the nobleman Gilbert, returned from the Holy Land, who was its first abbot.—Privilege of Clement III, 1188, CCIV, 1355.

NOVIACENSIS PRIORY. See above NOVEIENSE.

NOVIBURGENSE, otherwise VALLEY OF ST. GEORGE (Saint-George of Neubourg or Georgenthal, diocese of Mainz), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded in Thuringia by Count Sizzo in 1043.—Letter by which Cardinal Conon summoned Theoger, abbot of this monastery, 1118, CLXIII, 1435.

NOVIGENTENSE, OF ST. MARY (Notre-Dame of Nogent-sous-Coucy, Aisne), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded in 1076 by Alberic, lord of Coucy, and his wife Adela.—It was made illustrious by Abbot Guibert, CLVI, 9.—Abbots of this monastery, CLVI, 1125.—Donation of Hugh, bishop of Soissons, ibid.—Privilege of Alexander III, 1174, CC, 985, 1036.

NOVIENTENSE, or EBERSHEIMENSE (Neuvillers, Alsace), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded in the diocese of Strasbourg by Bishop Sigebald in the seventh century.—Diploma of King Theodoric, 683, LXXXVII, 1334.—Charter of King Carloman, 770, XCVI, 1578.—Diploma of Charlemagne, 810, XCVII, 995, 1080.—Of Louis the Pious, 814, CIV, 1000, 1082, 1180.—Privilege of Lucius III, 1183, CCI, 1217.

NOVIGENTENSE, OF ST. DENIS (Nogent-le-Rotrou), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in 1094 by Geoffrey, count of Mortagne, on the Huisne in the diocese of Chartres.—Privilege of Urban II, 1095, CLI, 435.—Concerning the foundation of this monastery, CLXXII, 1405.—Privilege of Clement III, 1190, CCIV, 1472.

NOVIGENTENSE (Saint-Cloud, formerly Nogent), a monastery founded near Paris in 560 by St. Clodoald, son of King Chlodomer, who, escaping the slaughter of his brothers, became a monk and priest; he died and was buried there. It was destroyed by the Northmen, and a collegiate church now stands on that site, LXXVI, 258 note; CXXXVIII, 204.

NOVIOMENSIS CONVENT OF NUNS, founded by St. Eligius, bishop, and King Dagobert in 660, LXXXVII, 515.—St. Godebertha was its first abbess, CL, 1520.—This convent appears to have passed to monks in the twelfth century.—Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1211, CCXVI, 401; CCXVII, 264.

NOVI PORTUS S. MARIAE (Saint Mary of Porto Nuovo, Papal States), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose possessions and privileges Alexander III confirmed in 1177, CC, 1123.—Privilege of Lucius III, 1184, CCI, 1262.

NOVO BURGO (de) (Newbury, county of Berkshire, England), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, to which Innocent III granted a privilege in 1199, CCXIV, 640.—Letter of Innocent to the abbot, 1207, CCXV, 1128.

NOVO CASTRO (de) S. MARIAE (St. Mary of Neuchâtel, Switzerland), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, whose property Celestine III confirmed in 1119, CCVI, 1119.—Letters of Innocent III, 1203, CCXV, 174; CCXVI, 822; CCXVII, 176.

NOVUM MONASTERIUM. See Afflighemense, Cabilonense, Pictaviense.

NUEMBURGENSE. See St. Mary of Castro Novo.

NUGARULENSE S. NICOLAI (St. Nicholas of Nogaroulet, diocese of Auch), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, whose property and privileges Alexander III confirmed in 1169, CC, 574.

NUGUBIENSE and NURKIENSE, small houses of canons [Col. 1114], founded by the nobleman Gunnarius in the dioceses of Torres and Empúries, in the kingdom of Naples, in 1117.—Privilege of Paschal II, CLXIII, 423.

NUTSCELLENSE (Nutcell, county of Southampton, England), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, to which St. Boniface was sent as a youth for study at the beginning of the eighth century, LXXXIX, 638.

NUNDRIACENSIS (probably Néris, former diocese of Bourges, Allier), a priory whose abbot Innocent III addressed in 1203, CCXV, 222.

OBAZINAE (Obazine or Aubazine, near Brive, Corrèze), a nunnery mentioned in Innocent’s letter to the abbot of La Sauve-Majeure, 1206, CCXV, 1051.

OBERMUNSTERIENSIS S. MARIAE (St. Mary of Obermünster, diocese of Regensburg), a nunnery founded at Regensburg by Emperor St. Henry II in 1010, CXL, 289.

OBONNENSE S. MARIAE or S. MICHAELIS (St. Mary of Obonne), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in Spain by Adelgaster, son of King Silo, in 780, XCVI, 889.

OCRIENSE. See St. Damian.

OFFONIS CELLA. See Schulteranense.

OLLONA (de). See St. Christina.

OMENSE (Om, Denmark), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, transferred from a place called Dear Island; Alexander III granted it a privilege in 1174, CC, 1004.—Privilege of Urban III, 1186, CCII, 1463.

OMNIUM SANCTORUM IN NIGRA SILVA (All Saints Abbey in the Black Forest, diocese of Strasbourg), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, to which Innocent III granted a privilege in 1204, CCXVII, 103.

ONIENSE, or DE ONIA SILVAE (Abbey of the Forest of Heugne, diocese of Bourges), a monastery founded by St. Abbot Ursus around 500, LXX, 1085.

ONIENSE S. SALVATORIS (St. Saviour of Oña, diocese of Burgos, Spain), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by King Sancho; its governance was entrusted to St. Odilo, abbot of Cluny, in the eleventh century, CXLII, 857.—Privilege of Innocent III, 1210, CCXVI, 249, 250.

ORATORIO (de) S. MARIAE (Our Lady of Loroux or Louroir, former diocese of Angers), a monastery of the Cistercian Order built by Fulk, count of Anjou, in 1121.—Charter of Henry II, king of England, 1175, CCVII, 1161.—Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1207, CCXV, 1122.

ORATORIO (de) S. EBRULFI or S. ANGARISMAE (Oroër, diocese of Beauvais), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, first dedicated in honour of St. Ebrulf (St. Evre), then of St. Angarisme; it is mentioned in the testament of St. Ansegisus, abbot of Fontenelle, 833, CV, 745.

ORBACENSE S. PETRI (St. Peter of Orbaix, diocese of Soissons), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by St. Reolus or Reulus (St. Rigule), archbishop of Rheims, in 680.—The monk Gottschalk here recanted his heresy in 868, CXXI, 345.

ORBIONENSE or URBIONENSE. See Crassense.

ORDORFENSE S. MICHAELIS (St. Michael of Ordorf, diocese of Mainz), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict founded by St. Boniface, bishop of Mainz, about 740, LXXIX, 646; CXIX, 686.

ORGANO (in) S. MARIAE. See the Veronese nunnery.

ORICOLI (S.) DE SENUCO (St. Oriol of Senuc, near Grandpré, Ardennes), a small monastery subject to St. Remigius of Rheims, whose prior was Robert, formerly abbot of St. Remigius. Letter of Pope Calixtus II, 1122, CLXIII, 1247.

ORIENTII (S.) AUSCIENSE (St. Orientius of Auch) was originally merely a church in which St. Orientius, bishop, was buried; later an abbey, bearing the same abbot’s name, was attached to it, sixth century, LXXI, 907.—It passed to the Cluniacs and became a simple priory.—Privilege of Pope St. Leo IX, 1154, CXLIII, 743.—Letter of Alberic, bishop of Ostia, concerning the agreement between this monastery and the bishop of Auch, 1100, CLV, 1631.—Privilege of Paschal II, 1104, CLXIII, 132.

ORTEGA DE S. JOANNIS (St. John of Ortega, diocese of Burgos, Spain), a monastery on whose behalf Innocent III wrote in 1210, CCXVI, 254.

ORTICARIENSE S. MICHAELIS (St. Michael of Orticaria, in the Pisan territory, Tuscany), a Camaldolese monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, to which Pope Clement III granted a privilege in 1188, CCIV, 1282.

OSENSE. See Augense.

OSITHAE. See Chusense.

OSPELLENSE S. SILVESTRI (St. Silvester of Ospello, diocese of Foligno, Umbria), a Camaldolese monastery whose prior Celestine III recalled to obedience to the Camaldolese monks in 1195, CCVI, 1076.

[Col. 1115] OSTERHOLTENSE (Osterholz, diocese of Bremen), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, to which Clement III granted a privilege in 1188, CCIV, 1382.

OSTERHOLTENSIS, a nunnery apparently attached to the preceding monastery, mentioned in the same privilege of Clement III. Ibid.—Privilege of Innocent III, 1216, CCXVI, 258.

OSTERHOWENSE S. MARGARETAE (St. Margaret of Osterhofen, Bavaria), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, formerly built by St. Firmin under Duke Otto, later restored by Odo, bishop of Bamberg, in 1110; and in 1127 it passed to the Premonstratensians, CLXXIII, 1282.—Privilege of Eugenius III, 1146, CLXXX, 1167.

OSWALDI (S.) BARDENIENSE, a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in the diocese of Lincoln, to which Bishop Hugh made many gifts in 1200, CLIII, 1118.

OTHMARSHEIMENSIS S. MARIAE (Our Lady of Othmarsheim, Alsace), a nunnery built by the nobleman Rudolf under Pope Leo VIII, tenth century.—Privilege of Eugenius III, 1153, CLXX, 1597.

OTHONIENSE (Ottenbevern, Swabia), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by King Nicholas and Bishop Hubald before 1138, when Paschal II granted it a privilege, CLXIII, 439.

PADERSBORNENSE S. MARIAE (Our Lady of Paderborn), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict situated in the suburb, to which Emperor St. Henry II granted immunities in 1023, CXL, 378.

PADERSBORNENSE SS. CHILIANI ET LIBORII, a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict built by Empress Gisela and endowed with a diploma of Emperor Conrad II in 1030, CLI, 1054, 1060.

PADERSBORNENSE SS. PETRI ET PAULI (St. Peter of Paderborn), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose rights and possessions Eugenius III confirmed in 1146, CLXXX, 1137.

PADOLIRONNENSE S. BENEDICTI (St. Benedict of Padolirone, diocese of Mantua), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in the Mantuan territory, where Blessed Simeon, canonized in the tenth century, was a monk.—Privilege of Benedict VIII, 1024, CXXXIX, 1033.—On the consecration of the church of St. Simeon the Confessor.—Privilege of Leo IX, 1051, CXLIII, 739.—Of St. Gregory VII, 1085, CXLVIII, 718.—Privilege of Urban II, 1088–1099, CLI, 527.—Privilege of Paschal II, 1107, CLXIII, 226.—Honorius subjects this monastery to Cluny, 1125, CLXVI, 1229.—Privilege of Innocent II, 1134, CLXXIX, 208.—Lucius II likewise subjects the monastery to Cluny, 1144, CLXXIX, 930.—Letter of Eugenius III concerning the monastery’s obedience to Cluny, CLXXX, 1306.—Decree of Alexander III by which the abbot of this monastery is elected from Cluny, 1166, CC, 435.—Privilege of Clement III, 1188, CCIV, 1310.—Letter of Innocent III concerning election, visitation, and correction, 1209, CCXVI, 86.

PALARIA (de). See St. Sebastian.

PALATIOLO (de) S. PETRI (St. Peter of Palatiole, Tuscany), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in Pisan territory, founded by St. Valfredus (Valfroy), a native of Lucca, in 754, LXXXVII, 1384.—Its brethren built a nunnery nearby, ibid.

PALATIOLO (de) TREVIRENSI (Palz, near Trier), a nunnery founded in 690 by Adela, daughter of Dagobert and abbess, LXXXVII, 1312.—Adela’s testament for the benefit of her monastery, 732, LXXXVIII, 1286.

PALMI (de), in the diocese of Tuy (Galicia, Spain), a monastery to which Innocent III wrote in 1213, CCXVI, 852.

PALNATUM S. SALVATORIS (St. Saviour of Pannat, diocese of Périgueux), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict built before the ninth century, governed by Abbot Adalgasius, and subsequently transferred to Vabres, CXXXIII, 710.

PANCRATII (S.) DE LEWES (St. Pancras of Lewes, county of Sussex, England), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict founded in 1077 by Count William de Warenne and his wife Gundreda.—Letter of Celestine III, 1196, CCVI, 1162.

PANCRATII (S.) (St. Pancras, Rome), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict built in Rome and mentioned by St. Gregory the Great. It is now a seminary of the Discalced Carmelites, LXXVII, 657. See among the Roman monasteries.

PANCRATII (S.) (St. Pancras, diocese of Chichester, England), a monastery formerly dependent on Cluny, mentioned in the life of Peter the Venerable, CLXXXIX, 25.—William de Warenne is named as its founder, CXCII, 1119.—For a time it had as prior Hugh, later archbishop of Rouen, ibid.

PANORMITANUM S. MARIAE (St. Mary of Palermo, [Col. 1116] Sicily), a nunnery whose tithes, conveyed by Tustin, bishop of Mazara, Alexander III confirmed in 1175, CC, 1015.

PANORMITANUM S. SPIRITUS (Monastery of the Holy Spirit, Palermo, Sicily), a monastery mentioned in Innocent III’s letter regarding the monastery of St. Mary of the Wood, subject to it, 1202, CCXIV, 1167.

PANORMITANUM S. HERMAE (St. Erme of Palermo), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, one of six monasteries built by St. Gregory the Great around 596, LXXV, 257; LXXVII, 833.

PANORMITANUM S. THEODORI (St. Theodore of Palermo), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose abbot St. Gregory the Great protected, LXXV, 300.

PAPIENSE S. JOANNIS A CIMITERIO (St. John of the Cemetery, suburb of Pavia), a monastery whose property Innocent III confirmed in 1198, CCXIV, 439.

PAPIENSE S. JUVENCI (St. Juventius of Pavia), a college of canons to whom Innocent III wrote concerning a canon specially commended by him, 1198, CCXIV, 104.

PAPIENSE S. PETRI COELI AUREI (St. Peter in the Golden Heaven), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict near Pavia in Lombardy, founded by King Liutprand shortly before 722; its property and privileges were confirmed by John XV in 986, CXXXVII, 827.—Diploma of Conrad II, 1033, CLI, 1065.—Privilege of Alexander II, 1069, CXLVI, 1353.—Privileges of Paschal II, 1102, CLXIII, 84, 148, 368.

PAPIENSE S. SALVATORIS (St. Saviour, Pavia), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict founded and endowed by Empress Adelaide near the Ticino; John XIII granted it extensive immunities in 972, CXXXV, 993, 995.—Letter of Paschal II, CLXIII, 200.—Privilege of Calixtus II, 1120, CLXIII, 1174.—Privilege of Innocent II, 1132, CLXXIX, 138.—Privilege of Eugenius III, 1145, CLXXX, 1026.—Privilege of Urban III, 1186, CCII, 1391.

PARACLITENSE S. THOMAE. See Ebleholtense.

PARACLITENSIS SS. TRINITATIS (the Paraclete or Holy Trinity, Saint-Aubin, diocese of Troyes), a nunnery founded by Peter Abelard in 1127 under Bishop Alton for Heloise and her companions, expelled from his monastery, CLXXVIII, 15.—Privileges of the Supreme Pontiffs for that nunnery, ibid., 1847.—Catalogue of the abbesses of the Paraclete, ibid., 1849.—Innocent II received it under his protection in 1131, CLXXIX, 114, 239, 569.—Privilege of Lucius II, 1144, CLXXIX, 830.—Of Eugenius III, CLXXX, 1291.—Privilege of Anastasius IV, 1153, CLXXXVIII, 1028.—Of Adrian IV, 1156, CLXXXVIII, 1448, 1529, 1539.—Of Alexander III, 1163, CC, 207.

PARASIO (de) (Paray-le-Moineau, Seine-et-Oise), a nunnery of the Cistercian Order, whose property, granted to it by Robert de Malovicino, Innocent III confirmed in 1209, CCXVI, 157.

PARCENSE S. MARIAE (Our Lady of Park, near Louvain, Belgium), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, founded in 1129 by Godfrey the Bearded, count of Flanders, and entrusted to Walter, abbot of St. Martin.—Privilege of Innocent II, 1142, CLXXIX, 602.—Letters of St. Hildegard, abbess, to Abbot Philip, CXCXIII, 271, 277.

PARCI DOMINARUM (Parc-aux-Dames, or Parc Bouille, near Crépy, Oise), a nunnery of the Cistercian Order, founded in 1205 by Eleanor, countess of St. Quentin, and King Philip Augustus.—Privilege of Innocent III, 1210, CCXVII, 204.

PARISIACENSE IN ALSACIA (Paris, diocese of Strasbourg, Alsace), a monastery of the Cistercian Order whose property and privileges Lucius III confirmed in 1185, CCI, 1339.—The monk Gunther flourished there in 1212, CCXII, 9.

PARISIENSE COLLEGIUM CANONICORUM S. MARIAE (the chapter of Notre-Dame, Paris), whose property John XVIII confirmed in 1006, CXXXIX, 483.—Charter of Stephen, bishop of Paris, 1124, CLXXIII, 1421.—Privileges of Alexander III, 1164, CC, 323, 353, 760, 998.—Peter the Chanter flourished in 1197, CCV, 9.—Certain authentic instruments of that church, 1169, CCV, 909, 910, 911.—Privilege of Celestine III, 1190, CCVI, 1168.

PARISIENSES S. OPPORTUNAE (St. Opportuna, Paris), Regular Canons whose property Adrian IV confirmed in 1159, CLXXXVIII, 1630.—Privilege of Alexander III, 1178, CC, 1185.—Of Urban III, 1187, CCII, 1479.

PARISIENSE S. PETRI (St. Peter), a monastery whose basilica was built by Clovis II and St. Clotilde and was later dedicated to St. Genevieve, 545, LXXI, 269.

PARISIENSE S. THOMAE (St. Thomas of the Louvre), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order founded by St. Norbert himself, [Col. 1117] as the privilege of Urban II relates, 1187, CCII, 1487.—Privilege of Clement III, 1189, CCIV, 1414.

PARISIENSE S. VINCENTII. See St. Germain-des-Prés. See also the monasteries of St. Denis, St. Eligius, St. Genevieve, St. Germanus of Auxerre, St. Maglorius, St. Martin-in-the-Fields, St. Marcellus, Montmartre, Holy Trinity, St. Victor, etc.

PARISIENSE SS. TRINITATIS (Monastery of the Holy Trinity, Paris), a monastery established by Brother John, whose rule Innocent III mentions and approves in 1198, CCXIV, 444.

PARMENSE S. MARIAE (St. Mary of Parma), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine whose possessions and privileges Innocent II confirmed in 1141, CLXXIX, 556.—Privilege of Eugenius III, 1146, CLXXX, 1111.

PARMENSIS S. ALEXANDRI (St. Alexander of Parma), a nunnery built before 1138, when Innocent II, at the request of the pious Abbess Agnes, granted it a privilege, 1138, CLXXIX, 357.—Privilege of Celestine III concerning the new church of St. Cecilia assigned to this monastery, 1195, CCVI, 1081; another letter of the same pope, 1219.

PARMENSE SANCTAE FELICULAE (St. Felicula or Feliciola of Parma), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, which Pope Adrian IV received under his protection in 1562.

PARMENSE S. JOANNIS (St. John of Parma), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict subject to Monte Cassino, whose possessions and rights Pope Lucius II confirmed in 1144, CLXXIX, 833.—Privilege of Eugenius III, 1145, CLXXX, 1059.—Letter of Innocent III, 1212, CCXVI, 622.

PARMENSIS S. PAULI (nuns of St. Paul, Parma), a nunnery to which Urban III subjected the nunnery of St. Mary of Castello Godo because of the nuns’ evil conduct, 1187, CCII, 1480.

PARRASIO (de). See above, PARASIO.

PARVA PONTE (de). See Brundusinum.

PASSENSE S. MARTINI (St. Martin of Pas, whose location is not specified, perhaps St. Martin of Parc, Eure), a priory of the Order of St. Augustine detached from Marmoutier and granted to St. Martin-in-the-Fields by Alexander III in 1164, CC, 318.

PASSINIANUM (Passignano, Tuscany), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict between Florence and Siena. Its prior Peter and Abbot Rusticus fled to St. John Gualbert; after entrusting their monastery to him, they lived under his direction around 1045, CXLVI, 773.—Privilege of Gregory VII, 1085, CXLVIII, 721.—Of Alexander III, 1179, CC, 1193.—Letter of Celestine III concerning the translation of St. John Gualbert, 1194, CCVI, 1033.

PASSU (de). See Dionysius.

PATAVIENSIS CANONIA (chapter of Padua), whose property and possessions Emperor Henry III confirmed in 1047, CLI, 1102.
