PATAVIENSE S. JUSTINAE (St. Justina of Padua), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded outside the city by the patrician Opilio; Emperor Henry IV confirmed its privileges, CLI, 1161.—Privilege granted by Alexander III to the abbot of this monastery, 1177, CC, 1146.

PATAVIENSIS S. PETRI (nuns of St. Peter, Padua), a nunnery which, at the request of Abbess Theophila, obtained a privilege from Pope Clement III in 1091.

PATERNIACUM (Payerne, diocese of Lausanne, Switzerland), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict built by Adelaide, wife of Emperor Henry II, and the nobleman Rudolf; rebuilt by Odilo, abbot of Cluny, on the shore of Lake Yverdon in the bishopric of Lausanne, in 1022, CXLI, 54 note; CXLII, 858, 75.

PATERNIANI (S.). See Fulignatense.

PATRICIACUM or PRINCIACUM S. EUSITII (Pressy-sur-Cher), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in the diocese of Bourges, where St. Eusitius first professed the monastic life, 531, LXXI, 890 note.—There also lived the recluse Marianus under Abbot Faterius, about 513, LXXI, 888.

PATRICII (S.) monastery. See Ynswytrinense.

PAULI (S.) NARBONNENSE (St. Paul, Narbonne), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine established before 1093.—Letter of Urban II to William, abbot of this monastery, 1093, CLI, 360.

PAULI (S.) IN CARINTHIA (the monastery of St. Paul in Carinthia, Germany), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in the diocese of Passau, once violently occupied by a certain count under Emperor Rudolf; the emperor was informed of that crime in 1279, XCVIII, 765.—Privilege of Innocent II, 1140, CLXXIX, 322.

PAULI (S.) ROMANUM. See Romanum.

PAULI (S.) IN ARGONNA (St. Paul in Argonne), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict near Verdun, restored by Bishop Wicfrid in 1131 for canons of the Premonstratensian Order.—Privilege of Calixtus, 1120, CLXIII, 1176. See Virdunense.

[Col. 1118] PAULIACENSE IN ARVERNIS appears to be the monastery in which the relics of St. Saturninus the martyr were long kept hidden, fourth century, LXXI, 750.

PAUSENSE S. MARIAE (Our Lady of Pauso, diocese of Cirenza, Naples), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in the diocese of Acerenza, endowed with a privilege of Urban II; but the instrument is apocryphal, CLI, 114, 365.

PAVILIACENSIS and PAULIACENSIS (St. Austrebertha of Pavilly, former diocese of Rouen), a nunnery founded by St. Austrebertha, abbess, in the diocese of Rouen in 650; it was later transferred near the village commonly called Montreuil-sur-Mer in the eleventh century, at the urging of Pope Urban II, letter of 1091, CLI, 335.

PEGAVIENSE (Pégan, diocese of Merseburg, Meissen), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict built shortly before 1104, when Pope Paschal II received it under his protection, CLXIII, 126.—Letters of Innocent III concerning the dispute between the bishop of Merseburg and that monastery, 1198, CCXIV, 279, 283; 1205, CCXV, 603, 645; 1210, CCXVI, 305, 871.

PENNENSE. See St. Bartholomew.

PENSAURIENSIS S. MARIAE (St. Mary of Pesaro, Papal States), a canonry whose property Celestine III confirmed in 1197, CCVI, 1217.

PENTALE, the name sometimes given to the monastery of Dol. See Dolense.

PEONENSE or PHAEONENSE, a monastery in Galicia built by St. Fructuosus in 670, LXXXVII, 1089.

PERCENSE or PERTICENSE. See Novigentum.

PEROALLO (de) S. MARIAE (St. Mary of Perallo, diocese of Genoa, Piedmont), a monastery of the Cistercian Order built before 1211, when Innocent III received it under his protection, CCXXI, 514.

PERSENIA (de) S. MARIAE (St. Mary of Perseigne, former diocese of Le Mans), a monastery of the Cistercian Order founded in 1145 by William III, count of Bellême.—Abbot Adam flourished there in 1203, CCXI, 579.—Letters of Innocent III to the abbot, 1203, CCXV, 255, 1360; CCXVI, 620.—On the reform of St. Martin of Tours, CCXVII, 109, 187.

PERSHORENSE (Pershore, diocese of Worcester, England), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in the diocese of Worcester, whose Abbot Fulbert owed his recovery to the merits of St. Oswald in 980, CXLVII, 1194.—Abbot Guy attended the council held in London by Blessed Anselm under King Henry in 1102, CLIX, 438.

PERUSINUM S. PETRI (St. Peter of Perugia), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict outside the city, whose property and rights Paschal II confirmed in 1115, CLXIII, 374.—Privilege of Innocent II, 1137, CLXXIX, 314.—Of Lucius II, 1144, CLXXIX, 828.—Privilege of Eugenius III, 1145, CLXXX, 1029.—Letter of Innocent III, 1199, CCXIV, 711.

PERUSINUM. See St. Anastasius.

PERUSINUM S. MARIAE. See Vallis Pontis.

PERUSINUM S. SALVATORIS (St. Saviour of Perugia), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, to whose abbot St. Gregory VII wrote concerning the monastery of St. Anastasius, then ruled by an unworthy abbot, 1074, CXLVIII, 375.

PETERSHAUSENSE or PETERSHUSANUM S. GREGORII (St. Gregory of Petershausen, diocese of Constance), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict on the Rhine in the diocese of Constance, built by Bishop Gebhard and subjected to Reichenau in 983; its beginnings are described, CXLIII, 306 ff.—Charter of John XVI, 989, CXLIII, 312.—Privilege of Gregory V, 323.

PETIS (de) (Petz or Pest, diocese of Veszprém, Hungary), a monastery whose abbot Innocent III addressed concerning Greek churches in 1204, CCXV, 332.

PETINGENSE (Petegem-by-Oudenaarde, Belgium), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, into which Rainald, archbishop of Rheims, introduced monks in 1130, CLXXII, 1341.

PETRAGORICENSES CANONICI (regular chapter of Périgueux), whose abbot was the bishop himself and whose patron was St. Front. In 1104 they granted to Blessed Robert of Arbrissel, for the support of the nuns of Fontevraud, a portion of the forest of Eadun, called Salvitas, CLXII, 1093.

PETRI (S.) or AEGIDII NEMAUSENSE (St. Peter, and more commonly St. Giles of Nîmes), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict founded by Blessed Aegidius before 886.—Letter of Adrian III, 886, CXXVI, 974.—Privilege of Urban II, 1095, CLI, 425.—Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1202, CCXIV, 1053.

PETRI (S.). See Aurea Valle.

PETRI (S.) DE LANDELINA (St. Peter of Landelin, diocese of Foligno, Umbria), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict [Col. 1119], founded in 1153 by the counts of Monaldo and Rudolf son of Lambert, who granted it to the bishop of Foligno.—Privilege of Anastasius IV, CLXXXVIII, 1043.

PETRI (S.) AD MONTES or DE MONTIBUS (St. Peter-aux-Monts, diocese of Châlons-sur-Marne), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict founded by Bishop Robert I in 1028. Decree of Alexander III, 1172, CC, 775.

PETRI (S.) MONASTERIUM (St. Peter-le-Moûtier, diocese of Nevers), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict built about 840.—Letter of Innocent III to the abbot concerning the subjection of the monastery of Menat, disputed between the bishop of Clermont and the Cluniacs, 1213, CCXVI, 965.

PETRI (S.) DE MONTIBUS (St. Peter of the Mountains, diocese of Alcalá), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in the district of Complutum, Spain, founded by St. Fructuosus in 640; St. Valerius was its abbot, LXXXVII, 417, and it was restored by Abbot Gennadius in the eleventh century, ibid.

PETRI (S.) DE MONTE (St. Peter of the Mount, diocese of Metz), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order founded in 1090 by Matilda, daughter of Boniface, duke of Lorraine.—Decree of Adrian IV concerning the wearing of the surplice, 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1372.

PETRI (S.) DE REGULA (St. Peter of La Réole, former diocese of Lescar, Béarn), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict built in 977 and assigned to the bishop of Lescar by Paschal II in 1114, CLXIII, 355.

PETRI (S.) PUELLARIS (St. Peter-le-Puellier, diocese of Poitiers), a nunnery founded by the noblewoman Monegundis, who was its first abbess, LXXI, 1087.—It later passed to the secular canons of St. Martin of Tours, ibid., 1089 note.

PETRI (S.) IN PIXIDE (St. Peter-au-Bassin, diocese of Florence), a monastery whose abbot Innocent III addressed in 1206, CCXV, 973.

PETRI (S.) IN CAMPO (St. Peter del Campo, diocese of Chieti, Naples), a monastery in the diocese of Chieti, mentioned in a privilege of Innocent III, 1208, CCXVII, 180.

PETRI (S.) COELI AUREI. See Papiense.

PETRI (S.) DE CELLARIA (St. Peter of Cellaria, Lombardy), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict subject to the monastery of St. Mary at Pulsano; mentioned in the privilege of Alexander III, 1177, CC, 1097.

PETRI (S.) DE VALERIIS (St. Peter-les-Vallières, diocese of Narbonne), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict built by the nobleman Rainard Amatus before 1114, when Paschal II endowed it with a privilege, CLXIII, 360.

PETRI (S.) MILIONNENSIS (St. Peter of Melun), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict rebuilt from its foundations by Seguin, archbishop of Sens, in 999, CXLII, 772.

PETRI (S.) VIVI (St. Peter-le-Vif, diocese of Sens), a nunnery built by Queen Theodechild about 564, LXXI, 290.—The nun Ingoara bestowed many goods upon it in 711, LXXXVIII, 1258.—Diploma of Louis the Pious, 822, CIV, 1111.—When it lay almost ruined, it was restored in the tenth century by Archbishop Seguin, who introduced monks there in 999.—Odorannus flourished there in 1048, CXLII, 766, 773.—Letter of Hugh, bishop of Lyons, to the archbishop of Sens, 1099, CLVII, 522.—Letter of Cardinal Cono to the bishop of Langres for Abbot Arnald, 1119, CLXIII, 1437.—Writings of Abbot Arnald, 1473.—On St. Abbo, abbot and later bishop, eighth century, CLXXXV, 1397.

PETRI (S.). See Cabilonense, Carnotense, Gandense, Eugubinense, Faventinum, Florentinum, Heisterbacense, Mellicense, Mutinense, Padersbornense, Papiense, Viennense, and many others besides.

PETRIBURGENSE (Petersbury, England), a celebrated monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, to which King Edward made many grants and whose rights and possessions William the Conqueror confirmed in 1081, CXLIX, 1333.—Privileges of Eugenius III, 1146, CLXXX, 1160, 1163.

PETRONILLAE (S.) DE DUOBUS CASTELLIS (St. Petronilla of the Two Castles, diocese of Poreč, Italy), a monastery discussed in a privilege of Alexander III, 1177, CC, 1101.

PETROSA (de) SANCTAE MARIAE (Our Lady of Peyrouse, diocese of Périgueux), a monastery of the Cistercian Order built in 1153; its abbot is the subject of a question in Innocent III’s letter of 1207, CCXV, 1101.

PHALEMPINO (de) S. CHRISTOPHORI (St. Christopher of Phalempin, Pas-de-Calais), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine built shortly before 1110 by Count Roger and his wife Ogiva, when Paschal II granted it a privilege, CLXIII, 270.—Privilege of Alexander III, 1159, CC, 110.

PHARENSIS PARTHENON: for **FARENSE**, which see.

PHYUTWANGENSE S. SALVATORIS (St. Saviour of Phyutwangen, diocese of Augsburg, Bavaria), a monastery [Col. 1120] of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by Wigo, dean and abbot, and entrusted to Empress Adelaide in 970, CXXXVII, 9.

PICTAVIENSE S. HILARII (St. Hilary of Poitiers), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, which Pope St. Gregory VII endowed with privileges in 1074, CXLVIII, 651.—Letter of Innocent III, 1311, CCXVI, 445.

PICTAVIENSIS SS. TRINITATIS (Holy Trinity of Poitiers), a nunnery whose Abbess Elizabeth received a privilege from Calixtus II in 1119, CLXIII, 1119.

PICTAVIENSIS S. CRUCIS (Convent of Holy Cross, Poitiers), a nunnery founded and endowed by St. Radegund after, as a deaconess, she received the veil from the hands of St. Medard at Noyon in 535, LXXI, 522; LXXII, 655.—Privilege of Urban II, 1090, CLI, 328.

PICTAVIENSIS S. RADEGUNDIS (St. Radegund of Poitiers), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict built in the sixth century by Blessed Queen Radegund.—Letter of Innocent III to the prior, 1212, CCXVI, 798.

PICTAVIENSE S. CYPRIANI (St. Cyprian, near Poitiers), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict built by King Pippin in 838 and rebuilt in 931 in the suburb beside the river Clain.—Privilege of John XI, 931, CXXXII, 1062.—Likewise, of Urban II, 1093, CLI, 368, 369.

PICTAVIENSE SS. JOANNIS, SIMONIS ET JUDAE (the New Monastery, or St. John of Poitiers), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict founded in the suburb of that city by the pious William, count of Poitiers, and later subjected by the same man to Cluniac governance.—Privilege of Pope St. Gregory VII, CXLVIII, 666.—Privilege of Urban II, by which he granted it the church of St. Nicholas built by Countess Agnes, 1093, CLI, 367.—Privilege of the same pope, CLI, 461.—Decree of Innocent, 1211, CCXVI, 542.

PIGAVIENSE. See above, Pegaviense.

PILLERENSE S. SALVATORIS (St. Saviour of Pillero), a monastery in Italy whose location is not stated.—Privilege of Innocent III, 1203, CCXV, 50.

PINEROLENSE S. MARIAE (Our Lady of Pinerolo, Savoy), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict founded in Savoy by Countess Adelaide, which Pope St. Gregory VII endowed with privileges in 1083, CXLVIII, 705.—Privilege of Pope Calixtus II, 1122, CLXIII, 1261.

PINETA (de) S. MARIAE (St. Mary of Pineta, Tuscany), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine whose property and privileges Adrian IV confirmed in 1156, CLXXXVIII, 1481.

PINETUM (Convent of Pineto, in the Roman countryside), a very ancient monastery in Roman territory, made illustrious by Macarius and Rufinus at the end of the fourth century, XXI, 116.

PINCHONIO (de) HOSPITALIS DOMUS DEI (Hospitaller Brothers of the House of God; Hôtel-Dieu of Picquigny, Somme).—Privilege of Innocent III, 1212, CCXVII, 216.

PINNA (de), a monastery in the diocese of Genoa, mentioned in a letter of Adrian IV, 1155, CLXXXVIII, 1443.

PINNA (de) S. JOANNIS, a monastery in Spain restored by King Sancho and endowed with a privilege by Pope Alexander II in 1071, CXLVI, 1362.—Letter of Urban II to the abbot concerning the tithes of St. Saturninus, which were not to be taken away, 1094, CLI, 374.

PINU (de) S. MARIAE (Our Lady of the Pine, diocese of Poitiers), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, built in 1120–1141 by Giraldus de Salis.—Letter of Innocent III, 1208, CCXV, 1360.

PIRO (de) S. PETRI (St. Peter of Poirier, in the county of Treviso), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, to which Emperor St. Henry II granted a privilege in 1017, CXL, 335.

PISANUM S. MICHAELIS (St. Michael of Verruca, near Pisa), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict which Pope St. Gregory VII took under his protection and whose possessions he confirmed by privilege in 1077, CXLVIII, 681.—Privilege of Adrian IV, 1155, CLXXXVIII, 1436.—Of Innocent III, 1209, CCXVI, 187.

PISANUM S. ZENONIS (St. Zeno of Pisa), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict whose property and rights Pope Gregory VII confirmed by privilege in 1080, CXLVIII, 698.

PISANUM S. MARIAE (St. Mary of Pisa), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine whose property John XVIII confirmed by privilege in 1007, CXXXIX, 1486.—Privilege of Victor II, 1055, CXLIII, 812.—Of Pope Alexander II, 1062, CXLVI, 1283.—Of Innocent II, 1137, CLXXIX, 321.—Of Anastasius IV, 1153, CLXXXVIII, 989.—Letter of Adrian IV, 1161, CLXXXVIII, 998.—Letters of Alexander III, [Col. 1121] 1168, CC, 556, 561, 663, 1052.—Privilege of Urban III, 1186, CCII, 1445.

PISCARIENSE (S.) CLEMENTIS (St. Clement of Pescara, kingdom of Naples), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built under Leo IX, whose rights and possessions Calixtus II confirmed in 1121, CLXIII, 1201.—Privilege of Adrian IV, 1159, CLXXXVIII, 1625.—Of Alexander III, 1166, CC, 409, 558, 682, 866, 1235, 1286.—Of Celestine III, 1191, CCVI, 881.

PISINO (de) S. MICHAELIS (St. Michael of Pisino, diocese of Poreč, Italy), a monastery mentioned in a privilege of Alexander III, 1177, CC, 1101.

PISTORIENSE S. ANGELI (St. Angelo of Pistoia), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict mentioned in the charter of the priest Aivaldus, eighth century, LXXXVII, 1430.—Rebuilt, the same monastery joined the Vallombrosan congregation about 1074, CXLVI, 806.—Privilege of Clement III, 1183, CCIV, 1292.—Likewise, of Innocent III, 1211, CCXVI, 554.

PISTORIENSE S. BARTHOLOMAEI (St. Bartholomew of Pistoia), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, to which various donations were made from 748 to 784, LXXXVII, 1430, 1432, 1439, 1441.—Diploma of Charlemagne under Abbot Adalard, 812, XCVII, 1046.

PISTORIENSE (another monastery at Pistoia), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine. At the request made by Abbot Hugh, Pope Urban II granted it a privilege confirming its rights and possessions in 1094, CLI, 390.—Privilege of Eugenius III, 1151, CLXXX, 1480.—Of Anastasius IV, 1153, CLXXXVIII, 1032.—Of Alexander III, 1174, CC, 999.—Of Lucius III, CCI, 1347.

PISTOIA, ST PETER’S (Saint-Pierre de Pistoia): a hospital for nuns, founded by Ratefrid, son of Gulichisius, in the reign of Rachis, in 748, LXXXVII, 1377.—The same institution seems to have been rebuilt by the canons of the same city for the use of pilgrims.—Privilege of Urban II, 1090, CLI, 317.

PISTOIA, SS PETER AND PAUL (Nuns of Saint-Pierre, near Pistoia): a convent for women outside the city, founded by the same Ratefrid in 748, LXXXVII, 1380. See the preceding entry.

PIACENZA, ST ANTONINUS (Saint-Antoine de Plaisance): monastery of the Order of St Augustine, to which Innocent II granted a privilege at the request of Azo, provost, in 1132, CLXXIX, 148.—The canons of St Antoninus carried on litigation with the Greater Church; Innocent wrote concerning its settlement, 1133, CLXXIX, 403.—Privilege of Eugenius III, 1148, CLXXX, 1361.—Alexander III, 1159, CC, 132.—Lucius III, 1182, CCI, 1126.—Urban III, 1187, CCII, 1485.

PIACENZA, OF MERCY (Brothers Hospitallers of Mercy, at Piacenza).—A hospital whose possessions and privileges Pope Anastasius IV confirmed, 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1062.

PIACENZA, ST MARY AND ST JUSTINA (Saint Mary or Saint Justina of Piacenza): monastery of the Order of St Augustine, which Calixtus II confirmed by privilege at the request of Bishop Arduino, 1126, CLXVI, 1253.—Privileges of Innocent II, 1132, CLXXIX, 152, 230.

PIACENZA, ST SIXTUS (Saint-Sixte, at Piacenza): a convent for women or hospital, which later became a monastery of men, founded by the Empress Angilberga about 876, according to a privilege granted to it by Pope John VIII in 877, CXXVI, 737, 821.—She entrusted that monastery to Gisulf, abbot of St Christina, in 880.—Privilege of Adrian III, 884, CXXVI, 971.—Diploma of Emperor Conrad II, 1038, CLI, 1074.—Privilege of Paschal II, 1115, CLXIII, 390.—Of Innocent II, 1131, CLXXIX, 146.—Privilege of Anastasius IV concerning the use of the mitre by the abbot of St Sixtus, 1153, CLXXXVIII, 1026.—Decree of Adrian IV settling a dispute between the monks and the bishop of Lodi, 1157, CLXXXVIII, 1490.—Privilege of Urban III, 1185, CCII, 1353.—Of Celestine III, 1192, CCVI, 922.

PIACENZA, ST SABINUS or SAVINUS (Saint-Sabin or Savin of Piacenza): monastery of the Order of St Benedict, built by Bishop Sigefrid and entrusted to Abbot Winpert, with a privilege of Pope Benedict VIII, 1024, CXXXIX, 1632.—Letter of St Gregory VII concerning the election of an abbot, 1074, CXLVIII, 382.—Of Pope Paschal II, 1101, CLXII, 62.—Letter of Innocent II, 1143, CLXXIX, 630.—Alexander III, 1173, CC, 905, 1054.—Decree of Urban III, 1187, CCII, 1478.

PIACENZA, HOLY SEPULCHRE (Saint-Sépulcre de Plaisance): monastery of the Order of St Augustine, built by Dionysius, bishop of Piacenza, before 1186, when Urban III confirmed it by privilege, CCII, 1465.

PIACENZA, ST BENEDICT [Col. 1122] (Saint-Benoît de Plaisance): monastery of the Order of St Benedict and of Vallombrosa, to which Eugenius III granted a confirming bull, 1149, CLXXX, 1411.—Decree of Celestine III, 1195, CCVI, 1065.

PLANA SILVA (Plène-Selve or Saint-Geniès de la Plaine, diocese of Bordeaux): monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, built in 1148 by Geoffrey, bishop of Bordeaux.—Letter of Innocent III, 1204, CCXV, 300.

PLORIZANO, ST FIRMUS (Saint-Firme of Plorizano, diocese of Bergamo): convent for women, whose possessions and privileges Anastasius IV confirmed, 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1046.

PODIA. ST MARY AT PODIA (Notre-Dame de la Puye, between Chauvigny and Les Angles, in Poitou): monastery founded by St Robert of Arbrissel and subject to the abbey of Fontevraud; it was entrusted by him to Peter, bishop of Poitiers, together with the other monasteries which he had established, 1115, CLXII, 1072, 1087.—Charter of donation of land at Podia, CLXII, 1096.—Perhaps identical with the church of Roffiac, 1092.

POELDEN (Sankt Pölten or Saint-Hippolyte, Lower Austria): monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, formerly of the Order of St Benedict, whose possessions and privileges Innocent II confirmed, 1153.

POJI, SS MICHAEL AND EUSEBIUS (Saint-Michel de Poji, diocese of Florence): monastery of the Order of St Augustine in the diocese of Florence, whose possessions Pope Nicholas II confirmed by privilege, 1069, CXLIII, 1330.

POLLING (Polling, diocese of Augsburg in Bavaria): monastery of the Order of St Augustine. Formerly a convent for women, founded in the eighth century and restored by Bishop Walter, who at the same time granted it to regular canons.—Privilege of Innocent II, 1136, CLXXIX, 207.

POLIGNY, HOLY SAVIOUR or ST NICHOLAS (Poligny in Franche-Comté): ancient monastery of the Order of St Benedict, handed over by Rudolf, king of Burgundy, to St Odilo, abbot of Cluny, 1029, CLI, 1024.

POMARIO. See BAUMGARTEN.

POMPOSA ISLAND, ST MARY (Sainte-Marie de Pomposa, diocese of Ravenna): monastery of the Order of St Benedict, whose possessions and privileges St Leo IX upheld, 1052, CXLIII, 695.—Privilege of Calixtus II, 1124, CLXIII, 1328.—Of Anastasius IV, 1153, CLXXXVIII, 1048.—Of Adrian IV, 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1401.—Of Celestine III, 1192, CCVI, 958.

POMPOSA, ST AURELIAN: monastery of the Order of St Benedict in the territory of Comacchio and the diocese of Ravenna, whose first foundations appear to have been laid by St Aurelian, bishop, about 460, CVI, 567, 570.—Letter of St Peter Damian, CXLIX, 388.—Likewise of Benedict VIII, 1022, CXXXIX, 1626.—Letter of Innocent III concerning correction of the abbot’s corrupt life, 1199, CCXIV, 820.

PONGARTENBERG, ST MARY (Notre-Dame de Pongartenberg on the Enns, Upper Austria): Cistercian monastery built before 1151, when Eugenius III confirmed its possessions by privilege, CLXXX, 1478.—It is the same as Baumgarten or Baumgartenberg, otherwise called Pomarium. See Baumgartenberg.

PONTELEUVA, ST MARTIN. See MARTIN.

PONTIANUS, ST. See LUCENSE.

PONTIDA, ST JAMES (Saint-Jacques de Pontidio, diocese of Bergamo in the Milanese): monastery of the Order of St Benedict, built by Blessed Albert, a Cluniac monk, who was its first abbot, in 1087; Blessed Liprand, priest of Milan, died there in 1095, CLXXIII, 1490, 1492.—Order of Adrian IV concerning the payment of tithes, 1153, CLXXXVIII, 1386.—Urban III, 1186, CCII, 1360.

PONTLEVOY (formerly in the diocese of Chartres): monastery of the Order of St Benedict, built by Gildan of Chaumont in 1034 and confirmed under King Philip I in 1075.—There the archdeacon and other priests, deputed by Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, suffered grave injury on account of the election of an abbot, CLXXIII, 1413.—Privilege of Pope Lucius II, 1143, CLXXIX, 852.

PONTIUS, ST: monastery of the Order of St Benedict at the foot of Mount Cemelus (Cimiez), founded by Charlemagne in 777; his grandson Siagrius was its first abbot. This monastery is mentioned in the notes on Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 379.—Letter of Innocent III, 1203, CCXV, 272.

ST PONS OF THOMIÈRES (Saint-Pons de Thomières, Hérault): monastery of the Order of St Benedict, built by Raymond, count of Toulouse, in 936.—Privilege of Pope Urban, 1089, CLI, 54, 302.—Letter of the same pope to Abbot Frothard, CLI, 315.

PONTIGNY, ST MARY (Sainte-Marie de Pontigny, diocese of Auxerre): celebrated monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded in 1114 by Thibaut IV, count of Champagne, under Bishop Humbald and on an allod of Canon Hildebert; its abbot was Hugh of Mâcon, [Col. 1123] 1151, CLXXIX, 614.—Privilege of Innocent II, 1139, CLXXIX, 412, 614.—Of Adrian IV, 1157, CLXXXVIII, 1500.—The monk Roger wrote the Life of Blessed Thomas in the twelfth century, CXC, 55.—Privileges and letter of Alexander III, 1159, CC, 85, 368.—Thomas, driven from his see, withdrew to this monastery in 1166, CC, 414.—Privilege of Alexander III, 1166, CC, 85.

PONTINIACUM for MONTINIACUM.

PONTOISE (Pontoise, Seine-et-Oise): monastery of the Order of St Benedict, dependent upon the abbey of Bec.—Privilege of Urban II, 1089, by which it was permitted to ring bells, CSI [perhaps OCR for CLI], 52, 574.

PONTOISE, ST MELLON (Saint-Mellon de Pontoise): monastery of the Order of St Augustine, built in 899, in which St Mello, archbishop of Rouen, was buried. It is mentioned in the Life of Pope Urban II, CLI, 52.

POPOLI, ST HILARY. See GALEATA.

POBLET, ST MARY (Sainte-Marie de Poblo or Pobleto, diocese of Tarragona): Cistercian monastery founded in 1153 by Raymond Berengar, count of Barcelona.—Privilege of Alexander III, 1162, CC, 166.—Letter of Innocent III to the abbot against the bishop of Vic, 1206, CCXV, 988.

POPOLONIA, HOLY SAVIOUR AND ST QUIRICUS (Saint-Sauveur de Popolo, in the Exarchate of Ravenna): monastery of the Order of St Augustine, whose possessions and rights Celestine II confirmed, 1143, CLXXIX, 777.

PORCARIANA. See ST MICHAEL.

CHARTREUSE OF THE GATES. See CHARTREUSE.

PORTA, ST MARY (Sainte-Marie de Porta, in Saxony): Cistercian monastery originating from Morimond, founded shortly before 1137. In that year Innocent II wrote to Abbot Adelbert that hunting should not be tolerated within the precincts of the monastery, CLXXIX, 343.

PORTA ST LEONIS, ST MARY (Notre-Dame de la Porte-Saint-Léon, perhaps at Toul): monastery in defence of which Alexander III wrote to King Louis, 1164, CC, 275.

PORTA MILETI, ST ANTHONY OF CAEN (Saint-Antoine de la porte Milly at Caen): hospital of the Order of St Augustine, whose possessions and privileges Innocent III confirmed, 1210, CCXVI, 142.

ST POURÇAIN (Saint-Pourçain, diocese of Clermont): ancient monastery, built among the Auvergnats and Bourbonnais by St Porcian, abbot, about 527, LXXI, 1026.—Letter of Innocent III concerning restoration of the church of Bayu., 1206, CCXV, 902.

PORT, monastery of the Order of St Benedict (commonly Le Pont-Saint-Esprit), in the diocese of Uzès, built on the Rhône. Blessed William, who later became abbot of St-Germain-des-Prés, was its prior for some time, 1034, CXLI, 833.

PORTO (near Rome): one of the six monasteries of the Order of St Benedict built by St Gregory the Great, and devastated by a dreadful plague under that pope, about 598, LXXVII, 360.

PORTO. See RAVENNA.

PORT-ROYAL or PORROIS (Porrois, and more commonly Port-Royal-des-Champs near Paris, Seine-et-Oise): convent for women built by Odo of Sully, bishop of Paris, about 1204.—Charter by which he granted certain things to it, CCXII, 82.

PORT-SUAVI, ST MARY (Notre-Dame-du-Poussey): convent for women in the diocese of Toul, founded by Herman, bishop of Toul, and consecrated in 1049 by his successor Bruno, who later became Pope Leo IX.—Privilege of St Leo IX, CXLIII, 614.

ST POTENTIANUS OF CHÂTEAU-CENSOIR (Saint-Potentien de Château-Censoir, diocese of Auxerre): monastery of the Order of St Benedict, founded before 1157 near Vézelay.—Letter of Alexander III concerning the election of Seguin as abbot, 1172, CC, 834, 836.

PREACHING BRETHREN: originating from the diocese of Elne, founded by Bernard I in the diocese of Cremona, formerly converts from the Albigensian heresy; Innocent III confirmed their institutions in 1212, CCXVI, 289, 601, 648, 668.

ST PRAEJECTUS. See CAMBRAI.

PRÉMONTRÉ, ST MARY (Prémontré, diocese of Laon): monastery and new order founded by Blessed Norbert under the Venerable Bartholomew, bishop of Laon, in a place in the Forest of Vosges called Prémontré, in 1121; an account of its foundation is found at CLVI, 991 ff.—Privilege of Pope Honorius II, 1126, CLXVI, 1249.—Vivian, a Premonstratensian canon, flourished in 1130, CLXVI, 1319.—Life of St Norbert by an anonymous author, CLXX, 1253.—Privileges of Bartholomew, bishop of Laon, 1121, CLXX, 1359, 1362.—Privileges of Innocent II, 1131, CLXXIX, 87, 204, 384, 386, 387, 393.—Of Celestine II, 1143, CLXXIX, 778, 781.—Of Lucius [Col. 1124] II, 1144, CLXXIX, 880.—Of Eugenius III, 1145, CLXXX, 1076, 1217.—Of Adrian IV, 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1373, 1375, 1682, 1583, 1632.—Adrian the Scot flourished in 1180, CXCVIII, 31.—Letters of Alexander III, 1170, CC, 514, 620, 823, 1052, 1105, 1288.—Lucius III, 1183, CCI, 1238.—Urban III, 1187, CCII, 1486, 1488, 1520, 1521.—Clement III, 1188, CCIV, 1326, 1333, 1383.—Letters and privileges of Innocent III, 1198, CCXIV, 173, 176, 297; 1207, CCXV, 1341; CCXVII, 138.

PRAGUE, ST WENCESLAS (St Wenceslas of Prague in Bohemia): monastery of the Order of St Augustine, whose dean was Cosmas of Prague, author of the Bohemian Chronicle, 1120, CLXVI, 54.

PRAGUE, ST GEORGE (the convent of Saint-George at Prague): convent for women built by Vladislaus, duke of the Bohemians, shortly before 1145, when Eugenius III confirmed it by privilege, CLXXX, 1032.—Letter of the same pope, 1470.

PRATO, ST MARY (Sainte-Marie des Prés, near Padua): monastery of the Order of St Benedict, built by Count Maltraverso of Montebello before 1122, when Calixtus II honoured it with a privilege, CLXIII, 1243.

PRATO, ST MARY (Santa-Maria del Prato): monastery of the Order of St Benedict between Florence and Pistoia, built on the bank of the Bisenzio at the foot of Monte Acuto by Marquis Hugh; confirmed by privilege by Emperor St Henry II in 1020, CXL, 352.—Privilege of Adrian IV, 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1343.—The same pope subjects this monastery to Camaldoli, 1551.

LA PRÉE, ST MARY (Notre-Dame de la Prée-sur-Arnon, diocese of Bourges): Cistercian monastery built by Ralph of Issoudun in 1128.—Letter of Innocent III to Abbot Evrard, 1203, CCXV, 222.

PRATENSE. See ST-GERMAIN-DES-PRÉS.

PRÉAUX (diocese of Lisieux): monastery of the Order of St Benedict in Normandy, founded in the eighth century, CV, 744.—Devastated by the Northmen, it was rebuilt by the illustrious Humphrey in 1035. Richard of Du Mesnil flourished there in 1100, CLV, 1657.—Richard, abbot of Préaux, 1147, CLXVI, 1357.—On the foundation of this monastery, CCII, 1317.

DES PRÉS (Abbey of the Meadows, diocese of Besançon): monastery of the Order of St Benedict, rebuilt by monks from Boscodon, as a privilege of Alexander III reports, 1176, CC, 1077.

PRATO, ST MARY (St Mary of the Meadow, at Leicester, England): Cistercian monastery to which Innocent III commended a certain converted Jew, 1199, CCXIV, 792.

PRATO LONGO, ST MARY (Notre-Dame de Pralon, diocese of Langres): convent for women of the Order of St Benedict, founded in 1149 by Guy and Hervé of Sombernon and St Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXV, 1409.—Charter of Garner of Fontaines, 1210, CLXXXV, 1423, 1426.—Charter of Arveus of Saffra, 1449.

PRATO, ST STEPHEN (Saint-Étienne de Prato, Tuscany): monastery of the Order of St Augustine, built by Abbot Hildeprand and confirmed by Innocent II, 1133, CLXXIX, 178.—Privilege of Lucius III, 1183, CCI, 1184.

PRIFLINGEN, ST GEORGE (Saint-Georges de Prefflingen, between Regensburg and the Danube, Bavaria): monastery of the Order of St Benedict, whose abbot Herbo obtained a privilege from Innocent II, 1136, CLXXIX, 289.

PRINCIACO (Pressy-en-Berry). See PATRICIACUM.

ST PROCULUS (Saint-Procule, in the diocese of Bologna): monastery whose abbot Innocent III answers in a matrimonial matter, 1198, CCXIX, 340.

ST PROSPER. See REGGIO.

PRÜFENING, ST GEORGE (Saint-George de Prüfening, between the Danube and Regensburg): monastery of the Order of St Benedict, to which Pope Honorius II granted a privilege at the request of Otto, bishop of Bamberg, 1130, CLXVI, 1307; CLXXIII, 1279.—Privilege of Innocent II, 1139, CLXXIX, 425.—Of Eugenius III, 1146, CLXXX, 1165.—Of Adrian IV, 1159, CLXXXVIII, 1628.—Letter of Innocent III, 1210, CCXVI, 390.

PRÜFLINGEN: the same as the preceding.

PRÜLL, ST VITUS (Saint-Vite de Prüll, diocese of Regensburg): monastery of the Order of St Benedict, built in 1145 by Bishop Henry, whose first abbot was Wernher.—Privilege of Eugenius III, 1147, CLXXX, 1280.—Privilege of Innocent III, 1215, CCXVII, 249.

PRÜLL, ST BARTHOLOMEW (Saint-Barthélemy de Prüll): monastery of the Order of St Benedict, apparently founded by Emperor St Henry II in Rupert’s county, in accordance with the wish of Abbot Boniface; he granted it immunities and privileges in 1009, CXL, 283.

PRULLY, ST MARY (Notre-Dame de Prully, [Col. 1125] Seine-et-Marne): Cistercian monastery originating from Cîteaux, founded by Theobald, count of Champagne, in 1118.—Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1212, 718. Testimony of the abbot in the matrimonial case between Erard of Brienne and Philip, son of Count Henry, 1213, CCXVI, 981.

PRÜM (Prüm, diocese of Trier): monastery of the Order of St Benedict, founded in the diocese of Trier in 721 by Duchess Bertrada or Bertha, grandmother of Bertha, wife of Pippin, LXXXVIII, 1274.—Testament of King Pippin in favour of this monastery, 762, XCVI, 1545, 1546.—Charter of Aegidius, illustrious man and monk of this monastery, 764, XCVI, 1552.—Diploma of King Carloman, 770, XCVI, 1576.—Privileges of Charlemagne, 775, XCVII, 953, 1053, 1054, 1064, 1068, 1073, 1075.—Diplomas of Louis the Pious, CIV, 1035, 1058, 1098, 1120, 1122, 1158, 1192, 1254, 1265.—The monk Wandalbert flourished in 870, CXXI, 573.—Regino became abbot in 915, CXXXII, 9.—Precept of Emperor St Henry II, 1020, CXL, 354.—Of Emperor Henry III, 1056, CXL, 1123.—Privilege of Pope Innocent II, 1133, CLXXIX, 189.

PRÜM (diocese of Trier): monastery of the Order of St Augustine, founded by Virold, abbot of Prüm, and endowed with privileges by Emperor St Henry II in 1017, CXL, 337.

PROVINS, ST JAMES (Saint-Jacques de Provins, Seine-et-Marne): monastery of the Order of St Augustine, founded in 1146 by Count Henry.—Bull of Celestine III in its favour, 1193, CCVI, 1026.—Privilege of Innocent III, 1198, CCXVII, 20.

PSALMODY, ST PETER (St Pierre de Psalmodi): monastery of the Order of St Benedict in the diocese of Nîmes, built before 791. It was restored by Charlemagne, and Louis the Pious granted a privilege to its abbot Theodemir in 815, CIV, 1030.—Privilege of Urban II, 1099, CLI, 545.—Privilege of Richard, archbishop of Narbonne, to Abbot Bertrand, 1117, CLXII, 1603.—Privilege of Innocent III, 1212, CCXVI, 620.

PUELLE-MONSTIER (diocese of Reims): convent for women founded in the forest of Der by the noblewoman Matilda and St Richarius, in the diocese of Reims, not far from the monastery over which he himself presided, 680, CXXXVII, 681.

PULCHICA VALLIS (convent of Hospitaller Brothers near Magliano in the Sabine): monastery built by Peter, lord of Magliano, in 1204, to which Innocent III granted a privilege, CCXV, 328.

BEAULIEU (near Lyons): convent for women, apparently founded in the diocese of Lyons by Theotard, archdeacon of Lyons, and several other noblemen. It was given to Petronilla, abbess of Fontevraud, according to a privilege of Calixtus II, 1125, CLXIII, 1156.

IN PULSANO, ST MARY (Saint Mary called In-Pulsano, diocese of Piacenza): monastery of the Camaldolese Order, on which many other monasteries depended.—Privilege of Alexander III, 1177, CC, 1097.

POULTIÈRES: monastery of the Order of St Benedict in the diocese of Langres, founded by Gerard of Rumilly and his wife Bertha shortly before 838. Lambert was its abbot in 843, CVI, 394.—Privilege of John VIII, 879, CXXVI, 879, 880.—Letter of Pope Gregory XII [the date and papal name are inconsistent as printed] to Humbert, archbishop of Lyons, concerning this monastery, 1074, CXLVIII, 375.—On the foundation of this monastery, CLVI, 1188.—Letter of Innocent III, 1206, CCXV, 850.

PUTEI DE CHARTARIIS. See ROCCA MAGGIORE.

POUZOLLES, ST PETER (Saint-Pierre de Pouzolles): monastery of the Order of St Benedict in the territory of Lucca, founded before 1095, when Urban II granted it a bull of confirmation, CLI, 398.—Privilege of Eugenius III, 1147, CLXXX, 1193.—Letter of Celestine III, 1195, CCVI, 1078, 1079.

POZZUOLI: monastery distinguished by the name of Falcidis, annexed by St Gregory the Great to the monastery of Grattere near Naples, under the rule of Abbot Adeodatus, about 600, LXXVII, 1113.

MUDDY PUTEOLI, SS MAURICE AND MARTIN, or LITTLE MONASTERY (Montreuil): ancient monastery of the Order of St Benedict, built near Der in the diocese of Laon by St Bercharius about 680; later transformed into a distinguished Cistercian convent for women, CXXXVII, 681, 682.

QUARANTE, ST MARY (Notre-Dame de Quarante, former diocese of Narbonne): monastery of the Order of St Augustine, consecrated by Archbishop Ermengaud in 982.—Privilege of Innocent II, 1135, CLXXIX, 247.

CELL OF THE FOUR CROWNED ONES at Trier: assigned to the archbishop of Trier by Pope Benedict VII in 975, CXXXVII, 318.—Likewise by Leo IX in 1049, CXLIII, 597.—Innocent III confirms a certain agreement in 1210, CCXVI, 367.

QUEDLINBURG, CONVENT FOR WOMEN (Quedlinburg, Upper Saxony): founded by Duke Henry, commonly called the Fowler, and Queen St Matilda became its first abbess, 936, CLI, 1319 ff.—Privilege of Innocent III, 1207, CCXV, 1106.

QUEDLINBURG (Upper Saxony): monastery built by St Matilda not far from her convent for women, in the tenth century, HCLI [probably OCR corruption], 1321.—Privilege of Innocent II, 1139, CLXXIX, 1189.—Perhaps the same is treated by Eugenius III, CLXXX, 1140.—Privilege of Lucius III, 1183, CCI, 1168.—Letter of Innocent III in its favour, 1209, CCXVII, 195.

QUIMPERLÉ. See KIMPERLÉ.

QUINÇAY, ST MARY (Notre-Dame de Quinçay, Yonne): Cistercian monastery built by E. [uncertain OCR] of Rubromont and other distinguished men in 1134, when Innocent II confirmed this foundation, CLXXIX, 209.

QUINÇAY, ST BENEDICT (Saint-Benoît de Quinçay, diocese of Poitiers): monastery of the Order of St Benedict, built in 654 and rebuilt in 878.—Letter of Alexander III ordering the abbot to pay tithes to the prior of Lanariac, 1175, CC, 1032.—Testimony of the abbot in the celebrated case litigated under Innocent III between the counts of Champagne and Erard of Brienne, 1213, CCXVI, 979.

ST QUENTIN-LES-BEAUVAIS: monastery of the Order of St Augustine, built near Beauvais by Bishop Guy in 1067.—Privileges of Urban II, 1093, CLI, 116, 370.—Letter of Paschal II concerning settlement of Abbot Odo’s case, 1105, CLXIII, 180.—Privilege of Eugenius III, 1147, CLXXX, 1245.—Of Clement III, 1189, CCIV, 1450.—Decree of Innocent III against promising benefices which are not vacant, 1211, CCXVI, 404, 414.

ST QUENTIN IN VERMANDOIS or OF THE MOUNT (Saint-Quentin-en-Vermandois, otherwise Saint-Quentin du Mont near Péronne): monastery of the Order of St Augustine, whose dean was Dudo, author of the *Deeds of the Norman People*, 1026, CXLI, 605.—Bull of Gregory in a Roman council, 1044, CXLII, 575.—Chronology of the abbots of St Quentin, CLVI, 1117.—Letter of Cono, 1115, CLXIII, 1433.—Letters of Alexander III, 1169, CC, 530, 896, 1046, 1047.—Lucius III, 1182, CCI, 1130.—Celestine III, 1195, CCVI, 1101.

ST QUIRICUS OF ROSES (Saint-Cyr-aux-Roses, in the Milanese): monastery of the Camaldolese Order, whose possessions Eugenius III confirmed, 1150, CLXXX, 1466.

ST QUIRICUS OF RIETI (Saint-Cyr de Riéti, Italy): monastery of the Order of St Benedict, whose goods had been taken by the Joseppingi; St Gregory VII orders that they be restored to it, 1074, CXLVIII, 341.

ST QUIRINUS. See TEGERNSEE.

ST QUITERIA. See ARDURENSE.

RACEBURG (Racembourg in Bavaria): monastery of the Order of St Augustine, built by Henry, duke of Bavaria and Saxony, shortly before 1158, when Adrian IV confirmed it by privilege, CLXXXVIII, 1530.

RADEFORD. See ST CUTHBERT.

ST RADEGUND. See POITIERS.

RADESDORF, ST JOHN THE BAPTIST AND ST CECILIA (Saint-Jean-Baptiste de Radesorf, on the Reder in Meissen): monastery of the Order of St Augustine, whose possessions Clement III confirms by privilege, 1189, CCIV, 1456.—Privilege of Celestine III, 1191, CCVI, 867.

READING (county of Berkshire, England): monastery of the Order of St Benedict, built by King Henry I in 1126, where two hundred monks lived under the Rule.—Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1205, CCXV, 740, 1115.

REUIL, ST PETER (Saint-Pierre de Reuil, diocese of Meaux): monastery of the Order of St Benedict, built in the seventh century and subsequently made subject to Cluny.—Privilege of Lucius III, 1184, CCI, 1280.—The monk Thomas flourished at the beginning of the thirteenth century, CCIX, 1007.

ST RAGNIBERT. See JURA.

RAITENBUCH, in Bavaria: monastery of the Order of St Augustine, founded by Duke Welf and his wife, and taken under Urban II’s protection in 1090.—Privilege of Eugenius III, 1150, CLXXX, 1429.—Alexander III, 1173, CC, 1022.

RAITTENHASELACH (abbey of Raittenhaselach, diocese of Salzburg): Premonstratensian monastery built by Bishop Conrad shortly before 1146, when Eugenius [Col. 1127] III confirmed it by privilege, CLXXX, 1186.—Privilege of Lucius III, 1185, CCI, 1338.—Of Celestine III, 1195, CCVI, 1072.

RAMSEY (Ramsay or Ramsée, England): monastery of the Order of St Benedict in Huntingdonshire, founded by St Oswald, bishop, in 972. Bridfert, disciple of Abbo, flourished there in 1008, CXXXIX, 1423.—The beginnings of this monastery are described, CLXVII, 1193.—Abbot Ealdwine attended the Council of London held under St Anselm and King Henry in 1102, CLIX, 430.

RAMSLOH (in the principality of Celle): monastery of the Order of St Augustine, on behalf of whose abbot Clement III wrote in 1188, CCIV, 1381.

RANDAN: monastery of the Order of St Benedict among the Auvergnats, made famous by the pious priest Justin in the time of Gregory of Tours, about 571, LXXI, 295.

RANINGEN: a cell given by Hugh of Longue-Eau to the Cluniacs, whose possession Pope St Leo IX confirmed to Hugh of Cluny in 1050, CXLIII, 658.

RASBACH. See RESBACH.

RASPENBERG (Raspemberg or Rapserg in Saxe-Weimar): monastery whose abbot cultivated the outstanding piety of Blessed Hildegard, CXCVII, 367.

RANSHOFEN, ST PANCRAS (Saint-Pancrace de Rantzow, in Holstein): monastery of the Order of St Augustine, whose rights and possessions Eugenius III confirmed in 1147, CLXXX, 1201.—Adrian IV likewise granted a privilege at the request of Henry, duke of Bavaria, 1158, CLXXXVIII, 1156.—Privilege of Celestine III, 1195, CCVI, 1091.

RASTEDT, ST MARY (Sainte-Marie de Rastedt, near Oldenburg): monastery of the Order of St Benedict, built by Count Huno and his wife Willa before 1124, when Calixtus confirmed it by privilege, CLXIII, 1324.—Privilege of the antipope Anacletus, CLXXIX, 692.

REGENSBURG, ST MARY (Canons of Our Lady at Regensburg): their possessions were confirmed by Lucius III in 1185, CCI, 1336.

REGENSBURG, LOWER MONASTERY, ST MARY (Le Bas-Moutier): convent for women founded by the Empress Judith; at the request of Abbess Oda, St Henry took it under his protection in 1002, CXL, 242.—Another privilege of the same emperor, 260.—The abbess commended herself to the prayers of St Hildegard in the twelfth century, CXCVII, 323.

REGENSBURG, ST JAMES (the convent of the Scots of St James at Regensburg): monastery of the Order of St Benedict, whose rights and possessions Eugenius III confirmed by privilege in 1148, CLXXX, 1378.—Privilege of Adrian IV, 1157, CLXXXVIII, 1494.—Of Alexander III, 1177, CC, 1094.—Of Lucius III, 1185, CCI, 1349.—Of Celestine III, 1144 [probably an erroneous year as printed], CCVI, 1059.

REGENSBURG, ST PETER: monastery of the Order of St Augustine, whose possessions Eugenius III confirmed by privilege in 1145, CLXXX, 1078.—Privilege of Lucius III, 1183, CCI, 1200.

REGENSBURG, ST JOHN: college of canons, founded in 1127.—Privilege of Urban III, 1186, CCI, 1418.

REGENSBURG, ST MAGNUS. See ST MAGNUS OF SALZBURG.

RAWENGIRSBURG (Rauschenbourg, Alsace): monastery of the Order of St Augustine, built by the nobleman Bertulf and his wife Aldewide shortly before 1139, when Innocent II honoured it with a privilege, CLXXIX, 491.

RAVENNA, ST MARY IN PORT (Sainte-Marie du Port, diocese of Forlimpopoli, Exarchate of Ravenna): monastery of the Order of St Augustine, to which Paschal granted a privilege in 1114, CLXIII, 357.—The same pope imposed a rule drawn up by a certain canon Peter, 1116, CLXIII, 414.—Peter de Honestis flourished there in 1119, 689.—Privilege of Honorius II, 1125, CLXVI, 1234.—Of Innocent II, 1138, CLXXIX, 378.—Privilege of Adrian IV, 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1393.—Of Celestine III, 1191, CCVI, 867, 1059, 1165.

RAVENNA, BLESSED THEODORE THE DEACON (Saint-Theodore de Ravenne): monastery of the Order of St Benedict, founded by Theodore the exarch not far from the monastery of St Martin, about 680, CVI, 684.

RAVENNA, ST JOHN THE EVANGELIST (Saint-Jean de Ravenne): monastery of the Order of St Benedict, founded and endowed by archbishops, which Eugenius III adorned with a privilege in 1145, CLXXX, 1077.

RAVENNA, ST ANDREW (Saint-André de Ravenne): [Col. 1128] monastery built by St Peter Chrysologus, bishop, beside the Tricolitan church, about 450, CXI, 557, 566.

RAVENNA, ST ANDREW (Saint-André de Ravenne): convent for women of the Order of St Benedict, whose possessions and rights Alexander III confirmed in 1177, CC, 1125.

RAVENNA, ST ZECHARIAH (Saint-Zacharie): monastery of the Order of St Benedict, founded near the church of the Holy Cross in the fifth century by Singledia, niece of the Empress Galla Placidia, mother of Valentinian, CVI, 536.

RAVENNA, ST ADELBERT (Saint-Adelbert, diocese of Ravenna): monastery for whose reform Innocent III wrote to Archbishop Hugbald, 1209, CCXVI, 24.

RAVENNA, ST PETRONILLA (Sainte-Petronille): ancient monastery, built beside the church of the Holy Apostles, in which St Florentius, bishop, was buried at the end of the fourth century, CVI, 506.

RAVENNA, ST SEVERUS (Saint-Sévère): monastery of the Order of St Benedict, built or restored by Peter the Elder in 578, CVI, 635.—Privilege of Lucius III, 1183, CCI, 1249.

RAVENNA, ST BARTHOLOMEW (Saint-Barthélemy de Ravenne): monastery of the Order of St Benedict, whose abbot was Agnellus, called Andrew, in 842, CVI, 442; later Maurus, who dared to resist the pope, CVI, 670, 674.—There was another monastery of St Bartholomew at Ravenna within the walls, ibid.

RAVENNA, ST VITALIS (Saint-Vital de Ravenne): ancient monastery founded by St Ecclesius, bishop, and Julian the Banker, about 480, CVI, 584.—Privilege of Adrian IV, 1157, CLXXXVIII, 1495.

RAVENNA, ST PETER IN CHAINS (Saint-Pierre-aux-Liens at Ravenna): monastery whose possessions and privileges Pope Lucius III confirmed, 1181, CCI, 1071.

RAVENNA, ST PULLIO (Saint-Pollio de Ravenne): very ancient monastery founded not far from the gate called New Gate, in which St Liberius, bishop, was buried about the end of the fourth century, CVI, 506.

RAVENNA, ST MARTIN (Saint-Martin de Ravenne): monastery founded by King Theodoric in the fifth century; later called St Apollinaris and inhabited by different monks, LXXI, 627; CVI, 619, 620, 740.

RAVENNA, ST NAZARIUS (Saint-Nazaire de Ravenne): monastery in which Galla Placidia, mother of Emperor Valentinian, was buried in 450, CVI, 537.

RAVENNA, SS STEPHEN, GERVASIUS, AND PROTASIUS (Saint-Gervais-et-Protais de Ravenne): convent for women built by the architect Lauricius under Emperor Honorius in 450, CVI, 52, 605 note.

RAYGRAD: monastery situated in the district of Prague, for whose defence Lucius II wrote to Bishop Otto in 1144, CLXXIX, 929.

REDON. See ST SULPICIUS.

REFLORE (diocese of Braga in Portugal): monastery whose abbot and prior Innocent III addressed concerning burial of excommunicated persons who had shown signs of repentance, 1213, CCXVI, 852.

RIÉVAL, ST MARY OF THE ROYAL VALLEY (Notre-Dame de Riéval, former diocese of Toul, Meuse): Premonstratensian monastery built in the twelfth century, whose possessions Innocent II confirms in 1141, CLXXIX, 545.—Likewise Lucius III, 1181, CCI, 1107.—Privilege of Clement III, 1188, CCIV, 1278.

REGGIO (duchy of Modena): monastery of the Order of St Augustine, whose possessions and rights the antipope Clement III confirmed by privilege in 1092, CXLVIII, 839.—Privilege of Urban III, 1187, CCII, 1474.

KNIGHTS TEMPLAR OF REGGIO (Templars of Reggio): established in the suburb of the city, in the duchy of Modena; Alexander III wrote to their master Boniface in 1179, CC, 613.

REGGIO, ST PROSPER (Saint-Prosper de Reggio): monastery of the Order of St Benedict, whose possessions Pope Stephen confirmed in 1059, CXLIII, 376.—Likewise Alexander II, 1072, CXLVI, 1370.—Alexander III, 1166, CC, 495.—Lucius III, 1183, CCI, 1222.—Celestine III, 1194, CCVI, 1062.—Decree of Innocent III annulling alienations formerly made by Abbot Guy, 1198, CCXIV, 44.—Privilege of Innocent III, 1208, CCXV, 1589.

REGGIO, ST THOMAS (Nuns of St Thomas of Reggio): convent for women to which Pope Lucius III granted a privilege at the request of Abbess Beatrice in 1184, CCI, 1276.

REGINSDERF. See WÜRZBURG.

**REGNIACENSE OF ST MARY** (Notre-Dame de Régny, former diocese of Autun near Vermenton, Yonne), a monastery of the Cistercian order, founded in 1104 by the hermits Gerard and Guarin. William, count of Nevers, granted it to Cîteaux in 1134. Privilege of Pope Innocent II, [col. 1129], in 1131, CLXXIX, 116.—Of Eugenius III, in 1147, CLXXX, 1269.—Adrian’s threatening letter against Milo of Nugerio, because of damage which he had inflicted upon the monastery, in 1157, CLXXXVIII, 1544.—Privilege of Alexander III, in 1165, CC, 356.—Of Innocent III, in 1199, CCXVII, 47.

**REICHENBACENSE OF ST MARY** (Notre-Dame of Reichenbach in Saxony), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, founded by Margrave Diepold and his wife Adelaide; Pope Calixtus II confirmed its possessions and rights in 1122, CLXIII, 1238.—Of Lucius III, in 1182, CCI, 1134.

**REICHENBERGENSE** (Reichenberg, near Goslar in Saxony), a monastery of the Order of St Augustine, perhaps identical with that of Goslar.—Privilege of Innocent II, in 1139, CLXXIX, 487.

**REICHENHALLENSE OF ST ZENO** (Saint-Zeno of Reichenhall in Bavaria, Munich district), a monastery of the Order of St Augustine, established by Conrad, archbishop of Salzburg, in 1144, CLXXIX, 850.—Privilege of Eugenius III, in 1146, CLXXX, 1099, 1156.—Of Celestine III, in 1195, CCVI, 1073.

**REICHERSPERGENSE** (Reichersberg on the Inn, in Bavaria), a monastery of the Order of St Augustine, founded and endowed by the distinguished man Wenner; Innocent II confirmed its goods and privileges in 1142, CLXXIX, 575.—Privilege of Eugenius III, in 1146, CLXXX, 1134.—Of Adrian, in 1159, CLXXXVIII, 1639.—The venerable provost Gerohus flourished in 1169, CXCIII, 462.—Likewise Arno, provost, in 1175, CXCIV, 1490.

**REINSBURGENSIS** (Rendsburg, in Holstein), a convent of nuns, established by Count Theodoric and his wife Petronilla and entrusted to the abbot of Egmond.—Privilege of Innocent II, in 1140, CLXXIX, 504.

**REINHARSBORNENSE OF ST MARY AND ST JOHN** (Reinhersborn in Thuringia), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, established by Count Louis in the Luiba Forest in the eleventh century. Urban II granted it a privilege at the request of Abbot Giselbert in 1092, CLI, 342.—Privilege of Paschal II, CLXIII, 37.—Of Innocent II, in 1139, CLXXIX, 423.—Of Lucius III, in 1184, CCI, 1305.

**REITENBACENSIS OF ST MARY** (Notre-Dame of Reitenbach in Bavaria), a canonry of the Order of St Augustine, founded by Welf, duke of Bavaria, and his wife Judith, and entrusted to Provost Uldaric, with a privilege of Pope Urban II, in 1092, CLI, 337.

**OF ST REMIGIUS.** See **RHEMENSE**.

**OF RENO.** See **ST MARY**.

**REOMAENSE OF ST JOHN** (Moutier-Saint-Jean at Réome, diocese of Langres), a noble monastery of the Order of St Benedict. It took its name from the river Reomaus beside which it was built in 442 by John, son of the senator Hilary, who is mentioned by Gregory of Tours. It later joined the Congregation of St Maur. Among its more celebrated abbots were John, Mummolus, Silvester, Leupardinus, and others, LXXI, 266, 894.—Privilege of Eugenius III, in 1147, CLXXX, 1295.—Of Alexander III, in 1164, CC, 316.—Of Lucius III, in 1185, CC, 1321.—Letter of Innocent III to the abbot against episcopal exactions, in 1211, CCXVI, 421.—Letter of the same pope concerning the reform of this monastery, ibid. Privilege of the same, 425.

**REPSHOLTENSE OF ST MAURICE** (Saint-Maurice of Ripsholten in the diocese of Bremen), a monastery of the Order of St Augustine. Pope Lucius III assigns it an income once established by Bishop Liemar, in 1182, CCI, 1143.

**RESBACENSE or RASBACENSE OF ST PETER** (Saint-Pierre of Rebaix, diocese of Meaux), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, called Jerusalem at Resbacus (Rebaix), founded by Dado in the territory of Meaux with a privilege of King Dagobert, in 635, LXXX, 537.—The foundation charter was confirmed by St Faro, bishop, in a synod of bishops at Clippiacum (Clichy), LXXXVII, 1134.—St Agilus was the first abbot of this monastery, CX, 745.—Privilege of Pope Innocent II, in 1133, CLXXIX, 194.—Decree of Alexander III, in 1163, CC, 290.—Privilege of Innocent III, in 1207, CCXV, 1203.

**RESSENSE or RENSENSE** (Rens, diocese of Cologne), a monastery of the Order of St Augustine, established by the Blessed Countess Irmintrude and Bishop Anno.—Privilege of Adrian IV, in 1159, CLXXXVIII, 1637.

**RETORTENSE OF ST MARY** (Notre-Dame de la Retorta, five leagues from Valladolid, Spain), a monastery of the Premonstratensian order, founded by the Countess of Assuris in 1143.—Privilege of Alexander III, in 1163, CC, 201.

**RHEDONENSE.** See **ST MELANIUS**.

**RHEGIENSE.** See above, **REGIENSE**.

**RHEMENSIS OF ST PETER** (the convent of Saint-Pierre at Reims), a convent of nuns to which Guy of Châtillon, archbishop of Reims, gave the altar of St Stephen in 1035, CXLII, 1400.

**RHEMENSE OF ST REMIGIUS** (Saint-Remi of Reims), a very celebrated monastery of the Order of St Benedict, founded by St Remigius and King Clovis I before 533. See the testament of Remigius, CXXXV, 60, 70.—Charter of Abbot Ado, in 715, LXXVII, 1261.—Privilege of Pope John XIII to Albero, in 972, CXXXV, 992.—The monk Richer flourished there in 999, CXXXVIII, 9.—From the time of Rudolf, the abbots of St Remigius enjoyed the title of primate and the right to sit in a *cliothedrum*, a kind of folding chair, CXXXVIII, 98.—Charter of Arnulf, archbishop of Reims, in 989, CXXXIX, 1547.—Precept of Emperor Henry, in 1002, CXL, 237.—Charter of Guy of Châtillon, archbishop, in 1053, CXLI, 1408.—Airard was the first regular abbot, in 954, CXLII, 1417, note.—Privilege of Leo IX, in 1049, 616.—Of Paschal II, in 1109, CLXIII, 216, 265, 322.—Privilege of Calixtus II, in 1119, CLXIII, 1138, 1216.—Diploma of Ralph, archbishop of Reims, by which he granted this monastery the church of Registetense (Rhège, Meurthe), in 1118, CLXIII, 1421.—The same confirms to the monastery of St Remigius the altar of St Julian, in 1124, CLXIII, 1430.—Privilege of Eugenius III, in 1145, CLXXX, 169.—Letter of Adrian IV to Abbot Hugh, in 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1363.—Privilege of the same, 1365.—Letters and privileges of Alexander III, in 1165, CC, 330, 331, 568, 620, 934, 968.—Of Lucius III, in 1182, CCI, 1168, 1324, 1329.—Privilege of William, archbishop of Reims, in 1182, CCIX, 832, 857.—Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, in 1212, CCXVI, 723; CCXVII, 74, 195.

**RHEMENSE OF ST NICASIUS** (Saint-Nicaise of Reims), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict. It began with a basilica erected in honour of the holy martyrs Agricola and Vitalis by Jovinus, commander of the forces in Gaul, at the beginning of the fourth century; a monastery dedicated to St Nicasius was later added to it. It subsequently joined the Congregation of St Maur, LXXI, 746, note.—Privilege of Alexander II, CXLVI, 1333.—The beginnings and development of this monastery, CLVI, 1142.—Chronological survey of the abbots, ibid., 1146.—Privilege of Paschal II, in 1112, CLXIII, 317, 318.—Release granted by Rainald, archbishop of Reims, in 1129, CLXXII, 1349.—Privilege of Innocent II, in 1146, CLXXIX, 291.—Of Eugenius III, in 1146, CLXXX, 1127.—Letters of Alexander III to the abbot, in 1172, CC, 778, 960.—Privilege of William, archbishop and cardinal, in 1196, CCIX, 857.

**RHEMENSE OF SS DIONYSIUS, ELEUTHERIUS, AND RUSTICUS** (Saint-Denis of Reims), a monastery restored by Archbishop Gervasius according to the Rule of St Augustine and endowed with privileges by Alexander II, in 1067, CXLVI, 1332.—Diploma of Ralph, archbishop of Reims, in 1123, CLXIII, 1427.—Letter of Alexander III to the abbot of this monastery, in 1172, CC, 795.—Privilege of William, archbishop and cardinal of Reims, in 1196, CCIX, 857.—Peter of Riga flourished there about 1212, CCXII, 9.—Letter of Innocent III concerning an accusation against the abbot, in 1208, CCXV, 1587.

**RHEMENSE OF ST THEODORIC** (Saint-Thierry of Reims), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, founded outside the city about 530 by the holy Abbot Theodoric, disciple of St Remigius, CXXXV, 85, 86.—King Theodoric, son of Clovis the Great, assisted it, ibid.—It passed to regular canons in the tenth century, 93.—Privilege of King Henry I of France, in 1050, CDI, 1029.—Privilege of Pope Honorius II, in 1126, CLXVI, 1247.—Diploma of Rainald, archbishop of Reims, in 1137, CLXXII, 1355.—Abbot William flourished in 1148, CLXXX, 185.—Privilege of Eugenius III, in 1148, CLXXX, 1338.

**RHEMENSE OF ST SIXTUS** (Saint-Sixte of Reims), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict outside the walls, over which St Ansegisus, abbot of Fontenelle, presided for some time, in 808, CV, 736.—Archbishop Ralph settled a dispute between this monastery and the brethren of St Timothy, in 1123, CLXIII, 1430.

**RHEMENSE OF ST SYMPHORIANUS** (Saint-Symphorien of Reims), a college of canons whose goods and privileges were confirmed by Ralph, archbishop of Reims, in 1119, CLXIII, 1425.

**RHEMENSE OF ST BASOLUS.** See **BASOLUS**.

**RHEMENSIS OF ST MARY**, a convent of nuns founded by St Baldric in the tenth century, CXXXV, 313.

**RHEMENSE OF ST MAURICE** (Saint-Maurice of Reims), a monastery of the Order of St Augustine, whose cause Alexander III formerly defended against the abbot of St Remigius, in 1165, CC, 355.

**RHEMENSE OF SS TIMOTHY AND APOLLINARIS** (the convent of St Timothy and Apollinaris at Reims), a monastery of the Order of St Augustine, restored by Archbishop Gerard in 1064, CXLIII, 1401.—Ralph extinguished the dispute which had arisen with the brethren of St Sixtus, CLXIII, 1430.

**RHEMENSIS OF ST PETER** (the convent of Saint-Pierre at [col. 1131] Reims), a convent of nuns whose abbess wrote to Alexander III in 1170, CC, 692, 797, 836.

**RHENAUGIENSE OF ST MARY, or OF ST PETER AND ST OLASIUS** (Rheinau or Rhinau, canton of Zurich, Switzerland), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, founded by Count Wolferad of Kyburg in 778 and still extant today.—Privilege of Honorius II, in 1135, CLXVI, 1319.—Letter of the same concerning the vexations of Count Rudolf, in 1129, CLXVI, 1283.

**OF RHENO, ST MARY.** See **ST MARY**.

**OF RHODIGIO**, a monastery of clerics established in the Venetian territory. When it began building a new church in a certain place, the brethren of St Cyprian of Murano contended that it was being built to their detriment.—Letter of Lucius III, in 1185, CCV, 1364.

**OF RIBODIMONTE.** See **ST NICHOLAS**.

**OF ST RICHARIUS, AMIENS MONASTERY.** See **CENTULENSE**.

**OF ST RICHARIUS.** See **CONSTANTIENSE**.

**OF ST RICHARIUS OF SCAMELLI-VILLA**, a monastery in Normandy, whose abbot, named Gervin, having been charged by the abbess of Villars, brought his case before William the Conqueror and obtained justice in 1047, CXLIX, 1373.

**OF ST RICMIR** (Saint-Ricmir on the Sarthe, diocese of Le Mans), a small monastery built in the district of Le Mans beyond the Sarthe before 800.—Diploma of Charlemagne, in 802, XCVII, 99.

**RIESBYARGENSIS** (Riesbyarghen in Sweden), a convent of nuns whose possessions Innocent III confirmed in 1216, CCXVII, 263.

**RIEVALLENSIS OF ST MARY** (Sainte-Marie of Rievaulx or Ridal, county of York, England), a Cistercian monastery founded in 1131 by the noble Walter Espec, with the consent of Thurstan, archbishop of York. It was made illustrious by Abbot Aelred in 1166, CXCV, 195.—Privilege of Alexander III, in 1159, CC, 92.—Innocent III assigned a certain church to this monastery in 1210, CCXVI, 374.

**OF ST RIGALD** (Saint-Rigaud, diocese of Mâcon), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, established in the forest commonly called *Silva adversa*, in the diocese of Mâcon, by Eustorgius, a monk from the monastery of St Austremonius in Auvergne; Alexander II granted it privileges in 1071, CXLVI, 1360.

**RIGENSE OF ST NICHOLAS** (Saint-Nicholas of Riga in Livonia, Prussia), a monastery whose abbot and prior Innocent III wrote to in 1213 concerning certain cases entrusted to them, CCXVI, 916, 918.

**RIGNIACENSE.** See **REGNIACENSE**.

**RINGELHEIMENSE** (Ringelheim, diocese of Hildesheim, Saxony), a monastery which seems to us identical with that of Goslar. See that entry.

**RINGSTADENSE** (Ringstadt in Denmark), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, built before 1139; in that year, at the request of Abbot Orm, Innocent II confirmed it by privilege, CLXXIX, 405.—Privilege of Celestine III, in 1192, CCVI, 975.

**RIPATORII OF ST MARY** (Notre-Dame de l’Arivour, diocese of Troyes), a Cistercian monastery founded by monks of Clairvaux under Bishop Hatto in 1140. It was distinguished by Abbot Alan, who afterward became bishop of Auxerre, in 1203, CCX, 9.

**RIPENSE** (Rippen, diocese of Worcester, England), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict in Northumbria and the diocese of Worcester, established in the seventh century by Alfrid, son of King Oswy. St Willibrord was educated there under Abbot Wilfrid, CI, 965. When it had been wholly destroyed and its ruins were excavated, the bodies of St Wilfrid and the other abbots were found; St Oswald honourably buried them in 658, CXLVIII, 1196.

**RIVIPULLENSE or RIOPULENSE OF ST MARY** (Notre-Dame of Rieux, near Aussonne, Haute-Garonne), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, built before 951, when Pope Agapetus II granted it a privilege, CXXXIII, 907.—Privilege of Sergius IV, in 1011, enumerating its innumerable monastic possessions, CXXXIX, 1509.—Of Benedict VIII, CXXXIX, 1630.—Bull of Pope Alexander II, in 1062, CXLI, 1282.—Privilege of Urban II, in 1096, CLI, 472.—Of Innocent II, in 1136, CLXXIX, 256.—Letters of Alexander III, in 1176, CC, 1049, 1051.

**RIVIPULLENSE.** See **ST JOHN**.

**OF ST ROBERT.** See **ST RUPERT**.

**OF ROCCA BOVIS CURTIS** (Roche-Beaucourt, diocese of Périgueux), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, concerning which there was long a controversy between Cluny and the canons of Périgueux.—Letter of Adrian IV, in 1159, CLXXXVIII, 1519, 1620.

**OF ROCCA MAJORE, ST MARY** (Notre-Dame de la Roche, also called Bois-Guyon, Seine-et-Oise), a monastery of the [col. 1132] Order of St Augustine or of St Victor of Paris, built by Guy de Lévis in 1190.—Diploma of Odo of Sully, archbishop of Paris, confirming this gift, in 1204, CCXII, 75.—Privilege of Innocent III, in 1199, CCXIV, 651.

**OF ROCCA MATURA** (Rocquemur in the diocese of Otranto, Naples), a monastery whose abbot Innocent III entrusted with a certain monk in 1212, CCXVI, 793.

**OF RODA** (Kloster-Rath, diocese of Cologne), a monastery of the Order of St Augustine, situated between Jülich and Maastricht on the Meuse, flourishing in the twelfth century.—Mentioned in the Life of Blessed Robert, CLXX, 1269, note.

**RODENSE OF ST PETER** (Saint-Pierre de la Rode, Aveyron), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, built in the county of Petralata (Peyrelatte), beneath the castle of Verdaria (Verdier), on the mountain called Rodas, before 974, when Pope Benedict VI granted it extensive privileges, CXXXV, 1086.—Privilege of Benedict VII, CXXXVII, 333.—Privilege of John XV, CXXXVII, 839.

**ROFFENSE OF ST ANDREW** (Saint-André of Rochester, county of Kent, England), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, founded in 600 by King Æthelberht.—An episcopal see was later established there. Various donations made to this monastery, CLXIII, 1447.—What St Lanfranc did, 1452. What King William did, ibid., 1153.—Privilege of Eugenius III, in 1146, CLXXX, 1113.

**OF ROFFIACO or ROSIACO** (Moutier-Roudeil, diocese of Tours), a monastery founded by St Aredius, abbot, and subjected by him to St Martin of Tours, in 572, LXXI, 1145.

**ROGGENBURGENSE OF ST MARY** (Roggenburg near Ulm in Bavaria), a Premonstratensian monastery built by Counts Siegfried and Berthold in 1126.—Privilege of Pope Lucius II, in 1144, CLXXIX, 908.

**ROMANENSE OF ST BARNARD** (St Barnard of Romans-sur-Isère), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, whose foundation derives from St Barnard, bishop of Vienne, in 640.—Gregory VII wrote to those monks, promising his protection if they lived according to the Rule, in 1074, CXLVIII, 411.—Guy, archbishop of Vienne, retained this monastery against the will of Pope Urban II, in 1097, CLI, 494.

**OF ST ROMANUS** (Saint-Romain near Blaye, diocese of Bordeaux), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, built on the Garonne, where St Romanus was buried in 580. It later passed to canons of St Augustine, LXXI, 863.

**OF ST ROMANUS.** See **BALMENSE**.

**ROMANUM-MONASTERIUM** (Romainmôtier, Switzerland), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, built in the district of Bern by St Lupicinus and his companion St Romanus in 530, LXXI, 1013, note.—Privilege of Innocent II, in 1139, CLXXIX, 469.—Privilege of Lucius III, in 1185, CCI, 1345.

### Roman monasteries

From the time of Pope St Innocent I, in 402, many monasteries existed, as Anastasius states, CXXVIII, 145, 149.

**ROME, ST ADRIAN**, a monastery of the Order of St Benedict near the Manger, mentioned in the Life of Pope St Leo III, in 795, CXXXVIII, 1233.

**ST AGAPETUS**, a monastery of the Order of St Benedict near the title of Eudoxia, built before 795, CXXVIII, 1235.

**ST AGATHA**, a monastery built on the Subura before 795, mentioned in the Life of Pope St Leo III, CXXVIII, 1233.

**ST AGNES**, a Roman monastery also called *Duorum-Furnorum* (“of the Two Furnaces”), founded before 795, CXXXIII, 1234.

**ST ANASTASIUS AT AQUAE SALVIAE**, a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, built at Rome before 795, CXXVIII, 1235.—Privilege of Pope Celestine III, in 1191, CCVI, 886.

**SS ANDREW AND BARTHOLOMEW**, a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, called *Honori*, founded and endowed by St Gregory the Great around 595, LXXI, 527.—From it was chosen the monk St Augustine, who under that pope was to become the apostle of England, LXXV, 366.—It was restored by Gregory II in 714, CXXVIII, 975, 1233.

**ST ANDREW**, a monastery of the Order of St Benedict called *Massa Juliana*, mentioned in the Life of St Leo III in 795, CXXVIII, 1233.—Perhaps identical with that given by Clement to the Fulda monks in 1044, CXLII, 578.

**AQUAE FLAVIAE**, a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, built in 795. See the Life of St Leo III, CXXVIII, 1234.

**ST BONIFACE**, a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, founded by St Boniface IV in his own house in 697, CXXVIII, 677.

[col. 1133] **SS BONIFACE AND ALEXIUS**, a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, built on the side of the Aventine Hill overlooking the Tiber. St Adalbert, fleeing his homeland, took refuge there and began the monastic life about 975, CXXXVII, 859.

**ST CAESARIUS.** This monastery of the Order of St Benedict was built near St Paul and is mentioned by Anastasius the Librarian in 795, CXXVIII, 1233.

**ST CASSIAN**, a monastery near Blessed Laurence Outside the Walls, mentioned in the same place.

**ST CHRYSOGONUS**, a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, built at Rome before 795, ibid.

**OF THE CORSICANS, or DE CORSAS**, a monastery mentioned there, built before 795 near the basilica of St Sixtus and restored by Leo IV in 854, CXV, 635.

**SS COSMAS AND DAMIAN**, a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, founded at Rome before 795 near the Manger, CXXVIII, 1233.

**ST DONATUS**, a monastery of the Order of St Benedict near the title of St Prisca, built before 795, CXXVIII, 1234.

**ST ERASMUS**, a monastery on the Caelian Hill, founded and endowed by Pope St Adeodatus in 669, CXXVIII, 791, 1233.

**ST EUGENIA**, a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, built outside the Latin Gate. It is mentioned in the Life of Pope St Leo III in 795, CXXVIII, 1234.

**SS EUPHEMIA AND THE ARCHANGEL**, a monastery which existed before 795 near the title of Pudens, CXXVIII, 1234.

**ST EUSTACE**, a diaconia established for the relief of the poor, before 795, ibid.

**ST GEORGE**, a diaconia mentioned in the same Life of St Leo III, CXXVIII, 1233.

**ST GREGORY**, a monastery or oratory in the Campus Martius, ibid.

**ST GREGORY**, a monastery of the Order of St Benedict founded by St Gregory the Great in his own house in 590, CXXVIII, 645.

**OF JERUSALEM**, a monastery of the Order of St Benedict built near Blessed Peter before 795. It is discussed in the Life of Pope St Leo III, CXXVIII, 1235.

**ST ISIDORE**, a monastery mentioned as in the preceding entry.

**ST JOHN**, a monastery of the Order of St Benedict built on the Aventine before 795, mentioned by Anastasius the Librarian in the Life of St Leo III, CXXVIII, 1235.

**SS JOHN AND PAUL**, a monastery of the Order of St Augustine near St Peter, or the Vatican basilica, discussed at CXXVIII, 1233.—Founded by St Leo the Great in 461, CXXVIII, 302.—Rebuilt by St Gregory II in 726, CXXVIII, 975; LXXXIX, 570.—Privilege of Pope St Leo IX, in 1053, CXLIII, 723.—Innocent II confirmed this monastery to the church of St Peter in 1138, CLXXIX, 364.—Privilege of the antipope Anacletus, in 1143, 692.—Of Adrian IV, in 1158, CLXXXVIII, 1557.—Of Urban III, in 1186, CCII, 1402.—Letter of Clement III, in 1188, CCIV, 1353.

**ST JOHN THE EVANGELIST, ST JOHN THE BAPTIST, AND ST PANCRAS**, a monastery of the Order of St Augustine near the Lateran basilica, rebuilt and enriched with gifts by Pope St Gregory II in 726, CXXVIII, 1827; LXXXIX, 568.—Privilege of Anastasius IV, in 1153, CLXXXVIII, 1019.—Privilege of Innocent III concerning the boundaries of the Lateran church, in 1212, CCXVI, 673.

**ST JUVENAL**, a monastery of the Order of St Benedict founded and endowed by the patrician Belisarius under Pope Vigilius, on the Via Flaminia near the city gate, in 540, CXXVIII, 577.

**ST LAURENCE WITHIN THE WALLS**, a monastery at *Luna*, or at the site of an old temple dedicated to the Moon; perhaps the same as that called *Pallacini* (now the Esquiline district), built by Pope St Hilary in 460, CXXVIII, 350, 358, 1233.—Privilege of the antipope Anacletus, in 1130, CLXXIX, 713.

**ST LAURENCE OUTSIDE THE WALLS**, a monastery at the *Balneum*, or praetorium, founded by Pope St Hilary in 460, CXXVIII, 350, 358.

**ST LUCY**, a monastery of the Order of St Benedict also called *de Renati*, mentioned in the Life of Pope St Leo, in 795, CXXVIII, 1235.

**ST MARY, or ST AMBROSE**, a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, cited ibid.

**ST MARY AT THE MANGER**, a monastery or home for the aged founded by Pope St Gregory II in 714, CXXVIII, 975.

**ST MARY OF JULIA**, a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, mentioned in the Life of Pope St Leo III, in 795, CXXVIII, 1234.

[col. 1134] **ST MARY ACROSS THE TIBER**, a monastery of the Order of St Benedict whose abbot was Anastasius the Librarian and cardinal, in 888, CXXVII, 9.

**ST MARY IN MINERVA** (Sainte-Marie de la Minerve), a convent of nuns in the middle of Rome, on the site of an old shrine dedicated to Minerva.—Privilege of Innocent II, in 1140, CLXXIX, 535.

**ST MARTIN**, a monastery of the Order of St Augustine which Innocent II confirmed to St Peter in 1138, CLXXIX, 364.—Privilege of Adrian IV, in 1158, CLXXXVIII, 1557.—Of Urban III, in 1186, CCII, CCII, 1402.—Letter of Clement III, in 1188, CCIV, 1353.

**ST MARTIN**, a diaconia of the Order of St Augustine existing at Rome before 795, CXXVIII, 1134.—The basilica of St Peter now stands on the same site.—Privilege of Pope St Leo IX, in 1053, CXLIII, 704.

**ST MICHAEL**, a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, mentioned by Anastasius the Librarian, built before 795, CXXVIII, 1235.

**ST PANCRAS**, a monastery of the Order of St Benedict built near the basilica of the Holy Saviour before 795, CXXVIII, 1234. It is mentioned by St Gregory the Great about 600, LXXVII, 657.—It later passed to regular canons, to whom Pope Lucius II granted a privilege in 1144, CLXXIX, 934 (or, more correctly, Lucius III, CCI, 1173).

**ST PAUL.** See above, **ST JOHN**.

**ST PAUL OUTSIDE THE WALLS**, a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, whose abbot was St Hildebrand before ascending the papal throne, in 1079, CXLVIII, 9.—Innocent III granted it possession of Monte Porzio in the Tusculan territory in 1203, CCXV, 63.—Letter of the same to the abbot concerning the division of parishes, in 1212, CCXVI, 600.

**ST PEREGRINUS**, a monastery or hospice beneath the Vatican palace, founded near the city gate called Angelica; an oratory of the same name also exists at the Naumachia. See the note on the privilege of St Leo IX, in 1053, CXLIII, 717.

**SS PETER AND LUCY** (perhaps Luke), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, for whose benefit Abbot Probus made a testament in the eleventh century, LXXV, 254, note.—It was founded in the fifth century by St Leo the Great, CXXVIII, 1414.

**SS PETER AND PAUL**, a college of canons in the Vatican. It seems to have been instituted by Blessed Leo IX; Eugenius III granted it a privilege in accordance with the tenor of Adrian IV’s privilege, CLXXXVIII, 1382.—Urban III, in 1186, CCII, 1402.—Privilege of Innocent III, in 1198, CCXIV, 254.

**ST PRISCA**, a monastery on the Aventine Hill, given by Alexander II to the monastery of the Holy Trinity at Vendôme in 1066, CXLVI, 1343.

**ST SABA**, a monastery of the Order of St Benedict built before 795, discussed in the Life of St Leo III, CXXVIII, 1234.

**THE HOLY SAVIOUR OF THE LATERAN**, a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, to which those withdrew who refused to follow the party of the antipope Constantine and pretended to be monks, in 768, CXXVIII, 1149.—Privilege of Paschal II, 1099–1118, CLXIII, 445.

**OF SARDAS.** See below, **ST VITUS**.

**SS SERGIUS AND BACCHUS**, a monastery—or rather an oratory—built at Rome in Callinicum before 795, for the support of the poor, in 740, LXXXIX, 570.—See also CXXVIII, 1233.

**ST SILVESTER**, a monastery of the Order of St Benedict in whose case Innocent III issued a judgment in 1199, CCXIV, 797.

**ST STEPHEN THE GREATER**, a monastery of the Order of St Augustine, also called *Catagalla patricia*, that is, “in the house of the patrician Galla,” discussed by Anastasius the Librarian in the Life of Pope St Leo III, in 795, CXXVIII, 1233.—It stood near the Vatican basilica of St Peter.—Privilege of Leo IX, in 1053, CXLIII, 717.—Innocent II confirmed this canonry to the church of St Peter in 1138, CLXXIX, 364.—Privilege of Adrian IV, in 1158, CLXXXVIII, 1457.—Of Urban III, in 1186, CCII, 1402.—Letter of Clement III, in 1188, CCIV, 1353.

**ST STEPHEN THE LESSER**, a hospice of canons for Hungarians, so called either because it may have been founded by St Stephen, king of the Hungarians, or because he was buried there; it was situated south of the basilica of St Peter.—Privilege of Leo IX, in 1053, CXLIII, 714.—It was also called St Stephen *Cata Barbara patricia*, ibid., note.—Innocent II confirmed this monastery to the Church of St Peter in 1138, CLXXIX, 364.—Privilege of Adrian IV, in 1158, CLXXXVIII, 1557.—Of Urban III, in 1186, CCII, 1402.—Letter of Clement III, in 1188, CCIV, 1353.

[col. 1135] **SS STEPHEN, LAURENCE, AND CHRYSOGONUS**, a monastery of the Order of St Benedict founded by Gregory III in 735, CXXVIII, 1027, 1233.

**SS STEPHEN AND SILVESTER**, a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, built by St Paul I in his own house and enriched with many possessions in 756, CXXVIII, 1137; LXXXIX, 1190.—Privilege of Agapetus II, in 955, CXXXIII, 916.

**ST VICTOR**, a monastery near St Pancras, mentioned by Anastasius the Librarian in the Life of St Leo III, in 795, CXXVIII, 1238.

**ST VITUS, or DE SARDAS**, a monastery built before 795, mentioned as in the preceding entry.

**ST VIVIANA, or BIBIANA**, a Roman monastery built before 795, mentioned as in the preceding entry.

**Note.** On the aforementioned monasteries of Rome, see the privilege of Adrian IV, in 1158, CLXXXVIII, 1557.—Four Roman hospices were restored by Pope Stephen II, and a fifth was founded by the same pontiff at the place called Plantana or Plataria, in 750, CXXVIII, 1983.

**ROMARICENSIS MONTIS**, a convent of nuns. See **ABENDENSE**.

**ROMARICENSIS MONTIS** (Remiremont), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, founded not far from the convent of nuns by St Arnulf, bishop of Metz, about 630, LXXI, 644, note.

**OF RONCAGLIA** (a priory in the diocese of Piacenza), a priory built by Bishop Arduinus, granted by him to the canons of St Antoninus, and confirmed by Innocent through a privilege in 1134, CLXXIX, 218.

**RORENSE** (Rorens, diocese of Regensburg), a monastery of the Order of St Augustine founded by Bishop Henry before 1136; in that year Innocent II adorned it with a privilege, CLXXIX, 275.—Privilege of Eugenius III, in 1152, CLXXX, 1511.

**RONCEVALLENSE** (Roncevaux, diocese of Pamplona), a monastery or hospice built by the bishop of Pamplona shortly before 1137; in that year Innocent II honoured it with a privilege, CLXXIX, 325.

**ROSATENSE** (Rosate, in the Milanese), a monastery of canons to whom Celestine II formerly wrote, commanding them not to harass the nuns of St Mary of Montano, in 1143, CLXXIX, 768.

**ROSENFELDENSE OF ST MARY** (Notre-Dame of Rosenfeld, duchy of Württemberg), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, built by Margrave Udo, his brother Rudolf, and their mother Oda, in 1087.—Privilege of Paschal II, in 1102, CLXIII, 88.—Of Adrian IV, in 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1409.

**ROSEVELDENSE OF ST MARY** (Notre-Dame of Roseweld, diocese of Hamburg), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, built by the distinguished man Odo, his brother Rudolf, and their mother Odda, at the urging of Archbishop Albero, before 1208; Innocent III confirmed it by privilege in that year, CCXV, 1507.

**OF ROSIACO.** See **OF ROFFIACO**.

**OF ROSIS.** See **ST QUIRICUS**.

**ROSSLEBIENSE** (Rossleben in Thuringia), a monastery of the Order of St Augustine, founded by Count Louis and his wife Matilda before 1142; Innocent II confirmed it by privilege in that year, CLXXIX, 580.

**ROSTENSE**, a monastery of the Order of St Benedict on the borders of Spain and Gaul, in the place called Rostas, where Sancho, king of Aragon, introduced monks brought from La Sauve-Majeure in 1092, CXLVII, 1014.

**OF ROTA, or ROTENSE OF ST MARY.** See **ST MARY**.

**ROTENSE OF SS MARINUS AND ANIANUS** (Roda, in the principality of Aldembourg, Bavaria), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict. At the request of Abbot Bertric, Innocent II confirmed its possessions by privilege in 1142, CLXXIX, 607.—Letter of the same pope on behalf of that monastery, ibid., 609.—Privilege of Celestine II, in 1144, CLXXIX, 788.—Lucius III commends it in 1185, CCI, 1335.

**OF ROTHA**, a cell or small monastery in the diocese of Würzburg, which Agnes of the Palatinate and her sister Adelaide granted to Otto, bishop of Bamberg, in 1120–1130, CLXXIII, 1280.
