**ROTHONENSE OF THE HOLY SAVIOUR** (Saint-Sauveur of Redon), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, founded in the district of Broërec, at the place called Bain, by the venerable Abbot Conwoïon; Louis the Pious confirmed certain donations to him in 834.—Abbot Cathwallon flourished there in 1038.—Privilege of Pope St Leo IX, in 1049, CXLIII, 596.—Likewise of St Gregory VII, in 1085, CXLVIII, 715.—An interdict imposed upon the abbot, in 1117, CLXIII, 416.—Letter of Calixtus to the abbot concerning the restoration of Belle-Île to the monastery of Quimperlé, CLXIII, 1117.—Letter of Paschal concerning the same abbot of Redon, CLXXII, 1326.—Decree of Innocent concerning this monastery’s exemption from episcopal jurisdiction, in 1210, CCXVI, 202, 204.

[col. 1136] **ROTNASCENSE OF ST ERMETES** (Renaix, between Oudenaarde and Grammont), a monastery of the Order of St Augustine, founded by St Amand in 545 and later subjected by Louis the Pious to the monastery of Inde, near Aachen, CXLIX, 141.

**OF ROTTIO MONASTERY** (Munchroth, diocese of Constance), a Premonstratensian monastery built in 1126.—Privilege of Eugenius III, in 1152, CLXXX, 1611.

**ROTHOMAGENSE.** See **ST AUDOENUS**.

**ROTHOMAGENSIS OF ST AMAND** (nuns of Saint-Amand in the city of Rouen), a convent of nuns built by Goslin, viscount of Arques, about 1041, CCII, 1316.

**OF ST ROTRUDE.** See **ANDRENSE**.

**RUEGGIRSBERGENSE OF ST MARY** (Notre-Dame of Rüeggisberg, diocese of Bern), a Cistercian monastery derived from Clairvaux before 1148; Eugenius confirmed it by privilege in that year, CLXXX, 1354.

**RUESPERRENSIS** (perhaps Riupeyrous near Pau in Béarn), a convent of nuns whose goods Innocent III received under his protection in 1204, CCXV, 302.

**OF ST RUF, VALENCE** (Saint-Ruf-lès-Valence, Dauphiné), a monastery of the Order of St Augustine, originally founded at Avignon in 1030; but, after its destruction by the Albigensians, it was transferred by Abbot Raymond to below Valence about 1210.—Abbot Lietbert had flourished before these times, in 1110, CLVII, 711, 715, note.—Decree of Innocent III confirming the sentence pronounced by the archbishop of Lyons in the controversy of this monastery with the Hospitallers of St James of that city, in 1199, CCXIV, 552.—Privilege of Innocent III, in 1206, CCXV, 885.

**OF ST RUF, AVIGNON**, the same as the preceding.

**OF ST RUF, PATRAS** (Saint-Ruf of Patras, in the Morea), a monastery of the Order of St Augustine, whose goods Innocent III confirmed in 1200, CCXVI, 338.

**OF ST RUF, VIVIERS** (Saint-Ruf of Viviers, Ardèche), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict. Bishop Leodegarius had granted it the church of St Andeolus; when certain clerics took this away from them, Pope Paschal II ordered by letter that it be restored, in 1210, CLXIII, 2280.

**OF RUFFIACO.** See **OF ROFFIACO**.

**OF ST RUFFILIUS.** See **FOROPOMPILIENSE**.

**RUFFINIANENSE, RUFFIANENSE, or ST PETER OF THE MOUNTAINS.** See **PETER**.

**RUGENSE OF ST GILDAS** (Saint-Gildas of Rhuys, Brittany, near Nantes), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, founded in 1026 by Simon de la Roche-Bernard. It chose Abelard as its abbot in 1126, CLXXVIII, 15.

**RUGGIANENSE OF ST NICHOLAS** (Saint-Nicholas of Royans), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, built in the territory of the Saintonge by Elias of Didonia and his wife Avicia in 1092, and later subjected to Gerald, abbot of La Sauve-Majeure, CXLVIII, 1011.

**RUMINIACENSIS or RUMILLIACENSIS PRIORY OF ST PETER** (Saint-Pierre of Rumigny in Thiérache, former diocese of Reims), formerly built by Odo called the Strong; afterward Nicholas ceded it by hereditary right to Ralph, archbishop of Reims, who subjected it to the monastery of St Nicasius in 1112, CLXIII, 1423.—Privilege of Lucius III, in 1182, CCI, 1133.

**RUMERSDORBENSE or ROMERSDORFENSE** (Romersdorf, diocese of Cologne), a monastery whose abbot Innocent III instructed to restore peace, if possible, between two counts of the province, in 1205, CCXV, 649.

RUPENSE, ST. MARY’S (Notre-Dame des Roches, near Cosne, Nièvre), a monastery of the Cistercian order, built by the barons of Douzy in 1136. — Privilege of Innocent II, 1142, CLXXIX, 613. — Of Alexander III, 1165, CC, 345. — Of Urban III, 1186, CCII, 1385.

ST. RUPERT’S OF SALZBURG. See SALZBURG.

ST. RUPERT’S ON THE HILL AT BINGEN (Convent of St. Rupert at Bingen, diocese of Liège), a nunnery built by Saint Hildegard, abbess, in 1147, CXCVII, 21.

RURICOURT, ST. MARTIN’S (Saint-Martin de Ruricourt, diocese of Beauvais), a monastery of the Augustinian order, on whose behalf Eugenius III wrote to Henry, bishop of Beauvais, in 1152, CLXXX, 1511.

RUTHENIAN. See ST. ANTONINUS and ST. AMANTIUS.

RUTHENIAN (the Augustinian convent at Rodez), a monastery of the Augustinian order, founded and endowed, apparently, by the bishops of that city before 1099, in which year Urban II confirmed its goods and rights, CLI, 546.

RYSEBIARGENSE. See RIESBYARGENSE.

ST. SABAS’S (Saint-Sabas in the March of Ancona), [Col. 1137] a monastery of the Benedictine order situated in the Italian March, concerning which there is discussion in letters of Pope Gregory VII of 1074, CXLVIII, 397, 399. — It was transferred to the Cluniac monks by Pope Lucius II in 1144, CLXXIII, 1501, note.

ST. SABIRIUS’S OR ST. SAVIN’S OF POITIERS (Saint-Savin, diocese of Poitiers), a monastery of the Benedictine order, built under Charlemagne and Louis the Pious, whose care was entrusted to St. Benedict of Aniane. Later it was restored by Abbot Gervase in the time of St. Bernard, about 1136, CLXXII, 1376.

ST. SABINUS’S. See PLACENTINE.

SAFFIACENSE. See SESSIACENSE.

SACCARGIA, MONASTERY OF THE HOLY TRINITY, of the Camaldolese order in Italy, confirmed by privilege of Innocent II in 1137, CLXXIX, 307.

SACRED WOOD. See HOLY WOOD.

SÉEZ, ST. MARTIN’S (Saint-Martin de Séez, Eure), a monastery of the Benedictine order, built by Roger of Montgomery in the eleventh century, CCII, 1317. — Letter of Hugh, prior, to Geoffrey of St. Barbara, 1170, CCV, 874. — Letter of Innocent III against the prior and bishop, 1212, CCXVI, 620.

SAHAGÚN, SS. FACUNDUS AND PRIMITIVUS (Saint Facond of Sahagún, kingdom of León, Spain), a monastery of the Benedictine order, whose possessions and rights Paschal II confirmed in 1116, CLXIII, 400, 402. — Subjected to Cluny by Pope Innocent II in 1132, CLXXIX, 166. — Privilege of Eugenius III, 1148, CLXXX, 1332. — Privilege of Alexander III, 1159, CC, 109, 228, 244. — Of Celestine III, 1194, CCVI, 1050. — Letter of Innocent III concerning a dispute with the chapter of Zamora, 1198, CCXIV, 216.

SALCIACO (Sauzet). See ST. MARCELLUS.

SALE, ST. MARY’S AND ST. GERMANUS’S, a monastery of the Benedictine order founded in England by William the Conqueror at the end of the eleventh century, CXLIX, 1361.

SALEM OR SOLOMON’S VILLAGE (Sa Monschweiler, former diocese of Constance), a monastery of the Cistercian order, built in 1137 near Überlingen by Guntram, baron of Adelsreuth. The abbot of this monastery wrote to St. Hildegard about 1150, CXCVII, 285. — Letters of Innocent III, 1203, CCXV, 174, 738; CCXVI, 803, 819, 822.

SALERNO, ST. BENEDICT’S (Saint-Benoît de Salerne, kingdom of Naples), a monastery subject to the abbey of Monte Cassino, flourished in the eleventh century under Archbishop Alphanus, 1078, CXLVII, 1217.

SALERNO, THE HOLY TRINITY (Convent of the Trinity at Salerno), a monastery of the Benedictine order, built before the time of Urban II, who restored it to Archbishop Alphanus in 1099, CLI, 547.

SALFELD (Salfeld in Thuringia), a monastery of the Benedictine order, founded by Hanno of Cologne and Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, shortly before 1125, in which year Honorius II honored it with a privilege, CLXVI, 219.

SALIGINENSE. See below, SANTONIAN.

ST. MARY OF THE SALT-WORKS VALLEY (Notre-Dame de Salival, near Vic, Meurthe), a monastery of the Premonstratensian order, founded in 1187 by Matilda, countess of Hamburg. — Privilege of Urban III, 1186, CCII, 1426.

SALION, ST. MARY’S (Sainte-Marie de Saux in Burgundy), a house of canons founded in the twelfth century by the noble Guy of Salion, lord of the place, which Celestine III confirmed by privilege, CCVI, 1232.

SALES, ST. MARY’S (Notre-Dame de Sales, diocese of Bourges), a house of canons founded about 632, whose statutes Innocent III confirmed in 1210, CCXVI, 357.

SAUMUR, ST. FLORENTIUS’S. See FLORENTIUS.

SALONE (Salone in Lombardy), a monastery of the Benedictine order, made subject by Charlemagne to the monastery of St. Denis at Paris in 777, XCVII, 958.

SAULT, ST. MARY’S (Notre-Dame-du-Sault at Fréjus), a nunnery at Forum Julii (Fréjus), built in 768 by the noble brothers Erfo and Zaneto, whose mother Piltrude was its first abbess, XCIX, 629.

SALTERS’ [SALSEREY] (Salserey, county of Huntingdon, England), a monastery of the Cistercian order, built in 1147 and made illustrious by Henry, a monk to whom is attributed the treatise on St. Patrick’s Purgatory, 1159, CLXXX, 971.

NEW GROVE, a monastery in the diocese of Zamora, Spain, to whose abbot Innocent III wrote in 1198, CCXIX, 62.

ST. SAVIOUR’S OF CAORLE (Saint-Sauveur de Caorla, in the Venetian territories), a monastery mentioned [Col. 1138] in a letter of Alexander III to the bishop of Caorle in 1179, CC, 1234, 1289.

ST. SAVIOUR’S (Saint-Sauveur, in the diocese of Piacenza), a monastery of the Camaldolese order dependent on the abbey of St. Mary at Pulsano, mentioned in a privilege of Alexander III of 1177, CC, 1097.

ST. SAVIOUR’S OF NEVERS, a monastery of the Benedictine order, was subjected to Cluny by Hugh, bishop of that city, in 1045. It was solemnly given to Odilo, abbot of Cluny, in the holy synod; ibid.

ST. SAVIOUR’S AT RIALTO (Saint-Sauveur du Rialto, Venice), a monastery of the Augustinian order built by an abbot and his brethren shortly before 1141. In that year Innocent II received it under his protection and confirmed it by privilege, CLXXIX, 744. — Privilege of Eugenius III, 1148, CLXXX, 1361; of Anastasius IV, 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1074; of Alexander III, 1169, CC, 563. — The same pope granted an indulgence of twenty days to those visiting the church of St. Saviour in 1179, CC, 1242. — Lucius III, 1181, CCI, 1091. — Urban III, 1185, CCII, 1357, 1552, 1553. — Clement III, 1188, CCIV, 1329, 1332. — Celestine III, 1195, CCVI, 1066, 1181. — Letter of Innocent III reconciling this monastery with the church of St. Bartholomew, 1198, CCXIV, 235.

ST. SAVIOUR’S ON THE TREBBIA (Saint-Sauveur-sur-la-Trébie, diocese of Piacenza), a monastery of the Benedictine order founded under Alexander III. — Privilege of Urban III, 1187, CCII, 1505.

ST. SAVIOUR’S. See ANDRES, BOCONIENSE, OF THE CELL, ON MOUNT AMIATA, ÉVREUX, MILSTAD, VIRTUENSE.

ST. SALVIUS’S OR ST. SAVIOUR’S at Bray or Brajac on the Seine (Bray-sur-Seine between Nogent and Montereau), a monastery discussed in the testament of St. Ansegisus, abbot of Fontenelle, 833, CV, 746. — Diploma of Henry I, king of France, 1042, CLI, 1025.

ST. SALVIUS’S (Saint-Sauve near Valenciennes), a monastery of the Benedictine order, built by St. Salvius himself, bishop of Amiens, 1112, CXLIX, 136.

ST. SALVIUS’S (Saint-Salvio, diocese of Chieti, Abruzzo, Naples), a monastery mentioned in a privilege of Innocent III, 1208, CCXVII, 180.

ST. SALVIUS’S. See ALBI, FLORENCE, MONSTERIOL.

ST. SALVINUS’S. See TARBES.

SALZBURG, ST. PETER’S (Saint-Pierre de Salzbourg), a monastery of the Benedictine order founded by St. Rupert, bishop of Worms, in the eighth century. Privilege of Eugenius III, 1146, CLXXX, 1125, 1387. — Letter of Celestine III concerning compensation for damage inflicted upon this monastery by certain persons, 1195, CCVI, 1078. — Another letter on behalf of the monastery of Gurk, 1188. — Letter of Innocent III to its abbot, 1206, CCXV, 872.

SALZBURG, ST. RUPERT’S (Saint-Rupert de Salzbourg), a monastery of the Augustinian order, established by Conrad, archbishop of Salzburg, shortly before 1123; in that year Pope Calixtus II confirmed it by privilege, CLXIII, 1265. — Privilege of Adrian IV, 1157, CLXXXVIII, 1529.

SAULZ, BLESSED MARY’S (Notre-Dame de Saulz, Côte-d’Or), a monastery of canons built by Guy of Saulz, 1197, CLXXXV, 1437, 1438. — Donations of James, knight of Saulz, to that monastery, 1438. — Foundations of Mary of Mont-Saint-Jean, lady of the place, and of various others, 1139.

SALZETO. See MARCELLUS.

SAMBLERIES PRIORY. See THE HOLY SEPULCHRE.

SAMBUCI (diocese of Syracuse), a monastery of the Benedictine order to which Innocent III wrote a sorrowful letter because of Saracen victories over Christians, 1198, CCXIV, 263, 470.

ORLÉANS, SS. SAMSON AND SYMPHORIANUS (Saint-Samson d’Orléans), a monastery of the Augustinian order built in 1067, to which Adrian IV granted a privilege in 1158, CLXXXVIII, 1564.

HOLY CROSSES (Saintes-Croix or Santa-Cruz, on the borders of the dioceses of Barcelona and Tarragona, Spain), a monastery of the Benedictine order, on whose behalf Urban III wrote in 1187, CCII, 1467.

SAINTONGE OR SALIGNAC, ST. MARTIN’S (Saint-Martin de Salignac, diocese of Saintes), a monastery of the Benedictine order founded and governed about 400 by Abbot Martin, disciple of St. Martin of Tours, LXXI, 869.

SARREBOURG (Sarrbourg, Electorate of Trier), [Col. 1139] a monastery of the Benedictine order, endowed with various properties by King Dagobert II in 577, LXXXVII, 314.

SARRAZAC NUNNERY (Sarrazac, Lot), near Cazillac in the district of Cahors, built by Ralph, bishop of Bourges; his sister Emesiana was its first abbess, 840, CXIX, 701.

SARAN OR SARIANS (Sarrians, arrondissement of Carpentras in the Comtat Venaissin), a monastery of the Benedictine order in the diocese of Arles, founded by a certain Leodegarius, a Cluniac monk, and William, duke of Provence, and consecrated by Regimbald, archbishop of Arles, in the eleventh century, in the time of St. Mayeul, abbot of Cluny, CXLII, 863.

SAREN (Saren in Galicia, Spain), perhaps the same monastery as Mount Ramo, of the Cistercian order, to which Innocent III subjected the monastery of Innchari in 1199, CCXIV, 720.

SARESBURY, SS. PETER AND PAUL (Saint-Pierre de Saresbury, England), a monastery of the Benedictine order, rebuilt much more splendidly by King William the Conqueror and his wife Adelaide at the end of the eleventh century, CXLIX, 1362.

SARLAT, ST. SAVIOUR’S (Saint-Sauveur de Sarlat, Dordogne), a monastery of the Benedictine order, whose foundation is attributed to St. Sacerdos, bishop, in 720. It was later enlarged by Pippin the Short and Charlemagne; but, after its buildings had collapsed, Bernard, count of Périgueux, restored and endowed it from the foundations in 936, CLXIII, 981, note. — Privilege of Eugenius III, 1153, CLXXX, 1591.

SATHANAC, ST. DAGOBERT’S (Stenay in Lorraine), a priory founded by Duke Godfrey the Bearded and his wife Beatrice before 1070. — Privilege of Godfrey of Bouillon, later king of Jerusalem, 1096, CLV, 395.

ST. SATYRUS OR ST. SATURUS OF THE CASTLE OF SACRO-CAESAR (Saint-Satur near Sancerre, diocese of Bourges), a monastery of the Augustinian order built before 1131, in which year Pope Innocent II granted it a privilege, CLXXIX, 112. — Letter of Alexander III, 1177, CC, 1092. — Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1212, CCXVI, 718.

SATZAV (Satz or Zadeck in Bohemia), a monastery of the Augustinian order, one of whose monks was a twelfth-century continuator of the Chronicle of Cosmas of Prague, CLXVI, 273.

SAVIGNY OR SAVIGNY, THE HOLY TRINITY (Savigny, former diocese of Avranches, Manche), a monastery of the Cistercian order, founded about 1112 by the noble Ralph, lord of Silgeria, his wife Amicia, and the devout hermit Vitalis, CLXII, 1030. — Privilege of Honorius II, 1125, CLXVI. — Of Lucius II, 1144, CLXXIX, 917, 920. — Eugenius transferred it to the Cistercians, 1147, CLXXX, 1282, 1398. — Privilege of Anastasius IV, 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1054; of Alexander III, 1163, CC, 200. — On the foundation of this monastery, CCII, 1312. — Charter of its founder Ralph, 1112, CCVII, 1163. — Charter of confirmation by Henry II, king of England, 1157, CCVII, 1164. — Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1205, CCXV, 594; CCXVII, 187.

SAVIGNY (Savigny, in the Bresse district, Rhône), a monastery of the Benedictine order, said to have been founded by St. Maurus. Destroyed by barbarians in 934, it was later restored and flourished for a long time. — Charter of Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, 1106, CLVII, 527, 528. — Paschal II removed in 1115 an interdict imposed upon these monks by Hugh, CLXIII, 370. — Letter of John, bishop of Coutances, to Abbot Geoffrey, 1435, CLXIII, 1479.

SAVIGLIANO (in the territory of Siena), a monastery on whose behalf Celestine III wrote to the monks of Chiusi in 1191, CCVI, 898. — Privilege of the same, ibid., 901. — Privilege of Innocent III, 1211, CCXVII, 206.

ST. SAVIN’S (Saint-Savin near Barèges, diocese of Tarbes), a monastery of the Benedictine order built by St. Savin about 700. — Charlemagne, or rather Louis the Pious, rebuilt it; but after it was again destroyed by the Northmen, it was repaired by Raymond, count of Bigorre. — Privilege of Alexander III, 1166, CC, 451, 1049, 1262.

ST. SAVIN’S. See PLACENTINE.

SAVINIO (near Lodi), a monastery of the Benedictine order in Tuscany, built before 883, in which year Pope Marinus honored it with a privilege, CXXVI, 968.

SAVINIENSE. See above, SAVIGNY.

SAXENENSE. See ST. DAMIAN.

SASSO-MONTE, ST. BENEDICT’S (Saint-Benoît de Sasso-Monte, Italy), a monastery of the Camaldolese order, whose goods Eugenius III confirmed in 1153, CLXXX, 1603.

SASSOVIVO, HOLY CROSS (Sainte-Croix de Sassovivo, diocese of Florence, Tuscany), a monastery of the Augustinian order to which Innocent III attached the monastery of St. Apollinaris for reform in 1208, CCXV, 1409. — Letter of the same pope to the abbot, ibid., 490. — On the reform of the monastery of Sassovivo, 1210, CCXVI, 373, 747.

SEYNE, ST. MARY’S (Notre-Dame de Seyne, diocese [Col. 1140] of Trier), a monastery of the Premonstratensian order, built in 1202. — Privilege of Innocent III, 1205, CCXVII, 156.

SAZETANUM. It appears to be the same as SEIZENSE.

ECHÂLIS OR SCARLEY, ST. MARY’S (Notre-Dame d’Echâlis, diocese of Sens, Yonne), a monastery of the Cistercian order, built in 1131 by the noble Vivian of La Ferté-Lopière. — Letter of Innocent III concerning the settlement between this monastery and the Hospitallers of Cerisy, 1202, CCXIV, 1094.

SCELDICE (diocese of Paderborn), a monastery granted by Emperor Henry II to the church of Paderborn in 1019, CXL, 346.

SÉLESTAT, ST. FAITH’S (Sainte-Foi de Schelestadt, Alsace), a monastery of the Benedictine order, also called that of the Holy Sepulchre, built by Duke Frederick and subjected by him to the abbey of Conques before 1106, in which year Paschal II confirmed it by privilege, CLXIII, 185.

SCHAFFNABURGENSE, for SCHAFFUSENSE.

SCHAFFHAUSEN, ST. SAVIOUR’S (Saint-Sauveur de Schaffouse), a monastery of the Benedictine order. St. Gregory VII wrote in 1080 to William, abbot of Hirsau, concerning the election of its abbot, CXLVIII, 567. — Letter of Urban II concerning protection of this monastery against Tato, 1092, CLI, 334. — Privilege of the same pope, 519. — Of Pope Calixtus II, 1120, CLXIII, 1149, 1150, 1156. — Letter of Innocent III concerning the election of an abbot, 1199, CCXIV, 560.

SCHARDBURG (Schardburg, diocese of York, England), a monastery of the Cistercian order founded by Richard, king of England, in 1192. — Privilege of Celestine III, 1192, CCXVI, 961.

SCHEFFLAREN, ST. DIONYSIUS’S (Saint-Denys de Schefflaren, diocese of Freising, Bavaria), a monastery of the Premonstratensian order, built chiefly through the efforts of Bishop Otto shortly before 1140; in that year Innocent II honored it with a privilege, CLXXIX, 527.

SCHEIDEN (Scheiden, Sceiden, or Ségor, diocese of Cologne), a monastery of the Premonstratensian order derived from Cappenberg. — Letter of Innocent III to its abbot concerning the provostship of the church of Cologne, 1203, CCXV, 36.

SCHENINGEN, ST. LAWRENCE’S (Saint-Laurent de Scheningen, diocese of Halberstadt), a monastery of the Augustinian order built by Bishop Reinhard before 1140, in which year Innocent II confirmed it by privilege, CLXXIX, 217.

SCHIREN, ST. MARY’S (Sainte-Marie de Schiren, diocese of Freising, Bavaria), a monastery of the Benedictine order to which Eugenius III granted a privilege confirming earlier donations, 1145, CLXXX, 1034.

ST. SCHOLASTICA’S (Sainte-Scholastique, former diocese of Le Mans, Orne), a monastery of the Benedictine order built before 802, in which year Charlemagne assigned it to the bishop of Le Mans; his diploma, XCVII, 995.

SCHÖNAU (diocese of Trier), a monastery of the Benedictine order founded by Abbot Hildelin and Count Rupert in 1124, made illustrious by Blessed Florinus and Abbot Eckbert in 1168, CXCV, 9.

SCHÖNAU NUNNERY, of the Benedictine order, built in 1124 by the same Abbot Hildelin. Blessed Elizabeth, abbess and sister of Eckbert, flourished there in the twelfth century, CXCV, 9.

SCHULTEREN, ST. MICHAEL’S (Saint-Michel de Schulteren, Alsace), a monastery of the Benedictine order built by Otto the Englishman in 603 and later endowed by King Dagobert II in 677. — Privilege of Innocent II, 1136, CLXXIX, 293.

SCHWARTZACH, ST. SAVIOUR’S (Saint-Sauveur de Schwartzach, Franconia), a monastery of the Benedictine order founded at the beginning of the ninth century in the diocese of Würzburg by Regimbald, governor of that region. Louis the Pious granted it a privilege under Abbot Waldo in 828, CIV, 1169. — Emperor Henry II gave it to the bishop of Strasbourg in 1014, CXL, 317.

SCILLENSE, of the Carthusian order. It appears to be the same as SQUILLACENSE.

SCIROS, ST. LUKE’S (Sciro, an island of the Archipelago, in the diocese of Danalia, in Romania or Thrace), a monastery concerning whose subjection Innocent III wrote in 1210, CCXVI, 303.

SCRINIOLO. See MARY.

ÉCUILLÉ (Maine-et-Loire), a small monastery or cell which Charlemagne assigned to the bishop of Le Mans by diploma of 802, XCVII, 995.

SS. SEBASTIAN AND ZOSIMUS OF PALARIA, a monastery of the Benedictine order in Italy, granted to the monastery of Monte Cassino by Alexander II in 1061, CXLVI, 1395.

SECKAU (in Lower Styria), a monastery of the Augustinian order transferred hither from Feistritz under Provost Wernher [Col. 1141] in 1143; Innocent II granted it a privilege in the same year, CLXXIX, 645. — Privilege of Alexander III, 1171, CC, 717.

SÉGUR, ST. MICHAEL OF THE NEEDLE (Saint-Michel de l’Aiguille at Ségur, near Le Puy), a monastery of the Augustinian order. Its church was founded in 962, but the monastery itself only in the twelfth century; Innocent III wrote to its prior in 1208, CCXV, 1544.

SÉMOY, ST. BARTHOLOMEW’S (Saint-Barthélemi de Sémoy, near Orléans), a monastery of the Benedictine order built by the noble Teeclin and subjected, at the end of the eleventh century, to the monastery of La Sauve-Majeure, then ruled by Abbot Gerald, CXLVII, 1012.

SAINT-SEINE OR ST. SEQUANUS’S (Saint-Seine, Côte-d’Or), a monastery of the Benedictine order founded by St. Sequanus, abbot, in 580, later transferred to the congregation of St. Maurus, LXXI, 894. — The monks of this monastery were excommunicated by Innocent II in 1133, CLXXIX, 176. — Letter of Innocent III concerning absolution of the abbot from a vow to cross the sea to the Holy Land, 1202, CCXIV, 970.

SIGÜENZA (New Castile, Spain), a monastery whose certain revenues Innocent III secured in 1200, CCXIV, 943.

SUSA, ST. JUSTUS’S (Sainte-Juste at Susa in Piedmont), a monastery of the Benedictine order founded before 1037 by the Venerable Bishop Alric and Marquis Mainfred; in that year Emperor Conrad II confirmed its rights and possessions, CLI, 1072.

SEILLINENSIS (Silley, Doubs), a priory whose prior Innocent III forbade in 1198 to demand money at the celebration of marriages or for burials, CCXIV, 191.

SEITENSTETTEN, ST. MARY’S (Sainte-Marie de Seitenstetten, diocese of Passau, Bavaria), a monastery of the Cistercian order founded by the noble Ulscalch shortly before 1186, CCII, 1431.

SEITZ, VALLEY OF ST. JOHN (Charterhouse of Val-Saint-Jean at Seitz, Styria), an abbey built by Count Otakar in the time of Alexander III, who confirmed it by privilege in 1177, CC, 1100. — Privilege of Lucius III, 1185, CCI, 1335, 1342.

SEIZA OR SAZETANUM (Seiza, diocese of Coimbra, Portugal), a monastery of the Cistercian order, apparently built, like Alcobaça, by King Alfonso I. Innocent III wrote to its abbot concerning the right of the church of Coimbra in 1198, CCXIV, 194.

SELBOLD (Selboldst in Hesse-Darmstadt, diocese of Mainz), a monastery of the Premonstratensian order built by Count Deitmar shortly before 1108, in which year Paschal II granted it a privilege, CLXIII, 246. — Privilege of Innocent II, 1139, CLXXIX, 451; of Adrian IV, 1158, CLXXXVIII, 1568.

SELIGENSTADT (diocese of Mainz), a monastery of the Benedictine order in the diocese of Mainz founded by Abbot Einhard in 836, CXIX, 524.

SÉLAINCOURT, ST. PETER’S (Saint-Pierre de Sélaincourt, arrondissement of Toul), a monastery of the Augustinian order founded by Guarin, bishop of Amiens, and confirmed by Rainald, archbishop of Reims, in 1135, CLXXI, 1331. — Privilege of Innocent II, CLXXIX, 310.

SEMPLINGHAM, A HOUSE OF CANONS in the diocese of Lincoln, whose goods St. Hugh, bishop, confirmed at the end of 1200, CLIII, 1122.

SÉNEVIÈRE (diocese of Tours), a monastery of the Benedictine order founded by St. Ursus in the territory of Tours about 560, whose first abbot was St. Leobatius. It was later called St. Leobatius’s, Saint-Leubasse, or Libesse, LXXI, 1085.

SENESE. See ST. EUGENIUS.

ST. SENOCH’S (Saint-Senoch, near Loches), a monastery founded or rebuilt by Abbot Senoch about 576, LXXI, 324.

SENS, ST. JOHN’S (Saint-Jean-lès-Sens), a monastery of the Augustinian order founded for women in the suburb by Heraclius, bishop of Sens, in 496, but rebuilt in the ninth century and granted to the Canons Regular of St. Augustine. — Diploma of Louis the Pious, 822, CIX, 1111. — Privilege of Innocent II, 1136, CLXXIX. — Of Innocent III, 1202, CCXIV, 1064. — Letter of the latter to the abbot, 1205, CCXV, 678.

SENS, ST. COLUMBA’S (Saint-Colombe-lès-Sens). This monastery of the Benedictine order was founded by King Clothar II about 620, and the body of St. Columba rested there. — Louis the Pious granted privileges to Abbot Sulpicius in 833, CIX, 1227, 1288. — Mention is made of that monastery, CXIX, 455. — Privilege of Innocent II, 1143, CLXXIX, 643.

[Col. 1142] SENS, ST. REMIGIUS’S (Saint-Rémy de Sens), a monastery of the Benedictine order, first dedicated to St. Maurice in 623; it was rebuilt in 535, not within the walls as before, but at the estate called Vallilias, by Aldric, archbishop of Sens. Diploma of Louis the Pious, 822, CIV, 1111. — Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1205, CCXV, 678.

SENS, ST. PETER’S (Saint-Pierre de Sens), a monastery of the Benedictine order founded in 505, to which the nun Ingoara made many gifts. — Charter of 711, LXXXVIII, 1258. See ST. PETER THE LIVING.

SENONES OR SENONA, ST. STEPHEN’S (Senones-en-Vosges), a monastery of the Benedictine order founded in 661 by St. Gondelbert, bishop of Senones, who retired there after resigning his office. — Diploma of King Childeric II, 661, LXXXVII, 1287. — Privilege of Calixtus II asserting to this monastery certain churches, 1123, CLXII, 1280. — Of Innocent II, 1139, CLXXIX, 464.

SEON OR SEUVA CELLA (Séon, Bavaria), ST. LAMBERT’S, a monastery of the Benedictine order founded among the Bavarians by Count Aribo under Emperor Otto III in 999, CXXXIX, 269. — Privilege of Sylvester II, ibid.

SEPT-FONTS, ST. MARY’S (Notre-Dame de Sept-Fonts or Saint-Lieu, diocese of Moulins), a monastery of the Cistercian order originating from Fontenay, built in 1132 by Wichard and William of Bourbon. — Charter of Haimo of Marmagne, knight, by which he gave for its foundation the place called Pratum Belet (“the beautiful meadow”), CLXXXV, 1479.

SEPT-FONTS, ST. NICHOLAS’S (Saint-Nicolas de Sept-Fonts, diocese of Langres), a monastery of the Premonstratensian order built by the priest Gosbert under Bishop Josceran in 1126. — Privilege of Innocent II, 1138, CLXXIX, 391. — Of Eugenius III, 1146, CLXXX, 1176.

SEPT-FONTS (Sept-Fonts, diocese of Reims, Ardennes), a monastery of the Premonstratensian order founded in 1129 by Elias, castellan of Mézières, and his wife Oda, at the place called Runiacum (Ruguéry). — Privilege of Innocent II, 1138, CLXXIX, 372.

SEPTIME, ST. SAVIOUR’S (Saint-Sauveur de Septime), a monastery of the Benedictine order founded by a certain Hugh, who had built seven monasteries in Tuscany as reparation for his former life. It later passed to the Cistercians in 1236 and became very famous. — Pope Gregory VII confirmed the rights and possessions of this monastery in 1078 at the request of Abbot Azo, CXLVIII, 682.

THE HOLY SEPULCHRE. See CAMBRAI, PIACENZA.

THE HOLY SEPULCHRE OF SAMBLERIES (Saint-Sépulcre, diocese of Troyes), a monastery of the Augustinian order, whose possessions and privileges Innocent III received under his protection in 1207, CCXV, 1335.

THE HOLY SEPULCHRE OF JERUSALEM (Convent of the Holy Sepulchre at Jerusalem), a monastery of the Augustinian order, for whose benefit innumerable donations were made and the holy pontiffs granted countless privileges. William became its first prior at the end of the eleventh century. See the cartulary of that monastery, CLV, 1111. — Privilege of Calixtus II, 1121, CLXIII, 1215; of Honorius II, 1128, CLXVI, 1281. — Letter of Innocent II concerning the reverence due to the canons of the Holy Sepulchre, 1137, CLXXIX, 329, 370, 548. — Privilege of Celestine II, 1144, CLXXIX, 903, 927. — Privileges of Alexander III, 1159, CC, 73, 471, 472, 473, 554, 695, 1196, 1257. — Of Celestine III, 1141, CCVI, 1142. — Decree of Innocent III confirming a certain composition of statutes, 1212, CCXVI, 605; CCXVII, 39.

SULLY, THE HOLY SEPULCHRE (Sully near Chinon in Touraine), a monastery of the Benedictine order founded by Walter of Montsoreau before 1114. In that year Robert of Arbrissel made an agreement with the monks of this monastery regarding the site of the monastery of Fontevraud, CLXII, 1087.

ST. SEQUANUS’S. See SEGESTRENSE.

SERENA, ST. MARY’S (Sainte-Marie Sereine, diocese of Lucca), a monastery to whose abbot Innocent III wrote in 1209, CCXVI, 107.

SEROPESBERIENSE. See SARESBURY.

ST. SERVANDUS’S (Saint-Servan or Servian of Segovia, diocese of Toledo), a monastery of the Benedictine order, formerly dependent upon St. Victor’s of Marseille. Later left vacant, it was granted by Paschal II to Bernard, bishop of Toledo, in 1116, CLXIII, 393.

ST. SERVATIUS’S, a monastery of the Benedictine order, whose construction is attributed to St. Manulf, bishop of Liège, on this side of the Rhine. Einhard held the office of abbot there for some time in 821, CIV, 607.

SESSIA, ST. PATERNUS’S (Saint-Pair-du-Mont, Calvados), perhaps the same monastery as St. Michael’s on Mount Jumba. [Col. 1143] It was begun by St. Paternus in 485 in the diocese of Coutances, LXXXVIII, 490, 498, note.

SERVIT, ST. DONATUS’S (Saint-Donat de Servit), in the province of Valencia, Spain. St. Donatus, abbot, fleeing Africa with monks because of persecution inflicted by the Moors, built this monastery with the aid of a noblewoman named Minchea. Shortly afterward St. Eutropius flourished there before being made bishop of Valencia, 600, LXXX, 9.

SEUMICH, ST. GILES’S OF VALLEFLAVIANA, a monastery of the Benedictine order founded in Poland by King Ladislaus. Privilege of Paschal II, 1106, CLXIII, 198.

ST. SEVERUS’S. See CLASSE.

ST. SEVERUS’S (Saint-Séver de Roustang, diocese of Tarbes), a monastery of the Benedictine order founded by St. Severus Sulpicius in 500, LXXI, 865. (See ADURANUM.) — Letter of Gregory VII concerning the dispute of this monastery with the monks of Holy Cross at Oloron, 1079, CXLVIII, 532. — Letter of Abbot Suavius to Pope Paschal II, 1107, CLXIII, 461. — Letter of Innocent III, 1204, CCXV, 300. — Privilege of the same, 1212, CCXVI, 566.

ST. SEVERINUS’S OF BORDEAUX (Saint-Seurin de Bordeaux), a monastery of the Benedictine order built before 593, of which St. Gregory of Tours speaks; it later passed to the Canons Regular of St. Augustine, LXXI, 863.

SEXENA (Sexena, diocese of Huesca, Spain), a nunnery whose goods and privileges Innocent III confirmed in 1207, CCXV, 1155. — Privilege of Celestine III, 1193, CCVI, 1001.

SESTO, ST. SAVIOUR’S (Saint-Sauveur du Sexto, Italy), a monastery of the Camaldolese order, belonging by right to the Holy Roman Church, and whose abbot Calixtus II elected in 1120, CLXIII, 1178.

SESTO OR ST. MARY’S OF SESTO (Notre-Dame du Sexto or Sesto), a monastery of the Benedictine order at Forum Julii (Fréjus), founded by the brothers Erfo and Zaneto in 762, XCIX, 629.

SHERBORNE, ST. MARY’S (Notre-Dame de Sherbourne, county of Dorset, England), a monastery of the Benedictine order founded by the ancient kings of England. — Privilege of Alexander III, 1163, CC, 334.

SIBETON (Sibeton, in the vicinity of Norfolk, England), a monastery founded in 1150, mentioned in a letter of Innocent III to the archbishop of Canterbury in 1204, CCXV, 315.

SICHEM OR SICHEN (Sichem or Sichen, diocese of Halberstadt, Germany), a monastery of the Cistercian order founded in 1141, whose first abbot was Wulkin. — Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1206, CCXV, 1101; 1210, CCXVI, 220, 413, 558, 870.

SICILIAN MONASTERIES were founded by St. Gregory the Great before he became pope, 594, LXXI, 527.

SECLIN, ST. PIATUS’S (Scklen or Séclin in the Low Countries), a monastery of the Augustinian order concerning which Alexander III wrote to Henry, archbishop of Reims, in 1168, CC, 542. — Privilege of Clement III, 1188, CCIV, 1328. — Letter concerning the provostship of this house of canons, 1199, CCXIV, 927. — Decree of Innocent III, 1211, CCXVII, 207.

SIGEBURG OR SIEGBURG, ST. MICHAEL’S (Saint-Michel de Sigeberg, diocese of Cologne), a monastery of the Benedictine order founded and consecrated by St. Anno, bishop, in 1066. — Reginhard was its abbot in 1072, CXLIII, 1517. — Privilege of Alexander II, 1063, CXLVI, 1312; of Paschal II, 1108, CLXIII, 237, 263; of Lucius III, 1181, CCI, 1077, 1213.

SIGNY, ST. MARY’S (Notre-Dame de Signy, diocese of Reims, Ardennes), a monastery of the Cistercian order built in 1135. — Privilege of William, archbishop of Reims, 1191, CCIX, 853.

LA SAUVE-MAJEURE (Grand-Selve, Saulve-Majeure, or La Séoube, Haute-Garonne), a famous monastery of the Benedictine order founded not far from Toulouse by Blessed Abbot Gerald in 1080, according to his charter of 1144, CXLVII, 1007. — Charter for the benefactors of the same monastery, CXLVII, 1078. — Diploma of Amatus, archbishop of Bordeaux, 1099, CLV, 1648. — Privilege of Innocent II, 1142, CLXXIX, 588. — Much concerning that monastery is related by Herbert, CLXXXV, 1353. — Alexander III, 1162, CC, 143, 769, 942. — Celestine III enrolled Blessed Gerald, founder of this monastery, among the saints in 1197, CCVI, 1211. — Privilege of the same, ibid., 1213. — Privilege of Innocent III, 1204, CCXV, 344. — Letters of the same, CCXV, 1051, 1168; 1212, CCXVI, 767.

SILVA MUNDA, a monastery of the Camaldolese order, built under Leo IX in the eleventh century by the noble Griffon in the county of Arezzo; later rebuilt elsewhere, it was confirmed by Innocent II in 1135, CLXXIX, 225.

[Col. 1144] BLACK FOREST, ST. GEORGE’S (Saint-George in the Black Forest), a monastery of the Benedictine order built and endowed by the noblemen Hetsilo and Hesso. Paschal II granted a privilege to its abbot Dieker in 1105, CLXIII, 172. — Privilege of Alexander III, 1179, CC, 1216; of Lucius III, 1183, CCI, 1237, 1328. — Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1201, CCXVII, 81.

BLACK FOREST, ST. BLAISE’S. See ST. BLAISE.

BLACK FOREST, ST. PETER’S (Saint-Pierre de la Forêt-Noire), a monastery of the Benedictine order built by Duke Berthold in the diocese of Constance. Pope Urban II granted it a privilege in 1075, CLI, 404. — Honorius II renewed the aforementioned privilege in 1125, CLXI, 1235. — Privilege of the same pope, 1129, CLXVI, 1304. — Privilege of Eugenius III, 1148, CLXXX, 1302.

SILVANENSE. See LA SAUVE-MAJEURE.

SENLIS, ST. MARY’S (Notre-Dame de Senlis), a college of canons whose goods Pope Lucius III confirmed in 1182, CCI, 1151.

SENLIS, ST. VINCENT’S (Saint-Vincent de Senlis, Oise), a monastery of the Augustinian order built in 1059 by Queen Anne, wife of Henry I. — Letter of Innocent III to the abbot concerning the chapter of St. Fraubald, 1203, CCXVII, 119. — The same pope secured possession of the church of Alvers, ibid., 138, 144.

HOLY WOOD, SS. PHILIP AND JAMES, OTHERWISE ST. WALBURGA’S (Sainte-Walburge d’Heiligsfort, Haut-Rhin), a monastery of the Benedictine order founded by Duke Frederick and the noble Peter before 1120. In that year Calixtus II confirmed its possessions and privileges, CLXIII, 1197. — Privilege of Innocent II, 1139, CLXXIX, 410.

SILVINIACENSE, or DE SILVANIACO (Souvigny, Allier), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, subject to the abbey of Cluny, when it was still merely a cell frequented by a few monks. There Saint Maiolus, abbot of Cluny, died while journeying to Paris, in 994.---Privilege of Pope Urban II, 1092, CLI, 344, 430. Of Paschal II, CLXIII, 50.---Of Eugenius III, 1152, CLXXX, 1515.---Of Lucius III, 1184, CCI, 1262.

SIMIGIENSE (Sümeg or Simegh in Hungary), a monastery founded before 1210, in which year Innocent III confirmed it by privilege, CCXVI, 368.

SINE MURO, DE (Samerey, Côte-d’Or), a priory dependent upon the monastery of Flavigny; Innocent III wrote concerning their reconciliation, 1198, CCIV, 257.

SINNINGTHWAITHENSIS, ST. MARY’S nunnery (St. Mary of Sinningthwaite, county of York, England), a monastery of the Cistercian Order to which Alexander III granted a privilege, 1172, CC, 890.

SINSHEIMENSE (Sintzheim, district of Swabia), a monastery to which Paschal II granted a privilege in 1115, CLXIII, 391.

SION. See MONTIS SION.

SIRICENSE (Siricken, diocese of Pécs [Five Churches], Hungary), a monastery whose abbot Innocent III charged with settling a dispute between the bishop and the abbot of Feldvár, 1198, CCXIV, 497.

SISTARICENSE, ST. MARY’S (Saint-Mary of Sisteron), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict in the diocese of that name, on the borders of Provence, founded about 500, LXXX, 27.

SITHIVENSE, or DE SITHIU, ST. BERTIN’S (Saint-Bertin of Sithiu), a most celebrated monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded by Saint Audomar, bishop of Thérouanne, at the place where Saint Winoc had lived a solitary life. He brought there Saints Mommolinus, Bertin, and Ebertram from the monastery of Luxeuil, who successively performed the office of abbot, in 638.---The foundation is likewise attributed to Count Blessed Adrowald, who made many grants.---Diploma of King Theuderic, LXXXVII, 1333; CXLVII, 1185.---Of Clovis III, LXXXVIII, 1079.---Charter of Chilperic II and Theuderic IV, 718, LXXXVIII, 1129, 1132.---Of Childeric III, 743, 1148.---Charter of Adrowald the founder, 748, LXXXVIII, 1155.---Of Bishop Audomar, 662, 1174.---Charter of Eodebert, ibid., 248.---Of Darmund, ibid., 125.---Of Felix the priest, 745, ibid., 1304, 1305.---Of Charlemagne, 769, XCVII, 917, 976.---Diploma of Louis the Pious and his son Lothair, 830, CIV, 1190, 1264.---Cartulary of Saint-Bertin from 748 to 808, by Folquin, a monk, 975, CXXXVI, 1183.---Privilege of Pope Victor II, 1057, CXLIII, 829.---The monk Folcard flourished in 1080, CXLVII, 1084.---Privilege of Urban II, 1096, CLI, 453.---Urban II entrusts this monastery to Hugh, abbot of Cluny, ibid., 522.---Letters of Paschal II, 1106, CLXIII, 165, 233, 301, 340, 415.---Privileges of Calixtus II, CLXIII, 1133, 1275, 1327.---Decree of Honorius II subjecting it to Cluny, CLXVI, 1220.---Privilege of Innocent II freeing Sithiu from Cluniac authority, 1139, CLXXIX, 459, 462.---Privilege of the antipope Anacletus, at the request of Abbot John, 1130, CLXXIX, 714.---Privilege of Celestine II, [Col. 1145] 1144, CLXXIX, 794.---Privilege of Pope Lucius II, 1144, CLXXIX, 891.---Of Eugenius III, 1145, CLXXX, 1031, 1032.---Of Anastasius IV, 1153, CLXXXVIII, 1021; of Adrian IV, 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1436.---Of Alexander III, 1163, CC, 227, 1041, 1207, 1221.---Of Lucius III, 1184, CCI, 1307, 1316.---Letters and privileges of Innocent III, 1199, CCXIV, 577; 1205, CCXV, 605, 1258; CCXVI, 40, 372, 375; CCXVII, 46, 94, 115, 116, 118, 160, 167, 171, 244.

SIXENENSIS (Sixena, diocese of Huesca in Aragon, Spain), a nunnery whose goods and privileges Celestine III confirmed, 1193, CCVI, 1001 (the same as SEXENENSE).

SNIAPENSE, ST. MARY’S (St. Mary of Sniapps, Germany), a monastery whose location is not specified, and which Pope Alexander III confirmed by privilege, 1163, CC, 227.

SOFENENSE, ST. SAVIOUR’S, a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict in Tuscany. It adopted the rule and governance of Saint John Gualbert about 1074, CXLVI, 806.

SOKSARDIENSE (Soksárd in Hungary, diocese of Pécs), a monastery of the Cistercian Order. Innocent III wrote to its abbot concerning the dispute of the monks of Saint Martin with the bishop of Veszprém, 1211, CCXVI, 545.

SOLACO, DE, CELL OF BLESSED MARY. See ST. MARY’S.

SOLEMNIS, ST., monastery. See MALLIACENSE.

SOLEMNIACENSE, OF SAINTS PETER AND PAUL (Solignac, diocese of Limoges), a celebrated monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded by Saint Eligius and King Dagobert; its first abbot was Saint Remaclus, 631, LXXI, 740 note; LXXXVII, 492, 657.---Diploma of Louis the Pious, 817, CIV, 1064.---Privilege of Pope Marinus, 883, CXXVI, 967.---Abbot Amblard flourished there in the tenth century, CXXXVIII, 187.

SOLENHOFFENSE (Solenhofen, diocese of Eichstätt), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded by Blessed Solo or Suolo in the diocese of Eichstätt in the eighth century, and subject to the abbey of Fulda, CVII, 51.

SONNEBECCENSE, ST. MARY’S (Our Lady of Sonnebeck, diocese of Ypres in Belgium), a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine, founded in the district of Ypres among the Belgians by the nobleman Fulbold and his wife Ramburga, and later endowed by their son Theobald before 1110; in that year Paschal confirmed it by privilege, CLXIII, 278.---Privilege of Innocent II, 1142, CLXXIX, 606.

SORENSE, or SOROENSE, ST. MARY’S (St. Mary of Sorø, Zealand, Denmark), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded by Absalon, bishop of Roskilde, shortly before 1181; in that year Lucius III confirmed it by privilege, CCI, 1164.---Privilege of Urban III, 1186, CCII, 1461.---Of Celestine III, 1197, CCVI, 1195.---Privilege of Innocent III, 1198, CCXIV, 399.

SORICINENSE, ST. MARY’S (Our Lady of Sorèze, diocese of Lavaur), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded by King Pippin and originally called *De Pace*, or Pacense.---Abbot Bertrand obtained a privilege from Louis the Pious, 817, CIV, 1059.

SOUTHWELLENSE, ST. MARY’S (St. Mary of Southwell, diocese of York, England), a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine, to which Alexander III granted a privilege, 1171, CC, 732.

SPANHEIMENSE, ST. MARY’S (Our Lady of Spanheim, diocese of Mainz), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded in 1047 by Count Eberhard of Spanheim.---Abbot John composed a eulogy of the Life of Rupert, abbot of Deutz, CLXVII, 11.---It is discussed in CXCVII, 15.

SPARMALIA, DE, ST. MARY’S, or New Jerusalem near Hunkewliet (Convent of Our Lady, or of the New Jerusalem, at Honkeliet, diocese of Bruges), a nunnery of the Cistercian Order, founded in 1200 by the noblewoman Gela.---Privilege of Innocent III, in the same year, CCXVII, 65.

SPARNACENSE, ST. MARTIN’S (Saint-Martin of Épernay, Marne), a monastery first granted to secular canons; afterwards, through Saint Bernard’s efforts, Raynald, archbishop of Reims, replaced them with regular monks of the Order of Saint Augustine, 1128, CLXXII, 1349.

SPECU, DE, ST. BENEDICT’S (Saint Benedict’s Grotto, near Subiaco), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict. Innocent III granted it a rent for the support of its monks, 1203, CCXV, 9.

SPELLENSIS, ST. LAWRENCE’S (Saint-Laurent of Spello, diocese of Spoleto), a priory of the Order of Saint Augustine, whose possessions Innocent III confirmed, 1198, CCXIV, 499.

SPINA, DE, PLACENTINUM (l’Épine, diocese of Piacenza, Spain), a monastery whose abbot Innocent III addressed concerning the absolution of the king of Portugal, 1213, CCXVI, 855.

SPINALENSE (community of canons at Épinal, [Col. 1146] diocese of Saint-Dié), a college of canons to which Lucius III granted a privilege, 1185, CCI, 1368.

SPINALENSIS nunnery (religious women of Épinal, diocese of Saint-Dié), whose constitution, issued by Stephen, bishop of Metz, concerning the weekly officiants who were to celebrate the services, Lucius III confirmed, 1185, CCI, 1360.

SPINENSE, or DE SPINETO (l’Épine-au-Bois near Guise, Aisne), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded by Bishop Bartholomew, who placed over it as abbot Odo, originally from the monastery of Foigny, 1122, CLVI, 1000.

HOSPITALLERS OF THE HOLY SPIRIT (Hospitallers of the Holy Spirit, diocese of Halberstadt), established by the count of Blankenburg in 1208 beside the monastery of Saint Michael of the Rock.---Privilege of Innocent III, ibid., 1383.

HOSPITALLERS OF THE HOLY SPIRIT IN SAXONY (Order and Teutonic Convent of the Holy Spirit in Saxony), whose new constitutions Innocent III confirmed, 1198, CCXIV, 525.---Grant, 1206, CCXV, 818.---Privilege, ibid., 1270.

HOSPITALLERS OF THE HOLY SPIRIT OF MONTPELLIER, or MAGALONENSES (Hospitallers of the Holy Spirit, a military order at Montpellier), an order founded by the nobleman Guy, to whom Innocent III wrote, 1198, CCXIV, 85; CCXV, 113, 1424.

SPISSI CAMPI (Épécamps, Somme), a priory of the Order of Saint Augustine, established by the abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin of Les Jumelles.---Letter of Innocent III commanding that discipline be established among the canons, 1198, CCXIV, 221.

SPOLETANUM, ST. MARY’S (Our Lady of Spoleto), a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine which Pope Alexander II took under his protection and whose goods he confirmed, 1069, CXLVI, 1351.---Privilege of Urban III, 1186, CCII, 1362.

SPOLETANUM, ST. PETER’S (Saint Peter of Spoleto), a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine, built outside the city gate.---Judgment of Innocent III in its controversy with the bishop of Spoleto, 1199, CCXIV, 547.

SPOLETANUM, ST. GREGORY’S (Saint Gregory of Spoleto), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict dependent on the monastery of Saint Julian. Letter of Innocent III, 1199, CCXIV, 547, 952; CCXV, 29, 125.

SPOLETANUM, ST. JULIAN’S (Saint Julian of Spoleto), a monastery whose abbot Innocent III addressed on behalf of the priory of Saint Gregory, 1199, CCXIV, 547.

SPONHEIMENSE, ST. MARTIN’S (Saint Martin of Spanheim or Sponheim, diocese of Mainz), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict. It appears to have been founded shortly before the pontificate of Honorius, who confirmed it by privilege in 1127, CLXVI, 1274.

SPRINCKIRSBACENSE, ST. MARY’S (Our Lady of Springiersbach, diocese of Trier), a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine, founded in 1107 by the noblewoman Benigna, widow of Rudger, whose son Richard was its first abbot. Letter of Gelasius II to Richard, 1118, CLXIII, 396.---Of Pope Calixtus II, 1119, CLXIII, 1138, 1298.---Privilege of Innocent II, 1143, CLXXIX, 642.---Of Eugenius III, 1145, CLXXX, 1080, 1532.---Abbot Absalon flourished in 1203, CCXI, 9.

SQUILLACENSIS CHARTERHOUSE. See TURRITANA.

STABULENSE, or DE STABULAUS (Stavelot), a most celebrated monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict in the Ardennes Forest, founded by King Sigebert and Grimoald, mayor of the palace, in 656. Saint Remaclus was its first abbot, LXXXVII, 311, 315.---Diploma of Sigebert, ibid., 321.---Likewise of Grimoald, ibid., 325.---Of Childeric, ibid., 1291, 1293.---Of Theuderic, ibid., 1331.---Of Clovis III, LXXXVIII, 1084.---Of Childeric III, 744, ibid., 1152.---Of Carloman, mayor of the palace, 746, ibid., 1307, 1310.---Of Louis the Pious, 814, CIV, 991.---Diploma of Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, 965, CXXXIV, 987.---Privilege of Gregory V, CXXXVII, 906.---Of Sylvester II, 1003, 282.---Life of Saint Remaclus by Notger, CXXXIX, 1147.---Privilege of Saint Leo IX, 1049, CXLIII, 611, 618, 678.---Emperor Henry III confirms all the preceding privileges, 1040, CLI, 1091, 1093.---Of Emperor Henry IV, 1065, CLI, 1143, 1160.---Decree of Celestine II against the despoilers of this monastery, 1143, CLXXIX, 784, 785.---Of Eugenius III, 1146, CLXXX, 1144.---Letter of the same pope against the plunderers of the monastery’s goods, ibid., 1206, 1490.---Privilege of Adrian IV, 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1419.---Concerning its possessions under Abbot Poppo, 1130, CLXXXIX, 1459.---Diploma of Lothair I, 1131, CLXXXIX, 1460.---Charter of Abbot Wibald, ibid., 1461, 1162, 1471, 1174.---Charter of the monastery, ibid., 1463.---Of Emperor Lothair, ibid., 1465, 1467.---Of Emperor Conrad, ibid., 1473, 1478 and following.---Of Albero, bishop of Liège, ibid., 1477.---Of Arnold, bishop of Cologne, ibid., 1480.

STAMPENSE, BLESSED MARY’S (Our Lady of Étampes), a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine, whose rights and possessions Calixtus II confirmed, 1119, CLXIII, 1145.---Diploma of Matthew, bishop and cardinal of Albano, concerning the agreement between Henry, bishop of Sens, and the monks, 1127, CLXIII, 1261.---Decree of Celestine III, 1191, CCVI, 898.

STAMPENSIS, BLESSED MARY OF THE HEATHS (Our Lady of Les Bruyères at Étampes), a nunnery founded in 672 under Chlothar III by a noblewoman named Chlotildis, LXXXVII, 1341.

STAMPENSE, HOLY CROSS (Holy Cross of Étampes), a college of canons to which Lucius III granted a privilege, 1185, CCI, 1315, 1316.---Decree of Celestine III, 1191, CCVI, 898.---Privilege of Innocent III, 1204, CCXV, 312.

STANFORDENSIS, ST. MICHAEL’S, a nunnery in Lincolnshire, England, founded and made subject to the abbey of Peterborough; it is mentioned in the Life of Saint Hugh, bishop, 1206, CLIII, 1109.---Charter of Bishop Hugh, CLIII, 1118.

STEINENSE, ST. MARY’S (Our Lady of Stein, diocese of Mainz), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict in the duchy of Lüneburg and diocese of Mainz, founded in the eleventh century, CXL, 261; CXLIII, 319.

STEINENSE, OF SAINTS GEORGE AND CYRIL (Saint George of Stein on the Rhine, Switzerland), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, transferred from Dwiehl in Hegau to Stein on the right bank of the Rhine near Schaffhausen, under Emperor Saint Henry II, in 1005, CXL, 261; CXLIII, 319.---The same monastery was enriched with estates by him, ibid.---Privilege of the same emperor, 271.

STEINFELDENSE, ST. MARY’S (St. Mary of Steinfeld, diocese of Cologne), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict begun by Count Sigebodo and later completed by Saint Wicfrid. Privilege of Pope Honorius II, 1129, CLXVI, 1288. Regular canons of Saint Augustine were introduced into this monastery; privilege of Innocent II, 1136, CLXXIX, 299, 940.

STEINGADENSE, ST. JOHN THE BAPTIST’S (Saint John of Steingaden, situated on the borders of the dioceses of Augsburg and Freising), a monastery founded by Welf, duke of Bavaria, which Alexander III took under his protection, 1177, CC, 1119.

STEINGADENSE, ST. MARY’S (Our Lady of Steingaden, diocese of Roth, Bavaria), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, founded in 1147 by Welf VI, duke of Bavaria. Privilege of Adrian IV, 1156, CLXXXVIII, 463.---Of Celestine III, 1194, CCVI, 1028, 1229.

STEKEDORENSE, or SIKEDORENSE (Stekedor, diocese of Csanád, Hungary), a monastery whose abbot Innocent III charged with the cause of the bishop of Pécs, 1205, CCXV, 667, 931; 1210, CCXVI, 211, 545.

STELLENSE, ST. MARY’S (Our Lady of l’Étoile, diocese of Poitiers), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded in 1124 by Isembert of Lusignan, and made illustrious by Abbot Isaac, a distinguished preacher, 1169, CXCIV, 1683.

STENDALENSE, ST. NICHOLAS’S (Saint Nicholas of Stendal, in the March of Brandenburg), a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine, founded shortly before 1189 by the nobleman and count Henry; in that year Clement III confirmed it by privilege, CCIV, 1446, 1448, 1449.---Privilege of Celestine III, 1191, CCVI, 895.

STENWELTENSE. See above, STEINFELDENSE.

STEPHEN, ST., OF THE SQUARE (Saint Stephen of Viterbo, called *in Platea*, “in the Square”), a monastery whose abbot Innocent III addressed, 1211, CCXVI, 472.

STEPHEN, ST., OF THE VALLEYS (Saint Stephen of Vaux, former diocese of Saintes), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded by the brothers Peter and Arnald of Mortagne in 1075; the monastery voluntarily subjected itself to Mallezais in 1093. Privilege of Alexander III, 1170, CC, 688.

STEPHEN, ST. See DIVIONENSE, NIVERNENSE, ROMANUM, etc.

STEPHEN, ST., OF THE WOOD (Saint Stephen of the Bocage, Calabria), a Carthusian monastery built in the wilderness of Calabria called Turritana by Saint Bruno himself and Count Roger, 1092, CLI, 385.

STILLANTIS PETRAE, TRIEFFENSTEINIENSE (Abbey of the Dripping Stone at Triefenstein, near Würzburg), a monastery in which a certain provost Folmar formerly preached errors, about 1170, CXCIV, 1481.

STIVAGIENSE, ST. PETER’S (Saint Peter of Estival or Estivay, Vosges), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, founded about 840. It was at first a nunnery subject to Andlau, but later passed to Premonstratensian canons in 1147. Innocent II granted a privilege in 1140, CLXXIX, 524.---Privilege of Eugenius III, 1147, CLXXX, 1274.---Of Lucius III, 1181, CCI, 1098.

STOKENSE, ST. MARY’S (St. Mary of Stok, in Norfolk, England), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, [Col. 1148] founded by various founders and taken under the protection of Alexander III, 1174, CC, 990.

STOKECURSY, DE, ST. ANDREW’S (Saint Andrew of Stoke Courcy, Devonshire, England), a priory dependent upon the monastery of St. Mary of Lonlay in the diocese of Le Mans, whose possessions Innocent III confirmed, 1204, CCXV, 370.

STOMENSE, incorrectly for STOVENSE below, CXLIX, 1354.

STOVENSE, ST. MARY’S (St. Mary of Stowe), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict in England, which William the Conqueror granted to the bishop of Stowe about 1082, CXLIX, 1353, 1354.

STRATENSE, ST. MARY’S (Our Lady of Estrées, near Dreux, Eure-et-Loir), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded in 1144 by Rabier, lord of Muzy. Privilege of Alexander III, 1164, CC, 292.

STRAHOWENSE (Strahov Abbey at Prague, Bohemia), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, founded in 1140 by Henry Zdík, bishop of Olomouc, and John, bishop of Prague. Letter of Eugenius III concerning certain fugitive brethren, 1146, CLXXX, 1085.

STREANSHALCENSIS nunnery in England, founded by Blessed Heiu, or Hilda, abbess of Hartlepool and daughter of King Oswin, in the district of Durham, where she became a teacher, 656, XCV, 157, 208; CXXXVII, 947.

STREANSHALCENSE, a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict in Yorkshire, founded by King Oswin, from which came many outstanding abbots and bishops, 658, XCV, 157, 208.

STROMBERCHENSE, ST. MARY’S (Our Lady of Stromberg, in the diocese of Mons), a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine, founded and endowed by Arnold, bishop of Cologne. Privilege of Innocent II, 1142, CLXXIX, 596.---Of Celestine II, 1145, CLXXIX, 804.

STRUMENSE (Estrun, diocese of Arras, Pas-de-Calais), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded in the time of Saint John Gualbert and adopting his rule in 1074, CXLVI, 806.---The monk Andrew wrote the life of this holy founder, 1080, CXLVI, 766.

STUDIENSE. See CONSTANTINOPOLITANUM.

SUALENBURGENSE, ST. MARY’S (Sualenburg, diocese of Paderborn), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded shortly before 1137 by the nobleman Widukind; in that year Innocent II confirmed it by privilege, CLXXIX, 334.

SUANENSE (Suana), a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine in the territory of Siena, whose goods Pope Nicholas II confirmed by privilege, 1061, CXLIII, 1355.

SUBENENSE, ST. LAMBERT’S (Saint Lambert of Suben, Bavaria), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, founded shortly before 1145 by Conrad, bishop of Salzburg; in that year Eugenius III confirmed it by privilege, CLXXX, 1091.

SUBLACENSE (Subiaco), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded among the Apennines by the holy founder and his holy sister Scholastica. Originally consisting of three, then of twelve monasteries, it was founded about 520, LXVI, 128.---Privilege of Nicholas I, 860, CXXIX, 1015.---Privilege of Leo VII, 936, CXXXVI, 1067, 1078.---John XII reproves these monks, 958, CXXXIII, 1019.---Gregory V confirmed their possessions, CXXXVII, 915.---Privilege of John XVIII, CXXXIX, 1481.---Privilege of Paschal II, 1114, CLXIII, 345, 424.---Of Alexander III, 1179, CC, 1263.---Of Clement III, 1189, CCIV, 1432.---Letter of Innocent III concerning certain matters to be corrected among these monks, 1202, CCXIV, 1064.

SUBTERRA, DE, ST. MICHAEL’S (Saint Michael of the Underground, diocese of Poreč, Istria), a monastery mentioned in a privilege of Alexander III, 1177, CC, 1101.

SUESSIONENSIS, ST. MARY’S (Our Lady of Soissons), a nunnery founded by Ebroin, mayor of the palace, and his wife Leutrude in 666, and endowed with a privilege by Saint Drausius, bishop, LXXXVIII, 1183.---Sigrada, mother of Saint Leodegar [Saint Léger], was received there in 668, XCVI, 373.---Privilege of Eugenius III, 1147, CLXXX, 1223.---Letters of Alexander III, 1176, CC, 1079, 1128.---Of Lucius III, 1181, CCI, 1077.---Of Celestine III, 1197, CCVI, 1203.

SUESSIONENSE, ST. PETER’S (Saint Peter of Soissons), a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine. Lucius III wrote to the abbess of Saint Mary’s on behalf of its canons, 1185, CCI, 1322.

SUESSIONENSE, OF SAINTS CRISPIN AND CRISPINIAN (Saints Crispin and Crispinian of Soissons), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict. See ST. CRISPIN IN CAVEA.

SUESSIONENSE. See ST. MEDARD.

SUFFOLCIENSE, ST. EDMUND’S (Saint Edmund of Suffolk, England), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict in the diocese of Norwich. Bishop Arfast brought suit against its abbot, [Col. 1149] but the abbot’s case prevailed. Charter concerning this judgment, 1081, CXLIX, 1355.

SULBISIENSIS (Soubise, diocese of Saintes, Charente), a priory of the Order of Saint Augustine, long deserted and half-ruined. When it was being restored by the bishop, Innocent III granted him a privilege, 1212, CCXVI, 687.

SULLIENSE. See ST. SEPULCHRE.

SULPICIUS, ST., NEAR RENNES (Saint-Sulpice near Rennes), a monastery of religious women, apparently of the same institution as the monastery of Saint Robert of Arbrissel at Fontevraud, founded in 1115 by Ralph of La Futaie, monk of the abbey of Saint Jovinus of Marnes, CLXII, 1033.

SULPICIUS, ST. (Saint-Sulpice of Bourges), a monastery built in the suburb of Bourges by Saint Sulpicius. See NAVENSE.

SUMMAQUENSE (Sommacqua, in the diocese of Concordia, duchy of Mirandola, Italy), a monastery mentioned in the privilege which Urban III granted to the bishop of Concordia, 1187, CCII, 1470.

SUNGEIACENSE, or DE SONEGIIS, ST. VINCENT’S (Soignies, Hainaut), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded by Blessed Vincent, count and monk, who was later buried there, 640, CXLIX, 142.

SUPPENTONIA, DE, a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict in Etruria, in which Saint Anastasius, abbot, flourished in the sixth century, LXXVII, 185.

SURICINENSE. See SORICINENSE.

SUSTERENSE, or DE SUESTRA (Susteren, duchy of Jülich), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded in Frisia by Saint Willibrord from the gifts of Pippin of Herstal before 714. After it was destroyed by the Northmen, a nunnery was built on the same site in the ninth century, CI, 702.

SWERINENSE, OF ST. MARY AND ST. JOHN (Saint John of Schwerin, duchy of Mecklenburg), a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine, whose goods Celestine III confirmed, 1191, CCVI, 896.

SWINENSIS (Swine, diocese of York, England), a nunnery on behalf of which Alexander III wrote to the archbishop of York, 1177, CC, 1136.

SYMPHORIANUS, ST. (Saint-Symphorien of Bourges), founded in the suburb of Bourges by Saint Ursinus in the fifth century and enlarged in the following century by Saint Desiderius, bishop; its abbot from the beginning was Augustus, LXXI, 887 note.---It was later annexed to a college of canons, ibid.

SYMPHORIANUS, ST. (Saint-Symphorien of Metz), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, built outside the walls of Metz by Saint Pappolus, bishop of Metz, in 608.---Abbot Constantine flourished there, author of the Life of Bishop Adalbero, 1024, CXXXIX, 1551.---And the monk Albert, CXL, 443.

SYMPHORIANUS, ST. See AUGUSTODUNENSE.

SYRACUSANUM, ST. LUCY’S (Saint Lucy at Syracuse), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded before the time of Saint Gregory the Great; that illustrious pontiff wrote to its abbot, LXXVII, 605.

THE MONASTERIES OF TABENNA IN EGYPT. See Rufinus, vol. XXI, and the *Lives of the Fathers*, LXXIII and LXXIV.

TALANTO, DE, VALLEY OF ST. MARY (Val-Notre-Dame near Talant, otherwise called Bonvaux, Côte-d’Or), a monastery of the Order of the Valley of Scholars of Langres, to which Alexander of Montaigu made gifts; his charter, 1272, CLXXXV, 1431, 1432.---Its founder was Garnier of Fontaines, 1215, CLXXXV, 1478.

TALIACOTIENSIS, ST. COSMAS’S (Saint-Côme of Tailliacosta, diocese of the Marsi, Naples), a nunnery which Pope Clement III confirmed by privilege, 1190, CCIV, 1458.---Privilege of Celestine III, 1192, CCVI, 948.

TANNIBACENSE (Tennenbach, grand duchy of Baden, diocese of Constance), a monastery of the Cistercian Order in the Black Forest, founded in 1156 by the counts of Stühlingen and Baar. Letter of Innocent III concerning the confirmation of the elected provost of Constance, 1210, CCXV, 377.

TARASCONENSE. See ST. NICHOLAS.

TARENTASIENSE (Augustinian convent at Taranto), a monastery founded by Peter, bishop of Taranto, before 1146; Eugenius III confirmed this foundation in that year, CLXXX, 1113, 1114.

TARRETANNENSE, an English monastery about whose location and order nothing is supplied. Letter of Innocent III to the abbot of this monastery, 1203, CCXV, 100.

TARTENSIS, ST. MARY’S (Our Lady of Tart-l’Abbaye, Côte-d’Or), a celebrated nunnery of the Cistercian Order, founded in 1132 by Arnulf the Horned and his wife Ameline, at the expense of Hugh, duke of Burgundy.---Privilege of Eugenius III, 1147, CLXXX, 1199.---Charter of foundation, CLXXXV, 1409.---Charter of Matthew, duke of Lorraine, 1142, CLXXXV, 1411.---Of Frederick, count of Toul, ibid., 1412.---Of Guy, abbot of Cîteaux, ibid., 1413.

[Col. 1150] TARVISINUM, ST. THEONESTUS’S (Treviso, Venetian States), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, subject to the abbey of Saint Zeno and taken under the protection of Emperor Conrad II in 1037, CLI, 1070.

TARVISINUM, ST. PETER’S (Saint Peter of Treviso), a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine, which Alexander III endowed with a privilege, 1171, CC, 722.---Privilege of Lucius III, 1184, CCI, 1285.---Of Urban III, 1187, CCII, 1524.

TARVISINUS, ST. CHRISTINA’S (religious women of Saint Christina at Treviso), a nunnery of the Camaldolese Order. Letter of Clement III concerning the rebuilding of this monastery, 1189, CCIV, 1429.

TAUNIACENSE, ST. MARY’S (St. Mary of Tonnay, diocese of Saintes, Charente), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded by Geoffrey, lord of Tonnay, and confirmed by Urban II in a privilege, 1099, CLI, 79.

TAURINENSE, OF SAINTS SOLUTOR AND ADVENTOR (Saint-Solutor at Turin), a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine, whose goods and privileges Emperor Henry III confirmed, 1047, CLI, 1193.---It is also mentioned in CLXXIII, 1493.---Privilege of Eugenius III, 1147, CLXXX, 1196.

TAURINUS, ST. (Saint-Taurin of Évreux), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded in the seventh century and rebuilt by Richard II, duke of Normandy, CCII, 1315.

TAUSIRIACUM, or TAUSILIACUM (Toiselay in Berry), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded by Saint Ursus in the diocese of Bourges about 500, LXXI, 1085.

TAWISLOCIENSE, OF ST. MARY AND RUMON (St. Mary of Tavistock, Devonshire, England), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, whose abbot Wimund attended the council of London held under Saint Anselm and King Henry in 1102, CLIX, 438.---Privilege of Pope Celestine III, 1193, CCVI, 999.

TEGERNSEENSE, ST. QUIRINUS’S (Saint Quirinus of Tegernsee, Bavaria), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded by Duke Henry at the beginning of the eleventh century and entrusted by him to Abbot Gozpert, CXXXIX, 365.---Precept of Emperor Saint Henry II, 1002, CXL, 240, 292, 343, 344.---Abbot Froumund flourished in 1040, CXLI, 1283.---About the same time, Eberhard, Ellinger, Peringer, and Udalric, abbots of the same monastery, flourished, CXLI, 1307 and following.---Shortly thereafter Leifrid flourished, LXLII, 719.---Privilege of Eugenius III, 1150, CLXXX, 1425, 1484.---Of Alexander III, 1177, CC, 1122.---Of Urban III, 1186, CCII, 1383, 1560.

TEGRENSENSE, the same as the preceding, CCII, 1560.

TELEQUI, DE, a monastery which appears to be situated in the further province of the kingdom of Naples. Innocent III wrote to its abbot concerning its reform and restoration, 1198, CCXIV, 5.

THE PRINCIPAL HOUSE OF THE KNIGHTS TEMPLAR AT JERUSALEM, whose grand preceptor or master was Bertrand de Blanquefort. He wrote to Louis VII, king of the Franks, at the end of the eleventh century, CLV, 1269, 1270, 1272, 1277.---John of Michaelis, who appears to have been the author of this order’s rule, flourished in 1128, CLXVI, 855.---Ulger, bishop of Angers, commends the Knights Templar, 1148, CLXXX, 1655.---Letter of Adrian IV to the archbishop of Reims on behalf of the Knights Templar, 1158, CLXXXVIII, 1537.---Letter of Alexander III to Louis VII commending the Knights Templar to him, ibid., 774.---The same pope granted privileges to Odo, master of the Temple, 1163, CC, 919.---The same Alexander III establishes peace between the Hospitaller brethren and the Knights Templar, 1179, CC, 1243.---He commends the knights, ibid., 1296.---Privilege of Lucius III, 1183, CCI, 1195.---The donations of Godfrey I and II and Henry I, dukes of Brabant, are confirmed by Lucius III, ibid., 1262.---Privilege of Urban III, 1187, CCII, 1468.---Letter of Celestine III concerning the dispute between the knights and the canons of the Holy Sepulchre, 1195, CCVI, 1154.---Letters and privileges of Innocent III from 1198 to 1216, CCXIV, 64, 467, 521, 641; 1206, CCXV, 861, 1427.

KNIGHTS TEMPLAR OF ARLES. Letter of Innocent III, 1212, CCXVI, 693.

KNIGHTS TEMPLAR established on the Aventine near Rome. Privilege and letters of Innocent III, 1211, CCXVI, 455, 456.---In Hungary, confirmed by Innocent III, 1210, CCXVI, 368.---In Romania: privileges and letters of Innocent III, 1210, CCXVI, 327, 329.---In Livonia: privilege of Innocent III, 1210, CCXVI, 327, 919, 921.---At Saint Philip of the Plain, diocese of Osimo (Osimo, March of Ancona): letter of Innocent III, 1211, CCXVI, 397.---At Riga (the same as those above in Livonia): Innocent III, CCXVI, 509.---In the diocese of Reims: letter of Innocent III concerning the non-burial of persons under interdict or excommunication, 1212, CCXVI, 645.

TENALIAE, THENOLIAE; THENILIOTENSE AND THENOLIENSE (Thenailles, near Vervins, Aisne), a monastery [Col. 1151] of the Premonstratensian Order in the diocese of Laon, founded by Bishop Bartholomew, who placed Abbot Walfrid over it, 1122, CLVI, 1000.

TENEBACENSE, ST. MARY’S (Our Lady of Tennenbach, called the Gate of Heaven, diocese of Constance), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded in the twelfth century. Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1201, CCXVII, 81.

TENERAEMUNDAE (Dendermonde, Belgium), a canonry in the diocese of Cambrai, founded by Remigius or Ringot the Bald, lord of Dendermonde, and his wife Adelwide, and confirmed by the privilege of Odard or Odo, bishop of Cambrai, 1108, CLX, 1154.

TEPLENSE, ST. MARY’S (St. Mary of Teplá, Bohemia), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, founded shortly before 1197 by the nobleman Hroznata, duke of Bohemia; in that year Celestine III confirmed it by privilege, CCVI, 1229.

TERRACINENSE, ST. STEPHEN’S (Saint Stephen of Terracina), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, situated in the Roman Campagna and founded by Saint Father Benedict himself; it was later united to Monte Cassino, 542, LXVI, 174.---When it was again separated, Saint Leo IX restored it to the Cassinese monks in 1052, CXLIII, 691.

TERRASCHENSE, ST. MICHAEL’S. See ST. MICHAEL IN THIERACHIA.

TERRAE-MAJORIS IN SAMNIUM (Terramajor in Samnium, Italy), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict. It once had a controversy with Monte Cassino, which was settled by the judgment of Pope Paschal II in 1113, CLXIII, 312.

TERTIO, DE, ST. MARTIN’S (Saint Martin of Terzo), a monastery formerly built near the Tower in Italy, in the sixth century, LXXI, 927.

TERWANENSE, OF ST. SAVIOUR AND ST. ROTRUDE (Saint-Sauveur or Sainte-Rotrude of Thérouanne, Pas-de-Calais), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, also called Hamense from the place where it was built in 1084.---Privilege of Innocent III, 1207, CCXV, 1196.

TEUTONIC. See HOSPITAL.

TEWKESBERIENSE (Tewkesbury, Gloucestershire, England), a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine. Its abbot Alan wrote the Life of Blessed Thomas of Canterbury in the twelfth century, CXC, 193, 1475.---Letter of Clement to the abbot, 1188, CCIV, 1328.---Letter of Innocent III to the abbot concerning the expulsion of the monks of Coventry from his monastery, 1198, CCXIV, 208.

THABOR. See MOUNT.

THANGMARSFELDENSE, ST. MARY’S (St. Mary of Thangmarsfeld, Saxony), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded by Archbishop Gero and his brother Thietmar; John XIII confirmed its goods and privileges, 971, CXXXV, 986.

THARAUCANUM (Tarouca, Portugal, province of Beira), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded by King Afonso and John Ciritta with his companions, 1108, CLXXXVIII, 1664.---Diploma of King Afonso, ibid.---Concerning the foundation of the same monastery, 1120, CLXXXVIII, 1665.---Privilege of Afonso, king of Portugal, 1122, CLXXXVIII, 1675.

THARISIENSE (Tharise near Wenkheim, diocese of Würzburg), a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, which Clement II himself had begun before being elevated to the papacy at Wenkheim in the diocese of Würzburg, and later confirmed by privilege, 1047, CXLII, 585.---Letter of Abbot Wigand to Otto, bishop of Bamberg, 1127, CLXXIII, 1342.

THELA, DE, ST. MARY’S (Our Lady of Théla, two leagues north of Lausanne), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded in 1133 by Guy, bishop of Lausanne. His successor Blessed Amadeus granted it many things, CLXXXVIII, 1290.

THELES, DE, ST. NICHOLAS’S, or ST. MARY’S (Saint Nicholas or Our Lady of Thil near Beauvais), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, whose possessions Eugenius III confirmed by privilege in 1147, CLXXX, 1221.

THELONIENSE, THENONIENSE, or DE TENALLIIS, OF ST. MARY (Sainte-Marie de Thenailles, Aisne), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, built in 1130 by Bartholomew of Viry, bishop of Laon. Privilege of Celestine II, 1143, CLXXIX, 774.---Privilege of Eugenius III, 1147, CLXXX, 1206, 1343.---Letter of Alexander III, 1174, CC, 941.---Letter of Innocent III to the abbot concerning the reform of the monastery of Alba Terra, 1203, CCXV, 245.

THE PRIORY OF ST. THEOBALD (Saint-Thiébault de Méréville, diocese of Toul), founded by the noble Hugh and his brother Haimo, and made subject to the monastery of St. Mansuetus, 1094.---Privilege of Pibo, bishop of Toul, CLVII, 433.

ST. THEODARD. See AUDARD.

ST. THEODERIC. See RHEIMS, VIENNE.

ST. THEODOTUS. See PAVIA.

[Col. 1152] THEOKESBERIENSE. See TEWKESBERIENSE.

ST. THEOFREDUS OF CALMICIACUM (Saint-Chaffre de Chemilly, Allier), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in the ancient diocese of Le Puy, built by Berengar Raymond, count of Provence and of Melgueil, shortly before 1090, the year in which Urban II honored it with a privilege, CLI, 822.---Privilege of Lucius II, 1144, CLXXIX, 844.

ST. MAURICE OF THEOLOGIUM. See DOLOCIENSE.

ST. DEMETRIUS OF THESSALONICA (Saint-Demetrius of Thessalonica), a monastery whose prior was addressed by Innocent III, 1210, CCXVI, 297, 303, 307.

ST. PETER OF THIERHAUPTEN (Saint-Pierre de Thierhaupten, diocese of Augsburg), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in the eighth century by Tassilo, duke of Bavaria, whose first abbot was Ulinus. Privilege of Lucius III, 1183, CC, 1226.

ST. THOMAS OF THE PARACLETE. See ELLEHOLTENSE.

ST. THOMAS OF EDESSA, a Syrian monastery renowned for miracles, existed in the fourth century, LXXI, 733.

ST. MARY AND ST. ROTHULF OF THORNEY (Saint-Mary of Thorney, county of Cambridge, England), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by King Sebert in 604 and rebuilt by St. Ethelwold, bishop, in 970.---Privilege of Alexander III, 1163, CC, 190.

THE NUNNERY OF THORN (Thoren or Tourne, Belgium), of the Order of St. Benedict, in the diocese of Liège, founded in 992 by the noble Hilsuind, wife of Count St. Ansfrid, who afterward became bishop; this nunnery was made subject to the bishop by Emperor Henry II in 1007, CXL, 275.---The bishop granted certain estates to the same nunnery, ibid.

THE HOSPITAL OF THUREGANUM (Hospitallers of Thurn, Upper Carniola), a house founded by a nobleman, duke of Thuringia, and honored with a privilege by Innocent III, 1204, CCXV, 300.

ST. PETER OF THURGARTON (Saint-Pierre of Thurgarton, diocese of York, England), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, to which Innocent III granted certain churches, 1205, CCXV, 611.

ST. TIBERIUS. See AGDE.

THE NUNNERY OF ST. MARY OF PAVIA (Our Lady of Pavia), called the nunnery of Senator; it was founded by Emperor Otto III and commended to the bishop by Pope Sylvester II, 1001, CXXXIX, 285.---Privilege of Alexander II, 1061, CXLVI, 1421.

ST. THEODOTUS, or DODOSUS, OF PAVIA (Saint-Theodosius of Pavia), a nunnery within the walls, founded in 986, which, under the administration of Abbess Asia, obtained immunities from Emperor Lothar in 833, CIV, 1240, 1307.

ST. PETER OF PAVIA AT THE GOLDEN HEAVEN. See PAVIA.

ST. SAVIOR OF TILESIUM (Saint-Sauveur of Télèse, in the Principato Ultra, Naples), a monastery concerning whose worthy election of an abbot Innocent III wrote in 1198, CCXIV, 266.

ST. MARY OF TILETO or TILIETO (Our Lady of Tilletto, diocese of Acqui, Sardinian States), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded in 1120; under Bishop Azo, Innocent II granted a privilege to this monastery in 1132, CLXXIX, 151.---Letters of Innocent III, 1205, CCXV, 777, 848, 1000, 1503; 1209, CCXVI, 25.

OF TILLIDI (perhaps Théligny, near Mamers, diocese of Le Mans), a monastery situated in the diocese of Le Mans, mentioned in a diploma of Charlemagne, 802, XCVII, 993.

TINENWAHE (Tinenwahe, diocese of Worcester, England), a monastery dependent upon the monastery of St. Alban, built and endowed by Kings Richard and John, whose possessions Innocent III confirmed in 1208, CCXV, 1526.

TINUMETUM, or THE CELL OF ST. ALBAN (Tinem, Northumberland, England), a monastery concerning whose dispute Innocent III wrote to the bishop of Worcester in 1205, CCXV, 591.

THRONENSE, or THIRONENSE (Thiron, diocese of Chartres), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, established by Bishop Ivo, Abbot Bernard, and the former prior of St. Savin. Charter of Ivo, 1110, CLXII, 290, 1033.---On the foundation of this monastery by Count Rotrou, CLXXII, 1412.---Privilege of Innocent II, 1132, CLXXIX, 132.---Of Eugenius III, 1147, CLXXX, 1228.---St. Adjutor, monk of this monastery, whose life is described, CXC, 1345.---On the foundation of this monastery, CCII, 1312.

TITAS-MONTE, an ancient monastery situated near Rimini in Italy, mentioned by Abbot Eugyppius, fifth century, LXXII, 1167.

ST. PETER OF TOLLA (Saint-Pierre de Tolla, diocese of Piacenza), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by Blessed Tobias in the eighth century; at the request of Abbot Aribert, Pope Stephen VIII took it under his protection in 939, CXXXI, 1089.---Privilege of Eugenius III, 1148, CLXXXX [sic], 1356.

ST. STEPHEN OF TOULOUSE (Saint-Étienne of Toulouse), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, which acquired the title of abbey in 1073.---Privilege of Alexander III, 1162, CC, 129.

ST. COLUMBA OF TOULOUSE (Convent of Sainte-Colombe at Toulouse), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict. It was restored by Bishop Amelius to the monks of Cluny in 1110, under Abbot Pons, CXLII, 866.

ST. SATURNINUS OF TOULOUSE (Saint-Saturnin of Toulouse), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, which under Urban II reached an agreement with the bishop in a certain dispute, 1096, CLI, 478.

ST. MARY OF THE GOLDEN ONE OF TOULOUSE (Notre-Dame de la Dorade at Toulouse), originally a nunnery, into which Rigunthis, daughter of King Chilperic, retired; afterward it passed to the monks of St. Benedict, and finally to the Congregation of St. Maur. It was founded about 585, LXXX, 422.---Privilege of Clement III, 1190, CCIV, 1470.

ST. GILES OF TOULOUSE. See ST. GILES.

ST. PONTIUS OF TOMERIARUM. See PONTIUS.

TOMOLATENSE (Les-Tombes, diocese of Périgueux), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in the territory of Périgueux and made subject to St. Eparchius of Angoulême in the tenth century, CXLI, 53.---It is improperly given by Abbot Aymeric to the duke of Moxeda, ibid.

ST. MARY OF TONGERLO (Sainte-Marie de Tongerlo, diocese of ’s-Hertogenbosch, Holland), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, founded in 1133 by Guilbert, who himself became a monk. Privilege of Eugenius III, CLXXX, 1120.---Of Urban III, 1186, CCII, 1436.

ST. PETER OF TORGATONA (Saint-Pierre of Torgatona, perhaps Tortona in Lombardy), a monastery of regular canons; Innocent III wrote to its prior concerning the establishment of canons in parish churches, 1209, CCXVI, 113.

ST. NICHOLAS AND ST. MEDARD OF TOURNAI (Saint-Nicolas-des-Prés or St. Médard of Tournai), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, founded by the nobleman Monin, 1125.

ST. MARY OF TOURNAI (Canons of Our Lady at Tournai). Various decrees of Innocent III concerning the administration of property, 1198, CCXIV, 1198.

ST. MARTIN OF TOURNAI (Saint-Martin of Tournai), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by St. Eligius, bishop of Noyon, in 652, LXXXVII, 562.---It later passed to the monks of St. Augustine in the ninth century. Privilege of Louis the Pious, 817, CIV, 170.---The monk Hermann flourished in 1147, CLXXX, 9.

ST. TORNAC (Saint-Tornac, diocese of Braga, Portugal), a monastery which Innocent III ordered to obey its bishop, 1199, CCXIV, 704.

ST. MICHAEL OF TONNERRE (Saint-Michel of Tonnerre, on the Armançon, Yonne), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded about 800. Restored by Milo, count of Tonnerre, in 980, under Wedric, bishop of Langres. Privilege of Alexander III, 1179, CC, 1219.---Privilege of Innocent III, 1211, CCXVI, 427.

ST. PHILIBERT OF TORNUS. See below, TRENORCIENSE.

TRAGURIENSE (Trau, Dalmatia), a monastery whose abbot Innocent III addressed concerning the election of the bishop of Hvar, 1199, CCXIV, 862.

OF TRAJECTUM (perhaps Tréjoux, arrondissement of Moissac), a small monastery founded by St. Gerald, abbot of La Sauve-Majeure, on the Garonne, 1084, CXLVII, 1014.
