ST. MARTIN OF UTRECHT, a monastery apparently founded by King Pepin and Charlemagne in 770. Their diplomas, ibid., 1047, 1058.---Diploma of Louis the Pious, 823, CIV, 1131.

TRANSALIACENSE. See below, TRESALLIACENSE.

OF TREBIA. See ST. SAVIOR.

TREBICENSE (Trébiz or Trebnitz, Moravia), a monastery whose abbot Eugenius III exhorts to punish the bishop’s enemies, 1145, CLXXX, 1044.

ST. LUPUS OF TROYES (Saint-Loup of Troyes), a double monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, one part outside and another within the city; it was built about 841, LXXI, 877 note.---Regular canons were established through the efforts of St. Bernard and Theobald, count of Troyes, 1135, CLXXXV, 980.---Gift of Hugh, count of Troyes, 1104, CLXXXV, 1477.---Privilege of Innocent III, 1203, CCXV, 11.

ST. JOHN OF THE CASTLE OF TROYES (Saint-Jean-du-Château-sous-Troyes), a monastery to which Hugh, count of Jerusalem, made a donation upon his second return, 1122, CLXXXV, 1477.

ST. MARTIN OF TROYES. See ST. MARTIN IN THE FIELDS.

ST. MARY OF THE TREMITI ISLANDS (Our Lady of the Tremiti Islands, [Col. 1154] kingdom of Naples), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built before the time of Innocent II.---Privilege of Alexander III, 1172, CC, 880.

ST. PHILIBERT OF TRENORCIUM (Tournus, diocese of Chalon), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, originally dedicated to St. Valerian, in the ninth century. Charles the Bald granted it to the monks of St. Benedict, and it became distinguished for very great wealth. At the request of Abbot Geilo, John VIII confirmed its possessions by privilege in 877, CXXVI, 686, 772.---Privilege of Urban II, 1096, CLI, 451.---Of Paschal II, 1105, CLXIII, 161.---Privilege of Calixtus II addressed to Abbot Franco, CLXIII, 1096, 1207, 1208.---Altars there consecrated by Pope Calixtus II, CLXIII, 1155.---Diploma of Gerard, bishop of Angoulême, 1109, CLXXII, 1317.---Privilege of Innocent II, 1132, CLXXIX, 131, 537.---Of Lucius II, 1144, CLXXIX, 896.---Of Eugenius III, 1146, CLXXX, 1093, 1600.---Decree of Adrian IV concerning the investiture of the church of Petraficta (Pierrefitte), CLXXXVIII, 1602.---Letter of Alexander III concerning payment of debts, 1164, CC, 304, 307, 1165, 1197, 1225.---Lucius III on churches taken away from this monastery, 1183, CCI, 1171.

TRESSALLIACENSE or TRANSALIACENSE (Trézay or Trézel, diocese of Clermont), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, subject to the abbey of Trenorcium (at Thiers) before 1056, LXXI, 1065.

THE MONASTERIES OF TRIER: concerning these, read in the book *On the Deeds of the Treveri*, CLIV, 1148 ff.

ST. BENEDICT OF TRIER: the same as ST. MARTIN below.

ST. EUCHARIUS, or ST. MATTHIAS, OF TRIER (Saint-Eucher of Trier), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict. King Dagobert made it subject to the church of St. Peter at Trier in 623, LXXX, 503.---Diploma of Sigebert, LXXXVII, 323.---Likewise of Pepin, 761, XCVI, 1534.---The monk Theodoric flourished in 1006, CLIV, 1233.---Privilege of Eugenius III, 1148, CLXXX, 1303.---Letter of the abbot of St. Eucharius to St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 286, 287.---Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1168, CCXIV, 212.

ST. JOHN OF TRIER, afterward ST. HILARY, and finally ST. MAXIMINUS (Saint-Maximin of Trier), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by St. Maximinus, whose body it possessed about 500, LXXI, 455, 898.---Charter of King Dagobert, LXXX, 501, 522.---Diploma of Sigebert, LXXXVII, 323.---Of Pepin, XCVI, 1534, 1565.---Diploma of Charlemagne, 779, XCVII, 1061.---Of Louis the Pious, 814, CIV, 1005.---Privilege of Pope Agapetus II, 950, CXXXIII, 902.---Of John XIII, CXXXV, 960.---Of John XV, CXXXVIII, 827.---The Emperor St. Henry II received certain estates from the abbot in 1023, CXI, 368.---Privilege of Pope St. Leo IX, 1050, CXLIII, 669.---Diploma of Emperor Henry III, 1051, CLI, 1110, 1115.---Abbot Beringosus flourished in 1112, CLX, 935.---Letter of Innocent II concerning the expulsion of a bad abbot, 1136, CLXXIX, 251, 252, 255.---His privilege, ibid., 511, 514, 529.---Of Eugenius III, 1147, CLXXX, 1212.

ST. SIMEON OF TRIER (Saint-Siméon of Trier), a monastery. Its provost Heldericus wrote to St. Hildegard to seek her counsel, CXCVII, 312.

ST. MARTIN OF TRIER (Saint-Martin of Trier), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded in the suburb of Trier by St. Magnerius, bishop, in 587, LXXI, 458 note.---Precept of King Pepin, 753, XCVI, 1522, 1534.---The monks of St. Benedict were restored by Pope Benedict VII in 975, CXXXVII, 319, 323.---Precept of Emperor St. Henry II, 1005, CXL, 266.---The monk Eberwin flourished in the eleventh century, CLIV, 1243.

TRIEFFENSTEIN. See STILLANTIS PETRAE.

THE HOLY TRINITY OF CURBA FOSSA. See LUCERNE.

THE HOLY TRINITY OF THE MOUNT (Holy Trinity of the Mount, near Rouen), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded about 1040 by Goscelin, viscount of Arques, CCII, 1316.

THE HOLY TRINITY. See Cervifrigidense, Lucanense, Parisiense, Pictaviense, Vindocinense.

ST. BARTHOLOMEW OF TRISULTO (Saint-Barthélemy of Trisulto, diocese of Veroli, Papal States), a Carthusian monastery founded by Innocent III. Privilege of foundation, 1211, CCXVI, 467.

ST. MARY OF THREE FOUNTAINS (Our Lady of Trois-Fontaines, diocese of Châlons-sur-Marne), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded by Hugh of Vitry in 1116 under Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny. Charters of Geoffrey, bishop of Châlons, and of Benedict, abbot of St. Peter, CLXXIII, 1397.---Privilege of Alexander III, 1170, CC, 624.---Letter of Innocent [Col. 1155] III to the abbot concerning the nunnery of Jotrense, 1202, CCXIV, 1144; CCXV, 16.

ST. ANASTASIUS OF THREE FOUNTAINS (Saint-Athanasius of Trois-Fontaines, or of Acque Salvie, near Rome), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, to which Charlemagne made the noble gift of the city of Ansidonia with its ports in Tuscany during the pontificate of Leo III, 805, XCVII, 1031.

ST. MARTIN OF TROARN (Saint-Martin of Troarn, diocese of Bayeux), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by Roger of Montgomery; its first abbot was Durand, a monk of Fécamp, 1060, CXLIX, 1374; CCII, 1317.---Privilege of Innocent III, 1210, CCXVI, 277.

TROCLARENSE (Le Truel, near Chrameaux, Tarn), the name of a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict built in the diocese of Albi about 770 by Chramlicus, father of St. Sigolena. It was double, one house for men and another for women. The monk Evantius flourished there in the eighth century, LXXXVIII, 718.

ST. TRUDO (Saint-Trond or Saint-Truyen, Belgium), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by St. Trudo himself, a nobleman of the Belgian region, and consecrated in honor of St. Quentin by Theodard, bishop of Maastricht, in 662.---It was distinguished by Abbot Rodulf in 1138, CLXXIII, 9.---The *Deeds of the Abbots of St. Trudo* by the same Rodulf, ibid., 11 ff.

ST. MARY OF TRUNCHINIUM, or OF THE TRUNK OF BERENGAR (Drongheim, near Ghent, Belgium), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, built about 944 through the efforts of Simon, bishop of Noyon; it passed to the Premonstratensians in 1141, when Innocent II took it under his protection, CLXXIX, 551.---Privilege of Eugenius III, 1147, CLXXX, 1259.---A settlement between the abbot and Count Baldwin arranged by St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 715.

ST. TRUTHBERT (Saint-Trupt, in the Black Forest near Freiburg), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by the counts Otpert and his nephew Rampert in 780, ibid., 813.---Privilege of Lucius II, 1144, CLXXIX, 849.

TRUTENHUSEN (Trultenhausen, diocese of Strasbourg), a monastery and hospice of regular canons, founded by Herrad, abbess of Landsberg, in 1182, near Mount St. Odile, about 1185, when Lucius III confirmed it, CCI, 1350.

TUCKELNHAUSEN, a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict dependent on the bishop of Bamberg in 1125, CLXXIII, 1280.

TUCIONENSE (La Touche, near Fontevraud, Vienne), a monastery for men founded by Blessed Robert of Arbrissel, on a site granted by the most illustrious Fulco of Frenicard.---Diploma of Peter, bishop of Poitiers, 1112, CLXII, 1093.

ST. JOHN AND ST. PAUL OF TODI (Saint-Jean of Todi, Papal States), a priory of the Order of St. Augustine, to which Innocent III adjudged the church of St. Hilary in 1208, CLXII, 1442.

OF TUFFIACUM (Tuffé, arrondissement of Mamers, or Tuffeaux, Maine-et-Loire), a nunnery in the territory of Le Mans, founded by the Venerable Abbess Loppa and assigned by King Theodoric to the bishop of Le Mans in 675, LXXXVII, 1321.---Diploma of Charlemagne, 802, XCVII, 995.

ST. MARY OF TUITIUM (Our Lady of Deutz or Duite, diocese of Cologne), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by St. Heribert, archbishop of Cologne, in 1002.---The Venerable Abbot Rupert flourished there in 1135, CLXVII, 11.---On the founder of this monastery, by Rupert, CLXX, 390, 403.---Privilege of Eugenius III, 1147, CLXXX, 1244.---Order of Celestine III concerning the restoration of certain things to this monastery, 1193, CCVI, 1022.

THE NUNNERY OF ST. LAMBERT OF TULB (Saint-Lambert of Tolba or Tolna, Austria), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by the noble Gerlach and his wife Regelind and handed over to the monastery of Fulda before 1142, CLXXIX, 587.

ST. APER OF TOUL. See APER.

ST. MANSUETUS OF TOUL (Saint-Mansuy-lez-Toul, Meurthe), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by St. Gerard, bishop of Toul, in 965.---Pope St. Leo IX, formerly Bruno, bishop of Toul, confirmed its possessions and privileges in 1050, CXLIII, 654.---Privilege of Adrian IV, 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1384.

ST. LEO OF TOUL (Convent of Saint-Léon, Toul), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by Luctulf, canon and dean of Toul, and dedicated in 1091 to Pope St. Leo IX, formerly bishop of Toul, CLVII, 427.---Privilege of Pibo, bishop of Toul, 1091, CLVII, 431.---Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1203, CCXV, 271.

ST. STEPHEN OF TOUL (Saint-Étienne-lez-Toul), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, whose possessions and rights [Col. 1156] were confirmed by Pope St. Leo IX in 1050, CXLIII, 656.

ST. THEOBALD OF TOUL. See THEOBALD.

THE NUNNERY OF TOUL (Religious women of Toul), of the Order of St. Dominic, founded by Emperor Rudolf in Lower Austria in 1273, XCVIII, 706, note 707.

ST. GENGULF OF TOUL (Saint-Gengoux, near Toul, Meurthe), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by Pibo, bishop of Toul, in 1105, CLVII, 442.

THE MONASTERY OF TURONIUM (La Torre, diocese of Braga), built in the territory of Braga in Spain by St. Fructuosus in 665, LXXXVII, 1089.

ZURICH, or TIGURINUM (Fraumünster, diocese of Constance), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in 823, whose possessions and privileges Clement III confirmed in 1188, CCIV, 1414.

ST. MARTIN OF TOURS. See MAJUS-MONASTER.

ST. VENANTIUS OF TOURS (Saint-Venant of Tours), a monastery built before 506, in which Licinius was abbot and afterward bishop. It was later transformed into a college of canons, LXXI, 568 note.

ST. COSMAS OF TOURS (Saint-Côme of Tours), a monastery whose prior Robert was commended to Pope Lucius II by Ulgerius, bishop of Angers, 1144, CLXXIX, 937.

ST. JULIAN OF THE STAIRS AT TOURS (Saint-Julien des Échelles, Tours), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in the sixth century and distinguished by miracles; later destroyed by the Northmen, it was rebuilt by Archbishop Theodolus, or Tetolus, and finally joined to the Congregation of St. Maur, LXXI, 820.---Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1207, CCXV, 1121, 1459, 1575; 1210, CCXVI, 246.

ST. RADEGUND OF TOURS (Convent of Sainte-Radegonde, Tours), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict founded by Radegund, in which the wood of the Holy Cross was kept, 555, LXXI, 518.

ST. MARY OF TURPINIACUM (Our Lady of Turpenay or Turpigny, diocese of Tours), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by the lords of Île-Bouchard before 1205, in which year Innocent III referred a certain case to its prior, CCXV, 580.

OF TURRE. See MILETENSE.

ST. MAURICE OF THE TOWERS (Saint-Maurice of Tours-sur-Marne, near Épernay), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict dependent on Cluny, treated in a letter of Alexander III, 1174, CC, 949.

TURRITANA, or SQUILLACENSIS (the Charterhouse of Squillace, Calabria), a charterhouse founded by St. Bruno in Calabria and in the diocese of Scyllacium, commonly Squillace, with the assistance of Count Roger, 1092, CLII, 338 ff.---At first it comprised two distinct monasteries: one of Blessed Mary and St. John the Baptist, the other of St. Stephen, called “of the Wood” or “of the Grove,” ibid., 385.---Master Lambert, prior of the monastery of St. Stephen and successor of Blessed Lanuin, flourished in 1125, CLIII, 1150.---Privilege of Calixtus II, 1120, CLXIII, 1189, 1279.---Letter of Innocent III by which the prior is appointed to Gaul to suppress certain abuses, 1203, CCXV, 189.

ST. PETER OF TURTURIACUM (Saint-Pierre of Tourtoirac or Tourcy, diocese of Périgueux), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by Viscount Guy in 1025 and entrusted by him to Richard, abbot of Uzerche.---Privilege of Pope Calixtus II, 1119, CLXIII, 1117.

TUSSIACENSE. See TUFFIACUM.

THE VALLEY OF TUSSON, a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose location is uncertain (perhaps Thoury or Thusey near Vaucouleurs in Champagne), where a council was later held and the kings of the Franks held court; it depended on the abbey of St. Denis and had been founded under Childebert III by Abbot Orderic in 696, LXXXVIII, 1092.

TUTELENSE (Tulle, Corrèze), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built about 700 by Count Calminius and his wife Namadia.---It was restored by Viscount Adémar in the ninth century; later it became an episcopal see in the fourteenth century.---Privilege of Urban II, 1096, CLI, 444.---Charter of Raymond of Curamonta, 1076, CLV, 483.---Privilege of Paschal II, 1105, CLXIII, 171, 341.---Of Adrian IV, 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1369.---Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1207, CCXV, 1184.

TYRONENSE. See TIRONENSE.

ST. UDALRIC (Saint-Udalric in the former diocese of Constance), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded before 1125, when Pope Honorius II confirmed it by privilege, CLXVI, 1240.---Privilege of Alexander III, 1177, CC, 1137.

ULCIENSE (Ulcia, diocese of Vercelli, Sardinian States), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, whose rights and privileges Pope Calixtus II confirmed in 1120, CLXIII, 1173.---Letter of the same pope concerning a certain restitution to be made to it, [Col. 1157] CLXIII, 1189.---Decree of Eugenius III granting it the church of Susa, CLXXX, 1192.---Privileges of the same, 1350, 1358, 1419.---Grant of Celestine, 1192, CCVI, 934, 1136.

ST. VINCENT OF LISBON (Saint-Vincent of Lisbon, Portugal), a monastery whose settlement with the bishop Innocent III confirmed in 1200, CCXV, 1001; CCXVI, 475.

ST. ULRIC OF AUGSBURG (Saint-Ulric of Augsburg), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, distinguished by Udalricus in 1135, CLXX, 835.

ST. MICHAEL OF THE FURTHER PORT (Saint-Michel of Le Tréport, diocese of Rouen), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by Robert, count of Eu, in 1056, CLVI, 1133.---Abbots of this monastery, ibid., 1137; CCII, 1318.

ULTRAJECTENSE. See TRAJECTENSE.

ST. PETER OF UNDERSDORF (Saint-Pierre of Undensdorf, diocese of Freising, Bavaria), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, built by Count Palatine Otto shortly before 1131, CXXIX, 80.

ST. MARY OF UNDERSFORD (Sainte-Marie of Undersfort, Bavaria), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, founded by the same Count Palatine Otto.---Privilege of Pope Celestine II, 1144. Perhaps the same as the preceding, CLXXIX, 803.---The abbot of this monastery commends himself to the prayers of St. Hildegard, abbess of St. Rupert, CXCVII, 305.

ST. MARY OF UNGIACUM (Our Lady of Oigny, Côte-d’Or), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, built in 1106 by Gaudin, lord of Bruis, and his wife Adeline. Letter of Innocent III to the abbot concerning the affairs of the church and monastery, 1198, CCXIV, 201.

ST. PETER OF URAH (Saint-Pierre of Aurach or Hohenaurach, Württemberg), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by St. Otto, bishop of Bamberg, in 1108, CLXXIII, 1279.

URANENSE (Urano, diocese of Ravenna), a monastery of the Camaldolese Order, which Pope Lucius III ordered to obey the archbishops of Ravenna in 1183, CCI, 1171.

ST. VINCENT OF URATISLAVIA (Saint-Vincent of Uratislaw, Poland), a monastery first granted to Black Monks; but after they were expelled because of their misconduct, it passed to the Premonstratensian Order.---Privilege of Pope Celestine III, 1193, CCVI, 986, 987.

ST. LAWRENCE OF URAUGE (Saint-Laurent of Urauge), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in the diocese of Würzburg, built by St. Otto, bishop, on the river Saale in 1102; its first abbot was Ekkerard, a monk of Hirsau, CLIV, 435; CLXXIII, 1279.---Charter of Otto, the founder, CLXXIII, 1331.

ST. URBAN OF JOINVILLE (Saint-Urbain of Joinville, diocese of Châlons-sur-Marne), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, formerly involved in a dispute with the monastery of Der concerning the church of St. Desiderius.---Letter of Alexander III, 1171, CC, 723, 779.

ST. SATURNINUS OF URGEL (Saint-Saturnin of Urgel), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by Charlemagne and confirmed by Pope Leo, on the river Valira in the diocese of Urgel. Privilege of Urban II, 1099, CLI, 512.

ST. MARY OF URSANUM (Our Lady of Ourchamp, diocese of Blois), a monastery of the same order as the community of Fontevraud, where both men and women lived separately under the governance of an abbess, built in the old diocese of Bourges, now that of Blois, by Blessed Robert of Arbrissel, where he himself died, 1117, CLXII, 1026, 1069.---Charter of Leodegarius, bishop of Bourges, 1113, CLXII, 1103.---Charters concerning the same priory, ibid., 1118.

URSARIENSE (Orsario, diocese of Caldas de Orense, suffragan of Santiago, Spain), a monastery whose abbot Innocent III addressed concerning the absolution of the king of Portugal, 1213, CCXVI, 855.

ST. MARY OF URSICAMP (Our Lady of Orcamp, diocese of Noyon, Oise), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded by Simon, bishop of Noyon, in 1129. Letter of Alexander III to the abbot of this monastery, 1168, CC, 544.---Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1208, CCXV, 1559.

SS. URSMARUS AND ERMINUS OF ALNENSE (Saint-Ursmard of Alno or Arno, Lombardy), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in Lombardy at the village of Alna, in the diocese of Verona; Ratherius, deposed from the episcopate, became its abbot in 968, CXXXVI, 66.

SS. URSMARUS AND ERMINUS IN THERASCIA. See ERMINUS.

URSPERGENSE (Ursperg, between Ulm and Vienna, Austria), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, founded in 1125 by Vernesius, born of noble blood; Hermann, bishop of Augsburg, and Pope Innocent II confirmed this foundation in 1139, CLXXIX, 433.

[Col. 1158] USENHOVENSE (Husenhow, Austria, circle of Bavaria), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded before 1104 by Counts Berthold and Otto and the noblewoman Azeca, when Paschal II honored it with a privilege, CLXIII, 134.---Privilege of Calixtus II, 1123, CLXIII, 1272.

ST. MARY OF THE VALLEY OF UTERINA (Sainte-Marie of Uzerthal, diocese of Speyer), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, built near Landau in 1148 by Stephen of Mertheim and his wife Gutta.---Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1207, CCXV, 1417.

ST. EBRULFUS OF UTICA (Saint-Évroul of Ouche, diocese of Lisieux), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by St. Abbot Ebrulf himself in 560. He dedicated it to St. Peter; rebuilt in the eleventh century, it passed to the Congregation of St. Maur in 1628. It was distinguished by Orderic, or Odelerius, Vitalis, English by origin, in 1143, CLXXXVIII, 9.---A survey of this monastery’s dues is described by Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 417 ff.---Charter of William, king of England, 457.---On the life and death of Blessed Ebrulf, by the same author, 472, 481.---The monastery is destroyed and rebuilt, 493.---On its foundation, CCII, 1315.

ST. PETER OF UZERCHE (Saint-Pierre of Uzerche, Corrèze), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built about 991 by Hildegarius, bishop of Limoges. Charter of Gerard, bishop of Angoulême, settling a dispute between Bernard of Comborn and the abbot of St. Peter, 1116, CLXXII, 1330.---Decree of Eugenius III concerning an agreement with the monks of Meymac, 1147, CLXXX, 1242.

ST. MARY OF UZNAM (Saint-Mary of Huesne or Huène, an island in the Baltic Sea, Denmark), a monastery whose possessions and rights Celestine III confirmed in 1195, CCVI, 1077.

ST. MARY AND ST. DIONYSIUS OF VABRES (Vabres near Saint-Affrique, Aveyron), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict at Vabres in the diocese of that name, founded under Charles the Bald in 864 by Count Raymond of Toulouse and entrusted to Blessed Abbot Adalgisus.---Privilege of Charles the Bald, 864, CXXXII, 784.---History of this foundation by Agio, ibid.---Charter of Count Raymond, 786.---See also CXXXIII, 709.

VAGIANUM (Veies or Vagiano, Tuscany), a monastery which joined the Vallombrosan congregation under the rule of Abbot Rodulf in 1074, CXLVI, 806.

VAISLIACENSE (Vaillac, diocese of Cahors, Lot), a monastery whose possessions Innocent III confirmed in 1206, CCXV, 1019.

ST. RUFUS OF VALENCE. See RUFUS.

ST. JAMES OF VALENCE (Saint-Jacques of Valence, Drôme), a house of the Hospitallers established shortly before 1199, when Innocent III confirmed the judgment rendered by the archbishop of Lyons in its dispute with the monastery of St. Rufus, CCXIV, 552.

ST. VALENTINUS IN THE SABINE COUNTRY, a cell or small monastery which Pope John VIII ordered Abbot Anastasius to restore to Bishop Gaugericus in 879, CXXVI, 849.

ST. JOHN THE BAPTIST OF VALENCIENNES, a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, founded by Count Arnulf under Bishop Rothard in the ninth century, CXLIX, 135.---Privilege of Odo, bishop of Cambrai, 1107, CXL, 1151.---Of Alexander III, 1173, CL, 926.

ST. VALERICUS OF AMIENS (Saint-Valery-sur-Mer, Somme), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by Chlothar II in 611; its first abbots were Valdolenus and Valericus, brought from Luxeuil. Its privileges are discussed, CLVI, 1031.---Privilege of Alexander III, 1166, CC, 477.

ST. PETER OF VALERIIS. See PETER.

ST. MARY MAGDALENE OF THE VALLEY OF FARA (Sainte-Marie-Madeleine of Vulfare, Papal States), a monastery to which Innocent III granted a church in 1204, CCXV, 465.

ST. GILES OF FLAVIAN VALLEY. See SEUMICHENSE.

ST. MICHAEL OF THE VALLEY (Saint-Michel du Val, diocese of Poreč, Istria), a monastery mentioned in a privilege of Alexander III, 1177, CC, 1101.

ST. JOHN IN VALLEIA. See JOHN.

VALLENSE. See CUCUPHATIS.

ST. STEPHEN OF THE VALLEYS. See STEPHEN.

OF THE HIGH VALLEY (Alta Valle or Val Profond, diocese of Bergamo, Lombardy), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, built by the Venerable Bishop Gregory shortly before 1138, when Innocent II honored it with a privilege, CLXXIX, 303.---Privilege of Urban III, 1187, CCII, 1494.

[Col. 1159] GOLDEN VALLEY. See AUREA VALLE.

ST. PETER OF VALBONNE (Saint-Pierre of Valbonne [Vallebuona], diocese of Piacenza), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict subject to the abbey of St. Mary at Pulsano. It is mentioned in a privilege of Alexander III, 1177, CC, 1097.

ST. MARY OF VALBUENA (Our Lady of Valbuena, diocese of Valladolid, Spain), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded in 1144 under Alfonso VIII, king of Castile.---Privilege of Eugenius III, 1153, CLXXX, 1388.

THE HOSPITAL FOR LEPERS OF THE VALLEY OF BUGNE (Le Val-de-Pouilly, Oise), which Celestine III took under his protection, CCVI, 1240.

VALLEY OF CABBAGES (Le Val-des-Choux, diocese of Langres, Côte-d’Or), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, built by Odo, duke of Burgundy, whose first abbot was the hermit Viard, formerly a Carthusian, in 1193.---Privilege of Innocent III, 1204, CCXV, 531.

VALLIS-CAVAE, a monastery situated near Astorga in Spain, which St. Beatus is believed to have governed for some time in the eighth century, XCVI, 890.

THE VALLEY OF CERNAY, or SARNAY (Vaux-Cernay, Seine-et-Oise), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, built by Simon, lord of Neauphle, in 1128.---Letter of Alexander III to Henry, archbishop of Reims, on behalf of this monastery, 1174, CC, 1008.---The monk Peter flourished in 1218, CCXIII, 541.

ST. MARY OF THE CHRISTIAN VALLEY (Our Lady of Vauchrétien, diocese of Soissons), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, built in 1134 by Rodulf, son of Gilbert and Gilla.---Privilege of Eugenius III, 1147, CLXXX, 1260.

ST. MARY OF THE HOLLOW VALLEY (Our Lady of Valeros, Var), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, founded before 1164, when Alexander III joined the monastery of Fontis Calidi to it, CC, 308, 394.

ST. MARY OF THE CLEAR VALLEY (Our Lady of Vauclair, former diocese of Laon), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, built in 1134 by Walter of Ruciacum and his wife Hermengard.---Letters of Innocent III, 1209, CCXVI, 46, 366.

THE NUNNERY OF ST. MARY OF THE VALLEY OF THE CITY OF AUSTRIA, within the walls of Forum Julii (Fréjus), whose foundation Emperors Louis and Lothar confirmed by diploma in 829, XCIX, 637; CIV, 1190.

VALLIS DEI (Val-Dieu, diocese of Mainz), a monastery whose provost commended himself to the prayers of St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 306.—The same as St. Disibod’s, which see.

VALLIS GALILEAE. See S. DEODATI.

VALLIS S. GEORGII. See NOVIBURGENSE.

VALLIS S. GREGORII (Saint-Grégoire du Val in Alsace), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded in 664 by Childeric, son of Grimoald, LXXXVII, 313.

VALLIS GRATIAE, otherwise VALLIS PROFUNDAE (Val-de-Grâce or Val-profond at Bièvre-le-Châtel near Paris), a convent of nuns of the Order of St. Benedict, built in the eleventh century. It was united with Givensis in 1207, under Innocent III, CCXV, 1250.

VALLIS LAUREAE (Valloro between Tarragona and Barcelona, Spain), a Cistercian monastery, concerning which the bishops of Barcelona and Tarragona disputed with one another.—Letter of Alexander III, 1166, CC, 509.

VALLIS LUCENTIS S. MARIAE (Notre-Dame de Vauluisant, diocese of Sens, Yonne), a Cistercian monastery founded in 1129 by the distinguished Artald of Anset and King Louis VII. Letter of Henry of Clairvaux, 1188, CCIV, 229.—Testimony of its abbot in the case concerning the succession of the counts of Champagne against Erard of Brienne, 1213, CCXVI, 979.

VALLIS MAGNAE S. MARIAE (Notre-Dame de Valmagne or Vaugrain, diocese of Agde, Hérault), a monastery first of the Order of St. Benedict, but later adopting the Cistercian Rule, in 1138.—Letter of Eugenius III, 1149, CLXXX, 1390.—The abbey of Cadouin granted this to the monastery of Bonnes-Vallées under Adrian IV, 1159, CLXXXVIII, 1599.—Letter of Innocent III, 1202, CCXIV, 1055; 1205, CCXV, 642.

VALLIS S. MARIAE. See MARIAE.

VALLIS S. MARIAE (Val-Sainte-Marie or Marienthal, diocese of Halberstadt), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by Count Palatine Frederick and devout women; Adrian IV granted it a privilege in 1159, CLXXXVIII, 1623.

VALLIS S. MARIAE. See TALANTO.

VALLIS MASSONIS S. LEODEGARII (Saint-Léger de Masmünster, or Moisevaux), a monastery founded by Masso, brother of Duke Lutfried; Louis the Pious granted it immunity in 823, CIV, 1126.

VALLIS-MONTIS S. MARIAE (Notre-Dame de Valmont). See GALLOMONTENSE.

[Col. 1160] VALLIS PONTIS S. MARIAE (Notre-Dame du Val-del-Ponte near Perugia), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, exempted by St. Leo IX from episcopal jurisdiction in 1049, CXLIII, 593.

VALLIS RICHERIAE S. MARIAE (Notre-Dame du Val-Richer, Calvados), a Cistercian monastery founded in 1150 by Simon de Bosville, whose possessions and rights Alexander III confirmed by privilege in 1164, CC, 295.

VALLIS S. PETRI (Val-Saint-Pierre), a Carthusian house in the diocese of Laon, founded in 1140. Its first prior was Engelbert, who afterwards became bishop of Chalon; Hugh, bishop of Lincoln, visited this charterhouse in 1199, CLIII, 1088.

VALLIS S. PETRI (Val-Saint-Pierre, diocese of Cologne), a Cistercian monastery. See HEISTERBACENSE.

VALLIS S. SALVATORIS ET S. MARIAE (Val-Saint-Sauveur, near Poligny, Doubs), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in the diocese of Besançon, built by Otto-William and granted to Cluny in 1029 by King Rudolf, CXLII, 863, 864.

VALLIS S. SALVATORIS ET S. MARIAE (Notre-Dame du Val-Saint-Sauveur, near Courmont, Côte-d’Or), a Cistercian monastery built at the beginning of the thirteenth century by Raynald de Grancey and his wife Agnes, together with Count Ebal of Saulx, CLXXXV, 1434.—The brothers of this monastery submit themselves to the monastery of Alba Ripa under Geoffrey, bishop of Langres, ibid.

VALLIS SECRETAE S. MARIAE (Notre-Dame de Val-Secret, diocese of Soissons), a Premonstratensian monastery built in 1060 by Count Odo II of Champagne and his wife Ermengard.—Privilege of Innocent II, 1142, CLXXIX, 575, 577.—Letter of Alexander III, 1172, CC, 771.—Letter of Innocent III to the abbot concerning an accusation against the abbot of St. Denis of Reims, 1208, CCXV, 1587.

VALLIS SENI S. LAMBERTI (Saint-Lambert du Val-de-Seine, diocese of Salzburg), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose goods and privileges Innocent II confirmed in 1139, CLXXIX, 423.

VALLIS SEITZENSIS. See SEITZENSIS.

VALLIS SEREN (Valséry, diocese of Soissons, Aisne), a Premonstratensian monastery, otherwise called Vivariensis, built in 1124 by Joachim Rufus; it is mentioned in the Life of St. Norbert, CLXX, 1309.—Privilege of Adrian IV, 1154, CLXXXVIII, 1380.

VALLIS UMBROSAE (Vallombrosa in the territory of Florence, Tuscany), an order established by St. John Gualbert about 1073, CXLVI, 667. Its beginnings, ibid.—Letter of Pope Gregory VII to the monks of Vallombrosa, 1073, CXLVIII, 644.—Privilege of Urban II, 1090, CLI, 322.—Paschal II, 1114, CLXIII, 372.—Privileges of Innocent II, 1130, CLXXIX, 57, 190.—Anastasius IV, 1153, CLXXXVIII, 997.—Privilege of Alexander III, 1169, CC, 569, 1067.—Urban III, 1186, CCII, 1389, 1413.—Clement III, 1188, CCIV, 1279.—Celestine III, 1193, CCVI, 1018.—Letter of Innocent III to the abbot of the diocese of Fiesole, 1205, CCXV, 746.

VALVENSE S. CLEMENTIS (Saint-Clément de Valvi), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in Italy. Pope Alexander II wrote in 1073 against certain persons who were harming this monastery, CXLVI, 1401.

VANGADIACENSE or VANDAGITIENSE S. MARIAE (Sainte-Marie de Vangadice on Mount Silicano in Venetian Lombardy), a Camaldolese monastery built by the noble Marquis Hugh shortly before 1123, when Callixtus II confirmed it by privilege, CLXIII, 1267.—Privilege of Innocent II, 1139, CLXXIX, 419.—Alexander III, 1177, CC, 1112.—Celestine III, 1196, CCVI, 1176.—Letter of Innocent III concerning the reform of this monastery, 1212, CCXVI, 801, 908.

VARENAS (AD) S. VALERIANI (Saint-Valérien de Varennes), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in the district of Auxerre, which the faithful visited in procession under Aunarius, bishop, in the seventh century, CXXXVIII, 234.

VARIVILLA (de) (Varville, diocese of Beauvais), a convent of nuns built by the noble lady Adelaide de Bulles before 1175, in which year Alexander III confirmed it by privilege, CC, 1050.

VARLARIENSE S. MARIAE (Notre-Dame de Vallencourt, or Varleaucourt, Pas-de-Calais), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, whose goods and rights Innocent II confirmed in 1142, CXXIX, 599.—Privilege of Eugenius III, 1146, CLXXX, 1141.

VASATENSIS (Bazas, diocese of Bordeaux), a convent of nuns built before the eleventh century; it is mentioned by St. Gregory, bishop of Tours, LXXI, 388.

VEDASTI (S.). See ATREBATENSE.

[Col. 1161] VEDOGIO (de) S. NICOLAI (Saint-Nicolas de Vidou or Wiège, former diocese of Arras near Bapaume), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict. Eugenius III wrote to its abbot concerning a dispute with the priest of Bapaume in 1145, CLXXX, 1053.

VENANTII (S.). See TURONENSE.

VENERE (in) S. JOANNIS. See JOANNIS.

VENETIARUM S. DANIELIS (Saint-Daniel of Venice), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, whose goods and privileges Alexander III confirmed in 1165, CC, 388.

VENETUM. See S. MARIAE DE CHARITATE.

VENETUM S. SALVATORIS IN RIVO ALTO. See SALVATORIS.

VENETUM S. GEORGII (the convent of Saint George the Greater in the vicinity of Venice), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded near the end of the seventh century by Cunibert, king of the Lombards, on the very spot where he had defeated Duke Alahis.—Callixtus II granted a privilege to Abbot Tribunus in 1123, CLXXXIII, 1294.—Privilege of Innocent II, 1132, CLXXIX, 160.

VENETUM S. MARCI (Saint Mark’s of Venice), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, whose possessions and rights in the cities of Tyre and Acre Alexander III confirmed in 1165, CC, 362.—Bull of the same pope, granting indulgences—namely, remission of one seventh of the punishment deserved—to those praying in the church of St. Mark, 1180, CC, 1319.

VENETUS S. ZACHARIAE (the convent of Saint Zacharias at Venice), a convent of nuns. At the request of Abbess Giseldruda, Eugenius III granted it a privilege in 1151, CLXXX, 1479.—Privilege of Adrian IV, 1157, CLXXXVIII, 1493.—Alexander III, 1169, CC, 604.—Lucius III, 1183, CCI, 1215, 1320.—Urban III, 1187, CCII, 1496.

VENETUM S. NICOLAI DE LITTORE (Saint Nicholas of Venice at the Rialto), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by the nobleman Domenico Contarini, doge of Venice, with the cooperation of Domenico, bishop of Grado, and Domenico, bishop of Olivolo.—Privilege of Urban III, 1187, CCII, 1492.—Letter of Clement, 1188, CCIV, 1390.

VENLOCHIENSIS convent of nuns. See WENELOCENSIS.

VERCELLENSE S. GEORGII (Saint George of Vercelli), a monastery to which Atto, bishop of Vercelli, gave certain estates in his will in 960, CXXXIV, 896.

VERCELLENSIS S. MARIAE MAJORIS (Santa Maria Maggiore), a convent of nuns, whose abbess Bertruda received certain estates from Bishop Abbo in 960, CXXXIV, 897.

VERCELLENSE S. EUSEBII (Saint Eusebius of Vercelli), a college of canons whose possessions Innocent II confirmed in 1142, CLXXIX, 593.—Privilege of Lucius III, 1183, CCI, 1177.

VERDENSE, for WERTHINENSE, which see.

VERNOLIO (de) HOSPITAL OF THE HOLY TRINITY (Brothers of the hospice of the Holy Trinity at Verneuil, Seine-et-Oise), a monastery endowed by Hervey the Little and honored with a privilege by Innocent III in 1205, CCXV, 662.

VERONENSE SS. NAZARII ET CELSI (Saints Nazarius and Celsus of Verona), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, mentioned in the privilege granted by Eugenius III to the bishop of Verona in 1145, CLXXX, 1038.—Privilege of Adrian IV, 1158, CLXXXVIII, 1567.

VERONENSE, a college of canons whose goods and privileges Callixtus II, and later Innocent II, confirmed in 1140, CLXXIX, 508.—Privilege of Eugenius III concerning the gift of the castle of Ceretensis, CLXXX, 1151.—Lucius III, 1184, CCI, 1302, 1320.—Urban III, 1187, CCII, 1473.

VERONENSE S. ZENONIS (Saint Zeno of Verona), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built under the Lombard kings; later destroyed by barbarians, it was rebuilt by Pippin in the eighth century.—Abbot Austrebert obtained a diploma from Louis the Pious confirming a privilege formerly granted by Pippin, 815, CIV, 1027.—Diploma of Emperor Lothair, 833, CIV, 1223, 1238.—Emperor Henry III, 1084, CLI, 1159, 1162.—Eugenius III, 1145, CLXXX, 1038.—Letter of Alexander concerning a dispute with certain citizens of Ferrara, 1726 [probably an erroneous date], CC, 770.—Privilege of Urban III, 1187, CCII, 1532.—Decree of Innocent III in favor of this monastery, 1198, CCXIV, 237.

VERONENSIS S. MARIAE, a convent of nuns (Notre-Dame called in Organo at Verona), built in 744 by the noblewomen Auteunda and Natalia, LXXXVII, 1374.—Privilege of Charlemagne, 805, XCVII, 1030.—Alexander III, 1177, CC, 1126.

VERONENSIS, a convent of nuns founded by St. Zeno, apparently the first in all the West, XI, 153; XVI, 897.

[Col. 1162] VERONENSE SS. FIRMI ET RUSTICI (Saints Firmus and Rusticus of Verona), a monastery mentioned in the privilege granted by Eugenius III to the bishop of Verona in 1145, CLXXX, 1038.

VERONENSE (Convent of Vemagara, diocese of Verona), the monastery of Vemagara, mentioned in the privilege granted by Eugenius III to the bishop of Verona in 1145, CLXXX, 1038.

VERRUCENSE S. MICHAELIS. See MICHAELIS.

VERZIACENSE S. VIVENTII (Saint-Vivant-sous-Vergy, near Nuits, Burgundy), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded in 890 or 924 by Count Manasses and his brother Walo, bishop of Autun.—Instrument of Callixtus II, 1117, CLXIII, 1146.

VESSERANUM (Vessera or Vesra in Franconia), a monastery begun by Count Gotebold and completed by Otto, bishop of Bamberg, in 1138, CLXXII, 1289.—Charter of Otto concerning the foundation of this monastery, 1138, CLXXII, 1350.

VETERINENSE (Vieux, near Ambazac), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in the district of Limoges, built in 840 by Rudolf, bishop of Bourges, CXIX, 701.

VETUS-MONASTERIUM S. MARIAE (Notre-Dame de Montières), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in the diocese of Thérouanne in 682 by St. Omer, bishop, and Count Adrowald; later rebuilt by Bishop Ermenfrid and consecrated in 1049 by Pope Leo IX, who granted it a privilege, CXLIII, 630.

VEZUNTIONENSE S. JOANNIS (Saint John of Besançon), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, whose goods and privileges Callixtus II confirmed in 1120, CLXIII, 1162, 1235, 1286.—Concerning the remission of customary dues made by Count Raynald, 1314.

VEZUNTIONENSE S. MARIAE MAGDALENAE (Saint Mary Magdalene at Besançon), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict on the river Doubs, which Pope Alexander II honored with a privilege in 1073, CXLVI, 1418.—Privilege of Callixtus II, 1120, CLXIII, 1172.—Celestine II, 1144, CLXXIX, 814.

VEZUNTIONENSE S. STEPHANI (Canons of Saint Stephen at Besançon). When a dispute arose between this monastery and the canons of St. John, it was settled by Callixtus II in 1123, CLXIII, 1286.

VICENTINUM SS. FELICIS ET FORTUNATI (Saint Felix and Fortunatus of Vicenza, Venetian States), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose goods and privileges Alexander III confirmed in 1166, CC, 499.

VICHPACENSE S. MARTINI (Saint Martin of Wibbach or Wippach, Carniola), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built by Countess Hazica and her sons Hecard, Bernard, and Otto before 1102, when Paschal II confirmed it by privilege, CLXIII, 101.

VICONIENSE S. SEBASTIANI, or DE CASA-DEI (Saint Sebastian of Vigogne, otherwise Case-Dieu, Nord), a Premonstratensian monastery built in 1125 near Valenciennes by a Breton priest.—Privilege of Innocent II, 1138, CLXXIX.—Letter of Alexander III, 1170, to Henry, archbishop of Reims, and the count of Flanders, on behalf of that monastery, CC, 666.

VICOVARIO (de) S. COSMAE (Saint Cosmas of Vicovaro, Lombardy), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, whose possessions and rights Innocent II took under his protection in 1212, CCXVI, 633.

VICTORIS (S.) IN CALETRICIS (Saint-Victor-en-Caux), a priory built by Roger de Mortemart in 1055. At his request it was raised to abbey rank and attached to the monastery of St. Ouen by John, archbishop of Rouen, in 1074, CXLVII, 263.—Privilege of Alexander III, 1179, CC, 1267.

VICTORIS (S.) PARISIENSIS (Saint-Victor near Paris), the celebrated monastery of canons of the Order of St. Augustine, founded in 1113 by King Louis the Fat and William of Champeaux. Privilege of Paschal II, 1114, CLXIII, 359.—Sentence of excommunication pronounced by Stephen, bishop of Paris, against the killers of Thomas, prior of St. Victor, 1132, CLXXIII, 1415.—Charter of Stephen, bishop of Paris, 1124, CLXXIII, 1421.—*Essay on the Foundation of Saint-Victor of Paris*, CLXXV, 9.—Hugh, the celebrated doctor, flourished before 1138, CLXXV; XL.—Decree of Innocent II concerning a prebend to be granted to St. Victor, 1143, CLXIX, 620.—Garnerius, prior, flourished in 1166, CXCIII, 9.—Richard, distinguished canon, flourished in 1173, CXCVI, 1.—Likewise, around the same time, Guarin flourished, ibid., 1387.—Odo, prior of St. Victor and afterwards abbot of St. Geneviève, ibid., 1397.—Godfrey, ibid., 1418.—Adam, ibid., 1421.—Walter, ibid., CXCIX, 1127.—Letters of Alexander III to Prior Robert, 1170, CC, 675, 772, 773, [Col. 1163] 876, 877.—Charter of Maurice de Sully, 1171, CCV, 989.—Odo de Sully, bishop of Paris, 1197, CCXII, 69, 75.—Letters of Innocent III, 1205, CCXV, 791, 793, 823, 980, 1366, 1445; CCXVI, 155, 351, 510, 549, 602.

VICTORIS (S.) GENEVENSIS (Saint Victor of Geneva), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, first founded in the sixth century by Queen Seleuba, sister of St. Clotilde, and restored in 1024 by Empress Adelaide; Cluniac monks were introduced there, CXLII, 858.

VICTORIS (S.). See Cenomanense, Massiliense, Mediolanense, etc.

VIENNENSE S. ANDREAE (Abbey of Saint Andrew at Vienne in Dauphiné), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, bought by Ansemund and his wife Ansleubana and immediately given to Bernard, bishop of Vienne, with the privileges of Theuderic and King Guntram; finally confirmed by Louis the Pious in 831, CIV, 1194.—Letter of Pope Urban II to the monks of St. Andrew against Archbishop Guy, ibid., 1099; CLI, 537.—Diploma of Rudolf, king of Burgundy, 994, CLI, 1021.—Letter of Innocent III, 1212, CCXVI, 823.

VIENNENSE S. FERREOLI (Saint-Ferréol of Vienne, Dauphiné), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict founded in the sixth century, later rebuilt in 1036 by Leodegarius, bishop of Vienne, CXLIII, 1403, 1406.—Letter of Innocent III, 1212, CCXVI, 823.

VIENNENSE S. MARCELLI (Saint-Marcel, in and near the diocese of Vienne in Dauphiné), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, where Pope Paschal II stayed in 1107, CLXIII, 224.—Letter of Innocent III, CCXVI, 823.

VIENNENSE S. PETRI (Saint Peter of Vienne), a celebrated monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in the city about 515 by St. Leonianus, abbot and brother of St. Anianus, bishop of Orléans, who at first had constructed for himself a simple cell.—Later restored by Bishop Leodegarius in 1036, CXLIII, 1403.—Privilege of Lucius III, 1184, CCI, 1288.—Letter of Innocent III, 1212, CCXVI, 823.

VIENNENSE S. THEUDERII (Saint-Theudère, or Saint-Chef of Vienne), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built on the hill of Rupianum by St. Theuderius himself, its abbot, in the sixth century. In the ninth century, the monks of Dervensis were received there after their monastery had been devastated by the Northmen. Privilege of Pope Formosus, 892, CXXIX, 837.

VIGORIS (S.) CERASIENSE (Saint-Vigor of Cérisy near Bayeux), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by St. Vigor, bishop of Bayeux, on land granted by King Childebert in 538. Destroyed by the Northmen, it was restored by Bishop Odo and eventually passed to the Congregation of St. Maur. Robert, called “of Tumbalena,” became abbot of St. Vigor in 1092, CL, 1359.—Urban II assigned it to the monastery of St. Benignus at Dijon in 1097, CLI, 500.—Charter of Odo, bishop of Bayeux, 1096, CLV, 475.

VILLAE MAGNAE SS. MARTINI ET MAJANI (Saint Martin and Majan of Villemagne-l’Argentière, Hérault), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, rebuilt by Louis the Pious in the ninth century. Privilege of Innocent III, 1203, CCXV, 140.

VILLAE MAJORIS S. MICHAELIS (Saint Michael of Villamajor, Spain), a Premonstratensian monastery, whose possessions Innocent III took under his protection in 1199, CCXIV, 607.

VILLALUPPENSE (Villeloin, near Loches, Indre-et-Loire), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded or enlarged in the diocese of Tours by Odacrus, abbot of Cormery, and consecrated by Bishop Herard in 859, CI, 1431.—Abbot Guy, who had acted badly, later restored what had been unjustly taken away, 996, CXXXVII, 853.—Grant of this monastery for the benefit of the Carthusian brethren, at the request of Henry, king of England and count of Anjou, about 1173, CCVII, 1162.

VILLA LUTOSA (Leuze between Ath and Tournai, diocese of Cambrai), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, founded by St. Amand in 615, CXLIX, 140.

VILLA SANCTIS, S. SATURNINAE (Saints-les-Marquions, former diocese of Arras), a convent of nuns founded in the diocese of Arras in the sixth century, CXLIX, 130.

VILLARENSE. See FULRADO-VILLARENSE.

VILLARENSIS (Montivilliers, diocese of Rouen), a notable Benedictine convent of nuns in the diocese of Rouen, founded by St. Philibert in 682, CV, 44 note.—Ansegisus made certain grants to this monastery in 833, ibid.

VILTHINENSE (Vilthina, diocese of Brixen in Tyrol), a Premonstratensian monastery founded by Regenbert, bishop of Brixen, shortly before 1138, when Innocent II honored it with a privilege, CLXXIX, 359.

[Col. 1164] VIMANENSE, a Portuguese monastery in the diocese of Braga, whose prior Innocent III addressed concerning the subjection owed to the bishop, 1199, CCXIV, 704.

VINCENTII (S.) AD VULTURNUM APUD BENEVENTUM (Saint-Vincent-sur-Vulturne), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded about 760 by three noble brothers, Paldon, Tason, and Tuto, LXXXIX, 1319; XCV, 651.—St. Ambrose Autpert, abbot, flourished there in 778, LXXXIX, 1265.—Diploma of Charlemagne, 774, concerning the foundation of this monastery, XCVII, 1006, 1016.—Diploma of Louis the Pious, 831, CIV, 1196.—Bull of Paschal I, 819, CXXIX, 980.—Privilege of Stephen VII, 930, CXXXII, 1051.—Marinus II, CXXXIII, 869.—Benedict VII, CXXXVII, 343.—Sergius IV, CXXXIX, 1522.—Nicholas II, CXLIII, 1304.—Diploma of Emperor Conrad II, 1038.—Bull of Callixtus II, 1128, CLXIII, 1184.

VINCENTII (S.) DE OVETO (Saint Vincent of Oviedo, Spain), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded in 791 by Abbot Fromista and his cousin Maximus, XCVI, 889.

VINCENTII (S.) LAUDUNENSIS (Saint Vincent of Laon), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, said to have been founded in 580 by Queen Brunhild, wife of Sigebert. It had long been abandoned when Adelelm restored it and introduced twelve canons; Roric then replaced them with twelve Benedictine monks from the monastery of Fleury in 961, CXXXIII, 951.—On Abbot Anselm, CLVI, 1003, 1152.—Charter of Guy of Anco (d’Eu), dean of Laon, ibid., 1154.—Charter of restoration by Bishop Rorico, 1169.—Diploma of Emperor Lothair, 975, CLVI, 1171.—List of abbots, 1172.

VINCENTII (S.) (Saint Vincent, diocese of Trivento, in Principato Ultra, Naples), to which Innocent III awarded tithes in 1208, CCXV, 1474.

VINCENTII (S.). See CENOMANENSE, METENSE, PARISIENSE, SILVANECTENSE, etc.

VINDICIACENSE (Venzat or Pansat in Auvergne), a monastery founded about 538 by Abbot Bracchio (St. Bravius) and the noble lady Ragnachild, LXXI, 1063, 1063 note.

VINDICIANI (S.) IN MONTE ELIGII (Saint Vindician of Mont-Saint-Éloi, diocese of Arras), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine near Arras, mentioned in the deeds of the bishops of Cambrai and Arras, CXLIX, 131.

VINDOCINENSE SS. TRINITATIS (Holy Trinity of Vendôme), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by Geoffrey, count of Anjou, and his wife Agnes, and confirmed by privilege of Pope Clement II in 1047, CXLII, 584.—Privilege of Pope Victor II, 1055, CXLIII, 819.—Nicholas II, 1061, CXLIII, 1352.—Alexander II, 1063, CXLVI, 1291.—Privilege of Gregory VII, 1085, CXLVIII, 729.—Urban II, 1093, CLI, 372, 380, 385, 537.—Geoffrey, abbot and cardinal, descended from the count of Anjou, 1107, CLVII, 9.—Privilege of Theuderic, bishop of Chartres, 1040, CLVII, 289.—Privilege of Paschal II, CLXIII, 36.—Callixtus II, CLXIII, 1125, 1306.—Honorius II, 1129, CLXVI, 1294.—Privilege of Innocent II, 1135, CLXXIX, 223.—Letter of the same concerning an agreement with Ulger, bishop of Angers, ibid., 261.—Privilege of Innocent III, 1205, CCXV, 747.—Letter of the same, 1459, CCXVI, 766, 814.

VINEIS (de). See S. JOANNIS.

VIRDUNENSE S. MICHAELIS (Saint Michael of Verdun), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded in 709 by Count Wulfald and his wife Adalsinda. In defense of this monastery Gregory VII wrote to the archbishop of Trier in 1047, CXLIII, 626.—Privilege of Paschal II, 1106, 165.

VIRDUNENSE S. PETRI (Saint Peter of Verdun), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built before 1065, when Pope Nicholas II ordered the count of Rethel to restore to it certain estates wrongfully withheld, CXLIII, 1346.

VIRDUNENSE. See S. VITONI and S. AGERICI.

VIRDUNENSE S. PAULI (Saint Paul of Verdun), a monastery first of the Order of St. Benedict and later Premonstratensian, built in the suburb by Wicfrid, bishop of Verdun, in 962–965; it was reformed by St. Norbert in 1137.—Privilege of Callixtus II, 1120, CLXIII, 1176.—Privilege of Innocent II, 1136, CLXXIX, 277.

VIRDUNENSIS S. MAURI (Saint Maur of Verdun), a convent of nuns situated in the suburb, restored by Bishop Heymo; St. Leo IX confirmed its privileges and goods in 1049, CXLIII, 626.

VIRIZIACUM. See S. BASOLI.

VIRTUENSE S. SALVATORIS (Saint-Sauveur des Vertus, diocese of Châlons-sur-Marne), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, CC, 629 note.—Letter of Alexander III to Henry, [Col. 1165] archbishop of Reims, concerning a dispute between the abbot and a certain priest, 1172, CC, 791.

VIRTUENSE S. MARIAE (Notre-Dame des Vertus, diocese of Châlons-sur-Marne), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, built before 1132.—Letter of Alexander III concerning the abbot of this monastery, 1169, CC, 568, 629, 776, 904.

VIRTUENSE (Les Vertus or Aubervilliers near Saint-Denis, Seine), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, subject to St. Victor of Paris; Stephen, bishop of Paris, gave it an abbot in 1132, CLXXIII, 1413.

VIRZILIACENSE, VIRZILIENSE. See VIZELIACENSE.

VIRZIONENSE S. PETRI (Saint Peter at Vierzon), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, formerly called Doverense, founded in the ninth century by Radulf, bishop of Bourges; later attached to the Congregation of St. Maur, LXXX, 579.

VISBECCENSIS (Visbec, a convent in Germany whose location is unknown to us), a convent of nuns whose possessions Adrian IV confirmed by privilege in 1158, CLXXXVIII, 1365. Is it perhaps Visberg, an estate belonging to the monastery of Fulda?

VISUMENSE, a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in Spain, between Galicia and Bierzo, founded by St. Fructuosus in 660, LXXXVII, 1089.

VITENSE S. MARIAE (Notre-Dame des Vignes in the diocese of Osma, Old Castile, Spain), a Premonstratensian monastery founded by King Alfonso shortly before 1163, when Alexander III honored it with a privilege, CC, 241.

VITERBIENSE. See S. GEMINI, S. MARIAE NOVAE, S. ANGELI de SPADA, S. STEPHANI de PLATEA.

VITESCOLENSE S. MARIAE (Notre-Dame des Vignerons, in the diocese of Aarhus, Jutland), a monastery built by Bishop Eskil shortly before 1164, when Alexander III wrote to its abbot, CC, 304.

VITI (S.) IN SARDINIA, a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict founded by a noblewoman named Vitula in the fourth century, in the times of St. Gregory the Great; it is mentioned in LXXVII, 511.

VITI (S.) (Saint Vito, near Etna in Sicily), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict near Mount Etna in Sicily, concerning which St. Gregory the Great complains, LXXVII, 1081.

VITI (S.). See PRULLENSE.

VITTONI (S.) VIRDUNENSIS (Saint-Vanne of Verdun), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, originating in a basilica bearing that name because the holy bishop had been buried there in 507; he himself had established some canons of St. Augustine in it. In the tenth century Berengar introduced monks of the Order of St. Benedict into this abbey.—Emperor St. Henry II confirmed its possessions and privileges in 1015, CXL, 321.—Charter of Guy of Châtillon, archbishop of Reims, 1040, CXLII, 1407.—Letter of Urban II in favor of this monastery, 1096, CLI, 447.—Paschal, 1114, CLXIII, 355.—Letter of Honorius II, CLXVI, 1225.—*On the Abbots of Saint-Vanne*, by Laurence of Liège, 1250, CCIV, 915.—Privilege of Innocent III, 1207, CCXVII, 164.

VIVARIENSE (Viviers near Squillace, Calabria), a monastery formerly founded by Cassiodorus in his old age, where he withdrew among the brethren in 560, LXIX, 421.

VIVARIENSE, a monastery called “of the pilgrims,” situated in the duchy of Alsace. Lothair, son of Louis the Pious, wrote to its abbot Sigimar, granting him the monastery of Lucerne in 839, CIV, 1308.

VIVARIENSE. See VALLIS SERENAE.

VIVENSE (Vivo, near Camaldoli in Tuscany), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, which Celestine II reconciled with the Camaldolese over the election of an abbot in 1144, CLXXIX, 806.—Privilege of Eugenius III, 1146, CLXXX, 1185.

VIZELIACENSE S. MARIAE (Notre-Dame de Vézelay, diocese of Auxerre), first a convent of nuns, founded in Burgundy near Vézelay in 867 by the noblewoman Bertha; later it passed to Benedictine monks, CXIX, 1116.—Privilege of Pope John VIII, CXXVI, 803.—Likewise of Stephen VI, CXXIX, 858.—John XI, CXXX, 1859.—Pope Marinus II, CXXXIII, 863.—Benedict VI, CXXXV, 1085.—Sylvester II, 1001, CXXXIX, 279.—St. Leo IX, CXLIII, 642.—On the foundation of this monastery, CLVI, 1192.—Paschal II, 1102, CLXIII, 102, 122.—His letters against the killers of the abbot, ibid., 196, 410.—Privilege of Callixtus II, 1120, CLXII, 1145.—Cardinal Conon excommunicates the count of Nevers for injuries inflicted upon the monastery of Vézelay, 1120, CLXIII, 1438.—Letter of Innocent II to Abbot Stephen, 1139, CLXXIX, 394, 633, 637.—Letter of the Cistercian general chapter concerning this monastery’s opposition to the bishop, CLXXIX, 671.—Letter of Lucius II against the killers of Abbot Artald, 1144, CLXXIX, 852, 887, 910.—Letters of Eugenius, [Col. 1166] 1146, CLXXX, 1179 and following, 1423, 1537, 1550, 1575.—Letter of Anastasius against the oppressors of this monastery, 1153, CLXXXVIII, 1008, 1009.—Letters of Adrian IV on the same matter, CLXXXVIII, 1423 and following, 1438, 1592.—Hugh of Poitiers, author of the history of Vézelay, flourished in 1167, CXCIV, 1559.—Privilege of Alexander III, 1162, CC, 153, 309, 372.—Lucius III, 1181, CCI, 1094.—Urban III, granting the abbot the use of the mitre, 1187, CCII, 1424.—Clement III, 1188, CCIV, 1292.—Celestine III, 1193, CCVI, 1023.—Privileges and letters of Innocent III, 1198, CCXIV, 122, 124, 132, 168.—The same pope granted an indulgence of forty days to those visiting the body of St. Mary Magdalene deposited in this monastery, 1199, CCXIV, 865; 1211, CCXVI, 478, 479, 481, 602, 810, 946.

VOLDARICI (S.) (Saint-Woldaric, diocese of Mainz), a monastery whose abbot Innocent III addressed in 1199, CCXIV, 824.

VOLTA (de) (La Voulte, Ardèche), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict founded in 1024 by St. Odilo, abbot of Cluny, and his nephews upon his hereditary estate, CXLII, 862.

VOLUSIANI (S.) (Saint-Volusien, Ariège), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine in the county of Foix; initially only a basilica was built, and later a monastery was attached to it, LXXI, 567.

VOLVICENSE (Volvic, near Riom, Puy-de-Dôme), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, to which the relics of St. Austremonius were translated in the eighth century, LXXI, 567.

VOSIDENSE (Le Vigeois, Vienne), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in the diocese of Limoges, founded before 550, LXXI, 1148.

VOTO (de). See MARIAE.

VULFINI (S.) (Saint-Vulfin of Auxerre), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine in the diocese of Auxerre, to which the faithful went in litanies during the time of Bishop Aunarius in the seventh century, CXXXVIII, 233, 234.

VULGANI (S.). See LENSENSE.

VULMARI (S.) BONONIENSE (Saint-Vulmer of Boulogne), a monastery restored within the walls of Boulogne about 1070 by Blessed Ida, duchess of Boulogne, CLV, 454.—Letter of Paschal II concerning the expulsion of its abbot by the count of Boulogne, CLXIII, 127.

VULMARI (S.) DE NEMORE (Saint-Vulmer-les-Bois, former diocese of Boulogne-sur-Mer), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in the district of Boulogne, likewise restored by Blessed Ida in 1070, CLV, 454.—Charter of Rainald, archbishop of Reims, 1132, CLXXII, 1352.—Letters and privilege of Innocent III, 1199, CCXVII, 49, 41, 208.

VULTENSE. Emperor Henry II formerly made an exchange with the abbot of this monastery in 1015, CXL, 325, 386.

VULTURNENSE. See above, S. VINCENTII.

WADEGOZINGENSE S. MARIAE (Notre-Dame de Wadegotra or Wadegasten, diocese of Trier), a Premonstratensian monastery founded in 1137. Privilege of Eugenius III, 1152, CLXXX, 1529.—Its abbot commends himself to the prayers of St. Hildegard, abbess of St. Rupert’s, CXCVII, 304.—Privilege of Celestine III, 1197, CCVI, 1108.

WALARICI (S.) (Saint-Walric, in the county of Witman), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict founded in the county of Witman by Count Hugh; Benedict VII confirmed its privileges in 981, CXXXVII, 338.—Privilege of Paschal II, 1106, CLXIII, 184.—Alexander III, 1165, CC, 552.

WALBURGENSE. See HEINHENHEIMENSE, CESTRENSE, FURNENSE, SILVASACRA.

WALERICI, or WALARICI. See VALERICI.

WALCHENRIETENSE (Walchenreith, diocese of Mainz), a Cistercian monastery originating from Kamp, built by Countess Adelaide of Lanterberg in 1124–1128.—Letter of Innocent III concerning a monk of this monastery, 1199, CCXIV, 741.

WALDEDRUDIS (S.). See MONTE CASTRILOCENSI (de).

WALDERBACENSE (Walderbach, diocese of Regensburg), a monastery against which Innocent III protects the church of Rickofen in 1199, CCXVII, 39.

WALLARENSE. See below, WASLARENSE.

WALTHANENSE S. CRUCIS (Holy Cross of Waltham, Berkshire, England), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, to which Innocent III granted a privilege in 1199, CCXIV, 665, 673 and following.

WARDONENSE (Wardon, Bedfordshire, England), a monastery founded in 1136, mentioned in a letter of Innocent III in 1205, CCXV, 593.

WARIVILLA (de) (Varville, diocese of Beauvais), a convent of nuns to which Alexander III granted a privilege at the request of Prioress Matilda in 1175, CC, 1030.

WARWICENSE S. SEPULCRI (Holy Sepulchre of [Col. 1167] Warwick, England), a monastery of the Order of St. Augustine, whose abbot Clement III addressed in 1185, CCIV, 1325.

WASLARENSE (Walers-en-Fagne, former diocese of Cambrai), a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, built in 657 by Blessed Landelin. The monastery of Lobbes, upon which it depended, gave it in 968 to Ratherius, formerly bishop of Verona and then abbot of Aulne, CXXXVI, 75.

WASTENSE. See below, WATINENSE.

WATERFORD, ST CATHERINE’S (St Catherine’s of Waterford, in the diocese of the same name, Ireland), a monastery of the same institution as St Victor’s, Paris. Innocent III confirmed its goods and privileges, 1210, CCXVI, 275, 293.—See also CLV, 1454.

WATEN, or WASTEN (Wast, Pas-de-Calais), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, rebuilt by the venerable Abbot Alfred between Calais and Saint-Omer under the invocation of St Michael, 1072. Its history was transmitted to us by Ebrard, disciple of the same abbot, CXLIX, 1513.

WATTUN (Wattun, diocese of York, England), a convent built by the Venerable Abbot Gilbert, mentioned among the writings of Abbot Aelred, twelfth century, CXCV, 789.

WAVERLEY, ST MARY’S (Our Lady of Waverley, Surrey, England), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded in 1129 by Gilbert de Gaunt, Count of Lincoln. Privilege of Eugenius III, 1147, CLXXX, 1226.

WECHTERSWINKEL, an English convent whose protection Eugenius III undertook, 1150, CLXXX, 1423.

WEDINGHAUSEN, ST LAWRENCE’S or ST MARY’S (Wedinghausen or Arnsberg, diocese of Cologne), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, founded in 1157 by the nobleman Henry, Count of Arnsberg.—Privilege of Celestine III, 1196, CCVI, 1156.

WEINGARTEN, or ST MARTIN OF THE VINES (St Martin’s of Weingarten, near Ravensburg, diocese of Constance), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, founded in 1053 by Welf, Duke of Bavaria, CLXXIV, 9.—Privilege of Innocent II, 1143, CLXXIX, 649.

WEISSENBURG, SS PETER AND STEPHEN (St Peter’s or St Stephen’s of Weissenburg, Bavaria), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, founded by King Dagobert in 623. Dagobert II later granted it baths during the rule of Abbot Ratefrid, LXXXVII, 301.—Privilege of Innocent II, 1141, CLXXIX, 559.

WEISSENOE (Weissnau, diocese of Bamberg), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, whose goods and possessions Paschal II confirmed, 1109, CLXIII, 257; CLXXIII, 1322.—Privilege of Eugenius III, 1140, CLXXX, 1444.

WELEGRAD (Wellehrad, diocese of Olomouc, Moravia, Austrian States), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded by Ottokar, King of the Bohemians, shortly before 1208; in that year Innocent III confirmed its possessions, CCXVII, 173.

WELMAR. See WULMAR.

WENLOCK (Venlock, county of Shropshire or Salop, England), originally a convent built by the Blessed Milburga, of royal Mercian blood; later destroyed by the Normans in the eleventh century. Roger of Montgomery rebuilt it and brought Cluniac monks there. Letter of Innocent III to the abbot, 1203, CCXV, 81.

WERBE (Werbe in the Margraviate of Brandenburg, Saxony), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, which Adrian IV subjected to Corbie when Wibald had become abbot there, 1155, CLXXXVIII, 1434.—Letter of the same pope to the Archbishop of Mainz, that he protect this monastery against the injuries of Count Bobbo.

WERDEN, HOLY CROSS, a convent founded at Werden in Alsace by the illustrious Manegald. Its abbess was Gunderada, the founder’s daughter; St Leo IX granted her privileges, 1049, CXLIII, 637.

WERDEN, or WERTHEN, ST SAVIOUR’S (St Saviour’s of Werden, diocese of Cologne), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, founded by St Ludger, XCIX, 745.—Subjected to St Mary’s, Strasbourg, by Bishop Remigius, 778, XCVI, 1582.—Diploma of Charlemagne, 802, XCVII, 1071.—Cartulary of Werden, XCIX, 795.—Privilege of Pope Stephen V, CXXIX, 814.—Of Eugenius III, 1153, CLXXX, 1584.—Letters of Innocent III, 1204, CCXV, 350, 644.

WESSOBRUNN, ST PETER’S (St Peter’s of Wessobrunn, Bavaria), a monastery of the Order of St Augustine, one of eight built in the diocese of Freising by the counts of Lanfredo, Waldram, and Eilando. Letter of Alexander III concerning the refusal to admit a schismatic abbot, 1176, CC, 1059.

WESTBURY, or WESTSBURY (Westbury, [Col. 1168] diocese of Worcester, England), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, founded in his diocese of Worcester by St Oswald, bishop, 962, CXLVII, 1193.

WESTMINSTER (near London), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, founded by King Sigebert near the city of London; rebuilt by St Edward the Confessor in 1061 and confirmed in its privileges by Pope Nicholas II, CXLIII, 1358.—Privilege of St Edward, 1066, CLI, 1195, 1198, 1200.—The monk Sulcard flourished about 1100, CLV, 1633.—He wrote the foundation-history of this monastery, 1635.—Letters of Innocent II, 1141, CLXXIX, 567, 568.—Privilege of Eugenius III, 1146, CLXXX, 1115.—On the restoration of this monastery under Edward the Confessor, by Aelred, CXCV, 752 et seq.—Indulgence of one year and forty days granted by Innocent III to the church of St Edward, 1208, CCXVII, 177.

WETHDERSWINKELE, a monastery whose location is unknown to us. Letter of its abbess to St Hildegard, twelfth century, CXCVII, 319.

WEZZINBRUNN. It appears to be the same as Weissenburg. See above.

WIBERG, or WIBURG, ST MARY’S (Our Lady of Wiberg or Wibourg, Jutland, Denmark), a monastery of the Order of St Augustine, founded by Nicholas, bishop of Viborg, shortly before 1170; in that year Alexander III confirmed it by privilege, CC, 649.—Letter of Clement III concerning the beatification of Ketil, formerly provost of this monastery, 1188, CCIV, 1360.

WIBLINGEN, ST MARTIN’S (St Martin’s of Wiblingen, diocese of Constance), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, built in the Black Forest by Count Hartmann and his brother Otto shortly before 1098; in that year Urban II confirmed it by privilege, CLI, 501.—Privilege of Pope Honorius II, 1126, CLXVI, 1257.

WIDDERGOLDESDORF, a convent in Germany, whose location we have not found. Its abbess wrote to St Hildegard, abbess of St Rupert’s, commending herself to her prayers, twelfth century, CXCVII, 329.

WORCESTER, ST MARY’S (Our Lady of Worcester), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict in the diocese of the same name, built by St Oswald beside the episcopal see, 966, CXLVII, 1195.—The monk Hemming, 1095, CL, 1489.

WILBACH (Wilbach, or Wilbolden, diocese of Paderborn), a convent of the Order of St Benedict, built before 1183, when Lucius III confirmed it by privilege, CCI, 1186.

ST WILFRID’S (St Wilfrid’s of Inhripp, Scotland), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict among the Scots, built in the place called Inhrypo by Abbot Wilfrid and King Alfred, whose teacher he was, 682, XCV, 159.

WILICH (Wilica, diocese of Cologne), a convent of the Order of St Benedict, founded in the tenth century by Megingoz, Count of Guelders. Privilege of Celestine III, 1195, CCVI, 1093.

WILMAR. See ST VULMAR.

WILTON, ST EADGITH’S or EDITH’S, a convent founded and made illustrious by this holy abbess Edith, daughter of King Edgar, tenth century, CLV, 109.

WILZACCHARIA, ST CAESARIUS’S (St Caesarius of Wilzacchar, near Modena), a monastery of the Order of St Augustine, built by Countess Matilda in the time of Pope Calixtus II and granted by her to the canons of Modena. Privilege of Calixtus II, 1123, CLXIII, 1266.

WINDEBERG (Weinsberg, duchy of Württemberg), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, built by Otto, bishop of Bamberg, about 1132, CLXXIII, 1279.—Privilege of Eugenius III, 1146, CLXXX, 1168.

WINDGARTEN. See WEINGARTEN.

WINNBURG, or WINNINBURG, a convent (Winburn, Dorset), whose founder and abbess was Eadburga, or Bugga, 740, LXXXIX, 711.

WINCHESTER, a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, called Hyde and New Minster, founded by the pious King Edgar in 966 and entrusted to St Æthelwold, bishop, to govern, CXXXVII, 92; CXXXVIII, 487, 496.—Privilege of Innocent III, 1205, CCXV, 561.

WINCHESTER, ST MARY’S (Nunnaminster at Winchester, England), a convent in which St Æthelwold gathered nuns, 960, CXXXVII, 92.—Privilege of Alexander II, 1073, CXLVI, 1416.

WIRRMOUTH (Wearmouth, England), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, formerly founded in England by Naitan, king of the Picts, at the confluence of the Wear and Tyne, about 674.—Ceolfrith was abbot of this monastery after Benedict, 709, CLXXXIX, 347, 349.—The Venerable [Col. 1169] Bede flourished there about 690, XC, 10, and later Alcuin, eighth century, ibid.

WÜRZBURG, UPPER CELL (Altencell, diocese of Würzburg), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, built in the twelfth century.—Privilege of Pope Celestine II, 1143, CLXXIX, 770.—Of Eugenius III, 1150, CLXXX, 1566.—Of Lucius III, 1182, CCI, 1156.

WÜRZBURG, or REGENSDORF (Reginstauf, Bavaria), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict in the diocese of Halberstadt, later granted by Emperor Henry to Otto, bishop of Bamberg, about 1130, CLXXIII, 1279.—Privilege of Celestine III, 1195, CCVI, 1080.

WISEBIK (Wisebick, Westphalia), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, built in the diocese of Minden before 1025. In that year Emperor Conrad, granting the petition of Abbess Abuga, issued a diploma, CLI, 1043.

WISSEGRAD (Wissegrad, Bohemia), a monastery of the Order of St Augustine, flourishing in the twelfth century, which supplied a continuator of Cosmas of Prague for 1124–1140, CLVI, 24, 245.

WITHAM (Witteham, Somerset, England), a Carthusian house founded by King Henry II, 1154–1189. Its first prior was Hugh, later bishop of Lincoln, CLIII, 961.—Charters of Hugh, ibid., 1115, 1118.

WOFFENHEIM, HOLY CROSS (Woffenheim, Alsace), a convent built by Hugh and Heilwig, parents of Pope St Leo IX. Leo himself confirmed its rights and privileges in 1049, CXLIII, 636.

WORMS, ST MARTIN’S (St Martin’s of Worms), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict. Privilege by which Celestine III exempted it from episcopal jurisdiction, 1142, CCVI, 953.

WLMAR. See VULMAR.

WROCŁAW. See ST MARY IN THE ARENA.

WLRIDESHUSEN IN GERMANY, a convent which Alexander III received under his protection, 1162, CC, 172.

YERQUA (St Peter’s of Illiergue, Tarn), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, whose Abbot Raymond received a privilege from Eugenius III, 1147, LXXX, 1278.

[Col. 1170] YNSWYTRIN (of) (Inswitrin, British Isles), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, founded by Saints Phagan and Deruvian under Pope Eleutherius, on the island of that name situated between Ireland and Britain. This monastery was later made illustrious by St Patrick, as is evident from his charter, 425, LIII, 827.

YPRES, or MORINES, ST JOHN’S (St John’s of the Mount, diocese of Ypres or Thérouanne), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, founded by King Theuderic II in 686.—Privilege of Innocent III, 1208, CCXV, 1343.

ZABERDOWI (Zaberdowiz, Moravia), a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, whose goods and privileges Innocent III confirmed, 1209, CCXVII, 192.

ST ZACHARIAS’S, a convent. See VENICE.

ZELLINGEN (Zellinghen on the Main), a convent mentioned in the Life of Rabanus Maurus, situated near Resbach, CVII, 59.

ST ZENO’S. See Pisa, Richenhall, Verona.

ZURZACH (Zurzach on the Rhine, former diocese of Constance), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict on the Rhine, subject to Reichenau Abbey, which St Gebhard, bishop, gave in exchange for Petershausen Abbey, 983, CXLIII, 307.—It later became a collegiate church, ibid., note.

ZWEITAL (Zwethl, Austria), a monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded in the duchy of Austria in 1138 by Count Hadmar and his wife Gertrude. For this monastery Abbot Ebro obtained a privilege from Emperor Rudolf in 1281, XCVIII, 829.—Letter of this monastery’s abbot to St Hildegard, CXCVII, 290.

ZWIFALTEN, ST MARY’S (Our Lady of Zwifalten, Swabia), a monastery of the Order of St Benedict, founded by Counts Liutold and Cono before 1122, when Calixtus II honoured it with a privilege, CLXIII, 1239.—The prior wrote to St Hildegard, abbess of St Rupert’s, CXCVII, 370.

ZWIFELDEN, or ZWIFALTEN, a convent whose nuns composed a letter to St Hildegard, abbess of St Rupert’s at Bingen, twelfth century, CXCVII, 371.

[Col. 1169]

CLXXX. INDEX OF DIOCESES MENTIONED IN THE COURSE OF PATROLOGY, IN WHICH THE DIOCESES ARE ARRANGED BY PROVINCES, AND ALPHABETICALLY WITHIN EACH PROVINCE.

PRELIMINARY NOTE.

The arrangement of the index of dioceses is as follows:

The dioceses are arranged by provinces, and alphabetically within each province. Connected with each diocese considered separately are letters, privileges, bulls, and diplomas pertaining to it; monasteries and councils founded or held within it; distinguished men belonging to it by holiness or learning; and surviving liturgical, historical, and biographical writings concerning it. Roman numerals refer the reader to the volume of the *Patrology*, Arabic numerals to the column. With these preliminaries, no one will fail to perceive the great usefulness of this index, and the pleasure it affords in investigating subjects. For what is more useful or more delightful to a priest than to possess separately the documents of Catholic tradition relating to the regions in which he himself lives; to know the names and deeds of holy men who cultivated in the early ages of the Church the same vineyard which he now waters with his labours; and to examine the history of churches and monasteries whose ruins he still has before his eyes?

CLXXXII. BIOGRAPHICAL INDEX, COMPRISING THE LIVES OF SAINTS AND DISTINGUISHED MEN REPRINTED IN THE *Patrologia*, ARRANGED ACCORDING TO THE INITIAL LETTER OF THE AUTHORS.

ABBO (St.), abbot of Fleury (tenth century).—1. *Life of St. Edmund, King of the English and Martyr*, CXXXIX, 507.—2. *Epitome on the Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*, 536.

ADAMNAN (St.), abbot of Iona (seventh century).—Three books *On the Life of St. Columba*, LXXXV, III, 726.

ADELBOLD, bishop of Utrecht (eleventh century).—1. *Life of Emperor St. Henry*, CXL, 88.—2. *Life of St. Walpurga*, ibid., 1092.

Wolphelmus (B.).—Life of Blessed Wolphelmus, abbot of Brauweiler near Cologne, by Conrad, monk of the same place and disciple of Blessed Wolphelmus, CLIV, 408.

Amalric, king of Jerusalem.—On Amalric, king of Jerusalem, William of Tyre, CCI, 748.

Baldwin III, king of Jerusalem.—On Baldwin III, king of Jerusalem, ibid., 640.

Baldwin IV, king of Jerusalem.—On Baldwin IV, ibid., 813.

Burchard, count.—Life of the venerable lord Count Burchard, who flourished under Kings Hugh Capet and his son Robert, by Odo, monk of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés, CXLIII, 848.

Charlemagne.—Life of the Emperor Charlemagne, by Einhard, XCVII, 25.

Charles the Good.—On the life of Blessed Charles the Good, count of Flanders, by Gualter, archdeacon of the Church of the Morini, CLXVI, 944.

Chunradus Salicus.—Life of the Emperor Chunradus Salicus, by Wipo, priest, CXLII, 1217.

Edmund (St).—Life of St Edmund, king of the English and martyr, by St Abbo, abbot of Fleury, CXXXIX, 508.

Edward (St).—Life of St Edward, king and confessor, by Blessed Aelred, CXCV, 740.

Gerald (St).—Four books on the life of St Gerald, count of Aurillac, by St Odo of Cluny, CXXXIII, 639.

Louis the Pious.—On the deeds of Louis the Pious, CV, 570.

Otto the Great.—On the deeds of Emperor Otto the Great, CXXXVI, 897.

Robert the Pious.—Life of Robert the Pious, king of the Franks, CXLI, 904.

Mary (St.) of Egypt.—Life of St. Mary of Egypt, LXXIII, 671; CLXXI, 1322.

Mary (St.) Magdalene.—Life of Blessed Mary Magdalene and of her sister St. Martha, Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1432.

Taso (St.).—Life of Saints Paldon, Taso, and Tato, St. Ambrose Autpertus, LXXXIX, 1320.

Thais (St.).—Life of St. Thais, Marbod of Rennes, CLXXI, 1629.

Valerius (St.).—On the Passion of Saints Valerius and Ruffinus, by St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 1489.

Vincent (St.).—History of the translation of St. Vincent, deacon and martyr, from Spain to the monastery of Castres in Gaul, by Aimoin, monk of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, CXXVI, 1012.

Waldetrudis (St.).—Life of St. Waldetrudis, by Philip of Harveng, CCIII, 1376.

Wereburga (St.).—Life of St. Wereburga, virgin, daughter of the king of the Mercians, by Goscelin, CLV, 94.
